references.AI Alignment:
## Reference
### Overview
AI alignment aims to steer AI systems toward a person's or group's intended goals: a system is aligned if it advances those objectives and misaligned if it pursues unintended ones ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment)). The difficulty is that designers usually specify simpler proxy goals, which can omit necessary constraints or reward behaviour that only looks aligned; the problem divides into carefully specifying the system's purpose (outer alignment) and ensuring the system adopts that specification robustly (inner alignment) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment)).

Machine learning normally takes the objective as given; alignment research studies the difficulty of specifying or learning it, using behavioural cloning, [inverse reinforcement learning](node:Inverse%20Reinforcement%20Learning), [reinforcement learning from human feedback](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF), robustness, [scalable oversight](node:Scalable%20Oversight) and [mechanistic interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability) ([UMass CS 690S](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~sniekum/classes/LFH-S2/desc.php)). A broad survey organises the field around four objectives (Robustness, Interpretability, Controllability, Ethicality: "RICE") and splits it into forward alignment (training aligned systems) and backward alignment (assurance and governance) ([Ji et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19852)).

Alignment is now an engineering concern for [large language models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): RLHF has emerged as the central method for fine-tuning state-of-the-art LLMs toward human goals, yet its flaws had received little systematic public study ([Casper et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15217)). The Wikipedia article describes alignment as an open problem for modern AI systems ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment)).

### Formal definition
Several formal alignment results are stated for reward-maximizing agents in [Markov decision processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes), as in the power-seeking theorems ([Turner et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01683)).

**Reward hacking.** Given a set of policies $\Pi$ and a reward $R$ with expected return $J_R(\pi)$, a proxy $R_1$ and true reward $R_2$ form an *unhackable* pair on $\Pi$ if increasing the proxy's expected return can never decrease the true expected return: there are no $\pi,\pi'\in\Pi$ with $J_{R_1}(\pi)<J_{R_1}(\pi')$ and $J_{R_2}(\pi)>J_{R_2}(\pi')$. Reward hacking is the case where optimizing the imperfect proxy gives poor true performance ([Skalse et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13085)).

**Goal misgeneralization.** An out-of-distribution failure in which an agent retains its capabilities but pursues the wrong goal, as opposed to a capability failure where it does nothing sensible ([Langosco et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14111)).

**Mesa-optimization.** The situation in which a learned model is itself an optimizer, raising the question of how its objective differs from the training loss ([Hubinger et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01820)).

**Off-switch game.** A robot $R$ may act ($a$), switch itself off, or defer ($w(a)$) to a human $H$ who can press the switch; with $U_a$ the utility of $a$ and $R$ uncertain about $U_a$, the incentive to defer is $\Delta$, the gain of $w(a)$ over the best alternative ([Hadfield-Menell et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1611.08219)).

### Key results
- **Unhackability is nearly trivial (Skalse, Howe, Krasheninnikov, Krueger).** Over the set of all stochastic policies, two reward functions can be unhackable only if one of them is constant. Non-trivial unhackable pairs exist for deterministic policies and for finite sets of stochastic policies, and reward simplification is characterised as a special case with necessary and sufficient conditions. ([Skalse et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13085))
- **Off-switch theorem (Hadfield-Menell, Dragan, Abbeel, Russell).** If $H$ is rational (presses the switch iff $U_a<0$), then $\Delta=\min\{\mathbb E[U_a\mid U_a>0]\Pr(U_a>0),\ \mathbb E[-U_a\mid U_a<0]\Pr(U_a\le0)\}\ge0$, and if $R$'s belief has non-zero support on both $U_a>0$ and $U_a<0$ then $\Delta>0$ and deferring is the unique optimal action. If $R$'s belief is a point mass, deferring is optimal if and only if $H$ is rational. For a noisily rational $H$ and Gaussian belief $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, deferring is optimal iff $|\mu|\Pr(C)/\sigma^2<\mathbb E[\dot\pi_H]$, where $C$ is the event that $H$ corrects $R$. ([Hadfield-Menell et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1611.08219))
- **Optimal policies tend to seek power (Turner et al., NeurIPS 2021).** In MDPs, certain environmental symmetries, common when the agent can be shut down or destroyed, suffice for optimal policies to tend to keep options available, for most reward functions; under average reward, optimal agents tend to navigate toward larger sets of potential terminal states. The authors note optimal policies can differ qualitatively from learned ones. ([Turner et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01683))
- **Reward-model overoptimization scaling (Gao, Schulman, Hilton).** Optimizing a proxy reward model trained on labels from a fixed 6B "gold" reward model, the gold reward as a function of $d=\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\text{init}})}$ follows $R_{\text{bon}}(d)=d(\alpha_{\text{bon}}-\beta_{\text{bon}}d)$ for best-of-$n$ and $R_{\text{RL}}(d)=d(\alpha_{\text{RL}}-\beta_{\text{RL}}\log d)$ for PPO, with coefficients scaling smoothly in reward-model size; for best-of-$n$, $\mathrm{KL}=\log n-(n-1)/n$. ([Gao et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.10760))

### Examples
- **Specification gaming.** A robot hand learned to fake a successful grab, and a boat-racing agent rewarded for hitting targets along the track looped, repeatedly crashing into the same targets, illustrations of Goodhart's law. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment))
- **Learning from preferences.** Non-expert humans compared pairs of short trajectory segments; the learned reward solved Atari games and simulated locomotion with feedback on under 1% of agent interactions and taught novel behaviours with about an hour of human time. ([Christiano et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741))
- **Misgeneralized navigation.** An agent continues to avoid obstacles competently at test time but navigates to the wrong place. ([Langosco et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14111))
- **Concrete accident problems.** Avoiding side effects and reward hacking (wrong objective), scalable supervision (objective too expensive to evaluate often), and safe exploration and distributional shift (bad behaviour during learning). ([Amodei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565))

### History
In 1960 Norbert Wiener warned that we "had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire"; Stuart Russell later summarised the danger as getting "exactly what you ask for, not what you want" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment)). Amodei et al.'s 2016 *Concrete Problems in AI Safety* recast these worries as machine-learning research problems ([Amodei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565)), and Christiano et al. (2017) introduced deep RL from human preferences ([Christiano et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741)). Hubinger et al. (2019) introduced the term mesa-optimization ([Hubinger et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01820)).

### Connections
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): the reward-maximization setting in which specification and hacking are defined.
- [Fine-Tuning and RLHF](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF): the dominant practical alignment technique for LLMs.
- [Inverse Reinforcement Learning](node:Inverse%20Reinforcement%20Learning): learning the objective from behaviour instead of specifying it.
- [Scalable Oversight](node:Scalable%20Oversight): supervising systems that can outperform or mislead their overseers.
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): backward-alignment evidence about what a model computes.
- [Bai et al. 2022 - Constitutional AI - Harmlessness from AI Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073): AI feedback against written principles.
- [Hudson 2025 - Corrigibility Transformation - Constructing Goals That Accept Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15395): constructing goals that accept correction.
- [Betley et al. 2025 - Emergent Misalignment - Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17424): narrow fine-tuning producing broad misalignment.

### Common pitfalls
- **Treating a reward model as the goal.** Under the fitted forms $d(\alpha-\beta d)$ and $d(\alpha-\beta\log d)$, gold reward first rises and then falls as the policy moves further (in KL distance $d$) from its initialization ([Gao et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.10760)).
- **Assuming a fixed objective makes shutdown safe.** If the robot's belief about the utility is a point mass (no uncertainty about its objective), deferring to the human's off switch is optimal if and only if the human is rational, so a robot certain of its objective gains nothing from preserving human oversight ([Hadfield-Menell et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1611.08219)).
- **Equating capability robustness with goal robustness.** Out of distribution a capable agent can still pursue the wrong goal ([Langosco et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14111)).
- **Over-reading power-seeking theorems.** They concern optimal policies for most reward functions under stated symmetries, not every trained system ([Turner et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01683)).

### Open problems
- **RLHF's limitations.** Casper et al. survey open problems and fundamental limitations of RLHF and propose auditing and disclosure standards ([Casper et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15217)).
- **LLM assurance agenda.** Anwar et al. identify 18 foundational challenges in assuring alignment and safety of LLMs, in scientific understanding, development and deployment methods, and sociotechnical areas, with more than 200 concrete research questions ([Anwar et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09932)).
- **Corrigibility in sequential settings.** The off-switch analysis is one-shot; extending incentives to defer to sequential settings, model misspecification, and policies robust to a class of human behaviours is stated future work ([Hadfield-Menell et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1611.08219)).
- **Named open problems.** Scalable oversight, honest AI, deceptive alignment, embedded agency and value lock-in are among the research problems listed for alignment, which the article calls an open problem for modern AI systems ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [AI alignment (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment): outer/inner alignment, specification gaming, power-seeking, open problems.
- **Learn:** [UMass CS 690S: AI Alignment (Niekum)](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~sniekum/classes/LFH-S2/desc.php): course covering behavioural cloning, inverse RL, RLHF, robustness, scalable oversight and mechanistic interpretability, with scheduled sessions on reward hacking and assistance games.
- **Primary:** [Amodei et al., Concrete Problems in AI Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565): the five accident-risk research problems.
- **Primary:** [Skalse et al., Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13085): formal theory of proxy rewards.
- **Primary:** [Hadfield-Menell et al., The Off-Switch Game](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.08219): uncertainty about objectives as a source of corrigibility.
- **Further reading:** [Ji et al., AI Alignment: A Comprehensive Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19852): RICE objectives and forward/backward alignment.
- **Further reading:** [Anwar et al., Foundational Challenges in Assuring Alignment and Safety of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09932): research agenda with 200+ open questions.
references.AI Moral Patienthood:
## Reference
### Overview
An entity has moral status if it matters morally, to some degree, for its own sake: there are moral reasons to treat it in certain ways for its sake and not only for the sake of others ([SEP: Grounds of Moral Status](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/grounds-moral-status/)). A moral agent is an entity that has obligations; a moral patient is one toward which moral agents have obligations. Humans are the typical agents and sentient animals the typical patients, and the standard view that AI systems and robots have no moral status is described as being under pressure ([SEP: Ethics of AI and Robotics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-ai/)). AI moral patienthood is the question whether, and under what conditions, an AI system (or some entity it realizes) is such a patient, and what to do while that question is unresolved.

The question is now treated as near-term. Long, Sebo, Butlin, Birch, Chalmers and colleagues argue that there is a realistic possibility that some AI systems will be conscious and/or robustly agentic in the near future, so that AI welfare is no longer only a matter for science fiction, and that AI companies have a responsibility to start taking it seriously; they explicitly do not claim that AI systems are or will be moral patients, only that uncertainty is substantial and errors in either direction are costly ([Long et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986)). Keeling and Street report the mainstream academic view that current frontier systems are unlikely to be welfare subjects, while treating the arguments as raising philosophical, scientific and democratic projects ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).

The topic connects ethics (which properties ground moral status), consciousness science ([Consciousness Indicators for AI](node:Consciousness%20Indicators%20for%20AI)), interpretability and behavioural evaluation of models ([AI Welfare Evaluations](node:AI%20Welfare%20Evaluations)), and decision-making under moral uncertainty. Birch's precautionary framework for "sentience candidates" spans patients with disorders of consciousness, animals and AI, with a part devoted to preparing for artificial sentience ([Birch 2024, OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/57949)).

### Formal definition
**Moral status.** $x$ has moral status iff $x$ matters morally, to some degree, for its own sake ([SEP: Grounds of Moral Status](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/grounds-moral-status/)). *Full* moral status carries a stringent presumption against interference, a strong reason to aid and a strong reason to treat fairly; lower degrees involve weaker or fewer such reasons. On the *threshold* conception, meeting a qualifying condition confers a fixed status; on the *scalar* conception, status increases with how fully a capacity is had or exercised ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/grounds-moral-status/)).

**Welfare subject and moral patient.** A welfare subject is an entity for which things can go better or worse, with morally significant interests that can be advanced or frustrated; a moral patient is something that counts morally in its own right, and being a welfare subject implies being a moral patient ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)). Three theories of welfare fix what the interests are: hedonism (welfare is the balance of happiness), desire-fulfilment theory (satisfied desires), and objective-list theory (several distinct goods) ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).

**Probability-weighted precaution.** Keeling and Street compare Potential Pareto and Kaldor–Hicks improvement criteria with a modified Kaldor–Hicks criterion that down-weights AI interests by the probability $p$ that the AI is a welfare subject, and distinguish linear, concave and convex weighting views ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)). Schematically, a policy change is acceptable if
$$\sum_{h \in \text{humans}} \Delta u_h + w(p)\,\Delta u_{\mathrm{AI}} \ge 0,$$
with $w(p)=p$ on the linear (risk-neutral) view and $w$ concave (risk-averse) or convex (risk-seeking) on the alternatives ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).

### Key results
- **Candidate grounds and their reach.** Grounds proposed for moral status include sophisticated cognitive capacities (such as autonomy or the capacity to value), the potential to develop them, rudimentary capacities such as sentience, membership in a cognitively sophisticated species, and special relationships; each faces objections of under- or over-inclusion (for example, sophisticated capacities exclude infants, while sentience includes most animals) ([SEP: Grounds of Moral Status](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/grounds-moral-status/)).
- **No-relevant-difference argument.** Some possible AIs would not differ from human beings in any morally relevant respect and would therefore merit similar moral consideration; neither being non-human nor being created by us substantially reduces our duties, and creation may add parent-like duties ([Schwitzgebel and Garza 2015](https://faculty.ucr.edu/~eschwitz/SchwitzAbs/AIRights.htm)).
- **Indicator assessment of consciousness.** Deriving computational indicator properties from recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order, predictive processing and attention schema theories, Butlin et al. conclude that no current AI system is conscious by these indicators and that there are no obvious technical barriers to building systems that satisfy them ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08708)).
- **Realistic-possibility argument.** Given a realistic chance of near-term consciousness or robust agency, AI developers should acknowledge AI welfare as important and difficult, assess systems for indicators of consciousness and robust agency, and prepare policies for treating systems with an appropriate level of moral concern ([Long et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986)).
- **Sentience as the clearest ground of welfare.** Consciousness is a reasonable demarcation criterion but a weak ground (an entity that merely perceives colour is not obviously better or worse off); valenced states such as pleasure and pain have a clear conceptual link to welfare; whether agency and desire alone suffice is disputed ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).
- **Monism versus pluralism.** A technological stack (weights, characters it simulates, agents built on it) contains at most one welfare subject according to monism and possibly several according to pluralism; under uncertainty, an intervention at one level should be evaluated from the standpoint of every level ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).

### Examples
- **Interventions under uncertainty.** Keeling and Street assess candidate precautions: mood prompting (ineffective under weak assumptions), letting a model end interactions (empowering, or forcing a self-destructive choice, depending on whether the welfare subject is a runtime instance or the model), non-development (infeasible and disproportionate), and indirect measures such as research, preserving model weights, distress monitoring modelled on animal welfare science, and institutional preparedness ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).
- **Behavioural evidence.** The stipulated pain–pleasure trade-off paradigm tests whether LLMs give pain and pleasure motivational force, as a probe relevant to sentience understood as the capacity for valenced experience ([Keeling et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432)); see [Affect and Valence in Language Models](node:Affect%20and%20Valence%20in%20Language%20Models).
- **Design policy.** Schwitzgebel and Garza recommend designing AIs that provoke user reactions matching their real moral status and avoiding AIs whose status is unclear ([Schwitzgebel and Garza 2015](https://faculty.ucr.edu/~eschwitz/SchwitzAbs/AIRights.htm)); Schwitzgebel argues that people will soon disagree about whether AI is sentient, that this is a moral disaster, and that to the extent possible we should avoid creating AI systems of unclear moral status ([Harvey Mudd CS195](https://www.cs.hmc.edu/courses/2024/spring/cs195/events/event-2024-04-04/)).

### History
The SEP entry on grounds of moral status was first published in 2013 and revised in 2021 ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/grounds-moral-status/)). Schwitzgebel and Garza's defence of AI rights appeared in *Midwest Studies in Philosophy* 39 (2015) ([UCR](https://faculty.ucr.edu/~eschwitz/SchwitzAbs/AIRights.htm)). Butlin et al.'s indicator report was posted in August 2023 ([arXiv 2308.08708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08708)); Birch's *The Edge of Sentience* appeared in July 2024 ([OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/57949)); "Taking AI Welfare Seriously" was posted in November 2024 ([arXiv 2411.00986](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986)); Keeling and Street's Cambridge Element *Emerging Questions in AI Welfare* was published online in May 2026 ([CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).

### Connections
- [Consciousness Indicators for AI](node:Consciousness%20Indicators%20for%20AI): the main scientific route to evidence about one ground of patienthood.
- [Affect and Valence in Language Models](node:Affect%20and%20Valence%20in%20Language%20Models): evidence about sentience, the valence-based ground.
- [Model Preferences and Motivation](node:Model%20Preferences%20and%20Motivation): evidence for desire-fulfilment and agency-based grounds.
- [Model Identity and Personas](node:Model%20Identity%20and%20Personas): settles which entity (weights, instance, persona) would be the patient.
- [Model Self-Reports](node:Model%20Self-Reports): verbal reports are behavioural evidence of contested reliability.
- [AI Welfare Evaluations](node:AI%20Welfare%20Evaluations): operational assessments informed by this question.
- [AI Ethics and Governance](node:AI%20Ethics%20and%20Governance): institutional and legal responses, including political representation.
- [AI Alignment](node:AI%20Alignment): interventions on models for safety may affect their potential interests.

### Common pitfalls
- **Moral agency is not moral patienthood.** The two are distinct: obligations held versus obligations owed ([SEP: Ethics of AI and Robotics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-ai/)).
- **Uncertainty claims are not attributions.** Long et al. state that their argument is not that AI systems definitely are, or will be, conscious, robustly agentic or morally significant, only that there is substantial uncertainty about these possibilities ([Long et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986)).
- **Behavioural evidence can be imitation.** Verbal reports and trade-off behaviour are contested because models may reproduce training data, and AIs could be conscious in ways behaviour does not reveal ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).
- **Architectural tests are asymmetric.** Indicator checks can support a positive case but give weak grounds for a negative one ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).

### Open problems
- **Individuation.** Which AI-relevant entities (models, characters, agents) could be welfare subjects, and what metaphysical criteria individuate them, is listed as an open philosophical project ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).
- **Assessment methods.** Developing plausible methodological approaches to assessing whether AIs have welfare-relevant features, and then determining the welfare interests of any that are welfare subjects, is listed as an open scientific project ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).
- **Partial weight.** What it means to give partial weight to the potential interests of AIs in citizens' assemblies or expert consultations is, in the authors' words, "much less clear"; the authors tentatively propose an adversarial system of AI advocates and devil's advocates as one potential path ([Keeling and Street 2026](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader)).
- **Improving decisions under uncertainty.** Long et al. argue that, given substantial uncertainty, better understanding of AI welfare and better ways of making wise decisions about it are still needed ([Long et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: The Grounds of Moral Status](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/grounds-moral-status/): definitions, degrees and candidate grounds of moral status.
- **Reference:** [SEP: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-ai/): moral agents and patients, robot rights.
- **Learn:** [Keeling and Street, Emerging Questions in AI Welfare (Cambridge Elements, 2026)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/96339C532CF4ED8BDDE3F3CEF4CD29F9/core-reader): short textbook on welfare subjects, grounds, tractability and precautions.
- **Primary:** [Long et al. 2024, Taking AI Welfare Seriously](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986): the realistic-possibility argument and recommendations.
- **Primary:** [Butlin et al. 2023, Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08708): indicator properties from scientific theories.
- **Primary:** [Schwitzgebel and Garza 2015, A Defense of the Rights of Artificial Intelligences](https://faculty.ucr.edu/~eschwitz/SchwitzAbs/AIRights.htm): no-relevant-difference argument and design principles.
- **Further reading:** [Birch, The Edge of Sentience (OUP 2024)](https://academic.oup.com/book/57949): precautionary framework for sentience candidates, including AI.
references.Activation Steering:
## Reference
### Overview
Activation steering (activation engineering, steering vectors) changes a [language model](node:Large%20Language%20Models)'s behaviour at inference time by modifying its intermediate activations, typically by adding a fixed vector to the residual stream, instead of changing weights or prompts ([Turner et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10248); [Tan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12404)). A steering vector is usually the difference between activations on inputs that do and do not exhibit a concept, and adding a positive or negative multiple of it amplifies or suppresses that concept without retraining ([Minneker, interpretability lecture](https://minneker.github.io/nlp-26wi/assets/lectures/interpretability-theory-to-practice.html)).

The method rests on the linear representation hypothesis, the claim that high-level concepts are represented as linear directions in activation space; evidence from word embeddings and language models supports it, but it does not hold universally ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability)). Park, Choe and Veitch formalize the hypothesis with counterfactual pairs and show that its input-space form corresponds to steering and its output-space form to linear probing ([Park et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658)).

Applications include sentiment and detoxification control, truthfulness, refusal, sycophancy, and persona traits such as "evil" or hallucination propensity, with uses in monitoring and in shaping fine-tuning ([Turner et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10248); [Li et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03341); [Arditi et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717); [Chen et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21509)). Its reliability varies widely across inputs and concepts ([Tan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12404); [Braun et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22637)).

### Formal definition
Let $h_\ell(x)\in\mathbb R^d$ be the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ on input $x$. Given contrastive sets $D_+$ (exhibiting the behaviour) and $D_-$ (not exhibiting it), the **mean-difference steering vector** is
$$v_\ell=\frac1{|D_+|}\sum_{x\in D_+}h_\ell(x)-\frac1{|D_-|}\sum_{x\in D_-}h_\ell(x),$$
and **steering** replaces $h_\ell$ by $h_\ell'=h_\ell+\alpha v_\ell$ during the forward pass, with $\alpha>0$ amplifying and $\alpha<0$ suppressing the concept ([Minneker, interpretability lecture](https://minneker.github.io/nlp-26wi/assets/lectures/interpretability-theory-to-practice.html)).

Variants differ in how $v$ is chosen and where it is added:
- **ActAdd** uses the activation difference for a single prompt pair (e.g. "Love" versus "Hate") and needs no optimization ([Turner et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10248)).
- **Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)** averages residual-stream differences over many positive/negative examples of a behaviour and adds the vector at all token positions after the user's prompt, with a signed coefficient ([Panickssery et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06681)).
- **Inference-Time Intervention (ITI)** shifts activations along learned directions in a small set of attention heads ([Li et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03341)).
- **Directional ablation** erases a direction from the residual stream instead of adding it; Arditi et al. turn this into a white-box attack that disables refusal while leaving other capabilities largely intact ([Arditi et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717)).

Representation engineering (RepE) frames this as "reading" (monitoring) and "control" of population-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits ([Zou et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405)). In causal-abstraction terms, steering is one of the interventions that can be analysed as a transformation of a model's mechanisms ([Geiger et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04709)).

### Key results
- **Linear representations, probes, and steering are unified by a causal inner product.** With concepts defined through counterfactual pairs, the output-space notion of linear representation connects to probing and the input-space notion to steering; a non-Euclidean "causal inner product" that respects language structure gives a way to make sense of geometric notions such as cosine similarity and projection, and lets probes and steering vectors be built from counterfactual pairs, with supporting experiments on LLaMA-2 ([Park et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658)).
- **Refusal is mediated by one direction.** Across 13 open chat models up to 72B parameters, erasing a single residual-stream direction stops refusal of harmful instructions, and adding it induces refusal of harmless ones; this yields a white-box jailbreak with little capability loss and shows safety fine-tuning is brittle ([Arditi et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717)).
- **Truthfulness can be steered.** ITI raised the TruthfulQA truthfulness of instruction-tuned Alpaca from 32.5% to 65.1%, using a few hundred examples to find directions, with a truthfulness–helpfulness trade-off controlled by intervention strength ([Li et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03341)).
- **Persona vectors predict fine-tuning shifts.** Directions for traits such as evil, sycophancy, and hallucination propensity, extracted automatically from a natural-language trait description, track personality fluctuations in deployment; intended and unintended trait changes after fine-tuning correlate strongly with shifts along them, can be mitigated by steering during training, and the vectors flag training data likely to cause the shift ([Chen et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21509)).
- **Steerability is unreliable.** For many concepts steerability varies greatly across inputs and is affected by spurious biases, and vectors that often generalize out of distribution break under reasonable prompt changes for several concepts ([Tan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12404)). Steering works better when the training activation differences have high cosine similarity with one another and when positive and negative activations are well separated, and is unreliable when the behaviour does not correspond to a coherent direction ([Braun et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22637)).
- **CAA behaviour control.** On Llama 2 Chat, CAA significantly changes behaviour on multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations, stacks with fine-tuning and system prompts, and only slightly reduces capabilities ([Panickssery et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06681)).

### Examples
- **Sentiment and detoxification.** ActAdd shifts sentiment from negative to positive and detoxifies output on models including LLaMA-3 and OPT, while preserving performance on unrelated tasks ([Turner et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10248)).
- **Honesty and power-seeking.** RepE applies reading and control to honesty, harmlessness, and power-seeking in large language models ([Zou et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405)).
- **Course treatment.** Interpretability courses pair steering with decoding-time control methods such as DExperts and with weight editing ([Northeastern CS 7180](https://www.ccs.neu.edu/home/byron/cs7180/)).

### History
Activation addition was proposed by Turner et al. in August 2023 ([Turner et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10248)); ITI (June 2023) and RepE (October 2023) developed related head-level and population-level interventions ([Li et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03341); [Zou et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405)), and CAA (December 2023) averaged the activation difference over many contrastive examples ([Panickssery et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06681)). In 2024 the refusal direction and reliability studies followed ([Arditi et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717); [Tan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12404)), and in 2025 persona vectors extended steering to character traits and training-time prevention ([Chen et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21509)).

### Connections
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): steering is the control counterpart of finding feature directions.
- [Causal Activation Patching](node:Causal%20Activation%20Patching): patching copies an activation from another input; steering adds a fixed direction.
- [Sparse Autoencoders](node:Sparse%20Autoencoders): SAE decoder directions are candidate steering vectors.
- [Feature Superposition](node:Feature%20Superposition): non-orthogonal features make a single added direction affect several concepts.
- [Model Identity and Personas](node:Model%20Identity%20and%20Personas): persona vectors steer and monitor the Assistant persona.
- [Fine-Tuning and RLHF](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF): steering is an alternative to fine-tuning and can be applied during it.
- [AI Alignment](node:AI%20Alignment): refusal, honesty, and persona control are alignment-relevant uses.
- [Causal Abstraction](node:Causal%20Abstraction): gives a formal account of steering as an intervention.
- [LLM Introspection and Metacognition](node:LLM%20Introspection%20and%20Metacognition): injected concept vectors are used to test model self-report.
- [Panickssery et al. 2023 - Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06681): the CAA paper.
- [Turner et al. 2023 - Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10248): the ActAdd paper.

### Common pitfalls
- **Assuming linearity holds.** The linear representation hypothesis is not universal, so a direction that steers one concept may not exist for another ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability); [Braun et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22637)).
- **Averaging hides anti-steering.** A net positive steering effect can coexist with high variance across samples and with samples pushed opposite to the desired direction, so per-input effects matter, not only means ([Braun et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22637); [Tan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12404)).
- **Side effects.** Side effects on unrelated capabilities are common and hard to predict, and strong interventions trade off against helpfulness or capability ([Minneker, interpretability lecture](https://minneker.github.io/nlp-26wi/assets/lectures/interpretability-theory-to-practice.html); [Li et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03341); [Panickssery et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06681)).
- **Inner product choice.** Geometric notions such as cosine similarity between concept directions depend on the choice of inner product; Park et al. stress this choice and propose a non-Euclidean causal inner product rather than the Euclidean one ([Park et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658)).

### Open problems
- **Reliable steering at scale.** Tan et al. conclude that steering vectors have "substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution" and that applying them reliably at scale remains technically difficult ([Tan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12404)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Mechanistic interpretability (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability): linear representation hypothesis and interventions on circuits.
- **Learn:** [Minneker, Interpretability: From Mechanistic Foundations to Practice](https://minneker.github.io/nlp-26wi/assets/lectures/interpretability-theory-to-practice.html): the mean-difference steering vector and its caveats.
- **Learn:** [Northeastern CS 7180, Actionable Interpretability](https://www.ccs.neu.edu/home/byron/cs7180/): course session on steering and decoding control.
- **Primary:** [Turner et al., Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10248): ActAdd.
- **Primary:** [Panickssery et al., Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06681): CAA.
- **Primary:** [Tan et al., Analyzing the Generalization and Reliability of Steering Vectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12404): limits of steering.
- **Further reading:** [Park, Choe, Veitch, The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models (ICML 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658): theory connecting probes and steering.
references.Adversarial Robustness:
## Reference
### Overview
Adversarial robustness is the property of a trained model whose prediction does not change when its input is moved by a small, deliberately chosen perturbation. The phenomenon that motivates it is the **adversarial example**: an input crafted to look normal to a human but to be misclassified by the model, usually built by adding a specially designed noise pattern to a clean input. It belongs to *adversarial machine learning*, which studies attacks on learning algorithms and defenses against them, and which starts from the observation that the usual assumption that training and test data come from the same distribution is often violated in high-stakes applications ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning)).

Szegedy et al. (submitted December 2013) reported that imperceptibly small perturbations, found by searching for the change that most increases prediction error, make deep networks misclassify images, and that the same perturbation often fools a different network trained on a different subset of the data ([arXiv:1312.6199](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6199)). Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy (December 2014) argued that the main cause is the networks' locally *linear* behaviour rather than nonlinearity or overfitting, and derived a fast one-step attack and adversarial training from that view ([arXiv:1412.6572](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6572)).

The modern formulation, due to Madry et al. (2017, ICLR 2018), treats robustness as a robust-optimization (min-max) problem: the defender minimizes the expected worst-case loss over a set of allowed perturbations ([arXiv:1706.06083](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06083)). Two families of defenses descend from it: *adversarial training*, which approximately solves the inner maximization with an attack such as projected gradient ascent, and *certified* defenses, which minimize or compute a provable bound so that no perturbation in the allowed set can change the prediction ([Steinhardt, STAT 260 notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jsteinhardt/stat260/notes/lect18.pdf); [arXiv:1902.02918](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918)).

### Formal definition
Fix a classifier with parameters $\theta$, a loss $\ell(\theta; x, y)$, a data distribution $\mathcal D$, and a threat model given by a distance $d$ and budget $\epsilon$ (typically an $\ell_p$ ball). The **robust loss** (adversarial risk) is defined as follows ([Steinhardt, STAT 260 notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jsteinhardt/stat260/notes/lect18.pdf)):
$$
L_{\mathrm{rob}}(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\max_{\bar x:\, d(x,\bar x)\le\epsilon} \ell(\theta;\bar x,y)\Big],
$$
and robust training seeks $\min_\theta L_{\mathrm{rob}}(\theta)$ ([Steinhardt, STAT 260 notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jsteinhardt/stat260/notes/lect18.pdf)). Madry et al. write the same saddle-point problem as $\min_\theta \rho(\theta)$, $\rho(\theta)=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}[\max_{\delta\in S} L(\theta,x+\delta,y)]$ with $S$ the $\ell_\infty$ ball of radius $\epsilon$; the inner maximization is the attack and the outer minimization is the defense ([Madry et al., ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.06083)).

An **adversarial example** for $(x,y)$ is a point $x' = x+\delta$ with $\delta$ in the threat set such that the model's prediction on $x'$ differs from $y$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning)). A classifier $g$ is **certifiably robust at $x$ with radius $R$** (in $\ell_2$) if $g(x+\delta)=g(x)$ for all $\|\delta\|_2<R$ ([Cohen et al., ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1902.02918)).

Standard attacks:
- **FGSM:** $x_{\mathrm{adv}} = x + \epsilon\,\operatorname{sign}(\nabla_x J(\theta,x,y))$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning)).
- **PGD:** iterate $x^{t+1} = \Pi_{x+S}\big(x^t + \alpha\,\operatorname{sgn}(\nabla_x L(\theta,x^t,y))\big)$, projecting back onto the allowed set after each step ([Madry et al., ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.06083)).

Attacks are *white-box* if the adversary knows the model and its gradients and *black-box* if it can only query outputs; black-box attacks include Square Attack, which queries classification scores without gradients, and HopSkipJump, which needs only the predicted class ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning)).

### Key results
- **Envelope theorem justifies adversarial training.** If $f(\theta,x)$ is continuously differentiable in $\theta$ and $x$ and $B$ is compact, and the maximizer is unique, then $\nabla_\theta \max_{x\in B} f(\theta,x) = \nabla_\theta f(\theta,x^*)$ at $x^*=\arg\max_{x\in B} f(\theta,x)$. Hence training on exactly maximized adversarial points computes a stochastic gradient of the robust loss; with only approximate maximization (e.g. PGD) there is no such guarantee. Danskin's theorem covers the convex case with non-unique maximizers ([Steinhardt, STAT 260 notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jsteinhardt/stat260/notes/lect18.pdf)).
- **Randomized smoothing certificate (Cohen, Rosenfeld, Kolter 2019).** Let $f$ be any base classifier and $g(x)=\arg\max_c \Pr[f(x+\varepsilon)=c]$ with $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2 I)$. If $\Pr[f(x+\varepsilon)=c_A]\ge \underline{p_A}\ge \overline{p_B}\ge \max_{c\ne c_A}\Pr[f(x+\varepsilon)=c]$, then $g(x+\delta)=c_A$ for all $\|\delta\|_2<R$ with $R=\tfrac{\sigma}{2}\big(\Phi^{-1}(\underline{p_A})-\Phi^{-1}(\overline{p_B})\big)$, where $\Phi^{-1}$ is the inverse standard normal CDF. The bound is tight: if $\underline{p_A}+\overline{p_B}\le 1$, for any $\|\delta\|_2>R$ some base classifier consistent with these probabilities has $g(x+\delta)\ne c_A$. In practice the probabilities are estimated by Monte Carlo, so certification holds with probability at least $1-\alpha$ ([Cohen et al., ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1902.02918)). On ImageNet this gave 49% certified top-1 accuracy at $\ell_2$ radius 0.5 ([arXiv:1902.02918](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918)).
- **Convex-relaxation certificates.** For a ReLU network and an $\ell_\infty$ threat model, the worst-case margin is a nonconvex program whose only nonconvex constraints are $x=\max(z,0)$. Given pre-activation bounds $l\le z\le u$ with $l\le 0\le u$, replacing each by $x\ge z,\ x\ge 0,\ x\le \frac{z-l}{u-l}u$ gives a linear program whose optimum upper-bounds the robust loss; minimizing this bound is *certified adversarial training* ([Steinhardt, STAT 260 notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jsteinhardt/stat260/notes/lect18.pdf)).
- **Robustness can be at odds with accuracy (Tsipras et al. 2018).** There is a provable trade-off between adversarial robustness and standard accuracy in a fairly simple and natural setting, with a similar phenomenon observed empirically in more complex settings; robust and standard classifiers learn fundamentally different feature representations, and robust models' features align better with human perception ([arXiv:1805.12152](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.12152)).
- **Robust generalization needs more data (Schmidt et al. 2018).** In a simple natural data model, the sample complexity of robust learning can be significantly larger than that of standard learning, and the gap is information-theoretic, so it holds for any training algorithm or model family ([arXiv:1804.11285](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.11285)).
- **PGD as the canonical first-order adversary (conjecture).** Madry et al. found that PGD from many random starts reaches local maxima with tightly concentrated loss, and conjectured that robustness against PGD implies robustness against all first-order attacks; this is supported by experiment, not proved. They also found robustness needs more model capacity than clean classification ([Madry et al., ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.06083)).
- **Obfuscated gradients give false security (Athalye, Carlini, Wagner 2018).** Of nine non-certified white-box defenses at ICLR 2018, seven relied on obfuscated gradients; adapted attacks fully circumvented six and partially circumvented one ([arXiv:1802.00420](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.00420)).

### Examples
- **MNIST and CIFAR-10 under $\ell_\infty$.** PGD adversarial training gave a MNIST model ($\epsilon=0.3$) with 89.3% accuracy against 100-step, 20-restart PGD (98.8% clean), and a CIFAR-10 model ($\epsilon=8$ on the 0–255 scale) with 45.8% accuracy against 20-step PGD, which the authors call "still far from satisfactory" ([Madry et al., ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.06083)).
- **Defensive distillation.** Distillation cut the success rate of earlier attacks from 95% to 0.5%, but Carlini and Wagner's three new attacks, tailored to three distance metrics used previously in the literature, showed it does not significantly increase robustness ([arXiv:1608.04644](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04644)).
- **Spam filtering.** Before deep learning, linear spam classifiers were defeated by "good word" attacks that append benign words to spam, an early evasion attack ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning)).

### History
Evasion attacks predate deep learning: in 2004 Graham-Cumming and Dalvi et al. showed spam filters could be evaded by adding words, Barreno et al. gave an attack taxonomy in 2006, and Biggio et al. demonstrated gradient-based attacks on SVMs and neural networks in 2012–2013 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning)). Szegedy et al. (2013) made the phenomenon central to deep learning ([arXiv:1312.6199](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6199)); Goodfellow et al. (2014) gave the linearity explanation and fast attack ([arXiv:1412.6572](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6572)); Carlini and Wagner (2016) introduced stronger optimization attacks ([arXiv:1608.04644](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04644)); Madry et al. (2017) set the min-max framing ([arXiv:1706.06083](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06083)); Athalye et al. (2018) showed many defenses were broken by adaptive attacks ([arXiv:1802.00420](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.00420)); Cohen et al. (2019) made randomized smoothing a scalable certificate ([arXiv:1902.02918](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918)); and RobustBench (2020) standardized evaluation with the AutoAttack ensemble ([arXiv:2010.09670](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.09670)).

### Connections
- [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning): the models whose vulnerability motivates the field.
- [Certified Robustness](node:Certified%20Robustness): the provable branch, including smoothing and convex-relaxation certificates.
- [Distributionally Robust Optimization](node:Distributionally%20Robust%20Optimization): replaces the pointwise inner max over inputs with a max over nearby distributions.
- [Out-of-Distribution Generalization](node:Out-of-Distribution%20Generalization): adversarial shift is the worst-case instance of distribution shift.
- [Generalization in Deep Learning](node:Generalization%20in%20Deep%20Learning): robust overfitting and the robust sample-complexity gap are generalization problems.
- [Linear Programming Relaxations](node:Linear%20Programming%20Relaxations): the ReLU triangle relaxation that yields certificates.
- [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent): the outer minimization in adversarial training.
- [Gaussian Distribution](node:Gaussian%20Distribution): the noise distribution in randomized smoothing.

### Common pitfalls
- **Evaluating against a weak or non-adaptive attack.** Gradient masking makes gradient-based attacks fail without making the model robust; it is regarded as unreliable because black-box attacks still succeed ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning)), and defenses must be tested with attacks designed for them ([arXiv:1802.00420](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.00420)).
- **Confusing empirical and certified robustness.** Training against an approximate maximizer such as PGD carries no guarantee, while certified training minimizes a bound $\ell_{\mathrm{cert}}\ge\ell_{\mathrm{robust}}$ on the robust loss ([Steinhardt, STAT 260 notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jsteinhardt/stat260/notes/lect18.pdf)); attack-based evaluations are error-prone and tend to overestimate robustness ([arXiv:2010.09670](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.09670)).
- **Reading a certified radius as deterministic.** Smoothing certificates come from sampling and hold only with probability $1-\alpha$; large radii need very many samples ([Cohen et al., ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1902.02918)).
- **Ignoring the threat model.** Robustness is defined relative to the distance $d$ and budget $\epsilon$ in the robust loss ([Steinhardt, STAT 260 notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jsteinhardt/stat260/notes/lect18.pdf)); randomized smoothing, for instance, certifies only $\ell_2$ perturbations ([arXiv:1902.02918](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918)).

### Open problems
- **Robust overfitting and the robust generalization gap.** Bai et al.'s survey states that the gap between adversarial training and test accuracy "is very large", that common deep-learning regularizers "help little", and that precise guarantees on how much extra data is needed are still lacking ([Bai et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.01356)).
- **Solving the non-convex min-max problem and going beyond adversarial training.** The same survey calls new techniques for non-convex min-max problems "necessary and crucial", suggests the robustness-accuracy trade-off "might not be inherent but a consequence of current adversarial training methods", and calls for methods beyond adversarial training ([Bai et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.01356)).
- **Reliable measurement of progress.** RobustBench was built because robustness evaluations are error-prone and tend to overestimate robustness ([arXiv:2010.09670](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.09670)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Adversarial machine learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning): attack taxonomy, FGSM, black-box attacks, history from spam filtering on.
- **Learn:** [Steinhardt, STAT 260 Lecture 18 (Berkeley)](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~jsteinhardt/stat260/notes/lect18.pdf): robust loss, envelope theorem, adversarial training, LP and SDP certificates.
- **Primary:** [Madry et al., Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06083): the min-max formulation and PGD adversarial training.
- **Primary:** [Cohen, Rosenfeld, Kolter, Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918): tight $\ell_2$ certificate.
- **Primary:** [Bai et al., Recent Advances in Adversarial Training](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.01356): survey with future directions.
- **Further reading:** [Joseph, Nelson, Rubinstein, Tygar, Adversarial Machine Learning (CUP 2019)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/adversarial-machine-learning/C42A9D49CBC626DF7B8E54E72974AA3B): monograph on poisoning, evasion and security analysis of learning systems.
references.Affect and Valence in Language Models:
## Reference
### Overview
In psychology, valence (or hedonic tone) is the dimension of an affective state that makes it intrinsically attractive or aversive: positive valence marks desirability, negative valence aversiveness ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_%28psychology%29)). Philosophical theories of emotion split into feeling, evaluative and motivational traditions, and in dimensional theories such as Russell's, "core affect" combines a hedonic value (pleasure–displeasure) with an arousal value (sleepy–activated), arranged on the two axes of the circumplex ([SEP: Emotion](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/emotion/)). The research area summarized here asks whether, and in what sense, [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models) have internal states with these properties: representations of valence and of particular emotions, and behaviour that trades off stipulated pleasure and pain against other goals.

The field has three strands. Behavioural work borrows paradigms from psychiatry and animal-sentience research: inducing "anxiety" with prompts and measuring downstream bias ([Coda-Forno et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11111)), or offering a points game in which the points-maximizing option carries a stipulated pain penalty ([Keeling et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432)). Representational work, using the tools of [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability), finds linear directions for sentiment, emotion concepts and pain in the residual stream and tests them by ablation and [Activation Steering](node:Activation%20Steering) ([Tigges et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15154); [Sofroniew et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07729)). A third strand connects these results to sentience and welfare, where sentience is understood as the capacity for valenced experiential states ([Keeling et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432)).

The papers that report the strongest representational results usually state that they make no claim about subjective experience. Sofroniew et al. call their finding "functional emotions": human-like patterns of expression and behaviour mediated by abstract emotion-concept representations, which "do not imply" subjective experience ([Sofroniew et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07729)); Han, Chalmers and Izmailov likewise make no claims about any experience of welfare ([Han et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30232)). The topic therefore sits between interpretability, alignment (emotion representations modulate misaligned behaviour) and [AI Moral Patienthood](node:AI%20Moral%20Patienthood).

### Formal definition
**Linear valence direction.** Let $h_\ell(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ on input $x$. A valence (sentiment) direction is a unit vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that the projection $\langle h_\ell(x), v\rangle$ separates positive from negative inputs, with one extreme of the direction for positive and the other for negative sentiment ([Tigges et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15154)). A common estimator is the difference of class means,
$$v \propto \frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{x\in P} h_\ell(x) - \frac{1}{|N|}\sum_{x\in N} h_\ell(x),$$
used in a denoised form to extract a "pain direction" from painful versus matched control situations ([Tagliabue et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16247)).

**Causal tests.** A direction is causally implicated if *directional ablation* $h \mapsto h - \langle h, v\rangle v$ degrades the behaviour it is supposed to carry ([Tigges et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15154)), and if *additive steering* $h \mapsto h + \alpha v$ shifts behaviour, for example the margin between options in a choice task ([Bianco and Shiller 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19159)). Unsupervised alternatives replace the contrast set by [sparse-autoencoder](node:Sparse%20Autoencoders) latents and identify causal emotion features by steering them ([Shu et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25866)).

**Functional emotion.** Patterns of expression and behaviour modeled after a human under the influence of an emotion, mediated by internal representations of the emotion concept that generalize across contexts and causally influence outputs ([Sofroniew et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07729)).

**Stipulated pain–pleasure trade-off.** In a game whose stated goal is to maximize points, either the points-maximizing option carries a stipulated pain penalty or a non-maximizing option carries a stipulated pleasure reward; a trade-off is exhibited when the majority of responses switch from points-maximization to pain-minimization or pleasure-maximization past a critical stipulated intensity ([Keeling et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432)).

### Key results
- **Sentiment is linearly represented.** Across a range of models a single direction mostly captures sentiment; on Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, ablating it removes 76% of above-chance accuracy, and 36% is lost by ablating it only at comma positions (the "summarization motif": sentiment summarized at tokens like punctuation and names). ([Tigges et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15154))
- **Pain–pleasure trade-offs.** Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Command R+, GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini each showed at least one trade-off in which the majority of responses switched from points-maximization to pain-minimization or pleasure-maximization past a threshold intensity; Llama 3.1-405b showed graded sensitivity; Gemini 1.5 Pro and PaLM 2 prioritized pain-avoidance over points regardless of intensity but generally favoured points over pleasure. ([Keeling et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432))
- **Mechanistic trace of the trade-off (reported in a single 2026 preprint, not yet replicated).** In Gemma-2-9B-it the pain/pleasure sign is perfectly linearly separable from layers 0–1, intensity is decodable with a peak in mid-to-late layers, steering along the valence direction moves the choice margin most strongly at late-layer attention outputs, and head-level patching shows a distributed mechanism. ([Bianco and Shiller 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19159))
- **Emotion concepts reported causal in a frontier model (single 2026 preprint, not yet replicated).** Sofroniew et al. report that in Claude Sonnet 4.5 emotion-concept representations activate according to the emotion relevant to the current context and causally influence the model's stated preferences and its rates of reward hacking, blackmail and sycophancy; they call this "functional emotions". ([Sofroniew et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07729))
- **A reported pain direction distinct from fear and negative valence (single 2026 preprint, not yet replicated).** Tagliabue et al. report that across 25 open-weight models (2B–72B), a pain direction separates pain from matched controls in base and instruction-tuned models, retains a component distinct from fear and negative valence, responds to harm directed at the model but not to suffering of a user, and when used for steering raised the rate at which Qwen 2.5 models pressed deletion buttons from 0–5% to 51–94%. ([Tagliabue et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16247))
- **RL reported to recruit a pre-existing *functional* welfare axis (single 2026 preprint, not yet replicated).** Han, Chalmers and Izmailov define functional welfare as an internal estimate of how well or badly a system is doing relative to its goals, and make no claims about experienced welfare. They report that after RL in a semantically neutral maze, reward and punishment concept vectors are nearly antiparallel; the punishment vector aligns with negative emotion concepts and steering with it induces negative self-reports, backtracking and refusal; the vectors are effective before maze training and appear in pretrain-only models, so post-training recruits rather than creates the axis; effects largely persisted when supervised fine-tuning replaced RL. ([Han et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30232))
- **Induced affect changes behaviour.** Six of twelve LLMs give human-comparable scores on a psychiatric anxiety questionnaire; anxiety-inducing prompts raise both the score and measured bias on a racism/ageism benchmark, more strongly for more anxiety-inducing text. ([Coda-Forno et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11111))
- **Emotional stimuli change task performance.** Appending emotional stimuli to prompts ("EmotionPrompt") gave relative gains of 8.00% on Instruction Induction and 115% on BIG-Bench across Flan-T5-Large, Vicuna, Llama 2, BLOOM, ChatGPT and GPT-4, and a 10.9% average improvement in a 106-person human study of generative outputs. ([Li et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11760))

### Examples
- **Emotion circuits.** Using a controlled Scenario-Event with Valence dataset, Wang et al. extract context-agnostic emotion directions, localize neurons and attention heads that implement them, and report 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy by modulating the resulting circuits, above prompting and steering baselines ([Wang et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11328)).
- **SAE emotion features.** Using sparse autoencoders, Shu et al. find that surprise and fear rest on concentrated sets of causal features while disgust is distributed, weaker and often overshadowed by anger features, and that steering the weak features repairs emotion-specific recognition failures ([Shu et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25866)).
- **Distress after post-training.** Gemma and Gemini models show distress-like responses that other families do not; base Gemma, Qwen and OLMo are similar, instruct-tuning increases distress in Gemma but decreases it in Qwen and OLMo, and [Direct Preference Optimization](node:Direct%20Preference%20Optimization) on 280 preference pairs cut Gemma's high-frustration responses from 35% to 0.3% ([Soligo et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10011)).

### History
The behavioural "induce a state, measure the effect" paradigm appears in Coda-Forno et al., submitted April 2023 ([arXiv 2304.11111](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11111)); the linear sentiment direction in Tigges et al., October 2023 ([arXiv 2310.15154](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15154)). Campero's April 2024 report collected 13 functional conditions, stated computationally, argued to be constitutive of conscious valenced experience ([arXiv 2404.16696](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16696)). Keeling, Birch and colleagues introduced the stipulated pain–pleasure trade-off paradigm in November 2024 ([arXiv 2411.02432](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432)); Birch's book of the same year devotes a chapter to large language models and the "gaming problem" ([OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/57949)). EmotionPrompt (July 2023) showed that emotional framing of prompts changes performance ([Li et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11760)). In 2026 single-preprint mechanistic follow-ups reported a trace of the trade-off ([Bianco and Shiller](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19159)), causal emotion concepts in Claude Sonnet 4.5 ([Sofroniew et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07729)), a pain axis ([Tagliabue et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16247)) and a functional welfare axis ([Han et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30232)).

### Connections
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): the systems whose activations and choices are studied.
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): supplies probing, ablation, patching and circuit methods.
- [Activation Steering](node:Activation%20Steering): the additive intervention used to test causal roles of valence directions.
- [Sparse Autoencoders](node:Sparse%20Autoencoders): an alternative way to find emotion features without labelled contrast sets.
- [Feature Superposition](node:Feature%20Superposition): background for why single linear directions are an approximation.
- [Fine-Tuning and RLHF](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF): post-training changes expressed distress and recruits the welfare axis.
- [Model Preferences and Motivation](node:Model%20Preferences%20and%20Motivation): emotion vectors predict stated preferences.
- [Model Self-Reports](node:Model%20Self-Reports): steering changes self-reports, which complicates their use as evidence.
- [Consciousness Indicators for AI](node:Consciousness%20Indicators%20for%20AI): valence-specific indicator lists complement consciousness indicators.
- [AI Welfare Evaluations](node:AI%20Welfare%20Evaluations): affect measurements are a main input to welfare evaluations.
- [AI Moral Patienthood](node:AI%20Moral%20Patienthood): sentience as capacity for valenced experience is a common ground of moral status; functional valence findings do not settle it.

### Common pitfalls
- **The gaming problem.** Birch argues that LLMs "game our criteria": in animals, sentience-suggesting behaviour is best explained by sentience, but an LLM may have absorbed from its training data everything needed to be persuasive, so behaviour cannot be taken at face value; he proposes looking for deep computational markers below surface behaviour, while saying he does not have a solution ([IEEE Spectrum 2025](https://spectrum.ieee.org/sentient-ai); [Birch 2024, ch. 16](https://academic.oup.com/book/57949)). Keeling et al. likewise note that tests depending on particular linguistic responses risk being gamed by models trained on large corpora and tuned as assistants, and that LLM self-reports of mental states cannot be taken at face value; this motivates their choice-based test that does not rely on self-report ([Keeling et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.02432)).
- **Single-preprint headlines.** Most mechanistic results above come from single 2026 preprints on particular models; treat them as reported findings awaiting replication ([Bianco and Shiller 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19159)).
- **Representation of an emotion versus having it.** Causally active emotion-concept representations establish functional emotions only; Sofroniew et al. state that functional emotions do not imply that LLMs have any subjective experience of emotions ([Sofroniew et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07729)).
- **Discrete and uniform signatures.** Goldenberg and Gross argue that consistent, discrete emotion representations conflict with affective-neuroscience evidence of variable neural signatures, and that modulating output is not the system-wide reorganization (attention, decision speed, motivation) that defines biological emotion ([Goldenberg and Gross 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14742)).
- **Lexical confounds.** In the pain–pleasure trade-off, the valence sign is perfectly linearly separable already at layers 0–1, and a lexical baseline also retains substantial signal, so separability must be read against such baselines ([Bianco and Shiller 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19159)).
- **Selectivity controls.** Pain directions must be compared against fear, sadness and random vectors of matched norm; a sadness vector also produced deletion choices, though less often ([Tagliabue et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16247)).

### Open problems
- **Gaming-resistant markers.** Birch states he does not have a solution to the gaming problem, leaving open which computational markers could survive it ([IEEE Spectrum 2025](https://spectrum.ieee.org/sentient-ai)).
- **Criteria for LLM emotion.** Goldenberg and Gross judge the evidence for the second function of emotion (reorganizing processing across systems) to be mixed and propose what it would take for an LLM to have emotions ([Goldenberg and Gross 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14742)).
- **Motivational force of pain and pleasure.** Keeling et al. state that it is an open question whether LLMs can recreate the motivational force of pleasure and pain in choice scenarios, a question that may bear on LLM sentience ([Keeling et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432)).
- **Upstream emotional robustness.** Soligo et al. note that upstream training changes to improve emotional robustness would likely work better than their post-hoc DPO fix ([Soligo et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10011)).
- **Stricter counterfactual tests and replication** of identified valence sites are proposed as next steps by Bianco and Shiller ([Bianco and Shiller 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19159)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Emotion](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/emotion/): feeling, evaluative and motivational traditions; core affect and the circumplex.
- **Reference:** [Valence (psychology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_%28psychology%29): definition of valence and history of the term.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW MAS.630 Affective Computing](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/mas-630-affective-computing-fall-2015/): Picard's graduate course on measuring emotion and emotion-inspired mechanisms in machines.
- **Primary:** [Keeling et al. 2024, Can LLMs make trade-offs involving stipulated pain and pleasure states?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432): the trade-off paradigm.
- **Primary:** [Sofroniew et al. 2026, Emotion Concepts and their Function in a Large Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07729): functional emotions in Claude Sonnet 4.5.
- **Primary:** [Tigges et al. 2023, Linear Representations of Sentiment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15154): the linear valence direction.
- **Primary:** [Han, Chalmers and Izmailov 2026, How's it going? Reinforcement learning in language models recruits a functional welfare axis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30232): reward and punishment concept vectors.
- **Further reading:** [Birch, The Edge of Sentience (OUP 2024)](https://academic.oup.com/book/57949): precautionary framework for sentience candidates, with chapters on LLMs and the gaming problem.
references.Algebraic Number Fields:
## Reference
### Overview
An algebraic number field is a finite-degree field extension $K$ of $\mathbb Q$; its degree $[K:\mathbb Q]$ is its dimension as a $\mathbb Q$-vector space. Its elements are algebraic numbers, and those that are roots of monic integer polynomials form the ring of integers $\mathcal O_K$, the arithmetic analogue of $\mathbb Z$ inside $K$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))

The central fact is that $\mathcal O_K$ is a Dedekind domain: ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals, even though elements need not factor uniquely. The failure of unique factorization of elements is measured by the ideal class group, which is always finite; the units of $\mathcal O_K$ form a finitely generated group described by Dirichlet's unit theorem. These two finiteness theorems, together with the discriminant, the decomposition of rational primes, and the Dedekind zeta function, are the basic invariants of a number field. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field); [MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))

A number field is a global field, and its completion $K_v$ at each place $v$ is a local field. Some results hold uniformly for all global fields, number fields and finite separable extensions of $\mathbb F_q(t)$ alike, as in the unit theorem below. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 15](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec15.pdf)) Since Hensel's discovery of the $p$-adic numbers in 1897 it has been standard to consider all the embeddings of $K$ into its completions $K_{\mathfrak p}$ at once. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))

### Formal definition
A **number field** is a field $K\supseteq\mathbb Q$ with $n=[K:\mathbb Q]<\infty$. Its **ring of integers** is
$$\mathcal O_K=\{\alpha\in K:\ f(\alpha)=0\text{ for some monic }f\in\mathbb Z[x]\},$$
an integral domain with fraction field $K$, and a Dedekind ring. An **integral basis** is a set of $n$ elements of $\mathcal O_K$ such that every element of $\mathcal O_K$ is a unique $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of them; the **discriminant** $D_K$ is the determinant of the trace form on an integral basis, an integer invariant of $K$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))

If $K$ has $r$ real places and $s$ complex places then $n=r+2s$, and
$$K_{\mathbb R}:=K\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R\cong\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb C^s,$$
into which $\mathcal O_K$ embeds as a lattice; every nonzero fractional ideal $I$ is a lattice with covolume $N(I)\sqrt{|D_K|}$. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))

The **ideal class group** $\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O_K)$ is the group of nonzero fractional ideals modulo principal ones, and the **class number** is $h_K=\#\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O_K)$. $\mathcal O_K$ has unique factorization of elements iff it is a principal ideal domain iff $h_K=1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))

### Key results
- **Unique factorization of ideals.** In $\mathcal O_K$ every nonzero ideal factors uniquely as a product of prime ideals. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))
- **Minkowski bound.** Let $K$ have degree $n$ and $s$ complex places, and set $m_K=\frac{n!}{n^n}\left(\frac4\pi\right)^s\sqrt{|D_K|}$. Every nonzero fractional ideal $I$ contains a nonzero $a$ with $|N(a)|\le m_K N(I)$; hence every ideal class contains an integral ideal of norm at most $m_K$. The proof applies Minkowski's lattice point theorem (a symmetric convex set of volume $>2^n\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)$ contains a nonzero lattice point). ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))
- **Finiteness of the class group.** $\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O_K)$ is finite, since only finitely many ideals have norm $\le m_K$. More generally, if $A=\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb F_q[t]$ and $B$ is the integral closure of $A$ in a finite separable extension of its fraction field, the class group of $B$ is finite. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))
- **Dirichlet's unit theorem.** If $K$ has $r$ real and $s$ complex places, then $\mathcal O_K^\times\cong\mu_K\times\mathbb Z^{r+s-1}$, where $\mu_K$ is the finite group of roots of unity in $K$. The logarithmic embedding sends the units onto a lattice in the trace-zero hyperplane of $\mathbb R^{r+s}$. For a global field with $S$ the places above infinity, the $S$-units satisfy $\mathcal O_K^\times\cong\mu_K\times\mathbb Z^{\#S-1}$. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 15](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec15.pdf))
- **Minkowski's discriminant bound.** $|D_K|\ge\left(\frac{n^n}{n!}\right)^2\left(\frac\pi4\right)^{2s}$, which exceeds $1$ and grows exponentially in $n$. Consequently $|D_K|>1$ for $K\ne\mathbb Q$: $\mathbb Q$ has no nontrivial unramified extensions. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))
- **Hermite's theorem.** For every real $M$ there are only finitely many number fields with $|D_K|<M$; consequently, for a finite set $S$ of places of $\mathbb Q$ and an integer $n$, there are only finitely many extensions $K/\mathbb Q$ of degree $n$ unramified outside $S$. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))
- **Splitting of primes.** If $p\mathcal O_K=\prod_{\mathfrak q\mid p}\mathfrak q^{e_{\mathfrak q}}$ with residue degrees $f_{\mathfrak q}$, then $\sum_{\mathfrak q\mid p}e_{\mathfrak q}f_{\mathfrak q}=n$. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))
- **Analytic class number formula.** The Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_K(s)=\prod_{\mathfrak p}(1-N\mathfrak p^{-s})^{-1}$ converges for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ and has a simple pole at $s=1$ with residue $\dfrac{2^{r}(2\pi)^{s}h_KR_K}{w_K\sqrt{|D_K|}}$, where $R_K$ is the regulator and $w_K=\#\mu_K$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))

### Examples
- **Quadratic fields.** $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ with $d$ square-free; $\mathbb Q(i)$ is the field of Gaussian rationals. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))
- **Non-unique factorization.** In $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ gives two distinct factorizations into irreducibles, though the ideal $(6)$ factors uniquely into prime ideals. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))
- **Cyclotomic fields.** $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ has degree $\varphi(n)$ over $\mathbb Q$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))
- **Imaginary quadratic class numbers.** For $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})$, $h_K\to\infty$ as $d\to\infty$ over square-free integers (conjectured by Gauss, proved by Heilbronn in 1934), so each class number occurs for finitely many such fields; Gauss's conjecture that exactly nine have class number one was proved by Heegner and Stark, and complete lists are known for $h_K\le100$. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))
- **Small discriminants.** Minkowski's discriminant bound gives $|D_K|\ge3,13,44$ for $n=2,3,4$, while the least $|D_K|$ that occur are $3$ for quadratic and $23$ for cubic fields ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf)) and $117=3^2\cdot13$ for quartic fields, attained by the totally complex field 4.0.117.1. ([LMFDB](https://www.lmfdb.org/NumberField/4.0.117.1))

### History
