Gauss's Disquisitiones Arithmeticae already contains the class number conjectures for quadratic fields. Nineteenth-century mathematicians treated algebraic numbers as complex numbers; this changed with Hensel's 1897 discovery of the $p$-adic numbers, after which number fields were studied through all their completions. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field)) Heegner's 1952 solution of the class number one problem contained gaps and was accepted only after Stark's complete proof in 1967. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))

### Connections
- [p-adic Numbers](node:p-adic%20Numbers): completions of $K$ at its finite places are finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_p$.
- [Hensel's Lemma](node:Hensel's%20Lemma): lifts factorizations mod $p$, computing how primes split.
- [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals): $\mathcal O_K$ is the prototypical Dedekind domain.
- [Unique Factorization Domains](node:Unique%20Factorization%20Domains): $\mathcal O_K$ is a UFD exactly when $h_K=1$.
- [Lattices and Minkowski's Theorem](node:Lattices%20and%20Minkowski's%20Theorem): geometry of numbers proves finiteness of the class group and the unit theorem.
- [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory): Galois number fields and decomposition groups of primes.
- [Separable Field Extensions](node:Separable%20Field%20Extensions): number fields are separable over $\mathbb Q$, so the trace form is nondegenerate.
- [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function): the case $K=\mathbb Q$ of the Dedekind zeta function.
- [L-Functions](node:L-Functions): Dedekind zeta functions factor into Artin $L$-functions.
- [Quadratic Forms over Number Fields](node:Quadratic%20Forms%20over%20Number%20Fields): classical motivation via Gauss's binary forms.
- [K-Theory of Number Fields](node:K-Theory%20of%20Number%20Fields): higher invariants extending class group and units.
- [Diophantine Equations](node:Diophantine%20Equations): solved by passing to number fields where they factor.

### Common pitfalls
- **$\mathcal O_K$ is not always $\mathbb Z[\alpha]$.** The polynomial discriminant of a generator can exceed $D_K$: for the cubic field defined by $x^3-11x^2+x+1$, the field discriminant is $1304=2^3\cdot163$ while the polynomial discriminant is $5216$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))
- **Elements versus ideals.** Unique factorization holds for ideals, not elements, unless $h_K=1$; an argument that factors elements of $\mathcal O_K$ as if it were a UFD is valid only when the class number is one. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field))
- **Function field analogues differ in detail.** In the function field version of Minkowski's lattice point theorem, convexity is not needed and the factor $2^n$ disappears; Hermite's theorem there requires a fixed constant field. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Real quadratic class number one.** Gauss predicted that infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number $1$; this "remains completely open". The Cohen–Lenstra heuristics predict $h_K=1$ for about $75.446\%$ of real quadratic fields of prime discriminant. ([MIT 18.785 Lecture 14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/mit18_785f21_lec14.pdf))
- **Leopoldt's conjecture.** For a number field $K$ and prime $p$, the $p$-adic regulator map on the global units is conjectured injective (Leopoldt defect $0$). It is known for abelian extensions of $\mathbb Q$ or an imaginary quadratic field and some other cases; Waldschmidt's bound $\delta^L_K\le(|S_\infty(K)|-1)/2$ is the best general bound, and Maksoud extends it to relative extensions and proves new cases of the related Gross–Kuz'min conjecture. ([Maksoud 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.08203))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Algebraic number field (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field): definitions, ring of integers, discriminant, class number, zeta function, examples.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.785 Number Theory I (Sutherland, Fall 2021)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/pages/lecture-notes): full graduate course; Lecture 14 (geometry of numbers, Minkowski, Hermite) and Lecture 15 (Dirichlet's unit theorem).
- **Primary:** [Maksoud, On the rank of Leopoldt's and Gross's regulator maps (Doc. Math. 28, 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.08203): research paper on $p$-adic regulators of number fields and the state of Leopoldt's conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory (Springer Grundlehren, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-03983-0): standard graduate monograph.
references.Algebraic Varieties:
## Reference
### Overview
Algebraic varieties are the geometric objects defined by polynomial equations and the central objects of algebraic geometry. Affine varieties are cut out in affine space, projective varieties by homogeneous polynomials in projective space, and quasi-projective varieties are Zariski-open subsets of projective ones, so every affine variety is quasi-projective. Abstract varieties drop the requirement of an embedding: Nagata gave early examples of varieties that are not quasi-projective, and there are complete toric varieties that are not projective. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety))

The subject studies varieties up to isomorphism (regular maps with regular inverses) and up to the coarser relation of birational equivalence, which only sees the function field. Its basic invariants are dimension, degree and singularities; its organizing correspondence is Hilbert's Nullstellensatz between radical ideals and algebraic sets, which links the subject to [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals). ([Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety); [Wikipedia: Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry); [Wikipedia: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_Nullstellensatz))

Conventions differ. Classically (over an algebraically closed field) an affine variety is an irreducible affine algebraic set, but some authors do not require irreducibility and speak of algebraic sets instead. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety)) In scheme language the Stacks Project defines a variety over an arbitrary field $k$ as an integral scheme, separated and of finite type over $k$. ([Stacks, Definition 33.3.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/020C))

### Formal definition
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and $J\subseteq k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ an ideal. Its zero set is $V(J)=\{a\in k^n: f(a)=0\ \forall f\in J\}$, and for $W\subseteq k^n$, $I(W)$ is the ideal of polynomials vanishing on $W$. The sets $V(J)$ are the closed sets of the Zariski topology. An **affine variety** (classical convention) is an irreducible affine algebraic set $V$: one not the union of two proper closed subsets. Its coordinate ring is $k[V]=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V)$, an integral domain, and its function field $k(V)$ is the fraction field of $k[V]$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety); [Wikipedia: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_Nullstellensatz); [Wikipedia: Dimension of an algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_of_an_algebraic_variety))

A **projective variety** is the zero locus in $\mathbb P^n$ of homogeneous polynomials that is irreducible; a **quasi-projective variety** is a Zariski-open subset of one. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety)) A **rational map** $X\dashrightarrow Y$ is a morphism defined on a nonempty open subset of $X$; it is **birational** if it has a rational inverse, and two varieties over $k$ are birational iff their function fields are isomorphic over $k$. ([Wikipedia: Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry))

### Key results
- **Nullstellensatz (Hilbert, 1893).** For $k$ algebraically closed, $I(V(J))=\sqrt J$. Hence $V$ and $I$ give an inclusion-reversing bijection between algebraic subsets of $k^n$ and radical ideals; irreducible sets correspond to prime ideals and points to maximal ideals, every maximal ideal having the form $(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_Nullstellensatz))
- **Dimension.** For an affine variety $V$ the following agree: the maximal length of a chain of distinct nonempty irreducible closed subvarieties; the Krull dimension of $k[V]$; the transcendence degree of $k(V)$ over $k$; the dimension of the tangent space at any nonsingular point; the degree of the Hilbert polynomial. The transcendence-degree description shows dimension is a birational invariant. ([Wikipedia: Dimension of an algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_of_an_algebraic_variety))
- **Bézout's theorem.** Over an algebraically closed field, $n$ hypersurfaces in $\mathbb P^n$ of degrees $d_1,\dots,d_n$ meet either in infinitely many points or in exactly $d_1\cdots d_n$ points counted with multiplicity; two plane curves of degrees $d_1,d_2$ without common component meet in $d_1d_2$ points. More generally, intersecting a projective algebraic set of dimension $\delta$ and degree $d_1$ with a hypersurface of degree $d_2$ containing none of its components gives dimension $\delta-1$ and degree $d_1d_2$. ([Wikipedia: Bézout's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zout%27s_theorem))
- **Jacobian criterion and the singular locus.** A point $P$ of $V$ is nonsingular when its local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is regular, $\dim_k\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=\dim R$, and singular otherwise; the tangent space at $P$ is cut out by the linear parts at $P$ of the equations of the ideal defining $V$. ([Wikipedia: Zariski tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zariski_tangent_space)) Hence, for $V$ defined by $f_1,\dots,f_m$, a point is singular when the rank of the Jacobian matrix $(\partial f_i/\partial x_j)$ there is lower than at other points of the variety; the nonsingular points form a Zariski open dense subset. ([Wikipedia: Singular point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_point_of_an_algebraic_variety))
- **Birational models.** Every variety is birational to a projective variety (Chow's lemma), and over a field of characteristic $0$ every variety is birational to a smooth projective variety (Hironaka, 1964). Every surface is birational to $\mathbb P^1\times C$ for a curve $C$ or to a unique minimal surface; Mori proved the existence of minimal models in dimension 3, and Birkar, Cascini, Hacon and McKernan proved that every variety of general type over a field of characteristic zero has a minimal model; the minimal model conjecture in higher dimensions remains open. ([Wikipedia: Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry))
- **Products.** If $k$ is algebraically closed and $X,Y$ are varieties over $k$, then $X\times_kY$ is a variety; the hypothesis matters, see Examples. ([Stacks, Lemma 33.3.3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/020C))

### Examples
The affine line, the twisted cubic, and the projective elliptic curve $y^2z=x^3-xz^2$ (genus one) are varieties; the Grassmannian is a projective variety via the Plücker embedding. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety)) The circle $x^2+y^2=1$ is birational to the affine line, which systematically produces the Pythagorean triples. ([Wikipedia: Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry)) Over $\mathbb Q$, $X=Y=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Q(i)$ are varieties in the Stacks sense, but $X\times_{\mathbb Q}Y$ is a disjoint union of two copies of $X$, hence reducible and not a variety. ([Stacks, Example 33.3.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/020C)) The real variety $x^2+y^2+z^2=0$ has dimension two but only one real point. ([Wikipedia: Dimension of an algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_of_an_algebraic_variety))

### History
Hilbert proved the Nullstellensatz in 1893. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_Nullstellensatz)) Bézout published his general theorem in 1779 without a proof meeting modern standards; Serre's algebraic definition of intersection multiplicity (1958) made it valid over any algebraically closed field. ([Wikipedia: Bézout's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zout%27s_theorem)) Weil gave an early definition of abstract varieties; Serre's 1955 paper *Faisceaux Algébriques Cohérents* (FAC) also worked with these objects, and Chevalley and Grothendieck developed schemes, Grothendieck's version becoming the accepted foundation. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety)) Hironaka resolved singularities in characteristic $0$ in 1964; Abhyankar treated surfaces in positive characteristic (1956) and Cossart and Piltant threefolds in all characteristics (2008-2009). ([Wikipedia: Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))

### Connections
- [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals): coordinate rings, the Nullstellensatz, Krull dimension.
- [Projective Geometry](node:Projective%20Geometry): projective space and homogeneous coordinates host projective varieties.
- [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory): function fields, transcendence degree, and the behaviour of varieties under field extension.
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): nonsingular complex varieties are complex manifolds; the Jacobian criterion mirrors the regular value theorem.
- [MSC 14Exx - Birational geometry](node:MSC%2014Exx%20-%20Birational%20geometry): rational maps, minimal models, rationality questions.
- [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry): parent field map.

### Common pitfalls
Whether "variety" includes irreducibility, or requires an algebraically closed ground field, depends on the author; state the convention. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety)) Products and base changes can leave the class of varieties over a non-closed field, as the $\mathbb Q(i)$ example shows. ([Stacks, Example 33.3.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/020C)) Bézout's count needs projective space, an algebraically closed field and multiplicities: plane-curve intersection points may lie at infinity or have complex coordinates. ([Wikipedia: Bézout's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zout%27s_theorem)) Real points can badly undercount the dimension. ([Wikipedia: Dimension of an algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_of_an_algebraic_variety))

### Open problems
- **Resolution of singularities in positive characteristic.** For varieties of dimension at least 4 over fields of characteristic $p>0$, whether every variety admits a resolution of singularities "is an open problem". ([Wikipedia: Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities)) Hauser's survey in the *Bulletin of the AMS* (2010) is subtitled "A proof we are still waiting for". ([Hauser, Bull. AMS 47 (2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0273-0979-09-01274-9))
- **Rationality of cubic hypersurfaces.** Smooth cubic threefolds are non-rational (Clemens-Griffiths, 1972), but Wikipedia records that "it is not known whether there is any smooth cubic hypersurface in $\mathbb P^{n+1}$ with $n\ge4$ which is not rational". ([Wikipedia: Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry)) For $n=4$, Katzarkov, Kontsevich, Pantev and Yu reported in a 2025 preprint (revised March 2026, no journal reference yet) a proof, via "Hodge atoms" built from quantum multiplication, that a very general cubic fourfold is not rational; treat this as a reported claim pending refereeing. ([arXiv:2508.05105](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05105))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety): conventions, affine/projective/abstract varieties, examples and history.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Section 33.3 Varieties](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/020C): scheme-theoretic definition and products.
- **Learn:** [Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry](https://math.stanford.edu/~vakil/216blog/): free notes (published by Princeton University Press) developing varieties through schemes.
- **Primary:** [Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry (Springer GTM, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3849-0): graduate text in Springer's Graduate Texts in Mathematics.
- **Primary:** [Hauser, On the problem of resolution of singularities in positive characteristic](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0273-0979-09-01274-9): survey of the open positive-characteristic case.
- **Further reading:** [Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3849-0) and [Vakil, The Rising Sea](https://math.stanford.edu/~vakil/216blog/): graduate textbooks developing varieties and schemes.

## Reference
### Overview
Analytic number theory uses mathematical analysis to study the integers. It is often dated to Dirichlet's 1837 introduction of $L$-functions to prove that arithmetic progressions contain infinitely many primes. It has two main branches: *multiplicative* number theory, which studies the distribution of primes (the prime number theorem, Dirichlet's theorem), and *additive* number theory, which studies representations of integers as sums (Goldbach's conjecture, Waring's problem). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_number_theory)) See [Prime Numbers](node:Prime%20Numbers) and [additive number theory](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions).

The multiplicative theory encodes arithmetic in Dirichlet series such as $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$ and $L(s,\chi)$, whose Euler products tie them to the primes, and then uses [complex analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) (analytic continuation, zero-free regions, contour integration) to extract asymptotics. Riemann (1859) linked the error in prime counting to the zeros of $\zeta$, and Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin (1896) proved the prime number theorem by showing $\zeta(s)\ne0$ on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_number_theory); [MIT 18.785, Lecture 16](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes16.pdf))

Three further toolkits shape the modern subject: sieve methods, which bound how many integers survive the removal of residue classes and became central after 1950; the Hardy–Littlewood circle method for additive problems; and estimates for exponential sums, which drive both equidistribution and bounds for $\zeta$ on the critical line. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_number_theory); [Elkies, sieve notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/sieve.pdf); [Elkies, exponential sums](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/weyl.pdf))

### Formal definition
The basic counting functions are $\pi(x)=\#\{p\le x\}$, Chebyshev's $\psi(x)=\sum_{p^k\le x}\log p=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)$ (with $\Lambda$ the von Mangoldt function), and for $\gcd(a,q)=1$ their restrictions $\pi(x;q,a)$, $\psi(x;q,a)$ to $n\equiv a\pmod q$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Vinogradov_theorem); [MIT 18.785, Lecture 16](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes16.pdf))

The Riemann zeta function is $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$; it extends meromorphically with a simple pole at $s=1$. For a Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $q$ (a homomorphism $(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times\to\mathbb C^\times$, extended by $0$ on non-units), $L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 16](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes16.pdf); [MIT 18.785, Lecture 18](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes18.pdf)) See [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) and [L-Functions](node:L-Functions).

### Key results
- **Euler product.** For $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, $\zeta(s)=\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$, with absolute convergence; consequently $\zeta$ has no zeros in $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, and by a further argument none on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$. ([MIT 18.785, Thm 16.2 and Cor 16.5](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes16.pdf))
- **Prime number theorem with classical error term.** There is an effective constant $C>0$ such that $\psi(x)=x+O\bigl(x\exp(-C\sqrt{\log x})\bigr)$ and $\pi(x)=\operatorname{li}(x)+O\bigl(x\exp(-C\sqrt{\log x})\bigr)$. The proof uses the de la Vallée Poussin zero-free region: $\zeta(\sigma+it)\ne0$ for $1-\sigma<c/\log|t|$ ($|t|$ large). In particular $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$. ([Elkies, PNT notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/pnt.pdf); [MIT 18.785, Thm 16.15](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes16.pdf)) See [Prime Number Theorem](node:Prime%20Number%20Theorem).
- **Explicit formula.** With $\psi_0(x)$ the average of the left and right limits of $\psi$ at $x$, the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula reads $\psi_0(x)=x-\sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho-\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2})$, the sum running over nontrivial zeros $\rho$ of $\zeta$ in order of increasing $|\operatorname{Im}\rho|$; von Mangoldt gave the first rigorous proof in 1895. Each zero contributes an oscillation of size $x^{\operatorname{Re}\rho}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explicit_formulae_for_L-functions))
- **Zeros and error terms are equivalent.** If every zero satisfies $\operatorname{Re}\rho\le\theta$ with $1/2\le\theta<1$, then $\psi(x)=x+O(x^\theta\log^2x)$ and $\pi(x)=\operatorname{li}(x)+O(x^\theta\log x)$; conversely $\psi(x)=x+O_\varepsilon(x^{\theta+\varepsilon})$ for all $\varepsilon>0$ forces $\zeta$ to have no zeros with real part $>\theta$. Hence the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to $\pi(x)=\operatorname{li}(x)+O(x^{1/2}\log x)$. ([Elkies, PNT notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/pnt.pdf))
- **Dirichlet's theorem and primes in progressions.** For coprime $a,m$ there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv a\pmod m$ (Dirichlet, 1837). ([MIT 18.785, Thm 18.1](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes18.pdf)) Quantitatively, for every $C>0$ there is $c>0$ such that for $\gcd(a,q)=1$ and $x>\exp(C\log^2q)$, $\psi(x;q,a)=\bigl(1+O(e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})\bigr)x/\varphi(q)$, unless some $L(s,\chi)$ mod $q$ has an exceptional real zero $\beta$, which then contributes a secondary term $-\chi(a)x^{\beta}/(\beta\varphi(q))$. ([Elkies, zero-free regions for $L(s,\chi)$](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/free_q.pdf)) Siegel's theorem below removes the exceptional term for small moduli, giving the **Siegel–Walfisz theorem** (Walfisz, 1936): for every $N>0$ there is $C_N>0$ with $\psi(x;q,a)=x/\varphi(q)+O\bigl(x\exp(-C_N\sqrt{\log x})\bigr)$ whenever $(a,q)=1$ and $q\le(\log x)^N$; $C_N$ is not effectively computable. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%E2%80%93Walfisz_theorem))
- **Siegel's theorem.** For each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C_\varepsilon>0$ with $L(1,\chi)>C_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$ for every real Dirichlet character $\chi$ mod $q$, so any real zero $\beta$ satisfies $1-\beta>C'_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$. The constants are ineffective for every $\varepsilon<1/2$. With Dirichlet's class number formula this gives $h(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-q}))\gg_\varepsilon q^{1/2-\varepsilon}$. ([Elkies, zero-free regions for $L(s,\chi)$](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/free_q.pdf))
- **Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem.** For $x^{1/2}(\log x)^{-A}\le Q\le x^{1/2}$, $\sum_{q\le Q}\max_{y\le x}\max_{(a,q)=1}\bigl|\psi(y;q,a)-y/\varphi(q)\bigr|=O\bigl(x^{1/2}Q(\log x)^5\bigr)$. On average over moduli $q$ up to about $\sqrt x$, primes in progressions are as well distributed as the generalized Riemann hypothesis would give for each modulus individually. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Vinogradov_theorem))
- **Selberg's sieve and Brun's theorem.** Selberg's upper-bound sieve gives, for example, that the number of $p\le x$ with $p+2n$ also prime is $O_n(x/\log^2x)$; hence the sum of reciprocals of twin primes converges, a result first obtained by Brun with his own sieve. ([Elkies, sieve notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/sieve.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime))
- **Bounded gaps between primes.** Zhang (2013) proved that some gap $N<7\times10^7$ occurs between infinitely many pairs of primes. Maynard proved $\liminf_n(p_{n+m}-p_n)<\infty$ for every fixed $m$ and $\liminf_n(p_{n+1}-p_n)\le600$; assuming the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture he obtained $\le12$. Polymath and Maynard–Tao work reduced the unconditional bound to $246$. ([Maynard](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.4600); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime))
- **Circle method and ternary Goldbach.** The Hardy–Littlewood method writes the number of representations as a coefficient integral of a generating function over the circle, split into major arcs near roots of unity, which supply the main term, and minor arcs, which must be bounded; Vinogradov recast it with finite exponential sums. Vinogradov (1937) proved that every sufficiently large odd number is a sum of three primes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_circle_method); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_weak_conjecture))

### Examples
Weyl's equidistribution criterion turns a counting question into an exponential-sum bound: $(nr)$ is equidistributed modulo $1$ exactly when $r\notin\mathbb Q$, because for irrational $r$ the sums $\sum_{n\le N}e^{2\pi i mnr}$ stay bounded. The same philosophy applies to $\zeta$ on the critical line: the Lindelöf hypothesis would follow, by partial summation, from good estimates for $\sum_{n\le M}n^{-it}=\sum_{n\le M}e^{i(-t\log n)}$, an exponential sum with phase $t\log n$. ([Elkies, exponential sums](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/weyl.pdf)) See [Exponential and Character Sums](node:Exponential%20and%20Character%20Sums) and [Equidistribution Modulo One](node:Equidistribution%20Modulo%20One).

The sign of $\pi(x)-\operatorname{li}(x)$ illustrates the explicit formula: $\psi(x)-x$ oscillates symmetrically, but $\pi(x)$ involves $\sum_{p<x}\log p$, which differs from $\psi(x)$ by about $x^{1/2}$, so $\pi(x)<\operatorname{li}(x)$ for all computed $x$. Littlewood nevertheless proved that the difference changes sign infinitely often; no explicit crossing has been found. ([Elkies, PNT notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/pnt.pdf))

### History
Legendre, Gauss and Dirichlet conjectured that $\pi(x)\sim x/\ln x$; Chebyshev (1848, 1850) proved that $\pi(x)\ln x/x$ lies between two constants near $1$ and that a limit, if it exists, equals $1$. Riemann's 1859 memoir introduced $\zeta$ as a function of a complex variable and conjectured the Riemann hypothesis; Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved the prime number theorem in 1896. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_number_theory)) Hardy and Ramanujan's 1916–17 work on the [partition function](node:Additive%20Bases%20and%20Integer%20Partitions) $p(n)$ began the circle method, and Siegel's theorem on $L(1,\chi)$ appeared in 1935. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_circle_method); [Elkies, zero-free regions for $L(s,\chi)$](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/free_q.pdf)) The bounded-gaps theorems of 2013 used the Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım method. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_number_theory); [Maynard](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.4600); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime))

### Connections
- [Prime Numbers](node:Prime%20Numbers): the primary object of the multiplicative theory.
- [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) and [L-Functions](node:L-Functions): the analytic encodings whose zeros govern prime distribution.
- [Prime Number Theorem](node:Prime%20Number%20Theorem): the model theorem; its error term is controlled by the zero-free region.
- [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) and [Residue Theorem](node:Residue%20Theorem): contour integration underlies Perron's formula and the explicit formula.
- [Tauberian Theorems](node:Tauberian%20Theorems): Newman's short proof of the PNT uses a Tauberian theorem for Laplace transforms.
- [Laplace and Mellin Transforms](node:Laplace%20and%20Mellin%20Transforms): Dirichlet series are Mellin transforms of counting functions.
- [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function): appears in the functional equation of $\zeta$.
- [Exponential and Character Sums](node:Exponential%20and%20Character%20Sums): the minor-arc and Weyl-sum input.
- [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields): Siegel's theorem bounds class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields.
- [Zeta and L-functions](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory) and [additive number theory](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions).

### Common pitfalls
- The defining series and Euler product of $\zeta$ converge only for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$; values elsewhere come from analytic continuation, not from the series. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 16](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes16.pdf))
- $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$ is a ratio statement; $\operatorname{li}(x)$ is the much better approximation, and the error relative to $x/\log x$ is only of order $x/\log^2x$. ([Elkies, PNT notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/pnt.pdf))
- Siegel's theorem is ineffective: it shows $h(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-q}))>1$ for all but finitely many $q$ without yielding a finite computation that finds them. ([Elkies, zero-free regions for $L(s,\chi)$](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/free_q.pdf))
- Bounded gaps (gap $\le246$ infinitely often) is not the twin prime conjecture (gap $2$ infinitely often). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime))

### Open problems
- **Riemann hypothesis.** All nontrivial zeros of $\zeta$ have real part $1/2$; equivalently $\pi(x)=\operatorname{li}(x)+O(x^{1/2}\log x)$. It is a Clay Millennium Problem, listed as unsolved. ([Clay](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/); [Elkies, PNT notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/pnt.pdf)) Its generalization to $L(s,\chi)$ (GRH), and the possible existence of Siegel zeros, are likewise open; Elkies notes that Siegel's constants remain ineffective eighty years later. ([Elkies, zero-free regions for $L(s,\chi)$](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/free_q.pdf))
- **Lindelöf hypothesis.** $\zeta(1/2+it)=O(t^\varepsilon)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$; implied by RH and unproved; the best listed exponent is $13/84$ (Bourgain, 2017). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindel%C3%B6f_hypothesis))
- **Twin primes and Goldbach.** The twin prime conjecture is unsolved, as is the strong (binary) Goldbach conjecture, verified by computer only to a bound of order $10^{18}$. Helfgott released a proof of the weak (ternary) conjecture in 2013; it was accepted for the *Annals of Mathematics Studies* and has been under further review. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_weak_conjecture))
- **Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (1968).** For every $\theta<1$ and $A>0$, $\sum_{q\le x^\theta}\max_{(a,q)=1}\bigl|\pi(x;q,a)-\pi(x)/\varphi(q)\bigr|\ll_{\theta,A}x/(\log x)^A$. Bombieri–Vinogradov gives every $\theta<1/2$, and the statement fails at $\theta=1$; the conjecture is open. Under it Maynard's method gives consecutive prime gaps $\le12$ infinitely often, and Polymath obtained $6$ under a generalized form. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott%E2%80%93Halberstam_conjecture); [Maynard](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.4600))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Analytic number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_number_theory): branches, history, landmark problems.
- **Learn:** [Elkies, Math 229: Introduction to Analytic Number Theory (Harvard, 2015)](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/index.html): zero-free regions, PNT with error term, Siegel's theorem, Selberg sieve, exponential sums.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.785 Lecture 16](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes16.pdf) and [Lecture 18](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes18.pdf) (Sutherland): Euler product, PNT, Dirichlet's theorem.
- **Primary:** [Maynard, Small gaps between primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.4600): the multidimensional sieve and bounded gaps.
- **Further reading:** [Davenport, Multiplicative Number Theory (Springer GTM, 1980)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-5927-3) and [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory (AMS Colloquium Publications 53, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/coll/053): the standard graduate texts.

## Reference
### Overview
Anti-de Sitter space $\mathrm{AdS}_n$ is the maximally symmetric Lorentzian manifold of constant negative curvature, the Lorentzian analogue of hyperbolic space. With Minkowski space (zero curvature) and de Sitter space (positive curvature) it is one of the three maximally symmetric vacuum solutions of Einstein's equations with cosmological constant, here $\Lambda<0$. Its conformal boundary is timelike, so it behaves like a box: momentarily parallel timelike geodesics eventually intersect, and well-posed evolution needs boundary conditions at infinity. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space))

AdS arises as a vacuum of gauged supergravities and preserves as many supersymmetries as flat space. Since Maldacena's 1997 work it is best known as the bulk of the AdS/CFT correspondence: string or M-theory on $\mathrm{AdS}\times$(compact space) is conjectured to be dual to a conformal field theory on the boundary, with $\mathrm{AdS}_5\times S^5$ dual to four-dimensional $\mathcal N=4$ super-Yang–Mills. ([Aharony et al., §§2.2.3–2.2.4 and ch. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111); [Maldacena, hep-th/9711200](https://export.arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9711200))

**Convention.** Below, $\mathrm{AdS}_n$ has dimension $n$ and radius $\alpha$ (also written $R$ or $l$); in holography one writes $n=d+1$, with $d$ the dimension of the boundary CFT. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space); [Aharony et al., §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111))

### Formal definition
$\mathrm{AdS}_n$ of signature $(n-1,1)$ is the quasi-sphere
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}x_i^2-t_1^2-t_2^2=-\alpha^2\qquad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^{n-1,2},\quad ds^2=\sum dx_i^2-dt_1^2-dt_2^2,$$
with the induced metric. It is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times S^1$, its isometry group is $O(n-1,2)$, and it contains closed timelike curves (e.g. $t_1=\alpha\sin\tau$, $t_2=\alpha\cos\tau$); physics usually uses the universal cover, which unrolls the time circle. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space); [nLab: anti de Sitter spacetime](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/anti+de+Sitter+spacetime))

It solves $G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=0$ for $\mathcal L=(R-2\Lambda)/(16\pi G)$ with
$$\Lambda=-\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2\alpha^2}\qquad\bigl(=-\tfrac{d(d-1)}{2\alpha^2}\text{ for }n=d+1\bigr).$$
([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space); [de Haro–Skenderis–Solodukhin, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0002230))

Global coordinates cover the whole space: $ds^2=\alpha^2(-\cosh^2\rho\,d\tau^2+d\rho^2+\sinh^2\rho\,d\Omega_{n-2}^2)$, with $\tau$ periodic on the hyperboloid and $\tau\in\mathbb R$ on the cover. Poincaré coordinates cover a patch bounded by a Killing horizon at $r=0$:
$$ds^2=-\frac{r^2}{\alpha^2}dt^2+\frac{\alpha^2}{r^2}dr^2+\frac{r^2}{\alpha^2}d\vec x^{\,2},\qquad \vec x\in\mathbb R^{n-2};$$
with $z=\alpha^2/r$ this becomes $ds^2=\frac{\alpha^2}{z^2}(dz^2-dt^2+d\vec x^{\,2})$, conformal boundary at $z=0$. nLab writes this chart as an embedding $\mathbb R^{1+p}\times\mathbb R_{>0}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{AdS}_{p+2}$ with metric of the form $(r^2/R^2)\,ds^2_{\text{flat}}+(R^2/r^2)\,dr^2$, and notes that it arises as the near-horizon geometry of black $p$-branes in supergravity. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space); [nLab: anti de Sitter spacetime](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/anti+de+Sitter+spacetime))

### Key results
- **Curvature.** $R_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}=-\alpha^{-2}(g_{\mu\alpha}g_{\nu\beta}-g_{\mu\beta}g_{\nu\alpha})$, $R_{\mu\nu}=-(n-1)\alpha^{-2}g_{\mu\nu}$, $R=-n(n-1)/\alpha^2$; $\mathrm{AdS}_n$ is the homogeneous space $O(2,n-1)/O(1,n-1)$. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space))
- **Causal structure.** Momentarily parallel timelike geodesics eventually intersect. Because conformal infinity is timelike, initial data on a spacelike slice do not determine the evolution without boundary conditions at infinity. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space))
- **Breitenlohner–Freedman bound.** A scalar of mass $m$ on $\mathrm{AdS}_{d+1}$ has normalizable modes with real frequencies only if
$$m^2R^2\ge-\frac{d^2}{4}.$$
Slightly tachyonic scalars are therefore stable. For $-\tfrac{d^2}{4}\le m^2R^2\le-\tfrac{d^2}{4}+1$ both falloffs are normalizable and two quantizations exist; the supersymmetric vacua of supergravity satisfy the bound. ([Aharony et al., eqs. 2.41–2.42](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111))
- **Positive energy and stability.** With suitable boundary conditions, supergravity on AdS has energy bounded below; Gibbons, Hull and Warner gave a non-perturbative stability proof generalizing Witten's positive-energy argument, and Abbott and Deser studied the stability of gravity with a cosmological constant. ([Aharony et al., §2.2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111); [Abbott–Deser 1982](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0550-3213%2882%2990049-9))
- **Brown–Henneaux central charge.** For $\mathrm{AdS}_3$ the asymptotic symmetries preserving the boundary falloff form two Virasoro algebras, whose finite-dimensional subalgebra generates the exact isometry group $SO(2,2)$, with classical central charge
$$c=\frac{3R}{2G_N^{(3)}},$$
which must equal the central charge of the dual two-dimensional CFT. ([Aharony et al., §5.1, eq. 5.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111); [Brown–Henneaux 1986](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01211590))
- **Fefferman–Graham expansion.** Near the boundary, any asymptotically AdS metric can be written
$$ds^2=l^2\Bigl(\frac{d\rho^2}{4\rho^2}+\frac1\rho g_{ij}(x,\rho)dx^idx^j\Bigr),\quad g=g_{(0)}+\rho g_{(2)}+\dots+\rho^{d/2}g_{(d)}+h_{(d)}\rho^{d/2}\log\rho+\dots,$$
with the log term only for even $d$. The $g_{(n)}$ with $n<d$ are fixed by $g_{(0)}$; the holographic stress tensor is $\langle T_{ij}\rangle=\frac{d\,l^{d-1}}{16\pi G_N}g_{(d)ij}+X_{ij}[g_{(n<d)}]$, where $X_{ij}$ encodes the conformal anomaly and vanishes for odd $d$. ([de Haro–Skenderis–Solodukhin, eqs. 1.1–1.3, 2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0002230))
- **Holographic dictionary.** CFT correlators are generated by the dependence of the on-shell supergravity action on boundary values of bulk fields (Gubser–Klebanov–Polyakov; Witten); a scalar of mass $m$ in $\mathrm{AdS}_{d+1}$ behaves as $z^{d-\Delta}$ and $z^\Delta$ near the boundary, and is dual to an operator of dimension $\Delta=\tfrac d2+\sqrt{\tfrac{d^2}{4}+m^2R^2}$. ([GKP, hep-th/9802109](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9802109); [Witten, hep-th/9802150](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9802150); [Aharony et al., eq. 3.14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111))
- **Hawking–Page transition.** In Euclidean $\mathrm{AdS}_5$ with boundary $S^3\times S^1$ there are two saddles, thermal AdS and the AdS–Schwarzschild black hole; their action difference $I(X_2)-I(X_1)=\pi^2r_+^3(R^2-r_+^2)/\bigl(4G_5(2r_+^2+R^2)\bigr)$ changes sign at $r_+=R$, and the black hole dominates for $r_+>R$. Witten interpreted this as a confinement–deconfinement transition of the boundary gauge theory on $S^3$. ([Aharony et al., §3.6.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111); [Witten, hep-th/9803131](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9803131))

### Examples
- **$\mathrm{AdS}_5\times S^5$.** The near-horizon geometry of $N$ D3-branes, with equal radii $R^4\sim g_sN\,l_s^4$. Classical supergravity is reliable when $R$ is large in string units, $R^4/l_s^4\sim g_{\rm YM}^2N=\lambda\gg1$, and string loops are suppressed at large $N$; holding $\lambda$ fixed as $N\to\infty$ gives classical string theory, which reduces to supergravity only at large $\lambda$. Perturbative gauge theory needs $\lambda\ll1$, the opposite regime. ([Aharony et al., §3.1, eqs. 3.9–3.10, and §6.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111))
- **$\mathrm{AdS}_3$.** In global coordinates $ds^2=R^2(-\cosh^2\rho\,d\tau^2+\sinh^2\rho\,d\phi^2+d\rho^2)$; its asymptotic symmetry analysis gives the Brown–Henneaux Virasoro algebras. ([Aharony et al., §5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111))
- **Open FRW slicing.** $ds^2=-dt^2+\alpha^2\sin^2(t/\alpha)\,dH_{n-1}^2$, with $dH_{n-1}^2$ the hyperbolic metric; these coordinates do not cover all of AdS. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space))

### History
Dirac's 1963 paper constructed a representation of the $3+2$ de Sitter group, the isometry group of $\mathrm{AdS}_4$, in which one cyclic generator has integral eigenvalues and three have half-odd eigenvalues; Wikipedia credits him as the first to explore anti-de Sitter space rigorously. ([Dirac 1963](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1063/1.1704016); [Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space))

Breitenlohner and Freedman's stability bound (1982) and Hawking and Page's thermodynamics of AdS black holes (1983) predate holography; Brown and Henneaux found the $\mathrm{AdS}_3$ central charge in 1986. Maldacena's 1997 conjecture, made precise by Gubser–Klebanov–Polyakov and Witten in 1998, turned AdS into the main laboratory of quantum gravity. Gibbons' 1998 Samos lectures review its global properties and stress the difference between AdS and its covering space. ([Aharony et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9905111); [Brown–Henneaux 1986](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01211590); [Maldacena, hep-th/9711200](https://export.arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9711200); [Gibbons, arXiv:1110.1206](https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.1206))

### Connections
- [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space) and [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime): the other maximally symmetric vacua ($\Lambda>0$, $\Lambda=0$).
- [Hyperbolic Space](node:Hyperbolic%20Space): constant-time slices of the Poincaré patch, and the Euclidean continuation of AdS.
- [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry), [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors), [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): constant negative curvature and refocusing geodesics.
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations), [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action), [Gibbons–Hawking–York Boundary Term](node:Gibbons–Hawking–York%20Boundary%20Term): AdS as the $\Lambda<0$ vacuum and the boundary terms of its on-shell action.
- [Penrose Diagrams](node:Penrose%20Diagrams) and [Global Hyperbolicity](node:Global%20Hyperbolicity): AdS is not globally hyperbolic because its boundary is timelike.
- [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence), [Holographic Principle](node:Holographic%20Principle), [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory): the holographic dictionary.
- [String Theory](node:String%20Theory), [Supergravity](node:Supergravity), [D-Branes](node:D-Branes), [Supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry): $\mathrm{AdS}_5\times S^5$ from D3-branes.
- [Asymptotic Gravitational Charges](node:Asymptotic%20Gravitational%20Charges): Brown–Henneaux asymptotic symmetries and AdS mass.
- [Black Hole Thermodynamics](node:Black%20Hole%20Thermodynamics), [Black Holes](node:Black%20Holes), [Hawking Radiation](node:Hawking%20Radiation): the Hawking–Page transition.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): the boundary side of the duality, including confinement.
- [Quantum Gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity): AdS/CFT as a non-perturbative definition of quantum gravity in AdS.
- [Renormalization](node:Renormalization): holographic renormalization of the on-shell action.
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model) and [Warped Products](node:Warped%20Products): a slice of $\mathrm{AdS}_5$ along an extra dimension.
- [QFT in Curved Spacetime](node:QFT%20in%20Curved%20Spacetime) and [Breitenlohner–Freedman Bound](node:Breitenlohner–Freedman%20Bound): fields on AdS and their stability bound.
- [Thermodynamics](node:Thermodynamics): free energies of competing Euclidean saddles.
- [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): the observed $\Lambda$ has the opposite sign.
- [Physics Subsection - Holographic dualities and conformal fields](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Holographic%20dualities%20and%20conformal%20fields): field map.

### Common pitfalls
- **Hyperboloid versus cover.** The embedded quasi-sphere has periodic time and closed timelike curves; most physics uses its universal cover. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space); [Gibbons, arXiv:1110.1206](https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.1206))
- **Poincaré coordinates are incomplete.** They cover only a patch bounded by a Killing horizon; global coordinates cover the whole space. ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space))
- **Dimension labels.** $\mathrm{AdS}_n$, $\mathrm{AdS}_{d+1}$ and $\mathrm{AdS}_{p+2}$ all occur in the literature for the same family; so check which dimension a formula such as the BF bound refers to. ([nLab: anti de Sitter spacetime](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/anti+de+Sitter+spacetime); [Aharony et al., §2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111))
- **Negative mass squared is not an instability.** Scalars with $-d^2/4\le m^2R^2<0$ are stable on AdS. ([Aharony et al., eq. 2.42](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111))
- **Supergravity needs strong coupling.** Large $N$ alone is necessary but not sufficient for a supergravity description; large 't Hooft coupling is also required. ([Aharony et al., §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9905111))

### Open problems
- **AdS instability conjecture.** Bizoń and Rostworowski (2011) conjectured that AdS is unstable under arbitrarily small generic perturbations, an instability triggered by resonant mode mixing that moves energy from low to high frequencies; their evidence is numerical evolution of the spherically symmetric Einstein–massless-scalar system with negative cosmological constant in four dimensions. ([Bizoń–Rostworowski, arXiv:1104.3702](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.3702)) Wikipedia describes it as small perturbations of certain shapes leading to black-hole formation and records the general conjecture as unproven, with proofs by Moschidis only for spherically symmetric Einstein–null dust with an inner mirror (2017) and Einstein–massless Vlasov (2018). ([Wikipedia: Anti-de Sitter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Anti-de Sitter space (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-de_Sitter_space): embeddings, coordinates, curvature, instability.
- **Reference:** [anti de Sitter spacetime (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/anti+de+Sitter+spacetime): quadric definition and horospheric chart.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 8.821 String Theory and Holographic Duality (Hong Liu, Fall 2014)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-821-string-theory-and-holographic-duality-fall-2014/): graduate course on AdS/CFT.
- **Learn:** [Gibbons, Anti-de-Sitter spacetime and its uses (arXiv:1110.1206)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.1206): lectures on global structure and covering space.
- **Primary:** [Aharony, Gubser, Maldacena, Ooguri, Oz, Large N field theories, string theory and gravity (hep-th/9905111)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9905111): the standard review, including AdS geometry, the BF bound, the dictionary, Hawking–Page and Brown–Henneaux.
- **Primary:** [Maldacena, The large N limit of superconformal field theories and supergravity (hep-th/9711200)](https://export.arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9711200): the original conjecture.
- **Primary:** [de Haro, Skenderis, Solodukhin, Holographic reconstruction of spacetime and renormalization (hep-th/0002230)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0002230): Fefferman–Graham expansion and holographic renormalization.
- **Further reading:** [Witten, Anti-de Sitter space and holography (hep-th/9802150)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9802150) and [Gubser, Klebanov, Polyakov (hep-th/9802109)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9802109): the dictionary papers.
references.Artificial Neural Networks:
## Reference
### Overview
An artificial neural network is a parametrized function built by composing simple units: each artificial neuron multiplies its inputs by connection weights, sums them, adds a bias, and applies a nonlinear activation function. Neurons are arranged in layers (input, hidden, output); in a feedforward network information flows only from one layer to the next, while recurrent networks also allow connections within a layer or back to earlier layers. A network with at least two hidden layers is usually called deep. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_network_%28machine_learning%29))

Networks are trained by adjusting the weights to reduce a loss that measures the gap between predictions and targets; [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation) computes the gradient of the loss with respect to all weights, and the weights are then updated, typically with [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_network_%28machine_learning%29)) Mathematically, the realization of a network is a composition of affine maps and componentwise nonlinearities, and the map from parameters to realized functions is highly non-injective. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

Neural networks are the hypothesis classes of [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning). Their theory splits into approximation (what functions can be represented), optimization (whether gradient methods find good parameters), and generalization (why fitted networks predict well on new data), and in each part classical theory leaves central questions unanswered. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026))

### Formal definition
**Fully connected feedforward network.** An architecture is $a=(N,\varrho)$ with $L\in\mathbb N$ layers, widths $N=(N_0,\dots,N_L)\in\mathbb N^{L+1}$, and activation $\varrho:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Parameters are $\theta=((W^{(\ell)},b^{(\ell)}))_{\ell=1}^L$ with $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{N_\ell\times N_{\ell-1}}$, $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{N_\ell}$, so there are $P(N)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L(N_\ell N_{\ell-1}+N_\ell)$ parameters. The realization $\Phi_a(\cdot,\theta):\mathbb R^{N_0}\to\mathbb R^{N_L}$ is
$$\Phi^{(1)}=W^{(1)}x+b^{(1)},\qquad \Phi^{(\ell+1)}=W^{(\ell+1)}\varrho\big(\Phi^{(\ell)}\big)+b^{(\ell+1)},\quad \ell\in[L-1],$$
with $\varrho$ applied componentwise and $\Phi_a=\Phi^{(L)}$. Width is $\|N\|_\infty$, depth is $L$; the architecture is shallow if $L=2$ and deep if $L>2$. ([Berner et al. 2021, Def. 1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

**Activations.** Common choices are $\mathrm{ReLU}(x)=\max(x,0)$, the logistic sigmoid $1/(1+e^{-x})$ with derivative $\sigma(1-\sigma)\le 1/4$, and $\tanh$ with derivative $1-\tanh^2$. Without a nonlinearity, stacked affine layers collapse to a single affine map. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/mlp.html))

**Perceptron.** Rosenblatt's perceptron is $f(x)=h(w\cdot x+b)$ with $h$ the Heaviside step; the learning rule updates $w_i\leftarrow w_i+r(d_j-y_j)x_{j,i}$, changing weights only on mistakes. ([Wikipedia: Perceptron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceptron))

### Key results
- **Perceptron convergence (Novikoff 1962).** If the data are linearly separable with margin $\gamma$ and $\max\|x\|=R$, the perceptron algorithm makes at most $(R/\gamma)^2$ mistakes, independent of learning rate and ordering; on non-separable data it never converges. ([Wikipedia: Perceptron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceptron))
- **[Universal Approximation Theorem](node:Universal%20Approximation%20Theorem) (Leshno–Lin–Pinkus–Schocken 1993).** Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact and $\varrho\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ have a Lebesgue-null closure of discontinuities. Then two-layer networks $\bigcup_n\mathcal F((d,n,1),\varrho)$ are dense in $C(K)$ for the sup norm if and only if $\varrho$ is not a.e. equal to a polynomial. Cybenko (1989) proved the sigmoidal case. ([Berner et al. 2021, Thm 1.15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_approximation_theorem); [Cybenko 1989 metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02551274); [Leshno et al. 1993 metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/S0893-6080%2805%2980131-5))
- **Finite-sample interpolation.** For distinct $x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(m)}\in\mathbb R^d$ and continuous non-polynomial $\varrho$, a two-layer network with $m$ hidden neurons can fit any labels $y^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^k$ exactly, using $O(m(d+k))$ parameters. ([Berner et al. 2021, Prop. 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Rates for smooth targets (Mhaskar).** For $\varrho\in C^\infty$ non-polynomial there is $c$ such that for every $n$ a width-$n$ shallow network approximates every $g\in W^{k,p}((0,1)^d)$ with $L^p$ error at most $c\,n^{-k/d}\|g\|_{W^{k,p}}$, matching spline rates. ([Berner et al. 2021, Thm 1.16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Bounded width, arbitrary depth.** ReLU networks of width exactly $\max\{n+1,m\}$ are dense in $L^p(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^m)$, and this width is necessary for some targets (Park et al.); for continuous non-affine $\varrho$ that is continuously differentiable with nonzero derivative at some point, width $n+m+2$ suffices for uniform approximation on compacta (Kidger–Lyons 2020). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_approximation_theorem))
- **Depth separation (Telgarsky 2016).** For every positive integer $k$ there are networks with $\Theta(k^3)$ layers and $\Theta(1)$ nodes per layer that cannot be approximated by networks with $O(k)$ layers unless these have $\Omega(2^k)$ nodes; the result is proved for "semi-algebraic gates", which include ReLU, maximum, indicator and piecewise-polynomial units. ([Telgarsky](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04485))
- **VC dimension.** For piecewise-polynomial $\varrho$, $\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal F_{(N,\varrho),\mathrm{sgn}})\le c\,(P(N)L\log P(N)+P(N)L^2)$ (Bartlett–Maiorov–Meir). ([Berner et al. 2021, Thm 1.18](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

### Examples
- **XOR.** A single perceptron cannot compute exclusive-or, as Minsky and Papert emphasized in 1969, but a multilayer perceptron can. ([Wikipedia: Perceptron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceptron))
- **One-hidden-layer MLP.** $H=\sigma(XW^{(1)}+b^{(1)})$, $O=HW^{(2)}+b^{(2)}$; with $\sigma$ removed, the model equals one affine layer with $W=W^{(1)}W^{(2)}$. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/mlp.html))
- **Piecewise-linear networks.** ReLU and maxout networks compute piecewise-linear functions whose complexity can be measured by their number of linear regions; the compositional structure of deep networks lets them re-use pieces of computation exponentially often in terms of depth. ([Montúfar et al. 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.1869))

### History
McCulloch and Pitts (1943) considered a non-learning computational model for neural networks; Hebb proposed a plasticity-based learning hypothesis in the late 1940s; Rosenblatt described the perceptron in 1958; Ivakhnenko and Lapa's group method of data handling (1965) is described as the first working deep-learning algorithm; Amari (1967) trained a multilayer perceptron with SGD; Minsky and Papert's 1969 analysis of XOR reduced interest; Linnainmaa (1970) published modern backpropagation, applied to networks by Werbos (1982) and popularized by Rumelhart et al. (1986). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_network_%28machine_learning%29)) The Mark I Perceptron, with 400 photocells, was first publicly demonstrated in 1960. ([Wikipedia: Perceptron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceptron))

### Connections
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): every layer is an affine map $x\mapsto Wx+b$.
- [Differential Calculus](node:Differential%20Calculus): gradients of the loss with respect to weights drive training.
- [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation): the algorithm that computes those gradients.
- [Universal Approximation Theorem](node:Universal%20Approximation%20Theorem): density of shallow networks in $C(K)$.
- [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning): training deep networks at scale.
- [Convolutional Neural Networks](node:Convolutional%20Neural%20Networks), [Recurrent Neural Networks](node:Recurrent%20Neural%20Networks), [Transformers](node:Transformers): architectures obtained by weight sharing or other structure.
- [VC Dimension](node:VC%20Dimension) and [Rademacher Complexity](node:Rademacher%20Complexity): capacity measures used to bound generalization.
- [Logistic Regression](node:Logistic%20Regression): a network with no hidden layer and sigmoid output.
- [Neural Tangent Kernel](node:Neural%20Tangent%20Kernel): the infinite-width linearized regime.

### Common pitfalls
- **Existence is not learnability.** Universal approximation theorems guarantee that a network exists but not how large it must be or how to find its weights. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_approximation_theorem); [d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/mlp.html))
- **Parameters are not functions.** Different $(a,\theta)$ can realize the same function (set $W^{(L)}=0$), so statements about weights do not transfer directly to functions. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Saturating activations.** Sigmoid derivatives vanish for large $|x|$, which slows optimization; ReLU has largely replaced them in hidden layers. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/mlp.html))
- **Parameter-count bounds can be vacuous.** CNNs fit random labels on CIFAR-10 yet generalize on real labels, so VC bounds scaling with parameter count do not explain their performance. ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530))

### Open problems
- **Why overparametrized networks generalize.** Berner et al. list this as an open question: networks with more parameters than samples interpolate noisy data yet generalize, contradicting classical bias-variance reasoning (the "generalization puzzle"). ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **The role of depth and the curse of dimensionality.** Whether there is a mathematically quantifiable benefit of depth in general, and why networks perform well on very high-dimensional inputs, are posed as open questions in the same survey. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026))
- **Non-convex optimization.** Why SGD reaches good minima despite non-convex empirical risk is open. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Neural network (machine learning), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_network_%28machine_learning%29): structure, training, history, criticism.
- **Reference:** [Universal approximation theorem, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_approximation_theorem): width and depth versions with hypotheses.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, Multilayer Perceptrons](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/mlp.html): MLPs and activation functions with code.
- **Primary:** [Berner, Grohs, Kutyniok, Petersen, The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026): survey of approximation, optimization, and generalization theory.
- **Primary:** [Telgarsky, Benefits of depth in neural networks (COLT 2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04485): depth separation.
- **Further reading:** [Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press 2016)](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/): standard text; chapter 6 covers deep feedforward networks.
references.Asymptotic Analysis:
## Reference
### Overview
Asymptotic analysis compares functions, typically the running time or space of an algorithm as a function of input size $n$, by their growth rate as $n\to\infty$, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. The notations $O$, $\Omega$ and $\Theta$ express upper, lower and tight bounds; $o$ and $\omega$ express strict domination; and $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to 1$. In a sum the fastest-growing term dominates, powers dominate logarithms, and exponentials dominate powers. ([Wikipedia: Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation))

Upper bounds come from exhibiting an algorithm, such as merge sort's $O(n\log n)$ comparisons; lower bounds hold for every algorithm in a model, such as the $\Omega(n\log n)$ bound for comparison sorting, which merge sort meets up to a linear term. ([Wikipedia: Comparison sort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_sort))

The analysis of algorithms also seeks concise and precise estimates of quantities of interest, using recurrences, generating functions and asymptotic approximations; analytic combinatorics obtains coefficient asymptotics of generating functions from their singularities by complex analysis, including singularity analysis and the saddle-point method. ([Sedgewick and Flajolet, An Introduction to the Analysis of Algorithms](https://aofa.cs.princeton.edu/home/); [Flajolet and Sedgewick, Analytic Combinatorics](https://ac.cs.princeton.edu/home/))

### Formal definition
For $f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}$:
$$g\in O(f)\iff \exists\, c,n_0>0\ \forall n\ge n_0:\ g(n)\le c\,f(n),$$
$$g\in \Omega(f)\iff \exists\, c,n_0>0\ \forall n\ge n_0:\ g(n)\ge c\,f(n),$$
$$g\in\Theta(f)\iff g\in O(f)\ \text{and}\ g\in\Omega(f)\iff \exists\, c_1,c_2,n_0>0\ \forall n\ge n_0:\ c_1 f(n)\le g(n)\le c_2 f(n).$$
([Toronto CSC110 notes](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~david/course-notes/csc110-111/09-runtime/03-asymptotic-notation.html))

Little-o and little-omega are defined by limits: $f=o(g)$ means $f/g\to0$, $f=\omega(g)$ means $f/g\to\infty$, and $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to1$. The $\Omega$ above is Knuth's; the older Hardy–Littlewood $\Omega$, still used in [analytic number theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory), only asserts that $f/g$ does *not* tend to 0. ([Wikipedia: Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation))

### Key results
- **Algebra of $O$.** $O$, $\Omega$, $\Theta$ are reflexive and transitive; $g\in O(f)\iff f\in\Omega(g)$; if $f,g\in O(h)$ then $f+g\in O(h)$; if $f\in\Theta(h)$ and $g\in O(h)$ then $f+g\in\Theta(h)$; $a f\in\Theta(f)$ for constants $a>0$; and $g_1\in O(f_1)$, $g_2\in O(f_2)$ imply $g_1g_2\in O(f_1f_2)$ (likewise for $\Omega$, $\Theta$). ([Toronto CSC110 notes](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~david/course-notes/csc110-111/09-runtime/03-asymptotic-notation.html))
- **Growth hierarchy.** For $a,b>0$: $\log_a n\in\Theta(\log_b n)$ when $a,b>1$; $n^a\in O(n^b)\setminus\Omega(n^b)$ when $a<b$; $a^n\in O(b^n)\setminus\Omega(b^n)$ when $a<b$; $\log_a n\in O(n^b)\setminus\Omega(n^b)$; and $n^a\in O(b^n)\setminus\Omega(b^n)$ when $b>1$. ([Toronto CSC110 notes](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~david/course-notes/csc110-111/09-runtime/03-asymptotic-notation.html))
- **Master theorem.** Let $T(n)=a\,T(n/b)+f(n)$ with constants $a\ge1$, $b>1$, $T(n)=\Theta(1)$ below a fixed threshold, and $c_{\text{crit}}=\log_b a$. (1) If $f(n)=O(n^c)$ for some $c<c_{\text{crit}}$, then $T(n)=\Theta(n^{c_{\text{crit}}})$. (2) If $f(n)=\Theta(n^{c_{\text{crit}}}\log^k n)$ with $k\ge0$, then $T(n)=\Theta(n^{c_{\text{crit}}}\log^{k+1}n)$. (3) If $f(n)=\Omega(n^c)$ for some $c>c_{\text{crit}}$ and the regularity condition $a f(n/b)\le k f(n)$ holds for some $k<1$ and all large $n$, then $T(n)=\Theta(f(n))$. ([Wikipedia: Master theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_theorem_%28analysis_of_algorithms%29))
- **Akra–Bazzi theorem.** For $T(x)=g(x)+\sum_{i=1}^k a_iT(b_ix+h_i(x))$ with constants $a_i>0$, $0<b_i<1$, $|g'(x)|\in O(x^c)$, and perturbations $|h_i(x)|\in O(x/\log^2x)$, let $p$ solve $\sum_i a_ib_i^p=1$. Then $T(x)\in\Theta\big(x^p\big(1+\int_1^x \frac{g(u)}{u^{p+1}}\,du\big)\big)$; the $h_i$ absorb floors and ceilings. ([Wikipedia: Akra–Bazzi method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akra%E2%80%93Bazzi_method))
- **Comparison-sorting lower bound.** Any comparison sort needs at least $\lceil\log_2 n!\rceil$ comparisons in the worst case, and at least $\log_2 n!$ on average over uniformly [random permutations](node:Random%20Permutations) of distinct keys; since $\log_2 n!\ge \tfrac n2\log_2\tfrac n2$, this is $\Omega(n\log n)$, asymptotically tight, since merge sort comes within a linear term of it. By Stirling, $\log_2 n!\approx n\log_2 n-1.4427\,n$. ([Wikipedia: Comparison sort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_sort))

### Examples
- $10n+5\in\Theta(n)$ but $\notin\Theta(n^2)$; $n+10\in O(n^{100})$ is true but uninformative; $\tfrac1{n+1}\in O(1)$ but $\notin\Omega(1)$. ([Toronto CSC110 notes](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~david/course-notes/csc110-111/09-runtime/03-asymptotic-notation.html))
- Typical orders: $O(\log n)$ for binary search, $O(n\log n)$ for merge sort, $O(n^2)$ for bubble sort. ([Wikipedia: Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation))
- **Matrix multiplication.** Strassen's 1969 discovery that $2\times2$ matrix multiplication has rank 7 gave the first subcubic algorithm, running in $O(n^{\log_2 7})\approx O(n^{2.807})$. Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu and Zhou proved $\omega<2.371339$ by a more asymmetric version of the laser method. ([Alman et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16349v1)) Dupont, Eisenberger, Kozlovskii, Mehrabian, Ruiz, See, Zhou, Alman, Vassilevska Williams and Balog (2026) solved the underlying optimization problem over a larger search space, using machine-learning-based optimization refined with AlphaEvolve, and improved this to $\omega<2.371177$, the best upper bound listed as of 2026. ([Dupont et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16884); [Alman et al., v3](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.16349); [Wikipedia: Computational complexity of matrix multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication))

### History
Du Bois-Reymond used an early growth notation in 1870; Bachmann introduced $O$ in 1894, Landau added $o$ in 1909, and Hardy and Littlewood introduced $\Omega$ in 1914. Knuth popularized $O$ in computer science in the 1970s, and in 1976 introduced $\Theta$ and redefined $\Omega$ as a lower bound. ([Wikipedia: Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation)) The master method was first presented in 1980 by Bentley, Haken and Saxe as a "unifying method" for divide-and-conquer recurrences, and the name "master theorem" spread through Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein's *Introduction to Algorithms*. ([Wikipedia: Master theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_theorem_%28analysis_of_algorithms%29)) Akra and Bazzi published their generalization in 1998. ([Wikipedia: Akra–Bazzi method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akra%E2%80%93Bazzi_method))

### Connections
- [Proof Techniques](node:Proof%20Techniques): $O$-bounds are proved by exhibiting witnesses $c,n_0$; recurrences are solved by induction.
- [Amortized Analysis](node:Amortized%20Analysis): bounds the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence.
- [Divide and Conquer](node:Divide%20and%20Conquer): its recurrences are the master theorem's domain.
- [Sorting and Searching](node:Sorting%20and%20Searching): the comparison lower bound and the $O(\log n)$ search bound.
- [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory): complexity classes are defined by asymptotic resource bounds.
- [Average-Case Complexity](node:Average-Case%20Complexity): asymptotic analysis of expected rather than worst-case cost.
- [Fine-Grained Complexity](node:Fine-Grained%20Complexity): asks for exact exponents, such as whether $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ is possible.
- [Generating Functions](node:Generating%20Functions): the main tool for precise asymptotics of combinatorial counts.
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): little-o, little-omega and $\sim$ are limit statements.
- [Matched Asymptotic Expansions](node:Matched%20Asymptotic%20Expansions): the analysts' counterpart, asymptotics of differential-equation solutions.

### Common pitfalls
- "$f=O(g)$" is a one-way statement: the equals sign is really membership or an inequality, which is why some authors write $f\in O(g)$. ([Wikipedia: Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation))
- Informal "Big-O" often means a tight bound; strictly, $O$ is only an upper bound, and $\Theta$ should be used for tight bounds. ([Toronto CSC110 notes](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~david/course-notes/csc110-111/09-runtime/03-asymptotic-notation.html))
- The two $\Omega$s (Knuth's and Hardy–Littlewood's) differ; check which convention a source uses. ([Wikipedia: Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation))
- The master theorem's third case needs the regularity condition; without it the theorem may give no conclusion. ([Wikipedia: Master theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_theorem_%28analysis_of_algorithms%29))
- $\lceil\log_2 n!\rceil$ is not always attained: it is 33 for $n=13$, but sorting 13 elements has been proven to need 34 comparisons. ([Wikipedia: Comparison sort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_sort))

### Open problems
- **The matrix multiplication exponent.** The trivial bound is $\omega\ge2$, no larger lower bound is known, and many conjecture $\omega=2$; the best upper bounds come from refinements of the laser method. ([Alman et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.16349)) Whether $\omega=2$ is described as a major open question in theoretical computer science. ([Wikipedia: Computational complexity of matrix multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Big O notation, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation): definitions, variants, conventions and history.
- **Learn:** [Toronto CSC110/111 notes, Asymptotic notation](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~david/course-notes/csc110-111/09-runtime/03-asymptotic-notation.html): quantifier definitions and proved properties.
- **Primary:** [Sedgewick and Flajolet, An Introduction to the Analysis of Algorithms (2nd ed., 2015)](https://aofa.cs.princeton.edu/home/): recurrences, generating functions and asymptotic approximations for algorithm analysis.
- **Primary:** [Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu and Zhou, More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16349): current-generation bounds on $\omega$.
- **Further reading:** [Flajolet and Sedgewick, Analytic Combinatorics](https://ac.cs.princeton.edu/home/): singularity analysis and saddle-point methods for coefficient asymptotics. [Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming](https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html): multivolume treatment of fundamental, seminumerical, sorting and searching, and combinatorial algorithms.
references.Attention Mechanism:
## Reference
### Overview
An attention mechanism computes, for a query, a weighted average of a set of values, where each weight measures how well the query matches the key attached to that value. Given a database $\mathcal D = \{(\mathbf k_i,\mathbf v_i)\}_{i=1}^m$, attention pooling returns $\sum_i \alpha(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)\,\mathbf v_i$; the most common setting in deep learning takes nonnegative weights summing to 1 (a convex combination), for instance a softmax over a score. ([Dive into Deep Learning, §11.1](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/queries-keys-values.html))

Attention was introduced into neural [machine translation](node:Machine%20Translation) to remove the bottleneck of compressing a whole source sentence into one fixed-length vector: the decoder instead "softly searches" the encoder states for the parts relevant to each target word. ([Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473)) The [Transformer](node:Transformers) then dropped recurrence entirely and built sequence models from self-attention and feed-forward layers, which is the form behind modern [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models). ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))

Without positional information attention is permutation-invariant, and dot-product softmax attention costs $O(L^2)$ over a sequence of length $L$, which has motivated many cheaper variants, including [linear attention](node:Linear%20Attention). ([Wikipedia: Attention (machine learning)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_%28machine_learning%29)) A self-attention layer connects any two positions by a path of length $O(1)$. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))

### Formal definition
**Attention pooling.** For a query $\mathbf q$ and key–value pairs $(\mathbf k_i,\mathbf v_i)_{i=1}^m$ with scoring function $a$,
$$\operatorname{Attention}(\mathbf q,\mathcal D)=\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)\,\mathbf v_i,\qquad \alpha(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)=\frac{\exp a(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)}{\sum_{j}\exp a(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_j)}.$$
Taking a similarity kernel $\alpha(\mathbf q,\mathbf k)$ (Gaussian, boxcar, Epanechnikov) normalized over the keys, $f(\mathbf q)=\sum_i \mathbf v_i\,\alpha(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)/\sum_j\alpha(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_j)$, with training features as keys and labels as values, gives the Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression estimator (Nadaraya 1964; Watson 1964). ([Dive into Deep Learning, §11.2](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/attention-pooling.html))

**Scoring functions.** Additive (Bahdanau) attention uses $a(\mathbf q,\mathbf k)=\mathbf w_v^\top\tanh(\mathbf W_q\mathbf q+\mathbf W_k\mathbf k)$, a one-hidden-layer MLP that allows queries and keys of different dimensions. Scaled dot-product attention uses $a(\mathbf q,\mathbf k)=\mathbf q^\top\mathbf k/\sqrt d$. Masked softmax sets the scores of padded or disallowed positions to a large negative number so their weights vanish. ([Dive into Deep Learning, §11.3](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/attention-scoring-functions.html))

**Matrix form and multi-head attention.** For query, key and value matrices $Q, K, V$,
$$\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)V,$$
$$\operatorname{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1,\dots,\mathrm{head}_h)W^O,\quad \mathrm{head}_i=\operatorname{Attention}(QW_i^Q,KW_i^K,VW_i^V).$$
In **self-attention** $Q,K,V$ are all projections of the same sequence; in **cross-attention** (encoder–decoder attention) queries come from the decoder and keys/values from the encoder; **causal** self-attention masks future positions to $-\infty$ before the softmax. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))

### Key results
- **Why scale by $\sqrt{d_k}$.** If the components of $\mathbf q$ and $\mathbf k$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then $\mathbf q^\top\mathbf k$ has mean 0 and variance $d_k$; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance and keeps the softmax out of its small-gradient saturated regime. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))
- **Path length versus cost.** A self-attention layer over $n$ positions of width $d$ costs $O(n^2 d)$ with $O(1)$ sequential operations and $O(1)$ maximum path length between positions, against $O(nd^2)$, $O(n)$ and $O(n)$ for a recurrent layer. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))
- **Quadratic time is necessary under SETH.** Computing self-attention, even approximately and for several attention variants, requires time quadratic in the input length unless the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis fails. ([Keles, Wijewardena and Hegde 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04881))
- **Sharp threshold for fast attention.** For $Q,K,V\in[-B,B]^{n\times d}$ with $d=O(\log n)$: if $B=o(\sqrt{\log n})$ there is an $n^{1+o(1)}$-time algorithm approximating attention to $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ additive error; if $B=\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$, no truly subquadratic $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$ algorithm exists assuming SETH. ([Alman and Song 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13214))
- **Linear attention is an RNN.** Writing the similarity as a dot product of kernel feature maps, $\operatorname{sim}(\mathbf q,\mathbf k)=\phi(\mathbf q)^\top\phi(\mathbf k)$, and reassociating the matrix products reduces the cost from quadratic to linear in length, and causal linear attention can be computed recurrently. ([Katharopoulos et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16236))
- **Fixed-size self-attention cannot model periodic or hierarchical languages.** With a fixed number of layers and heads, both soft and hard self-attention cannot model periodic finite-state languages or hierarchical structure as input length grows, unless layers or heads grow with input length. ([Hahn 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.06755)) Under leftmost-hard attention, this includes PARITY and Dyck-1; under softmax attention the PARITY negative result needs Lipschitz position-wise functions and a KL generation criterion, and Chiang and Cholak exhibit PARITY constructions when either assumption is dropped. ([Strobl et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.00208v3))

### Examples
- **Bahdanau alignment.** In English–French translation, the learned attention weights form soft alignments between source and target words that agree with intuition, and the model was comparable to the best phrase-based system of the time. ([Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473))
- **Special weightings.** One-hot weights reduce attention to an exact database lookup, and uniform weights $1/m$ reduce it to average pooling. ([Dive into Deep Learning, §11.1](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/queries-keys-values.html))
- **Transformer base.** $h=8$ heads with $d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h=64$ and $d_{\text{model}}=512$. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))

### History
Multiplicative units such as sigma-pi units predate attention, and in Schmidhuber's 1992 fast-weight controllers a slow network learns to generate keys and values, which amounts to dot-product attention without softmax (Schlag et al. 2021).
