Bahdanau et al. (2014) introduced additive attention for sequence-to-sequence translation, Luong et al. (2015) compared scoring functions including the dot-product form, and Vaswani et al. (2017) built the Transformer from attention alone. FlashAttention later partitioned the attention computation into blocks that fit in the GPU's faster on-chip memory, reducing memory needs without sacrificing accuracy. ([Wikipedia: Attention (machine learning)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_%28machine_learning%29))

### Connections
- [Transformers](node:Transformers): stacks of multi-head self-attention and MLP blocks.
- [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning): attention is a differentiable layer trained end to end by [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation).
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): queries, keys and values are learned linear projections; attention is a row-stochastic matrix times $V$.
- [Recurrent Neural Networks](node:Recurrent%20Neural%20Networks): attention was introduced to relieve their fixed-vector bottleneck; linear attention is itself recurrent.
- [Kernel Methods](node:Kernel%20Methods): softmax attention generalizes Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoothing, and linear attention uses kernel feature maps.
- [Linear Attention](node:Linear%20Attention), [Multi-Head Latent Attention](node:Multi-Head%20Latent%20Attention), [Paged Attention](node:Paged%20Attention): efficiency variants.
- [Rotary Positional Embeddings](node:Rotary%20Positional%20Embeddings): supplies position information to a permutation-invariant operator.
- [Graph Neural Networks](node:Graph%20Neural%20Networks) and [Graph Transformers](node:Graph%20Transformers): attention restricted to, or biased by, graph edges.
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): analyzes attention heads as circuit components.

### Common pitfalls
- Without positional encoding attention is permutation-invariant: the pooled sum $\sum_i\alpha(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)\mathbf v_i$ does not depend on the order of the key–value pairs, so sequence order must be injected by positional encodings. ([Wikipedia: Attention (machine learning)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_%28machine_learning%29); [Dive into Deep Learning, §11.1](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/queries-keys-values.html))
- Omitting the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor at large $d_k$ saturates the softmax and shrinks gradients. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))
- Random Fourier feature approximations can have negative entries even though the RBF kernel they approximate is always positive; Performer's feature maps are chosen so that all features are positive. ([Wikipedia: Attention (machine learning)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_%28machine_learning%29))

> [!warning] Contested
> Whether attention weights explain a model's predictions is disputed. Jain and Wallace report that attention weights are often uncorrelated with gradient-based importance and that very different attention distributions can yield the same predictions, and conclude that standard attention modules largely do not provide meaningful explanations. ([Jain and Wallace 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10186)) Wiegreffe and Pinter argue that the answer depends on the definition of explanation, propose four alternative tests, and conclude that the earlier work does not show attention is useless for explainability. ([Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.04626))

### Open problems
- **Exact logical characterization of softmax attention.** Strobl et al. list as open whether softmax-attention transformers can be characterized more tightly, or exactly, in terms of a logic, and whether the effects of positional encodings, average-hard versus softmax attention, and pre- versus post-norm on expressivity can be clarified. ([Strobl et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.00208v3))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Attention (machine learning), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_%28machine_learning%29): history, variants, efficiency methods.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, Ch. 11](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/queries-keys-values.html): queries, keys and values, scoring functions, with code.
- **Primary:** [Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio, Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473): the original additive attention.
- **Primary:** [Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7): scaled dot-product and multi-head attention.
- **Further reading:** [Strobl, Merrill, Weiss, Chiang and Angluin, What Formal Languages Can Transformers Express? (TACL 2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.00208v3): survey of expressivity results for attention-based models.
references.Automatic Differentiation:
## Reference
### Overview
Automatic differentiation (AD), also called algorithmic differentiation, evaluates partial derivatives of a function specified by a computer program. It applies the chain rule to each elementary operation the program executes and carries derivative values alongside function values. It is neither symbolic differentiation, which must turn the program into one closed-form expression, nor finite differencing, which introduces truncation and round-off errors; AD derivatives are accurate to working precision ([Wikipedia: Automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation); [Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)). AD applies to ordinary code with branching, loops and recursion, at a small constant-factor overhead ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)).

There are two basic modes. Forward mode propagates directional derivatives in evaluation order; reverse mode first evaluates the program, records the intermediate values, and then propagates adjoints backward. Forward mode suits functions with few inputs and many outputs, reverse mode the opposite, so reverse mode is the method for gradients of scalar losses ([Wikipedia: Automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation)). Deep-learning "autograd" builds a computational graph of the operations applied to the data and traverses it backward with the chain rule ([Dive into Deep Learning §2.5](https://d2l.ai/chapter_preliminaries/autograd.html)).

AD has applications in engineering design optimization, [computational fluid dynamics](node:Computational%20Fluid%20Dynamics), optimal control, atmospheric sciences and computational finance. The AD and machine-learning communities developed partly independently and in some cases rediscovered each other's results ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)). Beyond the chain rule, the subject includes combinatorial questions (which order of chain-rule products is cheapest), memory–recomputation trade-offs, higher-order and implicit derivatives, and the semantics of differentiating nonsmooth programs ([arXiv:2107.05355](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05355); [Blondel and Roulet](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14606); [arXiv:1909.10300](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.10300)).

### Formal definition
A program computing $y=f(x)$, $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, is written as an evaluation trace (Wengert list): inputs $v_{i-n}=x_i$ for $i=1,\dots,n$, working variables $v_i=\varphi_i\big((v_j)_{j\prec i}\big)$ for $i=1,\dots,l$ built from elementary operations $\varphi_i$ with known derivatives, and outputs $y_{m-i}=v_{l-i}$ ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)).

**Forward (tangent) mode** seeds $\dot x=r$ and computes
$$\dot v_i=\sum_{j\prec i}\frac{\partial\varphi_i}{\partial v_j}\,\dot v_j$$
alongside $v_i$, which yields the Jacobian–vector product $J_f(x)\,r$ in one sweep. Equivalently, evaluate $f$ on dual numbers $v+\dot v\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon^2=0$, so that $(u+\dot u\varepsilon)(v+\dot v\varepsilon)=uv+(\dot uv+u\dot v)\varepsilon$ ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767); [Wikipedia: Automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation)).

**Reverse (adjoint) mode** runs the trace forward, stores it, seeds $\bar y=r$, and computes in reverse order
$$\bar v_j=\sum_{i:\,j\prec i}\bar v_i\,\frac{\partial\varphi_i}{\partial v_j},$$
which yields the transposed Jacobian–vector product $J_f(x)^{\top} r$ in one reverse sweep ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)).

**Implementation styles.** *Source transformation* rewrites the program into derivative code before compilation (ADIFOR and ADIC for Fortran and C; Tapenade, which does forward and reverse mode for Fortran and C; Tangent for a subset of Python). *Operator overloading* redefines the elementary operations on AD-enabled types: ADOL-C in C++ records operations on a tape that is played back in reverse mode ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)). Operator overloading is the most straightforward implementation in languages with polymorphism ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)); source transformation can be implemented for all programming languages, while operator overloading usually has weaker speed performance ([Wikipedia: Automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation)).

### Key results
- **Cost of the two modes.** If $\mathrm{ops}(f)$ is the operation count of $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, the full $m\times n$ Jacobian costs $n\,c\,\mathrm{ops}(f)$ by forward mode and $m\,c\,\mathrm{ops}(f)$ by reverse mode, where $c<6$ is guaranteed and typically $c\approx2$–$3$ (Griewank–Walther). For $m=1$ the gradient costs a constant multiple of evaluating $f$, independent of $n$. ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767))
- **Baur–Strassen theorem (1983).** For arithmetic circuits: for every polynomial $f$, the minimal circuit size of its gradient satisfies $S(\nabla f)\le 5\,S(f)$. Morgenstern (1985) gave a simpler proof by backward induction, and analogous bounds hold for computation graphs with more primitives than $+$ and $\times$. ([Blondel and Roulet, §8.3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14606); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0304-3975%2883%2990110-X))
- **Memory of reverse mode and optimal checkpointing.** Reverse mode's storage grows, in the worst case, in proportion to the number of operations of $f$ ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)). For a chain $f=f_K\circ\cdots\circ f_1$ with $s$ memory slots, the minimal number $C^*(k,s)$ of function evaluations for a chain of length $k$ satisfies
  $$C^*(k,s)=\min_{1\le l\le k-1}\{C^*(k-l,s-1)+C^*(l,s)+l\},\quad C^*(1,s)=0,\ C^*(k,1)=\tfrac{k(k-1)}2;$$
  recursive halving reverses a chain of length $K=2^j$ with $\log_2K$ slots, and Griewank (1992) found the optimal schedule analytically ([Blondel and Roulet, §8.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14606)). The binomial schedule gives, for a given number of checkpoints, the minimal number of recomputed time steps; it is implemented in `revolve` (Griewank and Walther, ACM TOMS 2000) ([Walther and Narayanan](https://eecs.wsu.edu/~assefaw/CSC16/abstracts/walther-CSC16_paper_6.pdf); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/347837.347846)). This optimality assumes the chain length is known in advance and the steps cost the same; online schemes for unknown length are nearly optimal ([Blondel and Roulet, §8.5.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14606)).
- **Hessian–vector products (Pearlmutter 1994).** For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, computing the directional derivative $\nabla f\cdot v$ by forward mode and then differentiating it by reverse mode gives $\nabla^2f\,v$ at $O(n)$ cost, without forming the $n\times n$ Hessian ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)). The same product can be formed by reverse-on-reverse, forward-on-reverse (the JVP of the gradient, using symmetry of the Hessian) or forward-on-forward ([Blondel and Roulet, §9.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14606)).
- **Implicit differentiation.** If $F:\mathcal W\times\Lambda\to\mathcal W$ is $C^1$ near $(w_0,\lambda_0)$, $F(w_0,\lambda_0)=0$ and $\partial_1F(w_0,\lambda_0)$ is invertible, then locally $F(w^\star(\lambda),\lambda)=0$ with $\partial w^\star(\lambda)=-\partial_1F(w^\star,\lambda)^{-1}\partial_2F(w^\star,\lambda)$. For $w^\star(\lambda)=\arg\min_wf(w,\lambda)$ with $f$ strictly convex in $w$, take $F=\nabla_1f$, assuming the Hessian $\nabla_1^2f$ is invertible at $(w^\star(\lambda),\lambda)$ ([Blondel and Roulet, §11.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14606)). Blondel et al. apply AD to a user-written optimality map $F$ and use the implicit function theorem to differentiate the solution of any solver ([arXiv:2105.15183](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.15183)).
- **Optimal Jacobian accumulation is NP-complete (Naumann).** Computing a Jacobian with the fewest operations, by choosing how to order chain-rule products over the computational graph, is NP-complete ([Wikipedia: Automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation)); the general "Chain Rule Differentiation" problem is NP-complete as well ([arXiv:2107.05355](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05355)).
- **Nonsmooth AD.** TensorFlow and PyTorch do not compute generalized subderivatives correctly even on simple examples; under restrictions on the nonsmooth elementary functions standard in nonlinear programming, provably correct generalized subderivatives cost a dimension-free factor of at most 6 times the function ([arXiv:1809.08530](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.08530)). Bolte and Pauwels's conservative fields admit a calculus; path-differentiable functions include convex, concave, Clarke regular and semialgebraic Lipschitz functions, and the model proves convergence of nonsmooth SGD as used in practice ([arXiv:1909.10300](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.10300)). For locally Lipschitz semialgebraic or definable elementary functions the backward-mode overhead is independent of the dimension, extending Baur–Strassen's smooth cheap gradient principle, while finding two subgradients in the Clarke subdifferential is NP-hard ([arXiv:2206.01730](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.01730)).

### Examples
- **Dual numbers.** For $z=x(x+y)+y^2$ at $(x,y)=(2,3)$, forward evaluation on dual numbers gives $\partial z/\partial x=7$ and $\partial z/\partial y=8$ ([Wikipedia: Automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation)).
- **Neural networks.** A scalar loss has $m=1$, so one reverse sweep gives the gradient in all parameters; backpropagation has become the default method for computing gradients ([Dive into Deep Learning §2.5](https://d2l.ai/chapter_preliminaries/autograd.html)).
- **Checkpointed BPTT.** A checkpointing variant of backpropagation through time saved up to 95% of memory at a 33% increase in computation in one instance ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)).
- **Stopping gradients.** If $u=x^2$ is detached, then for $z=u\cdot x$ the computed $\partial z/\partial x$ is $u$, not $3x^2$ ([Dive into Deep Learning §2.5](https://d2l.ai/chapter_preliminaries/autograd.html)).

### History
Ideas underlying AD go back to the 1950s (Nolan 1953; Beda et al. 1959), and Wengert (1964) essentially discovered forward mode. The continuous-time essence of reverse mode is the Pontryagin maximum principle; control theorists (Bryson and Denham 1962; Bryson and Ho 1969) used it, Linnainmaa (1970, 1976) is often cited as the first published description of reverse mode, Werbos (1974) gave it in discrete-time form, and Speelpenning (1980) built the first truly automatic implementation. Griewank's work revived the field in the 1980s ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)). Baur and Strassen's complexity paper appeared in *Theoretical Computer Science* 22 (1983) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0304-3975%2883%2990110-X)), and Griewank and Walther's *Evaluating Derivatives* (2nd ed., SIAM, 2008) is the standard monograph ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898717761)).

### Connections
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): the chain rule for Jacobians supplies the local derivative rules; the cost, ordering and memory questions are algorithmic.
- [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation): reverse-mode AD specialized to neural networks.
- [Checkpointing for Automatic Differentiation](node:Checkpointing%20for%20Automatic%20Differentiation): the recomputation–memory trade-off made optimal by binomial schedules.
- [Implicit Function Theorem](node:Implicit%20Function%20Theorem): the basis of implicit differentiation through solvers and fixed points.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): the complexity class of optimal Jacobian accumulation.
- [Semialgebraic Sets](node:Semialgebraic%20Sets): the function class on which nonsmooth AD is well behaved.
- [Differentiable Programming](node:Differentiable%20Programming) and [Differentiable Simulation](node:Differentiable%20Simulation): AD applied to general programs and simulators.
- [Adjoint Sensitivity Methods](node:Adjoint%20Sensitivity%20Methods): the continuous-time analogue of reverse mode for ODE and PDE constraints.
- [Neural ODEs](node:Neural%20ODEs): trained by adjoint methods instead of storing the full trace.
- [Hyperparameter Optimization](node:Hyperparameter%20Optimization): nested AD gives exact hypergradients.
- [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent) and [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent): the optimizers that consume AD gradients.
- [Newton's Method](node:Newton's%20Method) and [Second-Order Optimization for Learning](node:Second-Order%20Optimization%20for%20Learning): consume Hessian–vector products from nested modes.
- [Combinatorial Optimization](node:Combinatorial%20Optimization): the setting of optimal derivative accumulation.

### Common pitfalls
- **Arithmetic bounds are not wall-clock bounds.** Naively allocating dual-number structures costs memory traffic on every operation, and operator-overloading method dispatch can amount to a slowdown of an order of magnitude ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)).
- **Perturbation confusion.** In nested forward mode the infinitesimals of different differentiations must be kept distinct; confusing them is an easy bug ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)).
- **Nonsmooth points.** Frameworks may return values that are not generalized subgradients ([arXiv:1809.08530](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.08530)).
- **The executed branch is differentiated.** For piecewise code the derivative is that of the branch taken ([Dive into Deep Learning §2.5](https://d2l.ai/chapter_preliminaries/autograd.html)).
- **Checkpointing optimality has hypotheses.** The optimal analytic schedule needs the chain length in advance and ignores varying step costs ([Blondel and Roulet, §8.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14606)).

### Open problems
- **Nested AD in machine learning.** Baydin et al. name making use of nested AD, differentiation nested arbitrarily deep with referential transparency, as an important direction for future work, with exact hypergradients and higher-order samplers as applications ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)).
- **Formalizing new AD modes.** Modes from the machine-learning community, such as direct propagation of the inverse Jacobian (Srinivasan and Todorov 2015), "have yet to be examined and formalized by the AD community" ([Baydin et al., JMLR 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation): modes, dual numbers, implementation approaches, history.
- **Learn:** [Blondel and Roulet, The Elements of Differentiable Programming](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14606): book-length treatment of autodiff, Baur–Strassen, checkpointing, Hessian–vector products and implicit differentiation.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, §2.5 Automatic Differentiation](https://d2l.ai/chapter_preliminaries/autograd.html): hands-on reverse-mode autograd with control flow and detaching.
- **Primary:** [Kakade and Lee, Provably Correct Automatic Subdifferentiation for Qualified Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.08530): a cheap subgradient principle.
- **Primary:** [Bolte, Boustany, Pauwels, Pesquet-Popescu, On the complexity of nonsmooth automatic differentiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.01730): nonsmooth extension of the cheap gradient principle.
- **Primary:** [Blondel et al., Efficient and Modular Implicit Differentiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.15183): automatic implicit differentiation of optimization solutions.
- **Further reading:** [Baydin, Pearlmutter, Radul, Siskind, Automatic differentiation in machine learning: a survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05767): survey (JMLR 2018) of AD modes, history, tools and future directions.
- **Further reading:** [Griewank and Walther, Evaluating Derivatives, 2nd ed. (SIAM, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898717761): the standard monograph on algorithmic differentiation.
- **Further reading:** [Griewank and Walther, Algorithm 799: revolve (ACM TOMS 26, 2000)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/347837.347846): the binomial checkpointing implementation.
references.Autonomous Scientific Research:
## Reference
### Overview
Autonomous scientific research is the attempt to automate the loop of science (forming hypotheses, designing and running experiments, interpreting results, and reporting them) with little or no human guidance. The idea predates language models: the "Robot Scientist" Adam, built by a group led by Ross King from 2004, hypothesized, devised experiments, ran them with laboratory robotics, interpreted the results and repeated the cycle in yeast functional genomics; a 2009 *Science* paper reported it as the first machine to discover new scientific knowledge independently of its creators. Its successor Eve works on drug screening. ([Wikipedia: Robot Scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot_Scientist))

The current wave builds on [LLM Agents](node:LLM%20Agents). Boiko, MacKnight and Gomes combined several LLMs into an agent that designs, plans and carries out chemistry experiments, the most complex being catalyzed cross-coupling reactions. ([Boiko et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05332)) "The AI Scientist" generates ideas, writes code, runs experiments, plots results, writes a full paper and then runs a simulated review, at under \$15 per paper. ([Lu et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292)) Benchmarks now measure pieces of the loop, such as ML engineering on Kaggle tasks and replication of published papers. ([Chan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095); [Starace et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848))

Producing a paper-shaped artifact is distinct from producing a verified result. A 2026 survey argues that the field's central bottleneck is no longer only whether agents can complete research tasks but also whether reviewers can verify the claims they produce, which are "often harder to verify than their code is to run." ([Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179)) This is why the topic sits next to [Reproducible Research Computing](node:Reproducible%20Research%20Computing) and [Scientific Claim Verification](node:Scientific%20Claim%20Verification).

### Formal definition
There is no single formal definition; the field is organized by which stages of the research lifecycle a system automates and how much autonomy it has at each. Ding et al. code systems along seven audit dimensions: lifecycle stage, autonomy level, evaluation method, released artifacts, human-in-the-loop points, novelty verification, and result-selection disclosure; their autonomy levels run from L0 (assistive) through L1 (tool-augmented), L2 (stage-local) and L3 (pipeline) to L4 (closed-loop, a system whose results are fed back to condition the next step), split into mechanical L4-m and externally validated L4-v; L5 (open-ended) is called aspirational and left unpopulated. ([Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179); [Ding et al. 2026, §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.05179)) The classical robot-scientist definition is the cycle hypothesize → design experiment → execute → interpret → repeat, run without human guidance. ([Wikipedia: Robot Scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot_Scientist))

Benchmarks evaluate the artifacts such systems produce against an external standard: hierarchical rubrics co-developed with paper authors and graded by an LLM judge in PaperBench, or human baselines from Kaggle's public leaderboards in MLE-bench. ([Starace et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848); [Chan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095))

### Key results
- **End-to-end ML papers at low cost.** The AI Scientist produces complete papers for under \$15 each; its automated reviewer is reported to reach near-human performance in scoring papers, and by that reviewer's judgment some generated papers exceed the acceptance threshold of a top ML conference. ([Lu et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292))
- **A workshop paper through peer review.** The AI Scientist-v2 replaces human-written code templates with agentic tree search managed by an experiment-manager agent; of three fully autonomous manuscripts submitted to a peer-reviewed ICLR workshop, one scored above the average human acceptance threshold. ([Yamada et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08066))
- **ML engineering.** On 75 Kaggle competitions, with human baselines from public leaderboards, the best setup (o1-preview with AIDE scaffolding) reached at least a bronze medal in 16.9% of competitions. ([Chan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095))
- **Replication is far from solved.** PaperBench asks agents to replicate 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers from scratch, graded on 8,316 rubric tasks co-developed with the papers' authors; the best agent (Claude 3.5 Sonnet with open-source scaffolding) averaged 21.0%, and models did not outperform top ML PhD students on a subset. ([Starace et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848))
- **Hidden pitfalls.** Controlled experiments on two open-source AI-scientist systems found failures of varying severity from inappropriate benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse and post-hoc selection bias; trace logs and code detected them far more effectively than the final paper alone. ([Luo, Kasirzadeh and Shah 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08713))
- **Auditability gap.** Of 24 runnable systems coded by Ding et al., 83% release code, 38% release seeds or execution traces, and 38% report any novelty-verification method; of nine closed-loop L4 systems, seven are mechanical reruns, and no LLM-era system in their corpus shows an externally validated in-loop oracle. ([Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179))

### Examples
- **Adam (Robot Scientist).** Yeast functional genomics with laboratory robotics; reported in *Science* in 2009. ([Wikipedia: Robot Scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot_Scientist))
- **Coscientist-style chemistry agent.** Multiple LLMs plan and execute experiments, including catalyzed cross-couplings; the authors discuss misuse risks and propose safeguards. ([Boiko et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05332))
- **The AI Scientist and v2.** Template-based and tree-search pipelines for ML research papers. ([Lu et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292); [Yamada et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08066))
- Teaching: Stanford's CS329A (Self-Improving AI Agents, Autumn 2025) reads The AI Scientist alongside automated agent design and AlphaEvolve, and covers deep-research benchmarks. ([Stanford CS329A](https://cs329a.stanford.edu/index.html))

### History
The Robot Scientist project began in 2004 with EPSRC and BBSRC funding, and Adam's discovery was published in 2009. ([Wikipedia: Robot Scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot_Scientist)) Boiko et al.'s LLM-based chemistry agent was posted in April 2023 ([Boiko et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05332)); end-to-end paper-writing systems followed in August 2024 ([Lu et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292)), along with benchmarks for ML engineering (October 2024) and paper replication (April 2025). ([Chan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095); [Starace et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848)) Systematic audits of these systems and of the verifiability of their claims followed in 2025 and 2026. ([Luo, Kasirzadeh and Shah 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08713); [Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179))

### Connections
- [LLM Agents](node:LLM%20Agents): the planning, tool-use and memory substrate of modern research agents.
- [Reproducible Research Computing](node:Reproducible%20Research%20Computing): released code, seeds and traces are what make agent claims checkable.
- [Scientific Claim Verification](node:Scientific%20Claim%20Verification): checking that a manuscript's claims follow from its evidence.
- [Closed-Loop Experiment Agents](node:Closed-Loop%20Experiment%20Agents): the L4 regime in which agents act on their own results.
- [Evidence-Gated Research Agents](node:Evidence-Gated%20Research%20Agents) and [Witness-First Scientific Workflows](node:Witness-First%20Scientific%20Workflows): designs that gate claims on verifiable artifacts.
- [Scientific Benchmark Validity](node:Scientific%20Benchmark%20Validity), [Data Leakage and Temporal Evaluation](node:Data%20Leakage%20and%20Temporal%20Evaluation), [Benchmark Contamination Detection](node:Benchmark%20Contamination%20Detection): the pitfalls Luo et al. find in AI-scientist outputs.
- [Code Generation](node:Code%20Generation) and [Agent Planning and Replanning](node:Agent%20Planning%20and%20Replanning): core capabilities for experiment implementation.
- [Automated Theorem Proving](node:Automated%20Theorem%20Proving): the setting in which machine-produced claims can be checked formally.
- Key papers: [Lu et al. 2024 - The AI Scientist - Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292), [Starace et al. 2025 - PaperBench - Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848), [Ding et al. 2026 - Autonomous Research Agents - A Survey of AI Scientists and the Verification Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179).

### Common pitfalls
- An automated reviewer's acceptance score is not peer review; The AI Scientist's above-threshold claims are judged by its own automated reviewer. ([Lu et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292))
- Judging only the final paper misses benchmark misselection, leakage, metric misuse and selective reporting; audit logs and code. ([Luo, Kasirzadeh and Shah 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08713))
- Re-running an agent's code is not independent verification: most closed-loop systems in Ding et al.'s corpus are mechanical reruns rather than externally validated checks. ([Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179))
- Benchmark scores depend on the scaffold as well as the model (AIDE in MLE-bench, open-source scaffolding in PaperBench). ([Chan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095); [Starace et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848))

### Open problems
- **The verification gap.** Ding et al. close with six open problems: proxy-to-truth validation for closed loops (when a proxy tracks scientific validity and how to detect when it does not); closed-loop verifiers that test whether results actually revise hypotheses rather than whether a pipeline re-ran; novelty auditing at literature scale; independent agent review, separate from the generator and robust to prompt injection and self-preference; contamination-resistant evaluation; and preregistration for AI-generated hypotheses to curb result selection. ([Ding et al. 2026, §16](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.05179))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Robot Scientist, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot_Scientist): the pre-LLM autonomous discovery systems Adam and Eve.
- **Learn:** [Stanford CS329A, Self-Improving AI Agents (Autumn 2025)](https://cs329a.stanford.edu/index.html): course with readings on The AI Scientist and research agents.
- **Primary:** [Lu et al., The AI Scientist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292): an end-to-end pipeline from idea generation to written paper and simulated review.
- **Primary:** [Ding et al., Autonomous Research Agents: A Survey of AI Scientists and the Verification Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179): coded survey of 26 systems and studies.
- **Further reading:** [Starace et al., PaperBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848) and [Luo, Kasirzadeh and Shah, Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08713): evaluation and auditing of research agents.
references.Backpropagation:
## Reference
### Overview
Backpropagation computes the gradient of a scalar loss with respect to every weight of a neural network by applying the chain rule layer by layer from the output back to the input. It is a special case of reverse accumulation, i.e. reverse-mode [Automatic Differentiation](node:Automatic%20Differentiation), which extends to general computational graphs. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation)) The gradients it produces are then used by [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent) or [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent) to update the weights. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

Its importance is economic: for $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, forward-mode differentiation needs work proportional to $n$ function evaluations to form the Jacobian, reverse mode work proportional to $m$. A training loss has $m=1$ output and millions of parameters, so reverse mode yields the full gradient at a small constant multiple of the cost of evaluating the loss. ([Baydin et al. 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-468/17-468.pdf))

Conceptually, the network is a computational graph of simple gates. The forward pass computes and caches each gate's output; the backward pass multiplies the upstream gradient by each gate's local gradient and sends the result to the gate's inputs, adding contributions where a variable feeds several gates. ([CS231n notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/))

### Formal definition
Consider a feedforward [network](node:Artificial%20Neural%20Networks) with $a^{0}=x$, pre-activations $z^{\ell}=W^{\ell}a^{\ell-1}+b^{\ell}$, activations $a^{\ell}=\sigma(z^{\ell})$ for $\ell=1,\dots,L$, and loss $C(a^{L},y)$. Define the error $\delta^{\ell}=\partial C/\partial z^{\ell}$. Backpropagation computes
$$\delta^{L}=\nabla_{a^{L}}C\odot\sigma'(z^{L}),\qquad \delta^{\ell}=\big((W^{\ell+1})^{\top}\delta^{\ell+1}\big)\odot\sigma'(z^{\ell}),$$
$$\frac{\partial C}{\partial W^{\ell}}=\delta^{\ell}(a^{\ell-1})^{\top},\qquad \frac{\partial C}{\partial b^{\ell}}=\delta^{\ell}.$$
Each layer's error is obtained from the next layer's by multiplying by the transposed weight matrix and the activation derivative, and each weight gradient is that error times the previous layer's activations. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation)) For a single matrix product $D=WX$ with upstream gradient $dD$, the local rules are $dW=dD\,X^{\top}$ and $dX=W^{\top}dD$. ([CS231n notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/))

**General reverse mode.** For a program $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ written as a sequence of elementary operations $v_i$, reverse mode propagates adjoints $\bar v_i=\partial y/\partial v_i$ backwards through the trace; seeding $\bar y=r$ yields the vector–Jacobian product $J_f^{\top}r$. ([Baydin et al. 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-468/17-468.pdf))

### Key results
- **Cheap gradient principle.** If evaluating $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ costs $\mathrm{ops}(f)$, the full Jacobian costs $n\,c\,\mathrm{ops}(f)$ in forward mode and $m\,c\,\mathrm{ops}(f)$ in reverse mode, with $c<6$ guaranteed and typically $c\in[2,3]$ (Griewank–Walther). Hence for a scalar loss ($m=1$) the gradient costs a constant multiple of one loss evaluation, independent of $n$. ([Baydin et al. 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-468/17-468.pdf))
- **Memory cost.** Reverse mode's storage grows, in the worst case, in proportion to the number of operations in the evaluated function, because intermediate values must be kept for the backward pass. Checkpointing trades recomputation for memory; a checkpointed backpropagation-through-time scheme saved up to 95% memory at a 33% time increase in one instance (Gruslys et al. 2016). ([Baydin et al. 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-468/17-468.pdf))
- **Vector–Jacobian products.** Reverse mode with seed $\bar y=r$ computes $J_f^{\top}r$ without forming $J_f$; forward mode analogously computes $J_f v$. ([Baydin et al. 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-468/17-468.pdf))
- **Vanishing and exploding gradients.** The backward recursion multiplies one Jacobian per layer (or time step), so gradient magnitudes can shrink or grow exponentially with depth; Hochreiter's 1991 thesis identified this as an obstacle to training deep networks. ([Wikipedia: Vanishing gradient problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanishing_gradient_problem)) Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio make this precise for $x_t=W_{\rm rec}\,\sigma(x_{t-1})+W_{\rm in}u_t+b$ with $\|\mathrm{diag}(\sigma'(x_k))\|\le\gamma$ ($\gamma=1$ for $\tanh$, $\gamma=1/4$ for the sigmoid). The one-step Jacobian $W_{\rm rec}^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(\sigma'(x_k))$ has 2-norm at most $\|W_{\rm rec}^{\top}\|\,\gamma$, so if the largest singular value $\lambda_1$ of $W_{\rm rec}$ satisfies $\lambda_1<1/\gamma$, every one-step Jacobian has norm at most some $\eta<1$ and the contribution from $t-k$ steps back is bounded by $\eta^{t-k}$ times its size at step $t$: a sufficient condition for vanishing gradients. Inverting the argument, $\lambda_1>1/\gamma$ is a necessary (not sufficient) condition for exploding gradients. ([Pascanu et al. 2013](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/pascanu13.pdf))
- **Local convergence only.** Gradient descent driven by backpropagated gradients is guaranteed at best to reach a local minimum and can stall on plateaus; LeCun et al. argue local minima are not a major problem in many practical settings. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation))

### Examples
- **Scalar circuit.** For $f=(x+y)z$ at $x=-2,y=5,z=-4$: with $q=x+y=3$, $\partial f/\partial z=q=3$ and $\partial f/\partial x=\partial f/\partial y=z=-4$. Add gates pass the upstream gradient unchanged, multiply gates swap in the other input, and max gates route the gradient to the larger input. ([CS231n notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/))
- **Sigmoid gate.** Since $\sigma'(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$, treating the sigmoid as a single gate is more efficient and has fewer numerical issues than backpropagating through its primitive operations. ([CS231n notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/))
- **Backpropagation through time.** A recurrent network is unfolded into a deep feedforward network with one layer per time step, and backpropagation is applied to the unfolded graph; the vanishing-gradient problem affects both such unfolded recurrent networks and many-layered feedforward networks. ([Wikipedia: Vanishing gradient problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanishing_gradient_problem))

### History
The essence of the reverse mode appears in continuous time in the [Pontryagin Maximum Principle](node:Pontryagin%20Maximum%20Principle) (Rozonoer 1959; Boltyanskii et al. 1960) and in control theory (Bryson and Denham 1962; Bryson and Ho 1969). Linnainmaa (1970, 1976) is often cited as the first published description of the reverse mode; Werbos (1974) cast it in discrete time; Speelpenning (1980) gave the first automatic implementation. In machine learning it was reinvented several times, e.g. by Parker (1985), before Rumelhart et al. (1986) made it famous. ([Baydin et al. 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-468/17-468.pdf)) Kelley (1960) and Dreyfus (1962) gave related control-theory derivations, Werbos's application to multilayer perceptrons was published in 1982, and LeCun proposed an alternative form in his 1987 thesis. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation)) The 1986 paper is Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams, "Learning representations by back-propagating errors", *Nature* 323, 533–536. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/323533a0))

### Connections
- [Automatic Differentiation](node:Automatic%20Differentiation): backpropagation is reverse-mode AD on a network's computational graph.
- [Artificial Neural Networks](node:Artificial%20Neural%20Networks): the models whose gradients it computes.
- [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent) and [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent): the optimizers that consume the gradients.
- [Checkpointing for Automatic Differentiation](node:Checkpointing%20for%20Automatic%20Differentiation): the memory–recomputation trade-off.
- [Adjoint Sensitivity Methods](node:Adjoint%20Sensitivity%20Methods): the continuous-time analogue, used for [Neural ODEs](node:Neural%20ODEs).
- [Recurrent Neural Networks](node:Recurrent%20Neural%20Networks): trained by backpropagation through time; prone to vanishing gradients.
- [Residual Networks](node:Residual%20Networks): identity paths that ease gradient flow.
- [Hypergradients](node:Hypergradients): nested differentiation through a training procedure.
- [Pontryagin Maximum Principle](node:Pontryagin%20Maximum%20Principle): the continuous-time optimal-control ancestor of the reverse mode.
- [Predictive Coding](node:Predictive%20Coding): a candidate biologically plausible approximation to backpropagated errors.

### Common pitfalls
- **Backprop is not the optimizer.** It computes gradients only; the update rule (SGD, momentum, Adam) is separate. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Forgetting to accumulate.** When a variable feeds several branches, gradients from each branch must be summed (`+=`), following the multivariable chain rule. ([CS231n notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/))
- **Input scaling changes gradient scale.** Multiply gates make weight gradients proportional to input magnitudes, so rescaling inputs by $1000$ scales weight gradients by $1000$ and may require a new learning rate. ([CS231n notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/))
- **Differentiability assumptions.** The method needs activation derivatives known at design time; nondifferentiable points (e.g. ReLU at $0$) use a conventional value, usually $0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation); [d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/mlp.html))

### Open problems
- **Memory-efficient reverse mode.** Baydin et al. state that improving the storage requirements of reverse-mode implementations, via checkpointing and data-flow analysis, "is an active area of research", and name nested AD for exact hypergradients as an important direction for future work. ([Baydin et al. 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-468/17-468.pdf))
- **Does the brain learn by something like backpropagation?** Backprop has long been seen as biologically problematic; Lillicrap et al. propose that cortical feedback connections may induce activity differences that locally approximate the required error signals, which remains a hypothesis. ([Lillicrap et al. 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41583-020-0277-3?error=cookies_not_supported&code=58a7fe0e-7669-4b87-bb17-5d63b026afa4))
- **Backprop-free training.** Hinton's Forward-Forward algorithm replaces the backward pass with two forward passes on positive and negative data, each layer optimizing a local "goodness" objective; it is presented as preliminary work that merits further study. ([Hinton 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13345))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Backpropagation, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation): matrix formulation, history, limitations.
- **Learn:** [CS231n: Backpropagation, Intuitions](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/): computational graphs, gate patterns, vectorized gradients.
- **Primary:** [Baydin, Pearlmutter, Radul, Siskind, Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: a Survey (JMLR 2018)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v18/17-468.html): forward and reverse modes, costs, history.
- **Primary:** [Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams, Learning representations by back-propagating errors (Nature 1986)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/323533a0): the paper that popularized backpropagation.
- **Further reading:** [Griewank and Walther, Evaluating Derivatives, 2nd ed. (SIAM 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898717761): the standard monograph on algorithmic differentiation.
