## Reference
### Overview
A Banach space is a normed vector space that is complete for the metric $d(x,y)=\|y-x\|$: every Cauchy sequence converges. Banach, Hahn and Helly studied the notion in 1920–1922; Fréchet coined the name "Banach space". Completeness is equivalent to the statement that every absolutely convergent series converges, and it is unchanged under passage to an equivalent norm; on a finite-dimensional space all norms are equivalent, so the theory is genuinely infinite-dimensional. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

Banach spaces carry the four basic principles of linear analysis (Hahn–Banach, open mapping, closed graph, uniform boundedness), which makes them the default setting for operator theory and for the function spaces of analysis, such as [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces), $C(K)$ and [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces). A first course covering normed spaces, completeness, Hahn–Banach, Baire-category arguments, $L^p$ theory, and compact operators on [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) is MIT 18.102. ([MIT OCW 18.102](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/pages/lecture-notes-and-readings/))

The research area "Banach space theory" (the isomorphic and isometric geometry of these spaces) studies which subspaces, quotients, bases and operators a space must have. Gowers and Maurey (1992) constructed a Banach space with no infinite unconditional basic sequence, and Argyros and Haydon (2009) a hereditarily indecomposable space on which every operator is a scalar multiple of the identity plus a compact operator. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space); [Gowers–Maurey, arXiv:math/9205204](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9205204); [Argyros–Haydon, arXiv:0903.3921](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3921))

### Formal definition
A **norm** on a real or complex vector space $X$ is a map $\|\cdot\|:X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\|x\|=0\iff x=0$, $\|\lambda x\|=|\lambda|\,\|x\|$, and $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$. $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ is a **Banach space** if every sequence with $\|x_n-x_m\|\to0$ has a limit in $X$. Two norms are **equivalent** if $c\|x\|_1\le\|x\|_2\le C\|x\|_1$ for constants $0<c\le C$; this happens exactly when they induce the same topology. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

The dual $X'$ is the space of continuous linear functionals with $\|f\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|f(x)|$. $X$ is **reflexive** if the canonical map $X\to X''$ is onto. A **Schauder basis** is a sequence $(e_n)$ such that every $x$ has a unique expansion $x=\sum_n x_ne_n$ converging in norm. $X$ has the **approximation property** (AP) if every compact operator into $X$ is a norm limit of finite-rank operators. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space); [Wikipedia: Approximation property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_property))

### Key results
- **Hahn–Banach theorem.** Let $Y$ be a subspace of a real or complex vector space $X$, $p$ a sublinear functional, and $f$ linear on $Y$ with $\operatorname{Re} f\le p$ on $Y$. Then $f$ extends to a linear $F$ on $X$ with $\operatorname{Re}F\le p$. Hence continuous functionals on subspaces extend without increase of norm, and for each $x$ there is $f\in X'$ with $\|f\|\le1$ and $f(x)=\|x\|$. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Open mapping, closed graph, uniform boundedness.** A continuous linear surjection between Banach spaces is open, so a continuous linear bijection has a continuous inverse. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ between Banach spaces is continuous iff its graph is closed. If $X$ is Banach, $Y$ normed and $\mathcal F$ a family of bounded operators with $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|Tx\|<\infty$ for each $x$, then $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|T\|<\infty$. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Reflexivity criteria.** $X$ is reflexive iff its closed unit ball is weakly compact; iff every bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence (Eberlein–Šmulian); iff every $f\in X'$ attains its norm on the unit ball (James). Uniformly convex spaces are reflexive (Milman–Pettis). James's space $J$ is isometrically isomorphic to $J''$ yet not reflexive, with $\dim J''/J=1$. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Dvoretzky's theorem.** For every $k\in\mathbb N$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N(k,\varepsilon)$ such that every normed space of dimension $N(k,\varepsilon)$ has a $k$-dimensional subspace $E$ with Banach–Mazur distance $d(E,\ell_2^k)\le1+\varepsilon$. Milman's 1971 concentration-of-measure proof gives $k\ge C(\varepsilon)\log N$ for every $N$-dimensional space. ([Wikipedia: Dvoretzky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvoretzky%27s_theorem))
- **Enflo's theorem.** There is a separable Banach space without the approximation property, hence without a Schauder basis. Enflo published it in 1973; Szankowski later showed that $B(\ell_2)$ fails the AP. ([Wikipedia: Approximation property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_property))
- **Lindenstrauss–Tzafriri complemented subspace theorem.** A Banach space in which every closed subspace is complemented is isomorphic to a Hilbert space. Kwapień characterized spaces isomorphic to a Hilbert space by parallelogram-type inequalities averaged over signs. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Gowers–Maurey and the Gowers dichotomy.** There is a Banach space containing no infinite unconditional basic sequence. Every infinite-dimensional Banach space contains either a subspace with an unconditional basis or a hereditarily indecomposable subspace. As a consequence, a space isomorphic to all its infinite-dimensional closed subspaces is isomorphic to $\ell_2$ (Banach's homogeneous space problem). ([Gowers–Maurey, arXiv:math/9205204](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9205204); [Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Argyros–Haydon.** There is a hereditarily indecomposable Banach space $X$ with $X^*\cong\ell_1$ on which every bounded operator has the form $\lambda I+K$ with $K$ compact. This solved the scalar-plus-compact problem. ([Argyros–Haydon, arXiv:0903.3921](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3921))
- **Topological classification.** By the Anderson–Kadec theorem, all infinite-dimensional separable Banach spaces are homeomorphic, so the theory is about linear (or Lipschitz) structure, not topology. The Mazur–Ulam theorem states that a surjective isometry between real Banach spaces is affine. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

### Examples
- $\ell_p$ and $L^p(\mu)$ for $1\le p\le\infty$, $c_0$, and $C(K)$ with the sup norm. $L^p$ is reflexive for $1<p<\infty$, while $c_0$, $\ell_1$, $L^1[0,1]$ and $C[0,1]$ are not. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- Universality: every Banach space embeds isometrically in some $C(K)$, and every separable Banach space is isomorphic to a quotient $\ell_1/M$. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- The disk algebra $A(\mathbb D)$ has a Schauder basis (Bočkarev, 1974, using the Franklin system), which settled a question open for more than forty years. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

### History
Enflo's 1973 counterexample answered a question that Mazur had posed in 1936, offering a live goose as the prize, which Enflo received in 1972. Much of the early theory of the AP and of tensor norms is due to Grothendieck (1955). Pisier (1983) disproved Grothendieck's conjecture that the projective and injective tensor norms on $X\otimes X$ always differ for infinite-dimensional $X$. ([Wikipedia: Approximation property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_property); [Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

Gowers and Maurey's unconditional basic sequence paper was submitted in May 1992. Argyros and Haydon's scalar-plus-compact space appeared on arXiv in March 2009. ([Gowers–Maurey, arXiv:math/9205204](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9205204); [Argyros–Haydon, arXiv:0903.3921](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3921))

### Connections
- [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces): a Banach space is a vector space with a complete norm.
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): completeness generalizes the completeness of $\mathbb R$.
- [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces): the norm metric; completeness and Baire category drive the open mapping and uniform boundedness theorems.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): Banach spaces whose norm satisfies the parallelogram law; characterized isomorphically by Lindenstrauss–Tzafriri and Kwapień.
- [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces): the main family of examples, with duality $(L^p)'=L^q$.
- [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem): contraction mappings on complete metric spaces, used constantly in Banach spaces.
- [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory): spectra of bounded operators on Banach spaces.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces): Banach spaces of weakly differentiable functions used in PDE.
- [Dual Vector Space](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space): the algebraic dual, of which $X'$ is the continuous part.
- [MSC 46 - Functional analysis](node:MSC%2046%20-%20Functional%20analysis) and [MSC 46Bxx - Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices](node:MSC%2046Bxx%20-%20Normed%20linear%20spaces%20and%20Banach%20spaces;%20Banach%20lattices): the MSC home of the topic.

### Common pitfalls
- Reflexivity is not the same as $X\cong X''$: James's space is isometric to its bidual by a map other than the canonical embedding, yet it is not reflexive. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- A separable space need not have a Schauder basis (Enflo), although every space with a basis is separable and has the AP. ([Wikipedia: Approximation property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_property))
- Banach–Alaoglu gives weak* compactness of the dual ball; it is metrizable only when $X$ is separable, so sequential compactness can fail otherwise. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

### Open problems
- **Separable quotient problem (open).** Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have an infinite-dimensional separable quotient? Ferrando–Kąkol–López-Pellicer–Śliwa attribute the question to Mazur (1932). Known positive cases include reflexive and weakly compactly generated spaces, all dual spaces (Argyros–Dodos–Kanellopoulos), and spaces $X$ where $X$ or $X^*$ contains $c_0$ or $\ell_1$. By Saxon–Wilansky the problem is equivalent to $X$ containing a dense non-barrelled subspace. ([Ferrando et al., arXiv:1709.09646](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09646); [ar5iv text](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1709.09646))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space): long survey of the basic theorems, reflexivity, bases, tensor products, and classification results.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102 Introduction to Functional Analysis](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/): lecture notes and videos on normed spaces, Baire category, Hahn–Banach, $L^p$, and compact operators. [Garrett, Functional Analysis course notes (UMN)](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/fun/): graduate notes including Banach spaces and Banach–Steinhaus.
- **Primary:** [Gowers and Maurey, The unconditional basic sequence problem (arXiv:math/9205204)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9205204): a Banach space with no infinite unconditional basic sequence. [Argyros and Haydon (arXiv:0903.3921)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3921): the scalar-plus-compact solution. [Ferrando et al., On the separable quotient problem (arXiv:1709.09646)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09646): survey of the main open problem.
- **Further reading:** [Albiac and Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory, GTM, Springer 2016](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-31557-7): graduate text (GTM). [Lindenstrauss and Tzafriri, Classical Banach Spaces I and II, Springer Classics 1996](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-53294-2): two-volume monograph on sequence spaces and function spaces.
references.Bayesian Inference:
## Reference
### Overview
Bayesian inference treats unknown parameters and hypotheses as random quantities and updates a prior distribution over them into a posterior distribution using [Bayes' Theorem](node:Bayes'%20Theorem): the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior. Predictions integrate over the posterior rather than plugging in a single estimate, and competing models are compared by their posterior probabilities ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)).

The approach goes back to Bayes and Laplace, was called "inverse probability" in its early uniform-prior form, and was largely displaced by frequentist methods after the 1920s; it later split into objective and subjective schools ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)). Its large-scale use followed the arrival of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods in the late twentieth century, and the twenty-first century added pseudo-marginal MCMC, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, [sequential Monte Carlo](node:Sequential%20Monte%20Carlo), and approximate methods ([Martin, Frazier, Robert 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.00646)).

The theory has two layers. Within a model, Bayesian updating is exact conditioning, and conjugate families make it closed-form ([MIT 18.05](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class15-prep.pdf)). Viewed from outside, as a frequentist procedure, its behaviour is described by asymptotic results: posterior normality in regular parametric models, and a more delicate picture in nonparametric and high-dimensional models ([Wikipedia: BvM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93von_Mises_theorem); [Castillo and Nickl](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.2484)).

### Formal definition
Let data $X=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ have density $p(X\mid\theta)$ and let the parameter have prior $p(\theta\mid\alpha)$ with hyperparameter $\alpha$. The posterior is
$$p(\theta\mid X,\alpha)=\frac{p(X\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid\alpha)}{p(X\mid\alpha)},\qquad p(X\mid\alpha)=\int p(X\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid\alpha)\,d\theta,$$
where the marginal likelihood (evidence) $p(X\mid\alpha)$ must be positive. For i.i.d. data $p(X\mid\theta)=\prod_k p(x_k\mid\theta)$, and updating one observation at a time gives the same posterior as a single batch update ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)).

The posterior predictive distribution of a new observation is
$$p(\tilde x\mid X,\alpha)=\int p(\tilde x\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid X,\alpha)\,d\theta,$$
and the prior predictive replaces the posterior by the prior ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)). For models $M_1,M_2$ of equal prior probability, the ratio of posterior probabilities equals the Bayes factor $p(X\mid M_1)/p(X\mid M_2)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)).

**Conjugacy.** If the prior belongs to a parametrized family and, for a given likelihood, the posterior always lies in the same family, the family is conjugate to that likelihood ([MIT 18.05](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class15-prep.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Bernstein–von Mises theorem.** Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^k\}$ be well specified with $X_1,\dots,X_n$ i.i.d. $P_{\theta_0}$; assume densities exist, the Fisher information $I(\theta_0)$ is nonsingular, the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$, uniformly consistent tests separate $\theta_0$ from $\{\|\theta-\theta_0\|>\varepsilon\}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, and the prior has a continuous positive density at $\theta_0$. Then, with $\hat\theta_n$ an asymptotically efficient estimator such as the maximum likelihood estimator under its usual regularity conditions,
$$\big\|\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X_1,\dots,X_n)-N\big(\hat\theta_n,\tfrac1n I(\theta_0)^{-1}\big)\big\|_{TV}\to0$$
in $P_{\theta_0}$-probability ([Wikipedia: BvM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93von_Mises_theorem); [CMU 36-705](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~larry/=stat705/Lecture24.pdf)).
- **Freedman's negative result.** For a countably infinite sample space, Freedman (1965) showed that for a dense set of priors the Bernstein–von Mises conclusion fails and almost surely there is no asymptotic convergence; the result relies on allowing a very broad range of priors ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference); [Wikipedia: BvM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93von_Mises_theorem)).
- **Misspecification.** If the model is misspecified, the posterior is still asymptotically Gaussian with the correct centring, but its covariance need not be the inverse Fisher information, so credible sets are not confidence sets of the same level ([Wikipedia: BvM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93von_Mises_theorem)).
- **Nonparametric Bernstein–von Mises (Castillo–Nickl 2014).** On suitable multiscale spaces, BvM theorems hold for a range of priors in Gaussian nonparametric regression and i.i.d. density estimation; consequences include Donsker- and Kolmogorov–Smirnov-type results for posterior CDFs and multiscale credible bands that are optimal frequentist confidence bands ([Castillo and Nickl](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.2484)).
- **Normal–normal and beta–binomial conjugacy.** For $x\sim N(\theta,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2$ known and prior $\theta\sim N(\mu_{\rm prior},\sigma^2_{\rm prior})$, the posterior is normal with $a=1/\sigma^2_{\rm prior}$, $b=1/\sigma^2$, $\mu_{\rm post}=(a\mu_{\rm prior}+bx)/(a+b)$, $\sigma^2_{\rm post}=1/(a+b)$. A $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ prior with $x$ successes in a $\mathrm{binomial}(N,\theta)$ experiment gives a $\mathrm{Beta}(a+x,\,b+N-x)$ posterior ([MIT 18.05](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class15-prep.pdf)).

### Examples
- **Coin with a beta prior.** A $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ prior updated by a Bernoulli success becomes $\mathrm{Beta}(a+1,b)$ and by a failure $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b+1)$; the same family is also conjugate to the geometric likelihood ([MIT 18.05](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class15-prep.pdf)).
- **Normal measurement.** With prior $N(0,1)$, likelihood variance $4/9$ and one observation $x=6.5$, the formulas give $a=1$, $b=9/4$, $\sigma^2_{\rm post}=4/13$ and $\mu_{\rm post}=4.5$, so the posterior is narrower than both prior and likelihood and its mean lies between the prior mean and the datum ([MIT 18.05](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class15-prep.pdf)).
- **Intractable likelihoods.** When the likelihood cannot be evaluated, simulation-based inference approximates the posterior, likelihood, or likelihood ratio from simulator draws ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)).

### History
Thomas Bayes (1701–1761) showed how to place probabilistic bounds on an unknown event; Pierre-Simon Laplace introduced the theorem now named after Bayes and applied it widely, using uniform priors justified by the principle of insufficient reason ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)). Bayesian computation runs from Bayes's one-dimensional integral of 1763 through Laplace, Metropolis and co-authors, Hammersley and Handscomb, and Hastings to the MCMC revolution ([Martin, Frazier, Robert 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.00646)). The twenty-first century added approximate methods for models with unavailable likelihoods, high dimension, or very large data ([Martin, Frazier, Robert 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10342)).

### Connections
- [Bayes' Theorem](node:Bayes'%20Theorem): the update rule.
- [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): priors, likelihoods and posteriors are distributions.
- [Maximum A Posteriori Estimation](node:Maximum%20A%20Posteriori%20Estimation): the posterior mode as a point estimate.
- [Maximum Likelihood Estimation](node:Maximum%20Likelihood%20Estimation): the BvM theorem centres the posterior at an efficient estimator such as the MLE.
- [Fisher Information](node:Fisher%20Information): sets the asymptotic posterior covariance.
- [Markov Chain Monte Carlo](node:Markov%20Chain%20Monte%20Carlo): the main tool for sampling posteriors.
- [Variational Inference](node:Variational%20Inference): optimization-based posterior approximation.
- [Approximate Bayesian Computation](node:Approximate%20Bayesian%20Computation) and [Simulation-Based Inference](node:Simulation-Based%20Inference): inference without tractable likelihoods.
- [Gaussian Processes](node:Gaussian%20Processes): Bayesian nonparametric priors over functions.
- [Bayesian Neural Networks](node:Bayesian%20Neural%20Networks): posterior inference over network weights.
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing): the frequentist counterpart of Bayes-factor model comparison.

### Common pitfalls
- **Cromwell's rule.** A prior probability of $0$ (or $1$) cannot be changed by any evidence: if $P(M)=0$ then $P(M\mid E)=0$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)).
- **"The data swamp the prior."** In finite but large problems convergence may be slow, and the prior's influence need not wash out quickly ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)).
- **Credible sets are not confidence sets.** In nonparametric models the BvM theorem usually fails (the Dirichlet process is an exception), and under misspecification posterior spread can be wrong ([Wikipedia: BvM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93von_Mises_theorem)).
- **Plug-in prediction.** Predicting with a MAP or maximum-likelihood point estimate ignores parameter uncertainty and can underestimate predictive variance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference)).

### Open problems
- **Scalable Bayesian deep learning.** Papamarkou et al. identify posterior computation and prior specification as the main obstacles for Bayesian [deep learning](node:Deep%20Learning), call demonstrating that it works at practical cost in modern settings "one of the most important problems that remains to be addressed," and describe achieving time efficiency, memory efficiency, and high model utility (predictive performance and uncertainty calibration) simultaneously as "the grand challenge" and "the holy grail" of approximate Bayesian inference ([Papamarkou et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00809v5); [PMLR](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/papamarkou24b.html)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bayesian inference (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference): definitions, prediction, model comparison, asymptotics, history.
- **Reference:** [Bernstein–von Mises theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93von_Mises_theorem): precise statement and failure modes.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.05, Conjugate priors: beta and normal](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class15-prep.pdf): worked conjugate updating.
- **Primary:** [Castillo and Nickl, On the Bernstein–von Mises phenomenon for nonparametric Bayes procedures](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.2484): nonparametric BvM theory.
- **Primary:** [Martin, Frazier, Robert, Approximating Bayes in the 21st Century](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10342): review of modern approximate Bayesian computation.
- **Further reading:** [Ghosal and van der Vaart, Fundamentals of Nonparametric Bayesian Inference (CUP, 2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/fundamentals-of-nonparametric-bayesian-inference/C96325101025D308C9F31F4470DEA2E8): graduate text on priors, computation and posterior asymptotics.
references.Beta Function:
## Reference
### Overview
The beta function is Euler's integral of the first kind, $B(a,b)=\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt$. Its basic identity writes it as a quotient of gamma functions, $B(a,b)=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)$, so integrals of endpoint-weighted powers can be evaluated through factorial-like algebra. The integral converges when both real parts are positive. ([DLMF §5.12](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.12); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function))

It is symmetric in its arguments, has several equivalent integral representations (over $(0,\infty)$, over $(0,\pi/2)$ with trigonometric weights, and a Pochhammer contour form that continues $B$ analytically to all complex parameters), and is related to binomial coefficients, to the incomplete beta function $I_x(a,b)$, and to the beta distribution of probability theory, where $B(\alpha,\beta)$ is the normalizing constant of the density. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function); [Wikipedia: Beta distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_distribution))

The $n$-dimensional generalization is the Selberg integral, which has a closed product form in gamma functions and has played a role in random matrix theory and the Macdonald conjectures. ([Wikipedia: Selberg integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_integral); [Forrester–Warnaar](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.3981))

### Formal definition
For $\Re a>0$ and $\Re b>0$,
$$B(a,b)=\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}.$$
Both endpoint conditions are needed for convergence. ([DLMF 5.12.1](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.12))

The incomplete beta function is $B_x(a,b)=\int_0^x t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}dt$ and the regularized form is $I_x(a,b)=B_x(a,b)/B(a,b)$; at $x=1$ the incomplete function equals the complete one. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function))

### Key results
- **Symmetry and alternative representations.** For $\Re a,\Re b>0$: $B(a,b)=B(b,a)$ (substitute $u=1-t$), $B(a,b)=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2a-1}\theta\cos^{2b-1}\theta\,d\theta$ (substitute $t=\sin^2\theta$), and $B(a,b)=\int_0^\infty \frac{t^{a-1}}{(1+t)^{a+b}}\,dt$. ([DLMF 5.12.2–5.12.3](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.12); [Rozman notes, eqs. 19–23](https://www.phys.uconn.edu/~rozman/Courses/P2400_25S/downloads/eulers-integrals.pdf))
- **Beta–gamma identity (proof sketch).** For $x,y>0$, write $\Gamma(x)=2\int_0^\infty u^{2x-1}e^{-u^2}du$. Then $\Gamma(x)\Gamma(y)=4\iint_{u,v>0}u^{2x-1}v^{2y-1}e^{-(u^2+v^2)}du\,dv$, writing the product of the two integrals as a double integral. Polar coordinates $u=r\cos\theta$, $v=r\sin\theta$ factor this as $\Gamma(x+y)\cdot 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2y-1}\theta\cos^{2x-1}\theta\,d\theta=\Gamma(x+y)B(x,y)$. ([Rozman notes, eqs. 24–27](https://www.phys.uconn.edu/~rozman/Courses/P2400_25S/downloads/eulers-integrals.pdf)) For nonnegative integrands on $\sigma$-finite spaces, [Tonelli's Theorem](node:Tonelli's%20Theorem) guarantees that the double integral equals the iterated integrals. ([Wikipedia: Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- **Pochhammer contour and analytic continuation.** For all $a,b\in\mathbb C$, with $P$ the Pochhammer double-loop contour around $0$ and $1$ based in $(0,1)$, $\int_P t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}dt=-4e^{\pi i(a+b)}\sin(\pi a)\sin(\pi b)\,B(a,b)$. This contour integral gives the analytic continuation of $B$ to all complex parameters. ([DLMF 5.12.12](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.12); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function))
- **Asymptotics.** As $x,y\to\infty$, $B(x,y)\sim\sqrt{2\pi}\,x^{x-1/2}y^{y-1/2}/(x+y)^{x+y-1/2}$; for fixed $y$ and large $x$, $B(x,y)\sim\Gamma(y)x^{-y}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function))
- **Selberg integral.** For $\Re\alpha>0$, $\Re\beta>0$, $\Re\gamma>-\min\{1/n,\Re\alpha/(n-1),\Re\beta/(n-1)\}$,
$$S_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=\int_{[0,1]^n}\prod_i t_i^{\alpha-1}(1-t_i)^{\beta-1}\prod_{i<j}|t_i-t_j|^{2\gamma}\,dt=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+j\gamma)\Gamma(\beta+j\gamma)\Gamma(1+(j+1)\gamma)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+(n+j-1)\gamma)\Gamma(1+\gamma)}.$$
For $n=1$ this is the beta integral. ([Forrester–Warnaar, (1.1)–(1.2)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.3981); [Wikipedia: Selberg integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_integral))
- **Aomoto and Macdonald–Opdam.** Aomoto (1987) proved that multiplying the Selberg integrand by $\prod_{i=1}^k t_i$ multiplies the value by $\prod_{j=1}^k\frac{\alpha+(n-j)\gamma}{\alpha+\beta+(2n-j-1)\gamma}$, under the same conditions. Mehta's integral follows from Selberg's by setting $\alpha=\beta$, changing variables, and letting $\alpha\to\infty$; Macdonald's extension to all finite [root systems](node:Root%20Systems) was proved uniformly by Opdam for crystallographic reflection groups. ([Wikipedia: Selberg integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_integral))

### Examples
For positive integers $m,n$, $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$ gives $B(m,n)=(m-1)!(n-1)!/(m+n-1)!$, and consequently $\binom nk=\frac1{(n+1)B(n-k+1,k+1)}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function))

Taking $a=b=\tfrac12$ in the sine form gives $B(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)=\pi$, hence $\Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi$. The area of $x^4+y^4=1$ is $4\int_0^1(1-x^4)^{1/4}dx=B(\tfrac14,\tfrac54)$ after $u=x^4$, which equals $\Gamma(\tfrac14)^2/(2\sqrt\pi)$. ([Rozman notes, Examples](https://www.phys.uconn.edu/~rozman/Courses/P2400_25S/downloads/eulers-integrals.pdf))

In probability, the beta density on $[0,1]$ is proportional to $x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}$ with $B(\alpha,\beta)$ as the normalizing constant; its mean is $\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$, and it is the conjugate prior of the Bernoulli and binomial distributions. Its CDF is $I_x(\alpha,\beta)$. ([Wikipedia: Beta distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_distribution); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function))

### History
Euler and Legendre studied the function, and Binet gave it its name. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function)) Atle Selberg published the multidimensional generalization in 1944; it became prominent only decades later after a question from Bombieri, when it was used to prove a random matrix conjecture and cases of the Macdonald conjectures. ([Wikipedia: Selberg integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_integral); [Forrester–Warnaar](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.3981))

### Connections
- [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function): the beta function is defined through and evaluated by it.
- [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus): Euler integrals and substitutions.
- [Fubini's Theorem](node:Fubini's%20Theorem): Tonelli's form justifies the double integral in the beta–gamma proof.
- [Hypergeometric Functions](node:Hypergeometric%20Functions): Euler's integral representation of ${}_2F_1$ is a beta integral.
- [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions): the beta function is a basic member of the family.
- [Stirling's Formula](node:Stirling's%20Formula): underlies the asymptotics of $B(x,y)$.
- [Binomial Theorem](node:Binomial%20Theorem): $B(m,n)$ gives reciprocal binomial coefficients.
- [Laplace and Mellin Transforms](node:Laplace%20and%20Mellin%20Transforms): the $(0,\infty)$ form is a Mellin-type integral.

### Common pitfalls
- The integral definition needs $\Re a,\Re b>0$; the gamma quotient continues $B$ beyond that region, but the integral then diverges. ([DLMF 5.12.1](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.12))
- $B_x(a,b)$ is not normalized; the probability CDF is the regularized $I_x(a,b)$, with $I_1=1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function))
- Selberg's condition on $\gamma$ is not just positivity of the real parts of $\alpha,\beta$; the lower bound on $\Re\gamma$ must hold too. ([Wikipedia: Selberg integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_integral))

### Open problems
- **Finite-field Kadell integral.** Forrester and Warnaar state that finding and proving a finite-field analogue of Kadell's integral (a Selberg-type integral with a Jack polynomial insertion) is an open problem, settled only in the 2-variable case. ([Forrester–Warnaar survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0710.3981))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [DLMF §5.12](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.12): beta integrals and Pochhammer contour. [Wikipedia: Beta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function): properties and history.
- **Learn:** [Rozman, Euler's integrals (UConn)](https://www.phys.uconn.edu/~rozman/Courses/P2400_25S/downloads/eulers-integrals.pdf): course notes proving the beta–gamma identity with polar coordinates.
- **Primary:** [Forrester and Warnaar, The importance of the Selberg integral](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.3981): survey of the Selberg integral and its generalizations.
- **Further reading:** Andrews, Askey and Roy, *Special Functions* (Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications 71, CUP, 1999; [review by Beukers, Bull. LMS](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-the-london-mathematical-society/article/special-functions-encyclopedia-of-mathematics-and-its-applications-71-by-george-e-andrews-richard-askey-and-ranjan-roy-664-pp-5500-us8500-isbn-0521623219-cambridge-university-press-1999/005D757B7C74672E7285CF4CCE8FDF23)): Chapter 8 gives a proof of Aomoto's integral. ([Wikipedia: Selberg integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_integral))
references.Bias–Variance Tradeoff:
## Reference
### Overview
The bias–variance decomposition writes the expected prediction error of a learning algorithm, averaged over random training sets, as a sum of three terms. Bias measures how far the average learned predictor is from the expected label. Variance measures how much the learned predictor fluctuates from one training set to another. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote12.html)) Noise, the irreducible error, forms a lower bound on the expected error on unseen samples. The tradeoff is that it is typically impossible to lower bias and variance simultaneously. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias%E2%80%93variance_tradeoff))

In practice the decomposition diagnoses two regimes. High variance shows up as training error well below test error and is treated with more data, a simpler model, or bagging. High bias shows up as high training error and is treated with a richer model, more features, or boosting. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote12.html)) Regularization of linear models lowers variance at the cost of bias, and dimensionality reduction or feature selection reduces variance. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias%E2%80%93variance_tradeoff))

The classical U-shaped test-error curve predicted by the tradeoff conflicts with modern practice: very large models that interpolate their training data often generalize well. Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal reconcile the two with a "double descent" curve, in which performance improves again once capacity passes the point of interpolation. ([Belkin et al., arXiv:1812.11118](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118)) Measured directly in neural networks, both bias and variance can decrease as the number of parameters grows. ([Neal et al., arXiv:1810.08591](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08591))

### Formal definition
Let $D\sim P^n$ be a training set, $h_D$ the predictor learned from it, and $(x,y)\sim P$ a test point. Define the expected label $\bar y(x)=\mathbb{E}_{y\mid x}[y]$ and the expected predictor $\bar h=\mathbb{E}_{D\sim P^n}[h_D]$. Under squared loss, the expected test error decomposes as
$$\mathbb{E}_{x,y,D}\big[(h_D(x)-y)^2\big]=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{x,D}\big[(h_D(x)-\bar h(x))^2\big]}_{\text{variance}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\big[(\bar y(x)-y)^2\big]}_{\text{noise}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_x\big[(\bar h(x)-\bar y(x))^2\big]}_{\text{bias}^2}.$$
Both cross terms vanish because $\mathbb{E}_D[h_D(x)]-\bar h(x)=0$ and $\mathbb{E}_{y\mid x}[\bar y(x)-y]=0$. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote12.html)) In the model $y=f(x)+\varepsilon$ with zero-mean noise of variance $\sigma^2$ independent of $x$, this reads $\mathbb{E}[(y-\hat f(x;D))^2]=\mathrm{Bias}^2+\mathrm{Var}+\sigma^2$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias%E2%80%93variance_tradeoff))

**Domingos's definitions for an arbitrary loss $L$.** Let $y_*$ be the optimal prediction, minimizing $\mathbb{E}_t[L(t,y_*)]$, and let the main prediction be $y_m=\arg\min_{y'}\mathbb{E}_D[L(y,y')]$, which is the mean under squared loss, the median under absolute loss, and the mode under zero-one loss. Then
$$B(x)=L(y_*,y_m),\qquad V(x)=\mathbb{E}_D[L(y_m,y)],\qquad N(x)=\mathbb{E}_t[L(t,y_*)].$$
([Domingos 2000](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~pedrod/papers/aaai00.pdf))

### Key results
- **Unified decomposition (Domingos).** For certain losses, $\mathbb{E}_{D,t}[L(t,y)]=c_1N(x)+B(x)+c_2V(x)$. **Theorem 1:** this holds for squared loss with $c_1=c_2=1$, recovering the standard decomposition of Geman et al. **Theorem 2:** it holds for zero-one loss in two-class problems with $c_1=2P_D(y=y_*)-1$, $c_2=1$ if $y_m=y_*$, and $c_2=-1$ otherwise. So variance adds to the error on unbiased examples and subtracts from it on biased ones. ([Domingos 2000](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~pedrod/papers/aaai00.pdf))
- **Exact asymptotics of ridgeless regression (Hastie, Montanari, Rosset, Tibshirani).** Assume $y=x^\top\beta+\varepsilon$ with noise variance $\sigma^2$, features $x$ with i.i.d. entries of zero mean, unit variance, and a finite moment of order $4+\eta$, and $\|\beta\|_2^2=r^2$. Then for the minimum-$\ell_2$-norm least-squares estimator, as $n,p\to\infty$ with $p/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$, almost surely the bias tends to $r^2(1-1/\gamma)$ and the variance to $\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$ for $\gamma>1$. The risk tends to
$$R(\gamma)\to\begin{cases}\sigma^2\dfrac{\gamma}{1-\gamma},&\gamma<1,\\[2mm] r^2\Big(1-\dfrac1\gamma\Big)+\sigma^2\dfrac1{\gamma-1},&\gamma>1.\end{cases}$$
On $(0,1)$ there is no bias and variance increases with $\gamma$. On $(1,\infty)$ bias increases and variance decreases with $\gamma$. When $\mathrm{SNR}=r^2/\sigma^2>1$, the risk has a local minimum at $\gamma=\sqrt{\mathrm{SNR}}/(\sqrt{\mathrm{SNR}}-1)$ and beats the null risk $r^2$ iff $\gamma>\mathrm{SNR}/(\mathrm{SNR}-1)$. ([Hastie et al., arXiv:1903.08560](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08560))
- **Double descent.** Across a range of models and datasets, test error first follows the classical U-shape and then decreases again when capacity passes the point at which the model interpolates the training data. ([Belkin et al., arXiv:1812.11118](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118))
- **Variance can fall with width.** In neural networks both bias and variance can decrease as the number of parameters grows, and test error keeps decreasing in wider networks. A new decomposition of the variance separates the effects of optimization and of data sampling. ([Neal et al., arXiv:1810.08591](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08591))

### Examples
- **$k$-nearest neighbours.** The bias–variance decomposition of $k$-NN regression has a closed form in which bias rises monotonically with $k$ and variance falls as $k$ grows. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias%E2%80%93variance_tradeoff))
- **Ensembles.** Boosting combines high-bias weak learners to reduce bias, and bagging averages strong learners to reduce variance. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias%E2%80%93variance_tradeoff))
- **Zero-one loss.** If $0.6$ of the classifiers trained on different training sets predict class 1 and $0.4$ predict class 0, the main prediction under zero-one loss is class 1. Under squared loss, the main prediction of $Y=\{1,1,2,2\}$ is $1.5$, which no individual model outputs. ([Domingos 2000](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~pedrod/papers/aaai00.pdf))

### History
Geman, Bienenstock and Doursat's "Neural Networks and the Bias/Variance Dilemma" appeared in Neural Computation in 1992. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1162/neco.1992.4.1.1)) They argued that generic abilities such as object recognition cannot be learned from scratch with model-free methods, which would need impractically large training sets, so some structure must be built in. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias%E2%80%93variance_tradeoff)) The decomposition was developed for squared loss. Kong and Dietterich, Breiman, Kohavi and Wolpert, Tibshirani, and Friedman then proposed versions for zero-one loss in the 1990s, and Domingos's 2000 unified definition reduces to the squared-loss case and nearly to Kong and Dietterich's. ([Domingos 2000](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~pedrod/papers/aaai00.pdf)) Later work revisited the classical picture through double descent and through measurements of bias and variance in wide networks. ([Belkin et al., arXiv:1812.11118](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118); [Neal et al., arXiv:1810.08591](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08591))

### Connections
- [Supervised Learning](node:Supervised%20Learning): the setting whose test error the decomposition analyses.
- [Expectation and Variance](node:Expectation%20and%20Variance): the decomposition is the variance identity applied over random training sets.
- [Regularization](node:Regularization): trades a little bias for a reduction in variance.
- [Cross-Validation](node:Cross-Validation): the empirical way to locate the best point on the tradeoff.
- [Decision Trees and Ensembles](node:Decision%20Trees%20and%20Ensembles): bagging and boosting target variance and bias respectively.
- [Deep Ensembles](node:Deep%20Ensembles): averaging networks to reduce variance.
- [Kernel Ridge Regression](node:Kernel%20Ridge%20Regression): a model where the ridge parameter tunes bias against variance.
- [Linear Regression](node:Linear%20Regression): the setting of the exact ridgeless asymptotics.
- [Generalization in Deep Learning](node:Generalization%20in%20Deep%20Learning): where interpolation and double descent challenge the classical picture.
- [Statistical Learning Theory](node:Statistical%20Learning%20Theory): capacity-based bounds as an alternative account of generalization.
- [VC Dimension](node:VC%20Dimension): a classical complexity measure that parameter counts only crudely track.

### Common pitfalls
- Assuming complex models must have high variance is a fallacy, and parameter count is a poor measure of complexity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias%E2%80%93variance_tradeoff))
- The additive "loss = bias + variance + noise" form is special to squared loss. Under zero-one loss, variance can lower the error on examples where the main prediction is wrong. ([Domingos 2000](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~pedrod/papers/aaai00.pdf))
- Bias and variance are properties of a learning algorithm averaged over training sets, not of a single fitted model. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote12.html))
- With $p>n$ the minimum-norm interpolator is biased even though it fits the training data exactly. Its bias grows with $\gamma$ while its variance shrinks. ([Hastie et al., arXiv:1903.08560](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08560))

### Open problems
- **Interpolation beyond linear models.** For a nonlinear model linearized around its initialization, studying the minimum-$\ell_2$-norm interpolator under an i.i.d. data model in any generality is described as an outstanding mathematical challenge. Understanding the bias that gradient-based algorithms induce on fully nonlinear models is a broadly open problem. ([Hastie et al., arXiv:1903.08560](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08560))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bias–variance tradeoff (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias%E2%80%93variance_tradeoff): the decomposition, classification variants, ways to manage the tradeoff, and history.
- **Learn:** [Cornell CS4780 Lecture 12, Bias–Variance Decomposition](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote12.html): full derivation and the high-bias/high-variance diagnosis.
- **Primary:** [Domingos, A Unified Bias-Variance Decomposition for Zero-One and Squared Loss (AAAI 2000)](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~pedrod/papers/aaai00.pdf): loss-general definitions and theorems.
- **Primary:** [Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal, Reconciling modern machine learning practice and the bias-variance trade-off](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118): the double-descent curve.
- **Primary:** [Hastie, Montanari, Rosset and Tibshirani, Surprises in High-Dimensional Ridgeless Least Squares Interpolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08560): exact bias and variance of minimum-norm interpolation.
- **Primary:** [Geman, Bienenstock and Doursat, Neural Networks and the Bias/Variance Dilemma (1992)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1162/neco.1992.4.1.1): the classic statement for neural networks.
- **Further reading:** [Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning (Springer, 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-84858-7): graduate text on statistical learning.

## Reference
### Overview
Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN, also called primordial nucleosynthesis) is the model for the production of the light nuclei $^2$H (D), $^3$He, $^4$He and $^7$Li in the first minutes of cosmic history; elements heavier than lithium are instead made in appreciable amounts later, in stars. Its predictions combine thermodynamic arguments with laboratory-measured nuclear reaction rates, and it is one of the key concepts of standard cosmology. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis))

The Particle Data Group review calls BBN "the deepest reliable probe of the early Universe", because it rests on well-understood Standard Model physics at temperatures $T \sim 1$ MeV (age $t \sim 1$ s). The predicted abundances, which span nine orders of magnitude from $^4\text{He/H} \sim 0.08$ to $^7\text{Li/H} \sim 10^{-10}$ by number, agree well overall with the primordial abundances inferred from observation. That agreement makes BBN a strong constraint on deviations from standard cosmology and on new physics. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))

Because the universe is radiation dominated during BBN, the expansion rate is set by the energy density of relativistic species such as photons and neutrinos, so the light-element abundances are sensitive to the energy densities of these species. BBN is also a baryometer: it measures the baryon-to-photon ratio, one of the inputs of the Lambda-CDM model, independently of the cosmic microwave background. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis))

### Formal definition
Standard BBN (SBBN) assumes Standard Model physics with $N_\nu = 3$ neutrino species, so the only free parameter is the baryon-to-photon ratio ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf)):
$$
\eta \equiv \frac{n_b}{n_\gamma}, \qquad \eta_{10} \equiv 10^{10}\,\eta .
$$

At high temperature the weak reactions $n + e^+ \leftrightarrow p + \bar\nu_e$ and $n + \nu_e \leftrightarrow p + e^-$ keep neutrons and protons in equilibrium, with $n/p = e^{-Q/T}$ and $Q = 1.293$ MeV the neutron-proton mass difference ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf); [Cambridge lecture notes](https://people.ast.cam.ac.uk/~pettini/Intro%20Cosmology/Lecture08.pdf)).

Freeze-out happens when the interconversion rate $\Gamma_{n\leftrightarrow p} \sim G_F^2 T^5$ drops below the Hubble rate $H \sim \sqrt{g_*\,G_N}\,T^2$, where $g_*$ counts relativistic degrees of freedom. This gives $T_{\rm fr} \sim (g_* G_N / G_F^4)^{1/6} \simeq 1$ MeV and $n/p = e^{-Q/T_{\rm fr}} \simeq 1/6$, which falls to $n/p \simeq 1/7$ through $\beta$-decay before nuclei form. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))

Since nearly all surviving neutrons end up in $^4$He, the primordial helium fraction is estimated by counting ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf)):
$$
Y_p \equiv \frac{\rho(^4\text{He})}{\rho_b} \approx \frac{2(n/p)}{1+n/p} \simeq 0.25 .
$$

### Key results
- **Deuterium formation is delayed.** The chain starts with $p(n,\gamma)D$, but the huge photon number density photo-dissociates deuterium until $\eta^{-1}e^{-\Delta_D/T}$, the number of photons per baryon above the threshold $\Delta_D = 2.23$ MeV, falls below unity at $T \simeq 0.1$ MeV. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Why BBN stops near lithium.** No stable nuclei exist with mass number 5 or 8, and Coulomb barriers suppress reactions such as $^3$He$(^4$He$,\gamma)^7$Be, so heavier nuclei do not form in significant amounts. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Observed abundances.** PDG recommends $\text{D/H}|_p = (25.08 \pm 0.29)\times 10^{-6}$ from high-redshift quasar absorbers, $Y_p = 0.245 \pm 0.003$ from metal-poor extragalactic H II regions, and $\text{Li/H}|_p = (1.45 \pm 0.25)\times 10^{-10}$ from metal-poor halo stars. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Baryon density.** Excluding lithium, D/H and $^4$He agree on $(\eta_{10})_{\rm SBBN} = 6.040 \pm 0.118$, that is $(\Omega_b h^2)_{\rm SBBN} = 0.02205 \pm 0.00043$ (1σ). This implies that baryons cannot close the universe and that most matter is non-baryonic. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Agreement with the CMB.** Planck gives $(\Omega_b h^2)_{\rm CMB} = 0.02237 \pm 0.00015$, i.e. $(\eta_{10})_{\rm CMB} = 6.12 \pm 0.04$, consistent with BBN even though the two measurements probe different physics at widely separated epochs. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Expansion rate and extra radiation.** Extra relativistic species raise $g_*$ and the expansion rate, so freeze-out happens earlier and $Y_p$ is larger. At $T = 1$ MeV, $g_* = 5.5 + \tfrac{7}{4}N_\nu$ and $\Delta Y_p \simeq 0.013\,\Delta N_\nu$. A joint $^4$He + D fit gives $N_\nu = 2.898 \pm 0.141$, consistent with the Standard Model. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Deuterium is the best baryometer.** $Y_p$ depends only weakly on $\eta$ because almost all neutrons end up in $^4$He, whereas D/H falls steeply as $\eta$ rises because denser plasma burns deuterium more efficiently. ([Cambridge lecture notes](https://people.ast.cam.ac.uk/~pettini/Intro%20Cosmology/Lecture08.pdf))

### Examples
- **Neutron-lifetime coincidence.** In one lecture-note estimate, freeze-out at $T_d \simeq 0.8$ MeV ($t \simeq 2.6$ s) gives $n/p \approx e^{-1.3/0.8} \approx 1/5$. Neutron decay over the roughly 300 s before deuterium survives then lowers it to about $1/7$, giving $Y_p \approx 0.25$. The notes remark that if the neutron lifetime were much shorter, only hydrogen would remain. ([Cambridge lecture notes](https://people.ast.cam.ac.uk/~pettini/Intro%20Cosmology/Lecture08.pdf))
- **Sensitivity of deuterium.** Lowering $\eta$ by a factor of 10 raises the primordial deuterium abundance by a factor of roughly 50. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis))
- **Measuring D/H.** Deuterium is observed through its isotope-shifted Lyman-series absorption in high-redshift, low-metallicity quasar absorption systems, where astration (stellar destruction of D) is estimated at only 0.1–1%. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))

### History
Alpher, Bethe and Gamow published "The Origin of Chemical Elements" in *Physical Review* in April 1948 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis)). It proposed non-equilibrium nuclear processes in a radiation-dominated early universe to explain the abundances of all the elements. The model was fundamentally flawed, but it started the path to the modern theory, which explains only the lightest elements. ([Turner 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.14254))

Attempts by Fermi and Turkevich to follow specific reactions ran into the "mass gap" at masses 5 and 8. After the CMB was discovered in 1965, Peebles used its temperature in detailed calculations of primordial abundances, and Wagoner, Fowler and Hoyle followed in 1967. From 1972 the Copernicus satellite measured deuterium, and by the 1990s deuterium data implied that there must be non-baryonic mass. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis))

In 1998 Schramm and Turner described BBN as a cornerstone of the Big Bang alongside the Hubble expansion and the CMB. They wrote that high-redshift deuterium measurements were pinning down the last BBN parameter, the baryon density, and that CMB anisotropies would provide an independent test. ([Schramm & Turner](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9706069))

### Connections
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): the radiation-dominated Friedmann expansion sets the clock that competes with weak and nuclear rates.
- [Nuclear Physics](node:Nuclear%20Physics): laboratory cross sections (e.g. D(p,γ)³He, D(D,n)³He) and the neutron lifetime are the inputs.
- [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background): gives an independent value of $\eta$ and $Y_p$ that BBN must match.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): BBN fixes the baryon density, one of its parameters.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): $\Omega_b \ll \Omega_m$ from BBN is evidence for non-baryonic matter.
- [Dark Radiation](node:Dark%20Radiation): extra relativistic species are bounded through $N_\nu$ / $N_{\rm eff}$.
- [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology): modified early expansion rates in brane models are constrained by BBN.
- [Supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry): late-decaying particles and gravitinos are constrained by light-element abundances.

### Common pitfalls
> [!warning] Contested
> **What delays and ends BBN.** Standard reviews explain the delay through photo-dissociation of deuterium until $T \simeq 0.1$ MeV and the end of BBN through the lack of stable mass-5 and mass-8 nuclei plus Coulomb barriers ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf)). Turner argues that blaming the "deuterium bottleneck" is misleading. On his account the real causes are the universe's high entropy (about 2 billion photons per baryon) and Coulomb barriers, and he likewise rejects the mass-5/8 gap as the reason BBN stops beyond helium ([Turner 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.14254)).

- **Mass fraction versus number ratio.** $Y_p \simeq 0.25$ is a mass (strictly baryon) fraction, which corresponds to $^4\text{He/H} \approx 1/12$ by number. The other light elements are usually quoted by number relative to H. ([Cambridge lecture notes](https://people.ast.cam.ac.uk/~pettini/Intro%20Cosmology/Lecture08.pdf); [PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Helium-3 is not a clean probe.** It has been measured only in the Solar System and in solar-metallicity Galactic H II regions, and stellar $^3$He models conflict with observations, so PDG does not use $^3$He as a cosmological probe. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Observed lithium is a lower bound.** $^7$Li in Population II stars may have been partly destroyed by mixing, so the inferred primordial value should be read as a lower bound. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Cosmological lithium problem.** The predicted $\text{Li/H}|_p = (4.72 \pm 0.7)\times 10^{-10}$ exceeds the observed value by a factor of 3.3, a 4.4σ discrepancy. PDG calls it unresolved: nuclear fixes look increasingly unlikely, stellar depletion is described as the leading explanation, and new physics during BBN is still possible. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))
- **Nuclear-rate uncertainty in D/H.** Nuclear uncertainties still leave the D/H prediction errors larger than the observational ones, with D(D,n)³He and D(D,p)³H dominating, and PDG says more experimental data is needed. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Big Bang nucleosynthesis (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis): physical sequence, parameters, measurements, and history.
- **Learn:** [M. Pettini, Introduction to Cosmology, Lecture 8 (Cambridge)](https://people.ast.cam.ac.uk/~pettini/Intro%20Cosmology/Lecture08.pdf): worked estimates of $n/p$, $Y_p$, and the abundance measurements.
- **Primary:** [Fields, Molaro & Sarkar, PDG review "Big Bang Nucleosynthesis" (2025)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf): standard review with current abundances, η, and $N_\nu$ bounds.
- **Primary:** [Schramm & Turner, "Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis Enters the Precision Era"](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9706069): classic *Rev. Mod. Phys.* colloquium.
- **Primary:** [Turner, "Understanding BBN: the physics and its history"](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.14254): physics and history, including common misconceptions.
references.Binary Decision Diagrams:
## Reference
### Overview
A binary decision diagram (BDD) is a data structure for Boolean functions: a rooted directed acyclic graph whose decision nodes are labelled by Boolean variables and have a low child and a high child, with terminal nodes $0$ and $1$. In common usage "BDD" means a reduced ordered BDD (ROBDD), in which variables appear in a fixed order along every path and redundant structure has been removed; the ROBDD of a function under a given order is canonical (unique up to isomorphism), which makes it useful for functional equivalence checking. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram))

Bryant's 1986 paper turned earlier decision-graph representations of Lee and Akers into a practical tool by imposing a variable ordering and giving manipulation algorithms whose running time is proportional to the sizes of the graphs involved. A function can need a graph exponential in the number of arguments, but many functions met in practice have small graphs, and Bryant reported experiments in logic design verification. ([Bryant 1986](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf))

OBDDs underlie symbolic analysis: system parameters and operating conditions are encoded with Boolean variables, and the system is evaluated for all variations by a sequence of OBDD operations. This approach has been used in digital system design, finite-state system analysis (symbolic model checking), artificial intelligence and mathematical logic. ([Bryant 1992](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/acmcs92.pdf)) BDDs are used extensively in CAD software for logic synthesis and in formal and network verification; lesser-known applications include fault tree analysis, Bayesian reasoning and product configuration. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram))

### Formal definition
**If-then-else normal form.** Write $x\to t_1,t_0$ for "if $x$ then $t_1$ else $t_0$". The Shannon expansion
$$t \;=\; x\to t[1/x],\,t[0/x]$$
shows that every Boolean expression is equivalent to one built only from $\to$ and the constants $0,1$, with tests only on variables. ([Andersen, An Introduction to BDDs](https://dang.cs.technion.ac.il/courseCG/S1-S2-bdd97.pdf))

**BDD, OBDD, ROBDD.** A BDD over variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is a DAG with two sinks labelled $0$ and $1$ and internal nodes labelled by variables, each with a $0$-edge (low) and a $1$-edge (high); an input selects a root-to-sink path whose sink label is the output. Given a variable ordering $\pi$ (a bijection from variables to $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$), an OBDD respects $\pi$ when every edge from a node labelled $x_i$ to a node labelled $x_j$ has $\pi(x_i)<\pi(x_j)$. It is reduced when (i) no two distinct nodes have identical subgraphs (isomorphic subgraphs are merged) and (ii) no node has identical low and high children. ([Qin 2026](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.30664); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram))

**Size.** $|B_\pi(f)|$ is the number of nodes of the ROBDD of $f$ under $\pi$, and $|B(f)|=\min_\pi|B_\pi(f)|$. ([Qin 2026](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.30664))

### Key results
- **Canonicity.** For every $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ and ordering $x_1<\dots<x_n$ there is exactly one ROBDD $u$ with $f_u=f$. ([Andersen](https://dang.cs.technion.ac.il/courseCG/S1-S2-bdd97.pdf)) Bryant's Theorem 1 adds minimality: the reduced function graph of $f$ is unique up to isomorphism, and every other function graph for $f$ (with the same ordering) has more vertices. ([Bryant 1986](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf))
- **Complexity of operations.** With graphs $G,G_1,G_2$ over $n$ variables: Reduce runs in $O(|G|\log|G|)$; Apply $f_1\,\langle op\rangle\,f_2$ in $O(|G_1|\cdot|G_2|)$; Restrict $f|_{x_i=b}$ in $O(|G|\log|G|)$; Compose $f_1|_{x_i=f_2}$ in $O(|G_1|^2|G_2|)$; Satisfy-one in $O(n)$; Satisfy-all in $O(n\cdot|S_f|)$; Satisfy-count in $O(|G|)$. ([Bryant 1986](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf)) Existential quantification $\exists x.t=t[0/x]\vee t[1/x]$ is two Restricts and one Apply. ([Andersen](https://dang.cs.technion.ac.il/courseCG/S1-S2-bdd97.pdf)) Quantifying out many variables at once is NP-complete in general, while model counting is polynomial in the BDD size. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram))
- **Variable ordering can be exponential.** For $a_1b_1+a_2b_2+\dots+a_nb_n$, the order $a_1<b_1<\dots<a_n<b_n$ gives an OBDD with $2n$ nonterminal vertices, while $a_1<\dots<a_n<b_1<\dots<b_n$ gives $2(2^n-1)$. ([Bryant 1992](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/acmcs92.pdf))
- **Optimal ordering is hard.** Finding a variable order minimizing BDD size is NP-hard, and so is approximating the optimum within any constant factor $c>1$; practice relies on heuristics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram))
- **Integer multiplication.** For every ordering of the $2n$ input bits, some output bit of the $n$-bit product needs an OBDD with at least $2^{n/8}$ vertices (Bryant 1986). ([Bryant 1986](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf)) Bryant (1991) showed the middle bit $\mathrm{Mul}^n_{n-1}$ alone needs $2^{n/8}$ nodes under every ordering; Woelfel (2005) raised the lower bound to $2^{n/2}/61$ and gave an upper bound $\tfrac73\,2^{4n/3}$ on $|B(\mathrm{Mul}^n_{n-1})|$. ([Qin 2026](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.30664))
- **Symmetric functions.** Every symmetric function of $n$ arguments has a reduced function graph with $O(n^2)$ vertices. ([Bryant 1986](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf))

### Examples
- **Equality of bit strings.** The ROBDD for $(x_1\Leftrightarrow y_1)\wedge(x_2\Leftrightarrow y_2)$ is obtained from the decision tree of its Shannon expansions by identifying the many identical subexpressions and removing redundant tests, giving a much smaller graph. ([Andersen](https://dang.cs.technion.ac.il/courseCG/S1-S2-bdd97.pdf))
- **$N$ queens.** With a variable $x_{ij}$ per square, the constraints that no queen shares a row, column or diagonal with another, and that each row holds a queen, are conjoined into a predicate $\mathrm{Sol}_N$ true exactly at the solutions; Andersen sets building its ROBDD and tabulating the number of solutions as an exercise. ([Andersen](https://dang.cs.technion.ac.il/courseCG/S1-S2-bdd97.pdf))
- **Adders.** Circuits with constant forward cross-section and zero reverse cross-section, such as a ripple adder, have OBDDs linear in the word size under a suitable ordering. ([Bryant 1992](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/acmcs92.pdf))
- **Multipliers.** Exponential under every ordering (above); Bryant found that for $n\le 8$ output functions need at most about 5000 vertices, but beyond $n=10$ some need more than 100,000. ([Bryant 1986](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf))

### History
The construction rests on the Shannon expansion; Lee introduced binary decision diagrams in 1959 and Akers studied them further in 1978. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram)) Bryant's 1986 *IEEE Transactions on Computers* paper added a fixed variable ordering and sharing, proved canonicity, and gave the operation algorithms and the multiplication lower bound. ([Bryant 1986](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf)) His 1992 *ACM Computing Surveys* article surveyed applications including symbolic model checking (Burch, Clarke, Dill, McMillan) and efficient BDD packages (Brace, Bryant, Rudell 1990). ([Bryant 1992](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/acmcs92.pdf)) Later variants include zero-suppressed (ZDD), free (FBDD, each variable read at most once per path), multi-terminal/algebraic (MTBDD/ADD) and multi-valued (MDD) diagrams. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram))

### Connections
- [Boolean Algebras](node:Boolean%20Algebras): ROBDDs give canonical forms for elements of finitely generated free Boolean algebras.
- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic): satisfiability, tautology and equivalence of formulas become constant-time checks once the ROBDD is built.
- [Digital Logic and Logic Synthesis](node:Digital%20Logic%20and%20Logic%20Synthesis): BDDs are a core data structure in synthesis and combinational equivalence checking.
- [Model Checking](node:Model%20Checking): symbolic model checking represents state sets and transition relations as BDDs.
- [SAT and SMT Solving](node:SAT%20and%20SMT%20Solving): a SAT solver searches for one assignment; a BDD represents all of them, at a possibly exponential size cost.
- [Boolean Circuits](node:Boolean%20Circuits): OBDDs are a restricted branching-program model of Boolean function complexity.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): most problems BDDs are applied to are NP-hard or PSPACE-hard, so BDD-based methods are not expected to have polynomial worst-case behaviour.

### Common pitfalls
- Canonicity holds only relative to a fixed variable order; two ROBDDs of the same function under different orders can differ in size exponentially. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram))
- Each Apply is polynomial, but a sequence of operations can still blow up exponentially, since the output of Apply can be as large as the product of its inputs. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram))
- Building an ROBDD directly from an expression by recursive Shannon expansion (the `build` algorithm) always makes on the order of $2^n$ calls for $n$ variables, even though `mk` prevents duplicate nodes. ([Andersen](https://dang.cs.technion.ac.il/courseCG/S1-S2-bdd97.pdf))
- BDDs do not escape NP-hardness: most problems they are applied to are NP-hard or PSPACE-hard, so no method with polynomial worst case is expected. ([Bryant 1992](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/acmcs92.pdf))

### Open problems
- **OBDD complexity of the middle bit of multiplication.** The best lower bound $2^{n/2}/61$ and upper bound $\tfrac73 2^{4n/3}$ (Woelfel 2005) still have different exponents; Qin (2026) states that closing this gap is the goal, proves $\Theta(2^{s_*(n)})$ width bounds only for a restricted input domain, and leaves an exact closed form of $s_*(n)$ for future research, calling the extension to arbitrary $n$-bit inputs significantly more challenging. ([Qin 2026](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.30664))
- **Better representations and methods.** Bryant's survey notes that although many problems have been solved with OBDDs, many cases still require improved methods, and names improving on the representation itself as one possibility, since OBDDs quickly become impractically large for systems with multipliers. ([Bryant 1992](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/acmcs92.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Binary decision diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_decision_diagram): definitions, ordering complexity, variants, applications.
- **Learn:** [Andersen, An Introduction to Binary Decision Diagrams (DTU lecture notes)](https://dang.cs.technion.ac.il/courseCG/S1-S2-bdd97.pdf): canonicity proof, mk/build/apply/restrict algorithms, N-queens.
- **Primary:** [Bryant 1986, Graph-Based Algorithms for Boolean Function Manipulation](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf): the ROBDD paper (IEEE Trans. Computers C-35).
- **Primary:** [Bryant 1992, Symbolic Boolean Manipulation with Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/acmcs92.pdf): survey of OBDDs and applications (ACM Computing Surveys).
- **Primary:** [Qin 2026, Upper and lower bounds on the OBDD-width of a special integer multiplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30664): recent status of multiplication bounds.
- **Further reading:** [Bryant 1992 survey](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/acmcs92.pdf): the standard entry point to the literature, with an extensive bibliography.

## Reference
### Overview
A black hole is a region of spacetime from which no information-carrying signal or object can escape; its boundary, the event horizon, was described by Finkelstein in 1958 as "a perfect unidirectional membrane". Because the definition refers to the whole future of spacetime, confirming it would require waiting an infinite time at infinite distance, so astrophysical identifications rely on indirect signatures. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole))

Within four-dimensional Einstein–Maxwell theory, stationary black holes are expected to be described by just mass, angular momentum and charge (the Kerr–Newman family). The proven uniqueness theorems carry hypotheses, including non-degenerate horizons and real analyticity, and because no general proof exists the statement is still called the no-hair conjecture; it fails with other matter fields or in higher dimensions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-hair_theorem)) ([Chruściel, Costa and Heusler](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.6112))

Black holes are also where gravity, [thermodynamics](node:Thermodynamics) and quantum theory meet: horizons obey laws formally analogous to thermodynamics, [quantum fields](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory) on a black-hole background radiate thermally at a temperature proportional to the surface gravity, and string theory reproduces the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy for some extremal black holes by counting microstates. ([Wikipedia: Black hole thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole_thermodynamics)) ([Strominger and Vafa](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9601029))

### Formal definition
For an asymptotically flat spacetime $(M,g)$ with future null infinity $\mathscr{I}^+$, the black-hole region is
$$\mathcal{B} = M \setminus J^-(\mathscr{I}^+),$$
and the event horizon is $\mathcal{H}=\partial J^-(\mathscr{I}^+)$. Defined through the causal past of $\mathscr{I}^+$, it is highly non-local, and teleological: its location is fixed by the future. ([Booth](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0508107)) ([Wikipedia: Event horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_horizon))

The rotating vacuum black hole is the Kerr metric, in Boyer–Lindquist coordinates
$$ds^2 = -\Big(1-\frac{r_s r}{\Sigma}\Big)c^2dt^2 + \frac{\Sigma}{\Delta}dr^2 + \Sigma\, d\theta^2 + \Big(r^2+a^2+\frac{r_s r a^2\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma}\Big)\sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2 - \frac{2 r_s r a\sin^2\theta}{\Sigma}\,c\,dt\,d\phi,$$
with $\Sigma=r^2+a^2\cos^2\theta$, $\Delta=r^2-r_sr+a^2$, $r_s=2GM/c^2$, $a=J/(Mc)$. In units $G=c=1$ the horizons are the roots $r_\pm=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-a^2}$ of $\Delta$; for $a>M$ there is no horizon (a naked singularity), $a=M$ is extremal, and $a=0$ gives Schwarzschild. The ergosphere lies between the outer horizon and $r_E=M+\sqrt{M^2-a^2\cos^2\theta}$; inside it every observer must co-rotate. ([Wikipedia: Kerr metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerr_metric))

### Key results
- **Penrose singularity theorem (1965).** If the null energy condition holds, the spacetime has a noncompact connected Cauchy surface, and it contains a closed trapped surface, then it is null geodesically incomplete. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems)) Published as "Gravitational Collapse and Space-Time Singularities", Phys. Rev. Lett. 14, 57 (1965). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.14.57))
- **Uniqueness theorems.** Israel showed that static vacuum and electrovacuum black-hole spacetimes satisfying a set of restrictive conditions are spherically symmetric; in vacuum, Robinson constructed an identity from which uniqueness of the Kerr metric followed, and Mazur generalized it to the Einstein–Maxwell case. The resulting classification covers analytic, connected, mean non-degenerate, asymptotically flat stationary electrovacuum black holes, and the review calls the analyticity and non-degeneracy hypotheses highly unsatisfactory, believing them unnecessary. ([Chruściel, Costa and Heusler](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.6112)) The papers are Israel, "Event Horizons in Static Vacuum Space-Times", Phys. Rev. 164, 1776 (1967) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.164.1776)), and Robinson, "Uniqueness of the Kerr Black Hole", Phys. Rev. Lett. 34, 905 (1975) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.34.905)). The pure-gravity results also assume real analyticity, and counterexamples exist with non-abelian Yang–Mills fields, skyrmions, some non-minimally coupled scalars and in higher dimensions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-hair_theorem))
- **Laws of black hole mechanics (Bardeen, Carter, Hawking 1973).** Surface gravity $\kappa$ is constant on a stationary horizon; $dM=\frac{\kappa}{8\pi}dA+\Omega\,dJ+\Phi\,dQ$; under the weak energy condition the horizon area is non-decreasing. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole_thermodynamics)) For two initially near-stationary non-rotating holes of masses $M_1,M_2$ that merge into one of mass $M_3$, the area theorem gives $M_3\ge\sqrt{M_1^2+M_2^2}$, so the fraction of mass radiated is at most $1-\sqrt{M_1^2+M_2^2}/(M_1+M_2)\le1-1/\sqrt2$. ([Townsend](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/9707012)) Hawking's 1971 letter on this is "Gravitational Radiation from Colliding Black Holes", Phys. Rev. Lett. 26, 1344. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.26.1344))
- **The third law is false.** The proposed third law says a subextremal black hole cannot become extremal in finite time by any continuous process in which spacetime and matter stay regular and obey the weak energy condition (Israel's formulation). Kehle and Unger construct regular one-ended asymptotically flat data for the spherically symmetric Einstein–Maxwell–charged scalar field system (which satisfies the dominant energy condition) that collapse to an exactly Schwarzschild apparent horizon and later form an exactly extremal Reissner–Nordström event horizon. ([Kehle and Unger](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.15742))
- **Hawking radiation (1974–75).** Quantum fields on a collapse background are emitted thermally at $T_H=\kappa/2\pi$ ($G=c=\hbar=k_B=1$), fixing $S_{BH}=k_BA/(4\ell_P^2)$. ([Wikipedia: Black hole thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole_thermodynamics)) For Schwarzschild $T_H=\hbar c^3/(8\pi GMk_B)$ and the evaporation time is $t_{ev}=5120\pi G^2M^3/(\hbar c^4)$, over $10^{67}$ years for a solar mass. ([Wikipedia: Hawking radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_radiation)) Paper: Commun. Math. Phys. 43, 199–220 (1975). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02345020))
- **Microscopic entropy (Strominger–Vafa 1996).** For a class of five-dimensional extremal black holes in string theory, counting degenerate BPS soliton bound states reproduces $S_{BH}=A/4$. ([Strominger and Vafa](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9601029))
- **Naked singularities in scalar collapse (Christodoulou).** In spherically symmetric collapse of a scalar field, regular asymptotically flat data can form singularities not preceded by a trapped region, so naked singularities occur; but the data that form them have positive codimension, so they are unstable in this model. ([Christodoulou](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901147))
- **Stability of Kerr.** Klainerman, Szeftel and collaborators establish nonlinear stability of Kerr with small angular momentum. ([Klainerman and Szeftel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14400)) Dafermos, Holzegel, Rodnianski and Taylor prove nonlinear asymptotic stability of Schwarzschild for data on a codimension-3 submanifold of moduli space; nearby data off it should settle to Kerr with $a\neq0$. ([Dafermos et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08222))
- **$C^0$-stability of the Kerr Cauchy horizon.** Dafermos and Luk show that, if the Kerr exterior is stable, the interior of a dynamical rotating vacuum black hole extends continuously across a piece of Cauchy horizon, so the $C^0$-inextendibility form of strong cosmic censorship is false. ([Dafermos and Luk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.01722))

### Examples
- **Schwarzschild, Kerr, Kerr–Newman.** Static, rotating, and rotating charged stationary black holes; charge and spin are bounded by mass, and those saturating the bound are extremal. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole))
- **Penrose process.** Particles splitting in the ergosphere can escape with more energy than they brought in; at most $E_{rot}=c^2(M-M_{irr})$ is extractable. ([Wikipedia: Kerr metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerr_metric))
- **Astrophysical black holes.** Cygnus X-1 was generally accepted as a black hole by the end of 1973; LIGO and Virgo detected the merger GW150914 in 2015; the Event Horizon Telescope imaged M87* (10 April 2019) and Sagittarius A* (2022). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole))

### History
Michell (1784) and Laplace (1796) imagined stars too compact for light to escape; Schwarzschild's 1916 solution was the first in general relativity to characterise a black hole; Oppenheimer and Snyder modelled collapse in 1939; the name "black hole" was suggested to Wheeler in a December 1967 lecture. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole)) Kerr published the rotating solution as "Gravitational Field of a Spinning Mass as an Example of Algebraically Special Metrics", Phys. Rev. Lett. 11, 237 (1963). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.11.237)) Penrose shared the 2020 Nobel Prize "for the discovery that black hole formation is a robust prediction of the general theory of relativity". ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems)) Bekenstein proposed area-proportional entropy in 1972, and Hawking's 1974 discovery of thermal emission fixed the constant at $1/4$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole_thermodynamics))
