- [Black Hole Thermodynamics](node:Black%20Hole%20Thermodynamics): the laws of black hole mechanics and entropy.
- [Hawking Radiation](node:Hawking%20Radiation): the quantum emission behind $T_H=\kappa/2\pi$.
- [Singularity Theorems in Relativity](node:Singularity%20Theorems%20in%20Relativity) and [Raychaudhuri Equation](node:Raychaudhuri%20Equation): focusing arguments behind incompleteness.
- [Penrose Diagrams](node:Penrose%20Diagrams): read off horizons and $\mathscr{I}^+$.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) and [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): the theory these solutions solve.
- [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves) and [Black Hole Quasinormal Modes](node:Black%20Hole%20Quasinormal%20Modes): mergers and ringdown.

- [Holographic Principle](node:Holographic%20Principle), [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence) and [Ryu–Takayanagi Formula](node:Ryu–Takayanagi%20Formula): the tools of Page-curve computations.
- [Primordial Black Holes](node:Primordial%20Black%20Holes): black holes formed in the early universe.

### Common pitfalls
- **The horizon is not local.** It cannot be located by finite measurements; Hawking proposed apparent horizons instead, and quasilocal horizons are built from two-surfaces of zero outward null expansion. ([Wikipedia: Event horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_horizon)) ([Booth](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0508107))
- **Existence of extremal black holes is not the issue for the third law.** The law concerns forming them in finite time from subextremal ones; the counterexample is a dynamical collapse construction. ([Kehle and Unger](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.15742))
- **"No hair" carries hypotheses.** The proofs assume non-degenerate horizons and real analyticity, among other conditions. ([Chruściel, Costa and Heusler](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.6112)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-hair_theorem))
- **Stellar black holes are not evaporating.** They are colder than the 2.7 K microwave background. ([Wikipedia: Hawking radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_radiation))
- **Singularity theorems prove incompleteness, not curvature blow-up.** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems))

### Open problems
- **Weak cosmic censorship.** That realistic collapse does not produce naked singularities has not been proven. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole)) Christodoulou's scalar-field results support it in spherical symmetry by showing naked singularities are non-generic there, and he frames whether they can form with positive probability as an open question. ([Christodoulou](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9901147))
- **Strong cosmic censorship.** Both the weak and strong versions remain mathematical conjectures, and the hypothesis is described as more of a research program proposal. ([Wikipedia: Cosmic censorship hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_censorship_hypothesis)) Dafermos and Luk's work suggests generic Cauchy horizons are weak null singularities and proposes a revised formulation. ([Dafermos and Luk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.01722))
- **Kerr stability for all $|a|<M$.** A 2026 preprint (v2, November 2026) reports a proof for the full subextremal range, "completing the proof of the Kerr stability conjecture"; it is recent and should be treated as reported pending community verification. ([Szeftel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40068))
- **No-hair conjecture.** No rigorous general proof exists. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-hair_theorem))
- **Information paradox and the Page curve.** If evaporation is unitary, the radiation's entropy rises then falls (the Page curve), turning at about half the lifetime. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole_information_paradox)) Penington, and Almheiri, Engelhardt, Marolf and Maxfield, found a phase transition of the quantum extremal surface at the Page time in holographic models of evaporation (absorbing boundary conditions in AdS/CFT; Jackiw–Teitelboim gravity with one boundary coupled to a heat sink). ([Penington](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08255)) ([AEMM](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08762)) A review describes the resulting fine-grained entropy corrections. ([Almheiri et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.06872)) Raju argues such bath models may misrepresent the information rate for asymptotically flat black holes, and examines state-dependent interior reconstruction, firewalls and fuzzballs. ([Raju](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.05770))
- **Schwarzschild microstates.** Microscopic counts agree for extremal and near-extremal holes, but the Schwarzschild case remains uncharacterized. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole_thermodynamics))

references.Boolean Algebras:
## Reference
### Overview
A Boolean algebra is the algebraic form of two-valued propositional logic with only sentential connectives, or equivalently an algebra of sets closed under union and complementation. Its axioms are the commutative, associative and distributive laws together with absorption and complement laws, and an equation holds in every Boolean algebra exactly when it holds in the two-element algebra of truth values. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))

In lattice-theoretic terms a Boolean algebra is a complemented distributive lattice: a set with meet, join, complement and constants $0,1$ satisfying self-dual axioms, so every Boolean algebra has a dual obtained by swapping meet with join and $0$ with $1$. Standard examples are the two-element algebra used for truth values and circuit bits, power sets, finite–cofinite algebras, the Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra of propositional logic, interval algebras, and the clopen sets of a topological space. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))

The subject sits where logic, algebra and topology meet. Stone's representation theorem identifies Boolean algebras with totally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces, which makes Boolean algebras the prototype of a duality between algebra and topology; complete Boolean algebras are central in set theory, and Boolean algebras of projections appear in the study of abelian von Neumann algebras. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Stone+duality); [Lurie, Math 261y lecture 14](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/261ynotes/lecture14.pdf))

### Formal definition
**Lattice form.** A Boolean algebra is a structure $(B,\wedge,\vee,\neg,0,1)$ that is a distributive lattice with least element $0$ and greatest element $1$ in which every element has a complement: for all $x,y,z\in B$,
$$x\vee(y\wedge z)=(x\vee y)\wedge(x\vee z),\qquad x\vee\neg x=1,\qquad x\wedge\neg x=0,$$
together with associativity, commutativity, absorption and identity laws for $\wedge,\vee$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))

**Ring form.** A Boolean ring is a commutative ring $B$ with identity in which every element is idempotent, $x^2=x$; such a ring has characteristic 2 since $2=2^2=4$. Ordering $B$ by $x\le y \iff xy=x$ makes it a complemented distributive lattice with $x\wedge y=xy$, $x\vee y=x+y-xy$ and complement $1-x$; conversely a complemented distributive lattice becomes a Boolean ring with $xy=x\wedge y$ and $x\oplus y=(x\vee y)\wedge(x'\vee y')$. ([Lurie, lecture 14](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/261ynotes/lecture14.pdf)) The two notions are definitionally equivalent. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))

**Ultrafilters and atoms.** A filter is a subset closed under meets, containing $1$, and upward closed; an ultrafilter is a filter $F$ with $0\notin F$ that contains, for each $a$, either $a$ or $\neg a$. An atom is a nonzero element $a$ with no $b$ such that $0<b<a$, and a Boolean algebra is atomless if it has no atoms. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/)) In a Boolean algebra prime and maximal ideals coincide, ultrafilters are exactly the duals of prime ideals, and they can be described as homomorphisms to the two-element algebra. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))

**Completeness.** $B$ is complete if every subset has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))

**Stone space.** For a Boolean algebra $B$, its Stone space $\operatorname{Spec}B$ is the set of prime ideals (equivalently ultrafilters, or homomorphisms $B\to 2$) with the topology generated by the sets $\{P : a\notin P\}$, $a\in B$; these basic sets are clopen. ([Harding, ESSLLI lecture 3](https://math.nmsu.edu/people/personal-pages/files/ESSLLI3.pdf); [Lurie, lecture 14](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/261ynotes/lecture14.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))

### Key results
- **Two-element completeness.** An equation in the Boolean operations holds in all Boolean algebras if and only if it holds in the two-element algebra $\{0,1\}$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))
- **Stone representation theorem.** Every Boolean algebra $B$ is isomorphic to a field of sets, via $a\mapsto\{U : U \text{ an ultrafilter},\ a\in U\}$; the image is exactly the algebra of clopen sets of a totally disconnected compact Hausdorff space. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))
- **Stone duality.** $B\mapsto\operatorname{Spec}B$ induces an equivalence between the category of Boolean algebras (a full subcategory of commutative rings) and the opposite of the category of totally disconnected compact (Stone) spaces; the inverse sends $X$ to its algebra of clopen sets, and $\operatorname{Hom}(B,\mathrm{Clopen}(X))\cong\operatorname{Hom}(X,\operatorname{Spec}B)$ for every space $X$. ([Lurie, lecture 14](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/261ynotes/lecture14.pdf)) Applied to topological spaces this needs the ultrafilter theorem or another form of the axiom of choice; the corresponding statement for locales holds constructively. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Stone+duality))
- **Finite Boolean algebras.** If $B$ is finite with $n$ coatoms, its prime ideals are the principal ideals ${\downarrow}c$ for coatoms $c$, its Stone space is an $n$-point discrete space, and $B\cong\mathcal P(\{1,\dots,n\})$; in particular $|B|=2^n$. ([Harding, ESSLLI lecture 3](https://math.nmsu.edu/people/personal-pages/files/ESSLLI3.pdf))
- **Completions.** Every Boolean algebra $A$ embeds in a complete Boolean algebra $B$ in which every element is the least upper bound of a set of elements of $A$; $B$ is unique up to $A$-isomorphism and is called the completion of $A$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/)) The category of Stonean spaces (compact extremally disconnected Hausdorff spaces, with open continuous maps) is contravariantly equivalent to the category of complete Boolean algebras with continuous Boolean homomorphisms. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Stone+duality))
- **Sikorski extension theorem.** If $f$ is a homomorphism from a Boolean algebra $A$ into a complete Boolean algebra $B$ and $A$ is a subalgebra of $C$, then $f$ extends to a homomorphism from $C$ into $B$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))
- **Free Boolean algebras.** The free Boolean algebra on $\kappa$ generators is the algebra of clopen subsets of $2^\kappa$ (the two-point discrete space raised to the power $\kappa$); every infinite free Boolean algebra is atomless. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))
- **Tarski's decidability theorem.** The elementary (first-order) theory of Boolean algebras is decidable, and stays decidable with a distinguished ideal added; the theory of Boolean algebras with a distinguished subalgebra is undecidable. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))
- **Robbins problem.** Robbins asked whether a dual variant of Huntington's 1933 equation also axiomatizes Boolean algebras; McCune proved in 1996, using the automated prover EQP, that it does. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))

### Examples
- **Two-element algebra** $\{0,1\}$: the algebra of truth values and of circuit bits. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))
- **Power sets** $\mathcal P(S)$ under $\cup,\cap$ and complement; by the finite case above every finite Boolean algebra has this form. ([Harding, ESSLLI lecture 3](https://math.nmsu.edu/people/personal-pages/files/ESSLLI3.pdf))
- **Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra** of propositional formulas modulo provable equivalence, which is the free Boolean algebra on the propositional variables. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))
- **Interval algebras**: every countable Boolean algebra is isomorphic to one. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))
- **Divisors of a square-free integer** under $\gcd$ and $\operatorname{lcm}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29))
- **Projections of a commutative $*$-algebra** $A$: the set $P(A)=\{e: e^*=e^2=e\}$ of projections is a Boolean algebra, and an abelian von Neumann algebra is determined by its Boolean algebra of projections. ([Lurie, lecture 14](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/261ynotes/lecture14.pdf))

### History
The structure is named after George Boole. Jevons and Peirce developed the algebra in the 1860s, Schröder gave the first systematic presentation in 1890, Whitehead gave the first general axiomatization in 1898, and Huntington gave a more economical system in 1904 and one with a single binary operation and complement in 1933. Stone's work in the 1930s and Birkhoff's *Lattice Theory* (1940) established the subject as mainstream mathematics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29)) Stone's representation paper is "The theory of representations for Boolean algebras", *Transactions of the AMS* 40 (1936), 37–111. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1936-1501865-8)) Stone duality predates category theory and is a guide to the other dualities of lattice theory: Birkhoff (finite distributive lattices and finite posets), Priestley (distributive lattices and certain ordered topological spaces) and Esakia (Heyting algebras and certain ordered topological spaces). ([Harding, ESSLLI lecture 3](https://math.nmsu.edu/people/personal-pages/files/ESSLLI3.pdf))

- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic): the Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra is the free Boolean algebra on the variables.
