### Common pitfalls
- Only equations transfer from the two-element algebra; structural properties of finite examples need not. Every finite Boolean algebra is atomic and isomorphic to a power set ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/); [Harding, ESSLLI lecture 3](https://math.nmsu.edu/people/personal-pages/files/ESSLLI3.pdf)), whereas every infinite free Boolean algebra is atomless. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))
- The ring addition is not the join: in the ring form, join is $x+y-xy$, while the ring sum of the lattice form is $(x\vee y)\wedge(x'\vee y')$, i.e. symmetric difference. ([Lurie, lecture 14](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/261ynotes/lecture14.pdf); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))
- The point-set form of Stone duality uses the ultrafilter theorem, a weak form of choice. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Stone+duality))

### Open problems
- **Monk's problems on cardinal invariants.** Monk's book *Cardinal invariants on Boolean algebras* posed 97 problems; his 2004 status report lists many as still open in their original form at that date (including problems 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 15, 17, 19). For Problem 1 (cellularity of free products), it states that it is still, evidently, open whether, for $\kappa$ inaccessible but not weakly compact with every stationary subset reflecting in an inaccessible, there is a Boolean algebra $A$ with $c'(A)=\kappa$ but $c'(A\oplus A)>\kappa$, and that the case $c'(A)\ne c'(B)$ is not fully described. ([Monk 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0401343))
- **Irredundance and spread.** Rosłanowski and Shelah answered several of Monk's questions on irredundance and spread with ZFC and consistency results (Ann. Pure Appl. Logic 103, 2000). ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9808056)) Monk's report still classes Problems 73, 77, 78 as only partially solved. ([Monk 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0401343))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: The Mathematics of Boolean Algebra](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/): definitions, Stone representation, completions, free algebras, decidability.
- **Reference:** [nLab: Stone duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Stone+duality): categorical statement, role of choice, generalizations.
- **Learn:** [Harding, Lattice Theory Lecture 3: Duality (NMSU)](https://math.nmsu.edu/people/personal-pages/files/ESSLLI3.pdf): Birkhoff and Stone duality with proofs.
- **Learn:** [Lurie, Math 261y lecture 14](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/261ynotes/lecture14.pdf): Boolean rings, Spec, Stone duality, projections in von Neumann algebras.
- **Primary:** [Stone 1936, The theory of representations for Boolean algebras](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1936-1501865-8): the original representation paper (Trans. AMS 40).
- **Primary:** [Monk 2004, Concerning problems about cardinal invariants on Boolean algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0401343): status of Monk's 97 problems.
- **Further reading:** [Givant and Halmos, Introduction to Boolean Algebras (Springer 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-68436-9): standard graduate text.
references.Bootstrap Methods:
## Reference
### Overview
The bootstrap estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by resampling: the unknown data-generating distribution is replaced by an estimate of it, usually the empirical distribution of the sample, and the statistic is recomputed on many samples drawn from that estimate. The resulting bootstrap distribution gives standard errors, bias estimates, confidence intervals, and test critical values without a closed-form sampling distribution; in practice the resampling is typically repeated 1,000 or 10,000 times ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)).

The method was introduced by Bradley Efron in 1979, building on the jackknife of Quenouille and Tukey ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)). Its theory explains when the approximation is valid: for smooth (Hadamard-differentiable) functionals the bootstrap works whenever the functional delta method does, and for studentized statistics it can be more accurate than the normal approximation ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)). It is not universally valid: extremes and heavy-tailed means are standard failures ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)).

Since about 2013 a high-dimensional theory has shown that Gaussian-multiplier and empirical bootstraps approximate the distribution of maxima of sample mean vectors with errors depending on the dimension $p$ only through $\log p$, which underlies simultaneous inference with $p\gg n$ ([Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, Kato, Koike 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09691)).

### Formal definition
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{iid}{\sim}F$, let $\hat F_n$ be the empirical distribution function, and let $\hat\theta_n=\theta(\hat F_n)$ estimate a functional $\theta(F)$. The **empirical (nonparametric) bootstrap** draws $X_1^*,\dots,X_n^*$ i.i.d. from $\hat F_n$, i.e. with replacement from the data, and computes $\hat\theta_n^*=\theta(\hat F_n^*)$. Repeating $B$ times gives $\hat\theta^{*(1)}_n,\dots,\hat\theta^{*(B)}_n$ and, for example,
$$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_B(\hat\theta_n)=\frac1{B-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^B\big(\hat\theta_n^{*(\ell)}-\bar\theta_B^*\big)^2,\qquad \bar\theta^*_B=\frac1B\sum_{\ell=1}^B\hat\theta_n^{*(\ell)},$$
and the **percentile interval** $[t_{\alpha/2},t_{1-\alpha/2}]$ with $t_\beta$ the $\beta$-quantile of the bootstrap values ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)).

The bootstrap is **consistent** for $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)$ with limit law $L$ if
$$\sup_t\Big|P\big(\sqrt n(\theta(\hat F_n^*)-\theta(\hat F_n))\le t\,\big|\,X_1,\dots,X_n\big)-P(L\le t)\Big|=o_P(1),$$
that is, convergence in Kolmogorov distance conditionally on the data ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)).

Variants replace $\hat F_n$ by another estimate of $F$: the **parametric bootstrap** samples from a fitted parametric model; the **residual bootstrap** resamples regression residuals; the **wild bootstrap** multiplies residuals by mean-zero, unit-variance weights, suiting heteroskedastic errors; the **smooth bootstrap** adds noise, i.e. samples a kernel density estimate; and **block bootstraps** (moving block, stationary) resample blocks to preserve dependence in time series ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)).

### Key results
- **Consistency for the mean with a Berry–Esseen rate.** If $E|X_1|^3<\infty$, $Z_n=\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)$ and $Z_n^*=\sqrt n(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)$, then $\sup_t|P(Z_n^*\le t\mid\hat F_n)-P(Z_n\le t)|=O_P(n^{-1/2})$. The proof applies the finite-sample Berry–Esseen bound both to $F$ and to $\hat F_n$ ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)).
- **Bootstrap functional delta method.** If $\theta$ is Hadamard differentiable at $F_0$ with respect to the sup norm, then $\sqrt n(\theta(\hat F_n)-\theta(F_0))\Rightarrow\dot\theta_{F_0}(\mathbb B)$ for a Gaussian process $\mathbb B$, and the bootstrap $\sqrt n(\theta(\hat F_n^*)-\theta(\hat F_n))$ converges conditionally to the same limit; so the bootstrap is consistent whenever the delta method applies ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)).
- **Higher-order accuracy of the studentized bootstrap.** Writing the error in the consistency bound as $O_P(n^{-k})$, the percentile method attains $k=1/2$, the same as the normal approximation, while the bootstrap-$t$ (studentized) method can attain $k=1$; the analysis uses Edgeworth expansions of the bootstrap distribution ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)). Bootstrap interval methods are accordingly classified as first-order or second-order accurate ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)).
- **Failure at extremes.** For $X_i\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$ and $\hat\theta_n=\min_iX_i$, $n\hat\theta_n\Rightarrow\mathrm{Exp}(1)$, but $P(\hat\theta^*_n=\hat\theta_n)=1-(1-1/n)^n\to1-e^{-1}$, so the bootstrap law has an atom of mass about $0.63$ and cannot approximate the continuous limit ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)).
- **Failure under infinite variance (Athreya 1987).** For populations with infinite variance, such as power laws, the naive bootstrap of the sample mean does not converge to the same limit as the sample mean ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)).
- **High-dimensional CLT and bootstrap over rectangles.** Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent mean-zero vectors in $\mathbb R^p$, $S_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_iX_i$, $\Sigma=E[S_nS_n^\top]$, and $\mathcal R$ the closed rectangles. If $\max_{i,j}E[e^{|X_{ij}|/B_n}]\le2$, $\min_j n^{-1}\sum_iE X_{ij}^2>\underline\sigma^2$ and $\max_jn^{-1}\sum_iEX_{ij}^4\le B_n^2\bar\sigma^2$, then
$$\sup_{R\in\mathcal R}|P(S_n\in R)-P(N(0,\Sigma)\in R)|\le C\Big(\frac{B_n^2\log^5(pn)}{n}\Big)^{1/4},$$
with $C$ depending only on $\underline\sigma,\bar\sigma$, and no restriction on the correlation structure ($\Sigma$ may be singular). Under the same assumptions the Gaussian-multiplier and empirical bootstraps satisfy the same bound with probability at least $1-C\delta_{1,n}$, where $\delta_{1,n}$ is the right-hand side above. Both are consistent when $B_n^2\log^5(pn)=o(n)$, allowing $p\gg n$ ([Chernozhukov et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2205.09691)).

### Examples
- **Median.** The standard error of the sample median has no simple closed form; the bootstrap estimates it by the sample variance of the medians of $B$ resamples, and a percentile interval follows from their quantiles ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)).
- **Small-sample undercoverage.** For a variance, percentile-type intervals tend to be too narrow for samples below about 50; with 20 points, a nominal 90% interval covers the true variance only about 78% of the time ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)).
- **Simultaneous confidence sets.** Taking $\hat t_\alpha$ as the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the bootstrap maximum $\|\bar X^*_n-\bar X_n\|_{\max}$ gives a simultaneous confidence rectangle for a $p$-dimensional mean, valid in high dimension by the rectangle bootstrap theorem; the same idea drives stepdown multiple testing ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf); [Chernozhukov et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09691)).

### History
Efron's "Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife" appeared in *The Annals of Statistics* 7(1), pp. 1–26, in 1979 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aos/1176344552)). It was inspired by the jackknife (Quenouille 1949, Tukey 1958, Jaeckel 1972); further theory followed (Bickel and Freedman 1981; Singh 1981), Efron (1987) introduced BCa intervals, and dependent-data versions followed with Künsch's moving block bootstrap (1989) and Politis and Romano's stationary bootstrap (1994) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)). Hall's monograph *The Bootstrap and Edgeworth Expansion* (Springer, 1992) systematized the higher-order theory ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4384-7)). High-dimensional CLTs over rectangles with $\log p$ dependence began with Chernozhukov, Chetverikov and Kato (2013) ([Chernozhukov et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2205.09691)).

### Connections
- [Sampling Distributions](node:Sampling%20Distributions): the bootstrap estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic.
- [Nonparametric Estimation](node:Nonparametric%20Estimation): the empirical bootstrap plugs in the nonparametric estimate $\hat F_n$.
- [Monte Carlo Methods](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Methods): the bootstrap distribution is computed by Monte Carlo resampling.
- [Limit Theorems (LLN and CLT)](node:Limit%20Theorems%20%28LLN%20and%20CLT%29): consistency proofs use the CLT, Berry–Esseen bounds, and Glivenko–Cantelli.
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing): bootstrap critical values and p-values replace analytic null distributions.
- [Multiple Testing and False Discovery Control](node:Multiple%20Testing%20and%20False%20Discovery%20Control): the multiplier bootstrap for maxima gives stepdown FWER control in high dimensions.
- [Statistical Time Series](node:Statistical%20Time%20Series): block and stationary bootstraps keep serial dependence.
- [Cross-Validation](node:Cross-Validation): also resamples the data, but to estimate prediction error rather than sampling variability.
- [Decision Trees and Ensembles](node:Decision%20Trees%20and%20Ensembles): bagging fits models to bootstrap resamples and averages them.
- [Machine Learning Evaluation](node:Machine%20Learning%20Evaluation): bootstrap intervals quantify uncertainty in benchmark scores.

### Common pitfalls
- **Treating the bootstrap as assumption-free.** It can be inconsistent (extremes, infinite variance) and has no general finite-sample guarantee; check that the statistic is smooth or asymptotically normal ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29); [Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)).
- **Ignoring dependence.** Resampling individual observations from a time series or clustered data destroys the dependence the sampling distribution depends on; resample blocks or clusters ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)).
- **Expecting more accuracy than first order from percentile intervals.** The percentile method has the same $n^{-1/2}$ accuracy as the normal approximation; the studentized bootstrap-$t$ can attain $n^{-1}$ ([Chen, UW STAT 535 notes](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf)).
- **Uniformity.** The $O(\cdot)$ error terms in bootstrap accuracy statements are not necessarily uniform in the parameters or the true distribution, as Gleser pointed out in discussion of DiCiccio and Efron ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29)).

### Open problems
- **Ranking bootstrap schemes in high dimension.** The same error bounds hold for Gaussian-multiplier, empirical, and Mammen's wild bootstraps, although the latter two perform slightly better numerically; deriving bounds that certify one scheme over another is named as a future research direction ([Chernozhukov et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2205.09691)).
- **Sharp rates for dependent data.** Error bounds for high-dimensional bootstraps with temporal or graph dependence are substantially slower than in the independent case, and the review says more research is needed on sharp bounds ([Chernozhukov et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2205.09691)).
- **Non-Gaussian limits.** Extending the high-dimensional bootstrap to statistics with non-Gaussian approximating distributions, such as degenerate U-statistics, is stated to be open apart from one exception ([Chernozhukov et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2205.09691)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bootstrapping (statistics), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_%28statistics%29): resampling schemes, interval types, history, and failure cases.
- **Learn:** [Yen-Chi Chen, Lecture 12: The Bootstrap (UW STAT 535)](https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/25A_stat535/Lec12_bootstrap.pdf): definitions, Berry–Esseen consistency proof, functional delta method, failure for extremes.
- **Primary:** [Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, Kato, Koike, High-dimensional Data Bootstrap (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09691): review of high-dimensional CLTs and bootstrap consistency with open directions.
- **Primary:** [Efron, Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife (Ann. Statist. 1979)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aos/1176344552): the founding paper.
- **Further reading:** [Hall, The Bootstrap and Edgeworth Expansion (Springer, 1992)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4384-7): the standard monograph on higher-order bootstrap theory.
references.Braneworld Cosmology:
## Reference
### Overview
Brane cosmology covers theories, tied to [String Theory](node:String%20Theory) and [M-Theory](node:M-Theory), in which the visible four-dimensional universe is a brane embedded in a higher-dimensional "bulk". In bulk models some [extra dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions) are extended rather than compact, and other branes may move through the bulk and affect ours. ([Wikipedia: Brane cosmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brane_cosmology))

In the standard picture, Standard Model fields are confined to a 1+3-dimensional brane while gravity propagates in the bulk. Maartens and Koyama's review concentrates on warped five-dimensional Randall–Sundrum (RS) models, where gravity is localized at low energy and recovers [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) but becomes five-dimensional at high energy, and on Dvali–Gabadadze–Porrati (DGP) models, where gravity is modified at low energy instead. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))

The main cosmological signature is a modified Friedmann equation on the brane: the brane energy density enters quadratically at high energy, and the bulk geometry feeds back as a radiation-like term. Both corrections must be negligible by the time of [Big Bang Nucleosynthesis](node:Big%20Bang%20Nucleosynthesis), which bounds the brane tension. ([Langlois, arXiv:hep-th/0209261](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0209261))

### Formal definition
In five dimensions the bulk obeys Einstein's equations with cosmological constant $\Lambda_5$, and the brane at $y=0$ carries matter $T_{\mu\nu}$ and tension $\lambda$, $T^{\rm brane}_{\mu\nu}=T_{\mu\nu}-\lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)):
$$
{}^{(5)}G_{AB} = -\Lambda_5\,{}^{(5)}g_{AB} + \kappa_5^2\left[{}^{(5)}T_{AB} + T^{\rm brane}_{AB}\,\delta(y)\right].
$$

Projecting the 5D curvature onto the brane with the [Gauss–Codazzi Equations](node:Gauss–Codazzi%20Equations) and using the $Z_2$-symmetric [Israel Junction Conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions), which fix the brane's [Extrinsic Curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature) in terms of its matter, Shiromizu, Maeda and Sasaki obtained effective equations that reduce to the Einstein equations at low energy ([Shiromizu, Maeda & Sasaki, arXiv:gr-qc/9910076](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/9910076); [Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)). With no bulk matter they read ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)):
$$
G_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu} + \kappa^2 T_{\mu\nu} + \frac{6\kappa^2}{\lambda}\mathcal{S}_{\mu\nu} - \mathcal{E}_{\mu\nu}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \tfrac{1}{6}\lambda\kappa_5^4, \qquad \Lambda = \tfrac12\left(\Lambda_5 + \kappa^2\lambda\right),
$$
with $\mathcal{S}_{\mu\nu}=\tfrac1{12}TT_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac14T_{\mu\alpha}T^\alpha{}_\nu+\tfrac1{24}g_{\mu\nu}(3T_{\alpha\beta}T^{\alpha\beta}-T^2)$ quadratic in $T_{\mu\nu}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{\mu\nu}$ the projected bulk Weyl tensor. The effective cosmological constant vanishes when the RS balance between $\Lambda_5$ and $\lambda$ holds ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)). See [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane).

For a Friedmann–Robertson–Walker brane with curvature index $K$ the **modified Friedmann equation** is ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)):
$$
H^2 = \frac{\kappa^2}{3}\rho\left(1 + \frac{\rho}{2\lambda}\right) + \frac{m}{a^4} + \frac{\Lambda}{3} - \frac{K}{a^2},
$$
where $m$ is the mass parameter of a bulk Schwarzschild–AdS$_5$ black hole; energy conservation $\dot\rho+3H(\rho+p)=0$ is unchanged ([Langlois](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0209261)).

### Key results
- **Non-conventional early expansion.** Binétruy, Deffayet and Langlois showed that cosmology on a brane differs from standard cosmology ([BDL, arXiv:hep-th/9905012](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9905012)). With no bulk cosmological constant and no Weyl term, a brane fluid with $p=w\rho$ gives $a\propto t^{1/(3(1+w))}$, so radiation gives $a\sim t^{1/4}$ instead of $t^{1/2}$, which cannot be reconciled with nucleosynthesis. ([Langlois](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0209261))
- **RS-tuned Friedmann equation.** With a bulk cosmological constant, Einstein's equations have a first integral playing the role of the Friedmann equation; when the tension cancels the bulk cosmological constant, standard evolution follows an early non-standard phase, and a small mismatch gives a late-time cosmological constant ([Binétruy, Deffayet, Ellwanger & Langlois, arXiv:hep-th/9910219](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9910219)). Cline, Grojean and Servant obtained normal expansion at nucleosynthesis with faster expansion in the very early universe ([arXiv:hep-ph/9906523](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9906523)), and Csáki, Graesser, Kolda and Terning found the non-compact scenario could be viable while the two-brane hierarchy scenario predicted a contracting universe ([arXiv:hep-ph/9906513](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9906513)).
- **Recovery of 4D gravity in RS2.** A single brane in five dimensions reproduces 4D Newtonian and general-relativistic gravity even though the [Kaluza–Klein](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes) spectrum has no gap ([Randall & Sundrum, arXiv:hep-th/9906064](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9906064)). The 1-brane model has a continuum $m>0$ of KK modes, and for $r\gg\ell$ (the AdS curvature length) the potential is $V(r)\approx\frac{GM}{r}\left(1+\frac{2\ell^2}{3r^2}\right)$, becoming $V\approx G\ell M/r^2$ for $r\ll\ell$ ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)). Garriga and Tanaka showed that Einstein gravity is recovered to leading order on a single positive-tension wall, whereas two-brane models give Brans–Dicke gravity on each wall ([arXiv:hep-th/9911055](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9911055)).
- **Dark radiation.** The $m/a^4$ term is the Coulomb effect of the bulk black hole through $\mathcal E_{\mu\nu}$; it behaves like radiation and nucleosynthesis and CMB data limit it to $\rho_{\mathcal E}/\rho_{\rm rad}\lesssim0.05$ at nucleosynthesis ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)). See [Dark Radiation](node:Dark%20Radiation).
- **Tension bounds.** The high-energy regime must end before nucleosynthesis, so $\lambda>(1\,\text{MeV})^4$ and $M_5>10^4$ GeV. Table-top tests finding no deviation from Newton's law down to about $0.1$ mm give $\ell\lesssim0.1$ mm and the much stronger RS 1-brane limits $\lambda>(1\,\text{TeV})^4$, $M_5>10^5$ TeV, which do not apply to the 2-brane case ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)); see [Tests of the Inverse-Square Law](node:Tests%20of%20the%20Inverse-Square%20Law).
- **Inflation on the brane.** For $\rho\gg\lambda$, $H$ is larger at fixed energy density, adding Hubble damping: steep potentials that do not inflate in general relativity can inflate the brane and stop when $V$ falls below $\lambda$, typically ending in a kinetic-dominated phase with a blue gravitational-wave spectrum. At high energy the tensor-to-scalar ratio is suppressed, $A_T^2/A_S^2\approx\frac{M_p^2}{16\pi}\frac{V'^2}{V^2}\frac{6\lambda}{V}$, and $n_t=-3\epsilon$, yet the general-relativistic consistency relation $n_t=-2A_T^2/A_S^2$ still holds to lowest order in slow roll. High-energy quadratic and quartic potentials are under more pressure from WMAP data than their 4D versions. ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)) Brane effects matter for chaotic inflation when $M_5\lesssim10^{17}$ GeV and allow inflation at field values below the 4D Planck mass $M_p$ though above $M_5$ ([Maartens, Wands, Bassett & Heard, arXiv:hep-ph/9912464](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9912464)). See [Cosmic Inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation).
- **DGP branches.** In DGP, $H^2+K/a^2-r_c^{-1}\sqrt{H^2+K/a^2}=\tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho$, which tends to de Sitter with $H_\infty=1/r_c$; this self-accelerating branch has a scalar ghost and is effectively ruled out by observations. The ghost-free normal branch ($r_c\to-r_c$) needs a $\Lambda$ term to accelerate and screens it, $\Lambda_{\rm eff}=\Lambda-\frac3{r_c}\sqrt{H^2+K/a^2}<\Lambda$, but best-fit flat models from geometric data admit only insignificant screening. ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)) See [DGP Gravity](node:DGP%20Gravity).

### Examples
- **Mirage cosmology.** The FRW brane can be placed in a static Schwarzschild–AdS$_5$ bulk, so cosmic expansion is the brane's motion along the fifth dimension; in Gaussian normal coordinates the brane is fixed and the bulk evolves instead ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962); [Langlois](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0209261)). Kehagias and Kiritsis proposed that motion through a curved bulk produces "mirage" energy densities on the brane ([arXiv:hep-th/9910174](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9910174)). For $m=0$ and $da/dT=0$ the brane is fixed with Minkowski geometry, the original RS 1-brane model ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)).
- **Exact solution.** For $\rho_{\mathcal E}=0$, $K=\Lambda=0$ and constant $w>-1$, $a\propto[t(t+t_\lambda)]^{1/(3(w+1))}$, interpolating between $a\propto t^{1/(3(w+1))}$ for $t\ll t_\lambda$ and the standard $a\propto t^{2/(3(w+1))}$ for $t\gg t_\lambda$ ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)).
- **Ekpyrotic universe.** Khoury, Ovrut, Steinhardt and Turok proposed that the hot big bang results from a bulk brane striking a boundary brane in heterotic M-theory, producing nearly scale-invariant perturbations without inflation and a strongly blue gravitational-wave spectrum ([arXiv:hep-th/0103239](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0103239)). Brane collisions mediated by a 5D scalar can instead induce inflation ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)).

### History
Rubakov and Shaposhnikov's 1983 domain-wall proposal is one of the earliest; Randall and Sundrum's RS1 and RS2 followed in 1999, and the ekpyrotic and cyclic models later ([Wikipedia: Brane cosmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brane_cosmology)). Langlois cites the Hořava–Witten model and the ADD proposal as motivations for confining matter to a 3-brane ([Langlois](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0209261)). The quadratic Friedmann equation (Binétruy–Deffayet–Langlois) and its RS-tuned form with a bulk cosmological constant appeared in 1999 ([arXiv:hep-th/9905012](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9905012); [arXiv:hep-th/9910219](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9910219)). Large static RS2 [black holes](node:Black%20Holes) were constructed numerically by Figueras and Wiseman in 2011 ([arXiv:1105.2558](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2558)).

### Connections
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model): the warped AdS$_5$ setup whose cosmological generalization is the main case studied.
- [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane): the Shiromizu–Maeda–Sasaki equations behind the modified Friedmann equation.
- [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space): the RS bulk geometry.
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): recovered at low energies; the brane is an FRW slice of the bulk.
- [Cosmological Perturbation Theory](node:Cosmological%20Perturbation%20Theory): brane perturbations couple to the bulk through $\mathcal E_{\mu\nu}$.
- [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence): the RS 1-brane model and its black holes are studied through AdS/CFT.
- [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions): the flat ADD alternative motivating brane confinement.
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem): the motivation for the two-brane RS model.

### Common pitfalls
- **RS1 vs RS2 naming.** "RS1" is the two-brane model and "RS2" the single positive-tension brane; Shiromizu, Maeda and Sasaki argue that the negative-tension brane of RS1 is an anti-gravity world ([arXiv:gr-qc/9910076](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/9910076)). Maartens and Koyama say "RS 2-brane" and "RS 1-brane" instead ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)).
- **RS dimensions are not "large" in the ADD sense.** RS2 has one infinite extra dimension whose warp factor makes its volume contribution finite ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)), and four-dimensional gravity without a gap in the KK spectrum ([Randall & Sundrum](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9906064)); its sub-millimetre bound is on the curvature length $\ell$ ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)).
- **The brane equations are not closed.** $\mathcal{E}_{\mu\nu}$ is nonlocal from the brane viewpoint, so the bulk must be solved; the open problems all stem from this ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)).
- **Tightest bound is not cosmological.** In the RS single-brane model, sub-millimetre gravity tests give $M>10^8$ GeV versus $M>10^4$ GeV from nucleosynthesis ([Langlois](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0209261)).

### Open problems
- **Cosmological perturbations on all scales.** Maartens and Koyama name as a key open problem developing realistic approximation schemes and manageable numerical codes for brane perturbations on all scales, to compute [CMB](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background) anisotropies and [large-scale structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure) and confront precision data. ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962))
- **Realistic black holes on the brane.** In 2010 no known solution described a realistic, stable black hole on the brane without naked singularity, and they reported contradictory indications about its nature, for example a non-static exterior for collapsing homogeneous dust; their list asks to settle its staticity, [Hawking radiation](node:Hawking%20Radiation) and horizon ([Maartens & Koyama](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962)). Static RS2 black holes have since been constructed numerically, up to about 20 AdS lengths and apparently stable to axisymmetric perturbations ([Figueras & Wiseman, arXiv:1105.2558](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2558)), and independently confirmed, with Hawking temperature and entropy close to Schwarzschild values at large mass ([Abdolrahimi et al., arXiv:1206.0708](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.0708)). A 2014 survey notes that no line element describing a stable, regular, realistic brane black hole has been found and calls finding a smoothly behaved one the core of the "black hole challenge" ([Pappas, arXiv:1409.0817](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0817)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Brane cosmology (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brane_cosmology): overview of models, history and empirical status.
- **Learn:** [D. Langlois, "Brane cosmology: an introduction"](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0209261): lecture notes deriving the modified Friedmann equation and its constraints.
- **Primary:** [R. Maartens & K. Koyama, "Brane-World Gravity", Living Rev. Relativ. 13 (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962): standard review of RS and DGP cosmology, perturbations and open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Brax, van de Bruck & Davis, "Brane World Cosmology", Rep. Prog. Phys. 67 (2004)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0404011): invited review of RS cosmology, two-brane systems, cyclic models and CMB signatures; [Figueras & Wiseman, "Gravity and large black holes in Randall–Sundrum II braneworlds"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2558): numerical brane black holes.
references.Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus:
## Reference
### Overview
Brownian motion (the Wiener process) is the real-valued continuous-time stochastic process with independent, stationary, centred Gaussian increments and continuous paths. It is a centred Gaussian process with covariance $\min(s,t)$, one of the best known Lévy processes, a martingale, and the scaling limit of rescaled random walks ([Wikipedia: Wiener process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_process)); it is also a strong Markov process ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)). Its paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable and of unbounded variation (see [Bounded Variation](node:Bounded%20Variation)), while their quadratic variation is finite, a fact of crucial importance for stochastic integration ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).

Stochastic calculus builds on this. Because Brownian paths are not of bounded variation, integrals $\int V\,dW$ cannot be defined pathwise as Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals; Itô's construction defines them as $L^2$ limits for adapted integrands, and Itô's formula replaces the chain rule with a second-order correction ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)). Stochastic differential equations $dX_t=\mu(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dB_t$ then model systems driven by noise; Kiyosi Itô developed this theory in the 1940s ([Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation)).

Brownian motion has rich relations to harmonic analysis and its own potential theory (the [Dirichlet problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem), equilibrium measures, polar sets and capacities). Bachelier first studied the mathematical process, modelling stock market fluctuations, and an international society for mathematical finance is named after him ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).

### Formal definition
**Brownian motion.** A real-valued process $\{B(t):t\ge0\}$ is a Brownian motion started at $x$ if $B(0)=x$; for $0\le t_1\le\dots\le t_n$ the increments $B(t_n)-B(t_{n-1}),\dots,B(t_2)-B(t_1)$ are independent; for all $t\ge0,h>0$, $B(t+h)-B(t)\sim N(0,h)$; and almost surely $t\mapsto B(t)$ is continuous. It is standard if $x=0$ ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)). A $k$-dimensional Wiener process has independent one-dimensional Wiener components ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).

**Itô integral.** For an elementary adapted process $V_t=\sum_j\xi_j\mathbf 1_{(t_j,t_{j+1}]}(t)$ with $\xi_j$ $\mathcal F_{t_j}$-measurable,
$$\int_0^tV_s\,dW_s:=\sum_j\xi_j\big(W(t_{j+1}\wedge t)-W(t_j\wedge t)\big),$$
and the integral extends by $L^2$ limits to all adapted square-integrable integrands ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).

**Quadratic variation.** For nested partitions of $[0,t]$ with mesh tending to $0$, almost surely $\sum_j\big(B(t_j^{(n)})-B(t_{j-1}^{(n)})\big)^2\to t$ ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)). For an Itô process $X_i=\int\sum_lV_{il}\,dW_l+\dots$, $d[X_i,X_j]_t=\sum_lV_{il}V_{jl}\,dt$ ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).

**Strong solution of an SDE.** For measurable drift $\mu$ and diffusion $\sigma$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n$ driven by an $m$-dimensional Brownian motion, a strong solution is a $t$-continuous process adapted to the filtration of the initial condition and the Brownian motion that satisfies the integral equation $X_t=Z+\int_0^t\mu\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma\,dB_s$ ([Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation)).

### Key results
- **Existence (Wiener 1923).** Standard Brownian motion exists; Mörters and Peres give Lévy's construction ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).
- **Path regularity.** Brownian paths are Hölder continuous of every order $\gamma<1/2$ and almost surely nowhere Lipschitz, hence nowhere differentiable (Paley–Wiener–Zygmund 1933) ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)). Lévy's modulus of continuity (1937): almost surely $\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\sup_{0\le t\le1-h}|B(t+h)-B(t)|/\sqrt{2h\log(1/h)}=1$ ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).
- **Law of the iterated logarithm.** For standard linear Brownian motion, almost surely $\limsup_{t\to\infty}B(t)/\sqrt{2t\log\log t}=1$ ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).
- **Reflection principle.** With $M(t)=\max_{s\le t}B(s)$ and $a>0$, $P_0\{M(t)>a\}=2P_0\{B(t)>a\}=P_0\{|B(t)|>a\}$ ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).
- **Donsker's invariance principle.** The linearly interpolated, diffusively rescaled random walk $S_n^*$ converges in distribution on $C[0,1]$ with the sup-norm to standard Brownian motion, for i.i.d. steps of any distribution with mean $0$ and variance $1$ ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).
- **Itô isometry.** $V\mapsto\int_0^tV\,dW$ extends from bounded elementary integrands to a linear isometry from the space of adapted processes with $E\int_0^tV_s^2ds<\infty$ into $L^2(P)$, so $E\big(\int_0^tV\,dW\big)^2=E\int_0^tV_s^2\,ds$ ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).
- **Itô's formula.** If $u(t,x)$ is $C^1$ in $t$ and $C^2$ in $x$ and $X$ is an Itô process, then $du(t,X_t)=u_t\,dt+u_x\,dX_t+\tfrac12u_{xx}\,d[X]_t$; for $X=W$, $u(t,W_t)-u(0,0)=\int_0^tu_s\,ds+\int_0^tu_x\,dW_s+\tfrac12\int_0^tu_{xx}\,ds$ ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).
- **Lévy's characterization and time change.** A continuous local martingale with $W_0=0$ is a Wiener process iff its quadratic variation is $t$ ([Wikipedia: Wiener process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_process)). If $X_t=\int_0^tV\,dW$ has $[X]_t=\int_0^t|V_s|^2ds<\infty$ for finite $t$ and $[X]_\infty=\infty$ a.s., then with $\tau(s)=\inf\{t:[X]_t=s\}$ the process $X(\tau(s))$ is a standard Wiener process ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).
- **Martingale representation.** If $W$ is $d$-dimensional with minimal filtration $\mathcal F^W$, every $\mathcal F^W_T$-measurable $Y$ with mean zero and finite variance equals $\int_0^TV_s\cdot dW_s$ for some adapted $V$; hence every $L^2$-bounded $\mathcal F^W$-martingale is an Itô integral and has a continuous version ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).
- **Girsanov's theorem.** Let $Z_t=\exp\{\int_0^tV_s\cdot dW_s-\tfrac12\int_0^t|V_s|^2ds\}$ be a martingale (true if $V$ is bounded, or under Novikov's condition $E\exp\{\tfrac12\int_0^T|V_s|^2ds\}<\infty$), and define $Q(F)=E_P(Z_T\mathbf 1_F)$ on $\mathcal F_T$. Then under $Q$, $\tilde W_t=W_t-\int_0^tV_s\,ds$, $t\le T$, is a standard Wiener process ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).
- **Existence and uniqueness for SDEs.** If $\mu,\sigma$ are measurable and satisfy a linear growth bound and a Lipschitz condition in $x$, uniformly in $t\in[0,T]$, and the initial condition $Z$ is independent of the Brownian motion with $E|Z|^2<\infty$, then the SDE has a $P$-a.s. unique $t$-continuous adapted solution with $E\int_0^T|X_t|^2dt<\infty$ ([Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation)).
- **Tanaka's formula.** For linear Brownian motion and $a\in\mathbb R$, almost surely for all $t>0$, $|B(t)-a|-|B(0)-a|=\int_0^t\operatorname{sign}(B(s)-a)\,dB(s)+L^a(t)$, where $L^a$ is the local time at $a$; with $\operatorname{sign}x=\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{x\le0\}}$; Lévy showed that the local time at zero $\{L(t)\}$ and the maximum process $\{M(t)\}$ have the same distribution ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).

### Examples
- **Martingales of Brownian motion.** $W_t$, $W_t^2-t$ and $\exp(\theta W_t-\theta^2t/2)$ are martingales ([Wikipedia: Wiener process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_process)). By Itô's formula the exponential martingale solves the linear SDE $dZ=\theta Z\,dW$ ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).
- **Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.** $dX_t=-\alpha X_t\,dt+dW_t$ has the unique solution $X_t=X_0e^{-\alpha t}+e^{-\alpha t}\int_0^te^{\alpha s}\,dW_s$, obtained by applying Itô's formula to $e^{\alpha t}X_t$ ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)). For $dx_t=-\theta x_t\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t$ the stationary process is centred Gaussian with $\operatorname{cov}(x_s,x_t)=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}e^{-\theta|t-s|}$, so with $\sigma=1$ the stationary variance is $1/(2\alpha)$, not $1$ ([Wikipedia: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornstein%E2%80%93Uhlenbeck_process)).
- **Geometric Brownian motion.** $dX_t=\mu X_t\,dt+\sigma X_t\,dB_t$ models share prices in the Black–Scholes model ([Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation)).
- **Sample-path facts.** The zero set of Brownian motion is perfect, nowhere dense, Lebesgue-null and of Hausdorff dimension $1/2$; $d$-dimensional Brownian motion is recurrent for $d\le2$ and transient for $d\ge3$ ([Wikipedia: Wiener process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_process)).

### History
Bachelier first modelled Brownian motion in 1900, Einstein and Smoluchowski modelled it in 1905, and Langevin's equations were early linear SDEs ([Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation)). Wiener proved existence in 1923; Paley, Wiener and Zygmund proved nowhere differentiability in 1933; Lévy found the exact modulus of continuity in 1937 ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)). Itô developed the stochastic integral and the theory of SDEs in the 1940s, and Stratonovich later proposed an alternative integral obeying the ordinary chain rule ([Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation)).

### Connections
- [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes): Brownian motion is the central continuous-time example.
- [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): the probability-space framework for path space and $L^2$ integration.
- [Martingales](node:Martingales): Brownian motion and Itô integrals are continuous martingales.
- [Itô Integration](node:Itô%20Integration): the integral defined above, treated in its own note.
- [Stopping Times](node:Stopping%20Times): needed for the strong Markov property and localization.
- [Gaussian Processes](node:Gaussian%20Processes): Brownian motion is the Gaussian process with covariance $\min(s,t)$.
- [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation): the transition density of Brownian motion is the heat kernel.
- [Feynman–Kac Formula](node:Feynman–Kac%20Formula): represents solutions of parabolic PDEs as Brownian expectations.
- [Martingale Pricing](node:Martingale%20Pricing): Girsanov's theorem underlies risk-neutral pricing.
- [Numerical Stochastic Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Stochastic%20Differential%20Equations): discretization of SDEs.
- [Rough Paths](node:Rough%20Paths): a pathwise theory of integration against rough signals such as Brownian paths.
- [Brownian Motion in Physics](node:Brownian%20Motion%20in%20Physics): the physical phenomenon behind the model.
- [Langevin Dynamics](node:Langevin%20Dynamics): SDE models in physics and sampling.
- [Abstract Wiener Space](node:Abstract%20Wiener%20Space): the Gaussian-measure framework for Wiener measure.
- [Path Integral Formulation](node:Path%20Integral%20Formulation): Wiener measure is the Euclidean path integral of a free particle.

### Common pitfalls
- The Itô integral does not obey the ordinary fundamental theorem of calculus: the second-order term $\tfrac12u_{xx}\,d[X]$ is required ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).
- Itô and Stratonovich SDEs give the same solutions for additive noise but different ones for multiplicative noise ([Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation)).
- "Finite quadratic variation" refers to limits along partitions with mesh tending to zero; the supremum over arbitrary partitions with mesh going to zero is infinite (Lévy), so the analogy with bounded variation is imperfect ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).
- Girsanov's theorem assumes the exponential $Z_t$ is a martingale; $E Z_T=1$ is what makes $Q$ a probability measure, and boundedness of $V$ or Novikov's condition guarantees it ([Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Curves in the planar Brownian path.** Pemantle showed the range of planar Brownian motion almost surely covers no line segment; which curves can be covered by a Brownian path is, in general, an open question in Mörters and Peres (2008 draft), and the minimal Hausdorff dimension of curves contained in the range is unknown, although the outer boundary is a curve of dimension $4/3$ (Lawler–Schramm–Werner) ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Wiener process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_process): characterizations, martingales and path properties.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation): SDEs, existence and uniqueness, history.
- **Learn:** [S. Lalley, Notes on the Itô Calculus (University of Chicago, Stat 385)](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/ItoIntegral.pdf): Itô integral, isometry, Itô formula, time change, representation, Girsanov.
- **Primary:** [P. Mörters and Y. Peres, Brownian Motion (draft of the CUP monograph)](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf): construction, path properties, Markov property, Donsker, stochastic integrals, local time.
- **Primary:** [R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples (5th ed.)](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf): graduate probability text with a chapter on Brownian motion.
- **Further reading:** [I. Karatzas and S. E. Shreve, Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus (Springer GTM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0949-2): the standard graduate text.
- **Further reading:** [P. Mörters and Y. Peres, Brownian Motion (Cambridge University Press)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511750489): published version of the monograph.
references.Bullet Cluster:
## Reference
### Overview
The Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-56, also written 1E 0657-558) is a pair of colliding galaxy clusters in Carina at redshift $z \approx 0.296$. Strictly, the name refers to the smaller subcluster, which is moving away from the larger one. Similar evidence comes from other colliding clusters such as MACS J0025.4-1222. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_Cluster))

In the collision the three main mass components behaved differently. The galaxies are effectively collisionless and passed through each other. The X-ray-emitting plasma, which holds most of the ordinary matter, was slowed by drag. The total mass, mapped by [weak gravitational lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing), follows the galaxies, not the gas. ([Chandra/Harvard-CfA](https://chandra.harvard.edu/photo/2006/1e0657/); [Clowe et al. 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0608407))

This spatial separation of the dominant baryons from the inferred mass is why Clowe et al. called the system a detection of [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter) "independent of assumptions regarding the nature of the gravitational force law". The same geometry turns the cluster into a laboratory for the dark-matter self-interaction cross-section per unit mass $\sigma/m$, the parameter of [Self-Interacting Dark Matter](node:Self-Interacting%20Dark%20Matter). ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407); [Markevitch et al. 2004](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0309303))

### Formal definition
The basic observable is the offset between peaks of the weak-lensing convergence $\kappa$ and peaks of the X-ray plasma mass. Clowe et al. reconstruct $\kappa$ from the reduced shear $\vec g=(g_1,g_2)$ of background galaxies via ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407))
$$
\nabla \ln(1-\kappa) = \frac{1}{1-g_1^2-g_2^2}\begin{pmatrix} 1+g_1 & g_2 \\ g_2 & 1-g_1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} g_{1,1}+g_{2,2} \\ g_{2,1}-g_{1,2} \end{pmatrix},
$$
integrated over the data field into a two-dimensional $\kappa$ map. The integration constant, effectively the true mean of $\ln(1-\kappa)$ at the edge of the reconstruction, has to be fixed separately. ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407))

Collisionality is quantified by the scattering depth of the subcluster's dark matter ([Markevitch et al. 2004, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0309303)),
$$
\tau_s = \frac{\sigma}{m}\,\Sigma_s ,
$$
with $\Sigma_s$ the subcluster's dark-matter surface density. Markevitch et al. argue that $\tau_s$ "cannot be much greater than 1" for a clump that survives the passage and stays ahead of its gas. ([Markevitch et al. 2004, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0309303)) Tulin and Yu describe this optical-depth (halo-survival) argument as the first and most conservative of the merger approaches, alongside mass-loss and offset limits. ([Tulin & Yu 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.02358))

### Key results
- **8σ mass–baryon offset (Clowe et al. 2006).** Wide-field ground-based and HST/ACS weak-lensing maps show the potential tracing the galaxies. The centre of total mass is offset from the centre of baryonic (plasma) mass at $8\sigma$. The subcluster lensing peak is detected at $8\sigma$, against $3\sigma$ in the 2004 analysis. They conclude that "any non-standard gravitational force that scales with baryonic mass will fail to reproduce these observations". ([Clowe et al. 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0608407); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407))
- **κ ratio versus mass ratio.** Within 100 kpc apertures the mean convergence of the galaxy+dark-matter components is $\bar\kappa \approx 0.36\pm0.06$ (main) and $0.20\pm0.05$ (sub), against about 0.05 and 0.02 for the plasma: roughly a 7:1 ratio in $\kappa$. In general relativity $\kappa$ is linear in surface density. In non-standard gravity $\kappa$ grows more slowly than mass, as mass to a power down to $1/2$ for a constant-acceleration model, so the true mass ratio would be even higher, up to about 49:1. ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407))
- **Combined strong + weak lensing map.** Bradač et al. combined many new HST/ACS arc candidates (one with a known redshift) with weak-lensing shapes. The result is an absolutely calibrated, high-resolution mass map of the core made without assuming a form for the potential. It confirms the Clowe et al. offset. ([Bradač et al. 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0608408))
- **Bow shock.** The first Chandra data gave a density jump with Mach number $M = 3.2^{+0.8}_{-0.6}$, read as a subcluster velocity of about $4500^{+1100}_{-800}$ km/s ([Markevitch et al. 2004, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0309303)). A 500 ks Chandra observation gave $M = 3.0 \pm 0.4$ ([Markevitch 2005](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0511345)). Randall et al. quote the corresponding shock velocity $4700 \pm 630$ km/s from that work. ([Randall et al. 2008, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0704.0261))
- **Shock speed exceeds subcluster speed.** In Springel and Farrar's hydrodynamical models (10:1 mass ratio) the shock moves at 4500 km/s. The subcluster's mass centroid moves at only 2600 km/s in the rest frame. The difference comes from gas ahead of the shock falling inward at about 1100 km/s, and from the shock front outrunning the subcluster. A generic ΛCDM collision on a zero-energy orbit reproduces the main features. ([Springel & Farrar 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0703232)) N-body/SPH runs by Mastropietro and Burkert prefer an offset 1:6 merger, with the subcluster at about twice the main cluster's virial velocity. ([Mastropietro & Burkert 2008](https://arxiv.org/abs/0711.0967))
- **Analytic σ/m limits.** Three arguments give upper limits. The gas–dark-matter offset gives $\sigma/m < 5\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$, and drag (velocity loss under 1000 km/s) gives $< 7$. Matching the subcluster's mass-to-light ratio to the main cluster's gives $< 1$, since the subcluster can have lost at most a fraction $f\approx0.2$–$0.3$ of its mass. The last limit excludes most of the $0.5$–$5\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ range proposed to flatten galaxy cores. ([Markevitch et al. 2004, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0309303))
- **Simulation σ/m limits (Randall et al. 2008).** SIDM N-body runs compared with the observed galaxy–mass offset of $25\pm29$ kpc give $\sigma/m < 1.25\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ (68%). Assuming equal pre-merger mass-to-light ratios gives $\sigma/m < 0.7\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$. These runs assume the subcluster moves at the shock velocity, although a run at about 3100 km/s changed the results little. ([Randall et al. 2008](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.0261); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0704.0261))
- **Those limits are overstated (Robertson, Massey & Eke 2017).** Bullet Cluster simulations with elastic SIDM, and the first with both SIDM and gas, show that the method used to locate the components matters more than reasonable changes to initial conditions. Shrinking-circle centroids like those of Randall et al. give much larger dark-matter–galaxy offsets than parametric fits to the density or shear. The authors call the $1.25\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ constraint "strongly overstated". For $\sigma/m = 2\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ they find an offset of about 20 kpc, allowed by the observed $25\pm29$ kpc. Gas stripping can also produce spurious offsets. ([Robertson et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.04307); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1605.04307))
- **Ensemble limit (Harvey et al. 2015).** Chandra and HST data on 72 cluster collisions detect dark mass at $7.6\sigma$, lying $5.8\pm8.2$ kpc from the stars. This gives $\sigma/m < 0.47\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ (95%). ([Harvey et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.07675)) Tulin and Yu call it the strongest merger-derived limit but point to Wittman et al. (2017) as disputing it. ([Tulin & Yu 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.02358))

### Examples
- **Geometry.** The two galaxy concentrations are 0.72 Mpc apart on the sky: a less massive western subcluster ($T\sim6$ keV) and a more massive eastern main cluster ($T\sim14$ keV). The line-of-sight velocity difference is only about 600 km/s, so the merger lies nearly in the plane of the sky; the cores passed through each other about 100 Myr ago. ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407))
- **Mass budget.** In clusters, stars make up about 1–2% of the mass and plasma about 5–15%, so the plasma is the dominant baryonic component whose displacement matters. ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407))
- **Composite image.** In the Chandra release image the X-ray gas is pink, galaxies are orange and white, and the lensing mass is blue, with the blue clumps clearly apart from the pink gas. ([Chandra/Harvard-CfA](https://chandra.harvard.edu/photo/2006/1e0657/))
- **Electron–ion equilibration.** Temperatures across the bow shock are consistent with near-instant electron heating, faster than the Spitzer collisional time at 95% confidence. ([Markevitch 2005](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0511345)) Wikipedia reports a later analysis that allows a lower merger velocity of about 3950 km/s if electron and ion temperatures do not equilibrate instantly. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_Cluster))

### History
Chandra first observed 1E 0657-56 in October 2000 for 24 ks. Markevitch et al. (2002) found a bullet-like cool subcluster just leaving the main cluster core, and Clowe, Gonzalez and Markevitch (2004) found a lensing dark-matter clump coincident with the subcluster galaxies. ([Markevitch et al. 2004, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0309303)) The 2006 analysis added three optical data sets, including HST/ACS imaging, and raised the lensing significance by more than a factor of 3 ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407)). NASA released the result on August 21, 2006 as "NASA Finds Direct Proof of Dark Matter". ([Chandra/Harvard-CfA](https://chandra.harvard.edu/photo/2006/1e0657/))

The velocity question followed. Mastropietro and Burkert's simulations required an initial infall of about 3000 km/s at about $2R_{200}$. Using the MICE simulation, Lee and Komatsu put the ΛCDM probability of such an infall at $3.3\times10^{-11}$ to $3.6\times10^{-9}$ and called the cluster "incompatible" with ΛCDM unless a lower-velocity solution exists. ([Lee & Komatsu 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.0939)) Thompson, Davé and Nagamine found that friends-of-friends halo finders merge the two progenitors. With the velocity-aware ROCKSTAR finder, the probability of a high-velocity pair among $\ge10^{14}M_\odot$ haloes is $4.6\times10^{-4}$, and they conclude the cluster does not challenge ΛCDM. ([Thompson et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.7438)) Kraljic and Sarkar instead count expected systems: about $1.3^{+2.0}_{-0.6}$ pairs as extreme in mass, separation and velocity up to $z=0.3$, falling to about 0.1 if the haloes must already have collided. ([Kraljic & Sarkar 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7719))

### Connections
- [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing): weak and strong lensing map the total projected mass independently of light.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): the offset is the standard direct evidence for a dominant, nearly collisionless unseen component.
- [Self-Interacting Dark Matter](node:Self-Interacting%20Dark%20Matter): merging clusters bound $\sigma/m$, which SIDM models need at about 0.5–1 cm²/g on dwarf scales.
- [Modified Newtonian Dynamics](node:Modified%20Newtonian%20Dynamics): the system is the canonical challenge to purely baryonic modified gravity.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): the pairwise-velocity question tests the tail of ΛCDM halo statistics.
- [N-body Simulations](node:N-body%20Simulations): used both for σ/m limits and for the frequency of Bullet-like pairs.
- [Weakly Interacting Massive Particles](node:Weakly%20Interacting%20Massive%20Particles): a collisionless candidate consistent with the observed behaviour.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the lensing-to-mass conversion assumes it; changing the theory changes the inferred mass ratio.

### Common pitfalls
- **Shock speed is not the subcluster speed.** The 4700 km/s shock speed was commonly read as the bullet's speed; in simulations the mass centroid moves at about 2600 km/s. ([Springel & Farrar 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0703232)) Wikipedia reports that early claims of conflict with standard cosmology rested on this erroneous infall velocity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_Cluster))
- **Galaxies are not a free-flight marker.** The galaxies are bound to the dark-matter clump and are dragged back with it, so they do not show where the subcluster would be without collisions. ([Markevitch et al. 2004, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0309303))
- **Centroiding defines the limit.** σ/m limits from offsets depend on how peaks are located; shrinking-circle methods inflate offsets compared with shear-based fits, and present weak-lensing data locate the bullet halo only to about ±40 kpc. ([Robertson et al. 2017, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1605.04307))
- **Lensing maps are projected.** Line-of-sight structure could mimic peaks; Clowe et al. estimate the probability of two suitably aligned gas filaments at about $10^{-6}$. ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407))
- **Dark matter evidence is not a refutation of all modified gravity.** Clowe et al. say the result "does not preclude non-standard gravity", though such a model still needs unseen mass. ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407))

> [!warning] Contested
> **Can MOND explain it?** Angus et al. find that the cluster is dominated by a collisionless component in both GR and MOND, and propose MOND plus ordinary neutrinos of about 2 eV instead of cold dark matter ([Angus et al. 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0609125)). Milgrom has argued that undetected cold gas could supply the mass, which Wikipedia notes AGN feedback makes unlikely. MOG and many-body-gravity proponents claim fits to the lensing ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_Cluster)). Against all of these, Clowe et al. show that any force scaling with baryonic mass fails without extra unseen mass ([Clowe et al. 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0608407)).

### Open problems
- **What σ/m the Bullet Cluster actually excludes.** Robertson, Massey and Eke argue that the published $1.25\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ bound is strongly overstated. They give no replacement bound, and they fit parametric halo models because shrinking circles give unstable results, stressing that simulations should be analysed in an observationally motivated way. They flag gas-induced asymmetries as a systematic that could fake an SIDM detection. They also leave open whether galaxy–dark-matter peak separations in colliding clusters can constrain isotropic SIDM at all. ([Robertson et al. 2017, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1605.04307)) Tulin and Yu note "some tension" between stacked-merger limits and the 0.5–1 cm²/g range favoured on dwarf scales. ([Tulin & Yu 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.02358))
- **Rarity in ΛCDM.** Kraljic and Sarkar find about 0.1 expected systems that have collided like 1E 0657-56 up to $z=0.3$, and state that "the discovery of more such systems would thus indeed present a challenge to the standard cosmology". ([Kraljic & Sarkar 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7719))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bullet Cluster (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_Cluster): properties, ΛCDM velocity debate and modified-gravity claims.
- **Learn:** [Chandra Photo Album: 1E 0657-56 (Harvard-Smithsonian CfA)](https://chandra.harvard.edu/photo/2006/1e0657/): annotated composite image and plain explanation.
- **Primary:** [Clowe et al., "A Direct Empirical Proof of the Existence of Dark Matter" (2006)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0608407): the 8σ lensing–plasma offset.
- **Primary:** [Markevitch et al. (2004)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0309303): analytic σ/m limits and scattering depth.
- **Primary:** [Randall et al. (2008)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.0261): SIDM simulation limits.
- **Primary:** [Robertson, Massey & Eke (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.04307): why the simulation limits are weaker than quoted.
- **Primary:** [Springel & Farrar (2007)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0703232): shock speed versus subcluster speed.
- **Further reading:** [Tulin & Yu, "Dark Matter Self-interactions and Small Scale Structure" (review)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.02358): SIDM constraints from mergers in context; [Harvey et al. (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.07675): ensemble limit from 72 mergers.
references.CMB Acoustic Peaks:
## Reference
### Overview
The angular power spectrum of [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background) temperature anisotropies shows a series of peaks: the first fixes the overall spatial curvature, the second and third carry the densities of ordinary and dark matter, and the odd-to-even peak ratio gives the reduced baryon density ([Wikipedia: CMB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background)). The peaks are acoustic: before recombination at $z\sim10^3$ (about 3000 K) photons and baryons formed a tightly coupled fluid in which pressure gradients act as a restoring force, and CMB anisotropies fall almost entirely under linear perturbation theory, which is why the pattern can be predicted precisely ([Hu & Dodelson, §§1, 3.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).

Hu and Sugiyama separated the ingredients analytically, Sachs–Wolfe effect, acoustic oscillations, diffusion damping, Doppler shifts and reionization, and showed that the acoustic oscillations are nearly model-independent, making them a tool for the matter content and for distinguishing adiabatic from isocurvature initial conditions ([Hu & Sugiyama 1995](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9411008)). Their 1996 paper explained how baryons drive alternating peak heights and gave an analytic small-scale transfer function ([Hu & Sugiyama 1996](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9510117)). Precision analyses use Boltzmann codes: CMBFAST introduced line-of-sight integration, CAMB is still regularly maintained, and CLASS was introduced as a new, more flexible code; parameter-extraction codes typically need about $10^4$–$10^6$ Boltzmann-code calls ([Lesgourgues, CLASS I](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1104.2932)). Lewis, Challinor and Lasenby applied the line-of-sight method to CMB anisotropy and polarization in nearly-FRW models with positive spatial curvature ([Lewis, Challinor & Lasenby](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9911177)).

The peak positions measure the acoustic angular scale: Planck 2018 finds $100\theta_*=1.0411\pm0.0003$, a 0.03% measurement, with $\Omega_ch^2=0.120\pm0.001$, $\Omega_bh^2=0.0224\pm0.0001$ and $H_0=67.4\pm0.5$ km s$^{-1}$Mpc$^{-1}$ in base [ΛCDM](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model) ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)).

### Formal definition
In Fourier space with conformal time $\eta$, an ideal photon fluid obeys $\ddot\Theta+c_s^2k^2\Theta=0$ with $c_s=1/\sqrt3$; the sound horizon is $s=\int c_s\,d\eta\approx\eta/\sqrt3$, and modes caught at an extremum at recombination give peaks at $k_n=n\pi/s_*$ ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)). Projected on the sky at comoving distance $D_*$, peaks lie at
$$\ell_n\approx n\,\ell_a,\qquad \ell_a=\pi D_*/s_*$$
([Hu & Dodelson, §3.1, eq. 11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).

With gravity (Newtonian-gauge potentials $\Psi,\Phi$) and baryon loading $R$, the sound speed becomes $c_s=1/\sqrt{3(1+R)}$ and, for slowly varying $R$ and potentials,
$$[\Theta+(1+R)\Psi](\eta)=[\Theta+(1+R)\Psi](\eta_{\rm md})\cos(ks),$$
so the effective temperature $\Theta+\Psi$ oscillates about a shifted zero point ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)). See [Cosmological Perturbation Theory](node:Cosmological%20Perturbation%20Theory) and the [Boltzmann Equation](node:Boltzmann%20Equation) for the underlying system.

Photon diffusion adds a damping term $\frac{k^2c_s^2}{\dot\tau}(A_v+A_h)\dot\Theta$ to the oscillator, with viscosity coefficient $A_v=16/15$ and heat-conduction coefficient $A_h=R^2/(1+R)$, so that the damping scale is of order $k_d\sim\sqrt{\dot\tau/\eta}$ ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)). The comoving sound horizon at recombination is
$$r_s=\int_0^{a_*}\frac{c_s\,da}{a^2H},\qquad c_s^2=\frac{1}{3(1+R)},\quad R=\frac{3\rho_b}{4\rho_\gamma}$$
([Hou et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1104.2333)).

### Key results
- **Sachs–Wolfe plateau.** In the matter-dominated limit $[\Theta+\Psi]=\tfrac13\Psi(\eta_{\rm md})\cos(ks)$; on large scales the observed fluctuation is $\Psi/3$, so overdense regions appear cold ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **First peak and flatness.** In a flat matter-dominated estimate $\ell_1\approx200$, and the observed first peak constrains the geometry to be nearly flat ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **Baryon loading.** Baryons boost compressional phases, enhancing the odd (first, third, fifth) peaks, while adiabatic damping scales the amplitude as $(1+R)^{-1/4}$ ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **Radiation driving and dark matter.** Decaying potentials in the radiation era drive the oscillations, raising the amplitude by a factor of about 4–5 across $k_{\rm eq}$; a high third peak is "a good indication that cold dark matter both exists and dominates the energy density at recombination" ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)); see [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter).
- **Doppler contribution.** The velocity term is a dipole source whose projection has no strong peak at $x=\ell$, so the [Doppler effect](node:Doppler%20Effect) cannot produce strong peak structure; the observed peaks are acoustic, not "Doppler peaks" ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **Integrated Sachs–Wolfe effect.** Residual radiation driving after decoupling adds $\int(\dot\Psi-\dot\Phi)j_\ell\,d\eta$, in phase with the monopole, shifting $\ell_1$ lower as the matter-to-radiation ratio decreases; at late times potentials decay again once dark energy or curvature dominates ([Hu & Dodelson, §§3.8, 4.2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **Diffusion damping.** Photon diffusion damps modes by $e^{-k^2\eta/\dot\tau}$, and detailed integration gives $k_ds_*\approx10$, suppressing peaks beyond the third ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.6, eq. 20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **Damping tail as a probe of $N_{\rm eff}$ and helium.** Extra relativistic species raise $H$; since $r_s\propto1/H$ and $\theta_s$ is fixed by data, $\theta_d$ grows and small-scale power is suppressed by increased Silk damping. The ratio $\theta_d/\theta_s=r_d/r_s\propto(1+f_\nu)^{0.28}/\sqrt{1-Y_P}$ is independent of $D_A$; because $Y_P$ also shifts it, $N_{\rm eff}$ and $Y_P$ are partly degenerate, and imposing BBN consistency shrinks the $N_{\rm eff}$ error by about 30% ([Hou et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1104.2333)). Planck+BAO give $N_{\rm eff}=2.99\pm0.17$ ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)).
- **Adiabatic versus isocurvature.** Adiabatic perturbations give peak positions in the ratio $1:2:3$, isocurvature ones $1:3:5$; observations favour adiabatic perturbations, supporting inflation ([Wikipedia: CMB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background)).

### Examples
- **Heavier spring.** Baryon loading is like adding mass to a spring hanging in a gravitational field: the zero point shifts to $\Theta=-(1+R)\Psi$ and compressions are enhanced relative to rarefactions ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **Polarization peaks.** Acoustic polarization comes from quadrupoles, has a polarized fraction of about ten percent of the anisotropy at its peak, is out of phase with the temperature peaks, and is pure $E$-mode; density perturbations produce no $BB$ at first order ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)); see [CMB Polarization](node:CMB%20Polarization).
- **ACT DR6.** ACT measured TT, TE and EE to arcminute scales over 10,000 deg² with polarization noise three times below Planck; P-ACT + lensing + DESI DR1 gives $H_0=68.22\pm0.36$, $\Omega_bh^2=0.0226\pm0.0001$, $\Omega_ch^2=0.118\pm0.001$, with no evidence for excess lensing in the power spectrum and no departure from flatness ([ACT DR6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14452)).
- **SPT-3G D1.** SPT-3G alone gives $H_0=66.66\pm0.60$, $6.2\sigma$ from SH0ES; the SPT+ACT+Planck combination gives $H_0=67.19\pm0.38$, and CMB data alone show no evidence for physics beyond ΛCDM ([SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707)).

### History
In the 1970s Harrison, Peebles and Yu, and Zel'dovich argued that primordial inhomogeneities would leave anisotropies at the $10^{-4}$–$10^{-5}$ level, and Sunyaev calculated their imprint; DASI announced the second and third acoustic peaks in 2001, and WMAP launched in June 2001 ([Wikipedia: CMB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background)). Hu and Sugiyama's analytic treatment appeared in 1995–1996 ([Hu & Sugiyama 1995](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9411008); [Hu & Sugiyama 1996](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9510117)). Planck's 2018 release gave the final full-mission parameters ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)), followed by the ground-based ACT DR6 and SPT-3G D1 spectra in 2025 ([ACT DR6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14452); [SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707)).

### Connections
- [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background): the peaks are the dominant feature of its anisotropy spectrum.
- [Recombination and Last Scattering](node:Recombination%20and%20Last%20Scattering): sets $\eta_*$, $s_*$ and the damping scale.
- [Cosmological Perturbation Theory](node:Cosmological%20Perturbation%20Theory) and [Boltzmann Equation](node:Boltzmann%20Equation): the linear Einstein–Boltzmann system.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter) and [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): the third peak and the six-parameter fit.
- [Cosmic Inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation): adiabatic initial conditions give $1:2:3$ spacing.
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): sets $D_*$ and the expansion rate.
- [Big Bang Nucleosynthesis](node:Big%20Bang%20Nucleosynthesis): independent $\Omega_b h^2$ and $Y_P$.
- [Baryon Acoustic Oscillations](node:Baryon%20Acoustic%20Oscillations) and [Large-Scale Structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure): the same sound waves in the galaxy distribution.
- [Dark Radiation](node:Dark%20Radiation) and [Neutrino Decoupling](node:Neutrino%20Decoupling): $N_{\rm eff}$ through the damping tail.
- [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing): the lensing-amplitude anomaly.
- [Damped and Driven Oscillations](node:Damped%20and%20Driven%20Oscillations), [Oscillations and Normal Modes](node:Oscillations%20and%20Normal%20Modes) and [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation): the forced, damped oscillator picture.
- [Spherical Harmonics](node:Spherical%20Harmonics) and [Bessel Functions](node:Bessel%20Functions): multipoles $\ell$ and projection kernels $j_\ell$.
- [Dark Acoustic Oscillations](node:Dark%20Acoustic%20Oscillations): analogous oscillations in interacting dark sectors.
- [Modified Newtonian Dynamics](node:Modified%20Newtonian%20Dynamics): no-dark-matter alternatives must reproduce the peak heights.

### Common pitfalls
- **Peaks count compressions and rarefactions.** The power spectrum measures variance, so both extrema give peaks; baryon loading boosts every other one ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **$\Theta$ is not the observed temperature.** The observed quantity is $\Theta+\Psi$, including the gravitational redshift out of potential wells ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **"Doppler peaks" is a misnomer.** The Doppler term cannot produce strong peaks ([Hu & Dodelson, §3.8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **Damping-tail suppression is not early ISW.** Hou et al. attribute the high-$\ell$ $N_{\rm eff}$ signal almost entirely to increased Silk damping from the faster expansion when BBN consistency fixes $Y_P$; the early ISW effect matters more when $Y_P$ is free ([Hou et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1104.2333)).

### Open problems
- **Hubble tension (open).** SH0ES measures $H_0=73.04\pm1.04$ km s$^{-1}$Mpc$^{-1}$, a $5\sigma$ difference from Planck+ΛCDM, and states that the source of the discrepancy remains unknown ([Riess et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04510)); SPT-3G alone is $6.2\sigma$ from SH0ES ([SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707)).
- **CMB versus BAO.** SPT-3G D1 reports a $2.8\sigma$ difference in ΛCDM between CMB and DESI DR2 BAO results ([SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707)).
- **Lensing amplitude.** Planck's spectra prefer a higher lensing amplitude than base ΛCDM at over $2\sigma$, not supported by lensing reconstruction ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)); ACT DR6 finds no evidence for excess lensing in its spectra ([ACT DR6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14452)).

- **Primary:** [Hu & Sugiyama, Toward understanding CMB anisotropies](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9411008) and [Small scale cosmological perturbations](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9510117): the analytic treatment.
- **Primary:** [Planck 2018 results VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209), [ACT DR6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14452), [SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707): current measurements.
- **Further reading:** [Lesgourgues, CLASS I](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.2932) and [Lewis, Challinor & Lasenby](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9911177): Boltzmann codes; [Hou et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1104.2333) on the damping tail.
references.Calculus of Variations:
## Reference
### Overview
The calculus of variations studies minima and maxima of functionals, typically integrals $J[y]=\int L(x,y,y')\,dx$ of a function and its derivatives, instead of functions of finitely many variables. Classical problems include shortest curves and geodesics, the brachistochrone, Dirichlet's principle for the Laplace equation and Plateau's least-area problem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations); [Stanford notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math63cm/calculus-of-variations.pdf))

The subject has three layers. The first-order theory gives the Euler–Lagrange equation, a necessary condition that a sufficiently smooth minimizer must satisfy. The second-order classical theory (Legendre, Jacobi, Weierstrass) gives further necessary and sufficient conditions for weak and strong minima. The modern theory asks whether minimizers exist at all and how regular they are: the direct method, convexity and Morrey's quasiconvexity, and Hilbert's nineteenth problem solved by De Giorgi and Nash. ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf); [Direct method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_method_in_the_calculus_of_variations); [Hilbert's 19th problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem))
