Optimal control grew out of the calculus of variations: Hamilton's canonical equations, Pontryagin's principle and the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation of [dynamic programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming) generalize the classical conditions to controlled systems. ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf); [Pontryagin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin%27s_maximum_principle))

### Formal definition
Let $L$ be $C^2$ and consider $J[y]=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}L(x,y,y')\,dx$ over $C^2$ functions with fixed endpoint values. If $J$ has a local extremum at $f$, then for every variation $\eta$ vanishing at the endpoints, $\Phi(\varepsilon)=J[f+\varepsilon\eta]$ has $\Phi'(0)=0$; integrating by parts gives the Euler–Lagrange equation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations); [Stanford notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math63cm/calculus-of-variations.pdf))
$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}-\frac{d}{dx}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}=0 .
$$
For $y:[x_0,x_1]\to\mathbb R^n$ it becomes the system $\partial L/\partial y_i-\frac{d}{dx}\partial L/\partial y_i'=0$. ([Stanford notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math63cm/calculus-of-variations.pdf))

**Weak and strong extrema.** On $C^1$ curves there are two natural norms, $\|y\|_0=\max|y|$ and $\|y\|_1=\max|y|+\max|y'|$. Extrema with respect to $\|\cdot\|_0$ are *strong*; extrema with respect to $\|\cdot\|_1$ are *weak*. A $C^0$-ball contains the $C^1$-ball of the same radius, so every strong extremum is a weak one, not conversely, and the Euler–Lagrange equation is necessary for both. Strong extrema can be posed over piecewise $C^1$ curves, which matters in optimal control. ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf))

**Second variation.** For $L\in C^3$, the second variation along $y$ is $\int_a^b\bigl(P\eta'^2+Q\eta^2\bigr)dx$ with $P=\tfrac12L_{y'y'}$ and $Q=\tfrac12\bigl(L_{yy}-\tfrac{d}{dx}L_{yy'}\bigr)$; its Euler–Lagrange equation is the Jacobi equation $Qv-\frac{d}{dx}(Pv')=0$. A point $c>a$ is conjugate to $a$ if the solution with $v(a)=0$, $v'(a)=1$ vanishes again at $c$. ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf))

### Key results
- **Fundamental lemma.** If $f$ is continuous on $(a,b)$ and $\int_a^bfh\,dx=0$ for every compactly supported smooth $h$ (in particular, $h$ vanishing at the endpoints), then $f\equiv0$. Du Bois-Reymond's version: for continuous $f,g$, if $\int(fh+gh')=0$ for all such $h$, then $g$ is differentiable with $g'=f$. ([Fundamental lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_lemma_of_the_calculus_of_variations))
- **Du Bois-Reymond regularity.** If $L$ has continuous first and second derivatives and $\partial^2L/\partial y'^2\ne0$, a function satisfying the weak (integrated) form of the first-variation condition has two continuous derivatives and satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation classically. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations))
- **First integrals.** If $L$ does not depend on $y$, then $\partial L/\partial y'$ is constant along extremals; if $L=L(y,y')$, a nonconstant $y$ solves Euler–Lagrange iff $y'\,\partial L/\partial y'-L$ is constant (Beltrami identity). ([Stanford notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math63cm/calculus-of-variations.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations))
- **Legendre's condition (1786).** If $y$ is a weak minimum, then $L_{y'y'}(x,y(x),y'(x))\ge0$ on $[a,b]$ (positive semidefinite in several degrees of freedom). ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf))
- **Jacobi sufficient condition.** An extremal $y$ is a strict weak minimum if $L_{y'y'}>0$ on $[a,b]$ and $[a,b]$ contains no point conjugate to $a$; absence of interior conjugate points is also necessary for the second variation to be positive semidefinite. On the sphere, conjugate points of great circles are antipodal points. ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf))
- **Weierstrass necessary condition.** With the excess function $E(x,y,z,w)=L(x,y,w)-L(x,y,z)-(w-z)L_z(x,y,z)$, a strong minimum satisfies $E(x,y(x),y'(x),w)\ge0$ at all non-corner points and all $w$: $L$ lies above its tangent line in the $y'$ variable. Weierstrass introduced it in his 1879 lectures; McShane removed his extra normality assumption in 1939. ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf))
- **Direct method.** Let $V$ be a subset of a separable reflexive Banach space that is closed under weak sequential limits (bounded sequences then have weakly convergent subsequences with limit in $V$). If $J$ is bounded below, its minimizing sequences are bounded (coercivity), and $J$ is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous, then $J$ has a minimizer on $V$. ([Direct method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_method_in_the_calculus_of_variations))
- **Convexity and quasiconvexity.** For $J(u)=\int_\Omega F(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx$ with $F$ Carathéodory and bounded below by an affine function, convexity of $A\mapsto F(x,y,A)$ implies sequential weak lower semicontinuity in $W^{1,p}$, and for scalar $u$ or one-dimensional $\Omega$ the converse holds. For vector-valued $u$ with $p$-growth, weak lower semicontinuity is equivalent to quasiconvexity of the integrand (Morrey 1952; Acerbi–Fusco in general), and convex $\Rightarrow$ polyconvex $\Rightarrow$ quasiconvex $\Rightarrow$ rank-one convex. ([Direct method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_method_in_the_calculus_of_variations); [Quasiconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconvexity_%28calculus_of_variations%29))
- **Hilbert's nineteenth problem.** Hilbert asked in 1900 whether solutions of regular variational problems with analytic integrands are analytic. Bernstein (1904) proved it for $C^3$ solutions in two variables; in 1956–1958 De Giorgi and Nash independently proved that the weak solutions have Hölder-continuous first derivatives, completing the solution, and Moser gave another proof. For vector-valued solutions, De Giorgi and Giusti–Miranda showed regularity can fail, with refinements by Nečas. ([Hilbert's 19th problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem))
- **Hamiltonian form and control.** With momentum $p=L_{y'}$ and $H=p\cdot y'-L$, extremals satisfy Hamilton's canonical equations $y'=H_p$, $p'=-H_y$ (Hamilton, 1835). ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf)) Pontryagin's principle (1956) gives necessary conditions for optimal controls through a Hamiltonian, costate equations and a pointwise extremum condition on $H$; the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation gives a necessary and sufficient condition but must hold over the whole state space. ([Pontryagin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin%27s_maximum_principle))
- **$\Gamma$-convergence.** $F_n$ $\Gamma$-converge to $F$ if $F(x)\le\liminf F_n(x_n)$ whenever $x_n\to x$ and every $x$ has a recovery sequence with $F(x)\ge\limsup F_n(x_n)$; then cluster points of minimizers of $F_n$ minimize $F$. De Giorgi introduced the notion. ([Γ-convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma-convergence))

### Examples
- **Shortest graph.** For $L=\sqrt{1+y'^2}$ the Euler–Lagrange equation forces $y'$ constant, so if a minimizer exists it is the straight line through the endpoints. ([Stanford notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math63cm/calculus-of-variations.pdf))
- **Catenoid.** Minimizing $\int_{x_0}^{x_1}x\sqrt{1+y'^2}\,dx$ (area of a surface of revolution) gives $x/c=\cosh((y-\hat c)/c)$; for two coaxial unit circles at distance $2h$ there are two such curves for small $h$ and none for large $h$, and the extremal need not be a graph $y(x)$. ([Stanford notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math63cm/calculus-of-variations.pdf))
- **[Brachistochrone](node:Brachistochrone%20Problem).** The curve of fastest frictionless descent between two points is a cycloid; Johann Bernoulli posed the problem in June 1696, and Newton, Jakob Bernoulli, Leibniz, Tschirnhaus and l'Hôpital responded with solutions. ([Brachistochrone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachistochrone_curve))
- **Dirichlet energy.** Minimizing $\tfrac12\iint|\nabla\varphi|^2$ with prescribed boundary values gives Laplace's equation; Riemann's assumption that a minimizer exists was undermined by Weierstrass and later justified by elliptic regularity theory. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations))
- **Weierstrass's non-existence example.** $W[\varphi]=\int_{-1}^1(x\varphi')^2dx$ with $\varphi(\pm1)=\pm1$ can be made arbitrarily small, but no admissible $\varphi$ achieves $W=0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations))

### History
Newton solved the minimal-resistance problem in 1685 (published in the *Principia*, 1687), and Johann Bernoulli's brachistochrone problem of 1696 drew several solutions. Euler began a systematic theory in 1733 and, after seeing Lagrange's 1755 work, adopted the analytic method and named the subject in 1756. Legendre (1786), Jacobi (1837) and Weierstrass developed second-order conditions, and Hilbert's twentieth and twenty-third problems (1900) encouraged further work; Morse applied the subject in Morse theory, and Pontryagin, Rockafellar and Clarke developed optimal control tools. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations)) Lavrentiev showed in 1926 that the infimum of a problem can depend on the class of admissible functions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations)) Morrey introduced quasiconvexity in "Quasi-convexity and the lower semicontinuity of multiple integrals", *Pacific J. Math.* **2** (1952), 25–53. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2140/pjm.1952.2.25); [Quasiconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconvexity_%28calculus_of_variations%29))

### Connections
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): the first variation is a directional derivative on a function space.
- [Euler–Lagrange Equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations): the first-order necessary condition, in mechanics and field theory.
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) and [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): Euler–Lagrange and Jacobi equations.
- [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics), [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics) and [Principle of Least Action](node:Principle%20of%20Least%20Action): physics as stationary action; the canonical equations.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) and [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws): symmetries of the action give conserved quantities.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): length-minimizing curves; conjugate points on the sphere.
- [Brachistochrone Problem](node:Brachistochrone%20Problem): the 1696 problem that launched the subject.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): Dirichlet's principle.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces), [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the setting of the direct method.
- [Convex Optimization](node:Convex%20Optimization): convexity in the gradient gives lower semicontinuity.
- [Dynamic Programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming): the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation.
- [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory), [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action) and [Path Integral Formulation](node:Path%20Integral%20Formulation): physical actions as functionals.
- Map: [MSC 49 - Calculus of variations and optimal control; optimization](node:MSC%2049%20-%20Calculus%20of%20variations%20and%20optimal%20control;%20optimization), [MSC 49Jxx - Existence theories in calculus of variations and optimal control](node:MSC%2049Jxx%20-%20Existence%20theories%20in%20calculus%20of%20variations%20and%20optimal%20control), [MSC 49Kxx - Optimality conditions](node:MSC%2049Kxx%20-%20Optimality%20conditions), [MSC 49Lxx - Hamilton-Jacobi theories](node:MSC%2049Lxx%20-%20Hamilton-Jacobi%20theories)

### Common pitfalls
- **Necessary, not sufficient.** A solution of Euler–Lagrange only passes the first-derivative test; it need not be a minimum, and a minimum need not exist. ([Stanford notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math63cm/calculus-of-variations.pdf))
- **Weak versus strong.** Weak minima are tested against competitors close in $C^1$; strong minima against competitors close only in $C^0$, a larger set, so strong $\Rightarrow$ weak. Legendre and Jacobi conditions concern weak minima; the Weierstrass condition is needed for strong minima. ([Liberzon](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf))
- **Existence.** A functional bounded below need not attain its infimum (Weierstrass's example); existence needs coercivity and lower semicontinuity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations); [Direct method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_method_in_the_calculus_of_variations))
- **Admissible class matters.** By the Lavrentiev phenomenon, the infimum can differ between classes of admissible functions, so the class (for example smooth, Lipschitz or Sobolev functions) is part of the problem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations))
- **Vector problems.** Convexity is too strong for vectorial problems (the [determinant](node:Determinant) is quasiconvex but not convex); the right condition is quasiconvexity, and regularity of minimizers can fail for systems. ([Quasiconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconvexity_%28calculus_of_variations%29); [Hilbert's 19th problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem))

### Open problems
- **Morrey's conjecture for $2\times2$ matrices.** Morrey conjectured that rank-one convexity does not imply quasiconvexity. For integrands on $m\times d$ matrices, Šverák gave a counterexample for $d\ge2$, $m\ge3$ (*Proc. Roy. Soc. Edinburgh A* **120** (1992), 185–189; [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/S0308210500015080)); the remaining case $m=2$, which includes $2\times2$ matrices, is still open and is known as Morrey's conjecture. Before Šverák's example the question was described as a major unsolved problem of the calculus of variations. ([Quasiconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconvexity_%28calculus_of_variations%29))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Calculus of variations (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations): Euler–Lagrange, examples, Dirichlet's principle and history.
- **Reference:** [Direct method in the calculus of variations (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_method_in_the_calculus_of_variations): existence theorems, convexity and quasiconvexity.
- **Learn:** [Liberzon, Calculus of Variations and Optimal Control Theory (UIUC notes)](http://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf): weak and strong extrema, Legendre, Jacobi and Weierstrass conditions, Pontryagin's principle and HJB.
- **Learn:** [Stanford Math 63CM, Calculus of Variations](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math63cm/calculus-of-variations.pdf): Euler–Lagrange with proof, conserved quantities, catenoids.
- **Primary:** [Morrey, Quasi-convexity and the lower semicontinuity of multiple integrals (1952)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2140/pjm.1952.2.25): the original quasiconvexity paper.
- **Further reading:** [Giaquinta & Hildebrandt, Calculus of Variations I (Springer Grundlehren)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-03278-7) and [Dacorogna, Direct Methods in the Calculus of Variations (Springer Applied Mathematical Sciences, 2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-55249-1): graduate monographs on classical and direct methods; the [Direct method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_method_in_the_calculus_of_variations) article uses Dacorogna as its main reference.
references.Cardinality:
## Reference
### Overview
Cardinality measures the size of a set by one-to-one correspondence rather than by counting a listed enumeration, length, or measure. For finite sets it agrees with counting; for infinite sets it separates different sizes of infinity, and a proper subset can have the same cardinality as the whole set. The notion was formulated by Georg Cantor between 1874 and 1884. ([Wikipedia, Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number))

Beyond comparison of sets, cardinality supports an arithmetic of infinite numbers. Addition, multiplication, and exponentiation are defined by disjoint unions, Cartesian products, and function sets, and in ZFC every infinite cardinal is an aleph. Sums and products of infinite cardinals then collapse to a maximum, so the real content of infinite cardinal arithmetic lies in exponentiation, above all in the value of $2^\kappa$. ([nLab, cardinal arithmetic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cardinal+arithmetic); [Shelah, Cardinal arithmetic for skeptics, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9201251))

The behaviour of $\kappa\mapsto 2^\kappa$ is where set theory meets independence. The continuum hypothesis $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1$ is neither provable nor refutable in ZFC (assuming ZFC is consistent), and Easton's theorem shows that ZFC imposes only two constraints on $2^\kappa$ for regular $\kappa$. For singular cardinals, by contrast, Silver and Shelah proved genuine ZFC theorems. ([SEP, The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/); [Shelah, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9201251))

### Formal definition
Sets $A$ and $B$ are equinumerous, $|A|=|B|$, if there is a bijection $A\to B$; write $|A|\le|B|$ if there is an injection $A\to B$, and $|A|<|B|$ if $|A|\le|B|$ but not $|A|=|B|$. Equinumerosity is an equivalence relation and $\le$ is a quasiorder. ([Zapletal, §2.3, Theorem 2.3.2](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf))

Assuming the axiom of choice, every set is in bijection with a unique cardinal number, namely its initial ordinal: the least ordinal $\alpha$ with a bijection $X\to\alpha$. ([Zapletal, Theorem 3.5.2](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf); [Wikipedia, Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number))

The aleph numbers are the cardinalities of well-orderable infinite sets; $\aleph_0=|\mathbb N|$ is the smallest, and under AC every infinite cardinal is an aleph. Cardinal operations are
$$|X|+|Y|=|X\sqcup Y|,\qquad |X|\cdot|Y|=|X\times Y|,\qquad |X|^{|Y|}=|X^Y|,$$
where $X^Y$ is the set of functions $Y\to X$. ([Wikipedia, Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number); [nLab, cardinal arithmetic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cardinal+arithmetic))

The cofinality $\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$ is the least order type of a cofinal subset of $\kappa$; $\kappa$ is regular if $\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)=\kappa$ and singular otherwise. ([Zapletal, Definition 3.5.6](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf); [Wikipedia, König's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nig%27s_theorem_%28set_theory%29))

### Key results
- **Schröder–Bernstein.** If $|A|\le|B|$ and $|B|\le|A|$, then $|A|=|B|$; the proof builds a bijection from the two injections without choice. ([Zapletal, Theorem 2.3.3](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf))
- **Cantor's theorem.** For every set $A$, $|A|<|\mathcal P(A)|$; in particular $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$, and hence $\mathbb R$, is uncountable, and $|\mathbb R|=2^{\aleph_0}$. ([Zapletal, Theorem 2.3.5 and Corollary 2.4.5](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf); [Wikipedia, Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number))
- **Idempotence of infinite cardinals (AC).** For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, $\kappa+\kappa=\kappa$ and $\kappa\cdot\kappa=\kappa$; hence if $\kappa,\lambda$ are nonzero and at least one is infinite, $\kappa+\lambda=\kappa\cdot\lambda=\max\{\kappa,\lambda\}$. Conversely, Tarski showed in ZF that if every infinite set is in bijection with its Cartesian square, every set can be well-ordered. ([nLab, cardinal arithmetic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cardinal+arithmetic))
- **Comparability is equivalent to choice (Hartogs).** In ZF, for every set $X$ there is an ordinal $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\not\le|X|$ (the least such is the Hartogs number). Consequently trichotomy for cardinals implies the well-ordering theorem, and AC is equivalent to: for all sets $X,Y$, $|X|\le|Y|$ or $|Y|\le|X|$. Hartogs proved this in 1915. ([Wikipedia, Hartogs number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs_number); [Wikipedia, Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number))
- **König's theorem (ZFC).** If $|A_i|<|B_i|$ for all $i$ in an index set $I$, then $\bigl|\bigsqcup_{i}A_i\bigr|<\bigl|\prod_i B_i\bigr|$. Corollaries: $\kappa<\kappa^{\operatorname{cf}\kappa}$ for infinite $\kappa$, and $\operatorname{cf}(2^\kappa)>\kappa$. In its strict form the theorem is equivalent to AC. ([Wikipedia, König's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nig%27s_theorem_%28set_theory%29))
- **Easton's theorem.** Let $G$ be a class function on ordinals such that $G$ is non-decreasing, $\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_{G(\alpha)})>\aleph_\alpha$, and $\aleph_\alpha$ is regular for every $\alpha$ in its domain. If ZFC is consistent, there is a model of ZFC with $2^{\aleph_\alpha}=\aleph_{G(\alpha)}$ for all such $\alpha$. So monotonicity and König's cofinality bound are the only ZFC constraints on $2^\kappa$ for regular $\kappa$. ([Wikipedia, Easton's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number))
- **Silver's theorem.** If $\kappa$ is singular of uncountable cofinality and $2^\lambda=\lambda^+$ for all infinite cardinals $\lambda<\kappa$, then $2^\kappa=\kappa^+$; for example, GCH below $\aleph_{\omega_1}$ forces $2^{\aleph_{\omega_1}}=\aleph_{\omega_1+1}$. ([Wikipedia, Singular cardinals hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_cardinals_hypothesis); [Shelah, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9201251))
- **Shelah's bound.** If $2^{\aleph_n}<\aleph_\omega$ for all $n$, then $2^{\aleph_\omega}<\aleph_{\omega_4}$. This is a ZFC theorem of pcf theory. ([Shelah, Theorem A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9201251))

### Examples
- $\mathbb Z$, the set of finite sequences from a countable set, and $\mathbb Q$ are countable; with AC a countable union of countable sets is countable. ([Zapletal, Theorems 2.4.2–2.4.3](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf))
- Since the algebraic reals are countable and $\mathbb R$ is not, transcendental numbers exist (Cantor). ([Zapletal, Corollary 2.4.5](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf))
- Every successor cardinal, such as $\aleph_1=\omega_1$, is regular (using AC), whereas $\aleph_\omega$ has cofinality $\omega$. By König, $\operatorname{cf}(2^{\aleph_0})>\aleph_0$. ([Zapletal, Theorem 3.5.7](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf); [Shelah, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9201251); [Wikipedia, König's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nig%27s_theorem_%28set_theory%29))

### History
Cantor formulated the continuum hypothesis in 1878, and in 1891 gave the diagonal argument, simpler than his 1874 proof that $\mathbb R$ is larger than $\mathbb N$. Kőnig presented his theorem at the 1904 Heidelberg ICM (published 1905), and Hartogs's theorem dates from 1915. ([Wikipedia, Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number); [Wikipedia, König's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nig%27s_theorem_%28set_theory%29); [Wikipedia, Hartogs number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs_number))

Gödel showed that ZFC + GCH is consistent if ZFC is, using the inner model $L$; Cohen (1963) introduced forcing to show ZFC + $\neg$CH is consistent. Easton extended forcing to all regular cardinals (published 1970), and Silver's 1974 theorem showed that singular cardinals obey real ZFC laws, leading to Shelah's pcf theory. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/); [Wikipedia, Easton's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton%27s_theorem); [Shelah, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9201251))

### Connections
- [Functions and Relations](node:Functions%20and%20Relations): injections, surjections, and bijections are the comparison maps.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): ZFC, ordinals, and forcing are the setting for infinite cardinal arithmetic.
- [Axiom of Choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice): equivalent to cardinal comparability (Hartogs) and needed for idempotence and König's theorem.
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): $|\mathbb R|=2^{\aleph_0}$ measures size, not metric structure.
- [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory): the Löwenheim–Skolem phenomena separate the size of a structure from its first-order theory.
- [MSC 03Exx - Set theory](node:MSC%2003Exx%20-%20Set%20theory): the MSC home of cardinal arithmetic and independence results.

### Common pitfalls
Cardinality is not order type: $\omega$ and $\omega+1$ are different ordinals of the same cardinality. Without AC, cardinals need not be comparable and need not be alephs, so rules such as $\kappa\cdot\kappa=\kappa$ do not transfer to ZF. König's theorem gives $\operatorname{cf}(2^{\aleph_0})>\aleph_0$, so $2^{\aleph_0}\ne\aleph_\omega$; that is a consequence, not an extra axiom. ([Wikipedia, Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number); [Wikipedia, Hartogs number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs_number); [nLab, cardinal arithmetic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cardinal+arithmetic); [Wikipedia, König's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nig%27s_theorem_%28set_theory%29))

### Open problems
- **Settling CH by new axioms.** CH is independent of ZFC, but whether it has a determinate answer, and whether new axioms should settle it, is unresolved. The SEP calls the status of local approaches "somewhat unsettled", describes Woodin's axiom $(*)$, which implies $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, and describes candidate ultimate inner models that would decide CH differently. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))
- **Sharpening Shelah's $\aleph_{\omega_4}$ bound.** When $\aleph_\omega$ is a strong limit, Shelah's bound is $2^{\aleph_\omega}<\aleph_{\omega_4}$, yet $2^{\aleph_\omega}<\aleph_{\omega_1}$ in all known models where SCH fails at $\aleph_\omega$. Garti (2024) says no significant progress has been made on this gap in either direction for decades. Shelah's survey also describes the subscript 4 as "admittedly very strange". ([Garti, Weak diamond and pcf theory](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.03142v1); [Shelah](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9201251))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cardinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number): definitions, alephs, arithmetic, history.
- **Learn:** [Zapletal, Undergraduate logic sequence notes](https://people.clas.ufl.edu/zapletal/files/notesset3.pdf): proofs of Schröder–Bernstein, Cantor, countability, and regularity of successor cardinals.
- **Primary:** [Shelah, Cardinal arithmetic for skeptics](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9201251): Bull. AMS survey of pcf theory, Silver's theorem, and the $\aleph_{\omega_4}$ bound.
- **Further reading:** [Jech, Set Theory](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL9076052W): the standard graduate text (Third Millennium edition, Springer); [SEP, The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/): independence and the search for new axioms.
references.Carleson's Theorem:
## Reference
### Overview
Carleson's theorem says that the Fourier series of a square-integrable periodic function converges to the function at almost every point. Hunt extended it to every periodic $f \in L^p$ with $1 < p \le \infty$ (the Carleson–Hunt theorem), and the analogous statement holds for Fourier integrals of $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R})$, $1 < p \le 2$. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))

Pointwise convergence of Fourier series is delicate. The Dirichlet kernel is not positive and its $L^1$ norm grows like $\tfrac{4}{\pi^2}\log N$; by a Baire-category argument the continuous functions whose Fourier series converge at a given point form a meager set, and there are integrable functions whose Fourier series diverge everywhere. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series)) Before Carleson the best general a.e. bound for $L^2$ was $S_N f(x) = o((\log N)^{1/2})$ (Kolmogorov–Seliverstov–Plessner). ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))

The substance of the theorem is a bound for a nonlinear maximal operator, the Carleson operator, which commutes with translations and dilations and is invariant under modulations. Fefferman's proof used both time and frequency information in an operator-theoretic fashion, and the study of the bilinear Hilbert transform led Lacey and Thiele to their proof by tiles, trees and size. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008)) A proof has been formalized in Lean. ([arXiv:2405.06423](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06423))

### Formal definition
For a $2\pi$-periodic integrable $f$ with Fourier coefficients $\hat f(n)$, the symmetric partial sums are
$$S_N f(x) = \sum_{|n| \le N} \hat f(n)\, e^{inx}.$$
**Theorem (Carleson 1966; Hunt).** If $f$ is periodic and $f \in L^p$ for some $p \in (1, \infty]$, then $S_N f(x) \to f(x)$ for almost every $x$. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))

On the line, Lacey's exposition uses the one-sided Carleson operator
$$\mathcal{C}f(x) = \sup_{N} \Bigl| \int_{-\infty}^{N} \hat f(\xi)\, e^{i x \xi}\, d\xi \Bigr|, \qquad x \in \mathbb{R},$$
and the core estimate is the weak-type bound $|\{\mathcal{C}f > \lambda\}| \lesssim \lambda^{-2}\|f\|_2^2$ for $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$. Almost-everywhere convergence follows by approximating $f$ by smooth compactly supported $g$, for which inversion holds exactly, and controlling the error by $\mathcal{C}(f-g)$. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008))

### Key results
- **Carleson–Hunt $L^p$ bound with constants.** For $1 < p < \infty$, the linearized Carleson operators $\mathcal{C}_N$ satisfy $|\{|\mathcal{C}_N \mathbf 1_E| > \lambda\}| \le K_p^p \lambda^{-p}|E|$ for every set $E$ of finite measure, and the constants satisfy $K_p \lesssim p^2/(p-1)$, which blow up as $p \to 1$. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008))
- **Stein–Sawyer continuity (maximal) principle.** Let $S_n : L^p(\mu) \to L^0(\mu)$, $1 \le p \le 2$, be continuous in measure and commute with a family of measure-preserving maps satisfying a mixing hypothesis (in Stein's original setting: translations on a compact abelian group). Then $\sup_n |S_n f| < \infty$ a.e. for every $f \in L^p$ if and only if $f \mapsto \sup_n|S_n f|$ is of weak type $(p,p)$. For $p > 2$ the same holds for positive operators (Sawyer). ([Weber, arXiv:1602.09025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1602.09025))
- **Failure at $p = 1$.** Kolmogorov (1923) constructed $f \in L^1$ whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere, later everywhere. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series))
- **Sharpness for continuous functions.** For every null set $E$ there is a continuous periodic function whose Fourier series diverges at every point of $E$ (Kahane–Katznelson). Combined with Carleson's theorem: a set is the divergence set of some continuous function's Fourier series iff it has measure zero. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series); [Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Below $L^p$.** Sjölin (1971) proved a.e. convergence on $L\log^+L\,\log^+\log^+L$ and Antonov (1996) on $L\log^+L\,\log^+\log^+\log^+L$; Konyagin (2000) found everywhere-divergent Fourier series in a space slightly larger than $L(\log^+L)^{1/2}$. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Walsh analogue.** For the Walsh–Paley system, Billard gave the analogous extension for $L^2$ and Sjölin extended it to all $1<p<\infty$. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008)) The Walsh functions $W_k$ take only the values $\pm1$ on dyadic intervals and form an orthonormal basis of $L^2[0,1]$, and every $f \in L^2[0,1]$ has an a.e. convergent Walsh series. ([Wikipedia: Walsh function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walsh_function)) Thiele's Walsh-model paper presents the full proof in a setting where many of the technical difficulties are minimized. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008))
- **Quadratic Carleson theorem (Lie 2009).** The generalized Carleson operator with polynomial phase function of degree two is of weak type $(2,2)$, via a new approach to the time-frequency analysis of the quadratic phase. ([arXiv:0710.2168](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.2168); [Crossref: GAFA 19 (2009) 457–497](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/s00039-009-0010-x))
- **Polynomial Carleson theorem (Lie 2020).** Stein conjectured that for each degree $d$, $\mathcal{C}_d f(x)=\sup_{\deg P \le d}\bigl|\int e^{iP(y)} f(x-y)\,\frac{dy}{y}\bigr|$ is bounded on $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$; the case $d=1$ is Carleson's theorem. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008)) Lie proved the one-dimensional case for all $1<p<\infty$, with a direct strong $L^2$ bound, using higher-order wave packets and a new tile discretization. ([Annals of Math. 192 (2020) 47–163](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2020/192-1/p02)) Earlier, Stein handled the purely quadratic case without linear term and Stein–Wainger all degrees without linear term, which does not contain Carleson–Hunt. ([Lie, arXiv:1105.4504](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1105.4504))

### Examples
- **Continuous functions.** A continuous periodic function is in $L^2$, so its Fourier series converges a.e., but du Bois-Reymond gave a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at a point. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series))
- **Bounded variation.** For functions of [bounded variation](node:Bounded%20Variation) the series converges at every point of continuity (Dirichlet–Jordan), with no need for Carleson's theorem. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series))
- **Norm versus pointwise.** For $1<p<\infty$, $S_Nf \to f$ in $L^p$; this fails for $p=1,\infty$. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series))
- **The Lacey–Thiele decomposition.** A tile is a dyadic rectangle $s = I_s \times \omega_s$ of area one in the time-frequency plane, split into halves $s_\pm$. Tiles are ordered by $s < s'$ iff $I_s \subset I_{s'}$ and $\omega_s \supset \omega_{s'}$; a tree is a set of tiles below a common top. The size of a collection measures $|I_{\mathbf T}|^{-1/2}\bigl(\sum_{s\in\mathbf T}|\langle f,\varphi_s\rangle|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$ over trees, and the density measures how much of the exceptional set $E$ the linearizing function $N(x)$ sends into each tile. The Size Lemma splits any collection into a part of half the size plus trees whose top intervals have total length $\sum|I_{\mathbf T}| \lesssim \mathrm{size}^{-2}$ (Lacey calls this sum the count), the Density Lemma does the same with $\sum|I_{\mathbf T}| \lesssim \mathrm{dense}^{-1}$, and the Tree Lemma bounds a single tree's contribution by $|I_{\mathbf T}|\cdot\mathrm{size}\cdot\mathrm{dense}$; iterating gives a summable bound. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008))

### History
Luzin conjectured a.e. convergence for $L^2$; Kolmogorov's 1923 example showed that the $L^1$ analogue fails, and Carleson said he first tried to find a continuous counterexample before proving the conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem)) The proof appeared as L. Carleson, "On convergence and growth of partial sums of Fourier series", *Acta Math.* 116 (1966), 135–157. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392815))

Hunt extended the proof to $L^p$. Carleson's paper is very hard to read; Charles Fefferman gave a new proof of Hunt's extension by bounding a maximal operator, and Lacey and Thiele gave a much simpler $L^2$ proof inspired by Fefferman's. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem)) Fefferman introduced the wave-packet discretization of the Carleson operator, and Lie's polynomial-phase work answers a question of Fefferman by proving a direct $L^2$ bound without interpolation. ([Lie, arXiv:1105.4504](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1105.4504))

A blueprint by Becker, van Doorn, Thiele and others (v1 2024, v2 2025) reduces the classical theorem for continuous functions to a new generalized theorem and proves it, as a guide to the Lean code. ([arXiv:2405.06423](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06423)) The formalization in Lean 4 was completed in 2025. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))

### Connections
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): the central pointwise-convergence theorem for Fourier series.
- [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration) and [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): "almost everywhere" and null divergence sets.
- [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces): holds for $1<p\le\infty$, fails on $L^1$; constants blow up as $p\to1$.
- [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence): norm, pointwise, and a.e. convergence separated sharply.
- [Cesàro and Abel Summation](node:Cesàro%20and%20Abel%20Summation): Fejér means converge where partial sums may not.
- [Littlewood–Paley Theory](node:Littlewood–Paley%20Theory) and [Singular Integral Operators](node:Singular%20Integral%20Operators): the Carleson operator is a modulated maximal Hilbert transform.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) and [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems): Stein's continuity principle links a.e. convergence to maximal inequalities for operators commuting with measure-preserving maps.
- [Orthogonal Expansions and Wavelets](node:Orthogonal%20Expansions%20and%20Wavelets): Walsh series, the dyadic model case.
- [Formal Verification and Proof Assistants](node:Formal%20Verification%20and%20Proof%20Assistants): the Lean formalization.
- [MSC 42Axx - Harmonic analysis in one variable](node:MSC%2042Axx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20one%20variable): its subject code.

### Common pitfalls
- **"Converges everywhere."** Only almost everywhere: continuous functions can diverge on any prescribed null set. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series))
- **Applying it to $L^1$.** Kolmogorov's example rules this out. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Confusing it with Fejér's theorem.** Cesàro means of the Fourier series of a continuous function converge uniformly; that is a statement about Fejér means, not the partial sums $S_Nf$. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Several variables.** For partial sums over dilates of a fixed polygon (squares, for example) the maximal operator is dominated by operators equivalent to the one-dimensional Carleson operator, so it is bounded on $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. Over arbitrary rectangles centred at the origin this fails: Fefferman gave a bounded compactly supported function whose rectangular maximal partial sum is infinite on a set of positive measure. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008)) Spherical partial sums are a separate, open case. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Linear terms matter.** Stein–Wainger bounds for polynomial phases without a linear term do not contain the Carleson–Hunt result, and the linear wave-packet framework is not invariant under quadratic modulations, so polynomial phases with linear terms need higher-order wave packets. ([Lie, arXiv:1105.4504](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1105.4504))

### Open problems
- **Spherical partial sums.** A.e. convergence of spherical partial sums of multiple Fourier series of $L^2$ functions is open. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **$L\log L$.** Whether the Fourier series of every $f \in L\log L(\mathbb T)$ converges a.e. is open; Lie states it as a conjecture, the "mystery of the story", with Antonov's $L\log L\log\log\log L$ the best known positive result. ([Lie, arXiv:1204.6542](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1204.6542)) Wikipedia names $L\log^+L$ as the simplest candidate for a largest natural space consistent with Antonov's and Konyagin's results. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Hardy's question.** Hardy showed that the partial sums of an integrable function are $o(\log N)$ a.e. and asked whether this is best possible; Lacey records that the question is still open, with the best lower bound coming from Konyagin's example. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008))
- **Product setting.** Lacey records that there are as yet no positive results relating to Carleson's theorem in a product (multiparameter) setting, where Fefferman's example shows the rectangular maximal operator can be infinite on a set of positive measure. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Carleson's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem): statement, history, extensions, open problems.
- **Learn:** [Lacey, Carleson's Theorem: Proof, Complements, Variations](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008): full Lacey–Thiele proof with tiles, trees, size and density lemmas, plus complements and conjectures.
- **Learn:** [Bonn summer school: Carleson theorems and Radon-like behavior](https://www.math.uni-bonn.de/~thiele/workshop15/topics.html): reading list from Lacey–Thiele through Lie's quadratic Carleson operator and Stein–Wainger.
- **Primary:** [Lie, The Polynomial Carleson operator, Annals of Math. 192 (2020)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2020/192-1/p02): proof of Stein's conjecture in one dimension.
- **Primary:** [Carleson 1966, Acta Math. 116 (Crossref record)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392815): the original paper.
- **Primary:** [Blueprint for the formalization of Carleson's theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06423): a modern proof written for Lean verification.
- **Further reading:** [Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis (GTM, Springer 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4939-1194-3) and [Grafakos, Modern Fourier Analysis (GTM, Springer 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4939-1230-8): graduate texts; Wikipedia cites *Modern Fourier Analysis* as a book containing a proof of Carleson's theorem ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem)).
references.Category Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Category theory studies [mathematical structures](node:Mathematical%20Structures) through objects, morphisms between them, and associative composition with identities. Functors are the structure-preserving maps between categories, and natural transformations compare two functors with the same source and target, compatibly with every morphism. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory); [Stacks, Yoneda section](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/001L))

The subject's central organizing idea is the universal property. Leinster's textbook presents three formulations of universal properties, namely adjoint functors, representable functors, and limits, and then shows how they are related. Characterizing a construction by how morphisms go into or out of it determines it up to unique isomorphism, independently of how it is built. ([Leinster, Basic Category Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.09375); [Stacks, Yoneda](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/001L))

Category theory grew out of algebraic topology and homological algebra, was developed extensively for scheme theory in algebraic geometry, and later reached logic and the semantics of programming languages. Its higher-dimensional extensions (2-categories, bicategories, $n$-categories, $\infty$-categories) form higher category theory. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory); [Lurie, Higher Topos Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608040))

### Formal definition
A **category** $\mathcal C$ consists of a class of objects; for objects $x,y$ a collection $\mathcal C(x,y)$ of morphisms $f:x\to y$; identities $1_x\in\mathcal C(x,x)$; and composition $\mathcal C(y,z)\times\mathcal C(x,y)\to\mathcal C(x,z)$, $(g,f)\mapsto g\circ f$, which is associative, $h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f$, and unital, $1_y\circ f=f=f\circ 1_x$. A category is **locally small** if each $\mathcal C(x,y)$ is a set, and a locally small category is **small** if its objects also form a set. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory); [Sharifi, §1.1](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch01.html))

A **functor** $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ assigns objects to objects and morphisms $f:x\to y$ to morphisms $F f:Fx\to Fy$, preserving identities and composition; a contravariant functor reverses the direction of morphisms. A **natural transformation** $\alpha:F\Rightarrow G$ is a family $\alpha_x:Fx\to Gx$ with $G(f)\circ\alpha_x=\alpha_y\circ F(f)$ for every $f:x\to y$; it is a natural isomorphism when every $\alpha_x$ is an isomorphism. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory))

An **adjunction** $F\dashv G$ between $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ is a bijection $\mathcal D(Fx,y)\cong\mathcal C(x,Gy)$ natural in $x$ and $y$. It determines a unit $\eta:1_{\mathcal C}\Rightarrow GF$ and a counit $\varepsilon:FG\Rightarrow 1_{\mathcal D}$, and the composites $F\eta$ followed by $\varepsilon F$, and $\eta G$ followed by $G\varepsilon$, are identities. ([Stacks, Definition 4.24.1 and Lemma 4.24.7](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0036))

A **limit** of a diagram $D:I\to\mathcal C$ is a universal cone over $D$; when all $I$-shaped limits exist, $\lim$ is right adjoint to the diagonal functor $\Delta:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C^I$ sending an object to the constant diagram. Colimits are the dual notion. ([Sharifi, Proposition 1.5.6](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch01.html))

### Key results
- **Yoneda lemma.** For an object $U$ of $\mathcal C$ and a presheaf $F:\mathcal C^{op}\to\mathrm{Set}$, the map $s\mapsto s_U(1_U)$ is a bijection $\mathrm{Nat}(h_U,F)\cong F(U)$, where $h_U=\mathcal C(-,U)$; for a small category the bijection is natural in $U$ and $F$. In particular every natural transformation $h_U\to h_V$ is $h(\phi)$ for a unique $\phi:U\to V$, so the Yoneda embedding $U\mapsto h_U$ is fully faithful and an object is determined up to unique isomorphism by the functor it represents. ([Stacks, Lemma 4.3.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/001L); [Sharifi, Theorem 1.3.6](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch01.html))
- **Adjoints preserve limits.** If $F\dashv G$, then $F$ preserves every colimit that exists in its domain and $G$ preserves every limit that exists in its domain. Also $F$ is fully faithful iff the unit is an isomorphism, and $G$ is fully faithful iff the counit is an isomorphism. ([Stacks, Lemma 4.24.4](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0036); [Stacks, Lemma 4.24.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0038))
- **Freyd's general adjoint functor theorem.** Let $\mathcal C$ be complete and locally small and let $R:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ preserve small limits. Then $R$ has a left adjoint iff it satisfies the solution set condition: for each object $d$ of $\mathcal D$ there is a set of morphisms $d\to R(c_i)$ through which every morphism $d\to R(c)$ factors. The **special adjoint functor theorem** replaces the solution set condition by hypotheses on the categories: $\mathcal C$ complete, locally small, well-powered, with a small cogenerating set, and $\mathcal D$ locally small. ([nLab, adjoint functor theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/adjoint+functor+theorem); [Wikipedia, Adjoint functors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_functors))
- **Recognition of equivalences.** A functor is an equivalence of categories iff it is fully faithful and essentially surjective. In classical mathematics the "if" direction uses the [axiom of choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice) to pick a quasi-inverse; the version with split essentially surjective functors does not need it. ([nLab, equivalence of categories](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+of+categories))
- **Construction of limits.** A category has all small limits as soon as it has all small products and equalizers, and has all finite limits once it has pullbacks and a terminal object. Covariant hom-functors preserve limits: $\mathcal C(c,\lim F)\cong\lim\,\mathcal C(c,F(-))$. ([nLab, limit](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/limit))
- **Kan extensions subsume the other universal constructions.** For $p:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C'$ and $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$, a left Kan extension $\mathrm{Lan}_pF$ is universal among functors $G$ with a transformation $F\Rightarrow G\circ p$; if $\mathcal C$ is small and $\mathcal D$ cocomplete, all left Kan extensions exist and are computed pointwise by colimits. A limit of $F$ is the right Kan extension along $\mathcal C\to 1$, and a functor has a left adjoint exactly when the right Kan extension of the identity along it exists and is preserved by it. ([nLab, Kan extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kan+extension); [Wikipedia, Kan extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kan_extension))

### Examples
- A group $G$ is a category with one object $x$ and $\mathrm{Mor}(x,x)=G$, composition being the group law; every one-object groupoid is of this form. ([Stacks, Example 4.2.6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0019))
- The free group functor $F:\mathrm{Set}\to\mathrm{Grp}$ is left adjoint to the forgetful functor; the unit includes generators, and the counit sends a generator to the group element it names. ([Wikipedia, Adjoint functors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_functors))
- For [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups), $-\otimes A$ is left adjoint to $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$: $\mathrm{Hom}(X\otimes A,Y)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(X,\mathrm{Hom}(A,Y))$ naturally (the tensor–hom adjunction). ([Wikipedia, Adjoint functors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_functors))
- Small categories, functors, and natural transformations form the 2-category $\mathbf{Cat}$; a 2-category with one object is essentially a monoidal category. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory))

### History
Eilenberg and Mac Lane used specific functors and natural transformations in their 1942 paper on [group extensions](node:Group%20Extensions) and homology, and introduced categories, functors, and natural transformations in general in "General theory of natural equivalences," Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 58 (1945), 231–294. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1945-0013131-6))

Daniel Kan introduced adjoint functors in "Adjoint functors," Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 87 (1958), 294–329, motivated by homological algebra; Kan extensions had appeared in Cartan and Eilenberg's 1956 *Homological Algebra* in the computation of derived functors. Freyd's adjoint functor theorems originate in the exercises of his 1964 book *Abelian Categories*. ([Wikipedia, Adjoint functors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_functors); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1958-0131451-0); [Wikipedia, Kan extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kan_extension); [nLab, adjoint functor theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/adjoint+functor+theorem))

Mac Lane's *Categories for the Working Mathematician* (Springer, Graduate Texts in Mathematics) contains the section "All Concepts Are Kan Extensions." Lurie's *Higher Topos Theory* develops $\infty$-category theory using quasicategories and applies it to higher analogues of Grothendieck topoi. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-4721-8); [Wikipedia, Kan extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kan_extension); [Lurie, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608040))

### Connections
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory): groups are exactly the one-object groupoids, and many constructions (free groups, abelianization) are adjoints.
- [Functions and Relations](node:Functions%20and%20Relations): the category of sets and functions is the basic example, and relations form another category.
- [Yoneda Lemma](node:Yoneda%20Lemma): the representability result at the core of the subject.
- [Adjoint Functors](node:Adjoint%20Functors): the most pervasive form of universal property.
- [Groupoids](node:Groupoids): categories in which every morphism is invertible.
- [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra): abelian categories and derived functors are its categorical setting; see [Abelian Categories](node:Abelian%20Categories).
- [Toposes](node:Toposes): categories that behave like categories of sheaves and support an internal logic.
- [Monads and Algebraic Theories](node:Monads%20and%20Algebraic%20Theories): [universal algebra](node:Universal%20Algebra) expressed through monads and Lawvere theories.
- [Higher Categories](node:Higher%20Categories): morphisms between morphisms, up to $\infty$-categories.
- [MSC 18Axx - General theory of categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20of%20categories%20and%20functors) and [MSC 18Gxx - Homological algebra in category theory, derived categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Gxx%20-%20Homological%20algebra%20in%20category%20theory,%20derived%20categories%20and%20functors): the corresponding MSC maps.

### Common pitfalls
- An isomorphism of categories requires inverse functors with composites equal to identities; an equivalence only requires them naturally isomorphic to the identities, and is detected by full faithfulness plus essential surjectivity. ([nLab, equivalence of categories](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+of+categories); [Sharifi, Definition 1.5.7](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch01.html))
- Preservation is not existence: a right adjoint preserves those limits that exist, but having an adjoint does not make a category complete. ([Stacks, Lemma 4.24.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0038))
- The general adjoint functor theorem needs the solution set condition; a limit-preserving functor on a complete category need not have a left adjoint without it. ([nLab, adjoint functor theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/adjoint+functor+theorem))

### Open problems
- **Homotopy hypothesis for Grothendieck $\infty$-groupoids.** The homotopy hypothesis says that a good notion of $\infty$-groupoid should model homotopy types. It is a theorem for Kan complexes (via Quillen's equivalence) and for several other models, while for some algebraic definitions nLab states that little is known about how to prove it. For Grothendieck's globular $\infty$-groupoids, Henry (2016) showed that a "seemingly simple conjecture" would imply the homotopy hypothesis and identified that conjecture as what remains to be proved; Henry and Lanari proved the 3-dimensional case. ([nLab, homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis); [Henry, arXiv:1609.04622](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04622); [Henry–Lanari, arXiv:1905.05625](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.05625); [nLab, Grothendieck ∞-groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Grothendieck+infinity-groupoid))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, adjoint functor theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/adjoint+functor+theorem): precise hypotheses for the GAFT and SAFT and their history.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Categories](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/001L): Yoneda lemma, adjunctions, limits with proofs.
- **Learn:** [Sharifi, Category theory (UCLA notes, ch. 1)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch01.html): categories, functors, Yoneda, limits, adjoints.
- **Learn:** [Leinster, Basic Category Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.09375): free introductory textbook organized around universal properties.
- **Primary:** [Henry, Algebraic models of homotopy types and the homotopy hypothesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04622): research paper on the Grothendieck homotopy hypothesis.
- **Primary:** [Eilenberg–Mac Lane, General theory of natural equivalences (1945)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1945-0013131-6): the founding paper.
- **Further reading:** [Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-4721-8): the standard graduate text.
- **Further reading:** [Lurie, Higher Topos Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608040): monograph on $\infty$-categories via quasicategories.
references.Causal Activation Patching:
## Reference
### Overview
Activation patching overwrites some internal activations of a model run with activations cached from a run on a different input, then measures how the output changes. It is also called causal tracing, resample ablation, interchange intervention, or causal mediation analysis ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)). It is the standard technique in [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability) of [transformer](node:Transformers) language models for localizing which components causally affect a behaviour, and it underlies automated circuit discovery ([Zhang and Nanda 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16042); [Conmy et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997)).

The method is an application of causal mediation analysis: the input is the treatment, an internal activation is the mediator, and the model output is the response. Vig et al. introduced this framing for neural NLP, decomposing gender-bias effects into direct effects of the input and indirect effects through individual neurons and attention heads ([Vig et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12265)). Geiger et al. place patching, path patching, causal tracing, and causal scrubbing inside the theory of causal abstraction ([Geiger et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04709)).

Results depend on choices that a careful study must specify: the clean and corrupted input distributions, the direction of patching, the patched site (component, position, subspace), and the metric. Different corruption methods and metrics can yield different localizations of the same behaviour ([Zhang and Nanda 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16042); [Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).

### Formal definition
Fix a model $M$, a clean input $x_c$ that elicits the behaviour (e.g. "The Colosseum is in" → "Rome") and a corrupted input $x_r$ differing in a key property (e.g. "The Louvre is in") ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)). For an internal site $a$ (a head output, MLP output, residual-stream vector at a position, or a subspace of one), write $a(x)$ for its value on input $x$ and $M(x\mid do(a=v))$ for the output when $a$ is set to $v$ and the rest of the computation proceeds normally ([Minneker, interpretability lecture](https://minneker.github.io/nlp-26wi/assets/lectures/interpretability-theory-to-practice.html)).

- **Denoising** (clean → corrupt): compute $m\big(M(x_r\mid do(a=a(x_c)))\big)$; this tests whether $a$ is *sufficient* to restore the clean behaviour ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).
- **Noising** (corrupt → clean): compute $m\big(M(x_c\mid do(a=a(x_r)))\big)$; this tests whether $a$ is *necessary* to maintain it ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).

The two are not complements and neither implies the other ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)). With the logit difference $m=\mathrm{logit}(y_c)-\mathrm{logit}(y_r)$ as metric, Zhang and Nanda normalize the denoising effect as
$$\mathrm{PE}(a)=\frac{m_{\text{patched}}-m_{\text{corrupt}}}{m_{\text{clean}}-m_{\text{corrupt}}},$$
which typically lies in $[0,1]$: 1 means fully restored and 0 means still corrupted ([Zhang and Nanda 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16042)).

In mediation terms with treatment $X$, mediator $M$ and output $Y$, the total effect is $\mathrm{TE}=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]$, the natural direct effect $\mathrm{NDE}=E[Y(1,M(0))-Y(0,M(0))]$ and the natural indirect effect $\mathrm{NIE}=E[Y(0,M(1))-Y(0,M(0))]$, with $\mathrm{TE}=\mathrm{NDE}-\mathrm{NIE}_r$ where $\mathrm{NIE}_r$ is the reverse transition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediation_%28statistics%29)). Patching a single internal site measures an indirect effect of the input through that mediator ([Vig et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12265)).

**Related interventions.** *Zero* and *mean ablation* replace activations with zeros or dataset means; *Gaussian-noise corruption* perturbs the clean input embeddings; *path patching* patches only the edge from one component to a chosen downstream component, separating direct from mediated effects ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)). *Attribution patching* applies a linear (first-order) approximation to activation patching, estimating the change in $m$ from a patch as $(a(x_c)-a(x_r))^\top\nabla_a m$, so that all edges are scored with two forward passes and one backward pass ([Syed et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10348)).

### Key results
- **Asymmetry of noising and denoising (AND/OR circuits).** If $C=A\wedge B$, denoising finds only $C$ (restoring $A$ alone leaves $B$ corrupted) while noising finds $A,B,C$; if $C=A\vee B$, noising finds only $C$ and denoising finds $A,B,C$. Redundant components such as backup heads produce the OR case ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).
- **Corruption method changes localization.** Gaussian noising (GN) of subject embeddings and symmetric token replacement (STR) often disagree: under GN the factual-recall MLP peaks are 2–5× higher and the IOI circuit found differs substantially. The authors tentatively attribute this to GN driving the model off-distribution and recommend STR when token alignment allows it ([Zhang and Nanda 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16042)).
- **Metric choice changes conclusions.** Probability can miss negative components when corruption drives the correct-token probability near zero, whereas logit difference detects them; sliding-window patching gives at least 20% more peak effect than summed single-layer effects, which the authors speculate may come from non-linear joint effects that inflate localization plots ([Zhang and Nanda 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16042)).
- **Localizing factual recall.** A causal intervention locates the neuron activations decisive for factual predictions in a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules while the model processes subject tokens; editing those weights is Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) ([Meng et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05262)).
- **Subspace patching illusion.** Patching a subspace can change the output by activating a dormant parallel pathway rather than by changing the feature the subspace was supposed to hold, so a successful subspace patch does not show the subspace contains the feature; the effect appears in IOI and factual recall, and helps explain past mismatches between fact localization and editing success ([Makelov et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17030)).
- **Patching-based circuit discovery.** ACDC automates the circuit-identification step that follows activation patching; on GPT-2 small's greater-than circuit it selected 68 of 32,000 edges, all previously identified by hand. Edge-level attribution patching achieves higher average circuit-recovery AUC than other methods ([Conmy et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997); [Syed et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10348)).

### Examples
- **Indirect effects of neurons on gender bias.** In pretrained transformers, gender-bias effects are sparse (concentrated in a few neurons and heads), synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects ([Vig et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12265)).
- **Path patching cost.** Each patch needs a forward pass, so full path patching costs $O(\text{components}\times\text{paths})$ forward passes, which motivates gradient approximations ([Minneker, interpretability lecture](https://minneker.github.io/nlp-26wi/assets/lectures/interpretability-theory-to-practice.html); [Syed et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10348)).
- **Exploratory versus confirmatory use.** Sweeps that patch one component at a time find candidate circuits; patching many components at once (as in causal scrubbing) tests a stated hypothesis ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).

### History
Vig et al. (2020) brought causal mediation analysis to neural NLP ([Vig et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12265)). Meng et al. (2022) developed a causal intervention to localize factual recall ([Meng et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05262)). Methodology papers in 2023–2024 compared corruptions and metrics and wrote down best practice ([Zhang and Nanda 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042); [Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15255)), while ACDC and attribution patching automated circuit search ([Conmy et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997); [Syed et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10348)). Course syllabi now treat patching as a basic method, alongside its interpretability illusions ([Northeastern CS 7180](https://www.ccs.neu.edu/home/byron/cs7180/)).

### Connections
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): patching is its main tool for causal localization.
- [Causal Inference](node:Causal%20Inference): patching is a do-intervention; effects are mediation quantities.
- [Causal Abstraction](node:Causal%20Abstraction): interchange interventions test whether a high-level model abstracts the network.
- [Causal Scrubbing](node:Causal%20Scrubbing): confirmatory resampling-ablation test of a full circuit hypothesis.
- [Circuit Tracing](node:Circuit%20Tracing): attribution graphs that approximate many patching effects at once.
- [Sparse Autoencoders](node:Sparse%20Autoencoders): SAE features can be patched instead of raw components.
- [Activation Steering](node:Activation%20Steering): adds a direction instead of copying an activation from another input.
- [Counterfactual Explanations](node:Counterfactual%20Explanations): clean/corrupted pairs are counterfactual inputs.
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing): patching effects across prompt sets need uncertainty quantification and multiplicity control.
- [Heimersheim and Nanda 2024 - How to use and interpret activation patching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15255): the practitioner's guide.
- [Zhang and Nanda 2023 - Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models - Metrics and Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042): the corruption/metric comparison.

### Common pitfalls
- **Off-distribution corruptions.** Gaussian noise can be ineffective and is highly sensitive to the noise scale; prefer in-distribution corruptions such as symmetric token replacement ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255); [Zhang and Nanda 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16042)).
- **Saturating metrics.** Probability and log-probability saturate once the answer is top-ranked; use at least one continuous, roughly logit-linear metric such as logit difference ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).
- **Backup behaviour.** When a component is disrupted, others may partially compensate (the Hydra effect), making it look less important ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).
- **Overgeneralizing scope.** Results hold only for the prompt distributions tested, and finding a sufficient set of components does not show it is minimal ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).
- **Gradient approximations.** Attribution patching uses gradients and so gives only a first-order approximation of the effect of ablating a component ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496)).

### Open problems
- **Negative components.** Components that hurt task performance can make circuit recovery look better than it is; Heimersheim and Nanda call this an unsolved problem; KL divergence addresses it at the cost of also tracking much variation one may not care about ([Heimersheim and Nanda 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15255)).
- **Principled corruptions.** The off-distribution explanation for Gaussian noising rests on tentative evidence, and more principled patching or localization methods are still needed ([Zhang and Nanda 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16042)).
- **Faithfulness depends on the intervention.** Existing faithfulness measures depend on the causal-intervention implementation, and identifying components by individual interventions is costly with many components; efficient and accurate attribution "remains an open problem" ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Mediation (statistics), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediation_%28statistics%29): counterfactual definitions of direct and indirect effects.
- **Learn:** [Minneker, Interpretability: From Mechanistic Foundations to Practice](https://minneker.github.io/nlp-26wi/assets/lectures/interpretability-theory-to-practice.html): clean/corrupted runs, do-interventions, path patching cost.
- **Learn:** [Northeastern CS 7180, Actionable Interpretability](https://www.ccs.neu.edu/home/byron/cs7180/): course readings on patching basics and interpretability illusions.
- **Primary:** [Heimersheim and Nanda, How to use and interpret activation patching (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15255): denoising vs noising, metrics, pitfalls.
- **Primary:** [Zhang and Nanda, Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching (ICLR 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042): systematic comparison of corruptions and metrics.
- **Primary:** [Vig et al., Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12265): the mediation framing.
- **Further reading:** [Geiger et al., Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04709): formal theory unifying patching-style interventions.
references.Causal Inference:
## Reference
### Overview
Causal inference is the problem of determining the effect of one component of a system on another: not whether two variables move together (association) but how an effect variable responds when its cause is changed. Randomized experiments are the ideal standard; when they are infeasible, researchers use quasi-experimental designs, structural causal models with causal diagrams and the do-calculus, structural equation modeling, or the Rubin potential-outcomes model, and in computer science causal-discovery methods that infer causal direction from data ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causal_inference)).

Two formal languages dominate. In the **structural** (graphical) approach, a system is a set of variables with equations giving each variable as a function of its direct causes, summarized by a directed acyclic graph; an intervention replaces a variable's equation by a fixed value, which graphically deletes the arrows into it ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)). In the **potential-outcomes** approach, each unit has an outcome under treatment and under control, and the causal effect is their difference; since only one is ever observed, unit-level effects are not directly observable (the "fundamental problem of causal inference") ([Wikipedia: Rubin causal model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_causal_model)).

The core technical question is *identification*: can a causal quantity such as $P(y\mid do(x))$ be computed from the observational distribution plus qualitative assumptions encoded in a graph? Pearl's do-calculus answers this for non-parametric models, and its completeness proofs (2006) together with later graphical criteria have, in Pearl's words, "laid this identification problem to rest"; current work extends the machinery to mediation, transportability across populations, and synthesis of studies ([Pearl 2012](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.4852)). In machine learning the frontier is learning the causal variables themselves from raw observations ([Schölkopf et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11107)).

### Formal definition
**Causal DAG and Markov condition.** Let $G$ be a DAG on variables $V$. $P$ satisfies the causal Markov condition relative to $G$ if every $X\in V$ is independent of its non-descendants given its parents: $P(X\mid \mathrm{PA}(X), Y)=P(X\mid\mathrm{PA}(X))$ for all $Y\subseteq V\setminus\mathrm{DE}(X)$. A set $Z$ *d-separates* $X$ and $Y$ if every path between them is blocked, i.e. contains a non-collider in $Z$ or a collider with no descendant in $Z$ ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)).

**Intervention.** $P(y\mid do(X=x))$ is the distribution obtained by removing the arrows into $X$ and setting $X=x$; under the Markov condition the post-intervention distribution keeps every other factor $P(v_i\mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$ of the factorization and replaces the factor for the intervened variable by a point mass at $x$ ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)).

**Back-door criterion.** $Z$ satisfies the back-door criterion relative to $(X,Y)$ if no member of $Z$ is a descendant of $X$ and $Z$ blocks every path between $X$ and $Y$ that contains an arrow into $X$; then $P(Y\mid do(X),Z)=P(Y\mid X,Z)$ ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)) and
$$P(y\mid do(x))=\sum_z P(y\mid x,z)\,P(z)$$
([Wikipedia: Confounding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confounding)).

**Potential outcomes.** For unit $u$, $Y_t(u)$ and $Y_c(u)$ are the outcomes under treatment and control; the unit effect is $Y_t(u)-Y_c(u)$ and the average treatment effect is $\mathrm{ATE}=\mathbb E[Y_t-Y_c]$. SUTVA requires that a unit's outcome depend only on its own treatment ([Wikipedia: Rubin causal model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_causal_model)).

### Key results
- **Rules of the do-calculus.** For disjoint sets $X,Y,Z,W$ in a causal DAG $G$: (1) $P(y\mid do(x),z,w)=P(y\mid do(x),w)$ if $Y$ and $Z$ are d-separated given $X,W$ in $G$ with arrows into $X$ removed; (2) $P(y\mid do(x),do(z),w)=P(y\mid do(x),z,w)$ if $Y$ and $Z$ are d-separated given $X,W$ in $G$ with arrows out of $Z$ and into $X$ removed; (3) $P(y\mid do(x),do(z),w)=P(y\mid do(x),w)$ if $Y$ and $Z$ are d-separated given $X,W$ in $G_{\overline{X}\,\overline{Z(W)}}$, the graph with arrows into $X$ and into $Z(W)$ removed, where $Z(W)$ is the set of $Z$-nodes that are not ancestors of any $W$-node in $G_{\overline X}$. ([Wikipedia: Do-calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do-calculus); [Rule 3 with $Z(W)$, appendix of arXiv:2511.15679](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.15679))
- **Completeness of the do-calculus (Huang and Valtorta; Shpitser and Pearl, 2006).** If repeated application of the three rules cannot eliminate the do-operator, the causal effect is not identifiable; Shpitser and Pearl give a necessary and sufficient graphical condition, with an algorithm, for when a conditional interventional distribution is uniquely computable from the graph and the observational distribution, and use it to prove completeness for that problem. ([Wikipedia: Do-calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do-calculus); [Shpitser and Pearl 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.6876))
- **Limits of observational structure learning.** Without assumptions on the functional form (e.g. for discrete variables, or linear Gaussian models), the distribution identifies in general only a Markov equivalence class of DAGs: those relative to which it satisfies the Markov and faithfulness conditions; the PC algorithm generates this class. Stronger functional assumptions (linear non-Gaussian errors, nonlinear additive noise) can identify the full DAG. With no latent common causes, interventions can recover the full DAG; with latent common causes single-variable interventions may not suffice but simultaneous multi-variable interventions can. ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/))
- **Randomization identifies the ATE.** Under random assignment the treated and control groups are equivalent on average, so the difference of group means estimates the ATE; for inference about a subject's effect the probability of treatment must lie strictly between 0 and 1 (positivity). ([Wikipedia: Rubin causal model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_causal_model))
- **Counterfactuals by abduction–action–prediction.** In a probabilistic structural model, a counterfactual probability is computed by conditioning on the observations, replacing the equation of the intervened variable, and computing the resulting distribution; quantities such as the probability of necessity are in general only bounded (e.g. between 0.45 and 1 in the SEP's asbestos example). ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/))

### Examples
- **Collider bias:** adjusting for a common effect of $X$ and $Y$ opens a path and creates bias (Berkson's paradox), so adding covariates is not always safe ([Wikipedia: Confounding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confounding)).
- **SUTVA violation:** Joe's blood pressure depending on whether his housemate Mary receives the drug requires extra potential outcomes ([Wikipedia: Rubin causal model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_causal_model)).
- **Cause–effect direction from noise models:** additive, linear and post-nonlinear noise models compare how well $X\to Y$ and $Y\to X$ fit ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causal_inference)).

### History
Neyman proposed potential outcomes for randomized experiments in his 1923 thesis; Rubin extended them to observational studies in 1974; Holland named the "Rubin causal model" in 1986 ([Wikipedia: Rubin causal model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_causal_model)). Spirtes, Glymour and Scheines developed the PC algorithm and treat the Markov condition as an empirical posit, while Pearl derives it from independent error terms ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)). The do-calculus dates from 1995 and was proved complete in 2006 ([Pearl 2012](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.4852)); Pearl's *Causality* appeared in a second edition with Cambridge University Press in 2009 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511803161)).

### Connections
- [Probabilistic Graphical Models](node:Probabilistic%20Graphical%20Models) and [Bayesian Networks](node:Bayesian%20Networks): causal DAGs are Bayesian networks with an interventional semantics.
