- [Conditional Probability](node:Conditional%20Probability): $P(y\mid x)$ versus $P(y\mid do(x))$ is the seeing/doing distinction.
- [Bayesian Inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference): Bayesian estimation of causal effects and structure.
- [Causal Discovery from Interventions](node:Causal%20Discovery%20from%20Interventions): learning the DAG beyond its Markov equivalence class.
- [Causal Representation Learning](node:Causal%20Representation%20Learning): learning the causal variables themselves.
- [Counterfactual Explanations](node:Counterfactual%20Explanations) and [Counterfactual Inference for Learning](node:Counterfactual%20Inference%20for%20Learning): counterfactual reasoning in ML.
- [Causal Abstraction](node:Causal%20Abstraction) and [Causal Activation Patching](node:Causal%20Activation%20Patching): interventions applied to neural networks.
- [Experimental Design and Information Gain](node:Experimental%20Design%20and%20Information%20Gain): choosing interventions.
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): actions are interventions; generalization in RL is a cited open question.

### Common pitfalls
- Equating $P(y\mid x)$ with $P(y\mid do(x))$; by the back-door criterion they coincide when the empty set blocks every back-door path, but not in general ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)).
- Adjusting for every available covariate, including colliders ([Wikipedia: Confounding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confounding)) or descendants of $X$, which the back-door criterion excludes ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)).
- Assuming faithfulness is guaranteed: it is a methodological principle, not a consequence of the Markov condition ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)).
- Expecting observational data to orient every edge: without functional-form assumptions only the Markov equivalence class is identified ([SEP: Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/)).

### Open problems
- **Causal representation learning.** Schölkopf et al. call the discovery of high-level causal variables from low-level observations a central problem for AI and causality, and list as critical areas for future research learning non-linear causal relations at scale, learning causal variables, understanding the biases of existing [deep learning](node:Deep%20Learning) approaches, and learning causally correct models of the world and the agent ([Schölkopf et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.11107)).
- **Generalization in reinforcement learning.** The same paper states that "there are still open questions about the right way to think about generalization in RL" ([Schölkopf et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.11107)).
- **Meta-synthesis.** Pearl highlights the challenges of combining studies on different populations and conditions to estimate a causal relation in an unstudied target environment ([Pearl 2012](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.4852)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Causal Models (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/): SEMs, Markov condition, d-separation, interventions, discovery, counterfactuals.
- **Learn:** [Penn State, Principles of Causal Inference (Honavar), study guide](https://faculty.ist.psu.edu/vhonavar/Courses/causality/studyguide.html): weekly path from potential outcomes through do-calculus, counterfactuals, discovery and transportability.
- **Primary:** [Shpitser and Pearl 2006, Identification of Conditional Interventional Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.6876): completeness of the do-calculus.
- **Primary:** [Schölkopf et al. 2021, Towards Causal Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11107): survey linking causality and ML.
- **Further reading:** [Pearl, Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference, 2nd ed. (CUP 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511803161): the standard monograph on structural causal models.
references.Cayley–Hamilton Theorem:
## Reference
### Overview
The Cayley–Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix over a commutative ring satisfies its own characteristic polynomial: $p_A(A)=0$. It converts the determinant defining $p_A$ into a polynomial identity among the powers of $A$, so the algebra $R[A]$ generated by an $n\times n$ matrix is spanned by $I,A,\dots,A^{n-1}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem); [Altman–Kleiman, §10](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf))

In commutative algebra the theorem is used in its module form, the "determinant trick": an endomorphism of a finitely generated module is annihilated by the characteristic polynomial of any matrix expressing it on generators. This yields Nakayama's lemma, the fact that surjective endomorphisms of finitely generated modules are isomorphisms, invariance of rank for free modules, and the basic properties of integral dependence. ([Altman–Kleiman, §10](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf); [Nakayama's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakayama%27s_lemma)) In linear systems theory, the same identity explains why the controllability matrix needs only $n$ block columns. ([Harvard notes](https://hankyang.seas.harvard.edu/OptimalControlReinforcementLearning/app-lti-system-theory.html))

### Formal definition
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ ([Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices)). Its characteristic polynomial is $p_A(T)=\det(TI_n-A)=T^n+c_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+c_n\in R[T]$ ([Determinant](node:Determinant)). The theorem asserts, in the ring of matrices, ([Altman–Kleiman, (10.1)](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf))
$$
p_A(A)=A^n+c_1A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_{n-1}A+c_nI_n=0 .
$$
Here a scalar polynomial $f(z)=\sum_j a_jz^j$ is evaluated as $f(A)=\sum_j a_jA^j$, with constant term $a_0I_n$. The minimal polynomial of $A$ (over a field) is the monic polynomial $m_A$ of least degree with $m_A(A)=0$. ([UNSW notes](https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~angell/2501/9.pdf))

Low-dimensional forms: for $n=2$, $A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+(\det A)I_2=0$; for $n=3$, $A^3-(\operatorname{tr}A)A^2+\tfrac12\big((\operatorname{tr}A)^2-\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\big)A-(\det A)I_3=0$. In general $c_1=-\operatorname{tr}A$ and $c_n=(-1)^n\det A$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))

### Key results
- **Determinant trick (equivalent module form).** Let $R$ be commutative, $M$ an $R$-module generated by $m_1,\dots,m_n$, and $\varphi\in\operatorname{End}_R(M)$ with $\varphi(m_i)=\sum_j a_{ij}m_j$. Then $p_{(a_{ij})}(\varphi)=0$ in $\operatorname{End}(M)$; the $m_i$ need not be a basis. Proof: the matrix $\Delta=(\delta_{ij}\varphi-a_{ij})$ over the commutative ring $R[\varphi]$ kills the column $(m_j)$, and multiplying by its adjugate gives $\det(\Delta)m_j=0$. Conversely the matrix theorem is the case $M=R^n$, so the two statements are equivalent. ([Altman–Kleiman, (10.2)](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf))
- **Refinement with an ideal.** If moreover $\varphi(M)\subseteq IM$ for an ideal $I$, one may take all $a_{ij}\in I$, so $\varphi$ satisfies a monic $p(t)=t^n+p_1t^{n-1}+\cdots+p_n$ with $p_k\in I^k$. ([Nakayama's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakayama%27s_lemma); [Altman–Kleiman, (10.1)](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf))
- **Nakayama's lemma.** For $M$ finitely generated and $I$ an ideal, $M=IM$ iff $(1+a)M=0$ for some $a\in I$ (apply the refinement to $\varphi=1_M$). Hence if $I\subseteq\operatorname{rad}R$ and $M=IM$, then $M=0$. ([Altman–Kleiman, (10.3), (10.11)](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf); [Nakayama's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakayama%27s_lemma))
- **Surjective endomorphisms and rank.** If $M$ is finitely generated over a commutative ring $R$ and $\varphi:M\to M$ is surjective, then $\varphi$ is an isomorphism (apply the previous result over $R[X]$ with $I=\langle X\rangle$). Consequently, for $R\neq0$, any $n$ generators of $R^n$ form a basis, and $R^m\cong R^n$ implies $m=n$. ([Altman–Kleiman, (10.4), (10.5)](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf))
- **Minimal polynomial and power reduction.** Over a field, $m_A$ divides $p_A$, and $\dim\mathbb C[A]=\deg m_A\le n$; every $A^m$ with $m\ge n$ lies in the span of $I,\dots,A^{n-1}$. For $A$ and $B$ of compatible sizes, every $A^kB$ with $k\ge n$ lies in the span of $B,AB,\dots,A^{n-1}B$, which is why the Kalman controllability matrix $[B\ AB\ \cdots\ A^{n-1}B]$ suffices (see [Linear Control Systems](node:Linear%20Control%20Systems)). ([UNSW notes](https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~angell/2501/9.pdf); [Harvard notes](https://hankyang.seas.harvard.edu/OptimalControlReinforcementLearning/app-lti-system-theory.html))
- **Inverse and adjugate.** If $\det A$ is invertible, then $c_n=(-1)^n\det A$ is a unit and the theorem gives $A^{-1}=-c_n^{-1}\big(A^{n-1}+c_1A^{n-2}+\cdots+c_{n-1}I\big)$, a polynomial of degree $n-1$ in $A$; for $n=2$, $A^{-1}=-(A+c_1I)/\det A$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))
- **Faddeev–LeVerrier algorithm.** With $M_0=0$ and $c_n=1$ (indexing $p_A(\lambda)=\sum_k c_k\lambda^k$), set $M_k=AM_{k-1}+c_{n-k+1}I$ and $c_{n-k}=-\tfrac1k\operatorname{tr}(AM_k)$ for $k=1,\dots,n$. This produces all coefficients, $\operatorname{adj}(A)=(-1)^{n-1}M_n$ and $A^{-1}=-M_n/c_0$; the derivation compares coefficients in $(\lambda I-A)\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I-A)=p_A(\lambda)I$ and itself yields $p_A(A)=0$. Each step divides by $k$, for $k=1,\dots,n$. ([Faddeev–LeVerrier algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faddeev%E2%80%93LeVerrier_algorithm))

### Proofs
- **Adjugate proof.** Write $B(\lambda)=\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I-A)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\lambda^iB_i$; then $(\lambda I-A)B(\lambda)=p_A(\lambda)I$. Comparing coefficients of each power of $\lambda$, multiplying the resulting equations by $A^n,A^{n-1},\dots,I$ and summing makes the left side telescope to $0$ and the right side to $p_A(A)$. ([Harvard notes](https://hankyang.seas.harvard.edu/OptimalControlReinforcementLearning/app-lti-system-theory.html))
- **Density proof over $\mathbb C$.** Diagonalizable complex matrices are dense, $p_A(A)=0$ is clear for them (see [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors)), and $A\mapsto p_A(A)$ is continuous, so the theorem holds for all complex, hence real and rational, matrices. The algebraic proofs are preferred because they work over any commutative ring. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))
- **Other proofs.** Proofs via matrix-coefficient polynomials, via endomorphisms of modules (adapted from Atiyah–Macdonald), via Hasse–Schmidt derivations, and a combinatorial proof from the Leibniz formula (Straubing) are known. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))

### Examples
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$, $\operatorname{tr}A=5$ and $\det A=-2$, so $p_A(z)=z^2-5z-2$ and $A^2=5A+2I$. Hence $A^3=10I+27A$ and $A^4=54I+145A$; every polynomial in $A$ is a combination of $I$ and $A$, and $\{I,A\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb C[A]$. ([UNSW notes](https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~angell/2501/9.pdf)) The theorem also gives $A^{-1}=(A-5I)/2$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))

### History
Hamilton proved a special case in 1853, in terms of inverses of linear functions of quaternions. Cayley in 1858 stated the result for $3\times3$ and smaller matrices but published a proof only for the $2\times2$ case. The general case was first proved by Frobenius in 1878. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem)) Le Verrier published the trace recursion in 1840, and Faddeev and Sominsky gave its present form in 1949. ([Faddeev–LeVerrier algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faddeev%E2%80%93LeVerrier_algorithm))

### Connections
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): the theorem is an identity in the endomorphism algebra.
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): the roots of $p_A$ are the eigenvalues; the density proof starts from diagonalizable matrices.
- [Determinant](node:Determinant): $p_A$ is a determinant, and the adjugate drives the main proof.
- [Jordan Canonical Form](node:Jordan%20Canonical%20Form): over an algebraically closed field the minimal polynomial, a divisor of $p_A$, is read off from Jordan blocks.
- [Modules over Commutative Rings](node:Modules%20over%20Commutative%20Rings): the determinant trick and Nakayama's lemma.
- [Local Rings](node:Local%20Rings): Nakayama's lemma with $I=\mathfrak m$ controls minimal generators.
- [Polynomial Identity Rings](node:Polynomial%20Identity%20Rings): Amitsur–Levitzki gives the minimal identity of matrix rings.
- [Linear Control Systems](node:Linear%20Control%20Systems): Kalman's rank condition.

### Common pitfalls
- Substituting $A$ for $\lambda$ in $\det(\lambda I-A)$ to get "$\det(A-A)=0$" is invalid: the result is a scalar, whereas $p_A(A)$ is a matrix, and $\lambda$ sits only on the diagonal. The analogous substitution in the permanent would "prove" $q(A)=0$ for $q(z)=z^2-5z+10$, but for the example above $q(A)=12I\neq0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem); [UNSW notes](https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~angell/2501/9.pdf))
- Commutativity of the coefficient ring matters: the module proof needs the entries of $\Delta$ to lie in the commutative ring $R[\varphi]$. Over the quaternions the theorem holds only with care in defining the determinant. ([Altman–Kleiman, (10.2)](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))
- No diagonalizability assumption is needed; the density argument is a proof device over $\mathbb C$, not a hypothesis. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))

### Noncommutative analogues
- **Amitsur–Levitzki theorem (1950).** For $n\times n$ matrices over a commutative ring, the standard polynomial $S_{2n}(x_1,\dots,x_{2n})=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{2n}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)x_{\sigma(1)}\cdots x_{\sigma(2n)}$ vanishes identically, and $2n$ is the least degree of a polynomial identity of $M_n$. Razmyslov (1974) gave a proof related to the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, and Procesi (2015) one via the Cayley–Hamilton identity for a generic Grassmann matrix. ([Amitsur–Levitzki theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amitsur%E2%80%93Levitzki_theorem))
- **Quaternions and octonions.** The theorem holds for quaternionic and split-quaternionic matrices, and a modified version holds for [octonions](node:Octonions) (Tian, 2000). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))
- **Quantum matrix algebras.** Ogievetsky and Pyatov (2025) establish Cayley–Hamilton identities for orthogonal $O(k)$-type quantum matrix algebras, with different forms for odd and even height and a spectral parametrisation of the coefficients by "eigenvalues" of the quantum matrix. ([Ogievetsky–Pyatov](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.12282v1))

### Open problems
The classical theorem is closed. Active research on its quantum analogues continues: Ogievetsky and Pyatov leave for future work low-dimensional examples of the orthogonal characteristic identities in the FRT and reflection-equation algebras, a BMW analogue of the Hecke-case basis whose multiplication reproduces the Littlewood–Richardson rule, and the $q$-orthosymplectic case; in Remark 3.4 they suspect that the accidental isomorphisms seen at $k=4$ hold more generally and say the question deserves further investigation. ([Ogievetsky–Pyatov, Introduction and Remark 3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.12282v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cayley–Hamilton theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem): statements, many proofs, history, generalizations.
- **Learn:** [UNSW MATH2501 notes, §9](https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~angell/2501/9.pdf): minimal polynomial, worked examples.
- **Learn:** [Harvard linear-system appendix](https://hankyang.seas.harvard.edu/OptimalControlReinforcementLearning/app-lti-system-theory.html): adjugate proof and controllability.
- **Primary:** [Altman and Kleiman, A Term of Commutative Algebra, §10](https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed-2up.pdf): Cayley–Hamilton over rings, determinant trick, Nakayama, integral dependence.
- **Primary:** [Ogievetsky and Pyatov, Cayley–Hamilton Theorem for Orthogonal Quantum Matrix Algebras](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.12282v1): research-level quantum analogue.
- **Further reading:** [Faddeev–LeVerrier algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faddeev%E2%80%93LeVerrier_algorithm) and [Amitsur–Levitzki theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amitsur%E2%80%93Levitzki_theorem): computation and noncommutative identities.
references.Centered Kernel Alignment:
## Reference
### Overview
Centered kernel alignment (CKA) is a normalized similarity score between two kernel (Gram) matrices computed on the same $n$ examples. Both matrices are first double-centered, and the score is the cosine of the angle between them in the Frobenius inner product. Cortes, Mohri and Rostamizadeh introduced centered alignment as a similarity measure between kernels for learning kernel combinations. They showed that the earlier uncentered alignment of Cristianini et al. (2001) "does not correlate well with performance", while the centered version does. ([Cortes et al., arXiv/ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550); [JMLR](https://jmlr.org/papers/v13/cortes12a.html))

In deep learning, CKA is the standard index for comparing the representations of two layers or two networks. Kornblith, Norouzi, Lee and Hinton (ICML 2019) argued that any similarity index invariant to invertible linear transformations, including CCA, cannot measure meaningful similarities between representations of higher dimension than the number of data points. They proposed CKA, which is invariant to orthogonal transformations and isotropic scaling but not to arbitrary invertible linear maps. They showed that CKA reliably identifies corresponding layers in networks trained from different initializations, where CCA-based indices do not. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00414))

Statistically, CKA is a normalized form of the Hilbert–Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC), the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the centered cross-covariance operator between two reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. With a characteristic kernel, HSIC vanishes exactly when the variables are independent. ([Wikipedia: Kernel embedding of distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_embedding_of_distributions); [Gretton, lecture notes](https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~gretton/coursefiles/lecture5_covarianceOperator.pdf))

### Formal definition
Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p_1}$ and $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p_2}$ be the activation matrices of two representations on the same $n$ examples. Let $K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)$ and $L_{ij}=l(y_i,y_j)$ be their Gram matrices, and let $H=I_n-\tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ be the centering matrix. The empirical HSIC used by Kornblith et al. is
$$\operatorname{HSIC}(K,L)=\frac{1}{(n-1)^2}\operatorname{tr}(KHLH),$$
and
$$\operatorname{CKA}(K,L)=\frac{\operatorname{HSIC}(K,L)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{HSIC}(K,K)\,\operatorname{HSIC}(L,L)}}.$$
([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))

Equivalently, write $K_c=HKH$ for the centered kernel matrix. Cortes et al. define the centered alignment of kernel matrices as
$$\hat\rho(K,K')=\frac{\langle K_c,K'_c\rangle_F}{\|K_c\|_F\,\|K'_c\|_F}.$$
The population version is $\rho(K,K')=\mathbb{E}[K_cK'_c]/\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[K_c^2]\,\mathbb{E}[K_c'^2]}$, where $K_c(x,x')=K(x,x')-\mathbb{E}_xK(x,x')-\mathbb{E}_{x'}K(x,x')+\mathbb{E}_{x,x'}K(x,x')$. ([Cortes et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550))

**Linear CKA.** With linear kernels $K=XX^\top$, $L=YY^\top$ and column-centered $X,Y$:
$$\operatorname{CKA}(XX^\top,YY^\top)=\frac{\|Y^\top X\|_F^2}{\|X^\top X\|_F\,\|Y^\top Y\|_F}.$$
In this case HSIC reduces to $\|\operatorname{cov}(X^\top,Y^\top)\|_F^2$. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))

**Population HSIC.** For kernels with feature maps into RKHSs $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$:
$$\operatorname{HSIC}(X,Y)=\|\mathcal C_{XY}-\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y\|_{HS}^2.$$
([Wikipedia: Kernel embedding of distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_embedding_of_distributions); [Gretton, lecture notes](https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~gretton/coursefiles/lecture5_covarianceOperator.pdf))

### Key results
- **Range.** For positive semidefinite kernels, the centered alignment lies in $[0,1]$, because the centered matrices are PSD and the Frobenius inner product of two PSD matrices is non-negative. ([Cortes et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550))
- **Invariance.** Linear CKA is invariant to orthogonal transformations, $s(X,Y)=s(XU,YV)$ for $U^\top U=I$ and $V^\top V=I$, and to isotropic scaling, $s(X,Y)=s(\alpha X,\beta Y)$. It is not invariant to arbitrary invertible linear transformations. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
- **Degeneracy of invertible-linear invariance (Kornblith et al., Theorem 1).** Suppose a similarity index $s$ is invariant to invertible linear transformation in its first argument, and $\operatorname{rank}(X)=\operatorname{rank}(Y)=n$. Then $s(X,Z)=s(Y,Z)$ for every $Z$. So such an index, CCA for example, gives the same value for every representation of width at least the dataset size. Orthogonal invariance avoids this. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
- **Relations to other indices.** Let $Q_X,Q_Y$ be orthonormal bases for the column spaces of centered $X$ (width $p_1$) and $Y$ (width $p_2$). ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
  - Mean squared CCA correlation: $R^2_{\mathrm{CCA}}=\|Q_Y^\top Q_X\|_F^2/p_1=\operatorname{CKA}(Q_XQ_X^\top,Q_YQ_Y^\top)\sqrt{p_2/p_1}$. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
  - Linear-regression fit of $X$ with design matrix $Y$: $R^2_{\mathrm{LR}}=\|Q_Y^\top X\|_F^2/\|X\|_F^2$, which equals linear CKA between $XX^\top$ and $Q_YQ_Y^\top$ times a data-dependent factor involving $\|X^\top X\|_F/\|X\|_F^2$. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
  - With linear kernels, CKA equals the RV coefficient of Robert and Escoufier (1976) and Tucker's congruence coefficient. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
- **Concentration (Cortes et al., Theorem 12).** Assume kernel values are bounded by $R^2$ and $R'^2$. For any $\delta>0$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample of size $m$,
$$|\rho(K,K')-\hat\rho(K,K')|\le 18\beta\Big[\tfrac{3}{m}+8\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(6/\delta)}{2m}}\Big],\qquad \beta=\max\!\Big(\tfrac{R^2R'^2}{\mathbb{E}[K_c^2]},\tfrac{R^2R'^2}{\mathbb{E}[K_c'^2]}\Big).$$
So the empirical alignment deviates from the population alignment by $O(1/\sqrt m)$. ([Cortes et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550))
- **High alignment implies a good predictor (Cortes et al., Theorem 13).** Assume centered, normalized labels ($\mathbb{E}[y]=0$, $\mathbb{E}[y^2]=1$). For the hypothesis $h^*$ built from $K_c$, $R(h^*)\le 1-\rho(K,K_Y)/\Gamma$, where $K_Y$ is the label kernel and $\Gamma=\max_x\gamma(x)$. ([Cortes et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550))
- **Maximum-alignment kernel learning is a QP (Cortes et al., Proposition 9).** Set $M_{kl}=\langle K_{kc},K_{lc}\rangle_F$ and $a_k=\langle K_{kc},yy^\top\rangle_F$, and let $v^*$ solve $\min_{v\ge0}v^\top Mv-2v^\top a$. Then $\mu^*=v^*/\|v^*\|$ maximizes alignment over convex combinations of base kernels. The problem is equivalent to a hard-margin SVM. ([Cortes et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550))
- **RSA equivalence.** Representational similarity analysis on dissimilarity matrices is "largely equivalent" to CKA once a mean-centering step is added to RSA. ([Williams 2024](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v285/williams24a.html))

### Examples
- **Layer-correspondence sanity check.** Kornblith et al. trained 10 CNNs on CIFAR-10 from different initializations. For each layer they asked whether the most similar layer in another network is the architecturally corresponding one. Accuracy was 99.3% for linear CKA, 99.3% for RBF CKA with bandwidth $\sigma=0.8\times$ median distance, and 80.6% for RBF CKA at $0.2\times$ median. CCA ($R^2_{\mathrm{CCA}}$) scored 10.6%, SVCCA 15.1%, PWCCA 11.1% and linear regression 45.4%. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
- **A case where uncentered alignment fails.** In a two-dimensional example of Cortes et al., the uncentered alignment equals $(\alpha^2+(1-\alpha)^2)^{1/2}$, which reaches 1 only at $\alpha\in\{0,1\}$. The centered alignment equals 1 for every $\alpha$. ([Cortes et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550))
- **HSIC feature selection.** With a linear kernel on features $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$, $K=\sum_\ell K_\ell$ with per-feature kernels $K_\ell=x[\ell]x[\ell]^\top$, so the biased estimate $\tfrac{1}{n^2}\operatorname{tr}(KHLH)$ is a sum of per-feature HSIC values. With suitably scaled binary labels and a linear label kernel, each term is $\tfrac1{n^2}$ times the squared difference between the two class means of feature $\ell$, which gives a per-feature score for selecting features. ([Gretton, lecture notes](https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~gretton/coursefiles/lecture5_covarianceOperator.pdf))

### History
- **Kernel–target alignment.** Cristianini et al. (2001) introduced the uncentered alignment as a similarity between a kernel and the target. ([Cortes et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550))
- **HSIC.** Gretton, Bousquet, Smola and Schölkopf introduced HSIC in 2005 ("Measuring statistical dependence with Hilbert–Schmidt norms", ALT). ([Wikipedia: Kernel embedding of distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_embedding_of_distributions))
- **Centered alignment.** Cortes, Mohri and Rostamizadeh developed centered alignment and its learning theory in JMLR vol. 13 (2012). ([JMLR](https://jmlr.org/papers/v13/cortes12a.html))
- **Representation similarity.** Kornblith et al. carried CKA into representation similarity in "Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited" (arXiv 1905.00414, ICML 2019). They noted that linear CKA is equivalent to the RV coefficient of Robert and Escoufier (1976). ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00414); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))

### Connections
- [Kernel Methods](node:Kernel%20Methods): CKA compares two Gram matrices and is built from kernel evaluations on a shared sample.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): HSIC is a Hilbert–Schmidt norm of a cross-covariance operator between RKHSs.
- [Representation Similarity Analysis](node:Representation%20Similarity%20Analysis): RSA with mean-centering is essentially CKA.
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): CKA is a common tool for comparing layers and models across training runs.
- [Independence of Random Variables](node:Independence%20of%20Random%20Variables): with characteristic kernels, population HSIC is zero iff the variables are independent.
- [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): CCA and SVCCA, the indices CKA was compared against, are computed from SVDs of the representations.
- [Support Vector Machines](node:Support%20Vector%20Machines): maximum-alignment kernel learning reduces to a hard-margin SVM problem.
- [Convolutional Neural Networks](node:Convolutional%20Neural%20Networks): the setting of the original layer-correspondence experiments.

### Common pitfalls
- **Invertible-linear invariance is not always a virtue.** When both representations have rank $n$ (possible only if width $\ge n$), an index with that invariance gives the same value for both, by Theorem 1 of Kornblith et al. CKA deliberately lacks this invariance. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
- **Outliers and manipulation.** Davari et al. characterize CKA's sensitivity to simple transformations. This explains its known sensitivity to outliers and to transformations that preserve linear separability. They show that CKA values can be "easily manipulated without substantial changes to the functional behaviour" of models. A CKA value alone does not certify functional similarity. ([Davari et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.16156))
- **Bandwidth matters.** RBF CKA with a small bandwidth ($0.2\times$ median distance) performed much worse in the sanity check than linear CKA. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
- **HSIC is not mutual information.** Kornblith et al. note that HSIC is not an estimator of mutual information. The $\operatorname{tr}(KHLH)$ estimator is biased; an unbiased U-statistic estimator exists. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414); [Gretton, lecture notes](https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~gretton/coursefiles/lecture5_covarianceOperator.pdf))
- **Centering is essential.** Uncentered alignment can stay below 1 for kernels that are equally good for the task. Earlier classification guarantees stated for uncentered alignment are, according to Cortes et al., erroneous. ([Cortes et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.0550))

### Open problems
- **Choice of kernel and weighting.** Kornblith et al. write that "it remains an open question whether there exist kernels beyond the linear and RBF kernels that would be better for analyzing neural network representations". They note that other weightings of scalar products between eigenvectors may be more appropriate in some settings and leave these questions to future work. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.00414))
- **Reliability and functional meaning.** CKA can change without a change in functional behaviour, so whether activation-alignment scores track functional similarity is unresolved. Davari et al. call for caution. Klabunde et al.'s survey of representational and functional similarity measures closes by pointing to open research problems in the area. ([Davari et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.16156); [Klabunde et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06329))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kernel embedding of distributions (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_embedding_of_distributions): HSIC as a Hilbert–Schmidt norm and its independence property.
- **Learn:** [Gretton, covariance operator and HSIC lecture notes (UCL Gatsby)](https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~gretton/coursefiles/lecture5_covarianceOperator.pdf): derivation of the biased and unbiased HSIC estimators.
- **Primary:** [Kornblith et al. 2019, Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00414): CKA for neural representations, invariance analysis, and the CCA comparison.
- **Primary:** [Cortes, Mohri, Rostamizadeh 2012, Algorithms for Learning Kernels Based on Centered Alignment (JMLR)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v13/cortes12a.html): centered alignment, concentration, and kernel-learning algorithms.
- **Primary:** [Klabunde et al., Similarity of Neural Network Models: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06329): survey of representational and functional similarity measures.
- **Further reading:** [Shawe-Taylor and Cristianini, Kernel Methods for Pattern Analysis (CUP, 2004)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/kernel-methods-for-pattern-analysis/kernel-methods-an-overview/5C8B31E83475594AAB48DA04AB835BB9): graduate text on kernel methods.
references.Central Force Motion and the Kepler Prob:
## Reference
### Overview
The central-force problem asks for the motion of a particle under a force directed along the line to a fixed centre whose magnitude depends only on the distance. Any two-body problem with a central interaction reduces exactly to one body of reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ obeying $\mu\ddot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf F$, and conservation of energy and angular momentum leave one radial degree of freedom in an effective potential ([Wikipedia: Classical central-force problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_central-force_problem)). Gravity ([Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity)) and [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics) are the key examples.

The Kepler problem is the inverse-square case, attractive or repulsive. Its orbits are conics with a focus at the centre, described by six orbital elements, and it is one of only two central problems (with the harmonic oscillator) whose bound orbits always close ([Wikipedia: Kepler problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_problem)). It is exceptionally symmetric: besides angular momentum it conserves the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector, and these generate $SO(4)$ for bound and $SO(3,1)$ for unbound motion ([Wikipedia: LRL vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%E2%80%93Runge%E2%80%93Lenz_vector)). Its five integrals (energy, angular momentum and the LRL vector) make it superintegrable ([Verrier–Evans](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0712.3677)).

Its time dependence is governed by the transcendental Kepler equation ([Wikipedia: Kepler's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_equation)); its collisions can be regularized by maps to harmonic oscillators or to geodesic flow on a sphere ([Zhao](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1308.2314); [Heckman–de Laat](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1007.3695)); and its action-angle (Delaunay) variables are used to simplify perturbative calculations in celestial mechanics ([Wikipedia: Delaunay variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaunay_variables)). In $d$ spatial dimensions with a Gauss-law force $\propto1/r^{d-1}$, stable circular orbits exist only for $d<4$ ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1011.4037)).

### Formal definition
A central force is $\mathbf F=F(r)\,\hat{\mathbf r}$; with $L=mr^2\dot\varphi$ conserved, the radial motion obeys
$$E=\tfrac12m\dot r^2+U_{\rm eff}(r),\qquad U_{\rm eff}(r)=U(r)+\frac{L^2}{2mr^2},$$
with turning points where $E=U_{\rm eff}(r)$ ([Wikipedia: Classical central-force problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_central-force_problem)). With $u=1/r$ the orbit satisfies $\frac{d^2u}{d\theta^2}+u=J(u)$, $J(u)=-\frac{m}{L^2}\frac{d}{du}V(1/u)$ ([Wikipedia: Bertrand's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand%27s_theorem)).

The Kepler problem has $\mathbf F=\frac{k}{r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}$, $V=k/r$ (attractive for $k<0$), and orbit
$$u=\frac1r=-\frac{km}{L^2}\big[1+e\cos(\theta-\theta_0)\big],$$
an ellipse for $E<0$, parabola for $E=0$ and hyperbola for $E>0$; a repulsive force allows only $e>1$ ([Wikipedia: Kepler problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_problem)).

**Kepler's equation.** With mean anomaly $M=n(t-t_0)$ ($n$ the mean motion, $t_0$ a periapsis passage), the eccentric anomaly $E$ solves $M=E-e\sin E$, and $x=a(\cos E-e)$, $y=b\sin E$; hyperbolic orbits use a $\sinh$ form ([Wikipedia: Kepler's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_equation)). Equivalently $r=a(1-e\cos E)$ and $(1-e)\tan^2(\theta/2)=(1+e)\tan^2(E/2)$ ([Wikipedia: Kepler's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion)).

### Key results
- **Area law for any central force.** The areal velocity is constant, with twice its value equal to $h=r^2\dot\varphi$ ([Wikipedia: Classical central-force problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_central-force_problem)).
- **Kepler's third law.** $T^2=4\pi^2a^3/\big(G(M+m)\big)$ ([Wikipedia: Kepler's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion)).
- **Virial theorem.** For a bounded system with conservative forces, $\langle T\rangle=-\tfrac12\sum_k\langle\mathbf F_k\cdot\mathbf r_k\rangle$ (time averages); for a power-law pair potential $V=\alpha r^n$, $2\langle T\rangle=n\langle V_{\rm tot}\rangle$, so inverse-square forces give $\langle T\rangle=-\tfrac12\langle V_{\rm tot}\rangle$ ([Wikipedia: Virial theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virial_theorem)); see [Virial Theorem](node:Virial%20Theorem).
- **Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector.** $\mathbf A=\mathbf p\times\mathbf L-mk\,\hat{\mathbf r}$ ($k>0$ attractive here) is conserved only for an exact inverse-square force; it points to periapsis with $e=|\mathbf A|/|mk|$, and $\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf r$ gives the conic $1/r=mk/L^2+(A/L^2)\cos\theta$. Under perturbations it rotates, producing apsidal precession ([Wikipedia: LRL vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%E2%80%93Runge%E2%80%93Lenz_vector)).
- **Hidden symmetry.** $\mathbf D=\mathbf A/p_0$, $p_0=\sqrt{2m|E|}$, and $\mathbf L$ close under Poisson brackets into $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ for $E<0$ and $\mathfrak{so}(3,1)$ for $E>0$; the Casimir $\mathbf D^2+\mathbf L^2=mk^2/(2|E|)$. Fock (1935) showed, using stereographic projection of momentum space, that the quantum bound problem is equivalent to a free particle on the unit 3-sphere in four dimensions ([Wikipedia: LRL vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%E2%80%93Runge%E2%80%93Lenz_vector)); see [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups) and [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem).
- **Hamilton–Jacobi separability.** The Hamilton–Jacobi equation separates in spherical polar coordinates for any central potential ([Wikipedia: Hamilton–Jacobi equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton%E2%80%93Jacobi_equation)); for the Kepler problem it separates also in rotational parabolic coordinates, and the two separations give the energy, $\mathbf L$ and the LRL vector, all at most quadratic in velocities ([Verrier–Evans](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0712.3677)). The orbit equation can be derived directly from the Hamilton–Jacobi equation ([Wikipedia: Classical central-force problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_central-force_problem)); see [Hamilton–Jacobi Theory](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Theory).
- **Bertrand's theorem (1873).** Perturbing a circular orbit gives $\beta^2=1-J'(u_0)$; closure at every radius forces $f(r)=-k/r^{3-\beta^2}$, and higher orders give $\beta^2(1-\beta^2)(4-\beta^2)=0$, so only $\beta=1$ (inverse square) and $\beta=2$ (harmonic oscillator) give all bound orbits closed ([Wikipedia: Bertrand's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand%27s_theorem); [Santos, Soares & Tort](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.2396)).
- **Moser regularization.** Swapping $x=p$, $y=-q$ (a "geometric Fourier transform") and applying stereographic projection on cotangent bundles, Moser's map sends the Kepler flow on the level $H=-\tfrac12$, with time reparametrized, to the geodesic flow on $S^n$, on $T^*(S^n\setminus\{n\})$ with $n$ the north pole. The Ligon–Schaaf map adapts this to the whole negative-energy region, makes the incomplete Kepler flow of collision orbits complete, and explains the extension of the visible $SO(n)$ symmetry to $SO(n+1)$ geometrically ([Heckman–de Laat](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1007.3695)). Moser's paper is "Regularization of Kepler's problem and the averaging method on a manifold" (CPAM 23, 1970) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/cpa.3160230406)).
- **Levi-Civita and Kustaanheimo–Stiefel regularization.** The two-to-one map $Q=z^2$, $P=w/(2\bar z)$ with a time change turns the planar Kepler problem into harmonic oscillators in $1{:}1$ resonance; the KS map $Q=\bar z\,i\,z$, $P=\bar z\,i\,w/(2|z|^2)$ on the bilinear cone turns the spatial problem into four oscillators in $1{:}1{:}1{:}1$ resonance; Kummer studied its link with Moser's regularization ([Zhao](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1308.2314)).
- **Stability of circular orbits and dimension.** A circular orbit at $r_0$ is stable iff $F'(r_0)<-3F(r_0)/r_0$. With $F=-\frac{4\pi G^{(3)}}{\mathrm{vol}(S^{d-1})}\frac{mM}{r^{d-1}}$, $\mathrm{vol}(S^{d-1})=2\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2)$, this gives $d<4$ spatial dimensions ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1011.4037)). For $n>3$ the two-body problem has no stable orbits: light particles escape or spiral into collision ([Tegmark](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/gr-qc/9702052)).

### Examples
- **Planets and Coulomb pairs.** Newtonian gravity and Coulomb's law are both inverse-square, so satellites, planets, binary stars and charges are Kepler problems ([Wikipedia: Kepler problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_problem)).
- **Rutherford scattering.** The repulsive problem gives hyperbolae with the nucleus at a focus, scattering angle $\Theta=2\arctan\!\big(kq_aq_g/(mv_0^2b)\big)$ for impact parameter $b$, and a cross-section $\propto\csc^4(\Theta/2)$ ([Wikipedia: Rutherford scattering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutherford_scattering)), which Geiger and Marsden confirmed in 1913 ([Wikipedia: Rutherford scattering experiments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutherford_scattering_experiments)).
- **Hydrogen atom.** Pauli (1926) used the LRL Casimir to derive the hydrogen spectrum before the [Schrödinger Equation](node:Schrödinger%20Equation) ([Wikipedia: LRL vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%E2%80%93Runge%E2%80%93Lenz_vector)); see [Hydrogen Atom](node:Hydrogen%20Atom).
- **Solving Kepler's equation.** Newton's method from $E_0=M$ and fixed-point iteration (Kepler's 1621 method) are standard; the Maclaurin series in $e$ converges for all $M$ only below the Laplace limit $e\approx0.66$ ([Wikipedia: Kepler's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_equation)); see [Newton's Method](node:Newton's%20Method) and [Bessel Functions](node:Bessel%20Functions).
- **Perihelion precession.** A [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) correction makes the LRL vector precess, with periapsis precession rate $6\pi k^2/(TL^2c^2)$ ([Wikipedia: LRL vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%E2%80%93Runge%E2%80%93Lenz_vector)).
- **Revolving orbits.** Newton showed that adding the inverse-cube force $F_2(r)-F_1(r)=L_1^2(1-k^2)/(mr^3)$, with $L_1$ the original angular momentum, multiplies the angular speed by $k$ and leaves the radial motion unchanged ([Wikipedia: Newton's theorem of revolving orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_theorem_of_revolving_orbits); [Wikipedia: Classical central-force problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_central-force_problem)).

### History
Kepler's *Astronomia nova* (1609) gave the first law from Tycho Brahe's Mars data, *Harmonice Mundi* (1619) the third, and the *Epitome* (1621) the modern area form of the second ([Wikipedia: Kepler's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion)); Kepler's equation dates from 1609 and appears earlier in a 9th-century work of Habash al-Hasib ([Wikipedia: Kepler's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_equation)). Newton's *Principia* showed that an inverse-square force yields the area law and conic orbits ([Wikipedia: Kepler problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_problem)). Jakob Hermann first showed the LRL vector is conserved in a special case of the inverse-square force, and Johann Bernoulli generalized this to its modern form in 1710; Laplace, Hamilton (1847), Gibbs, Runge and Lenz rediscovered or reused it ([Wikipedia: LRL vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%E2%80%93Runge%E2%80%93Lenz_vector)). Clausius stated the virial theorem in 1870 ([Wikipedia: Virial theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virial_theorem)), Bertrand his theorem in 1873 ([Wikipedia: Bertrand's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand%27s_theorem)), and Rutherford his scattering analysis in 1911 ([Wikipedia: Rutherford scattering experiments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutherford_scattering_experiments)). Ehrenfest (1917) showed that neither classical atoms nor planetary orbits are stable for $n>3$ ([Tegmark](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/gr-qc/9702052)).

### Connections
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity) and [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics): the two physical inverse-square laws.
- [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws), [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) and [Integrable Physical Systems](node:Integrable%20Physical%20Systems): energy, $\mathbf L$ and LRL make the problem superintegrable.
- [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics), [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics), [Canonical Transformations](node:Canonical%20Transformations) and [Hamilton–Jacobi Theory](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Theory): effective potential, separation, regularization.
- [Action-Angle Variables](node:Action-Angle%20Variables), [Orbital Elements and Perturbations](node:Orbital%20Elements%20and%20Perturbations) and [KAM Theory](node:KAM%20Theory): perturbations of nearly Keplerian systems.
- [Virial Theorem](node:Virial%20Theorem) and [Galaxy Rotation Curves](node:Galaxy%20Rotation%20Curves): averaged and circular-orbit dynamics in bound systems.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics) and [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere): Fock and Moser identify the bound problem with geodesic flow on $S^3$.
- [The N-Body Problem](node:The%20N-Body%20Problem): what remains when more bodies interact.
- [Hydrogen Atom](node:Hydrogen%20Atom) and [Schrödinger Equation](node:Schrödinger%20Equation): the quantum Kepler problem and its $SO(4)$ degeneracy.
- [Gauss's Law in n Dimensions](node:Gauss's%20Law%20in%20n%20Dimensions), [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions), [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions) and [Tests of the Inverse-Square Law](node:Tests%20of%20the%20Inverse-Square%20Law): orbit stability in other dimensions.
- [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution), [Tests of General Relativity](node:Tests%20of%20General%20Relativity) and [Binary Pulsars](node:Binary%20Pulsars): relativistic precession.

### Common pitfalls
- **Circular, closed and stable differ.** Every attractive central force allows circular orbits, but with radial velocity added orbits need not be stable or closed ([Wikipedia: Bertrand's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand%27s_theorem)).
- **Two dimensions is not three.** The $d=2$ Gauss-law force $\propto1/r$ satisfies $d<4$ ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1011.4037)), but $3-\beta^2=1$ gives $\beta=\sqrt2$, not a Bertrand value, so generic bound orbits do not close ([Wikipedia: Bertrand's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand%27s_theorem)).
- **Sign conventions.** $V=k/r$ with $k<0$ for attraction ([Wikipedia: Kepler problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_problem)) versus $\mathbf A=\mathbf p\times\mathbf L-mk\hat{\mathbf r}$ with $k>0$ for attraction ([Wikipedia: LRL vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%E2%80%93Runge%E2%80%93Lenz_vector)).
- **Spatial versus spacetime dimension.** The bound $d<4$ counts spatial dimensions; the title of Mota and Pérez-Guerrero refers to spacetime dimension $D=d+1>4$ ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1011.4037)).
- **Third law involves both masses.** $T^2$ depends on $G(M+m)$; dropping $m$ is an approximation ([Wikipedia: Kepler's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion)).

### Open problems
None found. The two-body Kepler problem is solved in closed form by Kepler orbits described by six orbital elements ([Wikipedia: Kepler problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_problem)), and none of the fetched sources names an open problem specific to it. Searches tried: "Kepler problem open problem", "central force problem unsolved", the Levi-Civita, Kustaanheimo–Stiefel, Moser and Ligon–Schaaf regularization literature, and Hamilton–Jacobi superintegrability; open questions begin with [The N-Body Problem](node:The%20N-Body%20Problem).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%E2%80%93Runge%E2%80%93Lenz_vector): conservation, $SO(4)$ symmetry, Fock's projection, history.
- **Reference:** [Bertrand's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand%27s_theorem): the perturbative proof.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 8.09 Classical Mechanics III (Stewart)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/): central forces, Hamilton–Jacobi theory, action-angle variables, perturbation theory.
- **Primary:** [Santos, Soares & Tort, An English translation of Bertrand's theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.2396): Bertrand's original theorem.
- **Primary:** [Mota & Pérez-Guerrero, Instability of the planetary orbits for space-time dimensions higher than four](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.4037): the dimension bound.
- **Primary:** [Heckman & de Laat, On the regularization of the Kepler problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.3695): Moser and Ligon–Schaaf regularization and the hidden symmetry.
- **Further reading:** [Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics (Springer GTM, 1989)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2063-1): Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics; Hamiltonian mechanics on manifolds.
- **Further reading:** [Zhao, Kustaanheimo–Stiefel regularization and the quadrupolar conjugacy](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1308.2314): Levi-Civita and KS regularization; [Tegmark, On the dimensionality of spacetime](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/9702052).
references.Certifying Algorithms:
## Reference
### Overview
A certifying algorithm returns, together with its output, a witness (certificate) proving that the output is correct for the given input. A separate, much simpler checker program verifies the triple (input, output, witness). If the checker accepts, the user can trust that this output was not compromised by a bug, whatever the complexity of the algorithm that produced it. If it rejects, either the output is wrong or the witness is not a proof. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462)) The proof must be simpler than the algorithm, since otherwise rerunning the algorithm would count as certification. A certifying algorithm is called efficient if the algorithm and checker together run within a constant factor of the best known non-certifying algorithm. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm))

The idea grew out of Blum and Kannan's programs that check their work. Mehlhorn and Näher introduced certifying algorithms, and they are a key design principle of the LEDA algorithm library, whose checkers may optionally be invoked after every execution of a LEDA algorithm. An extensive survey is McConnell, Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer (2011). ([Schmidt](https://algo.uni-rostock.de/storages/uni-rostock/Alle_IEF/Inf_ALGO/Publications/Schmidt2013.pdf); [Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.cosrev.2010.09.009)) Developing certifying algorithms is a major goal where the fastest known algorithms are complicated and their implementations error-prone; testing a graph for 3-connectivity is a prominent example. ([Schmidt](https://algo.uni-rostock.de/storages/uni-rostock/Alle_IEF/Inf_ALGO/Publications/Schmidt2013.pdf))

The concept sits between testing and full formal verification. Proving a complex algorithm correct is often intractable, but checkers are small enough to verify formally. Combining a verified checker with a proof of the witness property yields formal instance correctness: a machine-checked proof that each particular output is correct. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462)) In the vault this is the algorithmic counterpart of [Proof-Carrying Results](node:Proof-Carrying%20Results) and [Proof-Carrying Code](node:Proof-Carrying%20Code), and the formal analogy behind [Witness-First Scientific Workflows](node:Witness-First%20Scientific%20Workflows).

### Formal definition
Let $X$, $Y$, $\mathcal W$ be the sets of inputs, outputs and witnesses. A specification is a precondition $\varphi(x)$ and a postcondition $\psi(x,y)$; $y$ is a correct output for $x$ if $\psi(x,y)$ holds. A **witness predicate** for $(\varphi,\psi)$ is a relation $W\subseteq X\times Y\times\mathcal W$ with the **witness property**
$$\varphi(x)\wedge W(x,y,w)\ \Longrightarrow\ \psi(x,y).$$
A **certifying algorithm** for $(\varphi,\psi)$ computes on input $x$ an output $y$ and a witness $w$. A **checker** $C$ for $W$ receives $(x,y,w)$. If $\varphi(x)$ fails, $C$ may do anything; if $\varphi(x)$ holds, $C$ must halt, accept when $W(x,y,w)$ holds, and reject otherwise. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462))


### Key results
- **Formal instance correctness.** If the checker is proved correct (it halts on inputs satisfying $\varphi$ and decides $W$) and the witness property is proved, then every triple it accepts satisfies $\psi(x,y)$. Alkassar, Böhme, Mehlhorn and Rizkallah prove checker correctness in the VCC verifier for C and the witness property in Isabelle/HOL, applied to LEDA checkers. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462))
- **Edmonds' odd-set cover certificate for matching.** An odd-set cover of $G$ is a vertex labelling $L$ such that every edge is incident to a vertex labelled $1$ or joins two vertices with the same label $i\ge2$. If $M$ is a matching, $n_i$ is the number of vertices labelled $i$, and $|M|=n_1+\sum_{i\ge2}\lfloor n_i/2\rfloor$, then $M$ has maximum cardinality. Conversely, every maximum matching admits such a cover, so LEDA's maximum-matching algorithm certifies its output with one. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462))
- **Tutte sequences certify 3-connectivity.** Let $e=(x,y)$ be an edge of a simple graph $G$ whose endpoints have degree at least $3$. If $G/e$ is 3-connected, then $G$ is 3-connected. Hence a sequence of such contractions ending in $K_4$ (a Tutte sequence) certifies 3-connectivity, while a set $S$ with $|S|\le2$ and $G\setminus S$ disconnected certifies the opposite. Before Schmidt's work, a Tutte sequence could be found in $O(n^2)$ time. ([Mehlhorn and Schweitzer](https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/%7Epascal/docs/progress_on_certifying_algorithms.pdf))
- **Linear-time certifying 3-connectivity** (Schmidt). Every 3-connected graph on more than 4 vertices has a contractible edge (Tutte), and Barnette and Grünbaum give an analogous sequence of edge removals down to $K_4$. Both sequences can be computed in $O(|E|)$ time, improving the previous $O(|V|^2)$. This gives a certifying test of 3-connectivity in $O(n+m)$ time that returns the construction sequence if $G$ is 3-connected and a cut vertex or separation pair otherwise, and also a linear-time certifying test of 3-edge-connectivity. A subquadratic certifying 3-connectivity test had been listed as an open problem in the McConnell et al. survey. ([Schmidt](https://algo.uni-rostock.de/storages/uni-rostock/Alle_IEF/Inf_ALGO/Publications/Schmidt2013.pdf))
- **Planarity.** A Kuratowski subgraph certifies non-planarity, and a planar embedding certifies planarity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm))
- **Graph classes by forbidden subgraphs.** For graph classes with a forbidden induced subgraph characterization, a membership model certifies yes and a forbidden subgraph certifies no. Chaplick gives linear-time certifying recognition for intersection graphs of non-crossing paths in a tree. As a consequence, the presence or absence of an induced claw in a chordal graph can be certified in linear time, whereas the best deterministic claw detection for general graphs is superlinear. ([Chaplick](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.00272))

### Examples
- **GCD.** The extended Euclidean algorithm returns $g$ with integers $s,t$ such that $g=sa+tb$. The checker verifies $g\mid a$, $g\mid b$ and $g=sa+tb$. This suffices because any common divisor $d$ of $a$ and $b$ divides $sa+tb=g$. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462))
- **Bipartiteness.** The algorithm outputs a 2-colouring if $G$ is bipartite and an odd cycle otherwise; both are easier to check than bipartiteness is to decide. Similar two-sided certificates: a topological order or a directed cycle for acyclicity, and an elimination ordering or a chordless cycle for chordality. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm))
- **Shortest paths.** For single-source shortest paths with nonnegative edge weights, the returned witness is a shortest-path tree for the computed distances; Alkassar et al. verify such a checker formally. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462))

### History
- Blum and Kannan initiated programs that check their work; Mehlhorn and Näher introduced certifying algorithms and built them into LEDA. ([Schmidt](https://algo.uni-rostock.de/storages/uni-rostock/Alle_IEF/Inf_ALGO/Publications/Schmidt2013.pdf))
- 2011: McConnell, Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer publish the survey "Certifying algorithms" in *Computer Science Review* 5(2), 119–161. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.cosrev.2010.09.009))
- 2011–2013: Alkassar, Böhme, Mehlhorn and Rizkallah verify LEDA checkers formally, starting with a CAV 2011 version. The effort revealed that LEDA's matching checker failed to test that the matching is a subset of the graph's edges. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.7462); [full text](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462))
- Schmidt gives the first linear-time certifying 3-connectivity test. ([Schmidt](https://algo.uni-rostock.de/storages/uni-rostock/Alle_IEF/Inf_ALGO/Publications/Schmidt2013.pdf))

### Connections
- [Proof Complexity and Certificates](node:Proof%20Complexity%20and%20Certificates): certificates whose size and checking cost are the object of study; NP is the class of problems with polynomially checkable yes-certificates.
- [Graph Algorithms](node:Graph%20Algorithms): most developed certifying algorithms are graph algorithms.
- [Network Flow](node:Network%20Flow): a cut whose capacity equals the flow value certifies that the flow is maximum.
- [Shortest-Path Algorithms](node:Shortest-Path%20Algorithms): shortest-path trees with feasible distances are certificates.
- [Linear Programming](node:Linear%20Programming): a dual feasible solution of equal value certifies primal optimality.
- [Formal Verification and Proof Assistants](node:Formal%20Verification%20and%20Proof%20Assistants): checkers are verified in VCC and Isabelle/HOL.
- [Proof-Carrying Code](node:Proof-Carrying%20Code) and [Proof-Carrying Results](node:Proof-Carrying%20Results): ship a checkable proof with code or results instead of trusting the producer.
- [Witness-First Scientific Workflows](node:Witness-First%20Scientific%20Workflows): applies the witness-and-checker pattern to scientific discovery.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): yes-certificates for NP problems are short; certifying algorithms seek certificates for both answers.

### Common pitfalls
- A checker certifies only the particular output, not the algorithm: an accepted run yields an output that was not compromised by a bug, while a bug in the algorithm shows up as a rejection unless the algorithm and checker have masking bugs. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm))
- The checker itself can be wrong. The formal verification of LEDA's matching checker found that it did not check that $M\subseteq E$. ([Alkassar et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7462))
- A witness must be simpler to check than the problem is to solve. Rerunning the algorithm is not a certificate. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm))
- Non-certifying implementations of intricate algorithms do fail in practice: Gutwenger and Mutzel report that an implementation of the Hopcroft–Tarjan triconnectivity algorithm wrongly declared some non-3-connected graphs 3-connected, and they provided a correction. ([Mehlhorn and Schweitzer](https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/%7Epascal/docs/progress_on_certifying_algorithms.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Construction sequences for higher connectivity.** Schmidt asks whether construction sequences give a general new approach to testing higher vertex connectivity efficiently, noting that construction sequences for 4-connected graphs exist. He also poses as of practical interest whether his algorithm can be extended to produce an SPQR-tree directly in linear time. ([Schmidt](https://algo.uni-rostock.de/storages/uni-rostock/Alle_IEF/Inf_ALGO/Publications/Schmidt2013.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Certifying algorithm (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm): definition, efficiency, standard graph examples and checker reliability.
- **Learn:** [Mehlhorn and Schweitzer, Progress on Certifying Algorithms](https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/%7Epascal/docs/progress_on_certifying_algorithms.pdf): short expository introduction through Edmonds' matching certificate, checker verification, and Tutte sequences for 3-connectivity.
- **Primary:** [Alkassar, Böhme, Mehlhorn, Rizkallah, A Framework for the Verification of Certifying Computations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.7462): formal definitions and verified LEDA checkers.
- **Primary:** [Schmidt, Contractions, Removals and How to Certify 3-Connectivity in Linear Time](https://algo.uni-rostock.de/storages/uni-rostock/Alle_IEF/Inf_ALGO/Publications/Schmidt2013.pdf): resolves the certifying 3-connectivity problem.
- **Further reading:** [McConnell, Mehlhorn, Näher, Schweitzer, Certifying algorithms, Computer Science Review 5(2), 2011](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.cosrev.2010.09.009): the survey, pages 119–161 (Crossref bibliographic record).
references.Chaos Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Chaos theory studies deterministic systems whose orbits are irregular and unpredictable in practice: nearby initial states separate, orbits mix through the phase space, and periodic orbits are dense. There is no general agreement on a single definition. Some authors call a system chaotic when it has positive topological entropy; Milnor suggests also requiring transitivity, so that most orbits behave chaotically, and notes that definitions often involve Lyapunov exponents or homoclinic points. ([Milnor, §4D](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~jack/DYNOTES/dn4a.pdf)) A statement that a system is chaotic therefore needs its chosen meaning: topological (Devaney, Li–Yorke, positive entropy) or metric (positive Lyapunov exponent for typical orbits). ([Che Dzul-Kifli–Good, introduction](https://web.mat.bham.ac.uk/C.Good/research/pdfs/dense-periodic.pdf); [Klages, §§5.2–5.3](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/r.klages/teaching/mas424/intro_ds_v1.1.pdf))

The mechanisms are geometric. Stretching and folding, modelled by Smale's horseshoe near transverse homoclinic points, produce an invariant Cantor set coded by sequences of two symbols, which places chaos inside [hyperbolic dynamics](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems) and [symbolic dynamics](node:Symbolic%20Dynamics). ([Wikipedia, Horseshoe map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe_map)) Chaotic systems can carry strange attractors with fractal structure, in flows such as the Lorenz system and maps such as the Hénon map, and families of maps reach chaos by period-doubling cascades with universal scaling. ([Wikipedia, Chaos theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaos_theory); [Wikipedia, Feigenbaum constants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feigenbaum_constants))

### Formal definition
Let $X$ be a compact metric space and $f:X\to X$ continuous. $f$ is topologically transitive if for all nonempty open $U,V$ there is $n$ with $f^n(U)\cap V\ne\varnothing$. $f$ has sensitive dependence on initial conditions if there is $\delta>0$ such that for every $x\in X$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there are $y$ and $n$ with $d(x,y)<\varepsilon$ and $d(f^n(x),f^n(y))\ge\delta$. Devaney's definition: $f$ is chaotic if it is transitive, has a dense set of periodic points, and is sensitive. ([Che Dzul-Kifli–Good, introduction](https://web.mat.bham.ac.uk/C.Good/research/pdfs/dense-periodic.pdf)) The quantifier order matters: $\delta$ is independent of $x$, while $y$ and $n$ depend on $x$ and $\varepsilon$. ([Klages, §5.2](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/r.klages/teaching/mas424/intro_ds_v1.1.pdf))

For a $C^1$ interval map $M$, the Lyapunov exponent of the orbit of $x_0$ is $\lambda(x_0)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\tfrac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\ln|M'(x_i)|$ when the limit exists, a Birkhoff time average. $M$ is chaotic in Lyapunov's sense if it is transitive and $\lambda(x_0)>0$ for Lebesgue-almost every $x_0$. ([Klages, §§5.3, 9](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/r.klages/teaching/mas424/intro_ds_v1.1.pdf)) In higher dimensions the exponents come from the growth of the tangent propagator, and the Oseledets theorem gives conditions for the limits to exist. ([Wikipedia, Lyapunov exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_exponent))

### Key results
- **Sensitivity is redundant (Banks–Brooks–Cairns–Davis–Stacey).** If $X$ is infinite and $f$ is transitive with dense periodic points, then $f$ has sensitive dependence for every metric compatible with the topology; the hypothesis is topological but the conclusion is metric. ([Milnor, Theorem 4.8](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~jack/DYNOTES/dn4a.pdf)) For continuous maps of a compact interval, transitivity alone implies dense periodic points (Vellekoop–Berglund), so transitive interval maps are Devaney chaotic. ([Che Dzul-Kifli–Good, introduction](https://web.mat.bham.ac.uk/C.Good/research/pdfs/dense-periodic.pdf))
- **Many periods nearby.** If $X$ is a compact metric space without isolated points and $f$ is Devaney chaotic, then for every $n$ the points of least period at least $n$ are dense. Conversely, for a continuous self-map of a closed interval, density of the points of least period at least 3 gives a decomposition into closed subintervals on which $f$ or $f^2$ is Devaney chaotic. ([Che Dzul-Kifli–Good, abstract and Theorem 1](https://web.mat.bham.ac.uk/C.Good/research/pdfs/dense-periodic.pdf))
- **Sharkovskii's theorem.** Order the positive integers $3\triangleright5\triangleright7\triangleright\cdots\triangleright2\cdot3\triangleright2\cdot5\triangleright\cdots\triangleright4\cdot3\triangleright\cdots\triangleright8\triangleright4\triangleright2\triangleright1$. If $f$ is a continuous map of an interval with a point of least period $m$ and $m\triangleright n$, then $f$ has a point of least period $n$; conversely every tail of the ordering is the set of periods of some continuous interval map. Continuity and the interval domain are both necessary. ([Wikipedia, Sharkovskii's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem))
- **Period three implies chaos (Li–Yorke 1975).** A continuous interval map with a period-3 point has points of every period and an uncountable set of "chaotic" points that never map into any cycle. ([Wikipedia, Sharkovskii's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem); [Li–Yorke, Amer. Math. Monthly 82 (1975)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1080/00029890.1975.11994008))
- **Lyapunov exponents, entropy and their limits.** Positive Lyapunov exponent implies sensitivity, but not conversely, since sensitivity need not be exponential. ([Klages, §5.3](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/r.klages/teaching/mas424/intro_ds_v1.1.pdf)) Perron (1930) gave a system whose linearization has negative exponents but whose zero solution is unstable, and reverse examples exist, so the sign of the largest exponent alone settles neither stability nor chaos; by Pesin's theorem the sum of the positive exponents gives an estimate of the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy, and the Kaplan–Yorke dimension $D_{KY}=k+\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i/|\lambda_{k+1}|$, with $k$ the largest index whose partial sum of ordered exponents is nonnegative, is an upper bound for the information dimension. ([Wikipedia, Lyapunov exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_exponent)) [Topological entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy) is a conjugacy invariant and, for a continuous map of a compact metric space, equals the supremum of the measure-theoretic entropies of invariant measures. ([Wikipedia, Topological entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_entropy))
- **Horseshoes.** The orbits of Smale's horseshoe that stay in the square form a Cantor set coded by two-symbol sequences, with periodic orbits of all periods whose number grows exponentially; the horseshoe is an Axiom A diffeomorphism that models dynamics near a transverse homoclinic point. ([Wikipedia, Horseshoe map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe_map))
- **Feigenbaum universality.** In one-parameter families of one-dimensional maps with a single quadratic maximum, such as the logistic map, the gaps between successive period-doubling parameters shrink by the ratio $\delta\approx4.6692$, with a second scaling constant $\alpha\approx2.5029$. Lanford gave a computer-assisted proof in 1982, and Lyubich gave the first complete non-numerical proof. ([Wikipedia, Feigenbaum constants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feigenbaum_constants)) See [Bifurcation Theory](node:Bifurcation%20Theory).
- **The Lorenz attractor exists.** For $\dot x=\sigma(y-x)$, $\dot y=x(\rho-z)-y$, $\dot z=xy-\beta z$ with $\sigma=10$, $\rho=28$, $\beta=8/3$, Smale's 14th problem asks whether the attractor is strange; Tucker answered yes with a rigorous computer-assisted proof using interval arithmetic and normal forms. ([Wikipedia, Lorenz system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenz_system); [Tucker, C. R. Acad. Sci. 328 (1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/S0764-4442%2899%2980439-X))

### Examples
- The one- and two-sided full 2-shifts, the interval map $x\mapsto2x^2-1$, and the angle-doubling map on the circle are Devaney chaotic and topologically mixing. ([Milnor, §4D, Example 1](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~jack/DYNOTES/dn4a.pdf))
- The Bernoulli shift $B(x)=2x\bmod1$ is transitive, sensitive, and has Lyapunov exponent $\ln2$, since $|B'|=2$ away from the discontinuity at $\tfrac12$ (for orbits that never hit $\tfrac12$). ([Klages, §§5.1–5.3](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/r.klages/teaching/mas424/intro_ds_v1.1.pdf))
- The Hénon map $(x,y)\mapsto(1-ax^2+y,\,bx)$ at the classical values $a=1.4$, $b=0.3$ has the Hénon strange attractor, smooth in one direction and a Cantor set in another, with box-counting dimension estimated at $1.261\pm0.003$. ([Wikipedia, Hénon map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9non_map))
- Rotations are not chaotic: a rational rotation has dense periodic points but is not transitive, and an irrational rotation is transitive with no periodic points; neither is sensitive. ([Che Dzul-Kifli–Good, introduction](https://web.mat.bham.ac.uk/C.Good/research/pdfs/dense-periodic.pdf))

### History
Poincaré found bounded nonperiodic orbits in the three-body problem in the 1880s; Lorenz encountered sensitive dependence in weather simulations in 1961 and published his convection model in 1963; Yorke is credited with the mathematical term "chaos"; and Feigenbaum (1975) and Coullet–Tresser (1978) discovered universality. ([Wikipedia, Chaos theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaos_theory); [Wikipedia, Lorenz system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenz_system)) Sharkovskii published his theorem in 1964, and Li and Yorke's "Period three implies chaos" appeared in 1975. ([Wikipedia, Sharkovskii's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem))

### Connections
- [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems): supplies orbits, iteration and invariant sets.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory): Lyapunov exponents and Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy are ergodic averages.
- [Hyperbolic Dynamical Systems](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems) and [MSC 37Dxx - Dynamical systems with hyperbolic behavior](node:MSC%2037Dxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20with%20hyperbolic%20behavior): horseshoes and Axiom A give robust chaos.
- [Symbolic Dynamics](node:Symbolic%20Dynamics): coding by shifts gives the standard models.
- [Topological Entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy): one of the main criteria for chaos.
- [Bifurcation Theory](node:Bifurcation%20Theory): period-doubling and other routes to chaos.
- [Global Attractors](node:Global%20Attractors): strange attractors as attracting invariant sets.

### Common pitfalls
- Sensitivity depends on the metric: for $x\mapsto2x$ on $(0,\infty)$ the usual metric gives sensitivity everywhere, but in the metric $|\log x-\log y|$ the map is an isometry; on compact spaces all compatible metrics agree on sensitivity. ([Milnor, §4D](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~jack/DYNOTES/dn4a.pdf))
- Positive topological entropy alone allows maps like $z\mapsto z^2$ on the Riemann sphere, where most orbits converge to $0$ or $\infty$, to count as chaotic. ([Milnor, §4D](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~jack/DYNOTES/dn4a.pdf))
- A positive largest Lyapunov exponent does not in general indicate chaos, and a negative one does not guarantee stability. ([Wikipedia, Lyapunov exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_exponent))

### Open problems
- **Finiteness of attractors (Palis programme; active direction).** Palis conjectured local finiteness of attractors for Kolmogorov-typical one-dimensional maps and surface diffeomorphisms, and for one-dimensional dynamics that Lebesgue-almost every point lies in the basin of a physical measure; Berger reports the latter fully proved for one-dimensional maps with a single critical point. Berger constructs Baire-generic $C^d$-families of $C^r$ maps on manifolds of dimension $\ge2$ (families of diffeomorphisms when the dimension exceeds 3, local diffeomorphisms on the annulus) in which every small parameter gives infinitely many sinks, a counterexample to a conjecture of Pugh and Shub. ([Berger, Generic family with robustly infinitely many sinks](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1411.6441); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.6441))
- **Arithmetic of the Feigenbaum constants.** Both constants are believed transcendental, but no proof is known that either is even irrational. ([Wikipedia, Feigenbaum constants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feigenbaum_constants))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Chaos theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaos_theory): history, definitions, strange attractors and routes to chaos.
- **Learn:** [Milnor, Dynamics notes §4: basic concepts](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~jack/DYNOTES/dn4a.pdf): Devaney chaos, sensitivity, mixing.
- **Learn:** [Klages, Introduction to Dynamical Systems (QMUL)](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/r.klages/teaching/mas424/intro_ds_v1.1.pdf): transitivity, sensitivity, Lyapunov exponents.
- **Primary:** [Li and Yorke, Period Three Implies Chaos (1975)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1080/00029890.1975.11994008): the original Li–Yorke paper.
- **Primary:** [Che Dzul-Kifli and Good, On Devaney chaos and dense periodic points (Amer. Math. Monthly 2015)](https://web.mat.bham.ac.uk/C.Good/research/pdfs/dense-periodic.pdf): density of high periods.
- **Primary:** [Berger, Generic family with robustly infinitely many sinks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.6441): generic families with infinitely many sinks.
- **Further reading:** [Devaney, An Introduction to Chaotic Dynamical Systems, 3rd ed. (CRC, 2021)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9780429280801); [Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (CRC, 2018)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9780429492563); [Katok and Hasselblatt, Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems (Cambridge, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511809187).
references.Citation and Claim Graphs:
## Reference
### Overview
A citation graph is a directed graph on a collection of documents: each vertex is a document and each edge runs from a citing document to a document it cites (some implementations reverse the direction). Because documents can normally cite only earlier ones, the graph is ideally acyclic, and since citations are meant to be permanent, most of it is static and only its leading edge changes; apparent "backward" citations from asynchronous bibliography updates appear to be under 1% of links ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_graph)). Citation indexes were originally designed for information retrieval and are increasingly used for bibliometrics and research evaluation; systematic measurement of citation counts for journals was initiated by Eugene Garfield at the Institute for Scientific Information, who also pioneered using such counts to rank authors and papers ([Wikipedia: Citation analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_analysis)).

A citation edge records only that one work refers to another. It says nothing about *what* is being cited or *why*. A claim graph refines the unit from the document to the individual statement: nodes are claims, data and methods, and typed edges say that one representation supports or challenges another. The Micropublications model of Clark, Ciccarese and Goble is the reference formalisation: a micropublication argues a principal claim, and the supports relation among its elements forms a directed acyclic graph rooted at that claim, while statements in one work may cite individual statements in another ([Clark, Ciccarese, Goble](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1305.3506)). Nanopublications take the minimal end of the same idea, subdividing results into atomic assertions represented in RDF with provenance attached to each assertion and treating each as an individual publication ([Kuhn et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1411.2749)).

Keeping the layers apart matters because only the claim layer can show whether a chain of citations bottoms out in data. Greenberg's analysis of a claim-specific citation network on one neuromuscular disorder found extensive progressive citation distortion, with reviews in reputable journals presenting as facts statements ultimately based on no evidence, which is the failure that claim-level graphs are meant to expose ([Clark, Ciccarese, Goble](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1305.3506)). The topic therefore sits between [Knowledge Graphs and Ontologies](node:Knowledge%20Graphs%20and%20Ontologies), [Data Provenance and Lineage](node:Data%20Provenance%20and%20Lineage), [Information Retrieval](node:Information%20Retrieval) and [Computational Network Science](node:Computational%20Network%20Science).

### Formal definition
**Citation graph and adjacency matrix.** For $n$ papers, let $A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ with $A_{ij}=1$ when paper $i$ cites paper $j$ and self-citations excluded, so $\operatorname{diag}A=0$; the resulting graph is a directed acyclic graph because papers cite only earlier work ([Deng et al., StatCite](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.08063)).

**Co-citation and bibliographic coupling.** With this convention the co-citation matrix and bibliographic coupling matrix are
$$C=A^{\top}A,\quad C_{i_1i_2}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}A_{k i_1}A_{k i_2},\qquad B=AA^{\top},\quad B_{i_1i_2}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}A_{i_1 k}A_{i_2 k},$$
so $C_{i_1i_2}$ counts papers citing both $i_1$ and $i_2$ and $B_{i_1i_2}$ counts references shared by $i_1$ and $i_2$; both define undirected weighted networks ([Deng et al., StatCite](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.08063)). Bibliographic coupling was introduced by Kessler in 1963 ([Wikipedia: Bibliographic coupling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliographic_coupling)); co-citation by Small and, independently, Marshakova in 1973 ([Wikipedia: Co-citation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-citation)).
