## Reference
### Overview
Combinatorial optimization is the subfield of mathematical optimization that seeks an optimal object from a finite set of objects, where the feasible solutions are discrete or can be reduced to a discrete set; typical problems are the travelling salesman problem, the minimum spanning tree problem and the knapsack problem. Exhaustive search over the feasible set is usually intractable, so the field develops specialized exact algorithms and approximation algorithms, and it draws on operations research, algorithm theory and [computational complexity theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial_optimization)).

The field divides roughly into two parts. Many problems, including shortest paths, flows, spanning trees, matchings and matroid problems, are solvable in polynomial time, largely through linear programming theory; for NP-complete problems, research targets polynomial special cases, algorithms that work well on random instances, polynomial-time approximation algorithms, and practical solution of large instances by methods such as branch-and-bound, branch-and-cut, dynamic programming and tabu search ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial_optimization)).

A main technique is polyhedral combinatorics: describing the [convex hull](node:Convex%20Hull) of the incidence vectors of feasible solutions by linear inequalities so that the machinery of linear programming, including duality, applies ([Goemans, Polyhedral notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/polyhedral.pdf)). Goemans's MIT course is organized around exactly this material: bipartite and non-bipartite matching, matroids, linear programming and polyhedral combinatorics, flows and cuts, matroid intersection and the ellipsoid algorithm ([Goemans, MIT 18.433](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/18433.html)).

### Formal definition
An instance of a combinatorial optimization problem is a finite ground set $E$, a family $\mathcal F \subseteq 2^E$ of feasible sets, and a cost $c : E \to \mathbb R$; the task is to find $F \in \mathcal F$ maximizing (or minimizing) $c(F) = \sum_{e \in F} c(e)$. In the polyhedral approach one identifies $F$ with its incidence vector $\chi^F \in \{0,1\}^E$ and optimizes $c^{\mathsf T}x$ over the polytope $\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F : F \in \mathcal F\}$, whose vertices are the incidence vectors; a linear description of this polytope turns the problem into a linear program ([Goemans, Polyhedral notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/polyhedral.pdf); [Goemans, Matroid notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matroid-notes.pdf)).

In complexity theory, the class **NPO** of NP optimization problems consists of problems whose solutions are polynomially bounded in size, whose validity can be checked efficiently, and whose objective value is computable in polynomial time; NPO is subdivided by approximability, with knapsack in NPO(I), which equals FPTAS, and TSP in NPO(V) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial_optimization)).

A matrix $A$ is **totally unimodular** if every square submatrix has determinant $-1$, $0$ or $+1$; a polyhedron is **integral** if all its vertices are integral ([Goemans, Polyhedral notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/polyhedral.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Total unimodularity gives integral polyhedra.** If $A$ is totally unimodular, then for every integral $b$ the polyhedron $\{x : Ax \le b,\ x \ge 0\}$ is integral; conversely, if this polyhedron is integral for all integral $b$, then $A$ is totally unimodular. The vertex–edge incidence matrix of a bipartite graph is totally unimodular, which proves the integrality of the bipartite matching polytope and yields König's theorem ([Goemans, Polyhedral notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/polyhedral.pdf)).
- **Ghouila-Houri characterization.** A matrix with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$ is totally unimodular if and only if every subset $R$ of its rows can be split into $R_1, R_2$ with $\sum_{i \in R_1} a_{ij} - \sum_{i \in R_2} a_{ij} \in \{-1,0,1\}$ for every column $j$ ([Goemans, Polyhedral notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/polyhedral.pdf)); in sign form, every subset of rows admits a $\pm1$ signing whose column sums lie in $\{-1,0,1\}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodular_matrix)).
- **Max-flow min-cut.** In a capacitated network, the maximum value of an $s$–$t$ flow equals the minimum capacity of an $s$–$t$ cut; the two problems form a primal–dual pair of linear programs, and equality follows from strong duality ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max-flow_min-cut_theorem)).
- **Greedy algorithm and matroid polytope.** For any matroid $M = (E, \mathcal I)$ and weights $c$, the greedy algorithm returns, for every $k$, a maximum-weight independent set of size $k$; an independence system is a matroid if and only if greedy succeeds for every $k$ and every cost function. The convex hull of independent sets is $\{x \in \mathbb R^E_{\ge 0} : x(S) \le r(S)\ \forall S \subseteq E\}$, where $r$ is the (submodular) rank function ([Goemans, Matroid notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matroid-notes.pdf)).
- **Tutte–Berge formula and Edmonds's blossom algorithm.** For every graph $G = (V,E)$,
$$\max_M |M| = \min_{U \subseteq V} \tfrac12\bigl(|V| + |U| - o(G \setminus U)\bigr),$$
where $o(G \setminus U)$ is the number of odd components of $G \setminus U$; Edmonds's algorithm, which shrinks odd cycles (blossoms), finds a maximum matching in $O(n^2 m)$ time and proves the formula, and Tutte's perfect-matching theorem is the special case of value $|V|/2$ ([Goemans, Non-bipartite matching notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matching-nonbip-notes.pdf)). Edmonds's paper is "Paths, Trees, and Flowers", Canadian Journal of Mathematics 17, 449–467 (1965) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.4153/CJM-1965-045-4)).
- **Max-Cut: SDP approximation and its limits.** Max-Cut is NP-hard and APX-hard; the Goemans–Williamson semidefinite-programming relaxation with random hyperplane rounding achieves ratio about $0.878$; beating $16/17$ is NP-hard (Håstad); and if the Unique Games Conjecture holds, $0.878$ is optimal ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_cut)). The Goemans–Williamson paper appeared in J. ACM 42(6), 1115–1145 (1995) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/227683.227684)).
- **Metric TSP below 3/2.** For some $\varepsilon > 10^{-36}$ there is a randomized $(3/2 - \varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for metric TSP ([Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01409)), and the integrality gap of the subtour LP is at most $3/2 - \varepsilon$ ([Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10043)).

### Examples
- **Maximum spanning tree.** For the graphic matroid the greedy algorithm is Kruskal's algorithm: scan edges in non-increasing order of cost and add an edge unless it closes a cycle ([Goemans, Matroid notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matroid-notes.pdf)).
- **Bipartite assignment.** The perfect matching polytope of $K_{n,n}$ is $\{x \ge 0 : \sum_j x_{ij} = 1,\ \sum_i x_{ij} = 1\}$, integral by total unimodularity, so the assignment problem is a linear program ([Goemans, Polyhedral notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/polyhedral.pdf)).
- **Non-bipartite matching.** In a triangle any matching has at most one edge while covering all edges needs two vertices, so König's min–max equality fails outside bipartite graphs; the Tutte–Berge formula, with odd components, is the correct replacement ([Goemans, Non-bipartite matching notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matching-nonbip-notes.pdf)).
- **Max-Cut in planar graphs** is polynomial-time solvable through duality with the route inspection problem, although it is NP-hard in general ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_cut)).
- **Unit-job scheduling with deadlines and profits** is posed in the notes as an exercise in recognizing a matroid and applying greedy ([Goemans, Matroid notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matroid-notes.pdf)).

### History
Harris posed the maximum-flow problem in 1955, and Ford and Fulkerson's 1956 paper "Maximal flow through a network" established the max-flow min-cut theorem, with an independent 1956 note by Elias, Feinstein and Shannon ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max-flow_min-cut_theorem)). The blossom algorithm for general matching is due to Edmonds ([Goemans, Non-bipartite matching notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matching-nonbip-notes.pdf)), whose "Paths, Trees, and Flowers" appeared in 1965 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.4153/CJM-1965-045-4)); the Goemans–Williamson semidefinite-programming algorithm for Max-Cut ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_cut)) was published in J. ACM in 1995 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/227683.227684)); and the 3/2 approximation barrier for metric TSP was broken by a randomized algorithm of Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan ([Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01409)).

### Connections
- [Linear Programming](node:Linear%20Programming): duality turns polyhedral descriptions into min–max theorems and algorithms.
- [Integer Programming](node:Integer%20Programming): the general formulation; combinatorial problems are integer programs over $\{0,1\}^E$.
- [Approximation Algorithms](node:Approximation%20Algorithms): the main approach to NP-hard combinatorial problems.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): most natural combinatorial problems are NP-hard, which separates the polynomial and approximation sides of the field.
- [Network Flow](node:Network%20Flow) and [Minimum-Cost Flow](node:Minimum-Cost%20Flow): the prototypical polynomially solvable class.
- [Graph Matching](node:Graph%20Matching): bipartite and non-bipartite matching are the central polynomial problems.
- [Minimum Spanning Trees](node:Minimum%20Spanning%20Trees): the greedy algorithm on a graphic matroid.
- [Matroids and Geometric Closure](node:Matroids%20and%20Geometric%20Closure): matroids are the structures on which greedy is optimal.
- [Submodular Optimization](node:Submodular%20Optimization): matroid rank functions are submodular; submodular minimization generalizes matroid problems.
- [Polytopes](node:Polytopes): feasible sets are studied through their convex hulls.
- [Dynamic Programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming): exact method for knapsack and problems on trees or bounded treewidth.
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): supplies most of the problems.

### Common pitfalls
- A polyhedron $\{x : Ax = b, x \ge 0\}$ can be integral for all integral $b$ without $A$ being totally unimodular; the converse of the total-unimodularity integrality theorem holds for the form $Ax \le b, x \ge 0$ ([Goemans, Polyhedral notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/polyhedral.pdf)).
- Greedy is optimal on matroids, not on general independence systems; its success for every weight function characterizes matroids ([Goemans, Matroid notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matroid-notes.pdf)).
- Bipartite intuitions such as König's theorem fail for general graphs because of odd components: in a triangle the maximum matching has one edge but a vertex cover needs two vertices ([Goemans, Non-bipartite matching notes](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/matching-nonbip-notes.pdf)).
- General-purpose methods such as branch-and-bound and branch-and-cut give no guarantee of finding an optimum quickly, as expected for NP-complete problems unless P = NP ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial_optimization)).

### Open problems
- **The 4/3 conjecture for metric TSP.** The integrality gap of the subtour elimination LP (the linear relaxation of the Dantzig–Fulkerson–Johnson formulation) is conjectured to be $4/3$; it has been proved when the optimal LP solution has at most $n + 6$ non-zero components ([Villa et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07003v2)), while the general upper bound proved by Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan is $3/2 - \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon > 10^{-36}$ ([Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10043)).
- **Optimality of Goemans–Williamson.** That $0.878$ is the best polynomial-time ratio for Max-Cut is known only conditionally on the Unique Games Conjecture; unconditionally, NP-hardness is known only above $16/17$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_cut)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Combinatorial optimization (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial_optimization): scope, tractable and NP-hard problems, NPO classes, methods.
- **Learn:** [Goemans, MIT 18.433 Combinatorial Optimization](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18433S13/18433.html): lecture notes on matchings, matroids, polyhedral combinatorics, flows and matroid intersection.
- **Primary:** [Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan, A (Slightly) Improved Approximation Algorithm for Metric TSP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01409): a randomized $(3/2-\varepsilon)$-approximation for metric TSP.
- **Primary:** [Edmonds, Paths, Trees, and Flowers (1965)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.4153/CJM-1965-045-4): the blossom algorithm for maximum matching in general graphs (bibliographic record).
- **Primary:** [Goemans and Williamson, Improved approximation algorithms for maximum cut and satisfiability (J. ACM 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/227683.227684): semidefinite programming rounding (bibliographic record).
- **Further reading:** [Korte and Vygen, Combinatorial Optimization: Theory and Algorithms (Springer, Algorithms and Combinatorics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-56039-6): standard graduate text.

## Reference
### Overview
Combinatorics is the area of mathematics primarily concerned with counting and with properties of finite structures; its scope is not universally agreed, but it covers the enumeration, existence, construction and optimization of discrete structures. Its branches include enumerative, analytic, algebraic and probabilistic combinatorics, partition theory, [graph theory](node:Graph%20Theory), design theory and extremal combinatorics (including Ramsey theory). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics))

Two kinds of argument recur. Exact counting turns a family of objects into sets and maps and counts by bijection, product, division, inclusion–exclusion or generating functions. ([MIT 6.042 counting](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/fd14182dfb1a679eda5cbd38c48c8bb5_MIT6_042JF10_chap11.pdf); [Wikipedia: Inclusion–exclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclusion%E2%80%93exclusion_principle); [Wikipedia: Generating function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_function)) Existence arguments show that some configuration must occur (pigeonhole, Ramsey, Hall) or that a random object has a property with positive probability (the probabilistic method). ([Wikipedia: Pigeonhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonhole_principle); [Wikipedia: Probabilistic method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_method))

### Formal definition
For a family of finite sets $S_n$, the enumerative problem asks for $a_n = |S_n|$, compared through [cardinality](node:Cardinality): the bijection rule says a bijection $A\to B$ gives $|A|=|B|$. ([MIT 6.042 counting](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/fd14182dfb1a679eda5cbd38c48c8bb5_MIT6_042JF10_chap11.pdf)) The answer is often encoded as a formal power series, the **ordinary** or **exponential generating function** ([Wikipedia: Generating function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_function))
$$
A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n, \qquad \hat A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n\frac{x^n}{n!},
$$
which need not converge; $x$ is an indeterminate. Exponential generating functions suit labelled objects: if $C=AB$ then $c_n=\sum_k\binom nk a_kb_{n-k}$. ([Wikipedia: Generating function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_function))

### Key results
- **Sum, product and division rules.** For disjoint finite $A_i$, $|\bigcup A_i|=\sum|A_i|$; $|P_1\times\cdots\times P_n|=\prod|P_i|$; if $f:A\to B$ is exactly $k$-to-1 then $|A|=k|B|$. The number of $k$-subsets of an $n$-set is $\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$. ([MIT 6.042 counting](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/fd14182dfb1a679eda5cbd38c48c8bb5_MIT6_042JF10_chap11.pdf))
- **Inclusion–exclusion.** For finite $A_1,\dots,A_n$,
$$\Big|\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\Big| = \sum_{\emptyset\ne J\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|J|+1}\Big|\bigcap_{j\in J}A_j\Big|.$$
Equivalently, if $g(A)=\sum_{S\subseteq A}f(S)$ then $f(A)=\sum_{S\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|S|}g(S)$, Möbius inversion on the subset lattice. The number of derangements of $n$ elements is the nearest integer to $n!/e$. ([Wikipedia: Inclusion–exclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclusion%E2%80%93exclusion_principle))
- **Double counting.** Counting one set two ways gives identities: summing degrees counts each edge twice (the handshaking lemma), and sorting subsets by size gives $\sum_k\binom nk=2^n$; counting edge sequences that build rooted trees gives Cayley's formula $n^{n-2}$ for labelled trees. ([Wikipedia: Double counting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_counting_%28proof_technique%29))
- **Pigeonhole principle.** No injection exists from a finite set into a smaller one; more precisely, distributing $n$ objects into $m$ boxes puts at least $\lceil n/m\rceil$ in some box. ([Wikipedia: Pigeonhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonhole_principle))
- **Ramsey's theorem.** For all $r,s$ there is a least $R(r,s)$ such that every red–blue colouring of the edges of $K_{R(r,s)}$ has a blue $K_r$ or a red $K_s$. $R(3,3)=6$ and $R(4,4)=18$. The Erdős–Szekeres induction gives $R(r,s)\le\binom{r+s-2}{r-1}$, so $R(s,s)\le(1+o(1))4^{s-1}/\sqrt{\pi s}$, while Erdős (1947) proved $R(s,s)\ge(1+o(1))\frac{s}{e\sqrt2}2^{s/2}$. ([Wikipedia: Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem)) Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved $R(k)\le(4-\varepsilon)^k$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, the first exponential improvement on Erdős–Szekeres (1935). ([Campos et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521))
- **Probabilistic method.** If $\binom nr 2^{1-\binom r2}<1$, the expected number of monochromatic $K_r$ in a uniformly random 2-colouring of $K_n$ is below 1, so some colouring has none and $R(r,r)>n$. Erdős (1959) also used random graphs to show that for all $g,k$ there are graphs of girth at least $g$ and chromatic number at least $k$. ([Wikipedia: Probabilistic method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_method))
- **Hall's marriage theorem.** A finite family $\mathcal F$ of sets has a transversal (a system of distinct representatives) iff every subfamily $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ satisfies $|\mathcal G|\le|\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal G}S|$; equivalently, a finite bipartite graph $(X,Y,E)$ has a matching covering $X$ iff $|W|\le|N(W)|$ for all $W\subseteq X$. It is equivalent to the König and Dilworth theorems. ([Wikipedia: Hall's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%27s_marriage_theorem))

### Examples
- **Catalan numbers.** $C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}n$ satisfy $C_0=1$, $C_n=\sum_{i=1}^nC_{i-1}C_{n-i}$; their generating function $c(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}$ solves $c=1+xc^2$, and $C_n\sim4^n/(n^{3/2}\sqrt\pi)$. They count Dyck words of length $2n$, full binary trees with $n+1$ leaves, triangulations of a convex $(n+2)$-gon and noncrossing partitions of $[n]$: $1,1,2,5,14,42,\dots$ ([Wikipedia: Catalan number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_number))
- **No consecutive integers.** The number of subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with no two consecutive integers is $F_{n+2}$ (with $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$), as is the number of binary strings of length $n$ with no two consecutive 1s. ([Wikipedia: Fibonacci sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_sequence)) Splitting on whether $n$ is present gives the recurrence $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ with $a_0=1$, $a_1=2$.
- **$R(3,3)=6$ by pigeonhole.** A vertex of $K_6$ has at least three edges of one colour; among their endpoints either an edge of that colour closes a triangle or all three edges have the other colour. A 2-colouring of $K_5$ with no monochromatic triangle shows $R(3,3)>5$. ([Wikipedia: Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem))

### History
Early combinatorial problems appear in the Rhind papyrus; Mahāvīra (c. 850) gave formulas for permutations and combinations, and Gersonides a closed formula for binomial coefficients in 1321. Pascal, Newton, Jacob Bernoulli and Euler did foundational work, Sylvester and MacMahon laid groundwork for enumerative and algebraic combinatorics, and powerful general methods developed in the later twentieth century made it an independent branch of mathematics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics)) Dirichlet treated the pigeonhole principle as the *Schubfachprinzip* in 1834. ([Wikipedia: Pigeonhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonhole_principle)) Ramsey's theorem dates from 1930 ([Wikipedia: Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem)) and Hall's theorem from 1935. ([Wikipedia: Hall's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%27s_marriage_theorem)) The probabilistic method was pioneered by Erdős, whose 1947 Ramsey bound is a classic example, though others used it earlier (Szele, 1943, on tournaments with many Hamiltonian cycles). ([Wikipedia: Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Probabilistic method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_method))

### Connections
- [Proof Techniques](node:Proof%20Techniques): bijections, double counting and [induction](node:Mathematical%20Induction) are the basic tools.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory) and [Cardinality](node:Cardinality): counting compares finite sets by bijection.
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): Ramsey and Hall are graph-theoretic existence results.
- [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces) and [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): the probabilistic method uses expectation over random structures.
- [Stirling's Formula](node:Stirling's%20Formula): gives asymptotics of $n!$ and $\binom{2n}n$, e.g. for $C_n$.
- [MSC 05 - Combinatorics](node:MSC%2005%20-%20Combinatorics): field map.
- [MSC 05Axx - Enumerative combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Axx%20-%20Enumerative%20combinatorics): counting and generating functions.
- [MSC 05Bxx - Designs and configurations](node:MSC%2005Bxx%20-%20Designs%20and%20configurations): design theory.
- [MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory): graphs and matchings.
- [MSC 05Dxx - Extremal combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Dxx%20-%20Extremal%20combinatorics): Ramsey and extremal problems.
- [MSC 05Exx - Algebraic combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Exx%20-%20Algebraic%20combinatorics): algebraic methods.

### Common pitfalls
- **Division needs equal fibres.** The division rule applies only to a map that is exactly $k$-to-1; dividing by a guessed symmetry factor fails when objects have different numbers of representations. ([MIT 6.042 counting](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/fd14182dfb1a679eda5cbd38c48c8bb5_MIT6_042JF10_chap11.pdf))
- **The sum rule needs disjointness.** For overlapping sets use inclusion–exclusion. ([MIT 6.042 counting](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/fd14182dfb1a679eda5cbd38c48c8bb5_MIT6_042JF10_chap11.pdf); [Wikipedia: Inclusion–exclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclusion%E2%80%93exclusion_principle))
- **Ordinary versus exponential generating functions.** Products of ordinary generating functions give plain convolutions, products of exponential ones give binomial convolutions; use the latter for labelled objects. ([Wikipedia: Generating function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_function))
- **Probabilistic existence is not construction.** Erdős's Ramsey argument is nonconstructive, and finding such colourings explicitly has been open for more than 50 years. ([Wikipedia: Probabilistic method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_method))

### Open problems
- **$R(5,5)$.** The exact value is unknown and listed as an unsolved problem; it lies between 43 (Exoo, 1989) and 46 (Angeltveit and McKay, 2024), and McKay, Radziszowski and Exoo conjectured in 1997 that $R(5,5)=43$. ([Wikipedia: Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem))
- **Induced Ramsey numbers.** Erdős conjectured in 1974 that there is a constant $c$ such that the induced Ramsey number of every $k$-vertex graph $H$ satisfies $r_{\rm ind}(H)\le 2^{ck}$; this "is still open" and is described as one of the important problems of extremal graph theory. ([Wikipedia: Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Combinatorics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics): scope, branches and history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.042J, Chapter 11 "Cardinality Rules"](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-fall-2010/fd14182dfb1a679eda5cbd38c48c8bb5_MIT6_042JF10_chap11.pdf): bijection, sum, product, division and subset rules.
- **Primary:** [Campos, Griffiths, Morris & Sahasrabudhe, "An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey" (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521): the $(4-\varepsilon)^k$ upper bound.
- **Primary:** [R. Stanley, *Enumerative Combinatorics*, Vols. 1–2 (Cambridge University Press)](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/): the standard graduate text on enumeration.
- **Further reading:** [N. Alon & J. Spencer, *The Probabilistic Method*, 4th ed. (Wiley, 2016)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Probabilistic+Method%2C+4th+Edition-p-9781119061953): the standard monograph on probabilistic combinatorics.

## Reference
### Overview
Compactification gives a spacetime dimension that would otherwise be infinite a finite, often periodic, length. In the limit where that size goes to zero no field depends on the extra direction and the theory is dimensionally reduced; in this sense compactification generalizes [Kaluza–Klein Theory](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Theory). In string theory the extra dimensions are curled up on Calabi–Yau spaces or [orbifolds](node:Orbifolds), and flux compactification additionally threads the internal space with generalized electromagnetic fluxes, whose many integer choices underlie the landscape ([Wikipedia: Compactification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compactification_%28physics%29)).

A compactified theory contains a tower of massive Kaluza–Klein excitations and, generically, massless scalar fields called moduli: each independent deformation $\delta G_\alpha=\partial G(\vec t)/\partial t^\alpha$ of the internal metric that preserves the equations of motion gives a massless four-dimensional field ([Douglas and Kachru, §II.2](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)). Moduli are deformations that leave the four-dimensional energy unchanged, so a realistic vacuum must give them a potential; flux can do so at tree level for some moduli, while the overall volume stays massless at tree level, and constructing fully stabilized vacua with fluxes, branes and quantum corrections is the subject of moduli stabilization ([Denef, Les Houches lectures, §2.1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0803.1194)).

The size of the internal space sets the relation between higher- and lower-dimensional gravity: $M_{P,4}^2=M_{P,D}^{D-2}/M_{KK}^{D-4}$ with $M_{KK}=\mathrm{Vol}(M)^{-1/(D-4)}$, so a large internal volume makes the four-dimensional Planck mass much larger than the fundamental scale ([Douglas and Kachru, §II.1, eq. 1](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)). This is the mechanism behind [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions) and one approach to the [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem). Which compactifications can describe our universe is now framed partly by swampland conjectures, which propose that some low-energy effective theories admit no consistent quantum-gravity completion ([Palti, swampland review](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.06239)).

### Formal definition
**Circle reduction of gravity.** Kaluza's ansatz writes the five-dimensional metric as
$$ds^2=g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu+\phi^2\,(A_\nu dx^\nu+dx^5)^2,$$
giving a four-dimensional metric $g_{\mu\nu}$, a vector $A_\mu$ identified with the electromagnetic potential, and a scalar $\phi$. Kaluza imposed the cylinder condition (no dependence on $x^5$), which Klein explained in 1926 by taking the fifth dimension to be a small circle. The scalar obeys $\Box\phi=\tfrac14\phi^3F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}$, so it cannot be held constant without constraining the electromagnetic field ([Wikipedia: Kaluza–Klein theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluza%E2%80%93Klein_theory)).

**Kaluza–Klein tower.** On a circle of radius $R$, momentum is quantized as $p=n/R$ ([Wikipedia: T-duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-duality)), so a massless higher-dimensional field appears in lower dimensions as a tower of standing waves with masses $M_n\propto n/R$ ([Wikipedia: Kaluza–Klein theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluza%E2%80%93Klein_theory)). On a general compact space the eigenvalues of the internal Laplacian become the squared KK masses ([Douglas and Kachru, §II.2](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)); see [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes).

**Scherk–Schwarz reduction.** Scherk and Schwarz described a generalized dimensional reduction applicable to theories in curved space; for a class of Lie groups they call "flat groups" the result has no cosmological constant and arbitrary mass parameters, and reducing 11-dimensional supergravity this way gives an $N=8$ four-dimensional theory with three arbitrary masses ([Scherk and Schwarz 1979, INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20Scherk%20and%20a%20Schwarz%20and%20t%20%22How%20to%20get%20masses%20from%20extra%20dimensions%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts)).

**Calabi–Yau moduli.** For a Calabi–Yau threefold $M$ the Kähler moduli space has dimension $b_2=h^{1,1}$ and the complex-structure moduli space has dimension $h^{2,1}$, with $b_3=2h^{2,1}+2$; the Ricci-flat family has dimension $2h^{2,1}+h^{1,1}$. For the quintic, $\dim\mathcal M_C=101$ and $b_3=204$ ([Douglas and Kachru, §§II.1.2, II.3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)). These counts are cohomological, computed by [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory) on [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds).

### Key results
- **Supersymmetry from special holonomy.** A flux-free compactification on a Calabi–Yau threefold with full $SU(3)$ holonomy leaves one quarter of the original supersymmetry ([Wikipedia: Calabi–Yau manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi%E2%80%93Yau_manifold)). In six dimensions $SU(3)$ is the only special holonomy for which the $SO(6)$ spinor contains a unique singlet ([Douglas and Kachru, §II.1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)); see [Holonomy Groups](node:Holonomy%20Groups) and [Supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry).
- **Heterotic Calabi–Yau spectrum.** In the standard embedding the gauge connection equals the spin connection; then $248=(27,3)\oplus(\overline{27},\bar 3)\oplus(78,1)\oplus(1,8)$ under $E_6\times SU(3)$, giving an $E_6$ [grand unified theory](node:Grand%20Unification) with $n_{27}=h^{2,1}$, $n_{\overline{27}}=h^{1,1}$. Since $\chi=2(h^{1,1}-h^{2,1})$, the net number of generations is $|\chi|/2$, and three generations need $|\chi|=6$ ([Douglas and Kachru, §II.1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)).
- **T-duality.** For a closed string on a circle with winding $m$ and momentum $n/R$, the zero-mode energy contains $(mR)^2+(n/R)^2$, invariant under $R\to1/R$ with $m\leftrightarrow n$. By the SYZ conjecture, mirror symmetry of Calabi–Yau threefolds is T-duality applied simultaneously to $T^3$ fibres ([Wikipedia: T-duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-duality)). On one circle T-duality maps IIA to IIB, since dualizing $X^9$ flips the chirality of the right-moving ground states ([Polchinski, TASI lectures on D-branes, §3.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-th/9611050)). See [String Dualities](node:String%20Dualities).
- **Flux quantization and potentials.** Fluxes obey $\int_\Sigma F_{p+2}=n\in\mathbb Z$ and generate $V=\int_M F\wedge *F$ on moduli space; flux-fixed complex-structure moduli get masses $M_F\sim\alpha'/R^3$, below the KK scale at moderately large radius ([Douglas and Kachru, §§II.4, II.6.2](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)). The D3 tadpole $\frac{1}{\ell_s^4}\int F_3\wedge H_3+N_{D3}=Q_c=\chi(Z)/24$ makes the number of metastable F-theory flux vacua in any compact region of low-energy parameter space finite ([Denef, §3.5, eqs. 3.34–3.35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0803.1194)).
- **GKP warped flux compactifications.** In type IIB orientifolds and F-theory on Calabi–Yau fourfolds the choice of RR and NS fluxes fixes moduli and produces strongly warped throats (compactified Klebanov–Strassler regions) and hence large hierarchies ([GKP](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0105097)). The warped metric is $ds^2=e^{2A(y)}\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu+e^{-2A(y)}\tilde g_{mn}dy^mdy^n$ with $G_3=F_3-\phi H_3$, $\phi=C_0+ie^{-S}$ ([Douglas and Kachru, §IV.1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)).
- **KKLT.** With $W=\int G_3\wedge\Omega$ and no-scale $K=-3\ln[-i(\rho-\bar\rho)]$ the volume modulus is flat. Adding $W=W_0+Ae^{ia\rho}$ gives a supersymmetric AdS minimum with $W_0=-Ae^{-a\sigma}(1+\tfrac23a\sigma)$ and $V_{\rm AdS}=-a^2A^2e^{-2a\sigma}/(6\sigma)$; control needs $\sigma\gg1$, $a\sigma>1$ and fluxes tuned so $|W_0|\ll1$. An anti-D3-brane adds a term $\propto1/\sigma^3$ and lifts the minimum to a metastable de Sitter vacuum ([KKLT, §§II–III](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0301240)).
- **Large Volume Scenario.** Including $\alpha'$ corrections, the IIB potential at large volume approaches zero from below, giving a non-supersymmetric AdS minimum at exponentially large volume that fixes all Kähler and complex-structure moduli, with a tachyon-free uplift ([BBCQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0502058)).
- **M-theory on $G_2$ and F-theory.** M-theory on $G_2$-holonomy manifolds needs singularities to produce non-abelian gauge groups and chiral fermions ([Acharya and Gukov](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0409191)); see [G2 Manifolds](node:G2%20Manifolds) and [M-Theory](node:M-Theory). In F-theory GUTs the local geometry of singularities determines gauge group, matter and Yukawa couplings, the latter arising at intersection points of surface defects that carry chiral matter ([Beasley, Heckman and Vafa](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.3391)).
- **Bubble of nothing.** The Kaluza–Klein vacuum $\mathbb M^4\times S^1$ is unstable to a bubble of nothing whose bounce is the five-dimensional Euclidean [Schwarzschild solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution), with action $\pi^2m_{\rm Pl}^2R^2$; supersymmetric fermion boundary conditions can obstruct the decay, but not universally across internal manifolds ([Draper, Garcia Garcia and Lillard](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.08068)). At large radius, winding tachyons show no evidence of enhancing the rate ([Dine, Shomer and Sun](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0607003)).

### Examples
- **Freund–Rubin.** Six-dimensional Einstein–Maxwell theory on $S^2$ with $N$ flux units has $V(R)\sim N^2/R^6-1/R^4$, minimized near $R\sim N$; strictly, the original Freund–Rubin vacua are not compactifications yielding lower-dimensional effective theories ([Douglas and Kachru, §II.4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)).
- **Toric Calabi–Yau threefolds.** Kreuzer and Skarke classified all 473,800,776 reflexive polyhedra in four dimensions, which give Calabi–Yau hypersurfaces with 30,108 distinct Hodge-number pairs, all linked by singular transitions ([Kreuzer and Skarke](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0002240)); see [Toric Varieties](node:Toric%20Varieties).
- **The Z-manifold.** Resolving the 27 fixed points of $T^6/\mathbb Z_3$ by exceptional $\mathbb P^2$s and adding the 9 invariant cycles of the torus gives $h^{1,1}=36$, while $h^{2,1}=0$, so the manifold is rigid ([Aspinwall and Plesser](https://arxiv.org/html/1106.2998)).
- **Quintic.** 101 complex-structure moduli and $b_3=204$ ([Douglas and Kachru, §II.3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)).

### History
Kaluza sent his five-dimensional unification to Einstein in 1919 and published it in 1921; Klein proposed the small circle in 1926 ([Wikipedia: Kaluza–Klein theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluza%E2%80%93Klein_theory)). Scherk and Schwarz introduced their generalized reduction in 1979 ([INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20Scherk%20and%20a%20Schwarz%20and%20t%20%22How%20to%20get%20masses%20from%20extra%20dimensions%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts)). Detailed arguments for Calabi–Yau compactification were made around 1985, most notably by Candelas et al., whose 1985 paper also coined the name "Calabi–Yau" ([Wikipedia: Calabi–Yau manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi%E2%80%93Yau_manifold); [Douglas and Kachru](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)). The large/small-radius duality was first described for toroidal compactifications by Brink–Green–Schwarz (1982), Kikkawa–Yamasaki (Phys. Lett. B 149, 1984) and Sakai–Senda ([Alvarez, Alvarez-Gaumé and Lozano](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-th/9410237); [Kikkawa–Yamasaki, INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=t%20%22Casimir%20effects%20in%20superstring%20theories%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts)). In 1989 Dai, Leigh and Polchinski showed that the $R\to0$ limit connects IIA and IIB, introducing D-branes and orientifold planes ([INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=t%20%22New%20connections%20between%20string%20theories%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts)), and Dine, Huet and Seiberg found that the known type II theories are different ground states of one theory and that in bosonic and heterotic theories duality transformations are often gauge transformations ([INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=t%20%22Large%20and%20small%20radius%20in%20string%20theory%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts)). GKP appeared in 2001, KKLT in 2003 and the LVS in 2005 ([GKP](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0105097); [KKLT](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0301240); [BBCQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0502058)).

### Connections
- [Kaluza–Klein Theory](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Theory): the original circle reduction of five-dimensional gravity.
- [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes): the massive tower produced by any compactification.
- [Effective Field Theory of Compactification](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory%20of%20Compactification): the four-dimensional theory of moduli and KK modes.
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds) and [Moduli Spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces): internal spaces and their deformation spaces.
- [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds), [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory) and [Toric Varieties](node:Toric%20Varieties): Hodge numbers count moduli and generations; toric methods build examples.
- [Holonomy Groups](node:Holonomy%20Groups) and [G2 Manifolds](node:G2%20Manifolds): special holonomy controls preserved supersymmetry.
- [String Theory](node:String%20Theory), [M-Theory](node:M-Theory), [Supergravity](node:Supergravity) and [D-Branes](node:D-Branes): the theories and objects being compactified.
- [String Dualities](node:String%20Dualities): T-duality and mirror symmetry act on compactifications.
- [String Landscape](node:String%20Landscape): the vast set of flux vacua.
- [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions), [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions) and [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale): the volume relation for $M_{P,4}$.
- [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space), [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant) and [Cosmic Inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation): targets of uplift constructions and of the de Sitter conjecture.
- [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space) and [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence): Freund–Rubin-type flux vacua have AdS factors.
- [Supersymmetry Breaking](node:Supersymmetry%20Breaking): flux and anti-brane effects break supersymmetry in KKLT and LVS.

### Common pitfalls
- **Flux alone does not fix everything.** In GKP-type vacua the no-scale structure leaves the volume unfixed; KKLT needs nonperturbative terms, and LVS needs $\alpha'$ corrections ([KKLT, §II.1](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0301240); [BBCQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0502058)).
- **Small radius is not small physics.** Under $R\to1/R$, $m\leftrightarrow n$ the zero-mode energy is unchanged, so a very small circle is equivalent to a large one ([Wikipedia: T-duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-duality)).
- **Small $|W_0|$ is a tuning.** Generically $W_0\sim O(1)$ if fluxes break supersymmetry, and then the KKLT control conditions fail ([KKLT, §II.3](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0301240)).
- **Euler characteristic counts net generations.** $|\chi|/2$ counts $27$ minus $\overline{27}$ multiplets, not the total ([Douglas and Kachru, §II.1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)).

### Open problems
> [!warning] Contested
> **Do controlled de Sitter compactifications exist?** KKLT propose metastable de Sitter vacua from anti-D3 uplift and argue they are long-lived ([KKLT, §§III–IV](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0301240)). Obied, Ooguri, Spodyneiko and Vafa propose instead that any consistent quantum-gravity potential obeys $|\nabla V|\ge cV$, $c>0$, forbidding de Sitter vacua, motivated by the difficulty of controlled constructions and by no-go theorems ([Obied et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.08362)). Denef, Hebecker and Wrase find that in the simplest models adding decoupled quintessence to the Standard Model this bound is violated by 50 orders of magnitude, and only a very specific quintessence–Higgs coupling might evade it ([Denef, Hebecker and Wrase](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06581)). Garg and Krishnan refine the criterion so that slow roll must be violated at $O(1)$: $\epsilon_V$ need not be $O(1)$ if $\eta_V\lesssim-O(1)$ ([Garg and Krishnan](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05193)), and Ooguri, Palti, Shiu and Vafa derive a refined version from the distance conjecture and the covariant entropy bound in parametrically controlled regimes, evading the counterexamples at potential maxima ([OPSV](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.05506)).

- **Distance conjecture.** At infinite geodesic distance in moduli space an infinite tower of states becomes light, $M(Q)\sim M(P)e^{-\alpha d(P,Q)}$ with $\alpha>0$ ([Ooguri and Vafa](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0605264); [Palti](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.06239)). The swampland criteria are not proven from microscopic physics and are stated as conjectures ([Palti](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.06239)).
- **Landscape questions.** Douglas and Kachru write that it is "far from obvious" that the number of $\Lambda>0$ vacua is near $10^{120}$, that no general agreement exists on how to define a measure factor, and that string theory lacks natural definitions of off-shell quantities such as the effective potential ([Douglas and Kachru, §§III.1, III.5](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Compactification (physics) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compactification_%28physics%29): definition and flux compactification in brief.
- **Reference:** [Kaluza–Klein theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluza%E2%80%93Klein_theory): the circle ansatz, cylinder condition and history.
- **Learn:** [Denef, Les Houches Lectures on Constructing String Vacua](https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.1194): F-theory flux vacua, tadpoles, moduli stabilization and vacuum statistics.
- **Learn:** [Palti, The Swampland: Introduction and Review](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.06239): distance and de Sitter conjectures.
- **Learn:** [Douglas and Kachru, Flux compactification (review)](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0610102): moduli, Hodge-number counting, fluxes and vacuum statistics.
- **Primary:** [Giddings, Kachru and Polchinski](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0105097): warped IIB flux compactifications.
- **Primary:** [Kachru, Kallosh, Linde and Trivedi, De Sitter vacua in string theory](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0301240): the KKLT construction.
- **Primary:** [Kreuzer and Skarke, reflexive polyhedra in four dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0002240): the toric Calabi–Yau database.
- **Further reading:** [Polchinski, String Theory Vol. 2 (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/string-theory/2D456468D20AA8A9CE10CEB08B95B9DC): orbifold and Calabi–Yau compactification chapters.
- **Further reading:** [Ibáñez and Uranga, String Theory and Particle Physics (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/string-theory-and-particle-physics/preface/6F8A3122497E92C4A89097FE4B5313CA): heterotic, orbifold and intersecting-brane model building.
references.Complex Analysis:
## Reference
### Overview
Complex analysis is the branch of mathematical analysis that studies complex-valued functions of complex variables; this note concentrates on one variable. Unlike real differentiable functions, complex-differentiable (holomorphic) functions are automatically infinitely differentiable and locally equal to their Taylor series, which makes the theory far more rigid than real analysis. The subject is used in functional analysis, algebraic geometry, number theory and applied mathematics, and in physics in hydrodynamics, thermodynamics and quantum mechanics. ([Wikipedia: Complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis))

The central passage of the theory runs from a local derivative to integral formulas and global constraints. Cauchy's integral theorem says closed-contour integrals of holomorphic functions vanish, and Cauchy's integral formula recovers the values inside a disk from the values on its boundary. From these come power series expansions, Liouville's theorem, the identity theorem and analytic continuation, the residue theorem for evaluating integrals, and, on the geometric side, the Riemann mapping theorem on conformal equivalence of planar domains, which may be "the most important result in the one-dimensional theory." ([Wikipedia: Complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis))

### Formal definition
For an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb C$, a function $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is **holomorphic** on $U$ if it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$, i.e. the limit
$$f'(z_0)=\lim_{h\to 0,\ h\in\mathbb C}\frac{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}{h}$$
exists for each $z_0\in U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. ([Wikipedia: Holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function))

Writing $f=u+iv$ with $u,v$ real, complex differentiability forces the **Cauchy–Riemann equations** $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$. Conversely, if $u,v$ are real-differentiable at $z_0$ and satisfy these equations there, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z_0$; continuity of the partial derivatives is a common sufficient hypothesis but is not necessary. Real differentiability cannot be dropped from the pointwise converse: $\sqrt{|xy|}$, with imaginary part zero, satisfies the equations at the origin but is not real-differentiable there, hence not complex differentiable. The Looman–Menchoff theorem gives a global weakening: if $f$ is continuous on an open set $\Omega$, its partial derivatives exist, and the equations hold throughout $\Omega$, then $f$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy–Riemann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Riemann_equations))

### Key results
- **Cauchy's integral theorem.** If $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ is open and simply connected and $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, then $\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=0$ for every closed smooth curve $\gamma$ in $U$. Goursat showed that only existence of $f'$ everywhere in $U$ is needed, with no continuity assumption on the partial derivatives. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's integral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_integral_theorem))
- **Cauchy's integral formula.** If $f$ is holomorphic on an open set $U$ containing a closed disk $D$ whose boundary circle $\gamma$ is oriented counterclockwise, then for every $a$ in the interior of $D$, $f(a)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f(z)}{z-a}\,dz$ and $f^{(n)}(a)=\frac{n!}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^{n+1}}\,dz$. Consequently holomorphic functions are analytic (given locally by convergent power series) and infinitely differentiable. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's integral formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_integral_formula))
- **Identity theorem.** If $f,g$ are analytic on a domain $D$ (open and connected) and $f=g$ on a set $S\subseteq D$ having an accumulation point in $D$, then $f=g$ on all of $D$; connectedness is necessary. ([Wikipedia: Identity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_theorem))
- **Liouville's theorem.** Every bounded entire function is constant. Applied to $1/p$ for a nonconstant polynomial $p$ without roots, it proves the fundamental theorem of algebra. Picard's little theorem strengthens it: an entire function whose image omits two or more complex numbers is constant. ([Wikipedia: Liouville's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%27s_theorem_%28complex_analysis%29))
- **Morera's theorem and uniform limits.** A continuous $f$ on an open set $D\subseteq\mathbb C$ with $\oint_\gamma f\,dz=0$ for every closed piecewise $C^1$ curve $\gamma$ in $D$ is holomorphic on $D$. Combined with Cauchy's theorem, this shows that if holomorphic functions on an open set $\Omega$ converge uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega$ to $f$, then $f$ is holomorphic (Weierstrass's convergence theorem). ([Wikipedia: Morera's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morera%27s_theorem))
- **Residue theorem.** Let $U$ be simply connected and open, $a_1,\dots,a_n\in U$, $f$ holomorphic on $U\setminus\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$, and $\gamma$ a closed rectifiable curve in $U\setminus\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$. Then $\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{k=1}^n I(\gamma,a_k)\operatorname{Res}(f,a_k)$, where $I(\gamma,a_k)$ is the winding number of $\gamma$ about $a_k$. ([Wikipedia: Residue theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residue_theorem))
- **Argument principle and Rouché's theorem.** If $f$ is meromorphic inside and on a simple closed counterclockwise contour $C$ with no zeros or poles on $C$, then $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C f'(z)/f(z)\,dz=Z-P$, the number of zeros minus the number of poles inside $C$, counted with multiplicity and order. ([Wikipedia: Argument principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_principle)) Rouché's theorem follows: for $f,g$ holomorphic on and inside a simple closed contour with $|g|<|f|$ on the contour, $f$ and $f+g$ have the same number of zeros inside it. ([Wikipedia: Rouché's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouch%C3%A9%27s_theorem))
- **Open mapping theorem.** A non-constant holomorphic function on a domain $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ maps open subsets of $U$ to open subsets of $\mathbb C$. ([Wikipedia: Open mapping theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_mapping_theorem_%28complex_analysis%29))
- **Maximum modulus principle.** If $f$ is holomorphic on a bounded connected open set $D$ and $|f|$ has a local maximum at some $z_0\in D$, then $f$ is constant on $D$. If $f$ is continuous on $\overline D$ and holomorphic on $D$, then $|f|$ attains its maximum on the boundary of $D$. ([Wikipedia: Maximum modulus principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_modulus_principle))
- **Schwarz lemma.** If $f$ is holomorphic on the open unit disk $\mathbb D$ with $f(0)=0$ and $|f|\le 1$, then $|f(z)|\le|z|$ on $\mathbb D$ and $|f'(0)|\le 1$; if equality holds at some $z\neq 0$ or $|f'(0)|=1$, then $f(z)=az$ with $|a|=1$. ([Wikipedia: Schwarz lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarz_lemma))
- **Riemann mapping theorem.** If $U\subsetneq\mathbb C$ is a non-empty simply connected open set, there is a biholomorphic map of $U$ onto $\mathbb D$; for fixed $z_0\in U$ it is unique once $f(z_0)=0$ and $f'(z_0)>0$ are imposed, a consequence of the Schwarz lemma. The theorem fails in higher dimensions. ([Wikipedia: Riemann mapping theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem); [Wikipedia: Complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis))

### Examples
Polynomials and the exponential and trigonometric functions are entire; $1/z$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and the principal logarithm on the complement of the nonpositive real axis. The conjugate $\bar z$ and $|z|$ are not holomorphic ($\bar z$ is antiholomorphic). ([Wikipedia: Holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function)) For $z^2=(x^2-y^2)+2ixy$ one has $u_x=v_y=2x$ and $u_y=-v_x=-2y$, so the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold everywhere. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy–Riemann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Riemann_equations))

A residue computation: for $t>0$, $f(z)=e^{itz}/(z^2+1)$ has a single pole $z=i$ in the upper half-plane with residue $e^{-t}/(2i)$. Closing the segment $[-a,a]$ with an upper semicircle of radius $a>1$, whose contribution is at most $\pi a/(a^2-1)\to0$, gives $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{itx}}{x^2+1}\,dx=\pi e^{-|t|}$ (using the pole $-i$ when $t<0$); at $t=0$ this is the elementary value $\pi$. ([Wikipedia: Residue theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residue_theorem))

Analytic continuation: by the identity theorem, a holomorphic function on a connected domain is determined by its values on any smaller subdomain, which is what allows the [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) to be extended across the complex plane. ([Wikipedia: Complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis))

### History
The subject has roots in the 18th century and just before; Euler, Gauss, Riemann, Cauchy and Weierstrass are among its principal founders. ([Wikipedia: Complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis)) Riemann stated the mapping theorem in his 1851 thesis, relying on the Dirichlet principle, which Weierstrass showed is not universally valid. Osgood gave the first rigorous proof in 1900; Carathéodory's 1912 proof via Montel's normal families became the textbook approach, Koebe simplified it, and Fejér and Riesz (1922) obtained the map as the solution of an extremal problem. ([Wikipedia: Riemann mapping theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem)) Goursat showed that Cauchy's theorem needs only the existence of the complex derivative, not continuity of the partial derivatives. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's integral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_integral_theorem))

### Connections
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): real partial derivatives give the Cauchy–Riemann test, and line integrals underlie contour integration.
- [Residue Theorem](node:Residue%20Theorem): the main computational tool built on Cauchy's theorem.
- [Laurent Series](node:Laurent%20Series): expansions around isolated singularities that define residues.
- [Riemann Mapping Theorem](node:Riemann%20Mapping%20Theorem): the central existence theorem for conformal maps of simply connected domains.
- [Conformal Mapping](node:Conformal%20Mapping): the geometric side of holomorphic functions with nonzero derivative.
- [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces): the natural domains for multivalued functions and analytic continuation.
- [Entire and Meromorphic Functions](node:Entire%20and%20Meromorphic%20Functions): the global theory extending Liouville and Picard.
- [Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory): uses contour integrals and continuation of Dirichlet series.
- [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) and [Prime Number Theorem](node:Prime%20Number%20Theorem): the classic application to the primes.
- [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable): the field map for further directions.

### Common pitfalls
A hole in the domain can obstruct Cauchy's theorem: $1/z$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, which is not simply connected, and its integral over any circle centred at $0$ is $2\pi i$, not $0$. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's integral formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_integral_formula); [Wikipedia: Holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function))

The Cauchy–Riemann equations at a single point do not give holomorphy: $z^5/|z|^4$ satisfies them at $0$ but is not analytic there, so the equations must hold throughout an open set, with suitable regularity. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy–Riemann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Riemann_equations))

The Riemann mapping theorem requires $U\neq\mathbb C$ and is special to one variable: it fails in higher dimensions. ([Wikipedia: Riemann mapping theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem); [Wikipedia: Complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis))

### Open problems
- **Brennan's conjecture.** For a simply connected domain $W$ with at least two boundary points in the extended plane and a conformal map $\varphi$ of $W$ onto the unit disk, the conjecture is that $\int_W|\varphi'|^p\,dx\,dy<\infty$ for all $4/3<p<4$. Brennan proved it for $4/3<p<p_0$ with some $p_0>3$, Bertilsson (1999) for $4/3<p<3.422$, and the source states that the full result remains open. ([Wikipedia: Brennan conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennan_conjecture))

> [!warning] Contested
> The same page reports a recent preprint claiming a proof of Brennan's conjecture and notes that it is unverified; treat the claim as reported and unconfirmed. ([Wikipedia: Brennan conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennan_conjecture))

- **Riemann hypothesis.** The Clay Mathematics Institute lists as unsolved the conjecture that all "interesting" solutions of $\zeta(s)=0$ lie on a certain vertical line. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/)) The zeta function's definition is extended to a much larger domain by analytic continuation, so this is a question about the zeros of the analytically continued function. ([Wikipedia: Complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Complex analysis (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis): orientation, history and the main theorems, with links to each.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.04 Complex Variables with Applications (Orloff)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-04-complex-variables-with-applications-spring-2018/): full course with notes; its [calendar](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-04-complex-variables-with-applications-spring-2018/pages/calendar/) runs from analytic functions through Cauchy's theorem, Laurent series, residues, conformal maps and the argument principle.
- **Primary:** [Stein and Shakarchi, Complex Analysis (Princeton Lectures in Analysis II, 2003)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691113852/complex-analysis): standard graduate text covering Cauchy's theorems, residues, analytic continuation, the argument principle, the zeta function and the prime number theorem, and elliptic functions.
- **Further reading:** [Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I (Springer GTM, 1978)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-6313-5): canonical graduate text (bibliographic record).
