## Reference
### Overview
Computability theory (recursion theory) studies which functions on the natural numbers can be computed by an effective procedure at all, independent of time or memory bounds. Its founding models — Gödel's general recursive functions, Church's lambda calculus, and Turing and Post machines — were introduced in the 1930s and shown to define the same class of functions; Church proposed that this class coincides with the intuitive notion of "computable in principle", which is the Church–Turing thesis ([SEP: Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/)).

The basic negative result is that some well-posed problems have no algorithm. Turing showed that the halting problem is unsolvable, and Church and Turing independently showed in 1936 that Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem is not effectively decidable. A counting argument already guarantees non-computable sets — there are countably many Turing machines but uncountably many sets of naturals — but the halting problem gives an explicit, natural example ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)).

Beyond the computable/non-computable split, the subject measures *how* non-computable a set is. Turing's 1939 oracle machines lead to Turing reducibility and the Turing degrees; the arithmetical hierarchy classifies definable sets by quantifier complexity; and much modern research concerns the global structure of the degrees, [algorithmic randomness](node:Algorithmic%20Randomness), and connections with descriptive set theory ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)). It is the foundation on which complexity theory (resource-bounded computation) is built ([SEP: Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/)).

### Formal definition
**Partial recursive functions.** The partial recursive functions are the closure of the initial primitive recursive functions (zero, successor, projections) under composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded minimization
$$\mu y\,[g(\vec x,y)=0] = \text{least } y \text{ with } g(\vec x,y)=0 \text{ and } g(\vec x,z)\!\downarrow \text{ for } z<y .$$
(if no such $y$ exists, or $g$ is undefined somewhere along the search, the result is undefined) ([Wikipedia: General recursive function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_recursive_function)). A Turing machine $M$ computes the partial function $n \mapsto M(n)$, undefined when $M$ does not halt on $n$; the two classes coincide ([SEP: Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/)).

**Indices.** Fix an admissible numbering $(\varphi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}$ of the partial computable functions; write $\varphi_e(n)\!\downarrow$ if it is defined and $F \simeq G$ if two partial functions are defined on the same inputs with equal values ([Wikipedia: Kleene's recursion theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kleene%27s_recursion_theorem)).

**Decidable and c.e. sets.** $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ is *computable* (decidable, recursive) if its characteristic function is computable; it is *computably enumerable* (c.e., r.e.) if it is the range of some computable function ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)). The halting set is
$$K=\{e : \varphi_e(e)\!\downarrow\}$$
([SEP: Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/)).

**Reducibilities and degrees.** $A \le_m B$ (many-one) if there is a total computable $f$ with $n\in A \iff f(n)\in B$. $A\le_T B$ (Turing) if an oracle machine with oracle $B$ decides $A$. The Turing degree of $A$ is its class under $A\le_T B \le_T A$. The *jump* $A'$ is the halting problem for oracle machines with oracle $A$ ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)).

**Arithmetical hierarchy.** $A$ is $\Sigma^0_n$ if it is definable by a formula $\exists \vec y\,\psi$ with $\psi$ a $\Pi^0_{n-1}$ formula, $\Pi^0_n$ if its complement is $\Sigma^0_n$, and $\Delta^0_n$ if it is both; $\Sigma^0_0=\Pi^0_0$ are the sets defined with bounded quantifiers only ([Wikipedia: Arithmetical hierarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetical_hierarchy)).

### Key results
- **Unsolvability of the halting problem (Turing).** $K$ is c.e. but its complement is not c.e.; hence $K$ is not computable ([SEP: Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/)). More generally, for every set $A$, $A' $ has strictly higher Turing degree than $A$ ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)).
- **Rice's theorem.** Let $P\subseteq\mathbb N$ be non-trivial ($P\ne\emptyset,\mathbb N$) and extensional ($\varphi_m=\varphi_n \Rightarrow (m\in P\iff n\in P)$). Then $P$ is undecidable; the only decidable index sets are $\emptyset$ and $\mathbb N$ ([Wikipedia: Rice's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice%27s_theorem)). In the sharper form, for any nontrivial class of c.e. sets, $K$ or its complement is many-one reducible to its index set ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)).
- **Kleene's second recursion theorem (1938).** For every partial computable $Q(x,y)$ there is an index $p$ with $\varphi_p \simeq \lambda y.\,Q(p,y)$, and $p$ is obtained effectively from an index of $Q$. **Rogers' fixed-point form:** for every total computable $F$ there is $e$ with $\varphi_e\simeq\varphi_{F(e)}$ ([Wikipedia: Kleene's recursion theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kleene%27s_recursion_theorem)).
- **Post's theorem.** For $n\ge1$, $\emptyset^{(n)}$ is $m$-complete for $\Sigma^0_n$, its complement is $m$-complete for $\Pi^0_n$, and $\emptyset^{(n-1)}$ is Turing-complete for $\Delta^0_n$. Consequently the hierarchy is proper: $\Sigma^0_n\subsetneq\Sigma^0_{n+1}$, and $\Sigma^0_n\cup\Pi^0_n\subsetneq\Delta^0_{n+1}$ for $n\ge1$. In particular $\Sigma^0_1$ = c.e. and $\Delta^0_1$ = computable ([Wikipedia: Arithmetical hierarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetical_hierarchy)).
- **Friedberg–Muchnik theorem.** There are c.e. sets of Turing degree strictly between $\mathbf 0$ and $\mathbf 0'$, solving Post's 1944 problem on the existence of c.e. sets of intermediate degree; Kleene and Post (1954) had earlier produced intermediate degrees, not necessarily containing c.e. sets ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)).
- **Friedberg jump inversion; Shore–Slaman definability.** Every set computing $\emptyset'$ is the jump of some set; and the jump operator is definable in the partial order of the Turing degrees (Shore–Slaman 1999) ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)).

### Examples
- **Undecidable problems from mathematics.** Hilbert's tenth problem (solvability of [Diophantine equations](node:Diophantine%20Equations)) has no algorithm (Matiyasevich 1970); the word problem for semigroups is undecidable (Markov, Post 1947), as is the word problem for groups (Novikov, Boone, 1950s) ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)).
- **Hierarchy levels.** The set of indices of total computable functions is $\Pi^0_2$ ([Wikipedia: Arithmetical hierarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetical_hierarchy)).
- **Program analysis.** By Rice's theorem, "does program $e$ compute a total function?", "does $e$ terminate and return 0 on every input?" and "is $\varphi_e$ equal to a fixed $\varphi_a$?" are all undecidable, since each is a nontrivial extensional property ([Wikipedia: Rice's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice%27s_theorem)).

### History
The subject was founded in the 1930s by Gödel, Church, Péter, Turing, Kleene and Post. In 1936 Turing introduced his machine model and, with Church, showed the Entscheidungsproblem undecidable; Turing introduced oracle machines in 1939. Post posed his problem on c.e. degrees in 1944; Gödel endorsed the Church–Turing thesis as an absolute notion in 1946; Kleene named "Church's thesis" and "Turing's thesis" in 1952. Friedberg and Muchnik independently solved Post's problem ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)). Turing's paper "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem" appeared in *Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society* s2-42, pp. 230–265 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.230)). Rice's theorem dates from his 1951 Syracuse dissertation and 1953 *Transactions of the AMS* paper ([Wikipedia: Rice's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice%27s_theorem)).

### Connections
- [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines): the standard model defining "computable"; the halting problem is stated for it.
- [Lambda Calculus](node:Lambda%20Calculus): Church's equivalent model of computation behind the Church–Turing thesis.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): incompleteness and undecidability share the diagonal method; c.e. theories that are complete would be decidable.
- [Rice's Theorem](node:Rice's%20Theorem): the general undecidability of semantic program properties.
- [Hilbert's Tenth Problem](node:Hilbert's%20Tenth%20Problem): an undecidable problem in number theory via the MRDP theorem.
- [Kolmogorov Complexity](node:Kolmogorov%20Complexity): a non-computable measure of information built on universal machines; the base of algorithmic randomness.
- [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP): the resource-bounded analogue of decidability questions.

### Common pitfalls
- **Total vs. partial.** "Computable function" is total in Soare's convention but the basic objects $\varphi_e$ are partial; minimization can fail to terminate ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/)).
- **c.e. is not decidable.** $K$ is c.e. (we can confirm halting by running) but not decidable, because its complement is not c.e. ([SEP: Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/)).
- **Rice's theorem is about extensional properties.** Syntactic properties of programs (e.g. "the code contains an if-then-else statement") are decidable; Rice applies only to properties of the computed function ([Wikipedia: Rice's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice%27s_theorem)).
- **$\Delta^0_n$ needs two definitions.** A $\Delta^0_n$ set has a $\Sigma^0_n$ and a separate $\Pi^0_n$ definition, not necessarily one formula of both shapes ([Wikipedia: Arithmetical hierarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetical_hierarchy)).

### Open problems
- **Martin's conjecture.** Assume ZF+DC+AD and let $f:2^\omega\to2^\omega$ be Turing invariant. (I) if $f$ is not increasing a.e. (that is, $f(x)\ge_T x$ does not hold for Martin-almost every $x$), then $f$ is constant a.e.; (II) $\le_m$ prewellorders the a.e.-increasing invariant functions and the jump $f'(x)=f(x)'$ raises rank by one. Informally, the only nontrivial definable degree-invariant functions are the transfinite iterates of the jump. Marks, Slaman and Steel state that it "remains open"; Slaman and Steel proved Part I, and Steel proved Part II, for all uniformly Turing invariant functions ([Marks–Slaman–Steel, arXiv:1109.1875](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1109.1875)). The related Slaman–Steel question on writing Turing equivalence as an increasing union of Borel equivalence relations is studied by Day and Marks ([arXiv:2004.00174](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.00174)).
- **Automorphisms of the Turing degrees.** Whether the partial order of Turing degrees has a nontrivial automorphism is "still one of the main unsolved questions in this area"; Cooper's claimed construction is unverified ([Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/): models of computation, Church–Turing thesis, halting problem, and the transition to complexity.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory): reducibilities, degrees, Post's problem, history and open problems.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.404J Theory of Computation (Sipser, Fall 2020)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/): lectures on decidability, undecidability, reducibility and recursion theory.
- **Primary:** [Turing, "On Computable Numbers" (Proc. LMS, 1937)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.230): the founding paper on machines and the Entscheidungsproblem.
- **Primary:** [Marks, Slaman, Steel, "Martin's conjecture, arithmetic equivalence, and countable Borel equivalence relations"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.1875): survey of Martin's conjecture with open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Soare, *Turing Computability* (Springer, 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-31933-4): the standard graduate text on c.e. sets and degrees.
references.Computational Complexity Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Computational complexity theory classifies computational problems by the resources, chiefly time and space, needed to solve them on a fixed model of computation, usually the Turing machine. A complexity class is a set of problems of related complexity, determined by the type of problem, the machine model, and the bounded resource; the basic example is $\mathrm{DTIME}(f(n))$, the decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in time $f(n)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory)). Computability theory asks what problems can in principle be solved algorithmically; imposing restrictions on the available resources is what distinguishes complexity theory from it ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory)).

The working notion of feasibility is the Cobham-Edmonds thesis: a decision problem is feasibly decidable exactly when it lies in $\mathbf P$, polynomial time. The thesis relies on the informal notion of a "reasonable" model of computation, and it is what makes the classes robust across machine models ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)). The central tool for comparing problems is reduction: a problem is hard for a class if every problem in the class reduces to it, and complete if it is also in the class ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory)).

The field's defining question, whether $\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP}$, asks whether every problem whose solutions are easy to check is also easy to solve; it is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains unsolved ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/)). Most separations between the standard classes are open: of the chain $\mathbf L\subseteq\mathbf{NL}\subseteq\mathbf P\subseteq\mathbf{NP}\subseteq\mathbf{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathbf{EXP}\subseteq\mathbf{NEXP}\subseteq\mathbf{EXPSPACE}$, the only proper inclusions currently known are those forced by the hierarchy theorems, such as $\mathbf L\subsetneq\mathbf{PSPACE}$ and $\mathbf P\subsetneq\mathbf{EXP}$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)).

### Formal definition
For a function $t:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$, $\mathrm{TIME}(t)$ (resp. $\mathrm{NTIME}(t)$, $\mathrm{SPACE}(t)$, $\mathrm{NSPACE}(t)$) is the class of languages $X\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ decided by a deterministic (resp. nondeterministic) Turing machine within $O(t(n))$ steps (resp. cells of work tape). Then
$$\mathbf P=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}\mathrm{TIME}(n^k),\qquad \mathbf{NP}=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}\mathrm{NTIME}(n^k),$$
and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$, $\mathbf{EXP}$ are defined analogously ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)).

**Certificate characterization.** $X\in\mathbf{NP}$ iff there are a polynomial-time decidable relation $R$ and a polynomial $p$ with
$$x\in X\iff\exists y\,\big(|y|\le p(|x|)\wedge R(x,y)\big);$$
$\mathbf{coNP}$ is obtained by replacing $\exists$ with $\forall$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)).

**Reductions and completeness.** $X\le_P Y$ (polynomial-time many-one, or Karp, reducibility) iff there is a polynomial-time computable $f$ with $x\in X\iff f(x)\in Y$ for all $x\in\{0,1\}^*$. A language $Y$ is $\mathbf{NP}$-hard if $X\le_P Y$ for every $X\in\mathbf{NP}$, and $\mathbf{NP}$-complete if moreover $Y\in\mathbf{NP}$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)).

### Key results
- **Deterministic time hierarchy (Hartmanis-Stearns 1965).** If $t_1,t_2$ are time constructible, $t_2(n)\ge t_1(n)\ge n$, and $\lim_{n\to\infty} t_1(n)\log t_1(n)/t_2(n)=0$, then $\mathrm{TIME}(t_1)\subsetneq\mathrm{TIME}(t_2)$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)). The original 1965 theorem was sharpened a year later when Hennie and Stearns improved the efficiency of the universal Turing machine ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_hierarchy_theorem)).
- **Nondeterministic time hierarchy.** Under the same constructibility hypotheses with $\lim_{n\to\infty}t_1(n+1)/t_2(n)=0$, $\mathrm{NTIME}(t_1)\subsetneq\mathrm{NTIME}(t_2)$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)). Cook (1972) proved the first nondeterministic hierarchy theorem; Seiferas, Fischer and Meyer (1978) brought it to this form, and Žák (1983) gave the simple proof taught today ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_hierarchy_theorem)).
- **Space hierarchy (Stearns-Hartmanis-Lewis 1965).** If $s_1,s_2$ are space constructible, $s_2(n)\ge s_1(n)\ge n$ and $s_1(n)/s_2(n)\to 0$, then $\mathrm{SPACE}(s_1)\subsetneq\mathrm{SPACE}(s_2)$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/))
- **Simulations.** If $f$ is time and space constructible, then $\mathrm{NTIME}(f)\subseteq\mathrm{SPACE}(f)$ and $\mathrm{NSPACE}(f)\subseteq\mathrm{TIME}(2^{O(f)})$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/))
- **Savitch's theorem (1970).** For every space constructible $s(n)$ with $s(n)=\Omega(\log n)$, $\mathrm{NSPACE}(s(n))\subseteq\mathrm{SPACE}(s(n)^2)$; hence $\mathbf{PSPACE}=\mathbf{NPSPACE}$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savitch%27s_theorem)).
- **Cook-Levin theorem.** SAT is $\mathbf{NP}$-complete; Cook (1971) and Levin (1973) proved it independently. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/))
- **PSPACE-completeness of TQBF (Stockmeyer-Meyer 1973).** The set of true quantified Boolean formulas is $\mathbf{PSPACE}$-complete. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/))
- **Ladner's theorem (1975).** If $\mathbf P\ne\mathbf{NP}$, then there are problems in $\mathbf{NP}$ that are neither in $\mathbf P$ nor $\mathbf{NP}$-complete; hence $\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP}$ iff the class $\mathbf{NPI}$ of such problems is empty. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-intermediate))
- **Relativization barrier (Baker-Gill-Solovay 1975).** There exist oracles $A,B$ with $\mathbf P^A=\mathbf{NP}^A$ and $\mathbf P^B\ne\mathbf{NP}^B$, so no proof technique that relativizes can resolve $\mathbf P$ versus $\mathbf{NP}$. By contrast $\mathbf{IP}=\mathbf{PSPACE}$ holds although $\mathbf{IP}^A\ne\mathbf{PSPACE}^A$ for a random oracle $A$, so its proof does not relativize. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativization))
- **Randomness.** $\mathbf P\subseteq\mathbf{BPP}$, and Lautemann (1983) showed $\mathbf{BPP}\subseteq\Sigma_2^P$; PRIMES is in $\mathbf P$ by the AKS algorithm. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/))

### Examples
- **$\mathbf{NP}$-complete problems.** Karp (1972) showed 21 combinatorial problems $\mathbf{NP}$-complete by many-one reductions ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)).
- **Candidate $\mathbf{NP}$-intermediate problems.** Graph isomorphism and the decision versions of integer factoring (does $n$ have a factor in $[2,k]$?) and discrete logarithm; Ladner's own construction is artificial ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-intermediate)). Factoring has no known efficient classical algorithm but is solvable in quantum polynomial time by Shor's algorithm ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory)).
- **Separations by hierarchy.** The time and space hierarchy theorems give $\mathbf P\subsetneq\mathbf{EXPTIME}$ and $\mathbf L\subsetneq\mathbf{PSPACE}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory)).

### History
Gabriel Lamé analysed the running time of the Euclidean algorithm in 1844, and Turing defined his machines in 1936; in 1965 Hartmanis and Stearns defined time and space complexity and proved the hierarchy theorems, and Edmonds proposed polynomial time as the mark of a good algorithm ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory)). Cobham and Edmonds proposed polynomial time as the criterion of feasibility in 1965, and Edmonds gave an informal description of $\mathbf{NP}$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)). Cook's paper "The complexity of theorem-proving procedures" appeared at STOC 1971 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/800157.805047)); Cook and Levin formulated the $\mathbf P$ versus $\mathbf{NP}$ problem independently in 1971 ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/)). Cook introduced polynomial-time Turing reducibility, and Karp (1972) introduced many-one reducibility with his list of 21 $\mathbf{NP}$-complete problems ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)).

### Connections
- [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines): the standard machine model over which time and space are measured.
- [Asymptotic Analysis](node:Asymptotic%20Analysis): classes are defined up to $O(\cdot)$ and polynomial factors.
- [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory): complexity refines decidability by bounding resources; diagonalization is shared.
- [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP): the central open problem of the field.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): completeness under polynomial-time reductions, beginning with Cook-Levin.
- [Polynomial Hierarchy](node:Polynomial%20Hierarchy): generalizes $\mathbf{NP}$ and $\mathbf{coNP}$ by alternating quantifiers.
- [Circuit Complexity](node:Circuit%20Complexity) and [Boolean Circuit Lower Bounds](node:Boolean%20Circuit%20Lower%20Bounds): a non-uniform route to separations.
- [Descriptive Complexity](node:Descriptive%20Complexity): characterizes classes by logical definability.
- [Quantum Computational Complexity](node:Quantum%20Computational%20Complexity): classes such as BQP for quantum machines.
- [Fine-Grained Complexity](node:Fine-Grained%20Complexity) and [Parameterized Complexity](node:Parameterized%20Complexity): finer measures within $\mathbf P$ and for hard problems.
- [Randomized Algorithms](node:Randomized%20Algorithms): the algorithmic side of $\mathbf{BPP}$ and derandomization questions.
- [SAT and SMT Solving](node:SAT%20and%20SMT%20Solving): practical solvers for the canonical $\mathbf{NP}$-complete problem.

### Common pitfalls
- **"NP" does not mean "not polynomial".** $\mathbf{NP}$ is defined by nondeterministic polynomial time, equivalently polynomial-time verifiable certificates, and contains $\mathbf P$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)).
- **Reduction direction.** To show $Y$ is hard, reduce a known hard problem to $Y$, not $Y$ to it: hardness of $Y$ means every problem in the class reduces to $Y$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory)).
- **Random-oracle evidence is weak.** $\mathbf P^A\ne\mathbf{NP}^A$ for a random oracle with probability 1 (Bennett-Gill 1981), but statements true for random oracles can fail without oracles, as $\mathbf{IP}=\mathbf{PSPACE}$ shows ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativization)).

### Open problems
- **$\mathbf P$ versus $\mathbf{NP}$.** Unsolved Millennium Prize Problem ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/)).
- **$\mathbf{NP}$ versus $\mathbf{coNP}$, and the polynomial hierarchy.** Whether $\mathbf{NP}\ne\mathbf{coNP}$, whether PH is a proper hierarchy, and whether PH is properly contained in $\mathbf{PSPACE}$ are open; it is also unknown whether $\mathbf{NP}\subseteq\mathbf{BPP}$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/)).
- **$\mathbf L$ versus $\mathbf P$, $\mathbf P$ versus $\mathbf{PSPACE}$, $\mathbf{BPP}$ versus $\mathbf P$.** All open; it is suspected that $\mathbf P=\mathbf{BPP}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory)).
- **Natural NP-intermediate problems.** Whether any natural problem is $\mathbf{NP}$-intermediate is open ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-intermediate)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Computational Complexity Theory (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computational-complexity/): definitions, hierarchy theorems, Cook-Levin, Cobham-Edmonds thesis, open questions.
- **Reference:** [Computational complexity theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory): classes, reductions, open problems and history.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.404J Theory of Computation (Sipser)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/): lectures on time and space complexity, completeness, hierarchy theorems, oracles, probabilistic computation and interactive proofs.
- **Primary:** [Cook, The complexity of theorem-proving procedures (STOC 1971)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/800157.805047): the paper introducing NP-completeness.
- **Primary:** [Clay Institute, P vs NP](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/): official problem statement with Cook's description.
- **Further reading:** [Arora and Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/): Cambridge University Press graduate text, author page with draft.

## Reference
### Overview
Network science studies complex networks, systems represented as nodes joined by links, and the U.S. National Research Council defines it as "the study of network representations of physical, biological, and social phenomena leading to predictive models" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)). Its computational side combines three activities: measuring large empirical graphs (degree distributions, clustering, path lengths, centralities), fitting and simulating generative random-graph models, and running dynamical processes such as epidemics, cascades and percolation on networks ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)). Newman's review organises the field around the same themes: the small-world effect, degree distributions, clustering, degree correlations, random-graph models, growth by preferential attachment, and processes on networks ([Newman, SIAM Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0303516)).

The field builds on [graph theory](node:Graph%20Theory) and the probabilistic theory of random graphs, and interest surged around 2000 after Watts and Strogatz described small-world networks and Barabási and Albert proposed scale-free networks ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)). It sits between statistical physics, computer science and the social sciences: Easley and Kleinberg's text combines graph theory, game theory, web link analysis, cascades and the small-world phenomenon in one book ([Easley and Kleinberg](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/kleinber/networks-book/)).

For transportation and infrastructure, a recurring question is whether a real network is "small-world"; Latora and Marchiori noted that applying the standard small-world analysis to real transportation networks runs into problems, proposed a refined analysis based on transportation efficiency, and applied it to the Boston subway ([Latora and Marchiori 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0202299)).

### Formal definition
A network is a graph $G=(V,E)$ with $N=|V|$ nodes and $E$ links; in the undirected case the mean degree is $\langle k\rangle=2E/N$ and the degree distribution $P(k)$ is the fraction of nodes with degree $k$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)). The local clustering coefficient of node $i$ with degree $k_i$ and $e_i$ links among its neighbours is
$$C_i=\frac{2e_i}{k_i(k_i-1)},$$
and the average shortest-path length averages the graph distance $d_{ij}$ over all pairs ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)).

A network is **small-world** when its typical distance grows like $\log N$ while its clustering stays non-trivial; a common test is $\sigma=(C/C_r)/(L/L_r)>1$, comparing clustering $C$ and path length $L$ to an Erdős–Rényi graph with the same mean degree ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small-world_network)). A network is **scale-free** when $P(k)\sim k^{-\gamma}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)).

**Betweenness centrality** of $v$ is $g(v)=\sum_{s\ne v\ne t}\sigma_{st}(v)/\sigma_{st}$, where $\sigma_{st}$ counts shortest $s$–$t$ paths and $\sigma_{st}(v)$ those through $v$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betweenness_centrality)). **Modularity** of a partition $\{c_v\}$ is
$$Q=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{v,w}\Big[A_{vw}-\frac{k_vk_w}{2m}\Big]\delta(c_v,c_w),$$
which lies in $[-\tfrac12,1]$ for unweighted undirected graphs ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_%28networks%29)).

### Key results
- **Erdős–Rényi giant component.** In $G(n,p)$: if $np<1$, almost surely all components have size $O(\log n)$; if $np=1$, the largest component has order $n^{2/3}$; if $np\to c>1$, there is a unique giant component containing a positive fraction of vertices and every other component has $O(\log n)$ vertices. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93R%C3%A9nyi_model))
- **Connectivity threshold.** For any $\varepsilon>0$, if $p<(1-\varepsilon)\ln n/n$ then $G(n,p)$ almost surely has isolated vertices, and if $p>(1+\varepsilon)\ln n/n$ it is almost surely connected; $\ln n/n$ is a sharp threshold. Vertex degrees are $\mathrm{Bin}(n-1,p)$, tending to $\mathrm{Poisson}(np)$ with $np$ fixed. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93R%C3%A9nyi_model))
- **Configuration model and robustness.** A random graph with prescribed degree sequence has a giant component when $\mathbb{E}[k^2]-2\mathbb{E}[k]>0$; when $\mathbb{E}[k^2]$ is finite, removing a fraction $p_c=1-\mathbb{E}[k]/(\mathbb{E}[k^2]-\mathbb{E}[k])$ of edges destroys it. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science))
- **Preferential attachment.** In the Barabási–Albert model each new node attaches to node $i$ with probability $k_i/\sum_jk_j$, producing $P(k)\sim k^{-3}$; nonlinear attachment $k_i^\alpha$ departs from the linear case $\alpha=1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science))
- **Watts–Strogatz interpolation.** Rewiring each edge of a ring lattice ($N$ nodes, $K$ neighbours) with probability $\beta$ makes path length fall from about $N/2K$ toward $\ln N/\ln K$ already at small $\beta$, while clustering stays near $C(0)=3(K-2)/(4(K-1))$, with $C'(\beta)\sim C(0)(1-\beta)^3$; short paths and high clustering therefore coexist. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts%E2%80%93Strogatz_model))
- **Decentralized search.** On a 2D grid augmented with long-range links chosen with probability proportional to $d(v,w)^{-q}$, Kleinberg showed that greedy routing with only local information is most efficient at $q=2$ (an inverse-square law); at $q=0$ the shortcuts are too random to exploit. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small-world_routing))
- **Brandes' algorithm.** Betweenness of all nodes can be computed in $O(|V||E|)$ time on unweighted graphs and $O(|V||E|+|V|^2\log|V|)$ on weighted ones, against $\Theta(|V|^3)$ for a path-counting Floyd–Warshall approach; large graphs use sampling approximations. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betweenness_centrality))
- **Modularity resolution limit.** Because the null model lets any node connect to any other, maximizing $Q$ on a large network can merge even well-defined communities joined by a single edge, so modularity optimization can fail to resolve small communities (Fortunato and Barthélemy 2007). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_%28networks%29))

### Examples
- **Epidemics on networks.** The SIR model $\dot S=-\beta SI$, $\dot I=\beta SI-\gamma I$, $\dot R=\gamma I$ (Kermack–McKendrick 1927) is the base case for non-conserved spreading on networks. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science))
- **PageRank.** A page's score is $x_i=\sum_{j\to i}x_j/N_j$ over pages $j$ linking to $i$ with $N_j$ out-links, plus a random-jump term so that pages with few in-links do not score zero. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science))
- **Transport efficiency.** Latora and Marchiori introduced network efficiency, a measure of how efficiently a network exchanges information that applies to weighted and unweighted graphs, and found neural, communication and transportation networks globally and locally efficient. ([Latora and Marchiori 2001](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0101396))
- **Small worlds in practice.** Airline networks, power grids, food webs, metabolic and neural networks, and telephone call graphs are standard empirical examples. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small-world_network))

### History
Euler's 1736 analysis of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg is counted as the field's first paper; Moreno introduced the sociogram in 1933 and Kőnig wrote the first graph theory book in 1936 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)). Erdős and Rényi's 1960 paper established the giant-component transition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93R%C3%A9nyi_model)). Watts and Strogatz's 1998 *Nature* paper introduced the rewiring model of small worlds ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts%E2%80%93Strogatz_model)). Newman's 2003 *SIAM Review* survey reviewed the subject ([Newman](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0303516)), and his textbook *Networks* reached a second edition with Oxford University Press in 2018 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198805090.001.0001)).

### Connections
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): the underlying mathematics of nodes, edges, paths and components.
- [Community Detection in Networks](node:Community%20Detection%20in%20Networks): finding densely connected groups; modularity is its classic objective.
- [Percolation in Physical Systems](node:Percolation%20in%20Physical%20Systems): giant-component and robustness thresholds are percolation transitions.
- [Graph Neural Networks](node:Graph%20Neural%20Networks): learned node and graph representations built on the same graph data.
- [Queueing Theory](node:Queueing%20Theory): congestion and flow on network nodes, as in transport systems.
- [Latora and Marchiori 2002 - Is the Boston subway a small-world network](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0202299): efficiency-based small-world analysis of a transit system.

### Common pitfalls
- The small-world coefficient $\sigma$ depends strongly on network size, and tacit assumptions in its use can bias studies toward finding small-world structure ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small-world_network)).
- Applying the standard small-world analysis directly to real transportation networks runs into problems; an efficiency-based analysis was proposed instead ([Latora and Marchiori 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0202299)).
- Assuming a heavy-tailed network is scale-free: in nearly 1,000 datasets only 4% showed the strongest evidence for power-law degrees ([Broido and Clauset](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.03400)).
- Reading too much into centrality rankings: centrality measures are reliable mainly for the most important nodes ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)).

### Open problems
- **Community detection.** Fortunato's review calls the problem "very hard and not yet satisfactorily solved" despite large interdisciplinary effort ([Fortunato 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.0612)), and a 2022 retrospective still treats automated discovery of communities as a fundamental technical challenge ([Fortunato and Newman 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.00111)).
- **How universal is scale-free structure?** Broido and Clauset conclude that the universality of scale-free networks is not supported and that the structural diversity of real networks likely requires new explanatory mechanisms ([Broido and Clauset](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.03400)).

> [!warning] Contested
> Barabási and Albert's preferential-attachment account presents many real networks as scale-free ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science)); Broido and Clauset's statistical test of nearly 1,000 networks finds strong scale-free evidence in only 4% and at best weak evidence for social networks ([Broido and Clauset](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.03400)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Network science (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_science): measures, models, centralities, spreading and percolation.
- **Learn:** [Easley and Kleinberg, Networks, Crowds, and Markets (Cornell)](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/kleinber/networks-book/): Cambridge University Press 2010 textbook (pre-publication draft free online) covering graphs, game theory, link analysis, cascades and the small-world phenomenon.
- **Primary:** [Newman, The structure and function of complex networks (SIAM Review 2003)](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0303516): the standard survey of empirical properties and models.
- **Primary:** [Fortunato, Community detection in graphs (Physics Reports 2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.0612): comprehensive review of community detection.
- **Primary:** [Broido and Clauset, Scale-free networks are rare (Nature Communications 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.03400): large-scale test of power-law degree distributions.
- **Primary:** [Latora and Marchiori, Efficient behavior of small-world networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0101396): efficiency as a small-world measure.
- **Further reading:** [Newman, Networks, 2nd ed. (Oxford University Press 2018)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198805090.001.0001): Newman's textbook, second edition.

## Reference
### Overview
Computer architecture is the conceptual design and operational structure of a computer system: how its parts are organized and interact. It spans the instruction set architecture, the processor microarchitecture, memory and I/O, and it trades off performance, cost, power, reliability and security ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture)). The field sits between the logic level (gates and [Boolean Circuits](node:Boolean%20Circuits), built from [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic)) and the software that runs on the machine ([Compilers](node:Compilers), [Operating Systems](node:Operating%20Systems)).

The field is usually split into three layers. The **instruction set architecture** ([ISA](node:Instruction%20Set%20Architecture)) is the machine code a processor executes together with its word size, addressing modes, registers and data types; the **microarchitecture** (computer organization) is how a particular processor implements the ISA; and **systems design** covers the other hardware, such as DMA, [virtualization](node:Virtualization) and multiprocessing ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture)). A graduate course covers instruction set design, pipelining, cache and virtual-memory organization, protection, I/O and interrupts, in-order and out-of-order superscalar machines, VLIW, vector machines, multithreading, symmetric multiprocessors and parallel computers ([MIT OCW 6.823](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-823-computer-system-architecture-fall-2005/)).

Since the mid-2000s the field has been shaped by the end of [Dennard scaling](node:Dennard%20Scaling): power density stopped staying constant as transistors shrank, clock speeds stalled, and manufacturers shifted to multicore designs; Moore's law and Dennard scaling are both nearing diminishing returns ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennard_scaling); [Ceze, Hill and Wenisch, arXiv:1612.03182](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03182)).

### Formal definition
**Architecture vs. implementation.** The term "architecture" in computer literature traces to the 1959 work of Lyle R. Johnson and Frederick P. Brooks Jr. at IBM on the Stretch supercomputer; with IBM System/360 it became a noun for "what the user needs to know". Details such as cache size belong to the microarchitecture, not the ISA ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture)).

**Iron law of processor performance.** For a program,
$$\frac{\text{time}}{\text{program}} = \frac{\text{instructions}}{\text{program}}\times\frac{\text{cycles}}{\text{instruction}}\times\frac{\text{time}}{\text{cycle}} ,$$
where the instruction count and cycles per instruction (CPI) are affected by the choice of ISA and the cycle time is largely determined by manufacturing technology. The term was coined by Douglas Clark, based on research with Joel Emer in the 1980s, including a 1984 study of the VAX-11/780 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_law_of_processor_performance)). The related measure instructions per cycle (IPC) is about 0.1 on older computers and nearly 1 on modern processors, with superscalar designs said to reach 3–5 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture)).

**Pipeline hazards.** In a pipelined processor a *hazard* is a conflict that prevents the next instruction from executing in the following cycle or would give a wrong result: a **data hazard** (e.g. read-after-write, an instruction reading a register before an earlier write commits), a **structural hazard** (two instructions needing the same unit), or a **control hazard** (a mispredicted branch) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard_%28computer_architecture%29)).

**Caches.** A cache holds copies of frequently used memory locations; a *hit* finds the data in the cache, a *miss* fetches it from slower memory. In a **direct-mapped** cache with $n$ blocks, memory block $y$ can live only in cache block $y \bmod n$; in an **$N$-way set-associative** cache it can live in any of the $N$ entries of its set. A **write-through** cache writes every store to memory, while a **write-back** cache marks lines dirty and writes them only on eviction ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CPU_cache)). See [Memory Hierarchies](node:Memory%20Hierarchies).

### Key results
- **Amdahl's law (1967).** If a fraction $p$ of execution time benefits from an improvement that speeds that part up by a factor $s$, the overall speedup is
$$S(s)=\frac{1}{(1-p)+p/s}\ \xrightarrow{\ s\to\infty\ }\ \frac{1}{1-p}.$$
Hence the serial fraction bounds the gain from adding processors. The law comes from Amdahl's paper at the 1967 AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)).
- **Dennard scaling (1974) and its breakdown.** Each generation shrinks linear dimensions by about 30%, cutting device area and power per transistor by about 51% while allowing about 40% higher clock frequency, so power density stays constant and the transistor count can double without more power. Because leakage current and threshold voltage stopped scaling, this broke down around 2005–2007; power density rose, clock rates stalled near 4–6 GHz, and only part of a chip can switch at once ("dark silicon") ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennard_scaling)).
- **Tomasulo's algorithm (1967).** Dynamic scheduling with register renaming (tags in place of unavailable values), reservation stations per functional unit, and a common data bus that broadcasts results lets instructions execute out of order; it eliminates WAW and WAR hazards and minimizes RAW stalls. It was first implemented in the floating-point unit of the IBM System/360 Model 91 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasulo%27s_algorithm)).
- **Hazard remedies.** Data hazards are reduced by operand forwarding (passing a result from a later pipeline stage directly to a dependent instruction) or stalls; control hazards by [branch prediction](node:Branch%20Prediction), with mispredicted instructions discarded without affecting architectural state; data stalls also by out-of-order execution via scoreboarding or Tomasulo's algorithm with register renaming; structural hazards by adding resources such as ALUs or memory ports ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard_%28computer_architecture%29)).
- **Associativity vs. size.** As a rule of thumb, doubling associativity from direct-mapped to two-way, or from two-way to four-way, raises the hit rate about as much as doubling the cache size, with diminishing returns beyond that; higher associativity costs power, area and possibly time ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CPU_cache)).
- **Speculation leaks (Spectre, 2018).** Branch prediction and speculative execution can be induced to perform operations that correct execution never would, and their microarchitectural side effects (e.g. in caches) leak secrets through side channels; vulnerable speculation was found in Intel, AMD and ARM processors. This undermines assumptions behind operating-system process isolation, containers, JIT compilation, static analysis and defenses against cache-timing attacks ([Kocher et al., arXiv:1801.01203](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.01203)). See [Cache Side Channels](node:Cache%20Side%20Channels).

### Examples
- **RISC vs. CISC through the iron law.** CISC reduces instruction count with complex instructions that take more cycles each; RISC's regular instructions suited pipelining, letting a new instruction start roughly every cycle ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_law_of_processor_performance)).
- **Memory hierarchy latencies.** Typical latencies range from about 0.25 ns for the register file to about 82.5 ns for main memory and milliseconds for hard disks; each level is smaller and faster than the next ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_hierarchy)).
- **Locality-aware code.** Changing the iteration order over a three-dimensional array can improve locality of reference, which is the main bottleneck for most workloads ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_hierarchy)).

### History
- **1945:** von Neumann's "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" described the stored-program organization; Turing's Automatic Computing Engine design of the same year cited it, and Zuse had earlier (1936) described storing instructions in the same memory as data ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture)).
- **1959–1964:** Johnson and Brooks's work at IBM on Stretch introduced the term; with System/360 it came to mean "what the user needs to know" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture)).
- **1967:** Amdahl's law and Tomasulo's algorithm ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasulo%27s_algorithm)).
- **1974–2007:** Dennard scaling held and then broke down, ending frequency scaling ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennard_scaling)).
- **2016–2018:** the Arch2030 white paper framed research after Dennard scaling ([arXiv:1612.03182](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03182)); Spectre exposed speculative execution as a security problem ([arXiv:1801.01203](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.01203)).

### Connections
- [Instruction Set Architecture](node:Instruction%20Set%20Architecture): the programmer-visible contract that microarchitectures implement.
- [Memory Hierarchies](node:Memory%20Hierarchies): registers, caches, DRAM and storage, organized around locality.
- [Cache Coherence](node:Cache%20Coherence): keeping private caches consistent in a multiprocessor.
- [Memory Consistency Models](node:Memory%20Consistency%20Models): what orderings of loads and stores a multiprocessor guarantees.
- [Multicore Architecture](node:Multicore%20Architecture): the response to the end of Dennard scaling.
- [GPU Computing](node:GPU%20Computing): throughput-oriented data-parallel architecture.
- [Accelerator Architectures](node:Accelerator%20Architectures): domain-specific hardware.
- [Virtual Memory](node:Virtual%20Memory): address translation supported by the TLB and page tables.
- [Cache Side Channels](node:Cache%20Side%20Channels): microarchitectural state as an information leak.
- [Boolean Circuits](node:Boolean%20Circuits): the gate-level substrate of datapaths and control.
- [Parallel and Distributed Computing](node:Parallel%20and%20Distributed%20Computing): Amdahl's law and multiprocessors link the two fields.

### Common pitfalls
- **Clock rate is not performance.** By the iron law, runtime also depends on instruction count and CPI; clock rate alone is a misleading metric ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_law_of_processor_performance)).
- **Pipelining improves throughput, not latency.** A pipeline typically makes each instruction's latency worse while raising throughput ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture)).
- **"Simpler ISA is always faster" is false.** A single CISC instruction can beat its RISC equivalent if it performs several micro-operations in one cycle, and techniques such as macro-op fusion narrow the gap ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_law_of_processor_performance)).
- **Discarded speculative work is not invisible.** Squashing mispredicted instructions restores architectural state but not microarchitectural state such as cache contents, which is what Spectre exploits ([arXiv:1801.01203](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.01203)).

### Open problems
- **Sustaining performance growth after Moore's law and Dennard scaling.** With both reaching diminishing returns, the community must find how to keep IT progress going, and architecture research is positioned to bridge application and device domains ([Ceze, Hill and Wenisch, arXiv:1612.03182](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03182)); the power wall leaves part of every chip dark ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennard_scaling)).
- **Secure speculative execution.** Kocher et al. argue that processor-specific workarounds are only partial and that lasting fixes require changes to processor designs and ISAs, so that hardware and software developers share a clear understanding of what CPUs may leak ([arXiv:1801.01203](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.01203)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Computer architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_architecture): definition, subcategories, performance and power measures, history.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 6.823 Computer System Architecture](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-823-computer-system-architecture-fall-2005/): graduate course from ISA design to superscalar, vector and multiprocessor machines.
- **Primary:** [Kocher et al., Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution (arXiv:1801.01203)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.01203): the paper showing speculative execution leaks secrets.
- **Primary:** [Ceze, Hill and Wenisch, Arch2030 (arXiv:1612.03182)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03182): community white paper on research directions after Dennard scaling.
- **Further reading:** [Hennessy and Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach (Morgan Kaufmann, 2019)](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780128119051): textbook on quantitative processor and memory-system design.
