## Reference
### Overview
Conditional probability measures how the probability of an event changes once we learn that another event has occurred. For events $A, B$ in a probability space with $\mathbb P(B)>0$, Kolmogorov's definition is $\mathbb P(A\mid B)=\mathbb P(A\cap B)/\mathbb P(B)$; conditioning on $B$ produces a new probability measure that gives zero mass to outcomes outside $B$ and rescales outcomes inside $B$ by $1/\mathbb P(B)$. Some authors, such as de Finetti, instead take the product form $\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A\mid B)\,\mathbb P(B)$ as the axiom. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability))

The elementary ratio fails when $\mathbb P(B)=0$, which is the typical case for continuous random variables (for example, conditioning on $X=x$ when $X$ has a density). The measure-theoretic theory resolves this by conditioning on a $\sigma$-algebra rather than a single event: $\mathbb P(A\mid\mathcal G)=\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A\mid\mathcal G]$ is a random variable defined through the Radon–Nikodym theorem, and a *regular* version of it is a Markov kernel. Kolmogorov formalized conditional expectation this way in 1933, and Halmos and Doob generalized it to the modern sub-$\sigma$-algebra form in 1953. ([Wikipedia: Conditional expectation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_expectation); [Durrett, PTE](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

Conditional probability is the mechanism of Bayesian updating, the basis of independence and Markov properties, and the object computed by probabilistic-inference systems. Philosophers debate whether the ratio formula captures the pre-theoretic notion; Popper, Rényi, and others axiomatize conditional probability as primitive instead. ([SEP: Interpretations of Probability](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/probability-interpret/))

### Formal definition
**Elementary.** On a [probability space](node:Probability%20Spaces) $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, for $B\in\mathcal F$ with $\mathbb P(B)>0$,
$$\mathbb P(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)},\qquad A\in\mathcal F,$$
and $A\mapsto\mathbb P(A\mid B)$ is again a probability measure satisfying the Kolmogorov axioms. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability))

**Given a $\sigma$-algebra.** For a sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and integrable $X$, the conditional expectation $\mathbb E(X\mid\mathcal G)$ is any $\mathcal G$-measurable integrable $Y$ with $\int_G Y\,d\mathbb P=\int_G X\,d\mathbb P$ for all $G\in\mathcal G$; it exists by the Radon–Nikodym theorem and is unique almost surely. Conditional probability is $\mathbb P(A\mid\mathcal G)=\mathbb E(\mathbf 1_A\mid\mathcal G)$. ([Durrett, PTE §4.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Conditional expectation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_expectation))

**Regular conditional distribution.** For a measurable $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\mathcal S)$, a map $\mu:\Omega\times\mathcal S\to[0,1]$ is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ if (i) for each $A\in\mathcal S$, $\omega\mapsto\mu(\omega,A)$ is a version of $\mathbb P(X\in A\mid\mathcal G)$, and (ii) for a.e. $\omega$, $A\mapsto\mu(\omega,A)$ is a probability measure on $(S,\mathcal S)$. When $S=\Omega$ and $X$ is the identity, $\mu$ is a regular conditional probability. ([Durrett, PTE §4.1.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

### Key results
- **Multiplication rule and law of total probability.** $\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A\mid B)\mathbb P(B)$, and for a countable partition $(B_n)$ of $\Omega$ into events of positive probability, $\mathbb P(A)=\sum_n\mathbb P(A\mid B_n)\mathbb P(B_n)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability); [MIT 18.05 Reading 3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class03-prep.pdf))
- **[Bayes' Theorem](node:Bayes'%20Theorem).** If $\mathbb P(A),\mathbb P(B)>0$ then $\mathbb P(A\mid B)=\mathbb P(B\mid A)\mathbb P(A)/\mathbb P(B)$, which inverts a conditional probability when the reverse one is known. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability))
- **Independence.** $A$ and $B$ are independent iff $\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$; when $\mathbb P(B)\neq0$ this is equivalent to $\mathbb P(A\mid B)=\mathbb P(A)$. $A,B$ are conditionally independent given $C$ iff $\mathbb P(A\cap B\mid C)=\mathbb P(A\mid C)\mathbb P(B\mid C)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability))
- **Existence of regular conditional distributions.** If $(S,\mathcal S)$ is *nice* (there is a one-to-one map $\varphi:S\to\mathbb R$ with $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ measurable; every Borel subset of a complete separable metric space, with its Borel sets, is nice), then a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given any $\mathcal G$ exists. Without such a hypothesis they need not exist; the first counterexample is due to Dieudonné (1948), and Faden (1985) studied necessary and sufficient conditions for existence. ([Durrett, PTE Thm 4.1.17 and Thm 2.1.22](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Regular conditional probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_conditional_probability))
- **Integration against a regular version.** If $\mu$ is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal F$ and $\mathbb E|f(X)|<\infty$, then $\mathbb E(f(X)\mid\mathcal F)=\int\mu(\omega,dx)f(x)$ a.s. ([Durrett, PTE Thm 4.1.16](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Disintegration.** A regular conditional probability given $T:\Omega\to E$ is a transition kernel $\nu$ with $\mathbb P(A\cap T^{-1}(B))=\int_B\nu(x,A)\,(\mathbb P\circ T^{-1})(dx)$ for all measurable $A,B$. ([Wikipedia: Regular conditional probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_conditional_probability)) The regularity hypothesis falls on the space carrying the measure $\nu(x,\cdot)$, here $\Omega$: taking $X$ to be the identity in the existence theorem above, a regular conditional probability given any $\mathcal G$ exists when $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ is nice. ([Durrett, PTE §4.1.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Noncomputability of conditioning (Ackerman–Freer–Roy).** There are computable random variables $X,Y$ in $[0,1]$ whose conditional distribution of one given the other encodes the halting problem, so no general algorithm computes conditional distributions. Conditioning is computable in the discrete setting and when a conditional density exists (under computability hypotheses), and $\mathbb P[(U,V)\mid U+E=\cdot\,]$ is computable when $E$ is independent noise with a bounded computable density. ([Ackerman, Freer, Roy](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.3014))

### Examples
- **Coins.** Toss a fair coin three times; $\mathbb P(\text{3 heads})=1/8$, but given that the first toss is heads the reduced sample space has four equally likely outcomes, so the conditional probability is $1/4$. ([MIT 18.05 Reading 3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class03-prep.pdf))
- **Screening test (base-rate fallacy).** With prevalence $\mathbb P(D^+)=0.005$, false-positive rate $\mathbb P(T^+\mid D^-)=0.05$, and true-positive rate $\mathbb P(T^+\mid D^+)=0.9$, the law of total probability gives $\mathbb P(T^+)=0.05425$ and Bayes gives $\mathbb P(D^+\mid T^+)\approx 8.3\%$. ([MIT 18.05 Reading 3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class03-prep.pdf))
- **Joint densities.** If $(X,Y)$ has a density $f(x,y)>0$, then $\mu(y,A)=\int_A f(x,y)\,dx\big/\!\int f(x,y)\,dx$ gives a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, recovering the undergraduate conditional density. ([Durrett, PTE Ex. 4.1.6](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

### History
Kolmogorov's 1933 *Grundbegriffe* defined conditional expectation via the Radon–Nikodym theorem, building on Laplace's earlier use of conditional distributions; Halmos and Doob (1953) gave the general sub-$\sigma$-algebra form. ([Wikipedia: Conditional expectation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_expectation)) Kolmogorov also wrote that conditional probability "with regard to an isolated hypothesis whose probability equals 0 is inadmissible", explaining the Borel–Kolmogorov paradox. ([Wikipedia: Borel–Kolmogorov paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel%E2%80%93Kolmogorov_paradox)) Dieudonné (1948) produced the first example where no regular conditional distribution exists. ([Durrett, PTE §4.1.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

### Connections
- [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces): the setting; conditioning produces a new probability measure on the same space.
- [Conditional Expectation](node:Conditional%20Expectation): conditional probability given a $\sigma$-algebra is the conditional expectation of an indicator.
- [Bayes' Theorem](node:Bayes'%20Theorem): inverts conditional probabilities and drives [Bayesian Inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference).
- [Independence of Random Variables](node:Independence%20of%20Random%20Variables): defined by conditioning leaving probabilities unchanged.
- [Radon–Nikodym Theorem](node:Radon–Nikodym%20Theorem): supplies existence of conditional expectations.
- [Disintegration of Measures](node:Disintegration%20of%20Measures): the measure-theoretic form of regular conditional probabilities.
- [Law of Total Expectation](node:Law%20of%20Total%20Expectation): the expectation-level version of the law of total probability.
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains): defined by a conditional-independence (Markov) property.
- [Probabilistic Programming](node:Probabilistic%20Programming): systems whose core operation is conditioning, limited by the Ackerman–Freer–Roy theorem.

### Common pitfalls
- **Confusing $\mathbb P(A\mid B)$ with $\mathbb P(B\mid A)$.** They are approximately equal only when $\mathbb P(A)\approx\mathbb P(B)$; neglecting the base rate leads to the base-rate fallacy. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability))
- **Conditioning on a null event.** Limits over shrinking neighbourhoods depend on how the event is approached. For a uniform point on the sphere, conditioning on the equator gives a uniform longitude, but conditioning on a meridian gives a latitude density $\tfrac12\cos\varphi$, though both are great circles. ([Wikipedia: Borel–Kolmogorov paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel%E2%80%93Kolmogorov_paradox))
- **Mutual exclusivity is not independence.** Disjoint events of positive probability are never independent. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability))
- **Versions.** $\mathbb P(A\mid\mathcal G)$ is defined only up to null sets, and the exceptional null sets for countably many $A$ can accumulate, which is why regularity is a separate theorem. ([Durrett, PTE §4.1.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Complexity of conditioning beyond finite settings.** Ackerman, Freer, and Roy note that conditional probabilities of computable distributions on finite discrete sets are computable but may not be efficiently so, that this finite setting "already" has interesting questions of computational complexity, and they propose extending those complexity results to the general computable-Polish-space setting as a direction that "could bear on the practice of statistical AI and machine learning." ([Ackerman, Freer, Roy](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1005.3014))

> [!warning] Contested
> Whether the ratio formula is the right *definition* of conditional probability is debated. The ratio formula is often taken to be the definition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability)), but the SEP entry, citing Hájek (2003), calls this a technical usage that may not align perfectly with the pre-theoretic concept, and Popper, Rényi, van Fraassen, and others take conditional probability as primitive. Whether every possible event should receive positive probability (regularity), which would make conditioning always defined, is also contested. ([SEP: Interpretations of Probability](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/probability-interpret/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Conditional probability (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability): definition, total probability, Bayes, independence, fallacies.
- **Reference:** [Interpretations of Probability (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/probability-interpret/): ratio analysis versus primitive conditional probability.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.05 Reading 3: Conditional Probability, Independence and Bayes' Theorem](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class03-prep.pdf): Orloff and Bloom's worked introduction, including the base-rate fallacy.
- **Primary:** [Ackerman, Freer, Roy, On the computability of conditional probability (J. ACM 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.3014): noncomputable conditional distributions and positive computability results.
- **Further reading:** [Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/pte.html): graduate text; §4.1 covers conditional expectation and regular conditional probabilities.
references.Connections and Covariant Derivatives:
## Reference
### Overview
A covariant derivative is a rule for differentiating sections of a vector bundle (in the basic case, vector fields on a manifold) along tangent vectors in a coordinate-independent way. Partial derivatives of vector components do not transform as a tensor, because the chain rule produces a second-derivative term; connection coefficients $\Gamma$ compensate for it. ([Rajeev, Rochester PHY413 Lecture 9](https://www.pas.rochester.edu/~rajeev/phy413/Grav9.pdf); [Wikipedia: Covariant derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_derivative))

There are several equivalent pictures. A linear (Koszul) connection on a vector bundle $E\to M$ is an operator $\nabla$ on sections satisfying a Leibniz rule; locally it is $d$ plus a matrix of one-forms. An Ehresmann connection is a choice of horizontal subbundle of $TE$ complementary to the vertical bundle, and for a vector bundle with linear horizontal spaces it is the same thing as a covariant derivative; on a principal bundle the horizontal spaces are required to be $G$-invariant. ([Wikipedia: Connection (vector bundle)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_%28vector_bundle%29); [Wikipedia: Ehresmann connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehresmann_connection))

A connection determines [Parallel Transport](node:Parallel%20Transport) along curves, and parallel transport in turn determines the connection by differentiation. Transport around loops generates the holonomy group, which the Ambrose–Singer theorem relates to curvature. On a (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold the metric singles out one connection on the [Tangent Bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle), the Levi-Civita connection. ([Wikipedia: Parallel transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_transport); [Wikipedia: Levi-Civita connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi-Civita_connection))

### Formal definition
**Vector bundles.** A linear connection on $E\to M$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear map $\nabla:\Gamma(E)\to\Omega^1(M)\otimes\Gamma(E)$ with
$$\nabla(fs)=df\otimes s+f\,\nabla s .$$
Writing $\nabla_X s$ for the contraction with a vector field $X$, $\nabla_X s$ is $C^\infty$-linear in $X$. Over an open set with a local frame, $\nabla s=ds+As$ for a matrix $A$ of one-forms (the connection one-form). If the frame changes by a matrix-valued function $g$, then $A'=gAg^{-1}-(dg)g^{-1}$. ([Wikipedia: Connection (vector bundle)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_%28vector_bundle%29))

**Curvature and exterior covariant derivative.** $\nabla$ extends to an exterior covariant derivative $d_\nabla$ on $E$-valued forms. Unlike $d$, in general $d_\nabla^2\neq 0$; instead $d_\nabla^2$ is tensorial and is given by the curvature two-form $F_\nabla\in\Omega^2(M;\operatorname{End}E)$, locally
$$F_\nabla=dA+A\wedge A$$
(Cartan's structure equation). ([Wikipedia: Connection (vector bundle)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_%28vector_bundle%29))

**Tangent bundle, coordinates.** Convention used here (differentiation index first): $\nabla_{\partial_j}\partial_k=\Gamma^l{}_{jk}\partial_l$, so
$$\nabla_j u^l=\partial_j u^l+\Gamma^l{}_{jk}u^k,\qquad \nabla_j\theta_k=\partial_j\theta_k-\Gamma^l{}_{jk}\theta_l ,$$
and a tensor gets one $+\Gamma$ term per upper index and one $-\Gamma$ term per lower index. ([Rajeev, Rochester PHY413 Lecture 9](https://www.pas.rochester.edu/~rajeev/phy413/Grav9.pdf))

**Along a curve.** For a curve $\gamma$, the derivative along $\gamma$ is $D_t T=\nabla_{\dot\gamma(t)}T$; $T$ need only be defined on the curve. A section along $\gamma$ is parallel if $D_t X=0$; in a local trivialization this is a first-order linear ODE, so parallel transport exists, is unique, and is a linear isomorphism between fibres. ([Wikipedia: Covariant derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_derivative); [Wikipedia: Parallel transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_transport))

**Levi-Civita connection.** On a pseudo-Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$, an affine connection is Levi-Civita if it is metric, $X(g(Y,Z))=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$, and torsion-free, $\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$. It is given by the Koszul formula
$$g(\nabla_XY,Z)=\tfrac12\bigl\{X(g(Y,Z))+Y(g(Z,X))-Z(g(X,Y))+g([X,Y],Z)-g([Y,Z],X)-g([X,Z],Y)\bigr\}.$$
([Wikipedia: Levi-Civita connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi-Civita_connection)) In coordinates, $\nabla_\rho g_{\mu\nu}=0$ and $\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\mu\nu}=\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\nu\mu}$ give the Christoffel symbols
$$\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\mu\nu}=\tfrac12 g^{\sigma\rho}\bigl(\partial_\mu g_{\rho\nu}+\partial_\nu g_{\rho\mu}-\partial_\rho g_{\mu\nu}\bigr).$$
([Rajeev, Rochester PHY413 Lecture 9](https://www.pas.rochester.edu/~rajeev/phy413/Grav9.pdf))

**Frame bundle and Cartan connections.** An affine connection on $M$ is the same as a principal connection on the frame bundle of $M$. The frame bundle carries a canonical solder form, an $\mathbb R^n$-valued horizontal equivariant one-form identifying $TM$ with an associated bundle; a principal connection plus the solder form is an absolute parallelism. More generally, for a model Klein geometry $G/H$, a Cartan connection on a principal $H$-bundle $P\to M$ is a $\mathfrak g$-valued one-form $\eta$ that is $H$-equivariant, reproduces the generators of $\mathfrak h$ on vertical fields, and maps each $T_pP$ isomorphically onto $\mathfrak g$; its curvature is $\Omega=d\eta+\tfrac12[\eta,\eta]$, and it vanishes exactly when the geometry is locally equivalent to the model. ([Wikipedia: Cartan connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan_connection))

### Key results
- **Existence and affine structure.** Every vector bundle over a manifold admits a linear connection (by partitions of unity). Connections are not unique: the difference of two is $C^\infty$-linear, so the set of connections on $E$ is an affine space modelled on $\Omega^1(M;\operatorname{End}E)$. ([Wikipedia: Connection (vector bundle)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_%28vector_bundle%29))
- **Transformation law; torsion.** Under a coordinate change, $\Gamma'^{\mu}{}_{\rho\sigma}$ equals the tensorial transform of $\Gamma$ plus a term built from $\partial^2x'^\mu/\partial x^\beta\partial x^\gamma$, so $\Gamma$ is not a tensor and can vanish in one chart but not another. The inhomogeneous term is symmetric in the lower indices, so the antisymmetric part $\Gamma^\mu{}_{\rho\sigma}-\Gamma^\mu{}_{\sigma\rho}$ is a tensor, the torsion. ([Rajeev, Rochester PHY413 Lecture 9](https://www.pas.rochester.edu/~rajeev/phy413/Grav9.pdf)) For a torsion-free connection there are coordinates (geodesic normal coordinates) in which all Christoffel symbols vanish at a given point; with torsion only the symmetric part can be removed. ([Wikipedia: Christoffel symbols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christoffel_symbols))
- **Fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry.** Every pseudo-Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ has a unique Levi-Civita (metric, torsion-free) connection; the Koszul formula proves both existence and uniqueness. Its parallel transport maps are linear isometries between tangent spaces. ([Wikipedia: Levi-Civita connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi-Civita_connection))
- **Bianchi identity.** For any connection on a vector bundle, $d_\nabla F_\nabla=0$. There is no general analogue of the first (algebraic) Bianchi identity, which uses special symmetries of the Levi-Civita connection. ([Wikipedia: Connection (vector bundle)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_%28vector_bundle%29))
- **Curvature as non-integrability.** For an Ehresmann connection, curvature measures the failure of the horizontal distribution $H$ to be Frobenius integrable, and vanishes identically exactly when $H$ is integrable. ([Wikipedia: Ehresmann connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehresmann_connection)) For a connection on a vector bundle, $\nabla$ is flat if and only if the restricted holonomy group $\mathrm{Hol}^0(\nabla)$ (loops that are contractible) is trivial; the full holonomy group of a flat connection can still be nontrivial. ([Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy); [Wikipedia: Parallel transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_transport))
- **Ambrose–Singer theorem (1953).** For a connection $\omega$ on a principal $G$-bundle with curvature $\Omega$, the Lie algebra of $\mathrm{Hol}_p(\omega)$ is spanned by the values $\Omega_q(X,Y)$, where $q$ ranges over points joined to $p$ by horizontal curves and $X,Y$ over horizontal vectors at $q$. ([Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy); [Ambrose–Singer, Trans. AMS 75 (1953)](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1953-0063739-1))
- **de Rham decomposition (1952).** On a simply connected Riemannian manifold the tangent bundle splits into holonomy-irreducible pieces, and $M$ is locally isometric to a product $V_0\times V_1\times\cdots\times V_k$ with $V_0$ an open subset of Euclidean space; if $M$ is complete the splitting is global. ([Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy))
- **Berger's classification (1955).** If $M^n$ is simply connected, irreducible (not locally a product) and not locally symmetric, its Riemannian holonomy is one of: $SO(n)$; $U(n/2)$ (Kähler); $SU(n/2)$ (Calabi–Yau); $Sp(n/4)\cdot Sp(1)$ (quaternion-Kähler); $Sp(n/4)$ (hyperkähler); $G_2$ ($n=7$); $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ ($n=8$). $\mathrm{Spin}(9)$, on Berger's original list, was later shown to occur only for locally symmetric spaces. ([Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy))
- **Flat connections and representations of $\pi_1$ (Riemann–Hilbert).** Over each connected component of $M$, flat connections on vector bundles are equivalent to group homomorphisms out of the fundamental group, and more generally to functors out of the fundamental groupoid; for this reason flat bundles are called local systems. ([nLab: flat connection](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/flat+connection)) For a flat connection, holonomy is a type of monodromy, and for any connection there is a surjection $\pi_1(M)\to\mathrm{Hol}/\mathrm{Hol}^0$. ([Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy))
- **Chern–Weil homomorphism.** Let $P\to M$ be a principal $G$-bundle and $f$ a $G$-invariant homogeneous polynomial of degree $k$ on $\mathfrak g$. For any connection with curvature $\Omega$, $f(\Omega)$ descends to a closed $2k$-form on $M$, and its de Rham class is independent of the connection, giving an algebra homomorphism $\mathbb C[\mathfrak g]^G\to H^*(M;\mathbb C)$. For $G=GL_n(\mathbb C)$, $\det(I-tx/2\pi i)=\sum_k f_k(x)t^k$ gives the Chern classes $c_k(E)$; if $G$ is compact or semisimple, $H^*(BG;\mathbb C)\cong\mathbb C[\mathfrak g]^G$. ([Wikipedia: Chern–Weil homomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chern%E2%80%93Weil_homomorphism))

### Examples
- **Flat plane in polar coordinates.** For the Euclidean metric $dr^2+r^2d\varphi^2$ (the $z=\text{const}$ slice of cylindrical coordinates), the nonzero Christoffel symbols are $\Gamma^r{}_{\varphi\varphi}=-r$ and $\Gamma^\varphi{}_{r\varphi}=\Gamma^\varphi{}_{\varphi r}=1/r$. ([Wikipedia: Christoffel symbols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christoffel_symbols)) They are nonzero because the coordinate grid rotates, not because of curvature; they vanish in Cartesian coordinates. ([Wikipedia: Covariant derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_derivative); [Rajeev, Rochester PHY413 Lecture 9](https://www.pas.rochester.edu/~rajeev/phy413/Grav9.pdf))
- **Unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$.** Identifying $T_mS^2$ with $m^\perp$, $(\nabla_XY)(m)=d_mY(X(m))+\langle X(m),Y(m)\rangle m$ is a torsion-free metric connection, hence the Levi-Civita connection of the round metric; it is the tangential projection of the ambient derivative. In the coordinates $d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$, $\Gamma^\theta{}_{\varphi\varphi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\Gamma^\varphi{}_{\theta\varphi}=\cot\theta$. ([Wikipedia: Levi-Civita connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi-Civita_connection); [Wikipedia: Christoffel symbols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christoffel_symbols))
- **Induced connections.** A connection on $E$ induces connections on $E^*$, tensor products, direct sums and exterior powers by the product rule. ([Wikipedia: Connection (vector bundle)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_%28vector_bundle%29))

### History
In 1869 Christoffel showed how the components of the intrinsic derivative of a vector field transform, the start of tensor analysis. Levi-Civita and Ricci-Curbastro used Christoffel's symbols to define parallel transport and study its relation to curvature, which led to the modern notion of holonomy. Brouwer considered parallel transport in spaces of constant curvature in 1906, Levi-Civita (1917) treated hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, and Schouten and Weyl (1918) followed. ([Wikipedia: Levi-Civita connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi-Civita_connection)) Weyl, Schouten and Cartan defined connections without a metric; Koszul (1950) gave the algebraic definition. ([Wikipedia: Covariant derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_derivative)) Ehresmann formalized connections on arbitrary fibre bundles in 1950. ([Wikipedia: Ehresmann connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehresmann_connection)) Ambrose and Singer published "A theorem on holonomy" in Trans. AMS 75 (1953), 428–443. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1953-0063739-1)) Chern and Weil developed characteristic classes from curvature in the late 1940s, after the proofs of the generalized Gauss–Bonnet theorem. ([Wikipedia: Chern–Weil homomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chern%E2%80%93Weil_homomorphism)) Kobayashi and Nomizu's *Foundations of Differential Geometry* (1963, 1969) treat connections in bundles, holonomy and the de Rham decomposition (Vol. I) and Chern–Weil theory (Vol. II); reviewers called it the standard reference of the subject. ([Wikipedia: Foundations of Differential Geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundations_of_Differential_Geometry))

### Connections
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics) and [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry): the data that select the Levi-Civita connection.
- [Tangent Bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle) and [Tangent Spaces and Vector Fields](node:Tangent%20Spaces%20and%20Vector%20Fields): the bundle on which an affine connection acts.
- [Parallel Transport](node:Parallel%20Transport): the integrated form of $\nabla$ along curves.
- [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles) and [Principal Bundle Connections](node:Principal%20Bundle%20Connections): Ehresmann and principal connections; Ambrose–Singer.
- [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms): connection one-forms, $d_\nabla$, and $F=dA+A\wedge A$.
- [Frobenius Integrability Theorem](node:Frobenius%20Integrability%20Theorem): flatness as integrability of the horizontal distribution.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$ for the tangent bundle.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): curves with $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$.
- [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds): holonomy $U(n)$ and $SU(n)$ in Berger's list.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups) and [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras): holonomy groups as Lie subgroups of the structure group; Ambrose–Singer works at the Lie-algebra level.
- [Holonomy Groups](node:Holonomy%20Groups): the group generated by transport around loops; Berger's list.
- [Characteristic Classes](node:Characteristic%20Classes) and [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology): Chern–Weil theory produces characteristic classes from the curvature.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): flat connections are representations of $\pi_1$.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): gauge fields are connections on principal bundles; $A'=gAg^{-1}-(dg)g^{-1}$ is a gauge transformation.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): free fall as geodesic motion of the Levi-Civita connection.

### Common pitfalls
- **Index order of $\Gamma$.** Sources disagree on whether the differentiation index is the first or second lower index; even Wikipedia's covariant-derivative article uses both. The two orders give the same formulas only when $\Gamma$ is symmetric, i.e. for torsion-free connections. ([Wikipedia: Covariant derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_derivative); [Rajeev, Rochester PHY413 Lecture 9](https://www.pas.rochester.edu/~rajeev/phy413/Grav9.pdf))
- **Nonzero $\Gamma$ is not curvature.** Christoffel symbols are chart-dependent; flat space in polar coordinates has nonzero $\Gamma$ and trivial transport around contractible loops. Curvature, a tensor, is the invariant. ([Wikipedia: Christoffel symbols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christoffel_symbols); [Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy))
- **Flat does not mean trivial holonomy.** Flatness kills $\mathrm{Hol}^0$, but non-contractible loops can still have nontrivial holonomy. ([Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy))

### Open problems
- **Classification of torsion-free affine holonomy groups.** The hypothesis that matters is torsion-freeness: without it the question is trivial, since by Hano and Ozeki (1956) every connected Lie subgroup of $GL(n,\mathbb R)$, $n\ge 2$, is the holonomy group of some linear connection on $n$-dimensional affine space. ([Hano and Ozeki 1956](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0027763000000106/type/journal_article)) For torsion-free connections the de Rham decomposition fails and a complete classification is described as out of reach; the irreducible case was classified by Merkulov and Schwachhöfer (1999), completing work Berger began in the 1950s, with Bryant (2000) showing that every group on their list occurs. ([Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy); [Merkulov and Schwachhöfer 1999](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9907206)) 
- **Conceptual proof of prehomogeneity.** The complex irreducible holonomy representations are all prehomogeneous (an analogue of Simons's transitivity result for Riemannian holonomy); the source states that a conceptual proof of this fact is not known. ([Wikipedia: Holonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomy))

### Resources
