references.Consciousness Indicators for AI:
## Reference
### Overview
Consciousness indicators for AI are architectural and functional properties, derived from scientific theories of consciousness, whose presence in an AI system is taken to raise the probability that the system is conscious. The approach was set out in the 2023 report *Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness* by Butlin, Long and seventeen co-authors spanning neuroscience, philosophy and machine learning (including Bengio, Birch, Fleming, Frith, Kanai, Mudrik, Peters and Schwitzgebel). It is "theory-heavy": instead of judging from behaviour, it asks whether a system performs the functions that leading theories associate with consciousness ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).

The motivation is that behavioural tests are unreliable for AI. AI systems may be trained to mimic human behaviour while working in very different ways, so passing a Turing-style test does not show sentience, and some chatbots have been trained to say they are not conscious ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_consciousness)). The target notion is *phenomenal* consciousness, the "what it is like" character of experience, as opposed to *access* consciousness in Block's sense, a state's being generally available for use and guidance by the organism ([SEP: Consciousness](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/consciousness/)).

The indicator framework matters for AI welfare and policy because both errors are costly: failing to recognise conscious AI "may risk causing or allowing morally significant harms", while over-attribution, to which anthropomorphism toward language models makes people prone, could misallocate resources and interfere with valuable human relationships ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).

### Formal definition
**Computational functionalism (working hypothesis).** Implementing computations of the right kind is necessary and sufficient for consciousness; this makes consciousness in non-biological systems possible in principle. Butlin et al. adopt it pragmatically, not as established, and therefore exclude integrated information theory, which is incompatible with it ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).

**Indicator property.** A property that one or more scientific theories of consciousness hold to be necessary for consciousness, with some subsets held to be jointly sufficient. The 14 indicators of the 2023 report are ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)):

- **Recurrent processing theory.** RPT-1: input modules using algorithmic recurrence; RPT-2: input modules generating organised, integrated perceptual representations ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Global workspace theory.** GWT-1: multiple specialised systems operating in parallel (modules); GWT-2: a limited-capacity workspace with a bottleneck and selective attention; GWT-3: global broadcast of workspace contents to all modules; GWT-4: state-dependent attention that can query modules in succession ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Computational higher-order theories.** HOT-1: generative, top-down or noisy perception modules; HOT-2: metacognitive monitoring distinguishing reliable perceptual representations from noise; HOT-3: agency guided by a general belief-formation and action-selection system with a strong disposition to update on monitoring; HOT-4: sparse, smooth coding generating a "quality space" ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Attention schema theory.** AST-1: a predictive model representing and enabling control over the system's current state of attention ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Predictive processing.** PP-1: input modules using predictive coding ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Agency and embodiment.** AE-1: learning from feedback and selecting outputs to pursue goals, especially with flexible responsiveness to competing goals; AE-2: modelling output–input contingencies and using that model in perception or control ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).

**Scoring rule.** The indicators form a rubric: a system with more of them is a better candidate. The authors do not endorse the stronger claims that particular indicators are necessary or that particular combinations suffice ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)). Credence in a system's consciousness depends on how closely it implements the functions, confidence in each theory, and confidence in computational functionalism ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).

### Key results
- **No current system is a strong candidate; no obvious technical barrier.** Butlin et al. conclude that their analysis "suggests that no current AI systems are conscious", but also that there are no obvious technical barriers to building systems that satisfy the indicators, and that "conscious AI is not merely a remote possibility in the distant future" ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Transformers lack a global workspace.** The residual stream resembles a workspace written to and read by attention and MLP modules, but its dimensionality matches the input, so it is questionable as a bottleneck, and transformers are not recurrent: no module receives back what it broadcast. The report concludes that "Transformers lack the overall structure of a system with a global workspace" and gives only a "relatively weak case" for GWT indicators in LLMs ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Perceiver and embodied agents are partial matches.** The Perceiver arguably has GWT-1, GWT-2 and part of GWT-4 but lacks global broadcast; PaLM-E's agency and embodiment are doubtful because it imitates human data and is not trained end-to-end on the effects of its outputs ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Chalmers's assessment of LLMs.** Under mainstream assumptions, current LLMs face obstacles including lack of recurrent processing, a global workspace and unified agency, making them "somewhat unlikely" to be conscious; it is "quite possible" that these obstacles will be overcome in the next decade or so, so the possibility that successors to LLMs are conscious should be taken seriously ([arXiv:2303.07103](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07103)).
- **Probabilistic aggregation (Digital Consciousness Model).** Shiller et al. combine a range of theories and perspectives into a probabilistic assessment and find that the evidence is against 2024 LLMs being conscious, though not decisively, and much weaker than the evidence against consciousness in simpler AI systems ([arXiv:2601.17060](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17060)).

### Examples
- **RPT-1 is easy to build.** The report calls building systems with algorithmic recurrence (RPT-1) straightforward, and holds that reinforcement learning is arguably sufficient for agency in the sense of AE-1 ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Case-study systems.** The report assesses transformer LLMs, the Perceiver, PaLM-E, DeepMind's Adaptive Agent in a 3D environment, and a virtual-rodent controller ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **LaMDA (2022).** Blake Lemoine's claim that Google's LaMDA was sentient was judged by the scientific community to reflect mimicry, illustrating why behavioural evidence is discounted ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_consciousness)).

### History
Global workspace theory, due to Baars, had been implemented in cognitive architectures such as Franklin's LIDA well before LLMs ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_consciousness)). Chalmers's NeurIPS invited lecture of 28 November 2022, posted to arXiv in March 2023, framed the question for LLMs ([arXiv:2303.07103](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07103)). The Butlin–Long report appeared on arXiv in August 2023 ([arXiv:2308.08708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08708)). In 2025 Butlin and Lappas proposed five principles for responsible AI consciousness research covering objectives, procedures, knowledge sharing and public communication ([arXiv:2501.07290](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07290)), and in January 2026 Shiller et al. released the Digital Consciousness Model ([arXiv:2601.17060](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17060)).

### Connections
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): the systems most often assessed, and found to lack a global workspace.
- [LLM Introspection and Metacognition](node:LLM%20Introspection%20and%20Metacognition): HOT-2 metacognitive monitoring is the indicator closest to introspection research.
- [Model Self-Reports](node:Model%20Self-Reports): the behavioural evidence the theory-heavy approach discounts.
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): the report says interpretability may be needed to check indicators such as AE-2.
- [Transformers](node:Transformers): the architecture whose residual stream is evaluated as a candidate workspace.
- [Predictive Coding](node:Predictive%20Coding): the basis of indicator PP-1.
- [Attention Mechanism](node:Attention%20Mechanism): relevant to GWT-2, GWT-4 and AST-1.
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): the usual route to the agency indicator AE-1.
- [AI Moral Patienthood](node:AI%20Moral%20Patienthood): consciousness assessments feed into moral-status judgements.
- [AI Welfare Evaluations](node:AI%20Welfare%20Evaluations): practical evaluations that use indicator-style evidence.

### Common pitfalls
- **Treating the list as a checklist with a threshold.** The authors present indicators as raising probability, not as necessary or jointly sufficient conditions ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Forgetting the conditional.** Every conclusion is conditional on computational functionalism; biological naturalists such as Seth argue computation alone may not suffice and that consciousness depends on being a living organism, making conscious AI unlikely on current trajectories ([Seth, BBS](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A)).
- **Reading mimicry as evidence.** Schwitzgebel's mimicry argument holds that when a system was built or selected to display features that indicate consciousness in humans, "we the receivers cannot justifiably infer underlying consciousness"; this undercuts the case for consciousness without establishing the case against ([Schwitzgebel, draft](https://faculty.ucr.edu/~eschwitz/SchwitzPapers/AIConsciousness-260330.htm)).
- **Choosing an interpretation of each theory.** Restrictive readings require very specific features found in humans, while liberal readings give abstract conditions that surprisingly simple artificial systems may meet; moderate readings are attractive but lack clear empirical support over the alternatives ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).

### Open problems
- **Refining and extending the indicators.** Butlin et al.'s Box 4 lists open questions: examining further theories, refining indicators, scrutinising computational functionalism (including whether conventional hardware can support consciousness and how copyable systems should be individuated), developing computational theories of valence, and overcoming "our limited understanding of the inner workings of complex deep learning systems" ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)).
- **Whether the question can be settled at all.** Schwitzgebel argues that we cannot know through introspection, conceptual analysis or near-term scientific inquiry which of ten possibly essential features of consciousness are essential, so "we cannot reliably assess its presence or absence in sophisticated AI systems" ([Schwitzgebel, draft](https://faculty.ucr.edu/~eschwitz/SchwitzPapers/AIConsciousness-260330.htm)).

> [!warning] Contested
> Whether non-biological computation can be conscious at all is disputed. Butlin et al. assume computational functionalism as a working hypothesis ([Butlin et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.08708)); Seth's biological naturalism holds that consciousness depends on life ([Seth, BBS](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Consciousness (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/consciousness/): phenomenal and access consciousness, global workspace, higher-order and integrated-information theories.
- **Reference:** [Artificial consciousness (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_consciousness): survey of positions, tests and history.
- **Learn:** [Schwitzgebel, AI and Consciousness: A Skeptical Overview (UC Riverside draft)](https://faculty.ucr.edu/~eschwitz/SchwitzPapers/AIConsciousness-260330.htm): book-length introduction to the arguments, including the mimicry argument.
- **Primary:** [Butlin, Long et al., Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08708): the indicator properties and case studies.
- **Primary:** [Chalmers, Could a Large Language Model be Conscious?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07103): reasons for and against LLM consciousness.
- **Primary:** [Shiller et al., Initial results of the Digital Consciousness Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17060): probabilistic aggregation across theories.
- **Further reading:** [Birch, The Edge of Sentience (OUP, 2024)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/9780191966729.001.0001): Oxford University Press monograph by Jonathan Birch.
references.Conservation Laws:
## Reference
### Overview
A conservation law states that a measurable property of an isolated physical system does not change as the system evolves. The physically realized form is local: the amount of the quantity in a region changes only by what flows through its boundary, which is a continuity equation. A merely global law, in which an amount disappears at one point while an equal amount appears elsewhere, is not Lorentz invariant; local conservation implies global conservation. ([Wikipedia: Conservation law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_law))

For systems with an action principle, Noether's theorem ties each continuous symmetry to a conserved quantity: time-translation invariance gives energy, spatial translations give linear momentum, and rotations give angular momentum. The theorem is "on shell" (it uses the equations of motion) and does not apply to systems that cannot be described by a Lagrangian alone, such as those with a Rayleigh dissipation function. ([Wikipedia: Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem); [Harnew, Oxford Lecture 28](https://users.physics.ox.ac.uk/~harnew/lectures/lecture28-mechanics-handout.pdf))

Not every familiar conservation law is exact. In the Standard Model, baryon number is an accidental global symmetry rather than a consequence of a gauge symmetry, and it is violated (negligibly at low temperature) by sphaleron processes; electroweak sphalerons change baryon and lepton number in steps of three. In general relativity there is no invariant local energy density of the gravitational field; the standard global notions of mass use extra structure, a timelike Killing vector (Komar) or asymptotic flatness (ADM, Bondi). ([Wikipedia: Proton decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_decay); [Wikipedia: Chiral anomaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral_anomaly); [Wikipedia: Mass in general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_in_general_relativity))

### Formal definition
**Local form.** If $\rho$ is the density of a quantity and $\mathbf{j}$ its flux,
$$\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}=0 ,$$
the [Continuity Equation](node:Continuity%20Equation). ([Wikipedia: Conservation law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_law))

**Noether's theorem, mechanics.** Let $I=\int L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt$ be invariant under a continuous $N$-parameter family of transformations with generators $\delta t=\sum_r\varepsilon_rT_r$, $\delta q=\sum_r\varepsilon_rQ_r$. Then the $N$ quantities
$$\Bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\cdot\dot q-L\Bigr)T_r-\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\cdot Q_r$$
are constants of motion. Time translation ($T=1$, $Q=0$) gives $H=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\cdot\dot q-L$; translation of an ignorable coordinate ($T=0$, $Q_k=1$) gives $p_k=\partial L/\partial\dot q_k$; a rotation about $\mathbf{n}$ ($Q=\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{r}$) gives $\mathbf{n}\cdot(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{p})$. ([Wikipedia: Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))

**Noether's theorem, fields.** If the action $\int\mathcal{L}(\varphi,\partial\varphi,x)\,d^4x$ is invariant (the Lagrangian density is invariant or changes by a divergence) under $N$ independent continuous transformations, there are $N$ currents
$$j^\nu_r=\Lambda^\nu_r-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\nu\varphi)}\cdot\Psi_r,\qquad \partial_\nu j^\nu_r=0\ \text{on shell},$$
where $\Psi_r$ is the field variation and $\Lambda_r$ the divergence term. The Noether charge is the integral of the current over a spacelike slice; it is conserved provided the currents fall off fast enough at spatial infinity. Spacetime translations give the stress-energy tensor with $T^{\mu\nu}{}_{,\nu}=0$; the phase rotation $\psi\mapsto e^{i\theta}\psi$ of a complex Klein–Gordon field gives the current $j^\nu=i(\partial^\nu\psi\,\psi^*-\partial^\nu\psi^*\,\psi)$, which times the particle's charge is the electric current. ([Wikipedia: Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))

### Key results
- **Energy (Hamiltonian).** With $H=\sum_kp_k\dot q_k-L$, one has $dH/dt=-\partial L/\partial t$, so $H$ is conserved if $L$ has no explicit time dependence. For a particle with $T=\tfrac12m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2+\dot z^2)$ and $L=T-U(x,y,z)$, $H=2T-(T-U)=T+U=E$. ([Harnew, Oxford Lecture 28](https://users.physics.ox.ac.uk/~harnew/lectures/lecture28-mechanics-handout.pdf))
- **Cyclic coordinates.** If $q_k$ does not appear in $L$, then $\dot p_k=\partial L/\partial q_k=0$ and the conjugate momentum $p_k=\partial L/\partial\dot q_k$ is conserved. ([Harnew, Oxford Lecture 28](https://users.physics.ox.ac.uk/~harnew/lectures/lecture28-mechanics-handout.pdf))
- **Angular momentum and the third law.** The total angular momentum of a system on which zero net external torque acts is constant; the associated symmetry is rotational invariance. ([Wikipedia: Angular momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_momentum)) The Newtonian particle derivation needs the strong form of the third law (internal forces equal, opposite and central): Diaz and Herrera show that, under conditions common in classical mechanics and using the superposition principle in the second law, combined conservation of linear and angular momentum is equivalent to Newton's third law for central forces. ([Diaz and Herrera, arXiv:physics/0405099](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0405099)) Charged bodies need not obey the third law; the momentum balance is restored by momentum carried by the electromagnetic field. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws of motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
- **Noether's second theorem.** If the action admits an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra of local symmetries parametrized linearly by $q$ arbitrary functions and their derivatives, then there are $q$ linear differential relations among the Euler–Lagrange expressions: the field equations are not independent. This is the gauge-theory case. ([Wikipedia: Noether's second theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_second_theorem))
- **Anomalies.** A classical conservation law can fail after quantization. The chiral anomaly is the anomalous non-conservation of the axial current $j^\mu_5=\bar\psi\gamma^5\gamma^\mu\psi$; Adler, Bell and Jackiw (1969) used it to explain the $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$ decay rate. Gauge symmetry must be non-anomalous and exactly respected for consistency. The electroweak anomaly makes baryon number non-conserved through sphalerons. ([Wikipedia: Chiral anomaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral_anomaly)) The anomalies that break $B$ and $L$ separately cancel in $B-L$. ([Wikipedia: B − L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B_%E2%88%92_L))
- **Ward–Takahashi identities.** The quantum counterpart of current conservation is an identity among correlation functions that follows from global or gauge symmetry and survives [renormalization](node:Renormalization). In QED, an amplitude with an external photon of momentum $k$ satisfies $k_\mu\mathcal{M}^\mu=0$ when all external particles are on shell. ([Wikipedia: Ward–Takahashi identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward%E2%80%93Takahashi_identity))
- **Energy in general relativity.** There is no invariant local energy density for the gravitational field, and pseudotensors such as Landau–Lifshitz give gauge-dependent results. Precise global notions require structure: the Komar mass is defined only for stationary spacetimes (timelike Killing vector); the ADM energy–momentum is defined at spatial infinity of an asymptotically flat spacetime, and under suitable [energy conditions](node:Energy%20Conditions) its mass is non-negative and vanishes only for Minkowski space (positive energy theorem); the Bondi mass at null infinity can decrease as gravitational radiation is emitted. ([Wikipedia: Mass in general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_in_general_relativity); [Jaramillo and Gourgoulhon, arXiv:1001.5429](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.5429)) In expanding FLRW spacetimes energy conservation is not well defined. ([Wikipedia: Conservation of energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_of_energy))

### Examples
- **Bead on a free hoop.** $L=\tfrac12m(R^2\dot\theta^2+R^2\sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2)+mgR\cos\theta$ has no $\varphi$ or $t$, so $p_\varphi=mR^2\sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi=J_z$ and $H=T+U=E$ are both conserved. ([Harnew, Oxford Lecture 28](https://users.physics.ox.ac.uk/~harnew/lectures/lecture28-mechanics-handout.pdf))
- **Driven hoop.** If the hoop is forced to rotate at fixed $\omega$, $L=\tfrac12m(R^2\dot\theta^2+R^2\omega^2\sin^2\theta)+mgR\cos\theta$ still has no explicit $t$, so $H$ is conserved; but $E=H+mR^2\omega^2\sin^2\theta$ is not, because the drive supplies energy. ([Harnew, Oxford Lecture 28](https://users.physics.ox.ac.uk/~harnew/lectures/lecture28-mechanics-handout.pdf))
- **Central force.** If the net force on a body is always directed toward a fixed point, there is no torque about that point and the angular momentum about it is constant, as for planetary and satellite orbits. ([Wikipedia: Angular momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_momentum))
- **Electric charge.** The $U(1)$ phase symmetry gives a conserved current whose time component integrates to the charge; Weyl first noted this [gauge invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance). ([Wikipedia: Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Weak isospin is not conserved.** Weak interactions conserve $T_3$, but interactions with the Higgs field (whose vacuum value is nonzero) do not; fermion mass terms mix chiralities. Only the combination $Q=T_3+\tfrac12Y_W$ is conserved. ([Wikipedia: Weak isospin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_isospin))

### History
Huygens (1669) listed momentum and kinetic energy as invariants of collisions. Du Châtelet proposed and tested conservation of total energy, repeating 's Gravesande's 1722 experiment of dropping balls into soft clay. Mayer (1842) first stated the mechanical equivalent of heat in modern form; Joule (1843) used a falling weight turning a paddle in water; Helmholtz's *Über die Erhaltung der Kraft* (1847) became the basis of general acceptance. ([Wikipedia: Conservation of energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_of_energy))

Noether began the work in 1915 while helping Klein and Hilbert with general relativity, had the key ideas by March 1918, and published both theorems in 1918. ([Wikipedia: Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem)) An English translation, "Invariant variation problems", appeared in *Transport Theory and Statistical Physics* 1 (1971) 186–207. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1080/00411457108231446)) Ward published his QED identity in 1950 and Takahashi generalized it in 1957. ([Wikipedia: Ward–Takahashi identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward%E2%80%93Takahashi_identity))

### Connections
- [Newtonian Mechanics](node:Newtonian%20Mechanics): $F=dp/dt$ and $\tau=dL/dt$; the third law and its strong (central) form.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem): the symmetry–conservation dictionary in detail.
- [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics) and [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics): cyclic coordinates and $dH/dt=-\partial L/\partial t$.
- [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory): Noether currents and charges.
- [Continuity Equation](node:Continuity%20Equation): the local form.
- [Central Force Motion and the Kepler Problem](node:Central%20Force%20Motion%20and%20the%20Kepler%20Problem): angular momentum about the force centre.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor) and [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$ as local covariant conservation of matter energy–momentum.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity), [ADM Formalism](node:ADM%20Formalism) and [Landau–Lifshitz Pseudotensor](node:Landau–Lifshitz%20Pseudotensor): why global gravitational energy needs extra structure.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): local symmetries give Noether second-theorem identities among the field equations.
- [Standard Model of Particle Physics](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics), [Electroweak Theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory) and [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): exact, accidental, and broken symmetries.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): anomalies and Ward–Takahashi identities.
- [Four-Vectors and Relativistic Momentum](node:Four-Vectors%20and%20Relativistic%20Momentum): energy and momentum as one conserved four-vector.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Energy momentum and rotation](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Energy%20momentum%20and%20rotation)

### Common pitfalls
- **$H$ versus $E$.** With time-dependent constraints the Hamiltonian can be conserved while $T+U$ is not (driven hoop). ([Harnew, Oxford Lecture 28](https://users.physics.ox.ac.uk/~harnew/lectures/lecture28-mechanics-handout.pdf))
- **Dissipation.** Dissipative systems with continuous symmetries need not have a corresponding conservation law. ([Wikipedia: Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Discrete symmetries.** CPT is discrete, so Noether's theorem does not apply to it. ([Wikipedia: Conservation law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_law))
- **Local versus global symmetry.** For gauge symmetries parametrized by arbitrary functions, the second theorem gives linear differential relations among the [Euler–Lagrange equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations), so the field equations are not independent. ([Wikipedia: Noether's second theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_second_theorem))
- **Uncited symmetry tables.** Wikipedia's conservation-law article lists weak isospin and $B-L$ among exact gauge conservation laws, but that table is flagged as uncited; weak isospin is violated by Higgs interactions, and $B-L$ is described as a hypothetical symmetry that the seesaw mechanism requires to be spontaneously broken. ([Wikipedia: Conservation law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_law); [Wikipedia: Weak isospin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_isospin); [Wikipedia: B − L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B_%E2%88%92_L))

### Open problems
- **Quasi-local energy in GR.** Assigning mass–energy to a finite region bounded by a closed surface has many proposals (Hawking, Geroch, Bartnik, Brown–York, Liu–Yau, Penrose); "the search for a fully satisfactory definition of quasi-local mass remains an open problem." ([Wikipedia: Mass in general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_in_general_relativity))
- **Is baryon number violated at low energy?** Proton decay has never been observed (Super-Kamiokande: lifetime above about $2.4\times10^{34}$ years for $p\to e^+\pi^0$), while grand unified theories predict it; "Do protons decay?" is listed as unsolved. ([Wikipedia: Proton decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_decay))
- **Is total lepton number violated?** Observing neutrinoless double beta decay would be the first signal of violation of total lepton-number conservation; it has not been found, with the strongest listed half-life bound from KamLAND-Zen ($^{136}$Xe, $>3.8\times10^{26}$ yr). ([Wikipedia: Neutrinoless double beta decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrinoless_double_beta_decay))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Noether's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem): mechanics and field-theory statements, examples, history.
- **Reference:** [Mass in general relativity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_in_general_relativity): Komar, ADM, Bondi, quasi-local mass.
- **Learn:** [Harnew, Oxford Classical Mechanics Lecture 28](https://users.physics.ox.ac.uk/~harnew/lectures/lecture28-mechanics-handout.pdf): Hamiltonian, cyclic coordinates, Noether, hoop examples.
- **Primary:** [Jaramillo and Gourgoulhon, "Mass and Angular Momentum in General Relativity" (arXiv:1001.5429)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.5429): review of Komar, ADM, Bondi and quasi-local quantities.
- **Primary:** [Noether, "Invariant variation problems" (transl. 1971)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1080/00411457108231446): the 1918 paper with both theorems.
- **Further reading:** [Kosmann-Schwarzbach, The Noether Theorems (Springer, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-87868-3): history and content of both theorems.
references.Convex Optimization:
## Reference
### Overview
Convex optimization is the minimization of a convex function over a convex set (equivalently, maximization of a concave function over a convex set). Its importance comes from structure that general nonlinear programming lacks: every local minimum is a global minimum, the optimal set is convex, Lagrangian duality is exact under mild conditions, and many problem classes admit polynomial-time algorithms, whereas general mathematical optimization is NP-hard ([Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization)).

The standard classes form a hierarchy: linear programming, then quadratic programming, then second-order cone programming and semidefinite programming, with conic optimization (a linear objective over the intersection of an affine set and a closed pointed convex cone) the most general; a standard-form linear program is the conic case where the cone is the nonnegative orthant ([Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization)). Introductory courses stress recognizing and formulating convex problems in signal processing, control, machine learning, finance, circuit design and statistics, alongside optimality conditions and duality theory ([MIT OCW 6.079](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-079-introduction-to-convex-optimization-fall-2009/)).

The theory sits between [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus) and [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) on one side and algorithm design on the other: first-order methods ([Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent), subgradient and proximal methods), Newton-type and interior-point methods, and splitting methods such as ADMM are all covered in a graduate course built around duality and the KKT conditions ([CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/)).

### Formal definition
A convex optimization problem in standard form is
$$\begin{aligned}\text{minimize}\quad & f_0(x)\\ \text{subject to}\quad & f_i(x)\le 0,\quad i=1,\dots,m,\\ & Ax=b,\end{aligned}$$
with $f_0,\dots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ convex and the equality constraints affine. Any such problem can be put in epigraph form with a linear objective by adding a variable $t$ and the constraint $f_0(x)-t\le 0$ ([Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization), [Wikipedia: Slater's condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slater%27s_condition)).

**Lagrangian and dual.** With multipliers $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$ for the inequalities and $\nu$ for the equalities, the Lagrangian is $L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x)+\nu^\top(Ax-b)$ and the dual function is
$$g(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,\lambda,\nu),$$
which is concave even when the primal is not convex, being a pointwise infimum of affine functions. The dual problem maximizes $g$ over $\lambda\ge 0$; with $p^\star,d^\star$ the primal and dual optimal values, the duality gap is $p^\star-d^\star\ge 0$ ([Wikipedia: Duality (optimization)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duality_%28optimization%29)).

**KKT conditions.** For the standard form above with differentiable $f_0,\dots,f_m$, a point $x^\star$ with multipliers $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, $\nu$ satisfies the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions if
$$\nabla f_0(x^\star)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla f_i(x^\star)+A^\top\nu=0,\quad f_i(x^\star)\le0,\ Ax^\star=b,\quad \lambda_i\ge0,\quad \lambda_i f_i(x^\star)=0,$$
that is, stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility and complementary slackness ([Wikipedia: KKT conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karush%E2%80%93Kuhn%E2%80%93Tucker_conditions)).

**Slater's condition.** There is $x$ in the relative interior of $D=\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i$ with $f_i(x)<0$ for all $i$ and $Ax=b$; in the relaxed form, constraints with affine $f_i$ need only hold with $\le$ ([Wikipedia: Slater's condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slater%27s_condition)).

### Key results
- **Local equals global.** For a convex problem every local minimum is a global minimum and the optimal set is convex; if the objective is strictly convex there is at most one optimal point. ([Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization))
- **Weak duality.** For every $\lambda\ge0$ and every $\nu$, $g(\lambda,\nu)\le p^\star$; hence $d^\star\le p^\star$ for any optimization problem, convex or not. ([Wikipedia: Duality (optimization)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duality_%28optimization%29))
- **Strong duality under Slater (Slater 1950).** If $f_0,\dots,f_m$ are convex, the problem is bounded below, and Slater's condition holds, then $p^\star=d^\star$ and, when finite, the dual optimum is attained. The same holds for generalized inequalities $f_i(x)\preceq_{K_i}0$ with $K_i$-convex $f_i$ when a strictly feasible point exists. ([Wikipedia: Slater's condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slater%27s_condition))
- **KKT necessity and sufficiency.** If $x^\star$ is a local optimum and a constraint qualification holds (LICQ, MFCQ, or Slater's condition for convex problems, among others; LICQ implies MFCQ), KKT multipliers exist. Conversely, for a differentiable convex objective with convex inequality and affine equality constraints, any KKT point is globally optimal. ([Wikipedia: KKT conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karush%E2%80%93Kuhn%E2%80%93Tucker_conditions))
- **Multiplier theorem (convex form).** At an optimum there are multipliers $(\lambda_0,\lambda)\ge0$, not all zero, with complementary slackness and $x^\star$ minimizing $\lambda_0f_0+\sum_i\lambda_if_i$ over the domain; if a strictly feasible point exists one may take $\lambda_0=1$. ([Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization))
- **First-order rates.** For convex $f$ with Lipschitz gradient, gradient descent achieves objective error $O(1/k)$ after $k$ steps; Nesterov's acceleration improves this to $O(1/k^2)$, which is optimal for first-order methods; under strong convexity gradient descent converges linearly with a fixed step. ([Wikipedia: Gradient descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent))
- **Interior-point methods.** Karmarkar's 1984 method solves linear programs in polynomial time; Nesterov and Nemirovski introduced self-concordant barriers, a class that can encode any convex set, and short-step path-following methods using a barrier with self-concordance parameter $M$ need at most $O(1)\cdot\sqrt{M}\,\ln\!\big(\tfrac{M}{t_0\varepsilon}+1\big)$ Newton steps to reach an $\varepsilon$-approximate solution (potential-reduction methods have $M$ in place of $\sqrt M$). The ellipsoid method is polynomial in theory but slow in practice. ([Wikipedia: Interior-point method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior-point_method))
- **Log-barrier IPMs are not strongly polynomial.** Allamigeon, Benchimol, Gaubert and Joswig construct linear programs on which primal-dual log-barrier interior-point methods need a number of iterations exponential in the dimension, and show the total curvature of the central path can be exponential, disproving a continuous analogue of the Hirsch conjecture. ([arXiv:1708.01544](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01544))

### Examples
- **Linear programming** is the conic problem over the nonnegative orthant; semidefinite programming replaces the orthant by the cone of positive semidefinite matrices, and second-order cone programming lies between quadratic and semidefinite programming ([Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization)).
- **Equality-constrained quadratic programs.** For quadratic problems the KKT conditions are linear and can be solved analytically ([Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization)).
- **Standard modelling examples.** Least squares, linear and quadratic programs, and semidefinite programs are the standard modelling examples in an introductory course ([MIT OCW 6.079](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-079-introduction-to-convex-optimization-fall-2009/)); a graduate course adds stochastic gradient descent, coordinate descent, ADMM and Frank–Wolfe ([CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/)).

### History
Slater introduced his condition in 1950 in the Cowles Commission discussion paper "Lagrange Multipliers Revisited" ([Wikipedia: Slater's condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slater%27s_condition)). Kuhn and Tucker published the KKT conditions in 1951; William Karush had stated the necessary conditions in an unpublished 1939 master's thesis ([Wikipedia: KKT conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karush%E2%80%93Kuhn%E2%80%93Tucker_conditions)). Karmarkar's polynomial-time interior-point method for linear programming appeared in 1984, and Nesterov and Nemirovski's self-concordant barrier theory extended interior-point methods to general convex sets ([Wikipedia: Interior-point method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior-point_method)). Boyd and Vandenberghe's *Convex Optimization* (Cambridge University Press, 2004; 727 pages, 337 exercises) is a comprehensive introduction covering convex sets and functions, problem classes, duality, and statistical and geometric applications ([Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/convex-optimization/17D2FAA54F641A2F62C7CCD01DFA97C4)).

### Connections
- [Linear Programming](node:Linear%20Programming): the simplest convex problem class and the setting of strongly polynomial questions.
- [Convex Polarity and Duality](node:Convex%20Polarity%20and%20Duality): the convex-analytic duality behind Lagrangian and Fenchel duality.
- [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent), [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent), [Newton's Method](node:Newton's%20Method): the main algorithms, with rates guaranteed by convexity.
- [Numerical Optimization](node:Numerical%20Optimization): the broader nonconvex setting where KKT conditions are only necessary.
- [Second-Order Optimization for Learning](node:Second-Order%20Optimization%20for%20Learning) and [Variance Reduction in Stochastic Optimization](node:Variance%20Reduction%20in%20Stochastic%20Optimization): convex-analysis-driven methods in machine learning.
- [Linear Programming Relaxations](node:Linear%20Programming%20Relaxations) and [Combinatorial Optimization](node:Combinatorial%20Optimization): convex relaxations of discrete problems.
- [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices): the cone underlying semidefinite programming.
- [Distributionally Robust Optimization](node:Distributionally%20Robust%20Optimization): robust formulations that are often reformulated as convex programs.
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus) and [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): prerequisites for gradients, Hessians and affine constraints.

### Common pitfalls
- KKT conditions are necessary only under a constraint qualification and sufficient only under convexity; without a constraint qualification an optimum need not have KKT multipliers ([Wikipedia: KKT conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karush%E2%80%93Kuhn%E2%80%93Tucker_conditions)).
- Convexity alone does not give strong duality: Slater's condition (or another constraint qualification) is needed for a zero duality gap ([Wikipedia: Duality (optimization)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duality_%28optimization%29)).
- In the standard form the equality constraints are affine and the inequality constraints are convex functions $\le 0$; a problem is not in convex form merely because its objective is convex ([Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization)).
- Polynomial-time guarantees for interior-point methods do not make them strongly polynomial: primal-dual log-barrier methods are not ([arXiv:1708.01544](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01544)).

### Open problems
- **Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale's 9th problem).** Whether linear programming admits a strongly polynomial-time algorithm is open: weakly polynomial methods such as the ellipsoid and interior-point methods exist, but no algorithm is known whose running time is polynomial in the number of constraints and variables alone, and Smale listed the question among his problems for the 21st century ([Wikipedia: Linear programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_programming)). Natura (2026) proves a strongly polynomial $O(m^2\log m)$ bound on the circuit diameter of standard-form polyhedra and notes that an augmentation algorithm matching it "would yield a strongly polynomial time algorithm for linear programming, resolving Smale's 9th problem" ([arXiv:2602.06958](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06958)). The log-barrier result of Allamigeon et al. rules out one natural route ([arXiv:1708.01544](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01544)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization): definitions, properties, problem hierarchy, algorithms.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karush%E2%80%93Kuhn%E2%80%93Tucker_conditions): conditions, constraint qualifications, sufficiency.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 6.079 Introduction to Convex Optimization (Boyd, Parrilo)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-079-introduction-to-convex-optimization-fall-2009/): modelling, optimality conditions, duality.
- **Learn:** [CMU 10-725 Convex Optimization (Tibshirani)](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/): duality, KKT, Newton, barrier and primal-dual interior-point methods, proximal methods, ADMM.
- **Primary:** [Allamigeon, Benchimol, Gaubert, Joswig, Log-barrier interior point methods are not strongly polynomial](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01544): tropical lower bounds for interior-point methods.
- **Primary:** [Natura, Circuit Diameter of Polyhedra is Strongly Polynomial](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06958): recent progress on the strongly polynomial LP question.
- **Further reading:** [Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (Cambridge University Press, 2004)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/convex-optimization/17D2FAA54F641A2F62C7CCD01DFA97C4): the standard graduate text.
references.Convolutional Neural Networks:
## Reference
### Overview
A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a feedforward neural network that learns features by optimising filters (kernels); CNNs are the de-facto standard in deep-learning-based approaches to computer vision ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network)). Its layers are built from convolutional layers, pooling layers, elementwise nonlinearities such as ReLU, and fully connected layers; convolutional and fully connected layers carry parameters, ReLU and pooling do not ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/)).

Two structural assumptions distinguish a CNN from a generic multilayer perceptron on images. **Translation equivariance**: shifting the input should only shift the hidden representation, which forces the weights to be independent of position. **Locality**: each hidden unit depends only on a small window of the input. Imposing both on a fully connected layer turns it into a convolution and cuts the parameter count for a $1000\times1000$ image from about $10^{12}$ to $4\Delta^2$ for a window of radius $\Delta$ ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-neural-networks/why-conv.html)). Weight sharing drastically reduces the number of free parameters: a $5\times5$ shared tile has 25 weights, whereas a fully connected neuron on a $100\times100$ image has 10,000 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network)).

Mathematically, CNNs are the translation-group case of a general principle: for networks whose layers carry functions on homogeneous spaces of a compact group, equivariance holds exactly when every linear layer is a (generalised) group convolution ([Kondor and Trivedi 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1802.03690)). This places them inside [Geometric Deep Learning](node:Geometric%20Deep%20Learning) alongside [Equivariant Neural Networks](node:Equivariant%20Neural%20Networks) and [Graph Neural Networks](node:Graph%20Neural%20Networks).

### Formal definition
For $f,g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ the convolution is $(f*g)(x)=\int f(z)\,g(x-z)\,dz$; in two discrete dimensions $(f*g)(i,j)=\sum_a\sum_b f(a,b)\,g(i-a,j-b)$ ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-neural-networks/why-conv.html)).

A **convolutional layer** with $C$ input channels and $D$ output channels maps $X\in\mathbb R^{H\times W\times C}$ to
$$H_{i,j,d}=\sum_{a=-\Delta}^{\Delta}\sum_{b=-\Delta}^{\Delta}\sum_{c} V_{a,b,c,d}\,X_{i+a,\,j+b,\,c},$$
followed by a pointwise nonlinearity. Because the index is $i+a$ rather than $i-a$, this is technically a cross-correlation; the difference is cosmetic since the kernel is learned ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-neural-networks/why-conv.html); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network)).

**Hyperparameters and shapes.** A layer has $K$ filters of spatial size $F$, stride $S$ and zero-padding $P$. On an input of width $W_1$ and depth $D_1$ the output width is
$$W_2=\frac{W_1-F+2P}{S}+1,$$
(similarly for height), the output depth is $K$, and the layer has $F\cdot F\cdot D_1\cdot K$ weights and $K$ biases ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/)).

**Pooling** reduces spatial resolution by a fixed function (typically max, sometimes average) over windows, commonly $2\times2$ with stride 2, and has no parameters ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network)).

**Group equivariance.** A map $\varphi$ between function spaces carrying actions $\mathbb T_g$, $\mathbb T'_g$ of a group $G$ is $G$-equivariant if $\varphi(\mathbb T_g f)=\mathbb T'_g\,\varphi(f)$ for all $f$ and $g\in G$ ([Kondor and Trivedi 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1802.03690)).

### Key results
- **Convolution characterises equivariance (Kondor and Trivedi 2018).** Let $G$ be a compact group (stated for countable $G$, with continuous groups a stated straightforward extension) and let $\mathcal N$ be an $(L+1)$-layer feedforward network whose $\ell$-th layer carries functions on a quotient $\mathcal X_\ell=G/H_\ell$, with linear maps $\varphi_\ell$ and pointwise nonlinearities. Then $\mathcal N$ is $G$-equivariant if and only if each $\varphi_\ell$ is a generalised convolution $f_{\ell-1}*\chi_\ell$ with a filter $\chi_\ell$ on the double coset space $H_{\ell-1}\backslash G/H_\ell$ ([Kondor and Trivedi 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1802.03690)).
- **Universality of deep CNNs (Zhou 2018).** Let $2\le s\le d$. For any compact $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $f\in C(\Omega)$, a deep ReLU CNN with filters of length $s$ and no fully connected layers approximates $f$ uniformly on $\Omega$ to arbitrary accuracy as the depth $J\to\infty$ ([Zhou 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1805.10769)).
- **Approximation rate (Zhou 2018).** If moreover $\Omega\subseteq[-1,1]^d$, $J\ge 2d/(s-1)$, and $f=F|_\Omega$ with $F\in H^r(\mathbb R^d)$ for an integer $r>2+d/2$, then the uniform error is at most $c\,\|F\|\sqrt{\log J}\,(1/J)^{1/2+1/d}$ for an absolute constant $c$ ([Zhou 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1805.10769)).
- **Equivariance and invariance.** Translation equivariance of convolutional layers does not imply translation invariance, since fully connected layers are not invariant to shifts of the input, and layers with stride greater than one ignore the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem and can alias; proposed remedies include avoiding downsampling and applying global average pooling at the last layer ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network)). Empirically, small shifts or rescalings can substantially change a modern CNN's output because subsampling ignores the sampling theorem ([Azulay and Weiss 2019](https://jmlr.org/papers/v20/19-519.html)).
- **Convolutional and fully connected layers interconvert.** Any fully connected layer equals a convolutional layer whose filter covers the whole input (e.g. a 4096-unit layer on a $7\times7\times512$ volume is a conv layer with $F=7$, $P=0$, $S=1$, $K=4096$), and every conv layer is a (sparse, weight-tied) fully connected layer ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/)).
- **G-convolutions add capacity without parameters.** Group-equivariant CNNs replace translation convolution by convolution over a discrete group of translations, reflections and rotations, increasing weight sharing and expressive capacity at no extra parameter cost and negligible overhead ([Cohen and Welling 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07576)).

### Examples
- **LeNet:** LeCun's networks of the 1990s, trained end-to-end by [backpropagation](node:Backpropagation) from 1989, were used to read zip codes and digits; LeNet-5 (1998) became a standard baseline ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network); [CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/)).
- **AlexNet:** five convolutional layers (some followed by max pooling) and three fully connected layers ending in a 1000-way softmax, with 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons, trained on GPUs with non-saturating (ReLU) units and dropout; it reached 37.5% / 17.0% top-1 / top-5 error on the ILSVRC-2010 test set, and a variant won ILSVRC-2012 with 15.3% top-5 test error against 26.2% for the second-best entry ([Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton 2012](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/file/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Paper.pdf)). (The NeurIPS proceedings web abstract gives earlier figures: 500,000 neurons and 39.7% / 18.9% ([proceedings page](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2012/hash/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Abstract.html)).)
- **Parameter sharing at scale:** AlexNet's first conv layer has 34,944 parameters with sharing versus over 105 million without ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/)).
- **VGG, GoogLeNet and ResNet:** VGG uses only $3\times3$ convolutions and $2\times2$ pooling with about 140M parameters; GoogLeNet's Inception module cuts this to about 4M ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/)). [Residual Networks](node:Residual%20Networks) learn residual functions relative to the layer input, reach 152 layers, and an ensemble achieved 3.57% ImageNet test error, winning ILSVRC 2015 ([He et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385)).
- **Beyond images:** the time-delay neural network applied 1-D convolution over time for phoneme recognition; CNNs are also used in natural language processing, recommender systems and medical image analysis ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network)).

### History
Hubel and Wiesel's work on cat visual cortex identified neurons responding to small receptive fields, and their 1968 paper distinguished simple and complex cells. Fukushima's 1980 neocognitron introduced shared-weight receptive-field layers and downsampling layers; in the original neocognitron some weights were not trainable. Waibel et al.'s 1987 time-delay neural network was the first CNN to combine weight sharing with backpropagation. By 1989 LeCun's group had reported training CNNs end-to-end by backpropagation, culminating in LeNet-5 (1998). The GPU-trained AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet win is described as an early catalytic event for the AI boom ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network)). Residual connections followed in 2015 ([He et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385)), and group-equivariant generalisations from 2016 ([Cohen and Welling 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07576)).

### Connections
- [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning): CNNs are the architecture that launched modern deep learning in vision.
- [Artificial Neural Networks](node:Artificial%20Neural%20Networks): a CNN is a feedforward network with sparse, weight-tied linear layers.
- [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation): trains the shared filters end to end.
- [Residual Networks](node:Residual%20Networks): skip connections that made very deep CNNs trainable.
- [Equivariant Neural Networks](node:Equivariant%20Neural%20Networks) and [Steerable Neural Networks](node:Steerable%20Neural%20Networks): generalise translation equivariance to rotations, reflections and other groups.
- [Geometric Deep Learning](node:Geometric%20Deep%20Learning): frames CNNs as the grid/translation instance of symmetry-based architecture design.
- [Graph Neural Networks](node:Graph%20Neural%20Networks): replace the grid by a graph and convolution by message passing.
- [Group Fourier Transform](node:Group%20Fourier%20Transform) and [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory): the harmonic analysis behind generalised convolutions on compact groups.
- [Universal Approximation Theorem](node:Universal%20Approximation%20Theorem): Zhou's theorem is its analogue for deep convolutional architectures.
- [Vision Transformers](node:Vision%20Transformers): the main competing image architecture, with weaker built-in locality.
- [Adversarial Robustness](node:Adversarial%20Robustness): imperceptible perturbations can change CNN predictions.
- [Normalization in Neural Networks](node:Normalization%20in%20Neural%20Networks): batch normalisation is part of the ResNet design.

### Common pitfalls
- **"CNNs are translation-invariant."** They are equivariant layer by layer only without striding; downsampling aliases, so outputs can change under one-pixel shifts ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network); [Azulay and Weiss 2019](https://jmlr.org/papers/v20/19-519.html)).
- **Data augmentation does not give invariance in general:** networks learn invariance mainly for images resembling the training set ([Azulay and Weiss 2019](https://jmlr.org/papers/v20/19-519.html)).
- **Convolution vs cross-correlation:** modern implementations typically compute correlation and call it convolution, for convenience ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network)).
- **Shape arithmetic:** $(W_1-F+2P)/S+1$ must be an integer, or the hyperparameters are inconsistent ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/)).

### Open problems
- **Invariance to small transformations.** Azulay and Weiss find that antialiasing and wider augmentation give only partial improvements and conclude that keeping high accuracy while guaranteeing invariance to small shifts and rescalings remains open ([Azulay and Weiss 2019](https://jmlr.org/papers/v20/19-519.html)). Srinivas et al. likewise list invariance under extreme deformations as largely unstudied, and whether adversarial examples can be completely eliminated as unresolved ([Srinivas et al. 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.06615)).
- **Efficient non-redundant training:** how to train compact, non-redundant CNNs from the start, rather than compressing large ones, is listed as open ([Srinivas et al. 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.06615)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Convolutional neural network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network): history, equivariance caveats, building blocks, applications.
- **Learn:** [Stanford CS231n: Convolutional Networks](https://cs231n.github.io/convolutional-networks/): layer shapes, parameter counts, architectures.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, From fully connected layers to convolutions](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-neural-networks/why-conv.html): derives the conv layer from translation invariance and locality.
- **Primary:** [Kondor and Trivedi, On the Generalization of Equivariance and Convolution in Neural Networks to the Action of Compact Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03690): equivariance iff convolution.
- **Primary:** [Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, ImageNet Classification with Deep CNNs](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2012/hash/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Abstract.html): AlexNet.
- **Primary:** [He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385): ResNets.
- **Primary:** [Zhou, Universality of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.10769): approximation theory.
- **Further reading:** [Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press), Chapter 9 Convolutional Networks](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/): the standard graduate text.

## Reference
### Overview
Cosmic inflation is the hypothesis that the very early universe went through a brief period of accelerated, nearly exponential expansion, ending when the energy of the driving field was converted into hot, dense particles (reheating) that began the hot Big Bang ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_inflation)). It was proposed to explain the initial-condition puzzles of standard Friedmann–Robertson–Walker cosmology: why causally disconnected regions of the cosmic microwave background have the same temperature (horizon problem), why the density is so close to critical (flatness problem), and why relic magnetic monopoles are not observed ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_inflation)).

The unifying idea is a shrinking comoving Hubble radius $(aH)^{-1}$. In ordinary decelerating cosmology this radius only grows, which is the root of both the horizon and flatness problems; a phase in which it decreases sufficiently makes $\Omega = 1$ an attractor and puts all presently observed scales in causal contact before inflation ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)). The same mechanism stretches quantum zero-point fluctuations of the inflaton beyond the horizon, where they freeze into classical curvature perturbations that later seed the CMB anisotropies and large-scale structure ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).

Its basic predictions, a flat universe with nearly scale-invariant, Gaussian and adiabatic density fluctuations, agree with observations ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)); Planck gives $n_s = 0.9649 \pm 0.0042$ (68% CL) and, combined with BAO data, confirms spatial flatness to 0.4% (95% CL) ([Planck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06211)). The predicted background of primordial gravitational waves has not been detected: BICEP/Keck give $r_{0.05} < 0.036$ at 95% confidence ([BICEP/Keck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00483)), and combining Planck with BK18 and BAO tightens this to $r < 0.032$ ([Tristram et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.07961)).

### Formal definition
Inflation is a period with $\ddot a > 0$, equivalently a decreasing comoving Hubble radius, $\frac{d}{dt}(aH)^{-1} < 0$. Defining the Hubble slow-roll parameters with $dN = H\,dt = d\ln a$,
$$\varepsilon = -\frac{\dot H}{H^2} = -\frac{d\ln H}{dN}, \qquad \eta = -\frac{\ddot\phi}{H\dot\phi} = \varepsilon - \frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\frac{d\varepsilon}{dN},$$
accelerated expansion occurs when $\varepsilon < 1$, and it is sustained for a sufficiently long time when $|\eta| < 1$, which keeps the fractional change of $\varepsilon$ per e-fold small; the de Sitter limit is $\varepsilon \to 0$ ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).

In **single-field slow-roll inflation** a scalar inflaton $\phi$ with potential $V(\phi)$ is minimally coupled to gravity; in Baumann's conventions (with $M_{pl} = 1$) the action is
$$S = \int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\left[\tfrac12 R + \tfrac12 g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial_\nu\phi - V(\phi)\right].$$
The potential slow-roll parameters
$$\epsilon_v = \frac{M_{pl}^2}{2}\left(\frac{V_{,\phi}}{V}\right)^2,\qquad \eta_v = M_{pl}^2\frac{V_{,\phi\phi}}{V}$$
satisfy $\varepsilon \approx \epsilon_v$, $\eta \approx \eta_v - \epsilon_v$ in the slow-roll regime $\epsilon_v, |\eta_v| \ll 1$, where $H^2 \approx V/3$, $\dot\phi \approx -V_{,\phi}/(3H)$, and $a(t) \sim e^{Ht}$; inflation ends when $\epsilon_v(\phi_{\rm end}) \approx 1$ ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)). The number of e-folds remaining is $N(\phi) = \ln(a_{\rm end}/a) = \int_{\phi_{\rm end}}^{\phi} d\phi/\sqrt{2\epsilon_v}$; solving the horizon and flatness problems requires a total of roughly $N_{\rm tot} \gtrsim 60$, and CMB scales left the horizon about $N_{\rm cmb} \approx 40$–$60$ e-folds before the end, depending on reheating ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).

**Primordial spectra.** To leading order in slow roll, the dimensionless scalar and tensor power spectra evaluated at horizon crossing $k = aH$ are
$$\Delta_s^2(k) \approx \frac{1}{24\pi^2}\frac{V}{M_{pl}^4}\frac{1}{\epsilon_v},\qquad \Delta_t^2(k) \approx \frac{2}{3\pi^2}\frac{V}{M_{pl}^4},$$
with
$$n_s - 1 = 2\eta_v - 6\epsilon_v,\qquad n_t = -2\epsilon_v,\qquad r = \frac{\Delta_t^2}{\Delta_s^2} = 16\epsilon_v$$
([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).

### Key results
- **Slow-roll consistency relation.** In single-field slow-roll models the tensor-to-scalar ratio and tensor tilt satisfy $r = -8n_t$; together with large non-Gaussianity ($f_{NL} > 1$), nonzero isocurvature, and large running ($|\alpha_s| > 0.001$), its violation would falsify single-field slow-roll inflation ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- **Lyth bound.** Since $r = \frac{8}{M_{pl}^2}\left(\frac{d\phi}{dN}\right)^2$, the field excursion between CMB horizon exit and the end of inflation obeys $\Delta\phi/M_{pl} = \mathcal O(1)\times (r/0.01)^{1/2}$, so $r > 0.01$ requires super-Planckian (large-field) excursions ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- **Single-field squeezed-limit theorem (Maldacena; Creminelli–Zaldarriaga).** For any single-field model, the squeezed limit of the curvature bispectrum is
$\lim_{k_3 \to 0}\langle \mathcal R_{k_1}\mathcal R_{k_2}\mathcal R_{k_3}\rangle = (2\pi)^3\delta(\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2+\mathbf k_3)(1-n_s)P_{\mathcal R}(k_1)P_{\mathcal R}(k_3)$, so a detection of squeezed-limit non-Gaussianity would rule out single-field inflation; in slow roll, $f_{NL} = \mathcal O(\varepsilon,\eta)$ ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- **Energy scale from tensors.** The tensor amplitude measures $V$ directly; $r \geq 0.01$ corresponds to inflation at energies of order the GUT scale, about $10^{16}$ GeV ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- **Planck 2018 constraints.** Planck temperature, polarization and lensing give $n_s = 0.9649 \pm 0.0042$ (68% CL) with no evidence for running; $r_{0.002} < 0.10$ from Planck alone and $< 0.056$ combined with BICEP2/Keck BK15 (95% CL); slow-roll models with concave potentials ($V'' < 0$) are increasingly favored, and two methods of reconstructing the inflaton potential find no evidence for dynamics beyond slow roll ([Planck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06211)).
- **BICEP/Keck 2021.** Combining BICEP/Keck through the 2018 season with Planck and WMAP gives $r_{0.05} < 0.036$ (95% CL), with $\sigma(r) = 0.009$ ([BICEP/Keck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00483)).

### Examples
- **$m^2\phi^2$ inflation.** For $V = \tfrac12 m^2\phi^2$, $\epsilon_v = \eta_v = 2(M_{pl}/\phi)^2$, slow roll requires $\phi > \sqrt2 M_{pl}$, $N(\phi) = \phi^2/(4M_{pl}^2) - 1/2$, and CMB scales correspond to $\phi_{\rm cmb} = 2\sqrt{N_{\rm cmb}}\,M_{pl} \sim 15 M_{pl}$, a large-field model; with $N_{\rm cmb} \sim 60$ it predicts $n_s = 1 - 2/N_{\rm cmb} \approx 0.96$ and $r = 8/N_{\rm cmb} \approx 0.1$ ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)), above the BICEP/Keck bound $r_{0.05} < 0.036$ ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424); [BICEP/Keck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00483)).
- **Starobinsky inflation.** Starobinsky's model predicts $n_s \approx 1 - 2/N$ and $r \approx 12/N^2$ in terms of the number of e-folds $N$; for $N \approx 60$ this gives $n_s \approx 0.967$ and $r \approx 0.003$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_inflation)), well inside the Planck interval for $n_s$ and the bounds on $r$ ([Planck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06211)).
- **Small- versus large-field models.** Monomial potentials $V \propto \phi^p$ give super-Planckian excursions and large tensor amplitudes, while small-field models move less than $M_{pl}$ and predict small $r$ ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).

### History
Starobinsky noted that quantum corrections to general relativity, which generically give curvature-squared terms in the action, could drive an early de Sitter phase; Guth proposed inflation in January 1981 to explain the nonexistence of magnetic monopoles (his model became known as "old inflation"); Albrecht and Steinhardt and Linde developed new (slow-roll) inflation, Linde introduced chaotic inflation, Steinhardt gave the first example of eternal inflation in 1983, and Vilenkin showed that eternal inflation is generic ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_inflation)). Guth's paper is "Inflationary universe: A possible solution to the horizon and flatness problems", Physical Review D 23, 347–356 (1981) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.347)). In 2014 the BICEP2 team reported $r$ between 0.15 and 0.27, but confidence in the claim was later reduced and later bounds on $r$ tightened ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_inflation); [BICEP/Keck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00483)).

### Connections
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): inflation is a phase of the FLRW background with $\varepsilon < 1$, and it addresses the initial-condition problems of the FLRW model.
- [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory): the inflaton is a scalar field theory minimally coupled to gravity.
- [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space): slow-roll inflation is a quasi-de Sitter expansion.
- [QFT in Curved Spacetime](node:QFT%20in%20Curved%20Spacetime): primordial perturbations are computed by quantizing fluctuations in a quasi-de Sitter background (Bunch–Davies vacuum).
- [Cosmological Perturbation Theory](node:Cosmological%20Perturbation%20Theory): gauge-invariant curvature perturbations carry the inflationary signal to late times.
- [Reheating after Inflation](node:Reheating%20after%20Inflation): the transfer of inflaton energy to Standard Model particles that ends inflation.
- [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background) and [CMB Polarization](node:CMB%20Polarization): the main probes; B-modes would detect inflationary tensors.
- [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves): inflation predicts a primordial stochastic tensor background.
- [Magnetic Monopoles](node:Magnetic%20Monopoles): their absence motivated Guth's proposal.
- [Large-Scale Structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure): grows from the inflationary curvature perturbations.
- [String Theory](node:String%20Theory): proposed ultraviolet completions of inflationary models.
- [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): the present accelerated expansion is a late-time analogue.

### Common pitfalls
- The horizon and flatness problems are not strict inconsistencies of the Big Bang model but severe shortcomings in its predictive power: flatness and large-scale homogeneity must be assumed in the initial conditions rather than predicted ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- The comoving horizon $\tau$ and the comoving Hubble radius $(aH)^{-1}$ are different: regions farther apart than $(aH)^{-1}$ cannot communicate now but may have been in causal contact earlier ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- Hubble and potential slow-roll parameters differ beyond leading order ($\eta \approx \eta_v - \epsilon_v$), and formulas such as $n_s - 1 = 2\eta - 4\varepsilon$ versus $2\eta_v - 6\epsilon_v$ must not be mixed ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- Reported bounds on $r$ refer to a pivot scale ($k = 0.002$ or $0.05\ \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$), which must match when comparing results ([Planck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06211); [BICEP/Keck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00483)).

> [!warning] Contested
> Critics argue that inflation does not solve the initial-conditions problem: Penrose argued that, because thermalization increases entropy, the universe would have been even more special before inflation than after, and Steinhardt and coauthors argued that Planck data put the inflationary paradigm in trouble; Guth, Kaiser, Nomura and Linde replied that inflation is on a stronger footing than ever before ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_inflation)).

### Open problems
- **Primordial B-modes.** Detecting the CMB B-mode signature of inflationary tensor modes would fix the energy scale of inflation and show a super-Planckian field excursion; Baumann calls it the most distinctive confirmation still to be made ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)), and it remains undetected, with $r_{0.05} < 0.036$ ([BICEP/Keck Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00483)) and $r < 0.032$ when Planck and BAO data are added ([Tristram et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.07961)).
- **Initial conditions.** The overshoot problem (a non-negligible initial inflaton velocity carries the field past the inflating region, worse for small-field models) and the patch problem (the inflaton must be smooth over several Hubble lengths to start inflation) are listed as poorly understood ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- **Eternal inflation and the measure problem.** Because inflation globally never ends, predictions depend on the relative probabilities of inflating and non-inflating regions, and different measures change the predicted likelihood of flatness and scale invariance ([Baumann, TASI Lectures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.5424)).
- **Alternatives.** Whether ekpyrotic/cyclic models can produce the correct density-perturbation spectrum and pass through the Big Crunch/Big Bang transition is described as a topic of controversy and current research, and whether string gas cosmology can stabilize the compactified dimensions and produce the correct spectrum is still under study ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_inflation)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cosmic inflation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_inflation): motivation, history, observational status and criticisms.
- **Learn:** [Baumann, TASI Lectures on Inflation](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.5424): slow roll, derivation of the scalar and tensor spectra, CMB tests, non-Gaussianity and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Guth, Inflationary universe (Phys. Rev. D 23, 1981)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.347): the original proposal (bibliographic record).
- **Primary:** [Planck 2018 results X: Constraints on inflation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06211): current constraints on $n_s$, $r$ and the inflaton potential.
- **Primary:** [BICEP/Keck XIII](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00483): B-mode bound $r_{0.05} < 0.036$ on primordial gravitational waves.
- **Further reading:** [Liddle and Lyth, Cosmological Inflation and Large-Scale Structure (CUP 2000)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781139175180/type/book): graduate textbook on inflation and structure formation.
references.Cosmic Microwave Background:
## Reference
### Overview
The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is a nearly isotropic microwave glow filling the observable universe, leftover radiation from the hot Big Bang. It is not associated with any star or galaxy; its energy density exceeds that of all photons ever emitted by stars. Penzias and Wilson discovered it accidentally in 1964, following theoretical work in the 1940s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background))

In the expanding universe the early plasma was opaque: photons Thomson-scattered off free electrons. After about $380\,000$ years the temperature had fallen to roughly $3000\,\mathrm{K}$, electrons combined with protons into hydrogen, and the universe became transparent. Those photons have since redshifted to a $2.7\,\mathrm{K}$ blackbody. ([ESA Planck](https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Planck/Planck_and_the_cosmic_microwave_background)) The PDG review places this “recombination” at redshift $z\simeq 1100$, with little model dependence. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))

Tiny temperature variations, first mapped by COBE and then by WMAP and Planck, are a snapshot of density fluctuations at last scattering. Their angular power spectrum, together with polarization, has become the primary dataset of precision cosmology and a pillar of spatially flat $\Lambda$CDM. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))

### Formal definition
The CMB is well described by a blackbody of temperature $T=2.7255\,\mathrm{K}$, equivalently $kT_\gamma=0.234\,\mathrm{meV}$. A blackbody at that temperature has number density $n_\gamma=(2\zeta(3)/\pi^2)T_\gamma^3\simeq 411\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, energy density $\rho_\gamma=(\pi^2/15)T_\gamma^4\simeq 4.64\times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{g}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}\simeq 0.260\,\mathrm{eV}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, and $\Omega_\gamma\simeq 5.38\times 10^{-5}$. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf)) Wikipedia quotes $T=2.72548\pm 0.00057\,\mathrm{K}$ and $\rho_\gamma=0.260\,\mathrm{eV}/\mathrm{cm}^3$ with about $411$ photons/cm$^3$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background))

Temperature anisotropies are expanded in spherical harmonics,
$$T(\theta,\phi)=\sum_{\ell m}a_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi),$$
with power $C_\ell\equiv\langle|a_{\ell m}|^2\rangle$. For a statistically isotropic Gaussian sky the two-point function (the $C_\ell$s) exhausts the cosmological information. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf)) Polarization is decomposed into $E$ (gradient) and $B$ (curl) modes; $E$ is about ten times weaker than the temperature anisotropy. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background))

In an expanding universe the blackbody temperature scales as $T(z)=T_0(1+z)$. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))

### Key results
- **Spectrum.** FIRAS on COBE found a nearly perfect blackbody, $T=2.725\pm 0.002\,\mathrm{K}$, matching hot-Big-Bang predictions and implying that nearly all of the universe's radiant energy was released within the first year. ([NASA LAMBDA/COBE](https://lambda.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/cobe/)) No deviations from a Planck spectrum are seen over more than three decades in frequency, constraining energy release at $z\lesssim 10^7$. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))
- **Dipole.** The largest anisotropy is the $\ell=1$ dipole, amplitude $3.3621\pm 0.0010\,\mathrm{mK}$, interpreted as a Doppler boost from Solar-System motion $v=369.82\pm 0.11\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ toward Galactic $(l,b)=(264.021^\circ\pm 0.011^\circ,\,48.253^\circ\pm 0.005^\circ)$. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))
- **Higher multipoles.** After subtracting the dipole, rms variations are just over $100\,\mu\mathrm{K}$ (about one part in $10^5$). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background)) They originate in density perturbations at last scattering. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))
- **Acoustic peaks.** Before decoupling, photon-baryon plasma oscillated; the sound waves freeze in at last scattering and appear as a harmonic series in $\ell(\ell+1)C_\ell/2\pi$. The first peak measures spatial curvature, the second baryon density, the third dark-matter density. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background)) Hu's notes frame this as “cosmic ultrasound.” ([Hu, UChicago](https://background.uchicago.edu/~whu/intermediate/intermediate.html))
- **Planck 2018 base $\Lambda$CDM (68% CL).** $\Omega_c h^2=0.120\pm 0.001$, $\Omega_b h^2=0.0224\pm 0.0001$, $n_s=0.965\pm 0.004$, $\tau=0.054\pm 0.007$, $100\theta_*=1.0411\pm 0.0003$; derived $H_0=(67.4\pm 0.5)\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, $\Omega_m=0.315\pm 0.007$, $\sigma_8=0.811\pm 0.006$. ([Planck 2018, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))
- **Extensions.** With BAO, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=2.99\pm 0.17$ (SM prediction $3.046$), $\sum m_\nu<0.12\,\mathrm{eV}$, $\Omega_K=0.001\pm 0.002$; with BICEP/Keck, $r_{0.002}<0.06$.
