No compelling evidence for extensions of six-parameter $\Lambda$CDM. ([Planck 2018, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))

### Examples
- **COBE.** Launched 18 November 1989. DMR detected intrinsic anisotropy at a part in $10^5$; FIRAS confirmed the blackbody; DIRBE searched for the cosmic infrared background. Mather and Smoot received the 2006 Nobel Prize. ([NASA LAMBDA/COBE](https://lambda.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/cobe/))
- **WMAP.** NASA's 2001 full-sky mission; ESA credits its results with helping determine the Universe's constituents and with establishing the standard model of cosmology now in use. ([ESA Planck](https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Planck/Planck_and_the_cosmic_microwave_background))
- **Planck.** ESA mission launched 2009, observing $27\,\mathrm{GHz}$–$1\,\mathrm{THz}$ over the whole sky at higher sensitivity and frequency coverage than WMAP, enabling cleaner foreground separation. ([ESA Planck](https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Planck/Planck_and_the_cosmic_microwave_background))

### History
Alpher and Herman, correcting a 1948 Gamow paper, predicted leftover Big-Bang radiation at about $5\,\mathrm{K}$. Tolman had shown in 1934 that expansion cools a blackbody while preserving the thermal shape. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background)) ESA also credits Gamow, Alpher, and Herman with the late-1940s prediction, tied to Big-Bang nucleosynthesis. ([ESA Planck](https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Planck/Planck_and_the_cosmic_microwave_background))

On 20 May 1964 Penzias and Wilson measured a $4.2\,\mathrm{K}$ excess antenna temperature with the Holmdel horn; Dicke's Princeton group had been building a radiometer to search for the same signal. Penzias and Wilson received the 1978 Nobel Prize. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background))

COBE (1992) established the anisotropy; balloon and ground experiments (BOOMERanG, MAXIMA, DASI, …) resolved the first acoustic peak and showed the geometry is nearly flat. WMAP and Planck then turned the $C_\ell$s into percent-level cosmological parameters. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background))

### Connections
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): the expanding background that redshifts $T\propto 1/a$.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): six-parameter model that the CMB fits.
- [CMB Acoustic Peaks](node:CMB%20Acoustic%20Peaks): the harmonic series in the $C_\ell$s.
- [Cosmological Perturbation Theory](node:Cosmological%20Perturbation%20Theory): evolution of the fluctuations to last scattering.
- [Cosmic Inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation): origin of the nearly scale-invariant adiabatic perturbations.
- [Big Bang Nucleosynthesis](node:Big%20Bang%20Nucleosynthesis): independent early-universe test; Planck abundances agree.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter) and [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): $\Omega_c h^2$ and the late-time expansion from the peak structure plus distance data.
- [Spherical Harmonics](node:Spherical%20Harmonics): the $Y_{\ell m}$ basis for $a_{\ell m}$.
- [Large-Scale Structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure) and [Galaxy Formation](node:Galaxy%20Formation): the same primordial fluctuations, grown by gravity.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Microwave background and acoustic structure](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Microwave%20background%20and%20acoustic%20structure)

### Common pitfalls
- **Dipole is kinematic.** The $\ell=1$ moment is overwhelmingly our motion through the CMB frame, not a primordial fluctuation; it is removed before cosmological analysis. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))
- **Recombination is not “the Big Bang.”** The CMB last-scatters at $z\simeq 1100$, $\sim 380\,000$ years after $t=0$, not at the singularity. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))
- **Foregrounds.** Galactic dust, synchrotron, and point sources must be separated; Planck's extra frequency bands exist largely for that. ([ESA Planck](https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Planck/Planck_and_the_cosmic_microwave_background))
- **Cosmic variance.** Each $C_\ell$ is a $\chi^2$ with $2\ell+1$ degrees of freedom; at low $\ell$ sampling variance, not instrument noise, dominates. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))
- **$H_0$ from the CMB is model-dependent.** The quoted $67.4\pm 0.5$ assumes base $\Lambda$CDM; it is not a direct local measurement. ([Planck 2018, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))

### Open problems
- **Hubble tension.** Planck base $\Lambda$CDM is in $3.6\sigma$ tension with local distance-ladder $H_0$ (higher local value). Simple extensions that ease the tension are not favoured by Planck. ([Planck 2018, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))
- **Primordial $B$ modes.** The tensor-to-scalar ratio is only bounded ($r_{0.002}<0.06$ with BICEP/Keck); a detection would measure the inflationary energy scale. ([Planck 2018, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))
- **Spectral distortions.** Standard physics predicts small departures from a pure blackbody (dissipation of perturbations, inverse Compton, recombination lines) that have not yet been measured. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))
- **Large-angle anomalies.** Weak signatures of non-Gaussianity or statistical anisotropy at large scales appear in both WMAP and Planck but are not significant enough to reject Gaussian isotropy. ([PDG 2025](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cosmic microwave background (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background): discovery, spectrum, anisotropy, and experimental history.
- **Learn:** [Hu, CMB Intermediate](https://background.uchicago.edu/~whu/intermediate/intermediate.html): acoustic oscillations, peaks, and parameter estimation, aimed at working cosmologists.
- **Primary:** [PDG, Cosmic Microwave Background (2025)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-cosmic-microwave-background.pdf): spectrum, $C_\ell$s, and cosmological-parameter review.
- **Primary:** [Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209): final full-mission $\Lambda$CDM constraints.
references.Cosmological Perturbation Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Cosmological perturbation theory describes small departures from a homogeneous, isotropic Friedmann–Robertson–Walker (FRW) background and how they evolve. It has a Newtonian form, valid below the Hubble scale for slow, low-pressure matter, and general-relativistic forms: the gauge-invariant theory of Bardeen (1980) and Kodama and Sasaki (1984), the standard approach in cosmology, and the 1+3 covariant approach of Hawking (1966) and Ellis and Bruni (1989) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_perturbation_theory)). Bardeen's paper introduced a complete set of gauge-invariant variables that give perturbations larger than the particle horizon a clear meaning and simplify the linearized equations for arbitrary equations of state, entropy perturbations and anisotropic pressure ([Bardeen 1980, INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20Bardeen%20and%20t%20%22Gauge%20invariant%20cosmological%20perturbations%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts)).

Density perturbations $\rho=\bar\rho(1+\delta)$ grow by gravitational instability against pressure: slowly during radiation domination ($\delta\sim\ln a$) and efficiently during matter domination ($\delta\sim a$) ([Baumann, TASI Lectures on Inflation](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0907.5424)). A relativistic treatment is required for perturbations larger than the horizon, while late-time galaxy formation is well described by Newtonian gravity ([Ma & Bertschinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9506072)).

CMB anisotropies fall almost entirely under linear perturbation theory, with essentially no phenomenological parameters ([Hu & Dodelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)). Large-scale structure goes nonlinear on small scales; its weakly nonlinear regime is handled by Eulerian and Lagrangian (standard) perturbation theory and by an effective field theory ([Bernardeau et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551); [Carrasco, Hertzberg & Senatore](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.2926)).

### Formal definition
**Newtonian fluid in comoving coordinates.** With conformal time $\tau$, $\mathcal H=d\ln a/d\tau$, peculiar velocity $\mathbf u$ and $\rho=\bar\rho(1+\delta)$, a pressureless fluid obeys
$$\partial_\tau\delta+\nabla\cdot[(1+\delta)\mathbf u]=0,\qquad \partial_\tau\mathbf u+\mathcal H\mathbf u+(\mathbf u\cdot\nabla)\mathbf u=-\nabla\Phi,\qquad \nabla^2\Phi=\tfrac32\Omega_m\mathcal H^2\delta .$$
Linearizing gives $D_1''+\mathcal H D_1'=\tfrac32\Omega_m\mathcal H^2D_1$, defining the linear growth factor $D_1$ and growth rate $f=d\ln D_1/d\ln a$ ([Bernardeau et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551)). With pressure, a sound speed $c_s^2\equiv\delta P/(\bar\rho\,\delta)$ closes the system ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_perturbation_theory)).

**Lagrangian description.** Particles move from initial positions $\mathbf q$ to $\mathbf x(\tau)=\mathbf q+\boldsymbol\Psi(\mathbf q,\tau)$. At first order, $\nabla_q\cdot\boldsymbol\Psi^{(1)}=-D_1(\tau)\delta(\mathbf q)$; the Zel'dovich approximation uses this displacement as an approximate solution, giving $1+\delta=1/\prod_{i=1}^3(1-\lambda_iD_1)$ with $\lambda_i$ the eigenvalues of the initial tidal tensor ([Bernardeau et al., §2.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551)).

**Scalar–vector–tensor split.** $ds^2=-(1+2\Phi)dt^2+2aB_i\,dx^idt+a^2[(1-2\Psi)\delta_{ij}+E_{ij}]dx^idx^j$, decomposed into helicity $0,\pm1,\pm2$ parts that evolve independently at linear order ([Baumann, eq. 119](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0907.5424)).

**Gauges.** The synchronous gauge is $ds^2=a^2[-d\tau^2+(\delta_{ij}+h_{ij})dx^idx^j]$, the conformal Newtonian gauge $ds^2=a^2[-(1+2\psi)d\tau^2+(1-2\phi)dx^idx_i]$, whose potentials coincide up to sign with Bardeen's gauge-invariant variables ($\psi=\Phi_A$, $\phi=-\Phi_H$) ([Ma & Bertschinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9506072)).

**Curvature perturbations.** $-\zeta\equiv\Psi+(H/\dot{\bar\rho})\,\delta\rho$ on uniform-density slices and $\mathcal R\equiv\Psi-H\,\delta q/(\bar\rho+\bar p)$ on comoving slices ([Baumann, eqs. 136, 139](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0907.5424)).

### Key results
- **Linearized Einstein equations (conformal Newtonian gauge).** $k^2\phi+3\frac{\dot a}{a}(\dot\phi+\frac{\dot a}{a}\psi)=4\pi Ga^2\,\delta T^0{}_0$, $k^2(\dot\phi+\frac{\dot a}{a}\psi)=4\pi Ga^2(\bar\rho+\bar P)\theta$, and $k^2(\phi-\psi)=12\pi Ga^2(\bar\rho+\bar P)\sigma$, with $\delta T^0{}_0=-\delta\rho$; so $\phi=\psi$ unless there is anisotropic stress, which before recombination comes mainly from neutrinos ([Ma & Bertschinger, eqs. 23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9506072)).
- **Boltzmann hierarchy.** Massless neutrinos obey $\dot F_\ell=\frac{k}{2\ell+1}[\ell F_{\ell-1}-(\ell+1)F_{\ell+1}]$ for $\ell\ge2$, truncated by $F_{\ell_{\max}+1}\approx\frac{2\ell_{\max}+1}{k\tau}F_{\ell_{\max}}-F_{\ell_{\max}-1}$, which improves on setting $F_{\ell_{\max}+1}=0$. When $\tau_c/\tau\ll1$ and $k\tau_c\ll1$, with $\tau_c=(an_e\sigma_T)^{-1}$, photons and baryons form one tightly coupled fluid, expanded to second order in $\tau_c$ ([Ma & Bertschinger, eqs. 50–51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9506072)).
- **Superhorizon conservation.** For adiabatic perturbations ($\delta p_{\rm en}\equiv\delta p-(\dot{\bar p}/\dot{\bar\rho})\delta\rho=0$), $\zeta$ is constant for $k\ll aH$, and $-\zeta=\mathcal R+\frac{k^2}{(aH)^2}\frac{2\bar\rho}{3(\bar\rho+\bar p)}\Psi_B$, so $\zeta$ and $\mathcal R$ agree outside the horizon ([Baumann, eqs. 137, 141](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0907.5424)).
- **Separate-universe conservation.** Using only local energy–momentum conservation, without the field equations, Wands, Malik, Lyth and Liddle show that on sufficiently large scales the curvature perturbation on uniform-density hypersurfaces is conserved whenever non-adiabatic pressure is negligible, by treating long-wavelength regions as separate FRW universes ([Wands et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0003278)).
- **$\delta N$ formula.** Sasaki and Stewart show that, on superhorizon scales with negligible anisotropic stress and slow roll, the comoving curvature perturbation after reheating equals the perturbed number of e-folds from an initial flat slice, $\mathcal R_c=\delta N=\frac{\partial N}{\partial\phi^a}\delta\phi^a_f$ ([Sasaki & Stewart, eqs. 13–15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9507001)).
- **Weinberg's adiabatic-mode theorem.** Under a mild technical assumption on the wavelength dependence of the field equations, and none on the universe's contents, the Newtonian-gauge equations always admit an adiabatic solution with $\mathcal R$ nonzero and constant at large wavelength in all eras; with no anisotropic inertia its form is fixed by the scale factor ([Weinberg 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0302326)).
- **Mukhanov–Sasaki equation.** In single-field inflation $v\equiv z\mathcal R$, $z^2=2a^2\varepsilon$, obeys $v_k''+(k^2-z''/z)v_k=0$, giving $\Delta^2_{\mathcal R}=\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\frac{H^2}{M_{\rm pl}^2}\frac1\varepsilon$ and $\Delta_t^2=\frac{2}{\pi^2}\frac{H^2}{M_{\rm pl}^2}$ at $k=aH$, so $r=16\varepsilon$ and $n_s-1=2\eta_v-6\epsilon_v$ ([Baumann, eqs. 185, 222–236](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0907.5424)).
- **Mészáros effect.** For dark matter decoupled from radiation, with $y=a/a_{\rm eq}$, $\delta''+\frac{2+3y}{2y(1+y)}\delta'-\frac{3}{2y(1+y)}\delta=0$, whose growing mode is $\delta\propto1+\tfrac32y$: nearly frozen in radiation domination ([Wikipedia: Mészáros effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9sz%C3%A1ros_effect)).
- **Linear growth in ΛCDM.** In Einstein–de Sitter $D_1^{(\pm)}=a,\;a^{-3/2}$ and $f=1$; with matter, curvature and $\Lambda$, the growing mode is the Heath integral $D_1^{(+)}=\frac{5\Omega_m}{2}H(a)\int_0^a\frac{da'}{a'^3H(a')^3}$, with $H(a)=(\Omega_ma^{-3}+\Omega_ka^{-2}+\Omega_\Lambda)^{1/2}$ in units of $H_0$ and $\Omega_m$ its present value, normalized so that $D_1\to a$ as $a\to0$ ([Hamilton 2001, eq. 1 and footnote](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0006089)); and $f\approx\Omega_m^{5/9}$ for $\Omega_m+\Omega_\Lambda=1$ ([Bernardeau et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551)). Linder parametrizes growth by a growth index, $f\simeq\Omega_m(a)^\gamma$, with $\gamma=0.55+0.05[1+w(z=1)]$ for $w>-1$ (accurate to better than 0.2%) and $\gamma=0.55+0.02[1+w(z=1)]$ for $w<-1$; within GR growth is fixed by the expansion history, so a measured $\gamma$ tests gravity ([Linder 2005](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0507263)).
- **Second-order kernel.** In Einstein–de Sitter $\delta_2$ is a convolution of two linear fields with $F_2(\mathbf q_1,\mathbf q_2)=\frac57+\frac12\frac{\mathbf q_1\cdot\mathbf q_2}{q_1q_2}(\frac{q_1}{q_2}+\frac{q_2}{q_1})+\frac27\frac{(\mathbf q_1\cdot\mathbf q_2)^2}{q_1^2q_2^2}$ ([Bernardeau et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551)). Gauge transformations at second order are given by Malik and Wands ([Malik & Wands](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.4944)).
- **EFT of large-scale structure.** Treating long-wavelength matter as a fluid whose sound speed ($c_s^2\sim10^{-6}$) and viscosity absorb small-scale physics gives percent agreement with simulations up to $k\sim0.24\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ at order $\delta^4$, far better than standard perturbation theory ([Carrasco, Hertzberg & Senatore](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.2926)); the expansion requires $k/k_{\rm NL}\ll1$, $k_{\rm NL}^{-1}\sim5$ Mpc today ([Snowmass EFT white paper](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.08232)).

### Examples
- **CMB acoustic oscillations.** Neglecting baryons, the tightly coupled photon fluid obeys $\ddot\Theta+c_s^2k^2\Theta=-\frac{k^2}{3}\Psi-\ddot\Phi$ with $c_s^2=1/3$, oscillating about $\Theta+\Psi=0$; after recombination photons free-stream and the multipoles are a projection of the last-scattering source ([Hu & Dodelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0110414)).
- **Zel'dovich pancakes.** Collapse is planar, filamentary or spherical depending on the tidal eigenvalues; at shell crossing the Jacobian vanishes and the density diverges, and the approximation then lets matter stream through pancakes ([Bernardeau et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551)).
- **Einstein–Boltzmann codes.** CLASS solves the linear Boltzmann–Einstein system with systematic accuracy control ([Lesgourgues](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.2932)).
- **Measured initial conditions.** Planck base ΛCDM assumes a power-law spectrum of adiabatic scalar perturbations and finds $n_s=0.965\pm0.004$ ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)).

### History
Lifshitz developed the linear theory in synchronous gauge in 1946; its spurious gauge modes led Bardeen (1980) and Kodama and Sasaki (1984) to gauge-invariant formulations, and Mukhanov, Feldman and Brandenberger (1992) advocated the conformal Newtonian gauge ([Ma & Bertschinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9506072)). Bardeen's paper is Phys. Rev. D 22, 1882–1905 ([INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20Bardeen%20and%20t%20%22Gauge%20invariant%20cosmological%20perturbations%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts)); Kodama and Sasaki's review is Prog. Theor. Phys. Suppl. 78, 1–166 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1143/PTPS.78.1)); the Mukhanov–Feldman–Brandenberger review is Phys. Rep. 215, 203–333 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0370-1573%2892%2990044-Z)). Mészáros described frozen growth in 1974 ([Wikipedia: Mészáros effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9sz%C3%A1ros_effect)); Sasaki and Stewart gave the $\delta N$ formula in 1995 ([Sasaki & Stewart](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9507001)); Carrasco, Hertzberg and Senatore introduced the EFT of LSS in 2012 ([CHS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.2926)).

### Connections
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): the homogeneous background being perturbed.
- [Linearized Gravity](node:Linearized%20Gravity): the same first-order expansion, around FRW instead of Minkowski.
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations) and [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): linearized to relate metric and matter perturbations.
- [Newtonian Limit of General Relativity](node:Newtonian%20Limit%20of%20General%20Relativity): the sub-horizon regime.
- [Gauge Invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance): why $\zeta$, $\mathcal R$ and the Bardeen potentials are needed.
- [Boltzmann Equation](node:Boltzmann%20Equation): the photon and neutrino hierarchies.
- [Cosmic Inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation) and [Primordial Non-Gaussianity](node:Primordial%20Non-Gaussianity): the origin of $\mathcal R$ and its higher correlators.
- [CMB Acoustic Peaks](node:CMB%20Acoustic%20Peaks), [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background) and [Baryon Acoustic Oscillations](node:Baryon%20Acoustic%20Oscillations): linear-theory observables.
- [Matter Power Spectrum](node:Matter%20Power%20Spectrum), [Large-Scale Structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure) and [N-body Simulations](node:N-body%20Simulations): where perturbations go nonlinear.
- [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): the organizing principle of the EFT of LSS.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model) and [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): the standard growth history.
- [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves): tensor modes, and second-order induced waves.
- [Fluid Dynamics](node:Fluid%20Dynamics): continuity and Euler equations in an expanding background.

### Common pitfalls
- **Time variables and signs differ.** Ma and Bertschinger's overdots are conformal-time derivatives and $\delta T^0{}_0=-\delta\rho$ ([Ma & Bertschinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9506072)); Poisson's equation involves $\bar\rho\,\delta$, not the total density ([Bernardeau et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551)).
- **Gauge modes versus decaying modes.** In synchronous gauge two of the density solutions (the $A$ and $B$ modes) are gauge modes removable by a coordinate change; a separate physical mode becomes the decaying $\phi\propto\psi\propto\delta\propto(k\tau)^{-3}$ in conformal Newtonian gauge, where the gauge modes do not exist ([Ma & Bertschinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/9506072)).
- **$f\approx\Omega_m^{0.6}$ is not the ΛCDM value.** $\Omega_m^{3/5}$ holds for $\Omega_\Lambda=0$; with a cosmological constant $f\approx\Omega_m^{5/9}$ ([Bernardeau et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551)).
- **Lagrangian theory fails after shell crossing.** Beyond it the Zel'dovich mapping is no longer one-to-one, and with enough small-scale power Lagrangian PT breaks down at larger scales than Eulerian PT ([Bernardeau et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0112551)).
- **Hypersurface approaches and nonlinearity.** The gauge-invariant hypersurface approach does not deal well with GR nonlinearities; the 1+3 covariant approach can be nonlinear ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_perturbation_theory)).

### Open problems
> [!warning] Contested
> **Does backreaction of inhomogeneities matter?** Green and Wald argue that backreaction of inhomogeneities is irrelevant in cosmology; Buchert et al. reply that it is incorrect to infer that Green and Wald have proven a general result, calling the proof of their trace-free theorem physically unjustified and many of their arguments coordinate-dependent ([Buchert et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.07800)), and Green and Wald respond to these criticisms ([Green & Wald](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06452)).

- **Gauge dependence of induced gravitational waves.** At second order scalar perturbations source tensor modes, and these are gauge-ambiguous through mode mixing; Domènech's review calls the problem well understood "although the gauge issue persists in the strictest sense," and says that whether the infrared slope $\propto k^{3-2|b|}$ it derives (with $b$ set by the expansion history) is unique to induced waves "is something yet to explore" ([Domènech](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2109.01398)).
- **Higher-loop EFT predictions.** The Snowmass white paper states that the state-of-the-art EFT of LSS calculations "must be extended to higher loop orders" to use more modes, and its table of available calculations has gaps such as the biased-tracer trispectrum ([Snowmass EFT white paper](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.08232)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cosmological perturbation theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_perturbation_theory): Newtonian, gauge-invariant and 1+3 covariant approaches.
- **Learn:** [Baumann, TASI Lectures on Inflation](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.5424): SVT split, gauge-invariant variables, Mukhanov–Sasaki equation.
- **Learn:** [Hu & Dodelson, CMB Anisotropies](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0110414): linear theory applied to the CMB.
- **Primary:** [Bardeen, Gauge-invariant cosmological perturbations (1980)](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20Bardeen%20and%20t%20%22Gauge%20invariant%20cosmological%20perturbations%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts): the gauge-invariant formalism.
- **Primary:** [Ma & Bertschinger](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9506072): Einstein–Boltzmann equations in synchronous and conformal Newtonian gauges.
- **Primary:** [Carrasco, Hertzberg & Senatore](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.2926): the founding EFT of LSS paper.
- **Primary:** [Sasaki & Stewart](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9507001): the $\delta N$ formula.
- **Further reading:** [Bernardeau et al., review, Phys. Rep. 367 (2002)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0112551) and [Malik & Wands, review, Phys. Rep. 475 (2009)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.4944): nonlinear PT and gauge-invariant perturbations.
- **Further reading:** [Dodelson, Modern Cosmology; Mukhanov, Physical Foundations of Cosmology (Open Library)](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=isbn:9780521563987+OR+isbn:9780128159484&fields=title,author_name,publisher,first_publish_year,isbn): the standard textbooks.
references.Cross-Entropy Loss:
## Reference
### Overview
The cross-entropy of a distribution $q$ relative to a distribution $p$ on the same events is $H(p,q)=-\mathbb{E}_p[\log q]$. In coding terms it is the average number of bits needed to identify an event drawn from $p$ when the code is optimized for $q$ instead. It splits as the entropy of $p$ plus the Kullback–Leibler divergence from $p$ to $q$, so for fixed $p$, minimizing cross-entropy in $q$ is the same as minimizing KL divergence; the terms "log loss" and "cross-entropy loss" are used interchangeably. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy))

As a training loss, cross-entropy compares a model's predicted distribution with the observed label. For a classifier with scores $f_j$ and a softmax output, the per-example loss is the negative log of the probability assigned to the correct class. Minimizing it is maximum likelihood estimation, and adding an $L^2$ penalty corresponds to MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior on the weights. ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/linear-classify/)) For $N$ observations, the log-likelihood of a model $q_\theta$ equals $-N$ times the cross-entropy between the observed frequencies and $q_\theta$, so maximizing likelihood amounts to minimizing cross-entropy. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy)) In language modelling, the exponential of the held-out cross-entropy is the perplexity. ([Wikipedia: Perplexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity))

In statistics the same loss is the logarithmic scoring rule $\mathrm{LogS}(p,\omega)=\log p(\omega)$ (as a reward), proposed by Good in 1952. It is strictly proper: a forecaster maximizes the expected score only by reporting the true distribution. ([Gneiting and Raftery 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf)) In classification theory, binary cross-entropy (logistic loss) is one of the convex surrogates for the 0-1 loss whose consistency is governed by the classification-calibration theory of Bartlett, Jordan and McAuliffe. ([Bartlett, Jordan and McAuliffe, tech. report](https://statistics.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/tech-reports/638.pdf))

### Formal definition
For discrete distributions,
$$H(p,q)=-\sum_x p(x)\log q(x),$$
and for distributions with densities $P,Q$ with respect to a reference measure, $H(p,q)=-\int P(x)\log Q(x)\,dx$. In both cases
$$H(p,q)=H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,q).$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy))

**Binary cross-entropy (log loss).** For labels $y_i\in\{0,1\}$ and predictions $\hat y_i=\sigma(w\cdot x_i)=1/(1+e^{-w\cdot x_i})$,
$$J(w)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\big[y_i\log\hat y_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-\hat y_i)\big].$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy))

**Softmax cross-entropy.** For class scores (logits) $f=(f_1,\dots,f_K)$ and true class $y_i$,
$$L_i=-\log\frac{e^{f_{y_i}}}{\sum_j e^{f_j}}=-f_{y_i}+\log\sum_j e^{f_j}.$$
The target is a one-hot distribution with zero entropy, so here cross-entropy equals the KL divergence from target to prediction. ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/linear-classify/))

**Perplexity.** The perplexity of a distribution is $2^{H(p)}$. The perplexity of a model $q$ on a test sample $x_1,\dots,x_N$ is
$$b^{-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\log_b q(x_i)}=\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^N q(x_i)\Bigr)^{-1/N},$$
usually with $b=2$; the exponent is the cross-entropy $H(\tilde p,q)$ of $q$ relative to the empirical distribution $\tilde p$ of the test sample, so perplexity is minimized at $q=\tilde p$. Per-word perplexity of a language model normalizes by the number of words $N$ in the corpus. ([Wikipedia: Perplexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity))

**Scoring-rule form.** Write $S(P,Q)=\int S(P,\omega)\,dQ(\omega)$ for the expected score under $Q$ of the forecast $P$. A scoring rule is proper relative to a class $\mathcal P$ if $S(Q,Q)\ge S(P,Q)$ for all $P,Q\in\mathcal P$, and strictly proper if equality holds only when $P=Q$. The logarithmic score is $\mathrm{LogS}(p,\omega)=\log p(\omega)$, and cross-entropy loss is its negative. ([Gneiting and Raftery 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf))

**Classification calibration.** For a margin loss $\varphi$ and $\eta\in[0,1]$, let $C_\eta(\alpha)=\eta\varphi(\alpha)+(1-\eta)\varphi(-\alpha)$, $H(\eta)=\inf_\alpha C_\eta(\alpha)$ and $H^-(\eta)=\inf_{\alpha(2\eta-1)\le0}C_\eta(\alpha)$. Then $\varphi$ is *classification-calibrated* if $H^-(\eta)>H(\eta)$ for every $\eta\ne1/2$: restricting the score to the wrong sign strictly increases the optimal conditional $\varphi$-risk. ([Bartlett, Jordan and McAuliffe](https://statistics.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/tech-reports/638.pdf))

### Key results
- **Gibbs' inequality and the minimizer.** For fixed $p$, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\ge0$ with equality iff $q=p$. Hence $H(p,q)\ge H(p)$, with the minimum $H(p)$ attained exactly at $q=p$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy))
- **Equivalence with maximum likelihood.** For i.i.d. data $x_1,\dots,x_N$ and a model $q_\theta$, $\log L(\theta;x)=-N\,H(p,q_\theta)$, where $p(x)$ is the empirical frequency $\#x/N$. So maximizing likelihood over $\theta$ is minimizing cross-entropy. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy))
- **Strict propriety and Bernardo's characterization.** The logarithmic score is strictly proper relative to the class $\mathcal L_1$ of probability measures dominated by the reference measure $\mu$. Its expected-score function is negative Shannon entropy and its divergence is the Kullback–Leibler divergence. For categorical forecasts it is the McCarthy–Savage rule $S(p,i)=G(p)-\langle G'(p),p\rangle+G'_i(p)$ generated by $G(p)=\sum_j p_j\log p_j$. Under regularity conditions, Bernardo (1979) showed that every proper *local* scoring rule (one depending on the forecast density only through its value at the realized outcome) is equivalent to the logarithmic score. ([Gneiting and Raftery 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf))
- **Gradients.** For the summed binary loss $L(w)$ with $\hat y=\sigma(Xw)$, $\nabla_wL(w)=X^\top(\hat y-y)$, the same form up to a constant factor as the squared-error gradient for linear regression. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy)) In the multiclass case, the derivative of softmax cross-entropy with respect to the logit $o_j$ is $\mathrm{softmax}(o)_j-y_j$, the predicted probability minus the one-hot label. ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_linear-classification/softmax-regression.html))
- **Consistency of convex surrogates (Bartlett–Jordan–McAuliffe).** Let $R$ be the 0-1 risk with Bayes risk $R^*$, $R_\varphi$ the $\varphi$-risk with infimum $R_\varphi^*$, and $\psi$ the convex hull of $\tilde\psi(\theta)=H^-\bigl(\tfrac{1+\theta}2\bigr)-H\bigl(\tfrac{1+\theta}2\bigr)$. For any nonnegative $\varphi$, measurable $f$ and distribution, $\psi(R(f)-R^*)\le R_\varphi(f)-R_\varphi^*$; and $\varphi$ is classification-calibrated iff $R_\varphi(f_i)\to R_\varphi^*$ implies $R(f_i)\to R^*$ for every sequence $f_i$ and every distribution. If $\varphi$ is convex, it is classification-calibrated iff it is differentiable at $0$ with $\varphi'(0)<0$ (Theorem 6). The logistic loss $\varphi(\alpha)=\log(1+e^{-\alpha})$ is convex with $\varphi'(0)=-1/2$, so it qualifies. The paper describes its theorem as holding under weaker conditions than Zhang's earlier comparison theorem for convex losses. ([Bartlett, Jordan and McAuliffe](https://statistics.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/tech-reports/638.pdf))
- **Implicit bias on separable data (Soudry et al.).** Assume the data are linearly separable; the loss $\ell$ is positive, differentiable, $\beta$-smooth and monotonically decreasing to zero; and $-\ell'$ has a *tight exponential tail*, i.e. there are positive constants with $c(1-e^{-\mu_-u})e^{-au}\le-\ell'(u)\le c(1+e^{-\mu_+u})e^{-au}$ for large $u$ (logistic and exponential losses qualify). Then for any step size $\eta<2\beta^{-1}\sigma_{\max}^{-2}(X)$ and any initialization, gradient descent on the unregularized empirical loss of a homogeneous linear predictor satisfies $w(t)=\hat w\log t+\rho(t)$ with $\|\rho(t)\|=O(\log\log t)$, where $\hat w$ is the hard-margin SVM solution, so $w(t)/\|w(t)\|\to\hat w/\|\hat w\|$. ([Soudry et al., JMLR 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume19/18-188/18-188.pdf)) The exponential tail is needed: for convex, strictly decreasing losses whose risk does not attain its infimum, the gradient-descent path and the regularization path converge to the same direction whenever either converges to a direction; for exponentially tailed losses that direction is necessarily the maximum-margin one, while polynomially tailed losses may converge to a direction with a poor margin. ([Ji, Dudík, Schapire and Telgarsky 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11226))

### Examples
- **Numerically stable softmax.** Since $e^{f_{y}}/\sum_je^{f_j}$ is unchanged when every score is shifted by a constant, implementations subtract $\max_jf_j$ before exponentiating so that the largest score becomes $0$. ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/linear-classify/))
- **Softmax versus hinge loss.** A multiclass SVM is satisfied once the margin is met, so it treats scores $[10,-100,-100]$ and $[10,9,9]$ alike. Softmax cross-entropy accumulates much higher loss on $[10,9,9]$ and is never fully satisfied. ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/linear-classify/))
- **Label smoothing.** Training uses the cross-entropy between the network outputs $p_k$ and modified targets $y_k^{LS}=y_k(1-\alpha)+\alpha/K$, a mixture of the one-hot target with the uniform distribution over $K$ classes; it was introduced by Szegedy et al. Müller, Kornblith and Hinton find that it implicitly calibrates models but makes a teacher trained with it worse for knowledge distillation, because same-class penultimate-layer representations collapse into tight clusters. ([Müller et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.02629))
- **Focal loss.** Writing $p_t=p$ if $y=1$ and $1-p$ otherwise, binary cross-entropy is $\mathrm{CE}(p_t)=-\log p_t$; focal loss is $\mathrm{FL}(p_t)=-(1-p_t)^\gamma\log p_t$ with $\gamma\ge0$ ($\gamma=0$ recovers CE), which down-weights well-classified examples to counter extreme foreground-background imbalance in dense object detection. The authors found $\gamma=2$ to work best; at $p_t=0.9$ the loss is then $100\times$ lower than CE. ([Lin et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.02002))
- **Language-model evaluation.** When $p$ is unknown, $H(T,q)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\log_2q(x_i)$ over a test set $T$ is a Monte Carlo estimate of the cross-entropy, with the test set treated as samples from $p$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy)) Its base-2 exponential is the model's perplexity. ([Wikipedia: Perplexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity))

### History
The logarithmic score dates back at least to Good (1952). It has since gone by other names, including the predictive deviance and the ignorance score; the term "proper" was apparently coined by Winkler and Murphy (1968). ([Gneiting and Raftery 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf)) The coding interpretation rests on the Kraft–McMillan theorem: code lengths $\ell_i$ define an implicit distribution $q(x_i)=2^{-\ell_i}$, so cross-entropy is the expected message length under $p$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy)) Hui and Belkin note that the conceptual or historical reasons for the current prevalence of cross-entropy in neural-network training are not entirely clear. ([Hui and Belkin, arXiv:2006.07322](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.07322))

### Connections
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence): cross-entropy minus entropy; the two have the same minimizer in $q$.
- [Information Theory](node:Information%20Theory): entropy, coding length, and the Kraft–McMillan interpretation.
- [Maximum Likelihood Estimation](node:Maximum%20Likelihood%20Estimation): minimizing empirical cross-entropy is maximizing likelihood.
- [Proper Scoring Rules](node:Proper%20Scoring%20Rules): cross-entropy is the negative logarithmic score, the unique proper local rule.
- [Logistic Regression](node:Logistic%20Regression): the binary cross-entropy model with gradient $X^\top(\hat y-y)$.
- [Language Modeling](node:Language%20Modeling): next-token cross-entropy is the training loss; perplexity is its exponential.
- [Language Model Pretraining Objectives](node:Language%20Model%20Pretraining%20Objectives): objectives built on token-level cross-entropy.
- [Knowledge Distillation](node:Knowledge%20Distillation): trains on a teacher's soft targets with cross-entropy; label smoothing interacts badly with it.
- [Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent](node:Implicit%20Bias%20of%20Gradient%20Descent): max-margin limits of gradient descent on exponentially tailed losses.
- [Support Vector Machines](node:Support%20Vector%20Machines): the hinge-loss alternative and the max-margin limit.
- [Empirical Risk Minimization](node:Empirical%20Risk%20Minimization): cross-entropy as the surrogate risk being minimized.
- [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent): the optimizer whose behavior on logistic loss gives the max-margin limit.
- [Uncertainty Quantification](node:Uncertainty%20Quantification): calibration of probabilities trained with cross-entropy.

### Common pitfalls
- The two arguments play different roles: the expectation is taken over $p$, not $q$. Some authors redefine cross-entropy as $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)$, and the notation $H(p,q)$ is also used for joint entropy, a different quantity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy))
- "Softmax loss" is a misnomer: softmax is the squashing function and cross-entropy is the loss. ([CS231n](https://cs231n.github.io/linear-classify/))
- The logarithmic rule allows infinite scores (a forecast of probability $0$ for an event that occurs scores $-\infty$), and despite its popularity it has been criticized for this unboundedness. ([Gneiting and Raftery 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf))
- Minimizing a proper score does not guarantee calibrated deep networks in practice: modern networks are often poorly calibrated, with depth, width, weight decay, and batch normalization as contributing factors, and single-parameter temperature scaling fixes much of it post hoc. ([Guo et al., arXiv:1706.04599](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599))
- The max-margin limit is a property of the loss tail, not of "any decreasing loss": it requires an exponential tail, and polynomially tailed losses may converge to a poor-margin direction. ([Ji et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11226)) Even with an exponential tail the convergence in direction is only logarithmic in $t$, which the authors suggest explains why continuing to optimize cross-entropy after zero training error can still help. ([Soudry et al., arXiv:1710.10345](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10345))

### Open problems
- **Which training loss for classification.** Across architectures and datasets in NLP, speech recognition and vision, square loss performed comparably or better in most NLP and speech experiments, cross-entropy had a slight edge in vision, and square loss was less sensitive to the randomness of initialization. The authors find little compelling empirical or theoretical evidence for a clear-cut advantage of cross-entropy and write that new theoretical analyses and intuitions are needed to understand training-loss selection. ([Hui and Belkin, arXiv:2006.07322](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.07322); [full text](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.07322))
- **Optimal loss tails for implicit bias.** Soudry et al. report that Nacson et al. proved the exponential tail gives the optimal rate of directional convergence among tails with $\ell'(u)$ of the form $\exp(-u^\nu)$, $\nu>0.25$, and *conjectured*, from heuristic analysis, that the exponential tail is optimal among all possible tails. ([Soudry et al., JMLR 2018](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume19/18-188/18-188.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cross-entropy (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy): definitions, KL decomposition, maximum-likelihood link, and logistic loss.
- **Reference:** [Perplexity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity): perplexity as exponentiated cross-entropy.
- **Learn:** [CS231n, Linear classification (Softmax classifier)](https://cs231n.github.io/linear-classify/): softmax cross-entropy, its information-theoretic and probabilistic readings, and numerics.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, Softmax regression](https://d2l.ai/chapter_linear-classification/softmax-regression.html): loss, gradient, and information-theory view.
- **Primary:** [Gneiting and Raftery, Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation (JASA 2007)](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf): the log score among proper scoring rules.
- **Primary:** [Bartlett, Jordan and McAuliffe, Convexity, Classification, and Risk Bounds](https://statistics.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/tech-reports/638.pdf): classification calibration and the $\psi$-transform.
- **Primary:** [Soudry et al., The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data (JMLR 2018)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume19/18-188/18-188.pdf): max-margin limit under exponential tails.
- **Primary:** [Ji, Dudík, Schapire and Telgarsky, Gradient descent follows the regularization path for general losses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11226): role of the loss tail.
- **Primary:** [Hui and Belkin, Square Loss vs Cross-Entropy in Classification Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.07322): large empirical comparison of the two losses.
- **Further reading:** [Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016)](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/): deep-learning textbook for students and practitioners entering the field.
- **Further reading:** [Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed. (Wiley, 2006)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Elements+of+Information+Theory%2C+2nd+Edition-p-9780471241959): textbook covering entropy, data compression and source coding.
references.Cross-Sections of Higher-Dimensional Obj:
## Reference
### Overview
A cross section is the intersection of a solid with a plane, or, in $n$ dimensions, the intersection of an $n$-dimensional body with a hyperplane. If a four-dimensional ball passed through three-dimensional space, an observer there would see a 3-ball that grows to a maximum size and then shrinks. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_%28geometry%29)) This is the dimensional analogy of Abbott's 1884 *Flatland*, where a sphere moving through a plane appears to its inhabitants as a circle that grows and shrinks. ([Wikipedia: Flatland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flatland)) Banchoff's *Beyond the Third Dimension* applies the same idea one dimension up to the hyperball and the hypercube. ([Banchoff, Brown University](https://www.math.brown.edu/tbanchof/Beyond3d/chapter3/section03.html))

Beyond visualization, slicing is a basic tool of analysis and geometry. Cavalieri's principle and its generalization, Fubini's theorem, compute volumes by integrating the volumes of slices. ([Wikipedia: Cavalieri's principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalieri%27s_principle)) In convex geometry, Brunn's concavity principle controls how the volumes of parallel sections of a convex body vary, and it follows from the Brunn–Minkowski inequality. ([Wikipedia: Brunn–Minkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunn%E2%80%93Minkowski_theorem)) Sharp bounds for volumes of sections of the cube, simplex and $\ell_p$ balls form an active research area. ([Nayar & Tkocz, arXiv:2210.00885](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.00885))

Two further theories treat slicing systematically. The Radon transform records the integrals of a function over all hyperplanes and is the mathematical basis of computed tomography. ([Wikipedia: Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform)) Morse theory studies how the sublevel sets of a smooth function on a manifold change topology as the level passes critical values, which is the topological theory of a "slicing movie". ([Wikipedia: Morse theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_theory)) Geometric tomography, the recovery of a geometric object from its sections or projections, draws on convex and integral geometry. ([Gardner, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781107341029/type/book))

### Formal definition
For a set $S \subset \mathbb R^{n}$, a unit vector $\theta \in S^{n-1}$ and $t \in \mathbb R$, the section of $S$ by the affine hyperplane $H_{\theta,t} = \{x : \langle x,\theta\rangle = t\}$ is $S \cap H_{\theta,t}$; it is a central section when $t = 0$, i.e. $S \cap \theta^{\perp}$. The curve or surface where a hyperplane meets the boundary of a body is a plane section, and it bounds the cross section; for $z = f(x,y)$ the sections by $z = k$ are the contour lines. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_%28geometry%29))

The section function of a convex body $K$ in direction $\theta$ is $A_{K,\theta}(t) = \mathrm{Vol}_{n-1}(K \cap H_{\theta,t})$; Brunn's principle below concerns this function with $\theta = e_1$. ([Wikipedia: Brunn–Minkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunn%E2%80%93Minkowski_theorem))

The Radon transform of a function $f$ on $\mathbb R^n$ is the function on the space of hyperplanes
$$Rf(\alpha,s) = \int_{x\cdot\alpha = s} f(x)\,d\sigma(x), \qquad \alpha \in S^{n-1},\ s \in \mathbb R,$$
where $d\sigma$ is hypersurface measure. For $f = \mathbf 1_K$ it is exactly the section function of $K$. ([Wikipedia: Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform))

### Key results
- **Cavalieri and Fubini.** If two solids lie between two parallel planes and every parallel plane cuts both in sections of equal area, the solids have equal volume; this is a particular case of Fubini's theorem. ([Wikipedia: Cavalieri's principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalieri%27s_principle)) Fubini: if $X,Y$ are $\sigma$-finite measure spaces and $f$ is measurable on $X\times Y$ with $\int_{X\times Y}|f| < \infty$, then $\int_{X\times Y} f = \int_X\!\int_Y f\,dy\,dx = \int_Y\!\int_X f\,dx\,dy$; Tonelli gives the same for measurable $f \ge 0$ without integrability. ([Wikipedia: Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- **Ball volumes by slicing.** Each hyperplane section of an $n$-ball is an $(n-1)$-ball, so $V_n(R) = \int_{-R}^{R} V_{n-1}\big(\sqrt{R^2-x^2}\big)\,dx$, which yields $V_n(R) = \pi^{n/2}R^n/\Gamma(n/2+1)$. For fixed $R$ this tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$, and $V_n(1)$ is largest at $n = 5$. ([Wikipedia: Volume of an n-ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume_of_an_n-ball))
- **Brunn's concavity principle.** If $K \subset \mathbb R^n$ is a convex body and $K(x) = K \cap \{x_1 = x\}$, then $r(x) = \mathrm{Vol}_{n-1}(K(x))^{1/(n-1)}$ is concave on the set where $K(x) \neq \varnothing$. It follows from the Brunn–Minkowski inequality $\mu(A+B)^{1/n} \ge \mu(A)^{1/n} + \mu(B)^{1/n}$ (for nonempty compact $A,B\subset\mathbb R^n$) applied to $K(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \supseteq \lambda K(x) + (1-\lambda)K(y)$. For convex sets of positive measure, equality in Brunn–Minkowski forces $A$ and $B$ to be homothetic. ([Wikipedia: Brunn–Minkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunn%E2%80%93Minkowski_theorem))
- **Cube slicing (Hadwiger, Hensley, Ball).** Let $Q_n = [-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^n$. For every unit vector $a$, $1 \le \mathrm{Vol}_{n-1}(Q_n \cap a^{\perp}) \le \sqrt 2$. The lower bound (Hadwiger; Hensley) has equality only for $a = \pm e_j$; Ball's upper bound has equality iff $a = (\pm e_i \pm e_j)/\sqrt2$ for some $i<j$, confirming Hensley's conjecture. For a $k$-dimensional subspace $H$, Ball also proved $\mathrm{Vol}_k(Q_n \cap H) \le \min\{(n/k)^{k/2}, 2^{(n-k)/2}\}$, the first bound sharp when $k \mid n$ and the second when $k \ge n/2$. ([Nayar & Tkocz, arXiv:2210.00885](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.00885))
- **Busemann–Petty problem.** For origin-symmetric convex bodies $K,T \subset \mathbb R^n$ with $\mathrm{Vol}_{n-1}(K\cap A) \le \mathrm{Vol}_{n-1}(T\cap A)$ for every hyperplane $A$ through the origin, must $\mathrm{Vol}_n(K) \le \mathrm{Vol}_n(T)$? Posed in 1956, it has answer yes for $n \le 4$ and no for $n \ge 5$. Lutwak showed that the answer is positive in a given dimension iff every symmetric convex body there is an intersection body; Larman–Rogers (1975) gave the first counterexamples ($n \ge 12$), Gardner (1994) settled $n=3$, Zhang (1999) $n = 4$, and Gardner, Koldobsky and Schlumprecht (1999) gave a uniform solution. ([Wikipedia: Busemann–Petty problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busemann%E2%80%93Petty_problem))
- **Bourgain's slicing problem (resolved).** There is a universal constant $c>0$ such that every convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^n$ of volume one has a hyperplane $H$ with $\mathrm{Vol}_{n-1}(K\cap H) > c$. Klartag and Lehec completed the proof in a December 2024 preprint, combining Milman's $M$-ellipsoids, stochastic localization with a bound of Guan, and Eldan–Mikulincer stability for the Shannon–Stam inequality. ([Klartag & Lehec, arXiv:2412.15044](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15044))
- **Radon inversion and projection-slice theorem.** The one-dimensional Fourier transform of $s \mapsto Rf(\alpha,s)$ equals the Fourier transform of $f$ along the line in direction $\alpha$: $\hat f(r\alpha) = \int Rf(\alpha,s)e^{-2\pi i s r}\,ds$. Hence $f$ is determined by its hyperplane integrals, with inversion $c_n f = (-\Delta)^{(n-1)/2}R^*Rf$; in the plane this is filtered back-projection with the ramp filter $\hat h(k) = |k|$. If $f$ vanishes outside the ball of radius $A$, then $Rf(\alpha,s) = 0$ for $|s|>A$. ([Wikipedia: Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform))
- **Morse theory of level sets.** Let $f$ be smooth on a manifold $M$ and $M^a = f^{-1}(-\infty,a]$. If $f^{-1}[a,b]$ is compact and contains no critical points, then $M^a$ and $M^b$ are diffeomorphic and $M^b$ deformation retracts onto $M^a$. Passing a non-degenerate critical point of index $\gamma$ changes $M^a$ up to homotopy by attaching a $\gamma$-cell. For a Morse function on a closed manifold, the number $C_\gamma$ of index-$\gamma$ critical points satisfies the Morse inequalities $C_\gamma - C_{\gamma-1} + \dots \pm C_0 \ge b_\gamma - b_{\gamma-1} + \dots \pm b_0$, in particular $C_\gamma \ge b_\gamma$. ([Wikipedia: Morse theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_theory))

### Examples
- **Cube in 3D.** Planes perpendicular to the line joining opposite face centres give squares; planes perpendicular to a space diagonal give a point, a triangle, or a hexagon. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_%28geometry%29))
- **Tesseract, cell first.** The hypercube entering cube first shows an ordinary cube for a while. Square first, the slices are rectangular prisms on a fixed square base whose other side grows to the square's diagonal and shrinks back, the 16 vertices appearing in groups 4, 8, 4. Edge first, an edge expands to a triangular prism, becomes a hexagonal prism, reverts, and shrinks back to an edge, vertices in groups 2, 6, 6, 2. ([Banchoff, Brown University](https://www.math.brown.edu/tbanchof/Beyond3d/chapter3/section03.html))
- **Tesseract, vertex first.** A vertex grows into a tetrahedron, which is then truncated; three-eighths of the way through the slice has four equilateral triangles and four regular hexagons as faces, a semi-regular solid known to Archimedes (the truncated tetrahedron). Halfway, it is a regular octahedron whose vertices are six vertices of the hypercube, and the second half reverses the sequence. ([Banchoff, Brown University](https://www.math.brown.edu/tbanchof/Beyond3d/chapter3/section03.html))
- **Coordinates and Pascal's triangle.** Slicing $[0,1]^4$ perpendicular to the diagonal from $(0,0,0,0)$ to $(1,1,1,1)$, the slice of vertices with coordinate sum $k$ contains $\binom4k$ vertices: a point, a tetrahedron, the octahedron with vertices such as $(1,1,0,0)$, a tetrahedron, a point. For the $n$-cube the counts are the $n$th row of Pascal's triangle. ([Banchoff, Brown University](https://www.math.brown.edu/tbanchof/Beyond3d/chapter8/section04.html))
- **Torus by height.** For the height function on an upright torus, with critical points of index 0, 1, 1, 2, the sublevel sets are successively empty, a disk, a cylinder, a torus minus a disk, and the torus. ([Wikipedia: Morse theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_theory))
- **Projection is not slicing.** The tesseract's cell-first parallel projection into 3-space has a cubical envelope and its vertex-first projection a rhombic dodecahedral one; these are shadows, not slices. ([Wikipedia: Tesseract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesseract))

### History
Archimedes, in the 3rd century BC, found the volume of a sphere by a method resembling Cavalieri's principle; Cavalieri published his method of indivisibles in 1635 and 1647. ([Wikipedia: Cavalieri's principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalieri%27s_principle)) Fubini proved his general theorem in 1907, and Tonelli the non-negative version in 1909. ([Wikipedia: Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem)) Brunn proved the convex case of his inequality in his 1887 Munich dissertation, Minkowski published it in 1896, and Lyusternik extended it to compact non-convex sets in 1935. ([Wikipedia: Brunn–Minkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunn%E2%80%93Minkowski_theorem)) Radon introduced his transform and its inversion in 1917. ([Wikipedia: Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform))

*Flatland* was published in London by Seeley & Co. in 1884. ([Wikipedia: Flatland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flatland)) The word "tesseract" goes back to Charles Howard Hinton's 1888 *A New Era of Thought* (spelled "tessaract" there). ([Wikipedia: Tesseract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesseract)) Alicia Boole Stott, introduced to four-dimensional geometry at about eighteen through Hinton's wooden cubes, produced three-dimensional central cross-sections of all six regular 4-polytopes by Euclidean constructions, published "On certain series of sections of the regular four-dimensional hypersolids" in 1900, worked with Schoute for almost twenty years, and received an honorary doctorate from Groningen in 1914. ([MacTutor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Stott/)) The Busemann–Petty problem dates from 1956 and was completely answered in 1999. ([Wikipedia: Busemann–Petty problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busemann%E2%80%93Petty_problem))

### Connections
- [Higher-Dimensional Euclidean Geometry](node:Higher-Dimensional%20Euclidean%20Geometry): hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^n$ are the cutting sets.
- [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere) and [n-Ball](node:n-Ball): slices of balls are balls, giving the volume recursion.
- [Polytopes](node:Polytopes), [Hypercubes and Cross-Polytopes](node:Hypercubes%20and%20Cross-Polytopes), [Regular Four-Dimensional Polytopes](node:Regular%20Four-Dimensional%20Polytopes): slicing sequences and sharp section bounds.
- [Tesseract](node:Tesseract): the 4-cube whose slicing sequences are worked out above.
- [Visualizing Higher Dimensions](node:Visualizing%20Higher%20Dimensions): slicing, projection and unfolding as visualization tools.
- [Fubini's Theorem](node:Fubini's%20Theorem), [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus), [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): volumes from slices.
- [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function): appears in the $n$-ball volume.
- [Brunn–Minkowski Inequality](node:Brunn–Minkowski%20Inequality) and [Isoperimetric Inequalities](node:Isoperimetric%20Inequalities): concavity of section volumes.
- [Concentration of Measure](node:Concentration%20of%20Measure): another high-dimensional phenomenon of convex bodies alongside slicing bounds.
- [Radon Transform](node:Radon%20Transform): hyperplane integrals as the analytic theory of sections.
- [Morse Functions and Handle Decompositions](node:Morse%20Functions%20and%20Handle%20Decompositions): level sets as the topological theory of slicing.
- [Submanifolds and Embeddings](node:Submanifolds%20and%20Embeddings) and [Extrinsic Curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature): curved slices in curved ambient spaces.
- [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology): a brane as a slice to which matter is confined.
- Maps: [MSC 51 - Geometry](node:MSC%2051%20-%20Geometry), [MSC 52 - Convex and discrete geometry](node:MSC%2052%20-%20Convex%20and%20discrete%20geometry)

### Common pitfalls
- **Slices depend on orientation.** A hyperball gives the same sequence however it is rotated, whereas the hypercube's slices depend on the direction of passage, so "the" cross-section of a tesseract needs a direction. ([Banchoff, Brown University](https://www.math.brown.edu/tbanchof/Beyond3d/chapter3/section03.html))
- **Section versus projection.** A cross section is an intersection with a hyperplane, while "cross-sectional area" seen from a viewing angle is the area of the orthographic projection. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_%28geometry%29))
- **Larger sections do not imply larger volume.** By the Busemann–Petty answer, in dimension $n\ge5$ a symmetric convex body can have every central section smaller than another's and still have larger volume. ([Wikipedia: Busemann–Petty problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busemann%E2%80%93Petty_problem))
- **Normalization matters.** For the unit-radius ball, $V_n(1)\to0$, so its central sections, which are $(n-1)$-balls of radius 1, also have volume tending to $0$ ([Wikipedia: Volume of an n-ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume_of_an_n-ball)); the unit-volume cube's central sections stay between $1$ and $\sqrt2$ in every dimension. ([Nayar & Tkocz, arXiv:2210.00885](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.00885)) Comparing slice volumes of different bodies is meaningful only at a common normalization.

### Open problems
- **Maximal lower-dimensional sections of the cube.** Nayar and Tkocz state as a conjecture that, for each $k$, the maximal $k$-dimensional central section of $Q_n$ is attained at an explicit subspace $H^*$; they record it as confirmed only for planar sections ($k=2$). ([Nayar & Tkocz, arXiv:2210.00885](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.00885))
- **Non-central sections of the cube.** A conjecture attributed to V. Milman in the same survey asks for the extremal hyperplane sections of the cube at a fixed distance $t$ from the origin, predicted to occur in diagonal directions with a suitable number of equal non-zero coordinates. ([Nayar & Tkocz, arXiv:2210.00885](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.00885))
- **Sections of $\ell_p$ balls.** The survey states that sharp upper bounds for hyperplane sections of $\ell_p$ balls with $2<p<\infty$ remain open, and conjectures a single threshold $p_0(n)$ at which the maximiser switches from the main diagonal direction to $(1,1,0,\dots,0)$. ([Nayar & Tkocz, arXiv:2210.00885](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.00885))
- Gardner's monograph on geometric tomography collects 66 unsolved problems on recovering bodies from sections and projections. ([Gardner, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781107341029/type/book))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cross section (geometry) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_%28geometry%29): definition, 3D examples, higher-dimensional analogue.
- **Reference:** [Brunn–Minkowski theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunn%E2%80%93Minkowski_theorem): the inequality and Brunn's concavity of sections.
- **Learn:** [Banchoff, Beyond the Third Dimension: Slicing the Hypercube (Brown University)](https://www.math.brown.edu/tbanchof/Beyond3d/chapter3/section03.html): illustrated slicing sequences in every orientation.
- **Learn:** [Banchoff: Coordinates for Hypercube Slices](https://www.math.brown.edu/tbanchof/Beyond3d/chapter8/section04.html): coordinate-sum slices and Pascal's triangle.
- **Primary:** [Nayar & Tkocz, Extremal sections and projections of certain convex bodies: a survey (arXiv:2210.00885)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.00885): cube slicing, simplex and $\ell_p$ ball sections, open conjectures.
- **Primary:** [Klartag & Lehec, Affirmative Resolution of Bourgain's Slicing Problem (arXiv:2412.15044)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15044): the resolution of the slicing problem.
- **Primary:** [Abbott, Flatland (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/201): the original dimensional analogy.
- **Further reading:** [Gardner, Geometric Tomography, 2nd ed. (Cambridge University Press)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781107341029/type/book): sections, projections and intersection bodies, with unsolved problems.
references.Curvature Tensors:
## Reference
### Overview
The Riemann curvature tensor measures the failure of second covariant derivatives to commute for the Levi-Civita connection of a (pseudo-)Riemannian metric; it is the obstruction to the manifold being locally isometric to Euclidean space, since a Riemannian manifold has zero curvature if and only if it is locally isometric to $\mathbb R^n$. Geometrically, parallel transport of a vector around a small loop returns a vector that deviates from the original, and the curvature tensor is the infinitesimal form of this non-holonomy. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor)) In the language of connections, the Riemann curvature is simply the curvature $F_{\nabla_g}$ of the Levi-Civita connection $\nabla_g$. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Riemann+curvature))

Contractions produce the other standard curvature tensors. The Ricci tensor is a symmetric rank-two trace of the Riemann tensor, and its direction-wise value is an average of sectional curvatures; a further trace gives the scalar curvature. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature)) The Weyl tensor is the trace-free remainder, and the Riemann tensor splits orthogonally into Weyl, trace-free Ricci, and scalar parts. ([Wikipedia: Ricci decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_decomposition))

Curvature bounds are the main input of global Riemannian geometry. Comparison theorems such as Rauch, Toponogov and Bishop–Gromov compare a manifold with a model space of constant curvature, and they lead to Myers's diameter bound, the Cheeger–Gromoll splitting theorem, sphere theorems and Gromov's Betti number bound. ([Wikipedia: Comparison theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_theorem)) ([Wilking, arXiv:0707.3091](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3091)) In physics, the Ricci tensor enters the Einstein field equations through the Einstein tensor. ([Wikipedia: Einstein tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_tensor))

### Formal definition
Let $(M,g)$ be a (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$. The Riemann curvature tensor is
$$R(X,Y)Z = \nabla_X\nabla_Y Z - \nabla_Y\nabla_X Z - \nabla_{[X,Y]}Z, \qquad R(X,Y) = [\nabla_X,\nabla_Y] - \nabla_{[X,Y]},$$
a $(1,3)$-tensor field; some authors use the opposite sign. In coordinates,
$$R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu\Gamma^\rho{}_{\nu\sigma} - \partial_\nu\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\sigma} + \Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\lambda}\Gamma^\lambda{}_{\nu\sigma} - \Gamma^\rho{}_{\nu\lambda}\Gamma^\lambda{}_{\mu\sigma}.$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor))

For a 2-plane $\sigma \subset T_pM$ spanned by $u,v$, the sectional curvature is $K(\sigma) = \langle R(u,v)v,u\rangle/|u\wedge v|^2$, and the sectional curvatures determine $R$ completely. The curvature operator $Q:\Lambda^2 T_pM \to \Lambda^2T_pM$ is defined by $\langle Q(u\wedge v), w\wedge z\rangle = \langle R(u,v)z,w\rangle$. ([Wikipedia: Curvature of Riemannian manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature_of_Riemannian_manifolds))

The Ricci tensor is the trace $\mathrm{Ric}(Y,Z) = \operatorname{tr}(X\mapsto R(X,Y)Z)$; sources disagree on the sign of the Riemann tensor but not of the Ricci tensor. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature)) The scalar curvature is $\mathrm{Scal} = g^{ij}R_{ij}$, the sum of sectional curvatures over pairs from an orthonormal frame; it needs the metric to take the trace. ([Wikipedia: Scalar curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_curvature)) The Einstein tensor is $G_{\mu\nu} = R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12 R g_{\mu\nu}$, with trace $(1-n/2)R$. ([Wikipedia: Einstein tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_tensor))

**Ricci decomposition.** With the trace-free Ricci tensor $Z_{jk} = R_{jk} - \tfrac{R}{n}g_{jk}$, the curvature splits as $R_{ijkl} = S_{ijkl} + E_{ijkl} + W_{ijkl}$, where
$$S_{ijkl} = \frac{R}{n(n-1)}\,(g_{il}g_{jk} - g_{ik}g_{jl}), \qquad E_{ijkl} = \frac{1}{n-2}\,(Z_{il}g_{jk} - Z_{jl}g_{ik} - Z_{ik}g_{jl} + Z_{jk}g_{il}),$$
and $W$ is the Weyl part; $S$ lies in $\mathbb R\, g\owedge g$ and $E$ in $g\owedge S^2_0$ for the Kulkarni–Nomizu product $\owedge$. The three pieces are mutually orthogonal, so $|\mathrm{Rm}|^2 = |S|^2+|E|^2+|W|^2$, and for $n\ge4$ they are the unique irreducible pieces. These signs use the less common Ricci convention; the standard convention flips the signs of $\mathrm{Ric}$ and $R$. ([Wikipedia: Ricci decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_decomposition)) Equivalently $W = \mathrm{Rm} - P\owedge g$ with $P$ the Schouten tensor. ([Wikipedia: Weyl tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_tensor))

### Key results
- **Algebraic symmetries.** $R_{abcd} = -R_{bacd} = -R_{abdc}$, $R_{abcd} = R_{cdab}$, and the first Bianchi identity $R_{a[bcd]} = 0$; these identities characterize the possible curvature tensors at a point, which form a space of dimension $n^2(n^2-1)/12$ (20 when $n = 4$). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor))
- **Contracted Bianchi identity.** For the Levi-Civita connection, $\operatorname{div}\mathrm{Ric} = \tfrac12\,d\,\mathrm{Scal}$, equivalently $\nabla^\mu G_{\mu\nu} = 0$. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature)) ([Wikipedia: Einstein tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_tensor)) With non-zero torsion, the Bianchi identities acquire torsion terms. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor))
- **[Geodesic deviation](node:Geodesic%20Deviation).** For a family of geodesics with tangent $T$ and deviation vector $X$, $\frac{D^2X^\mu}{d\tau^2} = R^\mu{}_{\nu\rho\sigma}T^\nu T^\rho X^\sigma$; in the Newtonian limit the deviation acceleration of nearby slowly moving particles becomes $A_i = -\frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial x^i\partial x^j}X^j$, so the relevant Riemann components reduce to the tidal tensor of the Newtonian potential (their overall sign depends on the index convention). ([Wikipedia: Geodesic deviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic_deviation))
- **Weyl tensor and conformal flatness.** The $(1,3)$ Weyl tensor $C^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}$ is unchanged under a conformal change $g\mapsto fg$, $f>0$. It vanishes identically in dimensions 2 and 3. Vanishing Weyl tensor is necessary for conformal flatness in every dimension and sufficient for $n\ge4$; for $n=3$ the criterion is vanishing of the Cotton tensor. ([Wikipedia: Weyl tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_tensor))
- **Ricci determines Riemann only in low dimension.** Ricci curvature determines the full curvature tensor exactly in dimensions 2 and 3; in higher dimension the Weyl part is extra information. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature))
- **Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks.** For connected complete Riemannian manifolds $M,N$ and a linear isometry $I:T_xM\to T_yN$, the theorem builds a map $F$ by sending broken geodesics from $x$ to broken geodesics from $y$, using parallel transport along them, and requires that these transported isometries carry the curvature of $M$ to that of $N$. In the locally symmetric case one point suffices: if $M,N$ are connected, complete and locally symmetric, $M$ is simply connected, and $I(R(X,Y)Z) = \bar R(IX,IY)IZ$, then there is a locally isometric covering $F:M\to N$ with $F(x)=y$ and $dF_x = I$. As an application, a simply connected complete manifold of constant sectional curvature $+1$, $0$, $-1$ is isometric to $S^n$, $\mathbb R^n$, or $\mathbb H^n$. ([Wikipedia: Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%E2%80%93Ambrose%E2%80%93Hicks_theorem))
- **Rauch comparison (1951).** Let $\gamma,\tilde\gamma:[0,T]$ be unit-speed geodesics in $M,\tilde M$, with $\tilde\gamma(0)$ having no conjugate points along $\tilde\gamma$, and $J,\tilde J$ normal Jacobi fields with $J(0)=\tilde J(0)=0$ and $|D_tJ(0)| = |D_t\tilde J(0)|$. If every sectional curvature of planes containing $\dot\gamma(t)$ is at most every sectional curvature of planes containing $\dot{\tilde\gamma}(t)$, then $|J(t)|\ge|\tilde J(t)|$ on $[0,T]$. ([Wikipedia: Rauch comparison theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rauch_comparison_theorem))
- **Toponogov's theorem.** If $M$ is complete with sectional curvature $\ge\delta$, $pqr$ is a geodesic triangle with $pq$ minimal (and $|pr| < \pi/\sqrt\delta$ if $\delta>0$), and $p'q'r'$ is the hinge in the model space $M_\delta$ with the same two sides at $p$ and the same angle, then $d(q,r)\le d(q',r')$. ([Wikipedia: Toponogov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toponogov%27s_theorem))
- **Bishop–Gromov volume comparison.** If $M^n$ is complete with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge(n-1)K$, then $r\mapsto \mathrm{Vol}\,B(p,r)/\mathrm{Vol}\,B(p_K,r)$ is non-increasing, where $p_K$ lies in the simply connected space form of curvature $K$; in particular $\mathrm{Vol}\,B(p,r)\le \mathrm{Vol}\,B(p_K,r)$. It is the key point in the proof of Gromov's compactness theorem. ([Wikipedia: Bishop–Gromov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop%E2%80%93Gromov_inequality))
- **Myers's theorem (1941).** If $(M^n,g)$ is complete and connected with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge (n-1)/r^2$, then any two points are joined by a geodesic of length at most $\pi r$; so $M$ is compact and $\pi_1(M)$ is finite. Cheng (1975) showed equality of the diameter forces constant curvature. ([Wikipedia: Myers's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myers%27s_theorem))
- **Cheeger–Gromoll splitting (1971).** A connected complete Riemannian manifold with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge0$ that contains a line splits isometrically as $N\times\mathbb R$. ([Wikipedia: Splitting theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splitting_theorem))
- **Gromov's Betti number theorem (1981).** If $M^n$ is complete with non-negative sectional curvature and $F$ is a field, then $\sum_i b_i(M;F)\le 10^{10n^4}$ (Abresch's improvement of Gromov's original double-exponential bound). ([Wilking, arXiv:0707.3091](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3091))
- **Sphere theorems.** A complete simply connected $n$-manifold whose sectional curvatures lie in $(1,4]$ is homeomorphic to $S^n$ (Berger and Klingenberg, 1960, after Rauch's 1951 result for $[3/4,1]$ pinching); it fails for $[1,4]$, e.g. $\mathbb{CP}^n$ with the Fubini–Study metric. ([Wikipedia: Sphere theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_theorem)) Brendle and Schoen proved via Ricci flow that a compact manifold with pointwise $1/4$-pinched sectional curvature is diffeomorphic to a space form. ([Brendle & Schoen, arXiv:0705.0766](https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.0766))

### Examples
- **Surfaces.** In dimension 2, $R_{abcd} = K(g_{ac}g_{db} - g_{ad}g_{cb})$ with $K$ the Gaussian curvature, equal to half the scalar curvature; only one component is independent. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor))
- **Space forms.** Constant sectional curvature $K$ gives $R_{abcd} = K(g_{ac}g_{db} - g_{ad}g_{cb})$, and outside dimension 2 this form characterizes constant curvature. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor)) Then $\mathrm{Ric} = (n-1)Kg$. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature))
- **Cylinder.** A cylinder is intrinsically flat even though it is bent in $\mathbb R^3$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor))
- **Einstein metrics.** The trace-free Ricci tensor vanishes exactly when $g$ is Einstein, which in general relativity is the vacuum equation with cosmological constant. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature))
- **Tori.** By Gromov–Lawson, tori admit no metric of positive scalar curvature. ([Wikipedia: Scalar curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_curvature))

### History
Riemann introduced an abstract, rigorous way to define curvature for manifolds. ([Wikipedia: Curvature of Riemannian manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature_of_Riemannian_manifolds)) Ricci and Levi-Civita's memoir "Méthodes de calcul différentiel absolu et leurs applications" appeared in *Mathematische Annalen* 54 (1900), pp. 125–201. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01454201)) Myers proved his theorem in 1941, extending Bonnet's 1855 surface case. ([Wikipedia: Myers's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myers%27s_theorem)) Cheeger and Gromoll proved the splitting theorem in 1971, after Cohn-Vossen's 2-dimensional case of 1936. ([Wikipedia: Splitting theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splitting_theorem)) Hamilton introduced Ricci flow in 1982, and Perelman used it to prove the Poincaré conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature)) Schoen and Yau proved the positive mass theorem in the 1970s and Witten reproved it; the Yamabe problem was resolved by 1984. ([Wikipedia: Scalar curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_curvature))

### Connections
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives): curvature is the curvature of the Levi-Civita connection.
- [Parallel Transport](node:Parallel%20Transport): the loop holonomy whose infinitesimal form is $R$.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics) and [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry): settings for Ricci and scalar curvature.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): geodesic deviation, Jacobi fields, and comparison theorems.
- [Comparison Geometry](node:Comparison%20Geometry): Rauch, Toponogov, Bishop–Gromov and their consequences.
- [Alexandrov Spaces](node:Alexandrov%20Spaces): synthetic lower curvature bounds modelled on Toponogov.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): finite under positive Ricci curvature (Myers).
- [Homology](node:Homology): Betti numbers bounded under non-negative sectional curvature (Gromov).
- [Hyperbolic Space](node:Hyperbolic%20Space): the constant negative curvature model.
- [Ricci Flow](node:Ricci%20Flow): evolves the metric by its Ricci tensor; used for the differentiable sphere theorem.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): symmetries and traces behind the decomposition.
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations), [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity), [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action): Einstein tensor and scalar curvature in gravity.
- [Raychaudhuri Equation](node:Raychaudhuri%20Equation): Ricci curvature controls focusing of geodesic congruences.
- [Gauss–Codazzi Equations](node:Gauss–Codazzi%20Equations) and [Extrinsic Curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature): hypersurface versus ambient curvature.
- [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane): the projected bulk Weyl tensor as a source term.
- Map: [MSC 53 - Differential geometry](node:MSC%2053%20-%20Differential%20geometry)

### Common pitfalls
- **Sign conventions.** The sign of $R(X,Y)Z$ varies between authors, while the Ricci tensor's does not; some authors normalize scalar curvature as an average rather than a sum of sectional curvatures. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature)) ([Wikipedia: Scalar curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_curvature))
- **Which Weyl tensor is conformally invariant.** The invariance under $g\mapsto fg$ is stated for the $(1,3)$ form $C^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}$, with one index raised; a fully covariant form is not the invariant object. ([Wikipedia: Weyl tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_tensor))
- **Ricci-flat is not flat.** Outside dimensions 2 and 3 a vanishing Ricci tensor does not imply vanishing curvature, and non-zero sectional curvature does not by itself indicate local mass, since tidal effects can come from mass elsewhere. ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature))
- **Negative Ricci curvature is not an obstruction.** Unlike positive Ricci curvature, negative Ricci curvature has no topological implications in dimension above two (Lohkamp, 1994). ([Wikipedia: Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature))
- **Homeomorphic versus diffeomorphic.** The topological sphere theorem did not give a diffeomorphism because exotic smooth spheres exist; that required Brendle–Schoen. ([Wikipedia: Sphere theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Hopf conjecture.** A compact even-dimensional manifold of positive sectional curvature should have positive Euler characteristic, and a compact $2d$-dimensional manifold of negative sectional curvature should have Euler characteristic of sign $(-1)^d$. It holds in dimensions 2 and 4 and is open in dimension 6 and higher. ([Wikipedia: Hopf conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_conjecture))
- **Hopf product conjecture.** Whether $S^2\times S^2$ carries a metric of positive sectional curvature is not excluded; Bourguignon (1975) ruled out such metrics near the product metric. ([Wikipedia: Hopf conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_conjecture))
- **Optimal Betti bound.** Gromov posed the problem whether the best bound on the total Betti number of a non-negatively curved $n$-manifold is $2^n$, the total Betti number of the $n$-torus. ([Wilking, arXiv:0707.3091](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3091))
- **Positive scalar curvature.** Gromov and Lawson's nonexistence results support a conjecture that certain topological invariants vanish on closed spin manifolds of positive scalar curvature; it is a special case of the strong Novikov conjecture, itself a special case of the Baum–Connes conjecture for the fundamental group. ([Wikipedia: Scalar curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_curvature))

### Resources
