- **Reference:** [Riemann curvature tensor (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor): definition, coordinate formula, symmetries, holonomy meaning.
- **Reference:** [Riemann curvature (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Riemann+curvature): curvature as the curvature form of the Levi-Civita connection.
- **Learn:** [Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (arXiv:gr-qc/9712019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/9712019): graduate course notes deriving the curvature tensors and Einstein's equations.
- **Primary:** [Brendle & Schoen, Manifolds with 1/4-pinched curvature are space forms (arXiv:0705.0766)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.0766): the differentiable sphere theorem.
- **Primary:** [Wilking, Nonnegatively and positively curved manifolds (arXiv:0707.3091)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0707.3091): survey of sphere theorems, Betti bounds, and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Ricci & Levi-Civita, Méthodes de calcul différentiel absolu (Math. Ann. 1900)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01454201): founding memoir of tensor calculus.
- **Further reading:** [Petersen, Riemannian Geometry (Graduate Texts in Mathematics, 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-26654-1): standard graduate text on Riemannian geometry.
references.DGP Gravity:
## Reference
### Overview
The Dvali–Gabadadze–Porrati (DGP) model, proposed in 2000, takes ordinary 3+1-dimensional spacetime to be a brane in 4+1-dimensional Minkowski space. Its action has an Einstein–Hilbert term on the brane and one in the bulk. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DGP_model)) The original paper shows how four-dimensional [Newtonian gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity) emerges on the brane even though the extra dimension is flat and infinite. The potential is 4D at short distances and 5D at large distances. ([Dvali, Gabadadze & Porrati 2000](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0005016))

The [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model) modifies [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) at high energies. DGP instead modifies it at low energies and large distances. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2); [Maartens & Koyama, Living Reviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962)) Its cosmology produces "self-acceleration" of the late-time universe through a weakening of gravity at low energies, not through a negative-pressure field. The model remains a toy model for developing tests of modified gravity. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))

DGP shares the vDVZ discontinuity of massive gravity: from the 4D viewpoint gravity is carried by a continuum of massive Kaluza–Klein gravitons. Exact DGP cosmological solutions showed for the first time an interpolation between a GR-like regime and a modified one, a realization of the [Vainshtein Mechanism](node:Vainshtein%20Mechanism). The second-order equations of the DGP decoupling limit led to the Galileon family. ([Babichev & Deffayet 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.7240))

### Formal definition
In the original normalization, with bulk metric $G_{AB}$, induced metric $g_{\mu\nu}(x)=G_{\mu\nu}(x,y=0)$ and a tensionless brane at $y=0$, the action is ([DGP, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0005016))
$$S = M^3\int d^5X\,\sqrt{G}\,\mathcal R_{(5)} + M_P^2\int d^4x\,\sqrt{|g|}\,R .$$
With reduced Planck masses and brane matter $\mathcal L_{(M)}$, one writes $S_{(5)}=\tfrac{M_{(5)}^3}{2}\int d^5X\sqrt{g_{(5)}}R_{(5)}$ and $S_{(4)}=\int d^4x\sqrt{g_{(4)}}\big(\tfrac{M_P^2}{2}R_{(4)}+\mathcal L_{(M)}\big)$. The crossover distance is ([Babichev & Deffayet 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.7240))
$$r_c \equiv \frac{M_P^2}{2M_{(5)}^3}.$$
The [bulk term](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action) dominates at $r\gg r_c$, where gravity leaks into the infinite-volume bulk. The 5D Minkowski bulk has no normalizable 4D graviton zero mode. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))

**Transition (Vainshtein) radius.** Around a source of Schwarzschild radius $r_g$, Lue, Scoccimarro and Starkman find the transition scale ([Lue, Scoccimarro & Starkman 2004](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0401515))
$$r_* = \left(\frac{r_c^2\,r_g}{\beta^2}\right)^{1/3},\qquad \beta=\frac{1-2r_cH+2r_c^2H^2}{1-2r_cH}$$
on the self-accelerating branch (their lower sign); this is $\sim (r_g/H_0^2)^{1/3}$ for $r_c\sim H_0^{-1}$. Inside $r_*$ (the "Einstein phase") 4D GR is recovered on the brane; outside it gravity is modified. ([Lue, Scoccimarro & Starkman 2004](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0401515))

**The parameter β.** On a flat FLRW brane, Koyama and Maartens instead define ([Koyama & Maartens 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0511634))
$$\beta = 1 - 2r_cH\left(1+\frac{\dot H}{3H^2}\right),\qquad \omega_{BD} = \tfrac32(\beta-1).$$

### Key results
- **Crossover of the potential.** For a Minkowski brane, $\psi\propto r^{-1}$ for $r\ll r_c$ and $\psi\propto r^{-2}$ for $r\gg r_c$ ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2)). In the exact scalar toy model the brane propagator is $\tilde G_R(p,y)=e^{-p|y|}/(M_P^2p^2+2M^3p)$ with $r_0=M_P^2/(2M^3)$. ([DGP, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0005016))
- **vDVZ tensor structure.** The brane graviton propagator has the trace coefficient $1/3$ of a massive graviton, not the massless $1/2$. DGP calls this difference "vital for description of observations", since it changes light bending at linear order. ([DGP, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0005016))
- **Strong coupling (Luty–Porrati–Rattazzi).** A longitudinal Goldstone mode gets its kinetic term only through mixing with the transverse graviton, as in massive gravity. The theory is strongly interacting below $\lambda_3\sim(\lambda_{\rm DGP}^2/M_P)^{1/3}$, about 1000 km if $\lambda_{\rm DGP}$ is the Hubble length. They also find a classical negative-energy solution, removable by a cutoff at $\lambda_3$. ([Luty, Porrati & Rattazzi 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0303116))
- **Decoupling limit.** The helicity-0 Lagrangian is $\mathcal L_{\rm dgp}=3\tilde\phi\Box\tilde\phi-\Lambda_{\rm dgp}^{-3}(\partial_\mu\tilde\phi)^2\Box\tilde\phi+\tilde\phi T/(2M_P)$ with $\Lambda_{\rm dgp}=(M_P/r_c^2)^{1/3}$. Its field equations are second order, consistent with DGP having no Boulware–Deser ghost. ([Babichev & Deffayet 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.7240))
- **Modified Friedmann equation.** With $\dot\rho+3H(\rho+p)=0$, the self-accelerating branch obeys ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
$$H^2+\frac{K}{a^2}-\frac{1}{r_c}\sqrt{H^2+\frac{K}{a^2}}=\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho .$$
GR is recovered for $Hr_c\gg1$, and $H\to1/r_c$ at late times, so acceleration needs $r_c\gtrsim H_0^{-1}$. The normal branch is $r_c\to-r_c$ and needs a $\Lambda$ term. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2)) Deffayet derived these brane-Friedmann equations for a $Z_2$-symmetric metric. ([Deffayet 2000](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0010186))
- **Linear growth (Koyama–Maartens).** In the quasi-static sub-horizon regime outside the Vainshtein radius, DGP is a Brans–Dicke theory with $\omega_{BD}=\tfrac32(\beta-1)$, and CDM perturbations obey ([Koyama & Maartens 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0511634))
$$\ddot\Delta+2H\dot\Delta=4\pi G\left(1+\frac{1}{3\beta}\right)\rho\Delta .$$
This is the Brans–Dicke $G_{\rm eff}=G\,(1+1/(2\omega_{BD}+3))$. Lue, Scoccimarro and Starkman obtain the same form $G_{\rm eff}=G(1+1/(3\beta))$ with their β, which is negative and of order unity at present on the self-accelerating branch, so the effective [gravitational constant](node:Gravitational%20Constant) decreases with time (about $0.72\,G$ at $z=0$ for $\Omega_m^0=0.3$). ([Lue, Scoccimarro & Starkman 2004](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0401515)) Neglecting the 5D bulk field violates the 4D Bianchi identity and gives the wrong growth factor. ([Koyama & Maartens 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0511634))
- **Ghost on the self-accelerating branch.** On the de Sitter brane with $Hr_c>1$ (positive brane cosmological constant), the helicity-0 mode of the massive spin-2 graviton is a ghost, and mixing at $Hr_c=1$ likely keeps it ([Koyama 2005](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0503191)). Charmousis, Gregory, Kaloper and Padilla find a 4D ghost on the self-accelerating branch for any brane tension. The normal branch is ghost-free and "perturbatively safe at large distance scales". ([Charmousis et al. 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0604086))

### Examples
- **Crossover density parameter.** With $\Omega_{r_c}=1/[4(H_0r_c)^2]$, the sum rule $\Omega_m+\Omega_\Lambda+\Omega_K=1$ becomes $\Omega_m+2\sqrt{\Omega_{r_c}}\sqrt{1-\Omega_K}+\Omega_K=1$ for self-accelerating DGP. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
- **Growth index.** Writing $f=d\ln\Delta/d\ln a=\Omega_m(a)^\gamma$, $\gamma\approx0.68$ for DGP against $\gamma\approx0.55+0.05[1+w(z=1)]$ for GR with smooth dark energy. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
- **Normal branch and degravitation.** Rewriting the normal-branch equation in GR form gives $\Lambda_{\rm eff}=\Lambda-\tfrac{3}{r_c}\sqrt{H^2+K/a^2}<\Lambda$. The effective equation of state is phantom ($w_{\rm eff,0}<-1$) with no ghost and no big rip. On this branch $\omega_{BD}>0$, so structure formation is less suppressed than in ΛCDM. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))

### History
"4D Gravity on a Brane in 5D Minkowski Space" by Dvali, Gabadadze and Porrati was submitted in May 2000 and published in Phys. Lett. B 485 (2000) 208. ([Dvali, Gabadadze & Porrati 2000](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0005016)) Deffayet's "Cosmology on a Brane in Minkowski Bulk" followed in October 2000, finding a self-inflationary solution with late-time acceleration. ([Deffayet 2000](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0010186)) Vainshtein's nonlinear way out of the vDVZ discontinuity lacked a proper proof, as Boulware and Deser stressed in 1972; the mechanism was re-introduced in the framework of DGP gravity. ([Babichev & Deffayet 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.7240))

Strong coupling was found in 2003 ([Luty, Porrati & Rattazzi 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0303116)), and the self-accelerating ghost in 2005–2006 ([Koyama 2005](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0503191); [Charmousis et al. 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0604086)). Observational fits followed. Background expansion plus large-angle CMB data put self-accelerating DGP about $5\sigma$ worse than ΛCDM, and Maartens and Koyama call it "effectively ruled out" ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2)). Lombriser, Hu, Fang and Seljak found that both branches require brane tension or Λ at high significance, with $H_0r_c>3$ and $3.5$ (95% CL) depending on the treatment of curvature. ([Lombriser et al. 2009](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.1112))

### Connections
- [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions): DGP uses one infinite, flat extra dimension.
- [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action): the model is two Einstein–Hilbert terms, bulk and brane.
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model) and [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions): braneworlds that localize gravity by warping or [compactification](node:Compactification) rather than by an induced term.
- [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology) and [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): DGP is the standard low-energy braneworld modification of Friedmann cosmology.
- [Israel Junction Conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions) and [Gauss–Codazzi Equations](node:Gauss–Codazzi%20Equations): give the brane Friedmann equation.
- [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane): the RS-type counterpart, modified at high energies.
- [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes): the brane graviton is a continuum of massive KK modes.
- [Vainshtein Mechanism](node:Vainshtein%20Mechanism): nonlinear recovery of GR inside $r_*$.
- [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions) and [Gauss's Law in n Dimensions](node:Gauss's%20Law%20in%20n%20Dimensions): the $1/r\to1/r^2$ crossover is the change of Green's-function falloff.
- [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant), [Quintessence](node:Quintessence) and [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): self-acceleration was an alternative to Λ; quintessence can mimic DGP distances but not its growth.
- [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space): the late-time self-accelerating attractor, where the ghost lives.
- [Cosmological Perturbation Theory](node:Cosmological%20Perturbation%20Theory): growth requires the 5D perturbations.
- [Tests of General Relativity](node:Tests%20of%20General%20Relativity) and [Tests of the Inverse-Square Law](node:Tests%20of%20the%20Inverse-Square%20Law): vDVZ and screening decide solar-system viability.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Modified gravity and screening](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Modified%20gravity%20and%20screening)

### Common pitfalls
- **Sign of the 1/(3β) term.** The Living Review prints the growth equation as $\ddot\Delta+2H\dot\Delta-4\pi G(1-\tfrac{1}{3\beta})\rho\Delta=0$ with a different β ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2)). That is inconsistent with its own $\omega_{BD}$ and with the original derivation. Use $4\pi G(1+\tfrac{1}{3\beta})$ with $\beta=1-2r_cH(1+\dot H/3H^2)$. ([Koyama & Maartens 2006, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0511634); [Lue, Scoccimarro & Starkman 2004](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0401515))
- **Normalization of $r_c$.** Sources use $M^3,M_P^2$ without factors of 1/2, reduced masses with 1/2, or an overall $1/r_c$ on the bulk term. Match conventions before comparing $r_c$. ([DGP, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-th/0005016); [Babichev & Deffayet 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.7240))
- **Branch choice.** The square root in the Friedmann equation forces a sign choice. Self-acceleration comes with a ghost; the normal branch is ghost-free but needs Λ. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2); [Charmousis et al. 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0604086))
- **Linear theory is not the whole story.** No 4D linearized effective theory reproduces DGP for weak-field gravity, and non-perturbative effects matter in apparently linear regimes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DGP_model)) Below the Vainshtein radius, roughly cluster scale for cosmology, the spin-0 mode is strongly coupled and GR is recovered. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
- **Background fits are not enough.** Supernova distances use only the background equation, which quintessence can mimic. Treating DGP perturbations as 4D with a modified $H$ violates $\nabla^\nu G_{\mu\nu}=0$. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2); [Koyama & Maartens 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0511634))

### Open problems
- **Exact static spherically symmetric solutions.** Babichev and Deffayet state that exact static, spherically symmetric DGP brane solutions "are not known, despite a lot of effort". ([Babichev & Deffayet 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.7240))
- **Vainshtein screening beyond static cases.** Their conclusions list as open the endpoint of gravitational collapse of a star, and whether Vainshtein screening can hide time variation of Newton's constant in the solar system. They add that "very little is known about time dependent cases". They also note that the UV completion of these theories "is currently lacking". ([Babichev & Deffayet 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.7240))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [DGP model (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DGP_model): setup, motivation, criticisms.
- **Learn:** [Gabadadze, ICTP Lectures on Large Extra Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0308112): introductory summer-school lectures with a detailed treatment of infinite-volume extra dimensions and late-time acceleration.
- **Primary:** [Dvali, Gabadadze & Porrati (2000)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0005016): the original model.
- **Primary:** [Koyama & Maartens, Structure formation in the DGP cosmological model (2006)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0511634): correct 5D growth equation.
- **Primary:** [Luty, Porrati & Rattazzi (2003)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0303116): strong coupling and the Goldstone mode.
- **Primary:** [Charmousis, Gregory, Kaloper & Padilla, DGP Specteroscopy (2006)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0604086): the ghost spectrum on both branches.
- **Further reading:** [Maartens & Koyama, Brane-World Gravity (Living Reviews)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962), §9 on DGP; [Babichev & Deffayet, An introduction to the Vainshtein mechanism](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.7240).
references.Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constan:
## Reference
### Overview
Dark energy is the proposed form of energy responsible for the accelerating expansion of the universe; it also slows the rate of structure formation. In the [Lambda-CDM model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model) it makes up about 68% of the present mass–energy of the observable universe, with dark matter about 27% and ordinary matter about 5%. Its density, about $7\times10^{-30}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, is tiny but spatially uniform, so it dominates the cosmic average. ([Wikipedia: Dark energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy))

The simplest candidate is a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ in Einstein's field equations, equivalent as a source to a uniform vacuum energy density. Einstein introduced $\Lambda$ in 1917 to allow a static universe and discarded it after Hubble's 1929 expansion law; from the 1930s to the late 1990s most physicists took $\Lambda=0$, until Type Ia supernova observations in 1998 showed that the expansion is accelerating. Michael Turner coined the term "dark energy" in 1998. ([Guth, MIT 8.286 notes](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf); [Wikipedia: Cosmological constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant); [Wikipedia: Dark energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy))

In particle physics $\Lambda$ measures the energy density of the vacuum, and quantum field theory estimates of that density exceed the observed value by between 50 and about 122 orders of magnitude, depending on the cutoff. This is the cosmological constant problem, which Carroll calls "one of the most significant unsolved problems in fundamental physics". Current work asks both why $\Lambda$ is so small and whether dark energy is constant at all: since 2024 DESI baryon-acoustic-oscillation data combined with the CMB and supernovae have favoured a slowly evolving equation of state. ([Wikipedia: Cosmological constant problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant_problem); [Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075); [DESI DR2, arXiv:2503.14738](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738))

### Formal definition
Einstein's field equations with a cosmological constant are
$$R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12 R\,g_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\kappa T_{\mu\nu},\qquad \kappa=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4},$$
and $\Lambda$ has dimension length$^{-2}$. Moving $\Lambda$ to the source side is equivalent to a vacuum energy density $u_{\rm vac}=\rho_{\rm vac}c^2$ with $\Lambda=\kappa u_{\rm vac}$ and equation-of-state parameter $w\equiv p/(\rho c^2)=-1$. ([Wikipedia: Cosmological constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant); [Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075); [Guth, MIT 8.286 notes](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf)) See [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations).

With explicit $c$, Guth writes
$$u_{\rm vac}=\rho_{\rm vac}c^2=\frac{\Lambda c^4}{8\pi G},\qquad p_{\rm vac}=-\rho_{\rm vac}c^2=-\frac{\Lambda c^4}{8\pi G}.$$
([Guth, MIT 8.286 notes](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf))

The gravitational action with a bare cosmological term is $S=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int\mathrm d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\,(R-2\Lambda_0)$. ([Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075)) Its uniqueness is a statement about field equations (Lovelock's theorem): in four dimensions every symmetric divergence-free tensor whose components are functions of the metric and its first and second derivatives (linear in the second derivatives) is $aG_{\mu\nu}+bg_{\mu\nu}$, so $\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ is the only possible addition to the Einstein tensor in a metric theory with second-order equations. ([Wikipedia: Lovelock's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock%27s_theorem)) See [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action).

Dynamical dark energy is usually tested with the parametrisation $w(a)=w_0+w_a(1-a)$, where $a=(1+z)^{-1}$ is the scale factor; $w_0=-1$, $w_a=0$ is a cosmological constant. ([DESI DR2, arXiv:2503.14738](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14738v3))

### Key results
- **Acceleration from negative pressure.** In an FLRW universe the acceleration equation is $\ddot a/a=-\tfrac{4\pi G}{3}(\rho+3p)+\Lambda/3$, so $\Lambda>0$, or any component with sufficiently negative pressure, can make $\ddot a>0$. ([Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075); [Guth, MIT 8.286 notes](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf)) See [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology).
- **Supernova discovery (High-$Z$ team).** Riess et al. added 10 Type Ia supernovae at $0.16<z<0.62$ to earlier data (16 high-redshift, 34 nearby). The distant ones are 10–15% farther than expected in an $\Omega_M=0.2$ universe without $\Lambda$; with a flat prior they require $\Omega_\Lambda>0$ at $7\sigma$ and $9\sigma$ for two fitting methods ($3.0\sigma$ and $4.0\sigma$ with only $\Omega_M>0$), and $\Omega_M=1$ is ruled out at $7$–$8\sigma$. ([Riess et al., arXiv:astro-ph/9805201](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9805201)) See [Supernovae](node:Supernovae).
- **Supernova discovery (SCP).** Perlmutter et al., using 42 Type Ia supernovae, found for a flat cosmology $\Omega_M=0.28^{+0.09}_{-0.08}$ (stat) ${}^{+0.05}_{-0.04}$ (identified systematics) and $P(\Lambda>0)=99\%$ including systematics. ([Perlmutter et al., arXiv:astro-ph/9812133](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9812133))
- **Concordance from independent probes.** The location of the [CMB acoustic peaks](node:CMB%20Acoustic%20Peaks) constrains the spatial geometry to near-flatness, $\Omega_m+\Omega_\Lambda\simeq1$; with supernovae this gave $\Omega_m\simeq0.3$, $\Omega_\Lambda\simeq0.7$. The 2024 PDG review states that the CMB "shows no evidence for dynamics of the dark energy, being consistent with a pure cosmological constant", and that combining CMB, SN, RSD and BAO in a flat universe gives $w=-1.03\pm0.03$. ([PDG 2024, Cosmological Parameters](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))
- **Pantheon+ and BAO before DESI.** Pantheon+ (1,701 light curves of 1,550 SNe Ia) gives $\Omega_M=0.334\pm0.018$ in flat $\Lambda$CDM; in flat $w$CDM, SNe + CMB + BAO give $w_0=-0.978^{+0.024}_{-0.031}$, "consistent with a cosmological constant". (The 2024 PDG text quotes this as $w=-0.98^{+0.2}_{-0.3}$, an apparent dropped digit.) eBOSS with Planck, Pantheon and other probes gives $w_p=-1.020\pm0.032$ at pivot $z_p=0.29$. ([Brout et al., arXiv:2202.04077](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04077); [PDG 2024, Cosmological Parameters](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))
- **DESI evidence for evolving dark energy.** DESI DR1 BAO combined with the CMB prefers $w_0>-1$, $w_a<0$ at $2.6\sigma$, rising to $2.5\sigma$, $3.5\sigma$ and $3.9\sigma$ with Pantheon+, Union3 and DES-SN5YR supernovae. DESI DR2 (over 14 million galaxies and quasars) finds the $w_0w_a$ model preferred over $\Lambda$CDM at $3.1\sigma$ for DESI + CMB and at $2.8$–$4.2\sigma$ with supernovae, depending on the sample, together with a mild $2.3\sigma$ tension between DESI and CMB parameters within $\Lambda$CDM. ([DESI DR1, arXiv:2404.03002](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03002); [DESI DR2, arXiv:2503.14738](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738)) See [Baryon Acoustic Oscillations](node:Baryon%20Acoustic%20Oscillations).
- **Vacuum-energy estimates.** Using ordinary quantum field theory up to the [Planck scale](node:Planck%20Scale) gives a vacuum contribution of about $2\times10^{110}\,\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-3}}$; the electroweak and QCD scales give contributions of order $(200\,\mathrm{GeV})^4$ and $(0.3\,\mathrm{GeV})^4$. Observations bound the vacuum energy at about $(10^{-12}\,\mathrm{GeV})^4\approx2\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-3}}$, "the famous discrepancy of 120 orders of magnitude". ([Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075))

### Examples
- **Einstein static universe.** The static solution balances matter against $\Lambda$, but any small deviation from that balance grows into a runaway departure; Wikipedia describes it as unstable against matter-density perturbations. ([Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075); [Wikipedia: Cosmological constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant))
- **Quintessence.** A slowly evolving scalar field with nearly the same effect as $\Lambda$; many quintessence models show tracker behaviour, which addresses why acceleration began when it did. No evidence of quintessence is yet available, nor has it been ruled out. ([Guth, MIT 8.286 notes](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf); [Wikipedia: Dark energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy)) See [Quintessence](node:Quintessence). Copeland, Sami and Tsujikawa review quintessence, k-essence, tachyon, phantom and dilatonic fields, scaling solutions and coupled dark energy, and modified-gravity alternatives. ([Copeland–Sami–Tsujikawa, arXiv:hep-th/0603057](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0603057))
- **Fate if $\Lambda$ dominates.** If dark energy is a cosmological constant, galaxies outside the Local Group eventually pass beyond a cosmological event horizon now about 16 billion light years away; phantom dark energy can instead produce a Big Rip. ([Wikipedia: Dark energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy)) The asymptotic spacetime is [de Sitter space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space).

### History
Einstein proposed the cosmological term in 1917 ("Kosmologische Betrachtungen zur allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie") to permit a static universe, and discarded it after Hubble's 1929 paper. ([Guth, MIT 8.286 notes](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf)) Friedmann showed in 1922 that the field equations allow a dynamic universe. ([Wikipedia: Cosmological constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant)) Zel'dovich first addressed quantum-fluctuation contributions to $\Lambda$ in the 1960s, and around 1987 Weinberg estimated the largest vacuum energy compatible with the formation of gravitationally bound structures. ([Wikipedia: Cosmological constant problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant_problem))

The High-Z Supernova Search Team posted its evidence for acceleration on 15 May 1998 and the Supernova Cosmology Project on 8 December 1998; *Science* named the discovery Breakthrough of the Year, and Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. ([Guth, MIT 8.286 notes](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf)) DESI released BAO results from its first data release in 2024 and second in 2025. ([DESI DR1, arXiv:2404.03002](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03002); [DESI DR2, arXiv:2503.14738](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738))

### Connections
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): $\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ is the unique extra term allowed by Lovelock's theorem.
- [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action): the term $-2\Lambda$ in the gravitational Lagrangian.
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): the Friedmann equations with a $\Lambda/3$ term and a $w=-1$ fluid.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): the standard cosmology with a cosmological constant and cold dark matter.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): vacuum energy appears as $T_{\mu\nu}\propto g_{\mu\nu}$.
- [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background) and [CMB Acoustic Peaks](node:CMB%20Acoustic%20Peaks): geometry and the late-time expansion history.
- [Baryon Acoustic Oscillations](node:Baryon%20Acoustic%20Oscillations) and [Large-Scale Structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure): standard rulers and growth of structure.
- [Supernovae](node:Supernovae): Type Ia standard candles for the distance–redshift relation.
- [Quintessence](node:Quintessence) and [Scalar-Tensor Gravity](node:Scalar-Tensor%20Gravity): dynamical alternatives to $\Lambda$.
- [Cosmic Inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation): an earlier epoch of vacuum-like acceleration at a much higher energy scale.
- [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space): the vacuum-dominated, constant-$\Lambda$ spacetime.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory) and [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale): zero-point energy as a putative source of $\Lambda$.
- [String Landscape](node:String%20Landscape): the anthropic setting for a small $\Lambda$.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): the other unknown dominant component of $\Lambda$CDM.
- [GW170817](node:GW170817): the speed-of-gravity bound that eliminated many modified-gravity substitutes for dark energy.

### Common pitfalls
- **Treating the vacuum energy as an unobservable constant.** Without gravity the vacuum energy of a system is arbitrary and can be shifted by a constant, but in [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity) "the actual value of the vacuum energy has important consequences", which is why zero-point estimates conflict with observation. ([Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075))
- **Confusing $\ddot a>0$ with increasing $H$.** $H=\dot a/a$ can decrease while $\dot a$ increases, as long as $a$ grows; in our universe $H$ is decreasing even though recession velocities are accelerating. ([Guth, MIT 8.286 notes](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf))
- **"Dark energy is 68% of the matter."** It is 68% of the total mass–energy; most of the matter is dark matter. ([Wikipedia: Dark energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy))
- **Reading the PDG Pantheon+ error bar literally.** The PDG 2024 text prints $w=-0.98^{+0.2}_{-0.3}$, but the Pantheon+ paper's SNe + CMB + BAO result is $-0.978^{+0.024}_{-0.031}$; the SNe-only flat $w$CDM value is $-0.90\pm0.14$. ([PDG 2024, Cosmological Parameters](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf); [Brout et al., arXiv:2202.04077](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04077))
- **"The Einstein–Hilbert action with $\Lambda$ is the most general second-derivative action."** As a statement about Lagrangians this is loose, since higher-curvature scalars also exist; the precise statement is Lovelock's theorem about second-order field equations. ([Wikipedia: Lovelock's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock%27s_theorem))

### Open problems
- **The cosmological constant problem.** Why is the vacuum energy density so much smaller than the zero-point energy suggested by quantum field theory? Wikipedia lists this as unsolved, and Carroll calls it "one of the most significant unsolved problems in fundamental physics". ([Wikipedia: Cosmological constant problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant_problem); [Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075))
- **Anthropic and landscape explanations.** Weinberg's first anthropic estimate of the maximum vacuum energy compatible with bound structures seemed too large; later estimates put it close to the observed value, and anthropic arguments gained traction with the [string theory](node:String%20Theory) landscape. Carroll writes that accepting an anthropic explanation "will therefore (again) require advances in our understanding of fundamental physics". ([Wikipedia: Cosmological constant problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant_problem); [Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075))
- **Is $w$ exactly $-1$?** Wikipedia notes that there is not yet sufficient data to rule out a cosmological constant, while PDG 2024 says that detecting variation in the dark energy density ($w\ne-1$) "would provide much-needed experimental input into its nature" and points to surveys such as DESI and Euclid. ([Wikipedia: Dark energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy); [PDG 2024, Cosmological Parameters](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))
- **The coincidence problem.** The coincidence problem asks why the acceleration of the universe began when it did; the tracker behaviour of many quintessence models is proposed as a solution. ([Wikipedia: Dark energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy))

> [!warning] Contested
> DESI DR2 BAO combined with the CMB and supernovae prefers $w_0>-1$, $w_a<0$ over $\Lambda$CDM at $2.8$–$4.2\sigma$ depending on the supernova sample. ([DESI DR2, arXiv:2503.14738](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738)) Wikipedia presents this as evidence for evolving dark energy, not a confirmed finding, and notes that data are not yet sufficient to rule out a cosmological constant. ([Wikipedia: Dark energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy)) The pre-DESI PDG 2024 review found CMB data consistent with $w=-1$ and no evidence for evolution. ([PDG 2024, Cosmological Parameters](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Dark energy (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy): evidence, candidate models and the DESI results.
- **Reference:** [Cosmological constant problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant_problem): the vacuum-energy discrepancy and anthropic arguments.
- **Learn:** [Guth, MIT 8.286 Lecture Notes 7](https://web.mit.edu/8.286/www/lecn18/ln07-euf18.pdf): vacuum energy, $p=-\rho c^2$, the accelerating Friedmann equation and the 1998 discovery.
- **Primary:** [Carroll, The Cosmological Constant (Living Reviews in Relativity, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0004075): review of $\Lambda$, vacuum energy, observations and anthropic reasoning.
- **Primary:** [Copeland, Sami and Tsujikawa, Dynamics of dark energy (arXiv:hep-th/0603057)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0603057): standard review of dynamical dark-energy models.
- **Primary:** [Riess et al., arXiv:astro-ph/9805201](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9805201) and [Perlmutter et al., arXiv:astro-ph/9812133](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9812133): the discovery papers.
- **Primary:** [DESI DR1, arXiv:2404.03002](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03002) and [DESI DR2, arXiv:2503.14738](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738): BAO constraints and the $w_0w_a$ preference.
- **Primary:** [PDG, Cosmological Parameters (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf) and [Brout et al., Pantheon+ (arXiv:2202.04077)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04077): pre-DESI constraints on $\Omega_m$ and $w$.

## Reference
### Overview
Dark matter (DM) is a hypothetical form of matter that does not interact with electromagnetic radiation and is inferred from gravitational effects that ordinary matter cannot explain. The evidence includes galaxy rotation curves, velocity dispersions, galaxy clustering, the Bullet Cluster, gravitational lensing, the Lyman-alpha forest, the cosmic microwave background, structure formation, and [baryon acoustic oscillations](node:Baryon%20Acoustic%20Oscillations). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter))

For the benchmark $\Lambda$CDM cosmology adopted by the Particle Data Group, DM is 26.4% of the critical density, or 84.4% of the total matter density. The three Standard Model neutrinos make up at least 0.5% and at most 1.6% of the non-baryonic matter; the makeup of the large majority of the DM is unknown. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf)) The leading candidates are new particles such as WIMPs or axions, with primordial black holes the other main possibility; a minority of researchers pursue modified gravity instead. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter))

Laboratory searches comprise direct detection of DM scattering, axion searches, and searches at accelerators and colliders; indirect detection looks for the annihilation or decay products of DM in astrophysical systems. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf)) No laboratory experiment has confirmed a DM signal. ([Wikipedia: WIMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle))

### Formal definition
In cosmology DM is modelled as an electromagnetically close-to-neutral, non-baryonic species with negligible velocity from the standpoint of structure formation, "cold dark matter" (CDM). ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf)) Its abundance is quoted as the physical density $\omega_c = \Omega_c h^2$; Planck 2018 finds $\Omega_c h^2 = 0.120 \pm 0.001$, with $\Omega_m = 0.315 \pm 0.007$ and $H_0 = 67.4 \pm 0.5\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$ in base $\Lambda$CDM. ([Planck 2018 VI, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))

DM is called cold, warm or hot according to its free-streaming length. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter)) For a thermal relic of a species pair-annihilating via $2\to2$ processes, the number density obeys
$$\frac{dn}{dt} + 3Hn = -\langle\sigma v\rangle\left(n^2 - n_{\rm eq}^2\right),$$
with $H$ the Hubble rate and $\langle\sigma v\rangle$ the thermally averaged annihilation cross section times velocity; the $3Hn$ term is the dilution of the number density by the expansion. ([Lisanti, arXiv:1603.03797](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1603.03797)) A relic is hot if it freezes out while relativistic and cold if non-relativistic. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))

### Key results
- **Flat rotation curves.** If the mass were concentrated where the stars are, orbital speeds outside the bulge would fall roughly as $r^{-1/2}$; observed speeds stay nearly constant, so the enclosed mass grows roughly linearly with radius far beyond the stellar disk. Rubin and Ford reported this in 1975. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve))
- **Structure formation.** Baryonic fluctuations at recombination are at most $\delta\rho_b/\rho_b \sim 10^{-5}$; growing linearly with the scale factor they would reach only about $10^{-2}$ today, far short of the observed non-linear structure. A cold, pressureless component that decoupled earlier fixes this. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Freeze-out abundance.** Hot relics give $\Omega h^2 \simeq m/(93\ \mathrm{eV})$ for SM-like neutrinos. Cold relics give $\Omega h^2$ inversely proportional to the annihilation cross section, with freeze-out at $x = m/T \approx 10$–$50$; electroweak-scale cross sections $\sigma \simeq 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$ give the observed abundance, the origin of the WIMP's popularity, although the relation itself bears no intrinsic connection to the weak scale. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf)) The required self-annihilation rate is $\langle\sigma v\rangle \simeq 3\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$. ([Wikipedia: WIMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle))
- **Other production mechanisms.** In freeze-in, out-of-equilibrium collisional production accumulates over cosmic time, with an abundance set by the production rate times the Hubble time; it typically implies long-lived visible-sector particles decaying to DM. Non-thermal production (decays of a mother particle, defects, moduli, gravity) and asymmetric DM are further options. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf)) For axions, oscillations of the field about the minimum of the QCD potential (misalignment) generate a cosmological population of cold axions whose abundance depends on the axion mass. ([Wikipedia: Axion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axion))
- **Model-independent mass bounds.** Pauli blocking in dwarf galaxies (Tremaine–Gunn) gives fermionic DM $m_F > 70$ eV from Fornax, with stronger but thermal-history-dependent Lyman-$\alpha$ limits. Ultralight bosonic DM would erase small-scale structure in conflict with the CMB, large-scale structure, Lyman-$\alpha$ data and satellite counts, giving $m_B \gtrsim 10^{-22}$ eV. Wide halo binaries and the star cluster in Eridanus II limit a point-like constituent making up all the DM to below about $5\,M_\odot$. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Warm DM from the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest.** Combining XQ-100 with HIRES/MIKE data gives a thermal-relic warm DM mass above 5.3 keV at $2\sigma$, relaxed to 3.5 keV if abrupt IGM temperature changes are allowed. ([Iršič et al., arXiv:1702.01764](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.01764))
- **Fuzzy DM scales.** For an ultralight boson of mass $m\sim10^{-22}$ eV with de Broglie wavelength of order 1 kpc, halos lighter than about $10^7(m/10^{-22}\,\mathrm{eV})^{-3/2}M_\odot$ do not form, and halos have a solitonic core inside a CDM-like envelope. ([Hui et al., arXiv:1610.08297](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.08297))
- **Self-interaction limit.** Merging clusters and X-ray ellipticities of galaxies give $\sigma_{\rm DM\text{-}DM}/m_{\rm DM} < 0.47\ \mathrm{cm^2/g}$ at 95% C.L. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Direct-detection limits.** The strongest DM–nucleus limits come from multi-tonne xenon experiments, LZ, PandaX-4T and XENONnT. The PDG compilation lists spin-independent limits of $9.2\times10^{-48}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ at 36 GeV (LZ), $3.8\times10^{-47}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ at 40 GeV (PandaX-4T) and $2.6\times10^{-47}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ at 30 GeV (XENONnT). Coherent neutrino–nucleus scattering from ${}^8$B and atmospheric neutrinos will affect light ($\lesssim 6$ GeV) and heavy ($\gtrsim100$ GeV) searches below about $10^{-45}$ and $10^{-49}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ respectively. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf)) Because this background can be overcome statistically, it is called the "neutrino fog"; O'Hare defines its boundary through the derivative of a discovery limit with respect to exposure, so that it depends only on the neutrino-flux uncertainties. ([O'Hare, arXiv:2109.03116](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03116))
- **Indirect and collider limits.** Fermi-LAT gives some of the most stringent constraints on DM pair annihilation, chiefly from stacked observations of nearby satellite dwarf spheroidal galaxies. At the LHC, ATLAS and CMS search for [missing transverse momentum](node:Missing%20Transverse%20Momentum) and mediator resonances; no DM signal has been seen, and collider searches alone cannot prove a discovery is DM. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Problems for modified gravity without DM.** Such theories struggle with the spectrum of density perturbations, the CMB anisotropy spectrum, and the lensing and X-ray maps of merging clusters such as 1E 0657-558; GW170817's measurement that gravitational and electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed excludes many modified theories. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))

### Examples
- **Coma Cluster.** Zwicky applied the virial theorem to the Coma Cluster in 1933 and inferred unseen mass he called *dunkle Materie*; his estimate was off by more than an order of magnitude, mainly because of an obsolete Hubble constant. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter))
- **Milky Way halo.** Global (rotation-curve) methods give a local DM density of $0.2$–$0.6\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3}$, and Gaia-based studies $0.3$–$1.5\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3}$ depending on the tracer stars. Direct-detection analyses usually adopt the Standard Halo Model: an isotropic isothermal sphere with $\rho\propto r^{-2}$ and a Maxwellian velocity distribution truncated at the escape speed. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Simulated halos.** The Navarro–Frenk–White profile $\rho(r) = \rho_0/\big[(r/R_s)(1+r/R_s)^2\big]$ was proposed from N-body simulations in 1996; its central density diverges. ([Wikipedia: NFW profile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navarro%E2%80%93Frenk%E2%80%93White_profile))
- **Axion window.** Axions with a mass above about $5\ \mu\mathrm{eV}$ could account for the DM, and if inflation occurs at a low scale and lasts long enough the mass can be as low as about $1$ peV; the ADMX haloscope converts halo axions to microwave photons in a resonant cavity and has excluded parts of the few-$\mu$eV range. ([Wikipedia: Axion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axion))
- **Solar System.** All DM out to Neptune's orbit would total roughly $10^{17}$ kg, about the mass of a large asteroid. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter))

### History
Lord Kelvin discussed unseen stars near the Sun in 1884, Poincaré used the term *matière obscure* in 1906, and Kapteyn (1922) and Oort (1932) made stellar-kinematic arguments. Zwicky's 1933 Coma analysis followed. In the 1970s Rubin and Ford's optical rotation curves and 21 cm radio maps strengthened the case, and in 1974 groups in Princeton and Tartu independently concluded that galaxies are surrounded by dark halos. Steigman and collaborators' 1978 study set up the treatment of DM as a new particle species, later the basis for WIMP research. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter)) Lee and Weinberg's 1977 "Cosmological lower bound on heavy-neutrino masses" (Phys. Rev. Lett. 39, 165) is an early relic-abundance argument. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.39.165)) Bertone and Hooper note that this history is often ignored or condensed into a brief anecdotal account of a few pioneers. ([Bertone & Hooper, arXiv:1605.04909](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.04909))

Peccei and Quinn proposed their solution to the strong CP problem in 1977, and Weinberg and Wilczek showed in 1978 that it predicts the axion. ([Wikipedia: Axion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axion)) Standard reviews include Jungman, Kamionkowski and Griest on supersymmetric DM (Phys. Rept. 267, 1996) ([arXiv:hep-ph/9506380](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9506380)) and Bertone, Hooper and Silk on evidence, candidates and constraints (Phys. Rept. 405, 2005). ([arXiv:hep-ph/0404175](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0404175))

- [Galaxy Rotation Curves](node:Galaxy%20Rotation%20Curves) and [Virial Theorem](node:Virial%20Theorem): the classic galactic and cluster evidence.

### Common pitfalls
- **"85% of the universe."** DM is about 85% of the matter, not of the total energy: with the PDG benchmark it is 26.4% of the critical density. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf)) The 5% / 26.8% / 68.2% split in Wikipedia's lead, cited there to NASA and Planck overview pages, does not match the PDG benchmark; use one consistent set. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter))
- **Neutrinos are not the answer.** SM neutrinos are DM but at most 1.6% of the non-baryonic matter. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Limits are model-dependent.** Direct-detection rates assume the local density, velocity distribution and escape speed; the Standard Halo Model is a convention, not a measurement. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **A collider excess is not a DM discovery.** LHC searches look for missing energy and momentum from particles escaping the detector, and collider searches alone cannot prove that a discovery is of dark matter. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Local density is small.** DM dominates halos, but in the Solar System its density is much lower than that of ordinary matter. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter))

### Open problems
- **What DM is.** The fundamental makeup of the large majority of the DM is, in the PDG's words, as of yet unknown. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Small-scale structure.** Below about 1 Mpc, $\Lambda$CDM faces the cusp–core and too-big-to-fail problems; there is now scant evidence for a missing-satellites problem, but tensions such as the diversity of rotation curves remain. Baryonic feedback is the most likely resolution, though these issues could also call for extending $\Lambda$CDM. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Galactic Centre gamma-ray excess.** Its nature is described as quite controversial: its spectrum and morphology fit a WIMP of a few tens of GeV, while unresolved millisecond pulsars are a plausible alternative, and statistical discrimination methods may not be conclusive. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))
- **Primordial black hole bounds.** A lively debate continues over the accretion efficiency around PBHs at high redshift, which affects CMB constraints on them. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf))

> [!warning] Contested
> Most astrophysicists accept DM, but a minority argue for modified gravity (MOND, TeVeS, entropic gravity); none of these yet explains all the evidence. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter)) The PDG review lists the CMB spectrum, the [matter power spectrum](node:Matter%20Power%20Spectrum) and merging clusters as the main difficulties for modified gravity without DM. ([PDG Review: Dark Matter](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf)) The radial acceleration relation, which predicts rotation-curve accelerations from baryons alone, is consistent with MOND, and some but not all $\Lambda$CDM simulations reproduce it. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Dark matter (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter): evidence, history, candidates and alternatives.
- **Learn:** [Lisanti, Lectures on Dark Matter Physics (TASI 2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.03797): rotation curves, thermal relics, and detection for graduate students.
- **Primary:** [PDG Review 27: Dark Matter (Baudis & Profumo, 2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-dark-matter.pdf): the standard review of properties, production and searches.
- **Primary:** [Planck 2018 results VI: Cosmological parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209): the precision measurement of $\Omega_c h^2$.

references.Dark Matter Direct Detection:
## Reference
### Overview
Direct detection is the search for the effects of a dark-matter particle colliding with a target nucleus (or electron) in a laboratory detector. Because almost all dark-matter particles would pass through without interacting, detectors must be extremely sensitive, low-background and scalable to large target masses ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)). The canonical target is the [WIMP](node:Weakly%20Interacting%20Massive%20Particles), whose elastic scattering off a nucleus would deposit recoil energies of order 10 keV; experiments therefore sit in deep underground laboratories and fight radioactive, cosmogenic and neutrino backgrounds ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).

The signal rate depends on three ingredients: particle physics (the dark-matter–nucleon cross-section and its spin structure), nuclear physics (form factors), and astrophysics (the local density and velocity distribution of the [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter) halo) ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026); [Lin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1904.07915)). Direct detection complements collider searches and [indirect detection](node:Dark%20Matter%20Indirect%20Detection) of annihilation products.

As of the latest results there are no confirmed detections; experiments set upper limits on the cross-section as a function of mass ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)). LUX-ZEPLIN's 2024 analysis of 4.2 tonne-years of exposure found no excess over background and excludes cross-sections above $2.2\times10^{-48}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ at 90% CL for a 40 GeV/$c^2$ WIMP ([LZ Collaboration 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17036)). Next-generation xenon and argon TPCs aim at about $10^{-48}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$, roughly an order of magnitude above the floor set by coherent neutrino scattering ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).

### Formal definition
**Kinematics.** For a dark-matter particle of mass $m_\chi$ scattering elastically on a nucleus of mass $m_N$ with momentum transfer $q$, the recoil energy is $E_R=q^2/(2m_N)$, and energy conservation bounds $|q|\le 2\mu_{\chi N}v$, where $\mu_{\chi N}=m_\chi m_N/(m_\chi+m_N)$ and $v\sim10^{-3}c$ ([Lin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1904.07915)). The minimum dark-matter speed that can produce recoil energy $E_R$ is
$$v_{\min}=\sqrt{\frac{m_N E_R}{2\mu^2}}$$
([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).

**Differential rate.** Per unit detector mass,
$$\frac{dR}{dE_R}=\frac{\rho_0}{m_N m_\chi}\int_{v_{\min}}^{v_{\rm esc}} v\,f(v)\,\frac{d\sigma}{dE_R}\,dv,$$
with $\rho_0$ the local dark-matter density and $f(v)$ the speed distribution in the detector frame. For a Maxwellian halo with the Earth's velocity and the escape speed neglected (and no form factor), the spectrum is exactly exponential, $dR/dE_R=\frac{R_0}{E_0r}e^{-E_R/(E_0r)}$, where $R_0$ is the total rate, $E_0=m_\chi v_0^2/2$ is the most probable WIMP kinetic energy and $r=4m_\chi m_N/(m_\chi+m_N)^2\le1$, so the mean recoil energy is $E_0r$ (about 15 keV for $m_\chi=m_N=50$ GeV/$c^2$); including the Earth's motion and $v_{\rm esc}$, the spectrum is still approximately $c_1\frac{R_0}{E_0r}e^{-c_2E_R/(E_0r)}$ with $c_1\approx0.75$, $c_2\approx0.56$ ([Schnee 2011](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.5205)). (Schumann's eq. (8) prints the factor $r$ in the numerator of the exponent; the dimensionally consistent form, with $r$ dividing $E_0$, is the one above.) The velocity integral is controlled by the mean inverse speed above $v_{\min}$ ([Lin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1904.07915)).

**Spin-independent (SI) cross-section.** With proton and neutron couplings $f_p,f_n$,
$$\sigma_{\rm SI}=\sigma_n\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_n^2}\frac{\big(f_pZ+f_n(A-Z)\big)^2}{f_n^2}\ \xrightarrow{\,f_p=f_n\,}\ \sigma_n\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_n^2}A^2,$$
where $\sigma_n$ is the WIMP–nucleon cross-section and $\mu_n$ the WIMP–nucleon reduced mass. Loss of coherence at large $q$ is described by a form factor, commonly the Helm form $F(x)=\frac{3j_1(x)}{x}e^{-(xs)^2/(2R_N^2)}$, $x=qR_N/\hbar$, $R_N\approx1.2A^{1/3}$ fm, $s\approx0.5$ fm ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).

**Spin-dependent (SD) scattering** couples to the nuclear spin $J$ through a spin-structure function $S(|q|)$ and has no $A^2$ enhancement ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).

**Standard Halo Model (SHM).** A truncated Maxwellian with $v_0\approx220$ km/s and an escape speed of about 500–600 km/s ([Lin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1904.07915)); the canonical local density is $\rho_0=0.3\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2/\mathrm{cm^3}$ with roughly 50% uncertainty, and $v_{\rm esc}\simeq544$ km/s (90% range 498–608 km/s) ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).

### Key results
- **Coherent $A^2$ enhancement.** For isospin-conserving SI couplings the nuclear cross-section scales as $\mu^2A^2$, so heavy targets such as xenon give higher rates at lower recoil energies, suppressed at large $q$ by the form factor ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026); [Lin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1904.07915)).
- **Kinematic mass reach.** For $m_\chi\ll m_N$, $\mu_{\chi N}\approx m_\chi$ and the maximal recoil energy $\approx2m_\chi^2v^2/m_N$ falls rapidly; with thresholds $E_R^{\rm th}\gtrsim5$–$10$ keV, nuclear-recoil sensitivity drops steeply at low mass, motivating electron-recoil and other searches for sub-GeV dark matter ([Lin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1904.07915)).
- **Annual modulation.** The detector speed through the halo is $v_E=v_\odot+v_\oplus\cos\theta\cos[\omega(t-t_0)]$ with $v_\odot=v_c+12$ km/s, $v_\oplus=30$ km/s, $\theta\approx60^\circ$, $t_0=$ June 2. The modulated fraction is of order 5%, so a modulation-only discovery requires of order $10^4$ events ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **LZ 2024 SI exclusion.** LZ (280 live days, $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years) excludes SI WIMP–nucleon cross-sections above $2.2\times10^{-48}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ at 90% CL at 40 GeV/$c^2$, with median sensitivity $5.1\times10^{-48}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ ([LZ Collaboration 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17036)). In 2019 the leading limits were XENON1T above about 5 GeV/$c^2$ ($4.1\times10^{-47}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ at 30 GeV/$c^2$), DarkSide-50 from about 1.8 to 5 GeV/$c^2$, and CRESST-III below 1.8 GeV/$c^2$ ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **The neutrino floor.** Coherent neutrino–nucleus scattering cannot be rejected event by event; solar $^8$B neutrinos dominate at low WIMP mass and atmospheric neutrinos above about 10 GeV/$c^2$ ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)). Beyond it, sensitivity improves at best as the square root of exposure ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)). O'Hare redefines the floor as the boundary of a "neutrino fog" using the derivative of the discovery limit with respect to exposure, so that it depends only on systematic uncertainties of neutrino fluxes; it is not a hard limit and can be pushed past with enough statistics, and the new floor differs from earlier estimates by nearly an order of magnitude at sub-GeV masses and above about 20 GeV ([O'Hare 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03116)). Directional detectors could go beyond the floor provided a significant number of events are detected; XENONnT, LZ, PandaX-4T and DarkSide-20k aim at about $10^{-48}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$, and DARWIN proposes a 40 t xenon TPC to reach the neutrino-floor regime ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **DAMA/LIBRA tension.** DAMA/LIBRA reports a 12.9$\sigma$ annual modulation over 20 cycles (2.46 t·y) in single-scatter events below 6 keVee; interpreted as standard WIMP nuclear recoils it is excluded by more sensitive experiments by orders of magnitude, and xenon experiments exclude it directly ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)). COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 NaI results have not replicated it, and COSINE-100 reported in 2022 that DAMA's analysis method can produce a similar modulation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)).

### Examples
- **Dual-phase liquid-xenon TPCs** (XENON, LZ, PandaX) read prompt scintillation (S1) and delayed ionisation (S2); the S2/S1 ratio rejects electronic recoils at about $10^{-3}$ for 30% nuclear-recoil acceptance ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **Liquid argon** (DEAP, DarkSide) uses pulse-shape discrimination reaching ER rejection below $2\times10^{-8}$ at 90% nuclear-recoil acceptance, at the cost of ~30 keV$_{\rm nr}$ thresholds and the need for underground argon to suppress $^{39}$Ar ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **Cryogenic [bolometers](node:Bolometers)** (CDMS, CRESST, EDELWEISS) run at $\le50$ mK with simultaneous heat and ionisation or scintillation readout, reaching the lowest thresholds for sub-5 GeV WIMPs ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)).
- **Bubble chambers** (PICO-60, with $^{19}$F-containing C$_3$F$_8$) give the best limits on spin-dependent WIMP–proton couplings; **directional gas TPCs** (DRIFT) aim to measure recoil direction ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **CCDs** (DAMIC, SENSEI) search for light dark matter through the electron–hole pairs its interactions create ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)).

### History
Annual modulation, one of the predicted signatures of a WIMP signal, is credited to Drukier, Freese and Spergel's 1986 paper "Detecting cold dark-matter candidates" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)). LUX and SuperCDMS, then PandaX (2021) and XENONnT and LZ (2023), set the strongest exclusions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)), and LZ's 2024 analysis reached $2.2\times10^{-48}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ ([LZ Collaboration 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17036)). The "WIMP miracle" made supersymmetric WIMPs the original benchmark, but the absence of supersymmetry at the LHC has weakened the simplest WIMP hypotheses ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)); sub-GeV "light" dark matter and dark sectors are now a major theme of direct-detection theory ([Lin 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.07915)).

### Connections
- [Weakly Interacting Massive Particles](node:Weakly%20Interacting%20Massive%20Particles): the benchmark candidate the nuclear-recoil technique was designed for.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): direct detection tests whether the cosmological dark matter couples to nucleons.
- [Dark Matter Halo Profiles](node:Dark%20Matter%20Halo%20Profiles) and [Dark Matter Phase-Space Distributions](node:Dark%20Matter%20Phase-Space%20Distributions): supply $\rho_0$ and $f(v)$, the main astrophysical uncertainty.
- [Halo-Independent Dark Matter Inference](node:Halo-Independent%20Dark%20Matter%20Inference): compares experiments without assuming the Standard Halo Model.
- [Neutrino Backgrounds in Dark Matter Searches](node:Neutrino%20Backgrounds%20in%20Dark%20Matter%20Searches): the neutrino floor/fog limiting future sensitivity.
- [Directional Dark Matter Detection](node:Directional%20Dark%20Matter%20Detection): recoil-direction measurement as a route through the neutrino fog.
- [Dark Matter Electron Scattering](node:Dark%20Matter%20Electron%20Scattering): the sub-GeV extension where nuclear recoils are kinematically too soft.
- [Time Projection Chambers](node:Time%20Projection%20Chambers): the detector architecture of the leading noble-liquid experiments.
- [Bolometers](node:Bolometers) and [Cryogenic Physics](node:Cryogenic%20Physics): the low-threshold technologies for light WIMPs.
- [Dark Matter Indirect Detection](node:Dark%20Matter%20Indirect%20Detection): the complementary search for annihilation or decay products.
- [Dark Matter Detection Likelihoods](node:Dark%20Matter%20Detection%20Likelihoods): the statistical framework for setting limits and claiming signals.
- [Thermal Freeze-Out](node:Thermal%20Freeze-Out): sets the cross-section scale that motivated WIMP searches.
- [Axion Haloscopes](node:Axion%20Haloscopes): the analogous laboratory search for wave-like dark matter.
- [Supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry): source of the original WIMP benchmark models.

### Common pitfalls
- **Limits are model-dependent.** Exclusion curves assume the SHM, specific $f_p/f_n$ and SI or SD couplings; $\rho_0$ alone carries roughly 50% uncertainty ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **keVee vs keVnr:** electronic-equivalent (keVee) and nuclear-recoil (keVnr) energy scales are not interchangeable; DAMA quotes its signal in keVee, while liquid-argon thresholds are quoted in keVnr ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **The neutrino floor is not a wall:** discovery remains possible below it with sufficient statistics or directionality ([O'Hare 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03116); [Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).
- **Anomalies usually fade:** excess events in the field have typically disappeared within months of more data ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)).

### Open problems
- **Origin of the DAMA/LIBRA modulation.** The DAMA/LIBRA anomaly remains unexplained; Schumann notes serious concerns about its dark-matter nature and that COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 needed more data for definite conclusions, and in 2022 COSINE-100 reproduced a similar modulation using DAMA's analysis method ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle)).
- **Migdal effect in dark-matter targets.** Schumann (2019) described whether the Migdal effect, an extra ionisation signal from the recoiling atom that would extend nuclear-recoil searches into the sub-GeV range, is actually present, and how detector response to it can be calibrated, as unclear ([Schumann 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.03026)). A 2026 Nature paper reports its first direct observation in neutron–nucleus collisions, at 5 standard deviations from 6 candidate events, with a Migdal-to-nuclear-recoil cross-section ratio of $4.9^{+2.6}_{-1.9}\times10^{-5}$ consistent with theory ([Yi et al. 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09918-8)). A definitive confirmation in liquid xenon, the target of the leading experiments, still requires dedicated measurements with background mitigation ([Xu et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03174)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Weakly interacting massive particle (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle): direct-detection section, detector types, DAMA status.
- **Learn:** [Lin, TASI lectures on dark matter models and direct detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.07915): kinematics, rate formula, SHM, sub-GeV directions.
- **Primary:** [Schumann, Direct Detection of WIMP Dark Matter: Concepts and Status](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03026): the standard review of signals, detectors, backgrounds and status.
- **Primary:** [LZ Collaboration, results from 4.2 tonne-years](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17036): WIMP search results from 280 live days.
- **Primary:** [O'Hare, Fog on the horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03116): neutrino-fog definition of the floor.
- **Further reading:** [Bertone (ed.), Particle Dark Matter: Observations, Models and Searches (CUP, 2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511770739): graduate monograph covering direct detection.
references.Dark Radiation:
## Reference
### Overview
"Dark radiation" names two related ideas that share one observational signature: an energy density that redshifts like radiation, $\rho \propto a^{-4}$, but is not made of photons or Standard Model neutrinos. In braneworld cosmology it is the Kaluza–Klein (Weyl) energy density $\rho_{\mathcal E}$, the part of the projected bulk Weyl tensor $\mathcal E_{\mu\nu}$ that a Friedmann brane feels as an effective fluid. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))

In particle cosmology the term refers to an extra radiation density $\rho_X$ added to the early universe by physics beyond the Standard Model, such as new light particles. It is usually quoted as a shift $\Delta N_{\rm eff}$ in the effective number of neutrino species, even when the extra density $\rho_X$ has nothing to do with neutrinos. ([Baumann, arXiv:1807.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098)) A narrower usage is a hidden "dark electromagnetism," a radiation field that mediates interactions between dark-matter particles and, like dark matter, does not couple to Standard Model particles. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_radiation))

In both settings the constraint comes from the same place. Any extra relativistic energy speeds up the expansion rate during Big Bang nucleosynthesis and at recombination, so light-element abundances and the CMB damping tail bound it. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962)) ([Baumann, arXiv:1807.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098))

### Formal definition
**Braneworld (Weyl) dark radiation.** For a brane with unit normal $n^A$ in a 5D bulk, the projected bulk Weyl tensor is $\mathcal E_{\mu\nu} = {}^{(5)}C_{ACBD}\,n^C n^D g_\mu{}^A g_\nu{}^B$. It is symmetric, traceless, and orthogonal to $n^A$. Relative to a brane observer with 4-velocity $u^\mu$ it decomposes as
$$-\frac{1}{\kappa^2}\mathcal E_{\mu\nu} = \rho_{\mathcal E}\left(u_\mu u_\nu + \tfrac13 h_{\mu\nu}\right) + q^{\mathcal E}_\mu u_\nu + q^{\mathcal E}_\nu u_\mu + \pi^{\mathcal E}_{\mu\nu},$$
and the KK energy density $\rho_{\mathcal E}$, carrying the spin-0 mode, is what is often called the dark radiation. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))

On a Friedmann brane, conservation gives $\dot\rho_{\mathcal E} + 4H\rho_{\mathcal E} = 0$, so $\rho_{\mathcal E} = \rho_{\mathcal E 0}(a_0/a)^4$. The modified Friedmann equation is
$$H^2 = \frac{\kappa^2}{3}\rho\left(1 + \frac{\rho}{2\lambda}\right) + \frac{m}{a^4} + \frac{\Lambda}{3} - \frac{K}{a^2}, \qquad m = \frac{\kappa^2}{3}\rho_{\mathcal E 0}a_0^4,$$
where $\lambda$ is the brane tension and $m$ is the mass parameter of the bulk black hole. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))

**Extra relativistic species.** $N_{\rm eff}$ is defined so that, well after electron–positron annihilation, the non-photon relativistic energy density is
$$\rho_{\rm rad} = N_{\rm eff}\,\tfrac78\left(\tfrac{4}{11}\right)^{4/3}\rho_\gamma,$$
with Standard Model value $N_{\rm eff} \approx 3.046$ and $\Delta N_{\rm eff} \equiv N_{\rm eff} - 3.046$. ([Planck 2018 VI, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)) Equivalently, $\Delta N_{\rm eff} \equiv \rho_X/\rho_\nu$ measures the extra density relative to one Standard Model neutrino species. ([Baumann, arXiv:1807.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098))

### Key results
- **First integral with a free radiation-like constant.** For a 3-brane in a 5D bulk with a cosmological constant, Binétruy, Deffayet, Ellwanger and Langlois showed that Einstein's equations admit a first integral analogous to the first Friedmann equation, valid whatever the metric does along the fifth dimension. It contains a free constant $\mathcal C$, set by initial conditions in the whole spacetime, entering as $\mathcal C/a^4$, an effective radiation term. ([Binétruy et al., arXiv:hep-th/9910219](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9910219))
- **Origin in a bulk black hole.** The most general vacuum bulk containing a Friedmann brane is Schwarzschild–AdS$_5$, with $F(R) = K + R^2/\ell^2 - m/R^2$. The bulk black hole produces dark radiation on the brane through its "Coulomb" effect, and $\rho_{\mathcal E} = 0$ only if its mass vanishes. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))
- **Vanishing for conformally flat bulks.** $\mathcal E_{\mu\nu} = 0$ for a conformally flat bulk, including pure AdS$_5$. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))
- **Nucleosynthesis bound on Weyl dark radiation.** Nucleosynthesis and CMB observations limit it to about 5% of the radiation density at nucleosynthesis, $\rho_{\mathcal E}/\rho_{\rm rad} \lesssim 0.05$. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))
- **CMB constraint on $N_{\rm eff}$.** Planck 2018 with BAO finds $N_{\rm eff} = 2.99 \pm 0.17$, in agreement with the Standard Model value 3.046. ([Planck 2018 VI, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))
- **Minimal thermal contribution.** A light species once in equilibrium with the Standard Model contributes $\Delta N_{\rm eff} = 0.027\,g_{*,X}\,\big(106.75/g_*(T_{{\rm dec},X})\big)^{4/3}$, so $\Delta N_{\rm eff} > 0.027\,g_{*,X}$: 0.054 for a gauge boson, 0.047 for a Weyl fermion, and 0.027 for a Goldstone boson. ([Baumann, arXiv:1807.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098))
- **How the CMB sees it.** Extra radiation raises the expansion rate at recombination. At fixed acoustic scale $\theta_*$ this enlarges the damping scale and reduces power in the damping tail; the effect is partly degenerate with the helium fraction $Y_P$. ([Baumann, arXiv:1807.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098))

### Examples
- **Schwarzschild–AdS$_5$ braneworld.** A Friedmann brane moving radially through a static Schwarzschild–AdS$_5$ bulk with $R = a(T)$: the expansion of the universe can be read as the brane's motion, and the bulk black-hole mass shows up as the $m/a^4$ term. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))
- **Dark electromagnetism.** Ackerman, Buckley, Carroll and Kamionkowski studied a long-range $U(1)$ gauge field that couples only to dark matter. Requiring dark matter to stay effectively collisionless in galaxies gives $\hat\alpha \lesssim 10^{-3}$ for TeV-scale dark matter, compatible with structure-formation and nucleosynthesis limits. ([Ackerman et al., arXiv:0810.5126](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.5126))
- **Thermal axions.** Baumann uses thermal axions as the example that a future CMB-S4 experiment could test, if it reaches sensitivity to the minimal abundance $\Delta N_{\rm eff} > 0.027$. ([Baumann, arXiv:1807.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098))

### History
Binétruy, Deffayet, Ellwanger and Langlois derived the brane Friedmann equation with its $\mathcal C/a^4$ term in 1999, noting that the parameter can be constrained by nucleosynthesis because it acts like extra relativistic degrees of freedom. ([Binétruy et al., arXiv:hep-th/9910219](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9910219)) Maartens and Koyama's Living Review cites Mukohyama's 2000 paper "Brane-world solutions, standard cosmology, and dark radiation" (hep-th/9911165), and their own treatment identifies $\rho_{\mathcal E}$ with the dark radiation. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962)) Wikipedia attributes the "dark electromagnetism" usage to Ackerman et al. (2008). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_radiation))

### Connections
- [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane): the projected Weyl term $\mathcal E_{\mu\nu}$ that sources Weyl dark radiation.
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): dark radiation adds an $a^{-4}$ term to the Friedmann equation.
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model) and [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology): the setting of the braneworld meaning.
- [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space) and [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution): pure AdS$_5$ gives no dark radiation; a Schwarzschild–AdS$_5$ bulk black hole does.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): the Weyl tensor is the trace-free part of the Riemann tensor.
- [Gauss–Codazzi Equations](node:Gauss–Codazzi%20Equations) and [Israel Junction Conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions): used to derive the modified Friedmann equation.
- [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes): $\mathcal E_{\mu\nu}$ carries the effect of massive bulk graviton modes.
- [Big Bang Nucleosynthesis](node:Big%20Bang%20Nucleosynthesis) and [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background): the two main constraints on extra radiation.
- [Axions](node:Axions) and [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): sources of $\Delta N_{\rm eff}$ in the particle usage.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Dark energy and additional radiation](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Dark%20energy%20and%20additional%20radiation)

### Common pitfalls
- **Two meanings.** Braneworld dark radiation is a geometric effect of the bulk Weyl tensor, not a new particle; in particle cosmology the term means new light species. Both appear observationally as extra radiation, but the physics is different. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962)) ([Baumann, arXiv:1807.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098))
- **Sign.** Weyl dark radiation need not be positive. Assuming a non-negative bulk black-hole mass (to avoid a naked singularity) gives $\rho_{\mathcal E 0} \ge 0$, but for $K = -1$ a negative $m$ with $|m| \le \ell^2/4$ also avoids one. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))
- **Not strictly radiation.** In a non-vacuum Vaidya–AdS$_5$ bulk (a radiating bulk black hole or radiating brane), a varying mass parameter $m(t)$ feeds both $\mathcal E_{\mu\nu}$ and the bulk-stress term, and the dark-radiation term no longer behaves strictly like radiation. ([Maartens & Koyama, arXiv:1004.3962](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962))
- **$N_{\rm eff}$ is not 3.** The Standard Model value 3.046 exceeds 3 because the neutrinos were not completely decoupled at electron–positron annihilation; values below 3.046 would need photon heating after neutrino decoupling or incomplete thermalization. ([Planck 2018 VI, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))

### Open problems
- **Is there any?** No notable evidence for dark radiation exists; it is not known whether dark matter has multiple interacting components. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_radiation)) Current CMB data are consistent with $N_{\rm eff} = 3.046$, and future CMB observations could tighten $N_{\rm eff}$ constraints by an order of magnitude, enough to probe particles that decoupled before the QCD phase transition. ([Baumann, arXiv:1807.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098))
- **Relation to the $H_0$ tension.** Planck lists $N_{\rm eff} > 3.046$ among the $\Lambda$CDM extensions that allow larger $H_0$ values, but such models are not preferred by Planck data and tend to introduce other tensions such as a higher $\sigma_8$. ([Planck 2018 VI, arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Dark radiation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_radiation): short entry on the dark-sector meaning and $N_{\rm eff}$.
- **Learn:** [Baumann, Primordial Cosmology (TASI lectures)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03098): derivation of $N_{\rm eff}$, thermal-relic contributions, and CMB signatures.
- **Primary:** [Maartens & Koyama, Brane-World Gravity (Living Reviews)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962): the Weyl fluid, the modified Friedmann equation, and constraints.
- **Primary:** [Binétruy, Deffayet, Ellwanger & Langlois (1999)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9910219): original brane Friedmann equation with the $\mathcal C/a^4$ term.
