- **Primary:** [Planck 2018 results VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209): the $N_{\rm eff}$ constraint.
references.Data Curation for Machine Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Data curation in general is "the organization and integration of data collected from various sources", including annotation and publication, with the aim of preserving the data's value over time ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_curation)). In machine learning the term covers everything done to a dataset before and during training to make the resulting model better: filtering, deduplication, label cleaning, rebalancing, mixing sources, and documenting what was done. MIT's course on data-centric AI describes this as "an emerging science that studies techniques to improve datasets", treated as systematic engineering rather than ad hoc trial and error, in contrast to the usual model-centric practice of improving models on a fixed dataset ([MIT Data-Centric AI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)).

For large language models, Albalak et al. frame curation as *data selection*: deciding which candidate data points enter training and how they are sampled, motivated by the variable quality of web text and by the compute, carbon and cost savings of training on less data ([arXiv:2402.16827](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.16827)). Open benchmarks make this measurable: DataComp fixes the CLIP training code and lets only the data vary ([arXiv:2304.14108](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14108)), and FineWeb publishes ablations of deduplication and filtering choices for a 15-trillion-token web corpus ([arXiv:2406.17557](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557)).

Curation also has theoretical content. Sorscher et al. showed that with a good enough pruning metric, test error can in principle fall faster than the power law in dataset size that governs ordinary scaling ([arXiv:2206.14486](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14486)), and confident learning gives provably consistent procedures for finding mislabelled examples ([arXiv:1911.00068](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00068)).

### Formal definition
Following Albalak et al., a dataset is a collection of data points and a **data selection function** $\phi$ maps a raw dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{raw}}$ to a curated dataset $\mathcal{D}=\phi(\mathcal{D}_{\text{raw}})$, chosen so that a model trained on $\mathcal{D}$ maximises (or minimises) a stated objective; selection functions compose into pipelines $\phi=\phi_1\circ\cdots\circ\phi_n$ ([arXiv:2402.16827](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.16827)). Each method has three parts ([arXiv:2402.16827](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.16827)):
- a **utility function** $u:x\mapsto u(x)\in\mathbb{R}$ scoring each data point;
- a **selection mechanism** that uses $u(x)$ to decide whether $x$ is included and how many times it is repeated (binary output for filtering, natural-number output for what is commonly called data mixing);
- a **selection sensitivity**, a threshold where the mechanism needs one (for example keep $x$ iff $u(x)>0.9$).

Methods are further classified by whether they match a target distribution or diversify, whether they alter the set of points or edit points themselves, and the training stage (pretraining, instruction tuning, alignment, [in-context learning](node:In-Context%20Learning), task fine-tuning) ([arXiv:2402.16827](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.16827)).

### Key results
- **Beating power-law scaling by pruning (Sorscher et al. 2022).** In a teacher-student perceptron model with a probe student ranking examples by margin, the best strategy keeps the *easiest* examples when the initial dataset is small and the *hardest* when it is large; pruning more aggressively as data grows allows error to decay exponentially in the pruned dataset size. With an imperfect metric (probe angle $\theta>0$) the Pareto-optimal error crosses over from exponential to power-law scaling, and there is a minimum useful kept fraction $f_{\min}(\theta)$ (about 24% at $\theta=10^\circ$, 46% at $\theta=20^\circ$). Empirically, better-than-power-law scaling appeared for ResNets on CIFAR-10, SVHN and ImageNet, and a self-supervised pruning metric matched the best supervised ones. ([arXiv:2206.14486](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.14486))
- **Deduplication reduces memorisation (Lee et al., ACL 2022).** Standard LM datasets contain many near-duplicates and long repeated substrings (one 61-word sentence appeared over 60,000 times in C4); deduplicating cut the rate of emitting memorised text tenfold and reached the same or better accuracy in fewer steps, and train-test overlap affected over 4% of the validation sets of standard datasets. ([arXiv:2107.06499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499))
- **Data alone can beat a strong baseline (DataComp).** From a pool of 12.8 billion Common Crawl image-text pairs, the DataComp-1B filtered subset trained CLIP ViT-L/14 to 79.2% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy, 3.7 points above OpenAI's CLIP ViT-L/14 with the same training procedure and compute. ([arXiv:2304.14108](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14108))
- **Repetition versus fresh data (Muennighoff et al. 2023).** Training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data gave negligible change in loss compared with unique data, but with more repetition the value of added compute decays to zero; the authors fit a compute-optimal scaling law accounting for the declining value of repeated tokens. ([arXiv:2305.16264](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16264))
- **Consistent label-error detection (confident learning).** Under class-conditional label noise, estimating the joint distribution of noisy and true labels and pruning, counting and ranking examples is provably consistent, with sufficient conditions for exact identification of label errors; it estimated 645 ImageNet "missile" images mislabelled as "projectile". ([arXiv:1911.00068](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00068))
- **Classifier-based quality filtering at scale.** FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3-trillion-token educational subset of FineWeb, gave much better results on knowledge- and reasoning-heavy benchmarks such as MMLU and ARC than unfiltered pretraining data. ([arXiv:2406.17557](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557))

### Examples
A typical LLM pretraining pipeline, as surveyed by Albalak et al. ([arXiv:2402.16827](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.16827)):
- **Language filtering** with classifiers such as fastText, cld3 or langdetect (C4 used langdetect with a probability threshold of 0.99, RefinedWeb used fastText with 0.65).
- **Heuristic filters** on item counts, repetition counts, existence of particular items, ratios and statistics of each document.
- **Quality filtering** with a classifier or perplexity score relative to a high-quality reference corpus; GPT-3 used a stochastic Pareto rule that keeps some out-of-distribution text.
- **Domain selection** with Moore-Lewis methods, DSIR or datamodels, which pick auxiliary data resembling in-domain data.
- **Deduplication**, exact (URL match, hashing, substring matching) or approximate (MinHash, SimHash and other locality-sensitive hashing).

For supervised data, the MIT course treats label errors, [class imbalance](node:Class%20Imbalance), outliers and distribution shift, dataset creation, and curation for LLMs as the core topics ([MIT Data-Centric AI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)). Documentation is part of curation: Datasheets for Datasets proposes that each dataset ship with a datasheet covering motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses, modelled on electronic-component datasheets ([arXiv:1803.09010](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010)).

### History
Gebru et al. proposed datasheets in 2018 (published in CACM in 2021) ([arXiv:1803.09010](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010)). Confident learning appeared in 2019 and was published in JAIR in 2021 ([arXiv:1911.00068](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00068)). Large-scale LM curation studies followed: deduplication (2021) ([arXiv:2107.06499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499)), data pruning theory (NeurIPS 2022 Outstanding Paper) ([arXiv:2206.14486](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14486)), DataComp (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks) ([arXiv:2304.14108](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14108)) and FineWeb (2024) ([arXiv:2406.17557](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557)). MIT's IAP course, billed as the first course on data-centric AI, ran in 2023 and 2024 ([MIT Data-Centric AI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)).

### Connections
- [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): curation changes the effective data term; pruning theory predicts departures from power-law scaling.
- [LLM Privacy and Memorization](node:LLM%20Privacy%20and%20Memorization): deduplication reduces verbatim memorisation of training text.
- [Benchmark Contamination Detection](node:Benchmark%20Contamination%20Detection): train-test overlap removal is a curation step that protects evaluation.
- [Synthetic Data](node:Synthetic%20Data): generated data is curated with the same filters, and adds its own selection problems.
- [Dataset Distillation](node:Dataset%20Distillation): compresses a dataset into synthetic points, the extreme form of pruning.
- [Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining](node:Contrastive%20Language-Image%20Pretraining): the model class DataComp uses to compare filtering strategies.
- [Language Model Pretraining Objectives](node:Language%20Model%20Pretraining%20Objectives): the objective whose loss the curated corpus is chosen to improve.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): the main consumers of web-scale curation pipelines.
- [Fine-Tuning and RLHF](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF): instruction-tuning and alignment stages have their own data-selection problems.

### Common pitfalls
- **Assuming quality filtering always helps.** Whether quality filtering is beneficial is still an open question, some recent datasets (MassiveText, RefinedWeb, Dolma) were built without quality filters, and one quality filter was found to favour high-school newspapers from wealthier, more educated, urban areas. ([arXiv:2402.16827](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.16827))
- **Pruning savings that disappear.** The main cost argument assumes training on the pruned set for the same number of epochs as on the full set; training for the same number of iterations instead improves accuracy only up to a point that saturates before full-data training time. Class balancing was essential to keep performance on pruned subsets. ([arXiv:2206.14486](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.14486))
- **Using the wrong pruning direction.** Keeping hard examples is optimal only when data is abundant; with scarce data, keeping easy examples is better. ([arXiv:2206.14486](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.14486))
- **Inflated evaluation from overlap.** Without deduplication against evaluation sets, measured accuracy partly reflects memorised validation examples. ([arXiv:2107.06499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499))

### Open problems
- **Systematic comparison of heuristics and cheap validation.** Albalak et al. note that no systematic study compares the possible heuristic filters, that stochastic heuristics are unexplored, and that validating a filter currently needs manual inspection or model training; they call for methods that measure data quality directly. ([arXiv:2402.16827](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.16827))
- **Low-resource languages and embedded code.** Language identifiers cover only a limited set of languages, and there is no known method for detecting code embedded in natural-language documents. ([arXiv:2402.16827](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.16827))
- **Scalable pruning metrics and foundation datasets.** Sorscher et al. call scalable unsupervised pruning metrics the most promising future direction, say more work is needed to select the appropriate amount of class balancing, call for deployment-specific fairness tests of pruned datasets, and propose highly pruned "foundation datasets". ([arXiv:2206.14486](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.14486))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Data curation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_curation): general definition of data curation.
- **Learn:** [MIT Introduction to Data-Centric AI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/): lectures on label errors, dataset creation and curation, and curation for LLMs.
- **Primary:** [Albalak et al., A Survey on Data Selection for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.16827): framework and taxonomy of data selection.
- **Primary:** [Sorscher et al., Beyond neural scaling laws: beating power law scaling via data pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14486): theory and experiments on pruning.
- **Primary:** [Lee et al., Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499).
- **Further reading:** [Gadre et al., DataComp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14108); [Penedo et al., The FineWeb Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557); [Northcutt, Jiang and Chuang, Confident Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00068).
references.Data Leakage and Temporal Evaluation:
## Reference
### Overview
*Leakage* (data leakage, target leakage) is the use, during training or model selection, of information that would not be available when the model is used for prediction. It yields overly optimistic performance estimates and can lead to choosing the wrong model. The standard forms are: features that duplicate or proxy the label; preprocessing fitted on the full dataset before splitting; duplicated rows across splits; and splits that ignore non-i.i.d. structure. Non-i.i.d. structure covers *time leakage*, where a random split of time-ordered data lets the model train on the future, and *group leakage*, where records of one entity land on both sides of the split. ([Wikipedia: Leakage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29))

Leakage is a widespread cause of reproducibility failures in machine-learning-based science. Kapoor and Narayanan surveyed reviews across 17 fields that together identified errors in 329 papers, and every field surveyed was affected. Their project page has since grown to 41 papers from 30 fields reporting errors that together affect 648 papers. In their case study of civil-war prediction, every paper claiming that complex models beat [logistic regression](node:Logistic%20Regression) failed to reproduce because of leakage. After correction, the complex models were not substantively better. ([Kapoor and Narayanan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048); [Princeton reproducibility project](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/))

*Temporal evaluation* is the corresponding discipline for time-indexed data and for models trained on time-stamped corpora. The test set should lie strictly after the training period. For large language models the issue reappears as *benchmark contamination*: evaluation items that occurred in the pre-training corpus. The defence is to evaluate on material published after a model's training cutoff, a "model-vintage" control. Released or reported cutoffs are themselves unreliable. ([Kapoor and Narayanan, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2207.07048); [Roberts et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10628); [Cheng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12958))

### Formal definition
Let a model $\hat f$ be selected and fitted by a procedure $\mathcal A$ on a training set $S$ and evaluated on a test set $S'$. The holdout estimate $\frac1{|S'|}\sum_{(x,y)\in S'}\ell(\hat f(x),y)$ is a valid estimate of the population risk because $\hat f$ is independent of $S'$. Testing many predictors on one holdout, or choosing them adaptively from earlier results, breaks this independence and can overfit the holdout itself. ([Dwork et al., full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.02629))

Kapoor and Narayanan give an eight-way taxonomy ([Kapoor and Narayanan, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2207.07048)):
- **L1.1** no test set;
- **L1.2** preprocessing on train and test together;
- **L1.3** feature selection on train and test together;
- **L1.4** duplicates across the split;
- **L2** illegitimate features, which would not be available at prediction time;
- **L3.1** temporal leakage: "the test set should not contain any data from a date before the training set";
- **L3.2** non-independence between train and test samples;
- **L3.3** sampling bias in the test distribution relative to the population the claim is about.

([Kapoor and Narayanan, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2207.07048))

**Temporal split.** With data indexed by time $t$, pick a cutoff $T$. Training and all fitted preprocessing use only $\{t<T\}$, and evaluation uses only $\{t\ge T\}$. HindSight applies the same construction to idea generation: the system sees only literature before $T$, and its outputs are scored against papers published in the following 30 months. ([Wikipedia: Leakage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29); [Jiang 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15164))

### Key results
- **Reusable holdout via differential privacy (Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold and Roth, Theorem 25).** Let Thresholdout use threshold $T=3\tau/4$, noise rate $\sigma=\tau/(96\ln(4m/\beta))$ and overfitting budget $B$. Suppose
$$n \;\ge\; O\!\left(\frac{\ln(m/\beta)}{\tau^2}\right)\cdot\min\Big\{B,\ \sqrt{B\,\ln\big(\ln(m/\beta)/\tau\big)}\Big\}.$$
Then with probability at least $1-\beta$, every answer $a_i$ given before the budget is exhausted is within $\tau$ of the true mean $P[\phi_i]$, for all $m$ adaptively chosen queries. So $m$ may be exponential in $n$ as long as $B\le n^{2-c}$. ([Dwork et al., full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.02629))
- **Leaderboard accuracy (Blum and Hardt, the Ladder).** Leaderboard error is the largest gap, over $t\le k$, between the best true loss among the first $t$ submissions and the $t$-th released score. The Ladder mechanism reports a new score only after a significant improvement. For adaptively chosen submissions it achieves leaderboard error $O\big(\log^{1/3}(kn)/n^{1/3}\big)$ with high probability, for $k$ submissions and a holdout of size $n$. No estimator beats $\Omega(\sqrt{\log k/n})$ in the worst case. Reporting near-exact holdout losses is defeated by a "boosting" attack: submit random label vectors, then take the majority vote of those scoring at most 1/2. Against the Kaggle mechanism with rounding parameter $\alpha\le1/\sqrt n$, this forces leaderboard error $\Omega(\sqrt{k/n})$ with probability $2/3$. ([Blum and Hardt, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1502.04585))
- **Test-set reuse versus distribution shift (Recht, Roelofs, Schmidt and Shankar).** New CIFAR-10 and ImageNet test sets were built by replicating the original collection procedures. On them, accuracies fell by about 3–15% and 11–14% respectively. Yet improvements on the old test sets carried over, amplified, to the new ones. The authors attribute the drop to slightly "harder" images rather than to adaptive overfitting from years of test-set reuse. ([Recht et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10811))
- **Contamination through the lens of time (Roberts et al.).** Using GPT training cutoffs as a natural experiment on Codeforces and Project Euler, they find statistically significant trends between LLM pass rate and both a problem's GitHub popularity and its release date relative to the cutoff. They read this as strong evidence of contamination. ([Roberts et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10628))
- **Effective knowledge cutoffs differ from reported ones (Cheng et al.).** Probing models across versions of their training sources shows that a model's *effective* cutoff for a source often differs from the reported cutoff. Two causes are old content in newer CommonCrawl dumps and incomplete removal of semantic and near-duplicates. ([Cheng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12958))
- **Instance-level contamination detection without training data (Golchin and Surdeanu).** The model receives the dataset name, the split and the start of an instance, and its completion is compared with the true continuation. Calibrated against a prompt that omits the dataset name, this detects contamination with 92–100% agreement with human experts across seven datasets. It flagged GPT-4 as contaminated with AG News, WNLI and XSum. ([Golchin and Surdeanu 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08493))

### Examples
- **Feature leakage.** Predicting yearly salary with monthly salary as a feature. ([Wikipedia: Leakage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29))
- **Group leakage.** Several X-rays of the same patient split across train and test, so the model memorizes patients. ([Wikipedia: Leakage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29))
- **Premature featurization.** Fitting a scaler or an n-gram vocabulary on the full dataset before splitting. ([Wikipedia: Leakage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29))
- **Contamination-limited LLM benchmarks.** LiveBench draws questions from recent maths competitions, arXiv papers, news and datasets, adds and updates them monthly, and scores against objective ground truth rather than an LLM judge. ([White et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19314))
- **Future-impact evaluation of research ideas.** HindSight finds no significant difference between retrieval-augmented and vanilla idea generators under LLM-as-judge ($p=0.584$). Under its temporal future-publication match, the retrieval-augmented system scores 2.5x higher ($p<0.001$), and the score correlates negatively with LLM-judged novelty ($\rho=-0.29$). ([Jiang 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15164))

### History
Adaptive reuse of a holdout set as a source of overfitting goes back to Freedman's paradox, which Dwork et al. take as the motivating example. They link [adaptive data analysis](node:Adaptive%20Data%20Analysis) to [differential privacy](node:Differential%20Privacy), and their reusable holdout appeared in 2015. The same year, Blum and Hardt gave the Ladder for Kaggle-style leaderboards. ([Dwork et al., full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.02629); [Blum and Hardt 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04585)) Kapoor and Narayanan's 2022 survey framed leakage as a reproducibility crisis across ML-based science and proposed *model info sheets* to document its absence. The paper appeared in *Patterns* in 2023. ([Kapoor and Narayanan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048); [Princeton reproducibility project](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/)) From 2023 onward, contamination of LLM benchmarks drove cutoff-based analyses, detection methods and continuously refreshed benchmarks. ([Roberts et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10628); [Golchin and Surdeanu 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08493); [White et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19314))

### Connections
- [Supervised Learning](node:Supervised%20Learning): holdout risk estimates assume the test set is independent of the fitted model.
- [Cross-Validation](node:Cross-Validation): preprocessing and feature selection must happen inside each fold, and random folds leak on time-ordered or grouped data.
- [Reproducible Research Computing](node:Reproducible%20Research%20Computing): leakage is a main source of irreproducible ML-based findings, and model info sheets are a reporting control.
- [Benchmark Contamination Detection](node:Benchmark%20Contamination%20Detection): the LLM-era instance of train–test overlap.
- [Scientific Benchmark Validity](node:Scientific%20Benchmark%20Validity): leaderboards and test-set reuse threaten benchmark conclusions.
- [Machine Learning Evaluation](node:Machine%20Learning%20Evaluation): temporal and group-aware splits are part of sound evaluation design.
- [Time-Series Forecasting](node:Time-Series%20Forecasting) and [Statistical Time Series](node:Statistical%20Time%20Series): forecasting evaluation needs chronological splits.
- [Out-of-Distribution Generalization](node:Out-of-Distribution%20Generalization): the sampling-bias leakage type shades into distribution shift.
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing): Freedman's paradox and adaptive testing are multiple-comparison problems.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): training cutoffs and contamination govern how LLMs can be evaluated.

### Common pitfalls
- **Fitting anything before splitting.** Imputation, resampling, scaling and feature selection on the full data are leakage types L1.2–L1.3. ([Kapoor and Narayanan, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2207.07048))
- **Random splits of time-ordered or grouped data.** These are types L3.1–L3.2. ([Kapoor and Narayanan, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2207.07048))
- **Trusting a reported training cutoff.** Effective cutoffs differ from reported ones, so "published after the cutoff" is weaker evidence than it appears. ([Cheng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12958))
- **Reading an accuracy drop on a fresh test set as proof of test-set overfitting.** It may be distribution shift instead. ([Recht et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10811))
- **Warning signs.** Unusually high accuracy, a large train–test gap, unstable cross-validation results and reliance on counterintuitive features all suggest leakage. ([Wikipedia: Leakage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29))

### Open problems
- **Distribution-shift and non-independence leakage.** Kapoor and Narayanan's taxonomy runs from textbook errors to open research problems. They call robustness to distribution shift (related to L3.3) "as such an open problem", and handling unknown dependence between train and test (L3.2) "a hard problem". ([Kapoor and Narayanan, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2207.07048))
- **Mitigating benchmark contamination.** Xu et al. judge it "impracticable to fully remove the risks associated with contamination". They note that dynamic systems still leave "residual BDC risks" and that dynamic benchmarks "lack the guarantee of consistent results across successive assessments". They list human evaluation, content tags, adversarial evaluation and comprehensive evaluation systems as future directions. ([Xu et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.04244))
- **Systemic fixes for reproducibility.** The Princeton project states that no systemic solutions to leakage-driven reproducibility failures yet exist. ([Princeton reproducibility project](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Leakage (machine learning)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29): feature and row-wise leakage, time and group leakage, detection.
- **Learn:** [Princeton: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/): project page with the taxonomy, model info sheet template and the list of affected fields.
- **Primary:** [Kapoor and Narayanan, Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048): eight-type taxonomy and the civil-war case study.
- **Primary:** [Dwork et al., Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629): Thresholdout and the theory of adaptive holdout reuse.
- **Primary:** [Xu et al., Benchmark Data Contamination of Large Language Models: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04244): contamination definitions, detection and mitigation.
- **Further reading:** [Hardt and Recht, Patterns, Predictions, and Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05242): graduate textbook with a chapter on datasets as benchmarks.
references.Data Provenance and Lineage:
## Reference
### Overview
Data lineage tracks how data is generated, transformed, transmitted, and used across systems over time, so that errors in an analytics workflow can be traced back to their root causes. In industry usage, lineage usually describes the end-to-end flow of datasets through transformations, while provenance focuses on how specific data items were derived and to whom they are attributed; the two are complementary. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_lineage))

Database theory gives provenance a precise meaning for queries. For a tuple in a query result, *why-provenance* returns the relevant part of the database that justifies it, *how-provenance* records the individual derivations, and *where-provenance* keeps track of individual attribute values ([Chomicki, Buffalo CSE 636](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~chomicki/636/handout-provenance.pdf)). Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan's survey organizes the field around these three notions, their applications, and how they relate ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)). The semiring framework of Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen unifies them: annotating tuples with elements of a commutative semiring and propagating annotations through queries recovers set and bag semantics, lineage, why-provenance and provenance polynomials as instances, ordered by surjective homomorphisms ([Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen 2007](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf); [Green 2011](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/tocs11_containment.pdf)).

At the level of workflows and the web, the W3C PROV standards (W3C Recommendations, begun in 2013) define provenance as information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing, with a data model (PROV-DM), an OWL2 ontology (PROV-O), and a textual notation (PROV-N) ([Wikipedia: W3C PROV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W3C_Prov)).

### Formal definition
**Lineage (Cui, Widom and Wiener).** For an operator $\mathrm{Op}$ over relations $R_1,\dots,R_n$ and an output record $t\in\mathrm{Op}(R_1,\dots,R_n)$, the lineage of $t$ is a tuple $\langle R_1',\dots,R_n'\rangle$ of subsets $R_i'\subseteq R_i$ such that (1) $\mathrm{Op}(R_1',\dots,R_n')=\{t\}$; (2) for each $i$ and each $t_i\in R_i'$, $\mathrm{Op}(R_1',\dots,R_{i-1}',\{t_i\},R_{i+1}',\dots,R_n')\ne\varnothing$; and (3) the tuple is maximal among those satisfying (1) and (2). Condition (1) makes the lineage relevant, (2) excludes irrelevant records, and (3) makes it complete ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)). Lineage is a **set** of input tuples.

**Why-provenance (Buneman, Khanna and Tan).** A witness for $t\in Q(I)$ is a subinstance sufficient to produce $t$; the number of witnesses can be exponential, so why-provenance is defined as a particular set of witnesses, the witness basis ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)). For positive relational algebra, $\mathrm{Why}(Q,D,t)$ is a **set of sets** of facts defined by structural recursion: base relations give $\{\{R_i(t)\}\}$ if $t\in r_i$; selection passes the set through when $t$ satisfies the condition; projection takes the union over all preimages; union takes the union of the two sets; join combines witnesses pairwise, $\mathcal S\Cup\mathcal T=\{S\cup T: S\in\mathcal S,\ T\in\mathcal T\}$ ([Chomicki, Buffalo CSE 636](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~chomicki/636/handout-provenance.pdf)).

**$K$-relations (Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen).** Let $(K,+,\cdot,0,1)$ be a commutative semiring. A $K$-relation over attributes $U$ is a function $R:U\text{-Tup}\to K$ with finite support. Union is $(R_1\cup R_2)(t)=R_1(t)+R_2(t)$; projection sums the annotations of all tuples restricting to $t$; selection is $(\sigma_PR)(t)=R(t)\cdot P(t)$ for a $\{0,1\}$-valued predicate $P$; natural join is $(R_1\bowtie R_2)(t)=R_1(t_1)\cdot R_2(t_2)$. The Booleans give set semantics, $(\mathbb N,+,\cdot,0,1)$ gives bag semantics, and the provenance semiring is the polynomial semiring $\mathbb N[X]$ over the set $X$ of tuple ids ([Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen 2007](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf)).

**The semiring hierarchy.** Over tuple ids $X$ ([Green 2011](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/tocs11_containment.pdf)):
- $\mathbb B[X]$: polynomials with Boolean coefficients, obtained from $\mathbb N[X]$ by dropping coefficients;
- $\mathrm{Trio}(X)$: the quotient of $\mathbb N[X]$ by the congruence that drops exponents, modelling the lineage of the Trio system;
- $\mathrm{Why}(X)=(\mathcal P(\mathcal P(X)),\cup,\Cup,\varnothing,\{\varnothing\})$: why-provenance, with pairwise union as multiplication;
- $\mathrm{PosBool}(X)$: irredundant sets of sets (no member contains another), the free distributive lattice on $X$, isomorphic to positive Boolean expressions; it computes the minimal witness basis;
- $\mathrm{Lin}(X)$: subsets of $X$ plus a bottom element, where both sum and product are union on ordinary elements; it captures the data-warehousing lineage of Cui et al.

**Where-provenance.** In the relational setting a location is a cell (a column of a tuple in a relation). The where-provenance of a value at location $l$ in $Q(D)$ is the set of locations of $D$ from which that value was copied according to $Q$ ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)).

**PROV-DM.** The core types are *entities* (things in a particular state), *activities* (processes that use and generate entities) and *agents* (people or software executions linked to activities), connected by relations including `used` (activity consumed an entity), `wasGeneratedBy` (entity produced by an activity), `wasDerivedFrom`, `wasAssociatedWith` and `wasAttributedTo` ([Wikipedia: W3C PROV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W3C_Prov)).

### Key results
- **Homomorphisms commute with queries.** For commutative semirings $K,K'$ and a map $h:K\to K'$, applying $h$ to annotations commutes with every positive relational algebra query, $q(h(R))=h(q(R))$, if and only if $h$ is a semiring homomorphism. ([Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen 2007](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf))
- **Universality of provenance polynomials.** For any commutative semiring $K$ and valuation $v:X\to K$ there is a unique semiring homomorphism $\mathrm{Eval}_v:\mathbb N[X]\to K$ extending $v$. Hence for every positive query $q$ and $K$-relation $R$ with abstractly tagged version $\bar R$, $q(R)=\mathrm{Eval}_v\circ q(\bar R)$: evaluation in any semiring factors through $\mathbb N[X]$. For Datalog the paper uses formal power series over commutative $\omega$-continuous semirings. ([Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen 2007](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf))
- **The hierarchy is a chain of surjective homomorphisms.** Dropping coefficients gives $\mathbb N[X]\to\mathbb B[X]$; dropping exponents gives $\mathbb N[X]\to\mathrm{Trio}(X)$ and $\mathbb B[X]\to\mathrm{Why}(X)$; dropping coefficients gives $\mathrm{Trio}(X)\to\mathrm{Why}(X)$; and flattening, $h(I)=\bigcup_{S\in I}S$, gives $\mathrm{Why}(X)\to\mathrm{Lin}(X)$. All are surjective semiring homomorphisms, which yields bounds on query containment between the models. Containment of conjunctive queries is NP-complete for each of these provenance semirings, and containment of unions of conjunctive queries is decidable for all of them; for $\mathbb N[X]$ and $\mathrm{Trio}(X)$ on UCQs only a PSPACE upper bound is given, and that paper leaves the exact complexity of $\mathbb N[X]$-containment of UCQs open. ([Green 2011](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/tocs11_containment.pdf))
- **Lineage versus why-provenance.** The flat powerset semiring $(\mathcal P(X),\cup,\cup,\varnothing,\varnothing)$ of Green et al. 2007, which that paper calls lineage/why-provenance, annotates each output with the set of all contributing input tuples ([Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen 2007](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf)). Green 2011 separates the two: the data-warehousing lineage of Cui et al., the set of all contributing source tuples, is captured by $\mathrm{Lin}(X)=(\mathcal P(X)\cup\{\bot\},+,\cdot,\bot,\varnothing)$, while Buneman-style why-provenance, the set of sets of contributing tuples, needs $\mathrm{Why}(X)$ ([Green 2011](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/tocs11_containment.pdf)). The witness-set form is recovered with $K=(\mathcal P(\mathcal P(\mathrm{Facts})),\cup,\Cup,\varnothing,\{\varnothing\})$ ([Chomicki, Buffalo CSE 636](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~chomicki/636/handout-provenance.pdf)). Lineage summarizes why-provenance by collecting all tuples mentioned in any witness, and can be obtained from why-provenance but not from minimal why-provenance ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)).
- **Witness basis and invariance.** For an SPJRU query $Q$, every witness for $t$ contains some element of $\mathrm{Why}(Q,I,t)$. The witness basis is not invariant under query equivalence, but the minimal witness basis is: if $Q\equiv Q'$ then $\mathrm{MWhy}(Q,I,t)=\mathrm{MWhy}(Q',I,t)$. Where-provenance is likewise not invariant under equivalent rewritings. ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf))
- **Difference via monus, and its limits.** A commutative monoid is naturally ordered if $a\le b\iff\exists c\,(a+c=b)$ is an order. An m-semiring (Geerts and Poggi) is a commutative semiring whose additive monoid is naturally ordered and has a monus, $a\mathbin{\dot-}b$ the smallest $c$ with $a\le b+c$; the monus is then determined by $+$. Amsterdamer, Deutch and Tannen show that the monus semantics fails one of the expected equivalence axioms in general, and that for some semirings every extension of the framework to difference must fail some of these axioms. ([Amsterdamer, Deutch and Tannen 2011](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1105.2255)) Geerts and Poggi's paper is "On database query languages for $K$-relations", *Journal of Applied Logic* 8(2), 2010 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Geerts+Poggi+On+database+query+languages+for+K-relations&rows=2)).
- **First-order logic with negation.** Grädel and Tannen extend semiring provenance to full first-order model checking, handling negation with a semiring of polynomials with dual indeterminates, and use it for reverse provenance analysis. ([Grädel and Tannen 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.01980))

### Examples
- **Three derivations.** Tag input tuples with ids $p,r,s$ and evaluate a query in $\mathbb N[p,r,s]$. The output $(d,e)$ gets provenance $2r^2+rs$. With bag multiplicities $p=2$, $r=5$, $s=1$, evaluating it in $\mathbb N$ gives $55$, the multiplicity of $(d,e)$ under bag semantics. In the flat powerset semiring, $(f,e)$ and $(d,e)$ both get $\{r,s\}$, although $(f,e)$ can be computed from $s$ alone and $(d,e)$ from $r$ alone. ([Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen 2007](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf))
- **Where-provenance of a copied value.** In a join of an `Agencies` table with an `ExternalTours` table on `name`, an output value "HarborCruz" has where-provenance $(t_2,\texttt{name})$ in `Agencies` because it was copied from that cell; rewriting the select clause to read the equal column of the other table changes the answer ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)).
- **Pipelines.** Coarse-grained lineage is captured per job and file, fine-grained lineage per task and record. Eager capture records full lineage at run time; lazy capture records coarse lineage and replays the dataflow on demand. Backward tracing finds the inputs of an output (debugging), and forward tracing finds the outputs of an input (error propagation). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_lineage))

- **ProvSQL** is a provenance-tracking and probabilistic database system built as a PostgreSQL extension, covering bag semantics, full relational algebra and aggregation, with generic provenance circuits stored in memory-mapped files ([Sen, Maniu and Senellart 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12058)).
- **Titian** adds data provenance to Apache Spark to find the input records behind a bug or outlier, with modest overhead (Interlandi et al., VLDB) ([Titian repository](https://github.com/UCLA-SEAL/Titian)).

### History
Cui, Widom and Wiener's "Tracing the lineage of view data in a warehousing environment" appeared in *ACM Transactions on Database Systems* 25(2), 2000 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/357775.357777)), and the survey describes their lineage model as apparently the first provenance model for relational queries defined by a semantic criterion ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)). Buneman, Khanna and Tan's "Why and Where: A Characterization of Data Provenance" appeared at ICDT 2001 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/3-540-44503-X_20)), and "Provenance semirings" by Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen at PODS 2007 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/1265530.1265535)). Green placed the provenance models in a hierarchy of semirings ([Green 2011](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/tocs11_containment.pdf)); Amsterdamer, Deutch and Tannen extended the framework to aggregates by annotating values inside tuples ([Amsterdamer, Deutch and Tannen, arXiv:1101.1110](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.1110)). The W3C PROV Recommendations date from 2013 ([Wikipedia: W3C PROV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W3C_Prov)).

### Connections
- [Databases](node:Databases): provenance is defined relative to queries over stored relations.
- [Reproducible Research Computing](node:Reproducible%20Research%20Computing): lineage records are what make computed results re-derivable.
- [Provenance Semirings](node:Provenance%20Semirings): the algebraic framework for how-provenance.
- [Semirings](node:Semirings): the algebraic structure annotations live in.
- [Distributive Lattices](node:Distributive%20Lattices): $\mathrm{PosBool}(X)$ is the free distributive lattice on the tuple ids.
- [Relational Algebra](node:Relational%20Algebra): the query language whose positive fragment the core theory covers.
- [Relational Data Model](node:Relational%20Data%20Model): tuples, attributes, and cells, the units provenance refers to.
- [Datalog](node:Datalog): recursive queries whose provenance uses formal power series.
- [Model Checking](node:Model%20Checking) and [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): semiring provenance extends to first-order model checking with negation.
- [Computational Workflow Systems](node:Computational%20Workflow%20Systems): workflow provenance at the level of jobs and files.
- [Workflow Dependency Graphs](node:Workflow%20Dependency%20Graphs): coarse-grained lineage as a dependency graph.
- [FAIR Data Principles](node:FAIR%20Data%20Principles): provenance metadata supports reuse of data.
- [Witness-First Scientific Workflows](node:Witness-First%20Scientific%20Workflows): workflows that record evidence for results as they are produced.

### Common pitfalls
- **"Lineage" means different things.** In industry it usually means dataset-level flow through pipelines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_lineage)); in database theory it is Cui et al.'s set of contributing tuples, a summary of why-provenance ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)).
- **The 2007 terminology conflates lineage and why-provenance.** Green et al. 2007 call $\mathcal P(X)$ "lineage/why-provenance" ([Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen 2007](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf)); the witness-basis notion is $\mathrm{Why}(X)$, a set of sets ([Green 2011](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/tocs11_containment.pdf)).
- **Provenance can depend on how a query is written.** Witness bases and where-provenance change under equivalent rewritings; only the minimal witness basis is invariant ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)).
- **Difference does not come for free.** Monus-based difference breaks expected query-equivalence axioms in general ([Amsterdamer, Deutch and Tannen 2011](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1105.2255)).

### Open problems
- **Negation and aggregation.** The survey states that further work is needed to understand provenance in the presence of negation and aggregation ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)). Later work addresses parts of this: aggregates via value-level annotation ([Amsterdamer, Deutch and Tannen, arXiv:1101.1110](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.1110)), negation in first-order logic via dual indeterminates ([Grädel and Tannen 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.01980)), while every semiring extension to difference fails some expected axioms for some semirings ([Amsterdamer, Deutch and Tannen 2011](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1105.2255)).
- **Updates, querying and optimization (as of the survey).** The design space of provenance for update languages was not well understood; there had been little work on querying provenance alongside data or presenting large provenance records usefully; and query optimization under eager provenance propagation had only begun to be studied ([Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf)).
- **Systems challenges.** For lineage in big-data systems: scalability, fault tolerance, capture for black-box operators, efficient tracing, sophisticated replay, and automated anomaly detection ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_lineage)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Data lineage (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_lineage): lineage versus provenance, capture strategies, tracing, and systems challenges.
- **Reference:** [W3C PROV (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W3C_Prov): PROV-DM, PROV-O, PROV-N and the core relations.
- **Learn:** [Chomicki, Data Integration: Provenance (University at Buffalo)](https://cse.buffalo.edu/~chomicki/636/handout-provenance.pdf): recursive definitions of why- and how-provenance and $K$-semirings.
- **Primary:** [Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen, Provenance Semirings (PODS 2007)](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/pods07.pdf): $K$-relations, $\mathbb N[X]$ and the factorization theorem.
- **Primary:** [Buneman, Khanna and Tan, Why and Where: A Characterization of Data Provenance (ICDT 2001)](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-44503-X_20): the origin of why- and where-provenance.
- **Primary:** [Green, Containment of Conjunctive Queries on Annotated Relations](https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~green/papers/tocs11_containment.pdf): the semiring hierarchy and containment complexity.
- **Primary:** [Amsterdamer, Deutch and Tannen, On the Limitations of Provenance for Queries With Difference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2255): monus semirings and impossibility results.
- **Further reading:** [Cheney, Chiticariu and Tan, Provenance in Databases: Why, How, and Where (Foundations and Trends in Databases)](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/jcheney/publications/provdbsurvey.pdf): monograph-length survey of why-, how-, and where-provenance.
references.Data Structures:
## Reference
### Overview
A data structure is a way to organize and store data, usually chosen for efficient access: concretely, a representation of the data in memory together with the operations (insertion, deletion, traversal, lookup) that act on it ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure)). It is distinguished from an abstract data type (ADT), which specifies only which operations are allowed and what they return; one ADT can have several implementations, as a list can be a linked list or a resizable array, and the implementations differ in cost ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure)).

Two memory layouts underlie almost everything: contiguous storage (arrays, records), which gives constant-time indexed access, and linked storage (lists, trees), which stores addresses of related elements and allows flexible resizing ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure)). Standard structures built from these include stacks and queues, hash tables, heaps, search trees, tries and graphs; databases use B-tree indexes and compilers use hash tables ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure)).

As a research area, data structures study upper and lower bounds for maintaining information under updates and queries. Current directions include persistence and retroactivity ("time travel"), geometric data, dynamic optimality of binary search trees, cache-oblivious structures for the memory hierarchy, hashing, integer structures beating logarithmic time, dynamic graph connectivity, string indexing, and succinct structures that use little space beyond the raw data ([MIT 6.851](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring21/)). Lower bounds for dynamic data structures are proved in the cell-probe model ([arXiv:cs/0502041](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0502041)), where cost is counted as accesses to memory words, for example words of $O(\log n)$ bits ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint-set_data_structure)).

### Formal definition
An **abstract data type** fixes a set of operations and their semantics; a **data structure** is an implementation of it, specifying memory representation and algorithms for each operation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure)). Costs are stated per operation as worst-case, expected, or amortized bounds in terms of the number $n$ of stored items.

**Heap property.** A min-heap is a rooted tree in which, for every parent $P$ and child $C$, $\mathrm{key}(P)\le\mathrm{key}(C)$; a max-heap reverses the inequality, so the root holds the minimum (resp. maximum) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heap_%28data_structure%29)).

**Load factor.** For a hash table storing $n$ pairs in $m$ buckets, the load factor is
$$\alpha=\frac{n}{m},$$
and performance is governed by $\alpha$: open addressing needs resizing as $\alpha\to1$ (typical $\alpha_{\max}\approx0.6$–$0.75$), while separate chaining degrades gradually (typical $\alpha_{\max}$ between 1 and 3) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table)).

**Disjoint sets.** A disjoint-set (union-find) structure maintains a partition of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ under MakeSet, Union and Find ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint-set_data_structure)).

### Key results
- **Binary heaps.** An array-stored binary heap supports find-min in $\Theta(1)$ and insert and delete-min in $\Theta(\log n)$ worst case; Floyd's heapify builds a heap from an unsorted array in $\Theta(n)$, versus $O(n\log n)$ by repeated insertion. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heap_%28data_structure%29))
- **Fibonacci heaps (Fredman-Tarjan).** Insert, find-min, decrease-key and merge take $\Theta(1)$ amortized time and delete-min $O(\log n)$ amortized; consequently Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms run in $O(|E|+|V|\log|V|)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_heap))
- **Hash tables.** With well-distributed hash values, search, insert and delete take $\Theta(1)$ on average and $O(n)$ in the worst case; resizing (reallocating at double the size and rehashing) keeps lookups and insertions $O(1)$ amortized. Cuckoo hashing, with two tables and two hash functions, guarantees $O(1)$ worst-case lookup and constant amortized insertion. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table))
- **Union-find upper and lower bounds.** With path compression (or splitting/halving) and union by size or rank, any sequence of $m$ operations of which at most $n$ are MakeSet costs $\Theta(m\,\alpha(n))$, where $\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function (Tarjan; Tarjan-van Leeuwen). Fredman and Saks (1989) proved that any disjoint-set structure must make $\Omega(\alpha(n))$ amortized accesses to words of $O(\log n)$ bits per operation, so the bound is optimal in the cell-probe model. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint-set_data_structure))
- **Splay trees (Sleator-Tarjan 1985).** Search, insert and delete take $O(\log n)$ amortized time (a single operation can take $O(n)$). Over an access sequence of length $m$ in which element $x$ is accessed $q_x$ times, the total cost is $O\big(m+\sum_x q_x\log(m/q_x)\big)$ (static optimality); the working-set theorem bounds the total cost by $O\big(m+n\log n+\sum\log(t(x)+1)\big)$, with $t(x)$ the number of distinct elements accessed since $x$'s previous access, and the dynamic-finger theorem gives a bound, up to linear terms, of $\sum\log(|y-x|+1)$ over consecutive accesses $x,y$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splay_tree))
- **Logarithmic cell-probe lower bounds (Pătraşcu-Demaine).** For dynamic partial sums and dynamic connectivity (on paths, forests and graphs), any data structure needs $\Omega(\log n)$ amortized randomized cell probes per operation; this shows Sleator-Tarjan dynamic trees are optimal, and gives matching upper and lower bounds for partial sums parameterized by word size. ([arXiv:cs/0502041](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0502041))

### Examples
- **Arrays versus linked lists.** Arrays give constant-time access by index from contiguous memory; linked lists trade this for cheap insertion and resizing through stored addresses ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure)).
- **Priority queues.** Binary heaps, introduced by J. W. J. Williams in 1964 for heapsort, are stored in arrays with parent-child links implied by indices ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heap_%28data_structure%29)).
- **Hash tables with collisions.** Separate chaining keeps a list per bucket; open addressing stores entries in the array and probes linearly, quadratically or by double hashing ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table)).

### History
Hans Peter Luhn used hashing with chaining in an internal IBM memorandum of January 1953 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table)), and Williams introduced the binary heap in 1964 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heap_%28data_structure%29)). Tarjan proved the inverse-Ackermann bound for union-find in 1975 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint-set_data_structure)); Fredman and Tarjan developed Fibonacci heaps in 1984, published in 1987 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_heap)); Sleator and Tarjan introduced splay trees in 1985 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splay_tree)). Tarjan's monograph *Data Structures and Network Algorithms* was published by SIAM in 1983 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9781611970265)). Pătraşcu and Demaine broke the $\Omega(\lg n/\lg\lg n)$ barrier for dynamic cell-probe lower bounds in 2005 ([arXiv:cs/0502041](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0502041)).

### Connections
- [Asymptotic Analysis](node:Asymptotic%20Analysis): operation costs are stated asymptotically.
- [Amortized Analysis](node:Amortized%20Analysis): the method behind bounds for dynamic arrays, splay trees, Fibonacci heaps and union-find.
- [Hash Tables](node:Hash%20Tables), [Heaps and Priority Queues](node:Heaps%20and%20Priority%20Queues), [Search Trees](node:Search%20Trees), [B-Trees](node:B-Trees), [Tries](node:Tries), [Suffix Arrays](node:Suffix%20Arrays), [Bloom Filters](node:Bloom%20Filters), [Disjoint-Set Union](node:Disjoint-Set%20Union): individual structures.
- [Dijkstra's Algorithm](node:Dijkstra's%20Algorithm): its running time depends on the priority queue used.
- [Sorting and Searching](node:Sorting%20and%20Searching): heapsort and search trees connect sorting to data structures.
- [Database Indexing](node:Database%20Indexing): B-trees and hash indexes in databases.
- [Memory Hierarchies](node:Memory%20Hierarchies): cache-efficient and cache-oblivious structures.

### Common pitfalls
- **Amortized is not worst case.** A splay-tree operation has $O(\log n)$ amortized cost but a single operation can take $O(n)$ time ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splay_tree)); a hash table is $\Theta(1)$ on average but $O(n)$ in the worst case ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table)).
- **ADT versus implementation.** Statements such as "lists support $O(1)$ indexing" are about a particular implementation, not the ADT ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure)).
- **Lower bounds are model-specific.** The Fredman-Saks union-find bound holds in the cell-probe model, not for every conceivable algorithm ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint-set_data_structure)).

### Open problems
- **Dynamic optimality conjecture.** Sleator and Tarjan conjectured that splay trees perform within a constant factor of any binary search tree algorithm on every access sequence; it is unproven ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splay_tree)). MIT 6.851 describes whether a single binary search tree can be optimal as still unknown ([MIT 6.851](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring21/)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Data structure (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure): definition, ADTs, memory layouts, common structures.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 6.851 Advanced Data Structures (Demaine)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-851-advanced-data-structures-spring-2012/): graduate lectures on major results and research directions.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.851 Spring 2021 course page](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring21/): topic overview including open problems.
- **Primary:** [Pătraşcu and Demaine, Logarithmic Lower Bounds in the Cell-Probe Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0502041): $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bounds for dynamic partial sums and connectivity.
- **Further reading:** [Tarjan, Data Structures and Network Algorithms (SIAM, 1983)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9781611970265): monograph by a co-inventor of several structures above (splay trees, Fibonacci heaps, union-find analysis).
references.Databases:
## Reference
### Overview
A database system stores a large, shared collection of data and answers queries against it, while keeping the data consistent under concurrent use and failures. The dominant formal basis is the relational model, introduced by E. F. Codd in "A relational model of data for large shared data banks" (*Communications of the ACM* 13(6), 377–387, 1970), in which data are organised as relations (sets of tuples over named attributes) and queries return relations ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/362384.362685); [Wikipedia: Relational model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_model)).

The subject splits into a logical side and a systems side. On the logical side, query languages are fragments of [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): relational calculus is essentially first-order logic, relational algebra is equivalent to its domain-independent fragment (Codd's theorem), and conjunctive queries form the select-project-join core whose containment and evaluation are NP-complete in combined complexity ([Wikipedia: Codd's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codd%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Conjunctive query](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjunctive_query)). On the systems side, a standard course covers storage, indexes, join algorithms, query execution and optimisation, concurrency control (two-phase locking, timestamp ordering, [multi-version concurrency control](node:Multi-Version%20Concurrency%20Control)), logging and recovery ([CMU 15-445 schedule](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/schedule.html)).

Transactions tie the two sides together. The ACID properties (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) specify what a transaction must guarantee, and serializability makes isolation precise: a concurrent schedule is correct if its effect equals that of some serial execution ([Wikipedia: ACID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACID); [Wikipedia: Serializability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serializability)).

### Formal definition
**Relations and keys.** A header $H$ is a finite set of attribute names; a relation is a pair $(H,B)$ whose body $B$ is a set of tuples over $H$. A relation schema adds a predicate every admissible relation must satisfy. A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each tuple, and a foreign key is an attribute set required to match a key of another relation ([Wikipedia: Relational model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_model)).

**Functional dependencies and normal forms.** A functional dependency $X\to Y$ holds in a relation if tuples agreeing on $X$ agree on $Y$. Armstrong's axioms are reflexivity ($Y\subseteq X\Rightarrow X\to Y$), augmentation ($X\to Y\Rightarrow XZ\to YZ$) and transitivity ($X\to Y,\ Y\to Z\Rightarrow X\to Z$) ([Wikipedia: Armstrong's axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armstrong%27s_axioms)). A relation is in Boyce–Codd normal form if for every functional dependency $X\to Y$, either the dependency is trivial or $X$ is a superkey ([Wikipedia: BCNF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyce%E2%80%93Codd_normal_form)).

**Conjunctive queries.** A conjunctive query (CQ) has the form $q(\bar x)\;\text{:-}\;R_1(\bar u_1),\dots,R_k(\bar u_k)$, meaning $\{\bar x:\exists\bar y\,\bigwedge_iR_i(\bar u_i)\}$. The canonical database $D[q]$ has one fact per body atom. A homomorphism from $q_2$ to $q_1$ maps the variables of $q_2$ to terms of $q_1$, sending every atom of $q_2$ to an atom of $q_1$ and head to head. $q_1\subseteq q_2$ means $q_1(I)\subseteq q_2(I)$ for every instance $I$ ([Wisconsin CS 784, Lecture 2](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture2.pdf)).

**Acyclicity.** An *ear* of a hypergraph is a hyperedge whose vertices either occur only in it or lie in one other hyperedge; the GYO algorithm repeatedly deletes ears, and a CQ is acyclic if GYO empties its hypergraph. Equivalently, it has a join tree: a tree on the atoms in which every variable shared by two atoms occurs on the path between them ([Wisconsin CS 784, Lecture 4](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture4.pdf)).

**Schedules.** Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same object, and at least one is a write. A schedule is conflict-serializable if adjacent non-conflicting swaps turn it into a serial schedule; its precedence graph has an edge $T_i\to T_j$ when an operation of $T_i$ conflicts with and precedes one of $T_j$ ([Wikipedia: Serializability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serializability)). Under two-phase locking (2PL) a transaction acquires locks in a growing phase and releases them in a shrinking phase, never acquiring after releasing ([Wikipedia: Two-phase locking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_locking)). Under snapshot isolation each transaction reads a consistent snapshot taken at its start and commits only if its writes do not conflict with concurrent updates ([Wikipedia: Snapshot isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapshot_isolation)).

### Key results
- **Codd's theorem.** Relational algebra and domain-independent relational calculus have the same expressive power. It does not cover SQL's nulls or multisets, and relationally complete languages cannot express counting or transitive closure. ([Wikipedia: Codd's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codd%27s_theorem))
- **Homomorphism theorem (Chandra–Merlin 1977).** For CQs $q_1,q_2$ the following are equivalent: (1) $q_1\subseteq q_2$; (2) there is a homomorphism from $q_2$ to $q_1$; (3) $\mathrm{head}(q_1)\in q_2(D[q_1])$. Hence CQ containment is NP-complete, by reduction from 3-colourability. For unions of CQs, $q\subseteq q'$ iff each disjunct of $q$ is contained in some disjunct of $q'$ (Sagiv–Yannakakis 1980), and every CQ has a minimal equivalent obtained by deleting atoms, unique up to isomorphism. Containment for full relational algebra is undecidable by Trakhtenbrot's theorem. ([Wisconsin CS 784, Lecture 2](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture2.pdf))
- **Data versus combined complexity.** With the query fixed, CQ evaluation is in $\mathrm{AC}^0$; acyclic CQs (hypertree-width 1) have polynomial combined complexity, and evaluation and containment for them are LOGCFL-complete. ([Wikipedia: Conjunctive query](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjunctive_query))
- **Yannakakis's algorithm (1981).** A CQ is acyclic iff it admits a *full reducer*, a finite sequence of semijoins $R\ltimes S=\pi_{\mathrm{att}(R)}(R\bowtie S)$ removing all dangling tuples; the triangle query has none. Applying a full reducer and then joining bottom-up along a join tree, projecting onto $\mathrm{var}(R)\cup\mathrm{head}(q)$ after each join, evaluates an acyclic CQ in time polynomial in the query, input and output ([Wisconsin CS 784, Lecture 4](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture4.pdf)), essentially linear in input plus output ([Ngo–Ré–Rudra survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.3314)).
- **AGM bound and worst-case optimal joins.** For a natural join $Q$ with hypergraph $(V,E)$ and any fractional edge cover $x$ ($x_F\ge0$, $\sum_{F\ni v}x_F\ge1$ for all $v$), $|Q|\le\prod_{F\in E}|R_F|^{x_F}$. For some query classes, such as the Loomis–Whitney joins, every join-project plan runs polynomially slower than the AGM bound on worst-case instances ([Ngo–Ré–Rudra survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1310.3314)); Ngo, Porat, Ré and Rudra gave an algorithm that is worst-case optimal for all natural joins ([arXiv:1203.1952](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.1952)).
- **Armstrong's axioms are sound and complete.** They derive exactly the closure $F^+$ of functional dependencies implied by $F$ ([Wikipedia: Armstrong's axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armstrong%27s_axioms)). The chase decides, for instance, whether a decomposition under given FDs is lossless, and its result does not depend on the order of steps ([Wikipedia: Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chase_%28algorithm%29)). BCNF cannot always be reached while preserving dependencies: $\{AB\to C,\ C\to B\}$ has no dependency-preserving BCNF schema (Beeri–Bernstein) ([Wikipedia: BCNF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyce%E2%80%93Codd_normal_form)).
- **Precedence-graph test.** A schedule is conflict-serializable iff its precedence graph over committed transactions is acyclic; conflict-serializable schedules are view-serializable, not conversely. ([Wikipedia: Serializability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serializability))
- **Two-phase locking.** 2PL schedules are conflict-serializable; strict 2PL (write locks held to commit or abort) gives strict, cascadeless schedules; 2PL can deadlock unless all locks are taken up front (conservative 2PL). ([Wikipedia: Two-phase locking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_locking))
- **Snapshot isolation is not serializable.** Berenson et al. showed that the ANSI SQL-92 phenomena (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms) fail to characterise common isolation levels, and defined snapshot isolation ([Berenson et al. 1995](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)); SI avoids the ANSI anomalies but admits write skew, and serializable SI (Cahill et al. 2008) aborts dangerous patterns ([Wikipedia: Snapshot isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapshot_isolation)).
- **ARIES recovery.** For a steal/no-force buffer policy, ARIES uses write-ahead logging, repeats history during redo, and logs undo actions as compensation log records, recovering in three passes: analysis, redo, undo ([Wikipedia: ARIES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics)).
- **Cost-based optimisation.** Following System R, optimisers choose join orders by dynamic programming: best access path per relation, then best two-relation plans, then larger plans, keeping the cheapest plan for each useful sort order. Costs rest on cardinality estimates, whose errors are a main cause of bad plans. ([Wikipedia: Query optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Query_optimization))

### Examples
- **Containment by homomorphism.** For $q_1(x,y)$ :- $R(x,y),S(y,y),R(y,w)$ and $q_1'(x,y)$ :- $R(x,y),S(y,z),R(z,w)$, the map $z\mapsto y$ (identity elsewhere) is a homomorphism from $q_1'$ to $q_1$, so $q_1\subseteq q_1'$ ([Wisconsin CS 784, Lecture 2](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture2.pdf)).
- **Triangle join.** $x_R=x_S=x_T=\tfrac12$ in the AGM bound gives $|R\bowtie S\bowtie T|\le\sqrt{|R||S||T|}=N^{3/2}$ for relations of size $N$ ([Ngo–Ré–Rudra survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.3314)).
- **Write skew.** A customer has two accounts of 100 dollars each and the rule is that the combined balance stays non-negative; two concurrent transactions each withdraw 200 dollars, one from each account, and both commit under SI, leaving a combined balance of $-200$ ([Wikipedia: Snapshot isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapshot_isolation)).
- **Lossless decomposition.** $R(A,B,C,D)$ with $A\to B$, $B\to C$, $CD\to A$ decomposed into $\{A,D\},\{A,C\},\{B,C,D\}$: the chase produces a row equal to the original tuple, so the decomposition is lossless ([Wikipedia: Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chase_%28algorithm%29)).

### History
Codd described the relational model in 1969 and published it in 1970 ([Wikipedia: Relational model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_model)); the equivalence behind Codd's theorem was implicit in Chin and Tarski (1948) and Tarski and Thompson (1952), and Codd's 1972 paper coined "relationally complete" ([Wikipedia: Codd's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codd%27s_theorem)). Armstrong's axioms date from 1974 ([Wikipedia: Armstrong's axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armstrong%27s_axioms)). Chandra and Merlin settled CQ containment at STOC 1977 ([Wisconsin CS 784, Lecture 2](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture2.pdf)); Selinger et al.'s "Access path selection in a relational database management system" appeared at SIGMOD 1979 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/582095.582099)); Yannakakis's "Algorithms for acyclic database schemes" at VLDB 1981 ([Wisconsin CS 784, Lecture 4](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture4.pdf)). Reuter and Härder coined ACID in 1983 ([Wikipedia: ACID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACID)). ARIES appeared in *ACM TODS* 17(1), 1992 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/128765.128770)), and the critique of ANSI isolation levels at SIGMOD 1995 ([Berenson et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)). Worst-case optimal joins date from 2012 ([arXiv:1203.1952](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.1952)).

### Connections
- [Relational Data Model](node:Relational%20Data%20Model) and [Relational Algebra](node:Relational%20Algebra): the data model and operator language.
- [SQL](node:SQL): the practical language, which departs from the model through duplicates, ordered columns and nulls.
- [Finite Model Theory](node:Finite%20Model%20Theory) and [Descriptive Complexity](node:Descriptive%20Complexity): query expressiveness and Trakhtenbrot-style undecidability.
- [Datalog](node:Datalog): adds recursion, capturing transitive closure.
- [Constraint Satisfaction Problems](node:Constraint%20Satisfaction%20Problems): CQ containment is the same problem as CSP.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): the complexity of CQ containment and evaluation.
- [Join Algorithms](node:Join%20Algorithms) and [Database Query Optimization](node:Database%20Query%20Optimization): Yannakakis, AGM, cost-based optimisers.
- [B-Trees](node:B-Trees), [Database Indexing](node:Database%20Indexing), [Data Structures](node:Data%20Structures): index structures.
- [Database Transactions and Query Processing](node:Database%20Transactions%20and%20Query%20Processing), [Database Isolation Levels](node:Database%20Isolation%20Levels), [Write-Ahead Logging](node:Write-Ahead%20Logging), [Deadlock Detection and Avoidance](node:Deadlock%20Detection%20and%20Avoidance): transaction processing and recovery.
- [Database Normalization](node:Database%20Normalization): schema design from functional dependencies.
- [Data Provenance and Lineage](node:Data%20Provenance%20and%20Lineage): annotating query answers with their derivations.
- [Distributed Transactions](node:Distributed%20Transactions): transactions across sites.

### Common pitfalls
- **SQL is not the relational model.** SQL tables may have duplicate rows, ordered columns and nulls, so results proved for set semantics need not hold for SQL ([Wikipedia: Relational model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_model); [Wikipedia: Codd's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codd%27s_theorem)).
- **Direction of the homomorphism.** For $q_1\subseteq q_2$ the homomorphism goes from $q_2$ to $q_1$ ([Wisconsin CS 784, Lecture 2](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture2.pdf)).
- **"Serializable" may mean SI.** Oracle and PostgreSQL before 9.1 labelled snapshot isolation "serializable", although it permits write skew ([Wikipedia: Snapshot isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapshot_isolation)).
- **2PL is not deadlock-free.** It guarantees conflict-serializability, but not freedom from deadlock, and unlike strict 2PL it does not guarantee strict (cascadeless) schedules ([Wikipedia: Two-phase locking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_locking)).

### Open problems
- **Bag-semantics CQ containment.** Chaudhuri and Vardi (1993) observed that the set-semantics theory does not carry over to bag semantics, which SQL uses. Marcinkowski and Orda (PODS 2024, *Proc. ACM Manag. Data* 2(2)) call its decidability "one of the most intriguing open questions in database theory" and prove undecidability for several generalisations ([arXiv:2503.18003](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18003)).
- **Worst-case optimal joins in general-purpose systems.** In 2013 Ngo, Ré and Rudra posed as open whether worst-case optimal join ideas yield runtime gains in database systems, given decades of engineering of binary-join plans ([Ngo–Ré–Rudra survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.3314)). Later systems report gains. Worst-case optimal joins have been implemented in commercial systems, including LogicBlox ([Wikipedia: Worst-case optimal join algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worst-case_optimal_join_algorithm)). EmptyHeaded, a graph engine built around this new class of join algorithms with strong theoretical guarantees, outperforms high-level approaches by up to three orders of magnitude on graph pattern queries ([Aberger et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02368)). Freitag et al. give a hash-based worst-case optimal join for general-purpose relational systems, with a hybrid optimiser that combines binary and multi-way joins in one plan, and report that it far outperforms existing systems when such joins help while losing no performance when they do not ([Freitag et al., PVLDB 13(11), 2020](https://15721.courses.cs.cmu.edu/spring2024/papers/10-multiwayjoins/p1891-freitag.pdf); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.14778/3407790.3407797)). The survey's second open question, for theoreticians, notes that worst-case results may only describe pathological instances and asks for guarantees beyond the worst case ([Ngo–Ré–Rudra survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.3314)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Relational model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_model): relations, keys, operators, SQL deviations.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Conjunctive query](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjunctive_query): complexity of evaluation, containment, acyclicity, width.
- **Learn:** [Wisconsin CS 784 (Koutris), Lecture 2: Query Containment](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture2.pdf) and [Lecture 4: Acyclic Conjunctive Queries](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~paris/cs784-s17/lectures/lecture4.pdf): homomorphism theorem, GYO, full reducers, Yannakakis.
- **Learn:** [CMU 15-445/645 Intro to Database Systems](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/schedule.html): storage, indexes, joins, optimisation, concurrency control, logging and recovery.
- **Primary:** [Codd, A relational model of data for large shared data banks (CACM 1970)](https://doi.org/10.1145/362384.362685): the founding paper.
- **Primary:** [Mohan et al., ARIES (ACM TODS 1992)](https://doi.org/10.1145/128765.128770): the standard recovery method.
- **Primary:** [Berenson et al., A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157): isolation phenomena and snapshot isolation.
- **Primary:** [Ngo, Porat, Ré, Rudra, Worst-case Optimal Join Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.1952): the first worst-case optimal join algorithm.
- **Primary:** [Ngo, Ré, Rudra, Skew Strikes Back](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.3314): survey of the AGM bound and worst-case optimal joins.
- **Further reading:** [Abiteboul, Hull and Vianu, Foundations of Databases (Addison-Wesley, 1995)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL3483918W): the standard theory text, cited as the reference for proofs in the Wisconsin course.
- **Further reading:** [Arenas, Barceló, Libkin, Martens, Pieris, Principles of Databases](https://github.com/pdm-book/community): a book on the foundations of databases, released in parts with a full PDF, one chapter per lecture.
references.Deep Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Deep learning is the branch of machine learning that trains [neural networks](node:Artificial%20Neural%20Networks) with many layers, from three to thousands, for classification, regression, and representation learning. Its distinctive feature is that features are learned from data rather than hand-crafted: successive layers build increasingly abstract representations (in an image model: simple shapes, then arrangements of edges, then facial parts, then a whole face). Depth is measured by the credit assignment path, the chain of transformations from input to output; most researchers regard a CAP depth above two as deep. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning))

In practice a deep-learning algorithm minimizes an empirical risk over a network hypothesis class with [SGD](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent) or a variant, using gradients from [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation); the output is the network at the final (or averaged) iterate. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026)) Making this work for very deep networks required engineering of initialization, normalization, and architecture. Deeper networks are harder to train, and residual learning was introduced to ease the training of substantially deeper networks ([He et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385)); batch [normalization](node:Normalization%20in%20Neural%20Networks) permits higher learning rates and less careful initialization ([Ioffe and Szegedy 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167)); and variance-preserving initializations counter vanishing and exploding gradients ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/numerical-stability-and-init.html)).

AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton) won the large-scale ImageNet competition in 2012 by a significant margin over shallow machine-learning methods, and efficient GPU implementations of CNNs drove the growth of deep learning in the 2010s; Bengio, Hinton, and LeCun received the 2018 Turing Award for this work. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning)) Its theory lags its practice: why overparametrized networks generalize, what depth buys, and why non-convex optimization succeeds remain open. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026))

### Formal definition
**Learning setup.** Given training data $s=(z^{(i)})_{i=1}^m$, a loss $\mathcal L$, and a network architecture $a$ with realization $\Phi_a(\cdot,\theta)$, deep learning approximately solves $\min_\theta \widehat{\mathcal R}_s(\Phi_a(\cdot,\theta))=\frac1m\sum_{i}\mathcal L(\Phi_a(\cdot,\theta),z^{(i)})$ by mini-batch SGD,
