$$\Theta^{(k)}=\Theta^{(k-1)}-\frac{\eta_k}{m'}\sum_{z\in S'}\nabla_\theta\mathcal L\big(\Phi_a(\cdot,\Theta^{(k-1)}),z\big),$$
where $S'$ is a random mini-batch of size $m'$ and $(\eta_k)$ is the learning rate; an architecture is deep when it has $L>2$ layers. ([Berner et al. 2021, Def. 1.4 and eq. 1.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

**Residual block.** $f(x)=x+g(x)$, where the layers learn the residual $g=f-\mathrm{id}$; learning the identity reduces to driving $g$ to zero. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-modern/resnet.html); [He et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385))

**Batch normalization.** $\mathrm{BN}(x)=\gamma\odot\frac{x-\hat\mu_B}{\hat\sigma_B}+\beta$, with mini-batch mean $\hat\mu_B$, standard deviation $\hat\sigma_B$ (variance offset by a small $\epsilon$), and learned $\gamma,\beta$; at prediction time fixed population estimates replace batch statistics. Layer normalization instead normalizes within a single example, so it does not depend on batch size. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-modern/batch-norm.html))

**Xavier (Glorot) initialization.** For a layer with fan-in $n_{\rm in}$ and fan-out $n_{\rm out}$, draw weights with variance $\sigma^2=2/(n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out})$, e.g. $U\big(-\sqrt{6/(n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out})},\sqrt{6/(n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out})}\big)$. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/numerical-stability-and-init.html))

### Key results
- **Variance propagation.** For a linear layer with independent zero-mean weights of variance $\sigma^2$ and inputs of variance $\gamma^2$, outputs have variance $n_{\rm in}\sigma^2\gamma^2$; preserving forward variance needs $n_{\rm in}\sigma^2=1$, preserving backward gradient variance needs $n_{\rm out}\sigma^2=1$, and Xavier initialization averages the two. The gradient of an $L$-layer network is a product of $L$ Jacobian-type matrices, which explains vanishing and exploding gradients. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/numerical-stability-and-init.html)) Glorot and Bengio showed that logistic sigmoids with random initialization drive top hidden units into saturation and proposed this scheme. ([Glorot and Bengio 2010](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v9/glorot10a.html)) He et al. derived an initialization for rectifiers that allows extremely deep rectified models to be trained from scratch. ([He et al. 2015b](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01852))
- **Residual learning.** Residual networks with up to 152 layers are easier to optimize than plain networks and gain accuracy from depth; an ensemble reached 3.57% top-5 error on ImageNet and won ILSVRC 2015 classification. ([He et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385)) Only when larger function classes contain the smaller ones is enlarging them guaranteed to increase expressive power; a residual block that can learn the identity makes the enlarged class contain the old one. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-modern/resnet.html))
- **Batch normalization.** Normalizing layer inputs per mini-batch permits much higher learning rates, reduces sensitivity to initialization, and matched a state-of-the-art image classifier's accuracy in 14 times fewer training steps. ([Ioffe and Szegedy 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167))
- **Neural tangent kernel (Jacot–Gabriel–Hongler 2018).** In the infinite-width limit the NTK of a network converges to an explicit deterministic kernel and stays constant during training; for least squares the network function then follows a linear ODE, and the limiting kernel is positive definite when data lie on the sphere and the nonlinearity is non-polynomial. ([Jacot et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07572))
- **Benefits of depth.** For every positive integer $k$ there are networks with $\Theta(k^3)$ layers, $\Theta(1)$ nodes per layer and $\Theta(1)$ distinct parameters that networks with $O(k)$ layers can approximate only if they have $\Omega(2^k)$ nodes; the result holds for "semi-algebraic gates", a class including ReLU, maximum, indicator and piecewise-polynomial units. ([Telgarsky 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04485))
- **Memorization.** State-of-the-art image classifiers trained by stochastic gradient methods easily fit a random labeling of the training data, even when the images are replaced by random noise, with explicit [regularization](node:Regularization) not changing this qualitatively. ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530))
- **Empirical scaling laws.** For language models, [cross-entropy loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss) falls as a power law in parameters, data, and compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude, with width/depth mattering little within a wide range. ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)) Hoffmann et al., training over 400 models, found that compute-optimal training scales parameters and tokens equally; their 70B Chinchilla, trained on about four times more data than the 280B Gopher with the same compute, outperformed it. ([Hoffmann et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556))

### Examples
- **ImageNet classification.** AlexNet (2012) began the deep-learning era ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning)); PReLU networks reached 4.94% top-5 error in 2015, which the authors report as the first result below the 5.1% human-level estimate ([He et al. 2015b](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01852)).
- **Architectures.** Fully connected networks, [Convolutional Neural Networks](node:Convolutional%20Neural%20Networks), [Recurrent Neural Networks](node:Recurrent%20Neural%20Networks), [generative adversarial networks](node:Generative%20Adversarial%20Networks), and [Transformers](node:Transformers) are the main deep architectures. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning))

### History
Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958) and Ivakhnenko and Lapa's group method of data handling (1965) are early milestones; Fukushima introduced the ReLU in 1969; backpropagation was popularized in 1986 and LeNet (1989) applied convolutional networks to digits; GPU training (Raina, Madhavan, Ng 2009) and AlexNet (2012) triggered the modern era; ResNets (2015) addressed degradation in very deep networks. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning)) LeCun, Bengio, and Hinton's 2015 review "Deep learning" appeared in *Nature* 521, 436–444. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/nature14539))

### Connections
- [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation) and [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent): the gradient computation and optimizer underlying training.
- [Residual Networks](node:Residual%20Networks) and [Normalization in Neural Networks](node:Normalization%20in%20Neural%20Networks): the main tools that make depth trainable.
- [Universal Approximation Theorem](node:Universal%20Approximation%20Theorem): expressivity of networks, motivating depth–width questions.
- [Neural Tangent Kernel](node:Neural%20Tangent%20Kernel): the infinite-width linearized limit.
- [Generalization in Deep Learning](node:Generalization%20in%20Deep%20Learning) and [Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent](node:Implicit%20Bias%20of%20Gradient%20Descent): attempts to explain why trained networks generalize.
- [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): empirical regularities of loss in model size, data, and compute.
- [Adaptive Optimizers](node:Adaptive%20Optimizers) and [Dropout](node:Dropout): standard training components.
- [Supervised Learning](node:Supervised%20Learning): the most common setting in which deep networks are trained.

### Common pitfalls
- **"Deep" is not a sharp threshold.** There is no universal depth cutoff; CAP depth above two is a convention. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning))
- **Initialization by constants.** If all hidden weights start equal, units stay identical under gradient updates; random initialization is needed to break the symmetry. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/numerical-stability-and-init.html))
- **Train/test mode.** Batch normalization behaves differently in training and prediction, using batch versus population statistics. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-modern/batch-norm.html))
- **Scaling laws are empirical fits.** They are measured regularities for particular model families and setups, and the two major studies reach different conclusions on how to allocate a fixed compute budget between model size and data. ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361); [Hoffmann et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556))

> [!warning] Contested
> Why batch normalization works is disputed. Ioffe and Szegedy attributed it to reducing "internal covariate shift" ([Ioffe and Szegedy 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167)); d2l summarizes Santurkar et al. (2018) as finding that it succeeds despite behaviour in some ways opposite to that explanation ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-modern/batch-norm.html)).

### Open problems
- **The generalization puzzle.** Overparametrized networks interpolate (even noisy) training data yet generalize, and further overparametrization can improve test error, so classical uniform bounds do not explain performance; Berner et al. list this among the open questions of deep-learning theory. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Depth, dimension, and optimization.** Whether depth has a mathematically quantifiable general benefit, why networks escape the curse of dimensionality, why SGD finds good minima of non-convex risks, which features are learned, and which architectural details matter are posed as questions not answered by classical learning theory. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Deep learning, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning): definition, history, architectures.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning: Numerical Stability and Initialization](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/numerical-stability-and-init.html), [Batch Normalization](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-modern/batch-norm.html), [ResNet](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-modern/resnet.html): derivations with code.
- **Primary:** [He, Zhang, Ren, Sun, Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385): residual networks.
- **Primary:** [Berner, Grohs, Kutyniok, Petersen, The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026): survey of deep-learning theory and its open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press 2016)](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/): the standard graduate text.

## Reference
### Overview
A density matrix (density operator, statistical operator) is the general description of the state of a quantum system. It extends state vectors, which describe only pure states, to statistical mixtures, and it is the object from which all measurement probabilities are computed ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix)). For an ensemble in which $|\psi_j\rangle$ is prepared with probability $p_j$, the density operator is $\rho=\sum_j p_j|\psi_j\rangle\langle\psi_j|$, and every expectation value is $\langle A\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A\rho)$ ([Lancaster PHYS223 notes](https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/people/schomeru/lecturenotes/Quantum%20Mechanics/S20.html)).

Density matrices are unavoidable for subsystems. If a composite system is in an entangled pure state, no state vector describes one part alone; its local statistics are given by the reduced density matrix obtained by the partial trace ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix); [Lancaster PHYS223 notes](https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/people/schomeru/lecturenotes/Quantum%20Mechanics/S20.html)). Conversely, every mixed state can be viewed as the reduced state of a pure state on a larger system, a purification, which Smolin called "the doctrine of the Church of the larger Hilbert space" ([Steck, Oregon PHYS 610 notes](https://atomoptics.uoregon.edu/~dsteck/teaching/09spring/phys610/notes/entanglement.pdf)). Tracing out an environment that has become entangled with a system suppresses the off-diagonal coherences of the reduced state, a simple model of [decoherence](node:Decoherence) ([Steck, Oregon PHYS 610 notes](https://atomoptics.uoregon.edu/~dsteck/teaching/09spring/phys610/notes/entanglement.pdf); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/density+matrix)).

Density matrices are therefore the basic language of open quantum systems, [quantum information](node:Quantum%20Information) and [quantum statistical mechanics](node:Quantum%20Statistical%20Mechanics), where von Neumann entropy and entanglement are defined on them ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix); [Horodecki et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/quant-ph/0702225)).

### Formal definition
Let $\mathcal H$ be a Hilbert space. A **density operator** is a linear operator $\rho$ on $\mathcal H$ that is self-adjoint, positive semidefinite and of unit trace:
$$\rho=\rho^\dagger,\qquad \rho\ge0,\qquad \operatorname{tr}\rho=1.$$
An operator is the density operator of some ensemble $\{p_j,|\psi_j\rangle\}$ if and only if it is positive with trace one ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/density+matrix); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix)).

**Pure and mixed.** $\rho$ is pure if $\rho^2=\rho$, equivalently if the purity $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=1$; otherwise it is mixed ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix)). On an $N$-dimensional space the maximally mixed state $I/N$ has purity $1/N$ ([Lancaster PHYS223 notes](https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/people/schomeru/lecturenotes/Quantum%20Mechanics/S20.html)).

**Measurement and dynamics.** The probability of outcome $i$ of a projective measurement $\{P_i\}$ is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i)$, with post-measurement state $P_i\rho P_i/\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i)$ (Lüders rule). Closed-system evolution obeys the von Neumann equation $i\hbar\,\dot\rho=[H,\rho]$, so $\rho(t)=e^{-iHt/\hbar}\rho(0)e^{iHt/\hbar}$ for time-independent $H$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix)).

**Partial trace.** For $\rho_{AB}$ on $\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_B$ and an orthonormal basis $\{|\alpha_B\rangle\}$ of $\mathcal H_B$, the reduced density operator is
$$\rho_A=\operatorname{tr}_B\rho_{AB}=\sum_\alpha\langle\alpha_B|\rho_{AB}|\alpha_B\rangle .$$
A **purification** of $\rho=\sum_\alpha P_\alpha|\psi_\alpha\rangle\langle\psi_\alpha|$ is $|\Psi\rangle=\sum_\alpha\sqrt{P_\alpha}\,|\psi_\alpha\rangle|\alpha_E\rangle$, whose partial trace over the ancilla $E$ returns $\rho$ ([Steck, Oregon PHYS 610 notes](https://atomoptics.uoregon.edu/~dsteck/teaching/09spring/phys610/notes/entanglement.pdf)).

**Separability.** A bipartite density operator is separable if it can be written $\rho=\sum_\alpha P_\alpha\,\rho^{(A)}_\alpha\otimes\rho^{(B)}_\alpha$, and entangled otherwise ([Steck, Oregon PHYS 610 notes](https://atomoptics.uoregon.edu/~dsteck/teaching/09spring/phys610/notes/entanglement.pdf)).

**Qubits.** Every qubit state has the form $\rho=\tfrac12(I+\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)$ with $|\vec r|\le1$ (the Bloch ball): pure states on the sphere, mixed states inside ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix)).

**Von Neumann entropy.** $S(\rho)=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho)$, which vanishes exactly on pure states ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix)).

### Key results
- **Gleason's theorem.** Let $\mathcal H$ be a Hilbert space of dimension at least 3. If $f$ assigns to each projection a number in $[0,1]$ such that $\sum_i f(\Pi_i)=1$ whenever $\sum_i\Pi_i=I$ (noncontextual probabilities), then there is a density operator $\rho$ with $f(\Pi)=\operatorname{tr}(\Pi\rho)$. Counterexamples exist in dimension 2; the POVM version of Busch and of Caves et al. holds also for a single qubit ([Wikipedia: Gleason's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gleason%27s_theorem)). So the density-matrix form of the [Born rule](node:Born%20Rule) follows from noncontextuality.
- **Schmidt decomposition.** For $\dim\mathcal H_1=n\ge m=\dim\mathcal H_2$, every $w\in\mathcal H_1\otimes\mathcal H_2$ can be written $w=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\,u_i\otimes v_i$ with orthonormal $\{u_i\}$, $\{v_i\}$ and real $\alpha_i\ge0$ unique up to ordering; it is the singular value decomposition of the coefficient matrix. Both reduced states of $ww^*$ have the same nonzero spectrum $\{|\alpha_i|^2\}$, and the entanglement entropy $-\sum_i|\alpha_i|^2\log|\alpha_i|^2$ vanishes exactly for product states ([Wikipedia: Schmidt decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_decomposition)). For pure bipartite states, the reduced states are mixed exactly when the state is entangled ([Lancaster PHYS223 notes](https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/people/schomeru/lecturenotes/Quantum%20Mechanics/S20.html)).
- **Schrödinger–HJW theorem.** Let a system–ancilla pair be in a pure state $|\Psi_{SM}\rangle$ with reduced state $\rho_S$. Every $\rho_S$-ensemble of order $n\le\dim\mathcal H_M$ has a corresponding ancilla in $\mathcal H_M$ (unique if the ensemble is linearly independent), and every orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_M$ contains exactly one ancilla corresponding to exactly one $\rho_S$-ensemble; any two $\rho_S$-ensembles are related by a unitary transformation on $\mathcal H_M$, unique if the ensembles are linearly independent; and every vector in the support of $\rho_S$ appears in some $\rho_S$-ensemble ([Kirkpatrick](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/quant-ph/0305068)). Equivalently, any two purifications differ by a unitary $I\otimes U$ on the purifying system, so different ensembles can be realised by different measurements on it ([Wikipedia: Schrödinger–HJW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%E2%80%93HJW_theorem)).
- **Strong subadditivity (Lieb and Ruskai 1973).** For every tripartite state $\rho_{123}$, $S(\rho_{123})+S(\rho_2)\le S(\rho_{12})+S(\rho_{23})$. Subadditivity $S(\rho_{12})\le S(\rho_1)+S(\rho_2)$ and the Araki–Lieb inequality $S(\rho_{12})\ge|S(\rho_1)-S(\rho_2)|$ bound the joint entropy. SSA follows from the monotonicity of relative entropy under partial trace, and Hayden, Jozsa, Petz and Winter characterised the equality case as a direct sum of tensor products over subspaces of system 2 ([Wikipedia: SSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_subadditivity_of_quantum_entropy)).
- **Peres–Horodecki (PPT) criterion.** If $\rho$ is separable then its partial transpose $\rho^{T_B}$ has no negative eigenvalues. The converse holds if and only if the dimension is $2\times2$ or $2\times3$; in higher dimensions there are entangled PPT states, which are bound entangled (not distillable) ([Wikipedia: Peres–Horodecki criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres%E2%80%93Horodecki_criterion)).
- **Ensemble ambiguity.** Different ensembles can produce the same density operator, and no measurement distinguishes them, and a given $\rho$ has infinitely many purifications ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/density+matrix)).

### Examples
- **Bell state:** for $|\psi\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)$, tracing out qubit $B$ gives $\rho_A=\tfrac12(|0\rangle\langle0|+|1\rangle\langle1|)=I/2$, a completely incoherent mixture although the global state is a coherent superposition ([Steck, Oregon PHYS 610 notes](https://atomoptics.uoregon.edu/~dsteck/teaching/09spring/phys610/notes/entanglement.pdf)).
- **Mixture vs superposition:** an equal mixture of $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ has diagonal $\rho$ and shows no interference, whereas the superposition $(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ has nonzero off-diagonal coherences ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/density+matrix)).
- **Global phase:** state vectors differing only by a phase give the same density operator, so $\rho$ removes the unphysical phase redundancy of $|\psi\rangle$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/density+matrix)).

### History
Von Neumann and Landau introduced the formalism independently in 1927, Dirac coined the term "density" in 1931, and Felix Bloch developed it further in 1946 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix)). Schrödinger proved the ancilla (HJW) theorem in 1936; it was rediscovered by Jaynes (1957, extended by Hadjisavvas 1981), partially by Gisin (1989), and by Hughston, Jozsa and Wootters (1993), and Mermin (1999) simplified part of the HJW proof; Kirkpatrick (2003) remarks that none of these appear to have been aware of Schrödinger's work ([Kirkpatrick](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/quant-ph/0305068); [Wikipedia: Schrödinger–HJW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%E2%80%93HJW_theorem)). Gleason proved his theorem in 1957, answering a question of Mackey ([Wikipedia: Gleason's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gleason%27s_theorem)). Strong subadditivity was conjectured by Robinson and Ruelle (1966) and Lanford and Robinson (1968) and proved by Lieb and Ruskai in 1973 ([Wikipedia: SSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_subadditivity_of_quantum_entropy)).

### Connections
- [Postulates of Quantum Mechanics](node:Postulates%20of%20Quantum%20Mechanics): density operators generalise the state postulate; Gleason's theorem derives the trace form of the Born rule.
- [Operator Formulation of Quantum States](node:Operator%20Formulation%20of%20Quantum%20States): states as positive normalised functionals, of which density matrices are the trace-class representatives.
- [C-Star Algebras and von Neumann Algebras](node:C-Star%20Algebras%20and%20von%20Neumann%20Algebras): the algebraic setting in which states generalise density matrices.
- [Quantum Entanglement](node:Quantum%20Entanglement) and [Entanglement Measures](node:Entanglement%20Measures): defined on reduced and bipartite density matrices.
- [Decoherence](node:Decoherence): loss of off-diagonal coherences in the reduced state after system–environment entanglement.
- [Lindblad Dynamics](node:Lindblad%20Dynamics) and [Quantum Master Equations](node:Quantum%20Master%20Equations): open-system evolution of $\rho$ beyond the von Neumann equation.
- [Quantum Channels](node:Quantum%20Channels): completely positive trace-preserving maps on density matrices; relative entropy is monotone under them.
- [Quantum State Tomography](node:Quantum%20State%20Tomography): reconstructing $\rho$ from measurement statistics.
- [Quantum Statistical Mechanics](node:Quantum%20Statistical%20Mechanics): thermal states $\rho\propto e^{-\beta H}$ and von Neumann entropy.
- [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): the Schmidt decomposition is an SVD of the coefficient matrix.
- [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices): the convex cone in which density matrices live.
- [Bell's Theorem](node:Bell's%20Theorem): tests of entangled states described by bipartite density matrices.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the ambient space on which density operators act.

### Common pitfalls
- **A mixture is not a superposition:** superpositions can interfere, mixtures cannot ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix)).
- **$\rho$ does not determine the ensemble:** the decomposition into pure states is not unique, and attributing physical reality to one ensemble is contested; Penrose argues that this makes the density operator ambiguous for mixed states, while others argue the ensembles are observationally indistinguishable ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/density+matrix)).
- **PPT does not imply separable** beyond $2\times2$ and $2\times3$ ([Wikipedia: Peres–Horodecki criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres%E2%80%93Horodecki_criterion)); deciding separability of a general mixed state is NP-hard ([Steck, Oregon PHYS 610 notes](https://atomoptics.uoregon.edu/~dsteck/teaching/09spring/phys610/notes/entanglement.pdf)).
- **Gleason needs dimension $\ge3$** for projective measurements; in dimension 2 one needs POVMs ([Wikipedia: Gleason's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gleason%27s_theorem)).

### Open problems
- **NPT bound entanglement.** Whether there exist bound entangled (undistillable) states that violate the PPT criterion is described by Horodecki et al. as a long-standing and still open question whose answer would have severe consequences for quantum communication theory ([Horodecki et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/quant-ph/0702225)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Density matrix (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_matrix): definition, measurement, dynamics, Bloch ball, entropy, history.
- **Reference:** [density matrix (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/density+matrix): characterisation, purification, interpretive remarks.
- **Learn:** [Steck, Entanglement and open systems (Oregon PHYS 610)](https://atomoptics.uoregon.edu/~dsteck/teaching/09spring/phys610/notes/entanglement.pdf): partial trace, purification, decoherence.
- **Learn:** [Lancaster PHYS223, Composite systems and the density matrix](https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/people/schomeru/lecturenotes/Quantum%20Mechanics/S20.html): mixed states, purity, reduced states, entanglement.
- **Primary:** [Horodecki, Horodecki, Horodecki and Horodecki, Quantum entanglement](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/quant-ph/0702225): comprehensive review of entanglement of density matrices.
- **Primary:** [Kirkpatrick, The Schrödinger-HJW theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0305068): concise statement and history of the ensemble/purification theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Nielsen and Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information (CUP, 10th anniversary ed. 2012)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511976667): the standard graduate text.

## Reference
### Overview
The determinant assigns a scalar to each square matrix. It encodes whether the matrix is invertible (exactly when the determinant is nonzero), and for a real matrix its absolute value is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns, so it measures how the linear map scales volume. ([MIT 18.06, Properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/5dd3f8ec0a398fd74264fef3fd591f81_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.5sum.pdf); [MIT 18.06, Cramer and volume](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/f6e46da0d783d8f9c0a25c407c76166a_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.7sum.pdf))

Intrinsically, the determinant of an endomorphism of an $n$-dimensional space is the scalar by which it acts on the one-dimensional top exterior power. This definition is basis-free and functorial, which is why the determinant is multiplicative and invariant under conjugation. The same theory works over any commutative ring, where invertibility of a matrix is equivalent to its determinant being a unit. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/determinant); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))

The determinant appears throughout mathematics: in the characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues, in Cramer's rule, in the Jacobian of the change-of-variables formula, and in algebraic complexity theory, where the gap between the determinant and the permanent is a central open question. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant); [Kumar and Volk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.02452))

### Formal definition
**Axiomatic.** On $n\times n$ matrices, $\det$ is characterized by $\det I=1$, a sign change when two rows are exchanged, and linearity in each row separately; from these it follows that a matrix with two equal rows has determinant $0$ and that adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the determinant. Equivalently, it is the unique alternating multilinear form of the columns (or rows) taking the value $1$ on the identity. ([MIT 18.06, Properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/5dd3f8ec0a398fd74264fef3fd591f81_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.5sum.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))

**Leibniz formula.** For $A=(a_{ij})$,
$$\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
the sum over all permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$; for $n=2$ this is $ad-bc$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))

**Exterior power.** If $\dim V=n$, then $\Lambda^nV$ is one-dimensional, so for $f:V\to V$ the induced map $\Lambda^n f$ is multiplication by a scalar, which is $\det f$. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/determinant))

### Key results
- **Multiplicativity and transpose.** $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ and $\det A^{T}=\det A$; in the exterior-power picture multiplicativity is functoriality, and it gives $\det(UAU^{-1})=\det A$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/determinant))
- **Invertibility.** Over a field, $\det A=0$ exactly when $A$ is singular; over a commutative ring, $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det A$ is a unit. The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries, which is how elimination computes determinants. ([MIT 18.06, Properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/5dd3f8ec0a398fd74264fef3fd591f81_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.5sum.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))
- **Laplace (cofactor) expansion.** With cofactors $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$, where $M_{ij}$ is the minor obtained by deleting row $i$ and column $j$, one has $\det A=\sum_j a_{ij}C_{ij}$ for each row $i$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant); [MIT 18.06, Cramer and volume](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/f6e46da0d783d8f9c0a25c407c76166a_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.7sum.pdf))
- **Adjugate and Cramer's rule.** The adjugate $\operatorname{adj}A=C^{T}$ satisfies $A\,\operatorname{adj}A=\operatorname{adj}A\,A=\det(A)I$, so $A^{-1}=C^{T}/\det A$ when $\det A\neq0$. If $A$ is nonsingular, the solution of $Ax=b$ is $x_j=\det B_j/\det A$, where $B_j$ is $A$ with column $j$ replaced by $b$. ([MIT 18.06, Cramer and volume](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/f6e46da0d783d8f9c0a25c407c76166a_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.7sum.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))
- **Eigenvalues.** The characteristic polynomial $p_A(t)=\det(tI-A)$ has constant term $(-1)^n\det A$. Over an algebraically closed field it splits into linear factors, so $\det A$ is the product and $\operatorname{tr}A$ the sum of the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity. ([Wikipedia, Characteristic polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_polynomial))
- **Jacobi's formula.** For a differentiable matrix function, $\frac{d}{dt}\det A(t)=\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\operatorname{adj}(A)\,\tfrac{dA}{dt}\big)$; taking $A(t)=\exp(tB)$ yields $\det(e^{B})=e^{\operatorname{tr}B}$. ([Wikipedia, Jacobi's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi%27s_formula))
- **Change of variables.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and $\varphi:U\to\mathbb R^n$ injective with continuous partial derivatives and nonzero Jacobian determinant on $U$. For continuous $f$ with compact support in $\varphi(U)$, $\int_{\varphi(U)}f(v)\,dv=\int_U f(\varphi(u))\,|\det D\varphi(u)|\,du$. ([Wikipedia, Integration by substitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integration_by_substitution))
- **Block matrices.** If $A$ is invertible, $\det\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}=\det A\,\det(D-CA^{-1}B)$; if $C$ and $D$ commute, it equals $\det(AD-BC)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))

### Examples
- Gaussian elimination reduces a matrix to triangular form with pivots $d_1,\dots,d_n$, and $\det A=\pm d_1\cdots d_n$, the sign recording the parity of row exchanges. For $2\times2$ matrices with $a\ne0$, elimination gives $a(d-\tfrac{c}{a}b)=ad-bc$. ([MIT 18.06, Properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/5dd3f8ec0a398fd74264fef3fd591f81_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.5sum.pdf))
- An orthogonal matrix $Q$ has $Q^TQ=I$, so $\det Q=\pm1$: its columns span a unit cube in a different orientation. A permutation matrix has determinant $\pm1$ according to the parity of the row exchanges. ([MIT 18.06, Cramer and volume](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/f6e46da0d783d8f9c0a25c407c76166a_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.7sum.pdf); [MIT 18.06, Properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/5dd3f8ec0a398fd74264fef3fd591f81_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.5sum.pdf))
- Gaussian elimination computes $\det$ in $O(n^3)$ arithmetic operations, although intermediate bit lengths can grow; if matrices can be multiplied in time $M(n)\ge n^a$ with $a>2$, the determinant can be computed in $O(M(n))$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))

### History
Seki introduced determinants in Japan in 1683, and Leibniz, in a 1693 letter to de l'Hôpital, gave a determinant condition for a system of three equations and knew the expansion now named after Laplace. Cramer published his rule for $n\times n$ systems without proof in 1750. Vandermonde (1771) developed methods of calculation; Laplace (1772), calling the determinant the "resultant", gave the expansion now named after him. Cauchy (1812) was the first to use "determinant" in its modern sense and gave the first proof of the multiplication theorem. Jacobi's 1841 treatises made determinants widely known, and Cayley introduced the two-vertical-bar notation in 1841. ([MacTutor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Matrices_and_determinants/)) Binet stated the product theorem for rectangular matrices in 1811–1812, and Jacobi's functional determinant was later named the Jacobian by Sylvester. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))

### Connections
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): square matrices represent endomorphisms; the determinant detects invertibility.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): the top exterior power gives the basis-free definition.
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): the characteristic polynomial is a determinant.
- [Cayley–Hamilton Theorem](node:Cayley–Hamilton%20Theorem): every matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial.
- [Permutation Groups](node:Permutation%20Groups): the sign homomorphism on $S_n$ enters the Leibniz formula.
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): the Jacobian determinant in the change-of-variables formula.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): $\det$ is a homomorphism $GL_n\to K^\times$, and $\det e^B=e^{\operatorname{tr}B}$ relates it to the trace on the Lie algebra.
- [Fredholm Determinants](node:Fredholm%20Determinants): an infinite-dimensional extension for trace-class perturbations of the identity.
- [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices): positive definite matrices have positive determinant.

### Common pitfalls
- Linearity holds in one row at a time, not in the whole matrix: in general $\det(A+B)\neq\det A+\det B$, and scaling every row by $t$ scales the determinant by $t^n$. ([MIT 18.06, Properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/5dd3f8ec0a398fd74264fef3fd591f81_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.5sum.pdf))
- Over a ring such as $\mathbb Z$, $\det A\ne0$ does not make $A$ invertible; the determinant must be a unit. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))
- The product of eigenvalues equals $\det A$ only when the eigenvalues are taken in an algebraically closed field and counted with algebraic multiplicity. ([Wikipedia, Characteristic polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_polynomial))
- Cramer's rule is usually less efficient than elimination for computation. ([MIT 18.06, Cramer and volume](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/f6e46da0d783d8f9c0a25c407c76166a_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.7sum.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Determinant versus permanent.** The permanent has the Leibniz formula without signs. It is $\#P$-complete even for $0$–$1$ matrices (Valiant 1979) and is generally believed not to be computable in polynomial time, whereas the determinant is computable in polynomial time by Gaussian elimination. ([Wikipedia, Computing the permanent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_the_permanent))
- **Determinantal complexity lower bounds.** The determinantal complexity of a polynomial is the size of the smallest matrix with affine entries whose determinant is that polynomial. For an $n$-variate polynomial of degree $d$ it is trivially at least $d$, and proving a lower bound super-linear in $\max\{n,d\}$ (for an explicit polynomial) is a long-standing open problem. Kumar and Volk prove $1.5n-3$ for $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^n$, improving the earlier $n+1$ of Alper, Bogart and Velasco. ([Kumar and Volk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.02452))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Determinant (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant): Leibniz and Laplace formulas, adjugate, rings, complexity, history; [nLab, determinant](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/determinant): exterior-power definition.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.06 lecture summary, properties of determinants](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/5dd3f8ec0a398fd74264fef3fd591f81_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.5sum.pdf) and [Cramer's rule, inverse matrix and volume](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/f6e46da0d783d8f9c0a25c407c76166a_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.7sum.pdf).
- **Primary:** [Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right (Springer UTM, 2024)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-031-41026-0): standard linear algebra textbook.
- **Further reading:** [Lang, Algebra (Springer GTM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4613-0041-0): standard graduate algebra text; [Kumar and Volk, A Lower Bound on Determinantal Complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.02452): current research on determinantal complexity.

## Reference
### Overview
Differential calculus studies how the output of a function responds to small changes of its input. The derivative of $f$ at $a$ is the limit of difference quotients; geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line, physically an instantaneous rate of change, and analytically the coefficient of the best linear approximation to $f$ near $a$. That last viewpoint generalizes: for maps between Euclidean spaces the total derivative is the best linear approximation, represented by the Jacobian matrix. ([Wikipedia: Derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative))

The theory rests on the limit concept of [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits) and on the mean value theorem, which converts pointwise information about $f'$ into global information about $f$. Its main tools are the differentiation rules (above all the chain rule), Taylor's theorem, and theorems describing what derivatives can and cannot look like (Darboux's theorem, the existence of continuous nowhere-differentiable functions). It is paired with [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus) by the fundamental theorem of calculus and extends to several variables in [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus) and to infinite-dimensional spaces through the Fréchet derivative. ([Wikipedia: Derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative); [Wikipedia: Fréchet derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_derivative))

### Formal definition
Let $f$ be real-valued and defined on an open interval containing $a$. Then $f$ is differentiable at $a$ if the limit
$$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$$
exists (as a finite number). A function differentiable at $a$ is continuous there, but not conversely: $|x|$ is continuous and not differentiable at $0$. ([Wikipedia: Derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative))

**Fréchet derivative.** For normed spaces $V,W$ and $U\subseteq V$ open, $f:U\to W$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ if there is a bounded linear operator $A:V\to W$ with
$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\lVert f(x+h)-f(x)-Ah\rVert_W}{\lVert h\rVert_V}=0 .$$
Such $A$ is unique and written $Df(x)$. For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ it is the map $h\mapsto f'(x)h$, so this definition recovers the ordinary derivative and makes "best linear approximation" precise. Fréchet differentiability implies Gateaux (directional) differentiability, but not conversely: $f(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$, $f(0,0)=0$, has all directional derivatives at the origin but they do not form a linear map. ([Wikipedia: Fréchet derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_derivative))

### Key results
- **Chain rule.** If $g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(c)$, then $f\circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f\circ g)'(c)=f'(g(c))\,g'(c)$. For $g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, $f:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^k$ the total derivative of $f\circ g$ at $a$ is the composite of the total derivatives, i.e. the product of Jacobian matrices, and the rule holds for Fréchet derivatives between Banach spaces. ([Wikipedia: Chain rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_rule))
- **Mean value theorem.** If $a<b$, $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, then $f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ for some $c\in(a,b)$. Rolle's theorem is the case $f(a)=f(b)$; Cauchy's form gives $c$ with $(f(b)-f(a))g'(c)=(g(b)-g(a))f'(c)$ under the same hypotheses on $f,g$. Corollary: $f'=0$ on an interval forces $f$ constant there. ([Wikipedia: Mean value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_theorem))
- **Taylor's theorem.** If $f$ is $k$ times differentiable at $a$, then $f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^k\frac{f^{(i)}(a)}{i!}(x-a)^i+h_k(x)(x-a)^k$ with $h_k(x)\to0$ as $x\to a$ (Peano remainder). If moreover $f^{(k)}$ is continuous on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$ and $f^{(k+1)}$ exists on the open interval, the remainder equals $\frac{f^{(k+1)}(\xi)}{(k+1)!}(x-a)^{k+1}$ for some $\xi$ between them (Lagrange form). The case $k=1$ is the linear approximation. ([Wikipedia: Taylor's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor%27s_theorem))
- **Inverse function rule.** If $f$ is continuous and injective on an interval, differentiable at $a$ with $f'(a)\ne0$, then $f^{-1}$ is differentiable at $b=f(a)$ with $(f^{-1})'(b)=1/f'(a)$. ([Wikipedia: Inverse function rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_rule)) Its several-variable analogue is the [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem).
- **Darboux's theorem.** If $f$ is differentiable on an open interval $I$, then $f'$ has the intermediate value property: for $a<b$ in $I$, every value between $f'(a)$ and $f'(b)$ is attained by $f'$ on $[a,b]$. So derivatives have no jump discontinuities, although they can be discontinuous (the derivative of $x^2\sin(1/x)$, extended by $0$, is discontinuous at $0$). ([Wikipedia: Darboux's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darboux%27s_theorem_%28analysis%29))
- **L'Hôpital's rule.** Let $f,g$ be differentiable on an open interval $I$ around $c$ except possibly at $c$, with $g'\ne0$ on $I\setminus\{c\}$, and suppose $f,g\to0$ or $|f|,|g|\to\infty$ as $x\to c$. If $\lim f'/g'$ exists, then $\lim f/g=\lim f'/g'$; $c$ and the limit may be infinite. ([Wikipedia: L'Hôpital's rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27H%C3%B4pital%27s_rule))
- **Nowhere-differentiable functions.** Weierstrass's function $W(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a^n\cos(b^n\pi x)$, with $0<a<1$ and $b$ a positive odd integer, is continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere; Weierstrass assumed $ab>1+\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, and Hardy showed $ab\ge1$ suffices. Such functions are typical: they form a comeager set of continuous functions, and under Wiener measure the functions differentiable at even one point form a null set. ([Wikipedia: Weierstrass function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_function_%28nowhere-differentiable_function%29))

### Examples
For $f(x)=x^2$, $[(x+h)^2-x^2]/h=2x+h\to2x$, so $f'(x)=2x$. ([Wikipedia: Derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative)) The flat function equal to $e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x>0$ and $0$ for $x\le0$ is infinitely differentiable, yet its Taylor series at $0$ is identically zero, so smoothness does not imply that $f$ equals the sum of its Taylor series (see [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence)). ([Wikipedia: Taylor's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor%27s_theorem)) For $f(x)=x+\sin x$ and $g(x)=x$ as $x\to\infty$, $f'/g'=1+\cos x$ has no limit while $f/g\to1$, so the hypothesis that $\lim f'/g'$ exists in L'Hôpital's rule is needed for the rule, not for the limit. ([Wikipedia: L'Hôpital's rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27H%C3%B4pital%27s_rule))

### History
Leibniz introduced his $dy/dx$ notation in 1675, and Newton's dot notation for time derivatives survives in physics. ([Wikipedia: Derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative)) Leibniz first used the chain rule in a 1676 memoir (with a sign error); a modern version appears in Lagrange (1797) and in Cauchy's 1823 text. ([Wikipedia: Chain rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_rule)) Rolle proved a restricted mean value theorem for polynomials in 1691, and Cauchy proved the modern form in 1823. ([Wikipedia: Mean value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_theorem)) Johann Bernoulli found L'Hôpital's rule and communicated it in a letter of 22 July 1694; L'Hôpital published it in *Analyse des Infiniment Petits* (1696). ([Wikipedia: L'Hôpital's rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27H%C3%B4pital%27s_rule)) Brook Taylor stated his theorem in 1715, with an earlier version in Gregory (1671). ([Wikipedia: Taylor's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor%27s_theorem)) Darboux published his theorem in 1875, and Weierstrass his nowhere-differentiable function in 1872. ([Wikipedia: Darboux's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darboux%27s_theorem_%28analysis%29); [Wikipedia: Weierstrass function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_function_%28nowhere-differentiable_function%29))

### Connections
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): the derivative is a limit; completeness underlies the mean value theorem.
- [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus): linked to differentiation by the fundamental theorem of calculus.
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): partial and total derivatives, Jacobians, the multivariable chain rule.
- [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem): the several-variable version of the inverse function rule.
- [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence): Taylor series and the gap between smooth and analytic functions.
- [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces): the setting of the Fréchet derivative.
- [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis): complex differentiability is a much stronger condition (Cauchy-Riemann equations).

### Common pitfalls
Differentiability is stronger than continuity ($|x|$ at $0$), and Fréchet differentiability is stronger than the existence of all directional derivatives. ([Wikipedia: Derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative); [Wikipedia: Fréchet derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_derivative)) The mean value theorem fails for complex-valued functions: $e^{ix}$ on $[0,2\pi]$ has equal endpoint values but a derivative that never vanishes; for vector-valued functions only the inequality $|f(b)-f(a)|\le(b-a)|f'(c)|$ survives. ([Wikipedia: Mean value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_theorem)) A derivative need not be continuous, but by Darboux's theorem it cannot have a jump. ([Wikipedia: Darboux's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darboux%27s_theorem_%28analysis%29))

### Open problems
Ciesielski and Seoane-Sepúlveda's survey of differentiability versus continuity closes with a list of "currently open problems", including ([arXiv:1806.10994, §6](https://arxiv.org/html/1806.10994)):
- **Characterizing derivatives (Problem 6.1).** "Find a non-trivial characterization of the derivatives", i.e. of the functions $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $h=f'$ for some $f$. Darboux's theorem gives a necessary condition that is not sufficient. ([arXiv:1806.10994](https://arxiv.org/html/1806.10994); [Wikipedia: Darboux's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darboux%27s_theorem_%28analysis%29))
- **Compositions of derivatives (Problem 6.2).** If $f$ is a composition of finitely many derivatives from $[0,1]$ into itself, must the graph of $f$ be connected in $\mathbb R^2$? ([arXiv:1806.10994](https://arxiv.org/html/1806.10994))
- **Extension of higher-order differentiable functions (Problem 6.4).** For each $n\ge2$, characterize the $D^n$ functions from a perfect set $P\subseteq\mathbb R$ into $\mathbb R$ that extend to $D^n$ functions on $\mathbb R$. ([arXiv:1806.10994](https://arxiv.org/html/1806.10994))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative): definition, rules, higher derivatives and generalizations.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.01SC Single Variable Calculus (Jerison)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-01sc-single-variable-calculus-fall-2010/): lectures on differentiation, the mean value theorem, L'Hôpital's rule and Taylor series.
- **Primary:** [Ciesielski and Seoane-Sepúlveda, Differentiability versus continuity: restriction and extension theorems and monstrous examples](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.10994): research survey of the fine structure of derivatives, with open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Abbott, Understanding Analysis (Springer UTM, 2015)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4939-2712-8): undergraduate real analysis text in Springer's Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics.
references.Differential Forms:
## Reference
### Overview
A differential form is a geometric object on a manifold that can be integrated: a smooth $k$-form is a smooth section of the $k$-th exterior power of the cotangent bundle, so at each point it is an alternating multilinear function of $k$ tangent vectors ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+form); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)). Forms of all degrees make up a graded-commutative algebra under the wedge product, with a degree-one operator, the exterior derivative $d$, that squares to zero. Pulling forms back along smooth maps commutes with both operations, which is what makes forms the natural integrands of differential topology ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).

The central identity is the generalized Stokes theorem $\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega$. It contains the [fundamental theorem of calculus](node:Fundamental%20Theorem%20of%20Calculus), Green's theorem, the divergence theorem and the classical Stokes theorem as special cases ([Mazurowski, lecture notes](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)). Because $d^2=0$, the forms on a manifold make up a cochain complex, the de Rham complex. Its cohomology is a topological invariant: by de Rham's theorem it agrees with real singular cohomology ([Wikipedia: de Rham cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rham_cohomology)).

Forms sit between [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra) (pointwise, they are alternating tensors) and algebraic topology, through [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology). In physics they carry gauge fields: the electromagnetic field is a 2-form $F=dA$, and Maxwell's equations read $dF=0$, $d{\star}F=J$. In Yang–Mills theory the field strength $F=dA+A\wedge A$ is the curvature of a Lie-algebra-valued connection 1-form ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).

### Formal definition
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. The space of $k$-forms is
$$\Omega^k(M)=\Gamma\big(\Lambda^k T^*M\big),$$
and in local coordinates every $k$-form is uniquely $\omega=\sum_{I} f_I\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$ over increasing multi-indices $I$, giving $\binom{n}{k}$ terms ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+form); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).

- **Wedge product.** $\wedge:\Omega^k\times\Omega^\ell\to\Omega^{k+\ell}$ is bilinear over $C^\infty(M)$ and graded commutative: $\alpha\wedge\beta=(-1)^{k\ell}\beta\wedge\alpha$. In particular $\omega\wedge\omega=0$ for odd $k$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+form)).
- **Exterior derivative.** $d:\Omega^k\to\Omega^{k+1}$ is given in coordinates by $d\big(\sum_I f_I\,dx^I\big)=\sum_I df_I\wedge dx^I$ ([Mazurowski](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)). It satisfies $d\circ d=0$ and the graded Leibniz rule $d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge d\beta$ for $\alpha\in\Omega^k$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).
- **Pullback.** For smooth $f:M\to N$, the pullback $f^*$ preserves sums and wedge products and satisfies $f^*(d\omega)=d(f^*\omega)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).
- **Interior product.** For a vector field $X$, $(\iota_X\omega)(X_1,\dots,X_{p-1})=\omega(X,X_1,\dots,X_{p-1})$. It is the unique antiderivation of degree $-1$ with $\iota_X\alpha=\alpha(X)$ on 1-forms, and $\iota_X\circ\iota_X=0$ ([Wikipedia: Interior product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_product)).
- **Closed and exact.** $\omega$ is *closed* if $d\omega=0$ and *exact* if $\omega=d\eta$. Exact forms are closed because $d^2=0$ ([Mazurowski](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)).
- **Algebraic characterization.** The smooth forms $\Omega^\bullet(X)$ are the universal differential envelope of $C^\infty(X)$: they are generated from smooth functions by sums, wedge products and $d$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+form)).

### Key results
- **Generalized Stokes theorem.** If $M$ is an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $\partial M$ carries the induced orientation, and $\omega\in\Omega^{n-1}(M)$ has compact support, then $\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega$. Reversing the orientation flips the sign of the integral ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)). For a $k$-form $\omega$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and a $(k+1)$-cell $c$, $\int_{\partial c}\omega=\int_c d\omega$ ([Mazurowski](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)).
- **Poincaré lemma.** For $k\ge 1$, every closed $k$-form on $\mathbb R^n$ is exact ([Mazurowski](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)). Hence the de Rham complex is locally exact in positive degrees, and the kernel of $d$ on $\Omega^0$ is the locally constant functions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).
- **Cartan's magic formula.** For a vector field $X$, the [Lie derivative](node:Lie%20Derivative) on forms is $\mathcal L_X=d\,\iota_X+\iota_X\,d$, the anticommutator of $d$ and $\iota_X$. Also $\iota_{[X,Y]}=[\mathcal L_X,\iota_Y]$ ([Wikipedia: Interior product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_product)).
- **De Rham's theorem (1931).** For a smooth manifold $M$, integration $[\omega]\mapsto\big(c\mapsto\int_c\omega\big)$ induces an isomorphism $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\cong H^k(M;\mathbb R)$ with singular cohomology, carrying the wedge product to the cup product ([Wikipedia: de Rham cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rham_cohomology)). Consistently, the integral of a closed form over homologous chains is the same ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).
- **Hodge theorem.** On a compact oriented Riemannian manifold, every de Rham class contains exactly one harmonic form, so the space of harmonic $k$-forms has dimension equal to the $k$-th Betti number ([Wikipedia: de Rham cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rham_cohomology)). The codifferential $\delta$, of degree $-1$, is the formal adjoint of $d$ built from the Hodge star $\star:\Omega^k\to\Omega^{n-k}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).
- **Brouwer fixed point theorem via Stokes.** Every smooth map $f:D\to D$ of the closed unit ball $D\subset\mathbb R^n$ has a fixed point; the notes derive this from Stokes' theorem ([Mazurowski](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)).

### Examples
- **Rotation form.** On $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, $\alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}$ is closed but not exact. The integral of any exact 1-form over a closed curve vanishes, while $\alpha$ integrates to a nonzero value around a loop encircling the origin ([Mazurowski](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)).
- **Vector calculus.** On $\mathbb R^3$, the exterior derivative of the work 1-form of a field $F$ is the flux 2-form of $\operatorname{curl}F$. Green's, Stokes' and the divergence theorems are the cases $k=1,2$ of the general Stokes theorem ([Mazurowski](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)).
- **Spheres and tori.** $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(S^n)=\mathbb R$ for $k=0,n$ and $0$ otherwise ($n>0$), and $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(T^n)\cong\mathbb R^{\binom nk}$ ([Wikipedia: de Rham cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rham_cohomology)).
- **Electromagnetism.** $F=dA$, where the vector potential $A$ is the connection form of a $U(1)$ principal bundle and $F$ is its curvature form. Then $dF=0$ holds automatically, and $d{\star}F=J$ carries the sources ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).

### History
Grassmann's *Die Lineale Ausdehnungslehre* (1844) contains aspects of the exterior algebra. Élie Cartan is credited with the algebraic organization of differential forms, starting with his 1899 paper on the Pfaff problem ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)). Georges de Rham proved in 1931 that forms compute real cohomology ([Wikipedia: de Rham cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rham_cohomology)). Bott and Tu's *Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology* appeared in Springer's Graduate Texts in Mathematics in 1982 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3951-0)).

### Connections
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): forms are sections of bundles over a smooth manifold; integration needs an orientation.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): pointwise, a $k$-form is an alternating $k$-tensor.
- [Stokes' Theorem](node:Stokes'%20Theorem): the defining integral identity of the exterior derivative.
- [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology): closed forms modulo exact forms, isomorphic to real singular cohomology.
- [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory): harmonic representatives on compact Riemannian manifolds.
- [Tangent Spaces and Vector Fields](node:Tangent%20Spaces%20and%20Vector%20Fields): interior products and Lie derivatives along vector fields.
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives): vector-valued and Lie-algebra-valued forms give connection and curvature forms.
- [Characteristic Classes](node:Characteristic%20Classes): curvature forms represent characteristic classes in de Rham cohomology.
- [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations): $dF=0$, $d{\star}F=J$.
- [Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry): a symplectic structure is a closed nondegenerate 2-form.
- [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus): grad, curl and div are $d$ in degrees 0, 1, 2 on $\mathbb R^3$.

### Common pitfalls
- Closed does not imply exact. The obstruction is topological and is measured by de Rham cohomology. The rotation form on the punctured plane is the basic counterexample ([Mazurowski](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf)).
- Integration of top-degree forms needs an orientation, and reversing it changes the sign. Non-orientable manifolds need twisted forms (pseudoforms, densities) instead ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+form)).
- Signs: the Leibniz rule carries $(-1)^k$ and the wedge product is graded commutative, so $\alpha\wedge\beta\neq\beta\wedge\alpha$ when both degrees are odd ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)).
- Regularity drops: $d$ sends $C^k$ forms to $C^{k-1}$ forms ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+form)).

### Open problems
- **Singer conjecture.** If $M^n$ is a closed aspherical manifold with fundamental group $\pi$ and universal cover $\widetilde M$, then the $L^2$-Betti numbers satisfy $b_i^{(2)}(\widetilde M;\pi)=0$ for all $i\neq n/2$. These numbers are the $\pi$-dimensions of the reduced $L^2$-cohomology of $\widetilde M$, introduced into topology by Atiyah in the 1970s; Dodziuk and Singer formulated the conjecture shortly afterwards. Through Atiyah's formula $\chi(M)=\sum_i(-1)^i b_i^{(2)}$, it implies the Hopf conjecture $(-1)^k\chi(M^{2k})\ge 0$ for closed aspherical $2k$-manifolds. Both are stated as conjectures in Davis's 2008 note in *L'Enseignement Mathématique* ([Davis](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/papers/singer-hopf.pdf)). Recent work proves the Singer conjecture for aspherical complex surfaces with residually finite [fundamental group](node:Fundamental%20Group), and for all aspherical complex surfaces except possibly those of Class VII$_0^+$ ([Albanese, Di Cerbo and Lombardi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10226)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: differential form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+form): definitions (sections, universal differential envelope, twisted forms) and basic identities.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Differential form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form): operations, Stokes theorem, physics applications, history.
- **Learn:** [Mazurowski, Differential Forms Lecture Notes](https://e.math.cornell.edu/people/mazurowski/DifferentialFormsNotes.pdf): forms on $\mathbb R^n$, the winding number, Stokes, the Poincaré lemma, Brouwer.
- **Primary:** [Davis, The Hopf conjecture and the Singer conjecture](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/papers/singer-hopf.pdf): statements of the Hopf and Singer conjectures on Euler characteristics and $L^2$-Betti numbers of aspherical manifolds.
- **Further reading:** [Bott and Tu, Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology (Springer, Graduate Texts in Mathematics, 1982)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3951-0): the standard graduate text on forms and topology.
references.Digital Logic and Logic Synthesis:
## Reference
### Overview
Digital logic describes circuits whose signals take two values and whose behaviour is given by Boolean functions; Shannon showed in 1938 that two-valued Boolean algebra describes switching circuits. Logic synthesis is the step of electronic design automation that turns an abstract specification, usually at register-transfer level (RTL) in Verilog or VHDL, into a network of logic gates; the other steps of circuit design in electronic design automation are place and route and verification and validation. ([Wikipedia: Logic synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_synthesis))

A truth table specifies the outputs of a combinational device for each of the $2^N$ combinations of its $N$ inputs, which makes it a good specification only for devices with few inputs and outputs. Any truth table converts to a sum-of-products (SOP) expression, with one AND term per row where the output is 1, all ORed together, and such an expression is a recipe for a circuit of inverters, AND gates and an OR gate. ([MIT 6.004](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c4/c4s1))

Synthesis has two classical problem settings. Two-level minimization looks for a smallest SOP and is now of limited importance in VLSI because most designs use many levels of logic; multilevel synthesis builds a Boolean network from the RTL, optimizes it technology-independently (with literal count of the factored form as an area proxy), and then performs technology mapping onto a library of gates under delay, power and area constraints. ([Wikipedia: Logic synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_synthesis)) Berkeley's ABC, a system for synthesis and verification of binary sequential logic circuits, combines scalable logic optimization based on And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) with DAG-based technology mapping for look-up tables and standard cells. ([ABC](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/abc/starting.htm))

### Formal definition
**Combinational device.** A combinational device with $N$ digital inputs is specified by a truth table with $2^N$ rows giving its outputs for every input combination; it is implemented from a library of logic gates (inverters, AND, OR, NAND, NOR and others). ([MIT 6.004](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c4/c4s1))

**Implicants.** For $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$, a product term $p$ (conjunction of literals) is an implicant if $p\Rightarrow f$; it is prime if no literal can be deleted while keeping $p\Rightarrow f$; a prime implicant is essential if it covers some minterm of $f$ that no combination of other prime implicants covers. ([Wikipedia: Implicant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implicant)) Exact two-level minimization selects essential prime implicants and then further prime implicants until every minterm is covered. ([Wikipedia: Quine–McCluskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quine%E2%80%93McCluskey_algorithm))

**And-Inverter Graph.** An AIG is a Boolean network of two-input AND nodes with optional complemented edges; any combinational network can be factored and converted to an AIG with De Morgan's rule, and structural hashing ensures no two AND nodes have the same pair of inputs. A cut $C$ of node $n$ is a set of nodes through which every path from the primary inputs to $n$ passes; it is $K$-feasible if $|C|\le K$. Two functions are NPN-equivalent if one is obtained from the other by negating inputs, permuting inputs and negating the output. ([Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton 2006](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/publications/2006/dac06_rwr.pdf))

### Key results
- **Functional completeness.** NAND alone and NOR alone are universal; De Morgan's law turns NAND–NAND and NOR–NOR networks into SOP form. A multiplexer with $N$ select inputs implements any $N$-input function by wiring constants to its data inputs, at a size exponential in $N$. ([MIT 6.004](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c4/c4s1))
- **Shannon's counting bound.** Almost all Boolean functions of $n$ variables require circuits of size $\Theta(2^n/n)$ (Shannon 1949), yet no superlinear lower bound has been proved for any explicit function. ([Wikipedia: Circuit complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_complexity))
- **Exact two-level minimization.** Quine–McCluskey (Quine 1952, McCluskey 1956) finds all prime implicants by merging terms that differ in one variable and then solves a covering problem on the prime implicant chart; a function can have about $3^n/n$ prime implicants, the covering step is a set-cover problem, and running time grows exponentially in $n$, so functions with many variables are minimized with potentially non-optimal heuristics such as Espresso. ([Wikipedia: Quine–McCluskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quine%E2%80%93McCluskey_algorithm))
- **Complexity of formula minimization.** Minimum Equivalent Expression, a natural optimization problem in the second level of the [polynomial hierarchy](node:Polynomial%20Hierarchy), is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete under Turing reductions, both in its depth-$k$ version for every $k\ge3$ and in the unbounded-depth version; the depth-2 case had been shown $\Sigma_2^p$-complete in 1998. ([Buchfuhrer thesis, Caltech](https://thesis.caltech.edu/2264/))
- **Canonical representations.** Fixing a variable order, each Boolean function has a unique (up to isomorphism) reduced function graph, and every other function graph for it has more vertices; Bryant applied these graphs to logic design verification. ([Bryant 1986](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~bryant/pubdir/ieeetc86.pdf))
- **AIG rewriting.** DAG-aware rewriting enumerates 4-feasible cuts, looks up each cut function's NPN class (there are 222 NPN classes of 4-variable functions, of which about 40 gave improvements experimentally) and replaces subgraphs by precomputed smaller ones while accounting for logic sharing. In ABC's experiments, scripts built from rewriting, refactoring and balancing often matched or beat SIS and MVSIS scripts in quality measured after mapping while being one to two orders of magnitude faster. ([Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton 2006](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/publications/2006/dac06_rwr.pdf))

### Examples
- **Karnaugh maps.** Arranging a truth table in Gray-code order makes adjacent cells differ in one input; prime implicants appear as maximal power-of-two rectangles of 1s. The method is practical up to about four variables. ([MIT 6.004](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c4/c4s1))
- **Hazard-free (lenient) SOP.** Simplification can introduce glitches; including all prime implicants in the SOP makes the implementation lenient. ([MIT 6.004](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c4/c4s1))
- **Wide gates.** An $n$-input AND built from 2-input gates as a chain has delay linear in $n$, as a tree logarithmic in $n$. ([MIT 6.004](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c4/c4s1))
- **NPN equivalence.** $ab+c$ and $ac+b$ are NPN-equivalent (swap $b,c$); $ab+c$ and $ab$ are not. ([Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton 2006](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/publications/2006/dac06_rwr.pdf))

### History
Boole's algebra and Shannon's 1938 switching-circuit paper are the foundations; early designers minimized by hand with Karnaugh maps (1953), and Quine–McCluskey was the first step toward automation. IBM's LSS was an early multilevel system using local transformations, and work on LSS and the Yorktown Silicon Compiler drove 1980s research; academic systems SIS (UC Berkeley), RASP (UCLA) and BOLD (Colorado) followed, and the technology entered commercial tools within a decade. Commercial high-level synthesis from C/C++ or SystemC to RTL appeared in 2004. ([Wikipedia: Logic synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_synthesis); [Wikipedia: Logic optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_optimization)) AIG rewriting was published at DAC 2006 by Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/1146909.1147048))

### Connections
- [Boolean Algebras](node:Boolean%20Algebras): the algebra of switching functions.
- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic): a combinational circuit is a shared representation of a propositional formula.
- [Binary Decision Diagrams](node:Binary%20Decision%20Diagrams): canonical representation used for equivalence checking and synthesis.
- [Boolean Circuits](node:Boolean%20Circuits): the complexity-theoretic model of the same objects.
- [Circuit Complexity](node:Circuit%20Complexity): Shannon's counting bound and the absence of strong explicit lower bounds.
- [Boolean Circuit Lower Bounds](node:Boolean%20Circuit%20Lower%20Bounds): why minimization is hard to certify.
- [SAT and SMT Solving](node:SAT%20and%20SMT%20Solving): SAT-based equivalence checking and don't-care computation in synthesis.
- [Model Checking](node:Model%20Checking): sequential verification of synthesized designs.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): two-level covering and minimization are intractable in general.
- [Hardware-Software Co-Design](node:Hardware-Software%20Co-Design): high-level synthesis sits above logic synthesis in the flow.

### Common pitfalls
- Minimizing two-level SOP size is of limited importance in VLSI, where most designs use multiple levels of logic and the simple cost estimates of technology-independent optimization are replaced by implementation-driven estimates during and after technology mapping. ([Wikipedia: Logic synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_synthesis))
- Heuristic minimizers such as Espresso need not return an optimum; exact methods scale only to small functions. ([Wikipedia: Logic optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_optimization))
- A logically minimal SOP may glitch when an input changes; including all prime implicants, even redundant ones, removes such glitches. ([MIT 6.004](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c4/c4s1))
- Cost functions differ between flows: traditional synthesis counts literals in factored forms while AIG rewriting counts AIG nodes and levels, so Mishchenko et al. compared quality after technology mapping. ([Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton 2006](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/publications/2006/dac06_rwr.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP).** Given a truth table and $s$, decide whether the function has a circuit of size $\le s$. Allender, Ilango and Vafa state that whether MCSP is NP-hard under familiar reductions (polynomial-time many-one or Turing, or $AC^0$) is closely related to longstanding open questions in complexity theory; MCSP is provably not hard under certain local reductions computable in $\mathrm{TIME}(n^{0.49})$, and they prove that PARITY does not reduce to superlinear approximations of circuit size via $AC^0$-Turing reductions with $O(1)$ queries. ([Allender, Ilango, Vafa](https://people.cs.rutgers.edu/%7Eallender/papers/ilango.vafa.pdf))
- **Explicit circuit lower bounds.** No superlinear circuit lower bound is known for any explicit function. ([Wikipedia: Circuit complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_complexity))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Logic synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_synthesis): the design flow and history.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Quine–McCluskey algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quine%E2%80%93McCluskey_algorithm): exact two-level minimization.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.004 Computation Structures, Combinational Logic](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c4/c4s1): SOP, universality, simplification, Karnaugh maps, MUX and ROM implementations.
- **Primary:** [Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton 2006, DAG-aware AIG rewriting](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/publications/2006/dac06_rwr.pdf): AIG-based combinational synthesis in ABC (DAC 2006).
- **Primary:** [Buchfuhrer, The Complexity of Formula Minimization (Caltech)](https://thesis.caltech.edu/2264/): $\Sigma_2^p$-completeness of formula minimization.
- **Further reading:** [ABC: A System for Sequential Synthesis and Verification](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/abc/starting.htm): the reference academic synthesis tool and its documentation.
references.Directed Acyclic Graphs:
## Reference
### Overview
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph with no directed cycles, where a cycle is a walk whose only repeated vertex is its first and last vertex. DAGs are exactly the directed graphs whose vertices can be listed in a topological order, an ordering in which every edge points from an earlier vertex to a later one. The reachability relation of a DAG is a partial order, so every DAG presents a finite poset, and different DAGs (for example a chain $u\to v\to w$ with or without the extra edge $u\to w$) can present the same poset ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph)).

DAGs are the standard model of dependency: spreadsheet recalculation, makefiles, instruction scheduling, PERT charts (whose longest path is the critical path), dataflow programs, combinational circuits, feedforward neural networks, Bayesian networks and causal diagrams, citation graphs, and Git version histories are all DAGs. Compressed data structures such as binary decision diagrams and directed acyclic word graphs are also DAGs, obtained by merging identical substructures of trees ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph)).

Algorithmically DAGs are the case where many hard digraph problems become easy: recognition, topological sorting, and single-source shortest and longest paths all run in linear time, while longest path is NP-hard on general graphs. Any digraph reduces to a DAG by contracting its strongly connected components, the condensation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph); [Princeton algs4](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/42digraph/)).

### Formal definition
A digraph $G=(V,E)$, $E\subseteq V\times V$, is **acyclic** if there is no sequence $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k=v_0$ with $k\ge 1$ and $(v_{i-1},v_i)\in E$ for all $i$. A **topological ordering** is a bijection $\pi:V\to\{1,\dots,|V|\}$ with
$$(u,v)\in E \implies \pi(u)<\pi(v).$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph); [Princeton algs4](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/42digraph/))

The **reachability order** sets $u\le v$ iff there is a directed path from $u$ to $v$; for a DAG this is a partial order. The **transitive closure** $G^{+}$ is the DAG with the most edges having the same reachability relation, and the **transitive reduction** $G^{-}$ is the one with the fewest; the edges of $G^{-}$ are exactly the covering pairs of the order, and a Hasse diagram is a drawing of $G^{-}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph)).

### Key results
- **Characterization by topological order.** A digraph has a topological ordering if and only if it is acyclic. In a DAG, the reverse postorder of a depth-first search is a topological ordering, computable in time $O(|V|+|E|)$. ([Princeton algs4](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/42digraph/))
- **Uniqueness of the order.** A DAG has exactly one topological ordering if and only if some directed path contains all its vertices (a Hamiltonian path). The topological orderings of a DAG are exactly the linear extensions of its reachability partial order. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- **Transitive reduction and closure.** For a DAG the transitive reduction and the transitive closure are uniquely determined and the reduction is a subgraph of the original; for digraphs with cycles a minimal reachability-preserving subgraph need not be unique. Both can be computed in $O(|V||E|)$ by a search from every vertex, or in $O(n^{\omega})$ via fast matrix multiplication, the reduction to Boolean matrix multiplication being due to Munro and to Fischer and Meyer (1971). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph); [Wikipedia: Transitive closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitive_closure))
- **Paths in linear time.** In a DAG with real edge weights, single-source shortest and longest paths are computed in linear time by relaxing edges in topological order; on general digraphs longest path is NP-hard. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- **Gallai–Hasse–Roy–Vitaver theorem.** For every undirected graph $G$, $\chi(G)$ equals one plus the minimum, over all orientations of $G$, of the number of edges in a longest directed path; an optimal orientation can be taken acyclic. Restricted to an acyclic orientation, the statement is a form of Mirsky's theorem: the longest chain of a finite poset equals the minimum number of antichains partitioning it. ([Wikipedia: GHRV theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallai%E2%80%93Hasse%E2%80%93Roy%E2%80%93Vitaver_theorem))
