- **Counting labeled DAGs (Robinson 1973).** The number $a_n$ of DAGs on $n$ labeled vertices satisfies $a_0=1$ and
$$a_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k-1}\binom{n}{k}2^{k(n-k)}a_{n-k},$$
giving $1,1,3,25,543,29281,\dots$ (OEIS A003024). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- **McKay–Oggier–Royle–Sloane–Wanless–Wilf theorem.** The number of labeled DAGs on $n$ vertices equals the number of $n\times n$ $(0,1)$-matrices all of whose eigenvalues are positive real numbers (Weisstein's conjecture); $A$ is the adjacency matrix of a DAG exactly when $A+I$ is such a matrix. ([arXiv: McKay et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0310423); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- **Acyclic orientations.** The number of acyclic orientations of an undirected graph $G$ is $|\chi_G(-1)|$, where $\chi_G$ is the chromatic polynomial. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))

### Examples
- **Hasse diagrams.** The inclusion order on the subsets of a three-element set is drawn as a DAG whose edges are its covering relations; the drawing depicts the transitive reduction. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- **Critical path.** In a PERT chart, milestones are vertices and tasks are weighted edges; the longest path, computable in linear time, is the critical path that determines project length. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- **Condensation.** Contracting each strongly connected component of any digraph yields a DAG; Kosaraju–Sharir computes the components in time $O(|V|+|E|)$, and the condensation of a graph that is already acyclic is the graph itself. ([Princeton algs4](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/42digraph/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- **Shortcut sets.** Adding a set of transitive-closure edges can shrink the diameter of a digraph; a folklore construction gets diameter $\tilde O(\sqrt n)$ with $O(n)$ added edges, Kogan and Parter reached $\tilde O(n^{1/3})$, and Vassilevska Williams, Xu and Xu proved an $\Omega(n^{1/5})$ lower bound for shortcut sets of size $O(m)$. ([arXiv: Kogan and Parter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13240); [arXiv: Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12051))
- **Polytrees and multitrees.** Orienting an undirected tree gives a polytree; multitrees, in which no two directed paths share endpoints, were introduced by Furnas and Zacks (1994). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))

### History
The colouring–orientation theorem was found repeatedly, by Vitaver (1962), Hasse (1965), Roy (1967) and Gallai (1968); Roy attributed it to a conjecture in Berge's 1958 graph theory text, and it generalizes Rédei's 1934 theorem that every tournament has a Hamiltonian path ([Wikipedia: GHRV theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallai%E2%80%93Hasse%E2%80%93Roy%E2%80%93Vitaver_theorem)). Munro and Fischer–Meyer reduced transitive closure to matrix multiplication in 1971 ([Wikipedia: Transitive closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitive_closure)); Aho, Garey and Ullman's "The Transitive Reduction of a Directed Graph" appeared in SIAM Journal on Computing 1(2), 1972 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/0201008)). Robinson enumerated labeled DAGs in 1973, de Solla Price studied citation DAGs in 1965, and Weisstein's eigenvalue conjecture was proved by McKay and coauthors (arXiv 2003, published 2004) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0310423)).

### Connections
- [Topological Sorting](node:Topological%20Sorting): the algorithmic face of the characterization theorem.
- [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders): every DAG's reachability relation is a finite poset; the Hasse diagram draws its transitive reduction.
- [Strongly Connected Components](node:Strongly%20Connected%20Components): contracting them turns any digraph into a DAG.
- [Dynamic Programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming): DP recurrences are evaluated along a topological order of their subproblem DAG.
- [Bayesian Networks](node:Bayesian%20Networks): probabilistic models whose factorization follows a DAG.
- [Causal Inference](node:Causal%20Inference): causal diagrams are DAGs.
- [Binary Decision Diagrams](node:Binary%20Decision%20Diagrams): rooted DAG representations of Boolean functions.
- [Graph Colorings](node:Graph%20Colorings): linked through acyclic orientations and the Gallai–Hasse–Roy–Vitaver theorem.
- [Workflow Dependency Graphs](node:Workflow%20Dependency%20Graphs): build systems and pipelines scheduled as DAGs.
- [Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling](node:Resource-Constrained%20Project%20Scheduling): precedence constraints form a DAG.
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): the ambient subject.

### Common pitfalls
- A DAG need not be a tree or forest: a vertex may have several parents, and the underlying undirected graph may contain cycles (pedigree collapse in family trees is an example). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- Distinct DAGs can have the same reachability order; only the transitive reduction and transitive closure are canonical. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- Making a digraph acyclic by deleting few vertices or arcs (minimum feedback vertex or arc set) is NP-hard, unlike recognition. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph))
- The $O(n^{\omega})$ closure bound is of theoretical interest; constant factors and memory on sparse graphs make it impractical. ([Wikipedia: Transitive closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitive_closure))

### Open problems
- **The 1/3–2/3 conjecture.** For every finite poset that is not a chain — equivalently, the reachability order of any DAG without a Hamiltonian path — there are $x,y$ such that the probability that $x$ precedes $y$ in a uniformly random topological ordering lies in $[1/3,2/3]$. Stated by Kislitsyn (1968) and independently by Fredman and Linial, it remains unsolved; Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter proved the bound $1/2-\sqrt5/10\approx 0.276$, and Olson and Sagan proved it for Boolean, set-partition and subspace lattices and some dimension-2 posets. If true it would let sorting with $e$ consistent linear extensions finish in $\log_{3/2}e$ comparisons. ([Wikipedia: 1/3–2/3 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture); [arXiv: Olson and Sagan](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04985))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Directed acyclic graph (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph): definitions, reachability, closure/reduction, enumeration, applications.
- **Learn:** [Directed Graphs, Algorithms 4th ed. (Princeton)](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/42digraph/): DFS-based topological sort, cycle detection, Kosaraju–Sharir, closure.
- **Primary:** [McKay et al., Acyclic digraphs and eigenvalues of (0,1)-matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0310423): proof of Weisstein's conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Aho, Garey, Ullman 1972, The Transitive Reduction of a Directed Graph](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/0201008): the original transitive-reduction paper (bibliographic record).
- **Further reading:** [Bang-Jensen and Gutin, Digraphs (Springer Monographs in Mathematics, 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-84800-998-1): monograph on directed graphs, cited by Wikipedia for transitive reduction (bibliographic record).
references.Dirichlet Problem:
## Reference
### Overview
The Dirichlet problem prescribes the values of a function on the boundary of a domain and asks for a solution of an elliptic equation inside, usually Laplace's or Poisson's equation, that attains those values. It is the model boundary value problem of potential theory: uniqueness follows from the maximum principle, explicit solutions exist for balls and half-spaces, and existence on general domains depends on the fine geometry of the boundary. ([Hunter, ch. 2](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch2.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_problem))

Three existence methods dominate. Perron's method builds the solution as a supremum of subharmonic functions, and the question becomes which boundary points are regular. The variational method goes back to Riemann's use of Dirichlet's principle; after Weierstrass found a flaw, Hilbert gave a rigorous existence proof by the direct method in 1900, and today it yields weak solutions in $H^1_0$ through the Lax–Milgram theorem. The probabilistic method, going back to Kakutani, represents the solution through the exit distribution of Brownian motion, that is, through harmonic measure. ([Perron method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron_method); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_problem); [Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem); [Harmonic measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_measure))

Modern research concerns the Dirichlet problem for divergence-form operators $-\operatorname{div}A\nabla$ with rough coefficients on rough domains, and boundary data in $L^p$ rather than $C(\partial\Omega)$. Solvability there is tied to quantitative absolute continuity ($A_\infty$) of elliptic measure with respect to surface measure. ([Hofmann–Kenig–Mayboroda–Pipher](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.2405); [Auscher, §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.01068))

### Formal definition
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set, $f\in C(\Omega)$ and $g\in C(\partial\Omega)$. The classical Dirichlet problem for Poisson's equation asks for $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ with
$$-\Delta u=f\ \text{in }\Omega,\qquad u=g\ \text{on }\partial\Omega;$$
with $f=0$ it is the harmonic Dirichlet problem. ([Hunter, eq. 2.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch2.pdf))

**Weak formulation.** For $g=0$, $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution if $\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. ([Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem))

**Regular boundary points.** A point $y\in\partial\Omega$ is regular if it has a barrier: a superharmonic $w_y$ on $\Omega$ with $w_y(y)=0$ and $w_y(x)>0$ for $x\neq y$. ([Perron method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron_method))

### Key results
- **Uniqueness.** On a bounded connected open set, for $f\in C(\Omega)$ and $g\in C(\partial\Omega)$, the Dirichlet problem has at most one solution in $C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$. The proof: the difference of two solutions is harmonic with zero boundary values, and the weak maximum principle $\min_{\partial\Omega}u\le u\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u$ forces it to vanish. ([Hunter, Thms. 2.17–2.18](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch2.pdf))
- **Poisson integral on the ball.** For the ball of radius $r$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $P(x,\zeta)=\dfrac{r^2-|x|^2}{r\,\omega_{n-1}|x-\zeta|^n}$, with $\omega_{n-1}$ the area of the unit sphere. For continuous boundary data, the Poisson integral is harmonic in the ball, extends continuously to the closed ball, and equals the data on the sphere. ([Poisson kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_kernel))
- **Perron's method (1923).** For boundary data $\varphi$, let $S_\varphi$ be the subharmonic functions on $\Omega$ whose boundary values are at most $\varphi$. The Perron solution $\sup S_\varphi$ is always harmonic. It attains the boundary value at every regular point, $u(x)\to\varphi(y)$ as $x\to y$, but may fail to do so elsewhere. ([Perron method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron_method)) The Dirichlet problem is solvable for all continuous data if and only if every boundary point is regular. ([Smolić–Klajn, appendix](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2007.10251))
- **Wiener's criterion.** Let $C_j$ be the capacity of $B_{\lambda^j}(x_0)\cap\Omega^c$ for fixed $\lambda\in(0,1)$. In $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$, the boundary point $x_0$ is regular if and only if $\sum_jC_j/\lambda^{j(n-2)}$ diverges. ([Perron method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron_method))
- **Variational existence.** On a bounded domain, $a(u,v)=\int\nabla u\cdot\nabla v$ is bounded and coercive on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ by the Poincaré inequality. Lax–Milgram therefore gives a unique weak solution of $-\Delta u=f$, $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, with $\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\le\|f\|_{H^{-1}}$. ([Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem)) Hunter's strategy is the same: first prove existence of weaker $H^1$ solutions, then show they are smooth under suitable assumptions on $f$, $g$, $\Omega$. ([Hunter, §2.3.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch2.pdf))
- **Smooth domains.** If $\partial\Omega$ is $C^{1,\alpha}$ for some $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and the data are continuous, a solution exists and is unique. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_problem))
- **Harmonic measure and Brownian motion.** For a bounded domain $D$ and $x\in D$, the harmonic measure $\omega(x,D)$ is a probability measure on $\partial D$, and the solution with continuous data $f$ is $H_f(x)=\int_{\partial D}f\,d\omega(x,D)$. The harmonic measure of a boundary set is the probability that Brownian motion started at $x$ first exits $D$ through that set. Kakutani identified this connection in 1944. ([Harmonic measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_measure))
- **Non-symmetric coefficients.** For $L=-\operatorname{div}A(x)\nabla$ on the upper half-space of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge2$, with $A$ bounded, measurable, uniformly elliptic, independent of the vertical variable, and not necessarily symmetric, $L$-harmonic measure is $A_\infty$ with respect to surface measure. Equivalently, the Dirichlet problem is solvable with $L^p$ data for some $p<\infty$. ([Hofmann–Kenig–Mayboroda–Pipher](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.2405))

### Examples
- **Unit disk.** $P_r(\theta)=\dfrac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^2}$ for $0\le r<1$, and the harmonic extension of $f$ is the convolution of $f$ with $P_r$, normalized by $1/(2\pi)$. ([Poisson kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_kernel))
- **Zaremba's punctured ball (1911).** Take $\Omega=B\setminus\{0\}$, with $g=0$ on $\partial B$ and $g=1$ at the centre. The Dirichlet problem has no solution, because the isolated boundary point is not regular. ([Smolić–Klajn, appendix](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2007.10251))
- **Lebesgue's spine (1912).** In $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$, remove the thin spike $\{x_n>0,\ x_1^2+\cdots+x_{n-1}^2\le e^{-1/x_n^2}\}$, which narrows to the origin. The boundary is connected, yet the Dirichlet problem can fail: the boundary has a sharp edge protruding into the region. ([Lebesgue spine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_spine); [Smolić–Klajn](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2007.10251))

### History
Green's 1828 essay treated the problem through what are now Green's functions. Dirichlet's 1850 paper shows he knew the solution for the ball via the Poisson kernel. Riemann solved the variational problem using what he called Dirichlet's principle. Weierstrass found a flaw in the argument, and Hilbert gave a rigorous existence proof in 1900. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_problem)) Zaremba (1911) and Lebesgue (1912) gave the first counterexamples. ([Smolić–Klajn](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2007.10251); [Lebesgue spine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_spine)) Perron's method appeared in 1923, and Wiener's capacity test characterized regular points. ([Perron method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron_method)) Kakutani connected the problem with Brownian motion in 1944. ([Harmonic measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_measure)) For non-symmetric real coefficients, Kenig asked whether elliptic measure is $A_\infty$. Kenig, Koch, Pipher and Toro answered this in the plane in 2000, and Hofmann, Kenig, Mayboroda and Pipher settled it in all dimensions in 2014. ([Auscher, §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.01068))

### Connections
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): the interior equations of the basic problem.
- [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle): the mechanism behind uniqueness and Perron's method.
- [Perron's Method](node:Perron's%20Method): the subharmonic-function existence method.
- [Harmonic Measure](node:Harmonic%20Measure) and [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus): the probabilistic representation.
- [Capacity and Fine Topology](node:Capacity%20and%20Fine%20Topology): Wiener's criterion for regular points.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces), [Weak Solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) and [Lax–Milgram Theorem](node:Lax–Milgram%20Theorem): the variational formulation.
- [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions): explicit representation formulas on special domains.
- [Newtonian Potential Theory](node:Newtonian%20Potential%20Theory) and [MSC 31Bxx - Higher-dimensional potential theory](node:MSC%2031Bxx%20-%20Higher-dimensional%20potential%20theory): the potential-theoretic setting.
- [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems): the Dirichlet problem is the model well-posed elliptic problem.
- [MSC 35Jxx - Elliptic equations and elliptic systems](node:MSC%2035Jxx%20-%20Elliptic%20equations%20and%20elliptic%20systems): the elliptic PDE context.

### Common pitfalls
- **Uniqueness is not existence.** The uniqueness theorem says nothing about existence. Stronger conditions on a solution make uniqueness easier and existence harder, which is why existence proofs usually start from weak $H^1$ solutions. ([Hunter, §2.3.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch2.pdf))
- **The Perron solution need not attain its boundary values.** It is always harmonic, but it attains the data only at regular points. Zaremba's and Lebesgue's examples show that this failure really happens. ([Perron method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron_method); [Smolić–Klajn](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2007.10251))
- **Sufficient conditions are not the criterion.** Regularity is hard to verify directly, so sufficient conditions such as the exterior cone condition are used in practice; Wiener's criterion is the exact test. ([Smolić–Klajn](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2007.10251); [Perron method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron_method))

### Open problems
None found. Searches tried: arXiv and web searches for open problems on the $L^p$ Dirichlet problem for non-symmetric elliptic operators and $A_\infty$ elliptic measure, and on regularity of boundary points (Zaremba, Lebesgue spine, Wiener criterion). The best-known question found, Kenig's question on $A_\infty$ for real non-symmetric $t$-independent coefficients, was settled in 2014. ([Auscher, §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.01068); [Hofmann–Kenig–Mayboroda–Pipher](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.2405))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Dirichlet problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_problem): formulation, smooth-domain existence, and history.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, PDE notes ch. 2](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch2.pdf): Laplace's equation, maximum principles, Harnack's inequality, and uniqueness.
- **Primary:** [Hofmann–Kenig–Mayboroda–Pipher](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.2405): $L^p$ Dirichlet solvability for non-symmetric elliptic operators.
- **Further reading:** [Gilbarg–Trudinger, Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order (Springer Classics in Mathematics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61798-0): the standard graduate monograph. Also [Auscher, Impact of Yves Meyer's work on Kato's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01068): a survey of boundary value problems with rough coefficients.
references.Distributions (Generalized Functions):
## Reference
### Overview
Distributions, or generalized functions, extend functions so that every one of them can be differentiated any number of times and so that point sources such as the Dirac delta become legitimate objects. A distribution is not evaluated at points; it is paired with smooth compactly supported test functions, generalizing the integral $\int f\varphi$. Derivatives are defined by moving them onto the test function, generalizing integration by parts. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29); [nLab: distribution](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/distribution))

The theory is the standard language of linear PDE: Green's functions are cumbersome without delta functions, and physically natural data (a plucked string with a triangular profile, which is not twice differentiable) make the classical wave equation problematic, leading to weak solutions. ([Johnson, MIT 18.303 notes](https://math.mit.edu/~stevenj/18.303/delta-notes.pdf)) Fundamental solutions of the wave and Klein–Gordon equations are distributions (the propagators of free quantum fields), quantum fields themselves are operator-valued distributions, and the singularity structure of a distribution (singular support and wave front set) is the starting point of microlocal analysis. ([nLab: distribution](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/distribution))

The price is multiplication. Distributions form a module over $C^\infty$ functions, but there is no reasonable product of two arbitrary distributions; products exist under wave-front conditions (Hörmander) or in larger algebras that give up part of the classical structure (Colombeau). ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29); [nLab: product of distributions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/product+of+distributions); [Wikipedia: Colombeau algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombeau_algebra))

### Formal definition
Let $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be open. $\mathcal{D}(U)=C_c^\infty(U)$ is the space of smooth compactly supported functions, with the topology in which $\varphi_k\to\varphi$ iff all $\operatorname{supp}\varphi_k$ lie in one compact $K\subset U$ and $\partial^\alpha\varphi_k\to\partial^\alpha\varphi$ uniformly for every $\alpha$. It is complete, locally convex, and not metrizable. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))

A distribution is a continuous linear functional $T:\mathcal{D}(U)\to\mathbb{C}$; the space is $\mathcal{D}'(U)$. Continuity is equivalent to sequential continuity and to: for every compact $K\subset U$ there are $C_K\ge0$ and $N_K\in\mathbb{N}$ with
$$|T(\varphi)|\le C_K\sup\{|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|:x\in K,\ |\alpha|\le N_K\}\quad\text{for all }\varphi\in\mathcal{D}(U),\ \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset K .$$
([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))

Derivatives: $\langle\partial^\alpha T,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle T,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$; in one variable $\langle T',\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\varphi'\rangle$. The delta at $x_0$ is $\langle\delta_{x_0},\varphi\rangle=\varphi(x_0)$, with $\langle\delta^{(n)}_{x_0},\varphi\rangle=(-1)^n\varphi^{(n)}(x_0)$, and the Heaviside function satisfies $H'=\delta$. ([NIST DLMF 1.16](https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.16))

The support $\operatorname{supp}T$ is the complement of the union of all open $V\subset U$ on which $T$ vanishes. Distributions of compact support extend uniquely to continuous linear functionals on $C^\infty(U)$, and this identifies them with the dual $\mathcal{E}'(U)$ of $C^\infty(U)$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) The singular support is the complement of the set near which $T$ is a smooth function. The wave front set $\mathrm{WF}(T)\subset U\times(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus0)$ is the complement of those $(x_0,\xi_0)$ for which there are $\phi\in C_c^\infty$ with $\phi(x_0)\neq0$ and an open cone $\Gamma\ni\xi_0$ such that for each $N$, $|\widehat{\phi T}(\xi)|\le c_N(1+|\xi|)^{-N}$ for $\xi\in\Gamma$. Its projection to $U$ is the singular support. ([Wikipedia: Wave front set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_front_set))

### Key results
- **Regular distributions.** Each $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ defines $\langle T_f,\varphi\rangle=\int f\varphi$, and $T_f=T_g$ iff $f=g$ a.e.; Radon measures also define distributions. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **Structure theorem.** For every $T\in\mathcal{D}'(U)$ there are continuous functions $g_\alpha$ on $U$ with $T=\sum_\alpha\partial^\alpha g_\alpha$, where every compact set meets the supports of only finitely many $g_\alpha$; if $T$ has finite order, finitely many $g_\alpha$ suffice. On a fixed compact $K$, $T=\partial^\alpha F$ on $C_c^\infty(K)$ for one continuous compactly supported $F$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **Point support.** If $\operatorname{supp}T=\{P\}$, then $T=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}a_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta_P$ for some $m$ and constants $a_\alpha$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) In QFT this is the ambiguity in extending a distribution from the complement of a point, i.e. renormalization freedom. ([nLab: distribution](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/distribution))
- **Convolution.** If $S\in\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $T\in\mathcal{E}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then $\langle S*T,\varphi\rangle=\langle S,\psi\rangle$ with $\psi(x)=\langle T,\tau_{-x}\varphi\rangle$ defines $S*T\in\mathcal{D}'$, and $\partial^\alpha(S*T)=(\partial^\alpha S)*T=S*(\partial^\alpha T)$. Titchmarsh's theorem: for $f\in C_c^\infty$ and compactly supported $T$, the [convex hull](node:Convex%20Hull) of $\operatorname{supp}(f*T)$ is the sum of the convex hulls of $\operatorname{supp}f$ and $\operatorname{supp}T$ (Hörmander, Thm 4.3.3). ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem.** Every nonzero linear differential operator $P(\partial)$ with constant coefficients has a fundamental solution $E\in\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $P(\partial)E=\delta$; hence $P(\partial)u=f$ is solvable for every compactly supported distribution $f$ (take $u=E*f$). Proved independently by Ehrenpreis (1954–55) and Malgrange (1955–56). The analogue for polynomial coefficients is false (Lewy's example). ([Wikipedia: Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem))
- **Schwartz kernel theorem.** For open $X,Y\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, every $k\in\mathcal{D}'(X\times Y)$ defines a continuous linear $K:\mathcal{D}(Y)\to\mathcal{D}'(X)$ with $\langle k,u\otimes v\rangle=\langle Kv,u\rangle$, and conversely every such continuous $K$ arises from exactly one $k$. The identity has kernel $\delta$ on the diagonal. ([Wikipedia: Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem))
- **Paley–Wiener–Schwartz theorem.** An entire function $F$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is the Fourier–Laplace transform of a distribution of compact support iff $|F(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^Ne^{B|\operatorname{Im}z|}$ for some $C,N,B$; the distribution is then supported in the closed ball of radius $B$. It is smooth iff for every $N$, $|F(z)|\le C_N(1+|z|)^{-N}e^{B|\operatorname{Im}z|}$. ([Wikipedia: Paley–Wiener theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley%E2%80%93Wiener_theorem))
- **Schwartz impossibility theorem (1954).** There is no associative algebra $A$ such that (1) $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ embeds linearly in $A$ with the constant $1$ as unit, (2) $A$ carries a linear derivation satisfying the Leibniz rule, (3) which restricts to the distributional derivative, and (4) the product restricts to the pointwise product of continuous functions. Colombeau algebras satisfy (1)–(3) and preserve products of smooth functions only. ([Wikipedia: Colombeau algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombeau_algebra)) Even associativity fails naively: $(\delta\cdot x)\cdot\mathrm{p.v.}\tfrac1x=0$ but $\delta\cdot(x\cdot\mathrm{p.v.}\tfrac1x)=\delta$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **Hörmander's product criterion.** The product $uv$ of two distributions is well defined (extending the product of smooth functions) when $\mathrm{WF}(u)+\mathrm{WF}(v)$ does not meet the zero section, i.e. no direction in $\mathrm{WF}(u)$ at a point has its opposite in $\mathrm{WF}(v)$ at the same point (Hörmander, ALPDO I, Thm 8.2.10). ([nLab: product of distributions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/product+of+distributions))

### Examples
- **Delta and Heaviside.** $H'=\delta$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$, and $\delta^{(n)}$ acts by $(-1)^n\varphi^{(n)}(0)$; $\delta$ models a point source such as a point charge or point mass. ([NIST DLMF 1.16](https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.16); [Johnson, MIT 18.303 notes](https://math.mit.edu/~stevenj/18.303/delta-notes.pdf))
- **Approximating $\delta$.** With $f_k=k\,\mathbf{1}_{[0,1/k]}$, $T_{f_k}\to\delta$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$, even though no function represents $\delta$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29); [Johnson, MIT 18.303 notes](https://math.mit.edu/~stevenj/18.303/delta-notes.pdf))
- **Jump across a curve.** A function on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with a jump across a smooth curve has the curve as singular support; its wave front set there consists of the normal directions, since it is smooth along the tangent. ([Wikipedia: Wave front set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_front_set))
- **Fourier transform.** On tempered distributions, $\langle\mathcal{F}u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\mathcal{F}\varphi\rangle$ for $\varphi$ in the Schwartz class; $\mathcal{F}\delta$ is a constant (its value depends on the normalization). ([NIST DLMF 1.16](https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.16))
- **Thin shells in GR.** Classical distribution theory is too narrow for some physically relevant solutions of Einstein's (nonlinear) equations; the review presents nonlinear generalized functions based on Colombeau algebras for these cases and argues that some solutions with weak singularities can be treated as distributional solutions. ([Steinbauer and Vickers, arXiv:gr-qc/0603078](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0603078))

### History
Sobolev (1936) used generalized functions for second-order hyperbolic PDEs; Schwartz developed the theory in the late 1940s, named distributions by analogy with charge distributions, and wrote the monograph *Théorie des distributions*. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) Schwartz's impossibility note appeared in 1954, and Colombeau's books on nonlinear generalized functions in 1984–85. ([Wikipedia: Colombeau algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombeau_algebra)) The wave front set was introduced around 1970, with Hörmander's "Fourier integral operators I" (Acta Math., 1971). ([Wikipedia: Wave front set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_front_set)) Grothendieck developed much of the theory of nuclear spaces while studying the kernel theorem. ([Wikipedia: Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem))

### Connections
- [Tempered Distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions): the subspace $\mathcal{S}'$ on which the Fourier transform acts.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) and [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem): Fourier transform extended by duality.
- [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration) and [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces): $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ functions as regular distributions.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces): weak derivatives are distributional derivatives that happen to be functions.
- [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions): fundamental solutions $PE=\delta$; Malgrange–Ehrenpreis.
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations), [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation), [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): weak solutions and point sources.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory) and [Renormalization](node:Renormalization): fields as operator-valued distributions; extension across points.
- [Israel Junction Conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions): delta-supported curvature on thin shells.
- [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces): $\mathcal{D}(U)$ is locally convex but not metrizable, so not a Banach space.

### Common pitfalls
- **$\delta(0)=\infty$.** $\delta$ is a functional with no pointwise values; ever-thinner bumps converge to it only in $\mathcal{D}'$. ([Johnson, MIT 18.303 notes](https://math.mit.edu/~stevenj/18.303/delta-notes.pdf))
- **Products.** $H$ and $\delta$ both have wave front set $\{(0,k):k\neq0\}$, so Hörmander's criterion excludes their products with themselves and with each other (e.g. $\delta\cdot\delta$); products with smooth functions are always defined. ([nLab: product of distributions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/product+of+distributions))
- **Stating Schwartz's theorem loosely.** "No product of distributions" is wrong as stated: Colombeau algebras embed $\mathcal{D}'$ and satisfy the derivative and Leibniz conditions while preserving products of *smooth* functions only. The obstruction needs all four conditions, including agreement with products of *continuous* functions. ([Wikipedia: Colombeau algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombeau_algebra))
- **Global structure.** A general distribution is a *locally finite* sum of derivatives of continuous functions, not a single finite sum, unless it has finite order. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **Variable coefficients.** Malgrange–Ehrenpreis is special to constant coefficients; the analogue for polynomial coefficients is false (Lewy's example). Even with constant coefficients the fundamental solution is not unique in general. ([Wikipedia: Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem))

### Open problems
None found. Searches tried: "open problem distribution theory Schwartz distributions multiplication division fundamental solution survey" (web), nLab's distribution and product-of-distributions pages, Wikipedia's Distribution, Colombeau algebra, Wave front set and Malgrange–Ehrenpreis articles, and the abstract of Steinbauer–Vickers' review (arXiv:gr-qc/0603078); none states an open problem in the core theory. Active research uses the theory (nonlinear generalized functions in GR, microlocal analysis in QFT), but no fetched source names a specific unsolved problem. ([nLab: distribution](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/distribution); [Steinbauer and Vickers, arXiv:gr-qc/0603078](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0603078))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Distribution (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29): topology of test functions, structure theorem, support, convolution.
- **Reference:** [nLab: distribution](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/distribution): generalized densities, wave front sets, QFT uses.
- **Learn:** [Johnson, "Delta functions and distributions", MIT 18.303 notes](https://math.mit.edu/~stevenj/18.303/delta-notes.pdf): motivation from PDEs and weak solutions.
- **Primary:** [Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I: Distribution Theory and Fourier Analysis (Springer)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2): the standard monograph; structure, convolution, fundamental solutions, wave front sets.
- **Further reading:** [Steinbauer and Vickers, "The use of generalised functions and distributions in general relativity" (arXiv:gr-qc/0603078)](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0603078): review of limits of linear distribution theory and Colombeau methods in GR.
references.Dual Vector Space:
## Reference
### Overview
The dual of a vector space $V$ over a field $F$ is the space $V^*$ of all linear functionals $V\to F$, with pointwise addition and scaling. It is defined over any field and needs neither a basis nor an inner product; the same construction for modules over a commutative ring gives the dual module. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space); [Conrad](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf)) Categorically, $V^*$ is the internal hom $[V,F]$, and $T\mapsto T^*$ makes $V\mapsto V^*$ a contravariant functor. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dual+vector+space))

In finite dimensions $V^*$ has the same dimension as $V$, but an identification $V\cong V^*$ depends on a choice, whereas the evaluation map $V\to V^{**}$ is natural and is an isomorphism; this was historically the motivating example of a natural transformation. In infinite dimensions the algebraic dual is strictly bigger than $V$, and analysis works instead with the much smaller continuous dual of a topological vector space. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dual+vector+space); [Erdős–Kaplansky theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Kaplansky_theorem); [Conrad, Rem. 4.8](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))

Conrad notes that the importance of the dual as a space separate from the original was first recognized in functional analysis, where the dual of a space of continuous functions is a space of measures; on $\mathbb R^n$ the dot product hides the distinction. ([Conrad](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))

### Formal definition
For a vector space $V$ over a field $F$, $V^*=\operatorname{Hom}_F(V,F)$ with $(a\varphi+b\psi)(v)=a\varphi(v)+b\psi(v)$. If $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is a basis of $V$, the **dual basis** $e^1,\dots,e^n$ is defined by $e^i(e_j)=\delta_{ij}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space))

The **evaluation map** $\Psi:V\to V^{**}$ is $\Psi(v)(\varphi)=\varphi(v)$. For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the **dual (transpose) map** is $T^*:W^*\to V^*$, $T^*(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T$. The **annihilator** of $S\subseteq V$ is $S^0=\{\varphi\in V^*:\varphi(s)=0\ \forall s\in S\}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space))

For a topological vector space $V$, the **continuous dual** $V'$ is the space of continuous linear functionals; the **weak-\* topology** $\sigma(V',V)$ is the topology of pointwise convergence on $V$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space))

### Key results
- **Finite dimension.** If $\dim V=n<\infty$, the dual basis is a basis of $V^*$, so $\dim V^*=n$; over a commutative ring, the dual of a finite free module of rank $n$ is finite free of rank $n$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space); [Conrad, Thm. 2.4](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- **Double dual.** $\Psi:V\to V^{**}$ is always injective and natural; it is an isomorphism when $V$ is finite-dimensional, and more generally for finite free modules. Modules for which it is an isomorphism are called reflexive. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space); [Conrad, Thm. 4.2](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dual+vector+space))
- **Annihilators.** For a subspace $W\subseteq V$, $(V/W)^*\cong W^0$; $(A+B)^0=A^0\cap B^0$ and $(A\cap B)^0=A^0+B^0$; for finite-dimensional $V$, $W^{00}=W$ under $V\cong V^{**}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space)) If $V$ is finite-dimensional, $\dim W+\dim W^0=\dim V$. ([Lee, Math 110 notes on Axler §3F](https://seewoo5.github.io/teaching/2024Fall/notes/Math110_week6.pdf))
- **Dual maps.** For finite-dimensional $V,W$ and $T:V\to W$: $\operatorname{null}T^*=(\operatorname{range}T)^0$ and $\operatorname{range}T^*=(\operatorname{null}T)^0$; $T$ is surjective iff $T^*$ is injective, and injective iff $T^*$ is surjective. ([Lee, Math 110 notes on Axler §3F](https://seewoo5.github.io/teaching/2024Fall/notes/Math110_week6.pdf)) Also $\dim\operatorname{range}T^*=\dim\operatorname{range}T$, which is the equality of row rank and column rank. ([Conrad, Ex. 5.18](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf)) Relative to dual bases the matrix of $T^*$ is the transpose of the matrix of $T$, and $(ST)^*=T^*S^*$. Over a field, if $T$ is injective then $T^*$ is onto, for spaces of any dimension. ([Conrad, Thms. 5.7, 5.8, 5.14](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- **Exactness.** For modules over a commutative ring, dualizing turns an exact sequence $M\xrightarrow{f}N\xrightarrow{g}P\to0$ into an exact sequence $0\to P^*\xrightarrow{g^*}N^*\xrightarrow{f^*}M^*$. The dual of an injective map need not be surjective: over $\mathbb Z$, the dual of the inclusion $2\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb Z$ is not onto. Over a field the dual of an injection is a surjection (previous item), so $\operatorname{Hom}_F(-,F)$ is exact on vector spaces. ([Conrad, Ex. 5.13, Thms. 5.14, 5.17](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- **Sums and products.** $\big(\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i\big)^*\cong\prod_{i\in I}M_i^*$; so if $V$ has a basis indexed by $A$, then $V\cong F^{(A)}$ and $V^*\cong F^A$. ([Conrad, Thm. 3.3](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- **Erdős–Kaplansky theorem.** If $V$ is infinite-dimensional over $F$ with basis $I$, then $\dim V^*=|F^I|$. By Cantor's theorem this exceeds $|I|=\dim V$, so $V^*\not\cong V$ and the dual basis is linearly independent but not a basis. ([Erdős–Kaplansky theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Kaplansky_theorem); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space)) Hence $\dim V<\dim V^*<\dim V^{**}$ and $\Psi$ is not surjective. ([Conrad, Ex. 4.7](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- **Hom, tensors and trace.** For finite-dimensional $U,V$ there is an isomorphism $U^*\otimes V\cong\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)$, $(f\otimes v)(u)=f(u)v$. ([Wikipedia, Tensor product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product)) For $U=V$, composing the inverse of $V\otimes V^*\cong\operatorname{End}(V)$ with the evaluation pairing $v\otimes\varphi\mapsto\varphi(v)$ gives exactly the trace: trace is contraction. ([Wikipedia, Trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_%28linear_algebra%29))
- **Riesz representation.** For a Hilbert space $H$, every continuous linear functional $\varphi$ has a unique $f_\varphi\in H$ with $\varphi(x)=\langle x,f_\varphi\rangle$ and $\|f_\varphi\|=\|\varphi\|$; $\varphi\mapsto f_\varphi$ is an antilinear isometric bijection, and completeness is needed for surjectivity. ([Wikipedia, Riesz representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz_representation_theorem))
- **Concrete continuous duals.** For $1<p<\infty$ and $1/p+1/q=1$, $(L^p(\mu))'\cong L^q(\mu)$ via $g\mapsto(f\mapsto\int fg\,d\mu)$, an isometry by Hölder, and $L^p$ is reflexive; for $\sigma$-finite $\mu$, $(L^1)'\cong L^\infty$. ([Wikipedia, Lp space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space)) For sequence spaces, $(\ell^p)'=\ell^q$, $(\ell^1)'=\ell^\infty$ and $c_0'\cong\ell^1$; $\ell^1$ is separable while its dual $\ell^\infty$ is not. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space)) $(\ell^\infty)'$ is the space ba of bounded finitely additive measures on $\mathbb N$ ([Wikipedia, ba space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba_space)); with the [axiom of choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice) it is much bigger than $\ell^1$, while Shelah showed that in some models of ZF the dual of $\ell^\infty$ is $\ell^1$. ([Wikipedia, Lp space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space))
- **Banach–Alaoglu theorem.** For a normed space $X$, the closed unit ball of $X'$ is weak-\* compact; more generally the polar of any neighbourhood of $0$ in a topological vector space is weak-\* compact. If $X$ is separable the ball is weak-\* sequentially compact (choice-free, by diagonalization); the general theorem is equivalent to the ultrafilter lemma. ([Wikipedia, Banach–Alaoglu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach%E2%80%93Alaoglu_theorem))

### Examples
- On $\mathbb R^n$ the coordinate functions are functionals, and every functional is $x\mapsto\sum_ia_ix_i$, i.e. dotting with a fixed vector. ([Conrad, Ex. 2.1](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- Over $\mathbb Z$, the dual of a finite [abelian group](node:Abelian%20Groups) is $0$, and the $\mathbb Z$-dual of $\bigoplus_{k\ge1}\mathbb Z$ is not free, although the map to the double dual is still an isomorphism there. ([Conrad, Rem. 2.6, Exs. 3.5, 4.6](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- Pairings: the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ on $M_n(R)$, and $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1fg\,dx$ on $L^p[0,1]\times L^q[0,1]$ for $1/p+1/q=1$. ([Conrad, §6](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- On a smooth manifold, integration $([\omega],[\sigma])\mapsto\int_\sigma\omega$ pairs de Rham classes (closed forms modulo exact forms) with smooth singular homology classes; it is well defined because exact forms integrate to $0$ on cycles and cycles differing by a boundary give the same integral of a closed form (Stokes). De Rham's theorem says the pairing is perfect, so $H^k_{dR}$ is the dual of real homology. ([Wikipedia, De Rham theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rham_theorem)) See [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology).

### History
Early names for the dual include *polarer Raum* (Hahn, 1927), *transponierter Raum* (Schauder, 1930; Banach, 1932) and *adjoint space* (Alaoglu, 1940); the term "dual" is due to Bourbaki. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space)) The Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert spaces is often attributed to Riesz and Fréchet, both in 1907. ([Wikipedia, Riesz representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz_representation_theorem)) Helly (1912) proved countable weak-\* compactness of the dual ball of $C([a,b])$, Banach the separable sequential case (1932), and Alaoglu the general theorem (1940). ([Wikipedia, Banach–Alaoglu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach%E2%80%93Alaoglu_theorem)) The map $V\to V^{**}$ motivated the definition of natural transformation. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dual+vector+space))

### Connections
- [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces): the dual is a vector space over the same field.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): dual maps are represented by transposed matrices.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): tensors are built from $V$ and $V^*$; $\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)\cong U^*\otimes V$.
- [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces): an inner product identifies $V$ with $V^*$ in finite dimensions.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) and [Riesz Representation Theorems](node:Riesz%20Representation%20Theorems): identification of $H$ with its continuous dual.
- [Hahn–Banach Theorem](node:Hahn–Banach%20Theorem): supplies enough continuous functionals on normed spaces.
- [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces) and [Weak Topologies in Banach Spaces](node:Weak%20Topologies%20in%20Banach%20Spaces): continuous duals, reflexivity, weak-\* compactness.
- [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): $V\mapsto V^*$ is a contravariant functor and $V\to V^{**}$ the archetypal natural transformation.
- [Modules over Commutative Rings](node:Modules%20over%20Commutative%20Rings): dual modules and reflexive modules.
- [Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality): the analogous duality for locally compact abelian groups.

### Common pitfalls
- Finite-dimensional $V$ and $V^*$ are isomorphic, but not naturally; choosing a basis or a nondegenerate bilinear form chooses an isomorphism. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space))
- In infinite dimensions the "dual basis" is not a basis of $V^*$, and $V\to V^{**}$ is not onto. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space); [Conrad, Ex. 4.7](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))
- Algebraic and continuous duals differ: the continuous dual is much smaller, and for it $V\to V''$ is often an isomorphism (reflexive spaces). ([Conrad, Rem. 4.8](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dual+vector+space))
- $(\ell^\infty)'\neq\ell^1$ (under choice), even though $(\ell^1)'=\ell^\infty$ and $c_0'=\ell^1$. ([Wikipedia, Lp space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space))
- Integration does not pair arbitrary $1$-forms with homology classes: only closed forms give values independent of the representing cycle. ([Wikipedia, De Rham theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rham_theorem))
- The dual map $T^*$ needs no inner product or basis; only its matrix description, the transpose, uses dual bases. ([Conrad, §5](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf))

### Open problems
None found. Searches tried: "dual vector space open problem algebraic dual reflexivity unsolved conjecture linear functionals" and "open problem dual space linear functionals algebraic dual open question reflexive vector space"; the results were consistency results without choice and solved Banach-space questions, not open problems about duals of vector spaces. For vector spaces over a field, the dimension of the algebraic dual is determined exactly by the Erdős–Kaplansky theorem. ([Erdős–Kaplansky theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Kaplansky_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, dual vector space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dual+vector+space): internal hom, naturality, reflexivity; [Dual space (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space): algebraic and continuous duals, annihilators, transpose, sequence-space duals.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Dual Modules](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/dualmod.pdf): duals over commutative rings, double duals, dual maps, exactness, pairings; [Lee, Math 110 notes on Axler §3F](https://seewoo5.github.io/teaching/2024Fall/notes/Math110_week6.pdf): annihilators and dual maps.
- **Primary:** [Halmos, *Finite-Dimensional Vector Spaces* (Springer UTM, 1974)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-6387-6): the classic monograph on coordinate-free finite-dimensional linear algebra.
- **Further reading:** [Lang, *Algebra* (Springer GTM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4613-0041-0): standard graduate algebra text; [Brezis, *Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations* (Springer, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-70914-7): continuous duals, weak-\* topology and reflexivity.
references.Dynamic Programming:
## Reference
### Overview
Dynamic programming (DP) is both a mathematical optimization method and an algorithmic paradigm: a problem is broken into recursively nested subproblems, and the value of the whole is expressed through the values of the parts. It applies when two conditions hold. The first is *optimal substructure*: an optimal solution can be combined from optimal solutions of subproblems, as in shortest paths, where every sub-path of a shortest path is itself shortest. The second is *overlapping subproblems*: a naive recursion would solve the same subproblems over and over, as when the naive recursive call tree for $\mathrm{fib}(5)$ computes $\mathrm{fib}(2)$ three times. Storing each subproblem's answer once turns the exponential-time naive Fibonacci recursion into an $O(n)$-time computation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming)).

In the optimization literature the recursive relation between the value of a problem and the values of its subproblems is called the *Bellman equation*. Its infinite-horizon discounted form is a functional equation for an unknown value function, and it is the bridge from algorithm design to [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes), [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning), and [Stochastic Optimal Control](node:Stochastic%20Optimal%20Control) ([Wikipedia: Bellman equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellman_equation)).

In algorithms, DP underlies [Shortest-Path Algorithms](node:Shortest-Path%20Algorithms) such as the [Bellman–Ford Algorithm](node:Bellman–Ford%20Algorithm) and Floyd–Warshall, [Sequence Alignment](node:Sequence%20Alignment) and [Edit Distance](node:Edit%20Distance), and interval problems such as matrix-chain multiplication and optimal binary search trees ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming); [Wikipedia: Optimal BST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimal_binary_search_tree)). Two lines of theory refine it: speedups that exploit monotone or Monge structure in the recurrence, and [Fine-Grained Complexity](node:Fine-Grained%20Complexity) lower bounds showing that the textbook quadratic DPs for edit distance and LCS are essentially optimal under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis ([Backurs and Indyk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.0348); [Abboud, Backurs, Vassilevska Williams](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.07053)).

### Formal definition
**Principle of optimality (Bellman).** An optimal policy has the property that, whatever the initial state and initial decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision ([Wikipedia: Bellman equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellman_equation)).

**Bellman equation.** For a deterministic infinite-horizon problem with state $x$, feasible actions $\Gamma(x)$, payoff $F(x,a)$, transition $T(x,a)$ and discount $0<\beta<1$, the value function satisfies
$$V(x)=\max_{a\in\Gamma(x)}\bigl\{F(x,a)+\beta\,V(T(x,a))\bigr\}.$$
With a Markov shock $z$ the continuation term becomes an expectation, $V(x,z)=\max_{c\in\Gamma(x,z)}\{F(x,c,z)+\beta\int V(T(x,c),z')\,d\mu_z(z')\}$ ([Wikipedia: Bellman equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellman_equation)).

**Algorithmic form.** A DP algorithm specifies a family of subproblems, a recurrence expressing each in terms of strictly smaller ones, base cases, and an evaluation order consistent with the dependency DAG. It is run either top-down with memoization (recurse, consulting a table before solving any subproblem) or bottom-up (tabulate from the smallest subproblems upward); bottom-up Fibonacci uses constant space where the memoized version needs $O(n)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming)). MIT's 6.006 packages the design as SRTBOT: Subproblem definition, Relate subproblems recursively, Topological order on subproblems (giving the subproblem DAG), Base cases, Original problem from subproblems, Time analysis. In that framing an algorithm is dynamic programming exactly when the dependency graph of recursive calls is a DAG whose subproblems overlap (in-degree above one), whereas divide and conquer gives a tree; the slogan is "recurse but re-use" ([MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 15](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/9eb3e9a51a7b5b60b0f67c2277f8b0ee_MIT6_006S20_lec15.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Knuth's optimal BST speedup (1971).** For the static optimal binary search tree recurrence $E(i,j)=\min_{i\le r\le j}\{E(i,r-1)+E(r+1,j)+W(i,j)\}$, with $W(i,j)$ the total probability weight of keys $i..j$, the naive evaluation takes $O(n^3)$ time; a monotonicity property of the optimal roots lets Knuth restrict each minimisation and fill the table in $O(n^2)$. When only gap probabilities are nonzero (alphabetic trees), Hu and Tucker (1971) find the optimum in $O(n\log n)$, and Mehlhorn's bisection rule gives a near-optimal tree in $O(n)$ ([Wikipedia: Optimal BST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimal_binary_search_tree)).
- **SMAWK row minima.** A matrix is totally monotone if in every submatrix the column of each row's minimum is at or after the column of the previous row's minimum; every Monge array is totally monotone, but not necessarily conversely. For an implicitly given totally monotone matrix with $r$ rows and $c$ columns, the SMAWK algorithm of Aggarwal, Klawe, Moran, Shor and Wilber (Algorithmica, 1987) finds every row minimum with $O(c(1+\log(r/c)))$ time and evaluations, against $O(rc)$ naively. Beyond the original computational-geometry applications, later applications include line breaking in paragraphs, RNA secondary structure prediction, DNA and protein sequence alignment, prefix-code construction and image thresholding ([Wikipedia: SMAWK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMAWK_algorithm)).
- **Edit distance is SETH-hard to beat.** If edit distance between two length-$n$ strings can be computed in $O(n^{2-\delta})$ time for some constant $\delta>0$, then CNF-SAT on $N$ variables and $M$ clauses can be solved in $M^{O(1)}2^{(1-\varepsilon)N}$ time for some $\varepsilon>0$, contradicting SETH. So the classical quadratic DP cannot be improved by a polynomial factor unless SETH fails ([Backurs and Indyk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.0348)).
- **LCS and dynamic time warping.** For two strings over a constant-size alphabet, an $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithm for longest common subsequence or dynamic time warping distance would refute SETH; for $k$ strings over an alphabet of size $O(k)$, an $O(n^{k-\varepsilon})$ LCS algorithm would too ([Abboud, Backurs, Vassilevska Williams](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.07053)).
- **Pseudo-polynomial knapsack.** The 0-1 knapsack recurrence $m[i,w]=\max(m[i-1,w],\,m[i-1,w-w_i]+v_i)$ (for $w_i\le w$) runs in $O(nW)$ time and space. This is pseudo-polynomial, since $W$ takes only about $\log W$ bits, which is why the decision version is weakly NP-complete ([Wikipedia: Knapsack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knapsack_problem)).

### Examples
- **Matrix-chain multiplication:** $m[i,j]$, the minimum number of scalar multiplications for $A_i\cdots A_j$, is a minimum over split points $k$ of $m[i,k]+m[k+1,j]$ plus the cost of the final product ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming)).
- **Egg dropping:** $W(n,k)=1+\min_x\max(W(n-1,x-1),W(n,k-x))$ with $W(n,0)=0$ and $W(1,k)=k$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming)).
- **Sequence alignment:** cell $(i,j)$ stores the optimal alignment cost of the prefixes $A[1..i]$, $B[1..j]$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming)).
- **Fibonacci:** naive recursion takes $\Omega(2^{n/2})$ time because $F(k)$ is recomputed; with memoization there are $n+1$ subproblems and fewer than $2n$ dependencies, so $O(n)$ additions ([MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 15](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/9eb3e9a51a7b5b60b0f67c2277f8b0ee_MIT6_006S20_lec15.pdf)).

### History
Richard Bellman developed the method in the 1950s, using "dynamic" for its time-varying sense and "programming" in the sense of planning; his own account that he chose the name to shield RAND's research from Secretary of Defense Wilson cannot be strictly true, since his first paper using the term predates Wilson's appointment ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming)). Bellman's survey "The theory of dynamic programming" appeared in the *Bulletin of the AMS* 60(6):503–515 in 1954 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1954-09848-8)). Knuth's 1971 $O(n^2)$ algorithm for optimal BSTs ([Wikipedia: Optimal BST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimal_binary_search_tree)) and the 1987 SMAWK algorithm ([Wikipedia: SMAWK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMAWK_algorithm)) are early instances of DP speedups from monotone structure, and conditional lower bounds for textbook DP problems followed from 2014 ([Backurs and Indyk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.0348)).

### Connections
- [Divide and Conquer](node:Divide%20and%20Conquer): also recursive, but its subproblems are disjoint; DP is what to use when they overlap.
- [Greedy Algorithms](node:Greedy%20Algorithms): commit to one locally optimal choice instead of minimising over all choices; correct only with a greedy-choice property.
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes) and [Value Iteration](node:Value%20Iteration): value iteration and policy iteration are DP on the Bellman equation.
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): approximates the Bellman equation from samples when the model is unknown.
- [Hidden Markov Models](node:Hidden%20Markov%20Models): Viterbi decoding and the forward algorithm are DP over time steps.
- [Shortest-Path Algorithms](node:Shortest-Path%20Algorithms) and [Bellman–Ford Algorithm](node:Bellman–Ford%20Algorithm): DP over path length.
- [Edit Distance](node:Edit%20Distance) and [Sequence Alignment](node:Sequence%20Alignment): the standard quadratic string DPs.
- [Fine-Grained Complexity](node:Fine-Grained%20Complexity): explains why many DPs cannot be sped up polynomially.
- [Hamilton–Jacobi Equations](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Equations) and [Stochastic Optimal Control](node:Stochastic%20Optimal%20Control): the continuous-time analogue of the Bellman equation.
- [Search Trees](node:Search%20Trees): the optimal BST problem is a DP over key intervals.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): pseudo-polynomial DPs separate weakly from strongly NP-hard problems.

### Common pitfalls
- Optimal substructure is not automatic. The cheapest airline fare from A to B may route through C, while the cheapest fare from A to C routes through some other airport D; the problem acquires optimal substructure only once the number of layovers is a parameter. The longest path problem is also listed as lacking it ([Wikipedia: Optimal substructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimal_substructure)).
- "Polynomial in the table size" is not "polynomial in the input": the $O(nW)$ knapsack DP is exponential in the bit length of $W$ ([Wikipedia: Knapsack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knapsack_problem)).
- Numerical backward induction on the Bellman equation may be infeasible with many state variables, the *curse of dimensionality* ([Wikipedia: Bellman equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellman_equation)).

### Open problems
- **Subquadratic (min,+)-convolution.** $(\min,+)$-convolution is easily computed in $O(n^2)$ time, but no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithm is known for any $\varepsilon>0$; Cygan, Mucha, Węgrzycki and Włodarczyk take its hardness as an assumption and prove it equivalent to variants of knapsack and to problems on subadditive sequences, so a breakthrough on any one would speed up all of them. They also explain why basing these lower bounds on SETH instead might not be possible ([Cygan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.07669)).
- **LCS of $k$ strings over a constant alphabet.** Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams prove the $n^{k-o(1)}$ SETH lower bound for $k$-LCS only for alphabets of size $O(k)$; whether the same lower bound holds when the alphabet size is a constant independent of $k$ is "a main question we leave open", as a step toward it they prove a tight $n^{k-o(1)}$ bound, under a conjecture of theirs, for a variant they call Local-$k$-LCS even over an $O(1)$ alphabet ([Abboud, Backurs, Vassilevska Williams](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.07053)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Dynamic programming (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming): definitions, history, many worked recurrences.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.006 Lecture 15 notes (Demaine, Ku, Solomon)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/9eb3e9a51a7b5b60b0f67c2277f8b0ee_MIT6_006S20_lec15.pdf): the SRTBOT recipe, subproblem DAGs, memoization versus bottom-up.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.006 Lecture 15 video page](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/resources/lecture-15-dynamic-programming-part-1-srtbot-fib-dags-bowling/): first of four DP lectures.
- **Primary:** [Backurs and Indyk, Edit Distance Cannot Be Computed in Strongly Subquadratic Time (unless SETH is false)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.0348): the founding conditional lower bound for a textbook DP.
- **Primary:** [Cygan et al., On problems equivalent to (min,+)-convolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.07669): equivalence class of knapsack-type DPs.
- **Further reading:** [Bellman, The theory of dynamic programming, Bull. AMS 60 (1954)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1954-09848-8): Bellman's own survey of the theory.
references.Dynamical Systems:
## Reference
### Overview
A dynamical system is a rule of time evolution on a state space, and the theory asks about long-time behaviour: will orbits stay bounded, settle down, recur, or behave chaotically? Teschl's motivating example is whether planets eventually collide or the solar system persists for all times; stable quasi-periodic motions and their persistence under small perturbations are the subject of the KAM theorem. ([Teschl, §6.1 and §8.6](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

The subject has three overlapping branches. Smooth (differentiable) dynamics studies flows of [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) and diffeomorphisms through fixed points, linearization, invariant manifolds, [bifurcations](node:Bifurcation%20Theory) and [hyperbolicity](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems). Topological dynamics studies continuous maps, limit sets and [symbolic models](node:Symbolic%20Dynamics). [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) studies systems with an invariant measure through recurrence and the convergence of time averages. ([Teschl, chapters 6–13](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf); [Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory))

A recurring theme is which qualitative features survive perturbation of the system itself. Structural stability asks that $C^1$-small perturbations leave the qualitative behaviour unchanged; it is distinct from [Lyapunov stability](node:Lyapunov%20Stability), which concerns perturbations of initial conditions. ([Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability))

### Formal definition
A dynamical system is a semigroup $G$ with identity $e$ acting on a set $M$: a map $G\times M\to M$, $(g,x)\mapsto T_g(x)$, with
$$T_g\circ T_h=T_{g\circ h},\qquad T_e=I.$$
Discrete time is $G=\mathbb N_0$ (iterates of one map $f$, $T_n=f^n$) or $G=\mathbb Z$ (when $f$ is invertible); continuous time is $G=\mathbb R_+$ or $\mathbb R$. ([Teschl, §6.1, eqs. 6.1–6.5](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

For $\dot x=f(x)$ on open $M\subset\mathbb R^n$, let $I_x=(T_-(x),T_+(x))$ be the maximal interval of the integral curve $\varphi(\cdot,x)$ with $\varphi(0,x)=x$, and $W=\bigcup_xI_x\times\{x\}$. The flow is $\Phi:W\to M$, $\Phi(t,x)=\varphi(t,x)$. The $\omega_\pm$-limit set $\omega_\pm(x)$ is the set of $y$ with $\Phi(t_n,x)\to y$ for some $t_n\to\pm\infty$; it is closed and invariant. ([Teschl, §6.2 eqs. 6.8–6.9, §6.3 Lemma 6.5](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

A fixed point $x_0$ is hyperbolic if the Jacobian $A=df(x_0)$ has no eigenvalue with zero real part. ([Hartman–Grobman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem)) A Liapunov function near a fixed point $x_0$ is a continuous $L:U(x_0)\to\mathbb R$ vanishing at $x_0$, positive elsewhere, and nonincreasing along solutions; it is strict if it is strictly decreasing. ([Teschl, §6.6](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

### Key results
- **Local flow.** If $f\in C^k(M,\mathbb R^n)$, $k\ge1$, each $x\in M$ has a unique maximal integral curve $\Phi(\cdot,x)\in C^k(I_x,M)$; $W$ is open, $\Phi\in C^k(W,M)$, $\Phi(0,x)=x$ and $\Phi(t+s,x)=\Phi(t,\Phi(s,x))$ for $s,t+s\in I_x$. ([Teschl, Theorem 6.1](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Stability by linearization and by Liapunov functions.** If $f\in C^1$ and all eigenvalues of $df(x_0)$ have negative real part, $x_0$ is exponentially stable; if $df(x_0)=0$ the linearization gives no information ($\dot x=\mu x^3$). If a Liapunov function exists, $x_0$ is stable; if it is not constant on any orbit in $U(x_0)\setminus\{x_0\}$ (e.g. strict), $x_0$ is asymptotically stable (Krasovskii–LaSalle). ([Teschl, Theorems 6.10, 6.13, 6.14](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Hartman–Grobman.** Near a hyperbolic fixed point the flow is topologically conjugate to its linearization: there is a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $\varphi=I+h$, $h$ bounded, with $\varphi\circ e^{tA}=\Phi_t\circ\varphi$ near $0$ (Teschl, for differentiable $f$). The conjugacy need not be smooth, nor even locally Lipschitz, though it is Hölder continuous; for smooth $f$ in dimension two the conjugacy and its inverse are $C^1$ (but need not be $C^2$), and in any dimension it is differentiable at the equilibrium if $f'$ is Hölder continuous. Grobman (1959) and Hartman (1960). ([Teschl, Theorem 9.9](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf); [Hartman–Grobman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem))
- **[Stable manifold theorem](node:Stable%20Manifold%20Theorem).** If $f\in C^k$, $k\ge1$, has a fixed point $x_0$ with Jacobian $A$ and linear stable/unstable subspaces $E^\pm$, then near $x_0$ the stable and unstable sets are graphs $\{x_0+a+h^\pm(a):a\in E^\pm\cap U\}$ of $C^k$ maps $h^\pm$ vanishing to first order at $x_0$, and $|\Phi(t,x)-x_0|\le Ce^{\mp t\alpha}$ for $\pm t\ge0$, $x\in M^\pm$, for any $\alpha<\min\{|\operatorname{Re}\alpha_j|:\operatorname{Re}\alpha_j\ne0\}$. ([Teschl, Theorem 9.4](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Poincaré–Bendixson (generalized).** If $M\subset\mathbb R^2$ is open, $f\in C^1(M,\mathbb R^2)$, and $\omega_\sigma(x)\ne\emptyset$ is compact, connected and contains finitely many fixed points, then $\omega_\sigma(x)$ is a fixed point, a regular periodic orbit, or finitely many fixed points joined by non-closed orbits whose limit sets are among those fixed points. ([Teschl, Theorem 7.16](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Recurrence.** A volume-preserving bijection of a bounded region $D\subset\mathbb R^n$ has, in every neighbourhood $U\subset D$, a point returning to $U$ (Poincaré); measure-theoretically, $\mu(A)>0$ implies $\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A)>0$ for some $n$. ([Teschl, Theorem 8.11](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf); [Moreira, Theorem 2.1.1](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf))
- **Birkhoff's ergodic theorem.** If $T$ preserves a probability measure $\mu$ and $f\in L^1(\mu)$, the averages $\frac1n\sum_{k<n}f(T^kx)$ converge a.e. to an invariant limit, which equals $\int f\,d\mu$ when $T$ is ergodic. ([Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory))
- **[KAM theorem](node:KAM%20Theory).** Let $H_0,H_1$ be analytic on $D\times\mathbb T^n$ with $H_0$ nondegenerate in Teschl's sense (eq. 8.108), and let $\Omega_\alpha(D)$ be the frequencies with $|k\cdot\Omega|\ge\alpha|k|^{-n}$ for all $k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}$. Then for $|\varepsilon|<\delta\alpha^2$ all invariant tori of the unperturbed system with frequencies in $\Omega_\alpha(D)$ persist as slightly deformed tori depending continuously on $I$. ([Teschl, Theorem 8.13 and eq. 8.107](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) See [Hamiltonian Dynamical Systems](node:Hamiltonian%20Dynamical%20Systems).
- **Horseshoes and homoclinic chaos.** The Smale horseshoe has an invariant Cantor set on which the dynamics is equivalent to the two-sided shift on two symbols. Smale–Birkhoff: if a diffeomorphism has a hyperbolic fixed point with a transversal homoclinic point, some iterate has a hyperbolic invariant set on which it is topologically equivalent to that shift. ([Teschl, Theorems 13.1–13.2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) See [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory).
- **Sharkovskii.** A continuous interval map with an orbit of period $m$ has orbits of prime period $n$ for every $n$ with $m\succ n$ in Sharkovskii's ordering. ([Teschl, Theorem 11.2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Structural stability.** Andronov–Pontryagin: a $C^1$ vector field on the unit disk (transversal to the boundary) or on the two-sphere is structurally stable iff it has finitely many singular points and periodic orbits, all non-degenerate, and no saddle-to-saddle connections. Peixoto's theorem, due to Maurício and Marília Peixoto, was the first global characterization; Anosov diffeomorphisms and flows are structurally stable in every dimension; Smale found that structurally stable systems are not dense in higher dimensions. ([Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability))

### Examples
The equation $\dot x=\mu x^3$ is asymptotically stable for $\mu<0$ and unstable for $\mu>0$ although its linearization at $0$ vanishes. ([Teschl, eq. 6.30](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) Hyperbolic toral automorphisms such as Arnold's cat map are the basic structurally stable chaotic examples. ([Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability)) Mixing gives a hierarchy of statistical chaos: strong mixing implies weak mixing implies ergodicity, with neither converse true. ([Mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_%28mathematics%29))

### History
Grobman (1959) and Hartman (1960) proved the linearization theorem. ([Hartman–Grobman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem)) Birkhoff's ergodic theorem appeared in 1931 and von Neumann's mean ergodic theorem in 1932. ([Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory)) The Peixotos' work on structural stability dates from the late 1950s and early 1960s, and Smale's hope that structural stability is typical was refuted by his own higher-dimensional examples. ([Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability)) The KAM theorem is due to Kolmogorov, Arnold and Moser. ([Teschl, §8.6](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

### Connections
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations): source of continuous-time flows.
- [Lyapunov Stability](node:Lyapunov%20Stability): stability of fixed points under perturbation of initial data.
- [Stable Manifold Theorem](node:Stable%20Manifold%20Theorem): invariant manifolds at hyperbolic points.
- [Hyperbolic Dynamical Systems](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems) and [MSC 37Dxx - Dynamical systems with hyperbolic behavior](node:MSC%2037Dxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20with%20hyperbolic%20behavior): uniformly hyperbolic theory, Anosov systems, horseshoes.
- [Bifurcation Theory](node:Bifurcation%20Theory): qualitative change under parameter variation.
- [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory), [Symbolic Dynamics](node:Symbolic%20Dynamics), [Topological Entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy): complexity of orbits.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) and [MSC 37Axx - Ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037Axx%20-%20Ergodic%20theory): invariant measures and statistical behaviour.
- [KAM Theory](node:KAM%20Theory) and [Hamiltonian Dynamical Systems](node:Hamiltonian%20Dynamical%20Systems): perturbation of integrable systems.
- [Global Attractors](node:Global%20Attractors): long-time behaviour of dissipative systems.
- [MSC 37Bxx - Topological dynamics](node:MSC%2037Bxx%20-%20Topological%20dynamics): continuous maps on [topological spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces).

### Common pitfalls
Flows of ODEs are in general only local: $\Phi(t+s,x)=\Phi(t,\Phi(s,x))$ holds only for $s,t+s\in I_x$, and $\omega_\pm(x)$ is empty unless $x$ is $\pm$-complete. ([Teschl, Theorem 6.1, §6.3](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

Hartman–Grobman gives only a topological conjugacy; even for smooth $f$ the conjugacy need not be locally Lipschitz. ([Hartman–Grobman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem)) Linearization gives no information when the Jacobian vanishes at the fixed point, as for $\dot x=\mu x^3$. ([Teschl, §6.5](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

Structural stability and Lyapunov stability are different notions: the first perturbs the system, the second perturbs initial conditions. ([Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability))

### Open problems
- **Second part of Hilbert's sixteenth problem.** Find an upper bound $H(n)$ for the number of limit cycles of planar polynomial vector fields of degree $n$; whether a finite $H(n)$ exists "remains unsolved for any $n>1$", although Ilyashenko and Écalle proved that each individual polynomial vector field has finitely many limit cycles, and quadratic fields with four limit cycles are known. ([Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem))
- **Multiple mixing.** It is not known whether strong 2-mixing implies strong 3-mixing for measure-preserving systems. ([Mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_%28mathematics%29))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hartman–Grobman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem): precise statement and regularity of the conjugacy; see also [Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability).
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.385J Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (Rosales, 2014)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-385j-nonlinear-dynamics-and-chaos-fall-2014/): graduate course with lecture notes and problem sets.
- **Primary:** [Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS, author's version)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf): graduate text, chapters 6–13 on flows, stability, invariant manifolds, KAM and chaos.
- **Further reading:** [Katok–Hasselblatt, Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems (CUP, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511809187): the standard graduate monograph.
- **Further reading:** [Guckenheimer–Holmes, Nonlinear Oscillations, Dynamical Systems, and Bifurcations of Vector Fields (Springer, 1983)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1140-2): applied and bifurcation-theoretic standard text.
references.Effective Einstein Equations on the Bran:
## Reference
### Overview
Brane cosmology models the visible four-dimensional universe as a membrane-like brane inside a higher-dimensional bulk, with Standard Model forces confined to the brane and gravity free to spread into the bulk. No experimental evidence for the required [extra dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions) has been reported. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brane_cosmology))

The Shiromizu–Maeda–Sasaki (SMS) equations are the four-dimensional [Einstein equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations) that a brane observer infers. They are derived by projecting the 5D Einstein equations onto the brane with the [Gauss–Codazzi equations](node:Gauss–Codazzi%20Equations), and the [extrinsic curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature) is eliminated with the [Israel junction conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions) under $Z_2$ symmetry. Ordinary 4D gravity is recovered at low energy only if the brane tension is positive. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))

The result has two corrections to [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): a local term quadratic in brane stress-energy, important at high energy, and the projected bulk Weyl tensor $E_{\mu\nu}$, which is nonlocal and carries [Kaluza–Klein](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes) (5D graviton) effects.
