These equations are the starting point for [Randall–Sundrum](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model) cosmology and astrophysics. ([Maartens & Koyama, Living Reviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962); [PDF §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))

### Formal definition
Assume 5D Einstein gravity with bulk cosmological constant $\Lambda$ (negative), a timelike brane with induced metric $q_{\mu\nu}$, and brane stress-energy $S_{\mu\nu}=-\lambda q_{\mu\nu}+\tau_{\mu\nu}$, where $\lambda$ is the tension. Assume $Z_2$ symmetry about the brane and no bulk matter. The junction condition $[K_{\mu\nu}]=-\kappa_5^2(S_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac13 q_{\mu\nu}S)$ then gives $K^+_{\mu\nu}=-K^-_{\mu\nu}=-\tfrac12\kappa_5^2(S_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac13 q_{\mu\nu}S)$. Substituting this into the Gauss equation gives ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))
$$
{}^{(4)}G_{\mu\nu}=-\Lambda_4q_{\mu\nu}+8\pi G_N\tau_{\mu\nu}+\kappa_5^4\pi_{\mu\nu}-E_{\mu\nu},
$$
with
$$
\Lambda_4=\frac12\kappa_5^2\left(\Lambda+\frac16\kappa_5^2\lambda^2\right),\qquad
G_N=\frac{\kappa_5^4\lambda}{48\pi},
$$
$$
\pi_{\mu\nu}=-\frac14\tau_{\mu\alpha}\tau_\nu{}^\alpha+\frac1{12}\tau\tau_{\mu\nu}+\frac18q_{\mu\nu}\tau_{\alpha\beta}\tau^{\alpha\beta}-\frac1{24}q_{\mu\nu}\tau^2 .
$$
Here $E_{\mu\nu}$ is the electric part of the 5D Weyl tensor, $E_{\mu\nu}={}^{(5)}C^\alpha{}_{\beta\rho\sigma}n_\alpha n^\rho q^\beta{}_\mu q^\sigma{}_\nu$, taken as a limit approaching the brane from either side. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))

The **RS fine-tuning** is $\Lambda_4=0$, i.e. $\Lambda=-\kappa_5^2\lambda^2/6$. By choosing $\Lambda$ and $\lambda$ the effective $\Lambda_4$ can take any value. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076)) Maartens and Koyama write the same equations with $\kappa_4^2=\kappa_5^4\lambda/6$ and state that $\Lambda_4\neq0$ exactly when the RS balance between bulk cosmological constant and tension is broken. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))

### Key results
- **Low-energy limit.** The ratio of the quadratic term to the ordinary matter term is $\sim\rho/\lambda$ (SMS write $M^4/M_\lambda^4$). For $\rho\ll\lambda$ and negligible $E_{\mu\nu}$, the equations reduce to ${}^{(4)}G_{\mu\nu}\simeq-\Lambda_4q_{\mu\nu}+8\pi G_N\tau_{\mu\nu}$. $G_N>0$ requires $\lambda>0$, so a negative-tension brane does not give normal gravity. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076); [Maartens & Koyama, PDF §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
- **Constraint on the Weyl term.** With no bulk matter, $D^\nu\tau_{\mu\nu}=0$, and the contracted Bianchi identity forces
$$D^\mu E_{\mu\nu}=\tfrac14\kappa_5^4\Big[\tau^{\alpha\beta}(D_\nu\tau_{\alpha\beta}-D_\beta\tau_{\nu\alpha})+\tfrac13(\tau_{\mu\nu}-q_{\mu\nu}\tau)D^\mu\tau\Big].$$
So the longitudinal part of $E_{\mu\nu}$ is fixed by brane matter. The transverse-traceless part (5D [gravitational waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves)) is not, and the brane equations are not closed in general. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076)) The 9 components of the tracefree $E_{\mu\nu}$ reduce to 5 degrees of freedom, the polarizations of the 5D graviton. Closing the system requires the 5D evolution equations for $E_{\mu\nu}$ and the magnetic Weyl part, with boundary conditions at the brane. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
- **No inhomogeneous perfect fluid in pure AdS.** If $E_{\mu\nu}=0$ (pure AdS bulk) and brane matter is a perfect fluid, then $D^\nu\pi_{\mu\nu}=\tfrac16(\rho+P)h_{\mu\nu}D^\nu\rho=0$, so $\rho$ must be spatially homogeneous. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076)) Hence inhomogeneous density requires $E_{\mu\nu}\neq0$, while homogeneous density does not imply $E_{\mu\nu}=0$. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
- **Modified Friedmann equation.** For an FLRW brane with $\kappa^2=8\pi G$,
$$H^2=\frac{\kappa^2}{3}\rho\left(1+\frac{\rho}{2\lambda}\right)+\frac{m}{a^4}+\frac{\Lambda_4}{3}-\frac{K}{a^2},$$
where the dark-radiation term $m/a^4$ comes from $\dot\rho_E+4H\rho_E=0$ and is generated by the Coulomb effect of a bulk black hole. Nucleosynthesis and CMB data limit it to about 5% of the radiation density. At high energy $H^2\propto\rho^2$. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §3, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2)) Langlois's introductory review discusses this modified Friedmann equation in detail. ([Langlois 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0209261))
- **Truncations are not unique.** Anderson and Tavakol show that the split of the full brane–bulk system into "brane" and "bulk" terms is not unique. Different equivalent formulations give inequivalent results when the "bulk" terms are discarded, especially for anisotropic or inhomogeneous branes with non-AdS bulks. ([Anderson & Tavakol 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0305013))

### Examples
- **FLRW brane.** Homogeneity trivially satisfies the Weyl constraint, leaving $\rho_E=\rho_{E0}(a_0/a)^4$ (dark radiation), which vanishes when the bulk is exactly AdS$_5$. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §3, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
- **Static RSII [black holes](node:Black%20Holes).** Figueras and Wiseman constructed static black holes on an RSII brane numerically by perturbing an AdS$_5$/CFT$_4$ solution, with radii up to about 20 AdS lengths. At large radius they approach 4D behaviour; at small radius they become five-dimensional. Their numerics indicate stability against axisymmetric perturbations for all radii. ([Figueras & Wiseman 2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2558); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1105.2558)) Abdolrahimi et al. found an independent numerical solution agreeing with this, adding "further evidence for the existence of large RSII black holes". ([Abdolrahimi et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.0708))
- **Rotating RSII black holes.** Biggs and Santos constructed them numerically: large ones approach Kerr on the brane, and small ones approach a 5D Myers–Perry black hole with one rotation parameter along the brane. ([Biggs & Santos 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00016))

### History
SMS submitted "The Einstein Equations on the 3-Brane World" in 1999 (arXiv:gr-qc/9910076). It combined Israel's junction condition with the Gauss equation and gave the evolution of $E_{\mu\nu}$ in an appendix. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))

Emparan, Fabbri and Kaloper (2002) interpreted brane black holes solving the classical bulk equations as duals of quantum-corrected black holes of a CFT coupled to gravity, with the CFT's [Hawking radiation](node:Hawking%20Radiation) dual to classical gravitational bremsstrahlung in the AdS$_5$ bulk. ([Emparan, Fabbri & Kaloper 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0206155)) Tanaka (2002) asked, on the basis of AdS/CFT, whether brane black holes could evaporate through classical evolution. ([Tanaka 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0203082)) Figueras and Wiseman attribute to these authors the conjecture that static black holes cannot exist in RSII for radius much greater than the AdS length. ([Figueras & Wiseman 2011, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1105.2558)) Maartens and Koyama's 2010 review called a stable, realistic localized black hole "a key open question". ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2)) Figueras and Wiseman's 2011 numerical solutions extend to radii of about 20 AdS lengths, contradicting that conjecture. ([Figueras & Wiseman 2011, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1105.2558))

### Connections
- [Gauss–Codazzi Equations](node:Gauss–Codazzi%20Equations): project bulk curvature onto the brane.
- [Israel Junction Conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions): fix the brane extrinsic curvature from $S_{\mu\nu}$.
- [Extrinsic Curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature): eliminated in favour of brane matter, producing $\pi_{\mu\nu}$.
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model): the RSII single brane is the main application; $\Lambda_4=0$ is its fine-tuning.
- [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology) and [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): the modified Friedmann equation.
- [Dark Radiation](node:Dark%20Radiation): the $m/a^4$ term from $E_{\mu\nu}$.
- [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space) and [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence): the bulk and the holographic reading of brane black holes.
- [DGP Gravity](node:DGP%20Gravity): the other standard 5D braneworld, with an induced 4D curvature term and a Minkowski bulk; it modifies gravity at low energies rather than high. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): the 4D limit.

### Common pitfalls
- **Dropping $E_{\mu\nu}$ is an assumption.** It is not implied by low density or homogeneity, and setting $E_{\mu\nu}=0$ gives a closed but perturbatively unstable system that need not embed in a regular bulk. ([Maartens & Koyama, PDF §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2)) Equivalent rearrangements can change what a truncation discards. ([Anderson & Tavakol 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0305013))
- **$E_{\mu\nu}$ is a limit.** It is evaluated as $\chi\to\pm0$, not exactly on the brane, where the Weyl tensor is distributional. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))
- **Tension versus matter is ambiguous.** $G_N$ depends on $\lambda$, and SMS warn that splitting $S_{\mu\nu}$ into $\lambda q_{\mu\nu}$ and $\tau_{\mu\nu}$ can be ambiguous, particularly in cosmology. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))
- **Conventions.** SMS use $8\pi G_N=\kappa_5^4\lambda/6$ and $\Lambda_4$ with the bulk constant $\Lambda$ in the action normalization; the Living Review writes $\Lambda_4=\tfrac12(\Lambda_5+\kappa^2\lambda)$ with a differently normalized $\Lambda_5$. Compare only after matching normalizations. ([SMS 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076); [Maartens & Koyama, PDF §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.3962v2))

### Open problems
- **Stability, uniqueness and collapse end states of brane black holes.** In the first full dynamical simulations of collapse on an RSII brane, Wang and Choptuik note that, without proofs of stability and uniqueness of the static solutions, "it is not clear whether they describe the end states of matter collapse on the brane". They find preliminary evidence for a unique sequence. ([Wang & Choptuik 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.04832); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1604.04832)) Figueras and Wiseman's numerical stability evidence covers only axisymmetric perturbations. ([Figueras & Wiseman 2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2558))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Brane cosmology (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brane_cosmology): framework and vocabulary.
- **Learn:** [Langlois, Brane cosmology: an introduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0209261): introductory review with a detailed discussion of the modified Friedmann equation.
- **Primary:** [Shiromizu, Maeda & Sasaki, The Einstein Equations on the 3-Brane World](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076): the original derivation.
- **Primary:** [Figueras & Wiseman (2011)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2558): large static RSII black holes.
- **Further reading:** [Maartens & Koyama, Brane-World Gravity, Living Rev. Relativity 13 (2010) 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3962): the standard review, covering the covariant equations, cosmology, black holes and DGP.
references.Effective Field Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
An effective field theory (EFT) includes the degrees of freedom appropriate to physics at a chosen length or energy scale and ignores substructure at shorter distances; the short-distance degrees of freedom are removed systematically, which is often described as integrating them out. With a single heavy scale $M$, the EFT is an expansion in $1/M$, and each new order brings new free parameters. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_field_theory))

EFTs explain why non-renormalizable interactions still make well-defined predictions: to fixed order in the expansion the theory behaves like an ordinary QFT, and a more fundamental UV-complete theory may underlie it. Fermi's four-fermion theory of beta decay is the classic example, with the W boson effectively invisible at low energy. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863), [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/effective+quantum+field+theory))

EFT is the working language of modern particle and condensed-matter physics: chiral perturbation theory for low-energy QCD, heavy-quark and soft-collinear effective theories, general relativity as the low-energy theory of quantum gravity, the BCS and Fermi-liquid descriptions of metals, and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) for parametrizing heavy new physics in LHC data. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_field_theory), [Polchinski](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9210046), [Brivio–Trott](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08945))

### Formal definition
In $d=4$ an EFT with cutoff (new-physics scale) $\Lambda$ has Lagrangian
$$\mathcal L_{\rm EFT}=\sum_{D\ge0,\,i}\frac{c_i^{(D)}\,O_i^{(D)}}{\Lambda^{D-4}}=\mathcal L_{D\le4}+\frac{\mathcal L_5}{\Lambda}+\frac{\mathcal L_6}{\Lambda^2}+\cdots,$$
where $O_i^{(D)}$ are local operators of mass dimension $D$ built from the light fields and consistent with the low-energy symmetries, and $c_i^{(D)}$ are dimensionless Wilson coefficients; the sum must be treated as an expansion in powers of $1/\Lambda$. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))

**Matching.** When the EFT is the low-energy limit of a weakly coupled full theory, its coefficients are fixed by requiring it to reproduce the same S-matrix at low energy; the difference between full-theory and EFT loop integrals is absorbed into shifts of the EFT Lagrangian coefficients. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))

**Wilsonian cutoffs.** In the causal perturbation theory formulation, a UV cutoff is a family of non-singular distributions $\Delta_{F,\Lambda}$ converging to the Feynman propagator as $\Lambda\to\infty$, with an effective S-matrix scheme $S_\Lambda$ at each cutoff. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/effective+quantum+field+theory))

### Key results
- **Power counting.** A tree graph with insertions of operators of dimensions $D_i$ scales as $\mathcal A\sim(p/\Lambda)^n$ with $n=\sum_i(D_i-4)$, and the same formula holds for loop graphs in dimensional regularization, which has no power divergences. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))
- **Renormalizability order by order.** To fixed order in $p/\Lambda$, an EFT is like a regular QFT: for corrections up to a given order, non-renormalizable EFTs are as predictive as renormalizable theories. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))
- **Weinberg's folk theorem.** The most general Lagrangian consistent with the low-energy symmetries yields an EFT consistent with unitarity, analyticity and cluster decomposition. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_field_theory))
- **Decoupling (Appelquist–Carazzone, 1975).** In gauge theories coupled to massive fermions, heavy fields decouple at low momenta except for their contribution to renormalization effects; the paper states a decoupling theorem for general renormalizable theories. ([Appelquist–Carazzone](https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.11.2856))
- **Redundant operators.** A field redefinition leaves the S-matrix unchanged when the new field overlaps the one-particle state, so equation-of-motion operators can be dropped from the operator basis. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))
- **Dimension-six SMEFT basis.** Assuming baryon-number conservation and not counting flavour structure, there are $15+19+25=59$ independent dimension-six operators (with 0, 2 and 4 fermion fields), versus $16+35+29=80$ in Buchmüller and Wyler's earlier list; relaxing baryon-number conservation adds 4 four-fermion operators. ([Grzadkowski et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.4884))
- **Counterterm characterization.** Given UV cutoffs $\Delta_{F,\Lambda}$ there exist vertex redefinitions $Z_\Lambda$ such that $S_\infty=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}S_\Lambda\circ Z_\Lambda$ is a genuine S-matrix scheme, and every S-matrix scheme arises this way (claimed by Brunetti–Dütsch–Fredenhagen 2009, proof sketched by Dütsch–Fredenhagen–Keller–Rejzner 2014). ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/effective+quantum+field+theory))

### Examples
- **Fermi theory.** Integrating out the W boson gives $\mathcal L=-\frac{g^2}{2M_W^2}V_{cb}(\bar c\gamma^\mu P_Lb)(\bar\ell\gamma_\mu P_L\nu_\ell)+O(1/M_W^4)$, matching the Fermi form with $G_F/\sqrt2=g^2/(8M_W^2)$; $G_F\approx1.1663787(6)\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}$ from the muon lifetime. The contact theory fails well above about 100 GeV because its cross section grows like $E^2$. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863), [Wikipedia: Fermi's interaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi%27s_interaction))
- **Neutrino masses.** The lepton-number-violating dimension-five operator $(H^\dagger\ell)(H^\dagger\ell)/M_S$ gives $m_\nu\sim v^2/M_S$ with $v\sim246$ GeV; $m_\nu\sim10^{-2}$ eV implies $M_S\sim6\times10^{15}$ GeV. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))
- **Proton decay.** Baryon-number violation first appears at dimension six, $qqq\ell/M_G^2$, giving lifetimes $\tau\sim(M_G/10^{15}\,\mathrm{GeV})^4\times10^{30}$ years. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))
- **Large logarithms.** Fixed-order perturbation theory breaks down when $\alpha_s/(4\pi)$ multiplies a large log; RG running in the EFT resums $(\frac{\alpha_s}{4\pi}\ln\frac{M_W}{m_b})^n$. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))
- **Fermi liquid.** Polchinski derives Landau's Fermi-liquid theory as the low-energy EFT of a conductor and argues that high-temperature superconductors need a different EFT. ([Polchinski](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9210046))
- **Chiral perturbation theory and gravity.** The pions of chiral perturbation theory are Goldstone bosons of spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking, and general relativity is expected to be the low-energy EFT of quantum gravity with expansion scale the Planck mass. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_field_theory))

### History
Fermi proposed the four-fermion description of beta decay in 1933, with Italian and German versions published in 1933 and 1934 after *Nature* rejected it. ([Wikipedia: Fermi's interaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi%27s_interaction)) Appelquist and Carazzone's decoupling theorem appeared in 1975 ([Appelquist–Carazzone](https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.11.2856)), and Weinberg's "Phenomenological Lagrangians" in *Physica A* 96 (1979), 327–340 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0378-4371%2879%2990223-1)). Polchinski's 1992 introduction applied EFT to the Fermi surface of a conductor ([Polchinski](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9210046)); Grzadkowski, Iskrzyński, Misiak and Rosiek's 2010 reclassification of dimension-six operators corrected Buchmüller–Wyler ([Grzadkowski et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.4884)), and SMEFT and HEFT developed as the two EFT approaches to interpreting Higgs-like measurements at the LHC ([Brivio–Trott](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08945)).

### Connections
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): an EFT is a QFT treated as an expansion in $p/\Lambda$.
- [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group) and [Renormalization](node:Renormalization): running between matching scales resums large logarithms.
- [Wilsonian Effective Actions](node:Wilsonian%20Effective%20Actions): the cutoff-based picture of integrating out modes.
- [Electroweak Theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory) and [Standard Model of Particle Physics](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics): Fermi theory is their low-energy limit, and SMEFT extends them.
- [Neutrino Mass Mechanisms](node:Neutrino%20Mass%20Mechanisms): the dimension-five Weinberg operator.
- [Chiral Nuclear Effective Field Theory](node:Chiral%20Nuclear%20Effective%20Field%20Theory): EFT for nucleons and pions.
- [Fermi Liquid Theory](node:Fermi%20Liquid%20Theory) and [BCS Theory](node:BCS%20Theory): condensed-matter EFTs.
- [Quantum Gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity) and [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): gravity as an EFT below the Planck scale.
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem) and [Naturalness](node:Naturalness): questions about the sizes of EFT coefficients.
- [Effective Field Theory of Compactification](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory%20of%20Compactification): lower-dimensional EFTs from compactified theories.
- [Electroweak Precision Observables](node:Electroweak%20Precision%20Observables): the historical test case for EFT interpretation.

### Common pitfalls
- **The $1/\Lambda$ series is an expansion, not an exact Lagrangian.** Each order brings new parameters, and terms must be kept consistently to a fixed order. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_field_theory), [Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))
- **"Integrating out high-momentum modes" is not the right interpretation.** Manohar recommends thinking of EFTs in terms of the physical problem and matching S-matrices, rather than as obtained by literally integrating out modes above a cutoff. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863))
- **Operator bases contain redundancies.** Equation-of-motion operators do not contribute to the S-matrix, which is part of why the 2010 basis is smaller than the Buchmüller–Wyler list. ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863), [Grzadkowski et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.4884))

> [!warning] Contested
> Whether the Higgs mass suffers quadratically divergent corrections that demand new physics is disputed. The standard naturalness argument says superpartners would cancel quadratic corrections to the Higgs mass ([Wikipedia: Supersymmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry)); Manohar calls the quadratic-cutoff argument "completely bogus", noting that in dimensional regularization $\delta m_H^2\propto m_H^2[\log(m_H^2/\bar\mu^2)+1]$ and "there is no cutoff" ([Manohar](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.05863)).

### Open problems
- **UV constraints on IR physics.** The Snowmass white paper surveys how causality, unitarity and quantum gravity constrain EFTs, through S-matrix positivity and bootstrap bounds, time delays, CFT and holography, and swampland criteria such as the weak gravity conjecture ([de Rham et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.06805)). Its authors note that the swampland picture currently rests on surveys of string theory examples and qualitative arguments, call extending positivity bounds to higher-point amplitudes a major uncharted territory, and say that deriving universal CFT features from the bootstrap axioms is still an open question. ([de Rham et al., full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.06805))
- **EFT methods for the LHC.** Brivio and Trott review the challenges that remain in developing SMEFT and HEFT methods for interpreting LHC measurements. ([Brivio–Trott](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08945))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Effective field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_field_theory): definition and examples across particle and condensed-matter physics.
- **Reference:** [nLab: effective quantum field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/effective+quantum+field+theory): cutoff and counterterm formulation in causal perturbation theory.
- **Learn:** [Manohar, Introduction to Effective Field Theories (Les Houches 2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.05863): power counting, matching, running and SMEFT.
- **Learn:** [Polchinski, Effective Field Theory and the Fermi Surface](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9210046): EFT reasoning applied to metals.
- **Primary:** [Grzadkowski, Iskrzyński, Misiak and Rosiek, Dimension-Six Terms in the Standard Model Lagrangian](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.4884): the complete dimension-six operator basis.
- **Primary:** [Brivio and Trott, The Standard Model as an Effective Field Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08945): Physics Reports review of SMEFT and HEFT.
- **Primary:** [Appelquist and Carazzone, Infrared singularities and massive fields](https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.11.2856): the decoupling theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Burgess, Introduction to Effective Field Theory (Cambridge University Press, 2020)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/9781139048040): graduate monograph on EFT methods.
references.Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors:
## Reference
### Overview
An eigenvector of a square matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector $x$ that $A$ only rescales, $Ax=\lambda x$; the scalar $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue. Vectors with eigenvalue $0$ form the nullspace of $A$, so $0$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $A$ is singular. An $n\times n$ matrix has $n$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, their sum is the trace and their product is the [determinant](node:Determinant). ([MIT 18.06SC notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/1999c9f4accdbef05571a1014438f8dd_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.8sum.pdf))

Eigen-decompositions organize much of matrix theory. Diagonalizable matrices are those with a basis of eigenvectors; every complex matrix is unitarily triangularizable (Schur) and similar to a [Jordan form](node:Jordan%20Canonical%20Form); normal matrices are exactly the unitarily diagonalizable ones ([spectral theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem)); and nonnegative matrices have a dominant positive eigenvector (Perron–Frobenius). Computing eigenvalues is a central task of [numerical linear algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra), solved in practice by the QR algorithm. ([Wikipedia: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors); [Wikipedia: Schur decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_decomposition); [Wikipedia: Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem); [Wikipedia: QR algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_algorithm))

### Formal definition
For $A\in K^{n\times n}$, $\lambda\in K$ is an eigenvalue if $(A-\lambda I)x=0$ for some $x\neq0$, equivalently if $\lambda$ is a root of the characteristic polynomial $p_A(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda I)$; the eigenvectors are the nonzero vectors of $\ker(A-\lambda I)$. ([MIT 18.06SC notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/1999c9f4accdbef05571a1014438f8dd_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.8sum.pdf))

The **algebraic multiplicity** $\mu(\lambda)$ is the multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a root of $p_A$; the **geometric multiplicity** $\gamma(\lambda)=\dim\ker(A-\lambda I)$. Always $1\le\gamma(\lambda)\le\mu(\lambda)\le n$. A matrix whose eigenvectors do not span the space is called defective. ([Wikipedia: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors))

### Key results
- **Existence over $\mathbb C$; trace and determinant.** Over $\mathbb C$ the characteristic polynomial of an $n\times n$ matrix splits into $n$ linear factors, so $A$ has $n$ eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ counted with algebraic multiplicity, and $\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_i\lambda_i$, $\det A=\prod_i\lambda_i$. ([Wikipedia: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors))
- **Diagonalizability criterion.** $A$ is diagonalizable iff its eigenvectors form a basis, iff $\sum_\lambda\gamma(\lambda)=n$; when $p_A$ splits this is equivalent to $\gamma(\lambda)=\mu(\lambda)$ for every eigenvalue. ([Wikipedia: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors); [Wikipedia: Jordan normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form))
- **Schur decomposition.** Every complex $n\times n$ matrix can be written $A=QUQ^*$ with $Q$ unitary and $U$ upper triangular; the diagonal of $U$ lists the eigenvalues. For real $A$ there is an orthogonal $Q$ with $A=QHQ^{-1}$, $H$ block upper triangular with $1\times1$ and $2\times2$ diagonal blocks (real Schur form). ([Wikipedia: Schur decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_decomposition))
- **Jordan normal form.** If all eigenvalues of $A$ lie in $K$ (i.e. $p_A$ splits over $K$, always the case over $\mathbb C$), then $A=PJP^{-1}$ with $J$ block diagonal of Jordan blocks, unique up to block order. For each $\lambda$: the number of blocks is $\gamma(\lambda)$, their total size is $\mu(\lambda)$, and the largest block size is the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in the minimal polynomial. ([Wikipedia: Jordan normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form))
- **Spectral theorem (finite dimension).** A Hermitian (self-adjoint) operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and all its eigenvalues are real. A complex matrix is unitarily diagonalizable, $A=UDU^*$, iff it is normal ($A^*A=AA^*$); then $D$ may be non-real. If $A$ is normal, its Schur factor $U$ is diagonal and the columns of $Q$ are eigenvectors. ([Wikipedia: Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem); [Wikipedia: Schur decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_decomposition))
- **Perron–Frobenius theorem.** If $A$ has all entries positive, its spectral radius $r$ is a simple eigenvalue, strictly larger in modulus than every other eigenvalue, with an eigenvector having all entries positive (unique up to scaling among nonnegative eigenvectors), and $\min_i\sum_ja_{ij}\le r\le\max_i\sum_ja_{ij}$ (Perron, 1907). If $A$ is only nonnegative and irreducible, $r$ is still a simple positive eigenvalue with positive left and right eigenvectors, but exactly $h$ eigenvalues (the period) have modulus $r$, namely $r$ times the $h$-th roots of unity (Frobenius, 1912). ([Wikipedia: Perron–Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem))
- **Power iteration.** If $|\lambda_1|>|\lambda_2|\ge\dots\ge|\lambda_n|$ and the start vector $b_0$ has a nonzero component along an eigenvector for $\lambda_1$, the iterates $b_{k+1}=Ab_k/\|Ab_k\|$ have a subsequence converging to an eigenvector for $\lambda_1$ and the Rayleigh quotients converge to $\lambda_1$; for diagonalizable $A$ the convergence is geometric with ratio $|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|$. ([Wikipedia: Power iteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_iteration))
- **QR algorithm.** Starting from $A_0=A$, factor $A_k=Q_kR_k$ and set $A_{k+1}=R_kQ_k=Q_k^TA_kQ_k$; every iterate is orthogonally similar to $A$, and under suitable conditions the iterates approach the Schur form. In practice $A$ is first reduced to Hessenberg form (tridiagonal if symmetric), and shifts with deflation are used; the basic unshifted iteration is not guaranteed to converge. ([Wikipedia: QR algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_algorithm))

### Examples
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-6\lambda+8$, so $\lambda=4,2$ with eigenvectors $(1,1)^T$ and $(1,-1)^T$; the coefficient $6$ is the trace and $8$ the determinant. The rotation $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2+1$ and eigenvalues $\pm i$: a real matrix can have no real eigenvector. The triangular matrix $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue $3$ with $\mu=2$ but only one independent eigenvector, $(1,0)^T$, so $\gamma=1$ and it is not diagonalizable. ([MIT 18.06SC notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/1999c9f4accdbef05571a1014438f8dd_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.8sum.pdf))

Eigenvalues of sums and products are not in general sums and products of eigenvalues; that holds when $A$ and $B$ share eigenvectors. ([MIT 18.06SC notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/1999c9f4accdbef05571a1014438f8dd_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.8sum.pdf))

### History
Euler studied the principal axes of rotating rigid bodies, and Lagrange recognized them as eigenvectors of the inertia matrix. Cauchy coined "characteristic root"; Hermite extended the real symmetric result to Hermitian matrices in 1855; Hilbert introduced the German "eigen" in 1904. Von Mises published the power method in 1929, and Francis and Kublanovskaya independently proposed the QR algorithm in 1961, after Rutishauser's LR algorithm of the early 1950s. ([Wikipedia: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors); [Wikipedia: QR algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_algorithm))

### Connections
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): eigenvalues are similarity invariants of the operator a matrix represents.
- [Determinant](node:Determinant): the characteristic polynomial; $\det A=\prod\lambda_i$.
- [Jordan Canonical Form](node:Jordan%20Canonical%20Form): the complete similarity invariant when $p_A$ splits.
- [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem): orthonormal eigenbases for normal and self-adjoint operators.
- [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces): supply adjoints and orthogonality for the spectral theorem.
- [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices): Hermitian matrices with all eigenvalues positive.
- [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of $A^*A$.
- [QR Factorization](node:QR%20Factorization): the building block of the QR algorithm.
- [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): power iteration, QR algorithm, Hessenberg reduction.
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains): Perron–Frobenius governs stationary distributions of irreducible chains.
- [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory): the infinite-dimensional generalization.

### Common pitfalls
The zero vector is never an eigenvector, though it lies in every eigenspace. Real matrices can have non-real eigenvalues, which come in conjugate pairs. A repeated eigenvalue does not by itself prevent diagonalization; compare $\gamma$ with $\mu$. ([MIT 18.06SC notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/1999c9f4accdbef05571a1014438f8dd_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.8sum.pdf); [Wikipedia: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors)) For a merely nonnegative irreducible matrix the Perron root need not be the only eigenvalue of maximal modulus. ([Wikipedia: Perron–Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Nonnegative inverse eigenvalue problem (NIEP).** Given a list $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ of complex numbers, find necessary and sufficient conditions for an $n\times n$ entrywise nonnegative matrix with spectrum $\lambda$ to exist; the real (RNIEP) and symmetric (SNIEP) variants restrict to real lists and symmetric realizations. The question goes back to Kolmogorov (1937) and Suleimanova (1949). Jin, Ke and Sui write that all three are completely solved for $n\le4$ but that from $n=5$ on none has been completely solved, calling the NIEP one of the longstanding open problems of matrix theory. The survey by Johnson, Marijuán, Paparella and Pisonero calls it a known hard problem and surveys the work on it. ([Jin–Ke–Sui](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.19435); [Johnson et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.10992))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Eigenvalues and eigenvectors (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors): multiplicities, trace and determinant, history.
- **Reference:** [Jordan normal form (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form): block structure and multiplicities.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.06SC, Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/1999c9f4accdbef05571a1014438f8dd_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses2.8sum.pdf): computing eigenvalues, complex and repeated cases.
- **Primary:** [Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed. (CUP, 2012)](https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/matrix-analysis/FDA3627DC2B9F5C3DF2FD8C3CC136B48): standard graduate monograph organized around canonical forms.
- **Primary:** [Johnson, Marijuán, Paparella, Pisonero, The NIEP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.10992): survey of the nonnegative inverse eigenvalue problem.
- **Further reading:** [Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right (Springer UTM, 2024)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-031-41026-0): textbook treatment of eigenvalues, inner product spaces and the spectral theorem.
references.Einstein Field Equations:
## Reference
### Overview
The Einstein field equations (EFE) relate the geometry of spacetime, expressed by the Einstein tensor, to the energy, momentum and stress of matter, expressed by the stress–energy tensor. Written out, they are a system of ten coupled, nonlinear, hyperbolic-elliptic partial differential equations for the metric; they imply local conservation of energy–momentum, reduce to Newtonian gravity for weak fields and slow motion, and imply the geodesic motion of free test bodies. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))

Baez and Bunn give an equivalent verbal form: for a small ball of freely falling test particles initially at rest relative to each other, the rate at which it begins to shrink is proportional to its volume times the energy density plus the three principal pressures at its centre, $\ddot V/V|_{t=0} = -\tfrac12(\rho + P_x + P_y + P_z)$ in units $c = 8\pi G = 1$. ([Baez & Bunn, arXiv:gr-qc/0103044](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0103044))

Mathematically, the equations are essentially hyperbolic, so the natural framework is the Cauchy problem: initial data on a spacelike hypersurface, subject to constraint equations, determine the spacetime. ([Rendall, arXiv:gr-qc/0505133](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133)) The global questions this raises, including singularity formation, cosmic censorship and black hole stability, are central to mathematical relativity. ([Wikipedia: Cosmic censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_censorship_hypothesis))

### Formal definition
With the conventions of Misner, Thorne and Wheeler,
$$G_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \kappa T_{\mu\nu}, \qquad G_{\mu\nu} = R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12 R\,g_{\mu\nu}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{8\pi G}{c^4},$$
where $R_{\mu\nu}$ is the Ricci tensor, $R$ the scalar curvature, $\Lambda$ the cosmological constant and $T_{\mu\nu}$ the stress–energy tensor; $G_{\mu\nu}$ is symmetric, divergence-free, and depends only on the metric and its first and second derivatives. Taking the trace in $D$ dimensions gives the trace-reversed form
$$R_{\mu\nu} - \frac{2\Lambda}{D-2}g_{\mu\nu} = \kappa\left(T_{\mu\nu} - \frac{T}{D-2}g_{\mu\nu}\right),$$
which for $D=4$ reads $R_{\mu\nu} - \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \kappa(T_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12 T g_{\mu\nu})$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))

The equations follow from varying $S = \frac{1}{2\kappa}\int R\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x + S_M$ with respect to the inverse metric, with $T_{\mu\nu} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta(\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal L_M)}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}$; replacing $R$ by $R - 2\Lambda$ adds the $\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ term. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action))

**Constraints.** Vacuum-plus-matter initial data are a 3-manifold $S$, a Riemannian metric $h_{ab}$ and a symmetric tensor $k_{ab}$ (the future second fundamental form), satisfying
$$R - k_{ab}k^{ab} + (h^{ab}k_{ab})^2 = 16\pi\rho, \qquad \nabla^a k_{ab} - \nabla_b(h^{ac}k_{ac}) = 8\pi j_b,$$
with $R$ the scalar curvature of $h$ and $\rho$, $j_a$ projections of $T_{\mu\nu}$. ([Rendall, arXiv:gr-qc/0505133](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133))

### Key results
- **Conservation and counting.** The contracted Bianchi identity gives $\nabla^\beta G_{\alpha\beta} = 0$, so the EFE force $\nabla^\beta T_{\alpha\beta} = 0$. Each side has 10 independent components; the four Bianchi identities reduce the independent equations to 6, matching the four-fold coordinate freedom. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))
- **Lovelock's theorem.** In four dimensions the Einstein tensor is, up to a constant factor and the addition of a multiple of $g_{\mu\nu}$, the only tensorial, divergence-free function of $g_{\mu\nu}$ depending on at most its second derivatives. ([Wikipedia: Einstein tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_tensor)) The form often quoted additionally assumes symmetry and linearity in the second derivatives and concludes $A_{\mu\nu} = aG_{\mu\nu} + bg_{\mu\nu}$; changing the EFE thus requires extra fields, other dimensions, higher derivatives, non-locality, or giving up an action. ([Wikipedia: Lovelock's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock%27s_theorem))
- **Newtonian limit.** Matching the time–time component for static weak fields and slow motion to Poisson's equation fixes $\kappa = 8\pi G/c^4$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))
- **Birkhoff's theorem.** Every spherically symmetric vacuum solution is static and asymptotically flat, so the exterior of a spherical body is Schwarzschild (Jebsen 1921, Birkhoff 1923); a spherically pulsating star emits no gravitational waves. ([Wikipedia: Birkhoff's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_theorem_%28relativity%29))
- **Local existence and uniqueness.** Given smooth vacuum data there is a smooth solution inducing them in which $S$ is a Cauchy surface; the maximal Cauchy development is unique up to a diffeomorphism fixing $S$ (Choquet-Bruhat and Geroch). The proofs require coordinate or gauge conditions, which turn the equations into a reduced system determined uniquely by the data, for example the reduced Einstein equations in harmonic coordinates, a quasilinear hyperbolic system. ([Rendall, arXiv:gr-qc/0505133](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133)) The developments obtained are globally hyperbolic. ([Wikipedia: Initial value formulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_value_formulation_%28general_relativity%29))
- **Stability of Minkowski space.** Christodoulou and Klainerman proved that asymptotically flat vacuum data sufficiently close to Minkowski data have a geodesically complete maximal development; Lindblad and Rodnianski gave a shorter proof in harmonic coordinates using a weak null condition. ([Rendall, arXiv:gr-qc/0505133](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133))
- **Stability of black holes.** Hintz and Vasy proved global non-linear stability of slowly rotating Kerr–de Sitter black holes ($\Lambda>0$) without symmetry assumptions. ([Hintz & Vasy, arXiv:1606.04014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04014)) For $\Lambda = 0$, Klainerman and Szeftel proved unconditional non-linear stability of the Kerr family for $|a|/m \ll 1$ ([Klainerman & Szeftel, arXiv:2104.11857](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11857)), with Giorgi, Klainerman and Szeftel supplying the remaining wave-equation estimates. ([Giorgi, Klainerman & Szeftel, arXiv:2205.14808](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14808))
- **Penrose singularity theorem.** If spacetime has a non-compact Cauchy hypersurface and a closed future-trapped surface, and $R_{\mu\nu}k^\mu k^\nu \ge 0$ for null $k$, then there are future-incomplete null geodesics. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle, arXiv:1410.5226](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226)) Hawking's companion theorem uses the strong energy condition to show past incompleteness in cosmology; both rest on focusing via the Raychaudhuri equation and do not say what kind of singularity forms. ([Wikipedia: Penrose–Hawking theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems))
- **Positive energy theorem.** For initial data $(M,g,k)$ satisfying the dominant energy condition with finitely many asymptotically flat ends, the ADM energy of each end is non-negative, and if it vanishes Minkowski space is a development of the data under additional decay assumptions (Schoen–Yau 1979, 1981); Witten's 1981 spinor proof shows the ADM energy–momentum is future causal. ([Wikipedia: Positive energy theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_energy_theorem))

### Examples
- **Vacuum.** With $T_{\mu\nu} = 0$, $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$, or $R_{\mu\nu}$ proportional to $g_{\mu\nu}$ with $\Lambda$; Minkowski space is the simplest solution. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))
- **Vacuum energy.** Moving $\Lambda$ to the right gives a vacuum stress–energy with $\rho = -p = \Lambda/\kappa$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))
- **Einstein–Maxwell.** The source is the electromagnetic stress–energy tensor $T_{\alpha\beta} = -\frac{1}{\mu_0}\big(F_\alpha{}^\psi F_{\psi\beta} + \tfrac14 g_{\alpha\beta}F_{\psi\tau}F^{\psi\tau}\big)$ in the $(-+++)$ signature, so $G_{\alpha\beta} = \kappa T_{\alpha\beta}$, solved together with Maxwell's equations. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))
- **Newton and the big bang from a ball.** Baez and Bunn derive $a = -GM/r^2$ outside a uniform planet of radius much larger than its Schwarzschild radius, and for an isotropic universe $3\ddot R/R = -\tfrac12(\rho+3P)$, the basic equation of big-bang cosmology. ([Baez & Bunn, arXiv:gr-qc/0103044](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0103044))
- **Kerr interior.** Dafermos and Luk show that, for interior data modelling a dynamical black hole settling to Kerr, the maximal development extends across a piece of Cauchy horizon with a continuous metric. ([Dafermos & Luk, arXiv:1710.01722](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.01722))

### History
Einstein gave four lectures in Berlin on 4, 11, 18 and 25 November 1915, and his field-equations paper appeared on 2 December; it built on the 1913 *Entwurf* theory with Grossmann, which first described gravity by a pseudo-Riemannian metric. Hilbert's paper was submitted five days before Einstein's but published in 1916. ([Wikipedia: priority dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity_priority_dispute)) Janssen and Renn trace how Einstein returned to field equations he had considered and discarded in the Zurich Notebook. ([Crossref: Janssen & Renn 2007](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4020-4000-9_9))

Einstein's original coupling was $8\pi G/c^2$, with $T_{\mu\nu}$ in mass-density units. He added $\Lambda$ to allow a static universe, abandoned it after the static solution proved unstable and Hubble found expansion, and positive $\Lambda$ is now used for accelerated expansion. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations)) Penrose's 1965 theorem introduced closed trapped surfaces and brought in incompleteness to describe singular spacetimes, which became the standard definition of a singularity in GR. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle, arXiv:1410.5226](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226)) Fourès-Bruhat proved the existence theorem for the Cauchy problem in 1952. ([Wikipedia: Initial value formulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_value_formulation_%28general_relativity%29))

> [!warning] Contested
> Carroll's notes state that the equations "were first derived by Hilbert, not Einstein", by the action principle, with Einstein deriving them independently. ([Carroll, arXiv:gr-qc/9712019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019)) Corry, Renn and Stachel (1997) argued from Hilbert's printer's proofs that he had not anticipated Einstein's equations, and Sauer (1999) concluded Einstein did not plagiarize Hilbert; Winterberg disputed the 1997 reading because part of a proof page is missing. ([Wikipedia: priority dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity_priority_dispute))

### Connections
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the EFE are its dynamical core.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): the source; its conservation follows from the Bianchi identity.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): Ricci tensor, scalar curvature and Bianchi identities build $G_{\mu\nu}$.
- [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action): varying it gives the EFE.
- [Newtonian Limit of General Relativity](node:Newtonian%20Limit%20of%20General%20Relativity) and [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): fix $\kappa$.
- [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution) and [Kerr Black Holes](node:Kerr%20Black%20Holes): the basic vacuum black holes; [Black Holes](node:Black%20Holes) more generally.
- [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime) and [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space): the maximally symmetric vacua and their stability.
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): homogeneous isotropic solutions.
- [Linearized Gravity](node:Linearized%20Gravity) and [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves): the weak-field regime.
- [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): the $\Lambda$ term.
- [Energy Conditions](node:Energy%20Conditions), [Raychaudhuri Equation](node:Raychaudhuri%20Equation), [Singularity Theorems in Relativity](node:Singularity%20Theorems%20in%20Relativity): focusing and incompleteness.
- [ADM Formalism](node:ADM%20Formalism) and [Global Hyperbolicity](node:Global%20Hyperbolicity): the Cauchy problem and its constraints.
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) and [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation): the analytic setting of well-posedness.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): motion of free test bodies.
- [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations): coupled in Einstein–Maxwell theory; unlike them the EFE are nonlinear.
- [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane): braneworld modification.

### Common pitfalls
- **Sign conventions.** Signs depend on the metric signature, the Riemann sign and the Ricci contraction: MTW is $(+++)$, Weinberg (1972) $(+--)$, and Einstein's Ricci sign makes the right-hand constant negative. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))
- **Guessing $R_{\mu\nu} = \kappa T_{\mu\nu}$.** With $\nabla^\mu T_{\mu\nu} = 0$ and $\nabla^\mu R_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12\nabla_\nu R$, this forces $\nabla_\nu T = 0$, so $T$ would be constant throughout spacetime, which fails between vacuum and matter. ([Carroll, arXiv:gr-qc/9712019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Arbitrary data are not physical.** One cannot choose $h_{ab}$, $k_{ab}$ freely and define $\rho$, $j_a$ by the constraints; with the dominant energy condition $\rho \ge (j_aj^a)^{1/2}$ must hold. ([Rendall, arXiv:gr-qc/0505133](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133))
- **Nonlinearity.** The EFE are nonlinear, which distinguishes general relativity from many other fundamental theories; for Maxwell's equations, by contrast, the sum of two solutions is again a solution. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))
- **Singularity theorems do not describe singularities.** They prove geodesic incompleteness, not curvature blow-up. ([Wikipedia: Penrose–Hawking theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems))
- **Dafermos–Luk is conditional.** Their result falsifies $C^0$-inextendibility strong cosmic censorship only if the Kerr exterior is dynamically stable, which they describe as widely expected; the Cauchy horizons they construct carry weak null singularities. ([Dafermos & Luk, arXiv:1710.01722](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.01722))

### Open problems
- **Cosmic censorship.** Weak censorship asks that generic data have maximal developments with complete future null infinity; strong censorship that generic maximal developments be locally inextendible. Penrose proposed the hypothesis in 1969; it is framed more as a research program than a fully formal statement, and formalizing it must exclude known special and unphysical naked singularities. ([Wikipedia: Cosmic censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_censorship_hypothesis)) Dafermos and Luk show that the $C^0$-inextendibility version of strong censorship is false for Kerr interiors provided the Kerr exterior is dynamically stable. Dafermos and Luk suggest a revised formulation based on the weak null singularities they find. ([Dafermos & Luk, arXiv:1710.01722](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.01722))
- **Non-CMC constraint equations.** Rendall called it "an important open problem" to extend the non-CMC theory of the constraints to a picture comparable with the CMC case. ([Rendall, arXiv:gr-qc/0505133](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133)) Since then Holst, Nagy and Tsogtgerel obtained non-CMC solutions on closed manifolds without near-CMC assumptions (positive Yamabe class, small TT data) ([arXiv:0712.0798](https://arxiv.org/abs/0712.0798)), Maxwell gave vacuum solutions with freely specified mean curvature under a global supersolution condition ([arXiv:0804.0874](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.0874)), and Dahl, Gicquaud and Humbert showed non-existence forces a non-trivial solution of a limit equation. ([arXiv:1012.2188](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.2188))
- **Positive energy in all dimensions.** Whether the initial-data formulation of the positive energy theorem holds in arbitrary dimension is described as an open problem; Schoen and Yau's minimal-hypersurface proofs fail in dimension eight and above because of singularities, and a 2017 Schoen–Yau preprint proves the higher-dimensional case with $\operatorname{tr}_g k = 0$. ([Wikipedia: Positive energy theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_energy_theorem))
- **Two-body problem.** No complete solution is known for a spacetime containing two massive bodies; binaries are treated by post-Newtonian and numerical approximations. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Einstein field equations (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations): form, conventions, trace-reversed form, Newtonian limit, vacuum solutions.
- **Learn:** [Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/9712019): graduate notes deriving the EFE heuristically and from the Hilbert action.
- **Learn:** [Baez & Bunn, The Meaning of Einstein's Equation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0103044): the ball-of-test-particles formulation.
- **Primary:** [Rendall, Theorems on Existence and Global Dynamics for the Einstein Equations (Living Reviews)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133): review of the Cauchy problem, global results and open questions.
- **Primary:** [Klainerman & Szeftel, Kerr stability for small angular momentum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11857): non-linear stability of slowly rotating Kerr.
- **Primary:** [Senovilla & Garfinkle, The 1965 Penrose singularity theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.5226): review of the theorem and its legacy.
- **Further reading:** [Hawking & Ellis, The Large Scale Structure of Space-Time (Cambridge University Press)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511524646/type/book): causal structure, singularity theorems and the Cauchy problem.
- **Further reading:** [Janssen & Renn, Untying the Knot, in The Genesis of General Relativity (Springer, 2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4020-4000-9_9): history of how Einstein reached the final equations.
references.Einstein–Hilbert Action:
## Reference
### Overview
The Einstein–Hilbert action is the action functional whose stationary points under variation of the spacetime metric are the Einstein field equations of [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity). With signature $(-,+,+,+)$ the gravitational part is
$$S_{\rm EH}=\frac{1}{2\kappa}\int R\sqrt{-g}\,\mathrm{d}^4x,\qquad \kappa=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4},$$
where $g=\det(g_{\mu\nu})$ and $R$ is the Ricci scalar. If the integral over all of spacetime diverges, the field equations still arise as Euler–Lagrange equations by integrating over arbitrarily large relatively compact domains. Hilbert proposed the action in 1915, as part of a variational treatment of gravity combined with electromagnetism. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action))

Deriving the field equations from an action places gravity among the classical field theories of [Lagrangian field theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory), gives a variational definition of the matter stress–energy tensor, and connects diffeomorphism invariance to the contracted Bianchi identity. In the standard (metric) formulation the connection is Levi-Civita; the Palatini formulation varies metric and connection independently. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action); [Bertschinger, MIT 8.962 notes](https://web.mit.edu/edbert/GR/gr5.pdf))

nLab defines the vacuum functional on a compact smooth manifold $X$ (possibly with boundary) as $g\mapsto\int_X R(g)\,d\mathrm{vol}(g)$ on (pseudo-)Riemannian metrics, whose critical points are the physically realised metrics; in first-order form, with the metric encoded by a connection, the four-dimensional integrand is $\langle R\wedge e\wedge e\rangle$ with $R$ the curvature 2-form of the Lorentz part and $e$ the vielbein. ([nLab: Einstein-Hilbert action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Einstein-Hilbert+action)) The action is the starting point for the Hamiltonian ADM formulation, for semiclassical and path-integral approaches to [quantum gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity), and for modified-gravity theories that change the Lagrangian. ([Wikipedia: ADM formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADM_formalism); [Wikipedia: Gibbons–Hawking–York boundary term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbons%E2%80%93Hawking%E2%80%93York_boundary_term))

### Formal definition
In units $c=1$, Bertschinger writes the Hilbert action as a functional of the inverse metric,
$$S_G[g^{\mu\nu}]=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}\sqrt{-g}\,\mathrm{d}^4x .$$
The factor $\sqrt{-g}$ makes the volume element invariant, so $S_G$ is a scalar under general coordinate transformations. A scalar Lagrangian for the metric cannot depend only on first derivatives $\partial_\alpha g_{\mu\nu}$, since these can all be transformed to zero at a point; $R=g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}$ is the simplest scalar formed from second derivatives. ([Bertschinger, MIT 8.962 notes](https://web.mit.edu/edbert/GR/gr5.pdf))

Coupled to matter,
$$S=\int\left[\frac{1}{2\kappa}(R-2\Lambda)+\mathcal{L}_M\right]\sqrt{-g}\,\mathrm{d}^4x,\qquad T_{\mu\nu}:=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta(\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal{L}_M)}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}},$$
where including a cosmological constant replaces $R$ by $R-2\Lambda$. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action)) See [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor).

On a manifold with boundary the well-posed action adds the Gibbons–Hawking–York term (units $G=c=1$):
$$S_{\rm EH}+S_{\rm GHY}=\frac{1}{16\pi}\int_M R\sqrt{-g}\,\mathrm{d}^4x+\frac{1}{8\pi}\oint_{\partial M}\varepsilon\,K\sqrt{|h|}\,\mathrm{d}^3y,$$
with $h_{ab}$ the induced boundary metric, $K$ the trace of the [extrinsic curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature), and $\varepsilon=+1$ ($-1$) where the normal is spacelike (timelike). Holding $h_{ab}$ fixed on $\partial M$ then yields the Einstein equations. ([Wikipedia: Gibbons–Hawking–York boundary term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbons%E2%80%93Hawking%E2%80%93York_boundary_term))

### Key results
- **Einstein equations from $\delta S=0$.** Using $\delta\sqrt{-g}=-\tfrac12\sqrt{-g}\,g_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}$, the Palatini identity $\delta R_{\mu\nu}=\nabla_\alpha(\delta\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\mu\nu})-\nabla_\mu(\delta\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha\nu})$, and discarding a total derivative, variation with respect to $g^{\mu\nu}$ gives $R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12 g_{\mu\nu}R+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}$. Neglecting the surface term, $\delta S_G/\delta g^{\mu\nu}=(16\pi G)^{-1}G_{\mu\nu}$. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action); [Bertschinger, MIT 8.962 notes](https://web.mit.edu/edbert/GR/gr5.pdf)) These are the [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations), derived as [Euler–Lagrange equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations).
- **Boundary term.** $\delta S_G=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int(G_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}+\nabla_\mu v^\mu)\sqrt{-g}\,\mathrm{d}^4x$ with $v^\mu=\nabla_\nu(-\delta g^{\mu\nu}+g^{\mu\nu}g_{\alpha\beta}\delta g^{\alpha\beta})$; the flux of $v^\mu$ involves normal derivatives of $\delta g^{\mu\nu}$ on the boundary, so either the Palatini variation or an extrinsic-curvature boundary term is needed. ([Bertschinger, MIT 8.962 notes](https://web.mit.edu/edbert/GR/gr5.pdf)) York first recognised the need for the term (1972), Gibbons and Hawking refined it (1977); it is needed to reproduce the ADM energy and for the composition property of the gravitational path integral. ([Wikipedia: Gibbons–Hawking–York boundary term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbons%E2%80%93Hawking%E2%80%93York_boundary_term))
- **Lovelock's theorem (uniqueness).** In four dimensions, any symmetric, divergence-free tensor built locally from the metric and its derivatives up to second order (linear in second derivatives) has the form $aG_{\mu\nu}+bg_{\mu\nu}$; equivalently, a local action of the four-dimensional metric whose field equations contain at most second derivatives yields only the Einstein equations with a cosmological constant (Lovelock, 1971–72). To modify Einstein's equations one must add fields, change the dimension, allow higher derivatives or nonlocality, or abandon an action principle. ([Wikipedia: Lovelock's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock%27s_theorem)) Uniqueness is about field equations, not Lagrangians: $R^2$ or $R_{\mu\nu}R^{\mu\nu}$ are also covariant scalars built from second derivatives, but $f(R)$ theories have fourth-order field equations. ([Wikipedia: f(R) gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%28R%29_gravity))
- **Lovelock gravity in $D$ dimensions.** Lovelock's theory is a sum of dimensionally extended Euler densities: the zeroth-order term is the cosmological constant, the first-order term is the Einstein–Hilbert action, and the quadratic Gauss–Bonnet term is topological in four dimensions and contributes to the field equations only for $D\ge 5$. It is described as the most general metric theory of gravity with conserved second-order equations of motion; in $D=3,4$ it coincides with Einstein's theory. ([Wikipedia: Lovelock theory of gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock_theory_of_gravity))
- **Hamiltonian (ADM) form.** Writing $ds^2=-N^2dt^2+\gamma_{ij}(dx^i+N^idt)(dx^j+N^jdt)$ (Arnowitt, Deser, Misner, 1959), the Einstein–Hilbert Lagrangian becomes a function of the spatial metric $\gamma_{ij}$ and its conjugate momentum $\pi^{ij}$; the lapse $N$ and shift $N^i$ are Lagrange multipliers whose variation gives the Hamiltonian constraint $\mathcal H=0$ and momentum constraints $\mathcal P_i=0$. Quantising by replacing momenta with functional derivatives leads to the Wheeler–DeWitt equation. ([Wikipedia: ADM formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADM_formalism)) See [ADM Formalism](node:ADM%20Formalism).
- **Diffeomorphism invariance.** $S_{\rm EH}$ is invariant under diffeomorphisms; in the field-theory formulation the contracted Bianchi identities arise from this non-dynamical symmetry, while stress–energy conservation arises from a dynamical symmetry of the matter action. ([Bertschinger, MIT 8.962 notes](https://web.mit.edu/edbert/GR/gr5.pdf)) See [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem).
- **Perturbative non-renormalizability.** Quantised perturbatively, gravity is nonrenormalizable: infinitely many independent counterterm coefficients appear, although as an [effective field theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory) it still predicts low-energy quantum corrections such as the first correction to the Newtonian potential. ([Wikipedia: Quantum gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_gravity)) Pure gravity is finite at one loop because the only available counterterm is the Gauss–Bonnet term, while amplitudes with external matter diverge at one loop ('t Hooft and Veltman, 1974); at two loops pure gravity diverges, as Goroff and Sagnotti showed (1985–86), through an $R^3$ counterterm. ([Bern et al., arXiv:1507.06118](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.06118))

### Examples
- **Vacuum GR.** $\mathcal L_M=0$ gives $G_{\mu\nu}=0$, or $G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=0$ with a cosmological term. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action))
- **$f(R)$ gravity.** Replacing $R$ by a function: $S=\frac{1}{2\kappa}\int f(R)\sqrt{-g}\,\mathrm{d}^4x$, first proposed by Buchdahl in 1970. Starobinsky's choice $f(R)=R+R^2/(6M^2)$ drives [inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation). Metric $f(R)$ is equivalent in the Einstein frame to general relativity plus a scalar field. ([Wikipedia: f(R) gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%28R%29_gravity)) See [Scalar-Tensor Gravity](node:Scalar-Tensor%20Gravity).
- **Hilbert's world function.** In his note of 20 November 1915 Hilbert took a world function invariant under general coordinate transformations, of the special form $H=K+L$ with $K$ the curvature scalar and $L$ an electromagnetic part containing no derivatives of the metric, following Mie's programme of an electromagnetic theory of matter. ([arXiv:1912.03269](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1912.03269)) In his 1923 Hamburg lectures he again wrote the Lagrangian as $I=K+L$, with dynamical variables the ten $g_{\mu\nu}$ and four potentials $\varphi_l$. ([Majer & Sauer, arXiv:physics/0405110](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0405110))

### History
Einstein made four communications to the Prussian Academy in November 1915: on 4 November (non-covariant field equations), 11 November (covariant equations assuming a traceless energy–momentum tensor), 18 November (the perihelion advance of Mercury) and 25 November (the correct field equations). Hilbert lectured to the Göttingen academy on 20 November 1915, five days before Einstein's final paper, and rewrote his paper for publication in March 1916. Corry, Renn and Stachel (*Science*, 1997), using printer's proofs dated 6 December, concluded that Hilbert had not anticipated Einstein's equations: the proofs show an originally non-covariant theory that Hilbert dropped in revision. ([Wikipedia: General relativity priority dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity_priority_dispute); [Bertschinger, MIT 8.962 notes](https://web.mit.edu/edbert/GR/gr5.pdf))

Hilbert was motivated by an axiomatic action principle (his sixth problem) and by Mie's field theory. Born, as quoted by Reid, recalled that the coincidence led "not to a controversy over priority, but to a series of friendly encounters and letters", and Hilbert freely said the great idea was Einstein's. ([nLab: Einstein-Hilbert action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Einstein-Hilbert+action)) Arnowitt, Deser and Misner gave the Hamiltonian form in 1959 and Lovelock gave his uniqueness theorem and higher-dimensional theory in 1971–72. ([Wikipedia: ADM formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADM_formalism); [Wikipedia: Lovelock theory of gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock_theory_of_gravity))

### Connections
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): the Euler–Lagrange equations of this action.
- [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory): gravity as a classical field theory for $g_{\mu\nu}$.
- [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations): the variational principle $\delta S=0$.
- [Euler–Lagrange Equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations): the field equations as stationarity conditions.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): the Lagrangian density is the Ricci scalar.
- [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry) and [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): the metric whose scalar curvature is integrated ($\sqrt{g}$ in Riemannian signature).
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): defined by varying the matter action with respect to the metric.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem): diffeomorphism invariance and the Bianchi identity.
- [Extrinsic Curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature): the Gibbons–Hawking–York integrand.
- [ADM Formalism](node:ADM%20Formalism): the Hamiltonian form of the action.
- [Black Hole Thermodynamics](node:Black%20Hole%20Thermodynamics): the Euclidean action with boundary term in semiclassical gravity.
- [Quantum Gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity) and [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): non-renormalizability and its low-energy treatment.
- [Scalar-Tensor Gravity](node:Scalar-Tensor%20Gravity): $f(R)$ and other modifications that evade Lovelock's theorem with extra fields.
- [Kaluza–Klein Theory](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Theory): the higher-dimensional Einstein–Hilbert action.
- [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): the $-2\Lambda$ term.
- [DGP Gravity](node:DGP%20Gravity): Einstein–Hilbert terms on a brane and in the bulk.

### Common pitfalls
- **"The Einstein–Hilbert action is the most general second-derivative action."** False as a statement about Lagrangians: $R^2$ is a covariant scalar built from second derivatives, but as a nonlinear $f(R)$ Lagrangian it gives fourth-order field equations. The precise statement is Lovelock's theorem about second-order field equations, and in four dimensions the Gauss–Bonnet term can be added without changing them because it is topological. ([Wikipedia: Lovelock's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Lovelock theory of gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock_theory_of_gravity); [Wikipedia: f(R) gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%28R%29_gravity))
- **Dropping the boundary term casually.** Fixing $g_{\mu\nu}$ on the boundary does not make the Einstein–Hilbert variation well defined, because the surface term contains normal derivatives of $\delta g_{\mu\nu}$; the GHY term or a Palatini variation is required. ([Bertschinger, MIT 8.962 notes](https://web.mit.edu/edbert/GR/gr5.pdf); [Wikipedia: Gibbons–Hawking–York boundary term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbons%E2%80%93Hawking%E2%80%93York_boundary_term))
- **Conventions.** The formula assumes Lorentzian signature with $g<0$; prefactors $1/(2\kappa)$ and $1/(16\pi G)$ differ by the choice of units for $c$. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action))
- **Dating the priority question.** Hilbert's 20 November submission date does not by itself show that he had the final field equations: Corry, Renn and Stachel read the December 1915 proofs as containing a non-covariant theory, and Einstein's correct equations are from 25 November. ([Wikipedia: General relativity priority dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity_priority_dispute))

### Open problems
- **Ultraviolet completion of gravity.** Perturbatively quantised Einstein–Hilbert gravity is nonrenormalizable, and Wikipedia states that "there is still no complete and consistent quantum theory of gravity". Bern et al. write that "basic questions about their ultraviolet (UV) structure persist" and that "much more remains to be learned" about the ultraviolet structure of gravity theories. ([Wikipedia: Quantum gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_gravity); [Bern et al., arXiv:1507.06118](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.06118))
- **The cosmological constant problem.** The $\Lambda$ term in the action measures the vacuum energy, and the observed value is many orders of magnitude smaller than particle-physics estimates of zero-point and phase-transition contributions, a discrepancy Carroll calls "the famous discrepancy of 120 orders of magnitude" and describes as "one of the most significant unsolved problems in fundamental physics". ([Carroll, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/astro-ph/0004075))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Einstein–Hilbert action (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action): the action, its variation, $\Lambda$ and Palatini remarks.
- **Reference:** [nLab: Einstein-Hilbert action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Einstein-Hilbert+action): geometric definition, first-order form and Hilbert–Einstein history.
- **Reference:** [Lovelock's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovelock%27s_theorem): the uniqueness statement and ways around it.
- **Learn:** [Bertschinger, MIT 8.962 notes](https://web.mit.edu/edbert/GR/gr5.pdf): derivation of $\delta S_G$, the surface term and the link to Bianchi identities and [gauge invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance).
- **Primary:** [Bern, Cheung, Chi, Davies, Dixon, Nohle, arXiv:1507.06118](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.06118): research paper on the two-loop divergence of pure gravity and its history.
- **Primary:** [Majer & Sauer, arXiv:physics/0405110](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0405110): Hilbert's 1915 variational "world equations" and 1923 lectures.
- **Primary:** [Carroll, The Cosmological Constant (Living Reviews in Relativity, arXiv:astro-ph/0004075)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0004075): review of $\Lambda$ and the vacuum-energy problem.
references.Electromagnetic Waves:
## Reference
### Overview
An electromagnetic wave is a self-sustaining disturbance of the electric and magnetic fields that propagates through vacuum or a medium. In the absence of sources, Maxwell's equations imply that each Cartesian component of $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ obeys the three-dimensional wave equation, with propagation speed $c_0=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\approx 2.998\times10^8$ m/s in vacuum and phase velocity $1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$ in a linear medium ([Wikipedia: Electromagnetic wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_wave_equation)).

Maxwell derived a wave equation whose speed matched the measured speed of light, and in his 1865 paper "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field" concluded that light is "an electromagnetic disturbance propagated through the field according to electromagnetic laws" ([Wikipedia: Electromagnetic wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_wave_equation)). Radio waves were first produced deliberately by Hertz in 1887, and the electromagnetic spectrum now spans radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma radiation, all governed by the same equations ([Wikipedia: Electromagnetic radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_radiation)).

Electromagnetic waves carry energy and momentum, described by the Poynting vector and field momentum density, and they are generated by accelerating charges; their quantized excitations are photons with energy $hf$ and momentum $h/\lambda$ ([Wikipedia: Poynting vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poynting_vector); [Wikipedia: Electromagnetic radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_radiation)). Their reflection and transmission at an interface between two media are given by the Fresnel equations ([Wikipedia: Fresnel equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresnel_equations)).

### Formal definition
In vacuum without charges or currents, Maxwell's equations read
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=0,\quad \nabla\times\mathbf E=-\frac{\partial\mathbf B}{\partial t},\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\quad \nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}.$$
Taking the curl of the curl equations and using $\nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf V)=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf V)-\nabla^2\mathbf V$ gives
$$\frac{1}{c_0^2}\frac{\partial^2\mathbf E}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2\mathbf E=0,\qquad \frac{1}{c_0^2}\frac{\partial^2\mathbf B}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2\mathbf B=0,\qquad c_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} .$$
Covariantly, in Lorenz gauge $\partial_\mu A^\mu=0$, the four-potential $A^\mu=(\phi/c,\mathbf A)$ satisfies $\Box A^\mu=0$ with $\Box=\nabla^2-c^{-2}\partial_t^2$ ([Wikipedia: Electromagnetic wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_wave_equation)).

A **monochromatic plane wave** has $\mathbf E(\mathbf r,t)=\Re\{\mathbf E_0e^{i(\omega t-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r)}\}$ with dispersion relation $|\mathbf k|=\omega/c=2\pi/\lambda$; the general solution is a superposition of waves $g(\omega t-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r)$ ([Wikipedia: Electromagnetic wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_wave_equation)).

### Key results
- **Transversality and field relations.** In the far field $\mathbf E\perp\mathbf B\perp\hat{\mathbf n}$ with $\mathbf B=\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf E/c$, and in lossless media the two fields are in phase ([Wikipedia: Electromagnetic radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_radiation)).
- **Poynting's theorem.** With $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$ (microscopically $\mathbf S=\mu_0^{-1}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$) and, in linear nondispersive media, $u=\tfrac12(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H)$, energy conservation reads $\partial_t u=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf S-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$. A plane wave of peak amplitude $E_{\rm peak}$ in a medium of impedance $\eta$ carries mean intensity $\langle S\rangle=E_{\rm peak}^2/(2\eta)$, with $\eta_0\approx377\,\Omega$ in vacuum ([Wikipedia: Poynting vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poynting_vector)).
- **Momentum and radiation pressure.** In free space the field momentum density is $\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2$, and [radiation pressure](node:Radiation%20Pressure) on an absorbing surface is $P_{\rm rad}=\langle S\rangle/c$ ([Wikipedia: Poynting vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poynting_vector)).
- **Fresnel equations.** For non-magnetic media with Snell's law $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$,
  $$r_s=\frac{n_1\cos\theta_i-n_2\cos\theta_t}{n_1\cos\theta_i+n_2\cos\theta_t},\qquad r_p=\frac{n_2\cos\theta_i-n_1\cos\theta_t}{n_2\cos\theta_i+n_1\cos\theta_t}.$$
  $r_p=0$ at Brewster's angle $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1$, and for $n_1>n_2$ total internal reflection ($R_s=R_p=1$) occurs when $(n_1/n_2)\sin\theta_i>1$ ([Wikipedia: Fresnel equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresnel_equations)).
- **Radiation from accelerated charges (Larmor, 1897).** A nonrelativistic point charge $q$ with acceleration $a$ radiates total power $P=q^2a^2/(6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3)$ (SI); in Gaussian units the nonrelativistic formula reads $P=2q^2a^2/(3c^3)$, and Liénard's relativistic generalization is $P=\tfrac{2q^2\gamma^6}{3c^3}\big[a^2-(\mathbf v\times\mathbf a/c)^2\big]$ ([Wikipedia: Larmor formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larmor_formula)). In the Liénard–Wiechert fields the acceleration terms fall off as $1/r$ and form the radiation field, while $1/r^2$ terms are near-field ([Wikipedia: Electromagnetic radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_radiation)).
- **Momentum in media (Abraham–Minkowski).** Minkowski's energy–momentum tensor predicts that a wave's momentum increases on entering a dielectric, Abraham's that it decreases. Pfeifer et al. conclude that neither tensor is complete alone: once the accompanying material tensor is included, all proposed forms give the same experimental predictions ([Pfeifer et al., arXiv:0710.0461](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.0461)).

### Examples
