A 2026 survey of AI-scientist systems argues that the bottleneck is shifting from whether agents can complete research tasks to whether reviewers can verify what they produce; 83% of runnable systems release code, but only 38% release seeds or execution traces, and no LLM-era system in the corpus shows an externally validated in-loop oracle under the authors' coding rule ([Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179)). Self-evaluation is the weak point: [LLM Agents](node:LLM%20Agents) combine generation, execution and self-evaluation in one loop, and their completion claims exceeded official evaluator pass rates by 28.7–37.9 percentage points on SkillsBench ([Li et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29921)).

The design borrows from two established ideas. From program checking: a certifying algorithm outputs, with its answer, a proof that the answer is correct, which a simpler checker validates ([Wikipedia: Certifying algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm)); compare [Proof-Carrying Results](node:Proof-Carrying%20Results). From reproducibility of ML-based science: errors such as data leakage are common and can be caught with structured disclosure, such as the "model info sheets" that document why a claim is free of leakage ([Kapoor and Narayanan 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048)). Gates of this kind sit between [Data Provenance and Lineage](node:Data%20Provenance%20and%20Lineage), which records where each number came from, and [Machine Learning Evaluation](node:Machine%20Learning%20Evaluation), which says what a number means.

### Formal definition
**Certifying computation.** A certifying algorithm outputs a solution together with a proof of its correctness, and a proof checker validates the pair. It is efficient if running it plus the checker is at most a constant factor slower than the best non-certifying algorithm, and the proof should be simpler than the algorithm, otherwise rerunning the algorithm would count as checking ([Wikipedia: Certifying algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm)).

**Specification authority.** Li et al. separate the agent from the authority that certifies completion: agents may plan, act and request completion, but only admissible evidence from qualified providers can establish a specification-governed state; their SpecHarness compiles visible specifications into source-linked obligations and governs finalization through versioned obligation state, with verifiable requirements validated at runtime and ambiguous ones left advisory ([Li et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29921)).

**Evidence gate (as proposed here).** Combining the two: let a research output contain claims $c_1,\dots,c_n$, and let each claim carry an evidence bundle $E(c_i)$ (data identifiers, split specification, metric definition, run trace). A gate is a checker $V$ independent of the agent, and the output is released iff
$$\forall i:\ V\big(c_i, E(c_i)\big) = \mathsf{accept}.$$
This is the certifying-algorithm pattern applied to claims, with the specification-authority boundary of Li et al. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm); [Li et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29921)).

**Leakage, the main thing a split gate checks.** Leakage is the use during training of information that would not be available at prediction time; it includes feature leakage (proxies for the label) and training-example leakage (preprocessing fitted before the split, duplicates across splits, non-independent rows such as randomly split time series) ([Wikipedia: Leakage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29)).

### Key results
- **Reusable holdout.** In [adaptive data analysis](node:Adaptive%20Data%20Analysis), reusing a holdout set adaptively can overfit it; Dwork et al. give a mechanism that validates many adaptively chosen hypotheses on a holdout while provably limiting overfitting, using [Differential Privacy](node:Differential%20Privacy) and description-length arguments unified by approximate max-information. ([Dwork et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629))
- **Leakage is widespread in ML-based science.** Errors were found in 17 fields affecting 329 papers, with a taxonomy of 8 leakage types; in civil-war prediction, every paper claiming complex models beat [Logistic Regression](node:Logistic%20Regression) failed to reproduce because of leakage. ([Kapoor and Narayanan 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048)) The authors' maintained list later reached 41 papers across 30 fields reporting errors affecting 648 papers ([Princeton reproducibility page](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/)).
- **LLM verifiers miss real errors.** On SPOT, 83 published papers with 91 errors serious enough for errata or retraction, no LLM exceeded 21.1% recall or 6.1% precision (o3 best), and models rarely rediscovered the same errors across eight runs. ([Son et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11855))
- **Agents over-claim completion.** Across seven models on SkillsBench, only 79.6%–86.4% of requirements were satisfied across 509 task directions, and completion claims exceeded official pass rates by 28.7–37.9 points. ([Li et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29921))
- **Checker outcomes.** Running a certifying algorithm with its checker yields a correct output, a detected bug, or (rarely) bugs in algorithm and checker that hide each other. ([Wikipedia: Certifying algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm))
- **Claim–evidence linking is hard for LLMs.** On CLAIM-BENCH (300+ claim–evidence pairs, six LLMs), models show significant limitations; three-pass and one-by-one prompting improve linking of dispersed evidence at higher cost. ([Javaji et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08235))

### Examples
- **Graph certificates.** A certifying bipartiteness test returns a 2-colouring or an odd cycle; a planarity test returns an embedding or a Kuratowski subgraph; in each case a checker validates the returned witness, and the proof should be simpler than the algorithm itself ([Wikipedia: Certifying algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm)). An evidence gate asks for the analogue for a reported metric: the split manifest and run trace that let a checker recompute it.
- **Model info sheets.** A template documenting the arguments that justify absence of leakage for a predictive-modelling claim; it is voluntary, cannot stop false claims, and its verification needs a computationally reproducible analysis ([Princeton reproducibility page](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/)).
- **Audit checklist.** Ding et al. code AI-scientist systems on lifecycle stage, autonomy, evaluation method, released artefacts, human-in-the-loop points, novelty verification and result-selection disclosure, and propose a reviewer-facing reporting checklist ([Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179)).

### History
[Certifying Algorithms](node:Certifying%20Algorithms) are surveyed by McConnell, Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer (2011), cited in ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm)). The reusable holdout dates to 2015 ([arXiv 1506.02629](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629)); the leakage survey to July 2022 ([arXiv 2207.07048](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048)); The AI Scientist to August 2024 ([arXiv 2408.06292](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292)). Verification benchmarks and specification-governed agents followed in 2025–2026 ([SPOT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11855); [CLAIM-BENCH](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08235); [Ding et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179); [Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29921)).

### Connections
- [Autonomous Scientific Research](node:Autonomous%20Scientific%20Research): the systems whose outputs a gate would control.
- [Closed-Loop Experiment Agents](node:Closed-Loop%20Experiment%20Agents): in-loop oracles are where gates would sit.
- [Data Provenance and Lineage](node:Data%20Provenance%20and%20Lineage): supplies the evidence bundle each claim points to.
- [Proof-Carrying Results](node:Proof-Carrying%20Results): results shipped with checkable certificates, the pattern a gate generalizes.
- [Proof-Carrying Code](node:Proof-Carrying%20Code): the code-level precedent for untrusted producers and trusted checkers.
- [Runtime Verification](node:Runtime%20Verification): checks execution traces against specifications at run time.
- [Data Leakage and Temporal Evaluation](node:Data%20Leakage%20and%20Temporal%20Evaluation): the error class a split gate targets.
- [Benchmark Contamination Detection](node:Benchmark%20Contamination%20Detection): test-set exposure in pretraining, a leakage variant for LLMs.
- [Multiple Testing and False Discovery Control](node:Multiple%20Testing%20and%20False%20Discovery%20Control): gates on many claims need error-rate control.
- [Reproducible Research Computing](node:Reproducible%20Research%20Computing): reruns and traces make claims checkable.
- [Scientific Benchmark Validity](node:Scientific%20Benchmark%20Validity): what a metric must mean before a gate can check it.
- [Multi-Agent Critique](node:Multi-Agent%20Critique): the text-only reviewing alternative that gates are compared against.

### Common pitfalls
- **Process checks are not semantic checks.** Verifiable requirements can be enforced, but ambiguous or subjective requirements remain advisory in specification-governed agents ([Li et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29921)).
- **Reruns are not validation.** Of nine closed-loop L4 systems in the survey, seven are mechanical reruns and one is author-claimed without an external check ([Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179)).
- **Disclosure does not prevent false claims.** Model info sheets cannot stop researchers from making false claims and need a reproducible analysis to verify ([Princeton reproducibility page](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/)).
- **Automated reviewers judging their own pipeline.** The AI Scientist's acceptance-threshold results are judged by its own automated reviewer, not by human reviewers ([Lu et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292)).
- **Holdout reuse.** A gate that lets an agent query the test set repeatedly reintroduces adaptive overfitting ([Dwork et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629)).

### Open problems
- **Dependable automated verification.** Son et al. conclude that a substantial gap remains between current LLM capabilities and what dependable AI-assisted academic verification requires ([Son et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11855)).
- **Verifying agent-produced claims.** Ding et al. identify reviewer verification of AI-scientist output as the field's shifting bottleneck, with no externally validated in-loop oracle in their corpus ([Ding et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179)).
- **Leakage mitigation.** Kapoor and Narayanan describe mitigations for leakage in scientific ML as understudied and note the absence of systemic solutions to reproducibility failures ([Princeton reproducibility page](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Certifying algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certifying_algorithm): certificates, checkers and examples.
- **Reference:** [Leakage (machine learning)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29): types and detection of leakage.
- **Learn:** [Princeton: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science](https://reproducible.cs.princeton.edu/): taxonomy, affected-paper list and model info sheets.
- **Primary:** [Li et al. 2026, Who Holds the Pen? Let Specifications, Not Agents, Sign Off](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29921): specification authority over agent completion.
- **Primary:** [Son et al. 2025, SPOT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11855): benchmark for automated verification of published research.
- **Primary:** [Dwork et al. 2015, Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629): provable holdout reuse.
- **Further reading:** [Ding et al. 2026, Autonomous Research Agents: A Survey of AI Scientists and the Verification Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05179): coded survey and reviewer checklist.
- **Further reading:** [Kapoor and Narayanan 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048): leakage survey and model info sheets.
references.Expectation and Variance:
## Reference
### Overview
The expectation $EX$ of a random variable is its Lebesgue integral against the probability measure, a probability-weighted average of its values; the variance $\operatorname{var}(X)=E(X-EX)^2$ measures the spread around it. Because expectation is an integral, it inherits linearity, monotonicity, and the convergence theorems of [measure theory](node:Measure%20Theory), and computations reduce to integrals against the distribution of $X$. ([Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value))

Expectation and variance carry most of elementary probability. Markov's and Chebyshev's inequalities turn moments into tail bounds; additivity of variance for uncorrelated summands gives the $L^2$ weak law of large numbers; and the first two moments are what the central limit theorem keeps. Characteristic and moment [generating functions](node:Generating%20Functions) package all the moments, and under growth conditions the moments determine the distribution. ([Durrett](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance))

In high-dimensional geometry, variance inequalities are a current research topic. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture can be stated as a Poincaré inequality $\operatorname{Var}_\pi f\le C\,\|\Sigma\|\,E_\pi\|\nabla f\|^2$ for every log-concave measure $\pi$, with a dimension-free constant $C$. ([Kook and Vempala 2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.10848v1)) Preprints posted in October 2026 claim a proof; they had not been refereed at the time of writing (see Open problems). ([Song and Zhang 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01447); [Bizeul, Klartag and Lehec 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05474))

### Formal definition
For $X\ge0$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, $EX=\int X\,dP\in[0,\infty]$. In general write $x^+=\max\{x,0\}$, $x^-=\max\{-x,0\}$; $EX$ **exists** and equals $EX^+-EX^-$ whenever $EX^+<\infty$ or $EX^-<\infty$. ([Durrett, §1.6](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

With $\mu=EX$ finite, the **variance** is
$$\operatorname{var}(X)=E(X-\mu)^2=EX^2-\mu^2,$$
and $EX^k$ is the $k$-th **moment**. For $p\ge1$, $\|X\|_p=(E|X|^p)^{1/p}$. ([Durrett, §1.6](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Sheffield, MIT 18.175 Lecture 5](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture5.pdf))

For a random vector $X$ with mean $\mu$, the covariance matrix is $\Sigma=E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^{\mathsf T}]$, which is positive semidefinite, and $\operatorname{var}(c^{\mathsf T}X)=c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma c$. ([Wikipedia: Variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance))

The **characteristic function** is $\varphi(t)=Ee^{itX}=E\cos tX+iE\sin tX$. ([Durrett, §3.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

### Key results
- **Linearity and monotonicity.** If $X,Y\ge0$ or $E|X|,E|Y|<\infty$: $E(X+Y)=EX+EY$, $E(aX+b)=aEX+b$, and $X\ge Y$ implies $EX\ge EY$. Consequently $\operatorname{var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{var}(X)$. ([Durrett, Thm 1.6.1 and (1.6.4)](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Change of variables.** If $X$ is a random element of $(S,\mathcal S)$ with distribution $\mu$ and $f:S\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $f\ge0$ or $E|f(X)|<\infty$, then $Ef(X)=\int_S f(y)\,\mu(dy)$. ([Durrett, Thm 1.6.9](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Jensen and Hölder.** If $\varphi$ is convex and $E|X|,E|\varphi(X)|<\infty$, then $E\varphi(X)\ge\varphi(EX)$. If $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ with $1/p+1/q=1$, then $E|XY|\le\|X\|_p\|Y\|_q$. ([Durrett, Thms 1.6.2–1.6.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Chebyshev's inequality (general form).** If $\varphi\ge0$, $A$ is Borel, and $i_A=\inf\{\varphi(y):y\in A\}$, then $i_A P(X\in A)\le E(\varphi(X);X\in A)\le E\varphi(X)$. Taking $\varphi(x)=x^2$ and $A=\{|x-\mu|\ge a\}$ gives $P(|X-\mu|\ge a)\le\operatorname{var}(X)/a^2$. ([Durrett, Thm 1.6.4](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Convergence theorems.** Fatou: $X_n\ge0\Rightarrow\liminf EX_n\ge E\liminf X_n$. Monotone convergence: $0\le X_n\uparrow X\Rightarrow EX_n\uparrow EX$. Dominated convergence: $X_n\to X$ a.s. and $|X_n|\le Y$ with $EY<\infty$ imply $EX_n\to EX$. ([Durrett, Thms 1.6.5–1.6.7](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Sheffield, Lecture 5](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture5.pdf))
- **Products and sums under independence.** If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are independent and either all $X_i\ge0$ or all $E|X_i|<\infty$, then $E\prod X_i=\prod EX_i$. If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ have $EX_i^2<\infty$ and are uncorrelated, then $\operatorname{var}(X_1+\dots+X_n)=\sum\operatorname{var}(X_i)$ (Bienaymé). ([Durrett, Thms 2.1.13, 2.2.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Law of total variance.** $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y))+\operatorname{Var}(E(X\mid Y))$. ([Wikipedia: Variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance))
- **Tail formula.** For $X\ge0$, $EX=\int_0^\infty P(X>x)\,dx$. ([Wikipedia: Expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value))
- **Moments and the characteristic function.** If $\int|x|^n\mu(dx)<\infty$ then $\varphi$ has a continuous $n$-th derivative $\varphi^{(n)}(t)=\int(ix)^ne^{itx}\mu(dx)$; if $EX^2<\infty$ then $\varphi(t)=1+itEX-t^2EX^2/2+o(t^2)$. If $\limsup_k\mu_{2k}^{1/2k}/2k<\infty$, at most one distribution function has moments $\mu_k$ (moment determinacy). ([Durrett, Thms 3.3.18, 3.3.20, 3.3.25](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Thin-shell variance bound (Klartag–Lehec).** There is a universal constant $C$ such that every log-concave random vector $X$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with mean zero and identity covariance satisfies $E(|X|-\sqrt n)^2\le C$, confirming the thin-shell conjecture (arXiv v1 posted July 2025). ([Klartag and Lehec 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15495))

### Examples
- Exponential with rate $1$: $EX^k=k!$, so mean $1$ and variance $1$; with rate $\lambda$, mean $1/\lambda$ and variance $1/\lambda^2$. ([Durrett, Example 1.6.10](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- Standard normal: $EX=0$, $\operatorname{var}(X)=1$; $\sigma X+\mu$ has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. ([Durrett, Example 1.6.11](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- Bernoulli($p$): mean $p$, variance $p(1-p)$. Poisson($\lambda$): factorial moments $E[X(X-1)\cdots(X-k+1)]=\lambda^k$, so mean and variance both equal $\lambda$. ([Durrett, Examples 1.6.12–1.6.13](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- Uniform on $[a,b]$: variance $(b-a)^2/12$; geometric($p$): variance $(1-p)/p^2$. ([Wikipedia: Variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance))
- The Cauchy distribution has no expectation, and the St. Petersburg game has infinite expectation. ([Wikipedia: Expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value))

### History
The idea grew out of the "problem of points," which Pascal and Fermat solved in 1654. Huygens published the first systematic treatment in 1657, Laplace defined expectation explicitly in 1814, and Whitworth introduced the notation $E$ in 1901. ([Wikipedia: Expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value)) Ronald Fisher introduced the term "variance" in his 1918 paper on correlation between relatives under Mendelian inheritance. ([Wikipedia: Variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance))

### Connections
- [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): expectation is computed from the distribution via the change-of-variables formula.
- [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration): $EX$ is the Lebesgue integral $\int X\,dP$.
- [Monotone Convergence Theorem](node:Monotone%20Convergence%20Theorem), [Dominated Convergence Theorem](node:Dominated%20Convergence%20Theorem): justify exchanging limits and expectations.
- [Jensen's Inequality](node:Jensen's%20Inequality), [Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality](node:Cauchy–Schwarz%20Inequality): the basic moment inequalities.
- [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces): $\|X\|_p$ and Hölder's inequality; variance is a squared $L^2$ distance to the constants.
- [Independence of Random Variables](node:Independence%20of%20Random%20Variables): makes expectations of products factor and variances add.
- [Conditional Expectation](node:Conditional%20Expectation), [Law of Total Expectation](node:Law%20of%20Total%20Expectation): give the law of total variance.
- [Limit Theorems (LLN and CLT)](node:Limit%20Theorems%20%28LLN%20and%20CLT%29): means and variances are the parameters of both theorems.
- [Concentration of Measure](node:Concentration%20of%20Measure): sharper tail bounds than Chebyshev for nice functions of many variables.
- [Isoperimetric Inequalities](node:Isoperimetric%20Inequalities): equivalent to Poincaré-type variance bounds for log-concave measures (KLS).

### Common pitfalls
- $EX$ need not exist: it is undefined when $EX^+=EX^-=\infty$, as for the Cauchy distribution. ([Durrett, §1.6](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value))
- $E[XY]=EX\,EY$ holds for independent integrable $X,Y$, but it fails in general for dependent variables. ([Durrett, Thm 2.1.13](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value))
- Variances add for uncorrelated summands; independence is sufficient but not necessary, and without either the covariance terms remain. ([Wikipedia: Variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance))
- The formula $EX^2-(EX)^2$ suffers catastrophic cancellation in floating point; use a centered or online algorithm. ([Wikipedia: Variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance))
- Jensen needs integrability: both $E|X|$ and $E|\varphi(X)|$ must be finite. ([Durrett, Thm 1.6.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

### Open problems
- **The KLS conjecture (variance form): proof claimed in October 2026, not yet refereed.** For a log-concave probability measure $\pi$ on $\mathbb R^n$ with covariance $\Sigma$, let $C_{\mathrm{PI}}(\pi)$ be the best constant in $\operatorname{Var}_\pi f\le C_{\mathrm{PI}}(\pi)E_\pi\|\nabla f\|^2$. The conjecture is $C_{\mathrm{PI}}(\pi)\lesssim\|\Sigma\|$ with a universal constant; the lower bound $\|\Sigma\|\le C_{\mathrm{PI}}(\pi)$ always holds. The December 2025 survey of Kook and Vempala lists it as open, records the thin-shell and slicing conjectures as resolved, and gives the best proved bound as $C_{\mathrm{PI}}(n)\lesssim\log n$. ([Kook and Vempala 2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.10848v1)) That bound is Klartag's 2023 theorem that the slicing and KLS conjectures hold up to a factor $\sqrt{\log n}$ (in the isoperimetric normalization). ([Klartag 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.14938)) Klartag and Lehec resolved Bourgain's slicing problem in December 2024: every convex body of volume one in $\mathbb R^n$ has a hyperplane section of $(n-1)$-volume at least a universal constant. ([Klartag and Lehec 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15044)) They proved the thin-shell conjecture, which KLS implies, in July 2025. ([Klartag and Lehec 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15495)) On 1 October 2026 Song and Zhang posted a preprint claiming that $\psi_n$ is bounded by a universal constant and that the Poincaré constant of every isotropic log-concave measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is bounded by a universal constant, which would resolve KLS. ([Song and Zhang 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01447)) On 4 October 2026 Bizeul, Klartag and Lehec posted a proof of the KLS conjecture whose key step uses Song and Zhang's criterion on high-order derivatives of tilt averages. ([Bizeul, Klartag and Lehec 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05474)) Treat this as a claimed resolution until it is refereed.

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Expected value (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value) and [Variance (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance): definitions, properties, inequalities, history.
- **Learn:** [Sheffield, MIT 18.175 Lecture 5: More integration and expectation](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture5.pdf): Lebesgue integration, Jensen, Hölder, convergence theorems (course page [18.175](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/spring2014math175.html)).
- **Primary:** [Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*, §1.6, §2.2, §3.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf): graduate treatment of expectation, variance, and characteristic functions.
- **Primary:** [Kook and Vempala, *The Localization Method for High-Dimensional Inequalities*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10848): survey of KLS, thin-shell, and slicing, stated as variance and isoperimetric inequalities.
- **Further reading:** [Durrett's book page](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/pte.html): the 5th edition of the standard graduate probability text.
references.Extra Dimensions:
## Reference
### Overview
Extra dimensions are spatial dimensions beyond the three observed ones. Proposals date to the 1920s work of Kaluza and Klein, who tried to unify the forces; around 1980 string theory revived the idea as a requirement of a consistent quantum theory of gravity, with the extra dimensions compactified near the Planck scale and so beyond experimental reach. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

Two 1998–1999 proposals made extra dimensions testable. Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos and Dvali (ADD) explained the weakness of gravity by two or more flat extra dimensions, between roughly a millimetre and $1/\mathrm{TeV}$ in size, in which only gravity propagates. Randall and Sundrum (RS) used a warped five-dimensional anti-de Sitter geometry with compactification scale of order $1/\mathrm{TeV}$, where the gravitational redshift of the warp factor generates the ratio of the electroweak and Planck scales. In warped models the Standard Model gauge fields and fermions may also live in the bulk, and the AdS/CFT correspondence reinterprets such models as four-dimensional strongly coupled theories with composite states. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

In string theory the extra dimensions are sometimes conjectured to form a six-dimensional Calabi–Yau manifold, and flux compactifications place the internal manifold in a Calabi–Yau or generalized Calabi–Yau space with nonzero fluxes. The number of such choices is the origin of the string landscape. ([Wikipedia, Calabi–Yau manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi%E2%80%93Yau_manifold); [Wikipedia, Compactification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compactification_%28physics%29))

### Formal definition
**Kaluza–Klein reduction.** For a five-dimensional complex scalar on $M^4\times S^1$ with $y\sim y+2\pi R$,
$$\phi(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi R M_5}}\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}e^{iny/R}\phi^{(n)}(x).$$
Integrating over $y$ gives a 4D theory with a massless zero mode and a tower of KK modes of mass $|n|/R$; the zero-mode self-coupling is $\lambda_4=\lambda_5/(2\pi R M_5)$, so it weakens as $R$ grows. Below $1/R$ the KK modes can be neglected. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)) With a 5D mass $m_0$ the tower becomes $m_n^2=m_0^2+n^2/R^2$, and for several compact dimensions $m^2=m_0^2+\sum_i n_i^2/R_i^2$. ([Cheng, TASI 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/1003.1162))

**ADD.** Gravity is described by the [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action) in $D=4+\delta$ dimensions, the Standard Model by an action on a 3-brane with the induced metric:
$$S_D=-\frac{\bar M_D^{2+\delta}}{2}\int d^4x\,d^\delta y\,\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal R+\int d^4x\sqrt{-g_{\rm ind}}\,\mathcal L_{\rm SM}.$$
For flat extra dimensions of volume $V_\delta$ (e.g. $(2\pi R)^\delta$ for a torus) the graviton tower has $m_{\vec n}^2=|\vec n|^2/R^2$, and the zero-mode action identifies the reduced Planck mass $M_P\equiv1/\sqrt{8\pi G_N}\simeq2.4\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ as
$$M_P^2=V_\delta\,\bar M_D^{2+\delta}.$$
([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

**RS.** The extra dimension is the orbifold $S^1/\mathbb Z_2$, the segment $y\in[0,\pi R]$, with a bulk cosmological constant $\Lambda$ and boundary tensions $\Lambda_0,\Lambda_{\pi R}$. Einstein's equations give the $\mathrm{AdS}_5$ metric
$$ds^2=a(y)^2\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu+dy^2,\qquad a(y)=e^{-ky},\qquad k=\sqrt{-\Lambda/(6M_5^3)},$$
with consistency requiring $\Lambda_0=-\Lambda_{\pi R}=-\Lambda/k$. Scales of fields on the infrared (IR) boundary $y=\pi R$ are redshifted by $e^{-k\pi R}$ relative to the ultraviolet (UV) boundary $y=0$, and
$$M_P^2=\frac{M_5^3}{2k}\bigl(1-e^{-2k\pi R}\bigr).$$
([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

### Key results
- **ADD radius prediction.** With $M_D\sim\mathrm{TeV}$, $M_P^2=V_\delta\bar M_D^{2+\delta}$ gives $R\sim10^9\,\mathrm{km}$ for $\delta=1$ (excluded by solar-system tests of Newton's law), $R\sim0.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ for $\delta=2$, down to $R\sim0.1\,\mathrm{MeV}^{-1}$ for $\delta=6$. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)) ADD originally framed this as a solution of the hierarchy problem needing neither supersymmetry nor technicolor, with $n\ge2$ new dimensions and the Standard Model localized on a weak-scale 4D manifold. ([ADD 1998](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9803315))
- **Sub-millimetre gravity.** KK gravitons modify the potential to $V(r)=-G_Nm_1m_2r^{-1}[1+\alpha e^{-r/\lambda}]$, with $\alpha=16/3$ and $\lambda=R$ for a 2-torus. Torsion-balance data give $R<30\,\mu\mathrm m$ at 95% CL for $\delta=2$, i.e. $M_D>4.0\,\mathrm{TeV}$. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Astrophysical and cosmological bounds on ADD.** SN1987A cooling gives $M_D>27\,(2.4)\,\mathrm{TeV}$ for $\delta=2\,(3)$; heating of neutron stars by trapped KK gravitons gives $M_D>1700\,(76)\,\mathrm{TeV}$; avoiding overclosure by relic gravitons needs $M_D>7\,\mathrm{TeV}$ and the diffuse gamma background $M_D>100\,\mathrm{TeV}$ for $\delta=2$. Bounds from graviton decays to photons weaken if KK gravitons decay mainly to hidden-sector states. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **LHC bounds on ADD.** Each KK graviton couples with strength $1/M_P$, but summing over the near-continuum gives inclusive rates suppressed only by powers of $M_D$. ATLAS (CMS) jet plus missing-$p_T$ searches with $139\,(137)\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ at $13\,\mathrm{TeV}$ give $M_D>5.9$–$11.2\,(5.5$–$10.7)\,\mathrm{TeV}$ for $\delta=2$–$6$. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **RS hierarchy without large parameters.** Taking $M_5\sim k\sim M_P$, a radius $R\simeq11/k$ yields an IR scale $ke^{-k\pi R}\sim\mathrm{TeV}$; if the Higgs is localized at the IR boundary this solves the hierarchy problem. Unlike ADD, the proposed radius stabilization mechanisms need no new small or large parameter. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)) RS predict spin-2 excitations of weak-scale mass coupling with weak rather than gravitational strength, so large-extra-dimension constraints do not apply. ([Randall & Sundrum 1999](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9905221))
- **Goldberger–Wise stabilization.** A bulk scalar with quartic interactions localized on the two 3-branes generates a potential for the modulus that sets the size of the fifth dimension; its minimum gives a compactification scale solving the hierarchy problem without fine-tuning. ([Goldberger & Wise 1999](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9907447)) The radion is generically heavy once $R$ is stabilized, but under some conditions a light radion, identified with the dilaton of spontaneously broken scale invariance, can arise. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Bulk Standard Model and KK spectrum.** Only the Higgs need be IR-localized; gauge bosons and fermions can propagate in the bulk, and light fermions localized toward the UV boundary give the fermion mass hierarchy through order-one bulk-mass parameters $c_f$. KK masses are $m_n\simeq(n+\tfrac{\alpha}{2}-\tfrac14)\pi ke^{-\pi kR}$ with $\alpha=|c_f-\tfrac12|,0,1$ for KK fermions, gauge bosons and gravitons, so the gauge KK modes are lightest and gravitons heaviest. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Gauge-Higgs unification and holography.** In gauge-Higgs unified models the Higgs is the fifth component $A_5$ of a 5D gauge field, its mass protected by 5D [gauge invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance) and generated only by non-local one-loop effects; a bulk custodial $SU(2)_V$ is needed for $M_W^2\simeq M_Z^2\cos^2\theta_W$, and the simplest realization uses $G_5=SU(3)_c\times SO(5)\times U(1)_X$ broken to $SO(4)$ on the IR boundary. Via AdS/CFT the extra coordinate plays the role of the [renormalization](node:Renormalization) scale, IR-localized fields and KK states are composite resonances of a strongly coupled CFT, and the Higgs is a composite pseudo-Nambu–Goldstone boson. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Electroweak precision and LHC bounds on warped models.** Electroweak precision data give $m_{KK}\gtrsim10\,\mathrm{TeV}$ from $\hat T$, relaxed to $m_{KK}\gtrsim3\,\mathrm{TeV}$ from $\hat S$ with custodial symmetry. For RS with only gravity in the bulk, CMS diphoton data ($36\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$) exclude the lightest KK graviton below $2.3$–$4.6\,\mathrm{TeV}$ for $k/M_P=0.01$–$0.2$, ATLAS ($139\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$) gives $4.5\,\mathrm{TeV}$ for $k/M_P=0.1$, and CMS dileptons exclude $2.47$–$4.78\,\mathrm{TeV}$ for $k/M_P=0.01$–$0.1$. With the Standard Model in the bulk these couplings are suppressed; then KK gluons decaying to $t\bar t$ are excluded below $4.55\,\mathrm{TeV}$ (CMS, $36\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$). ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Universal extra dimensions.** If all Standard Model fields propagate in a flat $S^1/\mathbb Z_2$ with KK parity, the lightest KK state is stable and a dark-matter candidate. Reinterpreted LHC supersymmetry searches give $1/R>1.4$–$1.5\,\mathrm{TeV}$ for $\Lambda R=5$–$35$, and the minimal UED model is ruled out when LHC data are combined with the dark-matter relic density, though extensions with boundary terms can survive. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

### Examples
- **Kaluza–Klein circle.** Kaluza's classical 5D extension of general relativity yields Einstein's equations, [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations) and an equation for a scalar (the dilaton, later radion); Klein's compact microscopic circle explained Kaluza's cylinder condition and related charge quantization to standing waves. The theory fails experimentally, for example in its predicted electron mass. ([Wikipedia, Kaluza–Klein theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluza%E2%80%93Klein_theory))
- **ADD with two extra dimensions.** $R\sim0.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ for $M_D\sim\mathrm{TeV}$; current tabletop data already push $M_D$ above $4\,\mathrm{TeV}$. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **RS1 warp factor.** With $M_5\sim k\sim M_P$, a radius $R\simeq11/k$ turns a Planck-scale input into a TeV-scale IR boundary. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **The dark dimension.** Montero, Vafa and Valenzuela use the swampland distance/duality conjecture and the smallness of dark energy $\Lambda$ to propose a single mesoscopic extra dimension of length $l\sim\Lambda^{-1/4}\sim10^{-6}\,\mathrm m$, with massless fermions in it giving a tower of sterile neutrinos. ([Montero, Vafa & Valenzuela 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12293))

### History
Nordström proposed a 5D theory of electromagnetism and scalar gravity in 1914. Kaluza and Klein (1919–1926) showed that 5D Einstein gravity on a circle gives 4D gravity and electromagnetism. Supergravity and superstrings renewed interest with Planck-scale extra dimensions. Antoniadis (1990) proposed $\mathrm{TeV}^{-1}$ dimensions tied to [supersymmetry breaking](node:Supersymmetry%20Breaking); Polchinski's D-branes (1995) let Standard Model fields live on branes while gravitons fill all dimensions; Hořava and Witten (1996) showed an M-theory extra dimension could lower the string scale to the unification scale; ADD (1998) and RS (1999) followed. ([Cheng, TASI 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/1003.1162)) Kaluza sent his idea to Einstein in 1919 and published it in 1921; Klein's compact-dimension interpretation dates from 1926. ([Wikipedia, Kaluza–Klein theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluza%E2%80%93Klein_theory)) Goldberger and Wise proposed bulk-scalar stabilization in 1999. ([Goldberger & Wise 1999](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9907447))

### Connections
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) and [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): the $D$-dimensional theory reduces to 4D gravity, and KK gravitons modify Newton's law below $R$.
- [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action): the bulk action whose reduction fixes $M_P$.
- [Kaluza–Klein Theory](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Theory) and [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes): the original compactification and the 4D towers it produces.
- [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions) and [Tests of the Inverse-Square Law](node:Tests%20of%20the%20Inverse-Square%20Law): ADD and its tabletop tests; [Gauss's Law in n Dimensions](node:Gauss's%20Law%20in%20n%20Dimensions) explains the $1/r^{2+\delta}$ force.
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model), [Warped Products](node:Warped%20Products), [Goldberger–Wise Mechanism](node:Goldberger–Wise%20Mechanism) and [Radion Phenomenology](node:Radion%20Phenomenology): warped geometry, stabilization and the radion.
- [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space) and [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence): the holographic reading of warped models.
- [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): gauge-Higgs unification and composite Higgs models realize the Higgs in warped space.
- [Universal Extra Dimensions](node:Universal%20Extra%20Dimensions) and [Kaluza–Klein Dark Matter](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Dark%20Matter): KK parity and a stable lightest KK particle.
- [Compactification](node:Compactification), [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds), [String Theory](node:String%20Theory), [M-Theory](node:M-Theory), [Supergravity](node:Supergravity), [D-Branes](node:D-Branes) and [String Landscape](node:String%20Landscape): where extra dimensions are required.
- [Supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry): proposed for the bulk to address the ADD radius hierarchy; ADD and RS were offered as alternatives to it for the electroweak hierarchy.
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem) and [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale): the puzzles extra dimensions address.
- [Neutron Stars](node:Neutron%20Stars), [Sterile Neutrinos](node:Sterile%20Neutrinos) and [Collider Physics](node:Collider%20Physics): astrophysical, dark-dimension and LHC probes.
- [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology) and [Standard Model of Particle Physics](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics): brane-localized versus bulk fields.
- Sources: [Csaki 2004 - TASI Lectures on Extra Dimensions and Branes](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0404096), [Randall and Sundrum 1999 - A Large Mass Hierarchy from a Small Extra Dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9905221), [Kachru et al. 2003 - de Sitter Vacua in String Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0301240).
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Extra dimensions and compactification](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Extra%20dimensions%20and%20compactification)

### Common pitfalls
- **ADD versus RS sizes.** ADD needs $\delta\ge2$ flat dimensions up to sub-millimetre size; RS needs one warped dimension with $R\simeq11/k$, $k$ near the Planck scale. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Applying RS graviton bounds to bulk-SM models.** Diphoton and dilepton KK-graviton bounds assume gravity-only bulk; with the Standard Model in the bulk those couplings are suppressed and KK gauge bosons are the better channel. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Treating $M_P$ as fundamental in ADD.** It is derived from $\bar M_D$ and the volume $V_\delta$. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [ADD 1998](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9803315))
- **Assuming photon-decay bounds are model independent.** Neutron-star and gamma-ray limits on ADD weaken if KK gravitons decay to hidden sectors on other branes. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

> [!warning] Contested
> Lowering the fundamental scale to a TeV makes higher-dimension operators less suppressed. Critics argue that Pauli-term contributions to the electron magnetic moment and dimension-five neutrino-mass operators become too large, and that operators above dimension four generically violate CP, baryon and lepton number. Responses include split fermions, whose offset wavefunctions suppress couplings exponentially (Arkani-Hamed and Schmaltz), and new gauge symmetries. ([Wikipedia, Large extra dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_extra_dimension))

### Open problems
- **Radius stabilization and the new hierarchy in ADD.** Consistency requires a mechanism fixing the radii at the values implied by $M_D\sim\mathrm{TeV}$, and $R\gg1/M_D$ is a new hierarchy problem whose solution might require bulk supersymmetry. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kaluza–Klein theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluza%E2%80%93Klein_theory): the original five-dimensional unification and its problems; [Large extra dimension (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_extra_dimension) for the ADD debate.
- **Learn:** [Csaki, TASI Lectures on Extra Dimensions and Branes](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0404096): pedagogical lectures on large and warped extra dimensions, radius stabilization and bulk gauge bosons; [Cheng, TASI 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/1003.1162) for KK reduction and UED.
- **Primary:** [PDG Review 85: Extra Dimensions (Demiragli & Pomarol, rev. 2023)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf): KK formalism, ADD, warped and flat models, and current bounds; original papers [Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos & Dvali 1998](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9803315); [Randall & Sundrum 1999](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9905221); [Goldberger & Wise 1999](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9907447).
- **Further reading:** [Kachru, Kallosh, Linde & Trivedi, de Sitter vacua in string theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0301240) and [Montero, Vafa & Valenzuela, The dark dimension and the swampland](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12293).
references.Extrinsic Curvature:
## Reference
### Overview
Extrinsic curvature measures how a hypersurface bends inside the space containing it. It is encoded by the second fundamental form (shape tensor), a quadratic form on the tangent space which, with the first fundamental form (induced metric), determines the principal curvatures; the notion extends from surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ to submanifolds of any Riemannian manifold, where in higher codimension it takes values in the normal bundle. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form)) Principal and mean curvatures depend on the embedding, whereas the Gaussian curvature of a surface is intrinsic, independent of how the surface is embedded. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))

The Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci equations tie the second fundamental form, the intrinsic curvature and the ambient curvature together; they are the fundamental equations of an isometric immersion. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) Hypersurfaces whose extrinsic curvature satisfies a condition, such as zero mean curvature (minimal), constant mean curvature (CMC) or constant principal curvatures (isoparametric), are classical objects of study; CMC surfaces remain an active area of research. ([Wikipedia: CMC surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant-mean-curvature_surface)) The classification of isoparametric hypersurfaces in spheres has only recently been completed. ([Cecil & Ryan, arXiv:2411.04231](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04231v2))

In general relativity the extrinsic curvature $K_{ij}$ of a spacelike slice, together with the induced metric $\gamma_{ij}$, forms the initial data of the 3+1 formalism ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035)), and its jump across a brane is fixed by the brane's stress–energy through Israel's junction condition. ([Shiromizu–Maeda–Sasaki, arXiv:gr-qc/9910076](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))

### Formal definition
**Surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$.** For a parametrization $\mathbf r(u,v)$ with unit normal $\mathbf n$, $\mathrm{II} = L\,du^2 + 2M\,du\,dv + N\,dv^2$, where $L, M, N$ are the projections of $\mathbf r_{uu}, \mathbf r_{uv}, \mathbf r_{vv}$ onto $\mathbf n$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form))

**Hypersurfaces in a Riemannian manifold.** With unit normal $n$ and ambient Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$, the shape operator $S$ and second fundamental form satisfy $\mathrm{II}(v,w) = \langle S(v),w\rangle = -\langle\nabla_v n, w\rangle = \langle n, \nabla_v w\rangle$; $\mathrm{II}$ is symmetric for a torsion-free connection and changes sign with the normal. In arbitrary codimension, $\mathrm{II}(v,w) = (\nabla_v w)^\perp$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form)) The principal curvatures are the eigenvalues of $S$, and the mean curvature is their average. ([Wikipedia: Principal curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_curvature))

**Normal connection.** For a submanifold $M\subset\tilde M$ with second fundamental form $h$, shape operators $A_\xi$ for normal $\xi$, and normal connection $D$ (the normal part of $\tilde\nabla_X\xi$), the Gauss formula is $\tilde\nabla_XY = \nabla_XY + h(X,Y)$ and the Weingarten formula $\tilde\nabla_X\xi = -A_\xi X + D_X\xi$, with $\langle A_\xi X, Y\rangle = \langle h(X,Y),\xi\rangle$. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

**Relativity convention.** For a non-null hypersurface $\Sigma$ of spacetime, Gourgoulhon defines the Weingarten map $\chi(v) = \nabla_v n$, proves it self-adjoint with respect to $\gamma$, and sets $K(u,v) = -u\cdot\nabla_v n$, the MTW and [numerical-relativity](node:Numerical%20Relativity) sign; for a member of a foliation, $K = -\tfrac12\mathcal L_n\gamma$. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))

### Key results
- **Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci equations.** For an isometric immersion into a space of constant curvature $c$, $\langle R(X,Y)Z,W\rangle = \langle h(X,W),h(Y,Z)\rangle - \langle h(X,Z),h(Y,W)\rangle + c(\langle X,W\rangle\langle Y,Z\rangle - \langle X,Z\rangle\langle Y,W\rangle)$; Codazzi says $(\bar\nabla_Xh)(Y,Z)$ is symmetric in $X,Y$ (in a space form); and the Ricci equation reads $\langle\tilde R(X,Y)\xi,\eta\rangle = \langle R^D(X,Y)\xi,\eta\rangle - \langle[A_\xi,A_\eta]X,Y\rangle$, so in a flat or constant-curvature ambient space the normal curvature is $R^D$ measured by the commutators of shape operators. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) Mainardi and Codazzi found the Codazzi equation independently, after Peterson. ([Wikipedia: Gauss–Codazzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Codazzi_equations))
- **Scalar Gauss relation and Theorema Egregium.** For a spacelike hypersurface of a Lorentzian manifold, ${}^4R + 2\,{}^4R_{\mu\nu}n^\mu n^\nu = R + K^2 - K_{ij}K^{ij}$; for a surface in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ the sign of the $K$ terms flips and it reduces to $R = 2\kappa_1\kappa_2$. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035)) Gauss proved in 1827 that Gaussian curvature is invariant under local isometry. ([Wikipedia: Theorema Egregium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorema_Egregium))
- **Totally geodesic hypersurfaces.** For $u,v$ tangent to $\Sigma$, $D_uv = \nabla_uv + K(u,v)n$, so $K$ measures the failure of geodesics of $\Sigma$ to be ambient geodesics, and the two notions coincide exactly when $K = 0$. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))
- **Minimal hypersurfaces.** A surface has zero mean curvature everywhere if and only if it is a critical point of area under compactly supported deformations; such surfaces need not be globally area-minimizing. ([Wikipedia: Minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface)) Bernstein's problem, whether entire minimal graphs in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ are hyperplanes, has a positive answer for $n\le7$ (Bernstein, De Giorgi, Almgren, Simons) and a negative one for $n\ge8$ (Bombieri–De Giorgi–Giusti, 1969). ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))
- **Hopf and Alexandrov theorems.** Hopf proved (1951) that an immersed topological sphere of constant mean curvature in $\mathbb E^3$ is a round sphere; Alexandrov proved (1958) that the only compact embedded CMC surfaces in $\mathbb E^3$ are round spheres; Wente's 1984 CMC tori show embeddedness cannot be dropped. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) Hopf's 1956 conjecture that immersed compact CMC hypersurfaces must be round spheres was disproved by Hsiang in $\mathbb R^4$ (1982) and by Wente's tori in $\mathbb R^3$. ([Wikipedia: CMC surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant-mean-curvature_surface))
- **Simons' gap theorem.** If $M^n$ is a compact minimal submanifold of $S^{n+p}$ whose second fundamental form has squared length $S \le n/(2 - 1/p)$, then either $M$ is totally geodesic or $S = n/(2-1/p)$; in the equality case $M$ is a generalized Clifford torus or a Veronese surface in $S^4$. For hypersurfaces ($p=1$) the gap is $S\le n \Rightarrow S\in\{0,n\}$. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))
- **Peng–Terng pinching.** For a compact minimal hypersurface of $S^{n+1}$ with constant scalar curvature there is $\delta(n) > 1/(12n)$ such that $n\le S\le n+\delta(n)$ forces $S = n$; for $n=3$, $S > 3$ implies $S\ge6$, sharp by Cartan's isoparametric hypersurface. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) Without assuming constant scalar curvature, Ding and Xin proved that for a compact minimal hypersurface of $S^{n+1}$ there is $\delta(n)>0$ with $n\le S\le n+\delta(n) \Rightarrow S\equiv n$ (a Clifford hypersurface), with explicit $\delta(n) = n/23$ for $n\ge6$. ([Ding & Xin, arXiv:1012.1073](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.1073))
- **Isoparametric hypersurfaces (Cartan, Münzner).** A hypersurface of a space form is isoparametric if its principal curvatures are constant. Cartan showed that in the sphere $g=3$ distinct principal curvatures forces a common multiplicity $m\in\{1,2,4,8\}$ (tubes over projective planes); Münzner proved $g\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$, with multiplicities $m_i = m_{i+2}$ and focal submanifolds minimal. The classification in spheres has recently been completed. ([Cecil & Ryan, arXiv:2411.04231](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04231v2))
- **Israel junction condition.** For a brane with surface stress–energy $S_{\mu\nu}$ in a 5D bulk, $[q_{\mu\nu}] = 0$ and $[K_{\mu\nu}] = -\kappa_5^2(S_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac13 q_{\mu\nu}S)$; $Z_2$ symmetry then gives $K^+_{\mu\nu} = -K^-_{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac12\kappa_5^2(S_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac13q_{\mu\nu}S)$. ([Shiromizu–Maeda–Sasaki, arXiv:gr-qc/9910076](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))

### Examples
- **Plane.** A plane has $\mathrm{II} = 0$: it is totally geodesic. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form))
- **Cylinder of radius $r$.** With Gourgoulhon's sign, $K = -1/r$ and $K_{ij}K^{ij} = 1/r^2$, while the intrinsic curvature vanishes, consistent with the Euclidean Gauss relation. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))
- **Sphere of radius $r$.** $K = -2/r$, $K_{ij}K^{ij} = 2/r^2$ and $R = 2/r^2$, so both curvatures are non-zero; geodesics of the sphere are not ambient geodesics. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035)) For the unit sphere in the standard parametrization, $\mathrm{II} = -du^2 - \sin^2u\,dv^2$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form))
- **Delaunay surfaces.** The CMC surfaces of revolution are obtained by rotating roulettes of conics: plane, cylinder, sphere, catenoid, unduloid and nodoid (Delaunay, 1841). ([Wikipedia: CMC surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant-mean-curvature_surface))
- **Catenoid and helicoid.** These minimal surfaces are locally isometric and can be bent into one another, illustrating that Gaussian curvature is intrinsic while the embedding is not. ([Wikipedia: Theorema Egregium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorema_Egregium))
- **Clifford tori.** The generalized Clifford tori $S^k(\sqrt{k/n})\times S^{n-k}(\sqrt{(n-k)/n})\subset S^{n+1}$ are the minimal hypersurfaces with $S = n$ in Simons' gap. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

### History
Gauss introduced the second fundamental form for surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form)) His *General Investigations of Curved Surfaces* (1827 and 1825 papers) is available in English translation. ([Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/36856)) Monge studied lines of curvature and Darboux later analyzed them systematically. ([Wikipedia: Principal curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_curvature)) Lagrange formulated the minimal surface problem in 1762, and Meusnier showed in 1776 that the helicoid and catenoid satisfy it. ([Wikipedia: Minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface)) Cartan began the theory of isoparametric hypersurfaces, and Münzner's work restricted the number of principal curvatures. ([Cecil & Ryan, arXiv:2411.04231](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04231v2)) In relativity, Wheeler coined the names lapse and shift, and York developed the initial-data method used in numerical relativity. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))

### Connections
- [Submanifolds and Embeddings](node:Submanifolds%20and%20Embeddings): extrinsic curvature is defined for an immersed submanifold.
- [Curves and Surfaces](node:Curves%20and%20Surfaces): the classical theory of $\mathrm{II}$ and principal curvatures.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): the Gauss equation relates intrinsic to ambient Riemann curvature.
- [Gauss–Codazzi Equations](node:Gauss–Codazzi%20Equations): the integrability conditions linking $K$ with intrinsic and ambient curvature.
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives) and [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles): $\mathrm{II}$ is the normal part of the ambient derivative; the normal bundle carries its own connection.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics) and [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry): Riemannian versus Lorentzian sign changes.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): $K=0$ characterizes totally geodesic hypersurfaces.
- [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations) and [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle): minimal and CMC hypersurfaces as critical points; moving-plane arguments behind Alexandrov's theorem.
- [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere): Clifford tori, Simons' gap and Chern's conjecture live in spheres.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity), [ADM Formalism](node:ADM%20Formalism), [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): $(\gamma_{ij},K_{ij})$ as initial data subject to constraints.
- [Israel Junction Conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions) and [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane): jumps of $K_{\mu\nu}$ across branes.

### Common pitfalls
- **Sign conventions.** Gourgoulhon's minus sign follows MTW and numerical relativity; Carroll, Poisson and Wald use the opposite convention. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035)) The sign of $\mathrm{II}$ also depends on the choice of normal. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form))
- **Trace versus mean curvature.** Gourgoulhon defines $H$ as the mean $(\kappa_1+\kappa_2+\kappa_3)/3$ of the eigenvalues of the Weingarten map, so with his sign $K = \operatorname{tr}K = -3H$. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))
- **Gaussian curvature is not extrinsic.** A cylinder has non-zero $K_{ij}$ but zero intrinsic curvature. ([Gourgoulhon, arXiv:gr-qc/0703035](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))
- **Embedded versus immersed.** Alexandrov's rigidity needs embeddedness; Wente's immersed CMC tori are not spheres. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))
- **Minimal does not mean minimizing.** Zero mean curvature only makes area stationary; minimal surfaces may self-intersect and need not minimize area globally. ([Wikipedia: Minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface))

### Open problems
- **Chern's conjecture.** For compact minimal hypersurfaces of $S^{n+1}$ with constant scalar curvature, the possible values of the scalar curvature (equivalently of $S$) should form a discrete set; a stronger form asserts such hypersurfaces are isoparametric. The source calls it unsolved as of 2018. ([Wikipedia: Chern's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chern%27s_conjecture_for_hypersurfaces_in_spheres))
- **Third value of $S$.** Peng and Terng conjectured that, for compact minimal hypersurfaces of $S^{n+1}$ with constant scalar curvature, the third value of $S$ (after $0$ and $n$) should be $2n$, realized by Cartan's isoparametric minimal hypersurfaces; Yang and Cheng's bound $S > n + n/3$ for $S>n>3$ is partial progress. ([Chen, arXiv:1307.1875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Second fundamental form (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form): classical and Riemannian definitions, codimension, Gauss equation.
- **Learn:** [Gourgoulhon, 3+1 Formalism and Bases of Numerical Relativity](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0703035): lecture notes; chapter 2 treats the Weingarten map, $K_{ij}$, examples and Gauss–Codazzi.
- **Primary:** [Chen, Riemannian Submanifolds: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.1875): fundamental equations, minimal and CMC submanifolds, Simons and Chern-conjecture results.
- **Primary:** [Cecil & Ryan, On the Work of Cartan and Münzner on Isoparametric Hypersurfaces](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04231v2): survey of isoparametric theory and its classification.
- **Primary:** [Gauss, General Investigations of Curved Surfaces (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/36856): the founding papers of surface theory.
- **Further reading:** [Colding & Minicozzi, A Course in Minimal Surfaces (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 121, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/121): graduate text on minimal surfaces.
references.FLRW Cosmology:
## Reference
### Overview
The Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) metric describes a homogeneous, isotropic universe that may expand, contract or stay static. Its form follows from the geometric assumptions of homogeneity and isotropy alone; combined with the Einstein field equations it gives the Friedmann equations, the basis of the standard cosmological model. ([Wikipedia: FLRW metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann%E2%80%93Lema%C3%AEtre%E2%80%93Robertson%E2%80%93Walker_metric))

The Friedmann equations rest on three assumptions: the FLRW metric, Einstein's field equations of [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity), and a perfect-fluid source. Homogeneity and isotropy are justified empirically on scales larger than about 100 Mpc. ([Wikipedia: Friedmann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann_equations))

The Particle Data Group review calls the observed expansion a natural, almost inevitable, result of any homogeneous and isotropic model based on general relativity, and notes that homogeneity and isotropy let the geometry and evolution be described by two quantities: the spatial curvature and the scale factor. The Robertson–Walker metric is the most general metric with a three-dimensional maximally symmetric spatial subspace. ([PDG: Big-Bang Cosmology](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))

### Formal definition
In PDG's conventions ($c=1$, signature $(+,-,-,-)$) the Robertson–Walker metric is
$$ds^2 = dt^2 - R^2(t)\left[\frac{dr^2}{1-kr^2} + r^2\left(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right)\right] = dt^2 - R^2(t)\left[d\chi^2 + S_k^2(\chi)\,d\Omega^2\right],$$
with $k\in\{+1,0,-1\}$ (closed, flat, open) and $S_k(\chi) = (\sin\chi,\ \chi,\ \sinh\chi)$. Here $r$ and $\chi$ are dimensionless and $R(t)$ carries length; the dimensionless scale factor is $a = R/R_0$. Conformal time $\eta$ is defined by $d\eta = dt/R(t)$, and the proper distance at fixed $t$ is $R(t)\chi$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))

For a perfect fluid with energy density $\rho$ and pressure $p$, Einstein's equations reduce to
$$H^2 \equiv \left(\frac{\dot R}{R}\right)^2 = \frac{8\pi G_N\rho}{3} - \frac{k}{R^2} + \frac{\Lambda}{3},\qquad \frac{\ddot R}{R} = \frac{\Lambda}{3} - \frac{4\pi G_N}{3}(\rho + 3p),$$
together with the [Continuity Equation](node:Continuity%20Equation) $\dot\rho = -3H(\rho+p)$, which follows from $T^{\mu\nu}{}_{;\mu}=0$. The critical density is $\rho_c = 3H^2/(8\pi G_N)$ (the density giving $k=0$ when $\Lambda=0$) and $\Omega_{\rm tot} = \rho/\rho_c$, where the vacuum term is counted in $\rho$ as the effective density $\Lambda/(8\pi G_N)$; then $k/R^2 = H^2(\Omega_{\rm tot}-1)$, or in present-day parameters $k/R_0^2 = H_0^2(\Omega_m+\Omega_r+\Omega_v-1)$, so it is the sum of matter, radiation and vacuum densities that fixes the sign of the curvature. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))

**Distances.** A null radial geodesic obeys $R(t)\,d\chi = dt$, so the comoving coordinate distance travelled between $t_1$ and $t_2$ is $\Delta\chi = \int_{t_1}^{t_2}dt/R(t) = \Delta\eta$, an interval of conformal time. The angular-diameter and luminosity distances are
$$D_A = \frac{R_0 S_k(\chi)}{1+z},\qquad D_L = (1+z)\,R_0 S_k(\chi).$$
([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf)) In terms of the Hubble distance $d_H$ and $E(z)=H(z)/H_0$, the line-of-sight comoving distance is $d_C = d_H\int_0^z dz'/E(z')$, and $d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A$ (Etherington reciprocity). ([Wikipedia: Distance measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_measures_%28cosmology%29))

### Key results
- **Uniqueness of the metric.** Robertson and Walker proved that the FLRW metric is the only metric on a spacetime that is spatially homogeneous and isotropic, a geometric result independent of the field equations. ([Wikipedia: FLRW metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann%E2%80%93Lema%C3%AEtre%E2%80%93Robertson%E2%80%93Walker_metric)) The work spans 1935–37: Robertson's "Kinematics and World-Structure" appeared in *ApJ* 82 (1935) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/143681)) and Walker's "On Milne's Theory of World-Structure" in *Proc. London Math. Soc.* s2-42 (1937). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.90))
- **Curvature from density.** With $\Omega$ the total density parameter (vacuum included), $\Omega>1 \Leftrightarrow k=+1$ (closed), $\Omega=1 \Leftrightarrow k=0$ (flat), $\Omega<1\Leftrightarrow k=-1$ (open), by $\Omega - 1 = k/(H^2a^2)$. ([Carroll, GR lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019)) ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))
- **Redshift.** $1+z = \nu_1/\nu_2 = R_2/R_1$, the ratio of scale factors at observation and emission, holds without any non-relativistic approximation; at small distances it reduces to Hubble's law. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf)) The redshift is caused by the expansion of space, not by relative velocities of emitter and observer. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Single-component solutions.** For constant $w=p/\rho$, $\rho\propto R^{-3(1+w)}$; neglecting curvature and $\Lambda$, $R\propto t^{2/[3(1+w)]}$, so radiation gives $R\propto t^{1/2}$ and matter $R\propto t^{2/3}$, while vacuum energy gives exponential expansion. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))
- **Fate with $\Lambda = 0$.** If $\Lambda=0$, $\rho>0$ and $p\ge 0$, open and flat universes expand forever; for $k=-1$, $\dot a\to 1$, for $k=0$ the expansion continues ever more slowly; closed ($k=+1$) universes reach a maximum $a_{\max}$ and recollapse. With only a cosmological constant this link between geometry and fate is lost. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019)) PDG adds that for $\Lambda<0$ the universe eventually recollapses regardless of the sign of $k$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))
- **Big Bang singularity.** For $\Lambda=0$, $\rho>0$, $p\ge0$ the acceleration equation forces $\ddot a<0$; since $\dot a>0$ today, tracing back necessarily reaches $a=0$, and the age is less than $H_0^{-1}$. Carroll notes that the singularity theorems show this singularity is not an artifact of the exact symmetry of the FLRW models. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Raychaudhuri focusing.** For a geodesic, vorticity-free timelike congruence in $D$ dimensions obeying the strong energy condition, $d\theta/d\tau \le -\theta^2/(D-1)$, so the expansion never increases and an initially converging congruence ($\theta_0<0$) reaches a caustic within proper time $(D-1)/|\theta_0|$. The equation is a fundamental lemma for the Penrose–Hawking singularity theorems. ([Wikipedia: Raychaudhuri equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raychaudhuri_equation))
- **Ehlers–Geren–Sachs theorem (1968).** If all freely falling observers measure the background radiation to be exactly isotropic, and the radiation is described kinetically with vanishing collision term (or [detailed balance](node:Detailed%20Balance)), the spacetime is FLRW. Stoeger, Maartens and Ellis extended this to nearly isotropic radiation implying a nearly FLRW universe, under the assumption that derivatives of temperature multipoles are bounded by the multipoles; Wainwright, Hancock and Uggla gave a counterexample in the non-tilted perfect-fluid case when that assumption fails. ([Wikipedia: EGS theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehlers%E2%80%93Geren%E2%80%93Sachs_theorem))
- **Horizon and flatness.** If $\rho$ falls faster than $R^{-2}$, light travels only a finite comoving distance since the Big Bang (a particle horizon). At last scattering ($z\simeq1100$) the horizon was of order 100 Mpc, subtending about $1^\circ$; and $\Omega=1$ is unstable, so a universe with non-zero curvature today needs finely tuned initial conditions. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))

### Examples
- **Matter plus vacuum.** A flat universe of matter and vacuum energy has $a(t) = \sinh^{2/3}(\sqrt{3\Lambda}\,t/2)$, normalized so $a=1$ when the two densities are equal. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))
- **Density-parameter form.** $H^2/H_0^2 = \Omega_{0,R}a^{-4} + \Omega_{0,M}a^{-3} + \Omega_{0,k}a^{-2} + \Omega_{0,\Lambda}$. ([Wikipedia: Friedmann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann_equations))
- **Vacuum-only universes.** For $\Lambda>0$: $a=\sqrt{3/\Lambda}\sinh(\sqrt{\Lambda/3}\,t)$ for $k=-1$, $a\propto\exp(\pm\sqrt{\Lambda/3}\,t)$ for $k=0$, and a $\cosh$ solution for $k=+1$; all three are [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space) in different coordinates. $\Lambda<0$ forces $k=-1$ and $a=\sqrt{-3/\Lambda}\sin(\sqrt{-\Lambda/3}\,t)$, which is [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space). ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Age of the universe.** Within six-parameter ΛCDM, CMB and large-scale-structure data give $t_0 = 13.80\pm0.02$ Gyr. Assuming $k=0$, $\Omega_v = 0.685\pm0.007$ and $\Omega_m = 0.315\pm0.007$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))
- **Measured curvature.** Planck 2018 temperature, polarization and lensing combined with BAO give $\Omega_K = 0.0007\pm0.0019$ (68%), flat to a $1\sigma$ accuracy of 0.2%. ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.06209)) See [Collaboration et al. 2018 - Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209) and [Baryon Acoustic Oscillations](node:Baryon%20Acoustic%20Oscillations).

### History
Friedmann published his papers in 1922 and 1924, the second treating negative curvature; Einstein initially dismissed the work and was convinced after Hubble's evidence for expansion; McCrea and Milne showed in 1934 that the pressureless equations follow from Newtonian dynamics. ([Wikipedia: Friedmann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann_equations)) The 1922 paper is "Über die Krümmung des Raumes", *Z. Phys.* 10, 377–386. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01332580))

Lemaître arrived at results independently in 1927, and Robertson and Walker studied the problem rigorously in the 1930s. ([Wikipedia: FLRW metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann%E2%80%93Lema%C3%AEtre%E2%80%93Robertson%E2%80%93Walker_metric)) The hot Big-Bang model was developed by Gamow, Alpher and Herman; in 1948 Alpher and Herman predicted relic radiation of a few kelvin, later observed as the CMB. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))

### Connections
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): the Friedmann equations are the EFE reduced by homogeneity and isotropy.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the theory whose symmetric cosmological solutions these are.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): the perfect-fluid source.
- [Continuity Equation](node:Continuity%20Equation): energy conservation $\dot\rho=-3H(\rho+p)$ on the FLRW background.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): the Ricci tensor of the RW metric enters the reduced field equations.
- [Cosmological Distance Measures](node:Cosmological%20Distance%20Measures): $D_A$, $D_L$ and comoving distance built from the metric.
- [Raychaudhuri Equation](node:Raychaudhuri%20Equation), [Energy Conditions](node:Energy%20Conditions), [Singularity Theorems in Relativity](node:Singularity%20Theorems%20in%20Relativity): why the Big Bang singularity is generic.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): the standard model on an FLRW background.
- [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): the $\Lambda/3$ term and $w=-1$ component.
- [Cosmic Inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation): the standard proposed solution of the horizon and flatness problems.
- [Cosmological Perturbation Theory](node:Cosmological%20Perturbation%20Theory): fluctuations added on the FLRW background.
- [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background): relic radiation of the hot FLRW model; input to the EGS theorem.
- [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space), [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space): vacuum-only FLRW solutions.
- [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology), [Dark Radiation](node:Dark%20Radiation): brane models modify the Friedmann equation with $\rho^2$ and dark-radiation terms.
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): McCrea and Milne's derivation of the dust equations.
- [Quantum Gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity): expected to replace classical GR near $a\to0$.
- [Mathematical Cosmological Models](node:Mathematical%20Cosmological%20Models): the broader mathematical study of cosmological spacetimes.

### Common pitfalls
- **Curvature is not an energy density.** PDG calls the notation $\Omega_K = -k/(R_0^2H_0^2)$ "unfortunate", because it encourages thinking of curvature as a contribution to the energy density, which is not correct. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf))
- **Redshift as a velocity.** Reading $z$ as a Doppler velocity is wrong in general: the redshift comes from the expansion of space. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Conventions for $k$ and $a$.** Either $k$ has units of length$^{-2}$ with dimensionless $a$, or $k\in\{-1,0,+1\}$ with $a$ carrying length. ([Wikipedia: FLRW metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann%E2%80%93Lema%C3%AEtre%E2%80%93Robertson%E2%80%93Walker_metric))
- **Flat does not mean infinite.** Zero measured curvature does not imply the universe is infinite; it may just be much larger than the observable part. ([Wikipedia: Friedmann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann_equations))
- **Lumpiness.** A strict FLRW model contains no galaxies or stars; it is a first approximation with fluctuations added as extensions. ([Wikipedia: Friedmann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann_equations))
- **The Big Bang as an explosion.** The singularity at $a=0$ represents the creation of the universe from a singular state, not an explosion of matter into a pre-existing spacetime. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Isotropy alone is not enough.** The almost-EGS result needs extra assumptions on derivatives of the CMB multipoles; without them a nearly isotropic CMB does not guarantee a nearly isotropic universe. ([Wikipedia: EGS theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehlers%E2%80%93Geren%E2%80%93Sachs_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Hubble tension.** Distance-ladder measurements give $H_0\approx73\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, while CMB-based values are near 67.7 (Planck 2018: $67.4\pm0.5$); the disagreement exceeds $5\sigma$ and its cause is unknown. Proposals include unknown systematics, a violation of the cosmological principle, and new physics such as early dark energy or time-varying dark energy. ([Wikipedia: Hubble tension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_tension))
- **Evolving dark energy.** DESI DR2 BAO data combined with the CMB prefer a time-varying $w_0w_a$ dark-energy equation of state over ΛCDM at $3.1\sigma$, and at $2.8$–$4.2\sigma$ when [supernovae](node:Supernovae) are added, depending on the sample. ([DESI DR2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738))
- **Backreaction and averaging.** Whether the formation of nonlinear structure changes the average expansion rate and spatial curvature of an inhomogeneous universe, and whether this could account for observations without dark energy, is reviewed by Buchert and Räsänen, who highlight open questions. ([Buchert & Räsänen](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.5335))
- **Initial conditions and the singularity.** The horizon and flatness problems mean standard FLRW models need finely tuned initial conditions; inflation is described as the best modern solution. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf)) Classical GR is not expected to be accurate as $a\to0$; a consistent theory of quantum gravity is hoped to resolve this. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))

> [!warning] Contested
> Radio-galaxy and quasar tests of whether the CMB dipole is purely kinematic disagree in magnitude, which taken at face value is at odds with an FLRW description; it has also been argued that FLRW tolerates at most $H_0 = 71\pm1\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$. On the other side, observations combined with the EGS theorem and its generalization lead astrophysicists to agree that the early universe is almost homogeneous and isotropic. ([Wikipedia: FLRW metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann%E2%80%93Lema%C3%AEtre%E2%80%93Robertson%E2%80%93Walker_metric))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann%E2%80%93Lema%C3%AEtre%E2%80%93Robertson%E2%80%93Walker_metric): coordinate forms, naming, history, challenges.
- **Reference:** [Friedmann equations (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann_equations): equations, density parameters, exact solutions.
- **Learn:** [Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019): chapter 8 derives the RW metric, Friedmann equations, exact solutions and the Big Bang singularity.
- **Learn:** [Piattella, Lecture Notes in Cosmology](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.00070): graduate course from the expanding universe to CMB anisotropies.
- **Primary:** [Particle Data Group, "Big-Bang Cosmology" (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-cosmology.pdf): standard review of equations, distances, parameters and observational status.
- **Primary:** [Planck 2018 results VI: Cosmological parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209): base-ΛCDM parameters and curvature constraints.
- **Further reading:** [Buchert & Räsänen, "Backreaction in late-time cosmology"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.5335): review of averaging and the validity of the FLRW description.
references.Feature Stability and Absorption:
## Reference
### Overview
A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is trained to disentangle neural-network activations into sparse representations whose learned dimensions often correspond to human-understandable concepts. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability)) Feature stability asks whether those dimensions are properties of the model or artefacts of one training run: SAEs that differ only in random seed can learn different features, and an SAE latent that looks monosemantic can still fail to fire on cases it should cover. ([Paulo and Belrose 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615); [Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507))
