Three related phenomena are named. **Feature splitting**: a broad latent in a small SAE becomes several finer latents in a larger SAE (for example "starts with L" splitting into uppercase and lowercase variants). **Feature absorption**: a specific latent absorbs the direction of a more general concept, so the general latent has gaps in its recall. **Non-canonicity**: smaller SAEs are incomplete, since larger SAEs contain novel latents that improve them, and larger-SAE latents are not atomic, since they decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507); [Leask et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04878))

These issues bear on whether SAE latents can serve as reliable classifiers (for example for bias or deception detection) and as units for circuits, and stable features are argued to be needed for causal, safety and circuit-level claims. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507); [Song et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20254v1)) Sharkey et al. list among the open problems of sparse dictionary learning that sparsity is an imperfect proxy for interpretability, citing splitting, absorption and composition, and that learned latents depend on the training data. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))

### Formal definition
**Sparse coding model.** Data $y_i = A a_i$ with $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times m}$ (often $m > n$) and $k$-sparse codes $a_i \in \mathbb R^m$. $A$ satisfies the **spark condition** if $A a_1 = A a_2$ for $k$-sparse $a_1, a_2$ implies $a_1 = a_2$. ([Hillar and Sommer 2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.3616)) Dictionaries are only ever determined up to the symmetry $A \mapsto APD$ with $P$ a permutation and $D$ an invertible diagonal matrix. ([Hillar and Sommer 2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.3616); [Spielman et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.5882))

**Consistency across runs (PW-MCC).** For two SAE runs with decoder columns $\{d_j\}$ and $\{d'_j\}$, compute a one-to-one matching $\pi$ by the Hungarian algorithm maximizing $\sum_j |\cos(d_j, d'_{\pi(j)})|$, and define
$$\mathrm{PW\text{-}MCC} = \frac1m\sum_j \lvert\cos(d_j, d'_{\pi(j)})\rvert .$$
Values near 1 mean the runs learned the same dictionary up to permutation and scaling; GT-MCC is the same quantity against a known ground-truth dictionary. ([Song et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20254v1))

**Absorption rate.** On a task with a ground-truth linear probe (first-letter identification), an absorption is counted when the main feature latents stay silent on a true positive while a single other latent has a probe-aligned direction and a much larger ablation effect than all others. The absorption rate is the number of absorptions divided by the probe's true positives. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507))

### Key results
- **Uniqueness of sparse coding (Hillar–Sommer, Theorem 2 and Corollary 2).** Fix $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times m}$ satisfying the spark condition. If $k+1$ random $k$-sparse vectors are drawn for each of the $\binom mk$ supports, giving $N = (k+1)\binom mk$ samples, then with probability one every $B$ and $k$-sparse $b_i$ with $Aa_i = Bb_i$ satisfy $A = BPD$ and $b_i = PDa_i$. A random $A$ satisfies the spark condition with probability one when $n \ge Ck\log(m/k)$. ([Hillar and Sommer 2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.3616))
- **Uniqueness for square dictionaries from few samples (Spielman–Wang–Wright, Theorem 3).** For nonsingular $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and Bernoulli($\theta$)-subgaussian $X$ with $1/n \le \theta \le 1/C$ and $p > Cn\log n$ samples, with high probability any factorization of $Y = AX$ whose maximum row sparsity is at most that of $X$ equals $(A,X)$ up to permutation and diagonal scaling. ([Spielman et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.5882))
- **TopK SAEs and identifiability (Song et al.).** Song et al. argue that exact $k$-sparsity, zero reconstruction error on data covering a required witness set, and a round-trip property (encoding a decoded $k$-sparse vector returns it) put TopK SAEs under a Hillar–Sommer-type uniqueness theorem, so that two such SAEs trained on the same data learn the same dictionary up to permutation and scaling, even when overcomplete. In a matched-capacity synthetic setting TopK SAEs reach GT-MCC about 0.97 versus 0.63 for standard ReLU SAEs; on Pythia-160M layer 8 TopK reaches PW-MCC about 0.80, and rare features are far less consistent (mean matched cosine about 0.51 versus 0.96 for the most frequent). ([Song et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20254v1))
- **Seed dependence in practice.** For a 131K-latent SAE on a Llama 3 8B feedforward layer only 30% of features were shared across seeds, and seed dependence appeared across multiple layers of three LLMs; ReLU SAEs trained with $\ell_1$ were more stable across seeds than TopK SAEs, even when controlling for sparsity. ([Paulo and Belrose 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615))
- **Absorption is incentivized by hierarchy.** In toy models, independently firing features are recovered cleanly, but when a child feature fires only together with a parent, the SAE folds the parent direction into the child latent; analytically, absorption lowers the sparsity loss while keeping reconstruction perfect. Empirically on Gemma Scope SAEs for Gemma-2-2B, absorption rises with sparsity and width; it also occurs in SAEs trained on Qwen2 0.5B and Llama 3.2 1B and in TopK SAEs, which have no $\ell_1$ penalty, and is not removed by changing SAE size or sparsity alone. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507))
- **SAEs are incomplete and non-atomic.** SAE stitching shows that larger SAEs contain novel latents that improve smaller ones, and meta-SAEs trained on decoder matrices decompose larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents (an "Einstein" latent into "scientist", "Germany" and "famous person"). ([Leask et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04878))

### Examples
- **First-letter spelling.** On Gemma Scope residual-stream SAEs, no SAE matched a linear probe for first-letter identification; low-L0 SAEs gave high-precision, low-recall latents and high-L0 SAEs the reverse. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507))
- **Matryoshka SAEs.** Training nested dictionaries so that each prefix must reconstruct the input on its own removes the incentive to absorb high-level features into specific ones, improving sparse probing and concept erasure on Gemma-2-2B at a small reconstruction cost. ([Bussmann et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17547))
- **Capacity mismatch.** A dictionary much larger than the ground truth can score high GT-MCC but lower PW-MCC (about 0.77 in one synthetic setting) because which extra atoms are learned is ambiguous. ([Song et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20254v1))

### History
Uniqueness of sparse dictionaries was studied in signal processing well before interpretability: Hillar and Sommer's result was first posted in 2011 and published in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, and Spielman, Wang and Wright gave exact recovery for square dictionaries in 2012. ([Hillar and Sommer 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.3616); [Spielman et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.5882)) In SAE interpretability, absorption was named and measured in 2024, and seed dependence, non-canonicity, Matryoshka SAEs and the consistency position paper followed in 2025. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507); [Paulo and Belrose 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615); [Leask et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04878); [Bussmann et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17547); [Song et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20254v1))

### Connections
- [Sparse Autoencoders](node:Sparse%20Autoencoders): the method whose learned features this note evaluates.
- [Feature Superposition](node:Feature%20Superposition): the reason features must be recovered by overcomplete sparse dictionaries at all.
- [Dictionary Learning](node:Dictionary%20Learning): supplies the uniqueness theory (spark condition, permutation and scaling symmetry).
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): absorption and instability limit SAE latents as units of analysis.
- [Circuit Tracing](node:Circuit%20Tracing): circuits built from absorbed or seed-specific latents inherit their gaps.
- [Activation Steering](node:Activation%20Steering): steering with an SAE latent assumes the latent's effect is stable across runs.
- [Disentangled Representation Learning](node:Disentangled%20Representation%20Learning): the same question of whether recovered factors are identifiable.
- [Identifiability in Scientific Machine Learning](node:Identifiability%20in%20Scientific%20Machine%20Learning): identifiability up to symmetries as a general modelling requirement.

### Common pitfalls
- **Using a latent as a classifier without measuring recall.** Absorption leaves silent gaps, which matters for uses such as bias or deception detection. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507))
- **Reporting one run.** Features shared across seeds can be a minority, so consistency should be reported with reconstruction and sparsity. ([Paulo and Belrose 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615); [Song et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20254v1))
- **Expecting a canonical width.** No SAE size yields a complete, atomic set of units; choose size for the task. ([Leask et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04878))
- **Undercounting absorption.** The Chanin et al. metric is conservative, may undercount absorption, and could only be applied up to layer 17 of Gemma-2-2B. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507))

### Open problems
- **Consistency for rare features and across layers.** Song et al. list as future work consistent SAEs across layers and activation statistics, consistency for rare features, functional or subspace notions of equivalence, the effect of the encoder's amortization gap on dictionary stability, and stronger guarantees under realistic data assumptions. ([Song et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20254v1))
- **Fixing absorption.** Chanin et al. find that changing SAE size or sparsity alone does not remove absorption and point to Meta-SAEs, attribution dictionary learning and structured sparsity (group lasso, hierarchical sparse coding) as possible remedies. ([Chanin et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.14507))
- **Sharper and noisy uniqueness theory.** Hillar and Sommer state that it is an open problem how much their sample bounds can be strengthened, raise the question of conditions under which dictionary-learning algorithms are guaranteed to converge, and name noisy versions of uniqueness as a focus of future work. ([Hillar and Sommer 2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.3616))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Mechanistic interpretability (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability): SAEs, features, circuits, linear representation hypothesis.
- **Reference:** [Sparse dictionary learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_dictionary_learning): the underlying optimization problem.
- **Learn:** [Northeastern CS 7180, Actionable Interpretability (Spring 2026)](https://www.ccs.neu.edu/home/byron/cs7180/): course session and readings on sparse autoencoders.
- **Primary:** [Chanin et al. 2024, A is for Absorption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14507): defines and measures splitting and absorption.
- **Primary:** [Song et al. 2025, Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20254): PW-MCC and identifiability of TopK SAEs.
- **Primary:** [Hillar and Sommer, When can dictionary learning uniquely recover sparse data from subsamples?](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.3616): uniqueness theorems.
- **Further reading:** [Shu et al. 2025, A Survey on Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05613): architectures, training, explanation and evaluation of SAEs for LLMs.
references.Feature Superposition:
## Reference
### Overview
Feature superposition is the hypothesis that a neural network represents more sparse features than it has dimensions (or neurons) by assigning them overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions in activation space. Elhage et al. built toy models in which this can be analyzed fully and argued that superposition explains polysemanticity, the tendency of single neurons to respond to several unrelated concepts. They report a phase change, a connection between the learned arrangements and the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence linking superposition to adversarial examples. ([Elhage et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652))

Cunningham et al. present sparse autoencoders as a scalable, unsupervised method for resolving superposition: trained to reconstruct language-model activations, they recover features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than those of alternative methods. ([Cunningham et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600)) Such sparse dictionary learning assumes the linear representation hypothesis ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496)), that high-level concepts are directions in activation space, which has supporting evidence in word embeddings and LLMs but does not hold universally. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability))

An earlier instance appears in [word embeddings](node:Word%20Embeddings): Arora et al. argue that a polysemous word's embedding is a linear superposition of sense vectors, and that sparse coding over about 2,000 "discourse atoms" recovers the senses. ([Arora et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03764)) The geometry of packing many directions into few dimensions is governed by results such as the [Johnson–Lindenstrauss Lemma](node:Johnson–Lindenstrauss%20Lemma), proved via [random projections](node:Random%20Projections), and the Welch bound on the coherence of unit vectors ([Bandeira, Ten Lectures](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~abandeira/TenLecturesFortyTwoProblems.pdf)); Liu, Liu and Gore use the Welch bound to bound overlaps between feature representations. ([Liu, Liu and Gore 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.10465))

### Formal definition
Let $f_1,\dots,f_m$ be boolean features of the input and $\vec\phi_k\in\mathbb R^d$ feature vectors with $m>d$. The activations represent the features in superposition when
$$\vec a(x)=\sum_{k=1}^m \vec\phi_k\, f_k(x),$$
and the inputs are $s$-sparse when at most $s$ features are active. Feature $f_k$ is $\varepsilon$-linearly represented if there is a read-off vector $\vec r_k$ with $|\vec r_k\cdot\vec a(x)-f_k(x)|<\varepsilon$ for all inputs $x$; this is stronger than linear separability. ([Hänni et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.05451))

The standard toy model compresses a sparse input $x\in\mathbb R^n$ (feature $i$ active with frequency $p_i$) to $h=W^\top x\in\mathbb R^m$ with $m\ll n$ and reconstructs $y=\mathrm{ReLU}(Wh+b)$, minimizing the expected squared error $\mathbb E\|y-x\|^2$. "Weak" superposition represents only the most frequent features with non-overlapping directions; "strong" superposition represents many more features with overlapping vectors, so the loss is dominated by interference. ([Liu, Liu and Gore 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.10465))

### Key results
- **Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma.** For $0<\varepsilon<1$ and any $n$ points in $\mathbb R^d$, if $k\ge 4(\varepsilon^2/2-\varepsilon^3/3)^{-1}\log n$ there is a linear map $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ with $(1-\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|^2\le\|f(x_i)-f(x_j)\|^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|^2$, found by random projection in randomized polynomial time. ([Bandeira, Thm. 5.1](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~abandeira/TenLecturesFortyTwoProblems.pdf)) The dependence $\Omega(\log N/\varepsilon^2)$ is optimal up to a constant (Larsen–Nelson). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson%E2%80%93Lindenstrauss_lemma))
- **Welch bound and equiangular tight frames.** The coherence $\mu=\max_{k\ne l}|\langle v_k,v_l\rangle|$ of $N$ unit vectors in $M$ dimensions satisfies $\mu\ge\sqrt{\frac{N-M}{M(N-1)}}$, with equality for equiangular tight frames; in $\mathbb C^M$ an ETF requires $N\le M^2$. ([Bandeira, §6.5.2](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~abandeira/TenLecturesFortyTwoProblems.pdf)) For $N\gg M$ the bound is about $\sqrt{1/M}$, so the maximum overlap among many feature vectors in $m$ dimensions is at least about $\sqrt{1/m}$. ([Liu, Liu and Gore 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.10465))
- **Computation in superposition (U-AND).** A single ReLU layer of width $\tilde O_m(1/\varepsilon^2)$, polylogarithmic in $m$, $\varepsilon$-linearly represents all $\binom m2$ pairwise ANDs of $m$ basis-aligned boolean inputs on $s$-sparse inputs, and sufficiently wide randomly initialized one-layer MLPs also do so. Combining such layers with error-correction layers, the authors claim that width-$d$ networks can emulate sparse [boolean circuits](node:Boolean%20Circuits) of width $\tilde O(d^{1.5})$ at any polynomial depth. ([Hänni et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.05451))
- **Superposition and loss scaling.** In the toy model, weak superposition with power-law feature frequencies of exponent $\alpha>1$ gives loss scaling as $m^{-(\alpha-1)}$, while strong superposition with roughly even frequencies gives loss scaling as $1/m$; the authors measure mean squared overlaps between normalized rows of LLM output heads scaling roughly as $1/m$ and a fitted model-size exponent of about $0.91\pm0.04$. They note the toy model was not solved rigorously. ([Liu, Liu and Gore 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.10465))
- **Polysemy as superposition in embeddings.** Under a random-walk-on-discourses generative model, word-sense vectors combine linearly in the word embedding and are recoverable by sparse coding, across several embedding methods. ([Arora et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03764))

### Examples
- **Toy models of superposition.** When features are sparse, small ReLU toy models store additional features in superposition, the learned arrangements relate to the geometry of uniform [polytopes](node:Polytopes), and the behavior changes through a phase change. ([Elhage et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652))
- **Sparse autoencoders on a language model.** SAE features localize the components responsible for the indirect-object-identification behavior more precisely than earlier decompositions. ([Cunningham et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600))
- **Word senses.** The embedding of a polysemous word decomposes into sense vectors, each tagged with a discourse atom. ([Arora et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03764))

### History
Mikolov et al. (NAACL 2013) showed that simple word embeddings encode semantic relationships along linear directions; Chris Olah coined the term mechanistic interpretability, and key circuits articles appeared in Distill in 2018 and 2020. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability)) Arora et al.'s linear superposition of word senses was posted in 2016 and published in TACL in 2018. ([Arora et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03764)) Elhage et al.'s "Toy Models of Superposition" appeared in September 2022, and sparse autoencoders were proposed as a remedy in 2023. ([Elhage et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652); [Cunningham et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600)) The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma dates to 1984. ([Bandeira](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~abandeira/TenLecturesFortyTwoProblems.pdf))

### Connections
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): superposition is the main reason neuron-level analysis fails.
- [Sparse Autoencoders](node:Sparse%20Autoencoders): the dominant method for undoing superposition.
- [Dictionary Learning](node:Dictionary%20Learning): the general sparse-coding problem SAEs instantiate.
- [Feature Stability and Absorption](node:Feature%20Stability%20and%20Absorption): failure modes of recovered SAE features.
- [Johnson–Lindenstrauss Lemma](node:Johnson–Lindenstrauss%20Lemma): why many nearly orthogonal directions fit in few dimensions.
- [Frames and Wavelet Bases](node:Frames%20and%20Wavelet%20Bases): tight frames and coherence bound feature overlap.
- [Concentration of Measure](node:Concentration%20of%20Measure): the probabilistic engine behind random near-orthogonality.
- [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): superposition as a proposed mechanism for model-size scaling.
- [Activation Steering](node:Activation%20Steering): intervening along feature directions assumes linear representation.
- [Artificial Neural Networks](node:Artificial%20Neural%20Networks): the models whose activations are decomposed.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): the embedding $W$ and read-off vectors are linear maps.
- [Elhage et al. 2022 - Toy Models of Superposition](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/): the founding toy-model paper.
- [Bricken et al. 2023 - Towards Monosemanticity - Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features/): dictionary learning applied to a transformer.

### Common pitfalls
- **Equating polysemanticity with superposition.** Polysemanticity is an observation about neurons; Cunningham et al. treat superposition as one hypothesized cause. ([Cunningham et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600))
- **Assuming strict linearity.** The strong linear representation hypothesis has been shown false for some models, and SDL methods assume it inside nonlinear networks. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))
- **Over-trusting toy models.** Small model organisms risk results that fail to generalize to real settings, and the U-AND theory covers only binary, sparse features. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496); [Hänni et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.05451))
- **Treating sparsity as interpretability.** Under enough optimization pressure sparsity breaks down as a proxy, producing feature splitting and absorption. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))

### Open problems
- **Foundations of the superposition hypothesis.** Sharkey et al. state that how to decompose networks into atomic units "remains a central problem" and that without conceptual foundations it is unclear whether the superposition hypothesis is valid or merely useful. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))
- **Reconstruction error and feature geometry.** SDL reconstruction errors are too high and structured, and SDL leaves feature geometry unexplained. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))
- **Computation natively in superposition.** Comparatively little work examines how networks compute on superposed features; Hänni et al. list non-binary features, the sparsity assumption, and the right notion of "computed" as open. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496); [Hänni et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.05451))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Mechanistic interpretability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability): linear representation hypothesis, sparse autoencoders, history.
- **Reference:** [Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson%E2%80%93Lindenstrauss_lemma): statement and optimality.
- **Learn:** [Bandeira, Ten Lectures and Forty-Two Open Problems in the Mathematics of Data Science](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~abandeira/TenLecturesFortyTwoProblems.pdf): MIT 18.S096 notes on JL, coherence, Welch bound and ETFs.
- **Primary:** [Elhage et al. 2022, Toy Models of Superposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652): the toy model, phase change and polytope geometry.
- **Primary:** [Hänni et al. 2024, Mathematical Models of Computation in Superposition](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.05451): theorems on computing in superposition.
- **Primary:** [Sharkey et al. 2025, Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496): survey of open questions about features and SDL.
- **Further reading:** [MIT OCW 18.S096, Topics in Mathematics of Data Science (Bandeira)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-s096-topics-in-mathematics-of-data-science-fall-2015/pages/lecture-notes/): course notes consolidated into the monograph *Ten Lectures and Forty-Two Open Problems in the Mathematics of Data Science*; JL lemma, Gordon's theorem, compressed sensing.
- **Further reading:** [Cunningham et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600): sparse autoencoders as the practical response to superposition.
references.Feynman Diagrams:
## Reference
### Overview
Feynman diagrams are a graphical bookkeeping device for perturbation theory in [quantum field theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory). Expanding $e^{iS_I}$ in the interaction action and evaluating the free-field vacuum expectation values with Wick's theorem produces sums of products of propagators; each distinct pattern of Wick contractions is drawn as a graph whose edges are propagators and whose vertices are interaction insertions. ([MIT 8.323 Recitation 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/mit8_323_s23_rec06.pdf); [Wikipedia, Quantum electrodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_electrodynamics))

The diagrams compute correlation functions, which the LSZ formula converts into S-matrix elements, so they are the standard route from a Lagrangian to scattering amplitudes in [QED](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics) and other interacting field theories. The diagrams represent terms in an expansion, not the physical positions of particles, and the perturbation series of an interacting quantum field theory has zero radius of convergence. ([Wikipedia, Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram); [Wikipedia, LSZ reduction formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LSZ_reduction_formula))

### Formal definition
Interacting correlators are given by the Gell-Mann–Low formula
$$\langle\Omega|T\phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_n)|\Omega\rangle=\frac{\langle0|T\phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_n)\,e^{iS_I}|0\rangle}{\langle0|T\,e^{iS_I}|0\rangle},$$
with free fields on the right. For $S_I=\int d^dz\,\lambda\phi^k/k!$ the position-space rules are: an external point contributes $1$; an internal vertex has $k$ legs, contributes $i\lambda$ and its position is integrated; an edge from $x$ to $y$ contributes the Feynman propagator $G_F(x-y)$; diagrams containing vacuum bubbles (components with no external point) are dropped, since they cancel against the denominator. ([MIT 8.323 Recitation 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/mit8_323_s23_rec06.pdf))

In momentum space in four dimensions (in the MIT notes' conventions) each edge carrying momentum $p$ contributes $G_F(p)=-i/(p^2+m^2-i\epsilon)$ and each vertex contributes $i\lambda$ times a momentum-conserving delta function, which arises from integrating the vertex position over the Fourier phases; with the standard normalization this is $(2\pi)^4\delta^{(4)}(\sum p_{\rm in}-\sum p_{\rm out})$ per vertex and $\int d^4k/(2\pi)^4$ per undetermined momentum. The delta functions fix every internal momentum except those running around loops, which are integrated over, leaving one overall factor $(2\pi)^4\delta^{(4)}(\sum p_{\rm in}-\sum p_{\rm out})$. ([MIT 8.323 Recitation 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/mit8_323_s23_rec06.pdf); [Wikipedia, Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram))

**Symmetry factors.** The $1/k!$ of each vertex and the $1/r!$ of the $r$-th order term cancel against the permutations of legs and vertices unless distinct permutations give the same contraction; the diagram is then divided by its symmetry factor, e.g. $2$ for each propagator beginning and ending at the same vertex, $j!$ for $j$ propagators joining the same two vertices, and $j!$ for $j$ interchangeable vertices. Equivalently, each diagram is divided by the order of its automorphism group. ([MIT 8.323 Recitation 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/mit8_323_s23_rec06.pdf); [Wikipedia, Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram))

### Key results
- **Loop counting.** The number of independent loop momenta equals the number of independent cycles of the graph, its first Betti number. For a connected graph with $V$ vertices and $I$ internal edges this is $L=I-V+1$ (circuit rank $e-v+c$ with $c=1$); diagrams with $L=0$ are trees and those with $L\ge1$ are loop corrections. ([Wikipedia, Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram); [Wikipedia, Circuit rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_rank))
- **Vacuum bubbles and connected diagrams.** In the normalized Gell-Mann–Low ratio all vacuum bubbles cancel. The generating functional of connected correlators is $W[J]=-i\ln Z[J]$, the sum of connected diagrams (linked-cluster theorem). ([Wikipedia, Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram); [Wikipedia, Effective action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_action))
- **1PI diagrams and the effective action.** The quantum effective action $\Gamma[\phi]=W[J_\phi]-\int d^4x\,J_\phi\phi$, the Legendre transform of $W$, generates the one-particle-irreducible (1PI) correlators and equals the sum of all 1PI diagrams; its one-loop approximation is $\Gamma[\phi]\approx S[\phi]+\tfrac i2\operatorname{Tr}\ln(\delta^2S/\delta\phi\delta\phi)$, and $V(\phi)=-\Gamma[\phi]/\mathcal V_4$ for constant $\phi$ is the effective potential. ([Wikipedia, Effective action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_action))
- **LSZ reduction (Lehmann, Symanzik, Zimmermann 1955).** Leaving aside normalization factors, S-matrix elements are the residues of the poles of the Fourier-transformed time-ordered correlators as the external momenta go on shell: one multiplies by an inverse propagator for each external leg (amputation) and divides by $\sqrt Z$ per leg, where $Z$ is the field-strength renormalization of the asymptotic field $\sqrt Z\,\varphi_{\rm in}$. The derivation uses asymptotic in/out fields and does not cover bound states, massless particles or topological solitons. See [LSZ Reduction Formula](node:LSZ%20Reduction%20Formula). ([Wikipedia, LSZ reduction formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LSZ_reduction_formula))
- **Asymptotic divergence (Dyson's argument).** If the QED series in $\alpha$ had a nonzero radius of convergence, observables would be analytic at small negative $\alpha$, where the vacuum is unstable; hence the series has zero radius of convergence and is at best asymptotic. One source of factorial growth of coefficients is the multiplicity of Feynman diagrams at high order. ([Serone, *Lectures on Resurgence*](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.02224v1); [Wikipedia, Quantum electrodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_electrodynamics))
- **Renormalons.** A second source of divergence arises in theories with classically but not exactly marginal couplings: chains of one-loop bubbles inserted into a diagram give factorially growing coefficients and singularities of the Borel transform on the real axis (ultraviolet and infrared renormalons); infrared renormalons are tied to non-perturbative power corrections in asymptotically free theories such as QCD. ([Serone, *Lectures on Resurgence*](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.02224v1); [Beneke, *Renormalons*](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9807443))

### Examples
In $\lambda\phi^3/3!$ theory at order $\lambda^2$ the two-point function receives three diagram classes free of vacuum bubbles: the one-loop self-energy bubble (symmetry factor $2$), a tadpole attached through an internal line (factor $2$), and a diagram with a tadpole on each external line (factor $4$). In momentum space the bubble is $\tfrac12(i\lambda)^2 G_F(p)^2\int\frac{d^4k}{(2\pi)^4}G_F(k)G_F(p-k)$ times the overall delta function: one loop, as $I-V+1=2-2+1$ predicts for its internal lines. ([MIT 8.323 Recitation 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/mit8_323_s23_rec06.pdf); [Wikipedia, Circuit rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_rank))

QED has three divergent one-loop diagram types (vacuum polarization, electron self-energy and vertex correction), and because only finitely many constants must be fixed by experiment the theory is renormalizable; its diagrammatic predictions for the electron's magnetic moment agree closely with experiment. ([Wikipedia, Quantum electrodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_electrodynamics))

### History
Feynman introduced the diagrams in 1948 and published *Space-Time Approach to Quantum Electrodynamics* in Physical Review 76, 769 (15 September 1949). ([Wikipedia, Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram); [Crossref, Feynman 1949](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.76.769)) Dyson's *The Radiation Theories of Tomonaga, Schwinger, and Feynman*, Physical Review 75, 486 (1 February 1949), gave, in its own words, "a demonstration of the equivalence of the Feynman and Schwinger theories" ([APS abstract](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.75.486)); because Dyson's derivation from old-fashioned perturbation theory was easier to follow for physicists of the time, the graphs were historically also called Feynman–Dyson diagrams or Dyson graphs. Tomonaga, Schwinger and Feynman shared the 1965 Nobel Prize. ([Crossref, Dyson 1949](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.75.486); [Wikipedia, Quantum electrodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_electrodynamics); [Wikipedia, Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram))

### Connections
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): supplies the fields, propagators and interactions the rules encode.
- [Perturbation Theory in Quantum Mechanics](node:Perturbation%20Theory%20in%20Quantum%20Mechanics): the Dyson series is its field-theoretic version.
- [Path Integral Formulation](node:Path%20Integral%20Formulation): the generating functionals $Z[J]$, $W[J]$ and $\Gamma[\phi]$ are defined by path integrals.
- [Renormalization](node:Renormalization) and [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group): treat the divergent loop integrals.
- [LSZ Reduction Formula](node:LSZ%20Reduction%20Formula): turns amputated diagrams into S-matrix elements.
- [Quantum Electrodynamics](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics) and [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics): the main applications.
- [Scattering Amplitudes in Quantum Field Theory](node:Scattering%20Amplitudes%20in%20Quantum%20Field%20Theory): on-shell methods that bypass individual diagrams.
- [Green Functions in Physics](node:Green%20Functions%20in%20Physics): propagators are Green functions of the free field equation.
- [Asymptotic Analysis](node:Asymptotic%20Analysis): the perturbation series is asymptotic, not convergent.

### Common pitfalls
- Only bubble-free diagrams contribute to normalized correlators; including vacuum bubbles in the numerator without the denominator gives wrong answers. ([MIT 8.323 Recitation 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/mit8_323_s23_rec06.pdf))
- Signs and factors of $i$ depend on the metric signature and on the sign of $S_I$; the MIT conventions above use the propagator $-i/(p^2+m^2-i\epsilon)$ and vertex factor $i\lambda$ for $S_I=\int\lambda\phi^k/k!$. ([MIT 8.323 Recitation 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/mit8_323_s23_rec06.pdf))
- Perturbation theory has zero radius of convergence, and tunnelling and bound states do not appear at any finite order; non-perturbative effects show up only in how the number of diagrams and resummations diverges at high order. ([Wikipedia, Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram))

### Open problems
- **Resurgence in QFT.** Whether resurgence works in quantum field theory, "in particular in theories featuring renormalon singularities", is described by Serone as "a hard question in general"; he also notes that "we do not know the semi-classical configuration associated to renormalons" (it may not exist) and that resurgence "is not a fully rigorous mathematical subject yet". ([Serone, *Lectures on Resurgence*](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.02224v1)) The Aniceto–Başar–Schiappa primer develops the transseries framework intended to reconstruct non-perturbative data from divergent perturbative series. ([Aniceto, Başar, Schiappa, *A primer on resurgent transseries*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.10441))
- **On-shell amplitude methods.** Elvang and Huang review spinor-helicity variables, on-shell recursion, loop integrands, [Grassmannians](node:Grassmannians) and [polytopes](node:Polytopes) as ways to compute amplitudes without summing individual Feynman diagrams. They describe carrying out the loop integrations for planar $\mathcal N=4$ SYM amplitudes as "an area of active research", call whether the non-planar loop amplitudes are determined by their Leading Singularities "another current area of investigation", and state that UV finiteness of $\mathcal N=8$ [supergravity](node:Supergravity) "is not known" at eight loops or higher (as of the review). ([Elvang, Huang, *Scattering Amplitudes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.1697))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Feynman diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feynman_diagram): rules, symmetry factors, connected diagrams and the asymptotic nature of the series.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.323 Recitation 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/mit8_323_s23_rec06.pdf): Wick contractions versus position- and momentum-space rules, with symmetry factors worked out.
- **Primary:** [Elvang, Huang, *Scattering Amplitudes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.1697): review from Feynman rules to on-shell methods; [Beneke, *Renormalons*](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9807443): Physics Reports review of large-order behaviour.
- **Further reading:** [Feynman, *Space-Time Approach to Quantum Electrodynamics*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.76.769) and [Dyson, *The Radiation Theories of Tomonaga, Schwinger, and Feynman*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.75.486): the founding papers.
references.Fiber Bundles:
## Reference
### Overview
A fiber bundle is a space $E$ that maps onto a base $B$ so that over small open sets $U\subseteq B$ it looks like a product $U\times F$, while possibly being twisted globally. The Möbius strip is the standard example: a bundle of line segments over a circle whose twist is visible only globally. [Tangent](node:Tangent%20Bundle) and cotangent bundles, covering spaces (bundles with discrete fiber), mapping tori and the Hopf fibration $S^3\to S^2$ are all fiber bundles ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)).

Bundles organize much of topology and geometry. Global sections may fail to exist, and the obstruction is often a cohomology class: the hairy ball theorem follows because the Euler class of $TS^2$ obstructs a nowhere-vanishing section ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)). Principal bundles with structure group $G$ are pulled back from a universal bundle $EG\to BG$ ([Wikipedia: Principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)). Every fiber bundle has the homotopy lifting property for CW complexes, so it has a long exact sequence of homotopy groups and a Serre spectral sequence ([Wikipedia: Fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration)).

Principal bundles underpin physical gauge theories, with principal $U(1)$- and $SU(2)$-bundles as key cases ([Wikipedia: Principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)). Vector bundles over a fixed base are classified by homotopy classes of maps into a Grassmannian, which is the entry point to characteristic classes and K-theory ([Hatcher, VBKT](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).

### Formal definition
**Fiber bundle.** A fiber bundle is a tuple $(E,B,\pi,F)$ with $\pi:E\to B$ a continuous surjection such that every $x\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ and a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $\varphi:\pi^{-1}(U)\to U\times F$ with $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ\varphi=\pi$. A family $\{(U_i,\varphi_i)\}$ covering $B$ is a local trivialization ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)). Over a site, a locally trivial fibre bundle with fibre $F$ is a map $p:E\to B$ with a cover $(j_\alpha:U_\alpha\to B)$ such that each pullback $E_\alpha$ is isomorphic in the slice over $U_\alpha$ to $U_\alpha\times F$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fiber+bundle)).

**Structure group and cocycles.** A $G$-atlas has transition functions $t_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to G$, with $G$ acting on $F$, satisfying
$$t_{ii}=1,\qquad t_{ij}=t_{ji}^{-1},\qquad t_{ik}=t_{ij}\,t_{jk}\ \text{ on }U_i\cap U_j\cap U_k,$$
and these determine the bundle ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)).

**Principal and associated bundles.** A principal $G$-bundle is a fiber bundle $P\to X$ with a continuous right $G$-action preserving fibers and acting freely and transitively on each, so each fiber is a $G$-torsor. A linear representation $V$ of $G$ gives the associated vector bundle $P\times_G V$ under the diagonal action ([Wikipedia: Principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)).

**Sections.** A section is a continuous $s:B\to E$ with $\pi\circ s=\mathrm{id}_B$; local sections exist over trivializing neighbourhoods ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)).

### Key results
- **Homotopy invariance of pullbacks.** Let $p:E\to B$ be a vector bundle and $f_0\simeq f_1:A\to B$. If $A$ is compact Hausdorff, or more generally paracompact, then $f_0^*E\cong f_1^*E$. The theorem holds for fiber bundles with the same proof. Consequently a homotopy equivalence of paracompact spaces induces a bijection on $\mathrm{Vect}^n$, and every vector bundle over a contractible paracompact base is trivial ([Hatcher, VBKT, Thm 1.6, Cor 1.8](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)). Every fiber bundle over a contractible CW complex is trivial ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)).
- **Classification.** For paracompact $X$, $[X,G_n]\to\mathrm{Vect}^n(X)$, $[f]\mapsto f^*(E_n)$, is a bijection, where $E_n\to G_n=G_n(\mathbb R^\infty)$ is the universal bundle over the infinite Grassmannian ([Hatcher, VBKT, Thm 1.16](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)). For a topological group $G$, $BG$ is the quotient of a weakly contractible $EG$ by a free proper $G$-action, every principal $G$-bundle over a paracompact manifold is a pullback of $EG\to BG$, and representability of the bundle functor follows from Brown representability ([Wikipedia: Classifying space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classifying_space)).
- **Clutching.** Gluing trivial bundles over the hemispheres $D^k_\pm$ along a map $f:S^{k-1}\to GL_n$ gives a bundle $E_f\to S^k$, and homotopic $f$ give isomorphic bundles. The map $[S^{k-1},GL_n(\mathbb C)]\to\mathrm{Vect}^n_{\mathbb C}(S^k)$ is a bijection, as is $[S^{k-1},GL_n^+(\mathbb R)]\to\mathrm{Vect}^n_+(S^k)$ for oriented real bundles. For $k>1$ every vector bundle over $S^k$ is orientable with exactly two orientations, and forgetting orientation, $\mathrm{Vect}^n_+(S^k)\to\mathrm{Vect}^n(S^k)$, is surjective and at most two-to-one; $\mathrm{Vect}^n(S^1)$ has exactly two elements, the trivial bundle and the Möbius bundle (plus a trivial summand) ([Hatcher, VBKT, Props 1.11, 1.14](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)). The construction generalizes to any closed triad $(X;A,B)$, with a clutching map on $A\cap B$ ([Wikipedia: Clutching construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clutching_construction)).
- **Sections of principal bundles.** A principal bundle is trivial if and only if it admits a global section; sphere bundles can have many sections without being trivial, the Klein bottle being an example ([Wikipedia: Principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)).
- **Bundles are fibrations.** A fiber bundle with paracompact Hausdorff base has the homotopy lifting property for all spaces (a Hurewicz fibration); every fiber bundle has it for CW complexes (a Serre fibration). A Serre fibration $F\to E\to B$ gives a long exact sequence $\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\to\pi_n(E)\to\pi_n(B)\to\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots$ ([Wikipedia: Fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration)).
- **Serre spectral sequence.** For a Serre fibration $X\to B$ with path-connected fiber $F$ there is $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(B;H^q(F))\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X)$, with local coefficients that become ordinary when $B$ is simply connected; it is multiplicative, with differentials acting as graded derivations ([Wikipedia: Serre spectral sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre_spectral_sequence)). The construction works for any additive homology theory over a path-connected CW base, and for fibrations over $S^n$ it gives the Wang exact sequences ([Wikipedia: Fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration)).
- **Leray–Hirsch theorem.** Let $p:E\to B$ be a fiber bundle and $R$ a commutative ring. If each $H^n(F;R)$ is a free $R$-module of finite rank and $F\hookrightarrow E$ induces a surjection on $H^*(-;R)$, then $H^*(E;R)$ is a free $H^*(B;R)$-module, with basis any classes in $H^*(E;R)$ restricting to a basis of $H^*(F;R)$ ([Hatcher, VBKT](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)). Equivalently $H^*(F)\otimes H^*(B)\to H^*(E)$, $\alpha\otimes\beta\mapsto s(\alpha)\smile\pi^*\beta$, is an isomorphism of $H^*(B)$-modules ([Wikipedia: Leray–Hirsch theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leray%E2%80%93Hirsch_theorem)).
- **Gysin sequence.** A fiber-oriented sphere bundle $S^k\to E\to M$ has an Euler class $e\in H^{k+1}(M)$ and a long exact sequence $\cdots\to H^n(E)\xrightarrow{\pi_*}H^{n-k}(M)\xrightarrow{\smile e}H^{n+1}(M)\xrightarrow{\pi^*}H^{n+1}(E)\to\cdots$, introduced by Gysin (1942) ([Wikipedia: Gysin sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gysin_sequence)). For a real vector bundle it follows from the Thom isomorphism, which holds with $\mathbb Z$ coefficients for orientable bundles and with $\mathbb Z_2$ coefficients for all bundles ([Hatcher, VBKT](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).
- **Ehresmann-type criterion.** A submersion between compact connected manifolds is a fiber bundle; Ehresmann's theorem extends this to surjective submersions with compact connected fibers ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)).
- **Reduction of structure group.** Reductions need not exist. A manifold is orientable exactly when its frame bundle reduces to $SO(n)$, and a spin structure is a further reduction to $\mathrm{Spin}(n)$ ([Wikipedia: Principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)).

### Examples
- **Möbius strip and Klein bottle.** The Möbius strip is a nontrivial interval bundle over $S^1$; the Klein bottle is a twisted circle bundle over $S^1$ whose trivial counterpart is the torus ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)).
- **Homogeneous spaces.** For closed $H\le G$, $G\to G/H$ is a bundle if it admits local cross-sections; the Hopf fibration $S^1\to S^3\to S^2$ is an example ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)), and its long exact sequence gives $\pi_i(S^3)\cong\pi_i(S^2)$ for $i\ge3$ ([Wikipedia: Fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration)). In its Serre spectral sequence the only possible differential $d_2:E_2^{0,1}\to E_2^{2,0}$ must be an isomorphism ([Wikipedia: Serre spectral sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre_spectral_sequence)).
- **Classifying spaces.** $B\mathbb Z=S^1$ with $E\mathbb Z=\mathbb R$; $BS^1=\mathbb{CP}^\infty$; $B(\mathbb Z/2)=\mathbb{RP}^\infty$ with $E\mathbb Z_2=S^\infty$ ([Wikipedia: Classifying space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classifying_space)).
- **Projective space from a circle bundle.** $S^1\to S^{2n+1}\to\mathbb{CP}^n$ yields $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^n)\cong\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{n+1})$ ([Wikipedia: Serre spectral sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre_spectral_sequence)).
- **Frame bundle.** The fiber over $x$ is the set of ordered bases of $T_xM$; there is no canonical identity section ([Wikipedia: Principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)).
- **Sphere bundles.** A fiber-oriented $S^n$-bundle has an Euler class in $H^{n+1}$ of the base, which enters the Gysin sequence ([Wikipedia: Gysin sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gysin_sequence)); for circle bundles it equals the first Chern class ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)).

### History
Herbert Seifert introduced "fiber" and "fiber space" in 1933; Hassler Whitney gave the first general definition in 1935 as a "sphere space", renamed "sphere bundle" in 1940; Hopf, Feldbau, Steenrod, Ehresmann and Serre developed the theory ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)). Gysin introduced his sequence in 1942 ([Wikipedia: Gysin sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gysin_sequence)). Steenrod's *The Topology of Fibre Bundles* appeared in 1951 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle)) and is a standard reference ([Wikipedia: Norman Steenrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Steenrod)). Milnor and Stasheff's *Characteristic Classes* (1974) is based mostly on Milnor's 1957 lectures at Princeton ([Wikipedia: Characteristic Classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_Classes)).

### Connections
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): tangent, cotangent and frame bundles are the basic smooth bundles.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): structure groups, and the bundles $G\to G/H$.
- [Tangent Spaces and Vector Fields](node:Tangent%20Spaces%20and%20Vector%20Fields): vector fields are sections of the tangent bundle.
- [Principal Bundle Connections](node:Principal%20Bundle%20Connections): connections on principal bundles, the form of gauge potentials.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): gauge fields are connections on principal $U(1)$, $SU(2)$, ... bundles.
- [Characteristic Classes](node:Characteristic%20Classes): cohomological obstructions to sections and trivializations; Euler class in the Gysin sequence.
- [Grassmannians](node:Grassmannians): classifying spaces for vector bundles.
- [Bott Periodicity](node:Bott%20Periodicity): computes $\pi_{k-1}$ of the classical groups, hence clutching classes over spheres.
- [Homotopy Equivalence](node:Homotopy%20Equivalence): pullback along a homotopy equivalence of paracompact spaces is a bijection on bundles.
- [Holomorphic Vector Bundles](node:Holomorphic%20Vector%20Bundles): the complex-analytic counterpart.
- [Spectral Sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences): the Serre spectral sequence computes the (co)homology of total spaces.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): covering spaces are bundles with discrete fiber.
- [Eilenberg–MacLane Spaces](node:Eilenberg–MacLane%20Spaces): $BG=K(G,1)$ for discrete $G$.
- [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds): Halperin's conjecture is known for fibers with Kähler cohomology.

### Common pitfalls
- Local triviality says nothing about global triviality: the Möbius strip and the Hopf fibration are locally products but not globally ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle); [Wikipedia: Fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration)).
- A section makes a bundle trivial only when it is principal ([Wikipedia: Principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)).
- A principal bundle's fiber is homeomorphic to $G$ but has no preferred identity point ([Wikipedia: Principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)).
- Not every fibration is a bundle. The restriction map of mapping spaces $X^{I^k}\to X^{\partial I^k}$, induced by the inclusion $\partial I^k\hookrightarrow I^k$, is a fibration but not a fiber bundle; the fibration is the map of mapping spaces, not the inclusion ([Wikipedia: Fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration)).
- Homotopy invariance and classification are proved for paracompact bases ([Hatcher, VBKT](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)), and the lifting property for all spaces needs a paracompact Hausdorff base ([Wikipedia: Fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration)).
- The complex clutching bijection does not carry over directly to real bundles, because $GL_n(\mathbb R)$ is not path-connected; the real bijection is for oriented bundles via $GL_n^+(\mathbb R)$ ([Hatcher, VBKT](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Halperin conjecture.** Let $F$ be a simply connected CW complex of finite rational type that is positively elliptic: $\dim H^*(F;\mathbb Q)<\infty$, $\dim\pi_*(F)\otimes\mathbb Q<\infty$, and $\chi(F)>0$. The conjecture says every fibration $F\to E\to B$ is totally non-cohomologous to zero, i.e. $H^*(E;\mathbb Q)\to H^*(F;\mathbb Q)$ is onto, equivalently the Serre spectral sequence with rational coefficients collapses at $E_2$. Lupton states that it "remains open" in general. Meier showed it is equivalent to $\mathrm{Der}_{<0}H^*(F;\mathbb Q)=0$ and to the case $B=S^{2n+1}$; Shiga and Tezuka proved it for $G/H$ with $G$ compact connected and $H$ closed of maximal rank; Thomas proved it when the model for $F$ has $\dim V^{\mathrm{even}}=1$ or $2$, Lupton extended this to $3$, and Markl showed the class of spaces satisfying it is closed under fibrations ([Lupton](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0010124)). It is known when $H^*$ is the rational cohomology of a Kähler manifold or homogeneous space, and is listed first among seventeen open problems in Félix–Halperin–Thomas ([Kennard and Wu](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.04086)). Amann and Kennard proved it for positively elliptic manifolds in dimensions up to 16 or Euler characteristic up to 16 ([arXiv:1512.01302](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01302)), and Kennard and Wu extended this to formal dimension 20 ([Kennard and Wu](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04086)). Wikipedia reports it still open as of 2019 ([Wikipedia: Halperin conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halperin_conjecture)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Fiber bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle): definitions, structure groups, examples, sections, history.
- **Reference:** [nLab: fiber bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fiber+bundle): local triviality over a general site.
- **Learn:** [Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf): pullbacks, clutching, universal bundles, Leray–Hirsch, Gysin, characteristic classes, K-theory.
- **Primary:** [Lupton, Variations on a conjecture of Halperin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0010124): statement, reformulations and known cases of the Halperin conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Kennard and Wu, Halperin's conjecture in formal dimensions up to 20](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04086): current state of the algebraic form of the conjecture.
- **Further reading:** Steenrod, *The Topology of Fibre Bundles* (Princeton, 1951), the classical monograph ([Wikipedia: Norman Steenrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Steenrod)).
- **Further reading:** [Husemoller, Fibre Bundles (Springer GTM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2261-1): standard graduate text.
- **Further reading:** Milnor and Stasheff, *Characteristic Classes* (Annals of Mathematics Studies 76, 1974) ([Wikipedia: Characteristic Classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_Classes)).
references.Fields and Galois Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Galois theory studies a field extension $E/F$ through the group of automorphisms of $E$ that fix $F$. For suitable extensions, intermediate fields correspond exactly to subgroups of this group, so questions about fields, such as which equations are solvable by radicals, become questions in [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_theory))

The correspondence needs hypotheses. A finite extension can have too few automorphisms for two reasons: conjugate roots are missing (failure of normality), or minimal polynomials have repeated roots (failure of separability). Conrad shows these are the only obstructions: for a finite extension, $|\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)|=[L:K]$ exactly when $L/K$ is normal and separable. ([Conrad](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/galoiscorr.pdf))

The theory reaches well beyond polynomial equations. [Finite Fields](node:Finite%20Fields) have cyclic Galois groups generated by Frobenius. Infinite algebraic extensions are handled with a profinite topology on the Galois group. Which finite groups occur as Galois groups over $\mathbb{Q}$ remains a central open problem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem))

### Formal definition
A field extension $L/K$ is a pair of fields $K\subseteq L$ whose operations agree on $K$. $L$ is a $K$-[vector space](node:Vector%20Spaces) whose dimension is the degree $[L:K]$, and for a tower $M/L/K$ the tower law $[M:K]=[M:L][L:K]$ holds, with $M/K$ finite iff both steps are. An element $x\in L$ is algebraic over $K$ if it is a root of a nonzero polynomial in $K[X]$; its minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree with root $x$, and it is irreducible. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension))

An algebraic extension $L/K$ is normal if every irreducible polynomial in $K[X]$ with a root in $L$ splits into linear factors over $L$. It is separable if the minimal polynomial of every element has no repeated roots in an algebraic closure. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension)) A Galois extension is an algebraic extension that is normal and separable, equivalently one for which $F$ is exactly the fixed field of $\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)$. Its Galois group is $\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)=\operatorname{Aut}(E/F)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_extension)) See [Separable Field Extensions](node:Separable%20Field%20Extensions) and [Algebraic and Transcendental Field Extensions](node:Algebraic%20and%20Transcendental%20Field%20Extensions).

### Key results
- **Characterization of finite Galois extensions.** For a finite extension $L/K$ the following are equivalent: (a) $|\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)|=[L:K]$; (b) $L^{\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)}=K$; (c) $L/K$ is separable and normal; (d) $L$ is the splitting field over $K$ of a separable polynomial. In general $|\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)|$ divides $[L:K]$. ([Conrad, Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/galoiscorr.pdf))
- **Artin's theorem.** If $H$ is a finite group of automorphisms of a field $E$, then $E/E^H$ is finite and Galois with $\operatorname{Gal}(E/E^H)=H$. ([Conrad, Theorems 5.2–5.3](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/galoiscorr.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_extension))
- **Fundamental theorem.** If $E/F$ is finite Galois with group $G$, then $H\mapsto E^H$ and $K\mapsto\operatorname{Aut}(E/K)$ are mutually inverse, inclusion-reversing bijections between subgroups of $G$ and intermediate fields, with $|H|=[E:E^H]$ and $[E^H:F]=[G:H]$. $E^H/F$ is normal iff $H\trianglelefteq G$, and then $\operatorname{Gal}(E^H/F)\cong G/H$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory)) See [Quotient Groups](node:Quotient%20Groups) and [Galois Connections](node:Galois%20Connections).
- **Primitive element theorem.** Every finite separable extension is simple, $L=K(\alpha)$. Separability is needed: for $E=\mathbb{F}_p(T,U)$ over $F=\mathbb{F}_p(T^p,U^p)$, every $\alpha\in E\setminus F$ has $\alpha^p\in F$, so $F(\alpha)$ is a proper intermediate field and no primitive element exists. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_element_theorem))
- **Solvability by radicals.** Galois showed that a polynomial is solvable by radicals iff its Galois group is a [solvable group](node:Solvable%20Groups); classically, characteristic zero was implicitly assumed. Since $A_n$ is a simple, non-cyclic normal subgroup of $S_n$ for $n>4$, the general polynomial of degree at least five is not solvable by radicals (Abel–Ruffini). For example, $x^5-x-1$ has Galois group $S_5$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_theory))
- **Finite fields.** A field of order $q$ exists iff $q=p^n$ is a prime power, and it is unique up to isomorphism: the splitting field of $X^q-X$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$. Its multiplicative group is cyclic. $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}/\mathbb{F}_p$ is Galois with cyclic group of order $n$ generated by the Frobenius $x\mapsto x^p$. $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ contains a (unique) copy of $\mathbb{F}_{p^m}$ iff $m\mid n$. Every finite field is perfect. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field))
- **Infinite Galois theory.** For infinite Galois $E/F$, many subgroups fix the same field. With the Krull topology on $G=\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$ (the weakest making each restriction to a finite Galois subextension continuous, with discrete finite quotients), $L\mapsto\operatorname{Gal}(E/L)$ is a bijection from intermediate fields to closed subgroups. For finite $E/F$ the topology is discrete and this is the finite theorem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory)) $G$ is the inverse limit of the groups of the finite Galois subextensions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_extension)) See [Topological Groups](node:Topological%20Groups).

### Examples
- $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}$: the only $\mathbb{R}$-automorphisms are the identity and complex conjugation, since $\sigma(i)$ must be a root of $X^2+1$. ([Conrad, Example 1.1](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/galoiscorr.pdf))
- $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb{Q}$ has prime degree $3$ but trivial automorphism group, because the other roots of $X^3-2$ are not real. ([Conrad, Example 1.2](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/galoiscorr.pdf))
- $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/\mathbb{Q}$ has Klein four-group; its five subgroups match $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt3)$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt6)$ and the whole field. The splitting field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega)$ of $X^3-2$ has group $S_3$: the order-$3$ subgroup fixes the normal subfield $\mathbb{Q}(\omega)$, and the three order-$2$ subgroups fix the non-normal cubic fields $\mathbb{Q}(\omega^k\sqrt[3]{2})$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory))

### History
Lagrange's 1770 *Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique des équations* analysed cubic and quartic formulas through permutations of roots. Galois's memoir was rejected in 1831; he died in a duel in 1832, and Liouville published the work in 1846. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_theory)) Galois sketched the primitive element theorem for splitting fields over $\mathbb{Q}$. Steinitz proved it in modern form in 1910, and Artin reformulated Galois theory without primitive elements in the 1930s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_element_theorem)) The classification of finite fields was first proved in 1893 by E. H. Moore. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field))

### Connections
- [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals): extensions are built as quotients $K[X]/(f)$ by maximal ideals.
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), [Solvable Groups](node:Solvable%20Groups), [Permutation Groups](node:Permutation%20Groups), [Finite Simple Groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups): the group side of the correspondence and of radical solvability.
- [Finite Fields](node:Finite%20Fields): cyclic Galois groups generated by Frobenius.
- [Separable Field Extensions](node:Separable%20Field%20Extensions) and [Algebraic and Transcendental Field Extensions](node:Algebraic%20and%20Transcendental%20Field%20Extensions): the hypotheses behind the correspondence.
- [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields) and [Galois Cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology): arithmetic uses of Galois groups.
- [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields) and [Fundamental Theorem of Algebra](node:Fundamental%20Theorem%20of%20Algebra): $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}(i)$ as the algebraic closure of degree $2$.
- [Galois Connections](node:Galois%20Connections): the order-theoretic abstraction of the correspondence.
- Map: [MSC 12Fxx - Field extensions](node:MSC%2012Fxx%20-%20Field%20extensions)

### Common pitfalls
- **Inclusion reverses.** Larger subgroups fix smaller fields: $H_1\subseteq H_2$ iff $E^{H_1}\supseteq E^{H_2}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory))
- **Normality of the subextension.** $\operatorname{Gal}(E^H/F)\cong G/H$ only when $H$ is normal; for $X^3-2$ the cubic subfields are not normal over $\mathbb{Q}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory))
- **Inseparability is fatal.** If $L/K$ is inseparable or not normal then $|\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)|<[L:K]$, and for the inseparable extension $\mathbb{F}_p(u^{1/p})/\mathbb{F}_p(u)$ enlarging the top field cannot turn the inequality into an equality. ([Conrad, Corollary 4.3](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/galoiscorr.pdf))
- **Infinite extensions.** Without the Krull topology, the subgroup–subfield map is not a bijection. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory))

### Open problems
- **Inverse Galois problem.** Is every finite group the Galois group of a Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$? The problem is unsolved and "in no sense solved in general." Known cases include Shafarevich's theorem that every finite solvable group is realizable over $\mathbb{Q}$, Hilbert's realization of all symmetric and alternating groups, and the realization of [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) via cyclotomic fields. Main methods are Hilbert irreducibility applied to generic polynomials and Thompson's rigidity method, which applies to many simple groups including the Monster. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem))
- **Research example.** Zywina showed that $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ occurs as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ for all primes $p>3$, using the Galois action on the second [étale cohomology](node:Étale%20Cohomology) of an elliptic surface. ([arXiv:1303.3646](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.3646))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fundamental theorem of Galois theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory): finite and infinite correspondence with worked examples.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, The Galois Correspondence](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/galoiscorr.pdf): proofs of the automorphism bound, Artin's theorem, and the correspondence.
- **Primary:** [Zywina, The inverse Galois problem for PSL₂(F_p) (arXiv:1303.3646)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.3646): research paper realizing an infinite family of simple groups over $\mathbb{Q}$.
- **Further reading:** [Malle and Matzat, Inverse Galois Theory (Springer Monographs in Mathematics, 2018)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-55420-3): standard monograph on realizing groups as Galois groups.
references.Fine-Tuning and RLHF:
## Reference
### Overview
Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a target behaviour by continuing training on new data. For [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models) the standard post-training recipe has three stages: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human-written prompt–response demonstrations; training a reward model on human comparisons of model outputs; and optimising the policy against that reward with reinforcement learning, usually [Proximal Policy Optimization](node:Proximal%20Policy%20Optimization) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback); [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/blog/rlhf)). The last two stages are reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), a technique for aligning an agent with human preferences that suits tasks that are hard to specify but easy to judge ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback)).

In human evaluations in the InstructGPT study, outputs of the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT were preferred to those of the 175B-parameter GPT-3, with minimal regressions on public NLP datasets ([Ouyang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)). Casper and 31 coauthors call RLHF the central method for fine-tuning state-of-the-art LLMs ([Casper et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15217)). It combines [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning) (the policy is optimised by PPO against a learned reward) with [Preference Learning](node:Preference%20Learning) (the reward model is fit with a Bradley–Terry-type pairwise comparison loss) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback)).

Two families of alternatives matter in practice. *Direct alignment* methods, chiefly [Direct Preference Optimization](node:Direct%20Preference%20Optimization), drop the explicit reward model and RL loop and fit the policy to preference pairs with a classification loss; RLAIF replaces human labels with AI feedback, as in constitutional AI ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback); [Rafailov et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)). *Parameter-efficient* fine-tuning such as [Low-Rank Adaptation](node:Low-Rank%20Adaptation) trains a small number of added parameters instead of the full network ([Hu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)).

### Formal definition
**Reward model.** Given a prompt $x$ with preferred response $y_w$ and rejected response $y_l$, a reward model $r_\theta$ is fit by the Bradley–Terry (pairwise logistic) loss
$$\mathcal L(\theta)=-\mathbb E_{(x,y_w,y_l)}\bigl[\log\sigma\bigl(r_\theta(x,y_w)-r_\theta(x,y_l)\bigr)\bigr]$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback)). Rankings are used instead of absolute scores because human scalar ratings are uncalibrated and noisy ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/blog/rlhf)).

**KL-regularised policy objective.** The policy $\pi_\phi$ maximises
$$\mathbb E_{x,\,y\sim\pi_\phi(\cdot\mid x)}\Bigl[r_\theta(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\phi(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\mathrm{SFT}}(y\mid x)}\Bigr],$$
where the KL term keeps the policy near the SFT model, limiting over-fitting to the reward model and loss of diversity ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback)); without it the policy can drift to gibberish that still fools the reward model ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/blog/rlhf)). InstructGPT's PPO-ptx variant adds a pretraining-gradient term against forgetting ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback)).

**LoRA.** For a frozen weight $W_0\in\mathbb R^{d\times k}$, LoRA learns $\Delta W=BA$ with $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}$, $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times k}$, $r\ll\min(d,k)$, so $h=W_0x+BAx$, scaled by $\alpha/r$; $A$ starts Gaussian and $B$ zero, so training starts from the pretrained model. The motivating hypothesis is that weight updates during adaptation have low intrinsic rank ([Hu et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2106.09685)).

### Key results
- **Closed-form optimum of the KL-regularised objective.** For a reference policy $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $\beta>0$, the maximiser of $\mathbb E[r(x,y)]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\Vert\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ is $\pi_r(y\mid x)=Z(x)^{-1}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)$, equivalently $r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}+\beta\log Z(x)$. Substituting into the Bradley–Terry likelihood cancels $Z(x)$ and gives the DPO loss
$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\mathbb E\Bigl[\log\sigma\Bigl(\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}-\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\Bigr)\Bigr].$$
Rafailov et al.'s Theorem 1 states that, if $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)>0$ for all pairs and $\beta>0$, every reward equivalence class consistent with the Plackett–Luce (in particular Bradley–Terry) model can be represented by this reparameterisation ([Rafailov et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.18290v3)).
- **Scaling laws for reward over-optimisation.** With a fixed "gold" reward model standing in for humans and a proxy reward model trained on its labels, the gold reward as a function of $d=\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(\pi\Vert\pi_{\mathrm{init}})}$ (with $R(0)=0$) follows $R_{\mathrm{bon}}(d)=d(\alpha_{\mathrm{bon}}-\beta_{\mathrm{bon}}d)$ for best-of-$n$ sampling, where $\mathrm{KL}_{\mathrm{bon}}=\log n-\frac{n-1}{n}$, and $R_{\mathrm{RL}}(d)=d(\alpha_{\mathrm{RL}}-\beta_{\mathrm{RL}}\log d)$ for RL. The coefficients scale smoothly with reward-model size, with $\beta_{\mathrm{bon}}$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{RL}}$ decreasing as the reward model grows, and in their RL setup a KL penalty acts like early stopping rather than improving the gold-reward frontier ([Gao, Schulman, Hilton](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.10760)).
- **Preferences can replace a reward function.** Learning from non-expert human comparisons of pairs of trajectory segments solves Atari and simulated locomotion tasks without access to the reward, with feedback on under 1% of agent–environment interactions; about an hour of human time sufficed to train novel behaviours more complex than those previously learned from human feedback ([Christiano et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741)).
- **Low-rank adaptation suffices at scale.** Relative to full fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B with Adam, LoRA cuts trainable parameters by 10,000 times and GPU memory by 3 times and, unlike adapters, adds no inference latency ([Hu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)).

### Examples
- **InstructGPT:** GPT-3 fine-tuned on labeller demonstrations, then on rankings of its outputs with RLHF ([Ouyang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)).
- **Alternatives to PPO-based RLHF:** IPO regularises DPO against noisy preferences; KTO uses prospect-theory value functions and needs only binary good/bad labels ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback)).

### History
Christiano et al. (2017) learned agent behaviour from human preferences between trajectory segments ([Christiano et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741)). The language-model algorithm was introduced by OpenAI in work on text continuation and summarisation from human feedback, gained popularity when reused for InstructGPT (2022), and ChatGPT was built on InstructGPT ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback); [Ouyang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)). LoRA appeared in 2021 ([Hu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)) and DPO in 2023 ([Rafailov et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)).

### Connections
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): the models being post-trained.
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning) and [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): response generation is an episodic MDP with a terminal reward.
- [Policy Gradient Methods](node:Policy%20Gradient%20Methods) and [Proximal Policy Optimization](node:Proximal%20Policy%20Optimization): the usual RL optimiser.
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence): the regulariser tying the policy to its reference.
- [Preference Learning](node:Preference%20Learning): Bradley–Terry and Plackett–Luce models of comparisons.
- [Direct Preference Optimization](node:Direct%20Preference%20Optimization): the reward-model-free reformulation.
- [Inverse Reinforcement Learning](node:Inverse%20Reinforcement%20Learning): inferring a reward from behaviour rather than comparisons.
- [Low-Rank Adaptation](node:Low-Rank%20Adaptation) and [Transfer Learning](node:Transfer%20Learning): parameter-efficient adaptation of pretrained weights.
- [Catastrophic Forgetting](node:Catastrophic%20Forgetting): the reason for PPO-ptx and KL anchoring.
- [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): the over-optimisation laws are scaling laws in reward-model size.
- [Early Stopping](node:Early%20Stopping): Gao et al. find the KL penalty behaves like early stopping.
- [AI Alignment](node:AI%20Alignment): RLHF is its main deployed technique and a main object of its critique.

### Common pitfalls
- **The proxy is not the target.** Optimising an imperfect reward model increases proxy reward, while the fitted gold-reward curves above are concave in $d$ and eventually decline ([Gao, Schulman, Hilton](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.10760)); the policy can learn to sound confident or persuasive without being accurate ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback)).
- **A KL penalty is not a fix for over-optimisation.** In Gao et al.'s RL setup it does not improve the gold-score frontier; it only makes the gold score converge earlier, like early stopping, a result they note may be sensitive to hyperparameters ([Gao, Schulman, Hilton](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.10760)).
- **One reward function, many people.** A single reward function may fail to represent diverse groups and favour the majority view ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback)).

### Open problems
Casper et al. classify RLHF's open problems as *tractable* or *fundamental* ([Casper et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.15217)):
- **Fundamental, human feedback:** humans cannot evaluate performance on difficult tasks well and can be misled; there is an inherent cost/quality trade-off and a richness/efficiency trade-off between feedback types.
- **Fundamental, reward model:** an individual's values are hard to represent as a reward function and a single reward cannot represent a diverse society; reward models misgeneralise even from correctly labelled data, and optimising an imperfect proxy leads to reward hacking.
- **Fundamental, policy:** policies can misgeneralise in deployment even with correct training rewards.
- **Tractable:** evaluator selection and data poisoning, evaluating reward models, adversarial exploitability, mode collapse from RL, and distribution shift from joint training.
- **Practical questions** raised by Lambert et al.: the cost of human preference data, annotator disagreement with no ground truth, and whether optimisers other than PPO (for example offline RL methods such as ILQL) can avoid costly reward-model evaluations ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/blog/rlhf)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Reinforcement learning from human feedback (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning_from_human_feedback): pipeline, losses, alternatives, limitations.
- **Learn:** [Lambert et al., Illustrating RLHF (Hugging Face)](https://huggingface.co/blog/rlhf): the three stages, the KL-penalised PPO reward, open questions.
