- **Primary:** [Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155): InstructGPT.
- **Primary:** [Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290): closed-form optimal policy and the DPO loss.
- **Primary:** [Gao, Schulman, Hilton, Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760): Goodhart effects quantified.
- **Further reading:** [Casper et al., Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of RLHF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15217): survey of open problems, complementary techniques, and auditing standards.
references.First-Order Logic:
## Reference
### Overview
First-order logic extends [propositional logic](node:Propositional%20Logic) with predicates, function symbols, and quantifiers $\forall,\exists$ that range over the individuals of a domain. A formal language, a deductive system, and a semantics of interpretations are given separately, and an argument is valid when no interpretation makes its premises true and its conclusion false. ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/))

Its metatheory is unusually well behaved: deduction is sound and complete for semantic consequence, every finitely satisfiable set of sentences is satisfiable, and satisfiable countable theories have countable models. Applied to a first-order axiomatization of [set theory](node:Set%20Theory), the last property yields the Skolem paradox. Compactness, which Boney's [model theory](node:Model%20Theory) notes call "THE theorem of first order logic", is the main tool for building models. ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/); [Boney, Harvard Math 144 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~wboney/spring16/144-modeltheory-notes_02_05_2016.pdf))

The same properties bound its expressive power. Lindström's theorem shows that no strictly stronger logic (satisfying regularity conditions such as closure under classical negation) keeps both countable compactness and the downward Löwenheim–Skolem property, so stronger logics gain expressiveness only by losing one of these theorems. ([Wikipedia, Lindström's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindstr%C3%B6m%27s_theorem); [Siddiqi, UChicago REU](http://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/VIGRE/VIGRE2011/REUPapers/Siddiqi.pdf))

### Formal definition
A signature $\sigma$ consists of relation symbols, function symbols and constants, each with an arity. Terms and formulas are built from variables, symbols of $\sigma$, connectives and quantifiers. An interpretation $\mathcal M=\langle d,I\rangle$ has a nonempty domain $d$ and assigns to each nonlogical symbol an extension over $d$; satisfaction $\mathcal M,s\models\varphi$ is defined between interpretations, variable assignments $s$ and formulas, with $\mathcal M,s\models\forall x\,\varphi$ holding when $\varphi$ holds under every assignment that differs from $s$ at most at $x$. ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/))

A sentence is a formula with no free variables. For a set $\Gamma$ of sentences, $\Gamma\models\theta$ (semantic consequence) means every interpretation satisfying all of $\Gamma$ satisfies $\theta$, and $\Gamma\vdash\theta$ means $\theta$ is derivable from $\Gamma$ in the deductive system; $\Gamma$ is consistent when no contradiction is derivable from it. ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/))

### Key results
- **Soundness.** For every set $\Gamma$ of sentences and sentence $\theta$, if $\Gamma\vdash\theta$ then $\Gamma\models\theta$. ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/))
- **Gödel's completeness theorem (1930).** Every consistent set of sentences is satisfiable; with soundness, $\Gamma\vdash\theta$ if and only if $\Gamma\models\theta$. Gödel proved the resulting compactness theorem for countable theories in 1930, and Mal'tsev extended compactness to all theories in 1936. ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/); [Boney, Harvard Math 144 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~wboney/spring16/144-modeltheory-notes_02_05_2016.pdf))
- **Compactness theorem.** A set of sentences is satisfiable if and only if every finite subset is satisfiable. It follows from completeness because a derivation uses only finitely many premises. See [Compactness Theorem](node:Compactness%20Theorem). ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/); [Boney, Harvard Math 144 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~wboney/spring16/144-modeltheory-notes_02_05_2016.pdf))
- **Löwenheim–Skolem theorem.** Let $\mathcal M$ be an infinite $\sigma$-structure and $\kappa\ge|\sigma|$ an infinite cardinal. Then there is a structure $\mathcal N$ of [cardinality](node:Cardinality) $\kappa$ that is an elementary substructure of $\mathcal M$ if $\kappa<|\mathcal M|$ (downward) and an elementary extension of $\mathcal M$ if $\kappa\ge|\mathcal M|$ (upward). Consequently a first-order theory with an infinite model is not categorical, that is, it does not determine its models up to isomorphism. ([Wikipedia, Löwenheim–Skolem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%B6wenheim%E2%80%93Skolem_theorem))
- **Lindström's theorem (1969).** Let $\mathcal L$ be an abstract logic, at least as expressive as first-order logic, that is countably compact (a countable set of sentences has a model iff each finite subset does) and has Löwenheim number $\aleph_0$ (every sentence with a model has a countable model). Then $\mathcal L$ is equivalent to first-order logic $\mathcal L_{\omega\omega}$. ([Siddiqi, UChicago REU, Theorem 4.9](http://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/VIGRE/VIGRE2011/REUPapers/Siddiqi.pdf); [Wikipedia, Lindström's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindstr%C3%B6m%27s_theorem))
- **Church–Turing undecidability.** There is no algorithm deciding validity of first-order sentences: Church (1935–36) and Turing, by reduction to the halting problem, gave independent negative solutions to Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem. Since validity equals provability by completeness, the valid sentences are nevertheless those enumerated by proof search. Restricting to finite models does not help in general: Trakhtenbrot's theorem shows that truth in all finite models is also undecidable. Decidable fragments include the monadic predicate calculus (only unary predicates, no function symbols) and the Bernays–Schönfinkel class $[\exists^*\forall^*]_=$ (that prefix, with equality and relation symbols but no function symbols), whose satisfiability is decidable. See [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory) and [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines). ([Wikipedia, Entscheidungsproblem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entscheidungsproblem))
- **Contrast: Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931).** If a formal system $F$ (decidable axioms and rules) is consistent and contains Robinson arithmetic $Q$, there is a sentence $G_F$ that $F$ neither proves nor refutes; and if $F$ is consistent and contains somewhat more arithmetic, it does not prove its own consistency statement. Completeness concerns the proof system ($\Gamma\vdash\theta$ iff $\Gamma\models\theta$); incompleteness concerns particular theories, which have sentences true in some models and false in others. See [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems). ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/); [Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/))

### Examples
- **Finiteness is not axiomatizable.** If a theory $T$ has arbitrarily large finite models, it has an infinite model: add constants $c_n$ with axioms $c_n\neq c_m$ for $n\neq m$; each finite subset is satisfied by a large enough finite model of $T$, so compactness gives a model of the whole set. By the same method, being a torsion group and being well-ordered are not first-order axiomatizable. ([Boney, Harvard Math 144 notes, Props. 5.3–5.6](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~wboney/spring16/144-modeltheory-notes_02_05_2016.pdf))
- **Graph colouring.** A graph is $k$-colourable iff every finite induced subgraph is, and $k$-colourability is axiomatized by the sentences forbidding each finite non-$k$-colourable induced subgraph. ([Boney, Harvard Math 144 notes, Lemma 5.8, Thm 5.9](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~wboney/spring16/144-modeltheory-notes_02_05_2016.pdf))
- **Infinitesimals.** Realizing the type $\{x>1+\cdots+1\ (n\text{ times}) : n\in\mathbb N\}$ in a structure $\mathbb R^*$ that extends the ordered field $\mathbb R$ and models $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbb R)$ gives an infinite element, whose inverse is infinitesimal; this is the start of [nonstandard analysis](node:Hyperreal%20Numbers). ([Boney, Harvard Math 144 notes, Example 6.9](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~wboney/spring16/144-modeltheory-notes_02_05_2016.pdf))
- **Skolem's paradox.** A countable model of set theory satisfies "the reals are uncountable"; the resolution is that countability is not absolute between a model and the ambient universe. ([Wikipedia, Löwenheim–Skolem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%B6wenheim%E2%80%93Skolem_theorem))

### History
Löwenheim (1915) showed that a satisfiable sentence in a countable signature is satisfiable in a countable model; Skolem (1920, using choice; 1922 without) proved versions for countable theories, and Mal'tsev (1936) proved the theorem in full generality. Gödel's completeness paper *Die Vollständigkeit der Axiome des logischen Funktionenkalküls* appeared in 1930; he announced the first incompleteness theorem at Königsberg on 7 September 1930 and published it in January 1931. ([Wikipedia, Löwenheim–Skolem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%B6wenheim%E2%80%93Skolem_theorem); [Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/); [Stanford Encyclopedia, Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/)) Church settled the Entscheidungsproblem negatively in 1935–36, and Lindström published his characterization in *Theoria* in 1969. ([Wikipedia, Entscheidungsproblem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entscheidungsproblem); [Wikipedia, Lindström's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindstr%C3%B6m%27s_theorem))

### Connections
- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic): the quantifier-free fragment; its compactness theorem is the propositional analogue.
- [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory): studies structures through first-order theories, built on compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem.
- [Compactness Theorem](node:Compactness%20Theorem): the central tool for constructing models.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): limits of particular first-order theories of arithmetic.
- [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory): undecidability of validity and semi-decidability of provability.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): ZFC is a first-order theory, which makes Skolem's paradox possible.
- [Hilbert's Tenth Problem](node:Hilbert's%20Tenth%20Problem): another undecidability result about arithmetic definability.
- [MSC 03Bxx - General logic](node:MSC%2003Bxx%20-%20General%20logic) and [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory): the classification homes.

### Common pitfalls
- Completeness of the proof system does not make a theory complete: Gödel's completeness theorem holds for every theory, while a consistent theory containing enough arithmetic still leaves some sentence undecided. ([Stanford Encyclopedia, Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/); [Stanford Encyclopedia, Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- Validity is semi-decidable but not decidable: a proof search halts on valid sentences, yet no algorithm halts with the right answer on every sentence. ([Wikipedia, Entscheidungsproblem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entscheidungsproblem))
- Countability is relative to a model, so a countable model of set theory is not a contradiction. ([Wikipedia, Löwenheim–Skolem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%B6wenheim%E2%80%93Skolem_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Asser's spectrum problem.** The spectrum of a first-order sentence is the set of sizes of its finite models. Asser asked whether the complement of a spectrum is always a spectrum; the Durand–Jones–Makowsky–More survey states that this "remains open". Since spectra are exactly the sets in the complexity class NE (Jones–Selman), the question is equivalent to NE $=$ co-NE, and a negative answer would imply P $\neq$ NP. ([Durand, Jones, Makowsky, More, *Fifty years of the spectrum problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.5495); [Wikipedia, Spectrum of a sentence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_sentence))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stanford Encyclopedia: Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/): syntax, semantics, soundness, completeness, compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem.
- **Learn:** [Boney, Harvard Math 144 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~wboney/spring16/144-modeltheory-notes_02_05_2016.pdf): compactness applications and Lindström's theorem; [Siddiqi, Lindström's Theorem](http://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/VIGRE/VIGRE2011/REUPapers/Siddiqi.pdf): a full proof via abstract logics.
- **Primary:** [Durand, Jones, Makowsky, More, *Fifty years of the spectrum problem: survey and new results*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.5495): survey of first-order spectra and [finite model theory](node:Finite%20Model%20Theory) (Bull. Symb. Logic 2012).
- **Further reading:** [Ebbinghaus, Flum, Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-030-73839-6): Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics (2021), a graduate text in mathematical logic.
