## Reference
### Overview
Fisher information measures how much an observable random variable $X$ reveals about an unknown parameter $\theta$ of its distribution. It is the variance of the score, the derivative of the log-likelihood in $\theta$, and the expected value of the observed information, the negative second derivative of the log-likelihood ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information)). Large information means a sharply curved log-likelihood and an easier estimation problem ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)).

Its central role is to bound estimation accuracy. The inverse information lower-bounds the variance of unbiased estimators (the [Cramér–Rao Bound](node:Cramér–Rao%20Bound)), and under quadratic mean differentiability or local asymptotic normality no estimator can beat the Fisher bound in a uniform sense, one of Le Cam's main contributions ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)). The Hájek–Le Cam convolution theorem and the local asymptotic minimax theorem make this precise ([Chae 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.05247)).

Frequentists use it for confidence intervals and tests from MLEs, Bayesians to build the Jeffreys prior, and minimum description length to measure model complexity ([Ly et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.01064)). With several parameters it is a positive semidefinite matrix which, when positive definite, defines a Riemannian metric, the starting point of [Information Geometry](node:Information%20Geometry) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information)). For a density on $\mathbb R^n$ with no parameter, the location form $J(X)$ links Fisher information to entropy through de Bruijn's identity ([Rioul](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0704.1751)).

### Formal definition
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n\sim p(x;\theta)$ i.i.d., $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, with log-likelihood $\ell(\theta)=\sum_i\log p(X_i;\theta)$ and score $s(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta)$. The **Fisher information matrix** is
$$I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[s(\theta)s(\theta)^{\mathsf T}\right],$$
a $d\times d$ positive semidefinite matrix. When differentiation under the integral is allowed, $\mathbb E_\theta[s(\theta)]=0$, so $I(\theta)$ is the covariance of the score, and for one observation $I_1(\theta)=-\mathbb E_\theta[\nabla^2_\theta\log p(X;\theta)]$ ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)). The regularity conditions include that the support of $p(\cdot;\theta)$ not depend on $\theta$; $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,\theta)$ fails them ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information)).

**Observed information.** $\mathcal J(\theta^*)=-\nabla^2\ell(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta^*}$, the negative Hessian of the log-likelihood of the sample; the Fisher information is its expectation for a single observation ([Wikipedia: Observed information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observed_information)).

**Fisher metric.** On a statistical manifold, $g_{jk}(\theta)=\mathbb E[-\partial_j\partial_k\log p(x\mid\theta)]$ ([Wikipedia: Fisher information metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information_metric)).

**Location (nonparametric) form.** For a random $n$-vector with smooth density $p$, $S(X)=\nabla\log p(X)$ and $J(X)=\mathrm{Cov}(S(X))$, with scalar version $J(X)=\mathbb E\,\|\nabla p(X)\|^2/p(X)^2$ ([Rioul](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0704.1751)).

### Key results
- **Additivity.** $I(\theta)=nI_1(\theta)$ for $n$ i.i.d. observations ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)); more generally a chain rule holds ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information)).
- **Cramér–Rao bound.** Under the regularity conditions, an unbiased $\hat\theta$ of $\theta\in\mathbb R$ has $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge1/(nI_1(\theta))$; for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\succeq I(\theta)^{-1}$ in the Loewner order. The proof uses $\operatorname{cov}(\hat\theta,s(\theta))=1$ ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)).
- **van Trees (Bayesian Cramér–Rao) inequality.** Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, the model differentiable in $L^2(\mu)$ with information $I_P(\theta)$, and $Q$ a prior with absolutely continuous density $q$ and $I_Q=\int(q')^2/q<\infty$. For any, possibly biased, statistic $S$ and absolutely continuous $\psi$,
$$\int_\Theta\mathbb E_\theta\big[(S-\psi(\theta))^2\big]\,dQ(\theta)\ \ge\ \frac{\big(\int_\Theta\psi'\,dQ\big)^2}{I_Q+\int_\Theta I_P\,dQ},$$
under mild extra conditions such as $q$ vanishing at finite boundary points of $\Theta$ ([Gassiat and Stoltz](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.06431)).
- **Sufficiency.** $I_{X^n}(\theta)\ge I_T(\theta)$ for any statistic $T$, with equality if and only if $T$ is sufficient ([Ly et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.01064)); see [Sufficient Statistics](node:Sufficient%20Statistics).
- **LAN.** $P_{n,\theta}$ is LAN at $\theta$ if $\log dP_{n,\theta+r_n^{-1}h_n}/dP_{n,\theta}=h^{\mathsf T}\Delta_{n,\theta}-\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}I_\theta h+o_P(1)$ with $\Delta_{n,\theta}\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,I_\theta)$; an i.i.d. model with twice continuously differentiable likelihood is LAN with $I_\theta$ the Fisher information ([Wikipedia: LAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_asymptotic_normality)).
- **Hájek–Le Cam convolution theorem.** If $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ is open and the model is LAN at $\theta$ with nonsingular $I_\theta$, then for every regular estimator sequence the limit law $L_\theta$ of $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)$ satisfies $L_\theta=\mathcal N(0,I_\theta^{-1})*M_\theta$ for some distribution $M_\theta$ ([Chae 2015, Thm 2.1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.05247)). Efficient estimators, those with $M_\theta=\delta_0$, exist for regular parametric models ([Wikipedia: Hájek–Le Cam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A1jek%E2%80%93Le_Cam_convolution_theorem)), and an estimator is efficient if and only if $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)=n^{-1/2}\sum_iI_\theta^{-1}\dot\ell_\theta(X_i)+o_P(1)$ ([Chae 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.05247)).
- **Local asymptotic minimax theorem.** Under the same hypotheses, for any estimator sequence and any bowl-shaped loss $\ell$ (sublevel sets convex and symmetric about 0),
$$\sup_{I}\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sup_{h\in I}\mathbb E_{\theta+h/\sqrt n}\,\ell\big(\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta-h/\sqrt n)\big)\ \ge\ \int\ell\,d\mathcal N(0,I_\theta^{-1}),$$
the first supremum over finite $I\subset\mathbb R^p$ ([Chae 2015, Thm 2.1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.05247)).
- **Asymptotic normality of the MLE.** In regular models $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)\Rightarrow\mathcal N_d(0,I_1(\theta^*)^{-1})$ ([Ly et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.01064)).
- **Misspecification (sandwich).** If the data come from $P_0$ outside the model, the MLE converges to the pseudo-true $\theta^*$ minimizing $\mathbb E_{P_0}\log[p_0/p_\theta]$, and $\hat\theta-\theta^*$ is approximately $\mathcal N(0,nA^{-1}BA^{-1})$ with $A=\sum_i\ddot\ell(\hat\theta;x_i)$ and $B=\operatorname{Var}_{P_0}[\dot\ell(\theta^*;x)]$; White (1982) reviews the theory ([Hoff and Wakefield](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1211.0087)).
- **Curvature of relative entropy.** $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\theta_0}\|p_{\theta_0+\Delta\theta})=\tfrac12\sum_{j,k}\Delta\theta_j\Delta\theta_kg_{jk}(\theta_0)+O(\|\Delta\theta\|^3)$ ([Wikipedia: Fisher information metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information_metric)); see [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence).
- **Chentsov's theorem.** The Fisher metric is the unique Riemannian metric, up to scale, invariant under sufficient statistics ([Wikipedia: Fisher information metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information_metric)). Chentsov's result concerns finite sample spaces; Ay, Jost, Lê and Schwachhöfer give a full generalization to infinite sample spaces for parametrized measure models, also covering the Amari–Chentsov 3-tensor ([Ay et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.6736)), and on a closed manifold of dimension $>1$ every diffeomorphism-invariant smooth weak Riemannian metric on smooth positive densities is a multiple of the Fisher–Rao metric ([Bauer, Bruveris, Michor](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.5577)).
- **Stam's inequality and de Bruijn's identity.** For independent $X_i$ with finite Fisher information, $J^{-1}(\sum_ia_iX_i)\ge\sum_ia_i^2J^{-1}(X_i)$. If $Z$ is independent of $X$ with finite covariance, $\frac{d}{dt}h(X+\sqrt tZ)|_{t=0}=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(J(X)\operatorname{Cov}(Z))$. Also $J(X)\ge\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Cov}(X)^{-1})$ with equality iff $X$ is Gaussian ([Rioul](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0704.1751)). Together these give the entropy power inequality $N(X+Y)\ge N(X)+N(Y)$ for independent $X,Y$, whose equality case was settled by Stam (1959) ([Wikipedia: EPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entropy_power_inequality); [Rioul](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.1751)).
- **Reparametrization.** Information transforms as a Riemannian metric: $I_\eta=I_\theta\,(d\theta/d\eta)^2$ for a scalar parameter ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information)).
- **Stochastic complexity.** Rissanen's Fisher information approximation is $-\log f(x^n\mid\hat\theta)+\tfrac d2\log\tfrac n{2\pi}+\log\int_\Theta\sqrt{\det I(\theta)}\,d\theta$ ([Ly et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.01064)).

### Examples
- **Bernoulli.** $I(p)=1/(p(1-p))$; the sample mean attains the Cramér–Rao bound $p(1-p)/n$ ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)).
- **Normal location.** For $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, $\sigma$ known, $I(\mu)=1/\sigma^2$ ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)); see [Gaussian Distribution](node:Gaussian%20Distribution).
- **Exponential families.** $I(\theta)=n\nabla^2A(\theta)=n\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T(X))$ ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)).
- **Categorical.** With $p_i=y_i^2$ the Fisher metric is four times the Euclidean metric on the positive orthant of the unit sphere ([Wikipedia: Fisher information metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information_metric)).
- **Jeffreys priors.** $p(\theta)\propto|I(\theta)|^{1/2}$ gives $\mathrm{Beta}(1/2,1/2)$ for the Bernoulli, $\lambda^{-1/2}$ for the Poisson rate, a flat improper prior for a normal mean and $1/\sigma$ for a normal scale ([Wikipedia: Jeffreys prior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffreys_prior)).
- **Hodges estimator.** $\hat\theta_n=\bar X_n$ if $|\bar X_n|\ge n^{-1/4}$ and $\alpha\bar X_n$ otherwise ($0<\alpha<1$) is superefficient at 0, so is not regular; superefficiency sets have Lebesgue measure zero ([Chae 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.05247)).

### History
Edgeworth discussed the quantity early, and Fisher emphasized its role in the asymptotic theory of maximum likelihood ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information)). Ly et al. cite Fisher 1912, 1922 and 1925 for this conceptualization of the MLE ([Ly et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.01064)): "On the mathematical foundations of theoretical statistics", *Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A* 222 (1922) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rsta.1922.0009)), and "Theory of statistical estimation", *Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc.* 22 (1925) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/S0305004100009580)). The information lower bound is due to Fréchet (1943), Rao (1945) and Cramér (1946); Jeffreys proposed his prior in 1946 and Rissanen linked Fisher information to stochastic complexity in 1996 ([Ly et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.01064)). Le Cam introduced LAN in 1960 ([Wikipedia: LAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_asymptotic_normality)); Hájek (1970) characterized limits of regular estimates ([Janssen and Ostrovski](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.4984)), and the local asymptotic minimax theorem goes back to Hájek (1972) and Le Cam (1972) ([Chae 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.05247)). Van Trees stated his inequality in 1968 and Gill and Levit (1995) brought out its statistical uses ([Gassiat and Stoltz](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.06431)). Efron and Hinkley (1978) gave a frequentist case for observed over expected information when an ancillary statistic affects the MLE's precision ([Wikipedia: Observed information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observed_information)).

### Connections
- [Maximum Likelihood Estimation](node:Maximum%20Likelihood%20Estimation): inverse information is the asymptotic covariance of the MLE.
- [Cramér–Rao Bound](node:Cramér–Rao%20Bound): the finite-sample bound built from the information.
- [Sufficient Statistics](node:Sufficient%20Statistics): a statistic keeps all the information exactly when sufficient.
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence): the Fisher metric is its second-order term.
- [Information Geometry](node:Information%20Geometry) and [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): the Fisher metric, unique by Chentsov's theorem.
- [Information Theory](node:Information%20Theory): Stam's inequality and de Bruijn's identity tie $J$ to differential entropy.
- [Natural Gradient Methods](node:Natural%20Gradient%20Methods): steepest descent in the Fisher metric.
- [Conjugate Priors](node:Conjugate%20Priors): the Jeffreys prior is defined from the information, not by conjugacy ([Wikipedia: Jeffreys prior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffreys_prior)), yet in textbook cases it lands in a conjugate family: for the Bernoulli it is $\mathrm{Beta}(1/2,1/2)$ ([Wikipedia: Jeffreys prior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffreys_prior)), and the Beta family is conjugate to the Bernoulli likelihood ([Wikipedia: Conjugate prior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_prior)).
- [Catastrophic Forgetting](node:Catastrophic%20Forgetting): elastic weight consolidation weights parameters by their Fisher information ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information)).
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing): frequentist tests and confidence intervals built from the MLE's asymptotic normal law use the information.
- [Quantum Sensing](node:Quantum%20Sensing): the quantum Fisher information plays the same role for quantum states.
- [Physical Model Sloppiness](node:Physical%20Model%20Sloppiness): read off the eigenvalue spectrum of the Fisher matrix.

### Common pitfalls
- **Non-regular models.** When the support depends on $\theta$, as for $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,\theta)$, the usual properties fail ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information)).
- **Unbiasedness.** Bias trades off against variance, unbiased estimators can be bad, and many quantities have no unbiased estimator ([CMU 36-705 Lecture 15](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf)); the relevant optimality statements are the convolution and minimax theorems. Pointwise, a non-regular estimator such as Hodges's can beat $I^{-1}$, but only on a Lebesgue-null set of parameters ([Chae 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.05247)).
- **Observed versus expected.** They differ in finite samples; Efron and Hinkley's argument for observed information concerns one-parameter families with an informative ancillary ([Wikipedia: Observed information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observed_information)).
- **Wrong model, wrong variance.** Under misspecification $I^{-1}$ is not the MLE's variance; use the sandwich $A^{-1}BA^{-1}$ ([Hoff and Wakefield](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1211.0087)).
- **Chentsov's hypotheses.** The classical uniqueness theorem is a finite-sample-space result; infinite cases need separate theorems with specified topologies ([Ay et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.6736)).

### Open problems
- **Attainability of the multiparameter quantum Fisher information bound.** Whether the QFI precision limit can be attained with measurements on individual copies lacks a general criterion, and the question was highlighted by Horodecki et al. (PRX Quantum 2022) as one of five problems in quantum information theory. A September 2026 preprint proves that deciding exact attainability is NP-hard even for real, constant-rank models, by reduction from bipartite separability, so unless P = NP no efficiently computable necessary-and-sufficient criterion exists; it is recent and not yet refereed ([Conlon et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35975)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fisher information (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information): definitions, regularity, properties, applications.
- **Reference:** [Fisher information metric (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information_metric): geometry, KL expansion, Chentsov.
- **Learn:** [CMU 36-705 Lecture 15 (Balakrishnan)](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/705/lec15.pdf): score, both forms of information, Cramér–Rao with proof.
- **Learn:** [Ly et al., A Tutorial on Fisher Information](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.01064): frequentist, Bayesian and MDL uses.
- **Primary:** [Fisher, Theory of Statistical Estimation (1925)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/S0305004100009580): Fisher's estimation paper in *Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc.*
- **Primary:** [Ay, Jost, Lê, Schwachhöfer, Information geometry and sufficient statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.6736): Chentsov's theorem beyond finite sample spaces.
- **Primary:** [Gassiat and Stoltz, The van Trees inequality in the spirit of Hájek and Le Cam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06431): van Trees under minimal assumptions and a LAM proof.
- **Further reading:** [van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics (CUP, 1998)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/asymptotic-statistics/A3C7DAD3F7E66A1FA60E9C8FE132EE1D): LAN (Ch. 7) and efficiency of estimators (Ch. 8).
references.Floating-Point Arithmetic and Numerical:
## Reference
### Overview
Floating-point arithmetic represents a real number as a signed significand of fixed length $p$ in a base $\beta$ (usually 2) multiplied by an integer power of the base, so the radix point "floats"; it is a form of scientific notation suited to very large and very small values, though representable numbers are not evenly spaced ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic)). Because only finitely many reals are representable, every operation rounds, and floating-point addition and multiplication are commutative but not associative: $(a+b)+c$ and $a+(b+c)$ can differ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic)). The IEEE 754 standard (1985, revised 2008 and 2019) fixes the formats, rounding rules and exceptional values, and many hardware floating-point units implement it ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754)).

Numerical stability is the study of how these rounding errors propagate through an algorithm. The organising idea, developed and popularised by James H. Wilkinson, is backward error analysis: show that the computed answer is the exact answer to a slightly perturbed problem ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic)). Combined with the condition number of the problem, which is independent of the arithmetic, this bounds the forward error: forward error $\lesssim$ condition number $\times$ backward error ([MIT 18.335](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-335j-introduction-to-numerical-methods-spring-2019/pages/week-2)).

The subject matters wherever reals are simulated: [scientific computing](node:Scientific%20Computing), [numerical linear algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra), and machine learning, where low precision such as half precision, increasingly available in hardware, brings speed and reduced communication and energy costs at the price of lower accuracy ([Higham and Mary, Acta Numerica](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/acta-numerica/article/mixed-precision-algorithms-in-numerical-linear-algebra/43CA701BA29251B5790C653E66F46197)).

### Formal definition
A floating-point number is a signed significand, a digit string of fixed length $p$ in base $\beta$, times $\beta^{e}$ for a signed integer exponent $e$ in a bounded range ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic)). An ulp (unit in the last place) is the gap between consecutive representable numbers with the same exponent, and IEEE 754 requires each basic operation to be correctly rounded, i.e. accurate to within half an ulp under the default round-to-nearest-ties-to-even ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic)). The standard's five rounding attributes are round to nearest (ties to even or away from zero), toward $0$, toward $+\infty$ and toward $-\infty$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754)).

Two conventions coexist: the unit roundoff $u=\tfrac12\beta^{1-p}$ is the maximum relative rounding error under round-to-nearest, while the "interval" machine epsilon $\epsilon=\beta^{1-p}$ is the gap between 1 and the next larger float, so $u=\epsilon/2$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_epsilon)). For IEEE binary32 ($p=24$) $u=2^{-24}\approx5.96\times10^{-8}$; for binary64 ($p=53$) $u=2^{-53}\approx1.11\times10^{-16}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_epsilon)).

**Standard model.** For $\mathrm{op}\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$ and floating-point $a,b$ whose result neither overflows nor underflows,
$$\mathrm{fl}(a\ \mathrm{op}\ b)=(a\ \mathrm{op}\ b)(1+\delta),\qquad |\delta|\le u.$$
Allowing underflow adds an absolute term $\eta$; with subnormal numbers $|\eta|\le \mathrm{UN}\cdot u$ for $\times,\div$ and $\eta=0$ for $\pm$ ([Demmel, Ma221](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt)).

**Stability notions.** For a problem $y=f(x)$ and computed $\hat y$: the forward error is $\hat y-y$; the backward error is the smallest $\Delta x$ with $f(x+\Delta x)=\hat y$; an algorithm is backward stable if the backward error is small (of order $u$) for all inputs, mixed (forward–backward) stable if $f(x+\Delta x)-\hat y$ and $\Delta x$ are both small, and forward stable if its forward error is comparable to that of a backward stable method, i.e. forward error divided by the condition number is small ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability)). The relative condition number of a differentiable $f$ can be expressed through the induced norm of its Jacobian; for $f(x)=Ax$ it is $\|A\|\|x\|/\|Ax\|\le\kappa(A)=\|A\|\|A^{-1}\|$ ([MIT 18.335](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-335j-introduction-to-numerical-methods-spring-2019/pages/week-2)).

### Key results
- **Forward error ≤ condition × backward error.** To first order, the relative forward error of any algorithm is bounded by the relative condition number times its relative backward error; so a backward stable algorithm applied to a well-conditioned problem is accurate. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability); [MIT 18.335](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-335j-introduction-to-numerical-methods-spring-2019/pages/week-2))
- **Exact subtraction (Sterbenz) and gradual underflow.** If $\tfrac12<x/y<2$ then $\mathrm{fl}(x-y)=x-y$ exactly; and with subnormals, $\mathrm{fl}(a-b)=0$ if and only if $a=b$. ([Demmel, Ma221](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt))
- **Error-free 2-Sum.** With $M\ge|x|$, set $S=\mathrm{fl}(M+x)$, $q=\mathrm{fl}(S-M)$, $r=\mathrm{fl}(x-q)$; then $S+r=M+x$ exactly, so the rounding error of an addition is itself a floating-point number that can be recovered. ([Demmel, Ma221](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt))
- **Horner's rule is backward stable.** Evaluating $p(x)=\sum_{i=0}^d a_ix^i$ by Horner's rule returns the exact value of $\sum_i(1+e_i)a_ix^i$ with $|e_i|\le 2d\,u$, hence relative error at most $\kappa(p,x)\cdot 2d\,u$ with condition number $\kappa(p,x)=\sum_i|a_ix^i|/|p(x)|$, which blows up near roots. ([Demmel, Ma221](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt))
- **Summation.** Recursive summation is backward stable but not forward stable: cancellation can make the exact sum arbitrarily small ([MIT 18.335](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-335j-introduction-to-numerical-methods-spring-2019/pages/week-2)). With condition number $\kappa=\sum|x_i|/|\sum x_i|$, naive summation's relative error bound grows like $O(n\varepsilon)\kappa$, pairwise summation's worst-case error grows only like $O(\log n)$, and Kahan's compensated summation satisfies $|E_n|\le[2\varepsilon+O(n\varepsilon^2)]\sum|x_i|$, essentially independent of $n$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahan_summation_algorithm))
- **Gaussian elimination and the growth factor (Wilkinson).** With growth factor $\rho(A)=\max_{i,j,k}|A^{(k)}_{ij}|/\max_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$, the computed solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies $\|x-\hat x\|_\infty/\|x\|_\infty\le4n^2\varepsilon_{\text{machine}}\,\kappa_\infty(A)\rho(A)$. Partial pivoting gives $\rho(A)\le2^{n-1}$, attained by an explicit matrix; complete pivoting gives $\rho\le 2n^{\ln n/4+1/2}$, improved by Bisain, Edelman and Urschel to $n^{c\log n+0.91}$ with $c\approx0.20781$. ([Peca-Medlin, arXiv:2308.16146](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.16146v2))

### Examples
- **Cancellation.** In four-significant-digit arithmetic, $f(x)=x(\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt x)$ gives $f(500)=10$, while the algebraically equal $g(x)=x/(\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt x)$ gives $11.17$; the true value is $\approx11.174755$. The subtraction of nearly equal rounded square roots destroys the leading digits. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability))
- **IEEE special values.** $1/0=+\infty$, $1/(-0)=-\infty$, and invalid operations such as $0/0$, $\infty-\infty$, $\sqrt{-1}$ produce NaN, with status flags recording each exception. ([Demmel, Ma221](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt))
- **Low-precision formats.** IEEE half precision has $p=11$ ($u=2^{-11}$, overflow threshold of order $10^4$), while bfloat16 has $p=8$ ($u=2^{-8}$) with the exponent range of single precision by design, so conversion between bfloat16 and single cannot overflow or underflow; 16-bit formats have become popular for machine learning. ([Demmel, Ma221](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt))

### History
IEEE 754-1985 standardised binary floating-point arithmetic; William Kahan, its primary architect, received the 1989 Turing Award ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic)). The 2008 revision merged 754-1985 with IEEE 854-1987, and fused multiply–add is among the required operations of the current standard; the 2019 revision mainly clarified the text, fixed defects and added recommended operations such as augmented addition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754)). Kahan published compensated summation in 1965 in *Communications of the ACM*; Babuška found a similar algorithm independently and Neumaier improved it in 1974 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahan_summation_algorithm)). Goldberg's survey "What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic" appeared in 1991 in *ACM Computing Surveys* 23(1):5–48 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/103162.103163)).

### Connections
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): floating point is a finite, non-associative approximation of the real field.
- [Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers](node:Matrix%20Norms%20and%20Condition%20Numbers): the condition number converts backward error into forward error.
- [Backward Error Analysis](node:Backward%20Error%20Analysis): Wilkinson's method, the main tool for proving stability.
- [Floating-Point Error and Interval Arithmetic](node:Floating-Point%20Error%20and%20Interval%20Arithmetic): interval methods give rigorous enclosures instead of a-priori bounds.
- [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): growth factors, Householder QR and iterative refinement are its stability questions.
- [Quantized Language Models](node:Quantized%20Language%20Models): low-bit formats push machine learning to the coarse end of the precision spectrum.

### Common pitfalls
- Confusing the two "epsilons": MATLAB's `eps` is $2^{-52}=2u$ for double, not the unit roundoff $u=2^{-53}$ ([Demmel, Ma221](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt)).
- Expecting forward stability from summation or polynomial evaluation: both are backward stable, but their relative error can be arbitrarily large when the result nearly cancels ([MIT 18.335](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-335j-introduction-to-numerical-methods-spring-2019/pages/week-2); [Demmel, Ma221](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt)).
- Reordering floating-point expressions (e.g. compiler reassociation under "fast math" options) can change results because addition is not associative ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic)).
- Blaming the algorithm for an ill-conditioned problem: the condition number $\sum|x_i|/|\sum x_i|$ of a sum measures the problem's intrinsic sensitivity to errors, regardless of the algorithm used ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahan_summation_algorithm)).

### Open problems
- **Worst-case growth under complete pivoting.** The old conjecture that complete-pivoting growth never exceeds $n$ was refuted by Gould's floating-point counterexample for $n=13$ (1991) and Edelman's exact-arithmetic confirmation about a year later ([Peca-Medlin, arXiv:2308.16146](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.16146v2)). Edelman and Urschel's computed lower bounds exceed $3n$ at $n=100$; their numerical evidence suggests that maximal growth exceeds $n$ only when $n\ge11$ and that maximal growth divided by $n$ likely tends to infinity ([Edelman and Urschel, arXiv:2303.04892](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04892)). Peca-Medlin calls the gap between the known lower and upper bounds a "huge gulf" that leaves room for future improvements ([Peca-Medlin, arXiv:2308.16146](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.16146v2)).
- **Partial-pivoting growth on orthogonal matrices.** The maximal partial-pivoting growth factor over orthogonal $n\times n$ matrices is $c\,2^{n-1}(1+o(1))$ with $c\in[1/\sqrt3,1)$ proved; Peca-Medlin conjectures $c=1/\sqrt3$ ([Peca-Medlin, arXiv:2308.16146](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.16146v2)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Floating-point arithmetic (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic): formats, rounding, non-associativity, history of IEEE 754.
- **Reference:** [Numerical stability (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability): forward, backward and mixed stability definitions.
- **Learn:** [Demmel, Ma221 Lecture 2 (Berkeley)](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/ma221_Fall20/Lectures/Lecture_02.txt): rounding model, IEEE exceptions, Horner's rule analysis.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.335J week 2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-335j-introduction-to-numerical-methods-spring-2019/pages/week-2): summation, backward stability and condition numbers.
- **Primary:** [Goldberg, What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic (ACM Computing Surveys 23(1), 1991)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/103162.103163): survey of floating-point arithmetic for computer scientists.
- **Primary:** [Higham and Mary, Mixed precision algorithms in numerical linear algebra (Acta Numerica 2022)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/acta-numerica/article/mixed-precision-algorithms-in-numerical-linear-algebra/43CA701BA29251B5790C653E66F46197): survey of mixed precision algorithms (iterative refinement, precision adapted to the data, mixed precision block FMA) and what is known about their stability.
- **Primary:** [Edelman and Urschel, Some new results on the maximum growth factor in Gaussian elimination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04892): complete-pivoting growth beyond $n$.
- **Further reading:** [Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, 2nd ed. (SIAM 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898718027): Higham's monograph, second edition.
references.Fluid Dynamics:
## Reference
### Overview
Fluid dynamics is the part of fluid mechanics that describes the flow of liquids and gases; solving a problem usually means finding velocity, pressure, density and temperature as functions of space and time. The fluid is treated as a continuum, so these quantities are defined at every point, and the governing equations are the conservation of mass, momentum and energy, closed by an equation of state. Before the twentieth century "hydrodynamics" was a synonym. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics))

The subject is organized by a few dichotomies. Compressible versus incompressible: a flow is treated as incompressible when the density of a fluid parcel does not change as it moves, $D\rho/Dt=0$, which for gases is usually adequate below Mach 0.3. Viscous versus inviscid: the [Reynolds number](node:Reynolds%20Number) compares inertia with viscosity; at $\mathrm{Re}\ll1$ viscosity dominates ([Stokes flow](node:Stokes%20Flow)), while at $\mathrm{Re}\gg1$ the flow away from walls is often modelled as inviscid by the Euler equations, with thin [boundary layers](node:Boundary%20Layers) where viscosity matters. Laminar versus turbulent, and Newtonian versus non-Newtonian (as in blood, latex, honey or lubricants). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics))

Its idealized limit, the **perfect fluid**, is characterized completely by its rest-frame mass density and isotropic pressure, with no shear stress, viscosity or [heat conduction](node:Heat%20Conduction). Classically perfect fluids obey the Euler equations and feel no drag; in [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity) they model stellar interiors and, under the cosmological principle, lead to the Friedmann equations. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_fluid))

### Formal definition
With density $\rho$, velocity $\mathbf u$, pressure $p$, body force per unit mass $\mathbf F$, enthalpy $h$, thermal conductivity $k$, temperature $T$ and viscous dissipation function $\Phi$, the differential conservation laws are
$$\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf u)=0,\qquad \frac{D\mathbf u}{Dt}=\mathbf F-\frac{\nabla p}{\rho}+(\text{viscous terms}),\qquad \rho\frac{Dh}{Dt}=\frac{Dp}{Dt}+\nabla\cdot(k\nabla T)+\Phi,$$
where $D/Dt=\partial_t+\mathbf u\cdot\nabla$ is the material derivative; a perfect gas closes the system with $p=\rho R_uT/M$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics))

**Euler equations.** Dropping viscosity and heat conduction gives the Euler equations of adiabatic inviscid flow, published by Euler in 1757. In the incompressible case they are the momentum equation with the constraint $\nabla\cdot\mathbf u=0$; the compressible Euler equations (mass, momentum, energy plus an equation of state) form a hyperbolic system of conservation laws whose characteristic speeds are real and which can develop shocks, governed by the Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_equations_%28fluid_dynamics%29))

**Viscous flow.** Adding the Newtonian viscous stress gives the [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations). **Reynolds number:** $\mathrm{Re}=uL/\nu=\rho uL/\mu$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynolds_number))

### Key results
- **Bernoulli's theorem.** For steady, incompressible flow with negligible viscosity, $\tfrac12v^2+gz+p/\rho$ is constant along each streamline; if the flow is also irrotational, the constant is the same throughout the flow ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli%27s_principle)). For steady, inviscid, incompressible flow in a conservative external field, the total head along a streamline is constant ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_equations_%28fluid_dynamics%29)).
- **Kelvin's circulation theorem (1869).** In an inviscid, barotropic fluid with conservative body forces, the circulation $\Gamma=\oint_C\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf s$ around a closed curve moving with the fluid satisfies $D\Gamma/Dt=0$. It fails with viscous stresses, non-conservative forces such as the [Coriolis force](node:Coriolis%20Force), or non-barotropic pressure–density relations; in a frame rotating at constant $\boldsymbol\Omega$ the Poincaré–Bjerknes theorem conserves $\oint(\mathbf u+\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)\cdot d\mathbf s=\int(\boldsymbol\omega+2\boldsymbol\Omega)\cdot\mathbf n\,dS$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin%27s_circulation_theorem))
- **d'Alembert's paradox (1752).** A body moving at constant velocity through an incompressible, inviscid, irrotational fluid experiences zero drag; the proof combines Bernoulli's equation for unsteady potential flow with the divergence theorem. Prandtl's 1904 boundary-layer theory, in which thin viscous layers cause separation and form drag, is accepted as the physical resolution, though a formal mathematical proof is lacking. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%27Alembert%27s_paradox))
- **Kolmogorov 1941 theory.** At very high Reynolds number, small-scale motions are statistically isotropic and their statistics depend only on $\nu$ and the dissipation rate $\varepsilon$, giving the Kolmogorov length $\eta=(\nu^3/\varepsilon)^{1/4}$; in the inertial range dimensional analysis gives the energy spectrum $E(k)=K_0\varepsilon^{2/3}k^{-5/3}$ with $K_0\approx1.5$. High-order structure functions deviate from the theory (intermittency). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbulence))
- **Onsager's conjecture (Isett).** Energy is conserved by [weak solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) of the 3D incompressible Euler equations in $C^\alpha$ for $\alpha>1/3$ (Eyink; Constantin, E and Titi), and for every $\alpha<1/3$ there are weak solutions in $C_tC_x^\alpha$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^3$ with compact temporal support that do not conserve kinetic energy. ([Isett](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08301))
- **Blowup with boundary (Chen–Hou).** The 2D Boussinesq and 3D axisymmetric Euler equations with smooth finite-energy initial data and a boundary develop a finite-time, nearly self-similar blowup. ([Chen and Hou](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07191))

### Examples
- **Pipe flow.** Fully developed pipe flow is laminar below $\mathrm{Re}\approx2300$, fully turbulent above about $2900$, and intermittent in between. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynolds_number))
- **Airfoil lift.** For steady flow, Kelvin's theorem is applied to a fixed curve enclosing an airfoil, and the circulation around that curve enters the theory of airfoil lift. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin%27s_circulation_theorem))
- **Relativistic matter.** Dust (zero pressure) and radiation (a photon gas) are special perfect fluids; [quark–gluon plasma](node:Quark–Gluon%20Plasma) and graphene are laboratory examples of nearly perfect fluids. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_fluid))
- **Computation.** Direct numerical simulation resolves turbulence only at moderate Reynolds number; engineering practice uses RANS turbulence models, large-eddy and detached-eddy simulation. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics))

### History
Daniel Bernoulli published his principle in *Hydrodynamica* (1738) and Euler derived it in its usual form in 1752 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli%27s_principle)); d'Alembert's paradox dates from 1752 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%27Alembert%27s_paradox)); Euler published his equations in 1757 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_equations_%28fluid_dynamics%29)). Kelvin's circulation theorem appeared in 1869, Poincaré's rotating version in 1893 and Bjerknes's in 1898 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin%27s_circulation_theorem)). Stokes introduced the Reynolds number in 1851, Reynolds popularized it in 1883, and Sommerfeld named it in 1908 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynolds_number)). Prandtl proposed boundary layers in 1904 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%27Alembert%27s_paradox)), and Kolmogorov's similarity theory dates from 1941 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbulence)). Batchelor's *An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics* is published by Cambridge University Press (2000 printing) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511800955)).

### Connections
- [Continuum Mechanics](node:Continuum%20Mechanics): fluids are continua whose stress is set by pressure and, for viscous flow, by strain rate.
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): the governing equations are nonlinear PDE systems.
- [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations): the viscous momentum law.
- [Euler Equations for Incompressible Fluids](node:Euler%20Equations%20for%20Incompressible%20Fluids) and [Compressible Euler Equations](node:Compressible%20Euler%20Equations): the inviscid limits.
- [Bernoulli's Equation](node:Bernoulli's%20Equation) and [Potential Flow and Airfoil Theory](node:Potential%20Flow%20and%20Airfoil%20Theory): consequences of inviscid, irrotational flow.
- [Vorticity and Circulation](node:Vorticity%20and%20Circulation): Kelvin's and Helmholtz's theorems.
- [Turbulence](node:Turbulence) and [Statistical Closure of Turbulence](node:Statistical%20Closure%20of%20Turbulence): high-Re flow and its modelling.
- [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws): compressible Euler is a hyperbolic system of conservation laws.
- [Reynolds Transport Theorem](node:Reynolds%20Transport%20Theorem): converts control-volume balances into differential form.
- [Computational Fluid Dynamics](node:Computational%20Fluid%20Dynamics) and [Finite Volume Methods for Fluids](node:Finite%20Volume%20Methods%20for%20Fluids): numerical practice.
- [Constitutive Models of Non-Newtonian Fluids](node:Constitutive%20Models%20of%20Non-Newtonian%20Fluids): stress laws beyond Newtonian viscosity.
- [Relativistic Fluid Equations](node:Relativistic%20Fluid%20Equations) and [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): the perfect fluid in relativity and cosmology.
- [Magnetohydrodynamics](node:Magnetohydrodynamics): fluids coupled to electromagnetic fields.
- [Kinetic Theory of Gases](node:Kinetic%20Theory%20of%20Gases) and [Boltzmann Equation](node:Boltzmann%20Equation): the microscopic origin of the continuum description.

### Common pitfalls
- Eddies do not by themselves indicate turbulence; laminar flow can contain them. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics))
- Inviscid theory cannot predict drag (d'Alembert's paradox); viscosity must be kept near solid surfaces even at high Reynolds number. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics))
- Bernoulli's equation along a streamline requires steady, incompressible, effectively inviscid flow; only for irrotational flow does the constant hold across streamlines. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli%27s_principle))
- Superfluids have zero viscosity but are not accurately described as perfect fluids; the two-fluid model treats them as a mixture of a normal and a perfect fluid. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_fluid))

### Open problems
- **3D Euler blowup without boundary.** Whether smooth solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations can become singular in finite time remains open, though some special classes of solutions are known to blow up ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_equations_%28fluid_dynamics%29)). Chen and Hou's result concerns the axisymmetric problem with a boundary, and the paper is Part I of a two-part work, with ideas for rigorous weighted estimates in Part II ([Chen and Hou](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07191)).
- **Turbulence.** Feynman called turbulence "the most important unsolved problem in classical physics"; Kolmogorov's self-similarity fails for high-order statistics (intermittency), and a complete description of turbulence remains open ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbulence)).
- **Viscous resolution of d'Alembert's paradox.** A formal mathematical proof that boundary layers produce the observed drag is lacking. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%27Alembert%27s_paradox))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fluid dynamics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics): conservation laws, classification of flows, turbulence modelling.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 2.25 Advanced Fluid Mechanics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-25-advanced-fluid-mechanics-fall-2013/): graduate survey covering conservation laws, Navier–Stokes, similarity, boundary layers, vorticity theorems, potential flow and turbulence.
- **Primary:** [Isett, A Proof of Onsager's Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08301): energy-dissipating Hölder weak solutions of Euler below exponent 1/3.
- **Primary:** [Chen and Hou, Stable nearly self-similar blowup of the 2D Boussinesq and 3D Euler equations with smooth data I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07191): blowup with boundary.
- **Further reading:** [Batchelor, An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics (Cambridge University Press)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511800955): Batchelor's textbook (2000 printing).
references.Formal Verification and Proof Assistants:
## Reference
### Overview
Formal verification is the act of proving or disproving the correctness of a system with respect to a formal specification, using mathematical methods. Its two main styles are *model checking*, a systematic and exhaustive exploration of a mathematical model of the system that is often fully automatic but does not in general scale to large systems, and *deductive verification*, in which the system, its specification and user annotations generate proof obligations that are discharged by proof assistants (HOL, ACL2, Isabelle, Rocq, PVS) or by automatic provers such as SMT solvers ([Wikipedia: Formal verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_verification)). Deductive verification of imperative programs rests on Floyd–Hoare logic and Dijkstra's weakest preconditions, which reduce correctness of a program to the validity of first-order formulas ([Wikipedia: Hoare logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoare_logic); [Wikipedia: Predicate transformer semantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predicate_transformer_semantics)).

A proof assistant (interactive theorem prover) is a software tool for developing formal proofs by human–machine collaboration: the user guides proof search while the machine records details and supplies some steps ([Wikipedia: Proof assistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_assistant)). nLab distinguishes a *foundational* thread, seeking the best foundation for formal mathematics (from Automath's dependent types through the calculus of constructions and the calculus of inductive constructions to homotopy type theory), and a *coverage* thread, formalising as much existing mathematics as possible ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proof+assistant)). Type-theoretic systems such as Rocq and Lean rest on [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory) through the [Curry-Howard Correspondence](node:Curry-Howard%20Correspondence), under which a proof is a program and the proposition it proves is its type ([Wikipedia: Curry–Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence)).

The area matters for software and hardware assurance (verified compilers and kernels; formal verification is used by most or all leading hardware companies) and for mathematics, where the four colour theorem, the Feit–Thompson theorem, the Kepler conjecture and recent research results have machine-checked proofs ([Wikipedia: Formal verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_verification); [Wikipedia: Proof assistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_assistant); [Hales et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.02155)). Proof assistants are also proposed as the verifier for AI mathematical reasoning, since they check reasoning and give automatic feedback ([Yang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16075)).

### Formal definition
**Specification and soundness.** Given a system model $M$ and a formal property $\varphi$, verification establishes $M\models\varphi$ or refutes it. A sound technique gives a result only after covering the entire space of possibilities; an unsound (for example bounded) technique covers a subset and can be decidable where no decidable sound technique exists ([Wikipedia: Formal verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_verification)).

**Model checking.** Given a finite structure $M$ with initial state $s$ and a temporal-logic formula $p$, decide whether $M,s\models p$; for finite $M$ this reduces to graph search ([Wikipedia: Model checking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_checking)). Properties are written in temporal logics. LTL formulas are built from atomic propositions with $\neg,\vee$, next $\mathbf X$ and until $\mathbf U$, and are evaluated over infinite traces; safety has the form $\mathbf G\neg\varphi$ and liveness $\mathbf{GF}\psi$ ([Wikipedia: LTL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_temporal_logic)). CTL is branching-time: each temporal operator is paired with a path quantifier $\mathbf A$ (all paths) or $\mathbf E$ (some path) ([Wikipedia: CTL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computation_tree_logic)). In a finite computation structure $K=(W,\curvearrowright,v)$ the satisfaction sets are computed by fixpoints, e.g.
$$[\![\mathbf{EF}P]\!]=\mu Z.\,([\![P]\!]\cup\tau_{\mathbf{EX}}(Z)),\qquad [\![\mathbf{EG}P]\!]=\nu Z.\,([\![P]\!]\cap\tau_{\mathbf{EX}}(Z)),$$
$$[\![\mathbf{E}(P\,\mathbf U\,Q)]\!]=\mu Z.\,([\![Q]\!]\cup([\![P]\!]\cap\tau_{\mathbf{EX}}(Z))),$$
where $\tau_{\mathbf{EX}}(Z)=\{s\in W: s\curvearrowright t\text{ for some }t\in Z\}$ and $\mu,\nu$ denote least and greatest fixpoints ([CMU 15-414 notes](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s23/lectures/23-ctl-checking.pdf)).

**Hoare logic.** A Hoare triple $\{P\}\,C\,\{Q\}$ asserts that if precondition $P$ holds and command $C$ terminates, postcondition $Q$ holds afterwards; standard Hoare logic proves only this partial correctness, and total correctness needs a loop variant decreasing in a well-founded order. The system has axioms for skip and assignment and rules for composition, conditionals, while loops and consequence ([Wikipedia: Hoare logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoare_logic)). Dijkstra's weakest precondition $\mathrm{wp}(S,R)$ is the predicate $Q$ such that $\{P\}S\{R\}$ holds iff $P\Rightarrow Q$, where the triple is read in the total-correctness sense (the while rule for wp requires a variant and wp ensures termination); the weakest liberal precondition $\mathrm{wlp}(S,R)$, the weakest condition under which $S$ either does not terminate or establishes $R$, corresponds to partial-correctness Hoare logic and differs from wp only in not requiring loop variants. wp satisfies
$$\mathrm{wp}(x:=E,R)=R[x\leftarrow E],\quad \mathrm{wp}(S_1;S_2,R)=\mathrm{wp}(S_1,\mathrm{wp}(S_2,R)),$$
$$\mathrm{wp}(\textbf{if }E\textbf{ then }S_1\textbf{ else }S_2,R)=(E\Rightarrow\mathrm{wp}(S_1,R))\wedge(\neg E\Rightarrow \mathrm{wp}(S_2,R)),$$
so for loop-free code a triple is valid iff $P\Rightarrow\mathrm{wp}(S,Q)$, a first-order verification condition ([Wikipedia: Predicate transformer semantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predicate_transformer_semantics)).

**Propositions as types.** Implication, conjunction, disjunction, $\forall$ and $\exists$ correspond to function, product, sum, dependent product $\Pi_{x:A}B(x)$ and dependent sum $\Sigma_{x:A}B(x)$ types; $\top$ and $\bot$ to unit and empty types. In natural deduction versus simply typed lambda calculus, hypotheses are free variables, modus ponens is application, implication introduction is abstraction, normalisation of deductions is weak normalisation of terms, and provability is type inhabitation ([Wikipedia: Curry–Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence)).

**Trusted kernels.** A system meets the de Bruijn criterion when its proofs can be checked by a small program (some checkers have under a thousand lines of core code); the LCF approach, from Edinburgh LCF and inherited by the HOL family, uses a functional metalanguage as the theorem prover's metalanguage. Rocq uses the calculus of inductive constructions, Lean the same with non-cumulative universes, Isabelle/HOL a foundation close to HOL's, HOL Light is a minimalist HOL, and Mizar uses first-order logic with Tarski–Grothendieck set theory ([Wikipedia: Proof assistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_assistant)).

### Key results
- **Rice's theorem.** For an admissible numbering $\varphi$ of the partial computable functions, every $P\subseteq\mathbb N$ with $P\ne\emptyset,\mathbb N$ and $\varphi_m=\varphi_n\Rightarrow(m\in P\Leftrightarrow n\in P)$ is undecidable. So no program decides a non-trivial behavioural property of arbitrary programs, and verification either requires annotations (Hoare logic), restricts programs, accepts incompleteness ([Abstract Interpretation](node:Abstract%20Interpretation)), or restricts to finite-state systems (model checking) ([Wikipedia: Rice's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice%27s_theorem)).
- **Complexity of LTL.** LTL model checking and satisfiability are PSPACE-complete, and LTL synthesis is 2EXPTIME-complete. In the automata-theoretic approach the system and the negated property are converted to Büchi automata, and the system satisfies the property iff their product is empty ([Wikipedia: LTL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_temporal_logic)).
- **Expressiveness.** By Kamp's theorem LTL is equivalent to first-order logic of order $\mathrm{FO}[<]$ and to star-free languages. CTL and LTL are incomparable: $\mathbf{FG}\,p$ is LTL-expressible but not CTL-expressible, $\mathbf{AG\,EF}\,p$ the reverse; both are fragments of CTL* ([Wikipedia: LTL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_temporal_logic); [Wikipedia: CTL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computation_tree_logic)).
- **Fixpoint correctness of CTL checking.** In a finite computation structure the equations above hold, with $\mathbf{EF},\mathbf{EU},\mathbf{AU}$ as least and $\mathbf{EG},\mathbf{AG}$ as greatest fixpoints; the $\mathbf{AU}$ case uses Kőnig's lemma ([CMU 15-414 notes](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s23/lectures/23-ctl-checking.pdf)).
- **Verified compiler.** Leroy's CompCert back-end, from the Cminor intermediate language to PowerPC assembly, is written and proved in Coq to preserve semantics, so safety properties proved of the source also hold of the compiled executable ([Leroy 2009](https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.2137)). The full CompCert compiles a large subset of C99 (Clight) to ARM, PowerPC, RISC-V, x86 and x86-64 ([Wikipedia: CompCert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CompCert)).
- **Verified kernel.** seL4 (about 8,700 lines of C and 600 of assembler) was proved functionally correct against an abstract specification, implying it never crashes or performs an unsafe operation, assuming correctness of compiler, assembly code, hardware and boot code; the whole proof is about 200,000 lines of Isabelle script and cost about 20 person-years ([Klein et al. 2009](https://www.read.seas.harvard.edu/~kohler/class/cs260r-s17/klein10sel4.pdf)).
- **Formalised mathematics.** Kepler conjecture in HOL Light and Isabelle (Flyspeck, Hales and 21 coauthors) ([Hales et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.02155)); four colour theorem (Rocq, 2005) and Feit–Thompson (Rocq, 2012) ([Wikipedia: Proof assistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_assistant)); the Clausen–Scholze theorem $\mathrm{Ext}^i(\mathcal M_{p'}(S),V)=0$ for $i\ge1$, $0<p'<p\le1$, $S$ profinite and $V$ $p$-Banach, completed in Lean on 14 July 2022 (Liquid Tensor Experiment) ([Lean community](https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog/posts/lte-final)); and Marton's polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture over $\mathbb F_2^n$ in Lean 4 ([PFR project](https://teorth.github.io/pfr)).

### Examples
- **Proof-by-program:** a proof of $(\beta\to\alpha)\to(\gamma\to\beta)\to\gamma\to\alpha$ is the term $\lambda a.\lambda b.\lambda g.\,a\,(b\,g)$; a proof of $\alpha\to\alpha$ is $\lambda x.x$ ([Wikipedia: Curry–Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence)).
- **Verification condition:** for $\{x\ge0\}\;x:=x+1\;\{x>0\}$, $\mathrm{wp}=(x+1>0)$, and the triple holds because $x\ge0\Rightarrow x+1>0$, by the assignment rule ([Wikipedia: Predicate transformer semantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predicate_transformer_semantics)).
- **SMT-backed verifiers:** Dafny (Leino, Microsoft Research, 2009) takes `requires`/`ensures` contracts, loop `invariant`s and `decreases` measures, translates to the Boogie intermediate language, and discharges obligations with Z3 ([Wikipedia: Dafny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dafny)). F* (Microsoft Research and Inria, 2011) combines dependent, refinement and monadic-effect types, checked by SMT solving plus manual proofs, and extracts to OCaml, F#, C or WebAssembly ([Wikipedia: F*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F*_%28programming_language%29)). Since 2017 Firefox's NSS library uses code from the verified HACL* library ([Wikipedia: Formal verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_verification)).
- **Taming state explosion:** symbolic model checking with [Binary Decision Diagrams](node:Binary%20Decision%20Diagrams), bounded model checking that unrolls $k$ steps into a SAT instance, abstraction and CEGAR ([Wikipedia: Model checking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_checking)).

### History
Floyd (1967) and Hoare (1969) founded program logic, and Dijkstra introduced weakest preconditions in *Comm. ACM*, August 1975 ([Wikipedia: Hoare logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoare_logic); [Wikipedia: Predicate transformer semantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predicate_transformer_semantics)). Pnueli proposed LTL in 1977 ([Wikipedia: LTL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_temporal_logic)) and Clarke and Emerson CTL in 1981 ([Wikipedia: CTL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computation_tree_logic)); Pnueli received the 1996 Turing Award, and Clarke, Emerson and Sifakis shared the 2007 award for founding model checking, with Queille and Sifakis credited for early work ([Wikipedia: Model checking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_checking)). De Bruijn's Automath (from 1967) is often considered the first proof checker; Edinburgh LCF led to HOL ([Wikipedia: Proof assistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_assistant)). Mizar's library had 1,150 articles and about 52,000 theorems around 2012 ([Wikipedia: Mizar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizar_system)); nLab still calls it orders of magnitude larger than others ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proof+assistant)), but by May 2025 Lean's mathlib held over 210,000 theorems and 100,000 definitions ([Wikipedia: Lean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lean_%28proof_assistant%29)). The Imperial College FLT project, led by Kevin Buzzard, is an ongoing effort to formalise Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean ([FLT project](https://imperialcollegelondon.github.io/FLT)); Separately, in September 2026 Anthropic reported a Lean 4 formalisation of Fermat's Last Theorem produced largely by AI agents, which Buzzard compiled and checked ([Wikipedia: Lean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lean_%28proof_assistant%29)). Its public repository states that the theorem `fermat_last_theorem` (for $n\ge3$ and positive $a,b,c$, $a^n+b^n\ne c^n$) is built on Mathlib and depends only on Lean's three standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`, with no `sorry` or added axioms, and was rechecked by an independent kernel and a statement comparator; it adds that no tool can check that each intermediate theorem means what its name suggests. It is a research artifact, not peer-reviewed and not merged into Mathlib ([anthropics/fermats-last-theorem](https://github.com/anthropics/fermats-last-theorem); [Wikipedia: Lean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lean_%28proof_assistant%29)).

### Connections
- [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory) and [Homotopy Type Theory](node:Homotopy%20Type%20Theory): foundations of Rocq, Lean and Agda.
- [Curry-Howard Correspondence](node:Curry-Howard%20Correspondence) and [Lambda Calculus](node:Lambda%20Calculus): proofs are typed terms.
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic) and [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): Mizar's foundation and the language of verification conditions.
- [Rice's Theorem](node:Rice's%20Theorem) and [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory): why verification cannot be fully automatic.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): the kernel is trusted, not self-certified.
- [Model Checking](node:Model%20Checking), [Binary Decision Diagrams](node:Binary%20Decision%20Diagrams), [SAT and SMT Solving](node:SAT%20and%20SMT%20Solving): automatic back ends.
- [Program Logic](node:Program%20Logic) and [Separation Logic](node:Separation%20Logic): Hoare-style logics for programs and heaps.
- [Fixed Points in Complete Lattices](node:Fixed%20Points%20in%20Complete%20Lattices): CTL operators are least/greatest fixpoints.
- [Abstract Interpretation](node:Abstract%20Interpretation): sound but incomplete static analysis.
- [Automated Theorem Proving](node:Automated%20Theorem%20Proving), [Neural Theorem Proving](node:Neural%20Theorem%20Proving), [Learning Mathematical Proof](node:Learning%20Mathematical%20Proof): automation and ML on top of proof assistants.
- [Compilers](node:Compilers), [Operating Systems](node:Operating%20Systems), [Programming Language Semantics](node:Programming%20Language%20Semantics): CompCert and seL4.
- [Proof-Carrying Code](node:Proof-Carrying%20Code): shipping a checkable proof with code.
- [Sphere Packings and Tilings](node:Sphere%20Packings%20and%20Tilings): the Kepler conjecture.

### Common pitfalls
- **Verified against what?** Verification asks whether the product conforms to its specification ("Have we made what we were trying to make?"); validation asks whether it meets the user's actual needs ([Wikipedia: Formal verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_verification)); generated specifications must be neither too strong nor too weak ([Yang et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16075v1)).
- **Trusted base.** seL4's proof assumes a correct compiler, assembly code, hardware and boot code ([Klein et al. 2009](https://www.read.seas.harvard.edu/~kohler/class/cs260r-s17/klein10sel4.pdf)); kernel soundness bugs have been found and fixed in Lean, HOL Light and Rocq ([Wikipedia: Proof assistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_assistant)).
- **Partial correctness.** A Hoare triple says nothing about termination unless total-correctness rules with variants are used ([Wikipedia: Hoare logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoare_logic)).
- **Compiling is not correctness of autoformalisation.** Neither BLEU nor compile rate correlates with human judgement of autoformalised statements ([Yang et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16075v1)).

### Open problems
Yang et al. present these as open challenges ([Yang et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16075v1)):
- **Synthetic data beyond competition math.** AlphaProof autoformalised one million IMO-like problems into one hundred million formal theorems; generalising this beyond domains with many human-written problems, such as research mathematics, "remains an open question". Proof Pile gathered only about 500MB of formal proofs across six systems ([Yang et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16075v1)).
- **Evaluating autoformalisation.** No established automatic metric aligns with human evaluation of autoformalised statements, which the authors call the main obstacle to robust autoformalisation ([Yang et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16075v1)).
- **Verified generation.** Constrained decoding guarantees syntax, but ensuring other semantic properties of generated code "remains an open challenge"; AI-supported proof engineering for large systems like seL4 is an "underexplored direction" ([Yang et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16075v1)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Proof assistant (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_assistant): systems, foundations, de Bruijn criterion, landmark formalisations.
- **Reference:** [proof assistant (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proof+assistant): foundational versus coverage threads, type-theoretic systems.
- **Learn:** [Software Foundations (UPenn)](https://softwarefoundations.cis.upenn.edu/): seven machine-checked Rocq volumes, from logic through Hoare logic to separation logic and Verifiable C.
- **Learn:** [CMU 15-414 lecture notes on CTL model checking](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s23/lectures/23-ctl-checking.pdf): fixpoint algorithm with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Leroy, A formally verified compiler back-end (JAR 2009)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.2137): CompCert's semantic-preservation proof in Coq.
- **Primary:** [Klein et al., seL4: Formal Verification of an OS Kernel (SOSP 2009)](https://www.read.seas.harvard.edu/~kohler/class/cs260r-s17/klein10sel4.pdf): functional correctness of a general-purpose kernel.
- **Primary:** [Hales et al., A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.02155): Flyspeck.
- **Primary:** [The mathlib Community, The Lean mathematical library](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.09336): design of mathlib.
- **Further reading:** [Yang et al., Formal Mathematical Reasoning: A New Frontier in AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16075): survey of autoformalisation, neural proving and verified generation with open challenges.
references.Four-Vectors and Relativistic Momentum:
## Reference
### Overview
A four-vector is a quantity with four components that transforms under Lorentz transformations exactly as the event coordinates $(ct,x,y,z)$ do. The energy $E$ and three-momentum $\mathbf{p}$ of a particle form such a vector, the four-momentum $p^\mu=(E/c,\mathbf{p})$, and its Minkowski square is the same for all inertial observers: $-E^2/c^2+|\mathbf{p}|^2=-m^2c^2$ in signature $(-,+,+,+)$. ([Sheffield PHY206 Lecture 9](https://www.hep.shef.ac.uk/edaw/PHY206/Site/2011_course_files/phy206lec9.pdf); [Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum))

Packaging energy and momentum together turns conservation of energy and of momentum into conservation of one four-vector, and gives invariants (masses, scalar products, Mandelstam variables) that can be evaluated in whichever frame is convenient. This is the working language of particle kinematics: the Particle Data Group's kinematics review states centre-of-mass energies, decay momenta and scattering variables entirely in terms of four-momenta. ([PDG Review: Kinematics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-kinematics.pdf))

The invariant mass of a system is the norm of its total four-momentum and is not the sum of the constituents' rest masses; kinetic and binding energy contribute. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum))

### Formal definition
**Four-momentum.** With $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, $\mathbf{p}=\gamma m\mathbf{v}$, and $E=\gamma mc^2$,
$$p^\mu=(E/c,\ p_x,\ p_y,\ p_z)=m\,u^\mu,\qquad u^\mu=\gamma(c,\mathbf{v}),$$
and in signature $(-,+,+,+)$, $p\cdot p=\eta_{\mu\nu}p^\mu p^\nu=-E^2/c^2+|\mathbf{p}|^2=-m^2c^2$; the minus sign reflects that $p$ is timelike for massive particles. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum)) In the particle-physics signature $(+,-,-,-)$ with $c=1$, $p^2=E^2-|\mathbf{p}|^2=m^2$, and the scalar product $p_1\cdot p_2=E_1E_2-\mathbf{p}_1\cdot\mathbf{p}_2$ is frame independent. ([PDG Review: Kinematics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-kinematics.pdf))

**Covariant components and the action.** In $(-,+,+,+)$, $p_\mu=\eta_{\mu\nu}p^\nu=(-E/c,\mathbf{p})$, which equals $\partial S/\partial x^\mu$ for the action $S$ along classical paths, giving the relativistic Hamilton–Jacobi equation $\eta^{\mu\nu}\,\partial_\mu S\,\partial_\nu S=-m^2c^2$. In an electromagnetic potential $A^\mu=(\phi/c,\mathbf{A})$ the canonical four-momentum is $P^\mu=p^\mu+qA^\mu$, which is not gauge invariant. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum))

**Four-force.** $F^\mu=dp^\mu/d\tau$. For constant mass, $F=m\,a=(\gamma\,\mathbf{f}\cdot\mathbf{u}/c,\ \gamma\mathbf{f})$ with $\mathbf{f}=d\mathbf{p}/dt$ and $\mathbf{f}\cdot\mathbf{u}=dE/dt$. ([Wikipedia: Four-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-force)) Because $p\cdot p$ is constant, $p_\mu a^\mu=\frac{1}{2m}\frac{d(p\cdot p)}{d\tau}=0$: four-acceleration is orthogonal to four-velocity. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum)) The Lorentz force is $F^\mu=qF^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. ([Wikipedia: Four-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-force))

### Key results
- **Energy–momentum relation.** $E^2=(pc)^2+(mc^2)^2$; for $m=0$, $E=pc$; for $v\ll c$, $E\approx mc^2+\tfrac12mv^2$. ([Wikipedia: Energy–momentum relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy%E2%80%93momentum_relation))
- **Boost law.** For a frame moving with velocity $\boldsymbol\beta_f$ ($c=1$), $E^*=\gamma_f(E-\beta_fp_\parallel)$, $p^*_\parallel=\gamma_f(p_\parallel-\beta_fE)$, $\mathbf{p}^*_T=\mathbf{p}_T$; the particle velocity is $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{p}/E$. ([PDG Review: Kinematics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-kinematics.pdf))
- **Centre-of-mass energy.** For masses $m_1,m_2$ at angle $\theta$, $E_{\rm cm}=[(E_1+E_2)^2-(\mathbf{p}_1+\mathbf{p}_2)^2]^{1/2}=[m_1^2+m_2^2+2E_1E_2(1-\beta_1\beta_2\cos\theta)]^{1/2}$; on a target $m_2$ at rest, $E_{\rm cm}=(m_1^2+m_2^2+2E_{1,\rm lab}m_2)^{1/2}$. ([PDG Review: Kinematics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-kinematics.pdf)) Setting $E_{\rm cm}$ equal to the total final rest mass gives the fixed-target threshold, because at threshold the products are at rest in the centre-of-mass frame. ([Sheffield PHY206 Lecture 9](https://www.hep.shef.ac.uk/edaw/PHY206/Site/2011_course_files/phy206lec9.pdf))
- **Two-body decay.** In the rest frame of $M\to1+2$, $E_1=(M^2-m_2^2+m_1^2)/(2M)$ and $|\mathbf{p}_1|=|\mathbf{p}_2|=\lambda^{1/2}(M^2,m_1^2,m_2^2)/(2M)$ with the Källén function $\lambda(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2-2\alpha\beta-2\alpha\gamma-2\beta\gamma$. ([PDG Review: Kinematics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-kinematics.pdf))
- **Mandelstam variables.** For $1+2\to3+4$: $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$, $t=(p_1-p_3)^2$, $u=(p_1-p_4)^2$, with $s+t+u=m_1^2+m_2^2+m_3^2+m_4^2$, and $d\sigma/dt=|\mathcal{M}|^2/(64\pi s|\mathbf{p}_{1\rm cm}|^2)$. ([PDG Review: Kinematics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-kinematics.pdf))
- **Curved spacetime.** For a particle in general relativity the inner product keeps its form with the Minkowski metric replaced by $g$: $P^\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}P^\beta=(mc)^2$ in signature $(+,-,-,-)$. ([Wikipedia: Energy–momentum relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy%E2%80%93momentum_relation))

### Examples
- **Invariant mass of two particles.** Four-momenta $(5,4,0,0)$ and $(5,-4,0,0)$ GeV/$c$ each have rest mass $3$ GeV/$c^2$, but the pair has invariant mass $10$ GeV/$c^2$. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum))
- **Decay to a photon.** For $M_1\to m_2+\gamma$, equating the squares of the initial and final four-momenta gives, in the rest frame of the daughter, $E_\gamma=(M_1^2-m_2^2)c^2/(2m_2)$, with no Lorentz transformation needed. ([Sheffield PHY206 Lecture 9](https://www.hep.shef.ac.uk/edaw/PHY206/Site/2011_course_files/phy206lec9.pdf))
- **Maximum mass from a fixed target.** A 10 GeV electron on a proton at rest can create total rest mass at most $Mc^2=m_pc^2\sqrt{2E/(m_pc^2)+1}\approx4.43$ GeV (electron mass neglected), far less than 10 GeV. ([Sheffield PHY206 Lecture 9](https://www.hep.shef.ac.uk/edaw/PHY206/Site/2011_course_files/phy206lec9.pdf)) Similarly a 0.80 GeV/$c$ kaon on a proton gives $E_{\rm cm}=1.699$ GeV and $p_{\rm cm}=0.442$ GeV/$c$. ([PDG Review: Kinematics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-kinematics.pdf))
- **GZK threshold.** For $p+\gamma_{\rm CMB}\to\pi^++n$ head-on, with $E_\gamma=6\times10^{-4}$ eV, the threshold is $E_p=[2m_nm_\pi c^4+(m_\pi c^2)^2]/(4E_\gamma)\approx1.2\times10^{20}$ eV. ([Sheffield PHY206 Lecture 9](https://www.hep.shef.ac.uk/edaw/PHY206/Site/2011_course_files/phy206lec9.pdf))
- **Compton scattering.** Energy and momentum conservation for a photon scattering off an electron at rest give $\lambda'-\lambda=\frac{h}{m_ec}(1-\cos\theta)$, with $h/(m_ec)\approx2.43\times10^{-12}$ m; Compton reported the effect in 1923. ([Wikipedia: Compton scattering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compton_scattering))

### History
Poincaré's Palermo paper (published January 1906) showed that $x^2+y^2+z^2-c^2t^2$ is invariant, named the transformations the Lorentz group, treated a Lorentz transformation as a rotation in four-dimensional space, and already used four-vectors. Planck (1906) defined relativistic momentum and gave the correct longitudinal and transverse masses, correcting a small error in Einstein's 1905 expression. Minkowski (1907/08) developed the four-dimensional formalism, including a four-dimensional formulation of electrodynamics and the terms world line and proper time. ([Wikipedia: History of special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_special_relativity)) Poincaré's paper is "Sur la dynamique de l'électron", Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 21 (1906) 129–175. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF03013466)) The energy–momentum relation appears in Planck's 1906 article, and Gordon (1926) and Dirac (1928) used it. ([Wikipedia: Energy–momentum relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy%E2%80%93momentum_relation))

### Connections
- [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime) and [Light Cone](node:Light%20Cone): the metric that defines the invariant and the timelike/null split.
- [Lorentz Transformations](node:Lorentz%20Transformations) and [Special Relativity](node:Special%20Relativity): the transformation law defining a four-vector.
- [Four-Velocity](node:Four-Velocity): $p^\mu=mu^\mu$ and $u\cdot a=0$.
- [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws): conservation of the total four-momentum.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics) and [Principle of Least Action](node:Principle%20of%20Least%20Action): $p_\mu=\partial_\mu S$ and the relativistic Hamilton–Jacobi equation.
- [Electromagnetic Field Tensor](node:Electromagnetic%20Field%20Tensor) and [Magnetic Vector Potential](node:Magnetic%20Vector%20Potential): Lorentz four-force and canonical momentum $p+qA$.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): four-momentum density of fields and matter.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): $g_{\alpha\beta}P^\alpha P^\beta=(mc)^2$ along [geodesics](node:Geodesics).
- [Collider Physics](node:Collider%20Physics) and [Feynman Diagrams](node:Feynman%20Diagrams): invariant masses and Mandelstam variables.
- [Klein–Gordon Equation](node:Klein–Gordon%20Equation) and [Dirac Equation](node:Dirac%20Equation): wave equations built on the energy–momentum relation.
- [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background): the photon target behind the GZK threshold.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Relativistic kinematics and stress energy](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Relativistic%20kinematics%20and%20stress%20energy)

### Common pitfalls
- **Signature.** $p\cdot p=-m^2c^2$ in $(-,+,+,+)$ but $+m^2c^2$ in $(+,-,-,-)$; Wikipedia's four-momentum article and the PDG use opposite conventions. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum); [PDG Review: Kinematics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-kinematics.pdf))
- **Sign of $p_\mu=\pm\partial_\mu S$.** The sign depends on the signature and on the sign convention for the action; even Wikipedia's four-momentum article uses both $p_\mu=\partial S/\partial x^\mu$ and $p_\mu\leftrightarrow-\partial S/\partial x^\mu$ in different places, so fix conventions before using it. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum))
- **Conservation is per observer; invariants are not.** Energy and momentum before and after a process are equal only when measured by the same observer, whereas $p\cdot p$ of the total can be compared across frames. ([Sheffield PHY206 Lecture 9](https://www.hep.shef.ac.uk/edaw/PHY206/Site/2011_course_files/phy206lec9.pdf))
- **Adding rest masses.** A system's invariant mass can exceed the sum of its constituents' rest masses. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum))
- **Photons and $E=\gamma mc^2$.** For $m=0$ use $E=pc$. ([Wikipedia: Energy–momentum relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy%E2%80%93momentum_relation))
- **Continuous matter is a different construction.** The four-momentum article's section on continuous matter in curved spacetime relies on a single cited source and uses different sign conventions; it is not the standard particle treatment, which is $g_{\alpha\beta}P^\alpha P^\beta=(mc)^2$. ([Wikipedia: Four-momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-momentum); [Wikipedia: Energy–momentum relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy%E2%80%93momentum_relation))

### Open problems
- **What ends the cosmic-ray spectrum?** The GZK threshold above is a direct four-momentum calculation; the 2019 review "Open Questions in Cosmic-Ray Research at Ultrahigh Energies" lists the origin of the end of the cosmic-ray spectrum among its open questions. ([Alves Batista et al., arXiv:1903.06714](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06714))
