## Reference
### Overview
Fourier analysis studies how functions on the real line, the circle, the integers, a finite cyclic group, or more generally a locally compact abelian group can be represented or approximated by sums of trigonometric functions or complex exponentials; decomposing a function is analysis and rebuilding it is synthesis. Exponentials are eigenfunctions of differentiation, convolution becomes multiplication, and the discrete version is computed quickly by the FFT. ([Wikipedia, Fourier analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_analysis))

The variants are distinguished by whether the domain is continuous or discrete and whether the function is periodic: Fourier series on the circle, the Fourier transform on $\mathbb{R}$, the discrete-time transform on $\mathbb{Z}$, and the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) on a finite cyclic group. All are cases of the Fourier transform on a locally compact abelian (LCA) group, which takes functions on the group to functions on its Pontryagin dual. ([Wikipedia, Fourier analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_analysis); [Wikipedia, Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) For compact, possibly non-abelian groups, the Peter–Weyl theorem replaces exponentials by matrix coefficients of irreducible unitary representations. ([Wikipedia, Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))

The theory has an easy $L^2$ core and a hard $L^p$ and pointwise theory. In $L^2$ the transform is unitary (Parseval, Plancherel). The Fourier series of a continuous function can diverge at a point and that of an $L^1$ function everywhere, yet Carleson proved almost-everywhere convergence for $L^2$. Partial sums converge in $L^p$ norm for $1<p<\infty$ but not for $p=1$ ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf)); on $\mathbb{R}$, the boundedness of the Hilbert transform on $L^p$ implies $L^p$ convergence of the symmetric partial-sum operator of the Fourier integral. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform))

### Formal definition
For a $2\pi$-periodic $F$ integrable on $(-\pi,\pi)$, i.e. $F\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ with $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, the Fourier coefficients, partial sums, Cesàro (Fejér) means and Abel means are ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf))
$$
c_n=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}F(x)e^{-inx}\,dx,\quad s_N=\sum_{|n|\le N}c_ne^{inx},\quad \sigma_N=\sum_{|n|\le N}\Bigl(1-\frac{|n|}{N}\Bigr)c_ne^{inx},\quad A_r=\sum_{n}r^{|n|}c_ne^{inx}.
$$
One has $s_N=D_N*F$, $\sigma_N=K_N*F$, $A_r=P_r*F$ with $D_N(x)=\sin((N+\tfrac12)x)/\sin(x/2)$, $P_r(x)=(1-r^2)/|1-re^{ix}|^2$ and $f*g(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x-y)g(y)\,dy$. ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf)) The Fejér kernel is the average of Dirichlet kernels, with closed form $K_N(x)=\frac1N\bigl(\sin(Nx/2)/\sin(x/2)\bigr)^2\ge0$. ([Wikipedia, Fejér kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fej%C3%A9r_kernel)) For period $P$, $c_n=P^{-1}\int_0^Ps(x)e^{-2\pi inx/P}\,dx$. ([Wikipedia, Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series))

For $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, in the unitary ordinary-frequency convention ([Wikipedia, Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform)),
$$
\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\,dx,\qquad f(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i\xi x}\,d\xi,
$$
the inversion holding for almost every $x$ when $f$ and $\widehat f$ are both integrable. $\widehat f$ is uniformly continuous, bounded by $\|f\|_1$, and vanishes at infinity (Riemann–Lebesgue); it extends unitarily to $L^2$ and by duality to tempered distributions. ([Wikipedia, Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))

For an LCA group $G$ with Haar measure $\mu$, the dual $\widehat G$ is the group of continuous homomorphisms $G\to\mathbb{T}$ with the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets, and $\widehat f(\chi)=\int_G f(x)\overline{\chi(x)}\,d\mu(x)$. ([Wikipedia, Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) The DFT of $(x_0,\dots,x_{n-1})$ is $X_k=\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}x_me^{-2\pi ikm/n}$. ([Wikipedia, Fast Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Fourier_transform))

### Key results
- **Uniqueness and Riemann–Lebesgue.** If $F\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ and all $c_n=0$, then $F=0$ a.e.; and $c_n\to0$ as $|n|\to\infty$. ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf))
- **Fejér's theorem.** If $F\in C(\mathbb{T})$, then $\sigma_N\to F$ and $A_r\to F$ uniformly. If $F\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ is continuous at $x_0$, then $\sigma_N(x_0)\to F(x_0)$; at a point with one-sided limits, $\sigma_N(x_0)\to(F(x_0^+)+F(x_0^-))/2$. ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf))
- **Parseval and Hölder-type pointwise convergence.** If $F\in L^2(\mathbb{T})$, then $\frac1{2\pi}\int|F|^2=\sum|c_n|^2$ and $\|s_N-F\|_2^2=\sum_{|n|>N}|c_n|^2$. If $F\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ and $|F(x)-F(x_0)|\le C|x-x_0|^\alpha$ near $x_0$ for some $\alpha>0$, then $s_N(x_0)\to F(x_0)$. ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf))
- **$L^p$ norm convergence.** If $F\in L^p(\mathbb{T})$, $1\le p<\infty$, then $\|F-\sigma_N\|_p\to0$; for $1<p<\infty$ also $\|F-s_N\|_p\to0$, which can fail for $p=1$. ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf)) On $\mathbb{R}$ the corresponding statement for the symmetric partial sums $S_Rf$ of the Fourier integral follows from M. Riesz's 1928 theorem: the Hilbert transform (principal-value convolution with $1/(\pi t)$) is bounded on $L^p$ for $1<p<\infty$; at $p=1$ it is only weak type $(1,1)$, and it maps $L^\infty$ into BMO. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform))
- **Wiener's theorems.** If $\varphi$ on $\mathbb{T}$ has absolutely convergent Fourier series and no zeros, then $1/\varphi$ also has absolutely convergent Fourier series (and conversely). For $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, the translates of $f$ span a dense subspace of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ iff $\widehat f$ has no real zeros; for $f\in L^2(\mathbb{R})$, iff the real zero set of $\widehat f$ has measure zero (Wiener 1932). Gelfand reproved the first via the maximal ideals of the Wiener algebra $A(\mathbb{T})$. ([Wikipedia, Wiener's tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_tauberian_theorem))
- **Plancherel and Pontryagin duality.** If $f\in L^1\cap L^2(\mathbb{R})$, then $\|\widehat f\|_2=\|f\|_2$, and the map extends uniquely to a unitary operator on $L^2$ (Plancherel, 1910). ([Wikipedia, Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem)) Every LCA group is canonically isomorphic to its double dual; with dual Haar measures the transform is unitary $L^2(G)\to L^2(\widehat G)$. Examples: $\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}=\mathbb{T}$, $\widehat{\mathbb{T}}=\mathbb{Z}$, $\widehat{\mathbb{R}}\cong\mathbb{R}$; a finite cyclic group is non-canonically self-dual. ([Wikipedia, Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))
- **Paley–Wiener theorem.** $F\in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ is supported in $[-A,A]$ iff its transform extends to an entire function $f$ of exponential type $A$, $|f(\zeta)|\le Ce^{A|\zeta|}$, square-integrable on horizontal lines. Schwartz: an entire $F$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is the Fourier–Laplace transform of a distribution supported in the closed $B$-ball iff $|F(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^Ne^{B|\operatorname{Im}z|}$. ([Wikipedia, Paley–Wiener theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley%E2%80%93Wiener_theorem))
- **Riesz–Thorin and Hausdorff–Young.** For complex scalars on $\sigma$-finite spaces, if a linear $T$ is bounded $L^{p_0}\to L^{q_0}$ and $L^{p_1}\to L^{q_1}$, then for $0<\theta<1$ it is bounded $L^{p_\theta}\to L^{q_\theta}$ with $\|T\|\le\|T\|_0^{1-\theta}\|T\|_1^\theta$, where $1/p_\theta=(1-\theta)/p_0+\theta/p_1$ (likewise $q_\theta$). Interpolating $L^1\to L^\infty$ and $L^2\to L^2$ gives $\|\widehat f\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)}$ and $\|\widehat F\|_{\ell^q}\le\|F\|_{L^p(\mathbb{T})}$ for $1\le p\le2$, $1/p+1/q=1$; the constant $1$ is not optimal on $\mathbb{R}^d$. ([Wikipedia, Riesz–Thorin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Thorin_theorem))
- **Poisson summation.** If $s$ is continuous and integrable with $|s(x)|+|\widehat s(x)|\le C(1+|x|)^{-1-\delta}$ (e.g. Schwartz), then $\sum_{n}s(n)=\sum_{k}\widehat s(k)$, both sides converging absolutely. It gives the theta transformation law, the functional equation of the [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function), and the sampling theorem. ([Wikipedia, Poisson summation formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_summation_formula))
- **Carleson–Hunt.** If $F\in L^p(\mathbb{T})$, $1<p\le\infty$, then $s_N(x)\to F(x)$ for a.e. $x$ (Carleson 1966 for $p=2$; Hunt for $p>1$); a.e. convergence also holds in $L\log^+L\log^+\log^+\log^+L$ (Antonov 1996). For every null set $E\subset\mathbb{T}$ there is a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at every point of $E$ (Katznelson 1966); combined with Carleson's theorem, a set is contained in the divergence set of some continuous function's Fourier series iff it has measure zero. ([Wikipedia, Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem)) See [Carleson's Theorem](node:Carleson's%20Theorem).
- **Littlewood–Paley theory.** Split $f$ into frequency pieces $f_\rho$ over dyadic bands $\pm[2^k,2^{k+1}]$; the Littlewood–Paley theorem bounds $\|(\sum_\rho|f_\rho|^2)^{1/2}\|_p$ by a multiple of $\|f\|_p$. For the $g$-function $g(f)(x)=(\int_0^\infty|\nabla u(x,y)|^2y\,dy)^{1/2}$, with $u$ the Poisson integral of $f$, the ratio $\|g(f)\|_p/\|f\|_p$ is bounded above and below by constants depending only on $n,p$ for $1<p<\infty$. ([Wikipedia, Littlewood–Paley theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood%E2%80%93Paley_theory)) See [Littlewood–Paley Theory](node:Littlewood–Paley%20Theory).
- **Calderón–Zygmund theorem.** If a convolution operator $T$ is bounded on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and its kernel satisfies Hörmander's condition $\sup_{y\ne0}\int_{|x|\ge2|y|}|K(x-y)-K(x)|\,dx<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded on $L^p$ for $1<p<\infty$ and weak type $(1,1)$. The Riesz transforms, with multipliers $i\xi_j/|\xi|$ and $\sum_jR_j^2=-I$, are the basic examples. ([Wikipedia, Singular integral operators of convolution type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_integral_operators_of_convolution_type)) See [Singular Integral Operators](node:Singular%20Integral%20Operators).
- **Stein–Tomas restriction theorem.** The extension operator $Eg(x)=\int_{S^{n-1}}g(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\sigma(\xi)$ is bounded $L^2(S^{n-1})\to L^{2(n+1)/(n-1)}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The constant function shows $p>2n/(n-1)$ is necessary for any extension estimate; the Knapp cap example gives the other constraint. ([Wu, ANU lecture notes](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~plyung/math3349/Kai2.pdf)) See [Fourier Restriction Theory](node:Fourier%20Restriction%20Theory).
- **Peter–Weyl theorem.** For a compact group $G$, matrix coefficients of irreducible unitary representations are dense in $C(G)$; $L^2(G)$ is the Hilbert direct sum over irreducibles $\pi$, each occurring $\dim\pi$ times, and $\sqrt{d_\pi}\,u_{ij}^\pi$ form an orthonormal basis. For $G=S^1$ this is the Fourier basis $e^{in\theta}$ (Peter and Weyl, 1927). ([Wikipedia, Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem)) See [Peter–Weyl Theorem](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem).
- **FFT.** The DFT of length $n$ costs $O(n^2)$ operations directly and $O(n\log n)$ by an FFT (Cooley–Tukey 1965 for composite $n$, anticipated in unpublished work of Gauss from 1805). ([Wikipedia, Fast Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Fourier_transform)) See [Fast Fourier Transform](node:Fast%20Fourier%20Transform).

### Examples
- **Square wave.** The odd $2\pi$-periodic extension of $g=1$ on $(0,\pi)$ has the unit-amplitude square-wave series $g\sim\frac4\pi\sum_{n\text{ odd}}\frac{\sin nx}{n}$, containing only odd harmonics. ([Wikipedia, Square wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_wave_%28waveform%29)) The partial sums converge to $1$ on $(0,\pi)$ and $-1$ on $(-\pi,0)$, while $\max_x s_N\to\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin t}{t}\,dt\approx1.18$ (Gibbs phenomenon); Fejér and Abel means satisfy $\max|\sigma_N|\le\operatorname{ess\,sup}|g|$ and so do not overshoot. ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf))
- **Steady-state plate.** For a square plate $[0,\pi]^2$ with three edges at $0$ and $T(x,\pi)=x$, the steady-state temperature is $T(x,y)=2\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin(nx)\frac{\sinh(ny)}{\sinh(n\pi)}$. ([Wikipedia, Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series)) See [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations).
- **Gaussian and delta.** $e^{-\pi x^2}$ is its own transform; the Dirac delta transforms to $1$, by duality on [Tempered Distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions). ([Wikipedia, Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))

### History
Fourier presented his 1807 memoir on heat propagation in solids and published *Théorie analytique de la chaleur* in 1822. In 1811 a prize committee including Lagrange, Laplace, Malus and Legendre found the analysis lacking in generality and rigour; Dirichlet and Riemann later made the results precise. ([Wikipedia, Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series))

Du Bois-Reymond (1876) found a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at a point. Luzin conjectured a.e. convergence for $L^2$; Carleson proved it (Acta Math. 116, 1966), with later proofs by Fefferman (1973) and Lacey–Thiele (2000). ([Wikipedia, Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem); [Lacey, Carleson's theorem survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0307008)) Littlewood and Paley developed square-function methods in 1931–1938, extended by Zygmund and Marcinkiewicz and, to higher dimensions, by Stein. ([Wikipedia, Littlewood–Paley theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood%E2%80%93Paley_theory)) Pontryagin founded duality in 1934; van Kampen (1935) and Weil (1940) extended it to all LCA groups. ([Wikipedia, Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))

### Connections
- [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence) and [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus): the original setting.
- [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration) and [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces): the natural function classes for coefficients and convergence.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): $\{e^{inx}\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{T})$, giving Parseval.
- [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem) and [Carleson's Theorem](node:Carleson's%20Theorem): the $L^2$ isometry and a.e. convergence.
- [Littlewood–Paley Theory](node:Littlewood–Paley%20Theory) and [Singular Integral Operators](node:Singular%20Integral%20Operators): the real-variable machinery behind $L^p$ theory.
- [Fourier Restriction Theory](node:Fourier%20Restriction%20Theory) and [Kakeya Conjecture](node:Kakeya%20Conjecture): the central open problems of Euclidean harmonic analysis.
- [Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality), [Harmonic Analysis on Locally Compact Groups](node:Harmonic%20Analysis%20on%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups), [Peter–Weyl Theorem](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem), [Group Fourier Transform](node:Group%20Fourier%20Transform): abelian and non-abelian generalizations.
- [Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure): the measure defining the transform on an LCA group.
- [Banach Algebras](node:Banach%20Algebras) and [Tauberian Theorems](node:Tauberian%20Theorems): Gelfand's proof of Wiener's theorem.
- [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29) and [Tempered Distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions): the transform extended by duality; Paley–Wiener–Schwartz.
- [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation), [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation), [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations), [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): separation of variables and Fourier multipliers.
- [Fast Fourier Transform](node:Fast%20Fourier%20Transform): the algorithmic form of the DFT.
- [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function): functional equation via Poisson summation.
- Map: [MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces](node:MSC%2042%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20on%20Euclidean%20spaces)

### Common pitfalls
- **Continuity does not give pointwise convergence.** A continuous function's Fourier series may diverge at a point; a modest Hölder condition suffices, and Fejér means of continuous functions always converge uniformly. ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf))
- **Divergence sets.** The theorem on null sets gives a continuous function diverging *at every point of* a prescribed null set, not one whose divergence set *equals* it. ([Wikipedia, Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **$p=1$ is different.** $\|F-s_N\|_1$ need not tend to $0$ for $F\in L^1$, and an $L^1$ Fourier series can diverge everywhere. ([MIT 18.103 outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf))
- **Several variables: the summation method matters.** Rectangular and polygonal partial sums inherit one-dimensional results, but spherical summation does not converge in $L^p$ norm for $p\ne2$. ([Wikipedia, Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Bochner–Riesz mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Riesz_mean))
- **Conventions.** Angular-frequency conventions move factors of $2\pi$ and the transform is then not unitary, changing Plancherel and the convolution theorem. ([Wikipedia, Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))
- **Non-abelian groups.** The dual of a non-abelian group is not a group; Tannaka–Krein duality works with the category of representations instead. ([Wikipedia, Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))

### Open problems
- **Fourier restriction conjecture.** In adjoint form, for the extension operator $E$ from the paraboloid in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\|Ef\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}\le C_{n,p}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^{n-1})}$ for $p>2n/(n-1)$; Fefferman and Stein proved $n=2$, and it remains open for $n\ge3$. It is tied to the Kakeya problem, which Wang and Zahl resolved in $\mathbb{R}^3$; for $n\ge4$ only partial results are known. ([Zahl 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.09397v1); [Wang and Zahl](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655)) Lecture notes record Tao's theorem that the Bochner–Riesz conjecture implies the restriction conjecture. ([Wu, ANU lecture notes](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~plyung/math3349/Kai2.pdf))
- **Bochner–Riesz conjecture.** For multiplier $(1-|\xi|^2/R^2)_+^\delta$, the conjecture is that $\delta>\delta(p)=\max(n|1/p-1/2|-1/2,0)$ is necessary and sufficient for $L^p$ boundedness. Necessity is known and $n=2$ is resolved; for $n\ge3$ it is only partially answered. ([Wikipedia, Bochner–Riesz mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Riesz_mean))
- **Spherical summation and the largest a.e.-convergence space.** A.e. convergence of spherical partial sums of multiple Fourier series is open for $L^2$, and the largest natural space with a.e. convergence on $\mathbb{T}$ is unknown (simplest candidate $L\log^+L$; Konyagin's everywhere-divergent examples lie just above $L(\log^+L)^{1/2}$). ([Wikipedia, Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **FFT lower bound.** It is not proved that the DFT requires $\Omega(n\log n)$ operations. ([Wikipedia, Fast Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Fourier_transform))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fourier analysis (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_analysis): the family of transforms and their uses; see also [Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality) and [Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem).
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.103, Fourier Series: an outline](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.103/outline.pdf): kernels, Fejér, Parseval, pointwise and $L^p$ convergence, Gibbs, Carleson. [Wu, ANU lecture notes on restriction](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~plyung/math3349/Kai2.pdf): Stein–Tomas, Knapp example, the conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Wang and Zahl, Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655): proves every Kakeya set in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has Minkowski and Hausdorff dimension 3.
- **Further reading:** [Katznelson, An Introduction to Harmonic Analysis (3rd ed., CUP 2004)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781139165372/type/book): standard graduate text from Fourier series on the circle to LCA groups.
- **Further reading:** [Stein–Shakarchi, Fourier Analysis (Princeton Lectures in Analysis I, 2003)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691113845/fourier-analysis); [Lacey, Carleson's Theorem: Proof, Complements, Variations](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0307008) (survey with a full proof); [Zahl, A Survey of the Kakeya conjecture, 2000–2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.09397v1) (survey).
references.Fubini's Theorem:
## Reference
### Overview
Fubini's theorem turns an integral over a product of measure spaces into successive integrals over the factors, in either order. Its decisive hypothesis is absolute integrability on the product: if $\int|f|\,d(\mu\otimes\nu)<\infty$, the two iterated integrals of $f$ exist and both equal the product integral. Without it, both iterated integrals of a signed function can exist and still disagree. ([MIT 6.436J, lecture 9](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))

Tonelli's companion theorem handles nonnegative measurable functions and allows the common value to be $+\infty$. The two are usually combined into the Fubini–Tonelli theorem: compute an iterated integral of $|f|$ by Tonelli; if it is finite, $f$ is integrable on the product and Fubini applies to $f$. Because sums are integrals against counting measure, the same results govern interchanging double sums, or a sum and an integral. ([MIT 6.436J, lecture 9](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))

The three standing hypotheses are $\sigma$-finiteness of the factors, measurability of $f$ for the product $\sigma$-algebra (or its completion), and integrability (or nonnegativity). Each is needed: there are counterexamples when any one is dropped, including one due to Sierpiński under the continuum hypothesis, in which both iterated integrals of a bounded nonnegative function on the unit square exist but differ. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))

### Formal definition
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be measure spaces. The product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ is generated by measurable rectangles $A\times B$, and there is a measure $\mu\otimes\nu$ on it with $(\mu\otimes\nu)(A\times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B)$; if both spaces are $\sigma$-finite, it is the unique such measure. ([Hunter, theorem 5.14](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch5.pdf))

For $f:X\times Y\to\mathbb C$ the sections are $f_x(y)=f(x,y)$ and $f^y(x)=f(x,y)$. If $f$ is $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$-measurable, every section is measurable; if the spaces are also $\sigma$-finite, $x\mapsto\int f_x\,d\nu$ and $y\mapsto\int f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable. ([Hunter, theorem 5.15](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch5.pdf))

**Fubini's theorem.** Let the two spaces be $\sigma$-finite and $f:X\times Y\to\mathbb C$ be $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$-measurable. Then $f\in L^1(\mu\otimes\nu)$ if and only if either iterated integral $\int\!\big(\int|f^y|\,d\mu\big)d\nu$ or $\int\!\big(\int|f_x|\,d\nu\big)d\mu$ is finite, and in that case ([Hunter, theorem 5.18](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch5.pdf))
$$
\int_{X\times Y}f\,d(\mu\otimes\nu)
=\int_X\left(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)\right)d\mu(x)
=\int_Y\left(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\right)d\nu(y).
$$
More precisely, for $\mu$-almost every $x$ the section $f_x$ is $\nu$-integrable, and there is a $\mu$-integrable $h$ equal to $\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)$ except on a $\mu$-null set of $x$ where that integral is undefined or infinite; symmetrically in $y$. ([MIT 6.436J, lecture 9, theorem 3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf))

### Key results
- **Tonelli's theorem.** If $g:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\to[0,\infty]$ is measurable for the product $\sigma$-algebra and $P=P_1\times P_2$ is the product of $\sigma$-finite measures, then $\omega_1\mapsto\int g\,dP_2$ and $\omega_2\mapsto\int g\,dP_1$ are measurable and both iterated integrals equal $\int g\,dP$, possibly $+\infty$. The proof goes through simple functions and the monotone convergence theorem. ([MIT 6.436J, lecture 9, theorem 2 and remark 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- **Fubini–Tonelli criterion.** For $\sigma$-finite factors and product-measurable $f$, the iterated integrals of $|f|$ equal $\int|f|$; if any one of them is finite, the iterated integrals of $f$ agree with $\int f$. The same holds applied to the positive and negative parts of $f$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem); [Hunter, theorem 5.18](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch5.pdf))
- **Complete version.** Products of complete measure spaces need not be complete: if $N\subset\mathbb R$ is non-Lebesgue-measurable, $\{0\}\times N$ is Lebesgue-null in $\mathbb R^2$ but lies outside $\mathcal L(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal L(\mathbb R)$, since every section of a set in the product $\sigma$-algebra is measurable. The Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$ is the completion of $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$, and a Lebesgue measurable $f$ on $\mathbb R^{m+n}$ is integrable iff either iterated integral of $|f|$ is finite, in which case both iterated integrals equal $\int f$, with the inner integrals well defined and finite a.e. ([Hunter, example 5.20 and theorem 5.21](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch5.pdf)) In the general complete setting one uses the completion of the product, and the restriction of $f$ to a line may be non-measurable on a null set of lines. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- **Minkowski's integral inequality.** For $\sigma$-finite $(S_1,\mu_1)$, $(S_2,\mu_2)$, measurable $F:S_1\times S_2\to\mathbb R$ and $1\le p<\infty$,
  $$\Big(\int_{S_2}\Big|\int_{S_1}F(x,y)\,d\mu_1(x)\Big|^p d\mu_2(y)\Big)^{1/p}\le\int_{S_1}\Big(\int_{S_2}|F(x,y)|^p\,d\mu_2(y)\Big)^{1/p}d\mu_1(x).$$
  When $p>1$ and both sides are finite, equality forces $|F(x,y)|=\varphi(x)\psi(y)$ a.e. for nonnegative measurable $\varphi,\psi$. Taking $\mu_1$ to be counting measure on $\{1,2\}$ recovers the triangle inequality in $L^p$. ([Wikipedia, Minkowski inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski_inequality))
- **Fubini for the Bochner integral.** Let $\mu,\nu$ be $\sigma$-finite, $E$ a second-countable Banach space, and $f:X\times Y\to E$ be $\mu\times\nu$-a.e. measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if and only if $f_x$ is $\nu$-integrable for almost every $x$ and $x\mapsto\int_Y\|f(x,y)\|\,d\nu(y)$ is $\mu$-integrable; and if $f$ is integrable, the product integral equals both iterated Bochner integrals, all integrands being a.e. measurable. The author of the Lean/mathlib formalization reports that he could not find a good source for its proof other than the Isabelle formalization, and gives detailed proofs. ([van Doorn 2021, theorem 3 and §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.07636)) A Bochner-measurable $f$ is Bochner integrable exactly when $\int\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty$. ([Wikipedia, Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral))

### Examples
- **Double series.** With counting measure on $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$: if $\sum_m\sum_n|a_{mn}|<\infty$ then $\sum_m\sum_n a_{mn}=\sum_n\sum_m a_{mn}$. ([Hunter, example 5.19](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch5.pdf)) The version for absolutely convergent double series is due to Pringsheim. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- **Convolution.** For $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$, $(x,y)\mapsto f(y)g(x-y)$ is Lebesgue measurable on $\mathbb R^{2n}$; Tonelli applied to $|f(y)g(x-y)|$ shows $f*g(x)=\int f(y)g(x-y)\,dy$ exists for a.e. $x$ and $\|f*g\|_1\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_1$. ([MIT 18.125, lecture 20, theorem 0.1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/f1dba73e7df549914ba1c94cdd66e725_18125_lec20.pdf))
- **Integrability fails.** On $\{1,2,\dots\}^2$ with counting measure, let $f(m,m)=1$, $f(m,m+1)=-1$ and $f=0$ elsewhere. The two iterated sums are $0$ and $1$: $f$ is neither nonnegative nor integrable. ([MIT 6.436J, lecture 9, §3.1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf)) An arctangent-derivative example on a square has iterated integrals $\pi/4$ and $-\pi/4$, with $\int|f|=\infty$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- **$\sigma$-finiteness fails.** Take $(0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure on Borel sets and $(0,1)$ with counting measure on all subsets, and $f(x,y)=1$ if $x=y$, else $0$. Integrating in $y$ first gives $1$; integrating in $x$ first gives $0$. ([MIT 6.436J, lecture 9, §3.2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf))
- **Product measurability fails.** On the first uncountable ordinal $\omega_1$ with the measure giving countable sets measure $0$ and co-countable sets measure $1$, the set $E=\{(x,y):x<y\}$ is countable on every horizontal line and co-countable on every vertical line; the iterated integrals of $1_E$ are $1$ and $0$, and $1_E$ is not measurable for the product. Sierpiński showed that, assuming the continuum hypothesis, $\omega_1$ can be identified with the unit interval $I$, producing a bounded nonnegative function on $I\times I$ with both Lebesgue iterated integrals defined and unequal. CH and Martin's axiom each imply that such a function exists, while Friedman (1980) proved it consistent with ZFC that a strong Fubini-type theorem for $[0,1]$ holds in this setting of bounded nonnegative functions on the unit square not assumed measurable: whenever both iterated integrals exist, they are equal. Unboundedness is a separate obstruction, as the arctangent example shows. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))

### History
Euler knew the case of continuous functions on products of closed bounded sets. Lebesgue (1904) extended it to bounded measurable functions on products of intervals; Beppo Levi conjectured the extension to integrable functions, which Fubini proved in 1907; Tonelli gave the nonnegative version in 1909. Standard proofs, such as the MIT lecture's, establish the nonnegative (Tonelli) case first and derive the integrable case by splitting into positive and negative parts, the reverse of this chronology. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem); [MIT 6.436J, lecture 9](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf)) Product measures and Fubini for both the Lebesgue and the Bochner integral have since been formalized in Isabelle/HOL and in Lean's mathlib. ([van Doorn 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.07636))

### Connections
- [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration): supplies the integral; Tonelli is proved from simple functions.
- [Monotone Convergence Theorem](node:Monotone%20Convergence%20Theorem): the limit step in the proof of Tonelli.
- [Dominated Convergence Theorem](node:Dominated%20Convergence%20Theorem): the integrable version parallels it as Tonelli parallels monotone convergence.
- [Tonelli's Theorem](node:Tonelli's%20Theorem): the nonnegative companion result.
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): repeated Riemann integrals become a theorem with explicit hypotheses.
- [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): product measures and $\sigma$-finiteness are the ambient setting.
- [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces): Minkowski's integral inequality and Young's convolution inequality.
- [Vector Measures and Bochner Integration](node:Vector%20Measures%20and%20Bochner%20Integration): the Banach-valued Fubini theorem.
- [Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure): its uniqueness proof uses product measures and iterated integrals.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory): absolute continuity of foliations is a Fubini property along leaves.
- [MSC 28Axx - Classical measure theory](node:MSC%2028Axx%20-%20Classical%20measure%20theory): product measures and integration theory.

### Common pitfalls
- Existence of both signed iterated integrals does not imply integrability on the product, and their values can differ; check finiteness of an iterated integral of $|f|$ first. ([MIT 6.436J, lecture 9](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf))
- Measurable sections are not enough: the integrand must be measurable on the product or its completion, as the $\omega_1$ and Sierpiński examples show. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- For complete factors and functions measurable for the completed product, "every section is measurable" must be weakened to "almost every section". ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem); [Hunter, example 5.20](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch5.pdf))
- A smooth foliation of the square need not obey a Fubini property along its leaves: in Katok's example a full-measure set meets each analytic leaf in at most one point, because the foliation is not absolutely continuous. ([Wikipedia, Fubini's nightmare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_nightmare))

### Open problems
- **Genericity of Fubini's nightmare for center foliations.** Absolute continuity of the holonomies of a foliation is what makes Fubini's theorem valid along it: a set is null iff almost every leaf meets it in a leafwise-null set. Stable and unstable foliations of partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms have absolutely continuous holonomies, but Shub and Wilkinson found an open set of examples whose center foliation is not absolutely continuous. The 2006 survey of Rodriguez Hertz, Rodriguez Hertz and Ures states that failure is generally believed to be generic and poses, as Problem 12, to prove there is a $C^1$-open, $C^\infty$-dense set of diffeomorphisms whose center foliation fails to be absolutely continuous, and to characterize the absolutely continuous case at least for one-dimensional center; Problem 13 asks for the regularity of the center foliation. ([Rodriguez Hertz–Rodriguez Hertz–Ures, §§1, 3.2–3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609362)) Gogolev later proved that the center foliation is generically non-absolutely continuous for a large class of volume-preserving partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms of $\mathbb T^3$ with non-compact center leaves. ([Gogolev](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.3533))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fubini's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem): statements, counterexamples for each hypothesis, Sierpiński and Friedman, history.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, Measure Theory notes, ch. 5](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch5.pdf): product $\sigma$-algebras, product measures, monotone class proof, completion.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.436J, lecture 9](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-436j-fundamentals-of-probability-fall-2018/6fe5ce4d56945ce7241679998922fb3a_MIT6_436JF18_lec09.pdf): product measure, Tonelli and Fubini, cautionary examples.
- **Primary:** [van Doorn, *Formalized Haar Measure*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.07636): product measures and a full proof of Fubini for the Bochner integral.
- **Primary:** [Rodriguez Hertz–Rodriguez Hertz–Ures, *A survey on partially hyperbolic dynamics*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609362): absolute continuity of foliations and open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Tao, *An Introduction to Measure Theory*, AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 126 (2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/126); [Axler, *Measure, Integration & Real Analysis*, Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics (2020)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-030-33143-6).

## Reference
### Overview
A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns to each element of a set $X$ (the domain) exactly one element of a set $Y$ (the codomain). Functions began as a way to say how one quantity depends on another; they were formalized in set theory at the end of the 19th century, which greatly widened the class of objects that count as functions. Given domain and codomain, a function is uniquely represented by its graph, the set of pairs $(x,f(x))$. ([Wikipedia: Function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)))

A binary relation over sets $X$ and $Y$ is a subset of the Cartesian product $X\times Y$, or equivalently a set of ordered pairs. Functions are the special relations that are entire and functional: every domain element is related to exactly one codomain element. Homogeneous relations (on a single set) include equivalence relations and the various orders. nLab records the same picture: a relation on a family of sets is a subset of the product, and combining functional and entire yields functions, injections, surjections, and bijections. ([Wikipedia: Binary relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_relation); [nLab: relation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/relation); [nLab: function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/function); [SEP: Basic Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/Fall2012/entries/set-theory/primer.html))

Equivalence relations (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) partition a set into disjoint classes; the set of classes is the quotient. This is the mechanism by which one passes from “same image under $f$” to a well-defined map on a quotient, and it is the set-theoretic origin of many constructions (integers modulo $n$, projective space, and so on). ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation); [nLab: equivalence relation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+relation))

### Formal definition
Following Kuratowski, the ordered pair is the set $(a,b)=\{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}$; then $(a,b)=(a',b')$ if and only if $a=a'$ and $b=b'$. A set $R$ is a binary relation if every element of $R$ is an ordered pair. One writes $xRy$ for $(x,y)\in R$; $\mathrm{dom}\,R$ and $\mathrm{ran}\,R$ are the sets of first and second coordinates. ([SEP: Basic Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/Fall2012/entries/set-theory/primer.html))

A binary relation $F$ is a function if $aFb_1$ and $aFb_2$ imply $b_1=b_2$; equivalently, each $a\in\mathrm{dom}\,F$ has exactly one $b$ with $aFb$. That unique $b$ is written $F(a)$. In the formulation that records domain and codomain, a function $X\to Y$ is a relation $R\subseteq X\times Y$ such that ([SEP: Basic Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/Fall2012/entries/set-theory/primer.html); [Wikipedia: Function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)); [nLab: function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/function))
- for every $x\in X$ there exists $y\in Y$ with $(x,y)\in R$ (entirety);
- if $(x,y)\in R$ and $(x,z)\in R$, then $y=z$ (functionality).

nLab notes that in material set theory it is cleaner to take a function as an ordered triple $(f,A,B)$ so that the codomain is determined even when the map is not surjective. ([nLab: function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/function))

An equivalence relation on a set $X$ is a binary relation $\sim$ that is reflexive ($x\sim x$), symmetric ($x\sim y$ if and only if $y\sim x$), and transitive. The equivalence class of $a$ is $[a]=\{x\in X:x\sim a\}$; the quotient $X/{\sim}$ is the set of classes, which is a partition of $X$. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation); [nLab: equivalence relation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+relation))

A partial order is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation))

### Key results
- **Extensionality of functions.** Functions $F$ and $G$ are equal if and only if they have the same domain and $F(x)=G(x)$ for all $x$ in that domain. ([SEP: Basic Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/Fall2012/entries/set-theory/primer.html))
- **Injective, surjective, bijective.** $f:A\to B$ is injective if $f(a_1)=f(a_2)$ implies $a_1=a_2$; surjective if for every $y\in B$ there is $x\in A$ with $f(x)=y$; bijective if both. A bijective $f$ has an inverse $f^{-1}:B\to A$ sending each $y$ to the unique $x$ with $f(x)=y$. Two sets have the same cardinality if there is a bijection between them. ([MIT 18.100A, Lecture 2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/10eRBzxaDhmhDya7nrt4G50lMys37g_7m_transcript.pdf); [Wikipedia: Function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)); [SEP: Basic Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/Fall2012/entries/set-theory/primer.html))
- **Composition.** If $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$, the composite $g\circ f:A\to C$ is $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$. ([MIT 18.100A, Lecture 2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/10eRBzxaDhmhDya7nrt4G50lMys37g_7m_transcript.pdf); [nLab: function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/function))
- **Equivalence kernel.** For any function $f$, the relation $x\sim y$ iff $f(x)=f(y)$ is an equivalence relation; its classes are the fibres of $f$. If $f$ is a surjection, there is a unique bijection $g:X/{\sim}\to B$ with $g\circ\pi=f$. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation))
- **Well-defined maps on quotients.** A function $f:X\to Y$ factors through $\pi:X\to X/{\sim}$ if and only if $x\sim y$ implies $f(x)=f(y)$; then $f$ is a class invariant. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation))
- **Generated equivalence.** For any relation $R$ on $S$ there is a smallest equivalence relation containing $R$ (the intersection of all equivalences containing $R$). ([nLab: equivalence relation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+relation); [nLab: relation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/relation))
- **Partial functions.** Dropping entirety yields partial functions: each $x$ relates to *at most* one $y$. In analysis, “a function $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$” often means a partial function whose domain of definition is a subset of $\mathbb{R}$. ([Wikipedia: Function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)); [nLab: function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/function))

### Examples
- Equality on any set is an equivalence (and a partial order). Congruence modulo $n$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, similarity of triangles, and “has the same image under $f$” are equivalences. Equipollence of directed segments (same length and direction) is the geometric example that produces Euclidean vectors. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation))
- $\ge$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is a partial order, not an equivalence (not symmetric). “Has a common factor $>1$” on integers $>1$ is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive. Approximate equality of reals, unless defined asymptotically, fails transitivity. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation))
- The empty relation on a nonempty set is vacuously symmetric and transitive but not reflexive. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation))
- Divides, as a relation from primes to integers, is a heterogeneous binary relation: $3$ relates to $6,9,12,\dots$ but not to $4$ or $5$. ([Wikipedia: Binary relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_relation))

### History
The informal notion of a function is that of Leibniz, Newton, and Euler; it cannot be formalized without a definition of “assignment.” The set-theoretic definition, as a functional relation, appears at the end of the 19th century. Ordered pairs are encoded as sets by the Kuratowski formula used in Hrbacek–Jech. nLab records that functions are the morphisms of the category $\mathbf{Set}$. ([Wikipedia: Function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)); [SEP: Basic Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/Fall2012/entries/set-theory/primer.html); [nLab: function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/function))

### Connections
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): functions and relations are sets of ordered pairs built from the axioms.
- [Cardinality](node:Cardinality): two sets have the same size when a bijection exists.
- [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): functions are morphisms in $\mathbf{Set}$; relations form the allegory $\mathbf{Rel}$.
- [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory): function types $S\to T$ generalize functions of sets.
- [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces): addition and scalar multiplication are functions; linear maps are structure-preserving functions.
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory): homomorphisms are functions preserving the operation; congruence relations are kernels.
- [Proof Techniques](node:Proof%20Techniques): injectivity and surjectivity are typical proof obligations.
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): external relations are propositions in a context of variables.
- Map: [MSC 03 - Mathematical logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003%20-%20Mathematical%20logic%20and%20foundations).

### Common pitfalls
- Domain versus image: a formula such as $x\mapsto 1/f(x)$ defines a function from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ only after the zeros of $f$ are removed; in analysis one often means a partial function. ([Wikipedia: Function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)))
- Inverse function versus inverse image: $f^{-1}$ as a function exists only for bijections; $f^{-1}(A)$ as a set of preimages is defined for any function. ([MIT 18.100A, Lecture 2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/10eRBzxaDhmhDya7nrt4G50lMys37g_7m_transcript.pdf))
- A map on a quotient is not automatically well-defined: one must check that equivalent inputs give equal (or equivalent) outputs. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation))
- Material-set-theory graphs do not determine the codomain unless the function is packaged as $(f,A,B)$. ([nLab: function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/function))
- “Approximately equal” is not an equivalence on $\mathbb{R}$: small errors accumulate. ([Wikipedia: Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation))

### Open problems
The basic theory of functions, relations, equivalences, and orders is settled. One famous problem that *presents* as a question about a function's domain of definition is the Riemann hypothesis: determining the zeros of $\zeta$ is equivalent to determining where $z\mapsto 1/\zeta(z)$ is defined as a complex function. That is an open problem about $\zeta$, not about the general notion of function. ([Wikipedia: Function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Function (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)), [Binary relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_relation), and [Equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation); [nLab: function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/function), [relation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/relation), [equivalence relation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+relation).
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.100A Lecture 2 transcript](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/10eRBzxaDhmhDya7nrt4G50lMys37g_7m_transcript.pdf): injective, surjective, bijective maps and cardinality.
- **Primary:** [SEP: Basic Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/Fall2012/entries/set-theory/primer.html): Hrbacek–Jech textbook excerpt defining ordered pairs, relations, and functions in ZF.
references.Fundamental Group:
## Reference
### Overview
The fundamental group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ of a space $X$ with base point $x_0$ is the group of homotopy classes of loops at $x_0$, with concatenation as the operation. It is the first and simplest homotopy group, and it detects one-dimensional holes ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)). It is a functor: a continuous map induces a homomorphism $f_*$, and homotopy-equivalent path-connected spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups. This makes it a basic tool for telling spaces apart. The circle has $\pi_1\cong\mathbb Z$, while every sphere $S^n$ with $n\ge2$ is simply connected ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).

Unlike homology, $\pi_1$ can be non-abelian: the figure eight has the free group on two generators as its fundamental group ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)). Covering space theory turns $\pi_1$ into a Galois group. For nice spaces, connected coverings correspond to conjugacy classes of subgroups, and the deck group of the universal cover is $\pi_1(X)$ ([Wikipedia: Covering space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_space)). The Seifert–van Kampen theorem computes $\pi_1$ by gluing pieces ([Wikipedia: Seifert–van Kampen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93van_Kampen_theorem)).

The fundamental group links topology with combinatorial and geometric group theory. Every group is the fundamental group of a connected 2-dimensional CW complex, and every finitely presented group is that of a compact smooth manifold of dimension 4 or more ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)). Group-theoretic undecidability enters here: some finitely presented groups have unsolvable word problem ([Wikipedia: Word problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups)).

### Formal definition
Let $X$ be a space and $x_0\in X$. A loop at $x_0$ is a path $\gamma:[0,1]\to X$ with $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=x_0$. Two loops are equivalent if they are homotopic through loops at $x_0$. With
$$(\gamma\cdot\delta)(t)=\begin{cases}\gamma(2t)&0\le t\le\tfrac12\\ \delta(2t-1)&\tfrac12\le t\le1\end{cases},$$
the set $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ of equivalence classes is a group, and the operation is well defined on classes ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).

- **Base point.** If $X$ is path-connected, a path from $x_0$ to $x_1$ induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(X,x_0)\cong\pi_1(X,x_1)$. A different path changes it by an inner automorphism ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- **Fundamental groupoid.** The fundamental groupoid has all points as objects and homotopy classes of paths as morphisms, so no base point is chosen. $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is its endomorphism group at $x_0$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- **Covering space.** A continuous $p:\tilde X\to X$ such that each point of $X$ has a neighbourhood whose preimage is a disjoint union of sheets, each mapped homeomorphically onto it ([Wikipedia: Covering space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_space)).

### Key results
- **Seifert–van Kampen.** Let $X=U_1\cup U_2$ with $U_1,U_2$ open and path-connected and $U_1\cap U_2$ nonempty and path-connected, and let $x_0\in U_1\cap U_2$. Then $\pi_1(X,x_0)\cong\pi_1(U_1,x_0)*_{\pi_1(U_1\cap U_2,x_0)}\pi_1(U_2,x_0)$, the pushout of the inclusion-induced homomorphisms, which need not be injective ([Wikipedia: Seifert–van Kampen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93van_Kampen_theorem)). Brown's groupoid version uses a set of base points meeting every path component, and it computes $\pi_1(S^1)$ ([Wikipedia: Seifert–van Kampen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93van_Kampen_theorem)).
- **Covering spaces.** For a connected covering $p:E\to X$ with $X$ path-connected, $p_*:\pi_1(E)\to\pi_1(X)$ is injective. With $H=p_*\pi_1(E)$, the deck group is $N(H)/H$. For a connected, locally simply connected $X$, path-connected coverings up to equivalence correspond to subgroups of $\pi_1(X)$, and two coverings are equivalent exactly when their subgroups are conjugate ([Wikipedia: Covering space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_space)). If a group $\Gamma$ acts discontinuously on a simply connected space $E$ (every point has an open neighbourhood $V$ with $d_1V\cap d_2V\neq\varnothing$ only for $d_1=d_2$), then $E\to\Gamma\backslash E$ is a normal covering with deck group $\Gamma$, so $\pi_1(\Gamma\backslash E)\cong\Gamma$ ([Wikipedia: Covering space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_space)).
- **Hurewicz in degree one.** For path-connected $X$, the Hurewicz map $\pi_1(X)\to H_1(X)$ is surjective with kernel the commutator subgroup, so $H_1(X)\cong\pi_1(X)^{\mathrm{ab}}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group); [Wikipedia: Hurewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurewicz_theorem)).
- **Products, wedges, topological groups.** For path-connected spaces, $\pi_1(X\times Y)\cong\pi_1(X)\times\pi_1(Y)$. For a wedge of locally contractible spaces, $\pi_1$ is the free product. The fundamental group of a [topological group](node:Topological%20Groups) is abelian ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- **Fibrations.** A fibration gives a long exact sequence of homotopy groups. It shows $\pi_1(SU(n))\cong\pi_1(SU(n-1))$, so every $SU(n)$ is simply connected ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group); [Wikipedia: Fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration)).
- **Realizability.** Every group is $\pi_1$ of a connected 2-dimensional CW complex. Graphs realize exactly the free groups. Every finitely presented group is $\pi_1$ of a compact smooth manifold of any dimension $\ge4$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- **Undecidability.** There is a finitely presented group with unsolvable word problem (Novikov 1955; a different proof by Boone 1958) ([Wikipedia: Word problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups)).
- **3-manifold groups that are Kähler.** If $G$ is the fundamental group of both a closed 3-manifold and a compact Kähler manifold, then $G$ is finite. It is then one of the known finite subgroups of $O(4)$ ([Dimca and Suciu](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.4350)).

### Examples
- $\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb Z$, computed from the universal cover $\mathbb R\to S^1$ by path lifting ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group); [Wikipedia: Covering space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_space)).
- The torus has $\pi_1\cong\mathbb Z^2$. A closed orientable genus-$g$ surface has $\pi_1=\langle a_1,b_1,\dots,a_g,b_g\mid\prod_i[a_i,b_i]\rangle$ ([Wikipedia: Seifert–van Kampen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93van_Kampen_theorem); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- $\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)\cong\mathbb Z/2$ for $n\ge2$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- A connected graph has free $\pi_1$ of rank $|E|-|V|+1$, one generator per edge outside a spanning tree ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- Knot groups: $\pi_1$ of a knot complement. The trefoil's group is the braid group $B_3$, which is non-abelian ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- Applications: in dimension 2, $\pi_1$ gives proofs of the Brouwer fixed point and Borsuk–Ulam theorems ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).

### History
Henri Poincaré defined the fundamental group in *Analysis situs* (1895). The idea grew out of work of Riemann, Poincaré and Klein on Riemann surfaces ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)). Seifert published the gluing theorem in 1931 and van Kampen his version in 1933 ([Wikipedia: Seifert–van Kampen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93van_Kampen_theorem)). Novikov (1955) and Boone (1958) showed that the word problem for finitely presented groups is undecidable in general ([Wikipedia: Word problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups)). J. H. C. Whitehead posed his asphericity question in *Annals of Mathematics* in 1941 ([Wikipedia: Whitehead conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_conjecture)).

### Connections
- [Topological Spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces): $\pi_1$ is defined for any pointed space.
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory): $\pi_1$ is a group, typically non-abelian.
- [Group Presentations](node:Group%20Presentations): van Kampen produces presentations; every presentation is realized by a 2-complex.
- [Homology](node:Homology): $H_1$ is the abelianization of $\pi_1$.
- [Homotopy Equivalence](node:Homotopy%20Equivalence): $\pi_1$ is a homotopy invariant.
- [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles): covering spaces are bundles with discrete fiber; fibrations give long exact sequences.
- [Groupoids](node:Groupoids): the fundamental groupoid removes the base point.
- [Geometric Group Theory](node:Geometric%20Group%20Theory): studies groups through spaces they act on, e.g. universal covers.
- [Knot Invariants](node:Knot%20Invariants): the knot group is $\pi_1$ of the complement.
- [Three-Manifold Topology](node:Three-Manifold%20Topology): 3-manifolds are largely governed by their fundamental groups.
- [Eilenberg–MacLane Spaces](node:Eilenberg–MacLane%20Spaces): $K(G,1)$ spaces have $\pi_1=G$ and no higher homotopy.
- [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces): the historical source of the concept.

### Common pitfalls
- The group depends in general on the base point. For path-connected $X$ the groups at different base points are isomorphic, but the isomorphism depends on the chosen path, up to an inner automorphism ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).
- Van Kampen needs open sets with path-connected intersection. It cannot compute $\pi_1(S^1)$ from two arcs, whose intersection is disconnected, without the groupoid version ([Wikipedia: Seifert–van Kampen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93van_Kampen_theorem)).
- Universal covers need local hypotheses on the base. Wikipedia states existence for connected, locally simply connected spaces; without such conditions a universal cover can fail to exist ([Wikipedia: Covering space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_space)).
- $\pi_1$ detects only one-dimensional holes. All $S^n$ with $n\ge2$ are simply connected, and higher homotopy groups are needed to tell them apart ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group)).

### Open problems
- **Whitehead asphericity conjecture (1941).** Every connected subcomplex of an aspherical 2-dimensional CW complex is aspherical. Equivalently, every sub-presentation of an aspherical presentation is aspherical ($\pi_2=0$ for the presentation complex) ([Wikipedia: Whitehead conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_conjecture)). Bestvina and Brady (1997) built a group showing that the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture and the Whitehead conjecture cannot both be true ([Wikipedia: Whitehead conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_conjecture)). Costa and Farber (2015) state that "at the time of writing the Whitehead Conjecture is still open", and they prove a random-complex analogue: with probability tending to one, aspherical subcomplexes of random 2-complexes satisfy it ([Costa and Farber](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.04837)).

> [!warning] Contested
> Kawauchi's preprint (v1 2023, v2 2024, no journal reference listed) claims that the conjecture is true for every aspherical 2-complex ([arXiv:2303.04368](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04368)). The problem remains listed as unsolved ([Wikipedia: Whitehead conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_conjecture)), and the claim is unconfirmed here.

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Fundamental group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group): definition, examples, coverings, realizability, history.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Seifert–van Kampen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93van_Kampen_theorem): precise statement and the groupoid version.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.901 Introduction to Topology (Munkres)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-901-introduction-to-topology-fall-2004/): course on point-set topology through the fundamental group.
- **Primary:** [Costa and Farber, Large Random Simplicial Complexes II: the fundamental groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.04837): fundamental groups of random complexes and the random Whitehead conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Dimca and Suciu, Which 3-manifold groups are Kähler groups?](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.4350): fundamental groups shared by 3-manifolds and Kähler manifolds are finite.
- **Further reading:** [Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (Cambridge University Press, 2002; free online)](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html): graduate text.
references.GW170817:
## Reference
### Overview
GW170817 is the gravitational-wave signal recorded by Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo on 17 August 2017 at 12:41:04 UTC, the first observation of a binary neutron star inspiral. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 119, 161101](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05832)) It was the first gravitational-wave event with an electromagnetic counterpart, and the aftermath of the merger in the galaxy NGC 4993 was observed by more than 70 observatories on seven continents and in space. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817))

A short gamma-ray burst, GRB 170817A, arrived $(1.74\pm0.05)$ s after the merger. The delay bounds the fractional difference between the speeds of gravity and light to between $-3\times10^{-15}$ and $+7\times10^{-16}$, establishing binary neutron star mergers as short-GRB progenitors. ([LIGO/Virgo/Fermi/INTEGRAL, ApJL 848, L13](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05834)) A kilonova, the optical/infrared transient SSS17a (AT 2017gfo), followed in NGC 4993. ([Multi-messenger paper, ApJL 848, L12](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05833))

Its tidal signature constrains the dense-matter equation of state and neutron-star radii. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 121, 161101](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11581)) It gave a distance-ladder-free "standard siren" measurement of the Hubble constant ([Standard siren paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05835)), ruled out large classes of dark-energy models with a gravitational-wave speed different from $c$ ([Ezquiaga & Zumalacárregui](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05901)), and limited gravitational leakage into non-compact extra dimensions. ([Pardo et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.08160)) Its kilonova supported neutron-star mergers as a dominant site of r-process production. ([Kasen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05463))

### Formal definition
GW170817 is the designation of a transient gravitational-wave signal, named by its UTC date. In the discovery analysis it had combined signal-to-noise ratio 32.4 and a false-alarm rate below one per $8.0\times10^4$ years. Component masses lie between $0.86$ and $2.26\,M_\odot$; restricting spins to the range seen in Galactic binary neutron stars gives components between $1.17$ and $1.60\,M_\odot$ and total mass $2.74^{+0.04}_{-0.01}\,M_\odot$. The 90% sky region was 28 deg² and $d_L=40^{+8}_{-14}$ Mpc. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 119, 161101](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05832))

The chirp mass $\mathcal M=(m_1m_2)^{3/5}(m_1+m_2)^{-1/5}$ was measured in the detector frame as $\mathcal M^{\rm det}=1.1977^{+0.0008}_{-0.0003}\,M_\odot$. Detector-frame masses relate to source-frame masses by $m^{\rm det}=m(1+z)$, and the source-frame chirp mass is $\mathcal M=1.188^{+0.004}_{-0.002}\,M_\odot$ independently of waveform model and priors. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 119, 161101](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.05832))

### Key results
- **Speed of gravity.** From the observed delay of $(+1.74\pm0.05)$ s, $(v_{\rm GW}-c)/c$ lies between $-3\times10^{-15}$ and $+7\times10^{-16}$; the same delay gave new bounds on Lorentz-invariance violation and a test of the equivalence principle through the Shapiro delay. ([ApJL 848, L13](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05834)) This improved the previous estimate by about 14 orders of magnitude. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817))
- **Tidal deformability.** To leading order the phase depends on $\tilde\Lambda=\frac{16}{13}\frac{(m_1+12m_2)m_1^4\Lambda_1+(m_2+12m_1)m_2^4\Lambda_2}{(m_1+m_2)^5}$. With a uniform prior on $\tilde\Lambda$ the discovery paper set 90% upper limits $\tilde\Lambda\le800$ (low-spin prior) and $\tilde\Lambda\le700$ (high-spin prior), and regarded its post-Newtonian results as conservative upper limits because the model is expected to overestimate deformabilities. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 119, 161101](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.05832)) The reanalysis extending the band down to 23 Hz (from 30 Hz) found $\tilde\Lambda=300^{+420}_{-230}$ with restricted spins and $(0,630)$ with large spins allowed, a 16 deg² sky region, total mass $2.73\,M_\odot$, and no evidence for non-zero spins. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRX 9, 011001](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11579))
- **Neutron-star radii and equation of state.** Assuming a common equation of state and Galactic-like spins, the data alone give $R_1=10.8^{+2.0}_{-1.7}$ km and $R_2=10.7^{+2.1}_{-1.5}$ km; requiring the equation of state to support $1.97\,M_\odot$ stars gives $R_1=R_2=11.9\pm1.4$ km, and the pressure at twice nuclear saturation density is $3.5^{+2.7}_{-1.7}\times10^{34}$ dyn cm$^{-2}$ (90%). ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 121, 161101](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11581))
- **Maximum neutron-star mass.** Combining the absence of prompt collapse, the inferred $\gtrsim10^{-2}M_\odot$ of lanthanide-free kilonova ejecta, and energy limits that disfavor a long-lived supramassive remnant, Margalit and Metzger find $M_{\rm max}\lesssim2.17\,M_\odot$ at 90% confidence. ([Margalit & Metzger](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05938))
- **Consequences for dark energy.** Because $|c_g/c-1|\lesssim5\times10^{-16}$, the covariant Galileon cannot be the late-universe dark energy, and the same holds for Horndeski theory and most beyond-Horndeski extensions that change the tensor speed. ([Ezquiaga & Zumalacárregui](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05901)) Among the three functions describing quartic and quintic beyond-Horndeski theories only one survives, and for Horndeski theories it reduces to a standard conformal coupling to the Ricci scalar. ([Creminelli & Vernizzi](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05877))
- **Tests of general relativity.** With the binary neutron star signal the LVC constrained dipole radiation, deviations in the post-Newtonian inspiral coefficients, modified dispersion of gravitational waves and, combining with the counterpart, large extra dimensions, and studied the polarization content; all tests agreed with GR. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 123, 011102](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00364))
- **Hubble constant from a standard siren.** The gravitational-wave distance plus the host galaxy's recession velocity gives $H_0=70.0^{+12.0}_{-8.0}$ km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ without a distance ladder. ([Standard siren paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05835)) Using the viewing angle from radio imaging of the jet breaks the distance–inclination degeneracy and gives $H_0=68.9^{+4.7}_{-4.6}$ km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. ([Hotokezaka et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.10596))
- **Structured, off-axis jet.** VLBI showed the compact radio source moving superluminally between 75 and 230 days after the merger; early radio emission came from a wider-angle outflow (cocoon) and late emission most likely from an energetic narrow jet (opening angle $<5^\circ$) seen about $20^\circ$ off-axis. ([Mooley et al., Nature 561, 355](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.09693)) A source size below 2.5 milliarcseconds at 207.4 days rules out an isotropic outflow and shows that a structured relativistic jet was produced; at least about 10% of mergers may produce such jets. ([Ghirlanda et al., Science 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.00469))
- **Number of spacetime dimensions.** If gravity leaks into extra dimensions, flux conservation damps the strain as $h\propto 1/d_L^{\gamma}$ with $\gamma=(D-2)/2$, so $D=4$ gives $\gamma=1$; normalizing at a 1 Mpc crossing scale, Pardo et al. fit $d_L^{\rm GW}/\mathrm{Mpc}=(d_L^{\rm EM}/\mathrm{Mpc})^\gamma$. ([Pardo et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.08160)) They find $\gamma=1.01^{+0.04}_{-0.05}$, i.e. $D=4.02^{+0.07}_{-0.10}$ (SH0ES $H_0$), or $\gamma=0.99^{+0.03}_{-0.05}$, i.e. $D=3.98^{+0.07}_{-0.09}$ (Planck $H_0$); theories with $D>4$ and a screening scale need that scale to exceed about 20 Mpc. ([Pardo et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.08160))
- **Kilonova and heavy elements.** AT 2017gfo was found less than 11 hours after the merger, faded in the ultraviolet within 48 hours, and reddened over about 10 days; X-rays appeared after about 9 days and radio after about 16. ([Multi-messenger paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05833)) Kilonova models fit to the optical and infrared emission infer two ejecta components, one rich in light r-process elements (mass number below 140) and one rich in heavy ones (above 140), and with the merger rate suggest that such mergers are a dominant mode of r-process production. ([Kasen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05463)) The LIGO press release describes the Gemini, VLT and Hubble observations as revealing "signatures of recently synthesized material, including gold and platinum" ([LIGO Caltech press release](https://www.ligo.caltech.edu/page/press-release-gw170817)); this is a model-based inference, and a 2019 reanalysis of the spectra reported evidence for one specific element, strontium, which had not been robustly identified when the spectra were first published. ([Watson et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10510))

### Examples
- **The chirp.** The signal lasted about 100 s, from about 24 Hz through roughly 3,000 cycles; it reached Virgo first, LIGO-Livingston about 22 ms later, and LIGO-Hanford about 3 ms after that. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817))
- **Localization by a non-detection.** The signal was clear in both LIGO detectors but not in Virgo, placing the source where Virgo was insensitive and narrowing the region to about 28 deg² in Hydra. ([LIGO science summary](https://www.ligo.org/science-summaries/GW170817BNS/))
- **A subluminous burst.** GRB 170817A is the closest short GRB with a known distance yet between 2 and 6 orders of magnitude less energetic than other bursts with measured redshift. ([ApJL 848, L13](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05834)) The off-axis viewing angle of about 20° found by VLBI accounts for much of this. ([Mooley et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.09693))
- **Contrast: GW190425.** A compact binary coalescence whose component masses are consistent with neutron stars, observed on 25 April 2019 by LIGO Livingston alone (Virgo's signal-to-noise ratio was too low to contribute to detection), had total mass $3.4^{+0.3}_{-0.1}\,M_\odot$; assuming it was a binary neutron star, the inferred local merger rate is 250–2810 Gpc⁻³ yr⁻¹. ([LIGO/Virgo, GW190425](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.01761))

### History
The detection came during the second observing run (O2), three days after GW170814; Virgo had joined O2 on 1 August 2017. ([LIGO science summary](https://www.ligo.org/science-summaries/GW170817BNS/)) Fermi issued an automatic alert about 14 seconds after detecting the burst, and the results were announced on 16 October 2017. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817)) The refined source properties were published in 2019 together with the dedicated tests of general relativity. ([PRX 9, 011001](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11579); [PRL 123, 011102](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00364))

### Connections
- [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves): the first gravitational-wave source with an electromagnetic counterpart.
- [Gravitational-Wave Detectors](node:Gravitational-Wave%20Detectors): the three-detector network enabled the localization.
- [Neutron Stars](node:Neutron%20Stars) and [Nuclear Matter Equation of State](node:Nuclear%20Matter%20Equation%20of%20State): tidal deformability, radii, and maximum mass constrain dense matter.
- [r-Process Nucleosynthesis](node:r-Process%20Nucleosynthesis): the kilonova is the main evidence for mergers as an r-process site.
- [Gamma-Ray Bursts](node:Gamma-Ray%20Bursts): GRB 170817A tied short bursts to binary neutron star mergers.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) and [Tests of General Relativity](node:Tests%20of%20General%20Relativity): speed-of-gravity, dispersion, dipole-radiation and Shapiro-delay tests.
- [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle): the Shapiro-delay comparison of photons and gravitons.
- [Scalar-Tensor Gravity](node:Scalar-Tensor%20Gravity) and [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): models with $c_g\ne c$ are ruled out.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): the standard-siren $H_0$ is an independent expansion-rate check.
- [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions), [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions) and [DGP Gravity](node:DGP%20Gravity): leakage into non-compact extra dimensions is constrained.
- [Physics Subsection - Relativistic observations and precision tests](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Relativistic%20observations%20and%20precision%20tests): the map this note belongs to.

### Common pitfalls
- **The 1.7 s is not a measured speed difference.** The gamma rays need not have been emitted at the merger, so the published bound assumes emission 0 to 10 s after the gravitational-wave peak. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817))
- **Detector-frame versus source-frame masses.** Detector-frame masses are larger by $(1+z)$, as the chirp masses above show. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 119, 161101](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.05832))
- **"Gold in the spectra" overstates the evidence.** Gold and platinum production is inferred from heavy-r-process ejecta in kilonova light-curve and opacity models ([Kasen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05463)); the element reported from the spectra themselves is strontium. ([Watson et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10510))
- **Compact extra dimensions are not ruled out.** At these frequencies the diffraction limit restricts resolution to scales of thousands of kilometres, so the leakage test constrains only non-compact extra dimensions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817))
- **The components need not both be neutron stars.** A neutron star–black hole binary is not excluded, though the masses match known neutron stars. ([LIGO science summary](https://www.ligo.org/science-summaries/GW170817BNS/))
- **Early tidal limits were conservative.** The discovery paper's post-Newtonian tidal model was expected to overestimate deformabilities, so its bounds are upper limits later tightened by reanalysis. ([LIGO/Virgo, PRL 119, 161101](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.05832); [PRX 9, 011001](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11579))

### Open problems
- **Nature of the remnant.** The gravitational-wave data could not decide whether the merger left a very massive neutron star or a light black hole of about 3 $M_\odot$. ([LIGO science summary](https://www.ligo.org/science-summaries/GW170817BNS/)) As of 2025 the precise nature of the ultimately stable remnant remains uncertain. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817))
- **Hidden population of dim nearby bursts.** Whether similarly dim nearby bursts have been missed is left to continued joint gamma-ray and gravitational-wave observations. ([LIGO GRB science summary](https://www.ligo.org/science-summaries/GW170817GRB/))
- **More localized standard sirens.** Hotokezaka et al. estimate that about 15 more localized GW170817-like events with radio images and light curves (or 50 to 100 events without them) could potentially resolve the tension between the Planck and Cepheid–supernova $H_0$ values. ([Hotokezaka et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.10596)) As of January 2025 no further gravitational-wave neutron star merger had been localized by electromagnetic observation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817)). GW190425 was detected by LIGO Livingston alone, Virgo's signal being too weak to contribute to the detection. ([GW190425 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.01761))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [GW170817 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817): timeline, source properties, and scientific impact.
- **Learn:** [LIGO science summary: GW170817](https://www.ligo.org/science-summaries/GW170817BNS/): the chirp, localization, and source properties explained.
- **Primary:** [GW170817: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Neutron Star Inspiral (PRL 119, 161101)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05832): the discovery paper.
- **Primary:** [Multi-messenger Observations of a Binary Neutron Star Merger (ApJL 848, L12)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05833): the joint electromagnetic campaign.
- **Primary:** [Gravitational Waves and Gamma-rays from a Binary Neutron Star Merger (ApJL 848, L13)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05834): GRB association and speed-of-gravity bound.
- **Primary:** [Properties of the binary neutron star merger GW170817 (PRX 9, 011001)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11579): the refined parameter estimation.
- **Primary:** [GW170817: Measurements of Neutron Star Radii and Equation of State (PRL 121, 161101)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11581): radius and pressure constraints.
- **Primary:** [Tests of General Relativity with GW170817 (PRL 123, 011102)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00364): dipole radiation, PN coefficients, dispersion, polarizations.
- **Primary:** [Kasen et al., Origin of the heavy elements in binary neutron star mergers](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05463) and [Watson et al., Identification of strontium](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10510): kilonova modelling and the strontium identification.
- **Primary:** [Mooley et al., Superluminal motion of a relativistic jet in GW170817 (Nature 561, 355)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.09693): the off-axis structured jet.
- **Further reading:** [Maggiore, Gravitational Waves, Vol. 2: Astrophysics and Cosmology (OUP, 2018)](https://academic.oup.com/book/43950): graduate monograph on astrophysical and cosmological gravitational-wave sources.
references.Galaxy Rotation Curves:
## Reference
### Overview
The rotation curve of a disc galaxy is the orbital speed of its stars or gas as a function of distance from the centre.
