Observed curves are at significant variance with Newtonian gravity applied to the visible matter: stars orbit at equal or increasing speed over a large range of radii instead of falling off as Kepler's laws would suggest. Unseen dark matter is the main proposed explanation, with modified gravity (MOND) the leading alternative. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve))

Sofue and Rubin describe rotation curves as the major tool for determining how mass is distributed in spiral galaxies. The mismatch between the mass implied by the light and that implied by the velocities is the classic evidence that spirals sit in extended [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter) halos. ([Sofue & Rubin, ARA&A 2001](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594))

The effect is striking because most of a typical galaxy's light lies within the inner 10 kpc; if stars supplied all the mass, speeds would fall beyond that radius, but they stay constant. ([Ohio State: A162 Lecture 18](https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/weinberg.21/Intro/lec18.html))

### Formal definition
The circular velocity $v_{\rm circ}(R)$ is the speed of a circular orbit at radius $R$ in a potential $\Phi$ symmetric about the centre, $v_{\rm circ}^2/R = \partial\Phi/\partial R$; the rotation curve is the function $v_{\rm circ}(R)$. For a spherically symmetric mass distribution with mass $M(R)$ inside $R$,
$$v_{\rm circ} = \sqrt{\frac{GM(R)}{R}},\qquad M(R) = \frac{v_{\rm circ}^2R}{G};$$
axisymmetric discs need a full potential calculation. ([UMD: ASTR 620 notes](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf))

For a spherical profile, inverting Newton's form of Kepler's third law gives the density implied by a measured curve,
$$\rho(r) = \frac{v(r)^2}{4\pi Gr^2}\left(1 + 2\,\frac{d\log v}{d\log r}\right).$$
([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve))

Observationally, for a disc inclined at angle $i$, the rotation speed is recovered from the intensity-weighted line-of-sight velocity $V_{\rm int} = \int I(v)\,v\,dv/\int I(v)\,dv$ as $V_{\rm rot} = (V_{\rm int} - V_{\rm sys})/\sin i$, with $V_{\rm sys}$ the systemic velocity. ([Sofue & Rubin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594))

Common halo models used to fit curves are the pseudo-isothermal profile $\rho = \rho_0[1+(r/r_c)^2]^{-1}$ with finite central density, the Navarro–Frenk–White profile $\rho = \rho_{\rm crit}\delta_c/[(r/r_s)(1+r/r_s)^2]$, and the Einasto profile. ([Wikipedia: Dark matter halo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter_halo)) The pseudo-isothermal form gives a curve that rises and then flattens, but its total mass diverges; NFW fits halos in [N-body Simulations](node:N-body%20Simulations). ([UMD](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf))

### Key results
- **Flat instead of Keplerian.** If mass were concentrated like the light, outer speeds would fall as $V\propto R^{-1/2}$; disc-galaxy rotation curves instead become approximately flat. ([McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.05917))
- **Linear mass growth.** For spherical symmetry, constant $v_{\rm circ}$ implies $M(r)\propto r$ and $\rho\propto r^{-2}$, the simplest dark-halo interpretation. ([UMD](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf))
- **Flat beyond the optical disc.** Synthesis HI observations show that most spiral rotation curves stay flat beyond the optical disc; UGC 2885, with the largest known HI disc (radius 120 kpc for $H_0=50$, 85 kpc for $H_0=70$), is still flat. ([Sofue & Rubin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594))
- **Exponential discs and the need for HI.** For an exponential light distribution the disc's own rotation curve peaks at about 2.2 scale lengths (Freeman 1970). ([Bosma, NED](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/Bosma2/Bos1_4_1.html)) A bulge plus disc can give a fairly flat curve out to about 4 scale lengths with no halo, so confidence in a halo needs the curve beyond about 5 scale lengths, which in practice means 21 cm HI data; Kalnajs's point is that bulge+disc and disc+halo curves have similar shapes at different scales. ([UMD](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf))
- **Radial acceleration relation.** For 2693 points in 153 galaxies from the SPARC sample (galaxies with $i<30^\circ$ or asymmetric curves excluded), $g_{\rm obs}=V^2/R$ follows $g_{\rm obs} = g_{\rm bar}/(1-e^{-\sqrt{g_{\rm bar}/g_\dagger}})$ with $g_\dagger = 1.20\pm0.02\,(\mathrm{rand})\pm0.24\,(\mathrm{syst})\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; residuals are Gaussian with width 0.11 dex (rms 0.13 dex with outliers). The fit is linear at high acceleration and $g_{\rm obs}\propto\sqrt{g_{\rm bar}}$ at low acceleration. ([McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.05917))
- **Universal rotation curve.** From about 1100 rotation curves, Persic, Salucci and Stel find that luminosity alone sets the rotation velocity at any radius; the dark-to-luminous mass ratio at the optical radius scales inversely with luminosity, and the central halo density scales as $L^{-0.7}$. ([Persic, Salucci & Stel](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9506004)) Most luminous galaxies show slightly declining outer curves, intermediate ones are nearly flat, and less luminous ones rise monotonically across the optical disc. ([Sofue & Rubin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594))
- **Diversity at fixed velocity.** ΛCDM hydrodynamical simulations predict rotation-curve shapes that vary with mass but little at fixed maximum circular velocity, whereas observed dwarfs show a large diversity at fixed velocity; many "cored" galaxies show an inner mass deficit relative to cold-dark-matter halos, so the cusp–core issue is better described as an inner-mass-deficit problem. ([Oman et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.01437))

### Examples
- **UGC 12591.** Gas at 465 km/s at both 20 and 36 kpc implies about $10^{12}\,M_\odot$ inside 20 kpc and 1.8 times that inside 36 kpc. ([Ohio State](https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/weinberg.21/Intro/lec18.html))
- **Milky Way: current values.** GRAVITY measured the distance to the Galactic Centre as $R_0 = 8178\pm13\,(\mathrm{stat})\pm22\,(\mathrm{sys})$ pc. ([GRAVITY 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.05721)) Eilers et al. find a circular velocity at the Sun of $229.0\pm0.2$ km/s (systematics 2–5%), declining gently at $-1.7\pm0.1$ km/s/kpc between 5 and 25 kpc. ([Eilers et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.09466)) The older textbook pair $R_0=8.0$ kpc, $v_{\rm circ}=220$ km/s appears in many notes. ([UMD](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf))
- **Milky Way: Gaia DR3 decline.** Jiao et al. report a Keplerian decline from about 19 to 26.5 kpc, a velocity drop of about 30 km/s, rejecting a flat curve at $3\sigma$ and revising the total mass to $2.06^{+0.24}_{-0.13}\times10^{11}\,M_\odot$. ([Jiao et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00048))
- **NGC 4258.** VLBI water masers reveal Keplerian rotation on scales of 0.1 pc around a massive central black hole. ([Sofue & Rubin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594))
- **Too big to fail.** Dissipationless ΛCDM simulations predict that most of the Milky Way's most massive subhalos are too dense to host any of its bright satellites; baryonic feedback or different dark-matter physics that reduced their central densities by order unity on a scale of 0.3–1 kpc would avoid this. ([Boylan-Kolchin, Bullock & Kaplinghat](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.0007))

### History
Galaxy rotation was discovered in 1914, when Slipher detected inclined absorption lines in M31 and the Sombrero galaxy and Wolf did so in M81. Oort's 1939 remark at the McDonald Observatory dedication that the mass in NGC 3115 "appears to bear almost no relation to that of the light" attracted little attention. Early 21 cm work gave a slowly falling curve for M31 (van de Hulst et al. 1957) and a flat curve for M33 (Volders 1959), whose flatness was attributed to beam side lobes; by the 1970s flat curves were routine, and observers and theorists (Ostriker & Peebles 1973; Einasto et al. 1974) jointly argued that disc galaxies sit in extended dark halos. ([Sofue & Rubin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594))

Rubin and Ford announced at a 1975 AAS meeting that most stars in spiral galaxies orbit at roughly the same speed. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve)) Rubin, Thonnard and Ford published rotation curves of 21 Sc galaxies, from NGC 4605 to UGC 2885, in *ApJ* 238 (1980). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/158003)) The SPARC database later gave mass models for 175 disc galaxies with Spitzer 3.6 μm photometry and HI/Hα rotation curves. ([Lelli, McGaugh & Schombert](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.09251))

### Connections
- [Central Force Motion and the Kepler Problem](node:Central%20Force%20Motion%20and%20the%20Kepler%20Problem): the Keplerian $v\propto r^{-1/2}$ baseline that observed curves violate.
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity), [Gauss's Law for Gravity](node:Gauss's%20Law%20for%20Gravity): $v^2=GM(r)/r$ converts speeds into enclosed mass.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter), [Dark Matter Halo Profiles](node:Dark%20Matter%20Halo%20Profiles): flat curves are classic evidence for halos; NFW, Einasto, pseudo-isothermal and Burkert fits.
- [Core-Cusp Problem](node:Core-Cusp%20Problem): inner curves of dwarfs versus cuspy simulated halos.
- [Baryonic Feedback in Dark Matter Halos](node:Baryonic%20Feedback%20in%20Dark%20Matter%20Halos), [Supernova Feedback](node:Supernova%20Feedback): proposed baryonic route from cusps to cores.
- [Missing Satellites Problem](node:Missing%20Satellites%20Problem): a companion small-scale problem alongside too-big-to-fail.
- [Self-Interacting Dark Matter](node:Self-Interacting%20Dark%20Matter): a dark-matter-physics route to cored halos.
- [Modified Newtonian Dynamics](node:Modified%20Newtonian%20Dynamics): the main alternative explanation of flat curves.
- [Radial Acceleration Relation](node:Radial%20Acceleration%20Relation), [Baryonic Tully–Fisher Relation](node:Baryonic%20Tully–Fisher%20Relation): tight baryon–dynamics scaling laws read off rotation curves.
- [McGaugh et al. 2016 - The Radial Acceleration Relation in Rotationally Supported Galaxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05917), [Rubin et al. 1980 - Rotational properties of 21 Sc galaxies](https://doi.org/10.1086/158003): source notes.
- [Galaxy Formation](node:Galaxy%20Formation), [N-body Simulations](node:N-body%20Simulations), [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): the framework predicting halo structure.
- [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing), [Jeans Modeling of Galaxies](node:Jeans%20Modeling%20of%20Galaxies): independent mass probes.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): some authors claim full GR, not the Newtonian limit, changes the Milky Way's inferred curve; these claims are disputed.

### Common pitfalls
- **Applying Kepler's third law to a whole galaxy.** It holds for systems with most mass at the centre; galaxies have extended mass, so this expectation does not apply directly. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve))
- **Spherical formulas for discs.** $M=v^2R/G$ holds only for spherical symmetry. The peak of an exponential disc's curve is at about 2.2 scale lengths, not at one scale length. ([UMD](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf)) ([Bosma, NED](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/Bosma2/Bos1_4_1.html))
- **Non-unique decompositions.** Mass deconvolutions into bulge, disc and halo are far from unique, and a third of an Ursa Major sample did not follow the universal curve shape. ([Sofue & Rubin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594))
- **Tracer and geometry biases.** Old stars have larger velocity dispersion and rotate slightly below $v_{\rm circ}$, so gas and young stars are better tracers; face-on discs cannot be analysed. ([UMD](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf))
- **Dated Milky Way numbers.** $R_0=8.0$ kpc and 220 km/s are older conventions; current measurements give $R_0\approx8.18$ kpc and $v_c\approx229$ km/s. ([GRAVITY 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.05721)) ([Eilers et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.09466))

### Open problems
- **Cusp–core and diversity.** Inner rotation curves of dark-matter-dominated galaxies favour roughly constant-density cores rather than the cuspy NFW halos of ΛCDM simulations. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve)) Oman et al. conclude that at least one must hold: dark matter is more complex than in current models, simulations miss baryonic effects in dwarf centres, or the kinematic mass profiles are inaccurate. ([Oman et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.01437))
- **Baryonic feedback versus dark-matter physics.** Pontzen and Governato propose that rapid, supernova-driven fluctuations of the central potential irreversibly transfer energy to dark matter and turn cusps into cores; they predict cores in systems of a wide mass range if central starbursts or AGN phases are frequent and energetic. ([Pontzen & Governato 2012](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.0499)) Burkert instead argued that the flat cores of dwarf halos are not the result of later baryonic processes and may reveal the nature of dark matter. ([Burkert 1995](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9504041))
- **Origin of the scaling relations.** There is not yet a straightforward explanation of why the Tully–Fisher scaling exists, and ΛCDM simulations give different radial acceleration relations, some similar to the observed one and some not. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve))
- **Halo extent.** How far dark halos extend, and hence the total masses of disc galaxies, remains poorly constrained. ([UMD](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf)) Even for the Milky Way, the Gaia DR3 outer curve of Jiao et al. revises the total mass downward, to $2.06^{+0.24}_{-0.13}\times10^{11}\,M_\odot$ with an upper limit of $5.4\times10^{11}\,M_\odot$. ([Jiao et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00048))

> [!warning] Contested
> Dark halos require Newtonian gravity to hold over these distances; Sofue and Rubin note that proof is lacking, though most astronomers prefer halos to modified dynamics. ([Sofue & Rubin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594)) MOND, proposed by Milgrom in 1983, modifies the force law at low accelerations and predicts the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation $V\propto M^{1/4}$; GR-based alternative rotation-curve models have been disputed. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve)) The Gaia DR3 Keplerian decline in the outer Milky Way reported by Jiao et al. contrasts with the gently declining curve of Eilers et al. to 25 kpc. ([Jiao et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00048)) ([Eilers et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.09466))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Galaxy rotation curve (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve): history, halo profiles, dark-matter and modified-gravity interpretations.
- **Learn:** [UMD ASTR 620, ch. 5 "Rotation Curves"](https://pages.astro.umd.edu/~rmushotz/ASTRO620/QM_chap5.pdf): circular velocity, disc potentials (Kalnajs), halo profiles.
- **Learn:** [Ohio State A162, Lecture 18](https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/weinberg.21/Intro/lec18.html): introductory lecture on galaxy masses from rotation.
- **Primary:** [Sofue & Rubin, "Rotation Curves of Spiral Galaxies", ARA&A 39 (2001)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0010594): standard review of methods, results and history.
- **Primary:** [McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert, "The Radial Acceleration Relation in Rotationally Supported Galaxies"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05917): the SPARC radial acceleration relation.
- **Primary:** [Oman et al., "The unexpected diversity of dwarf galaxy rotation curves"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.01437): diversity / inner-mass-deficit problem.
- **Further reading:** [SPARC: Mass Models for 175 Disk Galaxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.09251): the rotation-curve database behind the RAR and BTFR.
references.Gamma Function:
## Reference
### Overview
The gamma function $\Gamma(z)$ is the standard meromorphic extension of the factorial: for $\operatorname{Re}z>0$ it is Euler's integral of the second kind, it satisfies $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!$ for positive integers $n$, and it continues analytically to $\mathbb{C}$ minus the non-positive integers. It has no zeros, so $1/\Gamma$ is entire. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function)) ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2))

It is not the only analytic function extending the factorial, and the recurrence alone does not determine it. It is singled out by the Bohr–Mollerup theorem as the unique positive, logarithmically convex solution of $f(x+1)=xf(x)$ with $f(1)=1$. Artin's 1931 monograph built the whole elementary theory from that characterization. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function)) ([Wikipedia, Bohr–Mollerup theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr%E2%80%93Mollerup_theorem)) ([Artin, The Gamma Function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Artin-TheGammaFunction.pdf))

$\Gamma$ appears in ball volumes, in the beta integral, as the archimedean factor completing the Riemann zeta function, and in transcendence theory, where its values at rational points are tied to periods of abelian varieties and remain largely mysterious: transcendence of $\Gamma(1/5)$ is unproved. ([Wikipedia, Volume of an n-ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume_of_an_n-ball)) ([Wikipedia, Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function)) ([Waldschmidt, Open Diophantine Problems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))

### Formal definition
For $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, Euler's integral is as follows. ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2))
$$
\Gamma(z)=\int_0^\infty e^{-t}t^{z-1}\,dt .
$$
Elsewhere $\Gamma$ is defined by analytic continuation; it is meromorphic with no zeros and simple poles of residue $(-1)^n/n!$ at $z=-n$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$. ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2)) ([Garrett notes](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/mfms/notes_2019-20/05b_Gamma.pdf)) Garrett writes the same integral as $\int_0^\infty t^se^{-t}\,dt/t$; integration by parts gives $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, which supplies the continuation strip by strip. ([Garrett notes](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/mfms/notes_2019-20/05b_Gamma.pdf))

Equivalent global definitions are Weierstrass's product and Hankel's loop integral below. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function)) ([DLMF §5.9](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.9))
$$
\Gamma(z)=\frac{e^{-\gamma z}}{z}\prod_{n=1}^\infty\Bigl(1+\frac{z}{n}\Bigr)^{-1}e^{z/n},\qquad
\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)}=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{-\infty}^{(0+)}e^tt^{-z}\,dt,
$$
where $\gamma=\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\tfrac12+\cdots+\tfrac1n-\ln n)\approx0.5772$ and the Hankel contour starts at $-\infty$, circles the origin once positively, and returns to $-\infty$. ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2)) ([DLMF §5.9](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.9))

The digamma function is $\psi(z)=\Gamma'(z)/\Gamma(z)$, and the polygamma functions are its derivatives $\psi^{(n)}$. ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2)) ([DLMF §5.15](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.15))

### Key results
- **Functional equations.** $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$; for $z\notin\mathbb{Z}$, $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin(\pi z)$; for $2z\ne0,-1,-2,\dots$, $\Gamma(2z)=\pi^{-1/2}2^{2z-1}\Gamma(z)\Gamma(z+\tfrac12)$; and for $nz\ne0,-1,-2,\dots$ Gauss's multiplication formula $\Gamma(nz)=(2\pi)^{(1-n)/2}n^{nz-1/2}\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\Gamma(z+k/n)$. ([DLMF §5.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.5)) Garrett proves the reflection formula with a Hankel-type contour and the duplication formula from Euler's integral. ([Garrett notes](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/mfms/notes_2019-20/05b_Gamma.pdf))
- **Bohr–Mollerup theorem.** If $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $f(x+1)=xf(x)$, $f(1)=1$, and $\ln f$ is convex, then $f=\Gamma$ on $(0,\infty)$. ([DLMF §5.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.5)) ([Wikipedia, Bohr–Mollerup theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr%E2%80%93Mollerup_theorem))
- **Hölder's theorem (1887).** $\Gamma$ satisfies no algebraic differential equation with rational-function coefficients: no nonzero polynomial in $z,\Gamma,\Gamma',\dots,\Gamma^{(n)}$ vanishes identically. ([Wikipedia, Hölder's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B6lder%27s_theorem))
- **Beta integral.** For $\operatorname{Re}a,\operatorname{Re}b>0$, $B(a,b)=\int_0^1x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}\,dx=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)$. ([Garrett notes](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/mfms/notes_2019-20/05b_Gamma.pdf)) See [Beta Function](node:Beta%20Function).
- **Stirling series.** As $z\to\infty$ in $|\operatorname{ph}z|\le\pi-\delta$, $\ln\Gamma(z)\sim(z-\tfrac12)\ln z-z+\tfrac12\ln(2\pi)+\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{B_{2k}}{2k(2k-1)z^{2k-1}}$, and $\Gamma(z)=e^{-z}z^z(2\pi/z)^{1/2}\Gamma^*(z)$ with $\Gamma^*(z)\sim1+\frac{1}{12z}+\frac{1}{288z^2}+\cdots$. ([DLMF §5.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11)) See [Stirling's Formula](node:Stirling's%20Formula).
- **Binet's formula.** For $|\operatorname{ph}z|<\pi/2$, $\ln\Gamma(z)=(z-\tfrac12)\ln z-z+\tfrac12\ln(2\pi)+\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\frac{1}{e^t-1}-\frac1t+\frac12\Bigr)\frac{e^{-zt}}{t}\,dt$; an equivalent form has remainder $2\int_0^\infty\frac{\arctan(t/z)}{e^{2\pi t}-1}\,dt$. ([DLMF §5.9](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.9))
- **Digamma and polygamma.** $\psi(z+1)=\psi(z)+1/z$; $\psi(z)-\psi(1-z)=-\pi\cot(\pi z)$; $\psi(1)=-\gamma$, $\psi(n)=H_{n-1}-\gamma$; $\psi(z+1)=-\gamma+\sum_{n\ge1}\bigl(\frac1n-\frac1{n+z}\bigr)$; and $\psi'(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}(k+z)^{-2}$. Gauss's digamma theorem evaluates $\psi(r/m)$ in closed form. ([DLMF §5.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.5)) ([DLMF §5.15](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.15)) ([Wikipedia, Digamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digamma_function))
- **Archimedean factor of $\zeta$.** $\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)=\pi^{-(1-s)/2}\Gamma((1-s)/2)\zeta(1-s)$ as meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}$; equivalently $\zeta(s)=2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin(\pi s/2)\Gamma(1-s)\zeta(1-s)$, and for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, $\Gamma(s)\zeta(s)=\int_0^\infty\frac{x^{s-1}}{e^x-1}\,dx$. ([Wikipedia, Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function))
- **Transcendence results.** Chudnovsky proved $\Gamma(1/3)$ and $\Gamma(1/4)$ transcendental; Nesterenko (1996) proved $\pi$, $\Gamma(1/4)$, $e^\pi$ algebraically independent (and likewise $\pi$, $\Gamma(1/3)$, $e^{\pi\sqrt3}$). By contrast Schneider (1940) proved every beta value $B(a,b)$ at rational non-integers $a,b,a+b$ transcendental. ([Wikipedia, Particular values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particular_values_of_the_gamma_function)) ([Waldschmidt, Open Diophantine Problems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))
- **Chowla–Selberg formula.** Products of $\Gamma$ at rational arguments evaluate the Dedekind eta function at imaginary quadratic points (essentially Lerch 1897; Chowla–Selberg 1949, 1967), e.g. $\eta(i)$ in terms of $\Gamma(1/4)$; it belongs to the theory of periods of CM abelian varieties. ([Wikipedia, Chowla–Selberg formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chowla%E2%80%93Selberg_formula))

### Examples
- **Half-integers.** $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ (reflection at $z=1/2$), and hence $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2}\,du=\sqrt\pi$ by $t=u^2$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function)) ([DLMF §5.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.5))
- **Ball volumes and sphere areas.** $V_n(R)=\pi^{n/2}R^n/\Gamma(n/2+1)$ and $A_{n-1}(R)=2\pi^{n/2}R^{n-1}/\Gamma(n/2)$, giving $V_2=\pi R^2$, $V_3=\tfrac43\pi R^3$, $V_4=\tfrac{\pi^2}{2}R^4$. ([Wikipedia, Volume of an n-ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume_of_an_n-ball)) See [n-Ball](node:n-Ball) and [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere).
- **Pochhammer symbol.** $(a)_n=a(a+1)\cdots(a+n-1)=\Gamma(a+n)/\Gamma(a)$, the building block of hypergeometric series. ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2))
- **Fourier transform.** For $\operatorname{Re}\alpha>-1$, $f(x)=x^\alpha e^{-x}$ ($x>0$), $0$ ($x<0$) has $\widehat f(\xi)=\Gamma(\alpha+1)/(1+2\pi i\xi)^{\alpha+1}$. ([Garrett notes](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/mfms/notes_2019-20/05b_Gamma.pdf))

### History
Extending the factorial to non-integers was first considered by Daniel Bernoulli and Christian Goldbach in the 1720s; Euler announced his infinite product in a letter of 13 October 1729; Legendre introduced the name and the symbol $\Gamma$ around 1811. Hölder proved the differential-transcendence theorem in 1887. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function)) Bohr and Mollerup published their characterization in a 1922 complex-analysis textbook, believing it already known. ([Wikipedia, Bohr–Mollerup theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr%E2%80%93Mollerup_theorem)) Artin's *Einführung in die Theorie der Gammafunktion* (1931) developed the theory from log-convexity; the English translation appeared in 1964. ([Artin, The Gamma Function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Artin-TheGammaFunction.pdf))

### Connections
- [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus): Euler's integral defines $\Gamma$ for $\operatorname{Re}z>0$.
- [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis): meromorphic continuation, Hankel contours, Weierstrass products.
- [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions): $\Gamma$ underlies hypergeometric and Bessel functions via Pochhammer symbols.
- [Beta Function](node:Beta%20Function): $B=\Gamma\Gamma/\Gamma$.
- [Stirling's Formula](node:Stirling's%20Formula): the leading term of the asymptotic series.
- [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) and [Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory): archimedean factor in the functional equation.
- [n-Ball](node:n-Ball), [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere), [Higher-Dimensional Euclidean Geometry](node:Higher-Dimensional%20Euclidean%20Geometry): volumes and areas.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): Mellin and Fourier transforms of $x^\alpha e^{-x}$.
- Map: [MSC 33 - Special functions](node:MSC%2033%20-%20Special%20functions)

### Common pitfalls
- **Off-by-one.** $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!$, so $\Gamma(1)=\Gamma(2)=1$. ([Garrett notes](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/mfms/notes_2019-20/05b_Gamma.pdf))
- **Poles, not zeros.** $\Gamma$ has simple poles at $0,-1,-2,\dots$ and no zeros; the zeros belong to $1/\Gamma$. ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2))
- **Recurrence does not determine $\Gamma$.** If $p$ has period $1$ and $p(1)=1$ (equivalently $p=1$ at every integer), then $p(x)\Gamma(x)$ satisfies the same recurrence and normalization; log-convexity on $(0,\infty)$ removes this freedom. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function)) ([DLMF §5.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.5))
- **Stirling's series diverges.** It is an asymptotic expansion in $|\operatorname{ph}z|\le\pi-\delta$, not a convergent series; Binet's integral gives an exact remainder for $\operatorname{Re}z>0$. ([DLMF §5.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11)) ([DLMF §5.9](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.9))
- **Beta versus gamma values.** Transcendence of all rational beta values (Schneider) does not give transcendence of individual gamma values. ([Waldschmidt, Open Diophantine Problems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))

### Open problems
- **Transcendence of $\Gamma(1/5)$.** Apart from $\Gamma(1/2),\Gamma(1/3),\Gamma(1/4)$, little is known; "there is no proof so far that $\Gamma(1/5)$ is transcendental": the algebraic-independence results for elliptic curves such as $x^3+y^3=1$ and $x^4+y^4=1$ that sufficed for $\Gamma(1/3)$ and $\Gamma(1/4)$ are not yet known for the higher-dimensional abelian varieties attached to $x^5+y^5=1$. Waldschmidt's Conjecture 3.18, that at least three of $\pi,\Gamma(1/5),\Gamma(2/5),e^{\pi\sqrt5}$ are algebraically independent, is stated as still open. ([Waldschmidt, Open Diophantine Problems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440)) Wikipedia likewise records that transcendence of $\Gamma$ at rationals is unknown in general and that no relations analogous to those for $1/3,1/4$ are known for $\Gamma(1/5)$. ([Wikipedia, Particular values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particular_values_of_the_gamma_function))
- **Rohrlich's conjecture and the general relations question.** With $G(z)=\Gamma(z)/\sqrt{2\pi}$ taken modulo $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^\times$, Rohrlich conjectures that $G$ is a universal odd distribution on $(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\setminus\{0\}$ with values in groups where multiplication by $2$ is invertible: every multiplicative relation $\pi^{b/2}\prod_a\Gamma(a)^{m_a}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ follows from the distribution (multiplication) relations, oddness (reflection), and the functional equation. The broader question is whether these relations generate all algebraic relations among the values. ([Waldschmidt, Open Diophantine Problems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gamma function (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function): definitions, functional equations, history; with [DLMF Chapter 5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2) for exact formulas and conditions.
- **Learn:** [Garrett, The Gamma function](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/mfms/notes_2019-20/05b_Gamma.pdf): Euler integral, beta integral, reflection by contour integration, duplication.
- **Primary:** [Waldschmidt, Open Diophantine Problems (2004), §3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440): what is known and conjectured about transcendence of gamma values.
- **Primary:** [Artin, The Gamma Function (Holt, Rinehart and Winston 1964; German 1931)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Artin-TheGammaFunction.pdf): the classic monograph developing $\Gamma$ from log-convexity.
- **Further reading:** [Artin, The Gamma Function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Artin-TheGammaFunction.pdf) and [DLMF Chapter 5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2).
references.Gauge Invariance:
## Reference
### Overview
In classical electromagnetism the fields $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ can be written in terms of a scalar potential $\phi$ and a vector potential $\mathbf A$, and these potentials are not unique: shifting $\mathbf A$ by the gradient of an arbitrary function $\psi(\mathbf r,t)$ while shifting $\phi$ by $-\partial_t\psi$ leaves $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ unchanged. Gauge invariance is the requirement that physical observables be unchanged under such transformations; calculations may be done in a fixed gauge, but their physical content must be gauge invariant. ([Wikipedia: Gauge fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_fixing))

Gauge invariance reflects a redundancy in the description rather than a change of physical state: both gauge invariance and diffeomorphism invariance reflect redundant degrees of freedom, and philosophers of physics describe local symmetries as "surplus" structure, with only gauge-invariant quantities serving as observables. How best to interpret gauge theories remains an open issue in the philosophy of physics. ([Wikipedia: Gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory)) ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/symmetry-breaking/))

In quantum theory the freedom acquires a second half: the wave function of a charged particle changes by a position-dependent phase, and demanding invariance under local phase changes forces the introduction of a gauge field through a covariant derivative. Generalised by Yang and Mills to non-abelian groups in 1954, this "gauge principle" underlies all of the Standard Model, and geometrically a gauge potential is a connection on a principal bundle. ([Wikipedia: Gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory)) ([Jackson and Okun](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012061))

### Formal definition
**Electromagnetic gauge transformation.** With $\mathbf B = \nabla\times\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf E = -\nabla\phi - \partial_t\mathbf A$, the transformation
$$\mathbf A \mapsto \mathbf A + \nabla\psi,\qquad \phi \mapsto \phi - \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}$$
leaves $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ unchanged for every function $\psi(\mathbf r,t)$. In covariant notation the potentials combine into a four-potential $A_\mu$ and the fields into $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$, i.e. $F = dA$; the transformation becomes $A_\mu\mapsto A_\mu + \partial_\mu\psi$ (up to sign conventions), and $F$ is unchanged because $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\psi$ is symmetric. ([Wikipedia: Gauge fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_fixing)) ([Wikipedia: Charge conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge_conservation)) ([Wikipedia: Electromagnetic tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_tensor))

**Gauge conditions.** The Coulomb gauge $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A = 0$ is a complete gauge but not Lorentz covariant. The Lorenz gauge $\partial_\mu A^\mu = 0$ is the unique constraint gauge that keeps manifest Lorentz invariance; it is incomplete, since gauge functions satisfying the wave equation $\partial_t^2\psi = c^2\nabla^2\psi$ preserve it. The temporal (Weyl) gauge $\phi = 0$ is also incomplete. $R_\xi$ gauges generalise the Lorenz gauge to non-abelian groups such as $SU(3)$, with $\xi=1$ the Feynman–'t Hooft gauge. ([Wikipedia: Gauge fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_fixing))

**Local gauge invariance in field theory.** A gauge theory is a field theory whose Lagrangian is invariant under local transformations forming a Lie group $G$, the gauge group; a global symmetry is a local one whose parameters are fixed in spacetime. For each generator of $G$ there is a gauge field, introduced so that the Lagrangian stays invariant. For $U(1)$ in QED the electron field's phase rotation $\theta$ becomes a function $\theta(x)$, and invariance requires replacing $\partial_\mu$ by the covariant derivative $D_\mu = \partial_\mu - ieA_\mu$ (in units with $\hbar = 1$). For non-abelian $G$ the field strength is the curvature $F = dA + A\wedge A$, which transforms covariantly rather than invariantly because the components of $A$ do not commute. ([Wikipedia: Gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory))

**Geometric form.** A gauge is a choice of local section of a principal bundle, a gauge transformation is a change between two such sections, and the gauge potential is the local connection form. ([Wikipedia: Gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory))

### Key results
- **Gauge invariance and charge conservation.** Taking the divergence of the Ampère–Maxwell law and using Gauss's law gives $\partial_t\rho + \nabla\cdot\mathbf J = 0$, so Maxwell's equations are consistent only with a conserved current; via Noether's theorem charge conservation is associated with global gauge invariance. ([Wikipedia: Charge conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge_conservation))
- **Aharonov–Bohm effect.** A charge $q$ moving along a path $P$ in a region where $\mathbf B = 0$ but $\mathbf A\neq 0$ acquires the phase $\varphi = \frac{q}{\hbar}\int_P \mathbf A\cdot d\mathbf x$; two paths enclosing magnetic flux $\Phi_B$ differ in phase by $q\Phi_B/\hbar$. The holonomy $e^{i\oint_\gamma A}$ around a closed loop depends only on the connection, not on the trivialisation, and a flat connection need not be trivial, its monodromy depending on the homology class of the loop. Gauge-invariant quantities are exactly the observable ones, and the phase is fixed by the potential along the path even where the field vanishes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aharonov%E2%80%93Bohm_effect))
- **Elitzur's theorem (1975).** In lattice gauge theory with a compact gauge group, local gauge symmetry cannot be spontaneously broken: integrating a gauge non-invariant observable over the group measure gives zero, so only gauge-invariant operators have nonzero expectation values. Positivity of the measure and gauge invariance suffice for the proof. Consequently the nonzero Higgs vacuum expectation value in unitary gauge is a gauge artefact, and confinement must be characterised by nonlocal invariants such as Wilson and Polyakov loops. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elitzur%27s_theorem))
- **Gribov ambiguity (1978).** In abelian gauge theory it suffices to choose a gauge, but for non-abelian theories a large class of gauge conditions intersect a gauge orbit more than once, and global gauge fixing is often impossible because of topological obstructions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gribov_ambiguity))
- **Higgs mechanism without breaking gauge invariance.** Gauge bosons acquire mass by "eating" Goldstone bosons without explicitly breaking the gauge invariance of the theory; a gauge-invariant reformulation is the Fröhlich–Morchio–Strocchi mechanism, which agrees with the usual Higgs picture for groups containing $SU(2)$ but can differ for other groups. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/symmetry-breaking/)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elitzur%27s_theorem))

### Examples
- **QED.** The $U(1)$ phase symmetry of the electron field, made local, requires the electromagnetic potential through $D_\mu$; gauge fixing in QED is straightforward because the group is abelian. ([Wikipedia: Gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gribov_ambiguity))
- **Yang–Mills theory.** Yang and Mills required invariance under local isotopic-spin rotations, which demands a field $b_\mu$ related to isotopic spin as the electromagnetic field is to charge; it obeys nonlinear equations and its quanta have spin 1, isotopic spin 1 and charge $\pm e$ or $0$. ([Yang and Mills](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.96.191))
- **Choosing a gauge for a calculation.** Radiation problems often use the Coulomb gauge, which is complete but not covariant, while covariant perturbation theory uses the Lorenz or $R_\xi$ gauges, with Faddeev–Popov ghosts appearing in the non-abelian case. ([Wikipedia: Gauge fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_fixing))

### History
Gauge freedom goes back to electrodynamics after the 1820 discovery of electromagnetism, when different forms of the vector potential were found to give the same observable forces, and L. V. Lorenz proposed the condition now bearing his name in the 1860s. In 1926 Schrödinger, Klein and Fock found a relativistic wave equation, and Fock observed its invariance under a phase multiplication of the wave function combined with a change of potential; in 1929 Weyl proclaimed this a general principle, Eichinvarianz or gauge invariance. ([Jackson and Okun](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012061))

The concept and name of gauge theory derive from Weyl's 1918 work. Yang and Mills generalised gauge invariance to non-abelian $SU(2)$ in "Conservation of Isotopic Spin and Isotopic Gauge Invariance", Phys. Rev. 96, 191 (1954). Ehrenberg and Siday predicted the Aharonov–Bohm effect in 1949, Aharonov and Bohm analysed it in 1959, and Tonomura and colleagues observed it unambiguously in 1986 with the magnetic field excluded by a superconducting shield. ([Wikipedia: Gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory)) ([APS](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.96.191)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aharonov%E2%80%93Bohm_effect))

### Connections
- [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations): the prerequisite; gauge freedom arises in their potential formulation.
- [Lorenz Gauge](node:Lorenz%20Gauge): the covariant gauge condition in detail.
- [Electromagnetic Field Tensor](node:Electromagnetic%20Field%20Tensor): the gauge-invariant $F_{\mu\nu}$.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): the general framework built on local gauge invariance.
- [Aharonov–Bohm Effect](node:Aharonov–Bohm%20Effect): the observable, gauge-invariant holonomy of the potential.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem): links global gauge symmetry to charge conservation.
- [Principal Bundle Connections](node:Principal%20Bundle%20Connections), [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles) and [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives): the geometric language of gauge fields.
- [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms) and [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology): $F = dA$ and the topology behind Aharonov–Bohm phases.
- [Quantum Electrodynamics](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics): the $U(1)$ gauge theory of electrons and photons.
- [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): mass generation that does not break gauge invariance.
- [Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap](node:Yang–Mills%20Existence%20and%20Mass%20Gap): the central open problem of non-abelian gauge theory.
- [Synthetic Gauge Fields](node:Synthetic%20Gauge%20Fields): engineered gauge potentials in cold-atom and photonic systems.
- [Transverse-Traceless Gauge](node:Transverse-Traceless%20Gauge): the analogous gauge freedom of linearised gravity.

### Common pitfalls
- **"Gauge symmetry breaking."** Local gauge symmetry cannot be spontaneously broken (Elitzur); the Higgs vacuum expectation value is an artefact of gauge choice. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elitzur%27s_theorem))
- **Lorenz gauge does not fix the gauge.** Residual transformations whose gauge functions satisfy the wave equation remain; a fully fixed gauge needs boundary conditions along the light cone. ([Wikipedia: Gauge fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_fixing))
- **Potentials are not physically meaningless.** Although $\mathbf A$ itself is not uniquely determined, its holonomy around a loop produces the measurable Aharonov–Bohm phase in regions where $\mathbf B=0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aharonov%E2%80%93Bohm_effect))
- **Lorenz, not Lorentz.** The gauge condition is due to L. V. Lorenz, distinct from H. A. Lorentz. ([Jackson and Okun](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012061))
- **Non-abelian field strength is not gauge invariant.** $F = dA + A\wedge A$ transforms covariantly rather than invariantly; nonlocal gauge-invariant quantities such as Wilson and Polyakov loops serve as observables, for example for confinement. ([Wikipedia: Gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elitzur%27s_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Yang–Mills existence and mass gap.** Prove that for every compact simple gauge group $G$ a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills theory exists on $\mathbb R^4$, satisfying axioms at least as strong as the Wightman or Osterwalder–Schrader axioms, and has a mass gap $\Delta>0$. The Clay Mathematics Institute lists the problem as unsolved and states that no proof of the mass gap is known. OpenAI announced an AI-generated proof of the existence part only, not the mass gap, on 26 October 2026. In a statement of 9 November 2026, a shepherding committee (Douglas, Gross as chair, Jaffe, Klebanov and Nekrasov) reported that it had checked the Lean code OpenAI submitted on 28 October and that it proves the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory according to the standard problem statements. This is a recent claim that the Clay Institute has not recognised, so it is recorded here as reported but not settled; the mass gap remains unproven. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/)) ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang%E2%80%93Mills_existence_and_mass_gap)) ([KITP shepherding committee](https://www.kitp.ucsb.edu/sites/default/files/3rd-Statement-About-Quantum-YangMills-Theory_Nov-9.pdf))
- **Elitzur's theorem in the continuum.** All current proofs use lattice formulations, so continuum exceptions are considered unlikely but not excluded; the theorem also does not cover residual or large gauge transformations. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elitzur%27s_theorem))
- **Interpretation of gauge theories.** Which quantities in a gauge theory are physically real, and how the Higgs mechanism should be understood, are described as open and actively debated issues in philosophy of physics. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/symmetry-breaking/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Gauge fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_fixing): gauge transformations of the potentials and standard gauge conditions.
- **Reference:** [SEP: Symmetry and Symmetry Breaking](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/symmetry-breaking/): local symmetry as surplus structure and the interpretation of the Higgs mechanism.
- **Learn:** [Alvarez-Gaume and Vazquez-Mozo, Lectures on Field Theory and the Standard Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08097): 2022 European School of High-Energy Physics lectures on symmetries and their realisation in the Standard Model.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 8.07, Electromagnetism II (Guth and Chen, 2012)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-07-electromagnetism-ii-fall-2012/): time-dependent fields, Maxwell's equations and relativistic electrodynamics.
- **Primary:** [Jackson and Okun, Historical roots of gauge invariance](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012061): Rev. Mod. Phys. 73 (2001) 663–680, review from the 1820s to 1954.
- **Primary:** [Yang and Mills, Conservation of Isotopic Spin and Isotopic Gauge Invariance](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.96.191): the founding non-abelian gauge theory paper.
- **Further reading:** [Weinberg, The Quantum Theory of Fields (Cambridge University Press, 1996)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139644174): graduate monograph on quantum field theory, including gauge theories.
- **Further reading:** [Clay Mathematics Institute: Yang–Mills and the Mass Gap](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/): official problem page.
references.Gauge Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
A gauge theory is a field theory whose description contains redundant degrees of freedom: a gauge symmetry is "not a true symmetry" but the statement that different field configurations are physically equivalent. In electromagnetism the phase of a charged field and the longitudinal part of $A_\mu$ are unphysical; a Lorentz-covariant $A_\mu$ has four components while a massless spin-one particle has two polarizations, so the redundancy must be handled in quantization. ([MIT 8.324 Lecture 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-324-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-ii-fall-2010/1b3e727b1edcd9b2f41182a3d8438701_MIT8_324F10_Lecture5.pdf))

The idea grew from Weyl's work; Yang–Mills theory replaces the $U(1)$ of electromagnetism by a compact nonabelian group $G$. Its quantum version is asymptotically free, which made it the basis of the theory of the strong force, while in electroweak theory a Higgs field reduces the structure group $SU(2)\times U(1)$ to a $U(1)$ subgroup, so only electromagnetism is long-ranged. ([Jaffe and Witten](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/yangmills.pdf)) Both parts of the [Standard Model](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics), [Electroweak Theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory) with gauge group $SU(2)\times U(1)$ and [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics) with gauge group $SU(3)$, are nonabelian gauge theories of this kind. ([Jaffe and Witten](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/yangmills.pdf))

Mathematically, gauge fields are connections on principal bundles and field strengths are curvatures. This geometric picture underlies both the physics and Donaldson's use of instanton [moduli spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces) in four-manifold topology. ([Wikipedia, Gauge theory (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory_%28mathematics%29))

### Formal definition
Let $G$ be a compact Lie group and $P\to X$ a principal $G$-bundle: a fibre bundle with a free right $G$-action transitive on fibres, locally trivial with transition functions satisfying the cocycle condition. A connection is a $G$-invariant choice of horizontal subspaces of $TP$, given locally by a [Lie-algebra](node:Lie%20Algebras)-valued one-form $A_\alpha$ with curvature $F=dA_\alpha+\tfrac12[A_\alpha,A_\alpha]$. The gauge group is the group of bundle automorphisms commuting with the projection and the $G$-action, i.e. sections of $\operatorname{Ad}(P)$; for matrix groups it acts by $A\mapsto gAg^{-1}-(dg)g^{-1}$. ([Wikipedia, Gauge theory (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory_%28mathematics%29)) See [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles) and [Principal Bundle Connections](node:Principal%20Bundle%20Connections).

The Yang–Mills functional is $\mathrm{YM}(A)=\int_X\|F_A\|^2\,d\mathrm{vol}$. Every connection satisfies the Bianchi identity $d_AF_A=0$, and the [Euler–Lagrange equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations) are $d_A{*F_A}=0$. ([Wikipedia, Gauge theory (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory_%28mathematics%29)) In the convention $F=dA+A\wedge A$, the source-free Yang–Mills equations read $0=d_AF=d_A{*F}$, reducing to [Maxwell's equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations) with $F=dA$ for $G=U(1)$; they are the variational equations of $L=\frac{1}{4g^2}\int\operatorname{Tr}F\wedge *F$, with $\operatorname{Tr}$ an invariant quadratic form on $\mathfrak g$. ([Jaffe and Witten](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/yangmills.pdf))

**Physics notation (minimal coupling).** With Hermitian generators $T^a$ normalized by $\operatorname{tr}(T^aT^b)=\tfrac12\delta^{ab}$ and structure constants $f^{abc}$, matter fields couple through the covariant derivative
$$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-igT^aA^a_\mu,\qquad F^a_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A^a_\nu-\partial_\nu A^a_\mu+gf^{abc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu,\qquad \mathcal L=-\tfrac14F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu}=-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}.$$
The term quadratic in $A$ makes the gauge field self-interacting, unlike the photon. ([Wikipedia, Yang–Mills theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang%E2%80%93Mills_theory))

### Key results
- **Faddeev–Popov gauge fixing.** The gauge-field kinetic operator $K_{\mu\nu}=\partial^2\eta_{\mu\nu}-\partial_\mu\partial_\nu$ annihilates every pure gauge $\partial_\nu\alpha$, so its inverse is not defined until gauge orbits are separated. Inserting $1=\int\prod_a d\Lambda_a\,\delta(f_a(A^\Lambda))\det[\delta f_a(A^\Lambda)/\delta\Lambda_b]$ for gauge conditions $f_a(A)=0$ factors out the gauge-orbit volume, leaving $Z=\int\mathcal DA\,e^{iS[A]}\delta(f(A))\det[\delta f/\delta\Lambda]$; the [determinant](node:Determinant) is written as an integral over ghost fields. ([MIT 8.324 Lecture 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-324-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-ii-fall-2010/1b3e727b1edcd9b2f41182a3d8438701_MIT8_324F10_Lecture5.pdf); [Wikipedia, BRST quantization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRST_quantization))
- **BRST symmetry.** The gauge-fixed action with ghosts has a symmetry found by Becchi, Rouet and Stora (culminating in 1976) and independently by Tyutin, generated by a nilpotent charge $Q^2=0$. Physical states are its cohomology, $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\ker Q/\operatorname{im}Q$, and the ghosts and other gauge-fixing fields do not appear in asymptotic states, though they can appear in intermediate states of perturbative calculations. ([Wikipedia, BRST quantization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRST_quantization))
- **Gribov ambiguity.** A gauge-fixing surface can meet a gauge orbit more than once. Gribov (1978) pointed out that for Yang–Mills theories uniqueness of the gauge-fixed representative fails for a large class of gauges (Singer's 1978 paper is cited for the same non-uniqueness); if two infinitesimally close copies both satisfy the Landau condition $\partial^\mu A^a_\mu=0$, the Faddeev–Popov operator has a zero mode. Gribov copies cause a nonperturbative failure of BRST symmetry. ([Wikipedia, Gribov ambiguity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gribov_ambiguity)) Restricting to the Gribov region leads to the Gribov–Zwanziger action, reviewed by Vandersickel and Zwanziger. ([Vandersickel and Zwanziger](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.1491))
- **Renormalizability ('t Hooft–Veltman).** In two 1971 papers 't Hooft showed how to renormalize massless Yang–Mills fields and then Yang–Mills theories whose gauge fields acquire mass by [spontaneous symmetry breaking](node:Spontaneous%20Symmetry%20Breaking); he and Veltman shared the 1999 Nobel Prize "for elucidating the quantum structure of the electroweak interactions". ([Wikipedia, Gerard 't Hooft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_%27t_Hooft)) Dimensional regularization came out of the collaboration that followed the first 1971 paper ([Wikipedia, Gerard 't Hooft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_%27t_Hooft)) and was published in 1972 ('t Hooft and Veltman, Nucl. Phys. B44, 189), alongside work by Bollini and Giambiagi. ([Wikipedia, Dimensional regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimensional_regularization)) See [Renormalization](node:Renormalization) and [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism).
- **[Asymptotic freedom](node:Asymptotic%20Freedom) (Gross–Wilczek, Politzer, 1973).** For a gauge group with Casimir $C_2(G)$ and $n_f$ Dirac fermions in a representation with index $T(R_f)$, the one-loop beta function is $\beta(g)=-\big(\tfrac{11}{3}C_2(G)-\tfrac43n_fT(R_f)\big)\tfrac{g^3}{16\pi^2}$ (without scalars); for $SU(3)$ it is $\beta(g)=-(11-\tfrac23n_f)\tfrac{g^3}{16\pi^2}$. ([Wikipedia, Beta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function_%28physics%29)) Equivalently $\mu^2\,d\alpha_s/d\mu^2=-(b_0\alpha_s^2+\cdots)$ with $b_0=(33-2n_f)/(12\pi)$; the minus sign makes the coupling weak at large momentum transfer. ([PDG, QCD review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)) QCD is asymptotically free for at most 16 flavours; Gross, Wilczek and Politzer shared the 2004 Nobel Prize. ([Wikipedia, Asymptotic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_freedom))
- **Elitzur's theorem (1975).** In a lattice gauge theory with compact gauge group, only gauge-invariant operators have nonzero expectation values, so a local gauge symmetry cannot be spontaneously broken; the proof uses positivity of the measure and gauge invariance, and does not cover large gauge transformations or residual gauge degrees of freedom. Consequently the Higgs vacuum expectation value is nonzero only after gauge fixing (e.g. unitary gauge), and the Higgs mechanism is not literally spontaneous breaking of a gauge symmetry. ([Wikipedia, Elitzur's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elitzur%27s_theorem))
- **Anomalies.** An anomaly is a symmetry of the classical action that is not a symmetry of any regularization of the quantum theory; the first was the Adler–Bell–Jackiw axial anomaly. Gauge anomalies make a theory inconsistent because gauge symmetry is needed to remove unphysical modes, so they must cancel. In the Standard Model, vanishing of the mixed anomaly with two $SU(2)$ generators and one $U(1)_Y$ hypercharge requires all charges in a fermion generation to add up to zero, linking quark and lepton charges. ([Wikipedia, Anomaly (physics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomaly_%28physics%29)) Two kinds of anomaly must be kept apart. In the ABJ case the axial current, conserved classically in electrodynamics, is broken in the quantized theory. ([Wikipedia, Anomaly (physics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomaly_%28physics%29)) A 't Hooft anomaly instead belongs to a global symmetry that stays an exact symmetry of the quantum theory but cannot be gauged; 't Hooft's matching condition (1980) says its value must be the same whether computed with UV or IR degrees of freedom, so in massless QCD the flavour-symmetry anomaly computed from quarks is reproduced by the Wess–Zumino–Witten term of the Nambu–Goldstone bosons. ([Wikipedia, 't Hooft anomaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%27t_Hooft_anomaly))
- **Instantons and theta vacua.** In four dimensions, connections with ${*F}=\pm F$ (self-dual or anti-self-dual) automatically solve the Yang–Mills equations by the Bianchi identity; these are instantons, with the BPST instanton the basic charge-one example. ([Wikipedia, Gauge theory (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory_%28mathematics%29)) In the quantum theory, vacua are labelled by a winding number $n$ shifted by large gauge transformations, instantons tunnel between them, and the gauge-invariant vacua are $|\theta\rangle=\sum_n e^{in\theta}|n\rangle$, found by Callan, Dashen and Gross and independently by Jackiw and Rebbi in 1976. The corresponding $\theta$-term is CP-violating, and in QCD the absence of a neutron electric dipole moment forces $\theta$ to be very small: the strong CP problem. ([Wikipedia, Theta vacuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theta_vacuum)) In the weakly coupled dilute instanton gas approximation the vacuum energy is $E(\theta)=-2|K|e^{-8\pi^2/g^2}\cos\bar\theta$, minimized at $\bar\theta=0$, with power corrections from instanton interactions and multi-instantons; this form is not exact, and in a softly broken supersymmetric $SU(2)$ model a first-order transition occurs at $\bar\theta=\pi$. ([Khoze 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.06827v2)) See [Axions](node:Axions).
- **Wilson loops and lattice gauge theory.** The Wilson loop $W[\gamma]=\operatorname{tr}\mathcal P\exp(i\oint_\gamma A_\mu dx^\mu)$ is gauge invariant, and the Wilson loops of all closed curves determine all gauge-invariant information of the connection (Giles 1981). In the confining phase of pure Yang–Mills $\langle W\rangle\sim e^{-a\,\mathrm{Area}}$ (area law), while in a Higgs phase it follows a perimeter law. ([Wikipedia, Wilson loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_loop)) Wilson's 1974 lattice formulation places group elements $U\in G$ on lattice links, builds the action from small Wilson loops, recovers the continuum action as the spacing $a\to0$, and turns the path integral into a finite-dimensional integral evaluated by Monte Carlo. ([Wikipedia, Lattice gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_gauge_theory)) See [Lattice QCD](node:Lattice%20QCD).

### Examples
For $U(1)$ gauge theory, $\psi\mapsto e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi$ and $A_\mu\mapsto A_\mu+\tfrac1e\partial_\mu\alpha$ leave the physics unchanged; the curvature is $F=dA$ and the Yang–Mills equations are Maxwell's equations. ([MIT 8.324 Lecture 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-324-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-ii-fall-2010/1b3e727b1edcd9b2f41182a3d8438701_MIT8_324F10_Lecture5.pdf); [Jaffe and Witten](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/yangmills.pdf))

In the [Aharonov–Bohm effect](node:Aharonov–Bohm%20Effect) a charge travelling along a path $P$ acquires phase $(q/\hbar)\int_PA\cdot dx$, so two paths enclosing flux $\Phi_B$ differ by $q\Phi_B/\hbar$ even where $E=B=0$; this is the holonomy of a flat connection around the loop, depending only on the enclosed flux and the loop's topological class. Predicted by Ehrenberg and Siday (1949) and by Aharonov and Bohm (1959), it was confirmed convincingly by Tonomura (1986); whether it shows that potentials are physical or reflects nonlocal gauge-invariant quantities is still argued (Vaidman versus Aharonov, Cohen and Rohrlich). ([Wikipedia, Aharonov–Bohm effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aharonov%E2%80%93Bohm_effect))

### History
Gauge theory evolved from Weyl's work. ([Jaffe and Witten](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/yangmills.pdf)) Yang and Mills published "Conservation of Isotopic Spin and Isotopic Gauge Invariance" in Phys. Rev. 96, 191 (1 October 1954). ([Crossref, Yang and Mills 1954](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.96.191)) It extended gauge theory from abelian to nonabelian groups, choosing $SU(2)$ to explain isospin conservation in strong interactions, and left the mass of the gauge quanta unresolved. ([Wikipedia, Yang–Mills theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang%E2%80%93Mills_theory)) Utiyama's "Invariant Theoretical Interpretation of Interaction" followed in Phys. Rev. 101 (1956). ([Crossref, Utiyama 1956](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.101.1597)) Asymptotic freedom was found in 1973. ([Wikipedia, Asymptotic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_freedom)) 't Hooft proved renormalizability in 1971, Wilson introduced lattice gauge theory in 1974, the BRST transformation was completed in 1976, and Gribov identified incomplete gauge fixing in 1978. ([Wikipedia, Gerard 't Hooft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_%27t_Hooft); [Wikipedia, Wilson loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_loop); [Wikipedia, BRST quantization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRST_quantization); [Wikipedia, Gribov ambiguity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gribov_ambiguity)) Donaldson used moduli spaces of anti-self-dual $SU(2)$ connections to prove a theorem on intersection forms of simply connected four-manifolds, for which he received the 1986 Fields Medal. Seiberg–Witten invariants, introduced by Witten in 1994 from the monopole equations for a spin$^c$ structure (a Dirac equation coupled to a curvature equation), have moduli spaces that tend to be compact, prove similar and sometimes stronger results, and are technically much easier than Donaldson invariants. ([Wikipedia, Gauge theory (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia, Seiberg–Witten invariants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiberg%E2%80%93Witten_invariants))

### Connections
- [Gauge Invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance): the redundancy principle behind the theory.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): supply gauge groups and representations of matter fields.
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives) and [Principal Bundle Connections](node:Principal%20Bundle%20Connections): the geometric formulation of gauge fields.
- [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory): Yang–Mills theory is a Lagrangian field theory.
- [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics), [Electroweak Theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory), [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): the physical gauge theories of the Standard Model.
- [Asymptotic Freedom](node:Asymptotic%20Freedom): the short-distance property of nonabelian Yang–Mills theory.
- [Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap](node:Yang–Mills%20Existence%20and%20Mass%20Gap): the Clay problem on the quantum theory.
- [Intersection Forms of Four-Manifolds](node:Intersection%20Forms%20of%20Four-Manifolds): Donaldson's application of instantons.
- [Feynman Diagrams](node:Feynman%20Diagrams): perturbative computation after gauge fixing.
- [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory): supplies the Hodge star used in the Yang–Mills equations.
- [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group): the running coupling and beta function behind asymptotic freedom.
- [Path Integral Formulation](node:Path%20Integral%20Formulation): the setting of Faddeev–Popov gauge fixing.
- [Aharonov–Bohm Effect](node:Aharonov–Bohm%20Effect): holonomy of a flat $U(1)$ connection.

### Common pitfalls
- Gauge transformations relate redundant descriptions, not physically distinct states, and gauge fixing is a computational choice. ([MIT 8.324 Lecture 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-324-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-ii-fall-2010/1b3e727b1edcd9b2f41182a3d8438701_MIT8_324F10_Lecture5.pdf))
- The Faddeev–Popov method assumes each orbit meets the gauge slice exactly once; Gribov copies violate this beyond perturbation theory. ([Wikipedia, Gribov ambiguity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gribov_ambiguity))
- "Spontaneously broken gauge symmetry" is shorthand: by Elitzur's theorem a local gauge symmetry cannot break, and the Higgs vev is a gauge-fixed quantity. ([Wikipedia, Elitzur's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elitzur%27s_theorem))
- A 't Hooft anomaly does not destroy a symmetry; it obstructs gauging it. Gauge anomalies, by contrast, render a theory inconsistent. ([Wikipedia, 't Hooft anomaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%27t_Hooft_anomaly); [Wikipedia, Anomaly (physics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomaly_%28physics%29))
- A local operator such as $A_\mu$ is not gauge invariant; gauge-invariant observables include traces of Wilson loops. ([Wikipedia, Wilson loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_loop))

### Open problems
- **Yang–Mills existence and mass gap.** Prove that for every compact simple gauge group $G$ a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills theory exists on $\mathbb R^4$, satisfying axioms at least as strong as the Wightman-type axioms cited, and has a mass gap $\Delta>0$ (no spectrum of the Hamiltonian in $(0,\Delta)$). This is a Clay Millennium Prize Problem, listed by the Clay Institute as unsolved. ([Jaffe and Witten](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/yangmills.pdf); [Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/))
- **Gribov problem.** Only the fundamental modular region removes all Gribov copies, and "it is unknown how to restrict the path integral to this region". ([Wikipedia, Gribov ambiguity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gribov_ambiguity)) Vandersickel and Zwanziger review the Gribov–Zwanziger approach and its relation to confinement. ([Vandersickel and Zwanziger](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.1491))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gauge theory (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory_%28mathematics%29): principal bundles, connections, Yang–Mills functional and instantons.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.324 Lecture 5 (Liu)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-324-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-ii-fall-2010/1b3e727b1edcd9b2f41182a3d8438701_MIT8_324F10_Lecture5.pdf): gauge redundancy and Faddeev–Popov quantization of nonabelian theories.
- **Primary:** [Yang and Mills, Conservation of Isotopic Spin and Isotopic Gauge Invariance, Phys. Rev. 96, 191 (1954)](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.96.191): the paper extending gauge theory to the nonabelian group $SU(2)$.
- **Reference:** [PDG Review of Particle Physics, Quantum Chromodynamics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf): running coupling, beta-function coefficients and the measured $\alpha_s$.
- **Further reading:** [Jaffe and Witten, *Quantum Yang–Mills Theory*](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/yangmills.pdf): the official Clay problem statement.
- **Further reading:** [Vandersickel and Zwanziger, *The Gribov problem and QCD dynamics*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.1491): Physics Reports review of Gribov copies and the Gribov–Zwanziger action.
- **Further reading:** [Weinberg, *The Quantum Theory of Fields*, Vol. II](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139644174): Cambridge University Press (1996); the volume applying quantum field theory methods to the weak, strong and electromagnetic interactions.
references.Gauss's Law for Gravity:
## Reference
### Overview
Gauss's law for gravity states that the flux of the gravitational field $\mathbf g$ through any closed surface equals $-4\pi G$ times the enclosed mass. It is the flux form of Newton's inverse-square law and stands to Newton's law as Gauss's law of electrostatics stands to Coulomb's law; both follow from inverse-square interactions in three-dimensional space. Because mass is never negative, the gravitational flux is never positive. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))

With $\mathbf g=-\nabla\phi$ the differential form becomes Poisson's equation $\nabla^2\phi=4\pi G\rho$, the field equation of Newtonian gravity. It contains no time derivative, so the potential responds instantaneously to the source ("action at a distance"); this is why Newton's theory is not relativistic, and why [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) replaces it. ([MIT 8.033 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/02415213222b845bbec6e734c64d1718_fieldeqs.pdf)) ([MIT 8.224 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-224-exploring-black-holes-general-relativity-astrophysics-spring-2003/7126f56028395a77443d487c3cf3d0b1_gravitymetricscoordinatesnotes2.pdf))

Gauss's law fixes only the divergence of $\mathbf g$. Recovering Newton's law also needs $\nabla\times\mathbf g=0$ and a boundary condition such as $\mathbf g\to0$ at infinity; the failure of that boundary condition in an infinite homogeneous medium is the origin of the "Jeans swindle", and nonlinear modifications of Poisson's equation define MOND. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity)) ([Kiessling 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/9910247)) ([Wikipedia, MOND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))

### Formal definition
For a closed outward-oriented surface $\partial V$ enclosing mass $M_{\rm enc}=\int_V\rho\,dV$, the integral and differential versions are as follows; they are equivalent by the divergence theorem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))
$$
\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf g\cdot d\mathbf A=-4\pi G\,M_{\rm enc},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf g=-4\pi G\rho .
$$
Writing $\mathbf g=-\nabla\phi$ gives Poisson's equation, Laplace's equation where $\rho=0$, and for a point mass $m$ the potential $\phi=-Gm/r$. ([Wikipedia, Poisson's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation))
$$
\nabla^2\phi=4\pi G\rho,\qquad \phi(\mathbf x,t)=-G\int\frac{\rho(\mathbf x',t)}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf x'|}\,d^3x' .
$$
The integral formula is the standard solution on all of space. ([MIT 8.224 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-224-exploring-black-holes-general-relativity-astrophysics-spring-2003/7126f56028395a77443d487c3cf3d0b1_gravitymetricscoordinatesnotes2.pdf)) For spherically symmetric $\rho(r)$ the equation reduces to $r^{-2}\,d/dr\,(r^2\,d\phi/dr)=4\pi G\rho(r)$ with $\mathbf g=-\hat{\mathbf e}_r\,d\phi/dr$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))

### Key results
- **Gauss is not enough for Newton.** Gauss's law says nothing about the curl of $\mathbf g$; Newton's law follows only with $\nabla\times\mathbf g=0$ and a boundary condition such as $\mathbf g\to0$ at infinity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity)) The underlying uniqueness statement is Helmholtz's: a vector field with prescribed divergence and curl that vanishes as $r\to\infty$ is unique; without decay one may add the gradient of any harmonic function. ([Wikipedia, Helmholtz decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_decomposition)) On a bounded domain, a solution of Poisson's equation with Dirichlet data is unique if it exists. ([Wikipedia, Poisson's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation))
- **Newton from Gauss.** For a point mass, spherical symmetry makes $g(r)$ constant on spheres, so $-g(r)\,4\pi r^2=-4\pi GM$ and $\mathbf g=-GM\hat{\mathbf e}_r/r^2$. ([Wikipedia, Shell theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_theorem))
- **Shell theorem.** A spherically symmetric body attracts external points as if its mass were at the centre; a spherical shell exerts no net force on anything inside; inside a uniform solid sphere the field is linear in $r$ and vanishes at the centre. Newton proved these by geometry in *Principia* (Props. 70–71); Gauss's law gives them in a line. ([Wikipedia, Shell theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_theorem)) See [Shell Theorem](node:Shell%20Theorem).
- **Planar and cylindrical symmetry.** Outside an infinite flat slab, $|\mathbf g|=2\pi G\sigma$ toward the slab ($\sigma$ = mass per unit area), independent of distance (Bouguer plate). For an infinite cylindrically symmetric distribution, $|\mathbf g|=2G\lambda(r)/r$ inward, with $\lambda(r)$ the mass per unit length inside radius $r$; the field vanishes inside a uniform hollow cylinder. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))
- **Variational form.** The Lagrangian density $\mathcal L=-\rho\phi-\frac{1}{8\pi G}(\nabla\phi)^2$ yields $\nabla^2\phi=4\pi G\rho$ by Hamilton's principle. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))
- **Exterior multipole expansion.** Outside the sources $\phi$ is harmonic, and the exterior potential of a body expands in spherical harmonics, $u=-\mu/r+\sum_{n\ge2}J_nP_{n0}(\sin\theta)/r^{n+1}+$ (tesseral terms), with $\mu=GM$. For Earth the oblateness term $J_2$ is by far the largest correction; $J_3$ is about two parts per thousand of it at 6600 km. ([Wikipedia, Geopotential model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopotential_model))
- **Infinite homogeneous medium: the Jeans swindle.** For a static medium with constant $\rho_0>0$ and $p_0$, Euler's equation forces $\nabla\Phi_0=0$ while Poisson's equation demands $\nabla^2\Phi_0=4\pi G\rho_0$; these are inconsistent unless $\rho_0=0$. Jeans removed the inconsistency by applying Poisson's equation only to perturbations and setting $\Phi_0=0$, obtaining $\omega^2=c_s^2|\mathbf k|^2-4\pi G\rho_0$ and the Jeans length $\lambda_J=\sqrt{\pi c_s^2/(G\rho_0)}$. Kiessling (1999) derived the same dispersion relation by a well-defined limiting procedure. ([Kiessling 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/9910247)) ([Wikipedia, Jeans instability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeans_instability))
- **Modified Poisson equation (MOND).** Bekenstein and Milgrom's AQUAL (1984) replaces Poisson's equation by $\nabla\cdot[\mu(|\nabla\Phi|/a_0)\nabla\Phi]=4\pi G\rho$ with $a_0\approx1.2\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; QUMOND (2010) first solves the Newtonian Poisson equation and then applies an algebraic step. The nonlinearity produces an external-field effect absent in Newtonian gravity. ([Wikipedia, MOND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics)) See [Modified Newtonian Dynamics](node:Modified%20Newtonian%20Dynamics).

### Examples
- **Uniform ball.** Outside, $M_{\rm enc}=M$ and $\mathbf g$ is that of a point mass; inside a ball of radius $R$ only the enclosed mass $M_{\rm enc}=Mr^3/R^3$ counts, so $|\mathbf g|=GM_{\rm enc}/r^2$ grows linearly in $r$. ([Wikipedia, Shell theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_theorem))
- **Electrostatic analogue.** In Gaussian units $\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=4\pi\rho_q$ and $\nabla^2\Phi_E=-4\pi\rho_q$; gravity has the opposite sign because like masses attract while like charges repel. ([MIT 8.224 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-224-exploring-black-holes-general-relativity-astrophysics-spring-2003/7126f56028395a77443d487c3cf3d0b1_gravitymetricscoordinatesnotes2.pdf)) In SI the point-charge solution is $\varphi=Q/(4\pi\varepsilon r)$. ([Wikipedia, Poisson's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation)) See [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics).
- **A gravito-Maxwell theory fails.** Adding Faraday- and Ampère-like equations by the substitution $\mathbf E\to\mathbf g$, $\rho\to\rho_m$, $\varepsilon_0\to-1/(4\pi G)$ does not give a consistent relativistic theory, because mass density and charge density transform differently under [Lorentz Transformations](node:Lorentz%20Transformations): total charge is a Lorentz scalar, while mass, being equivalent to energy, is not. ([MIT 8.033 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/02415213222b845bbec6e734c64d1718_fieldeqs.pdf))

### History
Gauss's law was first formulated by Lagrange in 1773 and then by Gauss in 1835, both in work on the attraction of ellipsoids. ([Wikipedia, Gauss's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law)) The underlying divergence theorem was found by Lagrange in 1762; Gauss proved special cases in 1813 while studying the attraction of an elliptical spheroid (and further cases in 1833 and 1839), and Ostrogradsky gave the first general proof in 1826. ([Wikipedia, Divergence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergence_theorem))

Poisson found that Laplace's equation holds only outside the attracting matter, and his equation was first published in the *Bulletin de la Société philomatique* in 1813; Gauss gave the first rigorous proof for masses of variable density in 1839. ([Wikipedia, Siméon Denis Poisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sim%C3%A9on_Denis_Poisson)) MacTutor likewise dates to 1813 his study of the potential in the interior of attracting masses. ([MacTutor, Poisson](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Poisson/))

### Connections
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): Gauss's law is the flux form of the inverse-square law.
- [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus): the divergence theorem connects the integral and differential versions.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations) and [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions): $\nabla^2\phi=4\pi G\rho$ and the kernel $-G/|\mathbf x-\mathbf x'|$.
- [Spherical Harmonics](node:Spherical%20Harmonics): exterior multipole expansion of the potential.
- [Shell Theorem](node:Shell%20Theorem): the spherical case.
- [Gauss's Law in n Dimensions](node:Gauss's%20Law%20in%20n%20Dimensions): in $d$ spatial dimensions the same argument gives a $1/r^{d-1}$ force.
- [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics) and [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations): the electric analogue and why gravity lacks Maxwell's time-dependent equations.
- [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29): point masses as $\rho=m\,\delta^3$.
- [Modified Newtonian Dynamics](node:Modified%20Newtonian%20Dynamics) and [Galaxy Rotation Curves](node:Galaxy%20Rotation%20Curves): the nonlinear modified Poisson equation.
- [Newtonian Limit of General Relativity](node:Newtonian%20Limit%20of%20General%20Relativity) and [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): Poisson's equation as the weak-field limit.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Newtonian gravitational fields and orbits](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Newtonian%20gravitational%20fields%20and%20orbits)

### Common pitfalls
- **Sign conventions.** With $\mathbf g=-\nabla\phi$, $\phi<0$ near masses and $\nabla^2\phi=+4\pi G\rho$, opposite to electrostatics. ([MIT 8.224 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-224-exploring-black-holes-general-relativity-astrophysics-spring-2003/7126f56028395a77443d487c3cf3d0b1_gravitymetricscoordinatesnotes2.pdf))
- **Symmetry is what makes Gauss's law compute fields.** Zero flux through a surface not enclosing mass does not mean $\mathbf g=0$ on it; without spherical, planar, or cylindrical symmetry the flux does not determine the field. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))
- **Boundary conditions matter.** Divergence and curl fix $\mathbf g$ only up to gradients of harmonic functions unless $\mathbf g\to0$ at infinity; in an infinite homogeneous medium no such solution exists. ([Wikipedia, Helmholtz decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_decomposition)) ([Kiessling 1999](https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/9910247))
- **Date of Poisson's equation.** Some accounts date the equation to Poisson's 1823 memoir on magnetism, ([Wikipedia, Poisson's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation)) but it was first published in 1813. ([Wikipedia, Siméon Denis Poisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sim%C3%A9on_Denis_Poisson))

### Open problems
- **Is the Newtonian Poisson equation correct at low accelerations?** Wikipedia lists as an unsolved problem in physics whether dark matter is a particle or whether the phenomena attributed to it require a modification of the laws of gravity, and calls distinguishing the alternatives a subject of current research.
