MOND's modified Poisson equation fits galaxy-scale data but is not widely accepted: it leaves a residual mass discrepancy in galaxy clusters and has difficulty with the [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background) and structure formation, while ΛCDM keeps Poisson's equation and adds [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter). ([Wikipedia, MOND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))

> [!warning] Contested
> Whether galactic dynamics require dark matter with standard Newtonian gravity or a modified law such as AQUAL/QUMOND is disputed; Wikipedia records MOND's galaxy-scale successes and its cluster and cosmological problems. ([Wikipedia, MOND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gauss's law for gravity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity): integral and differential versions, symmetric cases, Lagrangian.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.224, Gravity, Metrics and Coordinates](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-224-exploring-black-holes-general-relativity-astrophysics-spring-2003/7126f56028395a77443d487c3cf3d0b1_gravitymetricscoordinatesnotes2.pdf) and [MIT 8.033, Einstein's Field Equations](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/02415213222b845bbec6e734c64d1718_fieldeqs.pdf): Poisson's equation, its electrostatic analogue, and why it is not relativistic.
- **Primary:** [Kiessling, Mathematical Vindications of the "Jeans Swindle" (1999)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9910247): the inconsistency of Poisson's equation in an infinite homogeneous medium and a rigorous limiting procedure.
- **Further reading:** [Binney & Tremaine, Galactic Dynamics (2nd ed., Princeton 2008)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691130279/galactic-dynamics): the standard graduate text on the structure and dynamics of galaxies: orbits, equilibrium and stability of stellar systems, dark matter.
references.Gauss's Law in n Dimensions:
## Reference
### Overview
Gauss's law for gravity states that the gravitational flux through any closed surface is $-4\pi G$ times the enclosed mass, $\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf g\cdot d\mathbf A = -4\pi GM$. It is equivalent to Newton's inverse-square law only together with a curl-free field and boundary conditions; the law alone does not determine $\mathbf g$. Newton's and Coulomb's laws both describe inverse-square interactions in a 3-dimensional space. ([Wikipedia: Gauss's law for gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))

In $d$ spatial dimensions one demands that the flux through the sphere $S^{d-1}(r)$ still equal a constant times the enclosed mass. Since the area of $S^{d-1}(r)$ scales as $r^{d-1}$, the force between point masses must scale as $1/r^{d-1}$. ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.4037))

The counting argument has two celebrated consequences. Following Ehrenfest (1917), neither classical atoms nor planetary orbits can be stable in a space with more than three dimensions, and quantum hydrogen atoms cannot be stable either. ([Tegmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9702052)) And in the ADD large-extra-dimensions proposal, gravity is weak at long distances because its flux spreads into compact [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions). ([Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos & Dvali](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9803315))

### Formal definition
The surface area of the unit $(n-1)$-sphere in $\mathbb R^n$ is $S_{n-1} = 2\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2)$, and a sphere of radius $r$ has area $S_{n-1}r^{n-1}$. ([Wikipedia: n-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere))

With a dimension-dependent Newton constant $G^{(d)}$, the generalized Gauss law in $d$ spatial dimensions is
$$\oint_{S^{d-1}(r)}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf a = -\operatorname{vol}(S^{d-1})\,G^{(d)}M_{\rm enc},$$
satisfied by $\mathbf F = -G^{(d)}mM\,\hat r/r^{d-1}$; Mota and Pérez-Guerrero fix the normalization $\operatorname{vol}(S^{d-1})G^{(d)} = 4\pi G^{(3)}$. ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.4037))

The differential form is Poisson's equation: in 3D, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf g = -4\pi G\rho$ and, with $\mathbf g = -\nabla\phi$, $\nabla^2\phi = 4\pi G\rho$. ([Wikipedia: Gauss's law for gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity)) In $\mathbb R^d$ the fundamental solution of the Laplacian (Newtonian kernel) is
$$\Gamma(x) = \begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\log|x|, & d=2,\\[4pt] \dfrac{1}{d(2-d)\,\omega_d}|x|^{2-d}, & d\ne 2,\end{cases}$$
with $\omega_d$ the volume of the unit $d$-ball, so the point-mass potential goes as $r^{2-d}$ for $d>2$ and $\log r$ for $d=2$. ([Wikipedia: Newtonian potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_potential))

### Key results
- **Force law.** In the normalization above, $F = -\dfrac{2\Gamma(d/2)\,G^{(3)}}{\pi^{d/2-1}}\dfrac{mM}{r^{d-1}}$. ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.4037))
- **Shell theorem in all dimensions.** If $f$ is a rotationally invariant, compactly supported mass distribution with total mass $\lambda = \int f$, then outside its support $f*\Gamma(x) = \lambda\,\Gamma(x)$; in $d=3$ this is Newton's theorem. ([Wikipedia: Newtonian potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_potential)) See [Shell Theorem](node:Shell%20Theorem).
- **No stable circular orbits for $d\ge4$.** For a central force, a circular orbit at $r_0$ is stable iff $F'(r_0) < -3F(r_0)/r_0$. For $F\propto r^{-(d-1)}$ this reduces to $d-1<3$, so stable circular orbits require $d<4$. ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.4037))
- **Bertrand's theorem (complement).** Among central-force potentials, only the inverse-square force and the radial harmonic oscillator have all bounded orbits closed (Bertrand, 1873). ([Wikipedia: Bertrand's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand%27s_theorem)) Since the Gauss-law force is $F\propto r^{-(d-1)}$, among $d\ge2$ only $d=3$ gives an inverse-square force with closed bound orbits; for $d\ge4$ even circular orbits are unstable. ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.4037))
- **Hydrogen atom.** The [Schrödinger Equation](node:Schrödinger%20Equation) with the $d$-dimensional Coulomb potential gives no stable atoms for $d>3$: there is no ground state but time-dependent states of arbitrarily negative energy, with a finite "annihilation" cross section. ([Tegmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9702052)) Tangherlini (1963) showed that the stability constraint holds both in general relativity and for the quantum-mechanical [Hydrogen Atom](node:Hydrogen%20Atom). ([Caruso & Moreira Xavier](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.4916))
- **Schwarzschild–Tangherlini metric.** In $D$ spacetime dimensions the static vacuum black hole is
$$ds^2 = -\Big(1-\frac{\mu}{r^{D-3}}\Big)dt^2 + \frac{dr^2}{1-\mu/r^{D-3}} + r^2d\Omega_{D-2}^2,\qquad \mu = \frac{16\pi GM}{(D-2)\Omega_{D-2}},$$
which replaces the $1/r$ falloff of the Newtonian potential by $1/r^{D-3}$ (Tangherlini, 1963); the horizon is at $r_0 = \mu^{1/(D-3)}$. ([Emparan & Reall](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0801.3471)) With $D = d+1$, $r^{3-D} = r^{2-d}$ matches the Newtonian kernel. See [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution).
- **Crossover with compact extra dimensions (ADD).** With $n$ compact extra dimensions of radius $R$, masses at $r\ll R$ feel $V(r)\sim m_1m_2/(M_{Pl(4+n)}^{n+2}\,r^{n+1})$, while for $r\gg R$ the flux cannot penetrate the extra dimensions and $V\sim m_1m_2/(M_{Pl(4+n)}^{n+2}R^n\,r)$. ([ADD](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9803315)) For a torus of equal radii, volume $V_\delta = (2\pi R)^\delta$, the 4D reduced Planck mass is $M_P^2 = V_\delta\,\bar M_D^{2+\delta}$, with $M_P = 1/\sqrt{8\pi G_N}$; equivalently the $D$-dimensional coupling is the 4D one times the compact volume. ([PDG: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Kaluza–Klein origin of the Yukawa correction.** Compactification gives a massless 4D graviton plus a [Kaluza–Klein tower](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes) with masses $m_{\vec n}^2 = |\vec n|^2/R^2$; these modes cause deviations from Newton's law at distances $\lesssim R$, parameterized as $V = -G_Nm_1m_2[1+\alpha e^{-r/\lambda}]/r$, with $\alpha = 16/3$ and $\lambda = R$ for a 2-torus. ([PDG: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

### Examples
- **$d=3$.** The Gaussian sphere has area $4\pi r^2$, giving Newton's $g = GM/r^2$. Lower-dimensional sources in 3D: an infinite uniform line produces a field of $2G/r$ times the mass per unit length, and an infinite plate a field $2\pi G$ times the surface density, independent of distance. ([Wikipedia: Gauss's law for gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))
- **$d=4$.** Gravity becomes an inverse-cube law; test particles fired at a point mass either escape to infinity or spiral into it, with no stable orbits. ([Tegmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9702052))
- **ADD with $n=1,2$.** For $n=1$, $R\sim10^{13}$ cm, excluded by solar-system gravity; for $n=2$, $R\sim100\ \mu$m–1 mm, and gravity would change from $1/r^2$ to $1/r^4$ at those distances. ([ADD](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9803315)) PDG quotes $R<30\ \mu$m at 95% CL for $\delta=2$, corresponding to $M_D>4.0$ TeV. ([PDG: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Torsion-balance test.** Data at separations from 52 μm to 3.0 mm fit Newtonian gravity and limit gravitational-strength Yukawa interactions to ranges below 38.6 μm (95% CL). ([Lee et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.11761))

### History
Ehrenfest's 1917 paper "In what way does it become manifest in the fundamental laws of physics that space has three dimensions?" (Proc. KNAW 20) and his 1920 *Annalen der Physik* paper used the stability of the $n$-dimensional two-body problem to favour three dimensions. Tangherlini's 1963 "Schwarzschild Field in n Dimensions and the Dimensionality of Space Problem" (Nuovo Cimento 27) extended the argument to general relativity and the hydrogen atom. ([Caruso & Moreira Xavier](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.4916))

In 1998 Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos and Dvali turned the flux-counting argument into a proposal for the hierarchy problem with $n\ge2$ large compact dimensions in which only gravity propagates. ([ADD](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9803315)) A year later Randall and Sundrum proposed a warped five-dimensional anti-de Sitter alternative. ([PDG: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

### Connections
- [Gauss's Law for Gravity](node:Gauss's%20Law%20for%20Gravity): the $d=3$ special case.
- [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere): the area factor $2\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2)$.
- [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions), [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): the $r^{2-d}$ kernel is the potential form of the law.
- [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms): Gauss's law as [Stokes' Theorem](node:Stokes'%20Theorem) for the flux $(d-1)$-form.
- [Shell Theorem](node:Shell%20Theorem): holds in every dimension for rotationally invariant sources.
- [Central Force Motion and the Kepler Problem](node:Central%20Force%20Motion%20and%20the%20Kepler%20Problem): the stability criterion and Bertrand's theorem.
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): the $d=3$ point-mass law being generalized.
- [Hydrogen Atom](node:Hydrogen%20Atom): no bound states for $d>3$.
- [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution), [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the Tangherlini metric is the relativistic version.
- [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions), [Compactification](node:Compactification), [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions): flux leaking into compact dimensions.
- [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes): the graviton tower that produces the Yukawa correction.
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model): warped alternative to flat ADD dimensions.
- [Tests of the Inverse-Square Law](node:Tests%20of%20the%20Inverse-Square%20Law): experiments that bound deviations.
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem), [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale): what ADD addresses.

### Common pitfalls
- **Newton constants differ across dimensions.** Because the unit-sphere volume depends on $d$, $G^{(d)}$ is a different constant in each dimension; a normalization such as $\operatorname{vol}(S^{d-1})G^{(d)} = 4\pi G^{(3)}$ is a convention. ([Mota & Pérez-Guerrero](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.4037))
- **Gauss's law alone is not enough.** It fixes only the divergence; the point-mass law also needs zero curl and boundary conditions. ([Wikipedia: Gauss's law for gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity))
- **$d=2$ is special.** The potential is logarithmic, not a power law. ([Wikipedia: Newtonian potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_potential))
- **Spatial versus spacetime dimension.** The Tangherlini falloff $1/r^{D-3}$ uses spacetime dimension $D$; the Newtonian $r^{2-d}$ uses spatial $d = D-1$. ([Emparan & Reall](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0801.3471))
- **Yukawa bounds versus extra dimensions.** Reading Yukawa limits as extra-dimension limits is a reasonable approximation only when the minimum separation exceeds the size of the largest extra dimension. ([Lee et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.11761))

### Open problems
- **Gravity below tens of microns.** New phenomena could occur below the dark-energy length scale $\lambda_d = \sqrt[4]{\hbar c/\rho_d}\approx85\ \mu$m, and ultra-light scalar or vector [dark matter](node:Dark%20Matter) would also violate the inverse-square law, motivating tests in this regime. ([Lee et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.11761)) PDG notes that for $\delta\ge2$ observable consequences can still be sought in present and future experiments. ([PDG: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Radius stabilization.** ADD needs a mechanism stabilizing the extra-dimensional radii, and $R\gg1/M_D$ creates a new hierarchy problem whose solution might require bulk [supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry). ([PDG: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gauss's law for gravity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_law_for_gravity): integral and differential forms, 3D applications.
- **Reference:** [Newtonian potential (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_potential): the $d$-dimensional Laplacian kernel.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 8.251 lecture notes (Zwiebach)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-251-string-theory-for-undergraduates-spring-2007/pages/lecture-notes/): lectures 3–4 cover Gauss's law, gravitational potentials, compactification and large extra dimensions.
- **Learn:** [Mota & Pérez-Guerrero, Instability of planetary orbits for $D>4$](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.4037): didactic derivation of the force law and stability bound.
- **Primary:** [Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos & Dvali (1998)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9803315): the ADD proposal.
- **Primary:** [Emparan & Reall, "Black Holes in Higher Dimensions"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0801.3471): review including the Schwarzschild–Tangherlini solution.
- **Primary:** [PDG review "Extra Dimensions" (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf): KK reduction, Planck-mass relation and sub-mm bounds.
- **Further reading:** [Tegmark, "On the dimensionality of spacetime"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9702052): stability of orbits and atoms versus dimension.
references.Gaussian Processes:
## Reference
### Overview
A Gaussian process is a stochastic process in which every finite collection of the random variables has a multivariate normal distribution; equivalently, every finite linear combination of them is univariate normal. It is an infinite-dimensional generalization of the multivariate normal and can be read as a probability distribution over functions on its index set, determined entirely by its mean and covariance functions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).

In machine learning, Gaussian processes are used as priors over unknown functions. Williams and Rasmussen observed that a simple prior over neural-network weights induces a complicated prior over functions, whereas a Gaussian process prior placed directly on functions allows exact predictive Bayesian inference for fixed hyperparameters using only matrix operations ([Williams and Rasmussen](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1995/hash/7cce53cf90577442771720a370c3c723-Abstract.html)). The covariance function (kernel) encodes the prior's assumptions, such as smoothness, periodicity, and trend, and kernels can be added or multiplied to combine these features ([Görtler, Kehlbeck and Deussen, Distill](https://distill.pub/2019/visual-exploration-gaussian-processes/)).

Inference of continuous values with a Gaussian process prior is known as Gaussian process regression, or kriging; its posterior mean and variance give point predictions with error bars. Exact inference costs $O(n^3)$ in the number of data points, which motivates a large literature of sparse and local approximations ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process); [Liu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.01065)).

### Formal definition
A stochastic process $\{f(x)\}_{x \in \mathcal X}$ is a **Gaussian process** if for every finite set $x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathcal X$ the vector $(f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n))$ is multivariate normal. It is specified by a mean function $m(x) = \mathbb E[f(x)]$ and a covariance function $k(x, x') = \operatorname{Cov}(f(x), f(x'))$, written $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m, k)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)). The process is **stationary** if $k$ depends only on $x - x'$, and isotropic if it depends only on $|x - x'|$; for Gaussian processes, strict-sense and wide-sense stationarity coincide ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).

Standard kernels, with $d = |x - x'|$ and length scale $\ell$, are
$$k_{SE}(x,x') = \exp\!\left(-\frac{d^2}{2\ell^2}\right),\qquad k_{OU}(x,x') = \exp\!\left(-\frac{d}{\ell}\right),$$
$$k_{\text{Matérn}}(x,x') = \frac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu}\,d}{\ell}\right)^{\nu} K_\nu\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu}\,d}{\ell}\right),$$
where $K_\nu$ is the modified Bessel function; the squared exponential gives infinitely differentiable sample paths and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck gives nowhere-differentiable ones ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).

**GP regression.** Observe $y = f(X) + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, \psi^2 I)$ and prior mean zero. Conditioning the joint Gaussian of training outputs and test values $f_*$ uses the Gaussian conditioning rule $X \mid Y \sim \mathcal N(\mu_X + \Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(Y - \mu_Y),\ \Sigma_{XX} - \Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{YX})$ with $\Sigma_{YY}$ replaced by $K + \psi^2 I$ ([Distill](https://distill.pub/2019/visual-exploration-gaussian-processes/)), giving
$$\mathbb E[f_* \mid y] = K_{*X}(K + \psi^2 I)^{-1} y,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}[f_* \mid y] = K_{**} - K_{*X}(K + \psi^2 I)^{-1}K_{X*}.$$
In the noiseless case these are the formulas $A = K(x_*, x)K^{-1}f(x)$ and $B = K(x_*,x_*) - K(x_*,x)K^{-1}K(x_*,x)^{\mathsf T}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)). Kernel hyperparameters $\theta$ are usually chosen by maximizing the log marginal likelihood, written here for noiseless observations $y = f(X)$ with $K_\theta$ the kernel matrix of the training inputs,
$$\log p(y \mid \theta, X) = -\tfrac12\left(y^{\mathsf T}K_\theta^{-1}y + \log\det K_\theta + n\log 2\pi\right),$$
a procedure also called type-II maximum likelihood, evidence maximization or empirical Bayes, which trades data fit against model complexity ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).

### Key results
- **Sample continuity (Fernique; Dudley; Marcus–Shepp).** Fernique's sufficient condition: if the increment standard deviation satisfies $\bigl(\mathbb E[(X_t - X_s)^2]\bigr)^{1/2} \le \Psi(t - s)$ for a nondecreasing function $\Psi$ on $[0,\varepsilon]$ with $\int_0^\varepsilon \frac{\Psi(u)}{u\sqrt{\log(1/u)}}\,du < \infty$, then $X$ has continuous sample paths; finiteness of this integral is not necessary in general, whereas for stationary processes Dudley's metric-entropy condition is both necessary and sufficient ([Azmoodeh et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/1403.2215v1)). For a stationary Gaussian process on $\mathbb R$ whose increment function is continuous and monotone near $0$, the Fernique integral condition is necessary and sufficient for sample continuity: Fernique announced sufficiency in 1964, Dudley published a proof in 1967, and Marcus and Shepp proved necessity in 1970 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).
- **Driscoll's zero-one law.** For a mean-zero Gaussian process with covariance $K$ and a positive definite kernel $R$, let $K_n, R_n$ be the Gram matrices on $n$ points. If $\lim_n \operatorname{tr}[K_n R_n^{-1}] < \infty$ then $\Pr[f \in \mathcal H(R)] = 1$, and if the limit is infinite the probability is $0$. Taking $R = K$, the trace diverges, so almost every sample path lies outside the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of its own covariance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).
- **Posterior contraction (van der Vaart–van Zanten).** For nonparametric and semiparametric models with Gaussian process priors, the rate at which the posterior contracts around the true parameter is determined by the position of the truth relative to the prior's reproducing kernel Hilbert space and by the process's small-ball probabilities; this gives rates for density estimation, Gaussian regression and classification ([van der Vaart and van Zanten](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.3024)).
- **Infinite-width networks are GPs.** As the width of every layer tends to infinity, deep neural networks with random weights converge to Gaussian processes with a compositional kernel that can be computed efficiently, so exact GP inference reproduces infinitely wide Bayesian neural networks ([Lee et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00165); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).
- **GP-UCB regret.** For maximizing an unknown function that is either drawn from a GP or has bounded RKHS norm, from noisy evaluations, the upper-confidence-bound rule has cumulative regret bounded in terms of the maximal information gain of the kernel, which yields explicit sublinear regret bounds for commonly used covariance functions ([Srinivas et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.3995)).
- **Variational sparse GPs (Titsias).** Introducing $m$ inducing variables and treating their inputs as variational parameters yields a lower bound on the exact log marginal likelihood, so inducing inputs and kernel hyperparameters can be selected jointly by minimizing the KL divergence to the exact posterior ([Titsias](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v5/titsias09a.html)); such sparse approximations reduce training cost from $O(n^3)$ to $O(nm^2)$ ([Liu et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.01065)).

### Examples
- **Brownian motion** (the Wiener process) is the integral of white noise; it is a non-stationary Gaussian process with stationary increments ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).
- **Random trigonometric process.** $X_t = \cos(at)\xi_1 + \sin(at)\xi_2$ with independent standard normals $\xi_1,\xi_2$ is a stationary Gaussian process ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).
- **Composite kernels.** Adding a linear and a periodic kernel gives periodic functions with a linear trend; multiplying them gives periodic functions whose amplitude grows away from the linear kernel's hinge point; a stationary RBF prior reverts to its mean far from data ([Distill](https://distill.pub/2019/visual-exploration-gaussian-processes/)).
- **Bayesian optimization of sensor data.** GP-UCB was tested on real sensor-network data and compared favorably with other GP optimization heuristics ([Srinivas et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.3995)).

### History
The process is named after Gauss through the normal distribution; Kolmogorov was probably the first to note how subtle sample continuity is even for stationary processes, a question settled by the Dudley–Fernique and Marcus–Shepp results of 1964–1970 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)). Williams and Rasmussen's 1995 NeurIPS paper proposed Gaussian process priors over functions for regression, motivated by the difficulty of Bayesian analysis of neural networks, and handled hyperparameters either by optimization or by Hybrid Monte Carlo averaging ([Williams and Rasmussen](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1995/hash/7cce53cf90577442771720a370c3c723-Abstract.html)), and their 2006 MIT Press book gave a self-contained treatment covering regression, classification, model selection, connections to support vector machines and neural networks, learning curves, PAC-Bayesian analysis, and approximations for large datasets ([Edinburgh Informatics](https://www.inf.ed.ac.uk/publications/report/0583.html)).

### Connections
- [Kernel Methods](node:Kernel%20Methods): the GP covariance is a positive definite kernel; the GP posterior mean coincides with a kernel regression estimator.
- [Kernel Ridge Regression](node:Kernel%20Ridge%20Regression): has the same predictor as the GP posterior mean, with the noise variance as regularizer, but no posterior variance.
- [Bayesian Inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference): GP regression is conjugate Bayesian inference with a Gaussian prior on functions.
- [Gaussian Distribution](node:Gaussian%20Distribution): all GP computations reduce to marginalizing and conditioning multivariate normals.
- [Bayesian Optimization](node:Bayesian%20Optimization): GPs are the standard surrogate model, with acquisition rules such as GP-UCB.
- [Neural Tangent Kernel](node:Neural%20Tangent%20Kernel): a second infinite-width limit, describing training dynamics rather than the prior.
- [Bayesian Neural Networks](node:Bayesian%20Neural%20Networks): infinitely wide Bayesian neural networks reduce to GPs.
- [Variational Inference](node:Variational%20Inference): underlies sparse inducing-point approximations.
- [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus): Brownian motion is the basic Gaussian process.
- [Support Vector Machines](node:Support%20Vector%20Machines): related kernel machines without a probabilistic predictive distribution.
- [Uncertainty Quantification](node:Uncertainty%20Quantification): GP posteriors supply calibrated error bars when the prior is appropriate.

### Common pitfalls
- The kernel choice determines smoothness and stationarity of the prior and strongly shapes predictions; a stationary RBF kernel reverts to the prior mean away from data, so trends need extra kernel terms ([Distill](https://distill.pub/2019/visual-exploration-gaussian-processes/)).
- Sample paths generally do not lie in the RKHS of the covariance, so "GP prior" and "RKHS ball" are not interchangeable ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).
- Continuity in probability (equivalently mean-square continuity) does not imply continuous sample paths ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).
- The posterior marginal at a test point has variance equal to the diagonal entry of the posterior covariance; the standard deviation is its square root ([Distill](https://distill.pub/2019/visual-exploration-gaussian-processes/)).
- The $O(n^3)$ cost of exact inference rules out naive use on large datasets ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)).

### Open problems
- **High-dimensional and manifold GPs.** Liu et al. list scalable GPs for comparable $n$ and $d$, or $d \gg n$, as an open issue, with continued theoretical and empirical work needed on components such as convolutional kernels ([Liu et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.01065)).
- **Inference for deep GPs.** Inference in deep GPs is intractable and expensive; easier inference without loss of predictive accuracy is described as a major remaining challenge ([Liu et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.01065)).
- **Scalable GP classification.** Intractable posteriors and training cost that grows with the number of classes are named as the main challenges of scalable multi-class GP classification ([Liu et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.01065)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gaussian process (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process): definition, kernels, sample-path theory, regression formulas.
- **Learn:** [A Visual Exploration of Gaussian Processes (Distill)](https://distill.pub/2019/visual-exploration-gaussian-processes/): interactive introduction to conditioning, kernels and kernel combinations.
- **Primary:** [Williams and Rasmussen, Gaussian Processes for Regression (NeurIPS 1995)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1995/hash/7cce53cf90577442771720a370c3c723-Abstract.html): Gaussian process priors for regression as an alternative to Bayesian neural networks.
- **Primary:** [Liu, Ong, Shen and Cai, When Gaussian Process Meets Big Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.01065): survey of scalable GP approximations and open issues.
- **Primary:** [van der Vaart and van Zanten, Rates of contraction of posterior distributions based on Gaussian process priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.3024): frequentist theory of GP posteriors.
- **Further reading:** [Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (MIT Press 2006)](https://www.inf.ed.ac.uk/publications/report/0583.html): the standard monograph.
references.Gauss–Codazzi Equations:
## Reference
### Overview
The Gauss–Codazzi equations are the fundamental formulas linking the induced metric and the second fundamental form of a submanifold of (or immersion into) a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold. They were first found for surfaces in Euclidean 3-space, where the Gauss equation underlies Gauss's Theorema Egregium and the Codazzi–Mainardi equation says the covariant derivative of the second fundamental form is fully symmetric. ([Wikipedia: Gauss–Codazzi equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Codazzi_equations))

For a submanifold of codimension greater than one, a third identity, the Ricci equation, relates the curvature of the normal bundle to the shape operators. Together with the Gauss and Weingarten formulas, the three are the fundamental equations of an isometric immersion, and in a space form they are the conditions under which a submanifold can be reconstructed from its intrinsic metric, normal bundle and second fundamental form (on a simply connected domain). ([Chen, Riemannian submanifolds survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

In [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) the same identities split the spacetime Riemann tensor into the intrinsic curvature of a spacelike hypersurface and its extrinsic curvature $K_{ij}$; projecting Einstein's equation with them gives the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints of the 3+1 formalism. ([Gourgoulhon, 3+1 Formalism](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035)) In braneworld models they are the starting point for the effective 4D Einstein equations on a 3-brane in a 5D bulk. ([Shiromizu, Maeda & Sasaki](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))

### Formal definition
Let $f:(M,g)\to(\tilde M,\tilde g)$ be an isometric immersion, with Levi-Civita connections $\nabla,\tilde\nabla$. For tangent fields $X,Y$, the **Gauss formula** $\tilde\nabla_XY = \nabla_XY + h(X,Y)$ defines the second fundamental form $h$, a normal-bundle-valued symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor. For a normal field $\xi$, the **Weingarten formula** $\tilde\nabla_X\xi = -A_\xi X + D_X\xi$ defines the shape operator $A_\xi$ (with $g(A_\xi X,Y) = \tilde g(h(X,Y),\xi)$) and the normal connection $D$. ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

With $R,\tilde R,R^D$ the curvatures of $\nabla,\tilde\nabla,D$ and $\bar\nabla$ the induced connection on $TM\oplus T^\perp M$, the tangential and normal parts of the integrability condition give, for tangent $X,Y,Z,W$ and normal $\xi,\eta$:
$$\text{(Gauss)}\quad \langle R(X,Y)Z,W\rangle = \langle\tilde R(X,Y)Z,W\rangle + \langle h(X,W),h(Y,Z)\rangle - \langle h(X,Z),h(Y,W)\rangle,$$
$$\text{(Codazzi)}\quad (\tilde R(X,Y)Z)^\perp = (\bar\nabla_Xh)(Y,Z) - (\bar\nabla_Yh)(X,Z),$$
$$\text{(Ricci)}\quad \langle\tilde R(X,Y)\xi,\eta\rangle = \langle R^D(X,Y)\xi,\eta\rangle - \langle[A_\xi,A_\eta]X,Y\rangle.$$
([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) For a hypersurface the normal bundle is one-dimensional, so the normal curvature vanishes and the Ricci equation carries no extra information. ([Andrews, ANU Lecture 18](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~andrews/DG/DG_chap18.pdf))

If $\tilde M$ has constant sectional curvature $c$, the three equations become
$$\langle R(X,Y)Z,W\rangle = \langle h(X,W),h(Y,Z)\rangle - \langle h(X,Z),h(Y,W)\rangle + c\{\langle X,W\rangle\langle Y,Z\rangle - \langle X,Z\rangle\langle Y,W\rangle\},$$
$$(\bar\nabla_Xh)(Y,Z) = (\bar\nabla_Yh)(X,Z),\qquad \langle R^D(X,Y)\xi,\eta\rangle = \langle[A_\xi,A_\eta]X,Y\rangle.$$
([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

**Index form for a spacelike hypersurface $\Sigma$ in spacetime.** With unit timelike normal $n$, projector $\gamma^\alpha{}_\beta = \delta^\alpha{}_\beta + n^\alpha n_\beta$, extrinsic curvature defined by $\gamma^\mu{}_\alpha\gamma^\nu{}_\beta\nabla_\mu n_\nu = -K_{\alpha\beta}$, and $D$ the Levi-Civita connection of the induced metric:
$$\gamma^\mu{}_\alpha\gamma^\nu{}_\beta\gamma^\gamma{}_\rho\gamma^\sigma{}_\delta\,{}^4R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = R^\gamma{}_{\delta\alpha\beta} + K^\gamma{}_\alpha K_{\delta\beta} - K^\gamma{}_\beta K_{\alpha\delta},\qquad \gamma^\gamma{}_\rho n^\sigma\gamma^\mu{}_\alpha\gamma^\nu{}_\beta\,{}^4R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = D_\beta K^\gamma{}_\alpha - D_\alpha K^\gamma{}_\beta.$$
([Gourgoulhon](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))

### Key results
- **Scalar Gauss relation.** Contracting twice gives ${}^4R + 2\,{}^4R_{\mu\nu}n^\mu n^\nu = R + K^2 - K_{ij}K^{ij}$, a generalization of the Theorema Egregium; the contracted Codazzi relation is $\gamma^\mu{}_\alpha n^\nu\,{}^4R_{\mu\nu} = D_\alpha K - D_\mu K^\mu{}_\alpha$. ([Gourgoulhon](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035)) For a Riemannian hypersurface with unit normal $n$, second fundamental form $h$ and mean curvature $H$, the analogue is $R' = R + 2\operatorname{Ric}'(n,n) + \|h\|^2 - H^2$. ([Wikipedia: Gauss–Codazzi equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Codazzi_equations))
- **Theorema Egregium.** For a surface in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ the ambient curvature vanishes and the sign of the extrinsic term flips (the normal is spacelike), giving $R - K^2 + K_{ij}K^{ij} = 0$, i.e. $R = 2\kappa_1\kappa_2$ in terms of the principal curvatures. ([Gourgoulhon](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035)) Hence the Gaussian curvature is invariant under local isometry. ([Wikipedia: Theorema Egregium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorema_Egregium))
- **Fundamental theorem of submanifolds (existence).** Let $(M,g)$ be a **simply connected** Riemannian $n$-manifold with a Riemannian vector bundle $\nu$ of rank $m$ (curvature $R^D$) and a $\nu$-valued symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor $h$ satisfying the space-form Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci equations for curvature $c$. Then $M$ can be isometrically immersed in the complete simply connected space form $R^{n+m}(c)$ with normal bundle $\nu$ and second fundamental form $h$. ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))
- **Fundamental theorem (uniqueness).** Two isometric immersions of $M$ into $R^m(c)$ whose normal bundles, normal connections and second fundamental forms correspond under a bundle map covering an isometry of $M$ differ by an isometry of $R^m(c)$. Bonnet gave the first proof (1867). ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) For surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ this is Bonnet's theorem: two quadratic forms (the first positive definite) satisfying the Gauss–Codazzi equations determine a surface locally, unique up to a rigid motion. ([Wikipedia: Differential geometry of surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry_of_surfaces))
- **Einstein constraints.** The scalar Gauss relation and Einstein's equation give the Hamiltonian constraint $R + K^2 - K_{ij}K^{ij} = 16\pi E$; the contracted Codazzi relation gives the momentum constraint $D_jK^j{}_i - D_iK = 8\pi p_i$. ([Gourgoulhon](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))
- **Conformal method (Lichnerowicz–York).** The vacuum constraints are four equations for twelve unknowns $(\gamma,K)$. The conformal method splits data into free data (a conformal metric $\lambda$, a transverse-traceless $\sigma$, mean curvature $\tau$) and determined data (a conformal factor $\phi$, a vector field $W$), turning the constraints into a determined elliptic system whose scalar part is the Lichnerowicz equation. For asymptotically Euclidean data with $\tau = 0$, a solution exists iff $\lambda$ is a positive Yamabe metric. ([Bartnik & Isenberg](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0405092))
- **Classical isometric-embedding results.** Janet (1926) and Cartan (1927) proved that a real-analytic Riemannian $n$-manifold embeds locally isometrically in any real-analytic manifold of dimension $\tfrac12n(n+1)$, which is dimensionwise optimal. Nash (1956) proved that every compact Riemannian $n$-manifold embeds isometrically in $\mathbb E^N$ with $N = \tfrac12n(3n+11)$. Nirenberg (1953) solved Weyl's problem: a smooth metric on $S^2$ with $K>0$ has a smooth global isometric embedding in $\mathbb E^3$. Hilbert (1901) showed that a complete surface of constant negative curvature has no $C^4$ isometric immersion in $\mathbb E^3$. ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) See [Nash Embedding Theorem](node:Nash%20Embedding%20Theorem).

### Examples
- **Plane, cylinder, sphere in $\mathbb R^3$.** Cylinder of radius $r$: $R=0$, $K=-1/r$, $K_{ij}K^{ij} = 1/r^2$. Sphere: $R = 2/r^2$, $K=-2/r$, $K_{ij}K^{ij} = 2/r^2$. Both satisfy $R - K^2 + K_{ij}K^{ij} = 0$. ([Gourgoulhon](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))
- **Bending a flat sheet.** A flat slice of pizza has Gaussian curvature 0; bending it along one direction makes it rigid in the perpendicular direction, the principle behind corrugated materials. ([Wikipedia: Theorema Egregium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorema_Egregium))
- **Brane in a 5D bulk.** With induced metric $q_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} - n_\mu n_\nu$ and $K_{\mu\nu} = q_\mu{}^\alpha q_\nu{}^\beta\nabla_\alpha n_\beta$, the Gauss equation is ${}^{(4)}R^\alpha{}_{\beta\gamma\delta} = {}^{(5)}R^\mu{}_{\nu\rho\sigma}q^\alpha{}_\mu q_\beta{}^\nu q^\rho{}_\gamma q^\sigma{}_\delta + K^\alpha{}_\gamma K_{\beta\delta} - K^\alpha{}_\delta K_{\beta\gamma}$ and the Codazzi equation is $D_\nu K^\nu{}_\mu - D_\mu K = {}^{(5)}R_{\rho\sigma}n^\sigma q^\rho{}_\mu$. ([Shiromizu, Maeda & Sasaki](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))
- **Sign-changing curvature.** C. S. Lin (1986) proved that if the curvature of a $C^s$ ($s\ge6$) surface metric vanishes at $P$ with $\nabla K(P)\neq0$, a neighbourhood of $P$ has a $C^{s-3}$ isometric embedding in $\mathbb E^3$. ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

### History
Gauss gave the first equation (1828). Mainardi (1856) and Codazzi (1868–1869) derived the second independently; Karl Mikhailovich Peterson had found it earlier. The equations are also called the Gauss–Peterson–Codazzi or Gauss–Codazzi–Weingarten–Mainardi formulas. ([Wikipedia: Gauss–Codazzi equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Codazzi_equations)) The Theorema Egregium was proved by Gauss in 1827. ([Wikipedia: Theorema Egregium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorema_Egregium))

Chen's survey adds that Bonnet (1867) recognized the fundamental importance of the formulas, Voss first gave the Gauss and Codazzi equations for general submanifolds in 1880, and Ricci gave the Ricci equation in 1888; the Weingarten formula is named after Weingarten's 1861 paper. ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

### Connections
- [Extrinsic Curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature): $K_{ij}$ (the second fundamental form) is the extrinsic input.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): the equations decompose the ambient Riemann tensor.
- [Submanifolds and Embeddings](node:Submanifolds%20and%20Embeddings): the setting of induced metrics and normal bundles.
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives): the tangential, normal and combined connections.
- [Curves and Surfaces](node:Curves%20and%20Surfaces): the classical surface case, Theorema Egregium and Bonnet's theorem.
- [Nash Embedding Theorem](node:Nash%20Embedding%20Theorem): global isometric embedding, governed by this PDE system.
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): local isometric embedding is a nonlinear PDE problem.
- [ADM Formalism](node:ADM%20Formalism), [Einstein Constraint Equations](node:Einstein%20Constraint%20Equations): Hamiltonian and momentum constraints come from these relations.
- [Israel Junction Conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions): the jump in $K_{ij}$ across a thin shell.
- [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane), [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology): the SMS derivation starts here.
- [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry), [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the Lorentzian setting, where signs depend on the normal's causal type.

### Common pitfalls
- **Sign of $K$.** Gourgoulhon uses $\gamma\gamma\nabla n = -K$, while Shiromizu–Maeda–Sasaki use $K_{\mu\nu} = q q\nabla n$. ([Gourgoulhon](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035)) ([Shiromizu, Maeda & Sasaki](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076))
- **Causal type of the normal.** The sign of the $K^2 - K_{ij}K^{ij}$ term flips between a timelike normal (projector $\delta + nn$) and a spacelike one ($\delta - nn$). ([Gourgoulhon](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035))
- **Codimension.** In codimension $>1$ the Gauss and Codazzi equations are not enough: the normal connection and the Ricci equation are part of the data. ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))
- **Local versus global.** The global existence theorem assumes $M$ simply connected, and not every Riemannian 2-manifold can be isometrically immersed in $\mathbb E^3$. ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) The classical Bonnet statement for surfaces is local. ([Wikipedia: Differential geometry of surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry_of_surfaces))
- **Tautology.** For surfaces, whether the Gauss formula $K = (LN - M^2)/(eg - f^2)$ is a theorem or a definition depends on how Gaussian curvature is defined. ([Wikipedia: Gauss–Codazzi equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Codazzi_equations))

### Open problems
- **Local isometric embedding of surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$.** It is still an open question whether every (smooth) Riemannian metric on a 2-dimensional chart arises from an embedding in Euclidean 3-space; the analytic case is settled. ([Wikipedia: Differential geometry of surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry_of_surfaces)) Known smooth results need nonnegative curvature (Lin 1985) or a simple zero of the curvature with $\nabla K\neq0$ (Lin 1986); Greub and Socolescu claimed the gradient condition can be removed. ([Chen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))
- **Einstein constraints far from constant mean curvature.** The conformal method resolves existence for most CMC and near-CMC free data, but some near-CMC cases on closed manifolds remain unknown, and for non-CMC data with no control on $|\nabla\tau|$ Bartnik and Isenberg wrote in 2004 that almost nothing was known and there were no promising techniques. ([Bartnik & Isenberg](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0405092)) Later work gave sufficient conditions, on compact manifolds, under which the conformal method yields solutions with freely specified mean curvature (Holst, Nagy and Tsogtgerel with matter; Maxwell in vacuum, assuming a global supersolution), which is not a complete existence theory. ([Maxwell 2008](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.0874))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gauss–Codazzi equations (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Codazzi_equations): coordinate-free statement, surface form, history.
- **Learn:** [Andrews, Lecture 18: The Gauss and Codazzi equations (ANU)](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~andrews/DG/DG_chap18.pdf): proofs of the Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci identities for submanifolds of Euclidean space.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.950 Differential Geometry lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-950-differential-geometry-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/): chapter 2 on the local geometry of hypersurfaces.
- **Learn:** [Gourgoulhon, 3+1 Formalism and Bases of Numerical Relativity](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0703035): chapter 2 derives the Gauss and Codazzi relations for spacetime hypersurfaces.
- **Primary:** [Chen, "Riemannian Submanifolds: A Survey"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875): fundamental equations and theorems, isometric embedding results.
- **Primary:** [Bartnik & Isenberg, "The Constraint Equations"](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0405092): review of the Einstein constraints and the conformal method.
- **Primary:** [Shiromizu, Maeda & Sasaki, "The Einstein equations on the 3-brane world"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9910076): braneworld application.
references.General Relativity:
## Reference
### Overview
General relativity (GR) is Einstein's geometric theory of gravitation and the accepted description of the gravitation of macroscopic objects. It generalizes [Special Relativity](node:Special%20Relativity) and refines Newton's law by describing gravity as the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime, tied to the energy, momentum and stress of matter through the Einstein field equations; in Wheeler's summary, "Space-time tells matter how to move; matter tells space-time how to curve." Newton's law is GR's prediction for nearly flat spacetime around stationary masses, and GR also predicts the gravitational redshift, the Shapiro delay, singularities and black holes; so far all tests agree with it. ([Wikipedia: General relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity))

Mathematically, the field equations are nonlinear second-order [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) for the metric. ([Carroll, GR lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019)) Initial data on a 3-manifold must satisfy constraint equations; for such data there is a globally hyperbolic solution with the 3-manifold as a Cauchy surface, and this 3+1 formulation is the basis of numerical relativity. ([Wikipedia: Initial value formulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_value_formulation_%28general_relativity%29)) Uniqueness holds for the maximal such development, up to a diffeomorphism fixing the initial surface. ([Rendall](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133)) The modern mathematical theory studies this evolution problem: stability of Minkowski space, solutions with prescribed singularity structure, and cosmic censorship. ([Rendall, Living Reviews](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133))

### Formal definition
Spacetime is a four-dimensional manifold with a Lorentzian metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ ([Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry)). The field equations are
$$G_{\mu\nu}\equiv R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu}=\kappa T_{\mu\nu},\qquad\kappa=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4},$$
which in vacuum reduce to $R_{\mu\nu}=0$; a freely falling particle moves on a geodesic, $\ddot x^\mu+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta=0$. ([Wikipedia: General relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity)) The constant is fixed by the Newtonian limit $\nabla^2h_{00}=-8\pi GT_{00}$ ($c=1$). ([Carroll, GR lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))

**Einstein Equivalence Principle.** "In small enough regions of spacetime, the laws of physics reduce to those of special relativity; it is impossible to detect the existence of a gravitational field." ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))

**Action and the stress tensor convention.** With the standard definition $T_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta(\sqrt{-g}\mathcal L_M)}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}$, the [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action) is
$$S=\int\Big[\frac{1}{2\kappa}R+\mathcal L_M\Big]\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x,$$
i.e. coefficient $1/(16\pi G)$ for $c=1$. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action)) Carroll's notes instead write $S=\frac{1}{8\pi G}S_H+S_M$ together with $T_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta S_M}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}$, noting that the normalization is convention-dependent; the two pairs give the same field equations. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))

**3+1 (ADM) form.** In the ADM Hamiltonian formulation (1959), a lapse $N$ and shift $N^i$ act as Lagrange multipliers whose variation gives the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. ([Wikipedia: ADM formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADM_formalism)) Initial data are a Riemannian 3-metric $h_{ab}$ and a symmetric $k_{ab}$ on $S$; a solution is a spacetime in which they are the induced metric and second fundamental form of $S$. ([Rendall](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133))

### Key results
- **Counting degrees of freedom.** The ten equations are subject to the four Bianchi identities $\nabla^\mu G_{\mu\nu}=0$, leaving six independent equations for ten metric components; the remaining four functions are coordinate freedom. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019)) For linearized plane waves, harmonic gauge and the residual gauge freedom reduce the ten components of the amplitude to two, the $+$ and $\times$ polarizations. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Local well-posedness and global uniqueness.** For smooth vacuum data $(h,k)$ satisfying the constraints there is a smooth solution in which $S$ is a Cauchy surface (Choquet-Bruhat); the maximal Cauchy development is unique up to a diffeomorphism fixing $S$ (Choquet-Bruhat and Geroch, 1969), and solutions depend continuously on the data. ([Rendall](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133)) The original local existence proof used harmonic coordinates. ([Rendall](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133))
- **Positive mass theorem.** For asymptotically flat, geodesically complete initial data satisfying the dominant energy condition, the ADM energy is nonnegative, and zero only for data in Minkowski space. Schoen and Yau proved it in 1979 (for 3-manifolds, extendable to dimension less than eight); Witten gave a spinor proof in 1981. ([Wikipedia: Positive energy theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_energy_theorem))
- **Nonlinear stability of Minkowski space.** For vacuum, asymptotically flat data sufficiently close to Minkowski data on a hyperplane, Christodoulou and Klainerman (1993) proved that the maximal development is geodesically complete; the Bel–Robinson tensor is the central tool, and Lindblad–Rodnianski later gave a proof in harmonic coordinates. ([Rendall](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133))
- **Kerr stability.** Klainerman and Szeftel's main paper in a series proves the full nonlinear stability of the Kerr family for small angular momentum, for general perturbations of asymptotically flat vacuum solutions. ([Klainerman & Szeftel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11857))
- **Penrose singularity theorem (1965).** If spacetime has a non-compact Cauchy hypersurface and a closed future-trapped surface, and $R_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu\ge0$ for null $u$, then there are future-incomplete null geodesics. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226))
- **Hawking–Penrose theorem (1970).** If $R_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu\ge0$ and the generic condition hold for causal vectors, there are no closed timelike curves, and there is a closed achronal hypersurface, a closed trapped surface, or a point with reconverging [light cone](node:Light%20Cone), then spacetime has incomplete causal geodesics. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226)) The [Raychaudhuri Equation](node:Raychaudhuri%20Equation) is a fundamental lemma for the Penrose–Hawking theorems. ([Wikipedia: Raychaudhuri equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raychaudhuri_equation))
- **Birkhoff's theorem.** Any spherically symmetric vacuum solution is static and asymptotically flat, so the exterior of a spherical non-rotating body is Schwarzschild (Jebsen 1921, Birkhoff 1923). ([Wikipedia: Birkhoff's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_theorem_%28relativity%29))
- **Black-hole uniqueness.** Israel (1967) gave the first version, the uniqueness of the Schwarzschild metric; it was quickly generalized to charged black holes (Israel 1968, static electrovac space-times) and spinning ones (Carter 1971, axisymmetric black holes). The conjecture is that stationary Einstein–Maxwell black holes are characterized by mass $M$, angular momentum $J$ and charge $Q$, so an isolated black hole is described by the Kerr–Newman metric; even in pure vacuum it is only partially resolved, by results of Hawking, Carter and Robinson that assume non-degenerate event horizons and real analyticity of the spacetime. ([Wikipedia: No-hair theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-hair_theorem)) Unlike vacuum and electrovacuum black holes, not all black-hole equilibrium configurations of self-gravitating nonlinear field theories are characterized by mass, angular momentum and global charges. ([Chruściel, Costa & Heusler](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.6112))
- **Experimental tests.** Mercury's anomalous perihelion advance is 43 arcseconds per century; Cassini time-delay measurements agree with GR to $10^{-3}$ percent; gravitational-wave damping in the Hulse–Taylor binary pulsar agrees with GR to better than half a percent. ([Will, Living Reviews](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377)) LIGO observed GW150914 on 14 September 2015, a binary black-hole merger detected at more than $5.1\sigma$. ([LIGO/Virgo](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.03837))

### Examples
- **Exact solutions.** Schwarzschild, Reissner–Nordström and Kerr describe black holes; FLRW and de Sitter describe expanding universes; the Gödel universe contains closed timelike curves. ([Wikipedia: General relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity))
- **GW150914.** Source-frame initial masses $36^{+5}_{-4}$ and $29^{+4}_{-4}\,M_\odot$, final mass $62^{+4}_{-4}\,M_\odot$, with $3.0\pm0.5\,M_\odot c^2$ radiated. ([LIGO/Virgo](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.03837))
- **Naked-singularity thresholds.** Reissner–Nordström with mass $M$ and charge $Q$ is a black hole if $Q\le M$ and a naked singularity if $Q>M$; Kerr is a black hole if $J\le M^2$. Attempts to overcharge a black hole fail because the added energy increases $M$. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226))

### History
Einstein began his search in 1907 and presented the field equations to the Prussian Academy in November 1915, explaining Mercury's perihelion advance without arbitrary parameters. Eddington's expedition tested light deflection at the eclipse of 29 May 1919, Schwarzschild found the first non-trivial exact solution in 1916, and the "golden age" of GR ran from about 1960 to 1975. ([Wikipedia: General relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity)) Hilbert derived the field equations from an action principle; Einstein derived them independently. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))

Penrose's 1965 theorem introduced closed trapped surfaces and was the first modern singularity theorem, and Hawking and Penrose's 1970 theorem is still regarded as the preeminent one. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226))

### Connections
- [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle), [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry), [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): the physical and mathematical foundations.
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations), [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action): the dynamical law and its variational form.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics), [Newtonian Limit of General Relativity](node:Newtonian%20Limit%20of%20General%20Relativity): motion of test bodies; recovering Poisson's equation.
- [ADM Formalism](node:ADM%20Formalism), [Einstein Constraint Equations](node:Einstein%20Constraint%20Equations), [Numerical Relativity](node:Numerical%20Relativity): the Cauchy problem.
- [Energy Conditions](node:Energy%20Conditions), [Raychaudhuri Equation](node:Raychaudhuri%20Equation), [Singularity Theorems in Relativity](node:Singularity%20Theorems%20in%20Relativity): singularity formation.
- [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime), [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution), [Kerr Black Holes](node:Kerr%20Black%20Holes), [Black Holes](node:Black%20Holes): stability and uniqueness.
- [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space), [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space), [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): cosmological solutions.
- [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves), [Binary Pulsars](node:Binary%20Pulsars), [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing), [Tests of General Relativity](node:Tests%20of%20General%20Relativity): observations.
- [Quantum Gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity), [QFT in Curved Spacetime](node:QFT%20in%20Curved%20Spacetime): where the classical theory meets quantum physics.

### Common pitfalls
- **Action normalization.** The coefficient of $\int R\sqrt{-g}$ is $1/(16\pi G)$ only with $T_{\mu\nu}=-2(-g)^{-1/2}\delta S_M/\delta g^{\mu\nu}$; pairing $1/(8\pi G)$ with that $T$ gives equations off by a factor of 2. ([Wikipedia: Einstein–Hilbert action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein%E2%80%93Hilbert_action)) ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Geodesic incompleteness is physical.** For reasonable matter content (no negative energies), spacetimes are almost guaranteed to be geodesically incomplete; Schwarzschild and FRW both have singularities. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Nonlinearity.** Solutions cannot be superposed. ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Coordinates.** The field equations alone do not determine the metric's evolution without a coordinate condition. ([Wikipedia: General relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity))
- **Incompleteness versus curvature blow-up.** The singularity theorems prove geodesic incompleteness, not that curvature becomes infinite. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226))

### Open problems
- **Cosmic censorship.** Weak censorship asks whether singularities from gravitational collapse are hidden inside event horizons, strong censorship whether singularities are non-timelike; a precise mathematical formulation is itself part of the problem. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226)) No formal proof exists, though numerical simulations support it; the generic structure of singularities (e.g. the BKL conjecture) is an active research question. ([Wikipedia: General relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity))
- **No-hair conjecture.** There is no rigorous proof of the general uniqueness theorem; in the pure-vacuum case it is only partly resolved, and the analyticity assumption is restrictive. ([Wikipedia: No-hair theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-hair_theorem))
- **Constraint solutions and global dynamics.** The conformal method for the constraints is well understood only under constant mean curvature; Rendall's review highlights open questions on global existence and asymptotics. ([Rendall](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133))
- **Positive mass in high dimension.** Whether the positive energy theorem holds for initial data of arbitrary dimension is open in general: the Schoen–Yau argument extends to dimensions below eight, Witten's spinor argument needs a spin structure, and a 2017 Schoen–Yau preprint treats the case $\operatorname{tr}_gk=0$. ([Wikipedia: Positive energy theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_energy_theorem))
- **Quantum gravity.** No complete and consistent theory of quantum gravity is currently known. ([Wikipedia: General relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity))
- **Strong-field tests.** Current and future tests will centre on strong gravity and gravitational waves. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7377))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [General relativity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity): history, principles, solutions, open questions.
- **Learn:** [Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019): standard graduate course from manifolds through cosmology.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 8.962 General Relativity (Hughes, 2020)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-962-general-relativity-spring-2020/): graduate lecture videos and problem sets.
- **Primary:** [Rendall, "Theorems on Existence and Global Dynamics for the Einstein Equations"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/0505133): review of the Cauchy problem, stability and cosmic censorship.
- **Primary:** [Senovilla & Garfinkle, "The 1965 Penrose singularity theorem"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5226): precise singularity theorems and their legacy.
- **Primary:** [Will, "The Confrontation between General Relativity and Experiment"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7377): the standard review of tests.
- **Further reading:** [Wald, *General Relativity* (Chicago, 1984)](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/G/bo5952261.html): classic textbook with chapters on singularities and black holes; [Misner, Thorne & Wheeler, *Gravitation*](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691177793/gravitation): full-year graduate text.
references.Generalization in Deep Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Generalization in deep learning asks why networks with far more parameters than training examples, trained by stochastic gradient methods to near-zero training error, still predict well on new data. Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht and Vinyals showed that standard image classifiers trained with SGD can fit randomly labeled data, and even random-noise images, even with explicit regularization, so explanations that credit only the model family or regularization cannot account for the small train–test gap seen on real labels. ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530))

Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin organize the theoretical response around three conjectures: overparameterization lets gradient methods find interpolating solutions, those methods implicitly regularize, and overparameterization enables benign overfitting. Their survey reviews classical uniform-convergence results and their limits, examples of implicit regularization that yield minimum-norm solutions, benign overfitting in regression with quadratic loss, and the linear regime of neural networks, including an exact asymptotic analysis of two-layer networks. ([Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09177))

The empirical side includes double descent: test error first follows the classical U-shape in model capacity and then decreases again past the interpolation threshold, where the model first fits the training data. ([Belkin et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118)) The phenomenon also appears as a function of training epochs, and adding samples can hurt in some regimes. ([Nakkiran et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02292)) The question sits at the junction of [Statistical Learning Theory](node:Statistical%20Learning%20Theory), optimization, and [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning) practice.

### Formal definition
For a loss $\ell$, data distribution $\mathcal D$ and sample $S=(z_i)_{i=1}^n\sim\mathcal D^n$, the risk and empirical risk of a predictor $f$ are $\mathcal R(f)=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mathcal D}\,\ell(f,z)$ and $\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(f)=\frac1n\sum_i\ell(f,z_i)$; the generalization gap is $\mathcal R(f)-\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(f)$. Uniform-convergence approaches bound $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}(\mathcal R(f)-\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(f))$ over a hypothesis class $\mathcal F$, for example through the empirical [Rademacher Complexity](node:Rademacher%20Complexity) $\mathrm{URad}(\mathcal F_{|S})=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_i\varepsilon_i f(z_i)$ with i.i.d. Rademacher signs $\varepsilon_i$. ([Telgarsky, Deep learning theory notes](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/))

The interpolation threshold is, roughly, where the number of parameters equals the number of training points; more precisely, it is characterized by the maximum number of samples on which the model and training procedure reach approximately zero average training error, and the overparameterized regime lies beyond it. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_descent))

### Key results
- **Rademacher generalization bound.** If every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $f(z)\in[a,b]$ almost surely, then with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$,
$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\Big(\mathbb E f-\tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_i f(z_i)\Big)\le \tfrac{2}{n}\,\mathrm{URad}(\mathcal F_{|S})+3(b-a)\sqrt{\tfrac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2n}}.$$
A margin version (Theorem 13.4) holds for any margin $\gamma>0$ and bounds the zero-one risk by an empirical margin risk plus a Rademacher term. ([Telgarsky, Thm. 13.1 and 13.4](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/))
- **Spectrally normalized margin bound.** Bartlett, Foster and Telgarsky give a multiclass margin bound for networks that scales with a spectral complexity: the product of the layers' spectral norms (a Lipschitz constant) times a correction factor; on AlexNet trained on MNIST and CIFAR-10, the bound, the Lipschitz constants and the excess risks are closely correlated across true and random labels. ([Bartlett, Foster and Telgarsky 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08498))
- **Finite-sample expressivity.** A depth-two network can fit any labeling of a finite sample once its parameter count exceeds the number of data points. ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530))
- **Implicit bias on separable data.** For unregularized [logistic regression](node:Logistic%20Regression) with homogeneous linear predictors on linearly separable data, [gradient descent](node:Gradient%20Descent)'s iterates converge in direction to the hard-margin SVM solution, and this convergence is only logarithmic in the convergence of the loss; the result extends to other monotone decreasing losses and multiclass problems. ([Soudry et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10345))
- **Benign overfitting in linear regression.** For the minimum-norm interpolating predictor in [linear regression](node:Linear%20Regression), Bartlett, Long, Lugosi and Tsigler characterize near-optimal prediction in terms of two effective ranks of the data covariance; benign overfitting requires many low-importance directions whose number substantially exceeds the sample size. ([Bartlett et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11300))
- **Limits of uniform convergence.** Nagarajan and Kolter construct overparameterized linear classifiers and networks trained by gradient descent for which any uniform-convergence bound, even one restricted to the classifiers GD outputs, is vacuous (above $1-\varepsilon$) although the test error is a small $\varepsilon$. ([Nagarajan and Kolter 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04742))
- **Nonvacuous PAC-Bayes bounds.** Directly optimizing a PAC-Bayes bound yields nonvacuous generalization bounds for stochastic networks with millions of parameters trained on tens of thousands of examples. ([Dziugaite and Roy 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.11008))

### Examples
- **Linear regression double descent.** Double descent occurs already for linear regression with isotropic Gaussian covariates and noise. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_descent))
- **Epoch-wise and sample-wise double descent.** Nakkiran et al. define effective model complexity and observe regimes where up to four times more training samples hurt test performance. ([Nakkiran et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02292))
- **Random-label test.** State-of-the-art image classifiers trained with SGD fit randomly labeled training data, and even random-noise images, so a capacity measure that depends only on the architecture cannot distinguish them from the same networks trained on real labels. ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530))
- **Large-scale evaluation of measures.** Jiang et al. trained over 10,000 convolutional networks while varying hyperparameters and tested more than 40 complexity measures for potentially causal relationships with generalization, reporting failures of some popular measures. ([Jiang et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02178))

### History
Observations of what is now called double descent in specific models date to 1989; Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal named the phenomenon in their 2019 paper. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_descent); [Belkin et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118)) Work after the random-label experiments of Zhang et al. (ICLR 2017) includes nonvacuous PAC-Bayes bounds (UAI 2017), spectrally normalized margin bounds (NIPS) and the 2019 uniform-convergence critique. ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530); [Dziugaite and Roy 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.11008); [Bartlett, Foster and Telgarsky 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08498); [Nagarajan and Kolter 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04742)) Telgarsky's lecture notes summarize this line of work as suggesting that the classical perspective is loose, has poor explanatory power, and lacks correlation with good test error. ([Telgarsky](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/))

### Connections
- [Statistical Learning Theory](node:Statistical%20Learning%20Theory): supplies the uniform-convergence framework being tested.
- [Rademacher Complexity](node:Rademacher%20Complexity) and [VC Dimension](node:VC%20Dimension): classical capacity measures that are vacuous for large networks with architecture-only control.
- [PAC-Bayesian Bounds](node:PAC-Bayesian%20Bounds): the route to the first nonvacuous bounds for deep networks.
- [Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent](node:Implicit%20Bias%20of%20Gradient%20Descent): the optimizer selects low-norm or max-margin interpolants.
- [Neural Tangent Kernel](node:Neural%20Tangent%20Kernel): the linear regime where several generalization results are proved.
- [Bias–Variance Tradeoff](node:Bias–Variance%20Tradeoff): the classical U-curve that double descent extends.
- [Regularization](node:Regularization): explicit penalties play a smaller role than expected.
- [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent): the training algorithm whose dynamics carry the implicit bias.
- [Support Vector Machines](node:Support%20Vector%20Machines): the max-margin limit of GD on separable data.
- [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): empirical regularities of loss in model and data size.
- [Out-of-Distribution Generalization](node:Out-of-Distribution%20Generalization): generalization when test and training distributions differ.

### Common pitfalls
- **Equating parameter count with capacity.** Architecture-only capacity cannot explain behavior, because the same network fits both real and random labels. ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530))
- **Assuming any norm-based uniform bound will eventually work.** Some uniform-convergence bounds grow with sample size in practice, and constructions exist where they are provably vacuous. ([Nagarajan and Kolter 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04742))
- **Reading benign overfitting as universal.** Near-optimal interpolation in linear regression holds only under specific covariance conditions, over a much narrower range of distributions in infinite dimension than in finite but growing dimension. ([Bartlett et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11300))
- **Trusting popular complexity measures.** In controlled experiments over more than 10,000 networks, some widely discussed complexity measures fail to track generalization. ([Jiang et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02178))

### Open problems
- **Extending implicit-regularization and benign-overfitting theory beyond linear and two-layer regimes.** Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin state the three conjectures above and close by identifying the challenges of extending them to realistic deep learning. ([Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09177))
- **A generalized double-descent law.** Nakkiran et al. conjecture a generalized double descent with respect to effective model complexity. ([Nakkiran et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02292))
- **Data-dependent Lipschitz control.** Telgarsky notes that an "average Lipschitz" bound would be preferable to worst-case Lipschitz bounds and that it is unclear how to obtain one. ([Telgarsky, Remark 13.7](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Double descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_descent): definition, interpolation threshold, theoretical explanations.
- **Learn:** [Telgarsky, Deep learning theory lecture notes](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/): approximation, optimization and generalization (Rademacher, margin and covering bounds).
- **Primary:** [Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530): random-label experiments that set the problem.
- **Primary:** [Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin 2021, Deep learning: a statistical viewpoint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09177): survey of implicit regularization and benign overfitting.
- **Primary:** [Bartlett, Long, Lugosi and Tsigler, Benign overfitting in linear regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11300): sharp characterization in the linear case.
- **Further reading:** [Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/): textbook; Chapter 5 (machine learning basics) and Chapter 7 (regularization for deep learning).
references.Geodesics:
## Reference
### Overview
A geodesic is a curve that is, in some sense, the locally shortest path between two points on a surface or [Riemannian manifold](node:Riemannian%20Metrics). On a manifold with an affine connection, it is a curve whose tangent vector stays parallel when transported along the curve itself. In metric geometry it is a curve that locally minimizes distance. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic))

Geodesics connect local differential geometry to global topology. The exponential map sends tangent vectors to the endpoints of geodesics, and Jacobi fields measure how nearby geodesics spread. Conjugate points mark where minimization fails, and closed geodesics are critical points of the energy on the free loop space, which ties their existence to the [homology](node:Homology) of that space. ([Wikipedia: exponential map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_map_%28Riemannian_geometry%29); [Wikipedia: conjugate points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_points); [Oancea survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3107))

In [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity), timelike geodesics are the worldlines of freely falling test particles and light follows lightlike (null) geodesics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic); [Arias Abad et al., lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.13625)) Geodesic incompleteness is the working definition of a spacetime singularity in the Penrose–Hawking theorems. ([Wikipedia: singularity theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems))

### Formal definition
**Affine geodesic.** On a smooth manifold with affine connection $\nabla$, a curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$. In local coordinates this is
$$\frac{d^2\gamma^\lambda}{dt^2}+\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\frac{d\gamma^\mu}{dt}\frac{d\gamma^\nu}{dt}=0,$$
with $\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$ the Christoffel symbols. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic))

**Variational definition.** For a Riemannian metric $g$, set $L(\gamma)=\int_a^b\sqrt{g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)}\,dt$ and $E(\gamma)=\tfrac12\int_a^b g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)\,dt$. Geodesics of the Levi-Civita connection are the critical points of $E$; its [Euler–Lagrange equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations) are the geodesic equation. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic))

**Metric-space geodesic.** A curve $\gamma:I\to M$ in a [metric space](node:Metric%20Spaces) is a geodesic if there is $v\ge0$ such that each $t\in I$ has a neighbourhood $J$ with $d(\gamma(t_1),\gamma(t_2))=v|t_1-t_2|$ for all $t_1,t_2\in J$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic))

**Exponential map.** For $p\in M$ and $v\in T_pM$, $\exp_p(v)=\gamma_v(1)$, where $\gamma_v$ is the geodesic with $\gamma_v(0)=p$, $\dot\gamma_v(0)=v$. Its differential at $0$ is the identity, so by the [inverse function theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem) it is a local diffeomorphism near $0$; this gives normal coordinates. The injectivity radius at $p$ is the radius of the largest ball about $0\in T_pM$ that $\exp_p$ maps diffeomorphically. ([Wikipedia: exponential map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_map_%28Riemannian_geometry%29); [Arias Abad et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.13625))

**Jacobi fields and conjugate points.** A vector field $J$ along a geodesic $\gamma$ is a Jacobi field if
$$\frac{D^2J}{dt^2}+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0 .$$
The derivative of a one-parameter family of geodesics is a Jacobi field, and on a complete manifold every Jacobi field arises this way. $J$ is determined by $J$ and $DJ/dt$ at one point, so the Jacobi fields along $\gamma$ form a vector space of dimension $2\dim M$ ([Wikipedia: Jacobi field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_field)). Points $p,q$ on $\gamma$ are conjugate if a nonzero Jacobi field vanishes at both. ([Wikipedia: conjugate points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_points))

### Key results
- **Local existence and uniqueness.** Given $p$ and $v\in T_pM$, there is a unique geodesic with $\gamma(0)=p$, $\dot\gamma(0)=v$, by the theory of [ODEs](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic))
- **Length versus energy.** $L(\gamma)^2\le2(b-a)E(\gamma)$, with equality exactly when $\gamma$ has constant speed. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic))
- **Gauss lemma.** Radial geodesics from $p$ meet the images under $\exp_p$ of small spheres about $0\in T_pM$ orthogonally; this underlies geodesic normal coordinates. ([Wikipedia: exponential map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_map_%28Riemannian_geometry%29)) The differential of $\exp_p$ is given by Jacobi fields: with $\gamma(t)=\exp_p(tv)$ and $V$ the Jacobi field with $V(0)=0$, $V'(0)=w$, one has $D(\exp_p)(v)(w)=V(1)$. ([Arias Abad et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.13625))
- **[Hopf–Rinow Theorem](node:Hopf–Rinow%20Theorem).** For a connected smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary, the following are equivalent: (i) closed bounded subsets are compact; (ii) $M$ is a complete metric space; (iii) $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pM$ for every $p$. Any of them implies that any two points are joined by a length-minimizing geodesic. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf%E2%80%93Rinow_theorem))
