- **Minimization stops at the first conjugate point.** On a Riemannian manifold, a geodesic continued beyond a point conjugate to its starting point is no longer locally the shortest path: nearby curves are shorter. ([Wikipedia: conjugate points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_points)) **Morse index theorem:** for a geodesic $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, its $\Omega$-index as a critical point of energy equals the number of points conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$ with $0<t<1$, counted with multiplicity, and is finite. ([Oancea survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1406.3107))
- **Cartan–Hadamard theorem.** If $M$ is connected, complete, and has nonpositive sectional curvature, then $\exp_p$ is a covering map and the universal cover of $M$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%E2%80%93Hadamard_theorem)) Such manifolds have no conjugate points. ([Wikipedia: conjugate points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_points))
- **Geodesic deviation.** For a family of geodesics with tangent $T^\mu$ and deviation vector $X^\mu$, $A^\mu=\frac{D^2X^\mu}{d\tau^2}=R^\mu{}_{\nu\rho\sigma}T^\nu T^\rho X^\sigma$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic_deviation)). For slow motion ($T\approx(1,0,0,0)$) this gives $A^i=R^i{}_{00k}X^k=-R^i{}_{0k0}X^k$. Comparing with Newtonian tidal acceleration $\ddot s^i=-\partial_i\partial_k\Phi\,s^k$ gives $R^i{}_{0k0}\approx+\partial_i\partial_k\Phi$, and contracting gives $\mathrm{Ric}_{00}=\Delta\Phi=4\pi G\rho$. ([Arias Abad et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.13625))
- **Closed geodesics.** *Lyusternik–Fet (1951):* every compact Riemannian manifold has a closed geodesic ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyusternik%E2%80%93Fet_theorem)). Oancea notes that on a closed manifold that is not simply connected, minimizing energy in a nontrivial free homotopy class already produces one; the simply connected case is the subtle one that Lyusternik and Fet settled. *Gromoll–Meyer:* if $M$ is a simply connected closed manifold and for some prime $p$ the Betti numbers of the free loop space of $M$ with $\mathbb F_p$ coefficients are unbounded, every Riemannian metric on $M$ has infinitely many prime closed geodesics. For simply connected closed $M$, Vigué-Poirrier and Sullivan showed that rational unboundedness holds exactly when the rational cohomology ring of $M$ needs at least two generators. *2-sphere:* by work of Bangert, Franks, Angenent and Hingston, every Riemannian $S^2$ has infinitely many geometrically distinct prime closed geodesics. ([Oancea survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1406.3107))
- **Theorem of the three geodesics.** Every Riemannian manifold homeomorphic to $S^2$ has at least three simple closed geodesics. The bound is sharp: Morse showed that an ellipsoid with distinct but nearly equal axes has exactly three. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem_of_the_three_geodesics))
- **Singularity theorems.** Penrose (1965): if the null energy condition holds, there is a noncompact connected Cauchy surface, and there is a closed trapped surface, then spacetime contains incomplete null geodesics. The proof uses Raychaudhuri focusing, which forces conjugate points, together with a global-hyperbolicity argument about maximal geodesics. Hawking's cosmological version uses the strong energy condition. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems))

### Examples
- **Euclidean space and spheres.** Geodesics are straight lines and great circles. On a sphere, antipodal points are joined by infinitely many shortest paths. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic)) Antipodal points are conjugate, so a geodesic continued past the antipode stops minimizing. $\mathbb R^n$ has no conjugate points. ([Wikipedia: conjugate points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_points))
- **Constant curvature Jacobi fields.** Normal Jacobi fields are linear in $t$ for curvature $0$. For curvature $k^2$ they are combinations of $\sin(kt)e_i,\cos(kt)e_i$, and for curvature $-k^2$ of $e^{\pm kt}e_i$. ([Wikipedia: Jacobi field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_field))
- **Incompleteness.** On an open disc in $\mathbb R^2$ geodesics cannot be extended to all of $\mathbb R$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic))
- **Hyperbolic surfaces.** On a compact hyperbolic surface whose [fundamental group](node:Fundamental%20Group) has no torsion, closed geodesics correspond one-to-one to nontrivial conjugacy classes in its Fuchsian group. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_geodesic))
- **[Special Relativity](node:Special%20Relativity).** Straight timelike lines maximize proper time between causally related events (the twin paradox). Massless particles move on lightlike geodesics, which cannot be parametrized by proper time. ([Arias Abad et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.13625))

### History
Hopf and his student Rinow published the completeness theorem as "Ueber den Begriff der vollständigen differentialgeometrischen Fläche", Comment. Math. Helv. 3 (1931) 209–225. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01601813); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf%E2%80%93Rinow_theorem)) Von Mangoldt (1881) and Hadamard (1898) proved the Cartan–Hadamard theorem for surfaces, and Cartan extended it to Riemannian manifolds in 1928. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%E2%80%93Hadamard_theorem))

Poincaré conjectured the three-geodesics theorem in 1905. Lyusternik and Schnirelmann's 1929 proof relied on a flawed deformation lemma, and Grayson gave an accepted proof in the 1980s via curve-shortening flow, following a suggestion of Uhlenbeck. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem_of_the_three_geodesics)) The existence of closed geodesics on spheres was the original problem Morse addressed with his theory. ([Oancea survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1406.3107))

### Connections
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives): geodesics are autoparallel curves.
- [Parallel Transport](node:Parallel%20Transport): the tangent vector is parallel along the geodesic.
- [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations) and [Euler–Lagrange Equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations): geodesics are critical points of energy.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics) and [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry): the metric fixes the Levi-Civita connection and the causal type of geodesics.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): curvature drives Jacobi fields and geodesic deviation.
- [Hopf–Rinow Theorem](node:Hopf–Rinow%20Theorem): completeness and existence of minimizers.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): closed geodesics in free homotopy classes; Cartan–Hadamard universal covers.
- [Homology](node:Homology): loop-space Betti numbers force infinitely many closed geodesics.
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds) and [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces): the two settings for the definitions.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics) and [Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry): geodesic flow is a Hamiltonian flow on the cotangent bundle.
- [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) and [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory): geodesic flows are basic examples.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity), [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle) and [Newtonian Limit of General Relativity](node:Newtonian%20Limit%20of%20General%20Relativity): free fall is geodesic motion.
- [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution) and [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing): orbits and light bending are geodesics.
- [Energy Conditions](node:Energy%20Conditions) and [Black Holes](node:Black%20Holes): inputs and outputs of the singularity theorems.

### Common pitfalls
- **Sign of the Newtonian tidal term.** The Wikipedia geodesic-deviation article writes $A^i=R^i{}_{0j0}X^j$ and $R^i{}_{0j0}=-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic_deviation)). With its own deviation equation, the first line should read $A^i=R^i{}_{00j}X^j=-R^i{}_{0j0}X^j$, and then $R^i{}_{0j0}=+\partial_i\partial_j\Phi$. The physics (tidal acceleration $-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi X^j$) is the same. ([Arias Abad et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.13625))
- **Geodesics need not minimize.** The long arc of a great circle is a geodesic but not a shortest path. Conversely, $t\mapsto t^2$ on $[0,1]$ traces a shortest path but is not a geodesic, because its speed is not constant. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic))
- **Hopf–Rinow is Riemannian and finite-dimensional.** The compact Clifton–Pohl torus (Lorentzian) is not geodesically complete. The unit sphere of a separable Hilbert space can be given a Hilbert-manifold structure in which antipodal points cannot be joined by a length-minimizing geodesic. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf%E2%80%93Rinow_theorem))
- **Completeness does not make $\exp_p$ a diffeomorphism.** Even on a complete manifold, $\exp_p$ need not be a global diffeomorphism; the cut locus is where minimizing geodesics stop being unique. ([Wikipedia: exponential map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_map_%28Riemannian_geometry%29))
- **Finsler versus Riemannian.** Katok's non-symmetric Finsler metrics on $S^n$ have only finitely many prime closed geodesics, so results for Riemannian metrics need not carry over. ([Oancea survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1406.3107))

### Open problems
- **Infinitely many closed geodesics.** Whether every closed Riemannian manifold carries infinitely many geometrically distinct prime closed geodesics: "The answer is not known in full generality." For spheres $S^n$, $n\ge3$, the problem "remains open in full generality". ([Oancea survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1406.3107))
- **Quasigeodesics on polyhedra.** Every convex polyhedron has at least three simple closed quasigeodesics. Whether they can be constructed in polynomial time is open. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem_of_the_three_geodesics))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Geodesic (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic): affine, Riemannian and metric definitions, geodesic flow.
- **Reference:** [Hopf–Rinow theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf%E2%80%93Rinow_theorem): completeness and minimizers.
- **Learn:** [Arias Abad, Quintero Vélez & Vélez Caicedo, Relativity (lecture notes)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.13625): geodesics, Jacobi fields, the exponential map, and geodesic deviation as tidal forces, for mathematicians.
- **Primary:** [Oancea, Morse theory, closed geodesics, and the homology of free loop spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3107): survey of closed-geodesic existence, the index theorem, Gromoll–Meyer and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Hopf & Rinow (1931), Comment. Math. Helv. 3](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01601813): the original completeness paper.
- **Further reading:** [Milnor, Morse Theory (Annals of Mathematics Studies 51, Princeton)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691080086/morse-theory-am-51-volume-51): the standard exposition of Morse theory.
references.Geometric Deep Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Geometric deep learning (GDL) is a programme for deriving neural-network architectures from the symmetries of the domain on which the data live. Bronstein, Bruna, Cohen and Veličković present it as a "geometric unification" inspired by Felix Klein's Erlangen Program: since practical learning tasks inherit regularities from the underlying low-dimensionality and structure of the physical world, architectures such as CNNs, RNNs, GNNs and Transformers can be explained, and new ones designed, by asking which transformations of the input should leave the output invariant or change it predictably. The title of their 156-page text names the five domains covered: grids, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges. ([Bronstein et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.13478))

The core mathematical tools are group actions, invariance and equivariance, and group convolution; the 2025 review by Sáez de Ocáriz Borde and Bronstein collects the background the subject uses: groups and group actions, vector spaces, vector calculus, topology and manifolds (tangent bundles, Riemannian manifolds), functional analysis, [spectral theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) and [Fourier analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis), and [graph theory](node:Graph%20Theory). ([Sáez de Ocáriz Borde and Bronstein 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.02723)) In the graph setting the symmetry is the permutation group acting on node labels: a CNN layer is a GNN on a pixel grid graph, and a Transformer layer is a GNN on the complete graph of tokens. ([Wikipedia: Graph neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network))

Equivariance has been built into networks for discrete rotations and reflections of images ([Cohen and Welling 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07576)), for sets and graphs ([Zaheer et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06114); [Maron et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.09902)), for actions of general compact groups ([Kondor and Trivedi 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03690)), and, on curved manifolds, for local gauge transformations ([Cohen et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04615)). Cambridge's graduate course on the subject teaches these together, from group and representation theory and Deep Sets and PointNet through Weisfeiler–Leman expressivity to E(n)-equivariant GNNs, the SE(3)-Transformer and AlphaFold 2. ([Cambridge L65](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2324/L65/))

### Formal definition
A (left) **action** of a group $G$ on a set $X$ is a map $G\times X\to X$, $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$, with $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$. For $G$-sets $(X,\cdot_X)$ and $(Y,\cdot_Y)$, a function $f:X\to Y$ is
$$\text{$G$-invariant if } f(g\cdot_X x)=f(x),\qquad \text{$G$-equivariant if } f(g\cdot_X x)=g\cdot_Y f(x)\qquad\forall g\in G,\ x\in X.$$
An invariant function is constant on orbits. ([Sáez de Ocáriz Borde and Bronstein 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.02723))

**Group convolution.** For integrable functions $f,\psi$ on a locally compact group $G$ with left Haar measure $\lambda$,
$$(f*\psi)(x)=\int_G f(y)\,\psi(y^{-1}x)\,d\lambda(y).$$
For a fixed kernel $\psi$ this operation commutes with left translations, $L_h(f*\psi)=(L_hf)*\psi$, which is equivariance to the action of $G$ on signals by left translation; it is in general not commutative. ([Wikipedia: Convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution))

**Message passing on graphs.** For node $u$ with neighbourhood $\mathcal N_u$, node features $x_u$ and edge features $e_{uv}$, a message-passing layer computes
$$h_u=\phi\Bigl(x_u,\ \bigoplus_{v\in\mathcal N_u}\psi(x_u,x_v,e_{uv})\Bigr),$$
with $\bigoplus$ a permutation-invariant aggregator (sum, mean, max). The layer is equivariant to relabelling the nodes, and a graph-level readout must be permutation invariant. ([Wikipedia: Graph neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network))

### Key results
- **Convolution is necessary for equivariance (compact groups).** For the action of any compact group $G$, under some natural constraints convolutional structure (in a generalized, representation-theoretic sense) is required for $G$-equivariance: convolution is "not just a sufficient, but also a necessary condition for equivariance". ([Kondor and Trivedi 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03690))
- **Linear equivariant layers on graphs.** For data on $k$-tuples of nodes of an $n$-node graph (e.g. $k=2$: adjacency or edge features), the space of permutation-invariant linear maps has dimension equal to the Bell number $B_k$ and the space of permutation-equivariant linear maps $\mathbb R^{n^k}\to\mathbb R^{n^k}$ has dimension $B_{2k}$; for $k=2$ these are $2$ and $15$, independent of $n$. Networks built from these layers can approximate any message-passing network. ([Maron et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.09902))
- **Weisfeiler–Leman bound.** Message-passing GNNs are at most as powerful as the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman graph-isomorphism test at distinguishing graphs; GCN and GraphSAGE fail on some simple structures, while a simple architecture proposed by Xu et al. is provably the most expressive in this class, matching the WL test. ([Xu et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826); [Wikipedia: Graph neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network))
- **Characterization of permutation-invariant set functions.** Deep Sets proves that every permutation-invariant objective on sets belongs to a specific family whose special structure yields a network architecture for sets, and gives necessary and sufficient conditions for permutation equivariance of a layer. ([Zaheer et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06114))
- **Group equivariant CNNs.** Replacing planar convolution by convolution over a discrete group generated by translations, rotations and reflections increases weight sharing and expressive capacity without adding parameters, at negligible cost, and reached state of the art on CIFAR-10 and rotated MNIST. ([Cohen and Welling 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07576))
- **Gauge equivariance.** Equivariance can be extended from global symmetries to local gauge transformations (changes of tangent frame), giving convolutions on manifolds that depend only on intrinsic geometry; on an icosahedral approximation of the sphere this reduces to a single conv2d call. ([Cohen et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04615))

### Examples
- **Images.** Translation equivariance gives ordinary CNNs; adding rotations and reflections gives G-CNNs. ([Cohen and Welling 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07576))
- **Sets and point clouds.** Permutation-invariant models handle point-cloud classification, set expansion and outlier detection. ([Zaheer et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06114))
- **Physical systems.** Equivariant GNNs that respect rotations and translations of 3D space, such as NequIP and MACE, model interatomic potentials. ([Wikipedia: Graph neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network))
- **Sphere and climate data.** Gauge-equivariant icosahedral CNNs improved segmentation of omnidirectional images and global climate patterns. ([Cohen et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04615))

### History
Group-equivariant convolutional networks appeared in 2016 ([Cohen and Welling 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07576)); Deep Sets (2017) and invariant graph networks (2018) treated permutation symmetry ([Zaheer et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06114); [Maron et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.09902)); Kondor and Trivedi's 2018 result tied equivariance to convolution for compact groups ([Kondor and Trivedi 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03690)); gauge-equivariant CNNs followed in 2019 ([Cohen et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04615)). The 2021 text by Bronstein, Bruna, Cohen and Veličković presented the programme as a geometric unification ([Bronstein et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.13478)), and Cambridge taught it as course L65 in 2023–24 ([Cambridge L65](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2324/L65/)).

### Connections
- [Graph Neural Networks](node:Graph%20Neural%20Networks): the permutation-equivariant instance of the blueprint.
- [Equivariant Neural Networks](node:Equivariant%20Neural%20Networks): the general class of architectures GDL designs.
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory): groups and actions define the symmetries.
- [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory): equivariant linear layers are intertwiners between representations.
- [Harmonic Analysis on Locally Compact Groups](node:Harmonic%20Analysis%20on%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups): Fourier analysis behind generalized convolution.
- [Convolutional Neural Networks](node:Convolutional%20Neural%20Networks): the translation-equivariant special case on grids.
- [Transformers](node:Transformers): GNNs on complete graphs of tokens.
- [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning): GDL is a design principle for deep architectures.
- [Weisfeiler–Leman Graph Tests](node:Weisfeiler–Leman%20Graph%20Tests): the yardstick for GNN expressive power.
- [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles): the setting for gauge-equivariant convolution on manifolds.
- [Symmetry-Constrained Scientific Learning](node:Symmetry-Constrained%20Scientific%20Learning): application of equivariance to physical data.

### Common pitfalls
- **Invariant versus equivariant.** Intermediate layers should usually be equivariant, keeping track of how features transform; only the final readout should be invariant, since an invariant map collapses each orbit to a single value. ([Sáez de Ocáriz Borde and Bronstein 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.02723); [Wikipedia: Graph neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network))
- **Equivariance does not imply expressivity.** Permutation-equivariant message passing cannot separate graphs that 1-WL cannot separate. ([Xu et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826))
- **Depth problems on graphs.** Stacking message-passing layers causes oversmoothing (node features become indistinguishable) and oversquashing (long-range information squeezed into fixed-size vectors). ([Wikipedia: Graph neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network))

### Open problems
- **A balanced theory of graph learning.** Morris et al. state that the theory of expressivity is incomplete and mostly coarse-grained and combinatorial, that generalization theory is poorly aligned with practice for GNNs trained with stochastic first-order methods, and call for a theory of how expressivity, generalization and optimization interact. ([Morris et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02287))
- **Beyond message passing.** Whether future architectures will overcome the message-passing primitive is described as an open research question. ([Wikipedia: Graph neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Graph neural network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network): message passing, equivariance, WL expressivity, oversmoothing.
- **Learn:** [Cambridge L65 Geometric Deep Learning](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2324/L65/): course page (Liò, Veličković, 2023–24) with syllabus and links to materials and recordings.
- **Learn:** [Sáez de Ocáriz Borde and Bronstein, Mathematical Foundations of Geometric Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02723): 78-page review of the required mathematics.
- **Primary:** [Cohen and Welling 2016, Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07576): G-CNNs.
- **Primary:** [Kondor and Trivedi 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03690): convolution necessary for compact-group equivariance.
- **Primary:** [Maron et al. 2018, Invariant and Equivariant Graph Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.09902): Bell-number dimension of equivariant linear layers.
- **Further reading:** [Bronstein, Bruna, Cohen and Veličković, *Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.13478): the book-length text that set out the programme.
references.Gradient Descent:
## Reference
### Overview
Gradient descent is a first-order iterative method for minimizing a differentiable function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$: from a current point it moves a step of size $\eta_k$ in the direction of the negative gradient, $x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k\nabla f(x_k)$, and the step size may change from one iteration to the next. With suitable step sizes the objective values decrease monotonically. Too small a step makes progress slow, and too large a step overshoots and can diverge. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent))

The motivation is a first-order Taylor expansion, $f(x+\varepsilon)\approx f(x)+\varepsilon^\top\nabla f(x)$: choosing $\varepsilon=-\eta\nabla f(x)$ decreases $f$ to first order, and the negative gradient is the direction of steepest descent. On nonconvex functions an (unrealistically) high learning rate can lead to a poor local minimum. Second-order alternatives such as Newton's method rescale the step by the inverse Hessian. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/gd.html))

Bubeck's monograph on the complexity theory of convex optimization starts from black-box methods, including (accelerated) gradient descent, and continues to non-Euclidean methods such as mirror descent and to stochastic methods such as stochastic gradient descent. ([Bubeck, arXiv:1405.4980](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.4980)) On neural-network training objectives, full-batch gradient descent typically operates in a regime (the Edge of Stability) that is inconsistent with several common presumptions of optimization theory. ([Cohen et al., arXiv:2103.00065](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00065))

### Formal definition
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable. Gradient descent with step sizes $(\eta_k)_{k\ge0}$ from $x_0$ is the sequence
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k\nabla f(x_k),\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent))

The standard regularity classes are as follows. $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz if $\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $x,y$ (for twice-differentiable $f$, $\nabla^2 f(x)\preceq LI$). $f$ is $m$-strongly convex if $f(x)-\tfrac m2\|x\|_2^2$ is convex (for twice-differentiable $f$, $\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq mI$). The ratio $L/m$ is the condition number. For least squares $f(\beta)=\tfrac12\|y-X\beta\|_2^2$ one has $L=\lambda_{\max}(X^\top X)$ and $m=\lambda_{\min}(X^\top X)$, so a wide $X$ ($p>n$) gives $m=0$ and no strong convexity. ([Tibshirani, CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf))

A first-order method is any iteration with $x_k\in x_0+\operatorname{span}\{\nabla f(x_0),\dots,\nabla f(x_{k-1})\}$. Backtracking line search chooses $\eta_k$ adaptively by shrinking a trial step until a sufficient-decrease condition holds. ([Tibshirani, CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf))

The Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality with constant $\mu>0$ is
$$\tfrac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge\mu\,(f(x)-f^*)\quad\text{for all }x,$$
where $f^*$ is the optimal value. It implies every stationary point is a global minimizer but does not require convexity or a unique solution. ([Karimi, Nutini and Schmidt, arXiv:1608.04636](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04636))

### Key results
- **Convex, $L$-smooth: $O(1/k)$.** If $f$ is convex and differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $L$-Lipschitz gradient, gradient descent with fixed step $t\le 1/L$ satisfies $f(x_k)-f^*\le \|x_0-x^*\|_2^2/(2tk)$. The same holds for backtracking with $t$ replaced by $\beta/L$. So an $\epsilon$-suboptimal point takes $O(1/\epsilon)$ iterations. ([Tibshirani, CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf))
- **Strongly convex: linear convergence.** If in addition $f$ is $m$-strongly convex, gradient descent with fixed step $t\le 2/(m+L)$ (or backtracking) satisfies $f(x_k)-f^*\le\gamma^k\tfrac L2\|x_0-x^*\|_2^2$ for some $0<\gamma<1$, with $\gamma=O(1-m/L)$. The iteration count is $O\big((L/m)\log(1/\epsilon)\big)$, so a large condition number slows the method. ([Tibshirani, CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf))
- **Linear convergence under PL (Polyak 1963).** If $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the solution set is non-empty, and $f$ satisfies the PL inequality with constant $\mu$, then $x_{k+1}=x_k-\tfrac1L\nabla f(x_k)$ satisfies $f(x_k)-f^*\le(1-\mu/L)^k(f(x_0)-f^*)$. The PL inequality is weaker than the main conditions that have been used to prove linear convergence without strong convexity, and $f(x)=x^2+3\sin^2 x$ is a nonconvex example. ([Karimi, Nutini and Schmidt, arXiv:1608.04636](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04636))
- **Nonconvex: stationarity at rate $O(1/\sqrt k)$.** If $f$ is differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient (not necessarily convex), gradient descent with fixed step $t\le1/L$ satisfies $\min_{0\le i\le k}\|\nabla f(x_i)\|_2\le\sqrt{2(f(x_0)-f^*)/(t(k+1))}$. That is $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ iterations to an $\epsilon$-stationary point, and this rate cannot be improved by any deterministic algorithm over this function class (Carmon et al. 2017). ([Tibshirani, CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf))
- **Lower bound for first-order methods (Nesterov).** For every $k\le(n-1)/2$ and every starting point there is a convex $f$ with $L$-Lipschitz gradient such that every first-order method satisfies $f(x_k)-f^*\ge 3L\|x_0-x^*\|_2^2/(32(k+1)^2)$. Plain gradient descent's $O(1/k)$ is therefore not optimal, and Nesterov's accelerated method attains $O(1/k^2)$. ([Tibshirani, CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent))
- **Avoidance of strict saddles.** Let $f$ be $C^2$ with $L$-Lipschitz gradient and let $x^*$ be a strict saddle ($\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x^*))<0$). If $0<\alpha<1/L$, gradient descent with constant step $\alpha$ from a random initialization satisfies $\Pr(\lim_k x_k=x^*)=0$. Under the further hypotheses of their Theorem 4.8 (including that every saddle is strict), if $\lim_k x_k$ exists it is a local minimizer almost surely; the introduction summarizes this as convergence to a local minimizer or to $-\infty$ almost surely. The proof applies the Stable Manifold Theorem. ([Lee et al., arXiv:1602.04915](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04915))

### Examples
- **Quadratics and least squares.** On $f(x)=x_1^2+2x_2^2$ with $\eta=0.1$ the iterates converge to $0$, slowly, because the two coordinates have different curvatures. In one dimension on $f(x)=x^2$, $\eta=1.1$ diverges. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/gd.html)) For symmetric positive-definite linear systems the iteration count of gradient descent grows in proportion to the condition number $\kappa(A)$. Conjugate gradient depends on $\sqrt{\kappa(A)}$ instead. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent))
- **Ill-conditioning in practice.** On a log-barrier test problem, rescaling coordinates by a diagonal scaling as small as $10:1$ makes gradient descent with backtracking need more than a thousand iterations, and at $20:1$ or more the method becomes essentially useless. The iteration count grows with $\gamma$ in the same way as the Hessian's condition number, roughly $\max\{\gamma^2,1/\gamma^2\}$. ([Tibshirani, CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf))

### History
Cauchy is generally credited with the method and first suggested it in 1847. Hadamard independently proposed a similar method in 1907, and Haskell Curry first studied its convergence for nonlinear problems in 1944. Later modifications include Polyak's heavy-ball momentum and Nesterov's acceleration, which improves the error decrease from $O(k^{-1})$ to $O(k^{-2})$ on convex problems. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent)) Linear convergence under the gradient-domination (PL) inequality was proved by Polyak in 1963. ([Karimi, Nutini and Schmidt, arXiv:1608.04636](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04636))

### Connections
- [Convex Optimization](node:Convex%20Optimization): the setting of the classical rate and lower-bound theory.
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): gradients, Hessians, and the Taylor expansion behind the update.
- [Taylor's Theorem](node:Taylor's%20Theorem): the first-order expansion that justifies stepping against the gradient.
- [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent): replaces $\nabla f$ with an unbiased estimate from a sample or minibatch.
- [Newton's Method](node:Newton's%20Method): second-order counterpart that preconditions by the inverse Hessian.
- [Adaptive Optimizers](node:Adaptive%20Optimizers): per-coordinate step-size rules built on gradient steps.
- [Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent](node:Implicit%20Bias%20of%20Gradient%20Descent): which minimizer gradient descent selects in underdetermined problems.
- [Stable Manifold Theorem](node:Stable%20Manifold%20Theorem): the tool behind almost-sure avoidance of strict saddles.
- [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation): computes the gradients that gradient descent consumes in neural networks.

### Common pitfalls
- The $O(1/k)$ and linear rates need an $L$-Lipschitz gradient and a step at most $1/L$ (or $2/(m+L)$). Plain gradient descent cannot handle nondifferentiable functions, and it is slow on problems that are not strongly convex or well-conditioned. ([Tibshirani, CMU 10-725](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf))
- Linear convergence does not require convexity: the PL inequality suffices, but it does not give a unique minimizer. ([Karimi, Nutini and Schmidt, arXiv:1608.04636](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04636))
- The saddle-avoidance theorem is probabilistic over the initialization and assumes a constant step below $1/L$. The authors caution that greedy methods using precise line search may still get stuck at stationary points. ([Lee et al., arXiv:1602.04915](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04915))
- Monotone decrease of the loss is a consequence of the small-step regime. Full-batch training of neural networks often runs with the sharpness just above $2/\eta$ and a non-monotone loss. ([Cohen et al., arXiv:2103.00065](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00065))

### Open problems
- **Edge of Stability.** Full-batch gradient descent on neural networks typically drives the largest Hessian eigenvalue to hover just above $2/\eta$, where the loss is non-monotone over short horizons yet decreases in the long run. This is inconsistent with several common presumptions in optimization, and the authors present a rigorous understanding of optimization at the Edge of Stability as a goal for future work. ([Cohen et al., arXiv:2103.00065](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00065))
- **Step-size conditions for saddle avoidance.** Whether the restriction $\alpha<1/L$ is necessary for avoiding saddle points is unclear. Whether backtracking or Wolfe line search with random initialization also avoids saddles, and how to relax the assumption of isolated saddles, are left as future work. ([Lee et al., arXiv:1602.04915](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04915))
- **Implicit bias on nonlinear models.** Understanding the bias that gradient-based algorithms induce on fully nonlinear models is described as a broadly open problem. ([Hastie et al., arXiv:1903.08560](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08560))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gradient descent (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent): update rule, step-size choices, acceleration, momentum, and history.
- **Learn:** [Tibshirani, Gradient descent (CMU 10-725)](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt/lectures/grad-descent.pdf): convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex rates with proofs, plus the Nesterov lower bound.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, Gradient Descent](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/gd.html): Taylor-expansion derivation, learning-rate effects, Newton's method, and preconditioning, with code.
- **Primary:** [Karimi, Nutini and Schmidt, Linear Convergence of Gradient and Proximal-Gradient Methods Under the PL Condition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04636): the PL inequality and its relation to other linear-convergence conditions.
- **Primary:** [Lee, Simchowitz, Jordan and Recht, Gradient Descent Converges to Minimizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04915): almost-sure avoidance of strict saddles.
- **Further reading:** [Bubeck, Convex Optimization: Algorithms and Complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.4980): monograph on complexity results for gradient, accelerated, mirror, and stochastic methods.
- **Further reading:** [Nesterov, Lectures on Convex Optimization (Springer, 2018)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-91578-4): graduate text on convex optimization and the complexity of first-order methods.
references.Gram–Schmidt Process:
## Reference
### Overview
The Gram–Schmidt process takes a linearly independent list $v_1,v_2,\dots$ in an [inner product space](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces) and produces an orthogonal (after normalizing, orthonormal) list spanning the same subspaces at every stage. Each new vector is made orthogonal to the earlier ones by subtracting its projections onto them. It works for countably infinite sequences as well, and a transfinite version yields orthonormal bases of arbitrary [Hilbert spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces). ([Wikipedia: Gram–Schmidt process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process))

Applied to the columns of a matrix it computes the reduced [QR factorization](node:QR%20Factorization), the standard tool for [least squares](node:Least-Squares%20Problems). In floating point the classical algorithm can lose orthogonality badly; the modified variant and reorthogonalization repair much of this, while Householder QR is unconditionally stable. Gram–Schmidt remains the method of choice when the orthonormal basis must be built one vector (or block) at a time, as in Arnoldi and other [Krylov subspace methods](node:Krylov%20Subspace%20Methods) of [scientific computing](node:Scientific%20Computing). ([Harvard AM205 notes](https://courses.seas.harvard.edu/courses/am205/fall13/AM205_unit_2_chapter_3.pdf); [Wikipedia: Gram–Schmidt process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process); [Carson–Lund–Rozložník–Thomas](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.12058))

### Formal definition
Let $V$ have inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and let $\operatorname{proj}_u(v)=\frac{\langle v,u\rangle}{\langle u,u\rangle}u$. For linearly independent $v_1,\dots,v_k$ set
$$u_1=v_1,\qquad u_j=v_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\operatorname{proj}_{u_i}(v_j),\qquad e_j=\frac{u_j}{\|u_j\|}.$$
([Wikipedia: Gram–Schmidt process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process))

In matrix form, for $A=[a_1,\dots,a_n]\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, classical Gram–Schmidt (CGS) computes $r_{ij}=q_i^Ta_j$ for $i<j$, $v_j=a_j-\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}q_i$, $r_{jj}=\|v_j\|_2$, $q_j=v_j/r_{jj}$. Modified Gram–Schmidt (MGS) instead orthogonalizes all remaining columns against each $q_i$ as soon as it is computed, so $r_{ij}=q_i^Tv_j$ is taken against a vector from which $q_1,\dots,q_{i-1}$ have already been removed. In exact arithmetic the two are identical. ([Harvard AM205 notes](https://courses.seas.harvard.edu/courses/am205/fall13/AM205_unit_2_chapter_3.pdf))

### Key results
- **Correctness and nested spans.** For independent input, every $u_j\neq0$, the $e_j$ are orthonormal, and $\operatorname{span}(e_1,\dots,e_j)=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_j)$ for each $j$. If the input is dependent, some $u_j=0$; discarding the zero vectors gives an orthonormal basis of the span. ([Wikipedia: Gram–Schmidt process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process); [Harvard AM205 notes](https://courses.seas.harvard.edu/courses/am205/fall13/AM205_unit_2_chapter_3.pdf))
- **QR factorization.** Every full-rank $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ ($m\ge n$) has a unique reduced factorization $A=\hat Q\hat R$ with $\hat Q^T\hat Q=I_n$ and $\hat R$ upper triangular with $r_{ii}>0$; every $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$ has a full QR factorization. Gram–Schmidt (CGS or MGS) costs about $2mn^2$ flops. ([Harvard AM205 notes](https://courses.seas.harvard.edu/courses/am205/fall13/AM205_unit_2_chapter_3.pdf))
- **Orthonormal bases of Hilbert spaces.** Every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis (via Zorn's lemma and Gram–Schmidt, or transfinite recursion), and a Hilbert space is separable iff it has a countable one. Such a basis spans a dense subspace, not in general all of $H$, so in infinite dimensions it is not a Hamel basis. ([Wikipedia: Orthonormal basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthonormal_basis); [Wikipedia: Gram–Schmidt process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process))
- **Loss of orthogonality in floating point.** With unit roundoff $\varepsilon$ and $\kappa(A)$ the 2-norm condition number, the computed $\bar Q$ satisfies, up to constants polynomial in the dimensions: MGS, $\|I-\bar Q^T\bar Q\|_2=O(\varepsilon)\kappa(A)$ provided $O(\varepsilon)\kappa(A)<1$ (Björck 1967); CGS with Pythagorean computation of $r_{jj}$ (CGS-P), $O(\varepsilon)\kappa^2(A)$ provided $O(\varepsilon)\kappa^2(A)<1$ (Smoktunowicz–Barlow–Langou); plain CGS has only the bound $O(\varepsilon)\kappa^{n-1}(A)$ (Kiełbasiński). CGS with reorthogonalization (CGSI+) and MGS with reorthogonalization reach $O(\varepsilon)$ provided $O(\varepsilon)\kappa(A)<1$ (Giraud–Langou–Rozložník–van den Eshof 2005 and others), and Householder and Givens QR give $O(\varepsilon)$ with no condition. ([Carson–Lund–Rozložník–Thomas, Table 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.12058); [Björck 1967](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01934122))

### Examples
For two vectors, $q_1=a_1/\|a_1\|$ and $q_2$ is $a_2-(q_1^Ta_2)q_1$ normalized; the original vectors need not be perpendicular. ([Harvard AM205 notes](https://courses.seas.harvard.edu/courses/am205/fall13/AM205_unit_2_chapter_3.pdf))

Orthogonalizing $1,x,x^2,\dots$ on $[-1,1]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{-1}^1f(x)g(x)\,dx$ gives, up to scaling, the Legendre polynomials $P_0=1$, $P_1=x$, $P_2=\tfrac12(3x^2-1)$, $P_3=\tfrac12(5x^3-3x)$, each orthogonal to all lower-degree polynomials. With the normalization $P_n(1)=1$ they satisfy $\int_{-1}^1P_mP_n\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\delta_{mn}$, so they are orthogonal but not orthonormal. ([Wikipedia: Legendre polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_polynomials))

### History
The process is named after Jørgen Pedersen Gram and Erhard Schmidt. Schmidt gave it in his 1907 paper on integral equations and again in 1908 in the setting of infinitely many equations in infinitely many unknowns (an early Hilbert-space setting). The method predates both: it appears to go back to Laplace and was essentially used by Cauchy in 1836. ([MacTutor: Schmidt](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Schmidt/); [MacTutor: Gram](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Gram/)) Björck's 1967 paper on least squares by Gram–Schmidt is the source of the MGS bound $O(\varepsilon)\kappa(A)$. ([Björck 1967](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01934122); [Carson–Lund–Rozložník–Thomas](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.12058))

### Connections
- [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces): projections and normalization use the inner product.
- [QR Factorization](node:QR%20Factorization): Gram–Schmidt on columns is the reduced QR factorization.
- [Least-Squares Problems](node:Least-Squares%20Problems): QR solves them without squaring the condition number.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): countable and transfinite Gram–Schmidt give orthonormal bases.
- [Orthogonal Expansions and Wavelets](node:Orthogonal%20Expansions%20and%20Wavelets): orthogonal polynomial systems such as Legendre's.
- [Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers](node:Matrix%20Norms%20and%20Condition%20Numbers): $\kappa(A)$ controls the loss of orthogonality.
- [Floating-Point Error and Interval Arithmetic](node:Floating-Point%20Error%20and%20Interval%20Arithmetic): the rounding model behind the stability bounds.
- [Krylov Subspace Methods](node:Krylov%20Subspace%20Methods): Arnoldi and GMRES orthogonalize Krylov bases by (block) Gram–Schmidt.
- [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): the wider subject of stable factorizations.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): the matrix form of the construction.

### Common pitfalls
Dependent input gives a zero residual that cannot be normalized. CGS and MGS agree in exact arithmetic but not in floating point, and even MGS loses orthogonality in proportion to $\kappa(A)$; when orthogonality to working precision matters, reorthogonalize or use Householder QR. Householder is more stable, but unlike Gram–Schmidt it does not deliver the orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{span}(a_1,\dots,a_j)$ incrementally. A Cholesky-based QR is efficient but numerically unstable: its loss of orthogonality grows like $O(\varepsilon)\kappa^2(A)$. ([Harvard AM205 notes](https://courses.seas.harvard.edu/courses/am205/fall13/AM205_unit_2_chapter_3.pdf); [Wikipedia: QR decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_decomposition); [Wikipedia: Gram–Schmidt process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process); [Carson–Lund–Rozložník–Thomas, Table 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.12058))

### Open problems
- **Stability of block and low-synchronization Gram–Schmidt.** In their 2020 overview of block Gram–Schmidt methods used in communication-avoiding Krylov solvers, Carson, Lund, Rozložník and Thomas state that for many commonly used variants a rigorous treatment of stability "remains open"; several bounds in their tables are conjectures based on numerical evidence, with formal proofs left as future work. Later work has settled some cases: Carson and Ma (2024) give a provably stable one-synchronization reorthogonalized block CGS variant with $O(u)$ loss of orthogonality when $O(u)\kappa^2(X)\le1/2$ (and a two-synchronization variant needing only $O(u)\kappa(X)\le1/2$), while Carson, Lund, Ma and Oktay (2024) show that the one-synchronization variant obtained by removing synchronization points from a four-synchronization reorthogonalized BCGS cannot be guaranteed stable. ([Carson–Lund–Rozložník–Thomas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12058); [full text, §4 and Table 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.12058); [Carson–Ma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07077); [Carson–Lund–Ma–Oktay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.10109))
- **How much orthogonality GMRES can lose.** Although GMRES with MGS is backward stable despite loss of orthogonality (Paige–Rozložník–Strakoš), Carson, Lund, Rozložník and Thomas wrote in 2020 that it remains an open problem, even without blocking, to determine how far orthogonality can be lost in the orthogonalization while still obtaining a backward-stable GMRES solution. For the block setting, Carson and Ma (2024) have since analysed the backward stability of s-step GMRES with block modified and reorthogonalized block classical Gram–Schmidt, showing that s-step GMRES with the classical s-step Arnoldi process is unstable. ([Carson–Lund–Rozložník–Thomas, §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.12058); [Carson–Ma, s-step GMRES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.03079))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gram–Schmidt process (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process): definition, infinite version, stability, alternatives.
- **Learn:** [Harvard AM205, QR factorization](https://courses.seas.harvard.edu/courses/am205/fall13/AM205_unit_2_chapter_3.pdf): CGS, MGS, operation count, Householder.
- **Primary:** [Carson, Lund, Rozložník and Thomas, An overview of block Gram–Schmidt methods and their stability properties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12058): survey of known and conjectured loss-of-orthogonality bounds.
- **Primary:** [Björck, Solving linear least squares problems by Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization, BIT 7 (1967)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01934122): the original MGS error analysis.
- **Further reading:** [Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, 2nd ed. (SIAM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898718027): standard monograph on rounding-error analysis, including QR.
references.Graph Algorithms:
## Reference
### Overview
Graph algorithms solve computational problems on graphs $G=(V,E)$ with $n=|V|$ vertices and $m=|E|$ edges: exploring the graph (breadth-first and depth-first search), computing shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, and maximum flows and minimum cuts. The two traversals each run in $O(|V|+|E|)$ time and $O(|V|)$ space and differ mainly in the vertex orders they produce, which is what their applications exploit ([Wikipedia: Depth-first search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search)). A standard first course covers BFS, DFS, weighted shortest paths, Bellman–Ford, Dijkstra, and all-pairs shortest paths with Johnson's algorithm, in that order ([MIT OCW 6.006](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes/)).

These problems are old and still active. The first MST algorithm (Borůvka, 1926) predates computers, and the MST problem's exact deterministic complexity remains open ([Wikipedia: Minimum spanning tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_spanning_tree)). Maximum flow, first studied by Harris and Ross as a model of Soviet railway traffic and first solved algorithmically by Ford and Fulkerson in the mid-1950s, was solved in almost-linear time $m^{1+o(1)}$ in 2022 ([Wikipedia: Maximum flow problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_flow_problem); [Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00671)). In 2025 Duan et al. reported a deterministic directed single-source shortest-path algorithm faster than Dijkstra's $O(m+n\log n)$ on sparse graphs ([Duan et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17033)).

### Formal definition
**Shortest paths.** Given a directed graph with weights $w:E\to\mathbb R$ and source $s$, compute $d(s,v)=\min_{P:s\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}w(e)$ for every $v$ (single-source, SSSP) or for every pair (APSP); the problem is well defined when there are no negative cycles. BFS solves it for unweighted graphs by counting edges ([Wikipedia: Shortest path problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_path_problem); [Wikipedia: Breadth-first search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadth-first_search)).

**Minimum spanning tree.** For a connected undirected graph with edge weights, a spanning tree $T\subseteq E$ minimizing $\sum_{e\in T}w(e)$ ([Wikipedia: Minimum spanning tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_spanning_tree)).

**Maximum flow.** A flow network has capacities $c:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, a source $s$ and sink $t$. A flow $f$ satisfies $0\le f(e)\le c(e)$ on each edge and conservation $\sum_{(u,v)\in E}f(u,v)=\sum_{(v,w)\in E}f(v,w)$ at every $v\ne s,t$; its value is the net amount leaving $s$, and the problem is to maximize it. An $s$–$t$ cut is a partition $(S,V\setminus S)$ with $s\in S$, $t\notin S$; its capacity is the total capacity of edges from $S$ to $V\setminus S$ ([Wikipedia: Maximum flow problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_flow_problem); [Wikipedia: Max-flow min-cut theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max-flow_min-cut_theorem)).

### Key results
- **Max-flow min-cut and integrality.** In any flow network the maximum value of an $s$–$t$ flow equals the minimum capacity of an $s$–$t$ cut; if all capacities are integers, there is a maximum flow that is integral on every edge. ([Wikipedia: Maximum flow problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_flow_problem))
- **Cut and cycle properties of MSTs.** For any cut, an edge strictly lighter than every other edge crossing it belongs to every MST; an edge strictly heavier than every other edge on some cycle belongs to no MST. Borůvka, Prim and Kruskal run in $O(m\log n)$ (Prim in $O(m+n\log n)$ with suitable data structures); Karger–Klein–Tarjan is randomized linear time; Chazelle's deterministic comparison-based algorithm runs in $O(m\,\alpha(m,n))$. ([Wikipedia: Minimum spanning tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_spanning_tree))
- **Optimal MST (Pettie–Ramachandran).** There is a deterministic, comparison-based algorithm that runs on a pointer machine in time $O(T^*(m,n))$, where $T^*(m,n)$ is the number of edge-weight comparisons needed to determine the MST of any graph with $m$ edges and $n$ vertices, so it is provably optimal; its exact running time is not known, because it uses precomputed MST decision trees of unknown depth. The trivial lower bound is linear in $m$, and the best upper bound is Chazelle's $O(m\,\alpha(m,n))$. ([Pettie and Ramachandran](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall05/cos528/handouts/An%20Optimal%20Minimum.pdf); [Wikipedia: Minimum spanning tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_spanning_tree))
- **Classical shortest-path bounds.** Dijkstra with a Fibonacci heap runs in $O(m+n\log n)$ for non-negative weights; Bellman–Ford runs in $O(nm)$ and allows negative weights without negative cycles; Floyd–Warshall solves APSP in $O(n^3)$; Bernstein, Nanongkai and Wulff-Nilsen (2022) solved negative-weight SSSP with integer weights in near-linear time. ([Wikipedia: Shortest path problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_path_problem))
- **Breaking the sorting barrier for SSSP (Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu, Yin 2025).** In the comparison-addition model there is a deterministic algorithm for SSSP on directed graphs with real non-negative weights in $O(m\log^{2/3}n)$ time, improving on Dijkstra's $O(m+n\log n)$ for sparse graphs. Dijkstra remains optimal if the vertices must be output in sorted order of distance. ([Duan et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.17033v2))
- **Almost-linear max flow (Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg, Sachdeva 2022).** Exact maximum flow and [minimum-cost flow](node:Minimum-Cost%20Flow) on directed graphs with polynomially bounded integral capacities, costs and demands can be computed in $m^{1+o(1)}$ time, by a sequence of $m^{1+o(1)}$ approximate undirected minimum-ratio cycles maintained with a dynamic data structure in amortized $m^{o(1)}$ time each. ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00671))

### Examples
- **BFS applications:** shortest paths in unweighted graphs, bipartiteness testing, the Ford–Fulkerson method for maximum flow, and Cheney's copying garbage collector ([Wikipedia: Breadth-first search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadth-first_search)).
- **DFS applications:** connected and strongly connected components, [topological sorting](node:Topological%20Sorting), biconnectivity and bridges, and Hopcroft–Tarjan planarity testing (1974). DFS classifies edges as tree, back, forward or cross; in undirected graphs every edge is a tree or back edge ([Wikipedia: Depth-first search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search)).
- **Max-flow algorithms:** with integer capacities Ford–Fulkerson runs in $O(m f^*)$, where $f^*$ is the maximum flow value, since each augmenting path costs $O(m)$ and adds at least one unit ([Wikipedia: Ford–Fulkerson algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford%E2%80%93Fulkerson_algorithm)); Edmonds–Karp runs in $O(nm^2)$ using BFS augmenting paths, and Orlin's algorithm in $O(nm)$ ([Wikipedia: Maximum flow problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_flow_problem)).
- **Negative edges break Dijkstra:** a single edge of weight $-10$ can make it return a wrong distance ([Wikipedia: Dijkstra's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%27s_algorithm)).

### History
Trémaux studied a form of DFS for mazes in the 19th century ([Wikipedia: Depth-first search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search)); Zuse described BFS in his rejected 1945 Ph.D. thesis, not published until 1972, Moore reinvented it in 1959 for mazes, and Lee used it for wire routing in 1961 ([Wikipedia: Breadth-first search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadth-first_search)). Dijkstra conceived his algorithm in 1956 and published it three years later ([Wikipedia: Dijkstra's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%27s_algorithm)). MST algorithms appeared in 1926 (Borůvka) and 1930 (Jarník, rediscovered by Prim in 1957 and Dijkstra in 1959) ([Wikipedia: Minimum spanning tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_spanning_tree)). Tarjan's *Data Structures and Network Algorithms* (SIAM, 1983) consolidated the data-structure view of these problems ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9781611970265)).

### Connections
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): the objects and structural theorems (cuts, cycles, connectivity) that the algorithms exploit.
- [Data Structures](node:Data%20Structures) and [Heaps and Priority Queues](node:Heaps%20and%20Priority%20Queues): Dijkstra's and Prim's running times are determined by the heap.
- [Graph Traversal](node:Graph%20Traversal): BFS and DFS in detail.
- [Strongly Connected Components](node:Strongly%20Connected%20Components): a DFS application.
- [Shortest-Path Algorithms](node:Shortest-Path%20Algorithms) and [Dijkstra's Algorithm](node:Dijkstra's%20Algorithm): the SSSP/APSP family.
- [Minimum Spanning Trees](node:Minimum%20Spanning%20Trees): cut and cycle properties, greedy algorithms.
- [Greedy Algorithms](node:Greedy%20Algorithms): Prim, Kruskal and Dijkstra are greedy.
- [Dynamic Programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming): Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall are dynamic programs.
- [Linear Programming](node:Linear%20Programming): max-flow and min-cost flow are linear programs, and max-flow min-cut is an instance of LP duality.
- [Graph Matching](node:Graph%20Matching): bipartite matching reduces to maximum flow.

### Common pitfalls
- Running Dijkstra with negative edge weights ([Wikipedia: Dijkstra's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%27s_algorithm)).
- Calling Ford–Fulkerson polynomial: its $O(m f^*)$ bound depends on the magnitude of the flow value, and with irrational capacities it need not terminate or converge to the maximum flow ([Wikipedia: Ford–Fulkerson algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford%E2%80%93Fulkerson_algorithm)); Edmonds–Karp's BFS rule gives the strongly polynomial $O(nm^2)$ ([Wikipedia: Maximum flow problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_flow_problem)).
- Assuming DFS parallelizes like BFS: computing the lexicographic DFS order is P-complete, and as of 1997 it was unknown whether a deterministic NC algorithm computes some DFS ordering ([Wikipedia: Depth-first search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search)).
- Reading "Dijkstra is optimal" without its qualifier: it is optimal when the output must list vertices in distance order, not for computing distances alone ([Duan et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.17033v2)).

### Open problems
- **Deterministic linear-time MST.** Whether a deterministic comparison-based algorithm solves MST in linear time "remains an open question" ([Wikipedia: Minimum spanning tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_spanning_tree)); Pettie and Ramachandran state that the exact running time of their optimal algorithm is not known, and that it is still unknown whether more powerful models (random bits, or a unit-cost RAM with integer weights) are necessary to compute the MST in linear time ([Pettie and Ramachandran](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall05/cos528/handouts/An%20Optimal%20Minimum.pdf)).
- **Deterministic parallel DFS.** Whether a deterministic NC algorithm computes a DFS ordering was unknown as of 1997, while a randomized RNC algorithm exists ([Wikipedia: Depth-first search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Shortest path problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_path_problem): algorithm tables for SSSP and APSP; [Maximum flow problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_flow_problem).
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms (Spring 2020)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/): Demaine, Ku and Solomon; lectures 9–14 on BFS, DFS, Bellman–Ford, Dijkstra, Johnson.
- **Primary:** [Chen et al. 2022, Maximum Flow and Minimum-Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00671).
- **Primary:** [Duan et al. 2025, Breaking the Sorting Barrier for Directed Single-Source Shortest Paths](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17033); [Pettie and Ramachandran, An Optimal Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm (journal version, PDF)](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall05/cos528/handouts/An%20Optimal%20Minimum.pdf).
- **Further reading:** [Tarjan, Data Structures and Network Algorithms (SIAM 1983)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9781611970265): the classic monograph on graph algorithms and their data structures.
references.Graph Neural Networks:
## Reference
### Overview
A graph neural network (GNN) is a neural architecture that takes a graph, with feature vectors on its nodes and possibly its edges, and computes representations of nodes, edges, or the whole graph. Because a graph has no canonical ordering of its nodes, GNN layers are designed to be permutation equivariant: relabelling the input nodes permutes the output node representations in the same way, and graph-level outputs use a permutation-invariant readout ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)). Tasks come at three levels: graph-level (a property of a whole molecule), node-level (a label for each node), and edge-level (predicting whether or how two nodes are related) ([Distill](https://distill.pub/2021/gnn-intro/)).

The dominant design is *message passing*: each node repeatedly aggregates messages from its neighbours with a permutation-invariant operator (sum, mean, max) and updates its own state with a learned function, so after $k$ layers a node's representation depends on its $k$-hop neighbourhood ([Distill](https://distill.pub/2021/gnn-intro/)). Gilmer et al. named this the Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) framework, reformulating several existing models invariant to molecular symmetries in a single scheme and applying it to molecular property prediction ([arXiv:1704.01212](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01212)). Geometric deep learning offers a common mathematical framework, built on geometric principles in the spirit of Klein's Erlangen Program, for studying GNNs alongside CNNs, RNNs and Transformers ([arXiv:2104.13478](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.13478)).

Applications include molecules and drug design (atoms as nodes, bonds as edges), interatomic potentials for atomistic simulation and materials science (SchNet, DimeNet, NequIP, MACE), and representations of irregular particle-detector geometry in physics ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)). MeshGraphNets learn mesh-based simulators for aerodynamics, structural mechanics and cloth by passing messages over the simulation mesh, running one to two orders of magnitude faster than the simulators they were trained on ([arXiv:2010.03409](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03409)).

### Formal definition
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph with node features $\mathbf{x}_u$ and edge features $\mathbf{e}_{uv}$, and let $N_u$ be the neighbourhood of $u$. A message-passing layer computes
$$\mathbf{h}_u=\phi\Big(\mathbf{x}_u,\ \bigoplus_{v\in N_u}\psi(\mathbf{x}_u,\mathbf{x}_v,\mathbf{e}_{uv})\Big),$$
where $\psi$ (message) and $\phi$ (update) are differentiable functions and $\bigoplus$ is a permutation-invariant aggregation such as sum, mean or max ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)).

Equivalently, in the notation of Xu et al., layer $k$ computes
$$a_v^{(k)}=\mathrm{AGGREGATE}^{(k)}\big(\{\!\{h_u^{(k-1)}:u\in N(v)\}\!\}\big),\qquad h_v^{(k)}=\mathrm{COMBINE}^{(k)}\big(h_v^{(k-1)},a_v^{(k)}\big),$$
with $h_v^{(0)}=\mathbf{x}_v$, and a graph-level output $h_G=\mathrm{READOUT}(\{\!\{h_v^{(K)}:v\in G\}\!\})$ over the multiset of final node features ([arXiv:1810.00826](https://arxiv.org/html/1810.00826v3)).

The graph convolutional network (GCN) layer is the special case
$$\mathbf{H}'=\sigma\big(\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Theta}\big),$$
where $\tilde{\mathbf A}=\mathbf A+\mathbf I$ is the adjacency matrix with self-loops, $\tilde{\mathbf D}$ its degree matrix, and $\boldsymbol\Theta$ a learned weight matrix ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)). Kipf and Welling motivated it as a localized first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions; its cost scales linearly in the number of edges ([arXiv:1609.02907](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907)).

The graph isomorphism network (GIN) uses the update
$$h_v^{(k)}=\mathrm{MLP}^{(k)}\Big((1+\varepsilon^{(k)})\,h_v^{(k-1)}+\sum_{u\in N(v)}h_u^{(k-1)}\Big)$$
with a learnable or fixed scalar $\varepsilon^{(k)}$ ([arXiv:1810.00826](https://arxiv.org/html/1810.00826v3)). Graph attention networks (GAT) replace fixed aggregation weights with masked self-attention over each node's neighbours, so that different neighbours receive different importance ([arXiv:1710.10903](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10903)).

### Key results
- **Upper bound by Weisfeiler-Leman (Xu et al., Lemma 2).** Let $G_1,G_2$ be any two non-isomorphic graphs. If an aggregation-based GNN of the form above maps $G_1$ and $G_2$ to different embeddings, then the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) test also decides that $G_1$ and $G_2$ are not isomorphic. Hence message-passing GNNs are at most as powerful as 1-WL at distinguishing graphs. ([arXiv:1810.00826](https://arxiv.org/html/1810.00826v3))
- **Matching the bound (Xu et al., Theorem 3).** Let $\mathcal A$ be a GNN with sufficiently many layers. If the neighbour aggregation-and-update map acting on (node feature, multiset of neighbour features) is injective, and the graph-level readout acting on the multiset of node features is injective, then $\mathcal A$ maps any two graphs that 1-WL decides are non-isomorphic to different embeddings. ([arXiv:1810.00826](https://arxiv.org/html/1810.00826v3))
- **Sum aggregation is universal on multisets (Lemma 5, Corollary 6).** For a countable feature space $\mathcal X$, there is $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $X\mapsto\sum_{x\in X}f(x)$ is injective on bounded-size multisets $X\subset\mathcal X$, and any multiset function $g$ factors as $g(X)=\phi\big(\sum_{x\in X}f(x)\big)$; Corollary 6 extends this to pairs $(c,X)$ via $(1+\varepsilon)f(c)+\sum_{x\in X}f(x)$, which justifies GIN. Mean and max aggregators are not injective: mean captures only the proportions of a multiset and max captures neither its exact structure nor its distribution. ([arXiv:1810.00826](https://arxiv.org/html/1810.00826v3))
- **GNNs and 1-WL are equally expressive; higher-order GNNs (Morris et al.).** Message-passing GNNs have the same power as 1-WL in distinguishing non-isomorphic (sub)graphs, and therefore share its limitations; $k$-dimensional GNNs operating on higher-order structures are proposed to go beyond it. ([arXiv:1810.02244](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02244))
- **Over-squashing (Alon and Yahav).** When a task depends on long-range interactions, messages aggregated along long paths cause exponentially growing information to be squeezed into fixed-size vectors, so information from distant nodes fails to propagate; GNNs that absorb incoming edges equally, such as GCN and GIN, are more susceptible than GAT and gated GNNs, and breaking the bottleneck improved prior results without tuning or extra weights. ([arXiv:2006.05205](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05205))

### Examples
- **Molecular property prediction.** A molecule is a graph with atoms as nodes and bonds as edges ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)); MPNNs learn a message passing algorithm and aggregation procedure to compute a function of the entire input graph, used for molecular property prediction ([arXiv:1704.01212](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01212)).
- **Semi-supervised node classification.** GCNs classify nodes of citation networks from a few labelled nodes, with hidden layers encoding both local graph structure and node features ([arXiv:1609.02907](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907)).
- **Mesh simulation.** MeshGraphNets pass messages over a simulation mesh and adapt mesh resolution during the forward simulation ([arXiv:2010.03409](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03409)).
- **Global context.** A "master node" connected to every node lets distant parts of a graph exchange information without many layers ([Distill](https://distill.pub/2021/gnn-intro/)).

### History
Scarselli et al. introduced the GNN model in 2009 as a recursive approach, and Micheli proposed a contextual constructive approach ("Neural Network for Graphs: A Contextual Constructive Approach") the same year; Li et al. later introduced gated graph sequence neural networks with a GRU update ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)). Kipf and Welling's GCN (ICLR 2017) made spectral-motivated convolution scalable ([arXiv:1609.02907](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907)); Gilmer et al. unified existing models as MPNNs in 2017 ([arXiv:1704.01212](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01212)); Veličković et al. introduced graph attention networks, published at ICLR 2018 ([arXiv:1710.10903](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10903)). The expressivity theory relating GNNs to the Weisfeiler-Leman test came from Xu et al. ([arXiv:1810.00826](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826)) and Morris et al. (AAAI 2019) ([arXiv:1810.02244](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02244)).

### Connections
- [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning): GNNs are deep networks trained by gradient descent, specialised to graph inputs.
- [Transformers](node:Transformers): a Transformer layer can be considered a GNN applied to the complete graph on the tokens of a passage ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)).
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): the input domain; neighbourhoods, adjacency matrices and isomorphism drive both design and theory.
- [Geometric Deep Learning](node:Geometric%20Deep%20Learning): the symmetry-based framework in which GNNs are the permutation-equivariant case.
- [Convolutional Neural Networks](node:Convolutional%20Neural%20Networks): GCNs generalise convolution from grids to graphs.
- [Attention Mechanism](node:Attention%20Mechanism): GAT uses masked self-attention over neighbourhoods.
- [Graph Transformers](node:Graph%20Transformers): replace or augment local message passing with global attention, partly to avoid over-squashing.
- [Equivariant Neural Networks](node:Equivariant%20Neural%20Networks): E(n)-equivariant GNNs add geometric symmetry for molecules and particles.
- [Molecular Graph Generation](node:Molecular%20Graph%20Generation): generative models built on GNN encoders.
- [Neural Operators](node:Neural%20Operators): mesh- and graph-based learned simulators overlap with GNN simulators such as MeshGraphNets.
- [Weisfeiler–Leman Graph Tests](node:Weisfeiler–Leman%20Graph%20Tests): the colour-refinement test that bounds and matches the expressive power of message passing.
- [Graph Algorithms](node:Graph%20Algorithms): GNN layers resemble iterative neighbourhood algorithms such as colour refinement.

### Common pitfalls
- **Expressivity is not universal.** Standard message-passing GNNs cannot distinguish some non-isomorphic graphs, because they are bounded by 1-WL ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)); models such as GCN and GraphSAGE fail on certain simple structures ([arXiv:1810.00826](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826)).
- **Choice of aggregator matters.** Mean and max aggregation lose multiset information that sum aggregation keeps ([arXiv:1810.00826](https://arxiv.org/html/1810.00826v3)).
- **Depth does not simply help.** Oversmoothing makes node representations indistinguishable as layers are stacked, while over-squashing compresses long-range information; mitigations include skip connections, gating, jumping knowledge, and a fully adjacent final layer ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network)).

### Open problems
The ICML 2024 position paper of Morris et al. argues that GNN theory concentrates on coarse combinatorial expressivity and does not explain generalization under stochastic first-order training, and lists open directions ([arXiv:2402.02287](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02287)):
- **Fine-grained and uniform expressivity.** Move from binary isomorphism-based results to geometric measures of graph similarity, and bound the network size needed for a task independently of graph size ([arXiv:2402.02287](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.02287v4)).
- **Expressivity versus cost.** Establish formal lower bounds on the computational cost of a given expressive power ([arXiv:2402.02287](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.02287v4)).
- **Generalization and extrapolation.** Understand how expressiveness and graph structure affect generalization, and when GNNs extrapolate to larger graphs than those seen in training ([arXiv:2402.02287](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.02287v4)).
- **Optimization and depth.** Prove convergence guarantees without strong linearity assumptions, and learn to train deep GNNs so that depth gives real benefits ([arXiv:2402.02287](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.02287v4)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Graph neural network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_neural_network): message-passing definition, GCN/GAT layers, expressivity, oversmoothing and over-squashing, applications.
- **Learn:** [A Gentle Introduction to Graph Neural Networks (Distill)](https://distill.pub/2021/gnn-intro/): interactive introduction to graph representation, permutation invariance, message passing and pooling.
- **Primary:** [Xu et al., How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826): the WL upper bound and GIN.
- **Primary:** [Gilmer et al., Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01212): the MPNN framework.
- **Primary:** [Morris et al., Future Directions in the Theory of Graph Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02287): survey of open problems in expressivity, generalization and optimization.
- **Further reading:** [Hamilton, Graph Representation Learning](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-031-01588-5): monograph in the Synthesis Lectures on Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (Springer, 2020).
- **Further reading:** [Bronstein, Bruna, Cohen, Veličković, Geometric Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.13478): symmetry-based unification of GNNs with other architectures.
references.Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation:
## Reference
### Overview
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model consult a specified set of documents before it responds. It supplements training data with domain-specific or updated information and lets answers cite sources that a user can check. The term comes from Lewis et al. (2020), who combined a parametric language model with a non-parametric memory accessed by retrieval at inference time. Standard RAG converts data to embeddings in a vector store, and it can miss facts a question needs, misread context, or blend conflicting sources. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation))

Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) retrieves from a graph instead of, or as well as, a flat set of chunks. The graph may be a public knowledge graph or one constructed from proprietary sources such as text. GraphRAG uses structural information across entities to make retrieval more precise and comprehensive, and the retrieved elements can be entities, triplets, paths or subgraphs. The Peng et al. survey divides the pipeline into three stages: graph-based indexing, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-enhanced generation. ([Peng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08921))

Two kinds of system illustrate the range. *Knowledge-graph QA* systems retrieve entities, triples, paths, or subgraphs to answer factual and multi-hop questions. *Corpus sensemaking* systems, typified by Microsoft's GraphRAG, build an entity graph from documents, cluster it into communities, and summarize those communities so that "global" questions about a whole corpus can be answered. ([Peng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.08921); [Edge et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130)) For this vault the appeal is traceability: GraphRAG's indexer splits the corpus into text units that provide fine-grained references to the source text in its outputs. ([GraphRAG documentation](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/))

### Formal definition
Let $\mathcal G=(\mathcal V,\mathcal E,\mathbf A,\{x_v\},\{e_{ij}\})$ be a text-attributed graph with node set $\mathcal V$, edge set $\mathcal E$, adjacency matrix $\mathbf A$, and textual attributes $x_v$ on nodes and $e_{ij}$ on edges. For a query $q$, GraphRAG seeks
$$a^*=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A} p(a\mid q,\mathcal G),\qquad p(a\mid q,\mathcal G)=\sum_{G\subseteq\mathcal G} p_\phi(a\mid q,G)\,p_\theta(G\mid q,\mathcal G).$$
Here $p_\theta$ is a graph retriever and $p_\phi$ a generator. The sum over subgraphs is intractable, so it is approximated by one retrieved subgraph
$$G^*=\arg\max_{G\subseteq \mathcal R(\mathcal G)} \mathrm{Sim}(q,G),$$
where $\mathcal R$ prunes the candidate space. The generator then conditions on $\mathcal F(q,G^*)$, a translation of the subgraph into a form it can read, such as linearized text, triples, or GNN embeddings. ([Peng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.08921))

**Retrieval granularity.** The retrieved unit may be nodes, triplets, paths, subgraphs (for example ego graphs or prize-collecting Steiner trees), or a hybrid of these. ([Peng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.08921))

**Global (community) GraphRAG.** Index: split the corpus into text units, extract entities, relationships and claims, partition the graph hierarchically with the Leiden algorithm, and write bottom-up community reports. Query: map the question over community summaries to partial answers, then reduce them to a final answer. ([GraphRAG documentation](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/); [Edge et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130))

### Key results
- **Global sensemaking.** For global questions over datasets in the one-million-token range, community-summary GraphRAG substantially outperforms a conventional vector-RAG baseline on answer comprehensiveness and diversity. Such questions are query-focused summarization tasks, not explicit retrieval. ([Edge et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130))
- **Subgraph retrieval as PCST.** G-Retriever poses retrieval over a textual graph as a prize-collecting Steiner tree problem. The authors report that it mitigates hallucination, handles textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM's context window, scales well with graph size, and outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from several domains. They also introduce a GraphQA benchmark. ([He et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07630)) The GraphRAG survey describes it as extending the conventional PCST algorithm with edge prices. ([Peng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.08921))
- **Single-step multi-hop retrieval by graph diffusion.** HippoRAG combines LLMs, a knowledge graph and Personalized PageRank, modelled on the hippocampal indexing theory of long-term memory. On multi-hop QA it reports gains of up to 20% over prior methods. Its single-step retrieval matches or beats iterative retrieval (IRCoT) while being 10–30 times cheaper and 6–13 times faster. ([Gutiérrez et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831)) Ordinary PageRank solves $R=dMR+\frac{1-d}{N}\mathbf 1$ for a column-stochastic link matrix $M$ and damping $d\approx 0.85$. ([Wikipedia: PageRank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PageRank))
- **No uniform winner.** Under a unified protocol for preprocessing, retrieval and generation, RAG and GraphRAG show different strengths across question answering and query-focused summarization. Selection and integration strategies that combine the two give consistent performance improvements. ([Han et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11371))
