### Common pitfalls
- **Dipole radiation by analogy with electromagnetism.** The leading gravitational radiation is quadrupolar; the gravitational analogue of the electric dipole formula is the quadrupole formula. ([Hirata, Lecture XIV](https://hirata10.github.io/ph6820/lec14_gw_energy.pdf); [Barausse lectures](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2303.11713))
- **Local energy density of a wave.** There is no gauge-invariant local energy of a gravitational wave; only the averaged effective stress-energy is meaningful. ([Hirata, Lecture XIV](https://hirata10.github.io/ph6820/lec14_gw_energy.pdf); [Barausse lectures](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2303.11713))
- **Coordinate waves.** Some apparent wave solutions are gauge artifacts, as Eddington showed. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_wave))
- **Over-reading chirp masses.** The chirp mass is well measured at leading order; individual masses require higher post-Newtonian terms and are less constrained. ([Wikipedia: Chirp mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirp_mass))

### Open problems
- **Undetected source classes.** Continuous waves from rotating neutron stars and true burst sources have not yet been detected, and LIGO has not yet seen a stochastic background. ([LIGO Scientific Collaboration](https://ligo.org/gravitational-wave-science/))
- **Origin of the nHz background.** The frequency dependence of the 2023 pulsar-timing signal differs from models of merging supermassive black-hole binaries, though those cannot be ruled out as the source. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_wave))
- **Detecting memory.** The memory effect is predicted but weaker than the oscillatory signals LIGO observes; proposed routes include stacking many events and low-frequency detectors such as LISA. ([Wikipedia: Gravitational memory effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_memory_effect))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gravitational wave (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_wave): prediction, properties, sources, history and detectors.
- **Learn:** [Barausse, The physics of gravitational waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11713): graduate lecture notes deriving the quadrupole formula, post-Newtonian dynamics, chirp mass and effective stress-energy; [Hirata, lecture on wave energy and binary evolution](https://hirata10.github.io/ph6820/lec14_gw_energy.pdf); [Flanagan & Hughes, The basics of gravitational wave theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0501041).
- **Primary:** [Abbott et al., Observation of gravitational waves from a binary black hole merger (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.03837); [GWTC-4.0 catalogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18082).
- **Further reading:** [Anderson, Gauge invariant effective stress-energy tensors for gravitational waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/9609023).
references.Green's Functions:
## Reference
### Overview
A Green's function is the impulse response of an inhomogeneous linear differential operator on a domain with specified initial or boundary conditions: it solves the equation with a Dirac delta as the source, and by superposition the solution for a general source is an integral (a convolution, when the operator is translation invariant) of the source against the Green's function. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))

In the modern theory of linear PDEs the idea is usually phrased through fundamental solutions, which are distributions solving $LF = \delta$ and which, unlike Green's functions, do not address boundary conditions. Fundamental solutions also underlie the boundary element method for solving PDEs numerically. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution))

Finding the Green's function turns the study of a differential operator into the study of an integral operator: the Green's function of a boundary value problem is the kernel of the integral operator inverse to the differential operator with its homogeneous boundary conditions. ([Encyclopedia of Mathematics](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Green_function)) In physics the term is used more loosely, for example for propagators and two-point correlation functions in quantum field theory. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))

### Formal definition
Let $L$ be a linear differential operator acting on distributions on a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. A Green's function $G(x,s)$ is a solution of
$$L\,G(x,s) = \delta(x-s),$$
and then $u(x) = \int G(x,s)\,f(s)\,ds$ solves $Lu = f$ whenever the integral converges. If $L$ has constant coefficients, $G(x,s) = G(x-s)$ can be taken to be a convolution kernel. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))

For an elliptic operator $A$ of order $m$ with coefficients $a_\alpha(x)$ on a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ with homogeneous boundary conditions $B_j u = 0$, a Green's function is a $G(x,y)$ that satisfies $B_j G(x,y) = 0$ for each fixed $y \in \Omega$ and, as a generalized function, $a(x,D)\,G(x,y) = \delta(x-y)$. ([Encyclopedia of Mathematics](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Green_function))

The fundamental solution of the Laplacian on $\mathbb{R}^n$ solves $-\Delta \Phi = \delta_0$ in the sense of distributions and is
$$\Phi(x) = \begin{cases} -\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\ln|x|, & n = 2,\\[2mm] \dfrac{1}{n(n-2)\alpha(n)}\,\dfrac{1}{|x|^{n-2}}, & n \ge 3,\end{cases}$$
where $\alpha(n)$ is the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $n\alpha(n)$ is the surface area of the unit sphere. ([Stanford Math 220B notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220b/handouts/laplace.pdf))

### Key results
- **Solving Poisson's equation.** If $f \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ has compact support and $u(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Phi(x-y) f(y)\,dy$, then $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $-\Delta u = f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. ([Stanford Math 220B notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220b/handouts/laplace.pdf))
- **Power-law falloff in $n$ dimensions.** For $n > 2$ the Green's function of the Laplacian on a domain has the form $G(x,y) = -\frac{\Gamma(n/2)}{2\pi^{n/2}(n-2)}|x-y|^{2-n} + \gamma(x,y)$, and for $n = 2$ it is $\frac{1}{2\pi}\ln|x-y| + \gamma(x,y)$, where $\gamma$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and chosen to enforce the boundary condition. ([Encyclopedia of Mathematics](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Green_function))
- **Singularity estimate.** For an elliptic operator of order $m$ with smooth coefficients and normal boundary conditions ensuring uniqueness, a Green's function exists and satisfies $|G(x,y)| \le C|x-y|^{m-n}$ if $m < n$, $|G(x,y)| \le C + C\,\bigl|\ln|x-y|\bigr|$ if $m = n$, and is uniformly bounded if $m > n$. ([Encyclopedia of Mathematics](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Green_function))
- **ODE boundary value problems.** For an $n$th-order ordinary differential operator on $[a,b]$ whose homogeneous problem $Ly = 0$ has only the trivial solution, there is exactly one Green's function, and for every continuous $f$ the solution of $Ly = f$ is $y(x) = \int_a^b G(x,\xi) f(\xi)\,d\xi$; the $(n-1)$th derivative of $G$ jumps by $1/p_n(\xi)$ at $x = \xi$. If $L$ is self-adjoint, $G(x,\xi) = \overline{G(\xi,x)}$. ([Encyclopedia of Mathematics](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Green_function))
- **Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem.** Every non-zero linear differential operator with constant coefficients has a fundamental solution (a distributional solution of $P(\partial)u = \delta$); consequently $P(\partial)u = f$ is solvable for every compactly supported distribution $f$, though not uniquely in general. It was proved independently by Ehrenpreis (1954, 1955) and Malgrange (1955–1956). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem))
- **Eigenfunction expansion.** If $L$ has a complete set of eigenfunctions $\Psi_n$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_n$, then $G(x,x') = \sum_n \Psi_n^\dagger(x')\Psi_n(x)/\lambda_n$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))
- **Representation formula.** Green's second identity gives $\varphi(x) = -\int_V G(x,x')\rho(x')\,d^3x' + \int_S \bigl[\varphi\,\nabla' G - G\,\nabla'\varphi\bigr]\cdot d\hat\sigma'$ for $\nabla^2\varphi = -\rho$ with $\nabla^2 G = \delta$, so a Dirichlet Green's function (vanishing on $S$) leaves only one surface term. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))

### Examples
- **3D Laplacian.** With no boundary conditions, $G(x,x') = -\frac{1}{4\pi|x-x'|}$ for $\nabla^2 G = \delta$. Combined with Poisson's equation $\nabla^2\varphi = -\rho$, this gives $\varphi(x) = \int \frac{\rho(x')}{4\pi|x-x'|}\,d^3x'$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))
- **Screened Poisson (Yukawa).** For $[-\Delta + k^2]\Phi = \delta$ the fundamental solution is $\frac{1}{2\pi}K_0(k|x-x'|)$ in 2D and $\frac{e^{-k|x-x'|}}{4\pi|x-x'|}$ in 3D. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution))
- **Retarded wave and heat kernels.** The retarded Green's function of the 3D d'Alembertian is $\frac{1}{4\pi r}\delta(t - r/c)$, and that of $\partial_t - k\nabla^2$ in 3D is $\left(\frac{1}{4\pi k t}\right)^{3/2}\Theta(t)\,e^{-r^2/4kt}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))
- **One dimension.** For $L = d^2/dx^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $F(x) = \tfrac12|x|$ is a fundamental solution. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution))

### History
Green's functions are named after George Green, who first studied a special case in his 1828 work on potential theory. ([Encyclopedia of Mathematics](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Green_function)) Green, a self-taught miller from Nottingham, published *An Essay on the Application of Mathematical Analysis to the Theories of Electricity and Magnetism* by subscription in March 1828; the Essay introduced the term "potential", the surface-volume integral formula now called Green's theorem, and what became Green's function. Its importance went unnoticed until William Thomson, who had seen it cited, was given copies by his coach William Hopkins in 1845 and later arranged its republication (1850–54). ([MacTutor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Green/)) The Essay was reprinted in three parts in *Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik* (1850, 1852, 1854). ([arXiv transcription](https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.0088))

Fundamental solutions of the Laplacian were long used in two and three dimensions and were investigated in all dimensions by Marcel Riesz. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution))

### Connections
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): the fundamental solution $\Phi$ is exactly what makes $u = \Phi * f$ solve Poisson's equation.
- [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29): $\delta$ and $G$ only make sense as distributions; $-\Delta\Phi = \delta_0$ is a distributional identity.
- [Gauss's Law in n Dimensions](node:Gauss's%20Law%20in%20n%20Dimensions): the $r^{2-n}$ potential and the $r^{1-n}$ force follow from spreading flux over an $(n-1)$-sphere.
- [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere): the normalization constant is the surface area of the unit $(n-1)$-sphere.
- [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions): the dimension dependence of the Laplacian's Green's function is the reason gravity would be modified at short range.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): for constant-coefficient operators, $G$ is found by inverting a polynomial symbol in Fourier space.
- [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory): the eigenfunction expansion of $G$ is the resolvent kernel.
- [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics): the Coulomb potential is the Green's function of the 3D Laplacian.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): propagators are Green's functions of wave operators.
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): Green's functions are a main tool for linear boundary value problems.

### Common pitfalls
- **Sign conventions differ.** Mathematicians often use $-\Delta\Phi = \delta$ (so $\Phi > 0$ in 3D), while many physics sources use $LG = \delta$ with $L = \nabla^2$, giving $G = -1/(4\pi r)$. ([Stanford Math 220B notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220b/handouts/laplace.pdf)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))
- **Non-uniqueness.** If the homogeneous equation has non-trivial solutions, adding any of them to a Green's function gives another one; boundary conditions, symmetry, or causality (retarded versus advanced) pick one out. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))
- **Neumann problems.** One cannot demand $\partial_n G = 0$ on the whole boundary, because Gauss's theorem forces the normal derivative of $G$ to integrate to 1 over the surface; the simplest choice is the constant $1/S$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function))
- **Convergence of the convolution.** $F * g$ can diverge pointwise even when the equation has a nice solution: with $F = \tfrac12|x|$ and $g = \sin x$ the integral diverges, although it agrees with $-\sin x$ as a distribution. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution))
- **The case $n = 2$ is logarithmic.** The power law $r^{2-n}$ degenerates at $n = 2$, where the fundamental solution is $-\frac{1}{2\pi}\ln r$. ([Stanford Math 220B notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220b/handouts/laplace.pdf))

### Open problems
No major open problems are specific to this topic. The existence question is settled for constant-coefficient operators by the Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem, and the analogous statement for polynomial coefficients is known to be false (Lewy's example). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Green function (Encyclopedia of Mathematics)](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Green_function): ODE, elliptic, and parabolic Green's functions, estimates, and the Laplacian in $n$ dimensions.
- **Reference:** [Green's function (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_function): definitions, eigenfunction expansions, and a large table of Green's functions.
- **Learn:** [Stanford Math 220B: Laplace's equation](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220b/handouts/laplace.pdf): derivation of the fundamental solution in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and a full proof that $-\Delta\Phi = \delta_0$.
- **Primary:** [G. Green, An Essay on the Application of Mathematical Analysis to the Theories of Electricity and Magnetism (1828), arXiv transcription](https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.0088): the original Essay.
references.Group Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Group theory studies sets with an associative operation that has an identity and inverses. Groups arise as symmetries of objects, as permutations of roots of equations, as arithmetic structures such as the integers under addition, and as Lie groups; the abstract definition unifies these settings. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29))

The basic toolkit consists of subgroups, cosets, normal subgroups, quotients and homomorphisms, together with group actions, which let a group be studied through the sets it permutes. On this foundation rest the structure theory of finite groups (Sylow theory, composition series and the classification of finite simple groups) and the classification of finitely generated abelian groups. ([Wikipedia, Group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action); [Wikipedia, Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups))

The subject remains active: the Kourovka Notebook, published every two to four years since 1965, collects unsolved problems in group theory proposed by mathematicians worldwide, and its 21st edition adds 150 new problems. ([Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300))

### Formal definition
A **group** is a set $G$ with a binary operation $(a,b)\mapsto ab$ that is associative, has an identity element $e$, and gives each $g$ an inverse $g^{-1}$ with $gg^{-1}=g^{-1}g=e$. A group is **abelian** if in addition $ab=ba$ for all $a,b$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29))

A **homomorphism** $\varphi:G\to H$ satisfies $\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$. Coset multiplication $(aN)(bN)=abN$ is well defined exactly when the subgroup $N$ is normal, and then makes $G/N$ a group. ([Wikipedia, Quotient group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_group))

A **(left) action** of $G$ on a set $X$ is a map $G\times X\to X$, $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$, with $e\cdot x=x$ and $g\cdot(h\cdot x)=(gh)\cdot x$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $G\cdot x$ and its **stabilizer** is the subgroup $G_x=\{g:g\cdot x=x\}$. ([Wikipedia, Group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action))

### Key results
- **[Lagrange's Theorem](node:Lagrange's%20Theorem).** For a subgroup $H\le G$, $|H|\,[G:H]=|G|$; in particular, if $G$ is finite, $|H|$ divides $|G|$. ([MIT 18.703, Thm. 3.11](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-703-modern-algebra-spring-2013/df580757da0149c376f1fda29bf82a91_MIT18_703S13_pra_l_3.pdf))
- **[First Isomorphism Theorem](node:First%20Isomorphism%20Theorem).** If $\varphi:G\to G'$ is a surjective homomorphism with kernel $H$, then $G'\cong G/H$; applied to the image, any homomorphism gives $G/\ker\varphi\cong\operatorname{im}\varphi$. ([MIT 18.703, Thm. 10.1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-703-modern-algebra-spring-2013/b40d60898322bbd1d63410b0a925946a_MIT18_703S13_pra_l_10.pdf); [Wikipedia, Quotient group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_group))
- **Orbit–stabilizer theorem.** For an action of $G$ on $X$ and $x\in X$, $gG_x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is a bijection $G/G_x\to G\cdot x$, so $|G\cdot x|=[G:G_x]$; for finite $G$, $|G\cdot x|\,|G_x|=|G|$. **Burnside's lemma:** for finite $G$ and $X$, the number of orbits is $\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|X^g|$, where $X^g$ is the set of points fixed by $g$. ([Wikipedia, Group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action))
- **Cayley's theorem.** Left multiplication is a free transitive action of $G$ on itself, so every group embeds in a symmetric group. ([Wikipedia, Group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action))
- **Sylow theorems.** Let $G$ be finite with $|G|=p^nm$, $p$ prime, $p\nmid m$. (1) $G$ has a subgroup of order $p^n$ (a Sylow $p$-subgroup). (2) All Sylow $p$-subgroups are conjugate. (3) Their number $n_p$ satisfies $n_p\mid m$, $n_p\equiv1\pmod p$, and $n_p=[G:N_G(P)]$ for any Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$. ([Wikipedia, Sylow theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylow_theorems))
- **Jordan–Hölder theorem.** A composition series is a finite subnormal series whose successive quotients are simple. Any two composition series of a group have the same length and the same composition factors up to permutation and isomorphism. Every finite group has one; not every infinite group does ($\mathbb Z$ has none). ([Wikipedia, Composition series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_series))
- **Classification of finite simple groups.** Every finite simple group is isomorphic to a cyclic group of prime order, an alternating group of degree at least $5$, a member of one of 16 further infinite families of groups of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups (27 if the Tits group is counted as sporadic). ([Wikipedia, Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups))
- **Finitely generated abelian groups.** Every finitely generated abelian group is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^n\oplus\mathbb Z/q_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb Z/q_t$ with each $q_i$ a prime power, equivalently to $\mathbb Z^n\oplus\mathbb Z/k_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb Z/k_u$ with $k_1\mid k_2\mid\cdots\mid k_u$. The rank $n$ and the prime powers (up to order), or equivalently the invariant factors, are uniquely determined by the group. ([Wikipedia, Finitely generated abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_abelian_group))

### Examples
The integers form an abelian group under addition, with identity $0$ and inverse $-a$; the dihedral group $D_4$ of symmetries of a square is a finite nonabelian example. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29)) By the classification of finitely generated abelian groups, $\mathbb Z/6\cong\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/3$, because by the [Chinese Remainder Theorem](node:Chinese%20Remainder%20Theorem) $\mathbb Z/jk\cong\mathbb Z/j\oplus\mathbb Z/k$ exactly when $j$ and $k$ are coprime. ([Wikipedia, Finitely generated abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_abelian_group))

### History
Galois introduced the term "group" in the 1830s for the symmetry group of the roots of an equation; Cayley gave the first abstract definition of a finite group in 1854; Jordan's *Traité des substitutions et des équations algébriques* (1870) helped unify the strands; Klein's 1872 Erlangen program organized geometries by symmetry groups; and Lie founded the theory of Lie groups in 1884. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29)) Sylow published his theorems in 1872 in *Mathematische Annalen*. ([Wikipedia, Sylow theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylow_theorems)) Kronecker proved the finite abelian case of the structure theorem in 1870, and Frobenius and Stickelberger stated and proved it in group-theoretic language in 1878. ([Wikipedia, Finitely generated abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_abelian_group)) Gorenstein announced the classification of finite simple groups in 1983, prematurely because of a gap in the quasithin case; Aschbacher announced the completed proof in 2004 after Aschbacher and Smith's 1,221-page treatment of that case. The proof spans tens of thousands of pages, and a second-generation proof by Gorenstein, Lyons and Solomon is still being published. ([Wikipedia, Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups))

### Connections
- [Functions and Relations](node:Functions%20and%20Relations): operations, homomorphisms and actions are functions with extra conditions.
- [Quotient Groups](node:Quotient%20Groups): the quotient construction and isomorphism theorems.
- [Abelian Groups](node:Abelian%20Groups): the commutative case and its structure theory.
- [Sylow Theorems](node:Sylow%20Theorems): the existence and conjugacy theory of maximal $p$-subgroups.
- [Permutation Groups](node:Permutation%20Groups): groups acting on sets; Cayley's theorem realizes every group this way.
- [Finite Simple Groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups): the building blocks given by Jordan–Hölder and the classification.
- [Solvable Groups](node:Solvable%20Groups): for finite groups, exactly those whose composition factors are cyclic of prime order.
- [Group Presentations](node:Group%20Presentations): groups given by generators and relations, the setting of the Burnside problem.
- [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory): studies groups through linear actions on [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces).
- [Geometric Group Theory](node:Geometric%20Group%20Theory): studies finitely generated groups through actions on [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces).
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): groups with a compatible smooth-manifold structure.
- [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory): Galois groups of field extensions; the inverse Galois problem.

### Common pitfalls
- [Lagrange's Theorem](node:Lagrange's%20Theorem) gives a necessary condition only: a divisor of $|G|$ need not be the order of a subgroup. Sylow's first theorem guarantees a subgroup whose order is the full prime-power part $p^n$ of $|G|$ (and, via Cauchy's theorem, elements of order $p$ for each prime $p\mid|G|$). ([Wikipedia, Sylow theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylow_theorems))
- Cosets exist for every subgroup, but the left cosets of $H$ form a group only when $H$ is normal. ([Wikipedia, Quotient group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_group))
- Jordan–Hölder concerns groups that have a composition series; infinite groups such as $\mathbb Z$ may have none. ([Wikipedia, Composition series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_series))
- The same composition factors do not determine the group: $\mathbb Z/4$ and $\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/2$ both have factors $\mathbb Z/2,\mathbb Z/2$ but are not isomorphic, as their invariant factors ($4$ versus $2\mid2$) differ. ([Wikipedia, Finitely generated abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_abelian_group))

### Open problems
- **Burnside problem for $B(2,5)$.** The free Burnside group $B(m,n)$ is finite for exponents $n=2,3,4,6$, while Novikov and Adian showed it is infinite for odd $n>4381$ (later odd $n>665$), and Ivanov and Lysënok treated large even exponents. Whether $B(2,5)$ is finite remains open. ([Wikipedia, Burnside problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_problem)) Kourovka Problem 11.48 (Kostrikin) asks whether $[x,y,y,y,y,y,y]$ is a product of fifth powers in the free group $\langle x,y\rangle$; a negative answer would show that $B(2,5)$ is infinite. ([Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300))
- **Inverse Galois problem.** Whether every finite group is the Galois group of a Galois extension of $\mathbb Q$ is unsolved. Hilbert realized all symmetric and alternating groups, and Shafarevich realized all finite solvable groups. ([Wikipedia, Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem))
- **The Kourovka Notebook** is the standard collection of unsolved problems across group theory, in which problems with AI-proposed solutions not yet confirmed by mathematicians are marked and treated as unsolved. ([Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Group (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29): definitions, examples and history; see also [Group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action) and [Classification of finite simple groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups).
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.703 Modern Algebra lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-703-modern-algebra-spring-2013/df580757da0149c376f1fda29bf82a91_MIT18_703S13_pra_l_3.pdf): cosets and Lagrange; [Lecture 10](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-703-modern-algebra-spring-2013/b40d60898322bbd1d63410b0a925946a_MIT18_703S13_pra_l_10.pdf): isomorphism theorems.
- **Primary:** [Khukhro and Mazurov, Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300): the running research problem list of the field.
- **Further reading:** [Rotman, An Introduction to the Theory of Groups (Springer GTM, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4176-8): standard graduate text.
references.Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems:
## Reference
### Overview
Gödel's incompleteness theorems limit what an effectively axiomatized theory can derive about arithmetic and about its own proofs. The first theorem says, roughly, that any consistent formal system in which a certain amount of elementary arithmetic can be carried out is incomplete; the second says that such a system, with a little more arithmetic, cannot prove its own consistency statement. Both are statements about derivability in a specified theory: an undecidable sentence of $T$ may well be provable in a stronger theory, for instance $T$ plus its Gödel sentence, which in turn has its own Gödel sentence. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_incompleteness_theorems))

The proofs rest on arithmetization of syntax. Formulas and proofs receive Gödel numbers, provability in $T$ becomes a $\Sigma_1$ formula $\operatorname{Pr}_T(x)$, and the diagonal lemma produces sentences that are provably equivalent to statements about their own codes. The first theorem extends beyond arithmetic to any theory, such as ZFC, that defines the natural numbers and interprets Robinson arithmetic $\mathsf Q$. ([Freund, lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))

The theorems are usually read as blocking Hilbert's aim of a finitary consistency proof for abstract mathematics, although the extent of that conclusion is debated. They also opened the study of relative strength of theories through consistency statements, ordinal analysis, and natural independence results such as the Paris–Harrington theorem and Goodstein's theorem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_incompleteness_theorems); [Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2))

### Formal definition
Write $T\vdash\varphi$ when $\varphi$ has a formal derivation from $T$. $T$ is *consistent* if it proves no sentence together with its negation, and *complete* if it proves $\varphi$ or $\neg\varphi$ for every sentence $\varphi$. The standard hypotheses are that $T\supseteq\mathsf Q$ is a theory of first-order arithmetic whose set of axiom codes $\{\ulcorner\theta\urcorner:\theta\in T\}$ is $\Sigma$-definable (equivalently, $T$ is computably axiomatized). ([Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))

For such $T$ there is a $\Sigma$-formula $\operatorname{Pr}_T(x)$ of the form $\exists p\,\operatorname{Prf}_T(p,x)$, with $\operatorname{Prf}_T$ bounded, such that $T\vdash\varphi$ if and only if $\mathbb N\models\operatorname{Pr}_T(\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner)$. The consistency statement is $\operatorname{Con}(T):\equiv\neg\operatorname{Pr}_T(\ulcorner 0=S0\urcorner)$. ([Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2))

The **Hilbert–Bernays–Löb derivability conditions** for $T$ and $\operatorname{Pr}_T$, with $\Box\varphi$ abbreviating $\operatorname{Pr}_T(\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner)$, are ([Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Bernays_provability_conditions)):
$$
\text{(D1) } T\vdash\varphi\ \Rightarrow\ T\vdash\Box\varphi,\qquad
\text{(D2) } T\vdash\Box\varphi\to\Box\Box\varphi,\qquad
\text{(D3) } T\vdash\Box(\varphi\to\psi)\to(\Box\varphi\to\Box\psi).
$$
(D1) follows from $\Sigma$-completeness; (D3) holds for standard arithmetizations; (D2) is a formalized $\Sigma$-completeness, which can be verified in $\mathsf{I\Sigma_1}$ or PA with considerable technical work. Löb (1955) gave these conditions; Hilbert and Bernays (1939) had given the first detailed proof of the second theorem, for PA, with more awkward conditions. ([Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))

### Key results
- **Diagonal (fixed-point) lemma.** For every formula $\varphi(x)$ with no other free variables there is a sentence $\psi$ with $\mathsf Q\vdash\psi\leftrightarrow\varphi(\ulcorner\psi\urcorner)$. The equivalence is material; $\psi$ does not literally "say" $\varphi$ of itself. ([Freund, Prop. 3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **First incompleteness theorem (Gödel–Rosser).** If $T\supseteq\mathsf Q$ is consistent and its axioms are $\Sigma$-definable, there is a $\Pi_1$ sentence $\psi$ with $T\nvdash\psi$ and $T\nvdash\neg\psi$. Gödel's 1931 proof used $\omega$-consistency (or $\Sigma$-soundness) to refute $\neg\psi$; Rosser (1936) reduced the hypothesis to plain consistency using the sentence "for any proof of me there is a shorter proof of my negation". Since every consistent $T\supseteq\mathsf Q$ is $\Pi_1$-sound, the Gödel sentence is true in $\mathbb N$. ([Freund, Thm. 3.3.9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Tarski's undefinability of truth (1933).** If the interpreted language has negation and a Gödel numbering satisfying the diagonal lemma, no formula $\mathrm{True}(x)$ satisfies $\mathrm{True}(\ulcorner A\urcorner)\leftrightarrow A$ for all sentences $A$; apply the diagonal lemma to $\neg\mathrm{True}(x)$. Gödel found the result independently in 1930. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarski%27s_undefinability_theorem); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Löb's theorem (1955).** If $T\supseteq\mathsf Q$ and $\operatorname{Pr}_T$ satisfy (D1)–(D3), then $T\vdash\operatorname{Pr}_T(\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner)\to\varphi$ implies $T\vdash\varphi$, for every sentence $\varphi$. In provability logic this is the axiom $\Box(\Box P\to P)\to\Box P$ of the logic GL. It answered Henkin's question about sentences asserting their own provability. ([Freund, Thm. 3.3.10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%B6b%27s_theorem); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Second incompleteness theorem.** Under the same hypotheses, if $T$ is consistent then $T\nvdash\operatorname{Con}(T)$; this is Löb's theorem with $\varphi$ taken to be $0=S0$. SEP reports that Jeroslow (1973) showed the second theorem can be proved without the distribution condition $\Box(\varphi\to\psi)\wedge\Box\varphi\to\Box\psi$ (Freund's proof of Löb's theorem uses it twice). Under (D1)–(D3) the Gödel sentence is $T$-provably equivalent to $\operatorname{Con}(T)$. ([Freund, Cor. 3.3.11 and Ex. 3.3.12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Intensionality of $\operatorname{Con}(T)$.** The second theorem depends on how provability is expressed. For Rosser provability $\operatorname{Pr}^R_{\mathsf Q}$ one has $\mathsf Q\vdash\neg\operatorname{Pr}^R_{\mathsf Q}(\ulcorner 0=S0\urcorner)$, and (D2) can be expected to fail for it. Feferman (1960) proved a version for consistent extensions of PA whose axioms are weakly represented by a $\Sigma_1$ formula and regarded the first theorem as extensional and the second as intensional. ([Freund, Ex. 3.3.12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Strength of the base theory.** Standard proofs of the second theorem need at least PRA; a version for $\mathsf Q$ was given by Bezboruah and Shepherdson (1976), though whether its formula really expresses consistency is debated. Willard (2001) studied consistent arithmetics that prove their own consistency because they lack multiplication as a total function. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_incompleteness_theorems))
- **Comparing theories.** Equivalently, no consistent theory of this kind proves the consistency of a stronger one: $\mathsf{I\Sigma_1}\nvdash\operatorname{Con}(\mathrm{PA})$, while $\mathrm{PA}\vdash\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{I\Sigma_1})$. Gentzen proved $\operatorname{Con}(\mathrm{PA})$ using transfinite induction up to $\varepsilon_0$, which therefore is not provable in PA. ([Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Natural independence results.** The strengthened finite Ramsey theorem (for all positive integers $n,k,m$ with $m\ge n$ there is $N$ such that every $k$-colouring of the $n$-subsets of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ has a homogeneous set $Y$ with $|Y|\ge m$ and $|Y|\ge\min Y$) is true but unprovable in PA (Paris–Harrington 1977), since PA proves that it implies $\operatorname{Con}(\mathrm{PA})$. Goodstein's theorem (1944), that every Goodstein sequence in hereditary base notation reaches $0$, is unprovable in PA (Kirby–Paris 1982), as is termination of the Kirby–Paris hydra game. ([Wikipedia: Paris–Harrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Harrington_theorem); [Wikipedia: Goodstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodstein%27s_theorem); [Kirby & Paris, Bull. LMS 14 (1982)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/blms/14.4.285))
- **A lower-level example.** Termination of *non-hereditary* Goodstein sequences is provable in PA but not in $\mathsf{I\Sigma_1}$: the function measuring their length dominates every primitive recursive function, while $\mathsf{I\Sigma_1}$-provably total functions are primitive recursive. ([Freund, Thm. 4.2.22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2))

### Examples
- **PA.** If PA is consistent, $\mathrm{PA}\nvdash\operatorname{Con}(\mathrm{PA})$, yet Gentzen's argument proves $\operatorname{Con}(\mathrm{PA})$ in a theory with extra transfinite induction; the second theorem limits internal consistency proofs, not external ones. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **ZFC.** The theorems apply to ZFC because it defines $\mathbb N$ and interprets $\mathsf Q$. Hilbert's hope that PA would prove $\operatorname{Con}(\mathrm{ZFC})$, which via (D1)–(D3) would make every $\Pi_1$ theorem of ZFC provable in PA, is therefore unattainable. ([Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2))
- **A Goodstein step.** Freund's non-hereditary sequence starting at $42=2^5+2^3+2^1$ continues $272, 1089, 3250, 7991, 17091,\dots$ before eventually reaching $0$. ([Freund, Def. 4.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2))

### History
Gödel announced the first theorem at Königsberg on 7 September 1930; von Neumann wrote to him about the second theorem on 20 November 1930; the paper "On formally undecidable propositions of Principia Mathematica and related systems I" appeared in January 1931. Rosser's strengthening followed in 1936, Hilbert–Bernays's detailed proof of the second theorem in 1939, and Löb's theorem in 1955. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_incompleteness_theorems)) Mathematically natural independent statements came later: Paris–Harrington in 1977 and Kirby–Paris on Goodstein sequences in 1982. ([Wikipedia: Paris–Harrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Harrington_theorem); [Kirby & Paris](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/blms/14.4.285))

### Connections
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): the completeness theorem for the calculus contrasts with incompleteness of particular theories.
- [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory): supplies effective axiomatizability, representability of computable functions, and undecidability of $\mathsf Q$.
- [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines): the halting problem gives an alternative computability-theoretic route to incompleteness.
- [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory): undecidable sentences correspond to nonstandard models in which they fail.
- [Proof Theory](node:Proof%20Theory): ordinal analysis and provably total functions measure the strength the second theorem compares.
- [Ramsey Theory](node:Ramsey%20Theory): the Paris–Harrington variant of finite Ramsey is a natural PA-independent statement.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): ZFC is subject to both theorems; set-theoretic independence (CH) uses different, forcing-based methods.
- [MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics): the MSC home of incompleteness and fragments of arithmetic.

### Common pitfalls
- **Consistency versus soundness.** Gödel's original argument for unprovability of $\neg\psi$ needs $\omega$-consistency; Rosser's sentence removes this and works under plain consistency. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/); [Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2))
- **"True but unprovable" is relative.** The Gödel sentence is unprovable in $T$, not absolutely; its truth is established in a metatheory, and it is false in some nonstandard models of $T$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_incompleteness_theorems))
- **Which $\operatorname{Con}(T)$.** The second theorem concerns provability predicates meeting (D1)–(D3); a Rosser-style predicate yields a provable "consistency" sentence. ([Freund](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.09921v2); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Adding axioms does not help.** Every consistent axiomatizable extension of an incomplete theory of this kind is again incomplete, so incompleteness is essential rather than a defect of a particular axiom list. If the Gödel sentence $G_T$ is independent, $T$ has models of both $G_T$ and $\neg G_T$; the latter contain nonstandard elements coding a "proof" of $G_T$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))

### Open problems
The theorems themselves are settled. An active direction is finite or feasible incompleteness: Pudlák proposes conjectures, going beyond $\mathrm P\neq\mathrm{coNP}$, that link high computational complexity of a problem to unprovability or long proofs of corresponding sentences in weak theories, and proves new connections between them. ([Pudlák, Incompleteness in the finite domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01487)) Whether the $\mathsf Q$-version of the second theorem genuinely expresses consistency, and how natural independent statements are, remain debated rather than settled. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/): hypotheses, derivability conditions, Löb, Tarski, independence results, and interpretations.
- **Learn:** [Freund, An Introduction to Mathematical Logic (arXiv:2310.09921)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.09921): full proofs of the diagonal lemma, Gödel–Rosser, Löb, the second theorem, and Goodstein independence for $\mathsf{I\Sigma_1}$.
- **Primary:** [Kirby & Paris, "Accessible independence results for Peano arithmetic", Bull. LMS 14 (1982) 285–293](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/blms/14.4.285): Goodstein and hydra independence.
- **Primary:** [Smith, An Introduction to Gödel's Theorems, 2nd ed., CUP 2013](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-godels-theorems/D9B794ACDDB00EB0EF32A7D653053E23): monograph with several proofs of the first theorem, the diagonalization lemma, Rosser's proof, and the second theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Hájek & Pudlák, Metamathematics of First-Order Arithmetic, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/metamathematics-of-firstorder-arithmetic/E72D370D90F316D86CB9D0927377A1A3): fragments of PA, self-reference and incompleteness, bounded arithmetic.
references.Hamiltonian Mechanics:
## Reference
### Overview
Hamiltonian mechanics reformulates classical dynamics on phase space, the space of generalized coordinates $q_i$ and conjugate momenta $p_i$. The Hamiltonian $H(q,p,t)$ is obtained from the Lagrangian by a Legendre transform, and the second-order [Euler–Lagrange equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations) become $2n$ first-order equations. In canonical coordinates the phase space carries the symplectic form $\omega=\sum_i dp_i\wedge dq_i$, and the dynamics is the flow of the vector field determined by $dH$. ([Wikipedia: Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics))

The formulation matters because its structure (Poisson brackets, canonical transformations, phase-space volume) is what carries over to statistical mechanics, through Liouville's theorem, and to quantum mechanics, where the classical limit ($\hbar\to0$) of the Schrödinger equation becomes a form of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation. ([Wikipedia: Canonical transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_transformation); [Wikipedia: Hamilton–Jacobi equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton%E2%80%93Jacobi_equation))

It is also the natural setting for the qualitative theory of motion: integrable systems move linearly on invariant tori, KAM theory says many of these tori survive small perturbations, deformed, and with more than two degrees of freedom the surviving tori no longer separate phase space, so small perturbations can accumulate to large drifts in the actions (Arnold diffusion). ([Wikipedia: Integrable system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrable_system); [Wikipedia: KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem); [Wikipedia: Arnold diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_diffusion))

### Formal definition
Given a Lagrangian $L(q,\dot q,t)$, set $p_i=\partial L/\partial\dot q_i$. Assuming this can be inverted for the velocities (local invertibility of $\partial_2L$; explicit for quadratic Lagrangians), define
$$H(q,p,t)=\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L.$$
([Sussman and Wisdom, SICM ch. 3](https://mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/9579/sicm_edition_2.zip/chapter003.html)) Hamilton's equations are
$$\dot q_i=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i},\qquad \dot p_i=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i},\qquad \frac{\partial H}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}.$$
The Poisson bracket $\{F,G\}=\sum_i\big(\partial_{q_i}F\,\partial_{p_i}G-\partial_{p_i}F\,\partial_{q_i}G\big)$ is bilinear, antisymmetric, satisfies the Leibniz rule and the Jacobi identity, and $dF/dt=\{F,H\}+\partial F/\partial t$. ([Wikipedia: Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics))

Geometrically, phase space is a symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$ of dimension $2n$, and the Hamiltonian vector field $X_H$ preserves $\omega$: $\mathcal L_{X_H}\omega=0$. ([Wikipedia: Liouville's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%27s_theorem_%28Hamiltonian%29))

A **canonical transformation** $(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ preserves the form of Hamilton's equations; equivalently its Jacobian $M$ satisfies $M^{\mathsf T}JM=J$, or it preserves Poisson brackets. A type-2 generating function $G_2(q,P,t)$ produces one via $p=\partial G_2/\partial q$, $Q=\partial G_2/\partial P$, with new Hamiltonian $K=H+\partial G_2/\partial t$ (types 1, 3, 4 use the other pairs of old and new variables). ([Wikipedia: Canonical transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_transformation))

### Key results
- **Conservation of $H$.** Along solutions $dH/dt=\partial H/\partial t$, so a Hamiltonian with no explicit time dependence is conserved. More generally, $dF/dt=\{F,H\}+\partial F/\partial t$, so $F$ without explicit time dependence is conserved exactly when $\{F,H\}=0$, and the bracket of two conserved quantities is conserved. ([Wikipedia: Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics); [SICM ch. 3](https://mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/9579/sicm_edition_2.zip/chapter003.html))
- **Liouville's theorem.** The Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space volume: $\mathcal L_{X_H}(\omega^n)=0$, equivalently the phase-space density obeys $\partial\rho/\partial t=-\{\rho,H\}$ and is constant along trajectories. This holds for time-dependent Hamiltonians too, and fails once friction is present. ([Wikipedia: Liouville's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%27s_theorem_%28Hamiltonian%29); [SICM ch. 3](https://mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/9579/sicm_edition_2.zip/chapter003.html))
- **Poincaré recurrence.** If $T$ preserves a finite measure $\mu$ and $\mu(A)>0$, then almost every point of $A$ returns to $A$. Applied to a Hamiltonian flow on a bounded region of phase space (for example a bounded energy surface), almost all trajectories return arbitrarily close to their starting points, so bounded Hamiltonian systems have no attractors. ([Wikipedia: Poincaré recurrence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_recurrence_theorem); [SICM ch. 3](https://mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/9579/sicm_edition_2.zip/chapter003.html))
- **Hamilton–Jacobi equation.** Choosing a type-2 generating function $S$ so that the new Hamiltonian vanishes gives $-\partial S/\partial t=H(q,\partial S/\partial q,t)$; for time-independent $H$, $S=W(q)-Et$ with $H(q,\partial W/\partial q)=E$. ([Wikipedia: Hamilton–Jacobi equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton%E2%80%93Jacobi_equation))
- **Liouville–Arnold theorem.** On a $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold let $F_1=H,\dots,F_n$ be pairwise Poisson-commuting ($\{F_i,F_j\}=0$) and let $c$ be a regular value ($dF_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dF_n\neq0$ on $L_c=\{F=c\}$). Then $L_c$ is a smooth manifold invariant under the flow of $H$; if it is also compact and connected it is diffeomorphic to the torus $\mathbb T^n$, and near it there are action–angle coordinates in which the actions are constant and $\dot\theta_i=\omega_i$, so the motion is linear. ([Wikipedia: Liouville–Arnold theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%E2%80%93Arnold_theorem); [Wikipedia: Integrable system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrable_system))
- **KAM theorem.** For a sufficiently small perturbation of a nondegenerate integrable system (Kolmogorov 1954; Arnold 1963 for analytic Hamiltonians; Moser 1962 for smooth twist maps), the invariant tori whose frequency vector is Diophantine, $|\omega\cdot k|\ge\gamma\|k\|^{-\tau}$ for all nonzero $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, survive, deformed, carrying quasiperiodic motion; tori destroyed by the perturbation become invariant Cantor sets, named cantori by Percival in 1979. ([Wikipedia: KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem))
- **Nekhoroshev estimates.** For a nearly integrable Hamiltonian $H(I)+\varepsilon h(I,\theta)$ with $n$ degrees of freedom in action–angle variables, under technical assumptions, actions drift little for exponentially long times; in a simplified form $|I(t)-I(0)|<\varepsilon^{1/(2n)}$ for $|t|<\exp\big(c\,\varepsilon^{-1/(2n)}\big)$ (Nekhoroshev 1971). ([Wikipedia: Nekhoroshev estimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nekhoroshev_estimates))
- **Noether's theorem in Hamiltonian form.** For a Hamiltonian action of a Lie group $G$, a momentum map $\mu:M\to\mathfrak g^*$ satisfies $d\langle\mu,\xi\rangle=\iota_{\rho(\xi)}\omega$. If $H$ is $G$-invariant, each component of $\mu$ Poisson-commutes with $H$ and is conserved (rotations give angular momentum). If the action is equivariant and free and proper on $\mu^{-1}(0)$, then $\mu^{-1}(0)/G$ is a symplectic manifold of dimension $\dim M-2\dim G$ (Marsden–Weinstein reduction). ([Wikipedia: Moment map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_map))

### Examples
- **Charged particle.** For $L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2+q\dot x\cdot A-q\varphi$, the canonical momentum is $p=m\dot x+qA$ and $H=(p-qA)^2/(2m)+q\varphi$, so canonical momentum differs from $m\dot x$. ([Wikipedia: Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics))
- **Spherical pendulum.** $H=\dfrac{p_\theta^2}{2m\ell^2}+\dfrac{p_\varphi^2}{2m\ell^2\sin^2\theta}-mg\ell\cos\theta$; $\varphi$ is cyclic, so $p_\varphi$ is conserved. ([Wikipedia: Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics))
- **Hénon–Heiles.** $H=\tfrac12(p_x^2+p_y^2)+\tfrac12(x^2+y^2)+x^2y-y^3/3$. On the surface of section $x=0$, orbits lie mostly on curves at $E=1/12$, the phase space is divided between curves and area-filling orbits at $E=1/8$, and most orbits fill the region at $E=1/6$. ([SICM ch. 3](https://mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/9579/sicm_edition_2.zip/chapter003.html))
- **Standard map.** $I'=I+K\sin\theta$, $\theta'=\theta+I'$ (mod $2\pi$) is area preserving and reproduces the mixed regular/chaotic structure of Hamiltonian sections, with a transition to large-scale chaos near $K=1$. ([SICM ch. 3](https://mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/9579/sicm_edition_2.zip/chapter003.html); [Wikipedia: Standard map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_map))

### History
The formulation is named after William Rowan Hamilton, who introduced it in 1833 as a reformulation of Lagrangian mechanics. ([Wikipedia: Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics)) Delaunay's 1846 lunar theory was the first major application of canonical transformations. ([Wikipedia: Canonical transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_transformation)) Poincaré discussed the recurrence theorem in 1890 in his work on the three-body problem. ([Wikipedia: Poincaré recurrence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_recurrence_theorem)) Arnold's 1964 example (a rotator–pendulum system) showed solutions whose actions grow by arbitrarily large amounts, through the transition-chain mechanism now called Arnold diffusion. ([Wikipedia: Arnold diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_diffusion))

### Connections
- [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics): Legendre-transform starting point.
- [Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry): the geometric structure of phase space.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) and [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws): symmetries and conserved momentum maps.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): group actions behind momentum maps and reduction.
- [Statistical Mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics): built on Liouville's theorem.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory): Poincaré recurrence and invariant measures.
- [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory) and [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems): KAM, cantori, Arnold diffusion.
- [Schrödinger Equation](node:Schrödinger%20Equation): Hamilton–Jacobi as its semiclassical limit.
- [Central Force Motion and the Kepler Problem](node:Central%20Force%20Motion%20and%20the%20Kepler%20Problem): separable via Hamilton–Jacobi; angular momentum as momentum map.

### Common pitfalls
- $H=T+V$ only when $V$ is velocity-independent, $T$ has no explicit time dependence, and $T$ is quadratic in $\dot q$; with a Rayleigh dissipation function energy is not conserved. ([Wikipedia: Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics))
- Conservation of $H$ follows from $\partial H/\partial t=0$, whether or not $H$ is the physical energy. ([Wikipedia: Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics))
- A complete solution of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation does not by itself prove Liouville integrability; the integration constants must be reinterpretable as values of a complete set of Poisson-commuting functions on the leaves of a Lagrangian foliation. ([Wikipedia: Integrable system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrable_system))
- Volume preservation is weaker than being symplectic: the non-squeezing theorem restricts symplectic maps further. ([Wikipedia: Liouville's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%27s_theorem_%28Hamiltonian%29))
- Poincaré recurrence needs finite measure; it says nothing for unbounded phase space. ([Wikipedia: Poincaré recurrence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_recurrence_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Positive entropy of the standard map.** Whether the Chirikov standard map has positive Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy with respect to the invariant Lebesgue measure is open; Knill's revised preprint states "The entropy conjecture is open" and deletes the incorrect parts of a 1999 claimed lower bound. ([Knill, arXiv math/9908014](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9908014))
- **Quantum KAM.** Whether a KAM theorem holds for perturbations of integrable quantum many-body systems is an open question. ([Wikipedia: KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hamiltonian mechanics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics): equations, brackets, symplectic form, integrability.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.09 Classical Mechanics III lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/pages/lecture-notes/): canonical transformations, Hamilton–Jacobi, action–angle variables, perturbation theory, chaos.
- **Primary:** [Sussman and Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, ch. 3](https://mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/9579/sicm_edition_2.zip/chapter003.html): textbook development of Hamilton's equations, Liouville, recurrence, surfaces of section; [Cheng and Xue on Arnold diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.04153).
- **Further reading:** [Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics (Springer GTM 60)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_Methods_of_Classical_Mechanics): symplectic manifolds, canonical formalism, perturbation theory, KAM appendix; 2nd edition, Springer 1989 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2063-1)).

## Reference
### Overview
The heat equation $u_t=\Delta u$ is the model parabolic equation: it describes diffusion of heat or of a concentration, and its theory was first developed by Fourier in 1822. On a bounded interval with zero boundary values it is solved by a Fourier sine series whose modes decay exponentially in time. ([Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation)) On $\mathbb R^n$ it is solved by convolution with a Gaussian kernel, and it smooths arbitrary $L^p$ data instantly; from the Fourier side this is the damping of the mode of wavenumber $k$ by $e^{-t|k|^2}$. ([Hunter, ch. 5, §5.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf))

The same features make the equation irreversible and globally coupled. It cannot in general be solved backward in time, its solutions are not unique without a growth condition at infinity, and disturbances propagate instantaneously. ([Hunter, §§5.1.3-5.1.4](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf); [Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation)) The probability density of a Brownian particle solves the heat equation. ([Brownian motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownian_motion); [Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation)) On Riemannian manifolds the heat semigroup $e^{t\Delta}$ of the Laplace-Beltrami operator connects geometry with analysis, through the Li-Yau inequalities and the heat-kernel bounds that follow from them. ([Garofalo, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.6581))

### Formal definition
The initial value problem on $\mathbb R^n$ asks for $u$ with $u_t=\Delta u$ for $t>0$ and $u(x,0)=f(x)$. Its solution is
$$u(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(x,t)=\frac{1}{(4\pi t)^{n/2}}e^{-|x|^2/4t},\quad t>0,$$
and $\Gamma(\cdot,t)\to\delta$ in $\mathcal S'$ as $t\to0^+$, so $\Gamma$ is the solution for a unit point source. ([Hunter, §5.1.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf)) On a bounded domain with Dirichlet conditions the heat kernel is $K(t,x,y)=\sum_n e^{-\lambda_nt}\varphi_n(x)\varphi_n(y)$, where $\lambda_n,\varphi_n$ are the Dirichlet eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenfunctions of $-\Delta$. ([Heat kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_kernel)) See [Eigenvalue Problems for PDEs](node:Eigenvalue%20Problems%20for%20PDEs).

### Key results
- **Smoothing (Hunter, Theorem 5.5).** If $1\le p\le\infty$ and $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$, then $u=\Gamma(\cdot,t)*f$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$, decays with all derivatives as $|x|\to\infty$, and solves $u_t=\Delta u$; if $1\le p<\infty$ then $u(\cdot,t)\to f$ in $L^p$ as $t\to0^+$. For Schwartz data $f$ one has moreover $\|u(t)\|_{L^2}\le\|f\|_{L^2}$ and $\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}\le(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\|f\|_{L^1}$. ([Hunter, Theorems 5.5 and 5.8](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf))
- **Parabolic maximum principle.** For a domain $\Omega$ and the cylinder $Q_T=(0,T)\times\Omega$ with parabolic boundary $\partial_pQ_T=\{0\}\times\Omega\cup(0,T]\times\partial\Omega$: if $w\in C^{1,2}(Q_T)\cap C(\overline{Q_T})$ satisfies $w_t-D\Delta w=f\le0$, then $w$ attains its maximum over $\overline{Q_T}$ on $\partial_pQ_T$. Hence comparison holds, and (as proved there in one space dimension) two solutions with forcings $f,g$ obey $\max|v-w|\le\max_{\partial_pQ_T}|v-w|+T\max|f-g|$; in particular the initial-boundary value problem has at most one solution. ([Speck, MIT 18.152 class 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/da093b7265d1fc4fe9c6edf3e7825661_MIT18_152F11_lec_04.pdf)) See [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle).
- **Uniqueness class and Tychonoff's example.** On $\mathbb R^n$ a solution of the initial value problem is unique among functions growing more slowly than $Ce^{a|x|^2}$. Without such a bound uniqueness fails: Tychonoff's series $u(x,t)=\sum_{n\ge0}g^{(n)}(t)x^{2n}/(2n)!$ with $g(t)=\exp(-1/t^2)$ is a nonzero solution of $u_t=u_{xx}$ with zero initial data, growing very rapidly in $|x|$. The failure is tied to the initial surface $t=0$ being characteristic. ([Hunter, §5.1.4 and Example 5.7](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf))
- **Backward ill-posedness.** For general $f\in\mathcal S$ there is no solution on $[-T,0]$ with values in $\mathcal S$ or even $\mathcal S'$, for any $T>0$ (take $\hat f(k)=e^{-\sqrt{1+|k|^2}}$). Continuous dependence also fails: $u_n=e^{-n}\sin(nx)e^{n^2t}$ has data tending to 0 with all derivatives while $\sup_x|u_n(\cdot,t)|\to\infty$ for each $t>0$. Backward uniqueness does hold under suitable assumptions. ([Hunter, §5.1.3 and Example 5.6](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf))
- **Heat semigroup.** The solution operators $T(t)f=\Gamma_t*f$, $\widehat{T(t)f}(k)=e^{-t|k|^2}\hat f(k)$, form a strongly continuous contraction semigroup $e^{t\Delta}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$. The map $t\mapsto T(t)$ is not continuous in operator norm, and for $t>0$ it carries $L^2$ into $H^\infty$, which is why the flow cannot be reversed. ([Hunter, Theorem 5.27 and §5.4.2](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf)) See [Strongly Continuous Operator Semigroups](node:Strongly%20Continuous%20Operator%20Semigroups).
- **Li-Yau estimate and parabolic Harnack inequality.** On a complete connected $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge0$, every positive solution $f$ of $\Delta f-f_t=0$ satisfies $|\nabla\log f|^2-(\log f)_t\le n/(2t)$. Integrating along geodesics gives, for $0<s<t$, $f(x,s)\le f(y,t)\,(t/s)^{n/2}\exp\big(d(x,y)^2/4(t-s)\big)$. These yield Liouville theorems and Gaussian upper bounds for the heat kernel. ([Garofalo, Theorems 1.1-1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.6581)) Li and Yau's two-sided Gaussian bounds for the heat kernel when $\mathrm{Ric}\ge0$ have since been sharpened. ([Xu, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.12758)) See [Laplace–Beltrami Operator](node:Laplace–Beltrami%20Operator).

### Examples
A point source of $N$ particles at the origin diffusing with coefficient $D$ has density $\rho(x,t)=N(4\pi Dt)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/4Dt}$: a normal distribution with variance $2Dt$, so the mean squared displacement grows like $t$. This is Einstein's 1905 account of Brownian motion, which Wiener's 1923 analysis made mathematically rigorous. ([Brownian motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownian_motion)) The identity $\Gamma_{s+t}=\Gamma_s*\Gamma_t$ says that a sum of independent Gaussians is Gaussian with added variances. ([Hunter, proof of Theorem 5.27](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf)) See [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus) and [Feynman–Kac Formula](node:Feynman–Kac%20Formula).

### History
Fourier developed the theory in 1822. Minakshisundaram and Pleijel later tied the heat equation to spectral geometry, and an abstract form of the heat equation on manifolds gives a major approach to the Atiyah-Singer index theorem. ([Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation)) Hadamard and Pini independently discovered the Harnack inequality for the heat equation, and Li and Yau extended it to manifolds with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge0$ in their 1986 Acta Mathematica paper. ([Garofalo, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.6581)) Rauch seems to have first formulated the hot spots conjecture in 1974. ([Rohleder, introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.01890v1))

### Connections
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): diagonalizes the equation; modes decay like $e^{-t|k|^2}$.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): steady states are harmonic.
- [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle): parabolic version on the parabolic boundary.
- [Fundamental Solutions](node:Fundamental%20Solutions): $\Gamma$ extended by zero for $t<0$ is the fundamental solution of $\partial_t-\Delta$.
- [Strongly Continuous Operator Semigroups](node:Strongly%20Continuous%20Operator%20Semigroups): $e^{t\Delta}$ is a model contraction semigroup.
- [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus): the heat kernel is the transition density of Brownian motion.
- [MSC 35Kxx - Parabolic equations and parabolic systems](node:MSC%2035Kxx%20-%20Parabolic%20equations%20and%20parabolic%20systems): the general parabolic theory.

### Common pitfalls
- Infinite speed of propagation: solutions respond instantly everywhere, in conflict with relativity; some nonlinear parabolic models have finite propagation speed instead. ([Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation))
- For rough data the initial condition holds in an $L^p$ sense, not pointwise, and solutions are generally not differentiable in $t$ at $t=0$. ([Hunter, §5.1.2](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf))
- The parabolic maximum principle uses the parabolic boundary; the final-time slice is not part of it. ([Speck, class 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/da093b7265d1fc4fe9c6edf3e7825661_MIT18_152F11_lec_04.pdf))
- Without a growth bound, the whole-space problem is not uniquely solvable (Tychonoff). ([Hunter, Example 5.7](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Hot spots conjecture.** For a bounded domain with insulated (Neumann) boundary, the conjecture in its strongest form asserts that an eigenfunction of the smallest positive Neumann eigenvalue attains its maximum and minimum only on the boundary, which would mean that for generic initial data the hottest and coldest points move apart and tend toward the boundary over time. It is still open for general simply connected planar domains and in higher dimensions. ([Rohleder, introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.01890v1)) The conjecture fails for some domains: de Dios Pont, Hsu and Taylor determine the largest possible "hot spots ratio" measuring the failure over connected Lipschitz domains and show it tends to $\sqrt e$ as the dimension grows. ([de Dios Pont-Hsu-Taylor, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16321))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation): history, interval solutions, physical interpretation.
- **Reference:** [Heat kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_kernel): kernels on domains and manifolds, eigenfunction expansion.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, Notes on PDEs, ch. 5](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch5.pdf): smoothing, irreversibility, nonuniqueness, semigroups.
- **Learn:** [Speck, MIT 18.152 class 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/da093b7265d1fc4fe9c6edf3e7825661_MIT18_152F11_lec_04.pdf): weak maximum principle and comparison.
- **Primary:** [Garofalo, Curvature-dimension inequalities and Li-Yau inequalities in sub-Riemannian spaces](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.6581): survey of Li-Yau, Harnack and Gaussian bounds.
- **Primary:** [Rohleder, A variational approach to the hot spots conjecture](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.01890v1): status of the conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed. (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 19, 2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/019): graduate PDE textbook.
