## Reference
### Overview
A function of several complex variables $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ open, is holomorphic when it is complex differentiable: near each point $f(z+h)=f(z)+L(h)+o(\|h\|)$ for a complex-linear $L:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C$. Equivalently it is holomorphic in each variable separately (Hartogs), and it is represented locally by convergent power series via a Cauchy integral formula on polydiscs. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))

Many one-variable facts survive (identity theorem on open sets, the [maximum principle](node:Maximum%20Principle), Riemann extension), but the theory for $n\ge2$ differs sharply. Holomorphic functions on a domain minus a compact set always extend (the Hartogs phenomenon), so not every domain is the natural domain of some holomorphic function; the unit ball and the bidisc are not biholomorphic, so there is no Riemann mapping theorem. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))

These phenomena lead to the core problems of the field: which domains are domains of holomorphy (answered by pseudoconvexity, the Levi problem), solving $\bar\partial u=f$, the Cousin problems, and the sheaf-theoretic theory of coherent sheaves and Stein manifolds developed by Oka, Cartan, Grauert and Remmert. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))

### Formal definition
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open and write $z_j=x_j+iy_j$, with Wirtinger operators
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial z_j}=\tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}-i\frac{\partial}{\partial y_j}\Big),\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar z_j}=\tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}+i\frac{\partial}{\partial y_j}\Big).$$
A continuously differentiable $f$ is holomorphic iff it satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations, i.e. $\partial f/\partial\bar z_j=0$ for every $j$. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf)) The ring of holomorphic functions on $\Omega$ is denoted $\mathcal O(\Omega)$.

Equivalent definitions: $f$ is complex differentiable at every point; or $f$ is holomorphic in each variable separately (Hartogs's theorem; Osgood's lemma when $f$ is also continuous); or $f$ is locally a convergent power series $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha (z-a)^\alpha$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))

A **domain of holomorphy** is a domain $\Omega$ for which there are no open sets $V$ (connected, not contained in $\Omega$) and $\emptyset\ne U\subset\Omega\cap V$ such that every $f\in\mathcal O(\Omega)$ agrees on $U$ with some holomorphic function on $V$; informally, $\partial\Omega$ is the natural boundary of some holomorphic function. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables)) For $K\subset\Omega$ the **holomorphic hull** is $\hat K_\Omega=\{z\in\Omega:|f(z)|\le\sup_K|f|\ \forall f\in\mathcal O(\Omega)\}$, and $\Omega$ is **holomorphically convex** if $\hat K_\Omega\subset\subset\Omega$ whenever $K\subset\subset\Omega$. A complete Reinhardt domain is a domain of holomorphy iff it is the domain of convergence of a power series at the origin. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))

### Key results
- **Cauchy integral formula on polydiscs.** If $\Delta=\Delta_1\times\cdots\times\Delta_n\subset\mathbb C^n$ is a polydisc and $f$ is continuous on $\bar\Delta$ and holomorphic in $\Delta$, then for $z\in\Delta$
$$f(z)=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^n}\int_{\partial\Delta_1\times\cdots\times\partial\Delta_n}\frac{f(\zeta_1,\dots,\zeta_n)}{(\zeta_1-z_1)\cdots(\zeta_n-z_n)}\,d\zeta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\zeta_n,$$
which yields a unique power-series expansion in $\Delta$. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf)) Compare [Cauchy's Integral Formula](node:Cauchy's%20Integral%20Formula).
- **Domains of convergence.** The domain of convergence of any power series in $n$ variables is a logarithmically convex Reinhardt domain centred at $0$: invariant under $z_j\mapsto e^{i\theta_j}z_j$, with convex image under $z\mapsto(\log|z_1|,\dots,\log|z_n|)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))
- **Hartogs phenomenon.** Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ be a domain, $n\ge2$, and $K\subset\subset\Omega$ compact with $\Omega\setminus K$ connected. Every holomorphic $f:\Omega\setminus K\to\mathbb C$ extends uniquely to a holomorphic function on $\Omega$. The proof extends $f$ smoothly and corrects by solving a $\bar\partial$-problem with compact support. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf)) See [Hartogs Extension Theorem](node:Hartogs%20Extension%20Theorem).
- **Riemann extension theorem.** If $g\in\mathcal O(\Omega)$ is not identically zero, $X=g^{-1}(0)$, and $f\in\mathcal O(\Omega\setminus X)$ is locally bounded in $\Omega$, then $f$ extends uniquely to $\mathcal O(\Omega)$. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **Cartan–Thullen theorem.** For a domain $\Omega\subsetneq\mathbb C^n$ the following are equivalent: (i) $\Omega$ is a domain of holomorphy; (ii) for all $K\subset\subset\Omega$, $\operatorname{dist}(K,\partial\Omega)=\operatorname{dist}(\hat K_\Omega,\partial\Omega)$; (iii) $\Omega$ is holomorphically convex. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **Solution of the Levi problem.** A domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ is holomorphically convex if and only if it is Hartogs pseudoconvex; hence domains of holomorphy are exactly the [pseudoconvex](node:Pseudoconvexity) domains. The forward direction is Oka's lemma; the converse takes "some hundred pages" and is proved in Hörmander's book. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf)) E. E. Levi posed the problem and Oka solved it for unramified Riemann domains over $\mathbb C^n$; for ramified Riemann domains pseudoconvexity no longer characterizes holomorphic convexity, and for domains in arbitrary complex manifolds the statement fails in general. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))
- **Weierstrass preparation theorem.** Let $f\in\mathcal O(U)$, $0\in U\subset\mathbb C^{n-1}\times\mathbb C$, $f(0)=0$, and suppose $z_n\mapsto f(0,z_n)$ is not identically zero near $0$ with order of vanishing $k\ge1$. Then on a polydisc $V=V'\times D\ni 0$ there are a unique nonvanishing $u\in\mathcal O(V)$ and a unique Weierstrass polynomial $P(z',z_n)=z_n^k+\sum_{j<k}c_j(z')z_n^j$ with $c_j\in\mathcal O(V')$, such that $f=uP$ on $V$. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **Injective holomorphic maps.** If $f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ is holomorphic and one-to-one on an open $U\subset\mathbb C^n$, its Jacobian determinant never vanishes; in particular a holomorphic bijection between open subsets of $\mathbb C^n$ is biholomorphic. Compare the [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem). ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **Cartan's uniqueness theorem.** If $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ is bounded, $0\in\Omega$, and $f:\Omega\to\Omega$ is holomorphic with $f(0)=0$ and $Df(0)=I$, then $f$ is the identity. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **[Cartan's Theorems A and B](node:Cartan's%20Theorems%20A%20and%20B).** On a [Stein manifold](node:Stein%20Spaces), coherent analytic sheaves are generated by global sections (A) and have vanishing higher cohomology (B). Theorem B implies the first Cousin problem is solvable on any Stein manifold, and every second Cousin problem on a Stein manifold $M$ is solvable when $H^2(M,\mathbb Z)=0$ (an instance of the Oka principle). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))

### Examples
- **Ball versus bidisc.** There is no proper holomorphic map from the bidisc $\mathbb D^2$ to the unit ball $\mathbb B^2\subset\mathbb C^2$ (Rothstein 1935), so they are not biholomorphic. Poincaré first argued this via automorphism groups assuming boundary extension, and Henri Cartan gave the first complete proof in 1931. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **Failure of the one-variable identity theorem.** $f=0$ and $g=z_1$ agree on the whole hyperplane $\{z_1=0\}$ but differ; zeros are not isolated, and the identity theorem only holds for agreement on open sets. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))
- **Riemann surfaces.** A connected Riemann surface is Stein iff it is non-compact; every Stein manifold of dimension $n$ embeds properly in $\mathbb C^{2n+1}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables)) See [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces).
- **Entire injective maps.** The Jacobian conjecture fails if "polynomial" is replaced by "entire holomorphic", even for $n=1$. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))

### History
Hartogs, Cousin, E. E. Levi, Oka and others developed the theory before and during the 1930s; after 1945 Cartan's seminar, together with Grauert and Remmert, rebuilt it on a sheaf-theoretic footing, with Oka's "idéal de domaines indéterminés" becoming Cartan's coherent sheaves. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables)) The analytic $L^2$ approach to $\bar\partial$ grew into the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem, an elliptic operator with non-coercive boundary conditions that is globally regular on many but not all pseudoconvex domains. ([Straube 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601128))

### Connections
- [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis): the one-variable theory; several of its theorems carry over, others (Riemann mapping, isolated zeros) fail.
- [Cauchy's Integral Formula](node:Cauchy's%20Integral%20Formula): iterated on polydiscs gives power series in several variables.
- [Hartogs Extension Theorem](node:Hartogs%20Extension%20Theorem): the basic phenomenon with no one-variable analogue.
- [Pseudoconvexity](node:Pseudoconvexity): the geometric condition characterizing domains of holomorphy.
- [Levi Convexity](node:Levi%20Convexity): the boundary (Levi form) form of pseudoconvexity.
- [Plurisubharmonic Functions](node:Plurisubharmonic%20Functions): exhaustion functions that define pseudoconvexity.
- [Riemann Mapping Theorem](node:Riemann%20Mapping%20Theorem): fails for $n\ge2$ (ball versus bidisc).
- [Complex Manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds): holomorphic functions in charts; Stein manifolds generalize domains of holomorphy.
- [Oka Manifolds](node:Oka%20Manifolds): the Oka principle for maps from Stein manifolds.
- [Dolbeault Cohomology](node:Dolbeault%20Cohomology): cohomology of $\bar\partial$, the obstruction to solving $\bar\partial u=f$.
- [CR Structures](node:CR%20Structures): boundaries of domains carry CR structures; the Lewy extension theorem extends CR functions holomorphically.
- [Holomorphic Approximation](node:Holomorphic%20Approximation): Runge-type approximation on holomorphically convex sets.
- [Jacobian Conjecture](node:Jacobian%20Conjecture): an open problem about polynomial maps of $\mathbb C^n$.

### Common pitfalls
- **Separate holomorphy needs no continuity hypothesis.** Hartogs's theorem shows separately holomorphic functions are holomorphic with no continuity assumption; Osgood's lemma is the easier version that assumes continuity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))
- **Not every domain is a domain of holomorphy.** In $\mathbb C$ every domain is one; in $\mathbb C^n$, $n>1$, this fails, so "the domain of $f$" is a genuine constraint. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))
- **Boundedness is needed for extension.** In the Riemann extension theorem $1/g$ is not bounded near $g^{-1}(0)$ and does not extend. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **Cartan's uniqueness theorem needs boundedness.** It fails on unbounded domains such as $\mathbb C^n$. ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Jacobian conjecture.** If $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ is a polynomial map whose Jacobian determinant never vanishes, is $F$ invertible with a polynomial inverse? It is a converse, in a special case, to the injectivity theorem above, and Lebl describes it as "well-known and as yet unsolved". ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **Proper maps between balls.** Proper holomorphic self-maps of the disc are exactly the finite Blaschke products; for proper holomorphic maps between unit balls the classification is far more involved, and when the balls have different dimensions Lebl states it "is not solved in general". ([Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/scv.pdf))
- **Problem lists.** Buzzard, Fornæss, Gavosto and Krantz started a collected list of open problems in higher-dimensional complex analysis, including a prize-problem section. ([Several Complex Variables Problem List](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9509202))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Function of several complex variables (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables): broad survey from definitions to Stein manifolds and the Cousin problems.
- **Learn:** [Lebl, Tasty Bits of Several Complex Variables](https://jirilebl.github.io/scv/): free textbook from Oklahoma State Math 6283 course notes; holomorphic functions, pseudoconvexity, CR geometry, $\bar\partial$, integral kernels, varieties.
- **Primary:** [Straube, Aspects of the $L^2$-Sobolev theory of the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601128): survey of compactness and global regularity on pseudoconvex domains.
- **Primary:** [The Several Complex Variables Problem List](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9509202): open problems in the field.
- **Further reading:** [Range, Holomorphic Functions and Integral Representations in Several Complex Variables (Springer GTM, 1986)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-1918-5): graduate text on integral representations and pseudoconvexity.

## Reference
### Overview
Homological algebra studies chain complexes, their homology, and resolutions, together with the derived functors built from them. Its basic setting is an abelian category, such as modules over a ring or sheaves of abelian groups on a space, and derived functors organize the cohomological methods of algebraic geometry. ([Kedlaya, MIT 18.726 lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-726-algebraic-geometry-spring-2009/738060c0a52a5982c224dd62c3fd68c0_MIT18_726s09_lec16_homalg.pdf))

The motivating phenomenon is that useful additive functors preserve only part of an exact sequence: a left exact $F$ turns $0\to A\to B\to C\to 0$ into an exact $0\to F(A)\to F(B)\to F(C)$ with no guarantee on the right. A cohomological δ-functor continues this sequence into a long exact sequence, and Grothendieck's universality theorem makes the continuation canonical. ([Kedlaya](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-726-algebraic-geometry-spring-2009/738060c0a52a5982c224dd62c3fd68c0_MIT18_726s09_lec16_homalg.pdf); [Stacks, Tag 010P](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/010P))

The same formalism computes Ext and Tor for modules, group cohomology as $\mathrm{Ext}$ over the group ring, and sheaf cohomology as the derived functors of global sections. ([Wikipedia, Group cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology); [Wikipedia, Sheaf cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_cohomology)) The subject has played a large role in algebraic topology, and its influence extends to commutative algebra, algebraic geometry, algebraic number theory and [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory). ([Wikipedia, Homological algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_algebra))

### Formal definition
In an additive category a chain complex is a family $d_n:C_n\to C_{n-1}$ with $d_{n-1}\circ d_n=0$, and a chain map $f:C\to D$ satisfies $d^D_nf_n=f_{n-1}d^C_n$. In an abelian category the homology is $H_n(C)=\ker d_n/\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$, functorial in chain maps. ([Stacks, Tag 010V](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/010V))

Let $F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be a left exact additive functor between abelian categories, where $\mathcal A$ has enough injectives. For an injective resolution $A\to I^\bullet$, the right derived functors are $R^iF(A)=H^i(F(I^\bullet))$, independent of the resolution up to canonical isomorphism. Dually, if $F$ is right exact and $\mathcal A$ has enough projectives, $L_iF(A)=H_i(F(P_\bullet))$ for a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$. ([Sharifi, §§3.3–3.4](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch03.html))

A cohomological δ-functor $\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ is a sequence of additive functors $F^n$ ($n\ge0$) with connecting maps $\delta:F^n(C)\to F^{n+1}(A)$ for every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$, natural in the sequence, such that the long sequence is exact. It is universal if every natural transformation $F^0\to G^0$ to another δ-functor extends uniquely to a morphism of δ-functors. ([Stacks, Definitions 12.12.1 and 12.12.3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/010P))

The projective dimension $\mathrm{pd}(M)$ of a module is the minimal length of a projective resolution of $M$ (infinite if there is no finite one), and the left global dimension of a ring is the supremum of the projective dimensions of its left modules. ([Wikipedia, Projective module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_module); [Wikipedia, Global dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_dimension))

### Key results
- **Snake lemma.** In an abelian category, given a commutative diagram with exact rows $A\to B\to C\to0$ and $0\to A'\to B'\to C'$ and vertical maps $a,b,c$, there is an exact sequence $\ker a\to\ker b\to\ker c\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }\operatorname{coker}a\to\operatorname{coker}b\to\operatorname{coker}c$. If $A\to B$ is mono, so is $\ker a\to\ker b$; if $B'\to C'$ is epi, so is $\operatorname{coker}b\to\operatorname{coker}c$. ([Wikipedia, Snake lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake_lemma))
- **Five lemma.** In a commutative diagram with exact rows and vertical maps $l,m,n,p,q$, if $m$ and $p$ are isomorphisms, $l$ is an epimorphism and $q$ is a monomorphism, then $n$ is an isomorphism. It holds in any abelian category and in groups, and it splits into two four lemmas giving epi and mono separately. ([Wikipedia, Five lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_lemma))
- **Long exact homology sequence.** A short exact sequence $0\to A_\bullet\to B_\bullet\to C_\bullet\to0$ of complexes in an abelian category gives a canonical long exact sequence $\cdots\to H_i(A)\to H_i(B)\to H_i(C)\to H_{i-1}(A)\to\cdots$, with connecting maps from the snake lemma. ([Stacks, Lemma 12.13.6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/010V))
- **Grothendieck's universality theorem.** A cohomological δ-functor $T$ with $T^i$ effaceable for every $i>0$ (each $A$ admits a monomorphism $u:A\to B$ with $T^i(u)=0$) is universal. Hence, under the hypotheses of the definition above, the $R^iF$ form the universal δ-functor extending $F$. ([Kedlaya](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-726-algebraic-geometry-spring-2009/738060c0a52a5982c224dd62c3fd68c0_MIT18_726s09_lec16_homalg.pdf); [Sharifi, Theorem 3.4.10](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch03.html))
- **Balancing of Tor.** $\mathrm{Tor}^R_i(A,B)$ can be computed by resolving either variable, and for commutative $R$ one has $\mathrm{Tor}^R_i(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}^R_i(B,A)$. ([Sharifi, Proposition 3.5.9 and Corollary 3.5.10](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch03.html))
- **$\mathrm{Ext}^1$ classifies extensions.** Equivalence classes of extensions $0\to N\to E\to M\to0$ of $R$-modules form an abelian group under Baer sum, naturally isomorphic to $\mathrm{Ext}^1_R(M,N)$; extensions of length $n$ similarly describe $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R$. ([May, Notes on Tor and Ext, §§4.5–4.6, Theorem 4.12](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/MISC/TorExt.pdf))
- **Grothendieck spectral sequence.** Let $F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ and $G:\mathcal B\to\mathcal C$ be left exact additive functors of abelian categories, with $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ having enough injectives and $F$ sending injectives to $G$-acyclic objects. Then for each $A$ there is a spectral sequence $E_2^{p,q}=R^pG(R^qF(A))\Rightarrow R^{p+q}(G\circ F)(A)$. The Leray spectral sequence $H^p(Y,R^qf_*\mathcal F)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X,\mathcal F)$ is the case $F=f_*$, $G=\Gamma(Y,-)$. ([Wikipedia, Grothendieck spectral sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_spectral_sequence))
- **Global dimension.** A ring has global dimension $0$ iff it is semisimple; a principal ideal domain that is not a field has global dimension $1$; $K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over a field has global dimension $n$ (Hilbert's syzygy theorem). Serre's theorem: a commutative Noetherian local ring is regular iff it has finite global dimension, which then equals its Krull dimension. ([Wikipedia, Global dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_dimension))

### Examples
- **Tor over $\mathbb Z$.** For an [abelian group](node:Abelian%20Groups) $A$ and $n>0$, the resolution $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$ gives $\mathrm{Tor}_0^{\mathbb Z}(A,\mathbb Z/n)=A/nA$, $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{\mathbb Z}(A,\mathbb Z/n)=A[n]=\{a: na=0\}$, and $\mathrm{Tor}_i=0$ for $i\ge2$. ([Sharifi, Example 3.5.5](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch03.html))
- **Group cohomology.** For a group $G$ and $G$-module $M$, $H^n(G,M)$ are the right derived functors of the invariants $M\mapsto M^G$, and $H^n(G,M)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb Z[G]}(\mathbb Z,M)$. $H^2(G,M)$ classifies extensions $0\to M\to E\to G\to 1$ inducing the given action, up to equivalence. ([Wikipedia, Group cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology))
- **Sheaf cohomology.** Sheaves of abelian groups on a space $X$ have enough injectives, and $H^i(X,\mathcal E)$ is defined as the right derived functors of $\mathcal E\mapsto\mathcal E(X)$. On a paracompact [Hausdorff space](node:Hausdorff%20Space) these groups vanish above the covering dimension (Godement). ([Wikipedia, Sheaf cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_cohomology))

### History
The subject's origins lie in the theory of modules and syzygies at the end of the nineteenth century, chiefly in work of Poincaré and Hilbert. It became an independent field in the 1940s around Ext and Tor. Cartan and Eilenberg's 1956 book *Homological Algebra* used projective and injective resolutions, and Grothendieck's 1957 Tôhoku paper recast the theory in abelian categories. Derived categories date to Verdier's thesis. ([Wikipedia, Homological algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_algebra))

### Connections
- [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): naturality, adjunctions and universal properties drive the theory.
- [Abelian Categories](node:Abelian%20Categories): the general setting in which homology and derived functors are defined.
- [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals) and [Modules and Bimodules](node:Modules%20and%20Bimodules): module categories give the basic examples.
- [Tor and Ext over Commutative Rings](node:Tor%20and%20Ext%20over%20Commutative%20Rings): the commutative-algebra specialization of Ext and Tor.
- [Flat Modules](node:Flat%20Modules): flatness is the vanishing of $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ against all modules.
- [Spectral Sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences): the computational tool for composite derived functors and filtered complexes.
- [Derived Categories](node:Derived%20Categories): the modern framework in which derived functors become functors on complexes.
- [Group Cohomology](node:Group%20Cohomology) and [Hochschild Cohomology](node:Hochschild%20Cohomology): Ext over the group ring and over the enveloping algebra.
- [Simplicial Methods](node:Simplicial%20Methods): the Dold–Kan correspondence links simplicial objects and chain complexes.
- [MSC 18Gxx - Homological algebra in category theory, derived categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Gxx%20-%20Homological%20algebra%20in%20category%20theory,%20derived%20categories%20and%20functors): the corresponding MSC subfield map.

### Common pitfalls
A chain complex already makes sense in an additive category, but the homology quotients use abelian structure. Likewise, enough injectives (or projectives) must be established before the corresponding resolution recipe applies. ([Stacks, Tag 010V](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/010V); [Sharifi, §3.4](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch03.html))

For noncommutative $R$, $\mathrm{Tor}^R_n(M,N)$ takes a right module $M$ and a left module $N$, and the symmetry $\mathrm{Tor}(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}(B,A)$ is a statement about commutative rings only. The left and right global dimensions of a noncommutative ring can differ. ([Sharifi, Corollary 3.5.10](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch03.html); [Wikipedia, Global dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_dimension))

### Open problems
- **Finitistic dimension conjecture.** For a finite-dimensional algebra $\Lambda$ over a field, the little finitistic dimension $\operatorname{fin\,dim}\Lambda$ is the supremum of the projective dimensions of finitely generated modules of finite projective dimension; $\operatorname{Fin\,dim}\Lambda$ uses all modules. Bass publicized both as problems in 1960. The conjecture $\operatorname{fin\,dim}\Lambda=\operatorname{Fin\,dim}\Lambda$ is false, with counterexamples among monomial relation algebras (Huisgen-Zimmermann, 1992). The conjecture $\operatorname{fin\,dim}\Lambda<\infty$ is known for special classes, among them $J^2=0$, $J^3=0$ and monomial algebras. ([Huisgen-Zimmermann, The finitistic dimension conjectures – a tale of 3.5 decades](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1407.2383)) A 2024 paper states that "the question remains open for Artin algebras" and calls it the Finitistic Dimension Conjecture. ([Giatagantzidis, Radical preservation and the finitistic dimension](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2412.10965))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Homological algebra chapter](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/010V): complexes, long exact sequences and δ-functors in abelian categories.
- **Learn:** [Sharifi, Homological algebra, Chapter 3](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch03.html): derived functors, Tor and Ext with worked examples.
- **Learn:** [Kedlaya, MIT 18.726 lecture on homological algebra](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-726-algebraic-geometry-spring-2009/738060c0a52a5982c224dd62c3fd68c0_MIT18_726s09_lec16_homalg.pdf): δ-functors and universality for algebraic geometry.
- **Primary:** [Huisgen-Zimmermann, The finitistic dimension conjectures (survey)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.2383): review of the homological conjectures for finite-dimensional algebras.
- **Primary:** [May, Notes on Tor and Ext](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/MISC/TorExt.pdf): universal coefficients, Künneth, and the extension interpretation of Ext.
- **Further reading:** [Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra (CUP, 1994)](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Hbook-corrections.html): the standard graduate text; Cartan–Eilenberg's *Homological Algebra* (1956) is the classical monograph.
references.Homology:
## Reference
### Overview
Homology assigns to a space $X$ a sequence of abelian groups $H_n(X)$. The dimension of the $n$-th group counts the "holes" of $X$ in dimension $n$. These ranks are the Betti numbers, and they refine the Euler characteristic ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)). Algebraically, homology is defined for any chain complex as cycles modulo boundaries. Topologically, one builds a chain complex from a space: from its simplices (simplicial homology) or from all continuous maps of simplices into it (singular homology) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homology)).

Homology is the basic computable invariant of algebraic topology. It is a functor, homotopy invariant, and determined on nice spaces by the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms. It is computed through long exact sequences and Mayer–Vietoris sequences ([Wikipedia: Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Steenrod_axioms); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)). Classical applications include the Brouwer fixed point theorem and invariance of domain. Persistent homology, the study of homology across length scales, is used in data analysis ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)).

Homology sits between [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group) and homotopy groups on one side and cohomology on the other. The Hurewicz theorem identifies $H_1$ with the abelianized fundamental group ([Wikipedia: Hurewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurewicz_theorem)). In the stable-homotopy view, any spectrum $E$ defines a generalized homology theory $E_n(X)=\pi_n(\Sigma^\infty X\wedge E)$, and ordinary homology is one example ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homology)).

### Formal definition
**Chain complexes.** A chain complex is a sequence of abelian groups and homomorphisms $\cdots\to C_{n+1}\xrightarrow{\partial_{n+1}}C_n\xrightarrow{\partial_n}C_{n-1}\to\cdots$ with $\partial_n\circ\partial_{n+1}=0$. Its homology is
$$H_n(C)=\ker\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1},$$
cycles modulo boundaries. The complex is exact at $n$ exactly when $H_n(C)=0$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homology); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)).

**Singular homology.** $C_n(X)$ is the free abelian group on continuous maps $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$, with boundary the alternating sum of faces, $\partial\sigma=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^i\sigma|_{[e_0,\dots,\hat e_i,\dots,e_n]}$ ([Wikipedia: Singular homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_homology)). Simplicial homology uses the oriented $n$-simplices of a simplicial complex as generators instead ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)).

**Betti numbers and Euler characteristic.** $b_n=\operatorname{rank}H_n(X)$. For a finite complex, $\chi=\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}C_n=\sum_n(-1)^n b_n$: the alternating sum can be computed on chains or on homology ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)).

**Axioms (Eilenberg–Steenrod, 1945).** A homology theory is a sequence of functors $H_n$ from pairs $(X,A)$ to abelian groups with natural maps $\partial:H_n(X,A)\to H_{n-1}(A)$, satisfying the following ([Wikipedia: Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Steenrod_axioms)):
1. *homotopy*: homotopic maps induce equal homomorphisms;
2. *excision*: if $\overline U\subseteq\operatorname{int}A$, then $(X\setminus U,A\setminus U)\hookrightarrow(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms;
3. *dimension*: $H_n(\mathrm{pt})=0$ for $n\neq0$;
4. *additivity*: $H_n(\bigsqcup X_\alpha)\cong\bigoplus H_n(X_\alpha)$;
5. *exactness*: there is a long exact sequence $\cdots\to H_n(A)\to H_n(X)\to H_n(X,A)\to H_{n-1}(A)\to\cdots$.

Dropping the dimension axiom gives extraordinary theories, such as topological K-theory and cobordism ([Wikipedia: Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Steenrod_axioms)).

### Key results
- **Long exact sequence.** Every short exact sequence of chain complexes $0\to A_\bullet\to B_\bullet\to C_\bullet\to0$ induces a long exact sequence $\cdots\to H_n(A)\to H_n(B)\to H_n(C)\to H_{n-1}(A)\to\cdots$, with connecting maps given by the zig-zag lemma. Mayer–Vietoris sequences are an application ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)).
- **Homotopy invariance.** By the homotopy axiom, homotopy-equivalent spaces have isomorphic homology groups ([Wikipedia: Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Steenrod_axioms)).
- **Hurewicz theorem.** If $X$ is path-connected, the Hurewicz map induces $\pi_1(X)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X)$. If $n\ge2$ and $X$ is $(n-1)$-connected, then $\tilde H_i(X)=0$ for $i<n$, $\pi_n(X)\to H_n(X)$ is an isomorphism, and $\pi_{n+1}(X)\to H_{n+1}(X)$ is surjective ([Wikipedia: Hurewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurewicz_theorem)).
- **Universal coefficient theorem.** For any abelian group $A$ there is a short exact sequence $0\to H_i(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes A\to H_i(X;A)\to\operatorname{Tor}(H_{i-1}(X;\mathbb Z),A)\to0$, which splits, though not naturally. For a PID $R$ and an $R$-module $G$ there is a natural sequence $0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{i-1}(X;R),G)\to H^i(X;G)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_i(X;R),G)\to0$ ([Wikipedia: UCT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_coefficient_theorem)).
- **Poincaré duality.** If $M$ is a closed $R$-oriented $n$-manifold, cap product with the fundamental class gives $H^k(M;R)\cong H_{n-k}(M;R)$ for all $k$. Mod 2 no orientation hypothesis is needed. Consequences: $b_k=b_{n-k}$, and every closed odd-dimensional manifold has $\chi=0$ ([Wikipedia: Poincaré duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_duality)).
- **Approximation of $L^2$-Betti numbers (Lück).** If $G=G_0\supset G_1\supset\cdots$ is a residual chain, a decreasing sequence of finite-index *normal* subgroups with $\bigcap_i G_i=\{e\}$, then the $n$-th $L^2$-Betti number of any finite free $G$-CW complex $X$ is the limit of $b_n(G_i\backslash X)/[G:G_i]$ ([Linnell, Lück and Sauer](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1003.0434)). For a lattice $\Gamma$ in a semisimple Lie group $G$, the limit of $\dim H_j(\Gamma_N;\mathbb C)/[\Gamma:\Gamma_N]$ is the $j$-th $L^2$-Betti number of $\Gamma$, and it is nonzero only when the complex rank of $G$ equals that of a maximal compact subgroup $K$ ([Bergeron and Venkatesh](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.1083)).

### Examples
- **Spheres.** $H_k(S^n)\cong\mathbb Z$ for $k=0,n$ and $0$ otherwise. By the axioms this shows $S^{n-1}$ is not a retract of $D^n$, which gives Brouwer's fixed point theorem ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Steenrod_axioms)).
- **Torus.** $H_1(T^2)\cong\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)).
- **Real projective space (torsion).** $H_i(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb Z)$ is $\mathbb Z$ for $i=0$ and for $i=n$ odd, $\mathbb Z/2$ for odd $0<i<n$, and $0$ otherwise. With $\mathbb Z/2$ coefficients every $H^i$, $0\le i\le n$, is $\mathbb Z/2$, and the ring is $\mathbb Z/2[w]/(w^{n+1})$ ([Wikipedia: UCT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_coefficient_theorem)).
- **Torsion in hyperbolic 3-manifolds.** If $k\subset S^3$ is a hyperbolic knot whose Alexander polynomial has nontrivial Mahler measure (e.g. the figure-eight knot) and $M_N$ is the $N$-th cyclic branched cover, then $\lim_N \log|H_1(M_N)_{\mathrm{tors}}|/N>0$ (following Silver and Williams) ([Bergeron and Venkatesh](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.1083)).

### History
Riemann introduced genus and connectivity numbers in 1857. Betti showed in 1871 that his "homology numbers" do not depend on choices. Poincaré's *Analysis Situs* (1895) introduced homology classes and relations. Noether, Vietoris and Mayer recast homology algebraically in 1925–28 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)). Poincaré stated his duality for Betti numbers in 1893, and cup and cap products (Čech, Whitney) gave its modern form in the 1930s ([Wikipedia: Poincaré duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_duality)). Eilenberg and Steenrod axiomatized the theory in "Axiomatic Approach to Homology Theory" (PNAS 31, 1945) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1073/pnas.31.4.117); [Wikipedia: Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Steenrod_axioms)). K-theory and cobordism, found in the 1950s, were the first extraordinary theories ([Wikipedia: Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Steenrod_axioms)).

### Connections
- [Topological Spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces): singular homology is defined for every topological space.
- [Abelian Groups](node:Abelian%20Groups): homology groups are abelian groups.
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory): $H_1$ is the abelianized fundamental group.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): Hurewicz identifies $H_1$ with $\pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}$.
- [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra): chain complexes, exact sequences, Tor and Ext.
- [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology): dual real-coefficient theory computed by differential forms.
- [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms): integrating closed forms over cycles pairs de Rham cohomology with homology.
- [Poincaré Duality](node:Poincaré%20Duality): homology and cohomology of closed manifolds in complementary degrees.
- [Homotopy Equivalence](node:Homotopy%20Equivalence): homology is invariant under it.
- [Spectral Sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences): the main tool for computing homology of fibrations and filtered complexes.
- [Topological K-Theory](node:Topological%20K-Theory) and [Cobordism](node:Cobordism): extraordinary theories obtained by dropping the dimension axiom.
- [Group Cohomology](node:Group%20Cohomology): (co)homology of a group, which for arithmetic groups is studied below.
- [Simplicial Methods](node:Simplicial%20Methods): simplicial homology and the Dold–Kan correspondence.

### Common pitfalls
- Homology does not determine homotopy type. It is abelian and loses information that $\pi_1$ keeps: $H_1$ sees only the abelianization ([Wikipedia: Hurewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurewicz_theorem)).
- Betti numbers do not detect torsion. $\mathbb{RP}^2$ has $H_1\cong\mathbb Z/2$ and $b_1=0$, and field coefficients can change the answer ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: UCT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_coefficient_theorem)).
- The universal-coefficient splitting is not natural, so it cannot be used to define maps ([Wikipedia: UCT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_coefficient_theorem)).
- Poincaré duality in the form $H^k\cong H_{n-k}$ needs compactness. Non-compact manifolds need Borel–Moore homology or compactly supported cohomology ([Wikipedia: Poincaré duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_duality)).

### Open problems
- **Torsion growth for arithmetic groups (Bergeron–Venkatesh conjecture).** Let $\mathbf G$ be $\mathbb Q$-anisotropic semisimple, $\Gamma\subset\mathbf G(\mathbb Q)$ a congruence lattice, $M$ an arithmetic $\Gamma$-module, and $\Gamma_N$ a decreasing sequence of congruence subgroups with $\bigcap_N\Gamma_N=\{1\}$. Write $S=G/K$ and $\delta=\operatorname{rank}G-\operatorname{rank}K$. *Conjecture:* $\lim_N\log|H_j(\Gamma_N,M)_{\mathrm{tors}}|/[\Gamma:\Gamma_N]$ exists for each $j$, and it is zero unless $\delta(S)=1$ and $j=(\dim S-1)/2$, in which case it equals an explicit positive constant $c_{G,M}$ times $\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma\backslash S)$. The authors call the conjecture "somewhat speculative at this stage". The groups with $\delta=1$ include $SL_2(\mathbb C)$, so the conjecture covers arithmetic hyperbolic 3-manifolds ([Bergeron and Venkatesh](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.1083); [arXiv abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.1083)).

references.Hyperbolic Representation Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Hyperbolic representation learning embeds data in a space of constant negative curvature instead of Euclidean space. The motivation is a volume argument: in hyperbolic geometry the circumference and area of a disc grow exponentially with the radius, as the number of nodes of a tree grows exponentially with depth, so a tree can be laid out with depth proportional to radius in very few dimensions. ([Nickel and Kiela 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.08039)) Embeddings of the WordNet noun hierarchy in a 5-dimensional Poincaré ball outperformed 200-dimensional Euclidean embeddings on reconstruction and link prediction. ([Nickel and Kiela 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.08039))

The area has moved from shallow embeddings (one vector per node) to hyperbolic neural networks, which define layers, multinomial logistic regression and recurrent units through gyrovector operations, and then to hyperbolic graph neural networks, transformers and foundation models. ([Ganea et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1805.09112); [Peng et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.04562); [He et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17787v1)) Applications include recommender systems, knowledge graphs, and chemistry and biology. ([Zhou et al. 2022](https://hyperbolicgraphlearning.github.io))

The method's claims are conditional on the data being tree-like. Gromov $\delta$-hyperbolicity measures this ($\delta = 0$ for trees), and the gain of hyperbolic GCNs over Euclidean GNNs tracks it: on the citation graph Cora ($\delta = 11$, far from tree-like) HGCN did not outperform Euclidean GNNs in the main 16-dimensional experiments, though it remained more effective than GCN at small dimensions. ([Chami et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.12933))

### Formal definition
**Poincaré ball.** $\mathbb B^d = \{x \in \mathbb R^d : \lVert x\rVert < 1\}$ with metric $g_x = \big(\tfrac{2}{1-\lVert x\rVert^2}\big)^2 g^E$ and distance
$$d(u,v) = \operatorname{arcosh}\!\Big(1 + \frac{2\lVert u - v\rVert^2}{(1-\lVert u\rVert^2)(1-\lVert v\rVert^2)}\Big).$$
([Nickel and Kiela 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.08039))

**Hyperboloid (Lorentz) model.** With $B(x,y) = -x_0y_0 + x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n$, hyperbolic $n$-space is the sheet $\{x : B(x,x) = -1,\ x_0 > 0\}$ with $d(u,v) = \operatorname{arcosh}(-B(u,v))$; the Poincaré model is obtained from it by a stereographic-type projection. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperboloid_model))

**Gyrovector operations (ball of parameter $c > 0$).** Möbius addition
$$x \oplus_c y = \frac{(1 + 2c\langle x,y\rangle + c\lVert y\rVert^2)x + (1 - c\lVert x\rVert^2)y}{1 + 2c\langle x,y\rangle + c^2\lVert x\rVert^2\lVert y\rVert^2},$$
exponential map at the origin $\exp_0^c(v) = \tanh(\sqrt c\lVert v\rVert)\,\frac{v}{\sqrt c\lVert v\rVert}$, distance $d_c(x,y) = \tfrac{2}{\sqrt c}\tanh^{-1}(\sqrt c\lVert -x \oplus_c y\rVert)$, and Möbius matrix-vector multiplication $M \otimes_c x = \exp_0^c(M\log_0^c(x))$. ([Ganea et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1805.09112))

**Riemannian SGD on the ball.** $\theta_{t+1} = \mathrm{proj}\big(\theta_t - \eta_t\tfrac{(1-\lVert\theta_t\rVert^2)^2}{4}\nabla_E\big)$, where $\mathrm{proj}$ pulls points with norm $\ge 1$ back inside by $\varepsilon = 10^{-5}$. ([Nickel and Kiela 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.08039))

### Key results
- **Trees embed with arbitrarily low distortion (Sarkar's construction).** Every tree embeds in the hyperbolic plane with distortion as close to 1 as desired by scaling edge lengths by a factor $\tau$; the combinatorial construction extends to $r$ dimensions using error-correcting codes and reaches MAP 0.989 on WordNet in two dimensions. ([De Sa et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.03329))
- **Precision–distortion tradeoff.** In two dimensions, embedding a tree with longest path $\ell$ and maximum degree $\deg_{\max}$ to distortion $1+\varepsilon$ needs $O(\tfrac1\varepsilon\,\ell\log\deg_{\max})$ bits, and a matching lower bound $\Omega(\tfrac{\ell}{\varepsilon}\log\deg_{\max})$ holds for any construction; raising the dimension to $r$ cuts the bit cost by about a factor $r$ up to $r \approx \log\deg_{\max} + 1$. Long paths are expensive and high branching is cheap. ([De Sa et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.03329))
- **Exact recovery by h-MDS.** Given exact pairwise hyperbolic distances, points are recovered exactly by centering at a pseudo-Euclidean mean and solving an eigenproblem on $\cosh$ of the distances; dimension reduction by principal geodesic analysis is nonconvex, with a sufficient condition for local convexity. ([De Sa et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.03329))
- **Curvature is not expressive power (Chami et al., Theorem 4.1).** With infinite precision, embeddings at one negative curvature can be rescaled to another curvature and give the same reconstructed graph under the Fermi–Dirac decoder; trainable curvature helps only through finite precision and normalization, raising Disease link-prediction ROC AUC from 78.4 to 89.1. ([Chami et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.12933))
- **Gain tracks $\delta$-hyperbolicity.** On graphs with low $\delta$ (Disease and Disease-M have $\delta = 0$, Human PPI and Airport $\delta = 1$) HGCN reduced error relative to the best baselines by an average of 45.4% (link prediction) and 12.3% (node classification); on PubMed ($\delta = 3.5$) the reductions were 27.5% and 6.2%; on Cora ($\delta = 11$) it did not outperform Euclidean GNNs at the standard 16 dimensions. ([Chami et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.12933))
- **Numerical capacity of models.** Under 64-bit arithmetic the Poincaré ball can correctly represent points over a larger region than the Lorentz model; a Euclidean parametrization of hyperbolic space alleviates the limitations of both. ([Mishne et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00181))

### Examples
- **WordNet nouns.** 82,115 nouns and 743,241 hypernym relations: Poincaré embeddings at $d = 5$ reach reconstruction MAP 0.823 versus 0.168 for Euclidean at $d = 200$, trained with a softmax ranking loss over 10 sampled negatives. ([Nickel and Kiela 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.08039))
- **Hyperbolic multinomial logistic regression.** Class probabilities are proportional to $\exp$ of a signed hyperbolic distance from $x$ to a Poincaré hyperplane $\{x : \langle -p_k \oplus_c x, a_k\rangle = 0\}$ through $p_k$ with normal $a_k$. ([Ganea et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1805.09112))
- **Lexical entailment.** On HyperLex a 5-dimensional Poincaré embedding reaches Spearman $\rho = 0.512$ against 0.389 for Euclidean. ([Nickel and Kiela 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.08039))

### History
Poincaré embeddings (Nickel and Kiela, 2017) introduced learned hyperbolic embeddings of hierarchies; De Sa et al. (2018) gave combinatorial constructions and precision bounds; Ganea et al. (2018) built hyperbolic neural networks from gyrovector operations; Chami et al. (2019) introduced hyperbolic graph convolutions with trainable curvature. ([Nickel and Kiela 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.08039); [De Sa et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.03329); [Ganea et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1805.09112); [Chami et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.12933)) Surveys appeared from 2021, and by 2025 the work had reached hyperbolic LLMs of about a billion parameters. ([Peng et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.04562); [He et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17787v1))

### Connections
- [Hyperbolic Space](node:Hyperbolic%20Space): the constant-negative-curvature geometry used as the embedding space.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): the conformal metric of the Poincaré ball and the Minkowski form of the hyperboloid.
- [Riemannian Optimization for Learning](node:Riemannian%20Optimization%20for%20Learning): Riemannian SGD and retractions train hyperbolic parameters.
- [Manifold Learning](node:Manifold%20Learning): learning representations on a curved space rather than in $\mathbb R^n$.
- [Geometric Deep Learning](node:Geometric%20Deep%20Learning): hyperbolic GNNs are a non-Euclidean case of the programme.
- [Graph Neural Networks](node:Graph%20Neural%20Networks): HGCN is the hyperbolic analogue of a GCN.
- [Distance Matrices and Metric Embeddings](node:Distance%20Matrices%20and%20Metric%20Embeddings): distortion and h-MDS are metric-embedding questions.
- [Mixed-Curvature Representation Learning](node:Mixed-Curvature%20Representation%20Learning): generalizes to products of spaces with different curvatures.
- [Knowledge Graph Completion](node:Knowledge%20Graph%20Completion): hierarchical relations are a main application.
- [Vector Search and Embeddings](node:Vector%20Search%20and%20Embeddings): hyperbolic retrieval needs hyperbolic nearest-neighbour search.
- [Logistic Regression](node:Logistic%20Regression): hyperbolic MLR replaces Euclidean hyperplanes with Poincaré hyperplanes.
- [Recommender Systems](node:Recommender%20Systems): a main application area of hyperbolic graph models.
- [Transformers](node:Transformers): hyperbolic transformers and LLMs extend the approach to foundation models.

### Common pitfalls
- **No Euclidean control.** Gains depend on graph hyperbolicity, and a low-$\delta$ assumption should be measured, not assumed; Cora is a counterexample. ([Chami et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.12933))
- **Ignoring precision.** Distances near the boundary need many bits, and long paths are costly in low dimensions; floating-point limits hurt h-MDS MAP. ([De Sa et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.03329); [Mishne et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00181))
- **Confusing MAP with distortion.** MAP is local and ranking-based; distortion is global and distance-based, and methods can rank differently on the two. ([De Sa et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.03329))
- **Treating curvature as a capacity knob.** In exact arithmetic, changing negative curvature only rescales. ([Chami et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.12933))

### Open problems
- **Recovery from incomplete distances.** De Sa et al. state that the sample complexity of recovering hyperbolic embeddings from incomplete distance information is an open theoretical question, and leave noisy recovery guarantees to future work. ([De Sa et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.03329))
- **Hyperbolic foundation models.** He et al. list as open challenges fully hyperbolic pre-training at the scale of Euclidean models, missing tooling (no Riemannian AdamW, no hyperbolic FlashAttention), fully hyperbolic retrieval pipelines, and the under-explored geometric interpretation of operations. ([He et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17787v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hyperboloid model (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperboloid_model): the Lorentz model, its bilinear form and distance.
- **Learn:** [Hyperbolic Graph Representation Learning: A Tutorial (ECML-PKDD 2022)](https://hyperbolicgraphlearning.github.io): Riemannian preliminaries, shallow models, hyperbolic GNNs, applications.
- **Primary:** [Nickel and Kiela 2017, Poincaré Embeddings for Learning Hierarchical Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08039): the founding paper.
- **Primary:** [De Sa et al. 2018, Representation Tradeoffs for Hyperbolic Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.03329): constructions, precision bounds, h-MDS.
- **Primary:** [Ganea et al. 2018, Hyperbolic Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09112): gyrovector layers and hyperbolic MLR.
- **Further reading:** [Peng et al., Hyperbolic Deep Neural Networks: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.04562) and [He et al. 2025, Hyperbolic Deep Learning for Foundation Models: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17787v1).
references.Hypothesis Testing:
## Reference
### Overview
A statistical hypothesis test decides between a null hypothesis $H_0$ and an alternative $H_1$ about the distribution of the data, using a test statistic and a rejection region chosen so that the probability of wrongly rejecting a true null (a type I error) is at most a significance level $\alpha$, commonly 5% or 1%. Accepting $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true is a type II error with probability $\beta$, and $1-\beta$ is the power ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing)).

Two traditions are merged in modern practice. Fisher's significance test uses only a null hypothesis and treats the p-value as an informal index; Neyman and Pearson, in a series of papers beginning in 1928, compared two hypotheses with error rates fixed in advance. Textbooks from about 1940 combined the two into the hybrid now called null-hypothesis significance testing ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing)). The mathematical core is the theory of optimal tests (the Neyman–Pearson lemma, uniformly most powerful tests in monotone likelihood ratio families, unbiased tests) and the asymptotic theory of likelihood-based tests ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/testing-one-parameter.html); [Wikipedia: Wilks' theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilks%27_theorem)).

For discovery claims the main practical issues are multiplicity and searching. Running many tests without adjustment inflates the overall type I error ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing)); in particle physics the version that arises when a signal is searched for over a range of masses is the look-elsewhere effect ([Gross and Vitells 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.1891)). A recent line of work replaces p-values by e-values and test martingales, which stay valid under continuous monitoring and optional stopping ([Ramdas et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01948)).

### Formal definition
Let $X\sim P_\theta$, $\theta\in\Theta=\Theta_0\sqcup\Theta_1$, with $H_0:\theta\in\Theta_0$ and $H_1:\theta\in\Theta_1$. A (randomized) test is a measurable $\phi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, the probability of rejecting $H_0$ after observing $x$; its power function is
$$\beta_\phi(\theta)=E_\theta[\phi(X)].$$
The test has **level** $\alpha$ if $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta_\phi(\theta)\le\alpha$, and a level-$\alpha$ test $\phi^*$ is **uniformly most powerful (UMP)** if $\beta_{\phi^*}(\theta)\ge\beta_\phi(\theta)$ for all $\theta\in\Theta_1$ and every level-$\alpha$ $\phi$ ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/hypothesis-testing.html)). A non-randomized test is $\phi=\mathbf 1_R$ for a rejection region $R$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyman%E2%80%93Pearson_lemma)).

For a statistic $T$ whose large values are evidence against $H_0$, the **p-value** of an observed $t$ is the probability of a result at least as extreme under the null; for a simple null this is $P_{\theta_0}(T\ge t)$, and for a composite null it is computed under the least favorable null case,
$$p(t)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}P_\theta(T\ge t),$$
so that $P_\theta(p\le\alpha)\le\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. Under a simple null with continuous $T$, $p$ is uniform on $[0,1]$ ([Wikipedia: p-value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-value)).

An **e-value** for $H_0$ is a nonnegative statistic with expectation at most one under every null distribution; rejecting when it exceeds $1/\alpha$ is a level-$\alpha$ test by Markov's inequality ([Ramdas and Wang](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23614)).

### Key results
- **Neyman–Pearson lemma.** Let $H_0:X\sim P_0$, $H_1:X\sim P_1$ have densities $p_0,p_1$ and $\mathrm{LR}=p_1/p_0$. The test with $\phi=1$ if $\mathrm{LR}>c$, $\phi=\gamma$ if $\mathrm{LR}=c$, $\phi=0$ otherwise, with $E_0\phi=\alpha$, maximizes power among level-$\alpha$ tests ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/hypothesis-testing.html)). Uniqueness concerns the non-randomized form: if a region test $R_{NP}=\{p_1>\eta p_0\}$ (up to a null set) has size exactly $\alpha$ with $\eta>0$, then every most powerful level-$\alpha$ test $R$ has the same form with the same $\eta$ and agrees with $R_{NP}$ with probability 1 under both hypotheses ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyman%E2%80%93Pearson_lemma)). In the Lagrangian form of the proof the value of $\phi$ on $\{\mathrm{LR}=c\}$ does not matter; the randomization $\gamma$ there is used only to make the type I error exactly $\alpha$ ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/hypothesis-testing.html)).
- **UMP tests under monotone likelihood ratio (Karlin–Rubin).** If $\{P_\theta\}$ has monotone likelihood ratio in $T(X)$, the test rejecting for large $T$ (randomizing on the boundary for exact size at $\theta_0$) is UMP for $H_0:\theta\le\theta_0$ against $\theta>\theta_0$ ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/testing-one-parameter.html)). In a one-parameter exponential family the likelihood ratio is increasing in $\sum_iT(X_i)$ ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/hypothesis-testing.html)); Karlin–Rubin is the extension of the lemma to such composite one-sided hypotheses ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyman%E2%80%93Pearson_lemma)).
- **Two-sided alternatives: UMPU.** For $X\sim N(\theta,1)$, $H_0:\theta=0$ against $\theta\ne0$, no test beats both one-tailed tests, so no UMP test exists. A test is unbiased if its power is at least $\alpha$ on $\Theta_1$; UMPU tests exist at least for one-parameter exponential families, with power $\alpha$ at the null boundary and, for a point null, zero power derivative at $\theta_0$ ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/testing-one-parameter.html)).
- **Test–confidence set duality.** A level-$\alpha$ test of $\theta=\theta_0$ rejects exactly when $\theta_0$ lies outside the $1-\alpha$ confidence set obtained by collecting the non-rejected values, a one-to-one correspondence under which most powerful tests correspond to uniformly most accurate intervals and equal-tailed tests to central intervals ([Cousins, Lectures on Statistics in Theory, §7.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1807.05996)). Permutation tests can be inverted the same way ([Wikipedia: Permutation test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_test)).
- **Wilks' theorem (1938).** For nested models with the true parameter in the interior of the parameter space, $-2\log\Lambda\to\chi^2_d$ under $H_0$, $d=\dim\Theta-\dim\Theta_0$. On the boundary the theorem fails and the limit can be a mixture of chi-squared laws, as for variance components in mixed models ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilks%27_theorem)).
- **Wald and score tests.** The Wald statistic $W=(\hat\theta-\theta_0)^2/\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(\hat\theta)$ needs only the unrestricted fit and is not invariant to reparametrizing the restriction ([Wikipedia: Wald test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wald_test)). Rao's score statistic $S=U(\theta_0)^2/I(\theta_0)$, with $U$ the score and $I$ the [Fisher Information](node:Fisher%20Information), needs only the restricted estimate; under $H_0$ Wald, score and likelihood-ratio statistics are asymptotically equivalent $\chi^2$, and when the null is false they converge to noncentral $\chi^2$ laws with possibly different noncentrality parameters ([Wikipedia: Score test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Score_test)).
- **Exactness of permutation tests.** If labels are exchangeable under $H_0$, the permutation test has exact significance level; Monte Carlo versions that count the observed data as one permutation keep the p-value positive ([Wikipedia: Permutation test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_test)).
- **Chernoff–Stein lemma.** For i.i.d. data with the type I error held below a fixed level, the best type II error decays exponentially in $n$ with exponent $D(f_0\|f_1)$, the [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence); with prior weights, the optimal Bayes error has exponent equal to the Chernoff information $\max_{\lambda\in[0,1]}-\log\int f_0^\lambda f_1^{1-\lambda}$ ([Wikipedia: Error exponents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_exponents_in_hypothesis_testing)).
- **Bonferroni and Holm (FWER).** Bonferroni rejects $H_i$ when $p_i\le\alpha/m$. Holm (1979) sorts $p_{(1)}\le\dots\le p_{(m)}$ and rejects $H_{(k)}$ while $p_{(k)}\le\alpha/(m+1-k)$, stopping at the first failure; by Boole's inequality it controls the familywise error rate $P(V\ge1)$ at $\alpha$ in the strong sense without independence assumptions, and is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni ([Wikipedia: Holm–Bonferroni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holm%E2%80%93Bonferroni_method)).
- **Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR).** Rejecting $H_{(1)},\dots,H_{(k)}$ for the largest $k$ with $p_{(k)}\le k\alpha/m$ gives $\mathrm{FDR}\le(m_0/m)\alpha$ for independent statistics (equality for continuous ones) and under positive dependence (Benjamini–Yekutieli 2001); dividing by $c(m)=\sum_{i\le m}1/i$ controls FDR under arbitrary dependence ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_discovery_rate)).
- **Ville's inequality.** For a test martingale $(M_t)$ (nonnegative, $M_0=1$) under the null, $P(\sup_tM_t\ge1/\alpha)\le\alpha$; so rejecting when $M_t$ first crosses $1/\alpha$ is valid under any stopping rule ([Ramdas et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01948)).
- **Trial factor.** For a resonance search over a mass range, the ratio of global to local false-alarm probability grows asymptotically linearly with the local significance; Gross and Vitells give a fast estimate based on Davies' results ([Gross and Vitells 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.1891)).

### Examples
- **Binomial test and randomization.** For $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(100,\theta)$, testing $\theta=0.5$ against $\theta=0.51$ at $\alpha=0.05$: the LR increases in $X$; $P_{0.5}(X>58)=0.044$, and randomizing at $X=58$ with $\gamma\approx0.26$ uses the full budget. Since the test is optimal for every $\theta_1>0.5$, it is UMP for $\theta>0.5$ ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/hypothesis-testing.html)).
- **Unequal tails.** For an exponential scale family testing $\theta=1$ at $\alpha=0.1$, the equal-tailed test has power below $\alpha$ on $(1/2,1)$, so it is biased; the unbiased test puts about $0.08$ of the error in the left tail ([Berkeley Stat 210A reader](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/testing-one-parameter.html)).
- **Normal variance.** With known mean, testing $\sigma_0^2$ against $\sigma_1^2>\sigma_0^2$, the LR depends only on $\sum(x_i-\mu)^2$, a scaled $\chi^2$ variable, so the most powerful test rejects when it is large ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyman%E2%80%93Pearson_lemma)).
- **Bonferroni as a look-elsewhere correction.** With $n$ effectively independent tests, significance requires $p<\alpha/n$; the term gained media attention in 2011 in the LHC Higgs search ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look-elsewhere_effect)).

### History
Arbuthnot (1710) applied what is now a sign test to 82 years of London birth records, Laplace compared birth rates in the 1770s, and Karl Pearson introduced the chi-squared test in 1900 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing)). Neyman and Pearson's series of papers began in 1928 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing)); the lemma appeared in "On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses", *Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A* 231, 289–337 (1933) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rsta.1933.0009); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyman%E2%80%93Pearson_lemma)), and the terms "type I error" and "type II error" come from their 1933 paper in the *Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society* ([Wikipedia: Type I and type II errors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_I_and_type_II_errors)). The Fisher–Neyman dispute ran until Fisher's death in 1962 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing)). Wilks' theorem dates from 1938 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilks%27_theorem)), Ville's inequality from 1939 ([Ramdas et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01948)), Rao's score test from 1948 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Score_test)), and Holm's procedure from 1979 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holm%E2%80%93Bonferroni_method)).

### Connections
- [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): tests are statements about the distribution of a statistic under $H_0$ and $H_1$.
- [Limit Theorems (LLN and CLT)](node:Limit%20Theorems%20%28LLN%20and%20CLT%29): asymptotic null distributions (z-tests, Wilks' limit) come from the CLT.
- [Sampling Distributions](node:Sampling%20Distributions) and [Statistical Quantiles and Critical Values](node:Statistical%20Quantiles%20and%20Critical%20Values): critical values are quantiles of the null distribution.
- [Maximum Likelihood Estimation](node:Maximum%20Likelihood%20Estimation) and [Fisher Information](node:Fisher%20Information): likelihood-ratio, Wald and score tests.
- [Sufficient Statistics](node:Sufficient%20Statistics): in exponential families UMP tests depend only on a sufficient statistic.
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence) and [Information Theory](node:Information%20Theory): the Chernoff–Stein error exponent.
- [Statistical Decision Theory](node:Statistical%20Decision%20Theory): a test is a decision rule with 0–1 loss.
- [Multiple Testing and False Discovery Control](node:Multiple%20Testing%20and%20False%20Discovery%20Control): FWER and FDR procedures.
- [Martingales](node:Martingales) and [Sequential Analysis](node:Sequential%20Analysis): test martingales and anytime-valid testing.
- [Bayesian Inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference): Bayes factors are the Bayesian counterpart; a p-value is not $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$.
- [Bootstrap Methods](node:Bootstrap%20Methods): resampling approximates null distributions.
- [Machine Learning Evaluation](node:Machine%20Learning%20Evaluation): comparing models on benchmarks is a testing problem with multiplicity.

### Common pitfalls
- **The p-value is not $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$.** It does not give the probability that the null is correct; failing to reject is not evidence for $H_0$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing)).
- **Significance is not effect size.** Report intervals as well as tests; a result is often significant when the interval excludes 0 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing)).
- **Post hoc one-sided tests and unreported tests.** Switching to a one-tailed test at the analyst's whim can make a non-significant result significant, and leaving failed tests unpublished understates the number of tests and inflates significance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look-elsewhere_effect)).
- **Optional stopping.** Peeking at a p-value and stopping when it falls below $\alpha$ breaks its guarantee; test martingales survive this ([Ramdas et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01948)).
- **Boundary nulls.** Testing whether a variance component is zero puts the null on the boundary, where the naive $\chi^2$ reference is wrong ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilks%27_theorem)).
- **Exchangeability is the assumption.** A permutation t-test for location requires equal variances under normality, inheriting the Behrens–Fisher problem ([Wikipedia: Permutation test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_test)).
- **Wald is not invariant.** Algebraically equivalent restrictions can give different Wald statistics ([Wikipedia: Wald test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wald_test)).

### Open problems
- **Existence and admissibility of e-processes.** Ramdas, Grünwald, Vovk and Shafer list open questions: for which classes of distributions nontrivial test martingales, test supermartingales or e-processes exist (a separation "not yet fully understood in general"); when coarsening the filtration yields useful new e-processes; in the study of admissible e-processes, delineating exactly when their admissibility condition (a "need for agreement") is required, which they call "an important open problem"; and "understanding the power of universal inference is itself quite open" ([Ramdas et al., §8.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01948)).
- **Sequential testing with general filtrations.** Ramdas and Wang write that the optimality theory of sequential testing is "less well understood" and that "many fundamental questions related to filtrations remain open" ([Ramdas and Wang](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23614)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Statistical hypothesis testing (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing): terminology, history and criticisms of NHST.
- **Reference:** [Neyman–Pearson lemma (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyman%E2%80%93Pearson_lemma): statement with existence and uniqueness.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley Stat 210A reader: Hypothesis testing](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/hypothesis-testing.html): test functions, power, the Neyman–Pearson lemma.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley Stat 210A reader: Testing with one real parameter](https://stat210a.berkeley.edu/fall-2025/reader/testing-one-parameter.html): MLR, one-sided UMP and UMPU tests.
- **Learn:** [Cousins, Lectures on Statistics in Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05996): tests, intervals and their duality for physicists.
- **Primary:** [Neyman and Pearson, On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses (1933)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rsta.1933.0009): the original lemma.
- **Primary:** [Gross and Vitells, Trial factors for the look elsewhere effect (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.1891): trial-factor estimate for mass scans.
- **Further reading:** [Lehmann and Romano, Testing Statistical Hypotheses (Springer, 2022)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-030-70578-7): the standard graduate text on optimal tests.
- **Further reading:** [Ramdas, Grünwald, Vovk and Shafer, Game-theoretic statistics and SAVI (survey)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01948) and [Ramdas and Wang, Hypothesis testing with e-values (monograph)](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23614): e-values, test martingales and open questions.
