## Reference
### Overview
Information retrieval (IR) is the task of identifying and retrieving resources relevant to an information need. Classical models are set-theoretic (Boolean, fuzzy), algebraic (vector space, latent semantic indexing) or probabilistic (the binary independence model, BM25, language models); feature-based models combine many signals, usually by learning to rank, and data fusion merges ranked lists from several systems ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_retrieval)).

The basic data structure is the inverted index, the inversion of a forward (document-to-terms) index: it maps each term to the documents, and in a word-level index the positions, where it occurs ([Wikipedia: Inverted index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverted_index)). Large engines process thousands of queries per second over billions of documents, so compressed postings and early-termination algorithms such as WAND matter as much as the scoring function ([Ding and Suel 2011](https://research.engineering.nyu.edu/~suel/papers/bmw.pdf)).

Retrieval models are now commonly split into sparse methods that keep inverted indexes (BM25, and learned sparse models such as SPLADE), dense methods that map queries and documents to continuous vectors, and hybrids ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_retrieval); [Formal et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2107.05720)). A standard pipeline retrieves about 1,000 candidates with BM25 and then re-ranks them with a BERT cross-encoder ([Nogueira and Cho 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.04085)). On the zero-shot BEIR benchmark BM25 remained a strong baseline, and dense retrievers often generalized worse out of domain ([Thakur et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663)).

### Formal definition
Let $\mathcal D$ be a finite collection and $\mathcal Q$ a set of queries. A **ranked retrieval model** is a scoring function $s:\mathcal Q\times\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$; for $q$ the system returns documents in decreasing order of $s(q,d)$, truncated at depth $k$, and is judged against binary or graded relevance labels ([Wikipedia: Evaluation measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_measures_%28information_retrieval%29)).

**Probabilistic relevance.** With classes $w_1$ (relevant), $w_2$ (non-relevant) and document description $x$, retrieve $x$ when $P(w_1\mid x)>P(w_2\mid x)$. If binary index terms $x_i$ are independent given relevance, the discriminant is linear with weights
$$c_i=\log\frac{p_i(1-q_i)}{q_i(1-p_i)},\qquad p_i=P(x_i=1\mid w_1),\ q_i=P(x_i=1\mid w_2).$$
([van Rijsbergen, ch. 6](http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/Keith/Chapter.6/Ch.6.html); [Wikipedia: Binary independence model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_Independence_Model))

**Okapi BM25.** With $f(q_i,D)$ the count of $q_i$ in $D$, $|D|$ the length, $\mathrm{avgdl}$ the mean length, $N$ the collection size and $n(q_i)$ the document frequency,
$$\mathrm{score}(D,Q)=\sum_{i} \mathrm{IDF}(q_i)\,\frac{f(q_i,D)\,(k_1+1)}{f(q_i,D)+k_1\bigl(1-b+b\,\tfrac{|D|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\bigr)},\qquad \mathrm{IDF}(q_i)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{N-n(q_i)+0.5}{n(q_i)+0.5}+1\Bigr),$$
usually with $k_1\in[1.2,2.0]$ and $b=0.75$ ([Wikipedia: Okapi BM25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25)).

**Query-likelihood language models.** Build a language model $M_d$ for each document and rank by $P(q\mid M_d)$; by Bayes, $P(d\mid q)\propto P(q\mid d)P(d)$, so this is ranking by posterior under a uniform document prior (Ponte and Croft 1998) ([Wikipedia: Query likelihood model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Query_likelihood_model); [Cummins, Cambridge lecture 5](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1617/InfoRtrv/lecture5-language-models.pdf)). Maximum-likelihood unigram estimates give unseen terms probability zero, so they are smoothed with the collection model $\mathrm{cf}_t/|c|$:
$$\text{Jelinek–Mercer: }\hat P(t\mid M_d)=\lambda\frac{\mathrm{tf}_{t,d}}{|d|}+(1-\lambda)\frac{\mathrm{cf}_t}{|c|},\qquad \text{Dirichlet: }\hat P(t\mid M_d)=\frac{\mathrm{tf}_{t,d}+\mu\,\mathrm{cf}_t/|c|}{|d|+\mu},$$
and documents are ranked by $\sum_{t\in q}\log\hat P(t\mid M_d)$. Dirichlet smoothing, which trusts longer documents' estimates more, has been found more effective in IR ([Cummins, Cambridge lecture 5](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1617/InfoRtrv/lecture5-language-models.pdf)).

**Evaluation measures.** Precision $=|\mathrm{rel}\cap\mathrm{ret}|/|\mathrm{ret}|$, recall $=|\mathrm{rel}\cap\mathrm{ret}|/|\mathrm{rel}|$, $F_\beta=(1+\beta^2)PR/(\beta^2P+R)$; $\mathrm{AP}=\sum_k P(k)\,\mathrm{rel}(k)/|\mathrm{rel}|$, with MAP its mean over queries; $\mathrm{DCG}_p=\sum_{i=1}^p \mathrm{rel}_i/\log_2(i+1)$ and $\mathrm{nDCG}_p=\mathrm{DCG}_p/\mathrm{IDCG}_p$, IDCG being the DCG of the list sorted by relevance ([Wikipedia: Evaluation measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_measures_%28information_retrieval%29)).

### Key results
- **Bayes-optimal decision and the probability ranking principle (PRP).** Retrieving $x$ exactly when $P(w_1\mid x)>P(w_2\mid x)$ minimizes the average probability of error. Ranking by decreasing probability of relevance is optimal under the assumption that the relevance of a document is independent of the other documents in the collection, and the principle can only be shown for one query. ([van Rijsbergen, ch. 6](http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/Keith/Chapter.6/Ch.6.html))
- **Binary independence weights.** Under term independence given relevance, the decision function is linear in term presence with weights $c_i$; with full relevance information $p_i\approx r/R$ and $q_i\approx(n-r)/(N-R)$ ([van Rijsbergen, ch. 6](http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/Keith/Chapter.6/Ch.6.html)). Robertson and Spärck Jones showed that weighting by $\log\frac{p_i(1-q_i)}{(1-p_i)q_i}$ gives optimal retrieval effectiveness under that assumption ([Wikipedia: Binary independence model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_Independence_Model)), and BM25's IDF derives from this model ([Wikipedia: Okapi BM25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25)).
- **Rocchio relevance feedback.** The query maximizing $\mathrm{sim}(q,C_r)-\mathrm{sim}(q,C_{nr})$ under cosine similarity is the difference of the centroids of relevant and non-relevant documents. Since these sets are only partly known, Rocchio uses
$$\vec q_m=\alpha\vec q_0+\beta\tfrac1{|C_r|}\textstyle\sum_{d\in C_r}\vec d-\gamma\tfrac1{|C_{nr}|}\sum_{d\in C_{nr}}\vec d,$$
with reasonable values $\alpha=1$, $\beta=0.75$, $\gamma=0.15$ ($\gamma<\beta$, since positive feedback is worth more). Relevance-based language models (Lavrenko 2001) estimate a relevance model $\theta_R$ from known relevant documents and mix it with the original query model as $(1-\pi)\theta_R+\pi\theta_q$, where $\pi$ sets how much of the original query is retained; the variant **RM3** is among the best performing, for both relevance and pseudo-relevance feedback. ([Cummins, Cambridge lecture 7](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1617/InfoRtrv/lecture7-relevance-feedback.pdf))
- **Safe early termination (WAND, block-max WAND).** Document-at-a-time WAND (Broder et al.) stores a maximum impact score per term, keeps lists sorted by current docID, and sums the maxima until they reach the current top-$k$ threshold (the lowest score in the result heap); no docID below the resulting pivot can enter the top $k$, so the other lists skip ahead. The result equals exhaustive disjunctive evaluation. Block-max indexes store the maximum score of each compressed block of postings, letting WAND skip whole blocks, and docID reassignment narrows the gap to conjunctive query speed. ([Ding and Suel 2011](https://research.engineering.nyu.edu/~suel/papers/bmw.pdf))
- **Gap coding of postings.** Sorted docIDs are stored as gaps between consecutive IDs and coded with variable-length integer codes. In a back-of-envelope example with $2^{38}$ documents and a term in $2^{28}$ of them, raw IDs need 38 bits each, while Elias $\delta$-coding gaps of mean $2^{10}$ needs about 17 bits each, less than half the space ([Princeton COS 435 notes](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring15/cos435/notes/compressionSummaryPart2.pdf)). Byte-aligned codes use 7 payload bits per byte and the top bit to flag continuation ([Wikipedia: Variable-length quantity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable-length_quantity)); block codes such as PForDelta use 64-posting blocks in the block-max experiments ([Ding and Suel 2011](https://research.engineering.nyu.edu/~suel/papers/bmw.pdf)).
- **Learning to rank.** Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches score documents, pairs, or whole lists. RankNet models the probability that one document outranks another as a logistic function of the score difference; LambdaRank weights each pair's contribution by the change in the IR metric from swapping the pair; LambdaMART approximates listwise objectives and an ensemble of LambdaMART models won the 2010 Yahoo Learning to Rank challenge. Direct optimization is hard because most evaluation measures are not continuous functions of the scores. ([Wikipedia: Learning to rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learning_to_rank))
- **Cross-encoder re-ranking (monoBERT).** Feed the query as sentence A and the passage as sentence B (query at most 64 tokens, total 512), pass the [CLS] vector to a single-layer network for the probability of relevance, fine-tune with cross-entropy using BM25 top-1000 negatives, and re-rank. On MS MARCO this raised MRR@10 from 16.7 (BM25) to 36.5 on dev and 35.8 on eval. ([Nogueira and Cho 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.04085))
- **Learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE).** With MLM-head logits $w_{ij}$ of input token $i$ over vocabulary entry $j$, the document weight is $w_j=\sum_{i}\log(1+\mathrm{ReLU}(w_{ij}))$, so terms absent from the text can get weight (expansion). The FLOPS regularizer $\sum_{j}\bigl(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N w_j^{(d_i)}\bigr)^2$ is a smooth relaxation of the average scoring cost and keeps vectors sparse; scores are dot products, served from an inverted index. ([Formal et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2107.05720))
- **Dense and late-interaction retrieval.** A dual-encoder dense retriever trained on modest question–passage data beat Lucene-BM25 by 9–19 points absolute in top-20 passage accuracy on open-domain QA ([Karpukhin et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906)). ColBERT encodes query and document independently with BERT and applies a cheap late interaction, so documents can be precomputed; it was competitive with BERT re-rankers at about two orders of magnitude less latency ([Khattab and Zaharia 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832)).
- **Dimension limit of single-vector retrieval.** The number of top-$k$ document subsets that inner-product retrieval with $d$-dimensional embeddings can return is bounded in terms of $d$; the limit persists even when free embeddings are optimized directly on the test set ([Weller et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21038)).

### Examples
- **BM25.** A term occurring in most documents gets IDF near zero, and long documents are penalized through $b\,|D|/\mathrm{avgdl}$; $b=1$ gives BM11 and $b=0$ BM15 ([Wikipedia: Okapi BM25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25)).
- **Phrase queries.** A record-level index stores only document references for each term; phrase searches need a word-level index that also stores positions, which costs more space and processing to build ([Wikipedia: Inverted index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverted_index)).
- **WAND pivot.** For query "dog cat kangaroo monkey" with current docIDs 609, 273, 9007, 4866 and threshold 6.8, sorting by docID and adding maxima $2.3+1.8+3.3>6.8$ makes 4866 the pivot, so the first two lists jump to docID at least 4866 ([Ding and Suel 2011](https://research.engineering.nyu.edu/~suel/papers/bmw.pdf)).

### History
Bush's 1945 "As We May Think" anticipated automated search; Luhn began punch-card search for chemical compounds in 1947 and published on auto-encoding documents for retrieval in 1959; Salton's SMART system dates from the 1960s; Cleverdon's Cranfield studies (1962) developed a model for evaluating IR systems; NIST and the US Department of Defense cosponsored TREC from 1992; and Google introduced PageRank in 1998 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_retrieval)). Robertson, Spärck Jones and others developed the probabilistic framework in the 1970s and 1980s, and BM25 is named after City University London's Okapi system ([Wikipedia: Okapi BM25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25)). Van Rijsbergen's *Information Retrieval* (1975; 2nd ed. 1979) gave the decision-theoretic treatment ([van Rijsbergen](http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/Keith/Preface.html)). The MS MARCO dataset of Bing queries appeared in November 2016 ([Bajaj et al. 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.09268)). Google released BERT in October 2018 and announced on 25 October 2019 that it was using BERT for US English search queries ([Wikipedia: BERT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BERT_%28language_model%29)). ColBERT (SIGIR 2020) and SPLADE (SIGIR 2021) followed ([Khattab and Zaharia 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832); [Formal et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2107.05720)).

### Connections
- [Lexical Retrieval and BM25](node:Lexical%20Retrieval%20and%20BM25): the probabilistic-relevance branch in detail.
- [Vector Search and Embeddings](node:Vector%20Search%20and%20Embeddings): dense retrieval represents queries and documents as vectors.
- [Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search](node:Approximate%20Nearest-Neighbor%20Search): the index that makes dense retrieval scale.
- [Learning to Rank](node:Learning%20to%20Rank): learned scoring functions over many relevance features.
- [Precision and Recall](node:Precision%20and%20Recall): the basic set-based evaluation measures.
- [Language Modeling](node:Language%20Modeling): query likelihood ranks documents by a per-document language model.
- [Transformers](node:Transformers): cross-encoders, ColBERT and SPLADE are built on BERT.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss): the training loss for monoBERT re-rankers.
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation](node:Retrieval-Augmented%20Generation): uses an IR system to ground language-model outputs.
- [Recommender Systems](node:Recommender%20Systems): ranking without an explicit query.
- [Bayes' Theorem](node:Bayes'%20Theorem): turns the relevance decision into a comparison of class-conditional likelihoods.
- [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): underlies latent semantic indexing.
- [Huffman Coding](node:Huffman%20Coding): another variable-length code; postings use integer codes for gaps.
- [Private Information Retrieval](node:Private%20Information%20Retrieval): a cryptographic problem with the same name but a different goal.

### Common pitfalls
- **Reading the PRP as global optimality.** Its optimality rests on independent document relevance and holds for one query, not over a range of queries ([van Rijsbergen, ch. 6](http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/Keith/Chapter.6/Ch.6.html)).
- **Treating in-domain gains as general.** Dense retrievers that beat BM25 in domain may trail it zero-shot ([Thakur et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663)).
- **Assuming relevance is well defined.** Queries may be ill-posed and relevance comes in shades ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_retrieval)).
- **Over-trusting feedback.** Relevance feedback creates long, expensive queries and works best when relevant documents contain similar terms ([Cummins, Cambridge lecture 7](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1617/InfoRtrv/lecture7-relevance-feedback.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Overcoming the single-vector limit.** Weller et al. call the dimension bound a fundamental limitation of the single-vector paradigm and call for future research on techniques that resolve it; state-of-the-art embedders fail their LIMIT stress test ([Weller et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21038)).
- **Zero-shot generalization of neural retrievers.** On BEIR, re-ranking and late-interaction models do best zero-shot but at high computational cost, while the cheaper dense and sparse retrievers often underperform; the authors point to considerable room for improvement in these retrievers' generalization capabilities ([Thakur et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Information retrieval (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_retrieval): history, model families, neural retrieval.
- **Reference:** [Evaluation measures (information retrieval)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_measures_%28information_retrieval%29): precision, recall, MAP, nDCG.
- **Learn:** [Cummins, Cambridge Part II Information Retrieval, lecture 7](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1617/InfoRtrv/lecture7-relevance-feedback.pdf): Rocchio, relevance models, query expansion ([lecture 5](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1617/InfoRtrv/lecture5-language-models.pdf) covers language models).
- **Learn:** [van Rijsbergen, *Information Retrieval*, 2nd ed. (Univ. of Glasgow)](http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/Keith/Preface.html): classic textbook; chapter 6 derives probabilistic retrieval.
- **Primary:** [Ding and Suel 2011, Faster Top-k Document Retrieval Using Block-Max Indexes](https://research.engineering.nyu.edu/~suel/papers/bmw.pdf): WAND and block-max WAND.
- **Primary:** [Nogueira and Cho 2019, Passage Re-ranking with BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04085): the monoBERT cross-encoder.
- **Primary:** [Formal et al. 2021, SPLADE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720): learned sparse retrieval.
- **Primary:** [Karpukhin et al. 2020, Dense Passage Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906) and [Thakur et al. 2021, BEIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663): dense retrieval and its zero-shot evaluation.
- **Primary:** [Weller et al. 2025, On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21038): dimension bound for single-vector retrieval.
- **Further reading:** [Manning, Raghavan and Schütze, *Introduction to Information Retrieval* (CUP, 2008)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-information-retrieval/669D108D20F556C5C30957D63B5AB65C): textbook on classical and web retrieval, indexing and search systems, evaluation, and text classification and clustering.

## Reference
### Overview
Information theory is the mathematical study of the quantification, storage and communication of information. It was founded by Claude Shannon's "A Mathematical Theory of Communication", published in the *Bell System Technical Journal* in July and October 1948, building on Nyquist (1924) and Hartley (1928). Its central quantities are entropy, mutual information and relative entropy (KL divergence), and its central results identify the entropy of a source as the limit of lossless compression and the channel capacity as the limit of reliable communication ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)).

Shannon's 1948 paper defined the entropy $H=-K\sum_i p_i\log p_i$, proved that it is the unique measure satisfying three natural axioms, defined the capacity of a noisy channel as a maximum of transmitted information over input sources, and proved that rates up to capacity can be achieved with arbitrarily small error. He noted that the form of $H$ is that of entropy in statistical mechanics ([Shannon 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)).

As a graduate subject it covers information measures (entropy, divergence, mutual information and their inequalities), lossless and lossy compression, binary hypothesis testing and large deviations, channel coding with converses and error exponents, and multi-user problems such as the multiple-access channel ([MIT 6.441 lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-441-information-theory-spring-2016/pages/lecture-notes/)).

### Formal definition
For discrete random variables with joint law $p(x,y)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)):
$$H(X)=-\sum_x p(x)\log p(x),\qquad H(X\mid Y)=-\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log p(x\mid y)=H(X,Y)-H(Y),$$
$$I(X;Y)=\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)=I(Y;X).$$
Logarithms to base 2 give bits (shannons), base $e$ gives nats, base 10 gives hartleys ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)).

The **relative entropy** of $P$ from $Q$, defined when $P\ll Q$, is
$$D(P\,\|\,Q)=\int\log\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dP,$$
which in the discrete case is $\sum_x P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$; mutual information is $I(X;Y)=D(P_{XY}\,\|\,P_X\otimes P_Y)$ ([Wikipedia: KL divergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).

For a channel with input $X$ and output $Y$, the **capacity** is $C=\max_{p_X} I(X;Y)$, the maximum over input distributions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)); Shannon wrote it as $C=\max\big(H(x)-H_y(x)\big)$, the maximum over all input sources of entropy minus equivocation ([Shannon 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Uniqueness of entropy (Shannon's Theorem 2).** The only function $H(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ that is continuous in the $p_i$, increasing in $n$ for uniform distributions, and satisfies the grouping (decomposition-of-choice) rule is $H=-K\sum_i p_i\log p_i$ with $K>0$ ([Shannon 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)).
- **Gibbs' inequality.** $D(P\|Q)\ge 0$, with equality if and only if $P=Q$ as measures; consequently $I(X;Y)\ge0$ ([Wikipedia: KL divergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- **Data processing inequality.** If $X\to Y\to Z$ is a Markov chain, i.e. $p(x,y,z)=p(x)p(y\mid x)p(z\mid y)$, then $I(X;Y)\ge I(X;Z)$, with equality iff $I(X;Y\mid Z)=0$. The proof expands $I(X;Y,Z)$ by the chain rule in two ways and uses $I(X;Z\mid Y)=0$ ([Wikipedia: DPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_processing_inequality)).
- **Source coding theorem.** $N$ i.i.d. copies of $X$ can be compressed into slightly more than $NH(X)$ bits with vanishing probability of loss as $N\to\infty$, and with fewer than $NH(X)$ bits loss is virtually certain. For a single symbol and an optimal uniquely decodable code over an alphabet of size $a$, $\frac{H(X)}{\log_2 a}\le\mathbb E[S]<\frac{H(X)}{\log_2 a}+1$ ([Wikipedia: source coding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon%27s_source_coding_theorem)). Shannon's own form: a source of entropy $H$ bits/symbol can be sent over a noiseless channel of capacity $C$ at rate $C/H-\epsilon$ symbols per second, and not faster than $C/H$ ([Shannon 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)).
- **Noisy-channel coding theorem (Shannon's Theorem 11).** For a discrete channel of capacity $C$ and a source of entropy rate $H$: if $H\le C$ there is a coding system transmitting the source with arbitrarily small frequency of errors; if $H>C$ the equivocation can be made less than $H-C+\epsilon$ but never less than $H-C$ ([Shannon 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)). Equivalently, every rate $R<C$ admits codes with arbitrarily small block error, and no rate $R>C$ does ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)).
- **Gaussian channel.** For band-limit $W$, average signal power $P$ and white Gaussian noise power $N$, the capacity is $C=W\log\frac{P+N}{N}$ ([Shannon 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)).

### Examples
- **Binary symmetric channel** with crossover probability $p$: $C=1-H_b(p)$ bits per use, where $H_b(p)=-p\log_2p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)).
- **Binary erasure channel** with erasure probability $p$: $C=1-p$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)).
- **Uniform choice.** For $n$ equally likely messages $H=\log_2 n$ bits, the maximum possible entropy over $n$ messages; Hartley's earlier (1928) measure was $H=n\log S$ for $n$ symbols from an alphabet of size $S$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)).

### History
Nyquist (1924) related transmission speed to $\log m$ for $m$ signal levels and Hartley (1928) proposed $H=n\log S$; Shannon's 1948 paper then introduced the probabilistic theory ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)). Shannon credited Nyquist and Hartley and observed that formulas like $C=W\log\frac{P+N}{N}$ had been developed independently by several other writers ([Shannon 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)). Kullback and Leibler introduced relative entropy in 1951 as "mean information for discrimination"; Jeffreys had defined the symmetrized version in 1948 ([Wikipedia: KL divergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).

### Connections
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence): relative entropy, the parent quantity of mutual information.
- [Thermodynamic Entropy](node:Thermodynamic%20Entropy): Shannon's $H$ has the form of the Gibbs entropy of statistical mechanics.
- [Statistical Mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics): Gibbs entropy has the same functional form as Shannon entropy.
- [Rate-Distortion Theory](node:Rate-Distortion%20Theory): the lossy-compression counterpart of the source coding theorem.
- [Coding Theory](node:Coding%20Theory): explicit codes approaching the capacity promised by the channel coding theorem.
- [Huffman Coding](node:Huffman%20Coding) and [Arithmetic Coding](node:Arithmetic%20Coding): practical prefix and stream codes near the entropy bound.
- [Lossless Compression](node:Lossless%20Compression): the operational meaning of entropy.
- [Kolmogorov Complexity](node:Kolmogorov%20Complexity): an algorithmic, single-object analogue of entropy.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss) and [Maximum Likelihood Estimation](node:Maximum%20Likelihood%20Estimation): likelihood maximization minimizes cross-entropy and KL divergence.
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing): Stein and Chernoff exponents are divergences.
- [Quantum Channel Capacity](node:Quantum%20Channel%20Capacity): the quantum generalization of channel capacity.

### Common pitfalls
- KL divergence is not a metric: it is asymmetric and fails the triangle inequality ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory)).
- $D(P\|Q)$ is defined (finite) only when $Q(x)=0$ implies $P(x)=0$ ([Wikipedia: KL divergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- The data processing inequality requires the Markov structure $X\to Y\to Z$; it says post-processing cannot increase information about $X$, not that it cannot change it ([Wikipedia: DPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_processing_inequality)).
- Shannon's proof of the coding theorem shows that good codes exist in a random ensemble rather than exhibiting one, a point he flagged himself ([Shannon 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Capacity of the interference channel.** The capacity region of the two-user Gaussian interference channel "has been open for thirty years" (as of 2007); the best achievable region then known was the Han–Kobayashi scheme, and Etkin, Tse and Wang showed that a simplified Han–Kobayashi scheme achieves capacity only to within one bit ([Etkin, Tse and Wang 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0702045)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Information theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_theory): definitions, coding theorems, channel examples, history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.441 Information Theory (Polyanskiy, OCW 2016)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-441-information-theory-spring-2016/): graduate lecture notes on information measures, compression, hypothesis testing, channel coding, rate distortion.
- **Primary:** [Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf): the founding paper; Theorems 2, 9, 11 and the Gaussian channel.
- **Primary:** [Etkin, Tse, Wang, Gaussian Interference Channel Capacity to Within One Bit](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0702045): state of the interference-channel problem.
- **Further reading:** [Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed. (Wiley, 2006)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Elements+of+Information+Theory%2C+2nd+Edition-p-9780471241959): the standard graduate text covering entropy, compression, capacity, rate distortion, network information theory, hypothesis testing.

## Reference
### Overview
An inner product space is a real or complex vector space with an inner product: a conjugate-symmetric, positive-definite pairing that is linear in one argument. It generalizes the dot product on Euclidean space and supplies lengths, angles and orthogonality. Every inner product induces a norm, its canonical norm, so every inner product space is a normed and hence a metric space. Giuseppe Peano is credited with first using the concept, in 1898. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space))

A complete inner product space is a Hilbert space, and every inner product space can be completed to a Hilbert space in which it is dense. The study of positive-definite inner product spaces is, in nLab's words, essentially the study of Hilbert spaces; nLab also treats semidefinite, nondegenerate and indefinite variants. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/inner+product+space))

In finite dimensions the theory culminates in orthonormal bases, orthogonal projections, Gram–Schmidt and the spectral theorem for self-adjoint and normal operators. In infinite dimensions completeness becomes essential: the projection theorem, the Riesz representation theorem and the existence of adjoints all use it. ([Wikipedia, Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem); [Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space); [Wikipedia, Riesz representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz_representation_theorem))

### Formal definition
Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. An inner product is a map $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb{F}$ such that for all $x,y,z\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb{F}$: $\langle x,y\rangle=\overline{\langle y,x\rangle}$ (conjugate symmetry), $\langle ax+by,z\rangle=a\langle x,z\rangle+b\langle y,z\rangle$ (linearity in the first argument), and $\langle x,x\rangle>0$ for $x\neq0$ (positive-definiteness). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space))

Conjugate-linearity in the second argument follows. Over $\mathbb{R}$ this is a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space))

nLab uses the physicists' convention, antilinear in the *first* variable, and calls the mathematicians' choice the reverse; the two agree on real spaces. nLab's variants: the pairing is nondegenerate if $\langle x,y\rangle=0$ for all $y$ forces $x=0$, definite if $\|x\|^2=0$ forces $x=0$, and positive if $\|x\|^2\ge0$ always. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/inner+product+space))

The norm is $\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$; $x\perp y$ means $\langle x,y\rangle=0$; a family $(e_i)$ is orthonormal if $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space)) For a bounded operator $A$ on a Hilbert space, the adjoint $A^*$ is defined by $\langle x,A^*y\rangle=\langle Ax,y\rangle$, and $A^{**}=A$. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))

### Key results
- **Cauchy–Schwarz.** $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space))
- **Polarization.** The inner product is recovered from the norm: over $\mathbb{R}$, $\langle x,y\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2\bigr)$; over $\mathbb{C}$ one adds $\tfrac{1}{4i}\bigl(\|ix+y\|^2-\|ix-y\|^2\bigr)$, which is correct for an inner product linear in the first argument. ([Wikipedia, Parallelogram law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallelogram_law))
- **Jordan–von Neumann theorem.** A norm on a real or complex normed space satisfies the parallelogram law $\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2$ if and only if it is induced by an inner product, which is then unique and given by polarization. Consequently every Banach space satisfying the parallelogram identity is a Hilbert space. ([Wikipedia, Polarization identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarization_identity); [Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))
- **Pythagoras, Bessel and Parseval.** If $x_1,\dots,x_n$ are pairwise orthogonal, $\|\sum x_i\|^2=\sum\|x_i\|^2$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space)) For any orthonormal system $(f_i)$ in a Hilbert space, Bessel's inequality $\sum_i|\langle x,f_i\rangle|^2\le\|x\|^2$ holds; equality for every $x$ (Parseval's identity) holds if and only if the system is an orthonormal basis. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))
- **Gram–Schmidt and QR.** From linearly independent $v_1,\dots,v_k$ the recursion $u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\frac{\langle v_k,u_j\rangle}{\langle u_j,u_j\rangle}u_j$ gives an orthogonal family with the same span at every stage; normalizing yields an orthonormal one, so every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis. Applied to the columns of a full-column-rank matrix it gives the $QR$ decomposition. ([Wikipedia, Gram–Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process))
- **Projection theorem.** If $C$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space $H$, each $x\in H$ has a unique nearest point in $C$. If $V$ is a closed subspace, every $x$ decomposes uniquely as $v+w$ with $v\in V$, $w\in V^\perp$, so $H=V\oplus V^\perp$, and $V^{\perp\perp}=\overline V$ for any subspace. The orthogonal projection $P_V$ is self-adjoint, idempotent, of norm at most $1$, and $P_Vx$ is the point of $V$ closest to $x$. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))
- **Riesz (Fréchet–Riesz) representation theorem.** For every continuous linear functional $\varphi$ on a Hilbert space $H$ there is a unique $f_\varphi\in H$ with $\varphi(x)=\langle x,f_\varphi\rangle$ for all $x$, and $\|f_\varphi\|=\|\varphi\|$. It is usually attributed to Riesz and Fréchet in 1907. The existence half uses completeness of $H$; the map $H\to H^*$ is onto when $H$ is complete. ([Wikipedia, Riesz representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz_representation_theorem))
- **Orthonormal bases and $\ell^2$.** Every separable inner product space and every complete one has an orthonormal basis, but not every inner product space has one. For separable $V$ with orthonormal basis $(e_k)$, $x\mapsto(\langle x,e_k\rangle)_k$ (with the first-slot-linear convention used here) is an isometric linear map into $\ell^2$ with dense image. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space)) A Hilbert space is separable if and only if it has a countable orthonormal basis; every Hilbert space is isometrically isomorphic to $\ell^2(B)$ with $|B|$ its Hilbert dimension. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))
- **Spectral theorem.** If $A$ is Hermitian (self-adjoint) on a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, then $V$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $A$ and every eigenvalue is real. A complex matrix $A$ is normal if and only if $A=UDU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $D$ diagonal; the eigenvalues need not be real. For a compact self-adjoint operator on a real or complex Hilbert space there is again an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues. ([Wikipedia, Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))

### Examples
- **Euclidean and unitary space.** $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i x_i\overline{y_i}$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$, the dot product on $\mathbb{R}^n$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space))
- **Continuous functions.** $C[a,b]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_a^b f\,\overline g$ is an inner product space but not complete: continuous functions approximating a step on $[-1,1]$ form a Cauchy sequence with no continuous limit. Its completion is a Hilbert space. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space))
- **Frobenius inner product.** On complex square matrices, $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB^\dagger)$ is positive definite. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space))
- **Sequence space.** $\ell^2$ of square-summable sequences is the model infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space; every such space is isometrically isomorphic to it. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))

### History
Peano first used an inner product on a vector space in 1898. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space)) The Gram–Schmidt process is named for Gram and Schmidt, though Laplace knew it earlier; in Lie theory it is generalized by the Iwasawa decomposition. ([Wikipedia, Gram–Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process)) Riesz and Fréchet proved the representation theorem in 1907. ([Wikipedia, Riesz representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz_representation_theorem)) Von Neumann's 1930 *Mathematische Annalen* paper on Hermitian operators discussed Hermitian inner products in defining Hilbert space, and separability was originally part of his definition. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/inner+product+space); [Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space)) The parallelogram characterization is credited to von Neumann and named the Jordan–von Neumann theorem. ([Wikipedia, Polarization identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarization_identity))

### Connections
- [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces): the underlying algebraic structure.
- [Dual Vector Space](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space): in finite dimensions, and in Hilbert space by [Riesz](node:Riesz%20Representation%20Theorems), the inner product identifies $V$ with its dual (antilinearly over $\mathbb{C}$).
- [Gram–Schmidt Process](node:Gram–Schmidt%20Process) and [QR Factorization](node:QR%20Factorization): orthonormalization and its matrix form.
- [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices): on $\mathbb{R}^n$, inner products are $x^TMy$ with $M$ positive definite.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) and [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): adjoints and the [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem).
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): complete inner product spaces; [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) are the complete normed generalization.
- [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces): the metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$.
- [Compact and Selfadjoint Operators](node:Compact%20and%20Selfadjoint%20Operators) and [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory): the infinite-dimensional spectral theorem.
- [Lax–Milgram Theorem](node:Lax–Milgram%20Theorem): a coercive-form extension of the Riesz representation theorem.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) and [Orthogonal Expansions and Wavelets](node:Orthogonal%20Expansions%20and%20Wavelets): Bessel, Parseval and orthonormal expansions.
- [Lorentzian Vector Spaces](node:Lorentzian%20Vector%20Spaces) and [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime): indefinite, nondegenerate pairings.
- [Postulates of Quantum Mechanics](node:Postulates%20of%20Quantum%20Mechanics): state spaces are Hilbert spaces.
- Map: [MSC 15Axx - Basic linear algebra](node:MSC%2015Axx%20-%20Basic%20linear%20algebra)

### Common pitfalls
- **Which slot is antilinear.** Mathematics texts (and Wikipedia) are linear in the first argument; nLab and physics are antilinear in the first. Adjoint and polarization formulas change accordingly. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/inner+product+space))
- **Completeness hypotheses.** The projection theorem, the existence half of Riesz representation, and the existence of orthonormal bases are statements about Hilbert spaces; an incomplete inner product space can lack an orthonormal basis. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space); [Wikipedia, Riesz representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz_representation_theorem); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space))
- **Orthonormal basis means Hilbert basis.** In infinite dimensions an orthonormal basis has dense span, not full algebraic span; vectors are infinite sums of basis elements. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))
- **Classical Gram–Schmidt in floating point.** It is numerically unstable; the modified version subtracts projections sequentially and has smaller rounding errors. ([Wikipedia, Gram–Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process))
- **Normal is not Hermitian.** Normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable but may have non-real eigenvalues. ([Wikipedia, Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Invariant subspace problem.** Does every bounded linear operator on a separable complex Hilbert space of dimension greater than one have a non-trivial closed invariant subspace? Chalendar and Partington's 2025 survey states that the problem remains open for Hilbert spaces, with partial results for specific operator classes, and that it is still unknown whether every Hilbert-space operator has a hyperinvariant subspace. ([Chalendar and Partington](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.21834v1)) Enflo and later Read constructed operators on Banach spaces with no non-trivial invariant subspaces. Positive results include Aronszajn–Smith (1954) for compact operators and Lomonosov (1973) for operators commuting with a nonzero compact operator. ([Wikipedia, Invariant subspace problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Inner product space (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space): axioms, norm, polarization, orthonormal bases, examples; [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/inner+product+space) for conventions and variants.
- **Learn:** [Strang, MIT 18.06SC, Orthogonal matrices and Gram–Schmidt](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/pages/least-squares-determinants-and-eigenvalues/orthogonal-matrices-and-gram-schmidt/): lecture video, summary and problems; [MIT 18.102 Introduction to Functional Analysis](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/): Hilbert spaces, compact self-adjoint operators and the spectral theorem.
- **Primary:** [Axler, *Linear Algebra Done Right*, Springer Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics (2015)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-11080-6): textbook on finite-dimensional linear algebra (bibliographic record).
- **Further reading:** [Conway, *A Course in Functional Analysis*, Springer GTM](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-4383-8): graduate text in functional analysis (bibliographic record).

## Reference
### Overview
Integral calculus studies the definite integral of a function on an interval, first as signed area and then as the inverse of differentiation, together with the techniques (substitution, integration by parts) that turn integrals into antiderivative computations. In real analysis the standard elementary construction is the Riemann integral: one approximates the region under a graph by rectangles, forms Riemann sums, and takes a limit as the partitions become finer. Every continuous function on a closed bounded interval is Riemann integrable; in advanced analysis the Riemann integral is often replaced by the Lebesgue integral. ([Wikipedia: Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral); [MIT 18.100A notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/mit18_100af20_lec_full.pdf))

The fundamental theorem of calculus (FTC) identifies differentiation and integration as inverse operations. The first part says that the integral of a continuous $f$ from a fixed lower limit to a variable upper limit is an antiderivative of $f$; the second part (Newton–Leibniz) says that if $F'=f$ and $f$ is Riemann integrable, then $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$. The Riemann integrability hypothesis in the second part is not automatic: some functions with antiderivatives are not Riemann integrable (Volterra's function), and the Lebesgue and Henstock–Kurzweil integrals extend the theorem to broader classes. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_calculus))

Two further generalizations sit next to the Riemann integral. The Riemann–Stieltjes integral $\int f\,dg$ integrates against a function $g$ of bounded variation and was the setting of F. Riesz's original description of the dual of $C[a,b]$ ([Wikipedia: Riemann–Stieltjes integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Stieltjes_integral)); the Henstock–Kurzweil (gauge) integral replaces the constant mesh bound by a variable gauge, under which the derivative of every everywhere-differentiable function is integrable. ([Wikipedia: Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral))

### Formal definition
A partition of $[a,b]$ is a finite sequence $a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$, with mesh $\max_i(x_{i+1}-x_i)$; a tagged partition also chooses $t_i\in[x_i,x_{i+1}]$. The Riemann sum of $f$ is
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(t_i)\,(x_{i+1}-x_i).$$
The Riemann integral equals $s$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every tagged partition of mesh less than $\delta$ has Riemann sum within $\varepsilon$ of $s$. An equivalent formulation uses refinements instead of mesh, and a function is Riemann integrable exactly when it is Darboux integrable (upper and lower sums with $\sup$ and $\inf$ on each subinterval). ([Wikipedia: Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral)) For $f\in C([a,b])$, MIT 18.100A proves there is a unique number $\int_a^b f$ such that $S_f(x^r,\xi^r)\to\int_a^b f$ for every sequence of tagged partitions with $\|x^r\|\to0$. ([MIT 18.100A notes, Theorem 235](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/mit18_100af20_lec_full.pdf))

**Riemann–Stieltjes integral.** For $f,g$ on $[a,b]$, $\int_a^b f\,dg$ is the limit, as the mesh tends to zero, of $\sum_i f(c_i)\,[g(x_i)-g(x_{i-1})]$ with $c_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$. ([Wikipedia: Riemann–Stieltjes integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Stieltjes_integral))

**Henstock–Kurzweil integral.** A gauge is a positive function $\delta$ on $[a,b]$; a tagged partition is $\delta$-fine if each $[x_i,x_{i+1}]\subset[t_i-\delta(t_i),t_i+\delta(t_i)]$. Then $I$ is the integral if for every $\varepsilon>0$ some gauge $\delta$ makes every $\delta$-fine Riemann sum lie within $\varepsilon$ of $I$. Constant gauges give the Riemann integral, and Cousin's theorem guarantees that $\delta$-fine partitions exist for every gauge. ([Wikipedia: Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral))

### Key results
- **Lebesgue's criterion.** A bounded function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable if and only if its set of discontinuities has Lebesgue measure zero. Hence bounded functions with countably many discontinuities, and monotone functions, are Riemann integrable; every Riemann-integrable function is Lebesgue integrable with the same integral. ([Wikipedia: Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral)) Lebesgue states the criterion ("il faut et il suffit que l'ensemble de ses points de discontinuité soit de mesure nulle") in his 1904 *Leçons*, p. 29. ([Lebesgue 1904, OCR text](https://archive.org/download/leconegrarecher00leberich/leconegrarecher00leberich_djvu.txt))
- **First FTC.** If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$, then $F$ is uniformly continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $F'=f$. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_calculus))
- **Second FTC (Newton–Leibniz).** If $F$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, $F'=f$ on $(a,b)$, and $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$; continuity of $f$ is not assumed. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_calculus)) The proof applies the mean value theorem on each subinterval to choose tags with $F(x_j)-F(x_{j-1})=f(\xi_j)(x_j-x_{j-1})$, so the Riemann sums telescope to $F(b)-F(a)$. ([MIT 18.100A notes, Theorem 250](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/mit18_100af20_lec_full.pdf))
- **Integration by parts.** If $u,v$ are continuously differentiable on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b u v'\,dx=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b u'v\,dx$; it remains valid if $u$ is absolutely continuous and $v'$ is Lebesgue integrable. ([Wikipedia: Integration by parts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integration_by_parts); [MIT 18.100A notes, Theorem 252](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/mit18_100af20_lec_full.pdf))
- **Substitution.** If $g:[a,b]\to I$ is differentiable with continuous derivative and $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, then $\int_a^b f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx=\int_{g(a)}^{g(b)}f(u)\,du$; the proof only needs $g'$ integrable. ([Wikipedia: Integration by substitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integration_by_substitution)) MIT 18.100A proves the case $\varphi'>0$ via the FTC. ([MIT 18.100A notes, Theorem 256](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/mit18_100af20_lec_full.pdf))
- **Mean value theorems for integrals.** If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, there is $c\in(a,b)$ with $\int_a^b f=f(c)(b-a)$; if moreover $g$ is integrable and does not change sign, there is $c$ with $\int_a^b fg=f(c)\int_a^b g$. Second (Bonnet) form: if $G$ is positive and decreasing and $\varphi$ is integrable, there is $x\in(a,b]$ with $\int_a^b G\varphi=G(a^+)\int_a^x\varphi$. ([Wikipedia: Mean value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_theorem))
- **Riemann–Stieltjes existence and reduction.** If $f$ is continuous and $g$ has bounded variation on $[a,b]$, $\int_a^b f\,dg$ exists; $\int f\,dg=f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a)-\int g\,df$, with either side existing if the other does; and if $g$ is continuously differentiable, $\int f\,dg=\int f g'\,dx$. ([Wikipedia: Riemann–Stieltjes integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Stieltjes_integral))
- **FTC for the gauge integral.** If $F$ is differentiable everywhere on $[a,b]$, then $F'$ is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable and $\int_a^x F'=F(x)-F(a)$, even when $F'$ is not Lebesgue integrable. Conversely, the indefinite HK integral of $f$ has derivative $f$ almost everywhere. $f$ is Lebesgue integrable exactly when $f$ and $|f|$ are HK integrable. ([Wikipedia: Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral))
- **Uniform limits.** If $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$ and each $f_n$ is Riemann integrable, then $f$ is Riemann integrable and $\int f_n\to\int f$; there is no monotone convergence theorem for the Riemann integral. ([Wikipedia: Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral))

### Examples
- **Volterra's function.** $V$ is differentiable everywhere on $\mathbb R$ with bounded derivative, yet $V'$ is not Riemann integrable: $V$ is built from scaled copies of $x^2\sin(1/x)$ on the intervals removed in constructing the Smith–Volterra–Cantor set, and $V'$ is discontinuous on a set of positive measure. ([Wikipedia: Volterra's function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra%27s_function)) This is why the second FTC must assume $f$ Riemann integrable. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_calculus)) Lebesgue credits the first such example to Volterra (*Giornale di Battaglini*, 1881). ([Lebesgue 1904, OCR text](https://archive.org/download/leconegrarecher00leberich/leconegrarecher00leberich_djvu.txt))
- **A proper gauge integral that is improper for Riemann.** By Hake's theorem, $\int_0^1 \sin(1/x)/x\,dx$ is a proper Henstock–Kurzweil integral. ([Wikipedia: Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral))
- **Indicator of the rationals.** On $[0,1]$ it is discontinuous everywhere, hence not Riemann integrable, but Lebesgue integrable with integral $0$. ([Wikipedia: Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral))
- **Riemann–Lebesgue lemma by parts.** For $f,f'\in C([-\pi,\pi])$ with $f(-\pi)=f(\pi)$, integration by parts gives $|b_n|\le\frac1n\int|f'|\to0$ for the Fourier coefficients. ([MIT 18.100A notes, Lemma 254](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/mit18_100af20_lec_full.pdf))

### History
James Gregory published a geometric form of the fundamental theorem, Isaac Barrow proved a more general version, and Newton and Leibniz built the calculus, Leibniz supplying the modern notation. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_calculus)) Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift defined the integral via tagged sums to study trigonometric series; it was published in 1868 ([Wikipedia: Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral)), and an 1867 Dieterich printing is on the Internet Archive. ([Riemann, archive.org](https://archive.org/details/bub_gb__zcPAAAAQAAJ)) Stieltjes published his integral in 1894. ([Wikipedia: Riemann–Stieltjes integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Stieltjes_integral)) Lebesgue first published his integration theory in his 1902 dissertation *Intégrale, longueur, aire* ([Wikipedia: Henri Lebesgue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Lebesgue); [MacTutor: Lebesgue](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Lebesgue/)), and his 1904 *Leçons sur l'intégration et la recherche des fonctions primitives* ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/leconegrarecher00leberich)) states the measure-zero criterion for Riemann integrability. ([Lebesgue 1904, OCR text](https://archive.org/download/leconegrarecher00leberich/leconegrarecher00leberich_djvu.txt)) Vitali found the criterion independently: MacTutor dates his theorem on the discontinuity points of Riemann-integrable functions to 1903 ([MacTutor: Vitali](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Vitali/)). (The 1907 date sometimes given for both proofs is later than Lebesgue's 1904 *Leçons*, which already state the criterion. ([Lebesgue 1904, OCR text](https://archive.org/download/leconegrarecher00leberich/leconegrarecher00leberich_djvu.txt))) Denjoy introduced a more general integral in 1912, Kurzweil gave the gauge formulation in 1957, and Henstock developed it independently in 1961. ([Wikipedia: Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral))

### Connections
- [Differential Calculus](node:Differential%20Calculus): the FTC identifies integration with inversion of differentiation.
- [Fundamental Theorem of Calculus](node:Fundamental%20Theorem%20of%20Calculus): the central theorem of the subject, stated above in both parts.
- [Monotone Convergence Theorem](node:Monotone%20Convergence%20Theorem): holds for the Lebesgue integral but has no Riemann analogue.
- [Mean Value Theorem](node:Mean%20Value%20Theorem): chooses the tags in the proof of the second FTC.
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): the integral is a limit of Riemann sums.
- [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration) and [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): Lebesgue's criterion uses measure zero; Lebesgue's integral has monotone convergence.
- [Bounded Variation](node:Bounded%20Variation): the integrators of the Riemann–Stieltjes integral.
- [Riesz Representation Theorems](node:Riesz%20Representation%20Theorems): first stated with Riemann–Stieltjes integrals on $C[a,b]$.
- [Uniform Convergence of Series](node:Uniform%20Convergence%20of%20Series) and [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence): uniform convergence justifies term-by-term integration on compact intervals.
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus) and [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus): multiple integrals and Stokes-type formulas.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): Riemann's motivation was trigonometric series.
- [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions): integrals against kernels solve linear differential equations.
- Map: [MSC 26 - Real functions](node:MSC%2026%20-%20Real%20functions), [MSC 26Axx - Functions of one variable](node:MSC%2026Axx%20-%20Functions%20of%20one%20variable).

### Common pitfalls
- **First versus second FTC.** Apostol calls $F(x)=\int_a^x f\Rightarrow F'=f$ the first part; Larson and Edwards reverse the labels. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_calculus))
- **Every choice of tags counts.** The Riemann sums must converge as the mesh tends to zero for every choice of tags: for the indicator of the rationals, at any mesh the tags can be chosen so the sums stay within $\varepsilon$ of $0$ or of $1$, so no single value is approached. ([Wikipedia: Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral))
- **Having an antiderivative does not imply Riemann integrable**, and Riemann integrable does not imply having an antiderivative. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_calculus))
- **Improper integrals and limits.** For $f_n=1/n$ on $[0,n]$ each integral is $1$ while $f_n\to0$ uniformly, so uniform convergence does not justify exchanging limit and improper integral; for $\operatorname{sgn}$, symmetric and asymmetric expansions of the interval give different values. ([Wikipedia: Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral))
- **Substitution hypotheses.** The one-variable theorem needs $g$ with integrable derivative and $f$ continuous on the range of $g$. ([Wikipedia: Integration by substitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integration_by_substitution))

### Open problems

Searches tried: "open problem Riemann integral elementary real analysis unsolved", "Henstock-Kurzweil integral open questions survey"; the results were surveys of generalized and non-absolute integrals, not open problems about the Riemann integral or the FTC. references.Inverse Function Theorem:
## Reference
### Overview
The inverse function theorem converts a linear-algebra condition into a nonlinear conclusion: if a continuously differentiable map $f$ has invertible derivative at a point $a$, then $f$ is a bijection between small neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$, and the inverse is continuously differentiable with derivative $(f^{-1})'(f(a))=f'(a)^{-1}$. The theorem is strictly local; a map can be locally invertible at every point and still fail to be injective. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem))

Dontchev and Rockafellar place it at the base of a theory of solution mappings: solving $f(x)=y$ is studied through the set-valued inverse $f^{-1}$ and its single-valued localizations, and the classical theorem is the first of a family that includes the [Implicit Function Theorem](node:Implicit%20Function%20Theorem), strict-differentiability versions, and the Lyusternik–Graves theorems in Banach spaces. All of these rest on the same contraction or Newton-type iteration. ([Dontchev–Rockafellar, Ch. 1 and 5](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf))

In geometry the theorem supplies local normal forms for smooth maps, and through them the constant rank and submersion theorems and the fact that the preimage of a regular value is a manifold. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem)) In nonlinear PDE, inverting linearizations of maps between Fréchet spaces loses derivatives, which is the problem the Nash–Moser theorem addresses. ([Wikipedia, Nash–Moser theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash%E2%80%93Moser_theorem))

### Formal definition
**Classical theorem.** Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuously differentiable in a neighbourhood of $\bar x$, and let $\bar y=f(\bar x)$. If the Jacobian $\nabla f(\bar x)$ is nonsingular (equivalently $\det\nabla f(\bar x)\neq 0$, see [Determinant](node:Determinant)), then $f^{-1}$ has a single-valued localization $s$ around $\bar y$ for $\bar x$; $s$ is continuously differentiable on a neighbourhood $V$ of $\bar y$ and
$$\nabla s(y)=\nabla f(s(y))^{-1}\qquad (y\in V).$$
([Dontchev–Rockafellar, Theorem 1A.1](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf))

**$C^r$ form.** For $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ of class $C^r$, if $Df(a)$ is bijective there are neighbourhoods $U_1$ of $a$ and $V$ of $f(a)$ such that $f|_{U_1}:U_1\to V$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism, that is, a bijection whose inverse is also $C^r$. ([MIT 18.101, Lecture 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-101-analysis-ii-fall-2005/d2c8fc5fe57cd59efc99caa048983d4c_lecture6.pdf))

**Banach-space form.** Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, $U\subseteq X$ an open neighbourhood of $0$, and $F:U\to Y$ continuously (Fréchet) differentiable with $dF_0$ a bounded linear isomorphism of $X$ onto $Y$. Then $F$ has a continuously differentiable local inverse $G$ near $F(0)$, and $G(y)$ is the unique sufficiently small solution $x$ of $F(x)=y$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem))

### Key results
- **Higher regularity.** If $f$ is $C^k$ around $\bar x$ ($k\ge1$), the localization $s$ of $f^{-1}$ is $C^k$ around $\bar y$; the derivative formula and the chain rule give this. ([Dontchev–Rockafellar, Proposition 1B.5](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf)) The same holds for $k=\infty$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem))
- **Holomorphic version.** If $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ is open, $f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ is holomorphic, and the complex derivative $\partial f/\partial z(p)$ is bijective, then $f$ maps a neighbourhood of $p$ biholomorphically onto a neighbourhood of $f(p)$. The proof applies the real theorem and checks that the inverse preserves the $(1,0)/(0,1)$ splitting of 1-forms. ([MIT 18.117, Lecture 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/989bea2ba42545febc2830a2b5f59cf2_18117_lec07.pdf))
- **Converse (symmetric inverse function theorem).** For $f$ continuously differentiable around $\bar x$, $\nabla f(\bar x)$ is nonsingular if and only if $f^{-1}$ has a single-valued localization around $\bar y$ that is continuously differentiable around $\bar y$. More generally, if $f$ is differentiable at $\bar x$ and $f^{-1}$ has a single-valued localization that is calm at $\bar y$, then $\nabla f(\bar x)$ is nonsingular. ([Dontchev–Rockafellar, Theorems 1C.2–1C.3](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf))
- **Strict differentiability suffices.** If $f$ is merely strictly differentiable at $\bar x$ (a condition implied by continuous differentiability near $\bar x$, but not equivalent to it), then $\nabla f(\bar x)$ is nonsingular if and only if $f^{-1}$ has a single-valued localization strictly differentiable at $\bar y$, with $\nabla s(\bar y)=\nabla f(\bar x)^{-1}$. ([Dontchev–Rockafellar, Theorem 1D.9 and Exercise 1D.6](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf))
- **Equivalence with the implicit function theorem.** Dini's theorem says: if $f:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ is $C^1$ near $(\bar p,\bar x)$ with $f(\bar p,\bar x)=0$ and $\nabla_x f(\bar p,\bar x)$ nonsingular, then the solution map $p\mapsto\{x:f(p,x)=0\}$ has a $C^1$ localization $s$ with $\nabla s(p)=-\nabla_xf(p,s(p))^{-1}\nabla_pf(p,s(p))$. The inverse theorem is the special case $f(p,x)=-p+f(x)$, and conversely the implicit theorem follows from the inverse one, so the two are equivalent. ([Dontchev–Rockafellar, Theorem 1B.1 and §1B](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf)) The standard derivation applies the inverse theorem to $F(x,y)=(x,f(x,y))$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem))
- **Constant rank theorem and immersions.** If $f:M\to N$ is smooth and $Df$ has constant rank $k$ near $p$, there are charts with $\psi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}(x_1,\dots,x_m)=(x_1,\dots,x_k,0,\dots,0)$; the inverse function theorem is a special case. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem); [Wikipedia, Rank (differential topology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank_%28differential_topology%29)) A constant-rank map is an immersion when its rank equals $\dim M$ and a submersion when it equals $\dim N$. ([Wikipedia, Rank (differential topology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank_%28differential_topology%29))
- **Lyusternik–Graves (surjective derivative).** Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, $f$ continuous on $\mathbb B_\varepsilon(\bar x)$, $A\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ surjective with regularity modulus at most $\kappa$, and suppose $\|f(x)-f(x')-A(x-x')\|\le\mu\|x-x'\|$ on $\mathbb B_\varepsilon(\bar x)$ with $\mu\kappa<1$. Then for $\|y-f(\bar x)\|\le(\kappa^{-1}-\mu)\varepsilon$ the equation $f(x)=y$ has a solution in $\mathbb B_\varepsilon(\bar x)$. When $A$ is invertible, the iteration in the proof goes back to Goursat. ([Dontchev–Rockafellar, Theorem 5D.2 and §5D](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf))
- **Hadamard–Caccioppoli and Hadamard–Lévy (global inversion).** A local homeomorphism $f:X\to Y$ between path-connected Hausdorff spaces with $Y$ simply connected is a homeomorphism onto $Y$ if and only if it is proper. A continuous $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is proper if and only if $|f(x)|\to\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$. For a local diffeomorphism $f$ between Banach spaces, $f$ is a diffeomorphism onto $Y$ if $\|f'(x)^{-1}\|\le\beta(\|x\|)$ for a continuous nondecreasing $\beta$ with $\int_0^\infty ds/\beta(s)=\infty$, for example under linear growth $\|f'(x)^{-1}\|\le a+b\|x\|$. ([De Marco–Gorni–Zampieri, Theorems 0.1–0.2, Prop. 1.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.7902))
- **Clarke's Lipschitz inverse function theorem.** Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be Lipschitz near $x_0$, and let $\partial f(x_0)$ be the convex hull of all limits $\lim Jf(x_i)$ with $x_i\to x_0$ and $f$ differentiable at each $x_i$. If every matrix in $\partial f(x_0)$ has maximal rank, there are neighbourhoods $U$ of $x_0$ and $V$ of $f(x_0)$ and a Lipschitz $g:V\to\mathbb R^n$ with $g(f(u))=u$ on $U$ and $f(g(v))=v$ on $V$. ([Phien, statement of Clarke 1976 and Defs. 2.5–2.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1204.4916))
- **Nash–Moser (Hamilton's form).** Let $F,G$ be tame Fréchet spaces, $U\subseteq F$ open, and $P:U\to G$ a smooth tame map whose linearization $dP_f$ is invertible for every $f\in U$, with the family of inverses $U\times G\to F$ smooth tame. Then $P$ is locally invertible with smooth tame local inverses. The Banach theorem does not apply because inverting the linearization loses derivatives, as in Nash's isometric embedding problem. ([Wikipedia, Nash–Moser theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash%E2%80%93Moser_theorem))

### Examples
- $F(x,y)=(e^x\cos y,e^x\sin y)$ has Jacobian determinant $e^{2x}\neq0$ everywhere, so it is locally invertible at every point, yet $F(x,y)=F(x,y+2\pi)$, so it is not injective. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem))
- The map $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\mapsto(\lambda_1+\lambda_2,\lambda_1\lambda_2)$ (trace and determinant of $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$) has Jacobian determinant $\lambda_1-\lambda_2$. Its inverse has smooth localizations, in fact two, around every $y$ with $4y_2<y_1^2$, and none on the discriminant curve $4y_2=y_1^2$. ([Dontchev–Rockafellar, §1A](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf))

### History
Cauchy (1831) is credited with the first rigorous implicit function theorem, for analytic functions, and Dini (1877/78) with the $C^1$ form found in calculus texts. Dontchev and Rockafellar trace their first (contraction-type) proof of the inverse theorem to Goursat (1903), who used the iteration $x_{k+1}=x_k-A^{-1}f(p,x_k)$ with $A=\nabla_xf(\bar p,\bar x)$ fixed, inspired by Picard's successive approximations; this is a contraction argument, and in Kantorovich–Akilov it is called a modified [Newton's Method](node:Newton's%20Method). Lamson (1920) extended Goursat's iteration to what are now Banach spaces, Hildebrand and Graves (1927) developed it further, and Banach published the contraction principle in 1922. Lyusternik (1934) and Graves (1950) treated surjective derivatives. ([Dontchev–Rockafellar, Commentary to Ch. 1 and §5D](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr208-ImplicitFns-DontRock.pdf))

Nash (1956) proved the hard implicit function theorem for the isometric embedding problem. Moser (1966) applied the method to KAM problems in celestial mechanics, and Hamilton (1982) gave the most widely cited general formulation in the *Bulletin of the AMS* 7(1), 65–222. ([Wikipedia, Nash–Moser theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash%E2%80%93Moser_theorem); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0273-0979-1982-15004-2)) Clarke's Lipschitz version appeared in *Pacific J. Math.* 64(1), 97–102 (1976). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2140/pjm.1976.64.97))
