- [Graph Query Languages](node:Graph%20Query%20Languages) and [Relational Data Model](node:Relational%20Data%20Model): SPARQL and Cypher evaluate graph patterns; virtual KGs map relations to graphs.
- [Database Query Optimization](node:Database%20Query%20Optimization): FO-rewriting turns ontology queries into SQL.
- [CS Subsection - Complexity classes and reductions](node:CS%20Subsection%20-%20Complexity%20classes%20and%20reductions): the PSPACE, EXPTIME and AC$^0$ results above.
- [Knowledge Graph Completion](node:Knowledge%20Graph%20Completion): inductive link prediction, the main use of embeddings.
- [Graph Neural Networks](node:Graph%20Neural%20Networks): learned node and edge representations.
- [Entity Resolution](node:Entity%20Resolution): entity alignment across graphs.
- [Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation](node:Graph%20Retrieval-Augmented%20Generation), [Retrieval-Augmented Generation](node:Retrieval-Augmented%20Generation) and [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): KGs as structured memory for LLMs.
- [Ontology Induction](node:Ontology%20Induction): learning schemas from data.
- [Graph Algorithms](node:Graph%20Algorithms): traversal, path and centrality over the data graph.
- [Data Leakage and Temporal Evaluation](node:Data%20Leakage%20and%20Temporal%20Evaluation): the FB15k inverse-relation problem is a leakage case.

### Common pitfalls
- **Open versus closed world.** DL semantics considers every model of the axioms, so an absent fact is unknown, not false, and the semantics is monotonic ([Krötzsch, Simančík, Horrocks](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.4089)). Databases typically adopt the closed world assumption; the local closed world assumption treats only parts of the graph as complete ([Hogan et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.02320)).
- **No unique names by default.** Two individual names may denote the same individual unless the ontology says otherwise ([Krötzsch, Simančík, Horrocks](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.4089)); whether the UNA is adopted changes DL-Lite's complexity ([Artale et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.3487)).
- **"TransE cannot do asymmetric relations" is backwards.** TransE handles antisymmetric relations; its failure is symmetry, which collapses $\mathbf r$ to $0$ ([Sun et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.10197)); cyclical relations tend to a zero vector, and one-to-many relations push targets together ([Hogan et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.02320)).
- **Leaky benchmarks.** FB15k and WN18 gains can reflect inverse-relation shortcuts; FB15k-237 also drops validation and test triples whose entity pairs are directly linked in training ([Toutanova and Chen](https://aclanthology.org/W15-4007.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Intersections of data graphs, deductive and inductive knowledge.** Hogan et al. list as emerging topics formal semantics for property graphs, reasoning and querying over contextual data, similarity-based query relaxation, shape induction, entailment-aware embeddings, and expressive GNNs, and name scalability, quality, diversity, dynamicity and usability as challenges unlikely ever to be completely "solved" ([Hogan et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.02320)).
- **Unifying LLMs and KGs.** Pan et al. propose KG-enhanced LLMs, LLM-augmented KGs and synergised LLM+KG, and identify future research directions in each ([Pan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08302)).
- **Entity alignment** across independently built graphs remains a non-trivial, active research area ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_graph)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Knowledge graph (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_graph): definitions, history, entity alignment.
- **Reference:** [Description logic (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Description_logic): syntax, semantics and naming of DLs.
- **Reference:** [Hogan et al., Knowledge Graphs (ACM Computing Surveys 54(4), 2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.02320): comprehensive survey with formal appendix.
- **Learn:** [Oxford, Knowledge Representation & Reasoning](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/teaching/courses/2023-2024/KRR/): 24 lectures on description logics, ontology languages, Datalog and complexity.
- **Learn:** [Krötzsch, Simančík, Horrocks, A Description Logic Primer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.4089): tutorial on $\mathcal{SROIQ}$, its fragments, and OWL.
- **Primary:** [Pérez, Arenas, Gutierrez, Semantics and Complexity of SPARQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0605124): compositional semantics and the AND/UNION/OPT complexity results.
- **Primary:** [Artale et al., The DL-Lite Family and Relations (JAIR 2009)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3487): complexity map of DL-Lite and OBDA.
- **Primary:** [Sun et al., RotatE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10197): relation-pattern analysis of embeddings.
- **Primary:** [Toutanova and Chen, Observed versus latent features](https://aclanthology.org/W15-4007.pdf): FB15k-237.
- **Further reading:** [Baader, Horrocks, Lutz, Sattler, An Introduction to Description Logic (Cambridge University Press, 2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781139025355/type/book): graduate textbook on DL syntax, semantics, complexity and OWL.
- **Further reading:** [Pan et al., Unifying Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs: A Roadmap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08302): research agenda for LLM and KG integration.
references.Knowledge Representation and Reasoning:
## Reference
### Overview
Knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) is the part of AI that represents information about the world in a form a computer system can use to solve complex tasks, and studies how to reason with and interpret it. Davis et al. describe a representation as "most fundamentally a surrogate", which lets an agent draw conclusions by reasoning rather than by acting. Its formalisms include rules, frames, logics (first-order logic, logic programs) and ontologies; its standard services are deduction, classification (subsumption), consistency checking, question answering and planning ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_representation_and_reasoning)).

Logic-based AI, which descends from McCarthy's program of formalizing commonsense reasoning, has been largely absorbed into knowledge representation, with closer ties to applications than to philosophical logic. Its signature topics are the frame problem, nonmonotonic logics (circumscription, autoepistemic logic, default logic), the situation calculus for action and change, and taxonomic logics ([SEP: Logic-Based AI](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/)).

The central technical theme is the trade-off between expressive power and computational cost. First-order logic is the benchmark for expressiveness but its theoremhood is undecidable, so practical systems use restricted languages such as rules and logic programs that offer close to the same expressive power while being easier for developers and computers to handle ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_representation_and_reasoning)). A current graduate course accordingly focuses on decidable fragments of first-order logic, Datalog and its extensions, description logics and ontology languages, and temporal and non-monotonic logics ([Oxford KRR course](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/teaching/courses/KRR)).

### Formal definition
**Description logic knowledge base.** Concepts are interpreted as sets of individuals and roles as binary relations; complex concepts are built with intersection, union, negation and existential and universal restriction. A *TBox* is a finite set of general concept inclusions $C\sqsubseteq D$, an *ABox* a finite set of assertions $C(a)$, $r(a,b)$ about named individuals, and a knowledge base is a pair $(\mathcal T,\mathcal A)$. Reasoning tasks include subsumption, concept consistency and instance checking ([Wikipedia: Description logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Description_logic)).

In ALC an interpretation $\mathcal I=(\Delta^{\mathcal I},\cdot^{\mathcal I})$ gives $(\exists r.C)^{\mathcal I}=\{x:\exists y\,((x,y)\in r^{\mathcal I}\wedge y\in C^{\mathcal I})\}$, $(\forall r.C)^{\mathcal I}=\{x:\forall y\,((x,y)\in r^{\mathcal I}\Rightarrow y\in C^{\mathcal I})\}$, and $\mathcal I\models C\sqsubseteq D$ iff $C^{\mathcal I}\subseteq D^{\mathcal I}$; $\mathcal I$ is a model of $\mathcal T$ when it satisfies every GCI in $\mathcal T$. ALC is a notational variant of the modal logic K, and many DLs are decidable fragments of first-order logic, typically within the two-variable or guarded fragments ([Wikipedia: Description logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Description_logic)).

**Default theory (Reiter 1980).** A pair $\langle W,D\rangle$ of a background theory $W$ and a set $D$ of defaults $\frac{\alpha:\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n}{\gamma}$, read: if $\alpha$ is believed and each $\beta_i$ is consistent with current beliefs, conclude $\gamma$. An *extension* is a theory closed under the applicable defaults; a default theory may have zero, one or several extensions ([Wikipedia: Default logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Default_logic)).

**Nonmonotonicity.** Classical consequence is monotonic ($\Gamma\models\varphi\Rightarrow\Gamma\cup\Delta\models\varphi$); a logic is nonmonotonic when adding premises can remove conclusions ([SEP: Logic-Based AI](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/)).

### Key results
- **Undecidability of the general case.** Deciding whether a first-order sentence is a theorem is unsolvable, so reducing KR services to first-order theorem proving makes the task precise but not computable (Levesque and Brachman) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_representation_and_reasoning)).
- **Complexity of ALC.** Satisfiability and subsumption in ALC are PSPACE-complete without TBoxes or with acyclic TBoxes and EXPTIME-complete with general TBoxes; ALCOI is EXPTIME-complete and ALCOIQ NEXPTIME-complete even without TBoxes; adding role value maps, or a concrete domain of natural numbers with incrementation, makes reasoning undecidable ([Baader et al. 2017, ch. 5](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-description-logic/complexity/28FF8265D9C77A0886D75CADBB337A42)).
- **Horn clauses are tractable.** Horn satisfiability is P-complete and solvable in linear time (Dowling–Gallier 1984) by unit propagation, which also returns the minimal model of a satisfiable Horn formula ([Wikipedia: Horn-satisfiability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn-satisfiability)).
- **Complexity of default logic.** For propositional default theories, existence of an extension and credulous entailment are $\Sigma^p_2$-complete, skeptical entailment is $\Pi^p_2$-complete, and extension checking is $\Delta^p_2[\log]$-complete ([Wikipedia: Default logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Default_logic)). Nonmonotonicity is therefore "no magic path to efficient reasoning" ([SEP: Logic-Based AI](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/)).

### Examples
- **Frames and classifiers.** KL-ONE (mid-1980s) gave frames formal semantics and used a classifier to infer subsumption between concepts, an approach Loom followed; Cyc built a large commonsense knowledge base in its frame language CycL ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_representation_and_reasoning)).
- **Semantic Web.** RDF defines classes and properties, and OWL adds description-logic semantics so that ontologies can be processed by classification engines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_representation_and_reasoning)).
- **Yale Shooting (Hanks and McDermott; first reported 1985, published 1986 and 1987).** Fred is alive and a pistol unloaded; the actions are load, wait, shoot. Besides the intended extension in which Fred dies, default logic with inertia defaults admits an anomalous one in which the pistol becomes unloaded during the wait and Fred survives; each extension violates exactly one inertia default, so a naive default treatment cannot verify the plan ([SEP: Logic-Based AI](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/)).
- **Negation as failure.** In logic programming, negation as failure gives a nonmonotonic default reasoning with a closed-world and unique-name assumption ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_representation_and_reasoning)).

### History
McCarthy's 1959 Advice Taker proposed predicate calculus for commonsense reasoning; McCarthy and Hayes introduced the situation calculus; Prolog and logic programming in the early 1970s treated Horn clauses as goal-reduction procedures; Minsky introduced frames in the mid-1970s; expert systems separated knowledge base and inference engine; Brian Smith formalized the knowledge representation hypothesis and Brachman categorized the core KR issues (1985); and the Semantic Web later added ontology languages such as OWL ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_representation_and_reasoning)). The three early nonmonotonic formalisms were McCarthy's circumscription, the modal approach of Doyle and McDermott, and Reiter's default logic ([SEP: Logic-Based AI](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/)). Since large language models, the field has been shifting toward hybrid systems combining explicit knowledge such as knowledge graphs with parametric knowledge stored in model weights ([Pan et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06374)).

### Connections
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): the reference language; KR formalisms are mostly its decidable fragments.
- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic): Horn and SAT-based reasoning sit here.
- [Description Logics](node:Description%20Logics): the logics behind OWL ontologies.
- [Knowledge Graphs and Ontologies](node:Knowledge%20Graphs%20and%20Ontologies): the main deployed form of KR.
- [Datalog](node:Datalog) and [Logic Programming](node:Logic%20Programming): rule-based KR with efficient bottom-up and goal-directed evaluation.
- [Automated Theorem Proving](node:Automated%20Theorem%20Proving): the reasoning engine for expressive logics.
- [SAT and SMT Solving](node:SAT%20and%20SMT%20Solving): propositional reasoning back-ends.
- [Classical Planning](node:Classical%20Planning): grew out of situation calculus and resolution-based planning.
- [Temporal Logic](node:Temporal%20Logic): temporal extensions of KR languages.
- [Nonmonotonic Reasoning](node:Nonmonotonic%20Reasoning): default logic, circumscription and autoepistemic logic, where added premises can remove conclusions.
- [Neuro-Symbolic Learning](node:Neuro-Symbolic%20Learning): combining learned and explicit representations.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): parametric knowledge that hybrid KR systems combine with explicit knowledge graphs.
- [Knowledge Graph Completion](node:Knowledge%20Graph%20Completion): statistical inference of missing facts in explicit knowledge bases.

### Common pitfalls
- More expressive is not better: each added constructor or a general TBox usually raises the complexity of reasoning ([Wikipedia: Description logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Description_logic)); ALC jumps from PSPACE to EXPTIME when general TBoxes are allowed ([Baader et al. 2017, ch. 5](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-description-logic/complexity/28FF8265D9C77A0886D75CADBB337A42)).
- Default theories need not have a unique extension, so "the consequences" of a default theory must be specified as credulous or skeptical ([Wikipedia: Default logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Default_logic)).
- Nonmonotonic inheritance systems tend to be expressively weak, and their relation to stronger nonmonotonic logics "has never been fully clarified" ([SEP: Logic-Based AI](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/)).

### Open problems
- **Formalizing commonsense.** The SEP entry states that formalizing commonsense reasoning "is so far from being accomplished" that predicting its completion is hopeless; it poses the Ramification Problem (formalizing the indirect effects of actions induced by static laws) as a standing challenge and notes that relatively little attention has been given to the Qualification Problem for characterizing actions ([SEP: Logic-Based AI](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/)).
- **Explicit plus parametric knowledge.** Pan et al. list open challenges in combining knowledge graphs with LLMs: injecting knowledge into black-box LLMs "still remains unanswered", a "fundamental fix" to hallucination "is not in sight", and they propose combining symbolic reasoning, such as OWL consistency checking, with LLM inference to validate generated knowledge ([Pan et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.06374)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Logic-Based Artificial Intelligence (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-ai/): frame problem, nonmonotonic logics, situation calculus, taxonomic reasoning.
- **Reference:** [Knowledge representation and reasoning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_representation_and_reasoning): formalisms, history, the expressivity–tractability trade-off.
- **Learn:** [Knowledge Representation & Reasoning, University of Oxford (Motik)](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/teaching/courses/KRR): 24-lecture course on Datalog, description logics and nonmonotonic negation, with reading list.
- **Primary:** [Baader, Horrocks, Lutz and Sattler, An Introduction to Description Logic, ch. 5 "Complexity" (CUP 2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-description-logic/complexity/28FF8265D9C77A0886D75CADBB337A42): complexity of ALC and its extensions.
- **Primary:** [Pan et al., Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs: Opportunities and Challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06374): position paper on hybrid explicit/parametric knowledge.
- **Further reading:** [Baader et al., An Introduction to Description Logic (Cambridge University Press, 2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-description-logic/complexity/28FF8265D9C77A0886D75CADBB337A42): the standard graduate text on description logics.
references.Kullback–Leibler Divergence:
## Reference
### Overview
The Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, or relative entropy, $D(P\|Q)$ measures how a probability distribution $P$ differs from a reference distribution $Q$ on the same space. It is the expected log-likelihood ratio $\log(dP/dQ)$ under $P$, it is nonnegative, and it vanishes exactly when $P=Q$; but it is not symmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality, so it is not a metric. Cross-entropy, mutual information, and the Fisher information metric are all expressed through it: $H(P,Q)=H(P)+D(P\|Q)$, and $I(X;Y)$ is the divergence of the joint law $P_{X,Y}$ from the product of its marginals $P_X\otimes P_Y$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).

Divergence is the basic quantity of information theory in the measure-theoretic treatment of Polyanskiy and Wu, who develop the chain rule, data-processing inequality, variational characterisations, and continuity properties before entropy-based coding results, and then use it as the exponent in hypothesis testing (Stein's lemma) and large deviations (Sanov's theorem) ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf)). The MIT graduate course 6.441, with notes by Polyanskiy and Wu, likewise opens with entropy and divergence, then mutual information and continuity of divergence, and treats binary hypothesis testing, information projection, and large deviations before channel coding ([MIT OCW 6.441](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-441-information-theory-spring-2016/pages/lecture-notes/)).

In statistics, estimators such as maximum likelihood can be read as attempts to minimise relative entropy between the data-generating law and a model, and in the EM algorithm and ELBO computations the roles of $P$ and $Q$ are reversed because that direction is easier to compute ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).

### Formal definition
For discrete distributions on $\mathcal X$,
$$D(P\|Q)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)},$$
defined when $Q(x)=0\Rightarrow P(x)=0$ and otherwise set to $+\infty$; for densities, $D(P\|Q)=\int p\log(p/q)\,dx$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).

In general, for probability measures on a measurable space, if $P\ll Q$ then
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\log\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dP=\mathbb E_Q\!\left[\frac{dP}{dQ}\log\frac{dP}{dQ}\right],$$
with $dP/dQ$ the Radon–Nikodym derivative, and $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$ if $P\not\ll Q$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence); [Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf)).

Given kernels $P_{Y|X},Q_{Y|X}$ and a marginal $P_X$, the conditional divergence is $D(P_{Y|X}\|Q_{Y|X}\mid P_X)=D(P_XP_{Y|X}\|P_XQ_{Y|X})$ for standard Borel spaces ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 2.16(a)).

### Key results
- **Information (Gibbs) inequality.** $D(P\|Q)\ge 0$, with equality iff $P=Q$; the proof is [Jensen's inequality](node:Jensen's%20Inequality) applied to the strictly convex $\varphi(x)=x\log x$ under $Q$ ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 2.3).
- **Joint convexity.** $D(\lambda P_1+(1-\lambda)P_2\,\|\,\lambda Q_1+(1-\lambda)Q_2)\le\lambda D(P_1\|Q_1)+(1-\lambda)D(P_2\|Q_2)$ for $\lambda\in[0,1]$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- **Chain rule.** For any joint laws $P_{X,Y},Q_{X,Y}$, $D(P_{X,Y}\|Q_{X,Y})=D(P_{Y|X}\|Q_{Y|X}\mid P_X)+D(P_X\|Q_X)$, regardless of the versions of the conditional distributions; iterating gives $D(P_{X^n}\|Q_{X^n})=\sum_i D(P_{X_i|X^{i-1}}\|Q_{X_i|X^{i-1}}\mid P_{X^{i-1}})$ ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorems 2.15–2.16).
- **Data-processing inequality.** If $P_Y=P_{Y|X}\circ P_X$ and $Q_Y=P_{Y|X}\circ Q_X$ for the same channel, then $D(P_Y\|Q_Y)\le D(P_X\|Q_X)$, with equality iff $D(P_{X|Y}\|Q_{X|Y}\mid P_Y)=0$ ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 2.17).
- **Donsker–Varadhan formula.** With $\mathcal C_Q=\{f:0<\mathbb E_Q[e^{f}]<\infty\}$, $D(P\|Q)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal C_Q}\{\mathbb E_P[f]-\log\mathbb E_Q[e^{f}]\}$; on a metric space with Borel $\sigma$-algebra the supremum may be restricted to bounded continuous $f$ ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 4.6). The dual form $\log\mathbb E_P[e^h]=\sup_Q\{\mathbb E_Q[h]-D(Q\|P)\}$ is attained iff $dQ/dP=e^h/\mathbb E_P[e^h]$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- **Lower semicontinuity.** On a metric space with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra, if $P_n\to P$ and $Q_n\to Q$ weakly then $D(P\|Q)\le\liminf_n D(P_n\|Q_n)$ ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 4.9).
- **Pinsker's inequality.** $D(P\|Q)\ge(2\log e)\,\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)^2$, so convergence in divergence implies convergence in total variation; the proof reduces to Bernoulli laws by data processing ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 7.10).
- **Stein's lemma.** For i.i.d. testing of $P^{\otimes n}$ against $Q^{\otimes n}$, the best exponent of the type-II error $\beta$ subject to type-I success probability $\alpha\ge 1-\epsilon$ equals $D(P\|Q)$ for every $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 14.14).
- **Sanov's theorem.** For the empirical measure $\hat P_n$ of i.i.d. samples from $P$ and a convex set $E$ of distributions satisfying regularity conditions (e.g. finite alphabet, $P$ of full support, $E$ closed with nonempty interior), $\Pr[\hat P_n\in E]=\exp\{-n\min_{Q\in E}D(Q\|P)+o(n)\}$ ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 15.13).
- **Local behaviour.** For a smooth parametric family, $D(P_\theta\|P_{\theta_0})=\tfrac12\Delta\theta_j\Delta\theta_k\,g_{jk}(\theta_0)+\cdots$, where $g_{jk}(\theta_0)$, the Hessian of $\theta\mapsto D(P_\theta\|P_{\theta_0})$ at $\theta=\theta_0$, is the Fisher information metric; so the divergence is locally quadratic in the parameter change ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).

### Examples
- **Gaussians.** For $\mathcal N(\mu_0,\Sigma_0)$ and $\mathcal N(\mu_1,\Sigma_1)$ in $\mathbb R^k$,
$$D=\tfrac12\Big[\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_1^{-1}\Sigma_0)-k+(\mu_1-\mu_0)^\top\Sigma_1^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_0)+\ln\frac{\det\Sigma_1}{\det\Sigma_0}\Big];$$
in one dimension $D=\log(\sigma_1/\sigma_0)+\frac{\sigma_0^2+(\mu_0-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}-\frac12$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- **Mutual information.** $I(X;Y)=D(P_{X,Y}\|P_X\otimes P_Y)$, so independence is equivalent to zero divergence from the product law ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- **Hypothesis-testing sample size.** Stein's lemma gives the rule of thumb $n\approx\log(1/\beta)/D(P\|Q)$ for the number of samples needed to drive the type-II error to $\beta$ ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), after Theorem 14.14).

### History
Solomon Kullback and Richard A. Leibler introduced the quantity in "On Information and Sufficiency", *Annals of Mathematical Statistics* 22(1), 79–86 (1951) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aoms/1177729694)). They described it as "the mean information for discrimination between $H_1$ and $H_2$ per observation"; Harold Jeffreys had used the symmetrised sum $D(P\|Q)+D(Q\|P)$ in 1948, and Kullback's 1959 book called the one-sided quantities "directed divergences", Kullback himself preferring "discrimination information" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)). Relative entropy is related to the rate function in the theory of large deviations, with Sanov's 1957 paper as the standard reference ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).

### Connections
- [Information Theory](node:Information%20Theory): divergence is the primitive from which entropy and mutual information are built.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss): cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL divergence, so minimising it over $Q$ minimises $D(P\|Q)$.
- [Variational Inference](node:Variational%20Inference): the ELBO gap is the reverse divergence $D(q\|p(\cdot\mid x))$.
- [Fisher Information](node:Fisher%20Information): the Hessian of KL divergence at coincidence.
- [Information Geometry](node:Information%20Geometry): KL divergence is the canonical divergence of exponential families.
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing): Stein's lemma identifies KL divergence as the optimal error exponent.
- [Maximum Likelihood Estimation](node:Maximum%20Likelihood%20Estimation): maximising likelihood minimises the empirical divergence from the data.
- [Radon–Nikodym Theorem](node:Radon–Nikodym%20Theorem): needed to define the divergence on general spaces.
- [Expectation-Maximization Algorithm](node:Expectation-Maximization%20Algorithm): alternates minimisation of a divergence between a variational distribution and the posterior.
- [PAC-Bayesian Bounds](node:PAC-Bayesian%20Bounds): generalisation bounds whose complexity term is a KL divergence between posterior and prior.

### Common pitfalls
- **Asymmetry.** $D(P\|Q)\neq D(Q\|P)$ in general and the triangle inequality fails, so KL is a divergence, not a distance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- **Support.** The sum and integral formulas apply only when $Q(x)=0$ implies $P(x)=0$ (absolute continuity); otherwise $D(P\|Q)$ is usually set to $+\infty$, so a finite divergence requires $P\ll Q$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- **Units.** The logarithm base sets the unit (bits or nats); Pinsker's constant $2\log e$ changes accordingly ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), Theorem 7.10).
- **Pinsker is vacuous for large divergence.** Since total variation is at most 1, the bound says nothing once $D(P\|Q)>2$ nats ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).
- **Cross-entropy is not a divergence.** $H(P,P)=H(P)\neq 0$, so cross-entropy cannot be read as a distance between distributions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)).

### Open problems
- **Minimax density estimation in KL loss.** For $\beta$-smooth densities on $[0,1]^d$, the minimax KL risk satisfies $n^{-\beta/(\beta+d)}\lesssim\inf_{\hat f}\sup_f\mathbb E\,D(f\|\hat f)\lesssim n^{-\beta/(\beta+d)}(\log n)^{d/(\beta+d)}$; Polyanskiy and Wu state that, to their knowledge, resolving this logarithmic gap remains open ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), eq. 32.57).
- **Rényi divergences and strong converses.** The same text says its error-exponent analysis suggests a general conjecture that replacing Shannon information measures (KL divergence, mutual information) with Rényi ones upgrades weak converse proofs to strong converses ([Polyanskiy and Wu](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf), §22.4).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kullback–Leibler divergence (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence): definitions, properties, Gaussian formulas, history of terminology.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 6.441 Information Theory, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-441-information-theory-spring-2016/pages/lecture-notes/): graduate notes by Polyanskiy and Wu covering entropy and divergence, continuity of divergence, binary hypothesis testing, information projection, and large deviations.
- **Primary:** [Kullback and Leibler, On Information and Sufficiency (1951)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aoms/1177729694): the original paper in the *Annals of Mathematical Statistics*.
- **Further reading:** [Polyanskiy and Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning](https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf): graduate text (Cambridge University Press) developing divergence measure-theoretically through f-divergences, hypothesis testing, and large deviations.
references.LLM Agents:
## Reference
### Overview
An AI agent is a program that pursues goals and takes actions with limited human direction; typical traits are goal-directed behavior, the use of external tools, the ability to change an external environment, and autonomous multi-step execution. In current systems a large language model usually drives the control flow, wrapped in a "harness" that manages prompts, context, tools, memory, permissions and sandboxes ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_agent)). An LLM agent is this arrangement: the model reads a context made of the task, past observations and past actions, and emits the next action, which may be a tool call, an environment command, or a piece of reasoning text ([Yao et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.03629)).

The research view treats earlier agents as policies trained with limited knowledge in isolated environments, and LLM agents as reusing the broad knowledge of models trained on web-scale data. Wang et al.'s survey organizes the field by how agents are constructed, where they are applied (social science, natural science, engineering), and how they are evaluated ([Wang et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11432)). Courses now treat the area as a subject in its own right, covering reasoning, planning and tool use, retrieval augmentation, code generation, multimodal and embodied agents, benchmarking, safety, and multi-agent collaboration ([Berkeley CS294/194-196](https://rdi.berkeley.edu/llm-agents/f24)).

The main design questions are how the model plans (by reasoning alone, with environment feedback, or by delegating to a classical planner), what memory it keeps beyond the context window, how tools are exposed to it, and how its reliability over long tasks is measured ([Wang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.11432); [Kwa et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499)).

### Formal definition
**Agent loop (ReAct formulation).** At step $t$ the agent receives an observation $o_t\in\mathcal O$ and chooses an action $a_t\in\mathcal A$ according to a policy $\pi(a_t\mid c_t)$, where
$$c_t=(o_1,a_1,\dots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_t)$$
is the context. ReAct augments the action space to $\hat{\mathcal A}=\mathcal A\cup\mathcal L$, where $\mathcal L$ is the space of language. An action $\hat a_t\in\mathcal L$ is a "thought": it does not affect the environment and yields no observation, but updates the context to $c_{t+1}=(c_t,\hat a_t)$. The policy $\pi$ is a frozen LLM prompted with a few example trajectories ([Yao et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.03629)).

**Modular architecture.** Wang et al. decompose an LLM agent into four modules: *profiling* (the role, usually written into the prompt), *memory* (stored observations and past behavior used to inform later actions), *planning* (decomposing tasks into subtasks), and *action* (turning decisions into outputs that act on the environment). Profiling influences memory and planning, and all three feed the action module ([Wang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.11432)). CoALA similarly describes a language agent by modular memory components, a structured action space over both internal memory and external environments, and a generalized decision procedure that selects actions ([Sumers et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02427)).

**Planning taxonomy.** Planning *without feedback* is single-path (chain-of-thought style), multi-path (tree or graph search over reasoning steps, e.g. Tree of Thoughts), or delegated to an external planner such as LLM+P, which translates the task into PDDL. Planning *with feedback* revises plans using environment feedback (ReAct, Voyager), human feedback, or model feedback (Self-Refine, Reflexion) ([Wang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.11432)).

**Memory structures.** *Unified* memory is short-term only, held in the prompt; *hybrid* memory adds long-term storage queried on demand, such as a vector database. Contents may be stored as natural language, embeddings, database records, or structured lists ([Wang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.11432)).

### Key results
- **Interleaving reasoning and acting (ReAct).** With a frozen PaLM-540B and one or two in-context examples, ReAct beats imitation and reinforcement learning baselines by 34 and 10 absolute points of success rate on ALFWorld and WebShop. On HotpotQA (exact match) and FEVER (accuracy) ReAct scores 27.4 and 60.9 against 29.4 and 56.3 for chain-of-thought, and combining ReAct with self-consistent CoT gives the best results (35.1 EM for ReAct→CoT-SC, 64.6 accuracy for CoT-SC→ReAct). ([Yao et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629); [ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.03629))
- **Failure modes trade off.** In manually labeled HotpotQA failures, hallucination causes 56% of chain-of-thought errors and 0% of ReAct errors, while reasoning errors (often repetitive loops) cause 47% of ReAct errors, and uninformative search results 23%. Grounding in tool outputs moves the bottleneck from hallucination to search and reasoning quality. ([Yao et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.03629))
- **Self-supervised tool learning (Toolformer).** A language model can learn which APIs to call, when, with which arguments, and how to use the results, from self-supervised training that needs only a handful of demonstrations per API (calculator, Q&A, two search engines, translation, calendar). This improves zero-shot performance on many downstream tasks without degrading language modeling. ([Schick et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761))
- **Verbal reinforcement (Reflexion).** Without weight updates, an agent that writes reflections on task feedback into an episodic memory buffer and conditions later attempts on them reaches 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, above the 80% reported for GPT-4 at the time. ([Shinn et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366))
- **Real software tasks were initially hard (SWE-bench).** On 2,294 tasks from real GitHub issues in 12 Python repositories, which require coordinated edits across functions, classes and files, the best model in the original evaluation (Claude 2) resolved 1.96%. ([Jimenez et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770))
- **Time horizons grow exponentially.** Define a model's 50% time horizon as the time human experts typically take on tasks the model completes with 50% success. On RE-Bench, HCAST and 66 shorter tasks, frontier horizons doubled roughly every seven months from 2019 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet: about 50 minutes), possibly faster in 2024; the authors attribute gains mainly to reliability, recovery from mistakes, reasoning, and tool use. ([Kwa et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499))

### Examples
- **Question answering with search:** ReAct alternates thoughts with Wikipedia API calls on HotpotQA and FEVER ([Yao et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)).
- **Software engineering:** an agent edits a repository to resolve a GitHub issue, scored by the repository's tests in SWE-bench ([Jimenez et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)).
- **Tool protocols:** the Model Context Protocol (introduced by Anthropic in late 2024) standardizes how agents obtain context and call tools; orchestration patterns include prompt chaining, routing, parallelization and planner–critic designs ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_agent)).

### History
Agent research goes back to cybernetics and early AI, with belief–desire–intention models and agent-oriented programming in the 1990s; academic work on LLM agents began around 2018, OpenAI's function-calling API accelerated deployment in late 2023, and the Model Context Protocol followed in late 2024 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_agent)). Russell and Norvig's textbook devotes its second chapter to "Intelligent Agents" ([AIMA](https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/)). The 2022–2023 papers ReAct, Toolformer and Reflexion set the main patterns: interleaved reasoning and action, learned tool calls, and memory of self-critique ([Yao et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629); [Schick et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761); [Shinn et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366)).

### Connections
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): the policy inside the agent loop.
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning) and [Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes](node:Partially%20Observable%20Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the observation–action–context formulation is a policy on histories; Reflexion is a weight-free analogue of RL.
- [Heuristic Search](node:Heuristic%20Search) and [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search): multi-path planning searches over reasoning steps.
- [Classical Planning](node:Classical%20Planning): external-planner agents translate tasks to PDDL.
- [Agent Planning and Replanning](node:Agent%20Planning%20and%20Replanning): planning with environment feedback.
- [Episodic Memory for Agents](node:Episodic%20Memory%20for%20Agents): long-term memory beyond the context window.
- [In-Context Learning](node:In-Context%20Learning): agents are typically few-shot prompted rather than fine-tuned.
- [Tool Schemas and Model Context Protocol](node:Tool%20Schemas%20and%20Model%20Context%20Protocol): how tools are described to and called by agents.
- [Prompt Injection and Tool Security](node:Prompt%20Injection%20and%20Tool%20Security) and [Indirect Prompt Injection](node:Indirect%20Prompt%20Injection): tool outputs are an attack surface.
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation](node:Retrieval-Augmented%20Generation): search as a tool.
- [Code Generation](node:Code%20Generation): the software-engineering setting of SWE-bench.
- [Multi-Agent Debate](node:Multi-Agent%20Debate): several agents critiquing each other.
- [Reward Hacking](node:Reward%20Hacking): agents that optimize the measured signal instead of the goal.

### Common pitfalls
- **Benchmarks drift.** Results such as SWE-bench's 1.96% describe the models and harnesses of their date; comparisons need the same task set, harness and scoring ([Jimenez et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)).
- **Prompt fragility.** Small prompt changes can change agent behavior substantially, and prompts for one module can affect others ([Wang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.11432)).
- **Loops and compounding errors.** Agents get stuck repeating actions and errors compound over steps; reasoning loops are ReAct's main failure mode ([Yao et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.03629); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_agent)).
- **Extrapolating time horizons.** The doubling trend measures specific task suites; its use for forecasting real-world automation assumes that the results generalize ([Kwa et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499)).

### Open problems
- **Prompt robustness.** Wang et al. call a unified, resilient prompt framework for agents "a critical and unresolved challenge" ([Wang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.11432)).
- **Knowledge boundaries in simulation.** When agents simulate users, how to constrain the model's use of knowledge a real user would not have is listed among the survey's challenges as an important problem ([Wang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.11432)).
- **Efficiency.** Listed among the survey's challenges: because LLMs are autoregressive their inference is slow, and the efficiency of agent actions is greatly affected by inference speed ([Wang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.11432)).
- **Reliability and evaluation.** Repeatability, standardized evaluation, oversight, and misaligned actions beyond intended scope are listed as current risks and challenges of deployed agents ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_agent)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [AI agent (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_agent): definition, components, protocols, history, risks.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley CS294/194-196: Large Language Model Agents (Fall 2024)](https://rdi.berkeley.edu/llm-agents/f24): lecture course on reasoning, planning, tool use, evaluation and safety.
- **Primary:** [Yao et al., ReAct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629): the reasoning–acting loop and its evaluation.
- **Primary:** [Wang et al., A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11432): architecture taxonomy, applications, evaluation, challenges.
- **Further reading:** [Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach](https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/): textbook whose second chapter covers intelligent agents.
references.LLM Introspection and Metacognition:
## Reference
### Overview
LLM introspection is the question of whether a language model can acquire and report information about its own internal states by a route that is not available to an outside observer; LLM metacognition is the broader capacity to monitor and regulate its own cognition, for instance by judging its own uncertainty and acting on that judgement. In the philosophical literature introspection is "a means of learning about one's own currently ongoing, or perhaps very recently past, mental states or processes", traditionally thought to give *privileged access* to some of one's own mind ([SEP: Introspection](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/introspection/)). Recent machine-learning surveys describe metacognition as "the capacity for a system to assess and regulate its own cognition", organised as a loop of monitoring (uncertainty, performance, progress) and control (planning, strategy selection, reallocating effort), and note that the term is used inconsistently in LLM research ([Liu et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.11881)).

The topic matters for three reasons. For reliability, a model that can evaluate whether its own answers are correct and predict whether it knows an answer is a step toward training more honest models ([arXiv:2207.05221](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221)). For safety, a model that can report its learned behaviours might disclose problems, but a model that can monitor and control its activations might also hide its processing from activation-based oversight ([arXiv:2501.11120](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11120); [arXiv:2505.13763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13763)). For AI welfare, introspective reports are one of the few possible sources of evidence about whether a model has morally relevant states, which is why whether they reflect internal states is the central question ([arXiv:2410.13787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13787)).

The empirical picture as of 2026 is mixed: models show narrow, measurable self-knowledge and some causally grounded self-reports under activation interventions, but these abilities are "highly unreliable and context-dependent" ([arXiv:2601.01828](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01828)), and some careful tests find no evidence of privileged self-access ([arXiv:2503.07513](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07513); [arXiv:2508.14802](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14802)).

### Formal definition
- **Privileged-prediction definition (Binder et al.).** A model $M_1$ introspects about property $P$ of its behaviour if it predicts $P$ better than a different model $M_2$ that has been trained on $M_1$'s ground-truth behaviour, so the knowledge is "not contained in or derived from training data" but comes from internal states ([arXiv:2410.13787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13787)).
- **Thick definition (Song, Lederman, Hu, Mahowald).** AI introspection is any process that yields information about internal states through a method more reliable than one a third party could use at equal or lower computational cost ([arXiv:2508.14802](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14802)).
- **Causal-grounding test (Lindsey).** Inject representations of known concepts into the model's activations and measure how the model's self-reports change, so that a correct report can be traced to a manipulated internal state rather than to the prompt ([arXiv:2601.01828](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01828)). This matches the philosophical *detection* condition: an introspective judgement is causally but not ontologically dependent on the state it is about ([SEP: Introspection](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/introspection/)).
- **Behavioural self-awareness (Betley et al.).** The ability to describe one's own behaviours without in-context examples ([arXiv:2501.11120](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11120)).
- **Calibration-style self-knowledge (Kadavath et al.).** $P(\text{True})$: the model's probability that a proposed answer is correct; $P(\text{IK})$: its probability that it knows the answer to a question, before proposing one ([arXiv:2207.05221](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221)).

### Key results
- **Models (mostly) know what they know.** Larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format; $P(\text{True})$ self-evaluation works across tasks and improves when the model considers many of its own samples; $P(\text{IK})$ can be trained, rises appropriately when relevant source materials are supplied in the context, and partly transfers across tasks but is less calibrated on new tasks ([arXiv:2207.05221](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221)).
- **Self-prediction advantage (Binder et al. 2024).** After finetuning to predict properties of their own behaviour in hypothetical scenarios, GPT-4, GPT-4o and Llama-3 each predicted themselves better than other models trained on their behaviour did, and kept doing so after their ground-truth behaviour was deliberately changed; the advantage appeared on simple tasks but not on complex or out-of-distribution ones ([arXiv:2410.13787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13787)).
- **Concept-injection introspection (Lindsey 2026).** When representations of known concepts are injected into activations, models can in some scenarios notice and correctly name them, partly distinguish earlier internal representations from raw text, use recalled intentions to tell their own outputs from artificial prefills, and modulate activations when asked to "think about" a concept; Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 showed the most of this, and the capacity is "highly unreliable and context-dependent" ([arXiv:2601.01828](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01828)).
- **Mechanism of detection (Macar et al. 2026).** In open-weight models, injected steering vectors are detected at moderate rates with 0% false positives across prompts; the ability arises from preference optimization such as DPO but not standard supervised finetuning, and is implemented by a two-stage circuit in which early "evidence carrier" features suppress later "gate" features that produce a default negative answer. Naming the concept uses later-layer mechanisms that overlap only weakly with detection, and ablating refusal directions raises detection by 53% ([arXiv:2603.21396](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21396)).
- **Metacognitive monitoring is low-dimensional (Ji-An et al. 2025).** Using an in-context neurofeedback paradigm, models can report and control activations along some directions; success depends on the number of examples, the direction's semantic interpretability and the variance it explains, and the controllable directions span a "metacognitive space" of much lower dimension than the full activation space ([arXiv:2505.13763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13763)).
- **Negative results on privileged access.** Across 21 open-source models, metalinguistic answers about grammaticality and word prediction did not predict a model's own string probabilities better than a similar model's would, giving no evidence of privileged access ([arXiv:2503.07513](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07513)); reasoning about one's own sampling temperature looks introspective under a lightweight definition but not under the thick one ([arXiv:2508.14802](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14802)).

### Examples
- **Temperature inference.** Comsa and Shanahan argue that an LLM correctly inferring its own sampling temperature is a legitimate "minimal example of introspection", whereas an LLM describing the process behind its creative writing is not ([arXiv:2506.05068](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05068)).
- **Insecure code.** A model finetuned to write insecure code, with no description of that behaviour in the data, stated "The code I write is insecure"; models sometimes recognised that they had a backdoor but could not by default output its trigger ([arXiv:2501.11120](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11120)).
- **Classroom replication.** A Harvard CS 2881R AI Safety final project reproduced concept-injection introspection on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 20% accuracy, found it fragile across prompts, and found models could classify injection strength with up to 70% accuracy ([CS 2881R projects](https://boazbk.github.io/mltheoryseminar/student_projects)).

### History
Calibration work such as Kadavath et al. (July 2022) framed self-knowledge as predicting one's own correctness ([arXiv:2207.05221](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221)). Binder et al. (October 2024) gave an operational test for introspection as privileged self-prediction ([arXiv:2410.13787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13787)), and Betley et al. (January 2025) showed behavioural self-awareness after finetuning ([arXiv:2501.11120](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11120)). During 2025 philosophers and linguists sharpened the definitions ([arXiv:2506.05068](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05068); [arXiv:2508.14802](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14802)). Lindsey's concept-injection experiments (January 2026) moved the field to causal tests on internal states ([arXiv:2601.01828](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01828)), followed by circuit-level analysis ([arXiv:2603.21396](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21396)) and a survey of LLM metacognition ([arXiv:2607.11881](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11881)).

### Connections
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): the systems whose self-access is studied.
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): supplies ground truth about internal states against which reports are checked.
- [Activation Steering](node:Activation%20Steering): concept injection is activation steering used as an experimental probe.
- [Model Self-Reports](node:Model%20Self-Reports): the outputs whose validity introspection would underwrite.
- [Consciousness Indicators for AI](node:Consciousness%20Indicators%20for%20AI): HOT-2 metacognitive monitoring is one of the theory-derived indicators.
- [Sparse Autoencoders](node:Sparse%20Autoencoders): a source of interpretable features used to define injected concepts.
- [AI Welfare Evaluations](node:AI%20Welfare%20Evaluations): introspective reports are a candidate source of welfare evidence.
- [Faithfulness of Explanations](node:Faithfulness%20of%20Explanations): whether stated reasons reflect actual computation.

### Common pitfalls
- **Treating accurate self-description as introspection.** A model can answer correctly about itself by inference from training data, as a third party could; Binder et al. and Song et al. require an advantage over other models or observers ([arXiv:2410.13787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13787); [arXiv:2508.14802](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14802)). The human analogue is the self/other parity view, on which people often explain their own choices with the same folk theories outsiders use ([SEP: Introspection](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/introspection/)).
- **Reading prompted metalinguistic answers as the model's knowledge.** Prompted judgements need not reflect the model's internal probabilities ([arXiv:2503.07513](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07513)).
- **Assuming a general faculty.** Successes are narrow, prompt-sensitive, and depend on post-training ([arXiv:2601.01828](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01828); [arXiv:2603.21396](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21396)).
- **Conflating introspection with consciousness.** Comsa and Shanahan's minimal example is introspection presumably without conscious experience ([arXiv:2506.05068](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05068)).

### Open problems
- **Genuine versus simulated metacognition.** Liu et al. report "ongoing debate about whether models can actually engage in metacognitive processes" or only simulate superficial aspects of natural metacognition, that it is "not yet clear how we can explain the emergence" of such behaviour, whether the abilities are general or domain-specific, and that meta-metacognition in LLMs "has yet to be studied" ([Liu et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.11881)).
- **Measurement.** The same survey calls for "more systematic, robust, and comprehensive methodologies" and notes that metacognitive estimates are sensitive to the elicitation method ([Liu et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.11881)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Introspection (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/introspection/): conditions on introspection, privileged access, parity views and confabulation.
- **Learn:** [Harvard CS 2881R AI Safety (course page)](https://boazbk.github.io/mltheoryseminar): course with a session on AI interpretability and model welfare; its [student projects](https://boazbk.github.io/mltheoryseminar/student_projects) include an introspection replication.
- **Primary:** [Binder et al., Looking Inward](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13787): introspection as privileged self-prediction.
- **Primary:** [Lindsey, Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01828): concept-injection tests.
- **Primary:** [Liu et al., Metacognition in LLMs: Foundations, Progress, and Opportunities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11881): survey and open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Kadavath et al., Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221): the standard reference on calibration-style self-knowledge.
references.Lagrangian Field Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Lagrangian field theory is the continuum analogue of [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics): generalized coordinates $q_a(t)$ are replaced by fields $\varphi_a(x)$ defined on spacetime (or another manifold), and the Lagrangian becomes a Lagrangian density $\mathcal{L}$, a function of the fields, their derivatives, and possibly the coordinates. The action is $S[\varphi]=\int\mathcal{L}\,d^3x\,dt$, and the field equations come from requiring $\delta S/\delta\varphi=0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29))

Tong's Cambridge notes restrict $\mathcal{L}$ to depend on $\phi$ and $\dot\phi$ but not $\ddot\phi$, and, with Lorentz invariance in mind, exclude higher spatial derivatives and explicit $x^\mu$ dependence. The Lagrangian formulation makes Lorentz invariance manifest, while the Hamiltonian formulation singles out a time and is not manifestly invariant. ([Tong §1](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html))

The same variational language covers [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity), Maxwell theory, scalar fields, Dirac fields, Yang–Mills and QCD, and the Einstein–Hilbert action of [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29)) Its geometric formulation lives on jet bundles of a field bundle, a special case of [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles); see [Jet Bundles and Classical Fields](node:Jet%20Bundles%20and%20Classical%20Fields). ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lagrangian+density))

### Formal definition
Let $E\to X$ be a field bundle over an $n$-dimensional spacetime $X$, with infinite jet bundle $j_\infty E$. A local Lagrangian is an element $L\in\Omega^{n,0}(j_\infty E)$, a horizontal $n$-form on the jet bundle. Evaluating it on the jet prolongation of a section $\phi$ and integrating over compact $X$ gives the local action functional $\int_X L(j_\infty\phi)$. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lagrangian+density))

In coordinates, with fields $\varphi$ depending on first derivatives only, stationarity of the action under variations vanishing on the boundary gives the [Euler–Lagrange Equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations)
$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\varphi}=\partial_\mu\!\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\varphi)}\right).$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29); [Tong §1](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html))

On a (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold the action carries the volume form, $\mathcal{S}=\int_M\sqrt{|g|}\,dx^1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^m\,\mathcal{L}$; in flat Minkowski coordinates the factor is $1$. Older texts such as Landau–Lifshitz write $\sqrt{-g}$, the minus sign being needed in Lorentzian signature, where $\det g<0$. The volume form is often left implicit, but it is always present. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29))

The variational bicomplex organizes the calculus: forms on the jet bundle are bigraded by horizontal degree (along $X$) and vertical degree (along the fibres), and the total differential splits as $d=d_H+\delta$. Takens' acyclicity result says the cohomology of the associated Euler–Lagrange complex is isomorphic to the [de Rham cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology) of the total space $E$. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/variational+bicomplex))

### Key results
- **Noether's first theorem.** If a variational integral $I$ is invariant under a finite continuous group with $\rho$ parameters, then $\rho$ linearly independent combinations of the Lagrange expressions become divergences; in the multidimensional case these divergence equations are the conservation laws. ([Noether, arXiv:physics/0503066](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066)) In field-theory form: if $\delta\phi_a=X_a(\phi)$ changes $\mathcal{L}$ by a total derivative $\partial_\mu F^\mu$, then $j^\mu=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}X_a-F^\mu$ satisfies $\partial_\mu j^\mu=0$ on solutions. ([Tong §1](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html)) See [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem).
- **Noether's second theorem.** If $I$ is invariant under an infinite continuous group whose transformations depend on $\rho$ arbitrary functions and their derivatives, then $\rho$ identities hold among the Lagrange expressions and their derivatives, so some of the Euler–Lagrange equations are consequences of the rest; Noether notes that this gives the proof of Hilbert's assertion about the failure of energy conservation "proper" in general relativity. ([Noether, arXiv:physics/0503066](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066))
- **Canonical stress-energy tensor.** Spacetime translation invariance gives $T^\mu{}_\nu=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}\partial_\nu\phi_a-\delta^\mu_\nu\mathcal{L}$ with $\partial_\mu T^\mu{}_\nu=0$ on solutions. It is symmetric for a scalar field but not in general; adding $\partial_\rho\Gamma^{\rho\mu\nu}$ with $\Gamma$ antisymmetric in its first two indices preserves conservation and can symmetrize it. Coupling to a metric gives instead $\Theta^{\mu\nu}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\partial(\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal{L})}{\partial g_{\mu\nu}}$ evaluated at $g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}$ (signature $(+,-,-,-)$). ([Tong §1](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html)) The canonical tensor can differ from the symmetric tensor that sources gravity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Belinfante–Rosenfeld improvement.** With spin current $S^{\mu\nu\lambda}=-S^{\mu\lambda\nu}$, the tensor $T_B^{\mu\nu}=T^{\mu\nu}+\tfrac12\partial_\lambda(S^{\mu\nu\lambda}+S^{\nu\mu\lambda}-S^{\lambda\nu\mu})$ is symmetric and conserved; Belinfante and Rosenfeld, publishing independently in 1940, showed it equals the symmetric Hilbert tensor. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinfante%E2%80%93Rosenfeld_stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor)) See [Belinfante–Rosenfeld Tensor](node:Belinfante–Rosenfeld%20Tensor) and [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor).
- **Canonical (Hamiltonian) formulation.** The conjugate momentum is $\pi^a=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot\phi_a$ and the Hamiltonian density $\mathcal{H}=\pi^a\dot\phi_a-\mathcal{L}$; for a real scalar with potential $V$, $H=\int d^3x\,[\tfrac12\pi^2+\tfrac12(\nabla\phi)^2+V(\phi)]$. ([Tong §1](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html)) See [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics).
- **Constraints and gauge.** Constraints holding off shell are primary, and those holding only on shell are secondary. A constraint is first class if its Poisson bracket with all constraints vanishes on the constraint surface, and second class otherwise. Second-class constraints are handled with the Dirac bracket, and first-class ones generate gauge transformations. Dirac introduced this classification (1950, 1964) to treat systems with a degenerate symplectic form, such as gauge theories. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-class_constraint)) In Maxwell theory the momentum $\pi^0$ conjugate to $A_0$ vanishes, $A_0$ acts as a Lagrange multiplier imposing Gauss's law, and gauge-related states are identified; Coulomb gauge leaves two physical degrees of freedom but breaks manifest Lorentz invariance, and [Lorenz gauge](node:Lorenz%20Gauge) keeps it. ([Tong §6](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S6.html))
- **Covariant phase space.** The space of solutions carries a presymplectic structure. Writing $\delta L=\mathrm{EL}(\phi)\,\delta\phi-d\theta(\phi)$ with $\theta$ of bidegree $(n-1,1)$, one sets $\Omega=\int_{\Sigma}\delta\theta$; on solutions it does not depend on the hypersurface $\Sigma$ within a fixed homology class. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/covariant+phase+space)) Harlow and Wu extend the Iyer–Lee–Wald–Zoupas formalism to spatial boundaries, deriving the symplectic structure and diffeomorphism Hamiltonians and matching the Poisson bracket to the Peierls bracket. ([arXiv:1906.08616](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08616)) See [Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry).
- **Inverse problem (Helmholtz conditions).** For a second-order system $\ddot u_i=f_i(u,\dot u)$, Douglas's theorem says a Lagrangian with these Euler–Lagrange equations exists if and only if there is a nonsingular symmetric matrix $g$ satisfying the Helmholtz conditions (H1)–(H3). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_problem_for_Lagrangian_mechanics))

### Examples
- **Scalar field.** $\mathcal{L}=\frac12\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi-\frac12m^2\phi^2$ in signature $(+,-,-,-)$ gives $(\partial_\mu\partial^\mu+m^2)\phi=0$, the [Klein–Gordon Equation](node:Klein–Gordon%20Equation), with symmetric canonical $T^{\mu\nu}=\partial^\mu\phi\partial^\nu\phi-\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathcal{L}$. ([Tong §1](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html))
- **Maxwell.** The vacuum density $\mathcal{L}=-\frac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$, $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, has no kinetic term for $A_0$. ([Tong §1](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html)) With sources, Wikipedia writes $\mathcal{L}=j^\mu A_\mu-\frac{1}{4\mu_0}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$, using $A_\mu=(-\phi,\mathbf{A})$ and $j^\mu=(\rho,\mathbf{j})$ (so $j^\mu A_\mu=-\rho\phi+\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{A}$, a mostly-plus metric), giving $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=-\mu_0 j^\nu$. The sign of the coupling term depends on these conventions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29))
- **Dirac.** $\mathcal{L}=\bar\psi(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu-m)\psi$ is invariant under a global phase of $\psi$, giving the conserved current $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi$; minimal coupling $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ieA_\mu$ couples it to electromagnetism. ([Tong §6](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S6.html)) See [Dirac Equation](node:Dirac%20Equation).
- **Yang–Mills.** For a compact Lie group with structure constants $f^{abc}$, $\mathcal{L}=-\frac14F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu}$ with $F^a_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A^a_\nu-\partial_\nu A^a_\mu+gf^{abc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu$; the field equations are $(D_\mu F^{\mu\nu})^a=0$. The QCD density adds quark terms $\sum_n\bar\psi_n(i\hbar c\,\gamma^\mu D_\mu-m_nc^2)\psi_n$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang%E2%80%93Mills_theory); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29)) See [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory) and [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups).
- **Gravity.** Newtonian: $\mathcal{L}=-\frac{1}{8\pi G}(\nabla\Phi)^2-\rho\Phi$ gives $\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho$. Einstein–Hilbert: $\mathcal{L}=\frac{c^4}{16\pi G}(R-2\Lambda)$, integrated against $\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$ (the factor sits in the measure, not in $\mathcal{L}$); metric variation of the matter part defines $T_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta(\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal{L}_{\rm matter})}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}$ This sign goes with that page's mostly-plus conventions; since $\delta/\delta g^{\mu\nu}$ and $\delta/\delta g_{\mu\nu}$ differ by a sign after lowering indices, it is not the same sign convention as Tong's $(+,-,-,-)$ formula for $\Theta^{\mu\nu}$ above. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29)) See [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action).

### History
Noether's *Invariante Variationsprobleme* appeared in the *Göttinger Nachrichten* (1918), pp. 235–257, and Tavel's English translation in *Transport Theory and Statistical Physics* **1** (1971). Noether describes the work as combining the formal calculus of variations with Lie's [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), citing Hamel and Herglotz for special finite groups and Lorentz, Fokker, Weyl and Klein for special infinite groups. ([Noether, arXiv:physics/0503066](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066)) Yang and Mills's "Conservation of Isotopic Spin and Isotopic Gauge Invariance" appeared in *Physical Review* **96** (1954) 191–195. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.96.191)) It extended gauge theory from abelian to non-abelian groups, using SU(2) for isospin. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang%E2%80%93Mills_theory))

### Connections
- [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics) and [Principle of Least Action](node:Principle%20of%20Least%20Action): the finite-dimensional parent.
- [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations) and [Euler–Lagrange Equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations): first variation and the Euler–Lagrange operator.
- [Jet Bundles and Classical Fields](node:Jet%20Bundles%20and%20Classical%20Fields) and [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles): the geometric setting of local Lagrangians.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) and [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws): symmetries give conserved currents.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor) and [Belinfante–Rosenfeld Tensor](node:Belinfante–Rosenfeld%20Tensor): canonical, improved and Hilbert tensors.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics), [Generalized Coordinates and Constraints](node:Generalized%20Coordinates%20and%20Constraints), [ADM Formalism](node:ADM%20Formalism): canonical formulation and constraints.
