- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory), [Gauge Invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance), [Principal Bundle Connections](node:Principal%20Bundle%20Connections): local symmetries and Noether's second theorem.
- [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action), [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations), [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity), [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): gravitational actions.
- [Klein–Gordon Equation](node:Klein–Gordon%20Equation), [Dirac Equation](node:Dirac%20Equation), [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics): standard field Lagrangians.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory), [Path Integral Formulation](node:Path%20Integral%20Formulation), [Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap](node:Yang–Mills%20Existence%20and%20Mass%20Gap): quantizing these actions.
- [Special Relativity](node:Special%20Relativity), [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime), [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations).
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Relativistic fields and quantization](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Relativistic%20fields%20and%20quantization)

### Common pitfalls
- **Lagrangian versus density.** $L=\int\mathcal{L}\,d^3x$ and $S=\int L\,dt$; calling $\mathcal{L}$ "the Lagrangian" blurs the distinction. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29))
- **Canonical tensor is not the gravitational source.** The canonical Noether tensor need not be symmetric; the symmetric (Belinfante or Hilbert) tensor is what couples to gravity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinfante%E2%80%93Rosenfeld_stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))
- **Gauge symmetries are not ordinary symmetries.** Gauge symmetry is a redundancy of description and does not give extra conservation laws the way a global symmetry does. ([Tong §6](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S6.html))
- **Dissipation.** Systems needing a Rayleigh dissipation function lie outside Noether's theorem; dissipative systems with continuous symmetries need not have conservation laws. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Sign conventions.** Signature and the sign convention for $A^\mu$ change the sign of $j^\mu A_\mu$ and of kinetic terms; check them before comparing formulas from different sources. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29); [Tong §1](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html))

### Open problems
- **Yang–Mills existence and mass gap.** Quantum Yang–Mills particles have positive mass even though classical Yang–Mills waves travel at the speed of light. This mass gap is seen in experiment and computer simulation, but no proof or theoretical understanding is known; it is a Clay Millennium Prize Problem, listed by the Clay Institute as unsolved. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/))
- **Inverse problem in arbitrary dimension.** For second-order systems, condition (H1) together with the algebraic conditions (A) derived from (H2) may imply that the Lagrangian is singular; "as of 2006, there is no general theorem to circumvent this difficulty in arbitrary dimension," though certain special cases have been resolved; for a parallel connection, such as the canonical connection on a Lie group, the higher-order algebraic conditions hold automatically. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_problem_for_Lagrangian_mechanics))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Lagrangian (field theory) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_%28field_theory%29): densities, volume forms, and the standard Lagrangians of physics.
- **Reference:** [Lagrangian density (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lagrangian+density) and [covariant phase space (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/covariant+phase+space): jet-bundle definition and presymplectic structure on solutions.
- **Learn:** [Tong, QFT §1 Classical Field Theory](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S1.html) and [§6 Quantum Electrodynamics](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qfthtml/S6.html): Euler–Lagrange equations, Noether currents, stress-energy, Hamiltonian form, and Maxwell constraints.
- **Primary:** [Noether, Invariant Variation Problems (arXiv:physics/0503066)](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066): the 1918 paper containing both theorems.
- **Primary:** [Harlow and Wu, Covariant phase space with boundaries (arXiv:1906.08616)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08616): research-level account of symplectic structure and Hamiltonians in Lagrangian field theories.
- **Further reading:** [Yang and Mills, Phys. Rev. 96 (1954) 191](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.96.191): the original non-abelian gauge theory paper.
references.Lagrangian Mechanics:
## Reference
### Overview
Lagrangian mechanics describes a system by generalized coordinates $q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ and a single scalar function $L(q,\dot q,t)$, and obtains the equations of motion by requiring the action $S=\int L\,dt$ to be stationary (Hamilton's principle, $\delta S=0$). For conservative systems $L=T-V$. Because the formulation works in any coordinates adapted to the constraints, ideal constraint forces drop out of the equations. ([Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics); [MIT 8.09, Ch. 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf)) It reorganizes [Newtonian Mechanics](node:Newtonian%20Mechanics) through [D'Alembert's Principle](node:D'Alembert's%20Principle) and the [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations), and it is the starting point for [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics) and for [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory).

Its main structural payoff is the link between symmetry and conservation: by [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem), each continuous symmetry of the action yields a conserved quantity, with energy, momentum and angular momentum as the basic cases. ([Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem); [Noether 1918, trans. Tavel](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066))

### Formal definition
Let $r_k=r_k(q,t)$ express particle positions in terms of independent [generalized coordinates](node:Generalized%20Coordinates%20and%20Constraints). With $S[q]=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt$ and variations vanishing at the endpoints, $\delta S=0$ gives the [Euler–Lagrange equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations)
$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_j}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j}=0,\qquad j=1,\dots,n.$$
The generalized momentum is $p_j=\partial L/\partial\dot q_j$ and the energy function is $h=\sum_j\dot q_j\,\partial L/\partial\dot q_j-L$. ([Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics); [MIT 8.09, eqs. 1.76–1.78](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))

From d'Alembert's principle $\sum_i(\dot p_i-F_i)\cdot\delta r_i=0$ one gets $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial T}{\partial\dot q_j}-\frac{\partial T}{\partial q_j}=Q_j$ with generalized forces $Q_j=\sum_iF_i\cdot\partial r_i/\partial q_j$; this reduces to the Euler–Lagrange equations when $Q_j=-\partial V/\partial q_j+\frac{d}{dt}\partial V/\partial\dot q_j$ for some $V(q,\dot q,t)$. ([MIT 8.09, eqs. 1.64–1.70](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))

### Key results
- **Noether's theorem (mechanics form).** If the action is invariant under the smooth one-parameter family $t\to t+\varepsilon T$, $q_k\to q_k+\varepsilon Q_k$, then along solutions of the Euler–Lagrange equations $\big(\sum_kp_k\dot q_k-L\big)T-\sum_kp_kQ_k$ is constant. Time translation gives conservation of $E=\sum_kp_k\dot q_k-L$ when $\partial L/\partial t=0$; translation in a cyclic coordinate gives conservation of $p_k$; rotation about $\mathbf n$ gives conservation of $\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf r\times\mathbf p)$. ([Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem)) Noether published the theorem in 1918 in "Invariante Variationsprobleme". ([Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem); [Noether 1918, trans. Tavel](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066))
- **Energy function versus energy.** $dh/dt=-\partial L/\partial t$, so $h$ is conserved when $L$ has no explicit time dependence; in natural coordinates $h=T+V=E$, but in general they differ: in a moving frame $h$ can be conserved while $T+V$ is not. ([MIT 8.09, §1.3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf); [Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics))
- **Constraints and Lagrange multipliers.** Holonomic constraints have the form $f_\alpha(q,t)=0$; constraints such as rolling without slipping, $\sum_ja_{j\alpha}(q,t)\dot q_j+a_{t\alpha}=0$, are generally non-holonomic (non-integrable). For $k$ such constraints, $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_j}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j}=\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha a_{j\alpha}$, which together with the constraints gives $n+k$ equations for $q_j,\lambda_\alpha$; $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha a_{j\alpha}$ is the generalized constraint force. In the holonomic case $a_{j\alpha}=\partial f_\alpha/\partial q_j$ and the equations follow from $\delta\int(L+\lambda_\alpha f_\alpha)\,dt=0$; the velocity-constraint case cannot in general be derived from Hamilton's principle and needs d'Alembert's principle. ([MIT 8.09, eqs. 1.85–1.91](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))
- **Dissipation.** Non-potential forces $R_j$ enter as $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_j}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j}=R_j$. For friction $F_i=-h_i(v_i)\hat v_i$, $R_j=-\partial\mathcal F/\partial\dot q_j$ with dissipation function $\mathcal F=\sum_i\int_0^{v_i}h_i(v')\,dv'$. ([MIT 8.09, eqs. 1.71–1.74](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf)) For linear damping this is Rayleigh's $D=\tfrac12\sum_{j,k}C_{jk}\dot q_j\dot q_k$, giving $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_j}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j}+\frac{\partial D}{\partial\dot q_j}=0$. ([Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics))
- **Velocity-dependent potentials.** A charge $q$ in potentials $(\phi,\mathbf A)$ has $L=\tfrac12m v^2-q\phi+q\,\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf A$; the canonical momentum $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v+q\mathbf A$ differs from the kinetic momentum, and the Euler–Lagrange equations give the Lorentz force $q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)$. ([MIT 8.09, eq. 1.36 and §1.3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf); [Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics))
- **Total-derivative freedom.** $L'=L+\frac{d}{dt}f(q,t)$ changes the action only by endpoint terms and gives the same equations of motion. ([Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics))
- **Legendre transform and the tangent bundle.** Geometrically, $L$ is a function on the [tangent bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle) $TM$ of the configuration manifold. The fibre derivative $F_L:TM\to T^*M$ defines $H(p,q)=p\cdot v-L(v,q)$ with $v=F_L^{-1}(p)$; if $L$ restricted to each fibre is strictly convex and bounded below by a positive-definite quadratic form minus a constant, $F_L$ is a diffeomorphism and the Hamiltonian formulation is well defined. ([Legendre transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_transformation)) For $L=L_0+a_j\dot q_j+\tfrac12\dot q_jT_{jk}\dot q_k$ with $T$ positive definite, $H=\tfrac12(p-a)\cdot T^{-1}\cdot(p-a)-L_0$. ([MIT 8.09, eq. 1.35](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))
- **Stationary, not least.** The true path makes the action stationary; it may be a minimum or a saddle, but not a maximum. ([Stationary-action principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary-action_principle)) For the 1D harmonic oscillator of frequency $\omega$, the action is a minimum when the elapsed time $\tau<\pi/\omega$ (half a period) and a saddle point beyond it; at $\tau=\pi/\omega$ every $q(t)=A\sin\omega t$ solves the boundary problem $q(0)=q(\pi/\omega)=0$, so infinitely many solutions join those endpoints and the second variation vanishes along them (a kinetic focus). Legendre's condition $\partial^2L/\partial\dot q^2\ge0$ is necessary but not sufficient; Jacobi's conjugate-point condition is also needed. ([Moriconi, arXiv:2104.07475](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.07475))

### Examples
- **Pendulum on a sliding support.** A mass $m_1$ sliding on the $x$-axis carries a rigid pendulum of length $\ell$ and mass $m_2$. With coordinates $(x,\theta)$, $L=\tfrac{m_1+m_2}2\dot x^2+m_2\ell\cos\theta\,\dot x\dot\theta+\tfrac{m_2}2\ell^2\dot\theta^2+m_2g\ell\cos\theta$; $x$ is cyclic, so $p_x=(m_1+m_2)\dot x+m_2\ell\cos\theta\,\dot\theta$ (the centre-of-mass momentum) is conserved, and small oscillations have $\ddot\theta=-(m_2g/\mu\ell)\theta$ with reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$. ([MIT 8.09, eqs. 1.37–1.47](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))
- **Particle leaving a sphere.** For a mass sliding from the top of a sphere of radius $a$, imposing $r=a$ with a multiplier gives the radial constraint force $\lambda=mg(3\cos\theta-2)$, so the mass leaves the surface at $\cos\theta=2/3$ ($\theta\approx48^\circ$). ([MIT 8.09, eq. 1.94](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))
- **Rolling disk.** A vertical disk rolling without slipping on a plane obeys $dx-a\sin\theta\,d\phi=0$, $dy+a\cos\theta\,d\phi=0$, which no integrating factor makes holonomic; rolling along a fixed line is holonomic. ([MIT 8.09, §1.4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))
- **Stokes drag.** A sphere falling in a viscous fluid with $\mathcal F=3\pi\eta a\dot y^2$ obeys $m'\ddot y+m'g=-6\pi\eta a\dot y$. ([MIT 8.09, §1.4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf)) Compare [Damped and Driven Oscillations](node:Damped%20and%20Driven%20Oscillations).

### History
Lagrange presented the approach to the Turin Academy in 1760 and published it in *Mécanique analytique* in 1788. ([Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics)) Euler and Lagrange, building on Maupertuis, shaped the principle of least action, and Hamilton and Jacobi then developed the Hamilton–Jacobi formulation. ([Stationary-action principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary-action_principle)) Noether, who began the work in 1915 while helping Klein and Hilbert with [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity), published the symmetry–conservation theorem in 1918. ([Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem)) Douglas's 1941 paper gave necessary and sufficient conditions, now called the Helmholtz conditions, for a system of ODEs to be Euler–Lagrange equations, and solved the inverse problem for two equations. ([Inverse problem for Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_problem_for_Lagrangian_mechanics); [Do–Prince, arXiv:2001.06771](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.06771))

### Connections
- [Newtonian Mechanics](node:Newtonian%20Mechanics): Lagrange's equations follow from Newton's laws via d'Alembert's principle.
- [Principle of Least Action](node:Principle%20of%20Least%20Action): the variational principle behind the Euler–Lagrange equations.
- [Generalized Coordinates and Constraints](node:Generalized%20Coordinates%20and%20Constraints) and [D'Alembert's Principle](node:D'Alembert's%20Principle): how constraints are eliminated or enforced.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) and [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws): symmetries to conserved quantities.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics), [Hamilton–Jacobi Theory](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Theory) and [Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry): the Legendre-transformed phase-space picture.
- [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations): Euler–Lagrange equations, Legendre and Jacobi conditions.
- [Tangent Bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle): the geometric home of $L$.
- [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory): the same formalism for fields.

### Common pitfalls
- The action is stationary, not always least; minimality can fail beyond a conjugate point. ([Stationary-action principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary-action_principle); [Moriconi, arXiv:2104.07475](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.07475))
- Canonical momentum $p_j=\partial L/\partial\dot q_j$ need not be mechanical momentum (e.g. $m\mathbf v+q\mathbf A$). ([MIT 8.09, §1.3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))
- The conserved energy function $h$ is not always $T+V$; the two coincide only in natural coordinates. ([MIT 8.09, §1.3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))
- Velocity (non-holonomic) constraints cannot simply be substituted into $L$ or added via $\lambda f$ in the action; use the multiplier equations derived from d'Alembert's principle. ([MIT 8.09, eq. 1.91](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf))
- Lagrangians are not unique: adding $df(q,t)/dt$ leaves the dynamics unchanged. ([Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics))

### Open problems
- **Inverse problem of the calculus of variations.** Given second-order ODEs $\ddot x^a=F^a(t,x,\dot x)$, decide whether they are Euler–Lagrange equations of some $L$, i.e. whether a nondegenerate symmetric multiplier $g_{ab}$ satisfies the Helmholtz conditions. Douglas solved dimension two; Do and Prince report that until recently only the two easiest of Douglas's cases had been solved in arbitrary dimension, and they analyse only some dimension-3 subcases. Wikipedia notes that as of 2006 there was no general theorem in arbitrary dimension on when the algebraic conditions force the Lagrangian to be singular, only special cases. ([Do–Prince, arXiv:2001.06771](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.06771); [Inverse problem for Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_problem_for_Lagrangian_mechanics))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Lagrangian mechanics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics): equations, multipliers, dissipation, energy function, history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.09 Classical Mechanics III, Chapter 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/04c9b750af0e52b90121e2fe00edf434_MIT8_09F14_Chapter_1.pdf): d'Alembert's principle, constraints, Lagrange multipliers, friction, worked examples.
- **Primary:** [Noether, Invariant Variation Problems (1918; trans. Tavel)](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066): the original symmetry–conservation theorems.
- **Primary:** [Do and Prince, The inverse problem in the calculus of variations: new developments](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.06771): research survey of the Helmholtz-conditions problem.
- **Further reading:** [Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics (Springer GTM, 1989)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2063-1): the geometric treatment on manifolds and tangent bundles.
references.Lambda Calculus:
## Reference
### Overview
The lambda calculus is a formal system whose only constructs are function abstraction $\lambda x.M$ and application $MN$, with computation given by substituting arguments for bound variables. It serves at once as a minimal programming language, as a model of computation for studying computable functions, and, in its typed form, as an internal language for cartesian closed categories ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus)).

The untyped calculus is Turing complete: the lambda-definable functions on numerals are exactly the recursive functions, and the question whether two lambda terms are convertible was the first problem proved undecidable ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)). Typed variants trade expressive power for termination: the simply typed calculus and polymorphic System F are strongly normalizing, and types correspond to propositions of intuitionistic logic ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus); [Wikipedia: System F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_F); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)).

Functional programming languages implement the lambda calculus, typed variants underlie ML and Haskell, and Landin's 1965 paper related ALGOL 60 to Church's lambda notation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus)). Scott's construction of a domain of continuous functions that is isomorphic to its own function space gave the untyped calculus a mathematical model and underlies denotational semantics ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)). The standard comprehensive reference for the untyped theory is Barendregt's *The Lambda Calculus: Its Syntax and Semantics* (North-Holland, revised edition 1984) ([Barendregt 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02243); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/b978-0-444-87508-2.50014-9)).

### Formal definition
**Terms.** Given a countable set of variables, the set $\Lambda$ of lambda terms is the least set such that every variable is a term, and if $M,N$ are terms and $x$ is a variable then $(MN)$ (application) and $(\lambda x.M)$ (abstraction) are terms. Application associates to the left, so $PQR=(PQ)R$; $\lambda$ binds $x$ in $M$, and a term with no free variables is a combinator ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)).

**Substitution and conversion.** $M[x:=N]$ replaces the free occurrences of $x$ in $M$ by $N$, renaming bound variables of $M$ when needed so that no free variable of $N$ is captured. The basic relations are
$$\alpha:\ \lambda x.M \equiv \lambda y.M[x:=y]\ (y\notin FV(M)),\qquad \beta:\ (\lambda x.M)N \to M[x:=N],\qquad \eta:\ \lambda x.Mx \to M\ (x\notin FV(M)).$$
$\twoheadrightarrow_\beta$ is the reflexive–transitive closure of one-step $\beta$-reduction inside any context, and $=_\beta$ the equivalence it generates ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus)).

**Normal forms.** $M$ is in $\beta$-normal form if it contains no redex $(\lambda x.P)Q$. $M$ is weakly normalizing if some finite reduction sequence from $M$ ends in a normal form, and strongly normalizing if every reduction sequence from $M$ terminates ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus)). A term has a head normal form if it reduces to one of the shape $\lambda x_1\ldots x_n.\,yM_1\cdots M_m$; its Böhm tree $BT(M)$ is $\bot$ if $M$ has no head normal form, and otherwise $\lambda x_1\ldots x_n.\,y\,BT(M_1)\cdots BT(M_m)$, a possibly infinite tree ([Wikipedia: Böhm tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6hm_tree)).

**Church numerals.** $\bar n=\lambda f.\lambda x.f^n x$, so $\bar 0=\lambda f x.x$, $\bar 2=\lambda f x.f(fx)$, with successor $\mathrm{succ}=\lambda n f x.f(nfx)$. A term $M$ numeralwise represents $f:\mathbb N^k\to\mathbb N$ if $M\bar n_1\cdots\bar n_k\twoheadrightarrow_\beta \overline{f(n_1,\dots,n_k)}$ for all inputs ([Selinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0804.3434); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus)).

**Simply typed lambda calculus.** Types are built from base types by $\to$; $\lambda x{:}A.\,t$ has type $A\to B$ when $t:B$ under the assumption $x:A$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus)).

**System F.** Girard and Reynolds independently extended the simply typed calculus with universal quantification over types. Types include $\forall\alpha.\sigma$; if $M:\forall\alpha.\sigma$ then the type application $M\tau$ has type $\sigma[\alpha:=\tau]$, and if $M:\sigma$ with $\alpha$ not free in the context then $\Lambda\alpha.M:\forall\alpha.\sigma$. The polymorphic identity has type $\forall\alpha.\alpha\to\alpha$, and the natural numbers are encoded at type $\forall\alpha.\alpha\to(\alpha\to\alpha)\to\alpha$ by typed Church numerals ([Wikipedia: System F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_F)).

### Key results
- **Church–Rosser theorem.** Let $\twoheadrightarrow$ be $\twoheadrightarrow_\beta$ or $\twoheadrightarrow_{\beta\eta}$. If $M\twoheadrightarrow N$ and $M\twoheadrightarrow P$, there is $Z$ with $N\twoheadrightarrow Z$ and $P\twoheadrightarrow Z$. Corollaries: two $\beta$-equal $\beta$-normal forms are $\alpha$-equal (similarly for $\beta\eta$), and $x\ne_\beta\lambda y.xy$, so $\eta$ does not follow from $\beta$. ([Selinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0804.3434))
- **Consistency.** The theory $\lambda$ does not prove every equation; for example $K=I$ is not derivable, since $K$ and $I$ are distinct $\beta$-normal forms and Church–Rosser applies. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/))
- **Standardization theorem.** If $M\twoheadrightarrow_\beta N$, then there is a *standard* $\beta$-reduction sequence from $M$ to $N$. Its special case, the **leftmost reduction theorem**, says: if $M\twoheadrightarrow_\beta N$ and $N$ is a $\beta$-normal form, then leftmost (normal-order) reduction leads from $M$ to $N$. ([Kashima 2000](https://www.is.c.titech.ac.jp/~kashima/pub/C-145.pdf)) Standardization is the stronger statement: it concerns every reduction $M\twoheadrightarrow_\beta N$, not only reductions to normal form. The rightmost strategy is not normalizing: $KI\Omega$ has normal form $I$, but rightmost reduction loops on $\Omega$ ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)).
- **Fixed point theorem.** Every term $F$ has a fixed point: with $A=\lambda xy.y(xxy)$ and Turing's combinator $\Theta=AA$, $\Theta F\twoheadrightarrow_\beta F(\Theta F)$. This is how general recursion is encoded. ([Selinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0804.3434); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/))
- **Definability of recursive functions.** All recursive functions can be represented in the lambda calculus; the lambda-definable, Turing-computable and general recursive functions coincide. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus))
- **Undecidability (Church 1936).** There is no algorithm deciding whether $M=_\beta N$. Church's proof first reduces this to deciding whether a term has a normal form and then uses a Gödel numbering of terms, following the structure of Gödel's first incompleteness theorem. Deciding whether a term has a head normal form is also undecidable. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus); [Wikipedia: Böhm tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6hm_tree))
- **Böhm's theorem (1968).** If $M_0,M_1$ are closed terms with *different* $\beta\eta$-normal forms, then for all closed $P_0,P_1$ there are terms $\vec N$ with $M_0\vec N=_\beta P_0$ and $M_1\vec N=_\beta P_1$; the two terms are *separable*. Consequently adding $M_0=M_1$ to $\lambda\beta\eta$ makes it inconsistent. A full proof is Theorem 10.4.2 of Barendregt's book. For closed terms that have a $\beta$-normal form, separability, inconsistency of the equation $M_0=M_1$ with $\lambda\beta$, and having distinct $\beta\eta$-normal forms are equivalent. Böhm and his students generalized the theorem from two to finitely many terms with pairwise different $\beta\eta$-normal forms (Böhm, Dezani-Ciancaglini, Peretti and Ronchi della Rocca 1979). ([Barendregt 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02243))
- **Strong normalization of typed calculi.** The simply typed lambda calculus and many typed variants are strongly normalizing. Adding a natural numbers object with a recursor defines more functions (including Ackermann's) but not all computable ones; adding a fixpoint combinator or unbounded search reaches all partial recursive functions. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus))
- **Strong normalization of System F (Girard).** Every well-typed term of the second-order polymorphic lambda calculus is strongly normalizing, under $\beta$- and $\beta\eta$-reduction. The proof uses Girard's *candidats de réductibilité*, sets of terms satisfying closure conditions, generalizing Tait's reducibility method for simple types; Tait simplified it by taking candidates to be sets of untyped terms and erasing types. ([Gallier, On Girard's candidats de reductibilité](https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~jean/sngirard.pdf); [Wikipedia: System F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_F)) Type inference for the Curry-style (unannotated) System F is undecidable (Wells) ([Wikipedia: System F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_F)).
- **Intersection types.** In the Barendregt–Coppo–Dezani system, a term is strongly $\beta$-normalizing if and only if it is typable without the universal-type rule $(\omega)$ (Ghilezan 1996) ([Wikipedia: Intersection type discipline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_type_discipline); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus)).
- **Curry–Howard and Lambek.** If a type $\tau$ is inhabited by a simply typed term, $\tau$ is intuitionistically valid; the correspondence is with the implicational fragment of propositional intuitionistic logic ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)). Every cartesian closed category yields a simply typed calculus (its internal language) and conversely, and nLab states that the two constructions are adjoint in an appropriate sense; the standard reference for this syntax–semantics relation is Lambek and Scott, *Introduction to Higher Order Categorical Logic* (1986) ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus); [nLab: cartesian closed category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cartesian+closed+category)).

### Examples
- $\Omega=(\lambda x.xx)(\lambda x.xx)$ reduces to itself, so it has no normal form; it is the classic non-terminating program ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus)).
- Capture: $\lambda x.\lambda y.\,x(y-5)$ cannot be applied to $2y$ by naive textual substitution, since the $y$ in $2y$ would be captured; it must first be $\alpha$-renamed ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)).
- Böhm separation: $\lambda xy.x$ and $\lambda xy.y$ are distinct $\beta\eta$-normal forms, so equating them derives every equation ([Barendregt 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02243)).
- Models: no nontrivial set-theoretic model exists, since $X\cong X^X$ contradicts Cantor's theorem. A categorical model is a reflexive object $U$ in a cartesian closed category with application $a:U\to U^U$ and abstraction $\ell:U^U\to U$ such that $a\circ\ell=1_{U^U}$, i.e. the composite $U^U\xrightarrow{\ell}U\xrightarrow{a}U^U$ is the identity and $U^U$ is a retract of $U$; this validates $\beta$. Scott's $D_\infty$ (1969) is the first such model ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)).

### History
Church developed the lambda calculus around 1930 as part of a larger logical system, and Schönfinkel's 1920 combinatory logic was independently rediscovered by Curry ([Hindley and Seldin, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/lambdacalculus-and-combinators/preface/A8E6261F5D932DED3B52FD246EA66D71)). Church's original system was shown inconsistent by the Kleene–Rosser paradox in 1935; in 1936 he published the untyped calculus as a theory of computation, and in 1940 the simply typed calculus ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus)). Böhm proved his separability theorem in 1968 ([Barendregt 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02243)), and Barendregt introduced Böhm trees in 1977 ([Wikipedia: Böhm tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6hm_tree)). Scott's $D_\infty$ (1969) and the Plotkin–Scott graph model $P_\omega$ (1972, 1974) gave the calculus mathematical semantics ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)). System F was introduced by Girard (1972) and Reynolds (1974) ([Wikipedia: System F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_F)).

### Connections
- [Functions and Relations](node:Functions%20and%20Relations): abstraction and application formalize functions given by rules rather than as graphs.
- [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory) and [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines): lambda-definability is one of the equivalent definitions of computable function.
- [Functional Programming](node:Functional%20Programming): languages in the ML and Haskell families are typed lambda calculi with extensions.
- [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory) and [Type Inference](node:Type%20Inference): typed lambda calculi are the term languages of type theories; inference is decidable for simple types but not for Curry-style System F.
- [Curry-Howard Correspondence](node:Curry-Howard%20Correspondence): simply typed terms are proofs in intuitionistic implicational logic.
- [Proof Theory](node:Proof%20Theory): normalization proofs for typed calculi, such as Tait's and Girard's reducibility methods, are proof-theoretic results.
- [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): simply typed calculi are internal languages of cartesian closed categories.
- [Domain Theory](node:Domain%20Theory) and [Programming Language Semantics](node:Programming%20Language%20Semantics): Scott's models give the denotational semantics of the calculus.
- [Universal Algebra](node:Universal%20Algebra): the lattice of lambda theories is studied with universal-algebraic tools.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): Church's undecidability proof uses Gödel numbering.
- [Homotopy Type Theory](node:Homotopy%20Type%20Theory): a dependent type theory whose terms extend the lambda calculus.

### Common pitfalls
- **Naive substitution is wrong.** Substitution must avoid capturing free variables of the argument, which forces $\alpha$-renaming ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/)).
- **Strategy matters for termination.** A term can have a normal form that applicative-order (leftmost innermost) reduction never reaches; normal order (leftmost outermost) reaches it whenever it exists ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus)).
- **$\eta$ is an extra axiom.** $\beta$-conversion alone does not identify $x$ with $\lambda y.xy$ ([Selinger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0804.3434)), and Böhm's theorem needs distinct $\beta\eta$-normal forms, not merely distinct $\beta$-normal forms ([Barendregt 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02243)).
- **Retraction direction in models.** The model condition is that $U^U$ is a retract of $U$ ($a\circ\ell=1$), not that $U$ is a retract of $U^U$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus)).

### Open problems
- **The $\lambda\beta$ problem.** Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra call it a longstanding open problem whether there is a non-syntactical model of the untyped lambda calculus whose equational theory is exactly the least lambda theory $\lambda\beta$. They show that the order theory of an "effective" model is never recursively enumerable, so no effective model has $\lambda\beta$ or $\lambda\beta\eta$ as its theory ([Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra 2008](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.2264)).
- **Representability of lambda theories.** Manzonetto and Salibra's survey of the lattice of lambda theories and of models studied with universal algebra refers to long-standing open questions on the representability of lambda theories as theories of models and lists 26 open problems ([Manzonetto and Salibra, J. Logic Comput. 2010](https://academic.oup.com/logcom/article/20/4/877/971894)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [The Lambda Calculus (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/lambda-calculus/): syntax, conversion, Church–Rosser, consistency, representability, models, typed calculus.
- **Reference:** [lambda-calculus (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lambda-calculus): normalization, typed variants, reflexive objects, and cartesian closed categories.
- **Learn:** [Selinger, Lecture Notes on the Lambda Calculus](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0804.3434): course notes with proofs of Church–Rosser, the fixed point theorem, types, and PCF.
- **Primary:** [Barendregt, Gems of Corrado Böhm](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02243): Böhm's separability theorem and its extensions, with sketches.
- **Primary:** [Gallier, On Girard's "candidats de reductibilité"](https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~jean/sngirard.pdf): strong normalization of System F by reducibility candidates.
- **Primary:** [Manzonetto and Salibra, Applying Universal Algebra to Lambda Calculus](https://academic.oup.com/logcom/article/20/4/877/971894): survey of lambda theories and models, with 26 open problems.
- **Primary:** [Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra, Effective lambda-models vs recursively enumerable lambda-theories](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.2264): results on the $\lambda\beta$ problem.
- **Further reading:** [Barendregt, *The Lambda Calculus: Its Syntax and Semantics* (North-Holland, rev. ed. 1984)](https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-444-87508-2.50014-9): the standard monograph on the untyped calculus (link is its chapter "Classical Lambda Calculus"); its Theorem 10.4.2 gives the full proof of Böhm's theorem ([Barendregt 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02243)).
- **Further reading:** [Hindley and Seldin, *Lambda-Calculus and Combinators: An Introduction* (CUP 2008)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/lambdacalculus-and-combinators/preface/A8E6261F5D932DED3B52FD246EA66D71): an introduction to lambda calculus and combinatory logic for readers who know basic logic, recursive functions and induction but nothing of these fields.
references.Lambda-CDM Model:
## Reference
### Overview
The Lambda-CDM (ΛCDM) model is the standard form of Big Bang cosmology. It contains a cosmological constant Λ associated with dark energy, cold dark matter (CDM), and ordinary matter, and is the simplest model that gives a reasonably good account of the cosmic microwave background, the large-scale distribution of galaxies, the light-element abundances, and the accelerating expansion. It assumes [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity) holds on cosmological scales and became the accepted "concordance" model in the late 1990s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model))

In its minimal form the model is a spatially flat universe with a power-law spectrum of adiabatic scalar perturbations, described by six parameters. The final Planck analysis found good consistency with this spatially-flat six-parameter cosmology and no compelling evidence for extensions. ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)) The ACT DR6 temperature and polarization spectra are well fit by ΛCDM ([ACT DR6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14452)), and SPT-3G finds ΛCDM parameters consistent with Planck and ACT DR6 with comparable constraining power. ([SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707))

Dark matter makes up about 26.5% of today's mass–energy density and ordinary matter 4.9%, the remainder (about 68%) being dark energy. CDM is assumed cold (velocity far below $c$ at radiation–matter equality, which excludes neutrinos), non-baryonic, and collisionless, interacting through gravity and possibly the weak force. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model))

### Formal definition
The background is a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker universe obeying the Friedmann equation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model)):
$$
H^2=\left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2=\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho-\frac{kc^2}{a^2}+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3},\qquad \rho_{\rm crit}=\frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G}.
$$
With $\Omega_i=\rho_i/\rho_{\rm crit}$ today and zero curvature ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model)):
$$
H(a)=H_0\sqrt{\Omega_{\rm m}a^{-3}+\Omega_{\rm rad}a^{-4}+\Omega_\Lambda}.
$$

Primordial curvature perturbations have a power-law spectrum $\Delta^2_{\mathcal R}(k)=\Delta^2_{\mathcal R}(k_*)(k/k_*)^{n_s-1}$, with $n_s=1$ the scale-invariant Harrison–Zeldovich case. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))

The six base parameters are $\omega_b\equiv\Omega_bh^2$, $\omega_c\equiv\Omega_ch^2$, the acoustic angular scale $\theta_{\rm MC}$, the reionization optical depth $\tau$, the amplitude $A_s$ and the spectral index $n_s$; $H_0$ and other quantities are derived from them. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model)) The PDG counts seven parameters including the photon density, which is fixed by the measured CMB temperature $T=2.7255\pm0.0006$ K, so six are varied in fits; the neutrino mass sum is set to the minimal oscillation value 0.06 eV and the tensor ratio $r$ to zero. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))

**From parameters to observables.** Linear evolution of perturbations is computed with Boltzmann codes such as CAMB and CLASS; this suffices for the CMB up to the present, while small-scale density perturbations need nonlinear methods. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf)) Lewis, Challinor and Lasenby applied the efficient line-of-sight method to CMB anisotropies and polarization in closed (positively curved) FRW models ([Lewis et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9911177)), and CLASS is the Cosmic Linear Anisotropy Solving System. ([Lesgourgues](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.2932))

### Key results
- **Planck 2018 parameters.** $\Omega_ch^2=0.120\pm0.001$, $\Omega_bh^2=0.0224\pm0.0001$, $n_s=0.965\pm0.004$, $\tau=0.054\pm0.007$, $100\theta_*=1.0411\pm0.0003$ (0.03% precision), with derived $H_0=67.4\pm0.5$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, $\Omega_m=0.315\pm0.007$ and $\sigma_8=0.811\pm0.006$. ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))
- **ACT DR6.** P-ACT (ACT DR6 combined with Planck) with CMB lensing and DESI DR1 BAO gives $\Omega_bh^2=0.0226\pm0.0001$, $\Omega_ch^2=0.118\pm0.001$, $H_0=68.22\pm0.36$, $n_s=0.974\pm0.003$, $\sigma_8=0.813\pm0.005$, with no evidence for excess lensing or curvature. ([ACT DR6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14452))
- **SPT-3G.** SPT-3G alone gives $H_0=66.66\pm0.60$, $6.2\sigma$ from SH0ES; combined SPT+ACT+Planck gives $H_0=67.19\pm0.38$ and $\sigma_8=0.8137\pm0.0037$. ([SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707))
- **Relativistic species.** Planck with BAO finds $N_{\rm eff}=2.99\pm0.17$ and $\sum m_\nu<0.12$ eV. ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)) The Standard Model prediction, including flavour oscillations and finite-temperature QED, is $N_{\rm eff}^{\rm SM}=3.0440\pm0.0002$ ([Bennett et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.02726)), the baseline value now used by the PDG. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))
- **Baryon acoustic oscillations.** SDSS luminous red galaxies showed a peak in the correlation function at $100\,h^{-1}$ Mpc, demonstrating linear growth by gravitational instability between $z=1000$ and today and confirming "a firm prediction of the standard cosmological theory". ([Eisenstein et al. 2005](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0501171)) DESI DR2 BAO is well described by flat ΛCDM. ([DESI DR2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738))
- **Growth of structure.** The linear growth rate is $f(z)=d\ln\delta/d\ln a\simeq\Omega_m^\gamma(z)$ with $\gamma\simeq0.55$ in ΛCDM; measuring $f$ through redshift-space distortions constrains $\gamma$ and can rule out modified-gravity models. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf)) Linder introduced $\gamma$ to separate a smooth dark-energy component from a modification of gravity by comparing growth and expansion histories. ([Linder](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0507263))
- **Nucleosynthesis consistency.** The observed primordial deuterium abundance matches BBN with the CMB-measured baryon density. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model))
- **Extensions.** As of the 2024 PDG review there is no positive evidence for extensions of the standard model. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))

### Examples
- **Critical density.** $\rho_{\rm crit}=1.878\,47(23)\times10^{-26}\,h^2$ kg m$^{-3}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model))
- **Matter plus Λ.** Ignoring radiation, the flat model has $a(t)=(\Omega_m/\Omega_\Lambda)^{1/3}\sinh^{2/3}(t/t_\Lambda)$ with $t_\Lambda=2/(3H_0\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda})$, and deceleration turns into acceleration at $a=(\Omega_m/2\Omega_\Lambda)^{1/3}$, around $z\approx0.66$ for best-fit values. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model))
- **Amplitudes.** $\sigma_8$ is the linear mass dispersion in $8\,h^{-1}$ Mpc spheres, and weak-lensing surveys use $S_8\equiv\sigma_8(\Omega_m/0.3)^{0.5}$. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))

### History
The 1964 CMB discovery confirmed a key Big Bang prediction. In the 1970s attention focused on purely baryonic models; in the early 1980s CDM was found to solve the problem of [galaxy formation](node:Galaxy%20Formation); COBE's 1992 detection of CMB anisotropy sharpened problems of critical-density CDM and led to models including ΛCDM. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model))

ΛCDM became the leading model after the 1998 discovery of accelerating expansion, supported by BOOMERanG (total density, 2000) and 2dFGRS (matter density near 25%, 2001), then by WMAP (2003–2010) and Planck (2013–2015). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model)) Planck's final 2018 release measured the acoustic angular scale to 0.03% precision. ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))

### Connections
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): the "CDM" component.
- [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): the "Λ" component driving late acceleration.
- [CMB Acoustic Peaks](node:CMB%20Acoustic%20Peaks): the peak structure constrains the six parameters.
- [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background): the main data set.
- [CMB Polarization](node:CMB%20Polarization): polarization spectra fix $\tau$ and test the model.
- [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): the homogeneous background.
- [Cosmic Inflation](node:Cosmic%20Inflation): the usual source of the adiabatic, nearly scale-invariant spectrum.
- [Big Bang Nucleosynthesis](node:Big%20Bang%20Nucleosynthesis): an independent check on $\Omega_bh^2$.
- [Baryon Acoustic Oscillations](node:Baryon%20Acoustic%20Oscillations): a standard ruler testing the expansion history.
- [Large-Scale Structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure): galaxy surveys test growth.
- [Cosmological Perturbation Theory](node:Cosmological%20Perturbation%20Theory): links parameters to spectra.
- [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing): weak lensing measures $S_8$.
- [Galaxy Rotation Curves](node:Galaxy%20Rotation%20Curves): one motivation for dark matter.
- [Modified Newtonian Dynamics](node:Modified%20Newtonian%20Dynamics): the main galaxy-scale alternative to CDM.
- [Dark Radiation](node:Dark%20Radiation): extra relativistic species would shift $N_{\rm eff}$.

### Common pitfalls
- **Which six?** The six are the sampled base parameters; $H_0$, $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$ are derived and model-dependent. ([Planck 2018 VI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))
- **$N_{\rm eff}$ is not exactly 3.** The precision Standard Model value is $3.0440\pm0.0002$, from a calculation including flavour oscillations and finite-temperature QED ([Bennett et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.02726)); the PDG attributes the shift from 3 to a slight predicted deviation of the neutrinos from a thermal distribution. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))
- **Hidden assumptions.** Flatness, $w=-1$, minimal neutrino mass, no tensors and adiabatic Gaussian perturbations are choices, not results. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))
- **$\Omega_m$ includes baryons.** $\Omega_m=\Omega_c+\Omega_b$. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Nature of the dark sector.** Dark-matter particles have not been detected, and the measured dark-energy density is far below vacuum-energy estimates. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model))
- **Hubble tension.** The SH0ES distance-ladder $H_0$ deviates from Planck by about $5\sigma$; the tension is under intense investigation for systematic effects, and ongoing studies ask whether it reflects systematics in at least one probe or new physics. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf)) SPT-3G alone is $6.2\sigma$ from SH0ES. ([SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707))
- **Lithium and small scales.** Observed lithium is 3–4 times below prediction, and simulations predict cuspier halos and more small halos than observed dwarf galaxies. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda-CDM_model))

> [!warning] Contested
> **Evolving dark energy.** DESI DR2 BAO is well fit by flat ΛCDM but in $2.3\sigma$ tension with CMB-preferred parameters; $w_0>-1$, $w_a<0$ is preferred at $3.1\sigma$ for DESI+CMB and $2.8$–$4.2\sigma$ with [supernovae](node:Supernovae), depending on the sample. The collaboration states this holds barring an unknown systematic in one or more data sets. ([DESI DR2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738)) SPT-3G finds CMB and DESI DR2 BAO differing by $2.8\sigma$ within ΛCDM ([SPT-3G D1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20707)), while ACT finds P-ACT and DESI DR2 ΛCDM parameters agreeing at $1.6\sigma$. ([ACT DR6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14452))
>
> **$S_8$ tension.** KiDS, HSC and DES each gave $S_8$ below Planck, but a joint KiDS/DES analysis reduces the discrepancy to $1.7\sigma$. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmological-parameters.pdf))

- **Further reading:** [S. Weinberg, *Cosmology* (Oxford University Press, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198526827.001.0001): monograph, Oxford University Press, 2008.
references.Language Model Pretraining Objectives:
## Reference
### Overview
A pretraining objective is the loss used to train a language model on unlabeled text before it is fine-tuned on downstream tasks. The objective decides which tokens the model must predict and what context it may use: autoregressive (causal) objectives predict each token from its left context, masked objectives reconstruct corrupted tokens from both sides, and denoising objectives reconstruct corrupted spans with a decoder ([XLNet](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1906.08237); [Raffel et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.10683)). The choice is tied to architecture: decoder-only models use maximum-likelihood next-token prediction, while encoder-only and encoder-decoder models need what CS324 calls "ad-hoc" objectives such as [masked language modeling](node:Masked%20Representation%20Learning) ([Stanford CS324](https://stanford-cs324.github.io/winter2022/lectures/modeling/)).

The causal, masked and permutation objectives are all log-likelihoods of tokens given some context, differing in which positions are predicted and in the factorization order ([XLNet](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1906.08237)); ELECTRA instead trains a discriminator with a per-token binary loss on whether each token was replaced, defined over all input positions rather than only a masked subset ([ELECTRA](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.10555)). Minimizing such negative log-likelihoods is the same as minimizing the token-level [cross-entropy](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss), and all of these are forms of [self-supervised learning](node:Self-Supervised%20and%20Contrastive%20Learning), since the targets come from the unlabeled text itself.

Systematic comparisons show that the objective interacts with architecture and with the evaluation regime. In T5's text-to-text study, denoising objectives outperformed language-modeling objectives for fine-tuning ([Raffel et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.10683)), whereas for zero-shot use after unsupervised pretraining alone, causal decoder-only models trained autoregressively generalized best ([Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05832)). That is one reason the causal objective dominates in [large language models](node:Large%20Language%20Models).

### Formal definition
**Causal (autoregressive) language modeling.** For a token sequence $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_T)$,
$$\max_\theta\ \log p_\theta(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(x_t\mid\mathbf{x}_{<t}).$$
([XLNet](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1906.08237))

**Masked language modeling (BERT).** Corrupt $\mathbf{x}$ to $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ by masking a random subset (indicator $m_t=1$) and reconstruct the masked tokens $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$:
$$\max_\theta\ \log p_\theta(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\mid\hat{\mathbf{x}})\approx\sum_{t=1}^{T}m_t\log p_\theta(x_t\mid\hat{\mathbf{x}}),$$
where $\approx$ marks the assumption that masked tokens are reconstructed independently ([XLNet](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1906.08237)). BERT selects 15% of WordPiece tokens; each selected token is replaced by [MASK] 80% of the time, by a random token 10% of the time, and left unchanged 10% of the time ([Devlin et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04805)).

**Permutation language modeling (XLNet).** With $\mathcal{Z}_T$ the set of permutations of $[1,\dots,T]$,
$$\max_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{Z}_T}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(x_{z_t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{z}_{<t}})\Big].$$
([XLNet](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1906.08237))

**Span corruption (T5).** Drop a fraction of tokens (15% by default), replace each consecutive dropped span by a single sentinel token, and train an encoder-decoder to output the dropped spans ([Raffel et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.10683)).

**Replaced token detection (ELECTRA).** A small generator $G$ trained by masked LM fills masked positions with samples, giving $\mathbf{x}^{\rm corrupt}$; a discriminator $D$ predicts for every position whether the token is original. The joint loss is $\min_{\theta_G,\theta_D}\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{L}_{\rm MLM}(\mathbf{x},\theta_G)+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\rm Disc}(\mathbf{x},\theta_D)$ with
$$\mathcal{L}_{\rm Disc}=\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^{n}-\mathbb{1}(x^{\rm corrupt}_t=x_t)\log D(\mathbf{x}^{\rm corrupt},t)-\mathbb{1}(x^{\rm corrupt}_t\neq x_t)\log\big(1-D(\mathbf{x}^{\rm corrupt},t)\big)\Big],$$
$\lambda=50$, and 15% masking ([ELECTRA](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.10555)).

### Key results
- **Bidirectional MLM pretraining transfers broadly (Devlin et al. 2018).** Pretraining a deep bidirectional transformer encoder with MLM (plus next-sentence prediction, NSP) and fine-tuning with one extra output layer set new state of the art on eleven NLP tasks, including GLUE 80.5 (7.7 points absolute improvement) and SQuAD v1.1 test F1 93.2. In BERT's ablation, removing NSP hurt QNLI, MNLI and SQuAD 1.1. ([Devlin et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805); [Devlin et al., full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04805)) RoBERTa later kept the architecture but removed NSP. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BERT_%28language_model%29))
- **Denoising beats language modeling for transfer (Raffel et al. 2020).** In a controlled comparison within the text-to-text framework, denoising objectives outperformed language-modeling and deshuffling objectives; span corruption with mean span length 3 slightly but significantly outperformed i.i.d. token corruption on most non-translation benchmarks; and the corruption rate had limited effect except at 50%, which degraded GLUE and SQuAD. ([Raffel et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.10683); [JMLR](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v21/20-074.html))
- **Learning from every token (Clark et al. 2020).** Because replaced token detection is defined over all input tokens rather than the masked subset, ELECTRA is more compute-efficient than MLM: a model trained on one GPU for 4 days beat GPT (about 30 times more compute) on GLUE, and at scale it matches RoBERTa and XLNet with less than a quarter of their compute. ([ELECTRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.10555))
- **Objective versus architecture for zero-shot generalization (Wang et al. 2022).** Across causal decoder, non-causal decoder and encoder-decoder models of over 5B parameters trained on more than 170B tokens, causal decoders trained autoregressively gave the strongest zero-shot generalization after purely unsupervised pretraining, whereas non-causal models trained with MLM and then multitask-finetuned performed best overall; each can be adapted into the other. ([Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05832))
- **Repeated data (Muennighoff et al. 2023).** Under a fixed compute budget, training for up to 4 epochs of repeated data changes loss negligibly relative to unique data; beyond that the value of extra compute decays towards zero, and they fit a scaling law for this regime. ([Muennighoff et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16264))

### Examples
- **Next-sentence prediction and its successors.** BERT's NSP asks whether segment B follows segment A (50% of the time it does); ALBERT replaced NSP with sentence-order prediction. ([Devlin et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04805); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BERT_%28language_model%29))
- **Mixture-of-Denoisers (UL2).** UL2 separates architecture from objective, argues that objectives can be rewritten in terms of one another, and mixes several denoising paradigms in one objective, with "mode switching" tokens linking downstream fine-tuning to a pretraining scheme. ([Tay et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05131))
- **Causal LM in GPT-style models.** Decoder-only models such as GPT-2 and GPT-3 use plain next-token maximum likelihood and produce unidirectional contextual embeddings. ([Stanford CS324](https://stanford-cs324.github.io/winter2022/lectures/modeling/)) See [Autoregressive Models](node:Autoregressive%20Models).

### History
BERT (October 2018) popularized masked language modeling with NSP ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BERT_%28language_model%29)). XLNet (2019) proposed permutation LM to keep an autoregressive formulation while capturing bidirectional context, criticizing BERT's pretrain-finetune discrepancy and its neglect of dependencies among masked positions ([XLNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08237)). T5 (2019; JMLR 2020) compared objectives systematically ([JMLR](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v21/20-074.html)), ELECTRA (ICLR 2020) introduced replaced token detection ([ELECTRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.10555)), and UL2 (2022) argued for mixing objectives ([Tay et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05131)).

### Connections
- [Language Modeling](node:Language%20Modeling): the causal objective is language modeling itself.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss): the likelihood objectives here minimize token-level cross-entropy; ELECTRA's discriminator uses a binary loss.
- [Masked Representation Learning](node:Masked%20Representation%20Learning): MLM is the text instance of masked prediction, shared with masked image modelling.
- [Masked Autoencoders](node:Masked%20Autoencoders): the vision analogue of masked-token reconstruction.
- [Self-Supervised and Contrastive Learning](node:Self-Supervised%20and%20Contrastive%20Learning): pretraining objectives are self-supervised tasks.
- [Autoregressive Models](node:Autoregressive%20Models): causal and permutation LM factorize the joint distribution autoregressively.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): modern LLMs are pretrained with the causal objective.
- [Diffusion Language Models](node:Diffusion%20Language%20Models): an alternative family that trains by iterative denoising of discrete tokens.
- [Subword Tokenization](node:Subword%20Tokenization): objectives are defined over the tokenizer's units (WordPiece for BERT).
- [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): data-constrained scaling laws describe how objectives interact with repeated data.
- [Transfer Learning](node:Transfer%20Learning): pretraining objectives exist to produce transferable representations.

### Common pitfalls
- The MLM likelihood is only approximate: masked tokens are predicted independently given the corrupted input, and [MASK] tokens never appear at fine-tuning time. ([XLNet](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1906.08237))
- "Which objective is best" depends on the downstream regime: denoising wins for fine-tuning in T5's study, while causal LM wins for zero-shot use without multitask finetuning. ([Raffel et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.10683); [Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05832))
- Objective and architecture are often conflated in comparisons; UL2 argues they should be separated. ([Tay et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05131))
- ELECTRA's generator is trained by maximum likelihood, not adversarially, so it is not a GAN despite the generator/discriminator terminology. ([ELECTRA](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.10555))
- Autoregressive training on "A is B" does not reliably teach "B is A" (the reversal curse), a failure that data augmentation did not fix in the reported experiments. ([Berglund et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288))

### Open problems
- **No settled objective.** The UL2 authors state that the field has not reached consensus on the best architecture and pretraining setup, and that existing pretrained models are specialized to particular problem classes. ([Tay et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05131))
- **Pretraining cost and tokenizer reliance.** High pre-training costs and tokenizer reliance are listed in Kaddour et al.'s systematic set of open problems for LLMs. ([Kaddour et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.10169))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [BERT (language model) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BERT_%28language_model%29): MLM and NSP details and objective variants (RoBERTa, ALBERT, ELECTRA, DeBERTa).
- **Learn:** [Stanford CS324: Modeling lecture](https://stanford-cs324.github.io/winter2022/lectures/modeling/): encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder models and their objectives; tokenization.
- **Primary:** [Raffel et al., Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (JMLR 2020)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v21/20-074.html): systematic comparison of objectives.
- **Primary:** [Devlin et al., BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805); [Yang et al., XLNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08237); [Clark et al., ELECTRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.10555).
- **Primary:** [Wang et al., What Language Model Architecture and Pretraining Objective Work Best for Zero-Shot Generalization?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05832).
- **Further reading:** [Bommasani et al., On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.07258): book-length report on the capabilities, technical principles and risks of models trained on broad data at scale.
references.Language Modeling:
## Reference
### Overview
A language model is a computational model that predicts sequences in natural language, used in speech recognition, [machine translation](node:Machine%20Translation), [information retrieval](node:Information%20Retrieval) and, at scale, as the basis of large language models ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_model)). Formally it is a probability distribution over token sequences, which the chain rule factorizes left to right so that the modeling problem reduces to predicting the next token from its prefix ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/language-model.html)).

Language models are trained and evaluated with the log-loss. The cross-entropy $H(p,q)=-\mathbb E_p[\log q]$ of the model $q$ against the data distribution $p$ is estimated on a held-out test set as an empirical average of negative log-probabilities, a Monte Carlo estimate in which the test set is treated as samples from $p$ ([Wikipedia: Cross-entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy)). Its exponential, perplexity, is the standard intrinsic metric; IBM researchers including Frederick Jelinek introduced it in the 1970s alongside statistical n-gram models for speech recognition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_model)).

The modeling history runs from count-based n-gram models with smoothing, through neural models with learned distributed word representations (Bengio et al. 2003) and recurrent networks (Mikolov et al. 2010), to Transformers, which superseded recurrent models and underlie today's LLMs ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_model)). Empirically, the cross-entropy of Transformer language models falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute over many orders of magnitude ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)).

### Formal definition
Let $\mathcal V$ be a finite vocabulary. A (autoregressive) language model assigns to every sequence $x_{1:T}\in\mathcal V^T$ the probability
$$q(x_1,\dots,x_T)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1}),$$
which is exact by the chain rule; an $n$-gram model is the Markov approximation $q(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1})=q(x_t\mid x_{t-n+1:t-1})$ ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/language-model.html)).

**Cross-entropy and perplexity.** On a test sequence of $n$ tokens the average cross-entropy is $\ell=-\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n\log q(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1})$ and the perplexity is
$$\mathrm{PPL}=\exp\Big(-\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n\log q(x_t\mid x_{t-1},\dots,x_1)\Big),$$
the reciprocal of the geometric mean of the probabilities assigned to the actual tokens. A perfect model scores 1, a model that assigns probability zero to a target scores $\infty$, and a uniform model scores $|\mathcal V|$ ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/language-model.html)). For a distribution $p$, perplexity is $2^{H(p)}$ with $H$ in bits, so a fair $k$-sided die has perplexity $k$; in NLP the usual figure is perplexity per word ([Wikipedia: Perplexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity)).

**Smoothing.** Maximum-likelihood n-gram estimates give zero probability to unseen n-grams. Interpolated Kneser–Ney smoothing for bigrams, with discount $\delta\in(0,1)$, is
$$p_{KN}(w_i\mid w_{i-1})=\frac{\max(c(w_{i-1},w_i)-\delta,0)}{\sum_{w'}c(w_{i-1},w')}+\lambda_{w_{i-1}}\,p_{KN}(w_i),\quad p_{KN}(w_i)=\frac{|\{w':c(w',w_i)>0\}|}{|\{(w',w''):c(w',w'')>0\}|},$$
with $\lambda_{w_{i-1}}$ chosen so the distribution normalizes ([Wikipedia: Kneser–Ney smoothing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kneser%E2%80%93Ney_smoothing)).

### Key results
- **Cross-entropy decomposition (Gibbs' inequality).** For distributions $p,q$ on a discrete set, $H(p,q)=H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)$; for fixed $p$ the cross-entropy is minimized exactly at $q=p$, where it equals $H(p)$. Hence the expected log-loss is uniquely minimized by the true distribution, and the gap to the minimum is the KL divergence. ([Wikipedia: Cross-entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy))
- **Entropy rate of a stationary source.** The entropy rate $H(\mathcal X)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n H(X_1,\dots,X_n)$, when it exists, equals $\lim_{n\to\infty}H(X_n\mid X_{n-1},\dots,X_1)$ for strongly stationary processes, so for such sources the entropy rate is the limiting conditional entropy of the next symbol given its full prefix. ([Wikipedia: Entropy rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entropy_rate))
- **Distributed representations beat n-grams (Bengio et al. 2003).** Learning a vector for each word jointly with the sequence probability function counters the curse of dimensionality, since one sentence informs the model about many similar sentences; on two corpora it significantly improved on state-of-the-art n-gram models and exploited longer contexts. ([Bengio et al. 2003](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/bengio03a.html))
- **Neural scaling laws (Kaplan et al. 2020).** Test cross-entropy of Transformer language models follows a power law in model size, dataset size and training compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude; width and depth matter little within a wide range, and larger models are more sample-efficient. ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361))
- **Compute-optimal training (Hoffmann et al. 2022).** Fitting over 400 models from 70M to over 16B parameters on 5–500B tokens, model size and training tokens should be scaled equally: every doubling of parameters should double the tokens. Chinchilla (70B, about 4 times more data than Gopher at the same compute) outperformed Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B) and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B). ([Hoffmann et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556))

### Examples
- **Brown Corpus trigram baseline:** the lowest published perplexity as of 1992 was about 247 per word with a trigram model, i.e. a cross-entropy of about 7.95 bits per word; this does not mean 1/247 accuracy, since always guessing "the" is right about 7% of the time ([Wikipedia: Perplexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity)).
- **Laplace smoothing** adds a constant to all counts; as the constant grows the unigram estimate tends to uniform $1/|\mathcal V|$; it handles rare n-grams poorly and ignores word similarity ("cat" vs. "feline"), which motivates neural models ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/language-model.html)).
- **Transformer:** an attention-only sequence model, more parallelizable than recurrent encoder–decoders, introduced on machine translation (28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English–German) ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)).

### History
IBM's statistical n-gram models and perplexity (1970s), Chen and Goodman's empirical study of smoothing techniques (ACL 1996), Bengio et al.'s neural probabilistic language model (JMLR 2003), recurrent LMs (2010), the Transformer (2017), and GPT-style pretraining followed by instruction tuning trace the main line ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_model); [Chen and Goodman 1996](https://aclanthology.org/P96-1041/); [Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)). Scaling-law studies from 2020 onward turned the cross-entropy of next-token prediction into the quantity used to plan model and data size ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361); [Hoffmann et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)).

### Connections
- [Information Theory](node:Information%20Theory): entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence and entropy rate define the objective and its floor.
- [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces): the model is a probability measure on sequences.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss): the training objective.
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains): n-gram models are finite-order Markov chains over tokens.
- [Hidden Markov Models](node:Hidden%20Markov%20Models): earlier latent-state sequence models in speech.
- [Recurrent Neural Networks](node:Recurrent%20Neural%20Networks) and [Transformers](node:Transformers): the neural architectures that replaced n-grams.
- [Word Embeddings](node:Word%20Embeddings): the distributed representations introduced by neural LMs.
- [Subword Tokenization](node:Subword%20Tokenization): defines the vocabulary $\mathcal V$ over which perplexity is measured.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models) and [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): language modeling at scale.
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation](node:Retrieval-Augmented%20Generation): kNN-LM and RETRO modify the next-token distribution with retrieval.

### Common pitfalls
- Comparing perplexities across different tokenizers or vocabularies: perplexity is per token (or per word) and its uniform baseline is $|\mathcal V|$, so the unit must match ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/language-model.html); [Wikipedia: Perplexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity)).
- Reading perplexity as inverse accuracy ([Wikipedia: Perplexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity)).
- Unsmoothed n-gram models assign zero probability and therefore infinite perplexity to any test text containing an unseen n-gram ([Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/language-model.html)).
- Treating the compute-optimal recipe as settled: Kaplan et al. advised training very large models on relatively modest data, while Hoffmann et al. found models were undertrained and should scale tokens with parameters ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361); [Hoffmann et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)).

### Open problems
- **Length generalization.** Kaddour et al., who set out to establish a systematic set of open problems for LLMs, state that "the challenge of generalizing to sequences much longer than seen during training remains largely unsolved" ([Kaddour et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.10169)).
- **Tokenizer reliance.** The same survey lists tokenization, particularly for languages without whitespace segmentation such as Chinese and Japanese, as still challenging ([Kaddour et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.10169)).
- **Tasks not solvable by scale.** Kaddour et al. list "Tasks Not Solvable By Scale" among their open challenges, alongside brittle evaluations and hallucinations ([Kaddour et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2307.10169)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Language model (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_model): history from n-grams to LLMs; [Perplexity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perplexity): definitions and the Brown-corpus example.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, Language Models](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/language-model.html): chain rule, n-grams, Laplace smoothing, perplexity, with code.
- **Primary:** [Bengio et al. 2003, A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (JMLR)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/bengio03a.html): the first neural LM with learned word vectors.
- **Primary:** [Kaplan et al. 2020, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) and [Hoffmann et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556): how cross-entropy scales.
- **Further reading:** [Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press 2016)](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/): text with chapters on probability and information theory and on sequence modeling.
references.Laplace and Poisson Equations:
## Reference
### Overview
Laplace's equation $\Delta f=0$ is the basic second-order elliptic PDE, named for Pierre-Simon Laplace, who first studied its properties in 1786; its twice continuously differentiable solutions are the harmonic functions, which are real-analytic wherever the equation holds. It is the steady-state [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation), and in electrostatics and gravitation it is the equation satisfied by the potential $V$ of a conservative field $-\nabla V$ in a source-free region. ([Laplace's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%27s_equation))

Poisson's equation $\Delta\phi=f$ restores the sources: from Gauss's law it gives $\nabla^2\phi=4\pi G\rho$ for [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity) and $\nabla^2\varphi=-\rho_f/\varepsilon$ for [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics). ([Poisson's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation)) On $\mathbf R^n$ it is solved by convolution with the fundamental solution (the Newtonian potential); on a bounded domain one prescribes Dirichlet, Neumann or Robin data, and the theory splits into existence (Perron's method, the Dirichlet principle), uniqueness (the [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle)), and regularity, where the classical surprise is that a continuous $f$ does not guarantee a $C^2$ solution. ([Newtonian potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_potential); [Perron method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron_method); [Laplace's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%27s_equation))

They are also the model for general second-order elliptic operators: Schauder's interior estimate for $\sum a_{ij}\partial_i\partial_ju$ is proved by freezing coefficients so that locally the operator is $\Delta$ plus small terms, and Serrin and Moser extended Harnack's inequality to elliptic and parabolic equations. ([MIT 18.156, Lectures 1–2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-ii-partial-differential-equations-and-fourier-analysis-spring-2016/28b906907cba5b677e70eafe5e7da274_MIT18_156S16_Lec1-2.pdf); [Harnack's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harnack%27s_inequality))

### Formal definition
On an open set $\Omega\subset\mathbf R^n$,
$$\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x_i^2}=0\quad\text{(Laplace)},\qquad\Delta\phi=f\quad\text{(Poisson)},$$
and $u\in C^2(\Omega)$ with $\Delta u=0$ is called harmonic. ([Laplace's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%27s_equation); [Poisson's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation); [Harmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_function))

The Newtonian kernel
$$\Gamma(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\log|x|,&n=2,\\[4pt]\dfrac{1}{n(2-n)\omega_n}|x|^{2-n},&n\ge3,\end{cases}$$
with $\omega_n$ the volume of the unit ball, is the fundamental solution of Laplace's equation, and the Newtonian potential $w=\Gamma*f$ solves $\Delta w=f$ under suitable hypotheses on $f$; for $n=3$, $\Gamma(x)=-1/(4\pi|x|)$. ([Newtonian potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_potential)) With the opposite convention $-\Delta\Phi=\delta$ one has $\Phi=-\frac1{2\pi}\ln|x|$ in the plane and $\Phi=1/(4\pi|x|)$ in space. ([Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution))

### Key results
- **Mean-value property.** If $u$ is harmonic on $\Omega$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset\Omega$, then
  $$u(x)=\frac{1}{n\omega_nr^{n-1}}\int_{\partial B(x,r)}u\,d\sigma=\frac{1}{\omega_nr^n}\int_{B(x,r)}u\,dV.$$
  Conversely, every locally integrable function with the volume mean-value property is $C^\infty$ and harmonic. ([Harmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_function))
