- **$L^1$ is a space of classes.** Functions equal a.e. are identified; Wikipedia notes that $L^1$ is not literally “the space of integrable functions.” ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral))
- **Orientation.** The Lebesgue integral is over a set, with no $\int_b^a=-\int_a^b$ built in; that sign convention belongs to oriented integrals of forms. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral))

### Open problems
The monotone, Fatou, and dominated convergence theorems are standard and proved in textbook treatments of the Lebesgue integral. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral)) Wikipedia records later necessary-and-sufficient interchange criteria (Cafiero, generalizing Caccioppoli, Dubrovskii, and Fichera) as completed theorems, not open questions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral)) No major open problems are specific to the definition of the Lebesgue integral.

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Lebesgue integral (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral): simple-function definition, comparison with Riemann, and the basic convergence theorems.
- **Reference:** [Lebesgue Integral (MathWorld)](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LebesgueIntegral.html): supremum-of-simple-functions definition for nonnegative measurable functions.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, Measure Theory, Ch. 4 Integration](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes.pdf): graduate notes constructing the integral from simple functions.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.125 Measure and Integration, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/): course outline from the definition of the integral through MCT, Fatou, DCT, $L^p$, and Fubini.
- **Primary:** [Lebesgue, Intégrale, longueur, aire (1902)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592): original thesis, *Annali di Matematica* 7, 231–359; scan at the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/integralelongueu00lebe).

## Reference
### Overview
A Lie algebra is a vector space with a bilinear, alternating bracket satisfying the Jacobi identity. Its basic source is Lie theory: the tangent space at the identity of a [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) carries such a bracket, and every finite-dimensional real or complex Lie algebra arises this way from a connected Lie group, unique up to coverings. Lie introduced the notion in the 1870s to study infinitesimal transformations, Killing found it independently in the 1880s, and Weyl named it in the 1930s; older texts say "infinitesimal group". ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra))

The prototype is a space of matrices with the commutator $[X,Y]=XY-YX$, and much of the theory is about representing an abstract Lie algebra by such operators. The finite-dimensional theory over $\mathbb C$ has a complete structure theory: Engel's and Lie's theorems for nilpotent and solvable algebras, Cartan's criteria via the Killing form, Levi's decomposition reducing everything to a solvable radical and a semisimple part, and the Killing–Cartan classification of simple algebras by [root systems](node:Root%20Systems) and Dynkin diagrams. A Cambridge Part III course runs through this sequence from $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ representations to the classification. ([Stewart–Mehrle, contents](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra))

### Formal definition
A Lie algebra over a field $F$ is a vector space $\mathfrak g$ with a bilinear map $[\cdot,\cdot]:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g$ such that
$$[x,x]=0,\qquad [x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]]=0\quad(x,y,z\in\mathfrak g).$$
The same definition over a commutative ring $R$ (an $R$-module with an alternating $R$-bilinear bracket satisfying Jacobi) gives Lie algebras over $R$; over $\mathbb Z$ these are Lie rings. No finite-dimensionality or characteristic assumption is part of the definition. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra))

A representation of $\mathfrak g$ on a vector space $V$ (of any dimension, over the same field) is a Lie algebra homomorphism $\rho:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$, i.e. $\rho([x,y])=\rho(x)\rho(y)-\rho(y)\rho(x)$; the adjoint representation is $\operatorname{ad}x(y)=[x,y]$. The Killing form is $K(u,v)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}u\,\operatorname{ad}v)$. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra))

### Key results
- **Engel's theorem.** Over any field, if $\mathfrak g\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ ($V$ finite-dimensional) consists of nilpotent endomorphisms, there is $v\neq0$ with $Xv=0$ for all $X\in\mathfrak g$. Consequently a finite-dimensional Lie algebra is nilpotent iff every $\operatorname{ad}u$ is nilpotent. ([Stewart–Mehrle, Thm 4.8](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra))
- **Lie's theorem.** If $\mathfrak g\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ is a solvable Lie subalgebra over $\mathbb C$ ($V$ finite-dimensional), its elements have a common eigenvector; hence $\mathfrak g$ is upper-triangular in a suitable basis. ([Stewart–Mehrle, Thm 4.12](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf))
- **Cartan's criteria.** For finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$ over a field of characteristic $0$: $\mathfrak g$ is solvable iff $K(\mathfrak g,[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g])=0$ (Cartan's criterion for solvability; in the linear form, if $\mathfrak g\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=0$ for all $X\in[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]$, $Y\in\mathfrak g$, then $\mathfrak g$ is solvable), and $\mathfrak g$ is semisimple iff $K$ is nondegenerate (Cartan's criterion for semisimplicity). ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra); [Stewart–Mehrle, Thm 4.20](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra))
- **Levi decomposition.** Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic $0$ is a semidirect product of its solvable radical and a semisimple subalgebra. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra))
- **Ado's and Iwasawa's theorems.** Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic $0$ has a faithful finite-dimensional representation (Ado); Iwasawa extended this to finite-dimensional Lie algebras over fields of any characteristic. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra))
- **Weyl's complete reducibility.** Over a field of characteristic $0$, every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra is a direct sum of irreducible ones. ([Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra); [Stewart–Mehrle, Thm 5.6](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf))
- **Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt.** For a Lie algebra $L$ over any field with a totally ordered basis (more generally over a commutative ring when $L$ is a free module), the ordered monomials in the basis form a basis of the universal enveloping algebra $U(L)$. Hence $L\to U(L)$ is injective and $\operatorname{gr}U(L)\cong S(L)$; when the base ring contains $\mathbb Q$, symmetrization $S(L)\to U(L)$ is a linear isomorphism. The theorem can fail for some non-free modules over rings. ([Wikipedia: PBW theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Birkhoff%E2%80%93Witt_theorem))
- **Classification of simple Lie algebras.** Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, a semisimple $\mathfrak g$ decomposes as a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ plus one-dimensional root spaces, the roots form a root system, and by Serre's theorem $\mathfrak g$ is determined by it. The simple ones are $A_n\ (n\ge1)$, $B_n\ (n\ge2)$, $C_n\ (n\ge3)$, $D_n\ (n\ge4)$ and $E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,G_2$. ([Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra); [Stewart–Mehrle, Thm 6.9](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf))
- **Highest-weight theorem.** For complex semisimple $\mathfrak g$, finite-dimensional simple modules correspond bijectively to dominant integral weights, and their characters are given by the Weyl character formula. ([Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra))
- **Lie's third theorem and the correspondence.** Every finite-dimensional real or complex Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a connected Lie group, unique up to covering; on simply connected Lie groups, taking the Lie algebra is an equivalence of categories with finite-dimensional real Lie algebras. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra))

### Examples
$\mathfrak{gl}(n,F)$ is all $n\times n$ matrices with the commutator bracket; $\mathfrak{sl}(n,F)$, the trace-zero matrices, is simple for $n\ge2$ over a field of characteristic $0$ (type $A_{n-1}$); $\mathfrak{so}(n)$, the skew-symmetric real matrices, is the Lie algebra of $SO(n)$ (and of $O(n)$). Any vector space with zero bracket is an abelian Lie algebra. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra); [Stewart–Mehrle, Thm 6.9](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf))

Kac–Moody algebras, defined by generators $e_i,f_i,h_i$ and relations from a generalized Cartan matrix, are usually infinite-dimensional; positive-definite matrices give the finite-dimensional simple algebras, semidefinite ones the affine algebras central to two-dimensional [conformal field theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory). ([Wikipedia: Kac–Moody algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kac%E2%80%93Moody_algebra))

### History
Lie (1870s) and Killing (1880s) began the subject. Killing classified complex semisimple algebras in 1888–90, with gaps that Cartan fixed in his 1894 thesis; Dynkin gave the diagram classification in 1947. Poincaré stated PBW in 1900, and Birkhoff and Witt published proofs in 1937. Kac and Moody independently introduced Kac–Moody algebras around 1967–68. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra); [Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra); [Wikipedia: PBW theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Birkhoff%E2%80%93Witt_theorem); [Wikipedia: Kac–Moody algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kac%E2%80%93Moody_algebra))

### Connections
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): matrix Lie algebras and representations are built from linear operators.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): Lie algebras are their tangent spaces at the identity; [Lie Group Exponential Map](node:Lie%20Group%20Exponential%20Map) links the two.
- [Root Systems](node:Root%20Systems): classify complex semisimple Lie algebras.
- [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory): highest-weight theory and Weyl's theorem.
- [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras): the universal enveloping algebra turns Lie modules into associative modules.
- [MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras): the research map for the area, including superalgebras and infinite-dimensional algebras.
- [Quantum Groups](node:Quantum%20Groups): deformations of universal enveloping algebras.

### Common pitfalls
The alternating axiom $[x,x]=0$ implies $[x,y]=-[y,x]$; the converse holds only when the characteristic is not $2$, which is why the definition uses $[x,x]=0$. Positive characteristic has many more simple Lie algebras than characteristic $0$; the classification for $p>3$ is due to Block, Wilson, Premet and Strade. Most structure results above (Lie's theorem, Cartan's criteria, Levi, Weyl, the root-system classification) need characteristic $0$ and, for Lie's theorem and the classification, algebraic closure; Engel's theorem, PBW and Iwasawa's theorem hold in any characteristic. In characteristic $p>0$ the simple algebras include Cartan-type and Melikian algebras that do not come from characteristic $0$. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra); [Stewart–Mehrle](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf); [Premet–Strade](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601380))

### Open problems
- **Simple Lie algebras in characteristics 2 and 3.** Over algebraically closed fields of characteristic $p>3$, every finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra is classical, of Cartan type, or a Melikian algebra (only for $p=5$). Premet and Strade write that the classification problem in characteristics $2$ and $3$ "is wide open" and list related problems, including classifying the simple algebras of absolute toral rank two in characteristics $2$ and $3$ and their conjecture that every finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra in characteristic $p>0$ has an infinite automorphism group (open for $p\in\{2,3\}$). ([Premet–Strade, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0601380v2); [Premet–Strade, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601380))
- **Two-generation in characteristics 2 and 3.** Premet and Strade ask whether every finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$ is generated by two elements and call this out of reach for $p\in\{2,3\}$; Bois proved two-generation for simple Lie algebras in characteristic $0$ and $p>3$. ([Premet–Strade, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0601380v2); [Bois](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.1711))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Lie algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra): definitions, structure theorems, Lie correspondence, history.
- **Reference:** [Semisimple Lie algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra): root decomposition and classification.
- **Learn:** [Stewart–Mehrle, Lie Algebras and their Representations (Cambridge Part III)](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf): course notes from $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ to the classification.
- **Primary:** [Premet–Strade, Classification of finite dimensional simple Lie algebras in prime characteristics](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601380): survey of the modular classification with a list of open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Humphreys, Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory (Springer GTM, 1972)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2): the standard graduate text.

## Reference
### Overview
A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, with multiplication and inversion smooth. Lie groups are the mathematical model of continuous symmetry: rotation groups, groups of invertible matrices, the Lorentz and Poincaré groups of relativity, and the Heisenberg group of quantum mechanics are all examples. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group))

The central idea of the theory is that a Lie group is largely determined by its Lie algebra, the tangent space at the identity with the bracket coming from the commutator. Lie's three fundamental theorems make this precise: connected subgroups correspond to subalgebras, homomorphisms out of simply connected groups correspond to Lie algebra homomorphisms, and every finite-dimensional Lie algebra comes from a group. This reduces much of the structure theory to linear algebra, while the global topology is captured by coverings and discrete central subgroups. ([Etingof, §9.3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf))

For compact and semisimple groups the theory is especially complete: connected compact groups are classified, up to finite central quotients, by tori and Dynkin diagrams, every compact group carries a bi-invariant Haar probability measure, its representation theory is governed by the Peter–Weyl theorem, and noncompact semisimple groups admit the Cartan and Iwasawa decompositions. The unitary representation theory of noncompact reductive groups, by contrast, is still unfinished. ([Wikipedia, Compact Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Lie_group); [Mason-Brown](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.04994))

### Formal definition
A real (finite-dimensional) Lie group is a smooth manifold $G$ with a group structure such that multiplication $G\times G\to G$ and inversion $G\to G$ are smooth. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group); [Etingof, §2.1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf))

Its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=T_eG$; the bracket is read off from the quadratic term of $\mu(x,y)=\log(\exp x\exp y)=x+y+\tfrac12[x,y]+\cdots$, equivalently it is the bracket of left-invariant vector fields. The exponential map sends $X\in\mathfrak g$ to $\gamma(1)$, where $\gamma$ is the unique one-parameter subgroup with $\gamma'(0)=X$. ([Etingof, §§7, 14.3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group); [Wikipedia, Exponential map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_map_%28Lie_theory%29))

### Key results
- **Exponential map.** $\exp:\mathfrak g\to G$ is a diffeomorphism from a neighbourhood of $0$ onto a neighbourhood of $1$; $\exp((s+t)x)=\exp(sx)\exp(tx)$; for a homomorphism $\varphi$, $\varphi(\exp x)=\exp(\varphi_*x)$; and $g\exp(x)g^{-1}=\exp(\operatorname{Ad}_g x)$. ([Etingof, Thm. 7.5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf))
- **Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula.** Each Taylor coefficient of $\log(\exp x\exp y)$ is a universal $\mathbb Q$-linear combination of iterated brackets of $x,y$; explicitly $\log(e^Xe^Y)=X+Y+\tfrac12[X,Y]+\tfrac1{12}\big([X,[X,Y]]+[Y,[Y,X]]\big)+\cdots$, convergent for $X,Y$ sufficiently small (for matrices with a submultiplicative norm, convergence is guaranteed when $\|X\|+\|Y\|<\tfrac12\ln2$). Thus the group law near $1$ is determined by the Lie algebra. ([Etingof, Thm. 14.6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf); [Wikipedia, BCH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%E2%80%93Campbell%E2%80%93Hausdorff_formula))
- **Closed subgroup theorem.** Any closed subgroup of a real Lie group is a closed (embedded) Lie subgroup. ([Etingof, Thm. 3.13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf))
- **Lie correspondence.** (1) Connected Lie subgroups $H\subseteq G$ correspond bijectively to Lie subalgebras $\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak g$ via $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}H$ (the subgroups need not be closed). (2) If $G$ is simply connected, $\varphi\mapsto\varphi_*$ is a bijection $\operatorname{Hom}(G,K)\to\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Lie}G,\operatorname{Lie}K)$. (3) Every finite-dimensional real or complex Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a Lie group. Hence $G\mapsto\operatorname{Lie}G$ is an equivalence between simply connected Lie groups and finite-dimensional Lie algebras, and every connected Lie group is $\tilde G/\Gamma$ with $\tilde G$ simply connected and $\Gamma$ a discrete central subgroup. ([Etingof, Thms. 9.11–9.13, Cor. 9.14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf); [Wikipedia, Correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group%E2%80%93Lie_algebra_correspondence))
- **Maximal tori and the Weyl group.** In a connected compact Lie group $K$, every element lies in a maximal torus and all maximal tori are conjugate; consequently $\exp$ is surjective. For a maximal torus $T$, the Weyl group $W=N(T)/T$ is finite, generated by root reflections, and isomorphic to the Weyl group of the root system. The Weyl integration formula expresses $\int_K f$ for a class function $f$ as $\frac1{|W|}\int_T f(t)|\Delta(t)|^2\,dt$. ([Etingof, Thm. 44.3, Cor. 44.4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf); [Wikipedia, Maximal torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximal_torus))
- **Classification of compact Lie groups.** Every connected compact Lie group is the quotient, by a finite central subgroup, of the product of a torus and a simply connected compact Lie group; the latter is a product of simple factors from $SU(n)$ ($n\ge3$), $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ ($n\ge7$), $Sp(n)$ ($n\ge1$), $G_2,F_4,E_6,E_7,E_8$. Classifying the simply connected ones is equivalent to classifying complex semisimple Lie algebras (via compact real forms), whose simple factors correspond to connected Dynkin diagrams. ([Wikipedia, Compact Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Lie_group))
- **Haar measure.** Every locally compact Hausdorff group has a left Haar measure, unique up to a positive scalar; compact groups are unimodular, and on an $n$-dimensional Lie group Haar measure comes from a left-invariant $n$-form. A compact group with a countable base has a unique left-invariant probability measure (Haar, von Neumann). ([Wikipedia, Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure); [Etingof, Thm. 37.1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf))
- **Peter–Weyl theorem.** For a compact group $G$: matrix coefficients of finite-dimensional representations are uniformly dense in $C(G)$; every unitary representation on a Hilbert space is an orthogonal direct sum of irreducible finite-dimensional ones; and $L^2(G)$ decomposes as a sum over all irreducibles, with normalized matrix coefficients an orthonormal basis. Corollary: every compact Lie group has a faithful finite-dimensional representation, so it is a closed subgroup of some $GL_n(\mathbb C)$. ([Wikipedia, Peter–Weyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))
- **Cartan and Iwasawa decompositions.** For a real semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan involution $\theta$, $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak p$ (the $\pm1$ eigenspaces). For a noncompact semisimple Lie group $G$, $(k,X)\mapsto k\exp X$ is a diffeomorphism $K\times\mathfrak p\to G$, $K$ is maximal compact when the center is finite, and $G=KAK$ with $A=\exp\mathfrak a$ for a maximal abelian $\mathfrak a\subseteq\mathfrak p$. The Iwasawa decomposition $G=KAN$ gives an analytic diffeomorphism $K\times A\times N\to G$ (not a homomorphism), with $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n$. ([Wikipedia, Cartan decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan_decomposition); [Wikipedia, Iwasawa decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwasawa_decomposition); [Etingof, Thm. 44.12](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf))

### Examples
- $GL(2,\mathbb R)$ is a four-dimensional noncompact Lie group with two components; $SO(2)$ is a circle; $SU(2)$ is the 3-sphere of unit quaternions; the Heisenberg, Lorentz and Poincaré groups have dimensions 3, 6 and 10. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group))
- For $GL_n(\mathbb R)$, the Cartan decomposition $G=KAK$ says every invertible real matrix is $O_1DO_2$ with $O_i$ orthogonal and $D$ positive diagonal, and $K\exp\mathfrak p$ is the polar decomposition (orthogonal times positive definite); for $GL_n(\mathbb C)$ one gets $U_1DU_2$ with $U_i$ unitary. ([Etingof, Example 44.14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf); [Wikipedia, Cartan decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan_decomposition))
- For $SL_n(\mathbb R)$, the Iwasawa decomposition takes $K$ orthogonal, $A$ positive diagonal of [determinant](node:Determinant) $1$ and $N$ upper unipotent, an analogue of Gram–Schmidt (QR). ([Wikipedia, Iwasawa decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwasawa_decomposition))
- The centre of $SU(n)$ is cyclic of order $n$, and $G_2$ has trivial centre. ([Wikipedia, Compact Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Lie_group))

### History
Sophus Lie (1842–1899) founded the theory of continuous transformation groups, dating its birth to the winter of 1873–1874, to study continuous symmetries of differential equations. Killing published the first of his series of papers on continuous transformation groups in 1888, and Élie Cartan refined and generalized his work. Hermann Weyl classified the irreducible representations of semisimple groups; Chevalley later recast the theory in modern language. Hilbert's fifth problem (1900) was answered by Gleason, Montgomery and Zippin in 1952: a topological group that is a topological manifold has a unique analytic structure making it a Lie group. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group)) Peter and Weyl proved their theorem in 1927, Haar proved existence of invariant measure for second-countable locally compact groups in 1933, and Iwasawa's decomposition appeared in 1949. ([Wikipedia, Peter–Weyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem); [Wikipedia, Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure); [Wikipedia, Iwasawa decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwasawa_decomposition)) Dynkin gave the first explicit BCH formula with all coefficients in 1947. ([Wikipedia, BCH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%E2%80%93Campbell%E2%80%93Hausdorff_formula))

### Connections

- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): supplies charts, tangent spaces and smooth maps.
- [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras): the infinitesimal structure; equivalent to simply connected groups.

- [Root Systems](node:Root%20Systems): classify compact and complex semisimple groups; Weyl groups.
- [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory): highest-weight theory and the Peter–Weyl theorem.
- [Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure): invariant integration, essential for compact-group representation theory.
- [Peter–Weyl Theorem](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem): harmonic analysis on compact groups.
- [Unitary Representations of Locally Compact Groups](node:Unitary%20Representations%20of%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups): the setting of the unitary dual problem.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): coverings and discrete central subgroups govern the global form.
- [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras): construct the spin groups covering $SO(n)$.
- [Topological Groups](node:Topological%20Groups): Hilbert's fifth problem characterizes Lie groups among them.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): uses Lie groups to organize continuous local symmetries.

### Common pitfalls
- $\exp$ is a local diffeomorphism near $0$ but need not be globally injective or surjective: for the connected noncompact group $SL_2(\mathbb R)$ its image is not the whole group, and it may fail to be a local diffeomorphism at points away from $0$. ([Wikipedia, Exponential map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_map_%28Lie_theory%29); [Etingof, Thm. 7.5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf))
- The Lie algebra determines only the simply connected group; different connected groups with the same Lie algebra differ by discrete central subgroups. ([Etingof, Cor. 9.14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf))
- Connected Lie subgroups attached to subalgebras need not be closed. ([Wikipedia, Correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group%E2%80%93Lie_algebra_correspondence))
- BCH converges only near the identity. ([Wikipedia, BCH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%E2%80%93Campbell%E2%80%93Hausdorff_formula))
- Infinite-dimensional Lie groups modelled on [locally convex spaces](node:Locally%20Convex%20Spaces) can fail finite-dimensional results; for example $\exp$ may not cover a neighbourhood of the identity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group))

### Open problems
- **The unitary dual of real reductive groups.** Identifying the irreducible unitary representations of a real reductive group is open; Mason-Brown calls it "perhaps the most fundamental unsolved problem in the representation theory of Lie groups." The two main approaches are Arthur's conjectures and the Orbit Method, which he describes as "a conjectural scheme for classifying irreducible unitary representations." ([Mason-Brown](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.04994); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04994))
- **Unitarity of Arthur packets.** In the Adams–Barbasch–Vogan formulation of Arthur's conjectures for real groups, the unitarity of Arthur packets "remains an open problem in general and is an active area of research." ([Mason-Brown, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.04994))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Lie group (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group): examples, history, Hilbert's fifth problem; [Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group%E2%80%93Lie_algebra_correspondence).
- **Learn:** [Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras (MIT 18.755 notes)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf): from the exponential map and BCH to maximal tori, Haar measure, Peter–Weyl and Cartan/Iwasawa decompositions.
- **Primary:** [Hall, Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Representations (Springer GTM, 2015)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-13467-3): graduate textbook ("An Elementary Introduction").
- **Further reading:** [Mason-Brown, Arthur's Conjectures and the Orbit Method for Real Reductive Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04994): survey of the unitary dual problem.
references.Limit Theorems (LLN and CLT):
## Reference
### Overview
The law of large numbers (LLN) says that the sample mean $\bar X_n=S_n/n$ of i.i.d. random variables with finite mean $\mu$ converges to $\mu$: in probability (weak law) and almost surely (strong law). The central limit theorem (CLT) describes the fluctuations around that limit: if the variance $\sigma^2$ is finite and positive, $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ converges in distribution to a standard normal, whatever the shape of the summands' distribution. ([Wikipedia: Law of large numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_large_numbers); [Durrett, Thm 3.4.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

Both theorems sit inside a hierarchy of sharper statements. The three-series theorem characterizes a.s. convergence of independent series; the Lindeberg–Feller theorem gives Gaussian limits for triangular arrays; Berry–Esseen gives rates; the law of the iterated logarithm gives the exact size of a.s. fluctuations; Donsker's theorem lifts the CLT to whole random-walk paths; martingale CLTs drop independence; and Cramér's large deviation theorem gives the exponential rate at which $P(\bar X_n\ge x)$ vanishes for $x>\mu$. With infinite variance the Gaussian is replaced by stable laws. ([Durrett, Chs. 2, 3, 8](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Cramér's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cram%C3%A9r%27s_theorem_%28large_deviations%29))

These theorems justify reading probabilities as long-run relative frequencies and estimating expectations by averages. Research continues on quantitative and high-dimensional versions, such as dimension-explicit Berry–Esseen bounds. ([Wikipedia: Law of large numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_large_numbers); [Raič 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.06475))

### Formal definition
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be random variables, $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$. $Y_n\to Y$ **in probability** if $P(|Y_n-Y|>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$; **almost surely** if $P(Y_n\to Y)=1$; **in distribution** ($Y_n\Rightarrow Y$) if $F_{Y_n}(x)\to F_Y(x)$ at every continuity point $x$ of $F_Y$, equivalently $Ef(Y_n)\to Ef(Y)$ for every bounded continuous $f$. ([Durrett, §§2.2, 3.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

- **Weak LLN:** $S_n/n\to\mu$ in probability. **Strong LLN:** $S_n/n\to\mu$ almost surely.
- **CLT:** $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)\Rightarrow\chi$, where $\chi\sim N(0,1)$.
([Durrett, Thms 2.2.12, 2.4.1, 3.4.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

### Key results
- **$L^2$ weak law.** If $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are uncorrelated with $EX_i=\mu$ and $\operatorname{var}(X_i)\le C<\infty$, then $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. ([Durrett, Thm 2.2.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Weak law without a mean (Feller).** If $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $xP(|X_1|>x)\to0$ and $\mu_n=E(X_1\mathbf 1_{|X_1|\le n})$, then $S_n/n-\mu_n\to0$ in probability; the tail condition is necessary for some centring $a_n$ to work. ([Durrett, Thm 2.2.12](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **[Borel–Cantelli lemmas](node:Borel–Cantelli%20Lemmas).** If $\sum P(A_n)<\infty$ then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$; if the $A_n$ are independent and $\sum P(A_n)=\infty$ then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$. ([Durrett, Thms 2.3.1, 2.3.7](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Strong law (Etemadi's form).** If $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are *pairwise* independent and identically distributed with $E|X_i|<\infty$ and $EX_i=\mu$, then $S_n/n\to\mu$ a.s. Conversely, if the $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $E|X_i|=\infty$, then $P(|X_n|\ge n\text{ i.o.})=1$ and $\lim S_n/n$ exists in $\mathbb R$ with probability $0$. ([Durrett, Thms 2.4.1, 2.3.8](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Kolmogorov's three-series theorem.** Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be independent, $A>0$, $Y_i=X_i\mathbf 1_{|X_i|\le A}$. Then $\sum X_n$ converges a.s. iff (i) $\sum P(|X_n|>A)<\infty$, (ii) $\sum EY_n$ converges, and (iii) $\sum\operatorname{var}(Y_n)<\infty$. ([Durrett, Thm 2.5.8](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Glivenko–Cantelli.** For i.i.d. $X_i$ with distribution function $F$ and empirical distribution function $F_n$, $\sup_x|F_n(x)-F(x)|\to0$ a.s. ([Durrett, Thm 2.4.9](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Cramér's theorem (large deviations).** If $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $\Lambda(t)=\log Ee^{tX_1}<\infty$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$, and $\Lambda^*(x)=\sup_t(tx-\Lambda(t))$, then for $x>EX_1$, $\lim_n n^{-1}\log P(S_n\ge nx)=-\Lambda^*(x)$. A weak version is due to Cramér (1938). ([Wikipedia: Cramér's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cram%C3%A9r%27s_theorem_%28large_deviations%29); [Durrett, Thm 2.7.7](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Lévy continuity theorem.** Let $\mu_n$ have characteristic functions $\varphi_n$. If $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu_\infty$ then $\varphi_n\to\varphi_\infty$ pointwise; if $\varphi_n(t)$ converges pointwise to a limit $\varphi$ continuous at $0$, then $(\mu_n)$ is tight and converges weakly to the law with characteristic function $\varphi$. ([Durrett, Thm 3.3.17](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Classical CLT.** If $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $EX_i=\mu$ and $\operatorname{var}(X_i)=\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$, then $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma n^{1/2})\Rightarrow\chi$. ([Durrett, Thm 3.4.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Lindeberg–Feller.** For each $n$ let $X_{n,m}$, $1\le m\le n$, be independent with $EX_{n,m}=0$. If (i) $\sum_{m}EX_{n,m}^2\to\sigma^2>0$ and (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\sum_m E(X_{n,m}^2;|X_{n,m}|>\varepsilon)\to0$, then $X_{n,1}+\dots+X_{n,n}\Rightarrow\sigma\chi$. ([Durrett, Thm 3.4.10](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Lyapunov's condition.** For independent $X_m$ with $\alpha_n=\operatorname{var}(S_n)^{1/2}$, if for some $\delta>0$ $\alpha_n^{-(2+\delta)}\sum_{m=1}^nE|X_m-EX_m|^{2+\delta}\to0$, then $(S_n-ES_n)/\alpha_n\Rightarrow\chi$. In practice it is usually easiest to check with $\delta=1$. ([Durrett, Exercise 3.4.12](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Central limit theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_limit_theorem))
- **Multivariate CLT (Cramér–Wold).** $X_n\Rightarrow X_\infty$ in $\mathbb R^d$ if $\theta\cdot X_n\Rightarrow\theta\cdot X_\infty$ for every $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Hence if $X_i$ are i.i.d. random vectors with mean $\mu$ and finite covariance matrix $\Gamma$, then $(S_n-n\mu)/n^{1/2}\Rightarrow N(0,\Gamma)$. ([Durrett, Thms 3.10.6, 3.10.7](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Berry–Esseen.** If $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $EX_i=0$, $EX_i^2=\sigma^2$, $E|X_i|^3=\rho<\infty$, and $F_n$ is the distribution function of $S_n/(\sigma\sqrt n)$, then $|F_n(x)-\Phi(x)|\le C\rho/(\sigma^3\sqrt n)$ for all $x,n$. Durrett proves this with $C=3$; Shevtsova (2011) proved $C<0.4748$ for identically distributed summands, and Esseen (1956) showed that $C$ cannot be below about $0.4097$. ([Durrett, Thm 3.4.17](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Shevtsova 2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.6554); [Wikipedia: Berry–Esseen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berry%E2%80%93Esseen_theorem))
- **Multivariate Berry–Esseen (Raič).** Let $X_i$, $i\in I$ countable, be independent $\mathbb R^d$-valued with $EX_i=0$ and $\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=I_d$, and $W=\sum_iX_i$. For every measurable convex $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $|P(W\in A)-N(0,I_d)\{A\}|\le(42d^{1/4}+16)\sum_iE|X_i|^3$. ([Raič 2019, Thm 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.06475))
- **Donsker's invariance principle.** Let $X_i$ be i.i.d. with mean $0$ and variance $1$, and let $S(u)$ equal $S_k$ at integers $u=k$ and be linear on each $[k,k+1]$. Then $S(n\,\cdot)/\sqrt n\Rightarrow B(\cdot)$, a standard Brownian motion, as measures on $C[0,1]$; consequently $\psi(S(n\cdot)/\sqrt n)\Rightarrow\psi(B)$ for every $\psi:C[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ continuous a.s. under Wiener measure. ([Durrett, Thms 8.1.4, 8.1.5](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Martingale CLT.** Let $X_n$ be a martingale difference sequence for $\mathcal F_n$ and $V_k=\sum_{n\le k}E(X_n^2\mid\mathcal F_{n-1})$. If (i) $V_k/k\to\sigma^2>0$ in probability and (ii) $n^{-1}\sum_{m\le n}E(X_m^2\mathbf 1_{|X_m|>\varepsilon\sqrt n})\to0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, then $S(n\cdot)/\sqrt n\Rightarrow\sigma B(\cdot)$. ([Durrett, Thm 8.2.8](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Law of the iterated logarithm.** If $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $EX_i=0$ and $EX_i^2=1$, then $\limsup_n S_n/\sqrt{2n\log\log n}=1$ a.s. ([Durrett, Thm 8.5.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Stable limits.** If $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $P(|X_1|>x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x)$ for some $\alpha\in(0,2)$ and $L$ slowly varying, and $P(X_1>x)/P(|X_1|>x)\to\theta\in[0,1]$, then with $a_n=\inf\{x:P(|X_1|>x)\le n^{-1}\}$ and $b_n=nE(X_1\mathbf 1_{|X_1|\le a_n})$, $(S_n-b_n)/a_n$ converges to a nondegenerate law. The possible limits of normalized i.i.d. sums are exactly the stable laws, with index $0<\alpha\le2$, $\alpha=2$ being the normal. ([Durrett, Thm 3.8.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Stable distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_distribution))

### Examples
- **De Moivre–Laplace.** For simple random walk $S_m$, $P(a\le S_m/\sqrt m\le b)\to\int_a^b(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}dx$, a special case of the CLT. ([Durrett, Thm 3.1.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Cauchy counterexample.** The average of $n$ i.i.d. Cauchy variables has the same law as one of them, so no LLN holds. ([Wikipedia: Law of large numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_large_numbers))
- **Local limit theorem.** Let $X_i$ be i.i.d. with $EX_i=0$, $EX_i^2=\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$, and a lattice distribution with **span** $h$ (the largest $h$ with $P(X_i\in b+h\mathbb Z)=1$ for some $b$). With $p_n(x)=P(S_n/\sqrt n=x)$ on $L_n=\{(nb+hz)/\sqrt n:z\in\mathbb Z\}$ and $n(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$, $\sup_{x\in L_n}|(n^{1/2}/h)p_n(x)-n(x)|\to0$. The span hypothesis matters: $P(X=1)=P(X=-1)=1/2$ lies on $\mathbb Z$, but its span is $2$ (take $b=-1$), and the theorem holds with $h=2$, not $h=1$. ([Durrett, Example 3.5.1, Thm 3.5.3](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Why the parabola.** With $EX=0$, $EX^2=1$ and $L_X=-\log\varphi_X$, one has $L_X(0)=L_X'(0)=0$, $L_X''(0)=1$, and $L_{V_n}(t)=nL_X(n^{-1/2}t)$ for $V_n=n^{-1/2}S_n$; zooming in this way on a twice-differentiable function near $0$ gives the parabola $t^2/2$, the Gaussian exponent. ([Sheffield, MIT 18.175 Lecture 16](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture16.pdf))

### History
Jacob Bernoulli proved the binary LLN in *Ars Conjectandi* (1713), calling it his "golden theorem"; Poisson named it "la loi des grands nombres" in 1837. Khinchin showed in 1929 that a finite mean suffices for the i.i.d. weak law; Kolmogorov proved the i.i.d. strong law in 1930 and showed in 1933 that a mean is necessary for it. Etemadi (1981) gave an elementary proof. ([Wikipedia: Law of large numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_large_numbers))

De Moivre used the normal curve in 1733 to approximate coin-tossing counts, and Laplace extended this in 1812. Lyapunov proved a general form in 1901, Pólya first used the name "central limit theorem" in a 1920 paper title, and Lindeberg's condition dates from 1920, with his CLT paper appearing in 1922. Turing's 1934 King's College fellowship dissertation proved a result similar to Lindeberg's 1922 CLT and was left unpublished once he learned it was known, and Lévy published the first complete proof of the generalized CLT in 1937. ([Wikipedia: Central limit theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_limit_theorem); [Wikipedia: Stable distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_distribution)) Lindeberg's paper appeared in *Mathematische Zeitschrift* 15 (1922) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/bf01494395)). Berry (1941) and Esseen (1942) independently proved the rate bound, Esseen's original constant being $7.59$ ([Wikipedia: Berry–Esseen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berry%E2%80%93Esseen_theorem)).

### Connections
- [Expectation and Variance](node:Expectation%20and%20Variance): the mean and variance are the two parameters of the LLN and CLT.
- [Independence of Random Variables](node:Independence%20of%20Random%20Variables): the basic hypothesis; pairwise independence suffices for the strong law.
- [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): convergence in distribution is convergence of distribution functions.
- [Gaussian Distribution](node:Gaussian%20Distribution): the universal limit in the finite-variance CLT.
- [Characteristic Functions](node:Characteristic%20Functions): turn sums into products and give the continuity theorem.
- [Martingales](node:Martingales): martingale CLTs extend the CLT beyond independence.
- [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus): the scaling limit in Donsker's theorem; the LIL is proved by embedding walks in Brownian motion.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory): Birkhoff's ergodic theorem is the strong law for stationary sequences.
- [Concentration of Measure](node:Concentration%20of%20Measure): non-asymptotic, exponential versions of the weak law.
- [Monte Carlo Methods](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Methods): estimate expectations by sample means, with CLT error bars.
- [Sampling Distributions](node:Sampling%20Distributions): the CLT gives approximate laws of statistics.

### Common pitfalls
- The strong law implies the weak law, but the weak law holds in some situations where the strong law does not. ([Wikipedia: Law of large numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_large_numbers))
- Finite variance is not needed for the LLN; it is needed for the Gaussian CLT. With infinite variance the right scaling is $a_n$, not $\sqrt n$, and the limit is stable. ([Durrett, Thms 2.4.1, 3.8.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- In Lévy's continuity theorem, continuity of the limit at $0$ is essential: for $N(0,n)$ laws the characteristic functions converge to $\mathbf 1_{\{t=0\}}$, yet the laws do not converge. ([Durrett, Thm 3.3.17](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- The CLT does not say $S_n/\sqrt n$ converges almost surely; the LIL shows $S_n/\sqrt{2n\log\log n}$ oscillates with $\limsup$ equal to $1$. ([Durrett, Thm 8.5.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- For dependent stationary sequences the limiting variance is $\sigma^2=EX_1^2+2\sum_kEX_1X_{1+k}$, not $EX_1^2$, and the $\alpha$-mixing CLT gives $S_n/(\sigma\sqrt n)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$ only under its moment and mixing-rate conditions and $\sigma\ne0$. ([Wikipedia: Central limit theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_limit_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Dimension dependence in the multivariate Berry–Esseen bound.** For the class of convex sets, the Gaussian perimeter of convex sets in $\mathbb R^d$ is of exact order $d^{1/4}$ (Ball; Nazarov), and Raič's bound has constant $42d^{1/4}+16$. Raič writes that this does not necessarily mean $d^{1/4}$ is the optimal order of the constant, and that this "remains an open question". ([Raič 2019, Remark 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.06475); [Wikipedia: Berry–Esseen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berry%E2%80%93Esseen_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Central limit theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_limit_theorem) and [Law of large numbers (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_large_numbers): statements, variants, dependent cases, history.
- **Learn:** [Sheffield, MIT 18.175 Lecture 16](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture16.pdf): CLT heuristics via characteristic functions and CLT variants.
- **Learn:** [Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*, 5th ed. (PDF)](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf): Chapters 2, 3 and 8 prove every classical result above.
- **Primary:** [Lindeberg, Eine neue Herleitung des Exponentialgesetzes in der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, Math. Z. 15 (1922)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01494395): the Lindeberg condition.
- **Primary:** [Berry, The accuracy of the Gaussian approximation to the sum of independent variates, Trans. AMS 49 (1941)](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1941-0003498-3): the Berry–Esseen rate.
- **Primary:** [Raič, A multivariate Berry–Esseen theorem with explicit constants (Bernoulli 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.06475): dimension-explicit normal approximation via Stein's method.
- **Primary:** [Shevtsova, On the absolute constants in the Berry–Esseen type inequalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.6554): the bounds $\Delta_n\le0.33554(\beta_3+0.415)/\sqrt n$ and $C_0<0.4748$ for identically distributed summands.
- **Further reading:** [Durrett's book page](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/pte.html): the 5th edition of the standard graduate probability text.
references.Linear Integral Equations:
## Reference
### Overview
A linear integral equation is an equation in which an unknown function appears linearly under an integral sign, typically through an integral operator $(K\varphi)(x)=\int K(x,y)\varphi(y)\,dy$ with a given kernel $K$. They are classified as homogeneous or inhomogeneous; of the first, second or third kind; Fredholm (fixed limits of integration) or Volterra (at least one variable limit); and regular or singular. Integral and differential equations can often be converted into one another: the initial value problem $u'=2tu$, $u(0)=1$ is equivalent to $u(x)=1+\int_0^x 2t\,u(t)\,dt$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))

The subject matters for two reasons. Analytically, Fredholm's 1903 paper on integral equations is one of the landmarks in the founding of operator theory, and Hilbert developed the abstraction of Hilbert space in association with research on integral equations prompted in part by Fredholm's ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory)). Practically, integral equations model radiative transfer, electromagnetic scattering, [viscoelasticity](node:Viscoelasticity), ruin theory, option pricing, demography (Lotka's equation) and the rendering equation of [computer graphics](node:Computer%20Graphics) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation)).

For a square-integrable (Hilbert–Schmidt) kernel the integral operator on $L^2$ is compact ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator)), its nonzero spectrum consists of eigenvalues that can accumulate only at 0 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation)), and second-kind equations obey the Fredholm alternative ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)), so much of the subject is the [spectral theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) of compact operators applied to concrete kernels.

### Formal definition
Let $a<b$ and let $K$ be a kernel on $[a,b]^2$. The **Fredholm equation of the first kind** asks for $f$ with
$$g(t)=\int_a^b K(t,s)\,f(s)\,ds,$$
and the **Fredholm equation of the second kind** for $\varphi$ with
$$\varphi(t)=f(t)+\lambda\int_a^b K(t,s)\,\varphi(s)\,ds .$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation))

**Volterra equations** replace the upper limit by the variable: first kind $f(t)=\int_a^t K(t,s)x(s)\,ds$, second kind $x(t)=f(t)+\int_a^t K(t,s)x(s)\,ds$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation))

A kernel $k$ on $\Omega\times\Omega$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, is **Hilbert–Schmidt** if $\int\!\!\int|k(x,y)|^2\,dx\,dy<\infty$; the operator $(Tf)(x)=\int_\Omega k(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ on $L^2(\Omega)$ is then a Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator))

The **resolvent** of $K$ is $R(\lambda)=(I-\lambda K)^{-1}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory)). With iterated kernels $K_n$ ($K_0(x,z)=\delta(x-z)$, $K_{n+1}(x,z)=\int K(x,y)K_n(y,z)\,dy$), the resolvent kernel is $R(x,z;\lambda)=\sum_{n\ge0}\lambda^nK_n(x,z)$ and the solution of the second-kind equation is $\varphi(x)=\int R(x,z;\lambda)f(z)\,dz$ whenever the series converges, as it does for $\lambda$ small enough (the Liouville–Neumann series). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%E2%80%93Neumann_series))

### Key results
- **Compactness.** A Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator is bounded and compact, and its Hilbert–Schmidt norm equals the $L^2$ norm of its kernel, $\|T\|_{HS}=\|k\|_{L^2(\Omega\times\Omega)}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator)). For suitably regular kernels on a bounded interval, compactness of the integral operator can also be shown by equicontinuity and the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem, and the nonzero spectrum consists of eigenvalues tending to 0 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation)).
- **Fredholm alternative.** Let $K\in L^2([a,b]^2)$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. Either the homogeneous equation $\lambda\varphi-K\varphi=0$ has a nontrivial solution, or the inhomogeneous equation $\lambda\varphi-K\varphi=f$ has a solution for every $f$. The same dichotomy holds for every compact operator $K$ on a Banach space: a nonzero $\lambda$ is either an eigenvalue of $K$ or lies in its resolvent set. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative))
- **Index zero.** A bounded operator between Banach spaces is Fredholm if and only if it is invertible modulo compact operators; the index $\dim\ker T-\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{ran}T$ is locally constant and unchanged by compact perturbations. In particular a compact perturbation $T+K$ of a Fredholm operator $T$ is Fredholm with the same index, so $I-\lambda K$ with $K$ compact has the index of $I$, namely 0. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_operator))
- **Hilbert–Schmidt spectral theorem.** If $T$ is compact and self-adjoint on a Hilbert space (for an integral operator: $k(x,y)=\overline{k(y,x)}$), then $(\ker T)^\perp$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $T$ with real eigenvalues $\lambda_n\to0$, and $\sigma(T)$ consists of the eigenvalues together with 0. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_operator_on_Hilbert_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator))
- **Mercer's theorem.** Let $K:[a,b]^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, symmetric and positive-definite ($\sum_{i,j}K(x_i,x_j)c_ic_j\ge0$ for all finite choices). Then $L^2[a,b]$ has an orthonormal basis $\{e_j\}$ of eigenfunctions of $T_K$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j\ge0$, eigenfunctions with $\lambda_j\neq0$ are continuous, and $K(s,t)=\sum_j\lambda_je_j(s)e_j(t)$ with absolute and uniform convergence. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem))
- **Fredholm determinant.** The infinite-dimensional analogue of the [determinant](node:Determinant) is commonly defined as $\det(I-\lambda K)=\exp\!\big[-\sum_{n\ge1}\tfrac{\lambda^n}{n}\operatorname{Tr}K^n\big]$ with $\operatorname{Tr}K=\int K(x,x)\,dx$; Fredholm theory also uses the reciprocal $\zeta(s)=1/\det(I-sK)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory))
- **Volterra first kind to second kind.** A first-kind Volterra equation reduces to a second-kind one by differentiation whenever $K(t,t)\neq0$; convolution kernels $K(t-s)$ are solved by the Laplace transform. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation))

### Examples
- **Initial value problems.** $u'=2tu$, $u(0)=1$ is the Volterra equation $u(x)=1+\int_0^x2t\,u(t)\,dt$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))
- **Abel's equation.** A weakly singular kernel $(t^2-s^2)^{-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, turns a first-kind Volterra equation into an Abel integral equation. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation))
- **Convolution on the line.** If $K(t,s)=K(t-s)$ and the limits are $\pm\infty$, a first-kind equation is a convolution and is solved formally by Fourier transform; the operator is then not compact, so this case is usually not counted as Fredholm. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation))
- **Nyström discretization.** Replacing the integral in a second-kind equation by a quadrature rule with nodes $x_k$ and weights $w_k$ gives an $n\times n$ linear system, solved in $O(n^3)$ operations; Gaussian quadrature is normally a good choice for smooth, non-singular problems, and the discrete system can be ill-conditioned. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystr%C3%B6m_method))

### History
Fredholm's paper "Sur une classe d'équations fonctionnelles" appeared in Acta Mathematica 27 in 1903 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) and is counted among the major landmarks in establishing operator theory; Hilbert's abstraction of Hilbert space grew out of research on integral equations prompted partly by it ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory)). Mercer published his theorem in 1909 in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem)). Lalescu studied Volterra equations in his 1908 thesis and wrote the first book on integral equations in 1911 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)). Nyström's quadrature method appeared in Acta Mathematica in 1930 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystr%C3%B6m_method)). Kress's *Linear Integral Equations* appeared in Springer's Applied Mathematical Sciences series, in a 2014 edition ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4614-9593-2)).

### Connections
- [Fredholm Alternative](node:Fredholm%20Alternative): the solvability dichotomy for second-kind equations.
- [Fredholm Determinants](node:Fredholm%20Determinants): the determinant $\det(I-\lambda K)$ and its use in random matrix theory.
- [Volterra Integral Equations](node:Volterra%20Integral%20Equations): the variable-limit case, where the Neumann series is the main tool.
- [Compact Integral Operators](node:Compact%20Integral%20Operators): the operator-theoretic setting of the whole theory.
- [Eigenfunctions of Integral Operators](node:Eigenfunctions%20of%20Integral%20Operators): the Hilbert–Schmidt and Mercer expansions.
- [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem): compact self-adjoint case underlies Hilbert–Schmidt theory.
- [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the function spaces on which kernels act; [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces) supply $L^2$ kernels.
- [Singular Integral Operators](node:Singular%20Integral%20Operators): kernels that are not integrable, treated in 45E.
- [Integral Equation Inverse Problems](node:Integral%20Equation%20Inverse%20Problems): first-kind equations and their ill-posedness.
- [Numerical Quadrature for Integral Equations](node:Numerical%20Quadrature%20for%20Integral%20Equations): Nyström and related discretizations.
- [Kernel Methods](node:Kernel%20Methods) and [Gaussian Processes](node:Gaussian%20Processes): Mercer's theorem gives the feature expansion of a positive-definite kernel.
- [Random Matrices](node:Random%20Matrices): gap probabilities are Fredholm determinants of integral operators.

### Common pitfalls
- The Neumann series converges only for $|\lambda|$ small enough; the Fredholm alternative, not the series, governs solvability for other $\lambda$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%E2%80%93Neumann_series); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative))
- Convolution equations on the whole line are not compact-operator problems, so Fredholm theory does not apply directly. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation))
- Mercer's theorem needs a continuous, symmetric, positive-definite kernel on a compact interval to give uniform convergence of $K(s,t)=\sum_j\lambda_je_j(s)e_j(t)$; for a general compact self-adjoint operator the spectral theorem gives only an orthonormal eigenbasis of $(\ker T)^\perp$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_operator_on_Hilbert_space))
- A Nyström discretization can be ill-conditioned, depending on the original problem and the chosen quadrature rule. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystr%C3%B6m_method))

### Open problems
- **Constructive matrix Wiener–Hopf factorization.** For systems of convolution equations on a half-line, solvability reduces to factorizing a matrix symbol $G=G_+\Lambda G_-$ with $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(t^{\kappa_1},\dots,t^{\kappa_n})$, the $\kappa_j$ being the partial indices. The 2021 review of Kisil, Abrahams, Mishuris and Rogosin states that "there are no constructive factorisation procedures for matrix functions in general", that in general "there exists no method of determining the partial indices", and that matrix problems must be solved case by case; by contrast, the review notes that scalar factorization is always possible via integrals of Cauchy type, with factors unique up to a constant. ([Kisil et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fredholm integral equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation): definitions of the two kinds, compactness, applications.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102, Lecture 19](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2009/resources/mit18_102s09_lec19): Melrose's notes on Fredholm operators and the spectral theory of compact self-adjoint operators.
- **Primary:** [Kisil, Abrahams, Mishuris, Rogosin, The Wiener–Hopf technique, its generalizations and applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06088): review of constructive and approximate methods for Wiener–Hopf equations.
- **Further reading:** [Kress, Linear Integral Equations (Springer, Applied Mathematical Sciences)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4614-9593-2): Kress's monograph on linear integral equations, 2014 edition.

## Reference
### Overview
A linear map $f:V\to W$ between vector spaces over the same field $K$ is a function preserving addition and scalar multiplication. It sends $\mathbf 0$ to $\mathbf 0$. Its kernel is a subspace of $V$ and its image a subspace of $W$. The linear maps $V\to W$ themselves form a vector space $\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)=\mathcal L(V,W)$. For $V=W$ the endomorphisms form an associative algebra $\operatorname{End}(V)$ under composition, whose group of units is $GL(V)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map))

Once bases are chosen in finite-dimensional $V$ and $W$, every linear map is given by a matrix whose $j$th column holds the coordinates of the image of the $j$th basis vector. The same map has many matrices, one for each choice of bases. For an endomorphism with matrix $A$, changing basis by an invertible $B$ gives $B^{-1}AB$. The central structural question is therefore which properties of a matrix are invariant under similarity, and what normal form a similarity class has. The determinant, the trace, the characteristic and minimal polynomials, and the Jordan and rational canonical forms answer it. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_normal_form))

Over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with inner products, the relevant equivalence is unitary rather than general change of basis. The singular value decomposition and polar decomposition are the structure theorems for arbitrary (not necessarily square) matrices. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)) Arthur Cayley's "A memoir on the theory of matrices" appeared in *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London* (1858, pp. 17–37). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rstl.1858.0002)) Cayley stated the characteristic-equation theorem for matrices of size at most $3$ but published a proof only for $2\times2$ matrices. Frobenius gave the first general proof in 1878. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))

### Formal definition
Let $V,W$ be vector spaces over a field $K$. A function $f:V\to W$ is **linear** if for all $\mathbf u,\mathbf v\in V$ and $c\in K$,
$$f(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)=f(\mathbf u)+f(\mathbf v),\qquad f(c\mathbf u)=c\,f(\mathbf u).$$
Its **kernel** is $\ker f=\{\mathbf x\in V: f(\mathbf x)=\mathbf 0\}$ and its **image** is $\operatorname{im} f=f(V)$. The **rank** is $\dim\operatorname{im} f$ and the **nullity** is $\dim\ker f$. The **cokernel** is $\operatorname{coker} f=W/\operatorname{im} f$, giving the exact sequence $0\to\ker f\to V\to W\to\operatorname{coker} f\to 0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map))

**Matrix of a map.** If $(\mathbf v_1,\dots,\mathbf v_n)$ and $(\mathbf w_1,\dots,\mathbf w_m)$ are bases, the matrix $(a_{ij})$ of $f$ is defined by $f(\mathbf v_j)=\sum_i a_{ij}\mathbf w_i$. Composition of maps corresponds to matrix multiplication. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map))

**Dual map (transpose).** The transpose of $u:X\to Y$ is ${}^t u:Y'\to X'$, $f\mapsto f\circ u$, so $\langle {}^t u(f),x\rangle=\langle f,u(x)\rangle$. With respect to dual bases its matrix is the transpose of the matrix of $u$. Its kernel is the annihilator of $\operatorname{im} u$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpose_of_a_linear_map))

**Determinant and trace of an endomorphism.** The determinant of a square matrix can be characterized as the unique function of the columns that is multilinear, alternating, and equal to $1$ on $I$. Explicitly, $\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_i a_{i,\sigma(i)}$. Similar matrices have equal determinants, so $\det$ is defined for endomorphisms of a finite-dimensional space. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant)) The trace $\operatorname{tr} A=\sum_i a_{ii}$ is also similarity invariant. Coordinate-free, for finite-dimensional $V$ it is the map $V\otimes V^*\cong\operatorname{End}(V)\to K$ sending $v\otimes g\mapsto g(v)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_%28linear_algebra%29))

### Key results
- **Rank–nullity.** If $T:V\to W$ is linear and $V$ is finite-dimensional, then $\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim V$. No hypothesis is needed on $W$. It is the dimension count of the first isomorphism theorem $V/\ker T\cong\operatorname{im}T$, which with the splitting lemma gives $V\cong\ker T\oplus\operatorname{im}T$. Equivalently, with $\operatorname{index}T=\dim\ker T-\dim\operatorname{coker}T$, one has $\operatorname{index}T=\dim V-\dim W$ when both are finite. Consequently, a linear map between spaces of equal finite dimension is injective iff surjective iff bijective. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank%E2%80%93nullity_theorem))
- **Determinant is multiplicative.** $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$. A square matrix over a commutative ring is invertible iff $\det A$ is a unit; over a field, iff $\det A\ne0$. The characteristic polynomial $\det(XI-A)$ has constant term $(-1)^n\det A$ and $X^{n-1}$-coefficient $-\operatorname{tr}A$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant))
- **Trace identities.** $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ whenever both products are defined, so commutators have trace zero; $\operatorname{tr}A$ is the sum of the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity; and $\det(e^A)=e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$. Any linear functional $f$ on $n\times n$ matrices with $f(XY)=f(YX)$ is a scalar multiple of the trace. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_%28linear_algebra%29))
- **Cayley–Hamilton.** For a square matrix $A$ over a commutative ring with $p_A(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-A)$, one has $p_A(A)=0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem))
- **Rational canonical form.** Over any field $F$, an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ is similar to a block-diagonal matrix of companion matrices of monic invariant factors $f_1\mid f_2\mid\cdots\mid f_k$. These are uniquely determined, and they correspond to the $F[X]$-module decomposition $V\cong F[X]/(f_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus F[X]/(f_k)$ given by the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID. Two matrices are similar iff they have the same invariant factors. $f_k$ is the minimal polynomial and $f_1\cdots f_k$ the characteristic polynomial. The form does not change under field extension. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_normal_form))
- **Jordan normal form.** An operator on a finite-dimensional space over $K$ has a basis in which its matrix is block diagonal with Jordan blocks $\lambda I+N$ ($N$ the nilpotent shift) iff all its eigenvalues lie in $K$, i.e. iff the characteristic polynomial splits; this always holds for $K$ algebraically closed. The form is unique up to the order of the blocks and is determined by the ranks of $(A-\lambda I)^k$. The multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a root of the minimal polynomial is the size of the largest $\lambda$-block. For complex $A$: $A$ is diagonalizable iff for every eigenvalue the geometric and algebraic multiplicities coincide, and then all Jordan blocks are $1\times1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form))
- **Singular value decomposition.** Every complex $m\times n$ matrix factors as $M=U\Sigma V^*$ with $U$ ($m\times m$) and $V$ ($n\times n$) unitary and $\Sigma$ rectangular diagonal with nonnegative entries. The singular values are unique up to order, and the number of nonzero ones (with multiplicity) is $\operatorname{rank}M$. **Eckart–Young:** truncating to the $t$ largest singular values gives a best Frobenius-norm approximation of $M$ by matrices of rank at most $t$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition))
- **Polar decomposition.** Every square complex matrix is $A=UP$ with $U$ unitary and $P=(A^*A)^{1/2}$ positive semidefinite Hermitian. $P$ is always unique, and $U$ is unique iff $A$ is invertible. Over $\mathbb R$, $U$ is orthogonal and $P$ symmetric positive semidefinite. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_decomposition))
- **Hom as a tensor product.** For finite-dimensional $U,V$ over $K$, $U^*\otimes V\cong\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)$ via $(f\otimes v)(u)=f(u)v$, with inverse $F\mapsto\sum_i u_i^*\otimes F(u_i)$; hence $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)=\dim U\cdot\dim V$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product))

### Examples
- **Plane rotation.** Counterclockwise rotation of $\mathbb R^2$ by $\theta$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map))
- **Differentiation.** $\frac{d}{dx}(af+bg)=a f'+b g'$, so differentiation is linear on differentiable functions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map))
- **Shifts on sequence spaces.** The right shift $(a_1,a_2,\dots)\mapsto(0,a_1,a_2,\dots)$ has kernel of dimension $0$ and cokernel of dimension $1$. The left shift $(a_1,a_2,\dots)\mapsto(a_2,a_3,\dots)$ has kernel of dimension $1$ and cokernel $0$. So for endomorphisms of infinite-dimensional spaces, injective and surjective are no longer equivalent. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map))
- **A non-diagonalizable matrix.** The Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&1\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}$ is a single Jordan block of size $2$, so its minimal polynomial is $(x-\lambda)^2$; its eigenvalue $\lambda$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$ but a $1$-dimensional eigenspace, so it is not diagonalizable. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form))

### History
Cayley's memoir appeared in *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London* (dated 31 December 1858, pp. 17–37). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rstl.1858.0002)) In it Cayley stated the Cayley–Hamilton theorem for matrices of size at most $3$, published a proof only for $2\times2$, and wrote that he had not thought it necessary to undertake a formal proof in general. Hamilton had proved a special case for linear functions of quaternions in 1853. Frobenius gave the first general proof in 1878. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Hamilton_theorem)) Camille Jordan stated the Jordan decomposition in 1870. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form)) Beltrami (1873) and Jordan (1874) independently found the singular values of bilinear forms as invariants. Sylvester (1889) found the decomposition for real square matrices, Autonne (1915) arrived at it via the polar decomposition, and Eckart and Young (1936) gave the first proof for rectangular and complex matrices. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition))

### Connections
- [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces): domain and codomain; bases and dimension underlie matrix representations.
- [Dual Vector Space](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space): home of the transpose map and of the identification $\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)\cong U^*\otimes V$.
- [Determinant](node:Determinant): the multiplicative similarity invariant of endomorphisms.
- [Cayley–Hamilton Theorem](node:Cayley–Hamilton%20Theorem): a matrix annihilates its characteristic polynomial.
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): eigenstructure, minimal polynomial, and Jordan form.
- [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces): adjoints, unitary equivalence, SVD and polar decomposition.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): endomorphisms of finite-dimensional $V$ as $(1,1)$-tensors $V\otimes V^*$.
- [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): computing rank, SVD, and fast matrix multiplication.
- [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the infinite-dimensional continuation, where bounded operators and invariant subspaces replace matrices.
- [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals): the PID structure theorem behind the rational canonical form.
- [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory): linear maps as morphisms of representations.
- Map: [MSC 15 - Linear and multilinear algebra; matrix theory](node:MSC%2015%20-%20Linear%20and%20multilinear%20algebra;%20matrix%20theory)

### Common pitfalls
- **Rank–nullity in infinite dimensions.** The splitting $V\cong\ker T\oplus\operatorname{im}T$ holds for any vector space ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank%E2%80%93nullity_theorem)), so the dimension identity survives as an equation of cardinals. What fails is the consequence: for endomorphisms of infinite-dimensional spaces, injectivity and surjectivity are not equivalent, and kernel and cokernel dimensions need not agree, as the shift operators show. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map))
- **$\operatorname{Hom}\cong$ tensor product needs finite dimension.** The isomorphism $U^*\otimes V\cong\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)$ is stated for finite-dimensional spaces. Only endomorphisms of $V$ are $(1,1)$-tensors on $V$, and the coordinate-free trace uses $V\otimes V^*\cong\operatorname{End}(V)$ for finite-dimensional $V$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_%28linear_algebra%29))
- **Jordan form needs split characteristic polynomial.** A Jordan form over $K$ exists only if all eigenvalues lie in $K$; the Jordan form of a real matrix can be non-real. The rational canonical form needs no factorization and does not change under field extension. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_normal_form))
- **Continuity is extra in infinite dimensions.** A linear operator on a normed space is continuous iff bounded, which is automatic for finite-dimensional domains. Differentiation on smooth functions with the sup norm is discontinuous: $\sin(nx)/n\to0$ but the derivatives $\cos(nx)$ do not tend to $0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map))
- **Uniqueness in SVD.** The singular values are unique up to order, but $U$ and $V$ are not unique in general. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition))

### Open problems
- **Exponent of matrix multiplication.** Let $\omega$ be the infimum of exponents such that $n\times n$ matrices over a field can be multiplied in $n^{\omega+o(1)}$ operations. Trivially $\omega\ge2$, Strassen's 1969 algorithm gives about $O(n^{2.807})$, and the best bound reported is $\omega<2.371177$. "Whether ω = 2 is a major open question in theoretical computer science." ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication))
- **Invariant subspace problem.** Every operator on a finite-dimensional complex space of dimension at least $2$ has an eigenvector and hence a nontrivial invariant subspace. The infinite-dimensional analogue asks whether every bounded operator on a complex Banach space of dimension $>1$ has a nontrivial closed invariant subspace. Enflo and Read gave Banach-space counterexamples, and the problem "is still open for separable Hilbert spaces"; 2023 preprints claiming solutions are not recognized as verified there. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Linear map (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map): matrices, kernel, cokernel, index, continuity, infinite-dimensional examples.
- **Reference:** [Jordan normal form (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form) and [Frobenius normal form (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_normal_form): the two canonical forms under similarity.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.700 Linear Algebra (Vogan, 2013)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-700-linear-algebra-fall-2013/): proof-based course covering determinants, eigenvalues, inner products and canonical forms; [syllabus](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-700-linear-algebra-fall-2013/pages/syllabus/) uses Axler, *Linear Algebra Done Right*.
- **Primary:** [Horn and Johnson, *Matrix Analysis*, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2012/2013)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139020411): graduate monograph on matrix theory (2nd edition).
- **Primary:** [Cayley, "A memoir on the theory of matrices" (1858)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rstl.1858.0002): Cayley's 1858 memoir, where the Cayley–Hamilton theorem was first stated.
- **Further reading:** [Horn and Johnson, *Matrix Analysis* (CUP)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139020411); Axler, *Linear Algebra Done Right*, as listed in the [MIT 18.700 syllabus](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-700-linear-algebra-fall-2013/pages/syllabus/).
