**00Bxx Conference proceedings and collections of articles.** 00B05 collections of abstracts of lectures; 00B10 and 00B15 collections of articles of general or miscellaneous specific interest; 00B20 and 00B25 proceedings of conferences of general or miscellaneous specific interest; 00B30 Festschriften; 00B50 and 00B55 collections of translated articles; 00B60 collections of reprinted articles (with a cross-reference to 01A75); 00B99 other. ([MSC2020: 00Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=00Bxx))

**Neighbouring codes.**
- Each subject section has its own "-06" code for proceedings and collections, for example 03-06 "Proceedings, conferences, collections, etc. pertaining to mathematical logic and foundations" and 01-06 for history. ([MSC2020: 03-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03-XX); [MSC2020: 01-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01-XX))
- History of mathematics and mathematicians is 01Axx, not 00; 00B60 points there for reprinted collections. ([MSC2020: 01-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01-XX); [MSC2020: 00Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=00Bxx))
- Philosophy of mathematics in general is 00A30, while philosophical and critical aspects of logic and foundations are 03A05, which carries a see-also to 00A30. ([MSC2020: 03Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Philosophy of mathematics (00A30).** Asks what mathematical objects are and how we know about them; the main positions are logicism (Frege, Russell), intuitionism (Brouwer), formalism (Hilbert), predicativism (Poincaré, Weyl, Feferman), platonism, structuralism and nominalism. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/)) See [MSC 03Axx - Philosophical aspects of logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003Axx%20-%20Philosophical%20aspects%20of%20logic%20and%20foundations) for the logic side.
- **Hilbert's program and incompleteness.** Hilbert's formalism sought consistency proofs for mathematics; Gödel proved the existence of undecidable arithmetical statements in 1931, and the two incompleteness theorems together entail that the program fails. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/)) See [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems) and [MSC 03 - Mathematical logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003%20-%20Mathematical%20logic%20and%20foundations).
- **Benacerraf's problems.** The epistemological problem (1973: how can causally inert abstract objects be known?) and the identification problem (1965: the natural numbers can be modelled by sets in incompatible ways, suggesting numbers are not sets). ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/)) Relevant to [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory).
- **Indispensability argument (Quine–Putnam).** Since our best scientific theories quantify over mathematical entities, we should accept those entities; Field's nominalist reconstruction of [Newtonian mechanics](node:Newtonian%20Mechanics) (1980) is the main attempt to undermine it. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/))
- **Methodology and proof (00A35).** The SEP notes there is no agreement about what the standard for a mathematical proof is. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/)) See [Proof Techniques](node:Proof%20Techniques).
- **Lists of open problems (00A27).** Problem lists such as the Clay Millennium Prize Problems, announced on 24 May 2000 in Paris. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/))
- **General reference works (00A20).** The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, edited by Gowers, Barrow-Green and Leader, is a reference for pure mathematics with nearly 200 entries across number theory, algebra, analysis, geometry, logic and probability, plus history and biographies. ([Princeton University Press](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691118802/the-princeton-companion-to-mathematics))

### History
MSC is developed jointly by the staffs of Mathematical Reviews and Zentralblatt MATH; MSC2020, the revision after MSC2010, was released in January 2020 after a revision process that began collecting input in July 2016. ([Wikipedia: Mathematics Subject Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_Subject_Classification)) Within the philosophy of mathematics filed under 00A30, Russell communicated his paradox in Frege's system in a 1902 letter, Weyl developed predicative analysis in 1918, and Wright revived logicism in 1983 through Hume's Principle. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/))

### Open problems
- **Problem lists (00A27).** The Clay Institute's seven Millennium Prize Problems are the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, the Hodge conjecture, Navier–Stokes, P vs NP, the Poincaré conjecture, the Riemann hypothesis, and Yang–Mills and the mass gap. The Clay page lists the Poincaré conjecture as solved (Perelman) lists the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, the Hodge conjecture, P vs NP, the Riemann hypothesis and Yang–Mills as unsolved, and lists Navier–Stokes under "active problems". These problems belong to their own fields; 00A27 classifies the lists themselves. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/)) See [Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap](node:Yang–Mills%20Existence%20and%20Mass%20Gap).
- **Philosophy of mathematics (00A30).** The SEP states that whether Benacerraf's identification problem is solved "is not completely clear", that whether mathematics is conservative over physics (as Field's programme needs) is "currently a matter of controversy", and that many set theorists and philosophers believe the continuum hypothesis is "absolutely undecidable", that is, neither true nor false. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/): the main research topic filed under 00A30.
- **Learn:** [MIT 24.118 Paradox and Infinity](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/24-118-paradox-and-infinity-spring-2019/): a course on the higher infinite, Gödel's theorem and their philosophical implications.
- **Primary:** [MSC2020 section 00-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=00-XX): the classification itself, with [00Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=00Axx) and [00Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=00Bxx).
- **Further reading:** [The Princeton Companion to Mathematics (Princeton University Press, 2008)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691118802/the-princeton-companion-to-mathematics): the standard general overview of modern mathematics.
references.MSC 01 - History and biography:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 01 classifies the history of mathematics and the biographies of mathematicians. Its single section 01Axx, "History of mathematics and mathematicians", is organized along three axes: by culture and period (01A10–01A61), by kind of historical object (biographies, schools, universities, academies, collected works), and by method (sociology of the profession, historiography, bibliographic studies). The heading also refers the reader to the classification number $-03$ in the other sections. ([MSC2020 01Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01Axx))

The field studies mathematical practice in its historical setting. The earliest surviving mathematical texts come from Mesopotamia and Egypt, Greek mathematics introduced deductive proof from definitions and axioms, and the Hindu–Arabic numerals reached Europe through Islamic scholars by the twelfth century. ([Wikipedia: History of mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_mathematics)) Much of the research consists of reading such sources without importing modern concepts into them, a difficulty visible in the long debate over the Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322. ([Wikipedia: Plimpton 322](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plimpton_322))

### Scope
- **01A05, 01A07:** general histories and source books; ethnomathematics. ([MSC2020 01Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01Axx))
- **01A10–01A35, by culture:** Paleolithic and Neolithic; indigenous cultures of Africa, Asia and Oceania, of the Americas, and of pre-Greek Europe; Egyptian (01A16); Babylonian (01A17); Greek and Roman (01A20); Chinese (01A25); Japanese (01A27); other East and Southeast Asian (01A29); the Golden Age of Islam (01A30); Indian (01A32); Late Antiquity and medieval Europe (01A35). ([MSC2020 01Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01Axx))
- **01A40–01A67, by period:** the Renaissance and 15th–16th centuries, then one code per century from the 17th to the 21st, plus development of contemporary mathematics (01A65) and future perspectives (01A67). ([MSC2020 01Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01Axx))
- **01A70–01A75, people and texts:** biographies, obituaries, personalia and bibliographies (01A70); schools of mathematics (01A72); mathematics at specific universities (01A73) and at non-university institutions and academies (01A74); collected or selected works, reprints and translations of classics (01A75, see also 00B60). ([MSC2020 01Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01Axx))
- **01A80–01A90, method:** sociology and profession of mathematics (01A80), historiography (01A85), and bibliographic studies (01A90). ([MSC2020 01Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01Axx))

Neighbours, as the entry's cross-references show: the heading points to the $-03$ classification number in the other sections (for example in [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) or [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry)), and collected or selected works (01A75) point to 00B60 in [MSC 00 - General and overarching topics; collections](node:MSC%2000%20-%20General%20and%20overarching%20topics;%20collections). ([MSC2020 01Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Babylonian mathematics (01A17).** Babylonian mathematics, which MacTutor says developed from 2000 BC, used a place-value system in base 60 that could represent very large numbers and fractions. ([MacTutor overview](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/History_overview/)) Its best-known artefact, Plimpton 322 (Larsa, c. 1800 BC, now at Columbia University), is a sexagesimal table of four columns and fifteen rows in which each row relates to a Pythagorean triple. ([Wikipedia: Plimpton 322](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plimpton_322))
- **Egyptian mathematics (01A16).** The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (c. 1650 BC, likely a copy of an older Middle Kingdom text) and the Moscow Mathematical Papyrus (c. 1890 BC) are, with Plimpton 322, among the earliest surviving mathematical texts. ([Wikipedia: History of mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_mathematics))
- **Greek mathematics and Euclid (01A20).** Greek mathematicians derived conclusions from definitions and axioms, and Euclid's *Elements* made the axiomatic method the model of rigor ([Wikipedia: History of mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_mathematics)); see [Euclidean Geometry](node:Euclidean%20Geometry) and [Proof Techniques](node:Proof%20Techniques). Book I alone contains 23 definitions, 5 postulates, 5 common notions and 48 propositions, from the construction of an equilateral triangle (I.1) to the Pythagorean theorem (I.47). ([Euclid, Book I (Joyce)](https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/elements/bookI/bookI.html)) MacTutor places the major Greek progress between 300 BC and AD 200, including irrational numbers and conic sections. ([MacTutor overview](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/History_overview/))
- **Indian and Islamic mathematics and transmission (01A30, 01A32).** The Hindu–Arabic numeral system evolved in India during the first millennium AD, reached Islamic mathematicians through a translation of an Indian text around 770, and was carried to Europe by the twelfth century. ([Wikipedia: History of mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_mathematics)) Adelard of Bath and later Fibonacci brought Islamic mathematics, with the Greek mathematics it had preserved, back into Europe. ([MacTutor overview](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/History_overview/)) The Kerala school, founded by Madhava of Sangamagrama and active from the 14th to the 16th century, recorded infinite [series](node:Series%20and%20Convergence) for sine, cosine and arctangent in Neelakanta's *Tantrasangraha* (c. 1500), with proofs in Jyesthadeva's *Yuktibhasa* (c. 1530); the school also derived a series for $\pi$ related to the Gregory series. ([Wikipedia: Kerala school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_school_of_astronomy_and_mathematics))
- **Biography and reference works (01A70).** The *Dictionary of Scientific Biography* (Scribner's, 1970–1980, 16 volumes, editor in chief C. C. Gillispie) covers scientists, mathematicians included, from antiquity to modern times, and was supplemented in 1990 and by the *New DSB* (2007, ed. N. Koertge, 775 entries). ([Wikipedia: Dictionary of Scientific Biography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictionary_of_Scientific_Biography)) MacTutor provides free biographies alongside cultural histories (Babylonian, Egyptian, Greek, Islamic, Chinese, Indian, and others) and topic histories (algebra, analysis, number theory, geometry and topology, mathematical physics and astronomy). ([MacTutor history topics](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/))
- **Historiography (01A85).** A central methodological issue is anachronism: reading a past text through modern concepts. Robson calls the trigonometric reading of Plimpton 322 "conceptually anachronistic" because Babylonian mathematics lacked a concept of angle measure ([Wikipedia: Plimpton 322](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plimpton_322)), and Grattan-Guinness's article "The mathematics of the past: distinguishing its history from our heritage" (*Historia Mathematica* 31, 2004) names the distinction between the history of past mathematics and its heritage in present mathematics in its title. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/S0315-0860%2803%2900032-6))

### History
General histories of the whole subject, the material of 01A05, include Morris Kline's *Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times* (first published 1972; Oxford University Press three-volume edition 1990), running from Babylon and Egypt through Greek geometry, the calculus and nineteenth-century analysis, to abstract algebra, topology and Gödel. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780195061352.001.0001)) The first major theory of the tablet's construction came from Neugebauer and Sachs (1945), who read it as number theory on Pythagorean triples generated by a rule like Euclid's, and Bruins (1949) introduced the reciprocal-pair reading later developed by Robson. ([Abdulaziz, arXiv:1004.0025](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1004.0025); [Wikipedia: Plimpton 322](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plimpton_322))

### Open problems
- **Purpose and construction of Plimpton 322.** "The purpose of Plimpton 322 is not known," and scholars differ on how its numbers were generated: Neugebauer–Sachs's number-theoretic reading, reciprocal pairs (Bruins, Friberg, Robson), a teacher's set of exercise parameters (Robson), and a trigonometric reading, which Wikipedia reports is ruled out because the Babylonians apparently lacked a concept of angle measure. ([Wikipedia: Plimpton 322](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plimpton_322)) Abdulaziz writes that "scholars are divided on how and why the list was devised"; in contrast, Mansfield and Wildberger titled their 2017 *Historia Mathematica* article (vol. 44) "Plimpton 322 is Babylonian exact sexagesimal trigonometry". ([Abdulaziz, arXiv:1004.0025](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1004.0025); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.hm.2017.08.001))
- **Transmission of Kerala mathematics to Europe.** Whether the Kerala series reached Europe is "an ongoing topic of scholarly debate"; there is "currently no direct manuscript evidence" of such a transfer. Bag (1979) proposed transmission through trade routes and Jesuit missionaries, while Bressoud states there is no evidence that the Indian work on series was known beyond India before the nineteenth century. ([Wikipedia: Kerala school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_school_of_astronomy_and_mathematics))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [History of mathematics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_mathematics): chronological and cultural survey.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 01Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=01Axx): the classification by culture, period, people and method.
- **Learn:** [MacTutor History of Mathematics, history topics](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/): University of St Andrews essays by culture and topic, with biographies.
- **Primary:** [Abdulaziz, The Plimpton 322 tablet and the Babylonian method of generating Pythagorean triples (arXiv:1004.0025)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1004.0025): research paper comparing the main reconstructions of the tablet.
- **Primary:** [Euclid's Elements, Book I (Joyce, Clark University)](https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/elements/bookI/bookI.html): a translated primary text with definitions, postulates, and propositions.
- **Further reading:** [Kline, Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times (OUP)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780195061352.001.0001): comprehensive three-volume history; [Grattan-Guinness, The mathematics of the past (Historia Mathematica, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/S0315-0860%2803%2900032-6): historiography of history versus heritage.
references.MSC 03 - Mathematical logic and foundati:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 03, "Mathematical logic and foundations", classifies the mathematical study of formal languages, proofs, models, computability and sets. MSC2020 divides it into 03A philosophical aspects, 03B general logic, 03C model theory, 03D computability and recursion theory, 03E set theory, 03F proof theory and constructive mathematics, 03G algebraic logic, and 03H nonstandard models. ([MSC2020: 03-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03-XX))

The field is organized around a few metatheorems linking syntax and semantics. Derivability and truth coincide for first-order logic (soundness and completeness), but any consistent formal system containing a modest amount of arithmetic is incomplete, and first-order validity is undecidable. ([SEP: Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/); [SEP: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))

Set theory supplies the usual foundation, and its central phenomenon is independence: questions such as the continuum hypothesis cannot be settled in ZFC, and research asks which new axioms could settle them. ([SEP: The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))

### Scope
Subdivisions, with the vault's subfield maps ([MSC2020: 03-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03-XX)):
- [03A Philosophical aspects of logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003Axx%20-%20Philosophical%20aspects%20of%20logic%20and%20foundations): 03A05 philosophical and critical aspects (see also 00A30, philosophy of mathematics), 03A10 logic in the philosophy of science. ([MSC2020: 03Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Axx))
- [03B General logic](node:MSC%2003Bxx%20-%20General%20logic).
- [03C Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory).
- [03D Computability and recursion theory](node:MSC%2003Dxx%20-%20Computability%20and%20recursion%20theory).
- [03E Set theory](node:MSC%2003Exx%20-%20Set%20theory).
- [03F Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics).
- [03G Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic).
- [03H Nonstandard models](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models) (see also 03C62).

The section also has form codes: 03-03 history of logic (with a note to consider 01-XX) and 03-06 proceedings and collections in logic. ([MSC2020: 03-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03-XX)) Philosophy of mathematics in general sits in 00A30 rather than here, which is why 03A05 cross-refers to it. ([MSC2020: 03Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Axx))

### Key concepts
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): **Completeness** (Gödel 1930): a consistent set of sentences $\Gamma$ is satisfiable; with soundness, $\Gamma\vdash\theta$ iff $\Gamma\models\theta$. **Compactness**: $\Gamma$ is satisfiable iff every finite subset is. ([SEP: Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/))
- [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory): **Löwenheim–Skolem**. In a countable language, a satisfiable $\Gamma$ has a model that is finite or countably infinite; if $\Gamma$ has arbitrarily large finite models, then for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$ it has a model of size $\kappa$. Hence a first-order theory with an infinite model cannot force all its models to be countable, or all to be uncountable. ([SEP: Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/))
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): If $F$ is a consistent, effectively axiomatized formal system that interprets Robinson arithmetic $Q$, then some sentence is neither provable nor refutable in $F$ (Gödel 1931, with Rosser's 1936 improvement removing $\omega$-consistency); and such $F$ (with slightly more arithmetic) does not prove its own consistency statement $\mathrm{Cons}(F)$. Tarski: no formula $\mathrm{Tr}(x)$ of $F$ satisfies $F\vdash\mathrm{Tr}(\ulcorner A\urcorner)\leftrightarrow A$ for all sentences $A$. ([SEP: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory) and [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines): **Undecidability.** The halting set is recursively enumerable but not decidable (Turing 1936); Church (1936) showed that first-order validity is undecidable, which also follows because $Q$ is essentially undecidable. A set is decidable iff it and its complement are r.e. ([Wikipedia: Halting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halting_problem); [SEP: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/); [SEP: Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/))
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory) and [Cardinality](node:Cardinality): **Independence of CH.** CH says $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1$. Gödel (1938) showed CH holds in the constructible universe $L$, so ZFC + CH is consistent if ZFC is; Cohen (1963) invented forcing and built models of ZFC + $\neg$CH. Standard large-cardinal axioms do not settle CH (Levy–Solovay). ([SEP: The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))
- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic), [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory) and [Proof by Contradiction](node:Proof%20by%20Contradiction): **Classical versus intuitionistic logic**, central to 03F (constructive mathematics). Intuitionistic logic drops excluded middle and double-negation elimination, so reductio proves only negative statements; by Glivenko's theorem (1929) a propositional formula $A$ is classically provable iff $\neg\neg A$ is intuitionistically provable, and the Gödel–Gentzen negative translation embeds Peano arithmetic in Heyting arithmetic, which therefore has the same consistency strength. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/))

### History
Gödel proved completeness in 1930 and the incompleteness theorems in 1931, with Rosser's strengthening in 1936. ([SEP: Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/); [SEP: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/)) In 1936 Church published an unsolvability result using the [lambda calculus](node:Lambda%20Calculus), and Turing's paper (sent to press in May 1936, printed January 1937) proved three problems undecidable, including the Entscheidungsproblem; Turing never used the word "halting", and the term "halting problem" is attributed to Martin Davis. ([Wikipedia: Halting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halting_problem)) Hilbert placed CH first on his list of open problems for the 20th century; Gödel's inner model $L$ (1938) and Cohen's forcing (1963) together showed it independent of ZFC. ([SEP: The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))

### Open problems
- **Vaught's conjecture (03C).** A complete first-order theory in a countable language has either at most $\aleph_0$ or exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$ countable models. Proposed by Vaught in 1961 and listed as unsolved; Morley showed the number is finite, $\aleph_0$, $\aleph_1$ or $2^{\aleph_0}$, and Harrington–Makkai–Shelah (1984) proved it for $\omega$-stable theories. ([Wikipedia: Vaught conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaught_conjecture))
- **Martin's conjecture (03D, 03E).** A proposed classification of the definable functions on the Turing degrees, stated in $\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{AD}+\mathsf{DC}_{\mathbb R}$, in two parts. Slaman and Steel proved Part 2 for Borel order-preserving functions; Lutz and Siskind prove Part 1 for all order-preserving functions, and state that the conjecture "remains open", with several special cases proved. ([Lutz and Siskind](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.19646))
- **The continuum hypothesis and new axioms (03E).** CH cannot be settled in ZFC; the SEP calls it "one of the most central open problems in set theory", the open question being whether new axioms can settle it. Woodin's $\mathbb P_{\max}$ and $\Omega$-logic work makes a case for $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, while the Ultimate-$L$ theory ZFC + $V=L_\Omega$ + LCA would imply CH (a variant would imply $\neg$CH), and the entry calls the status of the local approaches to resolving CH (such as Woodin's) "somewhat unsettled". ([SEP: The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Classical Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/): syntax, semantics, completeness, compactness, Löwenheim–Skolem; [SEP: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/).
- **Learn:** [MIT 24.242 Logic II](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/24-242-logic-ii-spring-2004/): computability, Gödel's incompleteness theorems, Church's and Tarski's theorems, with lecture notes and problem sets.
- **Primary:** [Lutz and Siskind, Part 1 of Martin's Conjecture for order-preserving and measure-preserving functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19646): current research in 03D; [MSC2020 03-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03-XX): the classification.
- **Further reading:** [Shoenfield, Mathematical Logic (1967; Association for Symbolic Logic / Addison-Wesley)](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=shoenfield+mathematical+logic&fields=title,author_name,first_publish_year,publisher,key&limit=5) and [Barwise (ed.), Handbook of Mathematical Logic (North-Holland, 1977)](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=handbook+of+mathematical+logic+barwise&fields=title,author_name,first_publish_year,publisher,key&limit=5): the standard graduate text and handbook.
references.MSC 03Axx - Philosophical aspects of log:
## Reference
### Overview
This MSC2020 subfield of [MSC 03 - Mathematical logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003%20-%20Mathematical%20logic%20and%20foundations) covers philosophical and critical aspects of logic and foundations. It sits next to the purely mathematical sections of 03 (general logic, [model theory](node:Model%20Theory), computability, set theory, proof theory, algebraic logic, nonstandard models), and is cross-referenced with 00A30, "Philosophy of mathematics". ([MSC2020: 03Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Axx); [MSC2020: 03-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03-XX); [MSC2020: 00A30](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=00A30))

Its questions are what mathematical objects are, how mathematical knowledge is possible, and what foundational systems and metatheorems show. The major positions (logicism, formalism, intuitionism, predicativism, platonism, structuralism) are closely tied to technical results: Russell's paradox, Gödel's incompleteness theorems, Frege's theorem, and the independence of the continuum hypothesis. A second strand, the philosophy of mathematical practice, asks why mathematicians value particular proofs and methods beyond their establishing truth. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/); [Avigad, Mathematical method and proof](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~avigad/Papers/method.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists three codes: 03A05 "Philosophical and critical aspects of logic and foundations" (with "for philosophy of mathematics, see also 00A30"), 03A10 "Logic in the philosophy of science", and 03A99 for other work in the section. 00A30 "Philosophy of mathematics" in turn says "see also 03A05". ([MSC2020: 03Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Axx); [MSC2020: 00A30](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=00A30))

The sibling sections of 03 are [MSC 03Bxx - General logic](node:MSC%2003Bxx%20-%20General%20logic), [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory), [MSC 03Dxx - Computability and recursion theory](node:MSC%2003Dxx%20-%20Computability%20and%20recursion%20theory), [MSC 03Exx - Set theory](node:MSC%2003Exx%20-%20Set%20theory), [MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics), 03Gxx Algebraic logic and 03Hxx Nonstandard models. The key concepts below pair each philosophical question with the technical result it turns on. ([MSC2020: 03-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03-XX); [SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/))

### Key concepts
- **Logicism and neo-logicism.** Frege tried to derive arithmetic from logic, but his Basic Law V is inconsistent (Russell's paradox). Neo-logicists (Wright, Hale) instead use Hume's Principle, $\#F=\#G\leftrightarrow F\approx G$ (the number of $F$s equals the number of $G$s iff they are equinumerous). **Frege's theorem:** in second-order logic, Hume's Principle implies the Dedekind–Peano axioms; Parsons (1965) first noted that it suffices, and Wright (1983) carried out most of the derivation. Hume's Principle is consistent with second-order logic; whether it is a truth of logic is disputed. ([SEP: Frege's Theorem](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frege-theorem/); [SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/))
- **[Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems) and Hilbert's program.** Any consistent formal system with decidable axioms that interprets enough arithmetic (Robinson's Q) is incomplete; with slightly more arithmetic it cannot prove its own consistency. These pose, at least prima facie, serious problems for Hilbert's finitary consistency program; the Lucas–Penrose argument that they refute mechanism is widely judged to fail. See also [Formalism and Mathematical Platonism](node:Formalism%20and%20Mathematical%20Platonism). ([SEP: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Intuitionism and predicativism.** Brouwer took mathematics to be mental construction and rejected the unrestricted law of excluded middle, which ties the position to [proof by contradiction](node:Proof%20by%20Contradiction) and constructive logic. Predicativists (Poincaré, Russell, Weyl, later Feferman) reject impredicative definitions; Feferman and, independently, Schütte calibrated predicative strength by ordinals, and most twentieth-century analysis is predicatively acceptable, unlike transfinite [set theory](node:Set%20Theory). ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/))
- **Benacerraf's problems.** The identification problem (1965): two standard set-theoretic reductions of the natural numbers are equally good yet disagree, e.g. on whether $1\in3$, suggesting numbers are not sets (a motivation for structuralism). The epistemological problem (1973): if abstract objects are causally inert, it is unclear how we could know about them. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/))
- **Quine–Putnam indispensability argument.** (P1) We ought to be ontologically committed to all and only the entities indispensable to our best scientific theories; (P2) mathematical entities are so indispensable; hence we ought to be committed to them. Field denies (P2) by nominalizing Newtonian gravitation, Maddy attacks (P1) from scientific practice, and Sober questions whether mathematics is empirically confirmed. ([SEP: Indispensability Arguments](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathphil-indis/))
- **Independence and the continuum hypothesis.** CH is independent of ZFC: it holds in Gödel's constructible universe $L$ (1938) and fails in a Cohen generic extension (1963). Pluralists take independence to show CH has no answer; Gödel took it to show the weakness of current axioms. ([SEP: The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))
- **Formal frameworks.** [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic), [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory), [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory) and [Proof Theory](node:Proof%20Theory) are the systems whose philosophical status is at issue; computational proof assistants such as those in [Formal Verification and Proof Assistants](node:Formal%20Verification%20and%20Proof%20Assistants) express mathematics in formal languages, and Avigad asks how such formal models bear on the philosophy of mathematics; his paper uses a model of proof from the automated-deduction community to evaluate the methods proofs employ. ([Avigad, Mathematical method and proof](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~avigad/Papers/method.pdf); [CMU seminar](https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/avigad/Teaching/mathematics_and_language/))

### History
Frege's logicism foundered on Russell's paradox; Russell's type theory avoided the paradox, but deriving arithmetic in it required an axiom asserting an infinite collection of ground objects, which could hardly be regarded as a logical principle. Hilbert's formalism aimed at finitary consistency proofs, which Gödel's incompleteness theorems undercut in their original form. Brouwer's intuitionism and the predicativism of Poincaré and Weyl arose in the same foundational crisis. Later debates were set by Gödel's platonism, Quine and Putnam's indispensability argument, Benacerraf's papers of 1965 and 1973, Field's nominalism, Wright's 1983 neo-logicism, and the structuralism of Shapiro and Resnik. ([SEP: Philosophy of Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/); [SEP: Frege's Theorem](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frege-theorem/))

### Open problems
- **Does CH have a determinate truth value?** The SEP calls CH one of the most central open problems in set theory, reports that pluralists and non-pluralists disagree on whether independence leaves it without an answer, and says it is open whether the completeness theorem behind Woodin's $\Omega$-conjecture holds. ([SEP: The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))
- **The indispensability debate.** The SEP entry describes the debate as "very much alive" and says it is not clear how damaging the criticisms by Field, Maddy and Sober are. ([SEP: Indispensability Arguments](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathphil-indis/))
- **A theory of the value of proofs.** Avigad argues that the value of new proofs of known theorems depends on their methods, and that standard models of formal deduction cannot support such evaluations. He describes the broader program of a theory of mathematical understanding as "dauntingly vague, broad, and open-ended" and only begins it. ([Avigad, Mathematical method and proof](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~avigad/Papers/method.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Philosophy of Mathematics (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/philosophy-mathematics/): the main positions, Benacerraf's problems, and the incompleteness theorems' bearing on them.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 03Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Axx): the official sub-codes.
- **Learn:** [CMU seminar, Mathematics and Language (Avigad)](https://www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/avigad/Teaching/mathematics_and_language/): seminar (fall 2015) on what proof assistants show about the philosophy of mathematics.
- **Primary:** [Avigad, Mathematical method and proof (2005)](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~avigad/Papers/method.pdf): research paper on why proofs are valued beyond correctness.
- **Further reading:** [Benacerraf and Putnam (eds.), Philosophy of Mathematics: Selected Readings, 2nd ed. (CUP, 1984)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139171519): the standard anthology of classic papers.
references.MSC 03Bxx - General logic:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 03B, "General logic", is the part of [MSC 03 - Mathematical logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003%20-%20Mathematical%20logic%20and%20foundations) that studies logical systems themselves: classical propositional, first-order and higher-order logic, subsystems such as intuitionistic logic, abstract deductive systems, decidability of theories, foundations of classical theories including reverse mathematics, mechanized proof, type theory and lambda calculus, and the many nonclassical logics (modal, temporal, epistemic, substructural, many-valued, fuzzy, paraconsistent, intermediate, probabilistic), together with applications to language and computer science. ([MSC2020 03Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Bxx))

Its basic question is how a proof system relates to a semantics. For classical first-order logic the answer is Gödel's completeness theorem, and Lindström's theorem explains why first-order logic is singled out. ([Gödel's completeness theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_completeness_theorem); [Lindström's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindstr%C3%B6m%27s_theorem)) For a nonclassical logic the same questions are asked again, for example whether a modal logic is complete for a class of Kripke frames; this can fail: the logic H defines the same frames as GL yet cannot prove $\Box A\to\Box\Box A$, which is valid on them. ([SEP, Modal Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-modal/)) Decidability of the extensions of K by modal reduction principles $\Diamond^k p\to\Diamond^n p$ is a long-standing open problem, settled so far only for subclasses. ([Ostropolski-Nalewaja–Lyon, arXiv:2405.10094](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10094v2))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 03B05 classical propositional logic; 03B10 classical first-order logic; 03B16 higher-order logic; 03B20 subsystems of classical logic (including intuitionistic logic); 03B22 abstract deductive systems; 03B25 decidability of theories and sets of sentences (see also 11U05, 12L05, 20F10); 03B30 foundations of classical theories, including reverse mathematics (see also 03F35); 03B35 mechanization of proofs (see also 68V15); 03B38 type theory; 03B40 combinatory logic and lambda calculus (see also 68N18); 03B42 logics of knowledge and belief; 03B44 temporal logic; 03B45 modal logic; 03B47 substructural logics; 03B48 probability and inductive logic; 03B50 many-valued logic; 03B52 fuzzy logic; 03B53 paraconsistent logics; 03B55 intermediate logics; 03B60 other nonclassical logic; 03B62 combined logics; 03B65 logic of natural languages; 03B70 logic in computer science; 03B80 other applications; 03B99. ([MSC2020 03Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Bxx))

- **Neighbour 03F.** Proof-theoretic aspects go to [MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics): 03B30 cross-refers to 03F35 (second- and higher-order arithmetic), 03B45 sends provability logic to 03F45, and 03B47 sends proof theory of substructural logics to 03F52. ([MSC2020 03Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Bxx))
- **Neighbour 68.** 03B35 cross-refers to 68V15 (theorem proving), in [MSC 68Vxx - Computer science support for mathematical research and practice](node:MSC%2068Vxx%20-%20Computer%20science%20support%20for%20mathematical%20research%20and%20practice), and 03B40 to 68N18. ([MSC2020 03Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Bxx))
- **Neighbour 03C.** Model theory is the separate section [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory); its 03C80 (logic with extra quantifiers and operators) cross-refers back to 03B42, 03B44, 03B45 and 03B48. ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Completeness of [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic) (03B10).** For a first-order theory $T$ and a sentence $s$: if $s$ holds in every model of $T$, then $T\vdash s$; with soundness, semantic and syntactic consequence coincide. Gödel proved it in his 1929 dissertation; Henkin (1949) isolated the core as the model existence theorem: a syntactically consistent theory has a model. The [Compactness Theorem](node:Compactness%20Theorem) follows. Second-order logic with standard semantics has no complete proof system, and its validities are not recursively enumerable; Henkin semantics restores completeness. ([Gödel's completeness theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_completeness_theorem))
- **Lindström's theorem (03B10, abstract logic).** First-order logic is maximal among logics (closed under classical negation, etc.) having countable compactness and the downward Löwenheim–Skolem property: no such logic is stronger. Lindström published it in 1969; it is perhaps the best-known result of what later became abstract model theory. ([Lindström's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindstr%C3%B6m%27s_theorem))
- **Undecidability and decidable theories (03B25).** Hilbert and Ackermann (1928) asked for an algorithm deciding first-order validity; Church and Turing (1936) showed none exists, Turing by reduction to the halting problem for [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines). Validity in finite models is also undecidable (Trakhtenbrot). Decidable cases include Presburger arithmetic, the theory of [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields), monadic predicate logic and the Bernays–Schönfinkel class. ([Entscheidungsproblem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entscheidungsproblem)) The related negative answer to [Hilbert's Tenth Problem](node:Hilbert's%20Tenth%20Problem) is listed on the same page. ([Entscheidungsproblem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entscheidungsproblem))
- **Kripke semantics and canonical models (03B45).** A frame is $\langle W,R\rangle$ and $\Box A$ is true at $w$ iff $A$ is true at every $w'$ with $wRw'$. System K adds necessitation and $\Box(A\to B)\to(\Box A\to\Box B)$ to propositional logic; the axioms $\Box A\to A$, $\Box A\to\Box\Box A$, $A\to\Box\Diamond A$, $\Diamond A\to\Box\Diamond A$ correspond to reflexive, transitive, symmetric and Euclidean frames, S4 is $T+4$, and S5 is $T+5$. ([SEP, Modal Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-modal/)) Completeness is proved with the canonical model of a normal system $S$: worlds are maximal $S$-consistent sets, $wRu$ iff $\{\beta:\Box\beta\in w\}\subseteq u$, and $\alpha$ is valid in it iff $S\vdash\alpha$; so $S$ is complete for a frame class containing its canonical frame, which gives completeness of K, D, T, B, S4, S5. ([MIT 24.244, Completeness](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/24-244-modal-logic-spring-2015/a4ab6b46bc0763e9638ae325f1e6cc3b_MIT24_244S15_Completeness.pdf)) For these systems it suffices to test a formula $\alpha$ on frames of size at most $N(\alpha)$, which makes them decidable. ([MIT 24.244, Testing](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/24-244-modal-logic-spring-2015/956a64be6d3ebaf611182158628e0ab6_MIT24_244S15_Testing.pdf)) Knudstorp (preprint, 2025) states that whether the logics $K\oplus\Box^n p\to\Box^m p$ with $n>m>1$ have the finite model property was a long-standing open problem and claims a proof that every logic axiomatized by such formulas has it. ([Knudstorp, arXiv:2510.00864](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00864)) See [Temporal Logic](node:Temporal%20Logic) for 03B44.
- **Curry–Howard (03B38, 03B40).** Proofs correspond to programs and formulas to types. Howard (1969, published 1980) matched intuitionistic implicational natural deduction with simply typed lambda terms (hypotheses as variables, modus ponens as application, implication introduction as abstraction); Curry (1934) observed that types of combinators can serve as axiom schemes of intuitionistic implicational logic, and Curry and Feys (1958) matched the types of $K$ and $S$ with Hilbert-style axioms; normal deductions correspond to normal forms. System F covers second-order propositional logic, and Griffin (1990) extended the correspondence to classical logic through control operators. ([Curry–Howard correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence)) See [Lambda Calculus](node:Lambda%20Calculus) and [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory).
- **Substructural logics (03B47).** These drop structural rules of classical sequent calculus: relevant logic rejects weakening, contraction-free logics such as linear logic forbid reusing premises, and the Lambek calculus makes premise order significant by rejecting exchange. The relevant logic R is undecidable. ([SEP, Substructural Logics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-substructural/)) Linear logic in fact drops both weakening and contraction, keeping them only in controlled form. ([Linear logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_logic))
- **Classical propositional logic and subsystems (03B05, 03B20).** MSC lists classical propositional logic and its subsystems, including intuitionistic logic, as separate codes; see [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic), [Lindenbaum–Tarski Algebras](node:Lindenbaum–Tarski%20Algebras) for algebraic semantics, and the neighbouring [Proof Theory](node:Proof%20Theory), [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory) and [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory). ([MSC2020 03Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Bxx))

### History
C. I. Lewis founded modern modal logic, and Kripke's "Semantical Considerations on Modal Logic" (1963) gave its relational semantics. ([SEP, Modal Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-modal/)) Gödel's completeness theorem dates from 1929–1930, and Henkin's proof from 1949. ([Gödel's completeness theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_completeness_theorem)) The Entscheidungsproblem was posed in 1928 and answered negatively in 1936. ([Entscheidungsproblem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entscheidungsproblem)) Lindström's characterization appeared in 1969. ([Lindström's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindstr%C3%B6m%27s_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Decidability of modal reduction principles.** Whether every extension of K by axioms $\Diamond^k p\to\Diamond^n p$ is decidable "has remained a longstanding open problem" (first discussed by Wolter and Zakharyaschev). Ostropolski-Nalewaja and Lyon proved decidability, with an EXPSPACE procedure, for the quasi-dense case $0<k<n$, and describe their work as headway toward a complete solution; extensions of K4 by such principles were shown decidable by Zakharyaschev. ([Ostropolski-Nalewaja–Lyon, arXiv:2405.10094](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.10094v2))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, Modal Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-modal/): Kripke semantics, the systems K to S5, frame correspondence.
- **Reference:** [SEP, Substructural Logics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-substructural/): relevant, linear and Lambek logics.
- **Learn:** [MIT 24.244 Modal Logic (Yablo), lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/24-244-modal-logic-spring-2015/pages/lecture-notes/): semantics, decision procedures, canonical-model completeness, modal predicate logic.
- **Primary:** [Ostropolski-Nalewaja and Lyon, Decidability of Quasi-Dense Modal Logics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10094v2): recent progress on a longstanding decidability problem.
- **Further reading:** [Blackburn, de Rijke and Venema, Modal Logic (CUP, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781107050884): standard graduate monograph.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 03Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Bxx): official code list.
references.MSC 03Cxx - Model theory:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 03C, "Model theory", is the part of [MSC 03 - Mathematical logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003%20-%20Mathematical%20logic%20and%20foundations) that studies [mathematical structures](node:Mathematical%20Structures) through the sets definable in them by formulas of a logic, mostly [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic). Its codes run from basic properties of languages and structures, quantifier elimination, ultraproducts and other model constructions, through categoricity, classification theory and stability, abstract elementary classes and o-minimality, to model-theoretic algebra, models of arithmetic and [set theory](node:Set%20Theory), computable structures, continuous logic, and infinitary and abstract logics. ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx))

Two programmes shape the research field. Classification theory, after Morley and Shelah, asks which complete theories have few models and finds "dividing lines" such as stability that separate them from theories with many. ([SEP, First-order Model Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/); [Morley's categoricity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morley%27s_categoricity_theorem)) Geometric and applied model theory uses tame classes of structures, such as o-minimal expansions of the real field, to prove theorems in algebra, geometry and number theory; examples are the model-theoretic proof of the geometric Mordell–Lang conjecture and the o-minimal approach to the André–Oort conjecture. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/); [André–Oort conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9%E2%80%93Oort_conjecture))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 03C05 equational classes and universal algebra (see also 08A, 08B, 18C05); 03C07 basic properties of first-order languages and structures; 03C10 quantifier elimination and model completeness; 03C13 finite structures; 03C15 denumerable and separable structures; 03C20 ultraproducts; 03C25 model-theoretic forcing; 03C30 other constructions; 03C35 categoricity and completeness; 03C40 interpolation, preservation, definability; 03C45 classification theory and stability; 03C48 abstract elementary classes; 03C50 models with special properties (saturated, rigid); 03C52 properties of classes of models; 03C55 set-theoretic model theory; 03C57 computable structure theory; 03C60 model-theoretic algebra; 03C62 models of arithmetic and set theory; 03C64 ordered structures and o-minimality; 03C65 models of other theories; 03C66 continuous model theory and metric structures; 03C68 other first-order model theory; 03C70 admissible sets; 03C75 infinitary logic; 03C80 extra quantifiers; 03C85 higher-order model theory; 03C90 nonclassical models; 03C95 abstract model theory; 03C98 applications; 03C99. ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx))

- **Neighbour 08A.** 03C05 cross-refers to universal algebra in [MSC 08Axx - Algebraic structures](node:MSC%2008Axx%20-%20Algebraic%20structures). ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx))
- **Neighbour 03D.** 03C57 cross-refers to 03D45, in [MSC 03Dxx - Computability and recursion theory](node:MSC%2003Dxx%20-%20Computability%20and%20recursion%20theory). ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx))
- **Neighbour 12L.** 03C60 cross-refers to [MSC 12Lxx - Connections between field theory and logic](node:MSC%2012Lxx%20-%20Connections%20between%20field%20theory%20and%20logic) and 13L05. ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx))
- **Neighbour 03H.** 03C62 cross-refers to [MSC 03Hxx - Nonstandard models](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models). ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem (03C07).** If every finite subset of a first-order theory $T$ has a model, so does $T$ (the [Compactness Theorem](node:Compactness%20Theorem)). Downward: if $A$ is a structure and $\lambda$ is a cardinal at least the number of formulas and below $|A|$, then $A$ has an elementary substructure of [cardinality](node:Cardinality) $\lambda$ containing any given set of at most $\lambda$ elements. Upward: for $\lambda$ at least the number of formulas and at least $|A|$, $A$ has an elementary extension of cardinality $\lambda$. ([SEP, First-order Model Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/))
- **Łoś's theorem (03C20).** For an ultrafilter $U$ on $I$, structures $M_i$, a formula $\varphi(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and $s_1,\dots,s_n\in\prod_i M_i$, $\left(\prod_i M_i\right)/U\models\varphi(s_1/{\sim},\dots,s_n/{\sim})$ iff $\{i\in I: M_i\models\varphi(s_1(i),\dots,s_n(i))\}\in U$. In particular the diagonal embedding into an ultrapower is elementary. ([Pillay, Thm 1.16](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~apillay/pdf/lecturenotes_modeltheory.pdf); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/))
- **Tarski and quantifier elimination (03C10, 03C60).** The structures elementarily equivalent to $(\mathbb R,+,\cdot)$ are exactly the [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields), from Tarski's 1930 description of the theory of $\mathbb R$, which he proved by quantifier elimination; embeddings between algebraically closed fields are elementary (model completeness), a weaker property than quantifier elimination. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/)) See [Model Theory of Fields](node:Model%20Theory%20of%20Fields).
- **Morley's categoricity theorem and classification (03C35, 03C45).** If a complete theory in a countable language with infinite models is $\kappa$-categorical for one uncountable $\kappa$, it is $\kappa$-categorical for every uncountable $\kappa$ (Morley, 1965, confirming a conjecture of Łoś, 1954); Shelah (1974) extended this to uncountable languages, above the cardinality of the language. Algebraically closed fields of fixed characteristic are uncountably categorical but not $\omega$-categorical; [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) over a fixed countable field are another example categorical in an uncountable cardinal; dense linear orders without endpoints are $\omega$-categorical but not categorical in any uncountable cardinal. Shelah's classification theory uses dividing lines such as stability, superstability, DOP and OTOP: a theory is classifiable if it is superstable without DOP or OTOP. ([Morley's categoricity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morley%27s_categoricity_theorem)) For countable complete $T$, $T$ is $\omega$-categorical iff every type in $S_n(T)$ is isolated for each $n$. ([Pillay, Lemma 4.31](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~apillay/pdf/lecturenotes_modeltheory.pdf))
- **O-minimality (03C64).** An ordered structure is o-minimal if every definable subset of the line is a finite union of intervals and points. Examples are real closed fields, whose definable sets are the [Semialgebraic Sets](node:Semialgebraic%20Sets), the real field with restricted analytic functions, and the real exponential field (Wilkie, 1996); o-minimal structures have cell decomposition and a well-behaved dimension theory. ([O-minimal theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-minimal_theory)) Pila–Wilkie counting theorem: if $X\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is definable in an o-minimal expansion of $\mathbb R$ and $X^{\mathrm{tr}}$ is $X$ minus the union of its connected infinite semialgebraic subsets, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $c$ with $\#\{a\in X^{\mathrm{tr}}\cap\mathbb Q^n: H(a)\le T\}\le cT^{\varepsilon}$ for all $T\ge1$. ([Bhardwaj–van den Dries, Thm 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.14046)) Building on the Pila–Zannier strategy (2006), Pila used o-minimality to prove André–Oort unconditionally for arbitrary products of modular curves (2009); Pila, Shankar and Tsimerman claimed in 2021 the height bound that completes the conjecture via the Pila–Zannier strategy. ([André–Oort conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9%E2%80%93Oort_conjecture))
- **Applications to geometry (03C98).** In the early 1990s Hrushovski, with Zilber, gave a model-theoretic proof of the geometric Mordell–Lang conjecture in all characteristics. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/))
- **Universal algebra and model-theoretic algebra (03C05, 03C60).** MSC lists equational classes and universal algebra in model theory, and model-theoretic algebra, as separate codes; see [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory), [Universal Algebra](node:Universal%20Algebra) and, for fields, [Valued Fields](node:Valued%20Fields). ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx))

### History
Łoś isolated the possible categoricity patterns in 1954, Morley proved his theorem in 1965, and Shelah extended it in 1974. ([Morley's categoricity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morley%27s_categoricity_theorem)) Vaught posed his conjecture in 1961. ([Vaught conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaught_conjecture)) O-minimality was developed by Pillay and Steinhorn (1986, 1988) and Knight, Pillay and Steinhorn (1986), and Wilkie proved the o-minimality of the real exponential field in 1996. ([O-minimal theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-minimal_theory)) André stated a one-dimensional form of his conjecture in 1989. ([André–Oort conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9%E2%80%93Oort_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Vaught's conjecture.** A complete first-order theory in a countable language has at most $\aleph_0$ or exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$ countable models up to isomorphism. By Morley the number is finite, $\aleph_0$, $\aleph_1$ or $2^{\aleph_0}$, so the open case is exactly $\aleph_1$ models when the continuum hypothesis fails; the $\omega$-stable case was proved in 1984, and there is a topological version for Polish group actions. Wikipedia lists the conjecture as unsolved. ([Vaught conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaught_conjecture))
- **Cherlin–Zilber algebraicity conjecture.** Every simple group of finite Morley rank is the group of $K$-rational points of an algebraic group over an algebraically closed field $K$. Tent writes that it "is confirmed for groups of Morley rank at most 3 and the general case is still wide open", and discusses sharply 2-transitive groups as possible counterexamples. ([Tent, arXiv:2606.18207](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.18207)) Altınel, Borovik and Cherlin (2008) showed that an infinite simple group of finite Morley rank is either algebraic over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 2 or has finite 2-rank. ([Cherlin–Zilber conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherlin%E2%80%93Zilber_conjecture))
- **Shelah's categoricity conjecture for abstract elementary classes (03C48).** There should be a Hanf number for categoricity: an AEC categorical in some sufficiently large cardinal is categorical in all larger ones, with the threshold depending only on its Löwenheim–Skolem number. Wikipedia states that as of 2014 the original conjecture remained open, with partial results under large-cardinal or amalgamation and tameness assumptions. ([Abstract elementary class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_elementary_class))

> [!warning] Contested
> Pillay's 2002 lecture notes mention that "a negative solution was recently announced by Knight" for Vaught's conjecture ([Pillay](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~apillay/pdf/lecturenotes_modeltheory.pdf)), while Wikipedia still lists the conjecture among unsolved problems ([Vaught conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaught_conjecture)). Wikipedia also presents the 2021 Pila–Shankar–Tsimerman completion of André–Oort as a claim. ([André–Oort conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9%E2%80%93Oort_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, First-order Model Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/): compactness, Löwenheim–Skolem, ultraproducts, stability, applications.
- **Learn:** [Pillay, Lecture notes in model theory (Notre Dame Math 411)](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~apillay/pdf/lecturenotes_modeltheory.pdf): ultraproducts, types, countable models, categoricity.
- **Primary:** [Tent, From the Cherlin–Zilber Conjecture via sharply 2-transitive groups to the Burnside problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18207): survey of the algebraicity conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Bhardwaj and van den Dries, On the Pila–Wilkie theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.14046): expository proof of the counting theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Tent and Ziegler, A Course in Model Theory (CUP, 2012)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139015417): graduate text through stability and classification.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx): official code list.
references.MSC 03Dxx - Computability and recursion:
## Reference
### Overview
Computability theory (the older name is recursive function theory; Soare proposed the rename in 1996) studies which functions on the natural numbers can be computed by an effective procedure and, beyond that, how unsolvable problems compare with one another. Its founding results are the equivalence of the 1930s models of computation (Church, Kleene, Turing) and Turing's 1936–37 proof that the halting problem is unsolvable; Turing (1939) then defined relative computability, and Post (1944) introduced many-one and one-one reducibility and posed what became Post's problem. ([SEP, Recursive Functions, §§1.6–1.8](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/)) Church and Turing independently proved the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable, and Gödel's incompleteness theorem gives that no complete computable axiomatization of first-order arithmetic exists. ([SEP, Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/))

A central subject of the field is the structure of the degrees of unsolvability: the Turing degrees $\mathcal D_T$, the computably enumerable (c.e.) degrees below $\mathbf 0'$, the jump operator, and definability hierarchies. Around this core sit algorithmic randomness, computable structure theory, higher recursion theory on ordinals and sets, and computable analysis. ([SEP, Recursive Functions, §3.5](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/); [MSC2020, 03D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Dxx))

### Scope
MSC2020 03D lists: 03D03 Thue and Post systems; 03D05 automata and formal grammars in connection with logical questions (see also 68Q45, 68Q70, 68R15); 03D10 Turing machines and related notions (see also 68Q04); 03D15 complexity of computation, including implicit computational complexity (see also 68Q15, 68Q17); 03D20 recursive functions and relations, subrecursive hierarchies; 03D25 recursively (computably) enumerable sets and degrees; 03D28 other Turing degree structures; 03D30 other degrees and reducibilities; 03D32 algorithmic randomness and dimension (see also 68Q30); 03D35 undecidability and degrees of sets of sentences; 03D40 word problems (see also 06B25, 08A50, 20F10, 68R15); 03D45 theory of numerations, effectively presented structures (see also 03C57; intuitionistic approaches in 03F55); 03D50 recursive equivalence types, isols; 03D55 hierarchies of computability and definability; 03D60 computability on ordinals, admissible sets; 03D65 higher-type and set recursion theory; 03D70 inductive definability; 03D75 abstract and axiomatic computability; 03D78 computation over the reals, computable analysis (constructive aspects in 03F60); 03D80 applications; 03D99. ([MSC2020, 03D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Dxx))

Neighbours, by the cross-references: machine models and complexity as computer science go to [MSC 68Qxx - Theory of computing](node:MSC%2068Qxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20computing) (68Q04, 68Q15, 68Q30, 68Q45); effectively presented structures border computable [model theory](node:Model%20Theory) in [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory) (03C57); constructive and intuitionistic treatments of numerations and the reals go to [MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics) (03F55, 03F60); word problems for lattices, algebras and groups are shared with 06B25, 08A50 and 20F10. ([MSC2020, 03D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Dxx))

### Key concepts
- **s-m-n theorem and Kleene's recursion theorem (03D20).** For all $n,m$ there is a primitive recursive $s^m_n$ with $\varphi_{s^m_n(i,\vec x)}(\vec y)\simeq\varphi^{n+m}_i(\vec x,\vec y)$. Recursion theorem (Kleene 1938): if $f$ is a total computable function, there is an index $n$ with $\varphi_n\simeq\varphi_{f(n)}$. ([SEP, Recursive Functions, Thms 3.1, 3.5](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/))
- **[Rice's Theorem](node:Rice's%20Theorem) (03D25).** Every non-trivial index set (a set of indices closed under $\varphi_i=\varphi_j$, neither empty nor everything) is undecidable (Rice 1953). The diagonal halting set $K=\{i:\varphi_i(i)\downarrow\}$ is computably enumerable but not decidable, and its complement is not c.e. ([SEP, Recursive Functions, Thm 3.4, Cor. 3.1](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/))
- **Post's problem and the priority method (03D25).** Post asked whether there is a c.e. degree $\mathbf a$ with $\mathbf 0<_T\mathbf a<_T\mathbf 0'$. Friedberg (1957) and Muchnik (1956) independently answered yes: there are c.e. sets $A,B$ with $A\not\le_T B$ and $B\not\le_T A$. Their proof introduced the priority (injury) method, in which requirements $R_0,R_1,\dots$ are ranked and actions for higher-priority requirements may injure lower ones. ([SEP, Recursive Functions, §3.5.2, Thm 3.8](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/))
- **Structure of the degrees (03D25, 03D28).** The jump $A'=\{n:\varphi^A_n(n)\downarrow\}$ satisfies $\mathbf a<\mathbf a'$. There are $2^{\aleph_0}$ Turing degrees, each degree has only countably many predecessors, and $\mathcal D_T$ is a join-semilattice that is not a lattice. Sacks (1964): the c.e. degrees are dense. Lachlan (1966, the non-diamond theorem): no pair of c.e. degrees has meet $\mathbf 0$ and join $\mathbf 0'$. ([Wikipedia, Turing degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_degree); [SEP, Recursive Functions, §3.5.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/))
- **Undecidability of the degree theories (03D35, 03D28).** The first-order theory of $(\mathcal D_T,\le_T)$ is undecidable (Lachlan 1968), and Simpson (1977) showed it is many-one equivalent to true second-order arithmetic; the theory of the c.e. degrees is many-one equivalent to true first-order arithmetic (Harrington and Slaman; Nies, Shore and Slaman 1998). ([SEP, Recursive Functions, §3.5.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/); [Wikipedia, Turing degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_degree))
- **Arithmetical hierarchy and Post's theorem (03D55).** A set is $\Sigma^0_n$ if it is defined by a prenex formula beginning with an existential block and having $n$ alternating quantifier blocks over a bounded-quantifier matrix. Post's theorem: $B$ is $\Sigma^0_{n+1}$ iff $B$ is c.e. relative to $\emptyset^{(n)}$, and $\emptyset^{(n)}$ is $\Sigma^0_n$-complete for $n>0$. ([Wikipedia, Post's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post%27s_theorem))
- [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory), [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines) and [Lambda Calculus](node:Lambda%20Calculus) are the equivalent models behind 03D10 and 03D20; [Algorithmic Randomness](node:Algorithmic%20Randomness) and [Kolmogorov Complexity](node:Kolmogorov%20Complexity) are 03D32; [Automata and Formal Languages](node:Automata%20and%20Formal%20Languages) in connection with logic is 03D05, and undecidability of sets of sentences (03D35) is the setting of [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems). ([MSC2020, 03D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Dxx); [SEP, Computability and Complexity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/computability/))

### History
Recursive definitions go back to Dedekind (1888) and Peano (1889); Skolem (1923) wrote the first work devoted to recursive definability, Gödel used primitive recursion in 1931 and general recursive functions in 1934, and Church, Kleene and Turing gave equivalent analyses of computability in 1936–37. Kleene proved the recursion theorem (1938) and a hierarchy theorem by diagonalization (1943), and his papers of 1943 and 1955 contain the definitions of the arithmetical and analytical hierarchies. ([SEP, Recursive Functions, §§1.2–1.8](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/)) Post's 1944 question led to the Friedberg–Muchnik theorem and the priority method in 1956–57, and to Sacks's density theorem in 1964. ([SEP, Recursive Functions, §3.5.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/)) A modern graduate text is Soare's *Turing Computability* (Springer, 2016). ([Crossref, Soare](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-31933-4))

### Open problems
- **Rigidity of the Turing degrees.** Does $\mathcal D_T$ have a non-trivial automorphism? The SEP entry (2020 revision) states that this "remains a significant open problem in computability theory." ([SEP, Recursive Functions, Question 3.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/))
- **Martin's conjecture.** Work in ZF + DC + AD; call $f:2^\omega\to 2^\omega$ Turing invariant if $x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)$, and say a property holds almost everywhere if it holds on a cone of Turing degrees. Part I: if $f$ is not increasing a.e., it is constant a.e. Part II: $\le_m$ (a.e. reducibility) prewellorders the Turing-invariant functions that are increasing a.e., and if $f$ has rank $\alpha$ then $f'$ has rank $\alpha+1$. Marks, Slaman and Steel call it "one of the oldest and deepest open problems on the global structure of the Turing degrees" and say it "remains open". Known cases: Slaman and Steel proved Part I, and Steel proved Part II, for uniformly Turing-invariant functions; Lachlan showed there is no uniform degree-invariant solution to Post's problem. ([Marks–Slaman–Steel, arXiv 1109.1875](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1109.1875))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, Recursive Functions](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/): history, s-m-n and recursion theorems, Rice's theorem, Post's problem, priority method, degree theory.
- **Learn:** [Cambridge, Computation Theory (Part IB, 2025–26)](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2526/CompTheory/): register and Turing machines, universal machines, halting undecidability, partial recursive functions, lambda calculus.
- **Primary:** [Marks, Slaman and Steel, Martin's conjecture, arithmetic equivalence, and countable Borel equivalence relations (arXiv 1109.1875)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1109.1875): research paper and survey of Martin's conjecture and its partial results.
- **Further reading:** [Soare, Turing Computability (Springer, 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-31933-4): graduate text on Turing degrees, c.e. sets and the priority method.
references.MSC 03Exx - Set theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Set theory studies sets, membership, and the sizes and definable structure of infinite collections. ZFC serves as a common foundation for mathematics, and the research area investigates what ZFC does and does not decide, which additional axioms (large cardinals, forcing axioms, determinacy) settle those questions, and how such axioms compare in consistency strength. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [Marks, Berkeley notes](https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/notes/set_theory_notes_4.pdf))

Two methods dominate independence work. Large cardinal hypotheses raise consistency strength: an inaccessible $\kappa$ gives a model $V_\kappa$ of ZFC, so ZFC cannot prove an inaccessible exists. Forcing and inner models instead produce models of ZFC with different properties, starting from Gödel's constructible universe $L$ (1938) and Cohen's forcing (1963). Natural theories have empirically been found to be linearly, indeed well, ordered by consistency strength. ([Marks](https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/notes/set_theory_notes_4.pdf); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))

### Scope
MSC2020 03E lists: partition relations (03E02); ordered sets and their cofinalities, pcf theory (03E04); other combinatorial set theory (03E05); ordinal and cardinal numbers (03E10); descriptive set theory (03E15, see also 28A05, 54H05); cardinal characteristics of the continuum (03E17); other classical set theory, including functions, relations, and set algebra (03E20); the axiom of choice and related propositions (03E25); axiomatics of classical set theory and its fragments (03E30); consistency and independence results (03E35); other aspects of forcing and Boolean-valued models (03E40); inner models, including constructibility, ordinal definability, and core models (03E45); other notions of set-theoretic definability (03E47); the continuum hypothesis and Martin's axiom (03E50); large cardinals (03E55); generic absoluteness and forcing axioms (03E57); determinacy principles (03E60); other set-theoretic hypotheses and axioms (03E65); nonclassical and second-order set theories (03E70); fuzzy sets (03E72); applications of set theory (03E75). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Exx))

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory) ([Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory)) studies models of arbitrary first-order theories, while 03E studies models of set theory itself; [MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics) measures strength by proofs and ordinals rather than by large cardinals; [MSC 03Dxx - Computability and recursion theory](node:MSC%2003Dxx%20-%20Computability%20and%20recursion%20theory) concerns computable and arithmetical definability; [MSC 06Axx - Ordered sets](node:MSC%2006Axx%20-%20Ordered%20sets) covers order theory without the set-theoretic cofinality machinery of 03E04. Descriptive set theory is shared with classical measure theory (28A05) and topology (54H05), per the MSC cross-references. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Exx))

### Key concepts
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): ZF consists of first-order axioms, with Separation and Replacement as schemas; ZFC adds the axiom of choice. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))
- [Cardinality](node:Cardinality) and cardinal arithmetic (03E04, 03E10): the cofinality $\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)$ is the least $\lambda$ such that $\kappa$ is a union of $\lambda$ smaller ordinals. Shelah (1989) proved in ZFC, by pcf theory, that if $\aleph_\omega$ is a strong limit then $2^{\aleph_\omega}<\aleph_{\omega_4}$. For a set $A$ of regular cardinals, $\mathrm{pcf}(A)$ is the set of cofinalities $\mathrm{cf}(\prod A/D)$ over ultrafilters $D$ on $A$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [Wikipedia: pcf theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCF_theory))
- **Singular Cardinal Hypothesis (SCH):** it determines exponentiation of singular cardinals modulo regular ones and follows from GCH. Silver's theorem gives SCH for all singulars if it holds at countable cofinality. Solovay proved it holds above a supercompact cardinal. Magidor (1977) made GCH first fail at $\aleph_\omega$, and large cardinals beyond measurability are needed for SCH to fail. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))
- [Axiom of Choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice) and constructibility (03E25, 03E45): Gödel showed that inside any model of ZF the constructible universe $L$ satisfies AC and the CH (indeed GCH), so these are consistent relative to ZF. Cohen's forcing gave the consistency of $\neg$CH; together these show the CH is independent of ZFC. ([Marks](https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/notes/set_theory_notes_4.pdf); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))
- Descriptive set theory and determinacy (03E15, 03E60): the study of definable sets of reals. Martin proved in ZFC that every Borel set is determined. Martin and Steel (1989) proved, assuming infinitely many Woodin cardinals, that every projective set is determined (PD), and Woodin showed infinitely many Woodin cardinals equiconsistent with $\mathrm{AD}^{L(\mathbb R)}$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))
- Large cardinals (03E55): inaccessible, measurable (Ulam, 1930), Woodin, and supercompact cardinals, with Woodin cardinals between strong and supercompact. They form a linear hierarchy of increasing consistency strength. ZF + DC + "all sets of reals are Lebesgue measurable" (see [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory)) is equiconsistent with an inaccessible; a saturated ideal on $\omega_1$ is equiconsistent with a Woodin cardinal. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [Marks](https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/notes/set_theory_notes_4.pdf))
- Cardinal characteristics (03E17): $\mathrm{add}(I)$, $\mathrm{cov}(I)$, $\mathrm{non}(I)$, $\mathrm{cof}(I)$ are defined for a proper ideal $I$ on an infinite set containing the finite sets; for the meagre ideal $\mathcal M$ and null ideal $\mathcal N$ on the reals these, together with $\mathfrak b\le\mathfrak d$, all lie between $\aleph_1$ and $2^{\aleph_0}$. Cichoń's diagram for the null and meagre ideals records the ZFC inequalities, including $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal M)=\min\{\mathfrak b,\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal M)\}$ and $\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal M)=\max\{\mathfrak d,\mathrm{non}(\mathcal M)\}$.
