When $2^{\aleph_0}\le\aleph_2$, every assignment of $\aleph_1,\aleph_2$ respecting them is consistent, and Goldstern, Kellner, Mejía and Shelah made all entries different except the two determined ones. ([Wikipedia: Cichoń's diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicho%C5%84%27s_diagram))
- Forcing axioms (03E50, 03E57): MA follows from CH and matters only when CH fails. PFA and Martin's Maximum extend it to proper and to stationary-set-preserving forcings. MM (Foreman–Magidor–Shelah, 1988) is consistent relative to a supercompact cardinal and implies $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [Wikipedia: Martin's maximum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin%27s_maximum))
- [Ramsey Theory](node:Ramsey%20Theory): partition relations (03E02) include higher analogues of Ramsey's theorem; for example an uncountable $\kappa$ is weakly compact if every $f:[\kappa]^2\to 2$ has a homogeneous set of size $\kappa$, and weakly compact cardinals are strongly inaccessible. Related: by [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems), if ZFC is consistent then none of these large cardinals can be proved to exist from ZFC. ([Marks](https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/notes/set_theory_notes_4.pdf))

### History
Set theory began with Cantor's 1874 proof that $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb R$ have different cardinalities. Gödel's $L$ (1938) and Cohen's forcing (1963) established independence of the CH. ([Marks](https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/notes/set_theory_notes_4.pdf); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/)) Inner model theory grew from $L$: Scott showed $L$ has no measurable cardinal, prompting a search for canonical $L$-like models of larger cardinals. Work of Steel and Woodin linked determinacy and large cardinals, showing that $\mathrm{HOD}^{L(\mathbb R)}$ is fine-structural. ([Trang, survey](https://sites.math.unt.edu/~ntrang/IMTre.pdf); [Wikipedia: inner model theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_model_theory)) Shelah's pcf theory (1989 bound) and the forcing axioms of the 1980s set much of the modern agenda. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [Wikipedia: Martin's maximum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin%27s_maximum))

### Open problems
- **Continuum hypothesis.** "To this day, the CH remains open" in the sense that ZFC does not settle it. The search for new axioms (large cardinals, forcing axioms) to decide it is a central theme. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))
- **pcf conjecture.** The conjecture that $|\mathrm{pcf}(A)|=|A|$ for every set $A$ of regular cardinals with $|A|<\min A$ is unsolved. It would improve Shelah's bound to $2^{\aleph_\omega}<\aleph_{\omega_1}$ when $\aleph_\omega$ is a strong limit. ([Wikipedia: pcf theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCF_theory))
- **Consistency strength of PFA.** Whether PFA is equiconsistent with a supercompact cardinal is described as one of the most longstanding open problems in set theory; a supercompact is a known upper bound. ([Marks](https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/notes/set_theory_notes_4.pdf); [Trang](https://sites.math.unt.edu/~ntrang/IMTre.pdf))
- **Inner model problem for supercompacts and Ultimate-$L$.** Woodin argues that solving the inner model problem for one supercompact cardinal would yield an ultimate version of $L$, and that current approaches would need fundamental revision. His Ultimate-$L$ conjecture remains open: for extendible $\delta$, there is a weak extender model for the supercompactness of $\delta$ that is contained in HOD and satisfies "$V=$ Ultimate-$L$". Trang lists iterability of short-extender models and fine structure for HOD of $\mathrm{AD}^+$ models among other open questions. ([Woodin, BSL 2017](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-symbolic-logic/article/in-search-of-ultimatel-the-19th-midrasha-mathematicae-lectures/BDBD4F26AC73B54AA7CD76CD5808B957); [Trang](https://sites.math.unt.edu/~ntrang/IMTre.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/): ZFC, cardinal arithmetic, descriptive set theory, forcing, large cardinals, forcing axioms.
- **Learn:** [Marks, Set Theory (Berkeley notes)](https://math.berkeley.edu/~marks/notes/set_theory_notes_4.pdf): ordinals to $L$ and forcing, with optional sections on SCH, measurables, and Goodstein.
- **Primary:** [Woodin, "In search of Ultimate-L", Bull. Symb. Logic 23 (2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-symbolic-logic/article/in-search-of-ultimatel-the-19th-midrasha-mathematicae-lectures/BDBD4F26AC73B54AA7CD76CD5808B957): the inner model problem for supercompacts.
- **Primary:** [Trang, A brief account of recent developments in inner model theory](https://sites.math.unt.edu/~ntrang/IMTre.pdf): survey of open problems in inner model theory and PFA.
- **Further reading:** [Jech, Set Theory, 3rd ed., Springer (2003)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/3-540-44761-X) and [Kanamori, The Higher Infinite, 2nd ed., Springer Monographs in Mathematics (2003)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-88867-3): standard graduate references (editions as listed in the [SEP bibliography](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/)).
references.MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructiv:
## Reference
### Overview
[Proof theory](node:Proof%20Theory) treats formal derivations as mathematical objects. Its central themes are cut elimination and normal forms, the measurement of the strength of theories by ordinals, consistency proofs relative to restricted (finitist or constructive) means, and the extraction of computational content from proofs. Gentzen's cut-elimination theorem (Hauptsatz) states that a sequent derivable in his calculus is derivable without the cut rule, at a possibly hyper-exponential cost in proof size; for Peano arithmetic (PA) full cut elimination fails because induction axioms have unbounded complexity. ([SEP, Proof Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/proof-theory/))

Gödel's second incompleteness theorem refutes the general ambitions of Hilbert's program, and much later proof theory replaces "finitist consistency proof" by relative consistency proofs and exact calibrations of strength; the search for minimal subsystems sufficient for given theorems led to the research program of reverse mathematics. ([SEP, Proof Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/proof-theory/)) Constructive mathematics, the second half of 03F, reads "there exists" as "we can construct" and uses intuitionistic logic; its main varieties are Brouwer's intuitionism, Markov's recursive mathematics, Bishop's constructive analysis, and Martin-Löf type theory. ([SEP, Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/))

### Scope
MSC2020 03F lists: 03F03 proof theory in general (including proof-theoretic semantics); 03F05 cut-elimination and normal-form theorems; 03F07 structure of proofs; 03F10 functionals in proof theory; 03F15 recursive ordinals and ordinal notations; 03F20 complexity of proofs; 03F25 relative consistency and interpretations; 03F30 first-order arithmetic and fragments; 03F35 second- and higher-order arithmetic and fragments; 03F40 Gödel numberings and issues of incompleteness; 03F45 provability logics and related algebras (e.g., diagonalizable algebras); 03F50 metamathematics of constructive systems; 03F52 proof-theoretic aspects of linear logic and other substructural logics; 03F55 intuitionistic mathematics; 03F60 constructive and recursive analysis; 03F65 other constructive mathematics; 03F99. ([MSC2020, 03F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Fxx))

Neighbours named by the entry's cross-references: 03F35 points to 03B30 and 03F45 to 03B45 in [MSC 03Bxx - General logic](node:MSC%2003Bxx%20-%20General%20logic); 03F45 also points to 03G25 in [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic) and 06E25 in [MSC 06Exx - Boolean algebras (Boolean rings)](node:MSC%2006Exx%20-%20Boolean%20algebras%20%28Boolean%20rings%29); 03F60 (constructive and recursive analysis) points to 03B30, to 03D45 and 03D78 in [MSC 03Dxx - Computability and recursion theory](node:MSC%2003Dxx%20-%20Computability%20and%20recursion%20theory), and to 26E40, 46S30 and 47S30; 03F65 points to 03D45; 03F52 points to 03B47. ([MSC2020, 03F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Fxx)) All of these sit inside [MSC 03 - Mathematical logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003%20-%20Mathematical%20logic%20and%20foundations).

### Key concepts
- **Gentzen's consistency proof and $\varepsilon_0$ (03F05, 03F15, 03F30).** Gentzen proved that the consistency of first-order PA is provable in primitive recursive arithmetic (PRA) plus quantifier-free transfinite induction up to $\varepsilon_0$ (published 1936). ([Wikipedia, Gentzen's consistency proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentzen%27s_consistency_proof)) PA proves transfinite induction up to each $\omega_n$ ($\omega_0=0$, $\omega_{n+1}=\omega^{\omega_n}$), whose supremum is $\varepsilon_0$, but does not prove it over the whole notation system for $\varepsilon_0$, a second independence result for PA of a different nature from Gödel's ([Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems)); Gentzen's 1943 paper showed that the $\varepsilon_0$ bound is best possible. ([Rathjen, AMS Notices 2023](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/203713/1/AMSNotices-Ordinalanalysis_kurz.pdf); [SEP, Proof Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/proof-theory/)) Combined with Goodstein's 1944 theorem that every Goodstein sequence terminates, this yields that termination of primitive recursive Goodstein sequences is unprovable in PA; Kirby and Paris (1982) showed the same for special Goodstein sequences. ([Rathjen, AMS Notices 2023](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/203713/1/AMSNotices-Ordinalanalysis_kurz.pdf))
- **Proof-theoretic ordinals (03F15, 03F35).** The proof-theoretic ordinal of a theory $T$ is the supremum of the order types of recursive well-orderings that $T$ proves well-founded. ([Wikipedia, Ordinal analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_analysis)) Standard values: $|\mathrm{PA}|=|\mathrm{ACA}_0|=\varepsilon_0$, $|\mathrm{RCA}_0|=|\mathrm{WKL}_0|=\omega^\omega$, $|\mathrm{ATR}_0|=\Gamma_0$, and the ordinal of $\mathrm{ID}_1$ is the Bachmann–Howard ordinal, written $\psi_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega+1})$. ([Rathjen, AMS Notices 2023](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/203713/1/AMSNotices-Ordinalanalysis_kurz.pdf); [Wikipedia, Ordinal analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_analysis)) Feferman and Schütte independently (1964) identified $\Gamma_0$ as the least upper bound of the predicative hierarchy, the least ordinal unreachable by certain predicative means; Howard (1972) gave the first ordinal analysis of $\mathrm{ID}_1$; Takeuti's 1967 consistency proof for $\Pi^1_1$-comprehension was the first ordinal analysis of an impredicative theory. ([SEP, Proof Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/proof-theory/))
- **Reverse mathematics and the "Big Five" (03F35).** Founded by Harvey Friedman and developed by Stephen Simpson, reverse mathematics proves theorems equivalent to subsystems of second-order arithmetic over the base theory $\mathrm{RCA}_0$ (Robinson arithmetic, $\Sigma^0_1$ induction, $\Delta^0_1$ comprehension). Over $\mathrm{RCA}_0$: $\mathrm{WKL}_0$ is equivalent to Heine–Borel for $[0,1]$ and the Brouwer fixed point theorem; $\mathrm{ACA}_0$ to Bolzano–Weierstrass and Kőnig's lemma; $\mathrm{ATR}_0$ to comparability of countable well-orderings and the perfect set theorem; $\Pi^1_1\text{-}\mathrm{CA}_0$ to the Cantor–Bendixson theorem. ([Wikipedia, Reverse mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_mathematics)) Friedman, Robertson and Seymour showed that the graph minor theorem ([MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory)) is not provable in $\Pi^1_1\text{-}\mathrm{CA}_0$, a consequence of the ordinal analysis of that system. ([Rathjen, AMS Notices 2023](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/203713/1/AMSNotices-Ordinalanalysis_kurz.pdf))
- **Proof complexity (03F20).** Cook and Reckhow (1979) defined a propositional proof system as a polynomial-time checkable proof format for tautologies and showed that a polynomially bounded proof system exists if and only if $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$, linking the subject to [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory) and [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP). Haken (1985) proved exponential lower bounds for resolution proofs of the pigeonhole principle; Ajtai (1988) proved superpolynomial lower bounds for constant-depth Frege systems, later improved to exponential. ([Wikipedia, Proof complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity))
- **Functional interpretations and proof mining (03F10, 03F50).** Gödel's Dialectica interpretation (1958) maps each formula $A$ of Heyting arithmetic to a quantifier-free $A_D(x;y)$, read as $\exists x\forall y\,A_D(x;y)$, and its soundness theorem gives, for every HA-proof of $A$, closed terms $t$ of System T with $T\vdash A_D(t;y)$; with the negative translation this reduces the consistency of PA to that of T. ([Wikipedia, Dialectica interpretation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialectica_interpretation); [SEP, Proof Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/proof-theory/)) Proof mining is a research program that analyses formalized proofs, especially in analysis, to obtain explicit bounds or rates of convergence from proofs that appear nonconstructive; Kohlenbach's *Applied Proof Theory: Proof Interpretations and Their Use in Mathematics* (Springer, 2008) is its monograph. ([Wikipedia, Proof mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_mining); [Crossref, Kohlenbach](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-77533-1))
- **Provability logic (03F45).** GL is the modal logic K plus Löb's axiom $\Box(\Box A\to A)\to\Box A$. Solovay's arithmetical completeness theorem (1976): $\mathrm{GL}\vdash A$ iff $\mathrm{PA}\vdash f(A)$ for every arithmetical realization $f$ that reads $\Box$ as PA-provability. GL is complete for finite transitive irreflexive trees, and its decision problem is PSPACE-complete. ([SEP, Provability Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-provability/))
- **Constructive analysis (03F55, 03F60).** Bishop's *Foundations of Constructive Analysis* (1967) developed much of analysis, including Stone–Weierstrass, Hahn–Banach and the [spectral theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem), with intuitionistic logic and without LPO; under Brouwer's continuity principles every map $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is pointwise continuous, while in recursive mathematics Specker's theorem gives a strictly increasing sequence of rationals in $[0,1]$ such that every real number is bounded away from almost all of its terms. ([SEP, Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/)) The proofs-as-programs side of this connects to [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory) and [Lambda Calculus](node:Lambda%20Calculus).

### History
Hilbert turned foundational questions into questions about formal systems, and his second problem asked for a direct consistency proof of analysis; Gentzen obtained a first consistency proof for PA in 1935, whose original version was published only in 1974, and his second published proof appeared in 1938, and in 1938 wrote that a consistency proof for analysis was "still outstanding". ([SEP, Proof Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/proof-theory/)) Takeuti formulated his fundamental conjecture (a Hauptsatz for a sequent calculus encompassing second-order arithmetic $Z_2$) in the late 1940s and in 1967 analysed $\Pi^1_1$-comprehension with ordinal diagrams. ([Rathjen, AMS Notices 2023](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/203713/1/AMSNotices-Ordinalanalysis_kurz.pdf)) Friedman's reverse mathematics dates from his 1974–1976 papers, with Simpson's *Subsystems of Second Order Arithmetic* (1999; 2nd ed. 2009) as the standard reference. ([Wikipedia, Reverse mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_mathematics); [Crossref, Simpson](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511581007))

### Open problems
- **Ordinal analysis of full second-order arithmetic.** SEP states that "the goal of giving an ordinal analysis of full second order arithmetic has not been attained yet". ([SEP, Proof Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/proof-theory/)) Rathjen reports that the current state of the art handles subsystems of $Z_2$ with $\Pi^1_2$-comprehension (work of Arai and Rathjen) and calls $\Pi^1_3$-comprehension "the next barrier". ([Rathjen, AMS Notices 2023](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/203713/1/AMSNotices-Ordinalanalysis_kurz.pdf))
- **Frege lower bounds.** "It is a long-standing open problem to derive a nontrivial lower bound for the Frege system"; whether any p-bounded or p-optimal propositional proof system exists is likewise open. ([Wikipedia, Proof complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity))
- **Provability logic of weak arithmetic.** Whether GL is the provability logic of $I\Delta_0+\Omega_1$ is "still an open question", possibly tied to open problems in complexity theory. ([SEP, Provability Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-provability/))
- **Fan theorem and uniform continuity.** Finding a form of the fan theorem equivalent over BISH to the uniform continuity theorem for $[0,1]$ is called "a major open problem" in constructive reverse mathematics. ([SEP, Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, Proof Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/proof-theory/): Hilbert's program, Gentzen, ordinal analysis, functional interpretations.
- **Reference:** [SEP, Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/): varieties of constructivism, BISH, constructive reverse mathematics.
- **Learn:** [Freund, Unprovability in Mathematics: A First Course on Ordinal Analysis (arXiv 2109.06258)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06258): notes for 12 lectures, building to a complete proof that Kruskal's theorem for binary trees is unprovable in conservative extensions of PA.
- **Primary:** [Rathjen, The Art of Measuring the Strength of Theories (Notices AMS, 2023)](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/203713/1/AMSNotices-Ordinalanalysis_kurz.pdf): survey of ordinal analysis, independence results and the state of the art.
- **Further reading:** [Simpson, Subsystems of Second Order Arithmetic (CUP, 2nd ed. 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511581007): the monograph of reverse mathematics.
- **Further reading:** [Kohlenbach, Applied Proof Theory: Proof Interpretations and Their Use in Mathematics (Springer, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-77533-1): proof interpretations and proof mining.
references.MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic:
## Reference
### Overview
Algebraic logic studies logical systems through algebras: each logic is matched with a class of algebras that models it, such as Boolean algebras (via the Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra) for classical sentential logic, Heyting algebras for intuitionistic propositional logic, MV-algebras for Łukasiewicz logic, modal algebras for modal logic K, cylindric algebras for first-order logic with equality, and relation algebras for [set theory](node:Set%20Theory). ([Wikipedia: Algebraic logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_logic)) Abstract algebraic logic studies the process of algebraization itself; its Leibniz hierarchy classifies logics by the behaviour of the Leibniz operator. ([SEP: Algebraic Propositional Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-algebraic-propositional/))

The basic method is Lindenbaum–Tarski: for a theory $T$, the relation $\varphi\,\theta(T)\,\psi\iff(\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi)\in T$ is a congruence on the formula algebra, and the quotient is a reduced matrix whose algebra lies in the intended class; this yields algebraic completeness theorems. ([SEP: Algebraic Propositional Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-algebraic-propositional/)) In the classical case the classes $[A]$ of logically equivalent formulas form a Boolean algebra under $[A]\cdot[B]=[A\wedge B]$, $[A]+[B]=[A\vee B]$ and $\overline{[A]}=[\neg A]$, after checking that these operations do not depend on representatives. ([Lawson, A First Course in Logic](https://www.macs.hw.ac.uk/~markl/teaching/LOGIC/LOGIC-NOTES.pdf))

### Scope
Within [MSC 03 - Mathematical logic and foundations](node:MSC%2003%20-%20Mathematical%20logic%20and%20foundations), MSC2020 03Gxx has the codes 03G05 logical aspects of Boolean algebras, 03G10 logical aspects of lattices and related structures, 03G12 quantum logic, 03G15 cylindric and polyadic algebras and relation algebras, 03G20 logical aspects of Łukasiewicz and Post algebras, 03G25 other algebras related to logic, 03G27 abstract algebraic logic, 03G30 categorical logic and topoi, and 03G99. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msnhtml/msc2020.pdf))

Neighbouring codes, from the cross-references in MSC2020 ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msnhtml/msc2020.pdf)):
- 03G05 points to 06Exx (Boolean algebras), and 06E15 covers Stone spaces; the structure theory of Boolean algebras sits in [MSC 06Exx - Boolean algebras (Boolean rings)](node:MSC%2006Exx%20-%20Boolean%20algebras%20%28Boolean%20rings%29).
- 03G10 points to 06Bxx (lattices); see [MSC 06Bxx - Lattices](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices). Heyting algebras (06D20), Post algebras (06D25) and MV-algebras (06D35) as lattice-theoretic objects are in [MSC 06Dxx - Distributive lattices](node:MSC%2006Dxx%20-%20Distributive%20lattices).
- 03G30 points to 18B25 (topoi) and 18C05, 18C10; see [MSC 18Bxx - Special categories](node:MSC%2018Bxx%20-%20Special%20categories) and [MSC 18Cxx - Categories and theories](node:MSC%2018Cxx%20-%20Categories%20and%20theories).
- Syntax and semantics of particular logics, beginning with 03B05 classical propositional logic, are in [MSC 03Bxx - General logic](node:MSC%2003Bxx%20-%20General%20logic); model theory is 03Cxx, see [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory).

### Key concepts
- **Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra and [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic).** Classical sentential logic corresponds to Boolean algebras via the Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_logic))
- **Stone duality.** Every Boolean algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of clopen subsets of its Stone space (the space of its ultrafilters, compact, totally disconnected and Hausdorff), via $b\mapsto\{U: b\in U\}$; this gives a contravariant equivalence between Boolean algebras and Stone spaces. Stone proved it in 1936, and it is equivalent to the Boolean prime ideal theorem. ([Wikipedia: Stone representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%27s_representation_theorem_for_Boolean_algebras)) Compare [Topological Spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces).
- **Heyting algebras.** A bounded lattice with $c\wedge a\le b\iff c\le a\to b$; a formula is intuitionistically provable iff it takes the top value in every Heyting algebra, the open sets of any space form a complete Heyting algebra, and Boolean algebras are the Heyting algebras with $\neg\neg a=a$. The equational theory is decidable (Kripke 1965) and PSPACE-complete (Statman 1979). ([Wikipedia: Heyting algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heyting_algebra))
- **MV-algebras and Chang's completeness theorem.** MV-algebras $(A,\oplus,\neg,0)$ form a variety containing all Boolean algebras; the standard model is $[0,1]$ with $x\oplus y=\min(x+y,1)$, $\neg x=1-x$, and Chang's theorem says an equation holding in $[0,1]$ holds in every MV-algebra, so MV-algebras characterize infinite-valued Łukasiewicz logic. Mundici related them to lattice-ordered abelian groups with strong unit. ([Wikipedia: MV-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV-algebra))
- **Cylindric algebras and [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic).** Tarski's cylindric algebras of dimension $\alpha$ are Boolean algebras with cylindrifications $c_\kappa$ (modelling $\exists x_\kappa$) and diagonal elements $d_{\kappa\lambda}$ (modelling $x_\kappa=x_\lambda$), algebraizing first-order logic with equality; not every cylindric algebra is representable as a cylindric set algebra. ([Wikipedia: Cylindric algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylindric_algebra))
- **Relation algebras.** Residuated Boolean algebras with converse, axiomatized equationally by Tarski. Representable relation algebras form a variety (Tarski 1955) that is a proper subvariety of RA (Lyndon 1950) and has no finite axiomatization (Monk 1964). RA expresses exactly the first-order formulas with at most three variables, enough for Tarski and Givant's variable-free set theory, so [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems) apply to it. ([Wikipedia: Relation algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relation_algebra))
- **Undecidability of representability.** Hirsch and Hodkinson proved that it is undecidable whether a finite relation algebra is representable, confirming a conjecture of Maddux, by reducing a tiling problem; Hodkinson extended this to finite $n$-dimensional cylindric, diagonal-free cylindric, polyadic and polyadic equality algebras for every finite $n\ge3$. ([Hodkinson, Imperial College](https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~imh/frames_website/tiling.html); [Crossref: Trans. AMS 353](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-99-02264-3)) See [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory).
- **Algebraizable logics and the Leibniz hierarchy.** Blok and Pigozzi (1989) call a logic algebraizable if a class $K$ is an algebraic semantics via defining equations and equivalence formulas $\Delta(p,q)$ that recover identity in each $A\in K$; protoalgebraic logics are those whose Leibniz operator is monotone, equivalential logics have a set $\Delta$ defining the Leibniz congruence, and for finitely algebraizable logics with the deduction–detachment property, Craig interpolation is equivalent to amalgamation in the algebraic counterpart. ([SEP: Algebraic Propositional Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-algebraic-propositional/))
- **Categorical logic and topoi.** An elementary topos has finite limits, is cartesian closed and has a subobject classifier; its internal logic is intuitionistic higher-order logic, and Boolean toposes correspond to classical higher-order logic. ([nLab: topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topos); [nLab: internal logic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/internal+logic)) See [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory) and [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory).

### History
Leibniz's memoranda of the 1680s are often cited as the earliest algebraic logic; modern algebraic logic began with Boole and De Morgan in 1847, continued with Peirce and Schröder's calculus of relations, and Tarski revived interest in relations with his 1941 essay "On the Calculus of Relations", which initiated abstract algebraic logic with relation algebras; Tarski also invented cylindric algebras and co-discovered the Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_logic)) Blok and Pigozzi's memoir *Algebraizable logics* appeared in 1989 as Memoirs of the AMS 77, no. 396. ([Crossref: Blok & Pigozzi](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0396)) Hirsch and Hodkinson's monograph *Relation Algebras by Games* appeared in 2002 (North-Holland, Studies in Logic vol. 147). ([Hodkinson, Imperial College](https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~imh/frames_website/rabook.html))

### Open problems
- **Flexible Atom Conjecture.** Every finite integral relation algebra with a flexible atom (one in no forbidden diversity cycle) should be representable over a finite set. Jipsen, Maddux and Tuza showed that finite symmetric integral relation algebras in which every diversity atom is flexible are finitely representable, and Alm and Levet give finite representations for eleven further algebras and close with several open problems. ([Alm & Levet](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.06781))
- **Varieties versus quasivarieties.** For many finitary, finitely algebraizable logics, why the algebraic counterpart is a variety rather than merely a quasivariety is described as "still an open area of research", and the interplay between the Leibniz and Frege hierarchies is a current research direction. ([SEP: Algebraic Propositional Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-algebraic-propositional/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Algebraic Propositional Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-algebraic-propositional/): Lindenbaum–Tarski method, algebraizability, Leibniz hierarchy and bridge theorems.
- **Reference:** [Algebraic logic (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_logic): table of logic–algebra correspondences and history.
- **Learn:** [M. V. Lawson, A First Course in Logic (Heriot-Watt)](https://www.macs.hw.ac.uk/~markl/teaching/LOGIC/LOGIC-NOTES.pdf): Boolean algebras and the Lindenbaum algebra of propositional logic.
- **Primary:** [Alm & Levet, Directed Ramsey and Anti-Ramsey Schemes and the Flexible Atom Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.06781): current work on finite representability of relation algebras.
- **Primary:** [Hirsch & Hodkinson, Representability is not decidable for finite relation algebras, Trans. AMS 353](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-99-02264-3): the undecidability theorem.
- **Primary:** [MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msnhtml/msc2020.pdf): the official 03G codes and cross-references.
- **Further reading:** [Blok & Pigozzi, Algebraizable logics, Mem. AMS 396 (1989)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0396) and [Hirsch & Hodkinson, Relation Algebras by Games (2002)](https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~imh/frames_website/rabook.html): the founding memoir of abstract algebraic logic and the monograph on representability.
references.MSC 03Hxx - Nonstandard models:
## Reference
### Overview
Nonstandard models are structures that satisfy the same first-order theory as an intended "standard" structure (the reals, the natural numbers, a universe of sets) but contain additional, nonstandard elements: infinite natural numbers, infinitesimal reals. Abraham Robinson introduced nonstandard analysis in the early 1960s (a 1961 article and the 1966 book *Non-standard Analysis*), giving a rigorous treatment of infinitesimals through model theory. ([Wikipedia: Nonstandard analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis)) The two main strands of the area are this analytic one, in which a nonstandard extension of a mathematical universe is used as a tool to prove standard theorems, and the study of nonstandard models of arithmetic for their own sake, which goes back to Skolem's 1934 construction. ([Wikipedia: Non-standard model of arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-standard_model_of_arithmetic))

The method works because of two properties of a nonstandard extension $X\mapsto {}^*X$: *transfer* (a bounded first-order statement holds of standard objects exactly when it holds of their extensions) and *saturation* (for example, a decreasing sequence of nonempty internal sets has nonempty intersection). Bounded quantification with an internal bound never ranges over external sets such as the set of infinitesimals or of limited hyperreals, and the standard-part map is itself external. ([Wikipedia: Nonstandard analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis))

### Scope
MSC2020 03Hxx "Nonstandard models" (see also 03C62) has four codes: 03H05 nonstandard models in mathematics (see also 26E35, 28E05, 30G06, 46S20, 47S20, 54J05), 03H10 other applications of nonstandard models (economics, physics, etc.), 03H15 nonstandard models of arithmetic (see also 11U10, 12L15, 13L05), and 03H99. ([MSC2020 03Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Hxx))

Neighbours: 03C62 "Models of arithmetic and set theory" in [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory) points back to 03Hxx, and 03C20 covers ultraproducts and related constructions. ([MSC2020 03Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Cxx)) Nonstandard analysis as a topic in real functions is 26E35 in [MSC 26Exx - Miscellaneous topics in real functions](node:MSC%2026Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20real%20functions), and nonstandard measure theory is 28E05 in [MSC 28Exx - Miscellaneous topics in measure theory](node:MSC%2028Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20measure%20theory); each cross-references 03H05. ([MSC2020 26Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=26Exx); [MSC2020 28Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=28Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Ultrapower construction (03H05).** For a free ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $\mathbb N$, ${}^*\mathbb R=\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}/\mathcal U$, where sequences are identified when they agree on a set in $\mathcal U$. ([Wikipedia: Nonstandard analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis)) Keisler proves that for every free ultrafilter on a countable index set the ultrapower is a hyperreal number system satisfying his axioms, including the Transfer Axiom: if every real solution of a system of formulas $S$ is a solution of $T$, then every hyperreal solution of $S$ is a solution of $T$. ([Keisler, Foundations of Infinitesimal Calculus, §§1C, 1G](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~hkeisler/foundations.pdf))
- **Infinitesimals and standard part.** A hyperreal $\varepsilon$ is infinitesimal if $|\varepsilon|<r$ for every positive real $r$; every finite hyperreal $x$ is infinitely close to a unique real number $\operatorname{st}(x)$, its standard part, and $\operatorname{st}$ is undefined on infinite hyperreals. ([Keisler, Defs. 1.1, 1.10](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~hkeisler/foundations.pdf)) This underlies the infinitesimal treatment of [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits) and calculus.
- **Overflow and saturation.** If $B\subseteq{}^*\mathbb N$ is internal and $B\cap\mathbb N$ is infinite, then $B$ contains an infinite hypernatural; likewise a set $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ is infinite iff ${}^*A$ contains an infinite number. ([Di Nasso–Goldbring–Lupini, Prop. 2.66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1709.04076)) Countable saturation is what shows ${}^*\mathbb N\setminus\mathbb N\neq\varnothing$, and $\kappa$-saturated extensions exist for every cardinal $\kappa$. ([Wikipedia: Nonstandard analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis))
- **Loeb measure (03H05, 28E05).** Given an internal finitely additive measure $\nu$ on an internal algebra of sets, its standard part $\operatorname{st}\circ\nu$ is countably additive, because countable unions within the internal algebra reduce to finite ones; Carathéodory's theorem then extends it to a genuine measure on the generated $\sigma$-algebra. Loeb introduced the construction in 1975, in a paper on applications to probability theory. ([Wikipedia: Loeb space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loeb_space)) This links the area to [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory) and [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus).
- **Nonstandard models of arithmetic (03H15).** Adding a constant $c$ and the axioms $c>n$ for each numeral $n$ gives, by compactness, a nonstandard model of Peano arithmetic; every countable nonstandard model has order type $\omega+(\omega^*+\omega)\cdot\eta$. ([Wikipedia: Non-standard model of arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-standard_model_of_arithmetic)) **Tennenbaum's theorem** (1959): no countable nonstandard model of PA is recursive; indeed neither its addition nor its multiplication is recursive. ([Wikipedia: Tennenbaum's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennenbaum%27s_theorem)) Models of PA also arise from [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): a model of PA in which the Gödel sentence fails must be nonstandard. ([Wikipedia: Non-standard model of arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-standard_model_of_arithmetic))
- **End extensions.** The MacDowell–Specker theorem (presented at the 1959 Warsaw conference on Infinitistic Methods): every model of PA has an elementary extension in which all new elements exceed all old ones. ([Kossak, arXiv:2208.03156](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03156)) Gaifman's theory of minimal types implies that every model of PA has a minimal (conservative) elementary end extension, and Gaifman showed that for every set $I$ every model has an elementary end extension whose lattice of intermediate models is the Boolean algebra of subsets of $I$. ([Abdul-Quader–Kossak, arXiv:2406.06338](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.06338v3))
- **Internal set theory.** Nelson's IST (1977) adds a predicate "standard" to ZFC with three schemes, Idealisation, Standardisation and Transfer; separation and replacement apply only to internal formulas, and IST is a conservative extension of ZFC, so every internal theorem of IST is a theorem of ZFC. ([Wikipedia: Internal set theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_set_theory)) The approach is syntactic rather than model-theoretic; compare [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory) and [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory).
- **Applications.** Bernstein and Robinson proved with nonstandard analysis that every polynomially compact operator on a Hilbert space has an invariant subspace (Pacific J. Math., 1966); Halmos gave a standard proof in the same issue. Other applications include the individual ergodic theorem (Kamae) and Gromov's polynomial-growth theorem (van den Dries–Wilkie). ([Wikipedia: Nonstandard analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis)) In combinatorics, Jin proved that if $A,B\subseteq\mathbb N$ have positive upper Banach density then $A+B$ is piecewise syndetic, and later work refines this with a Lebesgue density theorem for measure spaces built on cuts of the nonstandard integers. ([Di Nasso et al., arXiv:1310.5729](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.5729)) The monograph of Di Nasso, Goldbring and Lupini develops the method for Ramsey's theorem, Hindman's theorem, the Hales–Jewett theorem, partition regularity of equations and density problems. ([arXiv:1709.04076](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.04076); [table of contents](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1709.04076)) See [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) and [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics).

### History
Ultrapowers were first applied to the natural numbers by Skolem (1934); Hewitt studied ultrapowers of the real field (1948), and Łoś applied them to arbitrary structures (1955). ([Keisler, §1G](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~hkeisler/foundations.pdf)) Robinson's nonstandard analysis followed in the early 1960s, with the 1966 book; Nelson's axiomatic IST appeared in the *Bulletin of the AMS* in 1977. ([Wikipedia: Nonstandard analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis)) On the arithmetic side, Tennenbaum's theorem and the MacDowell–Specker theorem both date from 1959, and Loeb's measure construction from 1975. ([Wikipedia: Tennenbaum's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennenbaum%27s_theorem); [Kossak, arXiv:2208.03156](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03156); [Wikipedia: Loeb space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loeb_space))

### Open problems
- **The lattice problem for models of PA.** For a model $\mathcal N$ of PA, $\operatorname{Lt}(\mathcal N)$ is the lattice of its elementary submodels. Abdul-Quader and Kossak call it "the most outstanding" open problem whether every finite lattice can be represented as $\operatorname{Lt}(\mathcal N)$ for some model $\mathcal N$ of PA; the problem has been studied for about 60 years. Known cases: a distributive lattice is $\operatorname{Lt}(\mathcal M)$ for some model $\mathcal M$ iff it is $\aleph_1$-algebraic (Mills; independently Paris), while $\mathbf M_3$ (Gaifman and Paris, independently) and the hexagon (Wilkie) cannot be interstructure lattices of elementary end extensions. ([Abdul-Quader–Kossak, arXiv:2406.06338](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.06338v3))
- **Further questions from the same survey.** Is every finite lattice that occurs as an interstructure lattice the congruence lattice of some finite algebra? If a finite lattice is an interstructure lattice, is its dual one as well? ([Abdul-Quader–Kossak, §10](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.06338v3))
- **MacDowell–Specker generalizations.** Kossak's survey of the theorem's 63-year history states that some open problems about its generalizations remain. ([Kossak, arXiv:2208.03156](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03156))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Nonstandard analysis (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis): ultrapower, transfer, saturation, internal sets, history and applications.
- **Reference:** [Non-standard model of arithmetic (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-standard_model_of_arithmetic): existence, order type and Tennenbaum's theorem.
- **Learn:** [Keisler, Foundations of Infinitesimal Calculus](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~hkeisler/foundations.pdf): axioms for the hyperreals, transfer, standard part, and the ultrapower construction.
- **Primary:** [Di Nasso, Goldbring, Lupini, Nonstandard Methods in Ramsey Theory and Combinatorial Number Theory (arXiv:1709.04076)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.04076): monograph on the modern nonstandard method in combinatorics.
- **Primary:** [Abdul-Quader, Kossak, The Lattice Problem for Models of PA (arXiv:2406.06338)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06338): survey of models of arithmetic with a list of open problems.
- **Primary:** [Kossak, 63 Years of the MacDowell–Specker Theorem (arXiv:2208.03156)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03156): survey of end extensions of models of PA.
references.MSC 05 - Combinatorics:
## Reference
### Overview
Combinatorics is primarily concerned with counting and with certain properties of finite structures; its main problem types are enumeration, existence, construction and optimization, and its subfields include enumerative, analytic, graph, design, order, matroid, extremal, probabilistic, algebraic and geometric combinatorics. In the second half of the 20th century it grew rapidly and developed "powerful and general theoretical methods", becoming an independent branch of mathematics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics))

Several phenomena organize the research area. Ramsey theory seeks regularity amid disorder: large enough complete graphs coloured with finitely many colours contain large monochromatic cliques. The probabilistic method proves existence non-constructively; for Erdős's exponential lower bound on diagonal Ramsey numbers no explicit construction achieving exponential growth is known. Szemerédi's regularity lemma partitions any large graph into boundedly many parts between which the edges behave in a random-like fashion. ([Wikipedia, Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Probabilistic method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_method); [Wikipedia, Regularity lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di_regularity_lemma)) The atomic entry points in this vault are [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) and [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory).

### Scope
MSC2020 section 05 has five subsections: [MSC 05Axx - Enumerative combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Axx%20-%20Enumerative%20combinatorics) (for enumeration in graph theory see 05C30), [MSC 05Bxx - Designs and configurations](node:MSC%2005Bxx%20-%20Designs%20and%20configurations) (for applications of design theory see 94C30), [MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory) (for computer science see 68R10), [MSC 05Dxx - Extremal combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Dxx%20-%20Extremal%20combinatorics), and [MSC 05Exx - Algebraic combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Exx%20-%20Algebraic%20combinatorics), plus general codes such as 05-02 research exposition and 05-03 history; finite fields are in 11Txx. ([MSC2020, 05](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05-XX))

Neighbouring areas: discrete mathematics as used in computer science is [MSC 68Rxx - Discrete mathematics in relation to computer science](node:MSC%2068Rxx%20-%20Discrete%20mathematics%20in%20relation%20to%20computer%20science); combinatorial probability is [MSC 60Cxx - Combinatorial probability](node:MSC%2060Cxx%20-%20Combinatorial%20probability); partitions in the number-theoretic sense are [MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; partitions](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions) and additive combinatorics of integers sits in [MSC 11Bxx - Sequences and sets](node:MSC%2011Bxx%20-%20Sequences%20and%20sets); ordered sets and lattices are [MSC 06 - Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures](node:MSC%2006%20-%20Order,%20lattices,%20ordered%20algebraic%20structures); [polytopes](node:Polytopes) are [MSC 52Bxx - Polytopes and polyhedra](node:MSC%2052Bxx%20-%20Polytopes%20and%20polyhedra). ([MSC2020, 05](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05-XX); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics))

### Key concepts
- **Ramsey's theorem.** For positive integers $r,s$ there is a least $R(r,s)$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_{R(r,s)}$ contains a red $K_r$ or a blue $K_s$; the same holds for any finite number of colours. Erdős and Szekeres (1935) gave a bound implying $R(k,k)\le(1+o(1))\,4^{k-1}/\sqrt{\pi k}$, and Erdős (1947) gave a lower bound of order $2^{k/2}$. ([Wikipedia, Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem)) Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved $R(k)\le(4-\varepsilon)^k$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, the first exponential improvement on Erdős–Szekeres. ([Campos et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521); [authors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521v1))
- **The probabilistic method.** To show an object exists, show a random object has the property with positive probability. Erdős's 1947 random colouring gives $R(r,r)$ exponential lower bounds non-constructively; his 1959 theorem gives, for all $g,k$, graphs with girth at least $g$ and chromatic number at least $k$. ([Wikipedia, Probabilistic method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_method)) It is closely tied to [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces) and [Randomized Algorithms](node:Randomized%20Algorithms).
- **Szemerédi's regularity lemma and theorem.** For every $\varepsilon>0$ and $m$ there is $M$ such that every graph on at least $M$ vertices has an $\varepsilon$-regular partition into $k$ parts, $m\le k\le M$; Gowers showed $M$ must be of tower type. With the counting lemma it yields the removal lemma and hence Roth's theorem. ([Wikipedia, Regularity lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di_regularity_lemma)) Szemerédi's theorem (1975, conjectured by Erdős and Turán in 1936): every subset of $\mathbb N$ of positive upper density contains arithmetic progressions of every length; Furstenberg (1977) and Gowers (2001) gave ergodic and Fourier-analytic proofs. ([Wikipedia, Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem))
- **Existence of designs.** Keevash proved the existence conjecture for combinatorial designs, answering Steiner's 1853 question: the natural divisibility conditions suffice for clique decompositions of suitably pseudorandom simplicial complexes. ([Keevash](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3665))
- **Matroids.** A matroid is a finite set $E$ with a nonempty family $\mathcal I$ of independent sets closed under subsets and satisfying augmentation: if $A,B\in\mathcal I$ and $|A|>|B|$, some $x\in A\setminus B$ has $B\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal I$. Whitney (1935) abstracted independence common to graphs and matrices; a subset-closed family is a matroid exactly when the greedy algorithm finds a maximum-weight member for every weighting. ([Wikipedia, Matroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matroid))
- **Algebraic combinatorics.** Symmetric functions, Young tableaux, association schemes and face rings; Stanley's *Enumerative Combinatorics* Vol. 2, Ch. 7 is the standard source on symmetric functions. ([Stanley, EC](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/); [Wikipedia, Algebraic combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_combinatorics); [Wikipedia, Stanley–Reisner ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley%E2%80%93Reisner_ring)) See [MSC 05Exx - Algebraic combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Exx%20-%20Algebraic%20combinatorics) and [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory).

### History
Enumerative problems are very old: problem 79 of the Rhind papyrus, Mahāvīra's formulas for permutations and combinations (c. 850), and Levi ben Gerson's closed formula for binomial coefficients (1321). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics)) Euler's 1736 solution of the Königsberg bridges problem laid the foundations of graph theory. ([Wikipedia, Königsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Bridges_of_K%C3%B6nigsberg)) Kirkman's schoolgirl problem (1850) is a classic of design theory, and Steiner's 1853 question on the existence of designs was answered by Keevash. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics); [Keevash](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3665)) Sylvester and MacMahon founded enumerative and algebraic combinatorics, and the four colour problem drove graph theory. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics)) Ramsey's 1930 paper, Erdős–Szekeres (1935), Whitney's matroids (1935), and Erdős's probabilistic method (1947) shaped the modern subject, followed by Szemerédi's theorem (1975). ([Wikipedia, Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Matroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matroid); [Wikipedia, Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Diagonal Ramsey growth.** The exponential base of $R(k,k)$ is unknown: lower bounds have base $\sqrt2$, unimproved for a long time, while a 2024 preprint of Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin and Wei claims an upper bound of about $3.8^k$; $R(5,5)$ is only known to lie in $[43,46]$. ([Wikipedia, Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem))
- **Union-closed sets conjecture (Frankl, 1979).** Every finite union-closed family other than $\{\emptyset\}$ has an element in at least half its sets; open, with Gilmer's 2022 breakthrough and follow-ups giving about $38\%$. ([Wikipedia, Union-closed sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union-closed_sets_conjecture))
- **Hadwiger's conjecture (1943).** Every graph with chromatic number $k$ has a $K_k$ minor; known for $k\le6$ (the case $k=5$ is equivalent to the four colour theorem) and unsolved for all $k>6$. Wikipedia also reports a claimed disproof released by OpenAI in October 2026; this is an unrefereed, unconfirmed claim, and the article still lists the conjecture as unsolved. ([Wikipedia, Hadwiger conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadwiger_conjecture_%28graph_theory%29))
- **Erdős–Hajnal conjecture.** For every graph $H$, graphs with no induced $H$ have a clique or independent set of size $\Omega(n^{\delta_H})$; open in general, known for all $H$ on at most five vertices. ([Wikipedia, Erdős–Hajnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Hajnal_conjecture))
- **Szemerédi bounds.** The growth rate of $r_k(N)$, the largest subset of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ with no $k$-term progression, is open. ([Wikipedia, Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Combinatorics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics): approaches, subfields, history.
- **Learn:** [Postnikov, MIT 18.212 Algebraic Combinatorics, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-212-algebraic-combinatorics-spring-2019/resources/lecture-notes/): Catalan numbers, hook walks, posets and Sperner, partition identities, Matrix–Tree, LGV lemma, plane partitions.
- **Primary:** [Campos, Griffiths, Morris & Sahasrabudhe, An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521): $R(k)\le(4-\varepsilon)^k$.
- **Primary:** [Keevash, The existence of designs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3665): existence conjecture for designs.
- **Further reading:** [Alon & Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, 4th ed. (Wiley)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Probabilistic+Method%2C+4th+Edition-p-9781119061953); [Diestel, Graph Theory (Springer GTM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-70107-2); [Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/).
references.MSC 05Axx - Enumerative combinatorics:
## Reference
### Overview
Enumerative combinatorics, the counting side of [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics), studies counting functions: given finite sets $S_i$ indexed by some set $I$ (often $\mathbb N$), determine $f(i)=|S_i|$ for all $i$ "simultaneously". Stanley stresses that what counts as a determination of $f$ is not fixed: a closed formula free of summations is the most satisfactory but rarely exists, and the alternatives are recurrences, generating functions and asymptotic formulas. ([Stanley, EC1 §1.1](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ec1.pdf)) When a closed form gives little insight into growth, one seeks $g$ with $f(n)/g(n)\to1$, written $f\sim g$. ([Wikipedia: Enumerative combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enumerative_combinatorics))

The organising tool is the generating function, ordinary $\sum f_nx^n$ or exponential $\sum f_nx^n/n!$. Constructions on combinatorial classes translate into operations on series: disjoint union into sum, Cartesian product into product, and sequences into $1/(1-F(x))$. For plane trees, $P=\{\bullet\}\times\mathrm{Seq}(P)$ gives $P(x)=x/(1-P(x))$, so $P(x)=(1-\sqrt{1-4x})/2$ and plane trees with $n$ nodes are counted by the Catalan number $C_{n-1}$. ([Wikipedia: Enumerative combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enumerative_combinatorics)) Flajolet and Sedgewick systematise this as the *symbolic method* and pair it with complex analysis of the generating function to extract coefficient asymptotics. ([Flajolet–Sedgewick, Analytic Combinatorics](https://ac.cs.princeton.edu/home/))

### Scope
MSC2020 05Axx has codes 05A05 permutations, words, matrices; 05A10 factorials, binomial coefficients, combinatorial functions; 05A15 exact enumeration problems, generating functions; 05A16 asymptotic enumeration; 05A17 combinatorial aspects of partitions of integers (see also 11P81–11P83); 05A18 partitions of sets; 05A19 combinatorial identities, bijective combinatorics; 05A20 combinatorial inequalities; 05A30 $q$-calculus and related topics; 05A40 umbral calculus; and 05A99. ([MSC2020 05Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Axx))

Neighbours: enumeration of graphs is 05C30 in [MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory), as the 05A heading itself directs. ([MSC2020 05Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Axx); [MSC2020 05Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Cxx)) The analytic and arithmetic theory of partitions belongs to [MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; partitions](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions), and $q$-series as [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions) to 33Dxx, both cross-referenced from 05A17 and 05A30. ([MSC2020 05Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Axx)) Symmetric functions (05E05) and combinatorial aspects of [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) (05E10) are in [MSC 05Exx - Algebraic combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Exx%20-%20Algebraic%20combinatorics). ([MSC2020 05Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Rational generating functions (05A15).** For complex $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d$ with $d\ge1$, $\alpha_d\neq0$, a function $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$ has $\sum_{n\ge0}f(n)x^n=P(x)/Q(x)$ with $Q(x)=1+\alpha_1x+\cdots+\alpha_dx^d$ and $\deg P<d$ if and only if $f(n+d)+\alpha_1f(n+d-1)+\cdots+\alpha_df(n)=0$ for all $n\ge0$, if and only if $f(n)=\sum_i P_i(n)\gamma_i^n$ where $Q(x)=\prod_i(1-\gamma_ix)^{d_i}$ and $\deg P_i<d_i$. ([Stanley, EC1 Thm 4.1.1](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ec1.pdf))
- **Exponential formula (labelled structures).** If $C(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nx^n/n!$ counts connected structures on $n$-element label sets and every structure splits uniquely into connected components on the blocks of a set partition, then all structures are counted by $F(x)=\exp C(x)$, i.e. $b_n=\sum_{\pi}a_{|S_1|}\cdots a_{|S_k|}$ over set partitions $\pi=\{S_1,\dots,S_k\}$ of $[n]$. Taking $b_n=2^{\binom n2}$ makes $a_n$ the number of connected labelled graphs; taking acyclic graphs makes $a_n$ count trees. ([Wikipedia: Exponential formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_formula)) This links 05A to [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory).
- **Lagrange inversion.** If $f(w)=w/\varphi(w)$ with $\varphi(0)\neq0$ as formal power series and $g$ is the compositional inverse of $f$, then $[z^n]g(z)=\tfrac1n[w^{n-1}]\varphi(w)^n$, and more generally $[z^n]H(g(z))=\tfrac1n[w^{n-1}]\big(H'(w)\varphi(w)^n\big)$. With $\varphi(w)=(1+w)^2$ it gives the Catalan numbers for binary trees. Lagrange's paper appeared in 1770 and Bürmann generalised it in the 1790s. ([Wikipedia: Lagrange inversion theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_inversion_theorem))
- **Pólya counting.** For a finite group $G$ acting on a finite set $X$, the number of $m$-colourings of $X$ up to $G$ is the average over $g\in G$ of $m^{c(g)}$, where $c(g)$ is the number of cycles of $g$; with weighted colours, the weight enumerator is the cycle index $Z_G(t_1,t_2,\dots)$ evaluated at $t_k=f(t^k)$. Redfield published it in 1927 and Pólya rediscovered it in 1937. ([Wikipedia: Pólya enumeration theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B3lya_enumeration_theorem)) See [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory).
- **Integer partitions (05A17).** $\sum_np(n)x^n=\prod_{k\ge1}(1-x^k)^{-1}$; Hardy and Ramanujan (1918) proved $p(n)\sim\frac{1}{4n\sqrt3}\exp\!\big(\pi\sqrt{2n/3}\big)$; Rademacher (1937) found an exact convergent series whose first term is this approximation; and Ramanujan's congruences give $p(5k+4)\equiv0\pmod5$, $p(7k+5)\equiv0\pmod7$, $p(11k+6)\equiv0\pmod{11}$. ([Wikipedia: Partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29))
- **RSK and bijective combinatorics (05A19).** The Robinson–Schensted–Knuth correspondence is a bijection between matrices with nonnegative integer entries and pairs $(P,Q)$ of semistandard Young tableaux of the same shape, with the weights of $P$ and $Q$ given by the column and row sums; on permutation matrices it pairs permutations of $[n]$ with pairs of standard tableaux, which yields $n!=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2$, and it gives a bijective proof of Cauchy's identity for Schur functions. ([Wikipedia: RSK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson%E2%80%93Schensted%E2%80%93Knuth_correspondence))
- **Analytic combinatorics (05A16).** Singularity analysis relates the asymptotics of $[z^n]F(z)$ to the behaviour of $F$ near its dominant singularities, with a transfer theorem for rational and meromorphic functions and the Flajolet–Odlyzko theorem for square-root and logarithmic singularities; the saddle-point method handles generating functions with no singularities. ([Flajolet–Sedgewick, Analytic Combinatorics](https://ac.cs.princeton.edu/home/)) This is where 05A meets [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis).
- **Permutation patterns (05A05).** The Stanley–Wilf conjecture, that for each permutation $\beta$ the number of length-$n$ permutations avoiding $\beta$ is at most $C^n$, was proved by Marcus and Tardos in 2004 via the Füredi–Hajnal conjecture, which Klazar had shown implies it. Arratia's guess $C=(k-1)^2$ fails for $\beta=4231$, and Fox showed that the growth rate is exponential in $k$ for almost all $\beta$. ([Wikipedia: Stanley–Wilf conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley%E2%80%93Wilf_conjecture)) Single patterns of length 3 all give the Catalan numbers; 1342-avoiders (Bóna) have an algebraic, non-rational generating function and 1234-avoiders (Gessel) a holonomic, non-algebraic one. ([Wikipedia: Enumerations of specific permutation classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enumerations_of_specific_permutation_classes))

### History
Redfield's 1927 and Pólya's 1937 counting theorem, Hardy–Ramanujan's 1918 partition asymptotics and Rademacher's 1937 series are early landmarks of the area's modern form. ([Wikipedia: Pólya enumeration theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B3lya_enumeration_theorem); [Wikipedia: Partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29)) Knuth's 1970 paper extended the Robinson–Schensted correspondence to integer matrices. ([Wikipedia: RSK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson%E2%80%93Schensted%E2%80%93Knuth_correspondence)) Stanley's *Enumerative Combinatorics* (first edition of volume 1 in 1986; author's second-edition version dated 2011) and Flajolet and Sedgewick's *Analytic Combinatorics* (Cambridge University Press) are the standard references for the algebraic and the analytic sides. ([Stanley, EC1 preface](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ec1.pdf); [Flajolet–Sedgewick](https://ac.cs.princeton.edu/home/)) Stanley and Wilf independently formulated their conjecture on pattern avoidance in the late 1980s; Marcus and Tardos proved it in 2004. ([Wikipedia: Stanley–Wilf conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley%E2%80%93Wilf_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Enumeration of 1324-avoiders.** No non-recursive formula counting permutations avoiding 1324 is known, and the growth rate is not known exactly; the best rigorous bounds place it in $[10.271,\,13.5]$. ([Wikipedia: Enumerations of specific permutation classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enumerations_of_specific_permutation_classes); [Bevan–Brignall–Elvey Price–Pantone, arXiv:1711.10325](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10325))
- **Self-avoiding walks.** The connective constant $\mu=\lim c_n^{1/n}$ of $n$-step self-avoiding walks is known exactly only for the hexagonal lattice, $\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}$ (Duminil-Copin–Smirnov); for other lattices it is only approximated numerically, and the asymptotic $c_n\approx\mu^nn^{11/32}$, with lattice-dependent $\mu$ and a universal power-law correction, is conjectural. ([Wikipedia: Self-avoiding walk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-avoiding_walk)) The exponent $11/32$ is the two-dimensional case of the predicted law $c_n\sim A\mu^nn^{\gamma-1}$, with $\gamma=43/32$ for $d=2$, $\gamma\approx1.16$ for $d=3$, a logarithmic correction for $d=4$, and $\gamma=1$ for $d\ge5$. ([Bauerschmidt–Duminil-Copin–Goodman–Slade, Lectures on self-avoiding walks, §1.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.2092))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Enumerative combinatorics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enumerative_combinatorics): counting functions, generating functions and the basic constructions.
- **Learn:** [Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. (author's copy)](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ec1.pdf): textbook covering counting, sieve methods, posets and rational generating functions, with many exercises.
- **Primary:** [Flajolet and Sedgewick, Analytic Combinatorics (Cambridge University Press)](https://ac.cs.princeton.edu/home/): the monograph on the symbolic method, singularity analysis and saddle-point asymptotics.
- **Primary:** [Bevan, Brignall, Elvey Price, Pantone, A structural characterisation of Av(1324) and new bounds on its growth rate (arXiv:1711.10325)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10325): research paper on the hardest small pattern class.
references.MSC 05Bxx - Designs and configurations:
## Reference
### Overview
Design theory studies finite incidence structures with prescribed balance. A design is a pair $(V,\mathcal B)$ of a finite point set $V$ and a collection $\mathcal B$ of subsets (blocks); the central class, the balanced incomplete block design (BIBD), has $|V|=v$, $b$ blocks of size $k$, every point in exactly $r$ blocks and every pair of points in exactly $\lambda$ blocks. The subject grew out of the statistical design of experiments, geometry and recreational mathematics and became an independent branch of [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) in the second half of the twentieth century, with deep ties to [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory), algebra, geometry and [number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory). ([Meszka, Combinatorial Designs](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf))

More generally a $t$-$(v,k,\lambda)$ design requires every $t$-subset of points to lie in exactly $\lambda$ blocks; a $t$-design with $t\ge2$ is also a $2$-design, and a $t$-$(v,k,1)$ design is a Steiner system $S(t,k,v)$. ([Block design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_design)) Within [MSC 05 - Combinatorics](node:MSC%2005%20-%20Combinatorics), the basic question is existence: for which parameters does a design exist? The arithmetic conditions are necessary but not sufficient, and the general existence question for BIBDs remains open for infinitely many parameter sets. ([Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 05Bxx "Designs and configurations" (for applications of design theory see 94C30) has these codes: 05B05 combinatorial aspects of block designs (see also 51E05, 62K10); 05B07 triple systems; 05B10 combinatorial aspects of difference sets (number-theoretic, group-theoretic, etc.; see also 11B13); 05B15 orthogonal arrays, Latin squares, Room squares; 05B20 combinatorial aspects of matrices (incidence, Hadamard, etc.); 05B25 combinatorial aspects of finite geometries (see also 51D20, 51Exx); 05B30 other designs, configurations (see also 51E30); 05B35 combinatorial aspects of matroids and geometric lattices (see also 52B40, 90C27); 05B40 combinatorial aspects of packing and covering (see also 11H31, 52C15, 52C17); 05B45 combinatorial aspects of tessellation and tiling problems (see also 52C20, 52C22); 05B50 polyominoes; 05B99 none of the above. ([MSC2020, 05B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Bxx))

Neighbouring codes, as the MSC cross-references indicate ([MSC2020, 05B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Bxx)):
- [MSC 51Exx - Finite geometry and special incidence structures](node:MSC%2051Exx%20-%20Finite%20geometry%20and%20special%20incidence%20structures): the geometric side of finite planes and incidence structures; 05B25 covers their combinatorial aspects.
- [MSC 62Kxx - Design of statistical experiments](node:MSC%2062Kxx%20-%20Design%20of%20statistical%20experiments): statistical design (62K10 for block designs), cross-referenced from 05B05.
- 94C30 in [MSC 94Cxx - Circuits, networks](node:MSC%2094Cxx%20-%20Circuits,%20networks): the 05Bxx header sends applications of design theory there.
- [MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory): 05C51 (graph designs and isomorphic decomposition) points back to 05B30. ([MSC2020, 05C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Cxx))
- [MSC 52Cxx - Discrete geometry](node:MSC%2052Cxx%20-%20Discrete%20geometry): geometric packing, covering and tiling, cross-referenced from 05B40 and 05B45.

### Key concepts
- **BIBD identities and Fisher's inequality.** Double counting gives $bk=vr$ and $\lambda(v-1)=r(k-1)$, so $v,k,\lambda$ determine $r$ and $b$; integrality of $r$ and $b$ is necessary but not sufficient. ([Block design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_design)) The incidence matrix $A$ satisfies $AA^{T}=(r-\lambda)I+\lambda J$, and Fisher's inequality states that a $(v,k,\lambda)$-BIBD with $2\le k<v$ has $b\ge v$; this rules out a $(21,6,1)$-BIBD ($b=14<21$) although its parameters are admissible. ([Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf))
- **Symmetric designs and Bruck–Ryser–Chowla.** A BIBD is symmetric if $b=v$ (then $r=k$ and $\lambda(v-1)=k(k-1)$); any two blocks then meet in exactly $\lambda$ points. ([Block design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_design)) Bruck–Ryser–Chowla: if a symmetric $(v,k,\lambda)$-BIBD exists and $n=k-\lambda$, then $n$ is a square when $v$ is even, and when $v$ is odd $z^2=nx^2+(-1)^{(v-1)/2}\lambda y^2$ has an integer solution with $x,y,z$ not all zero. The conditions are not sufficient: a symmetric $(111,11,1)$ design satisfies them but does not exist, as shown by structural analysis and exhaustive computer search. ([Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf))
- **Projective planes.** A projective plane of order $N$ is a symmetric $(N^2+N+1,N+1,1)$ design; the Fano plane is the $(7,3,1)$ case. Every known finite projective plane has prime-power order. Bruck–Ryser–Chowla is the only known general restriction: if $N\equiv1,2\pmod4$, $N$ must be a sum of two squares, which excludes $N=6$; $N=10$ was excluded by massive computer calculation (Lam, 1991). ([Projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane); [Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf)) See [Projective Geometry](node:Projective%20Geometry) and [MSC 51Exx - Finite geometry and special incidence structures](node:MSC%2051Exx%20-%20Finite%20geometry%20and%20special%20incidence%20structures).
- **Steiner and Kirkman triple systems.** For a Steiner triple system STS$(v)$ the arithmetic conditions reduce to $v\equiv1,3\pmod 6$, and Kirkman proved in 1847 that they are sufficient; simple direct constructions are due to Bose (from idempotent commutative quasigroups, for $v\equiv3\pmod6$) and Skolem (from half-idempotent commutative quasigroups, for $v\equiv1\pmod6$). A design is resolvable if its blocks split into parallel classes; a Kirkman triple system KTS$(v)$ (a resolvable STS) exists if and only if $v\equiv3\pmod6$, proved by Ray-Chaudhuri and Wilson in 1971. ([Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf)) Kirkman's 15-schoolgirl problem asks for a resolution of a $2$-$(15,3,1)$ design. ([Block design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_design))
- **Difference sets.** A $k$-subset $D$ of a group $G$ of order $v$ is a $(v,k,\lambda)$-difference set if every non-zero element of $G$ is a difference $d-d'$ of elements of $D$ in exactly $\lambda$ ways. A set of residues mod $v$ is a $(v,k,\lambda)$-difference set if and only if its translates form the blocks of a cyclic $(v,k,\lambda)$-BIBD; for example $\{0,1,3,9\}\subset\mathbb Z_{13}$ develops a cyclic $(13,4,1)$ design. ([Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf)) The automorphism groups involved connect the area with [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory).
- **Latin squares and MOLS.** A Latin square of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ array in which each of $n$ symbols occurs once per row and column, equivalently the multiplication table of a quasigroup. ([Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf)) Euler's 36 officers problem asks for two orthogonal Latin squares of order 6; Euler conjectured none exist for $n\equiv2\pmod4$, Tarry confirmed non-existence for $n=6$ by exhaustion (1900–01), and Parker, Bose and Shrikhande (1959) disproved the conjecture for all $n\ge7$, so orthogonal pairs exist for all $n>1$ except $2$ and $6$. At most $n-1$ mutually orthogonal Latin squares (MOLS) of order $n$ exist, and a complete set of $n-1$ MOLS$(n)$ is equivalent to a finite affine plane of order $n$. ([Graeco-Latin square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeco-Latin_square))
- **Hadamard matrices (05B20).** Paley's 1933 construction gives a Hadamard matrix of order $q+1$ for every prime power $q\equiv3\pmod4$, and of order $2(q+1)$ for $q\equiv1\pmod4$. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix))
- **Existence of designs.** Wilson proved the graph case ($r=2$) of the decomposition problem in 1975. ([Glock–Kühn–Lo–Osthus](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.06827)) Keevash (2014) proved the existence conjecture for combinatorial designs, answering a question of Steiner from 1853: the natural divisibility conditions suffice for large enough point sets. ([Keevash](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3665)) In particular nontrivial Steiner systems with $t\ge6$ exist, but the proof is non-constructive, and as of 2019 no explicit Steiner systems are known for large $t$. ([Steiner system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system)) Glock, Kühn, Lo and Osthus gave a new proof by iterative absorption and extended it to $F$-designs: for any $r$-uniform hypergraph $F$, the trivially necessary divisibility conditions suffice for a large complete $r$-graph to decompose into copies of $F$. ([Glock–Kühn–Lo–Osthus](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.06827))
- **Steiner systems and Mathieu groups.** The unique $S(5,6,12)$ has automorphism group $M_{12}$, and the Witt design $S(5,8,24)$ has automorphism group $M_{24}$; $M_{11}$ and $M_{23}$ arise from $S(4,5,11)$ and $S(4,7,23)$. ([Steiner system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system))

### History
Steiner raised the existence question in 1853. ([Keevash](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3665)) Kirkman settled Steiner triple systems in 1847, and Kirkman triple systems were settled by Ray-Chaudhuri and Wilson in 1971, more than 120 years after Kirkman posed the problem. ([Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf)) Euler's conjecture on orthogonal Latin squares stood until Parker, Bose and Shrikhande presented its disproof in April 1959. ([Graeco-Latin square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeco-Latin_square)) Lam's 1991 computation excluded projective planes of order 10. ([Projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane)) Wilson's 1975 theorem for graphs was followed by Keevash's 2014 general existence theorem and the 2016 iterative-absorption proof. ([Glock–Kühn–Lo–Osthus](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.06827); [Keevash](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3665))

### Open problems
- **Projective plane of order 12.** Whether a finite projective plane of order 12 exists is still open; such a plane is conjectured not to exist, and all known planes have prime-power order. ([Projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane))
- **Hadamard conjecture.** A Hadamard matrix of order $4k$ is conjectured to exist for every positive integer $k$; Wikipedia lists this as unsolved. As of 2014 the smallest order with no known Hadamard matrix was 668. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix)) A reported, not yet peer-reviewed result: an arXiv paper of September 2026 states that in August 2026 Alpöge, Voinov, Reynolds-Haertle and Claude (Anthropic) generated computationally verified Hadamard matrices for all 12 previously unknown orders below 2000, citing Epoch AI's tracker, which marks order 668 as solved only provisionally. Even if confirmed, this settles finitely many orders, not the conjecture. ([González-Regadera–Falcón](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.18380); [Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix))
- **MOLS of order 10.** The smallest $n$ for which the maximum number of MOLS$(n)$ is unknown is $n=10$: there are at least two and fewer than seven, and no set of three MOLS$(10)$ has been found. ([Graeco-Latin square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeco-Latin_square))
- **The $q$-analogue of the Fano plane.** Kiermaier calls the existence of a $q$-analogue of the Fano plane (a $q$-Steiner system $S_q(2,3,7)$) the most important open problem in the theory of $q$-analogues of designs; it is undecided for every prime power $q\ge2$. ([Kiermaier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.00365))
- **Explicit designs with large $t$.** Keevash's existence proof is non-constructive, and no actual Steiner systems are known for large $t$. ([Steiner system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system))
- **Small parameter sets.** The general existence question for BIBDs remains a crucial open problem for infinitely many parameter sets. ([Meszka](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Block design (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_design): BIBDs, $t$-designs, Fisher's inequality, symmetric and resolvable designs.
- **Learn:** [Meszka, Combinatorial Designs (lecture notes)](https://home.agh.edu.pl/~meszka/cd_lecturenotes.pdf): BIBDs, Fisher, Bruck–Ryser–Chowla, difference sets, Latin squares, Steiner and Kirkman triple systems with proofs and constructions.
- **Primary:** [Keevash, The existence of designs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3665): proof of the existence conjecture for combinatorial designs.
- **Primary:** [Glock, Kühn, Lo & Osthus, The existence of designs via iterative absorption](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.06827): $F$-designs for arbitrary uniform hypergraphs $F$.
- **Further reading:** [Kiermaier, On α-points of q-analogs of the Fano plane](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.00365): current state of the $q$-Fano problem.
references.MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 05C is the graph-theory subfield of [MSC 05 - Combinatorics](node:MSC%2005%20-%20Combinatorics): graphs, digraphs, hypergraphs and infinite graphs, studied structurally, extremally, probabilistically and algebraically. Much of the area is organised around theorems that control a global parameter by excluding finitely many local configurations: Kuratowski's planarity criterion, the strong perfect graph theorem, and the Robertson–Seymour theorem that every minor-closed class has finitely many forbidden minors. ([MSC2020, 05C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Cxx); [Wikipedia, Kuratowski's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuratowski%27s_theorem); [Chudnovsky–Robertson–Seymour–Thomas, Annals 2006](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2006/164-1/p02); [Wikipedia, Robertson–Seymour theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robertson%E2%80%93Seymour_theorem)) The elementary vocabulary and first theorems are in [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory); colouring is developed in [Graph Colorings](node:Graph%20Colorings).

A second axis is quantitative: how many edges force a subgraph (Turán, Erdős–Stone), how random graphs behave near thresholds, and how eigenvalues measure expansion. Szemerédi's regularity lemma connects these, approximating every large dense graph by boundedly many random-like pairs. ([Diestel, ch. 7](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch7.pdf); [Wikipedia, Erdős–Rényi model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93R%C3%A9nyi_model); [Wikipedia, Expander graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expander_graph))

### Scope
