MSC2020 05C has 41 codes: 05C05 trees; 05C07 vertex degrees; 05C09 graphical indices; 05C10 planar graphs, geometric and topological aspects; 05C12 distance; 05C15 colouring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C17 perfect graphs; 05C20 digraphs, tournaments; 05C21 flows; 05C22 signed and weighted graphs; 05C25 graphs and abstract algebra; 05C30 enumeration; 05C31 graph polynomials; 05C35 extremal problems; 05C38 paths and cycles; 05C40 connectivity; 05C42 density (toughness); 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs; 05C48 expander graphs; 05C50 graphs and linear algebra; 05C51 graph designs; 05C55 generalized Ramsey theory; 05C57 games on graphs; 05C60 isomorphism problems (reconstruction conjecture) and homomorphisms; 05C62 graph representations; 05C63 infinite graphs; 05C65 hypergraphs; 05C69 and 05C70 special vertex and edge subsets (independent sets, cliques, matchings, factorizations); 05C72 fractional and fuzzy graph theory; 05C75 structural characterization of families; 05C76 graph operations; 05C78 labelling; 05C80 random graphs; 05C81 random walks; 05C82 small-world graphs and complex networks; 05C83 graph minors; 05C85 graph algorithms; 05C90 applications; 05C92 chemical graph theory; 05C99. ([MSC2020, 05C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Cxx))

How it differs from its neighbours, following the code's cross-references ([MSC2020, 05C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Cxx)):
- **05D** ([MSC 05Dxx - Extremal combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Dxx%20-%20Extremal%20combinatorics)): 05C55 (generalized Ramsey theory) carries a see-also to 05D10 (see [Ramsey Theory](node:Ramsey%20Theory)).
- **05E and 05B** ([MSC 05Exx - Algebraic combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Exx%20-%20Algebraic%20combinatorics), [MSC 05Bxx - Designs and configurations](node:MSC%2005Bxx%20-%20Designs%20and%20configurations)): 05C07 carries a see-also to 05E30 and 05C51 to 05B30.
- **68R** ([MSC 68Rxx - Discrete mathematics in relation to computer science](node:MSC%2068Rxx%20-%20Discrete%20mathematics%20in%20relation%20to%20computer%20science)): the 05C heading says "For computer science, see 68R10", and 05C85 (graph algorithms, graph-theoretic aspects) points to 68R10 and 68W05 (see [Graph Algorithms](node:Graph%20Algorithms)).
- **20F** ([MSC 20Fxx - Special aspects of infinite or finite groups](node:MSC%2020Fxx%20-%20Special%20aspects%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups)): 05C25 (graphs and abstract algebra) carries a see-also to 20F65.
- **60B and 57K/57M**: 05C80 (random graphs) points to 60B20, and 05C10 (planar graphs; geometric and topological aspects) to 57K10 and 57M15.

### Key concepts
- **Kuratowski–Wagner and the Four Colour Theorem (05C10, 05C15).** A finite graph is planar iff it contains no subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$, equivalently no $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$ minor. Every planar graph is 4-colourable: Appel and Haken announced a computer-aided proof in 1976; Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas gave a simpler proof with 633 configurations and a quadratic-time 4-colouring algorithm; Gonthier and Werner formalised it in Coq in 2005. ([Wikipedia, Kuratowski's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuratowski%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Four colour theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_color_theorem))
- **Brooks and Vizing (05C15).** A connected graph that is neither complete nor an odd cycle has $\chi\le\Delta$ (Brooks 1941); every graph has $\Delta\le\chi'\le\Delta+1$ (Vizing 1964); planar graphs are 5-choosable (Thomassen 1994). ([Diestel, ch. 5](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch5.pdf)) Deciding $\chi'=\Delta$ is NP-complete (Holyer 1981). ([Wikipedia, Edge coloring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_coloring))
- **Strong perfect graph theorem (05C17).** $G$ is perfect if every induced subgraph $H$ has $\chi(H)=\omega(H)$. Chudnovsky, Robertson, Seymour and Thomas proved Berge's 1961 conjecture: $G$ is perfect iff no induced subgraph is an odd cycle of length at least five or the complement of one; they also proved the Conforti–Cornuéjols–Vušković decomposition conjecture for Berge graphs. ([Chudnovsky–Robertson–Seymour–Thomas, Annals 2006](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2006/164-1/p02))
- **Graph minors and tree-width (05C83).** Finite graphs are well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation (Robertson–Seymour, 1986–2004), so every minor-closed property has a finite set of forbidden minors; for every $r$ there is $k$ such that tree-width at least $k$ forces an $r\times r$ grid minor. ([Diestel, Thms 12.6.3, 12.7.1](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch12.pdf)) For fixed $H$, testing for an $H$ minor takes polynomial time (cubic, improved to quadratic by Kawarabayashi, Kobayashi and Reed), but the proof does not produce obstruction sets: that for the torus has at least 17,535 graphs. ([Wikipedia, Robertson–Seymour theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robertson%E2%80%93Seymour_theorem)) The graph structure theorem says that for every $H$ there is $k$ such that every $H$-minor-free graph is a $k$-clique-sum of graphs almost embeddable, with at most $k$ apices and vortices, in surfaces where $H$ does not embed; for planar $H$ this gives bounded tree-width. ([Wikipedia, Graph structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_structure_theorem))
- **Extremal graph theory (05C35).** Turán: the unique $K_r$-free graph on $n$ vertices with the most edges is the Turán graph $T_{r-1}(n)$. Erdős–Stone: $t_{r-1}(n)+\varepsilon n^2$ edges force $K^r_s$ for large $n$. Hence (Erdős–Simonovits 1966) for every $H$ with an edge, $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)/\binom n2\to(\chi(H)-2)/(\chi(H)-1)$. The regularity lemma: for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $m\ge1$ there is $M$ such that every graph of order at least $m$ has an $\varepsilon$-regular partition into $k$ parts with $m\le k\le M$. ([Diestel, Thms 7.1.1–7.1.2, Cor. 7.1.3, Thm 7.4.1](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch7.pdf)) Gowers (1997) showed $M$ can need an iterated exponential of height a power of $1/\varepsilon$; with counting, the lemma gives the removal lemma and Roth's theorem. ([Wikipedia, Szemerédi regularity lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di_regularity_lemma))
- **Random graphs (05C80).** In $G(n,p)$ each edge appears independently with probability $p$ (Gilbert 1959; $G(n,M)$ is Erdős–Rényi 1959). $\ln n/n$ is a sharp threshold for connectivity; at $np=1$ a phase transition occurs: for $np<1$ components have size $O(\log n)$, at $np=1$ the largest has order $n^{2/3}$, and for $np\to c>1$ a unique giant component holds a positive fraction of vertices. ([Wikipedia, Erdős–Rényi model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93R%C3%A9nyi_model))
- **Spectra and expanders (05C50, 05C48).** For $d$-regular $G$ the spectral gap $d-\lambda_2$ controls the edge expansion $h(G)$ from both sides (discrete Cheeger inequalities). Alon–Boppana: large $d$-regular graphs have $\lambda_2\ge2\sqrt{d-1}-o(1)$; Ramanujan graphs attain this, constructed explicitly by Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak and Margulis, and in the bipartite case for all degrees by Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava via lifts. ([Wikipedia, Expander graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expander_graph))
- **Ramsey numbers (05C55).** $R(k)$ is the least $n$ such that every red–blue colouring of $K_n$ has a monochromatic $K_k$. Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved $R(k)\le(4-\varepsilon)^k$, the first exponential improvement on Erdős–Szekeres (1935). ([Campos et al., arXiv 2303.09521](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521)) Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin and Wei improved the base to about $3.8$; Erdős's probabilistic lower bound is of order $2^{k/2}$. ([Wikipedia, Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem))

### History
Guthrie posed the four colour problem in 1852; Heawood exposed Kempe's flawed 1879 proof and proved the five colour theorem in 1890. ([Wikipedia, Four colour theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_color_theorem)) Kuratowski's criterion appeared in 1930 (Frink and Smith had an unpublished independent proof). ([Wikipedia, Kuratowski's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuratowski%27s_theorem)) Turán's theorem dates from 1941 and Erdős–Stone from 1946, though its main application came twenty years later. ([Diestel, ch. 7](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch7.pdf)) Robertson and Seymour proved the graph minor theorem in twenty papers totalling over 500 pages (1983–2004). ([Wikipedia, Robertson–Seymour theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robertson%E2%80%93Seymour_theorem)) The strong perfect graph theorem was published in 2006. ([Chudnovsky–Robertson–Seymour–Thomas, Annals 2006](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2006/164-1/p02))

### Open problems
- **Hadwiger's conjecture (05C15, 05C83).** Every loopless graph with no $K_t$ minor has $\chi<t$. Posed in 1943, proved for $t\le6$ ($t=5$ is equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem; $t=6$ by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas 1993), open for $t>6$; the best established bound is $O(t\log\log t)$ colours (Delcourt–Postle 2024). ([Wikipedia, Hadwiger conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadwiger_conjecture_%28graph_theory%29))

> [!warning] Contested
> Wikipedia reports that an October 2026 OpenAI release of preprints included a claimed counterexample, with no confirmation. ([Wikipedia, Hadwiger conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadwiger_conjecture_%28graph_theory%29)) Separately, Norin and Steiner's unrefereed preprint claims the linear bound: some $C$ makes every $K_t$-minor-free graph $Ct$-colourable, with a proof the abstract says was found by an AI system following the authors' directions. ([Norin–Steiner, arXiv 2610.05291](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05291)) Both are reported, unconfirmed claims.

- **Erdős–Hajnal conjecture (05C69, 05C75).** For every $H$ there is $\delta_H>0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph with no induced $H$ has a clique or independent set of size $n^{\delta_H}$. Posed in 1977; it is known for every graph $H$ on at most five vertices, including $C_5$ (Chudnovsky–Scott–Seymour–Spirkl) and $P_5$ (Nguyen–Scott–Seymour 2023), and for cographs, and is open in general. ([Wikipedia, Erdős–Hajnal conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Hajnal_conjecture))
- **Reconstruction conjecture (05C60).** Two graphs on at least three vertices with the same deck of vertex-deleted subgraphs are isomorphic (Kelly 1957, Ulam 1960). Unsolved; verified up to 13 vertices (McKay) and for regular graphs, trees and disconnected graphs. ([Wikipedia, Reconstruction conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_conjecture))
- **Colouring conjectures (05C15).** The list colouring conjecture $\mathrm{ch}'(G)=\chi'(G)$ (bipartite case Galvin 1995) and the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture that excluding any fixed forest as an induced subgraph gives a $\chi$-bounded class are stated as conjectures. ([Diestel, ch. 5](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch5.pdf))
- **Erdős–Sós conjecture (05C35).** Graphs of average degree greater than $k-1$ contain every tree with $k$ edges; a proof for large graphs announced in 2009 has not been made publicly available. ([Diestel, ch. 7 notes](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch7.pdf))
- **Diagonal Ramsey numbers (05C55).** The base of the exponential lower bound for $R(k)$ still stands at $\sqrt2$ while the upper bound's base is about $3.8$, and the exact value of $R(5,5)$ is unknown: it lies between 43 and 46. ([Wikipedia, Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Robertson–Seymour theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robertson%E2%80%93Seymour_theorem): graph minors, obstruction sets and algorithmic consequences.
- **Learn:** [Diestel, Graph Theory, ch. 7 (Extremal graph theory), free preview](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch7.pdf): Turán, Erdős–Stone, Hadwiger's conjecture, regularity lemma with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Chudnovsky, Robertson, Seymour & Thomas, The strong perfect graph theorem (Annals 164, 2006)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2006/164-1/p02): proof of Berge's conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Campos, Griffiths, Morris & Sahasrabudhe, An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521): $R(k)\le(4-\varepsilon)^k$.
- **Further reading:** [Bondy & Murty, Graph Theory (Springer GTM, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-84628-970-5) and [Diestel, Graph Theory, ch. 12 (Graph minors)](https://www.math.uni-hamburg.de/home/diestel/books/graph.theory/preview/Ch12.pdf): graduate texts.
references.MSC 05Dxx - Extremal combinatorics:
## Reference
### Overview
Extremal combinatorics, a branch of [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics), asks for the largest or smallest size of a finite structure subject to a restriction: how many $k$-subsets of an $n$-set can pairwise intersect, how large an antichain of subsets can be, how large $n$ must be before every 2-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$. In MSC2020, 05Dxx is the home of the set-system, Ramsey, transversal and probabilistic parts of this subject; extremal problems for graphs themselves are classified separately under 05C35. ([MSC2020 05Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Dxx); [MSC2020 05Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Cxx))

The typical answer is a sharp bound together with the extremal configurations attaining it, as in the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem, where the extremal intersecting families are stars. ([Wikipedia: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Ko%E2%80%93Rado_theorem)) Where exact answers are out of reach, the subject studies asymptotics, and much of its modern progress comes from methods: random constructions, the polynomial method, flag algebras and hypergraph containers. ([Zhao, Probabilistic Methods in Combinatorics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-226-probabilistic-methods-in-combinatorics-fall-2022/mit18_226_f22_lec_full.pdf); [Keevash, Hypergraph Turán problems](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/keevash/papers/turan-survey.pdf); [Wikipedia: Cap set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_set))

### Scope
MSC2020 05Dxx "Extremal combinatorics" has 05D05 extremal set theory; 05D10 Ramsey theory (see also 05C55); 05D15 transversal (matching) theory; 05D40 probabilistic methods in extremal combinatorics, including polynomial methods (combinatorial Nullstellensatz, etc.); and 05D99. ([MSC2020 05Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Dxx))

Neighbours in [MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory): 05C35 "Extremal problems in graph theory" (see also 90C35), the code for extremal graph theory, whose "fundamental theorem" is the Erdős–Stone theorem below, and 05C55 "Generalized Ramsey theory" holds graph Ramsey numbers, cross-referenced with 05D10. ([MSC2020 05Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Cxx); [Wikipedia: Erdős–Stone theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Stone_theorem)) Exact counting belongs to [MSC 05Axx - Enumerative combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Axx%20-%20Enumerative%20combinatorics).

### Key concepts
- **Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem (05D05).** If $n\ge2r$ and $\mathcal A$ is a family of distinct $r$-subsets of an $n$-set in which every two members intersect, then $|\mathcal A|\le\binom{n-1}{r-1}$; for $n>2r$ the only extremal families are stars (all $r$-sets through a fixed point). Proved in 1938, published in 1961; Katona (1972) gave the cyclic-order proof, and Hilton–Milner (1967) showed that maximal intersecting families that are not maximum have size at most $\binom{n-1}{r-1}-\binom{n-r-1}{r-1}+1$. ([Wikipedia: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Ko%E2%80%93Rado_theorem)) This is the founding result of extremal [set theory](node:Set%20Theory) for finite set systems.
- **Sperner's theorem and LYM (05D05).** An antichain (Sperner family) of subsets of an $n$-set has at most $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ members, with equality only for all $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$-subsets or all $\lceil n/2\rceil$-subsets (Sperner, 1928). The proof goes through the LYM inequality $\sum_k s_k/\binom nk\le1$, where $s_k$ is the number of $k$-sets in the antichain. ([Wikipedia: Sperner's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperner%27s_theorem)) Antichains are a notion from [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders).
- **Kruskal–Katona theorem (05D05).** Write $N=\binom{n_i}{i}+\binom{n_{i-1}}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{n_j}{j}$ with $n_i>\cdots>n_j\ge j\ge1$. If $\mathcal A$ consists of $N$ distinct $i$-sets, the family of $(i-r)$-sets contained in members of $\mathcal A$ has size at least $\binom{n_i}{i-r}+\cdots+\binom{n_j}{j-r}$; Lovász's form: if $|\mathcal A|=\binom xi$ for real $x$, the shadow has size at least $\binom{x}{i-r}$. It characterises the $f$-vectors of simplicial complexes. ([Wikipedia: Kruskal–Katona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kruskal%E2%80%93Katona_theorem))
- **Ramsey numbers (05D10).** Erdős (1947): if $\binom nk2^{1-\binom k2}<1$ then $R(k,k)>n$, which gives exponential growth $\sqrt2^{\,k}$ by a random colouring. ([Zhao, Thm 1.1.2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-226-probabilistic-methods-in-combinatorics-fall-2022/mit18_226_f22_lec_full.pdf)) Erdős and Szekeres's bound implies $R(k,k)\le(1+o(1))4^{k-1}/\sqrt{\pi k}$, and $R(5,5)$ is known only to lie in $[43,46]$. ([Wikipedia: Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem)) Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved $R(k)\le(4-\varepsilon)^k$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, the first exponential improvement on the 1935 Erdős–Szekeres bound. ([arXiv:2303.09521](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521))
- **Hall's theorem (05D15).** A finite family of finite sets has a system of distinct representatives (a transversal) iff every subfamily of $k$ sets has a union of at least $k$ elements (P. Hall, 1935); equivalently a bipartite graph has a matching saturating one side iff every subset of that side has at least as many neighbours. It is interderivable with the theorems of König, König–Egerváry and Dilworth. ([Wikipedia: Hall's marriage theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%27s_marriage_theorem))
- **Probabilistic and container methods (05D40).** Caro (1979) and Wei (1981) show by a random ordering that every graph has an independent set of size at least $\sum_v1/(d(v)+1)$. The hypergraph container method gives, for every $\varepsilon>0$, a family of at most $n^{Cn^{3/2}}$ graphs, each with at most $(\tfrac14+\varepsilon)n^2$ edges, containing every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices; this recovers the Erdős–Kleitman–Rothschild count $2^{n^2/4+o(n^2)}$ of triangle-free graphs. ([Zhao, Thm 2.3.2, Ch. 11](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-226-probabilistic-methods-in-combinatorics-fall-2022/mit18_226_f22_lec_full.pdf)) Compare [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces).
- **Polynomial method (05D40).** Ellenberg and Gijswijt (2016), building on Croot–Lev–Pach, proved that a cap set (no three points on a line) in $\mathbb Z_3^n$ has size at most $2.756^n$, while the best constructions give about $2.22^n$: $2.2202^n$ from a December 2023 paper, and Wikipedia reports $(2.2203+\varepsilon)^n$ from a 2026 preprint of Hametner and Tyrrell, whose abstract claims constructions beating direct products of a fixed cap set. ([Wikipedia: Cap set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_set); [arXiv:2606.12194](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12194))
- **Turán-type problems (05C35, for contrast).** For a graph $H$ with $\chi(H)=r>2$, Erdős–Stone (1946) gives $\operatorname{ex}(n;H)=\big(\tfrac{r-2}{r-1}+o(1)\big)\binom n2$; for bipartite $H$ it only gives $o(n^2)$, and the degenerate case leads to the Zarankiewicz problem. ([Wikipedia: Erdős–Stone theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Stone_theorem)) For $r$-uniform hypergraphs the same question becomes the hypergraph Turán problem, on which there are very few results, even asymptotically. ([Keevash](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/keevash/papers/turan-survey.pdf)) See [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory).

### History
Sperner's theorem (1928), Hall's theorem (1935) and the Erdős–Szekeres Ramsey bound (1935) are among the first results; Mantel's 1907 theorem that the largest triangle-free graph on a given vertex set is complete bipartite is earlier still. ([Wikipedia: Sperner's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperner%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Hall's marriage theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%27s_marriage_theorem); [arXiv:2303.09521](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521); [Keevash](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/keevash/papers/turan-survey.pdf)) Erdős's 1947 random-colouring bound is one of the earliest applications of the probabilistic method in combinatorics, and Erdős–Ko–Rado (proved 1938, published 1961) and Kruskal–Katona (1963, 1968) shaped extremal set theory. ([Zhao](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-226-probabilistic-methods-in-combinatorics-fall-2022/mit18_226_f22_lec_full.pdf); [Wikipedia: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Ko%E2%80%93Rado_theorem); [Wikipedia: Kruskal–Katona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kruskal%E2%80%93Katona_theorem)) Recent landmarks are the cap-set bound (2016), Gilmer's 2022 breakthrough on union-closed families, and the 2023 exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey numbers. ([Wikipedia: Cap set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_set); [Wikipedia: Union-closed sets conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union-closed_sets_conjecture); [arXiv:2303.09521](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521))

### Open problems
- **Turán's tetrahedron problem.** Determine the largest 3-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with no $K_4^{(3)}$. Turán's construction gives density $\pi(K_4^{(3)})\ge5/9$; Chung–Lu proved $\pi\le(3+\sqrt{17})/12\approx0.5936$, and Razborov's flag-algebra computations suggest $\pi\le0.561666$. Keevash calls the question, posed in 1941, still open. ([Keevash, Hypergraph Turán problems](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/keevash/papers/turan-survey.pdf))
- **Erdős jumping problem.** Whether $r!/r^r$ is a jump for $r$-graphs is a long-standing open problem of Erdős. ([Keevash](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/keevash/papers/turan-survey.pdf))
- **Sunflower conjecture.** Erdős–Rado proved that more than $k!(r-1)^k$ distinct $k$-sets contain a sunflower with $r$ petals; the conjecture that $C_r^k$ sets suffice is open even for $r=3$. Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang proved a bound $C^k$ with $C=O(r^3\log k\log\log k)$; Rao improved this to $C=O(r\log(rk))$, and the best known is $C=O(r\log k)$ (Bell, Chueluecha and Warnke, 2021). ([Wikipedia: Sunflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunflower_%28mathematics%29))
- **Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture.** Every finite union-closed family other than $\{\varnothing\}$ has an element in at least half of its sets. It remains open; Gilmer (2022) gave the first constant fraction ($0.01$), improved within a week to $(3-\sqrt5)/2$ and later to about $0.38271$. ([Wikipedia: Union-closed sets conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union-closed_sets_conjecture))
- **Diagonal Ramsey numbers and cap sets.** The exact value of $R(5,5)$ is unknown, and the gap between $\sqrt2^{\,k}$ and $(4-\varepsilon)^k$ remains. ([Wikipedia: Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem)) As of March 2023 there was no exponential improvement on the Ellenberg–Gijswijt cap-set upper bound. ([Wikipedia: Cap set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_set))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Ko%E2%80%93Rado_theorem): statement, extremal families, Katona's proof, Hilton–Milner.
- **Reference:** [Ramsey's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem): bounds and small Ramsey numbers.
- **Learn:** [Zhao, Probabilistic Methods in Combinatorics (MIT 18.226 notes)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-226-probabilistic-methods-in-combinatorics-fall-2022/mit18_226_f22_lec_full.pdf): graduate notes on random constructions, the local lemma and containers.
- **Primary:** [Keevash, Hypergraph Turán problems (survey)](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/keevash/papers/turan-survey.pdf): survey of hypergraph Turán densities, flag algebras and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Campos, Griffiths, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey (arXiv:2303.09521)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09521): the $(4-\varepsilon)^k$ bound.
references.MSC 05Exx - Algebraic combinatorics:
## Reference
### Overview
Algebraic combinatorics uses methods of abstract algebra, especially group theory and representation theory, to study combinatorial problems, and applies combinatorial techniques to algebra in return. Up to the mid-1990s its objects either had a high degree of symmetry (association schemes, strongly regular graphs, posets with group actions) or a rich algebraic structure coming from representation theory (symmetric functions, Young tableaux); the AMS created the category 05E in 1991. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_combinatorics))

Its core is the combinatorics of partitions and tableaux: Schur functions, the RSK correspondence, the Littlewood–Richardson rule and the hook-length formula give clean product formulas and positive combinatorial interpretations for quantities from [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) and geometry. A current theme is where such formulas stop, e.g. for Kronecker and plethysm coefficients, and whether computational complexity explains why. ([Panova](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17511)) A second strand, combinatorial commutative algebra, studies simplicial complexes and polytopes through face rings. ([Wikipedia, Stanley–Reisner ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley%E2%80%93Reisner_ring)) It is part of [MSC 05 - Combinatorics](node:MSC%2005%20-%20Combinatorics) and of [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) more broadly.

### Scope
MSC2020 05E covers: 05E05 symmetric functions and generalizations; 05E10 combinatorial aspects of representation theory (see also 20C30); 05E14 combinatorial aspects of algebraic geometry (see also 14Nxx); 05E16 combinatorial aspects of groups and algebras (see also 22E45, 33C80); 05E18 group actions on combinatorial structures; 05E30 association schemes, strongly regular graphs; 05E40 combinatorial aspects of commutative algebra; 05E45 combinatorial aspects of simplicial complexes; 05E99 none of the above. ([MSC2020, 05E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Exx))

Neighbouring codes: the representation theory of $S_n$ itself is 20C30 in [MSC 20Cxx - Representation theory of groups](node:MSC%2020Cxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20groups) (05E10 is its combinatorial side); Schubert calculus and enumerative geometry are [MSC 14Nxx - Projective and enumerative algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Nxx%20-%20Projective%20and%20enumerative%20algebraic%20geometry) (05E14 the combinatorial side); polytopes as geometric objects are [MSC 52Bxx - Polytopes and polyhedra](node:MSC%2052Bxx%20-%20Polytopes%20and%20polyhedra); designs and finite geometries are [MSC 05Bxx - Designs and configurations](node:MSC%2005Bxx%20-%20Designs%20and%20configurations); graph spectra outside association schemes are [MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory). ([MSC2020, 05E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Exx); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_combinatorics))

### Key concepts
- **Schur functions and the Littlewood–Richardson rule (05E05, 05E10).** In $s_\lambda s_\mu=\sum_\nu c^\nu_{\lambda\mu}s_\nu$, the coefficient $c^\nu_{\lambda\mu}$ is the number of Littlewood–Richardson tableaux: semistandard skew tableaux of shape $\nu/\lambda$ and weight $\mu$ whose reversed reading word is a lattice word. The same numbers are tensor-product multiplicities for $GL_n$, induction multiplicities for symmetric groups, and intersection numbers of Schubert classes on a Grassmannian. ([Wikipedia, LR rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood%E2%80%93Richardson_rule))
- **RSK correspondence.** RSK is a bijection between matrices with nonnegative integer entries and pairs $(P,Q)$ of semistandard Young tableaux of the same shape, with the column sums giving the weight of $P$ and the row sums that of $Q$; transposing the matrix swaps $P$ and $Q$. It gives a bijective proof of Cauchy's identity $\sum_\lambda s_\lambda(x)s_\lambda(y)=\prod_{i,j}(1-x_iy_j)^{-1}$. ([Wikipedia, RSK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson%E2%80%93Schensted%E2%80%93Knuth_correspondence)) On permutations it gives $\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!$, where $f^\lambda$ is the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$. ([Stanley, Algebraic Combinatorics, Cor. 8.5 and RSK appendix](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/algcomb/algcomb.pdf))
- **Hook-length formula.** For $\lambda\vdash n$, $f^\lambda=n!/\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}h_\lambda(i,j)$; $f^\lambda$ is also the dimension of the irreducible representation of $S_n$ indexed by $\lambda$. Frame, Robinson and Thrall found it in 1953. ([Wikipedia, Hook length formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_length_formula))
- **Association schemes (05E30).** An $n$-class scheme partitions $X\times X$ into relations $R_0=\mathrm{id},R_1,\dots,R_n$ such that the number of $z$ with $(x,z)\in R_i$, $(z,y)\in R_j$ depends only on the $k$ with $(x,y)\in R_k$. For a symmetric scheme the adjacency matrices span a commutative Bose–Mesner algebra with a basis of primitive idempotents; the Hamming and Johnson schemes are central in coding theory, where the [linear programming](node:Linear%20Programming) method gives upper bounds on the size of a code with given minimum distance ([MSC 94Bxx - Theory of error-correcting codes and error-detecting codes](node:MSC%2094Bxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20error-correcting%20codes%20and%20error-detecting%20codes)). ([Wikipedia, Association scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_scheme)) Strongly regular graphs, regular graphs in which adjacent vertices have $\lambda$ and non-adjacent vertices $\mu$ common neighbours, are the 2-class case studied with [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_combinatorics))
- **Stanley–Reisner rings and face numbers (05E40, 05E45).** For a simplicial complex $\Delta$ on vertices $x_1,\dots,x_n$, $k[\Delta]=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I_\Delta$, with $I_\Delta$ generated by the squarefree monomials of non-faces; its Hilbert series has numerator the $h$-vector. Reisner's criterion: $\Delta$ is Cohen–Macaulay over $k$ iff the link of every face has vanishing reduced homology below its top dimension; so simplicial spheres are Cohen–Macaulay, which Stanley used to prove the Upper Bound Conjecture for spheres. ([Wikipedia, Stanley–Reisner ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley%E2%80%93Reisner_ring)) Adiprasito proved McMullen's $g$-conjecture in full generality, characterizing the face numbers of simplicial rational homology spheres, via a hard Lefschetz theorem beyond positivity. ([Adiprasito](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10454)) This links to [Polytopes](node:Polytopes).
- **Linear algebra on graphs and posets.** For a finite graph $G$ with adjacency matrix $A$, $(A^\ell)_{ij}$ counts walks of length $\ell$ from $v_i$ to $v_j$; and for a finite connected loopless graph, deleting row and column $i$ of the Laplacian gives $\det L_0=\kappa(G)$, the number of spanning trees (Matrix–Tree Theorem). Sperner's theorem, that the Boolean lattice $B_n$ has no antichain larger than its largest rank, is proved there with [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) on [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders) and group actions ([Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory)). ([Stanley, Thm. 1.1, Ch. 4, Thm. 9.8](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/algcomb/algcomb.pdf))

### History
Young introduced tableaux in 1900 and Frobenius applied them to the symmetric group in 1903; MacMahon, Hodge, Robinson, Rota, Lascoux, Schützenberger and Stanley contributed to the theory, and the name "algebraic combinatorics" dates from the late 1970s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_combinatorics)) Littlewood and Richardson stated their rule in 1934; the first rigorous proofs came from Thomas (1974) and Schützenberger (1977). ([Wikipedia, LR rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood%E2%80%93Richardson_rule)) Association schemes go back to Bose and Nair (1939) and Bose and Shimamoto (1952), with the Bose–Mesner algebra (1959) and Delsarte's 1973 thesis linking them to coding theory. ([Wikipedia, Association scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_scheme)) Stanley's Enumerative Combinatorics, Vol. 2 (1999; 2nd ed. 2023), with Chapter 7 on symmetric functions, became the standard reference. ([Stanley, EC page](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/)) Recent landmarks include Adiprasito's 2018 proof of the $g$-conjecture. ([Adiprasito](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10454))

### Open problems
- **Kronecker coefficients.** Finding a positive combinatorial formula for the Kronecker coefficients of the symmetric group is an open problem roughly 85 years old; the analogous problem for plethysm coefficients of $GL_n$ is also open, and both matter for Geometric Complexity Theory. ([Panova](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17511))
- **Stanley's positivity problems.** In Stanley's list "Positivity problems and conjectures in algebraic combinatorics", a modified "full rank" version of Problem 9 (on plethysm) remains open and only partial progress (Reiner and collaborators) is reported on Problem 4, while others, such as Haiman's $(q,t)$-Kostka positivity, have been solved. ([Stanley, problem updates](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/papers/problems_update.html))
- **Circulant Hadamard conjecture.** A circulant $n\times n$ matrix with entries $\pm1$ and $HH^{T}=nI$ should have $n=1$ or $n=4$; Turyn excluded orders $8m$ and some orders $4(2m+1)$. ([Stanley, Hadamard notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-318-topics-in-algebraic-combinatorics-spring-2006/f75a88e2ffba8f27de52aeebebfb7fe8_hadamard.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Algebraic combinatorics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_combinatorics): scope, history, and key topics.
- **Learn:** [Stanley, Algebraic Combinatorics: Walks, Trees, Tableaux, and More (free text)](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/algcomb/algcomb.pdf): undergraduate route through walks, Sperner, tableaux, RSK, Matrix–Tree.
- **Primary:** [Panova, Computational Complexity in Algebraic Combinatorics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17511): survey of Kronecker/plethysm problems and complexity.
- **Primary:** [Adiprasito, Combinatorial Lefschetz theorems beyond positivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10454): proof of the $g$-conjecture for spheres.
- **Further reading:** [Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, Vols. 1–2 (Cambridge)](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/): the graduate reference; Vol. 2 Ch. 7 on symmetric functions.
references.MSC 06 - Order, lattices, ordered algebr:
## Reference
### Overview
Order theory studies binary relations of comparison. A partial order is a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation; a lattice is a poset in which every nonempty finite set has a supremum and an infimum, and a complete lattice one in which every set does. A Galois connection is a pair of maps in opposite directions that are not inverse but closely related; a monotone Galois connection is the same as a pair of adjoint functors between posets. ([Wikipedia, Order theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_theory)) See [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders) for the basic notions.

Lattice theory began with algebra: Dedekind, revising Dirichlet's lectures on number theory in the 1890s, asked how many subgroups can be generated from three subgroups of an abelian group by sums and intersections (the answer is 28) and developed lattices as "Dualgruppen" in papers of 1897 and 1900; Schröder's algebra of logic had already treated distributive lattices and Boolean algebras. ([Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) Order also underlies computer science: directed complete partial orders are central to domain theory, the Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem is used in the formal semantics of programming languages and in abstract interpretation, and formal concept analysis builds concept lattices from a collection of objects and their properties. ([Wikipedia, Order theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_theory); [Wikipedia, Knaster–Tarski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knaster%E2%80%93Tarski_theorem); [Wikipedia, Introduction to Lattices and Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Introduction_to_Lattices_and_Order))

### Scope
MSC2020 field 06 ("Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures", see also 18B35) has six sections. ([MSC2020, 06](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06-XX))
- [MSC 06Axx - Ordered sets](node:MSC%2006Axx%20-%20Ordered%20sets): total orders (06A05), partial orders (06A06), [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) of posets (06A07), algebraic aspects of posets (06A11), semilattices (06A12), Galois correspondences and closure operators (06A15), generalizations (06A75). ([MSC2020, 06A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Axx))
- [MSC 06Bxx - Lattices](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices) (see also 03G10): structure theory, ideals and congruences, representations of lattices, varieties of lattices, complete lattices and completions, free and projective lattices and word problems, topological lattices, continuous lattices and posets (06B05–06B75). ([MSC2020, 06B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Bxx))
- [MSC 06Cxx - Modular lattices, complemented lattices](node:MSC%2006Cxx%20-%20Modular%20lattices,%20complemented%20lattices): modular and Desarguesian lattices (06C05), semimodular and geometric lattices (06C10), complemented and orthocomplemented lattices and posets (06C15, see also 03G12 and 81P10), complemented modular lattices and continuous geometries (06C20). ([MSC2020, 06C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Cxx))
- [MSC 06Dxx - Distributive lattices](node:MSC%2006Dxx%20-%20Distributive%20lattices), [MSC 06Exx - Boolean algebras (Boolean rings)](node:MSC%2006Exx%20-%20Boolean%20algebras%20%28Boolean%20rings%29) (see also 03G05) and [MSC 06Fxx - Ordered structures](node:MSC%2006Fxx%20-%20Ordered%20structures). ([MSC2020, 06](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06-XX); [MSC2020, 06E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Exx))

Neighbours, by the listed cross-references: lattices (06B) point to 03G10 in [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic); continuous lattices and posets (06B35) point to 68Q55 in [MSC 68Qxx - Theory of computing](node:MSC%2068Qxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20computing); word problems for lattices (06B25) point to 03D40, 08A50 and 20F10; and the field as a whole points to 18B35 in [MSC 18Bxx - Special categories](node:MSC%2018Bxx%20-%20Special%20categories). ([MSC2020, 06B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Bxx); [MSC2020, 06](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Dilworth's theorem (06A07, 1950).** In a finite poset the maximum size of an antichain equals the minimum number of chains needed to cover the poset; more generally a poset has finite width $w$ iff it can be partitioned into $w$ chains, while for infinite width the two numbers can differ. The dual (Mirsky) says the length of a longest chain equals the minimum number of antichains partitioning the poset; Dilworth's theorem is equivalent to Kőnig's theorem on bipartite matchings. ([Wikipedia, Dilworth's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilworth%27s_theorem); [Nation, Thm 1.4](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))
- **Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem (06B23).** If $L$ is a complete lattice and $f:L\to L$ is monotone, the set of fixed points of $f$ is itself a complete lattice; in particular $f$ has a least fixed point. Conversely (Davis 1955), a lattice on which every order-preserving self-map has a fixed point is complete. ([Wikipedia, Knaster–Tarski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knaster%E2%80%93Tarski_theorem); [Nation, Thm 2.12](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) The theorem gives a short proof of the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem on [Cardinality](node:Cardinality). ([Wikipedia, Knaster–Tarski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knaster%E2%80%93Tarski_theorem))
- **Birkhoff, Stone and Priestley representation (06D).** Every finite distributive lattice is isomorphic to the lattice of down-sets of the poset of its join-irreducible elements (Birkhoff 1937). This may fail for infinite distributive lattices, which may have no join-irreducibles at all; instead Stone represents distributive lattices by compact open sets of spectral spaces, and Priestley represents bounded distributive lattices by Priestley spaces, Stone spaces with a partial order tied to the topology by the Priestley separation axiom. ([Wikipedia, Birkhoff's representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_representation_theorem)) Boolean algebras are the case handled by Stone duality in [MSC 06Exx - Boolean algebras (Boolean rings)](node:MSC%2006Exx%20-%20Boolean%20algebras%20%28Boolean%20rings%29).
- **Congruence lattices (06B10).** Grätzer and Schmidt (1963): every algebraic lattice is isomorphic to the congruence lattice of some algebra; every finite distributive lattice is the congruence lattice of a finite lattice (Dilworth). Dilworth's congruence lattice problem, whether every distributive algebraic lattice is the congruence lattice of a lattice, was answered negatively by Wehrung in 2007, with the counterexample size later lowered to $\aleph_2$ by Růžička. ([Wikipedia, Congruence lattice problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_lattice_problem)) This links field 06 with [MSC 08 - General algebraic systems](node:MSC%2008%20-%20General%20algebraic%20systems).
- **Free and modular lattices (06B25, 06C05).** Skolem (1920) and independently Whitman (1941) solved the word problem for free lattices. In the variety of modular lattices the free lattice on three generators has 28 elements (Dedekind), but Freese (1980) proved the word problem for the free modular lattice on five generators unsolvable, and Herrmann did the same for four; hence some lattice equation holds in all finite modular lattices but not in all modular lattices. ([Nation, ch. 6 and 7](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))
- **Galois connections and formal concept analysis (06A15).** Formal concept analysis builds "concept lattices" from a collection of objects and their properties; Davey and Priestley treat concept lattices, closure operators and Galois connections, and the embedding of a poset in the smallest complete lattice containing it (the Dedekind–MacNeille completion). ([Wikipedia, Introduction to Lattices and Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Introduction_to_Lattices_and_Order))
- **Domain theory (06B35).** Directed complete partial orders, in which directed subsets have suprema, are tied to domain theory, where function spaces between posets, ordered pointwise, play an important role; 06B35 cross-refers to 68Q55. ([Wikipedia, Order theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_theory); [MSC2020, 06B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Bxx)) See [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory) and [Functional Programming](node:Functional%20Programming) for the computational side.

### History
Explicit partial orders appear in the 19th century in Boole, Peirce, Dedekind and Schröder; the word "poset" is due to Birkhoff in the second edition of his book *Lattice Theory*. ([Wikipedia, Order theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_theory)) Dedekind's 1897 and 1900 papers on "Dualgruppen" are the classical starting point, and lattice theory had its "great awakening" in the 1930s. ([Nation](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) Birkhoff's representation theorem dates from 1937, Dilworth's chain theorem from 1950, and Tarski's general fixed-point theorem from 1955 (after Knaster and Tarski's earlier power-set case). ([Wikipedia, Birkhoff's representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_representation_theorem); [Wikipedia, Dilworth's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilworth%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Knaster–Tarski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knaster%E2%80%93Tarski_theorem)) Davey and Priestley's *Introduction to Lattices and Order* (first edition 1990) was substantially revised in a new edition that added Galois connections and fixpoint calculus, taking account of applications in computer science. ([Cambridge, preface to the second edition](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-lattices-and-order/preface-to-the-second-edition/783D25FF7EB33A7BCB0E60DCB8275470))

### Open problems
- **The 1/3–2/3 conjecture (06A07).** Every finite poset that is not a total order has two elements $x,y$ such that the probability that $x$ precedes $y$ in a uniformly random linear extension lies in $[1/3,2/3]$. Posed by Kislitsyn (1968) and independently by Fredman and Linial, it remains unsolved; Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter proved the bound $\tfrac12-\tfrac{\sqrt5}{10}\approx0.276$, and it is known for width two, height two, semiorders and posets with at most 13 elements. ([Wikipedia, 1/3–2/3 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture))
- **Finite lattice representation problem.** Is every finite lattice isomorphic to the congruence lattice of a finite algebra? It is among the oldest unsolved problems of universal algebra; Pálfy and Pudlák (1980) showed it is equivalent to asking whether every finite lattice is an interval in the subgroup lattice of a finite group. ([Wikipedia, Finite lattice representation problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_lattice_representation_problem)) DeMeo showed by computer that, with one possible exception, every lattice with at most seven elements is such a congruence lattice. ([DeMeo, arXiv:1204.4305](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4305))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Order theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_theory): definitions, Galois connections, history and applications.
- **Learn:** [Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf): Dilworth, fixed points, congruence lattices, free and modular lattices, with exercises.
- **Primary:** [DeMeo, Congruence lattices of finite algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4305): PhD thesis reviewing methods for finding a finite algebra with a given congruence lattice, with new results on small lattices.
- **Further reading:** [Davey and Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order (CUP, 2nd ed.)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-lattices-and-order/preface-to-the-second-edition/783D25FF7EB33A7BCB0E60DCB8275470): introduction to order and lattices, with Galois connections and fixpoint calculus. [Grätzer, Lattice Theory: Foundation (Springer Basel, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-0018-1): graduate monograph on lattice theory.
references.MSC 06Axx - Ordered sets:
## Reference
### Overview
A partially ordered set (poset) is a set with a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation; 06A studies posets in their own right, as opposed to lattices and ordered algebraic structures elsewhere in field 06. A finite relation can be viewed equivalently as a set of pairs, a bipartite graph, a directed graph, or an incidence matrix, a locally finite poset is determined by its Hasse diagram of covering pairs, and on a finite set the preorders correspond one-to-one with the topologies. ([Britz & Cameron, Partially ordered sets](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf)) Basic vocabulary is in [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders); this map covers the research area inside [MSC 06 - Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures](node:MSC%2006%20-%20Order,%20lattices,%20ordered%20algebraic%20structures).

Research in 06A is largely combinatorial: chain and antichain decompositions (Dilworth, Mirsky), linear extensions and their counting, order dimension, and the incidence algebra and Möbius function, developed in Rota's series of papers from 1964 and a tool of enumerative [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics). ([Wikipedia, Dilworth's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilworth%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Incidence algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_algebra)) Its best-known open problem, the 1/3–2/3 conjecture, comes from sorting under partial information. ([Wikipedia, 1/3–2/3 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture))

### Scope
MSC2020 06A lists: 06A05 total orders; 06A06 partial orders, general; 06A07 combinatorics of partially ordered sets; 06A11 algebraic aspects of posets; 06A12 semilattices (see also 20M10; for topological semilattices see 22A26); 06A15 Galois correspondences, closure operators (in relation to ordered sets); 06A75 generalizations of ordered sets; 06A99. ([MSC2020, 06A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Axx))

Neighbours: 06A12 cross-refers semilattices to 20M10 in [MSC 20Mxx - Semigroups](node:MSC%2020Mxx%20-%20Semigroups) and topological semilattices to 22A26 ([MSC2020, 06A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Axx)); the other sections of field 06 are [MSC 06Bxx - Lattices](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices), [MSC 06Cxx - Modular lattices, complemented lattices](node:MSC%2006Cxx%20-%20Modular%20lattices,%20complemented%20lattices), [MSC 06Dxx - Distributive lattices](node:MSC%2006Dxx%20-%20Distributive%20lattices), [MSC 06Exx - Boolean algebras (Boolean rings)](node:MSC%2006Exx%20-%20Boolean%20algebras%20%28Boolean%20rings%29) and [MSC 06Fxx - Ordered structures](node:MSC%2006Fxx%20-%20Ordered%20structures). ([MSC2020, 06](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Dilworth's and Mirsky's theorems (06A07).** In a finite poset the maximum size of an antichain (the width) equals the minimum number of chains in a partition into chains (Dilworth, 1950); dually, the maximum size of a chain equals the minimum number of antichains in a partition (Mirsky, 1971). Dilworth's theorem is equivalent to Kőnig's theorem on bipartite matchings and to Hall's marriage theorem, links to [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory). For infinite posets of finite width $w$ a partition into $w$ chains still exists (via the De Bruijn–Erdős theorem), but for infinite width the two quantities can differ greatly. ([Wikipedia, Dilworth's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilworth%27s_theorem)) The antichain partition is constructive: remove the maximal elements repeatedly. ([Britz & Cameron, §4](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- **Szpilrajn extension theorem (06A05, 06A06).** Every partial order on a set is contained in a total order on the same set (Szpilrajn, 1930); the infinite case uses Zorn's lemma, and some form of the axiom of choice is necessary. ([Wikipedia, Szpilrajn extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szpilrajn_extension_theorem)) The infinite version is not provable in ZF but is strictly weaker than the axiom of choice: there is a model of ZF in which it holds while Zorn's lemma fails, a point of contact with [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory). ([Britz & Cameron, §6](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- **Order dimension (06A07).** Every finite partial order is the intersection of its linear extensions; its dimension is the least number of total orders whose intersection is the order, and the crown (standard example) on $2n$ elements has dimension $n$. By the compactness theorem of [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory), a poset all of whose finite subposets have dimension at most $n$ has dimension at most $n$. ([Britz & Cameron, §6](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf)) The notion is due to Dushnik and Miller (1941); deciding whether dimension is at most $k$ is NP-complete for each fixed $k\ge3$ (Yannakakis, 1982) but polynomial for $k=2$; and Schnyder's theorem says a graph is planar iff its vertex–edge incidence poset has dimension at most 3. ([Wikipedia, Order dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_dimension))
- **Incidence algebra and Möbius inversion (06A07, 06A11).** For a locally finite poset $P$ the incidence algebra consists of functions on intervals $[x,y]$ with convolution $(f*g)(x,y)=\sum_{x\le z\le y}f(x,z)g(z,y)$; the zeta function $\zeta\equiv1$ is invertible, and its inverse is the Möbius function, $\mu(x,x)=1$ and $\mu(x,y)=-\sum_{x\le z<y}\mu(x,z)$ for $x<y$. On the Boolean lattice $\mu(S,T)=(-1)^{|T\setminus S|}$ (inclusion–exclusion), and on divisibility $\mu$ is the classical number-theoretic Möbius function. ([Wikipedia, Incidence algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_algebra)) Möbius inversion reads $f=g\zeta\iff g=f\mu$; on the subspace lattice of $\mathrm{GF}(q)^n$, $\mu(U,W)=(-1)^kq^{\binom k2}$ with $k=\dim W-\dim U$. ([Britz & Cameron, §8](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf)) The foundational paper is Rota, "On the foundations of combinatorial theory I. Theory of Möbius functions" (1964). ([Crossref, Rota 1964](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00531932))
- **Linear extensions and balance (06A07).** For a finite poset $P$ that is not a chain, let $\delta(P)$ be the largest $\delta$ such that some pair $x,y$ satisfies $\delta\le\Pr[x<y]\le1-\delta$ in a uniformly random linear extension. Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter (1995) proved $\delta(P)\ge(5-\sqrt5)/10\approx0.276$ for all finite non-chains, a bound that is optimal for infinite posets; Kahn and Saks (1984) observed that if the 1/3–2/3 conjecture holds, a poset with $E$ linear extensions can be sorted with at most $\log_{3/2}E$ further comparisons (ignoring the cost of choosing them). ([Wikipedia, 1/3–2/3 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture)) Aires, Chan, Pak and Panova (2026 preprint) report an $\varepsilon$-improvement of the Brightwell–Felsner–Trotter bound for finite posets, "the first general result towards the 1/3–2/3 conjecture in over 30 years". ([Aires–Chan–Pak–Panova, arXiv 2609.30888](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30888))
- **Finite posets and topology (06A06).** For finite $X$ there is a bijection between topologies on $X$ and preorders on $X$: $x\preceq y$ iff every open set containing $x$ contains $y$; this connects finite posets to [Topological Spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces). Down-sets of a finite poset form a distributive lattice, and every finite distributive lattice arises this way from its poset of join-irreducibles. ([Britz & Cameron, §§7, 10](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))

### History
Szpilrajn proved the extension theorem in 1930 and Dushnik and Miller introduced dimension in 1941. ([Wikipedia, Szpilrajn extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szpilrajn_extension_theorem); [Wikipedia, Order dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_dimension)) Dilworth's theorem appeared in 1950 in the *Annals of Mathematics* and Mirsky's dual in 1971. ([Wikipedia, Dilworth's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilworth%27s_theorem)) Rota's series of papers on incidence algebras began in 1964, and Kislitsyn formulated the 1/3–2/3 conjecture in 1968, and it was later made independently by Fredman and by Linial (1984). ([Wikipedia, Incidence algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_algebra); [Wikipedia, 1/3–2/3 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture)) Davey and Priestley's *Introduction to Lattices and Order* appeared in a second edition with Cambridge University Press in 2002. ([Crossref, Davey–Priestley](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511809088))

### Open problems
- **The 1/3–2/3 conjecture.** Every finite poset that is not totally ordered has elements $x,y$ with $1/3\le\Pr[x<y]\le2/3$ in a uniformly random linear extension; the constants are attained by the three-element poset with a single relation. The conjecture is open, called "one of the most intriguing problems in the combinatorial theory of posets"; it is known for width two, height two, semiorders, N-free posets, posets with at most 13 elements, and several other classes. ([Wikipedia, 1/3–2/3 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture)) The 2026 Aires–Chan–Pak–Panova preprint treats it as unresolved and improves only the general lower bound. ([Aires–Chan–Pak–Panova, arXiv 2609.30888](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30888))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Order dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_dimension): realizers, standard examples, complexity, planarity.
- **Learn:** [Britz & Cameron, Partially ordered sets (QMUL notes)](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf): relations, Dilworth, linear extensions, dimension, Möbius function, lattices.
- **Primary:** [Aires, Chan, Pak & Panova, Breaking the Infinite Barrier in the 1/3–2/3 Conjecture (arXiv 2609.30888)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30888): current research on balanced pairs.
- **Primary:** [Rota, On the foundations of combinatorial theory I (1964)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00531932): founding paper of Möbius functions of posets.
- **Further reading:** [Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order (CUP, 2nd ed. 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511809088): textbook on orders and lattices.
references.MSC 06Bxx - Lattices:
## Reference
### Overview
A lattice is a poset in which every pair of elements has a meet (greatest lower bound) and a join (least upper bound); equivalently, an algebra $(L,\wedge,\vee)$ with two idempotent, commutative, associative operations satisfying the absorption laws, the order being recovered by $x\le y\iff x\wedge y=x$. A complete lattice has meets and joins of all subsets. ([Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory, ch. 2](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) Dedekind developed the basic theory in the 1890s (as *Dualgruppen*) while asking how many subgroups three subgroups of an abelian group generate under sums and intersections, the answer being 28; the subject revived in the 1930s with [universal algebra](node:Universal%20Algebra) (Birkhoff, Ore). ([Nation, Introduction](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))

06B is general [lattice theory](node:Lattice%20Theory): structure, ideals and congruences, representations, varieties, completions, free lattices and their word problem, and topological and continuous lattices. Lattices with extra laws have their own codes ([MSC 06Cxx - Modular lattices, complemented lattices](node:MSC%2006Cxx%20-%20Modular%20lattices,%20complemented%20lattices), [MSC 06Dxx - Distributive lattices](node:MSC%2006Dxx%20-%20Distributive%20lattices), [MSC 06Exx - Boolean algebras (Boolean rings)](node:MSC%2006Exx%20-%20Boolean%20algebras%20%28Boolean%20rings%29)), and the underlying order theory is [MSC 06Axx - Ordered sets](node:MSC%2006Axx%20-%20Ordered%20sets) and [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders). ([MSC2020, 06B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Bxx); [MSC2020, 06](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06-XX))

### Scope
MSC2020 06B (see also 03G10) lists: 06B05 structure theory of lattices; 06B10 lattice ideals, congruence relations; 06B15 representations of lattices; 06B20 varieties of lattices; 06B23 complete lattices, completions; 06B25 free lattices, projective lattices, word problems (see also 03D40, 08A50, 20F10); 06B30 topological lattices (see also 06F30, 22A26, 54F05, 54H12); 06B35 continuous lattices and posets, applications (see also 06B30, 06D10, 06F30, 18B35, 22A26, 68Q55); 06B75 generalizations of lattices; 06B99. ([MSC2020, 06B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Bxx))

Neighbours named by the cross-references: the 06B section points to 03G10 in [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic); 06B25 (free lattices, word problems) points to 03D40 in [MSC 03Dxx - Computability and recursion theory](node:MSC%2003Dxx%20-%20Computability%20and%20recursion%20theory), to 08A50 in [MSC 08Axx - Algebraic structures](node:MSC%2008Axx%20-%20Algebraic%20structures) and to 20F10; 06B30 and 06B35 point to 06F30 in [MSC 06Fxx - Ordered structures](node:MSC%2006Fxx%20-%20Ordered%20structures) and to 22A26; 06B35 (continuous lattices and posets) also points to 06D10, 18B35 and 68Q55. ([MSC2020, 06B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Fixed points and completeness (06B23).** Knaster–Tarski: if $L$ is a complete lattice and $f:L\to L$ is order-preserving, the fixed points of $f$ form a complete lattice; in particular $f$ has a least fixed point, the least $x$ with $f(x)\le x$. Tarski stated the general form in 1955; Davis (1955) proved the converse, that a lattice on which every order-preserving self-map has a fixed point is complete. ([Wikipedia, Knaster–Tarski theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knaster%E2%80%93Tarski_theorem); [Nation, Thm 2.12](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))
- **Dedekind–MacNeille completion (06B23).** For a poset $P$ and $A\subseteq P$, let $A^u$ and $A^\ell$ be the sets of upper and lower bounds; the sets with $(A^u)^\ell=A$, ordered by inclusion, form the smallest complete lattice containing $P$ (MacNeille, 1937), characterized as the completion in which $P$ is both join-dense and meet-dense. Applied to $\mathbb Q$ it gives the [real line](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits) with $\pm\infty$. ([Wikipedia, Dedekind–MacNeille completion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind%E2%80%93MacNeille_completion)) Every join-dense completion preserves the meets that already exist in $P$; the MacNeille completion also preserves all existing joins. ([Nation, ch. 2](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))
- **Free lattices and Whitman's condition (06B25).** In the free lattice $FL(X)$, for generators $x,y$: $x\le y$ iff $x=y$; $x\le q_1\vee q_2$ iff $x\le q_1$ or $x\le q_2$; dually for meets; and Whitman's condition (W): $p_1\wedge p_2\le q_1\vee q_2$ iff $p_1\le q_1\vee q_2$ or $p_2\le q_1\vee q_2$ or $p_1\wedge p_2\le q_1$ or $p_1\wedge p_2\le q_2$. These rules decide the word problem for lattices. A finite lattice embeds in a free lattice iff it satisfies (W) and both semidistributive laws; every countable poset embeds in $FL(3)$, but every chain in a free lattice is countable. ([Nation, Thms 6.2, 6.9, 6.10](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) $FL(3)$ is infinite and contains free sublattices on countably many generators, and a complete free lattice on three generators does not exist as a set. ([Wikipedia, Free lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_lattice))
- **Congruences (06B10).** For every lattice $L$, $\mathrm{Con}\,L$ is a distributive algebraic lattice (the majority term $(x\wedge y)\vee(x\wedge z)\vee(y\wedge z)$ forces distributivity), and every lattice is a subdirect product of subdirectly irreducible lattices. ([Nation, Thms 5.7, 5.8](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) Conversely every finite distributive lattice is $\mathrm{Con}\,L$ for a finite lattice $L$ (Dilworth, c. 1940; published by Grätzer and Schmidt 1962), and Grätzer and Schmidt (1963) showed every algebraic lattice is the congruence lattice of some algebra. ([Wikipedia, Congruence lattice problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_lattice_problem)) Wehrung solved Dilworth's congruence lattice problem negatively: there is a distributive algebraic lattice with $\aleph_{\omega+1}$ compact elements that is not $\mathrm{Con}\,L$ for any lattice $L$ ([Wehrung, arXiv math/0601059](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601059)); Růžička lowered the bound to $\aleph_2$, which is optimal since every distributive algebraic lattice with at most $\aleph_1$ compact elements is representable. ([Wikipedia, Congruence lattice problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_lattice_problem))
- **Representations and varieties (06B15, 06B20).** Whitman (1946) proved that every lattice embeds in the lattice $\mathrm{Eq}\,X$ of equivalence relations on some set, and hence every lattice embeds in the subgroup lattice of a group, linking to [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory). ([Nation, ch. 4](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) Lattice varieties form a lattice dually isomorphic to the fully invariant congruences of $FL(\omega)$; Jónsson's lemma says a subdirectly irreducible lattice in $\mathrm{HSP}(\mathcal K)$ lies in $\mathrm{HSP_u}(\mathcal K)$, and the variety generated by a finite lattice is finitely based. ([Nation, Thms 7.3, 7.7, 7.10](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) This is the lattice case of [MSC 08Bxx - Varieties](node:MSC%2008Bxx%20-%20Varieties).
- **$M_3$ and $N_5$ (06B05).** A lattice is modular iff it has no sublattice isomorphic to the pentagon $N_5$, and distributive iff it has no sublattice isomorphic to $N_5$ or the diamond $M_3$; these are the gateways from 06B to 06C and 06D. ([Britz & Cameron, Thm 10.1](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf); [Nation, Thms 9.1, 9.2](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))

### History
Dedekind's papers of 1897 and 1900 founded the theory; Birkhoff and Ore developed it in the 1930s within universal algebra. ([Nation, Introduction](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) MacNeille's completion dates from 1937, Whitman's representation theorem from 1946, and Tarski's fixed-point theorem and Davis's converse from 1955. ([Wikipedia, Dedekind–MacNeille completion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind%E2%80%93MacNeille_completion); [Nation, ch. 4](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf); [Wikipedia, Knaster–Tarski theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knaster%E2%80%93Tarski_theorem)) Dilworth's congruence lattice problem, linked to his work of about 1940 and first stated in print by Grätzer and Schmidt in 1962, stayed open until Wehrung's 2007 solution in *Advances in Mathematics*. ([Wikipedia, Congruence lattice problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_lattice_problem); [Wehrung, arXiv math/0601059](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601059)) Grätzer's *Lattice Theory: Foundation* was published by Springer Basel in 2011. ([Crossref, Grätzer](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-0018-1))

### Open problems
- **Finite lattice representation problem.** Does every finite lattice occur as the congruence lattice of some finite algebra? Wikipedia calls it "among the oldest unsolved problems in universal algebra"; Pálfy and Pudlák (1980) showed it is equivalent to asking whether every finite lattice is an interval in the subgroup lattice of a finite group. ([Wikipedia, Finite lattice representation problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_lattice_representation_problem)) DeMeo's thesis describes it as "an important and long-standing open problem" and reports that, with one possible exception, every lattice with at most seven elements is the congruence lattice of a finite algebra. ([DeMeo, arXiv 1204.4305](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4305))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Congruence lattice problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_lattice_problem): history and solution of Dilworth's problem.
- **Learn:** [Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf): one-semester text through free lattices, varieties, congruences, modular and geometric lattices.
- **Primary:** [Wehrung, A solution to Dilworth's Congruence Lattice Problem (Adv. Math. 2007; arXiv math/0601059)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601059): the negative solution of the CLP.
- **Primary:** [DeMeo, Congruence lattices of finite algebras (arXiv 1204.4305)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4305): PhD thesis reviewing methods for the finite lattice representation problem.
- **Further reading:** [Grätzer, Lattice Theory: Foundation (Springer Basel, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-0018-1): monograph on lattice theory.
references.MSC 06Cxx - Modular lattices, complement:
## Reference
### Overview
A lattice is modular if $a\le b$ implies $a\vee(x\wedge b)=(a\vee x)\wedge b$; this is equivalent to an unconditional identity, so modular lattices form a variety (also called Dedekind lattices), and every distributive lattice is modular. Submodule lattices, subgroup lattices of [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) and normal-subgroup lattices are modular, whereas subgroup lattices of arbitrary groups need not be (the dihedral group of order 8 is a counterexample). ([Wikipedia, Modular lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_lattice)) In a bounded lattice a complement of $a$ is an element $b$ with $a\wedge b=0$ and $a\vee b=1$; in a complemented modular lattice every interval is again complemented. ([Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory, Lemma 12.1](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))

06C is where [lattice theory](node:Lattice%20Theory) meets geometry: the subspace lattice of a vector space is modular, complemented and geometric, and coordinatization theorems recover a vector space over a division ring, or a von Neumann regular ring, from such a lattice; in the Hilbert-space formulation of quantum logic the propositions of a system form the lattice of closed subspaces of a [Hilbert space](node:Hilbert%20Spaces). ([Nation, ch. 12](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf); [Wehrung, arXiv math/0409250](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0409250); [Wikipedia, Quantum logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_logic)) It sits between [MSC 06Bxx - Lattices](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices) and [MSC 06Dxx - Distributive lattices](node:MSC%2006Dxx%20-%20Distributive%20lattices) in [MSC 06 - Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures](node:MSC%2006%20-%20Order,%20lattices,%20ordered%20algebraic%20structures).

### Scope
MSC2020 06C lists: 06C05 modular lattices, Desarguesian lattices; 06C10 semimodular lattices, geometric lattices; 06C15 complemented lattices, orthocomplemented lattices and posets (see also 03G12, 81P10); 06C20 complemented modular lattices, continuous geometries; 06C99. ([MSC2020, 06C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Cxx))

Neighbours named by the cross-references: 06C15 (complemented and orthocomplemented lattices) points to 03G12 in [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic) and to 81P10 in [MSC 81Pxx - Foundations, quantum information and its processing, quantum axioms, and philosophy](node:MSC%2081Pxx%20-%20Foundations,%20quantum%20information%20and%20its%20processing,%20quantum%20axioms,%20and%20philosophy). ([MSC2020, 06C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **$N_5$, $M_3$ and the diamond isomorphism (06C05).** A lattice is modular iff it has no sublattice isomorphic to the pentagon $N_5$; a modular lattice is distributive iff it has no sublattice isomorphic to the diamond $M_3$ (Birkhoff). In a modular lattice the maps $x\mapsto x\wedge a$ and $y\mapsto y\vee b$ are mutually inverse isomorphisms between the intervals $[b,a\vee b]$ and $[a\wedge b,a]$. ([Nation, Thms 9.1–9.3](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf); [Britz & Cameron, Thm 10.1](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf)) A finite lattice is modular iff it is graded with rank function satisfying $\rho(a)+\rho(b)=\rho(a\vee b)+\rho(a\wedge b)$; Dedekind showed in 1900 that the free modular lattice on three generators has 28 elements. ([Wikipedia, Modular lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_lattice))
- **Semimodularity and the Jordan–Dedekind chain condition (06C10).** $L$ is (upper) semimodular if $a\succ a\wedge b$ implies $a\vee b\succ b$; modular lattices are both upper and lower semimodular. In a semimodular lattice, if some maximal chain from $a$ to $b$ is finite then all chains from $a$ to $b$ are finite and all maximal ones have the same length (first proved for modular lattices by Dedekind in 1897); the subnormal subgroups of a finite group form a lower semimodular sublattice of the subgroup lattice, so the dual chain theorems give the Jordan–Hölder theorem for composition series in [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory). ([Nation, Thms 9.4, 9.8](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))
- **Geometric lattices and matroids (06C10).** A geometric lattice is an algebraic semimodular lattice in which every element is a join of atoms; examples are subspace lattices of [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) and the lattice $\mathrm{Eq}\,X$ of equivalence relations. Mac Lane: a lattice is geometric iff it is the lattice of closed sets of an algebraic closure operator with the exchange property. Every geometric lattice is relatively complemented. ([Nation, Thms 11.2, 11.3](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) Finite geometric lattices correspond exactly to simple matroids via their lattices of flats, with semimodularity matching submodularity of the rank function. ([Wikipedia, Geometric lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_lattice))
- **Desarguesian lattices and projective geometry (06C05, 06C20).** Every algebraic complemented modular lattice is geometric, and every complemented modular lattice embeds in a geometric modular lattice (Jónsson, extending Frink). Subdirectly irreducible geometric modular lattices of dimension $>2$ correspond to projective geometries; those of dimension $\ge4$ are Arguesian, and (Birkhoff–Frink) a subdirectly irreducible geometric Arguesian lattice of dimension $\kappa\ge3$ is the subspace lattice of a $\kappa$-dimensional vector space over a division ring, the lattice form of coordinatization in [Projective Geometry](node:Projective%20Geometry). ([Nation, Thms 12.2–12.6](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf))
- **Von Neumann coordinatization and continuous geometries (06C20).** Von Neumann's coordinatization theorem: if a complemented modular lattice $L$ has a spanning finite homogeneous sequence with at least four elements, then $L$ is isomorphic to the lattice of principal right ideals of a von Neumann regular ring; Jónsson extended this to complemented Arguesian lattices with a large partial 3-frame. Wehrung proved that coordinatizability is nevertheless not first-order, answering a 1960 problem of Jónsson. ([Wehrung, J. Math. Logic 2006, arXiv math/0409250](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0409250)) A continuous geometry is an irreducible complete complemented modular lattice satisfying a continuity condition; it carries a dimension function $D$ into $[0,1]$ with $D(a\vee b)+D(a\wedge b)=D(a)+D(b)$, and the projections of a finite type II von Neumann algebra form one. Kaplansky (1955) showed every orthocomplemented complete modular lattice is a continuous geometry. ([Wikipedia, Continuous geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_geometry))
- **Orthocomplemented and orthomodular lattices (06C15).** An orthomodular lattice is an orthocomplemented lattice in which $a\le c$ implies $a\vee(a^\perp\wedge c)=c$, a weakening of modularity; the closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space form an orthomodular lattice. ([Wikipedia, Orthomodular lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthomodular_lattice)) Birkhoff and von Neumann's "The Logic of Quantum Mechanics" (*Annals of Mathematics*, 1936) introduced quantum logic; in its Hilbert-space formulation the propositions are the closed subspaces, the negation of $V$ is the orthogonal complement $V^\perp$, and the distributive law fails for non-commuting observables such as position and momentum. ([Wikipedia, Quantum logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_logic))

### History
Dedekind discovered the modular law in papers of 1894, 1897 and 1900. ([Wikipedia, Modular lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_lattice)) Birkhoff developed geometric lattices in the 1930s, with related work by Menger, Alt and Schreiber. ([Nation, ch. 11](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf)) Von Neumann introduced continuous geometries in 1936 as analogues of complex projective geometry with dimensions in $[0,1]$, and Birkhoff and von Neumann founded quantum logic the same year. ([Wikipedia, Continuous geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_geometry); [Wikipedia, Quantum logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_logic)) Jónsson's coordinatization work (1960) and Wehrung's 2006 negative answer to Jónsson's question whether coordinatizability is first-order continue the line. ([Wehrung, arXiv math/0409250](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0409250)) Grätzer's *Lattice Theory: Foundation* (Springer Basel, 2011) covers modular and semimodular lattices. ([Crossref, Grätzer](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-0018-1))

### Open problems
- **Borel complexity of coordinatizability.** Coding countable complemented modular lattices as points of a compact metrizable space, the set of codes of coordinatizable lattices is $\Sigma^1_1$; Wehrung poses as open whether it is Borel (Problem 1), and likewise for lattices admitting an orthocomplementation (Problem 2). ([Wehrung, arXiv math/0409250, §11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0409250))
- **Finite embeddings.** If a finite lattice embeds in some complemented modular lattice, does it embed in a finite complemented modular lattice? (Wehrung, Problem 6.) The same list asks whether the theory of 2-distributive complemented modular lattices is decidable (Problem 5). ([Wehrung, arXiv math/0409250, §11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0409250))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Continuous geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_geometry): von Neumann's theory, dimension functions and coordinatization.
- **Learn:** [Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/lat.pdf): chapters 9, 11 and 12 on modular, geometric and complemented modular lattices.
- **Primary:** [Wehrung, Von Neumann coordinatization is not first-order (J. Math. Logic 6, 2006; arXiv math/0409250)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0409250): coordinatization theorems, the solution of Jónsson's problem, and a list of open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Grätzer, Lattice Theory: Foundation (Springer Basel, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-0018-1): the standard graduate monograph.
references.MSC 06Dxx - Distributive lattices:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 06D, "Distributive lattices", is the part of [MSC 06 - Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures](node:MSC%2006%20-%20Order,%20lattices,%20ordered%20algebraic%20structures) devoted to lattices satisfying $x\wedge(y\vee z)=(x\wedge y)\vee(x\wedge z)$ and to the algebras of logic whose lattice reduct is distributive: pseudocomplemented lattices, Heyting algebras, frames and locales, Post, De Morgan and Łukasiewicz algebras, and MV-algebras, together with duality theory.
