([MSC2020 06Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Dxx); [Wikipedia, Distributive lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_lattice)) See [Distributive Lattices](node:Distributive%20Lattices) for the concept note and [Lattice Theory](node:Lattice%20Theory) for the general setting.

The area is dominated by representation and duality. Every distributive lattice embeds in a lattice of sets via its prime filters; for finite lattices this is Birkhoff's correspondence with finite [posets](node:Partial%20Orders), and for bounded distributive lattices it becomes Priestley duality with ordered Stone spaces, which restricts to Stone duality for [Boolean Algebras](node:Boolean%20Algebras) and Esakia duality for Heyting algebras. ([Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory, Ch. 8](https://math.hawaii.edu/~jb/math618/Nation-LatticeTheory.pdf); [Wikipedia, Birkhoff's representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_representation_theorem); [Wikipedia, Heyting algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heyting_algebra); [Bezhanishvili et al., arXiv:2103.02530](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.02530)) Gehrke and van Gool's course in Stone–Priestley duality applies it to the semantics of [propositional logics](node:Propositional%20Logic), [domain theory](node:Domain%20Theory) in logical form, and profinite monoids for regular languages. ([Gehrke–van Gool, arXiv:2203.03286](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.03286))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 06D05 structure and representation theory of distributive lattices; 06D10 complete distributivity; 06D15 pseudocomplemented lattices; 06D20 Heyting algebras (lattice-theoretic aspects; see also 03G25); 06D22 frames, locales (for topological questions see 54-XX); 06D25 Post algebras (see also 03G20); 06D30 De Morgan algebras, Łukasiewicz algebras (see also 03G20); 06D35 MV-algebras; 06D50 lattices and duality; 06D72 fuzzy lattices (soft algebras); 06D75 other generalizations of distributive lattices; 06D99. ([MSC2020 06Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Dxx))

- **Neighbour 06B** ([MSC 06Bxx - Lattices](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices)): a lattice is distributive iff it has no sublattice isomorphic to $M_3$ or $N_5$. ([Wikipedia, Distributive lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_lattice))
- **Neighbour 06C** ([MSC 06Cxx - Modular lattices, complemented lattices](node:MSC%2006Cxx%20-%20Modular%20lattices,%20complemented%20lattices)): every distributive lattice is modular, and a modular lattice is distributive iff it has no sublattice $M_3$. ([Nation, Thm 9.2](https://math.hawaii.edu/~jb/math618/Nation-LatticeTheory.pdf))
- **Neighbour 06E** ([MSC 06Exx - Boolean algebras (Boolean rings)](node:MSC%2006Exx%20-%20Boolean%20algebras%20%28Boolean%20rings%29)): Boolean algebras are the Heyting algebras satisfying $a\vee\neg a=1$. ([Wikipedia, Heyting algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heyting_algebra))
- **Neighbours 03G and 54**: 06D20 carries a see-also to 03G25 and 06D25, 06D30 to 03G20 ([MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic)); 06D22 says "For topological questions, see 54-XX". ([MSC2020 06Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Dxx))

### Key concepts
- **Characterizations (06D05).** The distributive law is equivalent to its dual and to the self-dual identity $(x\vee y)\wedge(x\vee z)\wedge(y\vee z)=(x\wedge y)\vee(x\wedge z)\vee(y\wedge z)$. A lattice is modular iff it has no pentagon $N_5$, and a modular lattice is distributive iff it has no diamond $M_3$ (Birkhoff). ([Nation, Lemma 8.2, Thms 9.1–9.2](https://math.hawaii.edu/~jb/math618/Nation-LatticeTheory.pdf))
- **Prime filter theorem and the variety.** If $D$ is distributive and $a\not\le b$, some prime filter contains $a$ but not $b$ (Zorn's lemma). Hence $x\mapsto\{F\text{ prime}:x\in F\}$ embeds $D$ in a power set, $\mathbf 2$ is the only subdirectly irreducible distributive lattice, and the variety is $HSP(\mathbf 2)$ and locally finite. ([Nation, Thms 8.4–8.5](https://math.hawaii.edu/~jb/math618/Nation-LatticeTheory.pdf)) The tool behind such results is Jónsson's lemma: if $\mathrm{Var}(K)$ is congruence-distributive, every subdirectly irreducible algebra in it lies in $HSP_U(K)$, and for a finite algebra $A$ in $HS(A)$. ([UCLA handout, Jónsson's lemma](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~baker/222a/handouts/dd_jonsson/node5.html))
- **Birkhoff's theorem (finite case).** For a finite distributive $D$ with poset $J(D)$ of nonzero join-irreducibles, every join-irreducible is join-prime, $a\mapsto{\downarrow}a\cap J(D)$ is an isomorphism $D\cong\mathcal O(J(D))$ onto the down-sets, and each $a$ has a unique irredundant join decomposition. ([Nation, Thm 8.6](https://math.hawaii.edu/~jb/math618/Nation-LatticeTheory.pdf); [Wikipedia, Birkhoff's representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_representation_theorem))
- **Priestley and Esakia duality (06D50, 06D20).** A Priestley space is a compact space with a partial order such that whenever $x\not\le y$ some clopen up-set contains $x$ but not $y$; Priestley spaces with continuous monotone maps form a category dual to (bounded) distributive lattices. ([nLab, Priestley space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Priestley+space); [Bezhanishvili et al., arXiv:2103.02530](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.02530)) Bezhanishvili et al. take the points of the dual space to be prime filters ordered by inclusion and recover the algebra as the clopen up-sets. ([Bezhanishvili et al., arXiv:2103.02530](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.02530)) An Esakia space is a Priestley space in which ${\downarrow}C$ is clopen for every clopen $C$; Esakia duality is a dual equivalence between Heyting algebras and Esakia spaces with Esakia morphisms, the continuous p-morphisms: ${\uparrow}f(x)=f({\uparrow}x)$. ([Bezhanishvili et al., arXiv:2103.02530](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.02530); [Wikipedia, Esakia space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esakia_space)) Both Stone's and Priestley's representations use the Boolean prime ideal theorem, a weak form of the [axiom of choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice). ([Wikipedia, Distributive lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_lattice))
- **Pseudocomplemented lattices (06D15).** $x^*$ is the greatest element with $x\wedge x^*=0$; a Stone algebra is a distributive p-algebra with $x^*\vee x^{**}=1$. ([Wikipedia, Pseudocomplement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudocomplement)) Lee's theorem: the subvarieties of distributive p-algebras form a chain of type $\omega+1$, $\mathsf{Pa}_{-1}\subsetneq\mathsf{Pa}_0\subsetneq\mathsf{Pa}_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathsf{Pa}$, with $\mathsf{Pa}_k=V(\overline{B}_k)$, where $\overline{B}_k$ is the $k$-atom Boolean algebra with a new top adjoined; $\mathsf{Pa}_0$ is Boolean algebras and $\mathsf{Pa}_1$ Stone algebras. ([Kowalski–Słomczyńska, arXiv:2409.08990](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.08990))
- **Heyting algebras and frames (06D20, 06D22).** A Heyting algebra is a bounded lattice with a greatest $x$ such that $a\wedge x\le b$, written $a\to b$; it is distributive, and every finite distributive lattice is Heyting. Heyting algebras model intuitionistic propositional logic, and validity of an equation in all of them is decidable and PSPACE-complete (Statman 1979). ([Wikipedia, Heyting algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heyting_algebra)) A frame is a complete lattice in which finite meets distribute over arbitrary joins; it is automatically Heyting, every space's open sets form one, and locales are the opposite category $\mathbf{Loc}=\mathbf{Frm}^{op}$. ([nLab, frame](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/frame))
- **MV-algebras (06D35).** Chang (1958) introduced them for Łukasiewicz logic; the standard model is $[0,1]$ with $x\oplus y=\min(x+y,1)$, $\neg x=1-x$, which generates the variety (Chang's completeness theorem), and Mundici proved a categorical equivalence with abelian $\ell$-groups with strong unit. ([Wikipedia, MV-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV-algebra))

### History
Peirce at first believed every lattice distributive; independence proofs were later given by Schröder, Voigt, Lüroth, Korselt and Dedekind. ([Wikipedia, Distributive lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_lattice)) Dedekind computed $|FD(3)|=18$ and $|FD(4)|=166$. ([Nation, Ch. 8](https://math.hawaii.edu/~jb/math618/Nation-LatticeTheory.pdf)) Birkhoff's "rings of sets" representation appeared in 1937, and Priestley reinterpreted Stone's theorem via ordered spaces in 1970–72. ([Wikipedia, Birkhoff's representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_representation_theorem)) Esakia introduced his spaces in 1974. ([Wikipedia, Esakia space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esakia_space)) The Dedekind number $M(9)$ was found independently in 2023 by Jäkel and by Van Hirtum et al. ([Wikipedia, Dedekind number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_number))

### Open problems
- **Representable posets.** Grätzer's problem asks for an internal characterization of the posets that are prime spectra of bounded distributive lattices; Esakia reformulated it for Heyting algebras. Bezhanishvili, Bezhanishvili, Moraschini and Stronkowski write that "it remains an interesting open problem to give a full characterization of Esakia representable posets of finite depth". ([Bezhanishvili et al., arXiv:2103.02530](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.02530))
- **Quasivarieties of p-algebras.** Although the subvarieties form an $\omega+1$ chain, the subquasivariety lattice is uncountable and Q-universal; Kowalski and Słomczyńska list as open the description of quasivarieties generated by free algebras $F_m(X)$ for $m\ge3$ and the covers of $\mathsf{Pa}_2$ and $\mathsf{Pa}_m$. ([Kowalski–Słomczyńska, arXiv:2409.08990](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2409.08990))
- **Dedekind's problem.** $M(n)$, the size of the free distributive lattice on $n$ generators with top and bottom, begins $2,3,6,20,168,7581,7828354,\dots$; $\log_2M(n)$ is asymptotic to $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ (Kleitman–Markowsky), but no closed form is known and exact values are known only for $n\le9$. ([Wikipedia, Dedekind number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_number))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Distributive lattice (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_lattice): characterizations, representations, free distributive lattices.
- **Reference:** [nLab, Priestley space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Priestley+space): Priestley spaces and the duality.
- **Learn:** [Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory, Chs. 8–9](https://math.hawaii.edu/~jb/math618/Nation-LatticeTheory.pdf): prime filter theorem, Birkhoff, Stone, $M_3$–$N_5$ criteria.
- **Primary:** [Gehrke and van Gool, Topological Duality for Distributive Lattices (arXiv:2203.03286)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.03286): graduate monograph on Stone–Priestley duality.
- **Primary:** [Bezhanishvili, Bezhanishvili, Moraschini, Stronkowski, Profiniteness and representability of spectra of Heyting algebras](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.02530): Esakia duality and representability.
- **Further reading:** [Balbes and Dwinger, Distributive Lattices (University of Missouri Press, 1974), JSL review record](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-symbolic-logic/article/abs/raymond-balbes-and-philip-dwinger-distributive-lattices-university-of-missouri-press-columbia1974-xiii-294-pp/BF8A1CD1148E68C60F502ACA5A9CBF4E): monograph on distributive lattices, reviewed by Urquhart in the Journal of Symbolic Logic (1977).
- **Further reading:** [Johnstone, Stone Spaces (Cambridge University Press, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 3, 1982), as listed in Wikipedia: Stone space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_space).
- **Further reading:** [Davey and Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order, 2nd ed. (CUP, 2002)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-lattices-and-order/preface-to-the-second-edition/783D25FF7EB33A7BCB0E60DCB8275470): chapters "Representation: the finite case" and "the general case".

## Reference
### Overview
A Boolean algebra (BA) is a set $A$ with binary operations $+$ (join), $\cdot$ (meet), a unary complement $-$ and constants $0,1$, satisfying the associative, commutative, absorption, distributive and complement laws; an equation holds in all Boolean algebras iff it holds in the two-element algebra $\{0,1\}$. Boolean algebras are definitionally equivalent to Boolean rings, i.e. rings with identity in which every element is idempotent: from a BA set $x\oplus y=(x\cdot -y)+(y\cdot -x)$, and from a Boolean ring recover $x+y=x\oplus y\oplus xy$ and $-x=1\oplus x$. ([SEP, The Mathematics of Boolean Algebra](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/)) For the power set of $X$, ring addition is symmetric difference and ring multiplication is intersection, so union is not the ring addition; Fremlin's convention allows the trivial algebra with $0=1$. ([Fremlin, §311A–B](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/chap31.pdf))

Beyond the elementary theory, the area is strongly set-theoretic and topological: Stone's representation matches Boolean algebras with totally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces, complete Boolean algebras give the Boolean-valued models equivalent to forcing, and many cardinal functions of infinite algebras (cellularity, independence, $\pi$-weight and others) are studied. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/); [Wikipedia, Complete Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Boolean_algebra)) The section sits inside [MSC 06 - Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures](node:MSC%2006%20-%20Order,%20lattices,%20ordered%20algebraic%20structures) beside [MSC 06Dxx - Distributive lattices](node:MSC%2006Dxx%20-%20Distributive%20lattices); with respect to the order $x\le y$, $+$ gives least upper bounds and $\cdot$ greatest lower bounds, and the two-element algebra and the Lindenbaum–Tarski algebras connect Boolean algebras directly with sentential [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic). ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/))

### Scope
MSC2020 06E ("Boolean algebras (Boolean rings)", see also 03G05) comprises: 06E05 structure theory of Boolean algebras; 06E10 chain conditions, complete algebras; 06E15 Stone spaces (Boolean spaces) and related structures; 06E20 ring-theoretic properties of Boolean algebras (see also 16E50, 16G30); 06E25 Boolean algebras with additional operations (diagonalizable algebras, etc.; see also 03G25, 03F45); 06E30 Boolean functions (see also 94D10); 06E75 generalizations of Boolean algebras; 06E99. ([MSC2020, 06E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Exx))

Neighbours, by those cross-references: the section as a whole points to 03G05 in [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic); 06E30 Boolean functions points to 94D10 in [MSC 94Dxx - Miscellaneous topics in information and communication theory](node:MSC%2094Dxx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20information%20and%20communication%20theory); 06E20 points to the ring-theoretic codes 16E50 and 16G30; 06E25 points to 03G25 and 03F45. ([MSC2020, 06E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Stone representation and Stone duality (06E15).** For a Boolean algebra $B$, let $S(B)$ be the set of ultrafilters of $B$ (equivalently, homomorphisms $B\to\{0,1\}$), topologized by the basis $\{x: b\in x\}$. Then $S(B)$ is compact, Hausdorff and totally disconnected (a Stone space), and $b\mapsto\{x\in S(B): b\in x\}$ is an isomorphism of $B$ onto the algebra of clopen subsets of $S(B)$. A homomorphism $A\to B$ corresponds to a continuous map $S(B)\to S(A)$, giving a dual equivalence between Boolean algebras and Stone spaces. The theorem needs a weak form of choice: it is equivalent to the Boolean prime ideal theorem. ([Wikipedia, Stone's representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%27s_representation_theorem_for_Boolean_algebras)) An undergraduate-level proof of the embedding into a power set via two-valued homomorphisms is in de Oliveira's exposition (Theorem 1.20). ([de Oliveira](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2015/REUPapers/deOliveira.pdf)) See [Topological Spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces) for the topological side.
- **Complete Boolean algebras and completions (06E10).** A Boolean algebra is complete if every subset has a supremum. Every Boolean algebra $A$ has an essentially unique completion: a complete Boolean algebra containing $A$ densely, in which every element is a supremum of elements of $A$ (as a poset, the Dedekind–MacNeille completion). A Boolean algebra is complete iff its Stone space is extremally disconnected. ([Wikipedia, Complete Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Boolean_algebra)) For any topological space $X$ the regular open sets ($G=\operatorname{int}\overline G$) form a complete Boolean algebra $\mathrm{RO}(X)$ with $G\wedge H=G\cap H$ and $G\vee H=\operatorname{int}\overline{G\cup H}$; the completion of $A$ can be realized as $\mathrm{RO}$ of its Stone space. ([Fremlin, 314P, 314S–T](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/chap31.pdf))
- **Sikorski extension theorem.** If $A$ is a subalgebra of $B$ and $C$ is a complete Boolean algebra, every homomorphism $A\to C$ extends to a homomorphism $B\to C$ (complete Boolean algebras are injective); the extension need not preserve infinite suprema. ([Wikipedia, Complete Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Boolean_algebra); [Fremlin, 314K](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/chap31.pdf))
- **Forcing and Boolean-valued models.** Complete Boolean algebras are used to build Boolean-valued models of [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory); the regular open algebra of a forcing poset gives Boolean-valued models equivalent to generic extensions by that poset. Unless the axiom of choice is relaxed, there is no free complete Boolean algebra on an infinite set of generators (Stavi 1974 built a model of ZF with an infinite free complete Boolean algebra), although free $\kappa$-complete algebras exist for each fixed $\kappa$. ([Wikipedia, Complete Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Boolean_algebra)) This is where 06E meets [MSC 03Exx - Set theory](node:MSC%2003Exx%20-%20Set%20theory).
- **Decidability (Tarski).** The elementary theory of Boolean algebras is decidable, and so is the theory of Boolean algebras with a distinguished ideal; the theory of Boolean algebras with a distinguished subalgebra is undecidable. ([SEP, §5](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/)) This places Boolean algebras in [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory) as a decidable but rich class.
- **Countable Boolean algebras (Ketonen).** Every countable Boolean algebra is isomorphic to an interval algebra. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/)) Ketonen (1978) characterized the isomorphism types of countable Boolean algebras completely by naturally defined invariants, and as an application showed that every countable commutative semigroup embeds in the semigroup of isomorphism types of countable Boolean algebras under direct product, solving Tarski's cube problem. ([Ketonen, Annals 108](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/1978/108-1/p02))
- **Cardinal invariants.** For infinite algebras one studies cellularity (sizes of pairwise disjoint families), independence, $\pi$-weight, incomparability and irredundance. By the Erdős–Tarski theorem, if the cellularity is singular it is attained by a disjoint family; every infinite complete Boolean algebra has an independent subset of the same size as the algebra. ([SEP, §4](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/)) Monk's notation $c'(A)$ is the least $\mu$ such that $A$ has no disjoint subset of size $\mu$; it is always regular. ([Monk 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0401343))

### History
Stone published *The Theory of Representation for Boolean Algebras* in the Transactions of the AMS, vol. 40, in 1936 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1989664)), the source of the representation theorem and an early nontrivial duality of categories. ([Wikipedia, Stone's representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%27s_representation_theorem_for_Boolean_algebras)) The SEP entry ties Boolean-valued models of set theory to Cohen's forcing method. ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/)) Ketonen's classification of countable algebras appeared in the Annals in 1978. ([Ketonen](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/1978/108-1/p02)) Volume 1 of the *Handbook of Boolean Algebras*, by Sabine Koppelberg, appeared in 1989, and Monk's 1996 book *Cardinal Invariants on Boolean Algebras* posed 97 open problems; Monk's 2004 report follows Koppelberg's notation. ([CU Boulder record](https://vivo.colorado.edu/display/pubid_44820); [Monk 2004](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0401343))

### Open problems
- **Monk's problems on cardinal invariants.** Monk's 2004 status report on the 97 problems of *Cardinal Invariants on Boolean Algebras* lists 26 as fully solved, 21 as partially solved, and the remaining 50 (for example Problems 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 15, 17) as still open in the form given in the book; Problem 3 (characterizing the subalgebra–cellularity relation) and Problem 6 (the homomorphism–cellularity relation) are described as still open. ([Monk 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0401343))
- **Cellularity of free products (Problem 1).** For which $\kappa,\lambda$ are there algebras with $c'(A)=\kappa$, $c'(B)=\lambda$ and $c'(A\oplus B)>\max(\kappa,\lambda)$? Results of Shelah settle the case $\kappa=\lambda$ a successor cardinal, but the report lists as still open: if $\kappa$ is inaccessible, not weakly compact, and every stationary subset of $\kappa$ reflects in an inaccessible, is there $A$ with $c'(A)=\kappa<c'(A\oplus A)$? and the general case $\kappa\ne\lambda$. ([Monk 2004, Problem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0401343))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [The Mathematics of Boolean Algebra (SEP, J. D. Monk)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/boolalg-math/): definitions, Stone representation, free and complete algebras, decidability, cardinal invariants.
- **Learn:** [de Oliveira, The Stone representation theorem for Boolean algebras (UChicago REU)](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2015/REUPapers/deOliveira.pdf): self-contained route through Boolean ideals, maximal ideals and two-valued homomorphisms to Stone's representation theorem (Theorem 1.20).
- **Primary:** [Ketonen, The structure of countable Boolean algebras (Annals 1978)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/1978/108-1/p02): classification of countable Boolean algebras.
- **Primary:** [Monk, Concerning problems about cardinal invariants on Boolean algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0401343): status of the 97 open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Koppelberg, Handbook of Boolean Algebras vol. 1 (1989)](https://vivo.colorado.edu/display/pubid_44820): general theory of Boolean algebras, whose notation Monk's problem report follows; [Fremlin, Measure Theory ch. 31](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/chap31.pdf): Boolean rings, Stone spaces, regular open algebras and completions.
references.MSC 06Fxx - Ordered structures:
## Reference
### Overview
Ordered algebraic structures are algebras (semigroups, groups, rings, lattices with a monoid operation) carrying a partial order compatible with the operations. The basic case is an ordered semigroup: a semigroup with a partial order such that $a\le b$ implies $ca\le cb$ and $ac\le bc$; ordered monoids and groups are defined the same way, and morphisms are monotone semigroup homomorphisms. ([Wikipedia, Ordered semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_semigroup)) The area joins [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders) and lattice theory ([MSC 06Bxx - Lattices](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices)).

Its theory of partially ordered and lattice-ordered groups grew from three sources: functional analysis (ordered spaces of real functions), the Hall–Malcev question of which groups are orderable, and generalizations of valuation theory initiated by Conrad; Holland's representation theorem married the group-theoretic and lattice-theoretic approaches. ([Bludov, Glass, Kopytov & Medvedev](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621)) A second major strand, residuated lattices, adds a residuated monoid operation to a lattice and covers lattice-ordered groups, ideal lattices of rings, and the algebraic semantics of linear and many-valued logics. ([Jipsen & Tsinakis](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/t2-my/my-prd/wp-content/uploads/sites/1171/2014/03/survey.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 06F covers: 06F05 ordered semigroups and monoids (see also 20Mxx); 06F07 quantales; 06F10 Noether lattices; 06F15 ordered groups (see also 20F60); 06F20 ordered abelian groups, Riesz groups, ordered linear spaces (see also 46A40); 06F25 ordered rings, algebras, modules (for ordered fields see 12J15; see also 13J25, 16W80); 06F30 ordered topological structures; 06F35 BCK-algebras, BCI-algebras (see also 03G25); 06F99. ([MSC2020, 06F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Fxx))

Neighbours, as the see-also notes indicate: orderability of groups as a group-theoretic property is 20F60 in [MSC 20Fxx - Special aspects of infinite or finite groups](node:MSC%2020Fxx%20-%20Special%20aspects%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups); ordered fields are 12J15 in [MSC 12Jxx - Topological fields](node:MSC%2012Jxx%20-%20Topological%20fields); ordered topological [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) are 46A40 in [MSC 46Axx - Topological linear spaces and related structures](node:MSC%2046Axx%20-%20Topological%20linear%20spaces%20and%20related%20structures); BCK/BCI-algebras as logic are 03G25 in [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic); plain lattices without extra operations are [MSC 06Bxx - Lattices](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices) within [MSC 06 - Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures](node:MSC%2006%20-%20Order,%20lattices,%20ordered%20algebraic%20structures). ([MSC2020, 06F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=06Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Hölder's theorem (06F15, 06F20).** A linearly ordered group is archimedean if for all $a,b>0$ there is $n$ with $b\le na$. Every archimedean linearly ordered group is order-isomorphic to a subgroup of $(\mathbb R,+)$, hence abelian. ([Wikipedia, Archimedean group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedean_group)) This is the algebraic core of the passage from ordered quantities to [real numbers](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits).
- **Hahn embedding theorem (1907).** Every linearly ordered abelian group $G$ embeds as an ordered subgroup of $\mathbb R^\Omega$ with the lexicographic order, where $\Omega$ is the set of archimedean classes of $G$ and $\mathbb R^\Omega$ consists of functions $\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with well-ordered support; for archimedean $G$ ($|\Omega|=1$) it reduces to Hölder's theorem. ([Wikipedia, Hahn embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hahn_embedding_theorem))
- **Lattice-ordered groups and Holland's theorem.** A partially ordered group is a group with a translation-invariant partial order ($a\le b\Rightarrow a+g\le b+g$ and $g+a\le g+b$); it is an $\ell$-group when the order is a lattice. Holland's embedding theorem (1963): every $\ell$-group embeds, preserving the lattice operations, in the $\ell$-group of order-preserving bijections of a chain. ([Wikipedia, Lattice-ordered group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice-ordered_group)) The variety of $\ell$-groups has decidable equational theory, but there is a one-relator finitely presented $\ell$-group with undecidable word problem; the universal theory of abelian $\ell$-groups is decidable (indeed co-NP-complete). ([Jipsen & Tsinakis, Thms. 7.5–7.8](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/t2-my/my-prd/wp-content/uploads/sites/1171/2014/03/survey.pdf))
- **Residuated lattices.** A residuated lattice is a lattice with a monoid $(L,\cdot,e)$ and residuals satisfying $x\cdot y\le z\iff x\le z/y\iff y\le x\backslash z$; residuated lattices form a variety. Ward and Dilworth introduced the concept in 1939; examples include ideal lattices of rings, Heyting algebras ($x\cdot y=x\wedge y$), totally ordered groups, binary relations under composition, and formal languages under concatenation. ([Wikipedia, Residuated lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residuated_lattice); [Jipsen & Tsinakis, §1](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/t2-my/my-prd/wp-content/uploads/sites/1171/2014/03/survey.pdf)) The equational theory of residuated lattices is decidable via a cut-free Gentzen system, while its quasi-equational theory is undecidable. ([Jipsen & Tsinakis, §7](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/t2-my/my-prd/wp-content/uploads/sites/1171/2014/03/survey.pdf)) Residuated lattices give algebraic semantics for substructural logics, the bridge to [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic). ([Jipsen, 2024 tutorial](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/Cagliari2024/Jipsen2024Intro2RL.pdf)) The survey proves that every lattice embeds in the lattice reduct of a simple integral cancellative residuated lattice (Theorem 5.3) and asks whether every lattice is a subreduct of a *commutative* cancellative one (Problem 8.1). ([Jipsen & Tsinakis, §8](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/t2-my/my-prd/wp-content/uploads/sites/1171/2014/03/survey.pdf)) Přenosil answered this open problem about cancellative commutative residuated lattices: every lattice is a subreduct of some integral cancellative commutative residuated lattice. ([Přenosil](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09392))
- **MV-algebras and Mundici's equivalence.** MV-algebras (Chang, 1958) are the algebraic semantics of Łukasiewicz logic; Chang's completeness theorem says an equation holds in all MV-algebras iff it holds in $[0,1]$ with $x\oplus y=\min(x+y,1)$, $\neg x=1-x$. ([Wikipedia, MV-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV-algebra)) For an abelian $\ell$-group $G$ with positive element $a$, the interval $\Gamma(G,a)=[e,a]$ is an MV-algebra; Mundici proved that $\Gamma$ is an equivalence between MV-algebras and abelian $\ell$-groups with strong unit. ([Jipsen & Tsinakis, §3](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/t2-my/my-prd/wp-content/uploads/sites/1171/2014/03/survey.pdf))
- **Ordered rings and fields (06F25, 12J15).** A field is orderable iff it is formally real ($0$ is not a sum of nonzero squares); orderings correspond bijectively to positive cones $P$ with $P+P\subseteq P$, $PP\subseteq P$, squares in $P$, $-1\notin P$ and $F=P\cup-P$. Artin and Schreier gave the positive-cone definition in 1926; the proof that every formally real field admits an ordering uses Zorn's lemma. ([Wikipedia, Ordered field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_field)) Compare [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory) and [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals).

### History
Hölder published his axiomatic theory of quantity, *Die Axiome der Quantität und die Lehre vom Mass*, in 1901. ([MacTutor, Hölder](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Holder/)) Hahn's embedding theorem dates from 1907. ([Wikipedia, Hahn embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hahn_embedding_theorem)) Hölder, Hahn and Hilbert abstracted ordered-field axioms from the reals, and Artin and Schreier gave the positive-cone definition in 1926. ([Wikipedia, Ordered field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_field)) Ward and Dilworth introduced residuated lattices in 1939, and Chang introduced MV-algebras in 1958. ([Wikipedia, Residuated lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residuated_lattice); [Wikipedia, MV-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV-algebra)) Conrad's structure theory of $\ell$-groups and Holland's 1963 representation theorem shaped the $\ell$-group programme; Kopytov and Medvedev's problem list, translated and extended with Bludov and Glass in 2009, is modelled on the Kourovka Notebook. ([Bludov et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621); [Wikipedia, Lattice-ordered group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice-ordered_group)) Blyth's *Lattices and Ordered Algebraic Structures* (Springer Universitext, 2005) is a textbook treatment, from residuated mappings through ordered groups, archimedean structures and ordered semigroups. ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b139095))

### Open problems
- **Archimedean lattice orders (Weinberg).** Problem 1.7 of the Bludov–Glass–Kopytov–Medvedev list asks whether every torsion-free abelian group has an archimedean lattice order; the list notes the answer is yes for groups of [cardinality](node:Cardinality) at most the continuum (embed in $\mathbb R$). ([Bludov et al., Problem 1.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621))
- **Unique addition (Conrad–Darnel).** Problem 1.21 of the same list: is every $\ell$-group with unique addition archimedean? ([Bludov et al., Problem 1.21](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Lattice-ordered group (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice-ordered_group): partially ordered groups, $\ell$-groups, Holland's theorem.
- **Learn:** [Jipsen, An introduction to residuated lattices (2024 tutorial)](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/Cagliari2024/Jipsen2024Intro2RL.pdf): residuals, examples, exercises.
- **Primary:** [Jipsen & Tsinakis, A Survey of Residuated Lattices](https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/t2-my/my-prd/wp-content/uploads/sites/1171/2014/03/survey.pdf): structure, varieties, decidability, open problems.
- **Primary:** [Bludov, Glass, Kopytov & Medvedev, Unsolved problems in ordered and orderable groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.2621): problem list with comments and solutions.
- **Further reading:** [Blyth, Lattices and Ordered Algebraic Structures (Springer, 2005)](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b139095): textbook on ordered groups, semigroups, and residuation.
references.MSC 08 - General algebraic systems:
## Reference
### Overview
Universal algebra (general algebra) studies the possible types of algebraic structures and their relationships rather than one class such as groups or rings. ([Wikipedia, Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra)) Its objects are algebras (a set with finitary operations of a fixed type), with subalgebras, homomorphic images and direct products; a class $K$ of algebras of one type is a variety if it is closed under $\mathsf H$, $\mathsf S$ and $\mathsf P$, equivalently $\mathsf{HSP}(K)=K$. ([Jipsen, Tutorial on Universal Algebras](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf)) Familiar examples are [groups](node:Group%20Theory), [rings](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals), lattices and Boolean algebras.

Major themes include the consequences of special assumptions about congruence lattices (permutability, modularity, distributivity), their characterization by term identities (Maltsev conditions), which finite algebras have a finite basis for their identities, and, through polymorphisms, the complexity of constraint satisfaction problems. ([Burris and Sankappanavar, §II.12](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf); [Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf); [Wikipedia, Constraint satisfaction problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constraint_satisfaction_problem))

### Scope
MSC2020 field 08 has three sections. ([MSC2020, 08](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08-XX))
- [MSC 08Axx - Algebraic structures](node:MSC%2008Axx%20-%20Algebraic%20structures) (see also 03C05): structure theory, subalgebras and congruences, automorphisms, operations and polynomials (clones, primal algebras), word problems, partial, unary, infinitary and heterogeneous algebras, and applications in computer science (08A70). ([MSC2020, 08A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Axx))
- [MSC 08Bxx - Varieties](node:MSC%2008Bxx%20-%20Varieties) (see also 03C05): equational logic and Maltsev conditions (08B05), congruence modularity and distributivity (08B10), lattices of varieties (08B15), free algebras (08B20), products and colimits (08B25), subdirect products and subdirect irreducibility (08B26), injectives and projectives (08B30). ([MSC2020, 08B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Bxx))
- [MSC 08Cxx - Other classes of algebras](node:MSC%2008Cxx%20-%20Other%20classes%20of%20algebras): categories of algebras (08C05, see 18C05), axiomatic model classes (08C10, see 03C60), quasivarieties (08C15), natural dualities (08C20, see also 06E15). ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))

Neighbours, by the listed cross-references: 08A and 08B point to 03C05 and 08C10 to 03C60 in [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory); 08C05 points to 18C05 in [MSC 18Cxx - Categories and theories](node:MSC%2018Cxx%20-%20Categories%20and%20theories); 08C20 natural dualities points to Stone spaces (06E15) in [MSC 06 - Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures](node:MSC%2006%20-%20Order,%20lattices,%20ordered%20algebraic%20structures). ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx); [MSC2020, 08A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Birkhoff's HSP theorem and subdirect representation.** A class of algebras is a variety (defined by identities) iff it is closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras and arbitrary direct products. ([Wikipedia, Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra)) Every algebra is a subdirect product of subdirectly irreducible homomorphic images of itself, so every variety satisfies $V=\mathsf{SP}(V_{SI})$, where $V_{SI}$ is its class of subdirectly irreducible members. ([Burris and Sankappanavar, Thm II.8.6](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf); [Jipsen](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf))
- **Maltsev conditions (08B05, 08B10).** A variety $V$ is congruence-permutable iff there is a term $p(x,y,z)$ with $V\models p(x,x,y)\approx y$ and $V\models p(x,y,y)\approx x$ (Maltsev; e.g. $p=xy^{-1}z$ for groups). $V$ is congruence-distributive iff for some $n$ there are terms $p_0,\dots,p_n$ with $p_i(x,y,x)\approx x$, $p_0\approx x$, $p_n\approx z$, $p_i(x,x,y)\approx p_{i+1}(x,x,y)$ for even $i$ and $p_i(x,y,y)\approx p_{i+1}(x,y,y)$ for odd $i$ (Jónsson). ([Burris and Sankappanavar, Thms II.12.2, II.12.6](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf))
- **Jónsson's lemma.** If $V(K)$ is congruence-distributive, its subdirectly irreducible members lie in $\mathsf{HSP_u}(K)$; in particular, if $K$ is a finite set of finite algebras then the subdirectly irreducibles of $V(K)$ are in $\mathsf{HS}(K)$ and $V(K)=\mathsf{IP_SHS}(K)$. ([Burris and Sankappanavar, Thm IV.6.8, Cor. IV.6.10](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf); [Jipsen](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf))
- **Commutator theory and tame congruence theory.** For congruence-modular varieties, commutator theory describes abelianness and the centrality relation among congruences (Freese and McKenzie, *Commutator Theory for Congruence Modular Varieties*). ([Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf); [McNulty, course resources](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/index.html)) Hobby and McKenzie's tame congruence theory (1988) analyses arbitrary finite algebras through minimal algebras, each of one of five types: unary, affine, Boolean, lattice or semilattice. ([Wikipedia, Minimal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_algebra))
- **Finite basis theorems.** A finite algebra is finitely based if its identities follow from finitely many. Every finite group, finite ring, finite lattice and two-element algebra of finite type is finitely based. Baker: if $\mathbf A$ is finite of finite type and $V(\mathbf A)$ is congruence-distributive, then $\mathbf A$ is finitely based. McKenzie (1987) extended this to congruence-modular varieties with a finite residual bound, Willard (2000) to congruence meet-semidistributive ones, and Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard to all varieties in a finite language with a difference term and a finite residual bound. McKenzie (1996) proved that whether a finite algebra is finitely based is undecidable, settling Tarski's finite basis problem. ([Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf))
- **CSP dichotomy (08A70).** For a finite set $\Gamma$ of relations on a finite domain, $\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma)$ is in P if some weak near-unanimity operation preserves $\Gamma$ (a polymorphism with $f(y,x,\dots,x)=\dots=f(x,\dots,x,y)$) and NP-complete otherwise; this Feder–Vardi dichotomy was proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017. ([Zhuk, Thm 1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.01914); [Bulatov](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03021); [Wikipedia, CSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constraint_satisfaction_problem)) See [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory).

### History
Whitehead's *A Treatise on Universal Algebra* (1898) used the term in essentially its modern sense, crediting Hamilton and De Morgan and attributing the name to Sylvester, but proved no general results. Birkhoff and Ore began publishing on the subject in the early 1930s; Maltsev's 1940s work went unnoticed during the war; Tarski's 1950 ICM lecture opened a model-theoretic period with Chang, Henkin, Jónsson and Lyndon; textbooks by Neumann, Cohn, Grätzer and Pierce appeared in the 1960s, and Lawvere's 1963 thesis brought in categorical methods. ([Wikipedia, Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra)) Maltsev initiated the study of Maltsev conditions in the 1950s, later advanced by Taylor. ([Burris and Sankappanavar, §II.12](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf)) Burris and Sankappanavar's *A Course in Universal Algebra* (1981) was reissued in a corrected Millennium Edition; *Algebras, Lattices, Varieties* by Freese, McKenzie, McNulty and Taylor appeared in three volumes (vol. I 1987, vols. II–III 2022). ([Burris and Sankappanavar, preface](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf); [ALV authors' page](https://math.hawaii.edu/~ralph/ALVIN/))

### Open problems
- **Jónsson's problem / Park's conjecture.** If a variety in a finite language has a finite residual bound (every subdirectly irreducible member has at most $r$ elements), must it be finitely based? The conjectured positive answer, Park's conjecture (Park's 1976 thesis), is known for congruence-distributive, congruence-modular, congruence meet-semidistributive and difference-term varieties, but Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard state that the problem remains open. ([Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf))
- **Finite lattice representation problem.** Is every finite lattice the congruence lattice of a finite algebra? It is among the oldest unsolved problems of universal algebra, equivalent (Pálfy–Pudlák 1980) to representing every finite lattice as an interval in the subgroup lattice of a finite group. ([Wikipedia, Finite lattice representation problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_lattice_representation_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Universal algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra): definitions, HSP theorem, history, CSP connection.
- **Learn:** [Jipsen, Tutorial on Universal Algebras](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf): precise slides on algebras, congruences, varieties and Jónsson's lemma; [McNulty's course page](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/index.html): problem sets and PDFs of texts including Burris–Sankappanavar, Hobby–McKenzie and Freese–McKenzie.
- **Primary:** [Burris and Sankappanavar, A Course in Universal Algebra (Millennium Edition)](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf): graduate text (originally Springer GTM, 1981) including Maltsev conditions and Jónsson's lemma.
- **Primary:** [Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard, A finite basis theorem for difference-term varieties with a finite residual bound](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf): research paper with a history of finite basis results and the status of Park's conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Freese, McKenzie, McNulty and Taylor, Algebras, Lattices, Varieties](https://math.hawaii.edu/~ralph/ALVIN/): three-volume monograph (vol. I 1987, vols. II–III 2022).
references.MSC 08Axx - Algebraic structures:
## Reference
### Overview
An $n$-ary operation on a set $A$ is a function $A^n\to A$, with 0-ary operations being constants; an algebra $\mathbf A=(A,f_1^{\mathbf A},f_2^{\mathbf A},\dots)$ is a set with operations of prescribed arities, its type is the list of arities, and a group $(G,\cdot,{}^{-1},1)$ is an algebra of type $(2,1,0)$. Subalgebras are subsets closed under all operations; a homomorphism between algebras of the same type commutes with every operation, and an isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism. ([Jipsen, Tutorial on Universal Algebras](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf)) Groups in the sense of [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), the rings of [ring theory](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals), and lattices are thus particular algebras.

Congruences (equivalence relations compatible with the operations) form an algebraic lattice $\operatorname{Con}\mathbf A$, and studying the consequences of special assumptions about congruence lattices is one of the major themes of universal algebra. ([Burris and Sankappanavar, §II.5](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf)) Finite algebras are studied locally through tame congruence theory ([Wikipedia, Minimal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_algebra)), and universal algebra gives a natural language for constraint satisfaction problems. ([Wikipedia, Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))

### Scope
MSC2020 08A ("Algebraic structures", see also 03C05) comprises: 08A02 relational systems, laws of composition; 08A05 structure theory; 08A30 subalgebras, congruence relations; 08A35 automorphisms and endomorphisms; 08A40 operations and polynomials, primal algebras; 08A45 equational compactness; 08A50 word problems (see also 03D40, 06B25, 20F10, 68R15); 08A55 partial algebras; 08A60 unary algebras; 08A62 finitary algebras; 08A65 infinitary algebras; 08A68 heterogeneous algebras; 08A70 applications of universal algebra in computer science; 08A72 fuzzy algebraic structures; 08A99. ([MSC2020, 08A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Axx))

Neighbours: the other sections of field 08 are [MSC 08Bxx - Varieties](node:MSC%2008Bxx%20-%20Varieties) (also cross-referred to 03C05) and [MSC 08Cxx - Other classes of algebras](node:MSC%2008Cxx%20-%20Other%20classes%20of%20algebras), both within [MSC 08 - General algebraic systems](node:MSC%2008%20-%20General%20algebraic%20systems); the model-theoretic side is 03C05 in [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory); 08A50 is cross-listed with word problems for groups (20F10) and lattices (06B25, in [MSC 06Bxx - Lattices](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices)). ([MSC2020, 08](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08-XX); [MSC2020, 08A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Isomorphism and correspondence theorems (08A30).** If $\alpha:\mathbf A\to\mathbf B$ is a surjective homomorphism, then $\mathbf A/\ker\alpha\cong\mathbf B$ (Homomorphism Theorem); for $\theta\in\operatorname{Con}\mathbf A$, the congruences of $\mathbf A/\theta$ correspond to the congruences of $\mathbf A$ containing $\theta$ (Correspondence Theorem). ([Burris and Sankappanavar, Thms 6.12, 6.20](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf))
- **Birkhoff's subdirect representation theorem.** Every algebra is isomorphic to a subdirect product of subdirectly irreducible algebras, each a homomorphic image of it; an algebra is subdirectly irreducible iff the identity relation is completely meet-irreducible in $\operatorname{Con}\mathbf A$. ([Burris and Sankappanavar, Thm 8.6](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf); [Jipsen](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf))
- **Congruence lattices: Grätzer–Schmidt (1963).** For every algebraic lattice $L$ there is an algebra $\mathbf A$ with $L\cong\operatorname{Con}\mathbf A$, so no abstract property beyond algebraicity is common to all congruence lattices; special classes do satisfy more, e.g. congruence lattices of lattices are distributive and those of groups and rings are modular. ([Burris and Sankappanavar, §II.5](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf)) Dilworth's congruence lattice problem for lattices was solved by Wehrung in 2007. ([Wikipedia, Congruence lattice problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_lattice_problem))
- **Clones and Post's lattice (08A40).** A clone on $A$ is a set of finitary operations containing all projections and closed under composition; the term operations of an algebra form a clone, and every clone arises this way. ([Wikipedia, Clone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clone_%28algebra%29)) On $\{0,1\}$ the clones form Post's lattice (1941), which is countably infinite with every member finitely generated, and whose five maximal proper clones yield Post's functional completeness criterion. ([Wikipedia, Post's lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post%27s_lattice)) On a finite set with at least three elements there are continuum many clones. ([Wikipedia, Clone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clone_%28algebra%29))
- **Tame congruence theory (08A05).** Hobby and McKenzie's theory (*The Structure of Finite Algebras*, AMS 1988) studies finite algebras locally through minimal algebras: finite algebras in which every non-constant unary polynomial is a permutation. By Pálfy's classification each minimal algebra is of one of five types: unary (a permutation group), affine (polynomially equivalent to a vector space), Boolean, lattice, or semilattice (polynomially equivalent to the two-element Boolean algebra, lattice or semilattice). ([Wikipedia, Minimal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_algebra))
- **Polymorphisms and the CSP dichotomy (08A70).** An operation $f:A^n\to A$ preserves a relation if applying $f$ coordinatewise to tuples of the relation gives a tuple of the relation; $f$ is a weak near-unanimity (WNU) operation if $f(y,x,\dots,x)=f(x,y,x,\dots,x)=\dots=f(x,\dots,x,y)$. For a finite set $\Gamma$ of relations on a finite set, $\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma)$ is solvable in polynomial time if some WNU preserves $\Gamma$, and NP-complete otherwise. ([Zhuk, Thm 1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.01914)) This settles the Feder–Vardi dichotomy conjecture, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017. ([Bulatov](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03021); [Wikipedia, Constraint satisfaction problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constraint_satisfaction_problem)) This is where 08A meets [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory).

### History
Whitehead's *A Treatise on Universal Algebra* (1898) used the name in essentially its modern sense; Birkhoff and Ore began publishing in the early 1930s, and papers from 1935 to 1950 dealt with free algebras, congruence and subalgebra lattices, and homomorphism theorems. Maltsev's results of the 1940s went largely unnoticed during the war, and textbooks by Grätzer, Cohn and others appeared in the 1960s. ([Wikipedia, Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra)) Post classified the two-element clones in 1941, Grätzer and Schmidt proved their representation theorem in 1963, and Hobby and McKenzie published tame congruence theory in 1988. ([Wikipedia, Post's lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post%27s_lattice); [Burris and Sankappanavar](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf); [Wikipedia, Minimal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_algebra))

### Open problems
- **Finite lattice representation problem.** Is every finite lattice isomorphic to $\operatorname{Con}\mathbf A$ for some finite algebra $\mathbf A$? Grätzer–Schmidt answers the infinite version, but the finite one is among the oldest unsolved problems in universal algebra; Pálfy and Pudlák (1980) proved it equivalent to asking whether every finite lattice is an interval in the subgroup lattice of a finite group. ([Wikipedia, Finite lattice representation problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_lattice_representation_problem)) DeMeo showed that every lattice with at most seven elements, with one possible exception, is the congruence lattice of a finite algebra, and analysed the remaining case. ([DeMeo, arXiv:1204.4305](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4305))
- **Infinite-domain CSPs.** The finite-domain dichotomy is proved, but the complexity of constraint satisfaction over infinite domains is still an active research area, with a conjectured dichotomy for reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. ([Wikipedia, Constraint satisfaction problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constraint_satisfaction_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Clone (algebra) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clone_%28algebra%29): clones, term operations, counts of clones.
- **Learn:** [Jipsen, Tutorial on Universal Algebras](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf): precise definitions of algebras, congruences, subdirect products and varieties.
- **Primary:** [Burris and Sankappanavar, A Course in Universal Algebra (Millennium Edition)](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/alglatvar/burrissanka.pdf): graduate text covering lattices, congruences, isomorphism theorems, subdirect representation and varieties, posted online.
- **Primary:** [Zhuk, A Proof of the CSP Dichotomy Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01914): the algebraic (WNU polymorphism) solution of the finite-domain CSP dichotomy.
- **Further reading:** [DeMeo, Congruence lattices of finite algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.4305): PhD thesis reviewing methods for representing finite lattices as congruence lattices of finite algebras.
references.MSC 08Bxx - Varieties:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 08B, "Varieties", is the part of [MSC 08 - General algebraic systems](node:MSC%2008%20-%20General%20algebraic%20systems) that studies varieties, also called equational classes: the classes of algebras of a fixed signature that satisfy a given set of identities $v\approx w$ between terms. Groups, rings, semigroups and left $R$-modules for a fixed ring $R$ are varieties; fields are not, because invertibility of nonzero elements is not an identity and a product of fields is not a field. ([Variety (universal algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29)) The concept note [Equational Classes of Algebras](node:Equational%20Classes%20of%20Algebras) and the general setting [Universal Algebra](node:Universal%20Algebra) cover the basics.

Research in 08B asks how the equational description of a class controls the structure of its members. The organising tools are Mal'tsev-type characterisations, which translate properties of congruence lattices such as permutability and distributivity into the existence of terms satisfying identities; Jónsson's lemma, which locates the subdirectly irreducible members of congruence-distributive varieties; and the finite basis problem, which asks which finite algebras have a finitely axiomatizable equational theory. ([UCLA Math 222A, Mal'tsev](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~baker/222a/handouts/cc_malcev/node2.html); [UCLA Math 222A, Jónsson](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~baker/222a/handouts/dd_jonsson/node5.html); [Kearnes–Szendrei–Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 08Bxx (see also 03C05) lists 08B05 equational logic, Mal'tsev conditions; 08B10 congruence modularity, congruence distributivity; 08B15 lattices of varieties; 08B20 free algebras; 08B25 products, amalgamated products, and other kinds of limits and colimits (see also 18A30); 08B26 subdirect products and subdirect irreducibility; 08B30 injectives, projectives; 08B99. ([MSC2020 08Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Bxx))

- **Neighbour 08A.** [MSC 08Axx - Algebraic structures](node:MSC%2008Axx%20-%20Algebraic%20structures) studies individual algebras (subalgebras, congruences, operations); 08B studies the classes they generate. ([MSC2020 08Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Bxx))
- **Neighbour 08C.** [MSC 08Cxx - Other classes of algebras](node:MSC%2008Cxx%20-%20Other%20classes%20of%20algebras) covers classes that are not varieties, such as [quasivarieties](node:Quasivarieties); cancellative semigroups are an example of a quasivariety that is not a variety. ([Variety (universal algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29))
- **Neighbour 03C.** The entry cross-refers to 03C05, equational classes in [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory). ([MSC2020 08Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Bxx))
- **Neighbour 18A.** 08B25 cross-refers to 18A30 in [MSC 18Axx - General theory of categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20of%20categories%20and%20functors) for limits and colimits. ([MSC2020 08Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Birkhoff's HSP theorem (08B05).** A class of algebras of one signature is a variety (equational class) if and only if it is closed under homomorphic images $H$, subalgebras $S$ and arbitrary direct products $P$; the variety generated by a class $K$ is $HSP(K)$. Birkhoff proved this in 1935. ([Variety (universal algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29); [Jipsen, UA tutorial](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf)) See [Birkhoff's Variety Theorem](node:Birkhoff's%20Variety%20Theorem).
- **Free algebras and subdirect irreducibility (08B20, 08B26).** In a nontrivial variety every set $S$ generates a free algebra $F(S)$ with the universal property, so every member is a homomorphic image of a free algebra. An algebra is subdirectly irreducible if it has more than one element and every subdirect representation has a factor isomorphic to it via the projection; every algebra is a subdirect product of its subdirectly irreducible quotients, so a variety is determined by its subdirectly irreducible members. The two-element chain is the only subdirectly irreducible [distributive lattice](node:Distributive%20Lattices), and an abelian group is subdirectly irreducible iff it is a cyclic $p$-group or a Prüfer group. ([Variety (universal algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29); [Subdirectly irreducible algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdirectly_irreducible_algebra))
- **Mal'tsev's theorem (08B05, 08B10).** A variety $V$ is congruence permutable (any two congruences of any algebra in $V$ permute) if and only if there is a term $p(x,y,z)$ with $V\models p(x,x,z)\approx z$ and $V\models p(x,z,z)\approx x$. Groups satisfy it with $p=xy^{-1}z$, and rings with $x-y+z$. A variety with such a term is called a Maltsev variety; Jónsson gave a characterisation of congruence distributivity in terms of identities of the same kind, and MSC 08B05 groups such characterisations under "Mal'tsev conditions". ([UCLA Math 222A, Mal'tsev](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~baker/222a/handouts/cc_malcev/node2.html); [Kearnes–Szendrei–Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf); [MSC2020 08Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Bxx))
- **Jónsson's lemma (08B10, 08B26).** If $K$ is a class of similar algebras and $HSP(K)$ is congruence distributive, then every subdirectly irreducible member of $HSP(K)$ lies in $HSP_u(K)$, the homomorphic images of subalgebras of ultraproducts of members of $K$ (Jónsson 1967). If $A$ is a finite algebra generating a congruence-distributive variety, every subdirectly irreducible member, finite or not, lies in $HS(A)$. Because the variety of lattices is congruence distributive, this applies to every variety of algebras with lattice reducts, such as Boolean and Heyting algebras. ([UCLA Math 222A, Jónsson](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~baker/222a/handouts/dd_jonsson/node5.html); [Jipsen, UA tutorial](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf); [Subdirectly irreducible algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdirectly_irreducible_algebra))
- **Finite basis theorems.** Every finite group, finite ring, finite commutative semigroup, finite lattice and two-element algebra in a finite language is finitely based, while some finite semigroups and some finite non-associative algebras are not. Baker's theorem (early 1970s): if $A$ is a finite algebra in a finite language and $V(A)$ is congruence distributive, then $A$ is finitely based. A variety in a finite language with a finite residual bound is finitely based if it is congruence modular (McKenzie, 1987), congruence meet-semidistributive (Willard, 2000), or more generally has a difference term (Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard). In 1996 McKenzie proved that it is undecidable whether a finite algebra is finitely based, settling Tarski's finite basis problem. ([Kearnes–Szendrei–Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf))
- **Varieties of lattices and residual bounds (08B15).** For a finite algebra $A$ with $V(A)$ congruence distributive, every subdirectly irreducible member of $V(A)$ has size at most $|A|$, so $V(A)$ is "residually $\le|A|$". The variety of distributive lattices is $HSP(\mathbf 2)$ and is locally finite. The subvarieties of a variety $V$ form a complete lattice $\Lambda V$ with meet given by intersection; Jipsen and Rose's monograph *Varieties of Lattices* (1992) treats varieties of lattices. ([Kearnes–Szendrei–Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf); [Nation, Notes on Lattice Theory, Ch. 8](https://math.hawaii.edu/~jb/math618/Nation-LatticeTheory.pdf); [Variety (universal algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29)) See [Lattice Theory](node:Lattice%20Theory).

### History
Birkhoff proved in 1935 that varieties are exactly the equational classes. ([Jipsen, UA tutorial](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf)) Mal'tsev's theorem characterises congruence permutability by a ternary term. ([UCLA Math 222A, Mal'tsev](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~baker/222a/handouts/cc_malcev/node2.html)) Jónsson's 1967 theorem on congruence-distributive varieties, together with his term characterisation of congruence distributivity, supplied the two ingredients of Baker's finite basis theorem in the early 1970s. Park's 1976 PhD thesis states the conjecture now named after him, McKenzie proved the congruence modular case in 1987 and the undecidability of the finite basis problem in 1996, and Willard proved the meet-semidistributive case in 2000. ([Jipsen, UA tutorial](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf); [Kearnes–Szendrei–Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Jónsson's problem (Park's conjecture).** If a variety in a finite language has a finite residual bound (every subdirectly irreducible member has size at most some $r<\omega$), must it be finitely based? A positive answer is sometimes called Park's conjecture, after R. E. Park's 1976 thesis. Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard write that "Jónsson's problem remains open to this day"; it is known for congruence distributive, congruence modular, congruence meet-semidistributive, and difference-term varieties. ([Kearnes–Szendrei–Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf))
- **Classifying finitely based finite algebras.** Since the finite basis property of finite algebras is undecidable, the same authors write that "the evidence suggests that a full classification of finitely based finite algebras is beyond reach", and research instead seeks finite basis theorems for natural classes of varieties. ([Kearnes–Szendrei–Willard](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Variety (universal algebra) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29): definition, Birkhoff's theorem, free algebras, examples.
- **Reference:** [Subdirectly irreducible algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdirectly_irreducible_algebra): subdirect representation and Jónsson's lemma.
- **Learn:** [UCLA Math 222A handouts: Mal'tsev's theorem](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~baker/222a/handouts/cc_malcev/node2.html) and [Jónsson's lemma](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~baker/222a/handouts/dd_jonsson/node5.html): graduate course notes.
- **Learn:** [Jipsen, Tutorial on Universal Algebra](https://math.chapman.edu/~jipsen/talks/BLAST2009/JipsenUAtutorial0.pdf): HSP, ultraproducts, congruence distributivity, lattices of subvarieties.
- **Primary:** [Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard, A finite basis theorem for difference-term varieties with a finite residual bound](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf): research paper with a history of the finite basis problem and Jónsson's problem.
- **Further reading:** [Burris and Sankappanavar, A Course in Universal Algebra (Springer GTM, 1981)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4613-8130-3): the standard graduate text.
references.MSC 08Cxx - Other classes of algebras:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 divides general algebraic systems into 08A (algebraic structures), 08B (varieties) and 08C (other classes of algebras). ([MSC2020, 08](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08-XX)) Where 08B studies equational classes, 08C collects classes of algebras organized in other ways: categories of algebras, axiomatic model classes, quasivarieties, and natural dualities. ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))

The common thread is a change of defining data. Varieties are the classes closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras and products (Birkhoff, 1935). ([Wikipedia, Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29)) Quasivarieties drop closure under homomorphic images and are axiomatized by implications between equations. ([Wikipedia, Quasivariety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasivariety)) Categorical approaches replace the signature by a Lawvere theory or a monad. Natural duality theory represents the quasivariety generated by a finite algebra as a category of topological structures. ([nLab, Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory); [Haviar](https://arxiv.org/html/1912.12901))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists the following codes. ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))
- **08C05 Categories of algebras** (see also 18C05). ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))
- **08C10 Axiomatic model classes** (see also 03Cxx, in particular 03C60). ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))
- **08C15 Quasivarieties.** ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))
- **08C20 Natural dualities for classes of algebras** (see also 06E15, 18A40, 22A30). ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))
- **08C99** None of the above, but in this section. ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))

Neighbouring codes, from the cross-references: 08B treats varieties, the equational special case. 18C05 (equational categories) and 18C10 (theories, structure and semantics) treat the same categorical material from the category-theory side, with 18C05 cross-referencing 08C05. 03C is model theory proper, while 08C10 concerns axiomatic classes of algebras. ([MSC2020, 08](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08-XX); [MSC2020, 18C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Cxx); [MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Quasi-identities and [Quasivarieties](node:Quasivarieties) (08C15).** A quasi-identity is an implication $s_1\approx t_1\wedge\cdots\wedge s_n\approx t_n\rightarrow s\approx t$. A class $K$ of algebras of a fixed signature is a quasivariety if equivalently: (i) $K$ is the class of models of a set of quasi-identities; (ii) $K$ contains a trivial algebra and is closed under isomorphisms, subalgebras and reduced products; (iii) $K$ contains a trivial algebra and is closed under isomorphisms, subalgebras, direct products and ultraproducts. Every variety is a quasivariety (take $n=0$). Cancellative semigroups form a quasivariety that is not a variety. ([Wikipedia, Quasivariety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasivariety); [Wikipedia, Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29))
- **Contrast with Birkhoff's HSP theorem.** A class of algebras of one signature is a variety if and only if it is closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras and arbitrary products; the hard direction is that such a class is equational. ([Wikipedia, Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29)) Quasivarieties keep $S$ and $P$ but need ultraproducts or reduced products in place of $H$. See [MSC 08Bxx - Varieties](node:MSC%2008Bxx%20-%20Varieties). ([Wikipedia, Quasivariety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasivariety))
- **Lawvere theories (08C05, 18C10).** A Lawvere theory is a category $T$ with finite products in which every object is isomorphic to a finite power of a generic object $x$. A model is a product-preserving functor $T\to\mathbf{Set}$, and homomorphisms are natural transformations. Lawvere theories correspond to finitary monads on $\mathbf{Set}$. A concrete category $U:C\to\mathbf{Set}$ is the category of models of a Lawvere theory exactly when $U$ is monadic and finitary (preserves filtered colimits). Lawvere introduced the method in his 1963 dissertation. ([nLab, Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory)) Monadic categories over $\mathbf{Set}$ go beyond finitary varieties: the forgetful functor from compact Hausdorff spaces to sets is monadic. ([Wikipedia, Monadic functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monadic_functor)) See [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory) and [Adjoint Functors](node:Adjoint%20Functors).
- **Natural dualities (08C20).** For a finite algebra $\mathbb{M}$, let $\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{ISP}(\mathbb{M})$ be the quasivariety it generates. An alter ego $\underset{\sim}{M}$ is a topological relational structure on $M$ that is algebraic over $\mathbb{M}$. The contravariant hom-functors $D(\mathbb{A})=\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{A},\mathbb{M})$ and $E(\mathbb{X})=\mathcal{X}(\mathbb{X},\underset{\sim}{M})$ are dually adjoint, and the alter ego yields a natural duality when each evaluation embedding $e_{\mathbb{A}}$ is an isomorphism; $\mathbb{M}$ is then dualisable. Stone's duality between [Boolean Algebras](node:Boolean%20Algebras) and Boolean spaces and Priestley's duality for [Distributive Lattices](node:Distributive%20Lattices) are the classical instances, and the NU-duality theorem gives a duality whenever $\mathbb{M}$ has a lattice reduct. Clark and Davey's monograph develops the theory in detail. ([Haviar](https://arxiv.org/html/1912.12901))
- **Non-dualisable algebras.** Dualisability is delicate: Szabó showed that the ring $\mathbb{Z}_8$ does not admit a natural duality (by showing its subring $2\mathbb{Z}_8$ is not dualizable), and Jackson used projective planes to show that almost all finite semigroups, in an asymptotic sense, are nondualisable, and gave an example of two dualisable finite semigroups whose product is inherently nondualisable. ([Szabó](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9709232); [Jackson](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3455))
- **Admissible rules and quasivarieties.** For a quasivariety generated by finitely many finite algebras, admissibility of a quasi-equation amounts to validity in a suitable finite free algebra, and is therefore decidable. Metcalfe and Röthlisberger give algorithms that replace the free algebra by a minimal finite set of algebras, which also check structural completeness, and adapt them to admissibility of rules in finite-valued logics. ([Metcalfe and Röthlisberger](https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.3530)) Cabrer and Metcalfe use natural dualities to axiomatize admissible quasi-identities of bounded distributive lattices, Stone, Kleene and De Morgan algebras. ([Cabrer and Metcalfe](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.06141)) See [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic).
- **Axiomatic model classes (08C10).** Classes of algebras defined by first-order axioms, studied with the tools of [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory); the MSC entry points to 03C60. ([MSC2020, 08C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=08Cxx); [Wikipedia, Quasivariety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasivariety))
- **[Universal Algebra](node:Universal%20Algebra)** supplies the common language, and [Congruence Relations on Algebras](node:Congruence%20Relations%20on%20Algebras) and [Lattice Theory](node:Lattice%20Theory) the structural tools used throughout the area. ([Wikipedia, Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29))

### History
Birkhoff proved the HSP theorem in 1935, fixing the equational picture against which 08C is defined. ([Wikipedia, Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29)) Stone (1936) gave the dual equivalence between Boolean algebras and Boolean spaces, the prototype of natural duality, later extended by Priestley to distributive lattices. ([Haviar](https://arxiv.org/html/1912.12901)) Lawvere's 1963 dissertation introduced categorical universal algebra via theories. ([nLab, Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory)) In 1998 two monographs appeared: Gorbunov's *Algebraic Theory of Quasivarieties* (Consultants Bureau, Siberian School of Algebra and Logic) and Clark and Davey's *Natural Dualities for the Working Algebraist*. ([Open Library, Gorbunov](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL1948104W); [Open Library, Clark and Davey](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=Natural+Dualities+for+the+Working+Algebraist))

### Open problems
- **Dualisability Problem.** Which finite algebras are dualisable? ([Haviar](https://arxiv.org/html/1912.12901))
- **Decidability of dualisability.** Is there an algorithm deciding whether a given finite algebra is dualisable? Haviar's survey states that both this and the Dualisability Problem remain open. ([Haviar](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.12901))
- **Admissibility in the modal logic K.** Decidability of admissibility for the basic modal logic $K$ is described as a major open problem. ([Wikipedia, Admissible rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admissible_rule))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Quasivariety (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasivariety): definitions and equivalent closure characterizations; [nLab, Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory) for the categorical side.
- **Learn:** [Haviar, On selected developments in the theory of natural dualities](https://arxiv.org/html/1912.12901): an introduction to alter egos, the duality functors and the main open problems.
- **Primary:** [Metcalfe and Röthlisberger, Admissibility in finitely generated quasivarieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.3530): research paper on admissible quasi-equations; [Szabó, Z_8 is not dualizable](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9709232).
- **Further reading:** [Gorbunov, *Algebraic Theory of Quasivarieties* (1998)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL1948104W) and [Clark and Davey, *Natural Dualities for the Working Algebraist* (1998)](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=Natural+Dualities+for+the+Working+Algebraist): the standard monographs.
references.MSC 11 - Number theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Number theory studies the integers and their properties and relations, including primes and objects built from integers such as rationals and algebraic integers. Its main subdivisions are elementary, analytic, algebraic and Diophantine-geometric number theory, with probabilistic, combinatorial, computational and applied branches alongside. ([Wikipedia: Number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory)) Analytic questions about primes are studied through objects such as the [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function), while algebraic number theory replaces $\mathbb Z$ by rings of integers of number fields. ([Wikipedia: Number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory))

Much current research is organized by the Langlands program, conjectured by Langlands in 1967 and 1970, which relates Galois representations to automorphic forms; its $\mathrm{GL}_1$ case is class field theory and Wiles's modularity theorem is an instance of reciprocity, but the general conjectures remain unproven. ([Wikipedia: Langlands program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_program)) Two Millennium Prize Problems, the Riemann hypothesis and the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, are number-theoretic. ([Clay: Riemann hypothesis](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/); [Clay: BSD](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/birch-and-swinnerton-dyer-conjecture/))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 11 has general codes 11-00 (reference works), 11-01 (introductory), 11-02 (research exposition), 11-03 (history), 11-04 (software), 11-06 (proceedings) and 11-11 (research data), and twenty second-level sections. ([MSC2020: 11-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11-XX)) By subject they group as follows (cross-references from the same entry):
- **Elementary and combinatorial:** [MSC 11Axx - Elementary number theory](node:MSC%2011Axx%20-%20Elementary%20number%20theory) (number-field analogues go to 11R04), [MSC 11Bxx - Sequences and sets](node:MSC%2011Bxx%20-%20Sequences%20and%20sets), [MSC 11Cxx - Polynomials and matrices](node:MSC%2011Cxx%20-%20Polynomials%20and%20matrices), [MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; partitions](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions).
- **Diophantine:** [MSC 11Dxx - Diophantine equations](node:MSC%2011Dxx%20-%20Diophantine%20equations) (see also 11G, 14G), [MSC 11Gxx - Arithmetic algebraic geometry (Diophantine geometry)](node:MSC%2011Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20algebraic%20geometry%20%28Diophantine%20geometry%29), [MSC 11Hxx - Geometry of numbers](node:MSC%2011Hxx%20-%20Geometry%20of%20numbers) (coding applications go to 94B75), [MSC 11Jxx - Diophantine approximation, transcendental number theory](node:MSC%2011Jxx%20-%20Diophantine%20approximation,%20transcendental%20number%20theory).
