- **Analytic and probabilistic:** [MSC 11Kxx - Probabilistic theory - distribution modulo 1; metric theory of algorithms](node:MSC%2011Kxx%20-%20Probabilistic%20theory%20-%20distribution%20modulo%201;%20metric%20theory%20of%20algorithms), [MSC 11Lxx - Exponential sums and character sums](node:MSC%2011Lxx%20-%20Exponential%20sums%20and%20character%20sums) (finite-field sums go to 11T), [MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory), [MSC 11Nxx - Multiplicative number theory](node:MSC%2011Nxx%20-%20Multiplicative%20number%20theory).
- **Algebraic and automorphic:** [MSC 11Exx - Forms and linear algebraic groups](node:MSC%2011Exx%20-%20Forms%20and%20linear%20algebraic%20groups), [MSC 11Fxx - Discontinuous groups and automorphic forms](node:MSC%2011Fxx%20-%20Discontinuous%20groups%20and%20automorphic%20forms) (see also 11R39, 11S37, 22E50, 22E55), [MSC 11Rxx - Algebraic number theory - global fields](node:MSC%2011Rxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20global%20fields) (complex multiplication goes to 11G15), [MSC 11Sxx - Algebraic number theory - local and p-adic fields](node:MSC%2011Sxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20local%20and%20p-adic%20fields), [MSC 11Txx - Finite fields and commutative rings (number-theoretic aspects)](node:MSC%2011Txx%20-%20Finite%20fields%20and%20commutative%20rings%20%28number-theoretic%20aspects%29).
- **Other:** [MSC 11Uxx - Connections of number theory and logic](node:MSC%2011Uxx%20-%20Connections%20of%20number%20theory%20and%20logic), [MSC 11Yxx - Computational number theory](node:MSC%2011Yxx%20-%20Computational%20number%20theory) (software goes to 11-04; see also 68W30), [MSC 11Zxx - Miscellaneous applications of number theory](node:MSC%2011Zxx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20applications%20of%20number%20theory).

### Key concepts
- **Prime number theorem ([Prime Numbers](node:Prime%20Numbers), 11N).** $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$, proved independently by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin in 1896 using Riemann's ideas on the zeta function; Selberg and Erdős found elementary proofs in 1949. Von Koch (1901) showed that the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to $\pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x)=O(\sqrt x\log x)$. ([Wikipedia: Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem)) See [Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory).
- **Dirichlet's theorem (11N, 11M).** If $\gcd(a,d)=1$, the progression $a,a+d,a+2d,\dots$ contains infinitely many primes; in fact the primes are asymptotically equidistributed among the $\varphi(d)$ reduced residue classes mod $d$ and $\sum 1/p$ over each class diverges. Dirichlet proved it in 1837 using $L$-series. ([Wikipedia: Dirichlet's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions)) See [Modular Arithmetic](node:Modular%20Arithmetic).
- **Modularity and Fermat's Last Theorem (11F, 11G, 11D).** Wiles, with Taylor (*Annals*, 1995), proved modularity of semistable elliptic curves over $\mathbb Q$; with Ribet's 1986 theorem that a Frey curve cannot be modular, this proves Fermat's Last Theorem. Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor (2001) proved modularity of all elliptic curves over $\mathbb Q$. ([Wikipedia: Wiles's proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiles%27s_proof_of_Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem))
- **Green–Tao theorem (11B, 11N).** If $A$ is a set of primes with $\limsup_N|A\cap[1,N]|/\pi(N)>0$, then $A$ contains arithmetic progressions of every length; in particular the primes do. The proof transfers Szemerédi's theorem to pseudorandom sets of positive relative density and uses Goldston–Yıldırım to place the primes in such a set. ([Wikipedia: Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem); [Green–Tao, Annals 167 (2008)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2008/167-2/p03))
- **Bounded gaps between primes (11N).** Zhang proved $\liminf_n(p_{n+1}-p_n)<7\times10^7$, refining Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım with a stronger Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem for smooth moduli. ([Zhang, Annals 179 (2014)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2014/179-3/p07)) Maynard and Tao's method and the Polymath project lowered the bound to 246, and to 12 (or 6) under the (generalized) Elliott–Halberstam conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Twin prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime))
- **Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer: known cases (11G).** For an elliptic curve $E/\mathbb Q$, BSD predicts $\mathrm{rank}\,E(\mathbb Q)=\mathrm{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)$. Gross–Zagier (1986) and Kolyvagin (1989) prove this rank statement when the analytic rank is $0$ or $1$ (for all $E/\mathbb Q$ after modularity), and Bhargava–Shankar bound the average rank by $7/6$; combined with other results, a positive proportion of curves have analytic rank zero and satisfy the conjecture. ([Wikipedia: BSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture))

### History
Euclid's *Elements* proves there are infinitely many primes and gives the Euclidean algorithm; Diophantus's *Arithmetica* studies rational solutions of polynomial equations; Fermat stated his little theorem and Last Theorem; Euler began serious work in 1729; Gauss's *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801) set the agenda of the nineteenth century. Dirichlet's 1837 theorem is a conventional starting point of analytic number theory and Riemann's 1859 paper of complex-analytic methods. ([Wikipedia: Number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory)) Wiles's corrected proof of modularity appeared in 1995, 358 years after Fermat's statement. ([Wikipedia: Wiles's proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiles%27s_proof_of_Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem); [Wikipedia: Number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory))

### Open problems
- **Riemann hypothesis.** Every nontrivial zero of $\zeta(s)$ has real part $1/2$; proposed in Riemann's 1859 paper and listed as unsolved by Clay. ([Clay: Riemann hypothesis](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/))
- **Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.** The rank of $E(\mathbb Q)$ equals the order of vanishing of $L(E,s)$ at $s=1$, with a formula for the leading coefficient; only special cases are proved (including the rank statement for analytic rank $\le1$), and it is an unsolved Millennium Prize Problem. ([Wikipedia: BSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture); [Clay: BSD](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/birch-and-swinnerton-dyer-conjecture/))
- **Twin prime conjecture.** Whether infinitely many $p$ have $p+2$ prime is unknown; improving the bounded-gaps constant from 246 to 2 would prove it. ([Wikipedia: Twin prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime))
- **Goldbach's conjecture.** Every even integer $>2$ is a sum of two primes (Goldbach, 1742); it is unproven, verified up to $4\times10^{18}$, partial results include Chen's theorem (1973: every sufficiently large even number is a sum of a prime and a prime or semiprime) and Helfgott's proof of the weak (ternary) conjecture, which does not imply the full conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Goldbach's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_conjecture))
- **Langlands reciprocity and functoriality.** The general conjectures remain unproven; even the full conjecture for $\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb Q)$ is open. ([Wikipedia: Langlands program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_program))

> [!warning] Contested
> **abc conjecture.** For coprime positive $a+b=c$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ only finitely many triples have $c>\mathrm{rad}(abc)^{1+\varepsilon}$ (Oesterlé–Masser, 1985). Mochizuki claimed a proof in 2012 via inter-universal Teichmüller theory, published in 2021 in a journal he edits; Scholze and Stix (2018) reported a gap "so severe that ... small modifications will not rescue the proof strategy", and the conjecture is still regarded as unproven by the mainstream community. ([Wikipedia: abc conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Number theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory): subdivisions, history and open problems.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.781 Theory of Numbers (Kumar, 2012)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-781-theory-of-numbers-spring-2012/): primes, congruences, quadratic reciprocity, Diophantine equations, continued fractions, partitions.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.785 Number Theory I (Sutherland, 2021)](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/lectures.html): graduate algebraic number theory through class field theory.
- **Primary:** [Green–Tao, *The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions*, Annals 167 (2008)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2008/167-2/p03) and [Zhang, *Bounded gaps between primes*, Annals 179 (2014)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2014/179-3/p07): two landmark results on prime distribution.
- **Further reading:** [Ireland–Rosen, *A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory*, GTM (1990)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2103-4), [Iwaniec–Kowalski, *Analytic Number Theory*, AMS Colloquium (2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/coll/053), and [Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory* (Springer, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-03983-0): standard graduate texts for the elementary, analytic and algebraic branches.
references.MSC 11Axx - Elementary number theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Elementary number theory, a section of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), covers the multiplicative structure of the integers and greatest common divisors, congruences and primitive roots, power residues and reciprocity, arithmetic functions, primes, factorization, continued fractions and number representations. ([MSC2020, 11A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Axx)) A basic tool is Bézout's identity: for nonzero integers $a,b$ there are $x,y\in\mathbb Z$ with $\gcd(a,b)=ax+by$, from which follow Euclid's lemma ($a\mid bc$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$ imply $a\mid c$) and the other basic facts about coprimality. ([Conrad, Divisibility and gcds, Thm 3.5, Cor 4.1](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ugradnumthy/divgcd.pdf))

Gauss's *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801) brought together results of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange and Legendre with much of his own, treating congruences systematically and making number theory rigorous and systematic. ([Wikipedia, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disquisitiones_Arithmeticae)) Some famous open questions, such as whether an odd perfect number exists, are stated entirely in this elementary language. ([Wikipedia, Perfect number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number))

### Scope
MSC2020 11A ("Elementary number theory"; for analogues in number fields see 11R04) comprises: 11A05 multiplicative structure, Euclidean algorithm, greatest common divisors; 11A07 congruences, primitive roots, residue systems; 11A15 power residues, reciprocity; 11A25 arithmetic functions, related numbers, inversion formulas; 11A41 primes; 11A51 factorization, primality; 11A55 continued fractions (for approximation results see 11J70; see also 11K50, 30B70, 40A15); 11A63 radix representation, digital problems (for metric results see 11K16); 11A67 other number representations; 11A99. ([MSC2020, 11A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Axx))

Neighbours, by those cross-references: number-field analogues go to 11R04 in [MSC 11Rxx - Algebraic number theory - global fields](node:MSC%2011Rxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20global%20fields); Diophantine approximation by continued fractions to 11J70 in [MSC 11Jxx - Diophantine approximation, transcendental number theory](node:MSC%2011Jxx%20-%20Diophantine%20approximation,%20transcendental%20number%20theory); metric theory of continued fractions and digits to 11K in [MSC 11Kxx - Probabilistic theory - distribution modulo 1; metric theory of algorithms](node:MSC%2011Kxx%20-%20Probabilistic%20theory%20-%20distribution%20modulo%201;%20metric%20theory%20of%20algorithms). ([MSC2020, 11A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Fundamental theorem of arithmetic (11A05, 11A51).** Every integer $n>1$ is prime or a product of primes, uniquely up to the order of the factors; existence is an induction, and uniqueness rests on Euclid's lemma. Unique factorization fails in other rings: in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$. ([Wikipedia, Fundamental theorem of arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_arithmetic)) Euclid IX.20 shows there are infinitely many [primes](node:Prime%20Numbers): for primes $p_1,\dots,p_k$, every prime divisor of $p_1\cdots p_k+1$ is new. ([Euclid IX.20, Joyce ed.](https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/elements/bookIX/propIX20.html))
- **Chinese remainder theorem (11A07).** If $n_1,\dots,n_k$ are pairwise coprime and $N=n_1\cdots n_k$, the system $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ has a solution, unique modulo $N$; equivalently $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\cong\prod_i\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$ as rings. ([Wikipedia, Chinese remainder theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_remainder_theorem)) See [Modular Arithmetic](node:Modular%20Arithmetic).
- **Fermat, Euler and Wilson (11A07).** For a prime $p$ and $p\nmid a$, $a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p$; more generally for $m\ge2$ and $\gcd(a,m)=1$, $a^{\varphi(m)}\equiv1\pmod m$, the coprimality hypothesis being essential. ([Conrad, Euler's theorem, Thms 1.1–1.2](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ugradnumthy/eulerthm.pdf)) For $n>1$, $n$ is prime iff $(n-1)!\equiv-1\pmod n$ (Wilson); Gauss showed that the product of the units modulo $m$ is $-1$ exactly when $m$ has a primitive root and $+1$ otherwise. ([Wikipedia, Wilson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson%27s_theorem))
- **Primitive roots (11A07).** $g$ is a primitive root modulo $n$ if every residue coprime to $n$ is a power of $g$. Primitive roots exist iff $n=1,2,4,p^k$ or $2p^k$ with $p$ an odd prime, and then there are $\varphi(\varphi(n))$ of them; Gauss gave the first rigorous existence proof for prime moduli. ([Wikipedia, Primitive root modulo n](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_root_modulo_n))
- **Quadratic reciprocity (11A15).** For distinct odd primes $p,q$, $\left(\tfrac pq\right)\left(\tfrac qp\right)=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}2\cdot\frac{q-1}2}$, with supplements $\left(\tfrac{-1}p\right)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$ and $\left(\tfrac2p\right)=(-1)^{(p^2-1)/8}$. Conjectured by Euler and Legendre, it was first proved by Gauss in 1796 and published in 1801; more than 240 proofs are now known. ([Wikipedia, Quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_reciprocity))
- **Arithmetic functions and Möbius inversion (11A25).** For arithmetic functions $f,g$, $g(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)$ for all $n\ge1$ iff $f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\,g(n/d)$; in Dirichlet-convolution form $g=\mathbf 1*f\iff f=\mu*g$, since $\mathbf 1*\mu=\varepsilon$. For example $\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n$. ([Wikipedia, Möbius inversion formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_inversion_formula)) Euclid–Euler theorem: an even number is perfect ($\sigma(n)=2n$) iff it is $2^{p-1}(2^p-1)$ with $2^p-1$ prime. ([Wikipedia, Perfect number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number))
- **Continued fractions (11A55).** A real number has an eventually periodic regular continued fraction iff it is a quadratic irrational (Euler for one direction, Lagrange for the converse); the expansion is purely periodic iff the quadratic irrational $\zeta$ is reduced, i.e. $\zeta>1$ and its conjugate lies in $(-1,0)$ (Galois). ([Wikipedia, Periodic continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_continued_fraction))

### History
Euclid's *Elements* contains Euclid's lemma (VII.30), existence of prime factorization (VII.32) and the infinitude of primes (IX.20); Gauss's *Disquisitiones* (art. 16) appears to give the first proof of uniqueness. ([Wikipedia, Fundamental theorem of arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_arithmetic); [Euclid IX.20](https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/elements/bookIX/propIX20.html)) The Chinese remainder theorem first appears in the *Sunzi Suanjing*, with a general method by Qin Jiushao (1247). ([Wikipedia, CRT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_remainder_theorem)) Wilson's theorem was announced by Waring in 1770 and first proved by Lagrange in 1771. ([Wikipedia, Wilson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson%27s_theorem)) Gauss wrote the *Disquisitiones* at 21 and published it in 1801, treating congruences, primitive roots, quadratic reciprocity, quadratic forms and cyclotomy. ([Wikipedia, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disquisitiones_Arithmeticae)) Möbius introduced his inversion formula in 1832. ([Wikipedia, Möbius inversion formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_inversion_formula))

### Open problems
- **Odd perfect numbers.** It is unknown whether any odd perfect number exists; any one must exceed $10^{1500}$ (Ochem–Rao 2012) and, by Euler, have the form $q^{\alpha}p_1^{2e_1}\cdots p_k^{2e_k}$ with $q\equiv\alpha\equiv1\pmod4$. It is also unknown whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes, hence infinitely many even perfect numbers. ([Wikipedia, Perfect number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number))
- **Lehmer's totient problem (1932).** Is there a composite $n$ with $\varphi(n)\mid n-1$? Unsolved; any such $n$ must be odd, squarefree and a Carmichael number, with at least 14 distinct prime factors (Cohen–Hagis 1980). ([Wikipedia, Lehmer's totient problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehmer%27s_totient_problem))
- **Carmichael's totient conjecture.** For every $m$, the equation $\varphi(x)=m$ has either no solutions or at least two. Ford calls it an open problem; a counterexample would have to exceed $10^{10^{10}}$, and if one exists then a positive proportion of totient values have multiplicity one. Ford also proved Sierpiński's conjecture that every multiplicity $k\ge2$ occurs. ([Ford, Annals 150 (1999)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9907204); [Wikipedia, Carmichael's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael%27s_totient_function_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fundamental theorem of arithmetic (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_arithmetic): statement, proofs, history, failure in other rings.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Divisibility and greatest common divisors](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ugradnumthy/divgcd.pdf) and [Conrad, Euler's theorem](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ugradnumthy/eulerthm.pdf): careful undergraduate notes with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Ford, The number of solutions of φ(x)=m (Annals 1999)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9907204): research paper on totient multiplicities, proving Sierpiński's conjecture and discussing Carmichael's.
- **Further reading:** [Hardy and Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, 6th ed. (OUP 2008)](https://india.oup.com/product/an-introduction-to-the-theory-of-numbers-sixth-edition-9780199219865): the classic text on congruences, arithmetic functions and continued fractions.
references.MSC 11Bxx - Sequences and sets:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11B, "Sequences and sets", is the part of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) that studies structured subsets of the integers and integer sequences. Its codes run from density and gaps (11B05), additive bases and sumsets (11B13), arithmetic progressions (11B25) and "arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity" (11B30), through recurrences (11B37), Fibonacci and Lucas numbers (11B39), sequences mod $m$ (11B50) and Farey sequences (11B57), to binomial coefficients (11B65), Bernoulli and Euler numbers (11B68), Bell and Stirling numbers (11B73), special sequences (11B83) and automata sequences (11B85). ([MSC2020 11Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Bxx))

Its research core is additive (arithmetic) [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics): when must a set of integers contain arithmetic progressions, and what structure is forced on a set $A$ whose sumset $A+A$ is small. The guiding results are Szemerédi's theorem, the Green–Tao theorem, Freiman's theorem and sum-product estimates; their proofs draw on [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis), [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory), [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory) (regularity lemmas), entropy methods and Gowers uniformity norms. ([Wikipedia, Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem); [Oxford C3.10](https://courses.maths.ox.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=5769)) A second strand is the arithmetic of special sequences: zero sets of linear recurrences, congruences for binomial coefficients and Bernoulli numbers, and automatic sequences. ([Wikipedia, Skolem–Mahler–Lech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skolem%E2%80%93Mahler%E2%80%93Lech_theorem); [Wikipedia, Automatic sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_sequence))

### Scope
- **Neighbour 11P** ([MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; partitions](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions)): Waring's problem (11P05), Goldbach-type problems (11P32), the Hardy–Littlewood method (11P55) and "inverse problems of additive number theory, including sumsets" (11P70) live there, while 11B13 is "Additive bases, including sumsets" (see [Additive Bases and Integer Partitions](node:Additive%20Bases%20and%20Integer%20Partitions)). ([MSC2020 11Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Pxx); [MSC2020 11Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Bxx))
- **Neighbour 11N** ([MSC 11Nxx - Multiplicative number theory](node:MSC%2011Nxx%20-%20Multiplicative%20number%20theory)): 11B25 cross-refers to 11N13, primes in congruence classes. ([MSC2020 11Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Bxx))
- **Neighbours 05 and 33**: 11B13 refers to 05B10 and 11B65 to 05A10, 05A30 in [MSC 05 - Combinatorics](node:MSC%2005%20-%20Combinatorics); 11B37 sends applications of recurrences to [special functions](node:Special%20Functions) to 33. ([MSC2020 11Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Szemerédi's theorem (11B25).** Every $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ of positive upper density contains a $k$-term arithmetic progression for every $k$; equivalently, with $r_k(N)$ the largest size of a $k$-AP-free subset of $\{1,\dots,N\}$, $r_k(N)=o(N)$. ([Wikipedia, Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem))
- **Kelley–Meka and the bounds for $r_3$.** Kelley and Meka proved that for some $\beta>0$, every $A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$ with $|A|\ge 2^{-O((\log N)^\beta)}N$ contains a nontrivial 3-term progression, where previous bounds only reached density $(\log N)^{-1-c}$. ([Kelley–Meka, arXiv:2302.05537](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05537)) Bloom and Sisask's account gives $|A|\le\exp(-c(\log N)^{1/12})N$ for 3-AP-free $A$. ([Bloom–Sisask, arXiv:2302.07211](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07211)) On the lower side, O'Bryant's form of the Behrend–Rankin–Elkin construction gives $r_3(N)>c\,N(2\log_2N)^{1/4}4^{-\sqrt{2\log_2N}}$ ([O'Bryant, arXiv:0811.3057](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.3057)), and Elsholtz, Hunter, Proske and Sauermann gave the first improvement of Behrend's 1946 construction beyond lower-order factors, together with lower bounds $(cp)^n$, $c>1/2$, for progression-free sets in $\mathbb F_p^n$. ([Elsholtz et al., arXiv:2406.12290](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12290))
- **Gowers norms and longer progressions (11B30).** Green, Tao and Ziegler proved the inverse theorem for the $U^{s+1}[N]$ norm for all $s\ge3$: a bounded function with large $U^{s+1}[N]$ norm correlates with a bounded-complexity $s$-step nilsequence. ([Green–Tao–Ziegler, arXiv:1009.3998](https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.3998)) Using quasipolynomial inverse bounds, Leng, Sah and Sawhney proved $r_k(N)\le N\exp(-(\log\log N)^{c_k})$ for $k\ge5$; for $k=4$, Green and Tao had $r_4(N)\le CN(\log N)^{-c}$. ([Leng–Sah–Sawhney, arXiv:2402.17995](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17995); [Wikipedia, Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem))
- **Green–Tao theorem (11B25, 11N13).** The [primes](node:Prime%20Numbers) contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. The proof combines Szemerédi's theorem, a transference principle to dense subsets of pseudorandom sets, and the Goldston–Yıldırım almost-prime majorant. ([Green–Tao, arXiv:math/0404188](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0404188))
- **Freiman's theorem and Marton's conjecture (11B13, 11B30).** If $A\subset\mathbb Z$ is finite with $|A+A|\le K|A|$, then $A$ lies in a generalized arithmetic progression whose dimension and size are bounded in terms of $K$ (Freiman 1964–66; Ruzsa's proof uses the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality and Ruzsa covering). ([Wikipedia, Freiman's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiman%27s_theorem)) Gowers, Green, Manners and Tao proved the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa (Marton) conjecture for $\mathbb F_2^n$ in a 2023 preprint, whose proof was formalised in Lean 4 ([Wikipedia, Freiman's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiman%27s_theorem)), and then for every abelian group of torsion $m$: if $|A+A|\le K|A|$, $A$ is covered by $(2K)^{O(m^3)}$ translates of a subgroup of size at most $|A|$. ([GGMT, arXiv:2404.02244](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02244))
- **Sum-product phenomenon.** Erdős and Szemerédi (1983) proved $\max(|A+A|,|A\cdot A|)\ge|A|^{1+\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$; Elekes reached exponent $1/4$ and Solymosi $1/3$ over the reals; Bourgain, Katz and Tao proved a version in $\mathbb F_p$ for $p^\delta<|A|<p^{1-\delta}$. ([Wikipedia, Sum-product phenomenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sum-product_phenomenon))
- **Special sequences.** Skolem–Mahler–Lech (11B37): for a linear recurrence over a field of characteristic $0$, $\{n:u_n=0\}$ is a finite set together with finitely many arithmetic progressions; known proofs are $p$-adic and non-constructive. ([Wikipedia, Skolem–Mahler–Lech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skolem%E2%80%93Mahler%E2%80%93Lech_theorem)) Lucas (1878, 11B65): $\binom mn\equiv\prod_i\binom{m_i}{n_i}\pmod p$ over base-$p$ digits, and Kummer: the exact power of $p$ dividing $\binom mn$ is the number of carries adding $n$ and $m-n$ in base $p$. ([Wikipedia, Lucas's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%27s_theorem)) Von Staudt–Clausen (1840, 11B68): $B_{2n}+\sum_{(p-1)\mid2n}1/p\in\mathbb Z$. ([Wikipedia, Von Staudt–Clausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Staudt%E2%80%93Clausen_theorem)) Cobham (11B85): for multiplicatively independent $h,k$, a sequence is both $h$- and $k$-automatic iff it is ultimately periodic; Christol: over $\mathbb F_q$ it is $q$-automatic iff its generating series is algebraic. ([Wikipedia, Automatic sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_sequence))

### History
Erdős and Turán conjectured Szemerédi's theorem in 1936; Roth proved $k=3$ in 1953 and Szemerédi $k=4$ in 1969 and the general case in 1975. Furstenberg gave an ergodic proof in 1977, Furstenberg–Katznelson the multidimensional and Bergelson–Leibman the polynomial versions, and Gowers (2001) a Fourier-analytic proof introducing the Gowers norms. ([Wikipedia, Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem)) Skolem (1935), Mahler (1935) and Lech (1953) proved the recurrence theorem in increasing generality. ([Wikipedia, Skolem–Mahler–Lech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skolem%E2%80%93Mahler%E2%80%93Lech_theorem)) Green and Tao posted their theorem on primes in 2004. ([Green–Tao, arXiv:math/0404188](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0404188)) Kelley and Meka's 3-AP bound appeared in February 2023. ([Kelley–Meka, arXiv:2302.05537](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05537))

### Open problems
- **Growth rate of $r_k(N)$.** The exact growth rate is open; for $k=3$ the Behrend-type lower bound $N2^{-O(\sqrt{\log N})}$ and the Kelley–Meka upper bound $N2^{-O((\log N)^\beta)}$ remain far apart. ([Wikipedia, Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem); [Kelley–Meka, arXiv:2302.05537](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05537))
- **Erdős–Turán conjecture on additive bases.** If $B$ is a basis of order 2, must $\limsup_n r_B(n)=\infty$? It "remains unsolved"; Borwein, Choi and Chu (2006) proved that for every additive basis the representation function eventually exceeds 7. ([Wikipedia, Erdős–Turán conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tur%C3%A1n_conjecture_on_additive_bases))
- **Skolem problem.** It is unknown whether an algorithm decides if a linear recurrence has any non-periodic zero. ([Wikipedia, Skolem–Mahler–Lech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skolem%E2%80%93Mahler%E2%80%93Lech_theorem))
- **Sum-product conjecture over the integers.** Erdős (1974) conjectured $\max(|A+A|,|A\cdot A|)\ge|A|^{2-o(1)}$; Wikipedia reports it disproved over the reals in 2026 and still open over the integers. ([Wikipedia, Sum-product phenomenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sum-product_phenomenon)) The disproof is the preprint of Bloom, Sawin, Schildkraut and Zhelezov, which builds sets of real algebraic integers in number fields of degree about $\log|A|$ with $\max(|A+A|,|AA|)\le|A|^{2-c}$; it is a recent preprint, not yet refereed. ([Bloom et al., arXiv:2605.28781](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28781))

> [!warning] Contested
> The Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions (if $\sum_{n\in A}1/n=\infty$ then $A$ contains arbitrarily long progressions; it would imply both Szemerédi and Green–Tao) is listed as unsolved, but the same page reports a 2026 claimed proof with a Lean formalization, released by OpenAI, without confirming it. ([Wikipedia, Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s_conjecture_on_arithmetic_progressions))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Szemerédi's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem): statements, $r_k(N)$ bounds and proof history.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 11Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Bxx): the official code list.
- **Learn:** [Oxford C3.10 Additive Combinatorics (Ben Green)](https://courses.maths.ox.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=5769): Roth, Freiman, Bogolyubov, entropy methods and Marton's conjecture, sum-product.
- **Primary:** [Kelley and Meka, Strong bounds for 3-progressions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05537): the bound $2^{-O((\log N)^\beta)}N$ for 3-AP-free sets.
- **Primary:** [Green and Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0404188): the transference method.
- **Further reading:** [Tao and Vu, Additive Combinatorics (CUP, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511755149): monograph.
references.MSC 11Cxx - Polynomials and matrices:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11C collects the number theory of individual polynomials and of matrices with arithmetic entries: polynomials with integer coefficients, their irreducibility, their roots and their heights (11C08), and matrices and determinants studied for their arithmetic (11C20). The section is small, but it is where questions such as Lehmer's problem on the Mahler measure, irreducibility criteria over $\mathbf Q$, and normal forms of integer matrices are filed. ([MSC2020, 11Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Cxx); [Smyth, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397))

A central object is the Mahler measure $M(P)$ of an integer polynomial, a height that is multiplicative and equals $1$ exactly on products of cyclotomic polynomials and powers of $z$ (Kronecker). How close $M(P)$ can come to $1$ without equalling it is Lehmer's problem, still unsolved. On the matrix side, the Smith and Hermite normal forms reduce integer matrices to canonical shapes under unimodular transformations, which is the arithmetic behind finitely generated abelian groups, lattices, and linear Diophantine systems. ([Smyth, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397); [Smith normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_normal_form); [Hermite normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_normal_form))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists three codes under 11Cxx: 11C08 "Polynomials in number theory" (see also 13F20), 11C20 "Matrices, determinants in number theory" (see also 15B36), and 11C99 for other work in the section. ([MSC2020, 11Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Cxx))

Neighbouring codes, as MSC2020 words them:
- **11T06** "Polynomials over finite fields" is a separate code in 11T, the finite-field section. ([MSC2020, 11Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Txx))
- **11R06** "PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure" and **11R09** "Polynomials (irreducibility, etc.)" are the algebraic-number-theory homes of closely related work; Smyth's Mahler-measure survey is itself classified primarily under 11R06. ([MSC2020, 11Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Rxx); [Smyth, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397))
- **15B36** "Matrices of integers" (cross-referenced to 11C20) and **15B34** "Boolean and Hadamard matrices" cover the matrix-theoretic side in [MSC 15 - Linear and multilinear algebra; matrix theory](node:MSC%2015%20-%20Linear%20and%20multilinear%20algebra;%20matrix%20theory). ([MSC2020, 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Mahler measure.** For $P(z)=a_0\prod_{i=1}^d(z-\alpha_i)\in\mathbf C[z]$, $M(P)=|a_0|\prod_{i}\max(1,|\alpha_i|)=\exp\int_0^1\log|P(e^{2\pi i t})|\,dt$; the two forms agree by Jensen's formula. $M$ is multiplicative, $M(PQ)=M(P)M(Q)$, and for $P\in\mathbf Z[z]$ one has $M(P)\ge1$. Only finitely many integer polynomials have bounded degree and bounded measure, so $M$ is a height. ([Smyth, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397); [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure)) See also [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) for Jensen's formula.
- **Kronecker's theorem.** For $P\in\mathbf Z[z]$, $M(P)=1$ only if $\pm P$ is a power of $z$ times a product of cyclotomic polynomials. In the form stated in the reference article: an irreducible monic $P\in\mathbf Z[z]$ with $M(P)=1$ is $z$ or a cyclotomic polynomial. ([Smyth, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397); [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure))
- **Lower bounds for $M$.** Smyth (1971): if $\alpha$ is a nonreciprocal algebraic integer then $M(\alpha)\ge M(z^3-z-1)=\theta_0=1.3247\ldots$, with $\theta_0$ best possible. Dobrowolski (1979): for an algebraic integer $\alpha$ of degree $d\ge2$, not a root of unity, $M(\alpha)>1+\tfrac{1}{1200}\left(\tfrac{\log\log d}{\log d}\right)^3$; later work improved the constant (Voutier: $1/4$ for all $d\ge2$) but not the dependence on $d$. ([Smyth, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397))
- **Cyclotomic polynomials.** $x^n-1=\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(x)$, $\Phi_n(x)=\prod_{d\mid n}(x^d-1)^{\mu(n/d)}$, and $\Phi_n\in\mathbf Z[x]$ is monic and irreducible over $\mathbf Q$ of degree $\varphi(n)$. Its coefficients need not lie in $\{0,\pm1\}$: $\Phi_{105}$ has a coefficient $-2$, and $105=3\cdot5\cdot7$ is the smallest product of three distinct odd primes. ([Cyclotomic polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotomic_polynomial)) Irreducibility of $\Phi_n$ is what makes $[\mathbf Q(\zeta_n):\mathbf Q]=\varphi(n)$ in [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).
- **Irreducibility criteria over $\mathbf Q$.** For monic $f\in\mathbf Z[T]$: if $f\bmod p$ is irreducible in $(\mathbf Z/p\mathbf Z)[T]$ for some prime $p$, then $f$ is irreducible in $\mathbf Q[T]$; if $p$ divides every non-leading coefficient and $p^2\nmid a_0$ (Eisenstein), then $f$ is irreducible. The mod-$p$ test can fail at every prime: $T^4-10T^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbf Q$ but reducible mod every $p$. A primitive $f$ of degree $d\ge1$ with $|f(a)|$ equal to $1$ or a prime for at least $2d+1$ integers $a$ is irreducible. ([Conrad, Irreducibility tests in Q[T]](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ringtheory/irredtestsoverQ.pdf)) Hilbert's irreducibility theorem: if $f\in\mathbf Q[X_1,\dots,X_r,Y_1,\dots,Y_s]$ is irreducible in $\mathbf Q(X_1,\dots,X_r)[Y_1,\dots,Y_s]$, then it stays irreducible in $\mathbf Q[Y_1,\dots,Y_s]$ after specializing $(X_1,\dots,X_r)$ to any rational $r$-tuple in a set (the Hilbert set) that is Zariski dense in $\mathbf Q^r$; this is how Galois groups over $\mathbf Q(X)$ descend to $\mathbf Q$. ([Hilbert's irreducibility theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_irreducibility_theorem))
- **Integer-valued polynomials.** (Pólya) A polynomial in $\mathbf Q[t]$ maps $\mathbf Z$ to $\mathbf Z$ iff it is an integer combination, uniquely, of $\binom{t}{k}=t(t-1)\cdots(t-k+1)/k!$. ([Integer-valued polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer-valued_polynomial))
- **Smith normal form.** For a nonzero $m\times n$ matrix $A$ over a PID $R$ (e.g. $\mathbf Z$) there are invertible $S,T$ with $SAT=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r,0,\dots)$, $\alpha_i\mid\alpha_{i+1}$, unique up to units, and $\alpha_i=d_i(A)/d_{i-1}(A)$ where $d_i(A)$ is the gcd of the $i\times i$ minors. It gives the invariant factors of $\mathbf Z^m/A\mathbf Z^n$, hence the structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups. ([Smith normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_normal_form)) Compare [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) and [Determinant](node:Determinant).
- **Hermite normal form.** Every full-row-rank integer matrix $A$ has a unique Hermite normal form $H=UA$ with $U$ unimodular; it decides whether two bases span the same lattice and reduces $Ax=b$ over $\mathbf Z$ to a triangular system, and it is computable in polynomial time. ([Hermite normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_normal_form))
- **Determinant bounds.** A complex $n\times n$ matrix with $|M_{ij}|\le1$ has $|\det M|\le n^{n/2}$ (Hadamard), with equality for real $M$ exactly when $M$ is a Hadamard matrix. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix))

### History
Lehmer introduced the measure (in the product form) while searching for large primes among the numbers $\prod_i(1\pm\alpha_i^m)$, which grow like $M(P)^m$; Mahler later gave the integral form and called $M(P)$ the "measure" of $P$, and Waldschmidt (1979) first referred to it as Mahler's measure ("mesure de Mahler"). Lehmer's polynomial $L(z)=z^{10}+z^9-z^7-z^6-z^5-z^4-z^3+z+1$, with $M(L)=1.176280818\ldots$, still has the smallest known measure above $1$. Smyth showed in 1981 that two-variable measures can be special values of $L$-functions, e.g. $m(1+x+y)$ is expressed through the Dirichlet $L$-value $L(\chi_{-3},2)$ and $m(1+x+y+z)$ through $\zeta(3)$, and Boyd conjectured that the set of all Mahler measures is closed. ([Smyth, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397); [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure)) Schinzel's monograph (CUP, 2000) systematized reducibility of polynomials over general fields, Ritt's theory of polynomial composition, and properties of the Mahler measure. ([CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511542916/type/book))

### Open problems
- **Lehmer's problem.** Is there $c>1$ such that every integer polynomial with $M(P)>1$ has $M(P)\ge c$? Smyth's survey states that no one has improved the degree dependence in Dobrowolski's bound, "so that Lehmer's problem remains unsolved", and that no measure in $(1, M(L))$ is known. ([Smyth, §§2, 4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397); [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure))
- **Boyd's conjecture.** The set of logarithmic Mahler measures of integer polynomials in any number of variables is conjectured to be closed in $\mathbf R$. ([Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure); [Smyth, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701397))
- **Hadamard conjecture.** That a Hadamard matrix (extremal for the determinant bound) exists of every order $4k$ is listed as unsolved. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix); [maximal determinant problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard%27s_maximal_determinant_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure): definitions, Kronecker, Lehmer, Boyd, entropy.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Irreducibility tests in Q[T]](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ringtheory/irredtestsoverQ.pdf): reduction mod $p$, Eisenstein, prime-value criterion, with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Smyth, The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey (arXiv:math/0701397)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0701397): Lehmer's problem, Dobrowolski-type bounds, nonreciprocal case.
- **Further reading:** [Schinzel, Polynomials with Special Regard to Reducibility (CUP, Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications 77)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511542916/type/book): standard monograph on reducibility.
- **Related maps:** [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), [MSC 11Txx - Finite fields and commutative rings (number-theoretic aspects)](node:MSC%2011Txx%20-%20Finite%20fields%20and%20commutative%20rings%20%28number-theoretic%20aspects%29), [MSC 11Rxx - Algebraic number theory - global fields](node:MSC%2011Rxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20global%20fields).
references.MSC 11Dxx - Diophantine equations:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11D, "Diophantine equations", is the subfield of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) devoted to integer and rational solutions of polynomial and exponential equations. Its codes are organized by the shape of the equation: linear equations and the Frobenius problem (11D04, 11D07), quadratic, cubic and quartic equations (11D09, 11D25), "higher degree equations; Fermat's equation" (11D41), counting solutions (11D45), norm form equations (11D57), Thue–Mahler equations (11D59), exponential equations (11D61), Egyptian fractions (11D68), equations in many variables (11D72), Diophantine inequalities (11D75), congruences (11D79), representation problems (11D85) and $p$-adic and power series fields (11D88). ([MSC2020 11Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Dxx))

The modern subject combines three toolkits: Diophantine approximation and linear forms in logarithms, which make finiteness theorems effective; local–global methods (the Hasse principle and the Hardy–Littlewood circle method) for forms in many variables; and the arithmetic of elliptic curves, modular forms and Galois representations, which settled Fermat's Last Theorem. ([Baker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem); [Hasse principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle); [Fermat's Last Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem))

### Scope
- **Neighbour 11G.** 11Dxx carries a see-also to [MSC 11Gxx - Arithmetic algebraic geometry (Diophantine geometry)](node:MSC%2011Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20algebraic%20geometry%20%28Diophantine%20geometry%29) (and 11Gxx back to 11Dxx), whose codes cover elliptic curves over global fields (11G05), curves of arbitrary genus or genus $\ne1$ over global fields (11G30), varieties over global fields (11G35), heights (11G50), and $L$-functions of varieties with the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture (11G40). ([MSC2020 11Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Gxx); [MSC2020 11Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Dxx))
- **Neighbour 11P.** 11D72 and 11D85 both cross-refer to 11P55, "Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method", in [MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; partitions](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions). ([MSC2020 11Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Dxx); [MSC2020 11Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Pxx))
- **Neighbour 11J.** Diophantine inequalities (11D75) cross-refer to 11J25 in [MSC 11Jxx - Diophantine approximation, transcendental number theory](node:MSC%2011Jxx%20-%20Diophantine%20approximation,%20transcendental%20number%20theory). ([MSC2020 11Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Dxx))

### Key concepts
- **Pell's equation (11D09).** For a positive nonsquare integer $n$, $x^2-ny^2=1$ has infinitely many integer solutions (Lagrange). The fundamental solution $(x_1,y_1)$, with smallest positive $x$, is read off from the continued fraction of $\sqrt n$, and all positive solutions come from powers $(x_1+y_1\sqrt n)^k$. ([Pell's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%27s_equation))
- **Hasse principle (11D09, 11D72).** Hasse–Minkowski: a quadratic form over $\mathbb Q$ (Hasse: over any number field) represents $0$ nontrivially iff it does so over $\mathbb R$ and every $\mathbb Q_p$. It fails for cubics: Selmer's $3x^3+4y^3+5z^3=0$ has real and $p$-adic solutions for all $p$ but no nontrivial rational one; the Brauer–Manin obstruction explains many such failures but, by Skorobogatov, not all. By the circle method, every integral cubic form in at least 14 variables represents $0$ (Heath-Brown, improving Davenport's 16); every non-singular cubic form over $\mathbb Q$ in at least 10 variables represents $0$ (Heath-Brown), which is best possible since some non-singular forms in 9 variables do not, and Hooley proved that the Hasse principle holds for non-singular cubic forms in at least 9 variables. ([Hasse principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle); [MIT 18.782, lecture 11](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-782-introduction-to-arithmetic-geometry-fall-2013/pages/lecture-notes/))
- **Thue equations (11D59) and Baker's method.** If $f\in\mathbb Q[x,y]$ is an irreducible binary form of degree $\ge3$ and $r\in\mathbb Q^\times$, then $f(x,y)=r$ has only finitely many integer solutions (Thue, 1909); Thue's proof was ineffective, but the equation is now effectively solvable with solutions bounded by $(C_1r)^{C_2}$, $C_i$ depending on $f$, using Baker's method. ([Thue equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thue_equation)) Baker's theorem: if $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are logarithms of nonzero algebraic numbers, linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, and $\beta_0,\dots,\beta_n$ are algebraic and not all zero, then $|\beta_0+\beta_1\lambda_1+\cdots+\beta_n\lambda_n|>H^{-C}$ with $H$ the maximum height of the $\beta_i$ and $C$ effectively computable; Baker used it for effective bounds on Diophantine equations and received the Fields Medal in 1970. ([Baker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem))
- **Fermat's Last Theorem (11D41).** $x^n+y^n=z^n$ has no solutions in positive integers for $n\ge3$. Frey (1984) attached to a putative solution a semistable elliptic curve; Ribet (1986) proved it could not be modular; Wiles proved modularity of semistable elliptic curves, published with a Taylor–Wiles paper in the *Annals* in 1995, and Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor completed the full modularity theorem by 2001. ([Fermat's Last Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem)) For the generalized equation $ax^p+by^q=cz^r$ with $1/p+1/q+1/r<1$ there are at most finitely many primitive solutions, and many parameter families have been solved individually. ([Ratcliffe–Grechuk survey, arXiv:2412.11933](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.11933))
- **Catalan's conjecture (11D61).** The only solution of $x^a-y^b=1$ in natural numbers with $a,b>1$, $x,y>0$ is $3^2-2^3=1$. Tijdeman (1976) used Baker's method to bound all variables effectively; Mihăilescu proved the conjecture in 2002 (published 2004) using cyclotomic fields and Galois modules. ([Catalan's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan%27s_conjecture))
- **Hilbert's tenth problem.** The MRDP theorem (completed by Matiyasevich, 1970) states that every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine, so no algorithm decides solvability of polynomial equations over $\mathbb Z$; Shapiro and Shlapentokh extended undecidability to rings of integers of abelian number fields. ([Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem)) Koymans and Pagano, via elliptic curves with full rational 2-torsion, additive [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) and 2-descent, proved a negative answer for every infinite ring finitely generated over $\mathbb Z$, in particular for the ring of integers of every number field ([Koymans–Pagano, arXiv:2412.01768](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01768)); Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman proved the number-field case independently via abelian varieties whose rank does not grow in a quadratic extension. ([Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman, arXiv:2501.18774](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18774)) This links 11D to [MSC 03Dxx - Computability and recursion theory](node:MSC%2003Dxx%20-%20Computability%20and%20recursion%20theory).

### History
Lagrange's general theory of Pell's equation via continued fractions dates to 1766–1769. ([Pell's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%27s_equation)) Catalan proposed his conjecture in 1842 and Thue proved his finiteness theorem in 1909. ([Catalan's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan%27s_conjecture); [Thue equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thue_equation)) Matiyasevich completed the negative solution of Hilbert's tenth problem in 1970. ([Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem)) Wiles announced his proof of Fermat's Last Theorem at the Isaac Newton Institute in June 1993, repaired a gap with Taylor in September 1994, and published in 1995. ([Fermat's Last Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem))

### Open problems
- **abc conjecture.** For coprime positive $a+b=c$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, only finitely many triples satisfy $c>\operatorname{rad}(abc)^{1+\varepsilon}$. It would imply Roth's theorem and the Fermat–Catalan conjecture, and an effective weak form would give Fermat's Last Theorem for $n\ge6$. ([abc conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture))
- **Fermat–Catalan and Beal conjectures.** Fermat–Catalan predicts finitely many coprime solutions of $a^m+b^n=c^k$ with $1/m+1/n+1/k<1$ (ten are known); Beal predicts none with $m,n,k>2$. Both are stated as conjectures. ([Fermat's Last Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem))
- **Pillai's conjecture.** Each positive integer occurs only finitely often as a difference of perfect powers; it remains open and would follow from abc. ([Catalan's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan%27s_conjecture))
- **Erdős–Straus conjecture (11D68).** For every $n\ge2$, $4/n=1/x+1/y+1/z$ has a solution in positive integers. It is unsolved; it has been verified for $n\le10^{17}$, and Mordell's identities cover all $n$ outside six classes mod $840$. ([Erdős–Straus conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Straus_conjecture))

> [!warning] Contested
> Mochizuki's claimed proof of abc (published in *Publ. RIMS* in 2021) is "still regarded as unproven by the mainstream mathematical community", after Scholze and Stix reported a gap in 2018 that Mochizuki disputes. ([abc conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture)) Hilbert's tenth problem over $\mathbb Q$ is presented as unresolved, while the same page reports a September 2026 preprint claiming a negative answer that it does not treat as verified. ([Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hasse principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle): local–global principle, Selmer's example, cubic forms in many variables.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.782 Introduction to Arithmetic Geometry, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-782-introduction-to-arithmetic-geometry-fall-2013/pages/lecture-notes/): rational points on conics, $p$-adics, Hasse–Minkowski, Mordell–Weil.
- **Primary:** [Ratcliffe and Grechuk, Generalised Fermat equation: a survey of solved cases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.11933): survey of solved cases of $ax^p+by^q=cz^r$.
- **Further reading:** [Bombieri and Gubler, Heights in Diophantine Geometry (CUP, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511542879): graduate monograph on heights and finiteness theorems.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 11Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Dxx): official code list.

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11E, "Forms and linear algebraic groups", is the part of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) that studies quadratic, bilinear, Hermitian and higher-degree forms over fields and rings of arithmetic interest (local, global, real, $p$-adic), their class numbers and analytic theory, and the arithmetic of classical groups, including the Galois cohomology of linear algebraic groups. ([MSC2020 11Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Exx))

Two questions run through the area. Over a field, when are two forms equivalent and when does a form represent $0$ or a given element? Over $\mathbf Q$ and number fields the answer is local–global: the Hasse–Minkowski theorem reduces it to the completions. ([Hasse–Minkowski theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Minkowski_theorem)) Over $\mathbf Z$ the local–global principle only determines the genus of a form, a genus may contain several classes, and counting or controlling those classes leads to the mass formula, the Siegel–Weil formula and the adelic theory of the orthogonal group, its Tamagawa number and strong approximation. ([Spinor genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinor_genus); [Smith–Minkowski–Siegel mass formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Minkowski%E2%80%93Siegel_mass_formula); [Strong approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_approximation_in_algebraic_groups))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 11E04 quadratic forms over general fields; 11E08 over [local rings](node:Local%20Rings) and fields; 11E10 forms over real fields; 11E12 quadratic forms over global rings and fields; 11E16 general binary quadratic forms; 11E20 general ternary and quaternary quadratic forms, forms of more than two variables; 11E25 sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms; 11E39 bilinear and Hermitian forms; 11E41 class numbers of quadratic and Hermitian forms; 11E45 analytic theory (Epstein zeta functions, relations with automorphic forms and functions); 11E57 classical groups; 11E70 $K$-theory of quadratic and Hermitian forms; 11E72 Galois cohomology of linear algebraic groups; 11E76 forms of degree higher than two; 11E81 algebraic theory of quadratic forms, [Witt groups](node:Witt%20Groups) and rings; 11E88 quadratic spaces, Clifford algebras; 11E95 $p$-adic theory; 11E99. ([MSC2020 11Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Exx))

- **Neighbour 15A.** Quadratic forms in linear algebra go to 15A63; 11E88 cross-refers to 15A63 and 15A66 ([Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras)), within [MSC 15Axx - Basic linear algebra](node:MSC%2015Axx%20-%20Basic%20linear%20algebra). ([MSC2020 11Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Exx))
- **Neighbour 19G.** The section as a whole cross-refers to [MSC 19Gxx - K-theory of forms](node:MSC%2019Gxx%20-%20K-theory%20of%20forms), and 11E81 to 19G12 and 19G24. ([MSC2020 11Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Exx))
- **Neighbours 14L and 20G.** Classical groups (11E57) cross-refer to [MSC 14Lxx - Algebraic groups](node:MSC%2014Lxx%20-%20Algebraic%20groups) and [MSC 20Gxx - Linear algebraic groups and related topics](node:MSC%2020Gxx%20-%20Linear%20algebraic%20groups%20and%20related%20topics), and Galois cohomology (11E72) to 20G10. ([MSC2020 11Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Hasse–Minkowski theorem (11E12).** A quadratic space over a number field is isotropic if and only if it is isotropic over every completion, and two quadratic forms over a number field are equivalent if and only if they are equivalent over every completion; the same holds for all global fields. Minkowski proved it over $\mathbf Q$ and Hasse extended it to number fields. ([Hasse–Minkowski theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Minkowski_theorem)) The principle fails for cubic forms: Selmer's $3x^3+4y^3+5z^3=0$ has real and $p$-adic solutions but no nontrivial rational one. ([Hasse principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle)) See [Quadratic Forms over Number Fields](node:Quadratic%20Forms%20over%20Number%20Fields).
- **Hilbert symbol and complete invariants (11E08, 11E95).** For a local field $K$, $(a,b)=1$ if $z^2=ax^2+by^2$ has a nonzero solution and $-1$ otherwise; for $a,b\in\mathbf Q^\times$, $(a,b)_v=1$ for almost all places $v$ and Hilbert reciprocity $\prod_v(a,b)_v=1$ holds, a statement equivalent to [Quadratic Reciprocity](node:Quadratic%20Reciprocity). ([Hilbert symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_symbol)) The Hasse invariant of $\sum a_ix_i^2$ is $\prod_{i<j}(a_i,a_j)$ in the Brauer group; over a local field, dimension, discriminant ([Determinant](node:Determinant) modulo squares) and Hasse invariant classify quadratic forms, and over a number field the complete invariants are dimension, discriminant, all local Hasse invariants and the signatures at the real places. ([Hasse invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_invariant_of_a_quadratic_form)) See [p-adic Numbers](node:p-adic%20Numbers).
- **Witt ring (11E81).** For $\operatorname{char}k\ne2$, $W(k)$ is the ring of nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms modulo hyperbolic (metabolic) ones, under $\perp$ and $\otimes$. The signature gives $W(\mathbf R)\cong\mathbf Z$; $W(\mathbf F_q)\cong\mathbf Z/4$ if $q\equiv3\pmod4$; for odd $p$, $W(\mathbf Q_p)$ has order $16$; and $W(\mathbf Q)\cong\mathbf Z\oplus\mathbf Z/2\oplus\bigoplus_{p\ne2}W(\mathbf F_p)$, with Hasse–Minkowski giving an injection $W(\mathbf Q)\to W(\mathbf R)\oplus\prod_pW(\mathbf Q_p)$. ([Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group))
- **Binary forms and the class group (11E16, 11E41).** For $ax^2+bxy+cy^2$ with discriminant $\Delta=b^2-4ac$, equivalence is under $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbf Z)$; Lagrange (1775) proved that each discriminant has finitely many classes, with a reduction algorithm, and Gauss showed that primitive classes of fixed discriminant (positive definite ones when $\Delta<0$) form a finite abelian group under composition. For a fundamental discriminant this group is the narrow class group of the quadratic field. ([Binary quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_quadratic_form)) Gauss's conjecture that the class number tends to infinity as $d\to-\infty$ was proved by Heilbronn (1934); the imaginary quadratic class-number-one list was settled by Heegner (1952), Baker (1966) and Stark (1967). ([Class number problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_problem))
- **Sums of squares and universality (11E25, 11E20).** Every nonnegative integer is a sum of four squares (Lagrange, 1770), and $n$ is a sum of three squares iff $n\ne4^k(8m+7)$ (Legendre). ([Lagrange's four-square theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange%27s_four-square_theorem)) Jacobi (1834): the number of representations of $n$ as a sum of four squares is $r_4(n)=8\sum_{m\mid n}m$ for odd $n$ and $r_4(n)=24\sum_{m\mid n,\ m\text{ odd}}m$ for even $n$. ([Jacobi's four-square theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi%27s_four-square_theorem)) The 15 theorem (Conway–Schneeberger 1993, simpler proof by Bhargava 2000): a positive definite form with integer matrix that represents $1,\dots,15$ represents every positive integer. The 290 theorem (conjectured by Conway, proved in a 2011 Bhargava–Hanke preprint): a positive definite integer-valued form representing $1,\dots,290$ is universal; both lists of critical numbers are sharp. ([15 and 290 theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_and_290_theorems))
- **Genus, spinor genus and the mass formula (11E41, 11E45).** Classes $\subseteq$ spinor genera $\subseteq$ genera; the number of spinor genera in a genus is a power of $2$, and for indefinite forms of dimension $\ge3$ each spinor genus is a single proper class; the spinor genus was introduced by Eichler. ([Spinor genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinor_genus)) For a positive definite lattice $f$ the mass $\sum_{\Lambda}1/|\mathrm{Aut}(\Lambda)|$ over the classes of the genus equals $2\pi^{-n(n+1)/4}\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(j/2)\prod_p2m_p(f)$ ($n\ge2$), a product of local densities; for $E_8$, the unique even unimodular lattice of rank $8$, it is $1/696{,}729{,}600$. Smith (1867) found it, Minkowski (1885) rediscovered it, Siegel (1935) corrected it. ([Mass formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Minkowski%E2%80%93Siegel_mass_formula)) The Siegel–Weil formula (Weil 1964–65, extending Siegel 1951–52) expresses an Eisenstein series as the $1/|\mathrm{Aut}|$-weighted average of theta series over a genus, linking 11E45 to [Modular Forms](node:Modular%20Forms). ([Siegel–Weil formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%E2%80%93Weil_formula))
- **Tamagawa numbers (11E57).** For a semisimple group $G$ over a global field $k$, $\tau(G)$ is the measure of $G(\mathbb A)/G(k)$ for the canonical Tamagawa measure. Weil conjectured $\tau(G)=1$ for simply connected simple groups over number fields; Kottwitz (1988) completed the proof over number fields and Gaitsgory–Lurie (2019) treated function fields. ([Tamagawa number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamagawa_number)) Tamagawa showed the mass formula is equivalent to $\tau(\mathrm{SO})=2$. ([Mass formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Minkowski%E2%80%93Siegel_mass_formula)) See [Algebraic Groups](node:Algebraic%20Groups).
- **Strong approximation (11E57).** For a non-solvable linear algebraic group $G$ over a global field $k$ and a finite set $S$ of places, $G(k)$ is dense in $G(\mathbb A^S)$ iff the radical $N$ of $G$ is unipotent, $G/N$ is simply connected, and every almost simple factor $H$ of $G/N$ has $H(k_s)$ noncompact for some $s\in S$. Kneser (1966) and Platonov (1969) proved it over number fields, Margulis and Prasad (1977) over function fields. ([Strong approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_approximation_in_algebraic_groups))
- **Galois cohomology and the Hasse principle (11E72).** For a simply connected group $G$ over a global field $k$, the map $H^1(k,G)\to\prod_vH^1(k_v,G)$ is injective; Kneser (1966) and others proved it case by case, and Chernousov (1989) completed the last case, $E_8$. ([Hasse principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle)) See [Galois Cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology) and [Reductive Algebraic Groups](node:Reductive%20Algebraic%20Groups).
- **Kneser–Tits problem (11E57).** For a semisimple, simply connected, isotropic group $G$ over $K$, is the Whitehead group $W(G,K)=G(K)/G(K)^+$ trivial, $G(K)^+$ being generated by $K$-subgroups isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$? Platonov (1969) proved triviality over local fields and gave fields where it fails; over global fields it is always trivial, by the combined work of several authors surveyed in Gille (2009). ([Kneser–Tits conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kneser%E2%80%93Tits_conjecture))

### History
Lagrange's 1775 *Recherches d'Arithmétique* created the general theory of binary forms, and Gauss's *Disquisitiones* introduced composition. ([Binary quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_quadratic_form)) Smith (1867), Minkowski (1885) and Siegel (1935) built the mass formula, and Eichler introduced the spinor genus. ([Mass formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Minkowski%E2%80%93Siegel_mass_formula); [Spinor genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinor_genus)) Eichler (1938) proved strong approximation for some classical groups, and the general adelic theory of algebraic groups (Kneser, Platonov, Kottwitz, Chernousov) followed in the 1960s–1980s. ([Strong approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_approximation_in_algebraic_groups); [Tamagawa number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamagawa_number))

### Open problems
- **Ramanujan's ternary form.** Ono and Soundararajan showed (1997) that, assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis, every odd integer $>2719$ is represented by $x^2+y^2+10z^2$ ([Kane–Sun, arXiv:0808.2761](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.2761)); the conjecture that the odd non-represented integers are exactly $3,7,21,\dots,679,2719$ "has not been fully resolved". ([Ramanujan's ternary quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%27s_ternary_quadratic_form))
- **Real quadratic class number one.** Gauss's question whether infinitely many real quadratic fields (equivalently, positive fundamental discriminants of binary forms) have class number one is still open. ([Class number problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 11Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Exx): official code list.
- **Reference:** [Hasse invariant of a quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_invariant_of_a_quadratic_form): complete local and global invariants.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.782 lecture notes (Sutherland)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-782-introduction-to-arithmetic-geometry-fall-2013/pages/lecture-notes/): lectures 9–11 on quadratic forms, Hilbert symbols, approximation and Hasse–Minkowski over $\mathbf Q$.
- **Learn:** [Hanke, Notes on "Quadratic Forms and Automorphic Forms" (2009 Arizona Winter School)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.5759): survey of the classical theory of quadratic forms over number fields and their rings of integers and their link with modular and automorphic forms.
- **Primary:** [Kane and Sun, On almost universal mixed sums of squares and triangular numbers (Trans. AMS, 2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.2761): research paper on representation of large integers by ternary forms, using modular forms and quadratic form theory.
- **Further reading:** [O'Meara, Introduction to Quadratic Forms (Springer, 1963)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-62031-7): standard monograph on forms over local and global fields and rings.
