## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11F, "Discontinuous groups and automorphic forms", is the part of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) that studies functions on symmetric spaces invariant (up to a factor of automorphy) under arithmetic groups. It runs from classical modular and automorphic functions (11F03, 11F11, 11F12), the structure of modular and arithmetic groups (11F06), eta functions and Dedekind sums (11F20), Hecke–Petersson operators (11F25, 11F60), theta series and the Weil representation (11F27) and Fourier coefficients (11F30), through Hilbert, Siegel and Jacobi forms (11F41, 11F46, 11F50), to Langlands $L$-functions (11F66), special values and periods (11F67), automorphic representations (11F70), trace formulas (11F72), cohomology of arithmetic groups (11F75), Galois representations (11F80) and $p$-adic theory (11F85). ([MSC2020 11Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Fxx))

The subject sits where [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups), and arithmetic geometry meet: Hecke eigenforms have Euler products, their coefficients carry Galois representations, and the modularity of elliptic curves over $\mathbb Q$ is the theorem behind Fermat's Last Theorem. ([Hecke operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_operator); [Modularity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_theorem))

### Scope
- **Neighbour 20H and 22E.** Discrete subgroups as groups are cross-referenced from 11F06 to 20H05, 20H10 and 22E40 in [group theory](node:Group%20Theory) and [MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups). ([MSC2020 11Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Fxx))
- **Neighbour 14G.** Hilbert modular surfaces (11F41) cross-refer to 14G35, perfectoid methods (11F77) to 14G45, and $p$-adic theory (11F85) to 14G20 and 22E50, in [MSC 14Gxx - Arithmetic problems in algebraic geometry; Diophantine geometry](node:MSC%2014Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20problems%20in%20algebraic%20geometry;%20Diophantine%20geometry). ([MSC2020 11Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Fxx))
- **Neighbour 11G.** Elliptic curves over global fields (11G05) and $L$-functions of varieties with the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture (11G40) sit in [MSC 11Gxx - Arithmetic algebraic geometry (Diophantine geometry)](node:MSC%2011Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20algebraic%20geometry%20%28Diophantine%20geometry%29); within 11F, Galois representations have their own code (11F80). ([MSC2020 11Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Gxx); [MSC2020 11Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Modular forms and $q$-expansions (11F11).** A modular form of weight $k$ for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ is a holomorphic $f$ on the upper half-plane $\mathcal H$ with $f\big(\tfrac{az+b}{cz+d}\big)=(cz+d)^kf(z)$ for all $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ that is bounded as $\operatorname{Im}z\to\infty$; then $f=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nq^n$ with $q=e^{2\pi iz}$, and $f$ is a cusp form if $a_0=0$. For even $k>2$ the Eisenstein series $G_k(\tau)=\sum_{(m,n)\ne(0,0)}(m+n\tau)^{-k}$ has weight $k$; $\Delta=q\prod_{n\ge1}(1-q^n)^{24}=\eta^{24}$ is a cusp form of weight 12; and for even $k\ge0$, $\dim M_k(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z))$ is $\lfloor k/12\rfloor$ if $k\equiv2\pmod{12}$ and $\lfloor k/12\rfloor+1$ otherwise. ([Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form))
- **Hecke operators (11F25).** On weight-$k$ forms for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, $T_m$ acts on coefficients by $b(n)=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(m,n)}d^{k-1}a(mn/d^2)$. The $T_m$ commute and preserve cusp forms; for $n$ prime to the level they are self-adjoint for the Petersson inner product, so cusp forms have a basis of eigenforms, a normalized eigenform has coefficients equal to its eigenvalues and an Euler product $L$-function, and for $\Delta$ this gives the multiplicativity of $\tau(n)$ (Mordell, 1917). ([Hecke operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_operator))
- **Newforms (Atkin–Lehner, 1970).** Oldforms of level $N$ are built from forms $g$ of level $M\mid N$, $M<N$, by $g(\tau)\mapsto g(d\tau)$ with $d\mid N/M$; newforms span the Petersson-orthogonal complement, which Hecke operators preserve and which has a basis of Hecke eigenforms. ([Atkin–Lehner theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atkin%E2%80%93Lehner_theory))
- **Ramanujan–Petersson and Deligne (11F30).** Ramanujan conjectured $|\tau(p)|\le2p^{11/2}$; Deligne proved it in 1974 via the Weil conjectures, and more generally coefficients of weight-$k$ holomorphic cusp forms satisfy $a_n=O(n^{(k-1)/2+\varepsilon})$ (weight 1 by Deligne–Serre). The bridge to geometry is the Eichler–Shimura congruence relation $T_p=\mathrm{Frob}+\mathrm{Ver}$ on the Jacobian $J_0(N)$ over $\mathbb F_p$ (Eichler 1954, Shimura 1958), which expresses the local $L$-factor of $X_0(N)$ at $p$ through Hecke eigenvalues. ([Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%E2%80%93Petersson_conjecture); [Eichler–Shimura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eichler%E2%80%93Shimura_congruence_relation))
- **Modularity theorem (11F80, 11F11).** Every elliptic curve $E/\mathbb Q$ admits a non-constant rational map $X_0(N)\to E$, the least such $N$ being the conductor of $E$. Wiles and Taylor proved it for semistable curves (1995), which implies Fermat's Last Theorem, and Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor completed it in 2001; elliptic curves over real quadratic fields are modular (Freitas–Le Hung–Siksek). ([Modularity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_theorem))
- **Selberg trace formula (11F72).** For a compact hyperbolic surface $X=\Gamma\backslash\mathcal H$ with Laplace eigenvalues $\mu_n=\tfrac14+r_n^2$, and $h$ even, analytic on $|\operatorname{Im}r|\le\tfrac12+\delta$ and polynomially decaying, $\sum_n h(r_n)=\frac{\mu(X)}{4\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}r\,h(r)\tanh(\pi r)\,dr+\sum_{\{T\}}\frac{\log N(T_0)}{N(T)^{1/2}-N(T)^{-1/2}}\,g(\log N(T))$, the sum over hyperbolic conjugacy classes, $g$ the Fourier transform of $h$ (Selberg, 1956); it yields Weyl-type eigenvalue asymptotics. Selberg proved $\lambda_1\ge 3/16$ for Maass forms on congruence subgroups, improved to $975/4096$ by Kim and Sarnak (2003). ([Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula); [Selberg's 1/4 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg%27s_1/4_conjecture))
- **Automorphic representations (11F70).** Langlands replaced automorphic forms by cuspidal automorphic representations of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over the adeles; functoriality predicts that a morphism of $L$-groups transfers automorphic representations compatibly with $L$-functions. ([Langlands program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_program))

### History
Hurwitz's work on modular correspondences anticipated Hecke operators; Mordell used them in 1917 for $\tau(n)$, and Hecke introduced the general theory in 1937. ([Hecke operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_operator)) Eichler (1954) and Shimura (1958) established the congruence relation, Selberg published his trace formula in 1956, and Atkin and Lehner developed newforms in 1970. ([Eichler–Shimura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eichler%E2%80%93Shimura_congruence_relation); [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula); [Atkin–Lehner theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atkin%E2%80%93Lehner_theory)) Deligne proved the Ramanujan conjecture in 1974, and modularity of elliptic curves over $\mathbb Q$ was completed between 1995 and 2001. ([Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%E2%80%93Petersson_conjecture); [Modularity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Ramanujan–Petersson for Maass forms.** "As of 2025, the version of the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for Maass forms is still open"; Deligne's method does not apply to real-analytic forms. Toward it, Luo–Rudnick–Sarnak give exponent $\tfrac12-\tfrac1{n^2+1}$ for $\mathrm{GL}_n$ and Kim–Sarnak give $7/64$ for $\mathrm{GL}_2$. ([Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%E2%80%93Petersson_conjecture)) Blomer and Brumley extended the best known bounds for $\mathrm{GL}_n$, $n=2,3,4$, to arbitrary number fields. ([Blomer–Brumley, arXiv:1003.0559](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.0559))
- **Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture.** The conjecture that $\lambda_1\ge\tfrac14$ for congruence subgroups would follow from the generalized Ramanujan conjecture for $\mathrm{GL}_2$; the best known bound $975/4096$ is below $1/4$. ([Selberg's 1/4 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg%27s_1/4_conjecture); [Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%E2%80%93Petersson_conjecture))
- **Langlands reciprocity and functoriality.** The full Langlands conjecture for $\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb Q)$ "remains unproved", and attempts at a direct construction of functoriality "have only produced some conditional results". ([Langlands program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_program))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form): definitions, Eisenstein series, $\Delta$, dimension formula.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.783 Elliptic Curves, lecture notes (Sutherland)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-783-elliptic-curves-spring-2021/pages/lecture-notes/): modular curves, the modular equation, modular forms and $L$-functions, Fermat's Last Theorem.
- **Primary:** [Blomer and Brumley, On the Ramanujan conjecture over number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.0559): research paper on bounds toward Ramanujan for $\mathrm{GL}_n$.
- **Further reading:** [A First Course in Modular Forms (Springer GTM, 2005)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-27226-9): standard graduate text on classical modular forms.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 11Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Fxx): official code list.
references.MSC 11Gxx - Arithmetic algebraic geometr:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11G, "Arithmetic algebraic geometry (Diophantine geometry)", is the part of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) that studies rational and integral points of varieties over global, local and [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields) with the tools of algebraic geometry: elliptic curves, abelian varieties, curves of higher genus, varieties over finite fields, complex multiplication, modular and Shimura varieties, heights, and $L$-functions of varieties including the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. ([MSC2020 11Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Gxx))

Its organizing results are finiteness theorems. The Mordell–Weil theorem makes the rational points of an abelian variety over a number field a finitely generated group, Faltings's theorem makes the rational points of a curve of genus $>1$ finite, and the Weil conjectures, now theorems, control point counts over finite fields. ([Mordell–Weil theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordell%E2%80%93Weil_theorem); [Faltings's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faltings%27s_theorem); [Weil conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_conjectures)) Its central open question is how the rank of $E(\mathbf Q)$ is read from the $L$-function, the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, which Clay lists as unsolved. ([Clay, BSD](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/birch-and-swinnerton-dyer-conjecture/))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 11G05 elliptic curves over global fields; 11G07 over local fields; 11G09 Drinfeld modules, higher-dimensional motives; 11G10 abelian varieties of dimension $>1$; 11G15 complex multiplication and moduli of abelian varieties; 11G16 elliptic and modular units; 11G18 arithmetic aspects of modular and Shimura varieties; 11G20 curves over finite and local fields; 11G25 varieties over finite and local fields; 11G30 curves of arbitrary genus or genus $\ne1$ over global fields; 11G32 dessins d'enfants, Belyi theory; 11G35 varieties over global fields; 11G40 $L$-functions of varieties over global fields, Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture; 11G42 arithmetic mirror symmetry; 11G45 geometric class field theory; 11G50 heights; 11G55 polylogarithms and relations with $K$-theory; 11G99. ([MSC2020 11Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Gxx))

- **Neighbour 11D.** The section cross-refers to [MSC 11Dxx - Diophantine equations](node:MSC%2011Dxx%20-%20Diophantine%20equations). ([MSC2020 11Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Gxx))
- **Neighbour 14G.** The section cross-refers to [14G](node:MSC%2014Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20problems%20in%20algebraic%20geometry;%20Diophantine%20geometry), and individual codes point to their geometric counterparts: 11G25 to 14G15 and 14G20, 11G35 to 14G25, 11G40 to 14G10, 11G18 to 14G35, 11G50 to 14G40. ([MSC2020 11Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Gxx))
- **Neighbours 14H and 14K.** 11G05 and 11G07 cross-refer to 14H52 in [MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Hxx%20-%20Curves%20in%20algebraic%20geometry), and 11G10 and 11G15 to [MSC 14Kxx - Abelian varieties and schemes](node:MSC%2014Kxx%20-%20Abelian%20varieties%20and%20schemes). 11G50 also points to 37P30 in [MSC 37Pxx - Arithmetic and non-Archimedean dynamical systems](node:MSC%2037Pxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20and%20non-Archimedean%20dynamical%20systems). ([MSC2020 11Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Gxx))

### Key concepts
- **Mordell–Weil theorem (11G05, 11G10).** For an [abelian variety](node:Abelian%20Varieties) $A$ over a number field $K$, $A(K)$ is a finitely generated abelian group, so $A(K)\cong\mathbf Z^r\oplus A(K)_{\mathrm{tors}}$. Mordell (1922) proved it for [elliptic curves](node:Elliptic%20Curves) over $\mathbf Q$ by showing $E(\mathbf Q)/2E(\mathbf Q)$ finite; Weil's 1928 dissertation extended it to Jacobians over number fields. The proof combines a weak Mordell–Weil theorem (finiteness of $A(K)/mA(K)$, via descent and Galois cohomology) with a height function. ([Mordell–Weil theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordell%E2%80%93Weil_theorem))
- **Heights (11G50).** For a very ample line bundle $L$, the Weil height $h_L(P)=h(\varphi(P))$ is defined via a projective embedding $\varphi$ and is well defined up to $O(1)$; only finitely many rationals have naive height below a given bound. The Néron–Tate height is a quadratic form on the Mordell–Weil group of an abelian variety over a global field, defined by Néron as a sum of local heights and globally by Tate. ([Height function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Height_function))
- **Torsion (11G05).** Mazur (1977–78): the torsion subgroup of $E(\mathbf Q)$ is one of the 15 groups $\mathbf Z/n$ ($1\le n\le10$ or $n=12$) or $\mathbf Z/2\times\mathbf Z/2n$ ($1\le n\le4$). Merel (1996): for elliptic curves over a number field of degree $d$, the torsion order is bounded by a constant depending only on $d$. ([Mazur's torsion theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazur%27s_torsion_theorem))
- **Faltings's theorem (11G30).** A nonsingular curve of genus $>1$ over $\mathbf Q$ has only finitely many rational points; Mordell conjectured it in 1922 and Faltings proved it in 1983. Its generalization to a subvariety meeting a finitely generated subgroup of an abelian variety, the Mordell–Lang conjecture, was proved by McQuillan (1995). ([Faltings's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faltings%27s_theorem)) See [Rational Points on Varieties](node:Rational%20Points%20on%20Varieties).
- **Hasse bound and Weil conjectures (11G20, 11G25).** For $E/\mathbf F_q$, $|\#E(\mathbf F_q)-(q+1)|\le2\sqrt q$ (Hasse, 1933); for a curve of genus $g$, $|\#C(\mathbf F_q)-(q+1)|\le2g\sqrt q$. ([Hasse's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%27s_theorem_on_elliptic_curves)) For a smooth projective $X/\mathbf F_q$ of dimension $n$, the zeta function is rational, $Z(X,T)=\prod_{i=0}^{2n}P_i(T)^{(-1)^{i+1}}$, satisfies a functional equation, and the reciprocal roots of $P_i$ have $|\alpha_{ij}|=q^{i/2}$; Dwork (1960) proved rationality, Grothendieck with Artin and Verdier the functional equation, and Deligne (1974) the Riemann hypothesis. ([Weil conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_conjectures))
- **Modularity and BSD (11G40).** Every elliptic curve over $\mathbf Q$ is modular: its $L$-series is that of a weight-$2$ newform of level $N$ equal to the conductor (Wiles 1995 for semistable curves, with Taylor; Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor 2001 in general), linking 11G to [Modular Forms](node:Modular%20Forms). ([Modularity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_theorem)) BSD asserts $\operatorname{rank}E(\mathbf Q)=\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)$, with a leading-coefficient formula involving Ш, the period, regulator, Tamagawa numbers and torsion. Known: Gross–Zagier (1986) gives a point of infinite order when $L$ has a simple zero; Kolyvagin (1989) proves rank $0$ if $L(E,1)\ne0$ and rank $1$ for a simple zero, for modular elliptic curves (a hypothesis now automatic over $\mathbf Q$). ([BSD conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture)) See [L-Functions](node:L-Functions).
- **Tate–Shafarevich group (11G05, 11G10).** Ш$(A/K)=\ker\bigl(H^1(K,A)\to\prod_vH^1(K_v,A)\bigr)$ measures failure of the Hasse principle for torsors under $A$; Lind's curve $x^4-17=2y^2$ has real and $p$-adic points but no rational point. The Cassels–Tate pairing is alternating for elliptic curves, so a finite Ш$(E)$ has square order. ([Tate–Shafarevich group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%E2%80%93Shafarevich_group)) See [Galois Cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology).
- **Complex multiplication (11G15).** For imaginary quadratic $\tau$, $j(\tau)$ is algebraic, and for an imaginary quadratic field $K$ the values $j(\mathfrak a)$ at ideals $\mathfrak a$ of $\mathcal O_K$ are algebraic integers generating the Hilbert class field of $K$, and CM elliptic curves generate the abelian extensions of $K$ (Kronecker's Jugendtraum), one of the few solved cases of Hilbert's twelfth problem. ([Complex multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_multiplication))

### History
Mordell's 1922 theorem answered a question apparently posed by Poincaré around 1901, and Weil generalized it in 1928. ([Mordell–Weil theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordell%E2%80%93Weil_theorem)) Hasse proved the elliptic bound in 1933, Weil proposed his conjectures in 1949, and Deligne finished them in 1974. ([Hasse's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%27s_theorem_on_elliptic_curves); [Weil conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_conjectures)) Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer formulated their conjecture in the 1960s from EDSAC-2 computations. ([BSD conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture)) Faltings proved Mordell's conjecture in 1983, and Taniyama–Shimura modularity, linked by Frey, Serre and Ribet to Fermat's Last Theorem, was proved in 1995–2001. ([Faltings's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faltings%27s_theorem); [Modularity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.** Unsolved and a Millennium Prize Problem. ([Clay, BSD](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/birch-and-swinnerton-dyer-conjecture/)) Bhargava and Shankar bound the average rank of $E/\mathbf Q$ by $7/6$, which with other work gives a positive proportion of curves of rank $0$ satisfying BSD. ([BSD conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture))
- **Finiteness of Ш.** Conjectured finite; proved only in special cases, for instance by Kolyvagin for modular elliptic curves over $\mathbf Q$ of analytic rank $\le1$. ([Tate–Shafarevich group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%E2%80%93Shafarevich_group))
- **Boundedness of ranks.** Whether ranks of elliptic curves over $\mathbf Q$ are bounded is open, with no consensus among experts. ([Rank of an elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank_of_an_elliptic_curve)) Park, Poonen, Voight and Wood give a heuristic suggesting ranks are bounded and that only finitely many curves have rank $>21$. ([Park–Poonen–Voight–Wood, arXiv:1602.01431](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01431)) Goldfeld, and later Katz and Sarnak, conjectured that the average rank is $1/2$. ([Rank of an elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank_of_an_elliptic_curve))
- **Bombieri–Lang conjecture.** For a variety $X$ of general type over a number field $k$, $X(k)$ should not be Zariski dense. ([Faltings's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faltings%27s_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 11Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Gxx): official code list.
- **Reference:** [Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture): statement and known cases.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.782 lecture notes (Sutherland)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-782-introduction-to-arithmetic-geometry-fall-2013/pages/lecture-notes/): lectures 23–26 on elliptic curves, torsion, Mordell–Weil, and Weil–Châtelet and Tate–Shafarevich groups.
- **Primary:** [Park, Poonen, Voight and Wood, A heuristic for boundedness of ranks of elliptic curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01431): research paper modelling ranks and Ш together.
- **Further reading:** [Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves (Springer GTM, 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-09494-6): standard graduate text.
- **Further reading:** [Hindry and Silverman, Diophantine Geometry (Springer GTM, 2000)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1210-2): graduate text on Diophantine geometry.

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11H, "Geometry of numbers", is the part of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) that studies lattices in $\mathbf R^n$ together with convex and nonconvex bodies: lattice points in bodies, packing and covering, products of linear forms, minima and reduction of quadratic forms, automorphism groups of lattices, mean value and transfer theorems, and relations with coding theory. ([MSC2020 11Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Hxx))

Minkowski founded the subject; his basic insight is that a symmetric convex body of large volume must contain a nonzero lattice point. Embedding the ring of integers of a number field as a lattice turns this into the finiteness of the class group and into norm bounds for ideals, and the same method underlies Dirichlet's approximation theorem and bounds on minima of positive definite quadratic forms. ([Geometry of numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry_of_numbers)) Its extremal problems, the densest lattice packing and the Hermite constant, are solved only in a few dimensions; in dimensions $8$ and $24$, work of 2016 showed that the $E_8$ and Leech lattice packings are densest among all sphere packings, lattice or not. ([Hermite constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_constant); [Viazovska, arXiv:1603.04246](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04246))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 11H06 lattices and convex bodies (number-theoretic aspects; see also 11P21, 52C05, 52C07); 11H16 nonconvex bodies; 11H31 lattice packing and covering (number-theoretic aspects; see also 05B40, 52C15, 52C17); 11H46 products of linear forms; 11H50 minima of forms; 11H55 quadratic forms (reduction theory, extreme forms, etc.); 11H56 automorphism groups of lattices; 11H60 mean value and transfer theorems; 11H71 relations with [coding theory](node:Coding%20Theory); 11H99. ([MSC2020 11Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Hxx))

- **Neighbour 52C.** The discrete-geometric side of lattices, packing and covering goes to [MSC 52Cxx - Discrete geometry](node:MSC%2052Cxx%20-%20Discrete%20geometry) (52C05, 52C07, 52C15, 52C17); 11H06 and 11H31 cover the number-theoretic aspects. ([MSC2020 11Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Hxx))
- **Neighbours 05B and 94B.** Combinatorial packing cross-refers to 05B40 in [MSC 05Bxx - Designs and configurations](node:MSC%2005Bxx%20-%20Designs%20and%20configurations), and applications in coding theory go to 94B75 in [MSC 94Bxx - Theory of error-correcting codes and error-detecting codes](node:MSC%2094Bxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20error-correcting%20codes%20and%20error-detecting%20codes); 11H71 keeps the relations with coding theory. ([MSC2020 11Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Hxx))
- **Neighbour 11P.** Lattice-point counting cross-refers to 11P21 in [MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; partitions](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions). ([MSC2020 11Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Hxx))

### Key concepts
- **Minkowski's first theorem (11H06).** If $K\subset\mathbf R^n$ is convex, symmetric about the origin, and $\operatorname{vol}(K)>2^n d(L)$, where $d(L)$ is the covolume of the lattice $L$, then $K$ contains a nonzero point of $L$ (Minkowski, 1889). Applied to the Minkowski embedding of a number field it gives Minkowski's bound: every ideal class contains an integral ideal of norm bounded in terms of the discriminant, so the class number is finite; it also gives Dirichlet's simultaneous approximation theorem and a proof of Lagrange's four-square theorem. ([Minkowski's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%27s_theorem)) See [Lattices and Minkowski's Theorem](node:Lattices%20and%20Minkowski's%20Theorem) and [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields).
- **Successive minima and Minkowski's second theorem (11H06, 11H50).** For a closed convex centrally symmetric body $K$ of positive finite volume and a lattice $\Gamma$, let $\lambda_k$ be the infimum of $\lambda$ such that $\lambda K$ contains $k$ linearly independent lattice vectors, so $0<\lambda_1\le\dots\le\lambda_n$. Then
  $$\frac{2^n}{n!}\operatorname{vol}(\mathbf R^n/\Gamma)\le\lambda_1\lambda_2\cdots\lambda_n\operatorname{vol}(K)\le2^n\operatorname{vol}(\mathbf R^n/\Gamma).$$
  ([Minkowski's second theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%27s_second_theorem))
- **Hermite's constant (11H50, 11H55).** $\gamma_n$ is the supremum of $\lambda_1(L)^2$ (squared length of a shortest nonzero vector) over lattices $L\subset\mathbf R^n$ of covolume $1$; equivalently it is the square of the maximal systole of a flat unit-volume $n$-torus. Exact values are known only for $n=1,\dots,8$ and $n=24$, for example $\gamma_2=2/\sqrt3$ (hexagonal lattice), $\gamma_8=2$ and $\gamma_{24}=4$; otherwise only upper bounds such as Blichfeldt's (for $n\ge18$) are available. ([Hermite constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_constant))
- **Minkowski–Hlawka and Siegel's mean value theorem (11H60, 11H31).** For $n>1$ there is a lattice whose sphere packing density satisfies $\Delta\ge\zeta(n)/2^{n-1}$; Minkowski stated it in 1911 and Hlawka proved it in 1943, and the proof is non-constructive. Siegel (1945): for a bounded set $S$, the average over lattices of covolume $D$ of the number of nonzero lattice points in $S$ is $\operatorname{vol}(S)/D$, and of primitive ones $\operatorname{vol}(S)/(D\zeta(n))$; Minkowski–Hlawka follows for symmetric star bodies such as balls. ([Minkowski–Hlawka theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%E2%80%93Hlawka_theorem)) See [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Lattice reduction (11H55).** A basis is LLL-reduced with parameter $\delta\in(1/4,1]$ if it is size-reduced (Gram–Schmidt coefficients of absolute value $\le1/2$) and satisfies the Lovász condition; the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász algorithm (1982) computes such a basis in polynomial time, and its first vector is within a bounded factor of a shortest nonzero vector (the original authors took $\delta=3/4$). Applications include factoring polynomials over $\mathbf Q$, integer relations, cryptanalysis, and Odlyzko and te Riele's disproof of the Mertens conjecture. ([LLL algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra%E2%80%93Lenstra%E2%80%93Lov%C3%A1sz_lattice_basis_reduction_algorithm)) See [Lattice-Based Cryptography](node:Lattice-Based%20Cryptography).
- **Optimal packings in dimensions 8 and 24 (11H31, 11H71).** Viazovska proved that no packing of unit balls in $\mathbf R^8$ is denser than the $E_8$ lattice packing. ([Viazovska, arXiv:1603.04246](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04246)) Building on this, Cohn, Kumar, Miller, Radchenko and Viazovska proved that the Leech lattice is the densest packing of congruent spheres in $\mathbf R^{24}$ and the unique optimal periodic packing, by finding an optimal auxiliary function for the [linear programming](node:Linear%20Programming) bounds. ([Cohn et al., arXiv:1603.06518](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.06518)) Gauss (1831) had found the optimal lattice packing in $\mathbf R^3$. ([Sphere packing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_packing)) See [Sphere Packings and Tilings](node:Sphere%20Packings%20and%20Tilings).
- **Products of linear forms (11H46).** Schmidt's subspace theorem (1972): for linearly independent linear forms $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with algebraic coefficients and $\varepsilon>0$, the nonzero integer points with $|L_1(x)\cdots L_n(x)|<|x|^{-\varepsilon}$ lie in finitely many proper subspaces of $\mathbf Q^n$. ([Geometry of numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry_of_numbers)) See [Diophantine Approximation](node:Diophantine%20Approximation).

### History
Minkowski proved his lattice-point theorem in 1889 and developed the subject in *Geometrie der Zahlen* (dated 1896; 1910 edition). ([Minkowski's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%27s_theorem); [Geometry of numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry_of_numbers)) He also showed that symmetric convex bodies induce norms, a line Kolmogorov extended to topological vector spaces. ([Geometry of numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry_of_numbers)) Hlawka (1943) and Siegel (1945) supplied the averaging theory, LLL reduction appeared in 1982, and the packing problems in dimensions $8$ and $24$ were solved in 2016. ([Minkowski–Hlawka theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%E2%80%93Hlawka_theorem); [LLL algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra%E2%80%93Lenstra%E2%80%93Lov%C3%A1sz_lattice_basis_reduction_algorithm); [Cohn et al., arXiv:1603.06518](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.06518))

### Open problems
- **Densest packings in other dimensions.** The densest sphere packings are proved only in dimensions $1$–$3$, $8$ and $24$; other dimensions remain open, while the asymptotic lower bounds continue to improve. ([Sphere packing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_packing)) Correspondingly, Hermite's constant is known exactly only for $n\le8$ and $n=24$. ([Hermite constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_constant))
- **Minkowski's conjecture on products of inhomogeneous linear forms.** For a unimodular lattice $\Lambda\subset\mathbf R^n$ and $N(u)=\prod_ju_j$, conjecturally $\sup_{u\in\mathbf R^n}\inf_{v\in\Lambda}|N(u-v)|\le2^{-n}$. Minkowski proved $n=2$, several authors $n\le5$, McMullen $n=6$, and Hans-Gill, Raka, Sehmi and Leetika proved the implying covering-radius bound for well-rounded lattices in dimensions $n=7,8,9$; Shapira and Weiss reduce the conjecture to a geometric question whose positive answer (a conjecture of Dutour-Sikirić, checked computationally for $n\le7$) would settle all dimensions. ([Shapira–Weiss, arXiv:1609.08481](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.08481))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 11Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Hxx): official code list.
- **Reference:** [Geometry of numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry_of_numbers): theorems, applications and history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.785 Number Theory I (Sutherland), lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-785-number-theory-i-fall-2021/pages/lecture-notes/): lecture 14 on the geometry of numbers and lecture 15 on Dirichlet's unit theorem.
- **Primary:** [Viazovska, The sphere packing problem in dimension 8](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04246): optimality of $E_8$.
- **Primary:** [Shapira and Weiss, Stable lattices and the diagonal group](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.08481): Minkowski's conjecture via dynamics on the space of lattices.
- **Further reading:** [Cassels, An Introduction to the Geometry of Numbers (Springer, 1959)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-62035-5): classical monograph.
- **Further reading:** [Conway and Sloane, Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups (Springer, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-6568-7): packing, lattices and codes.
references.MSC 11Jxx - Diophantine approximation, t:
## Reference
### Overview
Diophantine approximation studies how well real numbers can be approximated by rationals $p/q$, measured against the size of the denominator $q$; transcendental number theory asks which numbers are not roots of any nonzero integer polynomial. The two halves are linked because the quality of rational approximation detects arithmetic nature: Liouville showed in 1844 that an irrational algebraic number of degree $n$ satisfies $|x-p/q|>c(x)/q^n$, so numbers approximable faster than every power of $q$ are transcendental, and the Liouville constant was the first explicit transcendental number. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation))

A second source of unity is method. Irrationality is itself a quantitative property: a rational $a/b$ satisfies $|a/b-p/q|\ge 1/(bq)$ for $p/q\ne a/b$, so to prove $\theta$ irrational it suffices to produce, for every $\varepsilon>0$, a rational $p/q$ with $0<|\theta-p/q|<\varepsilon/q$. Waldschmidt's survey stresses that despite this weak requirement, few "interesting" constants are known to be irrational. ([Waldschmidt, §2.3](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312440)) Transcendence proofs from Hermite onward work with auxiliary functions and polynomials that are small at many points, and Baker's method gives effective lower bounds for linear forms in logarithms that feed back into [Diophantine Equations](node:Diophantine%20Equations). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number_theory); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem))

A third strand is metric: rather than asking about one number, one asks for which approximation rates almost every real number (in Lebesgue [measure](node:Measure%20Theory)) is approximable. This is where probabilistic and [ergodic-theoretic](node:Ergodic%20Theory) methods enter. ([Beresnevich–Ramírez–Velani](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01948))

### Scope
MSC2020 11Jxx is titled "Diophantine approximation, transcendental number theory". Its approximation codes are 11J04 (homogeneous approximation to one number), 11J06 (Markov and Lagrange spectra), 11J13 (simultaneous homogeneous approximation, linear forms), 11J17 (approximation by numbers from a fixed field), 11J20 (inhomogeneous linear forms), 11J25 (Diophantine inequalities), 11J54 (small fractional parts of polynomials), 11J61 (approximation in non-Archimedean valuations), 11J68 (approximation to algebraic numbers), 11J70 (continued fractions and generalizations), 11J71 (distribution modulo one) and 11J83 (metric theory). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Jxx))

Its transcendence codes are 11J72 (irrationality; linear independence over a field), 11J81 (transcendence, general theory), 11J82 (measures of irrationality and transcendence), 11J85 (algebraic independence; Gel'fond's method), 11J86 (linear forms in logarithms; Baker's method), 11J87 (Schmidt subspace theorem and applications), 11J89 and 11J91 (transcendence of elliptic, abelian and other [special functions](node:Special%20Functions)), 11J93 (Drinfel'd and $t$-modules), 11J95 (results involving [abelian varieties](node:Abelian%20Varieties)) and 11J97 (number-theoretic analogues of Nevanlinna theory, work of Vojta et al.). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Jxx))

Neighbouring codes: 11J70 cross-refers to 11A55 and 11K50 for continued fractions, and 11J71 cross-refers to 11K06 for distribution modulo one, so the probabilistic theory of those topics sits in [11Kxx](node:MSC%2011Kxx%20-%20Probabilistic%20theory%20-%20distribution%20modulo%201;%20metric%20theory%20of%20algorithms); 11J25 cross-refers to 11D75, the Diophantine-inequalities part of [11Dxx](node:MSC%2011Dxx%20-%20Diophantine%20equations). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Jxx))

### Key concepts
- **Dirichlet's and Hurwitz's theorems** ([Diophantine Approximation](node:Diophantine%20Approximation)). Every irrational $\alpha$ has infinitely many $p/q$ with $|\alpha-p/q|<1/q^2$ (Dirichlet, 1842, via the [pigeonhole principle](node:Pigeonhole%20Principle)); Hurwitz (1891) improved the constant to $1/(\sqrt5\,q^2)$, and $\sqrt5$ is sharp, as the golden ratio shows. Numbers for which $|\alpha-p/q|>c/q^2$ for some $c>0$ and all $p/q$ are *badly approximable*; they are exactly those with bounded continued-fraction partial quotients. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation); [Beresnevich–Ramírez–Velani, Thm 1.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01948))
- **Thue–Siegel–Roth theorem.** After Thue (1909), Siegel (1921) and Dyson (1947), Roth (1955) proved: for algebraic irrational $\alpha$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $c(\alpha,\varepsilon)>0$ with $|\alpha-p/q|>c(\alpha,\varepsilon)/q^{2+\varepsilon}$ for all $p/q$. Dirichlet's theorem shows the exponent $2$ cannot be lowered. Roth received a Fields Medal for this work. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation); [Fukshansky, §12](https://www1.cmc.edu/pages/faculty/lenny/papers/m662_notes.pdf))
- **Schmidt subspace theorem (simultaneous form).** If $x_1,\dots,x_n$ are algebraic and $1,x_1,\dots,x_n$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, then for each $\varepsilon>0$ only finitely many rational $n$-tuples $(p_1/q,\dots,p_n/q)$ satisfy $|x_i-p_i/q|<q^{-(1+1/n+\varepsilon)}$ for all $i$. This is the case of 11J87 most often quoted. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation))
- **Hermite–Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem** ([Algebraic and Transcendental Field Extensions](node:Algebraic%20and%20Transcendental%20Field%20Extensions)). Hermite proved $e$ transcendental (1873); Lindemann proved $e^\alpha$ transcendental for nonzero algebraic $\alpha$ (1882), hence $\pi$ transcendental, since $e^{\pi i}=-1$; Weierstrass completed the general theorem (1885): if $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ are algebraic and linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, then $e^{\alpha_1},\dots,e^{\alpha_n}$ are algebraically independent over $\mathbb Q$. Equivalently, for distinct algebraic $\alpha_i$ the $e^{\alpha_i}$ are linearly independent over the algebraic numbers. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number_theory); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindemann%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem))
- **Gelfond–Schneider theorem.** Solving Hilbert's seventh problem (Gelfond 1934, Schneider 1935): if $a,b$ are algebraic, $a\ne0,1$, and $b$ is irrational, then $a^b$ is transcendental. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number_theory))
- **Baker's theorem on linear forms in logarithms (11J86).** Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ be logarithms of nonzero algebraic numbers, linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, and let $\beta_0,\dots,\beta_n$ be algebraic, not all zero, of degree at most $d$ and height at most $H$. Then $|\beta_0+\beta_1\lambda_1+\cdots+\beta_n\lambda_n|>H^{-C}$ with $C$ effectively computable from $n$, the $\lambda_i$ and $d$; in particular the form is nonzero. Baker proved this in 1966–67, generalizing Gelfond–Schneider, used it to give effective bounds for Diophantine equations and to settle Gauss's class number one problem for imaginary quadratic fields, and received the 1970 Fields Medal. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem))
- **Khintchine's theorem (11J83).** For $\psi:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)$ let $W(\psi)$ be the set of $x\in[0,1)$ with $\|qx\|<\psi(q)$ for infinitely many $q$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the distance to the nearest integer. If $\psi$ is monotonic, $W(\psi)$ has Lebesgue measure $0$ if $\sum\psi(q)<\infty$ and $1$ if $\sum\psi(q)=\infty$. So almost every $x$ has infinitely many $q$ with $\|qx\|<1/(q\log q)$: Dirichlet's rate improves by a logarithm. Monotonicity cannot simply be dropped in the divergent case: Duffin and Schaeffer (1941) built a counterexample. ([Beresnevich–Ramírez–Velani, Thm 2.3 and §2.2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01948))
- **Duffin–Schaeffer theorem.** For arbitrary $\psi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, if $\sum_q \psi(q)\varphi(q)/q=\infty$ ($\varphi$ Euler's totient), then almost every real $\alpha$ has infinitely many reduced fractions $a/q$ with $|\alpha-a/q|\le\psi(q)/q$. Conjectured by Duffin and Schaeffer in 1941, it was proved by Koukoulopoulos and Maynard (announced 2019; *Annals of Mathematics* 192 (2020)). ([Koukoulopoulos–Maynard](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.04593); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duffin%E2%80%93Schaeffer_theorem))
- **Irrationality of $\zeta(3)$ (11J72).** Apéry proved that $\zeta(3)$ is irrational (talk June 1978, published 1979). Rivoal (2000) proved that infinitely many odd zeta values $\zeta(2n+1)$ are irrational, and Zudilin (2001) that at least one of $\zeta(5),\zeta(7),\zeta(9),\zeta(11)$ is irrational. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ap%C3%A9ry%27s_theorem)) See [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Mahler's classification and heights.** Mahler (1932) divided transcendental numbers into $S$-, $T$- and $U$-numbers by how small integer polynomials of each degree can be at the number; almost all complex numbers are $S$-numbers, and Schmidt showed in 1968 that $T$-numbers exist. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number_theory)) Heights measure the arithmetic complexity of algebraic numbers and control the number of good approximations in quantitative Roth-type theorems. ([Fukshansky, §§14–15](https://www1.cmc.edu/pages/faculty/lenny/papers/m662_notes.pdf))

### History
Best approximations by continued fractions were worked out in the 18th century, and the field is named after Diophantus of Alexandria. Liouville's 1844 construction began transcendence theory; Hermite (1873) and Lindemann (1882) followed, the latter settling the impossibility of squaring the circle. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number_theory))

The 20th century brought the Thue–Siegel–Roth line (1909–1955), Khintchine's metric theorem (1924) and the Duffin–Schaeffer problem (1941), Gelfond–Schneider (1934–35), Baker's linear forms (1966–67), Apéry's $\zeta(3)$ (1978) and Schmidt's subspace theorem. Margulis's 1990 ICM address and work of Kleinbock and Margulis brought ergodic theory on homogeneous spaces into metric Diophantine approximation, and Maynard's 2022 Fields Medal cited work in this area. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ap%C3%A9ry%27s_theorem); [Beresnevich–Ramírez–Velani, Thm 2.3 and §2.2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01948))

### Open problems
- **Schanuel's conjecture.** If $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\mathbb C$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, then $\mathbb Q(x_1,\dots,x_n,e^{x_1},\dots,e^{x_n})$ has transcendence degree at least $n$. It would imply most expected algebraic-independence statements for values of $\exp$ and $\log$, including the transcendence of $e+\pi$; it is unproved. Its special cases include the still-open four exponentials conjecture (Schneider, Lang, Ramachandra): for $\mathbb Q$-linearly independent $x_1,x_2$ and $y_1,y_2$, at least one of $e^{x_iy_j}$ is transcendental. ([Waldschmidt, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312440); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number_theory))
- **Irrationality of classical constants.** No proof of irrationality is known for Euler's constant $\gamma$, Catalan's constant, $e+\pi$, $e^\gamma$ or $\zeta(5)$. Whether each odd zeta value is irrational remains open beyond $\zeta(3)$. ([Waldschmidt, §2.3](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312440); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ap%C3%A9ry%27s_theorem))
- **Littlewood conjecture.** For all real $\alpha,\beta$, $\liminf_{n\to\infty} n\,\|n\alpha\|\,\|n\beta\|=0$. It is known when $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not badly approximable, and for $\alpha,\beta$ in the same cubic field (Cassels–Swinnerton-Dyer, 1955). Einsiedler, Katok and Lindenstrauss (*Annals*, 2006) proved that the set of possible counterexamples has Hausdorff dimension zero; the conjecture itself remains open. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood_conjecture); [Beresnevich–Ramírez–Velani, §4.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01948))
- **Lehmer's problem.** Is there an absolute constant $C>1$ such that every $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ that is not a product of cyclotomic polynomials and a power of $x$ has Mahler measure $M(f)\ge C$? Lehmer's degree-10 polynomial gives $M=1.1762808\ldots$, conjectured to be the minimum. Fukshansky calls it an outstanding conjecture, and Waldschmidt lists it as Conjecture 4.1. ([Fukshansky, §15](https://www1.cmc.edu/pages/faculty/lenny/papers/m662_notes.pdf); [Waldschmidt, §4.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312440))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Diophantine approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation) and [Transcendental number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number_theory): the classical theorems with dates.
- **Learn:** [Fukshansky, Diophantine approximations and geometry of numbers (Math 662 notes, 2006)](https://www1.cmc.edu/pages/faculty/lenny/papers/m662_notes.pdf): Dirichlet, Liouville and Roth, heights, Lehmer's problem.
- **Learn:** [Beresnevich, Ramírez and Velani, Metric Diophantine approximation: aspects of recent work](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01948): Khintchine, Jarník, Duffin–Schaeffer and Littlewood, with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Waldschmidt, Open Diophantine problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312440): a survey of open problems in approximation and transcendence (Schanuel, four exponentials, Lehmer, irrationality of constants).
- **Primary:** [Koukoulopoulos and Maynard, On the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.04593): the proof of the 1941 conjecture.
- **Further reading:** Baker's 1966–67 *Mathematika* papers on linear forms in logarithms, cited in [Baker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem).

## Reference
### Overview
This subfield applies probabilistic and measure-theoretic ideas to the integers and the reals. Its classical core is distribution modulo one: a real sequence $(c_n)$ is *equidistributed (uniformly distributed) mod 1* if its fractional parts $\langle c_n\rangle$ fall into each interval $[a,b]\subseteq[0,1]$ with limiting frequency $b-a$, that is $\lim_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\#\{n\le N: a\le\langle c_n\rangle\le b\}=b-a$. Weyl (1914) showed this is equivalent to convergence of averages $N^{-1}\sum f(c_n)\to\int_0^1 f$ for continuous $f$ on $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, and to the vanishing of exponential-sum averages, so that proving equidistribution becomes a problem of nontrivially estimating exponential sums. ([Elkies, Math 229 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/weyl.pdf)) See [Equidistribution Modulo One](node:Equidistribution%20Modulo%20One).

Its second half is the *metric* theory of digit-generating algorithms: continued fractions, radix expansions and related maps, studied for Lebesgue-almost every input. The Gauss map $h(x)=1/x-\lfloor 1/x\rfloor$ generates continued-fraction digits, preserves the measure with density $1/((1+x)\ln 2)$, and is ergodic, so the [ergodic theorem](node:Ergodic%20Theory) converts statements about typical digits into almost-everywhere limit laws. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Kuzmin%E2%80%93Wirsing_operator))

A recurring theme is the gap between metric and individual statements. Borel's theorem that almost every real is normal, or Koksma's theorem that $(\alpha^n)$ is equidistributed for almost every $\alpha>1$, says nothing about a named number such as $\sqrt2$, $e$ or $\pi$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence))

### Scope
MSC2020 11Kxx, "Probabilistic theory: distribution modulo $1$; metric theory of algorithms", has the codes 11K06 (general theory of distribution modulo 1), 11K16 (normal numbers, radix expansions, Pisot and Salem numbers, good lattice points), 11K31 (special sequences), 11K36 (well-distributed sequences and other variations), 11K38 (irregularities of distribution, discrepancy), 11K41 (continuous, $p$-adic and abstract analogues), 11K45 (pseudo-random numbers; [Monte Carlo methods](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Methods)), 11K50 (metric theory of continued fractions), 11K55 (metric theory of other algorithms and expansions; measure and Hausdorff dimension), 11K60 (Diophantine approximation in probabilistic number theory), 11K65 (arithmetic functions in probabilistic number theory) and 11K70 (harmonic analysis and almost periodicity in probabilistic number theory). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Kxx))

Neighbours, by the entry's own cross-references: 11K06 points to 11J71 and 11K60 to 11Jxx, the [Diophantine-approximation](node:Diophantine%20Approximation) subfield [11Jxx](node:MSC%2011Jxx%20-%20Diophantine%20approximation,%20transcendental%20number%20theory); 11K50 points to 11A55 and 11J70 for the non-metric theory of continued fractions; 11K16 points to 11A63 (radix representation); 11K38 and 11K65 point to 11Nxx (multiplicative number theory); 11K45 points to numerical analysis codes 65C05 and 65C10; and 11K55 points to 28Dxx, measure-theoretic [ergodic theory](node:MSC%2028Dxx%20-%20Measure-theoretic%20ergodic%20theory). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Kxx))

### Key concepts
- **Weyl's criterion (11K06).** $(c_n)$ is equidistributed mod 1 if and only if $\sum_{n\le N}e(mc_n)=o(N)$ for every nonzero integer $m$, where $e(x)=e^{2\pi i x}$. For $r\in\mathbb R$, $(nr)$ is equidistributed if and only if $r\notin\mathbb Q$, since for irrational $r$ the geometric sum $\sum_{n\le N}e(mnr)$ is bounded. ([Elkies, Math 229 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/weyl.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence))
- **Weyl's polynomial theorem and its relatives (11K31).** If $P\in\mathbb R[x]$ has at least one irrational non-constant coefficient, then $(P(n))$ is equidistributed mod 1; this was Weyl's main application in 1914. Van der Corput's difference theorem (if each difference sequence $(s_{n+h}-s_n)$ is equidistributed, so is $(s_n)$) gives the standard inductive proof. Vinogradov (1948) proved that $(p_n\alpha)$ over the primes is equidistributed for irrational $\alpha$, while $(\log n)$ is not equidistributed. ([Elkies, Math 229 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/weyl.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence))
- **Koksma's metric theorem.** $(\alpha^n)$ is equidistributed mod 1 for almost every $\alpha>1$; indeed $(\alpha,\alpha^2,\alpha^3,\dots)$ is completely uniformly distributed for almost all $\alpha>1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence))
- **Discrepancy and the Erdős–Turán and Koksma–Hlawka inequalities (11K38, 11K45).** The discrepancy $D(N)=\sup_{0\le a\le b\le1}\bigl|N^{-1}\#\{j\le N: a\le \langle s_j\rangle\le b\}-(b-a)\bigr|$ tends to $0$ exactly for equidistributed sequences. Erdős–Turán: for all $N,K\ge1$, $D(N)\le C\bigl(1/K+N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}k^{-1}\bigl|\sum_{j=1}^{N}e(ks_j)\bigr|\bigr)$ with an absolute constant $C$, a quantitative Weyl criterion. Koksma–Hlawka: if $f$ has bounded Hardy–Krause variation $V(f)$ on $[0,1]^s$, the quasi-Monte Carlo error $\bigl|N^{-1}\sum f(x_i)-\int f\bigr|$ is at most $V(f)\,D_N^*$, so integration quality depends only on the star discrepancy of the points. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tur%C3%A1n_inequality); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-discrepancy_sequence))
- **Irregularities of distribution.** No point set is perfectly distributed: in dimension 1, $D_N^*\ge 1/(2N)$ for every $N$-point set; in dimension 2, W. M. Schmidt proved $D_N^*\ge C\log N/N$ for every finite set; Roth proved a lower bound of order $(\log N)^{(s-1)/2}/N$ in every dimension $s$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-discrepancy_sequence))
- **Normal numbers (11K16).** $x$ is normal in base $b$ if each block of $n$ digits occurs with frequency $b^{-n}$, and absolutely normal if normal in every base $b\ge2$. Normality in base $b$ is equivalent to equidistribution of $(b^kx)$ mod 1. Borel (1909), using the Borel–Cantelli lemma, proved that almost every real number is normal; Champernowne's constant $0.123456789101112\ldots$ is normal in base 10. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number)) See [Borel–Cantelli Lemmas](node:Borel–Cantelli%20Lemmas).
- **Metric theory of continued fractions (11K50).** For $x$ uniformly distributed in $(0,1)$, Kuzmin's theorem gives that the $n$th partial quotient satisfies $P(a_n=k)\to-\log_2\bigl(1-1/(k+1)^2\bigr)$ (the Gauss–Kuzmin distribution); Kuzmin (1928) bounded the rate of convergence, Lévy (1929) improved the error to $O(0.7^n)$, and Wirsing (1974) showed the error behaves like a multiple of $(-\lambda)^n$ with $\lambda=0.3036630\ldots$, the Gauss–Kuzmin–Wirsing constant. For almost every $x$, the geometric mean $(a_1\cdots a_n)^{1/n}$ tends to Khinchin's constant $K_0=2.6854520\ldots$, and the convergent denominators satisfy $q_n^{1/n}\to e^{\pi^2/(12\ln2)}\approx3.2758$ (Khinchin 1935 for existence, Lévy 1936 for the value). Rationals, quadratic irrationals and $e$ are known exceptions to Khinchin's law. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Kuzmin_distribution); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khinchin%27s_constant); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy%27s_constant))
- **Multiples need not test equidistribution.** Myerson and Pollington (*J. Austral. Math. Soc.* 49 (1990), 264–272) exhibit a sequence $(u_n)$ that is not equidistributed mod 1 even though $(ku_n)$ is equidistributed for every integer $k\ge2$; conversely they show $(u_n)$ is equidistributed if suitable subsequences $(u_{kn})$ are, for squarefree $k$ built from a fixed set of primes. ([Myerson–Pollington](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/notes-on-uniform-distribution-modulo-one/48B489D94427D2404962DA76FBEF52B6))
- **Metric results along curves.** Bergelson and Moreira prove that for injective integer sequences $a_1,\dots,a_k$, the set of $(x_1,\dots,x_k)$ for which $(a_1(n)x_1,\dots,a_k(n)x_k)$ is uniformly distributed in $\mathbb T^k$ has full measure on every non-degenerate analytic curve in $\mathbb R^k$. ([Bergelson–Moreira](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.06909v1)) The ambient measure here is Lebesgue measure; see [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory).

### History
Weyl's 1914 paper introduced the exponential-sum criterion and proved equidistribution of polynomial sequences. ([Elkies, Math 229 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/weyl.pdf)) Borel's normal-number theorem dates from 1909, and Kuzmin's theorem on continued-fraction digits together with Khinchin's and Lévy's laws of the 1930s founded the metric theory of continued fractions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Kuzmin_distribution); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy%27s_constant)) Vinogradov's 1948 theorem on $(p_n\alpha)$ and the Erdős–Turán inequality brought the techniques of [analytic number theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory) to bear. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence)) The standard monograph is Kuipers and Niederreiter's *Uniform Distribution of Sequences* (Wiley, 1974). ([Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL7205325W))

### Open problems
- **Powers of specific numbers.** It is not known whether $(e^n)$ or $(\pi^n)$ is equidistributed mod 1, even though $(\alpha^n)$ is for almost every $\alpha>1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence)) For powers of $3/2$ even weaker questions are open: Mahler asked whether there is a nonzero real $\alpha$ (a "Z-number") with $\langle\alpha(3/2)^n\rangle<1/2$ for every $n\ge1$, and it is not known whether Z-numbers exist; Littlewood remarked that one cannot even prove that $\langle e^n\rangle$ does not tend to $0$. ([Waldschmidt, §2.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312440))
- **Normality of classical constants.** Normality of $\sqrt2$, $\pi$, $e$ and $\ln 2$ is conjectured but unproved; Borel conjectured that every irrational algebraic number is normal in every base, and no irrational algebraic number has been proved normal in any base. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number))
- **Khinchin's law for explicit numbers.** The geometric-mean law has not been proved for any real number not constructed for the purpose (numerical evidence suggests it for $\pi$ and Euler's $\gamma$), and it is unknown whether $K_0$ is rational, algebraic or transcendental. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khinchin%27s_constant))
- **Optimal discrepancy in dimension $s\ge3$.** The conjectured lower bound $D_N^*\ge c_s(\log N)^{s-1}/N$ for every $N$-point set in $[0,1]^s$ is proved only for $s\le2$ (W. M. Schmidt); for $s\ge3$ the optimal order is open, and the best known bounds (Bilyk, Lacey and Vagharshakyan) improve Roth's exponent $(s-1)/2$ only by some small $t>0$ depending on $s$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-discrepancy_sequence))
- **Joint distribution of powers.** Bergelson and Moreira formulate Conjectures 4.3–4.4 (equidistribution along analytic functions and along jointly scattered families) and note that either would imply that $(x^n,x^{2n})$ is uniformly distributed in $\mathbb T^2$ for almost every $x>1$, a statement they say they are unable to prove or disprove. ([Bergelson–Moreira, §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.06909v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Equidistributed sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence) and [Normal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number): definitions, classical theorems, open cases.
- **Learn:** [Elkies, Math 229 (Harvard): exponential sums and Weyl equidistribution](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M229.15/weyl.pdf): proof of Weyl's criterion and the $(nr)$ example.
- **Primary:** [Myerson and Pollington, Notes on uniform distribution modulo one (1990)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/notes-on-uniform-distribution-modulo-one/48B489D94427D2404962DA76FBEF52B6): counterexamples on multiples and subsequences.
- **Primary:** [Bergelson and Moreira, Metric uniform distribution on analytic curve (2025)](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.06909v1): current metric theory, with open conjectures.
- **Further reading:** [Kuipers and Niederreiter, Uniform Distribution of Sequences (Wiley, 1974)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL7205325W): the standard monograph.
