## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11L, "Exponential sums and character sums", is the part of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) concerned with bounding sums $\sum_n e(f(n))$, $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$, and sums $\sum_n\chi(n)$ of multiplicative characters. Its codes are the general theory of trigonometric and exponential sums (11L03), Gauss and Kloosterman sums (11L05), estimates on exponential sums (11L07), Jacobsthal, Brewer and other complete character sums (11L10), Weyl sums (11L15), sums over primes (11L20), sums over arbitrary intervals (11L26) and estimates on character sums (11L40). ([MSC2020 11Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Lxx))

The common goal is cancellation: a sum of $N$ terms of modulus one is trivially at most $N$, and nontrivial savings drive [Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory). Character sums enter the functional equation of Dirichlet $L$-functions and the distribution of quadratic residues; Weyl sums and Vinogradov's mean value theorem drive the Hardy–Littlewood method for Waring's problem and zero-free regions for the [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function); and Kloosterman sums feed bounds for coefficients of modular forms. ([Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum); [Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem); [Harvard Math 259](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M259.02/index.html))

### Scope
- **Neighbour 11T.** The 11L entry says "For finite fields, see 11Txx", pointing to [MSC 11Txx - Finite fields and commutative rings (number-theoretic aspects)](node:MSC%2011Txx%20-%20Finite%20fields%20and%20commutative%20rings%20%28number-theoretic%20aspects%29). ([MSC2020 11Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Lxx))
- **Neighbour 11P.** Waring's problem (11P05) and applications of the Hardy–Littlewood method (11P55) are classified in [MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; partitions](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions); Weyl sums have their own code in 11L (11L15), and Vinogradov's mean value theorem is central to the Hardy–Littlewood method for Waring's problem. ([MSC2020 11Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Pxx); [Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem))
- **Neighbour 11M.** Exponent pairs, estimates of the kind filed under 11L07 ("Estimates on exponential sums"), give bounds $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll t^{\theta}\log t$ for the Riemann zeta function, the subject of [MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory). ([MSC2020 11Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Lxx); [Exponent pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponent_pair))

### Key concepts
- **Gauss sums (11L05).** For a multiplicative character $\chi$ and additive character $\psi$, $G(\chi)=\sum_r\chi(r)\psi(r)$. For a primitive Dirichlet character mod $N$, $|G(\chi)|=\sqrt N$; Gauss showed the quadratic sum mod an odd prime $p$ equals $\sqrt p$ or $i\sqrt p$ according as $p\equiv1$ or $3\pmod 4$. Gauss sums appear in the functional equation of Dirichlet $L$-functions and in proofs of quadratic, cubic and quartic reciprocity. ([Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum))
- **Kloosterman sums and the Weil bound (11L05).** $K(a,b;m)=\sum_{0\le x<m,\ (x,m)=1}e\big((ax+b\bar x)/m\big)$, $x\bar x\equiv1\pmod m$. For a prime $p$ with $p\nmid ab$, Weil proved $|K(a,b;p)|\le2\sqrt p$ by viewing the sum on a curve over $\mathbb F_p$; in general $|K(a,b;m)|\le\tau(m)\gcd(a,b,m)^{1/2}\sqrt m$. The method extends to complete exponential sums along higher-dimensional varieties, where good estimates depend on the Weil conjectures proved by Deligne, and was pushed much further by Deligne, Laumon and Katz. Sums of Kloosterman sums are linked to automorphic spectra by the Kuznetsov formula. ([Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum)) The Weil bound is applied to estimate coefficients of cusp forms via Poincaré series, connecting 11L to [MSC 11Fxx - Discontinuous groups and automorphic forms](node:MSC%2011Fxx%20-%20Discontinuous%20groups%20and%20automorphic%20forms). ([Harvard Math 259](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M259.02/index.html))
- **Pólya–Vinogradov (1918) (11L40).** For a non-principal Dirichlet character $\chi$ mod $q$ and integers $M,N$, $\big|\sum_{M<n\le M+N}\chi(n)\big|=O(\sqrt q\log q)$; under GRH Montgomery and Vaughan (1977) improved this to $O(\sqrt q\log\log q)$, and Paley's lower bound shows $\log\log q$ cannot be removed. ([Pólya–Vinogradov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B3lya%E2%80%93Vinogradov_inequality))
- **Burgess (1963) (11L40, 11L26).** For a non-principal $\chi$ mod $q$, $r\ge2$, $\varepsilon>0$, and $q$ cube-free or $r\le3$, $\big|\sum_{N<n\le N+H}\chi(n)\big|\le C_{r,\varepsilon}H^{1-1/r}q^{(r+1)/(4r^2)+\varepsilon}$. ([Burgess inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgess_inequality)) For prime $q$ and every $r\ge2$, Kerr, Shparlinski and Yau prove $\sum_{M<n\le M+N}\chi(n)=O\big(N^{1-1/r}q^{(r+1)/4r^2}(\log q)^{1/4r}\big)$, sharpening earlier logarithmic refinements by a factor $(\log q)^{1/4r}$. ([Kerr–Shparlinski–Yau, arXiv:1711.10582](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10582)) Burgess also proved $n(p)\ll p^\theta$ for any $\theta>1/(4\sqrt e)$ for the least quadratic nonresidue. ([Pólya–Vinogradov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B3lya%E2%80%93Vinogradov_inequality))
- **Weyl's inequality (11L15).** If $f\in\mathbb R[x]$ has degree $k$ and leading coefficient $c$ with $|c-a/q|\le tq^{-2}$, $(a,q)=1$, $t\ge1$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$,
  $$\sum_{x=M}^{M+N}e(f(x))\ll N^{1+\varepsilon}\Big(\frac tq+\frac1N+\frac t{N^{k-1}}+\frac q{N^k}\Big)^{2^{1-k}},$$
  useful only when $q<N^k$. ([Weyl's inequality (number theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl%27s_inequality_%28number_theory%29))
- **Vinogradov's mean value theorem (11L15).** Let $J_{s,k}(X)$ count solutions of $\sum_{i\le s}x_i^j=\sum_{i\le s}y_i^j$ ($1\le j\le k$) with $1\le x_i,y_i\le X$. Then $J_{s,k}(X)\gg X^s+X^{2s-k(k+1)/2}$, and the main conjecture $J_{s,k}(X)\ll X^{s+\varepsilon}+X^{2s-k(k+1)/2+\varepsilon}$ is now a theorem: Bourgain, Demeter and Guth proved it for degrees above three via a sharp decoupling inequality for curves, and Wooley proved it by efficient congruencing. ([Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem); [Bourgain–Demeter–Guth, arXiv:1512.01565](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01565))
- **Exponent pairs (11L07).** $(k,l)$ with $0\le k\le\tfrac12\le l\le1$ is an exponent pair if for each $\sigma>0$, $\sum_{n=a}^{b} e(f(n))\ll(T/N^{\sigma})^kN^l$ uniformly over a class of smooth $f$ on $[N,2N]$ (with $T$ a size parameter of the derivatives); $(0,1)$ is trivial, the set is convex, and van der Corput's processes $A:(k,l)\mapsto\big(\tfrac k{2k+2},\tfrac{k+l+1}{2k+2}\big)$ and $B:(k,l)\mapsto(l-\tfrac12,k+\tfrac12)$ generate new pairs. Any pair gives $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll t^{\theta}\log t$ with $\theta=(k+l-\tfrac12)/2$. ([Exponent pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponent_pair))

### History
Gauss evaluated the quadratic Gauss sum; Pólya and Vinogradov proved their inequality independently in 1918; Vinogradov's mean value bound dates from 1935; Burgess's inequality from 1963; and Montgomery–Vaughan's conditional bound from 1977. ([Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum); [Character sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_sum); [Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem); [Burgess inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgess_inequality); [Pólya–Vinogradov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B3lya%E2%80%93Vinogradov_inequality)) Wooley proved the conjectured form of Vinogradov's bound for $s\ge k(k+1)$ in 2012, and Bourgain, Demeter and Guth's proof of the main conjecture appeared in the *Annals* in 2016. ([Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Exponent pair conjecture.** For every $\varepsilon>0$, $(\varepsilon,\tfrac12+\varepsilon)$ is conjectured to be an exponent pair; it would imply the Lindelöf hypothesis $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll t^{\varepsilon}$. ([Exponent pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponent_pair))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum): definitions, Weil bound, Kuznetsov formula.
- **Learn:** [Harvard Math 259, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory (Elkies)](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M259.02/index.html): notes on Weyl equidistribution, van der Corput estimates, Gauss sums, Kloosterman sums.
- **Primary:** [Bourgain, Demeter and Guth, Proof of the main conjecture in Vinogradov's mean value theorem for degrees higher than three](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01565): the decoupling proof.
- **Further reading:** [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory (AMS Colloquium Publications, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/coll/053): the standard graduate reference.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 11Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Lxx): official code list.
references.MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analy:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11M is the analytic theory of zeta and $L$-functions: Dirichlet series with Euler products whose continuation, functional equations, zeros and growth encode the distribution of primes and other arithmetic data. The prototypes are the [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) and Dirichlet $L$-functions $L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s}$, which Dirichlet introduced in 1837 to prove his theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions. ([MSC2020 11M](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Mxx); [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function))

The central questions are where the zeros lie (zero-free regions, the Riemann hypothesis and its generalizations), how large the functions are on the critical line (convexity, subconvexity, Lindelöf), and the statistics of zeros and values (moments, pair correlation, random matrix models). These feed directly into prime counting through explicit formulas. ([Riemann hypothesis, Clay](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/); [Lindelöf hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindel%C3%B6f_hypothesis); [CFKRS, arXiv:math/0206018](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0206018); [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 11M into: 11M06 $\zeta(s)$ and $L(s,\chi)$; 11M20 real zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ and results on $L(1,\chi)$; 11M26 nonreal zeros of $\zeta(s)$ and $L(s,\chi)$, Riemann and other hypotheses; 11M32 multiple Dirichlet series, zeta functions and multizeta values; 11M35 Hurwitz and Lerch zeta functions; 11M36 Selberg zeta functions and regularized determinants, with applications to [spectral theory](node:Spectral%20Theory), Dirichlet series and Eisenstein series (explicit formulas); 11M38 zeta and $L$-functions in characteristic $p$; 11M41 other Dirichlet series and zeta functions; 11M45 [Tauberian theorems](node:Tauberian%20Theorems); 11M50 relations with [random matrices](node:Random%20Matrices); 11M55 relations with noncommutative geometry; 11M99 other. ([MSC2020 11M](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Mxx))

Neighbouring codes: under 11M41 the entry sends zeta functions over local and global ground fields to 11R42, 11R52, 11S40 and 11S45, and algebro-geometric methods to 14G10, with see-also references to 11E45, 11F66, 11F70 and 11F72; 11M45 (Tauberian theorems) has a see-also to 40E05. ([MSC2020 11M](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Mxx))

### Key concepts
- [L-Functions](node:L-Functions) and Dirichlet $L$-functions: for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, $L(s,\chi)=\prod_p(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1}$. For the principal character $L(s,\chi)$ is $\zeta(s)$ times finitely many factors, with a simple pole at $s=1$; otherwise it is entire. For primitive $\chi$ mod $q>1$ a functional equation relates $L(s,\chi)$ to $L(1-s,\bar\chi)$ with a Gamma factor and a root number of modulus $1$ built from a Gauss sum. ([Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function))
- **Non-vanishing on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$.** $\zeta(1+it)\ne0$ (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin) is equivalent to the [Prime Number Theorem](node:Prime%20Number%20Theorem); $L(1,\chi)\ne0$ for nonprincipal $\chi$ is the key step in Dirichlet's theorem that every coprime progression $a+nd$ contains infinitely many primes. ([DLMF §25.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.10); [Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function); [Dirichlet's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions))
- **Zero-free regions and Siegel zeros.** De la Vallée Poussin's region $\sigma\ge1-c/\log|t|$ for $\zeta$ has an analogue for $L(s,\chi)$ with at most one exception, a real simple zero of a real character: the Landau–Siegel (exceptional) zero. Siegel's theorem: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C(\varepsilon)>0$ such that a real zero $\beta$ of the $L$-function of a real primitive character of conductor $q$ satisfies $\beta<1-C(\varepsilon)q^{-\varepsilon}$, with $C(\varepsilon)$ ineffective. ([Siegel zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_zero); [MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Landau-SiegelZero.html))
- **Explicit formula.** For non-integer $x>1$, $\psi(x)=x-\log2\pi-\sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho$ over all zeros of $\zeta$, trivial and nontrivial (the nontrivial-zero sum converging only conditionally), so zero-free regions translate into error terms for prime counting; de la Vallée Poussin's region gives $\pi(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)+O(xe^{-a\sqrt{\log x}})$, and RH is equivalent to $\pi(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)+O(\sqrt x\log x)$. ([Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))
- **GRH.** For every primitive Dirichlet character, all nontrivial zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ have real part $\tfrac12$; under GRH, $\pi(x;d,a)=\operatorname{Li}(x)/\varphi(d)+O(x^{1/2+\varepsilon})$. The function-field analogues are the only proven cases. ([GRH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Riemann_hypothesis))
- **Convexity and subconvexity.** Lindelöf's convexity bound gives $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll t^{1/4+\varepsilon}$; Hardy and Littlewood lowered the exponent to $1/6$; the best recorded exponent is Bourgain's $13/84$ (2017). Michel and Venkatesh solved the subconvexity problem for $L$-functions of $\mathrm{GL}_1$ and $\mathrm{GL}_2$ automorphic representations uniformly in all aspects. ([Lindelöf hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindel%C3%B6f_hypothesis); [Michel–Venkatesh, arXiv:0903.3591](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3591))
- **Selberg class.** Dirichlet series with meromorphic continuation (at most a pole at $s=1$), a Ramanujan bound $a_n\ll n^\varepsilon$, a functional equation with Gamma factors, and an Euler product. Kaczorowski and Perelli (2011) showed that the members of degree below $2$ come from Dirichlet $L$-functions of primitive characters, including $\zeta$. ([Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class))
- **Random matrices (11M50).** Montgomery's 1973 conjecture says normalized zero differences have pair correlation $1-(\sin\pi u/\pi u)^2$, that of GUE eigenvalues, supported by Odlyzko's numerics. ([Montgomery's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery%27s_pair_correlation_conjecture))

### History
Dirichlet introduced $L$-functions in 1837 for primes in progressions, modelling his proof on Euler's link between $\zeta$ and primes. Riemann's 1859 paper gave the continuation and functional equation of $\zeta$ and stated RH. Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved the prime number theorem in 1896, and von Koch tied RH to the error term in 1901. Selberg defined his axiomatic class in a 1992 paper, and Montgomery's 1973 pair correlation conjecture began the random-matrix connection. ([Dirichlet's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions); [Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function); [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem); [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class); [Montgomery's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery%27s_pair_correlation_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Riemann hypothesis** for $\zeta$: unsolved Clay Millennium Problem. ([Clay](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/))
- **GRH and ERH** for Dirichlet $L$-functions and Dedekind zeta functions: open outside the function-field case. ([GRH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Riemann_hypothesis))
- **Lindelöf hypothesis**, and the sixth moment of $\zeta$ on the critical line: open. ([Lindelöf hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindel%C3%B6f_hypothesis))
- **Selberg class conjectures**: Selberg's orthogonality conjectures, the conjecture that every degree is a nonnegative integer, and GRH for the class are unproven, and the class is conjectured to equal the class of automorphic $L$-functions. ([Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class))
- **Moment conjectures** of Conrey–Farmer–Keating–Rubinstein–Snaith for all main terms in families. ([CFKRS, arXiv:math/0206018](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0206018))

> [!warning] Contested
> **Landau–Siegel zeros.** The conjecture that $1-\beta\gg1/\log q$ for every real zero $\beta$ of a real primitive $L(s,\chi)$ has long been open. ([Siegel zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_zero)) An October 2026 preprint by Banks gives an explicit-constant account of an OpenAI manuscript's argument, proving $(1-\beta)\log q\ge3.0\times10^{-3}$ for conductors $q\ge10^{10}$, extended to $q\ge3$ using a computation of Lu, Zaman and Zhao. ([Banks, arXiv:2610.15483](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15483)) MathWorld notes that the extension to small conductors uses a cited computation Banks did not independently verify, that Banks calls for further independent scrutiny of the argument, and it presents these and follow-up claims as reported results requiring further verification. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Landau-SiegelZero.html))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Dirichlet L-function (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function): definitions, Euler product, functional equation, zeros.
- **Learn:** [Elkies, Math 259: Introduction to Analytic Number Theory](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M259.06/index.html): Harvard notes on functional equations of $\zeta$ and $L(s,\chi)$, zero-free regions with the exceptional zero, and primes in progressions.
- **Primary:** [Conrey, Farmer, Keating, Rubinstein, Snaith, Integral moments of L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0206018): the moment conjectures and their random-matrix origin; [Michel and Venkatesh, The subconvexity problem for GL₂](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3591).
- **Further reading:** [Davenport, Multiplicative Number Theory (Springer GTM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-5927-3); [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory (AMS Colloquium Publications 53, 2004)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL2686784W).
references.MSC 11Nxx - Multiplicative number theory:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11N, "Multiplicative number theory", is the part of [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) about the distribution of [primes](node:Prime%20Numbers) and of integers defined by multiplicative conditions. Its codes cover the distribution of primes (11N05), primes in congruence classes (11N13), integers with multiplicative constraints (11N25), Turán theory (11N30), primes represented by polynomials (11N32), sieves and their applications (11N35, 11N36), asymptotics and growth of arithmetic functions (11N37, 11N56), distribution functions of additive and multiplicative functions (11N60, 11N64), integers in special residue classes (11N69), applications of automorphic forms (11N75) and generalized primes (11N80). ([MSC2020 11Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Nxx))

The analytic engine is the theory of the [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) and Dirichlet $L$-functions: zero-free regions give the prime number theorem with error term and its analogue for progressions, while sieve methods bound primes in sparse sets. These are the core of [Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory) courses, which run from Chebyshev's method and the von Mangoldt function through the prime number theorem, Dirichlet's theorem, Siegel's theorem and the Selberg sieve. ([Harvard Math 259](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M259.02/index.html); [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))

### Scope
- **Neighbour 11B.** The 11B25 entry for arithmetic progressions cross-refers to 11N13, "Primes in congruence classes"; see [MSC 11Bxx - Sequences and sets](node:MSC%2011Bxx%20-%20Sequences%20and%20sets). ([MSC2020 11Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Bxx); [MSC2020 11Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Nxx))
- **Neighbour 11F.** 11N75 covers applications of automorphic forms to multiplicative problems and cross-refers to 11Fxx, [MSC 11Fxx - Discontinuous groups and automorphic forms](node:MSC%2011Fxx%20-%20Discontinuous%20groups%20and%20automorphic%20forms). ([MSC2020 11Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Nxx))
- **Neighbour 30B.** Turán theory (11N30) cross-refers to 30Bxx in [complex analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis). ([MSC2020 11Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **Arithmetic functions.** The Dirichlet convolution $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)g(n/d)$ makes arithmetic functions a commutative ring with identity $\varepsilon$; $f$ is invertible iff $f(1)\ne0$, the convolution of multiplicative functions is multiplicative, and $1*\mu=\varepsilon$ (Möbius inversion), $\tau=1*1$, $\sigma=\mathrm{Id}*1$, $\varphi*1=\mathrm{Id}$. Convolution corresponds to multiplying Dirichlet series. ([Dirichlet convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_convolution))
- **[Prime number theorem](node:Prime%20Number%20Theorem) (11N05).** $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$ (Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin, 1896). De la Vallée Poussin's error term $\pi(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)+O\big(xe^{-a\sqrt{\log x}}\big)$ has been improved to $O\big(x\exp(-A(\log x)^{3/5}(\log\log x)^{-1/5})\big)$, and von Koch showed that $\pi(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)+O(\sqrt x\log x)$ is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis. ([Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))
- **Primes in progressions (11N13).** Dirichlet (1837): if $\gcd(a,d)=1$, there are infinitely many primes $p\equiv a\pmod d$, and in fact primes are asymptotically equidistributed among the $\varphi(d)$ coprime classes. ([Dirichlet's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions)) Siegel–Walfisz (1936): with $\psi(x;q,a)=\sum_{n\le x,\,n\equiv a\,(q)}\Lambda(n)$, for every $N$ there is $C_N>0$ with $\psi(x;q,a)=x/\varphi(q)+O\big(x e^{-C_N\sqrt{\log x}}\big)$ uniformly for $q\le(\log x)^N$, $\gcd(a,q)=1$; $C_N$ is ineffective because Siegel's theorem is. ([Siegel–Walfisz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%E2%80%93Walfisz_theorem))
- **Bombieri–Vinogradov (mid-1960s).** For $x^{1/2}(\log x)^{-A}\le Q\le x^{1/2}$,
  $$\sum_{q\le Q}\max_{y\le x}\max_{(a,q)=1}\Big|\psi(y;q,a)-\frac{y}{\varphi(q)}\Big|\ll x^{1/2}Q(\log x)^5,$$
  so on average over moduli $q\le Q$ the error is about of the strength of the generalized Riemann hypothesis; it was proved as a major application of the large sieve. ([Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Vinogradov_theorem); [Large sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_sieve))
- **Sieves (11N35, 11N36).** Brun (1919) introduced sieve methods to prove that $\sum 1/p$ over twin primes converges, with $\pi_2(x)=O\big(x(\log\log x)^2/(\log x)^2\big)$. ([Brun's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brun%27s_theorem)) The large sieve goes back to Linnik (1941) and was given its definitive form in independent work of Roth and Bombieri. ([Large sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_sieve))
- **Bounded gaps between primes.** Zhang (2013) proved $\liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n)<7\times10^7$; Maynard's refinement of the GPY sieve gave $\liminf(p_{n+m}-p_n)<\infty$ for every $m$ and $\liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n)\le600$, and the Polymath project lowered this to $246$. ([Prime gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_gap); [Maynard, arXiv:1311.4600](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.4600))
- **Erdős–Kac (1940) (11N60).** For fixed $a<b$, the proportion of $n\le x$ with $(\omega(n)-\log\log n)/\sqrt{\log\log n}\in[a,b]$ tends to $\Phi(b)-\Phi(a)$, the standard Gaussian; it extends the Hardy–Ramanujan theorem that $\omega(n)$ has normal order $\log\log n$. ([Erdős–Kac theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Kac_theorem))
- **Divisor problem (11N37).** $D(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\tau(n)=x\log x+(2\gamma-1)x+\Delta(x)$. Dirichlet (1849) had $\Delta(x)=O(\sqrt x)$, Voronoi (1904) $O(x^{1/3}\log x)$, and Huxley (2003) $O(x^{131/416+\varepsilon})$; Hardy (1916) showed the exponent cannot be below $1/4$. ([Divisor summatory function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor_summatory_function))

### History
Dirichlet proved his theorem on progressions in 1837 and Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin the prime number theorem in 1896. ([Dirichlet's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_theorem_on_arithmetic_progressions); [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem)) Brun's sieve dates from 1919, Walfisz's theorem from 1936 (building on Siegel, 1935), and Bombieri–Vinogradov from the mid-1960s. ([Brun's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brun%27s_theorem); [Siegel–Walfisz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%E2%80%93Walfisz_theorem); [Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Vinogradov_theorem)) Zhang's bounded-gaps theorem (2013) and Maynard's sieve (November 2013) reshaped the study of small gaps. ([Prime gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_gap))

### Open problems
- **Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (1968).** For every $\theta<1$ and $A>0$, $\sum_{q\le x^\theta}\max_{(a,q)=1}|\pi(x;q,a)-\pi(x)/\varphi(q)|\ll x(\log x)^{-A}$. It is proven only for $\theta<\tfrac12$ (Bombieri–Vinogradov) and fails at $\theta=1$; it would give gaps at most $12$, and its generalized form gaps at most $6$. ([Elliott–Halberstam conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott%E2%80%93Halberstam_conjecture); [Maynard, arXiv:1311.4600](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.4600))
- **Twin prime and Cramér conjectures.** Both are unproven: twin primes asks for $p_{n+1}-p_n=2$ infinitely often, and Cramér for $p_{n+1}-p_n=O((\log p_n)^2)$. ([Prime gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_gap))
- **Dirichlet divisor problem.** The optimal exponent lies between $1/4$ and Huxley's $131/416\approx0.3149$, is widely conjectured to be $1/4$, and the problem "remains unsolved". ([Divisor summatory function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor_summatory_function))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Vinogradov_theorem): statement and relation to GRH and the large sieve.
- **Learn:** [Harvard Math 259, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory (Elkies)](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M259.02/index.html): PNT with error term, Dirichlet's theorem, Siegel's theorem, the Selberg sieve.
- **Primary:** [Maynard, Small gaps between primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.4600): the refined GPY sieve and bounded gaps between $m$ consecutive primes.
- **Further reading:** [Montgomery and Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I: Classical Theory (CUP, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511618314): the standard graduate text.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 11Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Nxx): official code list.
references.MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; part:
## Reference
### Overview
Additive number theory studies representations of integers as sums of elements from a given set — squares, $k$th powers, [primes](node:Prime%20Numbers), lattice points — and, inversely, what the size of a sumset $A+A$ says about the structure of $A$. Its central analytic tool is the Hardy–Littlewood circle method, whose analysis splits into major arcs, which produce the main term and the singular series, and minor arcs, which are controlled by bounds for exponential sums of $k$th powers; strong mean-value estimates are an important input for Waring's problem. ([MSC2020, 11Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Pxx); [Oxford C3.10 syllabus](https://courses.maths.ox.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=6233); [Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem))

Partition theory counts the ways of writing $n$ as an unordered sum of positive integers, the order of parts being disregarded. Its analytic side (Hardy–Ramanujan asymptotics, Rademacher's exact series) and arithmetic side (Ramanujan's congruences and their generalizations by Ono and Ahlgren) are both organized around the counting function $p(n)$ and its product generating function. ([Partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29); [Ramanujan's congruences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%27s_congruences))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 11P into: 11P05 Waring's problem and variants; 11P21 lattice points in specified regions; 11P32 Goldbach-type theorems and other additive questions involving primes; 11P55 applications of the Hardy–Littlewood method (see also 11D85); 11P70 inverse problems of additive number theory, including sumsets; 11P81 elementary theory of partitions (see also 05A17); 11P82 analytic theory of partitions; 11P83 partitions, congruences and congruential restrictions; 11P84 partition identities, identities of Rogers–Ramanujan type; 11P99 other. ([MSC2020, 11Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Pxx))

The entry's cross-references are 11D85 from 11P55 (applications of the Hardy–Littlewood method) and 05A17 in [MSC 05Axx - Enumerative combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Axx%20-%20Enumerative%20combinatorics) from 11P81 (elementary theory of partitions). ([MSC2020, 11Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Pxx))

### Key concepts
- **Waring's problem (11P05).** Hilbert (1909): for each $k$ there is $s$ such that every natural number is a sum of at most $s$ $k$th powers. $g(k)$ is the least such $s$, with $g(2)=4$, $g(3)=9$, $g(4)=19$, $g(5)=37$; $G(k)$ is the least $s$ that works for all sufficiently large $n$. For $k\ge2$ only $G(2)=4$ and $G(4)=16$ (Davenport, 1939) are known exactly; $4\le G(3)\le7$, and Wooley proved $G(k)\le k(\log k+\log\log k+C)$. ([Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem))
- **Vinogradov's mean value theorem.** Let $J_{s,k}(X)$ count solutions of the system $\sum_{i=1}^s(x_i^j-y_i^j)=0$, $1\le j\le k$, with $1\le x_i,y_i\le X$. The main conjecture $J_{s,k}(X)\ll X^{s+\varepsilon}+X^{2s-k(k+1)/2+\varepsilon}$ was proved for degrees $k>3$ by Bourgain, Demeter and Guth via a sharp decoupling inequality for curves, and by Wooley by efficient congruencing. Such estimates drive the minor-arc analysis for Waring's problem. ([Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem); [Bourgain–Demeter–Guth, arXiv:1512.01565](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01565))
- **Ternary Goldbach and Chen (11P32).** Hardy–Littlewood (1923) showed under GRH that every sufficiently large odd number is a sum of three primes; Vinogradov (1937) proved this unconditionally. Helfgott (2013) posted a proof that every odd integer $>5$ is a sum of three primes, using the circle method, an optimized large sieve and exponential-sum bounds; it was accepted for the *Annals of Mathematics Studies* in 2015 and has undergone further review and revision since. Chen (1966, proof 1973): every sufficiently large even number is $p+q$ with $p$ prime and $q$ prime or a product of two primes. Montgomery–Vaughan (1975): the even numbers up to $N$ that are not sums of two primes number $O(N^{1-c})$. ([Goldbach's weak conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_weak_conjecture); [Helfgott, arXiv:1312.7748](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.7748); [Chen's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen%27s_theorem); [Goldbach's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_conjecture))
- **Partition asymptotics (11P82).** $\sum_{n\ge0}p(n)q^n=\prod_{m\ge1}(1-q^m)^{-1}$; Hardy and Ramanujan (1918) proved $p(n)\sim\frac{1}{4n\sqrt3}\exp\!\left(\pi\sqrt{2n/3}\right)$, and Rademacher (1937) gave a convergent series for $p(n)$. ([Partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29))
- **Partition congruences (11P83).** Ramanujan: $p(5k+4)\equiv0\pmod5$, $p(7k+5)\equiv0\pmod7$, $p(11k+6)\equiv0\pmod{11}$. Dyson's rank (1944) and the Andrews–Garvan crank give combinatorial explanations; Atkin found further congruences such as $p(11^3\cdot13k+237)\equiv0\pmod{13}$; Ono (2000) proved that congruences of this kind exist for every prime modulus $\ge5$, extended to every modulus coprime to $6$ with Ahlgren. ([Ramanujan's congruences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%27s_congruences); [Partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29))
- **Rogers–Ramanujan identities (11P84).** $\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{q^{n^2}}{(q;q)_n}=\frac{1}{(q;q^5)_\infty(q^4;q^5)_\infty}$: partitions of $n$ into parts differing by at least $2$ are equinumerous with partitions into parts $\equiv\pm1\pmod5$ (Rogers 1894; Rogers–Ramanujan joint proof 1919). ([Rogers–Ramanujan identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers%E2%80%93Ramanujan_identities))
- **Freiman's theorem (11P70).** If $A\subset\mathbb Z$ is finite with $|A+A|\le K|A|$, then $A$ lies in a generalized arithmetic progression of dimension $\le d(K)$ and size $\le f(K)|A|$. Green–Ruzsa extended this to all abelian groups (coset progressions); Gowers–Green–Manners–Tao (2023) gave a proof of the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture for $\mathbb F_2^n$, since fully formalized in Lean 4. ([Freiman's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiman%27s_theorem))
- **Lattice points (11P21).** For $N(r)=\#\{(m,n)\in\mathbb Z^2:m^2+n^2\le r^2\}=\pi r^2+E(r)$, Gauss showed $E(r)=O(r)$; Hardy and Landau (1915) showed $E(r)$ is not $o\!\left(r^{1/2}(\log r)^{1/4}\right)$; Huxley (2000) proved $|E(r)|\le Cr^{t}$ with $t=131/208\approx0.6298$. ([Gauss circle problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_circle_problem))

### History
Goldbach's binary and ternary conjectures go back to the 1742 correspondence of Euler and Goldbach. ([Helfgott, arXiv:1312.7748](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.7748)) Lagrange proved the four-square theorem in 1770 and Hilbert settled Waring's problem in 1909. ([Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem)) Hardy and Ramanujan obtained the asymptotic for $p(n)$ in 1918; Hardy and Littlewood treated ternary Goldbach conditionally on GRH in 1923, and Vinogradov removed GRH in 1937. ([Partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29); [Goldbach's weak conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_weak_conjecture)) The inverse direction (Freiman, Ruzsa in 1992–1994, Green–Ruzsa) and decoupling (Bourgain–Demeter–Guth, 2015) are the main later developments. ([Freiman's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiman%27s_theorem); [Bourgain–Demeter–Guth](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01565))

### Open problems
- **Binary Goldbach conjecture.** Every even integer $>2$ is a sum of two primes; it "remains unproven", and has been verified up to $4\times10^{18}$ (Oliveira e Silva, Herzog, Pardi). ([Goldbach's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_conjecture))
- **Exact values of $G(k)$.** Apart from $G(2)=4$ and $G(4)=16$, $G(k)$ is unknown; even $G(3)$ is only known to lie in $[4,7]$. ([Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem))
- **Gauss circle problem.** The conjectured bound $|E(r)|=O(r^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ remains unproven. ([Gauss circle problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_circle_problem))
- **Newman's conjecture.** That for every modulus $m$ each residue class $r\bmod m$ contains $p(n)$ for infinitely many $n$ is an unsolved problem on partition congruences. ([Partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29))
- **Freiman-type theorems beyond abelian groups.** Extending Freiman's theorem to arbitrary nonabelian groups is described as open. ([Freiman's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiman%27s_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem): $g(k)$, $G(k)$, history and bounds.
- **Learn:** [Oxford C3.10 Additive Number Theory (Maynard)](https://courses.maths.ox.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=6233): sums of squares, Fourier methods, the circle method for Waring's problem, Roth's theorem.
- **Primary:** [Helfgott, The ternary Goldbach conjecture is true (arXiv:1312.7748)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.7748): the explicit circle-method proof; also [Bourgain–Demeter–Guth (arXiv:1512.01565)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01565) for Vinogradov's mean value theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Nathanson, Additive Number Theory (GTM, Springer 1996)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3845-2); [Vaughan, The Hardy–Littlewood Method (CUP, 2nd ed. 1997)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511470929); [Andrews, The Theory of Partitions (CUP)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511608650).
- **Related maps:** [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), [Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory), [MSC 11Nxx - Multiplicative number theory](node:MSC%2011Nxx%20-%20Multiplicative%20number%20theory), [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis).

## Reference
### Overview
Global algebraic number theory studies number fields (finite extensions of $\mathbb Q$) and global function fields (finite extensions of $\mathbb F_q(t)$) through their rings of integers, ideals, units, class groups, places, zeta functions and Galois extensions. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_theory); [MIT 18.785, Lecture 13](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes13.pdf)) Its central structural results are the finiteness of the class group, Dirichlet's unit theorem, the analytic class number formula, and class field theory, which describes all abelian extensions of a global field in terms of data attached to the field itself. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_theory); [Wikipedia: Class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_field_theory))

All places matter, archimedean and nonarchimedean together. For a global field $L$ and every $x\in L^\times$ the product formula $\prod_{v\in M_L}\|x\|_v=1$ holds over the normalized absolute values, and Artin and Whaples showed that fields whose completions are local fields and which satisfy such a product formula are exactly the finite extensions of $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_q(t)$. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 13](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes13.pdf)) The completions are the subject of [MSC 11Sxx - Algebraic number theory - local and p-adic fields](node:MSC%2011Sxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20local%20and%20p-adic%20fields); the idelic form of class field theory glues these local fields together. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 28](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes28.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 11Rxx (Algebraic number theory: global fields) sits in [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) and has the codes 11R04 algebraic numbers and rings of algebraic integers; 11R06 Pisot–Vijayaraghavan numbers, special algebraic numbers, Mahler measure; 11R09 polynomials, including irreducibility; 11R11 quadratic, 11R16 cubic and quartic, 11R18 cyclotomic, 11R20 other abelian and metabelian extensions, 11R21 other number fields; 11R23 Iwasawa theory; 11R27 units and factorization; 11R29 class numbers, class groups, discriminants; 11R32 Galois theory; 11R33 integral representations and Galois module structure of rings of integers; 11R34 Galois cohomology; 11R37 class field theory; 11R39 Langlands–Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory; 11R42 zeta and $L$-functions of number fields; 11R44 distribution of prime ideals; 11R45 density theorems; 11R47 other analytic theory; 11R52 quaternion and other division algebras; 11R54 other algebras and orders; 11R56 adèle rings and groups; 11R58 arithmetic theory of algebraic function fields; 11R59 zeta and $L$-functions of function fields; 11R60 cyclotomic function fields; 11R65 class groups and Picard groups of orders; 11R70 $K$-theory of global fields; 11R80 totally real fields; 11R99. ([MSC2020: 11Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Rxx))

Neighbouring codes, from the cross-references in MSC2020 ([MSC2020: 11Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Rxx); [MSC2020: 11-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11-XX)):
- Complex multiplication goes to 11G15, in [MSC 11Gxx - Arithmetic algebraic geometry (Diophantine geometry)](node:MSC%2011Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20algebraic%20geometry%20%28Diophantine%20geometry%29).
- 11R39 points to 11Fxx and 22E55: automorphic forms are in [MSC 11Fxx - Discontinuous groups and automorphic forms](node:MSC%2011Fxx%20-%20Discontinuous%20groups%20and%20automorphic%20forms).
- 11R42 points to 11M41 ([MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory)); 11R44 and 11R47 point to 11N05 and 11Nxx ([MSC 11Nxx - Multiplicative number theory](node:MSC%2011Nxx%20-%20Multiplicative%20number%20theory)).
- 11R34 points to 12Gxx ([MSC 12Gxx - Homological methods (field theory)](node:MSC%2012Gxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20%28field%20theory%29)) and 19F05; 11R70 points to 19Fxx ([MSC 19Fxx - K-theory in number theory](node:MSC%2019Fxx%20-%20K-theory%20in%20number%20theory)).
- 11R58 points to 14Gxx and 14H05 ([MSC 14Gxx - Arithmetic problems in algebraic geometry; Diophantine geometry](node:MSC%2014Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20problems%20in%20algebraic%20geometry;%20Diophantine%20geometry)).
- Elementary number theory analogues in number fields are filed under 11R04 rather than 11Axx ([MSC 11Axx - Elementary number theory](node:MSC%2011Axx%20-%20Elementary%20number%20theory)).

### Key concepts
- **Dirichlet's unit theorem (11R27).** If $K$ is a number field with $r$ real and $s$ complex places, then $\mathcal O_K^\times\simeq\mu_K\times\mathbb Z^{r+s-1}$; more generally, for $S$ the places above the infinite place of $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_q(t)$, the $S$-units form $\mu_K\times\mathbb Z^{\#S-1}$. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 15](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes15.pdf))
- **Finiteness of the class group and discriminant bounds (11R29).** With the Minkowski constant $m_K=\frac{n!}{n^n}\left(\frac4\pi\right)^s\sqrt{|D_K|}$, every ideal class of $\mathcal O_K$ contains an ideal of norm at most $m_K$, so $\mathrm{cl}\,\mathcal O_K$ is finite. Consequently $|D_K|>1$ for $K\ne\mathbb Q$ (no nontrivial unramified extensions of $\mathbb Q$), only finitely many number fields have $|D_K|<M$, and (Hermite) only finitely many degree-$n$ extensions of $\mathbb Q$ are unramified outside a finite set of places. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 14](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes14.pdf))
- **Analytic class number formula (11R42).** For a number field $K$ of degree $n$, $\zeta_K(z)$ extends meromorphically to $\mathrm{Re}(z)>1-\frac1n$ with only a simple pole at $z=1$, of residue $\lim_{z\to1^+}(z-1)\zeta_K(z)=\dfrac{2^r(2\pi)^s h_K R_K}{w_K|D_K|^{1/2}}$, where $h_K$ is the class number, $R_K$ the regulator and $w_K$ the number of roots of unity. Hecke later proved continuation to all of $\mathbb C$ with a functional equation. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 19](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes19.pdf); [Wikipedia: Class number formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_formula)) See [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Global class field theory (11R37).** For a global field $K$ with idele class group $C_K$, there is a continuous Artin homomorphism $\theta_K:C_K\to\mathrm{Gal}(K^{ab}/K)$ such that, for every finite abelian $L/K$, it induces $C_K/N_{L/K}(C_L)\simeq\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$; every finite-index open subgroup $H\le C_K$ is $N_{L/K}(C_L)$ for a unique such $L$ (existence theorem), giving an inclusion-reversing bijection. For number fields $\theta_K$ is surjective with kernel the connected component of the identity. In ideal-theoretic form, every finite abelian $L/K$ lies in a ray class field $K(\mathfrak m)$ exactly when its conductor divides $\mathfrak m$, with $\mathrm{Cl}_K^{\mathfrak m}\simeq\mathrm{Gal}(K(\mathfrak m)/K)$. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 28](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes28.pdf); [Lecture 22](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes22.pdf)) Compare [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).
- **Hilbert class field and class field towers.** The Hilbert class field $H$ of $K$ is its maximal unramified abelian extension; $[H:K]=h_K$, $\mathrm{Gal}(H/K)\cong\mathrm{Cl}_K$, and every ideal of $\mathcal O_K$ becomes principal in $\mathcal O_H$. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field)) Iterating can fail to terminate: Golod and Shafarevich proved in 1964 that infinite class field towers exist, for example over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-30030})$. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 22](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes22.pdf))
- **Chebotarev density theorem (11R45).** Let $L/K$ be a finite Galois extension of number fields with group $G$ and $C\subseteq G$ stable under conjugation. The set of primes of $K$ unramified in $L$ with Frobenius class in $C$ has density $\#C/\#G$ (Dirichlet density, and also natural density for number fields). ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 28](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes28.pdf)) Under GRH there is an effective version: the number of such primes of norm at most $x$ is $\frac{\#C}{\#G}\left(\mathrm{Li}(x)+O\!\left(\sqrt x\,(n\log x+\log|\Delta|)\right)\right)$ with an absolute implied constant, where $n=[L:\mathbb Q]$ and $\Delta$ is the discriminant of $L$. ([Wikipedia: Chebotarev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem))
- **Iwasawa theory (11R23).** For an odd prime $p$ and the cyclotomic $\mathbb Z_p$-extension $K_\infty=\bigcup_n K_n$ of a number field $K$, Iwasawa's class number formula gives constants $\mu,\lambda\ge0$ and $\nu$ with $\log_p\#H_n=\mu p^n+\lambda n+\nu$ for all sufficiently large $n$, where $H_n$ is the $p$-part of the class group of $K_n$. ([Chao Li, Columbia notes](https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chaoli/tutorial2012/Lecture14.pdf)) Ferrero and Washington (1979) proved $\mu=0$ for cyclotomic $\mathbb Z_p$-extensions of abelian number fields; Iwasawa had found non-cyclotomic $\mathbb Z_p$-extensions with $\mu\ne0$. ([Wikipedia: Ferrero–Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrero%E2%80%93Washington_theorem)) The main conjecture, identifying algebraic and analytic $p$-adic $L$-functions, was proved over $\mathbb Q$ by Mazur and Wiles (1984) and for totally real fields by Wiles (1990). ([Wikipedia: Iwasawa theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwasawa_theory))
- **Nonabelian class field theory (11R39).** The Langlands program extends Artin reciprocity by conjecturing that Artin $L$-functions of Galois representations equal $L$-functions of cuspidal automorphic representations; the $\mathrm{GL}_1$ case is class field theory, while the general conjectures remain unproven. ([Wikipedia: Langlands program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_program)) See [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory).

### History
Kummer's ideal numbers (1843), devised in work on Fermat's Last Theorem, led Dedekind to define ideals; Dirichlet proved the unit theorem and the first class number formula; Hilbert's 1897 *Zahlbericht* unified the subject and conjectured much of class field theory, which Takagi helped establish, with the main results proved by about 1930; Artin's reciprocity law appeared in papers from 1924 to 1930. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_theory)) Chevalley introduced ideles in the 1930s, and later presentations recast the theory with group cohomology. ([Wikipedia: Class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_field_theory)) The class number one problem for imaginary quadratic fields was settled by Heegner (1952), Baker and Stark: exactly nine fields, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ for $d=-1,-2,-3,-7,-11,-19,-43,-67,-163$. ([Wikipedia: Class number problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_problem))

### Open problems
- **Leopoldt's conjecture.** For a number field $K$ and prime $p$, the closure of the global units in the product of the local principal units above $p$ should have $\mathbb Z_p$-rank $r_1+r_2-1$; equivalently the $p$-adic regulator is nonzero. Ax's reduction together with Brumer's 1967 $p$-adic Baker theorem proves it for abelian extensions of $\mathbb Q$ and of imaginary quadratic fields; the general case is listed as unsolved. ([Wikipedia: Leopoldt's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopoldt%27s_conjecture))
- **Greenberg's conjecture.** For a totally real field $k$, the Iwasawa invariants $\lambda_p(k)$ and $\mu_p(k)$ of the cyclotomic $\mathbb Z_p$-extension should vanish for every prime $p$. Gras gives sufficient conditions and heuristics and argues that a proof needs deep $p$-adic results "probably out of reach now". ([Gras, arXiv:1611.09592](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1611.09592))
- **Real quadratic class number one.** Whether infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number one is open; the Cohen–Lenstra heuristics predict that about 75.45% of real quadratic fields $\mathbb Q(\sqrt p)$ with $p$ prime have class number one. ([Wikipedia: Class number problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_problem))
- **Inverse Galois problem (11R32).** Whether every finite group is a Galois group over $\mathbb Q$ is unsolved; it is known for solvable groups (Shafarevich) and for symmetric and alternating groups (Hilbert). ([Wikipedia: Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem)) See [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Class field theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_field_theory): idelic statements, history, nonabelian generalizations.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.785 Number Theory I (Sutherland, 2021)](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/lectures.html): complete lecture notes from Dedekind domains through the class number formula, ray class fields, and global class field theory with Chebotarev.
- **Learn:** [Chao Li, Iwasawa theory lecture (Columbia)](https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chaoli/tutorial2012/Lecture14.pdf): the cyclotomic $\mathbb Z_p$-extension and Iwasawa's class number formula.
- **Primary:** [Gras, *p-adic approach of Greenberg's conjecture*, arXiv:1611.09592](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.09592): current research on vanishing of Iwasawa invariants, with its link to Leopoldt's conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, Grundlehren (Springer, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-03983-0) and [Neukirch–Schmidt–Wingberg, *Cohomology of Number Fields*, Grundlehren (Springer, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-37889-1): the standard graduate text and the standard monograph on Galois cohomology of number fields.

## Reference
### Overview
A local field is a locally compact Hausdorff non-discrete topological field; up to isomorphism the archimedean ones are $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$, the nonarchimedean ones of characteristic $0$ are the finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_p$, and those of characteristic $p$ are the Laurent series fields $\mathbb F_q((t))$. ([Wikipedia: Local field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field); [MIT 18.785, Lecture 9](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes9.pdf)) Local fields are exactly the completions of global fields, so 11S is the local half of algebraic number theory; the global half is [MSC 11Rxx - Algebraic number theory - global fields](node:MSC%2011Rxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20global%20fields). ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 9](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes9.pdf))

For a nonarchimedean local field $F$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, the higher unit groups $U^{(n)}=1+\mathfrak m^n$ give a filtration with $\mathcal O^\times/U^{(n)}\cong(\mathcal O/\mathfrak m^n)^\times$ and $U^{(n)}/U^{(n+1)}\cong\mathcal O/\mathfrak m$ for $n\ge1$ (non-canonically). ([Wikipedia: Local field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field)) The algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q_p$ is not complete; its completion $\mathbb C_p$ is algebraically closed but not locally compact. ([Wikipedia: p-adic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number)) The research frontier of the area runs through Galois representations of local fields: local class field theory, $p$-adic Hodge theory, and the local Langlands correspondence. ([Wikipedia: p-adic Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_Hodge_theory); [Wikipedia: Local Langlands conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Langlands_conjectures))

### Scope
MSC2020 11Sxx (Algebraic number theory: local fields), in [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), has the codes 11S05 polynomials; 11S15 ramification and extension theory; 11S20 Galois theory; 11S23 integral representations; 11S25 Galois cohomology; 11S31 class field theory, $p$-adic formal groups; 11S37 Langlands–Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory; 11S40 zeta functions and $L$-functions; 11S45 algebras and orders, and their zeta functions; 11S70 $K$-theory of local fields; 11S80 other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, $p$-adic integration); 11S82 non-Archimedean [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems); 11S85 other nonanalytic theory; 11S90 prehomogeneous [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces); 11S99. ([MSC2020: 11Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Sxx))

Neighbouring codes, from the MSC2020 cross-references ([MSC2020: 11Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Sxx)):
- 11S25 points to 12Gxx ([MSC 12Gxx - Homological methods (field theory)](node:MSC%2012Gxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20%28field%20theory%29)) and 16H05.
- 11S31 points to 14L05 (formal groups); 11S37 points to 11Fxx ([MSC 11Fxx - Discontinuous groups and automorphic forms](node:MSC%2011Fxx%20-%20Discontinuous%20groups%20and%20automorphic%20forms)) and 22E50 ([MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups)).
- 11S40 points to 11M41 ([MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory)) and 19F27; 11S70 points to 19Fxx ([MSC 19Fxx - K-theory in number theory](node:MSC%2019Fxx%20-%20K-theory%20in%20number%20theory)).
- 11S45 points to 11R52, 11R54, 16Hxx ([MSC 16Hxx - Associative algebras and orders](node:MSC%2016Hxx%20-%20Associative%20algebras%20and%20orders)) and 16Kxx.
- 11S82 is mainly classified in 37Pxx: [MSC 37Pxx - Arithmetic and non-Archimedean dynamical systems](node:MSC%2037Pxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20and%20non-Archimedean%20dynamical%20systems).

### Key concepts
- **Hensel's lemma.** If $A$ is a complete DVR and $f\in A[x]$ is monic with reduction having a simple root $\bar a$ in the residue field, then $\bar a$ lifts to a root of $f$ in $A$. In Newton form: if $|f(a_0)|<|f'(a_0)|^2$, then $a_{n+1}=a_n-f(a_n)/f'(a_n)$ converges to the unique root $a$ with $|a-a_0|\le|f(a_0)|/|f'(a_0)|^2$. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 9](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes9.pdf))
- **Krasner's lemma and continuity of roots (11S15).** Let $K$ be the fraction field of a complete DVR and $\alpha$ separable over $K$. If $\beta$ is strictly closer to $\alpha$ than to any conjugate $\sigma(\alpha)\ne\alpha$, then $K(\alpha)\subseteq K(\beta)$. Consequently, for monic irreducible separable $f\in K[x]$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every monic $g$ with $\|f-g\|_1<\delta$ is irreducible, separable, and has the same splitting field as $f$. Although named after Krasner, the lemma was proved earlier by Ostrowski. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 11](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes11.pdf)) It is also used to show that $\mathbb C_p$ is algebraically closed. ([Wikipedia: Krasner's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krasner%27s_lemma))
- **Ramification filtration and Hasse–Arf (11S15).** For finite Galois $L/K$ with group $G$, the lower ramification groups are $G_s=\{\sigma: v_L(\sigma a-a)\ge s+1\ \forall a\in\mathcal O_L\}$; the Herbrand function $\eta_{L/K}(s)=\int_0^s dx/[G_0:G_x]$ and its inverse $\psi_{L/K}$ define the upper numbering $G^t=G_{\psi(t)}$. The Hasse–Arf theorem: if $L/K$ is a finite abelian extension of nonarchimedean local fields, every jump of the upper filtration is a rational integer; Hasse proved this case with finite residue fields and Arf generalized it. ([Wikipedia: Hasse–Arf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Arf_theorem))
- **Local class field theory (11S31).** For a local field $K$ there is a unique continuous homomorphism $\theta_K:K^\times\to\mathrm{Gal}(K^{ab}/K)$ such that, for every finite abelian $L/K$, $\theta_{L/K}$ is surjective with kernel $N_{L/K}(L^\times)$, giving $K^\times/N_{L/K}(L^\times)\simeq\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$, and $\theta_{L/K}(\pi)=\mathrm{Frob}_{L/K}$ for every uniformizer $\pi$ when $L/K$ is unramified. Every finite-index open subgroup $H\le K^\times$ equals $N_{L/K}(L^\times)$ for a unique such $L$, and $\theta_K$ induces $\widehat{K^\times}\simeq\mathrm{Gal}(K^{ab}/K)$. Norm groups see only the maximal abelian subextension (norm limitation theorem). ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 27](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes27.pdf))
- **Lubin–Tate theory (11S31).** Lubin and Tate (1965) introduced formal groups to isolate the local part of complex multiplication. Over a complete DVR with finite residue field, choosing a uniformizer, the $\pi^n$-division points generate abelian extensions with Galois group $U/(1+\mathfrak p^n)$, and together these give the ramified part of the abelian extensions. ([Wikipedia: Lubin–Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law)) One proof of local class field theory shows $K^{ab}=K_\pi K^{unr}$ using these fields and the Hasse–Arf theorem. ([MIT 18.785, Lecture 27](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes27.pdf)) See [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory).
- **Local Tate duality (11S25).** For a nonarchimedean local field $K$ and a finite $G_K$-module $A$ of order prime to $\mathrm{char}\,K$, with $A'=\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mu)$, the cup product $H^i(K,A)\times H^{2-i}(K,A')\to H^2(K,\mu)=\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is a perfect pairing for $i=0,1,2$, and the groups $H^i(K,A)$ vanish for $i\ge3$. ([Wikipedia: Local Tate duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Tate_duality)) See [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra).
- **$p$-adic Hodge theory.** Fontaine's period rings $B_{dR},B_{st},B_{cris}$ classify $p$-adic representations of $G_K$ for $K$ of characteristic 0 and residue characteristic $p$: crystalline $\subsetneq$ semistable $\subsetneq$ de Rham $\subsetneq$ Hodge–Tate. With finite residue field, de Rham equals potentially semistable (the $p$-adic monodromy theorem). Faltings proved Tate's Hodge–Tate comparison and Fontaine's $C_{dR}$, $C_{cris}$ conjectures; Tsuji proved $C_{st}$. ([Wikipedia: p-adic Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_Hodge_theory))
- **Local Langlands for $\mathrm{GL}_n$ (11S37).** Irreducible admissible representations of $\mathrm{GL}_n(F)$ correspond bijectively to $n$-dimensional Frobenius-semisimple Weil–Deligne representations, preserving $L$- and $\varepsilon$-factors of pairs and agreeing with the Artin map for $n=1$. Harris and Taylor (2001) and Henniart proved this in characteristic 0; Laumon, Rapoport and Stuhler (1993) in positive characteristic. ([Wikipedia: Local Langlands conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Langlands_conjectures)) Fargues and Scholze construct $L$-parameters for irreducible smooth representations of general $G(E)$ via geometric Langlands on the Fargues–Fontaine curve. ([Fargues–Scholze, arXiv:2102.13459](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.13459)) See [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory).

### History
Ostrowski's theorem shows that every nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value on a number field comes from a prime ideal of its ring of integers, the others coming from real or complex embeddings. ([Wikipedia: p-adic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number)) Lubin–Tate formal groups date from 1965. ([Wikipedia: Lubin–Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law)) Tate conjectured the Hodge–Tate decomposition in the mid-1960s and Faltings proved it in the late 1980s; Tsuji's proof of $C_{st}$ came in the late 1990s. ([Wikipedia: p-adic Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_Hodge_theory)) Arf's 1939 paper gave the general Hasse–Arf theorem. ([Wikipedia: Hasse–Arf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Arf_theorem))

### Open problems
- **$p$-adic local Langlands beyond $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_p)$.** The $p$-adic correspondence for $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_p)$ has "a very satisfactory shape", but no other group is as well understood, "not even $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb Q_p)$ or $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$ for $[F:\mathbb Q_p]<\infty$"; several competing approaches exist, and for groups not directly connected to $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_p)$ it is not known what to expect. ([Colmez–Dospinescu–Nizioł, arXiv:2408.02358](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.02358))
- **Local Langlands for general reductive groups.** Beyond $\mathrm{GL}_n$, the conjectures are proved in particular cases, for example (groups over $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$, $\mathrm{GSp}(4)$ and $\mathrm{Sp}(4)$), and for general reductive groups it is unclear what the best formulation should be. ([Wikipedia: Local Langlands conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Langlands_conjectures))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Local field (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field): definitions, classification, unit filtration.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.785 Number Theory I (Sutherland, 2021)](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/lectures.html): local fields and Hensel's lemmas (Lecture 9), Krasner's lemma (11), local class field theory (27).
- **Primary:** [Colmez–Dospinescu–Nizioł, *On the geometrization of the p-adic local Langlands correspondence*, arXiv:2408.02358](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02358): survey of the $p$-adic correspondence for $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_p)$ and approaches for other groups.
- **Primary:** [Fargues–Scholze, *Geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence*, arXiv:2102.13459](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.13459): $L$-parameters for general reductive groups.
- **Further reading:** [Serre, *Local Fields*, GTM (Springer, 1979)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9), [Fesenko–Vostokov, *Local Fields and Their Extensions* (AMS Translations of Mathematical Monographs 121)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/mmono/121), and [Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory* (Springer, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-03983-0): the standard texts on local fields, ramification and local class field theory.
references.MSC 11Txx - Finite fields and commutativ:
## Reference
### Overview
A finite field of order $q$ exists exactly when $q=p^n$ is a prime power, and is unique up to isomorphism (E. H. Moore, 1893). $\mathbb F_{p^n}/\mathbb F_p$ is Galois with cyclic group of order $n$ generated by Frobenius $x\mapsto x^p$, $\mathbb F_{p^m}\subseteq\mathbb F_{p^n}$ iff $m\mid n$, and every finite division ring is commutative (Wedderburn). ([Wikipedia: Finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field)) For irreducible $f\in\mathbb F_p[x]$ of degree $n$, $\mathbb F_p[x]/(f)\simeq\mathbb F_{p^n}$, which is the standard explicit representation; finite fields are perfect, and $\mathbb F_q^\times$ is cyclic. ([MIT 18.783, Lecture 3](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/LectureNotes3.pdf)) See [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).

The number-theoretic side of the subject, which 11T classifies, concerns polynomials over $\mathbb F_q$, cyclotomy, Gauss, Jacobi and Kloosterman sums, the arithmetic of $\mathbb F_q[T]$ as an analogue of $\mathbb Z$, and number-theoretic aspects of [coding theory](node:Coding%20Theory) and cryptography. ([MSC2020: 11Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Txx)) A fundamental technique is Weil's bounds, which control character sums and point counts by $\sqrt q$. ([Wikipedia: Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum); [Wikipedia: Hasse's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%27s_theorem_on_elliptic_curves))

### Scope
MSC2020 11Txx, in [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), has the codes 11T06 polynomials over finite fields; 11T22 cyclotomy; 11T23 exponential sums; 11T24 other character sums and Gauss sums; 11T30 structure theory for finite fields and commutative rings; 11T55 arithmetic theory of polynomial rings over finite fields; 11T60 finite upper half-planes; 11T71 algebraic coding theory, cryptography (number-theoretic aspects); 11T99. ([MSC2020: 11Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Txx))

How it differs from its neighbours: the 11Txx entry itself lists no cross-references, but the section 11Lxx (exponential sums and character sums) directs finite-field sums to 11Txx, so 11T23–11T24 cover sums over $\mathbb F_q$ while [MSC 11Lxx - Exponential sums and character sums](node:MSC%2011Lxx%20-%20Exponential%20sums%20and%20character%20sums) covers the general theory. ([MSC2020: 11-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11-XX)) The 11T30 and 11T71 titles restrict those codes to "number-theoretic aspects" of structure theory and of coding theory and cryptography. ([MSC2020: 11Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Txx))

### Key concepts
- **Irreducible polynomials (11T06).** Over $\mathbb F_p$, $X^{p^n}-X$ is the product of all monic irreducibles of degree dividing $n$, and the number of monic irreducible polynomials of degree $n$ over $\mathbb F_q$ is $N(q,n)=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\,q^{n/d}$. Irreducibility testing and factorization of polynomials over finite fields have efficient algorithms. ([Wikipedia: Finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field))
- **Primitive and normal elements (11T30).** $\mathbb F_q$ has $\varphi(q-1)$ primitive elements, and the minimal polynomial of a primitive element is a primitive polynomial. ([Wikipedia: Primitive element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_element_%28finite_field%29)) Every extension $\mathbb F_{q^n}/\mathbb F_q$ has a normal basis $\{\beta,\beta^q,\dots,\beta^{q^{n-1}}\}$, and Lenstra and Schoof (1987) proved that every extension of finite fields has a primitive normal basis; Davenport had settled the prime-field case. ([Wikipedia: Normal basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_basis))
- **Gauss sums (11T24).** For a multiplicative character $\chi$ and additive character $\psi$ of a finite commutative ring $R$, $G(\chi,\psi)=\sum_{r\in R}\chi(r)\psi(r)$. Over $\mathbb F_p$ with $\chi$ and $\psi$ both nontrivial, $|G|=\sqrt p$; for the Legendre symbol and $\psi(x)=e^{2\pi ix/p}$ Gauss showed $G=\sqrt p$ if $p\equiv1\pmod 4$ and $G=i\sqrt p$ if $p\equiv3\pmod4$. ([Wikipedia: Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum))
- **Kloosterman sums and the Weil bound (11T23).** $K(a,b;m)=\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/m)^\times}e^{2\pi i(ax+bx^{-1})/m}$. For prime $p$ and $ab\ne0$, Weil proved $|K(a,b;p)|\le2\sqrt p$; for general $m$, $|K(a,b;m)|\le\tau(m)\gcd(a,b,m)^{1/2}\sqrt m$. Kloosterman introduced the sums in 1926 to adapt the circle method to quaternary quadratic forms. ([Wikipedia: Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum)) More generally, Weil's results give square-root bounds for character sums of polynomials, with constants linear in the genus of the associated curve, and lead to Burgess's bounds for short sums. ([Wikipedia: Character sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_sum))
- **Point counts.** Hasse (1933): an elliptic curve over $\mathbb F_q$ has $N$ points with $|N-(q+1)|\le2\sqrt q$; Weil's generalization gives $|\#C(\mathbb F_q)-(q+1)|\le2g\sqrt q$ for a curve of genus $g$. ([Wikipedia: Hasse's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%27s_theorem_on_elliptic_curves))
- **Chevalley–Warning.** If $f_1,\dots,f_r\in\mathbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ have degrees summing to $d<n$, the number of common zeros in $\mathbb F_q^n$ is divisible by $p$; if the $f_j$ have no constant term there is a nontrivial zero (Chevalley, 1935), so finite fields are quasi-algebraically closed. Ax–Katz: $q^b$ divides the count with $b=\lceil(n-d)/d_{\max}\rceil$. ([Wikipedia: Chevalley–Warning theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevalley%E2%80%93Warning_theorem))
- **$\mathbb F_q[T]$ and the Carlitz module (11T55).** The Carlitz exponential $e_C(x)=\sum_i x^{q^i}/D_i$ satisfies $e_C(Tx)=Te_C(x)+e_C(x)^q$, defining the Carlitz module $T\mapsto T+\tau$, a Drinfeld $\mathbb F_q[T]$-module. ([Wikipedia: Carlitz exponential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlitz_exponential)) Carlitz described it in 1935; Drinfeld's general modules (1974), a function-field analogue of complex multiplication, and later shtukas led to the Langlands correspondence for $\mathrm{GL}_2$ and, by L. Lafforgue, $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over function fields. ([Wikipedia: Drinfeld module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drinfeld_module))
- **Discrete logarithms (11T71).** Deterministic generic algorithms in a cyclic group of prime order $N$ need at least $(\sqrt2+o(1))\sqrt N$ group operations (Shoup), while baby-step giant-step uses $(2+o(1))\sqrt N$. ([MIT 18.783, Lecture 9](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/LectureNotes9.pdf)) In $\mathbb F_p^\times$ index calculus with number-field-sieve techniques gives heuristic time $L_N[1/3,c]$; for fields $\mathbb F_{q^k}$ with $q\approx k$, Joux's 2013 index calculus heuristically achieves $L_N[1/4+o(1),c]$, and a recursive variant heuristically achieves quasi-polynomial time $k^{O(\log k)}$. ([MIT 18.783, Lecture 10](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/LectureNotes10.pdf)) See [Cryptography](node:Cryptography).

### History
Moore's 1893 classification fixed the structure theory. ([Wikipedia: Finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field)) Weil's 1948 paper "On some exponential sums" gave the Kloosterman bound. ([Wikipedia: Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum)) Lidl and Niederreiter's textbook organizes the subject into theory (structure, polynomials, factorization, exponential sums, linear recurring sequences) and applications to [information theory](node:Information%20Theory), coding, cryptology, finite geometry and [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics). ([Lidl–Niederreiter, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-finite-fields-and-their-applications/84CD611976678E270A2146652E1773D6))

### Open problems
- **Deterministic construction of irreducible polynomials.** Adleman and Lenstra gave an efficient deterministic construction assuming GRH, and Shoup's unconditional deterministic algorithm runs in $\tilde O(d^4p^{1/2}\log^4q)$, polynomial only for small characteristic; "the problem of efficient and unconditional deterministic construction of irreducible polynomials" remains open, as does its special case of deterministically constructing quadratic non-residues. Rai gives a pseudo-deterministic algorithm in time $\tilde O(d^4\log^4q)$. ([Rai, arXiv:2410.04071](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.04071v1))
- **Classical complexity of discrete logarithms.** Whether discrete logarithms can be computed in polynomial time on a classical computer is open; for black-box groups there is in general no subexponential-time solution (Shoup's lower bound); Shor's algorithm solves the problem on a quantum computer. ([Wikipedia: Discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_logarithm))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Finite field (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field): structure, irreducible-polynomial counts, applications.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.783 Elliptic Curves (Sutherland, 2023), Lectures 3, 9, 10](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/lectures.html): finite field arithmetic, generic discrete-log lower bounds, index calculus.
- **Primary:** [Rai, *Pseudo-Deterministic Construction of Irreducible Polynomials over Finite Fields*, arXiv:2410.04071](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04071): recent progress on a central open construction problem, with a survey of prior results.
- **Primary:** [Lidl–Niederreiter, *Introduction to Finite Fields and their Applications* (CUP, 2nd ed.)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-finite-fields-and-their-applications/84CD611976678E270A2146652E1773D6): standard monograph on structure, polynomials, exponential sums and applications.
- **Further reading:** [Rosen, *Number Theory in Function Fields*, GTM (Springer, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-6046-0): arithmetic of $\mathbb F_q[T]$ and global function fields.
references.MSC 11Uxx - Connections of number theory:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11U collects work where logic acts on number theory: decidability of arithmetic theories, model-theoretic transfer between fields, ultraproducts of finite and local fields, and nonstandard models of arithmetic. ([MSC2020 11U](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Uxx)) The founding example is [Hilbert's Tenth Problem](node:Hilbert's%20Tenth%20Problem): Hilbert asked in 1900 for an algorithm deciding whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution, and the Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem shows there is none. ([Shlapentokh, introduction](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/hilberts-tenth-problem/introduction/952F1814E85CD1A14FB5EF2696223110); [Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem))

The positive side is model-theoretic: the Ax–Kochen–Ershov theorem, proved in 1965–1966, transfers first-order statements between $\mathbb Q_p$ and $\mathbb F_p((t))$ for almost all $p$, and began the model theory of [valued fields](node:Valued%20Fields); Ax's pseudo-finite fields describe what is true in almost all finite fields. ([d'Elbée, course notes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14469); [Ax–Kochen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem); [Pseudo-finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-finite_field))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 11U05 decidability (number-theoretic aspects; see 03B25), 11U07 ultraproducts (see 03C20), 11U09 model theory (see 03Cxx), 11U10 nonstandard arithmetic (see 03H15), and 11U99. ([MSC2020 11U](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Uxx)) Each code is limited to the number-theoretic aspects of its topic and points to the corresponding logic code: 03B25 in [MSC 03Bxx - General logic](node:MSC%2003Bxx%20-%20General%20logic) for decidability, 03C20 and the rest of [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory) for ultraproducts and [model theory](node:Model%20Theory), and 03H15 in [MSC 03Hxx - Nonstandard models](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models) for nonstandard arithmetic. ([MSC2020 11U](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Uxx))

### Key concepts
- **MRDP theorem (11U05).** Every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine (Matiyasevich completed the proof in 1970), so Hilbert's tenth problem is unsolvable; 9 unknowns suffice over the natural numbers, and every Diophantine set has a definition of degree at most 4. ([Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem)) For any 1-consistent axiomatizable theory $F$ there are [Diophantine equations](node:Diophantine%20Equations) with no solutions that $F$ cannot prove unsolvable, a concrete form of [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems). ([SEP, §4.4](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/))
- **Other rings.** Shapiro and Shlapentokh proved H10 unsolvable for rings of integers of number fields with abelian Galois group, and Pheidas and Shlapentokh for fields with exactly one pair of complex embeddings. ([Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem)) Koymans and Pagano proved, unconditionally, that H10 has a negative answer for every infinite ring finitely generated over $\mathbb Z$, using [elliptic curves](node:Elliptic%20Curves) with full rational 2-torsion and no rank growth in quadratic extensions, combining additive combinatorics with 2-descent; Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman reached the number-field case by other methods. ([Koymans–Pagano, arXiv:2412.01768](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01768); [Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem))
- **Defining $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$.** Julia Robinson's 1949 paper "Definability and Decision Problems in Arithmetic" defined elementary number theory inside $\mathbb Q$, so the first-order theory of $\mathbb Q$ is undecidable. ([Julia Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Robinson)) Koenigsmann found a universal first-order definition of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$ and an $\forall\exists$-definition with one universal quantifier, and showed that, under a strong variant of the Bombieri–Lang conjecture, no existential definition exists. ([Koenigsmann, arXiv:1011.3424](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.3424))
- **Mazur's conjecture.** For a variety over $\mathbb Q$, the real topological closure of its rational points has only finitely many connected components; it implies that $\mathbb Z$ is not Diophantine over $\mathbb Q$. ([Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem))
- **Ax–Kochen theorem (11U07, 11U09).** For each $d\ge1$ there is a finite set of primes $Y_d$ such that for $p\notin Y_d$ every homogeneous form of degree $d$ over $\mathbb Q_p$ in more than $d^2$ variables has a nontrivial zero.
