The proof transfers Lang's theorem that $\mathbb F_p((t))$ is $C_2$ through ultraproducts, using that Henselian valued fields with residue characteristic $0$ and equivalent residue fields and value groups are elementarily equivalent. Terjanian's 2-adic quartic shows $Y_d$ can be nonempty, refuting Artin's conjecture. ([Ax–Kochen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem); [d'Elbée](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14469)) The series concluded with "Diophantine problems over local fields III. Decidable fields" (Ann. of Math. 83, 1966). ([JSL review](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-symbolic-logic/article/james-ax-and-simon-kochen-diophantine-problems-over-local-fields-i-american-journal-of-mathematics-vol-87-1965-pp-605630-james-ax-and-simon-kochen-diophantine-problems-over-local-fields-ii-a-complete-set-of-axioms-for-padic-number-theory-american-journal-of-mathematics-vol-87-1965-pp-631648-james-ax-and-simon-kochen-diophantine-problems-over-local-fields-iii-decidable-fields-annals-of-mathematics-vol-83-1966-pp-437456/51B55CE37F9314DCC9B260DE6FE4DDF3))
- **Pseudo-finite fields (11U07, 11U09).** A pseudo-finite field is an infinite model of the first-order theory of all [Finite Fields](node:Finite%20Fields), equivalently a perfect pseudo-algebraically-closed field with exactly one extension of each degree; every nonprincipal ultraproduct of finite fields is pseudo-finite (Ax, 1968). ([Pseudo-finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-finite_field)) In the same paper Ax proved the existential theory of the class of rings $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$ decidable and asked about the full theory; Derakhshan and Macintyre proved the class of all $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$ ($m>1$) decidable, by reduction to the decidability of the adele ring $\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q}$. ([Derakhshan–Macintyre, Forum Math. Sigma 2023](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S2050509423000622/type/journal_article))
- **Nonstandard arithmetic (11U10).** Skolem (1934) constructed nonstandard models of arithmetic; they also arise by compactness or as ultrapowers of $\mathbb N$ (the hypernaturals). Countable nonstandard models of PA have order type $\omega+(\omega^*+\omega)\cdot\eta$, and by Tennenbaum's theorem (1959) neither addition nor multiplication of such a model is computable under any coding. ([Non-standard model of arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-standard_model_of_arithmetic))

### History
Hilbert posed the tenth problem in 1900; Robinson's 1949 paper gave the undecidability of $\mathbb Q$, and her 1950 work on Diophantine exponentiation led to the J.R. hypothesis, which Matiyasevich proved in 1970 by showing an exponentially growing set of Fibonacci-related pairs Diophantine. ([Julia Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Robinson); [Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem); [Shlapentokh](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/hilberts-tenth-problem/introduction/952F1814E85CD1A14FB5EF2696223110)) Ax and Kochen, and independently Ershov, proved their transfer theorem in 1965–1966, and Ax introduced pseudo-finite fields in 1968. ([d'Elbée](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14469); [Pseudo-finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-finite_field)) Derakhshan's survey connects the model theory of adeles to zeta integrals and Tate's thesis. ([Derakhshan, arXiv:2007.09237](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.09237))

### Open problems
- **Hilbert's tenth problem over $\mathbb Q$.** Whether there is an algorithm deciding solvability of polynomial equations in rational numbers is open according to the standard references; Mazur's conjecture would rule out the classical route of a Diophantine definition of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$. ([Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem))
- **Existential definability of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$** is excluded only conditionally, under a strong Bombieri–Lang variant. ([Koenigsmann, arXiv:1011.3424](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.3424))
- **Questions on adeles.** Derakhshan formulates questions on Artin reciprocity for ideles, $p$-adic fields and adeles, and a completeness problem for identities between adelic integrals. ([Derakhshan, arXiv:2007.09237](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.09237))

> [!warning] Contested
> In October 2026 preprints claimed a negative solution of H10 over $\mathbb Q$: Sun's paper states that the problem was recently solved negatively in an OpenAI manuscript and reduces the number of variables for which it is undecidable to 48. ([Sun, arXiv:2610.20691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20691)) MathWorld reports that Sun's claims depend on arithmetic inputs from the OpenAI-related manuscripts, that a related Lean formalization is conditional on five unproved height and analytic premises, and that no independent specialist verification of the complete arguments has been reported; Wikipedia records the OpenAI claim together with OpenAI's caveat that not all results were formalized in Lean and unformalized results could contain errors. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/HilbertsTenthProblem.html); [Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, Gödel's incompleteness theorems, §4.4](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/goedel-incompleteness/): MRDP and its link to incompleteness; [Hilbert's tenth problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem): variants over other rings.
- **Learn:** [d'Elbée, The Ax-Kochen-Ershov Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14469): summer-school course notes proving AKE and the asymptotic $C_2$ property of $p$-adic fields.
- **Primary:** [Koymans and Pagano, Hilbert's tenth problem via additive combinatorics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01768); [Koenigsmann, Defining ℤ in ℚ](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.3424); [Derakhshan and Macintyre, Decidability of the class of all the rings ℤ/mℤ](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S2050509423000622/type/journal_article).
- **Further reading:** [Shlapentokh, Hilbert's Tenth Problem: Diophantine Classes and Extensions to Global Fields (CUP, 2006)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/hilberts-tenth-problem/introduction/952F1814E85CD1A14FB5EF2696223110).
references.MSC 11Yxx - Computational number theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Computational (algorithmic) number theory studies computational methods for problems in number theory and arithmetic geometry: primality testing, integer factorization, finding solutions to Diophantine equations, and explicit methods in arithmetic geometry. It supports cryptography, including RSA and elliptic curve cryptography, and is used to investigate conjectures such as the Riemann hypothesis, Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer, abc and Sato–Tate. Standard software includes PARI/GP, SageMath, Magma, NTL and FLINT. ([Wikipedia: Computational number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_number_theory)) See [Cryptography](node:Cryptography).

Complexity is measured in the bit length of the input. Subexponential running times are written $L_N[\alpha,c]=\exp\!\big((c+o(1))(\log N)^\alpha(\log\log N)^{1-\alpha}\big)$, which is polynomial in $\log N$ for $\alpha=0$, exponential for $\alpha=1$, and subexponential for $0<\alpha<1$. ([MIT 18.783, Lecture 10](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/LectureNotes10.pdf)) The central complexity contrast of the field is that primality is in deterministic polynomial time ([Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena, Annals](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2004/160-2/p12)), whereas no polynomial-time classical factoring algorithm is known. ([Wikipedia: Integer factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization)) See [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory).

### Scope
MSC2020 11Yxx, in [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), has the codes 11Y05 factorization; 11Y11 primality; 11Y16 number-theoretic algorithms, complexity; 11Y35 analytic computations; 11Y40 algebraic number theory computations; 11Y50 computer solution of Diophantine equations; 11Y55 calculation of integer sequences; 11Y60 evaluation of number-theoretic constants; 11Y65 continued fraction calculations; 11Y70 values of arithmetic functions, tables; 11Y99. ([MSC2020: 11Yxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Yxx))

Neighbouring codes, from the MSC2020 cross-references ([MSC2020: 11Yxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Yxx)):
- Software itself goes to 11-04, not 11Y.
- The section points to 68W30: see [MSC 68Wxx - Algorithms in computer science](node:MSC%2068Wxx%20-%20Algorithms%20in%20computer%20science).
- 11Y16 points to 68Q25: see [MSC 68Qxx - Theory of computing](node:MSC%2068Qxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20computing).

### Key concepts
- **AKS primality test (11Y11).** Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena give an unconditional deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether an integer is prime (received 24 January 2002, *Annals* 160 (2004) 781–793). ([Annals of Mathematics](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2004/160-2/p12)) The first bound was $\tilde O(\log^{12}n)$, later $\tilde O(\log^{7.5}n)$; a Lenstra–Pomerance variant runs in $\tilde O(\log^6 n)$. It is the first primality-proving algorithm that is simultaneously general, polynomial, deterministic and unconditional. ([Wikipedia: AKS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AKS_primality_test)) See [Prime Numbers](node:Prime%20Numbers).
- **Practical primality (11Y11).** Miller–Rabin: write $n-1=2^sd$ with $d$ odd; $n$ passes for base $a$ if $a^d\equiv1$ or $a^{2^rd}\equiv-1\pmod n$ for some $r<s$. At most $1/4$ of bases are strong liars for composite $n$, so $k$ random rounds err with probability at most $4^{-k}$; under GRH, testing all bases up to $2(\ln n)^2$ is deterministic (Bach). ([Wikipedia: Miller–Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test)) ECPP (Goldwasser–Kilian, Atkin–Morain) produces a quickly checkable certificate in heuristic time about $\tilde O(L^5)$ ($\tilde O(L^4)$ for fastECPP) in the bit length $L$; its worst case is not known. ([Wikipedia: ECPP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve_primality)) For Mersenne numbers, with $s_0=4$, $s_i=s_{i-1}^2-2$, $M_p=2^p-1$ ($p$ odd prime) is prime iff $s_{p-2}\equiv0\pmod{M_p}$ (Lucas 1878, Lehmer 1930). ([Wikipedia: Lucas–Lehmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%E2%80%93Lehmer_primality_test)) See [Randomized Algorithms](node:Randomized%20Algorithms) and [Modular Arithmetic](node:Modular%20Arithmetic).
- **Factoring algorithms (11Y05).** The quadratic sieve and ECM have heuristic running time $L_n[1/2,1+o(1)]$, and Lenstra and Pomerance proved the expected time $L_n[1/2,1+o(1)]$ rigorously for the Schnorr–Seysen–Lenstra algorithm. The general number field sieve, best for numbers above about 400 bits, runs heuristically in $\exp\!\big(((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln n)^{1/3}(\ln\ln n)^{2/3}\big)$. ([Wikipedia: Integer factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization)) Lenstra's elliptic curve method takes heuristic time $L_p[1/2,\sqrt2]\,M(\log N)$ where $p$ is the smallest prime factor, so it is used first to strip small factors before sieve methods. ([MIT 18.783, Lecture 10](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/LectureNotes10.pdf); [Wikipedia: ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra_elliptic-curve_factorization))
- **Discrete logarithms (11Y16).** Any deterministic generic algorithm in a cyclic group of prime order $N$ needs at least $(\sqrt2+o(1))\sqrt N$ group operations, nearly matched by baby-step giant-step. ([MIT 18.783, Lecture 9](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/LectureNotes9.pdf)) In $\mathbb F_p^\times$ index calculus gives heuristic $L_N[1/2,\sqrt2]$, improved to $L_N[1/3,c]$ by number-field-sieve methods; for fields $\mathbb F_{q^k}$ with $q\approx k$, Joux's 2013 index calculus heuristically achieves $L_N[1/4+o(1),c]$, and a recursive variant is heuristically quasi-polynomial, $k^{O(\log k)}$. ([MIT 18.783, Lecture 10](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/LectureNotes10.pdf))
- **Quantum algorithms.** Shor's 1994 algorithm factors $n$ in polynomial time in $\log n$ on a quantum computer, placing factoring in BQP, and has versions for discrete logarithms; both are instances of the hidden subgroup problem. Laboratory demonstrations have factored only very small numbers. ([Wikipedia: Shor's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shor%27s_algorithm)) See [Quantum Algorithms](node:Quantum%20Algorithms).
- **Algebraic number theory computations and the LMFDB (11Y40).** A graduate text for this code is Cohen's *A Course in Computational Algebraic Number Theory* (Springer, Graduate Texts in Mathematics, 1993). ([Crossref: Cohen](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-02945-9)) The LMFDB is an online database of number fields, $p$-adic fields, elliptic curves and higher-genus curves, modular forms, $L$-functions, Dirichlet characters, Artin representations and Galois groups, organized to illustrate the connections predicted by the Langlands program. ([LMFDB](https://www.lmfdb.org/))

### History
Lucas devised his Mersenne test in 1878 and Lehmer proved it in 1930; GIMPS used Lucas–Lehmer as its main test until 2021, when it switched to a Fermat-type probable-prime test with Lucas–Lehmer used for verification. ([Wikipedia: Lucas–Lehmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%E2%80%93Lehmer_primality_test)) Miller's test (1976) was made unconditional by Rabin (1980). ([Wikipedia: Miller–Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test)) Lenstra's ECM appeared in the *Annals* in 1987, Shor's algorithm in 1994, and AKS was announced in August 2002. ([Wikipedia: ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra_elliptic-curve_factorization); [Wikipedia: Shor's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shor%27s_algorithm); [Wikipedia: AKS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AKS_primality_test)) RSA-240 (795 bits) was factored in 2019 with about 900 core-years. ([Wikipedia: Integer factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization)) As of March 2021 the finite-field discrete-log record was in $\mathbb F_{2^{30750}}$ (2019, about 2900 core-years). ([MIT 18.783, Lecture 10](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/LectureNotes10.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Polynomial-time factoring.** No published classical algorithm factors all integers in polynomial time; "neither the existence nor non-existence of such algorithms has been proved." The decision problem lies in NP $\cap$ co-NP and is suspected to be NP-intermediate. ([Wikipedia: Integer factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization))
- **Polynomial-time discrete logarithms.** Whether discrete logarithms can be computed in polynomial time on a classical computer is listed as open; for black-box groups there is in general no subexponential-time solution (Shoup's lower bound). ([Wikipedia: Discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_logarithm))
- **Provable ECPP running time.** The running-time bounds for ECPP are heuristic, and its worst-case execution time is not known. ([Wikipedia: ECPP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve_primality))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Integer factorization (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization): algorithms, complexities and status.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.783 Elliptic Curves (Sutherland, 2023)](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2023/lectures.html): generic discrete-log algorithms, index calculus and factoring (Lectures 9–10), ECPP (Lecture 11).
- **Primary:** [Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena, *PRIMES is in P*, Annals of Mathematics 160 (2004)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2004/160-2/p12): deterministic polynomial-time primality.
- **Primary:** [LMFDB](https://www.lmfdb.org/): the main research database of computed arithmetic objects.
- **Further reading:** [Cohen, *A Course in Computational Algebraic Number Theory*, Graduate Texts in Mathematics (Springer, 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-02945-9): graduate text on computational algebraic number theory.
references.MSC 11Zxx - Miscellaneous applications o:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 11Zxx is the catch-all section of number theory for applications that have no more specific home. MSC2020 gives it a single substantive code, 11Z05 "Miscellaneous applications of number theory", plus 11Z99. The code title names no specific subject; the entry lists no cross-references. ([MSC2020, 11Zxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Zxx))

A book-length survey of such applications is Manfred Schroeder's *Number Theory in Science and Communication* (Springer, 2009), whose subtitle lists applications "in cryptography, physics, digital information, computing, and self-similarity". Schroeder, a physicist known for his contributions to acoustics, also invented number-theoretic sound diffusers in the 1970s. In the examples below, arithmetic of [residues modulo a prime](node:Modular%20Arithmetic) (quadratic residues, primitive roots, $k^2\bmod p$) fixes the design of a physical or combinatorial object. ([Manfred R. Schroeder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_R._Schroeder); [Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-85298-8); [Diffuser (acoustics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffuser_%28acoustics%29))

### Scope
- **11Z05** "Miscellaneous applications of number theory" and **11Z99** "None of the above, but in this section" are the only codes in 11Zxx; MSC2020 lists no cross-references for them. ([MSC2020, 11Zxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Zxx))
- **[Cryptography](node:Cryptography) is not here.** Number-theoretic cryptography and coding have their own code, **11T71** "Algebraic coding theory; cryptography (number-theoretic aspects)", and **94A60** "Cryptography" cross-references 11T71; signatures and secret sharing are **94A62**. RSA, the most familiar application of arithmetic, therefore belongs under 11T71/94A60, not 11Z. ([MSC2020, 11Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Txx); [MSC2020, 94Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=94Axx))
- **Algorithms are not here.** Factorization (11Y05), primality (11Y11), number-theoretic algorithms and complexity (11Y16) and the computation of sequences, constants and tables (11Y55–11Y70) sit in **11Y**, Computational number theory. ([MSC2020, 11Yxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Yxx))

### Key concepts
- **Quadratic Gauss sums.** For an odd prime $p$, $g(1;p)=\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}e^{2\pi i n^2/p}$ equals $\sqrt p$ if $p\equiv1\pmod4$ and $i\sqrt p$ if $p\equiv3\pmod4$; for $p\nmid a$, $g(a;p)=\left(\tfrac ap\right)g(1;p)$, so $|g(a;p)|^2=p$. Gauss proved $g(1;p)^2=\left(\tfrac{-1}{p}\right)p$ easily but needed several years to fix the sign; the evaluation of $g(1;p)^2$ led to one of his proofs of quadratic reciprocity. ([Quadratic Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Gauss_sum))
- **Number-theoretic diffusers.** Schroeder's diffusers set the depths of wells by number-theoretic sequences: maximum-length-sequence diffusers use two depths following an MLS, quadratic-residue diffusers widen the useful bandwidth and are still widely used, and primitive-root diffusers perform much like quadratic-residue ones. The article says Schroeder got the idea during a 1977 Göttingen lecture by André Weil. ([Diffuser (acoustics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffuser_%28acoustics%29))
- **Golomb rulers.** A Golomb ruler is a set of integer marks with all pairwise differences distinct (found independently by Sidon in 1932 and Babcock in 1953). For each odd prime $p$, the Erdős–Turán marks $2pk+(k^2\bmod p)$, $0\le k\le p-1$, form an asymptotically optimal ruler. Applications include radio-frequency selection, antenna placement, and error correction. Optimal rulers are known up to order 28 (length 585), confirmed by distributed.net in 2022. ([Golomb ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golomb_ruler))
- **Costas arrays.** An $n\times n$ permutation array in which all displacement vectors between points are distinct, giving an ideal "thumbtack" ambiguity function for sonar and radar (Costas, 1965). The Welch construction uses powers $g^i\bmod p$ of a primitive root of a prime $p$ and gives order $p-1$; the Lempel–Golomb construction uses primitive elements $\alpha,\beta$ of $\mathrm{GF}(q)$ with $\alpha^i+\beta^j=1$ and gives order $q-2$. ([Costas array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costas_array))
- **Euclidean rhythms.** Toussaint (2004–2005) observed that distributing $k$ onsets among $n$ pulses as evenly as possible is done by Euclid's gcd algorithm, and that the resulting patterns include traditional rhythms, e.g. the tresillo $E(3,8)=$ `x..x..x.`. ([Euclidean rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_rhythm))
- **Arithmetic behind public-key cryptography (classified in 11T71).** RSA takes $n=pq$ for distinct primes, $e$ coprime to $\lambda(n)=\operatorname{lcm}(p-1,q-1)$, $d\equiv e^{-1}\pmod{\lambda(n)}$, $c=m^e\bmod n$, $m=c^d\bmod n$; its security rests on the difficulty of factoring $n$. It was published by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman in 1977. ([RSA cryptosystem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_cryptosystem)) See [Prime Numbers](node:Prime%20Numbers).

### History
Gauss's evaluation of quadratic Gauss sums, and the long struggle over their sign, belong to the classical theory that later applications draw on. ([Quadratic Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Gauss_sum)) Sidon's 1932 sets with distinct differences reappeared as Babcock's 1953 rulers, and Costas's 1965 sonar arrays impose a distinct-displacement condition in two dimensions. ([Golomb ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golomb_ruler); [Costas array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costas_array)) Schroeder introduced number-theoretic acoustic diffusers in the 1970s; the cited account says he got the idea during a 1977 Göttingen lecture by André Weil. His book (Springer, 2009 edition) collects applications across science and communication. ([Diffuser (acoustics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffuser_%28acoustics%29); [Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-85298-8); [Manfred R. Schroeder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_R._Schroeder)) Toussaint's 2005 Bridges paper connected Euclid's algorithm to music. ([Euclidean rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_rhythm))

### Open problems
- **Enumeration of Costas arrays.** The general enumeration of Costas arrays is described as an open problem; complete counts are known only for orders $1$–$29$, and arrays of order above $29$ outside the known algebraic families may exist. ([Costas array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costas_array))
- **Optimal Golomb rulers.** The complexity of finding optimal Golomb rulers of arbitrary order is unknown, and optimality has been established only up to order 28. ([Golomb ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golomb_ruler))
- **RSA problem versus factoring.** Whether breaking RSA is as hard as factoring remains open (a question filed under 11T71/94A60 rather than 11Z). ([RSA cryptosystem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_cryptosystem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Costas array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costas_array): definition, Welch and Lempel–Golomb constructions, enumeration status.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.781 Theory of Numbers (OCW)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-781-theory-of-numbers-spring-2012/): primes, congruences, quadratic reciprocity, continued fractions and partitions, with lecture notes — the arithmetic these applications use.
- **Primary:** [Schroeder, Number Theory in Science and Communication (Springer, 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-85298-8): monograph on applications in cryptography, physics, digital information, computing, and self-similarity.
- **Further reading:** [Golomb ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golomb_ruler): constructions, optimal rulers, applications.
- **Related maps:** [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), [MSC 11Txx - Finite fields and commutative rings (number-theoretic aspects)](node:MSC%2011Txx%20-%20Finite%20fields%20and%20commutative%20rings%20%28number-theoretic%20aspects%29), [MSC 11Yxx - Computational number theory](node:MSC%2011Yxx%20-%20Computational%20number%20theory), [MSC 94Axx - Communication, information](node:MSC%2094Axx%20-%20Communication,%20information).
references.MSC 12 - Field theory and polynomials:
## Reference
### Overview
A field is a set closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero elements, whose nonzero elements form a group under multiplication. Every field has characteristic $0$ or a prime $p$ and contains a prime field isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$; every field has an algebraic closure, unique up to non-unique isomorphism; and two algebraically closed fields are isomorphic exactly when they have the same characteristic and transcendence degree. ([Wikipedia: Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_%28mathematics%29))

MSC 12 is the research area of fields as such: their extensions and Galois groups, polynomials over them, orderings and valuations, Galois cohomology, fields with a derivation, generalizations such as near-fields and semifields, and the connections between field theory and logic. ([MSC2020 12-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12-XX))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 12-XX into eight sections. ([MSC2020 12-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12-XX))

- **12D Real and complex fields:** factorization and algebraic location of zeros of real and complex polynomials (12D05, 12D10), and fields related with sums of squares, such as formally real and Pythagorean fields (12D15, see also 11E). ([MSC2020 12Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Dxx))
- **12E General field theory:** irreducibility and special polynomials, equations in general fields, skew fields (see also 16K), finite fields, Hilbertian fields and Hilbert's irreducibility theorem (12E25), and field arithmetic (12E30). ([MSC2020 12Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Exx))
- **12F Field extensions:** algebraic, separable (Galois theory), inseparable and transcendental extensions, with a separate code 12F12 for inverse Galois theory. ([MSC2020 12Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Fxx))
- **12G Homological methods:** Galois cohomology (12G05) and cohomological dimension of fields (12G10). ([MSC2020 12Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Gxx))
- **12H Differential and difference algebra:** differential algebra (see also 13N), difference algebra, abstract differential equations, and $p$-adic differential equations. ([MSC2020 12Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Hxx))
- **12J Topological fields:** normed, valued, formally $p$-adic and ordered fields, topological semifields, general valuation theory (see also 13A18), non-Archimedean valued fields, and Krasner–Tate algebras. ([MSC2020 12Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Jxx))
- **12K Generalizations of fields:** near-fields and semifields. ([MSC2020 12Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Kxx))
- **12L Field theory and logic:** decidability, ultraproducts, model theory of fields (see also 03C60), and nonstandard arithmetic. ([MSC2020 12Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Lxx))

Neighbours, by the cross-references in the entry: skew fields and division rings point to 16K and 11R52; differential algebra to 13N; difference algebra to 39A; sums of squares to 11E; the analytic theory of zeros of polynomials to 26C10 and 30C15; general valuation theory to 13A18; Galois cohomology to 14F22, 16H05 and 16K50; model theory of fields to 03C60. ([MSC2020 12Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Dxx); [MSC2020 12Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Exx); [MSC2020 12Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Gxx); [MSC2020 12Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Hxx); [MSC2020 12Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Jxx); [MSC2020 12Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Lxx))

### Key concepts
- [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory) (12F10): for a finite Galois extension $E/F$ with $G=\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$, $H\mapsto E^H$ is an inclusion-reversing bijection from subgroups to intermediate fields with $|H|=[E:E^H]$; $E^H/F$ is Galois iff $H\trianglelefteq G$, and then $\operatorname{Gal}(E^H/F)\cong G/H$. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory)) See [MSC 12Fxx - Field extensions](node:MSC%2012Fxx%20-%20Field%20extensions).
- **Infinite Galois theory:** for an infinite Galois extension, $\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)=\varprojlim \operatorname{Gal}(F'/F)$ over finite Galois subextensions is a profinite group in the Krull topology, and intermediate fields correspond bijectively to *closed* subgroups. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Galois_theory)) Every profinite group is isomorphic to the Galois group of an extension of some field (Waterhouse 1974), but not every profinite group is an absolute Galois group; every projective profinite group can be realized as the absolute Galois group of a pseudo-algebraically closed field (Lubotzky–van den Dries). ([Wikipedia: Profinite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profinite_group)) This uses [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory) and [topology](node:Topological%20Spaces).
- **Hilbertian fields** (12E25): Hilbert's irreducibility theorem says irreducible polynomials over $\mathbb Q$ in several variables stay irreducible under infinitely many rational (even integer) specializations of some variables. Hence a finite group realized as a Galois group over $\mathbb Q(X_1,\dots,X_r)$ is realized over $\mathbb Q$, which reduces inverse Galois problems to function fields. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert irreducibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_irreducibility_theorem))
- **Real fields** (12D15, 12J15): a field can be ordered iff it is formally real ($\sum a_i^2=0$ forces all $a_i=0$); if $F$ is not algebraically closed but its algebraic closure is a finite extension of $F$, then $F$ is real closed, the degree is 2, and $F(\sqrt{-1})$ is algebraically closed. Artin proved in 1927 that a nonnegative real polynomial is a sum of squares of rational functions (Hilbert's 17th problem), and Pfister showed $2^n$ squares suffice in $n$ variables. ([Wikipedia: Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Real closed field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_closed_field); [Wikipedia: Hilbert's 17th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_seventeenth_problem)) See [MSC 12Dxx - Real and complex fields](node:MSC%2012Dxx%20-%20Real%20and%20complex%20fields).
- **Differential Galois theory** (12H05): for a linear differential equation over a differential field, the Picard–Vessiot extension is generated by its solutions without new constants; its Galois group is a linear algebraic group, and the extension is Liouvillian iff the group's identity component is solvable. The Airy equation has group $SL(2,\mathbb C)$, so its solutions are not Liouvillian. ([Wikipedia: Differential Galois theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_Galois_theory)) See [MSC 12Hxx - Differential and difference algebra](node:MSC%2012Hxx%20-%20Differential%20and%20difference%20algebra) and [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups).
- **Valued fields and logic** (12J, 12L): Ax–Kochen: for each $d$ there is a finite set $Y_d$ of primes such that for $p\notin Y_d$ every degree-$d$ form over $\mathbb Q_p$ in at least $d^2+1$ variables has a nontrivial zero. The proof transfers Lang's theorem for $\mathbb F_p((t))$ to $\mathbb Q_p$ through ultraproducts, using that Henselian valued fields with residue characteristic 0 and equivalent value groups and residue fields are elementarily equivalent. Terjanian's 2-adic quartic in 18 variables shows $Y_d$ can be nonempty. ([Wikipedia: Ax–Kochen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem)) See [MSC 12Jxx - Topological fields](node:MSC%2012Jxx%20-%20Topological%20fields), [MSC 12Lxx - Connections between field theory and logic](node:MSC%2012Lxx%20-%20Connections%20between%20field%20theory%20and%20logic) and [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory).

### History
Hensel introduced the $p$-adic numbers in 1904, and Steinitz's 1910 work synthesized abstract field theory axiomatically, defining many of its basic notions. ([Wikipedia: Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_%28mathematics%29)) Artin settled Hilbert's 17th problem in 1927, and Motzkin gave the first explicit nonnegative polynomial that is not a sum of squares of polynomials in 1967. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's 17th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_seventeenth_problem)) In inverse Galois theory, Hilbert realized symmetric and alternating groups, Shafarevich all solvable groups, and Thompson's 1984 rigidity method many simple groups including the Monster. ([Wikipedia: Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem)) A 2026 preprint of Huang, Jackson, Lee, Poonen, Pries and Zhang realizes $M_{23}$, the last sporadic group not yet known to occur, with an explicit degree-23 polynomial, via a regular $M_{23}$-extension of $\mathbb Q(t)$ built from computed Belyi maps. ([arXiv 2608.08538](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08538))

### Open problems
- **Inverse Galois problem.** Is every finite group the Galois group of a Galois extension of $\mathbb Q$? It is unsolved. Every finite group is realizable over any function field in one variable over $\mathbb C$; over $\mathbb Q$, abelian and solvable groups, symmetric and alternating groups, and all sporadic simple groups are realized, as are all 4,953 transitive groups of degree at most 23, while as of June 2026 only 286 of the 25,000 transitive groups of degree 24 were known to be. ([Wikipedia: Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem); [arXiv 2608.08538](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08538))
- **Number of squares in Hilbert's 17th problem.** The least number $v(n,d)$ of squares of rational functions needed to write every nonnegative $n$-variate polynomial of degree $d$ is open; Pfister gives $v(n,d)\le 2^n$, and $v(n,d)=2^{\Omega(n)}$ holds conditionally on the exponential time hypothesis. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's 17th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_seventeenth_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Field (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_%28mathematics%29): definitions, invariants, ordered and valued fields, history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.702 Algebra II readings](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-702-algebra-ii-spring-2011/pages/readings/): field extensions, finite fields, splitting fields, the main theorem of Galois theory, Kummer extensions and quintics.
- **Primary:** [Huang–Jackson–Lee–Poonen–Pries–Zhang, The Mathieu group $M_{23}$ is a Galois group over $\mathbb Q$](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08538): the 2026 paper completing the sporadic groups.
- **Further reading:** [Fried–Jarden, *Field Arithmetic* (Springer Ergebnisse, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-77270-5): the Ergebnisse monograph on field arithmetic (12E30).
references.MSC 12Dxx - Real and complex fields:
## Reference
### Overview
[MSC 12](node:MSC%2012%20-%20Field%20theory%20and%20polynomials) subfield 12Dxx studies polynomials over the real and complex numbers from an algebraic point of view, together with the fields that share the order-theoretic and sums-of-squares behaviour of $\mathbb{R}$. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Dxx)) The central objects are formally real fields, those admitting an ordering, equivalently those in which $-1$ is not a sum of squares. Such fields have characteristic $0$, since in characteristic $p$ the element $-1$ is a sum of $1$s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formally_real_field))

The model case is the real closed field: a field with the same first-order properties as $\mathbb{R}$, for instance the real algebraic numbers, Puiseux series with real coefficients, or hyperreal fields. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_closed_field)) Two numerical invariants measure how far a field is from these: the level $s(F)$, the least number of squares summing to $-1$ ($s(F)=\infty$ exactly when $F$ is formally real) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stufe_%28algebra%29)), and the Pythagoras number $p(F)$, the least $p$ such that every sum of squares in $F$ is a sum of $p$ squares. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoras_number))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists three codes ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Dxx)):
- **12D05** Polynomials in real and complex fields: factorization.
- **12D10** Polynomials in real and complex fields: location of zeros (algebraic theorems); the analytic theory is referred to 26C10 and 30C15.
- **12D15** Fields related with sums of squares (formally real fields, Pythagorean fields, etc.), with a cross-reference to 11Exx (quadratic forms).

Neighbouring codes: real algebraic sets and semialgebraic sets belong to [14Pxx](node:MSC%2014Pxx%20-%20Real%20algebraic%20and%20real-analytic%20geometry), whose entry 14P05 points back to 12D15. ([MSC2020 14Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Pxx)) Analytic zero-location results go to 26C10 and 30C15, and quadratic-form theory proper to 11Exx. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Dxx))

### Key concepts
- [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields): equivalent definitions include an ordering in which every positive element is a square and every odd-degree polynomial has a root; an ordering with the polynomial intermediate value property; being formally real with no proper formally real algebraic extension; and being non-algebraically closed with $F(\sqrt{-1})$ algebraically closed. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_closed_field))
- **Artin–Schreier theory.** Every ordered field $F$ has a real closure: an algebraic extension that is real closed with ordering extending that of $F$, unique up to unique $F$-isomorphism (Artin and Schreier, 1926). Among the equivalent characterizations of real closed fields: $F$ is not algebraically closed but its algebraic closure is a finite extension of $F$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_closed_field)) The complex counterpart, that $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed, is the [Fundamental Theorem of Algebra](node:Fundamental%20Theorem%20of%20Algebra); see also [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).
- **Hilbert's 17th problem.** Hilbert (1888) showed that every nonnegative form of degree $2d$ in $n$ variables is a sum of squares of forms if and only if $n=2$, or $2d=2$, or $n=3$ and $2d=4$. The form $z^6+x^4y^2+x^2y^4-3x^2y^2z^2$ is nonnegative but not a sum of squares of polynomials; Motzkin (1967) constructed the first explicit counterexample. Artin (1927) proved that every positive semidefinite rational function over $\mathbb{R}$, or more generally over a real closed field, is a sum of squares of rational functions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_seventeenth_problem))
- **Pfister's theorems.** A positive semidefinite form in $n$ variables over $\mathbb{R}$ is a sum of $2^n$ squares of rational functions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_seventeenth_problem)) The level of a field, if finite, is a power of $2$, and every power of $2$ occurs; for a field that is not formally real, $s(F)\le p(F)\le s(F)+1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stufe_%28algebra%29)) Examples: $s(\mathbb{F}_q)=1$ if $q\equiv1\bmod4$ and $2$ if $q\equiv3\bmod4$; $s(\mathbb{Q}_2)=4$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stufe_%28algebra%29))
- **Pythagoras numbers.** $p(\mathbb{R})=1$, $p(\mathbb{Q})=4$ by Lagrange's four-square theorem, and $p=2$ for [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields) of odd characteristic. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoras_number)) Pfister (1967) gave $p(\mathbb{R}(X_1,\dots,X_n))\le2^n$, and $p(\mathbb{R}(X_1,X_2))=4$. ([Becher et al., arXiv:2302.11425](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.11425v3)) In a 2025 preprint, Benoist proves that every sum of squares in a field of transcendence degree $1$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is a sum of five squares, answering a question of Pop and Pfister. ([arXiv:2506.21380](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21380))
- **Positivstellensatz.** Let $R$ be real closed, $F,G$ finite sets of polynomials, $W=\{x\in R^n: f\ge0\ \forall f\in F,\ g=0\ \forall g\in G\}$, and $P(F,G)$ the preorder generated. Then $p>0$ on $W$ iff $q_1p=1+q_2$ for some $q_1,q_2\in P(F,G)$, and $p\ge0$ on $W$ iff $q_1p=p^{2s}+q_2$ for some such $q_1,q_2$ and integer $s$ (Krivine 1964; Stengle 1974). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stengle%27s_Positivstellensatz)) For compact semialgebraic sets, Schmüdgen (1991) and Putinar (1993) give representations with no denominators. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positivstellensatz)) See [Semialgebraic Sets](node:Semialgebraic%20Sets).
- **Zero location (12D10).** Sturm's theorem (1829): for square-free $P$ with Sturm sequence $P_0=P$, $P_1=P'$, $P_{i+1}=-\operatorname{rem}(P_{i-1},P_i)$, the number of distinct roots in $(a,b]$ equals $V(a)-V(b)$, the drop in sign variations; it holds over every real closed field. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%27s_theorem)) Descartes' rule: the number of positive roots, counted with multiplicity, equals the number of sign changes of the coefficients or is less than it by an even number. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descartes%27_rule_of_signs)) See [Real Polynomials and Rational Functions](node:Real%20Polynomials%20and%20Rational%20Functions).
- **Tarski's theorem.** The first-order theory of real closed fields is complete and decidable, proved by quantifier elimination using a generalization of Sturm's theorem; Collins' cylindrical algebraic decomposition is a practical algorithm, and doubly exponential complexity is nearly optimal (Davenport–Heintz). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_closed_field)) See [Model Theory of Fields](node:Model%20Theory%20of%20Fields).

### History
Sturm discovered his theorem in 1829. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%27s_theorem)) Artin and Schreier developed the theory of real closures in 1926. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_closed_field)) Artin's solution of Hilbert's 17th problem, "Über die Zerlegung definiter Funktionen in Quadrate," appeared in *Abh. Math. Sem. Univ. Hamburg* **5** (1927) 100–115. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02952513)) Krivine (1964) proved the Positivstellensatz, and Stengle rediscovered it in 1974. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stengle%27s_Positivstellensatz)) Delzell gave an algorithmic solution of Hilbert's 17th problem in 1984. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_seventeenth_problem))

### Open problems
- **Number of squares in Hilbert's 17th problem.** Let $v(n,d)$ be the least number of squares of rational functions needed for nonnegative forms of degree $d$ in $n$ variables. Pfister gives $v(n,d)\le2^n$; the smallest value is an open question. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_seventeenth_problem))
- **Pythagoras numbers of rational function fields.** "Can one bound $p(K(X))$ in terms of $p(K)$?" Becher, Daans, Grimm, Manzano-Flores and Zaninelli describe this question as still wide open, together with whether some field $K$ has $p(K(X))>p(K)+2$. ([arXiv:2302.11425](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.11425v3)) Becher and Zaninelli give a sufficient condition for $p(F)\le2^n+1$ that recovers the bound $3$ in some cases. ([arXiv:2210.02384](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02384))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Real closed field (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_closed_field): equivalent definitions, real closure, and Tarski's theorem.
- **Reference:** [Hilbert's seventeenth problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_seventeenth_problem): Hilbert, Artin, Motzkin, Pfister and open bounds.
- **Learn:** [Becher et al., The Pythagoras number of a rational function field in two variables](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.11425v3): introduction surveys known Pythagoras-number results and open questions.
- **Primary:** [Artin, Über die Zerlegung definiter Funktionen in Quadrate (1927)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02952513): solution of Hilbert's 17th problem.
- **Primary:** [Benoist, The Pythagoras number of fields of transcendence degree 1 over Q](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21380): proof of the five-squares bound.
- **Further reading:** [Lam, Introduction to Quadratic Forms over Fields (AMS GSM 67, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/067) and [Prestel and Delzell, Positive Polynomials (Springer, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-04648-7): standard monographs.
references.MSC 12Exx - General field theory:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 12E (general field theory) collects polynomials and equations over general fields, [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields) (field-theoretic aspects), skew fields and division rings, Hilbertian fields and Hilbert's irreducibility theorem (12E25), and field arithmetic (12E30). ([MSC2020 12Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Exx))

The organizing tension of field arithmetic is between "small" fields such as $\mathbb Q$, number fields and infinite finitely generated fields, which are Hilbertian, and "large" fields such as algebraically closed, PAC, real closed and Henselian fields, which are ample. Hilbert's irreducibility theorem transfers Galois-theoretic information from $\mathbb Q(t)$ down to $\mathbb Q$, while ampleness makes rational points plentiful and lets every finite split embedding problem be solved regularly. ([Hilbertian field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbertian_field); [Bary-Soroker–Fehm](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 12E05 polynomials in general fields (irreducibility, etc.), 12E10 special polynomials in general fields, 12E12 equations in general fields, 12E15 skew fields and division rings (see also 11R52, 16Kxx), 12E20 finite fields (field-theoretic aspects), 12E25 Hilbertian fields and Hilbert's irreducibility theorem, 12E30 field arithmetic, and 12E99. ([MSC2020 12Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Exx))

Neighbours inside [MSC 12](node:MSC%2012%20-%20Field%20theory%20and%20polynomials): 12D is real and complex fields; [12F](node:MSC%2012Fxx%20-%20Field%20extensions) is field extensions, including Galois theory and inverse Galois theory; [12G](node:MSC%2012Gxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20%28field%20theory%29) is homological methods; 12J is topological fields; 12L is connections between field theory and logic. ([MSC2020 12-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12-XX)) The division-ring code 12E15 carries see-also references to 11R52 and 16Kxx. ([MSC2020 12Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Hilbert's irreducibility theorem (12E25).** If $f_1,\dots,f_n$ are irreducible in $\mathbb Q(X_1,\dots,X_r)[Y_1,\dots,Y_s]$, there is $(a_1,\dots,a_r)\in\mathbb Q^r$ such that every $f_i(a_1,\dots,a_r,Y)$ is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[Y_1,\dots,Y_s]$; the good specializations are Zariski dense and can be chosen integral. Consequently, if a finite group $G$ is a Galois group over $\mathbb Q(X_1,\dots,X_r)$, it is a Galois group over $\mathbb Q$, which was Hilbert's motivation (1892). ([Hilbert's irreducibility theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_irreducibility_theorem)) This is the bridge to [inverse Galois theory](node:MSC%2012Fxx%20-%20Field%20extensions).
- **Hilbertian fields and thin sets.** A field $K$ is Hilbertian if $\mathbb P^1(K)$ is not a thin set in Serre's sense; Lang introduced the term in 1962. Number fields, finite extensions of Hilbertian fields and finitely generated infinite fields are Hilbertian; $\mathbb C$, $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb Q_p$ are not. Hilbertianity passes to finite separable and to abelian extensions, and Weissauer's theorem says that if $N$ is a Galois extension of a Hilbertian field then every proper finite extension of $N$ is Hilbertian (Haran's diamond theorem is the general form). Over $\mathbb Q$, a thin subset of $\mathbb Z^n$ has $O(H^{n-1/2}\log H)$ points of height at most $H$ (S. D. Cohen). ([Hilbertian field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbertian_field))
- **PAC fields (12E30).** $K$ is pseudo algebraically closed if every absolutely irreducible $K$-variety has a $K$-rational point (Ax, 1967). Examples: separably closed fields, nonprincipal ultraproducts of distinct finite fields (via the Riemann hypothesis for curves over finite fields), infinite algebraic extensions of finite fields. A PAC field has trivial Brauer group and projective absolute Galois group (cohomological dimension $\le1$), and a PAC field of characteristic $0$ is $C_1$. For a countable Hilbertian $K$ and $e\ge1$, the fixed field of the subgroup generated by almost all $e$-tuples in $G_K$ ([Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure)) is PAC. ([PAC field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo_algebraically_closed_field))
- **Ample fields and Pop's theorem.** $K$ is ample if every smooth $K$-curve with one $K$-point has infinitely many; equivalently $K$ is existentially closed in $K((t))$. PAC fields, fields complete for a nontrivial absolute value, and Henselian [valued fields](node:Valued%20Fields) are ample; finite fields, number fields and function fields are not, and the class is closed under algebraic extensions. Pop (1996) proved that over an ample field every finite split embedding problem has a regular solution, which in particular gives the regular inverse Galois problem over every ample field. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))
- **Finite fields (12E20) and irreducible polynomials (12E05).** A field of order $q$ exists iff $q$ is a prime power and is unique up to isomorphism; $\mathbb F_{p^n}\supseteq\mathbb F_{p^m}$ iff $m\mid n$; $\mathbb F_q^\times$ is cyclic; and for $q=p^n$, $X^q-X$ is the product of all monic irreducibles over $\mathbb F_p$ of degree dividing $n$; Möbius inversion gives the number of monic irreducibles of degree $n$ over $\mathbb F_q$ as $N(q,n)=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)q^{n/d}$. ([Finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field)) In particular a monic irreducible of every degree exists over every $\mathbb F_q$, and $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb F_{q^n}/\mathbb F_q)$ is cyclic, generated by Frobenius. ([Conrad, Thms 5.1, 5.6](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/finitefields.pdf)) Primitive polynomials (minimal polynomials of generators of $\mathbb F_{p^m}^\times$) exist in every degree, and there are $\varphi(p^m-1)/m$ of degree $m$ over $\mathbb F_p$. ([Primitive polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_polynomial_%28field_theory%29))
- **Equations over finite fields (12E12).** Chevalley–Warning: if $f_1,\dots,f_r\in\mathbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ have total degrees $d_j$ with $n>\sum d_j$, the number of common zeros in $\mathbb F_q^n$ is divisible by $p$; if the $f_j$ have no constant terms there is a nontrivial common zero, so finite fields are $C_1$ (Artin's 1935 conjecture). Ax–Katz sharpens the divisibility to $q^{\lceil (n-\sum d_j)/\max d_j\rceil}$. ([Chevalley–Warning theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevalley%E2%80%93Warning_theorem))
- **Wedderburn's little theorem (12E15).** Every finite division ring is commutative, hence a finite field; Witt's proof uses the class equation and the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n(q)$. The theorem is essentially equivalent to triviality of the Brauer group of a finite field. ([Wedderburn's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedderburn%27s_little_theorem)) The general ring language is in [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals), and Galois groups of finite fields in [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).

### History
Hilbert proved the irreducibility theorem in 1892 in *J. reine angew. Math.* 110, motivated by the inverse Galois problem. ([Hilbert's irreducibility theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_irreducibility_theorem)) Wedderburn proved that finite division rings are fields in 1905; Parshall argues that his first proof had a gap and that Dickson's gave the first correct proof, and Witt later simplified it. ([Wedderburn's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedderburn%27s_little_theorem)) Chevalley and Warning proved their theorems in 1935, confirming Artin's conjecture that finite fields are quasi-algebraically closed. ([Chevalley–Warning theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevalley%E2%80%93Warning_theorem)) Lang named Hilbertian fields in 1962, and Ax introduced PAC fields in 1967. ([Hilbertian field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbertian_field); [PAC field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo_algebraically_closed_field)) In the mid-1990s Pop observed that every field over which regular solvability of finite split embedding problems had been proved is ample, and in 1996 proved it for all ample fields. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310)) The standard monograph is Fried and Jarden's *Field Arithmetic* (Springer Ergebnisse, 2008 edition). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-77270-5))

### Open problems
All items below are posed as open in the survey of Bary-Soroker and Fehm (2011). ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))
- **Is $\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}$ ample?** A positive answer would, through Pop's results, prove Shafarevich's conjecture that the absolute Galois group of $\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is a free profinite group. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))
- **Is $\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{solv}}$ PAC?** Frey proved that $\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is not PAC, but whether the maximal solvable extension of $\mathbb Q$ is PAC (equivalently, whether every absolutely irreducible $\mathbb Q$-variety has a solvable point) is called a long-standing open question; even ampleness of $\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{solv}}$ is unknown. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))
- **Galois-theoretic criteria for ampleness.** Is every infinite field with prosolvable absolute Galois group ample? Is every infinite field with finitely generated absolute Galois group ample? Is every radically closed field ample (which would imply Podewski's conjecture that minimal fields are algebraically closed)? ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm, Questions II, III, V](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))
- **The Dèbes–Deschamps conjecture.** Does every finite split embedding problem over every field have a regular solution? Pop proved it for ample fields, and the survey asks whether it holds for any non-ample field at all. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm, §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))
- **Weak weak approximation.** Colliot-Thélène conjectures that every unirational variety has the WWA property, which would imply a positive answer to the inverse Galois problem. ([Hilbertian field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbertian_field))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hilbertian field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbertian_field): thin sets, permanence results, counting; with [PAC field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo_algebraically_closed_field) and [Finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field).
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Finite fields](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/finitefields.pdf): existence, uniqueness, irreducible polynomials and Frobenius, with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Bary-Soroker and Fehm, Open problems in the theory of ample fields (arXiv 1106.1310)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.1310): survey of ample, PAC and Hilbertian fields and their open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Fried and Jarden, *Field Arithmetic* (Springer, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-77270-5): the standard monograph on Hilbertian and PAC fields; [Lidl and Niederreiter, *Finite Fields*, 2nd ed. (CUP, 1996)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511525926): the standard reference on finite fields.
references.MSC 12Fxx - Field extensions:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 12F classifies work on field extensions $L/K$ as such: algebraic and transcendental extensions, separability and inseparability, Galois theory, and inverse Galois theory. ([MSC2020 12Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Fxx)) The basic invariants are the degree $[L:K]=\dim_K L$, multiplicative in towers, and for transcendental extensions the transcendence degree, the common size of all transcendence bases. ([Field extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension))

The research centre of the code is the inverse Galois problem: does every finite group occur as $\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)$? It remains open, although large families of groups are known to occur. ([Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem)) An August 2026 preprint (not yet refereed) realizes the last of the 26 sporadic simple groups, $M_{23}$, over $\mathbb Q$ by an explicit degree-23 polynomial. ([Huang–Jackson–Lee–Poonen–Pries–Zhang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08538)) Transcendental questions such as Lüroth's theorem and Noether's problem on the rationality of invariant fields connect the code to birational geometry, and generic polynomials and essential dimension measure how many parameters are needed to describe all $G$-extensions. ([Noether's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_problem); [Generic polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generic_polynomial); [Essential dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_dimension))

### Scope
The MSC2020 codes are 12F05 algebraic field extensions, 12F10 separable extensions and Galois theory, 12F12 inverse Galois theory, 12F15 inseparable field extensions, 12F20 transcendental field extensions, and 12F99; the entry lists no cross-references. ([MSC2020 12Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Fxx))

Neighbours inside [MSC 12](node:MSC%2012%20-%20Field%20theory%20and%20polynomials): [12E](node:MSC%2012Exx%20-%20General%20field%20theory) holds polynomials over general fields, [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields), Hilbertian fields and field arithmetic (where Hilbert's irreducibility theorem is classified); [12G](node:MSC%2012Gxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20%28field%20theory%29) holds [Galois cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology) and cohomological dimension; 12H is differential and difference algebra; 12J topological fields; 12L connections with logic. ([MSC2020 12-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Galois correspondence and primitive elements (12F05, 12F10).** An algebraic extension is Galois if it is normal and separable, and for a Galois extension intermediate fields correspond bijectively to subgroups of the Galois group. ([Field extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension)) A nonzero polynomial is separable iff it is coprime to its derivative; an irreducible polynomial is inseparable iff its derivative is $0$, so inseparability is a characteristic-$p$ phenomenon; and every finite separable extension is simple, $L=K(\gamma)$ (primitive element theorem). ([Conrad, Thms 2.1, 2.8, 3.6](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/separable1.pdf)) The first-course theory is in [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).
- **Inseparable extensions (12F15).** For algebraic $E/F$ the elements separable over $F$ form the separable closure $S$ of $F$ in $E$, the unique intermediate field separable over $F$ with $E/S$ purely inseparable, and for finite $E/F$, $[E:F]=[S:F]\,[E:S]$, the product of the separable degree and the inseparable degree, the latter a power of $p$. The separable closure of $F$ in an algebraic closure is unique up to non-unique isomorphism and is the maximal Galois extension of $F$; $F$ is perfect iff its separable and algebraic closures coincide. ([Separable extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separable_extension)) In characteristic $p$, a finite $L/K$ is purely inseparable iff every $\alpha\in L$ has minimal polynomial $X^{p^m}-a$, iff every $\alpha\in L$ is a root of some $X^{p^m}-a$ with $a\in K$. The model case is $X^p-u$ over $\mathbb F_p(u)$: irreducible, with a single root of multiplicity $p$. ([Conrad, Thm B.3, Ex. 2.11](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/separable1.pdf))
- **Transcendence degree and Lüroth's theorem (12F20).** All transcendence bases of $L/K$ have the same size, and $L/K$ is purely transcendental if $L=K(S)$ for a transcendence basis $S$. ([Field extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_extension)) $K/k$ is *separably generated* if some transcendence basis $\{x_i\}$ makes $K/k(x_i)$ separable algebraic; a finitely generated extension is separable iff it has such a separating transcendence basis. ([Stacks, Def. 10.42.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/030O); [Separable extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separable_extension)) Lüroth's theorem: for any field $K$, every intermediate field $K\subseteq M\subseteq K(X)$ is $K(f)$ for some rational function $f\in K(X)$. ([Lüroth's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCroth%27s_theorem))
- **Noether's problem.** If a finite group $G$ permutes indeterminates $y_1,\dots,y_n$, is $K(y_1,\dots,y_n)^G$ purely transcendental over $K$? Noether raised it in 1913 and proved it for $n=2,3,4$ in 1918; Swan (1969) gave a counterexample with $G$ cyclic of order $47$ permuting $47$ variables. ([Noether's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_problem)) For the regular action of $C_p$ over $\mathbb Q$, the invariant field $\mathbb Q(C_p)$ is known to be rational only for $p\le 43$ and $p=61,67,71$; Lenstra (1974) gave a necessary and sufficient condition for abelian $G$. ([Hoshi, arXiv 1402.3678](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.3678)) Hilbert's criterion links this to inverse Galois theory: if $G$ acts on an extension $K$ of $\mathbb Q$ and the invariant field $K^G$ is rational over $\mathbb Q$, then $G$ is realizable over $\mathbb Q$. ([Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem))
- **Known cases of inverse Galois theory (12F12).** Every finite abelian group is a quotient of a cyclotomic Galois group over $\mathbb Q$; Hilbert realized all $S_n$ and $A_n$ using $x^n-sx-s$ and his irreducibility theorem; all transitive [permutation groups](node:Permutation%20Groups) of degree at most $23$ are realized over $\mathbb Q$. ([Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem)) Shafarevich (1954) proved every finite solvable group occurs over $\mathbb Q$; A. Schmidt found a gap, which Shafarevich repaired in 1989. ([Shafarevich's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shafarevich%27s_theorem_on_solvable_Galois_groups))
- **The rigidity method.** For conjugacy classes $C_1,\dots,C_n$ of $G$, let $A$ be the set of tuples $(g_1,\dots,g_n)$ with $g_i\in C_i$ and $g_1\cdots g_n=1$; $A$ is rigid if it is nonempty, $G$ acts transitively on it by conjugation, and each tuple generates $G$. Thompson (1984) showed that a group with a rigid set can often be realized over the cyclotomic field generated by the character values of $G$ on the $C_i$; the Monster is realized over $\mathbb Q$ this way, using its generating triads of elements of orders $2,3,29$, all of which are conjugate. ([Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem)) Twenty-five of the 26 sporadic groups were realized over $\mathbb Q$ in 1984–1989; a 2026 preprint realizes $M_{23}$ through a regular extension of $\mathbb Q(t)$ built from a non-rigid triple and Belyi maps. ([Huang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08538)) The standard monograph is Malle–Matzat. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-55420-3))
- **Generic polynomials and essential dimension.** A generic polynomial for $G$ over $F$ is monic with coefficients in $F(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ and Galois group $G$, such that every $G$-extension arises as the splitting field of a specialization; $x^n+t_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+t_n$ is generic for $S_n$, cyclic groups $C_n$ have no generic polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ when $8\mid n$ (Lenstra), and G. W. Smith constructed one when $8\nmid n$. The generic dimension over $\mathbb Q$ is $1$ for $A_3,S_3$ and $2$ for $D_4,S_4,D_5,S_5$; the reference monograph is Jensen–Ledet–Yui (2002). ([Generic polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generic_polynomial)) Essential dimension (Buhler–Reichstein, 1997) is the least transcendence degree of a field of definition; $\operatorname{ed}(S_n)$ is known for $n\le5$, for $n=6$ outside characteristic $2$, and for $n=7$ in characteristic $0$. ([Essential dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_dimension))

### History
Lüroth proved his theorem in 1876. ([Lüroth's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCroth%27s_theorem)) Hilbert's 1892 irreducibility theorem was motivated by the inverse Galois problem; Noether raised her rationality problem in 1913, and Swan's 1969 counterexample gave it a negative answer in general. ([Hilbert's irreducibility theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_irreducibility_theorem); [Noether's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_problem)) Shafarevich's solvable-group theorem dates from 1954 (repaired 1989), and the rigidity method from Thompson's 1984 work. ([Shafarevich's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shafarevich%27s_theorem_on_solvable_Galois_groups); [Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem)) The sporadic programme was reported complete in a 2026 preprint realizing $M_{23}$. ([Huang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08538))

### Open problems
- **The inverse Galois problem over $\mathbb Q$.** Whether every finite group is a Galois group over $\mathbb Q$ remains open; the question is "in no sense solved in general". ([Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem))
- **The regular inverse Galois problem.** It has been conjectured that for every field $K$ and finite group $G$ there is a Galois extension $F/K(t)$ with group $G$ and $F/K$ regular. The stronger Dèbes–Deschamps conjecture, that every finite split embedding problem over any field has a regular solution, was proved by Pop for ample fields and, as of the survey, for no field known to be non-ample; Dèbes and Ghazi suggested a possible way to disprove the regular problem over $\mathbb Q$. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm, §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))
- **Noether's problem for cyclic groups of prime order.** It is unknown whether $\mathbb Q(C_p)$ is rational over $\mathbb Q$ for infinitely many primes $p$; Hoshi showed it is not (stably) rational for primes $p<20000$ apart from the $17$ rational cases and $46$ undetermined primes. ([Hoshi, arXiv 1402.3678](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.3678))
- **Shafarevich's conjecture.** The absolute Galois group of $\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is conjectured to be free profinite; Iwasawa's theorem (its maximal prosolvable quotient is free prosolvable) and the function-field analogue are evidence. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Inverse Galois problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Galois_problem): known cases and rigidity; with [Separable extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separable_extension) for inseparability.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Separability](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/separable1.pdf): derivative criterion, primitive element theorem and purely inseparable extensions, with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Huang, Jackson, Lee, Poonen, Pries, Zhang, The Mathieu group $M_{23}$ is a Galois group over $\mathbb Q$ (arXiv 2608.08538)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08538): completes the realization of the sporadic groups.
- **Further reading:** [Malle and Matzat, *Inverse Galois Theory* (Springer Monographs in Mathematics, 2018)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-55420-3): the standard monograph on rigidity and Galois realizations; [Fried and Jarden, *Field Arithmetic* (Springer, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-77270-5): embedding problems and Hilbertian fields.
