## Reference
### Overview
MSC 12G covers homological methods in field theory: [Galois cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology) (12G05, with see-also references to 14F22, 16H05 and 16K50) and the cohomological dimension of fields (12G10). ([MSC2020 12Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Gxx)) Galois cohomology applies [group cohomology](node:Group%20Cohomology) to modules over Galois groups; it measures the failure of taking Galois-invariants to be exact. For a separable closure $K^s$ one writes $G_K=\operatorname{Gal}(K^s/K)$ and $H^n(K,M)=H^n(G_K,M)$, with $H^0$ the invariants and $H^1$ defined also for nonabelian $M$, where it classifies twisted forms. ([Galois cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_cohomology))

The central themes of current research are the Bloch–Kato (norm residue) isomorphism between Milnor $K$-theory and Galois cohomology, proved by Voevodsky and Rost; the vanishing of $H^1(K,G)$ for [algebraic groups](node:Algebraic%20Groups) $G$ over fields of small cohomological dimension (Serre's Conjectures I and II); arithmetic duality; and the period–index problem for Brauer classes. ([Norm residue isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norm_residue_isomorphism_theorem); [Izquierdo–Lucchini Arteche](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.00903); [Hotchkiss et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.09774v2))

### Scope
The codes are 12G05 Galois cohomology [see also 14F22, 16H05, 16K50], 12G10 cohomological dimension of fields, and 12G99. ([MSC2020 12Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Gxx)) Neighbours inside [MSC 12](node:MSC%2012%20-%20Field%20theory%20and%20polynomials): [12F](node:MSC%2012Fxx%20-%20Field%20extensions) studies the extensions and Galois groups themselves, including inverse Galois theory; [12E](node:MSC%2012Exx%20-%20General%20field%20theory) holds field arithmetic (PAC and Hilbertian fields), whose Galois-theoretic invariants are often cohomological; 12J holds topological and [valued fields](node:Valued%20Fields). ([MSC2020 12-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12-XX)) The general machinery of derived functors is [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra), and the underlying Galois theory is [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).

### Key concepts
- **Hilbert 90 and the Brauer group.** For a Galois extension $L/K$, $H^1(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K),L^\times)=0$; this extends to $H^1(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K),GL_n(L))=1$ and to $SL_n$ and $Sp$. $H^2(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K),L^\times)=\operatorname{Br}(L/K)$, so $H^2(K,(K^s)^\times)$ is the Brauer group of central simple algebras. ([Galois cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_cohomology)) For a finite cyclic $L/K$ with generator $\sigma$, Hilbert 90 says $\ker N_{L/K}=\{\sigma(\beta)/\beta:\beta\in L^\times\}$; for a nonarchimedean local field $K$ the invariant map gives $\operatorname{Br}(K)\cong\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ (via $\operatorname{Br}(K^{\mathrm{ur}}/K)$). ([Sharifi, Thm 1.3.12, Prop. 9.1.7, Thm 9.1.13](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/algnum.pdf))
- **Norm residue isomorphism (Bloch–Kato).** For a field $k$ and $\ell$ invertible in $k$, the Galois symbol $K^M_n(k)/\ell\to H^n_{\text{ét}}(k,\mu_\ell^{\otimes n})$ is an isomorphism for all $n$. The case $\ell=2$ is the Milnor conjecture, and $n=2$ is the Merkurjev–Suslin theorem (Merkurjev 1981 for $\ell=2$; Merkurjev–Suslin 1982 for all $\ell$). It implies the Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture and is equivalent to the Beilinson–Lichtenbaum conjecture. ([Norm residue isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norm_residue_isomorphism_theorem))
- **Cohomological dimension (12G10).** $\operatorname{cd}_p(K)$ is the $p$-cohomological dimension of $G_K$ and $\operatorname{cd}(K)=\sup_p\operatorname{cd}_p(K)$. A field of characteristic $p>0$ has $\operatorname{cd}_p\le1$; [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields), and $k((t))$ for $k$ algebraically closed of characteristic $0$, have $G\cong\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ and $\operatorname{cd}=1$. ([Cohomological dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomological_dimension)) Tate proved that $\operatorname{cd}(\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}})=1$. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))
- **$C_1$ fields and Tsen's theorem.** $F$ is $C_1$ if every nonconstant homogeneous polynomial in more variables than its degree has a nontrivial zero. Finite fields (Chevalley–Warning), function fields of curves over algebraically closed fields (Tsen's theorem, 1936) and PAC fields of characteristic $0$ are $C_1$; a $C_1$ field has trivial Brauer group for every finite extension and cohomological dimension at most $1$. More generally a $C_k$ field requires a zero whenever $d^k<N$, and transcendence degree $n$ over a $C_k$ field gives $C_{k+n}$ (Lang–Nagata); Terjanian showed that $\mathbb Q_p$ is not $C_2$. ([Quasi-algebraically closed field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-algebraically_closed_field))
- **Serre's Conjecture I (Steinberg).** If $K$ is perfect with Serre dimension $\le1$ (Brauer group of every finite extension trivial), then $H^1(K,G)=1$ for every smooth connected linear algebraic group $G$; Steinberg proved it in 1965. Lourdeaux–Zidani (2026) extend it to $K$-unirational groups over imperfect fields with $[K:K^p]\le p$, while non-unirational unipotent groups can have infinite $H^1$ there. ([Lourdeaux–Zidani](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.05148))
- **Serre's Conjecture II.** For $K$ of cohomological dimension $\le2$, every principal homogeneous space under a semisimple simply connected $K$-group should have a rational point, i.e. $H^1(K,G)=1$. It is known for classical groups (types A, B, C, D without triality) and $F_4$, $G_2$ (Bayer-Fluckiger–Parimala over perfect fields; Berhuy–Frings–Tignol over imperfect ones), for quasi-split exceptional groups other than $E_8$, for $p$-adic and totally imaginary number fields (Kneser, Bruhat–Tits, Harder, Chernousov), and for function fields of complex surfaces (de Jong–He–Starr and others). ([Izquierdo–Lucchini Arteche](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.00903)) It is also known for complete discretely valued fields of dimension $2$. ([Gille–Izquierdo–Lucchini Arteche](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.01403))
- **Duality and local–global principles.** For a nonarchimedean local field $K$ and finite $G_K$-module $A$ of order prime to $\operatorname{char}K$, with $A'=\operatorname{Hom}(A,\mu)$, cup product gives perfect pairings $H^i(K,A)\times H^{2-i}(K,A')\to H^2(K,\mu)=\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ for $i=0,1,2$, and $G_K$ has cohomological dimension $2$. ([Local Tate duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Tate_duality)) Its global counterpart is Tate–Poitou duality. ([Galois cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_cohomology)) For a simply connected group over a global field, $H^1$ maps injectively to the product of local $H^1$'s (Kneser case by case, Chernousov for $E_8$ in 1989); central simple algebras over number fields satisfy the Albert–Brauer–Hasse–Noether local–global principle. ([Hasse principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle))

### History
Galois cohomology consolidated around 1950 as a formulation of class field theory, building on Hilbert 90 and Kummer theory; in the 1960s it became a foundation of [étale cohomology](node:Étale%20Cohomology). ([Galois cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_cohomology)) Serre formulated Conjecture I in 1962 and Steinberg proved it in 1965. ([Lourdeaux–Zidani](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.05148)) Serre's monograph *Galois Cohomology* appeared in English in Springer Monographs in Mathematics. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-59141-9)) Milnor (1970) proposed the $\ell=2$ isomorphism; Bloch and Kato conjectured the general case; Voevodsky proved the Milnor conjecture (preprints from 1995–96) and, using Rost's norm varieties, the full Bloch–Kato conjecture (Annals, 2011), with Weibel's 2009 account repairing a gap. ([Norm residue isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norm_residue_isomorphism_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Serre's Conjecture II.** The conjecture "remains open, although a lot has been done in particular cases"; Izquierdo and Lucchini Arteche (2023, revised 2025) show that the characteristic-$0$ case implies the positive-characteristic case. Quasi-split $E_8$ is excluded from the known quasi-split cases. ([Izquierdo–Lucchini Arteche](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.00903))
- **The period–index conjecture.** For a Brauer class $\alpha$ on a smooth projective complex variety $X$, the period $\operatorname{per}(\alpha)$ is its order in $\operatorname{Br}(X)$ and the index $\operatorname{ind}(\alpha)$ is the gcd of the square roots of ranks of Azumaya algebras of class $\alpha$; the longstanding period–index conjecture for the function field $\mathbb C(X)$ predicts $\operatorname{ind}(\alpha)\mid\operatorname{per}(\alpha)^{\dim X-1}$. De Jong proved $\operatorname{per}=\operatorname{ind}$ for surfaces, but in higher dimensions little is known, beyond the existence of a bound of this general form (Huybrechts–Mattei). ([Hotchkiss–Maulik–Shen–Yin–Zhang](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.09774v2))
- **Galois groups of cohomological dimension 1.** Shafarevich's conjecture that $G_{\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}}$ (which has $\operatorname{cd}=1$ by Tate) is free profinite remains open. ([Bary-Soroker–Fehm, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1310))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Galois cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_cohomology): definitions, Hilbert 90, Brauer groups, history; with [Norm residue isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norm_residue_isomorphism_theorem).
- **Learn:** [Sharifi, Algebraic Number Theory](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/algnum.pdf): course notes with Hilbert 90, Brauer groups of local fields and cohomological class field theory.
- **Primary:** [Izquierdo and Lucchini Arteche, Transfer principles for Galois cohomology and Serre's conjecture II (arXiv 2308.00903)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00903): research paper with a survey of known cases of Conjecture II.
- **Further reading:** [Serre, *Galois Cohomology* (Springer Monographs in Mathematics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-59141-9): the standard monograph on cohomology of profinite groups, cohomological dimension and nonabelian $H^1$.
references.MSC 12Hxx - Differential and difference:
## Reference
### Overview
Differential algebra studies algebraic differential equations through commutative rings equipped with one or more pairwise commuting derivations, additive maps obeying the Leibniz rule. Its basic objects are differential rings and fields, their constants (elements killed by every derivation, which form a subfield in a differential field), and differential ideals, ideals stable under the derivations. Ritt developed the theory because he regarded attempts to reduce systems of differential equations to canonical forms as unsatisfactory; his *Differential Algebra* appeared in 1950, and his student Kolchin's *Differential Algebra and Algebraic Groups* in 1973. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebra))

Difference algebra, initiated by Ritt and his student Cohn, replaces the derivation by a ring endomorphism $\sigma$ (often assumed injective); the model example is $\mathbb C(x)$ with $\sigma f(x)=f(x+1)$, and the Gamma function's functional equation places it in a difference variety. A proof of the Manin–Mumford conjecture by Hrushovski (2001) uses difference-algebraic methods. ([Wikipedia, Difference algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Difference_algebra))

The two theories meet in Galois theories for linear equations. Picard–Vessiot theory attaches a linear algebraic group to $Y'=AY$; van der Put and Singer laid the algebraic foundations of the analogous Galois theory of linear difference equations; and Hardouin and Singer built a Galois theory of difference equations that measures the *differential* dependencies among their solutions. ([Singer](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0712.4124); [van der Put–Singer](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/BFb0096118); [Hardouin–Singer](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.1493))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 12Hxx into 12H05 differential algebra (see also 13Nxx), 12H10 difference algebra (see also 39Axx), 12H20 abstract differential equations (see also 34Mxx), 12H25 $p$-adic differential equations (see also 11S80, 14G20), and 12H99. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Hxx))

Neighbouring codes, as given by the entry's cross-references: 12H05 points to [MSC 13Nxx - Differential algebra](node:MSC%2013Nxx%20-%20Differential%20algebra) (the commutative-ring side, close to [modules over commutative rings](node:Modules%20over%20Commutative%20Rings)), 12H10 to [MSC 39Axx - Difference equations](node:MSC%2039Axx%20-%20Difference%20equations), 12H20 to [MSC 34Mxx - Ordinary differential equations in the complex domain](node:MSC%2034Mxx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations%20in%20the%20complex%20domain), and 12H25 to 11S80 in [MSC 11Sxx - Algebraic number theory - local and p-adic fields](node:MSC%2011Sxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20local%20and%20p-adic%20fields) and to 14G20. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Hxx))

For 12H25, Kedlaya's monograph develops $p$-adic differential equations on discs and annuli, Frobenius structures, the $p$-adic local monodromy theorem and global theory, starting from Dwork's example linking the $p$-adic behaviour of Gauss's hypergeometric equation to point counts on an elliptic curve over a finite field. ([Kedlaya, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/padic-differential-equations/introductory-remarks/8494671FA6D05385ECEF8DBAC72566D0))

### Key concepts
- [Differential Fields](node:Differential%20Fields): a differential field is a differential ring that is a field; the constants form a subfield, and a radical (perfect) differential ideal is one equal to its radical, with prime differential ideals always radical. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebra))
- **Ritt–Raudenbush basis theorem.** If $R$ is a Ritt algebra (a differential ring containing $\mathbb Q$) satisfying the ascending chain condition on radical differential ideals, then so does the differential polynomial ring $R\{y\}$; iterating, $K\{y_1,\dots,y_n\}$ over a differential field $K\supseteq\mathbb Q$ satisfies the ascending chain condition on radical differential ideals, which yields Ritt's basis theorem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebra))
- **Differential Nullstellensatz.** For $K$ of characteristic zero with commuting derivations and $F\subseteq K\{y_1,\dots,y_n\}$: $1\notin[F]$ iff $F$ has a common zero in every differentially closed $L\supseteq K$; and $g\in\sqrt{[F]}$ iff $g$ vanishes on all common zeros of $F$ in every such $L$. ([Gustavson–Kondratieva–Ovchinnikov](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1411.1000))
- **Differentially closed fields.** Robinson introduced them in 1959; the theory $\mathrm{DCF}_0$ is complete, model complete and eliminates quantifiers. Every differentially perfect field has a differential closure (a prime model extension); Shelah proved it unique up to isomorphism over the field, and showed that the prime differentially closed field of characteristic $0$ is not minimal. ([Wikipedia, DCF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentially_closed_field))
- **Picard–Vessiot theory.** Over $k$ of characteristic zero with algebraically closed constants, a Picard–Vessiot ring for $Y'=AY$ is a simple differential ring generated by a fundamental matrix $Z$ and $1/\det Z$; it is unique up to isomorphism, its differential Galois group is a linear algebraic group $G\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_n(C_k)$ with $\dim G=\operatorname{tr.deg}(K/k)$, and Zariski-closed subgroups correspond bijectively to intermediate differential fields, normal subgroups to Picard–Vessiot subextensions. With only regular singular points, the monodromy group is Zariski dense in $G$ (Schlesinger). ([Singer](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0712.4124)) See [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory) and [Algebraic Groups](node:Algebraic%20Groups).
- **Liouvillian solutions and Kovacic's algorithm.** $L(y)=0$ is solvable in Liouvillian functions iff the identity component of its differential Galois group is solvable. For $L=\partial^2-s$ the group lies in $\mathrm{SL}_2$, and a Liouvillian solution exists iff the group has a finite-index subgroup fixing a line, of index $1,2,4,6$ or $12$; Kovacic's algorithm searches for the corresponding rational or algebraic $z'/z$. A general algorithm for computing differential Galois groups (Hrushovski) exists in principle. ([Singer](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0712.4124)) Compare [Monodromy of Complex Differential Equations](node:Monodromy%20of%20Complex%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Differential Galois theory of difference equations.** Hardouin and Singer's Galois theory, which measures differential dependencies among solutions of linear difference equations, reproves Hölder's theorem that the [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function) satisfies no polynomial differential equation over $\mathbb C(x)$, and shows that no differential relation holds among solutions of certain $q$-hypergeometric equations. ([Hardouin–Singer](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.1493)) See also [Difference Equations](node:Difference%20Equations).
- **Difference varieties.** Difference varieties over a difference field $K$ correspond one-to-one with perfect difference ideals of $K\{y\}$, and every ascending chain of perfect difference ideals is finite, a difference analogue of Hilbert's basis theorem. ([Wikipedia, Difference algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Difference_algebra))

### History
Ritt's 1930 paper on manifolds of functions defined by algebraic differential equations and his 1932 book *Differential Equations from the Algebraic Standpoint* preceded the 1950 *Differential Algebra*; Kolchin's 1973 monograph unified the theory with algebraic groups. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebra)) Cohn's *Difference Algebra* is a standard reference, cited in its 1979 Krieger edition. ([Wikipedia, Difference algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Difference_algebra)) Van der Put and Singer's *Galois Theory of Difference Equations* (Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1666, 1997) extended work of Birkhoff and Trjitzinsky, also covering the inverse problem, effective computation of Galois groups and $q$-difference equations. ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/BFb0096118)) Singer's 2006 London Mathematical Society lectures survey linear differential Galois theory. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/0712.4124))

### Open problems
- **Kolchin catenary problem.** Given a point $p$ of an irreducible differential variety $\Sigma$, does there exist a long gap chain of irreducible differential subvarieties beginning at $p$ and ending at $\Sigma$? Wikipedia calls this a fundamental open problem in differential algebra, and Freitag, León Sánchez and Simmons treat it among conjectural questions. ([Wikipedia, Kolchin's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolchin%27s_problems); [Freitag–León Sánchez–Simmons](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.6211))
- **Ritt problem and Jacobi bound.** The Ritt problem asks for an algorithm deciding whether one prime differential ideal, given by a characteristic set, is contained in another; the Jacobi bound conjecture predicts that the order of an irreducible component of a differential variety is bounded by its Jacobi number. Wikipedia lists both as open problems. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebra); [Golubitsky–Kondratieva–Ovchinnikov](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.1128))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Differential algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebra): definitions, basis theorem, history and open problems.
- **Learn:** [Singer, Introduction to the Galois Theory of Linear Differential Equations](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0712.4124): Picard–Vessiot theory, Liouvillian solutions and Kovacic's algorithm.
- **Primary:** [van der Put–Singer, Galois Theory of Difference Equations](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/BFb0096118): foundational monograph for difference Galois theory.
- **Primary:** [Hardouin–Singer, Differential Galois theory of linear difference equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.1493): differential relations among solutions of difference equations.
- **Further reading:** [Kedlaya, p-adic Differential Equations](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/padic-differential-equations/introductory-remarks/8494671FA6D05385ECEF8DBAC72566D0): graduate monograph for 12H25.
references.MSC 12Jxx - Topological fields:
## Reference
### Overview
A topological field is a field with a topology for which addition, multiplication, negation and inversion on nonzero elements are continuous. The basic examples are metric: $\mathbb Q$ with the usual absolute value completes to $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb Q$ with the $p$-adic valuation completes to $\mathbb Q_p$, and $F(t)$ with the $t$-adic valuation completes to the [Laurent series](node:Laurent%20Series) field $F((t))$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_field))

Two kinds of structure produce most field topologies studied under 12J: absolute values and Krull valuations on one side, and orderings on the other, since the order topology of an ordered field makes the operations continuous. ([Wikipedia, Valuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_%28algebra%29); [Wikipedia, Ordered field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_field)) The theory links number theory (local fields as completions of global fields), real algebra, non-Archimedean analysis and the [model theory](node:Model%20Theory) of valued fields. ([MIT 18.785](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2018fa/LectureNotes9.pdf); [Kuhlmann](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.06386))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 12J05 normed fields, 12J10 valued fields, 12J12 formally $p$-adic fields, 12J15 ordered fields, 12J17 topological semifields, 12J20 general valuation theory for fields (see also 13A18), 12J25 non-Archimedean valued fields (see also 30G06, 46S10), 12J27 Krasner–Tate algebras (see mainly 32P05; see also 46S10, 47S10), and 12J99. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Jxx))

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 11Sxx - Algebraic number theory - local and p-adic fields](node:MSC%2011Sxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20local%20and%20p-adic%20fields) covers local fields number-theoretically, including ramification, Galois theory and class field theory; [MSC 12Dxx - Real and complex fields](node:MSC%2012Dxx%20-%20Real%20and%20complex%20fields) covers the real and complex fields; [MSC 13Jxx - Topological rings and modules](node:MSC%2013Jxx%20-%20Topological%20rings%20and%20modules) covers topological rings and modules; and [MSC 32Pxx](node:MSC%2032Pxx%20-%20Non-Archimedean%20analysis%20%28should%20also%20be%20assigned%20at%20least%20one%20other%20classification%20number%20from%20Section%2032-XX%20describing%20the%20type%20of%20problem%29) is the main home of rigid-analytic Krasner–Tate algebras. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Jxx); [MSC2020, 11S](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Sxx))

### Key concepts
- **Absolute values and Ostrowski's theorem.** Two absolute values on a field $F$ induce the same topology iff $|\cdot|'=|\cdot|^e$ for some $e>0$; an absolute value is non-Archimedean iff $|x+y|\le\max(|x|,|y|)$, which always holds in positive characteristic. Ostrowski: the absolute values on $\mathbb Q$ are the trivial one, $|\cdot|_\infty^e$ for $0<e\le1$, and $|\cdot|_p^e$ for $e>0$ and $p$ prime. Every field with an absolute value has a completion, unique up to unique isometric isomorphism, in which it is dense. ([Conrad](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/248APage/handouts/ostrowski.pdf)) See [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces) and [p-adic Numbers](node:p-adic%20Numbers).
- [Valued Fields](node:Valued%20Fields) (12J10, 12J20): a Krull valuation is $v:K\to\Gamma\cup\{\infty\}$ into a totally ordered abelian group with $v(a)=\infty\iff a=0$, $v(ab)=v(a)+v(b)$ and $v(a+b)\ge\min(v(a),v(b))$; it has valuation ring $R_v=\{v\ge0\}$ with unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_v=\{v>0\}$ and residue field $R_v/\mathfrak m_v$, and two valuations are equivalent iff they have the same valuation ring. ([Wikipedia, Valuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_%28algebra%29))
- **Local fields.** A local field is a field with a nontrivial absolute value that is locally compact. For a discrete valuation with valuation ring $A$ and uniformizer $\pi$, $K$ is local iff it is complete and $A/\pi A$ is finite. Every local field is $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, or a finite extension of $\mathbb Q_p$ or $\mathbb F_q((t))$. ([MIT 18.785](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2018fa/LectureNotes9.pdf))
- [Hensel's Lemma](node:Hensel's%20Lemma): if $A$ is a complete DVR, $f\in A[x]$ and $a_0\in A$ with $|f(a_0)|<|f'(a_0)|^2$, then Newton's iteration $a_{n+1}=a_n-f(a_n)/f'(a_n)$ converges quadratically to the unique root $a$ of $f$ with $|a-a_0|\le|f(a_0)|/|f'(a_0)|^2$. A local ring in which the simple-root form holds is called Henselian. ([MIT 18.785](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2018fa/LectureNotes9.pdf)) A valued field is Henselian iff its valuation extends uniquely to every finite extension, and the henselization is an algebraic substitute for completion. ([Wikipedia, Henselian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henselian_ring))
- **Krasner's lemma.** Let $K$ be complete non-Archimedean, $\alpha$ separable over $K$ with conjugates $\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n$. If $\beta$ in a separable closure satisfies $|\alpha-\beta|<|\alpha-\alpha_i|$ for all $i\ge2$, then $K(\alpha)\subseteq K(\beta)$. It is used to show that $\mathbb C_p$, the completion of $\overline{\mathbb Q}_p$, is algebraically closed. ([Wikipedia, Krasner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krasner%27s_lemma))
- **Ordered fields (12J15).** An ordering can be given as a compatible total order or as a positive cone, with a bijection between the two. Every ordered field is formally real ($0$ is not a sum of nonzero squares) and, by Artin–Schreier and Zorn's lemma, every formally real field admits an ordering; fields of positive characteristic, $\mathbb C$ and $\mathbb Q_p$ admit none. An ordered field is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$ iff it is Dedekind complete. ([Wikipedia, Ordered field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_field)) See [Ordered Groups and Ordered Rings](node:Ordered%20Groups%20and%20Ordered%20Rings) and [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields).
- **Ax–Kochen–Ershov transfer.** Henselian valued fields with residue fields of characteristic $0$ are elementarily equivalent when their residue fields and value groups are; consequently nonprincipal ultraproducts of the $\mathbb Q_p$ and of the $\mathbb F_p((t))$ are elementarily equivalent, which yields the Ax–Kochen theorem that for each $d$, for all but finitely many $p$, every degree-$d$ form over $\mathbb Q_p$ in at least $d^2+1$ variables has a nontrivial zero. Terjanian's 1966 counterexample shows the exceptional set can be nonempty. ([Wikipedia, Ax–Kochen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem)) See [Model Theory of Fields](node:Model%20Theory%20of%20Fields).

### History
Artin and Schreier gave the positive-cone definition of an ordering in 1926, the start of the Artin–Schreier theory of formally real fields; Hilbert, Hölder and Hahn had earlier abstracted the order axioms from $\mathbb R$. ([Wikipedia, Ordered field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_field)) Ax and Kochen proved their theorem in 1965 using the transfer principle for Henselian fields. ([Wikipedia, Ax–Kochen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem)) Engler and Prestel's 2005 monograph develops valuation theory from absolute values to Krull valuations, explaining why henselization replaces completion, and includes definable valuation rings and a Galois-theoretic characterization of $\mathbb Q_p$. ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/3-540-30035-X))

### Open problems
- **Model theory of $\mathbb F_p((t))$.** Kuhlmann's 2025 survey lists as an open problem a complete axiomatization and the decidability of $\mathbb F_p((t))$; Anscombe and Fehm proved its existential theory in the language of valued fields decidable (with a constant for $t$ the existential theory is known decidable only under extra hypotheses), and Rigler's Oxford thesis obtains decidability only conditionally. ([Kuhlmann](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.06386); [Anscombe–Fehm](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.04522); [Rigler](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:37283d4a-148f-48c3-8622-b70dcf791c71))
- **Tame fields.** The same survey asks whether tame valued fields admit quantifier elimination in a suitable language. ([Kuhlmann](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.06386))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Valuation (algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_%28algebra%29): Krull valuations, valuation rings and residue fields.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.785, Lecture 9](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2018fa/LectureNotes9.pdf): local fields and Hensel's lemmas; [Conrad, absolute values](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/248APage/handouts/ostrowski.pdf): equivalence, Ostrowski and completion.
- **Primary:** [Kuhlmann, Model theory of tame valued fields and beyond](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.06386): survey with open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Engler–Prestel, Valued Fields](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/3-540-30035-X): standard monograph on valuations and Henselian fields.
references.MSC 12Kxx - Generalizations of fields:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 12Kxx, "Generalizations of fields", has exactly three codes: 12K05 Near-fields (see also 16Y30), 12K10 Semifields (see also 16Y60), and 12K99 for other material in the section. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Kxx)) Each weakens the axioms of a division ring while keeping division by nonzero elements. A near-field keeps associativity but has only one distributive law. A semifield in the finite-geometry sense keeps both distributive laws but drops associativity of multiplication; its nonzero elements form a loop. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semifield))

Both are special cases of quasifields, the coordinatizing algebras of translation planes, so the area's main application is finite projective geometry. A quasifield yields a planar ternary ring and a projective plane, and every translation plane can be coordinatized by a quasifield; nearfield planes and semifield planes are listed among the special classes of translation planes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasifield)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_plane)) Near-fields are also tied to permutation groups: they correspond to Frobenius groups $A\rtimes M$ with $|M|=|A|-1$, and to sharply 2-transitive groups that contain an abelian normal subgroup. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29)) ([Rips–Segev–Tent](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1406.0382))

Associative division rings (skew fields) are not in 12K. They are classified under 12E15 "Skew fields, division rings", which cross-references 11R52 and 16Kxx. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Exx))

### Scope
- **12K05 Near-fields.** Cross-referenced to 16Y30 Near-rings. A near-field is a near-ring with identity in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Kxx)) ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Yxx)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29))
- **12K10 Semifields.** Cross-referenced to 16Y60 Semirings. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Yxx)) The word has two meanings. In finite geometry a semifield is a nonassociative division ring with identity. In ring theory and [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) it is a semiring in which every nonzero element has an inverse, so there is no subtraction; tropical semirings $(\mathbb R,\max,+)$ are examples. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semifield))
- **12K99.** Other generalizations of fields not covered above. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Kxx))
- **Neighbouring codes.** 12E15 holds associative skew fields, with [16Kxx](node:MSC%2016Kxx%20-%20Division%20rings%20and%20semisimple%20Artin%20rings) for their ring theory ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Exx)). [16Y30 Near-rings and 16Y60 Semirings](node:MSC%2016Yxx%20-%20Generalizations) treat the ring-theoretic generalizations without the division requirement and cross-reference back to 12K05 and 12K10 ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Yxx)). The geometry of semifield planes is filed in 51A; Kantor's survey of finite semifields carries MSC2000 primary codes 51A40 and 17A35 ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf)), and work on semifields and rank-metric codes is filed under 12K10 together with 11T71, 17A35 and 94B60 ([Gluesing-Luerssen](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.11691)).

### Key concepts
- **Near-fields and Dickson near-fields.** A near-field is "similar to a division ring, except that it has only one of the two distributive laws". Dickson introduced near-fields in 1905 by twisting the multiplication of a field while keeping its addition. The smallest near-field that is not a field has order $9$. The additive group of every near-field is abelian, and every finite near-field is planar, while infinite ones need not be. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29)) See [Near-Fields and Semifields](node:Near-Fields%20and%20Semifields) and [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals).
- **Zassenhaus's classification of finite near-fields.** Every finite near-field is a field, a Dickson near-field, or one of exactly seven exceptional near-fields, each with additive group $C_p^2$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29)) Equivalently on the group side, Zassenhaus classified the finite sharply 2-transitive groups in 1936, and every finite sharply 2-transitive group has a non-trivial abelian normal subgroup. Kerby showed that this splitting statement for a sharply 2-transitive group is equivalent to the statement that every near-domain is a near-field. ([Rips–Segev–Tent](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1406.0382)) Compare [Permutation Groups](node:Permutation%20Groups) and [MSC 20Bxx - Permutation groups](node:MSC%2020Bxx%20-%20Permutation%20groups).
- **Presemifields, isotopy and Albert's theorem.** A presemifield $(F,+,*)$ is an additive group with a multiplication satisfying both distributive laws and $x*y=0\iff x=0$ or $y=0$; it is a semifield if it has an identity. An isotopism is a triple $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ of additive bijections with $(x*y)^\gamma=x^\alpha\circ y^\beta$, and every presemifield is isotopic to a semifield. **Albert's theorem:** two semifields coordinatize isomorphic planes iff they are isotopic. ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf)) Isotopy of nonassociative algebras was introduced by Albert in 1942 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopy_of_an_algebra)), in "Non-associative algebras I: Fundamental concepts and isotopy", Ann. of Math. 43 (1942) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1968960)). By Wedderburn's theorem every finite associative division algebra is commutative, so finite skew fields are [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields) ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf)); see [Artin–Wedderburn Theorem](node:Artin–Wedderburn%20Theorem) and [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).
- **Small dimension: Menichetti's theorems.** Semifields of order $p$ or $p^2$ are fields, and there are only two classes of semifields of order $p^3$. ([Pott–Schmidt–Zhou](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1401.3294)) Kantor records that for $p$ an odd prime all semifields of order $p^3$ are twisted fields and that their number is known, citing Menichetti's "Algebre tridimensionali su un campo di Galois" (Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. 1973) and his 1996 paper on $n$-dimensional algebras over a field with a cyclic extension of degree $n$. ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf))
- **Knuth's cubical arrays and computer classification.** Knuth's "Finite semifields and projective planes" (J. Algebra 2 (1965) 182–217) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0021-8693%2865%2990018-9)) writes a presemifield on $K^n$ as a cubical array $(a_{ijk})$ with $v_i\circ v_j=\sum_k a_{ijk}v_k$. Permuting the indices gives presemifields again, the source of Knuth's $S_3$ action on semifield planes. Knuth also gave "binary" presemifields over $GF(q^n)$, $q$ even and $n>1$ odd. Excluding fields, there are $2$ isotopy classes of semifields of order $16$ and $5$ of order $32$. ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf)) Rúa, Combarro and Ranilla classified all semifields of order $64$ by computer: $332$ isotopy classes (against $35$ previously known), $80$ classes under Knuth's $S_3$ action, completing the classification of finite semifields of order at most $125$. ([Rúa–Combarro–Ranilla](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0807.2994)) The same group classified order $243=3^5$: $23$ isotopy classes, giving four new semifield planes. ([Rúa–Combarro–Ranilla](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1010.0228))
- **Twisted fields and commutative semifields.** Albert's generalized twisted fields come from the presemifield $x*y=xy-jx^\alpha y^\beta$ on a finite field $F$ with nontrivial $\alpha,\beta\in\operatorname{Aut}F$, and Albert determined when two are isotopic. ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf)) Commutative semifields are equivalent to certain planar functions; in odd characteristic a Dembowski–Ostrom polynomial $f$ is planar iff it is 2-to-1. ([Pott–Schmidt–Zhou](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1401.3294))
- **Translation planes.** Finite quasifields and finite translation planes have prime-power order, because the kernel of a quasifield is a division ring and finite division rings are fields. All planes of order at most $8$ are Desarguesian, and the Hall plane is the unique non-Desarguesian translation plane of order $9$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasifield)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_plane)) Hall built that plane from the order-9 near-field. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29)) See [Projective Geometry](node:Projective%20Geometry), [Finite Projective Planes](node:Finite%20Projective%20Planes), [MSC 51Axx - Linear incidence geometry](node:MSC%2051Axx%20-%20Linear%20incidence%20geometry) and [MSC 51Exx - Finite geometry and special incidence structures](node:MSC%2051Exx%20-%20Finite%20geometry%20and%20special%20incidence%20structures).

### History
Wedderburn published the finite division algebra theorem in 1905 with three proofs; Artin noticed more than twenty years later that the first proof had a gap, and the other two used an idea from Dickson's 1905 paper. ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf)) Quasifields were first studied by Veblen and Wedderburn in 1907 and were called "Veblen–Wedderburn systems" until 1975. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasifield)) Dickson introduced near-fields in 1905 and Zassenhaus's classification appeared in 1935; Wähling's monograph is from 1987. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29)) Albert introduced isotopy in 1942 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopy_of_an_algebra)); Kantor describes it as introduced "for purely algebraic reasons" and cites Albert's plane-isomorphism theorem to a 1960 AMS symposium paper. Knuth introduced cubical arrays and two new families of semifields in his 1963 PhD research under Marshall Hall, Jr., and Walker and Knuth independently enumerated the semifields of order $32$ by computer in the early 1960s. ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf)) The order-64 classification was posted in 2008 ([Rúa–Combarro–Ranilla](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0807.2994)). In 2014 Rips, Segev and Tent built infinite sharply 2-transitive groups with no non-trivial abelian normal subgroup, answering "a long-standing open question" ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.0382)); Rips and Tent then did the same in characteristic $0$ ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00573)).

### Open problems
- **Kantor's conjecture on the number of semifields.** "The number of pairwise non-isomorphic semifield planes of order $N$ is not bounded above by a polynomial in $N$", equivalently for non-isotopic presemifields. Kantor proves it for $N$ even using the symplectic presemifields of his Section 5.2; for $N$ odd the number known is less than $N^3$. The isomorphism problem for the even-order planes is settled for $[F:F_1]>3$, but "the general case remains open". ([Kantor](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf))
- **Planar functions and semifield planes.** Pott, Schmidt and Zhou ask whether there are planar functions in characteristic $2$ that are not of Dembowski–Ostrom type (Problem 8.2), and say it "remains open" whether a planar function not of Dembowski–Ostrom type can give a semifield plane. ([Pott–Schmidt–Zhou](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1401.3294))
- **Non-split sharply 2-transitive groups of small characteristic.** Every near-domain being a near-field is equivalent to splitting of sharply 2-transitive groups ([Rips–Segev–Tent](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1406.0382)). Non-split examples now exist in characteristic $2$ (Rips–Segev–Tent), $0$ (Rips–Tent) and every sufficiently large prime $p$ (André–Amelio–Tent), while by Kerby every sharply 2-transitive group of characteristic $3$ splits; Amelio adds non-split examples of bounded exponent for every sufficiently large prime $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$. He notes the earlier methods need a very large $p$ and writes that the existence of non-split sharply 2-transitive groups of "small" characteristic $p\ge5$ "remains, to the best of our knowledge, open". ([Amelio](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11958)) ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11958))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Near-field (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29): definition, Dickson near-fields, Zassenhaus's classification, Frobenius groups, Hall plane.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 12Kxx (AMS)](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Kxx): the code list and cross-references.
- **Learn:** [Cordero, Math 5392 Finite Geometries (UT Arlington)](https://websites.uta.edu/cordero/?p=764): course schedule from projective planes through coordinatization and semifields.
- **Primary:** [Kantor, "Finite semifields" (survey)](https://pages.uoregon.edu/kantor/PAPERS/Pingree2005.pdf): isotopy, Albert and Knuth, the known families, and the counting conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Pott, Schmidt, Zhou, "Semifields, relative difference sets, and bent functions"](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1401.3294): commutative semifields, planar functions, and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Rúa, Combarro, Ranilla, "Classification of 64-element finite semifields"](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0807.2994): the computer classification of order 64.
- **Primary:** [Rips, Segev, Tent, "A sharply 2-transitive group without a non-trivial abelian normal subgroup"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.0382): the infinite counterexamples and the near-domain reformulation.
- **Further reading:** [Knuth, "Finite semifields and projective planes", J. Algebra 2 (1965)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0021-8693%2865%2990018-9): the founding paper on cubical arrays and semifield families.
- **Further reading:** [Wähling, "Ordered Nearfields", in Nearrings, Nearfields and K-Loops (1997)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-009-1481-0_5): chapter by the author of the monograph "Theorie der Fastkörper" (1987).

## Reference
### Overview
This area applies logic, chiefly [model theory](node:Model%20Theory) and decidability theory, to fields. In the ring language $\{+,-,\cdot,0,1\}$, first-order formulas express Boolean combinations of polynomial equations with quantifiers over field elements, so questions such as "is this theory decidable?" or "which sets are definable?" become questions about the solvability of polynomial systems. ([Berkeley notes](https://math.berkeley.edu/~ltomczak/notes/Lent2023/ModelTheory_Notes.pdf); [Marker](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/mt-intro.html))

The founding example is Tarski's theorem that the theory of the real field is decidable, for which he developed quantifier elimination; it contrasts with Gödel's incompleteness for the ring of integers. Later geometric model theory produced deep applications, including Hrushovski's model-theoretic proof of the Mordell–Lang conjecture for function fields, and differential algebra is where model-theoretic ideas have had the most fruitful impact. ([Marker](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/mt-intro.html))

At the arithmetic end the central questions concern $\mathbb Q$ and local fields: Julia Robinson's 1949 first-order definition of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$ shows, with Gödel, that $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbb Q)$ is undecidable, while the decidability of the *existential* theory of $\mathbb Q$ (Hilbert's tenth problem over $\mathbb Q$) is a different and much harder question. ([Koenigsmann](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.0441))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 12L05 decidability and field theory (see also 03B25), 12L10 ultraproducts and field theory (see also 03C20), 12L12 model theory of fields (see also 03C60), 12L15 nonstandard arithmetic and field theory (see also 03H15), and 12L99. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Lxx))

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory) holds general model theory, with 03C60 as the cross-reference for model-theoretic algebra; [MSC 03Hxx - Nonstandard models](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models) is the cross-reference for nonstandard arithmetic; [MSC 11Uxx - Connections of number theory and logic](node:MSC%2011Uxx%20-%20Connections%20of%20number%20theory%20and%20logic) and [MSC 13Lxx - Applications of logic to commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013Lxx%20-%20Applications%20of%20logic%20to%20commutative%20algebra) are the analogous logic-interface codes for number theory and commutative algebra. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Lxx))

### Key concepts
- **Algebraically closed fields.** $\mathrm{ACF}_0$ and $\mathrm{ACF}_p$ are complete and have quantifier elimination in the ring language; consequently they are strongly minimal: every definable subset of a model in one variable, with parameters, is finite or cofinite. ([Berkeley notes](https://math.berkeley.edu/~ltomczak/notes/Lent2023/ModelTheory_Notes.pdf)) See [Model Theory of Fields](node:Model%20Theory%20of%20Fields) and [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic).
- **Ax–Grothendieck theorem.** An injective polynomial map $\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ is bijective; more generally injective regular self-maps of varieties over algebraically closed fields are bijective. Ax (1968) and Grothendieck (EGA IV, 1966) proved it independently; the logical proof reduces to the trivial finite-field case and transfers it to characteristic $0$ by compactness. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Grothendieck_theorem))
- **Ultraproducts and Łoś's theorem (12L10).** For structures $M_i$ and an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $I$, a first-order formula holds in $\prod M_i/\mathcal U$ iff the set of $i$ where it holds in $M_i$ lies in $\mathcal U$; ultraproducts of ordered fields are ordered fields, and the hyperreals arise as an ultrapower of $\mathbb R$, the basis of transfer in nonstandard analysis (12L15). ([Wikipedia, Ultraproduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraproduct)) See [Ultraproducts of Commutative Rings](node:Ultraproducts%20of%20Commutative%20Rings).
- **Pseudo-finite fields.** Ax introduced them in 1968 as the infinite models of the theory of finite fields; equivalently they are perfect, have exactly one extension of each degree, and are pseudo-algebraically closed (every absolutely irreducible variety has a rational point). Every non-principal ultraproduct of [Finite Fields](node:Finite%20Fields) is pseudo-finite. ([Wikipedia, Pseudo-finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-finite_field))
- **Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle.** Henselian [Valued Fields](node:Valued%20Fields) with residue fields of characteristic $0$ are elementarily equivalent when their residue fields and value groups are; hence non-principal ultraproducts of the $\mathbb Q_p$ and of the $\mathbb F_p((t))$ are elementarily equivalent, and Lang's theorem that $\mathbb F_p((t))$ is $C_2$ transfers to give the Ax–Kochen theorem (1965): for each $d$, for all but finitely many primes $p$, every form of degree $d$ over $\mathbb Q_p$ in at least $d^2+1$ variables has a nontrivial zero. ([Wikipedia, Ax–Kochen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem)) In equal characteristic $p$, Anscombe and Fehm proved an existential AKE principle, giving decidability of the existential theory of $\mathbb F_q((t))$. ([Anscombe–Fehm](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.04522))
- **Definability of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$.** Robinson gave a first-order definition (1949), Poonen a $\forall\exists$ definition with two universal quantifiers (2009), and Koenigsmann a purely universal one; no quantifier-free definition exists, and whether an existential one exists is open. ([Koenigsmann](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.0441)) See [Hilbert's Tenth Problem](node:Hilbert's%20Tenth%20Problem).
- **Differentially closed fields.** $\mathrm{DCF}_0$ is complete, model complete and eliminates quantifiers (A. Robinson, 1959), and every differential field of characteristic $0$ has a differential closure unique up to isomorphism (Shelah). ([Wikipedia, DCF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentially_closed_field)) See [Differential Fields](node:Differential%20Fields), and [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields) for Tarski's theorem.

### History
Tarski proved the decidability of the real field by quantifier elimination; Julia Robinson defined $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$ in 1949; and Abraham Robinson introduced differentially closed fields in 1959. ([Marker](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/mt-intro.html); [Koenigsmann](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.0441); [Wikipedia, DCF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentially_closed_field)) Ax and Kochen proved their theorem in 1965, Terjanian found a 2-adic counterexample to Artin's conjecture in 1966, and Ax's 1968 Annals paper on the elementary theory of finite fields introduced pseudo-finite fields. ([Wikipedia, Ax–Kochen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem); [Wikipedia, Pseudo-finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-finite_field)) Matiyasevich completed the MRDP theorem in 1970, settling Hilbert's tenth problem over $\mathbb Z$ negatively. ([Wikipedia, H10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem))

### Open problems
- **Decidability of $\mathbb F_p((t))$.** Koenigsmann calls it one of the big open problems in model theory, and Kuhlmann's survey lists a complete axiomatization and decidability of $\mathbb F_p((t))$ as open; unconditionally, only its existential theory in the language of valued fields is known to be decidable. ([Koenigsmann](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.0441); [Kuhlmann](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.06386))
- **Existential definability of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$.** Koenigsmann states that whether $\mathbb Z$ is existentially definable in $\mathbb Q$ is open, and that Mazur's conjecture and the Bombieri–Lang conjecture each imply it is not; he also asks whether the ring of integers of $\mathbb T(\sqrt{-1})$, with $\mathbb T$ the totally real numbers, is decidable. ([Koenigsmann](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.0441))
- **Hilbert's tenth problem over $\mathbb Q$.** Koenigsmann's 2013 survey calls the solvability of H10 over $\mathbb Q$ the most prominent open problem in the field. ([Koenigsmann](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.0441))

> [!warning] Contested
> A preprint dated 24 September 2026, part of an OpenAI release of more than 700 manuscripts produced by an internal language model, claims a proof that Hilbert's tenth problem over $\mathbb Q$ is unsolvable; OpenAI stated that not all results in the release were formalized in Lean and that unformalized results could contain errors. ([Wikipedia, H10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem))
> MathWorld reports further 2026 manuscripts claiming a Diophantine (existential) definition of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q$, which would make solvability over $\mathbb Q$ undecidable: an AI-assisted manuscript by Glazer with a degree-four definition, a claimed unconditional degree-four definition by Burungale, a congruent-number twist approach by Jaswal, variable bounds by Z.-W. Sun that depend on arithmetic inputs from the OpenAI manuscripts, and a definition by Kozachinskiy, Pasten and Vidaux conditional on the abc conjecture, Dickson's conjecture and finiteness of 2-primary Tate–Shafarevich groups. It notes that the accompanying Lean formalization rests on unproved premises and that independent specialist verification has not been reported. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/HilbertsTenthProblem.html)) Since Mazur's conjecture and the Bombieri–Lang conjecture each imply that $\mathbb Z$ is not Diophantine in $\mathbb Q$ ([Koenigsmann](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.0441)), a correct Diophantine definition would refute both; treat both questions as open until expert review is published.

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Ax–Kochen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem): transfer principle and its arithmetic application.
- **Learn:** [Cambridge Part III model theory notes](https://math.berkeley.edu/~ltomczak/notes/Lent2023/ModelTheory_Notes.pdf): quantifier elimination and strong minimality of ACF.
- **Primary:** [Koenigsmann, Undecidability in number theory](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.0441): survey of definability and decidability in $\mathbb Q$ and related fields, with open questions.
- **Primary:** [Kuhlmann, Model theory of tame valued fields and beyond](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.06386): survey of valued-field model theory and open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Marker, Model Theory: An Introduction](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~marker/mt-intro.html): graduate text with fields as the central examples.
references.MSC 13 - Commutative algebra:
## Reference
### Overview
Commutative algebra studies commutative rings, their ideals, and modules over such rings. Polynomial rings, rings of algebraic integers, and $p$-adic integers are central examples, and the subject is "the main technical tool of algebraic geometry" while also underlying [algebraic number theory](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields). ([Commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra)) Its basic objects are [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals), [Modules over Commutative Rings](node:Modules%20over%20Commutative%20Rings), [localization](node:Localization%20of%20Rings), and the prime spectrum with its Zariski topology, which is the starting point of [scheme theory](node:Schemes). ([Commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra); [Lurie–Mathew, Lectures 2–4](https://math.uchicago.edu/~amathew/CAnotes.pdf))

The research core is the local and homological theory of Noetherian rings: dimension, depth, regularity, Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein rings, completions, and the "homological conjectures" relating these invariants, of which the direct summand conjecture was proved by André using perfectoid spaces. Standard treatments cover dimension theory, regular sequences, regular rings, flatness, and complete local rings. ([Matsumura, contents](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/commutative-ring-theory/02819830750568B06C16E6199F3562C1); [Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra))

### Scope
The MSC2020 section 13-XX, Commutative algebra, has thirteen subfields: [13A general commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Axx%20-%20General%20commutative%20ring%20theory); [13B ring extensions](node:MSC%2013Bxx%20-%20Commutative%20ring%20extensions%20and%20related%20topics); [13C modules and ideals](node:MSC%2013Cxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20modules%20and%20ideals%20in%20commutative%20rings); [13D homological methods](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory); [13E chain and finiteness conditions](node:MSC%2013Exx%20-%20Chain%20conditions,%20finiteness%20conditions%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory); [13F arithmetic and other special rings](node:MSC%2013Fxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20rings%20and%20other%20special%20commutative%20rings); [13G integral domains](node:MSC%2013Gxx%20-%20Integral%20domains); [13H local and semilocal rings](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings); [13J topological rings and modules](node:MSC%2013Jxx%20-%20Topological%20rings%20and%20modules); [13L applications of logic](node:MSC%2013Lxx%20-%20Applications%20of%20logic%20to%20commutative%20algebra); [13M finite rings](node:MSC%2013Mxx%20-%20Finite%20commutative%20rings); [13N differential algebra](node:MSC%2013Nxx%20-%20Differential%20algebra); and [13P computational aspects and applications](node:MSC%2013Pxx%20-%20Computational%20aspects%20and%20applications%20of%20commutative%20rings). ([MSC2020 13-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13-XX))

Its main neighbours are [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry), for which commutative algebra is the main technical tool, and [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), through rings of algebraic integers and $p$-adic integers. ([Commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra))

### Key concepts
- **Noetherian rings and Hilbert's basis theorem (13E).** A ring is Noetherian if every ideal is finitely generated; polynomial rings over a field are Noetherian (Hilbert's basis theorem). In a Noetherian ring every ideal $I$ is a finite intersection of primary ideals with distinct radicals, and the set of radicals is the same for every irredundant decomposition (Lasker–Noether). ([Commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra)) See [Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings).
- **Hilbert's Nullstellensatz.** For an algebraically closed field $K$ and any ideal $J\subseteq K[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, $I(V(J))=\sqrt J$; in weak form, a proper ideal has a common zero in $K^n$. Hilbert proved it in 1893. It follows from Zariski's lemma, that a field finitely generated as an algebra over $K$ is a finite extension of $K$, and it is subsumed by the theory of Jacobson rings, those in which every radical ideal is an intersection of maximal ideals: a finitely generated algebra over a Jacobson ring is again Jacobson. ([Hilbert's Nullstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_Nullstellensatz)) It is the dictionary between radical ideals and [Algebraic Varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties).
- **Krull's principal ideal and height theorems; dimension theory (13C, 13H).** In a Noetherian ring every minimal prime over a proper principal ideal has height at most one; more generally, every minimal prime over an ideal generated by $n$ elements has height at most $n$, and conversely a prime of height $n$ is minimal over some ideal generated by $n$ elements. ([Krull's principal ideal theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%27s_principal_ideal_theorem)) For a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ the fundamental theorem of dimension theory says $\dim R$ equals the least number of generators of an $\mathfrak m$-primary ideal and the order of the pole at $t=1$ of the Poincaré series of $\mathrm{gr}_{\mathfrak m}R$; in particular $\dim R\le\dim_k\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2<\infty$, and $\dim k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]=n$. ([Dimension theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_theory_%28algebra%29)) The commutative algebra article calls the principal ideal theorem "the single most important foundational theorem in commutative algebra". ([Commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra))
- **Regular local rings and the Auslander–Buchsbaum–Serre theorem (13H, 13D).** A Noetherian local ring is regular if the minimal number of generators of its maximal ideal equals its Krull dimension (equality in the bound above). Serre proved that a Noetherian local ring is regular if and only if it has finite global dimension, which then equals its Krull dimension; consequently every localization of a regular local ring at a prime is regular. Auslander and Buchsbaum proved that every regular local ring is a unique factorization domain. ([Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring); [Global dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_dimension)) A polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field has global dimension $n$, a result going back to Hilbert's foundational work on homological properties of polynomial rings. ([Global dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_dimension)) See [Local Rings](node:Local%20Rings), [Tor and Ext over Commutative Rings](node:Tor%20and%20Ext%20over%20Commutative%20Rings), and [Unique Factorization Domains](node:Unique%20Factorization%20Domains).
- **Completions and the Cohen structure theorem (13J, 13H).** The $I$-adic completion of $R$ is $\varprojlim R/I^n$; the completion of a Noetherian ring is flat over it, and the completion of a Noetherian local ring at its maximal ideal is a Noetherian local ring. ([Complete local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_local_ring)) Cohen structure theorem: if $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is a complete local ring with $\mathfrak m$ finitely generated, then $R\cong\Lambda[\![x_1,\ldots,x_n]\!]/I$, where $\Lambda$ is a field or a Cohen ring; if $R$ contains a field, $R\cong k[\![x_1,\ldots,x_n]\!]/I$ with $k$ the residue field. ([Stacks, Tag 032A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/032A); [Complete local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_local_ring)) See [Adic Completion](node:Adic%20Completion).
- **Direct summand conjecture (13D, 13B).** Hochster's conjecture: if a regular ring $R$ sits inside a module-finite extension ring $S$, then $R$ is a direct summand of $S$ as an $R$-module. Yves André proved it in mixed characteristic using Scholze's perfectoid spaces (arXiv 2016; Publ. Math. IHÉS 2018), and Bhatt gave a shorter proof and proved a derived variant proposed by de Jong. ([Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra); [André, arXiv:1609.00345](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00345); [Bhatt, arXiv:1608.08882](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08882))
- **Computational commutative algebra (13P).** [Gröbner Bases](node:Gröbner%20Bases), introduced by Buchberger in 1965, make ideal membership, elimination, and syzygy computations effective in polynomial rings. ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis))

### History
Dedekind's ideal theory, building on Kummer and Kronecker, started the subject. Hilbert introduced the term "ring" and the abstract approach; Emmy Noether recast the theory around the ascending chain condition; Lasker introduced primary ideals and proved the first form of the Lasker–Noether theorem; and Krull introduced localization, completion, and Krull dimension. Grothendieck's schemes, from the late 1950s, built algebraic geometry on prime spectra. ([Commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra)) Krull defined regular local rings in 1937, and Zariski later showed that they correspond to smooth points of varieties. ([Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring))

### Open problems
- **Serre's positivity conjecture.** Let $R$ be a regular local ring and $P,Q$ primes with $\ell_R(R/P\otimes_RR/Q)<\infty$, and $\chi(R/P,R/Q)=\sum_i(-1)^i\ell_R\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(R/P,R/Q)$. Serre proved $\dim R/P+\dim R/Q\le\dim R$; vanishing of $\chi$ when the inequality is strict was proved by Roberts (1985) and Gillet–Soulé (1987), and non-negativity by Gabber (1995). Positivity, $\chi(R/P,R/Q)>0$ when $\dim R/P+\dim R/Q=\dim R$, "remains open" in general. ([Serre's multiplicity conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_multiplicity_conjectures)) KC and Soto Levins (2024) prove new cases over ramified regular local rings for "Serre liftable" modules. ([KC–Soto Levins, arXiv:2404.17572](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.17572))
- **Remaining homological conjectures.** The list of homological conjectures includes the existence of small Cohen–Macaulay modules (for a complete local ring, a nonzero finitely generated module on which every system of parameters is a regular sequence), stated there as a conjecture. ([Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Commutative algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra): scope, history, basic theorems.
- **Reference:** [Homological conjectures in commutative algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra): list of conjectures and the direct summand theorem.
- **Learn:** [Lurie (lectures) and Mathew (notes), Commutative Algebra, Harvard 2010](https://math.uchicago.edu/~amathew/CAnotes.pdf): graduate course with proofs, including the Nullstellensatz, completions, dimension theory, and regular local rings.
- **Primary:** [André, La conjecture du facteur direct](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00345): perfectoid proof of the direct summand conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Bhatt, On the direct summand conjecture and its derived variant](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08882): shorter proof and derived variant.
- **Further reading:** [Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/commutative-ring-theory/02819830750568B06C16E6199F3562C1): dimension theory, regular sequences, regular rings, complete local rings.
- **Further reading:** [Eisenbud, Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry (Springer GTM, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-5350-1): the standard graduate text linking commutative algebra and geometry.

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 13A is general commutative ring theory. In MSC2020 it covers graded rings, divisibility and factorization, ideals and multiplicative ideal theory, valuations, Rees algebras and analytic spread, characteristic-$p$ (Frobenius) methods and tight closure, group actions and invariant theory, and the [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) of rings such as zero-divisor graphs. ([MSC2020 13Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Axx); [MSC2020 13-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13-XX))

Hochster and Huneke's tight closure (13A35) gives simple proofs of the Hochster–Roberts theorem, the Briançon–Skoda theorem, the Evans–Griffith syzygy theorem and the equicharacteristic monomial conjecture, and has applications to singularities, vanishing theorems and adjoint linear series in algebraic geometry. ([Smith, Introduction to Tight Closure](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209378); [Tight closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_closure)) In invariant theory (13A50), Hilbert's fourteenth problem asks when rings of invariants are finitely generated. ([Hilbert's fourteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fourteenth_problem))

### Scope
The codes are 13A02 graded rings [see also 16W50]; 13A05 divisibility and factorizations [see also 13F15]; 13A15 ideals and multiplicative ideal theory; 13A18 valuations and their generalizations [see also 12J20]; 13A30 associated graded rings of ideals (Rees ring, form ring), analytic spread; 13A35 characteristic $p$ methods (Frobenius endomorphism), reduction to characteristic $p$, tight closure [see also 13B22]; 13A50 actions of groups on commutative rings, invariant theory [see also 14L24]; 13A70 commutative ring theory and combinatorics (zero-divisor graphs, annihilating-ideal graphs) [see also 05C25, 05E40]; and 13A99. ([MSC2020 13Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Axx))

Neighbours in [MSC 13](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra): [13B](node:MSC%2013Bxx%20-%20Commutative%20ring%20extensions%20and%20related%20topics) ring extensions (including integral closure), [13C](node:MSC%2013Cxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20modules%20and%20ideals%20in%20commutative%20rings) modules and ideals, 13D homological methods, 13E chain and finiteness conditions, [13F](node:MSC%2013Fxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20rings%20and%20other%20special%20commutative%20rings) special rings such as Dedekind, Krull and factorial rings, [13G](node:MSC%2013Gxx%20-%20Integral%20domains) [integral domains](node:Integral%20Domains), and [13H](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings) [local rings](node:Local%20Rings). ([MSC2020 13-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Noetherian foundations.** $R$ is Noetherian if every ideal is finitely generated, equivalently if ascending chains of ideals stabilize. Hilbert's basis theorem: if $R$ is Noetherian so is $R[X]$, hence $R[X_1,\dots,X_n]$. A polynomial ring $K[X_1,X_2,\dots]$ in infinitely many variables over a field $K$ is not Noetherian; it is the standard example of a non-Noetherian ring. In a nonzero Noetherian ring every proper ideal is a finite intersection of primary ideals (Lasker 1905 for polynomial rings; Noether in general). ([Conrad, Thms 3.1, 3.6, 3.25](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ringtheory/noetherian-ring.pdf)) Basic ideal theory is in [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals).
- **Krull's principal ideal theorem and Nakayama's lemma (13A15).** In a Noetherian ring, every minimal prime over a proper ideal generated by $n$ elements has height at most $n$ (for $n=1$: height $\le1$); conversely a prime of height $n$ is minimal over some $n$-generated ideal. ([Krull's principal ideal theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%27s_principal_ideal_theorem)) Nakayama: if $M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module and $IM=M$, there is $r\equiv1\pmod I$ with $rM=0$; hence $J(R)M=M$ forces $M=0$, and over a local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$ any basis of $M/\mathfrak mM$ lifts to a minimal generating set of $M$. ([Nakayama's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakayama%27s_lemma))
- **Valuations (13A18).** A domain $V$ with fraction field $F$ is a valuation ring if $x\in V$ or $x^{-1}\in V$ for every $x\in F^\times$; equivalently its ideals are totally ordered, or (Krull) it is a local Bézout domain. A valuation ring is Noetherian iff it is a PID, and a Noetherian non-field valuation ring is a DVR with value group $\mathbb Z$. The integral closure of a domain $A$ is the intersection of the valuation rings of its fraction field containing $A$, and the Krull dimension of $V$ equals the height of its value group. ([Valuation ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_ring))
- **Factorization (13A05).** A domain is atomic if every nonzero nonunit is a product of irreducibles; UFDs and Noetherian domains are atomic. ACCP implies atomic but not conversely (Grams 1974, against a claim of Cohn), BFD is strictly stronger than ACCP, and HFD and FFD are strictly stronger than BFD without implying unique factorization. ([Atomic domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_domain))
- **Rees algebras and analytic spread (13A30).** For an ideal $I\subseteq R$, the Rees algebra is $R[It]=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}I^nt^n\subseteq R[t]$ and the associated graded ring is $\operatorname{gr}_I(R)=R[It]/IR[It]$; $\operatorname{Proj}R[It]$ is the blow-up of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ along $V(I)$. For $(R,\mathfrak m)$ Noetherian local, the analytic spread of $I$ is $\dim R[It]/\mathfrak mR[It]$, and for $J\subseteq I$ in a Noetherian ring, $R[Jt]\subseteq R[It]$ is integral iff $J$ is a reduction of $I$. ([Rees algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rees_algebra))
- **Tight closure (13A35).** For $R$ Noetherian containing a field of characteristic $p>0$, $z\in I^*$ if there is $c$ outside every minimal prime with $cz^{p^e}\in I^{[p^e]}$ for all $e\gg0$; $R$ is weakly F-regular if every ideal is tightly closed, and F-regular if this holds in every localization. ([Tight closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_closure)) Main properties: in a regular ring every ideal is tightly closed; $\overline{I^\mu}\subseteq I^*$ if $I$ has $\mu$ generators (and always $I^*\subseteq\bar I$), which gives the Briançon–Skoda theorem $\overline{I^\mu}\subseteq I$ for regular rings containing a field; colon capturing; persistence. If $R\subseteq S$ splits as $R$-modules and $S$ is (weakly) F-regular, so is $R$; hence a direct summand of a regular ring containing a field is Cohen–Macaulay. For an excellent local domain of characteristic $p$, the absolute integral closure $R^+$ is a Cohen–Macaulay $R$-module. ([Smith, §2, Thms 2.3, 2.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209378))
- **Invariant theory (13A50).** Invariant rings of reductive groups acting on finitely generated algebras are finitely generated (Hilbert, Weyl and successors), but Hilbert's fourteenth problem has a negative answer in general: Nagata gave counterexamples in 1958–59, Roberts in 1990, and Kuroda gave a counterexample in $n=3$ variables in 2005, the smallest possible since Zariski proved finite generation when the transcendence degree is at most $2$. ([Hilbert's fourteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fourteenth_problem)) Hochster–Roberts (1974): the invariant ring of a linearly reductive group acting linearly on a regular ring is Cohen–Macaulay; in characteristic $p$ even finite groups can have non-Cohen–Macaulay invariant rings. ([Hochster–Roberts theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochster%E2%80%93Roberts_theorem)) Tight closure gives a short proof via the Reynolds operator splitting. ([Smith, Cor. 2.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209378))
- **Zero-divisor graphs (13A70).** In the Anderson–Livingston graph, whose vertices are the nonzero zero divisors of the ring, $x\sim y$ iff $xy=0$; it is connected with diameter at most $3$ and girth at most $4$ when it has a cycle. Beck's 1988 conjecture that clique number equals chromatic number was disproved by Anderson and Naseer (1993). ([Zero-divisor graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-divisor_graph)) This is the commutative-algebra side of [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory).

### History
Noether's 1921 paper developed ideal theory from the finiteness condition, proving its equivalence with the ascending chain condition; Chevalley introduced the name "Noetherian ring" in 1943. ([Conrad](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ringtheory/noetherian-ring.pdf)) Krull's special case of Nakayama's lemma was generalized by Azumaya, and Nakayama introduced the present form in 1951. ([Nakayama's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakayama%27s_lemma)) Nagata's counterexamples to Hilbert's fourteenth problem appeared in 1958–59, and Hochster and Roberts proved their theorem in 1974. ([Hilbert's fourteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fourteenth_problem); [Hochster–Roberts theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochster%E2%80%93Roberts_theorem)) Hochster and Huneke introduced tight closure in 1988 and 1990, and Brenner and Monsky (2010) showed that tight closure does not commute with localization, settling what Smith had called probably the biggest open problem of the theory. ([Tight closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_closure); [Smith](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209378))

### Open problems
- **Weakly F-regular versus F-regular.** It is still unknown whether every weakly F-regular ring is F-regular, i.e. whether the property that all ideals are tightly closed passes to localizations. ([Tight closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_closure)) Smith records the known cases: Gorenstein rings (Hochster–Huneke), $\mathbb Q$-Gorenstein rings and rings with isolated non-$\mathbb Q$-Gorenstein points (MacCrimmon), dimension at most three (these under mild hypotheses such as excellence), and finitely generated $\mathbb N$-graded algebras over a field (Lyubeznik–Smith). ([Smith, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209378))
- **Log-canonical singularities and F-split type.** Smith poses, as an open problem with deep connections to number theory, whether a variety with log-canonical singularities has F-split type. ([Smith, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209378))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Tight closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_closure): definitions of tight closure and F-regularity; with [Valuation ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_ring) and [Hilbert's fourteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fourteenth_problem).
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.705 Commutative Algebra (Kleiman)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-705-commutative-algebra-fall-2008/): Noetherian rings, integral dependence, localization, primary decomposition, DVRs and dimension theory; with [Conrad, Noetherian rings](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ringtheory/noetherian-ring.pdf).
- **Primary:** [Smith, An Introduction to Tight Closure (arXiv math/0209378)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0209378): survey of tight closure, its main properties, applications and open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Atiyah and Macdonald, *Introduction to Commutative Algebra* (CRC reissue, 2018)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9780429493638) and [Matsumura, *Commutative Ring Theory* (CUP, 1987)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139171762): the standard texts.
references.MSC 13Bxx - Commutative ring extensions:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 13Bxx collects the study of a commutative ring $A$ together with an $A$-algebra $B$, usually an extension $A\subseteq B$: how primes, dimension, and finiteness properties of $A$ and $B$ compare. It generalizes the comparison of a field with an extension field. The central relation is integrality: $b\in B$ is integral over $A$ if it is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $A$, and $A\to B$ is integral if every element of $B$ is. ([MSC2020 13Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Bxx); [Stacks, integral ring maps](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00GH))

Beyond integrality, the section covers the extensions that algebraic geometry uses to pass between rings: localization, completion, flat and étale extensions, Henselization, and Artin approximation. Geometrically, a ring map $A\to B$ corresponds to a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$, and properties such as integrality, flatness, and étaleness become properties of that morphism.
