([MSC2020 13Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Bxx); [Stacks, étale ring maps](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00U0))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists these codes ([MSC2020 13Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Bxx)):
- **13B02** extension theory of commutative rings; **13B05** Galois theory and commutative ring extensions; **13B10** morphisms of commutative rings.
- **13B21** integral dependence, going up and going down; **13B22** integral closure of rings and ideals, integrally closed rings and related rings (Japanese, etc.).
- **13B25** polynomials over commutative rings; **13B30** rings of fractions and localization; **13B35** completion of commutative rings (see also 13J10).
- **13B40** étale and flat extensions, Henselization, Artin approximation (see also 13J15, 14B12, 14B25); **13B99** other.

Neighbouring sections of MSC 13 ([MSC2020 13](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13-XX)): [13Axx](node:MSC%2013Axx%20-%20General%20commutative%20ring%20theory) treats general ring theory of a single ring rather than the comparison along an extension; [13Cxx](node:MSC%2013Cxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20modules%20and%20ideals%20in%20commutative%20rings) treats modules and ideals; [13Hxx](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings) treats local rings themselves; [13Jxx](node:MSC%2013Jxx%20-%20Topological%20rings%20and%20modules) treats topological rings, where completion is also cross-listed; and [14Bxx](node:MSC%2014Bxx%20-%20Local%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) is the geometric counterpart of the étale-local material in 13B40.

### Key concepts
- **Finite versus integral.** A finite ring map is integral, and $A\to B$ is finite if and only if it is integral and of finite type. The elements of $B$ integral over $A$ form an $A$-subalgebra, the integral closure of $A$ in $B$. So $A[x]$ is of finite type over $A$ but not finite. See [Integral Ring Extensions](node:Integral%20Ring%20Extensions) and [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals). ([Stacks, integral ring maps](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00GH))
- **Cohen–Seidenberg theorems.** For an integral extension $A\subseteq B$: lying over ($\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ is surjective), going up (a chain $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak p'$ in $A$ and $\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak p$ extend to $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak q'$ over $\mathfrak p'$), and incomparability (distinct primes over the same prime are incomparable). Consequently $\dim A=\dim B$. ([Stacks, integral ring maps](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00GH); [Integral element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_element))
- **Going down.** Going down holds for $A\subseteq B$ if $B$ is integral over $A$, $B$ is a domain, and $A$ is integrally closed in its fraction field. Going down also holds for every flat ring map, with no integrality hypothesis. ([Going up and going down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Going_up_and_going_down); [Mustață, Prop. 10.13](https://websites.umich.edu/~mmustata/CAnotes.pdf))
- **Noether normalization.** If $k$ is a field and $A$ a finitely generated $k$-algebra, there are algebraically independent $y_1,\dots,y_d\in A$ with $A$ finite over $k[y_1,\dots,y_d]$; here $d=\dim A$, and for a domain $d$ is the transcendence degree of $\operatorname{Frac}A$ over $k$. ([Noether normalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether_normalization_lemma); [Mustață, Thm. 6.1](https://websites.umich.edu/~mmustata/CAnotes.pdf))
- **Finiteness of integral closure.** If $A$ is a finitely generated domain over a field and $L$ is a finite extension of $\operatorname{Frac}A$, the integral closure of $A$ in $L$ is a finite $A$-module (proved via Noether normalization). Krull–Akizuki: if $A$ is a one-dimensional reduced noetherian ring with total ring of fractions $K$, $L$ is finite over $K$, and $A\subseteq B\subseteq L$ with $B$ reduced, then $B$ is noetherian of dimension $\le1$; so the integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite extension of its fraction field is Dedekind. In general finiteness fails: Nagata gave a three-dimensional noetherian domain whose integral closure is not noetherian. ([Integral element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_element); [Krull–Akizuki theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%E2%80%93Akizuki_theorem))
- **Galois transitivity.** If $A$ is integrally closed with fraction field $K$, $L/K$ is finite normal with group $G$, and $B$ is the integral closure of $A$ in $L$, then $G$ acts transitively on the primes of $B$ over each prime of $A$. Compare [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory) and [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields). ([Integral element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_element))
- **Localization and completion.** See [Localization of Rings](node:Localization%20of%20Rings) and [Adic Completion](node:Adic%20Completion). The $I$-adic completion is $\hat R=\varprojlim R/I^n$; for noetherian $R$ it is noetherian and flat over $R$. A complete noetherian local ring containing a field is a quotient of a formal power series ring $k[\![x_1,\dots,x_n]\!]$, $k$ the residue field (Cohen structure theorem). ([Completion of a ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_of_a_ring))
- **Étale maps and Henselization.** $R\to S$ is étale if it is of finite presentation and its naive cotangent complex is quasi-isomorphic to zero; equivalently it is smooth of relative dimension zero, and it is flat. A local ring is Henselian if [Hensel's Lemma](node:Hensel's%20Lemma) holds for it; the Henselization of a local ring $A$ is the universal Henselian local ring under $A$, flat over $A$, with the same residue field and completion. See [Flat Modules](node:Flat%20Modules) and [Local Rings](node:Local%20Rings). ([Stacks, étale ring maps](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00U0); [Henselian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henselian_ring))
- **Artin approximation.** Artin (1968): if $F(x,y)$ is a vector of convergent power series over $\mathbb C$ and $\hat y(x)$ is a formal solution of $F(x,y)=0$, then for every $c$ there is a convergent solution agreeing with $\hat y$ modulo $(x)^c$. Popescu's general Néron desingularization theorem (a regular morphism $A\to B$ of noetherian rings lets any $A$-algebra map from a finitely generated $C$ to $B$ factor through a smooth finitely generated $A$-algebra) yields the same approximation for polynomial equations over any excellent Henselian pair. ([Rond, Artin approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04717))

### History
Cohen and Seidenberg published "Prime ideals and integral dependence" in the *Bulletin of the AMS* 52 (1946), 252–261; the going-up and going-down theorems for integral extensions are named after them. Noether introduced normalization in 1926; a widely used proof is due to Nagata. Azumaya introduced Henselian rings in 1951 and Nagata introduced Henselization in 1953. Artin proved his approximation theorem for convergent power series in 1968 and conjectured it for more general rings; Popescu's work of 1985–86 proved the general Néron desingularization theorem. ([Crossref, Cohen–Seidenberg](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1946-08552-3); [Going up and going down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Going_up_and_going_down); [Noether normalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether_normalization_lemma); [Henselian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henselian_ring); [Rond, Artin approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04717))

### Open problems
- **Effective bounds in strong Artin approximation.** Artin proved that the approximation order $\beta$ needed to lift an approximate solution to a true one can be chosen to depend only on the degrees of the equations, but Rond's survey states that "it is still an open problem to find effective bounds" on $\beta$. ([Rond, Artin approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04717))
- **Strong approximation for general ideals.** The survey states that it is "still an open question" under which conditions on an ideal $I$ the pair $(A,I)$ satisfies the strong approximation theorem when $A$ is a general excellent Henselian local ring; A. More settled the case of equicharacteristic excellent regular Henselian local rings (exactly when $I$ is $\mathfrak m$-primary). ([Rond, Artin approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04717))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, integral ring maps](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00GH) and [étale ring maps](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00U0): complete statements and proofs.
- **Learn:** [Mustață, Math 614 notes](https://websites.umich.edu/~mmustata/CAnotes.pdf): integral extensions, Noether normalization, flatness and going down.
- **Primary:** [Rond, Artin Approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04717): research survey of approximation, Henselian and excellent rings, with open problems; and [Cohen–Seidenberg 1946](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1946-08552-3), the original going-up/going-down paper.
- **Further reading:** [Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/commutative-ring-theory/02819830750568B06C16E6199F3562C1): the standard graduate text; its chapter 3 is on properties of extension rings.
references.MSC 13Cxx - Theory of modules and ideals:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 13C is the part of [commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra) that classifies modules and ideals over commutative rings: projective, free, injective, flat and torsion modules; Cohen–Macaulay modules; depth and dimension; class groups; and linkage, complete intersections and determinantal ideals. ([MSC2020 13Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Cxx))

Its organizing invariant is depth. For a finitely generated module $M$ over a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$, all maximal $M$-regular sequences in $\mathfrak m$ have the same length, the depth of $M$, and $\operatorname{depth}M\le\dim M$. Modules with equality are the Cohen–Macaulay modules; Cohen–Macaulay rings share some algebro-geometric properties of smooth varieties, such as local equidimensionality. ([Wikipedia: Depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth_%28ring_theory%29); [Wikipedia: Cohen–Macaulay ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Macaulay_ring))

### Scope
The MSC2020 codes in 13C are: ([MSC2020 13Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Cxx))
- **13C05** structure and classification theorems for modules and ideals;
- **13C10** projective and free modules and ideals (see also 19A13, $K_0$);
- **13C11** injective and flat modules; **13C12** torsion modules; **13C13** other special types;
- **13C14** Cohen–Macaulay modules (see also 13H10, Cohen–Macaulay local rings);
- **13C15** dimension theory, depth, and related rings such as catenary rings;
- **13C20** class groups (see also 11R29, class groups of number fields);
- **13C40** linkage, complete intersections and determinantal ideals (see also 14M06, 14M10, 14M12);
- **13C60** module categories; **13C70** modules and ideals described by combinatorial properties (see also 05C25, 05E40).

Neighbouring codes: free resolutions, Ext/Tor and homological dimensions are [13D](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory); local rings themselves, including Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein rings, are [13H](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings); class groups cross-reference 11R29; linkage, complete intersections and determinantal ideals cross-reference 14M06, 14M10 and 14M12. ([MSC2020 13Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Cxx); [MSC2020 13Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Dxx); [MSC2020 13Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Hxx))

### Key concepts
- **Modules over a PID** (13C05): every finitely generated module $M$ over a principal ideal domain $R$ is $M\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^n R/(d_i)$ with $(d_1)\supseteq\cdots\supseteq(d_n)$ proper, i.e. $d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots\mid d_n$, the $d_i$ unique up to units; equivalently a sum of $R/(p_i^{r_i})$ and free summands. Over a Dedekind domain the torsion part is still unique, but torsion-free modules are sums of rank-one projectives classified by rank and Steinitz class in the ideal class group. ([Wikipedia: Structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structure_theorem_for_finitely_generated_modules_over_a_principal_ideal_domain)) Generalizes [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) and the theory of abelian groups in [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory).
- **Projective modules: Quillen–Suslin** (13C10): every finitely generated projective module over $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, $k$ a field, is free. Serre asked this in 1955 and proved in 1957 that such modules are stably free; Quillen and Suslin independently proved freeness in 1976. ([Wikipedia: Quillen–Suslin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem); [Crossref: Quillen 1976](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01390008))
- **Depth and Auslander–Buchsbaum** (13C15): depth is also $\min\{i:\operatorname{Ext}^i_R(R/\mathfrak m,M)\ne0\}$. If $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is Noetherian local and $M\neq 0$ is finitely generated of finite projective dimension, then $\operatorname{pd}_R M+\operatorname{depth}M=\operatorname{depth}R$. ([Wikipedia: Depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth_%28ring_theory%29)) This ties 13C to [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra).
- **Cohen–Macaulay modules** (13C14): $M\ne0$ is Cohen–Macaulay if $\operatorname{depth}M=\dim M$, and maximal Cohen–Macaulay if moreover $\dim M=\dim R$. Regular local rings, Gorenstein rings (including complete intersections), and quotients of a regular local ring by the ideal of $r\times r$ minors of a matrix when that ideal has the expected codimension are Cohen–Macaulay. A Noetherian ring is Cohen–Macaulay iff every ideal generated by height-many elements is unmixed (Macaulay 1916 for polynomial rings, Cohen 1946 for power series rings). ([Wikipedia: Cohen–Macaulay ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Macaulay_ring)) By the Hochster–Roberts theorem (1974), rings of invariants of linearly reductive groups acting on regular rings are Cohen–Macaulay; Boutot's theorem on rational singularities recovers this in characteristic 0, while in characteristic $p>0$ there are reductive, even finite, groups acting on polynomial rings with non-Cohen–Macaulay invariant rings. ([Wikipedia: Hochster–Roberts theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochster%E2%80%93Roberts_theorem))
- **Injectives and Matlis duality** (13C11): for a complete Noetherian local ring $R$ with residue field $k$ and injective hull $E$ of $k$, $M\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,E)$ is an anti-equivalence between Noetherian and Artinian $R$-modules, restricting to finite-length modules. Matlis introduced the general theory of injective modules over Noetherian rings in 1958. ([Wikipedia: Matlis duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matlis_duality))
- **Class groups** (13C20): for a Krull domain $A$ (a domain that is the finite-character intersection of the DVRs $A_\mathfrak p$ over its height-one primes), the class group is Weil divisors modulo principal divisors, and $A$ is a UFD exactly when every height-one prime is principal. Every UFD and every integrally closed Noetherian domain is Krull. ([Wikipedia: Krull ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_ring)) The quadric cone $xy=z^2$ has class group $\mathbb Z/2$, generated by a line through the vertex that is not principal there. ([Wikipedia: Divisor class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor_class_group)) Compare [MSC 13Fxx - Arithmetic rings and other special commutative rings](node:MSC%2013Fxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20rings%20and%20other%20special%20commutative%20rings).

### History
Macaulay's 1916 unmixedness theorem for polynomial rings and Cohen's 1946 extension to power series rings gave Cohen–Macaulay rings their name. ([Wikipedia: Cohen–Macaulay ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Macaulay_ring)) Krull introduced Krull domains in 1931 as higher-dimensional analogues of Dedekind domains. ([Wikipedia: Krull ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_ring)) Serre's 1955 question on projective modules over polynomial rings was answered by Quillen and Suslin in 1976. ([Wikipedia: Quillen–Suslin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem)) Of the homological conjectures, the direct summand conjecture was proved by André using perfectoid spaces (*Publ. Math. IHÉS* 127, 2018). ([Wikipedia: Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra))

### Open problems
- **Hochster's small Cohen–Macaulay module conjecture.** Hochster conjectured (1975) that every complete Noetherian local domain has a small Cohen–Macaulay module: a nonzero finitely generated module whose depth equals $\dim R$. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SmallCohen-MacaulayModule.html); [Wikipedia: Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra)) Schoutens proved it for three-dimensional complete F-pure rings. ([arXiv 1408.6212](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.6212))

> [!warning] Contested
> A September 2026 preprint by Liang Chen proposes a local-cohomology obstruction and claims that a specific three-dimensional local ring has no nonzero finite maximal Cohen–Macaulay module, which would be a counterexample. MathWorld reports the claim without treating it as an established resolution; the preprint has not been shown to be verified. ([arXiv 2609.24142](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24142); [MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SmallCohen-MacaulayModule.html))

- **Bass–Quillen conjecture.** The generalization of Quillen–Suslin from fields to regular Noetherian rings $A$ (finitely generated projective $A[x_1,\dots,x_n]$-modules should be extended from $A$) is stated as a conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Quillen–Suslin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem)) Popescu records positive answers in dimensions 1 and 2 (Quillen, Suslin, Murthy), for many regular local rings by Lindel and Swan, and for a regular local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ when $p=\operatorname{char}k$ satisfies $p=0$ or $p\notin\mathfrak m^2$; he poses a question about regular local rings essentially smooth over $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ whose positive answer would give a complete positive answer to the conjecture. ([arXiv 1810.00617](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00617))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cohen–Macaulay ring (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Macaulay_ring): definitions, examples, unmixedness, miracle flatness.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.705 Commutative Algebra (Kleiman)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-705-commutative-algebra-fall-2008/): Noetherian modules, localization, primary decomposition, DVRs, length, Hilbert polynomials and dimension theory.
- **Primary:** [Quillen, Projective modules over polynomial rings, *Invent. Math.* 36 (1976)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01390008): the solution of Serre's problem.
- **Further reading:** [Bruns–Herzog, *Cohen–Macaulay Rings* (CUP, 1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511608681): the standard monograph on depth, Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein rings and modules.
references.MSC 13Dxx - Homological methods in commu:
## Reference
### Overview
Homological methods study a commutative ring $R$ and its modules through free and projective resolutions, the derived functors Tor, Ext and local cohomology, and the numerical invariants these produce (projective dimension, depth, Betti numbers, regularity). The early central results were homological characterizations of ring-theoretic properties: the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula (1957) relating projective dimension to depth, and Serre's theorem that a Noetherian local ring is regular exactly when it has finite global dimension. ([Wikipedia: Auslander-Buchsbaum formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auslander%E2%80%93Buchsbaum_formula); [Wikipedia: Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring))

The area has two research strands. One studies resolutions themselves: minimal free resolutions, their Betti numbers and lower bounds for them, and, over singular rings, infinite free resolutions, the topic of Avramov's "Infinite Free Resolutions" (in *Six Lectures on Commutative Algebra*, 1998); Poincaré series have their own code 13D40. ([Boocher-Grifo, Lower bounds on Betti numbers](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.05871); [Crossref record for Avramov](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0346-0329-4_1); [MSC2020 13Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Dxx)) The other is the cluster of "homological conjectures" for Noetherian local rings, which has its own MSC code 13D22 and saw the direct summand conjecture proved by André with perfectoid methods. ([MSC2020 13Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Dxx); [Wikipedia: Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra))

### Scope
MSC2020 13Dxx (for noncommutative rings see 16Exx; for general categories see 18Gxx) has these codes: 13D02 syzygies, resolutions, complexes; 13D03 (co)homology of commutative rings and algebras (Hochschild, André-Quillen, cyclic, dihedral); 13D05 homological dimension; 13D07 homological functors on modules (Tor, Ext); 13D09 derived categories; 13D10 deformations and infinitesimal methods (see also 14B10, 14B12, 14D15, 32Gxx); 13D15 Grothendieck groups and $K$-theory (see also 14C35, 18F30, 19Axx, 19D50); 13D22 homological conjectures (intersection theorems); 13D30 torsion theory (see also 13C12, 18E40); 13D40 Hilbert-Samuel and Hilbert-Kunz functions, Poincaré series; 13D45 local cohomology (see also 14B15); 13D99. ([MSC2020 13Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Dxx))

Neighbours: general [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) in arbitrary abelian categories is 18Gxx, and homological methods for noncommutative rings are 16Exx, per the 13Dxx header note. Local cohomology in algebraic geometry is cross-listed to 14B15 in [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry). Regular local rings (13H05) and Cohen-Macaulay and Gorenstein rings (13H10) are classified in [MSC 13Hxx - Local rings and semilocal rings](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings), while dimension theory and depth (13C15) and torsion modules (13C12, cross-referenced from 13D30) are in [MSC 13Cxx - Theory of modules and ideals in commutative rings](node:MSC%2013Cxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20modules%20and%20ideals%20in%20commutative%20rings). ([MSC2020 13Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Dxx); [MSC2020 13Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Hxx); [MSC2020 13Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Auslander-Buchsbaum formula (13D05).** Let $R$ be a Noetherian local ring and $M$ a nonzero finitely generated $R$-module of finite projective dimension. Then $\operatorname{pd}_R M+\operatorname{depth}M=\operatorname{depth}R$. ([Stacks, Proposition 10.111.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/090U)) Auslander and Buchsbaum proved it in "Homological dimension in local rings" (Trans. AMS, 1957). ([Wikipedia: Auslander-Buchsbaum formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auslander%E2%80%93Buchsbaum_formula))
- **Serre's regularity criterion.** A Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is regular when $\mathfrak m$ needs exactly $\dim R$ generators. Serre proved that $R$ is regular if and only if it has finite global dimension. Every localization of a regular local ring at a prime, and its completion, is again regular. Auslander and Buchsbaum proved that regular local rings are unique factorization domains. ([Wikipedia: Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring)) This ties the area to [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals).
- **Koszul complexes and regular sequences (13D02, 13D07).** For $f_1,\dots,f_r\in R$, the sequence is $M$-Koszul-regular if $H_i(K_\bullet(f_1,\dots,f_r)\otimes_RM)=0$ for $i\ne0$. Every $M$-regular sequence is $M$-Koszul-regular, and if $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is Noetherian local, $M\ne0$ is finite and all $f_i\in\mathfrak m$, then $M$-regular, $M$-Koszul-regular, $M$-$H_1$-regular and $M$-quasi-regular are equivalent. ([Stacks, Section 15.31](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/062D))
- **Local cohomology (13D45).** $H^i_I(M)$ are the right derived functors of the $I$-torsion functor $\Gamma_I$. Grothendieck's vanishing theorem gives $H^i_I(M)=0$ for $i>\dim M$; for $R$ local and $M$ finitely generated, $H^{\dim M}_{\mathfrak m}(M)\ne0$, and the least $i$ with $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M)\ne0$ is $\operatorname{depth}M$. Hence $M$ is Cohen-Macaulay iff exactly one $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M)$ is nonzero. Local duality: for $R$ Cohen-Macaulay local of dimension $d$ and a quotient of a Gorenstein local ring, $H^n_{\mathfrak m}(M)$ is dual to $\operatorname{Ext}^{d-n}_R(M,\omega_R)$. ([Wikipedia: Local cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_cohomology))
- **Betti numbers and regularity (13D02, 13D40).** For a finitely generated graded module over a polynomial ring with minimal graded free resolution whose $j$-th module has generators of maximal degree $b_j$, the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity is $\max_j(b_j-j)$; Mumford introduced $r$-regularity in 1966, attributing the key results to Castelnuovo (1893). ([Wikipedia: Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castelnuovo%E2%80%93Mumford_regularity)) Equivalently it is $\sup_i(\operatorname{end}H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M)+i)$ over $0\le i\le\dim M$. ([Wikipedia: Local cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_cohomology))
- **Homological conjectures (13D22).** The direct summand conjecture states that if $R\subseteq S$ is a module-finite extension with $R$ regular, then $R$ is a direct summand of $S$ as an $R$-module; it was proved by Yves André using perfectoid spaces (Publ. Math. IHÉS, 2018). ([Wikipedia: Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra)) André's argument reduces to unramified complete regular local rings of mixed characteristic and works in Scholze's perfectoid theory. ([André, arXiv:1609.00345](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00345))
- **Total rank theorem.** If $M$ is nonzero of finite length and finite projective dimension over a local ring of dimension $d$, Walker proved $\sum_i\beta_i(M)\ge2^d$ in a large number of cases (2017). ([Walker, arXiv:1702.02560](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.02560)) The Boocher-Grifo survey (2021) records that the bound holds whenever the residue characteristic is not 2, with only a weaker bound $2(\sqrt3)^{d-1}$ then known in residue characteristic 2. ([Boocher-Grifo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.05871)) VandeBogert and Walker subsequently proved a stronger form of the total rank conjecture for rings of characteristic two (to appear in Duke Math. J.). ([VandeBogert-Walker, arXiv:2305.09771](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.09771))

### History
Auslander and Buchsbaum's 1957 paper introduced the formula, and Serre's criterion characterized regular local rings homologically. ([Wikipedia: Auslander-Buchsbaum formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auslander%E2%80%93Buchsbaum_formula); [Wikipedia: Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring)) Grothendieck introduced local cohomology in a 1961 Harvard seminar, written up by Hartshorne, and in SGA 2. ([Wikipedia: Local cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_cohomology)) Bruns and Herzog's *Cohen-Macaulay Rings* (Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 39, revised edition 1998) covers local cohomology, canonical modules and Hochster's big Cohen-Macaulay modules with their applications to intersection theorems. ([Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cohenmacaulay-rings/938BC2204D8A7C99E2CEBA1695A692A4))

### Open problems
- **Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks conjecture.** If $M$ is a nonzero module of finite length and finite projective dimension over a local ring of dimension $d$, then $\beta_i(M)\ge\binom di$. ([Walker, arXiv:1702.02560](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.02560)) Boocher and Grifo state that it "remains widely open in the general setting"; it is known in codimension at most 4 and for multigraded modules and monomial ideals, but for codimension at least 5 it is open, and it is unknown, for example, whether $\beta_2\ge10$ for a cyclic module of codimension 5. ([Boocher-Grifo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.05871))
- **Serre's positivity conjecture.** For $R$ regular local of dimension $d$ and finitely generated $M,N$ with $\ell(M\otimes N)<\infty$, the intersection multiplicity $\chi(M,N)=\sum_i(-1)^i\ell(\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M,N))$ should be positive when $\dim M+\dim N=d$. ([Wikipedia: Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra)) Serre proved positivity for unramified regular local rings, and vanishing (Gillet-Soulé, Roberts) and nonnegativity (Gabber) are proved for all regular rings, but "positivity remains an open conjecture for ramified regular local rings"; recent work proves it there for "Serre liftable" modules. ([KC-Soto Levins, arXiv:2404.17572](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.17572); [KC-Soto Levins, §1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.17572))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Homological conjectures in commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra): list of the conjectures and their relations.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Local cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_cohomology): definition, vanishing theorems, local duality.
- **Learn:** [Stacks Project, Auslander-Buchsbaum](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/090U): complete proof of the formula; see also [Koszul-regular sequences](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/062D).
- **Primary:** [Boocher-Grifo, Lower bounds on Betti numbers](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.05871): survey of the Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks and total rank problems.
- **Primary:** [Walker, Total Betti numbers of modules of finite projective dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.02560): the total rank theorem.
- **Primary:** [André, La conjecture du facteur direct](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00345): proof of the direct summand conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Bruns-Herzog, Cohen-Macaulay Rings (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cohenmacaulay-rings/938BC2204D8A7C99E2CEBA1695A692A4) and [Avramov, Infinite Free Resolutions (1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0346-0329-4_1).
references.MSC 13Exx - Chain conditions, finiteness:
## Reference
### Overview
Chain and finiteness conditions control the ideals and submodules of a ring rather than the size of the ring itself. A commutative ring is Noetherian if every ascending chain of ideals stabilizes, equivalently if every ideal is finitely generated; it is Artinian if every descending chain of ideals stabilizes. The main structure theorems depend on them: Lasker-Noether primary decomposition is a theorem about Noetherian rings, dimension theory behaves poorly without the Noetherian hypothesis (Krull's principal ideal theorem depends on it), and the Krull intersection theorem fails without it. ([Wikipedia: Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring); [Wikipedia: Krull's intersection theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%27s_intersection_theorem))

Beyond the Noetherian world the area studies weaker finiteness conditions. A ring is coherent if every finitely generated ideal is finitely presented; much of the theory of finitely generated modules over Noetherian rings carries over to finitely presented modules over coherent rings. A monograph on the subject is Sarah Glaz, *Commutative Coherent Rings* (Lecture Notes in Mathematics, 1989). ([Wikipedia: Coherent ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_ring); [Crossref record for Glaz](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0084570))

### Scope
MSC2020 13Exx has four codes: 13E05 commutative Noetherian rings and modules; 13E10 commutative Artinian rings and modules, finite-dimensional algebras; 13E15 commutative rings and modules of finite generation or presentation, number of generators; 13E99. The entry lists no cross-references. ([MSC2020 13Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Exx))

Neighbours in [MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra): structure and classification of modules and ideals, projective and flat modules, and dimension theory and depth (13C05, 13C10, 13C11, 13C15) belong to [MSC 13Cxx - Theory of modules and ideals in commutative rings](node:MSC%2013Cxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20modules%20and%20ideals%20in%20commutative%20rings); regular, Cohen-Macaulay and Gorenstein local rings and multiplicity theory (13H05, 13H10, 13H15) to [MSC 13Hxx - Local rings and semilocal rings](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings); resolutions and homological dimension (13D02, 13D05) to [MSC 13Dxx - Homological methods in commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory). ([MSC2020 13Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Cxx); [MSC2020 13Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Hxx); [MSC2020 13Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Dxx))

### Key concepts
- **Hilbert basis theorem and stability (13E05).** If $R$ is Noetherian then $R[X]$ is, hence $R[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ is. Quotients and localizations of commutative Noetherian rings are Noetherian, and over a commutative Noetherian ring every ideal is a finite intersection of primary ideals (Lasker-Noether). ([Wikipedia: Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring)) This is the finiteness behind [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals).
- **Cohen's theorem and Eakin-Nagata (13E05, 13E15).** A commutative ring is Noetherian as soon as every prime ideal is finitely generated (Cohen); finite generation of the maximal ideals alone does not suffice. If $A\subseteq B$ with $B$ commutative Noetherian and finitely generated as an $A$-module, then $A$ is Noetherian (Eakin-Nagata); this fails for noncommutative rings. ([Wikipedia: Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring))
- **Artinian rings (13E10).** An Artinian ring is Noetherian (for one-sided Artinian rings this is the Akizuki-Hopkins-Levitzki theorem), and a commutative Noetherian ring is Artinian iff it has Krull dimension zero, iff it is a finite product of Artinian local rings; examples are $k[t]/(t^n)$, $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ and $A/I$ for a nonzero ideal $I$ of a Dedekind domain. ([Wikipedia: Artinian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artinian_ring)) An Artinian ring has finitely many maximal ideals and nilpotent Jacobson radical, and a ring is Artinian iff it has finite length as a module over itself. ([Stacks, Section 10.53](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00J4))
- **Krull's theorems.** *Principal ideal theorem:* in a Noetherian ring, every minimal prime over a proper principal ideal has height at most one; more generally a minimal prime over an ideal generated by $n$ elements has height at most $n$, and conversely every prime of height $n$ is minimal over some $n$-generated ideal. ([Wikipedia: Krull's principal ideal theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%27s_principal_ideal_theorem)) *Intersection theorem:* for $I$ an ideal of a commutative Noetherian ring $A$ and $M$ a finitely generated module, some $x\in1+I$ annihilates $N=\bigcap_nI^nM$; hence $\bigcap_nI^n=0$ for a proper ideal when $A$ is local or a domain. The proof uses the Artin-Rees lemma. ([Wikipedia: Krull's intersection theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%27s_intersection_theorem))
- **Dimension and its limits.** In a Noetherian ring every prime has finite height, and $\dim R[x]=\dim R+1$ for Noetherian $R$ (without the Noetherian hypothesis, if $\dim R=n$ then $\dim R[x]$ can be anything from $n+1$ to $2n+1$); yet Nagata gave a Noetherian ring of infinite Krull dimension. ([Wikipedia: Krull dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_dimension))
- **Coherent rings (13E15).** Every Noetherian ring is coherent but not conversely: a polynomial ring in infinitely many variables over a Noetherian ring is coherent and not Noetherian. Chase's theorem (1960): a ring is coherent iff every direct product of flat modules is flat. ([Wikipedia: Coherent ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_ring))

### History
Hilbert recognized the importance of the finiteness condition through his basis theorem, and the rings are named after Emmy Noether. ([Wikipedia: Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring)) Noether's "Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen" appeared in *Mathematische Annalen* 83 (March 1921), 24-66. ([Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01464225)) It treats decompositions of an ideal into irreducible and primary ideals, the associated primes, and the corresponding notions for modules; Berlyne's English translation was posted in 2014. ([arXiv:1401.2577](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.2577)) Chase's characterization of coherence dates from 1960. ([Wikipedia: Coherent ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_ring))

### Open problems
The collection "Open problems in commutative ring theory" (Cahen, Fontana, Frisch, Glaz; draft of 23 December 2013) lists the following problems on finiteness conditions ([Cahen-Fontana-Frisch-Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf)):
- **Vasconcelos' question (Problem 3).** Is the integral closure of a one-dimensional coherent domain in its field of quotients a Prüfer domain? The collection says it has been answered positively in many, but not all, cases. ([Cahen-Fontana-Frisch-Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf)) A 2026 preprint that answers several problems of the collection does not address it. ([arXiv:2605.25259](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25259))
- **Finite conductor versus quasi-coherent (Problem 4b).** $R$ is a finite conductor ring if $aR\cap bR$ and $(0:c)$ are finitely generated for all $a,b,c\in R$, and quasi-coherent if $a_1R\cap\dots\cap a_nR$ and $(0:c)$ are finitely generated for all $a_i,c$; both classes contain all coherent rings, UFDs and GCD domains. Are the two properties distinct? ([Cahen-Fontana-Frisch-Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf)) The same 2026 preprint gives negative answers to the companion ascent questions for group rings (Problem 4a) but does not address Problem 4b. ([arXiv:2605.25259](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25259))
- **Quasi-completeness (Problem 8a), recently answered.** A Noetherian local ring $(R,M)$ is quasi-complete if for every decreasing sequence of ideals $A_n$ and every $k$ there is $s_k$ with $A_{s_k}\subseteq(\bigcap_nA_n)+M^k$, and weakly quasi-complete if this holds for sequences with $\bigcap_nA_n=0$; complete local rings are quasi-complete (Chevalley). ([Cahen-Fontana-Frisch-Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf)) The 2026 preprint constructs a weakly quasi-complete ring that is not quasi-complete (its Theorem 3.3); this claim is recent and not yet refereed. ([arXiv:2605.25259](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25259))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring): equivalent definitions, Hilbert, Cohen and Eakin-Nagata theorems.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Artinian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artinian_ring): Hopkins-Levitzki and the structure theorem for commutative Artinian rings.
- **Learn:** [Stacks Project, Section 10.53 Artinian rings](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00J4): full proofs on Artinian rings and finite length.
- **Primary:** [Noether, Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen, Math. Ann. 83 (1921)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01464225); [English translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.2577).
- **Primary:** [Cahen-Fontana-Frisch-Glaz, Open problems in commutative ring theory](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf): problem list covering Noetherian and non-Noetherian rings.
- **Further reading:** [Glaz, Commutative Coherent Rings (LNM, 1989)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0084570): monograph on coherent rings.
references.MSC 13Fxx - Arithmetic rings and other s:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 13F collects classes of commutative rings singled out by arithmetic, valuation-theoretic or combinatorial structure: Dedekind, Prüfer, Krull and Mori rings; Euclidean and principal ideal rings; rings defined by factorization properties; polynomial and integer-valued polynomial rings; formal power series and valuation rings; Witt vectors; excellent and seminormal rings; Hodge algebras; Stanley–Reisner rings; cluster algebras; and binomial and toric rings. ([MSC2020 13Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Fxx))

### Scope
The MSC2020 codes are: ([MSC2020 13Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Fxx))
- **13F05** Dedekind, Prüfer, Krull and Mori rings and their generalizations; **13F07** Euclidean rings and generalizations; **13F10** principal ideal rings.
- **13F15** commutative rings defined by factorization properties (e.g., atomic, factorial, half-factorial) (see also 13A05, 14M05).
- **13F20** polynomial rings and ideals; rings of integer-valued polynomials (see also 11C08, 13B25); **13F25** formal power series rings (see also 13J05); **13F30** valuation rings (see also 13A18).
- **13F35** Witt vectors and related rings; **13F40** excellent rings; **13F45** seminormal rings; **13F50** rings with straightening laws, Hodge algebras.
- **13F55** commutative rings defined by monomial ideals; Stanley–Reisner face rings; simplicial complexes (see also 55U10); **13F60** cluster algebras; **13F65** commutative rings defined by binomial ideals, toric rings, etc. (see also 14M25); **13F70** other combinatorially defined rings; **13F99**.

Neighbours, one line each:
- [13G05](node:MSC%2013Gxx%20-%20Integral%20domains) is the catch-all for [integral domains](node:Integral%20Domains); 13F takes the named special classes. ([MSC2020 13Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Gxx))
- [13C](node:MSC%2013Cxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20modules%20and%20ideals%20in%20commutative%20rings) holds class groups (13C20) and projective modules (13C10). ([MSC2020 13Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Cxx))
- [13A](node:MSC%2013Axx%20-%20General%20commutative%20ring%20theory) holds divisibility and factorization in general rings (13A05, cross-referenced to 13F15) and valuations on rings (13A18, cross-referenced to 12J20). ([MSC2020 13Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Axx))
- Formal power series rings point to [13J05](node:MSC%2013Jxx%20-%20Topological%20rings%20and%20modules), and toric rings to [14M25](node:MSC%2014Mxx%20-%20Special%20varieties) (toric varieties). ([MSC2020 13Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Dedekind domains and Krull–Akizuki (13F05).** An integral domain in which every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely into primes; equivalently (for a non-field) an integrally closed Noetherian domain of Krull dimension one, or a Noetherian domain whose localizations at maximal ideals are DVRs. A Dedekind domain is a UFD iff it is a PID iff its class group is trivial; by Claborn's theorem every abelian group is the class group of some Dedekind domain; and $K_0(R)\cong\mathbb Z\oplus\operatorname{Cl}(R)$ via Steinitz classes. ([Wikipedia: Dedekind domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_domain)) **Krull–Akizuki theorem:** if $A$ is a one-dimensional reduced Noetherian ring with total ring of fractions $K$, $L$ a finite extension of $K$, and $A\subset B\subset L$ with $B$ reduced, then $B$ is Noetherian of dimension at most one, and $B/I$ is finite over $A$ for every nonzero ideal $I$; hence the integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite extension of its fraction field is Dedekind. ([Wikipedia: Krull–Akizuki theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%E2%80%93Akizuki_theorem)) Rings of integers are the motivating case: see [MSC 11Rxx - Algebraic number theory - global fields](node:MSC%2011Rxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20global%20fields) and [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals).
- **Prüfer and valuation domains (13F05, 13F30).** $V$ is a valuation domain if for every nonzero $x$ in its fraction field, $x\in V$ or $x^{-1}\in V$; its ideals are totally ordered, and by a theorem of Krull a domain is a valuation ring iff it is a [local](node:Local%20Rings) Bézout domain. The integral closure of a domain $A$ in its fraction field is the intersection of the valuation rings containing $A$. ([Wikipedia: Valuation ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_ring)) A Prüfer domain is one in which every nonzero finitely generated ideal is invertible; equivalently every localization at a prime is a valuation domain, or every torsion-free module is flat. Dedekind domains are exactly the Noetherian Prüfer domains; the ring of entire functions and $\operatorname{Int}(\mathbb Z)=\{f\in\mathbb Q[X]:f(\mathbb Z)\subseteq\mathbb Z\}$ are non-Noetherian Prüfer domains. ([Wikipedia: Prüfer domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%BCfer_domain))
- **Krull domains (13F05).** $A$ is Krull if $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a DVR for each height-one prime $\mathfrak p$, $A=\bigcap_{\mathfrak p}A_{\mathfrak p}$, and each nonzero element lies in finitely many height-one primes. [UFDs](node:Unique%20Factorization%20Domains) and integrally closed Noetherian domains are Krull; if $A$ is Krull so are $A[x]$ and the power series ring $A[\![x]\!]$; a polynomial ring in infinitely many variables over a UFD is Krull but not Noetherian; a Krull domain is a UFD iff every height-one prime is principal. **Mori–Nagata theorem:** the integral closure of a Noetherian domain in a finite extension of its fraction field is a Krull domain. ([Wikipedia: Krull ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_ring))
- **Factorization theory (13F15).** For domains, UFD $\Rightarrow$ HFD and FFD; HFD, FFD $\Rightarrow$ BFD $\Rightarrow$ ACCP $\Rightarrow$ atomic, all strict. ([Wikipedia: Atomic domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_domain)) **Carlitz's theorem:** a ring of algebraic integers has class number at most 2 iff it is half-factorial; $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, with class number 2 and $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$, is half-factorial but not a UFD. ([Chapman, arXiv 1903.04606](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1903.04606))
- **Witt vectors (13F35).** For a prime $p$ and a commutative ring $R$, a Witt vector is a sequence $(X_0,X_1,\dots)$ in $R$ with ring operations determined by the ghost components $W_n=\sum_{i=0}^np^iX_i^{p^{n-i}}$. $W(\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb Z_p$, and $W(\mathbb F_{p^n})$ is the ring of integers of the unramified extension of $\mathbb Q_p$ of degree $n$. $W$ is a representable functor, fully faithful on perfect rings of characteristic $p$. ([Wikipedia: Witt vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_vector)) Compare [p-adic Numbers](node:p-adic%20Numbers).
- **Stanley–Reisner rings (13F55).** For a simplicial complex $\Delta$ on $n$ vertices, $k[\Delta]=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I_\Delta$ with $I_\Delta$ generated by the squarefree monomials of non-faces; the numerator of its Hilbert series is the $h$-vector of $\Delta$; Stanley used face rings to prove the Upper Bound Conjecture for simplicial spheres. ([Wikipedia: Stanley–Reisner ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley%E2%80%93Reisner_ring)) **Reisner's theorem:** for a field $k$ and a finite complex $\Sigma$, $k[\Sigma]$ is Cohen–Macaulay iff $\tilde H_i(\operatorname{lk}\sigma;k)=0$ for every face $\sigma\in\Sigma$ and every $i<\dim\operatorname{lk}\sigma$, and $\tilde H_i(\Sigma;k)=0$ for every $i<\dim\Sigma$ (reduced homology, with $\dim\varnothing=-1$). ([Baggio, arXiv math/0505581, Prop. 1.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0505581)) See [MSC 05Exx - Algebraic combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Exx%20-%20Algebraic%20combinatorics).
- **Cluster algebras (13F60).** Introduced by Fomin and Zelevinsky "in an attempt to create an algebraic framework for dual canonical bases and total positivity in semisimple groups". ([arXiv math/0104151](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104151)) A cluster algebra is generated inside an ambient field by all clusters reachable from an initial seed by mutation, each mutation an exchange relation $xx'=M_1+M_2$ with coprime monomials $M_1,M_2$. **Laurent phenomenon (Thm 3.1):** every cluster variable is a Laurent polynomial in the variables of any given cluster; the authors conjectured that these Laurent polynomials have positive coefficients. ([Fomin–Zelevinsky, Cluster algebras I](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0104151)) Lee and Schiffler proved this positivity conjecture for all skew-symmetric cluster algebras. ([arXiv 1306.2415](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.2415v3)) Cluster algebras of finite type (finitely many seeds) are classified by Dynkin diagrams of finite-dimensional simple [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras). ([Wikipedia: Cluster algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluster_algebra))
- **Toric rings (13F65).** The affine [toric variety](node:Toric%20Varieties) of a cone $\sigma$ is the spectrum of the monoid algebra of the lattice points of the dual cone, and toric varieties built from fans are normal. ([Wikipedia: Toric variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toric_variety)) **Hochster's theorem** (Ann. Math. 96, 1972, Thm 1): if an affine semigroup $H$ is normal, $K[H]$ is Cohen–Macaulay. ([arXiv 1006.5670](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1006.5670))
- **Excellent rings (13F40).** Excellent means Noetherian, universally catenary and quasi-excellent (a G-ring and J-2). Nagata's examples (e.g. a normal Noetherian local ring that is not analytically normal) motivated the definition. Complete Noetherian local rings, Dedekind domains of characteristic 0, and finitely generated algebras over excellent rings are excellent. ([Wikipedia: Excellent ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excellent_ring))

### History
Lamé's 1847 claimed proof of Fermat's Last Theorem assumed $\mathbb Z[\zeta_n]$ is a UFD, which Kummer had shown fails for $n=23$; Kummer's ideal numbers led to Dedekind's notion of ideal. ([Wikipedia: Dedekind domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_domain)) Krull introduced Krull domains in 1931. ([Wikipedia: Krull ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_ring)) Carlitz's theorem (Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 11) began quantitative and qualitative research on non-unique factorization. ([Chapman, arXiv 1903.04606](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1903.04606)) Grothendieck introduced excellent rings in 1965. ([Wikipedia: Excellent ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excellent_ring)) Fomin and Zelevinsky's foundational cluster-algebra papers appeared in 2002 and 2003. ([Wikipedia: Cluster algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluster_algebra))

### Open problems
From the collection of Cahen, Fontana, Frisch and Glaz (2014), classified under 13F05, 13F20 and 13F30 among other codes. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf))
- **Dimension of $\operatorname{Int}(D)$ (Problem 14).** For the ring of [integer-valued polynomials](node:Integer-Valued%20Polynomials) it is known that $\dim\operatorname{Int}(D)\ge\dim D[X]-1$; the upper bound "remains open" and is conjectured to be $\dim D[X]$. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf))
- **Flatness and freeness of $\operatorname{Int}(D)$ (Problem 19).** $\operatorname{Int}(D)$ is free over Dedekind domains and locally free, hence flat, over Krull and TV PvMD domains; is it flat (19a), or free (19b), over every domain? ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf)) A 2026 arXiv preprint by Haotian Ma, whose proof it says was completed by the Rethlas automated reasoning system and checked by the author, claims a negative answer: an explicit one-dimensional Noetherian local domain $D$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with $\operatorname{Int}(D)$ not flat over $D$. It is unrefereed, so the problem is best regarded as reportedly answered, pending confirmation. ([arXiv 2604.05922](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05922))
- **Bouvier's conjecture (Problem 37).** A finite-dimensional domain is Jaffard if $\dim D[X_1,\dots,X_n]=n+\dim D$ for all $n$. Computing the dimension of polynomial rings over Krull domains is called open in general, and Bouvier conjectured that finite-dimensional Krull, or even factorial, domains need not be Jaffard; the collection calls this "still elusively open" (37a). Problem 37b asks whether David's three-dimensional factorial domain $J$ is locally Jaffard; a negative answer would have proved the conjecture for factorial domains. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf)) A 2026 arXiv preprint by Jiang, Li, Sun, Wang, Xiao and Yu reports proofs, generated by the Rethlas automated reasoning system and then checked by human experts, that $J$ is locally Jaffard (37b) and of answers to Problems 4a(i), 4a(ii), 8a, 21 and 35; it does not address 37a. ([arXiv 2605.25259](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25259))
- **Local tameness and factorization in $\operatorname{Int}(D)$ (Problems 38, 39; both since answered).** Problem 38 asked whether every one-dimensional local Mori domain is locally tame, which was known when the conductor $(R:\widehat R)\ne0$, when $R$ is Noetherian, and in some Krull cases; Problem 39 asks to describe non-unique factorization in $\operatorname{Int}(D)$ for $D$ a DVR with finite residue field. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf)) Geroldinger and Roitman proved that every strongly primary domain is locally tame (Thm 3.9); one-dimensional local Mori domains are strongly primary, which answers Problem 38 in the affirmative. ([Geroldinger–Roitman, arXiv 1807.10683](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1807.10683)) Fadinger and Windisch proved that if $D$ is a Krull domain with a prime element $\pi$ such that $D/\pi D$ is finite, then $\operatorname{Int}(D)$ has a full system of multisets of lengths: for all $k\ge1$ and $1<n_1\le\dots\le n_k$ some $H\in\operatorname{Int}(D)$ has exactly $k$ essentially different factorizations, of lengths $n_1,\dots,n_k$; this covers DVRs with finite residue field and, in their words, solves Problem 39. ([Fadinger–Windisch, arXiv 2308.14535](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.14535))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Prüfer domain (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%BCfer_domain): characterizations and examples.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.705 Commutative Algebra (Kleiman)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-705-commutative-algebra-fall-2008/): Noetherian rings, integral dependence, localization, DVRs and dimension theory.
- **Primary:** [Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz, Open problems in commutative ring theory (2014)](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf): research problems on Prüfer, Krull, Mori and Jaffard domains, integer-valued polynomials and factorization; [Fomin–Zelevinsky, Cluster algebras I](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104151): the founding paper of 13F60.
- **Further reading:** [Matsumura, *Commutative Ring Theory* (Cambridge University Press)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139171762): the standard graduate text, including Krull and valuation rings; [Geroldinger–Halter-Koch, *Non-Unique Factorizations* (Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9781420003208): the standard monograph on factorization theory.
references.MSC 13Gxx - Integral domains:
## Reference
### Overview
An integral domain is a nonzero commutative ring in which the product of two nonzero elements is nonzero; equivalently, its zero ideal is prime. Every domain embeds in its field of fractions, the smallest field containing it, and every finite domain is a field. ([Wikipedia: Integral domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain))

MSC2020 gives 13G a single substantive code, 13G05 "Integral domains". Named special classes (Dedekind, Prüfer, Krull and Mori rings in 13F05, valuation rings in 13F30, rings defined by factorization properties such as atomic, factorial and half-factorial in 13F15) have their own codes in [13F](node:MSC%2013Fxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20rings%20and%20other%20special%20commutative%20rings). ([MSC2020 13Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Gxx); [MSC2020 13Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Fxx))

### Scope
The codes are 13G05 (integral domains) and 13G99 (none of the above), with no cross-references in the MSC entry. ([MSC2020 13Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Gxx)) Problem lists in the area mix 13G05 with 13F05, 13F20, 13A15 and 13A18. Typical topics are straight and divided domains, GCD and almost-GCD domains, Prüfer $v$-multiplication domains (PvMDs), $v$-domains, composite rings $D+XD_S[X]$, stable and Mori domains, and Jaffard domains. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf))

Neighbours: specific classes of rings are 13F; modules, class groups and depth are [13C](node:MSC%2013Cxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20modules%20and%20ideals%20in%20commutative%20rings); ideals and multiplicative ideal theory in commutative rings are 13A15, and valuations and their generalizations 13A18; the parent field is [MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra). ([MSC2020 13Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Fxx); [MSC2020 13Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Cxx); [MSC2020 13Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Axx))

### Key concepts
- **The classical hierarchy.** Integral domains $\supset$ integrally closed domains $\supset$ GCD domains $\supset$ UFDs $\supset$ PIDs $\supset$ Euclidean domains $\supset$ fields. ([Wikipedia: Integral domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain)) The basic ideal theory is in [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals).
- **Factorization without uniqueness.** A domain is *atomic* if every nonzero nonunit is a product of irreducibles. With ACCP (no infinite strictly ascending chain of principal ideals), BFD (bounded factorization lengths), HFD (all factorizations of an element have the same length) and FFD (finitely many non-associate divisors), UFD $\Rightarrow$ HFD, FFD $\Rightarrow$ BFD $\Rightarrow$ ACCP $\Rightarrow$ atomic, and none of these implications reverses. Cohn claimed that atomic implies ACCP; Grams (1974) showed it does not. ([Wikipedia: Atomic domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_domain))
- **GCD and Bézout domains.** In a GCD domain any two elements have a gcd (equivalently an lcm). UFDs and Bézout domains are GCD domains; GCD domains are integrally closed and Schreier, their irreducibles are prime, and a GCD domain with ACCP is exactly a UFD. If $R$ is GCD, so is $R[X]$. The ring of entire functions is Bézout but not a UFD. ([Wikipedia: GCD domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCD_domain))
- **Divisorial ideals and the $v$-operation.** For a nonzero fractional ideal $I$ with $(R:I)=\{x\in K:xI\subseteq R\}$, set $I_v=(R:(R:I))$, the intersection of the principal fractional ideals containing $I$; $I$ is divisorial if $I_v=I$. A Mori domain is a domain with ACC on divisorial ideals, and a local Krull domain is a DVR iff its maximal ideal is divisorial. ([Wikipedia: Divisorial ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisorial_ideal)) A $v$-domain is one where every nonzero finitely generated ideal is $v$-invertible, and a PvMD one where every such ideal is $t$-invertible. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf)) Krull and Mori rings are classified under 13F05. ([MSC2020 13Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Fxx))
- **Composite constructions as a source of examples.** For a multiplicative set $S\subseteq D$, $R=D+XD_S[X]$ (polynomials over $D_S$ with constant term in $D$) is a GCD domain iff $D$ is GCD and $\gcd(d,X)$ exists for all $d\ne0$; $R$ is a PvMD iff $D$ is a PvMD and $(d,X)$ is $t$-invertible for all $d\ne0$; if $D$ is a $v$-domain, $D_S$ need not be one. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf))
- **Overrings and valuation rings.** The integral closure of a domain $A$ in its fraction field is the intersection of the valuation rings of that field containing $A$. ([Wikipedia: Valuation ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_ring)) Prüfer domains are those whose localizations at primes are valuation domains; the ring of all algebraic integers and $\operatorname{Int}(\mathbb Z)=\{f\in\mathbb Q[X]:f(\mathbb Z)\subseteq\mathbb Z\}$ are Prüfer, while $\mathbb Z[X]$ is not. ([Wikipedia: Prüfer domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%BCfer_domain))
- **Jaffard domains and dimension.** A finite-dimensional domain $D$ is Jaffard if $\dim D[X_1,\dots,X_n]=n+\dim D$ for all $n$, equivalently if its Krull dimension equals its valuative dimension (the supremum of dimensions of valuation overrings). Noetherian domains, Prüfer domains, and universally catenarian domains are locally Jaffard. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf))

### History
Krull introduced Krull domains in 1931 as higher-dimensional analogues of Dedekind domains. ([Wikipedia: Krull ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_ring)) Cohn's 1968 paper introduced the term "atom" and claimed atomic domains satisfy ACCP; Grams refuted this in 1974. ([Wikipedia: Atomic domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_domain)) Anderson, Anderson and Zafrullah's paper *Factorization in integral domains* appeared in *J. Pure Appl. Algebra* 69 (1990). ([Crossref: AAZ 1990](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0022-4049%2890%2990074-R); [Wikipedia: Atomic domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_domain)) In 2026 a machine-assisted paper reported a solution to the almost-GCD problem (Problem 35) of the Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz list. ([arXiv 2605.25259](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25259))

### Open problems
Both items are from the Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz collection (2014) and are not among the problems the 2026 machine-assisted paper reports solving (4a, 8a, 21, 35, 37b). ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf); [arXiv 2605.25259](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25259))
- **Straight versus locally divided (Problem 13).** $D$ is *straight* if for every overring $S$ and prime $P$, $S/PS$ is torsion-free over $D/P$; $D$ is *divided* if $PD_P=P$ for all primes $P$. Does there exist a straight domain that is not locally divided? Relatedly: if $R_P$ and $R/P$ are straight, is $R+PR_P$ straight? ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf))
- **$v$-domains among composite rings (Problem 34).** Find necessary and sufficient conditions for $D+XD_S[X]$, or more generally $A+XB[X]$ for an extension $A\subseteq B$, to be a $v$-domain; in particular, prove or disprove that $D+XD_S[X]$ is a $v$-domain iff $D$ is a $v$-domain and $(d,X)$ is $v$-invertible for all $d\ne0$. ([Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Integral domain (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain): definitions, fraction fields and the hierarchy of domains; see also [Atomic domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_domain).
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.705 Commutative Algebra](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-705-commutative-algebra-fall-2008/): integral dependence, localization, DVRs and dimension theory.
- **Primary:** [Anderson–Anderson–Zafrullah, Factorization in integral domains, *J. Pure Appl. Algebra* 69 (1990)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0022-4049%2890%2990074-R): the 1990 paper on factorization properties of integral domains; [Cahen–Fontana–Frisch–Glaz, Open problems in commutative ring theory](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~glaz/Publications_Selected%20Articles/OpenProblemsInCommutativeRingTheory.Springer14.pdf): research problems on domains.
- **Further reading:** [Geroldinger–Halter-Koch, *Non-Unique Factorizations*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9781420003208): monograph on factorization in domains and monoids.
references.MSC 13Hxx - Local rings and semilocal ri:
## Reference
### Overview
A commutative ring is local if it has a unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$; equivalently its nonunits form an ideal, and $k=R/\mathfrak m$ is its residue field. Localizing a commutative ring at a prime ideal gives a local ring, and rings of germs of functions at a point are local, so [local rings](node:Local%20Rings) are the algebraic model of a neighbourhood of a point. ([Wikipedia, Local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring)) A commutative ring is semilocal if it has finitely many maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_1,\dots,\mathfrak m_n$; then by the [Chinese Remainder Theorem](node:Chinese%20Remainder%20Theorem) $R/J(R)\cong\prod_i R/\mathfrak m_i$, where $J(R)=\bigcap_i\mathfrak m_i$ is the [Jacobson radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical). ([Wikipedia, Semi-local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-local_ring))

Local algebra measures how far a Noetherian local ring is from being "smooth". The basic chain of ring classes is regular $\subset$ complete intersection $\subset$ Gorenstein $\subset$ Cohen–Macaulay, and each class is defined by homological or numerical invariants: such as dimension, depth, embedding dimension and injective dimension. ([Wikipedia, Cohen–Macaulay ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Macaulay_ring); [Wikipedia, Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring))

### Scope
MSC2020 13Hxx has four codes: 13H05 regular local rings; 13H10 special types (Cohen–Macaulay, Gorenstein, Buchsbaum, etc.), see also 14M05; 13H15 multiplicity theory and related topics, see also 14C17; and 13H99. ([MSC2020, 13Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Hxx))

Neighbouring codes, from their MSC entries:
- [MSC 13Dxx - Homological methods in commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory) holds resolutions, homological dimension, Tor and Ext, local cohomology, Hilbert–Samuel and Hilbert–Kunz functions (13D40), and the homological conjectures (intersection theorems, 13D22). ([MSC2020, 13Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Dxx))
- [MSC 13Jxx - Topological rings and modules](node:MSC%2013Jxx%20-%20Topological%20rings%20and%20modules) holds power series rings, completion (13J10) and Henselian rings (13J15). ([MSC2020, 13Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Jxx))
- [MSC 14Bxx - Local theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Bxx%20-%20Local%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) holds singularities, deformations, Artin approximation and formal neighbourhoods from the geometric side. ([MSC2020, 14Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Bxx))
- [MSC 16Lxx - Local rings and generalizations](node:MSC%2016Lxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20generalizations), under associative rings and algebras, holds noncommutative local and semilocal rings and perfect rings (16L30) and quasi-Frobenius rings (16L60). ([MSC2020, 16Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Lxx))

### Key concepts
- **Nakayama's lemma and embedding dimension.** If $I\subseteq J(R)$ and $M$ is finitely generated with $IM=M$, then $M=0$; over $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ a basis of $M/\mathfrak mM$ lifts to a minimal generating set of $M$. Hence $\dim_k\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ is the minimal number of generators of $\mathfrak m$, and $\dim R\le\dim_k\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. The finiteness hypothesis is needed: it fails for $R=k[\![x]\!]$, $M=k((x))$. ([Jiang, Thm 1.1, Cor. 1.5, Cor. 3.6](https://scms.fudan.edu.cn/dfiles/summerschool/lecture_note_5.pdf)) See [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals) and [Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings).
- **Dimension theory and Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity (13H15).** For a Noetherian local ring, $\dim R$ equals the least number of elements of $\mathfrak m$ generating an $\mathfrak m$-primary ideal (a system of parameters), the length of a maximal chain of primes, and $1+\deg$ of the polynomial agreeing with $\dim_k\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}$ for $n\gg0$. ([Jiang, Thm 3.4](https://scms.fudan.edu.cn/dfiles/summerschool/lecture_note_5.pdf)) For an $\mathfrak m$-primary ideal $I$ in a local ring of dimension $d$, $\ell(R/I^n)$ is eventually a polynomial whose leading term is $\frac{e}{d!}n^d$; the integer $e=e(I)$ is the multiplicity of $I$, and $e(\mathfrak m)$ is the multiplicity of $R$. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert–Samuel function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Samuel_function))
- **Regular local rings (13H05).** $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ is regular if $\dim R=\dim_k\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$, i.e. $\mathfrak m$ is generated by $\dim R$ elements; a regular system of parameters is then a regular sequence and $R$ is a domain. Example: $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ localized at the origin is regular, while $k[x,y]/(x^2-y^3)$ localized at the origin (a cusp) is not. ([Jiang, Def. 3.9, Cor. 3.11–3.12, Ex. 3.10](https://scms.fudan.edu.cn/dfiles/summerschool/lecture_note_5.pdf)) Other examples are fields, DVRs such as $\mathbb Z_p$, $k[\![X_1,\dots,X_d]\!]$, and $\mathbb Z[X]_{(2,X)}$, a regular local ring containing no field. ([Wikipedia, Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring))
- **Auslander–Buchsbaum–Serre theorem.** A Noetherian local ring is regular if and only if it has finite global dimension; then $\operatorname{gldim}R=\dim R$. Consequently localizations of regular local rings at primes are regular. ([Jiang, Thm 4.13, Cor. 4.9](https://scms.fudan.edu.cn/dfiles/summerschool/lecture_note_5.pdf); [Wikipedia, Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring)) Auslander and Buchsbaum also proved that every regular local ring is a UFD. ([Wikipedia, Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring)) See [Projective Resolutions](node:Projective%20Resolutions) and [Tor and Ext over Commutative Rings](node:Tor%20and%20Ext%20over%20Commutative%20Rings).
- **Auslander–Buchsbaum formula.** If $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is local and $M\neq0$ is finitely generated of finite projective dimension, then $\operatorname{pd}M=\operatorname{depth}R-\operatorname{depth}M$. ([Jiang, Thm 4.12](https://scms.fudan.edu.cn/dfiles/summerschool/lecture_note_5.pdf))
- **Cohen–Macaulay rings (13H10).** A nonzero finitely generated module $M$ over a Noetherian local ring is Cohen–Macaulay if $\operatorname{depth}M=\dim M$, and $R$ is Cohen–Macaulay if it is so as a module over itself. Regular rings, Artinian rings and one-dimensional reduced rings are Cohen–Macaulay. A Noetherian ring is Cohen–Macaulay iff the unmixedness theorem holds for it; in particular Cohen–Macaulay rings are equidimensional and have no embedded components, so $k[x,y]/(x^2,xy)$ (a line with an embedded point) is not Cohen–Macaulay. ([Wikipedia, Cohen–Macaulay ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Macaulay_ring))
- **Gorenstein rings (13H10).** A Noetherian local ring is Gorenstein if it has finite injective dimension over itself; it is then Cohen–Macaulay, and a zero-dimensional local ring is Gorenstein iff its socle is simple. Every complete intersection (in particular every regular local ring) is Gorenstein; $k[x,y]/(x^2,xy,y^2)$ is Cohen–Macaulay but not Gorenstein because its socle is $2$-dimensional. ([Wikipedia, Gorenstein ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorenstein_ring))
- **Cohen structure theorem.** A complete Noetherian local ring containing a field is $k[\![x_1,\dots,x_n]\!]/I$ with $k$ its residue field; in general it is a quotient of a power series ring over a Cohen ring (a field or a complete characteristic-$0$ DVR with maximal ideal generated by $p$) with the same residue field. Hence every complete Noetherian local ring is a quotient of a complete regular local ring, and a complete regular equicharacteristic local ring is a power series ring over a field. ([Wikipedia, Cohen structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen_structure_theorem)) See [Adic Completion](node:Adic%20Completion).
- **Henselian local rings (13J15).** A local ring is Henselian if Hensel's lemma holds for it (factorizations of monic polynomials over $k$ lift to $R$), equivalently every finite extension is a product of local rings; complete local rings are Henselian, and every local ring has a Henselization, an algebraic substitute for completion. ([Wikipedia, Henselian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henselian_ring)) See [Hensel's Lemma](node:Hensel's%20Lemma).
- **Serre's intersection multiplicity.** For a regular local ring $R$ and primes $P,Q$ with $\ell(R/P\otimes R/Q)<\infty$, Serre defined $\chi(R/P,R/Q)=\sum_i(-1)^i\ell(\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(R/P,R/Q))$ and proved $\dim R/P+\dim R/Q\le\dim R$. Vanishing of $\chi$ when the inequality is strict was proved by Roberts (1985) and by Gillet–Soulé (1987), and nonnegativity by Gabber (1995). ([Wikipedia, Serre's multiplicity conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_multiplicity_conjectures)) See [Intersection Theory](node:Intersection%20Theory).

### History
Krull introduced local rings in 1938 as *Stellenringe*, and the English term is credited to Zariski. ([Wikipedia, Local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring)) Macaulay proved the unmixedness theorem for polynomial rings in 1916 and Cohen for power series rings in 1946, giving Cohen–Macaulay rings their name; Cohen introduced the structure theorem in 1946. ([Wikipedia, Cohen–Macaulay ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Macaulay_ring); [Wikipedia, Cohen structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen_structure_theorem)) Grothendieck introduced Gorenstein rings in his 1961 seminar and Bass publicized them in 1963. Azumaya introduced Henselian rings in 1951 and Nagata the Henselization in 1953. ([Wikipedia, Gorenstein ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorenstein_ring); [Wikipedia, Henselian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henselian_ring))

### Open problems
- **Lech's conjecture.** For a flat local homomorphism $(R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)$ of Noetherian local rings, $e(R)\le e(S)$. Ma proved it when $R$ is a standard graded ring over a perfect field localized at its homogeneous maximal ideal, and states that "in general the conjecture is wide open when $\dim R>3$, even in equal characteristic". ([Ma, *Lim Ulrich sequences and Lech's conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02338))
- **Serre's positivity conjecture.** With $R,P,Q$ as above and $\dim R/P+\dim R/Q=\dim R$, is $\chi(R/P,R/Q)>0$? This remains open in general, with partial results by Dutta (2008) and Skalit (2019). ([Wikipedia, Serre's multiplicity conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_multiplicity_conjectures))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring) and [Cohen–Macaulay ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Macaulay_ring): definitions, hierarchy and examples.
- **Learn:** [Jiang, Commutative Algebra Notes](https://scms.fudan.edu.cn/dfiles/summerschool/lecture_note_5.pdf): Nakayama, dimension, regular rings, Auslander–Buchsbaum formula and Serre's theorem with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Ma, *Lim Ulrich sequences and Lech's conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02338): research paper on multiplicities under flat local maps.
- **Further reading:** [Matsumura, *Commutative Ring Theory*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/commutative-ring-theory/02819830750568B06C16E6199F3562C1): Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 8, covering dimension, depth, Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein rings.
references.MSC 13Jxx - Topological rings and module:
## Reference
### Overview
A topological ring is a ring with a topology for which addition and multiplication $R\times R\to R$ are continuous; its additive group is then a topological group, and as a uniform space it can be completed to a complete ring containing it as a dense subring. In commutative algebra the central topologies are the $I$-adic ones: for an ideal $I\subseteq R$ a set $U$ is open when each $x\in U$ has some $n$ with $x+I^n\subseteq U$, and this topology is Hausdorff exactly when $\bigcap_n I^n=0$. ([Wikipedia, Topological ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_ring))

Completing $\mathbb Z$ at $(p)$ gives the $p$-adic integers and completing $K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ at $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ gives the formal power series ring $K[\![x_1,\dots,x_n]\!]$. Completion captures the formal neighbourhood of a point and is used to analyse the local structure of singularities. ([Wikipedia, Completion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_%28algebra%29)) The section also covers a second, order-theoretic strand: ordered rings and real algebra, where positivity rather than nearness is the organizing notion. ([MSC2020, 13Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Jxx))

### Scope
MSC2020 13Jxx (see also 16W60, 16W80) lists 13J05 power series rings (see also 13F25); 13J07 analytical algebras and rings (see also 32B05); 13J10 complete rings, completion (see also 13B35); 13J15 Henselian rings (see also 13B40); 13J20 global topological rings; 13J25 ordered rings (see also 06F25); 13J30 real algebra (see also 12D15, 14Pxx); and 13J99. ([MSC2020, 13Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Jxx))
