Neighbouring codes: [MSC 13Hxx - Local rings and semilocal rings](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings) covers regular local rings, special types (Cohen–Macaulay, Gorenstein, Buchsbaum) and multiplicity theory, while completion (13J10) and Henselian rings (13J15) are classified in 13J ([MSC2020, 13Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Hxx)); [MSC 12Jxx - Topological fields](node:MSC%2012Jxx%20-%20Topological%20fields) treats normed, valued and ordered fields ([MSC2020, 12Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Jxx)); and 13J30 cross-references 14Pxx, real algebraic and real-analytic geometry, whose code 14P05 (real algebraic sets) points back to 13J30. ([MSC2020, 13Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Jxx); [MSC2020, 14Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Pxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Adic Completion](node:Adic%20Completion) (13J10).** The $I$-adic completion of a module is $\widehat M=\varprojlim_n M/I^nM$. If $R$ is Noetherian, then $\widehat R$ is Noetherian (and local if $R$ is local), $\widehat R$ is a flat $R$-module, and for finitely generated $M$ one has $\widehat M\cong M\otimes_R\widehat R$, so completion is exact on finitely generated modules. ([Wikipedia, Completion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_%28algebra%29); [Dutta notes, Lemma 2.44, Thm 2.48](https://people.math.osu.edu/snapp/IntroCommAlg.pdf)) See [Flat Modules](node:Flat%20Modules).
- **Artin–Rees lemma.** If $A$ is Noetherian, $I$ an ideal, $M$ finitely generated and $N\subseteq M$, there is $m\ge0$ with $N\cap I^{m+n}M=I^n(N\cap I^mM)$ for all $n\ge0$; hence the $I$-adic topology of $M$ induces the $I$-adic topology on $N$, which is the key step in exactness of completion. ([Dutta notes, Lemma 2.31](https://people.math.osu.edu/snapp/IntroCommAlg.pdf))
- **Krull intersection theorem.** If $IM=M$ for a finitely generated module $M$, then $(1-a)M=0$ for some $a\in I$. Combined with Artin–Rees: if $A$ is Noetherian, $I\subseteq J(A)$ and $M$ is finitely generated, then $\bigcap_n I^nM=0$, so $M$ is $I$-adically separated. In particular $R\to\widehat R$ is injective for Noetherian local rings and Noetherian domains. ([Dutta notes, Thm 2.34, Cor. 2.41](https://people.math.osu.edu/snapp/IntroCommAlg.pdf); [Wikipedia, Completion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_%28algebra%29)) See [Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings).
- **Cohen structure theorem.** A complete Noetherian local ring containing a field is $k[\![x_1,\dots,x_n]\!]/I$ with $k$ its residue field; in mixed characteristic it is a quotient of a power series ring over a Cohen ring (a complete characteristic-$0$ DVR with maximal ideal $(p)$). Thus every complete Noetherian local ring is a quotient of a complete regular local ring. ([Wikipedia, Cohen structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen_structure_theorem)) See [Local Rings](node:Local%20Rings).
- **Henselian rings (13J15).** A local ring is Henselian if Hensel's lemma holds for it, equivalently if every finite extension is a product of local rings. Complete local rings such as $\mathbb Z_p$ and $k[\![x]\!]$ are Henselian, and every local ring has a universal Henselization, with the same completion and residue field, that serves as an algebraic substitute for completion; a Henselian local ring is called strictly Henselian when its residue field is separably closed. ([Wikipedia, Henselian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henselian_ring)) See [Hensel's Lemma](node:Hensel's%20Lemma).
- **Artin approximation.** MSC2020 places Artin approximation itself under 14B12, with a cross-reference to 13B40. ([MSC2020, 14Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Bxx)) Artin (1968): if $F(x,y)$ is a vector of convergent power series over $\mathbb C$ and $\hat y(x)$ is a formal solution of $F(x,\hat y(x))=0$, then for every $c$ there is a convergent solution $y(x)$ with $y\equiv\hat y\bmod (x)^c$. The strong form: for every $c$ there is $\beta$ such that any approximate solution with $F(x,\bar y(x))\equiv0\bmod (x)^\beta$ agrees modulo $(x)^c$ with an actual convergent solution. ([Rond, *Artin Approximation*, Thms 1.2, 1.9](https://arxiv.org/html/1506.04717)) Artin's 1969 algebraic version approximates formal solutions by algebraic power series, and more generally works over the Henselization at a prime of a finite-type algebra over a field or excellent DVR. ([Wikipedia, Artin approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_approximation_theorem))
- **Positivstellensatz (13J30).** Over a real closed field $R$, let $W=\{x: f(x)\ge0\ \forall f\in F,\ g(x)=0\ \forall g\in G\}$ for finite sets $F,G$ of polynomials, and let $P(F,G)$ be the cone generated by $F$ and sums of squares plus the ideal generated by $G$. Then $p>0$ on $W$ iff $q_1p=1+q_2$ for some $q_1,q_2\in P(F,G)$, and $p\ge0$ on $W$ iff $q_1p=p^{2s}+q_2$ for some $q_i\in P(F,G)$ and integer $s$ (Krivine 1964, Stengle 1974). ([Wikipedia, Stengle's Positivstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stengle%27s_Positivstellensatz)) See [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields) and [Semialgebraic Sets](node:Semialgebraic%20Sets).
- **Hilbert's 17th problem.** A real polynomial is nonnegative on $\mathbb R^n$ iff it is a sum of squares of real rational functions (Artin 1927); squares of polynomials do not suffice, as Motzkin's 1967 example shows. For compact semialgebraic sets the Schmüdgen and Putinar Positivstellensätze give certificates without denominators. ([Wikipedia, Positivstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positivstellensatz)) Schmüdgen's theorem: if $W=\{x\in\mathbb R^n: f(x)\ge0\ \forall f\in F\}$ is compact, every polynomial strictly positive on $W$ lies in $P(F,\emptyset)$; Putinar's version, under the stronger assumption that $L-\sum_i x_i^2$ lies in the quadratic module $Q(F,G)$ for some $L>0$, puts such polynomials in $Q(F,G)$. ([Wikipedia, Stengle's Positivstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stengle%27s_Positivstellensatz)) See [Ordered Groups and Ordered Rings](node:Ordered%20Groups%20and%20Ordered%20Rings).

### History
Artin solved Hilbert's seventeenth problem (posed in 1900) in 1927. ([Wikipedia, Positivstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positivstellensatz)) Cohen proved the structure theorem for complete local rings in 1946. ([Wikipedia, Cohen structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen_structure_theorem)) Azumaya introduced Henselian rings in 1951 and Nagata the Henselization in 1953. ([Wikipedia, Henselian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henselian_ring)) Krivine proved the Positivstellensatz in 1964 and Stengle rediscovered it in 1974. ([Wikipedia, Stengle's Positivstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stengle%27s_Positivstellensatz)) Artin's approximation theorems date from 1968 (analytic) and 1969 (algebraic). ([Wikipedia, Artin approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_approximation_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Effective Artin functions.** In the strong Artin approximation theorem, the integer $\beta$ depends on $c$ (the Artin function $c\mapsto\beta(c)$). Artin proved that, for each $c$, $\beta$ can be chosen to depend only on the degrees of the components of $F$, but Rond's survey states that "it is still an open problem to find effective bounds on $\beta$". ([Rond, *Artin Approximation*](https://arxiv.org/html/1506.04717))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Completion (algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_%28algebra%29): $I$-adic topology, completion, flatness and exactness.
- **Learn:** [Dutta, *Introduction to Commutative Algebra* (course notes, ch. 2)](https://people.math.osu.edu/snapp/IntroCommAlg.pdf): filtrations, Artin–Rees, Krull's intersection theorem and flatness of completion, with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Rond, *Artin Approximation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04717): survey of Artin approximation, strong approximation and Néron desingularization.
- **Further reading:** [Bochnak, Coste, Roy, *Real Algebraic Geometry*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-03718-8): Springer (1998), a monograph on real algebraic geometry.
references.MSC 13Lxx - Applications of logic to com:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 13L, "Applications of logic to commutative algebra", sits inside [MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra) and cross-refers to model theory (03C) and nonstandard models (03H). ([MSC2020 13Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Lxx)) Its central tool is the ultraproduct: a family of rings indexed by a set $I$ is glued along an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$, and Łoś's theorem says a first-order sentence holds in the ultraproduct exactly when it holds in $\mathcal U$-many factors. This turns "for all sufficiently large $p$" arguments and uniform-bound statements into statements about a single ring. ([Ultraproduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraproduct); [Knyszewski, G1 seminar notes](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~fk4805/ultra.pdf)) See [Ultraproducts of Commutative Rings](node:Ultraproducts%20of%20Commutative%20Rings) for the concept note, and [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory) and [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic) for the logical background.

Three strands dominate. First, nonstandard proofs that degree bounds in polynomial rings over fields depend only on the number of variables and the input degrees (van den Dries–Schmidt, 1984). ([Göral, arXiv:1210.1651](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1210.1651)) Second, transfer between residue characteristics, as in the Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle for Henselian valued fields. ([Ax–Kochen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem)) Third, Aschenbrenner and Schoutens's use of ultraproducts of rings of prime characteristic to give a characteristic-zero analogue of tight closure and canonical big Cohen–Macaulay algebras in equal characteristic zero. ([Aschenbrenner–Schoutens, arXiv:math/0411349](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411349))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists only 13L05 "Applications of logic to commutative algebra" (see also 03Cxx, 03Hxx) and 13L99. ([MSC2020 13Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Lxx))

- **Neighbour 03C.** [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory) studies the logic itself; 13L is for its use in proving algebraic theorems. ([MSC2020 13Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Lxx))
- **Neighbour 03H.** [MSC 03Hxx - Nonstandard models](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models) covers nonstandard analysis and models; 13L collects nonstandard methods applied to rings. ([MSC2020 13Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Lxx))
- **Neighbour 13A.** 13A35 in [MSC 13Axx - General commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Axx%20-%20General%20commutative%20ring%20theory) is "Characteristic $p$ methods (Frobenius endomorphism) and reduction to characteristic $p$; tight closure". ([MSC2020 13Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Axx)) Ultraproduct work such as Aschenbrenner–Schoutens's characteristic-zero tight closure, built from a nonstandard Frobenius, sits between the two codes. ([Aschenbrenner–Schoutens, arXiv:math/0411349](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411349))
- **Neighbour 13D.** The homological conjectures have their own code, 13D22 "Homological conjectures (intersection theorems) in commutative ring theory", in [MSC 13Dxx - Homological methods in commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory). ([MSC2020 13Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Dxx)) They include the existence of big Cohen–Macaulay modules and of weakly functorial big Cohen–Macaulay algebras. ([Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra))

### Key concepts
- **Ultraproducts and Łoś's theorem.** For structures $M_i$ ($i\in I$) and an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $I$, $\prod_{\mathcal U}M_i$ is $\prod_iM_i$ modulo $(a_i)\sim(b_i)$ iff $\{i:a_i=b_i\}\in\mathcal U$. Łoś: a first-order formula holds in the ultraproduct iff the set of $i$ where it holds is in $\mathcal U$. Non-first-order properties (such as the Archimedean property) need not transfer. ([Ultraproduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraproduct)) Compare [Hyperreal Numbers](node:Hyperreal%20Numbers) and the [Compactness Theorem](node:Compactness%20Theorem).
- **$\prod_{\mathcal U}\overline{\mathbb F}_p\cong\mathbb C$.** For a nonprincipal ultrafilter on the primes, the ultraproduct of the algebraic closures $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ is an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ and [cardinality](node:Cardinality) $|\mathbb C|$, hence isomorphic to $\mathbb C$. Through Łoś's theorem this proves the Ax–Grothendieck theorem: an injective regular self-map of a complex affine variety is surjective. ([Knyszewski, Prop. 0.3.3, Thm 0.4.1](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~fk4805/ultra.pdf))
- **Uniform bounds in polynomial rings (Hermann; van den Dries–Schmidt).** Hermann (1926): over a field $F$, if $f_0\in(f_1,\dots,f_n)\subseteq F[X_1,\dots,X_N]$ with all $\deg f_i\le d$, then $f_0=\sum g_if_i$ with $\deg g_i\le(2d)^{2^N}$; Mayr–Meyer examples show the doubly exponential growth is essentially unavoidable. ([Aschenbrenner, arXiv:math/0305172](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0305172)) Van den Dries and Schmidt (*Invent. Math.* 76, 1984) reproved the existence of such field-independent bounds by nonstandard methods and showed that primality of an ideal generated in degree $<D$ can be tested by a bound $B(n,D)$; a key step is that the extension $K^*[X_1,\dots,X_n]\subseteq(K[X_1,\dots,X_n])^*$, from the polynomial ring over the ultrapower field into the ultrapower of the polynomial ring, is faithfully flat (van den Dries–Schmidt, Thm 1.8), and that a prime ideal generated by finitely many polynomials extends to a prime ideal (their Thm 2.5). Harrison-Trainor, Klys and Moosa carry these nonstandard flatness and primality-transfer arguments over to differential polynomial rings. ([Göral, arXiv:1210.1651](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1210.1651); [Harrison-Trainor–Klys–Moosa, arXiv:1105.0600](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1105.0600)) Over $\mathbb Z$, Aschenbrenner obtained cofactor degrees $(2d)^{2^{O(N^2)}}(h+1)$ for inputs of height $\le h$. ([Aschenbrenner, Theorem A](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0305172)) See [Gröbner Bases](node:Gröbner%20Bases) for the computational side.
- **Ax–Kochen–Ershov transfer.** Henselian [valued fields](node:Valued%20Fields) with residue fields of characteristic $0$ and elementarily equivalent value groups and residue fields are elementarily equivalent. Comparing ultraproducts of $\mathbb F_p((t))$ and $\mathbb Q_p$ gives the Ax–Kochen theorem: for each $d$ there is a finite set of primes $Y_d$ such that for $p\notin Y_d$ every degree-$d$ form over $\mathbb Q_p$ in more than $d^2$ variables has a nontrivial zero. Terjanian's 2-adic quartic in 18 variables shows $Y_d$ can be nonempty, refuting Artin's conjecture. ([Ax–Kochen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem)) See [p-adic Numbers](node:p-adic%20Numbers).
- **Tight closure and its ultraproduct analogue.** In a Noetherian ring of characteristic $p$, $z\in I^*$ iff some $c$ outside all minimal primes has $cz^{p^e}\in I^{[p^e]}$ for all large $e$; Hochster and Huneke introduced this in 1988. ([Tight closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_closure)) A tight-closure Briançon–Skoda theorem holds in every equicharacteristic Noetherian ring. ([Hochster, Utah minicourse, Thm 13](https://www.math.utah.edu/vigre/minicourses/algebra/hochster.pdf)) Aschenbrenner and Schoutens attach to each equicharacteristic-zero Noetherian [local ring](node:Local%20Rings) a faithfully flat extension that is an ultraproduct of rings of prime characteristics; its nonstandard Frobenius defines a characteristic-zero tight closure, and for equidimensional universally catenary rings they build a canonical, weakly functorial balanced big Cohen–Macaulay algebra. The construction uses Rotthaus's characteristic-zero Artin approximation rather than Néron desingularization. ([Aschenbrenner–Schoutens, arXiv:math/0411349](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411349))

### History
Hochster's lectures record that several homological conjectures were proved in equal characteristic by reduction to characteristic $p$, for example the existence of big Cohen–Macaulay modules (Hochster, 1973), and that weak functoriality of big Cohen–Macaulay algebras in equal characteristic zero follows by such a reduction. ([Hochster, Utah minicourse](https://www.math.utah.edu/vigre/minicourses/algebra/hochster.pdf)) Schoutens's monograph *The Use of Ultraproducts in Commutative Algebra* appeared in Springer's Lecture Notes in Mathematics in 2010. ([Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-13368-8)) In mixed characteristic, where reduction to characteristic $p$ is unavailable, André proved the direct summand conjecture with Scholze's perfectoid spaces (arXiv 2016) and then the existence of weakly functorial big Cohen–Macaulay algebras for local homomorphisms of complete local domains (arXiv 2018). ([André, arXiv:1609.00345](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00345); [André, arXiv:1801.10010](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.10010); [Homological conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_conjectures_in_commutative_algebra)) Bhatt later proved that the absolute integral closure of an excellent Noetherian domain is Cohen–Macaulay modulo every power of $p$. ([Bhatt, arXiv:2008.08070](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.08070))

### Open problems
- **Small Cohen–Macaulay modules.** Hochster's conjecture that every complete local domain has a finitely generated maximal Cohen–Macaulay module remains a conjecture; Xie (2023) proves a special case. Hochster himself suspected it false in general, though possibly true in characteristic $p$. ([Xie, arXiv:2302.11011](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.11011); [Hochster, Utah minicourse, Conj. 1](https://www.math.utah.edu/vigre/minicourses/algebra/hochster.pdf))
- **Weakly F-regular versus F-regular.** Brenner and Monsky showed that tight closure does not commute with localization, but whether every weakly F-regular ring is F-regular remains open. ([Tight closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_closure))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Ultraproduct (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraproduct): definitions and Łoś's theorem.
- **Reference:** [Ax–Kochen theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ax%E2%80%93Kochen_theorem): transfer principle and the Artin conjecture.
- **Learn:** [Knyszewski, G1 seminar notes on ultraproducts](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~fk4805/ultra.pdf): $\prod_{\mathcal U}\overline{\mathbb F}_p\cong\mathbb C$ and Ax–Grothendieck.
- **Learn:** [Hochster, Current state of the homological conjectures (Utah, 2004)](https://www.math.utah.edu/vigre/minicourses/algebra/hochster.pdf): the conjectures, reduction to characteristic $p$, tight closure.
- **Primary:** [Aschenbrenner and Schoutens, Lefschetz extensions, tight closure, and big Cohen–Macaulay algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411349): ultraproduct construction of characteristic-zero tight closure.
- **Primary:** [Aschenbrenner, Ideal membership in polynomial rings over the integers](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0305172): Hermann's bound and its arithmetic analogue.
- **Further reading:** [Schoutens, The Use of Ultraproducts in Commutative Algebra (Springer LNM, 2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-13368-8): the standard monograph for the area.
references.MSC 13Mxx - Finite commutative rings:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 13M, "Finite commutative rings", is the part of [MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra) devoted to commutative rings with finitely many elements, with number-theoretic aspects referred to [11Txx](node:MSC%2011Txx%20-%20Finite%20fields%20and%20commutative%20rings%20%28number-theoretic%20aspects%29). ([MSC2020 13Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Mxx)) [Finite Fields](node:Finite%20Fields) are the most important special case, but a finite ring can have zero divisors and nilpotents, so the finite-field classification is only the starting point; the additive group of any finite ring is a finite abelian group. ([Finite ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_ring)) See [Finite Commutative Rings](node:Finite%20Commutative%20Rings) for the concept note.

The basic reduction is to local rings. A finite ring satisfies the descending chain condition, and a commutative [Artinian ring](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings) is a finite direct product of Artinian [local rings](node:Local%20Rings) $R/M_i^k$, obtained from the [Chinese Remainder Theorem](node:Chinese%20Remainder%20Theorem) once the nilradical is shown to be nilpotent. ([McGovern, Lecture 4-12](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~mcgovern/506sp17/4-12.pdf)) Research then splits into the structure of finite local rings (Galois rings, chain rings), counting rings of given order, and applications, above all codes over rings such as $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$. ([Keppens, arXiv:2003.02900](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.02900); [Hammons et al., arXiv:math/0207208](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0207208))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 13M05 structure of finite commutative rings; 13M10 polynomials and finite commutative rings; 13M99; with a cross-reference to 11Txx for number-theoretic aspects. ([MSC2020 13Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Mxx))

- **Neighbour 11T.** [MSC 11Txx - Finite fields and commutative rings (number-theoretic aspects)](node:MSC%2011Txx%20-%20Finite%20fields%20and%20commutative%20rings%20%28number-theoretic%20aspects%29): the MSC entry sends number-theoretic questions there; 13M is the ring-theoretic structure. ([MSC2020 13Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Mxx))
- **Neighbour 13H.** [MSC 13Hxx - Local rings and semilocal rings](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings) treats local and semilocal rings in general; a finite local ring is in particular an Artinian local ring, in which every prime ideal is maximal and the maximal ideal is nilpotent. ([McGovern, Lecture 4-12](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~mcgovern/506sp17/4-12.pdf))
- **Neighbour 94B.** Linear codes over Galois and chain rings are studied in [coding theory](node:Coding%20Theory), [MSC 94Bxx - Theory of error-correcting codes and error-detecting codes](node:MSC%2094Bxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20error-correcting%20codes%20and%20error-detecting%20codes). ([Keppens, arXiv:2003.02900](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.02900); [Hammons et al., arXiv:math/0207208](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0207208))

### Key concepts
- **Artinian structure theorem.** In a commutative Artinian ring every non-zero-divisor is a unit, every prime ideal is maximal, there are finitely many maximal ideals $M_1,\dots,M_n$, the nilradical is nilpotent, and $R\cong\prod_iR/M_i^k$ with each factor local Artinian. In a finite local ring the maximal ideal is nilpotent and the residue field is finite. ([McGovern, Lecture 4-12](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~mcgovern/506sp17/4-12.pdf)) If the maximal ideal is principal, generated by $x$, every element has the form $x^nu$ with $u$ a unit, like a discrete valuation ring with nilpotent uniformizer. ([McGovern](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~mcgovern/506sp17/4-12.pdf))
- **Invariants of a finite local ring (Raghavendran).** A finite local ring $R$ has unique parameters $p,n,r,k$ with $|R|=p^{nr}$, $|J(R)|=p^{(n-1)r}$, residue field of order $q=p^r$, and characteristic $p^k$ with $1\le k\le n$. ([Keppens, arXiv:2003.02900](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.02900)) In particular its order is a prime power, the [cardinality](node:Cardinality) of the residue field raised to $n$.
- **Galois rings.** $GR(p^n,r)\cong\mathbb Z[x]/(p^n,f(x))$ with $f$ monic of degree $r$ irreducible mod $p$; it has characteristic $p^n$ and $p^{nr}$ elements and depends only on $(p,n,r)$. It is local with maximal ideal $(p)$ and residue field $\mathbb F_{p^r}$, its ideals are exactly $(p^i)$, $0\le i\le n$, and it specializes to $\mathbb F_{p^r}$ ($n=1$) and $\mathbb Z/p^n\mathbb Z$ ($r=1$). Its unit group is $C_{p^r-1}\times(1+pR)$, with $1+pR\cong(C_{p^{n-1}})^r$ for $p$ odd (or $p=2$, $n\le2$) and $C_2\times C_{2^{n-2}}\times(C_{2^{n-1}})^{r-1}$ for $p=2$, $n\ge3$; $\operatorname{Aut}GR(p^n,r)$ is cyclic of order $r$, generated by a generalized Frobenius. ([Galois ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_ring)) Compare [Units and Idempotents in Rings](node:Units%20and%20Idempotents%20in%20Rings).
- **Finite chain rings.** A finite ring whose ideals form a chain. For finite rings, Clarke–Drake and Lorimer showed that the following are equivalent: chain ring, local principal ideal ring, local ring with principal maximal ideal; every ideal is then a power of the maximal ideal. Galois rings are the basic examples. ([Keppens, arXiv:2003.02900](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.02900))
- **$\mathbb Z_4$-linear codes.** Hammons, Kumar, Calderbank, Sloane and Solé showed that the Nordstrom–Robinson, Kerdock, Preparata, Goethals and Delsarte–Goethals codes (the Preparata and Goethals codes slightly modified), which are nonlinear as binary codes, are Gray-map images of linear codes over $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$; the $\mathbb Z_4$ Kerdock and Preparata codes are dual, explaining the duality of their binary weight enumerators. (*IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory* 40, 1994.) ([Hammons et al., arXiv:math/0207208](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0207208)) Such codes are naturally built over $GR(4,r)$. ([Galois ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_ring))
- **Enumeration.** There are eleven rings of order 4, four with identity (Bloom, answering Singmaster's 1964 question), and eleven rings of order $p^2$. ([Finite ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_ring)) Asymptotically, the number of commutative rings of order $p^n$ is $p^{\beta}$ with $\beta=\tfrac2{27}n^3+O(n^{5/2})$ (all rings: $\tfrac4{27}n^3+O(n^{5/2})$). ([Blackburn–McLean, arXiv:2107.13215](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13215)) Poonen derived the commutative count $p^{(2/27)n^3+O(n^{8/3})}$ from the dimension of the moduli scheme $\mathfrak B_n$ of rank-$n$ commutative algebras, and showed that over an algebraically closed field there are finitely many rank-$n$ algebras up to isomorphism iff $n\le6$. ([Poonen, arXiv:math/0608491](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0608491))
- **Zero-divisor graphs.** The Anderson–Livingston graph $\Gamma(R)$ has the nonzero zero divisors as vertices, joined when their product is $0$. It is connected of diameter at most $3$, its girth is at most $4$ when it has a cycle, and for $R$ not a domain $\Gamma(R)$ is finite iff $R$ is finite. Beck's conjecture that clique number equals chromatic number is false (Anderson–Naseer). ([Zero-divisor graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-divisor_graph)) See [MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory).

### History
Wedderburn's theorems of 1905 and 1907 show that finite division rings are commutative and that finite simple rings are matrix rings over finite fields (compare the [Artin–Wedderburn Theorem](node:Artin–Wedderburn%20Theorem)). ([Finite ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_ring)) Kruse and Price stated the $\tfrac4{27}n^3$ asymptotic for rings of order $p^n$ in 1969; Knopfmacher pointed out a flaw in 1973, and Poonen's 2008 commutative statement relied on the same step; Blackburn and McLean (2021) gave complete proofs with error term $O(n^{5/2})$. ([Blackburn–McLean, arXiv:2107.13215](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13215)) The $\mathbb Z_4$-linearity paper appeared in *IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory* in 1994. ([Hammons et al., arXiv:math/0207208](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0207208)) Beck introduced zero-divisor graphs in 1988 and Anderson and Livingston reformulated them in 1999. ([Zero-divisor graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-divisor_graph))

### Open problems
- **Classification of chain rings.** Keppens writes that the classification of all chain rings "is still an open problem but partial results are known", and that the number of non-isomorphic finite chain rings with given parameters is still open in general. ([Keppens, arXiv:2003.02900](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.02900))
- **The typical finite commutative ring (Poonen's Conjecture 11.4).** Poonen conjectures that as $N\to\infty$ almost all commutative rings of order $\le N$ have order $2^n$ ($2^n$ the largest power of 2 at most $N$), are local with residue field $\mathbb F_2$, satisfy $\mathfrak m^3=0\ne\mathfrak m^2$ and $\dim\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=2n/3+O(1)$, and have characteristic $8$. ([Poonen, arXiv:math/0608491](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0608491))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Finite ring (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_ring): Wedderburn's theorems, small-order enumeration.
- **Reference:** [Galois ring (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_ring): construction, ideals, unit group, automorphisms.
- **Learn:** [McGovern, Lecture 4-12 (Artinian rings)](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~mcgovern/506sp17/4-12.pdf): decomposition into local Artinian rings.
- **Primary:** [Blackburn and McLean, The enumeration of finite rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13215): asymptotic counts with complete proofs.
- **Primary:** [Poonen, The moduli space of commutative algebras of finite rank](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0608491): moduli-theoretic counting and Conjecture 11.4.
- **Primary:** [Hammons, Kumar, Calderbank, Sloane, Solé, The $\mathbb Z_4$-linearity of Kerdock, Preparata, Goethals and related codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0207208): the founding paper of codes over $\mathbb Z_4$.
- **Further reading:** [McDonald, Finite Rings with Identity (Dekker, 1974)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL5367601W): monograph on finite rings with identity (Pure and Applied Mathematics 28).
- **Further reading:** [Keppens, 50 years of finite geometry, the "geometries over finite rings" part](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.02900): survey of finite local, chain and Galois rings.
references.MSC 13Nxx - Differential algebra:
## Reference
### Overview
Despite its name, MSC 13Nxx is not the Ritt–Kolchin theory of differential equations; it classifies the commutative algebra of derivations, Kähler differentials, and rings of differential operators. Its subcodes are 13N05 modules of differentials, 13N10 commutative rings of differential operators and their modules, and 13N15 derivations and commutative rings, with cross-references to 12H05 and 14F10. ([MSC2020 13Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Nxx)) Ritt–Kolchin differential algebra (differential fields, differential ideals, differential polynomial rings) is classified under 12H05 "Differential algebra" in [MSC 12Hxx - Differential and difference algebra](node:MSC%2012Hxx%20-%20Differential%20and%20difference%20algebra), which points back to 13Nxx. ([MSC2020 12Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Hxx))

The central object is the module of Kähler differentials $\Omega_{S/R}$ of a ring map $R\to S$. It linearizes $S$ over $R$: derivations become module homomorphisms, and properties of $R\to S$ such as separability, unramifiedness, and smoothness can be read off from it. Erich Kähler introduced the notion in the 1930s. ([Wikipedia: Kähler differential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_differential)) Differential operators extend derivations to higher order. Grothendieck defined them over an arbitrary commutative ring by iterated commutators, and recent work uses them to measure singularities. ([Brenner–Jeffries–Núñez-Betancourt](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04476))

### Scope
- **13N05 Modules of differentials:** $\Omega_{S/R}$, its exact sequences, and its use to detect separable, unramified, and smooth maps. ([MSC2020 13Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Nxx); [Wikipedia: Kähler differential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_differential))
- **13N10 Rings of differential operators and their modules:** $D_{S/R}$, principal parts, and $D$-modules over commutative rings. The entry cross-references 16S32 (rings of differential operators as associative rings) and 32C38 (analytic $D$-modules). ([MSC2020 13Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Nxx))
- **13N15 Derivations and commutative rings:** the modules $\operatorname{Der}_R(S,M)$ and their structure, including freeness questions such as the Zariski–Lipman conjecture below. ([MSC2020 13Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Nxx))

Neighbours: [MSC 12Hxx - Differential and difference algebra](node:MSC%2012Hxx%20-%20Differential%20and%20difference%20algebra) takes differential fields and Ritt–Kolchin theory; [MSC 14Fxx - (Co)homology theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Fxx%20-%20%28Co%29homology%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) (14F10) takes sheaves of differentials on schemes; [MSC 16Sxx - Associative rings and algebras arising under various constructions](node:MSC%2016Sxx%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras%20arising%20under%20various%20constructions) (16S32) takes noncommutative structure of rings of differential operators; [MSC 32Cxx - Analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Cxx%20-%20Analytic%20spaces) (32C38) takes analytic $D$-modules. ([MSC2020 13Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **Kähler differentials (13N05).** For a ring map $R\to S$, an $R$-linear derivation $d:S\to M$ into an $S$-module satisfies $d(fg)=f\,dg+g\,df$. There is a universal derivation $d:S\to\Omega_{S/R}$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_S(\Omega_{S/R},M)\cong\operatorname{Der}_R(S,M)$ for every $S$-module $M$. Concretely $\Omega_{S/R}\cong I/I^2$, where $I=\ker(S\otimes_RS\to S)$, with $ds=1\otimes s-s\otimes1$. For $S=R[t_1,\dots,t_n]$, $\Omega_{S/R}$ is free on $dt_1,\dots,dt_n$, and $\Omega_{R[t]/(f)/R}\cong R[t]/(f,f')\,dt$. ([Wikipedia: Kähler differential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_differential))
- **Fundamental exact sequences.** For $R\to S\to T$ there is an exact sequence $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_ST\to\Omega_{T/R}\to\Omega_{T/S}\to0$. If $T=S/I$, the conormal sequence $I/I^2\xrightarrow{\ [f]\mapsto df\otimes1\ }\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_ST\to\Omega_{T/R}\to0$ is exact. Applied to $T=R[t_1,\dots,t_n]/(g_1,\dots,g_r)$, it presents $\Omega_{T/R}$ as the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix of the $g_i$. ([Wikipedia: Kähler differential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_differential))
- **Separability, unramifiedness, smoothness.** For a finite field extension $K/k$, $\Omega_{K/k}=0$ if and only if $K/k$ is separable (see [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory)). A morphism is unramified if and only if $\Omega_{X/Y}=0$, and a finite-type morphism is smooth if it is flat and $\Omega_{X/Y}$ is locally free of the appropriate rank. ([Wikipedia: Kähler differential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_differential)) For $X$ locally of finite type over a field $k$, $X$ is smooth if and only if $\Omega^1_{X/k}$ is a vector bundle of rank $\dim X$ near each point. In the Jacobian criterion, an affine $X\subset\mathbb A^n$ cut out by $g_1,\dots,g_r$ is smooth of dimension $m$ if it has dimension at least $m$ near each point and the Jacobian has rank at least $n-m$ everywhere on $X$. Over a perfect field, smooth is equivalent to regular. ([Wikipedia: Smooth scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_scheme)) These are the algebraic counterparts of the tangent and cotangent spaces of [Algebraic Varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties).
- **Grothendieck's differential operators (13N10).** For $R\to S$ and $S$-modules, an operator of order $0$ is an $S$-linear map. For $k\ge1$, an operator of order $k$ is an $R$-linear $D$ such that $m\mapsto D(gm)-gD(m)$ has order $k-1$ for every $g\in S$. Order-one operators $S\to N$ are sums of $R$-derivations and multiplications, and the first module of principal parts is $P^1_{S/R}=\Omega_{S/R}\oplus S$. ([Stacks Project, Section 10.133, Def. 10.133.1 and Ex. 10.133.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09CH)) In general $D^n_{R|K}\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(P^n_{R|K},R)$ with $P^n_{R|K}=(R\otimes_KR)/\Delta^{n+1}$. ([Brenner–Jeffries–Núñez-Betancourt, Prop. 2.9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04476))
- **Characteristic 0 versus $p$.** Over a field of characteristic $0$, the differential operators of a smooth algebra are generated by $R$ and the partial derivatives, and form a Noetherian ring. In characteristic $p$ one also needs the operators $\frac1{\alpha!}\partial^\alpha$ (defined formally, since the factorials are not invertible) and $D$ is not Noetherian when $\dim R>0$. ([Brenner–Jeffries–Núñez-Betancourt, Ex. 2.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04476)) For the polynomial ring in characteristic $0$ this gives the Weyl algebra $A_n$, with $[\partial_i,x_j]=\delta_{ij}$; it is a simple Noetherian domain of global dimension $n$. ([Wikipedia: Weyl algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_algebra)) These operators are the algebraic analogues of those studied in [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Differential operators as singularity invariants.** Brenner, Jeffries and Núñez-Betancourt define the differential signature using differential powers $\mathfrak m^{\langle n\rangle}=\{r:\delta(r)\in\mathfrak m\text{ for all }\delta\in D^{n-1}\}$. For reduced localizations of finitely generated algebras over a perfect field, it equals $1$ for regular rings, and positivity implies that $R$ is a simple $D$-module. For invariant rings $R^G$ of finite $G\subset SL_n$ of order invertible in $K$, it equals $1/|G|$. ([Brenner–Jeffries–Núñez-Betancourt](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04476))
- **Freeness of derivations.** For a complex variety $X$, Lipman proved that if the tangent sheaf $T_X=\mathcal{H}om(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal O_X)$ is locally free, then $X$ is normal. ([Graf–Kovács](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1301.7315)) Whether $X$ must then be smooth is the Zariski–Lipman conjecture (see Open problems). The commutative ring theory is that of [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals) in [MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra).

### History
Kähler introduced the module of differentials in the 1930s, and it became standard in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry somewhat later. ([Wikipedia: Kähler differential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_differential)) Grothendieck introduced the modules of principal parts (EGA IV, Définition 16.3.1), which represent differential operators of each order. ([Brenner–Jeffries–Núñez-Betancourt](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04476)) He also proved that smooth varieties have rings of differential operators generated by derivations, and Nakai conjectured the converse in 1961. ([Wikipedia: Nakai conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakai_conjecture)) Matsumura's standard graduate text gives derivations and $I$-smoothness a chapter each (Chapters 9–10). ([Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/commutative-ring-theory/02819830750568B06C16E6199F3562C1))

### Open problems
- **Zariski–Lipman conjecture.** Let $X$ be a complex variety whose tangent sheaf $T_X$ is locally free; then $X$ is smooth. Graf and Kovács note that, despite being almost 50 years old, it "remains open in general." Known cases include singular locus of codimension at least 3 (Flenner), complete intersections (Källström), klt spaces (Greb–Kebekus–Kovács–Peternell), and log canonical spaces and pairs (Graf–Kovács, and independently Druel). ([Graf–Kovács](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1301.7315); [Druel, arXiv:1301.5910](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.5910))
- **Nakai's conjecture (1961).** If the ring of differential operators of a complex algebraic variety is generated by its derivations, then the variety is smooth. It is unproven and known for algebraic curves (Mount–Villamayor, 1973) and Stanley–Reisner rings (Schreiner, 1994). A proof would also establish the Zariski–Lipman conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Nakai conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakai_conjecture)) Brenner, Jeffries and Núñez-Betancourt obtain a special case in characteristic $0$: $D$-simplicity together with generation by derivations forces regularity. ([Brenner–Jeffries–Núñez-Betancourt, Rem. 3.17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04476))
- **Differential signature as a limit.** The same authors could not show in general that the differential signature exists as a limit rather than a limsup. They prove existence and rationality only when the associated graded ring of the order filtration is finitely generated. ([Brenner–Jeffries–Núñez-Betancourt, Thm. 9.8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04476))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kähler differential (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_differential): construction, exact sequences, smoothness and separability.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Section 10.133 Finite order differential operators](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09CH): Grothendieck's definition and principal parts.
- **Learn:** [Smooth scheme (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_scheme): Jacobian criterion and smoothness via $\Omega^1$.
- **Primary:** [Brenner, Jeffries, Núñez-Betancourt, Quantifying singularities with differential operators (arXiv:1810.04476)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04476): current research on 13N10 with background on $D_{R|K}$.
- **Primary:** [Graf, Kovács, An optimal extension theorem for 1-forms and the Lipman–Zariski conjecture (arXiv:1301.7315)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1301.7315): status and known cases of the conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/commutative-ring-theory/02819830750568B06C16E6199F3562C1): Chapters 9 (Derivations) and 10 ($I$-smoothness).
references.MSC 13Pxx - Computational aspects and ap:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 13P, "Computational aspects and applications of commutative rings", is the part of [MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra) that makes constructions with ideals and modules over polynomial rings effective and applies them outside algebra. The basic question is ideal membership: given $f,f_1,\ldots,f_k\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, decide whether $f\in(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$. With a [Gröbner basis](node:Gröbner%20Bases) $G$ of the ideal for a fixed monomial order, $f$ lies in the ideal if and only if its remainder on division by $G$ is zero. ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis); [Stanford EE464, More Gröbner bases](https://lall.stanford.edu/ee464/lectures/more_groebner_bases.pdf))

The area combines exact symbolic algorithms (Gröbner bases, resultants, computation of syzygies and free resolutions), their complexity theory, and applications in statistics, optimization, chemistry, and coding theory. The MSC entry for 13P25 names statistics, control theory, and optimization as applications. ([MSC2020 13Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Pxx)) Its exact methods are implemented in general computer algebra systems such as Macaulay2, Singular, Magma, and Maple. Macaulay2, built by Daniel Grayson and Michael Stillman, is designed for computation in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry and has efficient algorithms for Gröbner bases and free resolutions in its core. Singular, developed at the Technische Universität Kaiserslautern, is "a computer algebra system for polynomial computations". ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis); [Macaulay2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macaulay2); [Singular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_%28software%29)) See also [Computer Algebra](node:Computer%20Algebra).

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 13Pxx (see also 14Qxx and 68W30; software-related material goes under 13-04) lists 13P05 polynomials, factorization in commutative rings (see also 12-08); 13P10 Gröbner bases and other bases for ideals and modules (for example Janet and border bases); 13P15 solving polynomial systems, resultants; 13P20 computational homological algebra (see also 13Dxx); 13P25 applications of commutative algebra (for example to statistics, control theory, optimization); and 13P99. ([MSC2020 13Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Pxx))

- **Neighbour 14Q.** The entry cross-refers to [MSC 14Qxx - Computational aspects in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Qxx%20-%20Computational%20aspects%20in%20algebraic%20geometry), the geometric counterpart ([Computational Algebraic Geometry](node:Computational%20Algebraic%20Geometry)). ([MSC2020 13Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Pxx))
- **Neighbour 68W30.** Symbolic computation and algebraic computation in [MSC 68Wxx - Algorithms in computer science](node:MSC%2068Wxx%20-%20Algorithms%20in%20computer%20science) is cross-referenced for the algorithmic side. ([MSC2020 13Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Pxx))
- **Neighbour 13D.** 13P20 points to [MSC 13Dxx - Homological methods in commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory), which holds the theory of resolutions ([Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra)); 13P20 holds their computation. ([MSC2020 13Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Pxx))
- **Neighbour 12.** 13P05 cross-refers to 12-08 in [MSC 12 - Field theory and polynomials](node:MSC%2012%20-%20Field%20theory%20and%20polynomials) for computational field theory. ([MSC2020 13Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Pxx))

### Key concepts
- **Gröbner bases and Buchberger's criterion (13P10).** Fix a monomial order on $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. A finite $G\subset I$ is a Gröbner basis of the ideal $I$ if the leading monomial of every nonzero element of $I$ is a multiple of the leading monomial of some element of $G$. A generating set $G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}$ is a Gröbner basis if and only if the remainder of every $S$-polynomial $S(g_i,g_j)$ on division by $G$ is zero. Buchberger's algorithm adjoins nonzero remainders until this holds; it terminates because the leading-term ideals form an ascending chain, which stabilizes since $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is Noetherian. For a fixed order the reduced Gröbner basis of an ideal is unique, so two ideals are equal exactly when their reduced Gröbner bases agree. ([Stanford EE464, More Gröbner bases](https://lall.stanford.edu/ee464/lectures/more_groebner_bases.pdf); [Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis)) See [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals) and [Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings).
- **Elimination (13P15).** If the variables are split as $X\cup Y$ and the monomial order is an elimination order for $X$, then for a Gröbner basis $G$ of $I$, the set $G\cap k[Y]$ is a Gröbner basis of the elimination ideal $I\cap k[Y]$. This computes implicit equations of parametrized curves and surfaces and reduces solving a zero-dimensional system to univariate problems. ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis))
- **Complexity of ideal membership.** Grete Hermann proved that if $f\in(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\subset\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg f_i\le d$, one can write $f=\sum r_if_i$ with $\deg r_i\le\deg f+(kd)^{2^n}$. Mayr and Meyer constructed ideals $J(n,d)$ for which a doubly exponential bound in $n$ is actually attained, and Bayer and Stillman showed that minimal syzygies of the same ideals have doubly exponential degree. ([Swanson, The first Mayr-Meyer ideal](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209154)) Mayr and Meyer showed that any decision procedure for the word problems for commutative semigroups and polynomial ideals "inherently requires computational storage space growing exponentially" with the input size. ([Mayr–Meyer, MIT technical memo](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/149010?show=full)) The worst-case complexity of a Gröbner basis computation is doubly exponential in $n$. ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis))
- **Linear-algebra and signature-based algorithms (13P10).** Faugère's F4 algorithm (1999) replaces many $S$-polynomial reductions by row reduction of one large Macaulay-type matrix. His F5 algorithm (2002) introduced signatures to discard useless data and performs no (signature) reduction to zero when the input is a regular sequence. A complete proof that F5 terminates was given only around 2012 (Galkin). ([Eder–Faugère, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.1774); [Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis))
- **Schreyer's theorem and free resolutions (13P20).** Let $G=\{f_1,\ldots,f_r\}\subset R^s$, $R=K[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, be a Gröbner basis for a monomial order $>$. For each pair write $S(f_i,f_j)=m_{ji}f_i-m_{ij}f_j=\sum_l g^{(ij)}_lf_l$ as a standard representation. Then the relations $m_{ji}e_i-m_{ij}e_j-\sum_l g^{(ij)}_le_l\in R^r$ form a Gröbner basis of the syzygy module $\mathrm{Syz}(G)$ for the order induced by $>$ and $G$. Iterating gives Schreyer's algorithm for free resolutions, needed for example to compute $\mathrm{Ext}$ modules. ([Erocal–Motsak–Schreyer–Steenpass](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.01654))
- **Numerical algebraic geometry (13P15).** Homotopy continuation joins a start system $g$, whose isolated solutions are known, to the target system $f$ by $H(z,t)=(1-t)f(z)+t\,g(z)$ and tracks solution paths by predictor–corrector steps. A positive-dimensional component is represented by a witness set: equations, a generic linear space of complementary dimension, and the finitely many intersection points, whose number is the degree of the component. Bertini, PHCpack, and HomotopyContinuation.jl implement these methods. ([Numerical algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_algebraic_geometry))
- **Applications (13P25).** Diaconis and Sturmfels (1998) used Gröbner bases to build [Markov Chain Monte Carlo](node:Markov%20Chain%20Monte%20Carlo) algorithms for conditional sampling from discrete exponential families; their theorem that a set of moves is a Markov basis if and only if the corresponding binomials generate the model's (toric) ideal is called the fundamental theorem of Markov bases. ([Algebraic statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_statistics); [Almendra-Hernández–De Loera–Petrović](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.06270)) In [Chemical Reaction Network Theory](node:Chemical%20Reaction%20Network%20Theory), complex-balanced mass-action systems are toric dynamical systems whose steady-state locus is a [toric variety](node:Toric%20Varieties) meeting each invariant polyhedron in one point. ([Craciun–Dickenstein–Shiu–Sturmfels](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.3431)) Gröbner bases are also used for algebraic decoding of error-correcting codes ([Coding Theory](node:Coding%20Theory)). ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis))

### History
Gröbner bases were introduced by Bruno Buchberger in his 1965 PhD thesis; Hironaka developed the analogous standard bases in 1964, and Günther had a similar notion in 1913. ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis)) Mayr and Meyer's lower bound appeared as an MIT technical memo in June 1981. ([Mayr–Meyer, MIT technical memo](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/149010?show=full)) Schreyer gave his syzygy algorithm in 1980. ([Erocal–Motsak–Schreyer–Steenpass](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.01654)) Faugère introduced F4 in 1999 and F5 in 2002, and from 2008 many signature-based variants (G2V, GVW, SB) followed. ([Eder–Faugère, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.1774))

### Open problems
- **Fröberg's conjecture.** Fröberg (1985) conjectured that for a generic homogeneous ideal $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subset K[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg f_i=d_i$, the Hilbert series of $K[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I$ is the truncation (at the first nonpositive coefficient) of $\prod_i(1-z^{d_i})/(1-z)^n$. Trung calls it "a longstanding conjecture"; it is known for $r\le n$, for $n\le 3$, and for $r=n+1$ in characteristic zero, and his paper gives a partial solution for $r\le n+2$. ([Trung, arXiv:1803.04997](https://arxiv.org/html/1803.04997v2)) A homogeneous sequence whose coordinate ring has the Hilbert series conjectured by Fröberg is called "cryptographic semi-regular"; Kudo and Yokoyama bound the Gröbner basis complexity of such sequences through the row reduction of a degree-$D$ Macaulay matrix, with $D$ bounded via the degree of regularity. ([Kudo–Yokoyama, arXiv:2410.23211](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.23211v2))
- **Signature-based algorithms.** Eder and Faugère (2014) list as open questions making the linear algebra in signature-based algorithms more flexible (row swaps are currently restricted by $s$-reductions; using further Gaussian-elimination techniques "is still an open problem"), and finding representations between signature–polynomial pairs and full module representations that reduce syzygies further without excessive overhead. ([Eder–Faugère, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.1774))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gröbner basis (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis): definitions, algorithms, complexity, applications.
- **Reference:** [Numerical algebraic geometry (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_algebraic_geometry): homotopy continuation and witness sets.
- **Learn:** [Stanford EE464, More Gröbner bases](https://lall.stanford.edu/ee464/lectures/more_groebner_bases.pdf): Buchberger's criterion and algorithm with worked example.
- **Primary:** [Eder and Faugère, A survey on signature-based Gröbner basis computations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.1774): F4, F5 and their variants, termination, open questions.
- **Primary:** [Erocal, Motsak, Schreyer, Steenpass, Refined algorithms to compute syzygies](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01654): Schreyer's theorem and algorithm.
- **Primary:** [Almendra-Hernández, De Loera, Petrović, Markov bases: a 25 year update](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.06270): algebraic statistics after Diaconis–Sturmfels.
- **Further reading:** [Cox, Little, O'Shea, Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms (Springer UTM, 2015)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-16721-3): the standard introduction to computational algebraic geometry and commutative algebra.
references.MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
Algebraic geometry studies the solution sets of systems of polynomial equations, algebraic varieties, using mainly commutative algebra. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz links algebraic sets to ideals, and birational geometry compares varieties through their function fields. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry)) Grothendieck's schemes generalize varieties so that points correspond to prime ideals. Stacks and derived algebraic geometry extend the framework further. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry)) Conventions matter: the Stacks Project calls a variety over $k$ an integral, separated scheme of finite type over $k$. Such a variety need not stay integral after a field extension. ([Stacks, Varieties](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/020C)) See [Algebraic Varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties) and [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals).

The field reaches into most of mathematics. Over $\mathbb C$, smooth projective varieties are compact Kähler manifolds, so Hodge theory applies (see [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds)). ([Wikipedia: Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_theory)) Over finite fields, Grothendieck's étale cohomology and Deligne's proof of the Weil conjectures tie point counts to topology. ([Wikipedia: Weil conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_conjectures)) Elliptic curves were instrumental in the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 14 has seventeen second-level areas: foundations (14A), local theory (14B), cycles and subschemes (14C), families and fibrations (14D), birational geometry (14E), (co)homology theory (14F, see also 13D), arithmetic problems and Diophantine geometry (14G, see also 11D, 11G), curves (14H), surfaces and higher-dimensional varieties (14J, with analytic theory in 32J), abelian varieties and schemes (14K), algebraic groups (14L, with linear algebraic groups in 20G), special varieties (14M), projective and enumerative geometry (14N), real algebraic and real-analytic geometry (14P), computational aspects (14Q), affine geometry (14R), and tropical geometry (14T). ([MSC2020 14-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14-XX))

Subfield maps for these areas: [MSC 14Exx - Birational geometry](node:MSC%2014Exx%20-%20Birational%20geometry), [MSC 14Jxx - Surfaces and higher-dimensional varieties](node:MSC%2014Jxx%20-%20Surfaces%20and%20higher-dimensional%20varieties) and [MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Hxx%20-%20Curves%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) for classification; [MSC 14Dxx - Families, fibrations in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Dxx%20-%20Families,%20fibrations%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) and [MSC 14Lxx - Algebraic groups](node:MSC%2014Lxx%20-%20Algebraic%20groups) (which contains geometric invariant theory, 14L24) for families and quotients; [MSC 14Fxx - (Co)homology theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Fxx%20-%20%28Co%29homology%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) and [MSC 14Cxx - Cycles and subschemes](node:MSC%2014Cxx%20-%20Cycles%20and%20subschemes) for cohomology and cycles; [MSC 14Gxx - Arithmetic problems in algebraic geometry; Diophantine geometry](node:MSC%2014Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20problems%20in%20algebraic%20geometry;%20Diophantine%20geometry) and [MSC 14Kxx - Abelian varieties and schemes](node:MSC%2014Kxx%20-%20Abelian%20varieties%20and%20schemes) for arithmetic; [MSC 14Nxx - Projective and enumerative algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Nxx%20-%20Projective%20and%20enumerative%20algebraic%20geometry), [MSC 14Txx - Tropical geometry](node:MSC%2014Txx%20-%20Tropical%20geometry) and [MSC 14Pxx - Real algebraic and real-analytic geometry](node:MSC%2014Pxx%20-%20Real%20algebraic%20and%20real-analytic%20geometry); and [MSC 14Rxx - Affine geometry](node:MSC%2014Rxx%20-%20Affine%20geometry). ([MSC2020 14-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14-XX); [MSC2020 14Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Lxx))

Neighbours: commutative algebra itself is [MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra); arithmetic of Diophantine equations is in [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory) (11D, 11G); analytic spaces are in [MSC 32 - Several complex variables and analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032%20-%20Several%20complex%20variables%20and%20analytic%20spaces). ([MSC2020 14-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Riemann–Roch and Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch.** For a divisor $D$ on a smooth projective curve of genus $g$, $h^0(\mathcal O(D))-h^1(\mathcal O(D))=\deg D+1-g$. For a holomorphic vector bundle $E$ on a compact complex manifold $X$, Hirzebruch (1954) proved $\chi(X,E)=\int_X\operatorname{ch}(E)\operatorname{td}(X)$. Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch followed a few years later. ([Wikipedia: Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirzebruch%E2%80%93Riemann%E2%80%93Roch_theorem))
- **Serre duality.** If $X$ is smooth and proper of dimension $n$ over a field $k$ and $E$ is a vector bundle, then $H^i(X,E)\cong H^{n-i}(X,K_X\otimes E^*)^*$. Serre proved it in 1955 for holomorphic vector bundles on compact complex manifolds; for nonsingular complex projective varieties this agrees with the algebraic version. Grothendieck extended it to Cohen–Macaulay schemes via a dualizing sheaf, and in general to proper schemes via a dualizing complex. ([Wikipedia: Serre duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre_duality))
- **GAGA and Chow's theorem.** For a complex projective variety $X$, analytification gives an equivalence between coherent algebraic sheaves on $X$ and coherent analytic sheaves on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, preserving cohomology (Serre, 1956). Chow's theorem says that a closed analytic subspace of complex projective space is algebraic. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic geometry and analytic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry_and_analytic_geometry))
- **Resolution of singularities.** Hironaka proved in 1964 that varieties over fields of characteristic $0$ admit resolutions, using repeated blowups along nonsingular centres. In characteristic $p$, Abhyankar resolved surfaces and Cossart and Piltant resolved threefolds. ([Wikipedia: Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))
- **Hodge decomposition.** For a compact Kähler manifold, $H^r(X,\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=r}H^{p,q}(X)$ with $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$, independent of the Kähler metric. Deligne's mixed Hodge structures extend this to arbitrary complex algebraic varieties. ([Wikipedia: Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_theory))
- **Weil conjectures.** For a smooth projective variety over a finite field, the zeta function is rational, satisfies a functional equation, and obeys a Riemann hypothesis. Weil proposed these in 1949. Dwork proved rationality (1960), Grothendieck with Artin and Verdier used étale cohomology for the functional equation and Betti numbers, and Deligne proved the Riemann hypothesis (1974). ([Wikipedia: Weil conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_conjectures)) Compare the classical [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Minimal model program.** For smooth $X$ with $\kappa(X)\ge0$ the goal is a birational model with nef canonical class, and for $\kappa=-\infty$ a Fano fibre space. Castelnuovo's contraction theorem handles surfaces, Mori (1988) proved existence of flips for threefolds, and Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan (2010) proved existence of minimal models for varieties of log general type. ([Wikipedia: Minimal model program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_model_program)) One consequence is that the canonical ring of a smooth projective variety is finitely generated. ([BCHM, arXiv:math/0610203](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610203))
- **Moduli via geometric invariant theory.** Many moduli spaces, including those of stable curves and of stable vector bundles on curves, are quotients of stable loci by reductive group actions, a method Mumford developed in 1965. ([Wikipedia: Geometric invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory))

### History
Descartes and Fermat introduced coordinates in the 17th century. In the 19th century, birational transformations, Riemann surfaces and Hilbert's work tied geometry to commutative algebra. Van der Waerden, Zariski and Weil gave rigorous foundations in the 20th century. Serre and Grothendieck then rebuilt the subject on sheaves and schemes. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry)) Italian geometers studied the birational classification of surfaces around 1900. ([Wikipedia: Minimal model program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_model_program))

### Open problems
- **Hodge conjecture.** On a non-singular complex projective variety $X$, every Hodge class in $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{k,k}(X)$ is a rational linear combination of classes of algebraic cycles. ([Wikipedia: Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_theory)) It is an unsolved Millennium Prize problem. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/hodge-conjecture/))
- **Abundance conjecture.** For a projective klt variety, if $K_X$ is nef then it is semiample. ([Wikipedia: Abundance conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_conjecture)) It is known for complex projective varieties of dimension at most $3$ and "is open in dimension $\ge4$." ([Jiang, arXiv:2604.03879](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.03879))
- **Resolution of singularities in positive characteristic.** For varieties of dimension at least $4$ over fields of characteristic $p$, resolution "is an open problem." ([Wikipedia: Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))
- **Termination of flips.** Termination of log flips in higher dimensions remains an active research area. ([Wikipedia: Minimal model program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_model_program))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/): open-source textbook and reference work on algebraic geometry.
- **Reference:** [Algebraic geometry (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry): broad orientation and history.
- **Learn:** [Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry](https://math.stanford.edu/~vakil/216blog/): free online foundations notes, also published by Princeton University Press.
- **Primary:** [Birkar, Cascini, Hacon, McKernan, Existence of minimal models for varieties of log general type (arXiv:math/0610203)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610203): landmark paper of the minimal model program.
- **Primary:** [Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry (Springer GTM, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3849-0): graduate text in Springer's GTM series.
- **Further reading:** [Griffiths and Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry (Wiley, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/9781118032527): graduate text on complex algebraic geometry.
references.MSC 14Axx - Foundations of algebraic geo:
## Reference
### Overview
14Axx classifies work on the basic objects and language of [algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry): varieties and schemes with their morphisms, the commutative algebra they rest on, and the generalizations of schemes (algebraic spaces and stacks, log schemes, noncommutative and derived geometry, geometry over the "field with one element"). ([MSC2020 14Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Axx))

A scheme enlarges the notion of an [algebraic variety](node:Algebraic%20Varieties): it is a ringed space covered by affine schemes $\operatorname{Spec}R$, whose points are the prime ideals of commutative rings, glued in the Zariski topology. Grothendieck gave the theory its definitive form in EGA (from 1960), continued in SGA, building on work of van der Waerden, Weil, Zariski, Chevalley, Nagata and Serre. ([Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_%28mathematics%29))

Since then the foundations have kept growing. Moduli problems need objects whose points carry automorphism groups (stacks); compactifications and degenerations need a record of boundary (log structures); and homotopical methods replace commutative rings by derived analogues. ([Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_%28mathematics%29); [Log structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log_structure); [Toën, Derived algebraic geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.1044))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists under 14Axx: 14A05 relevant commutative algebra (see also 13-XX); 14A10 varieties and morphisms; 14A15 schemes and morphisms; 14A20 generalizations (algebraic spaces, stacks); 14A21 logarithmic algebraic geometry, log schemes; 14A22 noncommutative algebraic geometry (see also 16S38); 14A23 geometry over the field with one element; 14A25 elementary questions in algebraic geometry; 14A30 fundamental constructions involving higher and derived categories (homotopical and derived algebraic geometry; for categorical aspects see 18Fxx, 18Gxx); 14A99 other. ([MSC2020 14Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Axx))

Neighbouring codes named in the entry's cross-references: 14A05 points to 13-XX ([MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra)); 14A22 points to 16S38; and 14A30 sends categorical aspects of higher and derived categories to 18Fxx and 18Gxx in [MSC 18 - Category theory; homological algebra](node:MSC%2018%20-%20Category%20theory;%20homological%20algebra). ([MSC2020 14Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Axx)) Local questions at a point (singularities, deformations, local cohomology) are classified separately in [MSC 14Bxx - Local theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Bxx%20-%20Local%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry). ([MSC2020 14Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Morphisms into affine schemes.** For a locally ringed space $X$ and an affine scheme $Y$, sending $f:X\to Y$ to $f^\sharp$ on global sections is a bijection $\operatorname{Mor}(X,Y)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}}(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y),\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X))$. In particular affine schemes are anti-equivalent to commutative rings. ([Stacks, Lemma 26.6.4](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01I1))
- **Functor of points.** A scheme $X$ over $R$ defines a functor $S\mapsto X(S)=\operatorname{Hom}_R(\operatorname{Spec}S,X)$ on $R$-algebras, and $X$ is determined by this functor; this generalizes the classical idea of solutions of the defining equations with values in a ring. Viewing spaces as functors leads to generalizations: the Artin representability theorem gives conditions for a functor to be represented by an algebraic space. ([Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_%28mathematics%29))
- **Separated and proper morphisms.** $f:X\to S$ is separated if the diagonal $\Delta_{X/S}:X\to X\times_SX$ is a closed immersion, and quasi-separated if it is quasi-compact. $f$ is proper if it is separated, of finite type and universally closed. ([Stacks, Definition 26.21.3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01KH); [Stacks, Definition 29.42.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01W0))
- **Valuative criterion of properness.** If a morphism of schemes $f:X\to Y$ is of finite type and quasi-separated, then $f$ is proper if and only if for every valuation ring $A$ with fraction field $K$ and every commutative square with $\operatorname{Spec}K\to X$ and $\operatorname{Spec}A\to Y$, there is a unique lift $\operatorname{Spec}A\to X$ making the diagram commute. ([Stacks, Lemma 29.43.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BX5))
- **Algebraic spaces (14A20).** An algebraic space over a scheme $S$ is a functor $F:(\mathit{Sch}/S)_{fppf}^{\mathrm{opp}}\to\mathit{Sets}$ that is an fppf sheaf, has representable diagonal, and admits a surjective étale map $h_U\to F$ from a scheme $U$. ([Stacks, Definition 65.6.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/025Y))
- **Algebraic stacks (14A20).** An algebraic stack over $S$ is a stack in [groupoids](node:Groupoids) over $(\mathit{Sch}/S)_{fppf}$ whose diagonal is representable by algebraic spaces and which admits a smooth surjective 1-morphism from a scheme. Stacks attach automorphism groups to points, which suits moduli problems; Deligne–Mumford stacks are a special case. ([Stacks, Definition 94.12.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/026O); [Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_%28mathematics%29))
- **Log structures (14A21).** A log structure on a scheme $X$ is a sheaf of commutative monoids $\mathcal M$ with a homomorphism $\alpha:\mathcal M\to\mathcal O_X$ (multiplicative) such that $\alpha$ restricts to an isomorphism $\alpha^{-1}(\mathcal O_X^\times)\to\mathcal O_X^\times$. It lets one study a smooth variety $U$ embedded in a proper variety $X$ by treating $X$ as a variety with boundary $D=X\setminus U$; standard examples are normal-crossings divisors and semistable schemes. ([Log structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log_structure))
- **Noncommutative algebraic geometry (14A22).** One replaces a space by its category of quasi-coherent sheaves; this is supported by the Gabriel–Rosenberg theorem that a commutative scheme is recovered up to isomorphism from that abelian category. Noncommutative $\operatorname{Proj}$ of a graded ring $R$ is the quotient of the category $\operatorname{Mod}\text{-}R$ of graded right $R$-modules by the finite-length modules. ([Noncommutative algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noncommutative_algebraic_geometry))
- **Derived algebraic geometry (14A30).** The structure sheaf is replaced by a homotopical analogue of commutative rings, retaining higher information. Toën's survey covers derived schemes and stacks, derived moduli, formal geometry of derived stacks, and shifted symplectic and Poisson structures. ([Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_%28mathematics%29); [Toën, contents](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.1044))
- **Field with one element (14A23).** $\mathbb F_1$ is a hypothetical object behaving like a field with one element, going back to Tits (1957). Weil proved the Riemann hypothesis for curves over [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields), and a base $\mathbb F_1$ over which $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ were a curve might let that method be adapted. Proposals include Soulé's, Deitmar's monoid schemes, Toën–Vaquié's, Connes–Consani's, Borger's construction by descent from the finite fields and the integers, and Lorscheid's blueprints. ([Field with one element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_with_one_element))

### History
The word "scheme" first appeared in the 1956 Chevalley Seminar; Martineau suggested the spectrum of an arbitrary commutative ring as a foundation, and Grothendieck developed it in EGA from 1960. Artin defined algebraic spaces as étale sheaves that are étale-locally affine schemes; Grothendieck introduced stacks for descent theory, and Artin defined the narrower class of algebraic stacks, which include Deligne–Mumford stacks. ([Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_%28mathematics%29)) Toën's 2014 survey has a first section on selected pieces of the history of derived algebraic geometry and is written with a view to its recent interface with deformation quantization. ([Toën, Derived algebraic geometry](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.1044)) Tits proposed geometry over a field of characteristic one in 1957 from degenerate projective geometries in his theory of buildings. ([Field with one element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_with_one_element))

### Open problems
- **A satisfactory geometry over $\mathbb F_1$.** "Many theories of $\mathbb F_1$ have been proposed, but it is not clear which, if any, of them give $\mathbb F_1$ all the desired properties"; for example, monoid schemes only reach [toric varieties](node:Toric%20Varieties). ([Field with one element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_with_one_element))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [The Stacks Project](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01KH): definitions and proofs for schemes, morphisms, algebraic spaces and stacks.
- **Learn:** [Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry](https://math.stanford.edu/~vakil/216blog/): free notes, published by Princeton University Press.
- **Primary:** [Toën, Derived Algebraic Geometry (survey, 2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.1044): survey of 14A30 foundations.
- **Further reading:** [Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry (Springer, Graduate Texts in Mathematics, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3849-0): standard graduate text on varieties and schemes.
references.MSC 14Bxx - Local theory in algebraic ge:
## Reference
### Overview
14Bxx collects the local theory of [algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry): the structure of a variety or scheme near a point, studied through [local rings](node:Local%20Rings), formal neighbourhoods and infinitesimal thickenings. Its main themes are singularities, deformations of singularities and local deformation theory, Artin approximation, local cohomology, and the local structure of morphisms (étale, flat). ([MSC2020 14Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Bxx))

The basic dichotomy is regular versus singular points. A point of an [algebraic variety](node:Algebraic%20Varieties) is called regular when its local ring is regular, and regular local rings have very rigid structure (a polynomial associated graded ring, the domain and Cohen–Macaulay properties). Zariski showed that, for a variety $Y\subseteq\mathbb A^n$ over a perfect field, $Y$ is nonsingular at $P$ in the Jacobian sense (the Jacobian matrix at $P$ has rank $n-\dim Y$) exactly when its local ring at $P$ is regular; over non-perfect fields this can fail. Singular points are measured by invariants such as the Milnor number and removed, when possible, by resolution of singularities. ([Stacks, Section 10.106](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00NN); [Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring); [Milnor number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor_number); [Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))

Deformation theory asks how an object, such as a singularity, a scheme or a sheaf, varies in families over Artin local rings. In Alper's description it studies the local geometry of a moduli space near a point. ([Alper, Notes on Deformation Theory](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~jarod/courses/math581J-fall21/def-theory-notes.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists: 14B05 singularities (see also 14E15, 14H20, 14J17, 32Sxx, 58Kxx); 14B07 deformations of singularities (see also 14D15, 32S30); 14B10 infinitesimal methods (see also 13D10); 14B12 local deformation theory, Artin approximation, etc. (see also 13B40, 13D10); 14B15 local cohomology (see also 13D45, 32C36); 14B20 formal neighbourhoods; 14B25 local structure of morphisms: étale, flat, etc. (see also 13B40); 14B99 other. ([MSC2020 14Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Bxx))

Neighbouring codes named in these cross-references: 14B05 points to 14E15 in [MSC 14Exx - Birational geometry](node:MSC%2014Exx%20-%20Birational%20geometry) and to [MSC 32Sxx - Complex singularities](node:MSC%2032Sxx%20-%20Complex%20singularities); 14B07 points to 14D15 in [MSC 14Dxx - Families, fibrations in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Dxx%20-%20Families,%20fibrations%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) and to 32S30; and 14B10, 14B12, 14B15 and 14B25 point to 13D10, 13B40 and 13D45 in [MSC 13 - Commutative algebra](node:MSC%2013%20-%20Commutative%20algebra). ([MSC2020 14Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Bxx)) Schemes and their morphisms as such are classified under 14A15 in [MSC 14Axx - Foundations of algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Axx%20-%20Foundations%20of%20algebraic%20geometry). ([MSC2020 14Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Regular local rings.** A Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ of dimension $d$ is regular if $\mathfrak m$ is generated by $d$ elements. Then $\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}\cong\kappa[X_1,\dots,X_d]$; $R$ is a domain; a minimal generating set $x_1,\dots,x_d$ of $\mathfrak m$ is a regular sequence, and each $R/(x_1,\dots,x_c)$ is regular of dimension $d-c$, so $R$ is Cohen–Macaulay.
