([Stacks, Lemmas 10.106.1–10.106.3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00NN)) By Serre, a Noetherian local ring is regular if and only if it has finite global dimension; consequently prime localizations of regular local rings are regular, and by Auslander–Buchsbaum every regular local ring is a unique factorization domain. ([Regular local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring)) See also [MSC 13Hxx - Local rings and semilocal rings](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings).
- **Resolution of singularities (14B05, 14E15).** A resolution of a variety $X$ is a nonsingular variety with a proper birational map onto $X$. Hironaka proved in 1964 that resolutions exist in every dimension over fields of characteristic $0$. In characteristic $p$, curves are classical, Abhyankar resolved surfaces (1956) and threefolds in characteristic $>6$ (1966), and Cossart and Piltant extended threefolds to all characteristics. ([Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))
- **Milnor number (14B05).** For a holomorphic germ $f:(\mathbb C^n,0)\to(\mathbb C,0)$, $\mu(f)=\dim_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}/(\partial f/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial x_n)$, finite if and only if $0$ is an isolated critical point. The Milnor fibre is homotopy equivalent to a bouquet of $\mu(f)$ spheres $S^{n-1}$. For example $\mu(x^3+xy^2)=4$; $x^3+y^3$ and $x^2+y^5$ both have $\mu=4$ but are not $\mathcal A$-equivalent, so $\mu$ is not a complete invariant. ([Milnor number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor_number))
- **Tangent–obstruction theory (14B10, 14B12).** Let $A'\to A$ be a surjection of Noetherian rings with square-zero kernel $J$ and $X\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ smooth and separated. Automorphisms of a deformation over $A'$ correspond to $H^0(X,T_{X/A}\otimes J)$; if a deformation exists, isomorphism classes form a torsor under $H^1(X,T_{X/A}\otimes J)$; and there is $ob_X\in H^2(X,T_{X/A}\otimes J)$ vanishing exactly when a deformation exists. For smooth projective curves of genus $g\ge2$ this gives $\dim\mathcal M_g=\dim H^1(C,T_C)=3g-3$. ([Alper, Proposition 2.5](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~jarod/courses/math581J-fall21/def-theory-notes.pdf); [Deformation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_theory))
- **Schlessinger's criterion (14B12).** For a functor $F$ from Artin local $k$-algebras to sets with $F(k)$ a point, consider $F(B_0\times_{A_0}A)\to F(B_0)\times_{F(A_0)}F(A)$. (H1) surjective when $A\to A_0$ is a small extension (kernel $k$); (H2) bijective when $A_0=k$, $A=k[\epsilon]$; (H3) $\dim_kF(k[\epsilon])<\infty$; (H4) bijective for all small extensions $A\to A_0$. Then $F$ has a miniversal formal deformation if (H1)–(H3) hold, and is pro-representable if (H3)–(H4) hold. ([Alper, Theorem 3.11 and Remark 3.12](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~jarod/courses/math581J-fall21/def-theory-notes.pdf))
- **Artin approximation (14B12, 14B25).** Let $R$ be a field or an excellent discrete valuation ring, $A$ the henselization at a prime of a finite-type $R$-algebra, $\mathfrak m$ a proper ideal, $\hat A$ the $\mathfrak m$-adic completion, and $F$ a functor commuting with filtered colimits. Then for every $c$ and every $\hat\xi\in F(\hat A)$ there is $\xi\in F(A)$ with $\xi\equiv\hat\xi\bmod\mathfrak m^c$. In its original form: formal power-series solutions of polynomial equations can be approximated to any order by algebraic solutions (Artin, 1969). ([Artin approximation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_approximation_theorem))
- **Local cohomology (14B15).** $H^i_I(M)$ is the $i$th right derived functor of $\Gamma_I(M)=\{m:I^nm=0\text{ for some }n\}$. For a Noetherian local ring and finitely generated $M$, $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M)=0$ for $i>\dim M$ and $\ne0$ at $i=\dim M$, and the smallest $i$ with $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M)\ne0$ is the depth; hence $M$ is Cohen–Macaulay exactly when only one $H^i_{\mathfrak m}(M)$ is nonzero. ([Local cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_cohomology))

### History
Kodaira and Spencer put the deformation theory of [complex manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds) on a firm basis, after tentative use in the Italian school. ([Deformation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_theory)) Schlessinger's "Functors of Artin rings" (1968) introduced the conditions (H1)–(H4). ([Alper, Remark 3.12](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~jarod/courses/math581J-fall21/def-theory-notes.pdf)) Grothendieck introduced local cohomology in Harvard seminars in 1961, written up by Hartshorne in 1967 and developed further in SGA 2. ([Local cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_cohomology)) Milnor introduced the Milnor number geometrically in his book *Singular Points of Complex Hypersurfaces*. ([Milnor number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor_number)) Hironaka's resolution theorem appeared in 1964. ([Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))

### Open problems
- **Resolution of singularities in positive characteristic.** For varieties of dimension at least $4$ over fields of characteristic $p>0$, existence of resolution "is an open problem". ([Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Regular local rings](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00NN): local algebra with complete proofs; local algebra used throughout 14B.
- **Learn:** [Alper, Notes on Deformation Theory (Univ. of Washington, Math 581J)](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~jarod/courses/math581J-fall21/def-theory-notes.pdf): first-order deformations, obstructions, Rim–Schlessinger criteria, Artin approximation and algebraization.
- **Primary:** [Schlessinger, Functors of Artin rings, Trans. AMS 130 (1968), 208–222](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1968-0217093-3): the original criterion.
- **Further reading:** [Hironaka, Resolution of singularities of an algebraic variety over a field of characteristic zero I, Ann. of Math. 79 (1964)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1970486): the characteristic-zero resolution theorem.
references.MSC 14Cxx - Cycles and subschemes:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14C, "Cycles and subschemes", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) that studies subvarieties of a variety both as formal combinations and as points of parameter spaces. Algebraic cycles, integer combinations of subvarieties, modulo rational equivalence form the Chow groups $\mathrm{CH}_i(X)$, the algebro-geometric analogues of homology; on a smooth variety they form a graded ring under intersection product, and $\mathrm{CH}^1$ is the divisor class group, isomorphic to the Picard group. ([Chow group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group)) See [Algebraic Cycles and Chow Groups](node:Algebraic%20Cycles%20and%20Chow%20Groups) and [Intersection Theory](node:Intersection%20Theory).

The area's research questions concern how much of a variety's cohomology comes from algebraic cycles (the Hodge and Tate conjectures), how large the Chow groups are (Mumford's theorem, Bloch's conjecture, the Bloch–Beilinson conjectures), and the theory of motives that organises them. ([Chow group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group); [Motive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motive_%28algebraic_geometry%29))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 14Cxx lists 14C05 parametrization (Chow and Hilbert schemes); 14C15 (equivariant) Chow groups and rings, motives; 14C17 intersection theory, [characteristic classes](node:Characteristic%20Classes), intersection multiplicities (see also 13H15); 14C20 divisors, linear systems, invertible sheaves; 14C21 pencils, nets, webs (see also 53A60); 14C22 Picard groups; 14C25 algebraic cycles; 14C30 transcendental methods, Hodge theory (algebro-geometric aspects), Hodge conjecture (see also 14D07, 32G20, 32J25, 32S35, 58A14); 14C34 Torelli problem (see also 32G20); 14C35 applications of algebraic K-theory (see also 19Exx); 14C40 Riemann–Roch theorems (see also 19E20, 19L10); 14C99. ([MSC2020 14Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Cxx))

- **Neighbours 58A14 and 14D07.** The Hodge conjecture is classified in 14C30, which cross-refers to 58A14 (Hodge theory in global analysis) and 14D07 (variations of Hodge structure). ([MSC2020 14Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Cxx))
- **Neighbour 13H15.** Intersection multiplicities in local algebra are cross-referenced from 14C17 to [MSC 13Hxx - Local rings and semilocal rings](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings). ([MSC2020 14Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Cxx))
- **Neighbour 19E.** K-theoretic methods (14C35) and Riemann–Roch (14C40) point to algebraic K-theory, 19Exx and 19E20; see [K-Theory of Schemes](node:K-Theory%20of%20Schemes). ([MSC2020 14Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Cxx))
- **Neighbour 32G20.** The Torelli problem and Hodge theory cross-refer to period matrices and variations of Hodge structure in 32G20. ([MSC2020 14Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Chow groups and rational equivalence (14C15, 14C25).** For a scheme $X$ locally of finite type over a base as in the Stacks project, a $k$-cycle is rationally equivalent to zero if it has the form $\sum_j(i_j)_*\mathrm{div}(f_j)$ for a locally finite family of integral closed subschemes $W_j$ of dimension $k+1$ and nonzero rational functions $f_j\in R(W_j)^*$; then $\mathrm{CH}_k(X)=Z_k(X)/\!\sim_{\mathrm{rat}}$. ([Stacks, Definition 42.19.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02RV)) For example $\mathrm{CH}^*(\mathbb P^n)\cong\mathbb Z[H]/(H^{n+1})$ with $H$ the hyperplane class. ([Chow group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group))
- **Divisors and intersection numbers (14C17, 14C20).** On a nonsingular projective surface $X$ over an algebraically closed field, distinct curves $C,D$ with local equations $f,g$ at $p\in C\cap D$ have intersection multiplicity $m_p(C\cap D)=\dim_k\mathcal O_p/(f,g)$, and $C\cdot D=\sum_p m_p(C\cap D)$. The pairing $L\cdot M=\chi(\mathcal O_X)-\chi(L^{-1})-\chi(M^{-1})+\chi(L^{-1}\otimes M^{-1})$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $\mathrm{Pic}\,X$ agreeing with $C\cdot D$ on distinct irreducible curves, and $\mathcal O_X(C)\cdot L=\deg L|_C$ for a nonsingular curve $C$. ([MIT 18.727, Lecture 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-algebraic-surfaces-spring-2008/cce30335f2f48854721e541f1c4cb536_lect1.pdf)) The standard reference for intersection theory in all dimensions is Fulton's *Intersection Theory*. ([Fulton, Springer 1998](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1700-8))
- **Picard and Néron–Severi groups (14C22).** The Néron–Severi group $\mathrm{NS}(V)=\mathrm{Pic}(V)/\mathrm{Pic}^0(V)$ is the group of divisors modulo algebraic equivalence. It is finitely generated (theorem of the base: Severi over $\mathbb C$, Néron over general fields), its rank is the Picard number $\rho(V)$, and for complex $V$, via the exponential sequence, it is the image of $c_1$ in $H^2(V,\mathbb Z)$. ([Néron–Severi group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A9ron%E2%80%93Severi_group))
- **Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch (14C40).** For a proper morphism $f:X\to Y$ of smooth quasi-projective schemes and a bounded complex $F^\bullet$ of sheaves on $X$,
$$\mathrm{ch}(f_!F^\bullet)\cdot\mathrm{td}(Y)=f_*\big(\mathrm{ch}(F^\bullet)\cdot\mathrm{td}(X)\big)\quad\text{in }\mathrm{CH}(Y)\otimes\mathbb Q,$$
where $f_!$ is the alternating sum of higher direct images. Grothendieck proved it in a 1957 manuscript, written up by Borel and Serre in 1958; Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch is the case $Y=\mathrm{pt}$ over $\mathbb C$. ([Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck%E2%80%93Riemann%E2%80%93Roch_theorem))
- **Torelli theorem (14C34).** A smooth projective curve is determined by its Jacobian as a principally polarized [abelian variety](node:Abelian%20Varieties) (Torelli, 1913); equivalently the period map from the moduli of curves of genus $g$ to principally polarized abelian varieties is injective on geometric points. Generalizations study period maps for other varieties, notably [K3 Surfaces](node:K3%20Surfaces) and hyperkähler manifolds. ([Torelli theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torelli_theorem))
- **Hilbert and Chow schemes (14C05).** Grothendieck's Hilbert scheme parametrizes closed subschemes of $\mathbb P^n$: its $T$-points are closed subschemes of $\mathbb P^n\times T$ flat over $T$, and it decomposes into pieces indexed by Hilbert polynomials, and each non-empty piece is connected (Hartshorne). The Hilbert–Chow morphism sends a zero-dimensional subscheme to its zero-cycle; it is birational for points on a smooth surface, where the Hilbert scheme of points is smooth, but in dimension at least three the Hilbert scheme of $n$ points is in general reducible for large $n$ and can have components of much larger dimension than the symmetric product. ([Hilbert scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_scheme)) See [Moduli Spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces).
- **Mumford's theorem on zero-cycles (14C25).** For a smooth complex projective surface with geometric genus $p_g\neq0$, the kernel of the degree map on $\mathrm{CH}_0$ is "infinite-dimensional". ([Chow group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group)) See [Algebraic Surfaces](node:Algebraic%20Surfaces).
- **Motives (14C15).** Grothendieck proposed motives in the 1960s as a universal cohomology theory of which Betti, de Rham, étale, and crystalline cohomology are realizations; pure motives are built from algebraic correspondences and idempotents. Jannsen proved that the category of pure motives is abelian and semisimple exactly when numerical equivalence is used, and Voevodsky's triangulated categories of mixed motives supply much of the expected formalism. ([Motive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motive_%28algebraic_geometry%29))

### History
Hodge presented his conjecture at the 1950 International Congress of Mathematicians; Atiyah and Hirzebruch later showed, using K-theory, that its integral version fails. ([Hodge conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_conjecture)) Torelli's theorem dates from 1913, Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch from 1957, and Tate formulated his conjecture in 1963. ([Torelli theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torelli_theorem); [Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck%E2%80%93Riemann%E2%80%93Roch_theorem); [Tate conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_conjecture)) Bloch, Kas and Lieberman (1976) proved Bloch's conjecture for surfaces not of general type, and Voisin (2012) proved it for Catanese and Barlow surfaces. ([Voisin, arXiv:1210.3935](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1210.3935))

### Open problems
- **Hodge conjecture (14C30).** On a non-singular complex projective variety $X$, every Hodge class, a class in $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{k,k}(X)$, should be a rational linear combination of classes of algebraic subvarieties. The case $k=1$ is Lefschetz's $(1,1)$ theorem, and the integral version is false. ([Hodge conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_conjecture)) The Clay Institute lists it as an unsolved Millennium Problem. ([Clay, Hodge conjecture](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/hodge-conjecture/)) See [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory) and [MSC 14Fxx - (Co)homology theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Fxx%20-%20%28Co%29homology%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry).
- **Tate conjecture.** For a smooth projective variety over a finitely generated field, the Galois-invariant part of $\ell$-adic cohomology in degree $2i$ should be spanned by classes of codimension-$i$ subvarieties. Even the case of divisors is called "a major open problem"; it is known for divisors on abelian varieties (Tate over [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields), Faltings over number fields) and for K3 surfaces over finitely generated fields of characteristic not 2. ([Tate conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_conjecture)) See [Étale Cohomology](node:Étale%20Cohomology).
- **Bloch's conjecture for zero-cycles.** For a surface with $p_g=q=0$, the Albanese kernel $\mathrm{CH}_0(X)_{\mathrm{alb}}$ should vanish, and more generally a correspondence acting trivially on holomorphic 2-forms should act trivially on $\mathrm{CH}_0(\cdot)_{\mathrm{alb}}$. Voisin states it as Conjecture 0.1; it is known for surfaces not of general type and for some families of surfaces of general type. ([Voisin, arXiv:1210.3935](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1210.3935); [Chow group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group))
- **Bloch–Beilinson conjectures and finite generation.** A conjectural filtration on rational Chow groups controlled by cohomology would imply Bloch's conjecture; whether Chow groups of varieties over number fields are finitely generated is open. ([Chow group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group))
- **Standard conjectures.** Grothendieck's standard conjectures on algebraic cycles remain open in general; Grothendieck and Bombieri gave a proof of the Weil conjectures conditional on them. ([Motive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motive_%28algebraic_geometry%29))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Chow group (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group): definitions, Mumford's theorem, main conjectures.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Rational equivalence](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02RV): rigorous definition of Chow groups.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.727 Algebraic Surfaces, Lecture 1 (Kumar)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-algebraic-surfaces-spring-2008/cce30335f2f48854721e541f1c4cb536_lect1.pdf): intersection multiplicities and the intersection form on surfaces.
- **Primary:** [Voisin, Bloch's conjecture for Catanese and Barlow surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.3935): research paper on zero-cycles of surfaces with $p_g=q=0$.
- **Further reading:** [Fulton, Intersection Theory (Springer, 1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1700-8): the standard monograph on Chow groups and intersection theory.
references.MSC 14Dxx - Families, fibrations in alge:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14D, "Families, fibrations in algebraic geometry", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) that studies how varieties and schemes vary over a parameter space, and the moduli spaces that classify them. Its codes run from the structure of families (monodromy, degenerations) through variations of Hodge structure and deformation theory to moduli problems, fine and coarse moduli spaces, stacks, and the geometric Langlands program. ([MSC2020 14Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Dxx))

The basic object is a morphism $f:X\to S$ viewed as the family of fibres $X_s$. Flatness is the standard condition that makes the fibres vary "continuously": $f$ is flat at $x$ when $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a flat $\mathcal O_{S,f(x)}$-module, and flat if it is flat at every point; nothing about smoothness of the fibres is built in. ([Stacks, Definition 29.26.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01U2)) A moduli problem asks for a space whose points are isomorphism classes of objects and whose maps from a test scheme $T$ correspond to families over $T$. The model case is [moduli of curves](node:Moduli%20Spaces), where automorphisms of the objects prevent a fine moduli scheme and lead either to coarse moduli spaces or to Deligne–Mumford stacks. ([MIT 18.727 notes, §1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 14Dxx lists: 14D05 structure of families (Picard–Lefschetz, monodromy, etc.); 14D06 fibrations, degenerations in algebraic geometry; 14D07 variation of Hodge structures (algebro-geometric aspects; see also 32G20); 14D10 arithmetic ground fields (finite, local, global) and families or fibrations; 14D15 formal methods and deformations in algebraic geometry (see also 13D10, 14B07, 32Gxx); 14D20 algebraic moduli problems, moduli of vector bundles (for analytic moduli problems see 32G13); 14D21 applications of vector bundles and moduli spaces in mathematical physics (twistor theory, instantons, [quantum field theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory)); 14D22 fine and coarse moduli spaces; 14D23 stacks and moduli problems; 14D24 geometric Langlands program (algebro-geometric aspects; see also 22E57); 14D99. ([MSC2020 14Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Dxx))

- **Neighbour 14H.** Moduli of curves as such is classified under 14H10 "Families, moduli of curves (algebraic)", and vector bundles on curves and their moduli under 14H60, in [MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Hxx%20-%20Curves%20in%20algebraic%20geometry); 14D holds the general theory of families and moduli. ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx); [MSC2020 14Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Dxx))
- **Neighbour 32G.** The analytic theory of deformations and analytic moduli problems is in [MSC 32Gxx - Deformations of analytic structures](node:MSC%2032Gxx%20-%20Deformations%20of%20analytic%20structures), which 14D07, 14D15 and 14D20 cross-refer to. ([MSC2020 14Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Dxx))
- **Neighbour 14C.** Chow and Hilbert schemes are classified under 14C05 "Parametrization (Chow and Hilbert schemes)" in [MSC 14Cxx - Cycles and subschemes](node:MSC%2014Cxx%20-%20Cycles%20and%20subschemes). ([MSC2020 14Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Cxx)) The Hilbert scheme is a basic tool for constructing moduli spaces: $\overline M_g$ is built as a GIT quotient of a locally closed subscheme of a Hilbert scheme of pluricanonically embedded curves. ([MIT 18.727 notes, §1–2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Flat families and base change (14D06).** The composition of flat morphisms is flat, the base change of a flat morphism is flat, and a flat morphism locally of finite presentation is universally open. These make flat families stable under pulling back along maps of parameter schemes. ([Stacks, Lemmas 29.26.6, 29.26.8, 29.26.10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01U2)) See [Flat Modules](node:Flat%20Modules) and [Schemes](node:Schemes).
- **Fine and coarse moduli (14D22).** A scheme $X(F)$ with a family $U(F)\in F(X(F))$ finely represents a functor $F$ if $g\mapsto g^*U(F)$ gives bijections $\mathrm{Hom}_S(Y,X(F))\to F(Y)$ for all $Y$. A coarse moduli space only requires a natural transformation $F\to\mathrm{Hom}_S(-,X(F))$ that is bijective on points over algebraically closed fields and universal among maps to schemes. The smooth-curve functor $M_g$ is not finely representable: a hyperelliptic curve $C$ and an Enriques surface give a non-trivial family over the Enriques surface all of whose fibres are isomorphic to $C$, which would have to correspond to the same constant map as the trivial family. ([MIT 18.727 notes, Example 1.1 and Definition 1.2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf))
- **Stacks (14D23).** An algebraic (Artin) stack is a category fibred in [groupoids](node:Groupoids) over $(\mathrm{Sch}/S)_{\mathrm{fppf}}$ that is a stack, has diagonal representable by algebraic spaces, and admits a smooth surjective atlas from a scheme; it is Deligne–Mumford when the atlas can be chosen étale. The moduli stack $\mathcal M_g$ of curves is a natural example of a Deligne–Mumford stack, while $B\mathrm{GL}_n=[*/\mathrm{GL}_n]$ is an Artin stack whose points have infinitesimal automorphisms, which points of a Deligne–Mumford stack never have. ([Algebraic stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_stack)) By Keel–Mori, any separated Deligne–Mumford stack of finite type has a coarse moduli space in the category of algebraic spaces. ([MIT 18.727 notes, Theorem 5.12](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf))
- **Deligne–Mumford theorem on stable curves.** For $2g-2+n>0$, a pointed nodal connected curve is stable if every rational component of its normalization has at least three special points and every genus-one component at least one; a stable curve over $S$ is a proper flat family whose geometric fibres are stable. ([MIT 18.727 notes, Definitions 1.5–1.6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf)) Deligne and Mumford showed that the moduli stack $\overline{\mathcal M}_g$ ($g\ge2$) is a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack, proper by stable reduction and the valuative criterion, of dimension $3g-3$, and that $\mathcal M_g$ is irreducible. ([Moduli of algebraic curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_of_algebraic_curves); [MIT 18.727 notes, §5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf); [Deligne–Mumford, Publ. Math. IHÉS 36 (1969)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684599)) Stable reduction: over a DVR $B$ with fraction field $K$, a stable pointed curve over $K$ extends, after a finite extension $L/K$, to a unique stable family over the base extended to $L$. The coarse space $\overline M_{g,n}$ is a projective variety containing $M_{g,n}$ as a Zariski open subset (Deligne–Mumford–Knudsen), and $M_g$ is irreducible over every algebraically closed field. ([MIT 18.727 notes, Theorems 1.7, 4.1, 6.28](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf))
- **Geometric invariant theory (14D20, 14D22).** For a reductive group $G$ acting linearly on a projective variety $X\subseteq\mathbb P^n$, the semistable locus $X^{ss}$ has a good quotient $Y$ that is projective, and an open $Y^s\subseteq Y$ is a geometric quotient of the stable locus $X^s$. Hilbert–Mumford criterion: $x$ is semistable iff $\mu(x,\lambda)\ge0$ and stable iff $\mu(x,\lambda)>0$ for every one-parameter subgroup $\lambda:\mathbb G_m\to G$. Finite generation of invariants comes from Haboush's theorem (reductive groups are geometrically reductive) and Nagata's theorem. ([MIT 18.727 notes, Theorems 6.2–6.4, 6.11, 6.13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf)) For $g\ge2$, $\overline M_g$ is a quotient of a locus in the Hilbert scheme of curves in $\mathbb P^{5g-6}$ by $\mathrm{PGL}(5g-5)$. ([Geometric invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory))
- **Moduli of vector bundles (14D20).** A vector bundle $W$ on a nonsingular projective curve with slope $\mu(W)=\deg W/\operatorname{rank}W$ is stable if $\mu(V)<\mu(W)$ for every proper nonzero subbundle $V$, and semistable with $\le$. Mumford introduced the notion and proved that stable bundles of fixed rank and degree have a quasi-projective moduli space; the Narasimhan–Seshadri theorem identifies stable bundles with bundles admitting projectively flat unitary irreducible connections, and degree-zero stable bundles with irreducible unitary representations of $\pi_1$. Gieseker stability, defined through Hilbert polynomials, extends this to higher dimension. ([Stable vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_vector_bundle)) See [Holomorphic Vector Bundles](node:Holomorphic%20Vector%20Bundles).
- **Deformation theory (14D15).** First-order deformations of a complex manifold are governed by $H^1(\Theta)$ of the tangent sheaf (Kodaira–Spencer), with obstructions in $H^2(\Theta)$, which vanishes for curves. Algebraically one studies functors $F$ on local Artin $k$-algebras with $F(k)$ a point and tangent space $F(k[\varepsilon])$. ([Deformation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_theory)) Schlessinger's theorem (1968): such a functor has a hull if it satisfies conditions (H1)–(H3), the last being that the tangent space is finite-dimensional, and is represented by a complete Noetherian local $k$-algebra if it also satisfies (H4). ([Schlessinger's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schlessinger%27s_theorem)) See [Deformations of Complex Structures](node:Deformations%20of%20Complex%20Structures).
- **Variation of Hodge structure (14D07).** A variation of Hodge structure of weight $n$ over a complex manifold $X$ is a local system $S$ of finitely generated [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) with a decreasing filtration $F^\bullet$ on $S\otimes\mathcal O_X$ inducing a Hodge structure on each fibre, such that the flat (Gauss–Manin) connection satisfies Griffiths transversality $\nabla F^p\subseteq F^{p-1}\otimes\Omega^1_X$. Variations of Hodge structure were first studied by Griffiths (1968), beginning with "Periods of integrals on algebraic manifolds I". ([Variation of Hodge structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variation_of_Hodge_structure)) See [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory).

### History
Deligne and Mumford introduced what are now called Deligne–Mumford stacks in "The irreducibility of the space of curves of given genus" (Publ. Math. IHÉS 36, 1969, 75–109), using them to prove irreducibility of $M_g$ in all characteristics. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684599); [MIT 18.727 notes, §6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf)) Mumford founded geometric invariant theory in a 1965 monograph, building on Hilbert's 1893 invariant theory. ([Geometric invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory)) Mumford introduced stable bundles in 1963, and Schlessinger's criterion appeared in 1968. ([Stable vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_vector_bundle); [Schlessinger's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schlessinger%27s_theorem)) Harris, Mumford and Eisenbud showed that $\overline M_g$ is of general type for $g\ge24$, and Farkas, Jensen and Payne extended this to $g=22,23$. ([Farkas–Jensen–Payne, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.00622))

### Open problems
- **Kodaira dimension of $\overline M_g$ for $16\le g\le21$.** Severi showed $M_g$ unirational for $g\le10$; later work gives unirationality for $g\le14$ and rational connectedness of $M_{15}$; $\overline M_g$ is of general type for $g\ge22$. Chang and Ran's argument that $M_{16}$ is uniruled was found to contain a fatal error, and Farkas, Jensen and Payne write that "the Kodaira dimension of $\overline M_g$ is unknown for $16\le g\le21$". They also note that all the standard moduli spaces (curves, [abelian varieties](node:Abelian%20Varieties), [K3 surfaces](node:K3%20Surfaces)), apart from spin curves, have components of unknown Kodaira dimension. ([Farkas–Jensen–Payne, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.00622))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Moduli of algebraic curves (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_of_algebraic_curves): stacks and coarse spaces of curves, Deligne–Mumford theorem, Kodaira dimension.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Flat morphisms](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01U2): exact hypotheses for flatness results.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.727, The moduli space of curves](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf): Hilbert schemes, stable reduction, Deligne–Mumford stacks, GIT construction of $\overline M_g$.
- **Primary:** [Deligne and Mumford, The irreducibility of the space of curves of given genus (1969)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684599): the original paper on stable curves and Deligne–Mumford stacks.
- **Primary:** [Farkas, Jensen and Payne, The Kodaira dimensions of $\overline M_{22}$ and $\overline M_{23}$](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.00622): research paper with the current status of the Kodaira dimension of $\overline M_g$.
- **Further reading:** [Mumford, Fogarty and Kirwan, Geometric Invariant Theory (Springer, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-57916-5) and [Harris and Morrison, Moduli of Curves (Springer GTM, 1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b98867): the standard monographs (authorship of the latter as in the [MIT 18.727 references](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-727-topics-in-algebraic-geometry-intersection-theory-on-moduli-spaces-spring-2006/c551b2cfe8816272aa54a51c6d04079e_const.pdf)).
references.MSC 14Exx - Birational geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14E, "Birational geometry", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) that classifies varieties up to birational equivalence, that is, up to isomorphism of dense open subsets. For varieties $X,Y$ over a field $k$ the following are equivalent: $X$ and $Y$ are birational; the function fields $k(X)$ and $k(Y)$ are isomorphic; $X$ and $Y$ have isomorphic nonempty open subsets. In fact the category of varieties with dominant rational maps is equivalent to that of finitely generated field extensions of $k$, with arrows reversed: a dominant rational map $X\dashrightarrow Y$ induces $k(Y)\to k(X)$. ([Stacks, Theorem 33.4.1 and Lemma 33.4.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BXM)) See [Birational Maps](node:Birational%20Maps) and [Algebraic Varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties).

The central question is to find a good representative in each birational class. For surfaces, contracting $(-1)$-curves gives a minimal model; in higher dimension Mori replaced $(-1)$-curves by extremal rays, and the resulting minimal model program (MMP) predicts that every variety is birational either to a minimal variety ($K$ nef) or to a Mori fibre space. ([Birkar, Lectures on Birational Geometry, §§1.6–1.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670)) Birational invariants, resolution of singularities, rationality questions, and birational automorphism groups complete the picture. ([Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 14Exx lists: 14E05 rational and birational maps; 14E07 birational automorphisms, Cremona group and generalizations; 14E08 rationality questions (see also 14M20); 14E15 global theory and resolution of singularities (algebro-geometric aspects; see also 14B05, 32S20, 32S45); 14E16 McKay correspondence; 14E18 arcs and motivic integration; 14E20 coverings (see also 14H30); 14E22 ramification problems (see also 11S15); 14E25 embeddings; 14E30 minimal model program (Mori theory, extremal rays); 14E99. ([MSC2020 14Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Exx))

- **Neighbour 14B and 32S.** Local theory of singularities is in [MSC 14Bxx - Local theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Bxx%20-%20Local%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) (14B05) and complex singularities in [MSC 32Sxx - Complex singularities](node:MSC%2032Sxx%20-%20Complex%20singularities); 14E15 holds the global theory of resolution. ([MSC2020 14Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Exx))
- **Neighbour 14J.** Classification of particular surfaces and higher-dimensional varieties is in [MSC 14Jxx - Surfaces and higher-dimensional varieties](node:MSC%2014Jxx%20-%20Surfaces%20and%20higher-dimensional%20varieties); 14E holds the general birational methods. 14E08 cross-refers to 14M20 for rational and unirational varieties. ([MSC2020 14Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Exx))
- **Neighbour 14H.** Coverings of curves specifically go to 14H30 in [MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Hxx%20-%20Curves%20in%20algebraic%20geometry). ([MSC2020 14Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Birational invariants (14E05).** For a smooth projective variety $X$ of dimension $d$ the plurigenera $P_m(X)=h^0(X,\omega_X^{\otimes m})$ and the Kodaira dimension $\kappa(X)\in\{-\infty,0,1,\dots,d\}$ (the largest $a$ with $\limsup_m P_m(X)/m^a>0$, or $-\infty$ if all $P_m=0$) are birational invariants. ([Birkar, Definition 1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670); [Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry)) For smooth complex projective varieties the Hodge numbers $h^{p,0}$ and the [fundamental group](node:Fundamental%20Group) are also birational invariants. ([Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry))
- **Minimal models of surfaces and the Enriques classification.** By Castelnuovo's theorem a $(-1)$-curve $E\cong\mathbb P^1$ with $E^2=-1$ on a smooth projective surface can be contracted to a smooth point; each contraction lowers the Picard number by one, so after finitely many steps one reaches $Y$ that is $\mathbb P^2$, a ruled surface, or has $K_Y$ nef. In characteristic zero, $\kappa(Y)=0$ gives a [K3 surface](node:K3%20Surfaces), an Enriques surface, or an étale quotient of an abelian surface; $\kappa(Y)=1$ a minimal elliptic surface; $\kappa(Y)=2$ general type. ([Birkar, §1.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670); [Minimal model program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_model_program))
- **Resolution of singularities (14E15).** Hironaka (1964): over a field of characteristic $0$, every variety has a resolution of singularities, obtained by repeatedly [blowing up](node:Blowups) along nonsingular subvarieties. In log form, for a variety $X$ and divisor $D$ in characteristic $0$ there is a log resolution $f:Y\to X$: $Y$ smooth and $\mathrm{exc}(f)\cup f^{-1}(\mathrm{Supp}\,D)$ a simple normal crossing divisor. ([Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities); [Birkar, Theorem 1.13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670))
- **Cone and contraction theorems (14E30).** Let $(X/Z,B)$ be a klt pair of dimension $d$ with $B$ rational (Birkar works over $\mathbb C$). Then there is a countable set of $(K_X+B)$-negative extremal rays $R_i$ with $\overline{NE}(X/Z)=\overline{NE}(X/Z)_{K_X+B\ge0}+\sum_iR_i$, the $R_i$ are discrete in the $(K_X+B)$-negative half, each can be contracted, and each contains the class of a rational curve $C_i$ with $-2d\le(K_X+B)\cdot C_i$. A contraction of an extremal ray is divisorial, small (then one needs a flip), or a fibration, the last giving a Mori fibre space. ([Birkar, Theorem 7.1, Remark 6.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670))
- **Existence of minimal models (BCHM).** Birkar, Cascini, Hacon and McKernan proved existence of minimal models for varieties of log general type, and that the canonical ring of a smooth projective variety is finitely generated. ([BCHM, arXiv:math/0610203](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610203); [Minimal model program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_model_program)) The minimal model conjecture for lc pairs was settled in dimension $3$ by Shokurov and Kawamata and in dimension $4$ by Shokurov and Birkar. ([Birkar, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670))
- **Weak factorization (14E05).** Abramovich, Karu, Matsuki and Włodarczyk: a birational map between complete nonsingular varieties over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero is a composite of blowings up and blowings down with smooth centres, and the factorization can be chosen functorially and compatibly with a normal crossings divisor. ([AKMW, arXiv:math/9904135](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9904135))
- **Rationality and the Cremona group (14E07, 14E08).** A variety is rational if it is birational to projective space. Smooth cubic threefolds (Clemens–Griffiths, 1972) and smooth quartic threefolds (Iskovskikh–Manin, 1971) are not rational, and quartic threefolds are birationally rigid. ([Birational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry)) The Cremona group $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb P^n)$ is generated for $n=2$ over $\mathbb C$ by $\mathrm{PGL}(3)$ and the standard quadratic transformation (Noether–Castelnuovo), while for $n\ge3$ it is not generated by elements of bounded degree (Hudson, 1927); Cantat and Lamy showed $\mathrm{Cr}_2(k)$ is not simple for $k$ algebraically closed. ([Cremona group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cremona_group))

### History
The Italian school (Enriques, Castelnuovo, Severi and others) worked out the birational classification of surfaces; Mumford and Bombieri obtained a similar statement in positive characteristic. Mori's extremal rays opened the higher-dimensional theory, and in dimension $3$ the program was established through work of Mori, Shokurov, Kawamata, Kollár, Reid and others. ([Birkar, §§1.6–1.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670)) Mori showed that flips exist for threefolds (1988), and BCHM generalized existence of flips and minimal models to higher dimension. ([Minimal model program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_model_program)) Hironaka proved resolution in characteristic zero in 1964. ([Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))

### Open problems
- **Abundance conjecture.** If $(X,\Delta)$ is a log canonical pair with $K_X+\Delta$ nef, then $K_X+\Delta$ is semi-ample. Meng writes that the log abundance conjecture "is only known to be true in dimensions up to 3" (Kawamata and Fujita in dimension $2$; Keel, Matsuki and McKernan in dimension $3$). ([Meng, arXiv:1906.11451, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.11451)) Birkar calls abundance "essentially the main problem". ([Birkar, §1.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670))
- **Nonvanishing and termination of flips.** Nonvanishing (for lc $(X/Z,B)$ with $K_X+B$ pseudo-effective, $K_X+B\sim_{\mathbb R}M\ge0$) is proved in dimension $3$, and "in higher dimension very little is known". Termination of flips is known in dimension $3$ (Kawamata, Shokurov), in dimension $4$ when $\kappa(K_X+B)\ge2$, and for flips with scaling in the klt big case (BCHM); "not much is known in higher dimension". ([Birkar, Conjectures 6.7, 6.15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670)) Later progress in dimension $4$ includes Moraga's termination of $(K_X+\Delta)$-flips for lc pairs with $K_X+\Delta$ pseudo-effective, and nonvanishing for lc pairs on uniruled $4$-folds. ([Meng, arXiv:1906.11451, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.11451))
- **Resolution in positive characteristic.** Resolution of singularities for varieties of dimension at least $4$ over fields of characteristic $p$ is an open problem; surfaces (Abhyankar, 1956) and threefolds (Abhyankar for $p>6$, Cossart–Piltant in general) are settled. ([Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Birational geometry (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry): invariants, rationality results, weak factorization, Cremona groups.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Varieties and rational maps](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BXM): field-theoretic characterization of birational equivalence.
- **Learn:** [Birkar, Lectures on Birational Geometry](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.2670): graduate lectures on the cone theorem, singularities of pairs, the main conjectures and their status.
- **Primary:** [Birkar, Cascini, Hacon and McKernan, Existence of minimal models for varieties of log general type](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610203): the BCHM paper.
- **Primary:** [Abramovich, Karu, Matsuki and Włodarczyk, Torification and factorization of birational maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9904135): weak factorization in characteristic zero.
- **Further reading:** [Kollár and Mori, Birational Geometry of Algebraic Varieties (Cambridge University Press, 1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511662560): the standard monograph on the MMP.
references.MSC 14Fxx - (Co)homology theory in algeb:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14F, "(Co)homology theory in algebraic geometry", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) that attaches cohomological invariants to schemes: coherent sheaf cohomology, derived categories, D-modules, vanishing theorems, étale and other Grothendieck topologies, Brauer groups, classical singular cohomology, $p$-adic and crystalline cohomology, fundamental groups and homotopy theory, de Rham cohomology, and motivic cohomology. ([MSC2020 14Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Fxx))

The field has two driving needs. Coherent cohomology controls linear systems, deformations and classification. A "Weil cohomology" for varieties over arbitrary fields, behaving like singular cohomology over $\mathbb C$, was needed to prove the Weil conjectures; Grothendieck introduced étale cohomology for this purpose, with foundations worked out with M. Artin in SGA 4. ([Étale cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tale_cohomology)) Over $\mathbb C$ the various theories are related by comparison isomorphisms, and Grothendieck's theory of motives aims to explain this parallelism; the Hodge conjecture and parallel conjectures such as Tate's, which predict the span of the classes of algebraic cycles, remain open. ([Deligne, The Hodge Conjecture, §5](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/hodge.pdf))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 14Fxx (see also 13Dxx) lists: 14F06 sheaves in algebraic geometry; 14F08 derived categories of sheaves, dg categories, and related constructions; 14F10 differentials and other special sheaves, D-modules, Bernstein–Sato ideals and polynomials; 14F17 vanishing theorems; 14F18 multiplier ideals; 14F20 étale and other Grothendieck topologies and (co)homologies; 14F22 Brauer groups of schemes; 14F25 classical real and complex (co)homology; 14F30 $p$-adic cohomology, crystalline cohomology; 14F35 homotopy theory and fundamental groups; 14F40 de Rham cohomology; 14F42 motivic cohomology, motivic homotopy theory (see also 19E15); 14F43 other (co)homologies (intersection, equivariant, Lawson, Deligne); 14F45 topological properties; 14F99. ([MSC2020 14Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Fxx))

- **Neighbour 13D and 18G.** Homological algebra of rings is in [MSC 13Dxx - Homological methods in commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory), and derived categories in general in [MSC 18Gxx - Homological algebra in category theory, derived categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Gxx%20-%20Homological%20algebra%20in%20category%20theory,%20derived%20categories%20and%20functors); 14F08 cross-refers to 18Gxx. ([MSC2020 14Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Fxx))
- **Neighbour 14C.** [Algebraic cycles and Chow groups](node:Algebraic%20Cycles%20and%20Chow%20Groups) are in [MSC 14Cxx - Cycles and subschemes](node:MSC%2014Cxx%20-%20Cycles%20and%20subschemes); 14F40 cross-refers to 14C30 (transcendental methods, Hodge theory). ([MSC2020 14Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Fxx))
- **Neighbour 19E.** Algebraic $K$-theory of schemes is in [MSC 19Exx - K-theory in geometry](node:MSC%2019Exx%20-%20K-theory%20in%20geometry), linked to motivic cohomology via 19E15. ([MSC2020 14Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Sheaf cohomology (14F06).** For an abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ with injective resolution $\mathcal F\to\mathcal I^\bullet$, $H^i(X,\mathcal F)=H^i(\Gamma(X,\mathcal I^\bullet))$, and for $f:X\to Y$ the higher direct images are $R^if_*\mathcal F=H^i(f_*\mathcal I^\bullet)$. ([Stacks, §20.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01DZ)) See [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) and [Derived Categories](node:Derived%20Categories).
- **Finiteness, vanishing and duality for coherent sheaves (14F06, 14F17).** For a proper scheme $X$ over a field $k$ and coherent $\mathcal F$, each $H^i(X,\mathcal F)$ is finite-dimensional. Grothendieck vanishing: on a Noetherian space of dimension $n$, $H^i=0$ for $i>n$. Serre vanishing: if $L$ is ample on a proper scheme over a Noetherian ring, then for $m\gg0$, $\mathcal F\otimes L^m$ is globally generated with $H^i(X,\mathcal F\otimes L^m)=0$ for $i>0$. Serre duality: on a smooth proper $X$ of dimension $n$ over $k$ there is a trace $H^n(X,K_X)\to k$ and a perfect pairing $H^i(X,E)\times H^{n-i}(X,K_X\otimes E^*)\to k$ for vector bundles $E$. Kodaira vanishing: for $X$ smooth projective in characteristic $0$ and $L$ ample, $H^j(X,K_X\otimes L)=0$ for $j>0$; it fails in positive characteristic. GAGA: for $X$ proper over $\mathbb C$, algebraic and analytic coherent cohomology agree (Grothendieck, generalizing Serre's projective case). ([Coherent sheaf cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf_cohomology))
- **Étale cohomology and base change (14F20).** Proper base change: if $f:X\to Y$ is proper, $g:Y'\to Y$ arbitrary, $X'=Y'\times_YX$, and $\mathcal F$ an abelian torsion sheaf on $X_{\text{ét}}$, then $g^{-1}Rf_*\mathcal F\to Rf'_*(g')^{-1}\mathcal F$ is an isomorphism. ([Stacks, Theorem 59.91.11](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095T)) Smooth base change: for a cartesian square with $f:X\to S$ smooth and $g:T\to S$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated, $f^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal F=R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal F$ for every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $T_{\text{ét}}$ whose stalks are torsion of orders invertible on $S$. ([Stacks, Theorem 59.89.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYU)) Artin comparison: for a complex variety, étale cohomology with finite coefficients is isomorphic to singular cohomology with finite coefficients, though not with integer coefficients. $\ell$-adic cohomology is the inverse limit over $k$ of étale cohomology with $\mathbb Z/\ell^k$ coefficients, for $\ell$ different from the characteristic $p$. ([Étale cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tale_cohomology)) See [Étale Cohomology](node:Étale%20Cohomology).
- **Weil conjectures (14F20, 14G10 neighbour).** For a nonsingular projective $n$-dimensional variety $X$ over the [finite field](node:Finite%20Fields) $\mathbb F_q$ with $N_m=\#X(\mathbb F_{q^m})$, the zeta function $Z(X,T)=\exp\big(\sum_m N_mT^m/m\big)$ is rational, $Z=\prod_i P_i(T)^{(-1)^{i+1}}$ with $P_0=1-T$, $P_{2n}=1-q^nT$; it satisfies a functional equation; the inverse roots of $P_i$ have absolute value $q^{i/2}$; and if $X$ is a good reduction mod $p$ of a nonsingular projective variety $Y$, $\deg P_i$ is the $i$-th Betti number of $Y(\mathbb C)$. ([Weil conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_conjectures))
- **$p$-adic and crystalline cohomology (14F30).** For $X$ over a field $k$ of characteristic $p$, crystalline cohomology $H^i(X/W)$ takes values in modules over the Witt vectors $W=W(k)$; for smooth proper $X$ with a smooth proper lift $Z$ over $W$ it is canonically the de Rham cohomology of $Z$. ([Crystalline cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystalline_cohomology)) For a smooth proper scheme over a $p$-adic field, Fontaine's period rings $B_{\mathrm{dR}}$, $B_{\mathrm{cris}}$, $B_{\mathrm{st}}$ give comparison isomorphisms between $p$-adic étale and de Rham or crystalline cohomology: the Hodge–Tate, de Rham and crystalline (good reduction) comparisons were proved by Faltings, and the semistable one by Tsuji (1999). ([p-adic Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_Hodge_theory)) See [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology).
- **Cycle classes and the Hodge conjecture (14F25, 14F40).** On a smooth projective complex variety a codimension-$p$ subvariety $Z$ has a class $\mathrm{cl}(Z)\in H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Z)$ whose image in $H^{2p}(X,\mathbb C)$ has type $(p,p)$; the Hodge classes are $H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{p,p}(X)$. For $p=1$ every integral $(1,1)$-class is the first Chern class of a line bundle (Lefschetz $(1,1)$, proved via the exponential sequence by Kodaira and Spencer). The integral version of the Hodge conjecture fails (Atiyah–Hirzebruch), and the conjecture fails for compact Kähler manifolds such as complex tori. ([Deligne, The Hodge Conjecture, §§1–2](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/hodge.pdf)) See [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory).

### History
Weil proposed his conjectures in 1949; Dwork proved rationality by $p$-adic methods in 1960; Grothendieck (1965) established the functional equation and the link to Betti numbers using étale cohomology; Deligne proved the Riemann-hypothesis analogue in "La conjecture de Weil I" (1974) and generalized it in "Weil II" (1980). ([Weil conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_conjectures); [Deligne, Publ. Math. IHÉS 43 (1974)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684373)) Deligne's simplified exposition of étale cohomology appeared as SGA 4½ in 1977. ([Étale cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tale_cohomology)) Grothendieck introduced crystalline cohomology, which Berthelot developed in his 1974 monograph. ([Crystalline cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystalline_cohomology)) Grothendieck formulated the standard conjectures in 1969. ([Standard conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_conjectures_on_algebraic_cycles))

### Open problems
- **Hodge conjecture.** On a projective non-singular variety over $\mathbb C$, every Hodge class is a rational linear combination of classes $\mathrm{cl}(Z)$ of algebraic cycles. ([Deligne, The Hodge Conjecture, §1](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/hodge.pdf)) It is a Clay Millennium Problem listed as unsolved. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/hodge-conjecture/)) Deligne notes it is not known even for the Künneth components of the diagonal or for the class inverting hard Lefschetz. ([Deligne, §4](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/hodge.pdf))
- **Tate conjecture.** For a smooth projective variety $V$ over a finitely generated field, the Galois-invariant part of $H^{2i}$ in $\ell$-adic cohomology (with the appropriate Tate twist) is spanned by classes of codimension-$i$ subvarieties. It is known for divisors on [abelian varieties](node:Abelian%20Varieties) (Tate over finite fields, Faltings over number fields, Zarhin in general) and for [K3 surfaces](node:K3%20Surfaces) in characteristic $\ne2$; the case of divisors on general varieties "is a major open problem". ([Tate conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_conjecture)) Deligne notes such conjectures "are open even for $H^2$". ([Deligne, §5](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/hodge.pdf))
- **Grothendieck's standard conjectures.** Conjecture B (Lefschetz type: the operator $\Lambda$ is algebraic), C (Künneth: the Künneth projectors are algebraic), D (numerical and homological equivalence coincide) and the Hodge standard conjecture would make pure motives a semisimple abelian category; they "remain open problems". The Hodge standard conjecture holds in characteristic $0$; Conjecture C is known for curves, surfaces, abelian varieties and varieties over finite fields; Conjecture D was shown by Lieberman over $\mathbb C$ in dimension at most $4$, and by Clozel for abelian varieties with étale $\ell$-adic cohomology. ([Standard conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_conjectures_on_algebraic_cycles))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Étale cohomology (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tale_cohomology): definitions, comparison, duality, history.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Proper base change](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095T) and [Smooth base change](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYU): precise statements and proofs.
- **Learn:** [Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry](https://math.stanford.edu/~vakil/216blog/): free notes from the author's page.
- **Primary:** [Deligne, The Hodge Conjecture (Clay Millennium Problem description)](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/hodge.pdf): precise statement, known cases, counterexamples to variants, and relation to motives.
- **Primary:** [Deligne, La conjecture de Weil I, Publ. Math. IHÉS 43 (1974)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684373): the proof of the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields.
- **Further reading:** [Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry (Springer GTM, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3849-0): the standard graduate text on schemes and coherent cohomology.
references.MSC 14Gxx - Arithmetic problems in algeb:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14G, "Arithmetic problems in algebraic geometry; Diophantine geometry", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) that studies varieties over fields that are not algebraically closed (finite, local, global and other fields), above all their rational points, together with zeta functions, local–global principles, modular and Shimura varieties, arithmetic schemes and heights, rigid and perfectoid geometry, and applications to [coding theory](node:Coding%20Theory) and [cryptography](node:Cryptography). ([MSC2020 14Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Gxx))

For a $k$-scheme $X$ the set of $k$-points is $X(k)=\mathrm{Hom}_k(\mathrm{Spec}\,k,X)$; for $X=\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ affine these are the $k$-algebra maps $A\to k$, that is, solutions of the defining equations in $k$. ([Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties, §2.3](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf)) The basic questions are whether $X(k)$ is empty, finite or infinite, and how to list or describe it; geometry (genus, Kodaira dimension) is expected to govern the answer, as Faltings' theorem and the Bombieri–Lang conjecture illustrate. ([Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties, §§2.6, 9.5](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf)) See [Rational Points on Varieties](node:Rational%20Points%20on%20Varieties).

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 14Gxx (see also 11Dxx, 11Gxx) lists: 14G05 rational points; 14G10 zeta functions and related questions (e.g. Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer; see also 11G40); 14G12 Hasse principle, weak and strong approximation, Brauer–Manin obstruction (see also 14F22); 14G15 finite ground fields; 14G17 positive characteristic ground fields; 14G20 local ground fields; 14G22 rigid analytic geometry; 14G25 global ground fields; 14G27 other nonalgebraically closed ground fields; 14G32 universal profinite groups; 14G35 modular and Shimura varieties (see also 11F41, 11F46, 11G18); 14G40 arithmetic varieties and schemes, Arakelov theory, heights (see also 11G50, 37P30); 14G45 perfectoid spaces and mixed characteristic; 14G50 applications to coding theory and cryptography (see also 94A60, 94B27, 94B40); 14G99. ([MSC2020 14Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Gxx))

- **Neighbour 11G and 11D.** The number-theoretic side of the same subject is [11G](node:MSC%2011Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20algebraic%20geometry%20%28Diophantine%20geometry%29) (elliptic curves, abelian varieties over number fields, [L-functions](node:L-Functions)) and explicit equations are [11D](node:MSC%2011Dxx%20-%20Diophantine%20equations); 14G cross-refers to both. ([MSC2020 14Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Gxx))
- **Neighbour 14F.** Brauer groups of schemes are classified at 14F22 in [MSC 14Fxx - (Co)homology theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Fxx%20-%20%28Co%29homology%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry), which 14G12 cross-refers to. ([MSC2020 14Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Gxx))

### Key concepts
- **Heights and Northcott finiteness (14G40).** For $t=a/b\in\mathbb Q$ in lowest terms, $H(t)=\max(|a|,|b|)$ and $h(t)=\log H(t)$; for every $B$ the set $\{t\in\mathbb Q:H(t)\le B\}$ is finite (Northcott). ([Poonen, 18.782 notes, §40](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/782/782notes.pdf)) Weil heights attach a height to each line bundle, well defined up to a bounded function, and the Néron–Tate canonical height is a quadratic form on the Mordell–Weil group of an abelian variety over a global field; heights were crucial to Weil's proof of Mordell–Weil and Faltings' proof of Mordell. ([Height function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Height_function))
- **Mordell–Weil theorem (14G05, 14G25).** For an [abelian variety](node:Abelian%20Varieties) $A$ over a number field $K$, $A(K)$ is a finitely generated abelian group (Mordell 1922 for [elliptic curves](node:Elliptic%20Curves) over $\mathbb Q$; Weil 1928/29 in general). ([Mordell–Weil theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordell%E2%80%93Weil_theorem)) So $E(\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Z^r\times T$ with $T$ finite; the proof combines the weak Mordell–Weil theorem ($E(\mathbb Q)/2E(\mathbb Q)$ finite) with heights, and it is not known whether an algorithm produces generators of $E(\mathbb Q)$. ([Poonen, 18.782 notes, Theorem 38.1, Remark 38.4](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/782/782notes.pdf))
- **Faltings' theorem (14G05).** If $X$ is a nice (smooth, projective, geometrically integral) curve of genus $>1$ over a number field $K$, then $X(K)$ is finite. Conjectured by Mordell in 1922 and proved by Faltings in 1983 via Parshin's reduction to Shafarevich's conjecture on abelian varieties with good reduction outside $S$; Vojta gave a Diophantine-approximation proof and Bombieri a more elementary version. All known proofs are ineffective. ([Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties, Theorem 9.5.1, Remark 9.5.2](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf)) Faltings later proved the Bombieri–Lang statements for subvarieties of abelian varieties. ([Poonen, §9.5.3](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf))
- **Hasse principle and the Brauer–Manin obstruction (14G12).** $X$ satisfies the local–global principle if $X(\mathbb A)\ne\emptyset$ implies $X(k)\ne\emptyset$. Quadrics satisfy it (Hasse–Minkowski), but Selmer's curve $3x^3+4y^3+5z^3=0$ has real and $p$-adic points for all $p$ and no nontrivial rational point. ([Hasse principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle)) For a nice variety over a global field, $X(k)\subseteq X(\mathbb A)^{\mathrm{Br}}$, so $X(\mathbb A)\ne\emptyset=X(\mathbb A)^{\mathrm{Br}}$ is an obstruction; the cubic surface $5x^3+9y^3+10z^3+12w^3=0$ (Cassels–Guy) violates the local–global principle. ([Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties, Corollary 8.2.6, Definition 8.2.7, §9.4.9](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf)) Skorobogatov showed the Brauer–Manin obstruction does not explain all failures of the Hasse principle. ([Hasse principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle))
- **Shimura varieties (14G35).** A Shimura datum $(G,X)$ is a reductive group $G$ over $\mathbb Q$ with a conjugacy class $X$ of homomorphisms satisfying three axioms; $X$ is a finite union of Hermitian symmetric domains, and the Shimura variety is the system of $G(\mathbb Q)\backslash X\times G(\mathbb A_f)/K$ over compact open $K$. Shimura introduced special cases in the 1960s, and examples include Shimura curves, Hilbert modular surfaces and Siegel modular varieties. Each has a canonical model over a number field, its reflex field, and they are the main testing ground for relating zeta functions to automorphic L-functions. ([Shimura variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimura_variety)) See [Modular Forms](node:Modular%20Forms).
- **Arakelov theory (14G40).** Arakelov (1974–75) defined [intersection theory](node:Intersection%20Theory) on arithmetic surfaces by adding archimedean fibres with Hermitian metrics; Faltings (1984) proved Riemann–Roch, Noether and Hodge index theorems there, and Gillet and Soulé extended the theory to higher dimension with an arithmetic Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem (1992). Vojta's 1991 proof of Mordell used it. ([Arakelov theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arakelov_theory)) See [Arithmetic Schemes](node:Arithmetic%20Schemes).
- **Rigid and perfectoid geometry (14G22, 14G45).** A perfectoid field is complete for a nondiscrete rank-one valuation with Frobenius surjective on $K^\circ/p$; Scholze (2012) proved that tilting $K\mapsto K^\flat$ gives an equivalence between perfectoid spaces over $K$ and over the characteristic-$p$ field $K^\flat$, and that the absolute Galois groups of $K$ and $K^\flat$ are isomorphic. ([Perfectoid space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfectoid_space)) See [Rigid Analytic Geometry](node:Rigid%20Analytic%20Geometry).

### History
Mordell conjectured finiteness for curves of genus $>1$ in 1922 and proved finite generation of $E(\mathbb Q)$ the same year; Weil generalized it in his 1928 thesis. ([Mordell–Weil theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordell%E2%80%93Weil_theorem); [Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties, §9.5.1](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf)) Faltings proved the Mordell conjecture in 1983 and Vojta reproved it in 1991. ([Poonen, 18.782 notes, §43](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/782/782notes.pdf)) Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer formulated their conjecture in the 1960s from numerical computations. ([Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture)) Vojta introduced his conjecture in 1987, and the abc conjecture arose from a 1985 discussion of Oesterlé and Masser. ([Vojta's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vojta%27s_conjecture); [abc conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.** For an elliptic curve $E$ over a number field, the rank of $E(K)$ should equal the order of vanishing of $L(E,s)$ at $s=1$, with a formula for the leading coefficient. The rank equality is known when the analytic rank over $\mathbb Q$ is $0$ or $1$ (Gross–Zagier, Kolyvagin, with modularity), and a positive proportion of curves over $\mathbb Q$ have analytic rank zero and so satisfy the conjecture (Bhargava–Shankar's average-rank bound combined with Skinner–Urban's main conjecture and parity results). ([Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture)) It is a Clay Millennium Problem listed as unsolved. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/birch-and-swinnerton-dyer-conjecture/))
- **Bombieri–Lang conjecture.** If $X$ is a geometrically integral variety of general type over a number field $k$ with $\dim X>0$, then $X(k)$ is not Zariski dense; Lang's stronger form asks for a proper closed $S\subsetneq X$ with $(X-S)(L)$ finite for all finite $L/k$. ([Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties, Conjectures 9.5.11–9.5.12](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf)) It is unsolved, and Caporaso, Harris and Mazur (with Pacelli for fixed degree) showed it implies a uniform bound on the number of rational points on genus-$g$ curves over number fields of fixed degree. ([Bombieri–Lang conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Lang_conjecture))
- **Effective Mordell.** It is not known whether there is an algorithm that, given a nice curve of genus $>1$ over a number field, outputs its rational points. ([Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties, Remark 9.5.2](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf)) Elkies showed the abc conjecture implies Mordell; abc remains "unproven" in the view of the mainstream community despite Mochizuki's claimed proof, to which Scholze and Stix raised an objection. ([abc conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture))
- **Vojta's conjecture and the Colliot-Thélène conjecture.** Vojta's height inequality would imply Bombieri–Lang and higher-dimensional abc-type statements, and is listed among unsolved problems. ([Vojta's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vojta%27s_conjecture)) Colliot-Thélène conjectured that for rationally connected nice varieties over number fields the Brauer–Manin obstruction is the only obstruction to the local–global principle. ([Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties, Conjecture 9.2.27](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hasse principle (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_principle) and [Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_and_Swinnerton-Dyer_conjecture): statements and status.
- **Learn:** [Poonen, Introduction to Arithmetic Geometry (MIT 18.782 notes)](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/782/782notes.pdf): $p$-adic numbers, Hasse principle, Mordell's theorem, heights, Faltings' theorem.
- **Primary:** [Poonen, Rational Points on Varieties](https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/Qpoints.pdf): author-hosted graduate text on local–global principles, the Brauer–Manin obstruction and rational points on varieties of general type.
- **Further reading:** [Hindry and Silverman, Diophantine Geometry (Springer GTM, 2000)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1210-2): a standard graduate text on Diophantine geometry.
references.MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14Hxx classifies the algebraic geometry of curves, the one-dimensional [Algebraic Varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties). Its subcodes run from function fields (14H05) and moduli (14H10, 14H15) through Jacobians and Prym varieties (14H40), theta functions and the Schottky problem (14H42), special divisors and Brill–Noether theory (14H51), elliptic curves (14H52), Weierstrass points (14H55), and vector bundles on curves (14H60), to relations with integrable systems and physics (14H70, 14H81). ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))

A smooth projective curve over $\mathbb C$ is the same thing as a compact Riemann surface, so the subject is shared with [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) and [MSC 30Fxx - Riemann surfaces](node:MSC%2030Fxx%20-%20Riemann%20surfaces). Its basic invariant is the genus $g$, which appears in Riemann–Roch, the degree $2g-2$ of the canonical divisor, and the dimension of the Jacobian. ([Guerzhoy, Ch. 25](https://math.hawaii.edu/~pavel/RR_course_notes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Jacobian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_variety)) Three of its codes carry the themes developed below: moduli of curves (14H10), Jacobians and Prym varieties (14H40), and special divisors, i.e. the linear series a curve carries (14H51). ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))

### Scope
- **14H05, 14H20, 14H25:** function fields of curves, singularities and local rings of curves, and curves over arithmetic ground fields (cross-referenced to 11R58, 13Hxx/14B05, and 11Dxx/11G05/14Gxx). ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))
- **14H10, 14H15:** families and moduli of curves, algebraic and analytic (the analytic code points to 30F10 and 32G15). ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))
- **14H30, 14H37, 14H57:** coverings and fundamental groups of curves, automorphisms, and dessins d'enfants (arithmetic aspects go to 11G32). ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))
- **14H40, 14H42:** Jacobians, Prym varieties, theta functions, and the Schottky problem, cross-referenced to 14K25 and 32G20. ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))
- **14H45, 14H50, 14H51, 14H55:** special and low-genus curves, plane and space curves, special divisors (gonality, Brill–Noether theory), and Weierstrass points and gap sequences. ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))
- **14H52, 14H60, 14H70, 14H81:** elliptic curves (see also 11G05, 14Kxx), vector bundles on curves and their moduli (see also 14D20, 14J60), integrable systems, and physics. ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))

Neighbours, as the entry's cross-references show: theta functions and the Schottky problem (14H42) point to 14K25 in [MSC 14Kxx - Abelian varieties and schemes](node:MSC%2014Kxx%20-%20Abelian%20varieties%20and%20schemes), and elliptic curves (14H52) point to 14Kxx and to 11G05/11G07 in [MSC 11Gxx - Arithmetic algebraic geometry (Diophantine geometry)](node:MSC%2011Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20algebraic%20geometry%20%28Diophantine%20geometry%29); vector bundles on curves (14H60) point to 14D20 in [MSC 14Dxx - Families, fibrations in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Dxx%20-%20Families,%20fibrations%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) and to 14F06, 14J60; Riemann surfaces and Weierstrass points (14H55) point to [MSC 30Fxx - Riemann surfaces](node:MSC%2030Fxx%20-%20Riemann%20surfaces). ([MSC2020 14Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Hxx))

### Key concepts
- **Riemann–Roch.** For a one-variable function field with curve $C$ of genus $g$ and a divisor $D$, $\ell(D)=\deg D+1-g+\ell(K-D)$ with $K$ canonical; hence $\ell(K)=g$ and $\deg K=2g-2$. ([Guerzhoy, Ch. 25](https://math.hawaii.edu/~pavel/RR_course_notes.pdf)) More generally, for $X$ proper, Gorenstein and equidimensional of dimension one over a field $k$, $\omega_X$ is invertible, $\deg\omega_X=-2\chi(X,\mathcal O_X)$, and for a locally free $\mathcal E$ of constant rank $\chi(X,\mathcal E)=\deg\mathcal E-\tfrac12\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal E)\deg\omega_X$, with $h^i(\mathcal E)=h^{1-i}(\mathcal E^\vee\otimes\omega_X)$. This duality is the curve case of [MSC 14Fxx - (Co)homology theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Fxx%20-%20%28Co%29homology%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry). ([Stacks, Lemma 53.5.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B5B))
- **Riemann–Hurwitz formula.** For a nonconstant holomorphic map $\pi:S'\to S$ of degree $N$ between compact Riemann surfaces with ramification indices $e_P$, $2g(S')-2=N\,(2g(S)-2)+\sum_{P\in S'}(e_P-1)$. In particular there is no nonconstant map from a curve of lower genus onto one of higher genus. ([Wikipedia: Riemann–Hurwitz formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hurwitz_formula))
- **Canonical embedding and Weierstrass points.** If $C$ is non-hyperelliptic of genus $g\ge3$, the canonical map is an isomorphism onto a curve of degree $2g-2$ in $\mathbb P^{g-1}$; for $g\ge4$ its ideal is generated by quadrics except for trigonal curves and smooth plane quintics (Petri). For hyperelliptic $C$ the canonical image is a rational normal curve doubly covered by $C$. ([Wikipedia: Canonical bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_bundle)) At every point of a complex curve of genus $g$ there are exactly $g$ gaps; points whose gap sequence is not $1,\dots,g$ are Weierstrass points, and their weights sum to $g^3-g$. On a hyperelliptic curve they are exactly the $2g+2$ ramification points of the double cover of $\mathbb P^1$. ([Wikipedia: Weierstrass point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_point))
- **Jacobians, Abel–Jacobi, Torelli (14H40).** For a compact Riemann surface $C$ of genus $g$, $J(C)=H^0(C,\Omega^1)^*/H_1(C,\mathbb Z)$ is a principally polarized abelian variety of dimension $g$, isomorphic to $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$. ([Wikipedia: Jacobian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_variety)) The Abel–Jacobi map $u(p)=\left(\int_{p_0}^p\omega_1,\dots,\int_{p_0}^p\omega_g\right)\bmod\Lambda$ extends linearly to divisors. On the group $\operatorname{Div}^0(C)$ of degree-zero divisors, Abel's theorem says its kernel is exactly the subgroup of principal divisors, and Jacobi inversion gives surjectivity, so degree-zero divisor classes form a group isomorphic to $J(C)$. ([Wikipedia: Abel–Jacobi map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%E2%80%93Jacobi_map)) Torelli's theorem: a smooth projective curve over an algebraically closed field is determined up to isomorphism by its Jacobian together with its principal polarization, so the period map from curves to principally polarized abelian varieties is injective on geometric points. ([Wikipedia: Torelli theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torelli_theorem))
- **Moduli of curves (14H10).** For $g\ge2$ the moduli stack $\mathcal M_g$ and the Deligne–Mumford stack $\overline{\mathcal M}_g$ of stable curves (connected, complete, only nodes, finite automorphism group) have dimension $3g-3$. Deligne and Mumford (1969) proved $\mathcal M_g$ irreducible and the stack smooth with finite stabilizers, and $\overline{\mathcal M}_g$ is proper by stable reduction. Severi proved $\mathcal M_g$ unirational for $g\le10$, while work of Harris–Mumford (1982) and Eisenbud–Harris (1987) shows the coarse space is of general type for $g>23$. ([Wikipedia: Moduli of algebraic curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_of_algebraic_curves)) Farkas, Jensen and Payne proved that $\overline{\mathcal M}_{22}$ and $\overline{\mathcal M}_{23}$ are of general type, using tropical methods for linear series. ([Farkas–Jensen–Payne, arXiv:2005.00622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00622))
- **Brill–Noether theory (14H51).** For a smooth projective curve of genus $g$, let $G^r_d$ parametrize linear series of degree $d$ and dimension $r$, and set $\rho=g-(r+1)(g-d+r)$. If $\rho\ge0$, $G^r_d\ne\emptyset$ and every component has dimension at least $\rho$ (Kempf), and it is connected if $\rho\ge1$ (Fulton–Lazarsfeld). For a general curve, $G^r_d$ has dimension exactly $\rho$, so it is empty when $\rho<0$ (Griffiths–Harris, 1980), and it is smooth (Gieseker). ([Wikipedia: Brill–Noether theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brill%E2%80%93Noether_theory)) The maximal rank conjecture for general curves in $\mathbb P^r$ was proved by Eric Larson (2017). ([Wikipedia: Brill–Noether theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brill%E2%80%93Noether_theory))
- **Clifford's theorem and gonality.** For an effective special divisor $D$ of degree $d$, $2(\ell(D)-1)\le d$, with equality only for $D=0$, $D=K$, or $C$ hyperelliptic and $D$ a multiple of the hyperelliptic divisor. ([Wikipedia: Clifford's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford%27s_theorem_on_special_divisors)) The gonality, the least degree of a nonconstant map $C\to\mathbb P^1$, is at most $\lfloor(g+3)/2\rfloor$, and it is $2$ for curves of genus $1$ and for hyperelliptic curves (including all curves of genus $2$). ([Wikipedia: Gonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonality_of_an_algebraic_curve))

### History
According to Amodeo's 1900 ICM talk, the notion (not the name) of gonality originated in Riemann's *Theory of Abelian Functions*, and Brill and Noether began the theory of special linear series in 1874. ([Wikipedia: Gonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonality_of_an_algebraic_curve); [Wikipedia: Brill–Noether theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brill%E2%80%93Noether_theory)) Torelli's paper "Sulle varietà di Jacobi" appeared in 1913, and Weil's "Zum Beweis des Torellischen Satzes" in 1957. ([Wikipedia: Torelli theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torelli_theorem)) Severi's unirationality result dates from 1915, Deligne–Mumford's irreducibility paper from 1969, and the general-type results of Harris–Mumford and Eisenbud–Harris from 1982 and 1987. ([Wikipedia: Moduli of algebraic curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_of_algebraic_curves)) Arbarello, Cornalba, Griffiths and Harris's *Geometry of Algebraic Curves* appeared in Springer's Grundlehren series in 1985. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-5323-3))

### Open problems
