- **Kodaira dimension of $\overline{\mathcal M}_g$ for $17\le g\le21$.** Barros and Mullane list "$\overline{\mathcal M}_g$ with $17\le g\le21$" among long-standing open cases of the Kodaira classification of moduli spaces of curves. ([Barros–Mullane, arXiv:2106.13774](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2106.13774)) Genera 22 and 23 were settled by Farkas–Jensen–Payne. ([arXiv:2005.00622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00622))
- **Green's conjecture.** For a non-hyperelliptic complex curve, the Clifford index should equal $a(C)+1$, where $a(C)$ is read from the linear syzygies of the canonical embedding. Green and Lazarsfeld proved the inequality and Voisin proved the case of generic curves; the conjecture for arbitrary curves remains open. ([Wikipedia: Clifford's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford%27s_theorem_on_special_divisors))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Moduli of algebraic curves (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_of_algebraic_curves): $\mathcal M_g$, stable curves, Kodaira dimension by genus.
- **Reference:** [Brill–Noether theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brill%E2%80%93Noether_theory): $\rho$, existence, connectedness, and generic results.
- **Learn:** [Guerzhoy, Riemann–Roch theorem for curves](https://math.hawaii.edu/~pavel/RR_course_notes.pdf): free course notes from function fields to Riemann–Roch, Hurwitz's formula, and hyperelliptic curves.
- **Primary:** [Farkas–Jensen–Payne, The Kodaira dimensions of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{22}$ and $\overline{\mathcal M}_{23}$](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00622): recent research on the birational geometry of $\overline{\mathcal M}_g$.
- **Primary:** [Stacks Project, Lemma 53.5.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B5B): Riemann–Roch and duality for proper Gorenstein curves.
- **Further reading:** [Arbarello–Cornalba–Griffiths–Harris, Geometry of Algebraic Curves (Springer, 1985)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-5323-3): Grundlehren monograph on the geometry of curves; [Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry (Springer GTM, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3849-0): standard graduate text.
references.MSC 14Jxx - Surfaces and higher-dimensio:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14J, "Surfaces and higher-dimensional varieties", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) devoted to varieties of dimension at least two: their classification, moduli, singularities, automorphisms, vector bundles and topology, with special classes (K3, Calabi–Yau, hyper-Kähler, Fano) given their own codes. The analytic theory of [compact complex spaces](node:Compact%20Complex%20Spaces) is referred to 32Jxx. ([MSC2020 14Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Jxx)) The concept notes [Algebraic Surfaces](node:Algebraic%20Surfaces) and [K3 Surfaces](node:K3%20Surfaces) treat the two-dimensional case.

The organising result for surfaces is the Enriques–Kodaira classification, which sorts minimal surfaces by Kodaira dimension; in higher dimension the same invariant organises the theory, but the role of the minimal model is taken by the minimal model program of [MSC 14Exx - Birational geometry](node:MSC%2014Exx%20-%20Birational%20geometry), and the "building blocks" are Fano varieties ($\kappa=-\infty$ side), Calabi–Yau varieties ($\kappa=0$) and varieties of general type. ([Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification); [Fano variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano_variety); [Calabi–Yau manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi%E2%80%93Yau_manifold))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 14Jxx (for analytic theory, see 32Jxx) lists: 14J10 families, moduli, classification: algebraic theory; 14J15 moduli, classification: analytic theory, relations with [modular forms](node:Modular%20Forms) (see also 32G13); 14J17 singularities of surfaces or higher-dimensional varieties (see also 14B05, 14E15, 32S05, 32S25); 14J20 arithmetic ground fields (see also 11Dxx, 11G25, 11G35, 14Gxx); 14J25 special surfaces (Hilbert modular surfaces go to 14G35); 14J26 rational and ruled surfaces; 14J27 elliptic surfaces, elliptic or Calabi–Yau fibrations; 14J28 K3 surfaces and Enriques surfaces; 14J29 surfaces of general type; 14J30 3-folds; 14J32 Calabi–Yau manifolds (algebro-geometric aspects; see also 32Q25); 14J33 mirror symmetry (algebro-geometric aspects; see also 11G42, 53D37); 14J35 4-folds; 14J40 $n$-folds ($n>4$); 14J42 holomorphic symplectic varieties, hyper-Kähler varieties; 14J45 Fano varieties; 14J50 automorphisms; 14J60 vector bundles and their moduli (see also 14D20, 14F06, 14H60, 32Lxx); 14J70 hypersurfaces; 14J80 topology of surfaces (Donaldson polynomials, Seiberg–Witten invariants); 14J81 relationships with physics; 14J99. ([MSC2020 14Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Jxx))

- **Neighbour 14H.** Curves (dimension one) are in [MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Hxx%20-%20Curves%20in%20algebraic%20geometry); 14J starts in dimension two. ([MSC2020 14Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Jxx); [MSC2020 14](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14-XX))
- **Neighbour 14E.** Singularities (14J17) cross-refer to 14E15, global theory and resolution of singularities; [rational and birational maps](node:Birational%20Maps) (14E05) and the minimal model program (14E30) are in [MSC 14Exx - Birational geometry](node:MSC%2014Exx%20-%20Birational%20geometry). ([MSC2020 14Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Jxx); [MSC2020 14Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Exx))
- **Neighbour 32J / 32Q.** The 14J entry sends analytic theory to [MSC 32Jxx - Compact analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Jxx%20-%20Compact%20analytic%20spaces), and cross-refers Calabi–Yau manifolds to 32Q25 in [MSC 32Qxx - Complex manifolds](node:MSC%2032Qxx%20-%20Complex%20manifolds). ([MSC2020 14Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Jxx); [MSC2020 32](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX))
- **Neighbour 14K.** Abelian surfaces appear as the $\kappa=0$ case $(p_g,q)=(1,2)$ of the classification, but [abelian varieties](node:Abelian%20Varieties) as such have their own code, [MSC 14Kxx - Abelian varieties and schemes](node:MSC%2014Kxx%20-%20Abelian%20varieties%20and%20schemes). ([Columbia notes](https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chaoli/docs/EnriquesClassification.html); [MSC2020 14](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Riemann–Roch and Noether's formula (14J10, 14J25).** For a divisor $D$ on a non-singular projective surface $X$ with canonical divisor $K$, $\chi(D)=\chi(\mathcal O_X)+\tfrac12 D\cdot(D-K)$, where $\cdot$ is the intersection pairing (see [Intersection Theory](node:Intersection%20Theory)). Noether's formula gives $12\chi(\mathcal O_X)=c_1^2+c_2=K\cdot K+e(X)$, with $e$ the topological Euler characteristic. ([Riemann–Roch theorem for surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Roch_theorem_for_surfaces); [Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification))
- **Castelnuovo's criteria and minimal models (14J26).** Castelnuovo's contractibility criterion: a curve $E\cong\mathbb P^1$ on a smooth projective surface with $E^2=-1$ is an exceptional curve; by Castelnuovo's contraction theorem, minimality is equivalent to having no such $(-1)$-curves. Every surface is birational to a minimal one, unique when $\kappa\ge0$ (or the surface is non-algebraic), while $\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1$ blown up at a point equals $\mathbb P^2$ blown up twice shows non-uniqueness for $\kappa=-\infty$. Castelnuovo's rationality criterion: a smooth complex projective surface with $q=P_2=0$ is rational. ([Columbia notes](https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chaoli/docs/EnriquesClassification.html); [Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification))
- **Enriques–Kodaira classification (14J25–14J29).** For smooth complex projective surfaces, $\kappa\in\{-\infty,0,1,2\}$: $\kappa=-\infty$ gives ruled surfaces (including rational ones); $\kappa=0$ minimal surfaces are, by $(p_g,q)$, Enriques $(0,0)$, hyperelliptic $(0,1)$, K3 $(1,0)$ and abelian $(1,2)$; minimal $\kappa=1$ surfaces are elliptic (admit an elliptic fibration over a curve); $\kappa=2$ is general type. Kodaira extended the classification to non-algebraic compact complex surfaces (adding class VII and Kodaira surfaces). ([Columbia notes](https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chaoli/docs/EnriquesClassification.html); [Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification))
- **Positive characteristic (14J20).** Mumford began and Bombieri and Mumford completed (1976–77) the classification over algebraically closed fields of positive characteristic. There are no Kodaira or class VII surfaces, but new families appear: non-classical Enriques surfaces (characteristic 2), quasi-hyperelliptic surfaces and quasi-elliptic fibrations (characteristics 2 and 3); Zariski's unirational non-rational surfaces also live here. ([Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification))
- **Bogomolov–Miyaoka–Yau inequality (14J29).** A compact complex surface of general type satisfies $c_1^2\le 3c_2$, equivalently (by Noether) $K^2\le 9\chi(\mathcal O_S)$, with equality exactly when the universal cover is the complex ball. Miyaoka proved the inequality in general and Yau when $K$ is ample; it fails in positive characteristic (Lang, Easton). ([Bauer–Catanese–Pignatelli, Thm 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.2583); [BMY inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogomolov%E2%80%93Miyaoka%E2%80%93Yau_inequality))
- **Gieseker moduli (14J10, 14J29).** For each pair $(x,y)$ there is a quasi-projective coarse moduli space $\mathcal M^{can}_{(x,y)}$ of minimal surfaces of general type with $\chi=x$, $K^2=y$; minimal surfaces of general type have $K^2\ge1$, $\chi\ge1$. See [Moduli Spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces). ([Bauer–Catanese–Pignatelli, Thm 2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.2583))
- **Calabi–Yau varieties and mirror symmetry (14J32, 14J33).** A compact Kähler manifold with vanishing first Chern class carries a Ricci-flat Kähler metric in each Kähler class (Yau's proof of the Calabi conjecture). The stronger definition asks for a trivial canonical bundle, which implies $c_1=0$ but not conversely (Enriques surfaces are Ricci-flat with non-trivial canonical bundle); for simply connected compact Kähler manifolds the two definitions agree. In dimension 1 these are tori; the compact simply connected ones in dimension 2 are the K3 surfaces; the smooth quintic threefold in $\mathbb P^4$ is the basic threefold example. Mirror symmetry predicted, via Candelas and collaborators, the 317,206,375 degree-three rational curves on the quintic; Kontsevich's homological mirror symmetry conjecture equates the derived category of one side with the Fukaya category of the mirror. See [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds). ([Calabi–Yau manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi%E2%80%93Yau_manifold); [Mirror symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_symmetry_%28string_theory%29))
- **Fano varieties (14J45, 14J30).** A Fano variety is a complete variety whose anticanonical bundle is ample. Del Pezzo surfaces are $\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1$ or $\mathbb P^2$ blown up in at most eight points in general position. Iskovskikh classified smooth Fano threefolds with $b_2=1$ (17 classes) and Mori–Mukai those with $b_2\ge2$ (88 deformation classes). Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, smooth Fano varieties of fixed dimension form a bounded family (Kollár–Miyaoka–Mori), and smooth Fano varieties are rationally chain connected (Campana; Kollár–Miyaoka–Mori). ([Fano variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano_variety))

### History
Max Noether began the systematic study of algebraic surfaces, Castelnuovo proved important parts of the classification, and Enriques described the classification of complex projective surfaces; Kodaira extended it to compact complex surfaces in papers of 1964–1968, and Bombieri–Mumford completed positive characteristic in 1976–77. ([Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification)) Max Noether asked whether $p_g=q=0$ forces rationality; Enriques and Castelnuovo gave counterexamples of special type, and Campedelli, Godeaux and Burniat found surfaces of general type with $p_g=0$. ([Bauer–Catanese–Pignatelli](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.2583)) The BMY inequality was proved by Miyaoka and Yau in 1977–78 after weaker constants by Van de Ven (8) and Bogomolov (4). ([BMY inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogomolov%E2%80%93Miyaoka%E2%80%93Yau_inequality))

### Open problems
- **Classification of Calabi–Yau threefolds.** Classification of the possible Calabi–Yau threefolds is an open problem; Yau suspects finitely many families, while Miles Reid conjectured infinitely many topological types. ([Calabi–Yau manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi%E2%80%93Yau_manifold))
- **Surfaces with $p_g=0$.** Understanding the moduli spaces $\mathcal M^{can}_{(1,n)}$, $1\le n\le 9$, is described as far from achievable; the survey lists open questions including which fundamental groups occur, whether every minimal surface with $p_g=0$, $K^2=8$ is a bidisk quotient, and Hirzebruch's question whether a surface of general type can be homeomorphic to $\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1$. ([Bauer–Catanese–Pignatelli, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.2583))
- **Bloch's conjecture.** For a smooth surface with $p_g=0$, the kernel of the Abel–Jacobi map $A_0^0(S)\to\mathrm{Alb}(S)$ should be trivial; proved for $\kappa<2$ by Bloch–Kas–Lieberman but verified in only a few cases of general type. ([Bauer–Catanese–Pignatelli, Conj. 3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.2583))
- **Class VII surfaces and mirror constructions.** The description of class VII rests on the global spherical shell conjecture, still unproved; homological mirror symmetry and the SYZ conjecture remain conjectures. ([Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification); [Mirror symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_symmetry_%28string_theory%29))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Enriques–Kodaira classification (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification): the ten classes, invariants, positive characteristic.
- **Reference:** [Fano variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano_variety) and [Calabi–Yau manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi%E2%80%93Yau_manifold): higher-dimensional special classes.
- **Learn:** [Columbia notes on the Enriques classification](https://www.math.columbia.edu/~chaoli/docs/EnriquesClassification.html): Castelnuovo's criteria, Kodaira dimension, the $\kappa=0$ cases.
- **Primary:** [Bauer, Catanese and Pignatelli, Surfaces of general type with geometric genus zero: a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.2583): moduli, BMY, fundamental groups, Bloch's conjecture, open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Barth, Hulek, Peters and Van de Ven, Compact Complex Surfaces (Springer, Ergebnisse, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-57739-0): the standard monograph on surface classification.
references.MSC 14Kxx - Abelian varieties and scheme:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14Kxx classifies abelian varieties, the proper connected group varieties, and their relative versions over a base, abelian schemes. Its subcodes cover isogenies (14K02), the algebraic theory (14K05), moduli and classification (14K10), subvarieties (14K12), arithmetic ground fields (14K15), the analytic theory and abelian integrals (14K20), complex multiplication (14K22), theta functions (14K25), and Picard schemes and higher Jacobians (14K30). ([MSC2020 14Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Kxx))

Over a field $k$, an abelian variety is a group scheme over $k$ that is a proper, geometrically integral variety. ([Stacks, Definition 39.9.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RO)) Over $\mathbb C$ these are exactly the complex tori $V/L$ that admit a Riemann form, a positive definite Hermitian form on $V$ whose imaginary part is integral on $L\times L$. ([Wikipedia: Abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety)) An abelian scheme over $S$ of relative dimension $g$ is a proper smooth group scheme over $S$ whose geometric fibres are connected of dimension $g$. ([Wikipedia: Abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety)) The subject joins geometry, through Jacobians of curves and moduli, with arithmetic, through rational points and Galois representations on torsion. ([Conrad, §§1.2–1.6](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf))

### Scope
- **14K02, 14K05, 14K12:** isogenies, the algebraic theory (line bundles, duality, endomorphisms), and subvarieties of abelian varieties. ([MSC2020 14Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Kxx))
- **14K10:** algebraic moduli and classification, with a cross-reference to 11G15. ([MSC2020 14Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Kxx))
- **14K15:** arithmetic ground fields, cross-referenced to 11Dxx, 11Fxx, 11G10 and 14Gxx. ([MSC2020 14Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Kxx))
- **14K20, 14K22, 14K25:** analytic theory and abelian integrals, complex multiplication (see also 11G15), and theta functions (see also 14H42). ([MSC2020 14Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Kxx))
- **14K30:** Picard schemes and higher Jacobians, cross-referenced to 14H40 and 32G20. ([MSC2020 14Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Kxx))

Neighbours, as the entry's cross-references show: theta functions (14K25) point to 14H42 and Picard schemes (14K30) to 14H40 in [MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Hxx%20-%20Curves%20in%20algebraic%20geometry); moduli (14K10) and complex multiplication (14K22) point to 11G15, and arithmetic ground fields (14K15) to 11G10 in [MSC 11Gxx - Arithmetic algebraic geometry (Diophantine geometry)](node:MSC%2011Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20algebraic%20geometry%20%28Diophantine%20geometry%29) and to [MSC 14Gxx - Arithmetic problems in algebraic geometry; Diophantine geometry](node:MSC%2014Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20problems%20in%20algebraic%20geometry;%20Diophantine%20geometry), as well as 11Dxx and 11Fxx. ([MSC2020 14Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Kxx))

### Key concepts
- **Structure and torsion.** Every complex torus is commutative and $A\cong T_0(A)/\Lambda_A$ with $\Lambda_A$ a lattice. For an abelian variety $A$ of dimension $g$ over $k$ and $n$ prime to $\operatorname{char}k$, $A[n](\bar k)\cong(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{2g}$, so the $\ell$-adic Tate module $T_\ell A=\varprojlim A[\ell^m]$ is free of rank $2g$ over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ for $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$. ([Conrad, Thm. 1.2.8, Prop. 4.2.2, §1.6](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf))
- **Isogenies, duality, polarizations (14K02, 14K05).** An isogeny is a finite flat surjective homomorphism. The dual abelian variety is $A^\vee=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{A/k}$, and for an ample line bundle $L$ the map $\varphi_L:A\to A^\vee$, $x\mapsto t_x^*L\otimes L^{-1}$, is an isogeny. A polarization is a symmetric isogeny $\varphi:A\to A^\vee$ with $(1,\varphi)^*\mathcal P_A$ ample; over $\bar k$ these are the $\varphi_L$ with $L$ ample. ([Conrad, Def. 5.1.3, §§5.2, 8](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf))
- **Poincaré reducibility and endomorphisms.** If $A'\subset A$ is an abelian subvariety over $k$, there is an abelian subvariety $A''\subset A$ over $k$ with $A'\times A''\to A$ an isogeny; hence the isogeny category is semisimple and $A$ is isogenous to $\prod A_i^{e_i}$ with $k$-simple $A_i$ unique up to isogeny. For abelian varieties $A,B$ over $k$, $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,B)$ is $\mathbb Z$-finite and $\mathbb Z_\ell\otimes\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,B)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z_\ell[G_k]}(T_\ell A,T_\ell B)$ is injective for $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$. ([Conrad, Thm. 7.6.1, Thm. 7.6.7](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf))
- **Mordell–Weil and the Tate/Faltings isogeny theorem (14K15).** If $A$ is an abelian variety over a global field $k$, then $A(k)$ is finitely generated, so $A(k)\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus A(k)_{\text{tors}}$. ([Wikipedia: Abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety); [Conrad, §1.4](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf)) The Tate conjecture for divisors on abelian varieties, equivalently the statement that homomorphisms of abelian varieties are determined by their Galois action on Tate modules, was proved by Tate over finite fields and by Faltings over number fields, and extended by Zarhin to finitely generated fields; in particular an abelian variety is determined up to isogeny by its $\ell$-adic Galois representation. ([Wikipedia: Tate conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_conjecture))
- **Moduli $\mathcal A_g$ and theta functions (14K10, 14K25).** The Siegel modular variety $\mathcal A_g$, a quotient of the Siegel upper half-space by a symplectic group, is the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties of dimension $g$; it has dimension $g(g+1)/2$ and is the basic example of a Shimura variety. Tai, Freitag and Mumford showed $\mathcal A_g$ is of general type for $g\ge7$. ([Wikipedia: Siegel modular variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_modular_variety)) Jacobians of curves give the basic examples: the analytic Jacobian $J_C=\Omega^1(C)^*/H_1(C,\mathbb Z)$ is a $g$-dimensional complex torus, and the Abel–Jacobi map embeds $C$ in it when $g>0$. ([Conrad, Def. 1.2.5](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf))
- **Néron models (the "schemes" half).** For a Dedekind domain $R$ with fraction field $K$ and a smooth separated $K$-scheme $A_K$, a Néron model is a smooth separated $R$-scheme $A_R$ with generic fibre $A_K$ such that every $K$-morphism $X_K\to A_K$ from a smooth separated $R$-scheme $X$ extends uniquely to an $R$-morphism $X\to A_R$. For abelian varieties Néron models exist and are unique commutative quasi-projective group schemes; Néron constructed them (1961, 1964) for abelian varieties over the fraction field of a Dedekind domain with perfect residue fields, and Raynaud (1966) extended the construction; Néron models also exist for some other commutative groups such as tori, but not for the additive group. ([Wikipedia: Néron model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A9ron_model))
- **Complex multiplication (14K22).** For a simple abelian variety, $\operatorname{End}^0_k(A)=\operatorname{End}_k(A)\otimes\mathbb Q$ is a finite-dimensional division algebra over $\mathbb Q$, and the polarization forces its centre to be a totally real or CM field. ([Conrad, Rem. 7.6.6](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf)) The Mumford–Tate conjecture is known for CM abelian varieties (Pohlmann). ([Kreutz, arXiv:2111.01126](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2111.01126))

### History
In the work of Abel and Jacobi the answer to the question that led to the subject was formulated through functions of two complex variables; Lefschetz appears to have been the first to use the name "abelian variety", and Weil gave the subject its modern algebro-geometric foundations in the 1940s. ([Wikipedia: Abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety)) Poincaré conjectured that the rational points of an elliptic curve over $\mathbb Q$ form a finitely generated group, Mordell proved it, and Weil's thesis extended finite generation to abelian varieties over global fields. ([Conrad, §1.4](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf)) Siegel introduced the Siegel modular varieties in 1943. ([Wikipedia: Siegel modular variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_modular_variety)) Abrashkin and Fontaine independently showed that there is no nonzero abelian variety over $\mathbb Q$ with good reduction at every prime. ([Wikipedia: Abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety))

### Open problems
- **Mumford–Tate conjecture.** For a smooth projective variety $X$ over a field $K\subset\mathbb C$ finitely generated over $\mathbb Q$, the conjecture predicts $G_{\ell,X}=G_X\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell$, where $G_{\ell,X}$ is the identity component of the Zariski closure of the Galois image on $\ell$-adic cohomology and $G_X$ is the Mumford–Tate group of the Hodge structure. Kreutz states that, despite partial results, "it is still open even for abelian varieties." ([Kreutz, arXiv:2111.01126](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2111.01126); [Wikipedia: Mumford–Tate group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumford%E2%80%93Tate_group))
- **Tate conjecture for divisors.** The Tate conjecture predicts that Galois-invariant $\ell$-adic classes are spanned by algebraic cycles; its case of divisors (codimension-1 cycles) is called "a major open problem", while abelian varieties are its most important known case. ([Wikipedia: Tate conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_conjecture))
- **Birational type of $\mathcal A_6$.** $\mathcal A_g$ is of general type for $g\ge7$ and has Kodaira dimension $-\infty$ for $g\le5$; Dittmann, Salvati Manni and Scheithauer write that the case $g=6$ "has been open for more than 30 years" and prove only that the Kodaira dimension of $\mathcal A_6$ is non-negative, without determining it. ([Dittmann–Salvati Manni–Scheithauer](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.07062))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Abelian variety (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety): complex tori, polarizations, Mordell–Weil, abelian schemes.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Definition 39.9.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RO): definition over an arbitrary field.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Abelian Varieties (Stanford course notes by T. Feng)](https://virtualmath1.stanford.edu/~conrad/249CS15Page/handouts/abvarnotes.pdf): Picard schemes, duality, Poincaré reducibility, Weil pairing, Mordell–Weil, heights.
- **Primary:** [Kreutz, ℓ-Galois special subvarieties and the Mumford–Tate conjecture (arXiv:2111.01126)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2111.01126): current research and status of the conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Dittmann–Salvati Manni–Scheithauer, Harmonic theta series and the Kodaira dimension of $\mathcal A_6$](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.07062): recent work on the moduli of abelian varieties.
- **Further reading:** [Mumford, Abelian Varieties (TIFR / Oxford University Press)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL2717253W): monograph published for TIFR (1970; 2nd ed. 1974), the 2nd edition with appendices by C. P. Ramanujam and Yuri Manin; [Bosch–Lütkebohmert–Raynaud, Néron Models (Springer, 1990)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-51438-8); [Milne, Abelian Varieties, in Arithmetic Geometry (Springer, 1986)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4613-8655-1_5).
references.MSC 14Lxx - Algebraic groups:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14Lxx classifies algebraic groups from the point of view of algebraic geometry: group varieties and group schemes, formal and $p$-divisible groups, geometric invariant theory, and actions of groups on varieties and their quotients. Its header sends linear algebraic groups to 20Gxx and Lie algebras to 17B45, and cross-references 11E57 (classical groups over arithmetic rings). ([MSC2020 14Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Lxx)) The structure theory of reductive groups (tori, roots, Weyl groups) is therefore mainly the subject of [MSC 20Gxx - Linear algebraic groups and related topics](node:MSC%2020Gxx%20-%20Linear%20algebraic%20groups%20and%20related%20topics). Within 14L, the emphasis falls on group schemes over general bases, non-smooth phenomena in positive characteristic, and the geometry of group actions.

A group scheme over $S$ is a group object in $S$-schemes: an $S$-scheme $G$ with multiplication, unit and inverse morphisms satisfying the group axioms. Over a field of characteristic $p$, $\mu_p$ is not smooth, so non-smooth group schemes appear naturally. ([Wikipedia: Group scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_scheme)) Abelian varieties are the projective smooth connected group schemes and are always commutative. ([Wikipedia: Linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group)) Chevalley's theorem shows that a general algebraic group is built from an affine group and an abelian variety. ([Wikipedia: Chevalley's structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevalley%27s_structure_theorem))

### Scope
The MSC2020 subcodes are: 14L05 formal groups and $p$-divisible groups (see also 55N22); 14L10 group varieties; 14L15 group schemes; 14L17 affine algebraic groups and hyperalgebra constructions; 14L24 geometric invariant theory (see also 13A50); 14L30 group actions on varieties or schemes (quotients); 14L35 classical groups (algebro-geometric aspects); 14L40 other algebraic groups (geometric aspects). ([MSC2020 14Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Lxx))

Neighbours: [MSC 20Gxx - Linear algebraic groups and related topics](node:MSC%2020Gxx%20-%20Linear%20algebraic%20groups%20and%20related%20topics) takes linear algebraic groups as groups; [MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras) takes their [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) (17B45); [MSC 14Kxx - Abelian varieties and schemes](node:MSC%2014Kxx%20-%20Abelian%20varieties%20and%20schemes) takes abelian varieties; [MSC 11Exx - Forms and linear algebraic groups](node:MSC%2011Exx%20-%20Forms%20and%20linear%20algebraic%20groups) holds the 11E57 cross-reference; [MSC 55Nxx - Homology and cohomology theories in algebraic topology](node:MSC%2055Nxx%20-%20Homology%20and%20cohomology%20theories%20in%20algebraic%20topology) (55N22) holds the topological use of formal groups. ([MSC2020 14Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Lxx)) Invariant rings themselves are in 13A50, cross-referenced from 14L24 and 14L30. ([MSC2020 14Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Lxx))

### Key concepts
- **Group varieties and affine groups (14L10, 14L15, 14L17).** In Conrad's course, a group variety over $k$ is a smooth group scheme of finite type; over imperfect $k$, reducedness does not imply geometric reducedness even for connected group schemes, so smoothness must be assumed rather than inferred. An algebraic $k$-group scheme is affine if and only if it is a closed $k$-subgroup scheme of some $\mathrm{GL}_n$. ([Conrad, Linear Algebraic Groups notes, §1.1](https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/249BW16Page/handouts/alggroups.pdf)) Linear algebraic groups can therefore be viewed either as matrix groups or as smooth affine group schemes. ([Wikipedia: Linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group))
- **Chevalley's structure theorem.** A smooth connected algebraic group $G$ over a perfect field has a unique normal smooth connected affine subgroup $H$ such that $G/H$ is an abelian variety. Over imperfect fields there is still a smallest normal connected linear subgroup with abelian-variety quotient, but it need not be smooth. ([Wikipedia: Chevalley's structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevalley%27s_structure_theorem)) Milne's text builds its first eight chapters to this result (the Barsotti–Chevalley theorem). ([Milne, Algebraic Groups (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/algebraic-groups/48D122BAEC63C2B70304E20F34482C8F))
- **Borel fixed point theorem; Borel and parabolic subgroups.** If a connected solvable linear algebraic group $G$ acts regularly on a non-empty complete variety $V$ over an algebraically closed field, then $V$ has a $G$-fixed point. Over a general field, the same holds for connected $k$-split solvable $G$ when $V$ has a $k$-rational point. ([Wikipedia: Borel fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_fixed-point_theorem)) Over an algebraically closed field, Borel subgroups (maximal smooth connected solvable subgroups) of a connected $G$ are all conjugate. $G/B$ is projective (the flag variety). A smooth subgroup $P$ is parabolic when $G/P$ is projective, and the parabolic subgroups are exactly the subgroups containing a Borel subgroup. ([Wikipedia: Linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group))
- **Root data.** A root datum $(X^*,\Phi,X_*,\Phi^\vee)$ has free abelian groups $X^*,X_*$ of finite rank in perfect $\mathbb Z$-valued duality, with a bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$, $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$, and reflections $x\mapsto x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ preserving the datum. A connected split reductive group is determined up to isomorphism by its (reduced) root datum, and every root datum arises; Demazure introduced root data in SGA 3 (1970). ([Wikipedia: Root datum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_datum)) Root data keep track of a split reductive group up to isomorphism, whereas root systems only keep track of it up to central isogeny. ([Conrad, Root datum handout](https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/249BW16Page/handouts/rootdatum.pdf)) This is the algebraic counterpart of the classification of compact [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups) and of the [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of reductive groups.
- **Geometric invariant theory (14L24).** For a linear action of $G$ on a vector space $V$, the affine quotient is $V/\!\!/G=\operatorname{Spec}R(V)^G$. Hilbert settled finite generation of invariants for $\mathrm{GL}$; it holds for reductive groups, and Nagata showed it fails for arbitrary groups (Hilbert's fourteenth problem). ([Wikipedia: Geometric invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory))
- **Stability and Hilbert–Mumford (14L24, 14L30).** For reductive $G$ acting linearly on $V$, a nonzero $x$ is unstable if $0\in\overline{G x}$, semistable otherwise, and stable if its orbit is closed and its stabilizer finite. The Hilbert–Mumford criterion says that $x$ is unstable if and only if some one-parameter subgroup has all its weights with respect to $x$ positive. Many moduli spaces are quotients of stable loci in projective space, such as those of stable curves and stable vector bundles on curves. ([Wikipedia: Geometric invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory))
- **Formal groups (14L05).** A one-dimensional formal group law over $R$ is $F(x,y)\in R[\![x,y]\!]$ with $F=x+y+\cdots$ and $F(x,F(y,z))=F(F(x,y),z)$; examples are $x+y$ and $x+y+xy$. Over a $\mathbb Q$-algebra a commutative law is strictly isomorphic to the additive one via a logarithm. In characteristic $p>0$, two one-dimensional laws over an algebraically closed field are isomorphic if and only if they have the same height. Lazard's universal ring is a polynomial ring over $\mathbb Z$, and Quillen identified it with the coefficient ring of complex cobordism. ([Wikipedia: Formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_group_law))
- **$p$-divisible groups (14L05).** Following Tate (1967), a $p$-divisible group of height $h$ is an inductive system $(G_n)$ of finite group schemes of order $p^{hn}$, with $G_n$ the $p^n$-torsion of $G_{n+1}$. Examples are $\mu_{p^\infty}$ (height $1$) and the $p$-power torsion of an abelian variety of dimension $d$ (height $2d$). Barsotti introduced them in 1962, and Grothendieck named them Barsotti–Tate groups. ([Wikipedia: p-divisible group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-divisible_group))

### History
Maurer, Chevalley and Kolchin founded the theory of algebraic groups, and Borel built much of the modern theory in the 1950s. ([Wikipedia: Linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group)) Borel proved his fixed point theorem in the 1956 *Annals* paper "Groupes linéaires algébriques". ([Wikipedia: Borel fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_fixed-point_theorem)) Chevalley announced his structure theorem in 1953 and proved it in 1960; Barsotti (1955) and Rosenlicht (1956) also proved it, and Conrad (2002) gave a scheme-theoretic proof. ([Wikipedia: Chevalley's structure theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevalley%27s_structure_theorem)) Mumford founded geometric invariant theory in a 1965 monograph, applying nineteenth-century invariant theory, including Hilbert's 1893 paper, to construct moduli spaces. ([Wikipedia: Geometric invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory)) Bochner introduced formal group laws in 1946. ([Wikipedia: Formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_group_law))

### Open problems
- **Grothendieck–Serre conjecture in mixed characteristic.** For a regular local ring $R$ with fraction field $K$ and a reductive $R$-group scheme $G$, no nontrivial $G$-torsor over $R$ becomes trivial over $K$. Česnavičius's survey records it as settled for tori (Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc), in dimension $\le1$ (Nisnevich, Guo), in equal characteristic (Fedorov–Panin for infinite residue fields, Panin for finite ones), and in the unramified mixed-characteristic case with a Borel subgroup. It "remains open in mixed characteristic, especially, over ramified regular local rings." ([Česnavičius, Problems about torsors over regular rings, §3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.06424))
- **Parahoric group schemes over discrete valuation rings.** The same survey flags as still open whether the corresponding injectivity holds over a discrete valuation ring when $G$ is merely a parahoric group scheme rather than reductive. ([Česnavičius, Problems about torsors over regular rings](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.06424))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Geometric invariant theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory): quotients, stability, Hilbert–Mumford criterion.
- **Reference:** [Linear algebraic group (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group): Borel and parabolic subgroups, history.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Linear Algebraic Groups course notes (Stanford)](https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/249BW16Page/handouts/alggroups.pdf): group schemes over fields, smoothness, embeddings in $\mathrm{GL}_n$.
- **Primary:** [Česnavičius, Problems about torsors over regular rings (arXiv:2201.06424)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.06424): survey of current problems on torsors under reductive group schemes.
- **Primary:** [Mumford, Fogarty, Kirwan, Geometric Invariant Theory (Springer, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-57916-5): the standard monograph on 14L24.
- **Further reading:** [Milne, Algebraic Groups: The Theory of Group Schemes of Finite Type over a Field (CUP, 2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/algebraic-groups/48D122BAEC63C2B70304E20F34482C8F): group schemes over fields through Barsotti–Chevalley, Borel subgroups and split reductive groups.
references.MSC 14Mxx - Special varieties:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14Mxx gathers classes of [Algebraic Varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties) singled out by extra structure rather than by dimension: varieties defined by ring conditions, complete intersections and determinantal varieties, Grassmannians, flag and homogeneous varieties, rational, unirational and rationally connected varieties, toric and spherical varieties, supervarieties, and character varieties. ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))

These classes are where explicit computation is possible. Toric varieties reduce geometry to fans and polytopes ([Telen](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.01690)); Grassmannians and Schubert varieties reduce it to partitions and Weyl groups ([Wikipedia: Grassmannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassmannian); [Wikipedia: Schubert variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_variety)); determinantal varieties reduce it to minors of matrices ([Wikipedia: Determinantal variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinantal_variety)). Rationality questions are hard even for simple examples: in Hassett's 2016 survey no cubic fourfold had been proven irrational ([Hassett](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.05501)), and a claimed proof that a very general cubic fourfold is not rational, by Katzarkov, Kontsevich, Pantev and Yu, is a 2025 preprint revised in 2026. ([KKPY, arXiv:2508.05105](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05105))

### Scope
- **14M05, 14M06, 14M07:** varieties defined by ring conditions (factorial, Cohen–Macaulay, seminormal), linkage, and low-codimension problems. ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))
- **14M10, 14M12:** complete intersections and determinantal varieties, both cross-referenced to 13C40. ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))
- **14M15, 14M17:** Grassmannians, Schubert varieties, flag manifolds, and homogeneous spaces (see also 32M10, 51M35, 53C30, 57T15). ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))
- **14M20, 14M22:** rational and unirational varieties (see also 14E08) and rationally connected varieties. ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))
- **14M25, 14M27:** toric varieties, Newton polyhedra and Okounkov bodies (see also 52B20); compactifications, symmetric and spherical varieties. ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))
- **14M30, 14M35:** supervarieties (see also 32C11, 58A50) and character varieties. ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))

Neighbours, as the entry's cross-references show: rational and unirational varieties (14M20) point to 14E08 in [MSC 14Exx - Birational geometry](node:MSC%2014Exx%20-%20Birational%20geometry); linkage, complete intersections and determinantal varieties (14M06, 14M10, 14M12) point to 13C40 in [MSC 13Cxx - Theory of modules and ideals in commutative rings](node:MSC%2013Cxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20modules%20and%20ideals%20in%20commutative%20rings); toric varieties (14M25) point to 52B20 in [MSC 52Bxx - Polytopes and polyhedra](node:MSC%2052Bxx%20-%20Polytopes%20and%20polyhedra); ring conditions (14M05) point to 13F15, 13F45 and 13H10. ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))

### Key concepts
- **Rationality hierarchy (14M20, 14M22).** A variety is rational if birational to projective space, stably rational if $V\times\mathbb P^m$ is rational for some $m\ge0$, unirational if dominated by a rational variety, and rationally connected if any two points lie on a rational curve in it. Lüroth's theorem says every subfield of a purely transcendental extension $K(X)$ of transcendence degree one containing $K$ is $K$ or rational, and Castelnuovo's theorem says a unirational complex surface is rational. In dimension 3 this fails: Clemens–Griffiths (1972) showed a general cubic threefold is not rational, Iskovskikh–Manin (1971) that all smooth quartic threefolds are irrational though some are unirational, and Artin–Mumford (1972) gave unirational non-rational threefolds. Kollár (published 2002) proved a smooth cubic hypersurface of dimension at least $2$ over $K$ is unirational if it has a $K$-point. ([Wikipedia: Rational variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety))
- **Fano varieties and rational curves.** A Fano variety is a complete variety with ample anticanonical bundle. Campana and Kollár–Miyaoka–Mori showed that a smooth Fano variety over an algebraically closed field is rationally chain connected, and Kollár–Miyaoka–Mori showed that smooth Fano varieties of fixed dimension in characteristic $0$ form a bounded family. Smooth Fano threefolds fall into 17 classes with $b_2=1$ (Iskovskikh) and 88 deformation classes with $b_2\ge2$ (Mori–Mukai). ([Wikipedia: Fano variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano_variety))
- **Grassmannians and Schubert varieties (14M15, 14M17).** $\operatorname{Gr}(k,V)$, $\dim V=n$, is a smooth projective variety of dimension $k(n-k)$, embedded in $\mathbb P(\Lambda^kV)$ by the Plücker map and cut out by the quadratic Plücker relations (for $\operatorname{Gr}(2,4)$, the single quadric $w_{12}w_{34}-w_{13}w_{24}+w_{14}w_{23}=0$). It is the homogeneous space $GL(V)/H$ with $H$ a parabolic subgroup, and relative to a complete flag it decomposes into Schubert cells indexed by partitions in a $k\times(n-k)$ box. ([Wikipedia: Grassmannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassmannian)) More generally $G/P$ has finitely many $B$-orbits indexed by Weyl group elements $w$, and the closure $X_w$ of the orbit of $w$ is a Schubert variety; their singularities are measured by Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials. ([Wikipedia: Schubert variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_variety)) This is where the geometry of [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups) enters the code.
- **Determinantal varieties (14M12).** For $r<\min(m,n)$, $Y_r\subset k^{m\times n}$ is the set of matrices of rank at most $r$, cut out by the $(r+1)\times(r+1)$ minors. The ideal of these minors in a generic matrix is prime (Bruns–Vetter), $\dim Y_r=r(m+n-r)$, and the singular locus of $Y_r$ is exactly $Y_{r-1}$. ([Wikipedia: Determinantal variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinantal_variety))
- **Toric varieties (14M25).** A fan in $N_{\mathbb R}$ is a finite collection $\Sigma$ of strongly convex rational polyhedral cones such that every face of a cone in $\Sigma$ is in $\Sigma$, and the intersection of any two cones $\sigma,\sigma'\in\Sigma$ is a face of each. Each rational cone $\sigma$ gives the affine toric variety $U_\sigma=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\sigma^\vee\cap M]$. ([Telen, Def. 3.45, Cor. 2.42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.01690)) Normal toric varieties $X_\Sigma$ correspond one-to-one with such fans; $X_\Sigma$ is complete iff the support of $\Sigma$ is all of $N_{\mathbb R}$, smooth iff every cone is generated by part of a lattice basis, and projective toric varieties are those of normal fans of rational [Polytopes](node:Polytopes). ([Wikipedia: Toric variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toric_variety))
- **Character varieties (14M35).** For a finitely generated group $\pi$ and a reductive group $G$ over $\mathbb C$, the $G$-character variety is the affine GIT quotient $\operatorname{Hom}(\pi,G)/\!/G$, whose points are homomorphisms up to the equivalence "orbit closures meet". Via holonomy, these spaces relate to flat connections, principal and vector bundles, and Higgs bundles. ([Wikipedia: Character variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_variety))

### History
Lüroth's and Castelnuovo's theorems settle unirational-versus-rational for curves and complex surfaces; the threefold examples of Iskovskikh–Manin (1971), Clemens–Griffiths (1972) and Artin–Mumford (1972) showed that unirational does not imply rational in dimension three. ([Wikipedia: Rational variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety)) Toric varieties were discovered in the early 1970s independently by several groups; Cox surveys their later links to [Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry), [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics), and mirror symmetry. ([Cox, arXiv:alg-geom/9606016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/alg-geom/9606016)) Cox, Little and Schenck's *Toric Varieties* appeared in the AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics series in 2011. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/124))

### Open problems
- **Rationality of cubic fourfolds.** Hassett (2016): "we expect that most cubic fourfolds should be irrational. However, no cubic fourfolds are proven to be irrational." ([Hassett, arXiv:1601.05501](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.05501)) Katzarkov, Kontsevich, Pantev and Yu's preprint (2025, revised 2026) states "we prove that a very general cubic fourfold is not rational" using new invariants called Hodge atoms; this is a reported claim in a preprint. ([KKPY, arXiv:2508.05105](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05105)) Which special cubic fourfolds are rational remains conjectural. Rational examples include the cubic fourfolds in $\mathcal C_{14}$, the closure of the Pfaffian locus, and cubics containing two disjoint planes; Kuznetsov's derived-category conjecture and Hassett's associated K3 surfaces (admissible discriminants $d$) predict which special cubics should be rational. ([Hassett, arXiv:1601.05501](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.05501))
- **Rationally connected versus unirational.** Unirational varieties are rationally connected, but it is not known whether the converse holds. ([Wikipedia: Rational variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Rational variety (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety): rationality hierarchy, classical theorems and counterexamples.
- **Reference:** [Grassmannian (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassmannian): Plücker embedding, Schubert cells, cohomology.
- **Learn:** [Telen, Introduction to Toric Geometry (arXiv:2203.01690)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.01690): free lecture notes with fans, polytopes, and computations.
- **Primary:** [Hassett, Cubic fourfolds, K3 surfaces, and rationality questions (arXiv:1601.05501)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.05501): survey of the cubic fourfold rationality problem.
- **Primary:** [Cox, Recent developments in toric geometry (arXiv:alg-geom/9606016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9606016): survey of toric constructions and applications.
- **Further reading:** [Cox–Little–Schenck, Toric Varieties (AMS GSM 124, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/124): graduate text on toric varieties.
references.MSC 14Nxx - Projective and enumerative a:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14Nxx covers projective techniques and enumerative questions in algebraic geometry: how many geometric objects satisfy given incidence conditions, and the projective varieties (Grassmannians, secant varieties, arrangements, varieties of low degree) that organize such counts. Its subcodes run from classical Schubert calculus (14N15) to Gromov–Witten, Gopakumar–Vafa and Donaldson–Thomas invariants (14N35), with a general cross-reference to geometry (51-XX). ([MSC2020 14Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Nxx))

The classical method computes a count as a product in a cohomology or Chow ring: the 27 lines on a cubic surface fall out of Schubert calculus on a Grassmannian, and putting this method on a rigorous foundation was the aim of Hilbert's 15th problem. ([Wikipedia: Schubert calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_calculus)) The modern method counts curves through intersection theory on moduli spaces of stable maps, which produces Gromov–Witten invariants and quantum cohomology. ([Wikipedia: Gromov–Witten invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gromov%E2%80%93Witten_invariant); [Halleck-Dubé](https://math.berkeley.edu/~chd/expo/kontsevich_formula.pdf))

### Scope
- **14N05:** projective techniques in algebraic geometry (see also 51N35). ([MSC2020 14Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Nxx))
- **14N07:** secant varieties, tensor rank, varieties of sums of powers. ([MSC2020 14Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Nxx))
- **14N10, 14N15:** enumerative (combinatorial) problems; classical problems and Schubert calculus. ([MSC2020 14Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Nxx))
- **14N20:** configurations and arrangements of linear subspaces. ([MSC2020 14Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Nxx))
- **14N25, 14N30:** varieties of low degree and adjunction problems. ([MSC2020 14Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Nxx))
- **14N35:** Gromov–Witten invariants, quantum cohomology, Gopakumar–Vafa and Donaldson–Thomas invariants in their algebro-geometric aspects (see also 53D45). ([MSC2020 14Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Nxx))

Neighbours, as the entry's cross-references show: the whole section points to 51-XX, projective techniques (14N05) to 51N35 in [MSC 51Nxx - Analytic and descriptive geometry](node:MSC%2051Nxx%20-%20Analytic%20and%20descriptive%20geometry), and Gromov–Witten and related invariants (14N35, algebro-geometric aspects) to 53D45 in [MSC 53Dxx - Symplectic geometry, contact geometry](node:MSC%2053Dxx%20-%20Symplectic%20geometry,%20contact%20geometry). ([MSC2020 14Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Nxx)) Grassmannians, Schubert varieties and flag manifolds as varieties also have their own code, 14M15, in [MSC 14Mxx - Special varieties](node:MSC%2014Mxx%20-%20Special%20varieties). ([MSC2020 14Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Mxx))

### Key concepts
- **Grassmannians and Schubert classes (14N15).** $\operatorname{Gr}(k,n)$ is a smooth projective variety of dimension $k(n-k)$, embedded in $\mathbb P(\Lambda^k\mathbb C^n)$ by Plücker coordinates and cut out by quadratic Plücker relations, a topic of [Projective Geometry](node:Projective%20Geometry). A complete flag decomposes it into Schubert cells indexed by partitions in a $k\times(n-k)$ box, whose closures are Schubert varieties; the cohomology ring is generated by the Chern classes of the tautological bundle. ([Wikipedia: Grassmannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassmannian)) The Schubert classes span the Chow ring and are linearly independent; the Pieri formula multiplies by a special class $\sigma_b$, the Giambelli formula writes $\sigma_\lambda$ as a [determinant](node:Determinant) in special classes (the same form as the Jacobi–Trudi identity), and the structure constants of the general product are Littlewood–Richardson coefficients. ([Wikipedia: Schubert calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_calculus))
- **Schubert polynomials and flag varieties.** For the full flag variety, Schubert polynomials $\mathfrak S_w$, defined from $x_1^{n-1}x_2^{n-2}\cdots x_{n-1}$ by divided differences $\partial_i\mathfrak S_w=\mathfrak S_{ws_i}$ when $w(i)>w(i+1)$, represent the Schubert classes. Their structure constants are non-negative integers by Kleiman's transversality theorem (1974). ([Wikipedia: Schubert polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_polynomial)) This links 14N15 with [MSC 05Exx - Algebraic combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Exx%20-%20Algebraic%20combinatorics).
- **Stable maps and Kontsevich's formula (14N35).** Fulton and Pandharipande's notes construct the moduli spaces of stable maps, Gromov–Witten invariants, and quantum cohomology. ([Fulton–Pandharipande, arXiv:alg-geom/9608011](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9608011)) The coarse space $\overline M_{0,n}(\mathbb P^r,d)$ of stable $n$-pointed degree-$d$ maps is a projective normal irreducible variety, locally a quotient of a smooth variety by a finite group. If $N_d$ is the number of rational plane curves of degree $d$ through $3d-1$ general points, then
  $$N_d=\sum_{\substack{d_A+d_B=d\\ d_A,d_B\ge1}}N_{d_A}N_{d_B}\left[d_A^2d_B^2\binom{3d-4}{3d_A-2}-d_A^3d_B\binom{3d-4}{3d_A-1}\right].$$
  More generally, all genus-0 Gromov–Witten invariants of $\mathbb P^r$ are determined recursively from the number of lines through two points (Kontsevich–Manin 1994, Ruan–Tian 1995). ([Halleck-Dubé, Thm. 1, Thm. 8](https://math.berkeley.edu/~chd/expo/kontsevich_formula.pdf)) Its first values are $N_1=1$, $N_2=1$, $N_3=12$, $N_4=620$, $N_5=87304$, and the invariants deform the cup product into the quantum cohomology ring. ([Wikipedia: Gromov–Witten invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gromov%E2%80%93Witten_invariant))
- **Secant varieties and Alexander–Hirschowitz (14N07).** The $k$-th secant variety $\Sigma_k$ of $V\subset\mathbb P^r$ is the closure of the union of linear spans of $k+1$ points of $V$; if $\dim V=d$, then $\dim\Sigma_k\le kd+d+k$, with Terracini's lemma the standard tool for computing it. ([Wikipedia: Secant variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secant_variety)) Alexander–Hirschowitz theorem: over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, for a general collection $X$ of $k$ double points in $\mathbb P^n$, the space $I_X(d)$ of degree-$d$ forms singular at $X$ has the expected codimension $\min\left((n+1)k,\binom{n+d}{n}\right)$, except for $d=2$, $2\le k\le n$, and $(n,d,k)=(2,4,5),(3,4,9),(4,3,7),(4,4,14)$. Equivalently the secant varieties of Veronese varieties have the expected dimension, and a general form of degree $d$ in $n+1$ variables is a sum of $\left\lceil\binom{n+d}{d}/(n+1)\right\rceil$ $d$-th powers of linear forms, with the same exceptions. ([Brambilla–Ottaviani, Thms. 1.1–1.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0701409))
- **Hyperplane arrangements (14N20).** For a finite set $\mathcal A$ of hyperplanes, the intersection semilattice $L(\mathcal A)$ consists of all intersections of hyperplanes, ordered by reverse inclusion. For a complex arrangement, the integral cohomology ring of the complement $M(\mathcal A)$ is isomorphic to the Orlik–Solomon algebra, a quotient of an exterior algebra determined by $L(\mathcal A)$. For a real affine arrangement in $\mathbb R^n$, Zaslavsky (1975) showed the number of regions is $(-1)^n\chi_{\mathcal A}(-1)$, where $\chi_{\mathcal A}$ is the characteristic polynomial. ([Wikipedia: Arrangement of hyperplanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement_of_hyperplanes)) These counts belong as much to [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) as to geometry.

### History
Hermann Schubert introduced his calculus in the nineteenth century to solve counting problems of projective geometry, and giving it a rigorous foundation was the aim of Hilbert's 15th problem. ([Wikipedia: Schubert calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_calculus)) Kleiman's transversality theorem (1974) gave the geometric reason that Schubert structure constants are non-negative. ([Wikipedia: Schubert polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_polynomial)) Fulton's *Intersection Theory* appeared in a 1998 Springer edition. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1700-8)) Kontsevich–Manin (1994) and Ruan–Tian (1995) established the recursive computation of genus-0 Gromov–Witten invariants of projective space. ([Halleck-Dubé, Thm. 8](https://math.berkeley.edu/~chd/expo/kontsevich_formula.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Combinatorial rule for Schubert structure constants.** The product of Schubert polynomials has non-negative integer structure constants, and it "is an outstanding problem in representation theory and combinatorics to give a combinatorial rule for these numbers." ([Wikipedia: Schubert polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_polynomial)) For Grassmannians the structure constants are the Littlewood–Richardson coefficients. ([Wikipedia: Schubert calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_calculus)) See [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory).
- **Interpolation with higher multiplicities.** Alexander–Hirschowitz settles general double points; Brambilla and Ottaviani write that "the higher multiplicity case is still open and it is a subject of active research." ([Brambilla–Ottaviani](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0701409))
- **McMullen problem.** In arrangement form: find the smallest arrangement of a given dimension, in general position in real projective space, with no cell touched by all hyperplanes. ([Wikipedia: Arrangement of hyperplanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement_of_hyperplanes)) In point form it asks for the largest $\nu(d)$ such that any $\nu(d)$ points in general position in affine $d$-space can be moved into convex position by a projective transformation; the conjecture $\nu(d)=2d+1$ is proven for $d=2,3,4$, and the problem "is still open." ([Wikipedia: McMullen problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMullen_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Schubert calculus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_calculus): Pieri, Giambelli, Littlewood–Richardson, 27 lines.
- **Reference:** [Gromov–Witten invariant (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gromov%E2%80%93Witten_invariant): stable maps, quantum cohomology, values of $N_d$.
- **Learn:** [Halleck-Dubé, Kontsevich's formula for rational plane curves (Berkeley)](https://math.berkeley.edu/~chd/expo/kontsevich_formula.pdf): elementary proof via boundary divisors on $\overline M_{0,n}(\mathbb P^2,d)$.
- **Primary:** [Fulton–Pandharipande, Notes on stable maps and quantum cohomology (arXiv:alg-geom/9608011)](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9608011): notes on the construction of stable-map moduli spaces, Gromov–Witten invariants and quantum cohomology.
- **Primary:** [Brambilla–Ottaviani, On the Alexander–Hirschowitz theorem (arXiv:math/0701409)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0701409): self-contained proof and open higher-multiplicity case.
- **Further reading:** [Fulton, Intersection Theory (Springer, 1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1700-8): monograph on intersection theory (Springer, 1998).
references.MSC 14Pxx - Real algebraic and real-anal:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14P, "Real algebraic and real-analytic geometry", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) that studies real solution sets: real algebraic sets, sets defined by polynomial inequalities, sets defined by real-analytic functions, Nash functions and manifolds, and the topology of real [algebraic varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties). ([MSC2020 14Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Pxx)) A projection of a real algebraic set along a coordinate axis need not be a real algebraic set, but it is always semialgebraic, so inequalities must be admitted from the start; the basic objects become the [semialgebraic sets](node:Semialgebraic%20Sets) over a [real closed field](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields). ([Real algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry); [Schweighofer, Thm 1.8.18](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04211))

Three threads run through the area: positivity (which polynomials are nonnegative on a semialgebraic set, and how to certify it by sums of squares), topology (how many components and what arrangements real curves and varieties can have), and tame geometry (finiteness theorems shared by semialgebraic, subanalytic and o-minimal sets). The algorithmic side, from Tarski's quantifier elimination to the computation of Betti numbers, overlaps with [MSC 14Qxx - Computational aspects in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Qxx%20-%20Computational%20aspects%20in%20algebraic%20geometry). ([Real algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry); [Basu](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1409.1534))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 14Pxx lists 14P05 real algebraic sets (see also 12D15, 13J30); 14P10 semialgebraic sets and related spaces; 14P15 real-analytic and semi-analytic sets (see also 32B20, 32C05); 14P20 Nash functions and manifolds (see also 32C07, 58A07); 14P25 topology of real algebraic varieties; 14P99. ([MSC2020 14Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Pxx))

- **Neighbour 12D / 13J.** 14P05 cross-refers to 12D15 (in [MSC 12Dxx - Real and complex fields](node:MSC%2012Dxx%20-%20Real%20and%20complex%20fields)) and to 13J30 (in [MSC 13Jxx - Topological rings and modules](node:MSC%2013Jxx%20-%20Topological%20rings%20and%20modules)). ([MSC2020 14Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Pxx))
- **Neighbour 32B / 32C.** Semi-analytic sets (14P15) and Nash functions (14P20) cross-refer to [MSC 32Bxx - Local analytic geometry](node:MSC%2032Bxx%20-%20Local%20analytic%20geometry) (32B20) and [MSC 32Cxx - Analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Cxx%20-%20Analytic%20spaces) (32C05, 32C07); 14P20 also cross-refers to 58A07. ([MSC2020 14Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Pxx))
- **Neighbour 14Q.** Computational real algebraic geometry is classified at 14Q30, which cross-refers back to 14Pxx. ([MSC2020 14Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Qxx))

### Key concepts
- **Tarski–Seidenberg and cylindrical decomposition (14P10).** The theory of real closed fields admits quantifier elimination (Tarski 1931, Seidenberg 1954); geometrically, a polynomial image (in particular a projection) of a semialgebraic set is semialgebraic. Collins's cylindrical algebraic decomposition (1975) made elimination implementable, with complexity $(sd)^{2^{O(k+\ell)}}$ for $s$ polynomials of degree $\le d$ in $k+\ell$ variables ($\ell$ of them free); Davenport and Heintz proved a doubly exponential lower bound for real quantifier elimination, using formulas whose number of quantifier alternations grows linearly in the number of variables. ([Real algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry); [Schweighofer, Thm 1.8.18](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04211); [Basu, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1409.1534))
- **Artin's theorem and the Positivstellensatz (14P05, 14P10).** Artin (1927, Hilbert's 17th problem): for $R$ real closed, $K\subseteq R$ an ordered subfield and $f\in K[X_1,\dots,X_n]$, $f\ge0$ on $R^n$ iff $f$ is a sum of terms $a\,g^2$ with $a\in K_{\ge0}$, $g\in K(X)$. Krivine–Stengle Positivstellensatz: if $T$ is a preorder of $K[X]$ finitely generated over $K_{\ge0}$ and $S=\{x\in R^n: p(x)\ge0\ \forall p\in T\}$, then $f>0$ on $S$ iff $tf\in1+T$ for some $t\in T$. ([Schweighofer, Thm 2.5.2, Cor 3.7.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04211); [Real algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry))
- **Schmüdgen and Putinar (14P10).** Schmüdgen: with $K\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $T$ as above, $T$ is Archimedean iff $S$ is compact, and then every $f$ with $f>0$ on $S$ lies in $T$ (no denominators). Putinar: if $S=\{g_1\ge0,\dots,g_m\ge0,\ \|x\|\le R\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $f>0$ on $S$, then $f=\sum_{i=0}^{m+1}\sigma_ig_i$ with sums of squares $\sigma_i$, $g_0=1$, $g_{m+1}=R^2-\sum X_i^2$. These underlie sum-of-squares relaxations in optimisation. ([Schweighofer, Thm 4.3.5, Cor 4.3.6, Ex 8.2.14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04211); [Positivstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positivstellensatz))
- **Harnack's theorem and Hilbert's sixteenth problem (14P25).** A real plane projective curve of degree $n$ has at most $\tfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}2+1$ connected components (Harnack 1876); curves attaining the bound are M-curves. The first part of Hilbert's sixteenth problem asks for the possible relative positions of the ovals; Hilbert found that the 11 components of a sextic M-curve are always grouped in a certain way, and the bound was later extended to all Betti numbers of real algebraic sets. Viro's patchworking technique (1980) was used to classify real [algebraic curves](node:Algebraic%20Curves) of low degree. ([Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem); [Real algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry))
- **Nash functions and the Nash–Tognoli theorem (14P20).** A Nash function is an analytic function $f$ on an open semialgebraic $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ satisfying a nontrivial polynomial equation $P(x,f(x))=0$; Nash manifolds are semialgebraic analytic submanifolds. Nash (1952) showed every compact [smooth manifold](node:Smooth%20Manifolds) is diffeomorphic to a Nash manifold (indeed to a nonsingular component of a real algebraic set), and Tognoli (1973) that it is diffeomorphic to a nonsingular real algebraic set. Germs of Nash functions at a point of an $n$-dimensional Nash manifold form a regular [local ring](node:Local%20Rings) of dimension $n$, and the ring of Nash functions on a Nash manifold, even a noncompact one, is Noetherian (Risler and Efroymson, independently, 1973). ([Nash functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_functions); [Real algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry))
- **Semianalytic and subanalytic sets, Łojasiewicz inequality (14P15).** Semianalytic sets are locally Boolean combinations of sets $\{f>0\}$, $f$ real analytic; projections of semianalytic sets need not be semianalytic, which leads to subanalytic sets (locally projections of relatively compact semianalytic sets). Łojasiewicz inequality: for $f$ real analytic on open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with nonempty zero set $Z$ and compact $K\subseteq U$, there are $\alpha,C>0$ with $\operatorname{dist}(x,Z)^\alpha\le C|f(x)|$ on $K$; the gradient form gives $|f(x)-f(p)|^\theta\le c|\nabla f(x)|$ near $p$ for some $\theta\in(0,1)$. Łojasiewicz triangulated semianalytic sets in 1964. ([Subanalytic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subanalytic_set); [Łojasiewicz inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%81ojasiewicz_inequality); [Real algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry))
- **O-minimality.** An ordered structure is o-minimal if every definable subset of the line is a finite union of points and intervals. The real field (definable sets: semialgebraic sets), the real field with restricted analytic functions $\mathbb R_{an}$, and the real exponential field (Wilkie) are o-minimal, and definable sets admit cell decompositions; this is the common framework for tame real geometry, linking 14P with [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory). ([O-minimal theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-minimal_theory))

### History
Harnack bounded the components of real plane curves in 1876, Hilbert posed the 16th and 17th problems in 1900, and Artin solved the 17th in 1927. Tarski (1931) and Seidenberg (1954) gave real quantifier elimination, Nash (1952) and Tognoli (1973) proved the algebraicity of smooth manifolds, Łojasiewicz (1964) triangulated semianalytic sets, Krivine (1964) and Stengle (1974) proved the Positivstellensatz, Rokhlin proved Gudkov's conjecture (1972), Collins introduced cylindrical algebraic decomposition (1975), and Schmüdgen (1991) and Putinar (1993) proved their representation theorems. ([Real algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry))

### Open problems
- **Hilbert's sixteenth problem, first part.** The classification of arrangements of ovals of real plane curves is unsolved for degree $n=8$. ([Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem))
- **Betti numbers in singly exponential time.** Basu calls it one of the most fundamental open questions of algorithmic semialgebraic geometry whether the Betti numbers of a semialgebraic set in $R^k$ defined by $s$ polynomials of degree $\le d$ can be computed in time singly exponential in $k$; only the first $\ell$ Betti numbers, for fixed $\ell$, are known to be. Related open questions: semialgebraic triangulations in singly exponential time, and lowering the $O(k^2)$ exponent of roadmap algorithms for connectivity to $O(k)$. ([Basu, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1409.1534))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Real algebraic geometry (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_algebraic_geometry): annotated timeline of the field.
- **Reference:** [Subanalytic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subanalytic_set) and [O-minimal theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-minimal_theory): the real-analytic and tame side.
- **Learn:** [Schweighofer, Real Algebraic Geometry, Positivity and Convexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04211): Konstanz lecture notes on real closed fields, quantifier elimination, Artin, Positivstellensätze.
- **Primary:** [Basu, Algorithms in Real Algebraic Geometry: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.1534): complexity of quantifier elimination, roadmaps, Betti numbers, open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Bochnak, Coste and Roy, Real Algebraic Geometry (Springer, 1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-03718-8): the standard graduate monograph.
references.MSC 14Qxx - Computational aspects in alg:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14Q, "Computational aspects in algebraic geometry", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) concerned with computing with varieties: algorithms for curves, surfaces and higher-dimensional varieties, effectivity and complexity bounds, computation over arithmetic ground fields, computational real algebraic geometry, and the geometry of numerical algebraic geometry. Software belongs under 14-04, and the section points to 12-08, 13Pxx and 68W30. ([MSC2020 14Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Qxx)) The overview note [Computational Algebraic Geometry](node:Computational%20Algebraic%20Geometry) gives the general picture.

There are two computational paradigms. Symbolic methods transform an ideal of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, given by generators, exactly; the main tool is [Gröbner bases](node:Gröbner%20Bases), and difficulty is measured by degree and regularity bounds. ([Bayer–Mumford](https://arxiv.org/src/alg-geom/9304003)) Numerical methods approximate solution sets by homotopy continuation and represent positive-dimensional components by witness sets; Sommese and Wampler began developing "numerical algebraic geometry" in a 1996 paper. ([Sommese–Verschelde–Wampler](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~jan/Articles/intro.pdf); [Numerical Nonlinear Algebra](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.08585v2))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists 14Q05 computational aspects of [algebraic curves](node:Algebraic%20Curves) (see also 14Hxx); 14Q10 of [algebraic surfaces](node:Algebraic%20Surfaces) (see also 14Jxx); 14Q15 of higher-dimensional varieties (see also 14Jxx, 14Mxx); 14Q20 effectivity, complexity and computational aspects; 14Q25 computation over arithmetic ground fields (see also 14Gxx, 14H25, 14Kxx); 14Q30 computational real algebraic geometry (see also 14Pxx); 14Q65 geometric aspects of numerical algebraic geometry (see also 65H14); 14Q99. ([MSC2020 14Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Qxx))

- **Neighbour 13P.** [13P](node:MSC%2013Pxx%20-%20Computational%20aspects%20and%20applications%20of%20commutative%20rings) (computational aspects of commutative rings) is one of the sections the 14Q header tells readers to see also, together with 12-08 and 68W30. ([MSC2020 14Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Qxx))
- **Neighbours 14H, 14J, 14M.** 14Q05–14Q15 cross-refer to [MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Hxx%20-%20Curves%20in%20algebraic%20geometry), [MSC 14Jxx - Surfaces and higher-dimensional varieties](node:MSC%2014Jxx%20-%20Surfaces%20and%20higher-dimensional%20varieties) and [MSC 14Mxx - Special varieties](node:MSC%2014Mxx%20-%20Special%20varieties). ([MSC2020 14Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Qxx))
- **Neighbours 65H and 14P.** 14Q65 cross-refers to 65H14 in [MSC 65Hxx - Nonlinear algebraic or transcendental equations](node:MSC%2065Hxx%20-%20Nonlinear%20algebraic%20or%20transcendental%20equations); 14Q30 cross-refers to [MSC 14Pxx - Real algebraic and real-analytic geometry](node:MSC%2014Pxx%20-%20Real%20algebraic%20and%20real-analytic%20geometry). ([MSC2020 14Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Qxx))

### Key concepts
- **Gröbner bases and Buchberger's criterion.** Fix a monomial order on $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. A finite $G\subseteq I$ is a Gröbner basis of $I$ ([Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals)) if the leading terms of $G$ generate $\langle\mathrm{LT}(I)\rangle$. By Dickson's lemma one exists; division by $G$ gives a unique remainder, so $f\in I$ iff that remainder is $0$; each nonzero ideal has a unique reduced Gröbner basis. With $x^\gamma=\operatorname{lcm}(\mathrm{LM}(f),\mathrm{LM}(g))$, $S(f,g)=\frac{x^\gamma}{\mathrm{LT}(f)}f-\frac{x^\gamma}{\mathrm{LT}(g)}g$. **Buchberger's criterion:** a generating set $G$ of $I$ is a Gröbner basis iff every $S(g_i,g_j)$ reduces to $0$ modulo $G$, and adding nonzero remainders until this holds terminates. ([O'Sullivan, Thm 2.1, Prop 2.6, Thm 3.3](https://mosullivan.sdsu.edu/Teaching/Algebra13s/groebner.pdf)) For an elimination order, the elements of $G$ in $K[Y]$ form a Gröbner basis of $I\cap K[Y]$, which computes projections. Faugère's F4 replaces many reductions by row reduction of one large matrix, F5 adds a criterion shrinking those matrices, and FGLM changes order for zero-dimensional ideals. ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis))
- **Degree bounds and complexity (14Q20).** **Hermann (1926):** if $g\in(f_1,\dots,f_k)\subseteq k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $d=\max\deg f_i$, then $g=\sum a_if_i$ with $\deg a_i\le\deg g+2(kd)^{2^{n-1}}$. Mayr and Meyer (1982) gave ideals $I_n$ in $10n$ variables with $10n-6$ binomial generators for which $S^{(n)}C_i^{(n)}-F^{(n)}M\in I_n$ forces $M=C_i^{(n)}(B_i^{(n)})^{e_n}$ with $e_n=2^{2^n}$, so doubly exponential degrees are unavoidable. ([Bayer–Mumford, §3](https://arxiv.org/src/alg-geom/9304003)) Ideal membership in $\mathbb Q[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is EXPSPACE-complete: Mayr and Meyer (1982) proved EXPSPACE-hardness by reducing the word problem for commutative semigroups to membership of binomials, and Mayr (1989) gave an exponential-space algorithm. The same holds for the decision problem whether a given polynomial belongs to the reduced Gröbner basis of $(f_1,\dots,f_s)$, and Kühnle and Mayr (1996) showed that the reduced Gröbner basis can be enumerated in exponential working space. Their algorithm uses **Dubé's bound** (1990): every element of the reduced Gröbner basis of $(f_1,\dots,f_s)\subseteq\mathbb Q[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $d=\max\deg f_i$ has degree at most $2\left(\tfrac{d^2}{2}+d\right)^{2^{n-1}}$. Conversely there are $O(k)$-size inputs whose reduced Gröbner basis has more than $2^{2^k}$ elements of degree more than $2^{2^k}$ (Möller–Mora 1984, Huynh 1986), so any algorithm computing the reduced Gröbner basis for a degree-compatible order needs space $2^{\Omega(\mathrm{size})}$ and time $2^{2^{\Omega(\mathrm{size})}}$ in the worst case; exponential space is therefore optimal. ([Kayser, Gröbner bases and their complexity](https://leokayser.github.io/assets/pdf/presentations/Groebner_Bases_and_Their_Complexity_THI.pdf)) For homogeneous ideals the complexity of membership drops into PSPACE (Mayr 1997), though Gröbner bases need not get smaller ([Kayser](https://leokayser.github.io/assets/pdf/presentations/Groebner_Bases_and_Their_Complexity_THI.pdf)); Mayr's paper is "Some complexity results for polynomial ideals", J. Complexity 13 (1997) 303–325 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1006/jcom.1997.0447)); Kühnle–Mayr is in ISSAC 1996 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/236869.236900)) and Dubé in SIAM J. Comput. 19 (1990) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/0219053)). Worst-case Gröbner cost is bounded by a polynomial in $d^{2^n}$. ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis))
- **Effective Nullstellensatz.** **Brownawell–Kollár:** let $I=(f_1,\dots,f_k)\subseteq k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over any field and $d=\max(\deg f_i,3)$ (replace $d$ by $2d-1$ if $n=1$).
