If $g\in\sqrt I$, then $g^s=\sum a_if_i$ with $s\le d^n$ and $\deg a_i\le(1+\deg g)d^n$; in particular $(\sqrt I)^{d^n}\subseteq I$. Degree bounds for membership in the radical are thus singly exponential, while the Mayr–Meyer ideals are bad only through high-degree primary components at infinity. ([Bayer–Mumford](https://arxiv.org/src/alg-geom/9304003)) Brownawell's 1987 proof was analytic and valid in characteristic $0$; Kollár's 1988 proof is algebraic and valid in any characteristic. ([Hilbert's Nullstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_Nullstellensatz))
- **Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity.** The regularity of a homogeneous ideal is the maximum over $i$ of (degree $-\,i$) of a minimal $i$-th syzygy. **Bayer–Stillman:** $I$ is $m$-regular iff its minimal generators have degree $\le m$ and there are linear forms $y_0,\dots,y_\ell$ satisfying a finite chain of conditions on the forms $f$ of degree $m$ (if $y_jf$ lies in $I$, then $f$ lies in $I+(y_0,\dots,y_{j-1})$, and finally $f\in I+(y_0,\dots,y_\ell)$); if such forms exist, they may be taken from a Zariski-open set. This makes $m$-regularity finitely checkable. For reverse lexicographic order in generic coordinates, $\operatorname{reg}(\operatorname{in}(I))=\operatorname{reg}(I)$ in any characteristic, and in characteristic $0$ this gives "the degree-complexity of a Gröbner basis computation is exactly the regularity of the input data". ([Bayer–Mumford, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/src/alg-geom/9304003))
- **Primary decomposition and normalisation.** By Lasker–Noether every ideal of a Noetherian ring is a finite intersection of primary ideals; Grete Hermann (1926) gave the first algorithm in characteristic $0$, and in nonzero characteristic the method needs irreducibility tests that are "not always algorithmically possible". ([Primary decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_decomposition)) Greuel, Laplagne and Seelisch give a normalisation algorithm, implemented in Singular, for reduced Noetherian rings. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/0904.3561))
- **Real algebraic geometry (14Q30).** Collins's cylindrical algebraic decomposition (1975) splits $\mathbb R^n$ into cells on which each input polynomial has constant sign, and gives effective quantifier elimination over the reals. ([CAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylindrical_algebraic_decomposition)) It costs $(sd)^{2^{O(k)}}$ for $s$ polynomials of degree $\le d$ in $k$ variables, and Davenport–Heintz proved a doubly exponential lower bound for quantifier elimination; the critical-points method gives singly exponential algorithms, e.g. a point in every connected component of every realizable sign condition in $s^{k'}d^{O(k)}$ operations, where $k'$ is the real dimension of the algebraic set on which the sign conditions are taken, and roadmaps for connectivity. ([Basu](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1409.1534)) See [Semialgebraic Sets](node:Semialgebraic%20Sets).
- **Homotopy continuation and witness sets (14Q65).** To solve $f=0$, a start system $g$ with known solutions is deformed by $H(z,t)=(1-t)f(z)+tg(z)$ and paths are tracked by predictor–corrector steps with [Newton](node:Newton's%20Method) correction. ([Numerical algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_algebraic_geometry)) Total-degree homotopies use the Bézout count; polyhedral homotopies rest on Bernstein's mixed-volume bound for Newton [polytopes](node:Polytopes). A witness set $W=(F,L,L\cap V)$ stores equations, a generic linear space of complementary dimension, and the $\deg V$ intersection points; one per component gives a numerical irreducible decomposition. Smale's $\alpha$-theory certifies output: if $\alpha(F,x)<(13-3\sqrt{17})/4\approx0.15767$, then $x$ is an approximate zero with associated zero $z$ and $\|x-z\|\le2\beta(F,x)$. ([Numerical Nonlinear Algebra, §§3–5](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.08585v2))
- **Software.** Gröbner bases are implemented in CoCoA, Macaulay 2, Magma, Maple, Mathematica, SINGULAR, SageMath and others ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis)); CAD in QEPCAD, Redlog, Maple and Mathematica ([CAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylindrical_algebraic_decomposition)); homotopy continuation in PHCpack, Bertini, HOM4PS, NAG4M2 and HomotopyContinuation.jl ([Numerical Nonlinear Algebra](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.08585v2)).

### History
Hermann's 1926 work gave the doubly exponential membership bound and the first primary decomposition algorithm. ([Bayer–Mumford](https://arxiv.org/src/alg-geom/9304003); [Primary decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_decomposition)) Buchberger introduced Gröbner bases in his 1965 PhD thesis. ([Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis)) Collins introduced CAD in 1975. ([CAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylindrical_algebraic_decomposition)) Mayr and Meyer's examples date from 1982, the Brownawell–Kollár bounds from 1987–88, and Bayer and Mumford's survey "What can be computed in algebraic geometry?" organised the subject around regularity. ([Bayer–Mumford](https://arxiv.org/src/alg-geom/9304003); [Hilbert's Nullstellensatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_Nullstellensatz)) Kühnle and Mayr's exponential-space Gröbner algorithm appeared at ISSAC 1996. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/236869.236900)) Membership is in EXPSPACE because Hermann's bound turns $f=\sum g_if_i$ into a linear system of doubly exponential size, which can still be solved in exponential space without writing it out. ([MIT lecture notes](https://people.csail.mit.edu/madhu/ST15/scribe/lect21/lect21.pdf)) Numerical algebraic geometry began with Sommese and Wampler's 1996 paper; PHCpack was the first widely used implementation, followed a decade later by Bertini. ([Sommese–Verschelde–Wampler](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~jan/Articles/intro.pdf); [Numerical Nonlinear Algebra](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.08585v2))

### Open problems
- **Certifying numerical irreducible decomposition.** Monodromy refines an empirical partition of a witness set toward the true one, but except when it has a single part there is no proof that the true partition has been found; the trace test is a heuristic because there is "no way to certify collinearity of traces of approximate solutions". ([Numerical Nonlinear Algebra, §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.08585v2))
- **Real equilibria of the Kuramoto model.** For four fully connected oscillators there are 20 complex equilibria; 18 real ones have been constructed (after 14 and then 16), and whether all 20 can be real remains unknown. ([Numerical Nonlinear Algebra, §6](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.08585v2))
- **Betti numbers in singly exponential time (14Q30).** Basu calls it "one of the most fundamental open questions in algorithmic semi-algebraic geometry" whether all Betti numbers of a semi-algebraic set can be computed in singly exponential time; current algorithms handle only the first few. ([Basu, §5](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1409.1534))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gröbner basis (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6bner_basis): definitions, Buchberger, F4, F5, FGLM, complexity, software.
- **Reference:** [Numerical algebraic geometry (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_algebraic_geometry): homotopy continuation, witness sets, software.
- **Learn:** [O'Sullivan, Lecture notes on Gröbner bases (SDSU)](https://mosullivan.sdsu.edu/Teaching/Algebra13s/groebner.pdf): monomial orders, Dickson's lemma, S-polynomials, Buchberger's criterion.
- **Learn:** [Sommese, Verschelde and Wampler, Introduction to Numerical Algebraic Geometry](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~jan/Articles/intro.pdf): homotopies, polyhedral methods, solution components.
- **Primary:** [Bayer and Mumford, What can be computed in algebraic geometry?](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9304003): Gröbner bases, regularity, Hermann, Mayr–Meyer and Brownawell–Kollár bounds.
- **Learn:** [Kayser, Gröbner bases and their complexity (slides)](https://leokayser.github.io/assets/pdf/presentations/Groebner_Bases_and_Their_Complexity_THI.pdf): EXPSPACE-completeness of ideal membership, Dubé's bound, Kühnle–Mayr.
- **Primary:** [Bates et al., Numerical Nonlinear Algebra](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.08585v2): homotopy continuation, witness sets, certification, applications.
- **Primary:** [Basu, Algorithms in real algebraic geometry: a survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1409.1534): CAD, critical points, roadmaps, Betti numbers, open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Cox, Little and O'Shea, Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms (Springer UTM, 2015)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-16721-3): the standard introduction to computational algebraic geometry.
references.MSC 14Rxx - Affine geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
Affine algebraic geometry, as MSC 14Rxx classifies it, asks how rigid affine space $\mathbb A^n$ and other affine varieties are. Its central questions concern recognizing $\mathbb A^n$ among affine varieties, describing its automorphisms and embeddings, and deciding whether $\mathbb A^n$ is determined by algebraic data such as its cylinder $X\times\mathbb A^1$ or the Jacobian of a map. ([MSC2020 14Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Rxx)) Gupta's ICM 2022 survey centres on the Zariski Cancellation Problem and treats the related characterization, affine fibration and epimorphism (embedding) problems, using locally nilpotent derivations and the invariants built from them as a principal tool. ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736))

These questions sit between [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) and commutative algebra: an affine variety corresponds to its coordinate ring, so a question about $\mathbb A^n$ becomes a question about polynomial rings $k[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ (see [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals) and [Algebraic Varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties)). The answers often depend on the characteristic. Cancellation fails for $\mathbb A^3$ in characteristic $p$, but is open for $n\ge3$ in characteristic $0$. ([Gupta, arXiv:1208.0483](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.0483); [Zaidenberg](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9801075)) The Jacobian conjecture has a trivial counterexample $x-x^p$ in characteristic $p$, and in characteristic $0$ an explicit map in three variables, announced by Alpöge in July 2026 and so far documented in preprints and an encyclopedia entry rather than a refereed paper, has constant Jacobian determinant and is not injective; the plane case is open. ([Wikipedia: Jacobian conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture); [Pissolato, arXiv:2608.19069](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19069))

### Scope
MSC2020 14Rxx has: 14R05 classification of affine varieties; 14R10 affine spaces (automorphisms, embeddings, exotic structures, cancellation problem); 14R15 Jacobian problem (see also 13F20); 14R20 group actions on affine varieties (see also 13A50, 14L30); 14R25 affine fibrations (see also 14D06). ([MSC2020 14Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Rxx))

Neighbours: polynomial rings as rings are in [MSC 13Fxx - Arithmetic rings and other special commutative rings](node:MSC%2013Fxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20rings%20and%20other%20special%20commutative%20rings) (13F20); invariant rings in [MSC 13Axx - General commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Axx%20-%20General%20commutative%20ring%20theory) (13A50); quotients by algebraic group actions in [MSC 14Lxx - Algebraic groups](node:MSC%2014Lxx%20-%20Algebraic%20groups) (14L30); families and fibrations in general in [MSC 14Dxx - Families, fibrations in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Dxx%20-%20Families,%20fibrations%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) (14D06). ([MSC2020 14Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Rxx))

### Key concepts
- **Jacobian problem (14R15).** For a field $k$ of characteristic $0$ and a polynomial map $F:k^n\to k^n$ whose Jacobian [determinant](node:Determinant) is a nonzero constant, must $F$ have a polynomial inverse? Keller posed the $n$-dimensional question in 1939, and Kraus stated the plane case in 1884. Bass, Connell and Wright reduced the general case to cubic homogeneous maps. For $n=2$, computer-assisted work excludes counterexamples of degree at most $100$. ([Wikipedia: Jacobian conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture)) For $n\ge3$ a counterexample has been reported. Alpöge's map $F=(f_1,f_2,f_3)$ on $\mathbb C^3$, with $f_1=(1+xy)^3z+y^2(1+xy)(4+3xy)$, $f_2=y+3x(1+xy)^2z+3xy^2(4+3xy)$, $f_3=2x-3x^2y-x^3z$, has Jacobian determinant $-2$. It sends $(0,0,-\tfrac14)$, $(1,-\tfrac32,\tfrac{13}2)$ and $(-1,\tfrac32,\tfrac{13}2)$ all to $(-\tfrac14,0,0)$, so it has no polynomial inverse; adding identity coordinates gives maps in every dimension $n\ge3$. ([Pissolato, arXiv:2608.19069, §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19069)) Alpöge presented the map on 19 July 2026, not in a journal paper, and its correctness is a finite computation that any computer algebra system can check. ([Wikipedia: Jacobian conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture)) This note's audit (2026-11-12) recomputed it symbolically with SymPy: $\det JF=-2$ identically, and the three points all map to $(-\tfrac14,0,0)$. Van den Essen's preprint derives the same map, up to linear coordinate changes, by elementary means. ([van den Essen, arXiv:2609.17795](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17795)) No refereed publication or formal expert statement on the example was found; its status rests on the published formula, which is directly checkable. Adjamagbo and van den Essen gave the chain $\mathrm{JC}_{2n}\Rightarrow\mathrm{PC}_n\Rightarrow\mathrm{DC}_n\Rightarrow\mathrm{JC}_n$ linking the Jacobian, Poisson and Dixmier conjectures, so the counterexample also refutes the Dixmier conjecture for the Weyl algebra $A_n$ when $n\ge3$. ([Wikipedia: Jacobian conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture))
- **Zariski Cancellation Problem (14R10).** Does $B[X]\cong k[X_1,\dots,X_{n+1}]$ imply $B\cong k[X_1,\dots,X_n]$? Abhyankar, Eakin and Heinzer settled transcendence degree one. In dimension two, cancellation holds in characteristic $0$ (Fujita, Miyanishi–Sugie), over perfect fields (Russell), and over all fields (Bhatwadekar–Gupta). ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736)) Gupta showed that it fails for $\mathbb A^3$ over every field of positive characteristic. Her counterexample is an Asanuma threefold $A$ with $A\not\cong k[X_1,X_2,X_3]$ but $A[T]\cong k[X_1,\dots,X_4]$. ([Gupta, arXiv:1208.0483](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.0483)) She later gave counterexamples in every dimension $\ge3$. ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736))
- **Embeddings and the Abhyankar–Moh–Suzuki theorem (14R10).** Every embedding of the complex line in $\mathbb C^2$ extends to an automorphism of the plane (Abhyankar–Moh, *J. reine angew. Math.* 1975), and the same holds over any algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$. ([Wikipedia: Abhyankar–Moh theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhyankar%E2%80%93Moh_theorem)) Algebraically, every epimorphism $k[X,Y]\to k[T]$ in characteristic $0$ is rectifiable. In positive characteristic, non-rectifiable epimorphisms exist (Segre, Nagata). Asanuma's construction turns such epimorphisms into cancellation counterexamples in positive characteristic; in characteristic $0$ it yields only potential candidates. ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736))
- **Exotic affine spaces (14R10).** An exotic $\mathbb C^n$ is a smooth affine variety diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^{2n}$ but not isomorphic to $\mathbb C^n$. By Ramanujam's theorem a smooth contractible affine surface is $\mathbb C^2$ exactly when it is simply connected at infinity, so there is no exotic $\mathbb C^2$. The Russell cubic $x+x^2y+z^2+t^3=0$ in $\mathbb C^4$ is an exotic $\mathbb C^3$. ([Zaidenberg, Lectures on exotic algebraic structures](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9801075)) Makar-Limanov's invariant distinguishes it from $\mathbb A^3$: $\mathrm{ML}=\mathbb C[x]$ for the cubic but $\mathbb C$ for $\mathbb A^3$. ([Wikipedia: Koras–Russell cubic threefold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koras%E2%80%93Russell_cubic_threefold)) Dubouloz showed that the cylinder over the cubic has trivial Makar-Limanov invariant. ([Dubouloz, arXiv:0807.4085](https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.4085))
- **Locally nilpotent derivations (14R20).** A derivation $D$ of $B$ is locally nilpotent if each element is killed by some power of $D$. The Makar-Limanov invariant $\mathrm{ML}(B)$ is the intersection of the kernels of all locally nilpotent derivations, and the Derksen invariant $\mathrm{DK}(B)$ is the subring generated by those kernels. ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736)) Derivations themselves are the subject of [MSC 13Nxx - Differential algebra](node:MSC%2013Nxx%20-%20Differential%20algebra).
- **Linearization and automorphism groups (14R20).** Kaliman, Koras, Makar-Limanov and Russell proved that every $\mathbb C^*$-action on $\mathbb C^3$ is linearizable. The Koras–Russell threefolds were the test cases. ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736); [Wikipedia: Koras–Russell cubic threefold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koras%E2%80%93Russell_cubic_threefold)) Automorphism groups of affine varieties carry the structure of ind-groups, introduced by Shafarevich in 1965. In this setting, Shestakov and Umirbaev's non-tame automorphisms of affine $3$-space give a strict closed subgroup of a connected ind-group with the same Lie algebra. ([Furter–Kraft, arXiv:1809.04175](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.04175))
- **Affine fibrations (14R25).** Is an $\mathbb A^n$-fibration over a regular Noetherian domain $R$ necessarily $\mathrm{Sym}_R(Q)$ for a projective $R$-module $Q$? For $n=1$ the answer is yes (Kambayashi, Miyanishi, Wright; Dutta). For $n=2$ over a one-dimensional ring containing $\mathbb Q$ it is yes (Sathaye). With positive-characteristic residue fields it is no for $n=2$ (Asanuma in dimension one, Gupta in higher dimensions). ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736))

### History
Kraus stated the plane Jacobian problem in 1884, and Keller posed the general question in 1939. The plane case has a long record of false proofs. ([Wikipedia: Jacobian conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture)) Abhyankar and Moh published their embedding theorem in 1975. ([Wikipedia: Abhyankar–Moh theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhyankar%E2%80%93Moh_theorem)) Shafarevich introduced ind-varieties and ind-groups in 1965. ([Furter–Kraft, arXiv:1809.04175](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.04175)) Gupta settled the cancellation problem in positive characteristic in 2012–2013 (to appear in *Inventiones*, per the arXiv record). ([Gupta, arXiv:1208.0483](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.0483)) Alpöge presented an explicit three-variable counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture on 19 July 2026. ([Wikipedia: Jacobian conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture)) Pissolato's August 2026 preprint reproduces the map, but gives no bibliographic reference for it. ([Pissolato, arXiv:2608.19069](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19069)) Freudenburg's monograph on locally nilpotent derivations appeared in Springer's Encyclopaedia of Mathematical Sciences in 2017. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-55350-3))

### Open problems
- **Plane Jacobian conjecture.** The case $n=2$ "is still an open problem"; the 2026 counterexample concerns only $n\ge3$. ([Pissolato, arXiv:2608.19069](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19069); [Wikipedia: Jacobian conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture)) Pissolato shows that for every $n$ the conjecture holds on a nonempty Zariski-open dense set of polynomial maps. He leaves open how far that set can be enlarged. ([Pissolato, arXiv:2608.19069](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.19069))
- **Cancellation in characteristic zero.** Gupta calls the Zariski Cancellation Problem in characteristic $0$ "still a challenging problem." In particular, whether the cylinder over the Russell cubic is isomorphic to $\mathbb C^4$ is "still open." ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736)) Zaidenberg also states cancellation for $n\ge3$ as open. ([Zaidenberg](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9801075))
- **Epimorphism problem (Abhyankar–Sathaye conjecture).** In characteristic $0$, if $f\in k[X,Y,Z]$ satisfies $k[X,Y,Z]/(f)\cong k^{[2]}$, must $f$ be a coordinate? Gupta records this case as open in general, with special cases settled by Sathaye, Russell, Wright and Das–Dutta. Her Question 2 asks whether Asanuma's ring $B$ over $\mathbb R$, which satisfies $B^{[1]}\cong\mathbb R^{[5]}$, is itself $\mathbb R^{[4]}$: a yes would give non-linearizable $\mathbb R^*$-actions on affine $4$-space, a no a counterexample to cancellation. ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736))
- **$\mathbb A^2$-fibrations.** For $n=2$ over a two-dimensional regular ring containing $\mathbb Q$, the affine fibration problem "is an open problem." ([Gupta, ICM 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.14736))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Jacobian conjecture (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture): statement, reductions, related conjectures.
- **Learn:** [Zaidenberg, Lectures on Exotic Algebraic Structures on Affine Spaces (arXiv:math/9801075)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9801075): lecture courses at Bochum and Toulouse on exotic $\mathbb C^n$ and cancellation.
- **Primary:** [Gupta, The Zariski Cancellation Problem and related problems in Affine Algebraic Geometry (ICM 2022, arXiv:2208.14736)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.14736): survey of cancellation and the related characterization, epimorphism and affine fibration problems, with open questions.
- **Primary:** [Gupta, A counter-example to the Cancellation Problem for $\mathbb A^3$ in characteristic $p$ (arXiv:1208.0483)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.0483).
- **Primary:** [Furter–Kraft, On the geometry of the automorphism groups of affine varieties (arXiv:1809.04175)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.04175): survey of ind-groups and automorphisms.
- **Further reading:** [Freudenburg, Algebraic Theory of Locally Nilpotent Derivations (Springer, 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-55350-3): monograph on locally nilpotent derivations.
references.MSC 14Txx - Tropical geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 14T, "Tropical geometry", is the part of [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry) that studies tropical varieties: polyhedral shadows of algebraic varieties obtained through a valuation, and the piecewise-linear geometry over the tropical semiring $(\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\},\min,+)$. ([MSC2020 14Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Txx); [Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry)) Tropical varieties are weighted polyhedral complexes, and plane tropical curves are dual to subdivisions of the Newton polygon of the defining polynomial, so they retain combinatorial information about the [algebraic varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties) they come from. ([Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry); [Brugallé–Itenberg–Mikhalkin–Shaw](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05950)) The concept note [Tropical Varieties](node:Tropical%20Varieties) treats the basic objects.

Interest in the field grew in the late 1990s through work of Kontsevich and Mikhalkin, and Speyer and Sturmfels's Gröbner-theoretic approach shows that the tropical variety of an ideal is a polyhedral subcomplex of the Gröbner fan; the subject now links algebraic geometry with polyhedral [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics), matroid theory, auction design and phylogenetics. ([Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry); [Speyer–Sturmfels, Tropical Grassmannian](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0304218); [Speyer–Sturmfels, Tropical Mathematics](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0408099))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 14Txx (see also 12K10, 14M25, 14N10, 52B20) lists 14T10 foundations of tropical geometry and relations with algebra (for algebraic aspects see 15A80); 14T15 combinatorial aspects of tropical varieties; 14T20 geometric aspects of tropical varieties; 14T25 arithmetic aspects of tropical varieties; 14T90 applications of tropical geometry; 14T99. ([MSC2020 14Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Txx))

- **Neighbour 14M25 / 52B20.** The entry cross-refers to 14M25 ([Toric Varieties](node:Toric%20Varieties)) and to 52B20 in [MSC 52Bxx - Polytopes and polyhedra](node:MSC%2052Bxx%20-%20Polytopes%20and%20polyhedra); plane tropical curves are dual to subdivisions of Newton [polygons](node:Polytopes). ([MSC2020 14Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Txx); [Brugallé–Itenberg–Mikhalkin–Shaw](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05950))
- **Neighbour 14N10.** The entry cross-refers to 14N10 in [MSC 14Nxx - Projective and enumerative algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Nxx%20-%20Projective%20and%20enumerative%20algebraic%20geometry). ([MSC2020 14Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Txx))
- **Neighbour 15A80 / 12K10.** 14T10 sends algebraic aspects of its foundations to 15A80, and the entry cross-refers to 12K10, semifields (a generalisation of fields; compare [semirings](node:Semirings)). ([MSC2020 14Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Txx); [MSC2020 12Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=12Kxx))

### Key concepts
- **Tropical hypersurfaces.** With $a\oplus b=\min(a,b)$ and $a\odot b=a+b$, a tropical polynomial is a minimum of finitely many affine-linear functions with integer slopes, hence continuous, concave and piecewise linear; its tropical hypersurface is the locus where the minimum is attained at least twice. Unique factorisation fails for tropical polynomials in two or more variables. ([Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry); [Speyer–Sturmfels, Tropical Mathematics](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0408099))
- **Fundamental theorem (14T10).** Let $K$ be the algebraic closure of $\mathbb C(t)$, with valuation $\deg$ given by order of vanishing at $t=0$, and let $I\subseteq K[x_1^{\pm1},\dots,x_n^{\pm1}]$ be an ideal. Then the following subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ coincide: (a) the closure of $\{(\deg u_1,\dots,\deg u_n): u\in V(I)\}$; (b) the intersection of the tropical hypersurfaces of $\mathrm{trop}(f)$ for $f\in I$; (c) the set of $w$ such that the initial ideal $\mathrm{in}_w(I)$ contains no monomial. This common set is the tropical variety $\mathcal T(I)$, and it is cut out by the finitely many tropical hypersurfaces of a universal Gröbner basis ([Gröbner Bases](node:Gröbner%20Bases)). Variants appeared earlier, with proof in work of Einsiedler, Kapranov, Lind and Ward; Wikipedia calls the equivalence the Fundamental Theorem of Tropical Geometry. ([Speyer–Sturmfels, Thm 2.1, Cor 2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0304218); [Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry))
- **Structure: Bieri–Groves and balancing (14T15, 14T20).** If $I$ is prime and $K[x]/I$ has Krull dimension $r$, then $\mathcal T(I)$ is a pure $r$-dimensional polyhedral complex (Bieri–Groves). Tropical varieties carry weights making them balanced (zero tension); in the plane every balanced rational graph is a tropical curve (Mikhalkin). Amoebas $\mathrm{Log}_t(C_t)$ of a family of complex curves whose coefficients behave like $\gamma\,t^{a}$ converge to the tropical curve of the tropicalised polynomial. ([Speyer–Sturmfels, Thm 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0304218); [Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry); [Brugallé–Itenberg–Mikhalkin–Shaw, Thms 2.9, 2.12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05950))
- **Mikhalkin's correspondence theorem (14T20, 14N10).** For $3d-1+g$ points in general position in $\mathbb R^2$, the number of irreducible nodal tropical curves of degree $d$ and genus $g$ through them, each counted with multiplicity the product over trivalent vertices of twice the area of the dual triangle, equals the number $N_{d,g}$ of complex plane curves of degree $d$ and genus $g$ through $3d-1+g$ general points; with real multiplicities and $g=0$ it gives Welschinger invariants $W_d$. For cubics this recovers $N_{3,0}=12$ and $W_3=8$. ([Brugallé–Itenberg–Mikhalkin–Shaw, Thm 4.11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05950); [Mikhalkin](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312530))
- **Tropical Riemann–Roch (14T20).** For a connected finite multigraph $G$ without loops, of genus $g=|E|-|V|+1$, with canonical divisor $K=\sum_v(\deg v-2)(v)$ and Baker–Norine rank $r$ defined via chip-firing, every divisor $D$ satisfies $r(D)-r(K-D)=\deg D+1-g$, mirroring Riemann–Roch for [algebraic curves](node:Algebraic%20Curves); tropical curves are closely tied to graphs and chip-firing, and Riemann–Roch has a tropical counterpart. ([Baker–Norine, Thm 1.12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0608360); [Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry))
- **Tropical Grassmannians and matroids (14T15).** Tropicalising the Plücker ideal gives the tropical Grassmannian, which parametrises tropical linear spaces; $\mathcal G_{2,n}$ is the space of phylogenetic trees of Billera–Holmes–Vogtmann, and $\mathcal G'''_{3,6}$ (the image of $\mathcal G_{3,6}$ modulo its lineality space, intersected with the unit sphere) is a 3-dimensional simplicial complex with 65 vertices, 550 edges, 1395 triangles and 1035 tetrahedra (see [Grassmannians](node:Grassmannians)). When all Plücker coordinates are $0$ or $\infty$, the tropical linear space is the Bergman fan of a matroid ([Matroids and Geometric Closure](node:Matroids%20and%20Geometric%20Closure)). Adiprasito, Huh and Katz proved hard Lefschetz and Hodge–Riemann relations for a ring attached to any matroid, settling the Heron–Rota–Welsh conjecture that the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial are log-concave. ([Speyer–Sturmfels, Thm 3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0304218); [Tropical Mathematics](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0408099); [Adiprasito–Huh–Katz](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.02888))

### History
The word "tropical" was coined by French mathematicians in honour of Imre Simon; Victor Maslov introduced early tropical ideas, and interest grew in the late 1990s through Kontsevich and Mikhalkin. ([Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry)) The dimension theorem is due to Bieri and Groves, and an alternative proof uses Gröbner basis methods; Speyer and Sturmfels's 2003 paper on tropical Grassmannians gave a self-contained proof of the fundamental theorem, and Mikhalkin's correspondence theorem for plane curves was first announced in 2002 (math.AG/0209253). ([Speyer–Sturmfels](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0304218); [Mikhalkin](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312530)) Baker and Norine's graph Riemann–Roch appeared in 2006 and Adiprasito–Huh–Katz in 2015. ([Baker–Norine](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608360); [Adiprasito–Huh–Katz](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.02888))

### Open problems
- **Complex and real analogues of tropical invariants.** According to these 2015 lecture notes, tropical enumeration produces many invariants, such as tropical Welschinger invariants in arbitrary genus and Block–Göttsche refined multiplicities, and the complex or real analogues of most of them are unknown. ([Brugallé–Itenberg–Mikhalkin–Shaw, §4.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.05950))
- **Quadratically enriched counts.** A 2026 survey states that developing effective means of computing quadratically enriched counts $N_{\mathbb A^1,d}(\sigma)$ of rational plane curves still poses challenges, that a full correspondence theorem for such counts with point conditions over quadratic field extensions has yet to be established, and that tropical counts with point conditions over extensions of degree greater than two are a task for further research. ([Jaramillo Puentes–Markwig–Pauli–Röhrle, §7](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.14216v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Tropical geometry (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry): conventions, definitions of tropical varieties, history, applications.
- **Learn:** [Brugallé, Itenberg, Mikhalkin and Shaw, Brief introduction to tropical geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.05950): Gökova lecture notes on tropical curves, amoebas, patchworking, enumeration, tropical homology.
- **Learn:** [Speyer and Sturmfels, Tropical Mathematics](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0408099): elementary introduction with research suggestions.
- **Primary:** [Speyer and Sturmfels, The Tropical Grassmannian](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0304218): fundamental theorem, Bieri–Groves, tropical Grassmannians and trees.
- **Primary:** [Mikhalkin, Enumerative tropical algebraic geometry in $\mathbb R^2$](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312530): the correspondence theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Maclagan and Sturmfels, Introduction to Tropical Geometry (AMS GSM 161, 2015)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/161): the standard graduate text.
references.MSC 15 - Linear and multilinear algebra;:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 15 classifies linear algebra, multilinear algebra and matrix theory. As a research area it is less about the axioms of [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) than about the fine structure of matrices: canonical forms, eigenvalue and singular-value inequalities, inverse and completion problems, linear preservers, structured matrix classes (nonnegative, Hadamard, Toeplitz, sign-pattern, random), and tensors and their ranks. ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx); [MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))

Several central results of the field are characterisation theorems: which diagonals, which spectra, or which sums of spectra a matrix class can have. The Schur–Horn theorem and Horn's problem on sums of Hermitian matrices are the model cases, the latter settled by Knutson and Tao's 1998 proof of the saturation conjecture, which rests on the [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of $GL_n$. ([Schur–Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur%E2%80%93Horn_theorem); [Knutson–Tao](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807160))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides the field into [MSC 15Axx - Basic linear algebra](node:MSC%2015Axx%20-%20Basic%20linear%20algebra) and [MSC 15Bxx - Special matrices](node:MSC%2015Bxx%20-%20Special%20matrices). ([MSC2020 15-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15-XX))

- **15Axx** covers rank and linear dependence (15A03), linear and semilinear transformations (15A04), generalized inverses (15A09, 15A10), conditioning (15A12, see also 65F35), determinants, permanents and traces (15A15), matrix functions (15A16), eigenvalues and singular values (15A18), Jordan and other canonical forms (15A20, 15A21), matrix pencils (15A22), factorizations (15A23), matrix equations (15A24), commutativity (15A27), inverse problems (15A29), eigenvalue and other matrix inequalities (15A39, 15A42, 15A45), norms and numerical range (15A60), quadratic and bilinear forms (15A63, "see mainly 11Exx"), [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras) and spinors (15A66, 15A67), multilinear algebra and tensor calculus (15A69), invariants (15A72), exterior algebra (15A75), max-plus algebra (15A80), matrix completion (15A83) and linear preserver problems (15A86). ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx))
- **15Bxx** covers Toeplitz and Cauchy matrices (15B05), orthogonal matrices (15B10), matrix [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) (15B30), matrices over special rings (15B33), Boolean and Hadamard matrices (15B34), sign patterns (15B35), integer matrices (15B36, see also 11C20), positive matrices and cones (15B48), stochastic matrices (15B51), random matrices in their algebraic aspects (15B52; probabilistic aspects go to 60B20) and Hermitian-type matrices (15B57). ([MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))

Neighbours, from the cross-references in the entry: conditioning and matrix norms point to numerical analysis (65F35, 65J05; see [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra)); quadratic forms go mainly to 11Exx and integer matrices also to 11C20; algebraic systems of matrices point to 16S50, 20Gxx and 20Hxx; matrix pencils point to 47A56; random matrices in their probabilistic aspects go to 60B20. ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx); [MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Jordan normal form (15A20).** Let $V$ be finite-dimensional over a field $K$ and $T:V\to V$ linear. A basis in which $T$ is block diagonal with Jordan blocks (eigenvalue $\lambda$ on the diagonal, $1$ on the superdiagonal) exists if and only if the characteristic polynomial of $T$ splits over $K$, which always holds for algebraically closed $K$; the form is unique up to the order of the blocks. See [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) and [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors). ([Jordan normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form)) Over a perfect field every operator has a Jordan–Chevalley decomposition $T=D+N$ with $D$ semisimple, $N$ nilpotent and $DN=ND$; over an imperfect field it can fail, e.g. multiplication by $x$ on $k[X]/(X^p-a)^2$ with $a$ not a $p$-th power. ([Jordan–Chevalley decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan%E2%80%93Chevalley_decomposition))
- **Spectral theorem (15A18, 15B57).** A complex square matrix $A$ is normal ($A^*A=AA^*$) if and only if $A=UDU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $D$ diagonal; $A$ is Hermitian exactly when, in addition, the diagonal of $D$ is real, and real symmetric matrices are orthogonally diagonalizable. The infinite-dimensional versions belong to [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory). ([Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))
- **Perron–Frobenius theorem (15B48, 15B51).** If $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix with all entries positive, its spectral radius $r$ is a simple eigenvalue, strictly larger in modulus than every other eigenvalue, with an eigenvector whose entries are all positive (Perron, 1907). If $A$ is only nonnegative but irreducible (its digraph is strongly connected) with period $h$, then $r>0$ is a simple eigenvalue with positive left and right eigenvectors, and exactly $h$ eigenvalues have modulus $r$, namely $r$ times the $h$-th roots of unity (Frobenius, 1912). This underlies the convergence theory of finite [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains). ([Perron–Frobenius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem))
- **Schur–Horn theorem (15A42).** For real non-increasing sequences $d$ and $\lambda$ of length $N$, there is a Hermitian matrix with diagonal $d$ and eigenvalues $\lambda$ if and only if $\sum_{i\le n} d_i\le\sum_{i\le n}\lambda_i$ for $1\le n<N$, with equality for $n=N$; that is, $d$ is majorized by $\lambda$. ([Schur–Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur%E2%80%93Horn_theorem))
- **Horn's problem (15A42).** Given the spectra of Hermitian matrices $A$ and $B$, which spectra can $A+B$ have? Horn conjectured an answer in 1962. Knutson and Tao proved the saturation conjecture for Littlewood–Richardson coefficients of $GL_n$ using honeycombs; combined with Klyachko's results this determines which Littlewood–Richardson coefficients are positive and yields Horn's conjecture. ([Knutson–Tao 1998](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807160); [Knutson–Tao survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0009048))
- **Tensor rank and border rank (15A69).** The rank of a tensor in $V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes V_k$ is the least $R$ such that it is a sum of $R$ decomposable tensors; its border rank is the least $r$ such that it is a limit of tensors of rank at most $r$. For matrices the two agree, but for order three and higher they may differ: for suitable vectors $u,v$ the tensor $u\otimes u\otimes v+u\otimes v\otimes u+v\otimes u\otimes u$ has rank $3$ but is a limit of rank-$2$ tensors, so its border rank is $2$. Computing tensor rank is NP-hard. See [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra). ([Tensor rank decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition))
- **Matrix multiplication exponent.** $\omega$ is the least real number such that two $n\times n$ matrices can be multiplied with $n^{\omega+o(1)}$ field operations; trivially $\omega\ge 2$. For bilinear algorithms the number of multiplications needed is the tensor rank of the matrix multiplication tensor, and for $2\times 2$ matrices seven multiplications are necessary, so Strassen's algorithm is optimal there. ([Matrix multiplication complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication))
- **Hadamard matrices (15B34).** A Hadamard matrix is a square $\pm1$ matrix with mutually orthogonal rows; its order must be $1$, $2$ or a multiple of $4$. For complex $M$ with $|M_{ij}|\le 1$, $|\det M|\le n^{n/2}$, with equality for a real matrix exactly when it is Hadamard; see [Determinant](node:Determinant). ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix))

### History
Leibniz used determinants to solve linear systems in 1693 and Cramer gave his rule in 1750; Grassmann's *Theory of Extension* (1844) contained foundational multilinear ideas; Sylvester introduced the word "matrix" in 1848, Cayley matrix multiplication and inverses in 1856, and Peano the modern definition of a vector space in 1888. ([Linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra)) Perron's theorem dates from 1907 and Frobenius's extension from 1912. ([Perron–Frobenius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem)) Horn posed his eigenvalue conjecture in 1962, and Knutson and Tao's saturation proof was posted in 1998. ([Knutson–Tao 1998](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807160))

### Open problems
- **Hadamard conjecture.** A Hadamard matrix of order $4k$ is conjectured to exist for every positive integer $k$; the conjecture is unsolved. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix))
- **Nonnegative inverse eigenvalue problem (NIEP).** Which lists of $n$ complex numbers are the spectrum of an $n\times n$ entrywise nonnegative matrix? The survey of Johnson, Marijuán, Paparella and Pisonero calls it long-standing and perhaps the most prominent problem in matrix analysis; it is settled for $n\le 3$, $n=4$ was handled by Meehan, and $n\ge 5$ remains open, as do the real and symmetric variants. ([The NIEP](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.10992); [arXiv abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.10992))
- **Is $\omega=2$?** Whether the matrix multiplication exponent equals $2$ is a major open question. ([Matrix multiplication complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication))
- **Tensor ranks.** The maximal rank of tensors in a given tensor space is unknown in general, and the Abo–Ottaviani–Peterson conjecture on generic ranks is proved only in special cases. ([Tensor rank decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition))
- **Crouzeix's conjecture.** For every complex square matrix $A$ and polynomial $p$, $\|p(A)\|\le 2\sup_{z\in W(A)}|p(z)|$, where $W(A)$ is the numerical range. Crouzeix and Palencia proved that $W(A)$ is a $(1+\sqrt2)$-spectral set, i.e. the bound with constant $1+\sqrt2$. In August 2026 Lorist and Schwenninger posted a claimed proof of the constant $2$, and Wikipedia reports an earlier independent preprint claim; neither has been refereed, so the conjecture's status awaits confirmation. ([Crouzeix–Palencia](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.00668); [Lorist–Schwenninger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03841); [Crouzeix's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crouzeix%27s_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra): orientation and history of the subject.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.06, Linear Algebra (Strang)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06-linear-algebra-spring-2010/): lectures on systems, vector spaces, determinants, eigenvalues, similarity and positive definite matrices.
- **Primary:** [Johnson, Marijuán, Paparella, Pisonero, The NIEP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.10992): research survey of the nonnegative inverse eigenvalue problem and its variants; [Knutson–Tao, Honeycombs and sums of Hermitian matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0009048): survey of the resolution of Horn's conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis (2nd ed., CUP 2012)](https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/matrix-analysis/FDA3627DC2B9F5C3DF2FD8C3CC136B48): standard graduate text organised around canonical forms; [Bhatia, Matrix Analysis (GTM, Springer 1997)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0653-8): graduate text on matrix inequalities.
references.MSC 15Axx - Basic linear algebra:
## Reference
### Overview
Alongside vector spaces, linear maps and canonical forms, MSC 15Axx covers eigenvalue and singular-value inequalities, matrix equations, matrix functions, factorizations, norms and numerical range, generalized inverses, multilinear and tensor algebra, Clifford algebras, max-plus algebra, matrix completion, and linear preserver problems. ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx))

The area has deep links outside linear algebra. Horn's 1962 conjecture on the spectra of sums of Hermitian matrices was settled through the representation theory of $\mathrm{GL}(n)$: Knutson and Tao proved the saturation conjecture for Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, extending results of Klyachko. ([Knutson–Tao, arXiv:math/9807160](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807160); [Knutson–Tao, Honeycombs and sums of Hermitian matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0009048)) The tensor rank of the matrix multiplication tensor is the minimum number of multiplications in a bilinear algorithm, which ties 15A69 to complexity theory. ([Wikipedia: Computational complexity of matrix multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication))

### Scope
MSC2020 15Axx subcodes, grouped:
- **Spaces and maps:** 15A03 vector spaces, linear dependence, rank, lineability; 15A04 linear and semilinear transformations; 15A06 linear equations; 15A09–15A10 generalized inverses; 15A12 conditioning; 15A15 determinants, permanents, traces. ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx))
- **Spectra and forms:** 15A18 eigenvalues, singular values and eigenvectors; 15A20 diagonalization and Jordan forms; 15A21 canonical forms and classification; 15A22 matrix pencils; 15A42 inequalities involving eigenvalues and eigenvectors; 15A45 other matrix inequalities; 15A60 norms of matrices and numerical range; 15A63 quadratic and bilinear forms (see mainly 11Exx). ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx))
- **Equations and functions:** 15A16 matrix exponential and similar functions; 15A23 factorization; 15A24 matrix equations and identities; 15A27 commutativity; 15A29 inverse problems; 15A30 algebraic systems of matrices; 15A39 linear inequalities; 15A54 matrices over function rings. ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx))
- **Multilinear algebra and other structures:** 15A66–15A67 Clifford algebras and spinors and their applications; 15A69 multilinear algebra and tensor calculus; 15A72 vector and tensor algebra and invariants; 15A75 exterior algebra; 15A78 other algebras built from modules; 15A80 max-plus algebra; 15A83 matrix completion; 15A86 linear preserver problems. ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx))

Neighbours: the sibling subfield is [MSC 15Bxx - Special matrices](node:MSC%2015Bxx%20-%20Special%20matrices); conditioning and computation are cross-referenced to 65F35; matrix pencils to 47A56; quadratic forms mainly to 11Exx; invariants to 13A50 and 14L24. ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx)) The parent map is [MSC 15 - Linear and multilinear algebra; matrix theory](node:MSC%2015%20-%20Linear%20and%20multilinear%20algebra;%20matrix%20theory).

### Key concepts
- **Weyl's inequalities (15A42).** Let $A,B$ be $n\times n$ Hermitian with eigenvalues ordered $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n$. If $i+j\le n+1$, then $\lambda_{i+j-1}(A+B)\le\lambda_i(A)+\lambda_j(B)$. Consequently $|\lambda_k(A+B)-\lambda_k(A)|\le\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, so the spectrum is stable under perturbation. For singular values, $|\sigma_k(M+\Delta)-\sigma_k(M)|\le\sigma_1(\Delta)$. ([Wikipedia: Weyl's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl%27s_inequality)) This is the matrix case of the perturbation theory in [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory), built on [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors) of self-adjoint maps on [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces).
- **Schur–Horn theorem (15A42).** A vector $d$ is the diagonal of a Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda$ if and only if $d$ lies in the [convex hull](node:Convex%20Hull) of the permutations of $\lambda$. Equivalently, $d$ is majorized by $\lambda$: with both sorted decreasingly, partial sums of $d$ are at most those of $\lambda$, and the totals agree. Schur proved necessity in 1923 and Horn sufficiency in 1954. ([Wikipedia: Schur–Horn theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur%E2%80%93Horn_theorem))
- **Horn's problem and saturation (15A42).** Which spectra can $A+B$ have, given the spectra of Hermitian $A$ and $B$? Horn's 1962 conjecture characterized them. Knutson and Tao's honeycomb model of the [polytopes](node:Polytopes) computing Littlewood–Richardson coefficients (the tensor product rule for $\mathrm{GL}(n)$) proved the saturation conjecture. Extending results of Klyachko, this gives a complete answer to which Littlewood–Richardson coefficients are positive and implies Horn's conjecture. ([Knutson–Tao, arXiv:math/9807160](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807160)) Their survey explains the proof through honeycombs and the [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of $U(n)$. ([Knutson–Tao, arXiv:math/0009048](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0009048))
- **Sylvester and Lyapunov equations (15A24).** For $A\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}$, $B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $AX+XB=C$ has a unique solution for every $C$ exactly when $A$ and $-B$ have no common eigenvalue. Vectorizing gives an $mn\times mn$ linear system, and the Bartels–Stewart algorithm solves it in $O(n^3)$ operations via Schur forms. The Lyapunov equation is a special case. Roth's removal rule says that $\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&B\end{pmatrix}$ are similar if and only if $AX-XB=C$ is solvable. ([Wikipedia: Sylvester equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester_equation))
- **Singular value decomposition (15A18, 15A23, 15A60).** Every complex $m\times n$ matrix factors as $M=U\Sigma V^*$ with $U,V$ unitary and $\Sigma$ rectangular diagonal with nonnegative entries. By Eckart–Young, keeping the $t$ largest singular values gives the best rank-$t$ approximation in the Frobenius norm. ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)) For a real matrix $A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}$, the columns of $V$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A^{\mathsf T}A$, and the squares $\sigma^2$ of the nonzero singular values are the nonzero eigenvalues of $A^{\mathsf T}A$ and $AA^{\mathsf T}$. ([MIT 18.065, Lecture 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-065-matrix-methods-in-data-analysis-signal-processing-and-machine-learning-spring-2018/resources/lecture-6-singular-value-decomposition-svd/)) Computation is the subject of [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra).
- **Tensor rank (15A69).** The rank of a tensor is the least $R$ such that it is a sum of $R$ rank-one tensors. Computing it is NP-hard. Unlike matrices, higher-order tensors can have border rank smaller than rank, so best low-rank approximations may not exist. Rank also depends on the field: a real tensor can have real rank $3$ but complex rank $2$. Matrices of rank above $1$ are generically not identifiable, whereas for tensors of order above $2$ generic tensors of rank below the generic rank are conjectured to be identifiable apart from a list of exceptions, which is proven for small spaces. ([Wikipedia: Tensor rank decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition)) See [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra).
- **Canonical forms and classical structure (15A20, 15A21, 15A66).** Jordan's canonical form appeared in 1870, for linear substitutions over a finite field of prime order. Frobenius introduced rank in 1878 and proved in general that a matrix satisfies its characteristic equation. ([MacTutor: Matrices and determinants](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Matrices_and_determinants/)) See [Cayley–Hamilton Theorem](node:Cayley–Hamilton%20Theorem), [Determinant](node:Determinant), [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices), [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces), and, for 15A66, [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras).

### History
Sylvester introduced the word "matrix" in 1850. Cayley's 1858 *Memoir on the theory of matrices* gave the first abstract definition of a matrix algebra with addition, multiplication and inverses. It proved the $2\times2$ case of the Cayley–Hamilton theorem and reported checking the $3\times3$ case without a formal proof. ([MacTutor: Matrices and determinants](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Matrices_and_determinants/)) Beltrami (1873) and Jordan (1874) found the singular value decomposition independently, and Eckart and Young proved it for rectangular complex matrices in 1936. ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)) Sylvester introduced his matrix equation in 1884. ([Wikipedia: Sylvester equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester_equation)) Horn's conjecture dates from 1962. Knutson and Tao's proof of saturation, which with Klyachko's results implies it, was posted to arXiv in 1998. ([Knutson–Tao, arXiv:math/9807160](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807160))

### Open problems
- **Exponent of matrix multiplication.** The exponent $\omega$ is the least real number such that two $n\times n$ matrices can be multiplied with $n^{\omega+o(1)}$ field operations. Known bounds give $2\le\omega<2.371177$, and whether $\omega=2$ is "a major open question." For bilinear algorithms, the minimal number of multiplications is the tensor rank of the matrix multiplication tensor. ([Wikipedia: Computational complexity of matrix multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication))
- **Maximal tensor rank.** The maximum rank of tensors of a given format is unknown in general. For real $2\times2\times2$ tensors, $2$ and $3$ are both typical ranks (each occurs on a Euclidean-open set), the generic rank is $2$, and the maximum rank is $3$; for complex $2\times2\times2$ tensors the generic rank is $2$. ([Wikipedia: Tensor rank decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Weyl's inequality (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl%27s_inequality): eigenvalue and singular-value perturbation bounds.
- **Reference:** [Tensor rank decomposition (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition): rank, border rank, identifiability.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.065 (Strang), Lecture 6: Singular Value Decomposition](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-065-matrix-methods-in-data-analysis-signal-processing-and-machine-learning-spring-2018/resources/lecture-6-singular-value-decomposition-svd/): university lecture on the SVD.
- **Primary:** [Knutson and Tao, The honeycomb model of GL(n) tensor products I: proof of the saturation conjecture (arXiv:math/9807160)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807160): resolution of Horn's problem.
- **Primary:** [Bhatia, Matrix Analysis (Springer GTM, 1997)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0653-8): graduate text in Springer's GTM series.
- **Further reading:** [Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed. (CUP, 2012)](https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/matrix-analysis/FDA3627DC2B9F5C3DF2FD8C3CC136B48): standard advanced matrix text organized around canonical forms.
references.MSC 15Bxx - Special matrices:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 15B, "Special matrices", is the part of [MSC 15 - Linear and multilinear algebra; matrix theory](node:MSC%2015%20-%20Linear%20and%20multilinear%20algebra;%20matrix%20theory) devoted to families of matrices singled out by a structural constraint: on the pattern of entries (Toeplitz, Cauchy, sign patterns), on the entries' values (Boolean, Hadamard, integer, positive, stochastic matrices), or by an algebraic identity (orthogonal, Hermitian and skew-Hermitian matrices, matrix Lie algebras); it also holds the algebraic side of random matrices. ([MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))

The research questions in the area are of three kinds: existence and classification of matrices with a prescribed combinatorial structure (Hadamard matrices, spectrally arbitrary sign patterns), [spectral theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) of structured families (Perron–Frobenius theory for nonnegative matrices), and asymptotics of structured matrices as their size grows (Szegő-type limit theorems for Toeplitz matrices, which grew up alongside the two-dimensional Ising model). ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix); [Perron–Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem); [Deift–Its–Krasovsky](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.4990))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists: 15B05 Toeplitz, Cauchy and related matrices; 15B10 orthogonal matrices; 15B15 fuzzy matrices; 15B30 matrix Lie algebras; 15B33 matrices over special rings (quaternions, finite fields, etc.); 15B34 Boolean and Hadamard matrices; 15B35 sign pattern matrices; 15B36 matrices of integers; 15B48 positive matrices and their generalizations, cones of matrices; 15B51 stochastic matrices; 15B52 random matrices (algebraic aspects); 15B57 Hermitian, skew-Hermitian and related matrices; 15B99. ([MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))

- **Neighbour 15A.** Matrix theory without a structural constraint (15A18 eigenvalues, singular values and eigenvectors; 15A21 canonical forms; 15A60 norms of matrices) is classified in [MSC 15Axx - Basic linear algebra](node:MSC%2015Axx%20-%20Basic%20linear%20algebra). ([MSC2020 15Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Axx))
- **Neighbour 11C.** 15B36 (matrices of integers) carries a see-also to 11C20, in [MSC 11Cxx - Polynomials and matrices](node:MSC%2011Cxx%20-%20Polynomials%20and%20matrices). ([MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))
- **Neighbour 60B.** 15B52 covers algebraic aspects of random matrices; probabilistic aspects go to 60B20, in [MSC 60Bxx - Probability theory on algebraic and topological structures](node:MSC%2060Bxx%20-%20Probability%20theory%20on%20algebraic%20and%20topological%20structures). ([MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Hadamard matrices (15B34).** A square matrix with entries $\pm1$ and mutually orthogonal rows, i.e. $HH^T=nI_n$. For complex $M$ with $|m_{ij}|\le1$, Hadamard's bound on the [determinant](node:Determinant) is $|\det M|\le n^{n/2}$, with equality for real $M$ exactly when $M$ is Hadamard. The order must be $1$, $2$ or a multiple of $4$. Sylvester's doubling $H\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}H&H\\H&-H\end{pmatrix}$ gives all orders $2^k$; Paley's construction (1933) uses [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields) to give order $q+1$ for a prime power $q\equiv3\pmod 4$ and $2(q+1)$ for $q\equiv1\pmod4$; the smallest order not reached by combining these is $92$, found by Baumert, Golomb and Hall in 1962 with Williamson's construction. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix))
- **Toeplitz and circulant matrices; Szegő's theorems (15B05).** $T_n(f)=[t_{k-j}]_{k,j=0}^{n-1}$ with $t_k$ the Fourier coefficients of a symbol $f$ on $[0,2\pi]$. Every circulant is diagonalized by the discrete Fourier vectors, with eigenvalues $\psi_m=\sum_k c_k e^{-2\pi i mk/n}$. If $\{t_k\}$ is absolutely summable and $f$ is real, the eigenvalues $\tau_{n,k}$ of $T_n(f)$ satisfy $\frac1n\sum_k F(\tau_{n,k})\to\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}F(f(\lambda))\,d\lambda$ for every $F$ continuous on $[\min f,\max f]$ (the Grenander–Szegő eigenvalue distribution theorem). ([Gray, Thms 3.1, 4.2](https://ee.stanford.edu/~gray/toeplitz.pdf)) Szegő's strong limit theorem (1952): for positive $\varphi\in C^{1+\varepsilon}$ on the unit circle, $D_n(\varphi)/e^{n(\log\varphi)_0}\to\exp\sum_{k\ge1}k|(\log\varphi)_k|^2$; Ibragimov gave necessary and sufficient conditions for positive symbols. ([Deift–Its–Krasovsky](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1207.4990); [Szegő limit theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szeg%C5%91_limit_theorems))
- **Fisher–Hartwig asymptotics (15B05).** For symbols with root and jump singularities, $f(z)=e^{V(z)}z^{\sum\beta_j}\prod_j|z-z_j|^{2\alpha_j}g_{z_j,\beta_j}(z)z_j^{-\beta_j}$ with $\operatorname{Re}\alpha_j>-1/2$, Fisher and Hartwig conjectured in 1968 that $D_n(f)\sim E\,n^{\sum_j(\alpha_j^2-\beta_j^2)}e^{nV_0}$. Widom proved the case $\beta=0$; Böttcher and Silbermann the case $|\operatorname{Re}\alpha_j|,|\operatorname{Re}\beta_j|<1/2$; Ehrhardt the case $\||\beta|\|<1$ for $C^\infty$ $V$ with $\alpha_j\pm\beta_j\ne-1,-2,\dots$; Deift, Its and Krasovsky gave a proof needing only finite smoothness of $V$, with error estimates. The motivating application is the [spontaneous magnetization](node:Spontaneous%20Magnetization) of the 2D [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model), a limit of Toeplitz determinants. ([Deift–Its–Krasovsky](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1207.4990))
- **Positive and nonnegative matrices (15B48).** Perron (1907): a matrix with all entries positive has a simple eigenvalue $r>0$ equal to its spectral radius and strictly larger in modulus than every other eigenvalue, with strictly positive left and right eigenvectors, and $A^k/r^k\to vw^T$. Frobenius (1912): if $A\ge0$ is irreducible with period $h$, then $r$ is still a simple eigenvalue with positive eigenvectors, and $A$ has exactly $h$ eigenvalues of modulus $r$, namely $r$ times the $h$-th roots of unity. ([Perron–Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem)) For a primitive matrix, i.e. a square nonnegative matrix some power of which is positive, the spectral radius is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial, strictly greater in modulus than every other root, with strictly positive eigenvectors. ([Boyle, Thm 2.2](https://math.umd.edu/~mboyle/courses/405sp10/specmay2011.pdf)) Totally positive matrices, all of whose minors are positive, include Vandermonde matrices with nodes $0<x_0<\dots<x_n$ (Gantmacher–Krein, 1941). ([Totally positive matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totally_positive_matrix))
- **Stochastic matrices (15B51).** For a row-stochastic matrix the all-ones vector is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $1$, which is the spectral radius; irreducibility gives the finite [Markov chain](node:Markov%20Chains) stationary distribution. ([Perron–Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem)) Birkhoff–von Neumann: the $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrices form a polytope of dimension $(n-1)^2$ whose vertices are exactly the permutation matrices. Van der Waerden's 1926 conjecture that the minimum permanent of an $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrix is $n!/n^n$, attained at $J_n/n$, was proved by Gyires (1980) and independently by Egorychev and Falikman (1981). ([Doubly stochastic matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubly_stochastic_matrix))
- **Random matrices (15B52), [Random Matrices](node:Random%20Matrices).** Wigner's semicircle law: for a Hermitian matrix with independent, mean-zero above-diagonal entries of common variance $\sigma^2$, the spectrum scaled by $\sqrt N\sigma$ converges in distribution to the density $\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{4-x^2}$ on $[-2,2]$. The Gaussian ensembles GOE, GUE and GSE are the real symmetric, Hermitian and quaternionic-Hermitian cases. ([Random matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_matrix))
- **Sign patterns (15B35).** An $n\times n$ sign pattern is spectrally arbitrary if every monic real polynomial of degree $n$ is the characteristic polynomial of some real matrix with entries of the prescribed signs. Shitov constructed a spectrally arbitrary pattern with a superpattern that is not spectrally arbitrary, disproving a 2000 conjecture of Drew, Johnson, Olesky and van den Driessche. ([Shitov, arXiv:1612.05818](https://arxiv.org/html/1612.05818))
- **Orthogonal, Hermitian and Lie-algebra classes (15B10, 15B57, 15B30).** MSC lists orthogonal matrices, Hermitian and skew-Hermitian matrices, and matrix Lie algebras as separate codes; see [Gram–Schmidt Process](node:Gram–Schmidt%20Process) and [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces) for orthonormal columns, [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices) for the Hermitian positive definite case, and [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) for the abstract setting. ([MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx))

### History
Sylvester gave the first Hadamard matrices in 1867, and Hadamard constructed orders 12 and 20 in 1893. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix)) Perron's theorem dates from 1907 and Frobenius's extension to irreducible matrices from 1912. ([Perron–Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem)) Szegő proved his first limit theorem in 1915 and the strong limit theorem in 1952; Onsager and Kaufman announced the formula $M_0=(1-k^2)^{1/8}$ for $0<k<1$, where $k=1/(\sinh(2J_1/k_BT)\sinh(2J_2/k_BT))$, for the Ising spontaneous magnetization in 1948–1949 without publishing a proof, and the Toeplitz-determinant problem it posed drove much of the later theory. ([Deift–Its–Krasovsky](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1207.4990)) Wishart introduced random matrices in multivariate statistics in 1928, and Wigner used them in the 1950s to model energy levels of heavy nuclei. ([Random matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_matrix))

### Open problems
- **Hadamard conjecture.** A Hadamard matrix of order $4k$ exists for every positive integer $k$; it is attributed to Paley and listed as unsolved. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix)) Cati and Pasechnik state the conjecture and report that below $1208$ the only orders with no known Hadamard matrix are $668$, $716$, $892$ and $1132$; they note that a similar conjecture exists for skew Hadamard matrices. ([Cati–Pasechnik, arXiv:2411.18897](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.18897v2))
- **Ising model in a magnetic field.** Deift, Its and Krasovsky call finding analogues of the explicit Toeplitz-determinant formulas for Ising correlations when the field $h\ne0$ "an outstanding problem in the theory of the Ising model". ([Deift–Its–Krasovsky](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1207.4990))

> [!warning] Contested
> Wikipedia reports an August 2026 announcement by Alpöge, Voinov and Reynolds-Haertle of constructions for all twelve orders below 2000 that were unknown in 2014 (beginning with 668); its citation is a social-media post, not a paper. Until a construction is published and checked, the smallest open order should be taken from the published record above. The Hadamard conjecture for all $4k$ is open either way. ([Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix); [Cati–Pasechnik](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18897))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Perron–Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem): positive and irreducible nonnegative matrices, with applications to Markov chains.
- **Reference:** [Hadamard matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_matrix): constructions, determinant bound, the Hadamard conjecture.
- **Learn:** [Gray, Toeplitz and Circulant Matrices: A Review](https://ee.stanford.edu/~gray/toeplitz.pdf): tutorial proofs of the circulant diagonalization and Szegő's eigenvalue distribution theorem.
- **Learn:** [Boyle, Notes on the Perron–Frobenius theory of nonnegative matrices](https://math.umd.edu/~mboyle/courses/405sp10/specmay2011.pdf): primitive and irreducible cases with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Deift, Its and Krasovsky, Toeplitz matrices and Toeplitz determinants under the impetus of the Ising model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.4990): survey of Szegő and Fisher–Hartwig asymptotics.
- **Primary:** [Cati and Pasechnik, A database of constructions of Hadamard matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18897): constructions of all known (skew) Hadamard matrices up to order 1208.
- **Further reading:** [Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/matrix-analysis/9CF2CB491C9E97948B15FAD835EF9A8B): graduate text with chapters on positive definite and nonnegative matrices.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 15Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=15Bxx): official code list.
references.MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 16 is noncommutative ring theory: associative rings and algebras, with the commutative case sent to 13-XX. An associative algebra over a commutative ring $K$ is a ring $A$ with a ring homomorphism $K\to Z(A)$; every ring is an algebra over $\mathbb Z$ and over its center. Unital algebras are the default, but non-unital ones (for example convolution algebras of functions) also occur. Standard examples are matrix algebras $M_n(K)$, group algebras $R[G]$, and the quaternions, a 4-dimensional real algebra that is not a $\mathbb C$-algebra because $\mathbb C$ is not central in it. ([MSC2020 16-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16-XX); [Wikipedia: Associative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra))

The subject is organized by structure theorems. The [Jacobson radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical) isolates the part of a ring invisible to simple modules; semisimple Artinian rings are classified by Artin–Wedderburn; Goldie's theorem reduces semiprime Noetherian rings to semisimple ones by noncommutative localization; and Kaplansky's and Posner's theorems do the same for rings satisfying a polynomial identity. Michael Artin's graduate course follows this route through Morita equivalence, localization, central simple algebras and the Brauer group, maximal orders, PI rings, and growth of algebras. ([Wikipedia: Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical); [Artin, Noncommutative Rings, contents](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/artinnotes.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 16 into: general and miscellaneous (16B); modules, bimodules and ideals (16D); homological methods (16E, with 13D for commutative rings and 18G for general categories); representation theory of rings and algebras (16G); algebras and orders (16H); division rings and semisimple Artin rings (16K); [local rings](node:Local%20Noncommutative%20Rings) and generalizations (16L); radicals (16N); chain, growth and other finiteness conditions (16P); polynomial-identity rings (16R); rings and algebras arising under various constructions (16S); Hopf algebras and quantum groups (16T); conditions on elements (16U); rings with additional structure (16W); generalizations (16Y, with nonassociative rings sent to 17-XX; see [MSC 16Yxx - Generalizations](node:MSC%2016Yxx%20-%20Generalizations)); and computational aspects (16Z). ([MSC2020 16-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16-XX))

Neighbouring areas: commutative rings are in 13; nonassociative rings, including [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras), in [17](node:MSC%2017%20-%20Nonassociative%20rings%20and%20algebras); arithmetic of orders in 11R/11S; and general [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) in 18G. ([MSC2020 16-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16-XX))

### Key concepts
- [Jacobson Radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical). $J(R)$ is the set of elements annihilating every simple right module; equivalently the intersection of all maximal right (or left) ideals, or the set of $y$ with $1+xy$ invertible for all $x$. Nakayama's lemma: if $M$ is a finitely generated module with $J(R)M=M$ then $M=0$. If $R$ is left or right Artinian, $J(R)$ is nilpotent. Jacobson introduced it for arbitrary rings in 1945. ([Wikipedia: Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical))
- [Artin–Wedderburn Theorem](node:Artin–Wedderburn%20Theorem). A semisimple (Artinian) ring is isomorphic to $\prod_{i=1}^r M_{n_i}(D_i)$ with $D_i$ division rings, the $n_i$ and $D_i$ unique up to order; over an algebraically closed field $k$ a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra is $\prod M_{n_i}(k)$; over an arbitrary field $k$, a finite-dimensional central simple $k$-algebra is $M_n(D)$ for a finite-dimensional central division algebra $D$ over $k$. Wedderburn (1908) proved the finite-dimensional case and Artin (1927) the Artinian case. ([Wikipedia: Artin–Wedderburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Wedderburn_theorem))
- **Ore localization and Goldie's theorem.** A right Ore set $S\subset A$ is multiplicative, consists of regular elements, and satisfies $sA\cap aS\neq\emptyset$ for all $a\in A$, $s\in S$; then the ring of right fractions $AS^{-1}$ exists. The free algebra $k\langle x,y\rangle$ fails the Ore condition. Goldie: in a semiprime right Noetherian ring (more generally a semiprime right Goldie ring) the regular elements form a right Ore set and the classical right ring of fractions is semisimple Artinian. See [Localization of Rings](node:Localization%20of%20Rings) and [Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings). ([Artin, II.2 and II.6](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/artinnotes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Goldie's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldie%27s_theorem))
- [Polynomial Identity Rings](node:Polynomial%20Identity%20Rings). Amitsur–Levitzki: for a commutative ring $R$, $n\times n$ matrices over $R$ satisfy the standard identity $S_{2n}=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{2n}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)x_{\sigma(1)}\cdots x_{\sigma(2n)}=0$, and no nonzero multilinear identity of lower degree. Kaplansky: a primitive algebra satisfying a multilinear identity of degree $2r$ is central simple over its center $K$ with $[A:K]\le r^2$. Posner: a prime PI algebra with center $Z$ has $A\otimes_Z\operatorname{Frac}(Z)$ central simple. ([Artin, V.3, V.6, V.8](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/artinnotes.pdf); [Wikipedia: PI ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_identity_ring))
- **Morita equivalence and growth.** Morita theory studies when the module categories of two rings are equivalent; and the [Gelfand–Kirillov dimension](node:Gelfand–Kirillov%20Dimension) measures growth, with Bergman's gap theorem stating that no algebra has GK dimension strictly between $1$ and $2$. ([Artin, I and VI.4](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/artinnotes.pdf))
- **Further subareas.** [Hopf Algebras](node:Hopf%20Algebras) and [Quantum Groups](node:Quantum%20Groups) (16T), homological methods such as [Hochschild Cohomology](node:Hochschild%20Cohomology) (16E), and the [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of algebras via [Quiver Representations](node:Quiver%20Representations) (16G) are separate MSC sections of 16. ([MSC2020 16-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16-XX))

### History
Wedderburn's 1908 paper "On hypercomplex numbers" classified finite-dimensional simple algebras, and Artin extended this to Artinian rings in 1927. Köthe posed his nil-ideal conjecture in 1930, Ore studied noncommutative fractions in the 1930s, Jacobson defined the radical of an arbitrary ring in 1945, and Goldie's theorems of 1958 and 1960 made fractions a cornerstone of noncommutative Noetherian ring theory. Higman's 1940 thesis formulated the unit and zero-divisor conjectures for group rings, later popularized by Kaplansky. ([Wikipedia: Artin–Wedderburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Wedderburn_theorem); [Wikipedia: Köthe conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture); [Artin, II.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/artinnotes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical); [Wikipedia: Goldie's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldie%27s_theorem); [Gardam](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.11818))

> [!warning] Contested
> Reported, not yet refereed. **Köthe's conjecture (1930)**, that the sum of two nil left ideals of a ring is nil, was long the best-known open problem of the area. Two September 2026 preprints claim to refute it. Adamczewski, Böhmler and Marczinzik construct, for every countable field $F$, a nil algebra $N$ and two nil left ideals of $M_2(F1+N)$ whose sum $M_2(N)$ is not nil; they report that the initial construction was found by an AI model working from a Lean formalization and that the authors checked all such material. Greenfeld, King and Vendramin give a short refutation via point modules. Wikipedia now lists the conjecture as disproved, attributing the first counterexample to the AI model GPT-6 Astra. Both papers are September 2026 arXiv preprints. ([Adamczewski–Böhmler–Marczinzik](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.07996); [Greenfeld–King–Vendramin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15080); [Wikipedia: Köthe conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Kaplansky's zero-divisor and idempotent conjectures (16S34).** For a field $K$ and torsion-free group $G$, the group ring $K[G]$ should have no nontrivial zero divisors, and no idempotents other than $0,1$. Gardam calls these, with the unit conjecture, long-standing open problems; he disproved the unit conjecture with an explicit nontrivial unit in $\mathbb F_2[P]$ for a virtually abelian torsion-free group $P$. The zero-divisor conjecture is known for elementary amenable groups and, over $\mathbb C$, for groups satisfying the strong Atiyah conjecture. ([Gardam](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.11818); [Wikipedia: Kaplansky's conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Associative algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_algebra): definitions and examples.
- **Reference:** [Jacobson radical (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical): characterizations and Nakayama's lemma.
- **Learn:** [M. Artin, Noncommutative Rings (course notes)](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/artinnotes.pdf): Morita theory, Goldie's theorem, central simple algebras, orders, PI theory, GK dimension.
- **Primary:** [Gardam, A counterexample to the unit conjecture for group rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11818): status of Kaplansky's group-ring conjectures.
