- **Primary:** [Adamczewski–Böhmler–Marczinzik, A counterexample to Köthe's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07996): the 2026 preprint.
- **Further reading:** [Lam, A First Course in Noncommutative Rings (Springer GTM, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-8616-0): the standard graduate text.
references.MSC 16Dxx - Modules, bimodules and ideal:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 16D, "Modules, bimodules and ideals in associative algebras", is the part of [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras) that studies a ring through its modules: general module theory, bimodules, one- and two-sided ideals, projective, flat and injective modules, simple and semisimple modules and primitive rings, decomposition and cancellation, and module categories with Morita equivalence and duality. ([MSC2020 16Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Dxx))

The organizing idea is that a ring is known through its category of modules. Two rings with equivalent module categories (Morita equivalent rings) share their ring-theoretic properties that are defined categorically, such as being simple, semisimple, Artinian or Noetherian, and have isomorphic centres, but not properties like commutativity or being a domain. ([Morita equivalence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morita_equivalence)) The classical structure theory runs from simple modules (Schur's lemma, the density theorem) to the Wedderburn decomposition of semisimple rings. ([Etingof, MIT 18.706](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_notes_by_pavel_etingof.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 16D10 general module theory; 16D20 bimodules; 16D25 ideals; 16D30 infinite-dimensional simple rings (except as in 16K); 16D40 free, projective and flat modules and ideals (see also 19A13); 16D50 injective modules and self-injective rings (see also 16L60); 16D60 simple and semisimple modules, primitive rings and ideals; 16D70 structure and classification of modules, bimodules and ideals (except as in 16G), direct sum decomposition and cancellation; 16D80 other classes of modules and ideals (see also 16G50); 16D90 module categories, module theory in a category-theoretic context, Morita equivalence and duality (see also 16G, 16S90); 16D99. ([MSC2020 16Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Dxx))

- **Neighbour 16G.** Classification of modules by representation-theoretic methods is excluded from 16D70 and sent to [MSC 16Gxx - Representation theory of associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016Gxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20associative%20rings%20and%20algebras). ([MSC2020 16Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Dxx))
- **Neighbour 16K.** Finite-dimensional simple rings and division rings belong to [MSC 16Kxx - Division rings and semisimple Artin rings](node:MSC%2016Kxx%20-%20Division%20rings%20and%20semisimple%20Artin%20rings); 16D30 takes only infinite-dimensional simple rings. ([MSC2020 16Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Dxx))
- **Neighbour 16L.** Self-injective rings in 16D50 cross-refer to 16L60, in [MSC 16Lxx - Local rings and generalizations](node:MSC%2016Lxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20generalizations). ([MSC2020 16Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Dxx))
- **Neighbour 16E.** Homological dimension (16E10) and homological functors such as Tor and Ext (16E30) are classified in [MSC 16Exx - Homological methods in associative algebras](node:MSC%2016Exx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20associative%20algebras). ([MSC2020 16Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Density and Wedderburn theorems (16D60).** Jacobson density theorem: let $U$ be a simple right $R$-module and $D=\operatorname{End}(U_R)$, a division ring by Schur's lemma; for every finite $D$-linearly independent $X\subset U$ and every $D$-linear map $A$ on $U$ there is $r\in R$ with $A(x)=xr$ for all $x\in X$. Hence every primitive ring is a dense ring of linear transformations of a vector space over a division ring. ([Jacobson density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_density_theorem)) For a simple module $M\cong D^n$ over $D=\operatorname{End}_A M$, the image of $A$ in $\operatorname{End}M$ is all of $\operatorname{Mat}_n(D)$, and a ring with the descending chain condition is semisimple iff it is a finite direct sum of matrix algebras over division algebras, with sizes and division algebras unique. ([Etingof, Cor. 1.6, Thm 1.9](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_notes_by_pavel_etingof.pdf)) This is the [Artin–Wedderburn Theorem](node:Artin–Wedderburn%20Theorem): a semisimple ring is $\prod_i M_{n_i}(D_i)$, with $n_i,D_i$ unique up to permutation. ([Artin–Wedderburn theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Wedderburn_theorem))
- **Morita theory (16D90).** Rings $R$ and $S$ are Morita equivalent if their categories of left modules are equivalent. This holds iff $S\cong\operatorname{End}_R(P)$ for a progenerator $P$ (a finitely generated projective generator), equivalently $S\cong eM_n(R)e$ for some $n$ and full idempotent $e$. So $R\sim M_n(R)$ for every $n$, while two commutative rings are Morita equivalent only if they are isomorphic. ([Morita equivalence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morita_equivalence))
- **Krull–Schmidt–Azumaya and cancellation (16D70).** A nonzero module of finite length is a direct sum of indecomposables, unique up to permutation and isomorphism. Azumaya: a decomposition, possibly infinite, into modules with local endomorphism rings is unique in the same sense. ([Krull–Schmidt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%E2%80%93Schmidt_theorem)) Without finite length the conclusion can fail: for $A$ the ring of smooth $1$-periodic real functions and $M$ the module of smooth $b$ with $b(x+1)=-b(x)$, $M$ is indecomposable and not isomorphic to $A$, yet $M\oplus M\cong A\oplus A$. ([Etingof, §1, exercise 17](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_notes_by_pavel_etingof.pdf)) Krull–Schmidt can fail for modules satisfying only one of the two chain conditions; Facchini, Herbera, Levy and Vámos (1995) showed it fails for Artinian modules. ([Krull–Schmidt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%E2%80%93Schmidt_theorem))
- **Projective modules (16D40).** $P$ is projective iff it is a direct summand of a free module. Kaplansky (1958): a projective module over a local ring is free. Bass (1963): big (non-finitely generated) projective modules over $K[X_1,\dots,X_n]$, $K$ a field or PID, are free; Quillen and Suslin settled the finitely generated case, so all projectives over these polynomial rings are free (Serre's problem). Raynaud–Gruson (1971): $M$ is projective iff it is flat, a direct sum of countably generated modules, and satisfies a Mittag-Leffler condition. ([Projective module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_module)) See also [Flat Modules](node:Flat%20Modules).
- **Injective modules (16D50).** Baer's criterion (1940): a left $R$-module $Q$ is injective iff every homomorphism from a left ideal of $R$ to $Q$ extends to $R$. Every module has an injective hull (Eckmann–Schopf, 1953). Bass–Papp: every direct sum of left (right) injective modules is injective iff $R$ is left (right) Noetherian. Matlis (1958): over a commutative Noetherian ring every injective is uniquely a direct sum of indecomposables $E(R/\mathfrak p)$. A right Noetherian right self-injective ring is quasi-Frobenius, and over it projective and injective modules coincide. ([Injective module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injective_module))
- **General modules, bimodules and ideals (16D10, 16D20, 16D25).** MSC lists general module theory, bimodules and ideals as separate codes; see [Modules and Bimodules](node:Modules%20and%20Bimodules), [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals), [Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings), [Jacobson Radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical), [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) and, for modules over a field, [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces). ([MSC2020 16Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Dxx))

### History
Wedderburn proved the structure theorem for finite-dimensional simple algebras (published 1908), and Artin generalized it in 1927 to Artinian rings. ([Artin–Wedderburn theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Wedderburn_theorem)) Uniqueness of direct decompositions goes back to Wedderburn (1909, finite groups), Remak (1911) and Schmidt (1913), and Krull (1925) extended it to operator groups in essentially module language. ([Krull–Schmidt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%E2%80%93Schmidt_theorem)) Jacobson's density theorem appeared in 1945, and Morita introduced equivalence and duality of module categories in 1958. ([Jacobson density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_density_theorem); [Morita equivalence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morita_equivalence)) Projective modules were introduced in Cartan and Eilenberg's *Homological Algebra* (1956). ([Projective module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_module))

### Open problems
- **Faith's conjecture (16D50, 16L60).** Every left or right perfect, left self-injective ring is quasi-Frobenius (Faith, 1976). Guil Asensio and Srivastava state that it "still remains open"; by Osofsky and Kato the conclusion holds when the ring is perfect and both left and right self-injective. ([Guil Asensio–Srivastava, arXiv:2205.01830](https://arxiv.org/html/2205.01830))

A related question of Faith asks which rings satisfy the dual Baer criterion ($R$-projectivity implies projectivity for all right $R$-modules). Right perfect rings do (Sandomierski), and it was known to be consistent with ZFC that only right perfect rings do; Trlifaj showed it is also consistent that some non-right-perfect ring does, so the question whether every such ring is right perfect is undecidable in ZFC. ([Trlifaj, arXiv:1710.10465](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10465))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Morita equivalence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morita_equivalence): progenerators, preserved properties, Morita duality.
- **Learn:** [Etingof, Rings, ideals and modules (MIT 18.706)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_notes_by_pavel_etingof.pdf): density theorem, Wedderburn, Krull–Schmidt with exercises.
- **Primary:** [Guil Asensio and Srivastava, MacWilliams extending conditions and quasi-Frobenius rings](https://arxiv.org/html/2205.01830): recent work around Faith's conjecture on self-injective rings.
- **Primary:** [Trlifaj, Faith's problem on R-projectivity is undecidable](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10465): set-theoretic resolution of the dual Baer criterion.
- **Further reading:** [Lam, Lectures on Modules and Rings (Springer GTM, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0525-8): graduate text by T. Y. Lam (bibliographic record).
- **Further reading:** [Anderson and Fuller, Rings and Categories of Modules (Springer GTM, 1992)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4418-9): graduate text by F. W. Anderson and K. R. Fuller (bibliographic record).
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 16Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Dxx): official code list.
references.MSC 16Exx - Homological methods in assoc:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 16E, "Homological methods in associative algebras", is the part of [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras) where noncommutative rings and algebras are studied through resolutions, homological dimensions, Tor and Ext, derived categories, Hochschild and cyclic (co)homology, and differential graded algebras, together with the ring classes defined homologically: von Neumann regular, hereditary and semihereditary rings, and Gorenstein and Cohen–Macaulay-type conditions. ([MSC2020 16Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx))

As a research area it has three centres. The first is homological dimension theory of finite-dimensional algebras, organized around the finitistic dimension conjecture and the Nakayama-type conjectures it implies. ([Guo–Igusa, arXiv:2311.00661](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.00661)) The second is Hochschild cohomology, which classifies extensions of an algebra and carries a Gerstenhaber algebra structure. ([Weibel, ch. 9](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/weibel/09-hochschild_and_cyclic_homology.pdf); [Gerstenhaber algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerstenhaber_algebra)) The third is derived equivalence: tilting theory and Rickard's Morita theory for derived categories. ([Tilting theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilting_theory))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 16E05 syzygies, resolutions, complexes; 16E10 homological dimension; 16E20 Grothendieck groups and $K$-theory (see also 18F30, 19Axx, 19D50); 16E30 homological functors on modules (Tor, Ext, etc.); 16E35 derived categories and associative algebras; 16E40 (co)homology of rings and algebras (Hochschild, cyclic, dihedral, etc.); 16E45 differential graded algebras; 16E50 von Neumann regular rings and generalizations; 16E60 semihereditary and hereditary rings, free ideal rings, Sylvester rings; 16E65 homological conditions on rings (generalizations of regular, Gorenstein, Cohen–Macaulay rings); 16E99. ([MSC2020 16Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx))

- **Neighbour 13D.** The section note sends homological methods for commutative rings to [MSC 13Dxx - Homological methods in commutative ring theory](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory). ([MSC2020 16Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx))
- **Neighbour 18G.** Homological algebra in general categories goes to [MSC 18Gxx - Homological algebra in category theory, derived categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Gxx%20-%20Homological%20algebra%20in%20category%20theory,%20derived%20categories%20and%20functors). ([MSC2020 16Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx))
- **Neighbour 19A.** Grothendieck groups of rings (16E20) cross-refer to algebraic $K$-theory in 19Axx; see [Grothendieck Groups](node:Grothendieck%20Groups). ([MSC2020 16Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Finitistic dimensions (16E10).** For a finite-dimensional algebra $\Lambda$, $\operatorname{Findim}\Lambda=\sup\{\operatorname{pd}M: M\in\operatorname{Mod}\Lambda,\ \operatorname{pd}M<\infty\}$ and $\operatorname{findim}\Lambda$ is the same supremum over finitely generated modules. The conjectures were (1) $\operatorname{Findim}\Lambda=\operatorname{findim}\Lambda$ and (2) $\operatorname{findim}\Lambda<\infty$. ([Guo–Igusa](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.00661)) Conjecture (1) is false: for each $n\ge2$ there is a monomial relation algebra with $\operatorname{findim}\Lambda=n$ and $\operatorname{Findim}\Lambda=n+1$ (Huisgen-Zimmermann, 1992). Conjecture (2) holds for monomial algebras (Green–Kirkman–Kuzmanovich, 1991), for $J^3=0$ (Green–Huisgen-Zimmermann, 1991), and when the category of finitely generated modules of finite projective dimension is contravariantly finite (Auslander–Reiten, 1991). ([Huisgen-Zimmermann, arXiv:1407.2383](https://arxiv.org/html/1407.2383v1)) It also holds for algebras of representation dimension three and special biserial algebras. ([Guo–Igusa](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.00661))
- **Hochschild cohomology (16E40), [Hochschild Cohomology](node:Hochschild%20Cohomology).** With $A^e=A\otimes A^{\mathrm{op}}$, $HH_n(A,M)=\operatorname{Tor}^{A^e}_n(A,M)$ and $HH^n(A,M)=\operatorname{Ext}^n_{A^e}(A,M)$ (Hochschild, 1945). ([Hochschild homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochschild_homology)) In low degrees: $H^0(R,M)=\{m: rm=mr\ \forall r\}$; $H^1(R,M)=\operatorname{Der}_k(R,M)/\operatorname{PDer}_k(R,M)$, derivations modulo inner ones; and $H^2(R,M)$ is in bijection with equivalence classes of $k$-split square-zero (Hochschild) extensions of $R$ by $M$. An algebra over a field is finite-dimensional separable iff it is projective over $R^e$ iff $H^n(R,M)=0$ for all $n\ne0$ and all bimodules $M$. ([Weibel, Lemma 9.2.1, Thms 9.2.11, 9.3.1](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/weibel/09-hochschild_and_cyclic_homology.pdf)) Gerstenhaber (1963) showed $HH^*(A,A)$ is a Gerstenhaber algebra: graded-commutative, with a Lie bracket of degree $-1$ satisfying the Poisson identity. ([Gerstenhaber algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerstenhaber_algebra)) For a smooth commutative algebra in characteristic $0$, Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg identifies $HH_n$ with Kähler $n$-forms. ([Hochschild homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochschild_homology)) The Hochschild cohomology object $\operatorname{Hom}_{A\otimes A^{\mathrm{op}}}(A,A)$ is the derived centre of $A$, and for $\mathcal O(X)$ it computes multivector fields. A first-order deformation $r_1\cdot_t r_2=r_1r_2+t\,f(r_1,r_2)$ with $t^2=0$ is a $k$-split extension of $R$ by itself, given by a Hochschild $2$-cocycle $f$, so such deformations are governed by $HH^2(R,R)$. ([nLab, Hochschild cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hochschild+cohomology))
- **Tilting and derived equivalence (16E35), [Derived Categories](node:Derived%20Categories).** A finitely generated module $T$ over a finite-dimensional algebra $A$ is tilting if $\operatorname{pd}T\le1$, $\operatorname{Ext}^1_A(T,T)=0$, and $A$ is the kernel of a surjection between finite sums of summands of $T$. Brenner–Butler (1980): with $B=\operatorname{End}_A(T)$, $T$ determines torsion pairs $(\mathcal T,\mathcal F)$ in $\operatorname{mod}A$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y)$ in $\operatorname{mod}B$, and the tilting functors give inverse equivalences $\mathcal T\simeq\mathcal Y$ and $\mathcal F\simeq\mathcal X$, swapping torsion and torsion-free classes; Happel (1988) and Cline–Parshall–Scott (1986) showed $A$ and $\operatorname{End}_A(T)$ are derived equivalent. Rickard (1989): two rings are derived equivalent iff one is the endomorphism ring of a tilting complex over the other. ([Tilting theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilting_theory)) Links to [Quiver Representations](node:Quiver%20Representations) and [MSC 16Gxx - Representation theory of associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016Gxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20associative%20rings%20and%20algebras).
- **Koszul algebras and duality.** A [graded algebra](node:Graded%20Algebras) is Koszul if the ground field has a linear minimal graded free resolution; polynomial rings are Koszul, and $k[x,y]/(xy)$ shows the resolution can be infinite. ([Koszul algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koszul_algebra)) The exterior and symmetric algebras form the basic Koszul dual pair, and Koszul duality relates parts of the two derived categories under finiteness conditions. ([nLab, Koszul duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Koszul+duality))
- **Regular and hereditary rings (16E50, 16E60).** $R$ is von Neumann regular if every $a$ has $x$ with $a=axa$; equivalently every left module is flat, or every finitely generated left ideal is generated by an idempotent; the Noetherian regular rings are exactly the semisimple ones. ([Von Neumann regular ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_regular_ring)) $R$ is left hereditary iff all left ideals are projective iff its left global dimension is at most $1$; path algebras of quivers are hereditary, and some triangular matrix rings are hereditary on one side only. ([Hereditary ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereditary_ring))
- **Resolutions and homological functors (16E05, 16E30).** MSC lists syzygies, resolutions and complexes, and Tor and Ext on modules, and sends the commutative case to 13Dxx; see [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra), [Projective Resolutions](node:Projective%20Resolutions) and [Tor and Ext over Commutative Rings](node:Tor%20and%20Ext%20over%20Commutative%20Rings). ([MSC2020 16Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx))

### History
Hochschild introduced his cohomology in 1945 for algebras over a field; Cartan and Eilenberg extended it to more general ground rings in 1956. ([Hochschild homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochschild_homology)) Von Neumann introduced regular rings in 1936 in his work on continuous geometry. ([Von Neumann regular ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_regular_ring)) Huisgen-Zimmermann traces the finitistic dimension conjectures to Bass (1960), while Guo and Igusa credit their first proposal to Rosenberg and Zelinsky. ([Huisgen-Zimmermann](https://arxiv.org/html/1407.2383v1); [Guo–Igusa](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.00661)) Tilting theory grew from Bernšteĭn–Gelfand–Ponomarev reflection functors (1973) through Brenner–Butler (1980), Happel–Ringel (1982) and Rickard (1989). ([Tilting theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilting_theory))

### Open problems
- **Finitistic dimension conjecture.** Whether $\operatorname{findim}\Lambda<\infty$ for every finite-dimensional algebra $\Lambda$: Guo and Igusa write that there is "no known counterexample" for finite-dimensional $\Lambda$ and that it "remains a very difficult question in general". It would imply the Wakamatsu tilting conjecture (and hence the Gorenstein symmetry conjecture) and the strong Nakayama conjecture, which implies the generalized Nakayama and Nakayama conjectures. ([Guo–Igusa, arXiv:2311.00661](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.00661))
- **Delooping level as an approach.** Gélinas showed $\operatorname{Findim}\Lambda^{\mathrm{op}}\le\operatorname{dell}\Lambda$, but Kershaw and Rickard gave an algebra with infinite delooping level; Guo and Igusa introduce derived delooping levels and list further directions. ([Guo–Igusa](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.00661)) Chen showed that finiteness of the delooping level is not preserved under derived equivalence, refuting a conjecture of Xi and Zhang. ([Chen, arXiv:2603.12974](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12974v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hochschild homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochschild_homology): definitions via Tor and Ext over $A^e$, HKR.
- **Reference:** [Tilting theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilting_theory): tilting modules, Happel and Rickard's derived equivalences.
- **Learn:** [Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, ch. 9](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/weibel/09-hochschild_and_cyclic_homology.pdf): Hochschild and cyclic homology, derivations, extensions, separable algebras.
- **Primary:** [Huisgen-Zimmermann, The finitistic dimension conjectures: a tale of 3.5 decades](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.2383): survey of the homological conjectures and known cases.
- **Primary:** [Guo and Igusa, Derived delooping levels and finitistic dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00661): recent work on the findim conjecture and its consequences.
- **Further reading:** [Happel, Triangulated Categories in the Representation of Finite Dimensional Algebras (CUP, 1988)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511629228): monograph on derived categories and tilting.
- **Further reading:** [Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra (CUP, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139644136): standard graduate text.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 16Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx): official code list.
references.MSC 16Gxx - Representation theory of ass:
## Reference
### Overview
This area of [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras) studies associative rings and algebras through their modules. For a unital algebra $A$ over a field $k$, a representation is a unital $k$-algebra homomorphism $A\to\operatorname{End}_k(V)$, equivalently a left $A$-module structure on the [vector space](node:Vector%20Spaces) $V$; neither $A$ nor $V$ need be commutative or finite dimensional in general. ([Etingof et al., §§1.1–1.3](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/replect.pdf)) The central problem for a finite-dimensional algebra is to classify its finite-dimensional indecomposable modules, since by the Krull–Schmidt theorem every finite-dimensional module is a direct sum of indecomposables, uniquely up to isomorphism and order of summands. ([Etingof et al., Theorem 2.19](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/replect.pdf)) See [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) for the wider subject.

Quivers make this concrete. For a quiver $Q$ the path algebra $kQ$ has the paths of $Q$ as a basis, with product given by concatenation when the paths compose and $0$ otherwise; $kQ$-modules are the same as representations of $Q$ (a vector space at each vertex, a linear map along each arrow), and $kQ$ is finite dimensional exactly when $Q$ has no oriented cycles. ([Crawley-Boevey, §1](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/quivlecs.pdf)) Crawley-Boevey notes that quiver representations touch linear algebra, invariant theory, finite-dimensional algebras and Kac–Moody [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras). ([Crawley-Boevey, introduction](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/quivlecs.pdf)) See [Quiver Representations](node:Quiver%20Representations).

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 16G10 representations of associative Artinian rings; 16G20 representations of quivers and partially ordered sets; 16G30 representations of orders, lattices, algebras over commutative rings (see also 16Hxx); 16G50 Cohen–Macaulay modules in associative algebras; 16G60 representation type (finite, tame, wild, etc.) of associative algebras; 16G70 Auslander–Reiten sequences (almost split sequences) and Auslander–Reiten quivers; and 16G99. ([MSC2020, 16G](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Gxx))

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 16Hxx - Associative algebras and orders](node:MSC%2016Hxx%20-%20Associative%20algebras%20and%20orders) treats orders and separable algebras themselves and sends their representation theory to 16G30 ([MSC2020, 16H](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Hxx)); [MSC 16Exx - Homological methods in associative algebras](node:MSC%2016Exx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20associative%20algebras) holds homological dimension (16E10) and derived categories and associative algebras (16E35) ([MSC2020, 16E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Exx)). See also [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) and [Derived Categories](node:Derived%20Categories).

### Key concepts
- **Gabriel's theorem (16G20, 16G60).** A finite connected quiver $Q$ has only finitely many isomorphism classes of indecomposable finite-dimensional representations iff its underlying graph is a Dynkin diagram $A_n,D_n,E_6,E_7,E_8$; in that case $M\mapsto\underline{\dim}\,M$ is a bijection from indecomposables to the positive roots of the corresponding root system. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel%27s_theorem); [Etingof et al., Theorem 5.23](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/replect.pdf)) Algebraic closure is not needed: Etingof et al. and Crawley-Boevey work over an algebraically closed field as a standing convention, while Schiffmann states the same criterion and root bijection for quiver representations over a field $k$ with no closure assumption. ([Etingof et al., §1](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/replect.pdf); [Crawley-Boevey, §1](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/quivlecs.pdf); [Schiffmann, Theorem 3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611617)) Over $\mathbb C$, nLab records the same ADE classification. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Gabriel%27s+theorem))
- **Euclidean quivers and Kac's theorem.** For a quiver without loops, the category of (nilpotent) representations is tame iff the symmetrized Euler form is positive semidefinite of corank $1$ (the affine, or Euclidean, case; Nazarova and Donovan–Freislich). For an arbitrary quiver over an algebraically closed field (Crawley-Boevey's standing convention), Kac proved that a dimension vector carries an indecomposable iff it is a positive root; for a real root the indecomposable is unique, and for an imaginary root there is more than one. Schiffmann's definition of tame excludes finite type. ([Schiffmann, Theorems 3.10 and 3.13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611617); [Crawley-Boevey, §10](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/quivlecs.pdf))
- **Auslander–Reiten theory (16G70).** For an Artin algebra $R$, a non-split exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ of finitely generated modules is almost split if $A$ and $C$ are indecomposable and every non-isomorphism from an indecomposable module to $C$ (respectively from $A$ to an indecomposable) factors through $B$. Every finitely generated indecomposable non-projective $C$ ends an almost split sequence, unique up to isomorphism, and its left end is $A\cong\tau C=D\operatorname{Tr}C$, the dual of the transpose. The Auslander–Reiten quiver has the indecomposables as vertices and irreducible morphisms as arrows. Example: for $R=k[x]/(x^n)$ and $1\le m<n$ the sequences are $0\to k[x]/(x^m)\to k[x]/(x^{m+1})\oplus k[x]/(x^{m-1})\to k[x]/(x^m)\to0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auslander%E2%80%93Reiten_theory)) Crawley-Boevey notes that these sequences exist for every finite-dimensional algebra. ([Crawley-Boevey, §6](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/quivlecs.pdf))
- **Tame–wild dichotomy (16G60).** Tame type means that in each dimension the indecomposables form finitely many one-parameter families and finitely many exceptions; wild type means that for every finite-dimensional algebra $\Lambda$ there is a representation embedding of $\operatorname{mod}\Lambda$, which ties classification to the classical unsolved problem of canonical forms for tuples of matrices up to simultaneous similarity. The dichotomy theorem (Drozd; Crawley-Boevey): a finite-dimensional algebra over an algebraically closed field is either tame or wild, and not both. ([Crabbe–Leuschke, §1 and Theorem 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1008.2465)) Bekkert and Drozd proved the analogue for derived categories: every such algebra is derived tame or derived wild. ([Bekkert–Drozd](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0310352))
- **Tilting theory.** A finitely generated module $T$ over a finite-dimensional algebra $A$ is tilting if $\operatorname{pd}T\le1$, $\operatorname{Ext}^1_A(T,T)=0$, and $A$ is the kernel of a surjection between finite direct sums of summands of $T$. With $B=\operatorname{End}_A(T)$, the Brenner–Butler theorem gives equivalences between torsion classes of $\operatorname{mod}A$ and $\operatorname{mod}B$, generalizing Morita equivalence; Happel (and Cline–Parshall–Scott) showed $A$ and $B$ are derived equivalent, and Rickard showed that two algebras are derived equivalent iff one is the endomorphism ring of a tilting complex over the other. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilting_theory))
- **Cohen–Macaulay representation type (16G50).** Over a complete local hypersurface $R=k[\![x_0,\dots,x_d]\!]/(f)$ with $d\ge1$, $f$ a nonzero non-unit and $k$ algebraically closed of characteristic not $2,3,5$, there are finitely many indecomposable maximal Cohen–Macaulay modules iff $R$ is a simple (ADE) singularity; Crabbe and Leuschke prove that for $d\ge2$ and $f$ of order at least $4$ the hypersurface has wild Cohen–Macaulay type. ([Crabbe–Leuschke, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1008.2465))

### History
Gabriel's classification appeared in "Unzerlegbare Darstellungen I" (Manuscripta Mathematica, 1972); Dlab and Ringel (1973) generalized it so that all Dynkin diagrams of finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebras occur, and Kac extended the root description to all quivers. ([Wikipedia, Gabriel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel%27s_theorem)) Bernstein, Gelfand and Ponomarev introduced reflection functors in 1973 ([Wikipedia, Tilting theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilting_theory)); Etingof et al. use them to prove Gabriel's theorem. ([Etingof et al., §§5.6–5.8](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/replect.pdf)) Auslander and Reiten introduced almost split sequences in "Representation theory of Artin algebras III" (1975) and developed them in later papers. ([Wikipedia, AR theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auslander%E2%80%93Reiten_theory)) Brenner and Butler generalized reflection functors to tilting functors in 1980, and Happel and Ringel defined tilted algebras in 1982. ([Wikipedia, Tilting theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilting_theory))

### Open problems
- **Finitistic dimension conjecture.** For a finite-dimensional algebra $A$, $\operatorname{findim}A=\sup\{\operatorname{pd}M: M\text{ finitely generated},\ \operatorname{pd}M<\infty\}$. The conjecture that $\operatorname{findim}A<\infty$, publicized as a question by Bass in 1960, was described by Rickard in 2018 as still open, as was the analogue for the big finitistic dimension over all modules. Rickard proves it for any algebra whose injective modules generate the unbounded derived category, and notes that it is known to imply other homological conjectures, including the generalized Nakayama conjecture. ([Rickard, §§1, 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.09801)) Cummings shows that it holds for all finite-dimensional algebras iff finiteness of $\operatorname{findim}A$ always implies finiteness of $\operatorname{findim}A^{\mathrm{op}}$. ([Cummings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.04394))
- **Injective generation.** Whether the injective modules generate the unbounded derived category of a non-commutative finite-dimensional algebra is open. ([Rickard, abstract](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.09801))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Auslander–Reiten theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auslander%E2%80%93Reiten_theory): almost split sequences, $D\operatorname{Tr}$, AR quiver.
- **Learn:** [Crawley-Boevey, Lectures on Representations of Quivers](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/quivlecs.pdf): path algebras, Dynkin and Euclidean classification; [Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/replect.pdf): Krull–Schmidt and a proof of Gabriel's theorem by reflection functors.
- **Primary:** [Schiffmann, Lectures on Hall algebras](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611617): Gabriel, Nazarova–Donovan–Freislich and Kac theorems with Hall algebras; [Rickard, Unbounded derived categories and the finitistic dimension conjecture](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.09801).
- **Further reading:** [Assem–Simson–Skowroński, Elements of the Representation Theory of Associative Algebras 1](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511614309) (CUP, 2006) and [Auslander–Reiten–Smalø, Representation Theory of Artin Algebras](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511623608) (CUP, 1995): the standard graduate texts.
references.MSC 16Hxx - Associative algebras and ord:
## Reference
### Overview
Orders are the noncommutative analogue of rings of integers. If $R$ is an integral domain with fraction field $K$ and $A$ is a finite-dimensional $K$-algebra, an $R$-order in $A$ is a subring $\mathcal O\subseteq A$ that is a full $R$-lattice, i.e. a finitely generated $R$-module with $\mathcal O\otimes_RK=A$. Examples are $M_n(R)\subseteq M_n(K)$, the integral closure of $R$ in a finite separable field extension $L/K$, and the group ring $R[G]\subseteq K[G]$ of a finite group, which makes integral group rings a central class of examples. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_%28ring_theory%29)) Every element of an order is integral over $R$, but in a noncommutative algebra the integral elements need not form a ring: in $M_2(\mathbb Q)$ the nilpotents $\alpha=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\beta=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1/2&0\end{pmatrix}$ are integral over $\mathbb Z$ while $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ are not. Maximal orders exist but need not be unique, and there is in general no largest order. ([Voight, §10.1](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_10); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_%28ring_theory%29))

The classical theory works over Dedekind rings: Reiner's monograph treats maximal orders in skewfields (local case), over discrete valuation rings and over Dedekind domains, then Morita equivalence, crossed-product algebras, simple algebras over global fields and hereditary orders, and its description adds Brauer groups and group rings. ([Reiner, OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/53330)) Quaternion orders are the most explicit case: Voight presents the Eichler mass formula for them as the quaternionic analogue of Dirichlet's analytic class number formula for imaginary quadratic fields, tying the area to the arithmetic of [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields). ([Voight, Ch. 25](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_25))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 16H05 separable algebras (e.g., quaternion algebras, Azumaya algebras, etc.); 16H10 orders in separable algebras; 16H15 commutative orders; 16H20 lattices over orders; and 16H99. The section note sends arithmetic aspects to 11R52, 11R54 and 11S45, and [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) to 16G30. ([MSC2020, 16H](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Hxx)) Within [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras) see also [Orders in Associative Algebras](node:Orders%20in%20Associative%20Algebras).

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 16Gxx - Representation theory of associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016Gxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20associative%20rings%20and%20algebras) contains 16G30, representations of orders, lattices and algebras over commutative rings ([MSC2020, 16G](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Gxx)); [MSC 16Kxx - Division rings and semisimple Artin rings](node:MSC%2016Kxx%20-%20Division%20rings%20and%20semisimple%20Artin%20rings) holds finite-dimensional division rings and Brauer groups ([MSC2020, 16K](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Kxx)); and [MSC 11Rxx - Algebraic number theory - global fields](node:MSC%2011Rxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20global%20fields) contains 11R52 and 11R54 from the section note.

### Key concepts
- **Existence and local–global principle for maximal orders.** If $R$ is a noetherian domain with fraction field $F$ and $B$ is a separable $F$-algebra, then $B$ has a maximal $R$-order, and every order lies in one. For $R$ a Dedekind domain, an $R$-order $\mathcal O$ is maximal iff each localization $\mathcal O_{(\mathfrak p)}$ is a maximal $R_{(\mathfrak p)}$-order (Lemma 10.4.3); likewise being an order can be checked locally (Lemma 10.2.10). If $R$ is integrally closed then $M_n(R)$ is a maximal order in $M_n(F)$. ([Voight, §§10.2–10.4](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_10); [Marseglia–Smit, Remark 5.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2211.13156)) Lattices over a Dedekind domain are determined by their localizations: $I=J$ iff $I_{\mathfrak p}=J_{\mathfrak p}$ for all primes $\mathfrak p$. ([Kirschmer–Voight, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0808.3833))
- **Local structure.** Where a quaternion algebra $B_{\mathfrak p}$ over a local field is a division algebra, the valuation extends to it and $B_{\mathfrak p}$ has a unique maximal order; where $B_{\mathfrak p}\cong M_2(F_{\mathfrak p})$, an Eichler order of level $\mathfrak p^e$ is conjugate to $\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb Z_{\mathfrak p}&\mathbb Z_{\mathfrak p}\\ \mathfrak p^e\mathbb Z_{\mathfrak p}&\mathbb Z_{\mathfrak p}\end{pmatrix}$. ([Kirschmer–Voight, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0808.3833))
- **Eichler and hereditary orders.** An Eichler order is the intersection of two (not necessarily distinct) maximal orders. In a quaternion algebra of discriminant $D$, an order is Eichler of level $M$, with $\gcd(D,M)=1$, when its reduced discriminant is $N=DM$ and it is locally Eichler of level $p^e$ at each $p^e\parallel M$. Every hereditary quaternion order is Eichler, an order is hereditary iff its reduced discriminant is squarefree, and Eichler orders of level $\mathfrak p^e$ correspond to paths of length $e$ in the Bruhat–Tits tree. ([Voight, Ch. 23](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_23))
- **Class numbers and Eichler's theorem.** For an Eichler order $\mathcal O$ in a quaternion algebra over a number field $F$, the set $\operatorname{Cl}\mathcal O$ of invertible right ideal classes is finite, and its size depends only on the level. If $B$ is indefinite (satisfies the Eichler condition: not totally definite), the reduced norm gives a bijection $\operatorname{Cl}\mathcal O\to\operatorname{Cl}_{S_\infty}\mathbb Z_F$ onto a ray class group, where $S_\infty$ is the set of real places ramified in $B$. ([Kirschmer–Voight, Props. 1.6, 4.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0808.3833))
- **Eichler mass formula.** Let $B$ be a definite quaternion algebra over $\mathbb Q$ of discriminant $D$ and $\mathcal O$ an Eichler order of level $M$. Then $\sum_{[J]\in\operatorname{Cls}\mathcal O}1/w_J=\varphi(D)\psi(M)/12$, where $w_J=\#\mathcal O_L(J)^\times/\{\pm1\}$, $\varphi(D)=\prod_{p\mid D}(p-1)$ and $\psi(M)=M\prod_{p\mid M}(1+1/p)$. It is a weighted class number; a maximal order has class number $1$ exactly for $D=2,3,5,7,13$. ([Voight, Thms. 25.1.1, 25.3.18, 25.4.1](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_25)) For a totally definite quaternion algebra over a totally real field $F$ of degree $n$, the mass is $2^{1-n}|\zeta_F(-1)|h(\mathbb Z_F)\Phi(\mathfrak D)\Psi(\mathfrak N)$. ([Kirschmer–Voight, §5](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0808.3833))
- **Hurwitz order.** In Hamilton's quaternions over $\mathbb Q$, the Lipschitz order $\mathbb Z+\mathbb Zi+\mathbb Zj+\mathbb Zk$ is not maximal; adjoining $(-1+i+j+k)/2$ gives the maximal Hurwitz order, of index $2$ over it. Its unit group has order $24$ and is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb F_3)$, it has a left and right [Euclidean algorithm](node:Euclidean%20Algorithm) for the reduced norm, so every right ideal is principal, and it yields a proof of Lagrange's four-square theorem. ([Voight, Ch. 11](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_11))
- **Azumaya algebras (16H05).** Over a commutative ring $R$, an algebra $A$ is Azumaya if it is finitely generated, faithful and projective as an $R$-module with $A\otimes_RA^{\mathrm{op}}\cong\operatorname{End}_R(A)$, equivalently central and separable over $R$. Over a field these are exactly the central simple algebras; over a [local ring](node:Local%20Rings) every automorphism is inner (Skolem–Noether), and Azumaya algebras up to similarity form the Brauer group of $R$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azumaya_algebra))

### History
Hurwitz developed the arithmetic of integral quaternions in a 1919 treatise. ([Voight, Ch. 11](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_11)) Brandt stated the mass formula in 1928, Hey, a doctoral student of Artin, proved it over $\mathbb Q$ in 1929, and Eichler developed the formula in 1955–56; Körner (1987, over number rings) and Brzezinski (1990, definite orders over $\mathbb Z$) proved general versions. ([Voight, Ch. 25](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_25)) Azumaya introduced Azumaya algebras over commutative [local rings](node:Local%20Rings) in 1951, and Grothendieck based his theory of the Brauer group of a scheme on them in 1964–65. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azumaya_algebra))

### Open problems
- **Condition (SEM).** Marseglia and Smit say an inclusion of orders $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathcal O'$ satisfies (SEM) if every invertible lattice $J$ with right order $\mathcal O'$ is $I\mathcal O'$ for some invertible lattice $I$ with right order $\mathcal O$; they use it to compute all right ideal classes, including non-invertible ones, of orders in quaternion algebras over global fields. Whether (SEM) can fail is open: they do not know whether the algebra of their Example 4.1 satisfies it, and know of no algebra that does not admit it. ([Marseglia–Smit, §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2211.13156))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Order (ring theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_%28ring_theory%29): definitions and standard examples.
- **Learn:** [Voight, Quaternion Algebras, Ch. 10 Orders](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-56694-4_10): open-access graduate text; continue with Chs. 23 and 25.
- **Primary:** [Kirschmer–Voight, Algorithmic enumeration of ideal classes for quaternion orders](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0808.3833): Eichler orders, Eichler's theorem and the mass formula in use; [Marseglia–Smit, Ideal classes of orders in quaternion algebras](https://arxiv.org/html/2211.13156).
- **Further reading:** [Reiner, Maximal Orders](https://academic.oup.com/book/53330) (OUP): the standard monograph on orders over Dedekind domains.
references.MSC 16Kxx - Division rings and semisimpl:
## Reference
### Overview
A division ring is a nonzero unital ring in which every nonzero element is invertible; multiplication need not commute. Division rings are the building blocks of semisimple rings: a ring $R$ is semisimple (every $R$-module is semisimple) iff $R\cong\prod_{i=1}^nM_{n_i}(D_i)$ with each $D_i$ a division ring, and a ring is simple and left or right Artinian iff it is $M_n(D)$ for a division ring $D$. ([MIT 18.706, Lecture 2, Thms. 2.10, 2.16](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec02.pdf)) The $n_i$ and $D_i$ are unique up to reordering, so the [Artin–Wedderburn Theorem](node:Artin–Wedderburn%20Theorem) reduces the classification of finite-dimensional central simple algebras over a field $k$ to that of central division algebras over $k$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Wedderburn_theorem))

Over a field the theory is organized by the Brauer group $\operatorname{Br}K$ of central simple algebras modulo Morita (Brauer) equivalence, with tensor product as the group law; it is always torsion and is isomorphic to the Galois cohomology group $H^2(\operatorname{Gal}(K_s/K),K_s^\times)$, see [Galois Cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology). ([Wikipedia, Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group); [Wikipedia, CSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_simple_algebra))

### Scope
MSC2020 16K, Division rings and semisimple Artin rings (see also 12E15, 15A30), comprises 16K20 finite-dimensional division rings (for crossed products, see 16S35); 16K40 infinite-dimensional and general division rings; 16K50 Brauer groups, algebraic aspects (see also 12G05, 14F22); and 16K99. ([MSC2020, 16K](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Kxx)) It sits in [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras).

Neighbouring codes, from these cross-references: crossed-product constructions are classified in [MSC 16Sxx - Associative rings and algebras arising under various constructions](node:MSC%2016Sxx%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras%20arising%20under%20various%20constructions) (16S35); cohomological aspects of Brauer groups of fields in [MSC 12Gxx - Homological methods (field theory)](node:MSC%2012Gxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20%28field%20theory%29) (12G05); the section heading also points to 12E15 and 15A30. ([MSC2020, 16K](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Kxx)) Separable algebras such as quaternion and Azumaya algebras, and orders in them, are classified in [MSC 16Hxx - Associative algebras and orders](node:MSC%2016Hxx%20-%20Associative%20algebras%20and%20orders). ([MSC2020, 16H](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Hxx))

### Key concepts
- **Central simple algebras.** A central simple algebra (CSA) over $K$ is a finite-dimensional simple $K$-algebra with center exactly $K$; it is $M_n(D)$ for a central division algebra $D$ unique up to isomorphism. Its dimension is a square $d^2$ (the degree $d$); the index is the degree of $D$; the period is its order in $\operatorname{Br}K$. The period divides the index and has the same prime factors, and a central division algebra decomposes uniquely as a tensor product of division algebras of prime-power index. Every CSA has a splitting field $E$ with $A\otimes_KE$ a matrix algebra; maximal subfields of a division algebra split it, and there is a separable splitting field of degree equal to the index (Wedderburn, Köthe). ([Wikipedia, CSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_simple_algebra))
- **Skolem–Noether and double centralizer.** If $A$ is a simple ring, $B$ a central simple $k$-algebra, and $f,g:A\to B$ are $k$-algebra homomorphisms, there is a unit $b\in B$ with $g(a)=bf(a)b^{-1}$ for all $a$; hence every automorphism of a CSA is inner. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skolem%E2%80%93Noether_theorem)) For a simple subalgebra $B$ of a CSA $A$ over $F$, $C_A(C_A(B))=B$ and $\dim_FB\cdot\dim_FC_A(B)=\dim_FA$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_centralizer_theorem))
- **Classical Brauer groups.** $\operatorname{Br}K=0$ for $K$ algebraically closed, finite (Wedderburn's little theorem: a finite division ring is a field), or the function field of a curve over an algebraically closed field (Tsen); $\operatorname{Br}\mathbb R\cong\mathbb Z/2$, generated by Hamilton's quaternions; $\operatorname{Br}K\cong\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ for a non-Archimedean local field. For a global field the Albert–Brauer–Hasse–Noether theorem gives an exact sequence $0\to\operatorname{Br}K\to\bigoplus_v\operatorname{Br}K_v\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to0$; over local and global fields the period equals the index. ([Wikipedia, Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group); [Wikipedia, Division algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_algebra))
- **Cyclic algebras and Merkurjev–Suslin.** If $n$ is invertible in $K$ and $K$ contains a primitive $n$th root of unity $\zeta$, the cyclic (symbol) algebra $(a,b)_\zeta$ is a CSA of degree $n$, and the Merkurjev–Suslin theorem says that the $n$-torsion $\operatorname{Br}_n K$ is generated by such algebras. ([Wikipedia, Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group); [Auel et al., §0](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1006.3304)) It is the degree-2 case (Merkurjev–Suslin, 1982) of the norm residue isomorphism $K^M_n(k)/\ell\cong H^n_{\text{ét}}(k,\mu_\ell^{\otimes n})$ for $\ell$ invertible in $k$, proved in general by Voevodsky using results of Rost. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkurjev%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem)) See [Higher Algebraic K-Theory](node:Higher%20Algebraic%20K-Theory).
- **Crossed products and Amitsur's theorem.** A degree-$n$ division algebra is a $G$-crossed product if it contains a maximal subfield Galois over the center with group $G$. In 1972 Amitsur produced noncrossed product division algebras of every degree divisible by $2^3$ or by $p^2$ for an odd prime $p$, provided the degree is prime to the characteristic. Albert's cyclicity criterion: a division algebra of prime degree $p$ over $F$ is a crossed product iff it contains a non-central $x$ with $x^p\in F$. ([Auel et al., §§0–2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1006.3304))
- **General division rings (16K40).** Division rings arise as rings of fractions: a domain satisfying the right Ore condition ($rS\cap sR\neq\varnothing$) has a classical ring of quotients, right Noetherian domains are right Ore, and a domain is right Ore iff it has finite uniform dimension (Goldie). The free monoid algebra on two generators satisfies no Ore condition yet still embeds in a division ring. ([Wikipedia, Ore condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore_condition)) Frobenius's theorem shows that the finite-dimensional associative division algebras over $\mathbb R$ are $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$ and the quaternions. ([Wikipedia, Division algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_algebra))

### History
Wedderburn proved the finite-dimensional structure theorem (main paper 1908) and Artin extended it to Artinian rings in 1927. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Wedderburn_theorem)) Skolem published his theorem in 1927 and Noether rediscovered it. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skolem%E2%80%93Noether_theorem)) Auslander–Goldman extended the Brauer group to commutative rings and Grothendieck to schemes (1968); de Jong's 2004 paper on the period-index problem for surfaces was an important advance. ([Wikipedia, Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group)) For much of the 20th century it was reasonable to conjecture that every central simple algebra is a crossed product; Amitsur's 1972 noncrossed product division algebras showed otherwise. ([Auel et al., §0](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1006.3304))

### Open problems
- **Albert's cyclicity problem.** Whether every division algebra of prime degree is cyclic is a major open problem; it holds in degrees 2 and 3 and over local and global fields, and is wide open for primes $p\ge5$. ([Wikipedia, Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group)) Auel et al. pose it as Problem 1.1: construct a non-cyclic division algebra of degree $p$ over some field. ([Auel et al., §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1006.3304))
- **Crossed product questions.** Determine whether division algebras of prime period are crossed products (Problem 2.1), whether $p$-algebras of degree $p^2$ are crossed products (Problem 2.2), and whether every CSA over a field of cohomological dimension at most 2 is a crossed product (Problem 2.3); and Albert's question whether $\operatorname{Br}_n F$ is generated by classes of cyclic algebras of degree dividing $n$ (Problem 3.1), which Merkurjev–Suslin answers when $F$ contains a primitive $n$th root of unity, so the open case is fields without one. ([Auel et al., §§2–3](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1006.3304))
- **Period-index problem.** For $K$ of transcendence degree $d$ over an algebraically closed field, the conjecture predicted $\operatorname{ind}(\alpha)\mid\operatorname{per}(\alpha)^{d-1}$ for $\alpha\in\operatorname{Br}K$; it is known for $d\le2$, with de Jong's work an important advance in the case $d=2$. ([Wikipedia, Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group))

> [!warning] Contested
> Perry's preprint (v1 4 August 2026, v2 3 September 2026) claims counterexamples in every dimension $d\ge3$: Brauer classes of period $2$ and index $2^d$, for instance over $\mathbb C$, and proposes a corrected conjecture with factors at small primes, proving only its Hodge-theoretic analogue. ([Perry, arXiv:2608.03684](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03684)) MathWorld reports that, as of 18 September 2026, independent specialist verification and peer review had not been reported. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Period-IndexConjecture.html)) MathWorld adds that the Hodge-theoretic analogue does not establish the corrected bound for the algebraic index.

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group): examples, Hasse sequence, open problems.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.706, Lecture 2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec02.pdf): semisimple modules and Wedderburn's theorem.
- **Primary:** [Auel–Brussel–Garibaldi–Vishne, Open problems on central simple algebras](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1006.3304): survey of cyclicity, crossed products, symbol length and period-index.
- **Further reading:** [Cohn, Skew Fields: Theory of General Division Rings](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139087193) (CUP, 1995): the standard text for 16K40.
references.MSC 16Lxx - Local rings and generalizati:
## Reference
### Overview
A ring $R$ is local if its non-invertible elements form an ideal; that ideal is then the [Jacobson radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical) $J(R)$ and $R/J(R)$ is a division ring. No commutativity or Noetherian hypothesis is involved. ([MIT 18.706, Lecture 4, Def. 4.10](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec04.pdf)) In the commutative case this is a ring with exactly one maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, equivalently a nonzero ring in which, for every $x$, either $x$ or $1-x$ is a unit; localizations $R_{\mathfrak p}$ at primes are local, and a local homomorphism is one with $\varphi(\mathfrak m_R)\subseteq\mathfrak m_S$. ([Stacks, §10.18](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07BH)) See [Local Rings](node:Local%20Rings) and [Local Noncommutative Rings](node:Local%20Noncommutative%20Rings).

Local rings matter in noncommutative algebra mainly as endomorphism rings: an indecomposable module of finite length has a local endomorphism ring (every endomorphism is nilpotent or invertible). ([MIT 18.706, Lecture 4, Prop. 4.15, Lemma 4.16](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec04.pdf)) Semiperfect and perfect rings, special cases of Bass's semilocal rings, were introduced in Bass's 1960 paper through projective covers, as [homological](node:Homological%20Algebra) generalizations of semiprimary rings. ([Lam, §§5–6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0002217))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 16L30 noncommutative local and semilocal rings, perfect rings; 16L60 quasi-Frobenius rings (see also 16D50); and 16L99. ([MSC2020, 16L](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Lxx)) It sits inside [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras).

Neighbouring code: [MSC 16Nxx - Radicals and radical properties of associative rings](node:MSC%2016Nxx%20-%20Radicals%20and%20radical%20properties%20of%20associative%20rings) studies the radicals themselves, including the Jacobson radical (16N20) and nil and nilpotent radicals (16N40). ([MSC2020, 16N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Nxx)) In commutative algebra, [MSC 13Hxx - Local rings and semilocal rings](node:MSC%2013Hxx%20-%20Local%20rings%20and%20semilocal%20rings) has 13H05 regular local rings, 13H10 special types (Cohen–Macaulay, Gorenstein, Buchsbaum, etc.) and 13H15 multiplicity theory. ([MSC2020, 13H](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Hxx))

### Key concepts
- **Nakayama's lemma.** If $U$ is a nonzero finitely generated right module over a unital ring $R$, then $UJ(R)$ is a proper submodule of $U$. Over a commutative local ring, a basis of $M/\mathfrak mM$ lifts to a minimal generating set of a finitely generated module $M$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakayama%27s_lemma)) Kaplansky used a related argument to show that every projective module over a local ring is free. ([Lam, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0002217))
- **Krull–Schmidt–Azumaya.** A nonzero module of finite length is a direct sum of indecomposables, unique up to permutation and isomorphism; Azumaya extended uniqueness to possibly infinite direct sums of modules with local endomorphism rings. The statement fails for modules that are only Noetherian or only Artinian. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull%E2%80%93Schmidt_theorem))
- **Semilocal and semiperfect rings (16L30).** $R$ is semilocal if $R/J(R)$ is semisimple Artinian (Bass's definition, which for noncommutative rings is not the same as having finitely many maximal ideals). Bass's Theorem: for any ring, the following are equivalent: $R$ is left semiperfect (every cyclic left module has a projective cover); every finitely generated left module has a projective cover; $R$ is semilocal and idempotents lift modulo $J(R)$. For commutative $R$ these are equivalent to $R$ being a finite product of local rings. Equivalently $1=e_1+\dots+e_n$ with orthogonal idempotents and each $e_iRe_i$ local, and $\operatorname{End}_S(M)$ is semiperfect iff $M$ is a finite direct sum of modules with local endomorphism rings. Every semilocal ring has stable range $1$. ([Lam, §§5, 8, Thms. 5.1, 5.2, 8.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0002217)) See [Units and Idempotents in Rings](node:Units%20and%20Idempotents%20in%20Rings).
- **Bass's Theorem P (perfect rings).** For a ring $R$ with $J=J(R)$, the following are equivalent: $R$ is left perfect (every left module has a projective cover); $R$ is semilocal and $J$ is left T-nilpotent (for any $a_1,a_2,\ldots\in J$, $a_1a_2\cdots a_n=0$ for some $n$); $R$ is semilocal and every nonzero left module has a maximal submodule; every flat left module is projective; $R$ satisfies DCC on principal right ideals; every right module satisfies DCC on cyclic submodules; $R$ is semilocal and every nonzero right module has a minimal submodule. Left and right perfect differ in general, and a semiprime left perfect ring is semisimple. ([Lam, Thm. 6.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0002217))
- **Quasi-Frobenius rings (16L60).** $R$ is QF if it is Noetherian and self-injective on one side, or Artinian on one side and self-injective on the other; equivalently projective and injective modules coincide. Frobenius algebras, semisimple rings and $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ ($n>1$) are QF; for commutative rings QF equals Frobenius and both mean finite products of local Artinian rings with a unique minimal ideal. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-Frobenius_ring)) Iovanov lists group algebras of finite groups among the examples and records Faith and Walker's characterization that all injective modules are projective (or all projective modules injective). ([Iovanov, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.2901))
- **Pseudo-Frobenius rings.** Right PF rings, in which every faithful right module is a generator, are semiperfect, and the rings admitting a Morita duality are semiperfect (Osofsky). ([Lam, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0002217)) Guil Asensio, Sahinkaya and Srivastava characterize PF and QF rings by tight modules using Osofsky's set-theoretic counting arguments. ([Guil Asensio et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.07815))

### History
Bass's 1960 paper introduced projective covers (dual to Eckmann–Schöpf injective hulls), defined perfect and semiperfect rings, and proved Theorem P; Lam notes that Theorem 6.1 is often misquoted because its conditions switch from left to right modules. ([Lam, §§5–6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0002217)) Nakayama defined QF rings in 1941 as Artinian rings with a Nakayama permutation, with Brauer, Morita, Nesbitt and Thrall among the early contributors. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-Frobenius_ring)) Jacobson treated the noncommutative Nakayama lemma for right ideals in 1945 and Azumaya and Nakayama gave general versions in 1951. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakayama%27s_lemma))

### Open problems
- **Faith's QF conjecture.** A left self-injective semiprimary ring is QF. Iovanov calls it one of the most interesting questions in ring theory and proves it for algebras over a field that are at most countable dimensional modulo the Jacobson radical, recovering other known cases (countable dimensional algebras; $|A/J|\le\aleph_0$ or $|A/J|<|A|$). ([Iovanov, abstract and §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.2901); [arXiv abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.2901))
- **Faith–Menal conjecture.** Every strongly right Johns ring is QF. Shen and Chen list it among three open conjectures on QF rings and prove it under the extra condition that every nonzero complement left ideal is not small. ([Shen–Chen](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0504068))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Quasi-Frobenius ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-Frobenius_ring): definitions, examples and generalizations.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.706, Lecture 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec04.pdf): Jacobson radical, local rings, indecomposable modules; [Stacks, Local rings](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07BH): commutative case.
- **Primary:** [Lam, Bass's work in ring theory and projective modules](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0002217): survey of semiperfect and perfect rings with the exact form of Theorem P.
- **Further reading:** [Nicholson–Yousif, Quasi-Frobenius Rings](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511546525) (CUP, 2003): the standard monograph on QF rings.
references.MSC 16Nxx - Radicals and radical propert:
## Reference
### Overview
A radical assigns to each ring an ideal that collects its "bad" elements, so that dividing it out leaves a ring that is semisimple for that radical. The leading example is the [Jacobson Radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical) $J(R)$, the intersection of the annihilators of all simple $R$-modules; for $a\in R$ this is equivalent to $a$ lying in every maximal left ideal, to $a$ lying in every maximal right ideal, and to $1-xay$ being invertible for all $x,y\in R$. ([MIT 18.706, Lecture 3, Def. 3.20, Lemma 3.21](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec03.pdf)) Nathan Jacobson first studied it for arbitrary rings in "The radical and semi-simplicity for arbitrary rings" (*Amer. J. Math.*, 1945). ([Wikipedia, Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical))

Alongside $J(R)$ sit the nil radicals: the lower nilradical (prime or Baer–McCoy radical), the intersection of the prime ideals; the Levitzki radical, the largest locally nilpotent ideal; and the upper nilradical, the ideal generated by all nil ideals, which is itself nil. The Levitzki radical lies between the lower and upper nilradicals, and $J(R)$ contains every nil ideal, so all three nil radicals lie in $J(R)$. ([Wikipedia, Nilradical of a ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilradical_of_a_ring); [Wikipedia, Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical)) The best-known question of the area, Köthe's conjecture (1930), concerns nil one-sided ideals and is equivalent to a statement about polynomial extensions of nil rings. ([Wikipedia, Köthe conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture); [Greenfeld–King–Vendramin, arXiv 2609.15080](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.15080))

### Scope
MSC2020 16N lists: 16N20 Jacobson radical, quasimultiplication; 16N40 nil and nilpotent radicals, sets, ideals; 16N60 prime and semiprime associative rings (see also 16D60, 16U10); 16N80 general radicals and associative rings (for radicals in module categories, see 16S90); 16N99. ([MSC2020, 16N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Nxx))

Neighbours: radicals of module categories and torsion theories belong to 16S90 in [MSC 16Sxx - Associative rings and algebras arising under various constructions](node:MSC%2016Sxx%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras%20arising%20under%20various%20constructions), whose entry says "for radicals of rings, see 16Nxx"; 16N60 points to 16D60 in [MSC 16Dxx - Modules, bimodules and ideals in associative algebras](node:MSC%2016Dxx%20-%20Modules,%20bimodules%20and%20ideals%20in%20associative%20algebras) and to 16U10 in [MSC 16Uxx - Conditions on elements](node:MSC%2016Uxx%20-%20Conditions%20on%20elements). ([MSC2020, 16N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Nxx); [MSC2020, 16S](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Sxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Jacobson Radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical) (16N20).** $J(R)$ is the intersection of maximal left ideals and also of maximal right ideals, so it is a two-sided ideal; Nakayama's lemma says that if $R$ is unital and $M$ is a finitely generated left $R$-module with $J(R)M=M$, then $M=0$. If $R$ is left or right Artinian, $J(R)$ is nilpotent; for upper triangular matrices over a field it is the strictly upper triangular matrices. ([Wikipedia, Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical); [MIT 18.706, Lemma 3.21](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec03.pdf))
- **Nil radicals and Levitzki's theorem (16N40).** Levitzki's theorem: if $R$ is right Noetherian, every nil one-sided ideal of $R$ is nilpotent (submitted 1939, published 1950; Utumi gave a short proof in 1963). In a Noetherian ring the lower, Levitzki and upper nilradicals coincide and are nilpotent; see [Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings). ([Wikipedia, Levitzky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levitzky%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Nilradical of a ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilradical_of_a_ring))
- **General (Kurosh–Amitsur) radicals (16N80).** A radical property $r$ is one whose class of $r$-rings is closed under homomorphic images, such that every ring $A$ has a largest $r$-ideal $r(A)$ and $r(A/r(A))=0$; a ring with no nonzero $r$-ideals is $r$-semisimple. Every class $\delta$ has a lower radical (the smallest radical class containing $\delta$), and a regular class has an upper radical. The Brown–McCoy radical, the intersection of the maximal two-sided ideals, is the upper radical of the class of simple unital rings. ([Wikipedia, Radical of a ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_of_a_ring))
- **Graded rings.** Bergman (1975 preprint) proved that the Jacobson radical of a $\mathbb Z$-graded ring is homogeneous and graded nil. Smoktunowicz proved the analogous statement for the nil radical, and that a subring generated by homogeneous elements of a graded Jacobson radical ring is Jacobson radical. ([Bell–Greenfeld, arXiv 1605.09585](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.09585); [Smoktunowicz, arXiv 1301.2835](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.2835)) See [Graded Algebras](node:Graded%20Algebras).
- **Köthe's conjecture and its equivalents (16N40, 16N20).** Köthe (1930): a ring with no nonzero nil ideal has no nonzero nil one-sided ideal. Equivalent forms include: the sum of two nil left ideals is nil; $M_n(J)$ is nil whenever $J$ is nil; and (Krempa, Amitsur) $R[t]$ is Jacobson radical for every nil ring $R$. It holds for PI rings and right Noetherian rings. ([Wikipedia, Köthe conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture); [Greenfeld–King–Vendramin, arXiv 2609.15080](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.15080)) Amitsur proved the conjecture, and indeed that $R[x]$ is nil for nil $R$, when $R$ is an algebra over an uncountable field; Smoktunowicz constructed nil rings $R$ over countable fields with $R[x]$ not nil. ([Bell–Greenfeld, arXiv 1605.09585](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.09585))
- **Prime and semiprime rings (16N60).** The lower nilradical is the intersection of the prime ideals; it lies below the Levitzki radical and the upper nilradical, and in commutative rings it is the set of nilpotent elements; see [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals). ([Wikipedia, Nilradical of a ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilradical_of_a_ring); [Wikipedia, Radical of a ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_of_a_ring))

### History
Köthe posed his conjecture in 1930. Levitzki used his nilpotence theorem in 1945 to answer a question of Köthe, and Jacobson's 1945 paper extended the radical to arbitrary rings. ([Wikipedia, Köthe conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture); [Wikipedia, Levitzky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levitzky%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Jacobson radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson_radical)) Amitsur settled the uncountable-field case in 1956, and Smoktunowicz's counterexamples to Amitsur's stronger conjecture showed that polynomial rings over nil rings need not be nil. ([Bell–Greenfeld, arXiv 1605.09585](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.09585)) Lam's *A First Course in Noncommutative Rings* (Springer GTM, 2001) is a graduate text in the area. ([Crossref, Lam](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-8616-0))

> [!warning] Contested
> In September 2026 two arXiv preprints claimed to refute Köthe's conjecture. Adamczewski, Böhmler and Marczinzik "construct a counterexample to Köthe's conjecture and use this to also answer a question due to Rowen" ([arXiv 2609.07996](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07996)). Greenfeld, King and Vendramin construct, over a countable algebraically closed field, a finitely generated, graded nil algebra $A$ admitting a point module, and show $A[t]$ is not Jacobson radical; they report that the first counterexample was found by an AI model and checked in Lean 4 ([arXiv 2609.15080](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.15080)). Neither arXiv page lists a journal reference, so the refutation has not yet appeared in refereed form. Earlier sources, such as Bell and Greenfeld (2017), describe the conjecture as "still open" ([arXiv 1605.09585](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.09585)), while Wikipedia now describes it as disproved ([Wikipedia, Köthe conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture)).

### Open problems
- **Nil algebras of finite [Gelfand–Kirillov dimension](node:Gelfand–Kirillov%20Dimension) over uncountable fields.** Lenagan, Smoktunowicz and Young construct, over any countable field, a two-generated infinite-dimensional nil algebra of GK dimension at most 3, note that their methods "depend crucially on the countability hypothesis", and ask whether a finitely generated infinite-dimensional nil algebra of finite GK dimension exists over an uncountable field. ([Lenagan–Smoktunowicz–Young, arXiv 1008.4461](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1008.4461))
- **Free subalgebras of polynomial rings over nil rings.** Bell and Greenfeld state that it is not known whether there is a nil algebra $R$ such that $R[x]$ contains a free noncommutative subalgebra. ([Bell–Greenfeld, arXiv 1605.09585](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.09585))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Radical of a ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_of_a_ring): Kurosh–Amitsur radicals and the standard examples.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.706 Noncommutative Algebra, Lecture 3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec03.pdf): characterizations of the Jacobson radical.
- **Primary:** [Bell and Greenfeld, Free subalgebras of graded algebras (J. Algebra 2017; arXiv 1605.09585)](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.09585): research paper with a survey of Köthe's and Amitsur's conjectures and graded radicals.
- **Primary:** [Greenfeld, King and Vendramin, The Köthe conjecture via point modules (arXiv 2609.15080)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.15080): 2026 preprint (not yet refereed) giving a construction that claims to refute Köthe's conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Lam, A First Course in Noncommutative Rings (Springer GTM, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-8616-0): graduate text on noncommutative ring theory.
references.MSC 16Pxx - Chain conditions, growth con:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 16Pxx collects finiteness conditions on associative rings and algebras: finite rings and finite-dimensional algebras, the Artinian and Noetherian chain conditions, Goldie-type conditions on annihilators, Krull dimension, and growth measured by Gelfand–Kirillov (GK) dimension. Within [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras), it is the place where size and finiteness hypotheses are turned into structure theorems. ([MSC2020, 16Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Pxx))

Two families of results dominate. On the chain-condition side, Hopkins–Levitzki shows that one-sided Artinian rings are Noetherian, and Goldie's theorem shows that semiprime Noetherian rings embed in semisimple Artinian quotient rings, so that Artin–Wedderburn applies. On the growth side, GK dimension behaves like Krull dimension for finitely generated algebras, and its small values are rigid: Bergman's gap theorem, the Small–Stafford–Warfield theorem, and the Smoktunowicz gap theorem. ([Wikipedia, Hopkins–Levitzki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins%E2%80%93Levitzki_theorem); [Wikipedia, Goldie's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldie%27s_theorem); [MIT 18.706, Lecture 24](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec24.pdf))

Growth also links ring theory to Burnside-type questions. The Kurosh problem asked whether finitely generated algebraic algebras are finite-dimensional; Golod and Shafarevich disproved it in 1964, and the modern question is how slowly such counterexamples can grow. ([Bell–Young, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1102.0362))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists: 16P10 finite rings and finite-dimensional associative algebras (semisimple ones go to 16K20, commutative ones to 11Txx and 13Mxx); 16P20 Artinian rings and modules; 16P40 Noetherian rings and modules; 16P50 localization and Noetherian rings (see also 16U20); 16P60 chain conditions on annihilators and summands, Goldie-type conditions, and Krull dimension; 16P70 chain conditions on other classes of submodules, ideals, and subrings, and coherence; 16P90 growth rate and GK dimension; 16P99 other. ([MSC2020, 16Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Pxx))

Neighbours: semisimple Artinian rings themselves belong to [MSC 16Kxx - Division rings and semisimple Artin rings](node:MSC%2016Kxx%20-%20Division%20rings%20and%20semisimple%20Artin%20rings), while Ore localization as an operation on multiplicative sets is 16U20 in [MSC 16Uxx - Conditions on elements](node:MSC%2016Uxx%20-%20Conditions%20on%20elements). Rings with polynomial identity, which appear here as the GK-dimension-one case, have their own code [MSC 16Rxx - Rings with polynomial identity](node:MSC%2016Rxx%20-%20Rings%20with%20polynomial%20identity). ([MSC2020, 16Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Pxx))

For a finitely generated $k$-algebra $A$ with finite-dimensional generating subspace $V\ni 1$, put $d_V(n)=\dim_k V^n$; then $\operatorname{GKdim}A=\inf\{\alpha: d_V(n)\le Cn^\alpha \text{ for some } C\}$, independent of $V$. For finitely generated commutative algebras it equals Krull dimension, and $\operatorname{GKdim}k[x_1,\dots,x_n]=n$. ([MIT 18.706, Definition 24.1 and Example 24.2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec24.pdf); [Wikipedia, GK dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand%E2%80%93Kirillov_dimension))

### Key concepts
- **Hopkins–Levitzki theorem.** For a unital semiprimary ring $R$ (with $R/J(R)$ semisimple and $J(R)$ nilpotent), a module is Noetherian iff Artinian iff of finite length. Right Artinian rings are semiprimary, so every right Artinian ring is right Noetherian. Hopkins and Levitzki published it independently in 1939. ([Wikipedia, Hopkins–Levitzki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins%E2%80%93Levitzki_theorem)) See [Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings) and [Jacobson Radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical).
- **Goldie's theorem.** A ring is right Goldie if it has finite right uniform dimension and ACC on right annihilators. A semiprime ring is right Goldie iff it has a semisimple Artinian right classical ring of quotients; every semiprime right Noetherian ring qualifies, and [Artin–Wedderburn](node:Artin–Wedderburn%20Theorem) then describes the quotient ring. ([Wikipedia, Goldie's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldie%27s_theorem)) See [Localization of Rings](node:Localization%20of%20Rings).
- **Krull dimension.** For a module over a possibly noncommutative ring, the Krull dimension is the deviation of its poset of submodules; for commutative Noetherian rings this agrees with the prime-chain definition. ([Wikipedia, Krull dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_dimension)) The definition now in use is due to Rentschler and Gabriel.
