([Goodearl–Warfield, Krull dimension chapter](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-noncommutative-noetherian-rings/krull-dimension/B8AB25B87819F3D958ADAB4FD66CC36B))
- **[Gelfand–Kirillov Dimension](node:Gelfand–Kirillov%20Dimension) and its gaps.** GK dimension in $[0,1)$ forces finite dimensionality (GK dimension 0). Bergman: no finitely generated algebra has GK dimension strictly between 1 and 2. Warfield: every real $r\ge2$ is the GK dimension of a 2-generated algebra. Smoktunowicz: no graded domain has GK dimension in the open interval $(2,3)$. Berele: finitely generated PI algebras have finite GK dimension. ([MIT 18.706, Lemma 24.5, Theorems 24.6, 24.8, 24.12, 24.13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec24.pdf))
- **GK dimension one and two.** Small and Warfield showed that a finitely generated prime algebra of GK dimension 1 is a finite module over its centre and hence PI. Small–Stafford–Warfield extended the PI conclusion to all affine algebras of GK dimension one. A graded domain with GK dimension in $[2,3)$ has quadratic growth. ([Bell, A dichotomy result for prime algebras of GK dimension two, §§1–2 and references](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0911.4214)) See [Polynomial Identity Rings](node:Polynomial%20Identity%20Rings).
- **Artin–Stafford classification.** Over an algebraically closed field, if $A$ is a finitely graded domain with $\operatorname{GKdim}A=2$, its graded quotient ring is $K[t,t^{-1};\sigma]$ with $\operatorname{tr.deg}(K/k)=1$. If $A$ is also generated in degree 1, it embeds in a twisted homogeneous coordinate ring $B(X,\mathcal L,\sigma)$ of a projective curve, isomorphically in large degrees. ([Rogalski, Theorem 5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065)) See [Graded Algebras](node:Graded%20Algebras).
- **Golod–Shafarevich and Kurosh.** Let $B=K\langle x_1,\dots,x_{d+1}\rangle/J$, where $J$ is generated by homogeneous relations of degrees $\ge2$ and $r_i$ of them have degree $i$. If $r_i\le d^2/4$ for all $i$, then $B$ is infinite-dimensional (1964). This gives finitely generated nil, hence algebraic, algebras that are infinite-dimensional, refuting Kurosh's conjecture, and also counterexamples to the generalized Burnside problem. ([Wikipedia, Golod–Shafarevich theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golod%E2%80%93Shafarevich_theorem); [Bell–Young](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1102.0362))
- **Slow-growth nil algebras.** Lenagan and Smoktunowicz built an infinite-dimensional affine nil algebra of finite nonzero GK dimension over a countable field (bound 20, later lowered to 3 with Young). Bell and Young showed that over any field and for any weakly increasing $\alpha\to\infty$, there is a finitely generated graded algebra with nil augmentation ideal and $\dim B(n)\le n^{\alpha(n)}$ for large $n$. ([Lenagan–Smoktunowicz](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0505141); [Bell–Young, Theorem 1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1102.0362))
- **Noetherian growth.** Stephenson–Zhang: a right (or left) Noetherian graded algebra has subexponential growth. ([MIT 18.706, Theorem 24.21](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec24.pdf))

### History
Hopkins and Levitzki (1939) linked the two chain conditions, after Akizuki's 1935 commutative case; Goldie's key papers on quotient rings date from 1958 and 1960. Golod and Shafarevich (1964) produced the first infinite-dimensional finitely generated algebraic algebras, and Lenagan and Smoktunowicz (2007) the first such nil algebra of finite GK dimension. Artin and Stafford's classification of graded domains of quadratic growth appeared in Inventiones in 1995, with the semiprime case following in 2000. ([Wikipedia, Hopkins–Levitzki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins%E2%80%93Levitzki_theorem); [Wikipedia, Goldie's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldie%27s_theorem); [Bell–Young](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1102.0362); [Rogalski, references AS1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065))

### Open problems
- **Kurosh problem with polynomial growth over uncountable fields.** Bell and Young pose as Question 1 whether, over an uncountable field $K$, there is an infinite-dimensional finitely generated algebraic $K$-algebra of finite GK dimension; the countable-field constructions do not transfer, and over uncountable fields "there has not been much progress since" Golod–Shafarevich. ([Bell–Young](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1102.0362))
- **Artin's conjecture on noncommutative surfaces.** The birational classification of noncommutative projective surfaces asks which division rings occur as $Q_{gr}(A)_0$ for finitely graded domains $A$ of GK dimension 3. Artin listed the known families and conjectured the list is complete; Rogalski calls this "still open" and "one of the important but elusive goals" of the subject. ([Rogalski, §5.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065))
- **Anick's conjecture.** If $A$ is an augmented connected graded algebra of polynomial growth and finite global dimension $d$, then $h_A(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}(1-t^{e_i})^{-1}$ for some positive integers $e_i$, the Hilbert series of a weighted polynomial ring. Gateva-Ivanova records it as a conjecture verified only in special cases: commutative algebras, enveloping algebras of [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras), monomial algebras, Noetherian PI rings, and algebras whose associated monomial algebra has finite global dimension. The MIT course states a right Noetherian version as Conjecture 24.25. ([Gateva-Ivanova, Conjecture 2.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.11281); [MIT 18.706, Conjecture 24.25](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec24.pdf))
- **Quadratic growth in GK dimension 2.** Bell notes there are no known examples of domains, simple rings, or prime Noetherian rings of GK dimension 2 without quadratic growth. ([Bell, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0911.4214))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Goldie's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldie%27s_theorem) and [Gelfand–Kirillov dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand%E2%80%93Kirillov_dimension): statements and basic facts.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.706, Lecture 24](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec24.pdf): GK dimension, Warfield and Bergman theorems with proofs, Noetherian growth.
- **Primary:** [Bell and Young, On the Kurosh problem for algebras over a general field](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1102.0362): research paper on subexponential nil algebras with a survey of the Kurosh problem.
- **Further reading:** [Krause and Lenagan, Growth of algebras and Gelfand–Kirillov dimension](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL80025W): AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 22, revised edition 2000; [McConnell and Robson, Noncommutative Noetherian rings](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL4962904W): the standard monograph on Noetherian ring theory (AMS edition 2001); [Rogalski, An introduction to noncommutative projective geometry](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065): graded algebras of low GK dimension.
references.MSC 16Rxx - Rings with polynomial identi:
## Reference
### Overview
A ring $R$ is a PI ring if some nonzero noncommutative polynomial $P\in\mathbb Z\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ vanishes on all substitutions from $R$; for an algebra over a field or commutative ring $k$ one asks for a nonzero $P\in k\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$. Commutative rings are PI rings via $xy-yx$. ([MIT 18.706, Lecture 22, Def. 22.5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec22.pdf)) Because $pX=0$ makes every ring of characteristic $p$ a PI ring, some authors require a monic identity; the identity can always be taken multilinear. Subrings, quotients, finite products, tensor products and matrix rings over PI rings are PI, and an algebra finitely generated as a module over its centre by $n$ elements satisfies the standard identity $s_N$ for $N>n$. ([Wikipedia, PI algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PI_algebra))

The theory says that a PI ring behaves much like a ring that is finite over its centre: primitive PI rings are finite-dimensional central simple, prime PI rings have central simple rings of fractions, and affine PI algebras over a field satisfy the Kurosh conjecture and a Nullstellensatz. ([MIT 18.706, Lecture 23, Thms 23.3–23.4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec23.pdf); [Wikipedia, PI algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PI_algebra)) The second strand is the [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) of the identities themselves: the set of identities of a ring is a T-ideal, an ideal of the free algebra stable under all its endomorphisms, and every T-ideal $I$ gives a PI ring $F/I$. ([Wikipedia, PI algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PI_algebra)) See [Polynomial Identity Rings](node:Polynomial%20Identity%20Rings).

### Scope
MSC2020 16R lists: 16R10 T-ideals, identities, varieties of associative rings and algebras; 16R20 semiprime p.i. rings, rings embeddable in matrices over commutative rings; 16R30 trace rings and invariant theory; 16R40 identities other than those of matrices over commutative rings; 16R50 other kinds of identities (generalized polynomial, rational, involution); 16R60 functional identities; 16R99. No individual 16R code carries a cross-reference; the whole of 16 points to 13 for the commutative case. ([MSC2020, 16R](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Rxx))

Neighbours: identities with involution are listed in 16R50, while rings with involution, graded rings and group actions as structures are 16W10, 16W22 and 16W50 in [MSC 16Wxx - Associative rings and algebras with additional structure](node:MSC%2016Wxx%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras%20with%20additional%20structure); the structure theory of prime and semiprime rings in general is [MSC 16Nxx - Radicals and radical properties of associative rings](node:MSC%2016Nxx%20-%20Radicals%20and%20radical%20properties%20of%20associative%20rings) (16N60). ([MSC2020, 16W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Wxx); [MSC2020, 16R](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Rxx))

### Key concepts
- **Amitsur–Levitzki theorem (16R10).** For every commutative ring $R$ and $n\ge1$, $M_n(R)$ satisfies the standard identity $s_{2n}=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{2n}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)x_{\sigma(1)}\cdots x_{\sigma(2n)}$, and if $R\ne0$ no nonzero homogeneous identity of smaller degree holds. Rosset's proof uses the [Cayley–Hamilton Theorem](node:Cayley–Hamilton%20Theorem), and another proof goes through the Lie algebra cohomology of $\mathfrak{gl}(n)$. ([MIT 18.706, Thm 22.9, §§22.6, 23.1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec22.pdf); [Lecture 23](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec23.pdf)) For $2\times2$ matrices the Hall identity $[[x,y]^2,z]=0$ holds; the infinite Grassmann algebra in characteristic 0 satisfies $[[x,y],z]=0$ but no $s_N$. ([Wikipedia, PI algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PI_algebra))
- **Kaplansky's theorem (16R20).** If $A$ is a primitive PI algebra over a field satisfying a homogeneous identity of degree $d$, then $A$ is a simple algebra of degree $m\le d/2$ over its centre, which is a field. ([MIT 18.706, Thm 23.3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec23.pdf))
- **Posner's and Rowen's theorems (16R20).** Posner (1960): if $A$ is a prime PI algebra with centre $Z$, then $Z$ is a domain and $A\otimes_Z\operatorname{Frac}(Z)\cong M_n(D)$ for a division ring $D$ finite-dimensional over $\operatorname{Frac}(Z)$. Rowen: in a semiprime PI algebra every nonzero two-sided ideal meets the centre. ([MIT 18.706, Thms 23.4–23.5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec23.pdf); [Wikipedia, Posner's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posner%27s_theorem))
- **Central polynomials.** A polynomial $p$ is central for $R$ if all its values lie in the centre of $R$ but $p$ is not an identity of $R$; a central polynomial for $n\times n$ matrices is moreover required to be non-constant, so that nonzero constants do not count. ([Kanel-Belov–Malev–Rowen–Yavich, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.07785); [Wikipedia, Central polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_polynomial)) Central polynomials for every $M_n$ were found independently by Formanek (J. Algebra 23, 1972) and Razmyslov; for $2\times2$ matrices $(xy-yx)^2=-\det(xy-yx)I$ is one, by Cayley–Hamilton. ([Crossref, Formanek 1972](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Formanek+Central+polynomials+for+matrix+rings&rows=3); [Wikipedia, Central polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_polynomial)) Razmyslov's polynomial built from Capelli polynomials takes scalar values on $M_n(k)$ and is not identically zero, and it is the tool behind Rowen's theorem. ([MIT 18.706, Def. 23.10, Thm 23.11](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec23.pdf))
- **Kemer theory (16R10).** Kemer proved that every affine PI algebra over an infinite field is PI-equivalent to a finite-dimensional algebra, and that in characteristic 0 every PI algebra is PI-equivalent to the Grassmann envelope of a finite-dimensional algebra; Kemer also solved Specht's finite basis problem in characteristic 0. Belov proved that relatively free affine PI algebras over an arbitrary field are representable; Specht's problem for affine algebras has a complete proof in every positive characteristic, while the non-affine case has counterexamples (Belov). ([Belov–Rowen–Vishne, arXiv 1805.04450](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1805.04450))
- **Codimension growth (16R10).** The codimension sequence $c_n(A)$ measures the quantity of multilinear identities of degree $n$ of an algebra $A$. Regev proved that for every associative PI algebra $A$ there is a constant $a$ with $c_n(A)<a^n$ for all $n\ge1$, and Giambruno and Zaicev confirmed Amitsur's conjecture that the PI-exponent $\exp(A)=\lim_{n\to\infty}c_n(A)^{1/n}$ exists and is a non-negative integer for every associative PI algebra over a field of characteristic zero. ([Zaicev–Repovš, arXiv 2407.17122, §1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.17122))

### History
The Hall identity goes back to Wagner (1937) and M. Hall (1943), and Rosset gave a proof of the Amitsur–Levitzki theorem through the Cayley–Hamilton theorem. ([Wikipedia, PI algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PI_algebra); [MIT 18.706, Lecture 23](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec23.pdf)) Posner's theorem appeared in *Proc. Amer. Math. Soc.* 11 (1960), and Formanek's central polynomials in 1972. ([Wikipedia, Posner's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posner%27s_theorem); [Crossref, Formanek 1972](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Formanek+Central+polynomials+for+matrix+rings&rows=3)) Standard monographs include Rowen, *Polynomial Identities in Ring Theory* (1980), Drensky–Formanek, *Polynomial Identity Rings* (2004), and Giambruno–Zaicev, *Polynomial Identities and Asymptotic Methods* (2005). ([Wikipedia, PI algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PI_algebra))

### Open problems
- **L'vov–Kaplansky conjecture.** For a multilinear polynomial $p$ and $M_n(K)$, the image of $p$ is one of $\{0\}$, the scalar matrices, $\mathfrak{sl}_n(K)$, or $M_n(K)$; equivalently, over an infinite field the set of values is a vector space. Kanel-Belov, Malev, Rowen and Yavich (SIGMA 2020) prove it for $n=2$ over quadratically closed fields and over $\mathbb R$, obtain only a list of six possible images for $n=3$ over algebraically closed fields ("we do not settle the L'vov–Kaplansky conjecture completely"), and work "while lacking a verification of this conjecture" in general. ([Kanel-Belov–Malev–Rowen–Yavich, arXiv 1909.07785](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.07785))
- **Specht's problem in positive characteristic.** The same survey states that Specht's finite basis problem "for multilinear polynomial identities is not yet settled in nonzero characteristic", and that Kemer's solution is non-computational, so explicit generators of the T-ideal of identities of $M_n$ for $n>2$ are not known. ([Kanel-Belov–Malev–Rowen–Yavich, §1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.07785))
- **Nonassociative representability.** Belov, Rowen and Vishne state that "the representability question remains open for nonassociative algebras"; see [Nonassociative Algebras](node:Nonassociative%20Algebras). ([arXiv 1805.04450](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1805.04450))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, PI algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PI_algebra): definitions, standard and Hall identities, T-ideals, monographs.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.706 Noncommutative Algebra, Lectures 22–23](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec23.pdf): Amitsur–Levitzki, Kaplansky, Posner and Rowen theorems, Razmyslov's central polynomial.
- **Primary:** [Kanel-Belov, Malev, Rowen and Yavich, Evaluations of noncommutative polynomials on algebras (SIGMA 2020; arXiv 1909.07785)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.07785): survey of polynomial images and the L'vov–Kaplansky conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Belov, Rowen and Vishne, Representability of affine algebras over an arbitrary field (arXiv 1805.04450)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1805.04450): Kemer's representability theory and its extension to [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields).
- **Further reading:** [Drensky and Formanek, Polynomial Identity Rings (Birkhäuser, 2004), Crossref records](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Formanek+Central+polynomials+for+matrix+rings&rows=3): graduate text with chapters on central polynomials for matrices; the same listing gives Formanek's 1972 paper.
references.MSC 16Sxx - Associative rings and algebr:
## Reference
### Overview
16S collects the standard ways of building associative rings: by universal properties (free algebras, tensor algebras, free products), by adjoining a variable with a twisted commutation rule (Ore extensions), from groups and group actions (group rings, skew group rings, crossed products), by inverting elements (rings of fractions), and by deforming a known algebra. Every algebra is a quotient of a free algebra, and the tensor algebra $T_R(V)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}V^{\otimes_R n}$ of a bimodule $V$ is the universal algebra generated by $V$ over $R$. ([Crawley-Boevey, Noncommutative algebra, §2.1](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/1617noncommalg/Noncommutative%20algebra.pdf))

A presentation by generators and relations does not by itself give a basis. Normal forms come from the Diamond Lemma and [Gröbner bases](node:Noncommutative%20Gröbner%20Bases), and PBW theorems compare a filtered algebra with its associated graded algebra; these techniques and their applications to [quantum groups](node:Quantum%20Groups), graded Hecke algebras and symplectic reflection algebras are surveyed by Shepler and Witherspoon. ([Shepler–Witherspoon, Abstract](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/shepler-witherspoon-pbw.pdf)) The constructions also produce some of the best-known open problems of ring theory, the Kaplansky conjectures for group rings and the Dixmier conjecture for the first Weyl algebras. ([Wikipedia, Kaplansky's conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures); [Wikipedia, Dixmier conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixmier_conjecture))

### Scope
MSC2020 16S lists: 16S10 rings determined by universal properties (free algebras, coproducts, adjunction of inverses); 16S15 finite generation, finite presentability, normal forms (diamond lemma, term-rewriting); 16S20 centralizing and normalizing extensions; 16S30 universal enveloping algebras of Lie algebras (see mainly 17B35); 16S32 rings of differential operators (see also 13N10, 32C38); 16S34 group rings (see also 20C05, 20C07), Laurent polynomial rings; 16S35 twisted and skew group rings, crossed products; 16S36 ordinary and skew polynomial rings and semigroup rings (see also 20M25); 16S37 quadratic and Koszul algebras; 16S38 rings arising from noncommutative algebraic geometry (see also 14A22); 16S40 smash products of general Hopf actions (see also 16T05); 16S50 endomorphism rings, matrix rings (see also 15-XX); 16S60 rings of functions, subdirect products, sheaves of rings; 16S70 extensions by ideals; 16S80 deformations (see also 13D10, 14D15); 16S85 rings of fractions and localizations (see also 13B30); 16S88 Leavitt path algebras; 16S90 torsion theories, radicals on module categories (see also 13D30, 18E40); 16S99. ([MSC2020, 16S](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Sxx))

Neighbours, by the cross-references: enveloping algebras are classified mainly in 17B35 of [MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras); Hopf actions border 16T05 in [MSC 16Txx - Hopf algebras, quantum groups and related topics](node:MSC%2016Txx%20-%20Hopf%20algebras,%20quantum%20groups%20and%20related%20topics); group rings border the [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) codes 20C05 and 20C07; and 16S90 states that radicals of rings themselves belong to [MSC 16Nxx - Radicals and radical properties of associative rings](node:MSC%2016Nxx%20-%20Radicals%20and%20radical%20properties%20of%20associative%20rings). ([MSC2020, 16S](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Sxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Ore Extensions](node:Ore%20Extensions) (16S36).** For a $K$-algebra $R$, $\sigma\in\operatorname{End}_K(R)$ and $\delta:R\to R$, the skew polynomial ring $R[x;\sigma,\delta]$ is the algebra of polynomials $\sum r_ix^i$ with $xr=\sigma(r)x+\delta(r)$; it exists iff $\sigma$ is an algebra endomorphism and $\delta$ is a $\sigma$-derivation, $\delta(rr')=\sigma(r)\delta(r')+\delta(r)r'$. ([Crawley-Boevey, §2.10](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/1617noncommalg/Noncommutative%20algebra.pdf)) If $\sigma$ is an automorphism and $R$ is left Noetherian, then $R[x;\sigma,\delta]$ is left Noetherian; Weyl algebras are iterated Ore extensions, and Ore extensions also arise in group algebras of polycyclic groups, enveloping algebras of solvable Lie algebras and coordinate rings of quantum groups. ([Wikipedia, Ore extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore_extension))
- **Weyl algebras and differential operators (16S32).** $A_n(K)$ is generated by $x_1,\dots,x_n,y_1,\dots,y_n$ with $y_ix_j-x_jy_i=\delta_{ij}$ and the $x$'s and $y$'s each commuting; by the Diamond Lemma the monomials $x^\alpha y^\beta$ form a basis, $A_n(K)\cong K[x_1,\dots,x_n][y_1;\partial/\partial x_1]\cdots[y_n;\partial/\partial x_n]$, and if $K$ is a field of characteristic 0 then $A_n(K)$ is a simple Noetherian domain. ([Crawley-Boevey, §2.11](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/1617noncommalg/Noncommutative%20algebra.pdf)) In characteristic 0 it has no finite-dimensional representations and is the ring of differential operators on $K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. ([Wikipedia, Weyl algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_algebra))
- **Rings of fractions (16S85).** A multiplicative set $S\subseteq R$ is left Ore if for all $s\in S$, $a\in R$ there are $s'\in S$, $a'\in R$ with $s'a=a's$. Ore's theorem: if $S$ is left Ore and left reversible, the universal localization $R_S$ is $S^{-1}R$, every element having the form $s^{-1}a$. Special case of Goldie's theorem: a left Noetherian domain embeds in a division ring of left fractions; the free algebra $K\langle x,y\rangle$ fails the Ore condition because $Rx\cap Ry=0$. ([Crawley-Boevey, §2.16](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/1617noncommalg/Noncommutative%20algebra.pdf)) Goldie: a domain is right Ore iff $R_R$ has finite uniform dimension. ([Wikipedia, Ore condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore_condition)) See [Localization of Rings](node:Localization%20of%20Rings).
- **Group rings and skew group rings (16S34, 16S35).** For $G$ acting on $R$, the skew group algebra $R\#G$ has multiplication $(a\#g)(b\#h)=a\,(g\cdot b)\#gh$; for the cyclic group of order $n$ permuting the factors of $K^n$, $K^n\#G\cong M_n(K)$. ([Crawley-Boevey, §2.14](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/1617noncommalg/Noncommutative%20algebra.pdf)) For torsion-free $G$ the Kaplansky conjectures predict that $K[G]$ has no zero divisors, no nontrivial idempotents, and only trivial units $kg$; unit $\Rightarrow$ zero-divisor $\Rightarrow$ idempotent. ([Wikipedia, Kaplansky's conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures)) Gardam disproved the unit conjecture: over $\mathbb F_2$, the torsion-free virtually abelian group $P=\langle a,b\mid b^{-1}a^2b=a^{-2},\ a^{-1}b^2a=b^{-2}\rangle$ (the Hantzsche–Wendt or Promislow group) has a nontrivial unit with 21-element support (*Ann. of Math.* 194, 2021). ([Gardam, arXiv 2102.11818](https://arxiv.org/html/2102.11818)) See [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory).
- **PBW deformations and Koszul algebras (16S30, 16S37, 16S80).** Let $A=T(V)/(P)$ with $P$ in filtration degree $\le 2$ and $S=T(V)/(R)$ its homogeneous quadratic version; $A$ is a PBW deformation of $S$ if $\operatorname{gr}A\cong S$. Theorem (Braverman–Gaitsgory, Polishchuk–Positselski): if $S$ is Koszul, $A$ is a PBW deformation iff (I) $P\cap F^1(T)=0$ and (J) $(F^1T\cdot P\cdot F^1T)\cap F^2T=P$. For $A=U(\mathfrak g)$, $S=S(\mathfrak g)$, (I) is antisymmetry of the bracket and (J) the Jacobi identity, recovering the classical PBW theorem for [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras). Priddy: a homogeneous quadratic algebra with a PBW basis is Koszul. ([Shepler–Witherspoon, Thms 3.1, 7.1, Ex. 7.3](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/shepler-witherspoon-pbw.pdf))
- **Leavitt path algebras (16S88).** The Leavitt path algebra $L_K(E)$ of a directed graph $E$ is universal for Cuntz–Krieger $E$-families; it is the algebraic analogue of the graph $C^*$-algebra, $L_{\mathbb C}(E)$ being isomorphic to a dense $*$-subalgebra of $C^*(E)$. It is simple if and only if $E$ satisfies Condition (L) and every vertex connects to every infinite path and every singular vertex. ([Wikipedia, Leavitt path algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leavitt_path_algebra))

### History
Ore introduced his condition while extending the field-of-fractions construction to noncommutative rings. ([Wikipedia, Ore condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore_condition)) Poincaré published the Lie-algebra embedding theorem in 1900; Birkhoff and Witt gave modern proofs in 1937. ([Shepler–Witherspoon, §1](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/shepler-witherspoon-pbw.pdf)) Dixmier posed his question on $A_1$ in 1968, and Bass, Connell and Wright recorded the version for $A_n$ in 1982; Tsuchimoto (2005) and Belov-Kanel–Kontsevich (2007) showed it stably equivalent to the Jacobian conjecture. ([Wikipedia, Dixmier conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixmier_conjecture)) Leavitt path algebras were introduced independently in 2005 by Abrams–Aranda Pino and by Ara–Moreno–Pardo, and received the code 16S88 in 2020. ([Wikipedia, Leavitt path algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leavitt_path_algebra)) Gardam's counterexample to the unit conjecture appeared in 2021. ([Gardam, arXiv 2102.11818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11818))

### Open problems
- **Kaplansky's zero-divisor and idempotent conjectures.** For $K$ a field and $G$ torsion-free, is $K[G]$ a domain, and does it have only the idempotents 0 and 1? Wikipedia records both as open; the zero-divisor conjecture is known for elementary amenable groups (whose group algebras are Ore domains) and, in characteristic 0, follows from the Atiyah conjecture, and the Kadison–Kaplansky version of the idempotent conjecture, for reduced group $C^*$-algebras, is known for a large class of groups including hyperbolic groups. ([Wikipedia, Kaplansky's conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures)) Gardam notes that the zero-divisor conjecture is known for his group $P$, so his unit does not affect it. ([Gardam, arXiv 2102.11818](https://arxiv.org/html/2102.11818))
- **Dixmier conjecture for $A_1$ and $A_2$.** Is every endomorphism of the Weyl algebra $A_1$ (respectively $A_2$) over a field of characteristic 0 an automorphism? Wikipedia lists these two cases as open, since the Jacobian conjecture in two variables is open; Zheglov announced a proposed proof for $A_1$ in 2024 whose acceptance the page does not report. ([Wikipedia, Dixmier conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixmier_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Kaplansky's conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures): statements, implications and status of the group-ring conjectures.
- **Learn:** [Crawley-Boevey, Noncommutative algebra (Bielefeld lecture notes), Ch. 2](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/1617noncommalg/Noncommutative%20algebra.pdf): tensor and free algebras, Diamond Lemma, skew polynomial rings, Weyl algebras, group and skew group algebras, Ore localization.
- **Primary:** [Shepler and Witherspoon, Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorems](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/shepler-witherspoon-pbw.pdf): survey of PBW theorems, Koszul algebras and PBW deformations.
- **Primary:** [Gardam, A counterexample to the unit conjecture for group rings (Ann. of Math. 2021; arXiv 2102.11818)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11818): the explicit nontrivial unit.
- **Further reading:** [McConnell and Robson, Noncommutative Noetherian Rings (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 30, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/030): graduate monograph on Noetherian rings and their constructions.
references.MSC 16Txx - Hopf algebras, quantum group:
## Reference
### Overview
A Hopf algebra over a field $k$ is simultaneously an algebra and a coalgebra, with compatible structure maps making it a bialgebra, together with an antipode $S$, the convolution inverse of the identity. The notion goes back to Hopf's 1941 structure theorem for the [cohomology of Lie groups](node:Cohomology%20of%20Lie%20Groups), where the cup product and the map induced by group multiplication give exactly this structure. ([Wikipedia, Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_algebra))

The comultiplication is what makes tensor products of modules into modules, so representation categories of Hopf algebras are monoidal. Quantum groups, introduced by Drinfeld and Jimbo from the theory of quantum integrable systems, add an R-matrix that makes this monoidal category braided and produces solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation and invariants of knots and braids. ([Schneider, Proposition 1.1](https://www.famaf.unc.edu.ar/~andrus/papers/Schn1.pdf); [Wikipedia, Quantum group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_group); [Wikipedia, Quasitriangular Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasitriangular_Hopf_algebra))

Modern work splits into structure theory of finite-dimensional Hopf algebras (integrals, freeness, the order of the antipode), classification programmes (semisimple and pointed Hopf algebras), and the categorical view in which a Hopf algebra is reconstructed from a tensor category with a fiber functor. ([Schneider, §§2–4](https://www.famaf.unc.edu.ar/~andrus/papers/Schn1.pdf); [Etingof–Gelaki–Nikshych–Ostrik, preface](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists: 16T05 Hopf algebras and their applications (see also 16S40, 57T05); 16T10 bialgebras; 16T15 coalgebras and comodules, corings; 16T20 ring-theoretic aspects of quantum groups (see also 17B37, 20G42, 81R50); 16T25 Yang–Baxter equations; 16T30 connections of Hopf algebras with [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) (see also 05Exx); 16T99 other. ([MSC2020, 16Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Txx))

The cross-references mark the boundaries. Quantum groups as quantized enveloping algebras and related deformations are 17B37, in [MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras). Quantum groups applied to problems in quantum theory are 81R50, within [MSC 81Rxx - Groups and algebras in quantum theory](node:MSC%2081Rxx%20-%20Groups%20and%20algebras%20in%20quantum%20theory). Smash products of general Hopf actions are 16S40, and Hopf algebras as aspects of the homology and homotopy of [topological groups](node:Topological%20Groups) are 57T05. Braided monoidal, fusion, and modular tensor categories have codes 18M15 and 18M20 in [MSC 18Mxx - Monoidal categories and operads](node:MSC%2018Mxx%20-%20Monoidal%20categories%20and%20operads). ([MSC2020, 16Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Txx); [MSC2020, 17Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Bxx); [MSC2020, 81Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=81Rxx); [MSC2020, 16Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Sxx); [MSC2020, 57Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=57Txx); [MSC2020, 18Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Mxx))

Definition: a bialgebra $(H,m,u,\Delta,\varepsilon)$ is a Hopf algebra if there is a linear $S:H\to H$ with $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=u\varepsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$. Then $S$ is unique, an anti-algebra map, and an anti-coalgebra map. Basic examples include the group algebra $kG$ with $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$ and $S(g)=g^{-1}$, its dual (functions on a finite group), and $U(\mathfrak g)$ with $\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x$ for $x\in\mathfrak g$. ([Schneider, Theorem 1.5](https://www.famaf.unc.edu.ar/~andrus/papers/Schn1.pdf); [Wikipedia, Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_algebra)) See [Hopf Algebras](node:Hopf%20Algebras).

### Key concepts
- **Drinfeld–Jimbo quantum groups.** For a Cartan matrix and $q\in\mathbb C^\times$ not a root of unity, $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ has generators $k_\lambda,e_i,f_i$ with $k_\lambda e_ik_\lambda^{-1}=q^{(\lambda,\alpha_i)}e_i$, $k_\lambda f_ik_\lambda^{-1}=q^{-(\lambda,\alpha_i)}f_i$, $[e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}\frac{k_i-k_i^{-1}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}$, and the quantum Serre relations. One coproduct is $\Delta(k_\lambda)=k_\lambda\otimes k_\lambda$, $\Delta(e_i)=1\otimes e_i+e_i\otimes k_i$, $\Delta(f_i)=k_i^{-1}\otimes f_i+f_i\otimes1$. As $q\to1$ the relations tend to those of $U(\mathfrak g)$; for $q$ not a root of unity, an irreducible highest-weight module has the same weight multiplicities as the irreducible $U(\mathfrak g)$-module with the same highest weight. ([Wikipedia, Quantum group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_group)) See [Quantum Groups](node:Quantum%20Groups) and [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras).
- **Quasitriangular structure and Yang–Baxter.** $(H,R)$ is quasitriangular if $R\in H\otimes H$ is invertible, $R\Delta(x)R^{-1}=(\tau\circ\Delta)(x)$, $(\Delta\otimes1)R=R_{13}R_{23}$, and $(1\otimes\Delta)R=R_{13}R_{12}$. Then $R$ solves the Yang–Baxter equation and $c(u\otimes v)=\tau(R(u\otimes v))$ braids the category of $H$-modules. $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ is only "nearly" quasitriangular, since its R-matrix is an infinite formal sum. ([Wikipedia, Quasitriangular Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasitriangular_Hopf_algebra); [Wikipedia, Quantum group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_group)) See [Monoidal Categories](node:Monoidal%20Categories).
- **Larson–Sweedler theorem (1969).** If $H$ is finite-dimensional over a field, the spaces of left and right integrals are one-dimensional, $S$ is bijective, and $H\cong H^*$ as $H$-modules via a nonzero integral of $H^*$, so $H$ is Frobenius. Maschke's theorem for Hopf algebras says that $H$ is semisimple iff $\varepsilon(\Lambda)\ne0$ for a left integral $\Lambda$. ([Schneider, Theorems 2.3, 3.1, 3.2](https://www.famaf.unc.edu.ar/~andrus/papers/Schn1.pdf))
- **Radford's $S^4$ formula (1976).** For finite-dimensional $H$ with modular elements $a\in G(H)$ and $\alpha\in\operatorname{Alg}(H,k)$, $S^4(h)=a(\alpha^{-1}\rightharpoonup h\leftharpoonup\alpha)a^{-1}$; hence the antipode has finite order. In characteristic 0 (Larson–Radford, 1988), $H$ is semisimple iff $H^*$ is semisimple iff $S^2=\mathrm{id}$. ([Schneider, Theorems 3.8, 3.14 and Corollary 3.9](https://www.famaf.unc.edu.ar/~andrus/papers/Schn1.pdf))
- **Nichols–Zoeller freeness theorem (1989).** A finite-dimensional Hopf algebra is free as a module over every Hopf subalgebra; hence $\dim R$ divides $\dim H$ ("[Lagrange's Theorem](node:Lagrange's%20Theorem) for Hopf algebras"). As an application, Zhu proved in 1994 that, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, a Hopf algebra of prime dimension $p$ is the group algebra of $\mathbb Z/p$. ([Schneider, Theorem 3.15, Corollary 3.16, Theorem 4.16](https://www.famaf.unc.edu.ar/~andrus/papers/Schn1.pdf))
- **Lifting method for pointed Hopf algebras.** For a pointed Hopf algebra $A$ with coradical $k\Gamma$, the graded algebra of the coradical filtration is $R\#k\Gamma$, where $R$ is a braided Hopf algebra (the Nichols algebra $\mathfrak B(V)$ in the generated-in-degree-one case). Classification then has three steps: determine the Nichols algebras $\mathfrak B(V)$, find all liftings $A$ with $\operatorname{gr}A\cong\mathfrak B(V)\#k\Gamma$, and decide generation in degree one. With this method Andruskiewitsch and Schneider classified finite-dimensional complex pointed Hopf algebras with abelian group of group-likes whose order has prime divisors $>7$; these are deformations of generalized small quantum groups (Annals, 2010). ([Andruskiewitsch–Schneider, Pointed Hopf algebras, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0110136); [Andruskiewitsch–Schneider, Ann. Math. 171](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0502157))
- **Tensor categories.** Hopf algebras can be viewed as structures arising from tensor categories with a fiber functor through reconstruction theory. Recent Hopf results, such as the classification of semisimple Hopf algebras of prime-power dimension and of triangular Hopf algebras, were proved with tensor-category methods. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, every semisimple Hopf algebra is defined over an algebraic number field. ([Etingof–Gelaki–Nikshych–Ostrik, preface and Corollary 9.1.8](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf))

### History
Hopf's 1941 Annals paper on the topology of group manifolds introduced the structure on the [cohomology of Lie groups](node:Cohomology%20of%20Lie%20Groups). Sweedler, Larson, and Radford developed the finite-dimensional theory (1969–1976), and Kaplansky posed ten conjectures in 1975 that organized much later work. Nichols and Zoeller proved freeness in 1989. Drinfeld and Jimbo formalized quantum groups as Hopf algebras out of quantum integrable systems. ([Wikipedia, Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_algebra); [Schneider, §3 and Appendix](https://www.famaf.unc.edu.ar/~andrus/papers/Schn1.pdf); [Wikipedia, Quantum group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_group))

### Open problems
- **Kaplansky's sixth conjecture.** Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Hopf algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0. Does the dimension of every simple $H$-module divide $\dim H$? Dai and Dong's survey says it "still remains open". It is known for quasitriangular $H$ (Etingof–Gelaki), for dimension $p^n$, for $pq$, $pq^2$, $pqr$, and for weakly group-theoretical $H$. Kaplansky's published version omitted the characteristic-zero hypothesis; without it divisibility fails already for the group algebra of $SL(2,p)$ over a field of characteristic $p$. ([Dai–Dong, On Kaplansky's sixth conjecture](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1409.2545))
- **Generation in degree one.** Andruskiewitsch and Schneider conjecture that every finite-dimensional pointed Hopf algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 is generated by group-like and skew-primitive elements (Conjecture 5.7, equivalent to Conjecture 2.7 on braided Hopf algebras). The statement fails in infinite dimension or in positive characteristic. ([Andruskiewitsch–Schneider, Pointed Hopf algebras, §§2, 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0110136)) Angiono proved it when the group of group-likes is abelian (J. Reine Angew. Math. 683, 2013); over non-abelian groups only partial cases are settled, and Angiono's 2025 survey lists braidings for which the Nichols algebras and the generation problem remain to be described. ([Angiono, Pointed Hopf algebras revisited, Conjecture 2.2, Theorems 2.9 and 2.16](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03124v1))
- **Non-abelian group-likes.** The 2001 survey calls the structure of pointed Hopf algebras with non-abelian $G(A)$ "largely unknown" and names as a basic open problem which finite groups $\Gamma$ admit Yetter–Drinfeld modules $V$ over $k\Gamma$ with $\mathfrak B(V)$ finite-dimensional. Angiono's 2025 survey still calls deciding when a Nichols algebra over a simple Yetter–Drinfeld module is finite-dimensional an open question. ([Andruskiewitsch–Schneider, introduction and Question 3.17](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0110136); [Angiono, Pointed Hopf algebras revisited](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03124v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hopf algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_algebra) and [Quantum group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_group): definitions, examples, Drinfeld–Jimbo relations.
- **Learn:** [Schneider, Lectures on Hopf algebras](https://www.famaf.unc.edu.ar/~andrus/papers/Schn1.pdf): five lectures from Larson–Sweedler to Zhu's theorem, with Kaplansky's conjectures.
- **Primary:** [Andruskiewitsch–Schneider, On the classification of finite-dimensional pointed Hopf algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0502157): Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), the lifting-method classification.
- **Further reading:** [Etingof, Gelaki, Nikshych, Ostrik, Tensor Categories](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf): AMS Mathematical Surveys and Monographs 205; [Andruskiewitsch–Schneider, Pointed Hopf algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0110136): MSRI survey of Nichols algebras and lifting.
references.MSC 16Uxx - Conditions on elements:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 16Uxx classifies associative rings by conditions imposed on individual elements: being a domain, Ore conditions on multiplicative sets, divisibility, idempotents, units, central and normalizing elements, weakened commutativity, and generalized inverses. Within [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras), it is where element-wise equations such as $axa=a$, $a=e+u$, or $ab=1\Rightarrow ba=1$ are related to the module and decomposition theory of the ring. ([MSC2020, 16Uxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Uxx); [Nielsen–Šter, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.03305))

A central thread runs from von Neumann regular rings through unit-regular, clean, and exchange rings. Regularity is an element condition ($a=axa$), but it is equivalent to every principal one-sided ideal being generated by an idempotent. For an endomorphism ring $\operatorname{End}(M)$, $a$ is regular exactly when $\ker a$ and $\operatorname{im}a$ are direct summands of $M$, and unit-regular exactly when, in addition, $\ker a\cong\operatorname{coker}a$. Element conditions therefore encode direct-sum decomposition and cancellation of modules. ([Wikipedia, Von Neumann regular ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_regular_ring); [Nielsen–Šter, Lemma 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.03305))

A long-standing open problem bearing on these conditions, the separativity problem for exchange rings, is a cancellation question for finitely generated projective modules. ([Ara–Goodearl–O'Meara–Pardo–Perera](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.06837v2))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists: 16U10 integral domains; 16U20 Ore rings, multiplicative sets, Ore localization; 16U30 divisibility and noncommutative UFDs; 16U40 idempotent elements; 16U60 units and groups of units; 16U70 center and normalizer (invariant elements); 16U80 generalizations of commutativity; 16U90 generalized inverses; 16U99 other. ([MSC2020, 16Uxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Uxx))

A multiplicative set $S$ satisfies the right Ore condition if $rS\cap sR\neq\varnothing$ for all $r\in R$, $s\in S$. A right Ore domain embeds in a division ring of right fractions $rs^{-1}$; right Noetherian domains are right Ore, while the free algebra on two generators satisfies neither Ore condition. Goldie showed that a domain is right Ore iff $R_R$ has finite uniform dimension. ([Wikipedia, Ore condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore_condition)) 16P50, localization and associative Noetherian rings, carries a cross-reference to 16U20; see [MSC 16Pxx - Chain conditions, growth conditions, and other forms of finiteness for associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016Pxx%20-%20Chain%20conditions,%20growth%20conditions,%20and%20other%20forms%20of%20finiteness%20for%20associative%20rings%20and%20algebras). ([MSC2020, 16Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Pxx)) See also [Localization of Rings](node:Localization%20of%20Rings) and [Ore Extensions](node:Ore%20Extensions).

Neighbours: nil and nilpotent radicals, sets, and ideals are 16N40, in [MSC 16Nxx - Radicals and radical properties of associative rings](node:MSC%2016Nxx%20-%20Radicals%20and%20radical%20properties%20of%20associative%20rings), which also holds the Jacobson radical (16N20). For the commutative case, MSC directs readers to 13-XX, which is where commutative [Local Rings](node:Local%20Rings) and [integral domains](node:Integral%20Domains) belong. ([MSC2020, 16Uxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Uxx); [MSC2020, 16Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **Regular and unit-regular rings.** $R$ is (von Neumann) regular if each $a$ has an inner inverse $x$ with $axa=a$; equivalently every principal one-sided ideal is generated by an idempotent ($e=ax$ gives $aR=eR$). Following Ehrlich, $R$ is unit-regular if $x$ can be chosen to be a unit. $\operatorname{End}_K(V)$ is regular for any vector space $V$; semisimple and commutative regular rings are unit-regular; strongly regular rings ($a=a^2x$) are exactly the reduced regular rings and are unit-regular. ([Wikipedia, Von Neumann regular ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_regular_ring); [Nielsen–Šter, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.03305))
- **Exchange, clean, and strongly clean rings.** Warfield's exchange rings, those whose finitely generated projective modules have the finite exchange property, are by Nicholson exactly the rings in which idempotents lift modulo every one-sided ideal. $a$ is clean if $a=e+u$ with $e^2=e$ and $u$ a unit, and strongly clean if moreover $eu=ue$. Clean rings are exchange rings, and abelian exchange rings are clean. Unit-regular rings are clean, but Bergman built a regular ring that is not clean, and Nielsen–Šter a unit-regular ring that is not strongly clean, answering Nicholson's question. A ring is local iff it is clean with only the idempotents $0,1$. ([Nielsen–Šter, §1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.03305); [Ara et al., introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.06837v2); [Wikipedia, Clean ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_ring)) See [Units and Idempotents in Rings](node:Units%20and%20Idempotents%20in%20Rings) and [Local Noncommutative Rings](node:Local%20Noncommutative%20Rings).
- **Sums of units.** An element is $k$-good if it is a sum of exactly $k$ units. Zelinsky (1954): every endomorphism of a vector space over a division ring is a sum of two automorphisms, except for a one-dimensional space over $\mathbb Z/2$. Henriksen (1974): for every ring $R$ with identity and $n\ge2$, every matrix in $M_n(R)$ is a sum of three units, and some such rings are not 2-good. Vámos extended this to endomorphism rings of free modules of any rank $\ge2$. ([Barroero–Frei–Tichy, §1 and Theorem 15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.0120v2); [Henriksen, J. Algebra 31](https://scholarship.claremont.edu/hmc_fac_pub/45)) If $R$ is unit-regular and $2$ is invertible, every element is a sum of two units. Indeed, $a=axa$ with $x$ a unit gives $a=ex^{-1}$ for the idempotent $e=ax$. Since $(2e-1)^2=1$, we get $a=(2e-1)2^{-1}x^{-1}+2^{-1}x^{-1}$, a sum of two units. ([Nielsen–Šter, definitions](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.03305))
- **Dedekind-finite (directly finite) rings.** $R$ is Dedekind-finite if $ab=1$ implies $ba=1$. Commutative, finite, one-sided Noetherian, and unit-regular rings are Dedekind-finite. $\operatorname{End}(V)$ for $V$ with a countably infinite basis is not, since the shifts satisfy $LR=1\ne RL$. The class is closed under subrings and products, and the property passes in both directions modulo the Jacobson radical. ([Wikipedia, Dedekind-finite ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind-finite_ring); [Wikipedia, Von Neumann regular ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_regular_ring)) See [Jacobson Radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical).
- **Reduced, reversible, semicommutative, and Armendariz rings.** $R$ is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotents (equivalently, $x^2=0\Rightarrow x=0$). It is reversible if $ab=0\Rightarrow ba=0$, semicommutative if $ab=0\Rightarrow aRb=0$, and Armendariz if $f(x)g(x)=0$ in $R[x]$ forces every product of coefficients $a_ib_j=0$. Reversible rings are semicommutative but not conversely, and reduced rings are Armendariz. ([Louzari, introduction](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1204.5205); [Wikipedia, Reduced ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduced_ring)) Reduced rings are reversible: if $ab=0$, then $(ba)^2=b(ab)a=0$, so $ba=0$. ([Louzari, definitions](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1204.5205))
- **Nilpotent perturbations of units.** If $a^n=0$, then $1-a$ is a unit with inverse $1+a+\cdots+a^{n-1}$; hence an element $a$ with $xay$ nilpotent for all $x,y$ lies in the Jacobson radical. Idempotents of $\operatorname{End}_R(M)$ correspond to direct-sum decompositions $M=eM\oplus(1-e)M$. ([MIT 18.706, Remarks 4.6 and 4.13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec04.pdf))

### History
Von Neumann introduced regular rings in 1936 in his work on continuous geometry and [operator algebras](node:Operator%20Algebras). Ehrlich defined unit-regularity, Warfield introduced exchange rings building on Crawley and Jónsson's decomposition theory, and Nicholson (1977) introduced clean rings and proved that clean rings are exchange rings. Zelinsky's 1954 two-automorphism theorem started the study of unit sums, which Henriksen's 1974 *Journal of Algebra* paper extended to matrix rings. ([Wikipedia, Von Neumann regular ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_regular_ring); [Nielsen–Šter, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.03305); [Wikipedia, Clean ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_ring); [Barroero–Frei–Tichy, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.0120v2); [Henriksen](https://scholarship.claremont.edu/hmc_fac_pub/45))

### Open problems
- **The separativity problem.** A ring is separative if, for finitely generated projective modules, $A\oplus A\cong A\oplus B\cong B\oplus B$ implies $A\cong B$. Ara, Goodearl, O'Meara, and Pardo asked in 1994 whether every exchange ring, or even every regular ring, is separative. Over a separative regular ring every square matrix is equivalent to a diagonal matrix. The 2024 paper of Ara, Goodearl, O'Meara, Pardo, and Perera calls it "the long standing Separativity Problem". It builds inverse-limit constructions that degrade unit-regularity, diagonalization, and finite stable rank, proposing them as a possible route to a negative answer, and notes that no counter-construction has worked to date. ([Ara–Goodearl–O'Meara–Pardo–Perera, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06837); [introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.06837v2))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Von Neumann regular ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Neumann_regular_ring): regular, unit-regular, and strongly regular rings.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.706, Lecture 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec04.pdf): units, nilpotents, idempotents, Jacobson radical, and local rings.
- **Primary:** [Nielsen and Šter, Connections between unit-regularity, regularity, cleanness, and strong cleanness](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.03305): research paper with a survey of the regular/clean/exchange hierarchy.
- **Further reading:** [Ara, Goodearl, O'Meara, Pardo, Perera, Regular ring properties degraded through inverse limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06837): current state of the separativity problem; [Barroero, Frei, Tichy, Additive unit representations in global fields](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.0120v2): survey of unit-sum numbers.
references.MSC 16Wxx - Associative rings and algebr:
## Reference
### Overview
16W covers associative rings carrying a second structure that the ring operations must respect: an involution, a group of automorphisms or a Lie algebra of derivations acting on the ring, a grading by a group, a filtration, a valuation or topology, or a super ($\mathbb Z/2$-graded) structure. ([MSC2020, 16W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Wxx)) The extra structure is part of the object: a filtration is weaker than a grading, since every $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$-grading gives a filtration but not every filtered algebra arises this way, and some properties pass from the associated graded algebra back to the original ring; for example, if $\operatorname{gr}A$ is a domain, so is $A$. ([Etingof, 18.745 notes, §10.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/lnlg.pdf))

Two lines of research in the code are the following. Group-graded ring theory studies strongly graded rings, crossed products and graded invariants such as the graded Grothendieck group $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}$, which is now used to classify Leavitt path algebras. ([Hazrat, Graded rings and graded Grothendieck groups, Ch. 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1405.5071); [Cortiñas–Hazrat, arXiv 2401.04262](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04262)) Rings with involution connect associative algebra to Jordan and Lie algebras through their symmetric and skew elements, and to polynomial-identity theory through identities with involution. ([Wikipedia, *-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/*-algebra); [Sviridova, arXiv 1410.2222](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.2222))

### Scope
MSC2020 16W lists: 16W10 rings with involution; Lie, Jordan and other nonassociative structures (see also 17B60, 17C50, 46Kxx); 16W20 automorphisms and endomorphisms; 16W22 actions of groups and semigroups, invariant theory; 16W25 derivations, actions of Lie algebras; 16W50 graded rings and modules; 16W55 "super" (or "skew") structure (see also 17A70, 17Bxx, 17C70; exterior algebras are 15A75, Clifford algebras 11E88 and 15A66); 16W60 valuations, completions, formal power series and related constructions (see also 13Jxx); 16W70 filtered associative rings, filtrational and graded techniques; 16W80 topological and ordered rings and modules (see also 06F25, 13Jxx); 16W99. ([MSC2020, 16W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Wxx))

Neighbours, by the cross-references: Lie and Jordan structures of rings with involution point to 17B60 and 17C50 ([MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras)); topological algebras with involution are [MSC 46Kxx - Topological (rings and) algebras with an involution](node:MSC%2046Kxx%20-%20Topological%20%28rings%20and%29%20algebras%20with%20an%20involution); commutative topological rings and completions are [MSC 13Jxx - Topological rings and modules](node:MSC%2013Jxx%20-%20Topological%20rings%20and%20modules); [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras) are sent to 11E88 and 15A66. Identities with involution are classified in 16R50 of [MSC 16Rxx - Rings with polynomial identity](node:MSC%2016Rxx%20-%20Rings%20with%20polynomial%20identity). ([MSC2020, 16W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Wxx); [MSC2020, 16R](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Rxx))

### Key concepts
- **Group-graded and strongly graded rings (16W50).** For an abelian group $\Gamma$, a $\Gamma$-graded ring is $A=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma}A_\gamma$ with $A_\gamma A_\delta\subseteq A_{\gamma+\delta}$; it is strongly graded if $A_\gamma A_\delta=A_{\gamma+\delta}$ for all $\gamma,\delta$, equivalently $1\in A_\gamma A_{-\gamma}$ for all $\gamma$. A crossed product is a graded ring with an invertible element in every homogeneous component; every crossed product is strongly graded but not conversely, and a strongly graded ring with $A_0$ local is a crossed product. If $A$ is strongly graded, $A$ is graded von Neumann regular iff $A_0$ is von Neumann regular, proved through an equivalence of module categories over $A$ and $A_0$ (Dade's theorem, Ch. 5). ([Hazrat, §§1.1, 1.9, Prop. 1.15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1405.5071)) See [Graded Algebras](node:Graded%20Algebras); homogeneous elements and graded modules are defined in ([Wikipedia, Graded ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graded_ring)).
- **Filtered rings and associated graded algebras (16W70).** A $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$-filtered algebra has $0=F_{-1}A\subset F_0A\subset F_1A\subset\cdots$ with $1\in F_0A$, $\bigcup F_nA=A$ and $F_iA\cdot F_jA\subseteq F_{i+j}A$; $\operatorname{gr}A=\bigoplus_n F_nA/F_{n-1}A$ with multiplication of leading terms. If $\operatorname{gr}A$ is a domain, so is $A$. For a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ is commutative and the PBW theorem says $S(\mathfrak g)\to\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ is an isomorphism; in characteristic 0 symmetrization identifies $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ with $S(\mathfrak g)^{\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak g}$. ([Etingof, §10.2, Prop. 10.6, Thm 11.1, Cor. 11.8](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/lnlg.pdf)) See [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras).
- **Rings with involution (16W10).** A $*$-ring has an antiautomorphism $*$ with $(xy)^*=y^*x^*$ and $x^{**}=x$; examples are $M_n(\mathbb C)$ with conjugate transpose, the quaternions, and group rings with $g\mapsto g^{-1}$. The Hermitian elements form a [Jordan algebra](node:Jordan%20Algebras) and the skew-Hermitian elements a Lie algebra; when 2 is invertible, $\tfrac12(1\pm *)$ split the ring into symmetric and skew parts, which are generally not associative subalgebras. ([Wikipedia, *-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/*-algebra)) See also [Involutive Topological Algebras](node:Involutive%20Topological%20Algebras).
- **Graded identities with involution (16W10, 16W50).** Sviridova works with associative algebras over a field of characteristic 0, graded by a finite abelian group, with an involution compatible with the grading; her representability theorem is proved for $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ with $q$ prime or $q=4$: a finitely generated such PI algebra has the same graded identities with involution as some finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$-graded algebra with involution. ([Sviridova, arXiv 1410.2222](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.2222))
- **Derivations (16W25).** A $K$-derivation $d$ of $R$ satisfies $d(rr')=r\,d(r')+d(r)\,r'$; $r\mapsto rm-mr$ is an inner derivation. On the Weyl algebra $A_n(K)$ the partial derivatives extend to inner derivations, $\partial/\partial x_j(a)=y_ja-ay_j$ and $\partial/\partial y_j(a)=ax_j-x_ja$, and these are what make $A_n(K)$ simple in characteristic 0. ([Crawley-Boevey, §§2.10–2.11](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~wcrawley/1617noncommalg/Noncommutative%20algebra.pdf))
- **Graded $K$-theory and Leavitt path algebras (16W50).** $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$, the [Grothendieck group](node:Grothendieck%20Groups) of graded finitely generated projective modules, carries a $\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$-module structure from shifting the grading; it is a complete invariant for graded ultramatricial algebras, and Leavitt path algebras of finite graphs with no sinks are graded von Neumann regular. ([Hazrat, §1.9, Ch. 5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1405.5071))

### History
Recent work using graded $K_0$ to classify Leavitt path algebras is part of the stated motivation for Hazrat's book on graded Grothendieck groups. ([Hazrat, Introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1405.5071)) For polycephaly graphs Hazrat proved that $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}$, as a pointed partially ordered group, determines the Leavitt path algebra up to graded isomorphism; Ara and Pardo proved it for finite essential graphs up to a twist by a locally inner automorphism, and Eilers, Ruiz and Sims proved it for amplified graphs. ([Cortiñas–Hazrat, §§8.1–8.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.04262)) Sviridova's 2014 work extends Kemer-type representability to graded algebras with involution. ([Sviridova, arXiv 1410.2222](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.2222))

### Open problems
- **Graded classification conjecture for Leavitt path algebras.** The conjecture asserts that for finite graphs $E,F$, an order-preserving $\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]$-module isomorphism $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(L(E))\cong K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(L(F))$ preserving the class of the identity is induced by a unital graded isomorphism $L(E)\cong L(F)$, extending the polycephaly case. Cortiñas and Hazrat (*Bull. London Math. Soc.* 2024) state that the conjectures in their survey "remain unsolved; in particular no counterexamples to them have been found". ([Cortiñas–Hazrat, arXiv 2401.04262, Introduction and Conj. 8.1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.04262))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, *-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/*-algebra): involutions, Hermitian and skew elements.
- **Learn:** [Etingof, 18.745 Lie groups and Lie algebras I (MIT notes), §§10.2–11](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/lnlg.pdf): filtered and graded algebras, PBW theorem.
- **Primary:** [Cortiñas and Hazrat, Classification conjectures for Leavitt path algebras (Bull. LMS 2024; arXiv 2401.04262)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04262): survey of graded classification results and open conjectures.
- **Primary:** [Sviridova, Identities of finitely generated graded algebras with involution (arXiv 1410.2222)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.2222): representability for graded identities with involution.
- **Further reading:** [Hazrat, Graded Rings and Graded Grothendieck Groups (arXiv 1405.5071)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1405.5071): monograph on group-graded rings, strongly graded rings, Dade's theorem and graded $K_0$.
references.MSC 16Yxx - Generalizations:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 16Yxx collects ring-like structures obtained by weakening or changing the axioms of an associative ring: hyperrings (16Y20), near-rings (16Y30), semirings (16Y60), and $\Gamma$- and fuzzy structures (16Y80), plus a catch-all 16Y99. The parent heading 16Yxx sends nonassociative rings to 17-XX, so the structures here keep an associative multiplication and modify instead the additive side, the distributive laws, or single-valuedness of the operations. ([MSC2020 16Yxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Yxx); [MSC2020 16-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16-XX))

Each weakening keeps a familiar class of examples in reach. Dropping additive inverses gives semirings such as $\mathbb N$, the Boolean semiring and the tropical semirings, which carry shortest-path computations. Dropping one distributive law gives near-rings such as the maps $G\to G$ on a group, which contain the near-fields used to coordinatize non-Desarguesian planes. Allowing set-valued addition gives hyperrings, which recent work uses for adele class spaces and for matroid theory. ([Wikipedia: Semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring); [Wikipedia: Near-ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-ring); [Connes–Consani](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.4260); [Baker–Bowler](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09707))

### Scope
- **16Y20 Hyperrings.** A hyperoperation sends each pair of elements of a nonempty set $H$ to a nonempty subset of $H$; a hypergroup is an associative hyperoperation satisfying the reproduction axiom $aH=Ha=H$. Krasner's hyperrings use such a set-valued addition with an ordinary multiplication; Krasner's hyperfields are the basic examples generalized by Baker–Bowler tracts. ([Wikipedia: Hyperstructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperstructure); [Connes–Consani](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.4260); [Baker–Bowler](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09707))
- **16Y30 Near-rings.** A (right) near-ring is a group $(N,+)$, not necessarily abelian, with an associative multiplication satisfying only $(x+y)z=xz+yz$. Then $0\cdot x=0$ always, but $x\cdot 0=0$ can fail. The MSC entry for 16Y30 adds "See also 12K05". ([Wikipedia: Near-ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-ring); [MSC2020 16Yxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Yxx))
- **16Y60 Semirings.** A semiring has a commutative additive monoid $(S,+,0)$, a multiplicative monoid $(S,\cdot,1)$, two-sided distributivity, and an absorbing zero $0a=a0=0$, which must be imposed because it no longer follows from the other axioms. The MSC entry for 16Y60 adds "See also 12K10". ([Wikipedia: Semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring); [MSC2020 16Yxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Yxx))
- **16Y80 $\Gamma$ and fuzzy structures; 16Y99 other.** These are listed in the MSC entry as separate codes within the section. ([MSC2020 16Yxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Yxx))

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 17 - Nonassociative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2017%20-%20Nonassociative%20rings%20and%20algebras) takes rings whose multiplication is not associative; 12K05 and 12K10 are the see-also targets of 16Y30 and 16Y60; the remaining 16 codes treat ordinary associative rings. ([MSC2020 16-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16-XX); [MSC2020 16Yxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Yxx))

### Key concepts
- [Semirings](node:Semirings) **and their examples.** The Boolean semiring $(\{0,1\},\vee,\wedge,0,1)$ is the smallest semiring that is not a ring; the tropical semiring $(\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\},\min,+,\infty,0)$ is the setting of Dijkstra's minimal-cost path algorithm; binary relations under union and composition, and languages $\mathcal P(\Sigma^\ast)$ under union and concatenation, are semirings; and $n\times n$ matrices over a semiring form a semiring. ([Wikipedia: Semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring); [Sutner, CMU](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~cdm/resources/30-semi-rings.pdf))
- **Idempotent semirings and the star operation.** If $x+x=x$ for all $x$ (equivalently $1+1=1$), then $x\le y\iff x+y=y$ is a partial order; max-plus is an example. In a closed idempotent semiring, $x^\ast=\sum_{i\ge0}x^i$ solves $x=ax+b$ by $x=a^\ast b$, which in the relation semiring is reflexive–transitive closure. Kleene algebras are star semirings with idempotent addition satisfying further axioms. ([Wikipedia: Semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring); [Sutner, CMU](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~cdm/resources/30-semi-rings.pdf))
- **$k$-ideals (subtractive ideals).** Henriksen (1958) defined a $k$-ideal of a semiring as an ideal $I$ with $x,\,x+y\in I\Rightarrow y\in I$. The $k$-closure $\{r: r+x\in I\text{ for some }x\in I\}$ characterizes them: $I$ is a $k$-ideal iff it equals its $k$-closure. Golan's monograph treats modules over semirings (semimodules), including subtractive semimodules. ([Dube–Goswami, Defs. 2.1–2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2304.04206))
- **Semifields and supertropical algebra.** A semifield is a semiring in which nonzero elements have multiplicative inverses; the tropical semirings are the algebra underlying [Tropical Varieties](node:Tropical%20Varieties). Izhakian and Rowen's supertropical algebra adds "ghost" elements to an ordered monoid to build a polynomial theory, with a Nullstellensatz analogue, in which tropical varieties appear as root sets of supertropical polynomials. ([Wikipedia: Semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring); [Izhakian–Rowen](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.1171))
- **Near-rings of maps.** For a group $G$, the set $M(G)$ of all maps $G\to G$ with pointwise addition and composition is a near-ring, not a ring once $|G|\ge2$ (a nonzero constant map $g$ has $g\cdot0=g$). Every near-ring embeds in some $M(G)$, the analogue of Cayley's theorem. Planar near-rings yield balanced incomplete [block designs](node:Block%20Designs). ([Wikipedia: Near-ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-ring))
- [Near-fields](node:Near-Fields%20and%20Semifields). A near-field is a near-ring with identity in which every nonzero element is invertible. Dickson (1905) built the first ones that are not division rings by modifying the multiplication of a division ring; Zassenhaus showed that all but seven finite near-fields are fields or Dickson near-fields; the smallest near-field that is not a field has order 9, and Marshall Hall used it to build the Hall plane. ([Wikipedia: Near-field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29))
- **Hyperrings and tracts.** Connes and Consani show that for a commutative ring $R$ and subgroup $G\subset R^\times$, the quotient $R/G$ is a hyperring extension of their hyperfield $\mathbf K$ exactly when $G\cup\{0\}$ is a subfield of $R$; and the adele class space of a global field inherits the structure of a hyperring extension of $\mathbf K$. Baker and Bowler's tracts generalize hyperfields and partial fields and give one theory of matroids covering linear subspaces, valuated, oriented and regular matroids. ([Connes–Consani](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.4260); [Baker–Bowler](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09707))

### History
Dickson introduced near-fields in 1905, and Zassenhaus classified the finite ones; Marshall Hall used the order-9 near-field for the Hall plane. Henriksen's 1958 paper on ideals in semirings introduced $k$-ideals. Golan's *Semirings and their Applications* (Kluwer/Springer, 1999), an update of his 1992 book, is the standard semiring monograph, and Pilz's *Near-rings, the Theory and its Applications* (2nd ed. 1983) and Clay's *Nearrings: Geneses and applications* (1992) are the near-ring books cited by Wikipedia; Pilz uses right near-rings and Clay left ones. ([Wikipedia: Near-field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-field_%28mathematics%29); [Dube–Goswami](https://arxiv.org/html/2304.04206); [Wikipedia: Semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring); [Wikipedia: Near-ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-ring); [Crossref: Golan](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-015-9333-5))

### Open problems
- **Infinite congruence-simple multiplicatively idempotent semirings.** Kepka, Korbelář and Landsmann study congruence-simple semirings $S$ satisfying $x^2=x$. They show that such an $S$ with a multiplicatively absorbing element has exactly two elements, and that a finite such $S$ has two elements or is isomorphic or anti-isomorphic to $\operatorname{End}(L)$ for the two-element semilattice $L$; they write that it seems to be an open question whether $S$ (without the absorbing-element hypothesis) can be infinite at all. ([Kepka–Korbelář–Landsmann](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.08160))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Semiring (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiring): axioms, standard examples, idempotent and star semirings, applications.
- **Reference:** [Near-ring (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-ring): axioms, $M(G)$, embedding theorem, designs.
- **Learn:** [Sutner, Semirings, Rings, Fields (CMU)](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~cdm/resources/30-semi-rings.pdf): course slides with relation, language, tropical and closed semirings.
- **Primary:** [Baker–Bowler, Matroids over partial hyperstructures](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09707): tracts, hyperfields and a unified matroid theory.
- **Primary:** [Connes–Consani (arXiv 1001.4260)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.4260): Krasner hyperrings in arithmetic.
- **Primary:** [Izhakian–Rowen, Supertropical algebra](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.1171): ghost elements and supertropical polynomials.
- **Further reading:** [Golan, Semirings and their Applications (Springer, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-015-9333-5): the standard semiring monograph.
references.MSC 16Zxx - Computational aspects of ass:
## Reference
### Overview
Computational associative algebra turns presentations and matrix data into effective answers. From generators and relations, it decides equality of elements, finds linear bases and Hilbert series, and computes growth. From a finite-dimensional algebra given by a basis, it computes the radical, the Wedderburn decomposition, and explicit matrix-algebra isomorphisms. In a free associative algebra $k\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ the monomials are words in noncommuting variables, ordered by an admissible order. ([Bremner, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.0920); [Rogalski, §§1.2, 1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065); [Ivanyos–Qiao, §3.5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.03495))

The central tool for presented algebras is the noncommutative Gröbner basis, also called the Gröbner–Shirshov basis. Its correctness criterion is the Diamond (Composition-Diamond) Lemma. Unlike Buchberger's algorithm in the commutative case, the completion procedure need not terminate. This is unavoidable: some finitely presented associative algebras have undecidable word problems. ([Wikipedia, Bergman's diamond lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergman%27s_diamond_lemma); [Bokut–Chen, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1303.5366))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 16Z05, computational aspects of associative rings (general theory; see also 68W30); 16Z10, Gröbner–Shirshov bases; and 16Z99, other. Software is classified under 16-04. ([MSC2020, 16Zxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Zxx))

The cross-references set the neighbours. Symbolic and algebraic computation in general is 68W30 in [MSC 68Wxx - Algorithms in computer science](node:MSC%2068Wxx%20-%20Algorithms%20in%20computer%20science), which cross-references 16Z05. Gröbner bases and other bases for ideals in commutative rings are 13P10, in [MSC 13Pxx - Computational aspects and applications of commutative rings](node:MSC%2013Pxx%20-%20Computational%20aspects%20and%20applications%20of%20commutative%20rings). Finite presentability and normal forms (diamond lemma, term-rewriting) as a ring-theoretic property are 16S15, in [MSC 16Sxx - Associative rings and algebras arising under various constructions](node:MSC%2016Sxx%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras%20arising%20under%20various%20constructions), which also holds free algebras (16S10), enveloping algebras (16S30), and quadratic and Koszul algebras (16S37). ([MSC2020, 16Zxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Zxx); [MSC2020, 68Wxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=68Wxx); [MSC2020, 13Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=13Pxx); [MSC2020, 16Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=16Sxx))

Setting: $A=k\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle/I$ with $I$ generated by $\{g_\sigma=w_\sigma-f_\sigma\}$, where $w_\sigma$ is the leading word for an admissible order. An admissible order is a total order on words, extending an order on the variables, such that $w<v$ implies $uw<uv$ and $wu<vu$, and only finitely many words lie below any given word. ([Rogalski, §1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065))

### Key concepts
- **Diamond Lemma (Bergman 1978).** For reductions $w_\sigma\mapsto f_\sigma$ under a fixed admissible order, the following are equivalent: (1) all overlap and inclusion ambiguities are resolvable; (2) every element is reduction-unique; (3) the images of the reduced (normal) words form a $k$-basis of $A$. Such a generating set is a Gröbner basis of $I$. ([Rogalski, Theorem 1.15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065); [Wikipedia, Bergman's diamond lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergman%27s_diamond_lemma)) See [Noncommutative Gröbner Bases](node:Noncommutative%20Gröbner%20Bases).
- **Gröbner–Shirshov bases and completion.** Shirshov (1962) introduced compositions (later Buchberger's s-polynomials) and an infinite completion algorithm for [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras), implicitly covering associative algebras. The Composition-Diamond lemma for associative algebras was stated explicitly by Bokut (1976), Bergman (1978), and Mora (1986). Completion either stops at a finite Gröbner basis or produces an infinite one, and the outcome depends even on the ordering: the Jordan plane $k\langle x,y\rangle/(yx-xy-x^2)$ has a finite basis for one degree-lex order and an infinite one when $y<x$. ([Bokut–Chen, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1303.5366); [Rogalski, Examples 1.18–1.19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065)) Compare [Gröbner Bases](node:Gröbner%20Bases).
- **Undecidability of the word problem.** Markov and Post constructed finitely presented semigroups with undecidable word problem. For a semigroup $P=\mathrm{sgp}\langle X\mid S\rangle$, the semigroup algebra $kP$ is presented as $k\langle X\mid S\rangle$ by the same generators and relations, so these give finitely presented associative algebras with undecidable equality of elements. Hence no general algorithm can produce finite Gröbner bases for all finite presentations. ([Bokut–Chen, §1 and §4.2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1303.5366)) See [Semigroups and Monoids](node:Semigroups%20and%20Monoids).
- **Hilbert series and growth.** For a graded algebra, a Gröbner basis makes $\dim A_n$ the number of normal words of degree $n$, so it gives the Hilbert series $h_A(t)=\sum_n(\dim A_n)t^n$; for example, $h_{k\langle x_1,\dots,x_m\rangle}(t)=1/(1-mt)$. For a finitely graded algebra, $\operatorname{GKdim}A=\limsup_n\log_n\sum_{i\le n}\dim A_i$, so GK dimension can be read off from the Hilbert series. Allowed (normal) words of length $d$ form the vertices of the Ufnarovskii graph, whose paths of length $n-d$ correspond to allowed words of degree $n$; the proof of Bergman's gap theorem can be read through this graph. ([Rogalski, §1.2 and Theorem 1.15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065); [MIT 18.706, §§24.3–24.4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-706-noncommutative-algebra-spring-2023/mit18_706_s23_lec24.pdf)) See [Gelfand–Kirillov Dimension](node:Gelfand–Kirillov%20Dimension).
- **Structure of finite-dimensional algebras.** Given a basis of a matrix algebra $A\subseteq M_n(\mathbb F_q)$, Rónyai's Las Vegas algorithm runs in time $\operatorname{poly}(n,\log q)$. It computes a basis of the [Jacobson radical](node:Jacobson%20Radical) and an epimorphism $A\to\bigoplus_i M_{n_i}(\mathbb F_{q_i})$ with kernel $\operatorname{Rad}A$, an explicit [Wedderburn decomposition](node:Artin–Wedderburn%20Theorem). Over a number field $E$, deterministic polynomial-time algorithms (Friedl–Rónyai, Eberly, Rónyai) compute $\operatorname{Rad}A$ and the simple components of $A\otimes_E\mathbb R$ and $A\otimes_E\mathbb C$. ([Ivanyos–Qiao, Theorems 18–19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.03495))
- **Software.** Rogalski's lectures use GAP with the GBNP package to compute noncommutative Gröbner bases. Singular's Letterplace subsystem computes Gröbner(–Shirshov) bases in free algebras, including over $\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$; over such coefficient rings, critical-pair formation and discarding criteria must be re-engineered compared with the commutative case. Bremner's lecture notes use computer algebra to build universal associative envelopes of nonassociative triple systems.
