([Rogalski, Exercise set 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065); [Levandovskyy–Metzlaff–Zeid](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.08518); [Bremner](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.0920)) See [Computer Algebra](node:Computer%20Algebra).

### History
Shirshov's 1962 paper gave the first Gröbner–Shirshov-type algorithm, a few years before Buchberger's commutative Gröbner bases (thesis 1965, paper 1970). Because Shirshov's work was little known outside Russia, Bokut proposed the name "Gröbner–Shirshov basis". The Composition-Diamond lemma for associative algebras was then stated explicitly by Bokut (1976), by Bergman in his 1978 *Advances* paper "The diamond lemma for ring theory", and by Mora (1986). ([Bokut–Chen, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1303.5366); [Wikipedia, Bergman's diamond lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergman%27s_diamond_lemma))

### Open problems
- **Gröbner–Shirshov bases of central algebras.** Bokut and Chen's 2014 survey lists cases where GS bases are still not known. For the elliptic algebras of Feigin and Odesskii, whose first example is the Sklyanin algebra, "GS bases are not known". For Markov's construction of semigroups with unsolvable isomorphism problem, the GS basis "is not known". ([Bokut–Chen, §1 list of examples](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1303.5366)) For three-dimensional Sklyanin algebras, Iyudu and Shkarin (2017) give explicit finite Gröbner bases only in degenerate parameter cases; in one case the basis does not appear to be finite, and the main case is handled through a central element and Gröbner basis members up to degree 4. ([Iyudu–Shkarin, §4](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1601.00564))
- **Derandomizing structure computation over finite fields.** Ivanyos and Qiao note that fully derandomizing Rónyai's radical-and-decomposition algorithm over $\mathbb F_q$ "is a difficult problem", because it relies on polynomial factorization over [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields). The known deterministic version costs time polynomial in the characteristic $p$, not in $\log p$. ([Ivanyos–Qiao, §3.5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.03495))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bergman's diamond lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergman%27s_diamond_lemma): statement and worked examples.
- **Learn:** [Rogalski, An introduction to noncommutative projective geometry, Lecture 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3065): Diamond Lemma, Hilbert series, and GAP/GBNP exercises.
- **Primary:** [Bokut and Chen, Gröbner–Shirshov bases and their calculation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.5366): survey in Bull. Math. Sci. 4 (2014) on Composition-Diamond lemmas and computed bases.
- **Further reading:** [Bremner, Free associative algebras, noncommutative Gröbner bases, and universal associative envelopes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.0920): course notes with computations; [Levandovskyy, Metzlaff, Zeid, Computing free non-commutative Gröbner bases over Z with Singular:Letterplace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.08518): implementation paper.
references.MSC 17 - Nonassociative rings and algebr:
## Reference
### Overview
A nonassociative algebra is a vector space with a bilinear product that is not assumed associative; MSC section 17 studies the classes singled out by identities, above all [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) (17B), [Jordan algebras](node:Jordan%20Algebras) (17C) and [alternative](node:Alternative%20Algebras) and Mal'tsev algebras (17D), together with general nonassociative rings (17A). ([MSC2020, 17](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17-XX); [Kaygorodov, §1.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2306.00425)) Each class is tied to associative algebra by a symmetrized or antisymmetrized product: an associative algebra $A$ gives a Lie algebra under $ab-ba$ and a Jordan algebra $A^+$ under $x\circ y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$, and an alternative algebra gives a Mal'tsev algebra under the commutator. ([Wikipedia, Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra); [Wikipedia, Malcev algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcev_algebra))

The [octonions](node:Octonions) are the meeting point of the classes. They are an 8-dimensional real normed division algebra that is alternative but not associative, their automorphism group is the 14-dimensional compact exceptional Lie group $G_2$, and $3\times3$ Hermitian octonionic matrices form the 27-dimensional exceptional Jordan algebra, whose automorphism group is $F_4$. ([Wikipedia, Octonion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octonion); [Wikipedia, G2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G2_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia, Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra)) Baez's survey relates them to [Clifford algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras) and spinors, [Bott periodicity](node:Bott%20Periodicity), projective and Lorentzian geometry, Jordan algebras and the exceptional Lie groups. ([Baez, The Octonions](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0105155))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 17 has four subsections: 17A general nonassociative rings, 17B Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras ("For Lie groups, see 22Exx"), 17C Jordan algebras (algebras, triples and pairs), and 17D other nonassociative rings and algebras; 17-08 carries a "See also 68W30" pointer to [computer algebra](node:Computer%20Algebra). ([MSC2020, 17](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17-XX))
- [MSC 17Axx - General nonassociative rings](node:MSC%2017Axx%20-%20General%20nonassociative%20rings): power-associative, flexible and noncommutative Jordan algebras, Leibniz algebras (17A32), nonassociative division algebras (17A35), $n$-ary compositions, free algebras, Gröbner–Shirshov bases, superalgebras and composition algebras (17A75). ([MSC2020, 17A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Axx))
- [MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras): structure, root systems, representations, exceptional algebras, universal enveloping algebras, [quantum groups](node:Quantum%20Groups) (17B37), modular Lie algebras (17B50), cohomology, Poisson algebras, Kac–Moody, Virasoro and vertex operator algebras (17B67–17B69). ([MSC2020, 17B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Bxx))
- [MSC 17Cxx - Jordan algebras (algebras, triples and pairs)](node:MSC%2017Cxx%20-%20Jordan%20algebras%20%28algebras,%20triples%20and%20pairs%29): structure, radicals, Peirce decompositions, exceptional Jordan structures, Jordan structures on [Banach spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) (see also 46H70, 46L70) and applications to physics. ([MSC2020, 17C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Cxx))
- [MSC 17Dxx - Other nonassociative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2017Dxx%20-%20Other%20nonassociative%20rings%20and%20algebras): alternative, Mal'tsev, right alternative, $(\gamma,\delta)$, Lie-admissible, non-Lie Hom and genetic algebras. ([MSC2020, 17D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Dxx))

Boundaries named by the entries: Lie groups go to 22E (see [MSC 22 - Topological groups, Lie groups](node:MSC%2022%20-%20Topological%20groups,%20Lie%20groups)), universal enveloping algebras are cross-listed with 16S30 and quantum groups with 16T20, 20G42, 81R50 and 82B23; the 16 codes belong to [MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras). ([MSC2020, 17B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Hurwitz's theorem (17A75).** A Hurwitz (composition) algebra is a finite-dimensional unital algebra with a nondegenerate quadratic form $q$ satisfying $q(ab)=q(a)q(b)$. Every finite-dimensional unital real algebra with a positive-definite multiplicative quadratic form is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, $\mathbb H$ or $\mathbb O$, so such algebras exist only in dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8; equivalently, multiplicative formulas for sums of squares exist only in these dimensions. Hurwitz proved the sums-of-squares form in 1898; the theorem was published posthumously in 1923. ([Wikipedia, Hurwitz's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz%27s_theorem_%28composition_algebras%29)) Every composition algebra is alternative. ([Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra))
- **Killing–Cartan classification (17B20, 17B22).** Every finite-dimensional simple complex Lie algebra is of type $A_n$ $(n\ge1)$, $B_n$ $(n\ge2)$, $C_n$ $(n\ge3)$, $D_n$ $(n\ge4)$, namely $\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}$, $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$, $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}$, $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$, or one of the five exceptional algebras $E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,G_2$. Killing gave the classification in 1888–90, Cartan made it rigorous in his 1894 thesis, and Dynkin's diagrams date from 1947; over characteristic 0, Weyl's theorem makes finite-dimensional modules of a semisimple Lie algebra completely reducible, and the Levi decomposition splits any finite-dimensional Lie algebra as a semidirect product of its solvable radical and a semisimple subalgebra. ([Wikipedia, Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra); [Wikipedia, Simple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Lie_algebra)) The bookkeeping is done by [root systems](node:Root%20Systems).
- **Modular Lie algebras (17B50).** Premet and Strade completed the classification for $p>3$: every finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>3$ is classical (coming from characteristic 0), a filtered Lie algebra of Cartan type, or a Melikian algebra, the last occurring only for $p=5$. ([Premet–Strade, survey abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601380); [Premet–Strade VI, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0711.2899)) The earlier Block–Wilson theorem proved the original Kostrikin–Shafarevich conjecture (1966) for $p>7$. ([Premet–Strade, §3.2, §4](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0601380))
- **Jordan algebras (17C).** A Jordan algebra is commutative with the Jordan identity; it is special if it embeds in some $A^+$, exceptional otherwise, and by the Shirshov–Cohn theorem every two-generated Jordan algebra is special. Jordan, von Neumann and Wigner (1934) classified the finite-dimensional formally real Jordan algebras: the simple ones are the self-adjoint $n\times n$ matrices over $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, $\mathbb H$, the spin factors, and the 27-dimensional Albert algebra. Zelmanov (1979) classified the infinite-dimensional simple (and prime nondegenerate) Jordan algebras: they are of Hermitian or Clifford type. ([Wikipedia, Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra)) The Tits–Kantor–Koecher construction (Tits 1962, Kantor 1964, Koecher 1967) makes $J\oplus J\oplus\mathrm{Inner}(J)$ into a Lie algebra; Kac used it in 1977 to classify simple Jordan superalgebras. ([Wikipedia, Kantor–Koecher–Tits construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kantor%E2%80%93Koecher%E2%80%93Tits_construction))
- **Alternative and Mal'tsev algebras (17D).** By Artin's theorem every two-generated subalgebra of an alternative algebra is associative, and by Kleinfeld's theorem every simple non-associative alternative ring is a generalized octonion algebra over its center. ([Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra)) Mal'tsev algebras, introduced in 1955, are to smooth Moufang loops what Lie algebras are to Lie groups. ([Wikipedia, Malcev algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcev_algebra))
- **Leibniz and pre-Lie algebras.** A (right) Leibniz algebra satisfies $[[a,b],c]=[a,[b,c]]+[[a,c],b]$, so right multiplications are derivations; it is a Lie algebra exactly when $[a,a]=0$. Bloh found them in 1965 and Loday's lift of the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex gives Leibniz homology. ([Wikipedia, Leibniz algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leibniz_algebra)) A pre-Lie algebra satisfies $(x y) z-x (y z)=(x z) y-x (z y)$, its commutator is a Lie bracket, and rooted trees with grafting form the free pre-Lie algebra on one generator; Gerstenhaber introduced the notion in deformation theory. ([Wikipedia, Pre-Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Lie_algebra))
- **$G_2$ and the octonions.** The compact form of $G_2$ is the automorphism group of the octonions; it has rank 2 and dimension 14, and Killing described a 14-dimensional simple Lie algebra to Engel in 1887. ([Wikipedia, G2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G2_%28mathematics%29)) Schafer's text closes its alternative-algebra chapter with "Derivations; Simple Lie Algebras of Type G" and its Jordan-algebra chapter with sections on simple Lie algebras of types $F$ and $E_6$. ([Schafer, contents](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf)) See also [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups) and [Projective Geometry](node:Projective%20Geometry), where alternative division rings give Moufang planes. ([Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra))

### History
Graves discovered the octonions in December 1843 and Cayley published them independently in 1845. ([Wikipedia, Octonion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octonion)) Killing's classification of complex semisimple Lie algebras (1888–90) was made rigorous by Cartan in 1894. ([Wikipedia, Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra)) Jordan introduced his algebras in 1933 to axiomatize quantum observables, the Jordan–von Neumann–Wigner classification followed in 1934, Albert renamed them Jordan algebras in 1946, and Zelmanov's classification dates from 1979. ([Wikipedia, Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra)) Mal'tsev defined his algebras in 1955, and the Premet–Strade completion of the $p>3$ classification of simple modular Lie algebras was announced in 2006. ([Wikipedia, Malcev algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcev_algebra); [Premet–Strade](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601380))

### Open problems
- **Simple Lie algebras in characteristics 2 and 3.** Premet and Strade write that "the classification problem in characteristics 2 and 3 is wide open", that it is unclear whether a complete classification can ever be achieved, and pose as Problem 1 the classification of simple Lie algebras of absolute toral rank two in characteristics 2 and 3. ([Premet–Strade, final sections](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0601380))
- **Infinite automorphism groups and two-generation.** Their Conjecture 1 (the automorphism group of a simple Lie algebra in characteristic $p>0$ is infinite) is proved for $p>3$ but open for $p\in\{2,3\}$, and their Question 1 asks whether every finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$ is generated by two elements; they call it out of reach for $p\in\{2,3\}$. ([Premet–Strade, final sections](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0601380)) For characteristic $0$ and $p>3$ Bois proved that every such algebra is generated by two elements, so the question remains open only in characteristics 2 and 3. ([Bois, arXiv 0708.1711](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.1711))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra): special and exceptional Jordan algebras, JvNW and Zelmanov classifications.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Hurwitz's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz%27s_theorem_%28composition_algebras%29): composition algebras and the dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8.
- **Learn:** [Schafer, An Introduction to Nonassociative Algebras](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf): alternative, Jordan and power-associative algebras and the exceptional Lie algebras of types $G$, $F$, $E_6$.
- **Primary:** [Premet–Strade, Classification of finite dimensional simple Lie algebras in prime characteristics (arXiv math/0601380)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601380): survey of the modular classification with open problems.
- **Primary:** [Baez, The Octonions (Bull. AMS 39, 2002; arXiv math/0105155)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0105155): survey of octonions, Jordan algebras and exceptional Lie groups.
- **Primary:** [Kaygorodov, Non-associative algebraic structures: classification and structure (arXiv 2306.00425)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00425): lecture notes on classification across nonassociative varieties.
- **Further reading:** [A Taste of Jordan Algebras (Springer Universitext, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b97489): graduate monograph on Jordan algebras.
references.MSC 17Axx - General nonassociative rings:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 17Axx is the general part of [nonassociative algebra](node:Nonassociative%20Algebras): algebras over a field (or rings) with a bilinear (biadditive) multiplication that need not be associative, studied either with no identity imposed or under identities weaker than associativity. The section covers general theory (17A01), power-associative rings (17A05), noncommutative Jordan algebras (17A15), flexible algebras (17A20), algebras with other identities (17A30) including Leibniz algebras (17A32), nonassociative division algebras (17A35), automorphisms and derivations (17A36), ternary and $n$-ary compositions (17A40, 17A42), quadratic algebras (17A45), free nonassociative algebras (17A50), structure theory (17A60), Gröbner–Shirshov bases (17A61), radicals (17A65), superalgebras (17A70), composition algebras (17A75) and valued algebras (17A80). ([MSC2020 17Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Axx))

The organizing measure is the associator $[a,b,c]=(ab)c-a(bc)$, which plays for associativity the role the commutator plays for commutativity. Three levels of associativity are distinguished: power-associative (each one-generated subalgebra is associative), alternative (each two-generated subalgebra is associative), and associative. The real division algebras $\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H,\mathbb O$ are the guiding examples, and the octonions connect the area to [Clifford algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras), [Bott periodicity](node:Bott%20Periodicity), Jordan algebras and the exceptional [Lie groups](node:Lie%20Groups). ([Baez, The Octonions §1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0105155); [Baez, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0105155))

### Scope
Schafer's standard text organizes the field as: arbitrary nonassociative algebras (basic concepts, the associative multiplication algebra $M(A)$ generated by left and right multiplications, the Lie multiplication algebra, trace forms and bimodules), then alternative algebras (Peirce decomposition, radical, Cayley algebras, Wedderburn principal theorem, derivations and Lie algebras of type $G_2$), Jordan algebras (types $F_4$ and $E_6$), and power-associative algebras including finite power-associative division rings and noncommutative Jordan algebras. ([Schafer, contents](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf))

Neighbouring codes: [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) and Lie superalgebras go to [17B](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras), (commutative) Jordan algebras to [17C](node:MSC%2017Cxx%20-%20Jordan%20algebras%20%28algebras,%20triples%20and%20pairs%29), and alternative, Mal'tsev, right alternative, Lie-admissible, Hom and genetic algebras to [17D](node:MSC%2017Dxx%20-%20Other%20nonassociative%20rings%20and%20algebras); 17A keeps the general theory and the classes listed above. ([MSC2020 17-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17-XX); [MSC2020 17Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Dxx); [MSC2020 17Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Alternative algebras and Artin's theorem.** An algebra is alternative iff $(aa)b=a(ab)$, $(ab)a=a(ba)$ and $(ba)a=b(aa)$ for all $a,b$; any two of these imply the third, and they say exactly that the associator is alternating. By Artin's theorem this is equivalent to every two-generated subalgebra being associative. The octonions are alternative but not associative. See [Alternative Algebras](node:Alternative%20Algebras) and [Octonions](node:Octonions). ([Baez §1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0105155))
- **Power-associativity (Albert).** An algebra is power-associative if the subalgebra generated by any single element is associative, so powers $x^n$ are well defined. Associative, alternative and [Jordan](node:Jordan%20Algebras) algebras are power-associative, as are the sedenions. Albert (*Trans. AMS* 1948) showed that over a field of characteristic $0$ an algebra is power-associative iff $[x,x,x]=0$ and $[x^2,x,x]=0$. ([Wikipedia: Power associativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_associativity))
- **Hurwitz's theorem (composition algebras, 17A75).** A finite-dimensional unital real algebra with a positive-definite quadratic form $q$ satisfying $q(ab)=q(a)q(b)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, $\mathbb H$ or $\mathbb O$; hence multiplicative sum-of-squares identities exist only in dimensions $1,2,4,8$. Hurwitz proved this in 1898 (published 1923), and the theory extends to arbitrary nondegenerate quadratic forms over other fields. Separately, $\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H,\mathbb O$ are the only alternative real division algebras (a version is due to Zorn, 1930). ([Wikipedia: Hurwitz's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz%27s_theorem_%28composition_algebras%29); [Baez, Theorems 1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0105155))
- **Bott–Milnor–Kervaire (17A35).** An algebra is a division algebra when left and right multiplication by any nonzero element are bijective; for nonassociative algebras this is not the same as having two-sided inverses (the sedenions have inverses but are not a division algebra). Every finite-dimensional real division algebra has dimension $1$, $2$, $4$ or $8$ (Kervaire and Bott–Milnor, independently, 1958, by topological methods), and every finite-dimensional real commutative division algebra has dimension $1$ or $2$ (Hopf, 1940). ([Wikipedia: Division algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_algebra); [Baez, Theorem 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0105155))
- **Free nonassociative algebras (17A50).** Kurosh proved that every subalgebra of a free nonassociative algebra is again free; Ismail generalizes this using an embedding of the free magma on $A$ into the product of the free magma on one generator and the free semigroup on $A$. ([Ismail](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.06380))
- **Evolution algebras (genetic algebras).** Tian and Vojtěchovský define an evolution algebra as a finite-dimensional algebra over a field $K$ with a basis $e_1,\dots,e_v$ such that $e_ie_j=0$ for $i\neq j$ and $e_ie_i=\sum_j a_{ij}e_j$; the coefficient $a_{ij}$ models the probability that allele $e_i$ becomes $e_j$ in the next generation. These algebras are commutative but not necessarily power-associative, hence not necessarily associative. MSC2020 places genetic algebras in 17D92. ([Tian–Vojtěchovský](https://cs.du.edu/~petr/data/papers/mathematical_concepts_of_evolution_algebras.pdf); [MSC2020 17Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Dxx))
- **Algebraic and geometric classification; degenerations.** For a variety of algebras defined by identities, the $n$-dimensional structures form a Zariski-closed subset $\mathfrak V_n\subset\operatorname{Hom}(V\otimes V,V)$ on which $GL(V)$ acts with orbits the isomorphism classes. $A_1$ degenerates to $A_2$ if the structure of $A_2$ lies in the orbit closure of $A_1$; an algebra is rigid if its orbit is open, and the closure of a rigid orbit is an irreducible component. Components need not contain a rigid algebra (Flanigan's 3-dimensional nilpotent associative example). Kaygorodov's survey collects many such algebraic and geometric classifications in small dimensions. ([Kaygorodov](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.00425v2))

### History
Hurwitz's 1898 paper gave the composition-algebra theorem, later reproved by Eckmann (1943), Lee (1948) and Chevalley (1954). Zorn treated alternative division algebras in 1930, Albert's "Power-associative rings" appeared in 1948, and Kervaire and Bott–Milnor proved the $1,2,4,8$ theorem in 1958. Schafer's *An Introduction to Nonassociative Algebras* organized the general theory alongside alternative, Jordan and power-associative algebras. ([Wikipedia: Hurwitz's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz%27s_theorem_%28composition_algebras%29); [Baez §1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0105155); [Wikipedia: Power associativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_associativity); [Schafer](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Classifying 8-dimensional real quadratic division algebras.** By the Hopf–Bott–Milnor–Kervaire theorem real division algebras have dimension $1,2,4,8$; those of dimension $1$ and $2$, and the $4$-dimensional quadratic ones, are classified, but Dieterich and Rubinsztein state that the problem of classifying all $8$-dimensional real quadratic division algebras is still open. They prove that every such algebra has degree $1$, $3$ or $5$. ([Dieterich–Rubinsztein](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.5071))
- **Active direction: geometric classification.** Kaygorodov poses, for each variety, the problems of finding the irreducible components of $\mathfrak V_n$, deciding which pairs of algebras admit a degeneration, and determining the algebras of a given level; the survey records answers in small dimensions for particular varieties. ([Kaygorodov](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.00425v2))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Division algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_algebra): associative and nonassociative division algebras, dimension theorems.
- **Reference:** [Hurwitz's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz%27s_theorem_%28composition_algebras%29): composition algebras and proofs.
- **Learn:** [Schafer, An Introduction to Nonassociative Algebras](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf): the standard textbook on general, alternative, Jordan and power-associative algebras.
- **Primary:** [Baez, The Octonions (Bull. AMS 2002)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0105155): survey of normed division algebras and their connections.
- **Primary:** [Kaygorodov, Non-associative algebraic structures: classification and structure](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.00425v2): survey of algebraic and geometric classification.
- **Primary:** [Dieterich–Rubinsztein](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.5071): degree theorem for 8-dimensional real quadratic division algebras.
- **Further reading:** [Schafer, An Introduction to Nonassociative Algebras (Pure and Applied Mathematics series)](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf): the canonical graduate text.
references.MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superal:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 17Bxx covers [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) and their $\mathbb Z/2$-graded analogues, Lie superalgebras, as algebraic objects; [Lie groups](node:Lie%20Groups) themselves are sent to 22Exx. Its codes run from identities and free Lie (super)algebras (17B01) and structure theory (17B05) through representations (17B10 algebraic, weights; 17B15 analytic), simple, semisimple and reductive algebras (17B20), [root systems](node:Root%20Systems) (17B22), exceptional algebras (17B25), solvable and nilpotent algebras (17B30), universal enveloping algebras (17B35), [quantum groups](node:Quantum%20Groups) (17B37), Yang–Baxter equations (17B38), modular Lie algebras (17B50), homology and cohomology (17B55, 17B56), Poisson algebras and Lie bialgebras (17B62, 17B63), infinite-dimensional algebras (17B65), Lie algebras of vector fields (17B66), Kac–Moody, extended affine and toroidal algebras (17B67), Virasoro algebras (17B68), vertex operator algebras (17B69), graded and color algebras (17B70, 17B75), and applications to integrable systems and physics (17B80, 17B81). ([MSC2020 17Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Bxx))

The centre of the area is the finite-dimensional theory in characteristic $0$: the Killing–Cartan classification of simple algebras by root systems and the highest-weight description of their representations. Research extends this in three directions: to infinite-dimensional algebras (Kac–Moody, affine, Virasoro), central to two-dimensional [conformal field theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory); to positive characteristic, where there are many more simple algebras; and to Lie superalgebras, used in physics to describe [supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry). ([Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra); [Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra); [Wikipedia: Lie superalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_superalgebra); [Wikipedia: Kac–Moody algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kac%E2%80%93Moody_algebra); [Wikipedia: Virasoro algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virasoro_algebra))

### Scope
A Lie superalgebra is a $\mathbb Z/2$-graded algebra $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_{\bar0}\oplus\mathfrak g_{\bar1}$ whose bracket (the supercommutator) is super skew-symmetric and satisfies a super Jacobi identity; $\mathfrak g_{\bar0}$ is an ordinary Lie algebra and $\mathfrak g_{\bar1}$ a representation of it. Some authors add axioms such as $[x,x]=0$ for even $x$, automatic when $2$ is invertible. Every associative superalgebra gives one via the supercommutator, e.g. $\mathfrak{gl}(p|q)$. ([Wikipedia: Lie superalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_superalgebra))

Neighbouring codes: Lie groups are sent to 22Exx; Lie algebras of linear [algebraic groups](node:Algebraic%20Groups) (17B45) point to 14Lxx and 20Gxx; enveloping algebras and quantum groups also have associative homes in 16S30 and 16T20 ([MSC 16 - Associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras)); and Lie algebras built from associative or Jordan structures (17B60) cross-refer to 16W10, 17C40 and 17C50. ([MSC2020 17Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Structure theorems (17B05, 17B30).** Engel: a finite-dimensional Lie algebra is nilpotent iff each $\operatorname{ad}u$ is nilpotent. Lie: a solvable $\mathfrak g\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ over $\mathbb C$ has a common eigenvector. Cartan: in characteristic $0$, $\mathfrak g$ is solvable iff $K(\mathfrak g,[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g])=0$ and semisimple iff the Killing form $K(u,v)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}u\operatorname{ad}v)$ is nondegenerate. Levi: in characteristic $0$ every finite-dimensional Lie algebra is a semidirect product of its solvable radical and a semisimple subalgebra. Ado: in characteristic $0$ every finite-dimensional Lie algebra has a faithful finite-dimensional representation (Iwasawa: any characteristic). ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra); [Stewart–Mehrle, Thms 4.8, 4.12](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf))
- **Killing–Cartan classification (17B20, 17B22, 17B25).** Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ a semisimple $\mathfrak g$ is a Cartan subalgebra plus one-dimensional root spaces; the roots form a root system that, by Serre's theorem, determines $\mathfrak g$. The simple algebras are $A_n\,(n\ge1)$, $B_n\,(n\ge2)$, $C_n\,(n\ge3)$, $D_n\,(n\ge4)$ and the exceptional $E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,G_2$. Killing (1888–90) found the list, Cartan (1894) made it rigorous, and Dynkin (1947) gave the diagram form. ([Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra); [Stewart–Mehrle, Thm 6.9](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf))
- **Representations (17B10).** Weyl's theorem: in characteristic $0$, finite-dimensional representations of a semisimple Lie algebra are completely reducible. Finite-dimensional simple modules of a complex semisimple algebra correspond bijectively to dominant integral weights, with characters given by the Weyl character formula. See [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory). ([Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra); [Stewart–Mehrle, Thm 5.6](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf))
- **Kac's classification of Lie superalgebras.** Kac (1977) classified the finite-dimensional simple complex Lie superalgebras: $\mathfrak{sl}(m|n)$ for $m\neq n$ (for $m=n\ge2$, its quotient by the ideal generated by the identity), $\mathfrak{osp}(m|2n)$, $D(2,1;\alpha)$, $F(4)$, $G(3)$, two "strange" series, and the Cartan types $W,S,\tilde S,H$. Among simple linearly compact infinite-dimensional ones there are ten series and five exceptional algebras $E(1,6),E(5,10),E(4,4),E(3,6),E(3,8)$. ([Wikipedia: Lie superalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_superalgebra))
- **Associated varieties of supermodules.** For a finite-dimensional complex Lie superalgebra let $X=\{x\in\mathfrak g_{\bar1}:[x,x]=0\}$, and for a module $M$ put $M_x=\ker x/xM$ and $X_M=\{x\in X:M_x\neq0\}$. Unlike the classical associated variety, $X_M$ can be nontrivial for finite-dimensional $M$; Duflo and Serganova show $X_{M\oplus N}=X_M\cup X_N$, $X_{M\otimes N}=X_M\cap X_N$, and $\operatorname{sdim}M=\operatorname{sdim}M_x$ for finite-dimensional $M$ and $x\in X$. ([Duflo–Serganova, §2](https://math.berkeley.edu/~serganov/papers/ass.pdf))
- **Kac–Moody algebras (17B67).** Defined by generators $e_i,f_i,h_i$ and relations from a generalized Cartan matrix $C$; for indecomposable symmetrizable $C$, a positive-definite form gives the finite-dimensional simple algebras, a semidefinite one the affine algebras, and an indefinite one indefinite type (the hyperbolic ones, of rank at most $10$, are classified). Kac and Moody introduced them independently around 1967–68, and Kac used affine representations to prove the Macdonald identities. ([Wikipedia: Kac–Moody algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kac%E2%80%93Moody_algebra))
- **Virasoro algebra (17B68).** Generators $L_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and central $c$ with $[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}+\tfrac{c}{12}(m^3-m)\delta_{m+n,0}$; it is the unique nontrivial central extension of the Witt algebra. A highest-weight representation is unitary iff $c\ge1,h\ge0$, or $c=1-\tfrac{6}{m(m+1)}$ ($m\ge2$) with $h=h_{r,s}(c)=\tfrac{((m+1)r-ms)^2-1}{4m(m+1)}$, $1\le r\le m-1$, $1\le s\le m$ (necessity by Friedan–Qiu–Shenker, sufficiency by Goddard–Kent–Olive). ([Wikipedia: Virasoro algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virasoro_algebra))
- **Modular Lie algebras (17B50).** Over algebraically closed fields of characteristic $p>3$, every finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra is classical, a filtered algebra of Cartan type, or a Melikian algebra ($p=5$ only); this is the Block–Wilson–Premet–Strade classification. ([Premet–Strade](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601380); [Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra))

### History
Lie (1870s) and Killing (1880s) started the theory, Weyl named it in the 1930s, Cartan completed the classification in 1894 and Dynkin recast it in 1947. Kac and Moody introduced Kac–Moody algebras around 1967–68, and Kac classified simple Lie superalgebras in 1977. ([Wikipedia: Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra); [Wikipedia: Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra); [Wikipedia: Kac–Moody algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kac%E2%80%93Moody_algebra); [Wikipedia: Lie superalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_superalgebra))

### Open problems
- **Simple Lie algebras in characteristics 2 and 3.** Premet and Strade state that the classification problem in characteristics $2$ and $3$ "is wide open" and list open problems: classify simple algebras of absolute toral rank two in characteristics $2$ and $3$; classify certain graded Lie algebras with reductive $G_0$ in those characteristics; their conjecture that every finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra in characteristic $p>0$ has infinite automorphism group (open for $p\in\{2,3\}$); determine absolute toral ranks and automorphism groups of all simple algebras for $p>3$; and whether every simple algebra is generated by two elements, which they call out of reach for $p\in\{2,3\}$. Bois later proved two-generation in characteristic $0$ and $p>3$. ([Premet–Strade, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0601380v2); [Bois](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.1711))
- **Finite-dimensional representations of Lie superalgebras.** Duflo and Serganova note that the finite-dimensional representation theory of superalgebras still has many open problems, and introduce associated varieties to study supercharacters and cohomology. ([Duflo–Serganova, §1](https://math.berkeley.edu/~serganov/papers/ass.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Semisimple Lie algebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra): root decomposition, classification, highest weights.
- **Reference:** [Lie superalgebra (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_superalgebra): definitions and Kac's classification.
- **Learn:** [Stewart–Mehrle, Lie Algebras and their Representations (Cambridge Part III)](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~dmehrle/notes/partiii/liealg_partiii_notes.pdf): structure theory through the classification.
- **Primary:** [Premet–Strade, Classification of finite dimensional simple Lie algebras in prime characteristics](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601380): survey and open problems for modular Lie algebras.
- **Primary:** [Duflo–Serganova, On associated variety for Lie superalgebras](https://math.berkeley.edu/~serganov/papers/ass.pdf): odd cohomology and associated varieties.
- **Further reading:** [Humphreys, Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory (Springer GTM, 1972)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2): the standard graduate text.
references.MSC 17Cxx - Jordan algebras (algebras, t:
## Reference
### Overview
A Jordan algebra is a commutative, not necessarily associative algebra satisfying the Jordan identity $(xx)(xy)=x((xx)y)$. Jordan algebras are power-associative. The basic source of examples is an associative algebra $A$ over a field of characteristic not $2$ with the symmetrized product $x\circ y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$, giving the Jordan algebra $A^+$; subalgebras of such $A^+$ are called special and all others exceptional. ([Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra))

MSC 17Cxx, a part of [MSC 17 - Nonassociative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2017%20-%20Nonassociative%20rings%20and%20algebras), covers Jordan algebras together with the trilinear generalisations named in its title: Jordan triple systems and Jordan pairs. The research area runs from pure structure theory (Zelmanov's classification of prime algebras) through Lie theory (the Tits–Kantor–Koecher construction) to analysis and geometry (JB-algebras, JB*-triples and bounded symmetric domains) and to the original motivation from quantum observables. ([MSC2020 17Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Cxx); [Brešar–Zelmanov survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16876v1); [Chu](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.05767); [Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists identities and free Jordan structures (17C05); structure theory (17C10); radicals (17C17); simple and semisimple algebras (17C20); idempotents and Peirce decompositions (17C27); associated groups and automorphisms (17C30), manifolds (17C36) and geometries (17C37); exceptional Jordan structures (17C40); Jordan structures associated with other structures (17C50, see also 16W10); finite-dimensional structures (17C55); division algebras (17C60); Jordan structures on Banach spaces and algebras (17C65, see also 46H70 and 46L70); super structures (17C70); and applications to physics (17C90). ([MSC2020 17Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Cxx))

Neighbouring codes, from the entry's cross-references: involutive associative rings whose symmetric elements carry Jordan structure are 16W10; Banach-algebraic and operator-algebraic Jordan theory is shared with 46H70 and 46L70 ([46Lxx](node:MSC%2046Lxx%20-%20Selfadjoint%20operator%20algebras%20%28C-star-algebras,%20von%20Neumann%20%28W-star-%29%20algebras,%20etc.%29)). ([MSC2020 17Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Cxx)) Lie theory ([MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras)) meets Jordan theory through the Tits–Kantor–Koecher construction below, which realises every unital Jordan algebra inside a $3$-graded Lie algebra. ([Brešar–Zelmanov survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16876v1))

### Key concepts
- **Jordan–von Neumann–Wigner classification (1934).** Every finite-dimensional formally real (Euclidean) Jordan algebra is a direct sum of simple ones, and the simple ones are: $n\times n$ self-adjoint matrices over $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$ or the quaternions $\mathbb H$; spin factors, generated by $\mathbb R^n$ with $x^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ (of [Clifford](node:Clifford%20Algebras) type); and the $27$-dimensional Albert algebra of $3\times3$ self-adjoint octonionic matrices, which is exceptional and has automorphism group $F_4$. ([Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra); [Symmetric cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_cone))
- **Zelmanov's structure theory.** In 1979 Zelmanov showed that infinite-dimensional simple (and prime nondegenerate) Jordan algebras are of Hermitian or Clifford type; the only exceptional simple Jordan algebras are the $27$-dimensional Albert algebras. His 1979 and 1983 papers "Prime Jordan algebras" are the basis of the modern structure theory, and his 1983 construction of a tetrad-eating T-ideal of the free Jordan algebra was later used by McCrimmon. ([Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra); [Brešar–Zelmanov survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16876v1))
- **Quadratic Jordan algebras.** McCrimmon (1966) axiomatised Jordan algebras through the identities of the quadratic representation $U_x$, which works over fields of any characteristic, including $2$, and reduces to the linear theory when the characteristic is not $2$. ([Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra))
- **Jordan triple systems and Jordan pairs.** A Jordan triple system is a space $V$ with a trilinear product satisfying $\{u,v,w\}=\{u,w,v\}$ and $\{u,v,\{w,x,y\}\}=\{w,x,\{u,v,y\}\}+\{w,\{u,v,x\},y\}-\{\{v,u,w\},x,y\}$. A Jordan pair is the generalisation involving two [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) $V_+,V_-$; Jordan triple systems are exactly the Jordan pairs with $V_+=V_-$ and equal trilinear maps. ([Jordan triple system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_triple_system))
- **Tits–Kantor–Koecher construction.** If a Lie algebra $L$ contains an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $e,f,h$ with $\operatorname{ad}h$ diagonalizable with eigenvalues $-2,0,2$, so $L=L_{-2}\oplus L_0\oplus L_2$, then $L_2$ with $a\circ b=[[a,f],b]$ is a Jordan algebra; Tits, Kantor and Koecher showed every unital Jordan algebra arises this way, with a universal Lie algebra $\mathrm{TKK}(J)$. This ties Jordan theory to [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras). ([Brešar–Zelmanov survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16876v1))
- **Koecher–Vinberg theorem.** Symmetric cones (open, convex, self-dual, homogeneous cones in a Euclidean space) correspond to the cones of squares of finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebras. For a Euclidean Jordan algebra $E$ with positive cone $C$, the tube $E+iC$ is a Hermitian symmetric space of tube type, biholomorphic via the Cayley transform to the unit ball of the complexification; the other irreducible bounded symmetric domains are described by Jordan triple systems. ([Symmetric cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_cone))
- **JB-algebras and JB*-triples.** A JB-algebra is a real Jordan Banach algebra with $\|a\circ b\|\le\|a\|\|b\|$, $\|a^2\|=\|a\|^2$ and $\|a^2\|\le\|a^2+b^2\|$ (Alfsen–Shultz–Størmer, 1978); the Albert algebra is the obstruction to realising every JB-algebra by self-adjoint operators on a [Hilbert space](node:Hilbert%20Spaces). A JB*-triple is a complex [Banach space](node:Banach%20Spaces) with a Jordan triple product such that each $a\,\square\,a$ is hermitian with non-negative spectrum and $\|a\,\square\,a\|=\|a\|^2$; every C*-algebra is one under $\{a,b,c\}=\tfrac12(ab^*c+cb^*a)$. ([Jordan operator algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_operator_algebra); [Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra); [Chu](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.05767); [Russo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.0694))
- **Kaup's Riemann mapping theorem (1983).** A complex Banach space is a JB*-triple if and only if its open unit ball is a bounded symmetric domain, and every bounded symmetric domain is biholomorphic to the open unit ball of a JB*-triple whose triple structure is unique up to isomorphism; Loos gave the finite-dimensional precursor. This is the bridge to [MSC 32Mxx - Complex spaces with a group of automorphisms](node:MSC%2032Mxx%20-%20Complex%20spaces%20with%20a%20group%20of%20automorphisms). ([Chu](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.05767))

### History
Jordan introduced these algebras in 1933 in an attempt to formalise the algebra of observables in [quantum electrodynamics](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics), Albert renamed them "Jordan algebras" in 1946, and the 1934 Jordan–von Neumann–Wigner paper classified the finite-dimensional formally real ones; see [MSC 81 - Quantum theory](node:MSC%2081%20-%20Quantum%20theory). McCrimmon's quadratic axioms date from 1966, and Zelmanov's classification of prime algebras from 1979 and 1983. ([Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra); [Brešar–Zelmanov survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16876v1)) Loos's *Jordan Pairs* appeared in Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics in 1975, and McCrimmon's *A Taste of Jordan Algebras* in Universitext in 2004. ([Loos](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0080843); [McCrimmon](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b97489); [Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra)) Kaup's Riemann mapping theorem was published in Math. Z. 183 (1983). ([Chu](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.05767))

### Open problems
- **Kaplansky's spectrum-preserver problem.** Brešar and Zelmanov list as not yet solved: is a bijective, unital, spectrum-preserving linear map between semisimple Banach algebras a Jordan isomorphism? ([Brešar–Zelmanov survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16876v1))
- **Jordan isomorphisms of general C*-algebras.** The same survey notes that the precise structure of a Jordan $*$-isomorphism (hence of an isometry) from a general C*-algebra is, to the authors' knowledge, unknown. ([Brešar–Zelmanov survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16876v1))
- **Cohomology of Jordan triples.** Russo notes that continuous cohomology of Banach Jordan triple systems has essentially no literature in infinite dimensions and that cohomology of Jordan algebras is far less developed than in the associative and Lie cases, and lists research projects in this direction. ([Russo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.0694))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_algebra): definitions, classification, Zelmanov's theorem and JB-algebras.
- **Learn:** [Schafer, An Introduction to Nonassociative Algebras](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf): chapter IV covers the radical, central simple Jordan algebras and their link to Lie algebras of types $F$ and $E_6$.
- **Primary:** [Brešar and Zelmanov, Jordan homomorphisms: a survey (2025)](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16876v1): research survey covering Herstein's theorems, the TKK construction and open questions; [Russo, Derivations and projections on Jordan triples](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.0694): introduction to Jordan triples and JB*-triples.
- **Further reading:** [McCrimmon, A Taste of Jordan Algebras (Springer Universitext, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b97489): standard graduate text including Zelmanov's theory; [Loos, Jordan Pairs (Springer LNM, 1975)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0080843): foundational monograph on pairs.
references.MSC 17Dxx - Other nonassociative rings a:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 17D collects the classes of nonassociative rings defined by identities other than the Lie and Jordan ones: alternative rings, Mal'tsev rings and algebras, right alternative rings, $(\gamma,\delta)$-rings, Lie-admissible algebras, (non-Lie) Hom algebras and genetic algebras. ([MSC2020, 17D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Dxx)) The two central classes are linked: an [alternative algebra](node:Alternative%20Algebras) is one in which the associator $[x,y,z]=(xy)z-x(yz)$ is alternating, and every alternative algebra becomes a Mal'tsev algebra under the commutator $xy-yx$, just as every associative algebra becomes a Lie algebra. ([Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra); [Wikipedia, Malcev algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcev_algebra))

The motivating examples are the [octonions](node:Octonions) and their relatives. The octonions are a non-associative alternative algebra and an 8-dimensional real normed division algebra, and their nonzero elements form a Moufang loop under multiplication. ([Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra); [Wikipedia, Moufang loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moufang_loop)) Mal'tsev algebras play for smooth Moufang loops the role that [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) play for [Lie groups](node:Lie%20Groups), which makes 17D the algebraic side of the theory of analytic loops. ([Wikipedia, Malcev algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcev_algebra); [Bremner et al., §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1008.2388))

### Scope
MSC2020 17D lists: 17D05 alternative rings; 17D10 Mal'tsev rings and algebras; 17D15 right alternative rings; 17D20 $(\gamma,\delta)$-rings, including $(1,-1)$-rings; 17D25 Lie-admissible algebras; 17D30 (non-Lie) Hom algebras and topics; 17D92 genetic algebras; 17D99 none of the above. The 17D entry itself carries no see-also cross-references. ([MSC2020, 17D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Dxx))

Neighbours inside section 17: composition algebras (17A75), nonassociative division algebras (17A35), power-associative rings (17A05), flexible algebras (17A20) and Leibniz algebras (17A32) belong to [MSC 17Axx - General nonassociative rings](node:MSC%2017Axx%20-%20General%20nonassociative%20rings), not to 17D, so Hurwitz algebras enter 17D only through the fact that every composition algebra is alternative. ([MSC2020, 17A](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Axx); [Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra)) Lie algebras themselves are [MSC 17Bxx - Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras) (Hom-Lie algebras are 17B61 there, while 17D30 is for non-Lie Hom algebras), and [Jordan algebras](node:Jordan%20Algebras) are [MSC 17Cxx - Jordan algebras (algebras, triples and pairs)](node:MSC%2017Cxx%20-%20Jordan%20algebras%20%28algebras,%20triples%20and%20pairs%29). ([MSC2020, 17D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=17Dxx)) The parent field is [MSC 17 - Nonassociative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2017%20-%20Nonassociative%20rings%20and%20algebras).

### Key concepts
- **Alternative identities and Artin's theorem (17D05).** An algebra is alternative if $x(xy)=(xx)y$ and $(yx)x=y(xx)$, equivalently $[x,x,y]=[y,x,x]=0$; any two of the left alternative, right alternative and flexible ($(xy)x=x(yx)$) identities imply all three. Artin's theorem: in an alternative algebra the subalgebra generated by any two elements is associative; more generally, if $x,y,z$ associate then the subalgebra they generate is associative. Hence alternative algebras are power-associative (the converse fails: the sedenions are power-associative but not alternative). Every alternative algebra satisfies the Moufang identities $a(x(ay))=(axa)y$, $((xa)y)a=x(aya)$ and $(ax)(ya)=a(xy)a$. ([Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra))
- **Structure of simple alternative rings (17D05).** Kleinfeld's theorem: every simple non-associative alternative ring is a generalized octonion (Cayley–Dickson) algebra over its center. The Artin–Zorn theorem: every finite alternative division ring is a [finite field](node:Finite%20Fields). Geometrically, the projective plane over any alternative division ring is a Moufang plane, which ties 17D05 to [projective geometry](node:Projective%20Geometry). ([Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra)) Schafer's text treats Cayley algebras, simple alternative algebras, the Wedderburn principal theorem and derivations giving the simple Lie algebras of type $G$ in its chapter on alternative algebras. ([Schafer, contents](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf))
- **Mal'tsev algebras (17D10).** A Mal'tsev algebra is an anticommutative algebra satisfying $(xy)(xz)=((xy)z)x+((yz)x)x+((zx)x)y$; every Lie algebra is one, and every alternative algebra $A$ gives one, $A^-$, under the commutator. ([Wikipedia, Malcev algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcev_algebra); [Bremner et al., §2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1008.2388)) Mal'tsev (1955) introduced them as the tangent algebras of analytic Moufang loops; a connected, simply connected real-analytic Moufang loop can be recovered from its Mal'tsev algebra. ([Wikipedia, Malcev algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcev_algebra); [Bremner–Douglas, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1108.4202)) The name is due to Sagle, and Kuzmin completed the basic theory in 1968: over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ there is a unique simple non-Lie Mal'tsev algebra, the commutator algebra of the 7-dimensional space of octonions with zero real part. ([Bremner–Douglas, §1, §2.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1108.4202))
- **Enveloping algebras of Mal'tsev algebras (17D10).** Pérez-Izquierdo and Shestakov extended the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem: for every Mal'tsev algebra $M$ over a field of characteristic $\ne 2,3$ there is a universal nonassociative algebra $U(M)$ and an injective map $M\to U(M)^-$ whose image lies in the generalized alternative nucleus. Shestakov showed that the universal alternative enveloping algebra of the real 7-dimensional simple Mal'tsev algebra (the traceless octonions under the commutator) is the real octonion division algebra. ([Bremner et al., §3, §6 and abstract](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1008.2388))
- **Lie-admissible algebras (17D25).** An algebra is Lie-admissible if the commutator $[a,b]=ab-ba$ makes it a Lie algebra; associative algebras, Lie algebras and Okubo algebras are examples. The notion is due to A. A. Albert (1948). ([Wikipedia, Lie-admissible algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie-admissible_algebra))
- **Hom algebras (17D30).** A Hom-associative algebra $(V,\mu,\alpha)$ satisfies $\mu(\alpha(x),\mu(y,z))=\mu(\mu(x,y),\alpha(z))$; a Hom-Lie algebra is skew-symmetric with the Hom-Jacobi identity $\circlearrowleft_{x,y,z}[\alpha(x),[y,z]]=0$; the commutator of a Hom-associative algebra is Hom-Lie (Makhlouf–Silvestrov, Prop. 1.6), and a Hom-algebra is Hom-Lie admissible when its commutator is Hom-Lie. Hom-Lie algebras go back to Hartwig, Larsson and Silvestrov. ([Makhlouf–Silvestrov, Defs 1.1, 1.3, 2.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0609501); [Makhlouf–Silvestrov, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0609501))
- **Genetic algebras (17D92).** A baric algebra is an algebra with a homomorphism (the weight) to the base field; train and special train algebras add polynomial and nilpotency conditions. Etherington began the subject in 1939, Schafer introduced genetic algebras in 1949, and Bernstein's 1923 work on the Hardy–Weinberg law underlies Bernstein algebras. ([Wikipedia, Genetic algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_algebra))

### History
Albert introduced Lie-admissible algebras in 1948 and Schafer genetic algebras in 1949. ([Wikipedia, Lie-admissible algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie-admissible_algebra); [Wikipedia, Genetic algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_algebra)) Mal'tsev defined his algebras in 1955, Sagle named them, and Kuzmin completed their basic theory in 1968. ([Bremner–Douglas, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1108.4202)) The structure theory of alternative rings was assembled in Zhevlakov, Slin'ko, Shestakov and Shirshov, *Rings That Are Nearly Associative*, reviewed by J. M. Osborn in the *Bulletin of the AMS* in 1983. ([Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra); [Crossref, Osborn review](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/s0273-0979-1983-15180-7)) Hom-associative and Hom-Lie-admissible algebras were introduced by Makhlouf and Silvestrov in 2006, building on the Hom-Lie algebras of Hartwig, Larsson and Silvestrov. ([Makhlouf–Silvestrov](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0609501))

### Open problems
- **Identities of the simple 7-dimensional Mal'tsev algebra.** Bremner and Douglas state as Conjecture 4.8, described as a "classical conjecture in the theory of Malcev algebras", that every polynomial identity of the simple 7-dimensional Mal'tsev algebra follows from the Mal'tsev identities and Filippov's degree-5 $h$-polynomial; they verify it computationally only through degree 7, and list further open problems on the identities of its binary–ternary (Lie–Yamaguti) structure. ([Bremner–Douglas, §4–§6](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1108.4202))
- **Phillips' problem (Moufang loops, the group side of 17D10).** Whether there is a finite Moufang loop of odd order with trivial nucleus is listed as open. ([Wikipedia, Moufang loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moufang_loop)) Moufang loops themselves are classified in [MSC 20Nxx - Other generalizations of groups](node:MSC%2020Nxx%20-%20Other%20generalizations%20of%20groups) and [Loops and Quasigroups](node:Loops%20and%20Quasigroups).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra): identities, Artin's theorem, Kleinfeld and Artin–Zorn theorems.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Malcev algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcev_algebra): definition and the Moufang-loop correspondence.
- **Learn:** [Schafer, An Introduction to Nonassociative Algebras](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/schafer-nonassociative-algebras.pdf): chapter III on alternative algebras (radical, Cayley algebras, simple alternative algebras, type $G$).
- **Primary:** [Bremner, Hentzel, Peresi, Tvalavadze, Usefi, Enveloping algebras of Malcev algebras (arXiv 1008.2388)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.2388): Pérez-Izquierdo–Shestakov envelopes and the universal property of the octonions.
- **Primary:** [Bremner–Douglas, The simple non-Lie Malcev algebra as a Lie–Yamaguti algebra (arXiv 1108.4202)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1108.4202): identities of the 7-dimensional algebra and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Makhlouf–Silvestrov, On Hom-algebra structures (arXiv math/0609501)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0609501): founding paper for Hom-associative and Hom-Lie-admissible algebras.
- **Further reading:** [Osborn's review of Zhevlakov–Slin'ko–Shestakov–Shirshov, Rings That Are Nearly Associative (Bull. AMS 9, 1983)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/s0273-0979-1983-15180-7): the standard monograph on alternative and nearly associative rings.
references.MSC 18 - Category theory; homological al:
## Reference
### Overview
[Category theory](node:Category%20Theory) studies objects through the morphisms between them: a category has objects, composable arrows with identities, functors map categories to categories preserving composition, and natural transformations compare functors. Riehl describes its purview as "mathematical analogy": constructions such as tensor products, free objects, localizations, kernels, completions and quotients are characterized by universal properties, limits or colimits rather than by their internal construction. ([Riehl, Preface and Ch. 1](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf)) Eilenberg and Mac Lane introduced the language in 1945 to make precise why a finite-dimensional real [vector space](node:Vector%20Spaces) $L$ is isomorphic to its [dual](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space) $T(L)$ only after a choice of basis, whereas the isomorphism with the double dual is natural. ([Eilenberg–Mac Lane, Introduction](https://people.math.osu.edu/cogdell.1/6112-Eilenberg%26MacLane-www.pdf))

The second half of section 18 is [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) in categorical form: abelian categories, resolutions and derived functors, Ext and Tor, [spectral sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences), and derived and triangulated categories. Abelian categories were introduced, by Buchsbaum (1955, as "exact categories") and by Grothendieck (1957), to unify the various cohomology theories. ([Wikipedia, Abelian category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_category)) Homological algebra over specific rings and groups is classified elsewhere: MSC directs commutative rings to 13D, associative rings to 16E, groups to 20J and [topological groups](node:Topological%20Groups) to 57T, with algebraic topology also at 55N and 55U. ([MSC2020, 18](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18-XX))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 18 has nine subsections: [18A general theory of categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20of%20categories%20and%20functors); [18B special categories](node:MSC%2018Bxx%20-%20Special%20categories); [18C categories and theories](node:MSC%2018Cxx%20-%20Categories%20and%20theories); [18D categorical structures](node:MSC%2018Dxx%20-%20Categorical%20structures); [18E categorical algebra](node:MSC%2018Exx%20-%20Categorical%20algebra); [18F categories in geometry and topology](node:MSC%2018Fxx%20-%20Categories%20in%20geometry%20and%20topology); [18G homological algebra in category theory, derived categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Gxx%20-%20Homological%20algebra%20in%20category%20theory,%20derived%20categories%20and%20functors) (see also 13Dxx, 16Exx, 20Jxx, 55Nxx, 55Uxx, 57Txx); [18M monoidal categories and operads](node:MSC%2018Mxx%20-%20Monoidal%20categories%20and%20operads); and [18N higher categories and homotopical algebra](node:MSC%2018Nxx%20-%20Higher%20categories%20and%20homotopical%20algebra). ([MSC2020, 18](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18-XX))

Within 18G the codes run from projectives and injectives (18G05), resolutions and derived functors (18G10), Ext and Tor and the Künneth formula (18G15), homological dimension (18G20) and relative homological algebra (18G25), through simplicial modules and Dold–Kan (18G31), chain complexes and dg categories (18G35), spectral sequences (18G40), crossed modules (18G45), nonabelian homological algebra (18G50), stable module categories (18G65), $A_\infty$-categories and homological mirror symmetry (18G70), derived and triangulated categories (18G80), graph complexes (18G85) and other (co)homology theories (18G90). ([MSC2020, 18G](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Gxx)) 18N covers 2-categories and bicategories, weak $n$-categories and coherence, categorification, strict $\omega$-categories, Quillen model categories and derivators (18N40), simplicial sets, localizations, $(\infty,1)$-categories, $\infty$-topoi and stable $\infty$-categories (18N60), $(\infty,n)$-categories and $\infty$-operads. ([MSC2020, 18N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Yoneda lemma](node:Yoneda%20Lemma) (18A).** For a functor $F:\mathcal C\to\mathbf{Set}$ with $\mathcal C$ locally small and any object $c$, evaluation at $\mathrm{id}_c$ gives a bijection $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal C(c,-),F)\cong Fc$, natural in $c$ and $F$; in particular these natural transformations form a set. ([Riehl, Thm 2.2.4](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf)) Dually, for a presheaf $X$ on $\mathcal C$, $\mathrm{Hom}(y(c),X)\cong X(c)$, so the Yoneda embedding $y:\mathcal C\to[\mathcal C^{op},\mathbf{Set}]$ is fully faithful; Mac Lane dates the name to a 1954 conversation with Yoneda. ([nLab, Yoneda lemma](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Yoneda+lemma))
- **[Adjunctions](node:Adjoint%20Functors) (18A).** Right adjoints preserve limits and left adjoints preserve colimits; the general and special adjoint functor theorems and Freyd's representability theorem give converses under solution-set or smallness conditions. ([Riehl, Thm 4.5.2, §4.7](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf)) Monads arise from adjunctions and categories of algebras recover them, the subject of [Monads and Algebraic Theories](node:Monads%20and%20Algebraic%20Theories) (18C). ([Riehl, Ch. 5](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf))
- **[Abelian categories](node:Abelian%20Categories) and Freyd–Mitchell (18E).** An abelian category is preadditive, has a zero object, binary biproducts, kernels and cokernels, and every monomorphism is a kernel and every epimorphism a cokernel; modules over a ring and sheaves of [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) on a space are the basic examples. ([Wikipedia, Abelian category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_category); [nLab, abelian category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/abelian+category)) Freyd–Mitchell embedding theorem: if $\mathcal A$ is a small abelian category, there is a ring $R$ and an exact, fully faithful functor $\mathcal A\hookrightarrow R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}$, which justifies diagram chases by elements. ([Riehl, Thm E.5.2](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf))
- **Derived functors, Ext and Tor (18G10, 18G15).** For a left exact functor $F$ between abelian categories with enough injectives, $R^iF(X)$ is the $i$-th cohomology of $F$ applied to an injective resolution of $X$; $R^0F=F$, $R^iF$ vanishes on injectives for $i>0$, and a short exact sequence yields a long exact sequence. The right derived functors of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ are $\mathrm{Ext}$, $\mathrm{Tor}$ is the left derived functor of $\otimes$, and sheaf cohomology is the right derived functor of global sections. ([Wikipedia, Derived functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derived_functor)) Riehl recasts derived functors as Kan extensions. ([Riehl, §6.4](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf)) See [Projective Resolutions](node:Projective%20Resolutions) and [Tor and Ext over Commutative Rings](node:Tor%20and%20Ext%20over%20Commutative%20Rings).
- **[Derived and triangulated categories](node:Derived%20Categories) (18G80).** The derived category $D(\mathcal A)$ is the localization of the category of chain complexes in $\mathcal A$ at the quasi-isomorphisms; every derived category is triangulated, and $D(\mathcal A)$ is the homotopy category of a stable $(\infty,1)$-category, presented by dg-model structures. Verdier introduced derived categories in his thesis under Grothendieck, originally to extend Serre duality to a relative setting. ([nLab, derived category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+category))
- **Coherence and higher structure (18M, 18N).** Mac Lane–Kelly coherence: every formal diagram of associators, unitors and symmetries in a symmetric [monoidal category](node:Monoidal%20Categories) commutes. ([Riehl, Thm E.2.2](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf)) The homotopy hypothesis, that $\infty$-groupoids model homotopy types, is a theorem for Kan complexes (Quillen's equivalence of $\mathbf{Top}$ with simplicial sets, 1967); see [Higher Categories](node:Higher%20Categories) and [Simplicial Methods](node:Simplicial%20Methods). ([nLab, homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis))

### History
Eilenberg and Mac Lane presented "General theory of natural equivalences" to the AMS in September 1942 and published it in the *Transactions of the AMS* 58 (1945); its final chapter applies functors to [homology](node:Homology), cohomology, duality, universal coefficient theorems and Čech homology. ([Eilenberg–Mac Lane, contents](https://people.math.osu.edu/cogdell.1/6112-Eilenberg%26MacLane-www.pdf)) Abelian categories followed with Buchsbaum (1955) and Grothendieck (1957), derived categories with Verdier's thesis, and Grothendieck formulated the homotopy hypothesis in *Pursuing Stacks* (1983). ([Wikipedia, Abelian category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_category); [nLab, derived category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+category); [nLab, homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis)) Mac Lane's *Categories for the Working Mathematician* appeared in Springer's Graduate Texts in Mathematics (1978 edition) and Weibel's *An Introduction to Homological Algebra* with Cambridge University Press in 1994. ([Crossref, Mac Lane](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-4721-8); [Crossref, Weibel](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139644136))

### Open problems
- **Freyd's generating hypothesis.** Freyd (1966) asked whether a map between finite spectra inducing zero on homotopy groups must be null; Barthel calls it "arguably one of the most important open problems in stable homotopy theory". ([Barthel, Introduction](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1603.09181)) Its triangulated-category analogue is settled in derived categories of rings: Lockridge proves the generating hypothesis holds in the derived category of a commutative ring $R$ if and only if $R$ is von Neumann regular. ([Lockridge, arXiv math/0511534](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511534))
- **Homotopy hypothesis for algebraic $\infty$-groupoids (18N).** Beyond Kan complexes, the nLab reports that for other algebraic definitions of $\infty$-groupoids "not much indication for how to prove the homotopy hypothesis is known", and points to a review of progress for Grothendieck–Maltsiniotis $\infty$-groupoids. ([nLab, homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, derived category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+category): derived categories, triangulated and $\infty$-categorical structure.
- **Reference:** [nLab, Yoneda lemma](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Yoneda+lemma): statement, corollaries and history.
- **Learn:** [Riehl, Category Theory in Context](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf): free textbook on universal properties, Yoneda, limits, adjunctions, monads, Kan extensions, with an epilogue on coherence and Freyd–Mitchell.
- **Primary:** [Eilenberg–Mac Lane, General Theory of Natural Equivalences (Trans. AMS 58, 1945)](https://people.math.osu.edu/cogdell.1/6112-Eilenberg%26MacLane-www.pdf): the founding paper.
- **Primary:** [Barthel, Auslander–Reiten sequences, Brown–Comenetz duality, and the K(n)-local generating hypothesis (arXiv 1603.09181)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1603.09181): the generating hypothesis and its local variants.
- **Further reading:** [Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician (Springer GTM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-4721-8): the standard graduate text on category theory.
- **Further reading:** [Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra (CUP, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139644136): the standard graduate text on homological algebra.
references.MSC 18Axx - General theory of categories:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 18Axx, "General theory of categories and functors," is the part of 18-XX (Category theory; homological algebra) devoted to the basic machinery of category theory itself: definitions of categories and functors, special classes of morphisms and functors, functor categories, limits and colimits, and adjoint functors with their universal constructions. ([MSC2020, 18Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Axx&btn=Current))

The unifying theme is the universal property. Representable functors, adjunctions, and limits are three formulations of it, and Kan extensions express all three: Mac Lane titled a section of *Categories for the Working Mathematician* "All Concepts Are Kan Extensions." ([Leinster, Basic Category Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.09375); [Wikipedia, Kan extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kan_extension))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists these codes ([MSC2020, 18Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Axx&btn=Current)):
- 18A05 Definitions and generalizations in theory of categories; 18A10 Graphs, diagram schemes, precategories; 18A15 Foundations, relations to logic and deductive systems (see also 03-XX).
- 18A20 Epimorphisms, monomorphisms, special classes of morphisms, null morphisms; 18A22 Special properties of functors (faithful, full, etc.); 18A23 Natural morphisms, dinatural morphisms.
- 18A25 Functor categories, comma categories; 18A30 Limits and colimits (products, sums, directed limits, pushouts, fiber products, equalizers, kernels, ends and coends, etc.); 18A32 Factorization systems, substructures, quotient structures, congruences, amalgams; 18A35 Categories admitting limits (complete categories), functors preserving limits, completions.
- 18A40 Adjoint functors (universal constructions, reflective subcategories, Kan extensions, etc.); 18A50 Graded categories (general), with dg categories sent to 18G35; 18A99 None of the above.

The 18-XX heading directs work on commutative rings, associative rings, groups, and [topological groups](node:Topological%20Groups) to 13Dxx, 16Exx, 20Jxx, and 57Txx, and points to 55Nxx and 55Uxx for algebraic topology. ([MSC2020, 18-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Axx&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- [Yoneda Lemma](node:Yoneda%20Lemma): for a presheaf $F$ on $\mathcal C$ and an object $U$, $s\mapsto s_U(1_U)$ gives a bijection $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathcal C(-,U),F)\cong F(U)$; hence the Yoneda embedding is fully faithful, and an object representing a functor is unique up to unique isomorphism. ([Stacks, Lemma 4.3.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/001L))
- [Adjoint Functors](node:Adjoint%20Functors): $F\dashv G$ means $\mathcal D(Fx,y)\cong\mathcal C(x,Gy)$ naturally in $x,y$, with unit $1\Rightarrow GF$ and counit $FG\Rightarrow 1$ satisfying the triangle identities; $F$ preserves all colimits that exist and $G$ all limits that exist, and $G$ is fully faithful iff the counit is an isomorphism. ([Stacks, Definition 4.24.1, Lemmas 4.24.4–4.24.7](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0036); [Stacks, Lemma 4.24.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0038))
- **Freyd's adjoint functor theorems.** If $\mathcal C$ is complete and locally small and $R:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ preserves small limits, then $R$ has a left adjoint iff it satisfies the solution set condition (general AFT). The special AFT drops the solution set condition when $\mathcal C$ is complete, locally small, well-powered, and has a small cogenerating set, and $\mathcal D$ is locally small. ([nLab, adjoint functor theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/adjoint+functor+theorem))
- **Limits and completeness (18A30, 18A35).** A category with all small products and equalizers has all small limits; pullbacks and a terminal object give all finite limits. When all $I$-shaped limits exist, $\lim:\mathcal C^I\to\mathcal C$ is right adjoint to the diagonal functor, and hom-functors $\mathcal C(c,-)$ preserve limits. ([nLab, limit](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/limit); [Sharifi, Proposition 1.5.6](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch01.html))
- **Kan extensions (18A40).** $\mathrm{Lan}_pF$, when it exists, is left adjoint to precomposition with $p$ evaluated at $F$: $[\mathcal C',\mathcal D](\mathrm{Lan}_pF,G)\cong[\mathcal C,\mathcal D](F,G\circ p)$. If $\mathcal C$ is small and $\mathcal D$ cocomplete, all left Kan extensions exist and are pointwise weighted colimits, given in the copowered case by the coend $\int^{c}\mathcal C'(pc,c')\cdot Fc$. Limits are right Kan extensions along $\mathcal C\to 1$, and a functor $F$ has a left adjoint iff $\mathrm{Ran}_F(1)$ exists and $F$ preserves it. ([nLab, Kan extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kan+extension); [Wikipedia, Kan extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kan_extension))
- **Factorization systems (18A32).** An orthogonal factorization system $(E,M)$ factors every morphism as $m\circ e$ with $e\in E$, $m\in M$, with unique diagonal fillers; each class determines the other, $E={}^{\perp}M$ and $M=E^{\perp}$. Examples are (epi, mono) in a topos and (regular epi, mono) in a regular category. ([nLab, orthogonal factorization system](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orthogonal+factorization+system))
- **Special functors (18A22).** A functor is an equivalence iff it is fully faithful and essentially surjective; in classical mathematics constructing a quasi-inverse from these two properties uses the [axiom of choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice). ([nLab, equivalence of categories](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+of+categories))
- [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): categories, functors, and natural transformations are the basic definitions (18A05, with natural morphisms under 18A23); a natural transformation $\alpha:F\Rightarrow G$ satisfies $G(f)\alpha_x=\alpha_yF(f)$ for every $f:x\to y$. ([Sharifi, §1.2](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch01.html))

### Neighbouring codes
- [MSC 18Bxx - Special categories](node:MSC%2018Bxx%20-%20Special%20categories) treats particular kinds of categories (sets, relations, topoi, [groupoids](node:Groupoids)), while 18Axx holds the general notions listed above. ([MSC2020, 18Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Bxx&btn=Current))
- [MSC 18Cxx - Categories and theories](node:MSC%2018Cxx%20-%20Categories%20and%20theories) holds [monads and algebraic theories](node:Monads%20and%20Algebraic%20Theories), sketches, and accessible and locally presentable categories. ([MSC2020, 18Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Cxx&btn=Current)) Every adjunction gives a monad, and Beck's monadicity theorem says when a functor $U:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ is monadic: iff $U$ has a left adjoint and creates coequalizers of $U$-split pairs. ([nLab, monadicity theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/monadicity+theorem))
- [MSC 18Exx - Categorical algebra](node:MSC%2018Exx%20-%20Categorical%20algebra) covers additive, regular and Barr-exact, and abelian categories (see [Abelian Categories](node:Abelian%20Categories)). ([MSC2020, 18Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Exx&btn=Current))
- [MSC 18Nxx - Higher categories and homotopical algebra](node:MSC%2018Nxx%20-%20Higher%20categories%20and%20homotopical%20algebra) covers 2-categories and bicategories, weak $n$-categories, model categories, and $(\infty,1)$-categories. ([MSC2020, 18Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx&btn=Current))

### History
Daniel Kan introduced adjoint functors in "Adjoint functors," Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 87 (1958), 294–329, a concept that grew out of [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra); the tensor–hom adjunction $\mathrm{Hom}(X\otimes A,Y)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(X,\mathrm{Hom}(A,Y))$ for [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) is a basic example. Kan constructed certain Kan extensions using limits in 1960, after an earlier appearance in Cartan–Eilenberg's 1956 treatment of derived functors.
