Freyd's adjoint functor theorems originate in the exercises of chapter 3 of his *Abelian Categories* (1964). ([Wikipedia, Adjoint functors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_functors); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1958-0131451-0); [Wikipedia, Kan extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kan_extension); [nLab, adjoint functor theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/adjoint+functor+theorem))

### Open problems
None found. The nLab list of open problems in category theory, which collects problems stated in the literature, has entries only under topos theory (Lawvere's 2009 list) and higher category theory (Simpson's conjecture, the [cobordism](node:Cobordism) and tangle hypotheses), none of them in the 18A subcodes. ([nLab, open problems in category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/open+problems+in+category+theory)) Searches tried: "open problems in category theory", "open problem factorization systems", "open problem Kan extensions"; the higher-categorical problems concern the objects listed under [MSC 18Nxx - Higher categories and homotopical algebra](node:MSC%2018Nxx%20-%20Higher%20categories%20and%20homotopical%20algebra). ([MSC2020, 18Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx&btn=Current))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, Kan extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kan+extension): definitions, pointwise formulas, existence.
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, adjoint functors](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0036): definitions and lemmas with proofs.
- **Learn:** [Sharifi, Category theory (UCLA notes, ch. 1)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch01.html): categories, Yoneda, limits, adjoints.
- **Learn:** [Leinster, Basic Category Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.09375): free textbook on adjoints, representables, and limits.
- **Primary:** [Kan, Adjoint functors (1958)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1958-0131451-0): the paper introducing adjunctions.
- **Further reading:** [Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-4721-8): the standard graduate reference, including Kan extensions.
references.MSC 18Bxx - Special categories:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 18Bxx, "Special categories," classifies work on particular kinds of categories (see [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory)) studied in their own right: categories of sets, of relations and spans, of automata, topoi, preorders and lattices viewed as categories, groupoids and semigroups viewed as categories, and extensive, distributive, and adhesive categories. ([MSC2020, 18Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Bxx&btn=Current))

The largest of these families is topos theory. An elementary topos is a category with finite limits that is cartesian closed and has a subobject classifier, and its internal logic is intuitionistic higher-order logic; Grothendieck topoi, the categories of sheaves on sites, are the geometric special case. A topos lets one use geometric and logical reasoning in settings with no underlying space, as with the étale topos of a scheme. ([nLab, topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topos); [Wikipedia, Topos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topos))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists ([MSC2020, 18Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Bxx&btn=Current)):
- 18B05 Categories of sets, characterizations (see also 03-XX); 18B10 Categories of spans/cospans, relations, or partial maps; 18B15 Embedding theorems, universal categories (see also 18E20).
- 18B20 Categories of machines, automata (see also 03D05, 68Qxx); 18B25 Topoi (see also 03G30, 18F10).
- 18B35 Preorders, orders, domains and lattices (viewed as categories) (see also 06-XX); 18B40 Groupoids, semigroupoids, semigroups, groups (viewed as categories) (see also 20Axx, 20L05, 20Mxx).
- 18B50 Extensive, distributive, and adhesive categories; 18B99 None of the above.

Neighbouring codes in 18Fxx: Grothendieck topologies and Grothendieck topoi are 18F10 (cross-referenced from 18B25), presheaves, sheaves, stacks, and descent conditions are 18F20, categories of topological spaces and continuous mappings are 18F60, and frames and locales are 18F70 (cross-referenced to 18B35). ([MSC2020, 18Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Fxx&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- [Toposes](node:Toposes) (18B25): an elementary topos has finite limits, is cartesian closed, and has a subobject classifier $\Omega$ (equivalently: finite limits and power objects). Its internal logic is intuitionistic higher-order logic. ([nLab, topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topos))
- **Lawvere–Tierney topologies.** A Lawvere–Tierney topology on an elementary topos is $j:\Omega\to\Omega$ with $j\circ\mathrm{true}=\mathrm{true}$, $j\circ j=j$, and $j\circ\wedge=\wedge\circ(j\times j)$; it is used to construct a topos of sheaves. Grothendieck topologies on a small category $C$ are essentially the same as Lawvere–Tierney topologies on the presheaf topos $[C^{op},\mathrm{Set}]$. Lawvere introduced the notion in 1971, with Tierney also credited. ([Wikipedia, Lawvere–Tierney topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawvere%E2%80%93Tierney_topology))
- **Giraud's theorem.** A category is a Grothendieck topos (equivalent to sheaves on a small site) iff it is locally presentable, its colimits are universal (stable under pullback), its coproducts are disjoint, and its quotients are effective. ([nLab, Giraud's theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Giraud%27s+theorem)) In the classical form of the axioms, local presentability appears as a small set of generators together with all small colimits, fibre products distribute over coproducts, and all [equivalence relations](node:Equivalence%20Relations) are effective. ([Wikipedia, Topos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topos))
- [Groupoids](node:Groupoids) (18B40): a groupoid is a category in which every morphism is an isomorphism; a group is the same as a one-object groupoid, with composition given by the group law. ([Stacks, Definition 4.2.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0018); [Stacks, Example 4.2.6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0019))
- **Brown's groupoid van Kampen theorem.** If $X=U\cup V$ with $U,V$ open and $X_0\subseteq X$ meets every path component of $U$, $V$, and $U\cap V$, then $\Pi_1(X,X_0)$ is the pushout of $\Pi_1(U,X_0)\leftarrow\Pi_1(U\cap V,X_0)\to\Pi_1(V,X_0)$ in groupoids. This removes the classical requirement that $U\cap V$ be path-connected, so it computes the [fundamental group](node:Fundamental%20Group) of the circle directly. It is due to R. Brown, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 17 (1967), 385–401. ([nLab, van Kampen theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/van+Kampen+theorem); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/plms/s3-17.3.385))
- **Relations and spans (18B10).** $\mathbf{Rel}$ has sets as objects and relations $R\subseteq X\times Y$ as morphisms, composed relationally; the transpose $R\mapsto R^\dagger$ makes it a dagger category, and products and coproducts coincide as disjoint unions. A span $X\leftarrow S\to Y$ generalizes a morphism; taking the image of $S\to X\times Y$ sends spans to relations, and for a regular category $C$ the same construction gives a category $\mathrm{Rel}(C)$. A cospan in $C$ is a span in $C^{op}$. ([nLab, Rel](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Rel); [nLab, span](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/span))
- **Preorders as categories (18B35).** A preorder is a thin category (at most one morphism between any two objects), and it is a partial order iff the category is skeletal. Monotone [Galois connections](node:Galois%20Connections) between posets are exactly [adjoint functors](node:Adjoint%20Functors) between the corresponding categories. ([nLab, preorder](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/preorder); [Wikipedia, Galois connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_connection))
- **Adhesive categories (18B50).** A category is adhesive if it has pullbacks and pushouts along monomorphisms, and pushouts of monomorphisms are van Kampen squares. Every topos is adhesive (Lack–Sobociński), while $\mathbf{Cat}$, posets, topological spaces, and groupoids are not. Adhesivity makes pushout complements unique when they exist, which double-pushout graph rewriting relies on. ([nLab, adhesive category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/adhesive+category))
- **Convenient categories of spaces (18F60, related).** The category $\mathbf{Top}$ of [topological spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces) is not cartesian closed. A convenient category is a full replete subcategory of $\mathbf{Top}$ containing CW complexes that is cartesian closed, complete, and cocomplete; compactly generated spaces are the main example. The name spread through Steenrod's "A convenient category of topological spaces," Michigan Math. J. 14 (1967), 133–152, but Brown had first proved that Hausdorff $k$-spaces form a cartesian closed category. ([nLab, convenient category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/convenient+category+of+topological+spaces); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1307/mmj/1028999711))

### History
Grothendieck topoi arose from sheaf theory in algebraic geometry, with Giraud's theorem characterizing them intrinsically; the elementary axioms came from Lawvere and Tierney, whose topologies date from Lawvere's 1971 "Quantifiers and sheaves." Brown's 1967 paper introduced fundamental groupoids on a set of base points for van Kampen-type pushout theorems. Lack and Sobociński's papers "Adhesive categories" (FoSSaCS 2004) and "Toposes are adhesive" (ICGT 2006) develop adhesive categories and show that every topos is one. ([Wikipedia, Topos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topos); [Wikipedia, Lawvere–Tierney topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawvere%E2%80%93Tierney_topology); [nLab, van Kampen theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/van+Kampen+theorem); [nLab, adhesive category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/adhesive+category))

### Open problems
- **Lawvere's open problems in topos theory (2009).** Lawvere listed seven problems he had "not yet been able to solve." The nLab list of open problems in category theory notes that some have since been resolved. In particular, problem (1), whether some Grothendieck topos has a proper class of connected surjective quotients, was answered positively by Kamio and Hora (2024), with the presheaf topos on the free monoid on countably many generators as an example. ([Lawvere, Open problems in topos theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Lawvere-OpenProblems.pdf); [nLab, open problems](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/open+problems+in+category+theory); [Kamio–Hora, arXiv:2407.17105](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.17105))
- Lawvere's problem (6), among those he posed as unsolved in 2009, concerns ATOMs: objects $D$ for which $(-)^D$ has a right adjoint $(-)^{1/D}$. In a presheaf topos the ATOMs form a small collection. The problem asks whether, in a general topos, the class of all ATOMs can be suitably parameterized, and whether there is a lower topos over which all the corresponding adjunctions are enriched. ([Lawvere, Open problems in topos theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Lawvere-OpenProblems.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topos): definitions, internal logic, and examples.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Topos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topos): Giraud's axioms and motivating examples.
- **Learn:** [Leinster, An informal introduction to topos theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.5647): short expository notes for readers who know basic category theory.
- **Primary:** [Kamio–Hora, Solution to Lawvere's first problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.17105): recent research on quotient topoi.
- **Primary:** [Brown, Groupoids and van Kampen's theorem (1967)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/plms/s3-17.3.385): groupoid methods in topology.
- **Further reading:** [Mac Lane–Moerdijk, Sheaves in Geometry and Logic](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0927-0): a standard graduate introduction to topos theory.
- **Further reading:** [Lurie, Higher Topos Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608040): higher-categorical analogues of Grothendieck topoi.
references.MSC 18Cxx - Categories and theories:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 18Cxx, "Categories and theories," covers the categorical treatment of algebraic and logical theories and their models. It includes equational categories, algebraic theories and functorial semantics, monads with their Eilenberg–Moore and Kleisli constructions, sketches, accessible and locally presentable categories, structured objects such as group objects, and categorical semantics of formal languages. ([MSC2020, 18Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Cxx&btn=Current))

The organizing idea, from Lawvere's 1963 thesis *Functorial Semantics of Algebraic Theories*, is that a theory is a category and a model is a structure-preserving functor out of it. For algebraic theories this gives a presentation-independent notion that is equivalent to finitary monads on $\mathrm{Set}$. ([Wikipedia, Lawvere theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawvere_theory); [nLab, Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists ([MSC2020, 18Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Cxx&btn=Current)):
- 18C05 Equational categories (see also 03C05, 08C05); 18C10 Theories (e.g., algebraic theories), structure, and semantics (see also 03G30).
- 18C15 Monads (= standard construction, triple or triad), algebras for monads, homology and derived functors for monads (see also 18Gxx; for functional programming, 68N18); 18C20 Eilenberg–Moore and Kleisli constructions for monads.
- 18C30 Sketches and generalizations; 18C35 Accessible and locally presentable categories; 18C40 Structured objects in a category (group objects, etc.); 18C50 Categorical semantics of formal languages (see also 68Q55, 68Q65); 18C99.

Cross-references tie 18C to [universal algebra](node:Universal%20Algebra) and logic: 18C05 points to 03C05 and 08C05 (see [MSC 08Cxx - Other classes of algebras](node:MSC%2008Cxx%20-%20Other%20classes%20of%20algebras)), 18C10 to 03G30 (see [MSC 03Gxx - Algebraic logic](node:MSC%2003Gxx%20-%20Algebraic%20logic)), 18C15 to 68N18 for functional programming, and 18C50 to 68Q55 and 68Q65. ([MSC2020, 18Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Cxx&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Lawvere theories and functorial semantics (18C10).** A Lawvere algebraic theory is a small category $\mathbb A$ with finite products whose objects are $A_0=1, A_1, A_2,\dots$ with $A_{n+1}=A_n\times A_1$; a model in a finite-product category $\mathcal C$ is a finite-product-preserving functor $\mathbb A\to\mathcal C$, and homomorphisms are natural transformations. Euclidean spaces with smooth maps form such a theory, whose $\mathrm{Set}$-models are $C^\infty$-algebras. ([Awodey–Bauer, Def. 1.2.10, Ex. 1.2.11](https://awodey.github.io/typetheory/notes/catlog2024.pdf)) Models of the theory of groups are groups in $\mathrm{Set}$, [topological groups](node:Topological%20Groups) in $\mathbf{Top}$, and [Lie groups](node:Lie%20Groups) in manifolds. ([Wikipedia, Lawvere theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawvere_theory))
- **Syntax–semantics duality.** For an algebraic theory $T$, the opposite of the category $\mathrm{mod}(T)$ of finitely generated free models classifies $T$-models: $\mathrm{Hom}_{FP}(\mathrm{mod}(T)^{op},\mathcal C)\simeq\mathrm{Mod}(T,\mathcal C)$ naturally in finite-product categories $\mathcal C$. Hence the syntactic category is equivalent to $\mathrm{mod}(T)^{op}$, and every Lawvere theory satisfies $\mathbb A\simeq\mathrm{mod}(\mathbb A)^{op}$. ([Awodey–Bauer, Thm. 1.2.1, Cor. 1.2.3, Thm. 1.2.15](https://awodey.github.io/typetheory/notes/catlog2024.pdf))
- **Monads and their algebras (18C15, 18C20).** For a monad $(T,\eta,\mu)$, a $T$-algebra is $\nu:TA\to A$ with $\nu\circ T\nu=\nu\circ\mu_A$ and $\nu\circ\eta_A=1_A$. The Eilenberg–Moore category $\mathcal C^T$ of algebras gives the terminal adjunction inducing $T$. The Kleisli category $\mathcal C_T$, with morphisms $a\to Tb$ composed through $\mu$, is equivalent to the free algebras and gives the initial one. ([nLab, Eilenberg–Moore category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Eilenberg-Moore+category); [nLab, Kleisli category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kleisli+category)) See [Monads and Algebraic Theories](node:Monads%20and%20Algebraic%20Theories).
- **Beck's monadicity theorem.** A functor $U:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ is monadic iff $U$ has a left adjoint and creates coequalizers of $U$-split pairs. A sufficient "crude" form: $U$ has a left adjoint, reflects isomorphisms, and $\mathcal D$ has and $U$ preserves coequalizers of reflexive pairs. The theorems go back to an untitled manuscript of Jon Beck circulated around 1966–68. ([nLab, monadicity theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/monadicity+theorem))
- **Algebraic categories over $\mathrm{Set}$.** For $U:\mathcal A\to\mathrm{Set}$ the following are equivalent: $\mathcal A$ is the category of $\mathrm{Set}$-models of a Lawvere theory with $U$ evaluation at the generator; $U$ has a left adjoint, preserves filtered colimits, and creates $U$-absolute coequalizers; $\mathcal A$ is monadic over $\mathrm{Set}$ for a finitary monad. So Lawvere theories correspond to finitary monads on $\mathrm{Set}$, while infinitary theories correspond to arbitrary monads. ([Awodey–Bauer, Thm. 1.2.19](https://awodey.github.io/typetheory/notes/catlog2024.pdf); [nLab, Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory))
- **Locally presentable and accessible categories (18C35).** A locally presentable category is an accessible category with all small colimits, equivalently an accessibly embedded reflective subcategory of a presheaf category; such categories are also complete. Examples include $\mathrm{Set}$, presheaf categories, Grothendieck [abelian categories](node:Abelian%20Categories) such as $R$-modules, and sheaf toposes. The notion is due to Gabriel–Ulmer (1971), with the textbook account by Adámek–Rosický (1994). ([nLab, locally presentable category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+presentable+category))
- **Gabriel–Ulmer duality.** $\mathcal C\mapsto\mathrm{Lex}(\mathcal C,\mathrm{Set})$ gives a biequivalence between small finitely complete categories (with finite-limit-preserving functors) and the opposite of locally finitely presentable categories with finitary right adjoints. ([nLab, Gabriel–Ulmer duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Gabriel-Ulmer+duality))
- **Sketches (18C30).** A sketch is a small category with a set of cones and a set of cocones; a model is a functor taking the cones to limit cones and the cocones to colimit cocones. The notion comes from Ehresmann's school; nLab cites Bastiani–Ehresmann (1972) for it. Categories of models of limit sketches are exactly the locally presentable categories (Adámek–Rosický, Cor. 1.52), and categories of models of general sketches are exactly the accessible categories. ([nLab, sketch](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sketch))
- **Semantics of computation (18C50).** Moggi (1989, 1991) proposed monads as "notions of computation" with effects such as state, input/output, and exceptions, with effectful programs as morphisms of the Kleisli category; MSC sends the functional-programming side to 68N18 (see [Functional Programming](node:Functional%20Programming)). Plotkin and Power's "Algebraic Operations and Generic Effects," Applied Categorical Structures 11 (2003), 69–94, relates algebraic operations to computational effects (see [Algebraic Effects and Handlers](node:Algebraic%20Effects%20and%20Handlers)). ([nLab, monad in computer science](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/monad+%28in+computer+science%29); [Crossref, Moggi 1991](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0890-5401%2891%2990052-4); [Crossref, Plotkin–Power 2003](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1023/A:1023064908962))

### History
Lawvere introduced functorial semantics in his 1963 doctoral dissertation. Beck's monadicity theorems date from the late 1960s, and Gabriel and Ulmer introduced locally presentable categories in 1971. Moggi's "Notions of computation and monads" appeared in *Information and Computation* 93 (1991), 55–92. Hyland and Power's 2007 paper "The Category Theoretic Understanding of Universal Algebra: Lawvere Theories and Monads" appeared in ENTCS 172, 437–458. ([nLab, Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory); [nLab, monadicity theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/monadicity+theorem); [nLab, locally presentable category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+presentable+category); [Crossref, Moggi](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0890-5401%2891%2990052-4); [Crossref, Hyland–Power](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.entcs.2007.02.019))

### Open problems
- **Colimit-density and Vopěnka's principle.** Adámek, Brooke-Taylor, Campion, Positselski, and Rosický proved, assuming Vopěnka's principle, that a category is locally presentable iff it is cocomplete and has a colimit-dense subcategory and a presentable generator. They say they do not know whether that [set-theoretic](node:Set%20Theory) assumption is needed. Their Open Problem 1.2 asks: if every category with a presentable generator and a colimit-dense subcategory is bounded, does Vopěnka's principle follow? ([ar5iv, Colimit-dense subcategories](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1812.10649); [arXiv:1812.10649](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10649))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, monadicity theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/monadicity+theorem): Beck's theorem in crude and precise forms.
- **Reference:** [nLab, locally presentable category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+presentable+category): definitions, characterizations, examples.
- **Learn:** [Awodey–Bauer, Introduction to Categorical Logic](https://awodey.github.io/typetheory/notes/catlog2024.pdf): lecture notes on algebraic theories, Lawvere duality, and categorical semantics.
- **Primary:** [Adámek et al., Colimit-dense subcategories](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10649): research on locally presentable categories and set theory.
- **Primary:** [Hyland–Power, The Category Theoretic Understanding of Universal Algebra (2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.entcs.2007.02.019): paper on Lawvere theories and monads.
- **Further reading:** [Moggi, Notions of computation and monads (1991)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0890-5401%2891%2990052-4): monads in programming semantics.
- **Further reading:** [Plotkin–Power, Algebraic Operations and Generic Effects (2003)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1023/A:1023064908962): algebraic theories of computational effects.
references.MSC 18Dxx - Categorical structures:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 18Dxx collects the structures that are added to, or built from, ordinary categories in [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): closed and enriched categories, actions of monoidal categories, fibered categories, internal categories and groupoids, profunctors, and the 2-categorical machinery of "formal category theory" (proarrow equipments, Yoneda structures, KZ doctrines). It sits in [MSC 18 - Category theory; homological algebra](node:MSC%2018%20-%20Category%20theory;%20homological%20algebra). ([MSC2020 18Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Dxx))

The unifying theme is that many arguments about categories (Yoneda, limits, Kan extensions, adjunctions) can be carried out in a more general setting: with hom-objects in a monoidal category $\mathcal V$, with categories varying over a base, with categories living inside another category, or abstractly inside a 2-category equipped with "proarrows". ([Kelly](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kelly-book.pdf); [proarrow equipment](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proarrow+equipment))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists: 18D15 closed categories (closed monoidal and cartesian closed categories); 18D20 enriched categories over closed or monoidal categories; 18D25 actions of a monoidal category and tensorial strength (for [functional programming](node:Functional%20Programming) see also 68N18); 18D30 fibered categories; 18D40 internal categories and groupoids; 18D60 profunctors (correspondences, distributors, modules); 18D65 proarrow equipments, Yoneda structures and KZ doctrines (lax idempotent monads); 18D70 formal category theory. ([MSC2020 18Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Dxx))

Boundaries stated by the classification: double categories go to 18N10, topological groupoids to 22A22 and Lie groupoids to 58H05 (from the 18D40 note). 2-categories, bicategories and double categories as such are classed at 18N10, and 2-dimensional monad theory at 18N15, in [MSC 18Nxx - Higher categories and homotopical algebra](node:MSC%2018Nxx%20-%20Higher%20categories%20and%20homotopical%20algebra); monoidal and symmetric monoidal categories themselves are 18M05, in [MSC 18Mxx - Monoidal categories and operads](node:MSC%2018Mxx%20-%20Monoidal%20categories%20and%20operads). ([MSC2020 18Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Dxx); [MSC2020 18Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx); [MSC2020 18Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Mxx))

### Key concepts
- **Enriched categories and weighted limits (18D15, 18D20).** For a monoidal $\mathcal V$, a $\mathcal V$-category has hom-objects $\mathcal A(x,y)\in\mathcal V$ with composition $\mathcal A(y,z)\otimes\mathcal A(x,y)\to\mathcal A(x,z)$ and units satisfying associativity and unit axioms. For this theory Kelly assumes $\mathcal V$ symmetric monoidal closed with complete and cocomplete underlying category $\mathcal V_0$. Ordinary conical limits are inadequate for general $\mathcal V$, so Kelly works with indexed (weighted) limits: for $F:\mathcal K\to\mathcal V$ and $G:\mathcal K\to\mathcal B$, the limit $\{F,G\}$ is defined by a $\mathcal V$-natural isomorphism $\mathcal B(B,\{F,G\})\cong[\mathcal K,\mathcal V](F,\mathcal B(B,G-))$. Kan extensions are expressed through such limits and colimits, and $[\mathcal A^{op},\mathcal V]$ is the free cocompletion of a small $\mathcal A$. ([Kelly, §§1.2, 3.1, 3.9, 4.1, 4.4](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kelly-book.pdf))
- **Lawvere metric spaces.** Lawvere observed that [metric spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces) are categories enriched in the monoidal poset $([0,\infty],\ge)$ with tensor $+$: composition is the triangle inequality, and such a Lawvere metric need not be symmetric or separated. The same pattern with the two-element Boolean preorder gives preorders. ([Lawvere metric space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+metric+space); [Baez, Lecture 29](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/act_course/lecture_29.html))
- **Grothendieck fibrations (18D30).** A morphism $f:x\to y$ in $\mathcal E$ is cartesian for $P:\mathcal E\to\mathcal B$ if every $g:z\to y$ with $P(g)=P(f)\circ w$ factors uniquely as $g=f\circ\hat w$ with $P(\hat w)=w$; $P$ is a fibration if every $f_0:x_0\to P(y)$ has a cartesian lift. The Grothendieck construction $F\mapsto\int F$ gives an equivalence between pseudofunctors $\mathcal B^{op}\to\mathbf{Cat}$ and fibrations over $\mathcal B$; Grothendieck introduced fibrations to describe stacks. ([Grothendieck fibration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Grothendieck+fibration))
- **Internal categories (18D40).** In a category $\mathcal A$ with pullbacks, an internal category consists of objects $C_0,C_1$ with source and target $s,t:C_1\to C_0$, identities $e:C_0\to C_1$ and composition $c:C_1\times_{C_0}C_1\to C_1$ satisfying the category laws as commuting diagrams; small categories are the categories internal to $\mathbf{Set}$. ([Internal category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/internal+category))
- **Profunctors (18D60).** A profunctor $\mathcal C\nrightarrow\mathcal D$ is a functor $\mathcal D^{op}\times\mathcal C\to\mathbf{Set}$, composed by the coend $(G\circ F)(e,c)=\int^{d}F(d,c)\times G(e,d)$. Small categories, profunctors and natural transformations form the bicategory $\mathbf{Prof}$; each functor $f$ yields representable profunctors $\mathcal D(1,f)\dashv\mathcal D(f,1)$, and profunctors correspond to colimit-preserving functors between presheaf categories. For one-object $\mathbf{Vect}$-enriched categories they are bimodules. ([Profunctor](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/profunctor))
- **Proarrow equipments and KZ doctrines (18D65, 18D70).** A proarrow equipment is a 2-functor $K\to M$, bijective on objects and locally fully faithful, sending each $f$ to a proarrow with a right adjoint; $\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{Prof}$ is the basic example. Equipments allow fully faithful morphisms, pointwise Kan extensions and weighted limits to be defined formally and to give the correct notions in $\mathcal V$-$\mathbf{Cat}$. A 2-monad is lax-idempotent (Kock–Zöberlein) when $T\eta_A\dashv\mu_A$ with invertible unit; then an object admits at most one pseudo-algebra structure, up to unique isomorphism, and free cocompletion 2-monads are the archetypes. ([Proarrow equipment](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proarrow+equipment); [Lax-idempotent 2-monad](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lax-idempotent+2-monad))

### History
Kelly's *Basic Concepts of Enriched Category Theory* was published as LMS Lecture Notes 64 by Cambridge University Press in 1982 and reprinted in Reprints in Theory and Applications of Categories in 2005. ([Kelly](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kelly-book.pdf)) Lawvere's "Metric spaces, generalized logic and closed categories" appeared in 1973. ([Lawvere metric space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+metric+space)) Kock's preprint on monads whose structures are adjoint to units dates from 1972/73 (published 1995) and Zöberlein's "Doctrines on 2-categories" from 1976; Street's "Fibrations and Yoneda's lemma in a 2-category" (1974) is among the early references on the subject. ([Lax-idempotent 2-monad](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lax-idempotent+2-monad)) Di Liberti and Loregian (2019) showed that cocomplete Yoneda structures correspond to certain proarrow equipments. ([Di Liberti–Loregian](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.01594))

### Open problems
None found. Searches tried: "formal category theory open problem", "Yoneda structure" / "proarrow equipment" / "enriched categories" with "remains open" on arXiv, and the nLab pages on fibrations, profunctors, proarrow equipments and lax-idempotent 2-monads. The closest active direction found is the comparison of formal frameworks: Di Liberti and Loregian relate Yoneda structures and equipments and recognise the presheaf construction as a relative lax idempotent monad and note that it "quite often" generates an ambidextrous Yoneda structure, in which a fully formal Isbell duality holds. ([Di Liberti–Loregian](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.01594))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, Grothendieck fibration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Grothendieck+fibration): cartesian morphisms, cleavages and the Grothendieck construction; see also [profunctor](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/profunctor).
- **Learn:** [Baez, Applied Category Theory, Lecture 29](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/act_course/lecture_29.html): enriched categories over monoidal preorders, from preorders to cost-enriched categories.
- **Primary:** [Kelly, Basic Concepts of Enriched Category Theory](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kelly-book.pdf): the standard monograph on enriched categories, indexed limits, Kan extensions and density.
- **Further reading:** [Di Liberti and Loregian, On the unicity of formal category theories](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.01594): research paper comparing Yoneda structures and proarrow equipments.
references.MSC 18Exx - Categorical algebra:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 18Exx, "Categorical algebra," classifies the study of categories (see [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory)) with algebraic exactness structure: preadditive and additive categories, regular and Barr-exact categories, abelian and Grothendieck categories, protomodular, semi-abelian and Mal'tsev categories, embedding theorems, localization, torsion theories, definable subcategories, and categorical Galois theory. ([MSC2020, 18Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Exx&btn=Current))

Two lines of development meet here. Abelian categories, introduced to unify cohomology theories for sheaves and for groups, have the category of abelian groups as their prototype and are the setting of [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra). Semi-abelian categories generalize them to capture the properties of non-additive categories such as groups, rings without unit, and Lie algebras, and axiomatic frameworks running from z-exact through homological and semi-abelian to abelian categories carry homological methods across this range. ([Wikipedia, Abelian category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_category); [nLab, semi-abelian category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/semi-abelian+category); [Peschke–Van der Linden, arXiv:2404.15896](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15896))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists ([MSC2020, 18Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Exx&btn=Current)):
- 18E05 Preadditive, additive categories; 18E08 Regular categories, Barr-exact categories; 18E10 Abelian categories, Grothendieck categories.
- 18E13 Protomodular categories, semi-abelian categories, Mal'tsev categories (see also 08B05, 08B10); 18E20 Categorical embedding theorems (see also 18B15).
- 18E35 Localization of categories, calculus of fractions (homotopical aspects go to 18N55, 55P60); 18E40 Torsion theories, radicals (see also 13D30, 16S90); 18E45 Definable subcategories and connections with [model theory](node:Model%20Theory) (see also 13C60); 18E50 Categorical Galois theory; 18E99.

Resolutions and derived functors, Ext and Tor, [spectral sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences), and derived and triangulated categories are classified in [MSC 18Gxx - Homological algebra in category theory, derived categories and functors](node:MSC%2018Gxx%20-%20Homological%20algebra%20in%20category%20theory,%20derived%20categories%20and%20functors). ([MSC2020, 18Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Gxx&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Additive categories (18E05).** An additive category has abelian-group hom-sets with composition distributing over addition, a zero object, and finite coproducts (which are then biproducts $A_1\oplus A_2$). A functor between additive categories is additive iff it is a homomorphism on hom-groups, equivalently iff it preserves biproducts. ([Sharifi, Defs. 2.1.1, 2.1.10, Lemma 2.1.13](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch02.html))
- [Abelian Categories](node:Abelian%20Categories) (18E10): an additive category in which all kernels and cokernels exist and the canonical map $\mathrm{Coim}(f)\to\mathrm{Im}(f)$ is an isomorphism for every $f$. Abelian categories have all finite limits and colimits, a morphism is an isomorphism iff it is mono and epi, and the opposite of an abelian category is abelian. ([Stacks, Def. 12.5.1, Lemmas 12.5.2–12.5.5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00ZX)) $P$ is projective iff $\mathrm{Hom}(P,-)$ is exact iff every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to P\to 0$ splits iff $\mathrm{Ext}(P,A)=0$ for all $A$. ([Stacks, Lemma 12.28.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/013A))
- **Grothendieck categories and Gabriel–Popescu.** A Grothendieck abelian category satisfies AB5 (it has direct sums and exact filtered colimits) and has a generator. Such a category has small limits, is locally presentable, and has an injective cogenerator. ([Stacks, Def. 19.10.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/079A); [nLab, Grothendieck category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Grothendieck+category)) If $G$ is a generator and $R=\mathrm{End}(G)$, then $S=\mathrm{Hom}(G,-):\mathcal A\to\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R$ is fully faithful and has an exact left adjoint (Gabriel–Popescu, 1964), so every Grothendieck category is a reflective localization of a module category. ([Wikipedia, Gabriel–Popescu theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel%E2%80%93Popescu_theorem); [nLab, Gabriel–Popescu theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Gabriel-Popescu+theorem))
- **Embedding theorems (18E20).** Freyd–Mitchell: every small abelian category admits a full, faithful, exact functor into $R$-$\mathrm{Mod}$ for some ring $R$ (Mitchell 1964; Freyd, *Abelian Categories*, Thm. 7.34). The smallness hypothesis is part of the theorem. ([nLab, Freyd–Mitchell embedding theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Freyd-Mitchell+embedding+theorem); [Sharifi, Thm. 2.5.9](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch02.html))
- **Regular and Barr-exact categories (18E08).** A category is regular if it is finitely complete, kernel pairs have coequalizers, and regular epimorphisms are pullback-stable; it is Barr-exact if moreover every congruence is a kernel pair. $\mathrm{Set}$, toposes, abelian categories, $\mathrm{Grp}$, and categories monadic over $\mathrm{Set}$ are regular, while $\mathbf{Cat}$, $\mathbf{Pos}$, and $\mathbf{Top}$ are not. The notion is from Barr, Grillet, and van Osdol (LNM 236, 1971). ([nLab, regular category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/regular+category))
- **Semi-abelian categories (18E13).** A category is semi-abelian if it is Barr-exact, has a zero object and finite coproducts, and is protomodular (Janelidze–Márki–Tholen, J. Pure Appl. Algebra 168 (2002)). Groups, rings and algebras without unit, [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras), crossed modules, and cocommutative [Hopf algebras](node:Hopf%20Algebras) over a field are examples. A semi-abelian category is abelian iff it is additive, iff its opposite is also semi-abelian. ([nLab, semi-abelian category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/semi-abelian+category); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/S0022-4049%2801%2900103-7))
- **Localization, Serre quotients, torsion theories (18E35, 18E40).** If a class $W$ admits a calculus of right fractions, morphisms of $\mathcal C[W^{-1}]$ are equivalence classes of roofs $a\leftarrow a'\to b$ with the left leg in $W$ (Gabriel–Zisman 1967). ([nLab, calculus of fractions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/calculus+of+fractions)) For a Serre subcategory $\mathcal C\subset\mathcal A$ (a nonempty full subcategory such that $B\in\mathcal C$ whenever $A\to B\to C$ is exact with $A,C\in\mathcal C$), there is an abelian quotient $\mathcal A/\mathcal C$ with an exact, essentially surjective functor with kernel $\mathcal C$, universal among exact functors killing $\mathcal C$, constructed as such a localization. ([Stacks, Def. 12.10.1, Lemma 12.10.6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02MN)) A torsion theory $(\mathcal T,\mathcal F)$ has $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal T,\mathcal F)=0$ and gives each $X$ an exact sequence $0\to Y\to X\to X/Y\to 0$ with $Y\in\mathcal T$, $X/Y\in\mathcal F$; torsion [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) form the basic example (Dickson 1966). ([nLab, torsion theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/torsion+theory))
- **Quillen exact categories.** An exact category is an additive category with a class of "exact" sequences (inflations, deflations) satisfying Quillen's axioms, for example an extension-closed full subcategory of an abelian category. Every small exact category embeds in an abelian category so that its exact sequences are exactly those exact there. Quillen introduced them in "Higher algebraic K-theory" (1973); see [Higher Algebraic K-Theory](node:Higher%20Algebraic%20K-Theory). ([nLab, Quillen exact category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Quillen+exact+category))

### History
Buchsbaum introduced the idea in 1955 under the name "exact category," and Grothendieck published the notion in his Tôhoku paper, "Sur quelques points d'algèbre homologique," Tôhoku Math. J. 9 (1957), 119–221, which listed the axioms AB1–AB6 and their duals and proved the existence of injectives in great generality; both aimed to unify the cohomology of sheaves and [of groups](node:Group%20Cohomology). ([Wikipedia, Abelian category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_category); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2748/tmj/1178244839); [Stacks, Section 19.10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/079A)) Gabriel–Popescu and Freyd–Mitchell date from 1964, Barr-exact categories from 1971, and semi-abelian categories from 2002. ([Wikipedia, Gabriel–Popescu theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel%E2%80%93Popescu_theorem); [nLab, Freyd–Mitchell](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Freyd-Mitchell+embedding+theorem); [nLab, regular category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/regular+category); [nLab, semi-abelian category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/semi-abelian+category))

### Open problems
None found. The nLab list of open problems in category theory has entries only in topos theory and higher category theory. ([nLab, open problems in category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/open+problems+in+category+theory)) Searches tried: "open problem semi-abelian categories", "open question Grothendieck abelian categories AB4*", "open problem categorical algebra survey"; these returned research papers and theses but no source stating an open problem in the 18E subcodes.

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, abelian categories](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00ZX): definitions and lemmas with proofs.
- **Reference:** [nLab, semi-abelian category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/semi-abelian+category): definition, examples, references.
- **Learn:** [Sharifi, Abelian categories (UCLA notes, ch. 2)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/homalg-ch02.html): additive and abelian categories, exactness, Freyd–Mitchell.
- **Primary:** [Peschke–Van der Linden, A Homological View of Categorical Algebra](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15896): monograph-length treatment from z-exact through homological, semi-abelian, and abelian categories.
- **Primary:** [Janelidze–Márki–Tholen, Semi-abelian categories (2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/S0022-4049%2801%2900103-7): the defining paper.
- **Further reading:** [Grothendieck, Sur quelques points d'algèbre homologique (1957)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2748/tmj/1178244839): the Tôhoku paper.

## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 subfield 18Fxx, "Categories in geometry and topology", collects the category-theoretic machinery that geometers and topologists use to pass from local to global information: Grothendieck topologies and toposes, sheaves, stacks and descent, categorical K-theory, synthetic differential geometry and tangent categories, functor calculus, and point-free topology. ([MSC2020, 18Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Fxx))

The unifying idea is the sheaf condition: data given on the members of a cover that agree on overlaps glue uniquely. For a presheaf $F$ of sets on a space $X$ and an open cover $U=\bigcup_i U_i$, $F$ is a sheaf when $F(U)\to\prod_i F(U_i)\rightrightarrows\prod_{i,j}F(U_i\cap U_j)$ is an equalizer. Grothendieck topologies replace open covers by abstract covering families, so the same condition makes sense on categories such as the étale site of a scheme. ([Stacks, Tag 0071](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0071); [Lurie, Lecture 8, Definition 6 and Example 11](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/278xnotes/Lecture8-Topologies.pdf))

A topos is then a category equivalent to sheaves on a small site, and Lurie's heuristic is that a topos is a generalized topological space; the classifying topos of a first-order theory is a kind of "space of all models" of the theory. Many different sites present the same topos, so the topos, not the site, is the invariant object. ([Lurie, Lecture 8, Definition 17 and Warning 20](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/278xnotes/Lecture8-Topologies.pdf))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists these codes: 18F05 local categories and functors; 18F10 Grothendieck topologies and Grothendieck topoi; 18F15 abstract manifolds and [fiber bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles) (category-theoretic aspects); 18F20 presheaves and sheaves, stacks, descent conditions; 18F25 algebraic K-theory and L-theory (category-theoretic aspects); 18F30 Grothendieck groups (category-theoretic aspects); 18F40 synthetic differential geometry, tangent categories, differential categories; 18F50 Goodwillie calculus and functor calculus; 18F60 categories of topological spaces and continuous mappings; 18F70 frames and locales, pointfree topology, Stone duality; 18F75 quantales; 18F99 other. ([MSC2020, 18Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Fxx))

Neighbouring codes divide the work differently. Topoi as a special kind of category are 18B25, which cross-refers to 18F10 and to 03G30 "Categorical logic, topoi"; 18F10 is the code for Grothendieck topologies and the toposes they generate. Algebraic K-theory proper is [MSC 19](node:MSC%2019%20-%20K-theory); 18F25 and 18F30 carry the qualifier "category-theoretic aspects". [Spectral Sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences) and [Derived Categories](node:Derived%20Categories) have their own codes in [18G](node:MSC%2018Gxx%20-%20Homological%20algebra%20in%20category%20theory,%20derived%20categories%20and%20functors), and $\infty$-topoi are listed under [18N60](node:MSC%2018Nxx%20-%20Higher%20categories%20and%20homotopical%20algebra). ([MSC2020, 18Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Fxx); [MSC2020, 18Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Bxx); [MSC2020, 03Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Gxx))

### Key concepts
- **Grothendieck topologies and sites (18F10)**, see [Sheaves and Categories of Spaces](node:Sheaves%20and%20Categories%20of%20Spaces) and [Toposes](node:Toposes). In Lurie's covering-family form, a Grothendieck topology on a category with finite limits specifies coverings $\{U_i\to X\}$ that are stable under base change (T1), closed under composition of coverings (T2), and include any family in which some map has a section (T3). A sheaf on the site is a presheaf $F$ for which $F(X)\to\prod_iF(U_i)\rightrightarrows\prod_{i,j}F(U_i\times_XU_j)$ is an equalizer for every covering. The equivalent sieve form asks covering sieves to be stable under pullback, to satisfy local character, and to include the maximal sieve. ([Lurie, Lecture 8, Definitions 6, 9, 13](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/278xnotes/Lecture8-Topologies.pdf); [nLab, Grothendieck topology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Grothendieck+topology))
- **Giraud's theorem (18F10).** A category is a Grothendieck topos exactly when it is locally presentable, its colimits are universal (stable under pullback), its coproducts are disjoint, and its quotients are effective. The Giraud–Rezk–Lurie theorem gives the analogous characterization of $(\infty,1)$-toposes, with effective groupoid objects in place of effective quotients. ([nLab, Giraud's theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Giraud%27s+theorem))
- **Direct and inverse image, geometric morphisms**, an instance of [Adjoint Functors](node:Adjoint%20Functors). For continuous $f:X\to Y$, $f_*F(V)=F(f^{-1}V)$ defines a sheaf on $Y$. The sheafified presheaf pullback $f^{-1}$ is left adjoint to $f_*$. A geometric morphism $E\to F$ of toposes is an adjunction $f^*\dashv f_*$ whose left adjoint $f^*:F\to E$ preserves finite limits. Every continuous map gives one $\mathrm{Sh}(X)\to\mathrm{Sh}(Y)$, and when $X$ and $Y$ are both sober every geometric morphism between their sheaf toposes comes from a unique continuous map. ([Stacks, Tag 008C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/008C); [nLab, geometric morphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometric+morphism))
- **Stacks and descent (18F20).** For a fibered category $F\to C$ over a site, a covering $\{U_i\to U\}$ gives a functor from $F(U)$ to the category $F(\{U_i\to U\})$ of objects with descent data. $F$ is a prestack if this functor is fully faithful for every covering, and a stack if it is an equivalence. Grothendieck's theorems state that every representable functor on $(\mathrm{Sch}/S)$ is an fpqc sheaf and that quasi-coherent sheaves form a stack for the fpqc topology. ([Vistoli, Definition 4.6, Theorems 2.55 and 4.23](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0412512))
- **Grothendieck groups (18F30)**, see [Grothendieck Groups](node:Grothendieck%20Groups). The Grothendieck group of a commutative monoid $M$ is the universal monoid map $M\to K$ into an abelian group. For an abelian category $\mathcal A$, $K_0(\mathcal A)$ has one generator $[A]$ per isomorphism class subject to $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for each short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$; for example $K_0$ of finite-dimensional [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) over a field is $\mathbb Z$, generated by $[k]$. ([Wikipedia, Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group))
- **Synthetic differential geometry and tangent categories (18F40)**, abstracting [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds). In a topos with a ring object $R$ and $D=\{x\in R\mid x^2=0\}$, the Kock–Lawvere axiom asks that $R\times R\to R^D$, $(x,d)\mapsto(\epsilon\mapsto x+\epsilon d)$, be an isomorphism: every map $D\to R$ is linear. The [Tangent Bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle) of a space $X$ is then the exponential $X^D$. Tangent categories instead axiomatize a tangent functor $T$ with projection, addition, zero, vertical lift $\ell:T\to T^2$ and canonical flip $c:T^2\to T^2$ satisfying a list of equations; the category of smooth manifolds is an example. The framework goes back to Rosický's *Abstract tangent functors* (1984) and to Cockett and Cruttwell's *Differential Structure, Tangent Structure, and SDG* (Appl. Categ. Structures 22, 2014), the source of the definition above. ([nLab, Kock–Lawvere axiom](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kock-Lawvere+axiom); [nLab, SDG](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/synthetic+differential+geometry); [Lucyshyn-Wright, §2.3.3 and Example 2.3.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.10857); [Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/s10485-013-9312-0))
- **Goodwillie calculus (18F50).** A functor is $n$-excisive if it sends strongly cocartesian $(n+1)$-cubes to cartesian cubes. A homotopy functor $F$ has a Taylor tower $F\to\cdots\to P_nF\to P_{n-1}F\to\cdots\to P_0F$ in which $P_nF$ is the universal $n$-excisive approximation. For functors to spectra the layers are $D_nF(X)\simeq(\partial_nF\wedge X^{\wedge n})_{h\Sigma_n}$, classified by the derivative spectra $\partial_nF$ with their $\Sigma_n$-actions. For analytic functors the tower converges on sufficiently highly connected inputs. ([nLab, Goodwillie calculus](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Goodwillie+calculus))
- **Frames and locales (18F70)**, related to [Lattice Theory](node:Lattice%20Theory) and [Topological Spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces). A frame is a poset with all joins and finite meets in which $x\wedge\bigvee_i y_i=\bigvee_i(x\wedge y_i)$. Frame maps preserve finite meets and arbitrary joins, and locales are defined by $\mathrm{Loc}=\mathrm{Frm}^{\mathrm{op}}$. Sending a space to its frame of opens embeds sober spaces fully into locales. Some theorems are better for locales than for spaces: products of compact locales are compact without the [Axiom of Choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice), and any intersection of dense sublocales is dense, so every locale has a smallest dense sublocale (Isbell's density theorem). There are also nontrivial locales with no points. ([nLab, locale](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locale); [Wikipedia, Pointless topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointless_topology))

### History
Grothendieck topologies were first motivated by algebraic geometry: the small étale site of a scheme (see [Schemes](node:Schemes) and [Étale Cohomology](node:Étale%20Cohomology)) has étale maps $U\to X$ as objects and jointly surjective families as coverings. ([Lurie, Lecture 8, Example 11](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/278xnotes/Lecture8-Topologies.pdf)) Vistoli's notes present Grothendieck's descent theory in the language of fibered categories and stacks, including fpqc descent for quasi-coherent sheaves. ([Vistoli](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0412512))

Point-free topology goes back to Stone's duality in the 1930s and to work of Menger and Wallman. Ehresmann and Bénabou made a major advance in the late 1950s with what are now called frames, and Isbell, Johnstone and Vickers developed it further. ([Wikipedia, Pointless topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointless_topology)) Synthetic differential geometry began with Lawvere's 1967 Chicago lectures *Categorical dynamics*, published in 1979. Kock's textbook *Synthetic Differential Geometry* (1981) and Moerdijk–Reyes's *Models for Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis* (1991) followed, and Dubuc constructed well-adapted models. ([nLab, SDG](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/synthetic+differential+geometry)) Goodwillie's calculus appeared in his papers *Calculus I–III* (1990–2003). ([nLab, Goodwillie calculus](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Goodwillie+calculus))

### Open problems
- **Lawvere's open problems in topos theory.** In April 2009 Lawvere listed seven problems he had "not yet been able to solve." They include the algebra of a topos's lattice of subquotients with its two closure operators (problem 2), the boundary operator on classes of models (problem 3), the relation between microlinearity and coverings defined by averaging (problem 5), the parameterization of all ATOMs (problem 6) and the computation of the "algebra of time" (problem 7). ([Lawvere, Open problems in topos theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Lawvere-OpenProblems.pdf))
- **Status of problem 1.** The first problem asked whether some Grothendieck topos has a non-small collection of quotient toposes. Kamio and Hora solved it in 2024, exhibiting presheaf toposes, among them presheaves on the free monoid on countably many generators, with a proper class of quotient topoi. ([Kamio–Hora, arXiv:2407.17105](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.17105))
- **Problem 4 has also been answered.** It asked for the "way below" (Aufhebung) relation between levels of the topos of presheaves on finite nonempty sets (symmetric simplicial sets). Hora, Kamio and Maehara computed it in 2025: for levels $l\ge3$ the answer is $2l-1$, as for ordinary simplicial sets. ([Hora–Kamio–Maehara, arXiv:2503.03439](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.03439))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, Grothendieck topology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Grothendieck+topology): sieves, sites and sheaves.
- **Reference:** [nLab, locale](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locale): frames, locales and their relation to spaces.
- **Learn:** [Lurie, Lecture 8: Grothendieck topologies](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/278xnotes/Lecture8-Topologies.pdf): Harvard lecture on sites, sheaves and toposes.
- **Primary:** [Vistoli, Notes on Grothendieck topologies, fibered categories and descent theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0412512): standard expository monograph on stacks and descent.
- **Primary:** [Stacks Project, Sheaves on spaces](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0071): sheaves of sets and of algebraic structures.
- **Further reading:** [Lawvere, Open problems in topos theory (2009)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Lawvere-OpenProblems.pdf); [Cockett–Cruttwell, Differential Structure, Tangent Structure, and SDG](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/s10485-013-9312-0): the paper whose definition of tangent category is now standard in the literature.
references.MSC 18Gxx - Homological algebra in categ:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 subfield 18Gxx covers [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) treated category-theoretically: projectives and injectives, resolutions and derived functors, Ext and Tor, homological dimension, relative homological algebra, simplicial modules, chain complexes and dg categories, spectral sequences, crossed modules, nonabelian homological algebra, stable module categories, $A_\infty$-categories, and derived and triangulated categories. ([MSC2020, 18Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Gxx))

Its central object is the derived category. Starting from the homotopy category $K(\mathcal A)$ of complexes in an [abelian category](node:Abelian%20Categories), one formally inverts quasi-isomorphisms, the maps inducing isomorphisms on all cohomology objects. The result keeps complexes as objects while identifying complexes with the same "homological content". Grothendieck and Verdier introduced it around 1960; Yekutieli notes that notions such as dualizing and tilting complexes have no counterpart in classical homological algebra. ([Stacks, Tag 05RR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05RR); [Yekutieli, Introduction to Derived Categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.06731))

Derived categories are triangulated rather than abelian, and the subfield studies triangulated categories, the t-structures that recover abelian hearts inside them, and the defects of the triangulated axioms (such as non-functorial cones) that have motivated alternatives such as derivators and stable $\infty$-categories. ([Wikipedia, Triangulated category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulated_category); [Wikipedia, t-structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-structure))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists: 18G05 projectives and injectives; 18G10 resolutions, derived functors; 18G15 Ext and Tor, generalizations, Künneth formula; 18G20 homological dimension; 18G25 relative homological algebra, projective classes; 18G31 simplicial modules and the Dold–Kan correspondence; 18G35 chain complexes, dg categories; 18G40 spectral sequences, hypercohomology; 18G45 2-groups, crossed modules, crossed complexes; 18G50 nonabelian homological algebra; 18G65 stable module categories; 18G70 $A_\infty$-categories and relations with homological mirror symmetry; 18G80 derived categories, triangulated categories; 18G85 graph complexes and graph homology; 18G90 other (co)homology theories; 18G99 other. Codes 18G05–18G25, 18G35, 18G50 and 18G90 carry the qualifier "category-theoretic aspects". ([MSC2020, 18Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Gxx))

Neighbouring subfields use the same tools in specific settings: [13D](node:MSC%2013Dxx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20commutative%20ring%20theory) for commutative rings, [16E](node:MSC%2016Exx%20-%20Homological%20methods%20in%20associative%20algebras) for associative algebras, [55T](node:MSC%2055Txx%20-%20Spectral%20sequences%20in%20algebraic%20topology) for spectral sequences in topology, and [14F](node:MSC%2014Fxx%20-%20%28Co%29homology%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) for cohomology of varieties and schemes. The MSC lists simplicial sets as such and homotopical model structures under [18N](node:MSC%2018Nxx%20-%20Higher%20categories%20and%20homotopical%20algebra) (18N50 and 18N40). ([MSC2020, 18Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Gxx); [MSC2020, 18Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **Derived category (18G80)**, see [Derived Categories](node:Derived%20Categories). $D(\mathcal A)=K(\mathcal A)/\mathrm{Ac}(\mathcal A)=\mathrm{Qis}(\mathcal A)^{-1}K(\mathcal A)$, where the localization kills exactly the acyclic complexes. $D^+$, $D^-$ and $D^b$ consist of complexes whose cohomology $H^n$ vanishes for $n\ll0$, for $n\gg0$, and for $|n|\gg0$; each is a full triangulated subcategory equivalent to the corresponding localization of its homotopy category. ([Stacks, Definition 13.11.3 and Lemma 13.11.6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05RR))
- **Triangulated categories (18G80).** A triangulated category is an additive category with a shift functor and a class of exact triangles satisfying TR1 (every morphism has a cone), TR2 (rotation), TR3 (completion of morphisms of triangles, not necessarily uniquely) and TR4 (the octahedral axiom). Verdier and Puppe introduced them independently, Puppe without the octahedral axiom. The homotopy category of complexes and $D(\mathcal A)$ are triangulated. A cone is unique only up to non-unique isomorphism and the cone construction is not functorial, which has motivated alternatives such as derivators and stable $\infty$-categories. ([Wikipedia, Triangulated category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulated_category))
- **t-structures.** A t-structure on a triangulated category $\mathcal D$ is a pair of full subcategories $(\mathcal D^{\le0},\mathcal D^{\ge0})$ with $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y[-1])=0$ for $X\in\mathcal D^{\le0}$, $Y\in\mathcal D^{\ge0}$, closed under the appropriate shifts, such that every object sits in a truncation triangle. Its heart $\mathcal D^{\le0}\cap\mathcal D^{\ge0}$ is always abelian. The standard t-structure on $D(\mathcal A)$ has heart $\mathcal A$, and perverse sheaves are the heart of the perverse t-structure. Beilinson, Bernstein and Deligne introduced the notion in *Faisceaux pervers* (1982). ([Wikipedia, t-structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-structure))
- **Derived functors via K-injective resolutions (18G10).** A complex $I$ is K-injective if $\mathrm{Hom}(N,I)$ is acyclic for every acyclic $N$. If $K(\mathcal M)$ has enough K-injectives, every triangulated functor $F$ on $K(\mathcal M)$ has a right derived functor with $RF(M)=F(I_M)$ for a K-injective resolution $M\to I_M$. Bounded-below complexes of injectives are K-injective, and every Grothendieck abelian category, including $\mathrm{Mod}\,A$ and modules over a sheaf of rings, has enough K-injectives. Dually, bounded-above complexes of projectives are K-projective and $K(\mathrm{Mod}\,A)$ has enough K-projectives. ([Yekutieli, Theorems 4.2, 4.4, 4.7 and Propositions 4.3, 4.8, 4.9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.06731))
- **Derived Morita theory.** For algebras $A,B$ over a field $K$, a two-sided tilting complex is $T\in D(\mathrm{Mod}\,A\otimes_KB^{\mathrm{op}})$ with a quasi-inverse $T^\vee$ such that $T\otimes^L_BT^\vee\cong A$ and $T^\vee\otimes^L_AT\cong B$. Rickard's theorem: $A$ and $B$ are derived Morita equivalent ($D(\mathrm{Mod}\,A)\simeq D(\mathrm{Mod}\,B)$ as $K$-linear triangulated categories) if and only if a two-sided tilting complex over $A$-$B$ exists. ([Yekutieli, Definition 8.2 and Theorem 8.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.06731); [nLab, derived Morita equivalence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+Morita+equivalence))
- **Reconstruction from the derived category.** Bondal and Orlov proved that a smooth projective variety with ample canonical or anticanonical sheaf is determined up to isomorphism by $D^b(\mathrm{Coh})$, and computed the group of exact autoequivalences of such categories. By contrast, an abelian variety and its dual have equivalent bounded derived categories via the Fourier–Mukai transform. ([Bondal–Orlov, arXiv:alg-geom/9712029](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9712029); [Wikipedia, Derived category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derived_category))
- **dg enhancements (18G35).** An enhancement of a triangulated category $\mathbf T$ is a pretriangulated dg category $\mathbf C$ with an exact equivalence $H^0(\mathbf C)\to\mathbf T$. An enhancement is unique if any two are related by a quasi-functor inducing an equivalence on $H^0$. Uniqueness can fail: by Canonaco and Stellari's Corollary 3.10, for the quasi-Frobenius rings $\mathbb Z/p^2$ and $\mathbb F_p[\epsilon]$ ($\epsilon^2=0$) the dg categories of acyclic complexes of injective modules are not isomorphic in $\mathrm{Hqe}$, yet both enhance the same triangulated category ($\mathrm{Mod}\,\mathbb F_p$ with identity shift). Keller's survey treats dg categories as a way to understand the triangulated categories of algebra and geometry. ([Canonaco–Stellari, Definitions 1.11 and 1.15 and Corollary 3.10](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1605.00490); [Keller, On differential graded categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601185))
- **Dold–Kan correspondence (18G31).** For an abelian category $\mathcal A$, the normalized chains functor $N$ is an equivalence between simplicial objects in $\mathcal A$ and chain complexes concentrated in nonnegative degrees, with inverse $\Gamma$. For [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) it is a Quillen equivalence between simplicial abelian groups and connective chain complexes with quasi-isomorphisms. See [Simplicial Methods](node:Simplicial%20Methods). ([nLab, Dold–Kan correspondence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Dold-Kan+correspondence))
- **Spectral sequences (18G40)**, see [Spectral Sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences). For left exact $F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$, $G:\mathcal B\to\mathcal C$, with enough injectives and $F$ sending injectives to $G$-acyclics, there is a spectral sequence $E_2^{p,q}=R^pG(R^qF(A))\Rightarrow R^{p+q}(GF)(A)$. ([Wikipedia, Grothendieck spectral sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_spectral_sequence))

### History
Grothendieck and his student Verdier developed derived categories shortly after 1960, motivated by Grothendieck's coherent duality. Verdier's thesis was published in *Astérisque* in 1996, after a summary had appeared in SGA 4½. ([Wikipedia, Derived category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derived_category)) Puppe (1962) and Verdier (1963) introduced triangulated categories independently. Puppe came from stable homotopy theory, and Verdier's main example was the derived category. ([Wikipedia, Triangulated category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulated_category)) K-injective and K-projective complexes, which allow unbounded derived functors, were introduced by Spaltenstein in 1988. ([Yekutieli, §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.06731)) The Dold–Kan correspondence goes back to Dold and to Kan (both 1958), with the general abelian version due to Dold and Puppe (1961). ([nLab, Dold–Kan correspondence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Dold-Kan+correspondence))

### Open problems
- **D-equivalence conjecture.** The conjecture predicts that birationally equivalent Calabi–Yau manifolds have equivalent derived categories of coherent sheaves. Halpern-Leistner (2020) proved it for projective Calabi–Yau manifolds birational to a smooth moduli space of Gieseker semistable sheaves on a K3 surface, the first known case for a birational class in dimension greater than three. The general statement remains a conjecture. See [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds). ([Halpern-Leistner, arXiv:2010.01127](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01127))
- **Uniqueness of enhancements.** Canonaco and Stellari state that the main geometric uniqueness problems are solved but pose further questions throughout their survey. One example is their Question 3.3: if $\mathbf S\subseteq\mathbf T$ is a full triangulated subcategory and $\mathbf S$ and $\mathbf T/\mathbf S$ are algebraic, is $\mathbf T$ algebraic? ([Canonaco–Stellari, A tour about existence and uniqueness of dg enhancements and lifts](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1605.00490))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stacks Project, Derived categories](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05RR): precise construction of $D(\mathcal A)$ and its bounded variants.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Triangulated category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulated_category): axioms, history and enhancements.
- **Learn:** [Yekutieli, Introduction to Derived Categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.06731): MSRI minicourse notes on resolutions, dualizing and tilting complexes.
- **Primary:** [Keller, On differential graded categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0601185): survey of the foundations of dg categories.
- **Primary:** [Bondal–Orlov, Reconstruction of a variety from the derived category](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9712029): the reconstruction theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Gelfand–Manin, Methods of Homological Algebra (Springer)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-12492-5); [Kashiwara–Schapira, Categories and Sheaves (Springer, Grundlehren)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/3-540-27950-4); [Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra (CUP)](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Hbook-corrections.html).
references.MSC 18Mxx - Monoidal categories and oper:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 subfield 18Mxx gathers two families of structures for composing things with several inputs. Monoidal categories carry a tensor product with associativity and unit isomorphisms, and the subfield covers their symmetric, braided, traced, rigid, fusion and Tannakian variants. Operads and their relatives (multicategories, PROPs, properads, cyclic and modular operads) encode operations with several inputs and the rules for substituting them into one another. ([MSC2020, 18Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Mxx))

Monoidal categories organize representation categories of groups, [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) and [Hopf algebras](node:Hopf%20Algebras). Operads arose in the recognition of iterated loop spaces ([homotopy theory](node:MSC%2055Pxx%20-%20Homotopy%20theory)) and now give a uniform language for algebras "of a given type": associative, commutative, Lie, and their homotopy-coherent versions. ([Etingof et al., Tensor categories, §§1.12, 1.22](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/tenscat.pdf); [May, Operads, algebras and modules](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/PAPERS/mayi.pdf))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists: 18M05 monoidal and symmetric monoidal categories; 18M10 traced monoidal, compact closed and star-autonomous categories; 18M15 braided monoidal and ribbon categories; 18M20 fusion categories, modular tensor categories, modular functors; 18M25 Tannakian categories; 18M30 string diagrams and graphical calculi; 18M35 categories of networks and processes, compositionality; 18M40 dagger categories, categorical quantum mechanics; 18M45 categorical aspects of linear logic; 18M50 bimonoidal, skew-monoidal and duoidal categories; 18M60 operads (general); 18M65 non-symmetric operads, multicategories, generalized multicategories; 18M70 algebraic operads, cooperads and Koszul duality; 18M75 topological and simplicial operads; 18M80 species, Hopf monoids, operads in [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics); 18M85 polycategories/dioperads, properads, PROPs, cyclic and modular operads; 18M90 globular operads; 18M99 other. ([MSC2020, 18Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Mxx))

The entry's cross-references mark the boundaries. Topological and simplicial operads (18M75) cross-refer to $(\infty,1)$-categories in [18N60](node:MSC%2018Nxx%20-%20Higher%20categories%20and%20homotopical%20algebra), and $\infty$-operads and higher algebra (18N70) cross-refer back to 18M75. Dagger categories (18M40) point to quantum computation in 81P68, linear logic (18M45) to 03B47, and monoidal categories (18M05) to 19D23 in K-theory. ([MSC2020, 18Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Mxx); [MSC2020, 18Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **Monoidal category (18M05)**, see [Monoidal Categories](node:Monoidal%20Categories). A monoidal category is $(\mathcal C,\otimes,a,\mathbf 1,\iota)$ with a bifunctor $\otimes$, a natural associativity isomorphism $a_{X,Y,Z}:(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z\to X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)$ satisfying the pentagon axiom, and a unit object $\mathbf 1$ with an isomorphism $\iota:\mathbf 1\otimes\mathbf 1\to\mathbf 1$ such that tensoring with $\mathbf 1$ on either side is an equivalence. ([Etingof et al., Definition 1.1.1](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/tenscat.pdf))
- **Mac Lane's coherence and strictness theorems.** Coherence: for objects $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and any two parenthesized products $P_1,P_2$ of them in this order, with units inserted anywhere, any two isomorphisms $P_1\to P_2$ built from associativity and unit isomorphisms, their inverses and identities tensored on are equal. Strictness: every monoidal category is monoidally equivalent to a strict one. Strictness is an equivalence, not a claim that the original associator is an identity: $\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega$ with cohomologically nontrivial 3-cocycle $\omega$ is not strict. ([Etingof et al., Theorems 1.8.5 and 1.9.1](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/tenscat.pdf))
- **Braided monoidal categories (18M15).** A braiding is a natural isomorphism $B_{x,y}:x\otimes y\to y\otimes x$ satisfying two hexagon identities with the associator; the category is symmetric if $B_{y,x}\circ B_{x,y}=\mathrm{id}$. Braided monoidal categories are equivalently algebras over the little 2-cubes operad $E_2$, and the braid category is the free braided strict monoidal category on one object. Joyal and Street developed the theory in *Braided tensor categories* (Adv. Math. 102, 1993). ([nLab, braided monoidal category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braided+monoidal+category))
- **Tensor and fusion categories, Drinfeld center (18M20).** A tensor category is a locally finite $k$-linear abelian rigid monoidal category with bilinear $\otimes$ and $\mathrm{End}(\mathbf 1)\cong k$; a fusion category is a semisimple tensor category with finitely many isomorphism classes of simple objects, such as the category $\mathrm{Vec}$ of finite-dimensional [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces). The Drinfeld center $Z(\mathcal C)$ has objects $(X,\Phi)$ with $\Phi:X\otimes(-)\to(-)\otimes X$ a half-braiding, and it is braided with $b_{(X,\Phi),(Y,\Psi)}=\Psi_X$. For a fusion category over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, $Z(\mathcal C)$ is again fusion, and $Z(\mathrm{Vec}_G)$ is the representation category of the Drinfeld double $D(G)$. ([Etingof et al., Definition 1.12.3 and Example 1.12.4](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/tenscat.pdf); [nLab, Drinfeld center](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Drinfeld+center))
- **Operads and their algebras (18M60).** In a symmetric monoidal category with unit $\kappa$, an operad $\mathcal C$ consists of objects $\mathcal C(j)$ with $\Sigma_j$-actions, a unit $\eta:\kappa\to\mathcal C(1)$, and composition maps $\gamma:\mathcal C(k)\otimes\mathcal C(j_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal C(j_k)\to\mathcal C(j_1+\cdots+j_k)$ that are associative, unital and equivariant. A $\mathcal C$-algebra is an object $A$ with compatible $\Sigma_j$-equivariant maps $\mathcal C(j)\otimes A^{\otimes j}\to A$, where $A^{\otimes0}=\kappa$. The operad with $\mathcal M(j)=\kappa[\Sigma_j]$ has monoids as algebras, and the operad with $\mathcal N(j)=\kappa$ has commutative monoids. Dropping the symmetric groups gives non-$\Sigma$ operads. ([May, §1, Examples 1.1–1.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/PAPERS/mayi.pdf))
- **Little cubes operads $E_n$ (18M75).** The operation spaces of $E_k$ are the rectilinear embeddings of disjoint $k$-cubes in a $k$-cube, and their algebras are "$k$-fold monoidal" objects. May's recognition theorem: a grouplike space with an action of the little $k$-cubes operad is homotopy equivalent to a $k$-fold loop space $\Omega^kX$. May's *The geometry of iterated loop spaces* (LNM 271, 1972) is the standard reference. ([nLab, little cubes operad](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/little+cubes+operad))
- **Koszul duality for operads (18M70).** Over a field of characteristic $0$, Ginzburg and Kapranov define the quadratic dual $\mathcal P^!$ of a quadratic operad and prove $\mathrm{Com}^!=\mathrm{Lie}$, $\mathrm{Lie}^!=\mathrm{Com}$ and $\mathrm{As}^!=\mathrm{As}$. A quadratic operad is Koszul iff its Koszul complex is exact, iff free $\mathcal P$-algebras have vanishing higher $\mathcal P$-homology, and $\mathcal P$ is Koszul iff $\mathcal P^!$ is. $\mathrm{As}$, $\mathrm{Com}$ and $\mathrm{Lie}$ are Koszul. The associated homology theories are Hochschild homology (see [Hochschild Cohomology](node:Hochschild%20Cohomology)) for $\mathrm{As}$, Chevalley–Eilenberg homology for $\mathrm{Lie}$ and Harrison homology for $\mathrm{Com}$. ([Ginzburg–Kapranov, Theorem 2.1.11, Proposition 4.1.4, Theorem 4.2.5, Examples 4.2.4, Corollary 4.2.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0709.1228); [nLab, Koszul duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Koszul+duality))
- **PROPs (18M85).** A PROP is a symmetric strict monoidal category whose objects are the natural numbers, with tensor product given by addition on objects. Adams and Mac Lane introduced them, and Boardman and Vogt gave the topological version. The PROP of matrices over a ring and the PROP $\mathrm{FinSet}$, whose algebras are commutative monoids, are examples, and an algebra of a PRO $P$ in a monoidal category $C$ is a strict monoidal functor $P\to C$. ([Wikipedia, PROP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PROP_%28category_theory%29))

### History
May coined the word "operad" to suggest both "operations" and "monads". The notion was first written up in a topological setting for the recognition principle for iterated loop spaces, and by 1971 it was understood to work in any symmetric monoidal category. May lists as precursors Lawvere's algebraic theories, Adams and Mac Lane's PROPs and PACTs, Stasheff's $A_\infty$-spaces and associahedra, and Boardman and Vogt's topological PROPs. ([May, introduction](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/PAPERS/mayi.pdf)) Mac Lane's coherence theorem is described as the first important result in the theory of monoidal categories. ([Etingof et al., §1.9](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/tenscat.pdf)) Kontsevich predicted Koszul duality for quadratic operads, and Ginzburg and Kapranov developed it in *Duke Math. J.* 76 (1994). ([nLab, Koszul duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Koszul+duality); [Ginzburg–Kapranov](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.1228))

### Open problems
- **Pivotal structures on fusion categories.** Etingof, Gelaki, Nikshych and Ostrik ask whether every semisimple tensor category admits a pivotal structure, and whether it admits a spherical one. They note that the answer is yes in all known examples and unknown in general, even in characteristic zero. ([Etingof et al., Question 1.41.4](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/tenscat.pdf))
- **Weakly integral versus weakly group-theoretical fusion categories.** Etingof, Nikshych and Ostrik show that weakly group-theoretical fusion categories have integer dimension and that every fusion category of integer dimension less than 84 is weakly group-theoretical; they note that all known fusion categories of integer dimension are weakly group-theoretical. They close the paper with Question 2: does there exist a weakly integral fusion category (one whose Frobenius–Perron dimension is an integer) which is not weakly group-theoretical? ([Etingof–Nikshych–Ostrik, arXiv:0809.3031](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.3031); [Etingof–Nikshych–Ostrik, §§2.3, 11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0809.3031))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, braided monoidal category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braided+monoidal+category): definitions, the relation with $E_2$, and references to Joyal–Street.
- **Learn:** [Etingof–Gelaki–Nikshych–Ostrik, Tensor categories (MIT lecture notes)](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/tenscat.pdf): monoidal, tensor and fusion categories with proofs.
- **Primary:** [May, Operads, algebras and modules](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/PAPERS/mayi.pdf): the inventor's account of the definitions and their origins.
- **Primary:** [Ginzburg–Kapranov, Koszul duality for operads](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.1228): the founding paper of operadic Koszul duality.
- **Further reading:** [Loday–Vallette, Algebraic Operads (Springer, Grundlehren, 2012)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-30362-3): the standard monograph on algebraic operads and Koszul duality.
references.MSC 18Nxx - Higher categories and homoto:
## Reference
