### Overview
MSC2020 subfield 18Nxx covers [categories with morphisms between morphisms](node:Higher%20Categories) (2-categories, bicategories, weak $n$-categories, $\omega$-categories, $(\infty,1)$- and $(\infty,n)$-categories) and homotopical algebra, the study of categories equipped with weak equivalences through Quillen model categories, derivators, simplicial objects and localizations. ([MSC2020, 18Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx))

The two halves meet in $(\infty,1)$-category theory. A homotopy category records morphisms only up to homotopy, while an $\infty$-category keeps the [mapping spaces](node:Mapping%20Spaces) and their higher coherences. In Lurie's quasi-categorical model, Kan complexes such as the singular complex of a space are $\infty$-categories (fundamental $\infty$-groupoids), and the nerve of any ordinary category is one, so ordinary [category theory](node:Category%20Theory) is a special case. ([Lurie, Higher Topos Theory, §1.1.2, Examples 1.1.2.5–1.1.2.6](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/papers/HTT.pdf))

Model categories, introduced by Quillen, present such homotopy theories by a category with three classes of maps, and Bergner's survey describes the various models of $(\infty,1)$-categories as "models for the homotopy theory of homotopy theories". ([Riehl, Categorical Homotopy Theory, §11.3](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/cathtpy.pdf); [Bergner, A survey of (∞,1)-categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610239))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists: 18N10 2-categories, bicategories, double categories; 18N15 2-dimensional monad theory; 18N20 tricategories, weak $n$-categories, coherence, semi-strictification; 18N25 categorification; 18N30 strict $\omega$-categories, computads, polygraphs; 18N40 homotopical algebra, Quillen model categories, derivators; 18N45 categories of fibrations, relations to K-theory and to [type theory](node:Type%20Theory); 18N50 simplicial sets, simplicial objects; 18N55 localizations (simplicial, Bousfield); 18N60 $(\infty,1)$-categories (quasi-categories, Segal spaces, etc.), $\infty$-topoi, stable $\infty$-categories; 18N65 $(\infty,n)$- and $(\infty,\infty)$-categories; 18N70 $\infty$-operads and higher algebra; 18N99 other. ([MSC2020, 18Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx))

The entry's cross-references set the boundaries with algebraic topology and with operads. 18N40 and 18N60 point to [55U35](node:MSC%2055Uxx%20-%20Applied%20homological%20algebra%20and%20category%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20topology), simplicial sets (18N50) to 55U10, localizations (18N55) to 18E35 and to 55P60 in [homotopy theory](node:MSC%2055Pxx%20-%20Homotopy%20theory), and $\infty$-operads (18N70) to topological operads in [18M75](node:MSC%2018Mxx%20-%20Monoidal%20categories%20and%20operads). ([MSC2020, 18Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **Bicategories and coherence (18N10, 18N20).** A bicategory has objects, hom-categories of 1-cells and 2-cells, and composition that is associative and unital only up to coherent isomorphisms satisfying the pentagon and triangle identities. Every bicategory is equivalent to a strict 2-category, by essentially the argument used for [monoidal categories](node:Monoidal%20Categories). One dimension up, the coherence theorem for tricategories, whose original source is Gordon, Power and Street's *Coherence for tricategories* (Mem. AMS 117, 1995), can be stated as: every tricategory is equivalent to a Gray-category, which is strict except for the interchange law. ([nLab, bicategory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/bicategory); [nLab, tricategory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tricategory))
- **Model categories and Quillen adjunctions (18N40).** In Riehl's formulation, a model structure on a complete and cocomplete homotopical category $(\mathcal M,\mathcal W)$ is a pair of classes $\mathcal C$ (cofibrations) and $\mathcal F$ (fibrations) such that $(\mathcal C\cap\mathcal W,\mathcal F)$ and $(\mathcal C,\mathcal F\cap\mathcal W)$ are weak factorization systems. A left Quillen functor preserves cofibrations and trivial cofibrations, a right Quillen functor preserves fibrations and trivial fibrations, and an adjoint pair of such functors is a Quillen adjunction. ([Riehl, Definition 11.3.1 and §11.3](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/cathtpy.pdf))
- **Quasi-categories and the Joyal model structure (18N50, 18N60).** An $\infty$-category (quasi-category) is a simplicial set $K$ such that every inner horn $\Lambda^n_i\to K$, $0<i<n$, extends to $\Delta^n$. Unlike for nerves of categories, the fillers need not be unique. There is a left proper combinatorial model structure on simplicial sets whose cofibrations are the monomorphisms and whose weak equivalences are the categorical equivalences. Its fibrant objects are exactly the $\infty$-categories, and $(\mathfrak C,N)$ is a Quillen equivalence with simplicial categories. ([Lurie, Definition 1.1.2.4, Theorems 2.2.5.1 and 2.4.6.1](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/papers/HTT.pdf))
- **Equivalence of models of $(\infty,1)$-categories (18N60).** Simplicial categories, Segal categories, complete Segal spaces and quasi-categories are four equivalent models. Joyal and Tierney proved that complete Segal spaces and Segal categories are Quillen equivalent to quasi-categories. ([Bergner, survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610239); [Joyal–Tierney, Quasi-categories vs Segal spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0607820))
- **Stable $\infty$-categories (18N60).** A stable $(\infty,1)$-category is pointed, every morphism has a kernel and a cokernel (fibres and cofibres formed as pullbacks and pushouts against the zero object), and exact and coexact triangles coincide, so $\Sigma$ and $\Omega$ are inverse equivalences. Its homotopy category is canonically triangulated. Spectra are the prototype, and every derived category of an abelian category is the homotopy category of a stable $\infty$-category; see [Derived Categories](node:Derived%20Categories). ([nLab, stable (∞,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stable+%28infinity%2C1%29-category))
- **$(\infty,n)$-categories and the cobordism hypothesis (18N65).** Let $\mathcal C$ be a symmetric monoidal $(\infty,n)$-category with duals. The framed cobordism hypothesis says that evaluation at the point is an equivalence from symmetric monoidal functors $\mathrm{Bord}_n^{\mathrm{fr}}\to\mathcal C$ to the core of $\mathcal C$, so fully extended framed TQFTs are classified by their fully dualizable values on a point. Baez and Dolan formulated it in 1995. Lurie's 2009 paper gives "an informal sketch of a proof", which nLab calls detailed but still incomplete. See [Cobordism](node:Cobordism). ([nLab, cobordism hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cobordism+hypothesis); [Lurie, On the classification of topological field theories](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.0465))
- **Homotopy hypothesis.** This principle says that $\infty$-[groupoids](node:Groupoids) are equivalent to spaces up to weak homotopy equivalence and that $n$-groupoids model homotopy $n$-types. For Kan complexes it is a theorem, via Quillen's equivalence between [topological spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces) and simplicial sets (see [Simplicial Methods](node:Simplicial%20Methods)). Henry and Lanari proved it for Grothendieck 3-groupoids, and for Grothendieck $n$-groupoids conditionally on the existence of a canonical left semi-model structure. See [Homotopy Equivalence](node:Homotopy%20Equivalence). ([nLab, homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis); [Henry–Lanari, arXiv:1905.05625](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.05625))

### History
Boardman and Vogt first formulated the inner-horn condition and called such simplicial sets "weak Kan complexes". Joyal developed their theory under the name quasi-categories, and Lurie's *Higher Topos Theory* builds on Joyal's work. ([Lurie, §1.1.2](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/papers/HTT.pdf)) Quillen's *Homotopical Algebra* (Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics, 1967) introduced model categories, and the Quillen equivalence between topological spaces and simplicial sets it contains is the classical case of the homotopy hypothesis. ([Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0097438); [nLab, homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis)) Joyal and Tierney's comparison of models dates from 2006 and Bergner's survey from the same year. ([Joyal–Tierney](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0607820); [Bergner](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610239))

### Open problems
- **Simpson's semistrictification conjecture.** Simpson conjectured that every weak $\infty$-category is equivalent to one in which composition and exchange laws are strict and only the unit laws hold weakly. He called it a conjecture because he had not checked it, and nLab records it as proven only up to the case of 3-categories with a single object (compare Joyal–Kock on weak units and homotopy 3-types). ([nLab, Simpson's conjecture](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Simpson%27s+conjecture))
- **Homotopy hypothesis for algebraic models.** For Trimble $\infty$-categories nLab says it "seems unclear at the moment how to make progress" on the homotopy hypothesis, and for other algebraic definitions "not much indication for how to prove" it is known. ([nLab, homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, homotopy hypothesis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+hypothesis): what is proven for which models of higher groupoids.
- **Learn:** [Riehl, Categorical Homotopy Theory](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/cathtpy.pdf): free textbook on derived functors, model categories and quasi-categories.
- **Primary:** [Lurie, Higher Topos Theory](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/papers/HTT.pdf): foundational monograph on quasi-categories and $\infty$-topoi.
- **Primary:** [Bergner, A survey of (∞,1)-categories](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610239): comparison of the four standard models.
- **Further reading:** [Quillen, Homotopical Algebra (LNM, Springer, 1967)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0097438): origin of model categories; [Lurie, On the classification of topological field theories](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.0465): $(\infty,n)$-categories and the cobordism hypothesis.
references.MSC 19 - K-theory:
## Reference
### Overview
$K$-theory studies invariants built from vector bundles, projective modules and related categories, by a Grothendieck-group construction: in topology it is a cohomology theory (topological $K$-theory), in algebra and geometry it is algebraic $K$-theory, and it is a basic tool for operator algebras (see [Operator Algebras](node:Operator%20Algebras) and [Grothendieck Groups](node:Grothendieck%20Groups)). ([Wikipedia: K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory))

The subject began with Grothendieck's formulation of his Riemann–Roch theorem (1957), continued with Atiyah and Hirzebruch's topological $K(X)$ in 1959, and was shaped by Whitehead torsion; Quillen gave two equivalent definitions of higher $K$-theory in 1969 and 1972. ([Wikipedia: K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory))

For a ring $R$, $K_0$ was originally the Grothendieck group of the symmetric monoidal category of projective modules, $K_1(R)$ maps to the unit group through the determinant, and Quillen defines $K(R)=BGL(R)^+$ via the plus construction, or $K(E)=\Omega BQ(E)$ for an exact category $E$. ([nLab: algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 19-XX has finer codes in eleven subfields: 19A Grothendieck groups and $K_0$, 19B Whitehead groups and $K_1$, 19C Steinberg groups and $K_2$, 19D higher algebraic $K$-theory, 19E $K$-theory in geometry, 19F $K$-theory in number theory, 19G $K$-theory of forms, 19J obstructions from topology, 19K $K$-theory and operator algebras, 19L topological $K$-theory, 19M miscellaneous applications; the entry cross-refers to 16E20 and 18F25. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- [MSC 19Axx - Grothendieck groups and K_0](node:MSC%2019Axx%20-%20Grothendieck%20groups%20and%20K_0): $K_0(R)$ is the group completion of finitely generated projectives under $\oplus$; $K_0(k)=\mathbb Z$ for a field or local ring, $K_0(A)=\mathrm{Pic}(A)\oplus\mathbb Z$ for a Dedekind domain $A$. Quillen–Suslin: every finitely generated projective module over $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is free. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory); [Wikipedia: Quillen–Suslin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem))
- [MSC 19Bxx - Whitehead groups and K_1](node:MSC%2019Bxx%20-%20Whitehead%20groups%20and%20K_1): $K_1(A)=GL(A)/[GL(A),GL(A)]$; Whitehead's lemma says $E(A)=[GL(A),GL(A)]$, and for commutative $A$ the determinant splits $K_1(A)\cong A^\times\oplus SK_1(A)$ with $SK_1(A)=SL(A)/E(A)$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) See [Algebraic K1 and Whitehead Groups](node:Algebraic%20K1%20and%20Whitehead%20Groups) and [Determinant](node:Determinant).
- [MSC 19Cxx - Steinberg groups and K_2](node:MSC%2019Cxx%20-%20Steinberg%20groups%20and%20K_2): Matsumoto's theorem gives $K_2(k)\cong(k^\times\otimes k^\times)/\langle a\otimes(1-a)\rangle$ for a field $k$; Tate computed $K_2(\mathbb Q)$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- [MSC 19Dxx - Higher algebraic K-theory](node:MSC%2019Dxx%20-%20Higher%20algebraic%20K-theory): $K(R)=BGL(R)^+$ and the $K$-groups are the homotopy groups of the $K$-theory spectrum ([nLab: algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory)); Quillen's two definitions of higher $K$-theory (1969, 1972) are equivalent. ([Wikipedia: K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory))
  Bass's fundamental theorem is a four-term exact sequence relating $K_0$ and $K_1$ of $R$, $R[t]$ and $R[t,t^{-1}]$. Quillen proved a localization sequence for $G$-theory, which coincides with $K$-theory for noetherian regular rings; for a Dedekind domain $A$ with fraction field $F$ it gives the exact sequence $K_2F\to\bigoplus_{\mathfrak p}K_1(A/\mathfrak p)\to K_1A\to K_1F\to\bigoplus_{\mathfrak p}K_0(A/\mathfrak p)\to K_0A\to K_0F\to0$, with $\mathfrak p$ over the nonzero primes. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- [MSC 19Exx - K-theory in geometry](node:MSC%2019Exx%20-%20K-theory%20in%20geometry): for a smooth scheme $X$, the Grothendieck group $G_0(X)$ of coherent sheaves is isomorphic to $K_0(X)$, and by Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch the Chern character $K_0(X)\otimes\mathbb Q\to A(X)\otimes\mathbb Q$ is a ring isomorphism. ([Wikipedia: K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory))
- [MSC 19Fxx - K-theory in number theory](node:MSC%2019Fxx%20-%20K-theory%20in%20number%20theory): the Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture, a spectral sequence from étale cohomology (see [Étale Cohomology](node:Étale%20Cohomology)) to $K$-theory, is now a theorem of Rost and Voevodsky. ([nLab: algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory))
- [MSC 19Gxx - K-theory of forms](node:MSC%2019Gxx%20-%20K-theory%20of%20forms): Witt and Grothendieck–Witt groups and $L$-theory; see [Witt Groups](node:Witt%20Groups). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))
- [MSC 19Jxx - Obstructions from topology](node:MSC%2019Jxx%20-%20Obstructions%20from%20topology): Whitehead torsion $\tau(f)\in\mathrm{Wh}(\pi_1)$ obstructs a [homotopy equivalence](node:Homotopy%20Equivalence) of finite CW complexes from being simple, and by the $s$-cobordism theorem an $h$-cobordism on a closed manifold of dimension $n>4$ is trivial iff the torsion vanishes. ([Wikipedia: Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion)) See [Whitehead Torsion](node:Whitehead%20Torsion).
- [MSC 19Kxx - K-theory and operator algebras](node:MSC%2019Kxx%20-%20K-theory%20and%20operator%20algebras): $K_0(A)$ via Murray–von Neumann classes of projections, with Bott periodicity and a cyclic six-term exact sequence. ([Wikipedia: Operator K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory))
- [MSC 19Lxx - Topological K-theory](node:MSC%2019Lxx%20-%20Topological%20K-theory): the topological index of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem is defined in $K$-theory, using [Bott Periodicity](node:Bott%20Periodicity) to identify $K(TY)$ with $\mathbb Z$ for a Euclidean space $Y$. ([Wikipedia: Atiyah–Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Singer_index_theorem))

### History
$K$-theory's two historical origins are Grothendieck's sheaf-theoretic construction and the torsion theory of J. H. C. Whitehead and others; Serre's 1955 analogy between vector bundles and projective modules led to the conjecture settled about twenty years later. ([Wikipedia: K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory)) The norm residue theorem, whose proof was finished mostly by Rost and Voevodsky, settles the Bloch–Kato, Beilinson–Lichtenbaum and Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjectures. ([Weibel, K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html))

### Open problems
- **Farrell–Jones conjecture.** For torsion-free $G$ and regular $R$ the assembly map $H_n(BG;K(R))\to K_n(RG)$ is conjectured an isomorphism; it would imply $\mathrm{Wh}(G)=0$ and $\widetilde K_0(\mathbb ZG)=0$ for torsion-free $G$ and the Borel conjecture in dimension $\ge5$. It is known for hyperbolic, finite-dimensional CAT(0), $S$-arithmetic groups and lattices, and no counterexample is known. ([Lück survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.11337v1); [Wikipedia: Farrell–Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrell%E2%80%93Jones_conjecture))
- **Baum–Connes conjecture.** Open without coefficients (unknown for $SL_3(\mathbb Z)$), false with coefficients. ([Wikipedia: Baum–Connes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture))
- **Bass's finite-generation conjecture.** $K_n(A)$ is finitely generated for regular finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebras $A$; Quillen proved it for dimension $\le1$, and it implies the Beilinson–Soulé vanishing conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Bass conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_conjecture))
- **Vandiver's conjecture and $K_*(\mathbb Z)$.** Equivalent (Kurihara) to $K_n(\mathbb Z)=0$ for $n\equiv0\pmod4$, and open. ([Wikipedia: Vandiver's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandiver%27s_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory): history and the three flavours.
- **Learn:** [Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html): free chapters on projective modules, $K_0$, $K_1$ and $K_2$, higher $K$-theory and fields.
- **Primary:** [Lück, K- and L-theory of group rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.5002): ICM survey of the Farrell–Jones conjecture and its consequences.
- **Further reading:** Weibel, *The K-book* (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 145, 2013), via the [author's page](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html); [Lück–Reich survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0402405) of the meaning, status and applications of the Baum–Connes and Farrell–Jones conjectures.
references.MSC 19Axx - Grothendieck groups and K_0:
## Reference
### Overview
A Grothendieck group turns additive data into an abelian group of formal differences. For a commutative monoid $M$ it is the abelian group $K$ with a monoid map $i:M\to K$ through which every monoid map from $M$ to an abelian group factors uniquely; $i$ is injective exactly when $M$ has the cancellation property. ([Wikipedia: Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group))

The construction was introduced by Grothendieck in his proof of the Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem, and it led to the development of K-theory. The same recipe applies to projective modules, vector bundles and exact categories, but the objects and the relations must always be specified. ([Wikipedia: Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group))

### Scope
This subfield treats degree zero of K-theory: the neighbouring subfields [MSC 19Bxx - Whitehead groups and K_1](node:MSC%2019Bxx%20-%20Whitehead%20groups%20and%20K_1), [MSC 19Cxx - Steinberg groups and K_2](node:MSC%2019Cxx%20-%20Steinberg%20groups%20and%20K_2) and [MSC 19Dxx - Higher algebraic K-theory](node:MSC%2019Dxx%20-%20Higher%20algebraic%20K-theory) handle $K_1$, $K_2$ and the higher groups, with $K_1(A)=GL(A)^{ab}$ and $K_2(A)$ the centre of the Steinberg group. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) For a ring $A$, $K_0(A)$ is the Grothendieck group of finitely generated projective $A$-modules under direct sum, and a ring map $A\to B$ induces $K_0(A)\to K_0(B)$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))

For a ringed space $(X,\mathcal O_X)$, $K_0(X)$ is the Grothendieck group of the exact category of locally free sheaves; $G_0$ is built from coherent sheaves (for an affine scheme, finitely generated modules over a noetherian ring). ([Wikipedia: Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group)) The up-level map is [MSC 19 - K-theory](node:MSC%2019%20-%20K-theory).

### Key concepts
- **Fields and local rings.** Projective modules over a field are vector spaces, so $K_0(k)\cong\mathbb Z$ by dimension; over a [local ring](node:Local%20Rings) finitely generated projectives are free, so again $K_0\cong\mathbb Z$ by rank. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Dedekind domains.** For a Dedekind domain $A$, $K_0(A)\cong \operatorname{Pic}(A)\oplus\mathbb Z$, so $K_0$ records the ideal class group. For commutative $A$ the tensor product makes $K_0(A)$ a commutative ring and $\operatorname{Pic}(A)$ embeds in its unit group. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Quillen–Suslin theorem.** Over $A=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $k$ a field, every finitely generated projective module is free, hence $K_0(A)\cong\mathbb Z$; Serre had shown in 1957 that such modules are stably free, and Quillen and Suslin proved freeness independently in 1976. The Bass–Quillen conjecture extends the question to polynomial rings over regular Noetherian rings. ([Wikipedia: Quillen–Suslin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem))
- **Serre–Swan theorem.** For compact Hausdorff $X$, finite-rank real or complex vector bundles on $X$ form a category equivalent to finitely generated projective $C(X)$-modules (Swan); the algebraic version is due to Serre. ([Wikipedia: Serre–Swan theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%E2%80%93Swan_theorem)) Consequently the topological K-theory of real vector bundles over $X$ (see [Topological K-Theory](node:Topological%20K-Theory)) coincides with $K_0$ of the ring of continuous real-valued functions on $X$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Wall finiteness obstruction.** For a finitely dominated space $X$, the alternating sum $w(X)=\sum_i(-1)^i[A_i]\in\tilde K_0(\mathbb Z[\pi_1X])$ of a finite-type projective chain complex $A_*$ for the universal cover vanishes exactly when $X$ is homotopy equivalent to a finite CW complex. ([Wikipedia: Wall's finiteness obstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%27s_finiteness_obstruction)) Ferry and Ranicki describe the obstruction as an algebraic K-theory invariant with applications to the surgery classification of manifolds. ([Ferry–Ranicki survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0008070))
- **Reduced $K_0$ and relative $K_0$.** For commutative $A$, $\tilde K_0(A)$ is the intersection over primes $\mathfrak p$ of the kernels of the rank maps, and $K_0(A,I)\cong K_0(I)$ for an ideal $I$ viewed as a rng, an excision-type statement. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Schemes and finite-dimensional algebras.** For a finite-dimensional algebra over a field, $G_0$ (the Grothendieck group of finitely generated modules) is free abelian on the isomorphism classes of simple modules. ([Wikipedia: Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group)) Weibel's K-book treats $K_0$ of schemes and varieties in Chapter II, §8. ([Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html)) Related vault notes: [K-Theory of Schemes](node:K-Theory%20of%20Schemes), [Algebraic Cycles and Chow Groups](node:Algebraic%20Cycles%20and%20Chow%20Groups), [Grothendieck Groups](node:Grothendieck%20Groups).

### History
Grothendieck introduced the construction in his proof of the Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem, originally for Euler characteristics. ([Wikipedia: Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group)) Serre posed his question on projective modules over polynomial rings in 1955, and it was settled in 1976. ([Wikipedia: Quillen–Suslin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem)) Wall formulated his finiteness obstruction in 1965. ([Ferry–Ranicki survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0008070))

### Open problems
- **Vanishing of $\tilde K_0(\mathbb ZG)$ for torsion-free $G$.** In Lück's survey of the Farrell–Jones conjecture, Conjecture 2.1 states that $\tilde K_0(\mathbb ZG)$ vanishes when $G$ is torsion-free; the survey says it implies Serre's conjecture on (FF) versus (FP) and that it fails without the torsion-free hypothesis. ([Lück, Survey on the Farrell–Jones Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.11337))
- **Bass–Quillen conjecture.** For a regular ring $A$ of finite Krull dimension, is every finitely generated projective $A[x_1,\dots,x_n]$-module extended from $A$? A 2025 preprint treats the conjecture as the $GL_m$ case of a generalized conjecture for reductive groups, records that the generalized version is known for regular rings containing a field and for rings ind-smooth over a discrete valuation ring, credits the dimension $\le 2$ case for $GL_n$ to Murthy, Suslin and Quillen, and proves the dimension $\le 2$ case for reductive groups whose derived group is split semisimple. ([Stavrova, On the generalized Bass–Quillen conjecture](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.18868v1)) Popescu proposes a question whose positive answer would give a complete positive answer to the conjecture. ([Popescu, On the Bass–Quillen Conjecture and Swan's question](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00617))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group): universal property, cancellation criterion, $K_0$ versus $G_0$.
- **Learn:** [Cortiñas, Algebraic v. topological K-theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3983): accessible lecture notes relating algebraic and topological $K$-theory; [Pedersen, Wall's finiteness obstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.07960): a self-contained exposition of the obstruction.
- **Primary:** [Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html): Chapter I (projective modules, Picard group, vector bundles) and Chapter II (group completion, $K_0$ of rings, schemes, $\lambda$- and Adams operations).
- **Further reading:** [Ferry–Ranicki, A survey of Wall's finiteness obstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0008070): applications to surgery classification of manifolds.
references.MSC 19Bxx - Whitehead groups and K_1:
## Reference
### Overview
Algebraic $K_1$ captures stable invertible matrices after abelianization: Bass defined $K_1(A)=GL(A)^{\mathrm{ab}}$, the abelianization of the infinite general linear group. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) Whitehead's lemma identifies the subgroup $E(A)$ generated by elementary matrices with the commutator subgroup $[GL(A),GL(A)]$, so $K_1(A)=GL(A)/E(A)$, and this quotient is the Whitehead group of $A$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))

The topologist's Whitehead group $\operatorname{Wh}(G)$ of a group $G$ is a further quotient: the cokernel of $G\times\{\pm1\}\to K_1(\mathbb Z[G])$, $(g,\pm1)\mapsto(\pm g)$. For a connected CW complex or manifold $M$ it is $\operatorname{Wh}(\pi_1 M)$ and it receives the Whitehead torsion of homotopy equivalences. ([Wikipedia: Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion)) The shared name hides different inputs, a point developed in [Algebraic K1 and Whitehead Groups](node:Algebraic%20K1%20and%20Whitehead%20Groups) and [Whitehead Torsion](node:Whitehead%20Torsion).

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 19Bxx into stable range conditions (19B10), stability for linear groups (19B14), $K_1$ of group rings and orders (19B28, see also 57Q10) and congruence subgroup problems (19B37, see also 20H05). ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Bxx)) For a commutative ring $A$ the [Determinant](node:Determinant) gives $K_1(A)\to A^\times$ with kernel $SK_1(A)=SL(A)/E(A)$, and the map splits, so $K_1(A)\cong A^\times\oplus SK_1(A)$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) The neighbouring subfields are [MSC 19Axx - Grothendieck groups and K_0](node:MSC%2019Axx%20-%20Grothendieck%20groups%20and%20K_0) (degree zero), [MSC 19Cxx - Steinberg groups and K_2](node:MSC%2019Cxx%20-%20Steinberg%20groups%20and%20K_2) (degree two, built from the Steinberg group) and [MSC 19Dxx - Higher algebraic K-theory](node:MSC%2019Dxx%20-%20Higher%20algebraic%20K-theory); the parent is [MSC 19 - K-theory](node:MSC%2019%20-%20K-theory).

### Key concepts
- **Euclidean domains and PIDs.** For Euclidean domains such as fields and $\mathbb Z$, $SK_1=0$ and the determinant is an isomorphism onto the units; this is false in general for PIDs, since Ischebeck (1980) and Grayson (1981) gave explicit PIDs with $SK_1\neq0$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Dedekind domains and number fields.** If $A$ is a Dedekind domain whose fraction field is a number field then $SK_1(A)=0$ (Milnor, 1971, Cor. 16.3) and $K_1(A)$ is generated by the images of $GL_1$ and $SL_2$; if all residue fields at maximal ideals are finite, $SK_1$ is torsion. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Central simple algebras.** For a central simple algebra $A$ over a field $F$, the reduced norm maps $K_1(A)\to F^\times$; Wang proved $SK_1(A)=0$ for prime degree, extended to square-free degree and to central simple algebras over number fields, while Platonov gave examples of prime-squared degree with $SK_1\neq0$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Finite groups.** For a finite group $G$, $\operatorname{Wh}(G)$ is finitely generated and its rank is the number of irreducible real representations minus the number of irreducible rational representations (Bass, 1965). ([Wikipedia: Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion))
- **s-cobordism theorem.** For a closed connected oriented manifold $M$ of dimension $n>4$, an h-cobordism $W$ from $M$ to $N$ is a product over $M$ if and only if the Whitehead torsion of $M\hookrightarrow W$ vanishes, and every element of $\operatorname{Wh}$ is realized by some h-cobordism. ([Wikipedia: Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion))
- **Exact sequence.** For an ideal $I$ the sequence $K_1(A,I)\to K_1(A)\to K_1(A/I)\to K_0(A,I)\to K_0(A)\to K_0(A/I)$ is exact, tying $K_1$ to [Grothendieck Groups](node:Grothendieck%20Groups). ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Congruence subgroup problem.** For $SL_n(\mathbb Z)$ with $n\ge3$ every finite-index subgroup is a congruence subgroup (Bass–Milnor–Serre, with Mennicke), while for $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ there are many non-congruence subgroups, already known to Klein. ([Wikipedia: Congruence subgroup problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_subgroup_problem))

### History
The geometric role of Whitehead torsion is the passage from Smale's h-cobordism theorem for simply connected manifolds of dimension $n\ge5$ to the s-cobordism theorem, due independently to Mazur, Stallings and Barden; an h-cobordism is a cylinder exactly when the Whitehead torsion of the inclusion vanishes. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) Milnor used Reidemeister torsion to disprove the Hauptvermutung. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))

### Open problems
- **Vanishing of $\operatorname{Wh}(G)$ for torsion-free $G$.** Lück's survey lists as Conjecture 3.6 that $\operatorname{Wh}(G)$ vanishes for torsion-free $G$ and notes that the Full Farrell–Jones Conjecture implies it; the Full Conjecture is known for classes including hyperbolic groups, finite-dimensional CAT(0) groups, certain lattices, fundamental groups of manifolds of dimension $\le3$ and $S$-arithmetic groups, and whether it holds for all groups is posed as a question in Section 11. ([Lück, Survey on the Farrell–Jones Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.11337)) No counterexample to Farrell–Jones is known. ([Wikipedia: Farrell–Jones conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrell%E2%80%93Jones_conjecture)) The vanishing of $\operatorname{Wh}$ for torsion-free groups is described as a well-known conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion))
- **Serre's congruence subgroup conjecture.** For an irreducible arithmetic lattice $\Gamma$ in a semisimple Lie group $G$, the conjecture says $\Gamma$ has the congruence subgroup property iff the real rank of $G$ is at least 2; in higher rank it is proven for non-anisotropic groups and several anisotropic classes, but the inner and outer forms of type $A_n$ are still open; in rank one the expected negative answer is known for all $SO(d,1)$ with $d\ne7$ and for many but not all lattices in $SU(d,1)$, while the remaining cases are described as completely open. ([Wikipedia: Congruence subgroup problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_subgroup_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion): the Whitehead group, torsion and the s-cobordism theorem.
- **Learn:** [Cortiñas, Algebraic v. topological K-theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3983): accessible lecture notes distinguishing algebraic and topological $K$-theory.
- **Primary:** [Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html): Chapter III treats $K_1$, relative $K_1$, the fundamental theorems and negative $K$-theory.
- **Further reading:** [Lück, Survey on the Farrell–Jones Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.11337): the conjectures on $\operatorname{Wh}(G)$, $\tilde K_0$ and negative $K$-groups of group rings; [Ferry–Ranicki, A survey of Wall's finiteness obstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0008070): the related $\tilde K_0$ obstruction.
references.MSC 19Cxx - Steinberg groups and K_2:
## Reference
### Overview
Milnor defined $K_2(A)$ as the center of the Steinberg group $\mathrm{St}(A)$; equivalently it is the kernel of $\mathrm{St}(A)\to GL(A)$, or the Schur multiplier of the group $E(A)$ of elementary matrices. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) In this way $K_2$ measures the relations among elementary matrices that are not consequences of the Steinberg relations, one degree above the quotient $GL/E$ of [MSC 19Bxx - Whitehead groups and K_1](node:MSC%2019Bxx%20-%20Whitehead%20groups%20and%20K_1).

For a field, $K_2$ has an explicit presentation by symbols, and the subject connects linear algebra over rings to Galois cohomology and Brauer groups through the symbol maps, as developed in [Milnor K2 and Steinberg Symbols](node:Milnor%20K2%20and%20Steinberg%20Symbols). ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory); [Wikipedia: Merkurjev–Suslin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkurjev%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 19Cxx into central extensions and Schur multipliers (19C09), symbols, presentations and stability of $K_2$ (19C20), $K_2$ and the Brauer group (19C30) and excision for $K_2$ (19C40). ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Cxx)) Commuting matrices $X,Y$ over $A$ give a commutator pairing in $K_2$, though the article notes this map is not always surjective. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) The adjacent codes are [MSC 19Axx - Grothendieck groups and K_0](node:MSC%2019Axx%20-%20Grothendieck%20groups%20and%20K_0), [MSC 19Dxx - Higher algebraic K-theory](node:MSC%2019Dxx%20-%20Higher%20algebraic%20K-theory) and [MSC 19Fxx - K-theory in number theory](node:MSC%2019Fxx%20-%20K-theory%20in%20number%20theory); the parent is [MSC 19 - K-theory](node:MSC%2019%20-%20K-theory).

### Key concepts
- **Matsumoto's theorem.** For a field $k$, $K_2(k)\cong (k^\times\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k^\times)/\langle a\otimes(1-a): a\ne0,1\rangle$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Milnor K-theory.** $K^M_n(k)$ is the degree-$n$ part of the tensor algebra of $k^\times$ modulo the ideal generated by $a\otimes(1-a)$; it agrees with $K_n$ for $n=0,1,2$ and differs in general for $n\ge3$. For finite fields $K^M_n(\mathbb F_q)=0$ for $n\ge2$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Computations.** $K_2$ of a finite field is zero; $K_2(\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/2$; $K_2$ of the ring of integers of a number field is finite; for a non-Archimedean local field $K_2(F)$ is a finite cyclic group plus a divisible group; $K_2(\mathbb Z/n)\cong\mathbb Z/2$ if $4\mid n$ and $0$ otherwise. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Tate's computation.** $K_2(\mathbb Q)\cong(\mathbb Z/4)^\times\times\bigoplus_{p\text{ odd}}(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, as the article writes it. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Localization sequence.** For a Dedekind domain $A$ with fraction field $F$ the sequence $K_2F\to\bigoplus_{\mathfrak p}K_1(A/\mathfrak p)\to K_1A\to K_1F\to\bigoplus_{\mathfrak p}K_0(A/\mathfrak p)\to K_0A\to K_0F\to0$ is exact; see also [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields). ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Merkurjev–Suslin theorem.** For a field $k$ and an integer $\ell$ invertible in $k$, the norm residue (Galois symbol) map $K_2^M(k)/\ell\to H^2_{\text{ét}}(k,\mu_\ell^{\otimes2})$ is an isomorphism; Merkurjev proved $\ell=2$ in 1981 and Merkurjev and Suslin the general case in 1982. The symbol is the Hilbert symbol, valued in the Brauer group when $k$ contains the $\ell$-th roots of unity; see [Galois Cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology). ([Wikipedia: Merkurjev–Suslin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkurjev%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem))
- **Norm residue theorem.** Merkurjev–Suslin is the case $n=2$ of the norm residue isomorphism (Milnor conjecture for $\ell=2$ proved by Voevodsky; the Bloch–Kato conjecture for odd primes by Voevodsky, Rost and others). ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory); [Wikipedia: Merkurjev–Suslin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkurjev%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem))
- **Bloch's formula.** For a smooth variety $X$ over a field, $CH^q(X)\cong H^q(X,\mathcal K_q)$; Bloch introduced it for $K_2$ and Quillen proved the general case, as in [Algebraic Cycles and Chow Groups](node:Algebraic%20Cycles%20and%20Chow%20Groups). ([Wikipedia: Bloch's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch%27s_formula))

### History
Milnor defined $K_2$ through the Steinberg group, and his book *Introduction to Algebraic K-theory* (Princeton, 1971) is listed among the historical references on algebraic $K$-theory. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) The Merkurjev–Suslin theorem dates to 1982. ([Wikipedia: Merkurjev–Suslin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkurjev%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem)) Thomason showed there is no analogue of Milnor $K$-theory for a general variety. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))

### Open problems
- **Bass's finite-generation conjecture.** The article lists the conjecture that $G_n(A)$ is finitely generated whenever $A$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebra. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) It is listed as unsolved; Quillen proved the cases of dimension at most one (curves over finite fields and rings of integers of number fields). ([Wikipedia: Bass conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_conjecture))
- **Mixed-characteristic Bloch formula.** The analogue of Bloch's formula for mixed characteristic rings is noted as still open. ([Wikipedia: Bloch's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch%27s_formula))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory): $K_2$, Milnor $K$-theory and computations.
- **Learn:** [Cortiñas, Algebraic v. topological K-theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3983): lecture notes on $K$-theory from the algebraic and topological sides.
- **Primary:** [Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html): Chapter III covers $K_2$ of rings and fields and Milnor $K$-theory; Chapter VI covers $K$-theory of fields.
- **Further reading:** [Merkurjev–Suslin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkurjev%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem): statement and relation to the norm residue theorem; Milnor, *Introduction to Algebraic K-theory* (Princeton University Press, 1971), listed in the bibliography of [Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory).
references.MSC 19Dxx - Higher algebraic K-theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Higher algebraic $K$-theory assigns to a ring, scheme or suitable category a sequence of groups $K_n$ extending $K_0$, $K_1$ and $K_2$. Quillen's plus-construction gives $K_n(R)=\pi_n(BGL(R)^+)$ for $n>0$, and Quillen's Q-construction gives $K_i(\mathcal P)=\pi_{i+1}(BQ\mathcal P,0)$ for an exact category $\mathcal P$; the "+ = Q" theorem says the two agree on finitely generated projective modules. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))

For a Waldhausen category $(C,wC)$ the S-construction gives a $K$-theory spectrum, and the construction extends to stable $(\infty,1)$-categories. ([nLab: algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory)) This is the machinery behind [Higher Algebraic K-Theory](node:Higher%20Algebraic%20K-Theory) and [Localization in Algebraic K-Theory](node:Localization%20in%20Algebraic%20K-Theory).

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 19Dxx into $Q$- and plus-constructions (19D06), algebraic $K$-theory of spaces (19D10), symmetric monoidal categories (19D23), Karoubi–Villamayor–Gersten $K$-theory (19D25), negative $K$-theory, NK and Nil (19D35), higher symbols and Milnor $K$-theory (19D45), computations of higher $K$-theory of rings (19D50), and $K$-theory and homology, including cyclic homology (19D55). ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Dxx)) In the K-book the foundations are in Chapter IV (BGL$^+$, finite coefficients, Q-construction, "+=Q", Waldhausen's $wS_\bullet$, non-connective spectra, homotopy $K$-theory) and the fundamental theorems in Chapter V (additivity, localization, resolution, dévissage, coniveau spectral sequence). ([Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html)) Degrees zero to two are in [MSC 19Axx - Grothendieck groups and K_0](node:MSC%2019Axx%20-%20Grothendieck%20groups%20and%20K_0), [MSC 19Bxx - Whitehead groups and K_1](node:MSC%2019Bxx%20-%20Whitehead%20groups%20and%20K_1) and [MSC 19Cxx - Steinberg groups and K_2](node:MSC%2019Cxx%20-%20Steinberg%20groups%20and%20K_2); $K$-theory of schemes is in [MSC 19Exx - K-theory in geometry](node:MSC%2019Exx%20-%20K-theory%20in%20geometry) and of number fields in [MSC 19Fxx - K-theory in number theory](node:MSC%2019Fxx%20-%20K-theory%20in%20number%20theory). The parent is [MSC 19 - K-theory](node:MSC%2019%20-%20K-theory).

### Key concepts
- **Finite fields (Quillen).** $K_0(\mathbb F_q)=\mathbb Z$, $K_{2i}(\mathbb F_q)=0$ for $i\ge1$, and $K_{2i-1}(\mathbb F_q)\cong\mathbb Z/(q^i-1)$ for $i\ge1$; reproved by Jardine in 1993. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) See [Finite Fields](node:Finite%20Fields).
- **Rings of integers (Quillen, Borel).** Quillen proved the $K$-groups of the ring of integers of a number field are finitely generated; Borel computed them modulo torsion, and for $\mathbb Z$, $K_i(\mathbb Z)/\mathrm{tors}=0$ for $i>0$ unless $i=4k+1$ with $k>0$, when it is $\mathbb Z$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) This is the content of [K-Theory of Number Fields](node:K-Theory%20of%20Number%20Fields).
- **Fundamental theorem and negative K-theory.** Bass proved a four-term exact sequence relating $K_0(R)$ to $K_1$ of $R$, $R[t]$ and $R[t,t^{-1}]$, and used it to define negative $K$-groups. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Weibel's vanishing conjecture (Kerz–Strunk–Tamme).** For a noetherian scheme $X$ of finite dimension $d$, $K_i(X)=0$ for $i<-d$; Weibel proposed this in 1980 and Kerz, Strunk and Tamme proved it in full generality in 2018. ([Wikipedia: Weibel's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibel%27s_conjecture)) Their proof derives it from pro-descent of $K$-theory for abstract blow-up squares of noetherian schemes. ([Kerz–Strunk–Tamme, arXiv:1611.08466](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.08466))
- **$G$-theory versus $K$-theory.** $G_n(R)$, built from finitely generated modules, agrees with $K_n(R)$ when $R$ is a noetherian regular ring. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Descent.** $K$-theory satisfies Zariski descent (Brown–Gersten for regular noetherian schemes, Thomason–Trobaugh for finite-dimensional noetherian schemes) and Nisnevich descent (Nisnevich, 1989, generalized by Thomason); Thomason–Trobaugh $K$-theory is the S-construction on perfect complexes. ([nLab: algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory))
- **Quillen–Lichtenbaum.** The Lichtenbaum–Quillen conjecture is now a theorem of Rost and Voevodsky, implying étale descent for $K$-theory in sufficiently large degrees. ([nLab: algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory)) It is implied by the norm residue isomorphism theorem. ([Wikipedia: Merkurjev–Suslin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkurjev%E2%80%93Suslin_theorem))
- **Trace methods.** The cyclotomic trace maps $K$-theory to topological cyclic homology and plays a role like a Chern character. ([nLab: algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory)) The Dundas–Goodwillie–McCarthy theorem says topological cyclic homology has the same local structure as algebraic $K$-theory. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))

### History
Waldhausen's S-construction extended the framework beyond exact categories after Quillen's constructions. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) Hesselholt and Nikolaus present the cyclotomic trace following Nikolaus and Scholze, together with a proof of Bökstedt periodicity. ([Hesselholt–Nikolaus survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08984))

### Open problems
- **Vandiver's conjecture and $K_n(\mathbb Z)$.** Whether $K_{4k+2}(\mathbb Z)$ is cyclic and whether $K_{4k}(\mathbb Z)$ vanishes depends on Vandiver's conjecture; Kurihara showed the conjecture is equivalent to $K_n(\mathbb Z)=0$ for $n$ a multiple of 4. The article lists it as open, with no strong evidence either way, and cites a verification for irregular primes below two billion (Hart–Harvey–Ong). ([Wikipedia: Vandiver's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandiver%27s_conjecture); [Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Gersten's conjecture.** For a regular local ring $R$ with fraction field $F$, $K_n(R)\to K_n(F)$ should be injective, and the general case remains open. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) Quillen proved it when $R$ is the local ring of a smooth variety over a field, Panin extended it to all equicharacteristic regular local rings, and the mixed-characteristic case is described as largely open, with Gillet and Levine's result for rings essentially smooth over a DVR the most general one at the time. ([Skalit, Regular morphisms and Gersten's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.00303))
- **Parshin's conjecture.** For a smooth projective variety $X$ over a finite field, $K_i(X)\otimes\mathbb Q=0$ for $i>0$; the cited cases are dimension 0 (Quillen's computation for finite fields) and dimension 1 (via Harder and Quillen's finite generation). ([Wikipedia: Parshin's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parshin%27s_conjecture))
- **Bass's conjecture.** $G_n(A)$ is finitely generated for every finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebra $A$. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) It is listed as unsolved, with Quillen's proof covering dimension at most one. ([Wikipedia: Bass conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_conjecture))
- **Farrell–Jones.** The assembly-map conjecture computing $K_*(R[G])$ from virtually cyclic subgroups has no known counterexample. ([Wikipedia: Farrell–Jones conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrell%E2%80%93Jones_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: algebraic K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory): Q, plus and S-constructions, descent, trace.
- **Learn:** [Hesselholt–Nikolaus, Topological cyclic homology](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08984): Handbook chapter on the cyclotomic trace and Bökstedt periodicity.
- **Primary:** [Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html): Chapters IV-VI on definitions, fundamental theorems and $K$-theory of fields, including $K$-theory of $\mathbb Z$.
- **Further reading:** [Kerz–Strunk–Tamme, Algebraic K-theory and descent for blow-ups](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.08466): proof of Weibel's conjecture.
references.MSC 19Exx - K-theory in geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 19Exx, "K-theory in geometry", has the sub-codes 19E08 ($K$-theory of schemes), 19E15 (algebraic cycles and motivic cohomology, $K$-theoretic aspects), 19E20 (relations of $K$-theory with cohomology theories) and 19E99 (none of the above, but in this section). ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Exx))

The central input is a choice of category of sheaves on a scheme $X$: vector bundles give $K(X)$, coherent sheaves on a noetherian scheme give $G(X)$, and perfect complexes give Thomason–Trobaugh K-theory, which coincides with Quillen's K-theory for schemes admitting an ample family of line bundles. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory); [Weibel, Ch. V](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf))

The general machinery is in [MSC 19Dxx - Higher algebraic K-theory](node:MSC%2019Dxx%20-%20Higher%20algebraic%20K-theory). Weibel's K-book treats $K_0$ of schemes and varieties (II.8), localization and the fundamental theorem for $K_*(X)$, the coniveau spectral sequence and Chern classes (Ch. V), and the relation to motivic cohomology (VI.4). ([Weibel, K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html))

### Scope
- **19E08, $K$-theory of schemes** (see also 14C35). ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Exx)) Weibel's Chapter V proves the resolution, localization, projective bundle and fundamental theorems for $K_*(X)$ and $G_*(X)$. ([Weibel, Ch. V](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf))
- **19E15, algebraic cycles and motivic cohomology ($K$-theoretic aspects)** (see also 14C25, 14C35, 14F42). ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Exx)) Motivic cohomology connects to $K$-theory through Bloch's formula and the motivic spectral sequence. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivic_cohomology))
- **19E20, relations of $K$-theory with cohomology theories** (see also 14Fxx). ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Exx)) One example is the cyclotomic trace from $K$-theory to topological cyclic homology, which works much like a Chern character. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory))
- **19E99** is the residual code "none of the above, but in this section". ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Exx))

The neighbouring subfield 19Dxx lists $Q$- and plus-constructions and computations of higher $K$-theory of rings. ([AMS MathSciNet: MSC2020 19Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Dxx))

### Key concepts
- [K-Theory of Schemes](node:K-Theory%20of%20Schemes): the groups $K_n(X)$ built from vector bundles or perfect complexes, versus $G_n(X)$ from coherent sheaves. ([Weibel, Ch. V](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf))
- [Localization in Algebraic K-Theory](node:Localization%20in%20Algebraic%20K-Theory): Quillen's theorem (Weibel attributes the higher localization theorem to Quillen) that for a Serre subcategory $\mathcal B$ of a small abelian category $\mathcal A$, $K(\mathcal B)\to K(\mathcal A)\to K(\mathcal A/\mathcal B)$ is a homotopy fibration, so there is a long exact sequence $\cdots\to K_{n}(\mathcal B)\to K_n(\mathcal A)\to K_n(\mathcal A/\mathcal B)\to K_{n-1}(\mathcal B)\to\cdots$. ([Weibel, Thm V.5.1](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf))
- Resolution and $K=G$: if $X$ is a separated regular noetherian scheme then $K_n(X)\cong G_n(X)$ for all $n$; the separatedness hypothesis is necessary, as the affine line with doubled origin shows. ([Weibel, Thm V.3.4 and Rem. 3.4.2](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf))
- Projective bundle formula: for a projective bundle $\mathbb P(E)$ of rank $r+1$ over a quasi-projective scheme $X$, the functors $N\mapsto N\otimes\mathcal O(-i)$, $0\le i\le r$, induce $K(X)^{r+1}\simeq K(\mathbb P(E))$. ([Weibel, Thm V.1.5](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf))
- [Algebraic Cycles and Chow Groups](node:Algebraic%20Cycles%20and%20Chow%20Groups) and Bloch's formula: $H^p(X,\mathcal K_p)\cong CH^p(X)$ for a smooth variety $X$ over a field, introduced by Bloch for $K_2$ and proved in general by Quillen; for mixed characteristic the formula is still open. ([Bloch's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch%27s_formula))
- Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch: for a proper morphism $f:X\to Y$ of smooth quasi-projective schemes over a field and $F^\bullet$ a bounded complex of sheaves, $\mathrm{ch}(f_!F^\bullet)\,\mathrm{td}(Y)=f_*\big(\mathrm{ch}(F^\bullet)\,\mathrm{td}(X)\big)$ in the rational Chow ring. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck%E2%80%93Riemann%E2%80%93Roch_theorem))

- **Fundamental theorem for schemes.** If $X$ is regular noetherian then $K_n(X)\cong K_n(X[s])$, $K_n(X[s,s^{-1}])\cong K_n(X)\oplus K_{n-1}(X)$ and $K_n(X\times\mathbb P^1)\cong K_n(X)\oplus K_n(X)$. ([Weibel, Cor. V.6.13.2](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf))
- **Weibel's conjecture (Kerz–Strunk–Tamme).** For a noetherian scheme $X$ of dimension $d<\infty$, $K_i(X)=0$ for $i<-d$; it was proposed by Weibel in 1980 and proved in full generality in 2018, as a consequence of pro-descent of K-theory for abstract blow-up squares of noetherian schemes. ([arXiv:1611.08466](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.08466); [Wikipedia: Weibel's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibel%27s_conjecture))
- **Beilinson–Lichtenbaum.** For a smooth scheme $X$ over a field $k$ and $m$ invertible in $k$, the cycle map $H^i(X,\mathbb Z/m(j))\to H^i_{et}(X,\mu_m^{\otimes j})$ is an isomorphism for $j\ge i$ and injective for $j\ge i-1$; this follows from the norm residue isomorphism theorem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivic_cohomology))
- **Motivic spectral sequence.** For smooth $X$ over a field there is a spectral sequence from motivic cohomology to algebraic K-theory, degenerating rationally. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivic_cohomology))

### History
Grothendieck's Riemann–Roch theorem was presented at the 1957 Bonn Arbeitstagung and written up by Borel and Serre in 1958; it was the origin of $K_0$ of schemes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck%E2%80%93Riemann%E2%80%93Roch_theorem)) The localization theorem for higher $K$-theory of abelian categories is due to Quillen. ([Weibel, Ch. V](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf)) Thomason–Trobaugh $K$-theory, built from perfect complexes, has better global descent properties. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory)) The Bloch–Kato conjecture was proved by Voevodsky, Rost and others ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)), and the Beilinson–Lichtenbaum statement is a consequence of the norm residue isomorphism theorem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivic_cohomology))

### Open problems
- **Gersten's conjecture.** For a regular local ring $R$ with fraction field $F$, the map $K_n(R)\to K_n(F)$ should be injective, and the general case remains open. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)) Quillen proved it for local rings of smooth varieties over a field, Panin extended it to all equicharacteristic regular local rings, and the mixed-characteristic case is described as largely open. ([Skalit, Regular morphisms and Gersten's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.00303)) Weibel states the version for discrete valuation rings as a conjecture known in low degrees and special cases. ([Weibel, Conj. V.6.9](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf))
- **Beilinson–Soulé vanishing.** Rational motivic cohomology $H^i(X,\mathbb Q(j))$ should vanish for $i<0$; it is known only in a few cases. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivic_cohomology))
- **Bass's conjecture.** $G_n(A)$ should be finitely generated for finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebras $A$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory)); it is listed as unsolved, with Quillen's proof covering dimension at most one. ([Wikipedia: Bass conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Algebraic K-theory (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+K-theory): Thomason–Trobaugh K-theory, descent, cyclotomic trace.
- **Reference:** [Bloch's formula (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch%27s_formula): $CH^p(X)\cong H^p(X,\mathcal K_p)$ for smooth varieties; mixed characteristic open.
- **Reference:** [Motivic cohomology (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivic_cohomology): Bloch formula, Beilinson–Lichtenbaum, Beilinson–Soulé.
- **Learn:** [Weibel, K-book Chapter V](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook/Kbook.V.pdf): additivity, resolution, localization, fundamental theorem and projective bundle theorem, with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Kerz–Strunk–Tamme, Algebraic K-theory and descent for blow-ups](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.08466): pro-descent and Weibel's conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html): Graduate Studies in Mathematics 145, AMS 2013; Chapter V is the fundamental theorems.
references.MSC 19Fxx - K-theory in number theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Arithmetic algebraic K-theory studies the $K$-groups of number fields, their rings of integers, and local and finite fields, and relates them to zeta values, étale cohomology and class field theory. Lichtenbaum conjectured a link between special values of the zeta function of a number field and the $K$-groups of its ring of integers; Quillen generalized this to a spectral sequence from étale cohomology to $K$-theory. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))

Much of that program is now a theorem: Voevodsky, using work of Rost, proved the Bloch–Kato (norm residue) conjecture, which implies the Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture at all primes. Weibel's book page records that the final steps of the proof of the norm residue theorem settled the Bloch–Kato, Beilinson–Lichtenbaum and Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjectures. ([Wikipedia: Quillen–Lichtenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Lichtenbaum_conjecture); [Weibel, K-book page](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html)) Weibel's Handbook survey uses the Rost–Voevodsky theorem to determine the odd torsion in the $K$-groups of local and global fields and their rings of integers. ([Weibel, K-theory of rings of integers](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf))

Still open are Vandiver's conjecture, which by Kurihara's theorem is equivalent to the vanishing of $K_{4k}(\mathbb Z)$ for all $k\ge1$, and the Beilinson and Bloch–Kato (Tamagawa number) conjectures on special values of $L$-functions, which are known only in special cases. ([Weibel, K-theory of rings of integers](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf); [Wikipedia: Special values of L-functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_values_of_L-functions))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists three finer codes under 19Fxx: 19F05 generalized class field theory ($K$-theoretic aspects), 19F15 symbols and arithmetic ($K$-theoretic aspects), and 19F27 étale cohomology, higher regulators, zeta and $L$-functions ($K$-theoretic aspects), plus 19F99; the section cross-refers to 11R70 and 11S70, and 19F27 to 11G40, 11R42, 11S40, 14F20 and 14G10. ([MSC2020, 19F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Fxx))

- **vs 11R70 / 11S70:** 11R70 ($K$-theory of global fields) is the number-theory code and refers back to 19Fxx, which in turn cross-refers to 11R70 and 11S70. ([MSC2020, 19F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Fxx); [MSC2020, 11R](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Rxx))
- **vs 11R37 and 11G45:** 19F15 (symbols and arithmetic) cross-refers to 11R37, class field theory, and 19F05 (generalized class field theory) to 11G45. ([MSC2020, 19F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Fxx); [MSC2020, 11R](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Rxx))
- **vs 11R42 / 14F20:** 19F27 cross-refers to 11R42 (zeta and $L$-functions of number fields), which refers back to 19F27, and to 14F20 (étale and other Grothendieck topologies and (co)homologies). ([MSC2020, 19F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Fxx); [MSC2020, 11R](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Rxx); [MSC2020, 14F](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Finite fields (Quillen).** For the finite field $\mathbb F_q$ (see [Finite Fields](node:Finite%20Fields)), $K_0=\mathbb Z$ and $K_{2i-1}(\mathbb F_q)\cong\mathbb Z/(q^i-1)$ for $i\ge1$; the even groups $K_{2i}(\mathbb F_q)$, $i\ge1$, vanish. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **Quillen–Borel theorem.** For a number field $F$ with $r_1$ real and $r_2$ complex places, the groups $K_n(\mathcal O_F)$ are finitely generated, with $\operatorname{rank}K_n(\mathcal O_F)=r_1+r_2$ for $n\equiv1\pmod 4$ ($n>1$) and $r_2$ for $n\equiv3\pmod4$; for even $n>0$, $K_n(\mathcal O_F)$ is finite, and for $n=2i-1$ the rank equals $\operatorname{ord}_{s=1-i}\zeta_F(s)$. Soulé showed $K_n(\mathcal O_F)\to K_n(F)$ is injective. ([Weibel, Theorem 6](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf); [Elmanto–Zhang](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.03578)) Zeta values enter via [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) and [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields).
- **$K_2$ of fields (Matsumoto, Tate).** For a field $k$, $K_2(k)\cong (k^\times\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k^\times)/\langle a\otimes(1-a)\rangle$; Tate computed $K_2(\mathbb Q)\cong(\mathbb Z/4)^\times\oplus\bigoplus_{p\text{ odd}}(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, and $K_2(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/2$. See [Milnor K2 and Steinberg Symbols](node:Milnor%20K2%20and%20Steinberg%20Symbols). ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory))
- **$K_3$ and the Bloch group (Suslin).** The Bloch group $B_2(K)$ is the kernel of $[x]\mapsto x\wedge(1-x)$ on the free abelian group on symbols modulo the five-term relation, whose cokernel is $K_2(K)$ by Matsumoto; for an infinite field Suslin proved an exact sequence $0\to\widetilde{\mathrm{Tor}}(K^\times,K^\times)\to K_3(K)^{\mathrm{ind}}\to B_2(K)\to0$. The Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm $D_2$ is well defined on it. ([Wikipedia: Bloch group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch_group))
- **Norm residue isomorphism theorem.** For a field $k$ and $\ell$ invertible in $k$, the norm residue map $K_n^M(k)/\ell\to H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(k,\mu_\ell^{\otimes n})$ is an isomorphism; $\ell=2$ is the Milnor conjecture and $n=2$ the Merkurjev–Suslin theorem. ([Wikipedia: Bloch–Kato conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch%E2%80%93Kato_conjecture)) See [Galois Cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology) and [Étale Cohomology](node:Étale%20Cohomology).
- **Quillen–Lichtenbaum.** For a finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebra $A$ and a prime $\ell$, Quillen predicted a spectral sequence, analogous to the Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence, with $E_2^{p,q}=H^p_{\mathrm{et}}(\operatorname{Spec}A[1/\ell],\mathbb Z_\ell(-q/2))$ (zero for $q$ odd) converging to $K_{-p-q}(A)\otimes\mathbb Z_\ell$ for $-p-q>1+\dim A$. Kahn and Rognes–Weibel proved it at the prime 2 for some number fields, and the Bloch–Kato theorem gives it at all primes. ([Wikipedia: Quillen–Lichtenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Lichtenbaum_conjecture))
- **Étale Chern classes.** Soulé's étale Chern classes, in the form of Dwyer–Friedlander's étale $K$-theory, map $K_{2i-1}(F;\mathbb Z/\ell^\nu)$ to $H^1_{\mathrm{et}}(F,\mu_{\ell^\nu}^{\otimes i})$ through étale $K$-theory and the edge map of its Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence; they detect the summands of $K_*(\mathcal O_F)$ related to the Picard and Brauer groups. ([Weibel, §5.4](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf))
- **Lichtenbaum's conjecture and regulators.** For $k\ge2$, up to sign and a power of 2, $\zeta_F^*(1-k)=\frac{\#K_{2k-2}(\mathcal O_F)}{\#K_{2k-1}(\mathcal O_F)_{\mathrm{tors}}}\,R^B_k(F)$, with $R^B_k(F)$ the Borel regulator; Borel and Beilinson regulators differ by powers of 2. ([Elmanto–Zhang](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.03578)) Borel proved that the leading coefficient of $\zeta_F$ at $1-m$ is the Borel regulator times a rational number; the cohomological form, with $\#H^2(\mathcal O_F[1/p],\mathbb Z_p(m))/\#H^1(\cdot)_{\mathrm{tors}}$ in place of $K$-groups, holds for abelian $F$ (Kolster–Nguyen Quang Do–Fleckinger, corrected by Benois–Nguyen Quang Do; also from Huber–Kings' Bloch–Kato theorem for Dirichlet characters). ([Sun, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.12314); [Huber–Kings](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0101071)) For totally real $F$, $\zeta_F(1-2k)=(-1)^{kr_1}\#K_{4k-2}(\mathcal O_F)/\#K_{4k-1}(\mathcal O_F)$ up to factors of 2 (from Wiles), and for $\mathbb Z$, $\#K_{4k-2}(\mathbb Z)/\#K_{4k-1}(\mathbb Z)=\lvert B_k/4k\rvert$ for $k\ge1$. ([Weibel, Theorem 77, Corollary 95](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf))
- **Birch–Tate theorem.** For totally real $F$, $\zeta_F(-1)=(-1)^{r_1}\#K_2(\mathcal O_F)/w_2(F)$. Wiles proved the odd part; the 2-part follows from the 2-adic main conjecture (Kolster), which Wiles proved for abelian extensions of $\mathbb Q$, so the full formula holds for all abelian $F$; e.g. $\zeta(-1)=-1/12$, $\#K_2(\mathbb Z)=2$, $w_2(\mathbb Q)=24$. ([Weibel, Conjecture 31](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf); [Wikipedia: Birch–Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch%E2%80%93Tate_conjecture))
- **$K_n(\mathbb Z)$ and Vandiver.** Kurihara: for an irregular prime $\ell$ and $1\le k\le(\ell-1)/2$, $K_{4k}(\mathbb Z)$ has no $\ell$-torsion iff the $(-2k)$-eigenspace of $\mathrm{Pic}(\mathbb Z[\zeta_\ell])/\ell$ vanishes; so Vandiver's conjecture is equivalent to $K_{4k}(\mathbb Z)=0$ for all $k\ge1$ ($K_0(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ is excluded). Assuming Vandiver, for $n\ge2$ and $k=\lfloor1+n/4\rfloor$, $K_n(\mathbb Z)$ is $\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/2$, $\mathbb Z/2c_k$, $\mathbb Z/2w_{2k}$, $0$, $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Z/c_k$, $\mathbb Z/w_{2k}$, $0$ for $n\equiv1,\dots,8\pmod8$, where $B_k/4k=c_k/w_{2k}$ in lowest terms. Unconditionally $K_3(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/48$, $K_4(\mathbb Z)=0$, $K_5(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$, $K_7(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/240$, $K_{22}(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/691$. ([Weibel, Theorem 105, Corollary 107, Table 5.1](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf))

### History
Lichtenbaum's 1973 conjectures on zeta values inspired Quillen's 1975 formulation of the Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Quillen–Lichtenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Lichtenbaum_conjecture)) Finite generation and the ranks of $K_n(\mathcal O_F)$ have been known since 1972, while the torsion was only conjectural until 1997; the 2-primary torsion of $K_*(\mathbb Z)$ was resolved in 1997 and the rest of the table follows from the Voevodsky–Rost theorem. Weibel notes that the content of Vandiver's conjecture was discussed by Kummer and Kronecker in 1849–1853. ([Weibel, K-theory of rings of integers](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf)) Weibel's K-book page records that the final steps of the proof of the norm residue theorem, spread over many papers mostly by Rost and Voevodsky, were finished during 2004–2008. ([Weibel, K-book page](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html))

### Open problems
- **Vandiver's conjecture.** Open; there is no particularly strong evidence either for or against it, and it has been checked computationally for all primes below 163,000,000 (Buhler–Harvey) and then below $2^{31}$ (Hart–Harvey–Ong, "Irregular primes to two billion"). ([Wikipedia: Vandiver's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandiver%27s_conjecture)) Weibel's 2005 survey records that the groups $K_{4k}(\mathbb Z)$ were then only known to have odd order, with $K_8(\mathbb Z)=0$ an open question. ([Weibel, §5.1](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf)) That case is now settled: Dutour Sikirić, Elbaz-Vincent, Kupers and Martinet computed cohomology of $GL_N(\mathbb Z)$ for $N\ge8$ via Voronoi complexes and proved $K_8(\mathbb Z)=0$, with consequences for the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture (J. Inst. Math. Jussieu, 2025). ([arXiv:1910.11598](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.11598); [Cambridge](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-institute-of-mathematics-of-jussieu/article/voronoi-complexes-in-higher-dimensions-cohomology-of-glnmathbbz-for-ngeqslant-8-and-the-triviality-of-k8mathbbz/6C1E2AA4FA1AD29554384C091A51D8E5)) The vanishing of $K_{4k}(\mathbb Z)$ for general $k$ remains equivalent to Vandiver's conjecture.
- **2-part of Birch–Tate for non-abelian fields.** Weibel's survey states that the two-primary part is still open in general, known only via the 2-adic main conjecture, proved for abelian extensions of $\mathbb Q$. ([Weibel, Conjecture 31](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf))
- **Tamagawa number conjectures.** The Beilinson and Bloch–Kato conjectures on special values of $L$-functions, and the equivariant Tamagawa number conjecture, are known only in special cases. ([Wikipedia: Special values of L-functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_values_of_L-functions))
- **Computing $K_*(\mathbb Z)$ and $K_*$ of local fields.** Computing the $K$-groups of the integers is described as an important outstanding problem; Weibel's survey notes that for a local field $E\supset\mathbb Q_p$ the $p$-completion of $K_*(E)$ is understood but the actual groups $K_*(E)$ are not. ([Wikipedia: Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory); [Weibel, §5.1](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quillen%E2%80%93Lichtenbaum_conjecture): statement, proofs and the conditional computation of $K_*(\mathbb Z)$.
- **Learn:** [Weibel, The K-book](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html): free chapter files; Chapter VI covers $K_3$ of a field, number fields and the $K$-theory of $\mathbb Z$.
- **Primary:** [Weibel, Algebraic K-theory of rings of integers in local and global fields](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/weibel-ints.pdf): Handbook of K-theory survey with the Quillen–Borel, Birch–Tate, Lichtenbaum and Vandiver results and the table of $K_n(\mathbb Z)$.
- **Primary:** [Dalawat, Some aspects of the functor $K_2$ of fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0311099): survey linking $K_2$ to reciprocity laws and special values of zeta and $L$-functions.
- **Further reading:** Weibel, *The K-book* (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 145, 2013), see the [author's page](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~weibel/Kbook.html).
references.MSC 19Gxx - K-theory of forms:
## Reference
### Overview
$K$-theory of forms studies projective modules or vector bundles that carry a nondegenerate symmetric, quadratic or hermitian form. Its basic invariants are the Grothendieck–Witt group $GW$, built from isometry classes of forms under orthogonal sum, and the Witt group $W$, the quotient of $GW$ by the ideal generated by hyperbolic spaces. ([Wikipedia: Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group))

Passing from forms to their "stable" classes leads to $L$-theory: for a ring with involution, $L_{2k}(R)$ is the Witt group of $\varepsilon$-quadratic forms with $\varepsilon=(-1)^k$, and $L_*(\mathbb Z[\pi])$ is central to surgery classification of manifolds of dimension $n>4$ and to the Novikov conjecture. ([Wikipedia: L-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-theory))

Higher Grothendieck–Witt (hermitian $K$-) groups are the homotopical refinement; Schlichting showed they are invariant under derived equivalences and proved Mayer–Vietoris sequences, while a nine-author programme recasts them through Poincaré $\infty$-categories and a fibre sequence linking $GW$, $K$-theory and $L$-theory. ([Schlichting](https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.0848); [Calmès et al. I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.07223); [Calmès et al. III](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.07225))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 19G05 stability for quadratic modules, 19G12 Witt groups of rings, 19G24 $L$-theory of group rings, and 19G38 hermitian $K$-theory and its relations with $K$-theory of rings. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

The entry cross-refers to 11Exx (forms and linear algebraic groups), and 19G12 and 19G24 cross-refer to 11E81; surgery obstructions ($K$-theoretic aspects) have their own code, 19J25, under obstructions from topology. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Witt ring of a field.** For a field $k$ of characteristic $\ne2$, $W(k)$ is the group of equivalence classes of nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms modulo hyperbolic planes; $W(\mathbb R)\cong\mathbb Z$ via signature, and for odd $q$, $W(\mathbb F_q)\cong\mathbb Z/4$ if $q\equiv3\pmod 4$ and $\cong(\mathbb Z/2)[\mathbb F_q^\times/\mathbb F_q^{\times2}]$ if $q\equiv1\pmod4$. See [Witt Groups](node:Witt%20Groups). ([Wikipedia: Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group))
- **Fundamental ideal and Pfister forms.** The kernel $I\subset W(k)$ of the rank-mod-2 map is the fundamental ideal; $I^n$ is additively generated by $n$-fold Pfister forms $\langle\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle\rangle$. ([Wikipedia: Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group))
- **Milnor conjecture on quadratic forms.** The map $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\mapsto\langle\langle a_1,\dots,a_n\rangle\rangle$ induces an isomorphism $K_n^M(k)/2\cong I^n/I^{n+1}$ for fields of characteristic $\ne2$ (Milnor showed surjectivity and conjectured bijectivity); Orlov, Vishik and Voevodsky proved it in characteristic $0$. The companion Milnor conjecture is the case $\ell=2$ of the norm residue theorem, $K_n^M(k)/2\cong H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(k,\mu_2^{\otimes n})$, proved by Voevodsky. See [Galois Cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology). ([Wikipedia: Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group); [Wikipedia: Bloch–Kato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch%E2%80%93Kato_conjecture); [Dugger](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0408436))
- **$L$-groups of $\mathbb Z$ and periodicity.** Quadratic and symmetric $L$-groups are 4-periodic; the quadratic groups of $\mathbb Z$ are $L_{4k}(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ (signature$/8$), $L_{4k+1}=0$, $L_{4k+2}=\mathbb Z/2$ (Arf invariant), $L_{4k+3}=0$. See [Surgery Theory](node:Surgery%20Theory). ([Wikipedia: L-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-theory))
- **Karoubi's fundamental theorem and descent.** Higher $GW$-groups are invariant under derived equivalences of dg categories with duality, which yields an algebraic Bott sequence and a new proof of Karoubi's fundamental theorem; for schemes with an ample family of line bundles and $2$ invertible there are Nisnevich and blow-up Mayer–Vietoris sequences. ([Schlichting](https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.0848))
- **Grothendieck–Witt groups of rings.** There is a fibre sequence relating $GW(R)$ to the homotopy $C_2$-orbits of $K(R)$ and Ranicki's symmetric $L$-theory; $GW$-groups of rings of integers are finitely generated, and the homotopy limit problem is solved for Dedekind rings with number-field fraction field. ([Calmès et al. III](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.07225))

### History
Milnor stated the conjecture relating $K^M_*(k)/2$ to the graded Witt ring in 1970; Orlov, Vishik and Voevodsky's proof was published in 2007 for characteristic $0$, and Dugger's notes explain the proofs of both Milnor conjectures by Voevodsky, Orlov–Vishik–Voevodsky and Morel. ([Wikipedia: Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group); [Dugger](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0408436))

### Open problems
- **The $u$-invariant.** Even for function fields of curves over number fields, whether $u(F)=2^{n+2}$ for finitely generated $F/K$ of transcendence degree $n$ over a nonreal number field $K$ is stated to be open already for $n=1$, as is bounding $u(F)$ in terms of $u(K)$ and the transcendence degree. ([Becher–Daans–Mehmeti](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.13086))

### Resources
