- **Reference:** [Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group): definitions, Pfister forms, the Milnor conjecture and $L$-theory pointers.
- **Learn:** [Dugger, Notes on the Milnor conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0408436): lecture notes covering both Milnor conjectures and their proofs.
- **Primary:** [Schlichting, Hermitian K-theory, derived equivalences and Karoubi's Fundamental Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.0848): higher $GW$-groups, descent and Bott sequences.
- **Further reading:** [Calmès et al., Hermitian K-theory for stable infinity-categories III](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.07225): $GW$-groups of rings, via $K$- and $L$-theory.
references.MSC 19Jxx - Obstructions from topology:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 19J collects the places where algebraic K-theory and L-theory of group rings $\mathbb Z[\pi]$ appear as obstructions in geometric topology: finiteness obstructions in $K_0$ (19J05), Whitehead torsion (19J10), surgery obstructions (19J25, see also 57R67) and obstructions to group actions (19J35). ([MSC2020, 19J](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Jxx)) The pattern is the same in each case: a geometric question about a space or manifold with [fundamental group](node:Fundamental%20Group) $\pi$ (is it finite up to homotopy, is an $h$-cobordism a product, is a homotopy equivalence a homeomorphism up to bordism) is answered by an element of an algebraic group built from $\mathbb Z[\pi]$. ([Ferry–Ranicki, Introduction, §6](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070); [Wikipedia, Surgery obstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgery_obstruction))

Ferry and Ranicki describe Wall's obstruction as generalizing Swan's application of algebraic K-theory to free group actions on spheres, and note that, for a finite complex $K$ in the homotopy type of $X$, Whitehead torsion governs the uniqueness of $K$ while the finiteness obstruction governs its existence. ([Ferry–Ranicki, Introduction, §6](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070)) The parent field is [MSC 19 - K-theory](node:MSC%2019%20-%20K-theory); the groups themselves are studied in [MSC 19Axx - Grothendieck groups and K_0](node:MSC%2019Axx%20-%20Grothendieck%20groups%20and%20K_0) and [MSC 19Bxx - Whitehead groups and K_1](node:MSC%2019Bxx%20-%20Whitehead%20groups%20and%20K_1).

### Scope
MSC2020 19J lists: 19J05 finiteness and other obstructions in $K_0$; 19J10 Whitehead (and related) torsion; 19J25 surgery obstructions ($K$-theoretic aspects), see also 57R67; 19J35 obstructions to group actions ($K$-theoretic aspects); 19J99 none of the above. ([MSC2020, 19J](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Jxx)) The cross-reference sends the geometric side of surgery to [MSC 57Rxx - Differential topology](node:MSC%2057Rxx%20-%20Differential%20topology), while 19J keeps the $K$-theoretic aspects. ([MSC2020, 19J](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Jxx))

### Key concepts
- **Wall's finiteness obstruction (19J05).** A space is finitely dominated if it is a homotopy retract of a finite complex: there are $d:K\to X$, $s:X\to K$ with $K$ finite and $d\circ s\simeq\mathrm{id}_X$. Wall: a finitely dominated connected CW complex $X$ has an obstruction $[X]\in\widetilde K_0(\mathbb Z[\pi_1X])$ that vanishes if and only if $X$ is [homotopy equivalent](node:Homotopy%20Equivalence) to a finite CW complex; and for finitely presented $\pi$ every element of $\widetilde K_0(\mathbb Z[\pi])$ is the obstruction of some finitely dominated complex with $\pi_1=\pi$. ([Ferry–Ranicki, Def. 1.1, Thm 3.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070)) Lurie defines it as $w(X)=(-1)^n[H_n(X,Z;\mathbb Z[G])]$, where $n\ge2$ bounds the homotopy dimension of $X$ and $Z\to X$ is an $(n-1)$-connected map from a CW complex $Z$ of dimension $<n$; since finitely generated projective $\mathbb Z$-modules are free, simply connected finitely dominated spaces have finite homotopy type. ([Lurie, Def. 20, Cor. 17](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/281notes/Lecture2-Wall.pdf))
- **Mather's trick and the product formula.** $X$ is finitely dominated if and only if $X\times S^1$ is homotopy equivalent to a finite CW complex; Gersten's product formula gives $[X\times S^1]=0$, an algebraic proof. ([Ferry–Ranicki, Prop. 1.5, §3](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070))
- **Siebenmann's end obstruction.** A tame end $\epsilon$ of an open $n$-manifold $W$ has an obstruction in $\widetilde K_0(\mathbb Z[\pi_1(\epsilon)])$ that vanishes if, and for $n\ge6$ only if, $\epsilon$ can be collared (Siebenmann's 1965 Princeton thesis). ([Ferry–Ranicki, Thm 5.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070))
- **[Whitehead torsion](node:Whitehead%20Torsion) (19J10).** The Whitehead group $\mathrm{Wh}(G)$ is the cokernel of $G\times\{\pm1\}\to K_1(\mathbb Z[G])$; a homotopy equivalence $f$ of finite CW complexes has a torsion $\tau(f)\in\mathrm{Wh}(\pi_1Y)$, a homotopy invariant that vanishes for [homeomorphisms](node:Homeomorphism) and measures whether $f$ is a simple homotopy equivalence. $\mathrm{Wh}$ of the trivial group and of free [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) vanishes (Bass–Heller–Swan, 1964), while $\mathrm{Wh}(\mathbb Z/5)\cong\mathbb Z$ (Higman, 1940). ([Wikipedia, Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion)) See [Algebraic K1 and Whitehead Groups](node:Algebraic%20K1%20and%20Whitehead%20Groups).
- **$s$-cobordism theorem.** For $n\ge5$ and a compact $(n+1)$-dimensional $h$-cobordism $W$ between $M$ and $N$, not necessarily simply connected, $W$ is a cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ if and only if $\tau(W,M)=0$; isomorphism classes of $h$-cobordisms on $M$ form a torsor for $\mathrm{Wh}(\pi)$. It holds in the smooth, PL and topological categories and is due independently to Mazur, Stallings and Barden. ([Wikipedia, s-cobordism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-cobordism_theorem)) The simply connected case is the [h-Cobordism Theorem](node:h-Cobordism%20Theorem).
- **Bass–Heller–Swan splitting.** $\mathrm{Wh}(\pi\times\mathbb Z)$ splits as $\mathrm{Wh}(\pi)\oplus\widetilde K_0(\mathbb Z[\pi])$ plus two Nil-terms, and the theorem involves a split injection $\widetilde K_0(\mathbb Z[\pi])\to\mathrm{Wh}(\pi\times\mathbb Z)$. Ferry identified the finiteness obstruction of $X$ with the Whitehead torsion in $\mathrm{Wh}(\pi\times\mathbb Z)$ of a self-homotopy equivalence, and Ranicki showed this corresponds to a sign-modified version of that split injection. ([Ferry–Ranicki, §6](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070))
- **Surgery obstructions (19J25).** For a degree-one normal map $(f,b)$ to an $n$-dimensional $X$ with $n\ge5$, the surgery obstruction $\theta(f,b)\in L_n(\mathbb Z[\pi_1X])$ vanishes exactly when $(f,b)$ is normally cobordant to a homotopy equivalence; simply connected, the obstruction is a signature difference for $n=4l$ and an Arf invariant for $n=4l+2$. ([Wikipedia, Surgery obstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgery_obstruction)) Wall's quadratic $L$-groups are 4-periodic and govern the surgery classification of manifolds of dimension $n>4$; $L_{4k}(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ (detected by the signature), $L_{4k+2}(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/2$ (Arf invariant), and the odd groups vanish. ([Wikipedia, L-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-theory)) See [Surgery Theory](node:Surgery%20Theory).

### History
Swan's 1960 work on periodic resolutions applied $K$-theory to free group actions on spheres; Wall's "Finiteness conditions for CW complexes" appeared in the *Annals of Mathematics* in 1965, and Siebenmann's thesis on finding a boundary for an open manifold dates from the same year. ([Ferry–Ranicki, Introduction and references](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070)) J. H. C. Whitehead's "Simple homotopy types" dates from 1950, Bass, Heller and Swan computed Whitehead groups of free abelian groups in 1964, and Milnor's survey "Whitehead torsion" appeared in 1966. ([Wikipedia, Whitehead torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_torsion)) Kirby and Siebenmann's structure theory showed every compact topological manifold has the homotopy type of a finite polyhedron. ([Ferry–Ranicki, §8](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070)) Whether every closed compact topological manifold is homeomorphic to a finite polyhedron was, when Ferry and Ranicki wrote, open in dimensions at least five, while Casson had shown it fails in dimension four. ([Ferry–Ranicki, §8, footnote 2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070)) Manolescu's Pin(2)-equivariant Seiberg–Witten Floer homology, combined with earlier work of Galewski–Stern and Matumoto, settled it negatively by producing non-triangulable high-dimensional manifolds. ([Manolescu, arXiv 1303.2354](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.2354))

### Open problems
- **Farrell–Jones and Novikov conjectures.** The Farrell–Jones conjecture (1993) asserts that the $K$- and $L$-theoretic assembly maps from the classifying space for virtually cyclic subgroups are isomorphisms; it is listed among unsolved problems, no counterexample is known, and it is proved for hyperbolic, CAT(0), virtually solvable and mapping class groups. ([Wikipedia, Farrell–Jones conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrell%E2%80%93Jones_conjecture)) The Novikov conjecture (1965), that higher signatures are oriented homotopy invariants, is unsolved, equivalent to rational injectivity of the $L$-theory assembly map, and proved for finitely generated abelian groups. ([Wikipedia, Novikov conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novikov_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, s-cobordism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-cobordism_theorem): statement and torsor classification of $h$-cobordisms.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, L-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-theory): Wall's $L$-groups and their periodicity.
- **Learn:** [Lurie, Math 281 Lecture 2: The Wall finiteness obstruction](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/281notes/Lecture2-Wall.pdf): finite domination and the construction of $w(X)$.
- **Primary:** [Ferry–Ranicki, A survey of Wall's finiteness obstruction (arXiv math/0008070)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/math/0008070): survey covering finiteness, end and splitting obstructions, Whitehead torsion and triangulation.
- **Further reading:** [Wall, Surgery on Compact Manifolds, ed. Ranicki (AMS Mathematical Surveys and Monographs 69, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/069): the standard monograph on surgery obstructions.
references.MSC 19Kxx - K-theory and operator algebr:
## Reference
### Overview
Operator $K$-theory is a noncommutative analogue of topological $K$-theory for Banach algebras (see [Banach Algebras](node:Banach%20Algebras)), used mainly for $C^*$-algebras. Its group $K_0(A)$ is the Grothendieck group of Murray–von Neumann equivalence classes of projections in matrix algebras over $A$, and $K_1$ and the higher groups come from suspension. ([Wikipedia: Operator K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory))

It matters because its invariants are computable and rigid: the Fredholm index enters the six-term exact sequence, Brown–Douglas–Fillmore used it to classify essentially normal operators, and Elliott's classification of AF $C^*$-algebras is by $K$-theory. ([Wikipedia: Operator K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory))

Bivariant theories (Kasparov's $KK$-theory, followed by similar bifunctors such as $E$-theory) extend the functor, and the Baum–Connes conjecture ties the $K$-theory of group $C^*$-algebras to topology. ([Wikipedia: KK-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KK-theory); [Wikipedia: Baum–Connes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 19K14 ($K_0$ as an ordered group, traces), 19K33 (Ext and $K$-homology), 19K35 (Kasparov theory, $KK$-theory) and 19K56 (index theory). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

The entry points mainly to 46L80 and also to 46M20; 19K35 cross-refers to 58J22 and 19K56 to 58J20 and 58J22. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **$K_0$ and $K_1$ of a $C^*$-algebra.** $K_0(A)$ is the Grothendieck group of Murray–von Neumann classes of projections; $K_n(A)=K_0(S^nA)$ for the $n$-fold suspension, and Bott periodicity (see [Bott Periodicity](node:Bott%20Periodicity)) forces $K_{n+2}\cong K_n$, so only $K_0$ and $K_1$ occur. See [Operator Algebra K-Theory](node:Operator%20Algebra%20K-Theory) and [C-Star Algebras and von Neumann Algebras](node:C-Star%20Algebras%20and%20von%20Neumann%20Algebras). ([Wikipedia: Operator K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory))
- **Six-term exact sequence.** For a closed two-sided ideal $J\subseteq A$, excision gives a cyclic exact sequence $K_0(J)\to K_0(A)\to K_0(A/J)\to K_1(J)\to K_1(A)\to K_1(A/J)\to K_0(J)$; the Fredholm index entered the classification of essentially normal operators. ([Wikipedia: Operator K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory)) The text of Rørdam–Larsen–Laustsen develops $K_0$, $K_1$, the index map, Bott periodicity and the six-term sequence in that order. ([Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-ktheory-for-calgebras/projections-and-unitary-elements/F93692DAB8A19EC94BEE58E158AC0C91))
- **Pimsner–Voiculescu sequence.** For a crossed product $A\rtimes_\alpha\mathbb Z$ there is a semisplit short exact sequence, the Pimsner–Voiculescu Toeplitz extension $0\to A\otimes\mathcal K\to T_\alpha\to A\rtimes_\alpha\mathbb Z\to0$, and applying $K$-theory gives the Pimsner–Voiculescu six-term cyclic sequence used to compute $K_*(A\rtimes_\alpha\mathbb Z)$. ([Hadfield](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0201093))
- **Kasparov $KK$-theory.** Introduced by Kasparov in 1980 as a common generalization of $K$-homology and $K$-theory: for separable $C^*$-algebras $A$ and $B$, $KK(A,B)$ is the set of homotopy classes of Kasparov cycles $(H,\rho,F)$; there is a bilinear Kasparov product $KK(A,B)\times KK(B,C)\to KK(A,C)$, $KK(\mathbb C,B)\cong K_0(B)$ and $KK(C_0(\mathbb R),B)\cong K_1(B)$. ([Wikipedia: KK-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KK-theory))
- **Index theory.** For an elliptic operator $D$ on a closed manifold $X$, analytic index equals topological index (Atiyah–Singer), and the topological index can be defined purely in $K$-theory; families of operators give an index in $K(Y)$. See [K-Theoretic Index Pairings](node:K-Theoretic%20Index%20Pairings) and [Elliptic Operators on Manifolds](node:Elliptic%20Operators%20on%20Manifolds). ([Wikipedia: Atiyah–Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Singer_index_theorem))
- **Baum–Connes conjecture.** The assembly map from the equivariant $K$-homology of the classifying space for proper actions to $K_*(C^*_r(G))$ is an isomorphism. It is proved for Haagerup groups, Gromov hyperbolic groups and discrete subgroups of $SO(n,1)$ and $SU(n,1)$. ([Wikipedia: Baum–Connes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture)) See [Group Cohomology](node:Group%20Cohomology).

### History
Brown, Douglas and Fillmore found that the Fredholm index was the missing ingredient in classifying essentially normal operators, and Elliott classified AF algebras by $K$-theory; Baum and Connes introduced their conjecture in 1982. ([Wikipedia: Operator K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory); [Wikipedia: Baum–Connes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Baum–Connes without coefficients.** The conjecture is open; $SL_3(\mathbb Z)$ is the simplest group for which it is unknown, and counterexamples with coefficients were found in 2002 by Higson, Lafforgue and Skandalis. ([Wikipedia: Baum–Connes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture))
- **The UCT problem.** A large class of simple nuclear $C^*$-algebras is classified, but only modulo the Universal Coefficient Theorem assumption; Brown, Browne, Willett and Wu argue it is unnecessary and propose a strategy to prove it. ([BBWW](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.03184))
- **Structure of nuclear $C^*$-algebras.** The 2025 problem collection of Schafhauser, Tikuisis and White gathers questions on structure and classification of nuclear $C^*$-algebras. ([Schafhauser–Tikuisis–White](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10902))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Operator K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_K-theory): definitions, periodicity, index.
- **Learn:** [Rørdam–Larsen–Laustsen, An Introduction to K-Theory for C*-Algebras](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-ktheory-for-calgebras/projections-and-unitary-elements/F93692DAB8A19EC94BEE58E158AC0C91): textbook; thirteen chapters from $K_0$ to dimension-drop algebras.
- **Primary:** [Lück–Reich, The Baum–Connes and the Farrell–Jones Conjectures in K- and L-Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0402405): survey of both conjectures, status and applications.
- **Further reading:** [Winter, Structure of nuclear C*-algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.00247): survey of structure and classification of separable simple nuclear $C^*$-algebras, quasidiagonality and the regularity conjecture; Rørdam–Larsen–Laustsen (CUP, 2000), linked above.
references.MSC 19Lxx - Topological K-theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Topological $K$-theory assigns to a compact Hausdorff space $X$ the Grothendieck group ([Grothendieck Groups](node:Grothendieck%20Groups)) $K(X)$ of finite-dimensional vector bundles; Atiyah and Hirzebruch applied Grothendieck's construction to vector bundles in 1959, and in topology $K$-theory is a cohomology theory. ([Wikipedia: K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory)) See [Topological K-Theory](node:Topological%20K-Theory) and [Hausdorff Space](node:Hausdorff%20Space).

Its tools are computational and structural: a Chern character relating the $K$-theory of a finite CW complex to its rational cohomology, the Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence from ordinary cohomology, and Adams operations playing the role of Steenrod operations (see [Steenrod Operations](node:Steenrod%20Operations)). ([Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory)) See [Characteristic Classes](node:Characteristic%20Classes) and [Spectral Sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences).

Its applications are classical: Adams used it to settle the Hopf invariant one problem and the number of vector fields on spheres, and the topological index in the Atiyah–Singer index theorem can be defined in $K$-theory. ([Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory); [Wikipedia: Atiyah–Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Singer_index_theorem))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 19L10 (Riemann–Roch theorems, Chern characters), 19L20 ($J$-homomorphism, Adams operations), 19L41 (connective $K$-theory, cobordism; see [Cobordism](node:Cobordism)), 19L47 (equivariant $K$-theory), 19L50 (twisted and differential $K$-theory) and 19L64 (geometric applications of topological $K$-theory). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

The entry cross-refers to 55N15, 55R50 and 55S25; 19L20 cross-refers to 55Q50, 19L41 to 55N22, and 19L47 to 55N91, 55P91, 55Q91, 55R91 and 55S91. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Negative degrees and the spectrum.** Reduced groups are $\widetilde K^{-n}(X)=\widetilde K(S^nX)$ for $n\ge0$ with $S^n$ the reduced suspension, and the representing space of $K$-theory is $BU\times\mathbb Z$ with $\mathbb Z$ discrete. ([Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory))
- **Serre–Swan theorem.** For compact Hausdorff $X$, the category of finite-rank complex vector bundles is equivalent, via sections, to the category of finitely generated projective $C(X)$-modules; hence the two Grothendieck groups agree, linking this note to algebraic $K_0$ and [Operator Algebra K-Theory](node:Operator%20Algebra%20K-Theory). ([Wikipedia: Serre–Swan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%E2%80%93Swan_theorem))
- **Bott periodicity.** $\Omega^2BU\simeq\mathbb Z\times BU$, so complex topological $K$-theory is 2-periodic; in the real case $\Omega^8BO\simeq\mathbb Z\times BO$, and $\pi_i(O)$ for $i=0,\dots,7$ is $\mathbb Z_2,\mathbb Z_2,0,\mathbb Z,0,0,0,\mathbb Z$. See [Bott Periodicity](node:Bott%20Periodicity). ([Wikipedia: Bott periodicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bott_periodicity_theorem))
- **Chern character and the AHSS.** For a finite CW complex the Chern character is a natural ring homomorphism $K^0(X)\to H^{2*}(X;\mathbb Q)$ that becomes an isomorphism after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$; the Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence computes $K$-groups from ordinary cohomology. ([Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory))
- **Adams' vector fields theorem.** The maximal number of pointwise linearly independent vector fields on $S^{n-1}$ is $\rho(n)-1$, where for $n=(2a+1)2^{4d+c}$ with $0\le c<4$, $\rho(n)=2^c+8d$; Adams proved the upper bound with homotopy theory and $K$-theory, the lower bound coming from Clifford-algebra constructions. See [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere) and [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras). ([Wikipedia: Vector fields on spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_fields_on_spheres))
- **Hopf invariant one.** Adams' theorem on the Hopf invariant, with its consequences for division algebras and parallelizable spheres, is proved in Chapter 2 of Hatcher's text, after complex Bott periodicity. ([Hatcher, VBKT](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VBpage.html))
- **Atiyah–Singer index theorem.** For an elliptic differential operator $D:E\to F$ on a compact smooth manifold without boundary, the analytic index $\dim\ker D-\dim\operatorname{coker}D$ equals the topological index, which can be defined in $K$-theory by embedding $X$ in $\mathbb R^n$ and pushing forward $K(TX)\to K(T\mathbb R^n)\cong\mathbb Z$, the last isomorphism by Bott periodicity; families of operators parametrized by a space $Y$ give an index in $K(Y)$ and group actions give equivariant $K$-theory. See [Elliptic Operators on Manifolds](node:Elliptic%20Operators%20on%20Manifolds). ([Wikipedia: Atiyah–Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Singer_index_theorem))
- **Twisted $K$-theory.** Twistings of a space $X$ correspond to $H^3(X;\mathbb Z)$, and to $H^3_G(X;\mathbb Z)$ for compact Lie group actions; the Freed–Hopkins–Teleman theorem relates loop group representations to twisted equivariant $K$-theory. See [Equivariant Topology](node:Equivariant%20Topology). ([Atiyah–Segal](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0407054); [Freed](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0206237))

### History
Grothendieck's work on Riemann–Roch gave the construction its start; Atiyah and Hirzebruch applied it to vector bundles in 1959, and $K$-theory played a major role in the second proof of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem. ([Wikipedia: K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory)) Adams' vector-fields result is dated 1962. ([Wikipedia: Vector fields on spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_fields_on_spheres))

### Open problems
- **Positive scalar curvature and the Gromov–Lawson–Rosenberg conjecture.** For closed spin manifolds, vanishing of the $KO$-valued index $\alpha$ obstructs positive scalar curvature; Stolz proved it is sufficient when $\pi_1=1$ and $n\ge5$, but the conjecture for general $\pi$ fails in some cases and there is no general characterization of the relevant subgroup; the "optimist's conjecture" that closed manifolds of dimension $\ge5$ with finite $\pi_1$ and non-spin universal cover admit such metrics is open. ([Stolz survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2202.05904))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory): variants, Chern character, Adams operations.
- **Learn:** [Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VBpage.html): free textbook; complex Bott periodicity and Adams' Hopf invariant theorem.
- **Primary:** [Atiyah–Segal, Twisted K-theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0407054): systematic treatment, including the equivariant version.
- **Further reading:** [Stolz, Positive scalar curvature](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2202.05904): survey where $KO$-theory obstructions arise; Hatcher's book (linked above).
references.MSC 19Mxx - Miscellaneous applications o:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 19Mxx is a residual code inside [MSC 19 - K-theory](node:MSC%2019%20-%20K-theory): it consists only of 19M05 "Miscellaneous applications of $K$-theory" and the catch-all 19M99. The K-theoretic subfields on which most applications rest have their own codes, for example topological K-theory (19Lxx) and K-theory and operator algebras (19Kxx). ([MSC2020 19Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Mxx); [MSC2020 19Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Lxx); [MSC2020 19Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Kxx))

Three well-developed applications are the gap-labelling theorem for aperiodic Schrödinger operators, the K-theoretic classification of D-brane charges in string theory, and the periodic table of topological insulators. Papers on them are often classified elsewhere: Kaminker and Putnam's proof of gap labelling carries the codes 46L87 and 52C23, with 19K14 and 82D25 as secondary codes. ([MSC2020 19Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Kxx); [Kaminker–Putnam](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0205102); [Witten](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9810188); [Kitaev](https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.2686))

### Scope
- **19M05:** miscellaneous applications of K-theory; **19M99:** none of the above. ([MSC2020 19Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Mxx))
- **Neighbour 19L ([MSC 19Lxx - Topological K-theory](node:MSC%2019Lxx%20-%20Topological%20K-theory)):** Riemann–Roch and Chern characters (19L10), Adams operations (19L20), connective K-theory (19L41), equivariant K-theory (19L47), twisted and differential K-theory (19L50) and geometric applications of topological K-theory (19L64). Twisted K-theory, which enters the D-brane and loop-group applications below, and equivariant K-theory thus have their own codes. ([MSC2020 19Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Lxx))
- **Neighbour 19K ([MSC 19Kxx - K-theory and operator algebras](node:MSC%2019Kxx%20-%20K-theory%20and%20operator%20algebras)):** $K_0$ as an ordered group and traces (19K14), K-homology (19K33), KK-theory (19K35) and index theory (19K56), with 46L80 as the main code. Gap labelling is a statement about traces on $K_0$, and Kaminker–Putnam list 19K14 as a secondary code. ([MSC2020 19Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=19Kxx); [Kaminker–Putnam](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0205102))

### Key concepts
- **Gap-labelling theorem.** Let $\Sigma$ be a Cantor set with a free minimal action of $\mathbb Z^n$ and an invariant probability measure $\mu$, and let $\tau$ be the induced traces on $C(\Sigma)$ and on $C(\Sigma)\rtimes\mathbb Z^n$. Then $\tau(K_0(C(\Sigma)))=\tau(K_0(C(\Sigma)\rtimes\mathbb Z^n))$, where the left side is the subgroup of $\mathbb R$ generated by the measures of clopen subsets of $\Sigma$. Bellissard formulated this as a statement about the possible gaps in the spectrum of Schrödinger operators in solid-state physics; Kaminker–Putnam proved it with the Moore–Schochet version of Connes' index theorem for foliated spaces, and Benameur–Oyono-Oyono independently with the measured index theorem for laminations and the longitudinal Chern character; Bellissard–Benedetti–Gambaudo proved a gap-labelling theorem for a large class of tilings by a different, branched-manifold route (next item). ([Kaminker–Putnam](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0205102); [Benameur–Oyono-Oyono](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0112113); [Bellissard–Benedetti–Gambaudo](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0109062)) See [Schrödinger Equation](node:Schrödinger%20Equation) and [Band Theory of Solids](node:Band%20Theory%20of%20Solids).
- **Tiling spaces.** For a large class of tilings, including the Penrose tiling and the $3$-dimensional icosahedral tilings, the continuous hull is a projective limit of branched, oriented, flat compact manifolds with a Cantor transversal; invariant measures form a cone inside the limit of their top homology, and this yields a gap-labelling theorem. ([Bellissard–Benedetti–Gambaudo](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0109062))
- **D-brane charge.** Witten argued, using stable non-supersymmetric D-brane states, that D-brane charge is classified by the K-theory of spacetime; Minasian and Moore had proposed the idea in 1997. In type IIB, configurations are built from D9 and anti-D9 branes by tachyon condensation, and K-theory detects torsion charges that BPS classifications miss. ([Witten](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9810188); [K-theory (physics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory_%28physics%29)) See [D-Branes](node:D-Branes) and [String Theory](node:String%20Theory).
- **Twisted K-theory and H-flux.** In a nontrivial Neveu–Schwarz 3-form background, Bouwknegt and Varghese Mathai proposed that D-branes are classified by twisted K-theory (19L50). Olsen and Szabo review how K-theory reproduces BPS and non-BPS spectra and how dualities act as isomorphisms of K-groups; Rosenberg's lectures treat twisted K-theory through continuous-trace algebras and crossed products. ([K-theory (physics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory_%28physics%29); [Olsen–Szabo](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9907140); [Rosenberg](https://math.umd.edu/~jmr/OberwolfachS05.pdf))
- **Freed–Hopkins–Teleman theorem.** For a compact connected [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) $G$ with torsion-free $\pi_1$, a Dirac family of Fredholm operators gives an isomorphism from the group of positive-energy representations of the loop group at a given level (the Verlinde ring) to the twisted equivariant K-theory of $G$; part III extends this to all compact Lie groups. ([Freed–Hopkins–Teleman II](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511232))
- **Periodic table of topological phases.** Kitaev classified gapped phases of noninteracting fermions, with or without charge conservation and time-reversal symmetry, by Bott periodicity: each symmetry class and dimension gives an invariant in $0$, $\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb Z_2$, the classes matching $2$ complex and $8$ real [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras); an interface between phases with different invariants carries gapless modes, and the classification survives disorder as long as states near the Fermi energy are absent or localized. ([Kitaev](https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.2686)) See [Topological Phases of Matter](node:Topological%20Phases%20of%20Matter).

### History
Witten's "D-Branes and K-Theory" was submitted on 23 October 1998, and Olsen and Szabo's review "Constructing D-Branes from K-Theory" on 16 July 1999. ([Witten](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9810188); [Olsen–Szabo](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9907140)) The three gap-labelling papers appeared on arXiv in 2001–2002. ([Bellissard–Benedetti–Gambaudo](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0109062); [Benameur–Oyono-Oyono](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0112113); [Kaminker–Putnam](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0205102)) Kitaev's periodic table was posted in January 2009 and Freed–Hopkins–Teleman's second loop-group paper in November 2005. ([Kitaev](https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.2686); [Freed–Hopkins–Teleman II](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511232))

### Open problems
- **Magnetic gap labelling.** For a constant magnetic field on $\mathbb R^p$ and the twisted crossed product $C(\Sigma)\rtimes_\sigma\mathbb Z^p$, Benameur and Mathai conjecture that the magnetic gap-labelling group is a subgroup of an explicit magnetic frequency group built from Pfaffians; they give evidence in dimensions $2$ and $3$ and in the periodic and block-diagonal cases. ([Benameur–Mathai](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.01064))
- **Beyond twisted K-theory in string theory.** The K-theory classification of D-brane charges and Ramond–Ramond fluxes is a conjecture: Diaconescu, Moore and Witten argued that twisted K-theory is incompatible with S-duality in type IIB, RR fluxes are not fully classified by K-theory, and elliptic cohomology has been proposed as a replacement. ([K-theory (physics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory_%28physics%29))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [K-theory (physics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-theory_%28physics%29): survey of D-brane, flux and condensed-matter applications and their open issues.
- **Learn:** [Rosenberg, Oberwolfach lectures on topological K-theory of noncommutative algebras (2005)](https://math.umd.edu/~jmr/OberwolfachS05.pdf): bivariant K-theory, continuous-trace algebras and twisted K-theory, crossed products, and applications to physics.
- **Primary:** [Kaminker and Putnam, A proof of the Gap Labeling Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0205102): precise statement and proof via the index theorem for foliated spaces; [Witten, D-Branes and K-Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9810188): the original charge argument.
- **Further reading:** [Freed, Hopkins and Teleman, Loop Groups and Twisted K-Theory II](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511232): twisted equivariant K-theory and the Verlinde ring; [Kitaev, Periodic table for topological insulators and superconductors](https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.2686).
references.MSC 20 - Group theory and generalization:
## Reference
### Overview
[Group theory](node:Group%20Theory) studies groups, the algebraic formalization of symmetry. Its research branches include finite group theory, culminating in the classification of finite simple groups; the [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of groups; Lie theory, the best-developed theory of continuous symmetry; and combinatorial and geometric group theory, which study groups through generators and relations and through Cayley graphs and actions on [metric spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces). ([Group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory))

MSC 20 covers abstract groups and several generalizations: semigroups, groupoids, loops, quasigroups and $n$-ary systems. Lie groups and topological groups as such are classified separately in [MSC 22](node:MSC%2022%20-%20Topological%20groups,%20Lie%20groups), and the arithmetic and geometric theory of linear algebraic groups is cross-referenced to 11E57, 14Lxx and 22Exx from 20G. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Scope
The MSC2020 subfields of 20 are: ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))
- [20A](node:MSC%2020Axx%20-%20Foundations) foundations; [20B](node:MSC%2020Bxx%20-%20Permutation%20groups) permutation groups (primitive and multiply transitive groups, symmetric groups, automorphism groups of structures).
- [20C](node:MSC%2020Cxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20groups) representation theory of groups (ordinary and modular characters, group rings, Hecke algebras, representations of symmetric, Lie-type and sporadic groups).
- [20D](node:MSC%2020Dxx%20-%20Abstract%20finite%20groups) abstract finite groups (finite simple groups and their classification, solvable and nilpotent finite groups, Sylow theory, subgroup structure).
- [20E](node:MSC%2020Exx%20-%20Structure%20and%20classification%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups) structure of infinite or finite groups (free groups and free products, groups acting on trees, profinite groups, residual properties, BN-pairs and buildings).
- [20F](node:MSC%2020Fxx%20-%20Special%20aspects%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups) special aspects (presentations, word problems, solvable and nilpotent groups, Burnside problems, braid, Artin and Coxeter groups, geometric group theory).
- [20G](node:MSC%2020Gxx%20-%20Linear%20algebraic%20groups%20and%20related%20topics) linear algebraic groups over fields, local and global fields and finite fields, quantum groups, Kac–Moody groups; [20H](node:MSC%2020Hxx%20-%20Other%20groups%20of%20matrices) other matrix groups (congruence subgroups, Fuchsian and crystallographic groups).
- [20J](node:MSC%2020Jxx%20-%20Connections%20of%20group%20theory%20with%20homological%20algebra%20and%20category%20theory) homological methods and group cohomology; [20K](node:MSC%2020Kxx%20-%20Abelian%20groups) abelian groups.
- [20L](node:MSC%2020Lxx%20-%20Groupoids%20%28i.e.%20small%20categories%20in%20which%20all%20morphisms%20are%20isomorphisms%29) groupoids as categories; [20M](node:MSC%2020Mxx%20-%20Semigroups) semigroups; [20N](node:MSC%2020Nxx%20-%20Other%20generalizations%20of%20groups) magmas, loops, quasigroups, hypergroups; [20P](node:MSC%2020Pxx%20-%20Probabilistic%20methods%20in%20group%20theory) probabilistic methods.

### Key concepts
- **Classification of finite simple groups.** Every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating of degree at least 5, a group of Lie type in one of 16 infinite families, or one of 26 sporadic groups (27 if the Tits group is counted as sporadic). The proof occupies tens of thousands of pages by about 100 authors, mostly published 1955–2004; Gorenstein announced completion in 1983 prematurely, and the quasithin case was closed by Aschbacher and Smith's 1,221-page work, with completion announced in 2004. The Feit–Thompson theorem (1963), that every group of odd order is solvable, was an early step. ([Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups))
- **Groups of Lie type.** These are finite groups closely related to the rational points of a reductive linear algebraic group over a finite field. Chevalley's 1955 construction, via a Chevalley basis of a complex simple Lie algebra, produced the untwisted families; Steinberg's twisted groups ($^2A_n$, $^2D_n$, $^2E_6$, $^3D_4$), Suzuki's series, and Ree's families $^2F_4$ and $^2G_2$ (using extra automorphisms in characteristics 2 and 3) complete the list. They account for all finite simple groups other than cyclic, alternating and sporadic ones. ([Group of Lie type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Lie_type))
- **Algorithmic problems.** There is a finitely presented group with unsolvable word problem (Novikov 1955; Boone 1958), and by Boone–Rogers (1966) there is no uniform algorithm solving the word problem for all finitely presented groups whose word problem is solvable. ([Word problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups)) Golod and Shafarevich (1964) gave an infinite finitely generated periodic group, and Novikov and Adian (1968) found infinite finitely generated groups of every odd exponent $n>4381$, a bound Adian later lowered to odd exponents above 665, while Zelmanov solved the restricted Burnside problem. ([Burnside problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_problem))
- **Geometric group theory.** A finitely generated group has polynomial growth if and only if it is virtually nilpotent (Gromov, 1981). ([Gromov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gromov%27s_theorem_on_groups_of_polynomial_growth)) A finitely generated group is hyperbolic if its Cayley graph is a hyperbolic metric space; hyperbolic groups are finitely presented, contain no $\mathbb Z^2$, and have word problem solvable by Dehn's algorithm. ([Bowditch](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/courses/8800/bbowditch-ggtcourse.pdf)) By the Tits alternative, a finitely generated subgroup of a Lie group with finitely many components is virtually solvable or contains a nonabelian free subgroup. ([Druţu–Kapovich](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~kapovich/EPR/ggt.pdf))
- **Profinite groups.** A profinite group is an inverse limit of finite groups, equivalently a compact Hausdorff totally disconnected group; examples are $\mathbb Z_p$, the profinite completion $\hat{\mathbb Z}$, and Galois groups of infinite Galois extensions with the Krull topology, linking group theory to [Galois theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory). In a topologically finitely generated profinite group every subgroup of finite index is open (Nikolov–Segal), a theorem whose proof uses the classification of finite simple groups. ([Profinite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profinite_group))
- **Representations.** A representation of $G$ on a vector space $V$ is a homomorphism $G\to GL(V)$, turning group elements into invertible linear maps so that abstract group operations become matrix multiplication; [Lie groups](node:Lie%20Groups), groups with a compatible smooth manifold structure, are the best-developed theory of continuous symmetry and a natural framework for the continuous symmetries of differential equations. ([Group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory))

### History
Galois coined the term "group" and connected groups with the solvability of polynomial equations; Cayley showed that every group is a permutation group acting on itself; Klein's Erlangen program made group theory the organizing principle of geometry; and in the 20th century Chevalley and Steinberg advanced the understanding of finite analogues of classical groups, while the complete classification of finite simple groups was achieved. ([Group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory)) Dehn's 1911 formulation of the word, conjugacy and isomorphism problems founded combinatorial group theory. ([Word problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups)) Since 1965 the Kourovka Notebook has collected open problems in group theory, reissued every two to four years. ([Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300))

### Open problems
- **The Kourovka Notebook.** The 21st edition collects open problems in all areas of group theory proposed by mathematicians worldwide, adding 150 new problems; problems with AI-proposed but unconfirmed solutions are flagged and are to be treated as unsolved. ([Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300))
- **Burnside group $B(2,5)$.** Whether the free Burnside group of rank 2 and exponent 5 is finite is open. ([Burnside problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_problem))
- **Hyperbolic groups.** Whether every hyperbolic group is virtually torsion-free is open, as is Cannon's question whether a hyperbolic group with 2-sphere boundary is virtually a hyperbolic 3-manifold group. ([Bowditch](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/courses/8800/bbowditch-ggtcourse.pdf))
- **Second-generation classification.** Gorenstein, Lyons and Solomon's revised proof of the classification is still being published; ten volumes had appeared by 2023, with more in preparation. ([Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory): branches, history and connections.
- **Learn:** [Bowditch, A course on geometric group theory](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/courses/8800/bbowditch-ggtcourse.pdf): presentations, quasi-isometries and hyperbolic groups.
- **Primary:** [Druţu and Kapovich, Geometric Group Theory](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~kapovich/EPR/ggt.pdf): monograph with proofs of Gromov's theorem and the Tits alternative; [Khukhro and Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300): the standard open-problem list.
- **Further reading:** [Robinson, A Course in the Theory of Groups](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-8594-1) (Springer GTM, 1996); [Lyndon and Schupp, Combinatorial Group Theory](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61896-3) (Springer Classics in Mathematics, 2001); [Bridson and Haefliger, Metric Spaces of Non-Positive Curvature](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-12494-9) (Springer Grundlehren, 1999).
references.MSC 20Axx - Foundations:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 20Axx is the foundations part of [MSC 20 - Group theory and generalizations](node:MSC%2020%20-%20Group%20theory%20and%20generalizations). It has three substantive codes: 20A05 axiomatics and elementary properties of groups, 20A10 metamathematical considerations in group theory, and 20A15 applications of logic to group theory. Topics under these headings include alternative axiom systems for groups, decidability of first-order theories of groups, elementary equivalence of groups, and the use of [model theory](node:Model%20Theory) to study groups. ([MSC2020 20Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Axx); [Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29); [Decidability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decidability_%28logic%29); [Tarski's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarski%27s_free_group_problem))

The basic object is a group in the sense of [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory): a set with an associative operation, an identity and inverses. Cayley's 1854 paper on the symbolic equation $\theta^n=1$ gave the first abstract definition of a finite group. ([Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29)) The foundational questions become research questions once the language is fixed: which axioms suffice, which first-order sentences hold in which groups, and which of these questions an algorithm can decide. ([Decidability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decidability_%28logic%29); [Tarski's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarski%27s_free_group_problem))

### Scope
- **20A05** "Axiomatics and elementary properties of groups". ([MSC2020 20Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Axx))
- **20A10** "Metamathematical considerations in group theory"; the entry sends word problems to 20F10. ([MSC2020 20Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Axx))
- **20A15** "Applications of logic to group theory". ([MSC2020 20Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Axx))

Neighbours: [MSC 20Fxx - Special aspects of infinite or finite groups](node:MSC%2020Fxx%20-%20Special%20aspects%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups) contains 20F05 (presentations), 20F10 (word problems, other decision problems, connections with logic and automata, group-theoretic aspects), 20F11 (groups of finite Morley rank, see also 03C45 and 03C60) and 20F65/20F67 (geometric group theory; hyperbolic and nonpositively curved groups). The model-theoretic cross-references point to [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory). ([MSC2020 20Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **One-sided axioms (20A05).** Assuming associativity, the existence of a left identity $e$ ($ea=a$ for all $a$) and of left inverses ($a'a=e$) already defines exactly the groups; requiring only a left identity and right inverses does not, as a two-element counterexample shows. ([Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29)) Course notes take the left-sided axioms as the definition and derive $aa'=e$, $ae=a$ and uniqueness of identity and inverses as exercises. ([Bristol notes, §1](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~majm/bib/talks/grouptheory.pdf))
- **Undecidability of group theory (20A10).** The [first-order](node:First-Order%20Logic) theory of groups is undecidable (Tarski, 1953), and so is the theory of finite groups (Mal'cev, 1961); by contrast the first-order theory of abelian groups is decidable (Szmielew, 1955). ([Decidability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decidability_%28logic%29))
- **Word problems (pointer to 20F10).** Novikov showed in 1955 that there is a finitely presented group $G$ whose word problem is undecidable; Boone gave a different proof in 1958. ([Word problem for groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups))
- **Tarski's problem on free groups (20A15).** Around 1945 Tarski asked whether all nonabelian free groups have the same first-order theory and whether that theory is decidable. Sela proved elementary equivalence (published 2006), and Kharlampovich and Myasnikov proved both elementary equivalence and decidability (2006). ([Tarski's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarski%27s_free_group_problem)) Sela's method studies solution sets of equations over a free group and classifies the finitely generated groups elementarily equivalent to a free group, with a generalization to hyperbolic groups. ([Sela, ICM 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0304209))
- **Groups of finite Morley rank.** A group has finite Morley rank if the formula $x=x$ has finite Morley rank; such groups are $\omega$-stable. Finite groups have rank $0$, and algebraic groups over algebraically closed fields have Morley rank equal to their dimension. Sela showed that free groups, and more generally torsion-free hyperbolic groups, are stable; free groups of rank at least $2$ are not superstable. ([Finite Morley rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_finite_Morley_rank))
- **Bad groups.** Frécon proved that bad groups in Cherlin's sense do not exist; equivalently, every simple group of Morley rank $3$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{PSL}_2(K)$ for an algebraically closed field $K$. ([Frécon](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.02994))

### History
Cayley's 1854 paper gave the first abstract definition of a finite group. ([Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29)) Tarski's undecidability result for the theory of groups dates from 1953, Szmielew's decidability of abelian groups from 1955, and Mal'cev's undecidability of finite groups from 1961. ([Decidability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decidability_%28logic%29)) Tarski's free-group questions (c. 1945) were answered in 2006. ([Tarski's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarski%27s_free_group_problem)) Zilber (1977) and Cherlin (1979) proposed the algebraicity conjecture for groups of finite Morley rank. ([Finite Morley rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_finite_Morley_rank))

### Open problems
- **Cherlin–Zilber algebraicity conjecture.** Infinite simple groups of finite Morley rank are conjectured to be simple algebraic groups over algebraically closed fields; Cherlin posed the question for all $\omega$-stable simple groups but remarked that even the finite Morley rank case seemed hard. Special cases are proved: Altınel, Borovik and Cherlin (2008) showed that such a simple group is either algebraic over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $2$ or has finite $2$-rank, and Frécon settled Morley rank $3$. ([Finite Morley rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_finite_Morley_rank); [Frécon](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.02994)) Tent's 2026 review surveys the current state of the conjecture and explains why sharply $2$-transitive groups are a possible source of counterexamples. ([Tent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18207))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Group (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_%28mathematics%29): axioms, the one-sided weakening and history.
- **Learn:** [Bristol MATH33300 Group Theory course notes](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~majm/bib/talks/grouptheory.pdf): group axioms in left-sided form through Sylow theory, solubility and Jordan–Hölder.
- **Primary:** [Sela, Diophantine geometry over groups and the elementary theory of free and hyperbolic groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0304209): ICM survey of the solution of Tarski's problems.
- **Further reading:** [Tent, From the Cherlin–Zilber Conjecture via sharply 2-transitive groups to the Burnside problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18207): 2026 review of the algebraicity conjecture; [Frécon, Bad groups in the sense of Cherlin](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.02994).
references.MSC 20Bxx - Permutation groups:
## Reference
### Overview
A permutation group is a subgroup of a symmetric group $\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)$; by Cayley's theorem every group is isomorphic to one, via the regular action of the group on itself by left multiplication. What distinguishes 20Bxx from abstract group theory is that the action is part of the data: transitivity (a single orbit) and primitivity (a transitive action preserving no nontrivial partition of $\Omega$) are properties of an action, not of the abstract group. ([Wikipedia: Permutation group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_group))

The modern finite theory is organized by two structural results. The O'Nan–Scott theorem sorts finite primitive groups into a short list of types, and the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) is what makes it useful; analysing the almost simple type requires knowledge of the maximal subgroups of almost simple groups. Classical problems such as the determination of all 2-transitive groups and Sims' conjecture on point stabilizers were settled this way. ([Wikipedia: O'Nan–Scott theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Nan%E2%80%93Scott_theorem); [Wildon, §7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.07502); [Wikipedia: Sims conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sims_conjecture))

On infinite sets the central class is the oligomorphic groups, those with finitely many orbits on $\Omega^n$ for every $n$. Through Fraïssé limits, their orbit-counting sequences are exactly the numbers of labelled and unlabelled finite structures in an amalgamation class, which ties 20Bxx to enumerative combinatorics and model theory. ([Cameron, CSG notes §§1–3](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/ipgn.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 20Bxx has the codes 20B05 (general theory for finite permutation groups), 20B07 (general theory for infinite permutation groups), 20B10 (characterization theorems), 20B15 (primitive groups), 20B20 and 20B22 (multiply transitive finite and infinite groups), 20B25 (finite automorphism groups of algebraic, geometric or combinatorial structures), 20B27 (infinite automorphism groups), 20B30 (symmetric groups), 20B35 (subgroups of symmetric groups) and 20B99. Code 20B25 carries cross-references to 05Bxx, 12F10, 20G40, 20H30 and 51-XX. ([MSC2020 20Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Bxx))

Related codes:
- **[MSC 05Bxx - Designs and configurations](node:MSC%2005Bxx%20-%20Designs%20and%20configurations), [MSC 05Cxx - Graph theory](node:MSC%2005Cxx%20-%20Graph%20theory) and other structures:** 20B25 (finite automorphism groups of algebraic, geometric or combinatorial structures) lists 05Bxx, 12F10, 20G40, 20H30 and 51-XX as related codes, and 20B27 (infinite automorphism groups) lists 12F10. ([MSC2020 20Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Bxx))
- **[MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory):** oligomorphic groups arise as automorphism groups of homogeneous structures, and recent classifications of slow orbit growth are stated in terms of first-order interpretability in $(\mathbb Q;<)$ and reducts. ([Bodor 2025, §1](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.16985))

### Key concepts
- **[Orbits, stabilizers and Schreier generators](node:Permutation%20Groups).** For $G\le\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ and $\alpha\in X$, the left cosets of $G_\alpha$ correspond bijectively to the orbit of $\alpha$. If $G=\langle Y\rangle$ and $T$ is a transversal of $G_\alpha$ with $\varphi(g)\alpha=g\alpha$, then $G_\alpha=\langle \varphi(yt)^{-1}yt : y\in Y,\ t\in T\rangle$ (a case of Schreier's theorem). Iterating along a chain of point stabilizers computes $|G|$. ([Cambridge CATAM project 16.5, §§4–5](https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/undergrad/catam/II/16pt5.pdf))
- **Bases and the Schreier–Sims algorithm.** A base is a sequence $(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_k)$ of points whose pointwise stabilizer in $G$ is trivial; $S_n$ has base size $n-1$. Sims' 1970 algorithm computes a base and strong generating set, from which the order and membership can be computed in polynomial time. Its deterministic version runs in $O(n^2\log^3|G|+tn\log|G|)$ for $t$ generators of degree $n$, and GAP and Magma typically use an optimized Monte Carlo variant. ([Wikipedia: Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_%28group_theory%29); [Wikipedia: Schreier–Sims algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schreier%E2%80%93Sims_algorithm))
- **O'Nan–Scott theorem.** A maximal subgroup of $S_n$ is intransitive ($S_k\times S_{n-k}$), imprimitive ($S_a\wr S_b$ with $n=ab$), or primitive of affine, product-action, diagonal or almost simple type. Finite primitive groups fall into eight types: HA, HS, HC, TW, AS, SD, CD and PA. An almost simple (AS) group $G$ satisfies $T\le G\le\operatorname{Aut}(T)$ for a nonabelian simple $T$. Praeger extended the theorem to quasiprimitive groups (1993). ([Wikipedia: O'Nan–Scott theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Nan%E2%80%93Scott_theorem))
- **2-transitive groups.** Every 2-transitive group is primitive. A finite 2-transitive group has a socle that is either a vector space over a finite field (the affine case) or a nonabelian simple group, in which case the group is almost simple. Huppert classified the solvable finite 2-transitive groups; CFSG made the complete classification possible, and the affine case is given by Hering's list of transitive finite linear groups. The classification of 2-transitive groups was one of the first applications of CFSG. ([Wikipedia: 2-transitive group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2-transitive_group); [Wikipedia: List of transitive finite linear groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_transitive_finite_linear_groups); [Wildon, §7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.07502))
- **Sims' conjecture (theorem, 1983).** There is a function $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ such that if $G$ is primitive and $h>1$ is the length of a nontrivial orbit of a point stabilizer $H$, then $|H|\le f(h)$. Cameron, Praeger, Saxl and Seitz proved it using CFSG; a consequence is that there are only finitely many connected distance-transitive graphs of each valency greater than 2. ([Wikipedia: Sims conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sims_conjecture))
- **Base size of primitive groups (Pyber's conjecture, proved).** There is a universal constant $c>0$ such that every primitive group $G$ of degree $n$ has minimal base size $b(G)$ with $\log|G|/\log n\le b(G)<45\log|G|/\log n+c$ (Duyan, Halasi and Maróti). ([Duyan–Halasi–Maróti](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.09487))
- **Oligomorphic groups and growth.** For $G$ on an infinite set, let $f_n(G)$ be the number of orbits on $n$-subsets. Macpherson proved, and Merola refined, that there is an absolute $c>1$ such that every primitive oligomorphic group that is not highly set-transitive has $f_n(G)\ge c^n/p(n)$ for some polynomial $p$. The random graph gives $f_n$ equal to the number of unlabelled $n$-vertex graphs. ([Cameron, CSG notes §§3, 7](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/ipgn.pdf))

### History
Lagrange studied permutations in 1770 in connection with the solution of polynomial equations, and Jordan codified the subject in his *Traité des substitutions et des équations algébriques* (1870), building on Galois's papers. ([Wikipedia: Permutation group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_group))

Scott stated the O'Nan–Scott theorem in an appendix to a 1979 Santa Cruz conference paper, noting O'Nan's independent proof. Aschbacher and Scott corrected it in 1985, Cameron (1981) recognized its value as a classification of primitive groups into types, and Liebeck, Praeger and Saxl (1988) gave a complete self-contained version. ([Wikipedia: O'Nan–Scott theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Nan%E2%80%93Scott_theorem); [Crossref: Liebeck–Praeger–Saxl 1988](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/S144678870003216X))

Sims's conjecture goes back to his 1967 paper *Graphs and finite permutation groups*; Cameron, Praeger, Saxl and Seitz proved it in 1983, and Pyber and Tracey (2021) later simplified the proof. ([Wikipedia: Sims conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sims_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Refined Sims conjecture.** Spiga proposes a refinement of Sims' conjecture concerning the cardinality of point stabilizers in finite primitive groups and makes partial progress towards it. ([Spiga 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.13614))
- **Growth of orbit counts.** Cameron's Problem 1 asks for a characterization of the sequences $(F_n(G))$, $(F^*_n(G))$, $(f_n(G))$ realized by oligomorphic groups. His Problem 3 asks whether $\lim_n f_n(G)^{1/n}$ exists for every primitive oligomorphic $G$, what values it takes, and what the smallest value above 1 is. ([Cameron, CSG notes, Problems 1 and 3](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/ipgn.pdf)) Some of the conjectures in this area are now proved: Falque and Thiéry classified closed P-oligomorphic groups, confirming Cameron's conjecture that a polynomially bounded profile is asymptotically polynomial and answering Macpherson's question on finite generation of the orbit algebra. ([Falque–Thiéry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.05296))
- **Thomas' conjecture and infinite-domain CSPs.** Thomas conjectured that every countable homogeneous structure in a finite relational language has finitely many reducts. Bodor lists the specific structures for which it has been verified (among them $(\mathbb Q;<)$, the random graph and the homogeneous $K_n$-free graphs), and he proves it for the class of structures whose unlabelled orbit growth $u_n$ satisfies $u_n\ge 2^n/p(n)$ for no polynomial $p$. The same paper restates the open conjecture that $\mathrm{CSP}(\mathfrak B)$ is in P or NP-complete for every reduct $\mathfrak B$ of a finitely bounded homogeneous structure. ([Bodor 2025, §1](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.16985))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: O'Nan–Scott theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Nan%E2%80%93Scott_theorem): the eight types of finite primitive group and the theorem's history.
- **Learn:** [Cameron, Counting problems from infinite permutation groups (CSG notes, QMUL)](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/ipgn.pdf): oligomorphic groups, orbit counting, Fraïssé classes and open problems.
- **Learn:** [Cambridge CATAM project 16.5](https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/undergrad/catam/II/16pt5.pdf): Sims' stripping algorithm, orbits with witnesses and Schreier generators, as a programming project.
- **Primary:** [Liebeck–Praeger–Saxl, On the O'Nan–Scott theorem for finite primitive permutation groups (1988)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/S144678870003216X): the self-contained version of the theorem.
- **Primary:** [Duyan–Halasi–Maróti, A proof of Pyber's base size conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.09487): the sharp base-size bound for primitive groups.
- **Further reading:** [Dixon–Mortimer, Permutation Groups (Springer GTM, 1996)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0731-3): the standard graduate text, including the O'Nan–Scott theorem.
- **In this vault:** [Permutation Groups](node:Permutation%20Groups), [Finite Simple Groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups), [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics), [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), [Random Permutations](node:Random%20Permutations), [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory), [MSC 20Dxx - Abstract finite groups](node:MSC%2020Dxx%20-%20Abstract%20finite%20groups), [MSC 20Cxx - Representation theory of groups](node:MSC%2020Cxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20groups), [MSC 20 - Group theory and generalizations](node:MSC%2020%20-%20Group%20theory%20and%20generalizations).
references.MSC 20Cxx - Representation theory of gro:
## Reference
### Overview
Group representation theory studies groups through homomorphisms $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$. In MSC2020, 20Cxx covers the representations of finite groups (ordinary, modular, integral and $p$-adic), group rings of finite and infinite groups, Hecke algebras, projective representations, and the representation theory of the symmetric groups, finite groups of Lie type and sporadic groups. ([MSC2020 20Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Cxx); [Wikipedia: Representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory))

The coefficient field determines the theory. If $\operatorname{char}k\nmid|G|$, Maschke's theorem makes $k[G]$ semisimple and characters determine everything. If $\operatorname{char}k=p$ divides $|G|$, modules need not be semisimple, and Brauer's block theory organizes them through $p$-subgroups and their normalizers. ([Etingof et al., Thm. 4.1.1](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf); [Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory))

The central research programme of the area is the family of local-global conjectures. These relate the representation theory of $G$ (counts of characters or Brauer characters in a block, or derived categories of blocks) to that of its $p$-local subgroups. Two of them have now been proved in work posted 2022–2024: McKay's conjecture, by completing the Isaacs–Malle–Navarro reduction to finite simple groups using the classification, and Brauer's height zero conjecture. ([Malle survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145); [Cabanes–Späth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20392); [Malle–Navarro–Schaeffer Fry–Tiep](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04736))

### Scope
MSC2020 20Cxx lists 20C05 (group rings of finite groups and their modules), 20C07 (group rings of infinite groups), 20C08 (Hecke algebras), 20C10 and 20C11 (integral and $p$-adic representations of finite groups), 20C12 (integral representations of infinite groups), 20C15 (ordinary representations and characters), 20C20 (modular representations and characters), 20C25 (projective representations and multipliers), 20C30 and 20C32 (finite and infinite symmetric groups), 20C33 (finite groups of Lie type), 20C34 (sporadic groups), 20C35 (applications to physics and other sciences) and 20C99. Representation rings and Burnside rings are cross-referenced to 19A22, and group rings to 16S34. ([MSC2020 20Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Cxx))

Related codes:
- **[MSC 19Axx - Grothendieck groups and K_0](node:MSC%2019Axx%20-%20Grothendieck%20groups%20and%20K_0):** the 20Cxx heading sends representation rings and Burnside rings to 19A22 as well. ([MSC2020 20Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Cxx))
- **[MSC 16Sxx - Associative rings and algebras arising under various constructions](node:MSC%2016Sxx%20-%20Associative%20rings%20and%20algebras%20arising%20under%20various%20constructions):** 20C05 and 20C07 cover group rings and their modules in their group-theoretic aspects, with 16S34 as the cross-reference. ([MSC2020 20Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Ordinary character theory](node:Representation%20Theory) (20C15).** Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic not dividing $|G|$, the irreducible characters form a basis of class functions. Their number equals the number of conjugacy classes, and $|G|=\sum_i(\dim V_i)^2$. Over $\mathbb C$ each $\dim V_i$ divides $|G|$. ([Etingof et al., Thms. 4.1.1, 4.2.1, 5.3.1, Cor. 4.2.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **Blocks, defect groups and Brauer's main theorems (20C20).** $k[G]$ splits into blocks, each with a defect group (a $p$-subgroup, unique up to conjugacy); the Sylow $p$-subgroups are defect groups of the principal block. *First main theorem:* for a $p$-subgroup $D$, blocks of $G$ with defect group $D$ correspond bijectively to blocks of $N_G(D)$ with defect group $D$. *Second:* a criterion, via generalized decomposition numbers, for a block of $C_G(t)$ ($t$ a $p$-element) to correspond to a given block of $G$. *Third:* for a $p$-subgroup $Q$ and $QC_G(Q)\subseteq H\subseteq N_G(Q)$, the principal block of $H$ is the only Brauer correspondent of the principal block of $G$. ([Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory); [Malle survey, §3.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145); [Wikipedia: Brauer's three main theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%27s_three_main_theorems))
- **Brauer characters and decomposition numbers.** Irreducible Brauer characters come from simple $kG$-modules. The decomposition matrix $D$ records multiplicities of Brauer characters in reductions of ordinary characters, and the Cartan matrix $C=D^TD$ is symmetric and nonsingular with determinant a power of $p$. ([Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory))
- **Deligne–Lusztig theory (20C33).** For a finite group of Lie type $G^F$, a maximal torus $T$ and a character $\theta$ of $T^F$, the virtual character $R_T^\theta$ is an alternating sum of compactly supported $\ell$-adic cohomology of a Deligne–Lusztig variety. Every irreducible character occurs in some $R_T^\theta$, and $\pm R_T^\theta$ is irreducible when $\theta$ is in general position. When the reductive group has connected centre, Lusztig's Jordan decomposition describes each irreducible character by a semisimple element of the dual group together with a unipotent representation of its centralizer, and its degree is the product of the degrees of its semisimple and unipotent components; the non-connected-centre case has extra complications. ([Wikipedia: Deligne–Lusztig theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deligne%E2%80%93Lusztig_theory))
- **Symmetric groups (20C30).** In characteristic $0$ (or $>n$) the irreducibles of $S_n$ are indexed by partitions of $n$, with dimension given by the hook length formula. In other characteristics the reductions mod $p$ of these modules (the Specht modules) are generally reducible, every irreducible appears inside some Specht module, and the dimensions of the irreducibles are not known in general. Williamson's torsion examples refute the James conjecture on decomposition numbers. ([Wikipedia: Representation theory of the symmetric group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory_of_the_symmetric_group); [Williamson](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.5055))
- **Group rings of infinite groups (20C07).** For a torsion-free group $G$ and field $K$, Kaplansky's unit conjecture (units of $K[G]$ are trivial) is false: Gardam's counterexample uses a virtually abelian group over $\mathbb F_2$. The zero-divisor and idempotent conjectures were open as of 2021. ([Gardam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11818); [Wikipedia: Kaplansky's conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures))
- **McKay and height zero theorems.** For every prime $\ell$, $G$ and $N_G(P)$ ($P\in\operatorname{Syl}_\ell G$) have equally many irreducible characters of $\ell'$-degree (Cabanes–Späth). For a $p$-block $B$ with defect group $D$, all characters of $B$ have height zero if and only if $D$ is abelian (completed by Malle–Navarro–Schaeffer Fry–Tiep). ([Cabanes–Späth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20392); [Malle–Navarro–Schaeffer Fry–Tiep](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04736); [Malle survey, Conj. 3.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145))

### History
Etingof et al. date the subject to Frobenius's 1896 character theory, triggered by Dedekind's letters on the group determinant. Brauer created modular representation theory from about 1940. ([Etingof et al., Introduction](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf); [Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory))

Deligne and Lusztig introduced their construction in 1976, and Lusztig's 1984 book *Characters of Reductive Groups over a Finite Field* set out the classification of irreducible characters of finite reductive groups. ([Wikipedia: Deligne–Lusztig theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deligne%E2%80%93Lusztig_theory))

McKay stated a limited form of his conjecture (for $p=2$ and simple groups) in 1971; Isaacs, Malle and Navarro reduced it to simple groups in 2007; Malle and Späth settled $p=2$ in 2016; and Cabanes and Späth announced the general case in October 2023. ([Wikipedia: McKay conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKay_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Alperin weight conjecture.** $|\mathrm{IBr}(B)|$ equals the number of $G$-classes of $B$-weights. It is open in general and reduced to an inductive blockwise condition on simple groups (Späth). Feng, Malle and Zhang (2025) describe their generic weights as a step towards an eventual proof. ([Malle survey, Conj. 4.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145); [Feng–Malle–Zhang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22064))
- **Alperin–McKay and Broué's abelian defect group conjectures.** Alperin–McKay asserts $|\mathrm{Irr}_0(B)|=|\mathrm{Irr}_0(b)|$ for the Brauer correspondent $b$ of $B$. Broué predicts that for abelian $D$, $B$ and $b$ are derived equivalent. Malle's survey reports both open in general, the second with no general reduction theorem. ([Malle survey, Conjs. 2.2, 6.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145))
- **Modular representations of symmetric groups.** Determining the simple modules of $S_n$ in positive characteristic, even their dimensions, is described as one of the most important open problems in representation theory. ([Wikipedia: Representation theory of the symmetric group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory_of_the_symmetric_group))
- **Kaplansky's zero-divisor and idempotent conjectures** for torsion-free groups: Wikipedia records both as open as of 2021. ([Wikipedia: Kaplansky's conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory): blocks, defect groups, Brauer characters, decomposition and Cartan matrices.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.712, Introduction to Representation Theory](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-712-introduction-to-representation-theory-fall-2010/pages/lecture-notes/): lecture notes from basic notions through finite groups, $S_n$, Schur–Weyl duality and quivers.
- **Learn:** [Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf): the book version of the course, with historical interludes.
- **Primary:** [Malle, Local-global conjectures in the representation theory of finite groups](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145): survey of the McKay, Alperin–McKay, height zero, Alperin weight and Broué conjectures and their reductions.
- **Primary:** [Cabanes–Späth, The McKay Conjecture on character degrees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20392) and [Malle–Navarro–Schaeffer Fry–Tiep, Brauer's Height Zero Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04736): the 2022–2024 proofs.
- **Further reading:** [Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups (Springer GTM, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-9458-7): standard graduate text covering characters, induction and Brauer theory.
- **In this vault:** [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory), [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras), [Algebraic Groups](node:Algebraic%20Groups), [Finite Simple Groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups), [Quiver Representations](node:Quiver%20Representations), [MSC 16Gxx - Representation theory of associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016Gxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20associative%20rings%20and%20algebras), [MSC 20Gxx - Linear algebraic groups and related topics](node:MSC%2020Gxx%20-%20Linear%20algebraic%20groups%20and%20related%20topics), [MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups), [MSC 20Dxx - Abstract finite groups](node:MSC%2020Dxx%20-%20Abstract%20finite%20groups), [MSC 20 - Group theory and generalizations](node:MSC%2020%20-%20Group%20theory%20and%20generalizations).
references.MSC 20Dxx - Abstract finite groups:
## Reference
### Overview
20Dxx studies finite groups as abstract objects: their simple groups, solvable and nilpotent groups, Sylow and special subgroups, series and automorphisms. ([MSC2020 20Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Dxx)) Every finite group has a composition series whose simple factors are unique up to order and isomorphism (Jordan–Hölder), and the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) lists the possible factors. ([Wikipedia: Composition series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_series); [Wikipedia: Classification of finite simple groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups))

Much of the theory is local analysis: deducing global structure from the Sylow subgroups and how their subgroups are conjugate (fused) in $G$. Fusion systems abstract this information, and Puig showed that the fusion system of a finite group at a Sylow subgroup is saturated. Fusion systems form a relatively new area with connections to local finite group theory, algebraic topology and modular representation theory. ([van Beek, §4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.11691); [Aschbacher–Oliver, Fusion systems, Bull. AMS 2016](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/72057))

### Scope
MSC2020 20Dxx has codes 20D05 (finite simple groups and their classification), 20D06 (alternating groups and groups of Lie type), 20D08 (sporadic groups), 20D10 (finite solvable groups, formations, Schunck and Fitting classes, $\pi$-length), 20D15 (finite nilpotent groups, $p$-groups), 20D20 (Sylow subgroups, $\pi$-structure), 20D25 (special subgroups such as Frattini and Fitting), 20D30 (series and lattices of subgroups), 20D35 (subnormal subgroups), 20D40 (products of subgroups), 20D45 (automorphisms), 20D60 (arithmetic and combinatorial problems) and 20D99. ([MSC2020 20Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Dxx))

Related codes:
- **[MSC 20Gxx - Linear algebraic groups and related topics](node:MSC%2020Gxx%20-%20Linear%20algebraic%20groups%20and%20related%20topics):** 20D06 (alternating groups and groups of Lie type) cross-references 20Gxx. ([MSC2020 20Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Dxx))
- **[MSC 20Fxx - Special aspects of infinite or finite groups](node:MSC%2020Fxx%20-%20Special%20aspects%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups):** 20D10 (finite solvable groups, formations, Schunck and Fitting classes) cross-references 20F17. ([MSC2020 20Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Dxx))
- **[MSC 20Cxx - Representation theory of groups](node:MSC%2020Cxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20groups):** Burnside's theorem that groups of order $p^aq^b$ are solvable, a statement about abstract finite groups, was proved with representation theory. ([Etingof et al., Thm. 5.4.3](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **[Sylow Theorems](node:Sylow%20Theorems) (20D20).** Let $|G|=p^rm$ with $p\nmid m$. Sylow $p$-subgroups exist and are all conjugate. Their number $n_p$ satisfies $n_p\mid m$, $n_p\equiv1\pmod p$ and $n_p=[G:N_G(P)]$ for any Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$; in particular $n_p=1$ exactly when $P\trianglelefteq G$. ([Conrad, The Sylow theorems, Thms. 1.7–1.10](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/grouptheory/sylowpf.pdf))
- **Composition series and [Finite Simple Groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups) (20D05–20D08).** Every finite group has a composition series, and by Jordan–Hölder any two have the same length and the same factors up to order and isomorphism; infinite groups such as $\mathbb Z$ may have none. Every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating of degree $\ge5$, one of 16 infinite families of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups. Feit–Thompson (1963): every group of odd order is solvable. ([Wikipedia: Composition series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_series); [Wikipedia: Classification of finite simple groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups))
