- **[Solvable Groups](node:Solvable%20Groups) and Hall subgroups (20D10).** Burnside: every group of order $p^aq^b$ is solvable, proved with characters. Hall (1928): if $G$ is finite solvable and $\pi$ is a set of primes, Hall $\pi$-subgroups (order a $\pi$-number, index prime to $\pi$) exist and are conjugate. Conversely, a finite group with a Hall $\pi$-subgroup for every $\pi$ is solvable. $A_4$ is solvable of order 12 yet has no subgroup of order 6, so the theorem does not give subgroups for every divisor of $|G|$. ([Etingof et al., Thm. 5.4.3](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf); [Wikipedia: Hall subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_subgroup))
- **Schur–Zassenhaus theorem.** If $N\trianglelefteq G$ with $\gcd(|N|,|G/N|)=1$, then $N$ has a complement and $G\cong N\rtimes G/N$. If $N$ or $G/N$ is solvable, all complements are conjugate; in general, conjugacy follows only via Feit–Thompson. Zassenhaus's 1937 textbook credited existence to Schur. ([Wikipedia: Schur–Zassenhaus theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur%E2%80%93Zassenhaus_theorem))
- **Fitting subgroup and $F^*(G)$ (20D25).** $F(G)$ is the largest normal nilpotent subgroup (Fitting's theorem makes the product of normal nilpotent subgroups nilpotent). If $G$ is solvable then $C_G(F(G))\le F(G)$. For arbitrary finite $G$ the generalized Fitting subgroup $F^*(G)=F(G)E(G)$, with $E(G)$ generated by the subnormal quasisimple subgroups, satisfies $C_G(F^*(G))\le F^*(G)$. ([Wikipedia: Fitting subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitting_subgroup))
- **Enumeration of $p$-groups (20D15).** Higman and Sims: the number of groups of order $p^n$ is $p^{\frac{2}{27}n^3+O(n^{8/3})}$, dominated by class-two groups. Of the $49{,}910{,}529{,}484$ groups of order at most $2000$, $49{,}487{,}367{,}289$ have order $1024$. ([Wikipedia: p-group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-group))
- **Fusion systems.** For $S\in\operatorname{Syl}_p(G)$, $\mathcal F_S(G)$ is the category whose objects are the subgroups of $S$ and whose morphisms are the maps induced by conjugation in $G$. By Puig, $\mathcal F_S(G)$ is always saturated, and a saturated fusion system not of this form is called exotic. ([van Beek, §4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.11691))

### History
In 1892 Hölder asked for a classification of the finite simple groups. ([Wikipedia: Classification of finite simple groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups)) Hall introduced Hall subgroups in 1928, generalizing Sylow's theorem to solvable groups. ([Wikipedia: Hall subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_subgroup))

Feit and Thompson proved the odd order theorem in 1963. Gorenstein announced the classification as complete in 1983, prematurely because the quasithin case was unfinished. Aschbacher and Smith's 1221-page quasithin work led Aschbacher to announce completion in 2004. Gorenstein, Lyons and Solomon (later with Capdeboscq) are publishing a second-generation proof, with ten volumes by 2023. Solomon's Bull. AMS article (2001) is a brief history of the classification. ([Wikipedia: Classification of finite simple groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups); [Crossref: Solomon 2001](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0273-0979-01-00909-0))

### Open problems
- **The Kourovka Notebook.** A collection of unsolved problems in group theory, published every 2–4 years since 1965; the 21st edition adds 150 new problems. Its current arXiv version marks problems with AI-proposed solutions that have not been confirmed by mathematicians as still unsolved. ([Khukhro–Mazurov, Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300))
- **Exotic fusion systems in Lie-type Sylow subgroups.** Van Beek's work belongs to a programme to classify all saturated fusion systems on Sylow $p$-subgroups of rank-2 groups of Lie type, with $\mathrm{PSU}_5(p^n)$, ${}^3D_4(p^n)$ and ${}^2F_4(2^n)$ still open as of that paper (2021). A cited conjecture (Parker–Semeraro) predicts that, apart from small cases, such Sylow subgroups support no exotic fusion systems. ([van Beek, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.11691))
- **"Almost all groups are 2-groups."** A folklore conjecture: the proportion of 2-groups among groups of order at most $n$ tends to $1$. ([Wikipedia: p-group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-group))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Classification of finite simple groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups): the statement, the families, the proof's history and the second-generation programme.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, The Sylow theorems (UConn expository notes)](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/grouptheory/sylowpf.pdf): statements, worked examples and proofs of Sylow I–III.
- **Primary:** [Solomon, A brief history of the classification of the finite simple groups, Bull. AMS 38 (2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0273-0979-01-00909-0): historical survey of the classification.
- **Primary:** [Aschbacher–Oliver, Fusion systems, Bull. AMS 53 (2016)](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/72057): survey of fusion systems and their links to local group theory, topology and representation theory.
- **Primary:** [Khukhro–Mazurov, Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300): the standard problem list.
- **Further reading:** [Oliver–Ruiz, Simplicity of fusion systems of finite simple groups (Trans. AMS 2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.07578): determines which known finite simple groups have simple $p$-fusion systems.
- **In this vault:** [Finite Simple Groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups), [Sylow Theorems](node:Sylow%20Theorems), [Solvable Groups](node:Solvable%20Groups), [Lagrange's Theorem](node:Lagrange's%20Theorem), [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), [MSC 20Bxx - Permutation groups](node:MSC%2020Bxx%20-%20Permutation%20groups), [MSC 20Exx - Structure and classification of infinite or finite groups](node:MSC%2020Exx%20-%20Structure%20and%20classification%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups), [MSC 20 - Group theory and generalizations](node:MSC%2020%20-%20Group%20theory%20and%20generalizations).

## Reference
### Overview
20Exx collects the general structural theory of groups, finite or infinite: how groups are assembled (extensions, semidirect and wreath products, free products with amalgamation, HNN extensions), how they are approximated (limits, profinite groups, residual properties), and their subgroup structure (subgroup theorems, maximal subgroups, chains of subgroups). It also covers varieties of groups, groups with a $BN$-pair and buildings, automorphisms of infinite groups, and conjugacy classes. ([MSC2020 20Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Exx))

The extension problem, determining all $G$ with $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $G/N\cong Q$, has been studied since the late nineteenth century. It matters because finite groups are built from finite simple groups by repeated extensions. ([Wikipedia: Group extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_extension)) Bass–Serre theory studies groups acting on trees: an action without inversions decomposes the group as the fundamental group of a graph of groups, built from vertex and edge groups by amalgamated free products and HNN extensions. ([Wikipedia: Bass–Serre theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass%E2%80%93Serre_theory))

### Scope
MSC2020 20Exx lists 20E05 (free nonabelian groups), 20E06 (free products, free products with amalgamation, HNN extensions), 20E07 (subgroup theorems; subgroup growth), 20E08 (groups acting on trees), 20E10 (quasivarieties and varieties), 20E15 (chains and lattices of subgroups, subnormal subgroups), 20E18 (limits, profinite groups), 20E22 (extensions, wreath products and other compositions), 20E25 (local properties), 20E26 (residual properties; residually finite groups), 20E28 (maximal subgroups), 20E32 (simple groups), 20E34 (general structure theorems), 20E36 (automorphisms of infinite groups), 20E42 (groups with a $BN$-pair; buildings), 20E45 (conjugacy classes) and 20E99. ([MSC2020 20Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Exx))

Related codes (cross-references in the MSC entry):
- **[MSC 20Dxx - Abstract finite groups](node:MSC%2020Dxx%20-%20Abstract%20finite%20groups):** 20E32 (simple groups) cross-refers to 20D05, and automorphisms of finite groups go to 20D45 rather than 20E36. ([MSC2020 20Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Exx))
- **[MSC 20Fxx - Special aspects of infinite or finite groups](node:MSC%2020Fxx%20-%20Special%20aspects%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups):** 20E08 (groups acting on trees) cross-refers to 20F65, and 20E15 (chains and lattices of subgroups) to 20F22. ([MSC2020 20Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Exx))
- **[MSC 20Jxx - Connections of group theory with homological algebra and category theory](node:MSC%2020Jxx%20-%20Connections%20of%20group%20theory%20with%20homological%20algebra%20and%20category%20theory):** 20E22 (extensions, wreath products) cross-refers to 20J05. ([MSC2020 20Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Exx))
- **[MSC 51Exx - Finite geometry and special incidence structures](node:MSC%2051Exx%20-%20Finite%20geometry%20and%20special%20incidence%20structures):** 20E42 (groups with a $BN$-pair; buildings) cross-refers to 51E24. ([MSC2020 20Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Exx))

### Key concepts
- **[Group Extensions](node:Group%20Extensions) and semidirect products (20E22).** An extension of $Q$ by $N$ is a short exact sequence $1\to N\to G\to Q\to1$. It splits, i.e. $G\cong N\rtimes_\varphi Q$ with multiplication $(n_1,q_1)(n_2,q_2)=(n_1\varphi_{q_1}(n_2),q_1q_2)$, if and only if $G\to Q$ has a homomorphic section. Central extensions by an abelian $A$ are classified by $H^2(Q,A)$; general extensions use homomorphisms to $\operatorname{Out}(N)$ together with $H^2$ and $H^3$. Inequivalent extensions can give isomorphic groups: there are 8 inequivalent extensions of the Klein four-group by $\mathbb Z/2$ but only 4 isomorphism types of groups of order 8 among them. ([Wikipedia: Semidirect product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semidirect_product); [Wikipedia: Group extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_extension))
- **Coprime extensions split (Schur–Zassenhaus).** If $G$ is finite, $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $\gcd(|N|,|G/N|)=1$, then $N$ has a complement, and all complements are conjugate if $N$ or $G/N$ is solvable (in general, using Feit–Thompson). ([Wikipedia: Schur–Zassenhaus theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur%E2%80%93Zassenhaus_theorem))
- **Wreath products and the Kaloujnine–Krasner theorem.** For $H$ acting on $\Omega$, $A\,\mathrm{Wr}_\Omega H=\bigl(\prod_\Omega A\bigr)\rtimes H$, and the restricted version uses $\bigoplus_\Omega A$. Every extension of $A$ by $H$ embeds in the unrestricted regular wreath product $A\wr H$ (Krasner–Kaloujnine, 1951). A Sylow $p$-subgroup of $S_{p^n}$ is the $n$-fold iterated wreath product $C_p\wr\cdots\wr C_p$. ([Wikipedia: Wreath product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreath_product))
- **Free groups and Nielsen–Schreier (20E05, 20E07).** Every subgroup of a free group is free. If $F$ has rank $n$ and $[F:H]=e<\infty$, then $H$ is free of rank $1+e(n-1)$ (Schreier index formula). A group is free if and only if it acts freely on a tree. ([Wikipedia: Nielsen–Schreier theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen%E2%80%93Schreier_theorem); [Manning, Bass–Serre theory notes, §1](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~jfmanning/teaching/notes/graph_of_groups.pdf))
- **Amalgams, HNN extensions and Bass–Serre theory (20E06, 20E08).** $A*_CB$ is the quotient of $A*B$ by the relations $\alpha(c)=\beta(c)$. With transversals chosen, every element has a unique normal form. $G\cong A*_CB$ if and only if $G$ acts on a tree with a single edge $e=[v,w]$ as strict fundamental domain and $\operatorname{Stab}(v),\operatorname{Stab}(e),\operatorname{Stab}(w)$ corresponding to $A,C,B$. For $\alpha:H\to K$ an isomorphism of subgroups of $G$, the HNN extension is $\langle G,t\mid tht^{-1}=\alpha(h)\ (h\in H)\rangle$, and Britton's lemma gives its normal form. The fundamental theorem says that a group acting on a tree without inversions is the fundamental group of the quotient graph of groups, and the Kurosh subgroup theorem follows. ([Manning, Thms. 2.3 and 4.1](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~jfmanning/teaching/notes/graph_of_groups.pdf); [Wikipedia: HNN extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HNN_extension); [Wikipedia: Bass–Serre theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass%E2%80%93Serre_theory))
- **Profinite groups and residual finiteness (20E18, 20E26).** A profinite group is an inverse limit of finite groups, equivalently a compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected group; examples are $\mathbb Z_p$ and infinite Galois groups. A group $G$ is residually finite if its finite-index normal subgroups intersect trivially, equivalently if its profinite topology is Hausdorff. Free groups, finitely generated linear groups and fundamental groups of compact 3-manifolds are residually finite, while $BS(2,3)$ is not. Finitely presented residually finite groups have solvable word problem. Nikolov–Segal (using CFSG): in a topologically finitely generated profinite group every finite-index subgroup is open. ([Wikipedia: Profinite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profinite_group); [Wikipedia: Residually finite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residually_finite_group))
- **Composition series (20E15).** A group with a composition series has a unique multiset of composition factors (Jordan–Hölder). Every finite group has one, but infinite groups such as $\mathbb Z$ need not. ([Wikipedia: Composition series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_series))

### History
Nielsen proved the finitely generated case of the subgroup theorem in 1921, and Schreier the general case in his 1926 habilitation, published 1927. Baer and Levi gave a topological proof in 1936, and Serre one via Bass–Serre theory in 1969. ([Wikipedia: Nielsen–Schreier theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen%E2%80%93Schreier_theorem))

Higman, B. H. Neumann and H. Neumann introduced HNN extensions in 1949 to show that two isomorphic subgroups of a group are conjugate in some overgroup. Krasner and Kaloujnine published the wreath-product embedding in 1951. ([Wikipedia: HNN extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HNN_extension); [Wikipedia: Wreath product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreath_product))

Serre developed the theory of groups acting on trees in the 1970s and published *Trees* (1977; English 1980), written with Bass. Bass later contributed foundational work, including a 1993 covering theory for graphs of groups. ([Wikipedia: Bass–Serre theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass%E2%80%93Serre_theory); [Crossref: Serre, Trees](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61856-7))

### Open problems
- **Are all hyperbolic groups residually finite?** Wilton writes that "in full generality, the question remains wide open", notes the widespread belief that a non-residually finite hyperbolic group exists, and cites Agol's positive answer for cubulable hyperbolic groups. Assuming a positive answer, the paper deduces the congruence subgroup property for mapping class groups of hyperbolic surfaces of finite type. ([Wilton–Sisto, introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.00556); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00556)) A 2019 claimed counterexample was withdrawn by its authors because of an error in its Section 4. ([Kim–Lee, arXiv 1903.00838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.00838))
- **The Kourovka Notebook** collects unsolved problems in group theory; its 21st edition adds 150 new problems. ([Khukhro–Mazurov](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Bass–Serre theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass%E2%80%93Serre_theory): graphs of groups, the fundamental theorem and its applications.
- **Learn:** [Manning, Bass–Serre theory and complexes of groups (Cornell)](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~jfmanning/teaching/notes/graph_of_groups.pdf): free products, amalgams and normal forms, amalgams as tree actions, graphs of groups.
- **Primary:** [Wilton–Sisto, The congruence subgroup property for mapping class groups and the residual finiteness of hyperbolic groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00556): current status of residual finiteness for hyperbolic groups and its consequences.
- **Primary:** [Khukhro–Mazurov, The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300): a list of unsolved problems in group theory, updated every 2–4 years.
- **Further reading:** [Serre, Trees (Springer, 1980)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61856-7): the founding monograph on groups acting on trees.
- **In this vault:** [Group Extensions](node:Group%20Extensions), [Group Presentations](node:Group%20Presentations), [Geometric Group Theory](node:Geometric%20Group%20Theory), [Group Cohomology](node:Group%20Cohomology), [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), [MSC 20Bxx - Permutation groups](node:MSC%2020Bxx%20-%20Permutation%20groups), [MSC 20 - Group theory and generalizations](node:MSC%2020%20-%20Group%20theory%20and%20generalizations).

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 20F collects special aspects of [groups](node:Group%20Theory), infinite or finite, alongside the neighbouring subfields [20E](node:MSC%2020Exx%20-%20Structure%20and%20classification%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups) (structure and classification of infinite or finite groups) and [20D](node:MSC%2020Dxx%20-%20Abstract%20finite%20groups) (abstract finite groups). Its codes run from generators and relations (20F05), cancellation theory and van Kampen diagrams (20F06) and decision problems (20F10), through groups of finite Morley rank (20F11), commutator calculus and central series (20F12, 20F14), solvable, supersolvable and nilpotent groups (20F16, 20F18), formations and Fitting classes (20F17), Engel conditions (20F45) and periodic and locally finite groups (20F50), to braid and Artin groups (20F36), reflection and Coxeter groups (20F55), ordered groups (20F60), automorphism groups (20F28), and geometric group theory (20F65, 20F67, 20F69). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Geometric group theory is therefore one part of 20F, not the whole of it. Its guiding idea is to give a finitely generated group a metric and study it as a geometric object; the word metric depends on the generating set only up to quasi-isometry. ([Druţu–Kapovich](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~kapovich/EPR/ggt.pdf)) The older combinatorial side is organized around the decision problems Dehn proposed in 1911: the word, conjugacy and isomorphism problems. ([Word problem for groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups))

### Scope
- **Presentations and algorithms (20F05, 20F06, 20F10, 20F70):** generators and relations, small cancellation and van Kampen diagrams, word and other decision problems with links to logic and automata, and equations over groups. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))
- **Classes defined by series and identities (20F12–20F24, 20F45, 20F50):** commutator calculus; derived and central series; solvable, supersolvable, nilpotent and generalized solvable groups; formations and Fitting classes (cross-referenced with finite solvable groups in 20D10); FC-groups; Engel conditions; periodic and locally finite groups. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))
- **Groups from topology, geometry and logic (20F11, 20F34, 20F36, 20F38, 20F55, 20F60):** groups of finite Morley rank (cross-referenced to [model theory](node:Model%20Theory), 03C45, 03C60), fundamental groups, braid and Artin groups, reflection and Coxeter groups, and ordered groups (mainly 06F15). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))
- **Geometric group theory (20F65, 20F67, 20F69):** general geometric group theory (with 05C25, 20E08, 57Mxx), hyperbolic and nonpositively curved groups, and asymptotic properties such as growth. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))
- **Automorphisms and Lie structures (20F28, 20F29, 20F40):** automorphism groups of groups (with 20E36), representations as automorphism groups of algebraic systems, and Lie rings associated with groups. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Neighbouring codes: 20F34 ([fundamental groups](node:Fundamental%20Group) and their automorphisms, group-theoretic aspects) and 20F06 are cross-referenced to 57M05 in low-dimensional topology; free groups, free products, profinite groups and groups acting on trees sit in 20E; finite solvable and nilpotent groups and $p$-groups in 20D10 and 20D15; semigroup word problems in 20M05; 20F55 (reflection and Coxeter groups) is cross-referenced to 22E40 and 51F15. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Word problem and Novikov–Boone.** For a finitely generated group $G$, the word problem asks for an algorithm deciding whether two words in the generators represent the same element; solvability does not depend on the finite generating set. Novikov (1955) constructed a finitely presented group with unsolvable word problem, and Boone (1958) gave a different proof. Solvable classes include one-relator groups (Magnus, 1932), polycyclic groups, finitely presented residually finite groups and automatic groups. Dehn (1912) solved the word and conjugacy problems for surface groups of genus at least 2. ([Word problem for groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups))
- **Hyperbolic groups (20F67).** A group is hyperbolic if it is finitely generated and its Cayley graph is a hyperbolic metric space; this does not depend on the finite generating set. Fundamental groups of compact hyperbolic manifolds and virtually free groups are examples, while $\mathbb Z^n$ for $n\ge 2$ is not, since a hyperbolic group contains no $\mathbb Z^2$ subgroup. Hyperbolic groups are finitely presented and their word problem is solvable in linear time by Dehn's algorithm. ([Bowditch](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/courses/8800/bbowditch-ggtcourse.pdf))
- **Growth (20F69) and Gromov's theorem.** Let $\beta_S(n)$ count elements of word length at most $n$. A finitely generated group has polynomial growth if and only if it has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index (Gromov, 1981). For finitely generated nilpotent $G$ with lower central series $G=G_1\supseteq G_2\supseteq\cdots$, the Bass–Guivarc'h formula gives the degree of growth $d(G)=\sum_{k\ge1}k\,\operatorname{rank}(G_k/G_{k+1})$. ([Gromov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gromov%27s_theorem_on_groups_of_polynomial_growth)) Milnor and Wolf asked whether every finitely generated group has polynomial or exponential growth; the Milnor–Wolf theorem answers yes for solvable groups, which have polynomial growth only when virtually nilpotent. ([Druţu–Kapovich](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~kapovich/EPR/ggt.pdf))
- **Burnside problems and periodic groups (20F50).** The general Burnside problem (is every finitely generated periodic group finite?) was answered negatively by Golod and Shafarevich in 1964. The free Burnside group $B(m,n)$ is finite for $n=2,3,4,6$; Novikov and Adian (1968) showed that infinite finitely generated groups of exponent $n$ exist for every odd $n>4381$, a bound Adian later lowered to odd exponents above 665; Ivanov (1994) and Lysënok (1996) treated large even exponents. Zelmanov's positive solution of the restricted Burnside problem earned a Fields Medal in 1994. ([Burnside problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_problem)) Grigorchuk's group (1980) is an infinite finitely generated 2-group; in 1984 it was shown to have intermediate growth, answering Milnor's 1968 question, and it is amenable but not elementary amenable. ([Grigorchuk group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grigorchuk_group))
- **Tits alternative.** If $\Gamma$ is a finitely generated subgroup of a Lie group with finitely many components, then $\Gamma$ is virtually solvable or contains a nonabelian free subgroup (Tits, 1972). Consequently a finitely generated subgroup of $GL(n,\mathbb R)$ is either virtually nilpotent or of exponential growth; over a field of characteristic zero finite generation is not needed. The alternative also holds for subgroups of hyperbolic groups, mapping class groups and $\mathrm{Out}(F_n)$. ([Druţu–Kapovich](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~kapovich/EPR/ggt.pdf)) For linear groups, nonamenability is equivalent to containing a nonabelian free group, although the von Neumann conjecture fails in general. ([Tits alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tits_alternative))
- **Coxeter and Artin groups (20F55, 20F36).** A Coxeter group has presentation $\langle r_1,\dots,r_n\mid (r_ir_j)^{m_{ij}}=1\rangle$ with $m_{ii}=1$ and $m_{ij}=m_{ji}\in\{2,3,\dots,\infty\}$ for $i\ne j$; the finite Coxeter groups are exactly the finite Euclidean reflection groups, classified by Coxeter in 1935 into types $A_n,B_n,D_n,I_2(p),E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,H_3,H_4$. ([Coxeter group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coxeter_group)) The associated Artin–Tits group drops the relations $r_i^2=1$ and keeps the braid relations $sts\cdots=tst\cdots$ (both of length $m_{st}$); type $A$ gives the braid group, whose Coxeter quotient is the symmetric group. ([Artin–Tits group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Tits_group))

### History
Dehn posed the word, conjugacy and isomorphism problems in 1911 and solved the first two for surface groups in 1912 using hyperbolic geometry; the undecidability results of Novikov (1955) and Boone (1958) followed. ([Word problem for groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups)) Burnside's questions on periodic groups drove the work of Golod–Shafarevich (1964), Novikov–Adian (1968) and Zelmanov (Fields Medal, 1994). ([Burnside problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_problem)) Gromov introduced hyperbolic groups around 1985, building on Thurston's work and earlier observations of Efremovich, Schwarz and Milnor that a group acting cocompactly and properly on a space is quasi-isometric to it. ([Bowditch](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/courses/8800/bbowditch-ggtcourse.pdf)) Gromov's polynomial growth theorem appeared in 1981 with an appendix by Tits, and Kleiner gave a relatively simple proof in 2010. ([Gromov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gromov%27s_theorem_on_groups_of_polynomial_growth))

### Open problems
- **Bounded Burnside problem for $B(2,5)$.** Whether the free Burnside group of rank 2 and exponent 5 is finite is open. ([Burnside problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_problem))
- **Artin groups.** For general Artin–Tits groups, decidability of the word and conjugacy problems, triviality of torsion, the structure of the centre, and the $K(\pi,1)$ conjecture remain open; they are settled in the spherical case. ([Artin–Tits group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Tits_group))
- **Hyperbolic groups.** Whether every hyperbolic group is virtually torsion-free is open, as is Cannon's question whether a hyperbolic group with boundary the 2-sphere is virtually a hyperbolic 3-manifold group. ([Bowditch](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/courses/8800/bbowditch-ggtcourse.pdf))
- **Gap Conjecture on growth.** Grigorchuk's Gap Conjecture on lower bounds for the growth of groups of intermediate growth remains a conjecture; his paper reduces it to simple and residually finite groups. ([Grigorchuk, arXiv:1202.6044](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.6044))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Word problem for groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups): decision problems, Novikov–Boone, and classes with solvable word problem.
- **Learn:** [Bowditch, A course on geometric group theory](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/courses/8800/bbowditch-ggtcourse.pdf): presentations, quasi-isometries and hyperbolic groups, with open questions.
- **Primary:** [Druţu and Kapovich, Geometric Group Theory](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~kapovich/EPR/ggt.pdf): author-hosted monograph with proofs of Gromov's theorem, the Tits alternative and the Milnor–Wolf theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Grigorchuk, On the Gap Conjecture concerning group growth](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.6044): growth of groups and the Gap Conjecture.

## Reference
### Overview
Linear algebraic groups are subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ cut out by polynomial equations; over an arbitrary field one takes smooth closed subgroup schemes of $\mathrm{GL}_n$. The subject joins [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory) with algebraic geometry; many [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups) can be viewed as linear algebraic groups over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and much of the theory was developed by analogy with Lie groups. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group))

Every affine [algebraic group](node:Algebraic%20Groups) is linear, and a reductive group is essentially a product of a central torus and a semisimple group; much of the theory parallels that of [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) and Lie groups. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_group)) Over a perfect field a connected linear algebraic group is uniquely an extension of a reductive group by a smooth connected unipotent group, its unipotent radical; only in characteristic zero is there the stronger Levi decomposition as a semidirect product. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group))

Several MSC 20G sub-codes (20G15 to 20G40) organise the subject by base field: arbitrary fields, the reals, complexes and quaternions, local fields, global fields, adèles and other rings, and finite fields. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Scope
The sub-codes of 20Gxx are: 20G05 Representation theory; 20G07 Structure theory; 20G10 Cohomology theory; 20G15 Linear algebraic groups over arbitrary fields; 20G20 over the reals, complexes, quaternions; 20G25 over local fields and their integers; 20G30 over global fields and their integers; 20G35 over adèles and other rings and schemes; 20G40 over [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields); 20G41 Exceptional groups; 20G42 [Quantum Groups](node:Quantum%20Groups) (quantized function algebras) and their representations; 20G43 Schur and $q$-Schur algebras; 20G44 Kac-Moody groups; 20G45 Applications to the sciences; 20G99 other. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

The MSC2020 entry directs arithmetic theory to 11E57 and 11H56, geometric theory to 14Lxx and 22Exx, and other methods in representation theory to 15A30 and 22E45 to 22E55; 20G42 cross-refers to 16T20, 17B37 and 81R50. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf)) Chevalley's structure theorem says a connected algebraic group over a perfect field is an extension of an abelian variety by a linear algebraic group. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_group))

### Key concepts
- **Jordan decomposition.** Each $g\in G$ is uniquely $g=g_{ss}g_u$ with $g_{ss}$ semisimple, $g_u$ unipotent, commuting; over a perfect field both parts lie in $G(k)$ when $g$ does. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group))
- **Borel subgroups and flag varieties.** Borel subgroups are maximal smooth connected solvable subgroups. Borel's fixed point theorem: a connected solvable group acting on a proper variety over an algebraically closed field $k$ has a fixed $k$-point. Hence, for $G$ connected over $k$ algebraically closed, any two Borel subgroups are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$, as are any two maximal tori; Borel subgroups are the minimal parabolic subgroups, and $G/B$ is projective. Conjugacy classes of parabolic subgroups of a simple group correspond to subsets of Dynkin diagram nodes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_subgroup); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group))
- **Reductive versus semisimple groups.** Over an algebraically closed field, a smooth connected $G$ is reductive if it has no nontrivial smooth connected unipotent normal subgroup, and semisimple if it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup; over a general field $k$ these are tested on $G_{\bar k}$. $\mathrm{SL}_n$ is semisimple, $\mathrm{GL}_n$ is reductive but not semisimple. See [Reductive Algebraic Groups](node:Reductive%20Algebraic%20Groups). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group))
- **Root data (Chevalley classification).** Theorem (Chevalley, 1958): connected reductive groups over an algebraically closed field are classified up to isomorphism by their root data. Split reductive groups (those containing a split maximal torus) have the same classification over any field, and over any field there is a unique simply connected split semisimple group for each Dynkin diagram. Demazure and Grothendieck extended this to pinned reductive group schemes over any nonempty base scheme, which includes the existence of Chevalley groups over $\mathbb Z$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductive_group); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group))
- **Bruhat decomposition.** For $G$ connected reductive over an algebraically closed field, $B$ a Borel subgroup and $W$ the Weyl group of a maximal torus in $B$, $G=\bigsqcup_{w\in W} BwB$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruhat_decomposition))
- **Galois cohomology (20G10).** The sets $H^1(k,G)$ classify forms and torsors; see [Galois Cohomology](node:Galois%20Cohomology). Serre's Conjecture II predicts $H^1(F,G)=0$ for $G$ simply connected semisimple over a perfect field $F$ of cohomological dimension at most 2. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_conjecture_II))
- **Strong approximation (20G30, 20G35).** For a global field $k$ and a nonsolvable linear group $G$, $G$ has strong approximation for a finite set $S$ of places if and only if the radical $N$ is unipotent, $G/N$ is simply connected, and each almost simple factor of $G/N$ has a noncompact component at some place in $S$ (Kneser). See also [Arithmetic Matrix Groups](node:Arithmetic%20Matrix%20Groups). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_approximation_theorem))
- **Modular representation theory (20G05).** Lusztig's conjecture on characters of simple rational $\mathrm{SL}_n$-modules in positive characteristic fails: Williamson found counterexamples using numbers from Schubert calculus that grow exponentially. See [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory). ([Williamson, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.5055))

### History
Maurer, Chevalley and Kolchin founded the theory, and Armand Borel built much of the modern theory in the 1950s; Killing and Cartan had classified simple Lie groups in the 1880s and 1890s without the algebraic structure. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group)) Strong approximation was proved by Eichler for some classical groups in 1938, by Kneser (1966) and Platonov (1969) for number fields, and over function fields by Margulis and Prasad in 1977. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_approximation_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Serre's Conjecture II.** Stated above; Serre posed it in 1962. ([Gille, survey](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/LAG/man/326.pdf)) It is known for local fields, totally imaginary number fields, classical groups, and groups of type $F_4$ and $G_2$, and for isotropic or quasi-split exceptional groups other than $E_8$ over perfect fields. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_conjecture_II)) Gille's survey reports that for exceptional groups (trialitarian $D_4$, $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$) the general conjecture is still open. ([Gille, survey](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/LAG/man/326.pdf)) Izquierdo and Lucchini Arteche show that the conjecture for characteristic 0 fields implies it for positive characteristic fields. ([arXiv:2308.00903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00903))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group): definitions, Jordan decomposition, Borel subgroups, classification.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Reductive groups over fields (notes by Feng)](https://math.berkeley.edu/~fengt/249B_2016.pdf): Stanford course developing the structure theory of reductive groups directly over arbitrary fields by dynamic methods; also [Ciappara-Williamson lectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14791) on modular representation theory of reductive groups.
- **Primary:** [Williamson, Schubert calculus and torsion explosion](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.5055): counterexamples to Lusztig's conjecture (J. AMS).
- **Further reading:** [Conrad, Reductive groups over fields](https://math.berkeley.edu/~fengt/249B_2016.pdf): graduate-level treatment, a sequel to Conrad's course on general linear algebraic groups; [Ciappara-Williamson](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14791): Lusztig character formula and geometric representation theory.
references.MSC 20Hxx - Other groups of matrices:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 20Hxx collects group-theoretic work on groups given concretely as matrix groups or as discrete groups of geometric transformations: unimodular and congruence subgroups, Fuchsian groups, crystallographic groups, and matrix groups over fields, rings, and finite fields. A group is linear if it has a faithful finite-dimensional representation over some field; finite groups, $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$, $\mathrm{SL}_n(K)$, and the classical groups are all linear. ([Wikipedia, Linear group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_group))

The area is where abstract [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory) meets arithmetic and geometry. Arithmetic groups such as $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)$ are lattices in Lie groups, Fuchsian groups are the discrete subgroups of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$ acting on the hyperbolic plane, and crystallographic groups are the discrete cocompact groups of Euclidean isometries. ([Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group); [Wikipedia, Fuchsian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuchsian_group))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 20Hxx carries the cross-reference 15A30; its subcodes are 20H05 unimodular groups and congruence subgroups (see also 11F06, 19B37, 22E40, 51F20); 20H10 Fuchsian groups and their generalizations (see also 11F06, 22E40, 30F35, 32Nxx); 20H15 other geometric groups, including crystallographic groups (see also 51-XX, especially 51F15, and 82D25); 20H20 other matrix groups over fields; 20H25 other matrix groups over rings; 20H30 other matrix groups over [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields); and 20H99 for everything else. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Both 20H05 and 20H10 cross-refer to 11F06 and to 22E40, the discrete-subgroup code within [MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Tits alternative:** a finitely generated linear group over a field is either virtually solvable or contains a non-abelian free subgroup. ([Wikipedia, Tits alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tits_alternative))
- **Strong Tits alternative (Breuillard):** for each $d$ there is $N(d)$ such that for any field $K$ and finite $F\subseteq \mathrm{GL}_d(K)$ generating a non-amenable subgroup, $F^{N(d)}$ contains two elements freely generating a non-abelian free subgroup. ([Breuillard](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.1395))
- **Malcev and Selberg:** a finitely generated linear group is residually finite (Malcev 1940), and over a field of characteristic zero it is virtually torsion-free (Selberg's lemma 1960); both follow from Platonov's theorem. ([Nica](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1306.2385))
- **Congruence subgroups (20H05):** a subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ containing the principal congruence subgroup $\Gamma(n)$ for some $n\ge1$; the congruence subgroup problem asks whether every finite-index subgroup of an arithmetic group is of this type. ([Wikipedia, Congruence subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_subgroup))
- **Fuchsian groups (20H10):** discrete subgroups of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$, equivalently groups acting discontinuously on the upper half-plane; the limit set is empty, one or two points, or infinite; an infinite limit set is either the whole boundary $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$ (first kind) or a nowhere dense perfect set, a Cantor set (second kind). ([Wikipedia, Fuchsian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuchsian_group))
- **Crystallographic groups (20H15):** see Bieberbach's theorems below. ([Wikipedia, Crystallographic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystallographic_group))

Related notes: [Arithmetic Matrix Groups](node:Arithmetic%20Matrix%20Groups), [Algebraic Groups](node:Algebraic%20Groups), [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups), [Geometric Group Theory](node:Geometric%20Group%20Theory), [Modular Forms](node:Modular%20Forms), [Algebraic K1 and Whitehead Groups](node:Algebraic%20K1%20and%20Whitehead%20Groups). ([Wikipedia, Linear group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_group))

### Key results
- **Tits alternative (1972).** If $G$ is a finitely generated subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ for a field $K$, then either $G$ has a solvable subgroup of finite index or $G$ contains a free group on two generators; the proof uses the Zariski closure and ping-pong. ([Wikipedia, Tits alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tits_alternative))
- **Breuillard's strong Tits alternative.** For every $d$ there is $N(d)$ such that for every field $K$ and finite $F\subset\mathrm{GL}_d(K)$ generating a non-amenable group, $F^{N(d)}$ contains two elements freely generating a free group of rank 2; consequences include growth and co-growth gaps. ([Breuillard](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.1395))
- **Malcev's theorem.** A finitely generated linear group (over any field) is residually finite. ([Nica](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1306.2385))
- **Selberg's lemma.** A finitely generated linear group over a field of characteristic zero is virtually torsion-free. This fails in positive characteristic, where torsion subgroups of finitely generated linear groups need not be finite; Platonov's theorem gives virtual residual $p$-finiteness for all but finitely many $p$ in characteristic 0 and for $p=\operatorname{char}K$ otherwise. ([Nica](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1306.2385))
- **Bieberbach's theorems.** For a crystallographic group in dimension $n$, the translation subgroup is free abelian of rank $n$, of finite index; there are only finitely many isomorphism classes in each dimension; and the affine action is unique up to affine conjugation. This partly answers Hilbert's 18th problem. There are 17 wallpaper groups in dimension 2 and in dimension 3 there are 219 space group types, or 230 if chiral copies are counted separately. ([Wikipedia, Crystallographic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystallographic_group))
- **Bass-Milnor-Serre.** For $n\ge3$ every finite-index subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)$ is a congruence subgroup, whereas this fails for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$; the proof by Bass, Milnor and Serre uses algebraic K-theory. ([Wikipedia, Congruence subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_subgroup))
- **Borel-Harish-Chandra.** An arithmetic subgroup of a semisimple Lie group has finite covolume (is a lattice), cocompact exactly when the defining $\mathbb Q$-group is anisotropic. ([Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group))

### History
Malcev's theorem dates from 1940, Selberg's lemma from 1960, Platonov's theorem from 1968, and Tits's alternative from 1972; Bieberbach's results on crystallographic groups answer part of Hilbert's 18th problem, and the 17 plane groups were completed by 1891. ([Nica](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1306.2385); [Wikipedia, Tits alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tits_alternative); [Wikipedia, Crystallographic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystallographic_group))

The congruence subgroup problem has been developed since the 1960s, beginning with integral unimodular groups. ([Raghunathan](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503088))

### Open problems
- **Serre's congruence subgroup conjecture.** It predicts that an irreducible arithmetic lattice in a semisimple Lie group has the congruence subgroup property if and only if the real rank is at least 2. It is confirmed in many cases, and in rank one negative answers are known for lattices in $\mathrm{SO}(d,1)$ with $d\ne7$ and for many lattices in $\mathrm{SU}(d,1)$, while the remaining cases are described as completely open. ([Wikipedia, Congruence subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_subgroup); [Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group))
- **Anisotropic groups.** A March 2026 arXiv preprint by A. S. Rapinchuk states that Serre's conjecture "remains completely open for some anisotropic groups" requiring noncommutative division algebras, such as norm-one groups of quaternion division algebras, and proves, assuming the Margulis-Platonov conjecture for an absolutely almost simple simply connected group $G$ over a number field $K$, that the congruence kernel $C^S(G)$ is trivial when $S$ contains the archimedean places, contains no nonarchimedean place where $G$ is anisotropic, and $S\cap\mathrm{Spl}(M/K)$ has positive Dirichlet density ($M$ the minimal Galois extension over which $G$ becomes an inner form). ([Rapinchuk, arXiv:2603.27472](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.27472v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Linear group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_group): definitions and the main theorems on finitely generated linear groups.
- **Learn:** [Dave Witte Morris, Introduction to Arithmetic Groups](https://www.mathi.uni-heidelberg.de/~wienhard/retreat10/references/morris_book.pdf): free text with sections on lattices in $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb R)$, the Borel density theorem, and the Margulis arithmeticity theorem.
- **Primary:** [Breuillard, A Strong Tits Alternative](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.1395): quantitative matrix-group alternative.
- **Further reading:** [Raghunathan, The congruence subgroup problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503088): survey of progress on the congruence subgroup problem since the 1960s.
references.MSC 20Jxx - Connections of group theory:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 20J covers homological methods in [group theory](node:Group%20Theory) (20J05), [cohomology of groups](node:Group%20Cohomology) (20J06) and the category of groups (20J15). ([MSC2020, 20J](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Jxx)) For a group $G$ and a $\mathbb ZG$-module $M$ there is a natural isomorphism $H^n(G,M)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb ZG}(\mathbb Z,M)$, with $H^0(G,M)=M^G$; $H^1$ is crossed homomorphisms modulo principal ones (just $\mathrm{Hom}(G,M)$ for trivial action), and $H^2$ classifies [extensions](node:Group%20Extensions) of $G$ by $M$ inducing the given module structure, central extensions when the action is trivial. ([Wikipedia, Group cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology))

The topological source is the aspherical space: Hurewicz (1936) showed that a space with $\pi_n=0$ for $n\ne1$ is determined up to homotopy by its [fundamental group](node:Fundamental%20Group) $\pi$, so $H_*(\pi):=H_*(X)$ is an invariant of the group; then $H_1(\pi)=\pi/[\pi,\pi]$ and $H_2(\mathbb Z^2)=\mathbb Z$ via the torus. Such an $X$ is a $K(\pi,1)$, an [Eilenberg–MacLane space](node:Eilenberg–MacLane%20Spaces). ([Brown, §0](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf)) The algebraic side is [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) over $\mathbb ZG$; the general categorical machinery sits in 18G, and MSC's section 18 sends homological algebra of groups to 20J. ([MSC2020, 18](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18-XX))

### Scope
MSC2020 20J lists 20J05 homological methods in group theory, 20J06 cohomology of groups, 20J15 category of groups and 20J99, with no see-also references. ([MSC2020, 20J](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Jxx)) The note to section 18 ("for groups, see 20Jxx") makes 20J the home of group-specific homological algebra, as 13D is for commutative rings and 16E for associative rings; [topological groups](node:Topological%20Groups) go to 57T, and algebraic topology to 55N and 55U. ([MSC2020, 18](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=18-XX)) The categorical viewpoint is as old as [category theory](node:Category%20Theory): Eilenberg and Mac Lane's founding paper has a section "Groups as categories". ([Eilenberg–Mac Lane, contents](https://people.math.osu.edu/cogdell.1/6112-Eilenberg%26MacLane-www.pdf)) Small categories in which all morphisms are invertible are [groupoids](node:Groupoids), classified in [20L](node:MSC%2020Lxx%20-%20Groupoids%20%28i.e.%20small%20categories%20in%20which%20all%20morphisms%20are%20isomorphisms%29). ([MSC2020, 20L](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Lxx)) Parent: [MSC 20 - Group theory and generalizations](node:MSC%2020%20-%20Group%20theory%20and%20generalizations).

### Key concepts
- **Restriction, transfer and Eckmann–Shapiro (20J06).** For $H\le G$ and an $H$-module $M$, $H_*(H,M)\cong H_*(G,\mathrm{Ind}_H^GM)$ and $H^*(H,M)\cong H^*(G,\mathrm{Coind}_H^GM)$. If $[G:H]<\infty$ and $M$ is a $G$-module, there is a transfer (corestriction) $H^*(H,M)\to H^*(G,M)$, and restriction followed by transfer is multiplication by $[G:H]$; consequently $H^*(G,M)$ of a finite group is annihilated by $|G|$ in positive degrees. The transfer on $H_1$ is Schur's Verlagerung $G^{ab}\to H^{ab}$, extended to (co)homology by Eckmann. ([Brown, Prop. 3.3, §3, §6.2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf)) Eckmann found the lemma in 1953 and Shapiro proved it in 1961. ([Wikipedia, Shapiro's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shapiro%27s_lemma))
- **Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence.** For $N\trianglelefteq G$ and a $G$-module $A$, $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(G/N,H^q(N,A))\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(G,A)$, with low-degree five-term inflation–restriction sequence $0\to H^1(G/N,A^N)\to H^1(G,A)\to H^1(N,A)^{G/N}\to H^2(G/N,A^N)\to H^2(G,A)$ (Lyndon 1948; Hochschild–Serre 1953). ([Wikipedia, LHS spectral sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon%E2%80%93Hochschild%E2%80%93Serre_spectral_sequence)) Topologically it is the Cartan–Leray spectral sequence of $K(N,1)\to K(G,1)$. ([Brown, (5.6)](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf)) See [Spectral Sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences).
- **Cohomological dimension (20J05).** $\mathrm{cd}\,G\le n$ when $\mathbb Z$ has a projective resolution of length $n$ over $\mathbb ZG$. Groups with torsion have $\mathrm{cd}=\infty$; $\mathrm{cd}\,G=0$ iff $G=1$; Stallings (finitely generated case, 1968) and Swan (1969) proved $\mathrm{cd}\,G=1$ iff $G$ is free and nontrivial; fundamental groups of closed aspherical $n$-manifolds have $\mathrm{cd}=n$. ([Brown, Examples 2.4](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf); [Wikipedia, Cohomological dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomological_dimension)) $\mathrm{cd}\,G\le\mathrm{gd}\,G$ (the least dimension of a $K(G,1)$), with equality except possibly when $\mathrm{cd}\,G=2$, $\mathrm{gd}\,G=3$; and by Serre, a torsion-free group has $\mathrm{cd}\,H=\mathrm{cd}\,G$ for every finite-index subgroup $H$. ([Brown, Thms 2.5, 4.4](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf))
- **Finiteness properties $F_n$ and $FP_n$.** $G$ is of type $F_n$ if it has a $K(G,1)$ with finite $n$-skeleton and $FP_n$ if $\mathbb Z$ has a projective resolution finitely generated through degree $n$: $F_1=FP_1$ is finite generation, $F_2$ is finite presentation, $FP_2$ is strictly weaker (Bestvina–Brady), and for $2\le n\le\infty$ a group is $F_n$ iff it is finitely presented and $FP_n$. A group is finitely presented and of type $FP$ iff $K(G,1)$ is finitely dominated, which connects these questions to Wall's finiteness obstruction. ([Brown, Defs 2.6, 2.8, Remarks 2.12](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf)) See [MSC 19Jxx - Obstructions from topology](node:MSC%2019Jxx%20-%20Obstructions%20from%20topology).
- **Tate cohomology and finite groups.** For finite $G$, Tate cohomology splices homology and cohomology via the norm map, and finite cyclic groups have 2-periodic Tate cohomology with $H^{2k}(C_m,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/m$ for $k\ge1$. ([Wikipedia, Group cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology)) A finite group acting freely on $S^{2k-1}$ has $\hat H^n\cong\hat H^{n+2k}$, and periodicity is equivalent to some $\hat H^d(G,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/|G|$ with $d\ne0$. ([Brown, §6.5, Prop. 6.6](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf))
- **Evens–Venkov and Quillen.** For a finite group $G$ and a field $k$ of characteristic $p$, $H^*(G,k)$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra, and $H^*(G,M)$ is a finitely generated $H^*(G,k)$-module for finitely generated $kG$-modules $M$ (Venkov 1959, Evens 1961). Quillen proved the Atiyah–Swan conjecture: the Krull dimension of the mod-$p$ cohomology ring equals the $p$-rank of $G$, the maximal rank of an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup; his stratification theorem glues the maximal ideal spectrum of $H^*(G,k)$ ($k$ algebraically closed) from those of the elementary abelian $p$-subgroups. ([Stephan, Thms 3.3, 3.5 and introduction](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/birep/activities/topics/files/ws20-stephan-quillen-stratification.pdf))

### History
Brown traces the subject to Hurewicz's 1936 paper on aspherical spaces and to Hopf's 1942 formula for $H_2$. ([Brown, §0](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf)) Group cohomology was then found independently in 1943–45 by Eilenberg and Mac Lane, Hopf and Eckmann, Freudenthal, and Faddeev. ([Wikipedia, Group cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology)) Lyndon's spectral sequence dates from 1948 and Hochschild–Serre's from 1953, Eilenberg and Ganea posed their problem in 1957, and Quillen's papers on the structure of the cohomology ring appeared in 1971–72. ([Wikipedia, LHS spectral sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon%E2%80%93Hochschild%E2%80%93Serre_spectral_sequence); [Wikipedia, Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Ganea_conjecture); [Stephan, introduction](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/birep/activities/topics/files/ws20-stephan-quillen-stratification.pdf)) Brown's *Cohomology of Groups* appeared in Springer's Graduate Texts in Mathematics in 1982. ([Crossref, Brown](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-9327-6))

### Open problems
- **Eilenberg–Ganea problem.** Does every group of cohomological dimension 2 have a 2-dimensional $K(G,1)$? Brown calls it "the famous Eilenberg–Ganea problem", and it is listed as unsolved; Bestvina and Brady (1997) built a group that is a counterexample either to it or to the Whitehead conjecture, so the two cannot both hold. ([Brown, §2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf); [Wikipedia, Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eilenberg%E2%80%93Ganea_conjecture))
- **$FP$ versus $F$.** Brown's Question 2.9 (is a finitely presented group of type $FP$ of type $F$?) and Question 2.11 ($FP$ implies $FL$?) are open; they would follow if finitely generated projective $\mathbb ZG$-modules were stably free for torsion-free $G$, which "a famous conjecture asserts". He also records as "still open" whether a finite-dimensional group of type $F_\infty$ is of type $F$. ([Brown, Remark 2.7, Questions 2.9, 2.11, Remark 2.12](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Group cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology): definitions, low-degree interpretations, Tate cohomology and history.
- **Learn:** [Brown, Lectures on the Cohomology of Groups](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/papers/cohomology_hangzhou.pdf): aspherical spaces, finiteness conditions, Eckmann–Shapiro, transfer, spectral sequences and Tate cohomology.
- **Learn:** [Stephan, Quillen's stratification theorem](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/birep/activities/topics/files/ws20-stephan-quillen-stratification.pdf): seminar notes on Evens–Venkov, Quillen–Venkov and Krull dimension.
- **Primary:** [Brown, Cohomology of Groups (Springer GTM, 1982)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-9327-6): the standard graduate monograph.
- **Further reading:** [Eilenberg–Mac Lane, General Theory of Natural Equivalences (Trans. AMS 58, 1945)](https://people.math.osu.edu/cogdell.1/6112-Eilenberg%26MacLane-www.pdf): founding paper, including groups as categories.
references.MSC 20Kxx - Abelian groups:
## Reference
### Overview
20K is the theory of [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups), equivalently $\mathbb Z$-modules, and its research content is overwhelmingly about infinite groups. The finitely generated case is closed: every finitely generated abelian group is $\mathbb Z^r\oplus F$ with $F$ finite, where $r$ and the prime-power orders of the cyclic summands of $F$ are invariants. Beyond that, the classical picture splits a group into torsion, torsion-free and mixed behaviour, and the classification theorems for divisible groups, countable torsion groups and rank-one torsion-free groups were all obtained before 1950. ([Wikipedia, Abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group))

The later subject is shaped by two facts. First, beyond those special classes there is no usable complete invariant: Paolini and Shelah proved that the isomorphism relation on countable torsion-free abelian groups is Borel complete, as complicated as an isomorphism relation can be. ([Paolini–Shelah, arXiv 2102.12371](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12371)) Second, natural questions such as the Whitehead problem turn out to be independent of ZFC, so [set theory](node:Set%20Theory) is a working tool in the field. ([Wikipedia, Whitehead problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_problem))

### Scope
MSC2020 20K lists: 20K01 finite abelian groups (for sumsets see 11B13, 11P70); 20K10 torsion groups, primary groups and generalized primary groups; 20K15 torsion-free groups, finite rank; 20K20 torsion-free groups, infinite rank; 20K21 mixed groups; 20K25 direct sums, direct products, etc.; 20K27 subgroups; 20K30 automorphisms, homomorphisms, endomorphisms, etc.; 20K35 extensions; 20K40 homological and categorical methods; 20K45 topological methods (see also 22A05, 22B05); 20K99. ([MSC2020, 20K](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Kxx))

Neighbours: the cross-references send additive [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) of sumsets to number theory (11B13, 11P70), and topological methods to [22A05](node:MSC%2022Axx%20-%20Topological%20and%20differentiable%20algebraic%20systems) and [22B05](node:MSC%2022Bxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20abelian%20groups%20%28LCA%20groups%29), where topological and locally compact abelian groups are classified. ([MSC2020, 20K](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Kxx)) Non-commutative [group theory](node:Group%20Theory) sits elsewhere in [MSC 20 - Group theory and generalizations](node:MSC%2020%20-%20Group%20theory%20and%20generalizations).

### Key concepts
- **Divisible groups (20K10, 20K40).** $D$ is divisible if multiplication by every $n\ge1$ is surjective; an abelian group is injective as a $\mathbb Z$-module if and only if it is divisible (via Baer's criterion). ([Sharifi, Algebra ch. 12, Def. 12.4.16, Prop. 12.4.17](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/algebra-ch12.html)) Every divisible group is a direct sum of copies of $\mathbb Q$ and Prüfer groups $\mathbb Z(p^\infty)$ with uniquely determined multiplicities, and a divisible subgroup is always a direct summand; a group with no nonzero divisible subgroup is called reduced. ([Wikipedia, Abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group))
- **Purity and the Prüfer–Kulikov theorems (20K10, 20K25, 20K27).** A subgroup $S\le A$ is pure if whenever $a\in S$ has an $n$th root (here $nx=a$) in $A$ it has one in $S$; direct summands and the torsion subgroup are pure, and Kulikov (1941) showed pure subgroups of finite exponent are direct summands. ([Wikipedia, Pure subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_subgroup)) First Prüfer theorem: an abelian group of bounded exponent is a direct sum of cyclic groups. Second Prüfer theorem: a countable abelian $p$-group whose nonzero elements have finite $p$-height is a direct sum of cyclic groups, and countability cannot be dropped. Kulikov's criterion: an abelian $p$-group is a direct sum of cyclic groups if and only if it is the union of an ascending sequence of subgroups $A_1\subseteq A_2\subseteq\cdots$ such that the heights of elements of each $A_i$ are bounded by a constant depending on $i$. ([Wikipedia, Prüfer theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%BCfer_theorems))
- **Basic subgroups (20K10, 20K27).** For a prime $p$, $B\le A$ is $p$-basic if $B$ is a direct sum of cyclic groups of order $p^n$ and infinite cyclic groups, $B$ is $p$-pure in $A$, and $A/B$ is $p$-divisible. Every abelian group has $p$-basic subgroups for each $p$, any two are isomorphic, and the quotient $A/B$ may depend on the choice. The notion is due to Kulikov for $p$-groups (his 1945 *Mat. Sb.* paper) and to Fuchs in general. ([Wikipedia, Basic subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_subgroup))
- **Ulm's theorem (20K10).** For a $p$-group $A$ set $U_0(A)=A$, $U_{\sigma+1}(A)=p^\omega U_\sigma(A)=\bigcap_n p^nU_\sigma(A)$, with intersections at limits; the Ulm factors are $U_\sigma/U_{\sigma+1}$. Ulm (1933): two countable abelian $p$-groups with isomorphic Ulm factors for every ordinal $\sigma$ and isomorphic $p$-divisible parts are isomorphic. In Kaplansky–Mackey form, a countable reduced torsion group is determined by the Ulm invariants $\dim_{\mathbb F_p}(p^\alpha A)[p]/(p^{\alpha+1}A)[p]$ over all primes $p$ and countable ordinals $\alpha$. The complementary existence theorem, realizing prescribed countable Ulm factors by a reduced $p$-group, was stated by Zippin (1935) and proved in Kurosh (1960). ([Wikipedia, Ulm's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulm%27s_theorem))
- **Torsion-free groups (20K15, 20K20).** The rank is $\dim_{\mathbb Q}(\mathbb Q\otimes A)$; rank-one torsion-free groups are exactly the subgroups of $\mathbb Q$, and for a nonzero $x$ the type function assigns to each prime $p$ the largest $k$ with $x\in p^kA$, or $\infty$ if there is none, and the choice of $x$ does not matter. Baer (1937) proved that two rank-one groups are isomorphic exactly when their type functions agree except at finitely many primes where both values are finite, so the type modulo this equivalence is a complete invariant. ([Wikipedia, Torsion-free abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torsion-free_abelian_group)) In finite rank the problem is genuinely harder: Baer's rank-one classification is already not smooth, Hjorth showed rank 2 is strictly more complicated than rank 1, and Thomas proved $\cong_n<_B\cong_{n+1}$ for every $n$. ([Coskey, arXiv 0909.0666, Introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0666)) The Baer–Specker group $\mathbb Z^{\mathbb N}$ is not free (Baer, 1937), although every countable subgroup of it is free (Specker, 1950), and its homomorphisms to $\mathbb Z$ form a free group of countable rank. ([Wikipedia, Baer–Specker group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baer%E2%80%93Specker_group))
- **Extensions and the Whitehead problem (20K35, 20K40).** $A$ is a Whitehead group if $\operatorname{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb Z)=0$ (in the sense of [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra)), i.e. every extension $0\to\mathbb Z\to B\to A\to0$ splits. Free groups are Whitehead, and Stein (1951) proved countable Whitehead groups are free. Shelah showed that under $V=L$ every Whitehead group is free, while under Martin's axiom plus $\neg$CH there is a non-free Whitehead group, so the problem is independent of ZFC, and it stays undecidable even assuming CH. ([Wikipedia, Whitehead problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_problem)) In a mixed group the torsion subgroup $T(A)$ is pure but need not be a direct summand, which is why 20K21 is separate. ([Wikipedia, Pure subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_subgroup); [Wikipedia, Abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group))

### History
Camille Jordan named abelian groups after Abel. Prüfer studied pure subgroups in 1923, Kulikov's 1941 work used them systematically, his 1945 paper treats basic subgroups of $p$-groups, and Ulm's theorem dates from 1933; Kaplansky and Mackey's 1951 proof became the model for later generalizations. ([Wikipedia, Abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group); [Wikipedia, Pure subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_subgroup); [Wikipedia, Basic subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_subgroup); [Wikipedia, Ulm's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulm%27s_theorem)) Shelah's independence results on the Whitehead problem date from 1974–1980. ([Wikipedia, Whitehead problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead_problem)) Paolini and Shelah's Borel-completeness theorem appeared in *Annals of Mathematics* 199 (2024), solving a problem going back to Friedman and Stanley (1989). ([Paolini–Shelah, arXiv 2102.12371](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12371)) Fuchs's *Abelian Groups* was published in Springer Monographs in Mathematics in 2015. ([Crossref, Fuchs 2015](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-19422-6))

### Open problems
- **Fuchs' problem on unit groups.** Which abelian groups occur as the group of units of a commutative ring? Fuchs asked this more than fifty years ago; Chebolu and Lockridge state that "the question remains open" and settle it for indecomposable abelian groups (see [Units and Idempotents in Rings](node:Units%20and%20Idempotents%20in%20Rings)). ([Chebolu–Lockridge, arXiv 1505.03508](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.03508))
- **Torsion-free groups of infinite rank.** Among torsion-free groups of finite rank only the finitely generated and rank-one cases are well understood, and many problems on torsion-free groups of infinite rank are unsolved; countable mixed groups are also much less developed than countable torsion groups. ([Wikipedia, Abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group): divisible, torsion, torsion-free and mixed groups, invariants, Whitehead problem.
- **Learn:** [Sharifi, Algebra notes ch. 12](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/notes/algebra-ch12.html): injective modules, Baer's criterion, divisible = injective for abelian groups.
- **Primary:** [Paolini–Shelah, Torsion-free abelian groups are Borel complete (Ann. Math. 2024; arXiv 2102.12371)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12371): the countable torsion-free classification problem is maximally complex.
- **Primary:** [Coskey, Borel reductions of profinite actions of SL(n,Z) (arXiv 0909.0666)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0666): introduction surveys Baer, Hjorth and Thomas on finite-rank classification.
- **Further reading:** [Fuchs, Abelian Groups (Springer Monographs in Mathematics, 2015)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-19422-6): current standard monograph on the subject.
references.MSC 20Lxx - Groupoids (i.e. small catego:
## Reference
### Overview
A groupoid is a small category in which every morphism is invertible; a groupoid with one object is a [group](node:Group%20Theory), so groupoids generalize groups to symmetries between several objects. ([Groupoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupoid)) In [categorical](node:Category%20Theory) terms the morphisms $x\to x$ form the automorphism (vertex) group $\mathrm{Aut}(x)$, and for a space $X$ the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(X)$ has the points of $X$ as objects and endpoint-preserving homotopy classes of paths as morphisms, so that $\pi_1(X,x)=\mathrm{Aut}(x)$ in $\Pi_1(X)$. ([nLab: groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/groupoid))

Weinstein describes groupoids as unifying "internal and external" symmetry: they can be read as generalized groups and also as generalized equivalence relations, recording not only which objects are equivalent but the different isomorphisms between them. ([Weinstein](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9602220)) In algebraic topology, Brown and Higgins used the fundamental groupoid on a set of base points to compute [fundamental groups](node:Fundamental%20Group), and crossed modules and double groupoids to obtain nonabelian invariants in dimension 2 and higher. ([Brown, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274))

### Scope
MSC 20L has a single research code, 20L05, for groupoids in the sense of small categories in which all morphisms are isomorphisms. The entry explicitly sends sets with a single binary operation (also historically called groupoids, i.e. magmas) to [20N02](node:MSC%2020Nxx%20-%20Other%20generalizations%20of%20groups), and topological groupoids to 22A22 and 58H05; conversely, 20N02 refers categorical groupoids back to 20L05. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf)) Lie groupoids, which carry topology and differentiable structure, are topological groupoids and so belong mainly to [22A22](node:MSC%2022Axx%20-%20Topological%20and%20differentiable%20algebraic%20systems) and 58H05 rather than here. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf); [Groupoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupoid)) Groupoids viewed as categories also appear in 18B40 ("groupoids, semigroupoids, semigroups, groups (viewed as categories)"), which cross-references 20L05. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Structure up to equivalence.** A groupoid is transitive (connected) if it has a single orbit. Each connected component is equivalent, though not in general isomorphic, to a one-object groupoid, i.e. to its vertex group, so every groupoid is equivalent to a collection of groups; a transitive groupoid is isomorphic to an action groupoid. ([Groupoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupoid)) The equivalence with a disjoint union of groups depends on the axiom of choice, and for topological, Lie and internal groupoids the theory is genuinely richer than that of groups. ([nLab: groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/groupoid))
- **Pair groupoids, equivalence relations and actions.** For a set $B$, the pair groupoid $B\times B$ has exactly one arrow $x\to y$ for each pair; its wide subgroupoids are exactly the equivalence relations on $B$. Every groupoid $G$ over $B$ maps to $B\times B$ with image the orbit equivalence relation and kernel the union of the isotropy groups. ([Weinstein](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9602220)) For a group acting on a set, the action groupoid has the points as objects and the group elements as arrows, with vertex groups the stabilizers. ([Groupoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupoid))
- **Groupoid van Kampen theorem (Brown, 1967).** Let $X=U\cup V$ with $U,V$ open and $W=U\cap V$, and let $X_0$ meet each path component of $U$, $V$ and $W$. Then $X_0$ meets each path component of $X$, and the square of fundamental groupoids $\pi_1(W,X_0)\to\pi_1(U,X_0),\pi_1(V,X_0)\to\pi_1(X,X_0)$ induced by inclusions is a pushout of groupoids. ([Brown, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274)) With two base points this computes $\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb Z$, where the one-base-point theorem fails because $S^1$ is not a union of two open sets with connected intersection. ([Seifert–van Kampen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93Van_Kampen_theorem))
- **Combinatorial groupoid theory.** Computing a fundamental group from the theorem uses the algebra of groupoids, developed in Higgins' *Categories and Groupoids* (1971), including the groupoid $f_*(G)$ induced from a groupoid $G$ by a function on objects, a change-of-base construction. ([Seifert–van Kampen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93Van_Kampen_theorem); [Brown, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274)) Covering spaces of a reasonable space $X$ are equivalent to functors $\pi_1(X)\to\mathbf{Set}$, giving a second route to van Kampen theorems through covering morphisms. ([Brown, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274))
- **Crossed modules and double groupoids.** A crossed module is a homomorphism $d:H\to G$ with an action of $G$ on $H$ such that $d(g\cdot h)=g\,d(h)\,g^{-1}$ and $d(h_1)\cdot h_2=h_1h_2h_1^{-1}$ (Peiffer identity); the classifying space of a crossed module $d:H\to G$ has $\pi_1=\operatorname{coker}d$, $\pi_2=\ker d$ and no higher homotopy, and (pointed, weak) homotopy 2-types are completely described by crossed modules. ([Crossed module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossed_module)) Whitehead introduced crossed modules (1941–50) to describe the boundary map $\pi_2(X,A,x)\to\pi_1(A,x)$, and Mac Lane and Whitehead used his theorem on free crossed modules in their proof that crossed modules capture all homotopy 2-types. ([Brown, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274)) Brown and Spencer proved that crossed modules are equivalent to double groupoids with connections and one vertex, and Brown and Higgins built a homotopy double groupoid of a filtered space $X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq X$ and proved a 2-dimensional van Kampen theorem (1978); the higher-dimensional versions were proved by 1979, with full details published in 1981. ([Brown, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274); [Seifert–van Kampen theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seifert%E2%80%93Van_Kampen_theorem))

### History
Brandt introduced and named groupoids in a paper on the composition of quadratic forms in four variables; Ehresmann added topological and differentiable structure, making them a tool in differential topology and geometry; Grothendieck used them for moduli problems and Mackey, as "virtual groups", for ergodic actions. ([Weinstein](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9602220)) Brandt's paper dates from 1927. ([Groupoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupoid)) The word "groupoid" is also used for a set with a single binary operation (a magma), which is a different notion classified in 20N02. ([Groupoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupoid); [MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf)) Higgins' 1964 paper led to Brown's 1967 groupoid van Kampen theorem; the search for higher homotopy groupoids produced the 2-dimensional theorem in 1975–78 and the general theorems by 1979. ([Brown, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274)) Brown's 1987 *Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society* article "From groups to groupoids: a brief survey" surveys the subject's development. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/blms/19.2.113))

### Open problems
Brown's survey closes with questions it poses as open: whether higher homotopy groupoids have applications in other settings where the fundamental groupoid is used, such as algebraic geometry; whether there is a nonabelian de Rham theory using an analogue of crossed complexes, given the uses of double groupoids in Poisson geometry and 2-dimensional holonomy; and whether there is a truly noncommutative integration theory based on limits of multiple compositions in multiple groupoids. It also records that interpretations of higher-dimensional van Kampen theorems via descent, analogous to the covering-morphism approach in dimension 1, are not known. ([Brown, survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/groupoid): definitions, the fundamental groupoid, and the equivalence with disjoint unions of groups.
- **Learn:** [Weinstein, Groupoids: unifying internal and external symmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9602220): example-driven introduction (Notices AMS, 1996).
- **Primary:** [Brown, Crossed complexes and homotopy groupoids as non commutative tools for higher dimensional local-to-global problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0212274): survey of the groupoid and higher van Kampen theorems, crossed modules and open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Brown, From groups to groupoids: a brief survey](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/blms/19.2.113): Bull. London Math. Soc. 19 (1987) 113–134.
- **Further reading:** Brown, *Topology and Groupoids* (2006; earlier editions 1968 and 1988) and Higgins, *Categories and Groupoids* (1971), books giving accounts of induced groupoids $f_*(G)$ and of covering spaces as functors $\pi_1(X)\to\mathbf{Set}$, as cited in [Brown's survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0212274).
references.MSC 20Mxx - Semigroups:
## Reference
### Overview
A semigroup is a set with an associative binary operation, and a monoid is a semigroup with identity; any semigroup embeds in a monoid by adjoining an identity. ([Wikipedia, Semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup)) 20M is the structure and [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of [semigroups and monoids](node:Semigroups%20and%20Monoids). Unlike [group theory](node:Group%20Theory), elements need not be invertible, so the basic invariants are ideals and the Green's relations they induce; groups reappear inside a semigroup as its maximal subgroups. ([Wikipedia, Green's relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_relations))

The field has two strong poles. One is the algebraic structure theory founded by Suschkewitsch, who determined the structure of finite simple semigroups, and developed by Rees, Green, Lyapin, Clifford and Preston. ([Wikipedia, Semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup)) The other is finite semigroup theory as the algebra of [finite automata](node:Finite%20Automata), organized by the syntactic monoid, Krohn–Rhodes decomposition and Eilenberg's correspondence between pseudovarieties and language varieties. ([Wikipedia, Krohn–Rhodes theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krohn%E2%80%93Rhodes_theory); [Urbat et al., arXiv 1602.05831](https://arxiv.org/html/1602.05831))

### Scope
MSC2020 20M lists: 20M05 free semigroups, generators and relations, word problems (see also 03D40, 08A50, 20F10); 20M07 varieties and pseudovarieties; 20M10 general structure theory; 20M11 radical theory; 20M12 ideal theory; 20M13 arithmetic theory; 20M14 commutative semigroups; 20M15 mappings of semigroups; 20M17 regular semigroups; 20M18 inverse semigroups; 20M19 orthodox semigroups; 20M20 semigroups of transformations, relations, partitions, etc. (see also 47D03, 47H20, 54H15); 20M25 semigroup rings, multiplicative semigroups of rings (see also 16S36, 16Y60); 20M30 representation of semigroups, actions on sets; 20M32 algebraic monoids; 20M35 semigroups in automata theory, linguistics, etc. (see also 03D05, 68Q70, 68T50); 20M50 connections with [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) and [category theory](node:Category%20Theory); 20M75 generalizations of semigroups; 20M99.
