([MSC2020, 20M](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Mxx))

Neighbours named by the cross-references: word problems are shared with [03D40](node:MSC%2003Dxx%20-%20Computability%20and%20recursion%20theory), [08A50](node:MSC%2008Axx%20-%20Algebraic%20structures) and [20F10](node:MSC%2020Fxx%20-%20Special%20aspects%20of%20infinite%20or%20finite%20groups); transformation semigroups are cross-referenced to [47D03](node:MSC%2047Dxx%20-%20Groups%20and%20semigroups%20of%20linear%20operators,%20their%20generalizations%20and%20applications), the code for semigroups of linear operators (see [Strongly Continuous Operator Semigroups](node:Strongly%20Continuous%20Operator%20Semigroups)); and the automata-theoretic side is shared with [68Q70](node:MSC%2068Qxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20computing). ([MSC2020, 20M](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Mxx))

### Key concepts
- **Green's relations (20M10).** With $S^1$ the semigroup with identity adjoined: $a\,\mathcal L\,b\iff S^1a=S^1b$, $a\,\mathcal R\,b\iff aS^1=bS^1$, $a\,\mathcal J\,b\iff S^1aS^1=S^1bS^1$, $\mathcal H=\mathcal L\cap\mathcal R$, and $\mathcal D=\mathcal L\circ\mathcal R=\mathcal R\circ\mathcal L$, the join of $\mathcal L$ and $\mathcal R$. In the egg-box picture of a $\mathcal D$-class, rows are $\mathcal R$-classes, columns $\mathcal L$-classes and cells $\mathcal H$-classes, all of the same size. Always $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal J$, with equality in finite semigroups. Green's theorem: for an $\mathcal H$-class $H$, either $H^2\cap H=\varnothing$ or $H$ is a subgroup; so $H_e$ is the maximal subgroup at an idempotent $e$ and no $\mathcal H$-class contains two idempotents. ([Wikipedia, Green's relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_relations))
- **Rees's theorem (20M10).** For a group $G$, sets $I,\Lambda$ and a $\Lambda\times I$ matrix $P$ over $G$, the Rees matrix semigroup $\mathcal M(G;I,\Lambda;P)$ is $I\times G\times\Lambda$ with $(i,g,\lambda)(j,h,\mu)=(i,\,g\,p_{\lambda j}\,h,\,\mu)$. Rees (1940): a semigroup is completely simple iff it is isomorphic to some $\mathcal M(G;I,\Lambda;P)$. In the version with zero, $\mathcal M(G^0;I,\Lambda;P)$ is regular iff every row and column of $P$ has a nonzero entry, and then it is completely 0-simple. ([Wikipedia, Rees matrix semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rees_matrix_semigroup)) Suschkewitsch (1928) had found the structure of finite simple semigroups and showed the minimal ideal of a finite semigroup is simple. ([Wikipedia, Semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup))
- **Inverse semigroups (20M18).** $S$ is inverse if each $x$ has a unique $y$ with $x=xyx$, $y=yxy$; equivalently $S$ is regular and its idempotents commute (form a semilattice). Wagner–Preston theorem: $a\mapsto(x\mapsto xa$ on $Sa^{-1})$ is a faithful representation of $S$ in the symmetric inverse semigroup of partial bijections of $S$, the analogue of Cayley's theorem. Munn showed elements of free inverse semigroups can be represented as trees (Munn trees); McAlister's covering theorem gives every inverse semigroup an $E$-unitary cover, and the $P$-theorem builds all $E$-unitary ones from McAlister triples. ([Wikipedia, Inverse semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_semigroup))
- **Transformation semigroups (20M20, 20M30).** The full transformation monoid $T_X$ of all maps $X\to X$ contains every transformation semigroup, and every finite semigroup $S$ is a transformation semigroup on a set of at most $|S|+1$ points ($|S|$ if $S$ is a monoid). A deterministic automaton with states $Q$ and alphabet $A$ gives a monoid morphism $A^*\to T_Q$ whose image is its transformation semigroup. ([Wikipedia, Transformation semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_semigroup))
- **Krohn–Rhodes theory (20M35).** Every finite semigroup divides an iterated wreath product of [finite simple groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups) dividing $S$ and finite aperiodic semigroups (Krohn and Rhodes, announced 1962, published 1965); for automata, every finite automaton is emulated by a cascade of permutation automata of simple groups and banks of flip-flops. The complexity of $S$ is the least number of group factors needed. ([Wikipedia, Krohn–Rhodes theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krohn%E2%80%93Rhodes_theory))
- **Syntactic monoids and Eilenberg's theorem (20M07, 20M35).** The syntactic monoid of a language $L$ is the smallest monoid recognizing it, equal to the transition monoid of the minimal automaton; Schützenberger proved $L$ is star-free iff its syntactic monoid is finite and aperiodic. ([Wikipedia, Syntactic monoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syntactic_monoid)) Eilenberg's variety theorem puts varieties of regular languages (closed under Boolean operations, quotients and inverse homomorphic images) in bijection with pseudovarieties of finite monoids (closed under quotients, submonoids and finite products), and Reiterman's theorem says pseudovarieties are defined by profinite equations. ([Urbat et al., arXiv 1602.05831](https://arxiv.org/html/1602.05831)) This is the algebraic side of [Automata and Formal Languages](node:Automata%20and%20Formal%20Languages) and [Regular Expressions](node:Regular%20Expressions).

### History
De Séguier first used the term (in French) in 1904 and Hinton in English in 1908; Suschkewitsch's 1928 paper gave the first non-trivial results. Clifford and Preston's two-volume monograph appeared in 1961 and 1967, and *Semigroup Forum* began in 1970. ([Wikipedia, Semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semigroup); [Crossref, Clifford–Preston vol. I](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/007.1)) Rees's theorem dates from 1940 and Green's relations from his 1951 *Annals* paper; inverse semigroups were introduced by Wagner (1952) and independently by Preston (1954). ([Wikipedia, Rees matrix semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rees_matrix_semigroup); [Wikipedia, Green's relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_relations); [Wikipedia, Inverse semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_semigroup))

> [!warning] Contested
> Decidability of Krohn–Rhodes complexity was long called a major open problem of finite semigroup theory; Margolis, Rhodes and Schilling announced an affirmative proof in June 2024, which Wikipedia describes as not yet confirmed as of 2025. ([Wikipedia, Krohn–Rhodes theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krohn%E2%80%93Rhodes_theory)) The authors' survey states that complexity is computable, solving a problem open for more than 50 years. ([Margolis–Rhodes–Schilling, arXiv 2501.00770](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00770))

### Open problems
- **Černý conjecture (20M20, 20M35).** A transformation semigroup is synchronizing if it contains an element of rank 1. Černý conjectured in 1969 that every synchronizing complete deterministic automaton with $n$ states has a synchronizing word of length at most $(n-1)^2$, a bound his 1964 examples attain. It is open; the best general upper bound, $\approx0.1654\,n^3$, is due to Shitov (2019). ([Wikipedia, Synchronizing word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronizing_word))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Green's relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_relations): definitions, egg-box picture, Green's theorem.
- **Learn:** [University of York, Semigroup Theory (MAT00100M)](https://www.york.ac.uk/students/studying/manage/programmes/module-catalogue/module/MAT00100M/2025-26): course syllabus covering Green's relations, Rees's theorem, inverse semigroups and bands, with Howie's *Fundamentals of Semigroup Theory* as indicative reading.
- **Primary:** [Margolis–Rhodes–Schilling, Complexity of Finite Semigroups: History and Decidability (arXiv 2501.00770)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00770): survey of Krohn–Rhodes complexity and its computability.
- **Primary:** [Urbat–Adámek–Chen–Milius, Eilenberg Theorems for Free (arXiv 1602.05831)](https://arxiv.org/html/1602.05831): Eilenberg, Schützenberger and Reiterman theorems and their generalizations.
- **Further reading:** [Clifford–Preston, The Algebraic Theory of Semigroups, Vol. I (AMS, 1961)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/007.1): the classic monograph on the algebraic theory.
references.MSC 20Nxx - Other generalizations of gro:
## Reference
### Overview
20N collects algebraic systems that keep part of the group axioms and drop the rest: sets with one binary operation and no axioms (magmas), quasigroups and loops (division without associativity), ternary heaps, $n$-ary groups, multivalued hypergroups and fuzzy groups. In the hierarchy of magma-like structures a quasigroup is a magma in which division is always possible, a loop is a quasigroup with identity, and a group is an associative loop. ([Wikipedia, Magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma_%28algebra%29); [MSC2020, 20N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Nxx))

The research core is the theory of [loops and quasigroups](node:Loops%20and%20Quasigroups) (20N05): loops studied through their multiplication groups, nuclei and identities such as Moufang's and Bol's, with active problem lists in each direction. ([Wikipedia, Problems in loop theory and quasigroup theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_loop_theory_and_quasigroup_theory)) Its central classification ties finite simple Moufang loops to split [octonion](node:Octonions) (Cayley) algebras over finite fields, the associative ones being the [finite simple groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups) ([Liebeck 1987](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/classification-of-finite-simple-moufang-loops/02FBE39338FC77C639059653939B48F4)), and smooth loops have a nonassociative Lie theory in which Akivis and Sabinin algebras play the role of Lie algebras. ([Pérez-Izquierdo, arXiv 1803.04441](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1803.04441))

### Scope
MSC2020 20N lists: 20N02 sets with a single binary operation (groupoids), with groupoids in the category-theoretic sense sent to 20L05 and topological groupoids to 22A22, 58H05; 20N05 loops, quasigroups (see also 05Bxx); 20N10 ternary systems (heaps, semiheaps, heapoids, etc.); 20N15 $n$-ary systems ($n\ge3$); 20N20 hypergroups; 20N25 fuzzy groups (see also 03E72); 20N99. ([MSC2020, 20N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Nxx))

Neighbours: Brandt-style [groupoids](node:Groupoids) (small categories with invertible morphisms) are [20L](node:MSC%2020Lxx%20-%20Groupoids%20%28i.e.%20small%20categories%20in%20which%20all%20morphisms%20are%20isomorphisms%29), not 20N02; Latin squares as combinatorial designs are [05B](node:MSC%2005Bxx%20-%20Designs%20and%20configurations); fuzzy [set theory](node:Set%20Theory) itself is 03E72 in [03E](node:MSC%2003Exx%20-%20Set%20theory); semigroups are [20M](node:MSC%2020Mxx%20-%20Semigroups). ([MSC2020, 20N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Nxx); [MSC2020, 05B15](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=05Bxx); [MSC2020, 03E72](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Exx); [MSC2020, 20M](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Mxx))

### Key concepts
- **Magmas (20N02).** A set with a closed binary operation and nothing else; the free magma on $X$ consists of non-associative words, equivalently full binary trees with leaves in $X$, and every map $X\to N$ into a magma extends uniquely to a morphism. The name "groupoid" (Hausmann and Ore, 1937) clashes with Brandt's 1927 groupoids. ([Wikipedia, Magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma_%28algebra%29))
- **Quasigroups, loops and Latin squares (20N05).** $(Q,\ast)$ is a quasigroup if $a\ast x=b$ and $y\ast a=b$ have unique solutions for all $a,b$, equivalently its table is a Latin square; an equational version uses divisions $\backslash,/$. An isotopy is a triple of bijections $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ with $\alpha(x)\beta(y)=\gamma(xy)$, and every quasigroup is isotopic to a loop. Up to isomorphism there are $1,1,5,35,1411,1130531$ quasigroups and $1,1,1,2,6,109$ loops of orders $1$–$6$. ([Wikipedia, Quasigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasigroup)) Latin squares are counted exactly only up to order 11, the total count being $n!(n-1)!$ times the number of reduced squares, and the best known upper and lower bounds for large $n$ are far apart. ([Wikipedia, Latin square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_square))
- **Multiplication groups and nuclei (20N05).** With $L_x(y)=xy$, $R_x(y)=yx$, the multiplication group is $\mathrm{Mlt}(Q)=\langle L_x,R_x\rangle$ and the inner mapping group $\mathrm{Inn}(Q)$ is the stabilizer of $1$; Bruck proved $\mathrm{Inn}(Q)=\langle L_{x,y},R_{x,y},T_x\rangle$ with $L_{x,y}(z)=(yx)\backslash(y(xz))$, $R_{x,y}(z)=((zx)y)/(xy)$, $T_x(y)=x\backslash(yx)$. A loop is automorphic if $\mathrm{Inn}(Q)\le\mathrm{Aut}(Q)$. Nuclei are always characteristic but not necessarily normal subloops; in automorphic loops characteristic subloops are normal. ([Vojtěchovský, Three lectures](https://cs.du.edu/~petr/data/papers/three_lectures_on_automorphic_loops.pdf))
- **Bol and Bruck loops (20N05).** A left Bol loop satisfies $a(b(ac))=(a(ba))c$ (Bol, 1937). A Bol loop with $(ab)^{-1}=a^{-1}b^{-1}$ is a Bruck loop (K-loop); positive definite Hermitian matrices form a left Bruck loop under $A\ast B=P$, the positive factor in the polar decomposition $AB=PU$, and left Bruck loops are equivalent to Ungar's gyrocommutative gyrogroups. A loop is Moufang iff it is left and right Bol, and a one-sided Bol loop is Moufang iff it is flexible. ([Wikipedia, Bol loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bol_loop)) **Glauberman's theorem:** a left Bruck loop of odd order is solvable, has the Lagrange property, has Sylow and Hall subloops and a left multiplication group of odd order, and is centrally nilpotent if its order is a power of an odd prime. ([Vojtěchovský, Thm 2.2](https://cs.du.edu/~petr/data/papers/three_lectures_on_automorphic_loops.pdf))
- **Moufang loops and their classification (20N05).** **Moufang's theorem:** if $x,y,z$ in a Moufang loop satisfy $(xy)z=x(yz)$, they generate a group; hence Moufang loops are diassociative. The nonzero octonions and the unit-norm octonions form Moufang loops. Every finite Moufang loop has the Lagrange property (Grishkov–Zavarnitsine; Gagola–Hall, 2003). Every finite nonassociative simple Moufang loop is a Paige loop over a [finite field](node:Finite%20Fields), the smallest $M^\ast(2)$ having order 120. ([Wikipedia, Moufang loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moufang_loop)) The Paige loop $M^\ast(F)$ is the loop $M(F)$ of norm-one elements of the split octonion algebra over $F$ modulo its centre, which is $\{\pm e\}$, or $\{e\}$ in characteristic 2. ([Wikipedia, Moufang loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moufang_loop)) Liebeck (1987) carried out the classification. ([Liebeck 1987](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/classification-of-finite-simple-moufang-loops/02FBE39338FC77C639059653939B48F4)) Nagy and Vojtěchovský reprove it with geometric loop theory, linking composition algebras, simple Moufang 3-nets and groups with triality. ([arXiv math/0701707](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0701707)) **Csörgő's theorem** (J. Algebra 603, 2022): a nontrivial Moufang loop of odd order has a nontrivial nucleus. ([Drápal–Vojtěchovský, arXiv 2301.03646, Thm 5.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2301.03646))
- **Commutative Moufang loops (20N05).** In a commutative Moufang loop every associator has order dividing 3 and $Q/Z(Q)$ has exponent 3. **Bruck–Slaby theorem:** for $n\ge3$, a commutative Moufang loop generated by $n$ elements is centrally nilpotent of class at most $n-1$. ([Sandu, arXiv 0804.3958, (1.4), Lemmas 1.5, 1.7](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0804.3958)) Commutative Moufang loops are automorphic. ([Vojtěchovský, Prop. 1.14](https://cs.du.edu/~petr/data/papers/three_lectures_on_automorphic_loops.pdf))
- **Analytic loops.** Hofmann and Strambach proved that the tangent algebra of a local analytic loop is an Akivis algebra, and Akivis algebras integrate to local analytic loops, but non-isomorphic local loops can share an Akivis algebra. Mikheev and Sabinin's finer Sabinin algebras fix this: two local loops are isomorphic iff their Sabinin tangent algebras are. Malcev extended Lie's fundamental theorems to some varieties of loops, and Kuzmin integrated Malcev algebras to local analytic Moufang loops. ([arXiv 1803.04441](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1803.04441)) Compare [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) and [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups).
- **Heaps and $n$-ary groups (20N10, 20N15).** A heap has a ternary operation with $[[a,b,c],d,e]=[a,[d,c,b],e]=[a,b,[c,d,e]]$ and $[h,h,k]=k=[k,h,h]$; a group gives a heap by $[x,y,z]=xy^{-1}z$, and fixing any $e$ recovers a group with $ab=[a,e,b]$, so a heap is a group with its identity forgotten (term from Sushkevich, 1937). ([Wikipedia, Heap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heap_%28mathematics%29)) An $n$-ary group is an $n$-ary semigroup that is an $n$-ary quasigroup; Dörnte (1928) showed that for $n>2$ some are not derived from binary groups, and Post (1940) proved a structure theorem relating each to an ordinary group. ([Wikipedia, n-ary group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-ary_group))
- **Hypergroups and fuzzy groups (20N20, 20N25).** Marty suggested hyperstructures in 1934; Krasner introduced hyperrings in 1956 to approximate valued fields, and Connes and Consani used Krasner's hyperfield in work connected to number theory. ([Jun, arXiv 1510.02979](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1510.02979)) A fuzzy subgroup of $G$ is $s:G\to[0,1]$ with $s(1)=1$, $s(x)\odot s(y)\le s(xy)$ and $s(x)\le s(x^{-1})$; for $\odot=\min$, $s$ is a fuzzy subalgebra iff every closed cut $\{x:s(x)\ge\lambda\}$ is a subalgebra. The article's references include Rosenfeld, "Fuzzy groups" (1971), and Zadeh, "Fuzzy sets" (1965). ([Wikipedia, Fuzzy subalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_subalgebra)) See [Fuzzy Sets and Information Measures](node:Fuzzy%20Sets%20and%20Information%20Measures).

### History
Moufang introduced her identities in 1935 and Bol his loops in 1937. ([Wikipedia, Moufang loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moufang_loop); [Wikipedia, Bol loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bol_loop)) Bruck's *A Survey of Binary Systems* appeared in 1958. ([Crossref, Bruck 1958](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-35338-7)) The study of automorphic loops began in earnest with Bruck and Paige in 1956, and automorphic loops became a focal area of loop theory after Jedlička, Kinyon and Vojtěchovský's work on commutative automorphic loops; Glauberman's 1960s papers on loops of odd order developed Bruck loops to study Moufang loops. ([Vojtěchovský, Three lectures](https://cs.du.edu/~petr/data/papers/three_lectures_on_automorphic_loops.pdf)) The Lagrange property for finite Moufang loops was settled in 2003, and Moufang loops of order 64 were classified by Nagy and Vojtěchovský (4262 nonassociative ones). ([Wikipedia, Problems in loop theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_loop_theory_and_quasigroup_theory))

### Open problems
- **Simple automorphic loops.** Is there a finite simple nonassociative automorphic loop (Problem 4.1)? Is there an automorphic loop of odd order with trivial middle nucleus (4.2)? Does every subloop of a finite automorphic loop have order dividing $|Q|$ (4.3)? No finite simple nonassociative automorphic loop has order less than 4096 (computer searches by Johnson–Kinyon–Nagy–Vojtěchovský and Cameron–Leemans). ([Vojtěchovský, Prop. 3.9, Problems 4.1–4.3](https://cs.du.edu/~petr/data/papers/three_lectures_on_automorphic_loops.pdf)) The first is also listed as open, with the remark that such a loop cannot be commutative or of odd order. ([Wikipedia, Problems in loop theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_loop_theory_and_quasigroup_theory))
- **Niemenmaa's conjecture.** If $\mathrm{Inn}(Q)$ is nilpotent, must $Q$ be nilpotent, and must it be solvable? Niemenmaa (2009) answered the first question affirmatively for finite $Q$; the general case is listed as open. ([Wikipedia, Problems in loop theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_loop_theory_and_quasigroup_theory))
- **Abelian inner mapping groups.** Finite loops with abelian $\mathrm{Inn}(Q)$ are nilpotent; for infinite loops nilpotency is open, as is whether the class is bounded: Csörgő-type loops of class 3 exist, none of higher class is known. ([Wikipedia, Problems in loop theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_loop_theory_and_quasigroup_theory))
- **Moufang loops.** Open: the restricted Burnside problem (is the order of a finite $m$-generated Moufang loop of exponent $n$ bounded by a function of $m,n$? known for prime and prime-power exponents); presentations of all finite simple nonassociative Moufang loops (each is 3-generated); whether the Frattini subloop of a finite Moufang loop is normal and nilpotent; and whether every finite commutative Moufang loop of period 3 embeds in a commutative alternative algebra. ([Wikipedia, Problems in loop theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_loop_theory_and_quasigroup_theory))
- **Analytic Bol loops and Latin squares.** Determining the Campbell–Hausdorff series of analytic Bol loops (partly solved for Bruck loops), and whether a matching-based procedure generates Latin squares uniformly, are listed as open. ([Wikipedia, Problems in loop theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_loop_theory_and_quasigroup_theory))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Quasigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasigroup): definitions, Latin squares, isotopy, small-order counts; [Problems in loop theory and quasigroup theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_loop_theory_and_quasigroup_theory): maintained problem list with status.
- **Learn:** [Vojtěchovský, Three lectures on automorphic loops (Loops '15)](https://cs.du.edu/~petr/data/papers/three_lectures_on_automorphic_loops.pdf): multiplication groups, nuclei, Bruck loops, Glauberman's theorems and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Nagy–Vojtěchovský, Octonions, simple Moufang loops and triality (Quasigroups Related Systems 10, 2003; arXiv math/0701707)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0701707): survey reproving that nonassociative finite simple Moufang loops are Paige loops; [Liebeck, The classification of finite simple Moufang loops (1987)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/classification-of-finite-simple-moufang-loops/02FBE39338FC77C639059653939B48F4); [Pérez-Izquierdo, arXiv 1803.04441](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1803.04441): nonassociative Lie theory of loops.
- **Further reading:** [Bruck, *A Survey of Binary Systems* (Springer, 1958)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-35338-7): the classic monograph; [Smith, *An Introduction to Quasigroups and Their Representations* (Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9781420010633): modern monograph.
references.MSC 20Pxx - Probabilistic methods in gro:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 section 20Pxx, "Probabilistic methods in group theory", (cross-referenced to 60Bxx) contains the two codes 20P05 (the same title) and 20P99 (none of the above, but in this section). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Pxx)) It collects work in which probability is used on groups: random elements and random generating tuples in finite or profinite groups, distributions of word maps, random walks and randomized algorithms on groups, and random presentations of infinite groups. ([Burness survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10434); [Annals 2019](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2019/190-2/p03); [Pak lecture](https://www.math.ucla.edu/%7Epak/courses/pg/l33.tex); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_group))

Both 20Pxx and 20P05 carry the cross-reference 60Bxx, in probability theory. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20Pxx)) The groups studied are often finite simple groups ([MSC 20Dxx - Abstract finite groups](node:MSC%2020Dxx%20-%20Abstract%20finite%20groups)) or alternating and symmetric groups ([MSC 20Bxx - Permutation groups](node:MSC%2020Bxx%20-%20Permutation%20groups)), and the product replacement algorithm is analysed as a reversible Markov chain, as in the theory of [Random Walks on Groups](node:Random%20Walks%20on%20Groups). ([Burness survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10434); [Pak lecture](https://www.math.ucla.edu/%7Epak/courses/pg/l33.tex))

### Scope
Within [MSC 20 - Group theory and generalizations](node:MSC%2020%20-%20Group%20theory%20and%20generalizations), 20P05 is the only substantive code. The area has several models: uniform random elements of a finite group (commuting probability, random generation), Haar-random tuples in a profinite group (positive finite generation, subgroup growth), values of word maps on finite simple groups, the product replacement chain for sampling, and random presentations (few-relator and Gromov density models). ([Segal](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0703885); [Larsen–Shalev–Tiep](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2011/174-3/p10); [Peres–Tanaka–Zhai](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1805.05025); [Duchin et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1412.8741); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_group))

### Key concepts
- **Commuting probability.** For a finite group $G$, $\Pr(xy=yx)=k(G)/|G|$ with $k(G)$ the number of conjugacy classes; $G$ is abelian iff this is $1$, and for nonabelian $G$ it is at most $5/8$ (attained by the dihedral group of order 8). For nonabelian simple $G$ it is at most $1/12$, with equality for $A_5$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting_probability))
- **Random generation.** Let $P_2(G)$ be the probability that two uniform random elements generate $G$. Dixon proved $P_2(A_n)\to1$ (Netto's prediction), and conjectured it for every finite simple group of order tending to infinity; Kantor–Lubotzky proved it for classical and low-rank exceptional groups, Liebeck–Shalev for the rest. See [Finite Simple Groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups). ([Burness survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.10434))
- **Maximal-subgroup union bound.** A non-generating pair lies in a common maximal subgroup, so $1-P_2(G)\le\zeta_G(2)=\sum_{H\text{ maximal}}|G:H|^{-2}$. For Lie-type groups, Aschbacher's theorem is used to show $\zeta_G(2)\to0$. ([Burness survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.10434))
- **Positively finitely generated (PFG) profinite groups.** A profinite group $G$ with normalised [Haar measure](node:Haar%20Measure) is PFG if $P(G,k)>0$ for some $k$. Mann–Shalev: $G$ is PFG iff it has polynomial maximal subgroup growth. A finitely generated nonabelian free profinite group is not PFG, so PFG is stronger than finite generation. ([Segal](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0703885))
- **Word maps.** Larsen–Shalev–Tiep: for any nontrivial word $w$ and nonabelian finite simple groups $G$ of sufficiently large order, every element of $G$ is a product of two values of $w$. ([Annals 2011](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2011/174-3/p10))
- **Product replacement.** On generating $n$-tuples of a finite group $G$, pick distinct $i\neq j$ uniformly and replace $\sigma(i)$ by $\sigma(i)\sigma(j)^{\pm1}$. For fixed $G$ and $n$ large enough for irreducibility, there is total-variation cutoff at $\tfrac32 n\log n$ with window of order $n$ (Peres–Tanaka–Zhai). This models sampling by [Randomized Algorithms](node:Randomized%20Algorithms); the chain is a [Markov chain](node:Markov%20Chains) with uniform stationary law. ([Peres–Tanaka–Zhai](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1805.05025))
- **Random groups.** In the Gromov density model with $m$ generators, $(2m-1)^{d\ell}$ random relators of length $\ell$ are taken. For $d<1/2$ the group is a.a.s. infinite, torsion-free and hyperbolic; for $d>1/2$ it is a.a.s. trivial or $\mathbb Z/2$. ([Duchin et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1412.8741)) Ollivier proved an isoperimetric inequality with constant $1-2d$ ([Ollivier](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0409226)), and for $d>1/3$ property (T) holds in the $\Gamma(n,k,d)$ model as $k\to\infty$. ([arXiv 2104.14986](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14986)) See [Geometric Group Theory](node:Geometric%20Group%20Theory).

### History
Dixon proved the alternating-group case of random generation in 1969 and conjectured the general simple-group case, settled by Kantor–Lubotzky (1990) and Liebeck–Shalev (1995). ([Burness survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.10434)) Mann and Shalev characterised PFG profinite groups, and the Jaikin-Zapirain–Pyber theorem shows open subgroups of PFG groups are PFG. ([Segal](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0703885)) Pak's lecture gives a polynomial-in-$\log|G|$ mixing bound for product replacement when $k$ is of order $\log|G|\log\log|G|$. ([Pak lecture](https://www.math.ucla.edu/%7Epak/courses/pg/l33.tex)) Larsen–Shalev–Tiep's Waring result (2011) was followed by a probabilistic version (2019). ([Annals 2019](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2019/190-2/p03)) Two conjectures listed as open in Burness's 2017 survey ([Burness survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.10434)) have since been proved: Burness, Guralnick and Harper showed that a finite group is $\tfrac32$-generated (has spread at least $1$) if and only if every proper quotient is cyclic, settling the Breuer–Guralnick–Kantor conjecture ([arXiv:2006.01421](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.01421)), and Lucchini, Marion and Tracey showed that every maximal subgroup of a finite almost simple group is $5$-generated ([arXiv:1807.05400](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05400)).

### Open problems
- **Sharp thresholds for random groups.** At density $1/2$ the density model has hyperbolic and trivial regimes with a gap between the proved bounds; the authors conjecture the two thresholds coincide and note that sharp hyperbolicity thresholds are not known for the density or triangular models. ([Duchin et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1412.8741))
- **Product replacement beyond fixed groups.** The cutoff theorem is for fixed $G$. For the closely related random walk on $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z/q)$, the best known mixing upper bound is $O(n^3)$ (Kassabov, improving Diaconis–Saloff-Coste's $O(n^4)$), while the Cayley-graph diameter of order $n^2/\log_q n$ gives the lower bound; Peres, Tanaka and Zhai call closing this gap an open problem. ([Peres–Tanaka–Zhai](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1805.05025))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Random group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_group): few-relator and density models, hyperbolicity and phase transition.
- **Learn:** [Pak, lecture on product replacement](https://www.math.ucla.edu/%7Epak/courses/pg/l33.tex): course lecture on mixing of the product replacement graph via blind algorithms.
- **Primary:** [Burness, Simple groups, generation and probabilistic methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10434): survey of random generation, spread and their proofs.
- **Further reading:** [Larsen–Shalev–Tiep, The Waring problem for finite simple groups](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2011/174-3/p10) and [Breuillard–Glazer, notes on word maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00417): word maps on finite simple and algebraic groups.
references.MSC 22 - Topological groups, Lie groups:
## Reference
### Overview
Section 22 studies [topological groups](node:Topological%20Groups), groups with a topology making multiplication and inversion continuous, and its largest part is the theory of [Lie groups](node:Lie%20Groups). Two analytic facts organize the locally compact theory: every locally compact Hausdorff group carries a left Haar measure, unique up to a positive scalar, and locally compact [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) satisfy [Pontryagin duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality), which generalizes [Fourier analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) to all of them. ([Wikipedia, Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure); [Wikipedia, Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))

The structural bridge between general locally compact groups and Lie groups is the solution of Hilbert's fifth problem: Lie groups are exactly the locally compact groups with no small subgroups, and every locally compact group has an open subgroup that is a projective limit of Lie groups. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert's fifth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem)) On the Lie side, research concentrates on the [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of reductive groups and on lattices, rigidity and arithmeticity. ([Wikipedia, Langlands classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_classification); [Wikipedia, Lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_%28discrete_subgroup%29))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 22 is "Topological groups, Lie groups", with transformation groups sent to 54H15, 57Sxx, 58-XX and abstract harmonic analysis to 43-XX. Its subject codes are: [22A](node:MSC%2022Axx%20-%20Topological%20and%20differentiable%20algebraic%20systems) topological and differentiable algebraic systems (topological rings and fields go to 12J, 13J, 16W80); [22B](node:MSC%2022Bxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20abelian%20groups%20%28LCA%20groups%29) locally compact abelian groups; [22C](node:MSC%2022Cxx%20-%20Compact%20groups) compact groups; [22D](node:MSC%2022Dxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20groups%20and%20their%20algebras) locally compact groups and their algebras; [22E](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups) Lie groups (topology of Lie groups and homogeneous spaces at 57S, 57T; analysis thereon at 43A80–43A90); and [22F](node:MSC%2022Fxx%20-%20Noncompact%20transformation%20groups) noncompact transformation groups. ([MSC2020, 22](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22-XX))

22E alone covers real, complex and $p$-adic Lie groups, discrete subgroups (22E40), representations over real, local and global fields (22E45–22E55), the geometric Langlands program (22E57) and infinite-dimensional and loop groups (22E65–22E67). ([MSC2020, 22E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Exx)) Abstract harmonic analysis itself is [43A](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis) and topological transformation groups [57S](node:MSC%2057Sxx%20-%20Topological%20transformation%20groups). ([MSC2020, 22](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22-XX))

### Key concepts
- **[Haar measure](node:Haar%20Measure) (22D).** On a locally compact Hausdorff group $G$ there is a nonzero left-invariant Radon measure, unique up to a positive constant; the modular function $\Delta:G\to\mathbb R_{>0}$, defined by $\nu(g^{-1}S)=\Delta(g)\nu(S)$ for a right Haar measure $\nu$, is a continuous homomorphism, and abelian, compact, discrete and semisimple Lie groups are unimodular ($\Delta\equiv1$), while the affine group of the line is not. Haar proved existence in 1933 for second-countable groups; Weil proved existence and uniqueness in general. ([Wikipedia, Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure))
- **Pontryagin duality (22B).** For a locally compact abelian group $G$, the dual $\widehat G$ of continuous homomorphisms $G\to\mathbb T$, with the compact-open topology, is again locally compact abelian, and evaluation $G\to\widehat{\widehat G}$ is a natural isomorphism; $G$ is compact iff $\widehat G$ is discrete, $\widehat{\mathbb Z}\cong\mathbb T$, $\widehat{\mathbb R}\cong\mathbb R$, and with dual Haar measures the Fourier transform satisfies inversion and Plancherel. Pontryagin (1934), van Kampen (1935) and Weil (1940) developed it. ([Wikipedia, Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) See [Harmonic Analysis on Locally Compact Groups](node:Harmonic%20Analysis%20on%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups).
- **[Peter–Weyl](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem) (22C).** For a compact group $G$: matrix coefficients of finite-dimensional representations are uniformly dense in $C(G)$; every unitary representation is an orthogonal direct sum of finite-dimensional irreducibles; and $L^2(G)\cong\widehat{\bigoplus}_{\pi}\operatorname{End}(E_\pi)$ (Peter and Weyl, 1927). Corollary: every compact Lie group has a faithful finite-dimensional representation, so is a closed subgroup of some $GL(n,\mathbb C)$. ([Wikipedia, Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))
- **Hilbert's fifth problem (22D, 22E15).** Gleason, Montgomery and Zippin (1950s) characterized Lie groups among locally compact groups as those with no small subgroups, so a topological group that is a topological manifold is a Lie group. Yamabe (1953): every connected locally compact group is a projective limit of Lie groups; with van Dantzig's theorem, every locally compact group has an open subgroup that is such a limit. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert's fifth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem))
- **Lie correspondence (22E60).** Every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a simply connected Lie group (Lie's third theorem); connected Lie subgroups correspond to subalgebras; and for simply connected $G$ every Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathrm{Lie}(G)\to\mathrm{Lie}(H)$ integrates uniquely. ([Wikipedia, Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group%E2%80%93Lie_algebra_correspondence)) Closed subgroups of Lie groups are Lie groups, and simply connected Lie groups are semidirect products of a solvable normal subgroup and a semisimple subgroup (Levi). ([Wikipedia, Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group)) The algebra side is [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras).
- **Representations of reductive groups (22E46).** Langlands (1973) classified irreducible admissible representations of real reductive groups as Langlands quotients of representations parabolically induced from tempered representations of Levi factors; Adams, van Leeuwen, Trapa and Vogan give a finite algorithm for the irreducible unitary representations. ([Wikipedia, Langlands classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_classification); [Adams et al., arXiv 1212.2192](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.2192)) Compare [Unitary Representations of Locally Compact Groups](node:Unitary%20Representations%20of%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups).
- **Lattices and rigidity (22E40).** For a semisimple linear algebraic group $G$ over $\mathbb Q$, $G\cap GL_n(\mathbb Z)$ is a lattice in $G(\mathbb R)$ (Borel–Harish-Chandra); by Margulis, lattices are arithmetic in most cases: non-arithmetic lattices exist in all $SO(n,1)$ and in $SU(2,1)$, $SU(3,1)$ (possibly in $SU(n,1)$, $n\ge4$), and all irreducible lattices in the other simple groups are arithmetic; and a lattice has Kazhdan's property (T) iff the ambient group does, lattices in $SO(n,1)$ and $SU(n,1)$ lacking it. ([Wikipedia, Lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_%28discrete_subgroup%29)) See [Arithmetic Matrix Groups](node:Arithmetic%20Matrix%20Groups).

### History
Lie dated his theory to the winter of 1873–74, Killing's structure papers began in 1888, and Weyl classified representations of compact and semisimple groups by highest weights; Hilbert posed his fifth problem in 1900. ([Wikipedia, Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group)) Hurwitz had an invariant integral for Lie groups in 1897; Haar's theorem (1933) let von Neumann solve Hilbert's fifth problem for compact groups the same year. ([Wikipedia, Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure)) Pontryagin duality dates from 1934 and the Peter–Weyl theorem from 1927. ([Wikipedia, Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality); [Wikipedia, Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem)) Tao's *Hilbert's Fifth Problem and Related Topics* appeared in the AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics in 2014. ([Crossref, Tao](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/153))

> [!warning] Contested
> The Hilbert–Smith conjecture says a locally compact group acting faithfully on a connected manifold is a Lie group; it reduces to showing the $p$-adic integers $\mathbb Z_p$ have no faithful action on a manifold. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert–Smith conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Smith_conjecture)) Pardon proved it for three-manifolds (*J. Amer. Math. Soc.* 2013). ([Pardon, arXiv 1112.2324](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.2324)) It is described as open in full generality ([Wikipedia, Hilbert's fifth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem)), but Wikipedia now also reports a manuscript released in October 2026 claiming a proof in every finite dimension, without saying that the claim has been verified. ([Wikipedia, Hilbert–Smith conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Smith_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Non-arithmetic lattices in $SU(n,1)$, $n\ge4$.** No non-arithmetic lattices are known in these groups, and whether they exist is an open question. ([Wikipedia, Lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_%28discrete_subgroup%29); [Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group))
- **Congruence subgroup problem.** Serre conjectured that irreducible arithmetic lattices in higher-rank groups have the congruence subgroup property and rank-one lattices do not; it is still open in this generality. ([Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Hilbert's fifth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem): Gleason–Montgomery–Zippin, Yamabe, Hilbert–Smith.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.755, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras II (Etingof, 2024)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/): Haar measure on locally compact groups, Peter–Weyl, Cartan and Iwasawa decompositions, real reductive groups.
- **Primary:** [Pardon, The Hilbert–Smith conjecture for three-manifolds (JAMS 2013; arXiv 1112.2324)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.2324): the three-dimensional case.
- **Primary:** [Adams–van Leeuwen–Trapa–Vogan, Unitary representations of real reductive groups (arXiv 1212.2192)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.2192): algorithm for the unitary dual.
- **Further reading:** [Tao, Hilbert's Fifth Problem and Related Topics (AMS GSM 153, 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/153): monograph on the structure of locally compact groups.
references.MSC 22Axx - Topological and differentiab:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 22Axx collects algebraic structures equipped with a compatible topology, or a compatible smooth structure: general topological groups, topological semigroups, topological groupoids (including differentiable and Lie groupoids), topological lattices, and their representations. The heading "Topological and differentiable algebraic systems" sends topological rings and fields to 12Jxx, 13Jxx and 16W80, and the parent section 22 sends transformation groups to 54H15, 57Sxx and 58-XX and abstract harmonic analysis to 43-XX. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Axx))

The basic object is a [topological group](node:Topological%20Groups), a group with a topology making multiplication and inversion continuous; equivalently a group object in the category of topological spaces. Many authors also demand the [Hausdorff](node:Hausdorff%20Space) property; any topological group has a Hausdorff quotient by the closure of the identity. Weaker notions are semitopological groups (each translation continuous), quasitopological groups (semitopological with continuous inversion) and paratopological groups (jointly continuous multiplication). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+group)) A current survey topic is when homomorphisms between Polish groups are automatically continuous, and how much choice is needed to build discontinuous ones. ([Rosendal–Suarez](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12143))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists the following sub-codes under 22Axx. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Axx))
- 22A05 Structure of general topological groups.
- 22A10 Analysis on general topological groups.
- 22A15 Structure of topological semigroups.
- 22A20 Analysis on topological semigroups.
- 22A22 Topological groupoids (including differentiable and Lie groupoids); see also 58H05.
- 22A25 Representations of general topological groups and semigroups.
- 22A26 Topological semilattices, lattices and applications; see also 06B30, 06B35, 06F30.
- 22A30 Other topological algebraic systems and their representations.
- 22A99 None of the above, but in this section.

Other sections of MSC 22 are [22Bxx](node:MSC%2022Bxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20abelian%20groups%20%28LCA%20groups%29) (locally compact abelian groups), [22Cxx](node:MSC%2022Cxx%20-%20Compact%20groups) (compact groups), [22Dxx](node:MSC%2022Dxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20groups%20and%20their%20algebras) (locally compact groups and their algebras), [22Exx](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups) (Lie groups) and [22Fxx](node:MSC%2022Fxx%20-%20Noncompact%20transformation%20groups) (noncompact transformation groups). 22A22 cross-references [58H05](node:MSC%2058Hxx%20-%20Pseudogroups,%20differentiable%20groupoids%20and%20general%20structures%20on%20manifolds), and 22A26 cross-references [06B30, 06B35](node:MSC%2006Bxx%20-%20Lattices) and 06F30. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Uniformities and basic facts.** A topological group carries a left and a right uniformity indexed by symmetric identity neighbourhoods; both induce the topology, and they coincide if $G$ is abelian or compact Hausdorff. Open subgroups are closed. For a homomorphism, continuity at one point, continuity, and [uniform continuity](node:Uniform%20Continuity) are equivalent. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+group))
- **Birkhoff–Kakutani.** For a topological group $G$ the following are equivalent: $G$ is Hausdorff and first countable; $G$ is metrisable; $G$ has a left-invariant (equivalently, right-invariant) compatible metric. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group))
- **Pettis's lemma, open mapping theorem, automatic continuity.** In a Baire topological group, if $U(A)$ denotes the largest open set in which $A$ is comeagre, then $U(A)U(B)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(AB)$. Consequences: every continuous epimorphism between Polish groups is open (**open mapping theorem**), and every Baire measurable homomorphism between Polish groups is continuous. ([Rosendal–Suarez, Lemma 2, Thm 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.12143); [Rosendal, Thm 2.2](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~rosendal/PapersWebsite/AutomaticContinuity06.pdf)) A Polish group is **Steinhaus** with exponent $k$ if $1\in\operatorname{int}A^k$ for every symmetric $\sigma$-syndetic $A\ni1$ (countably many left translates of $A$ cover $G$); Steinhaus groups have automatic continuity into separable groups. **Kechris–Rosendal:** a Polish group with ample generics (a comeagre orbit in every diagonal action on $X^n$) is Steinhaus with exponent $10$, so every homomorphism from it into a Polish group is continuous, and in any covering of it by countably many two-sided translates of subgroups some subgroup is open. Rosendal and Solecki showed $\mathrm{Homeo}(2^{\mathbb N})$ and $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb Q,<)$ are Steinhaus, and Rosendal did the same for $\mathrm{Homeo}(M)$, $M$ a compact 2-manifold. ([Rosendal, §5](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~rosendal/PapersWebsite/AutomaticContinuity06.pdf))
- **Ellis's joint continuity theorem.** A locally compact Hausdorff semitopological group is a topological group: separately continuous multiplication is automatically jointly continuous and inversion continuous. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semitopological_group)) The result goes back to Ellis (1957); in particular a compact semitopological semigroup that is algebraically a group is a compact group. ([Das–Mrozinski](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.02469))
- **Compact semigroups (22A15).** **Ellis–Numakura:** a non-empty compact Hausdorff semigroup in which every right translation is continuous has an idempotent; on $\beta\mathbb N$ this gives idempotent ultrafilters and Hindman's theorem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis%E2%80%93Numakura_lemma); [Fernández-Bretón](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1711.01304)) Every compact right-topological semigroup has a smallest two-sided ideal (kernel), which is completely simple; it is partitioned by minimal left ideals, each minimal left ∩ minimal right ideal is a group with a unique idempotent, all these groups are isomorphic, and the kernel has the Rees form $I\times H\times\Lambda$ with $(i,g,\lambda)(j,h,\mu)=(i,g\,a_{\lambda j}h,\mu)$. ([Kellendonk](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.07480)) See [Semigroups and Monoids](node:Semigroups%20and%20Monoids) and [Stone–Čech Compactification](node:Stone–Čech%20Compactification).
- **Topological semilattices (22A26).** Compact semilattices are tied to [domain theory](node:Domain%20Theory): the Lawson topology on a poset is the common refinement of the lower and Scott topologies ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawson_topology)), continuous lattices are the meet-continuous lattices with Hausdorff Lawson topology, and the "Fundamental Theorem of Compact Semilattices" relates the two. ([Erné](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.04721))
- **Topological and Lie groupoids (22A22).** A topological groupoid is an internal groupoid in $\mathbf{Top}$; it is open if the source map is open and étale if the source map is also a local [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism). ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+groupoid)) A [Lie groupoid](node:Lie%20Groupoids%20and%20Pseudogroups) (see [Groupoids](node:Groupoids)) has smooth structure maps with source and target surjective submersions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_groupoid))
- **Haar and Gleason–Montgomery–Zippin.** A locally compact Hausdorff group carries a nonzero left-invariant regular Borel measure finite on compacta, unique up to a positive constant ([Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure)); Weil first proved this in full generality. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure)) A locally compact group is a [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) iff it has no small subgroups, which settles Hilbert's fifth problem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem))
- **Kechris–Pestov–Todorcevic.** For a Fraïssé structure $F$, $\mathrm{Aut}(F)$ is extremely amenable (every compact $G$-flow has a fixed point) iff $\mathrm{Age}(F)$ has the Ramsey property ([Ramsey Theory](node:Ramsey%20Theory)) and consists of rigid structures. ([Nguyen Van Thé](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1201.1270)) Precompact Ramsey expansions extend this to compute universal minimal flows; Jasiński, Laflamme, Nguyen Van Thé and Woodrow showed that the age of every homogeneous directed graph in Cherlin's classification admits a Ramsey precompact expansion. ([JLNW](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1310.6466))

### History
Topological groups were studied extensively from about 1925 to 1940; Haar (1933) and Weil (1940) showed that integrals and Fourier series are special cases of a construction on a wide class of topological groups. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group)) Von Neumann solved Hilbert's fifth problem for compact groups (1933) and Pontryagin for locally compact abelian groups (1934); Gleason, Montgomery and Zippin settled it in the 1950s, and Yamabe showed in 1953 that every locally compact connected group is a projective limit of Lie groups. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem)) Numakura (1952) and Ellis (1958) proved the idempotent lemma ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis%E2%80%93Numakura_lemma)), and Ellis's joint continuity theorem is from 1957 ([Das–Mrozinski](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.02469)). Pestov's 1999 survey set research directions for actions on compacta and "massive" groups ([Pestov](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9910144)); the KPT correspondence appeared in 2005 ([Nguyen Van Thé survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1412.3254)), and the directed-graph test case proposed by Nguyen Van Thé in 2012 was later carried out ([JLNW](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1310.6466)).

### Open problems
- **Hilbert–Smith conjecture.** A locally compact group acting faithfully and continuously on a connected manifold must be a Lie group; equivalently, the $p$-adic integers $\mathbb Z_p$ have no faithful action on a topological manifold. It is proved for Lipschitz actions on Riemannian manifolds (Repovš–Ščepin 1997), quasiconformal actions (Martin 1999) and dimension three (Pardon 2013), and is described as open in general. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Smith_conjecture)) A manuscript released in October 2026 claims a proof in every finite dimension; this is reported and unconfirmed. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Smith_conjecture))
- **Choice and discontinuous homomorphisms.** Rosendal and Suarez pose, in ZF+DC, whether the failure of automatic continuity can be split into a case stipulating a Hamel basis of $\mathbb R$ over $\mathbb Q$ and a non-trivial condition on the "characteristic group" of every Polish group homomorphism (Problem 32), and the analogous dichotomy with non-principal ultrafilters on $\mathbb N$ (Problem 41). ([Rosendal–Suarez](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.12143))
- **Unique ergodicity.** For amenable non-Archimedean Polish groups with metrizable universal minimal flow, whether the flow is always uniquely ergodic: "The question of knowing whether this always holds is open." ([Nguyen Van Thé survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1412.3254))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Topological group (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+group): definition, uniformities, basic propositions.
- **Reference:** [Topological group (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group): Birkhoff–Kakutani, semitopological and paratopological groups, history.
- **Learn:** [Topological Groups, Oxford (Sanders)](https://courses.maths.ox.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=854): foundations, open mapping theorem, Haar integrals, duality.
- **Primary:** [Rosendal and Suarez, Aspects of automatic continuity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12143): Pettis's lemma, open mapping theorem, automatic continuity, open problems.
- **Primary:** [Pestov, Topological groups: where to from here?](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9910144): research survey.
- **Primary:** [Kechris, Pestov, Todorcevic](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0305241): Fraïssé limits, Ramsey theory, topological dynamics.
- **Further reading:** [Arhangel'skii and Tkachenko, Topological Groups and Related Structures](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2991/978-94-91216-35-0): Atlantis Studies in Mathematics, Atlantis Press, 2008.
- **Further reading:** [Hewitt and Ross, Abstract Harmonic Analysis](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-26755-4): Springer, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften, 1970.
references.MSC 22Bxx - Locally compact abelian grou:
## Reference
### Overview
Locally compact abelian (LCA) groups are Hausdorff [topological](node:Topological%20Groups) abelian groups that are locally compact. Examples include $\mathbb R^n$, $\mathbb Z$, the circle $\mathbb T$, finite abelian groups, $\mathbb Q_p$ and the adeles. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_compact_abelian_group)) The area is organised by Pontryagin duality: the group $\widehat G$ of continuous characters $G\to\mathbb T$, with the topology of uniform convergence on compacta, is again LCA, and $G\mapsto\widehat G$ is a contravariant self-equivalence of the category. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Pontryagin+duality))

Pontryagin duality places Fourier series of periodic functions, Fourier transforms on the real line, and discrete Fourier transforms on finite abelian groups in one context. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) A [Haar measure](node:Haar%20Measure) is unique up to a positive scalar; it can be normalised to total mass one on a compact group, and on a discrete group a Haar measure is counting measure. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure)) Duality exchanges compact and discrete groups. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists three codes under 22Bxx: 22B05 (general properties and structure of LCA groups), 22B10 (structure of group algebras of LCA groups) and 22B99 (none of the above but in this section). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf)) The neighbouring sections of MSC 22 are [22Axx](node:MSC%2022Axx%20-%20Topological%20and%20differentiable%20algebraic%20systems) (topological and differentiable algebraic systems), [22Cxx](node:MSC%2022Cxx%20-%20Compact%20groups) (compact groups) and [22Dxx](node:MSC%2022Dxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20groups%20and%20their%20algebras) (locally compact groups and their algebras); [43Axx](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis) is abstract harmonic analysis. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Pontryagin duality.** For an LCA group $G$, the evaluation map $G\to\widehat{\widehat G}$, $x\mapsto(\chi\mapsto\chi(x))$, is an isomorphism of topological groups; $G$ is compact iff $\widehat G$ is discrete. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) See [Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality).
- **Structure theorem (Pontryagin–van Kampen).** Every LCA group is isomorphic to $E\times\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge 0$ and $E$ an LCA group having a compact open subgroup. ([Prasad](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0912.0574)) The proof goes through the fact that every LCA group has an open subgroup $H$ with a compact subgroup $K$ such that $H/K\cong\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb Z^b\times\mathbb T^c\times F$ with $F$ finite. ([Morris, Cambridge](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/pontryagin-duality-and-the-structure-of-locally-compact-abelian-groups/duality-theorem-and-the-principal-structure-theorem/E850D3614B6D950DED429CEE3C872E88))
- **Annihilators.** If $U$ is a compact open subgroup of $E$, then its annihilator $U^\perp\subset\widehat E$ (characters trivial on $U$) is isomorphic to the dual of the discrete group $E/U$, hence compact and open, and $\widehat E/U^\perp\cong\widehat U$ is discrete. ([Prasad](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0912.0574))
- **Fourier inversion and Plancherel.** For each Haar measure $\mu$ on $G$ there is a unique dual Haar measure $\nu$ on $\widehat G$ for which inversion holds for $f\in L^1(G)$ with $\hat f\in L^1$, and $\int|f|^2d\mu=\int|\hat f|^2d\nu$ extends the transform to a unitary $L^2(G)\to L^2(\widehat G)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) See [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem) and [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis).
- **Bochner's theorem.** A continuous positive-definite function $f$ on $G$ with $f(0)=1$ is $f(g)=\int_{\widehat G}\xi(g)\,d\mu(\xi)$ for a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\widehat G$, and conversely every such Fourier transform is such a function. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%27s_theorem)) See [Positive-Definite Functions on Groups](node:Positive-Definite%20Functions%20on%20Groups).
- **Group algebra.** $L^1(G)$ is a commutative associative Banach algebra under convolution, and the Fourier transform takes convolution to multiplication of functions on $\widehat G$; the structure of such group algebras is the subject of 22B10. This connects to [Gelfand Representation](node:Gelfand%20Representation) and [Banach Algebras](node:Banach%20Algebras). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality); [MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### History
Pontryagin built the foundations in 1931–1934 for second-countable groups that are compact or discrete; van Kampen (1935) and Weil (1940) extended the theory to all LCA groups. Haar introduced his measure in 1933. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) Mackey (1948) proved that $A$ is connected iff its dual is the product of a discrete torsion-free group and a finite-dimensional real vector space. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Pontryagin+duality))

### Open problems
One active direction is duality beyond local compactness. A group is reflexive if the evaluation map into the double dual is a topological isomorphism, and strongly reflexive if all its subgroups and Hausdorff quotients are reflexive. Hofmann and Morris list as open: which abelian pro-Lie groups are reflexive (Question 3), and which are strongly reflexive (Question 4); they also state that nothing is known about the duality of prodiscrete abelian groups, and ask (Question 1) whether there is a satisfactory structure theory for nondiscrete prodiscrete groups. ([Hofmann–Morris survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.06852)) Via a Banaszczyk example of a nondiscrete prodiscrete abelian torsion group that is semireflexive but not reflexive, they conclude that the category of abelian pro-Lie groups is not self-dual under Pontryagin duality. ([Hofmann–Morris](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.06852)) Further directions include Barr's $*$-autonomous category of topological abelian groups containing all LCA groups, whose duality extends Pontryagin's ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Pontryagin+duality)), and Clausen's homotopy fibre sequence $K(\mathbb Z)\to K(\mathbb R)\to K(\mathrm{LCA})$ of algebraic K-theory spectra. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_compact_abelian_group))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Pontryagin duality (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality): duality, inversion, Plancherel, history.
- **Reference:** [Pontryagin duality (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Pontryagin+duality): categorical formulation and generalisations.
- **Learn:** [Haar measure (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure): existence, uniqueness, normalisations.
- **Learn:** [Bochner's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%27s_theorem): positive-definite functions on LCA groups.
- **Primary:** [Hofmann and Morris, Pro-Lie groups: a survey with open problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06852): survey including duality of abelian pro-Lie groups.
- **Primary:** [Prasad, An easy proof of the Stone-von Neumann-Mackey theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.0574): states the structure theorem and annihilator facts.
- **Further reading:** [Morris, Pontryagin Duality and the Structure of Locally Compact Abelian Groups](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/pontryagin-duality-and-the-structure-of-locally-compact-abelian-groups/duality-theorem-and-the-principal-structure-theorem/E850D3614B6D950DED429CEE3C872E88): LMS Lecture Notes, Cambridge University Press, 1977.
- **Further reading:** [Rudin, Fourier Analysis on Groups](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/9781118165621) (Wiley) and [Hewitt and Ross, Abstract Harmonic Analysis](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-26755-4) (Springer, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften): monographs on Fourier and abstract harmonic analysis.
references.MSC 22Cxx - Compact groups:
## Reference
### Overview
A compact group is a topological group whose underlying space is compact; such groups generalize finite groups (with the discrete topology), and their basic examples are the circle, tori, $SU(n)$, profinite groups such as Galois groups, and the $p$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$, which is compact but not a Lie group. Every compact group carries a Haar measure, is unimodular, and its Haar measure can be normalized to a probability measure. ([Wikipedia: Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group))

The theory has two layers. Compact Lie groups are classified up to finite central quotients by tori and simply connected simple compact groups, and their representations are controlled by maximal tori and highest weights. General compact groups are reached from Lie groups by inverse limits: the [Peter–Weyl Theorem](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem) implies that every compact Hausdorff group is an inverse limit of compact Lie groups, though it need not itself be Lie. ([Wikipedia: Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group); [Wikipedia: Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))

This makes compact groups a subclass of pro-Lie groups, the closed subgroups of products of finite-dimensional real Lie groups, a class that also contains all locally compact abelian groups and all almost connected locally compact groups. Hofmann and Morris show that pro-Lie groups are equivalently the projective limits of finite-dimensional Lie groups, and name Lie theory as the crucial tool for their structure theory. ([Hofmann–Morris, Pro-Lie groups survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06852))

### Scope
In MSC2020, 22Cxx has a single substantive code, 22C05 (Compact groups), plus the catch-all 22C99; the parent section [MSC 22 - Topological groups, Lie groups](node:MSC%2022%20-%20Topological%20groups,%20Lie%20groups) sends transformation groups to 54H15, 57Sxx and 58-XX and abstract harmonic analysis to 43-XX. ([MSC2020 22Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=22Cxx); [MSC2020 22-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22-XX))

Representation theory and harmonic analysis of compact groups also have codes in neighbouring sections. ([MSC2020 22Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Dxx); [MSC2020 43Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43Axx))
- **22Bxx** ([MSC 22Bxx - Locally compact abelian groups (LCA groups)](node:MSC%2022Bxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20abelian%20groups%20%28LCA%20groups%29)): compact abelian groups are studied through [Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality); for them, connectedness is equivalent to a torsion-free dual. ([Hofmann–Morris survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06852))
- **22Dxx** ([MSC 22Dxx - Locally compact groups and their algebras](node:MSC%2022Dxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20groups%20and%20their%20algebras)): unitary representations of locally compact groups are 22D10 and duality theorems are 22D35. ([MSC2020 22Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Dxx))
- **22Exx** ([MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups)): real Lie groups are 22E15, semisimple Lie groups and their representations are 22E46, and infinite-dimensional Lie groups (where the pro-Lie survey is filed) are 22E65. ([MSC2020 22Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Exx); [Hofmann–Morris survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06852))
- **43Axx** ([MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis)): harmonic analysis on specific compact groups is 43A75 and on general compact groups is 43A77. ([MSC2020 43Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43Axx))

### Key concepts
- **[Haar Measure on Compact Groups](node:Haar%20Measure%20on%20Compact%20Groups).** A compact group is unimodular and has finite Haar measure, normalized so that $\mu(G)=1$; averaging an inner product over $G$ shows that every continuous representation of a compact group on a Hilbert space admits an equivalent $G$-invariant inner product, so it is unitary. See also [Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure). ([Murnaghan, Ch. 2 §2 and Ch. 3 §1](https://www.math.toronto.edu/murnaghan/courses/mat1196/rnotes.pdf))
- **[Peter–Weyl Theorem](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem).** For a compact Hausdorff group $G$: matrix coefficients of finite-dimensional unitary representations are uniformly dense in $C(G)$; every unitary representation on a Hilbert space is an orthogonal direct sum of irreducible finite-dimensional ones; and $L^2(G)$ decomposes over all irreducibles, with suitably normalized matrix coefficients forming an orthonormal basis. This is the nonabelian extension of [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) on the circle. ([Wikipedia: Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))
- **Lie criterion and projective limits.** For a compact group $G$ the following are equivalent: some neighbourhood of $1$ contains no nontrivial subgroup; $G$ has a faithful finite-dimensional representation; $G$ is a real Lie group. Moreover, for every neighbourhood $U$ of $1$ there is a finite-dimensional representation with kernel inside $U$. Together these give the structure theorem that every compact group is an inverse limit of compact Lie groups. ([Murnaghan, Ch. 3 Cor. 1.14 and Prop. 2.2](https://www.math.toronto.edu/murnaghan/courses/mat1196/rnotes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))
- **Compact connected groups.** A connected compact Lie group is the quotient by a finite central subgroup of a product of a torus and a simply connected compact Lie group, the latter a product of groups of type $SU(n)$, $Sp(n)$, $\mathrm{Spin}(n)$ and the five exceptional groups. For general compact connected groups, Hofmann and Morris call such a group semisimple when its algebraic commutator subgroup is the whole group, and record that every element of a compact connected semisimple group is itself a commutator. ([Wikipedia: Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group); [Hofmann–Morris survey, §2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06852))
- **Maximal tori and the Weyl integration formula.** Let $G$ be a compact connected [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) with maximal torus $T$ and Weyl group $W=N_G(T)/T$. Any two maximal tori are conjugate, every element lies in a maximal torus, and $W$ is finite. With $D(t)=\lvert\det(\mathrm{Ad}(t^{-1})-I)|_{\mathfrak g/\mathfrak t}\rvert$ and normalized Haar measures, every continuous class function $f$ satisfies
  $$|W|\int_G f(g)\,dg=\int_T D(t)\,f(t)\,dt,$$
  where $D=|\delta|^2$ with $\delta(t)=\prod_{\alpha>0}\bigl(e^{\alpha(t)/2}-e^{-\alpha(t)/2}\bigr)$ over the positive roots. ([Murnaghan, Ch. 4 Thm. 1.3 and Thm. 1.7](https://www.math.toronto.edu/murnaghan/courses/mat1196/rnotes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Weyl integration formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_integration_formula))
- **Weyl character formula.** If $\Pi$ is irreducible with highest weight $\lambda$, $\rho$ is half the sum of the positive roots and $\varepsilon(w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$, then on $T$
  $$\chi_\Pi(e^H)=\frac{\sum_{w\in W}\varepsilon(w)\,e^{w(\lambda+\rho)(H)}}{\prod_{\alpha>0}\bigl(e^{\alpha(H)/2}-e^{-\alpha(H)/2}\bigr)},\qquad \dim V_\lambda=\prod_{\alpha>0}\frac{(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)}{(\rho,\alpha)}.$$
  For $SU(2)$ the character of the $(m+1)$-dimensional irreducible is $\sin((m+1)\theta)/\sin\theta$. The integration formula is a main tool in the proof of the character formula. ([Wikipedia: Weyl character formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_character_formula); [Wikipedia: Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group); [Murnaghan, Ch. 4 §1](https://www.math.toronto.edu/murnaghan/courses/mat1196/rnotes.pdf))
- **Tannaka–Krein duality.** Tannaka's theorem: for compact $G$, the group of tensor-preserving, conjugation-compatible natural automorphisms of the forgetful functor on finite-dimensional representations is canonically isomorphic to $G$. Krein's theorem characterizes which categories of finite-dimensional spaces arise this way (unit object, decomposition into minimal objects, Schur's lemma for Hom-spaces). For abelian groups this reduces to [Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality); for nonabelian groups the dual is a category, not a group. ([Wikipedia: Tannaka–Krein duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannaka%E2%80%93Krein_duality))

### History
Weyl proved his character formula in 1925–1926, and F. Peter and H. Weyl published the completeness theorem in *Mathematische Annalen* 97 (1927), pp. 737–755. ([Wikipedia: Weyl character formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_character_formula); [Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01447892))

Von Neumann answered Hilbert's fifth problem for compact groups in 1933 and Pontryagin for locally compact abelian groups in 1934; Gleason, Montgomery and Zippin settled the locally compact case in the 1950s by characterizing Lie groups as the locally compact groups with no small subgroups, and Yamabe (1953) showed every connected locally compact group is a projective limit of Lie groups. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's fifth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem))

Hofmann and Morris's monograph *The Structure of Compact Groups: A Primer for the Student – A Handbook for the Expert* has a 2023 De Gruyter edition. ([Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9783111172606))

### Open problems
- **Bergman's compact amalgamation problem.** Joswig, Kummer, Thom and Yun describe the amalgamation question raised by George Bergman in 1987 as an open problem about compact groups. They study its simplest instance (whether copies of $S^1$ in $SU(3)$ can be amalgamated in a compact group), report computational evidence for a positive answer there, and prove only a relaxed version. ([Joswig–Kummer–Thom–Yun 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08365))
- **Questions on pro-Lie groups.** Hofmann and Morris (2015) list 12 open questions on pro-Lie groups, the class that contains all compact groups; for example, Question 2 asks whether $G/G_0$ is complete (hence prodiscrete) for every pro-Lie group $G$ with identity component $G_0$. Their one question specifically about compact groups, Question 5 (whether every surjective morphism $\mathbb{Z}^I\to K$ onto a compact group is open), is not open: an added-in-proof note reports that Gabriyelyan and Morris announced a positive answer. ([Hofmann–Morris survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06852))
- **Hilbert–Smith conjecture.** A locally compact group acting faithfully on a connected manifold should be a Lie group; the problem reduces to excluding faithful actions of the compact group $\mathbb{Z}_p$. Pardon proved it for three-manifolds (2013). ([Pardon 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.2324); [Wikipedia: Hilbert–Smith conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Smith_conjecture))

> [!warning] Contested
> The general Hilbert–Smith conjecture is described as still open in full generality ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's fifth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_fifth_problem)). The Hilbert–Smith article reports an October 2026 manuscript claiming a proof in every finite dimension, and a separately registered Lean formal proof; both are reported claims, unconfirmed, with no peer review stated. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert–Smith conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Smith_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group): examples, classification of compact Lie groups, maximal tori, characters, and pointers to Tannaka–Krein duality.
- **Learn:** [Murnaghan, Representations of locally compact groups](https://www.math.toronto.edu/murnaghan/courses/mat1196/rnotes.pdf): Haar measure, Peter–Weyl, the Lie criterion, and compact Lie groups through the Weyl integral and character formulas (Chs. 1–4).
- **Primary:** [Hofmann–Morris, Pro-Lie Groups: A Survey with Open Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06852): survey of the structure theory containing compact groups, with 12 open questions.
- **Primary:** [Peter–Weyl 1927, Math. Ann. 97](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01447892): the original completeness theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Hofmann–Morris, The Structure of Compact Groups (De Gruyter, 2023)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9783111172606): the standard monograph on the structure theory of compact groups.
- **In this vault:** [Unitary Representations of Locally Compact Groups](node:Unitary%20Representations%20of%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups), [Harmonic Analysis on Locally Compact Groups](node:Harmonic%20Analysis%20on%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups), [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory), [Topological Groups](node:Topological%20Groups), [Root Systems](node:Root%20Systems).
references.MSC 22Dxx - Locally compact groups and t:
## Reference
### Overview
A locally compact group is a topological group whose topology is locally compact and Hausdorff; every such group carries a Haar measure, so Borel functions on it can be integrated invariantly ([Wikipedia: Locally compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_compact_group)). MSC2020 subfield 22Dxx collects the structure theory of these groups, their unitary and other representations, their group algebras, and the operator algebras ($C^*$- and $W^*$-algebras) generated by representations, together with induced representations, duality, [ergodic theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) on groups, rigidity, and Kazhdan's property (T) ([MSC2020 22Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Dxx)).

The organizing idea is to replace the group by an algebra. Convolution against Haar measure makes $L^1(G)$ a Banach $*$-algebra, and strongly continuous unitary representations of $G$ correspond bijectively to non-degenerate bounded $*$-representations of $C_c(G)$, with unitary equivalence and irreducibility preserved, so [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of $G$ becomes the representation theory of a $C^*$-algebra ([Wikipedia: Group algebra of a locally compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_algebra_of_a_locally_compact_group)). The irreducible representations of the group $C^*$-algebra then serve as a dual object for non-abelian groups, supporting a Fourier transform and a Plancherel theorem for unimodular separable type I groups ([Wikipedia: Spectrum of a C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_C*-algebra)).

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists: 22D05 general properties and structure of locally compact groups; 22D10 unitary representations; 22D12 other representations; 22D15 group algebras; 22D20 representations of group algebras; 22D25 $C^*$-algebras and $W^*$-algebras in relation to group representations; 22D30 induced representations; 22D35 duality theorems; 22D40 ergodic theory on groups; 22D45 automorphism groups; 22D50 rigidity; 22D55 Kazhdan's property (T), the Haagerup property, and generalizations; 22D99 other ([MSC2020 22Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Dxx)).

Neighbouring codes in [MSC 22 - Topological groups, Lie groups](node:MSC%2022%20-%20Topological%20groups,%20Lie%20groups) split off special cases: 22Bxx treats locally compact abelian groups, 22Cxx compact groups, 22Exx Lie groups, 22Axx topological and differentiable algebraic systems, and 22Fxx noncompact transformation groups; the 22-XX header refers abstract harmonic analysis to 43-XX ([MSC2020 22-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22-XX)).
