The corresponding notes are [MSC 22Bxx - Locally compact abelian groups (LCA groups)](node:MSC%2022Bxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20abelian%20groups%20%28LCA%20groups%29), [MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups) (structure and representations of [Lie groups](node:Lie%20Groups)) and [MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis); within 22Dxx, 22D25 cross-references operator algebras in [MSC 46Lxx](node:MSC%2046Lxx%20-%20Selfadjoint%20operator%20algebras%20%28C-star-algebras,%20von%20Neumann%20%28W-star-%29%20algebras,%20etc.%29) and 22D40 cross-references 28Dxx ([MSC2020 22-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22-XX); [MSC2020 22Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Dxx)).

### Key concepts
- **[Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure) and the modular function (22D05).** On a locally compact Hausdorff group there is a left-invariant Radon measure, unique up to a positive scalar (Haar proved existence in 1933; Weil gave existence and uniqueness in full generality). Right Haar measure also exists but can differ; the modular function $\Delta:G\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ is a continuous homomorphism, and $G$ is unimodular when $\Delta\equiv1$ (abelian, compact, discrete, semisimple Lie and connected nilpotent Lie groups), while the $ax+b$ group is not. For a closed subgroup $H$, $G/H$ carries a $G$-invariant measure if and only if $\Delta_G|_H=\Delta_H$. ([Wikipedia: Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure))
- **Group algebras (22D15, 22D20, 22D25).** $L^1(G)$ with $(f*g)(x)=\int_G f(y)g(y^{-1}x)\,dy$ and $f^*(x)=\Delta(x^{-1})\overline{f(x^{-1})}$ is a Banach $*$-algebra with a bounded approximate identity; it has an identity only when $G$ is discrete. $C^*(G)$ completes $C_c(G)$ in the largest $C^*$-norm, $C^*_r(G)$ in the norm of convolution operators on $L^2(G)$; the latter is a quotient of the former, and $C^*(G)=C^*_r(G)$ if and only if $G$ is amenable. For countable discrete $G$, the group von Neumann algebra is the hyperfinite II$_1$ factor if and only if $G$ is amenable and has infinite conjugacy classes. See [C-Star Algebras and von Neumann Algebras](node:C-Star%20Algebras%20and%20von%20Neumann%20Algebras). ([Wikipedia: Group algebra of a locally compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_algebra_of_a_locally_compact_group))
- **[Unitary Representations of Locally Compact Groups](node:Unitary%20Representations%20of%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups) and the Gelfand–Raikov theorem (22D10).** A unitary representation is strongly continuous when $g\mapsto\pi(g)\xi$ is norm continuous for every vector $\xi$ ([Wikipedia: Unitary representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_representation)). Gelfand and Raikov (1943) proved that the irreducible unitary representations of a locally compact group separate its points: for $g\neq h$ some irreducible $\rho$ has $\rho(g)\neq\rho(h)$ ([Wikipedia: Gelfand–Raikov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand%E2%80%93Raikov_theorem)).
- **Unitary dual, Fell topology, type I (22D10, 22D25).** The unitary dual $\widehat G$ is the set of equivalence classes of irreducible unitary representations, identified with the spectrum of $C^*(G)$; the topology pulled back from the hull-kernel topology on primitive ideals is the Fell topology. A group is type I when its $C^*$-algebra is, i.e. every separable factor representation is a multiple of an irreducible one; connected nilpotent and connected semisimple real Lie groups, compact groups and abelian groups are type I. Glimm (1961) proved that a separable $C^*$-algebra is type I if and only if its dual is a standard Borel space, settling a conjecture of Mackey, who called such Borel spaces smooth. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum of a C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_C*-algebra)) Bekka and de la Harpe's text also treats the primitive dual (weak-equivalence classes) and characters, with examples such as lamplighter and solvable Baumslag–Solitar groups ([Bekka–de la Harpe, arXiv:1912.07262](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.07262)).
- **Plancherel theorem and direct integrals (22D10, 22D35).** Through the group $C^*$-algebra, $C^*$-algebra theory gives a direct-integral decomposition theory for representations of separable locally compact groups ([Wikipedia: Direct integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_integral)). The dual supports a [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem) for separable unimodular type I groups ([Wikipedia: Spectrum of a C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_C*-algebra)); for abelian $G$ the picture comes from [Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality), and for compact $G$ the [Peter–Weyl Theorem](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem) describes the regular representation on $L^2(G)$, with discrete dual and each point carrying mass equal to its degree ([Wikipedia: Unitary representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_representation)). The first abstract Plancherel formulas for unimodular groups are due to Segal and Mautner; Harish-Chandra completed the spherical Plancherel theorem for semisimple groups in 1966 ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem for spherical functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem_for_spherical_functions)).
- **Induced representations and the Mackey machine (22D30).** For closed $H\le G$, a unitary representation of $H$ induces a unitary representation of $G$ on $L^2$ functions over $G/H$ ([Wikipedia: Induced representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induced_representation)). Imprimitivity: for $G$ locally compact second countable acting transitively on a standard Borel space $X$ with a quasi-invariant σ-finite measure, systems of imprimitivity based on $(G,X)$ correspond bijectively, preserving irreducibility, to representations of a stabilizer $G_x$. For $G=N\rtimes H$ with $N$ abelian, representations of $G$ correspond to systems of imprimitivity for the $H$-action on the characters of $N$; the Heisenberg and inhomogeneous Lorentz groups are standard examples. ([Wikipedia: System of imprimitivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_imprimitivity))
- **Amenability (43A07).** $G$ is amenable if $L^\infty(G)$ has a left-invariant mean. Equivalent: Følner sets, Reiter's condition, the trivial representation weakly contained in the regular representation, and (Kesten) symmetric random-walk operators on $L^2(G)$ of norm 1. Closed subgroups, quotients, extensions and directed unions of amenable groups are amenable; compact, abelian and solvable groups are amenable, and a discrete group containing a free subgroup of rank 2 is not. ([Wikipedia: Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group)) MSC2020 files means on groups and amenable groups under 43A07 in abstract harmonic analysis ([MSC2020 43Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43Axx)).
- **Kazhdan's property (T) (22D55).** $G$ has (T) when the trivial representation is isolated in $\widehat G$ for the Fell topology; equivalently there are $\varepsilon>0$ and compact $K$ such that any unitary representation with an $(\varepsilon,K)$-invariant unit vector has a nonzero invariant vector. A lattice $\Gamma$ in a Lie group $G$ has (T) iff $G$ does; (T) groups have compact abelianization, countable discrete (T) groups are finitely generated, and an amenable (T) group is compact. By Delorme–Guichardet, (T) is equivalent to property (FH) for σ-compact groups. Examples: $SL_n(\mathbb Z)$ for $n\ge3$, $Sp(n,1)$ for $n\ge2$, higher-rank simple Lie groups; non-examples: $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb R$, $SL_2(\mathbb R)$, nontrivial free groups. ([Wikipedia: Kazhdan's property (T)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhdan%27s_property_%28T%29))

### History
Hurwitz treated invariant integration on Lie groups in 1897, Haar proved the existence theorem in 1933, and Weil proved existence and uniqueness in full generality; in 1936 Weil showed that groups with a suitable invariant measure are essentially locally compact ([Wikipedia: Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure)). Von Neumann introduced amenability in 1929 in response to the Banach–Tarski paradox, and Day named it in 1949 ([Wikipedia: Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group)). Gelfand and Raikov's separation theorem appeared in 1943 ([Wikipedia: Gelfand–Raikov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand%E2%80%93Raikov_theorem)); von Neumann introduced direct integrals in 1949, and Mackey used them for systems of imprimitivity and induced representations of separable groups ([Wikipedia: Direct integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_integral)), in papers of 1951–1953 ([Wikipedia: Induced representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induced_representation)). Glimm's type I theorem dates from 1961 ([Wikipedia: Spectrum of a C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_C*-algebra)), Kazhdan introduced property (T) in 1967 ([Wikipedia: Kazhdan's property (T)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhdan%27s_property_%28T%29)), and Baum and Connes proposed their conjecture in 1982 ([Wikipedia: Baum–Connes conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture)).

### Open problems
- **Baum–Connes conjecture.** The conjecture asserts that the assembly map from the equivariant K-homology of the classifying space for proper actions to $K_*(C^*_r(G))$ is an isomorphism. It is known for Haagerup-property groups, hyperbolic groups, one-relator groups, real reductive groups (Wassermann 1987), almost connected groups (Chabert–Echterhoff–Nest 2003) and cocompact lattices in $SL_3(\mathbb R)$ (Lafforgue 1998); the version with coefficients has counterexamples (Higson–Lafforgue–Skandalis 2002), and $SL_3(\mathbb Z)$ is the simplest group for which it is not known whether the conjecture holds. See [Operator Algebra K-Theory](node:Operator%20Algebra%20K-Theory). ([Wikipedia: Baum–Connes conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture))
- **Dixmier's unitarizability problem.** Amenable groups are unitarizable (every uniformly bounded representation is similar to a unitary one); whether every unitarizable group is amenable is an open problem ([Wikipedia: Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group)). Dixmier asked in 1950 whether every non-amenable group has uniformly bounded representations that cannot be unitarised; Monod and Ozawa provide such representations after passing to extensions by abelian groups, giving a new characterisation of amenability, and showed certain Burnside groups are non-unitarisable ([Monod–Ozawa, arXiv:0902.4585](https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.4585)).
- **Unitary duals of real reductive groups.** Admissible representations of real reductive Lie groups are classified by the Langlands classification, and the difficulty in describing $\widehat G$ is deciding which of them are unitary; Wikipedia calls this one of the important unsolved problems in mathematics ([Wikipedia: Unitary representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_representation)). Adams, van Leeuwen, Trapa and Vogan give a finite algorithm that finds all irreducible unitary representations of a real reductive group, by tracking signatures of Hermitian forms under deformation, so the open part is an explicit, closed-form description rather than decidability ([Adams–van Leeuwen–Trapa–Vogan, arXiv:1212.2192](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.2192)).
- **Property (T) without computers.** Property (T) for $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$, $n\ge5$, is established by computer-assisted methods and no human proof is known ([Wikipedia: Kazhdan's property (T)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhdan%27s_property_%28T%29)). Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette end Part I of their monograph with a chapter "A short list of open questions" ([Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511542749/type/book)).
- **Active direction: $C^*$-simplicity of non-discrete groups.** Raum initiated research on locally compact $C^*$-simple groups, proving that every $C^*$-simple group is totally disconnected and giving the first simplicity result for reduced $C^*$-algebras of non-discrete groups ([Raum, arXiv:1505.07793](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.07793)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Group algebra of a locally compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_algebra_of_a_locally_compact_group): $L^1(G)$, $C^*(G)$, $C^*_r(G)$, von Neumann algebras and the amenability criterion.
- **Reference:** [Spectrum of a C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_C*-algebra): unitary dual, Fell topology, type I groups and Glimm's theorem.
- **Learn:** [Bekka and de la Harpe, Unitary representations of groups, duals, and characters](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.07262): free expository book on unitary, primitive and normal quasi-duals with worked examples.
- **Primary:** [Bekka, de la Harpe and Valette, Kazhdan's Property (T)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511542749/type/book): Cambridge New Mathematical Monographs 11 (2008); property (T) and (FH), with appendices on unitary representations, induced representations, Fell's topology and amenability.
- **Primary:** [Raum, C*-simplicity of locally compact Powers groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.07793): research paper opening $C^*$-simplicity for non-discrete groups.
references.MSC 22Exx - Lie groups:
## Reference
### Overview
A [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) is a group that is also a differentiable manifold, with smooth multiplication and inversion; closed subgroups of Lie groups are again Lie groups (Cartan's closed subgroup theorem). Beyond the real case the theory includes $p$-adic Lie groups, analytic manifolds over $\mathbb Q_p$ with analytic group laws, and infinite-dimensional Lie groups modelled on Banach or [locally convex spaces](node:Locally%20Convex%20Spaces), where many finite-dimensional results fail or become subtle. ([Wikipedia, Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group)) 22E covers all of these: structure, analysis, discrete subgroups, and representation theory of Lie and linear [algebraic groups](node:Algebraic%20Groups) over real, local and global fields. ([MSC2020, 22E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Exx))

The research centre of gravity is the harmonic analysis and [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) of semisimple and reductive groups (Harish-Chandra's discrete series, the Langlands classification, the unitary dual) and the rigidity and arithmeticity of lattices (Borel–Harish-Chandra, Margulis). ([Wikipedia, Discrete series representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_series_representation); [Wikipedia, Langlands classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_classification); [Adams–van Leeuwen–Trapa–Vogan, arXiv 1212.2192](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.2192); [Wikipedia, Lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_%28discrete_subgroup%29))

### Scope
MSC2020 22E lists: 22E05 local Lie groups; 22E10, 22E15, 22E20 general properties and structure of complex, real and other Lie groups; 22E25 nilpotent and solvable Lie groups and 22E27 their representations; 22E30 analysis on real and complex Lie groups; 22E35 analysis on $p$-adic Lie groups; 22E40 discrete subgroups; 22E41 continuous cohomology; 22E43 the Lorentz group; 22E45 representations over real fields, analytic methods; 22E46 semisimple Lie groups and their representations; 22E47 algebraic methods (Verma modules, etc.); 22E50 representations over local fields; 22E55 over global fields and adèle rings; 22E57 geometric Langlands program, representation-theoretic aspects; 22E60 Lie algebras of Lie groups; 22E65, 22E66 infinite-dimensional Lie groups, their Lie algebras, analysis and representations; 22E67 loop groups; 22E70 applications to the sciences; 22E99. ([MSC2020, 22E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Exx))

Neighbours named by the entry: the topology of Lie groups and homogeneous spaces is 57S and 57T (see [MSC 57Sxx - Topological transformation groups](node:MSC%2057Sxx%20-%20Topological%20transformation%20groups)); analysis on them is 43A80–43A90 in [MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis); the purely algebraic theory of [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) is [17B](node:MSC%2017Bxx%20-%20Lie%20algebras%20and%20Lie%20superalgebras); discrete subgroups also point to 20H and 32N, and representations over local and global fields to 11F70 and 20G05 (see [MSC 11Fxx - Discontinuous groups and automorphic forms](node:MSC%2011Fxx%20-%20Discontinuous%20groups%20and%20automorphic%20forms) and [MSC 20Gxx - Linear algebraic groups and related topics](node:MSC%2020Gxx%20-%20Linear%20algebraic%20groups%20and%20related%20topics)). ([MSC2020, 22E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Exx)) The parent section is [MSC 22 - Topological groups, Lie groups](node:MSC%2022%20-%20Topological%20groups,%20Lie%20groups).

### Key concepts
- **Lie correspondence (22E60).** Lie's third theorem: every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a simply connected Lie group. For a Lie subalgebra $\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathrm{Lie}(G)$ there is a unique connected Lie subgroup $H$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak h$, not necessarily closed. If $G$ is simply connected, every Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathrm{Lie}(G)\to\mathrm{Lie}(H)$ is the differential of a unique Lie group homomorphism $G\to H$; simple connectivity is needed, as $\mathfrak{so}(3)\cong\mathfrak{su}(2)$ but this isomorphism does not come from any homomorphism $SO(3)\to SU(2)$. For closed $G\le GL(n,\mathbb C)$, $\mathrm{Lie}(G)=\{X:e^{tX}\in G\ \forall t\in\mathbb R\}$, the link to the [exponential map](node:Lie%20Group%20Exponential%20Map). ([Wikipedia, Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group%E2%80%93Lie_algebra_correspondence)) Every simply connected Lie group is a semidirect product of a solvable normal subgroup and a semisimple one (Levi decomposition). ([Wikipedia, Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group))
- **Structure of semisimple groups (22E15, 22E46).** For a real semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan involution $\theta$ (with $-B(X,\theta Y)$ positive definite, $B$ the Killing form) exists and is unique up to inner automorphism, giving $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak p$ with $[\mathfrak k,\mathfrak p]\subseteq\mathfrak p$, $[\mathfrak p,\mathfrak p]\subseteq\mathfrak k$. For a noncompact semisimple $G$, with $K$ the analytic subgroup with Lie algebra $\mathfrak k$, $K$ is closed and $K\times\mathfrak p\to G$, $(k,X)\mapsto k\exp X$, is a diffeomorphism, $K$ is maximal compact when the centre is finite, and $G=KAK$ with $A=\exp\mathfrak a$, $\mathfrak a\subseteq\mathfrak p$ maximal abelian. ([Wikipedia, Cartan decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan_decomposition)) Iwasawa (1949): $(k,a,n)\mapsto kan$ is an analytic diffeomorphism $K\times A\times N\to G$, $N$ generated by the positive restricted root spaces; for $SL_n(\mathbb R)$ these are orthogonal, positive diagonal and upper unitriangular matrices. ([Wikipedia, Iwasawa decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwasawa_decomposition)) Bruhat: for connected reductive $G$ over an algebraically closed field with Borel $B$ and Weyl group $W$, $G=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB$; for $GL_n$ this is $A=U_1PU_2$ with $P$ a permutation matrix. ([Wikipedia, Bruhat decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruhat_decomposition)) Compare [Root Systems](node:Root%20Systems) and [Reductive Algebraic Groups](node:Reductive%20Algebraic%20Groups).
- **Representations of real reductive groups (22E45–22E47).** A representation on a Hilbert space is admissible if its restriction to $K$ is unitary with each $K$-type of finite multiplicity; irreducible unitary representations are the prototype, and one passes to $(\mathfrak g,K)$-modules. ([Wikipedia, Admissible representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admissible_representation)) Harish-Chandra (1965–66): a connected semisimple group with finite centre has discrete series iff $\operatorname{rank}G=\operatorname{rank}K$, and the discrete series is parametrized by regular elements of $L+\rho$ modulo $W_K$; Atiyah and Schmid (1977) realized them on harmonic spinors. ([Wikipedia, Discrete series representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_series_representation)) Langlands (1973) classified irreducible admissible $(\mathfrak g,K)$-modules as unique irreducible quotients of parabolically induced representations attached to triples $(F,\sigma,\lambda)$ with $\sigma$ tempered on a Levi factor; Knapp and Zuckerman classified the tempered representations. ([Wikipedia, Langlands classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_classification)) Compare [Unitary Representations of Locally Compact Groups](node:Unitary%20Representations%20of%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups).
- **Lattices and arithmeticity (22E40).** For a semisimple linear algebraic group $G$ over $\mathbb Q$, Borel and Harish-Chandra proved $\Gamma=G\cap GL_n(\mathbb Z)$ is a lattice in the real points $G(\mathbb R)$; it is cocompact iff the $\mathbb Q$-form is anisotropic. ([Wikipedia, Lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_%28discrete_subgroup%29); [Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group)) Margulis superrigidity: if $G$ is a simply connected semisimple real algebraic group whose real points have real rank at least 2 and no compact factors, $\Gamma\le G$ is an irreducible lattice, and $\rho:\Gamma\to GL_n(F)$ over a local field $F$ has unbounded image with connected Zariski closure, then $F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and $\rho$ extends to a rational representation of $G$. ([Wikipedia, Superrigidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superrigidity)) It is a key ingredient of Margulis arithmeticity: in higher rank irreducible lattices are arithmetic, e.g. every lattice in $SL_n(\mathbb R)$, $n\ge3$; non-arithmetic lattices exist in all $SO(n,1)$ and in $SU(2,1)$, $SU(3,1)$ (possibly in $SU(n,1)$, $n\ge4$), and all irreducible lattices in the other simple groups are arithmetic. Lattices in $SO(n,1)$, $SU(n,1)$ lack property (T), while irreducible lattices in other simple Lie groups have it. ([Wikipedia, Lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_%28discrete_subgroup%29); [Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group)) See [Arithmetic Matrix Groups](node:Arithmetic%20Matrix%20Groups).
- **Unitary dual algorithm (22E46).** Adams, van Leeuwen, Trapa and Vogan give a finite algorithm computing the irreducible unitary representations of a real reductive group, by tracking signatures of Hermitian forms (normalized so that the compact form acts skew-adjointly) through deformations, using the Langlands classification and Kazhdan–Lusztig theory. ([Adams–van Leeuwen–Trapa–Vogan, arXiv 1212.2192](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.2192))

### History
Lie dated his theory to the winter of 1873–74; Killing's structure papers began in 1888, Élie Cartan refined and generalized Killing's work, and Weyl classified representations of compact and semisimple groups by highest weights. Hilbert's fifth problem (1900) was answered in 1952 by Gleason, Montgomery and Zippin: a topological group that is a topological manifold has a unique compatible Lie group structure. ([Wikipedia, Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group)) Margulis's arithmeticity work dates from the 1970s (ICM Vancouver, 1974). ([Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group)) Knapp's *Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction* appeared with Birkhäuser in 1996. ([Crossref, Knapp](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2453-0))

### Open problems
- **Non-arithmetic lattices in $SU(n,1)$, $n\ge4$.** Whether they exist is an open question; none are known. ([Wikipedia, Lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_%28discrete_subgroup%29); [Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group))
- **Congruence subgroup problem.** Serre's conjecture: irreducible arithmetic lattices in higher-rank groups have the congruence subgroup property and rank-one lattices do not; it is still open in this generality, though many cases are settled. ([Wikipedia, Arithmetic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_group))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Lattice (discrete subgroup)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_%28discrete_subgroup%29): Borel–Harish-Chandra, arithmeticity, superrigidity, property (T).
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.755, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras II (Etingof, 2024)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/): Peter–Weyl, Cartan and Iwasawa decompositions, classification of real reductive groups, Lie's third theorem, Levi and Ado.
- **Primary:** [Adams–van Leeuwen–Trapa–Vogan, Unitary representations of real reductive groups (arXiv 1212.2192)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.2192): finite algorithm for the unitary dual.
- **Further reading:** [Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction (Birkhäuser, 1996)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2453-0): standard graduate text on structure and representations of semisimple groups.
references.MSC 22Fxx - Noncompact transformation gr:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 22F studies actions of noncompact (typically locally compact or Lie) groups on spaces: topological, smooth, measurable and homogeneous. For a [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) $G$ and a [smooth manifold](node:Smooth%20Manifolds) $M$, an action ([Transformation Group Actions](node:Transformation%20Group%20Actions)) $\sigma\colon G\times M\to M$ is a Lie group action when $\sigma$ is differentiable; in general the orbit space $M/G$ is not a manifold. ([Wikipedia, Lie group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group_action))

Two ideas organise the noncompact theory. The first is properness, which makes an action of a noncompact group behave like the action of a compact group; Palais introduced it in 1961 to prove slice theorems. ([nLab, proper action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proper+action)) The second is ergodic theory of measure-preserving group actions, including homogeneous flows; in the MSC, 37A15 (general groups of measure-preserving transformations) carries "see mainly 22Fxx" and 37A17 (homogeneous flows) "see also 22Fxx". ([MSC2020, 37Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Axx))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists five codes under 22Fxx ([MSC2020, 22Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Fxx)):
- **22F05** General theory of group and pseudogroup actions (cf. [Lie Groupoids and Pseudogroups](node:Lie%20Groupoids%20and%20Pseudogroups)); topological properties of spaces with an action go to 57S20.
- **22F10** Measurable group actions (see also 22D40, 28Dxx, 37Axx).
- **22F30** Homogeneous spaces (general actions on manifolds or preserving geometric structures go to 57M60, 57Sxx; discrete subgroups of Lie groups especially to 22E40).
- **22F50** Groups as automorphisms of other structures; **22F99** none of the above.

Neighbouring codes, one line each:
- **[57S](node:MSC%2057Sxx%20-%20Topological%20transformation%20groups)** takes the topology of spaces with an action, including 57S20 "noncompact Lie groups of transformations" and 57S30 "discontinuous groups of transformations". ([MSC2020, 57Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=57Sxx))
- **[22D](node:MSC%2022Dxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20groups%20and%20their%20algebras)** takes [unitary representations](node:Unitary%20Representations%20of%20Locally%20Compact%20Groups) (22D10), ergodic theory on groups (22D40), rigidity (22D50) and property (T) (22D55). ([MSC2020, 22Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Dxx))
- **[37A](node:MSC%2037Axx%20-%20Ergodic%20theory)** and [28D](node:MSC%2028Dxx%20-%20Measure-theoretic%20ergodic%20theory) take single transformations and flows; 37A20 holds cocycles and orbit equivalence. ([MSC2020, 37Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Axx))
- **[22E](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups)** takes discrete subgroups and lattices themselves (22E40). ([MSC2020, 22Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Proper actions and slices (22F05).** For $G$ acting on a locally compact Hausdorff $X$, the following are equivalent (Palais 1961): the map $(g,x)\mapsto(gx,x)$ is proper; $\{g:gK\cap K\neq\varnothing\}$ is compact for every compact $K$; and Palais's local condition. Stabilizers of proper actions are compact, and smooth actions of compact Lie groups are proper. ([nLab, proper action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proper+action)) **Palais's slice theorem:** if $G$ is a Lie group (not necessarily compact) and $X$ a proper $G$-space, each $x$ has a $G$-invariant neighbourhood $U$ with a $G$-equivariant map $U\to G/G_x$; every orbit is closed and every stabilizer compact. Mostow had proved the slice theorem for compact Lie groups. ([Antonyan, arXiv 1702.08093, Thm 1.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1702.08093)) If a Lie group acts smoothly, freely and properly on $M$, then $M/G$ has a unique smooth structure making $M\to M/G$ a principal $G$-bundle. ([Wikipedia, Lie group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group_action))
- **Proper actions on reductive homogeneous spaces (22F30).** For reductive $G\supset H$ and reductive $L$, $L$ acts properly on $G/H$ iff $\mathfrak a_H\cap W\cdot\mathfrak a_L=\{0\}$ in a Cartan subspace (Kobayashi 1989; the general criterion of Benoist and Kobayashi (1996) compares Cartan projections). **Calabi–Markus phenomenon:** for real reductive $G\supset H$, $G/H$ admits an infinite discontinuous group iff $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}G>\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}H$; for $(O(n,1),O(n-1,1))$ the ranks agree, so de Sitter space admits no infinite discontinuous group and its complete space forms $\Gamma\backslash G/H$ have $\Gamma$ finite, hence are non-compact. ([Kobayashi, arXiv 2506.15616, Thms 4.14, 4.17, Cor. 4.19](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.15616v2))
- **Howe–Moore and Moore ergodicity.** A group has the Howe–Moore property if all matrix coefficients of unitary representations without nonzero invariant vectors vanish at infinity; connected non-compact simple real Lie groups with finite centre have it. ([Ciobotaru, arXiv 1403.0223](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.0223v2)) **Moore's theorem** (Amer. J. Math. 1966): for a lattice $\Gamma$ in such a $G$ and a Lie subgroup $H$, $H$ acts ergodically on $G/\Gamma$ iff $\overline H$ is noncompact. ([Amerik–Verbitsky, arXiv 1408.3892, Thm 3.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1408.3892)) See [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) and [Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure).
- **Margulis superrigidity and arithmeticity.** For an irreducible lattice $\Gamma$ in a semisimple Lie group of real rank $\ge2$ (with $G$ simply connected), every linear representation $\sigma$ of $\Gamma$ almost extends: $\sigma=\tilde\sigma\cdot\bar\sigma$ with $\tilde\sigma$ a representation of $G$ and $\bar\sigma$ of bounded image. Arithmeticity: if $G$ is semisimple without compact factors and not locally isomorphic to $SO(1,n)$ or $SU(1,n)$, every irreducible lattice in $G$ is arithmetic; in real rank $\ge2$ this follows from superrigidity. ([Fisher 2008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0809.4849))
- **Orbit equivalence (22F10).** Free p.m.p. ([measure-preserving](node:Measure-Preserving%20Transformations)) actions are orbit equivalent if a measure-preserving isomorphism of conull sets carries orbits to orbits. ([Furman, Def. 2.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0901.0678)) All ergodic hyperfinite p.m.p. relations are orbit equivalent (Dye); p.m.p. actions of amenable groups are hyperfinite (Ornstein–Weiss 1980); every non-amenable group has continuum many orbit-inequivalent free ergodic actions (Epstein, completing Hjorth, Gaboriau–Popa, Ioana); free actions of $\mathbb F_n$ have cost $n$. ([Gaboriau survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.0132)) **Zimmer's OE rigidity:** if $G,G'$ are center-free simple Lie groups of real rank $\ge2$ with lattices $\Gamma,\Gamma'$ having orbit-equivalent essentially free p.m.p. actions, then $G\cong G'$; so $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)\curvearrowright\mathbb T^n$ and $\mathrm{SL}_m(\mathbb Z)\curvearrowright\mathbb T^m$ are not orbit equivalent for $2\le n<m$. ([Furman, Thm 3.14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0901.0678)) **Popa's OE superrigidity:** for ICC property (T) $\Gamma$, any free action orbit equivalent to the Bernoulli shift is conjugate to it. ([Gaboriau survey, Thm 12.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.0132))
- **Homogeneous dynamics: Ratner, EKL, Benoist–Quint.** For a lattice $\Gamma$ in a Lie group $G$ and a unipotent one-parameter subgroup $u_t$ on $\Gamma\backslash G$: every ergodic invariant probability measure is homogeneous, every orbit closure is homogeneous, and every orbit is equidistributed in its closure (Ratner, around 1990). ([Wikipedia, Ratner's theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratner%27s_theorems)) Margulis's Oppenheim theorem: a real indefinite nondegenerate quadratic form in $n\ge3$ variables, not a multiple of an integral form, has $Q(\mathbb Z^n)$ dense in $\mathbb R$. ([Witte Morris](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0310402)) **Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss:** for $k\ge3$, an $A$-invariant ergodic probability measure on $\mathrm{SL}(k,\mathbb R)/\mathrm{SL}(k,\mathbb Z)$ ($A$ the positive diagonal group) for which some one-parameter subgroup of $A$ has positive entropy is algebraic; hence the exceptions to Littlewood's conjecture have Hausdorff dimension zero. ([EKL, Thms 1.3, 1.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0612721)) **Benoist–Quint:** for $G$ connected almost simple, $\Lambda$ a lattice, and $\mu$ a compactly supported probability measure whose support generates a Zariski-dense subgroup, every non-atomic $\mu$-stationary probability measure on $G/\Lambda$ is Haar; and for a Zariski-dense subsemigroup $\Gamma$, every closed infinite $\Gamma$-invariant set is all of $G/\Lambda$. ([Benoist–Quint, Thm 1.1, Cor. 1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/1610.05912v1))
- **Zimmer program.** Zimmer's conjecture: for $n>2$ every homomorphism $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb Z)\to\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ has finite image when $\dim M<n-1$, sharp because of the action on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$; Zimmer's cocycle superrigidity extends Margulis's theorem to cocycles over measure-preserving actions. ([Fisher 2008, Conj. 1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0809.4849)) Brown, Fisher and Hurtado proved it for $C^2$ actions of finite-index subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}(m,\mathbb Z)$, $m>3$ ([arXiv 1710.02735](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.02735)), published in Inventiones 221 (2020). ([Wikipedia, Zimmer's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimmer%27s_conjecture))

### History
Palais's 1961 Annals paper on slices for non-compact Lie groups introduced proper actions. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1970335); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proper+action)) Moore's ergodicity theorem dates to 1966. ([Amerik–Verbitsky](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1408.3892)) Zimmer's orbit-equivalence rigidity appeared as "Strong rigidity for ergodic actions of semisimple Lie groups", Ann. of Math. 112 (1980) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1971090)), and his monograph *Ergodic Theory and Semisimple Groups* (Birkhäuser) appeared in 1984. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-9488-4)) Ornstein–Weiss (1980), Gaboriau's cost and Popa's superrigidity mark the growth of measured group theory. ([Gaboriau survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.0132)) Ratner's theorems date to around 1990 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratner%27s_theorems)), EKL to Annals 164 (2006) ([arXiv math/0612721](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0612721)), and Benoist–Quint to Annals 174 (2011). ([arXiv 1610.05912](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.05912))

### Open problems
- **Fixed price problem.** Is there a group with two free p.m.p. actions of different costs (Gaboriau Q6.3; Furman Question 3.3)? ([Gaboriau survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.0132); [Furman](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0901.0678)) Gaboriau's Q6.4 was answered: every countably infinite property (T) group has cost 1, while "it remains open if they have fixed price 1". ([Hutchcroft–Pete, arXiv 1810.11015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.11015))
- **Cost versus $\ell^2$-Betti numbers.** Is there an infinite countable group with $\mathcal C(\Gamma)>\beta_1^{(2)}(\Gamma)+1$? Equality holds in every computed case (Q8.2). ([Gaboriau survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.0132))
- **Margulis's measure-classification conjecture.** For $k\ge3$, every $A$-invariant ergodic probability measure on $\mathrm{SL}(k,\mathbb R)/\mathrm{SL}(k,\mathbb Z)$ should be algebraic, with no entropy assumption (Conjecture 1.1); EKL prove only the positive-entropy case. ([EKL](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0612721))
- **Zimmer program.** Fisher's survey conjectures that volume-preserving smooth actions of property (T) groups on surfaces are finite (Conj. 4.7) and that actions of lattices $\Gamma<\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb R)$ on compact manifolds preserving both a volume form and an affine connection can be classified (Conj. 1.2). ([Fisher 2008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0809.4849)) On his circle conjecture (Conj. 4.2: continuous actions of higher-rank lattices on $S^1$ are finite), Deroin and Hurtado show that irreducible lattices in finite-centre semisimple groups of real rank $\ge2$ are not left-orderable and that each of their circle actions has finite image or is semi-conjugate, up to finite index, to a projective action through a $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)$ factor. ([Deroin–Hurtado, arXiv 2008.10687](https://arxiv.org/html/2008.10687))
- **Proper $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R)$-actions.** Kobayashi asks which homomorphisms $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R)\to\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb R)$ induce proper actions on $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb R)/\mathrm{SL}(m,\mathbb R)$ (Questions 4.21–4.22). ([Kobayashi, arXiv 2506.15616](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.15616v2))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, proper action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proper+action): equivalent definitions of properness; [MSC2020, 22Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=22Fxx): official codes and cross-references.
- **Learn:** [Witte Morris, *Ratner's Theorems on Unipotent Flows*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0310402): lecture-note book on homogeneous dynamics and Oppenheim.
- **Primary:** [Furman, A survey of measured group theory](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0901.0678); [Gaboriau, Orbit equivalence and measured group theory](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.0132); [Fisher, Groups acting on manifolds: around the Zimmer program](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0809.4849); [Kobayashi, Proper actions and representation theory](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.15616v2); [Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss, Annals 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0612721).
- **Further reading:** [Zimmer, *Ergodic Theory and Semisimple Groups* (Birkhäuser, 1984)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-9488-4): Zimmer's monograph on ergodic theory of semisimple groups.
references.MSC 26 - Real functions:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 26 ("Real functions", see also 54C30) is the research classification for the fine theory of real-valued functions of real variables. It has five subdivisions: functions of one variable (26Axx), functions of several variables (26Bxx), polynomials and rational functions (26Cxx), inequalities (26Dxx), and miscellaneous topics (26Exx, see also 58Cxx). ([MSC2020 26](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26-XX))

Undergraduate real analysis ([Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits), [Differential Calculus](node:Differential%20Calculus), [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus)) is the entry point, but the section itself classifies research on questions such as which functions are derivatives, how far integration can be generalized beyond Lebesgue's, how real functions of bounded variation or given smoothness behave, how real zeros of polynomials are located, and which analytic inequalities hold. Abstract measure and integration are classified separately in [MSC 28 - Measure and integration](node:MSC%2028%20-%20Measure%20and%20integration), to which 26A42 explicitly points. ([MSC2020 26Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Axx); [MSC2020 26Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Cxx); [MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))

### Scope
- **26Axx Functions of one variable** ([map](node:MSC%2026Axx%20-%20Functions%20of%20one%20variable)): foundations and one-variable calculus; growth and slowly varying functions; continuity, Lipschitz (Hölder) classes; iteration of real functions (26A18); Baire classification (26A21); differentiation, nondifferentiability and singular (Cantor-type) functions (26A24–26A30); fractional derivatives and integrals (26A33); Denjoy, Perron and other special integrals (26A39); integrals of Riemann, Stieltjes and Lebesgue type (26A42, see also 28); bounded variation, absolute continuity, monotonicity and convexity (26A45–26A51). ([MSC2020 26Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Axx))
- **26Bxx Functions of several variables** ([map](node:MSC%2026Bxx%20-%20Functions%20of%20several%20variables)): continuity and differentiation; implicit function theorems and Jacobians (26B10); calculus of vector functions (compare [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus) and [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem)); integration (length, area, volume) and integral formulas of Stokes, Gauss and Green; convexity; absolute continuity and bounded variation; Hölder conditions; representation and superposition of functions (26B40). ([MSC2020 26Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Bxx))
- **26Cxx Polynomials, rational functions** ([map](node:MSC%2026Cxx%20-%20Polynomials,%20rational%20functions%20in%20real%20analysis)): analytic properties of real polynomials, location of their zeros, real rational functions. ([MSC2020 26Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Cxx))
- **26Dxx Inequalities** ([map](node:MSC%2026Dxx%20-%20Inequalities%20in%20real%20analysis)): inequalities for polynomials, for derivatives and operators, and for sums, series and integrals; maximal, functional and probabilistic inequalities are classified in 42B25, 39B72 and 60E15. ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))
- **26Exx Miscellaneous** ([map](node:MSC%2026Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20real%20functions)): real-analytic, $C^\infty$ and quasi-analytic functions; calculus on or with values in infinite-dimensional spaces; set-valued functions; non-Archimedean, nonstandard, constructive and fuzzy real analysis; means; analysis on time scales. ([MSC2020 26Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Bounded variation.** The total variation of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is the supremum over partitions of $\sum|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|$; $f$ has bounded variation iff $f=f_1-f_2$ with $f_1,f_2$ non-decreasing (Jordan decomposition), and then $f'(x)$ exists almost everywhere. Jordan introduced the class in 1881 in his work on convergence of Fourier series. ([Bounded variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_variation))
- **Henstock–Kurzweil (gauge) integral.** $I$ is the integral of $f$ on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positive function $\delta$ (a gauge) such that $|I-\sum_P f|<\varepsilon$ for every $\delta$-fine tagged partition $P$. If $F$ is differentiable everywhere on $[a,b]$, then $F'$ is integrable and $\int_a^bF'=F(b)-F(a)$; $f$ is Lebesgue integrable iff $f$ and $|f|$ are both gauge integrable. It can be viewed as a non-absolutely convergent version of [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration), and it is also called the narrow Denjoy or Perron integral (26A39). ([Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral))
- **Fractional calculus (26A33).** The Riemann–Liouville integral $I^\alpha f(x)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_a^x(x-t)^{\alpha-1}f(t)\,dt$, defined for locally integrable $f$ and $\operatorname{Re}\alpha>0$ using the [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function), satisfies the semigroup law $I^\alpha I^\beta f=I^{\alpha+\beta}f$; fractional derivatives are defined as $D^\alpha f=\frac{d^{\lceil\alpha\rceil}}{dx^{\lceil\alpha\rceil}}I^{\lceil\alpha\rceil-\alpha}f$. ([Riemann–Liouville integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Liouville_integral))
- **Sard's theorem.** If $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge\max\{n-m+1,1\}$, the image of its critical set (points where the Jacobian has rank $<m$) has Lebesgue measure zero. Morse proved the case $m=1$ in 1939 and Sard the general case in 1942. ([Sard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem))
- **Whitney extension theorem.** Given functions $f_\alpha$ on a closed set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ satisfying Whitney's compatibility condition, there is a $C^m$ function $F$ with $F=f_0$ and $\partial^\alpha F=f_\alpha$ on $A$, real-analytic off $A$ (Whitney 1934); Fefferman's 2005 paper is titled "A sharp form of Whitney's extension theorem". ([Whitney extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_extension_theorem))
- **Real zeros of polynomials (26C).** Sturm's theorem counts the distinct real roots of a square-free real polynomial in $(a,b]$ exactly by sign variations of its Sturm sequence. ([Sturm's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%27s_theorem))
- **Sharp inequalities (26D).** Hardy's inequality $\sum_n\big(\frac{a_1+\dots+a_n}{n}\big)^p\le(\frac{p}{p-1})^p\sum_na_n^p$ for $p>1$, $a_n\ge0$, with a constant that is sharp but attained only by the zero sequence when the right side is finite. ([Hardy's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%27s_inequality))

### History
Jordan's functions of bounded variation (1881) arose from Fourier series. Liouville first considered fractional calculus in 1832, and Riemann's essay on fractional integration is dated 1847. Denjoy defined his non-absolute integral in 1912 by transfinite induction; Kurzweil (1957) and Henstock (1961) independently found the simpler gauge definition. ([Bounded variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_variation); [Riemann–Liouville integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Liouville_integral); [Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral)) Whitney's extension theorem appeared in 1934 and Sard's theorem in 1942. ([Whitney extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_extension_theorem); [Sard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Sharp Landau–Kolmogorov constants on a half-line (26D).** In $\|f^{(k)}\|_\infty\le C\|f\|_\infty^{1-k/n}\|f^{(n)}\|_\infty^{k/n}$, the sharp constants are known on $\mathbb R$ (Kolmogorov), and Schoenberg found the extremal functions on the half-line, but explicit forms of the half-line sharp constants are still unknown. ([Landau–Kolmogorov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93Kolmogorov_inequality))
- **Kushnirenko's question (real zeros of sparse polynomial systems).** Whether the number of regular positive zeros of $n$ real polynomials in $n$ variables with $t_1,\dots,t_n$ terms admits a bound polynomial in the $t_i$ (to the power $n$) is described as "widely open", even in two variables. ([Ergür–Telek–Tonelli-Cueto](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.06784))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral): definition, properties and history of the gauge integral.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.100A Real Analysis (OCW)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/): sequences, series, continuity, differentiability, the Riemann integral and uniform convergence.
- **Primary:** [Gordon, The Integrals of Lebesgue, Denjoy, Perron, and Henstock (AMS GSM 4, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/004): monograph on the Lebesgue, Denjoy, Perron and Henstock integrals.
- **Primary:** [Ergür, Telek and Tonelli-Cueto (arXiv 2306.06784)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06784): current research on real zeros of sparse polynomial systems.
- **Further reading:** [Mitrinović, Pečarić and Fink, Classical and New Inequalities in Analysis (Springer, 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-017-1043-5) for 26D; [Rahman and Schmeisser, Analytic Theory of Polynomials (OUP, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198534938.001.0001) for 26C.
references.MSC 26Axx - Functions of one variable:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 26A covers real functions of one real variable. Its subjects range from foundations and one-variable calculus to Baire classes, generalized derivatives, nondifferentiable and singular functions, fractional calculus, Denjoy and Perron integrals, bounded variation, absolute continuity, monotonicity and convexity. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf)) It sits inside [MSC 26 - Real functions](node:MSC%2026%20-%20Real%20functions) and uses [measure theory](node:Measure%20Theory) and [Lebesgue integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration) as working tools.

A central theme is the gap between continuity and differentiability. Weierstrass presented a continuous nowhere differentiable function to the Prussian Academy in 1872 (published 1886), and a typical continuous function in the sense of Baire category is nowhere differentiable; on the other hand, every continuous $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ agrees with some $C^1$ function on an uncountable set (Agronsky–Bruckner–Laczkovich–Preiss, 1985). ([Ciesielski–Seoane](https://community.wvu.edu/~kciesiel/ProfessionalStuff/prepF/138DiffFunctionsBAMS.pdf))

### Scope
The 26A codes are: 26A03 foundations and topology of the line; 26A06 one-variable calculus; 26A09 elementary functions; 26A12 rates of growth and slowly varying functions; 26A15 continuity, moduli of continuity, semicontinuity; 26A16 Lipschitz (Hölder) classes; 26A18 iteration of real functions; 26A21 Baire classification; 26A24 differentiation, generalized derivatives, mean value theorems; 26A27 nondifferentiability and discontinuous derivatives; 26A30 singular and Cantor functions; 26A33 fractional derivatives and integrals; 26A36 antidifferentiation; 26A39 Denjoy and Perron integrals; 26A42 Riemann, Stieltjes and Lebesgue integrals; 26A45 bounded variation; 26A46 absolute continuity; 26A48 monotonic functions; 26A51 convexity. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Neighbouring codes: continuity properties determined by Fourier coefficients go to 42A16 and those determined by approximation to 41A25 and 41A27; iteration is cross-referenced to [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) (37Bxx, 37Cxx, 37Exx) and functional equations (39B12); differentiation (26A24) is cross-referenced to 28A15; several-variable questions are [26B](node:MSC%2026Bxx%20-%20Functions%20of%20several%20variables). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Bounded variation and Lebesgue's differentiation theorem (26A45, 26A48).** The total variation of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is $\sup\sum_i|f(x_{i+1})-f(x_i)|$ over partitions. Jordan: $f$ has bounded variation on $[a,b]$ if and only if $f=f_1-f_2$ with $f_1,f_2$ nondecreasing. BV functions have at most countably many discontinuities and are differentiable almost everywhere. ([Bounded variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_variation)) The a.e. differentiability of every monotone $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is Lebesgue's theorem; a standard proof uses F. Riesz's rising sun lemma (1932). ([Ciesielski–Seoane](https://community.wvu.edu/~kciesiel/ProfessionalStuff/prepF/138DiffFunctionsBAMS.pdf))
- **Absolute continuity and the Lebesgue fundamental theorem (26A46).** $f$ is absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $\sum|f(\beta_i)-f(\alpha_i)|<\varepsilon$ for every finite family of disjoint $(\alpha_i,\beta_i)$ of total length $<\delta$. Then: $f$ is absolutely continuous if and only if $f$ is differentiable a.e., $f'\in L^1$, and $f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt$. On a bounded interval, Lipschitz $\subseteq$ absolutely continuous $\subseteq$ BV. ([Absolute continuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_continuity)) For $f\in L^1$, $F(x)=\int_a^x f$ is differentiable a.e. with $F'=f$ a.e. ([MIT 18.125, lecture 22](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/31864359c21e7fd7f0559904c8876e7a_18125_lec22.pdf))
- **Singular functions (26A30).** The Cantor function is continuous, of bounded variation, with $f'=0$ a.e., yet not absolutely continuous, since $\int_0^1 f'=0\neq f(1)-f(0)=1$. ([Absolute continuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_continuity)) Minkowski's question-mark function $?(x)$ (1904) is continuous and strictly increasing but singular, with derivative 0 almost everywhere; it maps rationals to dyadic rationals and quadratic irrationals to non-dyadic rationals. ([Question-mark function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%27s_question-mark_function))
- **Henstock–Kurzweil (Denjoy–Perron) integration (26A39).** Replacing the mesh of Riemann sums by a positive gauge $\delta(x)$ on tagged partitions gives the gauge integral (Denjoy 1912; gauge form by Kurzweil 1957 and Henstock 1961). If $F$ is differentiable everywhere on $[a,b]$, then $F'$ is gauge integrable and $\int_a^x F'=F(x)-F(a)$; $f$ is Lebesgue integrable exactly when $f$ and $|f|$ are gauge integrable. ([Henstock–Kurzweil integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henstock%E2%80%93Kurzweil_integral))
- **Fractional calculus (26A33).** Generalizing Cauchy's formula for repeated integration with the [gamma function](node:Gamma%20Function), the Riemann–Liouville integral is $(J^\alpha f)(x)=\frac1{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^x(x-t)^{\alpha-1}f(t)\,dt$, satisfying $J^\alpha J^\beta=J^{\alpha+\beta}$; the Riemann–Liouville derivative is $D^\alpha f=\frac{d^n}{dx^n}J^{n-\alpha}f$ with $n=\lceil\alpha\rceil$, and the Caputo derivative applies $J^{n-\alpha}$ to $f^{(n)}$ instead. Non-integer derivatives are nonlocal, and different definitions need not agree even for smooth functions. ([Fractional calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_calculus))
- **Baire classes (26A21).** Class 0 functions are continuous and class $\alpha$ functions are pointwise limits of sequences from lower classes (Baire, 1899). Derivatives of differentiable functions are Baire class 1; a function is of class 1 exactly when its restriction to each nonempty closed set has a point of continuity, and the Dirichlet function is class 2 but not class 1. Lebesgue showed each class contains functions in no smaller class. ([Baire function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baire_function))

### History
Jordan introduced functions of bounded variation in 1881 while studying convergence of [Fourier series](node:Fourier%20Analysis). ([Bounded variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_variation)) Leibniz's 1695 letter to L'Hôpital is the first appearance of a fractional derivative; Abel (1823) and Liouville (1832) laid foundations, and Heaviside used fractional operators around 1890. ([Fractional calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_calculus)) Bolzano had a continuous nowhere differentiable function in 1822, before Weierstrass's published example. Around 1940 Ulam asked in the Scottish Book whether every continuous function agrees with a real analytic one on an uncountable set; Zahorski (1948) answered no and posed the Ulam–Zahorski problem, which the 1985 $C^1$ theorem settles for $C^1$, while Olevskiĭ (1994) built a continuous function agreeing with every $C^2$ function on at most countably many points. ([Ciesielski–Seoane](https://community.wvu.edu/~kciesiel/ProfessionalStuff/prepF/138DiffFunctionsBAMS.pdf))

### Open problems
- **$D^n$ extension.** For each $n\ge2$, characterize the $n$-times differentiable functions on a perfect $P\subseteq\mathbb R$ that extend to $n$-times differentiable functions on $\mathbb R$, a $D^n$ analogue of Whitney's $C^n$ extension theorem. ([Ciesielski–Seoane, Problem 6.4](https://community.wvu.edu/~kciesiel/ProfessionalStuff/prepF/138DiffFunctionsBAMS.pdf))
- **Ulam–Zahorski interpolation for $D^1,D^2$.** Is it true that for every differentiable $g$ there is a twice differentiable $f$ with $\{f=g\}$ uncountable? ([Ciesielski–Seoane, Problem 6.5](https://community.wvu.edu/~kciesiel/ProfessionalStuff/prepF/138DiffFunctionsBAMS.pdf))
- **Fixed points of $?(x)$.** It is conjectured that the question-mark function has exactly five fixed points: $0,\tfrac12,1$ and a symmetric pair, one near $0.42037$. ([Question-mark function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%27s_question-mark_function))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Absolute continuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_continuity): definitions, the Lebesgue fundamental theorem and the Cantor function.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.125 Measure and Integration, lecture 22](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/31864359c21e7fd7f0559904c8876e7a_18125_lec22.pdf): Lebesgue's differentiation theorem, absolute continuity and the Vitali covering theorem.
- **Primary:** [Ciesielski and Seoane-Sepúlveda, Differentiability versus continuity](https://community.wvu.edu/~kciesiel/ProfessionalStuff/prepF/138DiffFunctionsBAMS.pdf): survey of nowhere differentiable functions, restriction and extension theorems, with an open-problem list.
- **Further reading:** [Bruckner, Differentiation of Real Functions](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/crmm/005): AMS CRM Monograph Series, 1994; monograph on derivatives of real functions, cited by the survey above on the problem of characterizing derivatives.
