## Reference
### Overview
MSC 26B covers real functions of several real variables: continuity and differentiation, implicit functions and Jacobians, vector functions, length, area and volume, integral formulas of Stokes–Gauss–Green type, convexity, absolute continuity and bounded variation, Hölder-type regularity, and representation of functions by superposition. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

The basic regularity theorem is Rademacher's: Lipschitz maps are differentiable almost everywhere. Preiss and Speight, combining their theorem with announced work of Alberti–Csörnyei–Preiss and Csörnyei–Jones, settled when the converse holds: a Lebesgue null set can contain a differentiability point of every Lipschitz map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ exactly when $m<n$. ([Preiss–Speight](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1304.6916)) A second line, going back to Whitney in 1934, asks how to decide whether a function given on an arbitrary set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ extends to a $C^m$ function, and how small its norm can be. ([Fefferman](https://web.math.princeton.edu/facultypapers/Fefferman/WhitneyExtInterpolJul08.pdf))

### Scope
The 26B codes are: 26B05 continuity and differentiation questions; 26B10 implicit function theorems, Jacobians, transformations with several variables; 26B12 calculus of vector functions; 26B15 integration in several variables: length, area, volume (with 28A75, 51M25); 26B20 integral formulas (Stokes, Gauss, Green, etc.); 26B25 convexity of functions of several variables; 26B30 absolutely continuous functions of several variables and functions of bounded variation; 26B35 special properties, Hölder conditions; 26B40 representation and superposition of functions. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Neighbouring codes: one-variable questions are [26A](node:MSC%2026Axx%20-%20Functions%20of%20one%20variable); length, area and volume are cross-referenced to [measure theory](node:Measure%20Theory) (28A75) and to 51M25. 26B20 covers integral formulas of Stokes, Gauss and Green type (see [vector calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus) and [differential forms](node:Differential%20Forms)). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Inverse and implicit function theorems (26B10).** If $f$ is $C^1$ on an open set and $df_p$ is invertible, then $f$ restricts to a bijection between neighbourhoods of $p$ and $f(p)$ with $C^1$ inverse $g$ satisfying $dg_{f(p)}=(df_p)^{-1}$; the proof reduces to the contraction mapping fixed point theorem and holds for maps between affine spaces modelled on [Banach spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces). ([Freed](https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/dafr/multi-with-homework.pdf)) See [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem).
- **Rademacher's theorem and its converse (26B05, 26B35).** If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^m$ is locally Lipschitz, then $f$ is differentiable outside a Lebesgue null set (Rademacher, 1919). More generally (Calderón), for bounded open $\Omega$ and $p>n$, every function in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is differentiable a.e.; see [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces). ([Rademacher's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher%27s_theorem)) For $n>1$ there is a null set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ containing a differentiability point of every Lipschitz $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n-1}$ (Preiss–Speight); combined with Alberti–Csörnyei–Preiss and the announced Csörnyei–Jones theorem, the converse of Rademacher's theorem holds if and only if $m\ge n$. ([Preiss–Speight](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1304.6916))
- **Alexandrov's theorem (26B25).** A convex function on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ has a second-order Taylor expansion, with remainder $o(|h|^2)$, at almost every point. ([Alexandrov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandrov_theorem)) Its proof can be modelled on that of Rademacher's theorem. ([Rademacher's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher%27s_theorem))
- **Coarea formula and BV (26B15, 26B30).** For $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ Lipschitz on open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $g\in L^1$, $\int_\Omega g\,|\nabla u|\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{u^{-1}(t)}g\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}\,dt$; for Lipschitz $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R^k$, $k\le n$, $|\nabla u|$ is replaced by the Jacobian $J_ku=\sqrt{\det(Du\,Du^{T})}$ and $\mathcal H^{n-1}$ by $\mathcal H^{n-k}$ (Federer 1959; BV version by Fleming–Rishel 1960). ([Coarea formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coarea_formula)) In several variables, $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ has bounded variation when its distributional derivative is a finite Radon measure. ([Bounded variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_variation))
- **Whitney extension theorem (26B05).** Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be closed and let $(f_\alpha)_{|\alpha|\le m}$ be functions on $A$ satisfying the Taylor compatibility condition $f_\alpha(x)=\sum_{|\beta|\le m-|\alpha|}\frac{f_{\alpha+\beta}(y)}{\beta!}(x-y)^\beta+o(|x-y|^{m-|\alpha|})$ uniformly as $x,y\to a\in A$. Then there is $F\in C^m(\mathbb R^n)$ with $D^\alpha F=f_\alpha$ on $A$, real-analytic off $A$ (Whitney, 1934). ([Whitney extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_extension_theorem)) Fefferman's work, building on Glaeser, Brudnyi–Shvartsman and Bierstone–Milman–Pawłucki, completely answers when a function on an arbitrary $E$ (with no jet data) extends to $C^m(\mathbb R^n)$. ([Fefferman](https://web.math.princeton.edu/facultypapers/Fefferman/WhitneyExtInterpolJul08.pdf))
- **Sard's theorem.** If $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge\max\{n-m+1,1\}$, the set of critical values (images of points where $Df$ has rank $<m$) has Lebesgue measure zero (Morse 1939 for $m=1$; Sard 1942). ([Sard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem))
- **Superposition (26B40).** Every continuous $f$ on $[0,1]^n$ can be written $f(x)=\sum_{q=0}^{2n}\Phi_q\big(\sum_{p=1}^n\varphi_{q,p}(x_p)\big)$ with continuous one-variable $\Phi_q,\varphi_{q,p}$, where the inner functions do not depend on $f$ (Kolmogorov–Arnold). ([Kolmogorov–Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold_representation_theorem))

### History
Rademacher's theorem dates from 1919. ([Rademacher's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher%27s_theorem)) Tonelli introduced continuous functions of bounded variation in several variables in 1926, and Cesari replaced continuity by integrability in 1936. ([Bounded variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_variation)) Whitney's extension papers appeared in 1934. ([Fefferman](https://web.math.princeton.edu/facultypapers/Fefferman/WhitneyExtInterpolJul08.pdf)) Kolmogorov (1956) and Arnold (1957) answered the continuous version of Hilbert's thirteenth problem, showing that functions of two variables suffice. ([Hilbert's thirteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_thirteenth_problem)) Preiss's infinite-dimensional work first showed the converse of Rademacher's theorem fails for real-valued functions when $n>1$. ([Preiss–Speight](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1304.6916))

### Open problems
- **Hilbert's thirteenth problem, algebraic version.** Whether solutions of algebraic equations can be built from algebraic functions of fewer variables, the variant for algebraic functions, remains unresolved. ([Hilbert's thirteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_thirteenth_problem))
- **Near-optimal $C^m$ interpolation.** Given $f$ on a finite $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $\epsilon>0$, compute an interpolant whose $C^m$ norm is within a factor $1+\epsilon$ of the least possible; Fefferman posed this sharpened problem (Question 8) because the constants in the known efficient algorithms are likely very large, and described work on it as just beginning. ([Fefferman](https://web.math.princeton.edu/facultypapers/Fefferman/WhitneyExtInterpolJul08.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Rademacher's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher%27s_theorem): statement and Sobolev and convex generalizations.
- **Learn:** [Freed, Multivariable Analysis](https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/dafr/multi-with-homework.pdf): UT Austin lecture notes on differentials, the inverse and implicit function theorems.
- **Primary:** [Preiss and Speight, Differentiability of Lipschitz functions in Lebesgue null sets](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1304.6916): completes the converse of Rademacher's theorem; [Fefferman, Whitney's extension problems and interpolation of data](https://web.math.princeton.edu/facultypapers/Fefferman/WhitneyExtInterpolJul08.pdf): survey of the $C^m$ extension problem.
- **Further reading:** [Evans and Gariepy, Measure Theory and Fine Properties of Functions](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/b18333) (revised edition, CRC 2015): Rademacher, Alexandrov, area and coarea formulas, BV and Sobolev functions.
references.MSC 26Cxx - Polynomials, rational functi:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 26Cxx is the part of [MSC 26 - Real functions](node:MSC%2026%20-%20Real%20functions) devoted to real polynomials studied as functions: their analytic properties (26C05), the location of their real zeros (26C10), and real rational functions (26C15). The classification sends the algebraic theory of zeros to 12D10, complex-variable methods for locating zeros to 30C15, numerical root finding to 65H05, and refers 26C15 to real algebraic geometry (14Pxx) and 26C05 to field theory (12Dxx, 12Exx). ([MSC2020 26Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Cxx))

The central questions are quantitative. How many real zeros can a real polynomial have in a given interval, as a function of its coefficients, its degree, or only its number of monomials? How large can its derivative be compared with the polynomial itself on an interval? The classical answers are sign-variation rules (Descartes, Budan–Fourier, Sturm) and the Markov–Bernstein inequalities; Khovanskii's fewnomial theory generalizes Descartes' rule, and Kac's formula counts real roots of random polynomials on average. ([Descartes' rule of signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descartes%27_rule_of_signs); [Markov brothers' inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_brothers%27_inequality); [MathWorld, Kac formula](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/KacFormula.html))

### Scope
- **26C05, real polynomials: analytic properties, etc.**, with a pointer to field theory (12Dxx, 12Exx). ([MSC2020 26Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Cxx))
- **26C10, real polynomials: location of zeros**; the algebraic theory goes to 12D10, complex methods to 30C15 and numerical methods to 65H05. ([MSC2020 26Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Cxx)) Counting and isolating real roots by sign variations and Sturm sequences is the classical toolkit. ([Real-root isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-root_isolation))
- **26C15, real rational functions**, with a pointer to real algebraic geometry (14Pxx). ([MSC2020 26Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Cxx))

Neighbours: interpolation, approximation by polynomials, and Bernstein- and Jackson-type inequalities in approximation have their own codes 41A05, 41A10 and 41A17 in [MSC 41 - Approximations and expansions](node:MSC%2041%20-%20Approximations%20and%20expansions) ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=41Axx)); zeros of polynomials and analytic functions of one complex variable are 30C15 in [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable) ([MSC2020 30Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Cxx)); algebraic root theory is in [MSC 12 - Field theory and polynomials](node:MSC%2012%20-%20Field%20theory%20and%20polynomials); numerical methods are in [MSC 65 - Numerical analysis](node:MSC%2065%20-%20Numerical%20analysis) (65H05). ([MSC2020 26Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Descartes' rule of signs.** For a real polynomial $p(x)=\sum a_k x^k$, let $v(p)$ be the number of sign changes in its sequence of nonzero coefficients. Then the number of positive roots, counted with multiplicity, equals $v(p)$ or is less than it by an even number; applying the rule to $p(-x)$ bounds the negative roots. If all roots of $p$ are known to be real, the rule is exact. ([Descartes' rule of signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descartes%27_rule_of_signs))
- **Budan–Fourier theorem.** For real $\ell<r$, let $v_h(p)$ be the number of sign variations in the coefficients of $p(x+h)$, and $\#(\ell,r]$ the number of roots in $(\ell,r]$ with multiplicity. Then $v_\ell(p)-v_r(p)-\#(\ell,r]$ is a nonnegative even integer. Fourier's version uses the sequence $p(h),p'(h),p''(h),\dots$ instead, and each version implies the other by Taylor expansion; Descartes' rule is the case $\ell=0$, $r$ beyond all roots. ([Budan's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budan%27s_theorem))
- **Sturm's theorem.** For a square-free real polynomial $P$, set $P_0=P$, $P_1=P'$, $P_{i+1}=-\operatorname{rem}(P_{i-1},P_i)$. If $V(\xi)$ is the number of sign variations of $P_0(\xi),P_1(\xi),\dots$, then for $a<b$ the number of distinct real roots of $P$ in $(a,b]$ is exactly $V(a)-V(b)$. Unlike Budan–Fourier, this count is exact, which gave the first complete real-root isolation algorithm; algorithms derived from Descartes' rule of signs (Vincent's theorem, the Collins–Akritas bisection) are more efficient in practice. ([Sturm's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%27s_theorem); [Real-root isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-root_isolation))
- **Markov brothers' inequality.** If $P$ has degree at most $n$, then for every $k\ge0$
  $$\max_{[-1,1]}|P^{(k)}|\le\frac{n^2(n^2-1^2)(n^2-2^2)\cdots(n^2-(k-1)^2)}{1\cdot3\cdot5\cdots(2k-1)}\max_{[-1,1]}|P|,$$
  so $\max|P'|\le n^2\max|P|$ for $k=1$. Equality holds for the Chebyshev polynomial $T_n$. Andrey Markov proved $k=1$ and Vladimir Markov the higher cases. ([Markov brothers' inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_brothers%27_inequality))
- **Bernstein's inequality.** For a polynomial of degree $n$, $\max_{|z|=1}|P'(z)|\le n\max_{|z|=1}|P(z)|$, with equality only for $P(z)=\alpha z^n$; Lax proved Erdős's conjecture that the constant improves to $n/2$ when $P$ has no zeros in $|z|<1$. ([Bernstein's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_inequality_%28mathematical_analysis%29))
- **Real-rooted polynomials.** If a real polynomial of degree $n$ has $n$ distinct real zeros $x_1<\dots<x_n$, Rolle's theorem places the zeros of $P'$ in $[x_1,x_n]$, the real case of the Gauss–Lucas theorem. For nonnegative $a_1,\dots,a_n$ the normalized elementary symmetric means $S_k=e_k/\binom nk$ satisfy Newton's inequalities $S_{k-1}S_{k+1}\le S_k^2$, with equality iff all $a_i$ are equal. ([Gauss–Lucas theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Lucas_theorem); [Newton's inequalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_inequalities)) Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava used the method of interlacing families of polynomials, analysing the largest roots of mixed characteristic polynomials, to prove Weaver's conjecture KS$_2$, which implies a positive solution to the Kadison–Singer problem. ([Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.3969))
- **Fewnomials.** Khovanskii's theory bounds real roots by the number of monomials rather than the degree, generalizing Descartes' rule to systems and to Pfaffian functions. For a system of $n$ real polynomials in $n$ variables in which $t$ distinct monomials appear, Khovanskii's bound on the number of regular positive zeros is $2^{\binom{t-1}{2}}(n+1)^{t-1}$. ([Descartes' rule of signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descartes%27_rule_of_signs); [Ergür–Telek–Tonelli-Cueto](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.06784))
- **Random polynomials.** For $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_kx^k$ with independent standard normal $a_k$, Kac's integral formula gives the expected number $E_n$ of real roots, and $E_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\ln n+C_1+\frac{2}{\pi n}+O(n^{-2})$ with $C_1\approx0.6257$. Edelman and Kostlan derived Kac's formula geometrically, as the length of the projected moment curve $(1,t,\dots,t^n)$ on the sphere divided by $\pi$. ([MathWorld, Kac formula](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/KacFormula.html); [Edelman–Kostlan](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9501224))

### History
Descartes described the rule of signs in *La Géométrie*. Budan published his interval extension in 1807 and Fourier a similar theorem in 1820, which led to a priority dispute; Sturm solved the exact counting problem in 1829. Vincent's 1834 theorem showed that continued-fraction transformations of a square-free polynomial eventually yield one with at most one sign variation, which isolates its positive roots, and Collins and Akritas revived these methods for computer algebra in 1976. ([Budan's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budan%27s_theorem); [Sturm's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%27s_theorem); [Real-root isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-root_isolation)) The Markov inequalities date from the 1890s (A. Markov 1890, V. Markov 1892). Kac's work on real roots of random polynomials appeared in 1943. ([Markov brothers' inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_brothers%27_inequality); [MathWorld, Kac formula](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/KacFormula.html))

### Open problems
- **Kushnirenko's question.** Can the number of regular positive zeros of $n$ real polynomials in $n$ variables with $t_1,\dots,t_n$ monomials be bounded by a polynomial in $t_1,\dots,t_n$ raised to the power $n$, rather than by Khovanskii's exponential bound? Ergür, Telek and Tonelli-Cueto write that this conjecture "remains widely open", that even the bivariate case is open, and prove a version for random Gaussian coefficients: the expected number of positive zeros is at most $4^{-n}\prod_k t_k(t_k-1)$. ([Ergür–Telek–Tonelli-Cueto](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.06784); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06784))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Descartes' rule of signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descartes%27_rule_of_signs) and [Sturm's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%27s_theorem): statements, generalisations and history of real root counting.
- **Learn:** [Sottile, Real solutions to equations from geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0609829): lecture notes on upper and lower bounds for numbers of real solutions of polynomial systems, and on cases where all solutions are real.
- **Primary:** [Rahman and Schmeisser, Analytic Theory of Polynomials (OUP, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198534938.001.0001): monograph on the analytic theory of polynomials.
- **Primary:** [Ergür, Telek and Tonelli-Cueto, On the number of real zeros of random sparse polynomial systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06784): current research on Kushnirenko's question.
- **Further reading:** [Borwein and Erdélyi, Polynomials and Polynomial Inequalities (Springer GTM, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0793-1): Graduate Texts in Mathematics volume on polynomials and polynomial inequalities.
references.MSC 26Dxx - Inequalities in real analysi:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 26Dxx, a subfield of [MSC 26 - Real functions](node:MSC%2026%20-%20Real%20functions), classifies analytic inequalities for real functions: inequalities for trigonometric functions and polynomials, for other special classes of functions, for derivatives and differential and integral operators, and for sums, series and integrals. Three families of inequalities are sent elsewhere: maximal-function inequalities to 42B25, functional inequalities to 39B72, and probabilistic inequalities to 60E15. ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))

The typical problem is to prove an inequality with the best constant and to identify the extremal functions, or to show that none exist. Hardy's inequality, the Markov and Bernstein inequalities for polynomials, Opial's inequality and the Landau–Kolmogorov inequalities between derivatives are standard examples. Several of them are sharp with explicitly known constants, while some sharp constants are still unknown. ([Hardy's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%27s_inequality); [Landau–Kolmogorov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93Kolmogorov_inequality); [Klaassen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05150))

### Scope
- **26D05** Inequalities for trigonometric functions and polynomials. ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))
- **26D07** Inequalities involving other types of functions. ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))
- **26D10** Inequalities involving derivatives and differential and integral operators. ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))
- **26D15** Inequalities for sums, series and integrals. ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))
- **26D20** Other analytical inequalities; 26D99 collects the rest of the section. ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))

Neighbours: maximal inequalities belong to [MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces](node:MSC%2042%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20on%20Euclidean%20spaces) (42B25); functional inequalities to [MSC 39 - Difference and functional equations](node:MSC%2039%20-%20Difference%20and%20functional%20equations) (39B72); probabilistic inequalities to [MSC 60 - Probability theory and stochastic processes](node:MSC%2060%20-%20Probability%20theory%20and%20stochastic%20processes) (60E15). The $L^p$ inequalities below are also the basic tools of [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces). ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Dxx))

### Key concepts
- **Hölder and Minkowski.** On a measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, with $1\le p\le\infty$ and conjugate exponent $p'$ ($1/p+1/p'=1$, $1'=\infty$, $\infty'=1$), if $f\in L^p$ and $g\in L^{p'}$ then $fg\in L^1$ and $\int|fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_{L^p}\|g\|_{L^{p'}}$; $p=2$ is Cauchy–Schwarz. For $1\le p\le\infty$, Minkowski's inequality $\|f+g\|_{L^p}\le\|f\|_{L^p}+\|g\|_{L^p}$ makes $\|\cdot\|_{L^p}$ a norm. ([Hunter, Theorems 7.5 and 7.7](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch7.pdf))
- **Hardy's inequality.** For $p>1$ and a nonnegative sequence $(a_n)$,
  $$\sum_{n\ge1}\Big(\frac{a_1+\dots+a_n}{n}\Big)^p\le\Big(\frac{p}{p-1}\Big)^p\sum_{n\ge1}a_n^p,$$
  and for measurable $f\ge0$ on $(0,\infty)$, $\int_0^\infty\big(\frac1x\int_0^xf\big)^p\,dx\le(\frac{p}{p-1})^p\int_0^\infty f^p\,dx$. If the right side is finite, equality holds only for $f=0$, so the constant is sharp but not attained. Multidimensional versions include $(1-\frac1p)^p\int_\Omega|f|^p/\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^p\le\int_\Omega|\nabla f|^p$ for $f\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ on a convex domain $\Omega$, with a constant that cannot be improved. ([Hardy's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%27s_inequality))
- **Rearrangement inequalities.** For $x_1\le\dots\le x_n$, $y_1\le\dots\le y_n$ and any permutation $\sigma$, $x_1y_n+\dots+x_ny_1\le\sum x_iy_{\sigma(i)}\le\sum x_iy_i$. The continuous analogue (Hardy–Littlewood) states $\int_{\mathbb R^n}fg\le\int_{\mathbb R^n}f^*g^*$ for nonnegative measurable $f,g$ vanishing at infinity, where $f^*,g^*$ are the symmetric decreasing rearrangements. ([Rearrangement inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rearrangement_inequality); [Hardy–Littlewood inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_inequality))
- **Majorization (Karamata).** If $f$ is convex on an interval $I$ and $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ majorizes $(y_1,\dots,y_n)$ (both decreasing, partial sums of $x$ dominate those of $y$, equal totals), then $\sum f(x_i)\ge\sum f(y_i)$; for strictly convex $f$ equality holds iff $y$ is a permutation of $x$. Taking $y$ constant equal to the mean gives the finite Jensen inequality. ([Karamata's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karamata%27s_inequality))
- **Markov and Bernstein inequalities.** For a polynomial of degree at most $n$, $\max_{[-1,1]}|P'|\le n^2\max_{[-1,1]}|P|$, with equality for the Chebyshev polynomial $T_n$; for a polynomial of degree $n$, $\max_{|z|=1}|P'|\le n\max_{|z|=1}|P|$, with equality only for $\alpha z^n$. ([Markov brothers' inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_brothers%27_inequality); [Bernstein's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_inequality_%28mathematical_analysis%29))
- **Opial's inequality.** For differentiable $x$ on $[0,h]$ with $x(0)=x(h)=0$, $\int_0^h|x x'|\,dt\le\frac h4\int_0^h|x'|^2\,dt$, and $h/4$ is optimal; with only $x(0)=0$, Beesack's version holds with optimal constant $h/2$. Klaassen (2023) gives a sharp generalization containing both the continuous and discrete versions and extending to higher derivatives. ([Klaassen](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.05150); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05150))
- **Landau–Kolmogorov inequalities.** For $1\le k<n$ and $f$ on $T\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\|f^{(k)}\|_\infty\le C(n,k,T)\,\|f\|_\infty^{1-k/n}\|f^{(n)}\|_\infty^{k/n}$. The case $k=1,n=2$, first proved by Landau, has sharp constants $2$ on a half-line and $\sqrt2$ on $\mathbb R$; after contributions by Hadamard and Shilov, Kolmogorov found the sharp constants on $\mathbb R$ for all $n,k$. ([Landau–Kolmogorov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93Kolmogorov_inequality))

### History
Hardy, Littlewood and Pólya planned and began *Inequalities* in 1929, intending a Cambridge Tract; it grew into the 1934 book that organized the subject. Their preface notes that it is often difficult to trace the origin of a familiar inequality and that the inequalities of Schwarz, Hölder and Jensen "can be traced further back". ([MacTutor, Hardy's books](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Hardy_books/)) Hardy first published his inequality in 1920 with a weaker constant; Landau's derivative inequality dates from 1913, and Karamata's majorization inequality from 1932. ([Hardy's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%27s_inequality); [Landau–Kolmogorov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93Kolmogorov_inequality); [Karamata's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karamata%27s_inequality))

### Open problems
- **Sharp Landau–Kolmogorov constants on the half-line.** Schoenberg identified the extremal functions on $[0,\infty)$, but explicit forms for the sharp constants $C(n,k,[0,\infty))$ are still unknown. ([Landau–Kolmogorov inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93Kolmogorov_inequality))
- **Sharpness of weighted Opial inequalities.** Klaassen quotes Troy (2001): "It remains an open problem to determine the sharpness" of Troy's weighted Opial-type inequalities, and shows that one of them is not sharp. ([Klaassen, Remark 5.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.05150))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hardy's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%27s_inequality): discrete, integral and multidimensional forms with sharp constants.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, $L^p$ spaces (UC Davis notes)](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch7.pdf): Hölder and Minkowski inequalities with proofs on a general measure space.
- **Primary:** [Mitrinović, Pečarić and Fink, Classical and New Inequalities in Analysis (Springer, 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-017-1043-5): monograph on classical and new inequalities in analysis.
- **Primary:** [Klaassen, Sharp unifying generalizations of Opial's inequality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05150): recent research paper on sharp Opial-type inequalities.
- **Further reading:** Hardy, Littlewood and Pólya, *Inequalities* (1934), described in its [preface at MacTutor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Hardy_books/); [Borwein and Erdélyi, Polynomials and Polynomial Inequalities (Springer GTM, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0793-1) for polynomial inequalities.
references.MSC 26Exx - Miscellaneous topics in real:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 26Exx is the miscellaneous-topics subfield of [MSC 26 - Real functions](node:MSC%2026%20-%20Real%20functions), alongside functions of one variable ([26A](node:MSC%2026Axx%20-%20Functions%20of%20one%20variable)), functions of several variables ([26B](node:MSC%2026Bxx%20-%20Functions%20of%20several%20variables)), polynomials and rational functions (26C), and inequalities ([26D](node:MSC%2026Dxx%20-%20Inequalities%20in%20real%20analysis)). ([MSC2020 26-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26-XX)) Its eleven specific codes cover real-analytic functions, $C^\infty$ and quasi-analytic functions, calculus on and with values in infinite-dimensional spaces, set-valued functions, non-Archimedean, nonstandard, constructive and fuzzy real analysis, means, and analysis on time scales. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))

Most codes carry explicit "See also" pointers into other sections, among them logic (03E72, 03F60, 03H05), several complex variables (32B05, 32C05), functional analysis (46E40, 46G05, 46G10, 47A64), global analysis (58C25, 58Cxx) and dynamic equations (34N05). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))

### Scope
- **26E05 Real-analytic functions** (see also 32B05, 32C05). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))
- **26E10 $C^\infty$-functions, quasi-analytic functions** (see also 58C25). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx)) Quasi-analytic classes are the Denjoy–Carleman classes of smooth functions in which a function vanishing to infinite order at one point vanishes identically. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-analytic_function))
- **26E15 Calculus of functions on infinite-dimensional spaces** and **26E20 Calculus of functions taking values in infinite-dimensional spaces** (see also 46G05, 46G10, 46E40, 58Cxx; the 46G codes are in [46G](node:MSC%2046Gxx%20-%20Measures,%20integration,%20derivative,%20holomorphy%20%28all%20involving%20infinite-dimensional%20spaces%29)). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))
- **26E25 Set-valued functions** (see also 28B20, 49J53, 54C60); nonsmooth analysis is sent to 49J52, 58Cxx and 90Cxx instead. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))
- **26E30 Non-Archimedean analysis** (see also 12J25) and **26E35 Nonstandard analysis** (see also 03H05, 28E05, 54J05; 03H05 is in [03H](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models)). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))
- **26E40 Constructive real analysis** (see also 03F60, within [03F](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics)) and **26E50 Fuzzy real analysis** (see also 03E72, 28E10). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))
- **26E60 Means** (see also 47A64, operator means). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))
- **26E70 Real analysis on time scales or measure chains**; dynamic equations on time scales go to [34N05](node:MSC%2034Nxx%20-%20Dynamic%20equations%20on%20time%20scales%20or%20measure%20chains). **26E99** is the residual code. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Flat smooth functions (26E10).** $f(x)=e^{-1/x}$ for $x>0$, $f(x)=0$ for $x\le 0$, is $C^\infty$ with all derivatives $0$ at the origin, so its Taylor series does not represent it; by Borel's lemma every real sequence $(\alpha_k)$ is the sequence of derivatives at $0$ of some smooth function on $\mathbb{R}$. So the expansion in [Taylor's Theorem](node:Taylor's%20Theorem) does not determine a smooth function. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-analytic_smooth_function))
- **Denjoy–Carleman theorem (26E10).** For a sequence of positive reals $M=(M_k)$, the class $C^M([a,b])$ consists of $f\in C^\infty([a,b])$ with $|f^{(k)}(x)|\le A^{k+1}k!\,M_k$ for some $A$, all $x$ and all $k$; it is *quasi-analytic* if every $f$ in it whose derivatives all vanish at one point is identically zero. The class is quasi-analytic if and only if $\sum_j 1/L_j=\infty$, where $L_j=\inf_{k\ge j} k\,M_k^{1/k}$; equivalently $\sum_j 1/\bigl(j\,(M_j^*)^{1/j}\bigr)=\infty$ with $M^*$ the largest log-convex sequence bounded above by $M$. Taking $M_k=1$ gives the real-analytic functions, and Denjoy's sequences $(\ln n)^n,\ (\ln n)^n(\ln\ln n)^n,\dots$ give quasi-analytic classes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-analytic_function))
- **Structure of quasi-analytic classes.** Weierstrass division holds for analytic functions but fails in other quasi-analytic classes (with respect to $x_1+x_2^2$); nevertheless Bierstone and Milman proved a version of Hironaka's resolution of singularities for classes of $C^\infty$ functions that contain no flat functions and are closed under differentiation and implicit equations, with quasi-analytic classes as the main examples, yielding topological Noetherianity, Łojasiewicz inequalities and division properties. Belotto da Silva, Bierstone and Kiro showed that, for $M$ log-convex, a function that lands in $C_M$ after composition with a blowing-up generally lies only in the shifted class with $N_k=M_{2k}$, and that this loss is sharp. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-analytic_function); [Bierstone–Milman](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0108204); [Belotto–Bierstone–Kiro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10580))
- **Fréchet versus Gateaux derivatives (26E15, 26E20).** For normed spaces $V,W$ and open $U\subseteq V$, $f:U\to W$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ if there is a bounded linear $A$ with $\|f(x+h)-f(x)-Ah\|_W/\|h\|_V\to 0$; it is Gateaux differentiable if every directional derivative $\lim_{t\to 0}(f(x+tv)-f(x))/t$ exists. Fréchet implies Gateaux, but not conversely: $x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ has non-linear directional derivatives at $0$, and $x^3y/(x^6+y^2)$ has zero Gateaux derivative at $0$ but is discontinuous there. The chain rule $D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))\circ Df(x)$ holds for Fréchet derivatives, extending [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus) to normed spaces such as [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_derivative))
- **Convenient calculus (26E15).** Beyond normed spaces, Kriegl and Michor work on *convenient vector spaces* (locally convex and $c^\infty$-complete) and call a map smooth if it sends smooth curves to smooth curves. By Boman's theorem this agrees with other reasonable notions on Fréchet spaces; smooth maps form a cartesian closed category with exponential law $C^\infty(U,C^\infty(V,G))\cong C^\infty(U\times V,G)$, at the price that some smooth maps are not continuous. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convenient_vector_space))
- **Power means and their inequality (26E60).** For positive $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and $p\ne 0$, $M_p=\bigl(\tfrac1n\sum x_i^p\bigr)^{1/p}$, with $M_0=(\prod x_i)^{1/n}$ and $M_{+\infty}=\max$, $M_{-\infty}=\min$ as limits. If $p<q$ then $M_p\le M_q$, with equality iff all $x_i$ are equal; $p=-1,0,1$ gives HM $\le$ GM $\le$ AM. The proof applies [Jensen's Inequality](node:Jensen's%20Inequality) to the convex function $x^{q/p}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_mean))
- **Delta derivative on a time scale (26E70).** A time scale $\mathbb{T}$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$, with forward jump $\sigma(t)=\inf\{s\in\mathbb{T}:s>t\}$ and graininess $\mu(t)=\sigma(t)-t$. $f^\Delta(t)$ is the number such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some neighbourhood $U$ of $t$ has $|f(\sigma(t))-f(s)-f^\Delta(t)(\sigma(t)-s)|\le\varepsilon|\sigma(t)-s|$ for $s\in U$. On $\mathbb{R}$ this is $f'$; on $\mathbb{Z}$ it is the forward difference, so one theory covers differential and difference equations ([Dynamic Equations on Time Scales](node:Dynamic%20Equations%20on%20Time%20Scales)). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-scale_calculus))
- **Infinitesimals and standard part (26E35).** In Keisler's axiomatic treatment of the [Hyperreal Numbers](node:Hyperreal%20Numbers), $x\in{}^*\mathbb{R}$ is infinitesimal if $|x|<r$ for all positive real $r$ and finite if $|x|<r$ for some real $r$; the Standard Part Principle (Theorem 1.9) says every finite hyperreal is infinitely close to a unique real, and its proof uses completeness of $\mathbb{R}$. A real function is differentiable at a real $a$ iff $(f(a+\Delta x)-f(a))/\Delta x$ is finite with the same standard part for all nonzero infinitesimal $\Delta x$. ([Keisler, Foundations of Infinitesimal Calculus](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~hkeisler/foundations.pdf))
- **Constructive real analysis (26E40).** Working in intuitionistic logic, reals are rational sequences with an apartness relation; positive trichotomy is not provable in general, the intermediate value theorem only yields points $c_n$ with $|f(c_n)|<1/n$ unless $f$ is locally non-zero, and least upper bounds exist for located sets such as intervals and compact sets. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructive_analysis))

### History
Denjoy gave partial results on quasi-analyticity in 1921 and Carleman proved the full theorem in 1926. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-analytic_function)) Robinson's article "Non-Standard Analysis" appeared in 1961 and his book *Non-standard Analysis* in 1966; Keisler's infinitesimal calculus textbook followed in 1976. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis)) Bishop's *Foundations of Constructive Analysis* appeared in 1967 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructive_analysis)), and Bishop and Bridges published *Constructive Analysis* in Springer's Grundlehren series in 1985. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61667-9)) Stefan Hilger introduced time-scale calculus in 1988, and Bohner and Peterson's *Dynamic Equations on Time Scales* (Birkhäuser, 2001) is a standard reference. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-scale_calculus); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0201-1)) Kriegl and Michor's *The Convenient Setting of Global Analysis* appeared with the AMS in 1997. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/053))

### Open problems
- **Inverse variational problem on time scales (26E70).** Dryl and Torres obtain a necessary condition for a dynamic integro-differential equation to be an Euler–Lagrange equation on an arbitrary time scale (Helmholtz's problem) and state that the question of sufficiency remains open (as of their 2016 survey); they also name mixed delta–nabla variational problems on unbounded time scales (infinite horizon) as an open direction of research. This links 26E70 to the [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations). ([Dryl–Torres survey, §6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.05111))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Quasi-analytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-analytic_function): Denjoy–Carleman classes, the theorem's equivalent conditions, division failure.
- **Learn:** [Keisler, Foundations of Infinitesimal Calculus](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~hkeisler/foundations.pdf): free author text on hyperreals, standard part and transfer with full proofs.
- **Primary:** [Bierstone–Milman, Resolution of singularities in Denjoy–Carleman classes](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0108204): the structural theorem for quasi-analytic classes in several variables.
- **Primary:** [Dryl–Torres, Direct and Inverse Variational Problems on Time Scales: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.05111): survey of variational calculus on time scales, ending with open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Bohner–Peterson, Dynamic Equations on Time Scales](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0201-1) (Birkhäuser 2001); [Kriegl–Michor, The Convenient Setting of Global Analysis](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/053) (AMS 1997); [Bishop–Bridges, Constructive Analysis](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61667-9) (Springer 1985); [Krantz–Parks, A Primer of Real Analytic Functions](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-8176-8134-0) (Birkhäuser 2002).
references.MSC 28 - Measure and integration:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 28 classifies measure and integration as a research area, from classical measure theory on sets and real lines to measures on topological groups, infinite-dimensional spaces and [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems). Its five subdivisions are classical measure theory (28Axx), set functions and integrals with values in abstract spaces (28Bxx), set functions and measures on spaces with additional structure (28Cxx), measure-theoretic ergodic theory (28Dxx), and miscellaneous topics (28Exx); analysis on manifolds is sent to 58. ([MSC2020 28](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28-XX))

The foundational layer, [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory), [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration) and [Fubini's Theorem](node:Fubini's%20Theorem), is the common language; research under 28 extends it in three directions visible in the classification: geometric measure theory and fractals (28A75, 28A78, 28A80), measures adapted to topological, group or infinite-dimensional structure (28C), and the measure-theoretic study of measure-preserving transformations (28D). ([MSC2020 28Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Axx); [MSC2020 28Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Cxx); [MSC2020 28Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx))

### Scope
- **28Axx Classical measure theory** ([map](node:MSC%2028Axx%20-%20Classical%20measure%20theory)): classes of sets (Borel, Suslin, analytic sets), outer measures and capacities, abstract differentiation of set functions, modes of convergence, spaces of measures, product measures, disintegration, lifting, measure algebras, and geometric measure theory: length, area and volume (28A75), Hausdorff and packing measures (28A78), fractals (28A80, see also 37F). ([MSC2020 28Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Axx))
- **28Bxx Abstract-valued set functions** ([map](node:MSC%2028Bxx%20-%20Set%20functions,%20measures%20and%20integrals%20with%20values%20in%20abstract%20spaces)): vector-valued, group-valued, ordered-space-valued and set-valued measures and integrals, and measurable selections (28B20). ([MSC2020 28Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Bxx))
- **28Cxx Spaces with additional structure** ([map](node:MSC%2028Cxx%20-%20Set%20functions%20and%20measures%20on%20spaces%20with%20additional%20structure)): integration via linear functionals (Radon measures, Daniell integrals), Haar and invariant measures on topological groups (28C10), regularity of measures on [topological spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces), and measures in infinite-dimensional spaces such as Wiener and Gaussian measures (28C20). ([MSC2020 28Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Cxx))
- **28Dxx Measure-theoretic ergodic theory** ([map](node:MSC%2028Dxx%20-%20Measure-theoretic%20ergodic%20theory)): measure-preserving transformations, flows and group actions, entropy and other invariants (28D20); the dynamical-systems aspects go to 37A. ([MSC2020 28Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx))
- **28Exx Miscellaneous** ([map](node:MSC%2028Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20measure%20theory)). ([MSC2020 28](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28-XX))

Neighbours: [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory) takes the dynamical side of ergodic theory; [MSC 49 - Calculus of variations and optimal control; optimization](node:MSC%2049%20-%20Calculus%20of%20variations%20and%20optimal%20control;%20optimization) (49Q15) is cross-referenced from 28A75 for geometric measure theory; [MSC 26 - Real functions](node:MSC%2026%20-%20Real%20functions) holds integrals of Riemann, Stieltjes and Lebesgue type for functions of one variable (26A42, which points back to 28). ([MSC2020 28Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx); [MSC2020 28Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Axx); [MSC2020 26Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=26Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Carathéodory extension.** A pre-measure $\mu$ on a ring $R$ of subsets of $X$ ($\mu(\varnothing)=0$, countably additive on disjoint decompositions within $R$) extends to a measure on the $\sigma$-ring generated by $R$, uniquely if $\mu$ is $\sigma$-finite. The extension is the outer measure $\mu^*$ restricted to the Carathéodory-measurable sets $M$, those with $\mu^*(S)=\mu^*(S\cap M)+\mu^*(S\cap M^c)$ for all $S\subseteq X$. ([Carathéodory's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_extension_theorem); [Princeton MAT425 notes, §2.9](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~js129/PDFs/teaching/MAT425_spring_2025/MAT425_Lecture_Notes.pdf))
- **Radon–Nikodym and Lebesgue decomposition.** If $\mu,\nu$ are $\sigma$-finite measures on $(X,\Sigma)$ and $\nu\ll\mu$, there is a measurable $f\ge0$, unique $\mu$-a.e., with $\nu(A)=\int_Af\,d\mu$ for all $A\in\Sigma$. Without absolute continuity, a $\sigma$-finite signed $\nu$ splits uniquely as $\nu=\nu_a+\nu_s$ with $\nu_a\ll\mu$ and $\nu_s\perp\mu$. ([Radon–Nikodym theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym_theorem))
- **Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation.** For $X$ locally compact Hausdorff and $\psi$ a positive linear functional on $C_c(X)$, there is a unique positive Borel measure $\mu$, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular on open sets, with $\psi(f)=\int f\,d\mu$; uniqueness needs the regularity conditions. ([Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem))
- **Hausdorff measure and dimension (28A78).** $\mathcal H^d(S)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\inf\{\sum(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^d: S\subseteq\bigcup U_i,\ \operatorname{diam}U_i<\delta\}$. On $\mathbb R^d$ for integer $d$, $\lambda_d=2^{-d}\alpha_d\mathcal H^d$ on Borel sets ($\alpha_d$ the volume of the unit ball). $\mathcal H^d(S)$ is finite and nonzero for at most one $d$, and $\dim_H S=\inf\{d\ge0:\mathcal H^d(S)=0\}$. ([Hausdorff measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_measure))
- **Haar measure (28C10).** Every locally compact Hausdorff group carries a nonzero left-invariant Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular on open sets, unique up to a positive scalar; on compact groups it is normalized by $\mu(G)=1$. ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure))
- **Gaussian measures and Cameron–Martin (28C20).** For the abstract Wiener measure $\gamma$ on a separable Banach space $E$ with Cameron–Martin space $H$, translation by $h\in H$ yields a measure equivalent to $\gamma$ with an explicit Radon–Nikodym density, and $\gamma$ is quasi-invariant under translation by $v$ if and only if $v$ lies in (the image of) $H$. ([Cameron–Martin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Martin_theorem))
- **Ergodic theorems and entropy (28D).** If $T$ preserves $\mu$ and $f\in L^1(\mu)$, Birkhoff's theorem gives a.e. convergence of $\frac1N\sum_{n<N}f(T^nx)$ to a $T$-invariant integrable limit, constant a.e. (equal to the space average) when $T$ is ergodic and $\mu(X)=1$. [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) classifies such systems up to isomorphism: the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy $h_\mu(T)=\sup_Q h_\mu(T,Q)$ over finite partitions is an invariant, and Bernoulli shifts are classified by entropy (Sinai 1962, Ornstein 1970). ([Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory); [Measure-preserving dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_dynamical_system))

### History
Hausdorff introduced his measures in "Dimension und äusseres Mass" (1918). Radon proved the differentiation theorem on $\mathbb R^n$ in 1913 and Nikodym the general case in 1930; Riesz represented functionals on $C[0,1]$ in 1909, extended by Markov (1938) and Kakutani (1941). ([Hausdorff measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_measure); [Radon–Nikodym theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym_theorem); [Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem)) Haar constructed invariant measures in 1933, with Weil giving existence and uniqueness in full generality; Birkhoff proved the pointwise ergodic theorem in 1931, Cameron and Martin their translation theorem in 1944, and Sinai showed in 1959 that the entropy supremum is attained on generating partitions. ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure); [Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory); [Cameron–Martin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Martin_theorem); [Measure-preserving dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_dynamical_system))

### Open problems
- **Multiple mixing.** A measure-preserving system is mixing of all orders if it is strong $k$-mixing for every $k\ge2$. It is unknown whether strong 2-mixing implies strong 3-mixing. ([Mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_%28mathematics%29))

> [!warning] Contested
> **Falconer distance conjecture.** If a compact $S\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$, has $\dim_H S>d/2$, its distance set should have positive Lebesgue measure. Falconer (1985) proved this above $(d+1)/2$, and Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang above $5/4$ in the plane. Wikipedia calls the conjecture unsolved while noting a 2026 OpenAI preprint claiming a proof ([Falconer's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falconer%27s_conjecture)); MathWorld records the proof announced for all dimensions $d\ge2$ as a claim and does not report peer review or independent verification ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FalconerDistanceConjecture.html)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hausdorff measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_measure): definition, Lebesgue normalization and Hausdorff dimension.
- **Learn:** [Princeton MAT425 lecture notes](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~js129/PDFs/teaching/MAT425_spring_2025/MAT425_Lecture_Notes.pdf): abstract measures, Carathéodory construction, Riesz representation, Fubini–Tonelli and Radon–Nikodym with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Bogachev, Measure Theory (Springer, 2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-34514-5): two-volume monograph on measure theory.
- **Further reading:** [Federer, Geometric Measure Theory (Springer Classics in Mathematics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-62010-2) and [Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces: Fractals and Rectifiability (CUP, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511623813): texts on geometric measure theory, fractals and rectifiability (28A75–28A80).

## Reference
### Overview
Classical measure theory, MSC2020 28Axx within [MSC 28 - Measure and integration](node:MSC%2028%20-%20Measure%20and%20integration), covers classes of measurable sets (Borel, Suslin and analytic sets), real- and complex-valued set functions, contents, measures, outer measures and capacities, differentiation of set functions, measurable functions and modes of convergence, integration, spaces and convergence of measures, product spaces, disintegration, lifting theory, measure algebras, and a geometric part: length, area and volume, Hausdorff and packing measures, and fractals. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Axx))

The abstract framework of [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory) separates the domain of measurable sets, a $\sigma$-algebra, from the countably additive rule assigning sizes; measures need not be defined on all subsets, while outer measures are defined on all subsets but are only countably subadditive. ([Hunter, §§1.4–1.6](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch1.pdf)) Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is the central example: it is the unique complete translation-invariant measure on the Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebra normalized so the unit cube has measure 1, and it extends the length, area and volume of [Euclidean Geometry](node:Euclidean%20Geometry). ([Wikipedia: Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_measure))

The geometric end of 28A (28A75, 28A78, 28A80) is where much current research sits: the study of Hausdorff dimension, rectifiability and fractal sets in $\mathbb R^n$, which Mattila's monograph describes as the geometric structure of general Borel sets and measures, especially small irregular sets such as Cantor-type sets and nonrectifiable curves. ([Mattila, introduction](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/geometry-of-sets-and-measures-in-euclidean-spaces/introduction/63E907DE848320B7CBFB15A01EA7A973))

### Scope
- **28A05, 28A10, 28A12:** classes of sets (Borel fields, $\sigma$-rings, Suslin and analytic sets); real- or complex-valued set functions; contents, measures, outer measures, capacities. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Axx))
- **28A15, 28A20, 28A25:** abstract differentiation of set functions; measurable and nonmeasurable functions and modes of convergence; integration with respect to measures and other set functions. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Axx))
- **28A33, 28A35, 28A50, 28A51, 28A60:** spaces and convergence of measures; product spaces; integration and disintegration; lifting theory; measures on Boolean rings and measure algebras. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Axx))
- **28A75, 28A78, 28A80:** length, area, volume and other geometric measure theory (see also 49Q15); Hausdorff and packing measures; fractals (see also 37Fxx). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Axx))
- **Neighbours:** 28Bxx treats set functions and integrals with values in abstract spaces, 28Cxx measures on spaces with additional structure, 28Dxx measure-theoretic [ergodic theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory), and 28Exx miscellaneous topics; 28A is the scalar-valued classical core. ([MSC2020, section 28](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Outer measures and Carathéodory's construction:** an outer measure $\mu^*:\mathcal P(X)\to[0,\infty]$ satisfies $\mu^*(\varnothing)=0$, monotonicity and countable subadditivity. ([Hunter, Definition 1.2](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch1.pdf)) A set $M$ is Carathéodory-measurable if $\mu^*(S)=\mu^*(S\cap M)+\mu^*(S\setminus M)$ for every $S\subseteq X$; these sets form a $\sigma$-algebra on which $\mu^*$ is countably additive. **Extension theorem:** a premeasure $\mu$ on a ring $R$ (with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ and countable additivity on $R$) extends to a measure on $\sigma(R)$, and the extension is unique when $\mu$ is $\sigma$-finite; uniqueness can fail otherwise. ([Wikipedia: Carathéodory's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_extension_theorem))
- **Completeness:** a measure space is complete if every subset of a null set is measurable; every measure space has a unique completion obtained by adjoining subsets of null sets. This depends on the measure, not only on the $\sigma$-algebra, and is unrelated to metric completeness. ([Hunter, Definition 1.14 and Theorem 1.15](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch1.pdf)) Borel-restricted Lebesgue measure is translation-invariant but not complete. ([Wikipedia: Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_measure))
- **[Fubini's Theorem](node:Fubini's%20Theorem) and [Tonelli's Theorem](node:Tonelli's%20Theorem) (28A35):** if $X,Y$ are $\sigma$-finite measure spaces and $f:X\times Y\to[0,\infty]$ is measurable, both iterated integrals equal the integral over $X\times Y$ (Tonelli); if $f$ is measurable with $\int_{X\times Y}|f|<\infty$, the iterated integrals of $f$ exist and equal the double integral (Fubini). Without $\sigma$-finiteness (Lebesgue times counting measure on $[0,1]$, indicator of the diagonal) or without integrability, the iterated integrals can differ. ([Wikipedia: Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- **Differentiation (28A15):** the [Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem](node:Lebesgue%20Differentiation%20Theorem) says that for locally integrable $f$ on $\mathbb R^n$, $\frac1{|B|}\int_B|f(y)-f(x)|\,dy\to0$ for almost every $x$ as balls $B\ni x$ shrink, and more generally for families of sets of bounded eccentricity; the proof runs through the weak-$L^1$ bound for the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function via the Vitali covering lemma. ([Wikipedia: Lebesgue differentiation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_differentiation_theorem)) The abstract counterpart is the [Radon–Nikodym Theorem](node:Radon–Nikodym%20Theorem): if $\mu,\nu$ are $\sigma$-finite and $\nu\ll\mu$, then $\nu(A)=\int_A f\,d\mu$ for a measurable $f\ge0$ unique $\mu$-a.e.; with Lebesgue decomposition $\nu=\nu_a+\nu_s$, $\nu_a\ll\mu$, $\nu_s\perp\mu$. Counting measure on $\mathbb R$ versus Lebesgue measure shows $\sigma$-finiteness is needed. ([Wikipedia: Radon–Nikodym theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym_theorem))
- **Hausdorff measure and dimension (28A78):** for $S$ in a metric space, $\mathcal H^d_\delta(S)=\inf\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^d: S\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\ \operatorname{diam}U_i<\delta\}$ and $\mathcal H^d(S)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\mathcal H^d_\delta(S)$; $\dim_H S=\inf\{d\ge0:\mathcal H^d(S)=0\}=\sup\{d:\mathcal H^d(S)=\infty\}$. On $\mathbb R^n$, $\mathcal H^n$ is a constant multiple of Lebesgue measure. ([Wikipedia: Hausdorff measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_measure)) This is the basic tool of [Geometric Measure Theory](node:Geometric%20Measure%20Theory) and of fractal geometry.
- **Rectifiability (28A75):** rectifiable sets and measures are very general curve- and surface-like objects (generalizing [curves and surfaces](node:Curves%20and%20Surfaces)) that keep many measure-theoretic properties of smooth curves and surfaces; their contrast with purely unrectifiable fractal sets is a central theme of Mattila's monograph. ([Mattila, introduction](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/geometry-of-sets-and-measures-in-euclidean-spaces/introduction/63E907DE848320B7CBFB15A01EA7A973))

### History
Lebesgue described his measure in 1901 and his integral the following year; both appeared in his 1902 dissertation *Intégrale, Longueur, Aire*. ([Wikipedia: Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_measure)) Hausdorff introduced the measure now named for him in 1918 in "Dimension und äusseres Mass" (*Mathematische Annalen* 79). ([Wikipedia: Hausdorff measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_measure)) Besicovitch showed that the plane contains sets of measure zero containing a unit segment in every direction, and Dvir proved the finite-field analogue of the Kakeya conjecture by a polynomial method. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set)) Besicovitch's description of plane sets of finite one-dimensional Hausdorff measure and Marstrand's study of planar fractals of non-integer dimension are the starting points Mattila names for the geometric theory. ([Mattila, introduction](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/geometry-of-sets-and-measures-in-euclidean-spaces/introduction/63E907DE848320B7CBFB15A01EA7A973))

### Open problems
- **Kakeya conjecture in dimension $n\ge4$.** A Kakeya (Besicovitch) set in $\mathbb R^n$ contains a unit segment in every direction; the conjecture is that every such set has Hausdorff dimension $n$. It is known for $n\le3$ and remains open for $n>3$. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set)) The case $n=3$ was settled by Wang and Zahl, who show that Kakeya sets in $\mathbb R^3$ have Minkowski and Hausdorff dimension 3. ([Wang–Zahl, arXiv:2502.17655](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655))
- **Falconer distance conjecture.** If a compact $S\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$, has $\dim_H S>d/2$, its distance set $\{|x-y|:x,y\in S\}$ should have positive Lebesgue measure. Falconer (1985) proved this above $(d+1)/2$; Wikipedia calls the problem unsolved and records the planar threshold $5/4$. ([Wikipedia: Falconer's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falconer%27s_conjecture)) Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang proved that a compact planar set of dimension greater than $5/4$ has a point $x$ whose pinned distance set has positive measure. ([Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang, arXiv:1808.09346](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09346))

> [!warning] Contested
> Wikipedia records 2026 preprint claims of proofs of the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and of the Falconer conjecture, while still listing both problems as open; these claims had not been confirmed by the sources fetched here. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set); [Wikipedia: Falconer's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falconer%27s_conjecture))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hausdorff measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_measure): definition, normalization against Lebesgue measure, Hausdorff dimension.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, *Measure Theory*, chapter 1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch1.pdf): outer measures, $\sigma$-algebras, measures, null sets and completion.
- **Primary:** [Mattila, *Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/geometry-of-sets-and-measures-in-euclidean-spaces/introduction/63E907DE848320B7CBFB15A01EA7A973): monograph on the geometric structure of Borel sets and measures in $\mathbb R^n$: Hausdorff measures, fractals and rectifiability (CUP, 1995).
- **Further reading:** [Falconer, *Fractal Geometry: Mathematical Foundations and Applications*, 3rd ed.](https://research-portal.st-andrews.ac.uk/en/publications/fractal-geometry-mathematical-foundations-and-applications-2/): 3rd edition, Wiley, 2014; textbook on fractal geometry.
- **Further reading:** [Wang–Zahl, Kakeya sets in three dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655): the 2025 resolution of the three-dimensional case.

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 28Bxx is the part of [MSC 28 - Measure and integration](node:MSC%2028%20-%20Measure%20and%20integration) (see [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory)) for set functions, measures and integrals whose *values* lie in abstract spaces; its subdivisions cover vector-valued, group- or semigroup-valued, ordered-space-valued and set-valued set functions. Among the five second-level sections of 28, it sits beside classical measure theory (28Axx), measures on structured spaces (28Cxx), ergodic theory (28Dxx), and miscellaneous topics (28Exx). ([MSC2020 28Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Bxx); [MSC2020 28-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=28-XX&btn=Current))

The largest strand is vector measure theory, whose basic object is a finitely or countably additive map $\mu:\mathcal F\to X$ from a field of sets into a Banach space, together with the integrals of Banach-space-valued functions (Bochner, Pettis) and of scalar functions against vector measures (Bartle–Dunford–Schwartz). A second strand, code 28B20, integrates set-valued maps and proves the existence of measurable selections; it is the measure-theoretic side of set-valued analysis used in control theory and mathematical economics. ([Vector measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_measure); [Artstein–Burns 1975](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1975.58.297); [MSC2020 28Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Bxx))

The vector-valued theory is closely tied to Banach space geometry: whether the Radon–Nikodym theorem holds for $X$-valued measures is a property of $X$ (the Radon–Nikodym property), equivalent to geometric conditions such as dentability of bounded convex sets. In the classification, 28B05 points to 46G10 in functional analysis, see [MSC 46Gxx](node:MSC%2046Gxx%20-%20Measures,%20integration,%20derivative,%20holomorphy%20%28all%20involving%20infinite-dimensional%20spaces%29). ([Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral); [arXiv:2510.21234](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.21234v1); [MSC2020 46Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Gxx&btn=Current))

### Scope
- **28B05** Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals (see also 46G10). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Bxx))
- **28B10** Group- or semigroup-valued set functions, measures and integrals. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Bxx))
- **28B15** Set functions, measures and integrals with values in ordered spaces. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Bxx))
- **28B20** Set-valued set functions and measures; integration of set-valued functions; measurable selections (see also 26E25, 54C60, 54C65, 91B14). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Bxx))
- **28B99** None of the above, but in this section. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Bxx))

**Neighbouring codes.**
- [28Axx](node:MSC%2028Axx%20-%20Classical%20measure%20theory) is "Classical measure theory". ([MSC2020 28-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=28-XX&btn=Current))
- [28Cxx](node:MSC%2028Cxx%20-%20Set%20functions%20and%20measures%20on%20spaces%20with%20additional%20structure) covers "Set functions and measures on spaces with additional structure". ([MSC2020 28-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=28-XX&btn=Current))
- 46G10, "Vector-valued measures and integration", is the functional-analysis home of the same objects and cross-references 28B05 and 46B22; 46G12 covers measures *on* abstract linear spaces. ([MSC2020 46Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Gxx&btn=Current))
- In [54Cxx](node:MSC%2054Cxx%20-%20Maps%20and%20general%20types%20of%20topological%20spaces%20defined%20by%20maps), 54C60 (set-valued maps) and 54C65 (selections) are the general-topology counterparts of 28B20, which they cross-reference. ([MSC2020 54Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=54Cxx&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Vector measure; variation and semivariation.** For a $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$ and Banach space $X$, a countably additive $\mu:\Sigma\to X$ satisfies $\mu(\bigcup_i A_i)=\sum_i\mu(A_i)$ in norm for disjoint $A_i$. Its variation $|\mu|(A)=\sup\sum_i\|\mu(A_i)\|$ over finite partitions of $A$ may be infinite; if $|\mu|(\Omega)<\infty$, then $\mu$ is countably additive exactly when $|\mu|$ is. ([Vector measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_measure)) Bartle, Dunford and Schwartz use the semivariation $\|\mu\|(E)=\sup\|\sum_i a_i\mu(E_i)\|$ over scalars $|a_i|\le1$ and finite partitions of $E$, and show $\|\mu\|(E)\le 4\sup\{\|\mu(F)\|:F\subseteq E,\ F\in\Sigma\}<\infty$. ([Bartle–Dunford–Schwartz 1955](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/63F856B2D175E5432C06A284F7E388A7/S0008414X00030406a.pdf/weak_compactness_and_vector_measures.pdf))
- **Orlicz–Pettis theorem.** In a Hausdorff locally convex space $X$, a series that is weakly subseries convergent is subseries convergent in the original topology; equivalently, an additive $\mu:\mathcal A\to X$ on a $\sigma$-algebra that is weakly countably additive (each $x^*\circ\mu$ countably additive) is countably additive. So countable additivity of a vector measure can be tested one functional at a time. ([Orlicz–Pettis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlicz%E2%80%93Pettis_theorem))
- **Bartle–Dunford–Schwartz control measure.** If $\mu$ is a countably additive vector measure on a $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$ with values in a Banach space, there is a positive finite scalar measure $\nu$ on $\Sigma$ with $\lim_{\nu(E)\to0}\|\mu\|(E)=0$, and $\nu$ can be chosen so that $\nu(E)<\varepsilon$ whenever $\|\mu\|(E)<\varepsilon$. The proof rests on a weak-compactness criterion in $\mathrm{ca}(\Sigma)$ showing $\{x^*\mu:\|x^*\|\le1\}$ is conditionally weakly compact; the control measure is what makes a Lebesgue-type integral of scalar functions against $\mu$, with Vitali and dominated convergence theorems, possible. ([Bartle–Dunford–Schwartz 1955](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/63F856B2D175E5432C06A284F7E388A7/S0008414X00030406a.pdf/weak_compactness_and_vector_measures.pdf))
- **Lyapunov convexity theorem.** The range of a non-atomic vector measure with values in a finite-dimensional space is closed and convex. ([Vector measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_measure))
- **Pettis measurability theorem.** For a measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ and a Banach space $B$ with its Borel algebra, $f:X\to B$ is strongly (Bochner) measurable iff it is weakly measurable and almost surely separably valued, i.e. $f(X\setminus N)$ lies in a separable subset of $B$ for some $\mu$-null $N$; for separable $B$, weak and strong measurability coincide. ([Bochner measurable function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_measurable_function)) Helmer (1994) showed that measurability of $u\circ f$ is needed only for $u$ in a subset of $B^*$ separating the points of $B$, and that the separability hypotheses can also be weakened. ([Helmer 1994](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/on-the-pettis-measurability-theorem/7302CF3926AFFBE9893F184D3B8DFDD4))
- **Bochner integral.** A Bochner-measurable $f:X\to B$ into a Banach space is Bochner integrable iff $\int\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty$; the dominated convergence theorem holds, and Hille's theorem lets a closed operator $T$ pass under the integral when $f$ and $Tf$ are both Bochner integrable. ([Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral)) The vector-valued setting is developed in [Vector Measures and Bochner Integration](node:Vector%20Measures%20and%20Bochner%20Integration).
- **Pettis integral.** A weakly measurable $f$ is Pettis integrable if $x^*\circ f\in L^1(\mu)$ for every $x^*$ and, for each $A\in\Sigma$, some $e_A\in V$ satisfies $x^*(e_A)=\int_A x^*\circ f\,d\mu$ for all $x^*$; $e_A$ is then the Pettis integral of $f$ over $A$. ([Pettis integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pettis_integral))
- **Radon–Nikodym property (RNP).** $B$ has the RNP with respect to $\mu$ if every countably additive vector measure of bounded variation that is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ is $\gamma(E)=\int_E g\,d\mu$ for a $\mu$-integrable $g$. Reflexive [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) (hence Hilbert spaces), $\ell^1$ and separable dual spaces have it; $c_0$, $L^\infty(\Omega)$ and $L^1(\Omega)$ for open bounded $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and $C(K)$ for infinite compact $K$ do not. ([Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral)) Geometrically, $X$ has the RNP iff every nonempty bounded (convex) subset has slices of arbitrarily small diameter, equivalently every closed bounded convex set has a denting point; martingale convergence and representation of operators on $L^1(\mu)$ give further characterizations. ([arXiv:2510.21234](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.21234v1)) This is the vector-valued form of the scalar [Radon–Nikodym Theorem](node:Radon–Nikodym%20Theorem).
- **Kuratowski–Ryll-Nardzewski selection theorem (28B20).** Let $X$ be a Polish space, $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ a measurable space, and $\psi$ a multifunction from $\Omega$ with nonempty closed values in $X$ such that $\{\omega:\psi(\omega)\cap U\ne\emptyset\}\in\mathcal F$ for every open $U\subseteq X$. Then $\psi$ has an $\mathcal F$–$\mathcal B(X)$-measurable selection. ([Kuratowski–Ryll-Nardzewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuratowski_and_Ryll-Nardzewski_measurable_selection_theorem))
- **Aumann integral (28B20).** For a set-valued $F$ on $[a,b]$ with values in subsets of $\mathbb R^q$, a selection is a Lebesgue-measurable $f$ with $f(t)\in F(t)$ a.e., and the Aumann integral $(A)\int_a^bF$ is the set of $\int_a^b f$ over all Lebesgue-integrable selections $f$; it is defined for every $F$ and may be empty. Artstein and Burns prove, for compact-valued $F$ integrable in McShane's Riemann-type sense, that the integral is convex, that $F$ and its pointwise [convex hull](node:Convex%20Hull) have the same integral, and that this integral equals the Aumann integral; they describe the first two as analogues of Aumann's first and third theorems. ([Artstein–Burns 1975](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1975.58.297))

### History
Bochner's integral for vector-space-valued functions appeared in *Fundamenta Mathematicae* in 1933. ([Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral)) Orlicz proved the series form of the Orlicz–Pettis theorem in 1929 for weakly sequentially complete spaces; Banach stated it in his 1932 monograph; and Pettis and Dunford gave proofs in 1938, Pettis while showing that weak and strong measures coincide, before Grothendieck's 1953 locally convex generalization. ([Orlicz–Pettis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlicz%E2%80%93Pettis_theorem)) The measurability criterion is Pettis's; Helmer (1994) weakened its hypotheses. ([Helmer 1994](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/on-the-pettis-measurability-theorem/7302CF3926AFFBE9893F184D3B8DFDD4))

Bartle, Dunford and Schwartz's paper "Weak compactness and vector measures" (received 1954, published 1955 by Cambridge University Press) built the integration of scalar functions against Banach-valued measures, motivated by spectral theory, and used it to give a vector Riesz representation for operators on spaces of continuous functions. ([Bartle–Dunford–Schwartz 1955](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/63F856B2D175E5432C06A284F7E388A7/S0008414X00030406a.pdf/weak_compactness_and_vector_measures.pdf)) Aumann's "Integrals of set-valued functions" appeared in *J. Math. Anal. Appl.* 12 (1965); Artstein and Burns place it among the Hukuhara, Debreu and Aumann approaches to set-valued integration, motivated by control theory, mathematical economics and statistics. ([Artstein–Burns 1975](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1975.58.297)) Kuratowski and Ryll-Nardzewski published "A general theorem on selectors" in 1965. ([Kuratowski–Ryll-Nardzewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuratowski_and_Ryll-Nardzewski_measurable_selection_theorem)) Diestel and Uhl's *Vector Measures* appeared in 1977 as volume 15 of the AMS Mathematical Surveys. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/015))

Rieffel's 1970 Berkeley graduate notes, from courses taught in the late 1960s, treated the Bochner integral from the beginning and in an elementary way, without the [Hahn–Banach Theorem](node:Hahn–Banach%20Theorem); students had asked for written lectures during campus protests. ([Rieffel](https://math.berkeley.edu/~rieffel/measinteg.html))

### Open problems
- **Krein–Milman property versus Radon–Nikodym property.** Whether the Radon–Nikodym property and the Krein–Milman property (every closed bounded convex set is the closed convex hull of its extreme points) are equivalent for Banach spaces is described as "a longstanding open question"; the implication RNP ⇒ KMP is clear because denting points are extreme, and the converse has motivated a large literature since the 1980s. ([arXiv:2510.21234](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.21234v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Vector measure (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_measure): definitions, variation, Lyapunov's theorem, bibliography; with [Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral) and [Pettis integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pettis_integral).
- **Learn:** [Rieffel's Berkeley measure and integration notes](https://math.berkeley.edu/~rieffel/measinteg.html): a graduate course built around the Bochner integral.
- **Primary:** [Bartle, Dunford, Schwartz, "Weak compactness and vector measures" (1955)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/63F856B2D175E5432C06A284F7E388A7/S0008414X00030406a.pdf/weak_compactness_and_vector_measures.pdf): control measures and integration against vector measures.
- **Primary:** [Helmer, "On the Pettis measurability theorem" (1994)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/on-the-pettis-measurability-theorem/7302CF3926AFFBE9893F184D3B8DFDD4): weakened hypotheses for Pettis's criterion.
- **Primary:** [Artstein, Burns, "Integration of compact set-valued functions" (1975)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1975.58.297): Aumann, Debreu and Hukuhara integrals compared.
- **Further reading:** [Diestel and Uhl, *Vector Measures*, AMS Mathematical Surveys 15 (1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/015): AMS monograph (bibliographic record via Crossref), the reference text listed in the [Vector measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_measure) article.

## Reference
### Overview
This subfield of [MSC 28 - Measure and integration](node:MSC%2028%20-%20Measure%20and%20integration) studies [measures](node:Measure%20Theory) on sets that carry more than a $\sigma$-algebra: a topology, a group operation compatible with a topology, or the linear structure of an infinite-dimensional vector space. MSC2020 groups under it integration via linear functionals (Radon measures, Daniell integrals), measures on topological groups and semigroups (Haar and invariant measures), regularity of measures on topological spaces, and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces such as Wiener and Gaussian measure. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Cxx))

The extra structure changes which questions make sense. On a locally compact [Hausdorff space](node:Hausdorff%20Space), measures can be produced from positive linear functionals on continuous functions, and regularity conditions are what make that correspondence unique ([Riesz–Markov–Kakutani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem)). On a locally compact group one gets a canonical invariant measure ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure)). On an infinite-dimensional separable Banach space, by contrast, no nontrivial locally finite translation-invariant Borel measure exists, ([Infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite-dimensional_Lebesgue_measure); [Eldredge, Thm 1.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1607.03591)). Gaussian measures are studied instead; they are quasi-invariant only under translations by their Cameron–Martin space ([Eldredge, Thm 4.24](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1607.03591)).

### Scope
- **28C05 Integration via linear functionals:** Radon measures, Daniell integrals, representation of set functions and measures. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Cxx))
