- **28C10 Measures on topological groups or semigroups:** Haar measures and invariant measures; MSC cross-references 22Axx and 43A05. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Cxx))
- **28C15 Measures on topological spaces:** regularity of measures and related questions. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Cxx))
- **28C20 Measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces:** Wiener measure, Gaussian measure; cross-references 46G12, 58C35, 58D20, 60B11. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Cxx))
- **Neighbouring codes.** 28C10 cross-references [22Axx](node:MSC%2022Axx%20-%20Topological%20and%20differentiable%20algebraic%20systems) and 43A05 in [43Axx](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis); 28C20 cross-references 46G12, 58C35, 58D20 and 60B11 (see [MSC 60Bxx](node:MSC%2060Bxx%20-%20Probability%20theory%20on%20algebraic%20and%20topological%20structures)); the whole 28Cxx heading carries the cross-reference "See also 46G12, 58C35, 58D20". ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Cxx)) In [MSC 46Gxx](node:MSC%2046Gxx%20-%20Measures,%20integration,%20derivative,%20holomorphy%20%28all%20involving%20infinite-dimensional%20spaces%29), 46G12 is "Measures and integration on abstract linear spaces" and points back to 28C20. ([MSC2020 46Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Gxx&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Radon measures and regularity** (28C05, 28C15). A Radon measure on a Hausdorff [topological space](node:Topological%20Spaces) $X$ is a Borel measure that is locally finite and inner regular, meaning $m(U)=\sup\{m(K): K\subseteq U \text{ compact}\}$ for open $U$; outer regularity is not part of this definition. Every Suslin space is strongly Radon (every locally finite Borel measure is Radon), so in particular Borel probability measures on Polish spaces are Radon. ([Radon measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_measure))
- **[Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem](node:Riesz%20Representation%20Theorems)** (28C05). If $X$ is locally compact Hausdorff and $\psi$ is a positive linear functional on $C_c(X)$, there is a unique positive Borel measure $\mu$ with $\psi(f)=\int f\,d\mu$ that is finite on compact sets, outer regular on Borel sets, and inner regular on open sets and on Borel sets of finite measure; without these regularity conditions uniqueness can fail. Dually, every bounded linear functional on $C_0(X)$ is integration against a unique complex regular Borel measure, with operator norm equal to the total variation $|\mu|(X)$. ([Riesz–Markov–Kakutani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem))
- **[Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure)** (28C10). Every locally compact Hausdorff group $G$ has a nonzero left-invariant Borel measure that is finite on compact sets, outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular on open sets, unique up to a positive constant; it gives positive mass to nonempty open sets and can be normalised to $\mu(G)=1$ when $G$ is compact. A right Haar measure $\nu$ satisfies $\nu(g^{-1}S)=\Delta(g)\nu(S)$ for a continuous homomorphism $\Delta:G\to(0,\infty)$, the modular function; $G$ is unimodular when $\Delta\equiv1$, as for abelian, compact, discrete and semisimple Lie groups, but not for the affine group of the line. ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure))
- **No infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure** (28C20). If $X$ is an infinite-dimensional separable [Banach space](node:Banach%20Spaces) and $\mu$ is a locally finite translation-invariant Borel measure on $X$, then $\mu=0$. Proof idea: by Riesz's lemma a ball $B(r)$ contains infinitely many disjoint balls of radius $r/4$, all of equal measure by invariance, so each is null; separability (Lindelöf) then gives $\mu(X)=0$. Oxtoby (1946) showed that a non-locally-compact Polish group has no nonzero $\sigma$-finite left-invariant Borel measure. ([Infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite-dimensional_Lebesgue_measure))
- **Gaussian measures and the Cameron–Martin space** (28C20). A Borel probability measure $\mu$ on a separable Banach space $W$ is (centred) Gaussian if every continuous linear functional $f\in W^*$ pushes it forward to a centred normal law on $\mathbb R$; the pair $(W,\mu)$ is an abstract Wiener space. The Cameron–Martin space is $H=\{h\in W:\|h\|_H<\infty\}$ with $\|h\|_H=\sup_{f\neq0}|f(h)|/\sqrt{q(f,f)}$, where $q$ is the covariance form; $H$ is a Hilbert space densely embedded in $W$, and $\mu(H)=0$ when $H$ is infinite-dimensional. ([Eldredge, Def. 2.1, 4.1, 4.19, Thm 4.20, Prop. 4.22](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1607.03591))
- **Cameron–Martin theorem** (28C20). For $h\in H$ the translate $\mu_h=\mu(\cdot-h)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$, with density $\exp\big(\langle h,x\rangle^\sim-\tfrac12\|h\|_H^2\big)$, where $\langle h,\cdot\rangle^\sim$ is the Paley–Wiener integral; for $h\notin H$, $\mu_h$ and $\mu$ are mutually singular. Thus $\mu$ is quasi-invariant exactly under translations by the dense, $\mu$-null subspace $H$. ([Cameron–Martin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Martin_theorem); [Eldredge, Thm 4.24](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1607.03591))
- **Fernique's theorem** (28C20). If $\mu$ is a centred Gaussian measure on a separable Banach space $X$, there is $\alpha>0$ with $\int_X e^{\alpha\|x\|^2}\,d\mu(x)<\infty$; in particular the norm has moments of all orders and Gaussian tails. ([Fernique's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernique%27s_theorem); [Eldredge, Thm 4.10](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1607.03591))
- **Wiener measure** (28C20). The law of Brownian motion on $W=\{\omega\in C([0,1]):\omega(0)=0\}$ is a Gaussian measure whose Cameron–Martin space consists of the absolutely continuous $h$ with $\dot h\in L^2([0,1])$, with inner product $\int_0^1\dot h_1\dot h_2\,dt$. This is the measure-theoretic base for [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus). ([Eldredge, §4.4, Thm 4.32](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1607.03591))
- **Prokhorov's theorem** (weak convergence; shared with 60B). If $S$ is a separable metric space, a tight family of Borel probability measures has sequentially compact closure in the weak topology, and the weak topology on $\mathcal P(S)$ is metrisable. If $S$ is also complete (Polish), the converse holds: a family is tight if and only if its weak closure is sequentially compact. ([Prokhorov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prokhorov%27s_theorem))

### History
Riesz (1909) represented continuous linear functionals on $C[0,1]$ as Riemann–Stieltjes integrals against functions of bounded variation; Markov (1938) extended this to some non-compact spaces and Kakutani (1941) to compact Hausdorff spaces, so the combined name records successive generalisations. ([Riesz–Markov–Kakutani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem)) Hurwitz (1897) used an invariant integral for Lie groups; Haar (1933) proved existence for second-countable locally compact groups, Weil gave the general proof, and Cartan gave a proof without the axiom of choice establishing existence and uniqueness together; von Neumann used Haar's theorem on Hilbert's fifth problem for compact groups. ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure)) In infinite dimensions, Cameron and Martin published their translation formula for Wiener integrals in the *Annals of Mathematics* in 1944, Prokhorov's compactness criterion appeared in 1956, and Fernique proved Gaussian integrability in 1970 in a note in the *Comptes Rendus*. ([Cameron–Martin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Martin_theorem); [Prokhorov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prokhorov%27s_theorem); [Fernique's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernique%27s_theorem)) Gross's original development of abstract Wiener spaces started from the Hilbert space $H$ and chose a pair $(W,\mu)$ to match it, a choice that is not unique. ([Eldredge, remark after Def. 4.1, §4.6](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1607.03591))

### Open problems
- **Null sets without Haar measure.** Because non-locally-compact Polish groups have no invariant measure, Christensen (1972) defined a set $A$ in a Polish group to be Haar null if some Borel $B\supseteq A$ and Borel probability measure $\mu$ satisfy $\mu(gBh)=0$ for all $g,h$. The 2016 survey of Elekes and Nagy lists open questions about this notion, among them Solecki's question whether left Haar null sets coincide with right Haar null sets in amenable-at-1 Polish groups (Question 4.4.11), and whether generalized Haar null sets form a strictly larger class than Haar null sets in every non-locally-compact Polish group (Question 4.2.3, settled there only for abelian groups). ([Elekes–Nagy](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1606.06607))
- **Haar meager sets.** The same survey records Darji's questions whether every Haar meager set is strongly Haar meager and whether the strongly Haar meager sets form a $\sigma$-ideal (Questions 4.7.2, 4.7.7). ([Elekes–Nagy](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1606.06607)) The first has since been answered negatively: Elekes, Nagy, Poór and Vidnyánszky constructed a $G_\delta$ subset of $\mathbb Z^\omega$ that is Haar meager but not strongly Haar meager, and showed no $F_\sigma$ counterexample exists. They list Darji's $\sigma$-ideal question, and even whether strongly Haar meager sets form an ideal, as still open, together with the question of which Polish groups have every Haar meager set strongly Haar meager. ([Elekes–Nagy–Poór–Vidnyánszky, §6](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.11524))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem): precise regularity hypotheses and the $C_0(X)$ dual; see also [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure) and [Cameron–Martin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Martin_theorem).
- **Learn:** [Eldredge, *Analysis and Probability on Infinite-Dimensional Spaces*](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1607.03591): Cornell course notes on Gaussian measures, Cameron–Martin space, Fernique's theorem and Wiener measure.
- **Primary:** [Elekes and Nagy, *Haar null and Haar meager sets: a survey and new results*](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1606.06607): survey of measure-like smallness in non-locally-compact Polish groups with a list of open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Bogachev, *Gaussian Measures* (AMS, 1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/062) for 28C20, and [Bogachev, *Measure Theory* (Springer, 2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-34514-5) for topological measure theory and weak convergence.
references.MSC 28Dxx - Measure-theoretic ergodic th:
## Reference
### Overview
Measure-theoretic ergodic theory studies a measure-preserving system $(X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)$, a probability space with a measurable $T$ satisfying $\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)$, through its invariant sets, long-time averages, recurrence, mixing and isomorphism invariants such as entropy. It applies [measure theory](node:Measure%20Theory) to dynamics and is the measure-theoretic core of [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) and a branch of the theory of [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems). ([Wikipedia: Measure-preserving dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_dynamical_system); [Hochman, §2.1](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~bruin/Hochman_Ergodic_Notes.pdf))

Within [MSC 28 - Measure and integration](node:MSC%2028%20-%20Measure%20and%20integration), 28Dxx is cross-referenced to 11K50, 11K55, 22D40, 37Axx, 47A35, 60Fxx and 60G10, so its themes are shared with metric number theory, ergodic theory of group actions, operator ergodic theorems and stationary processes. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx)) The area's tools reach number theory: Furstenberg's 1977 ergodic proof of Szemerédi's theorem started ergodic [Ramsey theory](node:Ramsey%20Theory), and Einsiedler and Ward's graduate text develops the subject toward Szemerédi's theorem, continued fractions and equidistribution of horocycle orbits. ([Wikipedia: Ergodic Ramsey theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_Ramsey_theory); [Einsiedler–Ward](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-85729-021-2))

### Scope
- **28D05:** measure-preserving transformations (dynamical-systems aspects go to 37A05). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx))
- **28D10:** one-parameter continuous families of measure-preserving transformations (flows; dynamical aspects 37A10). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx))
- **28D15:** general groups of measure-preserving transformations (dynamical aspects 37A15). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx))
- **28D20:** entropy and other invariants. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx))
- **Neighbours:** the explicit pointers from 28D05–28D15 to 37A05–37A15 send dynamical-systems aspects to [MSC 37Axx - Ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037Axx%20-%20Ergodic%20theory); within section 28, 28Axx is classical measure theory and 28Cxx treats measures on spaces with additional structure. ([MSC2020, 28Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Dxx); [MSC2020, section 28](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28-XX))

### Key concepts
- **[Measure-Preserving Transformations](node:Measure-Preserving%20Transformations) and recurrence:** for a measure-preserving $T$ and $\mu(A)>0$, $\mu$-almost every $x\in A$ returns to $A$, indeed infinitely often (Poincaré recurrence). ([Hochman, Theorem 2.2.2 and Corollary 2.2.3](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~bruin/Hochman_Ergodic_Notes.pdf))
- **Ergodic theorems:** von Neumann's mean ergodic theorem: if $U$ is a linear contraction of a Hilbert space $V$ (for instance a unitary) and $\pi$ is the orthogonal projection onto the invariant vectors, then $\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U^nv\to\pi v$ in norm for every $v$. Birkhoff's pointwise theorem: for $f\in L^1(\mu)$ and $\mathcal I$ the $\sigma$-algebra of invariant sets, $\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f\circ T^n\to\mathbb E(f\mid\mathcal I)$ almost everywhere and in $L^1$; if $T$ is ergodic the limit is $\int f\,d\mu$. ([Hochman, Theorems 4.2.3 and 4.3.1](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~bruin/Hochman_Ergodic_Notes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory))
- **Mixing hierarchy and the [spectral](node:Spectral%20Theory) viewpoint:** $T$ is strongly mixing if $\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)\to\mu(A)\mu(B)$ for all $A,B$, and weakly mixing if the Cesàro averages of $|\mu(A\cap T^{-k}B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|$ tend to 0; strong mixing implies weak mixing, which implies ergodicity. ([Wikipedia: Mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_%28mathematics%29)) Equivalently, $T$ is weakly mixing iff $T\times T$ is ergodic, and an ergodic $T$ is weakly mixing iff $1$ is its only eigenvalue (no nonconstant eigenfunctions); irrational rotations are ergodic but not weakly mixing. ([Hochman, Definition 6.1.1, Example 6.1.2, Theorem 6.4.7](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~bruin/Hochman_Ergodic_Notes.pdf)) Above these sit K-automorphisms (an invertible $T$ with a sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal K\subset T\mathcal K$ whose iterates generate $\mathcal B$ and whose backward tail is trivial): Bernoulli shifts are K, the converse fails, and K-automorphisms are strongly mixing. ([Wikipedia: Kolmogorov automorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov_automorphism))
- **Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy (28D20):** for a finite partition $\alpha$, $h_\mu(T,\alpha)=\lim_n\frac1nH_\mu\big(\bigvee_{i=1}^nT^{-i}\alpha\big)$ with $H(\alpha)=-\sum_{A\in\alpha}\mu(A)\log\mu(A)$, and $h_\mu(T)=\sup_\alpha h_\mu(T,\alpha)$, an isomorphism invariant. **Kolmogorov–Sinai theorem:** if $\alpha$ is generating, $h_\mu(T)=h_\mu(T,\alpha)$. ([Hochman, §7.7, Proposition 7.7.2, Theorem 7.7.5](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~bruin/Hochman_Ergodic_Notes.pdf)) **Krieger's generator theorem:** for an invertible ergodic measure-preserving $T$ on a Lebesgue probability space with $h(T)<\log k$, there is a generator with $k$ atoms; when $h(T)=\log k$ exactly, a $k$-atom generator exists iff the system is isomorphic to the Bernoulli shift on $k$ symbols with equal weights. ([Wikipedia: Measure-preserving dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_dynamical_system)) The measure-theoretic notion parallels [Topological Entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy).
- **Ornstein isomorphism theorem:** two Bernoulli schemes with the same entropy are isomorphic (Ornstein, 1970); Kolmogorov and Sinai had shown that the Bernoulli scheme $BS(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ has entropy $-\sum p_i\log p_i$, so schemes of different entropy are not isomorphic. Factors of Bernoulli shifts are Bernoulli, and K-systems of equal entropy need not be isomorphic. ([Wikipedia: Ornstein isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornstein_isomorphism_theorem))
- **Multiple recurrence and Szemerédi:** Szemerédi's theorem (1975) says a set of positive integers with positive upper density contains arithmetic progressions of every length; Furstenberg gave an ergodic-theoretic proof in 1977, which Einsiedler–Ward present in a chapter of their text. ([Wikipedia: Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem); [Einsiedler–Ward, contents](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-85729-021-2))
- **Homogeneous dynamics and rigidity:** Ratner's theorems (proved around 1990, main papers 1990–1995) say that for unipotent flows on $\Gamma\backslash G$, $\Gamma$ a lattice in a Lie group $G$, every ergodic invariant probability measure is homogeneous (algebraic), orbit closures are homogeneous, and orbits equidistribute in their closures; unipotent dynamics was decisive in Margulis's proof of the Oppenheim conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Ratner's theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratner%27s_theorems)) Work on diagonal actions is driven by conjectures of Furstenberg and Margulis, with a partial result of Lindenstrauss under a positive-entropy hypothesis. ([Wikipedia: Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory))

### History
Birkhoff's "Proof of the ergodic theorem" appeared in *PNAS* in 1931 and von Neumann's "Proof of the quasi-ergodic hypothesis" in 1932. ([Wikipedia: Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory)) Sinai's 1959 theorem showed that the entropy supremum is attained on generators. ([Wikipedia: Measure-preserving dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_dynamical_system)) Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy answered negatively von Neumann's question whether $BS(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and $BS(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ are isomorphic, and Ornstein's 1970 theorem completed the classification of Bernoulli shifts by entropy. ([Wikipedia: Ornstein isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornstein_isomorphism_theorem)) Furstenberg's 1977 proof of Szemerédi's theorem created ergodic Ramsey theory. ([Wikipedia: Ergodic Ramsey theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_Ramsey_theory))

### Open problems
- **Multiple mixing.** As of 2020 it was not known whether 2-mixing implies 3-mixing. ([Wikipedia: Mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_%28mathematics%29))
- **Furstenberg's ×2 ×3 conjecture.** An atomless probability measure on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ invariant under multiplication by both $p$ and $q$, where $p,q>1$ are multiplicatively independent (not both powers of one integer), should be Lebesgue measure. Rudolph's theorem proves this for relatively prime $p,q$ when $\mu$ is ergodic for the joint action and some element of the semigroup $\langle p,q\rangle$ has positive entropy (Johnson extended it to multiplicatively independent $p,q$); Tal's survey records that not much is known in the zero-entropy case. ([Tal, survey, Conjecture 1.2 and Theorem 1.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2110.05989v16))
- **Diagonal actions.** Measure rigidity for higher-rank diagonalizable actions is an active direction motivated by conjectures of Furstenberg and Margulis, known only partially (Lindenstrauss, with positive entropy). ([Wikipedia: Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory): mean and pointwise ergodic theorems, history, homogeneous dynamics.
- **Learn:** [Hochman, *Notes on ergodic theory*](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~bruin/Hochman_Ergodic_Notes.pdf): Hebrew University course notes covering recurrence, ergodic theorems, weak mixing and spectral theory, Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy, Rokhlin's lemma.
- **Primary:** [Einsiedler–Ward, *Ergodic Theory with a view towards Number Theory*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-85729-021-2): Graduate Texts in Mathematics 259; mixing, conditional measures, joinings, Furstenberg's proof of Szemerédi's theorem, homogeneous dynamics.
- **Further reading:** [Tal, Furstenberg's ×2 ×3 conjecture (survey)](https://arxiv.org/html/2110.05989v16): the conjecture and the positive-entropy proofs of Rudolph, Host and Parry.
references.MSC 28Exx - Miscellaneous topics in meas:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 division 28Exx sits inside [MSC 28 - Measure and integration](node:MSC%2028%20-%20Measure%20and%20integration) next to [MSC 28Axx - Classical measure theory](node:MSC%2028Axx%20-%20Classical%20measure%20theory) and collects three branches: nonstandard measure theory (28E05), fuzzy measure theory (28E10), and other connections with logic and set theory (28E15), with 28E99 as the catch-all. The three branches are separate classifications, cross-referenced respectively to nonstandard models and nonstandard analysis (03H05, 26E35) and to fuzzy set theory, fuzzy real analysis and 94D05 (03E72, 26E50, 94D05). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Exx))

The nonstandard branch keeps countable additivity but starts from internal, hyperfinite data and converts it to a standard measure via Loeb's construction ([Loeb space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loeb_space)). The fuzzy branch drops additivity, keeping only monotonicity of the set function ([Fuzzy measure theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_measure_theory)). The set-theoretic branch asks which measures can exist at all, for instance whether Lebesgue measure extends to every set of reals, a question tied to large cardinals and the [Axiom of Choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice) ([Measurable cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_cardinal); [Solovay model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay_model)).

### Scope
- **28E05 Nonstandard measure theory** (see also 03H05, 26E35). Its basic tools are Loeb measures on hyperfinite probability spaces, used widely in probability theory and in mathematical economics. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Exx); [Anderson, ch. 4](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~anderson/Book.pdf))
- **28E10 Fuzzy measure theory** (see also 03E72, 26E50, 94D05). Its objects are monotone set functions (capacities), such as Sugeno $\lambda$-measures, and integrals against them. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Exx); [Fuzzy measure theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_measure_theory))
- **28E15 Other connections with logic and set theory.** Examples of such connections are models of ZF + DC in which all sets of reals are measurable, real-valued measurable cardinals, and extensions of Lebesgue measure to all sets of reals. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=28Exx); [Measurable cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_cardinal); [Solovay model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay_model))
- **Neighbours.** In [MSC 03Hxx - Nonstandard models](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models), 28E05's cross-reference 03H05 is "Nonstandard models in mathematics" ([MSC 03Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Hxx)). [MSC 26Exx - Miscellaneous topics in real functions](node:MSC%2026Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20real%20functions) holds nonstandard analysis (26E35) and fuzzy real analysis (26E50) ([MSC 26Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=26Exx)). [MSC 03Exx - Set theory](node:MSC%2003Exx%20-%20Set%20theory) holds large cardinals (03E55), consistency and independence results (03E35) and fuzzy set theory (03E72) ([MSC 03Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=03Exx)).

### Key concepts
- **Loeb's theorem (28E05).** Work in a saturated nonstandard extension. Let $(A,\mathcal A,\nu)$ be an internal probability space ($\mathcal A$ an internal $\sigma$-algebra, closed under unions and intersections of internal sequences indexed by ${}^*\mathbb N$, and $\nu$ internally ${}^*$-countably additive; closure under finite unions and finite additivity suffice). Put
$$\bar{\mathcal A}=\{B\subseteq A:\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{++}\ \exists C,D\in\mathcal A\ [C\subseteq B\subseteq D,\ \nu(D\setminus C)<\varepsilon]\},\qquad \bar\nu(B)=\inf\{{}^\circ\nu(D):B\subseteq D\in\mathcal A\}.$$
Then $\bar{\mathcal A}\supseteq\mathcal A$ is a $\sigma$-algebra, $\bar\nu$ is a countably additive probability measure, $\bar{\mathcal A}$ is complete for $\bar\nu$, $\bar\nu(B)={}^\circ\nu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal A$, and every $B\in\bar{\mathcal A}$ differs from some $A'\in\mathcal A$ by a $\bar\nu$-null set. Saturation enters the proof through the extension of a countable sequence of internal sets to an internal sequence (Anderson's Theorem 1.10.3) followed by overspill. ([Anderson, Thm 4.1.6 and Thm 1.10.3](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~anderson/Book.pdf)) The mechanism behind countable additivity: if a set in the internal algebra is a countable union of members of the algebra, it is already a finite union of them, so the standard part of $\nu$ is automatically countably additive on $\mathcal A$ and Carathéodory extension applies. ([Loeb space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loeb_space))
- **Lebesgue measure as a Loeb measure (Anderson, Henson).** Fix an infinite hypernatural $n$, let $A=\{k/n:1\le k\le n\}$ with counting measure $\nu(B)=|B|/n$ on internal subsets, and push the Loeb measure forward by the standard-part map: $\mu(C)=\bar\nu(\mathrm{st}^{-1}(C))$ on $\mathcal C=\{C\subseteq[0,1]:\mathrm{st}^{-1}(C)\in\bar{\mathcal A}\}$. Then $([0,1],\mathcal C,\mu)$ is exactly the Lebesgue measure space on $[0,1]$. More generally every Radon probability space $(X,\mathcal B,\mu)$ is the image of a hyperfinite Loeb space under a map $S:A\to X$, with $B$ in the completion of $\mathcal B$ iff $S^{-1}(B)\in\bar{\mathcal A}$. ([Anderson, Thms 4.2.2 and 4.3.3](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~anderson/Book.pdf))
- **Anderson's Brownian motion.** Anderson built a single object that, from the nonstandard point of view, has all the formal properties of a discrete random walk and, viewed measure-theoretically, is a standard Brownian motion; this gives a pathwise definition of the Itô integral and pathwise solutions of stochastic differential equations. The paper is R. M. Anderson, *Israel J. Math.* 25 (1976), 15–46. ([Robert M. Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_M._Anderson_%28mathematician%29); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02756559)) It is one of the starting points of an extensive literature on stochastic processes based on Loeb measure. ([Anderson, ch. 4 notes](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~anderson/Book.pdf)) See [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus).
- **Fuzzy measures and the Choquet integral (28E10).** A fuzzy measure (capacity) on a class $\mathcal C$ of subsets of $X$ is $g:\mathcal C\to\mathbb R$ with $g(\emptyset)=0$ and $E\subseteq F\Rightarrow g(E)\le g(F)$. On finite $X$ the Sugeno $\lambda$-measure ($\lambda>-1$) satisfies $g(X)=1$ and $g(A\cup B)=g(A)+g(B)+\lambda g(A)g(B)$ for disjoint $A,B$, with $\lambda+1=\prod_i(1+\lambda g_i)$ for densities $g_i=g(\{x_i\})$. Every fuzzy measure on finite $X$ has a Möbius representation $M(E)=\sum_{F\subseteq E}(-1)^{|E\setminus F|}g(F)$, recovered by $g(E)=\sum_{F\subseteq E}M(F)$. ([Fuzzy measure theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_measure_theory)) The Choquet integral of measurable $f$ with respect to a monotone $\nu$ is
$$(C)\!\int f\,d\nu=\int_{-\infty}^{0}\big(\nu(\{f\ge x\})-\nu(S)\big)\,dx+\int_0^{\infty}\nu(\{f\ge x\})\,dx;$$
it is monotone, positively homogeneous and additive on comonotone pairs, subadditive if $\nu$ is 2-alternating and superadditive if $\nu$ is 2-monotone. ([Choquet integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choquet_integral)) The Sugeno integral replaces sums by sup/min: $\sup_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\min(\alpha,g(A\cap\{h\ge\alpha\}))$ for $h:X\to[0,1]$. ([Sugeno integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugeno_integral)) Compare [Fuzzy Sets and Information Measures](node:Fuzzy%20Sets%20and%20Information%20Measures) and the potential-theoretic capacities in [Capacity and Fine Topology](node:Capacity%20and%20Fine%20Topology).
- **Solovay's model (28E15).** If there is an inaccessible cardinal, then inside a suitable forcing extension there is an inner model of ZF + DC in which every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable, has the Baire property and has the perfect set property. Shelah (1984) showed the inaccessible is necessary: if every $\Sigma^1_3$ set of reals is measurable then $\aleph_1$ is inaccessible in $L$. ([Solovay model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay_model))
- **Real-valued measurable cardinals (28E15).** $\kappa$ is real-valued measurable if some $\kappa$-additive probability measure on $\mathcal P(\kappa)$ vanishes on singletons. Ulam (1930): such $\kappa$ is weakly inaccessible. Banach–Kuratowski (1929): under CH, $\mathfrak c$ is not real-valued measurable. A real-valued measurable cardinal $\le\mathfrak c$ exists iff Lebesgue measure has a countably additive extension to all sets of reals; and Solovay (1971) showed measurable cardinals and real-valued measurable cardinals are equiconsistent over ZFC. ([Measurable cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_cardinal)) See [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory) and [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory).
- **Applications in combinatorics.** Loeb measure on hyperfinite sets gives nonstandard proofs of the triangle removal lemma, Szemerédi regularity and Jin's sumset theorem, and a nonstandard proof of Steinhaus' theorem on sets of reals of positive Lebesgue measure. ([Goldbring minicourse](https://webapps.math.uci.edu/~isaac/beijingcourse.html)) See [Nonstandard Measure Theory](node:Nonstandard%20Measure%20Theory) and [Hyperreal Numbers](node:Hyperreal%20Numbers).

### History
Choquet introduced capacities and the Choquet integral in "Theory of capacities" (1953), first used in statistical mechanics and potential theory and later in decision theory, including Tversky and Kahneman's cumulative prospect theory (1992). ([Choquet integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choquet_integral)) Sugeno independently defined fuzzy measures and the fuzzy integral (paper 1972, thesis 1974, Tokyo Institute of Technology). ([Sugeno integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugeno_integral); [Fuzzy measure theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_measure_theory)) On the set-theoretic side, Banach and Kuratowski (1929), Banach (1930) and Ulam (1930) began the study of real-valued measurable cardinals, and Solovay's model appeared in 1970. ([Measurable cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_cardinal); [Solovay model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay_model)) Loeb's construction appeared in *Trans. AMS* 211 (1975), 113–122, originally to solve a problem in potential theory; Anderson's Brownian motion followed in 1976. ([Loeb space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loeb_space); [Anderson, ch. 4](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~anderson/Book.pdf)) Cutland's *Loeb Measures in Practice: Recent Advances* appeared in Springer's Lecture Notes in Mathematics in 2000. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b76881))

### Open problems
- **Liftings in ZFC.** Fremlin's problem list (version 8.8.25) recalls that every complete probability space has a lifting, that under CH every probability space of Maharam type at most $\mathfrak c^+$ has one, and that it is consistent with ZFC that Lebesgue measure restricted to the Borel sets of $[0,1]$ has no lifting. It asks whether it is a theorem of ZFC that some probability space has no lifting; by Maharam's theorem it suffices to consider the usual measure on the Baire $\sigma$-algebra of $\{0,1\}^\kappa$, with $\kappa=\omega_3$ singled out. ([Fremlin, Problem D](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/problems.pdf))
- **Products of Radon spaces (L. Schwartz).** The same list asks whether the product of two Radon spaces can always be Radon; the answer is no if there is an atomlessly-measurable cardinal or if $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak c$ (Martin's axiom). ([Fremlin, Problem W](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/problems.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Loeb space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loeb_space): construction and original citation; [Fuzzy measure theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_measure_theory): definitions, Sugeno measures, Möbius and Shapley; [Measurable cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_cardinal): real-valued measurability and extensions of Lebesgue measure.
- **Learn:** [Goldbring, minicourse on nonstandard methods](https://webapps.math.uci.edu/~isaac/beijingcourse.html): UCI course page with lecture notes and videos introducing Loeb measure and its combinatorial uses.
- **Primary:** [Anderson, *Infinitesimal Methods in Mathematical Economics*](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~anderson/Book.pdf): monograph, chapter 4 proves Loeb's theorem and the Lebesgue and Radon representations; Anderson, "A non-standard representation for Brownian motion and Itô integration", *Israel J. Math.* 25 (1976) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02756559)).
- **Further reading:** [Fremlin, *Measure Theory*](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/mt.htm): five volumes, volume 5 is *Set-theoretic Measure Theory*; Cutland, *Loeb Measures in Practice: Recent Advances*, Springer LNM (2000) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b76881)).
references.MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 30 classifies research on functions of one complex variable. Beyond the foundational theory of [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), its second-level codes cover general properties of functions (30A), series expansions (30B), geometric function theory (30C), entire and meromorphic functions (30D), miscellaneous analysis in the plane including approximation and interpolation (30E), Riemann surfaces (30F), generalized function theory (30G), spaces and algebras of analytic functions (30H), function theory on the disc (30J), universal holomorphic functions (30K), and analysis on [metric spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces) (30L). ([MSC2020 30-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30-XX))

The research core rests on a few classical theorems. The Riemann mapping theorem reduces every proper simply connected plane domain to the disc; Picard's theorems say how few values an entire or essentially singular function can omit; Montel's theorems turn omitted values into compactness of families. ([Wikipedia: Riemann mapping theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem); [Wikipedia: Picard theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard_theorem); [Wikipedia: Montel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montel%27s_theorem)) From these grow quantitative theories: coefficient problems for univalent maps, Nevanlinna's value distribution theory for meromorphic functions, quasiconformal maps, and the uniformization of Riemann surfaces. ([Wikipedia: De Branges's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Branges%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory); [Wikipedia: Quasiconformal mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconformal_mapping))

The field is still producing problems: Hayman's *Research Problems in Function Theory*, in a new edition with Lingham (arXiv, 2018), collects over five hundred problems in nine chapters (meromorphic functions, entire functions, subharmonic and harmonic functions, polynomials, functions in the unit disc, univalent and multivalent functions, miscellaneous, spaces of functions, interpolation and approximation) with progress reports since 1967. ([Hayman–Lingham, arXiv:1809.07200](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1809.07200))

### Scope
The eleven second-level codes of 30-XX are listed above; history is 30-03 (consider also 01-XX) and computational methods 30-08 (see also 65Exx). ([MSC2020 30-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30-XX)) Subfield maps: [MSC 30Axx - General properties of functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Axx%20-%20General%20properties%20of%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable), [MSC 30Bxx - Series expansions of functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Bxx%20-%20Series%20expansions%20of%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable), [MSC 30Cxx - Geometric function theory](node:MSC%2030Cxx%20-%20Geometric%20function%20theory), [MSC 30Dxx - Entire and meromorphic functions of one complex variable, and related topics](node:MSC%2030Dxx%20-%20Entire%20and%20meromorphic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable,%20and%20related%20topics), [MSC 30Exx - Miscellaneous topics of analysis in the complex plane](node:MSC%2030Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20of%20analysis%20in%20the%20complex%20plane), [MSC 30Fxx - Riemann surfaces](node:MSC%2030Fxx%20-%20Riemann%20surfaces), [MSC 30Gxx - Generalized function theory](node:MSC%2030Gxx%20-%20Generalized%20function%20theory), [MSC 30Hxx - Spaces and algebras of analytic functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Hxx%20-%20Spaces%20and%20algebras%20of%20analytic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable), [MSC 30Jxx - Function theory on the disc](node:MSC%2030Jxx%20-%20Function%20theory%20on%20the%20disc), [MSC 30Kxx - Universal holomorphic functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Kxx%20-%20Universal%20holomorphic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable), [MSC 30Lxx - Analysis on metric spaces](node:MSC%2030Lxx%20-%20Analysis%20on%20metric%20spaces).

Examples of the fine structure: 30H contains Hardy, Bergman, Bloch, BMO and de Branges–Rovnyak spaces and corona theorems; 30J contains inner functions, Blaschke products and singular inner functions; 30K contains universal Taylor and Dirichlet series and compositional universality. ([MSC2020 30Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Hxx); [MSC2020 30Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Jxx); [MSC2020 30Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Kxx)) Neighbouring fields: several complex variables and analytic spaces is [MSC 32 - Several complex variables and analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032%20-%20Several%20complex%20variables%20and%20analytic%20spaces); potential theory, including two-dimensional potential theory (31A), is [MSC 31 - Potential theory](node:MSC%2031%20-%20Potential%20theory). ([MSC2020 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX); [MSC2020 31-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Riemann mapping theorem (30C).** Every nonempty simply connected open $U\subsetneq\mathbb C$ admits a biholomorphic map onto the open unit disc; it is unique once $f(z_0)=0$ and $\arg f'(z_0)$ are prescribed. Riemann stated it in his 1851 thesis with a proof resting on the Dirichlet principle; Osgood gave the first rigorous proof in 1900, and Carathéodory's 1912 proof via normal families became the textbook route. ([Wikipedia: Riemann mapping theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem))
- **Picard and Montel (30D).** A non-constant entire function omits at most one complex value; near an essential singularity a holomorphic function takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often. A locally uniformly bounded family of holomorphic functions on an open set is normal, and a family all of whose members omit the same two values $a,b\in\mathbb C$ is normal (Montel); the second statement corresponds to Picard's theorem and can be derived from it via Zalcman's lemma. ([Wikipedia: Picard theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard_theorem); [Wikipedia: Montel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montel%27s_theorem))
- **Bieberbach conjecture / de Branges's theorem (30C).** If $f(z)=z+\sum_{n\ge2}a_nz^n$ is univalent on the unit disc, then $|a_n|\le n$ for all $n\ge2$, with equality for the Koebe function. Bieberbach posed it in 1916; Littlewood (1925) proved $|a_n|\le en$; de Branges proved it (1985) by proving the stronger Milin conjecture, which implies Robertson's conjecture and hence Bieberbach's. ([Wikipedia: De Branges's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Branges%27s_theorem))
- **Nevanlinna theory (30D).** For meromorphic $f$ the characteristic $T(r,f)=m(r,f)+N(r,f)$ satisfies the first main theorem $T(r,f)=N(r,a,f)+m(r,a,f)+O(1)$ for every $a$ in the Riemann sphere, and the second main theorem implies that for distinct $a_1,\dots,a_k$, $(k-2)T(r,f)\le\sum_j\overline N(r,a_j,f)+S(r,f)$. Consequently the deficient values are at most countable and $\sum_a\delta(a,f)\le2$, a quantitative Picard theorem. Nevanlinna devised the theory in 1925. ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory))
- **Quasiconformal maps and the measurable Riemann mapping theorem (30C, 30F).** A quasiconformal map solves the Beltrami equation $\partial_{\bar z}f=\mu\,\partial_zf$ with measurable $\mu$, $\|\mu\|_\infty<1$, and has dilatation $K=(1+\|\mu\|_\infty)/(1-\|\mu\|_\infty)$. Ahlfors–Bers: for simply connected $D\subsetneq\mathbb C$ and any such $\mu$ there is a quasiconformal [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) of $D$ onto the disc in $W^{1,2}(D)$ solving the equation distributionally, unique up to three real parameters. Grötzsch introduced these maps in 1928 and Ahlfors named them in 1935. ([Wikipedia: Quasiconformal mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconformal_mapping))
- **Uniformization (30F).** Every simply connected Riemann surface is conformally equivalent to the disc, the plane, or the Riemann sphere; hence the compact surfaces covered by the disc are exactly those of genus greater than $1$, and every Riemann surface carries a constant-curvature metric. Poincaré and Koebe gave the first rigorous proofs in 1907. ([Wikipedia: Uniformization theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniformization_theorem))

### History
Riemann's 1851 thesis already contains the mapping theorem, though Weierstrass later showed that the Dirichlet principle it relied on is not universally valid. ([Wikipedia: Riemann mapping theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem)) Klein and Poincaré conjectured uniformization for algebraic curves in 1882–1883. ([Wikipedia: Uniformization theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniformization_theorem)) The twentieth century brought value distribution (Nevanlinna, 1925), quasiconformal maps (Grötzsch, 1928; Ahlfors, 1935), and the 1916–1985 arc of the Bieberbach conjecture. ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory); [Wikipedia: Quasiconformal mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconformal_mapping); [Wikipedia: De Branges's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Branges%27s_theorem))

In October 2026 two OpenAI preprints claimed to establish Brennan's conjecture and to disprove Kraetzer's more general $t^2/4$ conjecture on the universal integral means spectrum; Binder, Ivrii, Prause and Smirnov, while checking them, posted a drastically shorter proof of a significantly stronger statement. All three are unrefereed preprints, so the resolution of Brennan's conjecture is a reported claim, not yet an established result. ([Binder–Ivrii–Prause–Smirnov, arXiv:2610.23853](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23853))

### Open problems
- **Deficiency sums for finite-order meromorphic functions.** Hayman–Lingham Problem 1.26 (Drasin–Weitsman) conjectures a sharp upper bound for $\sum_a\delta(a,f)$ for meromorphic $f$ of finite order $\rho$; the correct bound is known for $0\le\rho\le1$, and the 2018 update reports no progress. ([Hayman–Lingham, Problem 1.26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1809.07200))
- **Minimum modulus of entire functions of large order.** Problem 2.33 asks for the exact value of $C_\infty$ (the analogous constant for functions of infinite order), or the asymptotics of $C(\lambda)/\log\lambda$ as $\lambda\to\infty$, where $C(\lambda)$ is the best lower bound for $\limsup_{r\to\infty}\log m_0(r,f)/\log M(r,f)$ over entire $f$ of lower order $\lambda$ ($C(\lambda)=\cos\pi\lambda$ for $0\le\lambda\le1$); the 2018 update reports no progress. ([Hayman–Lingham, Problem 2.33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1809.07200))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Riemann mapping theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem): statement, uniqueness and history.
- **Reference:** [Nevanlinna theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory): characteristic, main theorems, defect relation.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.112 Functions of a Complex Variable (Helgason, Fall 2008)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/): course with problem sets, exams and solutions.
- **Primary:** [Hayman–Lingham, Research Problems in Function Theory (arXiv:1809.07200)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.07200): over 500 problems with progress updates.
- **Primary:** [Binder–Ivrii–Prause–Smirnov, Brennan's conjecture and the universal integral means spectrum (arXiv:2610.23853)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23853): recent research preprint in geometric function theory.
- **Further reading:** [Stein–Shakarchi, Complex Analysis (Princeton Lectures in Analysis II)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691113852/complex-analysis) and [Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I (Springer GTM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-6313-5).
references.MSC 30Axx - General properties of functi:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 30Axx, a subfield of [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable), has two substantive codes: 30A05, monogenic and polygenic functions of one complex variable, and 30A10, inequalities in the complex plane; 30A99 collects the rest. It lists no cross-references. ([MSC2020 30Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Axx))

The first code concerns what it means for a function of $z=x+iy$ to have a derivative, and what happens when the limit of the difference quotient depends on the path. Examples of inequalities in the complex plane are Bernstein-type bounds for derivatives of polynomials on the unit circle, their refinements under hypotheses on the zeros, and extremal problems such as the length of polynomial lemniscates; see also [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis). ([Monogenic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogenic_function); [Bernstein's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_theorem_%28polynomials%29); [Tao](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.12455v2))

### Scope
- **30A05 Monogenic and polygenic functions.** Cauchy's term *monogenic* means a single finite derivative $f'(\zeta)=\lim_{z\to\zeta}\frac{f(z)-f(\zeta)}{z-\zeta}$, the same along all paths; a function monogenic on a domain is analytic there. ([Monogenic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogenic_function)) A function with infinitely many derivatives at a point is called polygenic there. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PolygenicFunction.html))
- **30A10 Inequalities in the complex plane.** ([MSC2020 30Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Axx))
- **30A99** Other general properties. ([MSC2020 30Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Axx))

**Related codes elsewhere.** In [MSC 30Cxx - Geometric function theory](node:MSC%2030Cxx%20-%20Geometric%20function%20theory), 30C80 holds "Maximum principle, Schwarz's lemma, Lindelöf principle, analogues and generalizations; subordination"; 30C10 holds polynomials and rational functions of one complex variable; and 30C15 holds zeros of polynomials, rational functions and other analytic functions, sending algebraic theory to 12D10 and real methods to 26C10. ([MSC2020 30Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Cxx)) 26D05 is "Inequalities for trigonometric functions and polynomials" ([26Dxx](node:MSC%2026Dxx%20-%20Inequalities%20in%20real%20analysis)), and 26C10 "Real polynomials: location of zeros" ([26Cxx](node:MSC%2026Cxx%20-%20Polynomials,%20rational%20functions%20in%20real%20analysis)) sends complex methods to 30C15 ([MSC2020 26Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=26Dxx); [MSC2020 26Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=26Cxx)). Erdélyi's paper on Lax-type inequalities on circular arcs carries the MSC2000 code 41A17 ([Erdélyi](https://people.tamu.edu/~terdelyi/papers-online/BPICA.pdf)); see [MSC 41Axx - Approximations and expansions](node:MSC%2041Axx%20-%20Approximations%20and%20expansions).

### Key concepts
- **Cauchy–Riemann criterion.** For $f=u+iv$ on an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$, $f$ is complex differentiable at $z_0=x_0+iy_0$ iff $(u,v)$ is real differentiable at $(x_0,y_0)$ and $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ there. ([Wang, Math 185 notes, Thm 2.1](https://math.berkeley.edu/~ruiwang/LN_185.pdf)) With $\partial_{\bar z}=\frac12(\partial_x+i\partial_y)$, the equations read $\partial f/\partial\bar z=0$, a first-order system of [PDE](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations). Pompeiu's "areolar derivative" (1912), a limit of normalized contour integrals over small circles, generalizes $\partial f/\partial\bar z$ and can exist where $f$ is not differentiable. ([Wirtinger derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wirtinger_derivatives))
- **Looman–Menchoff theorem (30A05).** If $f$ is continuous on an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ and $\partial f/\partial x$, $\partial f/\partial y$ exist at all but countably many points, then $f$ is holomorphic iff $\partial f/\partial\bar z=0$. Continuity cannot be dropped ($e^{-z^{-4}}$ with $f(0)=0$ satisfies the equations everywhere), and the result does not localize: $z^5/|z|^4$ satisfies them at $0$ without being analytic there. It generalizes Goursat's theorem, which assumes real differentiability instead of continuity. ([Looman–Menchoff theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looman%E2%80%93Menchoff_theorem))
- **Cauchy's inequality.** If $f$ is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\overline{D(z_0,R)}$, then $|f^{(n)}(z_0)|\le n!\,R^{-n}\sup_{|z-z_0|=R}|f(z)|$ for all $n\ge0$. ([Wang, Thm 1.7](https://math.berkeley.edu/~ruiwang/LN_185.pdf)) This is the prototype of the derivative bounds below; see [Cauchy's Integral Formula](node:Cauchy's%20Integral%20Formula).
- **Bernstein's inequality and the Erdős–Lax theorem (30A10).** For a polynomial $P$ of degree $n$, $\max_{|z|=1}|P'(z)|\le n\max_{|z|=1}|P(z)|$, with equality only for $P=\alpha z^n$. If $P$ has no zeros in $|z|<1$, the constant improves to $n/2$ (conjectured by Erdős, proved by Lax 1944); if $P$ has no zeros in $|z|<k$ with $k\ge1$, it is $n/(1+k)$ (Malik 1969). ([Bernstein's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_theorem_%28polynomials%29); [Bernstein's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_inequality_%28mathematical_analysis%29)) Erdélyi proves the right Lax-type inequality on subarcs of the unit circle for polynomials with no zeros in the open disk, via a Bernstein–Szegő–Videnskii inequality for trigonometric polynomials on intervals shorter than a period. ([Erdélyi](https://people.tamu.edu/~terdelyi/papers-online/BPICA.pdf))
- **Markov's inequality (real counterpart).** For real polynomials $P$ of degree at most $n$, $\max_{[-1,1]}|P^{(k)}|\le\frac{n^2(n^2-1^2)\cdots(n^2-(k-1)^2)}{1\cdot3\cdots(2k-1)}\max_{[-1,1]}|P|$, sharp for Chebyshev polynomials; A. Markov proved $k=1$ and V. Markov the higher cases. ([Markov brothers' inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_brothers%27_inequality)) Compare [Chebyshev Approximation](node:Chebyshev%20Approximation).
- **Lemniscate length (Erdős–Herzog–Piranian).** For monic $p$ of degree $n$, let $L_p=\{|p(z)|=1\}$ and $p_0(z)=z^n-1$. Fryntov and Nazarov showed that $|L_p|$ has a local maximum at $p=p_0$ and that $|L_p|\le2n+O(n^{7/8})$, using $|L|=2\iint_E\overline{\partial s}\,dx\,dy$ over $E=\{|p|<1\}$ with $s=|\varphi|/\varphi$, $\varphi=p'/p$. ([Fryntov–Nazarov](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0808.0717)) **Tao (2025, arXiv preprint):** $|L_p|\le2n+4\log2+o(1)$, and for all sufficiently large $n$, $|L_p|\le|L_{p_0}|$ with equality only for rotations and translations of $p_0$. Earlier bounds were $74n^2$ (Pommerenke), $8e\pi n$ (Borwein), $4\pi n$ (Dolženko) and $9.173n$ (Eremenko–Hayman), who also settled $n=2$. ([Tao, Thm 1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.12455v2)) Lemniscates are one topic of Richards's survey of the geometry of complex polynomials. ([Richards](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.01159))

### History
Cauchy coined *monogenic* and used *synectic* for what Briot and Bouquet named *holomorphic* in 1875. ([Monogenic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogenic_function); [Holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function)) Pompeiu's areolar derivative dates from 1912 and Wirtinger's systematic use of $\partial_z,\partial_{\bar z}$ from 1927. ([Wirtinger derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wirtinger_derivatives)) Looman (1923) and Menchoff (*Les conditions de monogénéité*, 1936) settled how weak the hypotheses for monogenicity can be. ([Looman–Menchoff theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looman%E2%80%93Menchoff_theorem)) Edward Kasner's work on polygenic functions occupied the period 1927–1940 of his career. ([MacTutor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Kasner/)) On the inequality side, A. Markov's inequality dates from 1890 and V. Markov's from 1892 ([Markov brothers' inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_brothers%27_inequality)); Lax proved Erdős's conjecture in 1944 and Malik extended it in 1969; Boas surveyed derivative inequalities for polynomials in 1969. ([Bernstein's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_theorem_%28polynomials%29)) Fryntov–Nazarov's lemniscate estimates were posted in 2008 ([Fryntov–Nazarov](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0808.0717)) and Tao's high-degree theorem in 2025 ([Tao](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.12455v2)).

### Open problems
- **Erdős–Herzog–Piranian lemniscate conjecture in small degree.** The conjecture that $z^n-1$ maximizes lemniscate length among monic degree-$n$ polynomials is trivial for $n=1$, settled for $n=2$ by Eremenko and Hayman, and proved by Tao for all sufficiently large $n$. Tao's constants are effectively computable, so the remaining cases reduce to finitely many degrees that the paper does not check; he notes that a competitor of exactly equal length could be hard to rule out by finite computation, since these lengths are likely transcendental. ([Tao](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.12455v2))
- **The set of maximizers.** Tao conjectures that rotations and translations of $p_0$ are the full set of maximizers in every degree (his Theorem 1.1(iv) gives this for large $n$), and says more elementary proofs of the existence and structure of maximizers would be of interest. ([Tao](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.12455v2))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Monogenic function (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogenic_function): Cauchy's notion of a single derivative and polygenic functions.
- **Reference:** [Bernstein's theorem (polynomials) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_theorem_%28polynomials%29): Bernstein, Erdős–Lax and Malik inequalities with references.
- **Learn:** [Wang, Math 185 Introduction to Complex Analysis notes (Berkeley)](https://math.berkeley.edu/~ruiwang/LN_185.pdf): Cauchy–Riemann criterion, Cauchy's inequality, Rouché, maximum modulus.
- **Primary:** [Tao, The maximal length of the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian lemniscate in high degree](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.12455v2): current research on an extremal inequality in the plane, with a survey of earlier bounds.
- **Primary:** [Fryntov and Nazarov, New estimates for the length of the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian lemniscate](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0808.0717): local maximality of $z^n-1$ and the $2n+O(n^{7/8})$ bound.
- **Primary:** [Richards, Some recent results on the geometry of complex polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.01159): survey of Gauss–Lucas, lemniscates and shape analysis.
- **Further reading:** [Rahman and Schmeisser, Analytic Theory of Polynomials (OUP, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198534938.001.0001): monograph on the analytic theory of polynomials.
- **Further reading:** [Milovanović, Mitrinović and Rassias, Topics in Polynomials: Extremal Problems, Inequalities, Zeros (World Scientific, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1142/1284): monograph on extremal problems, inequalities and zeros of polynomials.
references.MSC 30Bxx - Series expansions of functio:
## Reference
### Overview
Subfield 30Bxx studies what the series expansion of a function of one complex variable reveals about the function: where it converges, how it behaves on the boundary of convergence, whether and where it can be continued analytically, and which systems of functions (powers, exponentials, continued-fraction convergents) can represent or approximate others. Its codes cover power series including lacunary series, random power series, boundary behaviour and over-convergence, analytic continuation, Dirichlet and exponential series, completeness problems, and the complex-analytic side of continued fractions. ([MSC2020 30Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Bxx))

The textbook starting point is the Laurent expansion: a function holomorphic on an annulus $A$ around $c$ equals $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_n(z-c)^n$ there, with $a_n=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma f(z)(z-c)^{-n-1}\,dz$ for a counterclockwise Jordan curve $\gamma\subset A$ enclosing $c$, and the expansion is unique. ([Wikipedia: Laurent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_series)) The research questions of 30Bxx begin where this stops: at the circle of convergence. A central theme is the *natural boundary*: for a series with large gaps between its nonzero exponents, or with random coefficients, the circle of convergence is typically a barrier beyond which no continuation is possible at any point. ([Wikipedia: Ostrowski–Hadamard gap theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrowski%E2%80%93Hadamard_gap_theorem); [Breuer–Simon, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1002.0823))

Breuer and Simon draw an analogy between natural boundaries of power series and the absence of absolutely continuous spectrum for Schrödinger operators, and use spectral-theoretic notions (reflectionless, right limits) to prove natural-boundary theorems. ([Breuer–Simon, arXiv:1002.0823](https://arxiv.org/abs/1002.0823)) Dirichlet series connect the code to [MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory): via $z_j=p_j^{-s}$ an ordinary Dirichlet series becomes a function of infinitely many complex variables. ([Saksman–Seip, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1601.01616))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists: 30B10 power series (including lacunary series); 30B20 random power series; 30B30 boundary behaviour of power series, over-convergence; 30B40 analytic continuation; 30B50 Dirichlet series, exponential series and other series (see also 11M41, 42-XX); 30B60 completeness problems, closure of a system of functions; 30B70 continued fractions, complex-analytic aspects (see also 11A55, 40A15); 30B99 other. ([MSC2020 30Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Bxx))

Neighbours, by the cross-references in the entry: the number-theoretic theory of zeta and $L$-functions is 11M ([MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory)); trigonometric and Fourier series are 42-XX ([MSC 42Axx - Harmonic analysis in one variable](node:MSC%2042Axx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20one%20variable)); arithmetic continued fractions are 11A55 and convergence of continued fractions as limiting processes is 40A15 ([MSC 40Axx - Convergence and divergence of infinite limiting processes](node:MSC%2040Axx%20-%20Convergence%20and%20divergence%20of%20infinite%20limiting%20processes)). Universal Taylor and Dirichlet series have their own code, [MSC 30Kxx - Universal holomorphic functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Kxx%20-%20Universal%20holomorphic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable). ([MSC2020 30Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Hadamard gap theorem (30B10, 30B30).** If $0<n_0<n_1<\cdots$ are integers with $n_{k+1}/n_k\ge\lambda>1$ and $f(z)=\sum_k a_kz^{n_k}$ has radius of convergence $1$, then the unit circle is a natural boundary of $f$: $f$ cannot be continued analytically across any point of it. Hadamard proved it in his 1892 thesis; it is a special case of both Ostrowski's over-convergence theorem and Fabry's gap theorem. ([Wikipedia: Ostrowski–Hadamard gap theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrowski%E2%80%93Hadamard_gap_theorem)) The standard example is $\sum_n z^{a^n}$ for an integer $a\ge2$. ([Wikipedia: Lacunary function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacunary_function))
- **Fabry and Pólya gap theorems.** If the exponents satisfy $n_k/k\to\infty$ (density $D=\limsup k/n_k=0$) and the radius of convergence is $1$, the unit circle is a natural boundary (Fabry, 1896). Pólya's form: every arc of the circle of convergence longer than $2\pi D$ contains a singularity; and Pólya (1942) showed the converse, that for $D>0$ some series with these exponents and radius $1$ does not have the circle as natural boundary. ([Wikipedia: Fabry gap theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabry_gap_theorem))
- **Ostrowski over-convergence (30B30).** Call $\sum a_\nu z^\nu$ an Ostrowski series if there are $\delta>0$ and integers $0\le m_0<n_0\le m_1<n_1\le\cdots$ with $n_\nu-m_\nu>\delta m_\nu$ and $a_j=0$ for $m_\nu<j<n_\nu$. If such a series has radius $r>0$ and $A$ is the set of non-singular points of the circle $|z|=r$, then the subsequence of sections $s_{m_k}(z)=\sum_{\nu\le m_k}a_\nu z^\nu$ converges in a neighbourhood of $B(0,r)\cup A$, so it converges beyond the circle near every regular boundary point. Gaps need only occur "here and there". ([Alameer, Thm 1.5 and Def. 1.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1604.06654)) Hadamard's gap theorem is a special case of this over-convergence theorem. ([Wikipedia: Ostrowski–Hadamard gap theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrowski%E2%80%93Hadamard_gap_theorem))
- **Pólya–Carlson theorem (30B40).** If $f(z)=\sum a_nz^n$ with $a_n\in\mathbb Z$ converges on the unit disc and extends holomorphically beyond it, then $f=P/Q$ is rational with $P,Q\in\mathbb Z[z]$. Attributed to Pólya (1916) and Carlson (1921); multivariate versions are current research. ([Multivariate Pólya–Carlson, arXiv:2312.00428](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2312.00428)) Szegő's theorem is a relative: if the coefficients take values in a finite set, then either $a_n$ is eventually periodic (and $f$ is rational with poles at roots of unity) or $f$ has a strong natural boundary. ([Breuer–Simon, Thm 5.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1002.0823))
- **Random power series (30B20).** For coefficients $a_n(\omega)$ that are independent and uniformly bounded, with variances of positive $\limsup$ along some subsequence, $\sum a_n(\omega)z^n$ has a strong natural boundary on the unit circle for almost every $\omega$ (Breuer–Simon, Thm 6.1). They also prove this without independence, for translation-invariant ergodic nondeterministic processes with uniformly bounded values (Thm 1.7), noting that earlier random-series results relied on independence. ([Breuer–Simon, Thms 1.7, 6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1002.0823)) The classical monograph is Kahane's *Some Random Series of Functions* (CUP, 2nd ed. 1985). ([Crossref: review in Proc. Edinburgh Math. Soc.](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/s0013091500017521))
- **Abel's theorem and boundary behaviour (30B30).** If $\sum a_k$ converges, then $\sum a_kz^k\to\sum a_k$ as $z\to1$ inside any Stolz sector $|1-z|\le M(1-|z|)$, $M>1$; there is no exact converse, only Tauberian results under extra hypotheses ([MSC 40Exx - Inversion theorems](node:MSC%2040Exx%20-%20Inversion%20theorems)). ([Wikipedia: Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%27s_theorem))
- **Dirichlet series and their abscissas (30B50).** For $f(s)=\sum a_ne^{-\lambda_ns}$ with real $\lambda_n\uparrow\infty$, the abscissa of convergence $\sigma_c$ and of absolute convergence $\sigma_a$ bound half-planes of convergence; $f$ is holomorphic for $\operatorname{Re}s>\sigma_c$, if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sigma_c=\limsup_n\log|a_1+\cdots+a_n|/\lambda_n$, and $0\le\sigma_a-\sigma_c\le L=\limsup(\log n)/\lambda_n$. ([Wikipedia: General Dirichlet series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Dirichlet_series)) For ordinary series ($\lambda_n=\log n$) the gap can equal $1$: $(1-2^{1-s})\zeta(s)=\sum(-1)^{n-1}n^{-s}$ has $\sigma_c=0$, $\sigma_a=1$. ([Harvard Math 213b notes](https://legacy-www.math.harvard.edu/archive/213b_spring_05/dirichlet_series.pdf)) Bohr showed the strip of uniform but not absolute convergence has width at most $1/2$, and Bohnenblust and Hille proved this optimal. ([Saksman–Seip, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1601.01616)) See [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Müntz–Szász theorem (30B60).** For $S\subset\mathbb N$ and $0<a<b$, the monomials $x^n$, $n\in S$, span a uniformly dense subspace of $C[a,b]$ if and only if $\sum_{n\in S}1/n=\infty$; the same holds for strictly increasing positive real exponents, and (Szász) for complex exponents with the condition on real parts. Müntz proved it in 1914 and Szász in 1916, after a conjecture of Bernstein. ([Wikipedia: Müntz–Szász theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BCntz%E2%80%93Sz%C3%A1sz_theorem))
- **Continued fractions (30B70).** Worpitzky (1865): if $|a_i|\le1/4$ for $i\ge2$, the continued fraction $1/(1+a_2/(1+a_3/(1+\cdots)))$ converges, uniformly when the $a_i$ are complex variables. Consequently, if $|c_i|\le M$, the convergents of $1/(1+c_2z/(1+c_3z/\cdots))$ converge uniformly on $|z|<1/(4M)$ to an analytic function. Śleszyński–Pringsheim: $|b_n|\ge|a_n|+1$ for all $n$ implies convergence. ([Wikipedia: Convergence problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_problem))

### History
Weierstrass described the Laurent expansion in an 1841 paper not published until 1894; Laurent published it in 1843. ([Wikipedia: Laurent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_series)) Hadamard's gap theorem appeared in his 1892 thesis on functions given by their Taylor expansion. ([Wikipedia: Ostrowski–Hadamard gap theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrowski%E2%80%93Hadamard_gap_theorem)) Fabry proved his gap theorem in 1896 and the refinement in 1899; Pólya put it in modern form in 1929 and proved the converse in 1942. ([Wikipedia: Fabry gap theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabry_gap_theorem)) Müntz (1914) and Szász (1916) settled Bernstein's completeness question. ([Wikipedia: Müntz–Szász theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BCntz%E2%80%93Sz%C3%A1sz_theorem))

In recent decades Hardy spaces $\mathcal H^p$ of Dirichlet series have grown into a theory of their own: through the Bohr correspondence they are isometrically and multiplicatively isomorphic to $H^p(\mathbb T^\infty)$, the Hardy spaces of the infinite-dimensional torus. ([Saksman–Seip, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1601.01616)) A monograph on the subject is Queffélec and Queffélec, *Diophantine Approximation and Dirichlet Series* (Springer, 2020). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-981-15-9351-2))

### Open problems
- **Zero sets and duals in Hardy spaces of Dirichlet series.** Saksman and Seip list as open: whether zero sets of functions in $\mathcal H^p$, $p<2$, satisfy the Blaschke condition in the half-plane $\operatorname{Re}s>1/2$ (Problem 2.3); describing the dual spaces of $\mathcal H^p$ (Problem 2.8); and characterizing the compact composition operators on $\mathcal H^2$ (Problem 3.3). ([Saksman–Seip, arXiv:1601.01616](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1601.01616))
- **Point versus singular continuous analogues for power series.** Breuer and Simon ask what the power-series analogues are of the distinction between pure point and singular continuous spectra in their natural-boundary/spectral dictionary. ([Breuer–Simon, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1002.0823))
- **Multivariate Pólya–Carlson.** The authors of a multivariate Pólya–Carlson theorem state that they do not know whether Straube's higher-dimensional conditions are necessary for rationality. ([arXiv:2312.00428, Remark 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2312.00428))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fabry gap theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabry_gap_theorem): Fabry and Pólya gap theorems and the converse.
- **Reference:** [General Dirichlet series (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Dirichlet_series): abscissas and their formulas.
- **Learn:** [Dirichlet series and abscissas of convergence (Harvard Math 213b notes)](https://legacy-www.math.harvard.edu/archive/213b_spring_05/dirichlet_series.pdf): summation by parts, sector convergence, the alternating zeta example.
- **Primary:** [Breuer–Simon, Natural boundaries and spectral theory (arXiv:1002.0823)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1002.0823): natural boundaries, Szegő's theorem, random power series.
- **Primary:** [Saksman–Seip, Some open questions in analysis for Dirichlet series (arXiv:1601.01616)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01616): survey and problem list.
- **Further reading:** [Kahane, Some Random Series of Functions (CUP, 2nd ed.)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/s0013091500017521) and [Queffélec–Queffélec, Diophantine Approximation and Dirichlet Series (Springer 2020)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-981-15-9351-2).
references.MSC 30Cxx - Geometric function theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Geometric function theory is the study of geometric properties of analytic functions. Its main objects are conformal maps, quasiconformal maps, univalent (injective holomorphic) functions, and extremal problems built on the maximum principle and the Schwarz lemma. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_function_theory))

Typical results turn injectivity on the disk plus a normalization at one point into global quantitative control: the Koebe quarter theorem bounds the size of the image from below, and de Branges's theorem bounds every Taylor coefficient. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koebe_quarter_theorem), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Branges%27s_theorem)) The subject meets potential theory through capacity and harmonic measure (30C85, cross-referenced with 31A15) and probability through the stochastic Loewner equation. ([MSC2020 30Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Cxx), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loewner_differential_equation))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 30Cxx, "Geometric function theory", lists these sub-codes: 30C10 polynomials and rational functions; 30C15 zeros of polynomials, rational functions and other analytic functions; 30C20 conformal mappings of special domains; 30C25 covering theorems; 30C30 Schwarz-Christoffel-type mappings; 30C35 general theory of conformal mappings; 30C40 kernel functions and applications; 30C45 special classes of univalent and multivalent functions (starlike, convex, bounded rotation); 30C50 coefficient problems; 30C55 general theory of univalent and multivalent functions; 30C62 quasiconformal mappings in the plane; 30C65 quasiconformal mappings in $\mathbb R^n$; 30C70 and 30C75 extremal problems and variational methods; 30C80 maximum principle, Schwarz lemma, Lindelof principle, subordination; 30C85 capacity and harmonic measure in the plane. ([MSC2020 30Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Cxx))

Neighbouring codes: 30Dxx covers [entire and meromorphic functions](node:Entire%20and%20Meromorphic%20Functions), including growth estimates (30D15), Nevanlinna theory (30D35) and normal families (30D45); 30Jxx, "Function theory on the disc", covers inner functions and [Blaschke Products](node:Blaschke%20Products); 30Lxx, "Analysis on metric spaces", includes quasiconformal mappings in metric spaces (30L10); 31Axx is two-dimensional potential theory, whose 31A15 (capacity, harmonic measure, extremal length) cross-refers to 30C85. ([MSC2020 30Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Dxx), [MSC2020 30Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Jxx), [MSC2020 30Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Lxx), [MSC2020 31Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Axx))

### Key concepts
- [Conformal Mapping](node:Conformal%20Mapping): angle-preserving holomorphic bijections; the basic objects of 30C20 to 30C35. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_function_theory))
- [Riemann Mapping Theorem](node:Riemann%20Mapping%20Theorem): if $U\subsetneq\mathbb C$ is nonempty, open and simply connected, there is a biholomorphism $U\to\mathbb D$, unique once $f(z_0)=0$ and $\arg f'(z_0)$ are fixed. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem))
- Koebe quarter theorem: if $f$ is injective and analytic on $\mathbb D$, then $f(\mathbb D)\supseteq D(f(0),|f'(0)|/4)$; the Koebe function $z/(1-z)^2$ omits $-1/4$, so $1/4$ is sharp. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koebe_quarter_theorem))
- de Branges's theorem (Bieberbach conjecture): if $f(z)=z+\sum_{n\ge2}a_nz^n$ is univalent on $\mathbb D$ then $|a_n|\le n$ for all $n$, with equality for the Koebe function. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Branges%27s_theorem))
- Loewner chains: for a growing family of simply connected domains with Riemann maps $f_t$, $f_t(0)=0$, $f_t'(0)=e^t$, one has $\partial_tf_t(z)=z\,p_t(z)\,\partial_zf_t(z)$ with $\operatorname{Re}p_t>0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loewner_differential_equation))
- [Quasiconformal maps](node:Quasiconformal%20Maps%20of%20Metric%20Spaces): a homeomorphism with Beltrami coefficient $\mu$ is $K$-quasiconformal when $K=(1+\|\mu\|_\infty)/(1-\|\mu\|_\infty)<\infty$; $1$-quasiconformal means conformal. The measurable Riemann mapping theorem (Ahlfors-Bers) says that for measurable $\mu$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty<1$ the Beltrami equation $\partial_{\bar z}f=\mu\,\partial_zf$ has a unique quasiconformal solution of $\mathbb C$ fixing $0,1,\infty$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconformal_mapping), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_Riemann_mapping_theorem))
- [Harmonic Measure](node:Harmonic%20Measure): Makarov's theorem says that for a simply connected planar domain $D$, harmonic measure vanishes on boundary sets of Hausdorff dimension below $1$ and is singular to $t$-dimensional Hausdorff measure for every $t>1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_measure))
- Caratheodory's boundary theorem: a conformal map of $\mathbb D$ onto a bounded domain $U$ extends to a homeomorphism of the closed disk onto $\overline U$ if and only if $\partial U$ is a Jordan curve; for simply connected $U\subset\hat{\mathbb C}$, a continuous extension to the circle exists iff $\partial U$ is locally connected. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_theorem_%28conformal_mapping%29))

### History
Riemann stated the mapping theorem in his 1851 thesis using the Dirichlet principle; Osgood gave the first rigorous proof (1900), and Caratheodory (1912) the first proof by function theory alone, via Montel's normal families. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_mapping_theorem)) Koebe conjectured the quarter theorem in 1907 and Bieberbach proved it in 1916 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koebe_quarter_theorem)); in 1916 he also proved $|a_2|\le2$ and posed the coefficient conjecture. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Branges%27s_theorem)) Loewner introduced his equation in 1923 and used it to prove $|a_3|\le3$; de Branges proved the full conjecture in 1985, via the Milin conjecture and Askey-Gasper inequalities, with later simplifications by FitzGerald-Pommerenke and Weinstein. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Branges%27s_theorem)) Ahlfors and Bers proved the measurable Riemann mapping theorem in 1960. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_Riemann_mapping_theorem)) Schramm introduced the stochastic Loewner equation in the late 1990s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loewner_differential_equation))

### Open problems
- **Brennan conjecture and the universal integral means spectrum.** For univalent $f$ on $\mathbb D$ set $\beta_f(\tau)=\limsup_{r\to1^-}\log\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|f'(re^{i\theta})^\tau|\,d\theta/|\log(1-r)|$ and $B(\tau)=\sup_f\beta_f(\tau)$. By Carleson and Makarov there is $\tau_*<0$ with $B(\tau)=B_b(\tau)=|\tau|-1$ for $\tau\le\tau_*$; only $\tau_*\le-2$ is known, and it is conjectured that $\tau_*=-2$. Brennan's conjecture is equivalent to $B(-2)=1$. Kraetzer's conjecture asserts $B_b(\tau)=\tau^2/4$ for $|\tau|\le2$ and $|\tau|-1$ for $|\tau|>2$ for bounded univalent functions. The paper attributes the best current upper estimate for $B(-2)$ to Hedenmalm and Shimorin, and proves the Brennan conjecture only for the class of univalent rational functions. ([Jin, arXiv:2512.09330](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.09330v3))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Geometric function theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_function_theory): themes, standard theorems, and references (Ahlfors, Krantz).
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 30Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Cxx): the full 30Cxx code list.
- **Learn:** [Belyaev, Complex Analysis: conformal maps and geometry (Oxford)](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/belyaev/TCC/TCC.html): Riemann mapping, area theorem, Koebe 1/4 and distortion, extremal length, Loewner evolution.
- **Primary:** [Hedenmalm and Sola, Spectral notions for conformal maps: a survey](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF03321698): Comput. Methods Funct. Theory 8 (2008).
- **Primary:** [Jin, Complex exponential integral means spectra and the Brennan conjecture](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.09330v3): recent work with the open problems stated.
- **Further reading:** [Pommerenke, Boundary Behaviour of Conformal Maps](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-02770-7): Springer, 1992.
