- **Further reading:** P. L. Duren, *Univalent Functions* (Springer, 1983), listed among the references of [Univalent function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Univalent_function).

Related: [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), [Hardy and Bergman Spaces](node:Hardy%20and%20Bergman%20Spaces), [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem), [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces), [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable).
references.MSC 30Dxx - Entire and meromorphic funct:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 30Dxx is the part of one-variable complex analysis concerned with functions defined on all of $\mathbb C$: entire functions (holomorphic on $\mathbb C$) and meromorphic functions. The organizing question is how growth, the distribution of zeros and poles, and exceptional values constrain one another. The classical tools are Hadamard factorization for finite order, the maximum-term (Wiman–Valiron) method for local behaviour, and Nevanlinna's value-distribution theory. ([Wikipedia: Entire function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entire_function); [Wikipedia: Hadamard factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_factorization_theorem); [Wikipedia: Wiman–Valiron theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman%E2%80%93Valiron_theory); [Wikipedia: Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory))

Nevanlinna theory replaces the degree of a rational map by a characteristic $T(r,f)=m(r,f)+N(r,f)$, where $m$ is the mean of $\log^+|f|$ on $|z|=r$ and $N$ counts poles. It yields a quantitative form of Picard's theorem and a bound on how many values can be "deficient". ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory))

A second strand, now very active, treats transcendental entire and meromorphic functions as dynamical systems: iteration, Fatou and Julia sets, and the Eremenko–Lyubich class. MSC2020 classifies dynamics of entire and meromorphic functions and their Fatou and Julia sets under 37F10, and the 37Fxx heading cross-refers to 30D05 (functional equations, iteration and composition). ([MSC2020 37Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Fxx); [MSC2020 30Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Dxx); [Bergweiler, Iteration of meromorphic functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9310226))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists the following sub-codes under 30Dxx ([MSC2020 30Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Dxx)):
- 30D05: functional equations in the complex plane, iteration and composition of analytic functions (see also 34Mxx, 37Fxx, 39-XX);
- 30D10: representations of entire functions by series and integrals;
- 30D15: special classes of entire functions and growth estimates;
- 30D20: entire functions (general theory);
- 30D30: meromorphic functions (general theory);
- 30D35: value distribution of meromorphic functions, Nevanlinna theory;
- 30D40: cluster sets, prime ends, boundary behavior;
- 30D45: normal functions, normal families;
- 30D60: quasi-analytic and other classes of functions;
- 30D99: none of the above.

Neighbouring codes: [30Cxx](node:MSC%2030Cxx%20-%20Geometric%20function%20theory) covers univalent functions, conformal and quasiconformal maps, and extremal problems; [30Exx](node:MSC%2030Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20of%20analysis%20in%20the%20complex%20plane) covers moment and interpolation problems, approximation, and integrals of Cauchy type; [30Fxx](node:MSC%2030Fxx%20-%20Riemann%20surfaces) covers Riemann surfaces; 37Fxx covers dynamical systems over the complex numbers; 34Mxx, ODEs in the complex domain, cross-refers to 30Dxx and has its own code 34M05 for entire and meromorphic solutions. ([MSC2020 30Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Cxx); [MSC2020 30Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Exx); [MSC2020 30-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30-XX); [MSC2020 37Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Fxx); [MSC2020 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Mxx))

### Key concepts
- **Order and type** ([Entire and Meromorphic Functions](node:Entire%20and%20Meromorphic%20Functions)): the order is $\rho=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\log^+\log^+M(r,f)/\log r$ with $M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f|$; for $0<\rho<\infty$ the type is $\sigma=\limsup \log M(r,f)/r^\rho$. Order-1 functions with finite type have exponential type. ([Wikipedia: Entire function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entire_function))
- **Hadamard factorization** ([Weierstrass Factorization Theorem](node:Weierstrass%20Factorization%20Theorem)): an entire function $f$ of finite order can be written $f(z)=z^m e^{Q(z)}\prod_n E_p(z/a_n)$ with $Q$ a polynomial and $p$ the least integer with $\sum|a_n|^{-p-1}<\infty$. The genus $g=\max\{p,\deg Q\}$ satisfies $g\le\rho\le g+1$. ([Wikipedia: Hadamard factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_factorization_theorem))
- **First main theorem.** For nonconstant meromorphic $f$ and every $a\in\hat{\mathbb C}$, $T(r,f)=N(r,a,f)+m(r,a,f)+O(1)$, a consequence of Jensen's formula. ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory))
- **Second main theorem, defect relation, Picard.** For distinct $a_1,\dots,a_k$, $(k-2)T(r,f)\le\sum_j\overline N(r,a_j,f)+S(r,f)$ with $S(r,f)=o(T(r,f))$ outside a set of finite length. The defect $\delta(a,f)$ satisfies $\sum_a\delta(a,f)\le2$. For transcendental entire $f$, taking $k=3$ and $a_3=\infty$ gives Picard's theorem: $f$ takes every value of $\hat{\mathbb C}$ infinitely often, with at most two exceptions, one of which is $\infty$ (omitted by every entire function). ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory))
- **Wiman–Valiron theory.** With $\mu(r)=\max_k|a_k|r^k$ and central index $n(r)$, for $r$ outside a set of finite logarithmic measure $f(z)\approx (z/z_r)^{n(r)}f(z_r)$ with relative error $o(1)$ on a Wiman–Valiron disk centred at a point $z_r$ of maximum modulus. ([Wikipedia: Wiman–Valiron theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman%E2%80%93Valiron_theory))
- **Denjoy–Carleman–Ahlfors theorem.** A nonconstant entire function of order $\rho$ has at most $2\rho$ asymptotic values (conjectured by Denjoy in 1907, proved by Ahlfors in 1929). ([Wikipedia: Denjoy–Carleman–Ahlfors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denjoy%E2%80%93Carleman%E2%80%93Ahlfors_theorem))
- **Eremenko–Lyubich class $\mathcal B$:** entire functions $f$ for which the set $\operatorname{sing}(f^{-1})$ of singular values is bounded. ([Das–Nayak, Baker wandering domains survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.08264v1)) Sixsmith's survey describes their dynamics as the most similar to polynomial dynamics among transcendental entire functions. ([Sixsmith, Dynamics in the Eremenko–Lyubich class](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09095))
- **Related notes:** [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) is the general setting; [Julia and Fatou Sets](node:Julia%20and%20Fatou%20Sets) of entire and meromorphic functions are classified under 37F10. ([MSC2020 37Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Fxx))

### History
Denjoy conjectured the asymptotic-value bound $2\rho$ in 1907; Carleman proved $5\rho/2$ in 1921 and Ahlfors proved $2\rho$ in 1929. ([Wikipedia: Denjoy–Carleman–Ahlfors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denjoy%E2%80%93Carleman%E2%80%93Ahlfors_theorem)) Nevanlinna introduced his theory in 1925; Cartan, Weyl and Ahlfors extended it to holomorphic curves and Selberg and Valiron to algebroid functions, and Weyl called it one of the few great mathematical events of the twentieth century. ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory)) Bergweiler's 1993 survey organized the iteration theory of transcendental meromorphic functions, with Baker domains and wandering domains as the phenomena absent from rational dynamics. ([Bergweiler](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9310226))

### Open problems
- **Problem list.** Hayman's *Research Problems in Function Theory* (1967) has a new edition by Hayman and Lingham containing over five hundred function theory and complex analysis problems with progress updates over 51 years. ([Hayman–Lingham, arXiv 1809.07200](https://export.arxiv.org/abs/1809.07200))
- **Baker wandering domains.** Das and Nayak's 2026 survey ends with open questions, for example whether a function $g$ from their Example 2.2 has a Fatou component outside the grand orbit of the Baker wandering domains constructed there (Question 1), and whether for every meromorphic function with infinitely many poles and a Baker wandering domain the point $\infty$ is a local Baker omitted value (Question 9). ([Survey of Baker wandering domains](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.08264v1))
- **Resolved, not open.** Eremenko's conjecture (every component of the escaping set of a transcendental entire function is unbounded) was disproved by Martí-Pete, Rempe and Waterman, who also constructed Lakes of Wada for entire functions; the paper appeared in J. Amer. Math. Soc. 38 (2025). ([Martí-Pete–Rempe–Waterman](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.10256))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Nevanlinna theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna_theory): characteristic, main theorems, defect relation, history.
- **Learn:** [Sixsmith, Dynamics in the Eremenko–Lyubich class](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09095): survey introduction to the dynamics of class $\mathcal B$.
- **Primary:** [Bergweiler, Iteration of meromorphic functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9310226): Bull. AMS survey of transcendental iteration theory.
- **Primary:** [Martí-Pete, Rempe, Waterman, Eremenko's conjecture, wandering Lakes of Wada, and maverick points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.10256): JAMS 2025 paper settling several open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Hayman and Lingham, Research Problems in Function Theory](https://export.arxiv.org/abs/1809.07200): arXiv record of the new edition of Hayman's 1967 problem book.
references.MSC 30Exx - Miscellaneous topics of anal:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 30Exx collects planar function theory that fits none of the other 30-series codes: approximation of holomorphic functions by rational functions, polynomials or entire functions (30E10), interpolation and moment problems (30E05), asymptotic representations (30E15), integrals of Cauchy type (30E20) and boundary value problems (30E25); 30E20 and 30E25 cross-refer to integral equations (45Exx). ([MSC2020 30Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Exx)) The classical boundary value problem of this kind is the Riemann–Hilbert problem for a function holomorphic off an oriented contour. ([Wikipedia: Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem))

The approximation branch is the best developed. Runge's theorem (1885) gives rational approximation of functions holomorphic on an open set containing the approximated set. ([Wikipedia: Runge's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%27s_theorem)) Mergelyan's theorem (1951) asks only for continuity on a compact $K$ and holomorphy in its interior, provided $\mathbb C\setminus K$ is connected; when the complement is not connected, polynomials must be replaced by rational functions, and deep results on that problem are due to Vitushkin. ([Wikipedia: Mergelyan's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mergelyan%27s_theorem))

### Scope
- **Approximation (30E10).** Uniform approximation on compact or closed sets by polynomials, rational functions or entire functions; the topology of the complement of the set controls what is possible. ([Wikipedia: Runge's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%27s_theorem); [Bierstone–Ivrii lecture notes](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/~ivrii/ComplexAnalysis.pdf))
- **Interpolation and moment problems (30E05).** Nevanlinna–Pick interpolation asks for a holomorphic self-map of the disc with prescribed values at finitely many points, and has operator-theoretic generalizations to the bidisc and multiply connected regions. ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna–Pick interpolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna%E2%80%93Pick_interpolation))
- **Cauchy-type integrals (30E20).** Boundary values of Cauchy integrals are described by the Sokhotski–Plemelj jump formulas. ([Wikipedia: Sokhotski–Plemelj theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokhotski%E2%80%93Plemelj_theorem))
- **Boundary value problems (30E25).** The scalar Riemann–Hilbert problem seeks functions analytic off a contour with a prescribed linear relation between boundary values from the two sides. ([Wikipedia: Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem))
- **Neighbours.** The 41-XX heading of [MSC 41Axx - Approximations and expansions](node:MSC%2041Axx%20-%20Approximations%20and%20expansions) sends approximation theory in the complex domain to 30E05 and 30E10, and 41A60 (asymptotic approximations) cross-refers to 30E15. ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx)) The background is in [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis).

### Key concepts
- [Holomorphic Approximation](node:Holomorphic%20Approximation): **Runge's theorem.** If $K\subset\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$ is closed, $f$ is holomorphic on an open set containing $K$, and $A$ contains a point of each component of the complement of $K$, then $f$ is a uniform limit on $K$ of rational functions with poles in $A$; for compact $K$ with connected complement, polynomials suffice. ([Wikipedia: Runge's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%27s_theorem))
- [Rational Approximation](node:Rational%20Approximation): **Mergelyan's theorem.** If $K$ is compact with $\mathbb C\setminus K$ connected and $f$ is continuous on $K$ and holomorphic in its interior, then $f$ is a uniform limit of polynomials on $K$. ([Wikipedia: Mergelyan's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mergelyan%27s_theorem))
- [Hardy and Bergman Spaces](node:Hardy%20and%20Bergman%20Spaces): **Pick's theorem.** Points $\lambda_i,z_i\in\mathbb D$ admit a holomorphic $\varphi:\mathbb D\to\overline{\mathbb D}$ with $\varphi(\lambda_i)=z_i$ iff the Pick matrix $\big((1-\bar z_jz_i)/(1-\bar\lambda_j\lambda_i)\big)$ is positive semidefinite, using the Szegő kernel of $H^2$. ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna–Pick interpolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna%E2%80%93Pick_interpolation))
- [Cauchy Singular Integral Equations](node:Cauchy%20Singular%20Integral%20Equations): **Sokhotski–Plemelj jump relations** for Cauchy integrals across a contour. ([Wikipedia: Sokhotski–Plemelj theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokhotski%E2%80%93Plemelj_theorem))
- Analytic capacity: a compact set is removable for bounded analytic functions exactly when its analytic capacity vanishes; sets of zero length have zero capacity and sets of Hausdorff dimension above 1 have positive capacity. ([Wikipedia: Analytic capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_capacity))
- Arakelian sets: Arakelyan's theorem says that for a relatively closed $E$ in an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$, every $f$ continuous on $E$ and holomorphic in its interior can be uniformly approximated on $E$ by functions holomorphic in $\Omega$ iff $\Omega^*\setminus E$ is connected and locally connected, where $\Omega^*$ is the one-point compactification of $\Omega$. For $\Omega=\mathbb C$ this characterizes closed sets of uniform approximation by entire functions. ([Wikipedia: Arakelyan's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arakelyan%27s_theorem))

### History
Runge proved his theorem in 1885, published in Acta Mathematica. Mergelyan proved his in 1951 and suggested a step toward the non-connected-complement problem in 1952; Vitushkin later obtained deep results on rational approximation. ([Wikipedia: Runge's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Mergelyan's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mergelyan%27s_theorem))

Pick proved his interpolation theorem in 1916 and Nevanlinna in 1919, independently; Sarason later gave a Hilbert-space proof using contractions. ([Wikipedia: Nevanlinna–Pick interpolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevanlinna%E2%80%93Pick_interpolation))

Ahlfors introduced analytic capacity in the 1940s. Painlevé asked in 1880 which sets are removable. David (1998) proved Vitushkin's conjecture for sets of finite length, and Tolsa (2002) proved that analytic capacity is semiadditive, answering a question of Vitushkin; together these settle it for sets of $\sigma$-finite length. ([Wikipedia: Analytic capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_capacity); [Tolsa, arXiv:math/0204027](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0204027))

**Tolsa's theorem.** For compact $E$, analytic capacity $\gamma(E)$ is comparable with $\gamma_+(E)$ (capacity via Cauchy transforms of positive measures), with absolute constants; hence $\gamma$ is semiadditive and removability is characterized via curvature of measures. ([Tolsa, arXiv:math/0204027](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0204027))

### Open problems
- **Converse in Vitushkin's conjecture.** Jones and Murai found a set of zero Favard length and positive analytic capacity, disproving one direction (Mattila had shown in 1986 that the conjecture fails for non-$\sigma$-finite sets); Wikipedia reports that, as of 2023, whether the converse holds was unknown, with progress toward a positive answer by Chang and Tolsa. ([Wikipedia: Analytic capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_capacity)) Their paper proves lower bounds for analytic capacity in terms of orthogonal projections and relates them to Vitushkin's conjecture on Favard length. ([Chang–Tolsa, arXiv:1712.00594](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.00594))
- **Arakelian-type approximation on Riemann surfaces.** Characterizing sets of uniform approximation on [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces) of infinite genus is described as one of the outstanding open problems in complex approximation; citing Scheinberg, the authors note that such a characterization, if it exists, cannot be purely topological. ([Fournodavlos–Nestoridis–Pasias](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.00802v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Runge's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%27s_theorem): statement, history, Runge subsets.
- **Learn:** [Bierstone lectures, scribed by Ivrii](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/~ivrii/ComplexAnalysis.pdf): rational approximation and pole moving in a complex analysis course.
- **Primary:** [Tolsa, Painlevé's problem and the semiadditivity of analytic capacity](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0204027): comparability of $\gamma$ and $\gamma_+$.
- **Primary:** [Chang–Tolsa, Analytic capacity and projections](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.00594): lower bounds relating capacity to projections.
references.MSC 30Fxx - Riemann surfaces:
## Reference
### Overview
A Riemann surface is a connected one-dimensional complex manifold: a space locally modelled on the complex plane, with holomorphic transition maps. Compact examples are classified topologically by genus, and by uniformization every Riemann surface has a universal cover that is the sphere, the plane, or the disk. This lets one treat multivalued functions and algebraic curves as single-valued objects on a surface with its own topology. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_surface))

The MSC sub-codes cover both a function-theoretic side (compact surfaces, harmonic functions, differentials) and a geometric side (Fuchsian and Kleinian groups, conformal metrics, Teichmüller theory). ([MSC2020 30Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Fxx)) Eynard's lecture notes cover the first part: atlases and algebraic curves, meromorphic functions and forms, the Abel map, Jacobian and theta functions, Riemann–Roch, and the moduli space with its uniformization link to hyperbolic surfaces. ([Eynard](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.06405))

### Scope
The MSC2020 section 30Fxx lists: 30F10 compact Riemann surfaces and uniformization; 30F15 harmonic functions on Riemann surfaces; 30F20 classification theory; 30F25 ideal boundary theory; 30F30 differentials on Riemann surfaces; 30F35 Fuchsian groups and automorphic functions; 30F40 Kleinian groups; 30F45 conformal metrics (hyperbolic, Poincaré, distance functions); 30F50 Klein surfaces; 30F60 Teichmüller theory; 30F99 other. ([MSC2020 30Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Fxx))

Cross-references in the entry: 30F10 points to 14H15 in [MSC 14Hxx - Curves in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Hxx%20-%20Curves%20in%20algebraic%20geometry) and to 32G15 in [MSC 32Gxx - Deformations of analytic structures](node:MSC%2032Gxx%20-%20Deformations%20of%20analytic%20structures); 30F60 also points to 32G15; 30F35 points to [11Fxx](node:MSC%2011Fxx%20-%20Discontinuous%20groups%20and%20automorphic%20forms), 20H10, 22E40, 32Gxx and 32Nxx; 30F40 points to 20H10. Conformal mappings of plane domains are classified in [MSC 30Cxx - Geometric function theory](node:MSC%2030Cxx%20-%20Geometric%20function%20theory) (30C20, 30C35). ([MSC2020 30Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Fxx); [MSC2020 30Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Uniformization (30F10).** Every simply connected Riemann surface is conformally equivalent to the Riemann sphere, the complex plane, or the open disk; surfaces are elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic according to their universal cover, and carry a metric of constant curvature $+1,0,-1$ respectively. Compact surfaces: genus 0 is the sphere, genus 1 a complex torus, genus $\ge 2$ hyperbolic. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniformization_theorem)) Generalizes [Riemann Mapping Theorem](node:Riemann%20Mapping%20Theorem).
- **Riemann–Roch (30F10, 30F30).** For a compact Riemann surface $X$ of genus $g$ with canonical divisor $K$ and any divisor $D$, $\ell(D)-\ell(K-D)=\deg D-g+1$; consequently $\deg K=2g-2$, $h^0(K)=g$, and $\ell(D)=\deg D-g+1$ whenever $\deg D\ge 2g-1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Roch_theorem)) The genus equals the complex dimension of the space of holomorphic one-forms ([Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms)). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Roch_theorem))
- **Riemann–Hurwitz.** For a surjective map $\pi:S'\to S$ of degree $N$ between compact connected orientable surfaces with ramification indices $e_P$, $2g(S')-2=N(2g(S)-2)+\sum_{P\in S'}(e_P-1)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hurwitz_formula))
- **Abel–Jacobi.** The Jacobian of a genus-$g$ compact surface is $J(C)=\mathbb C^g/\Lambda$, $\Lambda$ the period lattice of $g$ holomorphic differentials over $H_1(C,\mathbb Z)$. Abel's theorem: for effective divisors $D,E$ of the same degree, $u(D)=u(E)$ iff $D$ and $E$ are linearly equivalent; Jacobi inversion: the map is surjective, so $J(C)$ is isomorphic to the group of degree-zero divisors modulo principal divisors. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%E2%80%93Jacobi_map), [Wikipedia: Jacobian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_variety)) Genus one recovers [Elliptic Curves](node:Elliptic%20Curves); the algebraic side is [Algebraic Curves](node:Algebraic%20Curves).
- **Fuchsian groups (30F35).** A Fuchsian group is a discrete subgroup of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)$ acting on the upper half-plane; it serves as the "Fuchsian model" of a hyperbolic surface $\mathbb H/\Gamma$, and $\mathbb H/\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb Z)$ is the moduli space of elliptic curves. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuchsian_group)) See [Hyperbolic Space](node:Hyperbolic%20Space) and [Modular Forms](node:Modular%20Forms).
- **Teichmüller theory (30F60).** The Teichmüller space $T(S)$ of a genus $g\ge2$ surface is homeomorphic to a ball of real dimension $6g-6$ and has complex dimension $3g-3$ via the Bers embedding. Teichmüller's theorem gives a unique extremal quasiconformal map in each isotopy class, defining the complete Teichmüller metric. The mapping class group acts properly discontinuously with quotient the moduli space, and by Royden's theorem it is the full isometry group of the Teichmüller metric. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teichm%C3%BCller_space))
- **Moduli of curves.** For $g>1$ the stack $\mathcal M_g$ has dimension $3g-3$ and can be compactified by adding boundary points corresponding to stable nodal curves; Deligne and Mumford (1969) introduced algebraic stacks as a tool to prove the irreducibility of the coarse moduli space of curves. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space)) See [Moduli Spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces) and [Complex Manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds).

### History
Klein and Poincaré conjectured uniformization for algebraic curves in 1882–1883; the first rigorous proofs of the general theorem were given by Poincaré and Koebe in 1907, and Weyl's 1913 book presented the theory in a modern setting. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniformization_theorem))

### Open problems
Schippers and Staubach's survey on comparison moduli spaces of Riemann surfaces includes a list of open problems in classical and modern function theory and Teichmüller theory, ranging from general theoretical questions to specific technical ones. ([Schippers–Staubach](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.09168), [arXiv abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.09168))
- **Resolved since the list: geometric characterization of Weil–Petersson quasicircles.** Their Problem 5.1 asked for analytic or geometric conditions on the set itself characterizing Weil–Petersson class quasicircles, and noted that no geometric characterization was known. ([Schippers–Staubach](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.09168)) Bishop has since given such characterizations: a curve is Weil–Petersson iff it is well approximated by polygons in a precise sense, iff it has finite Möbius energy, iff its arclength parametrization is in $H^{3/2}(\mathbb T)$, and iff its local curvature, measured for example by Jones's $\beta$-numbers, is square integrable over all locations and scales; planar Weil–Petersson curves are exactly the asymptotic boundaries of minimal surfaces in $\mathbb H^3$ with finite renormalized area. ([Bishop, Weil–Petersson curves, conformal energies, β-numbers, and minimal surfaces](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~bishop/papers/wpbeta.pdf))
- **Active direction.** Viklund and Wang characterize Weil–Petersson quasicircles quantitatively through the Loewner–Kufarev energy of foliations of the twice-punctured sphere. ([Viklund–Wang, arXiv:2012.05771](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.05771))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Riemann surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_surface): definitions, uniformization, genus, moduli.
- **Reference:** [Uniformization theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniformization_theorem): statement, classification of simply connected surfaces, history.
- **Learn:** [Eynard, Lecture notes on compact Riemann surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.06405): functions, forms, Abel map, Riemann–Roch, moduli.
- **Primary:** [Schippers and Staubach, Comparison moduli spaces of Riemann surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.09168): reviews comparison moduli spaces in geometric function theory and Teichmüller theory, with a list of open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces (Springer, 1981)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-5961-9) and [Farkas and Kra, Riemann Surfaces (Springer, 1992)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-2034-3); Farkas–Kra is one of the main sources of [Eynard's notes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.06405).

## Reference
### Overview
Generalized function theory, MSC2020 30Gxx within [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable), collects theories that keep the structure of holomorphic functions while changing the equation, the variable, the domain or the topology: non-Archimedean and nonstandard function theory, finely holomorphic functions, Bers–Vekua pseudoanalytic functions, discrete analytic functions, abstract-valued generalizations, and functions of hypercomplex variables. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Gxx))

The common thread is a replacement for the Cauchy–Riemann system of [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis). Pseudoanalytic theory replaces it by a first-order system with variable coefficients tied to equations of mathematical physics, preserving many features of analytic function theory. ([Kravchenko, *Applied Pseudoanalytic Function Theory*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-0346-0004-0)) In $\mathbb R^n$ the Dirac operator of Clifford analysis plays the role of $\partial_{\bar z}$, and its null solutions, the monogenic functions, carry a Cauchy integral formula. ([Wikipedia: Clifford analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_analysis)) On a lattice, discrete Cauchy–Riemann equations give preholomorphic functions, which Smirnov's ICM survey uses to prove conformal invariance in two-dimensional statistical physics. ([Smirnov, arXiv:1009.6077](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.6077))

### Scope
- **30G06:** non-Archimedean function theory (see also 12J25); nonstandard function theory (see also 03H05). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Gxx))
- **30G12:** finely holomorphic functions and topological function theory. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Gxx))
- **30G20:** generalizations of Bers and Vekua type (pseudoanalytic, $p$-analytic, etc.). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Gxx))
- **30G25:** discrete analytic functions. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Gxx))
- **30G30, 30G35:** other generalizations of analytic functions, including abstract-valued functions; functions of hypercomplex variables and generalized variables. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Gxx)) Slice regular quaternionic function theory is classified here (30G35). ([Colombo–Gentili–Sabadini–Struppa, arXiv:0905.1861](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0905.1861))

### Key concepts
- **Pseudoanalytic functions and the Vekua equation (30G20):** on a simply connected plane domain, a generating pair is a pair $F,G$ of complex functions with partial derivatives such that $\operatorname{Im}(\overline FG)>0$; every $W$ then has a unique representation $W=\phi F+\psi G$ with $\phi,\psi$ real. The $(F,G)$-derivative of $W$ exists iff $\phi_{\bar z}F+\psi_{\bar z}G=0$, equivalently iff $W$ solves the Vekua equation $W_{\bar z}=a_{(F,G)}W+b_{(F,G)}\overline W$ with characteristic coefficients determined by $F,G$; such $W$ are $(F,G)$-pseudoanalytic, and $(1,i)$ recovers ordinary analytic functions. The $(F,G)$-derivative of a pseudoanalytic function is pseudoanalytic for a successor pair, generally a different Vekua equation. ([Kravchenko, §2.1, Definition 1, Theorem 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611400)) Bers's formal powers generalize $(z-z_0)^n$, behaving like it only near the center, and under general conditions form a complete system of solutions. ([Kravchenko, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611400)) In Bers's real form, $f=u+iv$ is pseudoanalytic for an admissible $\sigma$ (for example $\sigma>0$ with Hölder-continuous partials) when $u_x=\sigma v_y$, $u_y=-\sigma v_x$. ([Wikipedia: Pseudoanalytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoanalytic_function))
- **Elliptic factorization:** Kravchenko factorizes $\operatorname{div}(p\nabla)+q$ with real $p,q$ by Vekua-type operators, reducing $(\operatorname{div}p\nabla+q)u=0$ to a homogeneous Vekua equation and constructing formal powers explicitly, which yields a complete system of exact solutions in a bounded domain. ([Kravchenko, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0611400))
- **Clifford analysis and monogenic functions (30G35):** with $e_1,\dots,e_n$ an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^n$ in the [Clifford algebra](node:Clifford%20Algebras) $Cl_n(\mathbb C)$, $e_j^2=-1$, the Dirac operator $D=\sum_je_j\partial_{x_j}$ satisfies $D^2=-\Delta_n$; solutions of $Df=0$ are (left) monogenic. The Cauchy kernel is $G(x)=\frac1{\omega_n}\frac{x}{\|x\|^n}$, $\omega_n$ the area of $S^{n-1}$, and the Cauchy integral formula is proved as in one variable using $x^{-1}=-x/\|x\|^2$. For $n=4$ the operator is the Cauchy–Riemann–Fueter operator. ([Wikipedia: Clifford analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_analysis)) Fueter's regular quaternionic functions satisfy a Liouville theorem: a regular function of bounded norm on $\mathbb E^4$ is constant. ([Wikipedia: Quaternionic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternionic_analysis))
- **Slice regular functions and the Fueter–Sce map (30G35):** a function $f$ on a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb H$ is slice (left) regular if for every imaginary unit $I$ ($I^2=-1$) its restriction to $L_I=\mathbb R+\mathbb RI$ has continuous partials and satisfies $\tfrac12(\partial_x+I\partial_y)f_I(x+yI)=0$. Unlike Cauchy–Fueter regular functions, this class contains polynomials and power series in $q$; axially symmetric domains play for it the role of domains of holomorphy. ([Colombo–Gentili–Sabadini–Struppa, Definition 2.1 and introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0905.1861)) The theory was introduced in 2006 and is surveyed in a Springer monograph. ([Gentili–Stoppato–Struppa](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-07531-5)) The Fueter–Sce theorem produces axially monogenic functions, in the kernel of a generalized Cauchy–Riemann operator on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, in two steps: the slice operator extends a holomorphic function of one complex variable to a slice monogenic function on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and a suitable power of the Laplacian in $n+1$ variables is then applied. ([De Martino–Diki–Guzmán Adán, arXiv:2305.06998](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06998))
- **Discrete analytic functions (30G25):** on the mesh-$\delta$ square lattice, a function is preholomorphic (Isaacs's second, rotation-symmetric definition) if $F(z+i\delta)-F(z+\delta)=i\big(F(z+\delta(1+i))-F(z)\big)$; restrictions of holomorphic functions satisfy this up to $O(\delta^3)$. Isaacs introduced such functions in 1941 and 1952, Ferrand named them preholomorphic and studied scaling limits, and Duffin and others followed; Smirnov and coauthors use them for the [Ising model](node:Ising%20Model) and self-avoiding walk. ([Smirnov, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.6077))
- **Finely holomorphic functions (30G12):** the fine topology on $\mathbb C$, introduced by H. Cartan as the weakest topology making all subharmonic functions continuous (see [Capacity and Fine Topology](node:Capacity%20and%20Fine%20Topology)), is locally connected (Fuglede). On a fine domain $D$, $f$ is finely holomorphic iff it is finely differentiable with finely continuous derivative; by Fuglede's theorem this is equivalent to each point having a fine neighbourhood on which $f$ is a uniform limit of rational functions, and to $f$ and $zf(z)$ both being finely harmonic. ([Fuglede–Groot–Wiegerinck, §1, Theorems 1.1 and 1.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.02498))

### History
Bers developed pseudoanalytic functions in *PNAS* notes from 1950 and 1951, a 1953 monograph and a 1956 *Bulletin of the AMS* outline. ([Wikipedia: Pseudoanalytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoanalytic_function)) Kravchenko names Bers and Vekua as the main founders and notes that Vekua's school calls these functions generalized analytic. ([Kravchenko, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611400)) Fueter's alternative theory of regular quaternionic functions began in the mid-1930s in *Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici*. ([Wikipedia: Quaternionic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternionic_analysis)) Gentili and Struppa introduced slice regularity in 2006 (*C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris*) and 2007 (*Adv. Math.* 216). ([Colombo–Gentili–Sabadini–Struppa, references](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0905.1861)) Brooks, Smith, Stone and Tutte used preholomorphic functions in 1940 to tile rectangles by squares, and Ferrand gave a discrete proof of the Riemann uniformization theorem. ([Smirnov, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.6077)) Finely holomorphic functions, introduced by Fuglede, are presented as the natural setting for Borel's ideas on monogenic functions. ([Fuglede–Groot–Wiegerinck, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.02498))

### Open problems
- **Discrete complex analysis beyond isoradial graphs.** Smirnov lists as an open question whether there is a discrete setup more general than isoradial graphs (rhombic lattices) with comparable estimates, in particular convergence of preholomorphic functions to holomorphic ones in the scaling limit; he also asks whether the "half-preholomorphic" parafermions found in other lattice models can be made fully preholomorphic. ([Smirnov, §6, Questions 1 and 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.6077))
- **Fine domains of existence.** Fuglede, Groot and Wiegerinck prove that fine domains that are both Euclidean $F_\sigma$ and $G_\delta$ are fine domains of existence for finely holomorphic functions, show that the $F_\sigma$ requirement cannot be dropped ($\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Q$ is not one), and ask whether every fine domain that is a Euclidean $F_\sigma$ is a fine domain of existence. ([Fuglede–Groot–Wiegerinck, Question 3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.02498))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Clifford analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_analysis): Dirac operator, monogenic functions, Cauchy kernel.
- **Learn:** [Kravchenko, Recent developments in applied pseudoanalytic function theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611400): free introduction to generating pairs, Vekua equations and formal powers.
- **Primary:** [Gentili–Stoppato–Struppa, *Regular Functions of a Quaternionic Variable*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-07531-5): Springer Monographs in Mathematics, 2nd ed. 2022; foundations of slice regularity.
- **Further reading:** [Kravchenko, *Applied Pseudoanalytic Function Theory*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-0346-0004-0): Birkhäuser, Frontiers in Mathematics, 2009.
- **Further reading:** [Smirnov, Discrete complex analysis and probability](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.6077): ICM 2010 survey of preholomorphic functions and conformal invariance.
references.MSC 30Hxx - Spaces and algebras of analy:
## Reference
### Overview
Section 30H of the MSC studies Banach and Hilbert spaces of holomorphic functions on the disc (or half-plane) and the algebras they form: bounded analytic functions, Hardy spaces, Nevanlinna and Smirnov spaces, Bergman and Fock spaces, Besov and $Q_p$ spaces, Bloch spaces and BMO-type spaces. ([MSC2020 30Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Hxx))

Hardy spaces measure boundary integral means, Bergman spaces impose area integrability, Dirichlet spaces control the energy of the derivative, and the Bloch space bounds $(1-|z|^2)|f'(z)|$. ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space); [Wikipedia: Dirichlet space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_space); [Wikipedia: Bloch space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch_space))

The area ties complex analysis to operator theory: shift-invariant subspaces of $H^2$ are classified by inner functions, and the maximal ideal space of $H^\infty$ is governed by the corona theorem. ([Wikipedia: Beurling's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beurling%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 30Hxx lists: 30H05 spaces of bounded analytic functions, 30H10 Hardy spaces (see also 42B30, 46E30), 30H15 Nevanlinna and Smirnov spaces, 30H20 Bergman and Fock spaces (see also 46E30, 46E35), 30H25 Besov and $Q_p$-spaces, 30H30 Bloch spaces, 30H35 BMO-spaces, 30H40 Zygmund spaces, 30H45 de Branges–Rovnyak spaces, 30H50 algebras of analytic functions, 30H80 corona theorems, 30H99 other. ([MSC2020 30Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Hxx))

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 30Cxx - Geometric function theory](node:MSC%2030Cxx%20-%20Geometric%20function%20theory) covers conformal maps and univalent and multivalent functions; [MSC 30Jxx - Function theory on the disc](node:MSC%2030Jxx%20-%20Function%20theory%20on%20the%20disc) covers inner functions, Blaschke products and singular inner functions; in [MSC 46Jxx - Commutative Banach algebras and commutative topological algebras](node:MSC%2046Jxx%20-%20Commutative%20Banach%20algebras%20and%20commutative%20topological%20algebras), 46J15 (Banach algebras of differentiable or analytic functions, $H^p$-spaces) cross-refers to 30H10. ([MSC2020 30Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Cxx); [MSC2020 30Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Jxx); [MSC2020 46Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Jxx))

### Key concepts
- [Hardy and Bergman Spaces](node:Hardy%20and%20Bergman%20Spaces): for $0<p<\infty$, $H^p(\mathbb D)$ is the set of holomorphic $f$ with bounded integral means $\sup_{r<1}\int|f(re^{it})|^p\,dt/2\pi$; $H^\infty$ is the bounded functions with the sup norm. ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space))
- Boundary values: for $p\ge1$ radial limits exist a.e., with $\|\tilde f\|_{L^p}=\|f\|_{H^p}$, and $H^p(\mathbb T)$ is the subspace of $L^p(\mathbb T)$ with vanishing negative Fourier coefficients. ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space))
- Inner-outer factorization: every nonzero $f\in H^2$ is $f=f_{\rm inn}f_{\rm out}$ with $f_{\rm inn}$ inner ($|f|=1$ a.e. on $\mathbb T$) and $f_{\rm out}$ outer (its shift-invariant span is all of $H^2$), and the factorization is unique up to a unimodular constant factor (Smirnov, 1928); in the canonical factorization $f=\lambda BS[f]$, $|\lambda|=1$, of $H^p$ functions ($p>0$) the inner part splits into a [Blaschke product](node:Blaschke%20Products) $B$ and a singular inner function $S$. ([Srivastava notes, Thms 4.5 and 5.32](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf))
- Bergman space $A^2$: reproducing kernel $k_z(\zeta)=1/(1-\bar z\zeta)^2$ on the disc (area measure normalized to total mass 1); a weighted $\ell^2$ space with weights $1/(n+1)$. ([Wikipedia: Bergman space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergman_space))
- Dirichlet space: $\|f\|^2=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)|a_n|^2$; $\mathcal D\cap H^\infty$ is a Banach algebra. ([Wikipedia: Dirichlet space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_space))
- Bloch space and BMOA: Bloch functions satisfy $\sup(1-|z|^2)|f'(z)|<\infty$; the analytic functions of bounded mean oscillation form BMOA, and $(H^1(\mathbb D))^*$ is identified with BMOA through an anti-linear pairing. ([Wikipedia: Bloch space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch_space); [Wikipedia: BMO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation))
- On the unit ball of $\mathbb C^n$ (the disc when $n=1$), weighted Bergman spaces with arbitrary real weight parameter give a unified scale containing Bergman, Besov, Lipschitz and Bloch spaces, with results on integral representations, complex interpolation, coefficient multipliers and Carleson measures. ([Zhao–Zhu](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0611093))

Key theorems:
- **Beurling's theorem.** If $E\ne\{0\}$ is a closed subspace of $H^2$ with $zE\subset E$, then $E=\Theta H^2$ for some inner $\Theta$ (Corollary 3.6 in the notes). ([Srivastava notes](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf); [Wikipedia: Beurling's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beurling%27s_theorem))
- **Carleson's corona theorem (1962).** $f_1,\dots,f_n\in H^\infty$ generate the unit ideal iff $|f_1|+\dots+|f_n|\ge\delta>0$ on $\mathbb D$; equivalently, the disc is dense in the maximal ideal space of $H^\infty$. ([Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem))
- **Fefferman duality (1971).** The dual of the Hardy space $H^1$ is BMO (Fefferman's original setting is the real-variable one: real BMO is dual to the real harmonic Hardy space on the upper half-space), via $(f,g)=\int fg$, an integral that need not converge absolutely and must be defined with care. ([Wikipedia: BMO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation))
- **John–Nirenberg.** For $f\in\mathrm{BMO}(\mathbb R^n)$ there are $c_1,c_2>0$ with $|\{x\in Q:|f-f_Q|>\lambda\}|\le c_1e^{-c_2\lambda/\|f\|_{BMO}}|Q|$ for every cube $Q$. ([Wikipedia: BMO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation))

### History
Riesz introduced Hardy spaces in 1923 and they were named for Hardy's 1915 work on integral means. ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space)) Kakutani conjectured the corona theorem in 1941 and Carleson proved it in 1962; Wolff gave a simplified proof in 1979 that was never published. ([Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem)) Beurling's invariant subspace theorem is credited to Beurling (1948) and Lax (1959). ([Wikipedia: Beurling's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beurling%27s_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Brown–Shields conjecture.** A function in the Dirichlet space $\mathcal D$ is cyclic iff it is outer and its boundary zero set has logarithmic capacity zero; Fricain and Lebreton (2024) state that it is still open despite significant progress. ([Fricain–Lebreton, arXiv:2403.04335](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.04335v1)) El-Fallah, Kellay and Ransford prove a special case. ([El-Fallah–Kellay–Ransford](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.4557)) A generalized conjecture for the spaces $\mathcal D(\mu)$ is proved for measures with countable support. ([El-Fallah–Elmadani–Kellay](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4977))
- **Corona problem beyond the disc.** Cole showed the theorem cannot be extended to all open [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces), and it is open whether it holds for every planar domain or for higher-dimensional domains. ([Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space): definitions, boundary values, factorization, duality.
- **Reference:** [Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem): statement, history, open cases.
- **Learn:** [Srivastava, Advanced Hardy Spaces (IIT Guwahati)](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf): course notes covering Beurling's theorem and inner-outer factorization.
- **Primary:** [Zhao–Zhu, Theory of Bergman Spaces in the Unit Ball of C^n](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0611093): 83-page unified treatment of weighted Bergman spaces covering Bergman, Besov, Lipschitz and Bloch spaces, $H^2$ and the Arveson space.
- **Primary:** [El-Fallah–Elmadani–Kellay, Cyclicity and invariant subspaces in Dirichlet spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4977): research paper on the generalized Brown–Shields conjecture.
- **Further reading:** Hedenmalm, Korenblum and Zhu, *Theory of Bergman Spaces* (Springer, 2000), and Duren and Schuster, *Bergman Spaces* (AMS, 2004), both listed in [Bergman space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergman_space).
references.MSC 30Jxx - Function theory on the disc:
## Reference
### Overview
Subfield 30Jxx is the theory of inner functions on the unit disc $\mathbb D$: bounded analytic functions $u$ with $|u(\zeta)|=1$ for almost every $\zeta$ on the unit circle $\mathbb T$. Its codes are inner functions (30J05), Blaschke products (30J10), and singular inner functions (30J15). ([MSC2020 30Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Jxx); [Garcia–Ross, Def. 2.6](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018))

Inner functions matter because they are the multiplicative building blocks of Hardy-space functions and because they parametrize the invariant subspaces of the shift operator. Every nonzero $f\in H^2$ factors uniquely as a Blaschke product times a singular inner function times an outer function, and Beurling's theorem identifies the nontrivial shift-invariant subspaces of $H^2$ as exactly $uH^2$ with $u$ inner. Inner functions originally arose in operator theory through Beurling's theorem. ([Garcia–Ross, Thms 2.16, 2.20](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018); [Chalendar–Gorkin–Partington, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1503.05461))

The complementary subspaces $K_u=(uH^2)^\perp$, the model spaces, carry compressed shifts and Toeplitz operators, so 30J sits at the junction of [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), and [MSC 47Axx - General theory of linear operators](node:MSC%2047Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20of%20linear%20operators). ([Garcia–Ross, §§1, 12](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018)) Boundary values on $\mathbb T$ link the subject with [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): the Hardy-space notes of Srivastava develop the theory through Fourier series, Poisson kernels and Fatou's theorem before canonical factorization. ([Srivastava, MA650 notes, contents](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 30Jxx lists 30J05 inner functions of one complex variable, 30J10 Blaschke products, 30J15 singular inner functions of one complex variable, and 30J99 other. ([MSC2020 30Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Jxx))

Neighbouring codes take the surrounding function spaces: Hardy spaces (30H10), Nevanlinna and Smirnov classes (30H15), BMO (30H35), de Branges–Rovnyak spaces (30H45), algebras of analytic functions (30H50), and corona theorems (30H80) belong to [MSC 30Hxx - Spaces and algebras of analytic functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Hxx%20-%20Spaces%20and%20algebras%20of%20analytic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable). ([MSC2020 30Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Hxx)) Moment problems and interpolation problems in the complex plane are classified under 30E05 in [MSC 30Exx - Miscellaneous topics of analysis in the complex plane](node:MSC%2030Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20of%20analysis%20in%20the%20complex%20plane). ([MSC2020 30Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Exx)) The parent field is [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable).

### Key concepts
- **Blaschke products (30J10).** For $a\ne0$ let $B(a,z)=\frac{|a|}{a}\frac{a-z}{1-\bar az}$ and $B(0,z)=z$. If $(a_n)\subset\mathbb D$ satisfies the Blaschke condition $\sum_n(1-|a_n|)<\infty$, then $B=\prod_nB(a_n,\cdot)$ is a bounded analytic function on $\mathbb D$ with exactly these zeros; conversely the zeros of every nonzero $f\in H^1$ satisfy the Blaschke condition. If $f$ is analytic on $\mathbb D$, continuous on $\overline{\mathbb D}$, and maps $\mathbb T$ into $\mathbb T$, then $f$ is a finite Blaschke product times a unimodular constant. ([Wikipedia: Blaschke product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blaschke_product))
- **Singular inner functions (30J15).** For a positive finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb T$ singular with respect to Lebesgue measure, $S_\mu(z)=\exp\!\big(-\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}\,d\mu(\zeta)\big)$ is inner and has no zeros in $\mathbb D$. ([Garcia–Ross, §2.4, eq. 2.10](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018); [Chalendar–Gorkin–Partington, §1.2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1503.05461))
- **Canonical (inner–outer) factorization.** Every $f\in H^2\setminus\{0\}$ has a unique factorization $f=BSF$ with $B$ a Blaschke product, $S$ a singular inner function and $F$ an outer function in $H^2$, and every such product lies in $H^2$. ([Garcia–Ross, Thm 2.16](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018)) More generally, for $0<p\le\infty$ every nonzero $f\in H^p$ is $f=Gh$ with $G$ outer and $h$ inner. ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space)) Smirnov's 1928 canonical factorization theorem is the version proved in Srivastava's notes (Thm 5.32). ([Srivastava, §5.10](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf))
- **Beurling's theorem.** A nontrivial closed subspace $\mathcal M\subset H^2$ satisfies $z\mathcal M\subset\mathcal M$ if and only if $\mathcal M=\theta H^2$ for some inner $\theta$; moreover $f$ is cyclic for the shift if and only if $f$ is outer. ([Chalendar–Gorkin–Partington, Cor. 1.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1503.05461); [Garcia–Ross, Thm 2.20](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018))
- **Frostman's theorem.** If $\theta$ is inner and $\alpha\in\mathbb D$, then $\theta_\alpha=(\theta-\alpha)/(1-\bar\alpha\theta)$ is inner, and it is a Blaschke product with distinct zeros for all $\alpha$ outside an exceptional set $E$ such that, for each $0<r<1$, $\{t: re^{it}\in E\}$ has measure zero; Frostman's stronger version makes $E$ of logarithmic capacity zero. ([Chalendar–Gorkin–Partington, Thm 3.2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1503.05461)) Consequently every inner function is a uniform limit of Blaschke products with simple zeros (Frostman, 1935). ([Srivastava, Thm 5.38](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf))
- **Interpolating Blaschke products.** A Blaschke product is interpolating if its zero sequence $(z_j)$ is an interpolating sequence for $H^\infty$; equivalently, $\inf_k\prod_{j\ne k}\left|\frac{z_j-z_k}{1-\bar z_kz_j}\right|>0$. ([Chalendar–Gorkin–Partington, §1.2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1503.05461)) Carleson's form in model spaces: for a Blaschke product $u$ with simple zeros $\lambda_i$, the normalized reproducing kernels form a Riesz basis of $K_u$ if and only if $\prod_{j\ne i}\left|\frac{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}{1-\bar\lambda_j\lambda_i}\right|>\delta$ for some $\delta>0$ and all $i$. ([Garcia–Ross, Thm 5.16](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018))
- **Douglas–Rudin theorem.** Quotients $\theta_1\overline{\theta_2}$ of inner functions are uniformly dense in the unimodular functions of $L^\infty(\mathbb T)$ (Douglas–Rudin, 1969); P. Jones showed the inner functions can be taken to be interpolating Blaschke products. ([Srivastava, Thm 5.37](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf); [Chalendar–Gorkin–Partington](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1503.05461))
- **Boundary behaviour of inner functions.** An inner function $u$ with zeros $\lambda_n$ and singular measure $\mu$, and all its divisors, has non-tangential limits of modulus one at $\zeta\in\mathbb T$ whenever $\sum_n\frac{1-|\lambda_n|}{|\zeta-\lambda_n|}+\int\frac{d\mu(\xi)}{|\xi-\zeta|}<\infty$. ([Garcia–Ross, §6.3](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018))

### History
Hardy introduced the spaces now named after him in a nine-page 1915 paper in the *Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society*. ([Srivastava, §1](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf)) Blaschke introduced his products in 1915, in a paper extending Vitali's theorem on sequences of analytic functions. ([Wikipedia: Blaschke product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blaschke_product)) Smirnov's canonical factorization dates from 1928 and Frostman's theorem from 1935. ([Srivastava, Thms 5.32, 5.38](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf)) Beurling's 1948 *Acta Mathematica* paper on two problems concerning linear transformations in Hilbert space is the reference behind the name "Beurling factorization" for the inner–outer factorization. ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space)) Garcia and Ross date a major breakthrough in model spaces to the 1970 paper of Douglas, Shapiro and Shields. ([Garcia–Ross, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018))

Standard monographs are Garnett's *Bounded Analytic Functions* (Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics, 2007) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/0-387-49763-3); [Srivastava, ref. 6](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf)) and Garcia, Mashreghi and Ross, *Introduction to Model Spaces and their Operators* (Cambridge University Press, 2016) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/cbo9781316258231)).

### Open problems
- **Approximation by interpolating Blaschke products.** Chalendar, Gorkin and Partington state that the question remains open whether every Blaschke product can be approximated uniformly on $\mathbb D$ by an interpolating Blaschke product; the best result they report is Hjelle and Nicolau's approximation in modulus. ([Chalendar–Gorkin–Partington, §1.2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1503.05461))
- **Model spaces and truncated Toeplitz operators.** Garcia and Ross describe clarifying the precise relationship between complex symmetric operators and truncated Toeplitz operators on model spaces as an ongoing effort. ([Garcia–Ross, §12](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Blaschke product (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blaschke_product): definition, Blaschke condition, finite Blaschke products.
- **Learn:** [Srivastava, Lecture notes on Hardy spaces (IIT Guwahati MA650)](https://fac.iitg.ac.in/rksri/MA650%20Advanced%20Hardy%20Spaces%20Notes.pdf): Beurling's theorem, canonical factorization, Frostman's theorem with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Garcia–Ross, Model spaces: a survey (arXiv:1312.5018)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.5018): inner functions, factorization, Beurling, Carleson's Riesz-basis theorem.
- **Primary:** [Chalendar–Gorkin–Partington, Inner functions and operator theory (arXiv:1503.05461)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1503.05461): survey of inner functions, Frostman, interpolating Blaschke products.
- **Further reading:** [Garnett, Bounded Analytic Functions (Springer GTM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/0-387-49763-3) and [Garcia–Mashreghi–Ross, Introduction to Model Spaces and their Operators (CUP 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/cbo9781316258231).
references.MSC 30Kxx - Universal holomorphic functi:
## Reference
### Overview
Subfield 30Kxx studies holomorphic functions and series whose iterates, translates, derivatives or partial sums approximate *every* function in a large class. Its codes are universal Taylor series (30K05), universal Dirichlet series (30K10), universal functions in general (30K15), and compositional universality (30K20). ([MSC2020 30Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Kxx))

The first instance is Birkhoff's 1929 theorem that translation $T_af(z)=f(z+a)$ on the space $H(\mathbb C)$ of entire functions (topology of locally uniform convergence) has a dense orbit for $a\ne0$: some entire function has translates approximating every entire function. MacLane (1952) proved the same for the differentiation operator. ([Aron–Bès, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9906199); [Shapiro, Notes on the dynamics of linear operators, §§1–2](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/shapiro/pubvit/Downloads/LinDynamics/lindynamics.pdf)) In operator language these functions are hypercyclic vectors: $x$ is hypercyclic for a continuous linear $T$ on $X$ if $\{T^nx\}$ is dense in $X$, which cannot happen in finite dimensions. ([Wikipedia: Hypercyclic operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercyclic_operator)) This ties 30K to linear dynamics in operator theory ([MSC 47Axx - General theory of linear operators](node:MSC%2047Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20of%20linear%20operators)).

The defining tools are Baire category and complex approximation. Mergelyan's theorem says that if $K\subset\mathbb C$ is compact with connected complement and $f$ is continuous on $K$ and holomorphic on its interior, then $f$ is a uniform limit of polynomials on $K$; universal Taylor series theorems are proved by combining it with a Baire argument, which also makes universality generic. ([Wikipedia: Mergelyan's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mergelyan%27s_theorem); [Tsirivas, §2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.01528)) The lack of comparable approximation theorems is what makes several-variable universal Taylor series hard. ([Daras–Nestoridis, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.4106))

### Scope
MSC2020 30Kxx: 30K05 universal Taylor series in one complex variable; 30K10 universal Dirichlet series in one complex variable; 30K15 universal functions of one complex variable; 30K20 compositional universality; 30K99 other. ([MSC2020 30Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Kxx))

Neighbours: ordinary convergence, boundary behaviour and over-convergence of power and Dirichlet series are [MSC 30Bxx - Series expansions of functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Bxx%20-%20Series%20expansions%20of%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable); approximation theorems such as Mergelyan's sit in approximation in the complex plane (30E10, [MSC 30Exx - Miscellaneous topics of analysis in the complex plane](node:MSC%2030Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20of%20analysis%20in%20the%20complex%20plane)). ([MSC2020 30Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Exx)) Universality of the [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function) belongs mainly to [MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory). The parent field is [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable).

### Key concepts
- **Birkhoff and MacLane universal entire functions (30K15).** For $b\ne0$ the translation operator $\tau_bf(z)=f(z+b)$ is hypercyclic on $H(\mathbb C)$ (Birkhoff, 1929), and so is differentiation $f\mapsto f'$: some entire function has a sequence of derivatives with every entire function as a limit point (MacLane, 1952). Godefroy and Shapiro (1991) unified both: if $\Phi$ is a non-constant entire function of exponential type on $\mathbb C^N$, then $\Phi(D)$ is hypercyclic on $H(\mathbb C^N)$. ([Aron–Bès, §1, Thm 1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9906199))
- **Birkhoff's transitivity theorem and the hypercyclicity criterion.** If $T$ is a continuous map of a complete separable metric space $X$ and for all nonempty open $U,V$ some $n\ge0$ gives $T^{-n}(U)\cap V\ne\emptyset$, then the points with dense orbit form a dense $G_\delta$. A sufficient condition (Kitai; Gethner–Shapiro): $T$ on an F-space is hypercyclic if $T^n\to0$ pointwise on a dense set and there is a map $S$ on a dense set $Z$ with $TS=I$ and $S^n\to0$ pointwise on $Z$. Rolewicz (1969): $\lambda B$ is hypercyclic on $\ell^p$ for every $|\lambda|>1$, $B$ the backward shift. ([Shapiro, Prop. 1.6, Thms 1.7, 2.1, 2.2](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/shapiro/pubvit/Downloads/LinDynamics/lindynamics.pdf))
- **Universal Taylor series in Nestoridis's sense (30K05).** For a simply connected proper subdomain $\Omega\subsetneq\mathbb C$ and $\xi\in\Omega$, $f\in H(\Omega)$ lies in $\mathcal U(\Omega,\xi)$ if for every compact $K\subset\mathbb C\setminus\Omega$ with connected complement and every $g$ continuous on $K$ and holomorphic on $K^\circ$, a subsequence of the partial sums $S_N(f,\xi)$ of the Taylor series at $\xi$ converges uniformly to $g$ on $K$. $\mathcal U(\Omega,\xi)$ is a dense $G_\delta$ in $H(\Omega)$ and does not depend on $\xi$ (Melas–Nestoridis; Müller–Vlachou–Yavrian). ([Gardiner, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1301.2082)) Nestoridis's 1996 paper proved the dense-$G_\delta$ statement on the disc, strengthening a result of Chui and Parnes. ([Crossref: Nestoridis, Ann. Inst. Fourier 46 (1996)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.5802/aif.1549))
- **Boundary behaviour and non-invariance.** Gardiner proved that universality of Taylor series is not conformally invariant: there is $f\in\mathcal U(S,0)$ on the strip $S=\{|\operatorname{Re}z|<1\}$ such that $f\circ F\notin\mathcal U(\mathbb D,F^{-1}(0))$ for every conformal $F:\mathbb D\to S$. He also showed that if $f\in\mathcal U(\mathbb D,0)$ then almost every point of the unit circle is a Plessner point of $f$, so the image under $f$ of every angular approach region at such a point is dense in $\mathbb C$. ([Gardiner, Thms 1–2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1301.2082))
- **Universal Dirichlet series (30K10).** Bayart established the existence of the first universal Dirichlet series (for compact sets he called admissible). Aron, Bayart, Gauthier, Maestre and Nestoridis removed that restriction: in the Fréchet space of Dirichlet series $\sum a_nn^{-s}$ absolutely convergent on $\operatorname{Re}s>0$, the series whose partial sums approximate every suitable function on every suitable compact set form a dense $G_\delta$ that contains a dense vector subspace apart from $0$. ([Aron–Bayart–Gauthier–Maestre–Nestoridis, Thm 3.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1608.06457))
- **Voronin universality.** If $U$ is a compact subset of the strip $1/2<\operatorname{Re}s<1$ with connected complement, and $f$ is continuous and zero-free on $U$ and holomorphic on its interior, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $t\ge0$ with $|\zeta(s+it)-f(s)|<\varepsilon$ on $U$, and the set of such $t$ has positive lower density (Voronin, 1975). Later work has focused on effective universality, which bounds the smallest such $t$. ([Wikipedia: Zeta function universality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_function_universality))

### History
Fekete showed before 1914 that a real power series can diverge "in the worst possible way". Seleznev (1951) produced a divergent power series with universal approximation properties in $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and Luh and Chui–Parnes (1970–1971) gave universal Taylor series with nonzero radius of convergence. Grosse-Erdmann (1987) showed that such universality is generic, so Baire's theorem simplifies the proofs. ([Daras–Nestoridis, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.4106)) Universal Taylor series on $[-1,1]$ are described as formal power series whose partial sums approximate every continuous function vanishing at $0$. ([Wikipedia: Universal Taylor series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Taylor_series))

Birkhoff's 1929 translation theorem was the first observed case of hypercyclicity for a linear operator, and Rolewicz gave the first Banach-space example in 1969. ([Shapiro, §1](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/shapiro/pubvit/Downloads/LinDynamics/lindynamics.pdf)) Grosse-Erdmann's survey "Universal families and hypercyclic operators" appeared in the *Bulletin of the AMS* in 1999 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/s0273-0979-99-00788-0)), and Grosse-Erdmann and Peris's *Linear Chaos* (Springer Universitext, 2011) is a textbook account ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4471-2170-1)).

### Open problems
- **Weighted universal Taylor series.** Tsirivas studies classes $\mathcal U(0,\mathbb D,K,(\beta_n))$ of $f\in H(\mathbb D)$ for which weighted partial sums $\beta_nS_n(f,0)$ are dense in $A(K)$, $K\subset\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb D$ compact with connected complement, and states that whether such classes are empty when the limit points of $|\beta_n|^{1/n}$ lie in certain explicit intervals remains open. ([Tsirivas, arXiv:1506.01528, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.01528))
- **Approximation by Dirichlet polynomials.** Aron et al. pose as Question 5.3 whether, for every compact $K$ with connected complement and every $f$ in their class $\tilde A(K)$, $f$ is a uniform limit on $K$, in the chordal metric, of Dirichlet polynomials; they prove this when $K$ is the closure of a Jordan domain (Thm 5.2) and state that it is open for general compact sets with connected complement. ([Aron–Bayart–Gauthier–Maestre–Nestoridis, §5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1608.06457))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hypercyclic operator (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercyclic_operator): definitions and early universal objects.
- **Reference:** [Zeta function universality (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_function_universality): Voronin's theorem.
- **Learn:** [Shapiro, Notes on the dynamics of linear operators (MSU)](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/shapiro/pubvit/Downloads/LinDynamics/lindynamics.pdf): lecture notes with Birkhoff's transitivity theorem, Birkhoff's and MacLane's theorems with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Gardiner, Universal Taylor series, conformal mappings and boundary behaviour (arXiv:1301.2082)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.2082): definitions, genericity, conformal non-invariance.
- **Primary:** [Aron–Bayart–Gauthier–Maestre–Nestoridis, Dirichlet approximation and universal Dirichlet series (arXiv:1608.06457)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1608.06457): universal Dirichlet series and open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Grosse-Erdmann, Universal families and hypercyclic operators (Bull. AMS 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/s0273-0979-99-00788-0) and [Grosse-Erdmann–Peris, Linear Chaos (Springer 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4471-2170-1).
references.MSC 30Lxx - Analysis on metric spaces:
## Reference
### Overview
Analysis on metric spaces, MSC2020 30Lxx within [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable), has three listed branches: geometric embeddings of metric spaces (30L05), quasiconformal mappings in metric spaces (30L10), and inequalities in metric spaces (30L15). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Lxx)) It develops first-order calculus on [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces) carrying a measure, where no smooth structure is assumed.

The theory replaces the derivative by an upper gradient, a purely metric notion, and the Sobolev space by the Newtonian space $N^{1,p}(X)$ of $p$-integrable functions with a $p$-integrable upper gradient; the upper gradient inequality serves as an abstract [fundamental theorem of calculus](node:Fundamental%20Theorem%20of%20Calculus). Its original motivation was the theory of quasiconformal and quasisymmetric mappings between metric spaces. ([Heinonen–Koskela–Shanmugalingam–Tyson, introduction and §14.1](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))

The central class is that of doubling metric measure spaces supporting a Poincaré inequality. Two landmark theorems describe them: Keith–Zhong self-improvement of the Poincaré inequality, and Cheeger's Rademacher-type differentiation theorem, which shows such spaces carry a rich infinitesimal linear structure. ([HKST, introduction](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))

### Scope
- **30L05 Geometric embeddings of metric spaces:** bi-Lipschitz and snowflake embeddings into Euclidean spaces, such as Assouad's theorem and the non-embeddability of the Heisenberg group. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Lxx); [Wikipedia: Doubling space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubling_space))
- **30L10 Quasiconformal mappings in metric spaces:** metric, analytic and geometric definitions of quasiconformality and their equivalence with quasisymmetry; see [Quasiconformal Maps of Metric Spaces](node:Quasiconformal%20Maps%20of%20Metric%20Spaces). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Lxx); [HKST, §14.1](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))
- **30L15 Inequalities in metric spaces:** Poincaré and Sobolev–Poincaré inequalities on metric measure spaces. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Lxx); [HKST, chapters 8–9](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))
- **Neighbours:** the MSC entry gives no cross-references. Heinonen–Koskela–Shanmugalingam–Tyson build the Sobolev theory on Lebesgue theory for Banach-space-valued functions, Lipschitz functions and embeddings, and the modulus of curve families, and also uses Gromov–Hausdorff convergence. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=30Lxx); [HKST, contents](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Lipschitz maps and extension:** $f:A\to\mathbb R^m$, $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, is $L$-Lipschitz if $|f(a)-f(b)|\le L|a-b|$, a purely metric condition. McShane–Whitney: every $L$-Lipschitz $f:A\to\mathbb R$ extends to an $L$-Lipschitz $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, for instance $F(x)=\inf_{a\in A}\big(f(a)+L|x-a|\big)$, the largest such extension. ([Heinonen, *Lectures on Lipschitz Analysis*, §1 and Theorem 2.3](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~shmuel/QuantCourse%20/Metric%20Space/Heinonen%2C%20Lecs%20on%20Lip%20Analysis.pdf))
- **Upper gradients and Newtonian Sobolev spaces:** a Borel $\rho\ge0$ is an upper gradient of $u:X\to Z$ if $d_Z(u(\gamma(a)),u(\gamma(b)))\le\int_\gamma\rho\,ds$ for every rectifiable curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to X$, and a $p$-weak upper gradient if this holds for $p$-almost every curve (outside a family of $p$-modulus zero). Shanmugalingam's thesis (1999) and paper (2000) built the space $N^{1,p}(X)$ on this notion, an extension of [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) to metric measure spaces, and it is a Banach space. ([HKST, §6.2, Chapter 7, introduction and bibliography](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))
- **Doubling measures and Poincaré inequalities (30L15):** $\mu$ is doubling if $0<\mu(B(x,2r))\le C\mu(B(x,r))<\infty$ for all $x\in X$, $r>0$. ([Wikipedia: Doubling space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubling_space)) $X$ supports a $p$-Poincaré inequality if balls have positive finite measure and there are $C>0$, $\lambda\ge1$ with $\fint_B|u-u_B|\,d\mu\le C\operatorname{diam}(B)\big(\fint_{\lambda B}\rho^p\,d\mu\big)^{1/p}$ for every ball $B$, every $u$ integrable on balls and every upper gradient $\rho$ of $u$. **Keith–Zhong theorem (2008):** if $X$ is complete, $\mu$ doubling and $X$ supports a $p$-Poincaré inequality for some $1<p<\infty$, then it supports a $q$-Poincaré inequality for some $1\le q<p$; the set of $p$ for which $X$ supports a $p$-Poincaré inequality is relatively open in $[1,\infty)$. ([HKST, Definition in §8.1 and Chapter 12](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))
- **Cheeger's differentiation theorem:** on a complete metric measure space with a doubling measure supporting a $p$-Poincaré inequality for some $p>1$, there is a countable family of measurable charts $U_\alpha$ covering $X$ up to a null set, each with at most $N$ coordinate Lipschitz functions $f^\alpha_1,\dots,f^\alpha_{N(\alpha)}$ ($N$ depending only on the data), such that every Lipschitz $u$ has for a.e. $x_0\in U_\alpha$ a unique vector $b^\alpha(u)(x_0)$ with $u(y)-u(x_0)-b^\alpha(u)(x_0)\cdot(f^\alpha(y)-f^\alpha(x_0))=o(d(x_0,y))$. This is the metric version of Rademacher's theorem (Cheeger 1999, *GAFA*); consequently $N^{1,p}(X)$ is reflexive for $p>1$. ([HKST, Chapter 13, Theorem 13.4.4 and Corollary 13.5.5](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))
- **Quasiconformal and quasisymmetric maps (30L10):** a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $f$ is $\eta$-quasisymmetric if $\frac{d(f(x),f(y))}{d(f(x),f(z))}\le\eta\big(\frac{d(x,y)}{d(x,z)}\big)$ for distinct $x,y,z$, and metrically $H$-quasiconformal if $\limsup_{r\to0}\frac{\sup_{d(x,y)\le r}d(f(x),f(y))}{\inf_{d(x,z)\ge r}d(f(x),f(z))}\le H$ at each point. **Heinonen–Koskela (1998):** a metrically quasiconformal map from an Ahlfors $Q$-regular space supporting a $Q$-Poincaré inequality onto a linearly locally connected Ahlfors $Q$-regular space, $Q>1$, is locally quasisymmetric; for maps between locally compact Ahlfors $Q$-regular spaces supporting a $Q$-Poincaré inequality, local quasisymmetry and the metric, analytic and geometric (modulus) definitions coincide. On Ahlfors $Q$-regular spaces the $Q$-Poincaré inequality is quantitatively equivalent to the Loewner condition on the modulus of curve families joining continua. ([HKST, Definitions 14.1.1–14.1.4 and §14.1](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))
- **Embeddings (30L05):** **Assouad's theorem:** if $(X,d)$ is doubling with constant $M$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$, the snowflake $(X,d^\varepsilon)$ admits an $L$-bi-Lipschitz map into $\mathbb R^N$ with $N,L$ depending only on $M,\varepsilon$. The Heisenberg group with its Carnot–Carathéodory metric is doubling but bi-Lipschitz embeds in no Euclidean space (Pansu). ([Wikipedia: Doubling space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubling_space)) Snowflaking destroys rectifiable curves, which limits Assouad's theorem in the upper-gradient theory. ([HKST, §4.5](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))
- **Conformal dimension and uniformization:** the Ahlfors regular conformal dimension of $X$ is the infimum of $Q$ such that $X$ is quasisymmetric to an Ahlfors $Q$-regular space. Bonk–Kleiner: if the Gromov boundary of a Gromov hyperbolic group, with a visual metric, is homeomorphic to $S^2$ and attains its Ahlfors regular conformal dimension, then it is quasisymmetric to $S^2$, a result toward Cannon's conjecture; it links the area to [Geometric Group Theory](node:Geometric%20Group%20Theory). ([HKST, §14.3 and Theorem 14.3.1](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))

### History
Fréchet addressed abstract spaces with metric properties in 1906, and Hausdorff coined the term metric space in 1914. ([Wikipedia: Metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space)) Assouad's embedding theorem appeared in 1983. Heinonen and Koskela's work on definitions of quasiconformality (1995) introduced spaces supporting a Poincaré inequality, and their 1998 *Acta Mathematica* paper developed quasiconformal maps in spaces with controlled geometry; Cheeger's differentiation theorem (1999), Shanmugalingam's Newtonian spaces (1999–2000) and Keith–Zhong (2008) followed. ([HKST, §14.1 and bibliography](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf)) Heinonen and Semmes's 1997 list of thirty-three yes-or-no questions helped direct the subject; David, Pankka and Tyson surveyed its status in 2025. ([David–Pankka–Tyson, arXiv:2510.19179](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19179))

### Open problems
- **Quasisymmetric characterization of spheres (Heinonen–Semmes Question 5).** If $(S^n,d)$, $n\ge2$, is linearly locally contractible, Ahlfors $n$-regular and quasisymmetrically three-point homogeneous, is it quasisymmetric to $S^n$? The survey records a yes for $n=2$: Bonk–Kleiner's theorem on the $n=2$ case of Question 3 (Theorem 2.5 there) already makes every linearly locally contractible Ahlfors 2-regular metric 2-sphere quasisymmetric to $S^2$, with no homogeneity assumption, and an earlier Bonk–Kleiner result covered the case where the homogeneity comes from uniformly quasi-Möbius homeomorphisms. The question remains open for $n\ge3$. ([David–Pankka–Tyson](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.19179))
- **Parametrizing chord-arc surfaces (Questions 6–7).** Whether smooth $n$-dimensional chord-arc surfaces with small constant in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ admit quasisymmetric parametrizations ($n\ge3$, Question 6) or bi-Lipschitz parametrizations ($n\ge2$, Question 7); the survey states both remain open, and notes Semmes's conjecture that both answers are no. ([David–Pankka–Tyson](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.19179))
- **Sierpiński carpet.** The standard carpet has the combinatorial Loewner property; whether it is quasisymmetric to a space with the classical Loewner property, or to one supporting a Poincaré inequality, is called a well-known open problem. The existence of Semmes curve pencils on sub-Riemannian spaces beyond the Heisenberg group is likewise called a challenging open problem. ([HKST, §§14.2–14.3](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf))

### Resources
