- **Reference:** [Doubling space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubling_space): doubling spaces and measures, Assouad embedding, Heisenberg group.
- **Learn:** [Heinonen, *Lectures on Lipschitz Analysis*](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~shmuel/QuantCourse%20/Metric%20Space/Heinonen%2C%20Lecs%20on%20Lip%20Analysis.pdf): Euclidean Lipschitz extension, Rademacher and Stepanov theorems, Whitney flat forms.
- **Primary:** [Heinonen–Koskela–Shanmugalingam–Tyson, *Sobolev Spaces on Metric Measure Spaces: An Approach Based on Upper Gradients*](https://homepages.uc.edu/~shanmun/book.pdf): monograph (author's draft); upper gradients, Poincaré inequalities, Keith–Zhong, Cheeger, quasiconformal maps.
- **Further reading:** [David–Pankka–Tyson, The Heinonen–Semmes problems after thirty years](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19179): status survey of the thirty-three questions.
references.MSC 31 - Potential theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Potential theory studies harmonic functions, the solutions of Laplace's equation, together with subharmonic functions, potentials of measures and boundary-value problems. Its name comes from nineteenth-century physics, where gravitational and electrostatic potentials satisfy Poisson's equation, or Laplace's equation in vacuum. The subject overlaps heavily with the theory of [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations). ([Wikipedia: Potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory))

Garnett and Marshall describe three classical methods for solving the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem) on an arbitrary plane domain. Wiener approximated the domain from inside and used energy to show that the limit harmonic measure is unique, which leads to capacity, equilibrium distributions and regular points. Perron took the upper envelope of subharmonic functions below the boundary data. Kakutani identified harmonic measure with the first-hitting distribution of Brownian motion. ([Garnett–Marshall, Harmonic Measure, Ch. III summary](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/harmonic-measure/potential-theory/C623B52A2EDB4891F79739A5D56736B2))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides field 31 into five subfields, with probabilistic potential theory sent to 60J45 ([MSC2020: 31-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31-XX)):
- [MSC 31Axx - Two-dimensional potential theory](node:MSC%2031Axx%20-%20Two-dimensional%20potential%20theory): harmonic and subharmonic functions, potentials and capacity, harmonic measure, extremal length, boundary behaviour and boundary-value problems in two dimensions. ([MSC2020: 31Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Axx))
- [MSC 31Bxx - Higher-dimensional potential theory](node:MSC%2031Bxx%20-%20Higher-dimensional%20potential%20theory): potentials and capacities, extremal length, boundary behaviour, boundary-value problems and polyharmonic functions in higher dimensions. ([MSC2020: 31Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Bxx))
- [MSC 31Cxx - Generalizations of potential theory](node:MSC%2031Cxx%20-%20Generalizations%20of%20potential%20theory): other spaces, pluriharmonic functions, Riemannian manifolds, discrete potential theory, Dirichlet forms, Martin boundary, fine potential theory and nonlinear potential theory. ([MSC2020: 31Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx))
- [MSC 31Dxx - Axiomatic potential theory](node:MSC%2031Dxx%20-%20Axiomatic%20potential%20theory): axiomatic potential theory (31D05); see [Harmonic Spaces](node:Harmonic%20Spaces). ([MSC2020: 31Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Dxx))
- [MSC 31Exx - Potential theory on fractals and metric spaces](node:MSC%2031Exx%20-%20Potential%20theory%20on%20fractals%20and%20metric%20spaces): potential theory on fractals and metric spaces (31E05). ([MSC2020: 31Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Exx))

Neighbouring fields:
- [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable) shares planar capacity; 31A15 cross-refers to 30C85. ([MSC2020: 31Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Axx))
- [MSC 60Jxx - Markov processes](node:MSC%2060Jxx%20-%20Markov%20processes) holds probabilistic potential theory (60J45), which cross-refers back to 31Cxx and 31D05. ([MSC2020: 60J45](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=60J45))

### Key concepts
- **Dirichlet problem.** For a bounded domain $D\subset\mathbb R^n$ and continuous $f$ on $\partial D$, one seeks $u$ continuous on $\overline D$, harmonic in $D$, with $u=f$ on $\partial D$; a solution, if it exists, is unique, by the [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle) applied to the difference of two solutions; uniqueness can fail on unbounded domains without a condition at infinity. ([Kuehn, Definition 3.1 and Theorem 3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.4689)) [Perron's Method](node:Perron's%20Method) produces the candidate solution.
- **Probabilistic solution and regular points.** For a bounded domain $U\subset\mathbb R^d$, with $\tau$ the first hitting time of $\partial U$, the function $u(x)=\mathbb E_x[\varphi(B_\tau)]$ is harmonic in $U$ and continuous at each boundary point regular for $U^c$. A solution exists iff $u$ is one, and if every boundary point is regular, $u$ is the unique solution. No regularity hypothesis is needed to define harmonic measure as the hitting distribution of $\partial U$ or for its harmonicity in $x$. ([Mörters–Peres, Theorem 8.5, Definition 3.38, Remark 3.40](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) See [Harmonic Measure](node:Harmonic%20Measure) and [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus).
- **Wiener's test.** For $d\ge3$, $x$ is regular for a closed set $\Lambda$ iff $\sum_k2^{k(d-2)}C_{d-2}\big(\Lambda\cap\{2^{-k-1}\le|y-x|\le2^{-k}\}\big)=\infty$. ([Mörters–Peres, Theorem 8.29](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) In the plane, for a compact set of positive capacity, irregular boundary points of the unbounded complementary component form a set of logarithmic capacity zero. ([Saff, Theorem 3.2 and Definition 3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760))
- **Capacity and polar sets.** A closed set is polar for $d$-dimensional Brownian motion iff it has zero capacity for the kernel $|x-y|^{2-d}$ ($d\ge3$) or $\log(1/|x-y|)$ ($d=2$) (Kakutani). Harmonic measure charges no polar set. ([Mörters–Peres, Theorem 8.19 and Notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) Fine-topology aspects are in [Capacity and Fine Topology](node:Capacity%20and%20Fine%20Topology).
- **Riesz decomposition and Frostman's theorem.** A superharmonic $f$ on a planar domain is locally a harmonic function plus the logarithmic potential of a positive measure. For compact $E$ with positive capacity, the equilibrium potential satisfies $U^{\mu_E}\le V_E$ everywhere and $=V_E$ quasi-everywhere on $E$. ([Saff, Theorems 1.12 and 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760)) See [Logarithmic Potentials](node:Logarithmic%20Potentials) and [Newtonian Potential Theory](node:Newtonian%20Potential%20Theory).
- **Green functions.** The Green function of a transient Brownian motion is the density of its expected occupation measure, $G(x,y)=\int_0^\infty p^*(t,x,y)\,dt$. ([Mörters–Peres, Definition 3.30](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) See [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions).

### History
The term dates from nineteenth-century gravitation and electrostatics. ([Wikipedia: Potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory)) Nevanlinna introduced the name harmonic measure for planar domains in 1928, and Kakutani linked it with Brownian motion in 1944. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_measure)) Frostman's thesis extended energy methods to Riesz potentials. ([Mörters–Peres, Notes to Chapter 8](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) Doob's account of the classical theory and its probabilistic counterpart was reissued in 2001 ([Crossref: Doob](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-56573-1)), the same year as Armitage–Gardiner's monograph ([Crossref: Armitage–Gardiner](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4471-0233-5)).

### Open problems
- **Dimension of harmonic measure in higher dimensions.** Jones–Wolff proved that harmonic measure in the plane has dimension at most 1. In $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge2$, Bourgain showed the sharp bound is below $n+1$, and finding its value is "an important open problem"; Jones conjectured $n+1-1/n$. ([Tolsa, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.07783))
- **Uniqueness of diffusions on self-similar fractals.** Uniqueness is proved for generalized Sierpinski carpets and nested fractals, but for p.c.f. self-similar sets "the general problem is still open". ([Barlow–Bass–Kumagai–Teplyaev, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.1802))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory): scope, symmetry, local behaviour, Harnack.
- **Reference:** [Harmonic measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_measure): definition and history.
- **Learn:** [Kuehn, Introduction to Potential Theory via Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.4689): free introductory notes. [Mörters–Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf): the probabilistic route through Kakutani's and Wiener's theorems.
- **Primary:** [Garnett–Marshall, Harmonic Measure, Ch. III](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/harmonic-measure/potential-theory/C623B52A2EDB4891F79739A5D56736B2): monograph chapter on the Dirichlet problem, capacity and Wiener series.
- **Primary:** [Saff, Logarithmic Potential Theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760): survey of the planar theory.
- **Further reading:** [Armitage–Gardiner, Classical Potential Theory (Springer, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4471-0233-5); [Doob, Classical Potential Theory and Its Probabilistic Counterpart (Springer, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-56573-1); [Ransford, Potential Theory in the Complex Plane (CUP, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511623776).
references.MSC 31Axx - Two-dimensional potential th:
## Reference
### Overview
Two-dimensional potential theory studies harmonic and subharmonic functions in plane domains together with logarithmic potentials, capacity and harmonic measure. In the plane every harmonic function is locally the real part of an analytic function, so the subject is tied closely to [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), while the conformal group in higher dimensions is only finite-dimensional. ([Wikipedia: Potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory))

Saff's review develops the logarithmic theory around three quantities attached to a compact set $E\subset\mathbb C$: the transfinite diameter, the logarithmic capacity and the Chebyshev constant. It proves their equality and uses equilibrium measures, Green functions and the Riesz decomposition to study polynomial approximation and the distribution of zeros. ([Saff, Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760)) The parent field is [MSC 31 - Potential theory](node:MSC%2031%20-%20Potential%20theory), and this map's planar objects reappear in [Logarithmic Potentials](node:Logarithmic%20Potentials), [Harmonic Measure](node:Harmonic%20Measure) and [Perron's Method](node:Perron's%20Method).

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 31Axx into: 31A05 harmonic, subharmonic and superharmonic functions in two dimensions; 31A10 integral representations, integral operators and integral-equation methods; 31A15 potentials and capacity, harmonic measure, extremal length and related notions (see also 30C85); 31A20 boundary behaviour (Fatou-type theorems); 31A25 boundary-value and inverse problems; 31A30 biharmonic and polyharmonic functions and Poisson's equation; 31A35 connections with differential equations; and 31A99. ([MSC2020: 31Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Axx))

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 31Bxx - Higher-dimensional potential theory](node:MSC%2031Bxx%20-%20Higher-dimensional%20potential%20theory) is the higher-dimensional counterpart, with a parallel list of topics ([MSC2020: 31Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Bxx)); 31A15 cross-refers to 30C85 in [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable); and potential theory on Riemannian manifolds, discrete potential theory and nonlinear generalizations are listed under [MSC 31Cxx - Generalizations of potential theory](node:MSC%2031Cxx%20-%20Generalizations%20of%20potential%20theory). ([MSC2020: 31Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Axx); [MSC2020: 31Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx))

For a positive unit Borel measure $\mu$ on a compact set, the logarithmic potential is $U^\mu(z)=\int\log\frac1{|z-t|}\,d\mu(t)$ and its energy is $I(\mu)=\iint\log\frac1{|z-t|}\,d\mu(t)\,d\mu(z)$. For compact $E$, $V_E=\inf\{I(\mu):\mu\text{ a probability measure on }E\}$ is the Robin constant and $\operatorname{cap}(E)=e^{-V_E}$; sets with $V_E=+\infty$ have capacity zero and are called polar, an arbitrary set is polar if every closed subset is, and a property holds quasi-everywhere (q.e.) if it fails only on a set of capacity zero. ([Saff, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760))

### Key concepts
- **Frostman's theorem.** If $E\subset\mathbb C$ is compact with $\operatorname{cap}(E)>0$ and $\mu_E$ is its equilibrium measure, then $U^{\mu_E}(z)\le V_E$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$, and $U^{\mu_E}(z)=V_E$ q.e. on $E$. For the closed disc $|z-a|\le r$ one has $\operatorname{cap}=r$ and $\mu_E$ is normalized arclength on the circle; for a segment $[a,b]$, $\operatorname{cap}=(b-a)/4$ and $\mu_E$ is the arcsine distribution. ([Saff, Examples 1.10–1.11 and Theorem 1.12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760))
- **Fundamental theorem (Fekete, Frostman, Szegő).** For every compact $E\subset\mathbb C$, $\operatorname{cap}(E)=\tau(E)=\operatorname{cheb}(E)$, where $\tau(E)=\lim_n\delta_n(E)$ with $\delta_n(E)=\max_{z_i\in E}\big(\prod_{i<j}|z_i-z_j|\big)^{2/n(n-1)}$ and $\operatorname{cheb}(E)=\lim_n t_n(E)^{1/n}$, $t_n(E)$ being the least sup-norm on $E$ of a monic polynomial of degree $n$. Fekete polynomials are asymptotically optimal: $\lim_n\|F_n\|_E^{1/n}=\operatorname{cap}(E)$. ([Saff, Theorem 1.18 and (1.1), (1.18)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760))
- **Riesz decomposition.** If $f$ is superharmonic in a domain $D$, there is a positive measure $\lambda$ on $D$ such that on every subdomain $D^*$ with $\overline{D^*}\subset D$, $f=h+\int_D\log\frac1{|z-t|}\,d\lambda(t)$ with $h$ harmonic in $D^*$; for smooth $f$, $d\lambda=-\frac1{2\pi}\Delta f\,dm_2$. A consequence is the unicity theorem: if $\mu,\nu$ are finite positive measures with compact support and $U^\mu=U^\nu+h$ a.e. on a region $D$ with $h$ harmonic there, then $\mu|_D=\nu|_D$. ([Saff, Theorems 2.4 and 2.10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760)) Subharmonic functions are the upper semicontinuous functions dominated by harmonic majorants on discs, and $\log|f|$ is subharmonic for holomorphic $f$. ([Wikipedia: Subharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subharmonic_function))
- **Green function with pole at infinity.** For compact $E$ with $\operatorname{cap}(E)>0$ and the unbounded component $\Omega$ of $\mathbb C\setminus E$, $g_\Omega(z,\infty)=V_E-U^{\mu_E}(z)$ is the unique function harmonic in $\Omega\setminus\{\infty\}$ and bounded outside each neighbourhood of $\infty$, with $g_\Omega(z,\infty)-\log|z|=O(1)$ at $\infty$ and boundary limit $0$ at q.e. point of $\partial\Omega$. Moreover $g_\Omega(z,\infty)-\log|z|\to\log\frac1{\operatorname{cap}(E)}$, and if $\Omega$ is simply connected, $g_\Omega=\log|\Phi|$ for the exterior Riemann map $\Phi(z)=z/\operatorname{cap}(E)+\dots$. ([Saff, Definition 3.4 and Theorem 3.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760)) This links capacity with the [Riemann Mapping Theorem](node:Riemann%20Mapping%20Theorem) and [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions).
- **Regularity and the Bernstein–Walsh lemma.** A point $z_0\in\partial_\infty E$ is regular when $U^{\mu_E}(z_0)=V_E$; irregular points form a set of capacity zero, and $g_\Omega(z,\infty)\to0$ at $\zeta$ exactly when $\zeta$ is regular. For any polynomial of degree $\le n$, $|p_n(z)|\le\|p_n\|_Ee^{ng_\Omega(z,\infty)}$ for $z\in\Omega$. ([Saff, Definition 3.3 and Lemma 3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760)) If every point of $\partial\Omega$ is regular, $\Omega$ is called regular with respect to the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem). ([Saff, Definition 3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760))
- **Harmonic measure and its dimension.** For a bounded domain, harmonic measure $\omega(x,D)$ represents the solution of the Dirichlet problem, $H_f(x)=\int f\,d\omega(x,D)$; Makarov showed that for simply connected planar domains it is singular to $t$-dimensional Hausdorff measure for $t>1$ and charges no set of $H^s$-measure zero for $s<1$. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_measure)) Jones and Wolff proved that in the plane the dimension of harmonic measure is at most 1. ([Tolsa, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.07783))

### History
The term potential theory dates from nineteenth-century gravitation and electrostatics. ([Wikipedia: Potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory)) Nevanlinna introduced the name harmonic measure for planar domains in 1928, and Kakutani linked it with Brownian motion in 1944. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_measure)) The equality of capacity, transfinite diameter and Chebyshev constant combines results of Fekete, Frostman and Szegő. ([Saff, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760)) Ransford's textbook on the planar theory was published by Cambridge University Press in 1995. ([Crossref: Ransford](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511623776))

### Open problems
- **Best constant in Hall's half-plane problem (Hayman's list, Problem 3.3).** For $u$ subharmonic and negative in the half-plane $|\theta|<\pi/2$ with $\inf_{|\theta|<\pi/2}u(re^{i\theta})\le-K$ for all $r$, Hall proved $u(r)\le-K/3$ on the positive axis and Hayman showed $-K/2$ fails; the best constant $\alpha$ with $u(r)<-\alpha K$ remains open. ([Hayman–Lingham, Research Problems in Function Theory, Problem 3.3](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1809.07200))
- **Sharpness of Maclane's condition (Problem 3.5).** For a positive subharmonic $u$ in the unit disc, bounded on arcs tending to an arc $\alpha\le\theta\le\beta$ of the circle, Maclane proved uniform boundedness on $\alpha+\delta\le\theta\le\beta-\delta$ under the radial condition (3.4) on a dense set of $\theta$ together with the growth condition $\int_0^1(1-r)B(r,u)\,dr<\infty$; Hornblower showed that the growth condition can be replaced by the much weaker $\int_0^1\log^+B(r)\,dr<\infty$, but it remains open whether (3.4) itself is sharp. ([Hayman–Lingham, Problem 3.5](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1809.07200))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Subharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subharmonic_function): definitions, Riesz representation, examples in the complex plane.
- **Learn:** [Kuehn, Introduction to Potential Theory via Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.4689): planar subharmonic functions, Riesz decomposition, Dirichlet problem, harmonic measure, Green function, capacity.
- **Primary:** [Saff, Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3760): survey with Frostman's theorem, the fundamental theorem and Green functions.
- **Primary:** [Hayman–Lingham, Research Problems in Function Theory](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1809.07200): problem list, Chapter 3 on subharmonic and harmonic functions.
- **Further reading:** [Ransford, Potential Theory in the Complex Plane (CUP, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511623776): standard graduate text on the planar theory; [Armitage–Gardiner, Classical Potential Theory (Springer, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4471-0233-5): Springer Monographs in Mathematics.
references.MSC 31Bxx - Higher-dimensional potential:
## Reference
### Overview
Higher-dimensional potential theory studies harmonic, subharmonic and superharmonic functions on domains in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$, together with Newtonian potentials, capacity, Green functions and boundary behaviour. Unlike the plane, where every harmonic function is the real part of an analytic function and the conformal group is infinite-dimensional, here the conformal group is finite-dimensional; conformal symmetry still explains classical techniques such as the Kelvin transform, and inequalities such as Harnack's inequality are basic tools. ([Wikipedia: Potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory))

A second route runs through Brownian motion: [harmonic measure](node:Harmonic%20Measure) is the first-hitting distribution of Brownian motion, polar sets are the sets it never hits, and regularity of a boundary point is the statement that Brownian motion started there leaves the domain immediately. Mörters and Peres develop the Dirichlet problem, Green kernels, capacity and Wiener's test in this language. ([Mörters–Peres, Brownian Motion, Chapters 3 and 8](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) The field map is [MSC 31 - Potential theory](node:MSC%2031%20-%20Potential%20theory); the classical entry points in this vault are [Newtonian Potential Theory](node:Newtonian%20Potential%20Theory), [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations) and [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem).

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 31Bxx into: 31B05 harmonic, subharmonic and superharmonic functions in higher dimensions; 31B10 integral representations, integral operators and integral-equation methods; 31B15 potentials and capacities, extremal length and related notions; 31B20 boundary-value and inverse problems for harmonic functions; 31B25 boundary behaviour of harmonic functions; 31B30 biharmonic and polyharmonic equations and functions; 31B35 connections with differential equations; and 31B99. ([MSC2020: 31Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Bxx))

Neighbouring codes: [MSC 31Axx - Two-dimensional potential theory](node:MSC%2031Axx%20-%20Two-dimensional%20potential%20theory) is the two-dimensional counterpart; [MSC 31Cxx - Generalizations of potential theory](node:MSC%2031Cxx%20-%20Generalizations%20of%20potential%20theory) lists potential theory on Riemannian manifolds (31C12), Dirichlet forms (31C25), Martin boundary theory (31C35), fine potential theory (31C40) and nonlinear potential theory (31C45). ([MSC2020: 31Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx)) The parent heading sends probabilistic potential theory to 60J45. ([MSC2020: 31Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Dirichlet problem and regular points.** A point $x\in A$ is regular for a closed set $A$ if Brownian motion started at $x$ hits $A$ at times arbitrarily close to $0$ almost surely. For a bounded domain $U$ and continuous $\varphi$ on $\partial U$, $u(x)=\mathbb E_x[\varphi(B(\tau))]$ is harmonic in $U$ and continuous at every boundary point regular for $U^c$; if all boundary points are regular, $u$ is the unique solution of the Dirichlet problem. The Poincaré cone condition at $x$ implies regularity. ([Mörters–Peres, Definition 8.1, Theorems 8.3 and 8.5](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) The harmonicity of $x\mapsto\mu_A(x,B)$ for the hitting distribution $\mu_A$ does not need any boundary condition. ([Mörters–Peres, Definition 3.38 and Remark 3.40](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf))
- **Wiener's test.** For $d\ge3$, with $\Lambda_x^k=\Lambda\cap\{y:2^{-k-1}\le|y-x|\le2^{-k}\}$, a point $x$ is regular for the closed set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ if and only if $\sum_{k\ge1}2^{k(d-2)}C_{d-2}(\Lambda_x^k)=\infty$, where $C_{d-2}$ is the Riesz $(d-2)$-capacity. ([Mörters–Peres, Theorem 8.29](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) Littman, Stampacchia and Weinberger showed that divergence-form uniformly elliptic operators with bounded measurable coefficients have the same regular points as the Laplacian. ([Lee–Lee, introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.00960)) See [Capacity and Fine Topology](node:Capacity%20and%20Fine%20Topology).
- **Polar sets (Kakutani).** A closed set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ is polar for Brownian motion if and only if it has zero capacity for the radial potential $f(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^{2-d}$ ($d\ge3$) or $|\log(1/\varepsilon)|$ ($d=2$). Nevanlinna proved that for $d\ge3$, $\mathbb R^d\setminus A$ carries non-constant bounded harmonic functions if and only if $A$ has positive Green capacity, and since in $d\ge3$ this Green kernel is the radial potential of Kakutani's theorem, such functions exist exactly when $A$ is not polar. Harmonic measure charges no polar set, so in $d\ge3$ it vanishes on Borel sets of dimension $<d-2$. ([Mörters–Peres, Theorem 8.19 and Notes to Chapter 8](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf))
- **Subharmonic functions, Riesz decomposition and Green functions.** An upper semicontinuous $\varphi:G\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$ on $G\subset\mathbb R^n$ is subharmonic if, for every closed ball in $G$ and every continuous $h$ on it that is harmonic inside and satisfies $h\ge\varphi$ on the boundary sphere, $\varphi\le h$ throughout the ball; a harmonic $v\ge u$ on $D$ is a harmonic majorant of $u$, and if one exists there is a least one. ([Wikipedia: Subharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subharmonic_function)) Riesz decomposition: on a bounded $C^2$ domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with Green function $G$ of the Laplacian, a nonnegative superharmonic $w$ can be written uniquely as $w=G(-\Delta w)+g$, where the distributional $-\Delta w$ is its Riesz measure and $g\ge0$ is its greatest harmonic minorant (Armitage–Gardiner, §4.4). ([Frazier–Verbitsky, §4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1509.09005)) Applied to $w=-u$, this writes a subharmonic $u\le0$ as its least harmonic majorant minus a Green potential. The Green function of a transient Brownian motion, $G(x,y)=\int_0^\infty p^*(t,x,y)\,dt$, is the density of its expected occupation measure. ([Mörters–Peres, Definition 3.30](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) See [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions).
- **Harnack inequality.** If $f\ge0$ is continuous on the closed ball $\overline B(x_0,R)\subset\mathbb R^n$ and harmonic inside, then for $|x-x_0|=r<R$, $\frac{1-r/R}{(1+r/R)^{n-1}}f(x_0)\le f(x)\le\frac{1+r/R}{(1-r/R)^{n-1}}f(x_0)$; on a bounded domain $\omega$ with $\overline\omega\subset\Omega$, $\sup_\omega u\le C\inf_\omega u$ for nonnegative harmonic $u$ on $\Omega$ with $C$ depending only on $\omega,\Omega$. Moser and Serrin extended it to elliptic and parabolic equations. ([Wikipedia: Harnack's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harnack%27s_inequality)) With the [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle) and Liouville's theorem it is used to prove convergence of families of harmonic functions. ([Wikipedia: Potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory))
- **Martin boundary.** Positive harmonic functions are integrals of Martin kernels $K_o(x,\gamma)$ against a measure supported on the minimal Martin boundary; for the unit disc this is the Poisson representation $f(z)=\int K(z,\xi)\,d\mu(\xi)$ with a unique $\mu$. ([Wikipedia: Martin boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_boundary)) Expansions on spheres use [Spherical Harmonics](node:Spherical%20Harmonics).

### History
Kakutani's 1944 papers introduced the probabilistic definition of harmonic measure and the polarity criterion, and Frostman's thesis extended energy methods to Riesz potentials. ([Mörters–Peres, Notes to Chapters 3 and 8](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) Nevanlinna, around 1920, characterized removable sets for bounded harmonic functions in $d\ge3$ by Green capacity. ([Mörters–Peres, Notes to Chapter 8](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)) Wiener's criterion was later extended to $p$-Laplacians, with sufficiency by Maz'ya and necessity for all $p>1$ by Kilpeläinen and Malý. ([Lee–Lee, introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.00960)) Doob's comparative treatment of the classical and probabilistic theories was reissued in 2001. ([Crossref: Doob](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-56573-1))

### Open problems
- **Dimension of harmonic measure.** In the plane harmonic measure has dimension at most 1 (Jones–Wolff); in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge2$, Bourgain proved the sharp upper bound is strictly below $n+1$, and "an important open problem consists of finding the sharp value". Jones conjectured the sharp bound $n+1-1/n$. ([Tolsa, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.07783)) Badger and Genschaw give explicit lower bounds on Bourgain's constant, e.g. $b_3\ge10^{-15}$ and $b_4\ge2\times10^{-26}$. ([Badger–Genschaw](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.15101))
- **Smooth escape paths (Hayman's list, Problem 3.2).** For non-constant harmonic $u$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$, Fuglede proved a path to infinity with $u\to+\infty$ exists; whether it can be taken smooth or polygonal is open. ([Hayman–Lingham, Problem 3.2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1809.07200))
- **Wiener criterion for fully nonlinear operators.** Lee and Lee prove necessity of their Wiener criterion for concave operators $F$ with $\alpha^*(F)<1$ (the analogue of $p>n-1$ for the $p$-Laplacian), and state that it is unknown whether the two conditions in their definition of a regular point are redundant. ([Lee–Lee](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.00960))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Harnack's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harnack%27s_inequality): ball and domain versions, extensions to elliptic equations.
- **Learn:** [Mörters–Peres, Brownian Motion (draft, Berkeley)](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf): Dirichlet problem, harmonic measure, polar sets, Kakutani's theorem and Wiener's test.
- **Primary:** [Tolsa, Mutual singularity of harmonic measure and Hausdorff measure](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.07783): research paper surveying the dimension of harmonic measure.
- **Primary:** [Lee–Lee, The Wiener criterion for fully nonlinear elliptic equations](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.00960): history of the Wiener criterion and its extensions.
- **Further reading:** [Armitage–Gardiner, Classical Potential Theory (Springer, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4471-0233-5); [Helms, Potential Theory (Springer Universitext, 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4471-6422-7); [Doob, Classical Potential Theory and Its Probabilistic Counterpart (Springer, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-56573-1).
references.MSC 31Cxx - Generalizations of potential:
## Reference
### Overview
Subfield 31Cxx collects potential theory outside the classical setting of the Laplacian on Euclidean domains: harmonic and subharmonic functions on other spaces, pluriharmonic and plurisubharmonic functions, potential theory on Riemannian manifolds, capacities on other spaces, discrete potential theory, Dirichlet forms, Martin boundary theory, fine potential theory, and nonlinear potential theory. ([MSC2020 31Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx))

Two broad kinds of generalization appear. The first is abstract and probabilistic: a Dirichlet form is a closed symmetric Markovian quadratic form on an $L^2$ space, generalizing the Dirichlet energy $\int|\nabla u|^2$, and Fukushima's theorem turns a regular Dirichlet form into a Markov process; the theory originated with Beurling and Deny. ([Wikipedia: Dirichlet form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_form); [Kassmann, arXiv:1412.7565](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1412.7565)) The second keeps the order structure of subharmonic functions but changes the operator: plurisubharmonic functions in several complex variables, the $p$-Laplacian, and the fully nonlinear "subequations" of Harvey and Lawson, in which subharmonicity is defined by a constraint set in the 2-jet bundle. ([DeMarco, Math 274 notes, §5](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~demarco/Math274/Math274_LectureNotes_draft.pdf); [Harvey–Payne, §§1–2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.14015))

Boundary theory and fine topology carry classical notions into these settings: the Martin boundary represents positive harmonic functions of random walks as boundary integrals, and the fine topology is the coarsest one making subharmonic functions continuous. ([Wikipedia: Martin boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_boundary); [Wikipedia: Fine topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_topology_%28potential_theory%29))

### Scope
MSC2020 31Cxx: 31C05 harmonic, subharmonic, superharmonic functions on other spaces; 31C10 pluriharmonic and plurisubharmonic functions (see also 32U05); 31C12 potential theory on Riemannian manifolds and other spaces (see also 53C20; Hodge theory is 58A14); 31C15 potentials and capacities on other spaces; 31C20 discrete potential theory; 31C25 Dirichlet forms; 31C35 Martin boundary theory (see also 60J50); 31C40 fine potential theory, fine properties of sets and functions; 31C45 other generalizations (nonlinear potential theory, etc.); 31C99 other. ([MSC2020 31Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx))

Neighbours within [MSC 31 - Potential theory](node:MSC%2031%20-%20Potential%20theory): two-dimensional and higher-dimensional classical theory are 31A and 31B, axiomatic potential theory is [MSC 31Dxx - Axiomatic potential theory](node:MSC%2031Dxx%20-%20Axiomatic%20potential%20theory), and 31E is [MSC 31Exx - Potential theory on fractals and metric spaces](node:MSC%2031Exx%20-%20Potential%20theory%20on%20fractals%20and%20metric%20spaces); probabilistic potential theory is 60J45. ([MSC2020 31-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31-XX)) Pluripotential theory proper is also [MSC 32Uxx - Pluripotential theory](node:MSC%2032Uxx%20-%20Pluripotential%20theory), as the 32U05 cross-reference indicates. ([MSC2020 31Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Dirichlet forms (31C25).** On a measure space $(X,\mu)$, a Dirichlet form is a symmetric bilinear form $\mathcal E$ on a dense subspace $D\subset L^2(\mu)$ with $\mathcal E(u,u)\ge0$, such that $D$ is a Hilbert space for $(u,v)_{L^2}+\mathcal E(u,v)$ (closedness) and the unit contraction $u^*=\min(\max(u,0),1)$ satisfies $u^*\in D$, $\mathcal E(u^*,u^*)\le\mathcal E(u,u)$ (Markov property). ([Wikipedia: Dirichlet form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_form)) It is regular if $C_c(X)\cap\mathcal F$ is dense in $\mathcal F$ for the $\mathcal E_1$-norm and dense in $C_c(X)$ for the sup norm; for $X$ a locally compact separable metric space, regular Dirichlet forms correspond to Hunt processes (Fukushima, 1971), the resolvent of the process being a quasi-continuous version of that of the form. The Beurling–Deny formula decomposes a closable symmetric Markovian form on $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ into a diffusion term $\int\partial_iu\,\partial_jv\,d\nu_{ij}$, a jump term $\iint(u(y)-u(x))(v(y)-v(x))\,J(dx,dy)$, and a killing term $\int uv\,d\kappa$. ([Kassmann, §§1–2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1412.7565)) This links 31C25 to [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains) and [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes).
- **Plurisubharmonic functions and Bedford–Taylor theory (31C10).** An upper semicontinuous $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$ on $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^N$ is plurisubharmonic if $\zeta\mapsto u(a+\zeta v)$ is subharmonic for all $a\in\Omega$, $v\in\mathbb C^N$; a set is pluripolar if it lies locally in $\{u=-\infty\}$ for such a $u$, e.g. $\{f=0\}$ for holomorphic $f\not\equiv0$. For locally bounded psh $u$ and a closed positive current $T$, $dd^cu\wedge T:=dd^c(uT)$ is closed and positive, which defines inductively the Monge–Ampère measure $(dd^cu)^N$; the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality bounds the local mass of $dd^cu_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dd^cu_m\wedge T$ by the product of the sup norms of the $u_j$ and the mass of $T$, and a strengthening, attributed in the notes to Bedford and Taylor, bounds the mass of $(-v)\,dd^cu_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dd^cu_m$ for psh $v\le0$ by $\|v\|_{L^1}$ times those sup norms. ([DeMarco, Math 274 notes, §§5, 8.2](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~demarco/Math274/Math274_LectureNotes_draft.pdf)) In several complex variables, plurisubharmonic functions are used to describe pseudoconvex domains, domains of holomorphy and Stein manifolds. ([Wikipedia: Plurisubharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurisubharmonic_function))
- **Martin boundary (31C35).** For a transient random walk with Green kernel $\mathcal G(x,y)=\sum_{n\ge1}p_n(x,y)$ and base point $o$, the Martin kernel is $\mathcal K_o(x,y)=\mathcal G(x,y)/\mathcal G(o,y)$; the embedding $y\mapsto\mathcal K_o(\cdot,y)$ has relatively compact image, and its closure adjoins the Martin boundary. Every positive harmonic function is $f(x)=\int\mathcal K_o(x,\gamma)\,d\nu(\gamma)$ for a measure on the boundary supported on the minimal Martin boundary, and with harmonic measure the Martin boundary is isomorphic to the Poisson boundary. ([Wikipedia: Martin boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_boundary))
- **Fine topology (31C40).** The fine topology on $\mathbb R^n$ is the coarsest topology making all subharmonic functions continuous; equivalently, a set is a fine neighbourhood of $\zeta$ when its complement is thin at $\zeta$. It is Hausdorff, Baire and locally connected but not locally compact, first countable or metrisable, and in $\mathbb R^n$ ($n\ge2$) its compact sets are finite. Cartan introduced it in 1940. ([Wikipedia: Fine topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_topology_%28potential_theory%29))
- **Discrete potential theory (31C20).** On a graph, $(\Delta\phi)(v)=\sum_{w\sim v}(\phi(v)-\phi(w))$, with weighted versions $\sum\gamma_{wv}(\phi(v)-\phi(w))$, and the closely related averaging operator $(M\phi)(v)=\frac1{\deg v}\sum_{w\sim v}\phi(w)$. ([Wikipedia: Discrete Laplace operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_Laplace_operator)) The Martin and Poisson boundary constructions are set up for random walks on discrete groups. ([Wikipedia: Martin boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_boundary))
- **Nonlinear potential theory (31C45).** For $1<p<\infty$, $\Delta_pu=\operatorname{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u)$; $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $\Delta_pu=0$ if $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0$ for all $\varphi\in C_0^\infty(\Omega)$, and the Dirichlet problem for $-\Delta_pu=f$ minimizes $\frac1p\int|\nabla u|^p-\int fu$; $p=2$ gives the Laplacian, while for $p>2$ solutions need not be twice differentiable. ([Wikipedia: p-Laplacian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-Laplacian)) See [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) and [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations).
- **Subequations (31C45).** Harvey–Lawson theory: a subequation is a closed set $F$ in the 2-jet bundle with positivity, negativity and topological stability; an upper semicontinuous $u$ is $F$-subharmonic if all its upper test jets lie in $F$ (a viscosity notion). The central question is the comparison principle, $u\le w$ on $\partial\Omega\Rightarrow u\le w$ on $\Omega$ for an $F$-subharmonic $u$ and an $F$-superharmonic $w$, which they obtain from monotonicity cones and fibre-regularity and which can fail without enough monotonicity. ([Harvey–Payne, §§1.3, 1.5, 2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.14015)) This frames fully nonlinear [Dirichlet problems](node:Dirichlet%20Problem) as potential theory.

### History
Beurling and Deny's 1958–1959 papers on Dirichlet spaces started the analytic theory of Dirichlet forms, and Fukushima's 1971 *Transactions AMS* paper gave the correspondence with strong Markov processes. ([Kassmann, §§1–2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1412.7565)) Oka and Lelong introduced plurisubharmonic functions in 1942. ([Wikipedia: Plurisubharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurisubharmonic_function)) Cartan introduced the fine topology in 1940, developing it through thinness in correspondence with Brelot. ([Wikipedia: Fine topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_topology_%28potential_theory%29)) Harvey and Lawson's three papers of 2009 began the subequation programme. ([Harvey–Payne, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.14015))

Standard monographs are Fukushima, Oshima and Takeda, *Dirichlet Forms and Symmetric Markov Processes* (De Gruyter, 2010) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9783110218091)) and Klimek, *Pluripotential Theory* (Oxford University Press, 1991) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198535683.001.0001)).

### Open problems
- **Comparison for the special Lagrangian potential equation.** Harvey and Payne state that for non-constant phases, comparison for the special Lagrangian potential equation is difficult and not completely settled. ([Harvey–Payne, §1.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.14015))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Dirichlet form (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_form): definition and classical references.
- **Reference:** [Martin boundary (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_boundary): Martin kernel and representation of positive harmonic functions.
- **Learn:** [DeMarco, Math 274 lecture notes (Harvard, 2023)](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~demarco/Math274/Math274_LectureNotes_draft.pdf): plurisubharmonic functions, currents, Bedford–Taylor Monge–Ampère measures.
- **Primary:** [Harvey–Payne, Interplay between nonlinear potential theory and fully nonlinear elliptic PDEs (arXiv:2203.14015)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.14015): survey of subequations and comparison.
- **Primary:** [Kassmann, On Dirichlet forms and semi-Dirichlet forms (arXiv:1412.7565)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7565): overview of Dirichlet form theory and its history.
- **Further reading:** [Fukushima–Oshima–Takeda, Dirichlet Forms and Symmetric Markov Processes](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9783110218091) and [Klimek, Pluripotential Theory](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198535683.001.0001).
references.MSC 31Dxx - Axiomatic potential theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Axiomatic potential theory starts from a sheaf of "harmonic" functions on a locally compact space, or from a cone of "superharmonic" functions, and derives regular sets (a local Dirichlet problem), superharmonic functions, potentials and the Riesz decomposition from a short list of axioms. One framework then covers the Laplacian, Schrödinger operators $\Delta-\mu$, hypoelliptic operators and the heat operator. ([Grigor'yan–Hansen, §7.1](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~grigor/liouv.pdf))

The axioms are designed so that potential-theoretic objects match those of Markov processes: in a balayage space with $1\in\mathcal W$ (which can be arranged by an $s$-transform) the cone of positive hyperharmonic functions is the cone of excessive functions of a Hunt process, and harmonic kernels are exit distributions. ([Bogdan–Hansen, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.13999)) The parent map is [MSC 31 - Potential theory](node:MSC%2031%20-%20Potential%20theory); the vault concept note is [Harmonic Spaces](node:Harmonic%20Spaces), and the probabilistic side is in [MSC 60Jxx - Markov processes](node:MSC%2060Jxx%20-%20Markov%20processes).

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 31D05 (axiomatic potential theory) and 31D99 under 31Dxx; the field heading points probabilistic potential theory to 60J45, whose entry in turn cross-refers to 31Cxx and 31D05. ([MSC2020: 31Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Dxx); [MSC2020: 60J45](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=60J45)) [MSC 31Cxx - Generalizations of potential theory](node:MSC%2031Cxx%20-%20Generalizations%20of%20potential%20theory) holds concrete non-Euclidean settings, Dirichlet forms (31C25), Martin boundary theory (31C35) and fine potential theory (31C40); 31D05 itself is titled axiomatic potential theory. ([MSC2020: 31Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Harmonic sheaf and regular sets.** On a locally compact space $X$ with countable base, a harmonic sheaf assigns to each open $U$ a linear subspace $\mathcal H(U)\subset C(U)$ that is stable under restriction and can be glued from local pieces. A relatively compact open $V$ is regular if every $f\in C(\partial V)$ has a unique continuous extension $H_Vf$ to $\overline V$, harmonic on $V$, with $H_Vf\ge0$ when $f\ge0$. ([Grigor'yan–Hansen, §7.1](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~grigor/liouv.pdf)) This abstracts the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem) on balls.
- **Bauer spaces and the three convergence axioms.** $(X,\mathcal H)$ is a Bauer space if (B1) each point has a local harmonic function not vanishing there, (B2) each point has a base of regular sets closed under intersection, and (B3) the supremum of an increasing sequence of positive harmonic functions is harmonic when it is locally bounded. Doob's axiom requires harmonicity whenever the supremum is finite on a dense set; Brelot's, on a domain, whenever it is not identically $\infty$. In the elliptic examples Brelot's axiom holds, and in the parabolic (heat-type) examples Doob's axiom holds. ([Grigor'yan–Hansen, §7.1](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~grigor/liouv.pdf))
- **Riesz decomposition and P-harmonic spaces.** A lower semicontinuous $s$ is hyperharmonic if $H_Vs\le s$ for all regular $V$, and a potential is a nonnegative superharmonic function whose largest harmonic minorant is $0$. Every $s\in\mathcal S^+(U)$ decomposes uniquely as $s=h+p$ with $h$ harmonic and $p$ a potential; $(X,\mathcal H)$ is P-harmonic if $X$ carries a strictly positive potential. ([Grigor'yan–Hansen, §7.1](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~grigor/liouv.pdf))
- **Hypoelliptic examples.** For $L=\tfrac12\sum_{k=1}^rA_k^2+A_0$ with smooth vector fields $A_k$ on open $X\subset\mathbb R^d$, the sheaf $\{h\in C^\infty(U):Lh=0\}$ is a Bauer space whenever the Lie algebra generated by $A_0,\dots,A_r$ spans $\mathbb R^d$ at each point (via Hörmander's theorem). In fact Doob's axiom holds, and if the spanning condition holds already without $A_0$, Brelot's axiom holds. ([Grigor'yan–Hansen, (7.1)–(7.2)](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~grigor/liouv.pdf)) See [Hypoelliptic Operators](node:Hypoelliptic%20Operators) and [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation).
- **Balayage spaces.** A convex cone $\mathcal W$ of positive numerical functions on $X$ forms a balayage space $(X,\mathcal W)$ if it has continuity (C), linear separation (S) and transience (T), is closed under increasing limits, is closed under finely regularized infima, and has the Riesz decomposition property $u\le v'+v''\Rightarrow u=u'+u''$ with $u'\le v'$, $u''\le v''$. For a P-harmonic space, the positive hyperharmonic functions form a balayage space. Isotropic $\alpha$-stable Lévy processes with $0<\alpha<2\wedge d$ also give balayage spaces, so jump processes are included. ([Bogdan–Hansen, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.13999))
- **Hunt-process correspondence.** If $(X,\mathcal W)$ is a balayage space with $1\in\mathcal W$ and $p$ is a bounded strict continuous potential, there is a Hunt process on $X$ whose excessive functions are exactly $\mathcal W$, whose potential kernel is $K_p$, and whose exit distributions give harmonic measures: $H_Vf(x)=\mathbb E^x(f\circ X_{\tau_V})$. Conversely, the excessive functions of a sub-Markov semigroup form a balayage space exactly when they satisfy (C), (S) and (T). ([Bogdan–Hansen, Theorems 3.2 and 3.9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.13999))
- **H-cones.** Grigor'yan and Hansen note that their results for harmonic spaces could even be done for balayage spaces or H-cones. ([Grigor'yan–Hansen, §7.1](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~grigor/liouv.pdf)) The H-cone volume *Order and Convexity in Potential Theory: H-Cones* (Lecture Notes in Mathematics, 1981) includes Boboc, Bucur, Cornea and Höllein's chapter on Markov processes associated with a standard H-cone of functions. ([Crossref: Boboc–Bucur–Cornea–Höllein](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0090455))

### History
Henri Cartan introduced the fine topology in 1940, and later noted to Marcel Brelot that the theory could be built from thinness. ([Wikipedia: Fine topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_topology_%28potential_theory%29)) Bauer's lecture notes on harmonic spaces appeared in Springer's Lecture Notes in Mathematics in 1966. ([Crossref: Bauer 1966](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0075360)) Constantinescu and Cornea's monograph on potential theory on harmonic spaces was published in 1972. ([Crossref: Constantinescu–Cornea](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-65432-9)) The H-cone theory appeared in Lecture Notes in Mathematics in 1981. ([Crossref: H-cones](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0090455)) Bliedtner and Hansen's 1986 Universitext presents balayage spaces analytically and probabilistically. ([Crossref: Bliedtner–Hansen](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-71131-2))

### Open problems
None found as a named open problem stated in a fetched source. Searches tried: "balayage spaces" or "harmonic spaces" with "open problem" or "open question" (Hansen, Netuka); "axiomatic potential theory harmonic spaces unsolved problem remains open"; and reading Hansen–Netuka's unavoidable-sets paper and Bogdan–Hansen for stated open questions. An active direction is to run classical results in balayage spaces so they apply to jump processes at once: Hansen proves a Liouville property and a Wiener test at infinity for unavoidable sets of Hunt processes with Green function $G\approx g\circ\rho$ ([Hansen 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.7532)), and Bogdan–Hansen solve semilinear problems $Lu=\varphi(\cdot,u)\mu$ in balayage spaces ([Bogdan–Hansen, arXiv 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13999)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fine topology (potential theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_topology_%28potential_theory%29): thinness, fine topology, Cartan and Brelot.
- **Learn:** [Grigor'yan–Hansen, §7 "Results for harmonic spaces"](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~grigor/liouv.pdf): short English exposition of Bauer spaces, the convergence axioms and examples. [Bauer, Harmonic Spaces and Associated Markov Processes](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-11084-9_2): English chapter in the Springer volume *Potential Theory* (2010) linking harmonic spaces and Markov processes.
- **Primary:** [Bogdan–Hansen, Positive harmonically bounded solutions for semi-linear equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13999): §3 gives the balayage-space axioms and the Hunt-process correspondence.
- **Further reading:** [Constantinescu–Cornea, Potential Theory on Harmonic Spaces (Springer, 1972)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-65432-9); [Bliedtner–Hansen, Potential Theory: An Analytic and Probabilistic Approach to Balayage (Springer, 1986)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-71131-2); [Bauer, Harmonische Räume und ihre Potentialtheorie (LNM, 1966)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BFb0075360).
references.MSC 31Exx - Potential theory on fractals:
## Reference
### Overview
Potential theory on fractals and metric spaces builds Laplacians, harmonic functions, energies and heat kernels on spaces that have no smooth structure, such as the Sierpinski gasket and carpet. Analysis on fractals begins by defining a Laplacian, and there are probabilistic, analytic and measure-theoretic approaches to doing so. ([Wikipedia: Analysis on fractals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_on_fractals)) The probabilistic route constructs a Brownian motion as a limit of random walks on graph approximations and defines the Laplacian as its generator. The analytic route, due to Kigami and to Fukushima–Shima, builds the energy (a Dirichlet form) directly. ([Barlow–Bass–Kumagai–Teplyaev, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.1802))

What separates these spaces from Euclidean space is anomalous diffusion. In regular cases $\mathbb E|X_t-X_0|\approx t^{1/d_w}$ with walk dimension $d_w>2$. As a result, energy measure and Hausdorff measure are mutually singular, the domain of the Laplacian is not an algebra, and distance functions are not in the domain of the Dirichlet form. ([BBKT, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.1802)) The parent map is [MSC 31 - Potential theory](node:MSC%2031%20-%20Potential%20theory), and the concept note is [Dirichlet Forms on Fractals](node:Dirichlet%20Forms%20on%20Fractals).

### Scope
MSC2020 lists only 31E05 (potential theory on fractals and metric spaces) and 31E99. ([MSC2020: 31Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Exx)) Neighbouring codes:
- [MSC 31Cxx - Generalizations of potential theory](node:MSC%2031Cxx%20-%20Generalizations%20of%20potential%20theory) contains Dirichlet forms in general (31C25), discrete potential theory (31C20) and nonlinear potential theory (31C45). ([MSC2020: 31Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx))
- [MSC 30Lxx - Analysis on metric spaces](node:MSC%2030Lxx%20-%20Analysis%20on%20metric%20spaces) covers geometric embeddings, quasiconformal mappings and inequalities in [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces). ([MSC2020: 30Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Lxx)) Kajino–Murugan's conformal walk dimension is defined through quasisymmetric changes of metric; see [Quasiconformal Maps of Metric Spaces](node:Quasiconformal%20Maps%20of%20Metric%20Spaces). ([Kajino–Murugan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.12836))

### Key concepts
- **Kigami's Laplacian on the Sierpinski gasket.** Let $V_n$ be the level-$n$ vertices and $E_n(f)=\sum_{x\sim y}(f(x)-f(y))^2$. Then $\tfrac53E_{n+1}(f)\ge E_n(f)$, with equality for harmonic functions. The energy $\mathcal E(f)=\lim_n(\tfrac53)^nE_n(f)$ is a local regular self-similar Dirichlet form with $\mathcal E(f)=\tfrac53\sum_{j=1}^3\mathcal E(f\circ F_j)$. The Laplacian is $\Delta_\mu f(x)=\lim_n5^n\Delta_nf(x)$ for the discrete Laplacians $\Delta_nf(x)=\tfrac14\sum_{y\sim x}(f(y)-f(x))$, whenever this limit exists and is continuous. ([Teplyaev, Gregynog lectures, pp. 37–38](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~teplyaev/gregynog/AT.pdf)) Kigami published this explicit analytic construction in 1989. ([Princeton University Press: Strichartz](https://press.princeton.edu/isbn/9780691127316))
- **Resistance forms.** A resistance form $(\mathcal E,\mathcal F)$ on a set $X$ satisfies (RF1)–(RF5): a nonnegative symmetric form vanishing exactly on constants, a Hilbert space modulo constants, separation of points, finiteness of $R(x,y)=\sup\{|u(x)-u(y)|^2/\mathcal E(u,u):\mathcal E(u,u)>0\}$, and the Markov property. Then $R$ is a metric and $|u(x)-u(y)|^2\le R(x,y)\,\mathcal E(u,u)$. ([Kigami, Definition 1.1 and Theorem 1.2](https://www-an.acs.i.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~kigami/vdrflecture.pdf)) Compatible forms on increasing finite sets $V_n$, each the trace of the next, define a resistance form on $\bigcup_nV_n$ as a nondecreasing limit. ([Teplyaev, Theorems of Kigami, p. 67](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~teplyaev/gregynog/AT.pdf))
- **Sub-Gaussian heat kernel estimates.** For Brownian motion on the Sierpinski gasket (Barlow–Perkins) and carpet (Barlow–Bass), the heat kernel satisfies $p(t,x,y)\asymp c_1t^{-\alpha/\beta}\exp\!\big(-c_2(d(x,y)^\beta/t)^{1/(\beta-1)}\big)$. Here $\alpha$ is the Hausdorff dimension and $\beta>2$ is the walk dimension. ([Kigami, introduction](https://www-an.acs.i.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~kigami/vdrflecture.pdf)) Under volume doubling, the elliptic Harnack inequality and a resistance estimate are equivalent to two-sided estimates of this type (Grigor'yan–Telcs). ([BBKT, Theorem 4.29](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.1802)) Compare the Gaussian case for the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation).
- **Uniqueness of Brownian motion on Sierpinski carpets.** On a generalized Sierpinski carpet $F\subset\mathbb R^d$, the local regular conservative Dirichlet forms invariant under all local symmetries form a set that is nonempty and, up to scalar multiples, has exactly one element, which is scale invariant. So the Barlow–Bass and Kusuoka–Zhou constructions give the same process, and the Laplacian is unique up to a constant. ([BBKT, Proposition 1.1, Theorem 1.2, Corollaries 1.3–1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.1802))
- **Spectral dimension.** For a p.c.f. self-similar set with weights $r_i$ and measure weights $\mu_i$, the spectral dimension $d_s$ of $\Delta_\mu$ is the unique solution of $\sum_{i=1}^k(r_i\mu_i)^{d_s/2}=1$ (Kigami–Lapidus). ([Teplyaev, p. 43](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~teplyaev/gregynog/AT.pdf))
- **Conformal walk dimension.** Kajino and Murugan define $d_{cw}$ as the infimum of walk dimensions over time changes and quasisymmetric changes of metric under which the parabolic Harnack inequality holds. They prove $d_{cw}<\infty$ iff metric doubling and the elliptic Harnack inequality hold, and then $d_{cw}=2$. The infimum is attained for the 2-dimensional Sierpinski gasket but not for the Vicsek set or for $N$-dimensional gaskets with $N\ge3$. ([Kajino–Murugan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.12836))

### History
Brownian motion on the gasket was first constructed probabilistically. Kigami and Fukushima–Shima then introduced analytic approaches, Barlow and Bass constructed Brownian motion on the carpet, and uniqueness for nested fractals was later proved by Sabot. ([BBKT, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.1802)) Kigami's *Analysis on Fractals* was published by Cambridge University Press in 2001 ([Crossref: Kigami](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511470943)), and Strichartz's tutorial appeared in 2006 ([Princeton University Press](https://press.princeton.edu/isbn/9780691127316)).

### Open problems
- **Uniqueness on p.c.f. self-similar sets.** Some sufficient conditions are known, but "the general problem is still open". ([BBKT, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.1802)) Teplyaev states as a conjecture that every p.c.f. fractal carries a self-similar local regular Dirichlet form giving positive capacity to boundary points. ([Teplyaev, Gregynog lectures, p. 44](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~teplyaev/gregynog/AT.pdf))
- **Energy measures of harmonic functions on carpets.** Kajino–Murugan list as open problems whether some non-constant harmonic function on a generalized Sierpinski carpet has an energy measure with volume doubling with respect to the Euclidean metric (Problem 7.5) or even with full support (Problem 7.6). They call it tempting to conjecture that every such energy measure has full support, a unique-continuation principle for harmonic functions on the carpet. They also ask for simple sufficient conditions for non-attainment of $d_{cw}$ on p.c.f. self-similar sets with a regular harmonic structure (Problem 7.3). ([Kajino–Murugan, §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.12836))
- **Attainment of Ahlfors regular conformal dimension of the carpet.** Kajino–Murugan call the attainment problem for the standard Sierpinski carpet a well-known open question. Bonk and Kleiner showed that Cannon's conjecture (a Gromov-hyperbolic group with 2-sphere boundary is Kleinian) is equivalent to attainment of the Ahlfors regular conformal dimension of the group's boundary. ([Kajino–Murugan, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.12836))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Analysis on fractals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_on_fractals): scope and approaches to fractal Laplacians.
- **Learn:** [Teplyaev, An Introduction to Analysis on Fractals (Gregynog, 2007)](https://www2.math.uconn.edu/~teplyaev/gregynog/AT.pdf): gasket energies, Laplacians, resistance forms, spectral dimension.
- **Primary:** [Barlow–Bass–Kumagai–Teplyaev, Brownian motion on the Sierpinski carpet (JEMS 2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.1802): uniqueness of Brownian motion and the Laplacian on generalized Sierpinski carpets.
- **Primary:** [Kajino–Murugan, On the conformal walk dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.12836): quasisymmetric uniformization and a list of open problems.
- **Primary:** [Kigami, Resistance forms, quasisymmetric maps and heat kernel estimates](https://www-an.acs.i.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~kigami/vdrflecture.pdf): lecture notes with precise axioms.
- **Further reading:** [Kigami, Analysis on Fractals (CUP, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511470943); [Strichartz, Differential Equations on Fractals (Princeton, 2006)](https://press.princeton.edu/isbn/9780691127316).
references.MSC 32 - Several complex variables and a:
## Reference
### Overview
Several complex variables studies holomorphic functions on open subsets of $\mathbb C^n$ and on complex manifolds and analytic spaces. For $n\ge2$ the theory departs sharply from [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) in one variable: by Hartogs's extension theorem (1906) a holomorphic function on $G\setminus K$, with $G\subset\mathbb C^n$ a domain, $K\subset G$ compact and $G\setminus K$ connected, extends holomorphically to $G$, so there are domains on which every holomorphic function continues to a strictly larger domain. Poincaré showed in 1907 that the ball and the polydisc in $\mathbb C^n$, $n>1$, are not biholomorphic, by comparing the dimensions of their automorphism groups as [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups). ([Wikipedia, Function of several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))

The field's organizing questions are which domains are "natural" (domains of holomorphy), how to characterize them geometrically (pseudoconvexity, the Levi problem), and how to solve the Cauchy–Riemann equation $\bar\partial u=f$ on them. Two of the main routes to these global results are Oka–Cartan sheaf theory, leading to Stein manifolds and [Cartan's Theorems A and B](node:Cartan's%20Theorems%20A%20and%20B), and the PDE method of Kohn and Hörmander for $\bar\partial$ with $L^2$ estimates, built on [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms) of type $(p,q)$; a third uses integral representations (Henkin, Grauert, Range). ([Jabbari, §§1.3, 3–4, 7](https://www.math.wustl.edu/~jabbari/SCV.pdf)) The local theory of zero sets via the Weierstrass preparation theorem leads to [Complex Analytic Spaces](node:Complex%20Analytic%20Spaces), the setting in which Grauert, Remmert and the Cartan seminar rebuilt the subject after 1945. ([Wikipedia, Function of several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))

### Scope
MSC2020 32-XX has twenty sections: 32A holomorphic functions of several complex variables; 32B local analytic geometry (see also 13-XX, 14-XX); 32C analytic spaces; 32D analytic continuation; 32E holomorphic convexity; 32F geometric convexity; 32G deformations of analytic structures; 32H holomorphic mappings and correspondences; 32J compact analytic spaces (for Riemann surfaces see 14Hxx, 30Fxx; for algebraic theory see 14Jxx); 32K generalizations of analytic spaces; 32L holomorphic fiber spaces (see also 55Rxx); 32M complex spaces with a group of automorphisms; 32N automorphic functions (see also 11Fxx, 20H10, 22E40, 30F35); 32P non-Archimedean analysis (always with a second 32 code); 32Q complex manifolds; 32S complex singularities (see also 58Kxx); 32T pseudoconvex domains; 32U pluripotential theory; 32V CR manifolds; 32W differential operators in several variables. ([MSC2020, 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX))

Neighbours, by the cross-references above: 32J sends [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces) to 14H and 30F (see [MSC 30 - Functions of a complex variable](node:MSC%2030%20-%20Functions%20of%20a%20complex%20variable)) and the algebraic theory of compact varieties to 14J; 32B cross-refers local analytic geometry to commutative algebra (13), where the algebra of [Local Rings](node:Local%20Rings) lives, and to [MSC 14 - Algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014%20-%20Algebraic%20geometry); 32N cross-refers automorphic functions to 11F, 20H10, 22E40 and 30F35; 32L to fibre bundles in 55R; 32S to singularities of maps in 58K. ([MSC2020, 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX)) Entry notes: [Holomorphic Functions of Several Variables](node:Holomorphic%20Functions%20of%20Several%20Variables), [Pseudoconvexity](node:Pseudoconvexity), [Stein Spaces](node:Stein%20Spaces), [Complex Manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds).

### Key concepts
- **Cartan–Thullen theorem (32D, 32E).** For open $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ the following are equivalent: $D$ is a domain of holomorphy (no boundary part across which every $f\in\mathcal O(D)$ continues); $\operatorname{dist}(K,\partial D)=\operatorname{dist}(\hat K_{\mathcal O(D)},\partial D)$ for every compact $K\subseteq D$; and $D$ is holomorphically convex, i.e. $\hat K_{\mathcal O(D)}=\{z\in D:|f(z)|\le\|f\|_K\ \forall f\in\mathcal O(D)\}$ is relatively compact in $D$ for every compact $K$. ([Jabbari, Theorem 44](https://www.math.wustl.edu/~jabbari/SCV.pdf))
- **Levi problem and pseudoconvexity (32T, 32U).** An open $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ is pseudoconvex if it has a continuous [plurisubharmonic](node:Plurisubharmonic%20Functions) exhaustion function; equivalently a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic one, or it satisfies the continuity principle for holomorphic discs (Hartogs–Oka). The solution of Levi's problem: $D$ is a domain of holomorphy iff it is pseudoconvex iff $\bar\partial u=f$ has a smooth solution for every smooth $\bar\partial$-closed $(p,q+1)$-form $f$, i.e. the [Dolbeault cohomology](node:Dolbeault%20Cohomology) $H^{p,q}(D)$ vanishes for $q\ge1$. ([Jabbari, Theorems 58, 70](https://www.math.wustl.edu/~jabbari/SCV.pdf)) Oka solved it for unramified Riemann domains over $\mathbb C^n$; Bremermann treated relatively compact, locally pseudoconvex open subsets of Stein manifolds by embedding into a high-dimensional $\mathbb C^N$ and reducing to Oka's result; Hörmander gave a proof by functional-analytic and PDE methods; for ramified Riemann domains pseudoconvexity does not characterize holomorphic convexity. ([Wikipedia, Function of several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables)) Grauert showed that a complex manifold is Stein iff it admits a smooth strongly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function, and Narasimhan extended this to complex spaces. ([Wikipedia, Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold))
- **Hörmander's $L^2$ estimates (32W).** Let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be pseudoconvex and $\varphi$ plurisubharmonic on $D$. For every $f\in L^2_{p,q+1}(D,e^{-\varphi})$ with $\bar\partial f=0$ there is $u\in L^2_{p,q,\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ with $\bar\partial u=f$ and
  $$\int_D|u|^2(1+|z|^2)^{-2}e^{-\varphi}\,d\mu\le\int_D|f|^2e^{-\varphi}\,d\mu;$$
  if $D$ is bounded, $\|u\|_\varphi\le C\|f\|_\varphi$ with $C$ depending only on $m$ and $\operatorname{diam}D$. Jabbari's notes apply it to interpolation, division and Cousin problems on pseudoconvex domains. ([Jabbari, Theorem 84, §§4.4–4.6](https://www.math.wustl.edu/~jabbari/SCV.pdf))
- **Stein manifolds and Cartan's Theorems A and B (32E, 32Q).** A complex manifold is Stein if it is holomorphically convex and holomorphically separable; Stein introduced the notion in 1951. Every Stein manifold of dimension $n$ admits a proper biholomorphic embedding into $\mathbb C^{2n+1}$, and a connected Riemann surface is Stein iff it is non-compact. ([Wikipedia, Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold)) For a coherent analytic sheaf $\mathcal F$ on a Stein manifold $X$, Theorem A says $\mathcal F$ is generated by its global sections and Theorem B says $H^p(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for $p>0$; conversely (Serre, 1956) a complex manifold with $H^1(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for all coherent $\mathcal F$ is Stein. ([Wikipedia, Cartan's theorems A and B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%27s_theorems_A_and_B)) Consequently the first Cousin problem is always solvable on a Stein manifold, and the second iff $H^2(M,\mathbb Z)=0$. ([Wikipedia, Function of several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))
- **Weierstrass preparation and Oka coherence (32B).** If $f$ is holomorphic near $0\in\mathbb C^n$, $f(0)=0$, and $f$ is not identically zero on the $z_1$-axis, then near $0$, $f=h\,W$ with $h(0)\ne0$ and $W=z_1^k+g_{k-1}z_1^{k-1}+\dots+g_0$, each $g_i$ holomorphic in $(z_2,\dots,z_n)$ and vanishing at $0$; the division theorem gives unique $f=gh+j$ with $\deg j<\deg g$ for a Weierstrass polynomial $g$, and these yield that the ring of germs $\mathcal O_n$ is Noetherian (Rückert basis theorem). ([Wikipedia, Weierstrass preparation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_preparation_theorem)) The Oka–Cartan coherence theorem makes $\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n}$ and the ideal sheaves of analytic subsets (Cartan, 1950) coherent. ([Wikipedia, Function of several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables))
- **Complex analytic spaces and proper maps (32C, 32H).** A complex analytic space is a locally ringed $\mathbb C$-space locally isomorphic to a model $(V(f_1,\dots,f_k)\cap U,\ \mathcal O_U/(f_1,\dots,f_k))$; the structure sheaf may have nilpotents, and the space is reduced when it has none. ([Wikipedia, Complex analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analytic_space)) Remmert's mapping theorem: the image of an analytic set under a proper holomorphic map is analytic. For a proper surjective $F:X\to Y$ with $X$ normal, Stein showed that the space of connected components of fibres carries a normal complex structure, giving the Stein factorization $F=f\circ\Phi$ with $f$ a finite ramified cover. ([Huckleberry, Karl Stein (1913–2000)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.6025)) See [Proper Holomorphic Maps](node:Proper%20Holomorphic%20Maps).

### History
Pierre Cousin posed special cases of the Cousin problems in 1895 and Hartogs proved his extension theorem in 1906. Oka's "idéaux de domaines indéterminés" were the precursor of coherent sheaves; Cartan recast them in sheaf language, and Serre (1955) carried coherent sheaves into algebraic geometry. ([Wikipedia, Function of several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables)) Cartan announced the Cartan–Serre vanishing theory for coherent sheaves at the 1953 Brussels colloquium on functions of several variables, where he named Stein's holomorphically complete spaces *variétés de Stein*. ([Huckleberry, Karl Stein (1913–2000)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.6025)) Grauert and Remmert's *Coherent Analytic Sheaves* (Springer Grundlehren, 1984) is a standard account of the resulting theory. ([Crossref, Grauert–Remmert](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-69582-7))

### Open problems
- **Local Steinness (singular Levi) problem and the union problem.** If $D\subset\subset X$ is an open subset of a Stein space $X$ with singularities and every boundary point has a neighbourhood $U$ with $U\cap D$ Stein, must $D$ be Stein? And is an increasing union of Stein open subsets of a Stein space Stein (the Behnke–Stein theorem for Stein spaces)? Both are described as unresolved; Colţoiu's survey discusses them as "well-known open problems". ([Wikipedia, Function of several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables); [Colţoiu, The Levi problem on Stein spaces with singularities. A survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343))
- **Green–Griffiths–Lang conjecture (32Q45).** For a projective variety of general type, all non-constant entire curves should lie in a fixed proper algebraic subvariety; it is open in general, and Demailly proves it only under a strong general type condition (jet-semistability of the [tangent bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle)). Kobayashi's conjecture that generic hypersurfaces of large degree are hyperbolic is proved for sufficiently large degree (Siu, Brotbek, Deng), and Demailly improves the degree bound to $d_n=\lfloor (en)^{2n+2}/5\rfloor$. ([Demailly, Recent results on the Kobayashi and Green–Griffiths–Lang conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.04765))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Function of several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_of_several_complex_variables): Hartogs, Cousin problems, Levi problem, coherence, Stein manifolds and history.
- **Learn:** [Jabbari, Analysis and Geometry of Several Complex Variables (WUSTL notes)](https://www.math.wustl.edu/~jabbari/SCV.pdf): Hartogs, Cartan–Thullen, pseudoconvexity, $\bar\partial$ with $L^2$ estimates, coherence, Cartan B.
- **Primary:** [Colţoiu, The Levi problem on Stein spaces with singularities. A survey (arXiv 0905.2343)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343): survey of the singular Levi and union problems.
- **Primary:** [Demailly, Recent results on the Kobayashi and Green–Griffiths–Lang conjectures (arXiv 1801.04765)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.04765): survey of hyperbolicity in complex geometry.
- **Further reading:** [Grauert & Remmert, Coherent Analytic Sheaves (Springer, 1984)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-69582-7): analytic spaces, coherence, Theorems A and B; and Hörmander's *An Introduction to Complex Analysis in Several Variables* (Van Nostrand, 1966) ([Crossref, review by Hervé](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/s0008439500028083)): the $L^2$ approach.
references.MSC 32Axx - Holomorphic functions of sev:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 32Axx, within [MSC 32 - Several complex variables and analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032%20-%20Several%20complex%20variables%20and%20analytic%20spaces), is the function theory of [Holomorphic Functions of Several Variables](node:Holomorphic%20Functions%20of%20Several%20Variables): power series, polynomials and entire and meromorphic functions, normal families and Nevanlinna theory, integral representations and canonical kernels (Bergman, Szegő, Cauchy–Fantappiè), residues, $H^p$, Bergman, BMOA and other function spaces, algebras of holomorphic functions, boundary behaviour, hyperfunctions, harmonic analysis, singular integrals and zero sets. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=32Axx))

Locally the theory resembles one variable: on polydiscs, holomorphic functions are given by convergent power series, and the identity and maximum principles hold. Globally it differs sharply: there is no Riemann mapping theorem, and the ball and the polydisc, although homeomorphic and simply connected, are not biholomorphic, so topology alone does not classify domains. ([Lebl, *Tasty Bits*, §§1.2, 1.4](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf)) The Hartogs phenomenon, by which compact singularities are removable when $n\ge2$, is the first sign of this rigidity. ([Wikipedia: Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem))

### Scope
- **32A05–32A20:** power series and series of functions; polynomials and rational functions; holomorphic functions; multifunctions; entire functions (compare one-variable [Entire and Meromorphic Functions](node:Entire%20and%20Meromorphic%20Functions)); special families; Bloch and normal functions; normal families and taut manifolds; meromorphic functions. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=32Axx))
- **32A22–32A30:** Nevanlinna theory and growth estimates (geometric theory goes to 32H25, 32H30); integral representations with canonical kernels (Szegő, Bergman) and constructed kernels (Cauchy, Fantappiè type); residues; other generalizations of one-variable function theory (hypercomplex variables go to 30G35). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=32Axx))
- **32A35–32A40:** $H^p$ and Nevanlinna spaces; Bergman spaces; BMOA, VMOA and other spaces; algebras of holomorphic functions; boundary behaviour. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=32Axx))
- **32A45–32A70:** hyperfunctions; harmonic analysis (mainly 43-XX); singular integrals; zero sets; Banach-algebra and functional-analysis techniques. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=32Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Power series and identity theorem:** if $f$ is continuous on the closure of a polydisc $\Delta=\Delta_r(a)$ and holomorphic in $\Delta$, then $f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ on $\Delta$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly on compact subsets; conversely such series are holomorphic. On a domain $U$, a holomorphic $f$ vanishing on a nonempty open subset vanishes identically, and $|f|$ cannot attain a local maximum unless $f$ is constant. ([Lebl, Theorems 1.2.1, 1.2.6, 1.2.7](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf))
- **Hartogs's theorem on separate holomorphicity:** a function $F$ on an open set in $\mathbb C^n$ that is holomorphic in each variable separately is continuous, hence holomorphic; no continuity or boundedness is assumed (with it, the result is Osgood's lemma). There is no real-variable analogue: $xy/(x^2+y^2)$ is separately real-analytic but discontinuous at $0$. ([Wikipedia: Hartogs's theorem on separate holomorphicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_theorem_on_separate_holomorphicity))
- **Hartogs phenomenon:** if $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge2$, is a domain and $K\subset U$ is compact with $U\setminus K$ connected, every holomorphic $f$ on $U\setminus K$ extends uniquely to $U$; Lebl proves it by solving a compactly supported $\bar\partial$-problem. ([Lebl, Theorem 4.3.1](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf)) Hence isolated singularities are removable in more than one variable. ([Wikipedia: Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem)) See [Hartogs Extension Theorem](node:Hartogs%20Extension%20Theorem); the domains on which this fails for some function are the domains of holomorphy studied under [Pseudoconvexity](node:Pseudoconvexity).
- **Ball versus polydisc:** $\mathbb B^n$ and $\mathbb D^n$ are homeomorphic but not biholomorphic for $n\ge2$; more strongly (Rothstein 1935) there is no proper holomorphic map $\mathbb D^2\to\mathbb B^2$, because $\partial\mathbb D^2$ contains analytic discs while the sphere $S^{2n-1}$ contains none. ([Lebl, §1.4, Theorem 1.4.4, Proposition 1.4.6](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf)) This contrasts with the one-variable [Riemann Mapping Theorem](node:Riemann%20Mapping%20Theorem).
