- **Bochner–Martinelli formula (32A26):** with the kernel $\omega(\zeta,z)=\frac{(n-1)!}{(2\pi i)^n}\frac{1}{\|\zeta-z\|^{2n}}\sum_{j=1}^n(\bar\zeta_j-\bar z_j)\,d\bar\zeta_1\wedge d\zeta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{d\bar\zeta_j}\wedge d\zeta_j\wedge\cdots\wedge d\bar\zeta_n\wedge d\zeta_n$ (the factor $d\bar\zeta_j$ is left out, so $\omega$ is an $(n,n-1)$-form), a smooth function $f$ on the closure of a bounded open set $U\subset\mathbb C^n$ with smooth boundary satisfies $f(z)=\int_{\partial U}f\,\omega(\cdot,z)-\int_U\bar\partial f\wedge\omega(\cdot,z)$ for $z\in U$, so $f(z)=\int_{\partial U}f\,\omega(\cdot,z)$ when $f$ is holomorphic; for $n=1$ it is the Cauchy–Pompeiu formula. ([Lebl, §5.1, Theorem 5.1.1](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf)) The kernel is written in [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms), and $\bar\partial$ enters exactly as in the one-variable generalized [Cauchy's Integral Formula](node:Cauchy's%20Integral%20Formula).
- **Bergman and Szegő kernels (32A25, 32A36):** the Bergman space $A^2(U)=\mathcal O(U)\cap L^2(U)$ is a closed subspace of $L^2(U)$ because $\sup_K|f|\le C_K\|f\|_{A^2}$ on compacts $K$; point evaluation is bounded, so there is a kernel with $f(z)=\int_Uf(\zeta)K_U(z,\bar\zeta)\,dV(\zeta)$, holomorphic in $z$, antiholomorphic in $\zeta$ and conjugate symmetric. For the ball, $K_{\mathbb B^n}(z,\bar\zeta)=\frac{n!}{\pi^n}\frac{1}{(1-\langle z,\zeta\rangle)^{n+1}}$. The Hardy space $H^2(\partial U)$ is the $L^2(\partial U,d\sigma)$-closure of boundary values of functions in $\mathcal O(U)\cap C(\bar U)$, and the Szegő kernel reproduces it through the Poisson extension; for an orthonormal basis $\{\varphi_j\}$, $S_U(z,\bar\zeta)=\sum_j\varphi_j(z)\overline{\varphi_j(\zeta)}$. ([Lebl, §§5.2–5.3, Lemma 5.2.1, Proposition 5.2.2](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf); [Wikipedia: Szegő kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szeg%C5%91_kernel)) In one variable the disc kernel is $\frac1\pi(1-z\bar\zeta)^{-2}$. ([Wikipedia: Bergman kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergman_kernel)) See [Hardy and Bergman Spaces](node:Hardy%20and%20Bergman%20Spaces).
- **Function theory on the ball:** Rudin's monograph organizes the ball theory around automorphisms of $\mathbb B$, integral representations, the invariant Laplacian, boundary behaviour of Poisson, Cauchy and $H^\infty$ functions, $L^p$ topics, the ball algebra and its interpolation sets, Möbius-invariant spaces, proper maps, the $\bar\partial$-problem and zeros of Nevanlinna functions. ([Rudin, contents](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-540-68276-9))

### History
Hartogs gave the original proof of his extension theorem in 1906. ([Wikipedia: Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem)) Lebl notes that this proof contained gaps: a complete proof was given by Fueter in 1939 for $n=2$ and independently by Bochner and Martinelli for higher $n$ in the early 1940s, and the standard modern proof via the compactly supported $\bar\partial$-problem is due to Ehrenpreis (1961). ([Lebl, §4.3](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf)) Poincaré first showed that the bidisc and the ball in $\mathbb C^2$ are inequivalent by computing their automorphism groups, assuming boundary extension; the first complete proof was Henri Cartan's in 1931. ([Lebl, §1.4](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf)) Martinelli introduced and proved his integral formula in 1938; Bochner published in 1943 and later withdrew his claim to the general form. ([Wikipedia: Bochner–Martinelli formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Martinelli_formula)) Carleson's corona theorem for the unit disc says the corona is empty: the open disc is dense in the spectrum of the algebra of bounded holomorphic functions. ([Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Corona problem in higher dimensions.** Carleson proved the corona theorem for the disc in 1962; whether versions of it hold for every planar domain, or for higher-dimensional domains, is stated to remain open, and Cole showed it cannot be extended to all open [Riemann surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces). ([Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem))
- **Rudin's problem list.** Rudin's monograph closes with a chapter of open problems on function theory in the ball (pp. 403–417); a Zentralblatt review quoted on the publisher's page says that problems and conjectures are continually underlined throughout the book. ([Rudin, contents and description](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-540-68276-9))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem): statement, history, removability of compact singularities.
- **Learn:** [Lebl, *Tasty Bits of Several Complex Variables* (OSU course notes, v3.0)](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/scv-s19/scv.pdf): power series, ball versus polydisc, Hartogs phenomenon via $\bar\partial$, Bochner–Martinelli, Bergman and Szegő kernels.
- **Primary:** [Rudin, *Function Theory in the Unit Ball of $\mathbb C^n$*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-540-68276-9): Grundlehren 241, reprinted in Classics in Mathematics; monograph on automorphisms, integral representations, function spaces, kernels and boundary behaviour on the ball, with a chapter of open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Bochner–Martinelli formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Martinelli_formula): attribution history of the formula (its kernel display omits $d\zeta_j$ where $d\bar\zeta_j$ should be omitted; use Lebl §5.1).
references.MSC 32Bxx - Local analytic geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
Local analytic geometry studies the zero sets of holomorphic (or real analytic) functions near a single point, through the ring $\mathcal O_n$ of convergent power series germs at $0\in\mathbb C^n$. An analytic set in an open $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ is a closed set cut out by finitely many holomorphic functions, and the local theory replaces it by its germ at a point and by the ideal of germs vanishing on it. The central goal of the classical theory is to describe the local structure of such a set, using Weierstrass preparation and division as the main tools in the way polynomial algebra is used in algebraic geometry. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Introduction](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf))

The subject has a complex half and a real half. On the complex side, the algebra of $\mathcal O_n$ (Noetherian, factorial, with a Nullstellensatz) controls the geometry of germs, which turn out to be finite branched coverings of coordinate polydiscs. On the real side, the semianalytic and subanalytic sets are the analytic counterparts of semialgebraic sets; the Tarski–Seidenberg theorem fails for semianalytic sets, which is why the larger subanalytic class is needed. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Thm 1.7, Thm 4.1](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf); [Subanalytic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subanalytic_set))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 32Bxx (with "See also 13-XX, 14-XX") lists: 32B05 analytic algebras and generalizations, preparation theorems; 32B10 germs of analytic sets, local parametrization; 32B15 analytic subsets of affine space; 32B20 semi-analytic sets, subanalytic sets, and generalizations (see also 14P15); 32B25 triangulation and topological properties of semi-analytic and subanalytic sets; 32B99. ([MSC2020, 32Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Bxx))

Neighbouring codes: the entry points to 13-XX and 14-XX, where the same local-ring methods appear for abstract commutative rings and [algebraic varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties); [MSC 14Pxx - Real algebraic and real-analytic geometry](node:MSC%2014Pxx%20-%20Real%20algebraic%20and%20real-analytic%20geometry) (cross-referenced at 32B20) handles semialgebraic and real-algebraic sets; [MSC 32Cxx - Analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Cxx%20-%20Analytic%20spaces) globalizes germs into ringed spaces; [MSC 32Sxx - Complex singularities](node:MSC%2032Sxx%20-%20Complex%20singularities) studies the singular points themselves. ([MSC2020, 32Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Bxx); [MSC2020, 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Weierstrass preparation theorem.** A Weierstrass polynomial of degree $k$ in $z_n$ is a monic $h=z_n^k+a_1z_n^{k-1}+\dots+a_k\in\mathcal O_{n-1}[z_n]$ with $a_i(0)=0$. If $f\in\mathcal O_n$ is regular of order $k$ in $z_n$ (that is, $f(0,\dots,0,z_n)$ has a zero of order exactly $k$ at $0$), then there is a unique Weierstrass polynomial $h$ of degree $k$ and a unit $u\in\mathcal O_n$ with $f=uh$. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Def. 1.4, Thm 1.5](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf))
- **Weierstrass division theorem.** If $h$ is a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $k$ in $z_n$, every $f\in\mathcal O_n$ can be written $f=gh+r$ with $g\in\mathcal O_n$ and $r\in\mathcal O_{n-1}[z_n]$ of degree at most $k-1$; the pair is unique. Many authors deduce preparation from division, and the two are equivalent. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Thm 1.6](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf); [Weierstrass preparation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_preparation_theorem))
- **Algebra of $\mathcal O_n$ ([Noetherian and Artinian Rings](node:Noetherian%20and%20Artinian%20Rings)).** By induction on $n$ using the two Weierstrass theorems, $\mathcal O_n$ is an integral domain, a unique factorization domain, and Noetherian; the Noetherian statement is the Rückert basis theorem. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Thm 1.7](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf); [Weierstrass preparation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_preparation_theorem))
- **Rückert Nullstellensatz.** For a prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset\mathcal O_n$, the ideal of germs vanishing on the germ $V(\mathfrak p)$ is $\mathfrak p$ itself: $I(V(\mathfrak p))=\mathfrak p$. Since $I(V(\mathfrak a))$ is always radical and a radical ideal is a finite intersection of primes, this gives $I(V(\mathfrak a))=\sqrt{\mathfrak a}$; a germ $V$ is irreducible exactly when $I(V)$ is prime. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Thms 2.5, 3.9, §4](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf))
- **Local parametrization ([Analytic Germs](node:Analytic%20Germs)).** For a prime $\mathfrak p$, after a choice of regular coordinates $(z_1,\dots,z_k,z_{k+1},\dots,z_n)$ there are Weierstrass polynomials $q_j\in\mathcal O_k[z_j]$, a discriminant $d\in\mathcal O_k$, and small polydiscs $\Delta=\Delta_1\times\Delta_2$ such that $V\setminus V(d)$ is a connected complex manifold of dimension $k$, the projection $\pi:V\setminus V(d)\to\Delta_1\setminus V(d)$ is an $s$-sheeted covering ($s=\deg q_{k+1}$), and $\pi:V\to\Delta_1$ is proper. This defines $\dim V=k$, and the regular points are dense. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Thm 4.1](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf))
- **Hypersurface germs.** If $f\in\mathcal O_n$, $f(0)=0$, $f\not\equiv0$, then every irreducible component of $V(f)$ has dimension $n-1$; in particular a holomorphic function of $n\ge2$ variables has no isolated zero. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Thm 4.2](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf); [Weierstrass preparation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_preparation_theorem))
- **Oka coherence.** The sheaf $\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n}$ of holomorphic functions is coherent (Oka, 1950), and more generally the structure sheaf of any complex analytic space is coherent; the main part of the proof is the case $\mathbb C^n$. The ideal sheaf of a closed analytic subspace is also coherent. Coherence is what turns pointwise statements about germs into statements valid on neighbourhoods. ([Oka coherence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oka_coherence_theorem); [Coherent sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf))
- **Semianalytic and subanalytic sets.** $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ is semianalytic if near every point $a$ it is a finite union of sets $\{g_{ij}>0,\ f_{ij}=0\}$ with $f_{ij},g_{ij}$ real analytic near $a$. Subanalytic sets are, locally, linear projections of relatively compact semianalytic sets; every semianalytic set is subanalytic, while projections of semianalytic sets need not be semianalytic. Subanalytic sets are locally finite unions of submanifolds. ([Valette, Def. 1.1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.23622); [Subanalytic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subanalytic_set)) These are the analytic analogue of [Semialgebraic Sets](node:Semialgebraic%20Sets).
- **Gabrielov's complement theorem.** The complement of a (globally) subanalytic set is subanalytic: if $A\in\mathcal S_n$ then $\mathbb R^n\setminus A\in\mathcal S_n$. Gabrielov's 1996 paper (received 1995) proves a version for subanalytic sets defined by functions from any subalgebra of real analytic functions closed under differentiation, and states its logical form: an expression built from such functions with both quantifiers is equivalent to an existential one, provided the variables stay away from infinity and from the boundary of the domain. ([Valette, Thm 1.8.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.23622); [Gabrielov 1995, abstract](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~agabriel/exist.pdf))
- **Łojasiewicz inequalities.** If $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is real analytic on open $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ with nonempty zero set $Z$, then for every compact $K\subset U$ there are $\alpha,C>0$ with $\operatorname{dist}(x,Z)^\alpha\le C|f(x)|$ on $K$. The gradient form: near each $p\in U$ there are $\theta\in(0,1)$, $c>0$ with $|f(x)-f(p)|^\theta\le c|\nabla f(x)|$. A definable (globally subanalytic) version compares two definable functions $f,g$ on a definable set $A$ with $f$ bounded: if $f(\gamma(t))\to0$ along every definable arc $\gamma$ on which $g(\gamma(t))\to0$, then there are $N\in\mathbb N^*$ and $C$ with $|f|^N\le C|g|$ on $A$. ([Łojasiewicz inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%81ojasiewicz_inequality); [Valette, Thm 2.2.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.23622))
- **Curve selection lemma.** If $A$ is globally subanalytic and $x_0\in\overline A$, there is an analytic arc $\gamma:[0,\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ with $\gamma(0)=x_0$ and $\gamma((0,\varepsilon))\subset A$. ([Valette, Lemma 2.2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.23622))
- **Subanalytic criteria for complex analyticity.** Viewing a complex manifold $M$ as a real one: if $f:M\to N$ is holomorphic, $A\subset M$ is complex analytic, and $f(A)$ is closed and subanalytic in $N$, then $f(A)$ is complex analytic. Remmert's proper mapping theorem follows, since a proper $f$ makes $f(A)$ closed and subanalytic; without subanalyticity the conclusion fails. ([Peterzil–Starchenko, Thm 2.1 and remarks](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410274))

### History
Siegel disputed the attribution of the preparation theorem to Weierstrass, noting that it had appeared under that name in late-nineteenth-century *Traités d'analyse* without justification; the sources cited for it include Stickelberger (1887) and Weierstrass's *Mathematische Werke* II (1895). Smooth analogues came much later: Malgrange's preparation theorem for $C^\infty$ functions, with the associated division theorem named after Mather. ([Weierstrass preparation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_preparation_theorem)) Oka proved the coherence of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n}$ in 1950. ([Oka coherence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oka_coherence_theorem))

On the real side, the first deep work on semianalytic geometry was Łojasiewicz's (papers of 1959 and 1964). Gabrielov introduced subanalytic sets in 1968 (*Projections of semi-analytic sets*, Funct. Anal. Appl. 2) and proved the complement theorem there, rewriting it in 1996; Hironaka, building on his 1964 resolution of singularities, introduced the term "subanalytic" and proved the rectilinearization and uniformization theorems (1973). Valette points to Bierstone and Milman's *Semianalytic and subanalytic sets* (Publ. Math. IHÉS 67, 1988, 5–42) alongside Hironaka's theorems. Denef and van den Dries (1988) proved a quantifier elimination result for globally subanalytic sets; that paper and van den Dries (1986) treat the complement theorem in logic, as model completeness and o-minimality of the real field with restricted analytic functions. ([Valette, Historical notes to Ch. 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.23622); [Gabrielov 1995, Introduction and references](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~agabriel/exist.pdf); [Bierstone–Milman, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02699126))

### Open problems
None found. Searched: the contents and historical notes of Valette's 2025 survey of subanalytic geometry (which states no open problems in the text read); the Several Complex Variables Problem List (Buzzard–Fornæss–Gavosto–Krantz, 1995), whose sections cover envelopes of holomorphy, the Levi problem, function theory, $\bar\partial$, mappings, dynamics, varieties and CR manifolds but have no section on germs, preparation, or subanalytic sets; and web searches for open problems on Gabrielov's complement theorem and on germs, local parametrization and the Rückert Nullstellensatz. ([Valette, arXiv:2507.23622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23622); [SCV Problem List, contents](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9509202))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Weierstrass preparation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_preparation_theorem): complex, smooth, formal and Tate-algebra versions, with history.
- **Reference:** [Subanalytic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subanalytic_set): definitions and failure of Tarski–Seidenberg for semianalytic sets.
- **Learn:** [Acquistapace–Broglia, Local properties of analytic sets (Sapporo lectures, 2017)](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf): preparation, division, $\mathcal O_n$ Noetherian/UFD, Rückert Nullstellensatz, germs as ramified coverings, with proofs.
- **Primary:** [Valette, On subanalytic geometry (survey, 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23622): complement theorem, cell decompositions, curve selection, Łojasiewicz inequalities, stratifications, Lipschitz geometry.
- **Primary:** [Gabrielov, Complements of subanalytic sets and existential formulas for analytic functions](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~agabriel/exist.pdf): the complement theorem for subalgebras closed under differentiation.

IHÉS, 1988)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02699126).
references.MSC 32Cxx - Analytic spaces:
## Reference
### Overview
An analytic space generalizes an analytic manifold by allowing singularities: it is a locally ringed space that is locally isomorphic to an analytic variety (the zero set of finitely many analytic functions in an open subset of $k^n$) with its structure sheaf. Over $\mathbb C$ these are the complex spaces of several complex variables; local models are analytic varieties rather than spectra of rings, and since these are finite-dimensional and defined over a field, analytic spaces behave much like schemes of finite type over a field. ([Analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_space))

The theory of complex spaces rests on coherence. Oka's theorem that the structure sheaf is coherent, together with coherence of ideal sheaves and of proper direct images, lets the local algebra of germs ([MSC 32Bxx - Local analytic geometry](node:MSC%2032Bxx%20-%20Local%20analytic%20geometry)) be assembled into global statements, most notably Cartan's Theorems A and B on Stein manifolds and Serre's GAGA comparison with algebraic geometry. ([Coherent sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf); [Shen–Yu, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12211v1); [Cartan's theorems A and B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%27s_theorems_A_and_B))

### Scope
MSC2020 32Cxx lists: 32C05 real-analytic manifolds, real-analytic spaces (see also 14Pxx, 58A07); 32C07 real-analytic sets, complex Nash functions; 32C09 embedding of real-analytic manifolds; 32C11 complex supergeometry; 32C15 complex spaces; 32C18 topology of analytic spaces; 32C20 normal analytic spaces; 32C22 embedding of analytic spaces; 32C25 analytic subsets and submanifolds; 32C30 integration on analytic sets and spaces, currents; 32C35 analytic sheaves and cohomology groups (see also 14Fxx, 18F20, 55N30); 32C36 local cohomology; 32C37 duality theorems; 32C38 sheaves of differential operators and their modules, $D$-modules; 32C55 the Levi problem in complex spaces; 32C81 applications to physics and other sciences; 32C99. ([MSC2020, 32Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Cxx))

Neighbours: 32B is the local theory of germs and semi/subanalytic sets; 32C covers complex and real analytic spaces and their sheaf cohomology; Stein spaces (32E10) and holomorphic convexity are classified in [MSC 32Exx - Holomorphic convexity](node:MSC%2032Exx%20-%20Holomorphic%20convexity); compact spaces in [MSC 32Jxx - Compact analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Jxx%20-%20Compact%20analytic%20spaces); singular points in [MSC 32Sxx - Complex singularities](node:MSC%2032Sxx%20-%20Complex%20singularities). The cross-references point to 14Pxx for real-algebraic geometry and 14Fxx for algebraic sheaf cohomology. ([MSC2020, 32Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Cxx); [MSC2020, 32Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Exx); [MSC2020, 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Complex spaces ([Complex Analytic Spaces](node:Complex%20Analytic%20Spaces)).** Each point has a local dimension and a Zariski tangent space whose dimension (the embedding dimension) is at least the local dimension; the non-smooth locus is a closed analytic subset. A space is reduced when its local models are defined by radical ideal sheaves, and normal when its stalks are normal rings; a normal space has singular locus of codimension at least two, and every space has a canonical normalization. ([Analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_space)) For a germ of an analytic set, the Rückert Nullstellensatz $I(V(\mathfrak p))=\mathfrak p$ for prime $\mathfrak p$ identifies irreducible germs with prime ideals. ([Acquistapace–Broglia, Thm 3.9](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf))
- **Coherence (Oka, Cartan).** The sheaf of holomorphic functions on a complex analytic space is a coherent sheaf of rings (Oka, 1950, for $\mathbb C^n$; the main part of the proof is the case $X=\mathbb C^n$). If $Z$ is a closed analytic subspace of $X$, the ideal sheaf $\mathcal I_{Z/X}$ is coherent. Coherence holds over algebraically closed fields and fails for real analytic spaces in general. ([Coherent sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf); [Oka coherence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oka_coherence_theorem); [Analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_space))
- **Cartan's Theorems A and B ([Cartan's Theorems A and B](node:Cartan's%20Theorems%20A%20and%20B)).** Let $X$ be a Stein manifold and $\mathcal F$ a coherent analytic sheaf on $X$. (A) $\mathcal F$ is generated by its global sections. (B) $H^p(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for all $p>0$. Consequently every holomorphic function on a closed complex submanifold of a Stein manifold extends to the whole manifold; conversely, a complex manifold on which $H^1$ of every coherent sheaf vanishes is Stein (Serre, 1956). ([Cartan's theorems A and B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%27s_theorems_A_and_B)) [Stein Spaces](node:Stein%20Spaces) are Stein manifolds with singularities allowed, the analytic analogue of [affine varieties](node:Affine%20Varieties); Grauert's characterization of Stein manifolds by a strongly pseudoconvex exhaustion (the solution of the Levi problem) was generalized to Stein spaces by Narasimhan. ([Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold))
- **Grauert's direct image theorem.** For a proper holomorphic morphism $f:X\to Y$ of complex analytic spaces and a coherent sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$, the higher direct images $R^qf_*\mathcal F$ are coherent. ([Shen–Yu, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12211v1)) Its set-theoretic counterpart is Remmert's proper mapping theorem (the image of a complex analytic set under a proper holomorphic map is complex analytic), which follows from a more general criterion: for a holomorphic $f:M\to N$ between complex manifolds and complex analytic $A\subset M$, if $f(A)$ is closed and subanalytic then it is complex analytic, and properness of $f$ guarantees this. ([Peterzil–Starchenko, Thm 2.1, Remark 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410274))
- **Remmert–Stein extension theorem.** Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ be open, $Y\subset\Omega$ an analytic subset of dimension at most $k-1$, and $X$ an analytic subset of $\Omega\setminus Y$ of pure dimension $k$. Then the closure of $X$ in $\Omega$ is an analytic subset of $\Omega$ (Remmert–Stein, 1953); applied to the cone over a projective analytic set, this gives a proof of Chow's theorem. ([Aguilar–Verjovsky, Thm 4 and §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2101.09872v1)) The dimension hypothesis is needed: the points $(1/n,0)$ form an analytic subset of $\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\}$ whose closure is not analytic. ([Remmert–Stein theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remmert%E2%80%93Stein_theorem))
- **GAGA and Chow.** For a complex projective variety $X$, $\mathcal F\mapsto\mathcal F^{an}$ is an equivalence between coherent algebraic sheaves on $X$ and coherent analytic sheaves on $X^{an}$, and $H^q(X,\mathcal F)\to H^q(X^{an},\mathcal F^{an})$ is an isomorphism for every $q$ (Serre, 1956). Chow's theorem (1949): a closed analytic subspace of complex projective space is algebraic. ([Algebraic geometry and analytic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry_and_analytic_geometry))
- **Resolution of singularities.** Hironaka proved resolution for varieties over fields of characteristic $0$ in 1964; Bierstone and Milman's constructive proof, by blowing up maximum strata of a local invariant, applies in particular to schemes of finite type and to analytic spaces. ([Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities); [Bierstone–Milman, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9508005))
- **Real analytic spaces (32C05–32C09).** Over $\mathbb R$ the theory changes: images of analytic sets under analytic maps need not be analytic (the projection of a circle is a closed interval), and coherence can fail; subanalytic sets are introduced to repair the first defect. ([Analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_space))
- **$D$-modules (32C38).** A $D$-module is a module over a ring $D$ of differential operators. A module whose dimension attains the least possible value $n$ is holonomic, equivalently its characteristic variety is Lagrangian in the cotangent bundle; Bernstein's inequality bounds the dimension between $n$ and $2n$. The Riemann–Hilbert correspondence links certain $D$-modules to constructible sheaves, with a derived-category version in all dimensions due to Mebkhout, and motivated perverse sheaves. ([D-module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-module))

### History
Oka proved coherence of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n}$ in 1950. ([Oka coherence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oka_coherence_theorem)) Cartan's Theorems A and B date from around 1951, with Serre supplying the cohomological form (Cartan's 1953 paper); Serre used them to prove GAGA (1956), and Chow's theorem dates from 1949. ([Cartan's theorems A and B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%27s_theorems_A_and_B); [Algebraic geometry and analytic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry_and_analytic_geometry)) Remmert and Stein published their extension theorem in *Math. Annalen* 126 (1953); Grauert and Remmert's paper *Komplexe Räume* appeared in *Math. Annalen* 136 (1958) and their monograph *Coherent Analytic Sheaves* (Grundlehren) in 1984. ([Remmert–Stein theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remmert%E2%80%93Stein_theorem); [Algebraic geometry and analytic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry_and_analytic_geometry); [Grauert–Remmert, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-69582-7)) $D$-module theory developed from around 1970, in response to Sato's algebraic analysis and Bernstein's work on the Bernstein–Sato polynomial. ([D-module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-module))

### Open problems
- **Local Steinness problem (singular Levi problem, 32C55).** Let $X$ be a Stein space and $D\subset X$ an open subset that is locally Stein (each boundary point has a neighbourhood $V$ with $V\cap D$ Stein). Is $D$ Stein? Colţoiu's survey calls this, together with the union problem, one of "the well-known open problems". Known cases: Stein spaces with isolated singularities (Andreotti–Narasimhan) and complements $X\setminus H$ of hypersurfaces in three-dimensional Stein spaces (Colţoiu–Diederich); the survey conjectures a positive answer when $\dim X=3$. ([Colţoiu, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343); [Colţoiu, Question 1 and Conjecture 1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0905.2343))
- **Union problem.** If $U_1\subset U_2\subset\cdots$ are Stein open subsets of a Stein space $X$, is $\bigcup_n U_n$ Stein? For [complex manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds) that are not Stein the answer is in general no. ([SCV Problem List, Problem 4.3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9509202); [Colţoiu, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_space): definitions, reduced/normal spaces, coherence and its failure over $\mathbb R$.
- **Reference:** [Coherent sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf): Oka coherence, ideal sheaves, coherence of proper direct images.
- **Learn:** [Acquistapace–Broglia, Local properties of analytic sets (Sapporo lectures)](https://www.math.sci.hokudai.ac.jp/~s.settepanella/Sapporo.pdf): the local algebra (preparation, Nullstellensatz, branched coverings) on which complex spaces are modelled.
- **Primary:** [Colţoiu, The Levi problem on Stein spaces with singularities. A survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343): survey of the local Steinness and union problems.
- **Primary:** [Bierstone–Milman, Canonical desingularization in characteristic zero](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9508005): resolution of singularities, including for analytic spaces.
- **Further reading:** [Grauert–Remmert, Coherent Analytic Sheaves (Springer Grundlehren, 1984)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-69582-7); [Gunning–Rossi, Analytic Functions of Several Complex Variables (AMS)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/chel/368).
references.MSC 32Dxx - Analytic continuation:
## Reference
### Overview
Analytic continuation in several complex variables studies how far holomorphic functions on an open set, or on a Riemann domain, can be continued, and what the maximal regions of existence look like. In one variable every open set is a domain of holomorphy ([Wikipedia: Domain of holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_holomorphy)). In $\mathbb C^n$ with $n\ge2$, by contrast, holomorphic functions on $G\setminus K$ ($K$ compact, $G\setminus K$ connected) always extend across $K$; in one variable $1/z$ on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ shows this fails. ([Wikipedia: Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem))

This "Hartogs phenomenon" makes the shape of the domain decisive. The domains that are maximal for some holomorphic function, the domains of holomorphy, are characterized by holomorphic convexity (Cartan–Thullen) and by pseudoconvexity (the Levi problem, solved by Oka). These characterizations organize the whole subject. ([Wikipedia: Domain of holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_holomorphy); [Noguchi, chronicle](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246))

When a domain is not a domain of holomorphy, the functions on it extend to its envelope of holomorphy, "the smallest Stein Riemann domain over $\mathbb C^n$ to which all functions holomorphic on our domain extend holomorphically". This envelope may be multi-sheeted over $\mathbb C^n$, even for a domain in $\mathbb C^n$. ([Jupiter 2004](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0404497))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry 32Dxx (Analytic continuation) lists these sub-codes ([MSC2020 32Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Dxx)):
- **32D05** Domains of holomorphy.
- **32D10** Envelopes of holomorphy.
- **32D15** Continuation of analytic objects in several complex variables.
- **32D20** Removable singularities in several complex variables.
- **32D26** Riemann domains.
- **32D99** None of the above, but in this section.

Neighbouring codes ([MSC2020 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX); [MSC2020 30Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Bxx)):
- [MSC 30Bxx - Series expansions of functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Bxx%20-%20Series%20expansions%20of%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable) contains 30B40, "Analytic continuation of functions of one complex variable"; the 32D codes are for several complex variables.
- [MSC 32Axx - Holomorphic functions of several complex variables](node:MSC%2032Axx%20-%20Holomorphic%20functions%20of%20several%20complex%20variables), [MSC 32Exx - Holomorphic convexity](node:MSC%2032Exx%20-%20Holomorphic%20convexity), [MSC 32Txx - Pseudoconvex domains](node:MSC%2032Txx%20-%20Pseudoconvex%20domains) and [MSC 32Vxx - CR manifolds](node:MSC%2032Vxx%20-%20CR%20manifolds) are sibling sections of 32-XX.

### Key concepts
- **Domain of holomorphy.** A domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ is a domain of holomorphy if there are no nonempty open $U\subset\Omega$ and connected open $V\not\subset\Omega$ with $U\subset\Omega\cap V$ such that every $f\in\mathcal O(\Omega)$ has a holomorphic $g$ on $V$ with $g=f$ on $U$. ([Wikipedia: Domain of holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_holomorphy))
- **Cartan–Thullen theorem (1932).** For the hull $\hat K_G=\{z\in G:|f(z)|\le\sup_K|f|\ \forall f\in\mathcal O(G)\}$, call $G$ holomorphically convex if $\hat K_G$ is compact in $G$ for every compact $K\subset G$. For a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ the following are equivalent: $\Omega$ is a domain of holomorphy; $\Omega$ is holomorphically convex; some $f\in\mathcal O(\Omega)$ has $\Omega$ as its exact domain of existence. ([Wikipedia: Holomorphically convex hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphically_convex_hull); [Wikipedia: Domain of holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_holomorphy); [Noguchi](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246))
- **Levi problem.** Every domain of holomorphy is pseudoconvex; the converse, "a pseudoconvex domain is a domain of holomorphy", is the Levi problem, solved by Oka. If $U\subset\mathbb C^n$ has smooth boundary and the Levi form has a negative eigenvalue at some $p\in\partial U$, every holomorphic function on $U$ extends to a neighbourhood of $p$, so $U$ is not a domain of holomorphy (the tomato can principle). See [Pseudoconvexity](node:Pseudoconvexity), [Levi Convexity](node:Levi%20Convexity), [Plurisubharmonic Functions](node:Plurisubharmonic%20Functions). ([Tasty Bits of SCV, §4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056); [Wikipedia: Domain of holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_holomorphy))
- **[Hartogs Extension Theorem](node:Hartogs%20Extension%20Theorem).** If $G\subset\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge2$, is open, $K\subset G$ compact and $G\setminus K$ connected, every $f\in\mathcal O(G\setminus K)$ extends uniquely to $F\in\mathcal O(G)$; in particular every holomorphic function on $\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$, $n>1$, is entire. ([Wikipedia: Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem); [Tasty Bits of SCV](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056))
- **Kontinuitätssatz (continuity principle).** If closed analytic discs $\varphi_k$ in $U$ converge to a disc $\varphi$ whose boundary $\varphi(\partial\mathbb D)$ lies in $U$, then there is a polyradius $s>0$ such that every $f\in\mathcal O(U)$ extends holomorphically to a polydisc of polyradius $s$ about each point of $\varphi(\mathbb D)$. Biswas describes the informal statements used in the literature as a folk theorem and gives a precise version. ([Tasty Bits of SCV](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056); [Biswas 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2325))
- **Removable singularities (Riemann extension).** If $g\in\mathcal O(U)$, $g\not\equiv0$, $N=g^{-1}(0)$, and $f\in\mathcal O(U\setminus N)$ is locally bounded in $U$, then $f$ extends uniquely to $U$. Bounded or $L^2$ singularities along analytic sets are removable, and a holomorphic function on the complement of an analytic set of codimension $\ge2$ extends with no boundedness hypothesis. ([Tasty Bits of SCV](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056); [Demailly 2015, §1](https://arxiv.org/html/1510.05230v1))
- **Bochner tube theorem.** If $\omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a connected open set, every holomorphic function on the tube $\omega+i\mathbb R^n$ extends holomorphically to its convex hull $\operatorname{ch}(\omega)+i\mathbb R^n$. ([Wikipedia: Bochner's tube theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%27s_tube_theorem))
- **Riemann domains and envelopes.** A Riemann domain over $\mathbb C^n$ is a reduced complex space $X$ with a holomorphic map $\pi:X\to\mathbb C^n$ with discrete fibres, unramified when $\pi$ is locally biholomorphic. Jupiter lists Reinhardt, Hartogs and tube domains among the classes whose envelopes are schlicht (single-sheeted). In $\mathbb C^2$, an envelope that is schlicht over $\Omega$ is schlicht everywhere, which fails in $\mathbb C^n$ for $n>2$. See [Stein Spaces](node:Stein%20Spaces). ([Noguchi](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246); [Jupiter 2004](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0404497); [Jupiter, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0404497))

### History
Hartogs found "simultaneous analytic continuation" in 1906. Osgood stated the global form in 1929. Levi showed in 1910–1911 that the boundary of a domain of holomorphy is pseudoconvex, and Cartan and Thullen proved in 1932 that domains of holomorphy are exactly the holomorphically convex domains. Behnke and Thullen's 1934 monograph posed the Levi (Hartogs inverse) problem among its "Three Big Problems". ([Noguchi](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246); [Merker–Porten](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610985))

Oka announced (1941) and published (1942) a solution of the Levi problem for univalent domains over $\mathbb C^2$, noting that it holds in all dimensions $n\ge2$. His unpublished 1943 reports treat unramified Riemann domains, published as Oka IX in 1953. Bremermann and Norguet independently solved the univalent case in $\mathbb C^n$ in 1954, and Grauert gave a simplified proof in 1958. ([Noguchi](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246); [Wikipedia: Several complex variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Several_complex_variables))

Ehrenpreis's 1961 proof of Hartogs extension via compactly supported solutions of $\bar\partial$ became the standard modern route. Merker and Porten (2006) addressed the long-standing question of proving global Hartogs extension with analytic discs alone, after Fornæss had shown in 1998 that some nonpseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb C^2$ cannot be filled by discs inside them. ([Wikipedia: Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem); [Merker–Porten](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610985))

### Open problems
- **Levi problem for ramified Riemann domains.** For a ramified Riemann domain $\pi:X\to\mathbb C^n$ that is locally Stein over $\mathbb C^n$, Noguchi poses "Find sufficient or necessary conditions for $X$ to be Stein" and says the problem is open even for nonsingular $X$. Fornæss (1978) built a smooth two-sheeted ramified domain over $\mathbb C^2$ that is locally Stein but not Stein. ([Noguchi](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246))
- **Local Steinness and union problems.** Coltoiu's survey poses two questions on Stein spaces with singularities. One asks whether a locally Stein open subset of a Stein space is Stein, which the survey calls the main open problem related to the Levi problem in the singular case (for Stein manifolds the answer is yes, by Docquier–Grauert); the other asks whether an increasing union of Stein open subsets of a Stein space is Stein, which the survey says is unsolved even for isolated singularities. ([Coltoiu survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343); [Coltoiu, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0905.2343))
- **Sheet number of envelopes.** Jupiter asks (Problem 1.1) whether a bounded domain in $\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge2$, with smooth boundary can have an infinitely sheeted envelope of holomorphy. The known bounded examples have highly nonsmooth boundaries. ([Jupiter 2004](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0404497))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Domain of holomorphy (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_holomorphy): definition and the equivalent characterizations (Cartan–Thullen, pseudoconvexity, Levi convexity).
- **Reference:** [Hartogs's extension theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem): statement, one-variable counterexample, proof history.
- **Learn:** [Records from the S-Matrix Marathon: Tasty Bits of Several Complex Variables](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056): lecture notes covering Hartogs figures, Riemann extension, Kontinuitätssatz, and the Levi problem.
- **Primary:** [Noguchi, A Brief Chronicle of the Levi (Hartogs' Inverse) Problem, Coherence and an Open Problem](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246): historical survey with the ramified-domain open problem.
- **Primary:** [Merker–Porten, A geometrical proof of the Hartogs extension theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610985): global Hartogs extension via analytic discs.
- **Primary:** [Jupiter, A schlichtness theorem for envelopes of holomorphy](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0404497): schlichtness of envelopes in $\mathbb C^2$ and counterexamples in $\mathbb C^n$, $n>2$.
- **Primary:** [Coltoiu, The Levi problem on Stein spaces with singularities. A survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343): local Steinness and union problems.
- **Further reading:** [Fritzsche–Grauert, From Holomorphic Functions to Complex Manifolds (Springer GTM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-9273-6): graduate text in several complex variables.
references.MSC 32Exx - Holomorphic convexity:
## Reference
### Overview
Holomorphic convexity tests a complex manifold or space $X$ by its algebra $\mathcal O(X)$ of global holomorphic functions. For compact $K\subset X$ the holomorphically convex hull $\widehat K_X$ is the set of points at which every $f\in\mathcal O(X)$ satisfies $|f|\le\sup_K|f|$, and $X$ is holomorphically convex when every such hull is compact. Replacing $\mathcal O(X)$ by polynomials on $\mathbb C^n$ gives the polynomially convex hull, which always contains the holomorphic hull. ([Cieliebak–Eliashberg](https://math.stanford.edu/~eliash/Public/269A/Stein-notes.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphically_convex_hull))

The central objects of the area are Stein manifolds and Stein spaces: holomorphically convex, holomorphically separable spaces; a Stein manifold is, equivalently, a closed complex submanifold of some $\mathbb C^N$. Stein theory joins three viewpoints that turn out to be equivalent: the function-theoretic one (hulls, domains of holomorphy), the sheaf-theoretic one (Cartan's Theorem B), and the potential-theoretic one (strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustions, which solve the Levi problem). ([Wikipedia, Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold); [Wikipedia, Cartan's theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%27s_theorems_A_and_B); [Cieliebak–Eliashberg](https://math.stanford.edu/~eliash/Public/269A/Stein-notes.pdf))

Approximation is the other main theme of the code: on Stein spaces, Runge-type approximation holds on $\mathcal O(X)$-convex compacta (Oka–Weil), while on $\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge2$, it is very difficult to decide whether a given compact set is polynomially convex. Modern work connects Stein geometry with differential topology through holomorphic embeddings, submersions, and the Oka principle. ([Wikipedia, Oka–Weil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oka%E2%80%93Weil_theorem); [Gorai 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.04094); [Forstnerič 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/1709.05630v5); [Forstnerič 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0211112))

### Scope
MSC2020 32E has six subject codes: 32E05 holomorphically convex complex spaces and reduction theory; 32E10 Stein spaces; 32E20 polynomial, rational and meromorphic convexity; 32E30 holomorphic, polynomial and rational approximation and interpolation, Runge pairs; 32E35 global boundary behavior of holomorphic functions; 32E40 the Levi problem (plus 32E99). ([MSC2020, 32E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Exx))

- **vs 32D (analytic continuation):** 32D has separate codes for domains of holomorphy (32D05), envelopes of holomorphy, continuation of analytic objects, removable singularities and Riemann domains. ([MSC2020, 32D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Dxx))
- **vs 32T (pseudoconvex domains):** 32T has codes for domains of holomorphy (32T05), strongly pseudoconvex, worm and finite-type domains, invariants of weakly pseudoconvex boundaries, exhaustion functions and peak functions; the Levi problem itself is 32E40. ([MSC2020, 32T](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Txx); [MSC2020, 32E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Exx))
- **vs 32F, 32U, 32C:** geometric convexity (32F), pluripotential theory (32U) and analytic spaces (32C) are separate sections of 32-XX. ([MSC2020, 32](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Cartan–Thullen theorem:** for a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ the following are equivalent: $\Omega$ is a domain of holomorphy; $\Omega$ is holomorphically convex; some function holomorphic on $\Omega$ cannot be analytically continued beyond $\Omega$. These are also equivalent to $\Omega$ being pseudoconvex, but the hard direction (pseudoconvex implies domain of holomorphy) is the Levi problem, not part of Cartan–Thullen. For $n=1$ every open set is a domain of holomorphy. See [MSC 32Dxx - Analytic continuation](node:MSC%2032Dxx%20-%20Analytic%20continuation) and [Pseudoconvexity](node:Pseudoconvexity). ([Wikipedia, Domain of holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_holomorphy); [Wikipedia, hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphically_convex_hull))
- **[Stein manifolds](node:Stein%20Spaces):** classically, $X$ is Stein if it is holomorphically convex, $\mathcal O(X)$ separates points, and global functions give local coordinates at every point. Remmert's theorem shows such $X$ admits a proper holomorphic embedding into some $\mathbb C^N$; conversely properly embedded submanifolds of $\mathbb C^N$ are holomorphically convex. Connected noncompact [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces) are Stein (Behnke–Stein). ([Cieliebak–Eliashberg](https://math.stanford.edu/~eliash/Public/269A/Stein-notes.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold))
- **[Cartan's Theorems A and B](node:Cartan's%20Theorems%20A%20and%20B):** on a Stein manifold every coherent analytic sheaf $\mathcal F$ is generated by global sections (A) and has $H^p(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for $p>0$ (B). Theorem B is sharp: a complex manifold with $H^1(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for all coherent $\mathcal F$ is Stein. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%27s_theorems_A_and_B))
- **Levi problem and Grauert's theorem:** a complex manifold is Stein if and only if it admits a smooth exhaustion $\psi$ with $i\partial\bar\partial\psi>0$ and compact sublevel sets $\{\psi\le c\}$ (Grauert 1958; Narasimhan 1962 for Stein spaces). For domains in $\mathbb C^n$ the Levi problem (pseudoconvex implies Stein) was solved by Oka, for univalent domains in $\mathbb C^2$ in 1942 (with a remark that the proof works for all $n\ge2$) and for unramified Riemann domains over $\mathbb C^n$ in 1953, with independent proofs for domains in $\mathbb C^n$ by Norguet and Bremermann (1954); in Oka's form an unbranched Riemann domain over $\mathbb C^n$ is Stein iff $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, $d$ the boundary distance. See [Plurisubharmonic Functions](node:Plurisubharmonic%20Functions) and [Levi Convexity](node:Levi%20Convexity). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold); [Coltoiu survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0905.2343); [Noguchi, chronicle](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246); [Cieliebak–Eliashberg](https://math.stanford.edu/~eliash/Public/269A/Stein-notes.pdf))
- **[Oka–Weil approximation](node:Holomorphic%20Approximation):** if $X$ is a Stein space and $K\subset X$ is a compact $\mathcal O(X)$-convex set, every function holomorphic near $K$ is a uniform limit on $K$ of functions in $\mathcal O(X)$; for polynomially convex $K\subset\mathbb C^n$ the approximants can be polynomials. Runge's theorem need not hold in several variables, which is why Oka–Weil is used instead. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oka%E2%80%93Weil_theorem))
- **Remmert reduction (32E05):** for a holomorphically convex manifold $X$, identifying points not separated by $\mathcal O(X)$ yields a quotient $\varphi:X\to Y$ with $\varphi_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y$; $Y$ is a Stein space whose holomorphic functions correspond to those of $X$. Mongodi applies it to a variant of the union problem: whether an increasing union of holomorphically convex subspaces is holomorphically convex. ([Boudreaux–Shafikov, §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.27100); [Mongodi](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08104))
- **Embedding dimension:** every Stein manifold of dimension $n>1$ embeds properly holomorphically into $\mathbb C^N$ with $N=[3n/2]+1$ (Eliashberg–Gromov 1992, improved by one for odd $n$ by Schürmann), and Forster showed this $N$ is minimal for every $n>1$. See [Proper Holomorphic Maps](node:Proper%20Holomorphic%20Maps). ([Forstnerič 2018, Thm 2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/1709.05630v5); [Cieliebak–Eliashberg](https://math.stanford.edu/~eliash/Public/269A/Stein-notes.pdf))
- **Noncritical functions:** every Stein manifold of dimension $n$ carries $[(n+1)/2]$ holomorphic functions with pointwise independent differentials, a number Forstnerič states is maximal, in particular a holomorphic function with no critical points, extending Gunning–Narasimhan (1967) for open Riemann surfaces. ([Forstnerič 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0211112))

### History
Cartan and Thullen gave the first results on domains of holomorphy through holomorphic convexity; Weil (1935) and Oka (1937) published the papers behind the Oka–Weil theorem. Behnke and Stein proved in 1948 that connected noncompact Riemann surfaces are Stein, and Stein introduced the manifolds in 1951. Cartan proved Theorems A and B around 1951, in a cohomological form attributed to Serre. Oka solved the Levi problem for univalent domains in 1942 and for unramified Riemann domains in 1953, Grauert for manifolds in 1958, and Narasimhan extended it to Stein spaces in 1962. ([Wikipedia, hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphically_convex_hull); [Wikipedia, Oka–Weil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oka%E2%80%93Weil_theorem); [Wikipedia, Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold); [Wikipedia, Cartan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%27s_theorems_A_and_B); [Coltoiu survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0905.2343); [Noguchi, chronicle](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1807.08246))

The optimal embedding dimension appeared in Eliashberg and Gromov's 1992 Annals of Mathematics paper, after intermediate work of Forster, with Schürmann's refinement for odd dimensions. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/2946547); [Cieliebak–Eliashberg](https://math.stanford.edu/~eliash/Public/269A/Stein-notes.pdf); [Forstnerič 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/1709.05630v5))

### Open problems
- **Unions of disjoint balls.** Whether every finite union of disjoint closed balls in $\mathbb C^n$ is polynomially convex is an old open problem. Kallin settled three balls; Gorai states that four balls in $\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge2$, is open. Khudaiberganov proved polynomial convexity when the centres lie in $\mathbb R^n$, Gorai extended this to centres in suitable Lagrangian configurations, and Nemirovski proved every such union is rationally convex. ([Gorai 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.04094); [Nemirovski](https://arxiv.org/html/0712.2948v2))
- **Local Steinness (singular Levi) problem.** If $X$ is a Stein space and $D\subset X$ is locally Stein, must $D$ be Stein? Coltoiu's 2009 survey calls this and the union problem (is an increasing union of Stein open subsets of a Stein space Stein?) well-known open problems. Both have positive answers on Stein manifolds (Docquier–Grauert; Behnke–Stein for $\mathbb C^n$), and the local problem was solved for isolated singularities by Andreotti–Narasimhan in 1964. ([Coltoiu survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0905.2343))
- **Embedding open Riemann surfaces in $\mathbb C^2$.** Forstnerič's 2018 survey states that it is still open whether every open Riemann surface embeds properly holomorphically into $\mathbb C^2$, the $n=1$ case not covered by the Eliashberg–Gromov bound. ([Forstnerič 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/1709.05630v5))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold): definitions, Behnke–Stein, Grauert's characterization, embeddings.
- **Reference:** [Holomorphically convex hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphically_convex_hull): hulls, domains of holomorphy, equivalent conditions.
- **Learn:** [Cieliebak and Eliashberg, Symplectic Geometry of Stein Manifolds (draft notes)](https://math.stanford.edu/~eliash/Public/269A/Stein-notes.pdf): chapter on complex analysis on Stein manifolds; hulls, three definitions of Stein, Remmert and Grauert theorems.
- **Primary:** [Forstnerič, Holomorphic embeddings and immersions of Stein manifolds: a survey](https://arxiv.org/html/1709.05630v5): embedding dimensions and open embedding problems.
- **Primary:** [Coltoiu, The Levi problem on Stein spaces with singularities. A survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2343): Levi, local Steinness and union problems.
- **Primary:** [Forstnerič, Noncritical holomorphic functions on Stein manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0211112): holomorphic submersions on Stein manifolds.
- **Further reading:** [Forstnerič, Stein Manifolds and Holomorphic Mappings (Springer, Ergebnisse der Mathematik und ihrer Grenzgebiete, 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-61058-0): monograph on Stein geometry and Oka theory.
- **Further reading:** [Polynomial Convexity (Birkhäuser, Progress in Mathematics, 2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-8176-4538-0): E. L. Stout's monograph on polynomial and rational convexity, as cited by [Gorai](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.04094).
references.MSC 32Fxx - Geometric convexity in sever:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 32Fxx collects the conditions on a domain or complex manifold that play the role convexity plays in real analysis, together with their analytic and topological consequences. The basic object is a real hypersurface $M=\partial U$ cut out by a defining function $r$ with $U=\{r<0\}$, $r=0$ and $dr\neq0$ on $\partial U$; the Levi form is the complex Hessian of $r$ restricted to the holomorphic tangent space $T^{1,0}_pM=\ker\partial r(p)$, and it is independent of the defining function up to a positive factor. Pseudoconvexity, the positive semidefiniteness of this form, is the weakest of the standard convexity notions and the only one invariant under biholomorphisms. ([Curry–Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV, §2.4, §4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056))

The subject branches in three directions. Weakening positivity to a count of positive Levi eigenvalues gives Andreotti–Grauert $q$-convexity, which controls finiteness and vanishing of coherent cohomology in degrees $\ge q$ ([Andreotti–Grauert theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreotti%E2%80%93Grauert_theorem)). Measuring how degenerate a weakly pseudoconvex boundary is leads to D'Angelo and Catlin finite type, which governs subelliptic estimates for the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem ([Nicoara, Notions of Higher Type](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03168v1)). Holomorphically invariant Finsler metrics, the Kobayashi and Carathéodory metrics, translate boundary convexity into intrinsic geometry ([Kim–Krantz, Complex scaling, §6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0610710)).

### Scope
The MSC2020 subdivisions of 32Fxx are: 32F10 $q$-convexity, $q$-concavity; 32F17 other notions of convexity in relation to several complex variables; 32F18 finite-type conditions for the boundary of a domain; 32F27 topological consequences of geometric convexity; 32F32 analytical consequences of geometric convexity (vanishing theorems, etc.); 32F45 invariant metrics and pseudodistances in several complex variables; 32F99 none of the above. ([MSC2020, 32Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Fxx))

Neighbouring sections of 32-XX include [MSC 32Exx - Holomorphic convexity](node:MSC%2032Exx%20-%20Holomorphic%20convexity), [MSC 32Txx - Pseudoconvex domains](node:MSC%2032Txx%20-%20Pseudoconvex%20domains) (which has its own codes for strongly pseudoconvex, worm and finite-type domains), [MSC 32Wxx - Differential operators in several variables](node:MSC%2032Wxx%20-%20Differential%20operators%20in%20several%20variables) and [MSC 32Qxx - Complex manifolds](node:MSC%2032Qxx%20-%20Complex%20manifolds). ([MSC2020, 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX); [MSC2020, 32Txx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Txx))

### Key concepts
- **Levi pseudoconvexity ([Levi Convexity](node:Levi%20Convexity), [Pseudoconvexity](node:Pseudoconvexity)).** For a $C^2$ domain $U=\{r<0\}$, $U$ is pseudoconvex at $p\in\partial U$ when $\sum_{j,k}a_j\bar a_k\,\partial^2 r/\partial z_j\partial\bar z_k(p)\ge0$ for all $a$ with $\sum_j a_j\,\partial r/\partial z_j(p)=0$, and strongly pseudoconvex when the Levi form is positive definite. Every convex domain is a domain of holomorphy, and a strongly pseudoconvex boundary is locally strongly convex after a biholomorphic change of coordinates. ([Curry–Lebl, §2.1–2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056)) For $C^2$ boundaries this agrees with Hartogs pseudoconvexity, the existence of a continuous [plurisubharmonic](node:Plurisubharmonic%20Functions) exhaustion. ([Wikipedia, Pseudoconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoconvexity))
- **$q$-convexity and the Andreotti–Grauert theorem (32F10, 32F32).** A real function is $q$-convex on an $n$-dimensional manifold if its Levi form has at least $n-q+1$ positive eigenvalues at every point; $X$ is $q$-complete if it has a $q$-convex exhaustion, so $1$-convex means strongly plurisubharmonic and $1$-complete manifolds are exactly [Stein manifolds](node:Stein%20Spaces). ([Forstnerič–Smrekar–Sukhov](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1404.2225)) **Theorem (Andreotti–Grauert 1962).** For a complex space $X$ and a coherent sheaf $\mathcal F$, $\dim_{\mathbb C}H^i(X,\mathcal F)<\infty$ for $i\ge q$ if $X$ is $q$-pseudoconvex, and $H^i(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for $i\ge q$ if $X$ is $q$-complete; in the $q$-pseudoconcave case finiteness holds for $i<\operatorname{codh}(\mathcal F)-q$. ([Wikipedia, Andreotti–Grauert theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreotti%E2%80%93Grauert_theorem))
- **Topological consequence (32F27).** A $q$-complete manifold of dimension $n$ is a handlebody with handles of index at most $n+q-1$ (Morse theory on a $q$-convex Morse exhaustion), so $H^k(M;G)=0$ for $k>n+q-1$ and any abelian group $G$; such a manifold contains no compact complex submanifold of dimension at least $q$. ([Forstnerič–Smrekar–Sukhov](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1404.2225))
- **Finite type (32F18).** D'Angelo's $1$-type at $x_0\in M$ is $\Delta_1(M,x_0)=\sup_\varphi \operatorname{ord}_0(\varphi^*r)/\operatorname{ord}_0(\varphi)$ over holomorphic curves $\varphi$ through $x_0$, with $q$-types $\Delta_q$ defined as an infimum of $1$-types over linear slices $\mathbb C^{n-q+1}\hookrightarrow\mathbb C^n$; Catlin's $D_q$ takes a supremum over germs of $q$-dimensional varieties through $x_0$. **Theorem (D'Angelo 1982).** $\Delta_q$ is independent of the defining function and, if $\Delta_q(M,x_0)<\infty$, then $\Delta_q(M,x)\le 2\Delta_q(M,x_0)^{n-q}$ near $x_0$, so the finite-type locus is open (no pseudoconvexity needed); $\Delta_q$ itself need not be upper semicontinuous. **Theorem (Brinzanescu–Nicoara 2023).** For a $q$-positive (e.g. pseudoconvex) domain, $\Delta_q\le D_q\le 2(\Delta_q)^{n-q}$, and Fassina gave an ideal with $\Delta_2=3$, $D_2=4$, so the two types differ in general. ([Nicoara](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03168v1))
- **Subelliptic estimates.** Kohn showed that for pseudoconvex domains with real-analytic boundary, subellipticity of the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem on $(p,q)$-forms is equivalent to finite order of contact of $q$-dimensional varieties with the boundary, building subelliptic multipliers algebraically; Catlin proved necessity (1983) and sufficiency (1987) of finite $q$-type for smooth pseudoconvex domains. ([Nicoara](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03168v1)) Consequently the Neumann operator $N$ and the Bergman projection $B$ are $C^\infty$ pseudolocal on domains of finite type, in particular on strictly pseudoconvex ones. ([Christ](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9511203)) See [Hardy and Bergman Spaces](node:Hardy%20and%20Bergman%20Spaces).
- **Worm domains.** Diederich and Fornæss constructed smoothly bounded pseudoconvex worm domains $W\subset\mathbb C^2$, strictly pseudoconvex off an annulus in the boundary. Barrett proved that for large $s$, $N$ and $B$ are unbounded on the Sobolev space $H^s(W)$; **Theorem (Christ).** On worm domains, $N$ on $(0,1)$-forms and $B$ do not preserve $C^\infty(\overline W)$, answering negatively whether smooth bounded pseudoconvexity alone gives global regularity. ([Christ, Global $C^\infty$ irregularity](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9511203))
- **Invariant metrics (32F45).** The Carathéodory metric is $F_C(z,\xi)=\sup\{|f_*(z)\xi|: f:\Omega\to\mathbb D \text{ holomorphic},\ f(z)=0\}$ and the Kobayashi–Royden metric is $F_K(z,\xi)=\inf\{|\alpha|: f:\mathbb D\to\Omega,\ f(0)=z,\ f'(0)=\xi/\alpha\}$. **Theorem (Graham 1975).** On a bounded strongly pseudoconvex domain with $C^2$ boundary, as $z\to P\in\partial\Omega$ nontangentially, $d_\Omega(z)F(z,\xi)\to\tfrac12|\xi_N|$ for both $F=F_C,F_K$, while complex-tangential directions blow up only like $d_\Omega^{-1/2}$ with a constant given by the Levi form. **Theorem (Wong–Rosay).** A bounded domain with an automorphism orbit accumulating at a $C^2$ strongly pseudoconvex boundary point is biholomorphic to the ball. ([Kim–Krantz, Thms 4.1, 6.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0610710)) A complex space is Kobayashi hyperbolic when its Kobayashi pseudodistance is a distance; bounded domains are hyperbolic, and a compact complex space is hyperbolic iff every holomorphic map $\mathbb C\to X$ is constant (Brody). ([Wikipedia, Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric))

### History
The Levi problem, whether pseudoconvex domains are domains of holomorphy, was solved principally by Oka in the early 1950s; the modern proof uses the $L^2$ $\bar\partial$-methods of Kohn, Hörmander, and Andreotti–Vesentini from the mid-1960s. ([Curry–Lebl, §4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056)) Andreotti and Grauert published their finiteness theorem in *Bull. Soc. Math. France* 90 (1962). ([Wikipedia, Andreotti–Grauert theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreotti%E2%80%93Grauert_theorem)) D'Angelo defined his types in 1982 and Catlin his in 1987, the year he completed the sufficiency half of the subellipticity theorem; Kohn's real-analytic theory appeared in *Acta Math.* in 1979. ([Nicoara](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03168v1)) Graham's boundary asymptotics date from 1975; Christ's worm-domain irregularity theorem built on Barrett's Sobolev counterexample. ([Kim–Krantz](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0610710); [Christ](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9511203))

### Open problems
- **Kohn conjecture.** Whether Kohn's algebraic construction of subelliptic multipliers, which proves the equivalence of subellipticity and finite order of contact for real-analytic boundaries, can be carried out for pseudoconvex domains with $C^\infty$ boundary; the obstruction is that no Nullstellensatz is known for the real radical in the $C^\infty$ category, and Nicoara records the problem as still open. ([Nicoara](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03168v1))
- **Bloom conjecture.** Commutator type with respect to $q$-dimensional subbundles should equal the order of contact with $q$-dimensional complex manifolds; proved for pseudoconvex hypersurfaces in $\mathbb C^3$ by Huang–Yin (2021), with only partial results for $n\ge4$. ([Nicoara](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03168v1))
- **Greene–Krantz conjecture.** If an automorphism orbit of a smoothly bounded domain accumulates at a boundary point $p$, then $p$ is of finite type; Kim and Krantz describe the full conjecture as open. ([Kim–Krantz, Conj. 5.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0610710))
- **Subelliptic estimates and finite type.** D'Angelo and Kohn close their survey (MSRI volume, 2000) with a list of nine open problems on subelliptic estimates, finite type, and their applications. ([D'Angelo–Kohn](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/several-complex-variables/subelliptic-estimates-and-finite-type/47B8058CB6222A781431EA9E70BC47B1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Pseudoconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoconvexity): Hartogs and Levi pseudoconvexity and their equivalence for $C^2$ boundaries.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Andreotti–Grauert theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreotti%E2%80%93Grauert_theorem): statement of finiteness and vanishing for $q$-convex spaces.
- **Learn:** [Curry–Lebl, Tasty Bits of Several Complex Variables (lecture notes)](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01056): defining functions, the Levi form, convexity notions, and the Levi problem.
- **Primary:** [Nicoara, Notions of Higher Type](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03168v1): survey of D'Angelo and Catlin $q$-types, their comparison, and open conjectures.
- **Primary:** [Christ, Global $C^\infty$ irregularity of the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem for worm domains](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9511203): the worm-domain counterexample to global regularity.
- **Primary:** [Kim–Krantz, Complex scaling and geometric analysis of several variables](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0610710): scaling, Wong–Rosay, invariant metrics and Graham's asymptotics.
- **Further reading:** [D'Angelo–Kohn, Subelliptic estimates and finite type (in Schneider–Siu, *Several Complex Variables*, MSRI/CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/several-complex-variables/subelliptic-estimates-and-finite-type/47B8058CB6222A781431EA9E70BC47B1): survey of the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem and finite type.
references.MSC 32Gxx - Deformations of analytic str:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 32Gxx studies how complex-analytic structures vary in families and how the resulting parameter spaces (deformation spaces, Teichmüller spaces, moduli and period spaces) are built. The basic object is a proper holomorphic submersion $\pi:\mathcal X\to\Delta$ over a small ball whose central fibre is a given compact complex manifold $M$; all fibres are diffeomorphic to $M$, but their complex structures can differ. A deformation is described by a tangent-valued $(0,1)$-form $\xi(t)\in A^{0,1}(M,T_M)$, built from [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms) with values in the holomorphic [Tangent Bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle), and the forms $\xi(t)$ define an integrable complex structure on the total space, that is, a holomorphic family, exactly when $\bar\partial\xi+\tfrac12[\xi,\xi]=0$ (each fibre's almost complex structure is integrable) and $\xi$ is holomorphic in $t$ (the structures vary holomorphically). ([Schnell, §2](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~cschnell/pdf/notes/kodaira.pdf))

The linear theory is controlled by sheaf cohomology of the tangent sheaf: first-order deformations live in $H^1(M,\Theta_M)$ and obstructions to extending them lie in $H^2(M,\Theta_M)$. Kodaira and Spencer put the deformation theory of complex manifolds on a firm basis, Spencer extended the techniques to other structures in differential geometry, and Grothendieck placed the theory in abstract algebraic geometry. ([Wikipedia: Deformation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_theory)) The local theory for a single manifold is in [Deformations of Complex Structures](node:Deformations%20of%20Complex%20Structures); this map covers the whole subfield, including Teichmüller theory and variations of Hodge structure.

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 32Gxx into: 32G05 deformations of complex structures; 32G07 deformations of special (e.g. CR) structures; 32G08 deformations of fiber bundles; 32G10 deformations of submanifolds and subspaces; 32G13 complex-analytic moduli problems; 32G15 moduli of Riemann surfaces and Teichmüller theory (complex-analytic aspects in several variables); 32G20 period matrices, variation of Hodge structure, and degenerations; 32G34 moduli and deformations for ordinary differential equations (e.g. the Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equation); 32G81 applications to the sciences; 32G99 other. ([MSC2020 32Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Gxx))

Neighbouring codes, as delimited by the classification's own cross-references:
- **[MSC 14Dxx - Families, fibrations in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Dxx%20-%20Families,%20fibrations%20in%20algebraic%20geometry):** the algebraic counterpart. Algebraic moduli problems go to 14D20/14D22 while analytic ones go to 32G13, formal and algebraic deformations to 14D15, and algebro-geometric variation of Hodge structure to 14D07 rather than 32G20. ([MSC2020 14Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Dxx); [MSC2020 32Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Gxx))
- **[MSC 30Fxx - Riemann surfaces](node:MSC%2030Fxx%20-%20Riemann%20surfaces):** 32G15 cross-refers to 30Fxx and 14H15 and keeps the several-variables, complex-analytic side of Teichmüller theory. ([MSC2020 32Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Gxx))
- **[MSC 32Jxx - Compact analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Jxx%20-%20Compact%20analytic%20spaces):** its codes cover compactification, algebraic dependence theorems, compact complex surfaces, 3-folds and $n$-folds, and compact Kähler manifolds (generalizations, classification). ([MSC2020 32Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Jxx))
- **[MSC 58Hxx - Pseudogroups, differentiable groupoids and general structures on manifolds](node:MSC%2058Hxx%20-%20Pseudogroups,%20differentiable%20groupoids%20and%20general%20structures%20on%20manifolds):** 32G05 cross-refers to 58H10 and 58H15 for deformations of general geometric structures on manifolds. ([MSC2020 32Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Gxx))

### Key concepts
- **Kodaira–Spencer map.** For a smooth proper family $\mathcal M\to B$ with special fibre $M=\mathcal M_0$, it is the connecting homomorphism $\mathrm{KS}:T_0B\to H^1(M,T_M)$ of the long exact sequence for $0\to T_M\to T_{\mathcal M}|_M\to T_0B\otimes\mathcal O_M\to 0$. ([Wikipedia: Kodaira–Spencer map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira%E2%80%93Spencer_map))
- **Kodaira–Nirenberg–Spencer theorem.** If $M$ is a compact complex manifold with $H^2(M,T_M)=0$, there is a deformation family of $M$ over a small ball in $H^1(M,T_M)$ whose Kodaira–Spencer map at the origin is the identity; it was conjectured by Kodaira and Spencer and proved with Nirenberg. ([Schnell, §3](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~cschnell/pdf/notes/kodaira.pdf))
- **Kuranishi's theorem.** Every compact complex manifold $Y$ has a Kuranishi family $(\mathcal Y,Y_0)\to(\mathfrak B(Y),0)$ that is semi-universal; its base $\mathfrak B(Y)$ is the germ at $0$ of the zero set of a holomorphic Kuranishi map $k:H^1(Y,\Theta_Y)\to H^2(Y,\Theta_Y)$ with $dk(0)=0$, whose quadratic term is the Schouten bracket. Hence $\dim\mathfrak B(Y)\ge h^1(\Theta_Y)-h^2(\Theta_Y)$. The family is universal if $H^0(Y,\Theta_Y)=0$. Grauert extended semi-universal deformations to compact complex spaces, with base a germ in $\mathbb T^1$ and obstructions in $\mathbb T^2$. ([Catanese, §§1.2–1.3, 2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.1368))
- **Stability of Kähler structures and unobstructedness.** If $Y$ is compact Kähler, every small deformation $Y_t$ is again Kähler (Kodaira–Morrow). For compact Kähler $Y$ with trivial canonical bundle, the Kuranishi space is smooth (Bogomolov–Tian–Todorov). ([Catanese, §1.4, Prop. 15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.1368)) In Auroux's formulation: a compact Calabi–Yau manifold with $H^0(X,T_X)=0$ has unobstructed deformations, and contraction with the holomorphic volume form gives $T_X\cong\Omega^{n-1}_X$. ([Auroux, MIT 18.969 Lecture 3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-969-topics-in-geometry-mirror-symmetry-spring-2009/1232012395d30aca2bf98aacbb7ad036_MIT18_969s09_lec03.pdf)) See [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds).
- **Teichmüller space (32G15).** $\mathcal T(M)=\mathcal C(M)/\mathrm{Diff}^0(M)$, complex structures modulo diffeomorphisms isotopic to the identity, with moduli space $\mathfrak M(M)=\mathcal T(M)/\mathrm{Map}(M)$. ([Catanese, §1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.1368)) For a closed surface of genus $g\ge2$, $\mathcal T_g$ is homeomorphic to a ball of real dimension $6g-6$ and, via the Bers embedding, a complex space of dimension $3g-3$. The mapping class group acts properly discontinuously with quotient the moduli space of [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces). The Kobayashi metric coincides with the Teichmüller metric, a fact used in Royden's proof that the mapping class group is the full isometry group of the Teichmüller metric. ([Wikipedia: Teichmüller space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teichm%C3%BCller_space)) See [Mapping Class Groups of Surfaces](node:Mapping%20Class%20Groups%20of%20Surfaces) and [Moduli Spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces).
- **Variation of Hodge structure (32G20).** Over a complex manifold $X$: a local system $S$ of finitely generated abelian groups, plus a decreasing filtration $F^\bullet$ on $S\otimes\mathcal O_X$ inducing weight-$n$ Hodge structures on the stalks. Griffiths transversality says the Gauss–Manin connection satisfies $\nabla F^p\subset F^{p-1}\otimes\Omega^1_X$. Variations of Hodge structure were first studied by Griffiths (1968). ([Wikipedia: Variation of Hodge structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variation_of_Hodge_structure)) For a Kähler manifold with trivial canonical bundle, the local period map on the Kuranishi space is injective, so the Kuranishi space maps locally homeomorphically to Teichmüller space. ([Catanese, §1.4, Prop. 15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.1368)) See [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory).
- **Douady space (32G10, 32G13).** For a separated complex space $X$, the set $H(X)$ of compact analytic subspaces of $X$ carries the structure of a complex space. The same holds for coherent quotients with compact support of a coherent sheaf; the proof required a theory of Banach analytic spaces. ([Douady 1966](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226))

### History
Riemann already counted $6g-6$ real parameters for genus-$g$ surfaces. Teichmüller introduced quasiconformal methods, and Ahlfors and Bers developed the analytic theory after World War II. ([Wikipedia: Teichmüller space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teichm%C3%BCller_space)) Kodaira and Spencer founded the deformation theory of higher-dimensional complex manifolds. Kodaira records that they could not prove convergence of the formal power-series solutions until Nirenberg joined them. ([Schnell, §3](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~cschnell/pdf/notes/kodaira.pdf); [Wikipedia: Deformation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_theory)) Douady's 1966 paper in *Annales de l'Institut Fourier* constructed the space of compact subspaces. ([Douady 1966](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226)) Griffiths' papers on periods of integrals on algebraic manifolds (1968–1970) began the study of variations of Hodge structure, and Deligne's mixed Hodge theory followed in papers of 1971–1974. ([Wikipedia: Variation of Hodge structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variation_of_Hodge_structure)) Catanese cites the unobstructedness theorem for Kähler manifolds with trivial canonical divisor to Bogomolov (1978), Tian (1986) and Todorov (1989). ([Catanese, §1.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.1368))

### Open problems
- **Teichmüller vs Kuranishi space.** Catanese asks when Teichmüller space is locally homeomorphic to Kuranishi space. He cannot settle this for all surfaces of general type, because it depends on whether complex automorphisms isotopic to the identity exist. His Proposition 15 gives a criterion (an injective local period map on a compact Kähler manifold), which applies to Kähler manifolds with trivial canonical divisor. ([Catanese, §1 and Prop. 15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.1368))
- **Rigidification.** $Y$ is *rigidified* if $\mathrm{Aut}(Y)\cap\mathrm{Diff}^0(Y)=\{\mathrm{Id}_Y\}$. Catanese calls it "an interesting question whether compact complex manifolds of general type are rigidified", and reports Jin Xing Cai's conjecture that simply connected surfaces of general type are rigidified. ([Catanese, §1.4, Def. 12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.1368))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kodaira–Spencer map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira%E2%80%93Spencer_map), [Teichmüller space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teichm%C3%BCller_space), and [Variation of Hodge structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variation_of_Hodge_structure): definitions for the three main subareas.
- **Learn:** [Schnell, Deformations of complex structures](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~cschnell/pdf/notes/kodaira.pdf): the integrability equation, the Kodaira–Spencer map, and the Kodaira–Nirenberg–Spencer theorem. Also [Auroux, Mirror Symmetry Lecture 3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-969-topics-in-geometry-mirror-symmetry-spring-2009/resources/mit18_969s09_lec03/): the Bogomolov–Tian–Todorov theorem and Calabi–Yau moduli.
- **Primary:** [Catanese, A superficial working guide to deformations and moduli](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1106.1368): survey covering Kuranishi and Grauert theory, Teichmüller vs Kuranishi spaces, period maps, and open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Douady, Le problème des modules pour les sous-espaces analytiques compacts (1966)](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226): the original construction of the Douady space.
references.MSC 32Hxx - Holomorphic mappings and cor:
## Reference
### Overview
