A holomorphic map between open sets of $\mathbb C^n$ is a map whose components are holomorphic; a holomorphic map between [complex manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds) is one whose expressions in compatible holomorphic charts are holomorphic. Locally the theory starts from the holomorphic inverse and implicit function theorems. ([MIT 18.117, Lecture 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/989bea2ba42545febc2830a2b5f59cf2_18117_lec07.pdf))

Rigidity is the dividing line from one variable. In $\mathbb C$, conformal maps between smoothly bounded domains extend to diffeomorphisms of the closures (Painlevé, Kellogg), and Fefferman generalized this to strictly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb C^n$ in 1974. In higher dimension proper self-maps of the ball are automorphisms, and proper maps between balls of different dimensions are often forced to be linear or to take values in a lower-dimensional ball. ([Krantz–Li, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9611202); [Huang–Ji–Yin, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.6440)) Value distribution and hyperbolicity ask instead when entire curves $\mathbb C\to X$ exist ([Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric)), and holomorphic dynamics studies iteration, for instance basins of attraction of automorphisms of $\mathbb C^n$. ([Fatou–Bieberbach domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatou%E2%80%93Bieberbach_domain))

### Scope
MSC2020 32Hxx lists: 32H02 holomorphic mappings, (holomorphic) embeddings and related questions; 32H04 meromorphic mappings; 32H12 boundary uniqueness of mappings; 32H25 Picard-type theorems and generalizations; 32H30 value distribution theory in higher dimensions (for function-theoretic properties see 32A22, also cross-referenced at 32H25); 32H35 proper holomorphic mappings, finiteness theorems; 32H40 boundary regularity of mappings; 32H50 iteration of holomorphic maps, fixed points of holomorphic maps and related problems; 32H99. ([MSC2020, 32Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Hxx))

Neighbours: 32A22 holds function-theoretic value distribution (per the entry's cross-reference); complex spaces with a group of automorphisms are [MSC 32Mxx - Complex spaces with a group of automorphisms](node:MSC%2032Mxx%20-%20Complex%20spaces%20with%20a%20group%20of%20automorphisms); the domains studied in boundary-regularity problems are classified under [MSC 32Fxx - Geometric convexity in several complex variables](node:MSC%2032Fxx%20-%20Geometric%20convexity%20in%20several%20complex%20variables) and [MSC 32Txx - Pseudoconvex domains](node:MSC%2032Txx%20-%20Pseudoconvex%20domains); [MSC 37Fxx - Dynamical systems over complex numbers](node:MSC%2037Fxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20over%20complex%20numbers), which cross-references 32H50, covers holomorphic dynamics from the dynamical-systems side, including one-variable Fatou and Julia sets (37F10) and higher-dimensional dynamics (37F80). ([MSC2020, 32Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Hxx); [MSC2020, 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX); [MSC2020, 37Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Holomorphic inverse and implicit function theorems ([Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem)).** If $f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ is holomorphic on open $U\subset\mathbb C^n$ and $\partial f/\partial z(p)$ is bijective, $f$ maps a neighbourhood of $p$ biholomorphically onto a neighbourhood of $f(p)$. If $f_1,\dots,f_k\in\mathcal O(U)$ have linearly independent differentials at $p$, there is a biholomorphism $\varphi:(V,0)\to(U_1,p)$ with $\varphi^*f_i=z_i$ for $i\le k$. ([MIT 18.117, Lecture 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/989bea2ba42545febc2830a2b5f59cf2_18117_lec07.pdf))
- **Proper maps and Remmert's theorem ([Proper Holomorphic Maps](node:Proper%20Holomorphic%20Maps)).** A holomorphic $F$ from $\mathbb B^n$ into $\mathbb B^N$ is proper if $F^{-1}(K)$ is compact for every compact $K$. ([Huang–Ji–Yin, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.6440)) For a holomorphic $f:M\to N$ of complex manifolds and complex analytic $A\subset M$, if $f(A)$ is closed and subanalytic in $N$ it is complex analytic; Remmert's proper mapping theorem is the case of proper $f$, which makes $f(A)$ closed and subanalytic. Without such a hypothesis the image can fail to be analytic: project $\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(1/n,n)\}\subset\mathbb C^2$ to the first coordinate. ([Peterzil–Starchenko, Thm 2.1 and remarks](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410274))
- **Fefferman's mapping theorem (32H40).** A biholomorphic map between smoothly bounded strictly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb C^n$ extends to a diffeomorphism of their closures (Fefferman, 1974). His proof used boundary asymptotics of the Bergman kernel and Kohn's regularity of the $\bar\partial$-Neumann operator; Bell and Ligocka gave a simpler proof, valid also for pseudoconvex domains of finite type, using regularity of the Bergman projection. ([Krantz–Li, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9611202))
- **Proper maps between balls (32H35).** For $n>1$, every proper holomorphic self-map of $\mathbb B^n$ is an automorphism (Alexander). For maps $\mathbb B^n\to\mathbb B^N$: Webster showed that a proper map into $\mathbb B^{n+1}$, $n>2$, which is $C^3$ up to the boundary, is a totally geodesic (linear) embedding; Faran showed linearity for $N<2n-1$ under real-analytic boundary regularity, and Huang reduced the regularity to $C^2$; Faran found four inequivalent proper maps $\mathbb B^2\to\mathbb B^3$ that are $C^3$ to the boundary. Forstnerič proved that proper maps $C^{N-n+1}$ up to the boundary are rational. ([Huang–Ji–Yin, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.6440))
- **Gap phenomena.** With $I_k=[kn+1,(k+1)n-k(k+1)/2-1]$, no new proper rational maps appear for $N\in I_1=[n+1,2n-2]$ (Faran), $N\in I_2=[2n+1,3n-4]$ (Huang–Ji–Xu, $n\ge4$, $C^3$ maps), and $N\in I_3=[3n+1,4n-7]$ for $n>7$ (Huang–Ji–Yin): every such map is equivalent to $(G,0)$ with $G$ into a lower-dimensional ball. D'Angelo's family $F_\theta$ gives inequivalent quadratic proper maps $\mathbb B^n\to\mathbb B^{2n}$. ([Huang–Ji–Yin, Thm 1.1 and §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.6440))
- **Kobayashi hyperbolicity and value distribution (32H25, 32H30).** The Kobayashi pseudometric $d_X$ is the largest pseudometric with $d_X(f(x),f(y))\le\rho(x,y)$ for all holomorphic $f:\mathbb D\to X$, $\rho$ the Poincaré distance; $X$ is hyperbolic if $d_X$ is a metric. Bounded domains, compact curves of genus $\ge2$, and $\mathbb C$ minus two points are hyperbolic. Brody: a compact complex space is hyperbolic if and only if every holomorphic map $\mathbb C\to X$ is constant. ([Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric)) Compare [Hyperbolic Space](node:Hyperbolic%20Space) for the real model.
- **Fatou–Bieberbach domains and dynamics (32H50).** A Fatou–Bieberbach domain is a proper subdomain of $\mathbb C^n$ biholomorphic to $\mathbb C^n$; none exist for $n=1$. If an automorphism $F$ of $\mathbb C^n$ fixes $p$ and all eigenvalues of $F'(p)$ have modulus $<1$, the basin of attraction of $p$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb C^n$ (Rosay–Rudin, 1988), giving such domains when the basin is proper, e.g. for $F(z,w)=(w+z^2,az)$, $0<|a|<1$. No Fatou–Bieberbach domain is bounded, and the inverse biholomorphism is never polynomial. ([Fatou–Bieberbach domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatou%E2%80%93Bieberbach_domain)) The one-variable analogue is [Julia and Fatou Sets](node:Julia%20and%20Fatou%20Sets).

### History
Rigidity of proper maps between balls goes back to Poincaré; Alexander's theorem, Webster's and Faran's work, and the gap theorems of Hamada, Huang, Ji, Xu and Yin form the modern line. ([Huang–Ji–Yin, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.6440)) Fefferman's boundary-extension theorem appeared in 1974, generalizing Painlevé and Kellogg; Bell–Ligocka and Bell simplified it. ([Krantz–Li, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9611202)) Fatou (1922) and Bieberbach (1933) first studied the domains named after them; the subject revived in the 1980s, and whether non-Runge Fatou–Bieberbach domains exist, a long-standing question, was answered affirmatively by Wold in 2008. ([Fatou–Bieberbach domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatou%E2%80%93Bieberbach_domain)) McQuillan (1998) proved the Green–Griffiths–Lang conjecture for surfaces with $c_1^2>c_2$, and Brotbek (2016; published 2017) proved Kobayashi's conjecture on the hyperbolicity of general hypersurfaces of high degree. ([Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric)) Siu's strategy from the early 2000s had been completed in 2015, and Brotbek's 2016 proof used a different method. ([Demailly 2018, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.04765))

### Open problems
- **Green–Griffiths–Lang conjecture.** For a projective variety $X$ of general type there should be a proper closed algebraic subset $Y\subsetneq X$ containing the image of every nonconstant holomorphic map $\mathbb C\to X$; the source calls this a central open problem. Known for surfaces of general type with $c_1^2>c_2$ (McQuillan); results for general hypersurfaces of high degree use jet differentials. ([Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric))
- **Huang–Ji–Yin gap conjecture.** For $n\ge3$, a proper rational map $\mathbb B^n\to\mathbb B^N$ is always equivalent to one of the form $(G,0)$ exactly when $N\in I_k$ for some $1\le k\le K(n)$. The 2014 paper states it as a conjecture, proved for $k=1,2,3$. ([Huang–Ji–Yin, Conjecture 1.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.6440))
- **Siu–Mok conjecture.** If $f:\mathbb B^n\to\mathbb B^N$, $1<n<N$, is proper and $M=f(\mathbb B^n)$ is invariant under a subgroup $\Gamma\subset\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb B^N)$ with $M/\Gamma$ compact, then $f$ is a linear embedding; described in 2014 as open for more than thirty years. ([Huang–Ji–Yin, Conjecture 1.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.6440))
- **Problem list items.** The 1995 Several Complex Variables Problem List asks whether every proper holomorphic self-map of a smooth bounded domain in $\mathbb C^n$, $n>1$, is biholomorphic, and asks for a classification of proper holomorphic correspondences of the disc. ([SCV Problem List, Problems 9.3.1–9.3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9509202))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric): hyperbolicity, Brody's theorem, Kobayashi and Green–Griffiths–Lang conjectures.
- **Reference:** [Fatou–Bieberbach domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatou%E2%80%93Bieberbach_domain): basins of attraction and known results.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.117, Lecture 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/989bea2ba42545febc2830a2b5f59cf2_18117_lec07.pdf): holomorphic inverse/implicit function theorems and complex manifolds, from Guillemin's course ([lecture notes index](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/pages/lecture-notes/)).
- **Primary:** [Huang–Ji–Yin, On the third gap for proper holomorphic maps between balls](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.6440): theorem plus a detailed survey of ball rigidity and the gap conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Krantz–Li, Application of the complex Monge–Ampère equation to proper holomorphic mappings](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9611202): a new proof of Fefferman's mapping theorem with history of the boundary-regularity problem.
- **Further reading:** [Buzzard–Fornæss–Gavosto–Krantz, The Several Complex Variables Problem List](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9509202): problems on maps, correspondences, and dynamics.
references.MSC 32Jxx - Compact analytic spaces:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 32Jxx collects the global theory of [compact complex analytic spaces](node:Compact%20Complex%20Spaces) and compact [complex manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds). Its subcodes cover compactification, algebraic dependence of meromorphic functions, compact complex surfaces, 3-folds and $n$-folds, the complex-analytic side of transcendental methods in algebraic geometry, and compact Kähler manifolds. The MSC sends [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces) to 14Hxx and 30Fxx and the algebraic theory of surfaces to 14Jxx. ([MSC2020, 32Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Jxx))

The central theme is how far a compact complex space is from being algebraic. Chow's theorem and Serre's GAGA show that closed analytic subspaces of projective space, and coherent analytic sheaves on them, are algebraic ([Wikipedia, GAGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry_and_analytic_geometry)). Kodaira's embedding theorem identifies projective manifolds among compact Kähler manifolds by an integrality condition on the Kähler class ([Wikipedia, Kodaira embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira_embedding_theorem)). Voisin's examples show that compact Kähler manifolds can be topologically different from all projective ones ([Voisin, arXiv:math/0312032](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312032)).

In dimension two the subject has a near-complete classification, the Enriques–Kodaira classification, and its one large unfinished piece is the class VII surfaces, which are never Kähler ([Wikipedia, Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification)). Compact analytic subspaces also form moduli: Douady gave the set of compact analytic subspaces of a complex space the structure of an analytic space ([Douady 1966](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226)).

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists these subcodes ([MSC2020, 32Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Jxx)):
- **32J05** Compactification of analytic spaces.
- **32J10** Algebraic dependence theorems.
- **32J15** Compact complex surfaces; **32J17** compact complex 3-folds; **32J18** compact complex $n$-folds.
- **32J25** Transcendental methods of algebraic geometry, complex-analytic aspects (see also 14C30).
- **32J27** Compact Kähler manifolds: generalizations, classification.
- **32J81** Applications to the sciences; **32J99** other.

Neighbouring codes:
- [MSC 14Jxx - Surfaces and higher-dimensional varieties](node:MSC%2014Jxx%20-%20Surfaces%20and%20higher-dimensional%20varieties): the 32J entry sends the algebraic theory there, and sends Riemann surfaces to 14Hxx and 30Fxx. ([MSC2020, 32Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Jxx))
- [MSC 32Qxx - Complex manifolds](node:MSC%2032Qxx%20-%20Complex%20manifolds), [MSC 32Gxx - Deformations of analytic structures](node:MSC%2032Gxx%20-%20Deformations%20of%20analytic%20structures) and [MSC 32Cxx - Analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Cxx%20-%20Analytic%20spaces) are sibling sections of 32-XX. ([MSC2020, 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Chow's theorem and GAGA.** Chow (1949): a closed analytic subspace of complex projective space is an algebraic subvariety. Serre (1956): for a complex projective variety $X$, the category of coherent algebraic sheaves on $X$ is equivalent to the category of coherent analytic sheaves on $X^{an}$, compatibly with cohomology. ([Wikipedia, GAGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry_and_analytic_geometry))
- **Kodaira embedding theorem.** Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $L$ a holomorphic line bundle. Then $L$ is positive if and only if some power $L^{\otimes m}$, $m>0$, equals $\varphi^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^N}(1)$ for a holomorphic embedding $\varphi:X\to\mathbb P^N$. Equivalently a compact Hodge manifold, one whose Kähler class is integral, embeds in projective space, and by Chow's theorem it is projective algebraic. ([Wikipedia, Kodaira embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira_embedding_theorem))
- **Hodge decomposition on compact Kähler manifolds ([Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory)).** For compact Kähler $X$, $H^r(X,\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=r}H^{p,q}(X)$ with $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$, so the odd Betti numbers are even. This fails for general compact complex manifolds; the Hopf surface, diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^3$, has $b_1=1$ and is not Kähler. ([Wikipedia, Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_theory); [Wikipedia, Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_manifold))
- **Kähler surfaces and the Kodaira problem ([Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds)).** A compact complex surface is Kähler if and only if $b_1$ is even (Kodaira and Siu, with later independent proofs by Buchdahl and Lamari). Kodaira showed every compact Kähler surface deforms to a projective surface. Voisin proved that in every dimension $\ge 4$ there are compact Kähler manifolds not homotopy equivalent to any projective manifold, so not deformation equivalent to one, which answers Kodaira's problem negatively. ([Wikipedia, Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_manifold); [Voisin, arXiv:math/0312032](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312032))
- **Algebraic dimension and Moishezon manifolds (32J10).** For compact complex $M$, the algebraic dimension $a(M)$ is the transcendence degree of the field of meromorphic functions over $\mathbb C$; $M$ is Moishezon when $a(M)=\dim_{\mathbb C}M$. Moishezon (1967): a Moishezon manifold is projective if and only if it admits a Kähler metric. Artin (1970): every Moishezon manifold carries the structure of an algebraic space. Hironaka's example is a smooth Moishezon 3-fold that is not an algebraic variety or scheme. ([Wikipedia, Moishezon manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moishezon_manifold))
- **Enriques–Kodaira classification (32J15).** Every surface is bimeromorphic to a minimal one, with no $(-1)$-curves, unique when $\kappa\ge0$ or the surface is non-algebraic. Every nonsingular minimal compact complex surface is of exactly one of ten types: for $\kappa=-\infty$, rational, ruled of genus $>0$, class VII; for $\kappa=0$, [K3 Surfaces](node:K3%20Surfaces), tori, Kodaira, Enriques, hyperelliptic; for $\kappa=1$, elliptic; for $\kappa=2$, general type. ([Wikipedia, Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification)) See also [Algebraic Surfaces](node:Algebraic%20Surfaces) and [Blowups](node:Blowups).
- **Non-Kähler surfaces.** Ornea, Verbitsky and Vuletescu give a mostly self-contained proof of the classification of non-Kähler surfaces based on the Buchdahl–Lamari theorem, and show that every non-Kähler surface not of class VII is locally conformally Kähler. ([Ornea–Verbitsky–Vuletescu, arXiv:1810.05768](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.05768))
- **Douady space ([Moduli Spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces)).** For a separated complex analytic space $X$, the set $H(X)$ of compact analytic subspaces carries a natural analytic-space structure, and more generally so does the set of coherent quotient sheaves with compact support of a coherent sheaf; the proof builds a theory of Banach analytic spaces. ([Douady 1966](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226))

### History
Max Noether began the systematic study of algebraic surfaces, Castelnuovo proved key parts of their classification, and Enriques described the classification of complex projective surfaces (1914; book 1949). Kodaira extended it to non-algebraic compact complex surfaces in papers from 1964 to 1968. ([Wikipedia, Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification)) Chow's theorem appeared in 1949 and Serre's GAGA in 1956 ([Wikipedia, GAGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry_and_analytic_geometry)). Douady's moduli paper appeared in the Annales de l'Institut Fourier, volume 16 (1966), pp. 1–95 ([Douady 1966](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226)). Moishezon's projectivity criterion dates from 1967 and Artin's algebraic-space result from 1970 ([Wikipedia, Moishezon manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moishezon_manifold)).

### Open problems
- **Classification of class VII surfaces and the global spherical shell (GSS) conjecture.** A recent survey calls the classification of class VII surfaces "the main open problem in the Kodaira classification of surfaces". It states the GSS conjecture, that all minimal class VII$_0$ surfaces with $b_2>0$ contain a global spherical shell, and says a proof would complete the classification; for class VII$_0$ surfaces with $b_2>2$ the survey calls even the existence of rational curves "still widely open, although progress has been done", and it reports that Teleman extended his $b_2=1$ result to a cycle of rational curves when $b_2=2$ ([survey, arXiv:2209.04229](https://arxiv.org/html/2209.04229)). Teleman used Donaldson theory to prove that class VII surfaces with $b_2=1$ contain curves, which he states settles the GSS conjecture in that case ([Teleman, arXiv:0704.2638](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.2638)). In a 2026 preprint, Kurnosov and Spicer prove, using Teleman's theorem on cycles of rational curves, that minimal class VII surfaces with $b_2=3$ carrying two distinct singular holomorphic foliations contain a GSS and are Inoue–Hirzebruch surfaces ([Kurnosov–Spicer, arXiv:2608.29047](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29047)).
- **Hodge conjecture (32J25 / 14C30).** For a projective manifold, rational $(p,p)$ classes are conjectured to be combinations of classes of subvarieties; the case $p=1$ holds by the Lefschetz $(1,1)$ theorem ([Wikipedia, Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_theory)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Enriques–Kodaira classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriques%E2%80%93Kodaira_classification): the ten classes of minimal compact complex surfaces and the history.
- **Reference:** [Moishezon manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moishezon_manifold): algebraic dimension, Moishezon and Artin theorems.
- **Learn:** [Auroux, MIT 18.966 Geometry of Manifolds, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-966-geometry-of-manifolds-spring-2007/pages/lecture-notes/): Kähler manifolds, Hodge decomposition, hard Lefschetz, and Donaldson's proof of Kodaira embedding (Lectures 13–19).
- **Primary:** [Voisin, On the homotopy types of compact Kähler and complex projective manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312032): the counterexample to the Kodaira problem.
- **Primary:** [Douady, Le problème des modules pour les sous-espaces analytiques compacts](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226): the Douady space.
- **Primary:** [A survey on rational curves on complex surfaces](https://arxiv.org/html/2209.04229): status of class VII and the GSS conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Barth, Hulek, Peters, Van de Ven, Compact Complex Surfaces (Springer, Ergebnisse, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-57739-0): monograph on the theory and classification of compact complex surfaces.
references.MSC 32Kxx - Generalizations of analytic:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 32K, Generalizations of analytic spaces, covers Banach analytic manifolds and spaces, formal and graded complex spaces, holomorphic maps with infinite-dimensional arguments or values, and differentiable functions on analytic spaces. ([MSC2020, 32K](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

The motivating example is a Banach analytic space: the local ambient space is an open set $U$ in a complex Banach space $E$, the defining equations are an analytic map $\Theta:U\to F$ into a Banach space, and the model is the zero locus $X=\Theta^{-1}(0)$ with the quotient sheaf generated by pairings $\langle \Theta(u),f(u)\rangle$ with analytic $F'$-valued maps $f$. ([Douady exposition, introduction](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~noonan/preprints/douady.pdf)) These spaces were developed by Douady in order to give the set of compact analytic subspaces of a complex space an analytic structure. ([Douady, abstract](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226))

The infinite-dimensional calculus underneath is subtler than the finite-dimensional one. A map between Banach spaces is holomorphic when it is Fréchet differentiable, such maps are locally analytic, but a Taylor series at the centre of a ball need not converge on the whole ball, and there are entire functions with finite radius of convergence. ([Wikipedia, Infinite-dimensional holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite-dimensional_holomorphy))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 32K05 (Banach analytic manifolds and spaces), 32K07 (formal and graded complex spaces), 32K12 (holomorphic maps with infinite-dimensional arguments or values), 32K15 (differentiable functions on analytic spaces, differentiable spaces) and 32K99. ([MSC2020, 32K](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Cross-references in the MSC entry: 32K05 points to 46G20 and 58Bxx, 32K07 to 58C50, 32K12 to 46G20 (in [MSC 46Gxx](node:MSC%2046Gxx%20-%20Measures,%20integration,%20derivative,%20holomorphy%20%28all%20involving%20infinite-dimensional%20spaces%29)), and 32K15 to 58C25. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf)) The ordinary theory being generalized is classified in [MSC 32Cxx - Analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Cxx%20-%20Analytic%20spaces), and Douady's application, spaces of compact analytic subspaces, is a moduli construction related to [MSC 32Gxx - Deformations of analytic structures](node:MSC%2032Gxx%20-%20Deformations%20of%20analytic%20structures). ([Douady, abstract](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226))

### Key concepts
- **[Banach Analytic Spaces](node:Banach%20Analytic%20Spaces):** local zero loci of analytic maps $\Theta:U\to F$ between Banach spaces, with the quotient structure sheaf above. ([Douady exposition](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~noonan/preprints/douady.pdf))
- **Douady space (main application).** For a complex separated analytic space $X$, the set $H(X)$ of compact analytic subspaces can be given the structure of an analytic space; more generally, for a coherent analytic sheaf $E$ on $X$ the set $H(E)$ of coherent quotients of $E$ with compact support is an analytic space. To obtain this, Douady lays the foundations of a theory of Banach analytic spaces. ([Douady, abstract](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226))
- **Pestov's realization theorem.** Every complete metric space is homeomorphic, and indeed isometric, to the zero locus of an analytic map between two Banach spaces; consequently a paracompact space carries a Banach analytic structure exactly when it is metrizable by a complete metric. This resolved a conjecture of Douady (1972). ([Pestov, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/funct-an/9406004))
- **[Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) holomorphy:** a function on an open $U\subset X$ is holomorphic if it is continuous and its restriction to every finite-dimensional subspace is holomorphic in the classical sense. ([Meylan, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.1726)) Gateaux holomorphy (holomorphic on each complex line) is the weakest notion in locally convex spaces. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite-dimensional_holomorphy))
- **Runge approximation in Banach spaces.** If $X$ is a complex Banach space and $f$ is holomorphic on the open unit ball $B(0,1)$ and bounded on each smaller ball $B(0,r)$, $0<r<1$, then for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is a holomorphic polynomial $h$ with $|f-h|<\varepsilon$ on $B(0,r)$. Boundedness is essential: on $\ell^1$, $f(z)=\sum_j 2^j z(j)^j$ is holomorphic on the unit ball but unbounded on $B(0,2/3)$ (take $z=\tfrac23 e_k$), so no polynomial can approximate it there. ([Meylan, Theorem 3.4 and Example 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.1726)) Note that [Holomorphic Approximation](node:Holomorphic%20Approximation) covers the finite-dimensional theory.
- **Formal and graded spaces (32K07).** A smooth supermanifold of dimension $p|q$ is a locally ringed space locally isomorphic to $(\mathbb R^p, C^\infty\otimes\Lambda(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_q))$; complex-analytic supermanifolds replace $C^\infty$ by holomorphic functions, with $\mathbb{CP}^{1|1}$ and super Riemann surfaces as basic examples. Batchelor's splitting theorem uses partitions of unity and does not extend to complex-analytic supermanifolds. ([Wikipedia, Supermanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermanifold))

### History
Douady's 1966 paper developed Banach analytic spaces to construct the analytic structure on spaces of compact subspaces. ([Douady, abstract](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226)) Pestov's 1994 paper proved the conjecture attributed to Douady in 1972. ([Pestov, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/funct-an/9406004)) Batchelor's theorem on the structure of smooth supermanifolds dates from 1979. ([Wikipedia, Supermanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermanifold))

### Open problems
**Runge approximation on Banach spaces.** For an infinite-dimensional complex Banach space $X$, ask (1) whether every holomorphic $f$ on $B(0,1)$ can be uniformly approximated by entire functions on each smaller ball, and (2) whether there is a radius $\rho\in(0,1)$ working for all $\varepsilon$ and all $f$. Lempert's counterexample ($\ell^\infty$ renormed with norms equivalent to the sup norm, combined with Dineen's bounding-set result) shows both fail in general, and the 2014 survey states that the Runge approximations are still open for $C[0,1]$ (into which every separable Banach space embeds isometrically) and for $L^1(0,1)$, asks whether (1) and (2) hold in every separable Banach space, and asks whether problem (2) holds in complex Banach spaces admitting an unconditional Schauder decomposition into spaces that themselves have a UFDD. The case where the decomposition pieces are finite-dimensional is covered by the survey's Theorem 6.5, which gives problem (1) for an equivalent norm. ([Meylan, survey, §§1, 4-6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.1726))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Infinite-dimensional holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite-dimensional_holomorphy): notions of holomorphy between Banach and locally convex spaces.
- **Reference:** [Supermanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermanifold): locally-ringed-space definition and complex-analytic examples.
- **Learn:** [Douady, The problem of moduli for complex analytic manifolds (following Kuranishi)](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~noonan/preprints/douady.pdf): exposition using Banach analytic models.
- **Learn:** [Meylan, Holomorphic approximation in Banach spaces: a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.1726): Runge problems, counterexample, and open questions.
- **Primary:** [Douady, Le problème des modules pour les sous-espaces analytiques compacts](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.226): construction of the analytic structure on $H(X)$.
- **Primary:** [Pestov, Douady's conjecture on Banach analytic spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/funct-an/9406004): realization of complete metric spaces as analytic zero loci.
- **Further reading:** [Mujica, Complex Analysis in Banach Spaces](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/s0304-0208%2808%2970888-0): monograph on holomorphic functions and domains of holomorphy in finite and infinite dimensions (North-Holland Mathematics Studies, Elsevier, 1986); bibliographic record via Crossref.
references.MSC 32Lxx - Holomorphic fiber spaces:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 32L, Holomorphic fiber spaces, covers holomorphic bundles and their generalizations, sheaves and cohomology of sections of holomorphic vector bundles, bundle convexity, vanishing theorems, twistor theory and double fibrations, and applications to the sciences. ([MSC2020, 32L](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

A holomorphic vector bundle is a complex vector bundle whose total space is a complex manifold and whose projection is holomorphic, equivalently one with holomorphic transition functions into $GL_k(\mathbb C)$. A holomorphic structure is the same as a Dolbeault operator $\bar\partial_E$ (by the Newlander–Nirenberg theorem), and holomorphic sections form a locally free sheaf $\mathcal O(E)$ whose cohomology is computed by Dolbeault's theorem. ([Wikipedia, Holomorphic vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_vector_bundle))

The central bridge to topology is the Oka principle, paraphrased by Forstnerič (2012) as: analytic problems on Stein spaces that can be formulated cohomologically have only topological obstructions. ([nLab, Oka principle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Oka+principle))

### Scope
The sub-codes are 32L05 (holomorphic bundles and generalizations), 32L10 (sheaves and cohomology of sections of holomorphic vector bundles), 32L15 (bundle convexity), 32L20 (vanishing theorems), 32L25 (twistor theory, double fibrations, complex-analytic aspects), 32L81 (applications to the sciences) and 32L99. ([MSC2020, 32L](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Neighbours: "Oka principle and Oka manifolds" has its own code 32Q56 in [MSC 32Qxx - Complex manifolds](node:MSC%2032Qxx%20-%20Complex%20manifolds). The 32L entry cross-references [55Rxx](node:MSC%2055Rxx%20-%20Fiber%20spaces%20and%20bundles%20in%20algebraic%20topology) as a whole; 32L10 points to 14F06, 14H60, 14J60, 18F20 and 55N30, 32L15 to 32F10 in [32Fxx](node:MSC%2032Fxx%20-%20Geometric%20convexity%20in%20several%20complex%20variables), and 32L25 to 53C28. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **[Holomorphic Vector Bundles](node:Holomorphic%20Vector%20Bundles):** the basic objects, with Dolbeault operator, Chern connection for a Hermitian metric, and $\mathrm{Pic}(X)\cong H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_vector_bundle)) See also [Dolbeault Cohomology](node:Dolbeault%20Cohomology) and [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles).
- **Grauert's Oka principle.** For a Stein manifold $S$, the holomorphic and topological classifications of $GL(n,\mathbb C)$-bundles agree, $H^1(S;GL(n,\mathbb C)_{hol})\simeq H^1(S;GL(n,\mathbb C)_{top})$. Oka proved the line-bundle case in 1939 (classification by the first Chern class), and Grauert extended it in 1958 to vector bundles and principal bundles with any complex Lie group as structure group. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Oka+principle)) Compare [Stein Spaces](node:Stein%20Spaces).
- **Gromov's Oka principle (sprays).** Let $Z\to X$ be a holomorphic fiber bundle over a Stein manifold. If the fiber admits a dominating holomorphic spray, then the inclusion of the space of holomorphic sections into the space of continuous sections is a weak homotopy equivalence; Grauert proved the case of a complex Lie group or homogeneous fiber. ([Forstnerič–Prezelj, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0305238)) Manifolds $Y$ for which every holomorphic map from a neighbourhood of a convex compact set in $\mathbb C^n$ into $Y$ is a uniform limit of entire maps are called Oka manifolds, and for Oka $Y$ every continuous map from a Stein manifold is homotopic to a holomorphic one, with relative and parametric versions. ([Forstnerič, Recent developments on Oka manifolds, Def. 1.1, Thm 1.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2006.07888))
- **Birkhoff–Grothendieck splitting.** Every holomorphic vector bundle $\mathcal E$ on $\mathbb{CP}^1$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal O(a_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathcal O(a_n)$, uniquely up to permutation. Grothendieck proved it in 1957; it is more or less equivalent to Birkhoff factorization (1909). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%E2%80%93Grothendieck_theorem))
- **Kodaira and Kodaira–Nakano vanishing (32L20).** For a compact Kähler manifold $M$ of dimension $n$ and a positive holomorphic line bundle $L$, $H^q(M,K_M\otimes L)=0$ for $q>0$; more generally $H^q(M,\Omega^r(L))=0$ for $q+r>n$. The algebraic version needs characteristic zero and fails in positive characteristic (Raynaud's counterexamples). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira_vanishing_theorem))
- **Twistor theory and the Penrose transform (32L25).** Via the double fibration $\mathrm{Gr}(2,4)\leftarrow Y\to\mathbb P^3$, the Penrose transform, a complex analogue of the Radon transform, identifies solutions of massless field equations on compactified complexified Minkowski space with sheaf cohomology groups on twistor space $\mathbb P^3$; its nonlinear version, the Penrose–Ward transform, relates holomorphic bundles on $\mathbb{CP}^3$ to self-dual Yang–Mills solutions on $S^4$. ([Wikipedia, Penrose transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose_transform))

### History
Oka's 1939 line-bundle result was extended by Grauert in 1958 to vector and principal bundles, and Gromov's 1989 paper on elliptic bundles gave the homotopy-theoretic form; Forstnerič and Prezelj supply a proof of that extension. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Oka+principle); [Forstnerič–Prezelj](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0305238)) Penrose introduced the transform in 1967-1969, and Ward (1977) and Atiyah–Ward (1977) the nonlinear version. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose_transform))

### Open problems
Forstnerič's 2025 survey lists open problems in Oka theory, including: Problem 3.5, whether every projective manifold satisfying the basic Oka property is Oka; Problem 3.10(a), the inverse Levi problem (if $\mathbb C^n\setminus K$ is Oka for compact $K$, must $bK$ be pseudoconvex?), answered affirmatively for $n=2$; whether every Fano manifold is Oka (stated as not known); and the conjecture that every projective rationally connected manifold is Oka-1. ([Forstnerič, 2025 survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.21197v1)) Forstnerič's "Recent developments on Oka manifolds" likewise lists open problems, e.g. whether the complement of a compact set in $\mathbb C^2$ can be an Oka domain that is neither elliptic nor subelliptic (Problem 4.8). ([Forstnerič, Recent developments on Oka manifolds](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2006.07888))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Holomorphic vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_vector_bundle): definitions, Dolbeault operator, Chern connection.
- **Reference:** [Oka principle (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Oka+principle): Oka–Grauert–Gromov statements and references.
- **Learn:** [Adamo, Lectures on twistor theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.02196): Modave summer-school lectures on the twistor correspondence for Minkowski space and its use for free fields and integrable systems.
- **Primary:** [Forstnerič–Prezelj, Oka's principle for holomorphic fiber bundles with sprays](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0305238): proof of Gromov's theorem.
- **Primary:** [Forstnerič, From Stein manifolds to Oka manifolds](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.21197v1): survey of the h-principle in complex analysis with open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Forstnerič, Stein Manifolds and Holomorphic Mappings (Springer, Ergebnisse der Mathematik vol. 34, 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-61058-0): monograph (bibliographic record via Crossref).
references.MSC 32Mxx - Complex spaces with a group:
## Reference
### Overview
This field studies complex manifolds and domains through their holomorphic symmetries. For a domain $\Omega$, $\operatorname{Aut}(\Omega)$ is the group of biholomorphic self-maps under composition with the compact-open topology; for bounded domains in $\mathbb C^n$ it is a real Lie group (Cartan), usually not a complex one. ([Krantz, §1](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4538.pdf); [Zaitsev, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9410025)) Poincaré's observation that the ball and polydisc in $\mathbb C^n$ are not biholomorphic shows there is no Riemann mapping theorem in several variables, which motivates classifying domains by their automorphism groups. ([Krantz, §1](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4538.pdf))

Two lines of study are prominent. Bounded symmetric and bounded homogeneous domains are classified through Lie theory (Cartan domains, Siegel domains). ([Viviani](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1310.3665); [Wikipedia, Siegel domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_domain)) A bounded domain with noncompact automorphism group has a boundary orbit accumulation point, and the boundary geometry there can force the domain to be the ball (Wong–Rosay) or an egg domain (Bedford–Pinchuk). ([Krantz, §§1, 3](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4538.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 32M05 (complex Lie groups, group actions on complex spaces), 32M10 (homogeneous complex manifolds), 32M12 (almost homogeneous manifolds and spaces), 32M15 (Hermitian symmetric spaces, bounded symmetric domains, Jordan algebras), 32M17 (automorphism groups of $\mathbb C^n$ and affine manifolds), 32M18 (automorphism groups of other complex spaces), 32M25 (complex vector fields, holomorphic foliations, $\mathbb C$-actions) and 32M99. ([MSC2020, 32M](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Neighbours: the next section, [MSC 32Nxx - Automorphic functions](node:MSC%2032Nxx%20-%20Automorphic%20functions), includes 32N15 (automorphic functions in symmetric domains). Within 32M, 32M05 cross-references 22E10 in [MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups); 32M10 points to 14M17 and 57T15; 32M12 to 14M17; and 32M15 to 22E10, 22E40, 53C35 and 57T15. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf)) Krantz's survey on automorphism groups of domains is itself classified under 30A99, 30F99, 32H02, 32H99, 32M17 and 32M99, alongside [MSC 32Hxx - Holomorphic mappings and correspondences](node:MSC%2032Hxx%20-%20Holomorphic%20mappings%20and%20correspondences). ([Krantz](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4538.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **[Homogeneous Complex Manifolds](node:Homogeneous%20Complex%20Manifolds) and [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups):** a bounded symmetric domain $\Omega$ is one in which each point $x$ has an involutive biholomorphism $\sigma_x$ with $x$ as an isolated fixed point; its Bergman metric is invariant, so $\Omega$ is a noncompact Hermitian symmetric space. ([Wikipedia, Bounded symmetric domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_symmetric_domain))
- **Cartan classification.** The irreducible bounded symmetric domains (Cartan domains) are of six types: $I_{p,q}$ ($p\times q$ complex matrices of operator norm $<1$), $II_n$ (antisymmetric), $III_n$ (symmetric), $IV_n$ (Lie ball), and the exceptional $V$ (dimension 16) and $VI$ (dimension 27). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_symmetric_domain))
- **Harish-Chandra embedding.** For a Hermitian symmetric space $M$ of noncompact type, the Harish-Chandra embedding into $\mathfrak p_+$ has image a bounded symmetric domain; conversely a bounded symmetric domain with its Bergman metric is a noncompact-type Hermitian symmetric space, and the two constructions are mutually inverse bijections (Theorems 2.25, 2.27, 2.30 of the cited notes). ([Viviani](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1310.3665))
- **Siegel domains and the homogeneous case.** Cartan showed that bounded homogeneous domains of dimension at most 3 are Hermitian symmetric; Piatetski-Shapiro found a non-symmetric homogeneous domain in dimension 4. Vinberg, Gindikin and Piatetski-Shapiro proved every bounded homogeneous domain is biholomorphic to a Siegel domain of the first or second kind. ([Wikipedia, Siegel domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_domain))
- **Wong–Rosay theorem.** If $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ is bounded, $P\in\partial\Omega$ is a boundary orbit accumulation point (some $\varphi_j\in\operatorname{Aut}\Omega$ and $X\in\Omega$ with $\varphi_j(X)\to P$), the boundary is $C^2$ near $P$ and $P$ is strongly pseudoconvex, then $\Omega$ is biholomorphic to the unit ball. ([Krantz, Theorem 1.1](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4538.pdf)) See [Pseudoconvexity](node:Pseudoconvexity).
- **Bedford–Pinchuk theorem.** A bounded pseudoconvex domain in $\mathbb C^2$ with real analytic boundary and noncompact automorphism group is biholomorphic to an egg domain $E_k=\{|z_1|^2+|z_2|^{2k}<1\}$, $k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$; Catlin observed the same holds for finite type domains in $\mathbb C^2$. ([Krantz, Theorem 3.1](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4538.pdf))
- **Andersén–Lempert theory (Forstnerič–Rosay theorem).** Here the shear group $\mathcal S(n)$ is generated by additive shears (Jacobian identically $1$) and multiplicative shears, together with their linear conjugates, and $\mathcal S_1(n)$ by additive shears alone. For a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$, $n>1$, and a continuous isotopy $\Phi_t$ of injective holomorphic maps starting at the identity with every image $\Phi_t(\Omega)$ Runge in $\mathbb C^n$, $\Phi_1$ is a uniform-on-compacta limit of elements of $\mathcal S(n)$; if moreover $\Omega$ is pseudoconvex, $H^{n-1}(\Omega,\mathbb C)=0$ and every $\Phi_t$ has Jacobian one, elements of $\mathcal S_1(n)$ suffice. ([Forstnerič–Kutzschebauch, Thm 1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.08802)) Andersén (1990) showed that for $n>1$ the group $\mathcal S_1(n)$ is dense in the volume-preserving automorphisms $\operatorname{Aut}_1(\mathbb C^n)$ but not equal to it, and Andersén and Lempert (1992) extended this to the density of $\mathcal S(n)$ in $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb C^n)$. ([Forstnerič–Kutzschebauch, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.08802); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.08802))

### History
The Lie group structure of $\operatorname{Aut}$ of a bounded domain goes back to H. Cartan. ([Zaitsev](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9410025)) Cartan asked whether bounded homogeneous domains are always symmetric; Piatetski-Shapiro answered no. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_domain)) Andersén and Lempert's 1992 result that the group generated by (additive and multiplicative) shears is dense in $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb C^n)$ began three decades of work on Stein manifolds with many automorphisms. ([Forstnerič–Kutzschebauch, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.08802); [§1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.08802))

### Open problems
**Greene–Krantz conjecture.** If $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ is a smoothly bounded domain and $P$ is a boundary orbit accumulation point, then $P$ is of finite type in the sense of Kohn, D'Angelo and Catlin. Krantz's 2025 survey says that although there are partial results, "the full result is still wide open." ([Krantz, Conjecture in §4](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4538.pdf)) Liu raises as questions, in $\mathbb C^2$, whether the model domain $\mathbb D\rtimes_\theta\mathbb H^+$ is biholomorphic to a smooth bounded domain, and whether boundary points of infinite type II exist. ([Analysis of orbit accumulation points, Remark 7](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1407.5546)) The conjecture is known for smoothly bounded convex domains in $\mathbb C^2$ (Krantz, Rocky Mountain J. Math. 2016, listed as Theorem 4.4 of the survey). ([Krantz, survey, Theorem 4.4](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4538.pdf); [Krantz, arXiv:1307.5350](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.5350))

**Density property of $(\mathbb C^*)^n$.** Whether $(\mathbb C^*)^n$, $n\ge 2$, has the density property is Problem 2.9 of the Andersén–Lempert survey, which calls it well known and notoriously difficult; the answer is conjectured to be negative. ([Forstnerič–Kutzschebauch](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.08802))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bounded symmetric domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_symmetric_domain): Cartan domains, Harish-Chandra and Borel embeddings.
- **Reference:** [Siegel domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_domain): Siegel domains and the homogeneous bounded case.
- **Learn:** [Viviani, A tour on Hermitian symmetric manifolds](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1310.3665): lecture notes with the embeddings and classification.
- **Primary:** [Krantz, The automorphism groups of domains and the Greene-Krantz conjecture](https://doi.org/10.7494/OpMath.2025.45.6.807): survey with the Wong–Rosay and Bedford–Pinchuk theorems.
- **Primary:** [Forstnerič and Kutzschebauch, The first thirty years of Andersén–Lempert theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.08802): survey with open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Zaitsev, On the automorphism groups of algebraic bounded domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9410025): Nash group structure on algebraic automorphisms of bounded domains.
references.MSC 32Nxx - Automorphic functions:
## Reference
### Overview
An automorphic form for a group $G$ acting on a complex domain $X$ is a holomorphic function $f$ with $f(g\cdot x)=j_g(x)f(x)$ for all $g$, where the factor of automorphy $j_g$ is an everywhere nonzero holomorphic function; an automorphic function is the case $j\equiv1$. The post-war interest in several complex variables made it natural to pursue automorphic forms beyond the upper half-plane. ([Automorphic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphic_form))

In several variables the central examples live on bounded symmetric domains (via the Harish-Chandra embedding, Hermitian symmetric spaces of noncompact type), and their quotients by arithmetic groups carry the Baily–Borel compactification. ([Hermitian symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_symmetric_space); [Baily–Borel compactification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baily%E2%80%93Borel_compactification)) Two basic families are Siegel modular forms on the Siegel upper half-space $\mathfrak H_g$, where $\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb Z)\backslash\mathfrak H_g$ is the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties, and Hilbert modular forms on products of upper half-planes attached to totally real fields. Van der Geer notes that, unlike the one-variable theory, the elementary theory of Siegel modular forms already needs the geometry of these quotients, in particular their compactifications. ([van der Geer, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346); [Hilbert modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_modular_form))

### Scope
MSC2020 32Nxx (see also 11Fxx, 20H10, 22E40, 30F35) lists: 32N05 general theory of automorphic functions of several complex variables; 32N10 automorphic forms in several complex variables; 32N15 automorphic functions in symmetric domains; 32N99. ([MSC2020, 32Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Nxx))

Neighbours named by the cross-references: [MSC 11Fxx - Discontinuous groups and automorphic forms](node:MSC%2011Fxx%20-%20Discontinuous%20groups%20and%20automorphic%20forms) holds the number-theoretic side, including holomorphic one-variable [Modular Forms](node:Modular%20Forms) (11F11), Hecke–Petersson operators (11F25), Hilbert modular forms (11F41), Siegel modular forms (11F46) and Langlands $L$-functions (11F66); 20H10 covers Fuchsian groups and their generalizations from the group-theoretic side; 22E40 and 30F35 are the other cross-references. ([MSC2020, 32Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Nxx); [MSC2020, 11Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=11Fxx); [MSC2020, 20H10](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=20H10)) Because $\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb Z)\backslash\mathfrak H_g$ is a moduli space of abelian varieties, the subject also meets [MSC 14Kxx - Abelian varieties and schemes](node:MSC%2014Kxx%20-%20Abelian%20varieties%20and%20schemes). ([van der Geer, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346))

### Key concepts
- **Bounded symmetric domains (32N15).** A bounded domain $\Omega$ in a complex vector space is symmetric if each $x\in\Omega$ is an isolated fixed point of an involutive biholomorphism $\sigma_x$ of $\Omega$. The Harish-Chandra embedding realizes every Hermitian symmetric space of noncompact type as a bounded symmetric domain; the irreducible ones (Cartan domains) are four classical types I–IV and two exceptional types built from the Cayley algebra. ([Hermitian symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_symmetric_space))
- **Siegel modular forms.** The Siegel upper half-space is $\mathfrak H_g=\{\tau\in\operatorname{Mat}_g(\mathbb C):\tau^t=\tau,\ \operatorname{Im}\tau>0\}$, on which $\Gamma_g=\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb Z)$ acts by $\tau\mapsto(A\tau+B)(C\tau+D)^{-1}$. For a representation $\rho$ of $\mathrm{GL}(g,\mathbb C)$ on $V$, a Siegel modular form of weight $\rho$ is a holomorphic $f:\mathfrak H_g\to V$ with $f(\gamma\tau)=\rho(C\tau+D)f(\tau)$ for all $\gamma\in\Gamma_g$, plus holomorphy at $\infty$ when $g=1$; the classical (scalar) case is $\rho=\det^k$. $\Gamma_g\backslash\mathfrak H_g$ is the moduli space $\mathcal A_g$ of principally polarized abelian varieties of dimension $g$ ([Abelian Varieties](node:Abelian%20Varieties)). ([van der Geer, §§2–3, 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346); [Siegel modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_modular_form))
- **Koecher principle.** If $f=\sum_n a(n)e^{2\pi i\operatorname{Tr}(n\tau)}\in M_\rho(\Gamma_g)$ with $g\ge2$, then $a(n)=0$ unless the half-integral matrix $n$ is positive semidefinite; so for $g>1$ holomorphy at the cusps is automatic, and a classical Siegel modular form of negative weight vanishes. ([van der Geer, Thm 4.4, Cor. 4.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346)) The same principle makes the cusp condition automatic for Hilbert modular forms over fields larger than $\mathbb Q$. ([Hilbert modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_modular_form))
- **Hilbert modular forms.** For a totally real field $F$ of degree $m$ with real embeddings $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_m$, $\mathrm{GL}_2^+(\mathcal O_F)$ acts on $\mathcal H^m$ componentwise; a Hilbert modular form of weight $(k_1,\dots,k_m)$ is a holomorphic function on $\mathcal H^m$ transforming by $\prod_i j(\sigma_i(\gamma),z_i)^{k_i}$ with $j(g,z)=\det(g)^{-1/2}(cz+d)$. ([Hilbert modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_modular_form))
- **Ring structure in genus 2 (Igusa).** The graded ring $\bigoplus_k M_k(\Gamma_2)$ of classical Siegel modular forms of genus 2 is generated by $E_4,E_6,\chi_{10},\chi_{12},\chi_{35}$, with the single relation $\chi_{35}^2=R(E_4,E_6,\chi_{10},\chi_{12})$ for an explicit isobaric polynomial $R$. ([van der Geer, Thm 9.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346))
- **Satake and Baily–Borel compactification.** Adding the quotients $\Gamma_i\backslash\mathfrak H_i$, $0\le i<g$, gives $\Gamma_g\backslash\mathfrak H_g^*=\bigsqcup_{i=0}^g\Gamma_i\backslash\mathfrak H_i$, which Satake made into a normal analytic space. Scalar Siegel modular forms of sufficiently high weight embed it in projective space, so $\Gamma_g\backslash\mathfrak H_g$ is quasi-projective and its compactification projective; this is a special case of Baily and Borel's theorem for arithmetic quotients of Hermitian symmetric spaces. For $g>1$ the boundary is very singular. ([van der Geer, §11, Thm 11.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346); [Baily–Borel compactification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baily%E2%80%93Borel_compactification))
- **Toroidal compactifications.** Mumford and his coworkers Ash, Rapoport and Tai constructed smooth (orbifold) compactifications $\tilde{\mathcal A}_g$, each depending on a cone decomposition of the cone of positive definite forms in $g$ variables; the boundary is a normal crossings divisor carrying a universal semi-abelian variety, and for $g\ge4$ there is no unique choice. ([van der Geer, §11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346))
- **Borcherds products.** Borcherds constructed families of automorphic forms on [Grassmannians](node:Grassmannians) with singularities along smaller sub-Grassmannians, via Harvey and Moore's extension of the Howe (theta) correspondence to modular forms with poles at cusps; the holomorphic ones are given by infinite products and yield new generalized Kac–Moody superalgebras. ([Borcherds, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9609022))
- **Birational geometry of $\mathcal A_g$.** $\mathcal A_g$ is unirational for $g\le5$ and of general type for $g\ge7$ (Tai for $g\ge9$, Freitag $g\ge8$, Mumford $g\ge7$). A Siegel cusp form of degree 6 and weight 14 (a harmonic theta series attached to the Leech lattice) vanishing to order 2 at the boundary defines a global section of $\omega^{\otimes2}$ on $\mathcal A_6$, so the Kodaira dimension of $\mathcal A_6$ is non-negative. ([Dittmann–Salvati Manni–Scheithauer, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.07062)) See [Moduli Spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces).

### History
Siegel introduced the forms named after him to study quadratic forms analytically; the reference article cites his 1939 work. ([Siegel modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_modular_form)) Hilbert considered Hilbert modular forms in unpublished work of 1893–94, and Blumenthal treated real quadratic fields in his 1901 Göttingen Habilitationsschrift, hence the name Hilbert–Blumenthal forms; the theory then lay dormant until complex manifold theory developed. ([Hilbert modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_modular_form)) The Koecher principle was observed by Götzky for Hilbert modular forms in 1928 and proved in general by Koecher in 1954. ([van der Geer, §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346)) Baily and Borel published their compactification in 1964 and 1966. ([Baily–Borel compactification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baily%E2%80%93Borel_compactification)) Borcherds's paper appeared in *Invent. Math.* 132 (1998). ([Borcherds, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9609022)) It was long believed that the $\mathcal A_g$ were unirational, until Freitag disproved this for some $g$. ([Dittmann–Salvati Manni–Scheithauer, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.07062))

### Open problems
- **Kodaira dimension of $\mathcal A_6$.** With $\mathcal A_g$ of Kodaira dimension $-\infty$ for $g\le5$ and of general type for $g\ge7$, the case $g=6$ was described in 2019 (published 2021) as "open for more than 30 years"; the cited paper proves only that $\kappa(\mathcal A_6)\ge0$, leaving its exact value (in particular whether $\mathcal A_6$ is of general type) undetermined there. ([Dittmann–Salvati Manni–Scheithauer, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.07062))
- **Geometric meaning of a lattice cusp form.** Theta series of the 24 Niemeier lattices span a 12-dimensional subspace of $M_{12}(\Gamma_{12})$ meeting the cusp forms in a line; van der Geer asks for the geometric meaning of this cusp form. ([van der Geer, Question 15.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Siegel modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_modular_form): definition, Koecher principle, moduli interpretation.
- **Reference:** [Hilbert modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_modular_form): definition and history.
- **Learn:** [van der Geer, Siegel Modular Forms (Nordfjordeid lectures)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0605346): Koecher principle, Igusa's ring, Satake and toroidal compactifications, Hecke theory, Harder's congruences.
- **Primary:** [Dittmann–Salvati Manni–Scheithauer, Harmonic theta series and the Kodaira dimension of A6](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.07062): research paper on $\kappa(\mathcal A_6)\ge0$ with a summary of the birational classification.
- **Primary:** [Borcherds, Automorphic forms with singularities on Grassmannians](https://arxiv.org/abs/alg-geom/9609022): the original Borcherds products paper.
- **Further reading:** Freitag's book on Siegel modular forms, which van der Geer calls the most accessible account of the Hecke theory for $g>1$. ([van der Geer, §16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605346))
references.MSC 32Pxx - Non-Archimedean analysis (sh:
## Reference
### Overview
Non-archimedean analytic geometry studies analytic spaces over fields complete for a non-archimedean absolute value, such as $\mathbb Q_p$ or Laurent-series fields. The classical theory of $k$-analytic manifolds has limited geometric interest because these spaces are totally disconnected; for global applications one wants a theory in which the closed unit ball is "connected" and coherent sheaves (hence analytic continuation) make sense. Tate first introduced such a theory in the early 1960s, rigid analytic spaces, whose admissible opens form a Grothendieck topology (the $G$-topology). ([Conrad, introduction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf); [Wikipedia, Rigid analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_analytic_space))

Tate introduced rigid spaces in 1962 while uniformizing $p$-adic elliptic curves with bad reduction. Later foundations are Raynaud's formal models (about 1970), Berkovich's spaces built from multiplicative seminorms (late 1980s), and Huber's adic spaces, which take a limit over all blow-ups to resolve the non-uniqueness of formal models. ([Wikipedia, Rigid analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_analytic_space)) Applications include Harris–Taylor's local Langlands for $GL_n$ (via étale cohomology of Berkovich spaces) and the Raynaud–Harbater solution of Abhyankar's conjecture (via rigid GAGA). ([Conrad, introduction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 has a single entry, 32P05, plus 32P99, and instructs that papers in 32P should also receive another 32-XX class describing the type of problem. ([MSC2020, 32P](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Neighbouring codes: MSC2020 has a separate code 14G22 (Rigid analytic geometry) in [MSC 14Gxx](node:MSC%2014Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20problems%20in%20algebraic%20geometry;%20Diophantine%20geometry), as well as 12J25 (Non-Archimedean valued fields), 30G06 (Non-Archimedean function theory) and 46S10 (functional analysis over fields other than $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$ or the quaternions; non-Archimedean functional analysis). ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf)) The complex-analytic counterpart of the theory is [MSC 32Cxx - Analytic spaces](node:MSC%2032Cxx%20-%20Analytic%20spaces); Conrad notes that the proofs of rigid GAGA closely follow Serre's complex-analytic ones. ([Conrad, introduction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf)) See also [Non-Archimedean Functional Analysis](node:Non-Archimedean%20Functional%20Analysis).

### Key concepts
- **Tate algebra and affinoids ([Rigid Analytic Geometry](node:Rigid%20Analytic%20Geometry), [p-adic Numbers](node:p-adic%20Numbers)).** For $k$ complete non-archimedean, $T_n=k\langle T_1,\dots,T_n\rangle=\{\sum a_IT^I:|a_I|\to0\}$ with Gauss norm $\|f\|=\max|a_I|$; affinoid algebras are quotients of $T_n$. $T_n$ is Noetherian, regular and a UFD; every maximal ideal has residue field of finite degree over $k$. ([Conrad, Defs. 1.1.2, 1.2.1 and Theorem 1.1.5](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf))
- **Gerritzen–Grauert theorem.** For a $k$-affinoid algebra $A$, every affinoid subdomain of $\mathcal M(A)$ is a finite union of rational domains; in particular affinoid subdomains are open in the canonical topology. ([Conrad, Theorem 2.2.5](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf))
- **Tate acyclicity.** For a $k$-affinoid algebra $A$, $U\mapsto A_U$ on affinoid subdomains of $\mathcal M(A)$ uniquely extends to a sheaf $\mathcal O_A$ for the Tate topology; in particular, for finite coverings by affinoid subdomains with affinoid union the sequence $0\to A_U\to\prod A_{U_i}\to\prod A_{U_i\cap U_j}$ is exact. ([Conrad, Theorem 2.3.3](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf))
- **Kiehl's theorems.** On an affinoid $X=\mathrm{Sp}(A)$ and a finite $A$-module $M$, $U\mapsto A_U\otimes_AM$ extends uniquely to an $\mathcal O_X$-module $\widetilde M$. For coherent $\mathcal F$ on affinoid $X$ and a finite admissible affinoid covering, Čech and sheaf cohomology $H^i$ vanish for $i>0$; for a proper map $f$ of rigid spaces, the $R^if_*\mathcal F$ are coherent, so $H^i(X,\mathcal F)$ is finite-dimensional for $X$ proper over $\mathrm{Sp}(k)$. ([Conrad, Theorems 3.1.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.7](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf))
- **Rigid GAGA.** For $X$ proper over $k$, the analytification gives an equivalence between coherent sheaves on $X$ and on $X^{an}$, comparison isomorphisms on cohomology, and full faithfulness of $X\mapsto X^{an}$, in analogy with Serre's theorem. ([Conrad, §3](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf))
- **Berkovich spaces.** The Berkovich spectrum of a normed ring $A$ is the set of bounded multiplicative seminorms with the weakest topology making evaluations continuous; it is nonempty for $A\neq0$ and compact when $A$ is complete. Berkovich affine space is locally compact, and over an algebraically closed complete non-archimedean field the Berkovich affine line is Hausdorff and uniquely path-connected. ([Wikipedia, Berkovich space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkovich_space)) The analytic spectrum construction underlying Berkovich spaces yields topological spaces that are locally connected and even locally contractible. ([nLab, Rigid analytic space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/rigid+analytic+space))
- **Adic and perfectoid spaces.** Huber's adic spaces arise by taking a limit over all blow-ups of Raynaud's formal models, which removes the non-uniqueness of those models and gives spaces functorial in the rigid space, though with fewer favourable topological features than other approaches. ([Wikipedia, Adic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adic_space)) Scholze's perfectoid spaces (2012) are adic spaces of a special kind; for a perfectoid field $K$ with tilt $K^\flat$ (characteristic $p$), tilting is an equivalence of categories between perfectoid spaces over $K$ and over $K^\flat$. ([Wikipedia, Perfectoid space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfectoid_space))

### History
Tate showed Grothendieck ad hoc $p$-adic theta-function computations in 1959, and Grothendieck was initially pessimistic that a global theory of such spaces existed; Tate then developed the theory in the early 1960s. ([Conrad, introduction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf)) Raynaud (c. 1970), Berkovich (late 1980s) and Huber gave the alternative foundations above. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_analytic_space))

### Open problems
**Weight-monodromy conjecture over $p$-adic fields.** For $X$ smooth proper over a finite extension $k$ of $\mathbb Q_p$ and $V=H^i(X_{\bar k},\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$ with monodromy operator $N$, the conjecture asserts $N^j:V_{i+j}\to V_{i-j}$ is an isomorphism for all $j\ge0$. Deligne proved the analogue over finite extensions of $\mathbb F_p((t))$; over $p$-adic fields Scholze's 2013 survey says it is known for $i=1$ and $i=2$ and "apart from that, little is known," with Scholze's Theorem 2.12 covering smooth complete intersections in $\mathbb P^n$ (extended in a cited follow-up to complete intersections in more general toric varieties). The survey reduces the general case to an approximation statement, Conjecture 2.15 (a closed subscheme $Y\subset\mathbb P^n_{K^\flat}$ of the same dimension as $X$ whose adic space lies in the preimage under the tilting map of a small neighbourhood of $X$), which is known locally but open globally. ([Scholze, Perfectoid spaces: a survey, §2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1303.5948))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Rigid analytic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_analytic_space): definitions and history of Tate, Raynaud, Berkovich and Huber.
- **Reference:** [Berkovich space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkovich_space): spectra and Berkovich affine line.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Several approaches to non-Archimedean geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Conrad-ApproachesNonArchGeometry.pdf): lecture notes with proofs-level statements of the foundations.
- **Primary:** [Scholze, Perfectoid spaces: a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.5948): survey with open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Bosch, Lectures on Formal and Rigid Geometry (Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics, 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-04417-0): textbook, bibliographic record via Crossref.
references.MSC 32Qxx - Complex manifolds:
## Reference
### Overview
A [complex manifold](node:Complex%20Manifolds) is a Hausdorff, second-countable space with an atlas of charts to open subsets of $\mathbb C^n$ whose transition maps are biholomorphic; every $n$-dimensional complex manifold is in particular a $2n$-dimensional smooth manifold whose tangent spaces carry a complex vector space structure, and holomorphic maps have $\mathbb C$-linear differentials. ([MIT 18.117, Lecture 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/989bea2ba42545febc2830a2b5f59cf2_18117_lec07.pdf)) MSC 32Q is the global geometry of these manifolds: curvature and Kähler metrics, Stein manifolds, hyperbolicity, embeddings, Oka theory, and almost complex structures. ([MSC2020, 32Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Qxx))

Two classes organize much of the subject. Compact Kähler manifolds, which include smooth projective varieties, carry Hodge theory and link complex geometry to topology and algebraic geometry. Stein manifolds, the closed complex submanifolds of some $\mathbb C^N$, instead have many holomorphic functions: they are holomorphically convex and holomorphic functions separate their points. ([Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_manifold); [Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold))

### Scope
MSC2020 32Qxx lists: 32Q02 special domains (Reinhardt, Hartogs, circular, tube, etc.) in $\mathbb C^n$ and complex manifolds; 32Q05 negative curvature and 32Q10 positive curvature complex manifolds; 32Q15 Kähler manifolds; 32Q20 Kähler–Einstein manifolds (see also 53Cxx); 32Q25 Calabi–Yau theory, complex-analytic aspects (see also 14J32); 32Q26 notions of stability; 32Q28 Stein manifolds; 32Q30 uniformization; 32Q35 complex manifolds as subdomains of Euclidean space; 32Q40 embedding theorems; 32Q45 hyperbolic and Kobayashi hyperbolic manifolds; 32Q55 topological aspects; 32Q56 Oka principle and Oka manifolds; 32Q57 classification theorems; 32Q60 almost complex manifolds; 32Q65 pseudoholomorphic curves; 32Q99. ([MSC2020, 32Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Qxx))

Neighbours named by the entry: 32Q20 cross-references [MSC 53Cxx - Global differential geometry](node:MSC%2053Cxx%20-%20Global%20differential%20geometry) and 32Q25 (complex-analytic aspects of Calabi–Yau theory) cross-references 14J32. Only Stein *manifolds* are in 32Q28; Stein spaces have their own code 32E10 under [MSC 32Exx - Holomorphic convexity](node:MSC%2032Exx%20-%20Holomorphic%20convexity). Deformations of analytic structures are a separate subfield, [MSC 32Gxx - Deformations of analytic structures](node:MSC%2032Gxx%20-%20Deformations%20of%20analytic%20structures). ([MSC2020, 32Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Qxx); [MSC2020, 32Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Exx); [MSC2020, 32-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Kähler manifolds ([Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds)).** Equivalently: a complex manifold with a Hermitian metric whose associated 2-form $\omega$ is closed; a symplectic manifold with a compatible integrable almost complex structure; or a Riemannian $2n$-manifold with holonomy in $U(n)$. Locally $\omega=\tfrac i2\partial\bar\partial\rho$ for a Kähler potential $\rho$. $\mathbb{CP}^n$ with the Fubini–Study metric is Kähler, and complex submanifolds of Kähler manifolds are Kähler, so Stein manifolds and smooth projective varieties are Kähler. ([Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_manifold))
- **Hodge decomposition ([Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory), [Dolbeault Cohomology](node:Dolbeault%20Cohomology)).** For a compact Kähler manifold $X$, $H^r(X,\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=r}H^{p,q}(X)$ with $H^{p,q}=\overline{H^{q,p}}$ and $H^{p,q}(X)\cong H^q(X,\Omega^p)$. Hence odd Betti numbers are even; this fails for general compact complex manifolds (the Hopf surface has $b_1=1$). ([Hodge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_theory))
- **Kodaira embedding theorem (32Q40).** Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $L$ a holomorphic line bundle. Then $L$ is positive if and only if there is a holomorphic embedding $\varphi:X\to\mathbb P^N$ with $\varphi^*\mathcal O(1)=L^{\otimes m}$ for some $m>0$. Hence Hodge manifolds (Kähler form with integral class) are projective, and by Chow's theorem algebraic. ([Kodaira embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira_embedding_theorem))
- **Newlander–Nirenberg theorem (32Q60).** An almost complex structure $J$ (a smooth field of endomorphisms with $J^2=-1$) is integrable, i.e. comes from a complex structure, if and only if its Nijenhuis tensor $N_J$ vanishes (1957). By Borel–Serre (1953) the only spheres with almost complex structures are $S^2$ and $S^6$. ([Almost complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_complex_manifold))
- **Calabi–Yau theorem (32Q20, 32Q25).** On a compact Kähler manifold, for every closed real $(1,1)$-form $R$ representing the first Chern class there is exactly one Kähler metric in each Kähler class whose Ricci form is $R$ (conjectured by Calabi 1954/57, proved by Yau 1977–78 via the complex Monge–Ampère equation). Consequences: a unique Ricci-flat metric in each Kähler class when $c_1=0$, and Kähler–Einstein metrics when $c_1<0$. ([Calabi conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi_conjecture)) For Fano manifolds ($c_1>0$), Chen, Donaldson and Sun announced in 2012 that a K-stable Fano manifold admits a Kähler–Einstein metric, with proofs in a series of three papers. ([Chen–Donaldson–Sun, announcement](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.7494); [CDS I](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.4566))
- **Stein manifolds (32Q28, [Stein Spaces](node:Stein%20Spaces)).** A complex manifold that is holomorphically convex and holomorphically separable; equivalently a closed complex submanifold of some $\mathbb C^N$. Grauert's solution of the Levi problem: Stein is equivalent to admitting a strongly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. A Stein manifold of dimension $n$ properly embeds in $\mathbb C^{2n+1}$, and a connected [Riemann surface](node:Riemann%20Surfaces) is Stein if and only if it is not compact. ([Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold))
- **Kobayashi hyperbolicity (32Q45).** $X$ is hyperbolic when the Kobayashi pseudometric (the largest pseudometric contracted by all holomorphic discs) is a metric; by Brody, a compact complex space is hyperbolic if and only if every holomorphic map $\mathbb C\to X$ is constant. ([Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric)) Kobayashi's 1970 conjecture that a generic hypersurface of sufficiently large degree in projective space is hyperbolic was proved by completing a strategy Siu proposed in the early 2000s (completed in 2015) and, by a different method, by Brotbek (2016), with explicit degree bounds by Deng and Demailly. ([Demailly 2018, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.04765))
- **Deformations (Kodaira–Spencer).** For a smooth proper family $\mathcal M\to B$ with fibre $M=\mathcal M_0$, the Kodaira–Spencer map $T_0B\to H^1(M,T_M)$ is the connecting homomorphism of the tangent sequence; first-order deformations correspond to $H^1(M,T_M)$. ([Kodaira–Spencer map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira%E2%80%93Spencer_map)) See [Deformations of Complex Structures](node:Deformations%20of%20Complex%20Structures).

### History
The reference cites Kodaira's 1954 paper *On Kähler varieties of restricted type* for the embedding theorem; in 1963 he showed every compact Kähler surface deforms to a projective one, and Buchdahl gave a classification-free proof in 2008. ([Kodaira embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira_embedding_theorem)) Borel and Serre settled which spheres are almost complex in 1953, and Newlander and Nirenberg's integrability theorem appeared in 1957 in *Annals of Mathematics*. ([Almost complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_complex_manifold)) Calabi posed his conjecture in 1954 and 1957 and Yau proved it in 1977–78, work cited for his Fields Medal; the Fano Kähler–Einstein case was resolved in the 2010s. ([Calabi conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi_conjecture)) McQuillan proved the Green–Griffiths–Lang conjecture for surfaces with $c_1^2>c_2$ in 1998. ([Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric))

### Open problems
- **Complex structures on $S^6$ (Hopf problem).** $S^6$ carries an almost complex structure from octonion multiplication; whether it admits an integrable one (Hopf, 1947) has long been a famous open problem, with a history of ultimately unverified claims. ([Almost complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_complex_manifold); [nLab, 6-sphere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/6-sphere))

> [!warning] Contested
> In August 2026 Alpöge presented an AI-generated proof proposal that $S^6$ admits a complex structure, and Alexeev claimed to have checked it in the Lean proof assistant. Neither reference treats the claim as confirmed, so the problem's status should be rechecked before relying on either answer. ([nLab, 6-sphere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/6-sphere); [Almost complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_complex_manifold))

- **Green–Griffiths–Lang conjecture.** For a projective variety $X$ of general type there should be a proper algebraic subvariety $Y\subsetneq X$ containing all nonconstant entire curves $\mathbb C\to X$; the reference calls it a central open problem, and Demailly proves it only under a strong general-type condition (jet-semistability of the [tangent bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle)). ([Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric); [Demailly 2018, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.04765))
- **Kähler groups.** Which groups are fundamental groups of compact Kähler manifolds is "wide open"; Hodge theory forces the abelianization to have even rank, so $\mathbb Z$ is not a Kähler group. ([Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_manifold))
- **Kobayashi's Calabi–Yau conjecture.** Kobayashi conjectured that the Kobayashi pseudometric vanishes identically on Calabi–Yau manifolds; the reference records it as known for [K3 Surfaces](node:K3%20Surfaces). ([Kobayashi metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_metric))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4hler_manifold): definitions, examples, Hodge decomposition, Kähler groups.
- **Reference:** [Almost complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_complex_manifold): Nijenhuis tensor, Newlander–Nirenberg, $S^6$.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.117 Topics in Several Complex Variables, lecture notes (Guillemin)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/pages/lecture-notes/): complex manifolds, Dolbeault cohomology, Kähler geometry, the Kähler–Einstein equation, Hodge theory on Kähler manifolds.
- **Primary:** [Demailly, Recent results on the Kobayashi and Green–Griffiths–Lang conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.04765): survey and research on entire curves and hyperbolicity.
- **Primary:** [Chen–Donaldson–Sun, Kähler–Einstein metrics and stability](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.7494): the K-stability criterion for Fano manifolds.
