references.MSC 32Sxx - Complex singularities:
## Reference
### Overview
Complex singularity theory studies the local behaviour of analytic spaces where the manifold description fails. The basic case is a hypersurface $V(f)=\{f=0\}$ for a non-locally-constant holomorphic $f$ on an open set of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$; at regular points the implicit function theorem gives a smooth hypersurface, and the critical locus $\Sigma f=V(\partial f/\partial z_0,\dots,\partial f/\partial z_n)$ records where it fails. ([Massey, lecture 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.3312))

For an isolated hypersurface singularity the general fiber of the Milnor fibration is the Milnor fiber; the Milnor number can be calculated algebraically as the dimension of the Jacobian ring, the Milnor fiber carries a canonical symplectic structure, and its boundary, the link, inherits a canonical contact structure. ([Peters, §§1.2-1.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.03475)) Milnor introduced these maps in *Singular Points of Complex Hypersurfaces* (1968), originally motivated by knots cut out by a small sphere around a plane-curve singularity. ([Wikipedia, Milnor map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor_map))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 32S05 (local complex singularities), 32S10 (invariants of analytic local rings), 32S15 (equisingularity), 32S20 (global theory, cohomological properties), 32S22 (arrangements of hyperplanes), 32S25 (surface and hypersurface singularities), 32S30 (deformations; vanishing cycles), 32S35 (mixed Hodge theory of singular varieties), 32S40 (monodromy; D-modules), 32S45 (modifications; resolution of singularities), 32S50 (topological aspects: Lefschetz theorems, classification), 32S55 (Milnor fibration; knot theory), 32S60 (stratifications; constructible sheaves; intersection cohomology), 32S65 (holomorphic vector fields and foliations), 32S70 and 32S99. ([MSC2020, 32S](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

Neighbours named in the MSC entry: 32Sxx as a whole and 32S60 cross-reference [MSC 58Kxx - Theory of singularities and catastrophe theory](node:MSC%2058Kxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20singularities%20and%20catastrophe%20theory); 32S15, 32S20 and 32S45 (whose resolution heading is marked "complex-analytic aspects") point to 14E15 in [MSC 14Exx - Birational geometry](node:MSC%2014Exx%20-%20Birational%20geometry); 32S05 and 32S25 to 14J17; 32S30 to 14B07 in [MSC 14Bxx - Local theory in algebraic geometry](node:MSC%2014Bxx%20-%20Local%20theory%20in%20algebraic%20geometry); 32S35 to 14C30 and 14D07; 32S22 to 52C35; and 32S55 to 57K10 and 57K45. ([MSC2020](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/pdfs/classifications2020.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Milnor fibration theorem.** For a non-constant polynomial $f$ in $n+1$ variables with $0\in V_f$, and small $\varepsilon$, $f/|f|:S_\varepsilon^{2n+1}\setminus V_f\to S^1$ is a fibration. ([Wikipedia, Milnor map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor_map)) See [Complex Analytic Singularities](node:Complex%20Analytic%20Singularities).
- **Milnor's bouquet and number.** If $f:(\mathbb C^{n+1},0)\to(\mathbb C,0)$ has an isolated critical point, the Milnor fiber is homotopy equivalent to a bouquet of $n$-spheres, and the number of spheres is
$$\mu(f)=\dim_{\mathbb C}\frac{\mathbb C\{z_0,\dots,z_n\}}{(\partial f/\partial z_0,\dots,\partial f/\partial z_n)}.$$
([Massey, Theorem 2.22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.3312)) For an isolated $m$-dimensional singularity with $m\ne2$, the Milnor fiber (a real $2m$-manifold) is obtained from the $2m$-ball by attaching $\mu$ disjoint handles of index $m$. ([Peters, Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.6](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.03475))
- **Lê–Ramanujam theorem.** If $n\neq2$ and $f,g$ lie in an analytic family of functions with isolated critical points, all with the same Milnor number, then $f$ and $g$ define hypersurfaces of the same local ambient topological type. ([Massey, Theorem 1.14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.3312))
- **Monodromy theorem.** Let $f$ have an isolated singularity on an isolated complete intersection singularity $(Y,0)$ with Milnor fiber of dimension $n$, and let $h_*$ be its Picard–Lefschetz monodromy on $H_n$. Then (a) the eigenvalues of $h_*$ are roots of unity; (b) the Jordan blocks have size at most $(n+1)\times(n+1)$; (c) if $(Y,0)$ is smooth, the Jordan blocks for eigenvalue $1$ have size at most $n\times n$. Many authors gave proofs (Borel, Brieskorn, Clemens, Deligne, Griffiths, Grothendieck, Katz, Landman, Lê, Malgrange, Schmid). ([Ebeling, Theorem 1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0507171)) Compare [Monodromy of Complex Differential Equations](node:Monodromy%20of%20Complex%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Du Val (ADE) singularities.** The isolated rational double points of complex surfaces are, up to analytic isomorphism, of types $A_n$, $D_n$ ($n\ge4$), $E_6,E_7,E_8$, each given by an equation in three variables; they are the quotients $\mathbb C^2/G$ for finite $G\subset SL_2(\mathbb C)$, and the minimal resolution has exceptional curves forming the corresponding Dynkin diagram. ([Wikipedia, Du Val singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du_Val_singularity))
- **Hironaka's resolution.** Over a field of characteristic $0$, every variety has a resolution of singularities, a proper birational map from a nonsingular variety (Hironaka, 1964); for embedded varieties one gets a strong desingularization by blow-ups of regular centres. ([Wikipedia, Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities)) See [Blowups](node:Blowups).
- **Mixed Hodge structures.** A mixed Hodge structure is a triple $(H_{\mathbb Z},W,F)$ with an increasing filtration $W$ on $H_\mathbb Q$ and decreasing $F$ on $H_\mathbb C$ whose $W$-graded pieces are pure Hodge structures; it is the framework of 32S35. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_Hodge_structure)) See [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory).

### History
Milnor introduced these maps in his 1968 book and earlier lectures; the book is AM-61 from Princeton University Press. ([Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9781400881819); [Wikipedia, Milnor map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor_map)) The Milnor number as a topological invariant is due to Teissier (1972-73) and Lê (1973), and Hironaka proved resolution in characteristic zero in 1964. ([Massey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.3312); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))

### Open problems
**Zariski's multiplicity conjecture** (Zariski, 1971, "Some open questions in the theory of singularities"): if a family $\{f_t\}$ of reduced hypersurface germs is topologically equisingular, then it is equimultiple, i.e. the multiplicity at $0$ is independent of $t$. Eyral and Ruas state that it "has been solved only in a few special cases": isolated singularities with $f_0$ weighted homogeneous (Greuel–O'Shea), isolated singularities with each $f_t$ Newton non-degenerate (Abderrahmane; Saia–Tomazella), and certain line singularities. ([Eyral–Ruas, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1602.05732)) The closely related question for single germs asks whether the embedded topological type of a reduced complex hypersurface germ determines its multiplicity. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ZariskiMultiplicityConjecture.html)) In the published literature cited here the conjecture remains open.

> [!warning] Contested
> Sampaio's October 2026 preprint reports that OpenAI announced a counterexample in dimension 4: two holomorphic germs on $(\mathbb C^4,0)$ with isolated singularities and multiplicities $4$ and $5$ whose zero sets are ambiently homeomorphic. Sampaio does not construct or verify it and writes that the conjecture would fail for all $n\ge4$ only "should these results be verified". The counterexample is therefore reported and unconfirmed here. ([Sampaio, arXiv:2610.41954](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.41954)) What the preprint proves is the metric version: if a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism of $(\mathbb C^n,0)$ carries $V(f)$ onto $V(g)$ and each irreducible component of the tangent cone has singular locus of dimension at most two, then the multiplicities agree; hence multiplicity is an embedded bi-Lipschitz invariant of hypersurface germs in $\mathbb C^n$ for $n\le4$, the cases $n=2,3$ being known before. ([Sampaio, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.41954); [MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ZariskiMultiplicityConjecture.html))

**Resolution in positive characteristic** (an algebraic neighbour of 32S45, under 14E15). The general problem is open in dimension at least $4$; it is known for surfaces (Abhyankar 1956) and for 3-folds in all characteristics (Cossart–Piltant). ([Wikipedia, Resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Milnor map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor_map): fibration, Milnor fiber, Milnor number.
- **Reference:** [Du Val singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du_Val_singularity): ADE surface singularities.
- **Learn:** [Massey, Non-isolated hypersurface singularities and Lê cycles](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.3312): lectures starting from Milnor fibers.
- **Learn:** [Ebeling, Monodromy](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0507171): survey on the Picard–Lefschetz operator, zeta function, spectrum.
- **Primary:** [Peters, On isolated hypersurface singularities](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.03475): survey of algebraic and symplectic aspects.
- **Further reading:** [Milnor, Singular Points of Complex Hypersurfaces (Princeton University Press)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9781400881819): Milnor's monograph (AM-61), bibliographic record via Crossref.
references.MSC 32Txx - Pseudoconvex domains:
## Reference
### Overview
A domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ is pseudoconvex when it carries a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function; for domains with $C^2$ boundary this is equivalent to the Levi condition on the boundary. Every convex domain is pseudoconvex but not conversely, and for $n=1$ every domain is pseudoconvex, so the notion only has content in several variables. ([Wikipedia, Pseudoconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoconvexity))

Pseudoconvexity is the boundary-geometric answer to the question of which domains are natural domains of existence of holomorphic functions. The Levi problem asks whether pseudoconvex domains are domains of holomorphy; its solution by Oka, Bremermann and Norguet, and the later $L^2$ proof via Hörmander's estimates for $\bar\partial$, made pseudoconvex domains the standard setting for function theory, the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem and the Bergman projection. ([Slatyer, The Levi problem in $\mathbb C^n$: a survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1411.0363); [Fornæss, lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.00562))

Much of the analytic difficulty lies at weakly pseudoconvex boundary points: finite-type conditions, the Diederich–Fornæss index, and the worm domains of Diederich and Fornæss, which are smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domains on which global regularity of the Bergman projection fails. ([Krantz–Peloso, Analysis and geometry on worm domains](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087); [Boas–Straube survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))

### Scope
MSC2020 32T has seven subject codes: 32T05 domains of holomorphy; 32T15 strongly pseudoconvex domains; 32T20 worm domains; 32T25 finite-type domains; 32T27 geometric and analytic invariants on weakly pseudoconvex boundaries; 32T35 exhaustion functions; 32T40 peak functions; plus 32T99. ([MSC2020, 32T](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Txx))

- **vs 32E (holomorphic convexity):** 32E lists holomorphically convex spaces, Stein spaces (32E10), polynomial and rational convexity, approximation, and the Levi problem itself (32E40). ([MSC2020, 32E](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Exx))
- **vs 32U (pluripotential theory):** 32U lists plurisubharmonic functions (32U05), plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions (32U10), capacities, Lelong numbers and currents. ([MSC2020, 32U](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Uxx))
- **vs 32W (differential operators):** the $\bar\partial$ and $\bar\partial$-Neumann operators are listed as 32W05. ([MSC2020, 32W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Wxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Pseudoconvexity](node:Pseudoconvexity) and exhaustion functions (32T35).** For a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ the following are equivalent: $\Omega$ has a continuous [plurisubharmonic](node:Plurisubharmonic%20Functions) exhaustion $u$ (each $\{u<c\}$ relatively compact in $\Omega$); $-\log d(z,\Omega^c)$ is plurisubharmonic. A pseudoconvex domain then carries a $C^\infty$ strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion, and is an increasing union of bounded strongly pseudoconvex domains with smooth boundary. ([Fornæss, Theorems 2.6.7 and 2.6.11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.00562); [Wikipedia, Proposition 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoconvexity))
- **Levi form ([Levi Convexity](node:Levi%20Convexity)).** If $\Omega=\{\rho<0\}$ with $\rho\in C^2$ and $d\rho\ne0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $\Omega$ is pseudoconvex iff for every $p\in\partial\Omega$ and every $w\in\mathbb C^n$ with $\sum_j \partial_{z_j}\rho(p)w_j=0$ one has $\sum_{i,j}\partial^2\rho(p)/\partial z_i\partial\bar z_j\,w_i\bar w_j\ge0$: the Levi form is positive semidefinite on the complex tangent space. Strong pseudoconvexity asks for positive definiteness there. ([Wikipedia, Pseudoconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoconvexity); [Wikipedia, CR manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_manifold))
- **Domains of holomorphy and the Levi problem (32T05, 32E40).** Domains of holomorphy in $\mathbb C^n$ are exactly the pseudoconvex domains; by Cartan–Thullen they are also exactly the holomorphically convex domains. Oka proved sufficiency of pseudoconvexity in dimension 2 in 1942, and Bremermann, Norguet and Oka gave independent proofs in all dimensions in 1953–54. The modern proof solves $\bar\partial u=f$ with Hörmander's $L^2$ estimates on a pseudoconvex domain. ([Slatyer survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1411.0363)) On manifolds, Grauert (Annals of Mathematics, 1958) proved that a complex manifold is a [Stein manifold](node:Stein%20Spaces) iff it carries a smooth exhaustion $\psi$ with $i\partial\bar\partial\psi>0$, and Narasimhan extended this to Stein spaces. ([Wikipedia, Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold))
- **Tube domains.** By Bochner's tube theorem a function holomorphic on a connected tube $T_A=A+i\mathbb R^n$ extends to the tube over the [convex hull](node:Convex%20Hull) of $A$, so the envelope of holomorphy of $T_A$ is $T_{\operatorname{ch}A}$; convex tubes are domains of holomorphy. ([Wikipedia, Tube domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tube_domain))
- **Finite type (32T25).** For a smooth real hypersurface $M\subset\mathbb C^n$ the set of points of finite D'Angelo 1-type is open, and the type is locally bounded but need not be upper semicontinuous. Catlin's theorem: on a bounded pseudoconvex domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, a subelliptic estimate for the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem on $(0,q)$-forms holds near $z_0\in\partial\Omega$ iff the D'Angelo $q$-type $D_q(z_0)$ is finite, and then the order satisfies $\varepsilon\le1/D_q(z_0)$. ([Boas–Straube, Theorems 9–10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))
- **Diederich–Fornæss exponent.** For a smoothly bounded pseudoconvex $\Omega$ there is a defining function $\tilde\varrho$ and $0<\delta\le1$ such that $-(-\tilde\varrho)^\delta$ is a bounded strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion; the supremum of admissible exponents is the Diederich–Fornæss index. Berndtsson–Charpentier and Kohn show that such $\delta$ gives Sobolev $H^s$ continuity of the Bergman projection for $0\le s<s_0(\Omega,\delta)$. ([Krantz–Peloso, Theorems 2.3–2.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087); [Krantz–Liu–Peloso](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02343); [Harrington](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1705.05815))
- **Worm domains (32T20).** The Diederich–Fornæss worm $\mathcal W=\{|z_1-e^{i\log|z_2|^2}|^2<1-\eta(\log|z_2|^2)\}$, with $\eta\ge0$ even and convex and $\eta^{-1}(0)=[-\mu,\mu]$, is smoothly bounded and pseudoconvex, strongly pseudoconvex off an annulus in $\{z_1=0\}$, and has no Stein neighbourhood basis; its Diederich–Fornæss exponents satisfy $\delta<\pi/(2\mu)$ for large $\mu$. Barrett showed that its Bergman projection fails to preserve $H^s$ for $s\ge\pi/(2\mu)$, and Christ showed that the Bergman projection and $\bar\partial$-Neumann operator fail to preserve $C^\infty(\overline{\mathcal W})$. ([Krantz–Peloso, Def. 1.2, Props. 1.3–1.4, Thms. 1.8–1.9, 2.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087); [Boas–Straube, Theorem 6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))

### History
Hartogs's 1906 extension phenomenon showed that not every domain in $\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge2$, is a domain of holomorphy, and Levi introduced his boundary condition in 1910–1911. Oka proved in 1942 that Levi pseudoconvexity suffices in dimension 2, and the general case was proved independently by Bremermann, Norguet and Oka in 1953–54. Plurisubharmonic functions were introduced by Oka and Lelong in 1942. ([Slatyer survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1411.0363); [Wikipedia, Plurisubharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurisubharmonic_function))

Hörmander's 1965 Acta Mathematica paper on $L^2$ estimates for $\bar\partial$ gave the existence theory on pseudoconvex domains that the modern solution of the Levi problem uses. Diederich and Fornæss published the worm domain in Mathematische Annalen in 1977, and Christ's irregularity theorem appeared in the Journal of the AMS in 1996. ([Fornæss notes](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.00562); [Crossref, Hörmander 1965](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02391775); [Slatyer survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1411.0363); [Crossref, Diederich–Fornæss 1977](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/bf01425243); [Crossref, Christ 1996](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/s0894-0347-96-00213-5))

### Open problems
- **Boundary behaviour of biholomorphisms.** Whether biholomorphic maps between smooth bounded pseudoconvex domains extend smoothly to the boundary is described as "a still open fundamental problem" by Monguzzi and Peloso (2020); Krantz and Peloso note that it is unknown whether a biholomorphic map of the smooth worm extends to a diffeomorphism of the closures; Monguzzi and Peloso record that the worm is the only known smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domain on which Condition R fails. ([Monguzzi–Peloso](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2003.00718); [Krantz–Peloso](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087))
- **Automorphisms of the worm.** Monguzzi and Peloso call characterizing the automorphism group of the smooth worm "an open and fundamental question"; Chen's claim that the automorphisms are only rotations in $z_2$ has a gap in its proof. ([Monguzzi–Peloso](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2003.00718))
- **Sharp Sobolev range.** The sharp value of $s_0(\Omega,\delta)$ in the Berndtsson–Charpentier–Kohn regularity theorem is not known. ([Krantz–Peloso](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087))
- **Optimal subelliptic order.** The optimal $\varepsilon$ in a subelliptic estimate, expressed through boundary invariants, is unknown in general. ([Boas–Straube](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Pseudoconvexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoconvexity): exhaustion and Levi-form definitions, approximation by strongly pseudoconvex domains.
- **Learn:** [Fornæss, Several Complex Variables (lecture notes)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.00562): a course following Hörmander, through $\bar\partial$ in $L^2$ and the Levi problem.
- **Learn:** [Slatyer, The Levi problem in $\mathbb C^n$: a survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1411.0363): expository proof via Hörmander's theorem, with history.
- **Primary:** [Krantz–Peloso, Analysis and geometry on worm domains](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087): worm geometry, Diederich–Fornæss exponents, Barrett and Christ theorems, open questions.
- **Primary:** [Boas–Straube, Global regularity of the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204): survey of finite type, Catlin's theorems and regularity.
- **Further reading:** [Krantz, Function Theory of Several Complex Variables (AMS, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/chel/340): graduate text, cited by Slatyer (chapter 4) for a self-contained proof of Hörmander's $L^2$ theorem used in the Levi problem.
- **Further reading:** [Hörmander, $L^2$ estimates and existence theorems for the $\bar\partial$ operator (Acta Math. 113, 1965)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02391775): the original $L^2$ method.
references.MSC 32Uxx - Pluripotential theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Pluripotential theory is the potential theory of plurisubharmonic functions: upper semicontinuous functions on a domain of $\mathbb C^n$ (or a [complex manifold](node:Complex%20Manifolds)) whose restriction to every complex line, or composition with every holomorphic disc, is subharmonic. The class was introduced independently by Oka and by Lelong in 1942. ([Wikipedia, Plurisubharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurisubharmonic_function)) It is tied to Stein manifolds by Grauert's 1958 solution of the Levi problem: a complex manifold is Stein iff it carries a smooth exhaustion $\psi$ with $i\partial\bar\partial\psi>0$; Narasimhan extended this to Stein spaces. ([Wikipedia, Stein manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_manifold))

Klimek's monograph describes the subject as a nonlinear complex counterpart of classical potential theory, centred on maximal plurisubharmonic functions and the complex Monge–Ampère operator $(dd^c u)^n$, which replaces the Laplacian. For $u\in C^2$ this operator is a constant multiple of $\det(\partial^2u/\partial z_j\partial\bar z_k)\,dV$. ([Klimek, OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/53331); [Guedj–Zeriahi 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16412))

Many current questions are motivated by complex differential geometry, where the same operator governs the Calabi conjecture and Kähler–Einstein metrics on compact [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds); the Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi problem list mixes local questions on domains with questions on compact complex manifolds. ([Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.00705); [Diller, Notre Dame course](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~jdiller/teaching/archive/spring11_80380/index.html))

### Scope
MSC2020 32U has eight subject codes: 32U05 plurisubharmonic functions and generalizations; 32U10 plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions; 32U15 general pluripotential theory; 32U20 capacity theory and generalizations; 32U25 Lelong numbers; 32U30 removable sets in pluripotential theory; 32U35 plurisubharmonic extremal functions and pluricomplex Green functions; 32U40 currents; plus 32U99. ([MSC2020, 32U](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Uxx))

- **vs 31C:** 31C (generalizations of potential theory) lists pluriharmonic and plurisubharmonic functions as 31C10, with a cross-reference to 32U05, and potentials and capacities on other spaces as 31C15. ([MSC2020, 31C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=31Cxx))
- **vs 32T:** 32T lists domains of holomorphy, strongly pseudoconvex, worm and finite-type domains, and exhaustion functions (32T35); plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions are 32U10. ([MSC2020, 32T](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Txx))
- **vs 32W:** the complex Monge–Ampère operator as a PDE is also listed as 32W20. ([MSC2020, 32W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Wxx))

### Key concepts
- **Bedford–Taylor operator and comparison principle (32U15).** Bedford and Taylor defined $(dd^cu)^n$ for every locally bounded [plurisubharmonic](node:Plurisubharmonic%20Functions) $u$ (1982); by Kiselman's example it cannot be defined on all plurisubharmonic functions when $n\ge2$. Comparison principle: if $u,v$ are bounded plurisubharmonic on a bounded domain $\Omega$ and $\liminf_{z\to\zeta}(u-v)(z)\ge0$ for every $\zeta\in\partial\Omega$, then $\int_{\{u<v\}}(dd^cv)^n\le\int_{\{u<v\}}(dd^cu)^n$. ([Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705); [Guedj–Zeriahi 2025, Thm 1.8](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16412))
- **Dirichlet problem (32W20).** For a bounded strictly [pseudoconvex](node:Pseudoconvexity) domain $\Omega$, boundary data $g\in C(\partial\Omega)$ and continuous $f\ge0$, the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem) $(dd^cu)^n=f\,dV$, $u=g$ on $\partial\Omega$ has a unique plurisubharmonic solution; Wang states this classical Bedford–Taylor result as the $u$-independent case of his Corollary 1.5. On a bounded hyperconvex domain a probability measure $\mu$ equals $(dd^c\varphi)^n$ for some bounded $\varphi$ with zero boundary values iff $\mu$ is dominated by the Monge–Ampère measure of a bounded plurisubharmonic function (Kołodziej). ([Wang](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1010.1292); [Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi, §2.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705))
- **Capacity and pluripolar sets (32U20, 32U30).** Following Bedford and Taylor, the relative capacity of a Borel set $E\subset\Omega$ is $\operatorname{cap}(E,\Omega)=\sup\{\int_E(dd^cu)^n: u\in PSH(\Omega),\,-1\le u\le0\}$. A set is pluripolar if it lies in $\{f=-\infty\}$ for some plurisubharmonic $f\not\equiv-\infty$; pluripolar sets have Lebesgue measure zero and Hausdorff dimension at most $2n-2$, and in a strictly pseudoconvex domain the outer capacity of $E$ vanishes iff $E$ is pluripolar (Pliś proves this on almost complex surfaces and notes that the $\mathbb C^n$ cases of his results are in Bedford–Taylor). Josefson's theorem: in open subsets of $\mathbb C^n$, locally pluripolar sets are globally pluripolar. ([Pliś](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1809.11006); [Wikipedia, Pluripolar set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluripolar_set); [arXiv 1611.03577, §2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1611.03577))
- **Extremal and Green functions (32U35).** For compact $K\subset\mathbb C^d$ the Siciak–Zaharjuta extremal function is $V_K(z)=\sup\{u(z):u\in\mathcal L,\ u\le0\text{ on }K\}$, where $\mathcal L$ is the Lelong class of plurisubharmonic $u$ with $u(z)-\log|z|=O(1)$; it can be computed from polynomials as $\max\{0,\sup_p \deg(p)^{-1}\log|p(z)|\}$ over $\|p\|_K\le1$, and $K$ is $L$-regular when $V_K$ is continuous. The pluricomplex Green function of a bounded hyperconvex $\Omega$ with pole $w$ is the supremum of $u\in PSH(\Omega)$, $u\le0$, with $u(z)\le\log\|z-w\|+C$ near $w$. ([arXiv 1911.03756](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.03756); [Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi, §3.7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705))
- **Lelong numbers and Siu's theorem (32U25, 32U40).** Siu's theorem implies that for a plurisubharmonic $\varphi$ on a complex manifold $X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ the upper level set $E_\varepsilon(\varphi)=\{x:\nu(\varphi,x)\ge\varepsilon\}$ of the Lelong number is a closed analytic subset. ([Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705))
- **Cegrell classes and Kołodziej's estimate.** $\mathcal E^p(\Omega)$ consists of plurisubharmonic $u$ that are decreasing limits of test functions $u_j$ with $\sup_j\int(-u_j)^p(dd^cu_j)^n<\infty$; Cegrell proved that a positive Radon measure $\mu$ is $(dd^cu)^n$ for a unique $u\in\mathcal E^p(\Omega)$ iff $\mathcal E^p(\Omega)\subset L^p(\Omega,\mu)$. Kołodziej's estimate: on the unit ball, for $p>1$, a smooth plurisubharmonic $\varphi$ vanishing on the boundary with $\det(\varphi_{j\bar k})=f$ satisfies $\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\le C(n,p)\|f\|_{L^p}^{1/n}$. ([Guedj–Zeriahi 2025, Thm 1.7](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16412); [Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi, Thm 3.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705))

### History
Oka and Lelong introduced plurisubharmonic functions in 1942, Lelong's note appearing in the Comptes Rendus and Oka's in the Tôhoku Mathematical Journal. Greene and Wu (1979) proved that every continuous plurisubharmonic function is a decreasing, even uniform, limit of smooth ones. ([Wikipedia, Plurisubharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurisubharmonic_function))

Bedford and Taylor's 1982 paper defined the Monge–Ampère operator for locally bounded functions; Guedj and Zeriahi place the birth of pluripotential theory "more than forty years" before 2025. Cegrell's energy classes (1998) extended the operator to classes of unbounded plurisubharmonic functions, and Kołodziej's work gave the $L^\infty$ estimate for $L^p$ densities (1996) and criteria on densities ensuring bounded solutions of the Dirichlet problem (2005). ([Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705); [Guedj–Zeriahi 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16412))

### Open problems
- **Range of the operator on bounded functions.** For a bounded strongly pseudoconvex domain $\Omega\Subset\mathbb C^n$, an integral characterization of the measures $(dd^cu)^n$ with $u$ bounded plurisubharmonic is called by Guedj and Zeriahi (October 2025) "an open problem since the birth of pluripotential theory"; a closely related question of Bedford, whether this range has a uniform-integrability characterization, is Question 13 of the 2015 list. ([Guedj–Zeriahi 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16412); [Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705))
- **Problem list.** Dinew, Guedj and Zeriahi list 45 questions, among them whether maximality is a local notion for arbitrary plurisubharmonic functions (Błocki), whether a Dirac mass of $(dd^c\varphi)^n$ at $0$ forces a positive Lelong number at $0$ (Guedj, Rashkovskii), ([Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705)) The same list asked for a PDE proof of Kołodziej's $L^\infty$ estimate; that question has since been answered by Guo, Phong and Tong (arXiv 2021), who give a PDE proof of the sharp $L^\infty$ estimates that previously required pluripotential theory. ([Guo–Phong–Tong](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02224))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Plurisubharmonic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurisubharmonic_function): definition, history, smoothing.
- **Learn:** [Diller, Math 80380: The complex Monge–Ampère operator (Notre Dame)](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~jdiller/teaching/archive/spring11_80380/index.html): graduate course outline from plurisubharmonic functions to the Dirichlet problem and Kähler geometry, with reading list.
- **Primary:** [Dinew, Guedj and Zeriahi, Open problems in pluripotential theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.00705): survey-style problem list with the main theorems stated.
- **Primary:** [Guedj and Zeriahi, High energy plurisubharmonic classes](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16412): comparison principle, Cegrell classes and the range problem.
- **Further reading:** [Klimek, Pluripotential Theory (OUP, 1991)](https://academic.oup.com/book/53331): standard monograph on maximal plurisubharmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem.
references.MSC 32Vxx - CR manifolds:
## Reference
### Overview
A CR manifold is a smooth manifold $M$ with a complex subbundle $L$ of the complexified [tangent bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle) that is formally integrable, $[L,L]\subset L$, and satisfies $L\cap\bar L=\{0\}$. CR functions are the solutions of the tangential Cauchy–Riemann equations $\bar\partial_bf=0$. The structure is modelled on a real hypersurface in complex space, for example the sphere $|z|^2+|w|^2=1$ in $\mathbb C^2$, where $L$ is spanned by $\bar w\,\partial/\partial z-\bar z\,\partial/\partial w$. ([Wikipedia, CR manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_manifold)) If a domain $U\subset\mathbb C^n$ (for instance a [pseudoconvex](node:Pseudoconvexity) one) has smooth boundary and $f$ is smooth on $\bar U$ and holomorphic in $U$, then $f|_{\partial U}$ is a CR function. ([Lebl, IAS 2024 lecture 3](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/ias-24-lec3.pdf))

The subject asks three kinds of question: when CR functions are boundary values of holomorphic functions (extension), when an abstract CR structure arises from an embedding in $\mathbb C^N$ (embeddability), and when two real submanifolds are equivalent under a biholomorphism (the equivalence problem of Poincaré, Cartan and Chern–Moser). Analysis of the tangential complex links the field to [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): Lebl notes that these extension ideas led Lewy to his 1957 non-solvable operator. ([MSC2020, 32V](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Vxx); [Lebl, IAS 2024 lecture 3](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/ias-24-lec3.pdf); [Kolář–Kossovskiy–Zaitsev](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1606.08091); [Wikipedia, Lewy's example](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy%27s_example))

### Scope
MSC2020 32V has eight subject codes: 32V05 CR structures, CR operators and generalizations; 32V10 CR functions; 32V15 CR manifolds as boundaries of domains; 32V20 analysis on CR manifolds; 32V25 extension of functions and other analytic objects from CR manifolds; 32V30 embeddings of CR manifolds; 32V35 finite-type conditions on CR manifolds; 32V40 real submanifolds in [complex manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds); plus 32V99. ([MSC2020, 32V](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Vxx))

- **vs 32T:** 32T lists strongly pseudoconvex, worm and finite-type domains, while 32V15 lists CR manifolds as boundaries of domains and 32V35 finite-type conditions on CR manifolds. ([MSC2020, 32T](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Txx); [MSC2020, 32V](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Vxx))
- **vs 32W:** the operators $\bar\partial_b$ and the $\bar\partial_b$-Neumann problem are filed under 32W10. ([MSC2020, 32W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Wxx))

### Key concepts
- **[CR Structures](node:CR%20Structures) and the Levi form (32V05).** The CR codimension of an abstract structure is $k=n-2\dim_{\mathbb C}L$, with $k=1$ the hypersurface type. For a hypersurface with defining function $F$, the Levi form is $i\partial\bar\partial F$ restricted to $L\wedge\bar L$, and strict pseudoconvexity means it is positive definite. Kohn and Rossi (1965) introduced the tangential complex, with $\bar\partial_b^2=0$ and Kohn Laplacian $\square_b=\bar\partial_b\bar\partial_b^*+\bar\partial_b^*\bar\partial_b$. ([Wikipedia, CR manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_manifold))
- **CR functions and Lewy extension (32V10, 32V25).** If $M\subset U\subset\mathbb C^n$ and $F$ is holomorphic on $U$, then $F|_M$ is CR; conversely, if $M$ and a CR function $f$ are real-analytic, $f$ extends holomorphically to a neighbourhood (Severi). Lewy's extension theorem: let $M$ be a smooth real hypersurface, $p\in M$, $r$ a defining function with sides $U_\pm=\{\pm r>0\}$ in a suitable neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and $f$ a smooth CR function. If the Levi form has a positive eigenvalue at $p$, then $f$ extends holomorphically to $U_-$, continuously up to $M$; a negative eigenvalue gives extension to $U_+$; eigenvalues of both signs give a holomorphic extension to all of $U$. Lebl notes that the result goes back to Kneser (1936). ([Lebl, IAS 2024 lecture 3](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/ias-24-lec3.pdf); [Eastwood–Graham](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9908009))
- **Hartogs–Bochner extension (32V15).** For a relatively compact domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge2$, with smooth connected boundary, every CR distribution on $\partial\Omega$ extends holomorphically into $\Omega$. For unbounded $\Omega$ this can fail, and Boggess, Dwilewicz and Porten show that it holds iff the envelope of holomorphy of $\mathbb C^n\setminus\overline\Omega$ is all of $\mathbb C^n$. Lebl remarks that neither Hartogs nor Bochner proved the CR version; Martinelli did. See [Hartogs Extension Theorem](node:Hartogs%20Extension%20Theorem) for the interior statement. ([Boggess–Dwilewicz–Porten](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.03425); [Lebl, IAS 2024 lecture 3](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/ias-24-lec3.pdf); [Wikipedia, Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem))
- **Wedge extension.** If $M$ is a $C^{2,\alpha}$ generic submanifold and the local CR orbit of $p$ has dimension $\dim M$, continuous CR functions extend holomorphically to a wedge with edge $M$ at $p$: Trépreau (1986) proved this for hypersurfaces and Tumanov (1988) in arbitrary codimension. ([arXiv math/0701531](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0701531))
- **Equivalence problem and Chern–Moser normal form.** Every real-analytic Levi-nondegenerate hypersurface can be brought by a convergent transformation into the form $v=\langle z,\bar z\rangle+\Psi(z,\bar z,u)$, with $\Psi$ satisfying trace conditions on its $(2,2)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,3)$ components; the normalizing maps are parametrized by the stability algebra of the quadric, of dimension $n^2+2n+2$ in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Cartan (1932–33) constructed the canonical connection for 3-dimensional strictly pseudoconvex structures and Chern and Moser (1974) extended it to higher dimensions; Tanaka (1975) and Webster (1978) gave the pseudo-Hermitian connection. ([Kolář–Kossovskiy–Zaitsev](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1606.08091); [Wikipedia, CR manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_manifold))
- **Embeddability (32V30).** Boutet de Monvel (1974): compact strongly pseudoconvex CR manifolds of real dimension $\ge5$ embed globally in some $\mathbb C^N$; for compact strictly pseudoconvex CR manifolds, global embeddability is equivalent to closed range of $\square_b$ on functions in $L^2$ (Kohn, 1986, for the converse direction). In dimension 3 the Rossi example, a family of perturbed CR structures on $S^3$ with parameter $\varepsilon\in\mathbb C$, $0<|\varepsilon|<1$, is locally but not globally embeddable, and Nirenberg (1974) perturbed Lewy's non-solvable vector field to get a structure that is not locally embeddable. Kuranishi proved local embeddability for strictly pseudoconvex structures in dimension $\ge9$, Akahori (1987) in dimension 7. ([Wikipedia, CR manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_manifold); [Brinkschulte–Hill–Nacinovich](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0711.0227))
- **Lewy's operator.** The equation $\partial u/\partial\bar z-iz\,\partial u/\partial t=F(t,z)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb C$, with suitable smooth $F$, has no solution on any open set (Annals of Mathematics, 1957); it shows that the $\bar\partial_b$-complex, unlike the Dolbeault complex, is almost never exact. ([Wikipedia, Lewy's example](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy%27s_example); [Wikipedia, Hans Lewy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Lewy))

### History
Poincaré's 1907 paper on analytic functions of two variables and conformal representation supplies the local realization on which Chern–Moser theory rests; the Levi form is named after E. E. Levi. Hartogs (1906) found the extension phenomenon, and Fichera (1957) gave a proof through CR functions. Lewy's non-solvable equation (1957) redirected the theory of linear PDE. Chern–Moser (1974), Boutet de Monvel (1974) and Kohn–Rossi (1965) set up the invariant geometry, embedding theory and $\bar\partial_b$-complex. ([Kolář–Kossovskiy–Zaitsev](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1606.08091); [Wikipedia, CR manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_manifold); [Wikipedia, Hartogs's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartogs%27s_extension_theorem); [Wikipedia, Hans Lewy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Lewy))

### Open problems
- **Local embeddability in dimension 5.** For abstract strictly pseudoconvex CR manifolds of real dimension 5, Brinkschulte, Hill and Nacinovich list local CR embeddability and the Poincaré lemma for $(0,1)$-forms as two open problems, and prove them equivalent; dimension $\ge7$ is settled and dimension 3 fails in general. ([Brinkschulte–Hill–Nacinovich](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0711.0227); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0711.0227))
- **Normal forms beyond the Levi-nondegenerate case.** Kolář, Kossovskiy and Zaitsev pose constructing a complete normal form for Levi-nondegenerate codimension-2 submanifolds of $\mathbb C^N$, $N\ge3$; a normal form for infinite-type hypersurfaces in $\mathbb C^2$; and a convergent normal form at isolated weakly pseudoconvex points. ([Kolář–Kossovskiy–Zaitsev, §5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1606.08091))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, CR manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_manifold): definitions, Levi form, embeddability results, Tanaka–Webster connection.
- **Learn:** [Lebl, Tasty Bits of SCV, IAS 2024 lecture 3](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/ias-24-lec3.pdf): CR functions, Severi and Lewy extension theorems; notes linked from [Lebl's page](https://math.okstate.edu/people/lebl/).
- **Primary:** [Kolář, Kossovskiy and Zaitsev, Normal forms in Cauchy–Riemann geometry](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1606.08091): survey of the Poincaré–Chern–Moser problem with open problems.
- **Primary:** [Brinkschulte, Hill and Nacinovich, The Poincaré lemma and local embeddability](https://arxiv.org/abs/0711.0227): equivalence of the two dimension-5 problems.
- **Further reading:** [Baouendi, Ebenfelt and Rothschild, Real Submanifolds in Complex Space and Their Mappings (Princeton, 1999)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691004983/real-submanifolds-in-complex-space-and-their-mappings): holomorphic extension, CR orbits, nondegeneracy and finite determination of mappings.
references.MSC 32Wxx - Differential operators in se:
## Reference
### Overview
On a complex manifold every complex $k$-form splits uniquely into $(p,q)$-forms, and the exterior derivative splits as $d=\partial+\bar\partial$ with $\bar\partial:\Omega^{p,q}\to\Omega^{p,q+1}$ and $\bar\partial^2=0$. The basic problem of the code is the inhomogeneous Cauchy–Riemann system $\bar\partial u=f$, for which $\bar\partial f=0$ is necessary; the MIT 18.117 notes pose as a basic problem the question of which open sets the [Dolbeault complex](node:Dolbeault%20Cohomology) is exact on, and prove that it is locally exact. ([Wikipedia, Complex differential form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_differential_form); [MIT 18.117, lecture 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/7d0d08a199dde69c878faab3bfbd4edc_18117_lec04.pdf))

The $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem gives a Hilbert-space approach: the complex Laplacian $\square=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial$ gives a boundary-value problem with an elliptic operator but non-coercive boundary conditions; its existence, subellipticity, compactness and global regularity theory depends on the boundary geometry of [pseudoconvex domains](node:MSC%2032Txx%20-%20Pseudoconvex%20domains). ([Boas–Straube survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))

The code also covers the tangential complex $\bar\partial_b$ on CR manifolds, the complex Monge–Ampère operator, [pseudodifferential operators](node:Pseudodifferential%20Operators) and heat kernels in several complex variables. ([MSC2020, 32W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Wxx))

### Scope
MSC2020 32W has six subject codes: 32W05 $\bar\partial$ and $\bar\partial$-Neumann operators; 32W10 $\bar\partial_b$ and $\bar\partial_b$-Neumann operators; 32W20 complex Monge–Ampère operators; 32W25 pseudodifferential operators in several complex variables; 32W30 heat kernels in several complex variables; 32W50 other partial differential equations of [complex analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) in several variables; plus 32W99. ([MSC2020, 32W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Wxx))

- **vs 35N:** the section for overdetermined problems in [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) has 35N15, $\bar\partial$-Neumann problems and formal complexes in the context of PDEs, which points to 32W05 and 32W10. ([MSC2020, 35N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Nxx))
- **vs 32U:** 32U lists plurisubharmonic functions, capacities, Lelong numbers and currents, while the complex Monge–Ampère operator itself is 32W20. ([MSC2020, 32U](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Uxx); [MSC2020, 32W](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=32Wxx))

### Key concepts
- **Local exactness (Dolbeault–Grothendieck).** If $V\subset U$ are polydiscs, $q\ge1$, and $\omega\in\Omega^{0,q}(U)$ is smooth with $\bar\partial\omega=0$, then $\omega=\bar\partial\mu$ on $V$ for a smooth $\mu\in\Omega^{0,q-1}(V)$. ([MIT 18.117, lecture 4, Theorem 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/7d0d08a199dde69c878faab3bfbd4edc_18117_lec04.pdf); [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms))
- **Hörmander's $L^2$ theorem (32W05).** On a bounded pseudoconvex $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$, the operator $\square$ on $(0,q)$-forms has a bounded inverse $N_q$ (the $\bar\partial$-Neumann operator) with constants $D^2e/q$, $D$ the diameter, and Kohn's formula $P_q=I-\bar\partial^*N_{q+1}\bar\partial$ expresses the Bergman projection through $N_{q+1}$. ([Boas–Straube, Theorem 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204); [Krantz–Peloso](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087)) Fornæss's course proves existence of $L^2_{\rm loc}$ solutions of $\bar\partial$ on pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb C^n$ and uses them to solve the Levi problem. ([Fornæss notes](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.00562); [Crossref, Hörmander 1965](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02391775); [The d-bar Problem](node:The%20d-bar%20Problem))
- **Weighted $L^2$ estimates and extension.** In the bundle form of Hörmander, Andreotti–Vesentini and Skoda: on a smoothly bounded domain $\Omega\Subset X$ with $q$-positive boundary in a Kähler manifold, if $-\sqrt{-1}(\Theta(h)+\mathrm{Ricci}(\omega))-\Xi$ is $q$-positive, then every $\bar\partial$-closed $E$-valued $(0,q)$-form $f$ with $\int_\Omega|f|^2_{\Xi,\omega;h}<\infty$ has a solution of $\bar\partial u=f$ with $\int_\Omega|u|^2_{\omega,h}\le\int_\Omega|f|^2_{\Xi,\omega;h}$; $\Xi=c\omega$ is the Hörmander case. The twisting technique, discovered by Donnelly and Fefferman in the mid-1980s, yields under a twisted curvature hypothesis a minimal-norm solution with $\int|u_o|^2e^{-\kappa}\le\int|\alpha|^2_{\Theta}e^{-\kappa}$. Ohsawa–Takegoshi: for bounded pseudoconvex $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$, a complex hyperplane $H$ and plurisubharmonic $\psi$, every holomorphic $f$ on $\Omega\cap H$ with $\int e^{-\psi}|f|^2<\infty$ extends to holomorphic $F$ on $\Omega$ with $\int_\Omega e^{-\psi}|F|^2\le C\int_{\Omega\cap H}e^{-\psi}|f|^2$, $C$ depending only on the diameter. ([McNeal–Varolin, Theorems 3.1.1, 3.4.1, 4.1.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.08047)) Guan–Zhou found the optimal constant in Ohsawa's generalized extension theorem and proved the extended Suita conjecture. ([Guan–Zhou](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.0054))
- **Kohn's estimates and Catlin's theorem.** On a bounded strictly pseudoconvex domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, $N_q$ gains one derivative and the estimates gain half a derivative (Kohn). A subelliptic estimate of order $\varepsilon$ gives local gains of $2\varepsilon$ derivatives for $N$. Catlin: on a bounded pseudoconvex domain with $C^\infty$ boundary a subelliptic estimate holds near $z_0$ iff the D'Angelo type $D_q(z_0)$ is finite, with $\varepsilon\le1/D_q(z_0)$. ([Boas–Straube, Theorems 7–10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))
- **Kohn's multiplier ideals.** A germ $f$ is a subelliptic multiplier if the subelliptic estimate holds with $f\varphi$ on the left. Kohn's algorithm builds real-radical ideals $I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\cdots$, starting from the defining function and the determinant of the Levi form and adjoining determinants of rows $(L_1f,\dots,L_{n-1}f)$. For a bounded pseudoconvex domain with real-analytic boundary, a subelliptic estimate holds at $p$ iff $1\in I_k$ for some $k$ iff no complex analytic variety through $p$ lies in the boundary (D'Angelo finite type), the last step using Diederich–Fornæss. ([Fassina, §1–2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.00128); [Boas–Straube](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))
- **Compactness and property (P).** $\Omega$ satisfies Catlin's property (P) if for every $M>0$ there is a plurisubharmonic $\lambda$ with $0\le\lambda\le1$ whose complex Hessian has eigenvalues $\ge M$ on $\partial\Omega$. Property (P) implies compactness of $N_q$ on $L^2$; by Kohn–Nirenberg a compactness estimate gives global regularity in every $W^s$. Strictly pseudoconvex and finite-type domains satisfy (P). ([Boas–Straube, Theorem 12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))
- **Global regularity and its failure.** Kohn's weighted theory gives $W^s$ regularity for the problem with weight $e^{-t|z|^2}$ when $t$ is large; $N_q$ and the Bergman projection are $W^s$-bounded for all $s$ when $\Omega$ has a defining function plurisubharmonic on the boundary (Boas–Straube). Christ proved that on worm domains the Bergman projection and $N_1$ fail to preserve $C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$. ([Boas–Straube, Theorems 4, 6, 14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204); [Crossref, Christ 1996](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/s0894-0347-96-00213-5))
- **Tangential complex and the Heisenberg group (32W10).** On a CR manifold $\bar\partial_b^2=0$ and the Kohn Laplacian $\square_b=\bar\partial_b\bar\partial_b^*+\bar\partial_b^*\bar\partial_b$ is non-negative and formally self-adjoint; on functions on the Heisenberg group $\square_b=\Delta_b+inT$ with $\Delta_b$ the sub-Laplacian and $T=\partial/\partial t$. Kohn showed that global embeddability implies that $\square_b$ on functions has closed range in $L^2$, and Boutet de Monvel that closed range implies global embeddability for compact strongly pseudoconvex CR manifolds of real dimension at least 5. See [MSC 32Vxx - CR manifolds](node:MSC%2032Vxx%20-%20CR%20manifolds). ([Wikipedia, CR manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_manifold)) Folland and Stein gave a closed-form expression for the complex Green operator of $\square_b$ on the Heisenberg group; e.g. on $(0,1)$-forms on the Heisenberg group in $\mathbb C^3$ the fundamental solution is $1/(\pi^3(|z|^4+|t|^2))$. ([Fundamental solutions to $\square_b$ on certain quadrics](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1110.5804); [Boggess–Raich, Part 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2101.08322))
- **Pseudodifferential and heat-kernel methods (32W25, 32W30).** Boutet de Monvel–Sjöstrand showed that the Bergman projection of a strictly pseudoconvex domain is a Fourier integral operator with complex phase, and gave a full asymptotic expansion of the Szegő projection on a strictly pseudoconvex CR manifold; Fefferman obtained the complete boundary expansion of the diagonal Bergman kernel. ([Hsiao–Marinescu](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.09820)) Christ's worm argument also uses a real-variable model with pseudodifferential operators. ([Krantz–Peloso](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087)) On quadrics, Boggess and Raich derive the fundamental solution of $\square_b$ from the $\square_b$-heat kernel; earlier sub-Laplacian heat-kernel formulas were known only up to a partial Fourier transform. ([Boggess–Raich, Part 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2101.08322))
- **Complex Monge–Ampère operators (32W20).** The nonlinear operator $(dd^cu)^n$ is defined for locally bounded [plurisubharmonic](node:Plurisubharmonic%20Functions) $u$ (Bedford–Taylor) but not for all plurisubharmonic functions when $n\ge2$ (Kiselman). Kołodziej: fix $p>1$; if $\varphi$ is smooth plurisubharmonic on the unit ball $\mathbb B\subset\mathbb C^n$ with $\varphi|_{\partial\mathbb B}=0$ and $\det(\varphi_{j\bar k})=f$, then $\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb B)}\le C\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb B)}^{1/n}$ with $C=C(n,p)$. For the Dirichlet problem $(dd^cu)^n=f\,dV$, $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, $f$ smooth with $f\ge\varepsilon>0$, the solution is smooth when $\Omega$ is smooth and strongly pseudoconvex (Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg–Spruck). See [MSC 32Uxx - Pluripotential theory](node:MSC%2032Uxx%20-%20Pluripotential%20theory). ([Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi, Theorem 3.1, Question 23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705)) On a compact Kähler manifold, Yau's solution of the Calabi conjecture solves $(\omega+i\partial\bar\partial\varphi)^n=e^F\omega^n$ for $e^F$ of average 1, uniquely up to a constant. ([Wikipedia, Calabi conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi_conjecture))

### History
Kohn solved the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem on strongly pseudoconvex manifolds in two Annals of Mathematics papers (1963, 1964), and Hörmander's 1965 Acta paper gave the $L^2$ existence theory on pseudoconvex domains; Kohn's weighted global regularity followed in 1973 (Trans. AMS). ([Boas–Straube, references](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204); [Crossref, Hörmander 1965](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02391775)) Andreotti–Vesentini introduced weighted estimates of the same type, and Donnelly–Fefferman, Ohsawa–Takegoshi and Berndtsson–Charpentier later gave alternative forms. ([Liu 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2401.16573)) Barrett showed loss of Sobolev regularity of the Bergman projection on the worm, and Christ's 1996 Journal of the AMS paper settled the $C^\infty$ question negatively. ([Krantz–Peloso](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0710.4087); [Crossref, Christ 1996](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/s0894-0347-96-00213-5)) Yau proved the Calabi conjecture in 1977–1978. ([Wikipedia, Calabi conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabi_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Characterizing global regularity.** Necessary and sufficient conditions for global regularity of the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem remain unknown, as stated in a 2024 paper of B. Liu, which also notes that the case of incomplete metrics is not yet understood. ([Liu 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2401.16573))
- **Compactness.** Boas and Straube's 1996 survey records that the boundary conditions characterizing compactness of $N_q$ are not understood, nor how property (P) relates to compactness. ([Boas–Straube](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204))
- **Optimal order of subellipticity and Kohn's algorithm.** The optimal $\varepsilon$ in terms of boundary data is unknown in general; Fassina shows Kohn's algorithm is not effective (the orders of the radicals taken cannot be bounded in terms of the type) on a family of pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb C^2$, and for smooth non-real-analytic boundaries it is open whether $1\in I_k$ is necessary for subellipticity. ([Boas–Straube](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204); [Fassina](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.00128))
- **Regularity for complex Monge–Ampère.** Whether the solution in the Dirichlet problem above is automatically smooth on bounded hyperconvex domains (Błocki's question) is open, among many problems in the Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi list. ([Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi, Question 23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Complex differential form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_differential_form): $(p,q)$-types and the operators $\partial,\bar\partial$.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.117 Topics in Several Complex Variables, lecture 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-117-topics-in-several-complex-variables-spring-2005/7d0d08a199dde69c878faab3bfbd4edc_18117_lec04.pdf): Dolbeault complex and local exactness; see also [Hodge theory](node:Hodge%20Theory).
- **Primary:** [Boas–Straube, Global regularity of the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem: a survey of the $L^2$-Sobolev theory](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9612204): existence, subellipticity, compactness, regularity and counterexamples.
- **Primary:** [McNeal–Varolin, $L^2$ estimates for the $\bar\partial$ operator](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.08047): survey of Hörmander, twisted and Ohsawa–Takegoshi estimates.
- **Primary:** [Dinew–Guedj–Zeriahi, Open problems in pluripotential theory](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1511.00705): complex Monge–Ampère estimates and open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Krantz, Function Theory of Several Complex Variables (AMS, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/chel/340): graduate text; Slatyer's [survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1411.0363) points to its chapter 4 for a self-contained proof of Hörmander's theorem.
references.MSC 33 - Special functions:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 33 is titled "Special functions (33-XX deals with the properties of functions as functions)": it studies named families such as the gamma, hypergeometric, Bessel and $q$-hypergeometric functions and the orthogonal polynomials built from them, while orthogonal functions in general go to 42C, combinatorial aspects to 05A, number-theoretic aspects to 11 and [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) to 22E. ([MSC2020, 33-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33-XX)) Theoretical questions about these functions include asymptotic analysis, analytic continuation and monodromy; Whittaker and Watson's 1902 textbook sought to unify the subject through [complex analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), and from 1950 on substantial parts of the classical theory were recast in terms of [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups), with Lie group representations generalizing spherical functions (Vilenkin, 1968). ([Wikipedia, Special functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_functions))

Hypergeometric structure organizes much of the field: 33C groups ${}_2F_1$, Bessel and Airy (${}_0F_1$), confluent (${}_1F_1$) and ${}_pF_q$ functions with the orthogonal polynomials of hypergeometric type, and the Askey scheme arranges those polynomials, and their $q$-analogues, by the type of their hypergeometric representation. ([MSC2020, 33C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Cxx); [Wikipedia, Askey scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Askey_scheme)) The NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions continues the 1964 National Bureau of Standards *Handbook of Mathematical Functions* (Applied Mathematics Series 55), with three methodology chapters followed by function chapters. ([DLMF, Introduction](https://dlmf.nist.gov/front/introduction)) Concept notes: [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions), [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function), [Hypergeometric Functions](node:Hypergeometric%20Functions).

### Scope
MSC2020 33-XX has five sections ([MSC2020, 33-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33-XX)):
- [MSC 33Bxx - Elementary classical functions](node:MSC%2033Bxx%20-%20Elementary%20classical%20functions): elementary classical functions.
- [MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Cxx%20-%20Hypergeometric%20functions): ${}_2F_1$, Bessel and Airy (${}_0F_1$), confluent (${}_1F_1$), ${}_pF_q$, orthogonal polynomials of hypergeometric type including the Askey scheme (33C45), spherical harmonics, Meijer-type integrals, Appell–Horn–Lauricella functions, root-system hypergeometric functions, connections with groups and algebras. ([MSC2020, 33C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Cxx))
- [MSC 33Dxx - Basic hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Dxx%20-%20Basic%20hypergeometric%20functions): $q$-gamma and $q$-beta functions, ${}_r\phi_s$, Askey–Wilson and Macdonald polynomials, connections with quantum groups and Hecke algebras. ([MSC2020, 33D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Dxx))
- [MSC 33Exx - Other special functions](node:MSC%2033Exx%20-%20Other%20special%20functions): other special functions.
- [MSC 33Fxx - Computational aspects of special functions](node:MSC%2033Fxx%20-%20Computational%20aspects%20of%20special%20functions): computation, with software at 33-04. ([MSC2020, 33-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33-XX))

Neighbours: by the cross-references above, general orthogonal systems belong to [MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces](node:MSC%2042%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20on%20Euclidean%20spaces) (42C), combinatorial aspects to [MSC 05 - Combinatorics](node:MSC%2005%20-%20Combinatorics) (05A; see [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics)), and arithmetic aspects to [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory), and representation theory to 22E. ([MSC2020, 33-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Equations with regular singularities.** Every second-order linear homogeneous ODE with at most three distinct singularities, all regular, transforms into the hypergeometric equation $z(1-z)w''+[c-(a+b+1)z]w'-abw=0$; its solutions with exponents $\{a_j\},\{b_j\},\{c_j\}$ at $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ (summing to 1) form Riemann's $P$-symbol. ([DLMF §15.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.11)) A confluent counterpart is Kummer's equation $zw''+(b-z)w'-aw=0$, with a regular singularity at $0$ and an irregular one of rank one at $\infty$, solved by $M(a,b,z)={}_1F_1(a;b;z)$ and by $U(a,b,z)\sim z^{-a}$ as $z\to\infty$ in $|\operatorname{ph}z|\le\tfrac32\pi-\delta$. ([DLMF §13.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/13.2)) See [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Integral representations.** For $\Re c>\Re b>0$ and $|\operatorname{ph}(1-z)|<\pi$, Euler's integral $\mathbf F(a,b;c;z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(b)\Gamma(c-b)}\int_0^1t^{b-1}(1-t)^{c-b-1}(1-zt)^{-a}\,dt$ expresses ${}_2F_1/\Gamma(c)$ through a [beta](node:Beta%20Function)-type integral; Barnes's integral $\frac{1}{2\pi i\,\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\int_{-i\infty}^{i\infty}\frac{\Gamma(a+t)\Gamma(b+t)\Gamma(-t)}{\Gamma(c+t)}(-z)^t\,dt$ gives the same function for $|\operatorname{ph}(-z)|<\pi$, $a,b\notin\{0,-1,\dots\}$. ([DLMF §15.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.6))
- **Askey scheme.** Hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials form a hierarchy from Wilson and Racah (${}_4F_3$) through the Hahn families (${}_3F_2$), Jacobi, Meixner, Krawtchouk and Meixner–Pollaczek (${}_2F_1$), and Laguerre, Bessel and Charlier, down to Hermite; drawn by Labelle and by Askey and Wilson (1985), it was extended to $q$-polynomials headed by Askey–Wilson and $q$-Racah (${}_4\phi_3$) by Koekoek and Swarttouw (1998) and Koekoek, Lesky and Swarttouw (2010). ([Wikipedia, Askey scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Askey_scheme))
- **$q$-series.** For $|q|<1$ and $|z|<1$ the $q$-binomial series gives ${}_1\phi_0(a;-;q,z)=(az;q)_\infty/(z;q)_\infty$ ([DLMF §17.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.5)), and Jacobi's triple product reads $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}(-z)^nq^{n(n-1)/2}=(q,z,q/z;q)_\infty$ ([DLMF §17.8](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.8)); Koornwinder's overview treats these $q$-analogues, with $q=1$ the classical case, together with Macdonald polynomials, elliptic hypergeometric series and applications to [Quantum Groups](node:Quantum%20Groups). ([Koornwinder, q-Special functions, an overview](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511148))
- **Asymptotics: saddle points and uniform approximation.** For $\int e^{-zp(t)}q(t)\,dt$ with large $z$, Laplace's method expands about an endpoint where $\Re(zp)$ is minimal; if the minimum is at an interior simple saddle point $p'(t_0)=0$, the expansion runs in powers $z^{-(s+1/2)}$ (the method of steepest descents), and when two saddle points coalesce, Chester, Friedman and Ursell's cubic change of variables gives uniform approximations in Airy or Scorer functions. ([DLMF §2.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.4)) See [Asymptotic Analysis](node:Asymptotic%20Analysis) and [Bessel Functions](node:Bessel%20Functions).
- **Painlevé transcendents.** The six Painlevé equations, e.g. $w''=6w^2+z$ (PI) and $w''=2w^3+zw+\alpha$ (PII), have the Painlevé property (no movable branch points; movable poles or isolated essential singularities may occur). For general parameters their solutions are transcendental, while for special parameter values PII–PVI have solutions in elementary or classical special functions. ([DLMF §32.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/32.2))

### History
The theory of [elliptic functions](node:Elliptic%20Functions) was the high point of nineteenth-century special-function theory; the twentieth century saw Whittaker and Watson's unification through complex analysis (1902), Watson's treatise on Bessel functions, the encyclopedic Bateman Manuscript Project edited by Erdélyi, and from 1950 the group-theoretic recasting surveyed by Vilenkin's *Special Functions and the Theory of Group Representations* (1968). ([Wikipedia, Special functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_functions)) The 1964 NBS *Handbook of Mathematical Functions*, created under Milton Abramowitz, was succeeded by the NIST DLMF. ([DLMF, Introduction](https://dlmf.nist.gov/front/introduction)) Askey and Wilson's 1985 AMS Memoir introduced the polynomials that head the $q$-Askey scheme. ([Crossref, Askey–Wilson 1985](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0319))

### Open problems
- **Usable uniform asymptotics for general orthogonal polynomials.** S. Olver asks in the OPSFA13 report whether uniform asymptotics with error bounds can be made easy to use for general weights; Riemann–Hilbert methods give such asymptotics but are hard for non-experts, and fast transforms and quadrature depend on them. The same list asks for an algorithm converting between values on a grid of $n$ points on the sphere and [spherical harmonic](node:Spherical%20Harmonics) coefficients in roughly $O(n\log n)$ operations. ([Cohl, Report from the Open Problems Session at OPSFA13](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06196))
- **Generalized linearization formulas.** Closed-form coefficients for $P_m(x;\mathbf a)P_n(x;\mathbf a)=\sum_k\gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)P_k(x;\mathbf b)$ are derived in the report for Laguerre, Gegenbauer, Jacobi, continuous $q$-ultraspherical/Rogers and continuous $q$-Jacobi polynomials; it states that further closed-form linearization formulae for other polynomials of the (q-)Askey scheme had yet to be found. ([Cohl, Report from the Open Problems Session at OPSFA13](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06196))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Special functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_functions): scope, history and the group-theoretic viewpoint.
- **Reference:** [NIST DLMF](https://dlmf.nist.gov/front/introduction): authoritative formulas with conventions; methods chapters 1–3.
- **Learn:** [Schlosser, Special Functions (Vienna course)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~schlosse/courses/SF/SF.html): gamma, beta, hypergeometric functions, orthogonal polynomials and, time permitting, $q$-series, theta and elliptic functions.
- **Primary:** [Cohl, Report from the Open Problems Session at OPSFA13 (SIGMA 2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06196): current research problems in orthogonal polynomials and special functions.
- **Primary:** [Koornwinder, q-Special functions, an overview (arXiv math/0511148)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511148): survey of the $q$-theory.
- **Further reading:** [Andrews, Askey & Roy, Special Functions (CUP, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781107325937); [Olver, Asymptotics and Special Functions (A K Peters, 1997 reprint)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9781439864548); [Gasper & Rahman, Basic Hypergeometric Series (CUP, 2nd ed. 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511526251).
references.MSC 33Bxx - Elementary classical functio:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 33Bxx (Elementary classical functions) is the part of the special-functions chapter 33 that covers exponential and trigonometric functions; gamma, beta and polygamma functions; incomplete beta and gamma functions, including error functions and Fresnel integrals; and higher logarithm functions. ([MSC2020 33Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Bxx)) The exponential $\exp(x)=e^x$ is the unique real function with value $1$ at $0$ and derivative equal to itself; it can equivalently be defined by a power series, by the limit $(1+x/n)^n$, or as the solution of $y'=y$, and it extends to complex arguments, to matrices, Banach algebras and Lie algebras. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_function))

The complex setting forces care about domains. $\exp$ is entire, zero-free and $2\pi i$-periodic, so its inverse is multivalued: the general logarithm $\operatorname{Ln}z=\ln z+2k\pi i$, while the principal branch $\ln z$ is single-valued analytic only on $\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. ([DLMF §4.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.2)) Gluing all branches gives a spiral Riemann surface biholomorphic to $\mathbb C$, the universal cover of $\mathbb C^*$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_logarithm))

The values of $\exp$ at algebraic points are the subject of transcendence theory: the Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem is extended by the Gelfond–Schneider and Baker theorems, and Schanuel's conjecture would generalize all of them. ([Wikipedia: Lindemann–Weierstrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindemann%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem)) Schanuel's conjecture opens the transcendence section of Waldschmidt's survey of open Diophantine problems. ([Waldschmidt, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists the following sub-codes under 33Bxx. ([MSC2020 33Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Bxx))
- **33B10** Exponential and trigonometric functions.
- **33B15** Gamma, beta and polygamma functions: see [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function), [Beta Function](node:Beta%20Function), [Stirling's Formula](node:Stirling's%20Formula).
- **33B20** Incomplete beta and gamma functions (error functions, probability integral, Fresnel integrals).
- **33B30** Higher logarithm functions.
- **33B99** None of the above, but in this section.

Neighbours: the other subdivisions of chapter 33 are [MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Cxx%20-%20Hypergeometric%20functions), [MSC 33Dxx - Basic hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Dxx%20-%20Basic%20hypergeometric%20functions), [MSC 33Exx - Other special functions](node:MSC%2033Exx%20-%20Other%20special%20functions) and [MSC 33Fxx - Computational aspects of special functions](node:MSC%2033Fxx%20-%20Computational%20aspects%20of%20special%20functions). The 33-XX header says the chapter deals with properties of functions as functions, and sends orthogonal functions to 42Cxx, combinatorial aspects to 05Axx, number-theoretic aspects to 11-XX, and representation theory to 22Exx. ([MSC2020 33-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Characterization of exp.** General exponentials are $f(x)=ae^{kx}$, characterized by constant $f'/f$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_function))
- **Euler's formula.** $e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x$ for real, and equally complex, $x$; it can serve as the definition of the trigonometric functions for complex arguments, and $t\mapsto e^{it}$ is a surjective morphism of topological groups $\mathbb R\to S^1$ with kernel $2\pi\mathbb Z$, exhibiting $\mathbb R$ as a covering space of $S^1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_formula))
- **Complex logarithm.** $w$ is a logarithm of $z\ne0$ iff $e^w=z$; no continuous logarithm exists on all of $\mathbb C^*$, each branch $L$ is holomorphic with $L'(z)=1/z$, and $\operatorname{Log}(z_1z_2)$ can differ from $\operatorname{Log}z_1+\operatorname{Log}z_2$ by an integer multiple of $2\pi i$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_logarithm))
- **Gamma function (33B15).** $\Gamma(z)=\int_0^\infty e^{-t}t^{z-1}\,dt$ for $\Re z>0$, continued analytically to a meromorphic function with no zeros and simple poles of residue $(-1)^n/n!$ at $z=-n$. ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2)) It satisfies $\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)$, the reflection formula $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin(\pi z)$ for $z\ne0,\pm1,\dots$, the duplication formula $\Gamma(2z)=\pi^{-1/2}2^{2z-1}\Gamma(z)\Gamma(z+\tfrac12)$, and Gauss's multiplication formula $\Gamma(nz)=(2\pi)^{(1-n)/2}n^{nz-1/2}\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\Gamma(z+k/n)$. ([DLMF §5.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.5)) Its large-argument asymptotics are [Stirling's Formula](node:Stirling's%20Formula).
- **Bohr–Mollerup theorem.** $\Gamma$ is the only positive function $f$ on $x>0$ with $f(1)=1$, $f(x+1)=xf(x)$ and $\log f$ convex; it first appeared in Bohr and Mollerup's 1922 complex analysis textbook and is treated in Artin's *The Gamma Function* (1964). ([Wikipedia: Bohr–Mollerup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr%E2%80%93Mollerup_theorem))
- **Digamma and polygamma functions.** $\psi(z)=\Gamma'(z)/\Gamma(z)$ for $z\ne0,-1,-2,\dots$ is meromorphic with simple poles of residue $-1$ at $z=-n$. ([DLMF §5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2)) Its derivatives $\psi^{(n)}$ are the polygamma functions; the trigamma function is $\psi'(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}(k+z)^{-2}$ for $z\ne0,-1,-2,\dots$. ([DLMF §5.15](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.15))
- **Incomplete gamma and error functions (33B20).** $\gamma(a,z)=\int_0^z t^{a-1}e^{-t}dt$ for $\Re a>0$ and $\Gamma(a,z)=\int_z^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}dt$, with $\gamma(a,z)+\Gamma(a,z)=\Gamma(a)$ for $a\ne0,-1,-2,\dots$. ([DLMF §8.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/8.2)) The error functions are the case $a=\tfrac12$: $\operatorname{erf}z=\pi^{-1/2}\gamma(\tfrac12,z^2)$ and $\operatorname{erfc}z=\pi^{-1/2}\Gamma(\tfrac12,z^2)$; the Fresnel integrals $C(z)$, $S(z)$ are expressed there through confluent hypergeometric functions. ([DLMF §7.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/7.11))
- **Polylogarithms (33B30).** $\operatorname{Li}_s(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}z^n/n^s$ for $|z|<1$, also convergent on $|z|=1$ when $\Re s>1$ and continued analytically elsewhere; $\operatorname{Li}_s(1)=\zeta(s)$. The dilogarithm satisfies $\operatorname{Li}_2(z)=-\int_0^z t^{-1}\ln(1-t)\,dt$ on $\mathbb C\setminus(1,\infty)$ and the inversion formula $\operatorname{Li}_2(z)+\operatorname{Li}_2(1/z)=-\pi^2/6-\tfrac12(\ln(-z))^2$ for $z\in\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$. ([DLMF §25.12](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.12)) See [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem.** If $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ are algebraic and $\mathbb Q$-linearly independent, then $e^{\alpha_1},\dots,e^{\alpha_n}$ are algebraically independent over $\mathbb Q$; hence $e$ and $\pi$ are transcendental. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindemann%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem))
- **Baker's theorem.** Linear forms in logarithms of algebraic numbers are bounded below effectively, a nonhomogeneous extension of the Gelfond–Schneider theorem; the bound is effectively computable. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem)) Gelfond–Schneider: if $a,b$ are algebraic with $a\notin\{0,1\}$ and $b\notin\mathbb Q$, every value of $a^b$ is transcendental. ([Wikipedia: Gelfond–Schneider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfond%E2%80%93Schneider_theorem))
- **Related concepts:** [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions), [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), [Taylor's Theorem](node:Taylor's%20Theorem), [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence), [Lie Group Exponential Map](node:Lie%20Group%20Exponential%20Map), [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): exp has a power series and extends to Lie algebras ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_function)), and $t\mapsto e^{it}$ makes $\mathbb R$ a covering space of the circle ([Wikipedia: Euler's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_formula)).

### History
Jacob Bernoulli's 1683 study of compound interest produced the number $e$, and Euler later gave the limit definition. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_function)) Euler published his formula in the 1748 *Introductio in analysin infinitorum*; Cotes had given an equivalent logarithmic form in 1714. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_formula)) Hermite proved the case of integer exponents, Lindemann extended this to algebraic numbers in 1882, and Weierstrass obtained the general theorem in 1885. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindemann%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem)) Baker received the Fields Medal in 1970 for his theorem on linear forms in logarithms. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Schanuel's conjecture.** For $\mathbb Q$-linearly independent complex $z_1,\dots,z_n$, the field $\mathbb Q(z_1,\dots,z_n,e^{z_1},\dots,e^{z_n})$ has transcendence degree at least $n$. It is open; the case of algebraic exponents is Lindemann–Weierstrass, and Ax proved a power-series analogue in 1971. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schanuel%27s_conjecture))
- **Algebraic independence of logarithms of algebraic numbers.** If $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are $\mathbb Q$-linearly independent complex numbers with $e^{\lambda_i}$ algebraic, then the $\lambda_i$ should be algebraically independent; Waldschmidt lists this as Conjecture 3.3, the most important special case of Schanuel's conjecture. ([Waldschmidt, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))
- **Four exponentials conjecture** (no homogeneous quadratic relations among logarithms of algebraic numbers) is listed as open. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Exponential function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_function): definitions, characterization, complex extension.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.112, Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/): lectures on the complex exponential, trigonometric functions and logarithm.
- **Primary:** [Waldschmidt, Open Diophantine Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0312440): survey of open transcendence questions including Schanuel's conjecture.
- **Reference:** [DLMF Chapters 5, 7, 8 and §25.12](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2): gamma, error, incomplete gamma and polylogarithm functions with conditions.
- **Further reading:** Artin, *The Gamma Function* (1964): treatment of the Bohr–Mollerup characterization. ([Wikipedia: Bohr–Mollerup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr%E2%80%93Mollerup_theorem))
- **Further reading:** [Baker, Transcendental Number Theory](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/transcendental-number-theory/21DDE8BFF5B527AF751D744736CE1CF2): monograph first published in 1975, with a chapter on linear forms in logarithms (Cambridge University Press).
references.MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions:
## Reference
### Overview
Hypergeometric functions are power series whose coefficients are ratios of shifted factorials $(a)_k=a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1)$. Gauss's function, for $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\dots\}$ and $|z|<1$,
$${}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k}\frac{z^k}{k!},$$
solves the hypergeometric equation $z(1-z)w''+[c-(a+b+1)z]w'-abw=0$, whose singularities at $0,1,\infty$ are all regular, with exponent pairs $\{0,1-c\}$, $\{0,c-a-b\}$, $\{a,b\}$. ([DLMF §15.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.10)) Euler's integral continues it to every $z$ that is not a real number $\ge1$. The subject combines three viewpoints: the series and its summation and transformation identities, integral representations (Euler, Barnes), and the differential equation with its monodromy, which Riemann used to characterize the function.
