([Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function))

MSC groups Bessel and Airy functions with ${}_0F_1$ (33C10) and confluent (Kummer, Whittaker) functions with ${}_1F_1$ (33C15), and the orthogonal polynomials of hypergeometric type (33C45) are organized by the Askey scheme into levels by the type of their hypergeometric representation. ([MSC2020, 33C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Cxx); [Wikipedia, Askey scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Askey_scheme)) This map sits inside [MSC 33 - Special functions](node:MSC%2033%20-%20Special%20functions) (see also [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions)); the concept note is [Hypergeometric Functions](node:Hypergeometric%20Functions).

### Scope
MSC2020 33C lists: 33C05 classical hypergeometric functions ${}_2F_1$; 33C10 Bessel and Airy functions, cylinder functions, ${}_0F_1$; 33C15 confluent hypergeometric functions, Whittaker functions, ${}_1F_1$; 33C20 generalized hypergeometric series ${}_pF_q$; 33C45 orthogonal polynomials and functions of hypergeometric type (Jacobi, Laguerre, Hermite, Askey scheme, etc.; for general orthogonal polynomials see also 42C05); 33C47 other special orthogonal polynomials and functions; 33C50 orthogonal polynomials in several variables expressible by one-variable special functions; 33C52 orthogonal polynomials associated with [root systems](node:Root%20Systems); 33C55 spherical harmonics; 33C60 hypergeometric integrals and functions defined by them ($E$, $G$, $H$, $I$ functions); 33C65 Appell, Horn and Lauricella functions; 33C67 hypergeometric functions associated with root systems; 33C70 other several-variable hypergeometric functions and integrals; 33C75 elliptic integrals as hypergeometric functions; 33C80 connections with groups and algebras; 33C90 applications; 33C99. ([MSC2020, 33C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Cxx))

Neighbours: $q$-analogues are in [MSC 33Dxx - Basic hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Dxx%20-%20Basic%20hypergeometric%20functions); the parent section sends general orthogonal functions to 42C (see [MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces](node:MSC%2042%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20on%20Euclidean%20spaces)), combinatorial aspects to 05A, number-theoretic aspects to 11, and [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) to 22E. ([MSC2020, 33-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33-XX)) Related concept notes: [Bessel Functions](node:Bessel%20Functions), [Spherical Harmonics](node:Spherical%20Harmonics), [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function).

### Key concepts
- **Euler and Barnes integrals (33C05, 33C60).** With $\mathbf F=F/\Gamma(c)$, for $\Re c>\Re b>0$ and $|\operatorname{ph}(1-z)|<\pi$,
  $$\mathbf F(a,b;c;z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(b)\Gamma(c-b)}\int_0^1\frac{t^{b-1}(1-t)^{c-b-1}}{(1-zt)^a}\,dt,$$
  and for $|\operatorname{ph}(-z)|<\pi$, $a,b\ne0,-1,-2,\dots$,
  $$\mathbf F(a,b;c;z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i\,\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\int_{-i\infty}^{i\infty}\frac{\Gamma(a+t)\Gamma(b+t)\Gamma(-t)}{\Gamma(c+t)}(-z)^t\,dt,$$
  where the contour separates the poles of $\Gamma(a+t)$ and $\Gamma(b+t)$ from those of $\Gamma(-t)$ and $(-z)^t$ has its principal value. ([DLMF §15.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.6)) The Euler integral (Euler, 1748), a [beta-type](node:Beta%20Function) integral, is valid for $z$ not real and $\ge1$. ([Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function)) Functions defined by such hypergeometric integrals (the $E$, $G$, $H$ and $I$ functions) form 33C60. ([MSC2020, 33C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Cxx))
- **Summation theorems.** Gauss: if $\Re(c-a-b)>0$, $F(a,b;c;1)=\dfrac{\Gamma(c)\Gamma(c-a-b)}{\Gamma(c-a)\Gamma(c-b)}$; Chu–Vandermonde: $F(-n,b;c;1)=(c-b)_n/(c)_n$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$ ([DLMF §15.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.4)). For ${}_3F_2(1)$: Pfaff–Saalschütz, ${}_3F_2(-n,a,b;c,d;1)=\dfrac{(c-a)_n(c-b)_n}{(c)_n(c-a-b)_n}$ when $c+d=a+b+1-n$ (balanced, terminating), together with the well-poised sums of Dixon, Watson and Whipple and the very-well-poised Rogers–Dougall ${}_5F_4$ and Dougall ${}_7F_6$ sums. ([DLMF §16.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/16.4))
- **Transformations and Kummer's 24 solutions.** For $|\operatorname{ph}(1-z)|<\pi$, Pfaff and Euler give
  $$F(a,b;c;z)=(1-z)^{-a}F\!\left(a,c-b;c;\tfrac{z}{z-1}\right)=(1-z)^{c-a-b}F(c-a,c-b;c;z);$$
  DLMF also lists quadratic and cubic transformations, the former existing only for restricted parameter groups. ([DLMF §15.8](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.8)) The six local solutions at $0,1,\infty$ yield, through these transformations, 24 expressions known as Kummer's solutions. ([DLMF §15.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.10))
- **Riemann's equation and monodromy.** Any second-order linear homogeneous ODE with at most three singularities, all regular, transforms into the hypergeometric equation; the solutions with exponents $\{a_1,a_2\},\{b_1,b_2\},\{c_1,c_2\}$ at $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, subject to $a_1+a_2+b_1+b_2+c_1+c_2=1$, are denoted by Riemann's $P$-symbol. ([DLMF §15.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.11)) Schwarz found the cases in which the solutions are algebraic. ([Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function)) Schwarz's list gives, in terms of the exponent differences $\lambda=1-c$, $\mu=c-a-b$, $\nu=b-a$ (determined up to permutation, sign changes and certain integer shifts), the 15 cases in which the equation has a finite non-cyclic monodromy group, equivalently two independent algebraic solutions; they are grouped as dihedral, tetrahedral, octahedral and icosahedral by the isomorphism class of the monodromy group. ([Wikipedia, Schwarz's list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarz%27s_list)) See [Monodromy of Complex Differential Equations](node:Monodromy%20of%20Complex%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Generalized and confluent functions (33C15, 33C20).** Provided no $b_j$ is a nonpositive integer, ${}_pF_q$ converges for all $z$ if $p\le q$; if $p=q+1$ it has radius 1 and on $|z|=1$, with $\gamma_q=\sum b_j-\sum a_j$, converges absolutely if $\Re\gamma_q>0$, converges except at $z=1$ if $-1<\Re\gamma_q\le0$, and diverges if $\Re\gamma_q\le-1$; if $p>q+1$ it diverges for $z\ne0$ unless it terminates. ([DLMF §16.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/16.2)) Kummer's equation $zw''+(b-z)w'-aw=0$ has a regular singularity at $0$ and an irregular singularity of rank one at $\infty$; $M(a,b,z)={}_1F_1(a;b;z)$ is entire in $z$, and $U(a,b,z)\sim z^{-a}$ as $z\to\infty$ in $|\operatorname{ph}z|\le\tfrac32\pi-\delta$ fixes the second solution. ([DLMF §13.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/13.2))
- **Askey scheme (33C45).** Hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials form a hierarchy: Wilson and Racah (${}_4F_3$) at the top; continuous dual Hahn, continuous Hahn, Hahn, dual Hahn (${}_3F_2$); Meixner–Pollaczek, Jacobi, Meixner, Krawtchouk (${}_2F_1$); Laguerre, Bessel, Charlier; Hermite at the bottom. It was drawn by Labelle and by Askey and Wilson in 1985. ([Wikipedia, Askey scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Askey_scheme)) Askey and Wilson's 1985 AMS Memoir introduced the $q$-polynomials generalizing Jacobi polynomials that head the $q$-scheme. ([Crossref, Askey–Wilson 1985](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0319))

### History
Wallis used the term "hypergeometric series" in *Arithmetica Infinitorum* (1655); Euler studied the series and found its integral representation (1748); Gauss gave the first full systematic treatment (1813); Kummer described the transformation group of order 24 (1836); and Riemann (1857) characterized the function by its differential equation with three regular singular points on the Riemann sphere. ([Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function)) Andrews, Askey and Roy's *Special Functions* (CUP, 1999) is a standard modern account of the hypergeometric theory. ([Crossref, Andrews–Askey–Roy](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781107325937))

### Open problems
- **Organizing hypergeometric identities.** There is no known system for organizing all identities among hypergeometric series, and the algorithmic discovery of identities is described as an active research topic. ([Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function))
- **Generalized linearization formulas.** Cohl's problem in the OPSFA13 open problems report asks for closed-form coefficients $\gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$ in $P_m(x;\mathbf a)P_n(x;\mathbf a)=\sum_k\gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)P_k(x;\mathbf b)$ for hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials; it derives such formulas for Laguerre, Gegenbauer, Jacobi, continuous $q$-ultraspherical/Rogers and continuous $q$-Jacobi polynomials, and says that further closed-form linearization formulae for other polynomials of the (q-)Askey scheme had yet to be found. ([Cohl, Report from the Open Problems Session at OPSFA13](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06196))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function): integrals, transformations, monodromy, Schwarz's list, history.
- **Reference:** [DLMF Chapter 15](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.8): conventions and formulas for ${}_2F_1$.
- **Learn:** [Schlosser, Special Functions (Vienna course)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~schlosse/courses/SF/SF.html): course on gamma, beta, hypergeometric functions and orthogonal polynomials using Andrews–Askey–Roy.
- **Primary:** [Askey & Wilson, Some basic hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials that generalize Jacobi polynomials (Mem. AMS 319, 1985)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0319): origin of the top of the Askey scheme.
- **Primary:** [Cohl, Report from the Open Problems Session at OPSFA13 (SIGMA 2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06196): research problems on hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials.
- **Further reading:** [Andrews, Askey & Roy, Special Functions (CUP, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781107325937): the standard graduate text.
references.MSC 33Dxx - Basic hypergeometric functio:
## Reference
### Overview
Basic hypergeometric ($q$-hypergeometric) series replace the shifted factorial $(a)_n$ by the $q$-shifted factorial $(a;q)_n=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1-aq^j)$; DLMF takes the base $q$ complex with $|q|<1$ unless stated otherwise ([DLMF §17.1](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.1)), with $(a;q)_\infty=\prod_{j\ge0}(1-aq^j)$ and $(a_1,\dots,a_k;q)_n=\prod_{j=1}^k(a_j;q)_n$. ([DLMF §17.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.2)) Heine (1846) first considered the series ${}_2\phi_1$, which tends to Gauss's ${}_2F_1$ as $q\to1$; besides the unilateral series ${}_r\phi_s$ there are bilateral series ${}_r\psi_s$ summed over all $n\in\mathbb Z$. ([Wikipedia, Basic hypergeometric series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_hypergeometric_series))

Koornwinder's overview describes the area as $q$-analogues of classical [special functions](node:Special%20Functions), usually with $0<q<1$ and $q=1$ the classical case: $q$-hypergeometric series with their evaluation and transformation formulas, $q$-hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials most notably the Askey–Wilson polynomials, Macdonald polynomials for [root systems](node:Root%20Systems), elliptic hypergeometric series, and applications in number theory, [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics), quantum groups and [statistical mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics). ([Koornwinder, q-Special functions, an overview](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511148)) The classical counterpart is [MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Cxx%20-%20Hypergeometric%20functions) (concept: [Hypergeometric Functions](node:Hypergeometric%20Functions)); the concept note is [Basic Hypergeometric Series](node:Basic%20Hypergeometric%20Series).

### Scope
MSC2020 33D lists: 33D05 $q$-gamma functions, $q$-beta functions and integrals; 33D15 basic hypergeometric functions in one variable, ${}_r\phi_s$; 33D45 basic orthogonal polynomials and functions (Askey–Wilson polynomials, etc.); 33D50 several-variable orthogonal polynomials expressible by one-variable basic hypergeometric functions; 33D52 basic orthogonal polynomials associated with root systems (Macdonald polynomials, etc.); 33D60 basic hypergeometric integrals and functions defined by them; 33D65 bibasic functions and multiple bases; 33D67 basic hypergeometric functions associated with root systems; 33D70 other several-variable basic hypergeometric functions and integrals; 33D80 connections with quantum groups, Chevalley groups, $p$-adic groups, Hecke algebras; 33D90 applications; 33D99. ([MSC2020, 33D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Dxx))

Neighbours: the parent section [MSC 33 - Special functions](node:MSC%2033%20-%20Special%20functions) sends combinatorial aspects to 05A ([MSC 05 - Combinatorics](node:MSC%2005%20-%20Combinatorics)), number-theoretic aspects to 11 (see [MSC 11Pxx - Additive number theory; partitions](node:MSC%2011Pxx%20-%20Additive%20number%20theory;%20partitions)), general orthogonal functions to 42C, and [representation theory](node:Representation%20Theory) to 22E. ([MSC2020, 33-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33-XX)) 33D80 is the meeting point with [Quantum Groups](node:Quantum%20Groups). ([MSC2020, 33D](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Dxx))

### Key concepts
- **$q$-binomial theorem (33D15).** For $|z|<1$,
  $${}_1\phi_0(a;-;q,z)=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(a;q)_n}{(q;q)_n}z^n=\frac{(az;q)_\infty}{(z;q)_\infty},$$
  and DLMF also gives ${}_0\phi_0(-;-;q,z)=\sum_n(-1)^nq^{\binom n2}z^n/(q;q)_n=(z;q)_\infty$, valid without the restriction on $|z|$. ([DLMF §17.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.5)) Wikipedia attributes the $q$-binomial theorem to Rothe (1811). ([Wikipedia, Basic hypergeometric series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_hypergeometric_series))
- **$q$-Gauss and $q$-Chu–Vandermonde sums.** For $|c|<|ab|$,
  $${}_2\phi_1(a,b;c;q,c/(ab))=\frac{(c/a,c/b;q)_\infty}{(c,c/(ab);q)_\infty},$$
  and for $n=0,1,2,\dots$, ${}_2\phi_1(a,q^{-n};c;q,cq^n/a)=(c/a;q)_n/(c;q)_n$ and ${}_2\phi_1(a,q^{-n};c;q,q)=a^n(c/a;q)_n/(c;q)_n$. ([DLMF §17.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.6))
- **Heine's transformations.** For $|z|<1$ and $|b|<1$,
  $${}_2\phi_1(a,b;c;q,z)=\frac{(b,az;q)_\infty}{(c,z;q)_\infty}\,{}_2\phi_1(c/b,z;az;q,b),$$
  and, for $|z|<1$, $|abz|<|c|$, Heine's third transformation ${}_2\phi_1(a,b;c;q,z)=\dfrac{(abz/c;q)_\infty}{(z;q)_\infty}{}_2\phi_1(c/a,c/b;c;q,abz/c)$. ([DLMF §17.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.6)) Gasper's notes start from $q$-extensions of the [binomial theorem](node:Binomial%20Theorem) and derive general summation and transformation formulas from them. ([Gasper, Lecture notes on q-series](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9509223))
- **Ramanujan's ${}_1\psi_1$ sum and Jacobi's triple product.** For $|b/a|<|z|<1$,
  $${}_1\psi_1(a;b;q,z)=\frac{(q,b/a,az,q/(az);q)_\infty}{(b,q/a,z,b/(az);q)_\infty},$$
  and Jacobi's triple product reads $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}(-z)^nq^{n(n-1)/2}=(q,z,q/z;q)_\infty$. ([DLMF §17.8](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.8)) Bailey gave analogous ${}_6\psi_6$ identities, and such bilateral sums generalize the Jacobi triple product, an identity for [theta functions](node:Jacobi%20Theta%20Functions). ([Wikipedia, Basic hypergeometric series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_hypergeometric_series))
- **Rogers–Ramanujan identities.** $\sum_{n\ge0}q^{n^2}/(q;q)_n=1/[(q;q^5)_\infty(q^4;q^5)_\infty]$ and $\sum_{n\ge0}q^{n^2+n}/(q;q)_n=1/[(q^2;q^5)_\infty(q^3;q^5)_\infty]$. Combinatorially, the partitions of $n$ into parts differing by at least 2 are equinumerous with partitions into parts $\equiv1,4\pmod5$. Rogers proved them in 1894, Ramanujan rediscovered them before 1913, and Schur independently proved them in 1917. ([Wikipedia, Rogers–Ramanujan identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers%E2%80%93Ramanujan_identities)) See [Additive Bases and Integer Partitions](node:Additive%20Bases%20and%20Integer%20Partitions).
- **Askey–Wilson polynomials and the $q$-Askey scheme (33D45).** With $x=\tfrac12(z+z^{-1})$,
  $$\frac{p_n(x;a,b,c,d\mid q)}{a^{-n}(ab,ac,ad;q)_n}={}_4\phi_3\!\left(\begin{matrix}q^{-n},\,abcdq^{n-1},\,az,\,az^{-1}\\ ab,\,ac,\,ad\end{matrix};q,q\right);$$
  $p_n$ is symmetric in $a,b,c,d$, orthogonal on $[-1,1]$ with an explicit weight when the parameters are real or form conjugate pairs and satisfy the stated modulus conditions, and has big and little $q$-Jacobi and Wilson polynomials as limits; Al-Salam–Chihara is the case $c=d=0$. ([DLMF §18.28](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.28)) Askey–Wilson and $q$-Racah (${}_4\phi_3$) head the $q$-Askey scheme, extended to basic polynomials by Koekoek and Swarttouw (1998). ([Wikipedia, Askey scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Askey_scheme)) The family was introduced in Askey and Wilson's 1985 AMS Memoir. ([Crossref, Askey–Wilson 1985](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0319))

### History
The systematic theory begins with Heine's ${}_2\phi_1$ (1846); Rothe's $q$-binomial theorem dates from 1811, and Watson later gave a contour-integral analogue of Barnes's integral, providing analytic continuation in $z$. ([Wikipedia, Basic hypergeometric series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_hypergeometric_series)) Rogers (1894), Ramanujan (before 1913) and Schur (1917) found the Rogers–Ramanujan identities, linking the series to partitions ([Wikipedia, Rogers–Ramanujan identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers%E2%80%93Ramanujan_identities)), and Askey and Wilson's 1985 Memoir introduced basic hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials generalizing the Jacobi polynomials. ([Crossref, Askey–Wilson 1985](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0319)) Gasper and Rahman's *Basic Hypergeometric Series* (CUP, 2nd ed. 2004) is the standard reference. ([Crossref, Gasper–Rahman](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511526251))

### Open problems
- **Generalized linearization in the $q$-Askey scheme.** The OPSFA13 open problems report asks for closed-form coefficients of generalized linearization formulas $P_m(x;\mathbf a)P_n(x;\mathbf a)=\sum_k\gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)P_k(x;\mathbf b)$; it treats the continuous $q$-ultraspherical/Rogers and continuous $q$-Jacobi polynomials and states that further closed-form formulas in the (q-)Askey scheme had yet to be found. ([Cohl, Report from the Open Problems Session at OPSFA13](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06196))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Basic hypergeometric series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_hypergeometric_series): definitions, $q$-binomial theorem, ${}_1\psi_1$, Watson's integral.
- **Reference:** [DLMF §17.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.6): ${}_2\phi_1$ summations and Heine transformations with conditions.
- **Learn:** [Gasper, Lecture notes for an introductory minicourse on q-series (arXiv math/9509223)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9509223): methods for deriving summation, transformation and expansion formulas.
- **Primary:** [Koornwinder, q-Special functions, an overview (arXiv math/0511148)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0511148): survey of the area and its applications.
- **Primary:** [Askey & Wilson, Mem. AMS 319 (1985)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0319): Askey–Wilson polynomials.
- **Further reading:** [Gasper & Rahman, Basic Hypergeometric Series (CUP, 2nd ed. 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511526251): the standard monograph.
references.MSC 33Exx - Other special functions:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 33Exx is the "other special functions" section of [MSC 33](node:MSC%2033%20-%20Special%20functions) ([Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions)): elliptic functions and integrals, the wave functions of Lamé, Mathieu and spheroidal type, Mittag-Leffler functions, Painlevé-type functions, other functions defined by series, integrals or differential, difference and integral equations, and special functions in characteristic $p$. The section heading of MSC 33 states that it deals with the properties of functions as functions, and sends orthogonal functions to 42Cxx and number-theoretic aspects to 11. ([MSC2020 33Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Exx))

Two families show the range of the section. The first is linear: Mathieu's equation arises when the Helmholtz equation (or the three-dimensional Laplace equation) is separated in elliptic cylinder coordinates, and its solutions are studied through Floquet theory, while the spheroidal equation comes from separating the [wave equation](node:Wave%20Equation) in spheroidal coordinates. ([Wikipedia: Mathieu function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathieu_function); [DLMF §30.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/30.2)) The second is nonlinear: the six Painlevé equations, whose solutions Clarkson describes as "nonlinear special functions" that now have their own chapter (§32) in the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. ([Clarkson, Open problems for Painlevé equations](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.10122)) Mittag-Leffler functions sit between these as the functions that solve linear equations of fractional order. ([Haubold–Mathai–Saxena survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0909.0230))

### Scope
The MSC2020 subcodes are 33E05 elliptic functions and integrals; 33E10 Lamé, Mathieu, and spheroidal wave functions; 33E12 Mittag-Leffler functions and generalizations; 33E15 other wave functions; 33E17 Painlevé-type functions; 33E20 other functions defined by series and integrals; 33E30 other functions coming from differential, difference and integral equations; 33E50 special functions in characteristic $p$ (gamma functions, etc.); and 33E99. ([MSC2020 33Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Exx))

Neighbours. Theta functions in their geometric role are classified under 14K25 "Theta functions and abelian varieties" in [MSC 14Kxx - Abelian varieties and schemes](node:MSC%2014Kxx%20-%20Abelian%20varieties%20and%20schemes). ([MSC2020 14Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=14Kxx)) The Painlevé equations as differential equations, their classification and hierarchies, are 34M55 and isomonodromic deformations 34M56, in [MSC 34Mxx - Ordinary differential equations in the complex domain](node:MSC%2034Mxx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations%20in%20the%20complex%20domain); 33E17 is for the transcendents as functions. ([MSC2020 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Mxx)) Hypergeometric functions, which supply the special-parameter solutions of Painlevé equations, are in [MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Cxx%20-%20Hypergeometric%20functions), and algorithms for evaluating all of these are in [MSC 33Fxx - Computational aspects of special functions](node:MSC%2033Fxx%20-%20Computational%20aspects%20of%20special%20functions). ([MSC2020 33Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Exx); [Wikipedia: Painlevé transcendents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_transcendents))

### Key concepts
- **Elliptic functions and the Weierstrass $\wp$ (33E05).** An elliptic function for a lattice $L\subset\mathbb C$ is a meromorphic function with every element of $L$ as a period. A nonzero elliptic function has as many zeros as poles, counted with multiplicity, in any fundamental parallelogram (Theorem 15.18), and an elliptic function holomorphic everywhere is constant by Liouville's theorem. For $L$, $\wp(z)=z^{-2}+\sum_{\omega\in L\setminus0}\big((z-\omega)^{-2}-\omega^{-2}\big)$ satisfies $\wp'(z)^2=4\wp(z)^3-g_2\wp(z)-g_3$ with $g_2=60G_4(L)$, $g_3=140G_6(L)$, $G_k=\sum_{\omega\ne0}\omega^{-k}$ (Theorem 15.29), and $z\mapsto(\wp(z),\wp'(z))$ maps $\mathbb C/L$ to the elliptic curve $y^2=4x^3-g_2x-g_3$, whose discriminant is nonzero (Lemma 15.32). ([MIT 18.783 Lecture 15](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2017/LectureNotes15.pdf)) This links the section to [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis).
- **Jacobi functions and theta quotients (33E05).** With nome $q=\exp(-\pi K'(k)/K(k))$ and $\zeta=\pi z/(2K)$, $\operatorname{sn}(z,k)=\frac{\theta_3(0,q)}{\theta_2(0,q)}\frac{\theta_1(\zeta,q)}{\theta_4(\zeta,q)}$, and similarly for $\operatorname{cn}$, $\operatorname{dn}$; for fixed $k$ each Jacobi function is meromorphic and doubly periodic in $z$ with simple poles and zeros, and $K(k)=\tfrac\pi2\theta_3^2(0,q)$. ([DLMF §22.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/22.2))
- **Elliptic integrals (33E05).** Legendre's forms are $F(\phi,k)=\int_0^\phi d\theta/\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2\theta}$ and $E(\phi,k)=\int_0^\phi\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta$; every elliptic integral reduces to integrals of rational functions and the three Legendre canonical forms, and $K(k)=\pi/\big(2\,\mathrm{agm}(1,\sqrt{1-k^2})\big)$. ([Wikipedia: Elliptic integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_integral)) Carlson's symmetric forms, e.g. $R_F(x,y,z)=\tfrac12\int_0^\infty dt/\sqrt{(t+x)(t+y)(t+z)}$ for $x,y,z\in\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$, are symmetric in their arguments and normalized by $R_F(1,1,1)=1$; $R_C(x,y)=R_F(x,y,y)$. ([DLMF §19.16](https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.16))
- **Mathieu functions and Floquet theory (33E10).** Mathieu's equation $w''+(a-2q\cos2z)w=0$ has, for every $\nu$, a solution with $w(z+\pi)=e^{\pi i\nu}w(z)$ exactly when $e^{\pi i\nu}$ is an eigenvalue of the monodromy matrix, i.e. $\cos\pi\nu=w_{\mathrm I}(\pi;a,q)$. The $\pi$- and $2\pi$-periodic solutions occur at the characteristic values $a_n(q)$, $b_n(q)$, with $a_n(0)=b_n(0)=n^2$ and, for $q>0$, the interlacing $a_0<b_1<a_1<b_2<a_2<\cdots$. ([DLMF §28.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/28.2)) A pair $(a,q)$ is stable if all solutions are bounded on $\mathbb R$: pairs with real non-integer $\nu$ are stable, while if $\Im\nu\ne0$ every nontrivial solution is unbounded. ([DLMF §28.17](https://dlmf.nist.gov/28.17)) These stability regions govern parametric resonance and the motion of the inverted pendulum and of ions in quadrupole traps. ([Wikipedia: Mathieu function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathieu_function))
- **Lamé and spheroidal equations (33E10).** Lamé's equation $w''+\big(h-\nu(\nu+1)k^2\operatorname{sn}^2(z,k)\big)w=0$ ($0<k<1$, $\nu\ge-\tfrac12$) has the Weierstrass form $w''+(g-\nu(\nu+1)\wp(\eta))w=0$, a special case of Heun's equation. ([DLMF §29.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/29.2)) The spheroidal equation $\frac{d}{dz}\big((1-z^2)w'\big)+\big(\lambda+\gamma^2(1-z^2)-\mu^2/(1-z^2)\big)w=0$ comes from separating the wave equation in prolate ($\gamma^2>0$) or oblate ($\gamma^2<0$) spheroidal coordinates. ([DLMF §30.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/30.2))
- **Mittag-Leffler functions (33E12).** $E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}z^k/\Gamma(\alpha k+\beta)$ for $\Re\alpha,\Re\beta>0$, with $E_\alpha=E_{\alpha,1}$; it is entire of order $1/\alpha$ and type 1, and $E_1(z)=e^z$. If $\Re\nu>0$, the fractional kinetic equation $N(t)-N_0=-c^\nu\,{}_0D_t^{-\nu}N(t)$ (Riemann–Liouville integral) has solution $N(t)=N_0E_\nu(-c^\nu t^\nu)$ (Theorem 13.1), which interpolates between exponential and power-law decay. ([Haubold–Mathai–Saxena](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0909.0230)) Its coefficients involve the [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function).
- **Painlevé transcendents (33E17).** Painlevé studied $y''=R(y',y,t)$ with $R$ rational and with only poles as movable singularities, finding 50 canonical forms, of which all but six reduce to known functions; Gambier completed the list (1910), and Fuchs found $P_{\mathrm{VI}}$ (1905) from isomonodromic deformations. Examples: $P_{\mathrm I}$: $y''=6y^2+t$; $P_{\mathrm{II}}$: $y''=2y^3+ty+\alpha$. Nishioka (1988) and Umemura (1989) proved irreducibility for generic parameters; for special parameters there are rational, algebraic, and Airy, Bessel, parabolic-cylinder, Whittaker or hypergeometric solutions. ([Wikipedia: Painlevé transcendents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_transcendents))

### History
Elliptic integrals were first studied by Fagnano and Euler around 1750 in connection with the arc length of the ellipse, and elliptic functions were discovered as inverse functions of elliptic integrals. ([Wikipedia: Elliptic integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_integral)) Weierstrass introduced the notation $\wp$ in his lectures of 1862–1863. ([Wikipedia: Weierstrass elliptic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_elliptic_function)) Mathieu introduced his functions in 1868 for vibrations of an elliptical membrane. ([Wikipedia: Mathieu function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathieu_function)) Mittag-Leffler introduced $E_\alpha$ in 1903 in connection with a summation method for divergent series, and Wiman the two-parameter function in 1905. ([Haubold–Mathai–Saxena](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0909.0230)) Painlevé's classification dates from 1900–1902, with Picard (1889) having met a special case of $P_{\mathrm{VI}}$. ([Wikipedia: Painlevé transcendents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_transcendents))

### Open problems
- **Painlevé equivalence problem.** Given an ordinary differential equation with the Painlevé property, how does one know whether it can be solved in terms of a Painlevé transcendent? (Clarkson's Open Problem 2.9). ([Clarkson 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.10122))
- **Numerics of Painlevé transcendents.** Develop numerical software that exploits integrability, for instance the isomonodromy method through the associated Riemann–Hilbert problem, rather than generic Runge–Kutta solvers (Open Problem 4.1). ([Clarkson 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.10122))
- **Notation and classification.** Find a notation for Painlevé transcendents reflecting their many solution types, and a complete, unified classification of their properties (Hamiltonian structure, special solutions, Bäcklund transformations, isomonodromy problems, connection formulae), which Clarkson calls fragmentary (Open Problems 3.1 and 5.1). ([Clarkson 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.10122))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Painlevé transcendents (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_transcendents): classification, special solutions, applications.
- **Reference:** [DLMF §28.2, Mathieu's equation](https://dlmf.nist.gov/28.2): Floquet theory and characteristic values; see also DLMF chapters 19, 22, 29, 30 linked above.
- **Learn:** [Sutherland, MIT 18.783 Lecture 15: Elliptic curves over C](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2017/LectureNotes15.pdf): elliptic functions, Eisenstein series, $\wp$ and its differential equation.
- **Learn:** [Schlosser, Special Functions course (Vienna)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~schlosse/courses/SF/SF.html): course built on Andrews–Askey–Roy, with theta and elliptic functions as the last topics, "as time permits".
- **Primary:** [Clarkson, Open Problems for Painlevé Equations, SIGMA 15 (2019) 006](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.10122): survey of Painlevé transcendents as nonlinear special functions and of open problems.
- **Primary:** [Haubold, Mathai, Saxena, Mittag-Leffler functions and their applications (J. Appl. Math. 2011)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.0230): survey of Mittag-Leffler-type functions and fractional kinetic equations.
- **Further reading:** [Whittaker and Watson, A Course of Modern Analysis, 5th ed. (CUP 2021, ed. Moll)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/9781009004091): the classical analysis text, cited by Weierstrass-function sources for its use of $\wp$.
references.MSC 33Fxx - Computational aspects of spe:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 33Fxx covers the computation of [special functions](node:Special%20Functions) in two senses: numerical approximation and evaluation (33F05), and symbolic computation, for which the classification itself names the Gosper and Zeilberger algorithms (33F10). Software as such goes to 33-04. ([MSC2020 33Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Fxx))

On the numerical side, the basic difficulty is that a formula correct in exact arithmetic can be useless in floating point: a three-term recurrence that a function satisfies may amplify rounding errors along the wanted solution, so the direction and form of the computation must be chosen with the analytic behaviour of all solutions in view. ([DLMF §3.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.6)) A current goal is rigorous evaluation, where each output carries a proven error bound; Johansson's Arb library implements midpoint-radius ("ball") arithmetic for real and complex numbers, polynomials, power series, matrices and many special functions, with speed competitive with non-interval libraries such as MPFR. ([Johansson, Arb](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02831))

On the symbolic side, the subject is the automatic discovery and proof of identities: given a summand or integrand, compute a recurrence or differential equation for the definite sum or integral, then solve it or use it to certify an identity. Chen and Kauers call creative telescoping "the method of choice" for definite sums and integrals, intensively studied since the early 1990s, now a classical technique of computer algebra and still the subject of ongoing research. ([Chen–Kauers, open problems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.03768))

### Scope
MSC2020 33Fxx has three codes: 33F05 numerical approximation and evaluation of special functions (see also 65D20), 33F10 symbolic computation of special functions (Gosper and Zeilberger algorithms, etc.; see also 68W30), and 33F99. ([MSC2020 33Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Fxx))

Neighbours. General algorithms for numerical approximation are in [MSC 65Dxx - Numerical approximation and computational geometry (primarily algorithms)](node:MSC%2065Dxx%20-%20Numerical%20approximation%20and%20computational%20geometry%20%28primarily%20algorithms%29) and symbolic computation in general is under [MSC 68Wxx - Algorithms in computer science](node:MSC%2068Wxx%20-%20Algorithms%20in%20computer%20science), the two cross-references of the MSC entry; 33Fxx keeps work in which the special function is the object. The properties of the functions themselves are in [MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Cxx%20-%20Hypergeometric%20functions), [MSC 33Exx - Other special functions](node:MSC%2033Exx%20-%20Other%20special%20functions) and the rest of [MSC 33 - Special functions](node:MSC%2033%20-%20Special%20functions). ([MSC2020 33Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Minimal solutions and stable recursion (33F05).** For a homogeneous three-term recurrence with independent solutions $w_n,g_n$ satisfying $w_n/g_n\to0$, $w_n$ is the recessive (minimal) solution, unique up to a constant factor. Forward recursion for $w_n$ is unstable because rounding introduces multiples of $g_n$; backward recursion from large $N$ is stable provided the coefficient $c_n\ne0$ for all $n$. Miller's algorithm starts from trial values such as $w_{N+1}=0$, $w_N=1$, recurs backward, normalizes with a known value or a sum $\sum\lambda_nw_n=1$, and repeats with larger $N$ until results agree. Olver's algorithm handles the inhomogeneous case by forward recurrence for an auxiliary solution, then backward recurrence, with a stopping test applied during the computation that fixes the starting index $N$; recessive solutions can also be computed by continued fractions. ([DLMF §3.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.6)) The classical analysis is Gautschi, "Computational aspects of three-term recurrence relations", SIAM Review 9 (1967) 24–82. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1009002))
- **Best uniform approximation (33F05).** For $f$ continuous on $[a,b]$ there is a unique minimax polynomial of degree $n$. ([DLMF §3.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.11)) Chebyshev's equioscillation theorem characterizes it: a polynomial $g$ of degree $\le n$ minimizes $\|f-g\|_\infty$ if and only if there are $n+2$ points $a\le x_0<\dots<x_{n+1}\le b$ with $f(x_i)-g(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^i\|f-g\|_\infty$, $\sigma=\pm1$; the Remez algorithm is the common way to compute it. ([Wikipedia: Equioscillation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equioscillation_theorem)) A truncated Chebyshev series is within a factor $1+L_n$ ($L_n$ the Lebesgue constant) of the minimax error, so in practice it is often used instead. ([DLMF §3.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.11))
- **Rigorous arbitrary-precision evaluation (33F05).** Johansson's implementation of ${}_0F_1$, ${}_1F_1$, ${}_2F_1$ and ${}_2F_0$ (Kummer $U$) in ball arithmetic covers unrestricted complex parameters and arguments, and thereby incomplete gamma and beta functions, error functions, Bessel, Airy and Legendre functions and complete elliptic integrals, giving provably correct results. ([Johansson, Computing hypergeometric functions rigorously](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06977)) This connects to [MSC 65Gxx - Error analysis and interval analysis](node:MSC%2065Gxx%20-%20Error%20analysis%20and%20interval%20analysis).
- **Gosper's algorithm (33F10).** A term $f(k)$ is hypergeometric if $f(k+1)/f(k)$ is a rational function of $k$. Given such an $f$, Gosper's algorithm decides whether there is a hypergeometric $F$ with $F(k+1)-F(k)=f(k)$, and finds it if so, giving $\sum_{k=a}^bf(k)=F(b+1)-F(a)$. ([Chen–Kauers–Koutschan, lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.05345v1)) For example, it finds $\sum_{k=0}^nk\,k!=(n+1)!-1$; it applies to indefinite sums only. ([Chen–Kauers](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.03768)) Gosper developed it in the 1970s while working on Macsyma and published it in *PNAS* in 1978. ([Wikipedia: Gosper's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosper%27s_algorithm))
- **Creative telescoping and Zeilberger's algorithm (33F10).** For a definite sum $F(n)=\sum_kf(n,k)$, creative telescoping finds polynomials $c_0(n),\dots,c_r(n)$, not all zero (the telescoper), and $g(n,k)$ (the certificate) with $\sum_{i=0}^rc_i(n)f(n+i,k)=g(n,k+1)-g(n,k)$; summing over $k$ yields an inhomogeneous recurrence for $F(n)$. Zeilberger's algorithm, a modification of Gosper's algorithm, was the first such algorithm for hypergeometric terms, and Zeilberger's holonomic vision led to Chyzak's operator algorithms and Schneider's difference-field methods. ([Chen–Kauers](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.03768); [Chen–Kauers–Koutschan, lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.05345v1))
- **WZ pairs (33F10).** $F,G$ form a WZ pair if $F(n+1,k)-F(n,k)=G(n,k+1)-G(n,k)$ and $G(n,M)\to0$ as $M\to\pm\infty$; then $\sum_kF(n,k)$ is independent of $n$, and $G=R\,F(n,k-1)$ with $R$ rational, the WZ proof certificate. For instance $R=(2k-1)/(2n+1)$ proves $\sum_k(-1)^k\binom nk\binom{2k}k4^{n-k}=\binom{2n}n$. ([Wikipedia: Wilf–Zeilberger pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilf%E2%80%93Zeilberger_pair)) Such identities are the subject of [MSC 05Axx - Enumerative combinatorics](node:MSC%2005Axx%20-%20Enumerative%20combinatorics).
- **Holonomic (D-finite) functions (33F10).** $f$ is holonomic if it satisfies a linear ODE with polynomial coefficients, and a sequence is P-recursive if it satisfies a linear recurrence with polynomial coefficients; holonomic functions are exactly the generating functions of P-recursive sequences. The class is closed, effectively, under sums, Cauchy and Hadamard products, integration and composition with algebraic functions, so identities among holonomic functions can be decided from annihilating operators. ([Wikipedia: Holonomic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomic_function))

### History
Gosper's decision procedure for indefinite hypergeometric summation came from Macsyma work in the 1970s and appeared in 1978. ([Wikipedia: Gosper's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosper%27s_algorithm)) Zeilberger propagated creative telescoping in the early 1990s and formulated the holonomic-systems approach, published in 1990. ([Chen–Kauers](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.03768); [Wikipedia: Holonomic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holonomic_function)) Petkovšek, Wilf and Zeilberger's book *A=B* (AK Peters, 1996) presents the theory. ([Wikipedia: Wilf–Zeilberger pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilf%E2%80%93Zeilberger_pair)) On the numerical side, Gautschi's 1967 survey of three-term recurrences and the 2007 SIAM monograph *Numerical Methods for Special Functions* of Gil, Segura and Temme are the references DLMF gives for computing recessive solutions by continued fractions. ([DLMF §3.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.6); [Crossref: Gautschi](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1009002); [Crossref: Gil–Segura–Temme](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898717822))

### Open problems
Chen and Kauers list eighteen open problems on creative telescoping, among them ([Chen–Kauers 2016](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.03768)):
- **Order-degree curves for D-finite functions.** For general D-finite functions bounds on the order of telescopers are known, but an order-degree curve (the trade-off between order and polynomial degree of telescopers) had not been worked out (Problem 3).
- **Bit size of telescopers.** Derive bounds for the bit size of telescopers for hyperexponential terms, as already done for hypergeometric input (Problem 4).

Their Problem 2, a reduction-based creative telescoping algorithm for (Fuchsian) D-finite functions, has since been addressed: Chen, van Hoeij, Kauers and Koutschan adapted Trager's Hermite reduction to Fuchsian D-finite functions ([arXiv:1611.07421](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.07421)), and Bostan, Chyzak, Lairez and Salvy extended Hermite reduction to arbitrary linear differential operators to treat definite integrals of D-finite functions ([arXiv:1805.03445](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.03445)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [DLMF §3.6, Linear difference equations](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.6): minimal solutions, Miller's and Olver's algorithms.
- **Reference:** [Wilf–Zeilberger pair (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilf%E2%80%93Zeilberger_pair): definition and a worked certificate.
- **Learn:** [Chen, Kauers, Koutschan, Creative Telescoping (IHP lecture notes, 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05345): lecture course from rational integration through Gosper's and Zeilberger's algorithms.
- **Primary:** [Chen and Kauers, Some open problems related to creative telescoping](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.03768): survey of the state of the art and eighteen open problems.
- **Primary:** [Koutschan, Creative telescoping for holonomic functions (2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.4554): introduction and survey of two decades of creative telescoping.
- **Primary:** [Johansson, Computing hypergeometric functions rigorously](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06977): rigorous arbitrary-precision evaluation.
- **Further reading:** [Gil, Segura, Temme, Numerical Methods for Special Functions (SIAM 2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898717822); [Gautschi, Computational aspects of three-term recurrence relations (SIAM Rev. 1967)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1009002).
references.MSC 34 - Ordinary differential equations:
## Reference
### Overview
An ordinary differential equation of order $n$ has the form $F(x,y,y',\dots,y^{(n)})=0$ for an unknown function $y$ of one independent variable $x$; "ordinary" contrasts with [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations), which involve several independent variables. Classical work tried to reduce solutions to quadratures; this is possible for linear equations with constant coefficients, but in the nineteenth century it appeared to be generally impossible in other cases, and Cauchy was the first to appreciate the importance of studying the solutions as functions in their own right. ([Ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation))

MSC 34 covers existence and dependence theory, boundary value and spectral problems, qualitative and stability theory, asymptotics, equations with randomness, equations in abstract spaces, control, functional-differential (delay) equations, [ordinary differential operators](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Operators), equations in the complex domain, and [dynamic equations on time scales](node:Dynamic%20Equations%20on%20Time%20Scales). Qualitative theory is cross-referenced to [MSC 37](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory) and stability theory to 37C75 and 93Dxx. ([MSC2020 34-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=34-XX)) The introductory concept note is [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations).

### Scope
- **34Axx General theory** ([map](node:MSC%2034Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations)): explicit solutions and first integrals (34A05); fractional, implicit and differential-algebraic equations (34A08, 34A09); initial value problems, existence, uniqueness, continuous dependence and continuation of solutions (34A12); linear and nonlinear systems (34A30, 34A34); discontinuous equations, impulses, hybrid systems; differential inequalities; inverse problems; differential inclusions (34A60). ([MSC2020 34Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=34Axx))
- **34Bxx Boundary value problems** ([map](node:MSC%2034Bxx%20-%20Boundary%20value%20problems%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations)); ordinary differential operators themselves go to **34Lxx** ([map](node:MSC%2034Lxx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20operators), see also 47E05). ([MSC2020 34-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=34-XX))
- **34Cxx Qualitative theory** ([map](node:MSC%2034Cxx%20-%20Qualitative%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations)): singular points and limit cycles (34C05); limit cycles of polynomial and analytic vector fields including Hilbert's 16th problem (34C07); oscillation and comparison theory (34C10); normal forms (34C20); bifurcation (34C23); periodic and almost periodic solutions (34C25, 34C27); chaotic behaviour (34C28); averaging (34C29); homoclinic and heteroclinic solutions (34C37); invariant manifolds (34C45). ([MSC2020 34Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=34Cxx))
- **34Dxx Stability** ([map](node:MSC%2034Dxx%20-%20Stability%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations)), **34Exx Asymptotic theory** ([map](node:MSC%2034Exx%20-%20Asymptotic%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations)), **34Fxx Randomness** (see also 60H10), **34Gxx Abstract spaces** (see also 47Jxx), **34Hxx Control** (see also 49J15, 93C15), **34Kxx Functional-differential equations** with delayed, advanced or state-dependent argument, and **34Nxx Time scales** (real analysis on time scales is 26E70). ([MSC2020 34-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=34-XX))
- **34Mxx Complex domain** ([map](node:MSC%2034Mxx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations%20in%20the%20complex%20domain)): linear and nonlinear equations in the complex domain; singularities and monodromy; Stokes phenomena and connection problems; Riemann–Hilbert and inverse differential Galois problems; Painlevé equations (34M55); isomonodromic deformations (34M56); complex WKB and turning points. ([MSC2020 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=34Mxx))

Neighbours: equations in several independent variables are [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) (MSC 35) ([Ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation)); 34Cxx cross-references [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) (37-XX), and 34Lxx cross-references 47E05 (ordinary differential operators in operator theory). ([MSC2020 34-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=34-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Picard–Lindelöf theorem (34A12).** If $f:D\to\mathbb R^n$ on a closed rectangle $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ is continuous in $t$ and Lipschitz in $y$ with a constant independent of $t$, and $(t_0,y_0)$ is interior to $D$, then $y'=f(t,y)$, $y(t_0)=y_0$ has a unique solution on some $[t_0-\varepsilon,t_0+\varepsilon]$; if the box $C_{a,b}=[t_0-a,t_0+a]\times\overline{B}_b(y_0)$ lies in $D$ and $M=\sup_{C_{a,b}}\lVert f\rVert$, one may take $\varepsilon=\min\{a,b/M\}$. If $f$ is only locally Lipschitz, solutions can fail to exist for all $t$ even when $f$ is smooth; if $f$ is globally Lipschitz, they extend to all of $\mathbb R$. Lindelöf's 1894 note generalized Picard's method of successive approximations. ([Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem))
- **Peano existence theorem.** For $f$ merely continuous on an open set, a local solution exists but need not be unique: $y'=y^{1/3}$, $y(0)=0$ has the solutions $y=0$ and $y=\pm(2t/3)^{3/2}$. Peano's 1886 proof was flawed; he published a corrected proof in 1890. Carathéodory's theorem weakens continuity further. ([Peano existence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_existence_theorem); [Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem))
- **Floquet theory (34A30, 34D).** For $x'=A(t)x$ with $A$ $T$-periodic, every fundamental matrix factors as $\Phi(t)=P(t)e^{tB}$ with $P$ $T$-periodic; the Floquet multipliers are the eigenvalues of the monodromy matrix $M=\Phi(0)^{-1}\Phi(T)$, solutions decay if all Floquet exponents have negative real part, and [Lyapunov stability](node:Lyapunov%20Stability) requires nonpositive real parts with unimodular multipliers semisimple. Floquet published this in 1883. ([Floquet theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floquet_theory))
- **Lyapunov's direct method (34D).** If $\dot x=f(x)$, $f(0)=0$, and $V$ is positive definite with $V(0)=0$ and $\dot V=\nabla V\cdot f\le 0$, the origin is Lyapunov stable; if $\dot V<0$ for $x\ne0$, it is asymptotically stable. If every eigenvalue of the Jacobian at an equilibrium has negative real part, the equilibrium is asymptotically stable. Lyapunov's thesis dates from 1892. ([Lyapunov stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_stability))
- **Poincaré–Bendixson theorem (34C).** For a differentiable flow on an open subset of the plane, a nonempty compact $\omega$-limit set containing only finitely many fixed points is a fixed point, a periodic orbit, or finitely many fixed points joined by homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits. ([Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem))
- **Sturm–Liouville theory (34B, 34L).** For $(py')'+qy=-\lambda wy$ on $[a,b]$ with $p,p',q,w$ continuous, $p,w>0$, and separated boundary conditions, the eigenvalues are real, simple, and form a sequence $\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\dots\to\infty$, and the normalized eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis of $L^2([a,b],w\,dx)$; this is an instance of [spectral theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) in the weighted [Hilbert space](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) $L^2([a,b],w\,dx)$. ([Sturm–Liouville theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%E2%80%93Liouville_theory))
- **Painlevé equations (34M55).** Second-order equations $y''=R(y',y,t)$, $R$ rational, whose only movable singularities are poles reduce to 50 canonical forms; six (PI–PVI, e.g. PI: $y''=6y^2+t$) define new transcendents. Painlevé's classification (1900, 1902) was completed by Gambier (1910), and R. Fuchs (1905) found PVI from isomonodromic deformations. ([Painlevé transcendents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_transcendents))

### History
Fuchs's memoirs of 1866 and 1868 began the theory of linear equations with regular singular points, developed by Thomé and Frobenius; from 1870 Lie's work put the theory of differential equations on a better foundation; Sturm and Liouville studied the eigenvalue problems now named after them in the mid-1800s. ([Ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation)) Floquet's periodic theory appeared in 1883, Lyapunov's stability thesis in 1892, a weaker version of the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem by Poincaré in 1892 with Bendixson's complete proof in 1901, and Hilbert posed his sixteenth problem in 1900. ([Floquet theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floquet_theory); [Lyapunov stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_stability); [Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem); [Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem))

### Open problems
- **Hilbert's 16th problem, second part (34C07).** For planar polynomial vector fields $\dot x=P(x,y)$, $\dot y=Q(x,y)$ of degree $n$, find an upper bound $H(n)$ for the number of limit cycles. Each individual field has finitely many limit cycles (Ilyashenko and Écalle, 1991/1992, after a gap was found in Dulac's 1923 proof), $H(1)=0$, and quadratic fields with four limit cycles exist, but whether $H(n)$ is finite is unsolved for every $n>1$. ([Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem)) Ilyashenko's survey records the century of work on the problem. ([Ilyashenko 2002](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0273-0979-02-00946-1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation): definitions, classical theories and their history.
- **Learn:** [Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS GSM 140, 2012; free author version)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/): existence and uniqueness, Floquet theory, complex domain and Frobenius method, Sturm–Liouville and oscillation theory, Lyapunov stability, Poincaré–Bendixson, Hartman–Grobman, KAM, chaos.
- **Primary:** [Ilyashenko, Centennial history of Hilbert's 16th problem, Bull. AMS 39 (2002) 301–355](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0273-0979-02-00946-1): survey of the limit-cycle problem.
- **Further reading:** [Hartman, Ordinary Differential Equations, 2nd ed. (SIAM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898719222): graduate monograph on ordinary differential equations.
references.MSC 34Axx - General theory for ordinary:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 34Axx is the general theory of [ordinary differential equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations): when an equation together with data determines a solution, how far the solution extends and how it depends on the data, and the structure of particular classes (linear, nonlinear, implicit, discontinuous, impulsive, fractional, set-valued). Its codes run from explicit solutions and first integrals (34A05) through initial value problems (34A12), linear systems (34A30), differential inequalities (34A40), inverse problems (34A55) and differential inclusions (34A60). ([MSC2020 34Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Axx))

The core is the theory of the initial value problem $\dot x=f(t,x)$, $x(t_0)=x_0$ on an open $U\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$: continuity of $f$ gives existence (Peano), a Lipschitz condition in $x$ gives uniqueness (Picard–Lindelöf), Gronwall's inequality turns integral estimates into continuous dependence, and every unique local solution extends to a maximal one that can only end by leaving every compact set. ([Teschl, ODE and Dynamical Systems, Ch. 2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) Several codes of the section concern weakening the regularity behind these results: Carathéodory solutions for right-hand sides measurable in $t$, Filippov solutions and differential inclusions for discontinuous ones, and Caputo-type fractional derivatives in place of $d/dt$. ([Wikipedia: Carathéodory's existence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_existence_theorem); [Wikipedia: Differential inclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_inclusion); [Diethelm et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.04241v1.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Axx: 34A05 explicit solutions, first integrals; 34A06 generalized ODEs (measure-differential, set-valued, etc.); 34A07 fuzzy ODEs; 34A08 fractional ODEs; 34A09 implicit ODEs, differential-algebraic equations; 34A12 initial value problems, existence, uniqueness, continuous dependence and continuation of solutions; 34A25 analytical theory (series, transformations, transforms, operational calculus); 34A26 geometric methods; 34A30 linear equations and systems; 34A33 lattice ODEs; 34A34 nonlinear equations and systems; 34A35 ODEs of infinite order; 34A36 discontinuous ODEs; 34A37 ODEs with impulses; 34A38 hybrid systems; 34A40 differential inequalities (see also 26D20); 34A45 theoretical approximation of solutions; 34A55 inverse problems; 34A60 differential inclusions (see also 49J21, 49K21); 34A99. ([MSC2020 34Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Axx))

Neighbours. The MSC entry sends numerical analysis to [MSC 65Lxx - Numerical methods for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2065Lxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations) (note under 34A45), differential inequalities in one real variable also to [MSC 26Dxx - Inequalities in real analysis](node:MSC%2026Dxx%20-%20Inequalities%20in%20real%20analysis), and control aspects of inclusions to [MSC 49Jxx - Existence theories in calculus of variations and optimal control](node:MSC%2049Jxx%20-%20Existence%20theories%20in%20calculus%20of%20variations%20and%20optimal%20control). ([MSC2020 34Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Axx)) Limit cycles, periodic solutions and bifurcations belong to [MSC 34Cxx - Qualitative theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Cxx%20-%20Qualitative%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations), equations in the complex domain to [MSC 34Mxx - Ordinary differential equations in the complex domain](node:MSC%2034Mxx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations%20in%20the%20complex%20domain), and equations with delayed, advanced or state-dependent argument to [MSC 34Kxx - Functional-differential equations (including equations with delayed, advanced or state-dependent argument)](node:MSC%2034Kxx%20-%20Functional-differential%20equations%20%28including%20equations%20with%20delayed,%20advanced%20or%20state-dependent%20argument%29). ([MSC2020 34Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Cxx); [MSC2020 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Mxx); [MSC2020 34Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Kxx))

### Key concepts
- **Picard–Lindelöf (34A12).** If $f\in C(U,\mathbb R^n)$ is locally Lipschitz in $x$ uniformly in $t$, the IVP has a unique local $C^1$ solution; if $V=[t_0,t_0+T]\times B_\delta(x_0)\subset U$ and $M=\max_V|f|$, it exists at least on $[t_0,t_0+T_0]$ with $T_0=\min\{T,\delta/M\}$ (Theorem 2.2). The proof applies the contraction principle (Theorem 2.1) to Picard iteration. ([Teschl, Ch. 2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) See [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem). The theorem is also called the Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem; Lindelöf's 1894 paper generalized an approach of Picard. ([Wikipedia: Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem))
- **Peano, Osgood and non-uniqueness (34A12).** If $f$ is merely continuous on $V$, at least one solution exists on $[t_0,t_0+T_0]$ (Theorem 2.19, proved via Euler polygons and Arzelà–Ascoli). Uniqueness survives under the Osgood condition: a modulus of continuity $\rho$ with $\int_0^1dr/\rho(r)=\infty$, such as $\rho(r)=r(1+|\log r|)$, but not Hölder moduli $r^\alpha$, $0<\alpha<1$ (Problem 2.25). ([Teschl, §2.7](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) Without such a condition uniqueness fails: $y'=y^{1/3}$, $y(0)=0$ has the solutions $0$ and $\pm(2t/3)^{3/2}$. ([Wikipedia: Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem))
- **Gronwall and continuous dependence (34A12, 34A40).** If $\psi(t)\le\alpha(t)+\int_0^t\beta(s)\psi(s)\,ds$ on $[0,T]$ with $\beta\ge0$ and $\alpha$ nondecreasing, then $\psi(t)\le\alpha(t)\exp\int_0^t\beta(s)\,ds$ (Lemma 2.7). Consequently, if $f$ has Lipschitz constant $L$ and $|f-g|\le M$ on a set containing both solutions, then $|x(t)-y(t)|\le|x_0-y_0|e^{L|t-t_0|}+\frac ML(e^{L|t-t_0|}-1)$ (Theorem 2.8); for $f\in C^k$ the flow is $C^k$ in initial data and parameters (Theorems 2.10–2.11). ([Teschl, §2.4](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) Grönwall proved the inequality in 1919 and Bellman a more general integral form in 1943. ([Wikipedia: Grönwall's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6nwall%27s_inequality)) This is the ODE case of [well-posedness](node:Well-Posed%20Problems).
- **Maximal solutions and blow-up alternative (34A12).** Under local uniqueness there is a unique maximal solution on an open interval $(T_-,T_+)$ (Theorem 2.13); if $T_+<\infty$ the solution eventually leaves every compact $C$ with $[t_0,T_+]\times C\subset U$, so for $U=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ it tends to infinity (Corollary 2.16). If $|f(t,x)|\le M(T)+L(T)|x|$ on $[-T,T]\times\mathbb R^n$ for every $T$, all solutions are global (Theorem 2.17). ([Teschl, §2.6](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Linear systems (34A30).** For $\dot x=A(t)x$ with $A$ continuous on an interval $I$, solutions exist on all of $I$ and form an $n$-dimensional space, given by a principal matrix solution $\Pi(t,t_0)$ (Theorems 3.9–3.10); the Wronskian satisfies Liouville's (Abel's) formula $W(t)=W(t_0)\exp\int_{t_0}^t\operatorname{tr}A(s)\,ds$ (Lemma 3.11). In general $\exp\big(\int_{t_0}^tA(s)\,ds\big)x_0$ is not the solution, because of noncommutativity; it is when $[A(t),A(s)]=0$ for all $t,s$. For $T$-periodic $A$, Floquet's theorem gives $\Pi(t,t_0)=P(t,t_0)\exp((t-t_0)Q)$ with $P$ periodic (Theorem 3.15). ([Teschl, Ch. 3](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Carathéodory solutions (34A12, 34A36).** If $f$ is continuous in $y$, measurable in $t$ and $|f(t,y)|\le m(t)$ with $m$ Lebesgue integrable on a rectangle, the IVP has a solution in the extended sense: absolutely continuous and satisfying the equation almost everywhere. Example: $y'=H(t)$ (Heaviside), $y(0)=0$, solved by the ramp function. ([Wikipedia: Carathéodory's existence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_existence_theorem))
- **Differential inclusions and Filippov solutions (34A60, 34A36).** For $\dot x\in F(t,x)$ with $F$ upper hemicontinuous in $x$, measurable in $t$, with closed convex values, solutions exist on a short interval; a one-sided Lipschitz condition $(x_1-x_2)^T(F(t,x_1)-F(t,x_2))\le C\|x_1-x_2\|^2$ gives uniqueness. Filippov's theory treats ODEs with discontinuous right-hand side (Coulomb friction, ideal switches) as inclusions, keeping $x$ continuous. ([Wikipedia: Differential inclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_inclusion))
- **Differential-algebraic equations (34A09).** A DAE $F(\dot x,x,t)=0$, e.g. in semi-explicit form $\dot x=f(x,y,t)$, $0=g(x,y,t)$, has differentiation index equal to the number of differentiations needed to obtain an ODE; the pendulum in Cartesian coordinates has index 3, typical for constrained mechanical systems. ([Wikipedia: Differential-algebraic system of equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential-algebraic_system_of_equations))

### History
The existence-and-uniqueness theorem carries the names of Cauchy, Lipschitz, Picard and Lindelöf; Lindelöf's 1894 paper generalized Picard's approach. ([Wikipedia: Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem)) Grönwall's inequality dates from 1919 and Bellman's extension from 1943. ([Wikipedia: Grönwall's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6nwall%27s_inequality)) The second edition of Hartman's *Ordinary Differential Equations* was published by SIAM in 2002. ([Crossref: Hartman](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898719222))

### Open problems
- **Non-convex differential inclusions.** Existence theory for $\dot x\in F(t,x)$ with non-convex values is described as an active area of research. ([Wikipedia: Differential inclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_inclusion))
- **Terminal value problems for fractional ODEs (34A08).** For ${}^CD^\alpha_{a+}y=f(t,y)$, $0<\alpha<1$, with the condition $y(b)=y^*$ imposed at $b>a$, uniqueness can be guaranteed for scalar problems but not in general for $y$ with values in $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$; the problem is equivalent to a Fredholm rather than a Volterra integral equation. Diethelm et al. state that many questions remain open, notably the best way to choose the next initial value in shooting methods. ([Diethelm et al., Trends and open problems of fractional calculus, §3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.04241v1.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Picard–Lindelöf theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem): statement, proof sketch, non-uniqueness examples.
- **Reference:** [Differential inclusion (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_inclusion): existence, uniqueness, Filippov theory.
- **Learn:** [Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS GSM 140, author's version)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf): Chapters 2–3 for existence, uniqueness, dependence, extensibility, linear and periodic systems.
- **Primary:** [Diethelm, Kiryakova, Luchko, Tenreiro Machado, Tarasov, Trends, directions for further research, and some open problems of fractional calculus (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.04241): survey with open problems on fractional ODEs.
- **Further reading:** [Hartman, Ordinary Differential Equations (SIAM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898719222): second edition of Hartman's monograph.
references.MSC 34Bxx - Boundary value problems for:
## Reference
### Overview
A boundary value problem (BVP) imposes conditions on a solution of an ordinary differential equation at two or more points, or at the ends of an interval, instead of all data at one initial point. The linear second-order model is the Sturm–Liouville equation $-(p y')'+(q-zr)y=0$ on $(a,b)$ with separated conditions $\cos\alpha\,f(a)-\sin\alpha\,p(a)f'(a)=0$, $\cos\beta\,f(b)-\sin\beta\,p(b)f'(b)=0$; Teschl calls it regular when $r,q\in C^0([a,b],\mathbb R)$, $p\in C^1([a,b],\mathbb R)$ and $p,r>0$ on $[a,b]$. ([Teschl, ODE and Dynamical Systems, §§5.3–5.4](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) Unlike an initial value problem, a linear BVP is governed by a Fredholm alternative: either the homogeneous problem $(L-\lambda)u=0$ has a nontrivial solution, or $(L-\lambda)u=f$ is uniquely solvable for every $f$. ([Wikipedia, Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) In the regular Sturm–Liouville case the resolvent is an integral operator whose continuous symmetric kernel is the Green's function of the problem. ([Wikipedia, Sturm–Liouville theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%E2%80%93Liouville_theory))

The area runs from this classical spectral theory, through singular problems on half-lines and with singular endpoints (Weyl's theory), to nonlinear problems (existence and multiplicity, positive solutions, shooting and lower–upper solution methods) and to differential equations on metric graphs. ([MSC2020, 34B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Bxx)) It sits in [MSC 34 - Ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations) and feeds [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) through separation of variables; concept entry: [Sturm–Liouville Problems](node:Sturm–Liouville%20Problems).

### Scope
MSC2020 34B (for ordinary differential operators see 34Lxx) lists: 34B05 linear BVPs; 34B07 linear BVPs with nonlinear dependence on the spectral parameter; 34B08 parameter-dependent BVPs; 34B09 boundary eigenvalue problems; 34B10 nonlocal and multipoint BVPs; 34B15 nonlinear BVPs; 34B16 singular nonlinear BVPs; 34B18 positive solutions to nonlinear BVPs; 34B20 Weyl theory and its generalizations; 34B24 Sturm–Liouville theory (see also 34Lxx); 34B27 Green's functions; 34B30 special equations (Mathieu, Hill, Bessel, etc.); 34B37 BVPs with impulses; 34B40 BVPs on infinite intervals; 34B45 BVPs on graphs and networks; 34B60 applications; 34B99. ([MSC2020, 34B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Bxx))

Neighbours: the operator-theoretic [spectral theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) of the same differential expressions is classified in [MSC 34Lxx - Ordinary differential operators](node:MSC%2034Lxx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20operators), per the cross-reference above ([MSC2020, 34B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Bxx)); see also [Spectral Theory of Ordinary Differential Operators](node:Spectral%20Theory%20of%20Ordinary%20Differential%20Operators) and [Ordinary Differential Operators](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Operators). Special equations of 34B30 such as Bessel's have their solutions classified as functions in 33C10, Bessel and Airy functions, within [MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Cxx%20-%20Hypergeometric%20functions). ([MSC2020, 33C](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **Green function and spectral theorem (34B24, 34B27).** Let $u_a(z,\cdot)$, $u_b(z,\cdot)$ solve the equation and satisfy the boundary condition at $a$, resp. $b$. Their Wronskian $W(z)$ is entire and vanishes exactly at the eigenvalues, and for $W(z)\ne0$ the solution of $(L-z)f=g$ is $f(x)=\int_a^bG(z,x,t)g(t)r(t)\,dt$ with the [Green function](node:Green's%20Functions)
  $$G(z,x,t)=\frac{1}{W(z)}\begin{cases}u_b(z,x)u_a(z,t),&x\ge t,\\ u_b(z,t)u_a(z,x),&x\le t,\end{cases}$$
  meromorphic in $z$ and symmetric in $x,t$. The resolvent is compact (Arzelà–Ascoli) and symmetric, so the regular problem has countably many simple eigenvalues accumulating only at $\infty$, with real eigenfunctions forming an orthonormal basis of $L^2((a,b),r\,dx)$; the expansion converges uniformly for $f$ in the domain. ([Teschl, Lemma 5.9, Theorem 5.11](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Fredholm alternative.** For a compact operator $K$ and $\lambda\ne0$, either $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $K$ or it lies in the resolvent set; for boundary value problems this reads: either $(L-\lambda)u=0$ has a nontrivial solution, or $(L-\lambda)u=f$ has a unique solution for every $f$. ([Wikipedia, Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) See [Fredholm Alternative](node:Fredholm%20Alternative).
- **Oscillation theory (34B24).** Ordering the eigenvalues $E_0<E_1<\cdots$, the eigenfunction $u_n$ has exactly $n$ zeros in $(a,b)$. Sturm's comparison theorem: if $p_1\le p_0$ and $\lambda_0r_0-q_0\le\lambda_1r_1-q_1$, $L_ju_j=\lambda_ju_j$, and at each end of $(c,d)\subseteq(a,b)$ either $W(u_1,u_0)=0$ or $u_0=0$, then $u_1$ vanishes in $(c,d)$ unless $u_1,u_0$ are proportional. If $pr\in C^1$, Weyl's asymptotics hold:
  $$E_n=\pi^2\Big(\int_a^b\sqrt{r(t)/p(t)}\,dt\Big)^{-2}n^2+O(n).$$
  On $(0,\infty)$, Kneser's theorem for $-u''+qu$: $\liminf x^2q(x)>-\tfrac14$ gives nonoscillation and $\limsup x^2q(x)<-\tfrac14$ gives oscillation. ([Teschl, Theorems 5.17, 5.20, 5.25, 5.26](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Weyl theory of singular problems (34B20, 34B40).** A problem is singular when the interval is unbounded or the coefficients are singular at an endpoint; the spectrum may then have a continuous part, with an eigenfunction expansion analogous to passing from Fourier series to the [Fourier transform](node:Fourier%20Analysis). ([Wikipedia, Sturm–Liouville theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%E2%80%93Liouville_theory)) Weyl's alternative (1910): at a singular endpoint, for non-real $\lambda$, either all solutions of $Df=\lambda f$ are square-integrable near it (limit circle) or exactly one non-zero solution up to scalars is (limit point). The Weyl–Titchmarsh function $m(\lambda)$ fixes the square-integrable solution $\Phi_\lambda+m(\lambda)\Psi_\lambda$, and the Titchmarsh–Kodaira formula recovers the spectral measure from $\operatorname{Im}m(t+i\varepsilon)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$; Titchmarsh (1946) and Kodaira (1949) obtained it independently. ([Wikipedia, Spectral theory of ODEs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_ordinary_differential_equations))
- **Nonlinear BVPs and shooting (34B15, 34B18).** For $y''=f(t,y,y')$, $y(t_0)=y_0$, $y(t_1)=y_1$, solve the initial value problem with $y'(t_0)=a$ and set $F(a)=y(t_1;a)-y_1$: roots of $F$ correspond one-to-one to solutions of the BVP, and $F$ may have several roots, so a nonlinear BVP can have several solutions. ([Wikipedia, Shooting method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shooting_method)) The lower and upper solutions method, with chapters on positive solutions and parametric multiplicity problems, is the subject of De Coster and Habets's monograph. ([Crossref, De Coster–Habets 2006](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=De+Coster+Habets+Two-Point+Boundary+Value+Problems+Lower+and+Upper+Solutions&rows=3&select=DOI,title,author,published,publisher,container-title))
- **BVPs on metric graphs (34B45).** A quantum graph is a metric graph equipped with a Schrödinger operator acting along the edges and vertex conditions; $\delta$ coupling of strength $\alpha_v$ at $v$ requires $f$ continuous at $v$ and $\sum_{j=1}^{\deg v}f_j'(v)=\alpha_vf(v)$, with $\alpha_v=0$ the continuity–Kirchhoff condition and $\alpha_v=\infty$ formally Dirichlet; $\delta'$ couplings of strength $\beta_v\ne0$ instead require the derivatives to agree at $v$, with $\sum_jf_j(v)=\beta_vf'(v)$. ([Rohleder & Seifert, survey, Definition 2.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01924)) Kuchment's survey introduces the basic notions and research directions. ([Kuchment, Quantum graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.3442))

### History
Papers of 1836–1837 by Sturm and Liouville on differential equations from the theory of heat, involving expansions of functions in series, founded what is now the Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem. ([MacTutor, Sturm](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Sturm/)) Weyl's limit-point/limit-circle dichotomy dates from his 1910 work, and Titchmarsh (1946) and Kodaira (1949) developed the spectral-measure formula, Kodaira using von Neumann's [spectral theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem) and extending the method to even-order singular equations in 1950. ([Wikipedia, Spectral theory of ODEs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_ordinary_differential_equations))

### Open problems
- **Eigenvalue bounds on quantum graphs (34B45).** Rohleder and Seifert pose as open problems: prove an upper bound for the principal eigenvalue of a Schrödinger operator with $\delta$ vertex couplings that is sharp, e.g. asymptotically as the coupling coefficients tend to $\infty$ (Open Problem 7.6); prove sharp upper and lower bounds for the lowest eigenvalue with $\delta'$ vertex conditions in terms of total length and coupling strengths (7.7); and decide whether unfolding parallel edges raises the principal eigenvalue in general for $\delta'$ conditions (5.11). ([Rohleder & Seifert, Spectral theory for Schrödinger operators on compact metric graphs with δ and δ' couplings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01924))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Sturm–Liouville theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%E2%80%93Liouville_theory): regular and singular problems, Green function, spectral theorem.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Spectral theory of ordinary differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_ordinary_differential_equations): Weyl alternative, $m$-function, Titchmarsh–Kodaira formula.
- **Learn:** [Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, Ch. 5](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf): Green function, regular Sturm–Liouville problems, oscillation theory, periodic problems.
- **Primary:** [Rohleder & Seifert, survey of Schrödinger operators on metric graphs (arXiv 2303.01924)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01924): recent results and open problems on graph BVPs.
- **Primary:** [Kuchment, Quantum graphs: an introduction and a brief survey (arXiv 0802.3442)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.3442): survey of the field.
- **Further reading:** [De Coster & Habets, Two-Point Boundary Value Problems: Lower and Upper Solutions (Elsevier, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=De+Coster+Habets+Two-Point+Boundary+Value+Problems+Lower+and+Upper+Solutions&rows=3&select=DOI,title,author,published,publisher,container-title): monograph on nonlinear two-point BVPs.
references.MSC 34Cxx - Qualitative theory for ordin:
## Reference
### Overview
Qualitative theory describes the solutions of an [ordinary differential equation](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) without solving it: the topology of the integral curves, singular points and their local type, periodic orbits and limit cycles, invariant manifolds, bifurcations as parameters vary, and complex or chaotic behaviour. MSC2020 34Cxx carries a "See also 37-XX" note, pointing to the theory of [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), with which it overlaps. ([MSC2020 34Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Cxx))

The central tools are local and global. Locally, the Hartman–Grobman and stable manifold theorems show that near a hyperbolic equilibrium the flow looks like its linearization; in the plane, Poincaré–Bendixson theory classifies the possible limit sets, so planar flows cannot be chaotic. ([Teschl, ODE and Dynamical Systems, Ch. 7 and 9](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf); [Wikipedia: Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem)) The section also contains one of the best-known open problems in mathematics: the second part of Hilbert's 16th problem, on the number of limit cycles of polynomial vector fields, named in the MSC entry under 34C07. ([MSC2020 34Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Cxx); [Wikipedia: Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Cxx: 34C05 topological structure of integral curves, singular points, limit cycles; 34C07 theory of limit cycles of polynomial and analytic vector fields (existence, uniqueness, bounds, Hilbert's 16th problem); 34C08 connections with real algebraic geometry (fewnomials, desingularization, zeros of abelian integrals); 34C10 oscillation theory, zeros, disconjugacy and comparison theory; 34C11 growth and boundedness; 34C12 monotone systems; 34C14 symmetries, invariants; 34C15 nonlinear oscillations and coupled oscillators; 34C20 transformation and reduction, normal forms; 34C23 bifurcation theory (see also 37Gxx); 34C25 periodic solutions; 34C26 relaxation oscillations; 34C27 almost and pseudo-almost periodic solutions; 34C28 complex behavior and chaotic systems (see also 37Dxx); 34C29 averaging; 34C37 homoclinic and heteroclinic solutions; 34C40 equations and systems on manifolds; 34C41 equivalence and asymptotic equivalence; 34C45 invariant manifolds; 34C46 multifrequency systems; 34C55 hysteresis; 34C60 qualitative investigation and simulation of models; 34C99. ([MSC2020 34Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Cxx))

Neighbours.
