The cross-references point to [MSC 37Gxx - Local and nonlocal bifurcation theory for dynamical systems](node:MSC%2037Gxx%20-%20Local%20and%20nonlocal%20bifurcation%20theory%20for%20dynamical%20systems) for bifurcations and [MSC 37Dxx - Dynamical systems with hyperbolic behavior](node:MSC%2037Dxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20with%20hyperbolic%20behavior) for chaos, and the section note to dynamical systems generally, e.g. [MSC 37Cxx - Smooth dynamical systems - general theory](node:MSC%2037Cxx%20-%20Smooth%20dynamical%20systems%20-%20general%20theory). ([MSC2020 34Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Cxx)) Stability of solutions, Lyapunov exponents and attractors have their own subfield, [MSC 34Dxx - Stability theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Dxx%20-%20Stability%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations); existence, uniqueness and continuation are in [MSC 34Axx - General theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations). ([MSC2020 34Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Dxx); [MSC2020 34Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Hartman–Grobman and stable manifolds (34C45, 34C41).** If $0$ is a hyperbolic fixed point of a differentiable vector field with Jacobian $A$, there is a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $\varphi=\mathrm{id}+h$, $h$ bounded, with $\varphi\circ e^{tA}=\Phi_t\circ\varphi$ near $0$ (Theorem 9.9). For $f\in C^k$ with a fixed point $x_0$, the stable and unstable manifolds $M^\pm(x_0)$ are locally $C^k$ graphs over the linear subspaces $E^\pm$ and tangent to them, and solutions on $M^\pm$ converge to $x_0$ exponentially as $t\to\pm\infty$ (Theorem 9.4); a center manifold also exists but need not be unique. ([Teschl, §§9.2–9.3](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Poincaré–Bendixson (34C05, 34C25).** Let $M\subset\mathbb R^2$ be open, $f\in C^1(M,\mathbb R^2)$, and suppose the limit set $\omega_\sigma(x)$ is nonempty, compact, connected and contains finitely many fixed points. Then it is a fixed point, a regular periodic orbit, or finitely many fixed points together with non-closed orbits whose limit sets are among those points (Theorem 7.16). Every periodic orbit encloses a fixed point (Lemma 7.17). ([Teschl, §7.3](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) The theorem fails in higher dimensions and on the torus, so chaos in continuous flows needs at least three dimensions. ([Wikipedia: Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem)) See [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory).
- **Liénard's theorem (34C15, 34C25).** For $\dot x=y-f(x)$, $\dot y=-x$ with $f$ differentiable and odd, $f<0$ on $(0,\alpha)$, $\liminf_{x\to\infty}f(x)>0$, there is at least one periodic orbit around $(0,0)$; if moreover $f$ is increasing for $x>\alpha$, the orbit is unique and attracts every other trajectory except the origin (Theorem 7.8). Van der Pol's equation $\ddot x-\mu(1-x^2)\dot x+x=0$, $\mu>0$, is equivalent to Liénard's equation with $f(x)=\mu(x^3/3-x)$, so it has a unique, globally attracting periodic orbit. ([Teschl, §7.2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Hopf bifurcation (34C23).** If at an equilibrium all eigenvalues of the Jacobian have negative real part except a complex pair $\rho\pm i\varepsilon$, and $\rho$ changes from negative to positive as parameters vary, a periodic orbit is born. In the normal form $\dot z=z((\lambda+i)+b|z|^2)$, $b=\alpha+i\beta$, the sign of the first Lyapunov coefficient $\alpha$ decides the type: for $\alpha<0$ a stable limit cycle exists for $\lambda>0$ (supercritical); for $\alpha>0$ an unstable one exists for $\lambda<0$ (subcritical). ([Wikipedia: Hopf bifurcation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_bifurcation)) Liénard's equation gives the prototype Poincaré–Andronov–Hopf bifurcation. ([Teschl, §7.2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Melnikov's method (34C37, 34C28).** For a perturbed planar Hamiltonian system, simple zeros of the Melnikov integral locate periodic orbits that persist; for the van der Pol equation it gives $\Delta_\varepsilon(q,0)=\frac{\pi q}{4}(q^2-4)$, whose simple zero $q=2$ shows that the unperturbed circular orbit of radius $2$ persists for small $\varepsilon$. The same method for homoclinic orbits leads, via the Smale horseshoe and the Smale–Birkhoff homoclinic theorem, to chaos in higher-dimensional systems. ([Teschl, §§12.4, 13.1–13.3](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Limit cycles of polynomial fields (34C07).** A limit cycle is an isolated periodic orbit. Every planar polynomial vector field has finitely many limit cycles (Ilyashenko; Écalle, 1991–1992), which is not automatic since $C^\infty$ fields can have infinitely many concentric ones; linear fields have none, and quadratic fields with four limit cycles are known. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem)) Each limit cycle of a quadratic field surrounds only one singular point, a focus; quadratic fields have at most two foci, and only one nest can contain more than one cycle (Zhang Pingguang). ([Ilyashenko–Llibre](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0910.3443))

### History
Poincaré formulated a weaker version of the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem in 1892 and Bendixson proved it in 1901. ([Wikipedia: Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem)) Hilbert posed the 16th problem in his 1900 Paris address; Dulac's 1923 finiteness proof was found in 1981 to have a gap, the Petrovsky–Landis claim of the 1950s was shown wrong in the early 1960s, and Ilyashenko and Écalle proved finiteness for individual fields in 1991/1992. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem)) Graduate references include Guckenheimer and Holmes, *Nonlinear Oscillations, Dynamical Systems, and Bifurcations of Vector Fields* (Springer, 1983), and Perko, *Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems* (Springer, 2001). ([Crossref: Guckenheimer–Holmes](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1140-2); [Crossref: Perko](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4613-0003-8))

### Open problems
- **Hilbert's 16th problem, second part (34C07).** Find an upper bound $H(n)$ for the number of limit cycles of planar polynomial vector fields of degree $n$, and their relative positions. No finite bound is known for any $n>1$. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem)) Ilyashenko and Llibre state that the answer is unknown even for $n=2$, where even the existence of a uniform bound for quadratic fields is not proved; they prove a restricted version, bounding the number of limit cycles of quadratic fields kept a distance from centers and from singular fields, with cycles kept away from singular points and infinity. ([Ilyashenko–Llibre](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0910.3443))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hilbert's sixteenth problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem): statement, history, finiteness theorem.
- **Reference:** [Hopf bifurcation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_bifurcation): normal form and Lyapunov coefficient.
- **Learn:** [Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS GSM 140, author's version)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf): Ch. 6–9 and 12–13 on flows, planar systems, Poincaré–Bendixson, invariant manifolds, Hartman–Grobman, Melnikov's method.
- **Primary:** [Ilyashenko and Llibre, A restricted version of Hilbert's 16th problem for quadratic vector fields (arXiv:0910.3443)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.3443): research paper with a summary of the state of the quadratic case.
- **Further reading:** [Guckenheimer–Holmes (Springer 1983)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1140-2); [Perko (Springer 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4613-0003-8).
references.MSC 34Dxx - Stability theory for ordinar:
## Reference
### Overview
Stability theory for ordinary differential equations asks how solutions of $\dot x=f(t,x)$ respond to perturbations of initial data or of the equation. An equilibrium $f_e$ is Lyapunov stable if for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that solutions starting within $\delta$ of $f_e$ stay within $\epsilon$ for all $t\ge t_0$; it is asymptotically stable if in addition nearby solutions converge to $f_e$. ([Wikipedia: Stability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_theory))

Two classical routes exist. Linearization at an equilibrium of a $C^1$ field with Jacobian having all eigenvalues of negative real part gives asymptotic stability, and for $x'=Ax$ the zero solution is asymptotically stable iff every eigenvalue has $\operatorname{Re}\lambda<0$. Lyapunov's second (direct) method instead uses a scalar function $V$ with $V(0)=0$, $V>0$ elsewhere and $\dot V\le 0$ along solutions to conclude stability without solving the equation. ([Wikipedia: Stability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_theory); [Wikipedia: Lyapunov stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_stability))

34Dxx is the stability subfield of [MSC 34 - Ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations); its heading cross-references 37C75 in dynamical systems and [MSC 93Dxx - Stability of control systems](node:MSC%2093Dxx%20-%20Stability%20of%20control%20systems). ([MSC2020 34Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Dxx)) The Lyapunov theorems assume only a continuous vector field $f$ and a continuously differentiable $V$, and Tedrake's notes apply them to general [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) described by [ordinary differential equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations). ([Tedrake, Lyapunov Analysis](https://underactuated.mit.edu/lyapunov.html))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Dxx lists: 34D05 asymptotic properties; 34D06 synchronization; 34D08 characteristic and Lyapunov exponents; 34D09 dichotomy, trichotomy; 34D10 perturbations; 34D15 singular perturbations; 34D20 stability; 34D23 global stability; 34D30 structural stability and analogous concepts; 34D35 stability of manifolds of solutions; 34D45 attractors; 34D99 none of the above. ([MSC2020 34Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Dxx))

Cross-references in the entry: the 34Dxx heading says see also 37C75 and [MSC 93Dxx - Stability of control systems](node:MSC%2093Dxx%20-%20Stability%20of%20control%20systems); 34D30 (structural stability) points to 37C20; and 34D45 (attractors) points to 37C70 and 37D45. ([MSC2020 34Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Dxx))

### Key concepts
- **Lyapunov function.** Under hypotheses $f$ continuous, $V\in C^1$ positive definite on a neighbourhood of $0$: $\dot V\le0$ gives stability and $\dot V<0$ off $0$ gives asymptotic stability; if $V$ is also radially unbounded and $\dot V<0$ off $0$ on all of $\mathbb R^n$, the origin is globally asymptotically stable. ([Tedrake](https://underactuated.mit.edu/lyapunov.html)) See [Lyapunov Stability](node:Lyapunov%20Stability) and [Lyapunov Functions for Control Systems](node:Lyapunov%20Functions%20for%20Control%20Systems).
- **LaSalle (Barbashin–Krasovskii–LaSalle) invariance principle.** For $\dot x=f(x)$, $f(0)=0$, $V\in C^1$ with $\dot V\le0$: accumulation points of trajectories lie in the union of complete trajectories contained in $\{\dot V=0\}$; if $V$ is positive definite with $V(0)=0$ and that set contains only the trivial trajectory, the origin is asymptotically stable, and globally so if $V$ is radially unbounded. ([Wikipedia: LaSalle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaSalle%27s_invariance_principle))
- **Hartman–Grobman theorem.** If $f$ is smooth and the Jacobian $A$ at an equilibrium $u^*$ has no eigenvalue with zero real part, then near $u^*$ the flow is topologically conjugate by a homeomorphism to that of $\dot U=AU$; the conjugacy is in general Hölder but not smooth. ([Wikipedia: Hartman–Grobman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem)) Eigenvalue input: [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors).
- **Stable manifold theorem.** For a smooth map with a hyperbolic fixed point $p$, the stable and unstable sets $W^s(p)$, $W^u(p)$ are smooth manifolds whose tangent spaces have the dimensions of the stable and unstable spaces of the linearization. ([Wikipedia: Stable manifold theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_manifold_theorem)) See [Stable Manifold Theorem](node:Stable%20Manifold%20Theorem) and [Hyperbolic Dynamical Systems](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems).
- **Converse Lyapunov theorems.** Massera: for periodic or autonomous systems with continuously differentiable right-hand side and unique solutions, asymptotic stability of the origin yields a continuously differentiable Lyapunov function, built as a semi-infinite integral along solutions. Kurzweil: with only a continuous right-hand side and no uniqueness assumption, uniform asymptotic stability in the large on the domain of attraction yields a smooth (infinitely differentiable) Lyapunov function. ([Kellett, survey](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.04809))
- **Quadratic certificates for linear systems.** For stable $\dot x=Ax$, a quadratic $V=x^\top Px$ exists, with $PA+A^\top P=-Q$ for any $Q\succ0$; sum-of-squares programming extends the search to polynomial systems. ([Tedrake](https://underactuated.mit.edu/lyapunov.html))
- **Markus–Yamabe conjecture.** If the Jacobian is Hurwitz everywhere, is the fixed point globally stable? True in dimension 2 (Gutierrez, Feßler, 1995), false for $n>2$ (polynomial counterexample of Cima et al., 1997). ([Wikipedia: Markus–Yamabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markus%E2%80%93Yamabe_conjecture))

### History
Lyapunov defended his thesis "The General Problem of Stability of Motion" at Moscow University on 12 September 1892. ([Wikipedia: Aleksandr Lyapunov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Lyapunov)) The work initially received little attention, and interest surged during the Cold War through aerospace guidance applications. ([Wikipedia: Lyapunov stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_stability)) Barbashin and Krasovskii communicated a special case of the invariance principle in 1952, Krasovskii the general result in 1959, and LaSalle independently in 1960. ([Wikipedia: LaSalle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaSalle%27s_invariance_principle)) Massera's converse theorem appeared in the *Annals of Mathematics* in 1949, and Kurzweil's converse results in the *Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal* in 1955–1957. ([Kellett](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.04809)) Grobman published his linearization theorem in 1959 and Hartman in 1960. ([Wikipedia: Hartman–Grobman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Constructive converse for absolute stability (Lur'e systems).** Kellett's survey states that a constructive converse has not been found; only existence results via frequency-domain conditions are available. ([Kellett](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.04809))
- **Robustness of strong KL-stability for inclusions.** Stated in the same survey as an open question outside special cases. ([Kellett](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.04809))
- **Necessary and sufficient conditions for global stability; Aizerman/Kalman problems.** Kuznetsov et al. call finding such conditions a challenging problem tied to hidden oscillations, with Kalman-conjecture counterexamples in a four-dimensional flutter model; extending first-approximation stability to non-periodic nonautonomous linearizations is likewise called challenging. ([Kuznetsov et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2107.13889))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_theory): definitions, linearization criteria, discrete maps.
- **Learn:** [Tedrake, Lyapunov Analysis (MIT)](https://underactuated.mit.edu/lyapunov.html): Lyapunov and LaSalle theorems, quadratic and SOS certificates, regions of attraction.
- **Primary:** [Kellett, Classical converse theorems in Lyapunov's second method](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1502.04809): survey of Massera, Kurzweil and Krasovskii converses.
- **Primary:** [Kuznetsov et al., The birth of the global stability theory and the theory of hidden oscillations](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2107.13889): historical survey with Aizerman/Kalman counterexamples.
- **Further reading:** [Perko, Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-0249-0): Lawrence Perko, Springer, Texts in Applied Mathematics (1996); bibliographic record.
references.MSC 34Exx - Asymptotic theory for ordina:
## Reference
### Overview
Asymptotic ODE theory describes solutions in limiting regimes: near a singular point, for a large parameter, or as a small parameter tends to zero. The right representation depends on local structure. At a regular singularity convergent Frobenius series exist, while at an irregular singularity of rank one the formal series solutions diverge unless they terminate (their coefficients grow factorially) and are only asymptotic in sectors, connected across sectors by Stokes multipliers. ([DLMF §2.7](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.7))

For equations with a large parameter, uniform approximations are built by comparing with a simpler equation whose solutions are elementary, Airy, or Bessel functions, chosen according to the transition points of the coefficient. These comparison functions belong to [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions). ([DLMF §2.8](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.8)) Singular perturbation problems, where a small parameter multiplies the highest derivative, are handled by inner and outer expansions that are then matched; see [Matched Asymptotic Expansions](node:Matched%20Asymptotic%20Expansions) and [Singular Perturbations of ODEs](node:Singular%20Perturbations%20of%20ODEs). ([Wikipedia: Matched asymptotic expansions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matched_asymptotic_expansions)) A geometric theory of fast-slow systems (Fenichel theory, blow-up) now treats many singular perturbation problems as problems about invariant manifolds of [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems). ([Jardón-Kojakhmetov–Kuehn survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.01402))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Exx lists: 34E05 asymptotic expansions of solutions; 34E10 perturbations, asymptotics of solutions; 34E13 multiple scale methods; 34E15 singular perturbations; 34E17 canard solutions; 34E18 methods of nonstandard analysis; 34E20 singular perturbations, turning point theory, WKB methods; 34E99 none of the above. The entry lists no "see also" cross-references. ([MSC2020 34Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Exx))

Neighbouring codes: complex-domain asymptotics sit in 34Mxx, which has its own codes 34M30 (asymptotics and summation methods), 34M40 (Stokes phenomena and connection problems) and 34M60 (complex WKB, turning points, steepest descent; see also 34E20) ([MSC2020 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Mxx)); 34D15 classifies singular perturbations under stability theory ([MSC2020 34Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Dxx)); and 41A60 covers asymptotic approximations and expansions of functions (steepest descent), not of ODE solutions. ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Singularity classification and formal solutions.** For $w''+f(z)w'+g(z)w=0$, $z_0$ is a regular singularity if $(z-z_0)f$ and $(z-z_0)^2g$ are analytic there; the rank is $\ell-1$ for the least $\ell$ with $(z-z_0)^\ell f$ and $(z-z_0)^{2\ell}g$ analytic. At a rank-one singularity at infinity, formal solutions $e^{\lambda_j z}z^{\mu_j}\sum_s a_{s,j}z^{-s}$ exist when $\lambda_1\neq\lambda_2$; the series generally diverge, and genuine solutions have them as asymptotic expansions in specified sectors. ([DLMF §2.7(i)–(ii)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.7))
- **Liouville–Green (WKB) approximation with error bounds.** For $w''=(f(x)+g(x))w$ on $(a_1,a_2)$ with $f>0$, $f\in C^2$ and $g$ continuous, there are solutions $w_j=f^{-1/4}\exp\left(\pm\int f^{1/2}dx\right)(1+\varepsilon_j(x))$ with
$$|\varepsilon_j(x)|,\ \tfrac12 f^{-1/2}|\varepsilon_j'(x)|\le \exp\left(\tfrac12\mathcal V_{a_j,x}(F)\right)-1,$$
where $F=\int\bigl(f^{-1/4}\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2}f^{-1/4}-gf^{-1/2}\bigr)dx$ is the error-control function and $\mathcal V$ denotes total variation. ([DLMF §2.7(iii)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.7)) See [WKB Approximation](node:WKB%20Approximation).
- **Turning-point theory.** For $w''=(u^2f(z)+g(z))w$ with $|u|\to\infty$, a Liouville transformation reduces the equation to $W''=(u^2\xi^m+\psi(\xi))W$ with $m=0,1,-1$ for no transition point, a simple zero of $f$ (turning point), or a simple pole. The approximants are $e^{\pm u\xi}$, Airy functions of $u^{2/3}\xi$, and Bessel functions of order $(1+4\rho)^{1/2}$, where $\rho=\lim_{\xi\to0}\xi^2\psi(\xi)$, respectively, with expansions uniform in $\xi$. ([DLMF §2.8](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.8)) Cf. [Bessel Functions](node:Bessel%20Functions).
- **Matched asymptotic expansions (worked example).** For $\varepsilon y''+(1+\varepsilon)y'+y=0$, $y(0)=0$, $y(1)=1$, the outer solution is $y_O=e^{1-t}$; in the boundary layer $\tau=t/\varepsilon$ the inner solution is $y_I=B(1-e^{-t/\varepsilon})$; matching $\lim_{\tau\to\infty}y_I=\lim_{t\to0}y_O$ gives $B=e$, and the composite $y=e(e^{-t}-e^{-t/\varepsilon})$ is uniformly valid. A layer placed at $t=1$ cannot be matched. ([Wikipedia: Matched asymptotic expansions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matched_asymptotic_expansions)) Cf. [Boundary Layers](node:Boundary%20Layers).
- **Fenichel's theorem.** For a fast-slow system $x'=f(x,y,\varepsilon)$, $y'=\varepsilon g(x,y,\varepsilon)$, let $S_0$ be a compact normally hyperbolic subset of the critical manifold $\{f(x,y,0)=0\}$. For small $\varepsilon>0$ there is a locally invariant slow manifold $S_\varepsilon$, diffeomorphic to $S_0$, at Hausdorff distance $O(\varepsilon)$, $C^k$-smooth, with the same fast-direction stability; distinct choices are $O(e^{-C/\varepsilon})$ close. ([Jardón-Kojakhmetov–Kuehn, Thm 2.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.01402)) Cf. [Hyperbolic Dynamical Systems](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems).
- **Canards (34E17).** A canard is a trajectory that follows the repelling part of the critical manifold for $O(1)$ time. At a planar canard point, Krupa and Szmolyan showed that the attracting and repelling slow manifolds connect if and only if the parameter equals $\omega_c(\sqrt\varepsilon)$ (the maximal canard), and that the transition map is defined only for parameters in an interval of size $O(e^{-C/\varepsilon})$ around $\omega_c$; for van der Pol, Dumortier and Roussarie showed that the transition from small canard cycles to relaxation oscillations occurs within an exponentially small parameter interval, the canard explosion. ([Jardón-Kojakhmetov–Kuehn, §3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.01402))
- **Stokes phenomenon, Borel summation, resurgence.** An analytic function can have different asymptotic expansions in different sectors because exponentially small terms switch on across Stokes curves; for $\operatorname{Ai}$ the expansions for $x\to+\infty$ and $x\to-\infty$ differ. ([Wikipedia: Stokes phenomenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokes_phenomenon)) The Borel transform $\sum a_kt^k/k!$ followed by Laplace integration resums factorially divergent series; Watson's theorem gives conditions (holomorphy in $|z|<R$, $|\arg z|<\pi/2+\epsilon$ and remainder bounds $C^{n+1}n!|z|^n$) under which a function is the Borel sum of its asymptotic series. ([Wikipedia: Borel summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_summation)) Loday-Richaud and Remy prove that solutions of level-one linear differential systems are summable-resurgent and express the Stokes–Ramis matrices through connection constants in the Borel plane, without genericity assumptions. ([Loday-Richaud–Remy](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.2613))

### History
Liouville and Green may be said to have founded the method in 1837, with Carlini (1817) among earlier essentially equivalent methods; Jeffreys gave a general method for linear second-order equations in 1923, and Wentzel, Kramers and Brillouin developed the method in 1926, their work and Jeffreys's including the treatment of turning points that connects evanescent and oscillatory solutions. ([Wikipedia: WKB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WKB_approximation)) Stokes's papers of 1847 and 1858 introduced the sectorial discontinuity of asymptotic constants. ([Wikipedia: Stokes phenomenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokes_phenomenon)) Fenichel's geometric theory dates from 1979; canards were explained with non-standard analysis in "Chasse au canard" (1981); Dumortier and Roussarie introduced blow-up for fast-slow systems in 1996; Krupa and Szmolyan's planar canard results appeared in 2001. ([Jardón-Kojakhmetov–Kuehn](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.01402))

### Open problems
- **Blow-up beyond low codimension and ODEs.** The survey of Jardón-Kojakhmetov and Kuehn names geometric studies of high-dimensional systems and high-codimension singularities as directions of growing relevance, and calls extending the blow-up method to partial, stochastic and stochastic-partial differential equations "a daunting challenge"; it lists torus canards, piecewise-smooth systems and maps with singularities as active extensions. ([Jardón-Kojakhmetov–Kuehn, §§3.6, 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.01402))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [DLMF §§2.7–2.8](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.7): singularities, Liouville–Green error bounds, turning-point approximants.
- **Learn:** [Matched asymptotic expansions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matched_asymptotic_expansions): the worked boundary-layer example.
- **Primary:** [Jardón-Kojakhmetov and Kuehn, A survey on the blow-up method for fast-slow systems](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.01402): Fenichel theory, canards, blow-up, further directions.
- **Primary:** [Loday-Richaud and Remy, Resurgence, Stokes phenomenon and alien derivatives for level-one linear differential systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.2613): summable-resurgence and explicit Stokes matrices.
- **Further reading:** [Olver, Asymptotics and Special Functions](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9781439864548): Frank Olver, A K Peters/CRC Press, 1997.
- **Further reading:** [Wasow, Asymptotic Expansions for Ordinary Differential Equations](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=wasow+asymptotic+expansions+ordinary+differential+equations): Wolfgang Wasow, first published 1965; later reprints.
references.MSC 34Fxx - Ordinary differential equati:
## Reference
### Overview
A random ordinary differential equation (RODE) is a pathwise ODE whose vector field contains a stochastic process: $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=f(\zeta_t(\omega),x)$ with $\zeta$ a process with continuous sample paths and $f$ continuous. For almost every fixed $\omega$ it is a nonautonomous deterministic [ODE](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations), so existence and uniqueness conditions are those of ODEs, and the solution sample paths are continuously differentiable. They are usually no smoother than that, because the driving noise is at most Hölder continuous in time, so $t\mapsto f(\zeta_t(\omega),x)$ is not differentiable in $t$. ([Jentzen–Kloeden, CBMS lectures, Lecture 2](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~mrasmuss/peter/nelderlectures.pdf)) See [Random Differential Equations](node:Random%20Differential%20Equations) and [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes).

RODEs and stochastic ODEs (SDEs) are closely linked. A RODE driven by a Wiener process can be rewritten as an SDE system: $x'=-x+\sin W_t$ becomes $d(X_t,Y_t)=(-X_t+\sin Y_t,\,0)\,dt+(0,1)\,dW_t$. Conversely, SDEs can be transformed into RODEs (the Doss–Sussmann approach, illustrated in the lectures for scalar additive noise), so deterministic calculus can be used pathwise to study SDE dynamics. ([Jentzen–Kloeden](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~mrasmuss/peter/nelderlectures.pdf)) The explicit Doss–Sussmann formula below is for a scalar equation and relies on a global Lipschitz assumption; for Stratonovich SDEs the link is made through conjugacy of the generated flows with RODE flows (Imkeller and Lederer). ([Milstein–Schoenmakers](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1312.0876); [Qiao–Duan](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1210.0675)) The natural long-time framework is that of [random dynamical systems](node:Random%20Dynamical%20Systems) ([MSC 37Hxx - Random dynamical systems](node:MSC%2037Hxx%20-%20Random%20dynamical%20systems)): a cocycle $\varphi$ over a measure-preserving base flow $\vartheta$ of the noise; unlike for deterministic [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), attractors must be defined by rewinding time, as for pullback attractors, and depend on the noise realization $\omega$. ([Wikipedia: Random dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_dynamical_system))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Fxx lists: 34F05 ordinary differential equations and systems with randomness; 34F10 bifurcation of solutions involving randomness; 34F15 resonance phenomena involving randomness; 34F99 none of the above. The heading says see also 34K50, 60H10 and 93E03. ([MSC2020 34Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Fxx))

Neighbouring codes ([MSC 60Hxx - Stochastic analysis](node:MSC%2060Hxx%20-%20Stochastic%20analysis)): SDEs as objects of stochastic analysis are 60H10 ("stochastic ordinary differential equations (aspects of stochastic analysis)", see also 34F05) and computational methods for stochastic equations are 60H35 (see also 65C30) ([MSC2020 60Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=60Hxx)); the general theory of random and stochastic dynamical systems, multiplicative [ergodic theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory), random bifurcation and stability is 37Hxx (37H05–37H30) ([MSC2020 37Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Hxx)); and stochastic functional-differential equations are 34K50 (see also 34Fxx, 60Hxx). ([MSC2020 34Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Kxx))

### Key concepts
- **Doss–Sussmann transformation.** For a scalar Stratonovich SDE $dV=b(V)\,dt+\gamma(V)\circ dw$, let $F(x,y)$ solve $\partial_yF=\gamma(F)$, $F(x,0)=x$. If $X$ solves the pathwise ODE $\dot X=b(F(X,w(t)))/\partial_xF(X,w(t))$, $X(0)=V(0)$, then $V(t)=F(X(t),w(t))$. The original Doss–Sussmann results (Doss 1977, Sussmann 1978) rely on a global Lipschitz assumption; for equations such as the Cox–Ingersoll–Ross SDE that violate it, the formula must be considered only formally until proved directly. ([Milstein–Schoenmakers](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1312.0876))
- **Additive noise via an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.** $dX_t=f(X_t)\,dt+dW_t$ is equivalent to the RODE $z'=f(z+O_t)+O_t$ with $z=X_t-O_t$ and $dO_t=-O_t\,dt+dW_t$. If $f$ is one-sided dissipative, $\langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le-L|x-y|^2$ with $L>0$, then any two RODE solutions satisfy $|z_1(t)-z_2(t)|^2\le e^{-2Lt}|z_1(0)-z_2(0)|^2$, giving a pathwise asymptotically stable stationary solution for the SDE. ([Jentzen–Kloeden](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~mrasmuss/peter/nelderlectures.pdf))
- **Conjugacy of random dynamical systems.** Two RDS $\varphi,\psi$ are conjugate if $\psi_t(\omega,\cdot)=H(\theta_t\omega,\cdot)\circ\varphi_t(\omega,\cdot)\circ H(\omega,\cdot)^{-1}$ for a random [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $H$; the cocycle property is $\varphi_{t+s}(\omega)=\varphi_t(\theta_s\omega)\circ\varphi_s(\omega)$. Qiao and Duan transform Itô SDEs driven by Lévy processes into random differential equations and prove the two cocycles conjugate, extending conjugacy methods previously applied to Brownian SDEs; they also prove a Hartman–Grobman theorem for discontinuous cocycles. ([Qiao–Duan](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1210.0675)) An earlier paper on this conjugacy is Imkeller and Schmalfuss, "The Conjugacy of Stochastic and Random Differential Equations and the Existence of Global Attractors" (J. Dyn. Diff. Equ. 13, 2001). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1023/A:1016673307045))
- **Random attractors.** A random compact set $A(\omega)$ is a global random attractor if $\varphi_t(\omega,A(\omega))=A(\theta_t\omega)$ for $t\ge0$ and it attracts every tempered random bounded set, in the pullback sense; existence follows from a compact absorbing set. ([Qiao–Duan, Def. 2.4, Thm 2.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1210.0675)) Cf. [Global Attractors](node:Global%20Attractors).
- **Numerical order for RODEs.** Classical ODE schemes applied pathwise rarely attain their usual order: for $x'=-x+\zeta_t$ with $\zeta$ Hölder of exponent $\tfrac12$, the Euler scheme has pathwise order $\tfrac12$, while an averaged Euler scheme using $\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\zeta_t\,dt$ does better. ([Jentzen–Kloeden](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~mrasmuss/peter/nelderlectures.pdf)) Kloeden and Rosa prove that if $f$ is globally Lipschitz in $x$, the noise is a semimartingale $Y=Y_0+F+Z$ (finite variation plus martingale) with suitable moments, $f$ is $C^1$ in $t$ and $C^2$ in $y$, and $\partial_tf$, $D_yf$, $D_{yy}f$ satisfy growth bounds, then the Euler method converges strongly with order 1; the proof does not rely on Hölder continuity of the noise paths. ([Kloeden–Rosa, Thm 7.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15418v8)) Cf. [Numerical Stochastic Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Stochastic%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Mean-square calculus and uncertainty quantification.** Soong's 1973 monograph develops a chapter on stochastic limits and calculus in mean square before treating random ODEs, random initial conditions, random inhomogeneous parts and random coefficients. ([Crossref: chapter 4](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Stochastic+Limits+and+Calculus+in+Mean+Square&filter=prefix:10.1016&rows=5); [Crossref: chapters 5–8](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Soong+Random+Differential+Equations+in+Science+and+Engineering&rows=5)) In modern [Uncertainty Quantification](node:Uncertainty%20Quantification), uncertainty in dynamical systems with uncertain parameters is tracked by polynomial chaos expansions in polynomials orthogonal for the input distribution (Wiener 1938; Askey-scheme generalization by Xiu and Karniadakis 2002), which become expensive with many random variables. ([Wikipedia: Polynomial chaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_chaos))

### History
Doss (1977) and Sussmann (1978) gave the pathwise link between stochastic and ordinary differential equations. ([Milstein–Schoenmakers references](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1312.0876)) Soong's *Random Differential Equations in Science and Engineering* appeared in 1973. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Soong+Random+Differential+Equations+in+Science+and+Engineering&rows=5)) Ludwig Arnold's monograph *Random Dynamical Systems* was published by Springer in 1998. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-12878-7)) Pathwise numerical schemes for RODEs were developed by Grüne and Kloeden (2001) and Jentzen and Kloeden (2007, 2009). ([Jentzen–Kloeden](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~mrasmuss/peter/nelderlectures.pdf)) Han and Kloeden collected the theory in a 2017 Springer monograph. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-981-10-6265-0))

### Open problems
- **Higher-order RODE schemes under semimartingale noise.** Kloeden and Rosa state that it is unclear whether their order-one technique would improve the order of higher-order methods, and suggest, without proving, that it could extend to pathwise convergence for non-globally Lipschitz vector fields (at least for finite-variation noise) and to random PDEs. ([Kloeden–Rosa](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15418v8))
- **Statistics of random error constants.** For pathwise convergence of Itô–Taylor schemes for SDEs (order $\gamma-\epsilon$ for a scheme of strong order $\gamma$, Kloeden–Neuenkirch) the error constant depends on $\omega$; Jentzen and Kloeden note that little is known theoretically about its statistical properties and that it requires further investigation. ([Jentzen–Kloeden](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~mrasmuss/peter/nelderlectures.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Random dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_dynamical_system): cocycles, the Wiener shift, random attractors.
- **Learn:** [Jentzen and Kloeden, Taylor approximations of stochastic PDEs (CBMS lectures)](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~mrasmuss/peter/nelderlectures.pdf): Lecture 2 on RODEs, RODE–SDE equivalence and pathwise schemes.
- **Primary:** [Kloeden and Rosa, Strong order-one convergence of the Euler method for RODEs](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15418v8): current numerical theory with stated open directions.
- **Primary:** [Qiao and Duan, Topological equivalence for discontinuous random dynamical systems](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1210.0675): SDE–RODE conjugacy and random attractors.
- **Further reading:** [Han and Kloeden, Random Ordinary Differential Equations and Their Numerical Solution](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-981-10-6265-0): Springer Singapore, 2017, Probability Theory and Stochastic Modelling.
- **Further reading:** [Arnold, Random Dynamical Systems](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-12878-7): Springer Monographs in Mathematics, 1998.
references.MSC 34Gxx - Differential equations in ab:
## Reference
### Overview
34Gxx studies differential equations whose unknown takes values in an infinite-dimensional space, typically a Banach space $X$: $u'(t)=Au(t)+f(t,u(t))$ with $A$ an unbounded operator. The basic linear object is the abstract Cauchy problem $u'=Au$, $u(0)=x$; its classical solutions are $C^1$ with values in $D(A)$, and its mild solutions are continuous with $\int_0^tu\in D(A)$ and $A\int_0^tu(s)\,ds=u(t)-x$. For closed $A$, unique mild solvability for every $x$ is equivalent to $A$ generating a $C_0$-semigroup $T$, and then $u(t)=T(t)x$. ([Wikipedia: C0-semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C0-semigroup)) See [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), [Strongly Continuous Operator Semigroups](node:Strongly%20Continuous%20Operator%20Semigroups), and [Evolution Equations in Banach Spaces](node:Evolution%20Equations%20in%20Banach%20Spaces).

Two features distinguish this field from finite-dimensional ODE theory. First, differential operators such as the Laplacian are treated as generators on a function space, so that diffusion equations such as the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation) become abstract evolution equations, and generation is characterized by resolvent estimates and dissipativity, using tools from [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory). ([Schnaubelt, KIT lecture notes, ch. 1–2](https://iana.math.kit.edu/downloads/iana3/schnaubelt/Skripten/evgl-skript.pdf)) Second, compactness fails: Peano's existence theorem for continuous right-hand sides is false in every infinite-dimensional Banach space. ([Hájek–Johanis](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0911.4860))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Gxx (see also 34K30, 47Jxx, 58D25) lists: 34G10 linear differential equations in abstract spaces (see also 47D06, 47D09); 34G20 nonlinear differential equations in abstract spaces (see also 34K30, 47Jxx); 34G25 evolution inclusions; 34G99 none of the above. ([MSC2020 34Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Gxx))

Neighbouring codes: operator-theoretic semigroup theory is [47Dxx](node:MSC%2047Dxx%20-%20Groups%20and%20semigroups%20of%20linear%20operators,%20their%20generalizations%20and%20applications), where 47D06 is "one-parameter semigroups and linear evolution equations" and 47D09 covers cosine functions and higher-order Cauchy problems, both cross-referenced back to 34G10. ([MSC2020 47Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Dxx)) 34G focuses on the equation and its solutions; 47D on the operator families; abstract functional-differential equations go to 34K30 and nonlinear operator equations to [47Jxx](node:MSC%2047Jxx%20-%20Equations%20and%20inequalities%20involving%20nonlinear%20operators). ([MSC2020 34Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Gxx))

### Key concepts
- **Hille–Yosida theorem.** Let $M\ge1$, $\omega\in\mathbb R$. A linear operator $A$ generates a $C_0$-semigroup with $\|T(t)\|\le Me^{\omega t}$ iff $A$ is closed, densely defined, $(\omega,\infty)\subset\rho(A)$ and $\|R(\lambda,A)^n\|\le M(\lambda-\omega)^{-n}$ for all $n\in\mathbb N$, $\lambda>\omega$. ([Schnaubelt, Thm 1.26](https://iana.math.kit.edu/downloads/iana3/schnaubelt/Skripten/evgl-skript.pdf)) For contractions only $n=1$ is needed, $\|R(\lambda,A)\|\le1/\lambda$; the general case is the Feller–Miyadera–Phillips theorem. ([Wikipedia: Hille–Yosida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hille%E2%80%93Yosida_theorem))
- **Lumer–Phillips theorem.** A densely defined, dissipative $A$ for which $\lambda_0I-A$ is surjective for some $\lambda_0>0$ generates a contraction semigroup; conversely every contraction generator is dissipative with $\|R(\lambda,A)\|\le1/\operatorname{Re}\lambda$. ([Schnaubelt, Thm 1.39](https://iana.math.kit.edu/downloads/iana3/schnaubelt/Skripten/evgl-skript.pdf); [Wikipedia: Lumer–Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumer%E2%80%93Phillips_theorem))
- **Inhomogeneous problem and variation of constants.** If $A$ generates $T$ and $u$ solves $u'=Au+f$, $u(0)=u_0$, then Duhamel's formula
$$u(t)=T(t)u_0+\int_0^tT(t-s)f(s)\,ds$$
holds, so solutions are unique; this formula defines the mild solution for any $u_0\in X$, $f\in C(J,X)$. It is a classical solution if $u_0\in D(A)$ and either $f\in C^1(J,X)$ or $f\in C(J,[D(A)])$. ([Schnaubelt, Prop. 2.6, Thm 2.9, Def. 2.11](https://iana.math.kit.edu/downloads/iana3/schnaubelt/Skripten/evgl-skript.pdf))
- **Analytic semigroups and parabolic problems.** For a closed operator $A$ the following are equivalent: $A$ is densely defined and sectorial of angle $>\pi/2$; $A$ is densely defined, $\mathbb C_+\subset\rho(A)$ and $\|R(\lambda,A)\|\le C/|\lambda|$ there; $A$ generates a bounded analytic $C_0$-semigroup; then $T(t)X\subset D(A)$ and $\|AT(t)\|\le M/t$. ([Schnaubelt, Thm 2.25](https://iana.math.kit.edu/downloads/iana3/schnaubelt/Skripten/evgl-skript.pdf)) If $A-\omega I$ is densely defined and sectorial of angle $>\pi/2$ for some $\omega\in\mathbb R$, then for Hölder continuous $f\in C^\alpha([0,b],X)$, the mild solution is a classical solution on $(0,b]$; with only continuous $f$ this can fail. ([Schnaubelt, Thm 2.31, Rem. 2.32](https://iana.math.kit.edu/downloads/iana3/schnaubelt/Skripten/evgl-skript.pdf)) Example: $A=d^2/ds^2$ on $C([0,1])$ with Dirichlet conditions is sectorial of angle $\pi$ but not densely defined (the closure of its domain is $C_0(0,1)$); its part in $C_0(0,1)$ is densely defined and sectorial of angle $\pi$. ([Schnaubelt, Ex. 2.20](https://iana.math.kit.edu/downloads/iana3/schnaubelt/Skripten/evgl-skript.pdf)) Analytic semigroups give better regularity and link growth type to spectrum. ([Wikipedia: Analytic semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_semigroup))
- **Failure of Peano's theorem.** Dieudonné built a counterexample in $c_0$ (1950); Godunov proved that the strong form (a local solution through every initial point for continuous $f$) fails in every infinite-dimensional Banach space. Hájek and Johanis proved that if $X$ has an infinite-dimensional separable quotient, there is a continuous $f:X\to X$ such that $x'=f(x)$ has no solution on any interval. ([Hájek–Johanis, Thm 8](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0911.4860))
- **Nonlinear evolution: Crandall–Liggett.** An operator $A$ is accretive if $\langle y_1-y_2,j\rangle\ge0$ for $(x_i,y_i)\in A$ and $j$ in the normalized duality map of $x_1-x_2$; its resolvents $(I+\gamma A)^{-1}$ are then single-valued and nonexpansive, and $A$ is m-accretive if also $\operatorname{ran}(I+\gamma A)=X$ for all $\gamma>0$. For m-accretive $A$ on any Banach space, $S(t)x=\lim_n(I+\tfrac tnA)^{-n}x$ exists for $x\in\overline{\operatorname{dom}A}$ and defines a nonexpansive semigroup; in reflexive $X$, $S(t)x$ solves $u'\in-Au$ for $x\in\operatorname{dom}A$, but in general the inclusion need not be solvable. ([Pinto–Pischke, Thm 2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2301.06880))

### History
Hille and Yosida proved the generation theorem independently around 1948; the general case with bound $Me^{\omega t}$ is named the Feller–Miyadera–Phillips theorem. ([Wikipedia: Hille–Yosida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hille%E2%80%93Yosida_theorem)) Lumer and Phillips published the dissipative-operator characterization in *Pacific J. Math.* in 1961. ([Wikipedia: Lumer–Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumer%E2%80%93Phillips_theorem)) Crandall and Liggett's generation theorem for nonlinear semigroups appeared in the *American Journal of Mathematics* in 1971. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/2373376)) Godunov's theorem on the strong form of Peano's theorem appeared in 1975. ([Hájek–Johanis references](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0911.4860)) Pazy's *Semigroups of Linear Operators and Applications to Partial Differential Equations* (Springer, 1983) became a standard reference. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-5561-1))

### Open problems
- **Weak Peano theorem and the separable quotient problem.** The weak form of Peano's theorem (a solution on some interval) is known to fail in spaces with an infinite-dimensional separable quotient (Hájek–Johanis), in spaces with a complemented subspace having an unconditional basis (Shkarin), and in Banach spaces with a fundamental biorthogonal system (Barroso–Rebouças–Marrocos, who also show that infinite-dimensional Fréchet spaces with such a system have a nontrivial separable quotient). Whether every infinite-dimensional Banach space has an infinite-dimensional separable quotient is the Separable Quotient Problem, called "one of the outstanding problems of the Banach space theory" by Hájek and Johanis and "still open" by Barroso, Rebouças and Marrocos; by Hájek–Johanis Theorem 8, a positive answer would extend their result to all infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. ([Hájek–Johanis](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0911.4860); [Barroso–Rebouças–Marrocos](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1207.6777))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [C0-semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C0-semigroup): abstract Cauchy problem, classical and mild solutions, well-posedness.
- **Learn:** [Schnaubelt, Evolution Equations (KIT lecture notes)](https://iana.math.kit.edu/downloads/iana3/schnaubelt/Skripten/evgl-skript.pdf): generation theorems, inhomogeneous problem, analytic semigroups.
- **Primary:** [Hájek and Johanis, On Peano's theorem in Banach spaces](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0911.4860): failure of Peano's theorem in infinite dimensions.
- **Primary:** [Pinto and Pischke, On computational properties of Cauchy problems generated by accretive operators](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2301.06880): accretive operators and the Crandall–Liggett theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Pazy, Semigroups of Linear Operators and Applications to Partial Differential Equations](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-5561-1): Springer, Applied Mathematical Sciences, 1983.
references.MSC 34Hxx - Control problems including o:
## Reference
### Overview
A control system adds an input $u(t)$ to an ODE, $\dot x=f(t,x,u)$, and asks how the choice of $u$ shapes trajectories. In optimal control the unknown being optimized is a time-dependent function, and admissible controls are taken piecewise continuous, or more generally measurable and locally bounded, rather than smooth. ([Liberzon, §3.3](https://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf)) See [Feedback Control of ODEs](node:Feedback%20Control%20of%20ODEs) and [Controllability and Observability](node:Controllability%20and%20Observability).

Optimal control extends the [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations): Liberzon develops the Pontryagin maximum principle and the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation as two routes, with [dynamic programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming) leading to the HJB partial differential equation for the optimal cost, which yields a sufficient condition for optimality. ([Liberzon, ch. 4–5](https://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf)) See [Hamilton–Jacobi Equations](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Equations). Computation replaces the continuous trajectory by finitely many decision variables; direct transcription keeps sampled states and inputs as variables with the dynamics as constraints, direct shooting keeps only inputs and simulates the states, and for nonlinear dynamics the resulting programs are generally nonconvex, so solvers return local solutions. ([Tedrake, Trajectory Optimization](https://underactuated.mit.edu/trajopt.html))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Hxx (see also 49J15, 49K15, 93C15) lists: 34H05 control problems involving ODEs; 34H10 chaos control; 34H15 stabilization of solutions; 34H20 bifurcation control; 34H99 none of the above. ([MSC2020 34Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Hxx))

Neighbouring codes: optimality conditions for problems with ODEs are 49K15 in [49Kxx](node:MSC%2049Kxx%20-%20Optimality%20conditions) ([MSC2020 49Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=49Kxx)); controllability as system structure is 93B05 and geometric methods 93B27 in [93Bxx](node:MSC%2093Bxx%20-%20Controllability,%20observability,%20and%20system%20structure) ([MSC2020 93Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=93Bxx)); stabilization by feedback in systems theory is 93D15 in [93Dxx](node:MSC%2093Dxx%20-%20Stability%20of%20control%20systems) ([MSC2020 93Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=93Dxx)).

### Key concepts
- **Bolza problem.** Minimize $J(u)=K(t_f,x_f)+\int_{t_0}^{t_f}L(t,x,u)\,dt$ subject to $\dot x=f(t,x,u)$; $K\equiv0$ gives the Lagrange problem and $L\equiv0$ the Mayer problem, and the forms are interconvertible. ([Liberzon, §3.3](https://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf))
- **Pontryagin maximum principle.** For the fixed-endpoint, free-time problem with time-independent $f,L$ such that $f,f_x,L,L_x$ are continuous: if $u^*$ is optimal with trajectory $x^*$, there exist $p:[t_0,t_f]\to\mathbb R^n$ and $p_0^*\le0$ with $(p_0^*,p(t))\ne(0,0)$ such that, with $H(x,u,p,p_0)=\langle p,f(x,u)\rangle+p_0L(x,u)$, (1) $\dot x^*=H_p$, $\dot p=-H_x$; (2) $u\mapsto H(x^*(t),u,p(t),p_0^*)$ attains its global maximum over $U$ at $u^*(t)$ for every $t$; (3) $H\equiv0$ along the optimal pair. The case $p_0^*=0$ is abnormal. For variable endpoints on a surface $S_1$, $p(t_f)$ is orthogonal to $T_{x^*(t_f)}S_1$ (transversality). ([Liberzon, §4.1](https://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf); [Wikipedia: PMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin%27s_maximum_principle))
- **Existence of time-optimal controls.** For a linear system $\dot x=Ax+Bu$ with compact convex $U$, if $x_1$ is reachable from $x_0$ at some time, a time-optimal control exists (via closedness of reachable sets, Filippov's theorem). ([Liberzon, Thm 4.3](https://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf))
- **Controllability.** $\dot x=Ax+Bu$ is controllable iff $\operatorname{rank}[B,AB,\dots,A^{n-1}B]=n$ (Kalman rank condition); for time-varying systems a transfer from $x_0$ to $x_1$ is possible iff $x_0-\varphi(t_0,t_1)x_1$ lies in the range of the controllability Gramian. For control-affine $\dot x=f(x)+\sum g_i(x)u_i$, local accessibility holds where the distribution generated by the $g_i$ and iterated Lie brackets with $f$ spans $\mathbb R^n$. ([Wikipedia: Controllability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controllability)) For driftless systems the Chow–Rashevskii theorem gives the global statement: on a connected manifold with a bracket-generating distribution, any two points are joined by a horizontal path. ([Wikipedia: Chow–Rashevskii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow%E2%80%93Rashevskii_theorem))
- **Brockett's necessary condition (34H15).** For $\dot x=f(x,u)$ with $f\in C^1$, if a $C^1$ feedback $u(x)$ makes $x_0$ asymptotically stable, then the image of $(x,u)\mapsto f(x,u)$ contains a neighbourhood of $0$. The nonholonomic integrator $\dot x=u$, $\dot y=v$, $\dot z=yu-xv$ fails this, so it has no continuous feedback with unique trajectories that asymptotically stabilizes the origin, although it is controllable; Kvalheim and Koditschek generalize the condition to compact sets with nonzero Euler characteristic. ([Kvalheim–Koditschek](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2106.00215)) Cf. [Lyapunov Stability](node:Lyapunov%20Stability).
- **Chaos control (34H10).** The Ott–Grebogi–Yorke method exploits the unstable periodic orbits embedded in a chaotic attractor, keeping the system near a chosen orbit with small perturbations applied once per cycle on a Poincaré section, without needing a detailed model; Pyragas's method instead injects a continuous feedback signal whose intensity is practically zero while the system stays near the target orbit. ([Wikipedia: Control of chaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_of_chaos)) Cf. [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory) and [Bifurcation Theory](node:Bifurcation%20Theory).

### History
The maximum principle was formulated in 1956 by Pontryagin and his students, with maximizing a rocket's terminal speed as an early application. ([Wikipedia: PMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin%27s_maximum_principle)) Bellman coined the term "dynamic programming" and published a book on it in 1957; the connection with the Hamilton–Jacobi equation was made explicit in the early 1960s by Kalman, apparently the first to use the name "HJB equation". ([Liberzon, §5.1](https://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf)) Rashevskii (1938) and Chow (1939) proved the bracket-generating connectivity theorem independently. ([Wikipedia: Chow–Rashevskii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow%E2%80%93Rashevskii_theorem)) Brockett's condition provided a counterexample to what was, in 1983, an oft-repeated conjecture that local controllability implies the existence of a stabilizing control law. ([Kvalheim–Koditschek](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2106.00215))

### Open problems
- **Regularity of time-optimal trajectories.** For single-input systems $\dot q=f(q)+u\,g(q)$, $|u|\le1$, with $(f,g)$ a generic pair, optimal trajectories cannot all be smooth; Agrachev asks whether they are piecewise smooth, known for $n=2$ and open for $n=3$. He also notes that the opinion that accumulating switching points survive generic perturbations in higher dimensions "was never supported by a proof", and asks whether, for analytic systems, time-optimal trajectories with at most countably many switching points always exist. ([Agrachev, Some open problems](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.2590))
- **Morse–Sard for endpoint maps.** Whether the endpoint map of a control system always has regular values is stated as open, together with whether optimal singular curves from a point can fill a set of positive measure. ([Agrachev](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.2590))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Pontryagin's maximum principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin%27s_maximum_principle): statement, Hamiltonian, transversality.
- **Learn:** [Liberzon, Calculus of Variations and Optimal Control Theory](https://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf): Bolza problem, proof of the maximum principle, HJB.
- **Learn:** [Tedrake, Trajectory Optimization (MIT)](https://underactuated.mit.edu/trajopt.html): direct transcription, shooting, collocation.
- **Primary:** [Kvalheim and Koditschek, Necessary conditions for feedback stabilization and safety](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2106.00215): Brockett's condition and topological generalizations.
- **Primary:** [Agrachev, Some open problems](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1304.2590): open questions in geometric control.
- **Further reading:** [Sontag, Mathematical Control Theory](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0577-7): Springer, Texts in Applied Mathematics, 1998.
- **Further reading:** [Agrachev and Sachkov, Control Theory from the Geometric Viewpoint](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-06404-7): Springer, Encyclopaedia of Mathematical Sciences, 2004.
references.MSC 34Kxx - Functional-differential equa:
## Reference
### Overview
Functional-differential equations (FDEs) let the rate of change depend on the state at other times. The basic case is the retarded equation with constant delay, $\dot u(t)=f(t,u(t),u(t-\tau))$, $\tau>0$; variants have time-dependent delays $\tau(t)$, state-dependent delays $\tau(t,u(t))$, delays defined implicitly by threshold conditions such as $\int_{t-\tau}^tV(u(s))\,ds=a$, distributed delays, and neutral terms $\dot u(t-\tau_2)$. ([Humphries, NZMRI lecture 1](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~hinke/meetings/NZMRI/materials/NZMRI16-Tony1.pdf)) Because the right-hand side needs the past, an initial value problem needs an initial function on $[t_0-\tau,t_0]$, and the phase space is a space of functions, so even a scalar delay equation is an infinite-dimensional [dynamical system](node:Dynamical%20Systems). ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang, arXiv:2510.17126](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126))

The classical theory treats DDEs as retarded functional differential equations (RFDEs) $\dot u(t)=F(t,u_t)$, where $u_t(\theta)=u(t+\theta)$, $\theta\in[-\tau,0]$, developed in the books of Bellman and Cooke (1963), Hale (1977), Hale and Verduyn Lunel (1993) and Diekmann et al. (1995), the last with the sun-star calculus. ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126)) State-dependent delays are the subject of much current research. ([Humphries, NZMRI lecture 1](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~hinke/meetings/NZMRI/materials/NZMRI16-Tony1.pdf)) For them $F$ is not even Lipschitz on the space of continuous histories, which has greatly impeded the development of bifurcation theory. ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Kxx has some forty codes, which mirror the ODE sections for functional equations: general theory (34K05), linear equations (34K06), [spectral theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) of functional-differential operators (34K08), inclusions (34K09), boundary value problems (34K10), oscillation (34K11), periodic and almost periodic solutions (34K13, 34K14), homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits (34K16), normal forms (34K17), bifurcation (34K18, see also 37Gxx), invariant manifolds (34K19), stability (34K20), chaos (34K23), synchronization (34K24), asymptotics and perturbations (34K25–34K27), equations in abstract spaces (34K30), control (34K35), fractional derivatives (34K37), neutral equations (34K40), the complex domain (34K41), time scales (34K42), state-dependent arguments (34K43), impulses (34K45), stochastic equations (34K50, see also 34Fxx, 60Hxx), and models (34K60). ([MSC2020 34Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Kxx))

Neighbours named by the MSC entry: [MSC 34Gxx - Differential equations in abstract spaces](node:MSC%2034Gxx%20-%20Differential%20equations%20in%20abstract%20spaces) for 34K30, [MSC 37Gxx - Local and nonlocal bifurcation theory for dynamical systems](node:MSC%2037Gxx%20-%20Local%20and%20nonlocal%20bifurcation%20theory%20for%20dynamical%20systems) for 34K18, and [MSC 34Fxx - Ordinary differential equations and systems with randomness](node:MSC%2034Fxx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations%20and%20systems%20with%20randomness) for 34K50. ([MSC2020 34Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Kxx)) [Ordinary differential equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) without delay are in [MSC 34Axx - General theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations) and [MSC 34Cxx - Qualitative theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Cxx%20-%20Qualitative%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations).

### Key concepts
- **Phase space and well-posedness (34K05).** For constant delay the state is $u_t\in C([-\tau,0],\mathbb R^d)$, a [Banach space](node:Banach%20Spaces) of continuous functions, infinite-dimensional even when $d=1$. If the initial function $\varphi$ is Lipschitz and $f(t,u,v)$ is Lipschitz in its arguments, the IVP $u=\varphi$ on $[t_0-\tau,t_0]$ has a unique local solution, also in the state-dependent case. ([Humphries, NZMRI lecture 1](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~hinke/meetings/NZMRI/materials/NZMRI16-Tony1.pdf)) The method of steps solves a constant-delay equation as a sequence of ODE problems on $[t_0+k\tau,t_0+(k+1)\tau]$. ([Wikipedia: Delay differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delay_differential_equation))
- **Breaking points and smoothing.** Generically $\dot\varphi(t_0)\ne f(t_0,\varphi(t_0),\varphi(t_0-\tau))$, so $\dot u$ jumps at $t_0$ and $u^{(k+1)}$ is discontinuous at $t_0+k\tau$; the solution is $C^{k+1}$ for $t>t_0+k\tau$. Neutral equations do not smooth in this way. ([Humphries, NZMRI lecture 1](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~hinke/meetings/NZMRI/materials/NZMRI16-Tony1.pdf)) For analytic $f$, solutions on compact invariant sets are analytic when the delay is constant (Nussbaum, 1973), but may fail to be analytic with time- or state-dependent delays (Mallet-Paret and Nussbaum, 2014), while Krisztin (2014) proved analyticity for threshold delays with analytic $f$ and $V$. ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126))
- **Characteristic equation and infinite spectrum (34K06, 34K08, 34K20).** Linearizing $\dot u=f(u(t),u(t-\tau))$ at a steady state gives $\dot u=\mu u(t)+\sigma u(t-\tau)$ and the transcendental characteristic equation $\lambda-\mu-\sigma e^{-\tau\lambda}=0$; it has infinitely many roots, only finitely many to the right of any vertical line, all with $\Re\lambda<|\mu|+|\sigma|$. In $\mathbb R^d$ with several delays it reads $\det\big(\lambda I-A_0-\sum_jA_je^{-\lambda\tau_j}\big)=0$, and state-dependent equations are linearized by freezing the delays. ([Humphries, NZMRI lecture 1](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~hinke/meetings/NZMRI/materials/NZMRI16-Tony1.pdf)) For $\dot x=-x(t-1)$ the roots are $\lambda=W_k(-1)$, the branches of the Lambert $W$ function. ([Wikipedia: Delay differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delay_differential_equation)) RFDEs have a principle of linearized stability: a steady state is stable if all characteristic values have negative real part and unstable if one has positive real part. ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126))
- **Hopf bifurcation and Wright's equation (34K18, 34K13).** For $y'(t)=-\alpha y(t-1)[1+y(t)]$, Wright's conjecture says that for every $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2]$ the origin is the global attractor; van den Berg and Jaquette completed its proof by a close analysis near the Hopf bifurcation at $\alpha=\pi/2$, and showed that the branch of slowly oscillating periodic orbits born there has no folds or further bifurcations for $\alpha\in(\pi/2,\pi/2+6.830\times10^{-3}]$. ([van den Berg–Jaquette, arXiv:1704.00029](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.00029)) Hopf bifurcation theorems for state-dependent delays were proved only recently (Eichmann 2006; Hu and Wu 2010; Sieber 2012). ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126))
- **State-dependent delays and solution manifolds (34K43, 34K19).** Example: the sawtooth equation $\varepsilon\dot u(t)=-\gamma u(t)-\kappa u(t-a-cu(t))$ of Mallet-Paret and Nussbaum, where $\tau=a+cu(t)$. ([Humphries, NZMRI lecture 1](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~hinke/meetings/NZMRI/materials/NZMRI16-Tony1.pdf)) State-dependent equations generally define a semiflow of continuously differentiable solution operators only on an associated submanifold (the solution manifold) of $C^1([-h,0],\mathbb R^n)$; Walther extends a recent result on the simplicity of these solution manifolds to algebraic-delay systems, where the delay is given implicitly by an extra equation (MSC 34K43, 34K19, 34K05). ([Walther, arXiv:2310.12845](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12845))
- **Neutral and threshold equations (34K40, 34K43).** An equation is neutral if derivatives of delayed terms appear, $\dot u(t)=f(t,u(t),u(t-\tau_1),\dot u(t-\tau_2))$; Humphries calls these an ongoing research area. Wheeler–Feynman electrodynamics gives a neutral equation with both advanced and retarded terms and implicitly defined delays. ([Humphries, NZMRI lecture 1](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~hinke/meetings/NZMRI/materials/NZMRI16-Tony1.pdf))

### History
Humphries, Eremin and Wang trace the theory of RFDEs through Bellman and Cooke (1963), Hale (1977), Hale and Verduyn Lunel (1993) and Diekmann et al. (1995), and point to the 2006 review of Hartung et al. for the theoretical issues raised by state-dependent delays. ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126)) *Introduction to Functional Differential Equations* by Hale and Verduyn Lunel appeared in Springer's Applied Mathematical Sciences in 1993, and *Delay Equations* by Diekmann, Verduyn Lunel, van Gils and Walther in the same series in 1995. ([Crossref: Hale–Verduyn Lunel](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4342-7); [Crossref: Diekmann et al.](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4206-2)) That review is the chapter "Functional differential equations with state-dependent delays: theory and applications" of the 2006 *Handbook of Differential Equations: Ordinary Differential Equations*. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/S1874-5725%2806%2980009-X)) The proof of Wright's conjecture was posted in 2017. ([van den Berg–Jaquette](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.00029))

### Open problems
- **Codimension-two bifurcations with state-dependent delay (34K18, 34K43).** Humphries, Eremin and Wang note that numerical continuation (DDE-Biftool) detects codimension-two bifurcations for state-dependent DDEs for which there is still no complete theory, because the centre manifold has not been shown to be smooth enough; their double-Hopf normal-form computations work "without any rigourous theory", and they expect a proof to exist. ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang, arXiv:2510.17126](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126))
- **Numerical software for RFDEs.** The same chapter notes that there are not yet widely available reliable numerical implementations for general RFDEs or threshold delays. ([Humphries–Eremin–Wang](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.17126))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Delay differential equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delay_differential_equation): method of steps, characteristic equation, Lambert $W$ solutions.
- **Learn:** [Humphries, Delay Differential Equations, NZMRI 2016 lecture 1](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~hinke/meetings/NZMRI/materials/NZMRI16-Tony1.pdf): IVPs, phase space, breaking points, linearization, numerics.
- **Primary:** [Humphries, Eremin, Wang, Practicalities of state-dependent and threshold DDEs (arXiv:2510.17126)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17126): survey chapter on modelling, linearization, bifurcation and numerics.
- **Primary:** [van den Berg and Jaquette, A proof of Wright's conjecture (arXiv:1704.00029)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.00029): global dynamics of Wright's equation near the Hopf bifurcation.
- **Primary:** [Walther, On solution manifolds for algebraic-delay systems (arXiv:2310.12845)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12845): solution manifolds for implicit state-dependent delays.
- **Further reading:** [Hale and Verduyn Lunel, Introduction to Functional Differential Equations (Springer 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4342-7); [Diekmann, Verduyn Lunel, van Gils, Walther, Delay Equations (Springer 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4206-2).
