## Reference
### Overview
MSC 34L is the part of the ODE classification devoted to ordinary differential operators as operators: their spectra, eigenfunction expansions, eigenvalue bounds and asymptotics, scattering and inverse problems, and nonlinear and particular operators such as Dirac and one-dimensional Schrödinger operators. The section cross-references 47E05, the operator-theory code for ordinary differential operators. ([MSC2020, 34Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Lxx))

The prototype is the Sturm–Liouville expression $\tau y=r^{-1}\bigl(-(py')'+qy\bigr)$ acting in $L^2((a,b),r\,dx)$. On a compact interval with continuous coefficients, $p,r>0$, and separated boundary conditions, the problem is regular and the spectrum is a discrete sequence of simple eigenvalues whose eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis. ([Teschl, ODE §5.4](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) When an endpoint is singular (infinite, or a point where the coefficients degenerate), the research questions change: which boundary conditions are needed, what the spectral measure looks like, and how the coefficients can be recovered from spectral data. Weyl's 1910 work began this singular theory, and Titchmarsh and Kodaira later gave the spectral-measure formula and the eigenfunction expansion. ([Spectral theory of ODEs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_ordinary_differential_equations))

The modern viewpoint treats $\tau$ as generating self-adjoint operators in a Hilbert space and studies them through Weyl–Titchmarsh $m$-functions, Herglotz representations, and subordinacy theory. Teschl's text develops this route for one-dimensional Schrödinger operators, including a proof of the local Borg–Marchenko theorem. ([Teschl, Mathematical Methods in QM, ch. 9](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists these subdivisions ([MSC2020, 34Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Lxx)):
- 34L05 general spectral theory; 34L10 eigenfunctions, eigenfunction expansions and completeness;
- 34L15 eigenvalues, their estimation, and upper and lower bounds; 34L16 numerical approximation of eigenvalues and other parts of the spectrum;
- 34L20 asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues and asymptotic theory of eigenfunctions;
- 34L25 scattering theory and inverse scattering; 34L30 nonlinear ordinary differential operators;
- 34L40 particular operators (Dirac, one-dimensional Schrödinger, etc.).

Neighbouring codes: 34B (boundary value problems for ODEs) contains 34B24, Sturm–Liouville theory, which points to 34L, and the 34B header sends ordinary differential operators to 34L. 47E05 is the general theory of ordinary differential operators within operator theory; it cross-references 34B and 34L and must be paired with another 47 code. ([MSC2020, 34Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Lxx); [MSC2020, 34Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Bxx); [MSC2020, 47Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Regular spectral theorem** ([Sturm–Liouville Problems](node:Sturm–Liouville%20Problems)): for $\tau$ on a finite interval $[a,b]$ with real $p\in C^1$, $q,r\in C$, $p,r>0$, and separated real boundary conditions, the eigenvalues are real, simple, and accumulate only at $+\infty$, and the normalized eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis of $L^2([a,b],r\,dx)$. ([Teschl, ODE Thm. 5.11](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf); [Sturm–Liouville theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturm%E2%80%93Liouville_theory))
- **Oscillation and comparison (34L10, 34L15):** for a regular problem the eigenvalues can be ordered $E_0<E_1<\cdots$, and the eigenfunction $u_n$ has exactly $n$ zeros in $(a,b)$; the zeros of $u_{n+1}$ interlace those of $u_n$. Sturm's comparison theorem: if $p_1\le p_0$ and $\lambda_0r_0-q_0\le\lambda_1r_1-q_1$, then between suitable zeros of a solution $u_0$ of $L_0u_0=\lambda_0u_0$ a solution $u_1$ of $L_1u_1=\lambda_1u_1$ must vanish, unless the two are multiples. On $(0,\infty)$, Kneser's theorem says $-u''+qu$ is nonoscillatory if $\liminf x^2q(x)>-\tfrac14$ and oscillatory if $\limsup x^2q(x)<-\tfrac14$. ([Teschl, ODE Thms. 5.17, 5.20, 5.26, Lemma 5.21](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Weyl asymptotics (34L20):** if $pr\in C^1$, the eigenvalues of a regular problem satisfy $E_n=\pi^2\Bigl(\int_a^b\sqrt{r(t)/p(t)}\,dt\Bigr)^{-2}n^2+O(n)$. ([Teschl, ODE Thm. 5.25](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Weyl limit-point/limit-circle alternative (34L05):** $\tau$ is limit circle at an endpoint if and only if, for one $z_0\in\mathbb C$, every solution of $(\tau-z_0)u=0$ is square integrable near that endpoint; this then holds for all $z\in\mathbb C$. In the limit-point case exactly one solution (up to multiples) is square integrable there for nonreal $z$, and no boundary condition is imposed at that endpoint. For $-f''+qf$ with $q-a/x^2$ continuous at $0$, the endpoint $0$ is limit point if and only if $a\ge 3/4$. ([Teschl, QM Thm. 9.9](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf); [Spectral theory of ODEs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_ordinary_differential_equations))
- **Weyl–Titchmarsh $m$-function and spectral measure (34L05, 34L10):** with a regular endpoint $a$ and boundary condition fixed there, the Weyl function $m_b$ is a Herglotz function, $m_b(z)=d+\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\lambda-z}-\tfrac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^2}\bigr)\,d\mu(\lambda)$ with $d\in\mathbb R$, and the operator is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by $\lambda$ in $L^2(\mathbb R,d\mu)$. The Titchmarsh–Kodaira formula recovers $\mu$ from boundary values of $\operatorname{Im}m$ (a case of Stieltjes inversion), and the spectrum equals the support of $d\mu$. ([Teschl, QM Thm. 9.17](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf); [Spectral theory of ODEs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_ordinary_differential_equations))
- **Subordinacy (34L05, 34L40):** if $b$ is limit point, the set of $\lambda$ at which no solution of $\tau u=\lambda u$ is subordinate at $b$ is a minimal support for the absolutely continuous spectrum, so $\sigma_{ac}$ is its essential closure. ([Teschl, QM Thm. 9.27](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf))
- **Inverse spectral theory (34L25):** the local Borg–Marchenko theorem says that if two Schrödinger operators on $(a,b)$ are regular at $a$ with the same boundary condition there, then $q_0=q_1$ on $(a,c)$ exactly when their Weyl $m$-functions differ by an exponentially small amount (of an order fixed by $c$) as $z\to\infty$ along a nonreal ray. The global Borg–Marchenko theorem, that the $m$-function determines the potential, follows as a corollary. ([Teschl, QM Thm. 9.22](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf); [Gesztesy–Simon](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9910089)) Constructive recovery uses the Gelfand–Levitan equation $G(x,t)+F(x,t)+\int_0^xF(t,s)G(x,s)\,ds=0$ for $0<t<x$, where $F$ is built from the spectral data and $G$ is the transmutation kernel, with $G(x,x)=h+\tfrac12\int_0^xq(t)\,dt$; the potential and boundary data can be recovered from two spectra or from a spectral density function. ([Kravchenko–Torba, eqs. 2.11, 2.13](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2010.15275); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15275))
- **Singular boundary values:** when the minimal operator is bounded below, generalized boundary values at a singular endpoint are defined through principal and nonprincipal solutions. Gesztesy, Littlejohn and Nichols illustrate this with Bessel, Legendre and Kummer/Laguerre operators. ([Gesztesy–Littlejohn–Nichols](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.13117))

### History
Sturm and Liouville developed the compact-interval theory in the nineteenth century. Hermann Weyl's 1910 work extended it to singular endpoints through the limit-point/limit-circle analysis. Von Neumann's spectral theorem for unbounded self-adjoint operators (1920s) and Stone's 1932 work recast part of Weyl's results. Titchmarsh (book, 1946) and Kodaira (1949–1950) independently gave the spectral-measure formula; Kodaira also extended the method to singular equations of even order. ([Spectral theory of ODEs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_ordinary_differential_equations)) Marchenko proved the uniqueness theorem in 1950 using spectral measures, and Borg gave a proof in 1952 using Weyl–Titchmarsh functions. Simon obtained the local version in 1998, and Gesztesy and Simon gave a short proof and a matrix-valued extension. ([Gesztesy–Simon, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9910089))

### Open problems
- **Non-real eigenvalues of indefinite Sturm–Liouville operators.** When the weight $r$ changes sign, the operator is self-adjoint only in a Krein space and can have non-real eigenvalues. Behrndt, Chen, Philipp and Qi describe bounding the non-real spectrum in terms of the coefficients as "a challenging open problem" (citing Mingarelli and Kong–Möller–Wu–Zettl), and prove bounds for the regular case. ([Behrndt–Chen–Philipp–Qi, intro](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.0323); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.0323)) For singular indefinite operators with limit-point endpoints, Behrndt, Schmitz, Teschl and Trunk note that even rank-one perturbations can produce non-real eigenvalues accumulating towards the essential spectrum. They record as an open problem whether accumulation of discrete eigenvalues of the definite half-line operators at the edges of their essential spectra forces non-real eigenvalues of the indefinite operator to accumulate at edge points that fail a condition the authors call (P). ([Behrndt–Schmitz–Teschl–Trunk, §§1, 3](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/articles/PertIndSL.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Spectral theory of ordinary differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_ordinary_differential_equations): Weyl alternative, Titchmarsh–Kodaira formula, history.
- **Learn:** [Teschl, ODE and Dynamical Systems, ch. 5](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf): regular Sturm–Liouville problems, oscillation theory, Weyl asymptotics.
- **Primary:** [Gesztesy–Simon, On local Borg–Marchenko uniqueness results](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9910089): the local inverse spectral theorem and its matrix extension.
- **Further reading:** [Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics (AMS GSM 157, 2014)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/): graduate text whose chapter on one-dimensional Schrödinger operators covers Weyl theory, $m$-functions, subordinacy and inverse theory; its bibliography points to Coddington–Levinson, Levitan, Marchenko, Naimark and Zettl. ([Teschl, bibliographical notes](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf))

Related notes: [MSC 34 - Ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations), [Ordinary Differential Operators](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Operators), [Spectral Theory of Ordinary Differential Operators](node:Spectral%20Theory%20of%20Ordinary%20Differential%20Operators), [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory), [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem), [Mathematical Schrödinger Operators](node:Mathematical%20Schrödinger%20Operators), [MSC 47Exx - Ordinary differential operators](node:MSC%2047Exx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20operators), [MSC 34Bxx - Boundary value problems for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Bxx%20-%20Boundary%20value%20problems%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations), [Wave Operators and Scattering Matrices](node:Wave%20Operators%20and%20Scattering%20Matrices).
references.MSC 34Mxx - Ordinary differential equati:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 34M covers ordinary differential equations whose independent variable is complex: linear and nonlinear equations, entire and meromorphic solutions, formal solutions and summation, singularities and monodromy, Stokes phenomena, inverse problems of Riemann–Hilbert type, Painlevé equations and isomonodromic deformations. The section cross-references 30D (entire and meromorphic functions) and 32G34. ([MSC2020, 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Mxx))

The basic phenomenon is that analytic continuation of a local solution along different paths around a singular point can give different solutions. For a linear system $w'=A(z)w$ with $A$ analytic on a simply connected domain $\Omega$, every initial value problem has a unique solution on all of $\Omega$, so solutions can be singular only where the coefficients are. ([Teschl, ODE Thm. 4.7](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) Around an isolated singularity a fundamental matrix has the form $U(z)(z-z_0)^M$, so the local datum is a monodromy matrix; at irregular points, asymptotic solutions are valid only in sectors and are linked by Stokes multipliers. ([Teschl, ODE Thm. 4.8](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf); [DLMF §2.7](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.7)) The global questions run in two directions: compute the monodromy and connection data of a given equation (34M35, 34M40), or construct an equation with prescribed data (34M50). ([MSC2020, 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Mxx))

Nonlinear equations add movable singularities, whose position depends on the initial data. Equations whose movable singularities are only poles have the Painlevé property; among Painlevé's 50 canonical forms of second-order equations with this property, the six Painlevé equations are those not solvable by known functions, and they arise as isomonodromic deformations of linear equations. ([Painlevé transcendents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_transcendents); [Clarkson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.10122))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists ([MSC2020, 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Mxx)):
- 34M03 linear and 34M04 nonlinear equations and systems in the complex domain; 34M05 entire and meromorphic solutions; 34M10 oscillation and growth of solutions;
- 34M15 algebraic aspects (differential-algebraic, hypertranscendence, group-theoretical);
- 34M25 formal solutions and transform techniques; 34M30 asymptotics and summation methods;
- 34M35 singularities, monodromy, local behaviour of solutions, normal forms; 34M40 Stokes phenomena and connection problems (linear and nonlinear);
- 34M45 equations on complex manifolds; 34M46 spectral theory of ordinary differential operators in the complex domain;
- 34M50 inverse problems (Riemann–Hilbert, inverse differential Galois, etc.);
- 34M55 Painlevé and other special equations, classification, hierarchies; 34M56 isomonodromic deformations;
- 34M60 singular perturbation problems (complex WKB, turning points, steepest descent), with a see-also to 34E20; 34M65 topological structure of trajectories.

Neighbouring codes, per the entry's cross-references: 30D is the function-theory section on entire and meromorphic functions of one complex variable, while 34M05 classifies entire and meromorphic solutions of ODEs; 34E20 (in 34E, asymptotic theory of ODEs) covers singular perturbations, turning points and WKB methods in general, while 34M60 classifies these problems in the complex domain. ([MSC2020, 34Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Mxx); [MSC2020, 30Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Dxx); [MSC2020, 34Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Analytic Cauchy problem (34M03, 34M04):** if $f$ is analytic and bounded by $M$ on $\{|z-z_0|<\varepsilon,\ |w-w_0|<\delta\}$, then $w'=f(z,w)$, $w(z_0)=w_0$ has a unique analytic solution on the disc of radius $\min(\varepsilon,\delta/M)$, and this radius cannot be improved in general. With parameters, the solution is analytic in all variables. ([Teschl, ODE Thms. 4.1–4.2](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Regular singularities and Fuchs' theorem (34M35):** for $w''+f(z)w'+g(z)w=0$, a point $z_0$ is a regular singularity when $(z-z_0)f$ and $(z-z_0)^2g$ are analytic there; otherwise it is irregular, and if $f,g$ have at worst poles there, the rank is $\ell-1$ for the least $\ell$ making $(z-z_0)^\ell f$ and $(z-z_0)^{2\ell}g$ analytic. At a regular singularity, with $f(z)=\sum_{s\ge0}f_s(z-z_0)^{s-1}$ and $g(z)=\sum_{s\ge0}g_s(z-z_0)^{s-2}$, the indices solve $\alpha(\alpha-1)+f_0\alpha+g_0=0$. ([DLMF §2.7](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.7)) Fuchs' theorem (at $z_0=0$): if $f$ and $g$ have poles of order at most one and two, then for exponents with $\alpha_1-\alpha_2\notin\mathbb N_0$ there is a fundamental system $z^{\alpha_j}h_j(z)$ with $h_j$ analytic, and when $\alpha_1-\alpha_2=m\in\mathbb N_0$ the second solution may contain a $\log z$ term. Conversely, two solutions of this form exist only if $f$ and $zg$ have at most first-order poles. ([Teschl, ODE Thms. 4.5–4.6](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Local monodromy for systems:** if $A(z)$ is analytic on a punctured disc around $z_0$, a fundamental matrix has the form $W(z)=U(z)(z-z_0)^M$ with $U$ analytic on the punctured disc. If $A$ has at most a simple pole, $U$ extends analytically to $z_0$. The converse fails for systems: a regular singularity forces only a pole of $A$, of unrestricted order. ([Teschl, ODE Thms. 4.8–4.9, Lemma 4.10](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Irregular singularities, Stokes phenomenon and summation (34M25, 34M30, 34M40):** at a rank-one irregular singularity at $\infty$, there are formal solutions $e^{\lambda_jz}z^{\mu_j}\sum_s a_{s,j}z^{-s}$ that diverge unless they terminate, but are asymptotic to actual solutions only within sectors. ([DLMF §2.7](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.7)) Across a Stokes curve an exponentially small term can switch on or off; the Airy function has Stokes lines at arguments $0,\pm2\pi/3$. ([Stokes phenomenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokes_phenomenon)) The Borel sum $\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\,\mathcal BA(tz)\,dt$, with $\mathcal BA(t)=\sum a_kt^k/k!$, resums such series. ([Borel summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_summation)) Ramis developed $k$-summability, Écalle introduced multisummability, and any formal power series solution of a linear or nonlinear meromorphic system at an irregular singularity is multisummable (Braaksma; Ramis–Sibuya; Balser). Malgrange's Newton-polygon method finds the orders involved. ([Lastra–Sanz–Sendra, intro](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1603.00689)) Resurgence theory describes the Stokes automorphism through alien derivatives. ([Dorigoni](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.3585))
- **Riemann–Hilbert problem / Hilbert's 21st problem (34M50):** Hilbert asked whether every prescribed set of singular points and monodromy group comes from a linear differential equation of Fuchsian class. Plemelj (1908) showed every monodromy can be realized by a system with regular singularities that is Fuchsian at all but possibly one point. Bolibrukh's 1989 counterexample showed that the stronger Fuchsian-system claim fails in general, using a reducible monodromy group. Bolibrukh and Kostov (1992) proved that every irreducible representation is realized by a Fuchsian system, and Dekkers (1979) settled rank 2 positively. Deligne (1970) developed the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence for algebraic connections with regular singularities. ([Hilbert's 21st problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_twenty-first_problem); [Yakovenko §16.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0104140)) The scalar Riemann–Hilbert boundary problem for functions analytic on two sides of a curve is a different problem with the same name. ([Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem))
- **Differential Galois theory (34M15):** a Picard–Vessiot extension is generated by the solutions of a homogeneous linear equation without adding constants. It is Liouvillian (solvable by integrals, exponentials of integrals and algebraic functions) if and only if the identity component of its differential Galois group is solvable. Kovacic's algorithm (1986) decides whether a second-order homogeneous linear equation can be solved by quadratures. ([Picard–Vessiot theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Vessiot_theory))
- **Painlevé equations and isomonodromy (34M55, 34M56):** of the fifty canonical second-order equations with the Painlevé property, 44 reduce to known functions and six define new transcendents, e.g. $\mathrm{P_{II}}:\ y''=2y^3+ty+\alpha$. Richard Fuchs (1905) found $\mathrm{P_{VI}}$ from isomonodromic deformations of linear equations with regular singularities. Nishioka (1988) and Umemura (1989) proved that the six are irreducible for generic parameters. ([Painlevé transcendents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_transcendents)) The Painlevé equations are the compatibility conditions of Lax pairs and are solvable by the isomonodromy method through an associated Riemann–Hilbert problem. ([Clarkson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.10122))

### History
Picard (1883–1898) and Vessiot (1892–1904) developed the Galois theory of linear ODEs, and Kolchin made it rigorous in 1946–1948. ([Picard–Vessiot theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Vessiot_theory)) Stokes's 1847 and 1858 papers, the latter "On the discontinuity of arbitrary constants which appear in divergent developments", introduced the phenomenon now named after him. ([Stokes phenomenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokes_phenomenon)) Hilbert posed his 21st problem in 1900. Plemelj's 1908 solution was accepted for decades, until Il'yashenko and Treibich Kohn located a gap in the early 1980s and Bolibrukh gave his counterexample in 1989. ([Hilbert's 21st problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_twenty-first_problem)) Painlevé (1900, 1902) classified the equations with the Painlevé property, and Gambier completed the classification in 1910. ([Painlevé transcendents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_transcendents))

### Open problems
- **Painlevé equivalence problem.** Given a nonlinear ODE with the Painlevé property, there is no general method for deciding whether it can be solved by a Painlevé transcendent, and no symbolic software exists even to identify the equation. Clarkson lists this, together with numerical solution, notation for solutions, and classification of properties, as open problems for the Painlevé equations. ([Clarkson, Open problems for Painlevé equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.10122); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.10122))
- **Quantitative Riemann–Hilbert problem.** Yakovenko observes that what is missing from all the solvability results (Plemelj, Bolibrukh–Kostov, Bolibrukh's counterexamples) is any upper bound on the norms of the residue matrices of the constructed Fuchsian system. For his programme of uniform bounds on zeros of solutions, he states that the positive results would have to be redone constructively, yielding such bounds, and that obstructions to solvability have to be circumvented. ([Yakovenko, §§15–16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0104140); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104140))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hilbert's twenty-first problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_twenty-first_problem): the three readings of the problem and its resolution.
- **Learn:** [Teschl, ODE and Dynamical Systems, ch. 4](https://radon.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf): analytic existence, Frobenius method, Fuchs' theorems, systems with singularities.
- **Primary:** [Clarkson, Open Problems for Painlevé Equations (SIGMA 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.10122): survey of Painlevé theory and its open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Ilyashenko–Yakovenko, Lectures on Analytic Differential Equations (AMS GSM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/086): graduate text on local and global theory of analytic ODEs, monodromy and Riemann–Hilbert questions. Also [Yakovenko, Quantitative theory of ODEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104140): lecture notes on zeros of solutions and the quantitative Riemann–Hilbert problem.

Related notes: [MSC 34 - Ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations), [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations), [Monodromy of Complex Differential Equations](node:Monodromy%20of%20Complex%20Differential%20Equations), [Entire and Meromorphic Functions](node:Entire%20and%20Meromorphic%20Functions) (34M05), [Complex Manifolds](node:Complex%20Manifolds) (34M45), [Spectral Theory of Ordinary Differential Operators](node:Spectral%20Theory%20of%20Ordinary%20Differential%20Operators) and [Ordinary Differential Operators](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Operators) (34M46, via [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory)), [Lax Pairs](node:Lax%20Pairs) (Painlevé equations), [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), [Hypergeometric Functions](node:Hypergeometric%20Functions), [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory), [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces), [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions), [MSC 34Exx - Asymptotic theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Exx%20-%20Asymptotic%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations).
references.MSC 34Nxx - Dynamic equations on time sc:
## Reference
### Overview
Time-scale calculus unifies differential and difference equations by letting time range over a time scale $\mathbb T$, an arbitrary nonempty closed subset of $\mathbb R$: examples are $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb Z$, $h\mathbb Z$, $q^{\mathbb N_0}$, unions of intervals and discrete sets, and the Cantor set. The delta derivative reduces to the ordinary derivative on $\mathbb R$, the forward difference quotient on $h\mathbb Z$, and the Jackson $q$-derivative on $q^{\mathbb N_0}$; Stefan Hilger introduced the calculus to unify discrete and continuous analysis. ([Bohner–Guseinov, Appendix A and §5](https://web.mst.edu/~bohner/papers/thlaqlt.pdf)) Hilger also introduced dynamic ($\Delta$-differential) equations on time scales to unify and extend the theories of [ordinary differential equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) and [Difference Equations](node:Difference%20Equations), including $q$-difference equations. ([Bohner–Guseinov, Appendix A](https://web.mst.edu/~bohner/papers/thlaqlt.pdf)) Time-scale calculus is described as a unification of difference and differential equations, and population models that grow in season and die off or lie dormant in winter are a standard application. ([Wikipedia: Time-scale calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-scale_calculus)) See [Dynamic Equations on Time Scales](node:Dynamic%20Equations%20on%20Time%20Scales).

The measure-chain viewpoint makes the link with [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory) precise. The forward jump $\sigma$ is the distribution function of a Borel measure whose atoms sit at right-scattered points with mass equal to the graininess; the delta integral is the Lebesgue–Stieltjes integral for this measure, and the Hilger derivative coincides with a [Radon–Nikodym](node:Radon–Nikodym%20Theorem) derivative. ([Eckhardt–Teschl, §2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/articles/TimeScales.pdf); [Wikipedia: Time-scale calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-scale_calculus))

### Scope
MSC2020 34Nxx contains 34N05 dynamic equations on time scales or measure chains and 34N99 none of the above; both the heading and 34N05 note that real analysis on time scales is 26E70. ([MSC2020 34Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Nxx))

Neighbouring codes: 26E70 "real analysis on time scales or measure chains" in [26Exx](node:MSC%2026Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20real%20functions) holds the calculus itself (derivatives, integrals, inequalities) and points back to 34N05 for dynamic equations ([MSC2020 26Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=26Exx)); purely discrete equations are [39Axx](node:MSC%2039Axx%20-%20Difference%20equations), with $q$-difference ("scaling") equations in 39A13, and the 39Axx heading sends dynamic equations on time scales to 34N05. ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Jump operators and graininess.** $\sigma(t)=\inf\{s\in\mathbb T:s>t\}$ and $\rho(t)=\sup\{s\in\mathbb T:s<t\}$ (with $\sigma=\sup\mathbb T$ at a maximum); the graininess is $\mu(t)=\sigma(t)-t$, and $t$ is right-scattered if $\sigma(t)>t$, left-scattered if $\rho(t)<t$. There are at most countably many scattered points, and the associated measure satisfies $\sigma(\{t\})=\mu(t)$. ([Eckhardt–Teschl, (2.1)–(2.5)](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/articles/TimeScales.pdf))
- **Hilger derivative as Radon–Nikodym derivative.** If $f$ is delta differentiable on $\mathbb T^\kappa=\mathbb T\setminus\{\sup\mathbb T\}$ and its extension $\bar f$ to $\mathbb R$ is locally of [bounded variation](node:Bounded%20Variation), then the Radon–Nikodym derivative of $\bar f$ with respect to the measure of $\sigma$ coincides with the Hilger derivative at every point of $\mathbb T^\kappa$; consequently the theory of generalized differential equations with measure-valued coefficients (Mingarelli) contains differential equations on time scales as a special case. ([Eckhardt–Teschl, Thm 2.2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/articles/TimeScales.pdf)) Cf. [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration).
- **Exponential function and regressivity.** $p:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$ is regressive if $1+\mu(t)p(t)\ne0$; regressive rd-continuous functions form an abelian group under $p\oplus q=p+q+\mu pq$. For such $p$, $y^\Delta=p(t)y$, $y(t_0)=1$ has a unique solution $e_p(\cdot,t_0)$. On $h\mathbb Z$, $e_z(t,t_0)=(1+hz)^{(t-t_0)/h}$; on $q^{\mathbb N_0}$, with $\sigma(t)=qt$ and $\mu(t)=(q-1)t$, $e_z(q^n,q^m)=\prod_{k=m}^{n-1}(1+(q-1)q^kz)$. ([Bohner–Guseinov, §§2, 4, 5](https://web.mst.edu/~bohner/papers/thlaqlt.pdf))
- **Laplace transform on time scales.** A single Laplace transform, defined through the time-scale exponential, on any time scale with $\sup\mathbb T=\infty$ specializes to a modified $Z$-transform on $h\mathbb Z$ and to a new $q$-Laplace transform on $q^{\mathbb N_0}$, with shifting, convolution, uniqueness and inversion theorems. ([Bohner–Guseinov, §§3–5](https://web.mst.edu/~bohner/papers/thlaqlt.pdf)) Cf. [Laplace and Mellin Transforms](node:Laplace%20and%20Mellin%20Transforms).
- **Nabla and diamond-$\alpha$ derivatives.** The nabla derivative $f^\nabla$ uses $\rho$ in place of $\sigma$; where both exist, the diamond-$\alpha$ derivative $f^{\diamond_\alpha}=\alpha f^\Delta+(1-\alpha)f^\nabla$, $\alpha\in[0,1]$, introduced by Sheng, Fadag, Henderson and Davis, interpolates between them. It has no antiderivative in general, so it is not a dynamic derivative, although a diamond-$\alpha$ integral is defined. ([Mozyrska–Torres](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0902.1380))
- **Stability by linear approximation.** For $x^\Delta=A(t)x+f(t,x)$ on an unbounded time scale with $A$ bounded and uniformly regressive, if the central upper exponent of $x^\Delta=A(t)x$ is negative and $|f(t,x)|\le\varepsilon|x|$ with $\varepsilon$ small, the zero solution is asymptotically stable. For constant $A$, the condition $\limsup_{t}\bigl(|1+\mu(t)\lambda_k|^2-1\bigr)/\mu(t)<0$ for all eigenvalues gives stability via a quadratic Lyapunov function; a Chetaev-type instability theorem holds on syndetic time scales. ([Kryzhevich–Nazarov, Thms 4.4, 7.6, 7.12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.02272))
- **Oscillation theory.** Classical Kamenev, Philos and Li oscillation criteria for linear second-order equations such as $x''+q(t)x=0$ use integral averaging and Riccati transformations (the Euler equation $x''+\lambda t^{-2}x=0$ is oscillatory iff $\lambda>1/4$); on time scales, generalized Riccati transformations give oscillation criteria for second-order half-linear delay dynamic equations $\bigl(r(t)(x^\Delta(t))^\gamma\bigr)^\Delta+q(t)f(x(\tau(t)))=0$ with rd-continuous coefficients, $\gamma>0$ a quotient of odd positive integers and $\tau$ a strictly increasing delay, under hypotheses avoiding earlier restrictions such as $\gamma\ge1$ or $r^\Delta\ge0$. Cf. [Lyapunov Stability](node:Lyapunov%20Stability) for the continuous-time stability counterpart. ([EJDE 2016/71, Oscillation of solution to second-order half-linear delay dynamic equations on time scales](https://ejde.math.txstate.edu/Volumes/2016/71/wu.pdf))

### History
Hilger introduced the theory in 1988 (thesis listed as 1989); the idea of unifying sums and integrals goes back to the Riemann–Stieltjes integral. ([Wikipedia: Time-scale calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-scale_calculus)) His paper "Analysis on Measure Chains: A Unified Approach to Continuous and Discrete Calculus" appeared in *Results in Mathematics* 18 (1990), 18–56. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF03323153)) Bohner and Peterson's *Dynamic Equations on Time Scales* (Birkhäuser, 2001) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0201-1)) is among the Bohner–Peterson textbooks recommended, with Hilger's paper, as a general introduction. ([Bohner–Guseinov, Appendix A](https://web.mst.edu/~bohner/papers/thlaqlt.pdf)) The diamond-$\alpha$ derivative dates from 2006. ([Mozyrska–Torres](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0902.1380))

### Open problems
- **Characterizing $h$- and $q$-Laplace transforms.** No function has $h$- or $q$-Laplace transform identically $1$; Bohner and Guseinov call finding conditions that guarantee a given function is a Laplace transform "an important theoretical question" and state that for time scales such as $h\mathbb N_0$ and $q^{\mathbb N_0}$, unlike $\mathbb T=\mathbb R$, "this problem awaits its investigation". ([Bohner–Guseinov, Concluding remarks](https://web.mst.edu/~bohner/papers/thlaqlt.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Time-scale calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-scale_calculus): definitions, measure viewpoint, applications.
- **Learn:** [Bohner–Guseinov, The h-Laplace and q-Laplace transforms](https://web.mst.edu/~bohner/papers/thlaqlt.pdf): Appendix A gives a compact introduction; §5 works out $q$-calculus.
- **Primary:** [Eckhardt and Teschl, On the connection between the Hilger and Radon–Nikodym derivatives](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/articles/TimeScales.pdf): measure-chain foundations.
- **Primary:** [Kryzhevich and Nazarov, Stability by linear approximation for time scale dynamical systems](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.02272): Lyapunov-exponent stability theory.
- **Further reading:** [Bohner and Peterson, Dynamic Equations on Time Scales](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0201-1): Birkhäuser Boston, 2001.
- **Further reading:** [Hilger, Analysis on Measure Chains](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF03323153): Results in Mathematics 18 (1990), the founding paper.
references.MSC 35 - Partial differential equations:
## Reference
### Overview
A PDE in one unknown $u$ is an equation $F(u,\partial u,\dots,\partial^Nu,x)=0$ involving $u$ and its partial derivatives; $N$ is its order. It is linear if it can be written $Lu=f$ for a linear differential operator $L$, and solutions of $Lu=0$ then superpose. The basic questions are whether solutions exist, what data determine them, whether they are unique, whether they develop singularities, how they depend on the data, and in which norms to measure them. ([Speck, MIT 18.152 lecture 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/15e3e62a513bb3bdc5de09374f03517d_MIT18_152F11_lec_01.pdf)) These questions organize the whole of MSC 35, the general theory of [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations).

Hadamard stated the principle of well-posedness: a solution should exist for all suitable data, be uniquely determined by them, and depend stably on them in appropriate norms. ([Brezis–Browder, §10](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/154-J.pdf)) The three criteria were introduced in 1902, and the backward heat equation is the standard ill-posed example. ([Wikipedia: Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem)) See [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems). Hadamard also classified second-order operators by their characteristic polynomials into elliptic, hyperbolic and parabolic, generalizing the Laplace, wave and heat operators. This classification, later extended to higher order, nonlinear equations and systems, "provides the basic framework" in which PDE theory has been studied. ([Brezis–Browder, §10](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/154-J.pdf)) The prototypes are [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations), the [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation) and the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation).

### Scope
The sections of MSC2020 Section 35, grouped here by theme: ([MSC2020 35-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35-XX))
- **General theory:** [35A](node:MSC%2035Axx%20-%20General%20topics%20in%20partial%20differential%20equations) general topics; [35B](node:MSC%2035Bxx%20-%20Qualitative%20properties%20of%20solutions%20to%20partial%20differential%20equations) qualitative properties; [35C](node:MSC%2035Cxx%20-%20Representations%20of%20solutions%20to%20partial%20differential%20equations) representations of solutions; [35D](node:MSC%2035Dxx%20-%20Generalized%20solutions%20to%20partial%20differential%20equations) generalized (weak, strong, viscosity) solutions.
- **By structure:** [35E](node:MSC%2035Exx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20and%20systems%20of%20partial%20differential%20equations%20with%20constant%20coefficients) constant coefficients; [35F](node:MSC%2035Fxx%20-%20General%20first-order%20partial%20differential%20equations%20and%20systems%20of%20first-order%20partial%20differential%20equations) general first-order; [35G](node:MSC%2035Gxx%20-%20General%20higher-order%20partial%20differential%20equations%20and%20systems%20of%20higher-order%20partial%20differential%20equations) general higher-order.
- **By type:** [35H](node:MSC%2035Hxx%20-%20Close-to-elliptic%20equations) close-to-elliptic; [35J](node:MSC%2035Jxx%20-%20Elliptic%20equations%20and%20elliptic%20systems) elliptic (global analysis in 58J10, 58J20); [35K](node:MSC%2035Kxx%20-%20Parabolic%20equations%20and%20parabolic%20systems) parabolic (58J35); [35L](node:MSC%2035Lxx%20-%20Hyperbolic%20equations%20and%20hyperbolic%20systems) hyperbolic (58J45); [35M](node:MSC%2035Mxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20of%20mixed%20type%20and%20mixed-type%20systems%20of%20partial%20differential%20equations) mixed type; [35N](node:MSC%2035Nxx%20-%20Overdetermined%20problems%20for%20partial%20differential%20equations%20and%20systems%20of%20partial%20differential%20equations) overdetermined.
- **Other:** [35P](node:MSC%2035Pxx%20-%20Spectral%20theory%20and%20eigenvalue%20problems%20for%20partial%20differential%20equations) [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) and eigenvalue problems (operator theory in 47A, 47B, 47F05); [35Q](node:MSC%2035Qxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20of%20mathematical%20physics%20and%20other%20areas%20of%20application) equations of mathematical physics and applications; [35R](node:MSC%2035Rxx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20partial%20differential%20equations) miscellaneous topics (stochastic PDE in 60H15; equations on manifolds in 32W, 58J); [35S](node:MSC%2035Sxx%20-%20Pseudodifferential%20operators%20and%20other%20generalizations%20of%20partial%20differential%20operators) [pseudodifferential operators](node:Pseudodifferential%20Operators) (operator theory in 47G30, 58J40).

### Key concepts
- **Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem.** A quasilinear first-order system with analytic coefficients and analytic Cauchy data on a noncharacteristic hypersurface has a unique analytic solution near the hypersurface. Cauchy proved a special case in 1842, and Kovalevskaya the general result. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Kovalevskaya_theorem)) The theorem covers the Laplace equation, but there the domain of existence varies drastically with the data and solutions are unstable, so the Cauchy problem for Laplace is ill-posed in Hadamard's sense. ([Brezis–Browder, §10](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/154-J.pdf)) The restriction on the orders of the time derivatives cannot be dropped: for the heat equation with analytic data $1/(1+x^2)$ at $t=0$, the formal power-series solution diverges for every $t\ne0$, so no analytic solution exists near the origin. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Kovalevskaya_theorem))
- **Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem and Lewy's example.** Every nonzero linear differential operator $P(D)$ with constant coefficients has a fundamental solution $E$, with $P(D)E=\delta$ in the sense of distributions (Ehrenpreis 1954–55, Malgrange 1955–56). Hence $P(D)u=f$ is solvable for every compactly supported distribution $f$. ([Wikipedia: Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem)) For variable coefficients this fails: Lewy (1957) found a smooth $F$ such that $\partial_{\bar z}u-iz\,\partial_tu=F(t,z)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb C$ has no solution on any open set. ([Wikipedia: Lewy's example](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy%27s_example))
- **Sobolev spaces and embeddings.** $W^{m,p}(\Omega)$ consists of $L^p$ functions whose distributional derivatives up to order $m$ lie in $L^p$; Meyers and Serrin (1964) showed it equals the completion of smooth functions. For bounded smooth $\Omega$, $W^{m,p}\subset W^{j,r}$ with $\frac1r=\frac1p-\frac{m-j}n>0$, compactly for smaller exponents, and $W^{m,p}\subset C^{k,\alpha}$ when $m-n/p>0$ (with $k$ and $\alpha$ the integer and fractional parts of $m-n/p$, when that is not an integer). Sobolev introduced these spaces in the mid-1930s. ([Brezis–Browder, §12](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/154-J.pdf)) See [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces).
- **Distributions.** Schwartz's theory (1950) defines $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ as the dual of $C_c^\infty$. Every $L^1_{\rm loc}$ function is a distribution, every distribution has derivatives of all orders, and any linear differential operator with smooth coefficients acts on distributions. A fundamental solution of $L$ is a distribution $E$ with $LE=\delta_0$. ([Brezis–Browder, §13](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/154-J.pdf)) See [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29) and [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions).
- **Regularity: De Giorgi–Nash.** [Weak Solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) $v\in H^1$ of $\operatorname{div}(A(x)\nabla v)=0$ with measurable $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$ are Hölder continuous. This solved Hilbert's nineteenth problem on the regularity of minimizers of $\int L(\nabla w)$ for uniformly convex $L$. ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, Thms. 3.2, 3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564)) For systems the analogue fails, as De Giorgi's 1968 counterexample shows. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem))
- **Characteristics and hyperbolic propagation.** First-order equations reduce to [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) along characteristic curves. ([Speck, lecture 1, §6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/15e3e62a513bb3bdc5de09374f03517d_MIT18_152F11_lec_01.pdf)) Solutions of hyperbolic equations depend only on Cauchy data in a finite cone of dependence. In odd space dimensions the wave equation obeys Huygens' principle, depending only on data on the boundary of that cone. ([Brezis–Browder, §10](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/154-J.pdf)) Hadamard's conjecture that this persists in all odd dimensions for variable coefficients is not correct in general, though it holds for certain families of coefficients. ([Wikipedia: Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation))

### History
Brezis and Browder trace the classical paradigm PDEs to the 18th and early 19th centuries, and the method of majorants for analytic solutions to Cauchy's work begun in 1840. They place Hadamard's well-posedness principle in his 1923 book on the Cauchy problem, and identify Sobolev spaces (1930s) and Schwartz distributions (1950) as the twentieth-century foundations. ([Brezis–Browder, §§2–13](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/154-J.pdf)) De Giorgi and Nash solved Hilbert's nineteenth problem in 1956–58. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem))

### Open problems
- **Navier–Stokes global regularity (35Q30).** Whether smooth, finite-energy solutions of the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations exist for all time, or can break down, is a Clay Millennium Problem. Fefferman notes that the analogous problems "are also open and very important for the Euler equations." ([Fefferman, Clay](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf)) See [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations) and the 35Q map.
- **Regularity of fully nonlinear elliptic equations (35J60).** Whether viscosity solutions of uniformly elliptic $F(D^2u)=0$ in $\mathbb R^3$ or $\mathbb R^4$ are $C^2$ "is one of the most remarkable open problems in elliptic PDEs"; non-$C^2$ solutions exist for $n\ge5$. ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, §4.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564)) Further problems are listed in the 35F, 35G and 35J maps.

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Well-posed problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem): Hadamard's criteria.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 35-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35-XX): official list of sections and cross-references.
- **Learn:** [Speck, MIT 18.152 Introduction to PDE, lecture 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/15e3e62a513bb3bdc5de09374f03517d_MIT18_152F11_lec_01.pdf): basic notions and the questions of the theory.
- **Primary:** [Brezis, Browder, Partial Differential Equations in the 20th Century (Adv. Math. 1998)](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/154-J.pdf): historical survey of the field's ideas.
- **Further reading:** [Evans, Partial Differential Equations, AMS GSM 19 (2nd ed. 2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/019): standard graduate text.
- **Further reading:** [Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I (Springer Classics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2): distribution theory and [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) for linear PDE.
- **Further reading:** [Gilbarg, Trudinger, Elliptic PDE of Second Order (Springer Classics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61798-0): standard elliptic monograph.
references.MSC 35Axx - General topics in partial di:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35A collects the general questions of [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) that are not tied to one equation type: existence and non-existence (35A01), uniqueness (35A02), [fundamental solutions](node:Fundamental%20Solutions) (35A08), Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorems (35A10), parametrices (35A17), wave front sets (35A18), analyticity and singularities (35A20, 35A21), and microlocal and sheaf-theoretic methods (35A27). ([MSC2020 35Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Axx))

A basic notion is Hadamard's well-posedness (1902): a solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the data; the backward [heat equation](node:Heat%20Equation) is not well-posed, since its solution is highly sensitive to changes in the final data. ([Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem)) See [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems). Even existence can fail for a smooth linear equation (Lewy, 1957); Hörmander's geometric interpretation and generalization of Lewy's example (1960) opened the study of local solvability. ([Lewy's example](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy%27s_example); [Lerner, ICM 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0304335))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists: existence problems (global, local, non-existence) and uniqueness problems; fundamental solutions; classical solutions; Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorems; variational methods (35A15); topological and monotonicity methods (35A16); parametrices; wave front sets; analyticity; singularity; transform methods (35A22); inequalities involving derivatives and integral operators (35A23); ODE methods applied to PDEs (35A24); microlocal methods and methods of sheaf theory and [homological algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) (35A27, see also 32C38, 58J15); geometric theory, characteristics and transformations (35A30, see also 58J70, 58J72); and theoretical approximation (35A35; numerical analysis goes to 65Mxx, 65Nxx). ([MSC2020 35Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Axx))

Neighbours inside [MSC 35](node:MSC%2035%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations): equation-type sections such as 35J (elliptic equations and systems), 35K (parabolic) and 35L (hyperbolic); [35E](node:MSC%2035Exx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20and%20systems%20of%20partial%20differential%20equations%20with%20constant%20coefficients) for constant-coefficient equations; and [35S](node:MSC%2035Sxx%20-%20Pseudodifferential%20operators%20and%20other%20generalizations%20of%20partial%20differential%20operators) for pseudodifferential operators and other generalizations of differential operators. ([MSC2020 35-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35-XX)) The microlocal and geometric codes 35A27 and 35A30 cross-reference [58J](node:MSC%2058Jxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20on%20manifolds;%20differential%20operators) (58J15, 58J70, 58J72). ([MSC2020 35Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem (35A10).** For analytic $F$ and analytic data $f_j$, the problem $\partial_t^k h=F(x,t,\partial_t^j\partial_x^\alpha h)$ with $j<k$, $|\alpha|+j\le k$, and $\partial_t^j h(x,0)=f_j(x)$ for $0\le j<k$ has a unique analytic solution near the origin. The restriction $|\alpha|+j\le k$ cannot be dropped: for $\partial_t h=\partial_x^2 h$, $h(0,x)=1/(1+x^2)$, the unique formal power series solution converges for no $t\ne0$. Cauchy proved a special case in 1842 and Kovalevskaya the full result. ([Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Kovalevskaya_theorem))
- **Holmgren's uniqueness theorem (35A02).** Let $P=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}A_\alpha(x)\partial^\alpha$ have real-analytic coefficients on a connected open $\Omega$, split by an analytic hypersurface $\Sigma$ that is noncharacteristic for $P$ at every point into $\Omega_\pm$. If a distribution $u$ satisfies $Pu=0$ and $u=0$ on $\Omega_-$, then $u=0$ near $\Sigma$. Holmgren's paper dates from 1901. ([Holmgren's uniqueness theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmgren%27s_uniqueness_theorem))
- **Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem (35A08).** Every nonzero linear differential operator $P(\partial)$ with constant coefficients has a fundamental solution: there is a distribution $E$ with $P(\partial)E=\delta$. Hence $P(\partial)u=f$ is solvable for every compactly supported distribution $f$. Proved independently by Ehrenpreis (1954–55) and Malgrange (1955–56), non-constructively via Hahn–Banach. See [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions). ([Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem))
- **Lewy's example and local solvability (35A01).** For a suitable $F\in C^\infty$, the equation $\partial_{\bar z}u-iz\,\partial_t u=F(t,z)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb C$ has no solution on any open set (Lewy 1957), although it is solvable for analytic $F$; so Malgrange–Ehrenpreis fails for polynomial coefficients. ([Lewy's example](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy%27s_example)) For operators of principal type the answer is condition $(\Psi)$: $\operatorname{Im}(ap_m)$ does not change sign from $-$ to $+$ along the oriented bicharacteristics of $\operatorname{Re}(ap_m)$ for any nonzero smooth $a$. ([Dencker, Operators of subprincipal type](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.05594)) Hörmander showed $(\Psi)$ necessary (1981), and Dencker proved it sufficient, resolving the Nirenberg–Treves conjecture (Ann. of Math. 163 (2006)); his estimate loses two derivatives relative to the elliptic case. ([Lerner, ICM 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0304335); [Dencker 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0303201))
- **Wave front set (35A18).** For a [distribution](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29) $u$, $(x_0,\xi_0)\notin WF(u)$ if there are $\varphi\in C_c^\infty$ with $\varphi(x_0)\ne0$ and an open cone $\Gamma\ni\xi_0$ such that $|\widehat{\varphi u}(\xi)|\le C_N(1+|\xi|)^{-N}$ for all $N$ and $\xi\in\Gamma$. Its projection to the base is the singular support. Hörmander coined the term around 1970. ([Wavefront set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavefront_set)) For compactly supported $u$, Melrose takes as definition that $WF(u)$ is the intersection of the characteristic sets of all order-zero [pseudodifferential operators](node:Pseudodifferential%20Operators) $A$ with $Au\in C^\infty$, and shows its projection is again the singular support; and pseudodifferential operators are pseudolocal: $\operatorname{sing\,supp}(Au)\subseteq\operatorname{sing\,supp}(u)$. ([Melrose, Introduction to Microlocal Analysis, §§4.3, 4.7](https://math.mit.edu/~rbm/iml90.pdf))
- **Propagation of singularities (35A21, 35A27).** If $P$ is a properly supported pseudodifferential operator of order $m$ with real homogeneous principal symbol $p_m$ and $Pu=f$, then $WF(u)\setminus WF(f)\subseteq\operatorname{char}p_m$, and $WF(u)\setminus WF(f)$ is invariant under the Hamiltonian flow of $p_m$ (Duistermaat–Hörmander, 1972). ([Propagation of singularities theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propagation_of_singularities_theorem))

### History
Cauchy's 1842 special case and Kovalevskaya's general theorem made analytic Cauchy problems solvable, and Holmgren (1901) added uniqueness among non-analytic solutions. ([Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Kovalevskaya_theorem); [Holmgren's uniqueness theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmgren%27s_uniqueness_theorem)) Hadamard introduced well-posedness in 1902. ([Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem)) Ehrenpreis and Malgrange proved existence of fundamental solutions in the mid-1950s; Lewy's 1957 example and Hörmander's 1960 generalization opened the solvability problem, Nirenberg and Treves proposed condition $(\Psi)$, and the 1970s brought wave front sets and Fourier integral operators. ([Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem); [Lerner, ICM 2002](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0304335); [Propagation of singularities theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propagation_of_singularities_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Optimal loss of derivatives under condition $(\Psi)$.** Condition $(\Psi)$ does not imply local solvability with a loss of one derivative; Lerner (2006) reduced Dencker's loss to $3/2$ derivatives and wrote that "one should probably expect a loss of $1+\epsilon$ derivatives", which was not proven there; he also noted that for his counterexamples it seems, but has not been proven, that only a logarithmic loss occurs. ([Lerner, Cutting the loss of derivatives](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0512455))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wavefront set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavefront_set): definition and basic properties of the microlocal singularity set.
- **Learn:** [Melrose, Introduction to Microlocal Analysis (MIT lecture notes)](https://math.mit.edu/~rbm/iml90.pdf): [tempered distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions), pseudodifferential calculus, elliptic regularity, wavefront sets.
- **Primary:** [Dencker, The resolution of the Nirenberg–Treves conjecture, Ann. of Math. 163 (2006)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0303201): sufficiency of condition $(\Psi)$ for principal-type pseudodifferential operators.
- **Primary:** [Lerner, Solving pseudo-differential equations (ICM 2002)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0304335): survey of local solvability from Lewy to condition $(\Psi)$.
- **Further reading:** [Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I (Springer Classics, 2003)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2): distribution theory and [Fourier analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis).

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35B classifies results about how solutions of [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) behave, rather than about a particular equation type: maximum and comparison principles, a priori estimates and regularity, Liouville theorems, symmetry, blow-up, long-time asymptotics and attractors, stability and bifurcation, homogenization and singular perturbations, and unique continuation. ([MSC2020 35Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Bxx))

An example of a qualitative estimate that recovers regularity is De Giorgi's and Nash's Hölder estimate, which settled Hilbert's nineteenth problem on the regularity of minimizers in the [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations). ([Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem)) For the Navier–Stokes equations, a fundamental problem in analysis is to decide whether smooth, physically reasonable solutions exist for all time or blow up. ([Fefferman, Clay problem description](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf))

### Scope
- **Structure of solutions:** oscillation, zeros and mean value theorems (35B05); symmetries (35B06) and axially symmetric solutions (35B07); entire (35B08), positive (35B09), periodic (35B10) and almost periodic (35B15) solutions. ([MSC2020 35Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Bxx))
- **Perturbation and parameters:** perturbations (35B20), singular perturbations (35B25), homogenization and media with periodic structure (35B27), dependence on data and parameters (35B30), bifurcations (35B32), critical exponents (35B33), resonance (35B34), stability (35B35), pattern formation (35B36), critical points of energy functionals (35B38). ([MSC2020 35Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Bxx))
- **Long time and singularities:** asymptotic behaviour (35B40), attractors (35B41, see also 37L30), inertial manifolds (35B42), blow-up (35B44). ([MSC2020 35Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Bxx))
- **Estimates and principles:** a priori estimates (35B45), maximum principles (35B50), comparison principles (35B51), Liouville and Phragmén–Lindelöf theorems (35B53), continuation and prolongation of solutions (35B60), smoothness and regularity (35B65). ([MSC2020 35Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Bxx))

Neighbours: the equation-type sections of [MSC 35](node:MSC%2035%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations) (35J elliptic, 35K parabolic, 35L hyperbolic) ([MSC2020 35-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35-XX)); [35A](node:MSC%2035Axx%20-%20General%20topics%20in%20partial%20differential%20equations), which holds existence and uniqueness problems, [fundamental solutions](node:Fundamental%20Solutions) and microlocal methods ([MSC2020 35Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Axx)); and infinite-dimensional dissipative dynamics, [37L](node:MSC%2037Lxx%20-%20Infinite-dimensional%20dissipative%20dynamical%20systems), which the attractor and inertial-manifold codes cross-reference (37L30, 37L25). ([MSC2020 35Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Hopf lemma and the strong [maximum principle](node:Maximum%20Principle) (35B50).** Let $L=a_{ij}\partial_{ij}+b_i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on a bounded domain (connected open set) $\Omega$ with $c\le0$, $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^1(\bar\Omega)$, $Lu\ge0$, and suppose $u$ attains $\max_{\bar\Omega}u\ge0$ at $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, where $\Omega$ satisfies an interior ball condition. Then either $u$ is constant or $\partial u/\partial\nu(x_0)>0$. Zaremba proved the Laplacian case (1910); Hopf and Oleinik proved the general case independently (1952). ([Hopf lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_lemma))
- **Harnack inequality (35B45).** A nonnegative harmonic function on a domain $\Omega$ satisfies $\sup_\omega u\le C\inf_\omega u$ for $\omega\Subset\Omega$, with $C$ depending only on $\omega,\Omega$ (Harnack 1887); Serrin (1955) and Moser (1961) extended it to elliptic equations, and Moser (1964) proved a parabolic version comparing the supremum at an earlier time with the infimum at a later time on a compact set. ([Harnack's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harnack%27s_inequality)) See [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations).
- **De Giorgi–Nash–Moser regularity (35B65).** [Weak solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) $u\in W^{1,2}$ of $\partial_i(a_{ij}(x)\partial_j u)=0$ with strictly elliptic coefficients are Hölder continuous (De Giorgi 1956–57; Nash 1957–58 via the parabolic equation; Moser gave another proof). Applied to the differentiated Euler–Lagrange equation, this (with a Lipschitz estimate when needed) plus a Schauder bootstrap shows minimizers of $\int L(Dw)$ are smooth. It fails for systems: De Giorgi (1968) gave an elliptic system with bounded coefficients with a non-analytic solution. ([Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem)) The coefficients need no regularity: in the parabolic setting, a bounded measurable matrix $A$ with $0<\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$ suffices for interior Hölder continuity of weak solutions, and Moser's 1960 approach gave a further proof. ([Guerand, quantitative parabolic De Giorgi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1903.07421)) See [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces).
- **Symmetry by moving planes (35B06).** Gidas–Ni–Nirenberg: if $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is locally Lipschitz and $u\in C^2(B_1)\cap C^0(\bar B_1)$ solves $-\Delta u=f(u)$, $u>0$ in the unit ball $B_1\subset\mathbb R^n$ ($n\ge2$), $u=0$ on $\partial B_1$, then $u$ is radially symmetric and strictly decreasing in $|x|$. The moving-plane method was pioneered by Alexandrov for constant mean curvature hypersurfaces and adapted by Serrin to overdetermined problems. ([Ciraolo–Cozzi–Perugini–Pollastro](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2308.00409))
- **Fujita exponent and blow-up (35B33, 35B44).** For $u_t-\Delta u=|u|^p$ on $\mathbb R^N$ let $p_F=1+2/N$. For $p<p_F$ Fujita (1966) showed that no nonnegative global solution exists for nontrivial data, Hayakawa completed the critical case $p=p_F$, and for $p>p_F$ global solutions exist for small nonnegative data. ([Fino, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.13627)) This is a model for the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation) with a nonlinear source; the monograph of Quittner and Souplet treats blow-up, global existence and steady states. ([Quittner–Souplet](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-030-18222-9))
- **Unique continuation (35B60).** The weak property: a solution vanishing on an open subset vanishes everywhere; the strong property: a solution vanishing to infinite order at a point, $\lim_{r\to0}r^{-m}\int_{B_r(x_0)}u^2=0$ for all $m$, vanishes everywhere. Carleman estimates, based on first works of Carleman, were developed as a major tool for these problems, and counterexamples (including those of Pliś and Miller) show that the standard regularity assumptions, such as a Lipschitz metric, are essentially sharp for both weak and strong unique continuation. ([Rüland, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1801.05563))

### History
Harnack's inequality dates from 1887 and Zaremba's boundary-point lemma for the Laplacian from 1910; Hopf and Oleinik's general boundary-point lemma (1952) completed the classical maximum-principle theory. ([Harnack's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harnack%27s_inequality); [Hopf lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_lemma)) Bernstein (1904) had solved Hilbert's nineteenth problem for $C^3$ solutions of nonlinear elliptic analytic equations in two variables; De Giorgi and Nash removed that assumption in 1956–58, and counterexamples for systems followed in 1968 (De Giorgi; Giusti–Miranda; Maz'ya for higher-order equations). ([Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem)) Fujita's blow-up theorem appeared in 1966. ([Fino, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.13627))

### Open problems
- **Global regularity versus blow-up for 3D Navier–Stokes (35B44, 35B65).** For $\nu>0$ on $\mathbb R^3$, prove that every smooth divergence-free $u_0$ with $|\partial^\alpha u_0(x)|\le C_{\alpha K}(1+|x|)^{-K}$ yields a smooth bounded-energy solution for all time, or exhibit breakdown. Global smooth solutions are known in two dimensions (Ladyzhenskaya) and in three dimensions for small data, and local smooth solutions exist up to a maximal "blowup time", near which the velocity becomes unbounded if it is finite. Fefferman notes the same questions are open for the Euler equations. ([Fefferman, Clay problem description](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf)) The Clay Institute's problem page says that for many decades no proof was found answering whether solutions exist and are unique. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/)) See [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hopf lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_lemma): boundary-point lemma, hypotheses and history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.152 lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/pages/lecture-notes/): weak maximum principle for the heat equation, Harnack's inequality and Liouville's theorem for Poisson's equation, energy estimates for the [wave equation](node:Wave%20Equation).
- **Primary:** [Ciraolo, Cozzi, Perugini and Pollastro, A quantitative version of the Gidas–Ni–Nirenberg theorem (arXiv 2308.00409)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00409): current research on symmetry and its stability.
- **Primary:** [Quittner and Souplet, Superlinear Parabolic Problems (Birkhäuser, 2019)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-030-18222-9): monograph on blow-up, global existence and steady states.
- **Further reading:** [Gilbarg and Trudinger, Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order (Springer Classics, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61798-0): monograph on second-order elliptic equations.
references.MSC 35Cxx - Representations of solutions:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35C classifies explicit and structured representations of solutions of [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): closed forms, self-similar and traveling-wave solutions, solitons, trigonometric, series and polynomial solutions, integral representations, and asymptotic expansions. ([MSC2020 35Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Cxx))

Three mechanisms recur. For linear equations, a Green's function $G$ with $LG(x,s)=\delta(s-x)$ turns $Lu=f$ into $u(x)=\int G(x,s)f(s)\,ds$ whenever the integral converges. ([Green's function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_function)) For nonlinear equations, symmetry reduces the PDE to an ODE: a self-similar ansatz exploits the absence of an intrinsic length or time scale, and a traveling-wave ansatz $u(x,t)=v(x-ct)$ looks for a fixed profile moving at constant speed $c$. ([Self-similar solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-similar_solution); [Fisher's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher%27s_equation)) Integrable equations such as KdV add a third mechanism, the inverse scattering transform. ([Korteweg–De Vries equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation))

### Scope
- **35C05** solutions in closed form; **35C06** self-similar solutions; **35C07** traveling wave solutions; **35C08** soliton solutions (see also 37K40); **35C09** trigonometric solutions. ([MSC2020 35Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Cxx))
- **35C10** series solutions; **35C11** polynomial solutions; **35C15** integral representations; **35C20** asymptotic expansions of solutions. ([MSC2020 35Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Cxx))

Neighbours: soliton solutions (35C08) cross-reference 37K40 ([37K](node:MSC%2037Kxx%20-%20Dynamical%20system%20aspects%20of%20infinite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems)) ([MSC2020 35Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Cxx)); [fundamental solutions](node:Fundamental%20Solutions) have their own code, [35A08](node:MSC%2035Axx%20-%20General%20topics%20in%20partial%20differential%20equations) ([MSC2020 35Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Axx)); stability, asymptotic behaviour and blow-up of solutions are classified in [35B](node:MSC%2035Bxx%20-%20Qualitative%20properties%20of%20solutions%20to%20partial%20differential%20equations) (35B35, 35B40, 35B44). ([MSC2020 35Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Poisson kernel (35C15).** For the ball $B_r\subset\mathbb R^n$ and $\zeta\in\partial B_r$, $P(x,\zeta)=\dfrac{r^2-|x|^2}{r\,\omega_{n-1}|x-\zeta|^n}$, with $\omega_{n-1}$ the area of the unit sphere. For continuous $u$ on $\partial B_r$, $P[u](x)=\int_{\partial B_r}u(\zeta)P(x,\zeta)\,d\sigma(\zeta)$ is harmonic in the ball, extends continuously to the closed ball, and equals $u$ on the boundary, so it solves the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem). On the upper half-space $\{(x,t):x\in\mathbb R^n,\ t>0\}$ the kernel is $c_n\,t/(t^2+|x|^2)^{(n+1)/2}$ with $c_n=\Gamma(\tfrac{n+1}2)/\pi^{(n+1)/2}$. ([Poisson kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_kernel)) See [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations) and [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions).
- **Heat kernel and eigenfunction series (35C15, 35C10).** On $\mathbb R^d$, $K(t,x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}$ solves the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation) with initial datum $\delta(x-y)$. For the Dirichlet Laplacian on a bounded domain with orthonormal eigenfunctions $\varphi_n$ and eigenvalues $0<\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots$, $K(t,x,y)=\sum_n e^{-\lambda_n t}\varphi_n(x)\varphi_n(y)$, the separation-of-variables series; convergence and regularity of the series are delicate. ([Heat kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_kernel))
- **Self-similar solutions (35C06).** A solution is self-similar if it is unchanged after suitable rescaling of independent and dependent variables; when a problem has no characteristic scale, an ansatz $T=f(\eta)$ in a similarity variable reduces the PDE to an ODE. For the heat equation on a half-line with constant surface temperature the solution is an error function of $x/(2\sqrt{\alpha t})$, and Rayleigh's moving-wall problem gives $u=U\bigl(1-\operatorname{erf}(y/(4\nu t)^{1/2})\bigr)$. Self-similar solutions "of the second kind" cannot be obtained from dimensional analysis. ([Self-similar solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-similar_solution))
- **Traveling waves (35C07).** For the Fisher–KPP equation $u_t-Du_{xx}=ru(1-u)$, monotone fronts $u=v(x\pm ct)$ connecting $0$ and $1$ exist exactly for $c\ge2\sqrt{rD}$; for a general KPP nonlinearity $F$ (in dimensionless form) the minimal speed is $2\sqrt{F'(0)}$. Fisher proposed the equation in 1937, and Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov introduced a more general form the same year. ([Fisher's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher%27s_equation))
- **Solitons and inverse scattering (35C08).** The KdV equation $\phi_t+\phi_{xxx}-6\phi\phi_x=0$ has the one-soliton solution $\phi=-\tfrac c2\operatorname{sech}^2\!\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt c}{2}(x-ct-a)\bigr)$. It is the compatibility condition $L_t=[L,A]$ of a Lax pair with the Sturm–Liouville operator $L=-\partial_x^2+\phi$, so the spectrum of $L$ is conserved and there are infinitely many conserved quantities; Gardner, Greene, Kruskal and Miura (1967) solved it by the inverse scattering transform. ([Korteweg–De Vries equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation); [GGKM 1967](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095))
- **Asymptotic (WKB) expansions (35C20).** For an equation whose highest derivative carries a small parameter, the ansatz $y\sim\exp\bigl[\delta^{-1}\sum_n\delta^nS_n\bigr]$ gives at leading order an eikonal equation and at next order an equation for the correction $S_1$; for the [Schrödinger Equation](node:Schrödinger%20Equation) with $\Psi=e^{iS/\hbar}$ these are $(\nabla S_0)^2=2m(E-V)$ and $2\nabla S_0\cdot\nabla S_1-i\nabla^2S_0=0$, singular at turning points $E=V$. ([WKB approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WKB_approximation))

### History
Green introduced his function in an 1828 essay on electricity and magnetism. ([Green's function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_function)) Liouville and Green (1837) used methods equivalent to WKB, Jeffreys gave a general approach in 1923, and Wentzel, Kramers and Brillouin developed it for quantum mechanics in 1926. ([WKB approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WKB_approximation)) Fisher and Kolmogorov–Petrovsky–Piskunov published their papers on the equation in 1937. ([Fisher's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher%27s_equation)) Zabusky and Kruskal's 1965 computations showed KdV solutions decomposing into solitons that pass through each other nearly unchanged, and the inverse scattering solution followed in 1967. ([Korteweg–De Vries equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation))

### Open problems
- **Soliton resolution for non-radial data (35C08, 35B40).** For the focusing energy-critical wave equation, the soliton resolution conjecture predicts that every global (or type II blow-up) solution decomposes into a sum of decoupled solitary waves, a linear free wave, and a small error. Duyckaerts, Kenig and Merle proved the radial case in three dimensions, and resolution along a sequence of times has also been proved; "the non-radial case of soliton resolution conjecture, however, is still an open problem." ([Shen, arXiv 2507.00391](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00391))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Green's function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_function): definition, integral representation of solutions, and Green's identities.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.152 lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/pages/lecture-notes/): the fundamental solution of the heat equation, Poisson's formula, and spherical means for the [wave equation](node:Wave%20Equation).
- **Primary:** [Gardner, Greene, Kruskal and Miura, Method for solving the Korteweg–de Vries equation, Phys. Rev. Lett. 19 (1967) 1095–1097](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095): the inverse scattering transform.
- **Primary:** [Shen, Dynamics of 3D focusing, energy-critical wave equation with radial data (arXiv 2507.00391)](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00391): current work on soliton resolution.
- **Further reading:** [Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed. (AMS GSM 19, 2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/019): graduate text.
