## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35D classifies notions of solution for [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) that do not require a classical (pointwise, sufficiently differentiable) solution. It has three codes: [weak solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) (35D30), strong solutions (35D35) and viscosity solutions (35D40). ([MSC2020 35Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Dxx))

Generalized solutions matter because many models have no smooth solutions, and existence is often proved first in a weak sense, with smoothness established afterwards. Different equation classes need different notions: distributional weak solutions suit linear and divergence-form problems; for hyperbolic systems weak solutions may be non-unique, so entropy conditions are added; for fully nonlinear equations such as [Hamilton–Jacobi Equations](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Equations), viscosity solutions are used instead. ([Weak solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_solution)) Uniqueness, and hence [well-posedness](node:Well-Posed%20Problems), depends on the class: for the transport equation, whether weak solutions are unique depends on the integrability exponents of the solution and of the vector field's derivative. ([Cheskidov–Luo](https://arxiv.org/html/2004.09538))

### Scope
- **35D30 Weak solutions.** Entropy solutions, for example, are weak solutions that satisfy additional entropy inequalities, which select the physically admissible weak solution. ([MSC2020 35Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Dxx); [Hashash](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.14565v2))
- **35D35 Strong solutions.** MIT's graduate course 18.156 studies elliptic equations with variable coefficients, building up to the minimal surface equation, and covers the Calderón–Zygmund inequality for the Laplacian. ([MSC2020 35Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Dxx); [MIT 18.156](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-ii-partial-differential-equations-and-fourier-analysis-spring-2016/))
- **35D40 Viscosity solutions:** continuous solutions of fully nonlinear degenerate elliptic equations defined by touching with smooth test functions. ([MSC2020 35Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Dxx); [Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution))

Related maps: [46F](node:MSC%2046Fxx%20-%20Distributions,%20generalized%20functions,%20distribution%20spaces) (distribution spaces), [35B](node:MSC%2035Bxx%20-%20Qualitative%20properties%20of%20solutions%20to%20partial%20differential%20equations) (regularity and other qualitative properties), [35A](node:MSC%2035Axx%20-%20General%20topics%20in%20partial%20differential%20equations) (existence and uniqueness), [49L](node:MSC%2049Lxx%20-%20Hamilton-Jacobi%20theories) (Hamilton–Jacobi theories, for which Crandall and Lions introduced viscosity solutions). ([MSC2020 35Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Axx); [MSC2020 35Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?btn=Current&t=35Bxx); [Weak solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_solution); [Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution))

### Key concepts
- **Distributional weak solution (35D30).** For a linear operator $P(x,\partial)$ with formal adjoint $Q$, an integrable $u$ is a weak solution of $Pu=0$ if $\int u\,Q(x,\partial)\varphi\,dx=0$ for every smooth compactly supported $\varphi$. Example: $u(t,x)=|t-x|$ is not differentiable on $t=x$, yet is a weak solution of $u_t+u_x=0$. ([Weak solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_solution)) See [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29).
- **Lax–Milgram theorem.** If $a$ is a bilinear form on a real Hilbert space $V$ that is bounded, $|a(u,v)|\le C\|u\|\|v\|$, and coercive, $a(u,u)\ge c\|u\|^2$ with $c>0$, then for every $f\in V'$ there is a unique $u\in V$ with $a(u,v)=f(v)$ for all $v\in V$, and $\|u\|\le\|f\|_{V'}/c$ (Lax and Milgram, 1954). For the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem) $-\Delta u=f$ in $\Omega$, $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, take $V=H^1_0(\Omega)$ normed by $\|\nabla v\|$ (valid by the Poincaré inequality) and $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v$; this gives a unique weak solution with $\|\nabla u\|\le\|f\|_{H^{-1}}$. ([Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem)) See [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) and [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations).
- **Viscosity solutions (35D40).** $F(x,u,p,X)$ is degenerate elliptic if $F(x,u,p,X)\ge F(x,u,p,Y)$ whenever $Y-X$ is positive definite. An upper semicontinuous $u$ is a subsolution of $F(x,u,Du,D^2u)=0$ if $F(x_0,\varphi(x_0),D\varphi(x_0),D^2\varphi(x_0))\le0$ whenever a $C^2$ function $\varphi$ touches $u$ from above at $x_0$; supersolutions are defined with touching from below and $\ge0$; a viscosity solution is a continuous function that is both. Uniqueness follows from comparison principles, and locally uniform limits of solutions are solutions. For $|u'|=1$ on $(-1,1)$, $u(\pm1)=0$, the viscosity solution is $1-|x|$, the $\varepsilon\to0$ limit of solutions of $|u'|^2-1=\varepsilon u''$. ([Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution)) Crandall, Ishii and Lions give a self-contained account of comparison, existence and continuous dependence for fully nonlinear second-order equations. ([Crandall–Ishii–Lions](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207212))
- **Entropy solutions of a scalar conservation law.** For $\partial_t u+\operatorname{div}f(u)=0$ on $\mathbb R^d\times(0,\infty)$, entropy solutions are weak solutions satisfying entropy inequalities for entropy pairs $(\eta,q)$, including Kruzhkov's $\eta=|u-k|$. Kruzhkov proved, by doubling of variables, that entropy solutions are $L^1$-contractive, which yields uniqueness of the entropy solution (not of arbitrary weak solutions), assuming the flux is continuously differentiable with spatial derivatives Lipschitz in the unknown. ([Hashash](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.14565v2))
- **Renormalized solutions of transport equations (DiPerna–Lions).** Let $u\in L^1(0,T;W^{1,q}(\mathbb T^d))$ be divergence-free and $\rho_0\in L^p$. Then $\partial_t\rho+u\cdot\nabla\rho=0$ has a unique renormalized solution, and if $1/p+1/q\le1$ it is unique among all weak solutions in $L^\infty(0,T;L^p)$. Cheskidov and Luo showed this is sharp: for $d\ge3$, $p>1$ and $1/p+1/q>1$, uniqueness fails in $L^1(0,T;L^p)$. ([Cheskidov–Luo](https://arxiv.org/html/2004.09538)) The Lagrangian side of the theory concerns flows of [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) with [Sobolev](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) vector fields, whose regular Lagrangian flow is unique. ([Cheskidov–Luo](https://arxiv.org/html/2004.09538))

### History
Lax and Milgram published their theorem in 1954. ([Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem)) Evans gave an early definition of viscosity solutions in 1980; Crandall and Lions named them in 1983 for Hamilton–Jacobi equations, Crandall, Evans and Lions refined the theory in 1984, and Jensen's 1988 comparison principle opened the second-order theory, with Ishii's work on Perron's method (1987) and fully nonlinear equations (1989). ([Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution)) The Crandall–Ishii–Lions survey appeared in 1992. ([Crandall–Ishii–Lions](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207212))

### Open problems
- **Smoothness of viscosity solutions in dimensions three and four.** Let $F:\mathrm{Sym}(n)\to\mathbb R$ be uniformly elliptic, $\lambda\operatorname{tr}N\le F(M+N)-F(M)\le\Lambda\operatorname{tr}N$ for $N\ge0$. Does every continuous viscosity solution of $F(D^2u)=0$ in the unit ball have empty singular set (that is, is $u$ $C^2$ near every point)? The answer is yes in two dimensions (Nirenberg) and no in dimensions five and higher (Nadirashvili–Tkachev–Vlăduţ), and the question "remains open in dimensions three and four." The same 2026 preprint calls it an important open problem whether the Armstrong–Silvestre–Smart bound $n-\varepsilon$ on the Hausdorff dimension of the singular set holds without their $C^1$ assumption on $F$, and reports a negative answer in dimensions five and higher; this is a recent, not yet refereed claim. ([Chu, arXiv 2608.18217](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.18217))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution): definitions, comparison, stability and history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.156 Differential Analysis II (OCW)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-ii-partial-differential-equations-and-fourier-analysis-spring-2016/): graduate course on elliptic equations with variable coefficients, up to the minimal surface equation, including the Calderón–Zygmund inequality.
- **Primary:** [Crandall, Ishii and Lions, User's guide to viscosity solutions of second order PDEs, Bull. AMS 27 (1992) 1–67](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207212): the standard survey of the viscosity theory.
- **Primary:** [Cheskidov and Luo, Nonuniqueness of weak solutions for the transport equation at critical space regularity (arXiv 2004.09538)](https://arxiv.org/html/2004.09538): sharpness of DiPerna–Lions uniqueness.
- **Further reading:** [Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed. (AMS GSM 19, 2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/019): graduate text.

## Reference
### Overview
A linear [differential operator](node:Partial%20Differential%20Operators) with constant coefficients has the form $P(D)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}a_\alpha D^\alpha$ with $a_\alpha\in\mathbb C$, and its complete symbol $P(\xi)=\sum_\alpha a_\alpha\xi^\alpha$ is a polynomial; regularity questions are then phrased through the complex zero set $N(P)=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C^n:P(\zeta)=0\}$. ([Bouzar-Dali, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3934)) The Fourier transform is what makes this work: it turns derivatives into multiplication by polynomials in the frequency variable. With the convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx$, one has $\widehat{\partial^\alpha f}(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\hat f(\xi)$ for $f\in C^k$ with $\partial^\alpha f\in L^1$ for $|\alpha|\le k$ and $\partial^\alpha f\in C_0$ for $|\alpha|\le k-1$. ([Speck, MIT 18.152 lectures 16-18](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/a2a21bfac16172f75f1448eeb973660c_MIT18_152F11_lec_16_18.pdf))

The classical theory, built in the 1950s and 1960s by Ehrenpreis, Malgrange, Hörmander and Palamodov, established that every nonzero operator has a fundamental solution, hypoellipticity has an algebraic characterization, and every solution of a homogeneous system on a bounded convex open domain is a superposition of exponential-polynomial solutions. ([Malgrange-Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem); [Bouzar-Dali, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3934); [Ait El Manssour-Härkönen-Sturmfels, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.10146)) A current line of work turns the Fundamental Principle into algorithms through computational commutative algebra. ([Ait El Manssour-Härkönen-Sturmfels, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.10146))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 35Exx into 35E05 (fundamental solutions to PDEs and systems with constant coefficients), 35E10 (convexity properties of solutions), 35E15 (initial value problems), 35E20 (general theory) and 35E99, with a cross-reference to 35N05 for overdetermined constant-coefficient systems. ([MSC2020, 35Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Exx))

How it differs from neighbouring codes:
- **35Hxx (close-to-elliptic equations):** a separate section with subcodes for hypoelliptic (35H10), subelliptic (35H20) and quasielliptic (35H30) equations. ([MSC2020, 35Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Hxx))
- **35N05 (overdetermined systems of PDEs with constant coefficients):** the 35Exx heading carries a "See also 35N05" cross-reference to this code in the overdetermined-problems section 35Nxx. ([MSC2020, 35Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Exx); [MSC2020, 35Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Nxx))
- **Variable-coefficient theory:** the analogous existence statement is false for operators with polynomial coefficients, as Lewy's example shows. ([Malgrange-Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem))

### Key concepts
- **Malgrange-Ehrenpreis theorem (35E05).** For every nonzero polynomial $P$ there is a distribution $E$ with $P(\partial)E=\delta$. Consequently $P(\partial)u=f$ is solvable for every compactly supported distribution $f$ (take $u=E*f$); the fundamental solution is not unique. ([Malgrange-Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem)) See [Fundamental Solutions](node:Fundamental%20Solutions) and [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29).
- **Model fundamental solutions.** For $-\Delta$: $-\frac1{2\pi}\ln|x|$ in $\mathbb R^2$ and $\frac{1}{4\pi|x|}$ in $\mathbb R^3$. ([Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution)) For $\partial_t-k\Delta$ in $\mathbb R^3$: $(4\pi kt)^{-3/2}\Theta(t)e^{-r^2/4kt}$. For $\frac1{c^2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ in $\mathbb R^3$, the retarded solution is $\frac{1}{4\pi r}\delta(t-r/c)$, supported on the light cone. ([Green's function table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_function)) Compare [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation), [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation) and [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations).
- **Hörmander's hypoellipticity theorem (1955).** For a constant-coefficient $P(D)$ the following are equivalent: (i) $P(D)$ is hypoelliptic; (ii) $|D^\alpha P(\xi)|/|P(\xi)|\to0$ as $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$, $|\xi|\to\infty$, for all $\alpha\ne0$; (iii) there are $C,\rho>0$ with $|D^\alpha P(\xi)|/|P(\xi)|\le C|\xi|^{-\rho|\alpha|}$ for large real $\xi$; (iv) the distance $d(\xi)$ from $\xi$ to the complex zero set of $P$ satisfies $|\xi|^{\delta}\le C\,d(\xi)$ for some $\delta>0$ and large $|\xi|$. ([Bouzar-Dali, Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3934); year from [Akhunov-Korobenko-Rios, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00161)) The heat operator is hypoelliptic but not elliptic, and the wave operator is not hypoelliptic. ([Hypoelliptic operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoelliptic_operator)) See [Hypoelliptic Operators](node:Hypoelliptic%20Operators).
- **Paley-Wiener-Schwartz theorem.** An entire function $F$ on $\mathbb C^n$ is the Fourier-Laplace transform of a distribution supported in the closed ball of radius $B$ iff $|F(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^Ne^{B|\operatorname{Im}z|}$; for a convex compact $K$ with support function $H$, $\operatorname{sing\,supp}v\subset K$ iff $|\hat v(\zeta)|\le C_m(1+|\zeta|)^Ne^{H(\operatorname{Im}\zeta)}$ holds in the logarithmic regions $|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|\le m\log(|\zeta|+1)$. ([Paley-Wiener theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley%E2%80%93Wiener_theorem)) See [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis).
- **P-convexity and solvability (35E10).** An open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ is $P$-convex for supports if for every compact $K\subset\Omega$ there is a compact $L\subset\Omega$ such that $u\in\mathcal E'(\Omega)$ and $\operatorname{supp}P(-D)u\subset K$ imply $\operatorname{supp}u\subset L$. Malgrange: $P(D)C^\infty(\Omega)=C^\infty(\Omega)$ iff $\Omega$ is $P$-convex for supports. Hörmander: $P(D)\mathcal D'(\Omega)=\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ iff $\Omega$ is also $P$-convex for singular supports. ([Kalmes, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0907.3037)) Convex open sets are $P$-convex for supports whenever $P\not\equiv0$, and every open set is when $P$ is elliptic. ([Ciaś-Kalmes, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.19272))
- **Ehrenpreis-Palamodov Fundamental Principle (35E20).** For a submodule $M\subseteq R^k$, $R=\mathbb C[\partial_1,\dots,\partial_n]$, (here $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ open, convex and bounded) there are irreducible varieties $V_1,\dots,V_s\subset\mathbb C^n$ and polynomial vectors $B_{ij}(x,z)$, independent of the domain, such that every smooth solution on $\Omega$ is $\psi(z)=\sum_i\sum_j\int_{V_i}B_{ij}(x,z)e^{x^tz}\,d\mu_{ij}(x)$ with bounded measures $\mu_{ij}$ supported on $V_i$. ([Ait El Manssour-Härkönen-Sturmfels, Theorem 2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.10146)) For the wave equation the varieties are two lines and the formula recovers d'Alembert's $\phi(z,t)=f(z+ct)+g(z-ct)$. ([same, §1-2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.10146)) The computation uses primary decomposition and [Gröbner Bases](node:Gröbner%20Bases); see also [Constant-Coefficient Differential Operators](node:Constant-Coefficient%20Differential%20Operators).

### History
Ehrenpreis proved the existence of fundamental solutions in 1954-1955 and Malgrange independently in 1955-1956; both proofs used the Hahn-Banach theorem and were non-constructive. Later proofs by Hörmander, Rosay and Wagner gave growth bounds or an explicit formula. ([Malgrange-Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem)) Hörmander classified hypoelliptic constant-coefficient operators in 1955, a question that goes back to Laurent Schwartz. ([Akhunov-Korobenko-Rios, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00161)) Ait El Manssour, Härkönen and Sturmfels date d'Alembert's travelling-wave solution to 1747 and the Fundamental Principle of Ehrenpreis and Palamodov to the 1960s. ([Ait El Manssour-Härkönen-Sturmfels, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.10146)) Volume II of Hörmander's *Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators*, subtitled *Differential Operators with Constant Coefficients*, was reprinted in Springer's Classics in Mathematics in 2005 from the 1983 original; its Chapter 10 treats $P$-convexity, including Hörmander's two-dimensional characterization (Theorem 10.8.3). ([Ciaś-Kalmes, introduction and references](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.19272)) One chapter of that volume is titled "Differential Operators of Constant Strength". ([Crossref, ALPDO II chapter](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/3-540-26964-9_5))

### Open problems
- **Geometric characterization of $P$-convexity for supports.** Malgrange's criterion is abstract. Hörmander gave a complete geometric characterization in two dimensions, and characterizations exist for second-order operators with wave principal part, for operators of real principal type under additional boundary-regularity conditions, and for polynomials acting along a subspace and elliptic there. In arbitrary dimension the problem "is far from being solved", in the words of Ciaś and Kalmes. ([Ciaś-Kalmes, introduction and §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.19272))
- **Computing solution spaces of special ideals.** The algorithmic program asks for the solution space of the ideal $J_{a,b,c}$ generated by three power sums $\partial_1^a+\partial_2^a+\partial_3^a,\dots$ (relatively prime $0<a<b<c$); the authors call computing solution spaces of power-sum ideals nontrivial even for $n=3$ and cite the conjecture of Conca, Krattenthaler and Watanabe that $V(J_{a,b,c})=\{0\}$ iff $abc$ is a multiple of 6. ([Ait El Manssour-Härkönen-Sturmfels, §7.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.10146))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Malgrange-Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem): statement, history of proofs, Lewy counterexample.
- **Learn:** [Speck, MIT 18.152 lectures 16-18](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/a2a21bfac16172f75f1448eeb973660c_MIT18_152F11_lec_16_18.pdf): Fourier transform and its derivative rules.
- **Primary:** [Ait El Manssour, Härkönen, Sturmfels, Linear PDE with Constant Coefficients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.10146): Fundamental Principle and its computation.
- **Primary:** [Ciaś, Kalmes (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19272): P-convexity for supports and Runge approximation.
- **Further reading:** [Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators II (Springer, Classics in Mathematics, 2005)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b138375): the volume on differential operators with constant coefficients, cited for Malgrange's surjectivity theorem and $P$-convexity in [Ciaś-Kalmes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.19272).
references.MSC 35Fxx - General first-order partial:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35Fxx classifies general first-order PDEs and systems of first-order PDEs. It is organised by linearity and problem type: linear equations (35F05) with their initial, boundary and initial-boundary value problems (35F10, 35F15, 35F16); nonlinear equations (35F20) with 35F25, 35F30, 35F31; and the corresponding codes for linear systems (35F35–35F46) and nonlinear systems (35F50–35F61). The one named equation is 35F21, [Hamilton–Jacobi Equations](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Equations), whose entry points to 49Lxx for calculus of variations and optimal control and to 70H20 for mechanics. ([MSC2020 35Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Fxx))

The classical tool is the [method of characteristics](node:Method%20of%20Characteristics), which reduces a first-order equation to a system of [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) along curves. For a fully nonlinear equation the solution is carried along characteristic strips that also transport the gradient. ([Stanford Math 220A, first-order notes §2.4–2.5](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/firstorder.pdf)) Characteristics can cross, so classical solutions generally exist only locally. For Hamilton–Jacobi equations the modern global theory is that of viscosity solutions, introduced by Crandall and Lions in 1983, with the definition given earlier by Evans in 1980. ([Wikipedia: Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution))

### Scope
- **Linear equations (35F05–35F16) and quasilinear equations (nonlinear, 35F20).** For the quasilinear equation $a(x,y,u)u_x+b(x,y,u)u_y=c(x,y,u)$ one solves $dx/ds=a$, $dy/ds=b$, $dz/ds=c$, and the solution surface is the union of these characteristic curves through the data curve; the linear case is the special case where $a,b$ do not depend on $u$. ([Stanford, first-order notes §§2.1–2.4](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/firstorder.pdf))
- **Fully nonlinear equations (35F20–35F31), including Hamilton–Jacobi equations (35F21).** Examples are the eikonal equation $u_x^2+u_y^2=1$ and $u_xu_y=1$. ([Stanford, first-order notes, Example 9](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/firstorder.pdf))
- **Systems (35F35–35F61).** Linear and nonlinear first-order systems with initial, boundary or initial-boundary data. ([MSC2020 35Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Fxx))

Neighbours: first-order *hyperbolic* problems are classified in 35L, for example 35L60 (first-order nonlinear hyperbolic equations), 35L65 (hyperbolic [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws)) and 35L67 (shocks and singularities), see [MSC 35Lxx - Hyperbolic equations and hyperbolic systems](node:MSC%2035Lxx%20-%20Hyperbolic%20equations%20and%20hyperbolic%20systems). ([MSC2020 35Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Lxx)) Viscosity solutions as a solution concept have their own code, 35D40, in [MSC 35Dxx - Generalized solutions to partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035Dxx%20-%20Generalized%20solutions%20to%20partial%20differential%20equations). ([MSC2020 35Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Dxx)) [Hamilton–Jacobi theory](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Equations) from the control side is [MSC 49Lxx - Hamilton-Jacobi theories](node:MSC%2049Lxx%20-%20Hamilton-Jacobi%20theories); from mechanics it is 70H20 in [MSC 70Hxx - Hamiltonian and Lagrangian mechanics](node:MSC%2070Hxx%20-%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20mechanics). ([MSC2020 35Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Characteristic strips and local existence.** For $F(x,u,Du)=0$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with $z=u(x(s))$ and $p=Du(x(s))$, the $2n+1$ characteristic equations are
$$\dot x_i=F_{p_i},\qquad \dot z=\sum_i p_iF_{p_i},\qquad \dot p_i=-F_{x_i}-F_zp_i .$$
Initial gradients $\psi$ on the data manifold $\Gamma$ must satisfy $F(\gamma,\varphi,\psi)=0$ and the tangential compatibility conditions. If the data are noncharacteristic, $\nabla_pF(\Gamma,\varphi,\Psi)\cdot N\neq0$ with $N$ normal to $\Gamma$, the map $(r,s)\mapsto x$ is locally invertible and $u(x)=z(r,s)$ solves the Cauchy problem near $\Gamma$ (local existence theorem, after Evans Ch. 3). ([Stanford, first-order notes §2.5, Theorem 12](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/firstorder.pdf)) In symmetric form these are the Lagrange–Charpit equations, and the solution graph is everywhere tangent to the Monge cone. ([Wikipedia: Method of characteristics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_of_characteristics))
- **Hamilton–Jacobi equations (35F21).** In mechanics, $-\partial_tS=H(q,\partial S/\partial q,t)$ is a single first-order nonlinear PDE for Hamilton's principal function, with $p_k=\partial S/\partial q_k$. It is equivalent to the $2N$ first-order Hamilton's equations: a solution with $N+1$ constants $\alpha_k$ yields further constants of motion $\beta_k=\partial S/\partial\alpha_k$, from which the motion $q(\alpha,\beta,t)$ is recovered. ([Wikipedia: Hamilton–Jacobi equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton%E2%80%93Jacobi_equation)) This links 35F21 with [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics) and [Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry).
- **Viscosity solutions.** For $F(x,u,Du,D^2u)=0$ with $F$ degenerate elliptic (every first-order $F$ is), an upper semicontinuous $u$ is a subsolution if $F(x_0,\varphi(x_0),D\varphi(x_0),D^2\varphi(x_0))\le0$ whenever a $C^2$ function $\varphi\ge u$ touches $u$ at $x_0$; supersolutions are defined with $\varphi\le u$ and $\ge0$; a continuous function that is both is a viscosity solution. Locally uniform limits of solutions are solutions, and uniqueness follows from a comparison principle. ([Wikipedia: Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution)) Example: $u=1-|x|$ is the viscosity solution of $|u'|=1$ on $(-1,1)$ with zero boundary values, and the vanishing-viscosity limit of $(u')^2-1=\varepsilon u''$; $|x|-1$ solves the same equation written with the opposite sign. ([Wikipedia: Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution))
- **Comparison principle.** Let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded and $H(p,z,x)$ nondecreasing in $z$ with $H(p,z,y)-H(p,z,x)\le\omega(|x-y|(1+|p|))$ for a modulus $\omega$. If $u\in USC(\bar U)$ is a viscosity solution of $H\le-\varepsilon$ and $v\in LSC(\bar U)$ of $H\ge0$ in $U$, and $u\le v$ on $\partial U$, then $u\le v$ in $U$. The proof doubles variables with $\Phi(x,y)=u(x)-v(y)-\tfrac\alpha2|x-y|^2$. ([Calder, Lecture notes on viscosity solutions, Thm. 3.1](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~jwcalder/8590F18/viscosity_solutions.pdf)) For $u_t+H(Du,x)=0$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$ with initial data $g$, under the continuity hypotheses on $H$ of Calder's theorem, a bounded subsolution with $u\le g$ at $t=0$ lies below a bounded supersolution with $v\ge g$ at $t=0$, which gives $\sup|u-v|\le\sup_x|u(x,0)-v(x,0)|$. ([Calder, Thm. 6.6, Cor. 6.7](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~jwcalder/8590F18/viscosity_solutions.pdf))
- **Hopf–Lax formula.** If $H=H(p)$ is convex and superlinear and $g$ is bounded and Lipschitz, the unique viscosity solution of $u_t+H(Du)=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=g$, is
$$u(x,t)=\min_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\Big\{tL\Big(\frac{x-y}{t}\Big)+g(y)\Big\},\qquad L(v)=\sup_p\{p\cdot v-H(p)\},$$
the Legendre transform of $H$. This links 35F21 to the [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations). ([Calder, §6.2](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~jwcalder/8590F18/viscosity_solutions.pdf))
- **Shocks for first-order conservation laws (pointer to 35L65).** [Weak Solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) of $u_t+f(u)_x=0$ satisfy the Rankine–Hugoniot condition $\sigma=[f(u)]/[u]$ across a jump. For uniformly convex $f$ the entropy condition $f'(u_-)>\sigma>f'(u_+)$ selects a unique admissible solution of the Riemann problem. For nonconvex $f$ the weaker condition $f'(u_-)\ge\sigma\ge f'(u_+)$ does not guarantee uniqueness, and the Oleinik entropy condition is needed. ([Stanford, conservation-law notes §§3.2–3.4, 3.6, Theorem 8](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/conservation.pdf))

### History
The equation is named after Hamilton (papers of 1833 and 1834) and Jacobi (*Vorlesungen über Dynamik*, cited there in the 1884 edition of his collected works). ([Wikipedia: Hamilton–Jacobi equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton%E2%80%93Jacobi_equation)) The characteristic relations for first-order equations bear the names of Lagrange and Charpit. ([Wikipedia: Method of characteristics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_of_characteristics)) Crandall and Lions's "Viscosity solutions of Hamilton–Jacobi equations" appeared in *Trans. AMS* 277 (1983), 1–42. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1983-0690039-8)) Crandall, Evans and Lions refined the theory in 1984, and Jensen's 1988 comparison method extended it to second order. ([Wikipedia: Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution)) The 1992 *Bull. AMS* "User's guide" by Crandall, Ishii and Lions is the standard exposition of the fully nonlinear second-order theory. ([arXiv:math/9207212](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207212))

### Open problems
- **Stochastic homogenization of nonconvex Hamilton–Jacobi equations.** For $u^\varepsilon_t+H(Du^\varepsilon,x/\varepsilon,\omega)=0$ with a stationary ergodic random Hamiltonian, homogenization was proved for convex $H$ by Souganidis and, independently, by Rezakhanlou and Tarver. Ziliotto gave a counterexample in the nonconvex case. Gao calls whether stochastic homogenization holds for a genuinely nonconvex Hamilton–Jacobi equation "one of the main open questions in this field." He conjectures homogenization for strict-saddle-point-free Hamiltonians built from nested max/min of quasiconvex and quasiconcave parts, and proves it under an extra monotonicity condition. ([Gao, arXiv:1803.08633](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1803.08633)) Homogenization and the perturbed test function method are introduced in Calder's notes, Ch. 10. ([Calder](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~jwcalder/8590F18/viscosity_solutions.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Viscosity solution (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution): definition, comparison, stability, history.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 35Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Fxx): official list of subcodes.
- **Learn:** [Stanford Math 220A, first-order equations](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/firstorder.pdf): characteristics from linear to fully nonlinear, with the local existence theorem.
- **Learn:** [Calder, Lecture notes on viscosity solutions](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~jwcalder/8590F18/viscosity_solutions.pdf): comparison principles, Hopf–Lax, vanishing viscosity, homogenization.
- **Primary:** [Crandall, Ishii, Lions, User's guide to viscosity solutions of second order PDE (arXiv:math/9207212)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207212): standard survey of the theory.
- **Primary:** [Gao, Stochastic homogenization of certain nonconvex Hamilton–Jacobi equations (arXiv:1803.08633)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1803.08633): current research and open question.
- **Further reading:** [Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed., AMS GSM 19 (2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/019): the standard graduate text. Its Chapter 3 treats nonlinear first-order equations (cited by the Stanford notes).
references.MSC 35Gxx - General higher-order partial:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35Gxx collects general higher-order PDEs and systems of higher-order PDEs. Its codes run parallel to 35F: linear higher-order equations (35G05) with initial, boundary and initial-boundary value problems (35G10, 35G15, 35G16); nonlinear equations (35G20) with 35G25, 35G30, 35G31; and the same pattern for linear systems (35G35–35G46) and nonlinear systems (35G50–35G61). The entry lists no cross-references. ([MSC2020 35Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Gxx))

Higher-order equations with a definite type have their own codes. Higher-order elliptic equations, their variational methods and boundary value problems are 35J30, 35J35 and 35J40; higher-order elliptic systems are 35J48 and 35J58; and semilinear equations with Laplacian, bi-Laplacian or poly-Laplacian are 35J91. ([MSC2020 35Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Jxx)) Higher-order parabolic equations are 35K25, 35K30 and 35K35, and higher-order parabolic systems 35K41, 35K46 and 35K52 ([MSC2020 35Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Kxx)), and higher-order hyperbolic equations and systems are 35L25–35L35 and 35L55–35L57 ([MSC2020 35Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Lxx)). Polyharmonic boundary value problems, such as the Boggio–Hadamard question below, thus fall under the higher-order elliptic codes of [MSC 35Jxx - Elliptic equations and elliptic systems](node:MSC%2035Jxx%20-%20Elliptic%20equations%20and%20elliptic%20systems), and higher-order parabolic problems under [MSC 35Kxx - Parabolic equations and parabolic systems](node:MSC%2035Kxx%20-%20Parabolic%20equations%20and%20parabolic%20systems).

### Scope
- **Linear problems (35G05–35G16, 35G35–35G46):** linear higher-order PDEs and systems, and their initial, boundary and initial-boundary value problems. ([MSC2020 35Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Gxx))
- **Nonlinear problems (35G20–35G31, 35G50–35G61):** nonlinear higher-order PDEs and systems, with the same three problem types. ([MSC2020 35Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Gxx))
- **What changes from second order:** the [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle) holds for higher-order equations only in relatively nice domains, and in general domains no direct analogue exists. Methods that work at second order fail, and the solutions themselves behave in more complicated ways. ([Barton–Mayboroda survey, §3](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~svitlana/HistoryWithComposition-Corrections.pdf))

### Key concepts
- **Complementing (Lopatinskii–Shapiro) condition and Agmon–Douglis–Nirenberg theory.** Consider $A(x,D)u=f$ in $\Omega$ with $A$ of order $2m$ and boundary conditions $B_j(x,D)u=g_j$ on $\partial\Omega$, $j=1,\dots,m$, where $B_j$ has order $m_j<2m$. Lopatinskii and Shapiro showed that solvability with a priori estimates is essentially equivalent to an algebraic condition on the symbols of $A$ and the $B_j$, now called the complementing or Lopatinskii–Shapiro condition. Work in Hölder and Lebesgue spaces culminated in the paper of Agmon, Douglis and Nirenberg. For smooth domains and coefficients this gives Schauder-type estimates of the form $\|u\|_{C^{2m,\alpha}(\Omega)}\le C(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\Omega)}+\sum_j\|g_j\|_{C^{2m-m_j,\alpha}(\partial\Omega)})$, together with the analogous $H^{2m}_p$ estimate in terms of $L^p$ norms. ([Danchin–Hieber–Mucha–Tolksdorf, arXiv:2011.07918, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.07918)) The function spaces involved are higher-order [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces).
- **Agmon–Miranda maximum principle.** Let $\Omega$ have $C^{2m}$ boundary, and let $L=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2m}a_\alpha\partial^\alpha$ be elliptic with $a_\alpha\in C^{|\alpha|}(\bar\Omega)$ and a uniquely solvable Dirichlet problem. If $Lu=0$, then $\max_{|\alpha|\le m-1}\|\partial^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le C\max_{|\beta|\le m-1}\|\partial^\beta u\|_{L^\infty(\partial\Omega)}$ (Agmon 1960). Pipher and Verchota extended this to $\Delta^m$ on bounded Lipschitz domains in $\mathbb R^2$ and $\mathbb R^3$. ([Barton–Mayboroda, Thm. 3.1](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~svitlana/HistoryWithComposition-Corrections.pdf))
- **Loss of positivity: Boggio–Hadamard.** For the clamped plate problem $\Delta^2u=f$, $u=\partial_\nu u=0$, positivity preservation ($f\ge0\Rightarrow u\ge0$) is equivalent to a nonnegative Green function. Boggio's explicit formula shows the Green function is positive on balls, even for the polyharmonic Dirichlet problem. Under Navier conditions $u=\Delta u=0$, applying the second-order comparison principle twice gives positivity. Coffman and Duffin showed positivity fails in any planar domain with a right angle, and Garabedian showed it fails in mildly eccentric ellipses. So positivity can fail even in smooth uniformly convex domains. ([Grunau–Robert, arXiv:0705.3301, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0705.3301)) Compare second-order [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions) and the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem).
- **Plate and biharmonic models.** A plate that resists bending obeys $\rho u_{tt}=-D\Delta^2u+f$, with bending modulus $D=Et^3/[12(1-\nu^2)]$; the steady state is biharmonic. The clamped plate problem is: find $w\in\mathring H^2(\Omega)$ with $b(w,v)=F(v)$ for all $v$, where $b(w,v)=D\int[(1-\nu)\nabla^2w:\nabla^2v+\nu\Delta w\Delta v]$. Coercivity of $b$ on this space makes the weak problem well posed. ([Arnold, UMN lecture notes, §1.3 and Ch. 6](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~arnold/8445-8446.17-18/notes.pdf)) In planar Stokes flow (Reynolds number $\ll1$, inertia neglected relative to viscous forces) the stream function satisfies $\Delta^2\psi=0$. This uses the linear Stokes system $\mu\Delta u-\nabla p+f=0$, $\nabla\cdot u=0$, not the full [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations). ([Wikipedia: Stokes flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokes_flow); [Wikipedia: Biharmonic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biharmonic_equation))
- **Cahn–Hilliard equation.** $\partial_tc=D\Delta(c^3-c-\gamma\Delta c)$ is in conservation form $\partial_tc=-\nabla\cdot j$, $j=-D\nabla\mu$, with $\mu=c^3-c-\gamma\Delta c$. It conserves $\int c$ and decreases $F[c]=\int\tfrac14(c^2-1)^2+\tfrac\gamma2|\nabla c|^2$, since (with $D=1$) $dF/dt=-\int|\nabla\mu|^2$. It was introduced by Cahn and Hilliard in 1958. ([Wikipedia: Cahn–Hilliard equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahn%E2%80%93Hilliard_equation))
- **Thin-film equation.** $\partial_th=-\frac1{3\mu}\nabla\cdot\big(h^n\nabla(\gamma\Delta h)\big)$ models the thickness of a viscous film; $n=3$ is surface-tension-driven flow, and $n<3$ can represent slip at the substrate. ([Wikipedia: Thin-film equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thin-film_equation)) With Navier slip the film has a free contact line moving at finite speed, and well-posedness is more delicate than for the porous-medium equation. Gnann and Petrache prove existence and uniqueness of classical solutions near a traveling-wave profile in two lateral dimensions. ([Gnann–Petrache, arXiv:1710.09903](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.09903))

### History
Schauder's work on the Laplacian in the 1930s began the search for maximal elliptic regularity. The systematic study of general elliptic boundary problems began with the work of Lopatinskii and Shapiro. ([Danchin et al., arXiv:2011.07918](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.07918)) Boggio (1901) and Hadamard (1908) conjectured positivity of the clamped-plate Green function. Hadamard knew by 1909 that it fails in annuli with small inner radius, and counterexamples on simply connected and convex domains began about forty years later. ([Grunau–Robert, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0705.3301)) The higher-order maximum principle was proved in two dimensions by Miranda (1948, 1958) and in all dimensions by Agmon (1960). ([Barton–Mayboroda, §3](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~svitlana/HistoryWithComposition-Corrections.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Uniqueness of [weak solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) of thin-film equations.** For the long-wave unstable thin-film equation $h_t=-a_0(|h|^nh_{xxx})_x-a_1(|h|^mh_x)_x$, Chugunova, Pugh and Taranets write that "uniqueness of nonnegative weak solutions ... is an open problem." They also note simple counterexamples to uniqueness for $h_t=-(h^nh_{xxx})_x$. ([Chugunova–Pugh–Taranets, arXiv:1008.0385](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1008.0385))
- **Boundedness of polyharmonic solutions in high dimension (35J).** For $\Delta^mu=h$ in an arbitrary bounded $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with $u\in\mathring W^m_2(\Omega)$, Maz'ya proved the Green-function bound $|G_m(X,Y)|\le C|X-Y|^{2m-n}$ for $n=2m+1,2m+2$ (and $n=7$ when $m=2$). Whether it holds for $n\ge2m+3$ ($n\ge8$ when $m=2$), and whether such solutions are bounded, is open. In particular it is not known whether solutions of $\Delta^2u=h$, $u\in\mathring W^2_2(\Omega)$, are bounded for $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge8$. ([Barton–Mayboroda, §3](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~svitlana/HistoryWithComposition-Corrections.pdf))
- **Pucci–Serrin conjecture (35J91).** Consider $\Delta^ku-\lambda u=|u|^{2^\star-2}u$ in the unit ball with Dirichlet data, where $2^\star=2n/(n-2k)$. For $2k<n<4k$, the conjecture says there is $\lambda_0(n,k)>0$ such that every radial solution vanishes when $0<\lambda<\lambda_0$. It is known for $k=1$ (Brezis–Nirenberg), for $k=2$ and for $k\ge2$ with $n=2k+1$ (Pucci–Serrin), for $k\ge2$ with $2k<n<2k+6$ (Bernis–Grunau, Grunau), and, restricted to positive solutions, by Grunau. Robert proves it for radial solutions with a fixed bound on $\|u\|_{2^\star}$ and says the sign-changing case "is much more involved." ([Robert, arXiv:2407.14893](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.14893v2))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 35Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Gxx): official list of subcodes.
- **Reference:** [Cahn–Hilliard equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahn%E2%80%93Hilliard_equation): model, energy and mass conservation.
- **Learn:** [Arnold, Numerical Analysis of PDEs lecture notes (UMN)](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~arnold/8445-8446.17-18/notes.pdf): plate equation and weak formulation of clamped and simply supported plates.
- **Primary:** [Barton, Mayboroda, Boundary-value problems for higher-order elliptic equations in non-smooth domains](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~svitlana/HistoryWithComposition-Corrections.pdf): survey of maximum principles, Wiener criteria, well-posedness and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Grunau, Robert, Positivity and almost positivity of biharmonic Green's functions (arXiv:0705.3301)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0705.3301): Boggio–Hadamard history and positivity results.
- **Further reading:** [Gazzola, Grunau, Sweers, Polyharmonic Boundary Value Problems, Springer LNM (2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-12245-3): monograph on positivity and nonlinear higher-order elliptic problems in bounded domains.
references.MSC 35Hxx - Close-to-elliptic equations:
## Reference
### Overview
The central notion of this section is hypoellipticity: an operator $P$ with smooth coefficients on an open $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ is hypoelliptic if, for every open $V\subseteq U$ and $u\in\mathcal D'(V)$, $Pu\in C^\infty(V)$ implies $u\in C^\infty(V)$. Elliptic operators with smooth coefficients are hypoelliptic; the heat operator $\partial_t-k\Delta_x$ ($k>0$) is hypoelliptic but not elliptic, while the wave operator is not hypoelliptic. ([Hypoelliptic operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoelliptic_operator))

Hörmander classified the hypoelliptic constant-coefficient operators in 1955; for variable coefficients the classification is incomplete, and much of the theory starts from his bracket condition of 1967. ([Akhunov-Korobenko-Rios, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00161)) The 1967 paper is *Hypoelliptic second order differential equations*, Acta Mathematica 119, 147-171. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392081)) The same operators arise as Kohn Laplacians and sublaplacians on CR, contact and Heisenberg manifolds, which are not elliptic and are studied with the Heisenberg pseudodifferential calculus. ([Ponge, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0509300))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 35Hxx into 35H10 (hypoelliptic equations), 35H20 (subelliptic equations), 35H30 (quasielliptic equations) and 35H99. ([MSC2020, 35Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Hxx))
- **35H10 versus 35H20.** A subelliptic operator gains $\varepsilon>0$ derivatives in the $L^2$ Sobolev scale, measured by $\|u\|_{H^\varepsilon}=\|\langle\xi\rangle^\varepsilon\hat u\|_{L^2}$, over what the quadratic form $(Lu,u)$ controls; for sums of squares satisfying Hörmander's bracket condition the gain is $\varepsilon=1/Q$ (see the sharp estimate below). Subelliptic operators are hypoelliptic, but the hypoelliptic class is much wider. ([Akhunov-Korobenko-Rios, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00161); [Chen, Theorem 1.1.2](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/attachments/Some%20Degenerate%20PDEs%20Lecture%20Notes%20Nov%202015.pdf))
- **35H30.** Multi-quasielliptic operators, a generalization of the classical quasielliptic operators (Mikhailov, Friberg, Gindikin-Volevich), (regular Newton polyhedron plus $|\xi|_P\le C(1+|P(\xi)|)$) are hypoelliptic, and the converse fails. ([Bouzar-Dali, Definition 5 and Remark 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3934))
- **Neighbour 35Exx.** Equations with constant coefficients have their own section 35Exx, with subcodes for fundamental solutions, convexity properties of solutions, initial value problems and general theory. ([MSC2020, 35Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Exx)) See [MSC 35Exx - Partial differential equations and systems of partial differential equations with constant coefficients](node:MSC%2035Exx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20and%20systems%20of%20partial%20differential%20equations%20with%20constant%20coefficients).

### Key concepts
- **Hörmander's constant-coefficient theorem.** For $P(D)$ with constant coefficients, hypoellipticity is equivalent to $|D^\alpha P(\xi)|/|P(\xi)|\to0$ as $|\xi|\to\infty$ in $\mathbb R^n$ for every $\alpha\ne0$, and to a polynomial lower bound $|\xi|^\delta\le C\operatorname{dist}(\xi,\{P=0\})$ for large real $\xi$. ([Bouzar-Dali, Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.3934))
- **Hörmander's sum-of-squares theorem (35H10).** Let $L=\sum_{j=1}^mX_j^2+X_0+c$ with real smooth vector fields $X_0,\dots,X_m$ and smooth $c$ on $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$. If $X_1,\dots,X_m$ and their iterated commutators $[X_{j_1},[X_{j_2},\dots]]$ span the tangent space at every point of $\Omega$, then $L$ is hypoelliptic on $\Omega$. ([Chen, Oxford lecture notes, Definition 1.1.1 and Theorem 1.1.1](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/attachments/Some%20Degenerate%20PDEs%20Lecture%20Notes%20Nov%202015.pdf)) This is the drift-free form of the condition. In Hörmander's condition the drift $X_0$ may also enter the brackets (in the parabolic version only $X_1,\dots,X_m$ may start a bracket), which is what makes the Kolmogorov operator below hypoelliptic. ([Hörmander's condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B6rmander%27s_condition); [Lucertini-Pagliarani-Pascucci, Assumption 1.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2204.14158)) Examples: the Kohn Laplacian on the Heisenberg group with $X_j=\partial_{x_j}+2y_j\partial_t$, $Y_j=\partial_{y_j}-2x_j\partial_t$, and the Grushin fields $\partial_{x_1},\dots,\partial_{x_{n-1}},x_1\partial_{x_n}$. ([same, Examples 1.1.1-1.1.2](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/attachments/Some%20Degenerate%20PDEs%20Lecture%20Notes%20Nov%202015.pdf)) See [Hypoelliptic Operators](node:Hypoelliptic%20Operators) and [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras).
- **Sharp subelliptic estimate (35H20).** If the bracket condition holds with Hörmander index $Q$ (the least bracket length needed), then $\||\nabla|^{1/Q}u\|_{L^2}^2\le C\big(\|Xu\|_{L^2}^2+\|u\|_{L^2}^2\big)$ for $u\in C_0^\infty(\Omega)$, and the exponent $1/Q$ is optimal. ([Chen, Theorem 1.1.2 and Remark 1.1.1](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/attachments/Some%20Degenerate%20PDEs%20Lecture%20Notes%20Nov%202015.pdf)) Fefferman and Phong (1981) showed that the subelliptic estimate holds exactly when the degeneracy has finite order. ([same, §2.1](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/attachments/Some%20Degenerate%20PDEs%20Lecture%20Notes%20Nov%202015.pdf)) These estimates are stated in [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces).
- **Rothschild-Stein lifting and approximation.** If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ on a manifold $M$ have brackets of length $\le r$ spanning the tangent space, they lift to fields $\tilde X_k=X_k+\sum_j f_{kj}(x,t)\partial_{t_j}$ on $M\times\mathbb R^\ell$ that are free up to step $r$, and in suitable coordinates $\tilde X_k=Y_k+R_k$ with $Y_k$ generators of the free nilpotent Lie algebra of step $r$. ([Ottazzi, Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.12239)) On a homogeneous group a left-invariant, degree-two homogeneous $L$ has a homogeneous [fundamental solution](node:Fundamental%20Solutions) (Folland), so singular-integral estimates on the group transfer back to the original operator. ([Bramanti-Brandolini-Pedroni, introduction](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1002.1331))
- **Kolmogorov operators.** The prototype $\frac{\delta}{2}\sum_{i\le d}\partial^2_{x_ix_i}+Y$, $Y=\partial_t+\langle Bx,\nabla\rangle$, has second-order part in only $d$ of the $N$ space variables; the drift $Y$ generates the rest through brackets, the rank condition is equivalent to Kalman's controllability condition, and under this rank condition the operator is hypoelliptic for every $\delta>0$. Kolmogorov wrote down its explicit Gaussian fundamental solution, the transition density of a linear SDE. ([Lucertini-Pagliarani-Pascucci, §1 and Remark 2.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2204.14158)) In SDE language the parabolic Hörmander condition gives solutions a smooth density. ([Hörmander's condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B6rmander%27s_condition)) See [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus).
- **Bracket condition is not necessary.** Fedii showed that $\partial_x^2+k(x)\partial_y^2$ with $k>0$ for $x\ne0$ and $\sqrt k$ smooth is hypoelliptic even when $k$ vanishes to infinite order at $0$; for such infinitely vanishing coefficients the operator is not subelliptic, so the bracket condition fails. ([Akhunov-Korobenko-Rios, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00161)) In $\mathbb R^3$, Kusuoka and Stroock proved that $\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2+(\varphi(x_1)\partial_{x_3})^2$ (with $\varphi\in C_b^\infty$ even, nonnegative, nondecreasing on $[0,\infty)$, vanishing only at $0$) is hypoelliptic iff $\lim_{x_1\to0}x_1\log|\varphi(x_1)|=0$. ([Chen, §2.1.2 and Theorem 2.1.1](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/attachments/Some%20Degenerate%20PDEs%20Lecture%20Notes%20Nov%202015.pdf))

### History
Schwartz raised the question of which operators are hypoelliptic in the 1950s, and Hörmander classified constant-coefficient operators in 1955. ([Akhunov-Korobenko-Rios, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00161)) The variable-coefficient bracket theorem followed in 1967. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392081)) The infinitely degenerate theory began with Fedii; Kusuoka and Stroock used Malliavin calculus, Morimoto (1987) and Christ (general case, 1997) proved hypoellipticity under logarithmic regularity estimates, and Kohn (2002) gave a geometric condition at infinite-type boundary points of pseudoconvex domains. ([Chen, §2.1](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/attachments/Some%20Degenerate%20PDEs%20Lecture%20Notes%20Nov%202015.pdf)) Ponge's memoir uses the Heisenberg calculus to derive spectral asymptotics of hypoelliptic operators on Heisenberg manifolds, with links to [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory). ([Ponge, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0509300))

### Open problems
- **Classifying degenerate elliptic hypoelliptic operators.** For variable coefficients the classification of hypoelliptic operators "is incomplete even for" second-order operators $-\sum a_{ij}\partial_{ij}+\sum a_i\partial_i+a_0$ with $(a_{ij})\ge0$. Current work seeks the widest class of operators $L_1+g(x)L_2$, with $g$ vanishing to infinite order, that are hypoelliptic, and shows examples where the hypotheses are necessary. ([Akhunov-Korobenko-Rios, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00161); [Korobenko-Rios](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.2339))
- **Regularity theory for rough Kolmogorov equations.** Lucertini, Pagliarani and Pascucci prove optimal regularity for Kolmogorov operators with coefficients measurable in time, and say the related martingale problem for the associated SDEs "will be addressed in a future work". ([Lucertini-Pagliarani-Pascucci, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2204.14158))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hypoelliptic operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoelliptic_operator): definition and basic examples.
- **Learn:** [Hua Chen, Some Results on Degenerate Elliptic Equations (Oxford mini-course, 2015)](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/attachments/Some%20Degenerate%20PDEs%20Lecture%20Notes%20Nov%202015.pdf): sum-of-squares theorem with proof, sharp subelliptic estimate, Carnot-Carathéodory geometry, infinite degeneracy.
- **Primary:** [Ponge, Heisenberg calculus and spectral theory of hypoelliptic operators on Heisenberg manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0509300): Mem. AMS 194 (2008).
- **Primary:** [Akhunov, Korobenko, Rios, Hypoellipticity without loss of derivatives for Fedii's type operators](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.00161): infinitely degenerate operators and the state of the classification.
- **Further reading:** [Hörmander, Hypoelliptic second order differential equations, Acta Math. 119 (1967)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392081): the original sum-of-squares paper.
- **Further reading:** [Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators II (Springer, Classics in Mathematics, 2005)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b138375): volume II of Hörmander's treatise.
references.MSC 35Jxx - Elliptic equations and ellip:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35Jxx covers linear and nonlinear elliptic equations and systems of first, second and higher order: their boundary value problems, variational methods, and named equations such as the Laplace, Helmholtz, Poisson, Schrödinger, $p$-Laplace, mean-curvature and Monge–Ampère equations. For global analysis on manifolds, the entry points to 58J10 and 58J20. ([MSC2020 35Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Jxx)) A linear second-order equation $\sum a_{ij}\partial_{ij}u+\dots=f$ is uniformly elliptic if $\sum a_{ij}\xi_i\xi_j\ge\theta|\xi|^2$ for some $\theta>0$. With smooth coefficients and smooth $f$, solutions are smooth. For nonlinear equations the regularity theory is much more subtle, and solutions need not be smooth. ([Wikipedia: Elliptic PDE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_partial_differential_equation))

The research core of the area is regularity theory. In Fernández-Real and Ros-Oton's summary, the sharp linear results say that $u$ is two derivatives more regular than $f$. Their nonlinear counterparts are the De Giorgi–Nash theorem, which solved Hilbert's nineteenth problem, and the Krylov–Safonov and Evans–Krylov theorems for fully nonlinear equations. ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, Regularity Theory for Elliptic PDE, Ch. 2–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564))

### Scope
- **Linear second-order equations (35J05–35J25):** the Laplace, Helmholtz and Poisson equations (35J05), [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions) (35J08), Schrödinger operators (35J10), general second-order equations, variational methods and boundary value problems (35J15–35J25). ([MSC2020 35Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Jxx))
- **Higher order and systems (35J30–35J58):** higher-order elliptic equations (35J30–35J40) and first-, second- and higher-order elliptic systems with their variational and boundary problems (35J46–35J58). ([MSC2020 35Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Jxx))
- **Nonlinear equations (35J60–35J75, 35J91–35J96):** semilinear (35J61), quasilinear (35J62), degenerate (35J70) and singular (35J75) equations; semilinear equations with Laplacian, bi- or poly-Laplacian (35J91), the $p$-Laplacian (35J92), the mean curvature operator (35J93), the infinity-Laplacian (35J94) and Monge–Ampère equations (35J96). ([MSC2020 35Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Jxx))
- **Unilateral problems and variational inequalities (35J86–35J88),** cross-referenced to free boundaries (35R35) and 49J40. ([MSC2020 35Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Jxx))

Neighbours: [MSC 35Kxx - Parabolic equations and parabolic systems](node:MSC%2035Kxx%20-%20Parabolic%20equations%20and%20parabolic%20systems) and [MSC 35Lxx - Hyperbolic equations and hyperbolic systems](node:MSC%2035Lxx%20-%20Hyperbolic%20equations%20and%20hyperbolic%20systems) cover the evolution types. [MSC 35Hxx - Close-to-elliptic equations](node:MSC%2035Hxx%20-%20Close-to-elliptic%20equations) is a separate section, and [elliptic operators on manifolds](node:Elliptic%20Operators%20on%20Manifolds) go to [MSC 58Jxx - Partial differential equations on manifolds; differential operators](node:MSC%2058Jxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20on%20manifolds;%20differential%20operators). ([MSC2020 35-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Weak solutions and Lax–Milgram.** If $\Omega$ is bounded in some direction and $f\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$, there is a unique [weak solution](node:Weak%20Solutions) $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ of $-\Delta u=f$ (Riesz representation). For $Lu=-\sum\partial_i(a_{ij}\partial_ju)+\sum b_i\partial_iu+cu$ with $a_{ij},b_i,c\in L^\infty$ and uniform ellipticity, the bilinear form satisfies a Gårding inequality $C_1\|u\|^2_{H^1_0}\le a(u,u)+\gamma\|u\|^2_{L^2}$. The Lax–Milgram theorem then gives a unique weak solution of the shifted problem $a(u,\varphi)+\mu(u,\varphi)=\langle f,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\mu\ge\gamma$, even though $a$ is not symmetric. ([Hunter, Ch. 4, Thms. 4.11, 4.20–4.22](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch4.pdf)) The natural spaces are [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces), and the model problem is the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem).
- **Schauder and Calderón–Zygmund estimates.** If $u\in C^{2,\alpha}$ solves $\sum a_{ij}(x)\partial_{ij}u=f$ in $B_1$ with $a_{ij},f\in C^{0,\alpha}$ and $\lambda I\le(a_{ij})\le\Lambda I$, then $\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(B_{1/2})}\le C(\|u\|_{L^\infty(B_1)}+\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_1)})$, with $C$ depending on $\alpha,n,\lambda,\Lambda$ and $\|a_{ij}\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$. For $\Delta u=f$, $f\in L^p$ gives $u\in W^{2,p}$ when $1<p<\infty$. Both fail at the endpoints: $u=(x^2-y^2)\log(x^2+y^2)$ has bounded Laplacian but unbounded second derivatives. ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, §2.2, Thm. 2.20](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564)) Boundary versions hold on $C^{2,\alpha}$ domains with $C^{2,\alpha}$ data. ([Wikipedia: Schauder estimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schauder_estimates)) For operators of order $2m$ with $m$ boundary operators, solvability with a priori estimates is essentially equivalent to the complementing (Lopatinskii–Shapiro) condition on the symbols, and the resulting Hölder and $L^p$ theory culminated in the paper of Agmon, Douglis and Nirenberg. ([Danchin–Hieber–Mucha–Tolksdorf, arXiv:2011.07918, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.07918))
- **De Giorgi–Nash–Moser and Hilbert's 19th problem.** Any weak solution $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ of $\operatorname{div}(A(x)\nabla v)=0$ with merely measurable $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$ is $C^{0,\alpha}$ in the interior, with $\alpha=\alpha(n,\lambda,\Lambda)>0$. Applied to derivatives of minimizers, it shows that local minimizers of $\int L(\nabla w)$ with $L$ uniformly convex and smooth are $C^{1,\alpha}$, and then $C^\infty$ by Schauder bootstrapping. ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, Thms. 3.2, 3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564)) Moser later gave an alternative proof. For systems the result fails: De Giorgi (1968) gave a discontinuous extremal for a vector-valued problem, Giusti–Miranda gave one with analytic coefficients, and Maz'ya gave non-smooth solutions of higher-order equations. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem)) This is the core link with the [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations) and the [Euler–Lagrange Equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations).
- **Harnack inequality and maximum principles.** A nonnegative harmonic $u$ in $B_1$ satisfies $\sup_{B_{1/2}}u\le C(n)\inf_{B_{1/2}}u$. ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, Thm. 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564)) Serrin (1955) and Moser (1961, 1964) extended Harnack's inequality to elliptic and parabolic equations. ([Wikipedia: Harnack's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harnack%27s_inequality)) Compare the [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle) for harmonic functions.
- **Fully nonlinear equations.** For uniformly elliptic $F$ with $F(0)=0$, viscosity solutions of $F(D^2u)=0$ in $B_1$ satisfy $\|u\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{1/2})}\le C\|u\|_{L^\infty(B_1)}$ (Krylov–Safonov, 1979). This rests on a $C^{0,\alpha}$ estimate for equations in non-divergence form with bounded measurable coefficients. If $F$ is convex or concave, $\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(B_{1/2})}\le C\|u\|_{L^\infty(B_1)}$ (Evans–Krylov, 1982). In two dimensions, for smooth $F$, all solutions are smooth (Nirenberg). Nadirashvili and Vladuts constructed solutions that are not $C^2$ in dimensions $n\ge5$. ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, Thms. 4.23–4.28](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564)) The Monge–Ampère equation $\det D^2u=f$ is elliptic when $f>0$, on uniformly convex solutions. ([Wikipedia: Elliptic PDE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_partial_differential_equation))
- **Critical exponents: Brezis–Nirenberg.** Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and smooth, and $2^*=2n/(n-2)$. The problem $-\Delta u=\lambda u+|u|^{2^*-2}u$, $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, has positive solutions for every $\lambda\in(0,\lambda_1(\Omega))$ when $n\ge4$. When $n=3$ there is $\lambda^*(\Omega)>0$ such that they exist for every $\lambda\in(\lambda^*(\Omega),\lambda_1(\Omega))$; for a ball they exist exactly when $\lambda\in(\lambda_1(B)/4,\lambda_1(B))$, and for strictly star-shaped $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ there are none for $\lambda$ close to $0$. ([Iacopetti, arXiv:1312.5871, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.5871)) Here $\lambda_1$ is the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the Laplacian, see [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations).

### History
Schauder's estimates appeared in 1934 and 1937. ([Wikipedia: Schauder estimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schauder_estimates)) Hilbert posed the nineteenth problem in 1900. Bernstein (1904) and Petrowsky (1939) gave partial answers, De Giorgi (1956–57) and Nash (1957–58) solved it, and counterexamples for systems followed in 1968. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem)) Crandall–Lions and Evans introduced viscosity solutions, and Jensen proved their uniqueness for the fully nonlinear Dirichlet problem. Nadirashvili and Vlăduţ's first nonclassical solution lived in dimension 12. ([Nadirashvili–Vlăduţ, arXiv:0912.3119](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0912.3119)) Monographs include Gilbarg–Trudinger on second-order elliptic equations (Springer Classics in Mathematics, 2001) and Caffarelli–Cabré, *Fully Nonlinear Elliptic Equations* (AMS Colloquium Publications, 1995). ([Crossref: Gilbarg–Trudinger](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61798-0); [Crossref: Caffarelli–Cabré](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/coll/043))

### Open problems
- **$C^2$ regularity of fully nonlinear equations in $\mathbb R^3$ and $\mathbb R^4$.** For uniformly elliptic $F$ and viscosity solutions of $F(D^2u)=0$ in $\mathbb R^3$ or $\mathbb R^4$, is $u\in C^2$? Fernández-Real and Ros-Oton write that "it is not known what happens in $\mathbb R^3$ and $\mathbb R^4$", calling it "one of the most remarkable open problems in elliptic PDEs". They also list as an important open problem whether the Armstrong–Silvestre–Smart partial regularity theorem ($C^2$ off a set of Hausdorff dimension at most $n-\varepsilon$) holds without assuming $F\in C^1$. ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, §§4.4–4.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564))
- **$C^1$ regularity of Lipschitz minimizers.** For strictly convex (not uniformly convex) $L$, Lipschitz minimizers of $\int L(\nabla u)$ are $C^1$ in the plane under extra hypotheses (De Silva–Savin), and can fail to be $C^1$ in $\mathbb R^4$ (Mooney). "It is currently an open question what happens in dimension $n=3$." ([Fernández-Real–Ros-Oton, §3.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01564))
- **De Giorgi's conjecture.** Let $n\le8$ and let $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^\infty$ solve $-\Delta u=u-u^3$ with $\partial_nu>0$. Must $u$ be one-dimensional? This is proven for $n\in\{2,3\}$ and "still open for $n\in\{4,\dots,8\}$". Savin proved it there under the extra assumption that the limits as $x_n\to\pm\infty$ are $\pm1$, and a counterexample in higher dimensions shows the dimensional restriction is needed. ([Dipierro–Valdinoci, arXiv:2207.04783, Conj. 5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.04783))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hilbert's nineteenth problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem): history of the regularity problem and counterexamples for systems.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 35Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Jxx): official list of subcodes.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, Elliptic PDEs (UC Davis notes, Ch. 4)](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch4.pdf): weak solutions, Sobolev spaces, Lax–Milgram.
- **Primary:** [Fernández-Real, Ros-Oton, Regularity Theory for Elliptic PDE (arXiv:2301.01564; EMS Zurich Lectures 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.01564): graduate text on Schauder theory, De Giorgi–Nash, fully nonlinear equations and the obstacle problem, with open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Gilbarg, Trudinger, Elliptic PDE of Second Order (Springer Classics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61798-0): the standard monograph on linear and quasilinear second-order theory.
- **Further reading:** [Caffarelli, Cabré, Fully Nonlinear Elliptic Equations (AMS Colloquium 43, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/coll/043): the regularity theory of viscosity solutions.
references.MSC 35Kxx - Parabolic equations and para:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35K covers parabolic equations and systems: the heat equation and heat kernel, linear second-order and higher-order parabolic equations and systems with their initial and initial–boundary value problems, nonlinear, semilinear, quasilinear, reaction–diffusion, degenerate and singular equations, unilateral problems, and abstract parabolic equations. Its geometric counterpart on manifolds is 58J35. ([MSC2020, 35Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Kxx))

The heat equation $u_t=\Delta u+f$ is the prototype. Like elliptic equations, parabolic equations have strong smoothing properties, parabolic maximum principles and Harnack inequalities, and a Schauder theory for Hölder continuous solutions; existence and regularity of weak solutions follow from $L^2$ energy estimates. ([Hunter, ch. 6](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch6.pdf)) The initial value problem for the heat equation is well-posed forward in time, while recovering earlier temperatures from later data is ill-posed. ([Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem)) Its solutions propagate disturbances instantaneously. ([Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation))

Research in the area divides roughly into the linear regularity theory for rough coefficients (Nash, Moser, Aronson), whose tools are Harnack inequalities and Gaussian heat-kernel bounds, and nonlinear parabolic problems: finite-time blow-up for reaction–diffusion equations, degenerate diffusions such as the porous medium equation, and geometric flows coded 35K93 and 35K96. ([Aronson, Gaussian estimates](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.04620); [del Pino–Musso–Wei](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.11461); [MSC2020, 35Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Kxx))

### Scope
The MSC2020 subdivisions are ([MSC2020, 35Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Kxx)):
- 35K05 heat equation; 35K08 heat kernel;
- 35K10–35K20 second-order parabolic equations (general, initial value, initial–boundary value); 35K25–35K35 the higher-order analogues;
- 35K40–35K52 second- and higher-order parabolic systems, with their initial and initial–boundary value problems;
- 35K55 nonlinear, 35K57 reaction–diffusion, 35K58 semilinear, 35K59 quasilinear equations; 35K60–35K61 nonlinear initial and boundary problems;
- 35K65 degenerate and 35K67 singular equations; 35K70 ultraparabolic and pseudoparabolic equations;
- 35K85–35K87 unilateral problems and parabolic variational inequalities (see also 35R35, 49J40); 35K90 abstract parabolic equations;
- 35K91 semilinear equations with Laplacian or poly-Laplacian; 35K92 quasilinear equations with $p$-Laplacian; 35K93 quasilinear equations with mean curvature operator; 35K96 parabolic Monge–Ampère equations.

Neighbouring codes, per the entry's cross-references: 58J35 holds heat equations on manifolds; 35R35 holds free boundary problems, beside the parabolic variational inequalities of 35K85–87; and for reaction–diffusion, 35K57 points to probabilistic diffusion processes (60J60, 60J70) and applied codes (80A23, 92E20). ([MSC2020, 35Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Kxx))

### Key concepts
- **Uniform parabolicity and weak solutions (35K10, 35K20):** for $u_t+Lu=f$ with $Lu=-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_ju)+b^j\partial_ju+cu$, the coefficients $a^{ij}=a^{ji},b^j,c\in L^\infty(\Omega\times(0,T))$ and $a^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j\ge\theta|\xi|^2$ with $\theta>0$. On a bounded open $\Omega$, for every $f\in L^2(0,T;H^{-1})$ and $g\in L^2(\Omega)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in C([0,T];L^2)\cap L^2(0,T;H^1_0)$ with $u_t\in L^2(0,T;H^{-1})$, and
$$\|u\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^2)}+\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;H^1_0)}+\|u_t\|_{L^2(0,T;H^{-1})}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{L^2(0,T;H^{-1})}+\|g\|_{L^2}\bigr).$$
The proof is by Galerkin approximation, and it rests on the energy identity $\tfrac12\frac{d}{dt}\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2=\int fu$ for the heat equation with zero Dirichlet data. ([Hunter, Assumption 6.1, Thm. 6.3, §6.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch6.pdf))
- **[Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation) and heat kernel (35K05, 35K08):** on $\mathbb R^n$ with unit diffusivity the fundamental solution is $\Phi(x,t)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/4t}$, and solutions are convolutions of $\Phi$ with the initial data. ([Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation))
- **Parabolic Harnack inequality:** let $M$ be a smooth bounded domain and $L$ a linear elliptic operator with smooth bounded coefficients and positive definite principal matrix. For a nonnegative $C^2$ solution of $u_t-Lu=0$ on $(0,T)\times M$, $K\Subset M$ and $0<\tau<T$, there is $C$ (depending on $K$, $\tau$, $t-\tau$ and the coefficients) with $\sup_Ku(t-\tau,\cdot)\le C\inf_Ku(t,\cdot)$ for $t\in(\tau,T)$. The waiting time matters: the supremum at an earlier time is controlled by the infimum at a later time. Harnack inequalities are used to prove interior regularity of weak solutions. ([Harnack's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harnack%27s_inequality)) Moser proved a parabolic Harnack inequality in 1964, with a correction in 1967. ([Aronson, Gaussian estimates](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1707.04620))
- **Nash continuity and Aronson's Gaussian bounds:** for uniformly parabolic divergence-form equations with bounded measurable coefficients, Nash (1958) proved Hölder continuity of solutions. Using Moser's Harnack inequality, Aronson (1967–68) proved two-sided bounds $C^{-1}g_1(x-\xi,t-\tau)\le\Gamma(x,t;\xi,\tau)\le Cg_2(x-\xi,t-\tau)$ for the fundamental solution, where $g_1,g_2$ are heat kernels with different diffusivities, under minimal regularity assumptions. Fabes and Stroock (1986) derived the Gaussian bounds from Nash's ideas and recovered Nash continuity and the Harnack inequality as consequences. ([Aronson, Gaussian estimates](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1707.04620); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.04620))
- **Fujita exponent (35K57, 35K58):** for $u_t=\Delta u+u^p$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with initial data $\phi\ge0$, $\phi\not\equiv0$, and $p>1$, let $p^*=1+2/n$. If $1<p\le p^*$, every solution blows up in finite time. If $p>p^*$, solutions with sufficiently small data are global. Fujita proved the case $p\ne p^*$, and the borderline $p=p^*$ was handled later (Aronson–Weinberger, Kobayashi–Sirao–Tanaka). ([Pinsky, intro](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0805.1313); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.1313))
- **Type I and type II blow-up:** for positive solutions of $v_t=\Delta v+|v|^{p-1}v$ in a smooth domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with $v=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, blow-up at time $T$ is type I if $(T-t)^{1/(p-1)}\|v(t)\|_{L^\infty}$ stays bounded, and type II otherwise. For $1<p<p_S=(d+2)/(d-2)$, only type I occurs (first proved by Giga–Kohn for convex domains, later extended to general domains). Radial type II blow-up exists for $p>p_{JL}(d)$, $d\ge11$ (Herrero–Velázquez), and is excluded radially for $p_S<p\le p_{JL}$ (Matano–Merle). ([del Pino–Musso–Wei, intro](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.11461)) In an October 2025 arXiv preprint, Miura, Takahashi and Zhanpeisov report a proof of nonexistence of type II blow-up for possibly sign-changing solutions in the subcritical range $(n-2)p<n+2$ on possibly non-convex, unbounded domains. ([Miura–Takahashi–Zhanpeisov](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17229))
- **Porous medium equation (35K65):** $u_t=\Delta(u^m)$, $m>1$, is a divergence-form equation with diffusion coefficient $D(u)=mu^{m-1}$, which vanishes where $u=0$. It has the Barenblatt self-similar solution. ([Porous medium equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porous_medium_equation)) Vázquez's monograph is the standard reference for its mathematical theory. ([Vázquez, OUP](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198569039.001.0001))

### History
Fourier developed the theory of the heat equation in 1822. ([Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation)) The regularity theory for rough coefficients came in the late 1950s and 1960s: Nash (1958) on continuity, Moser (1964, corrected 1967) on the parabolic Harnack inequality, and Aronson (1967–1968) on Gaussian bounds. Fabes and Stroock unified these in 1986. ([Aronson, Gaussian estimates](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1707.04620)) Fujita proved the critical-exponent dichotomy for $p\ne p^*$, and the borderline case was settled in the late 1970s. ([Pinsky](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0805.1313)) Giga–Kohn (1985), Herrero–Velázquez and Matano–Merle then obtained the type I and type II results above. ([del Pino–Musso–Wei](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.11461))

### Open problems
- **Type II blow-up in the Matano–Merle range.** For positive solutions of $v_t=\Delta v+|v|^{p-1}v$ on a domain with zero Dirichlet data, del Pino, Musso and Wei call the question of whether type II blow-up can occur for $p_S(d)<p<p_{JL}(d)$ "conspicuously open for many years". Such solutions must be non-radial. They answer yes only for $d\ge7$ and the single exponent $p=(d+1)/(d-3)$, in axially symmetric domains, with blow-up on a circle in a negatively curved part of the boundary. ([del Pino–Musso–Wei, intro](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.11461); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.11461))
- **Genericity of type I blow-up.** The same authors write that type I blow-up is *expected* to be the generic form of blow-up for every $p>1$, a statement they frame as an expectation rather than a theorem. ([del Pino–Musso–Wei, intro](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.11461))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation): fundamental solution, maximum principle, smoothing, and history.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, PDE notes ch. 6](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch6.pdf): energy estimates, weak solutions, Galerkin method, semilinear heat equation.
- **Primary:** [Aronson, Gaussian estimates: a brief history](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.04620): survey by the originator of the Gaussian bounds, covering Nash, Moser and Fabes–Stroock.
- **Further reading:** [Vázquez, The Porous Medium Equation (OUP, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198569039.001.0001): the monograph on degenerate diffusion. Also [del Pino–Musso–Wei](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.11461): a research paper on type II blow-up, whose introduction reviews the blow-up classification.

Related notes: [MSC 35 - Partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations), [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation), [MSC 35Jxx - Elliptic equations and elliptic systems](node:MSC%2035Jxx%20-%20Elliptic%20equations%20and%20elliptic%20systems) (the elliptic theory that parabolic theory parallels), [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle), [Weak Solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions), [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces), [Regularity of PDE Solutions](node:Regularity%20of%20PDE%20Solutions), [Strongly Continuous Operator Semigroups](node:Strongly%20Continuous%20Operator%20Semigroups) (35K90), [Reaction–Diffusion Models in Biology](node:Reaction–Diffusion%20Models%20in%20Biology), [Reaction–Advection–Diffusion Systems](node:Reaction–Advection–Diffusion%20Systems), [Darcy's Law and Porous Media Equations](node:Darcy's%20Law%20and%20Porous%20Media%20Equations), [Free Boundary Problems](node:Free%20Boundary%20Problems), [Ricci Flow](node:Ricci%20Flow) (a geometric parabolic flow).
