## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35L, "Hyperbolic equations and hyperbolic systems", is the part of [MSC 35 - Partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations) about evolution equations with finite propagation speed. Its codes are organised by order and type: first-order equations (35L02–35L04), the [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation) (35L05), second- and higher-order equations (35L10–35L35), first-, second- and higher-order systems (35L40–35L57), nonlinear equations (35L60, 35L70–35L77), hyperbolic conservation laws (35L65), shocks and singularities (35L67), degenerate, singular and pseudohyperbolic equations (35L80–35L82), unilateral problems and variational inequalities (35L85–35L87), and abstract hyperbolic equations (35L90). The section cross-refers global analysis to 58J45. ([MSC2020 35Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Lxx))

An equation is hyperbolic at a point when the Cauchy problem is uniquely solvable near that point for arbitrary data on a non-characteristic hypersurface; relative to a time coordinate, disturbances travel at finite speed along characteristics, which distinguishes hyperbolic from elliptic and parabolic problems. ([Hyperbolic PDE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_partial_differential_equation)) The research area splits into linear theory (energy estimates, well-posedness, propagation of singularities), nonlinear waves (local and global existence via dispersive estimates, with [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity) as a driving application), and hyperbolic conservation laws, where solutions develop shocks in finite time and must be understood in a weak, entropy-admissible sense. ([Bressan, §§1–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707); [Klainerman–Selberg](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0101118))

### Scope
- **Neighbour 58J.** Hyperbolic equations on manifolds belong to 58J45, which the 35L heading names as the place for global analysis; see [MSC 58Jxx - Partial differential equations on manifolds; differential operators](node:MSC%2058Jxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20on%20manifolds;%20differential%20operators). ([MSC2020 35Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Lxx))
- **Neighbours 76L and 74J.** Shocks and singularities (35L67) cross-refer to 58Kxx, 74J40 and 76L05, the fluid-mechanical side of shock waves in [MSC 76Lxx - Shock waves and blast waves in fluid mechanics](node:MSC%2076Lxx%20-%20Shock%20waves%20and%20blast%20waves%20in%20fluid%20mechanics). ([MSC2020 35Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Lxx))
- **Neighbours 35R and 49J.** Unilateral hyperbolic problems (35L85–35L87) cross-refer to [free boundary problems](node:Free%20Boundary%20Problems) (35R35) and variational inequalities (49J40); compare [MSC 35Rxx - Miscellaneous topics in partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035Rxx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20partial%20differential%20equations). ([MSC2020 35Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Lxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation) and finite speed.** For $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ on $\mathbb R$ with $u(x,0)=\phi(x)$, $u_t(x,0)=\psi(x)$, d'Alembert's formula
  $$u(x,t)=\tfrac12[\phi(x+ct)+\phi(x-ct)]+\frac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}\psi(s)\,ds$$
  gives the unique solution, so $u(x_0,t_0)$ depends only on data in $[x_0-ct_0,x_0+ct_0]$. For compactly supported data the energy $E(t)=\tfrac12\int(u_t^2+c^2u_x^2)\,dx$ is conserved, and the energy method proves finite propagation speed: if $\phi\equiv\psi\equiv0$ on $[x_0-ct_0,x_0+ct_0]$ then $u\equiv0$ in the backward cone. ([Stanford, §§5.3–5.4](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/waveequation1.pdf))
- **Hyperbolic systems and [energy estimates](node:Energy%20Estimates%20for%20PDEs).** The system $U_t+\sum_{i=1}^nA_i(x,t)U_{x_i}=F$ is hyperbolic if $A(x,t;\xi)=\sum_iA_i\xi_i$ is diagonalizable with real eigenvalues for all $\xi$; it is symmetric hyperbolic if every $A_i$ is symmetric and strictly hyperbolic if $A(x,t;\xi)$ has $m$ distinct real eigenvalues. For constant symmetric $A_i$, with $M=\max_{|\xi|=1}\max_i|\lambda_i(\xi)|$, a solution of $U_t+\sum A_iU_{x_i}=0$ vanishing on the ball $|x-x_0|\le Mt_0$ at $t=0$ vanishes on the cone over it, and the $L^2$ energy $\tfrac12\int|W|^2dx$ of the difference of two smooth solutions with compactly supported data is constant, giving uniqueness. ([Stanford systems notes, §§8.1, 8.3, Theorems 4–5](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/systems.pdf)) Strong hyperbolicity gives a well-posed initial value problem, and symmetric hyperbolic systems with maximally dissipative boundary conditions give well-posed initial-boundary value problems. ([Hilditch](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.2012))
- **[Hyperbolic conservation laws](node:Conservation%20Laws) (35L65, 35L67).** For $u_t+f(u)_x=0$, $u\in\mathbb R^n$, the gradient can blow up in finite time even for $C^1$ data, so one uses [weak solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions): $\iint(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x)\,dx\,dt=0$ for all $\varphi\in C^1_c$. A shock with states $u^\pm$ and speed $\lambda$ is a weak solution iff the Rankine–Hugoniot equations $\lambda(u^+-u^-)=f(u^+)-f(u^-)$ hold; weak solutions are not unique, so admissibility conditions (Liu's condition on intermediate shock speeds, vanishing viscosity, entropy dissipation) are imposed. ([Bressan, §§2, 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707)) For a scalar law, a shock with left and right states $u^-,u^+$ is stable under insertion of any intermediate state $u^*$ between them iff $\frac{f(u^*)-f(u^-)}{u^*-u^-}\ge\frac{f(u^+)-f(u^*)}{u^+-u^*}$ (the jump behind is at least as fast as the jump ahead); for $n\times n$ systems, an $i$-shock joining $u^-$ to $u^+=S_i(\sigma)$ on the $i$-shock curve is Liu-admissible if the speeds of all intermediate shocks satisfy $\lambda_i(s)\ge\lambda_i(\sigma)$ for $s\in[0,\sigma]$, and for a single shock this is equivalent to vanishing-viscosity admissibility. ([Bressan, §2.3, eqs. 2.16, 2.20, Definition 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707)) Kruzhkov proved a general existence–uniqueness theorem for scalar conservation laws in any number of space dimensions. ([Bressan, §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707))
- **Glimm's theorem.** For a one-dimensional strictly hyperbolic system in which each characteristic field is genuinely nonlinear or linearly degenerate, there is $\delta>0$ such that data $\bar u\in L^1$ with $\mathrm{Tot.Var.}\{\bar u\}\le\delta$ give a global weak solution, entropy-admissible if the system has a convex entropy; the proof uses the random-choice Glimm scheme, a uniform [total-variation](node:Bounded%20Variation) bound and Helly compactness. Smallness of the initial data has never been removed in these results. ([Bressan, Theorem 4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707))
- **Vanishing viscosity (Bianchini–Bressan).** For a strictly hyperbolic $n\times n$ system $u_t+A(u)u_x=\varepsilon u_{xx}$ with small total variation, solutions exist globally with BV bounds and $L^1$-Lipschitz dependence uniform in $\varepsilon$, and converge as $\varepsilon\to0$ to a Lipschitz semigroup; in conservation form $A=Df$ the limits are the unique entropy weak solutions. ([Bianchini–Bressan](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0111321); [Bressan, Theorem 5.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707)) Conversely, every Liu-admissible weak solution of small total variation coincides with a semigroup trajectory. ([Bressan, Theorem 6.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707))
- **Strichartz estimates and nonlinear waves (35L70–35L72).** For $\Box u=0$, $(u,\partial_tu)|_{t=0}=(f,0)$ in $\mathbb R^{1+n}$, the estimate $\|u\|_{L^q_tL^r_x}\lesssim\|f\|_{\dot H^s}$ holds for all $f\in\dot H^s$ iff $s=\tfrac n2-\tfrac nr-\tfrac1q$ and $(q,r)$ is wave admissible: $2\le q\le\infty$, $2\le r<\infty$, $\tfrac2q\le(n-1)(\tfrac12-\tfrac1r)$. The case $q=r=4$, $n=3$ is Strichartz's original inequality; such estimates, with null structure and bilinear estimates, drive low-regularity local well-posedness for nonlinear wave systems. ([Klainerman–Selberg, §2 Theorem A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0101118); [Strichartz estimate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strichartz_estimate))
- **Global stability of [Minkowski space](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime).** Christodoulou and Klainerman proved the global nonlinear stability of Minkowski space for the vacuum [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations); Lindblad and Rodnianski gave a new proof in harmonic (wave) gauge, showing that asymptotically flat data satisfying a global smallness condition give causally geodesically complete solutions converging to Minkowski space, also for the Einstein–scalar field system. ([Lindblad–Rodnianski](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411109); [Christodoulou–Klainerman, PUP 1994](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9781400863174))
- **Propagation of singularities.** The wave front set refines the singular support by recording singular directions in $T^*\mathbb R^n$; the term was coined by Hörmander around 1970. ([Wave front set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_front_set)) For a classical [pseudodifferential operator](node:Pseudodifferential%20Operators) $P$ of real principal type with principal symbol $p_m$, $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ (or $P$ properly supported and $u\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$) and $Pu\in C^\infty$, each null bicharacteristic of $p_m$ lies either entirely inside or entirely outside $\mathrm{WF}(u)$, so singularities of solutions travel along bicharacteristics. ([Ma, Theorem 9.13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12839))

### History
Strichartz's estimate dates from 1977 and arose from the Fourier restriction problem. ([Strichartz estimate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strichartz_estimate)) Glimm's random-choice theorem was for many years the only rigorous tool for weak solutions of systems; Liu removed the genuine nonlinearity/linear degeneracy hypothesis, front tracking gave alternative proofs, and the vanishing-viscosity approach removed it from the stability theory as well. ([Bressan, §§4–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707)) The Bianchini–Bressan paper was submitted in 2001. ([arXiv:math/0111321](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0111321)) Christodoulou and Klainerman's stability monograph appeared in 1994 and the harmonic-gauge proof was posted in 2004. ([Christodoulou–Klainerman](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9781400863174); [Lindblad–Rodnianski](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411109))

### Open problems
- **BV blow-up for physical systems.** For a strictly hyperbolic system of conservation laws with a strictly convex entropy, either construct an entropy-admissible solution whose total variation blows up in finite time, or prove that bounded variation persists for all time. Jenssen's blow-up example has no strictly convex entropy, and the question is "not resolved even for the $2\times2$ system of isentropic gas dynamics" (cf. [Compressible Euler Equations](node:Compressible%20Euler%20Equations)). ([Bressan, Open Problem #1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707))
- **Nonlinear viscosity.** Extend the Bianchini–Bressan theory to $u_t+A(u)u_x=\varepsilon(B(u)u_x)_x$ with a positive semidefinite viscosity matrix $B(u)$: prove uniform BV bounds for small-BV data and study the limit $\varepsilon\to0^+$. ([Bressan, Open Problem #2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707))
- **$L^\infty$ solutions.** Existence of $L^\infty$ solutions "remains a largely open problem" for general $n\times n$ systems; extending the vanishing-viscosity semigroup to data of unbounded variation, and the uniqueness of the Glimm–Lax solutions, are listed as open; and it is open to find a strictly hyperbolic system with a strictly convex entropy and $L^\infty$ data admitting two distinct entropy-admissible solutions. ([Bressan, §8, Open Problems #5–#6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.16707))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hyperbolic partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_partial_differential_equation): definitions, hyperbolic systems, conservation-law form.
- **Learn:** [Stanford Math 220A notes on the wave equation](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/waveequation1.pdf): d'Alembert, domain of dependence, energy methods; companion [notes on hyperbolic systems](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220a/handouts/systems.pdf).
- **Primary:** [Bressan, One dimensional hyperbolic conservation laws: past and future (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16707): survey of well-posedness theory with six stated open problems.
- **Primary:** [Bianchini–Bressan, Vanishing viscosity solutions of nonlinear hyperbolic systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0111321): the vanishing-viscosity well-posedness theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Dafermos, Hyperbolic Conservation Laws in Continuum Physics (Springer, Grundlehren, 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-49451-6): the standard monograph on conservation laws.
- **Further reading:** [Christodoulou–Klainerman, The Global Nonlinear Stability of the Minkowski Space (Princeton, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9781400863174): the original stability proof.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 35Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Lxx): official code list.

## Reference
### Overview
A partial differential equation is of mixed type when it is elliptic in one part of its domain and hyperbolic in another. The model is the Tricomi equation $\partial_{x_1x_1}u+x_1\partial_{x_2x_2}u=0$, which is elliptic for $x_1>0$, hyperbolic for $x_1<0$, and degenerates on the line $x_1=0$. ([Chen, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769)) In steady two-dimensional potential flow, $(c^2-u^2)\varphi_{xx}-2uv\varphi_{xy}+(c^2-v^2)\varphi_{yy}=0$ is elliptic where the Mach number $M=q/c<1$ and hyperbolic where $M>1$, so a transonic flow is governed by a nonlinear mixed-type equation. ([Wang, Oxford short course 2024, Part 1](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/inline-files/Euler%20Equations%20and%20Mixed-Type%20Problems%20in%20Gas%20Dynamics%20and%20Geometry%20WANG_Oxford2024.pdf)) In the transonic application the change of type is the passage between subsonic and supersonic speed, and the problem is typically formulated in the hodograph plane, where the unknown is a stream function and $x$, $y$ are the flow angle and a scaled flow speed. ([Perinati-Imbert-Gérard-Moiola-Stocker, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.06910))

For linear equations the transition curve is known in advance, and one may study the equation as a degenerate elliptic or degenerate hyperbolic problem on each side, or through its fundamental solution. For nonlinear equations the transition boundary is in general unknown and the nonlinearity creates further singularities, so the classical methods for each type no longer apply directly. Chen's survey argues that many hard questions in gas dynamics and geometry sit exactly at, or beyond, the boundaries of the elliptic/hyperbolic/parabolic classification. ([Chen, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769))

### Scope
MSC2020 divides 35Mxx into single equations (35M10 PDEs of mixed type; 35M11 initial value, 35M12 boundary value, 35M13 initial-boundary value problems), systems (35M30 mixed-type systems, with 35M31-35M33 for the corresponding problems), unilateral problems and variational inequalities of mixed type (35M85-35M87), and 35M99. ([MSC2020, 35Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Mxx))

How it differs from neighbouring codes:
- **Elliptic and hyperbolic theory:** a second-order equation in two variables is elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic according to the signs of the eigenvalues of its coefficient matrix, and a mixed-type equation contains regions of different type separated by a transition set. ([Wang, Part 1](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/inline-files/Euler%20Equations%20and%20Mixed-Type%20Problems%20in%20Gas%20Dynamics%20and%20Geometry%20WANG_Oxford2024.pdf)) The single-type theories have their own maps: [MSC 35Jxx - Elliptic equations and elliptic systems](node:MSC%2035Jxx%20-%20Elliptic%20equations%20and%20elliptic%20systems) and [MSC 35Lxx - Hyperbolic equations and hyperbolic systems](node:MSC%2035Lxx%20-%20Hyperbolic%20equations%20and%20hyperbolic%20systems).
- **35R35 and 49J40:** each of the unilateral-problem codes 35M85-35M87 carries a "See also 35R35, 49J40" cross-reference. ([MSC2020, 35Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Mxx)) See [Free Boundary Problems](node:Free%20Boundary%20Problems).

### Key concepts
- **Classification and degeneracy.** A second-order equation in two variables with principal coefficient matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}$ is elliptic where the eigenvalues of $A$ have the same sign, parabolic where $A$ is singular, and hyperbolic where they have opposite signs; type can also depend on the solution, as in $u_{xx}-uu_{yy}=0$, whose elliptic-hyperbolic interface $u=0$ is a free boundary. ([Wang, Part 1](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/inline-files/Euler%20Equations%20and%20Mixed-Type%20Problems%20in%20Gas%20Dynamics%20and%20Geometry%20WANG_Oxford2024.pdf)) The Tricomi equation $\partial_{x_1x_1}u+x_1\partial_{x_2x_2}u=0$ has *hyperbolic degeneracy* at $x_1=0$ (its two characteristic families meet the line perpendicularly), while the Keldysh equation $x_1\partial_{x_1x_1}u+\partial_{x_2x_2}u=0$ has *parabolic degeneracy* (characteristics are parabolas tangent to the line). Both reduce to Euler-Poisson-Darboux equations $\partial_{\tau\tau}u\pm\partial_{x_2x_2}u+\frac\beta\tau\partial_\tau u=0$, with $\beta=\frac13$ and $\beta=-\frac14$ respectively. ([Chen, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769)) Well-posedness results have also been proved for fractional elliptic problems of Tricomi-Gellerstedt-Keldysh type. ([Ruzhansky-Torebek-Turmetov](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03479))
- **The Tricomi problem.** For the Frankl (Chaplygin) operator $Lu=K(y)u_{xx}+u_{yy}$ with $K(y)y>0$ for $y\ne0$ and $K'>0$, take $\Omega$ bounded by an elliptic arc $\Gamma_0$ in $y>0$ and two characteristics $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ in $y<0$. The Tricomi problem is $Lu=f$ in $\Omega$, $u=g$ on $\Gamma_0\cup\Gamma_1$: Dirichlet data on only part of the boundary (an "open" problem). It is well posed under conditions such as star-shapedness of $\Gamma_0$ or a Frankl-type condition on $K$, whereas "closed" problems with data on the whole boundary are generally ill posed for strong solutions. Uniqueness proofs typically use Friedrichs' $abc$-method with Morawetz multipliers $av+bv_x+cv_y$. ([Perinati et al., §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.06910))
- **Morawetz's theorem on shockless airfoils.** Morawetz showed that specially designed shockless airfoils cannot in fact prevent shocks: shocks develop from even small disturbances, such as a gust of wind or an imperfection in the wing. Her 1956 paper is titled "On the non-existence of continuous transonic flows past profiles I". ([Cathleen Synge Morawetz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathleen_Synge_Morawetz)) This opened the problem of developing a theory for transonic flows with shocks. ([Cathleen Synge Morawetz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathleen_Synge_Morawetz)) See [Compressible Euler Equations](node:Compressible%20Euler%20Equations).
- **Shock reflection-diffraction (Chen-Feldman).** A planar shock hitting a wedge of half-angle $\theta_w$ leads, in self-similar variables, to a free-boundary problem for a nonlinear equation of mixed type whose sonic circle separates elliptic and hyperbolic regions. Chen and Feldman proved that if $v_1\le c_1$ (behind-shock speed at most sound speed) a regular reflection solution exists for every $\theta_w$ from the detachment angle $\theta_w^d$ up to $\pi/2$, giving a global entropy solution; the supersonic solution is $C^{1,1}$ but not $C^2$ across the sonic arc, which is optimal. ([Chen, Theorem 3.4 and §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769)) See [MSC 76Lxx - Shock waves and blast waves in fluid mechanics](node:MSC%2076Lxx%20-%20Shock%20waves%20and%20blast%20waves%20in%20fluid%20mechanics).
- **Isometric embedding.** For a surface with metric $g$, the Gauss equation and Codazzi equations for the second fundamental form form a system of mixed elliptic-hyperbolic type determined by the sign of the Gauss curvature $K$. Chen-Slemrod-Wang rewrite Codazzi as momentum balance laws and Gauss as a Bernoulli relation with Chaplygin pressure, so $K>0$, $K<0$, $K=0$ correspond to subsonic, supersonic and sonic flow. In higher dimensions the Gauss-Codazzi-Ricci system has no type, yet $L^p$-bounded ($p>2$) sequences of solutions have weak limits that are again solutions. ([Chen, §4 and Theorem 4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769))

### History
Chen's survey sets mixed-type equations against the elliptic/parabolic/hyperbolic classification as presented in Hadamard's 1923 lectures on the Cauchy problem, a classification into which they do not fit. ([Chen, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769)) Tricomi was the first to study PDEs of mixed type. ([Perinati et al., §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.06910)) Courant-Friedrichs (1948) and von Neumann's 1940s reports on shock reflection set out the transonic and shock problems, and Morawetz's work showed the generic presence of shocks. ([Chen, §§2-3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769); [Cathleen Synge Morawetz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathleen_Synge_Morawetz)) The Tricomi equation is also a limiting form of Chaplygin's equation of gas dynamics. ([Euler-Tricomi equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Tricomi_equation))

### Open problems
- **Transonic flow problems from the 1950s-60s.** Chen states that some fundamental problems for transonic flow posed then remain unsolved, although recent progress has been made. In the same section he describes two such settings governed by nonlinear mixed-type equations: subsonic flow through a de Laval nozzle, where a supersonic bubble with a transonic shock may form and the role of nozzle geometry in creating or (de)stabilizing the shock is not fully understood, and the Morawetz problem for steady subsonic flow past an airfoil, where experiments show a supersonic bubble may form. ([Chen, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769))
- **Multidimensional hyperbolic conservation laws.** Shock reflection-diffraction configurations are building blocks of general solutions of multidimensional hyperbolic conservation laws, whose theory Chen calls "in its infancy". ([Chen, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769)) See [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws).
- **Global isometric embedding for sign-changing curvature.** For surfaces whose Gauss curvature $K$ changes sign, so that the Darboux Monge-Ampère equation is of mixed type, the embedding problem "is still largely open for global results for general $K$", though local results exist. ([Chen, §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769))
- **Unified methods.** Chen names the lack of effective unified approaches for handling elliptic and hyperbolic phases together as a main obstacle, and lists variational approaches for transonic flow and analysis of viscosity, relaxation and numerical methods as directions to develop. ([Chen, §§1, 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06769))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Euler-Tricomi equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Tricomi_equation): the model equation, characteristics and polynomial solutions.
- **Learn:** [Dehua Wang, Euler Equations and Mixed-Type Problems in Gas Dynamics and Geometry (Oxford short course, 2024)](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/inline-files/Euler%20Equations%20and%20Mixed-Type%20Problems%20in%20Gas%20Dynamics%20and%20Geometry%20WANG_Oxford2024.pdf): classification, model equations, transonic flows in nozzles and past obstacles, isometric embedding.
- **Primary:** [Chen, Partial Differential Equations of Mixed Type: Analysis and Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.06769): survey of transonic flow, shock reflection and isometric embedding.
- **Primary:** [Perinati, Imbert-Gérard, Moiola, Stocker, A discontinuous Galerkin method for elliptic-hyperbolic equations: the Tricomi problem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.06910): formulation and well-posedness literature of the Tricomi problem.
- **Further reading:** [Chen, Feldman, The Mathematics of Shock Reflection-Diffraction and von Neumann's Conjectures (Princeton University Press, 2018)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/j.ctt1jktq4b): monograph on the free-boundary theory behind Theorem 3.4 of Chen's survey.
- See also [Mixed-Type Partial Differential Equations](node:Mixed-Type%20Partial%20Differential%20Equations).

## Reference
### Overview
An overdetermined problem prescribes more conditions than are needed to determine a solution, so a solution exists only when the data or the domain satisfy compatibility conditions. In the finite-dimensional model, a linear system with more equations than unknowns is overdetermined; it is usually inconsistent, but can be consistent when some equations are dependent. ([Wikipedia, Overdetermined system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdetermined_system)) In PDE the area has three strands. The first is boundary value problems with extra boundary data, where solvability forces rigidity of the domain: Serrin's problem adds a constant Neumann condition to the [Dirichlet problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem) for $\Delta u=-1$, and only balls admit solutions. ([Nitsch–Trombetti, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1711.10787))

The second strand is systems with more equations than unknowns, where integrability conditions are hidden in the system. Reducing a higher-order system to first order always produces an overdetermined system, and the classical definition of ellipticity fails for such systems unless all integrability conditions are included; Krupchyk, Seiler and Tuomela show that one should "complete first to an involutive system and then check for ellipticity", and that Douglis–Nirenberg weights decide ellipticity in many but not all cases. ([Seiler, Overdetermined Elliptic Systems](https://www.mathematik.uni-kassel.de/~seiler/Papers/HTML/Elliptic.html); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/s10208-004-0161-y)) A third strand is the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem of several complex variables, which MSC2020 files here as 35N15. ([MSC2020, 35N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Nxx))

### Scope
MSC2020 35N lists: 35N05 overdetermined systems of PDEs with constant coefficients; 35N10 overdetermined systems with variable coefficients; 35N15 $\bar\partial$-Neumann problems and formal complexes in the context of PDEs; 35N20 overdetermined initial value problems; 35N25 overdetermined boundary value problems; 35N30 overdetermined initial-boundary value problems; and 35N99. The section header points to 58Hxx, 58J10 and 58J15 for global analysis, and 35N15 cross-refers to 32W05, 32W10 and 58J10. ([MSC2020, 35N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Nxx))

- **vs [32W](node:MSC%2032Wxx%20-%20Differential%20operators%20in%20several%20variables):** 35N15 ($\bar\partial$-Neumann problems and formal complexes in the context of PDEs) carries a "see also" cross-reference to 32W05 and 32W10 (and 58J10). ([MSC2020, 35N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Nxx))
- **vs [58J](node:MSC%2058Jxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20on%20manifolds;%20differential%20operators) and [58H](node:MSC%2058Hxx%20-%20Pseudogroups,%20differentiable%20groupoids%20and%20general%20structures%20on%20manifolds):** the 35N header sends global analysis of overdetermined problems to 58Hxx, 58J10 and 58J15. ([MSC2020, 35N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **Serrin's theorem (35N25).** Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded, open, connected and of class $C^2$, with outer normal $\nu$, and let $u\in C^2(\bar\Omega)$ satisfy $\Delta u=-1$ in $\Omega$, $u=0$ and $\partial_\nu u=c$ on $\partial\Omega$. Then $\Omega$ is a ball of some radius $R$ and, up to translation, $u=(R^2-|x|^2)/(2n)$. Serrin's proof moves hyperplanes and reflects caps (after Alexandrov), using the strong [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle), Hopf's lemma, and a refined Hopf lemma at corner points where the plane meets $\partial\Omega$ orthogonally. ([Nitsch–Trombetti, Theorem 1.1 and §1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1711.10787))
- **Weinberger's proof.** The $P$-function $P=|Du|^2+\tfrac2n u$ satisfies $\Delta P\ge0$ and $P=c^2$ on $\partial\Omega$; the Pohozaev identity gives $(n+2)\int_\Omega u=nc^2|\Omega|$, which rules out $P<c^2$, so $P$ is constant, $D^2u=-\tfrac1n I$, and $\Omega$ is a ball. Payne and Schaefer's duality theorem gives an equivalent formulation: for the torsion function $u$, $\partial_\nu u$ is constant iff every $h\in C(\bar\Omega)$ harmonic in $\Omega$ has equal averages over $\Omega$ and $\partial\Omega$. ([Nitsch–Trombetti, §§1.2, 2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1711.10787))
- **Schiffer's conjecture and the Pompeiu problem.** Schiffer's conjecture: if a bounded simply connected smooth $\Omega$ carries a nontrivial solution of $\Delta u+\lambda u=0$ in $\Omega$ with $\partial_n u=0$ and $u=1$ on $\partial\Omega$ for some $\lambda>0$, then $\Omega$ is a ball. Pompeiu's problem (1929) asks whether a simply connected Lipschitz domain $K$ must be a ball if some nonzero continuous $f$ integrates to zero over every congruent copy of $K$. Williams (1976) showed the two are equivalent for smooth contractible domains. ([Wikipedia, Pompeiu problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeiu_problem))
- **Berestycki–Caffarelli–Nirenberg (BCN) conjecture.** For Lipschitz $f$ and a smooth domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with $\mathbb R^n\setminus\bar\Omega$ connected, if $\Delta u+f(u)=0$, $u>0$ in $\Omega$, $u=0$ and $\partial_\nu u$ constant on $\partial\Omega$ has a bounded solution, then $\Omega$ is a ball, a half-space, a generalized cylinder $B^k\times\mathbb R^{n-k}$, or the complement of one. Sicbaldi disproved it for $n\ge3$ with a periodic perturbation of the cylinder $B^{n-1}\times\mathbb R$ (taking $f(t)=\lambda t$), and Schlenk–Sicbaldi produced a smooth family of rotationally symmetric periodic counterexamples bifurcating from $B^n\times\mathbb R$ for $n\ge2$. ([Ros–Sicbaldi, §1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1202.5167); [Schlenk–Sicbaldi](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.3988)) In the plane, Ros and Sicbaldi prove the conjecture when $\Omega$ lies in a half-plane with $|\nabla u|$ bounded, or when $f(t)\ge\lambda t$ for some $\lambda>0$. ([Ros–Sicbaldi, Theorem 1.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1202.5167)) For epigraphs, Wang and Wei prove $\Omega$ is a half-space when $n=2$, when the graph is globally Lipschitz, or when $n\le8$ and $\partial_{x_n}u>0$, which is sharp by a counterexample for $n\ge9$. ([Wang–Wei](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04680))
- **Involution, Spencer cohomology, Cartan–Kuranishi and Cartan–Kähler (35N05, 35N10).** Spencer cohomology gives an intrinsic definition of involutive symbols and hence of involutive differential equations; Lambe and Seiler express it as a Cotor of comodules. ([Seiler, Spencer cohomology](https://www.mathematik.uni-kassel.de/~seiler/Papers/HTML/Spencer.html)) The Cartan–Kuranishi prolongation theorem says that after finitely many prolongations an exterior differential system either is in involution or is impossible; Kuranishi proved Cartan's conjecture in 1957. ([Wikipedia, Cartan–Kuranishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%E2%80%93Kuranishi_prolongation_theorem)) The Cartan–Kähler theorem then gives existence: for a real-analytic exterior differential system, a connected real-analytic regular $k$-dimensional integral manifold $P$ with $r(P)\ge0$, contained in a real-analytic $R$ of codimension $r(P)$ with $\dim(T_pR\cap H(T_pP))=k+1$, extends to a locally unique $(k+1)$-dimensional integral manifold $P\subseteq X\subseteq R$; the proof uses Cauchy–Kovalevskaya, so analyticity is essential. ([Wikipedia, Cartan–Kähler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%E2%80%93K%C3%A4hler_theorem))
- **The $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem (35N15).** On a domain $\Omega=\{r<0\}\subset\mathbb C^n$, a $(0,1)$-form $\phi$ lies in the domain of $\bar\partial^*$ when $\sum\phi_j\,\partial r/\partial z_j=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. A subelliptic estimate of order $\epsilon>0$ holds at $p\in\partial\Omega$ if $\|\phi\|_\epsilon^2\le C(\|\bar\partial\phi\|^2+\|\bar\partial^*\phi\|^2+\|\phi\|^2)$ for forms supported near $p$ in that domain. At strongly [pseudoconvex](node:Pseudoconvexity) points it holds with $\epsilon=\tfrac12$ (Kohn); Catlin proved it holds for some $\epsilon>0$ on smooth pseudoconvex boundaries of finite type, and conversely that $\epsilon$ bounds the order of contact of complex curves by $1/\epsilon$. Kohn's algorithm builds subelliptic multipliers, starting from $r$ and $\det(\lambda)$, and terminates for real-analytic boundaries. ([Catlin–D'Angelo, Definition 2.1, Proposition 4.1, Theorems 6.1–6.2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0906.0009))

### History
Serrin's paper "A symmetry problem in potential theory" and Weinberger's two-page "Remark on the preceding paper of Serrin" appeared consecutively in Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis 43 (1971), pp. 304–318 and 319–320. ([Crossref, Serrin](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00250468); [Crossref, Weinberger](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00250469)) Later proofs use duality, domain derivatives, and an integral approach through the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. ([Nitsch–Trombetti](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10787)) Pompeiu posed his problem in 1929, and the Cartan–Kuranishi theorem dates from Cartan's attempts in 1946 and Kuranishi's 1957 proof. ([Wikipedia, Pompeiu problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeiu_problem); [Wikipedia, Cartan–Kuranishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan%E2%80%93Kuranishi_prolongation_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Schiffer and Pompeiu conjectures, with reported 2026 counterexamples.** Wikipedia still lists the Pompeiu problem among unsolved problems in geometry. ([Wikipedia, Pompeiu problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeiu_problem)) In August 2026 two arXiv preprints, with no journal reference listed, reported planar counterexamples. Colbrook and Stepaniants construct a bounded, simply connected, non-circular planar domain with real-analytic boundary (the image of the disc under a ten-fold symmetric conformal map) carrying a Neumann eigenfunction constant on the boundary, at wavenumber near $31.967$, by a computer-assisted proof; it also fails the Pompeiu property. ([Colbrook–Stepaniants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01579)) Cao-Labora and de Dios Pont independently construct infinitely many non-disc planar domains with $N$-fold symmetry by a bifurcation argument. ([Cao-Labora–de Dios Pont](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05114)) Until they are refereed, these disproofs are reported and unconfirmed, and both concern planar domains only. ([Colbrook–Stepaniants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01579); [Cao-Labora–de Dios Pont](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05114))
- **Classifying unbounded extremal domains.** Ros and Sicbaldi (2012) ask whether the Schlenk–Sicbaldi Delaunay-type family extends to all parameters $s\in(0,1]$ with a union of balls as $s\to0$; whether a catenoid-like unbounded domain exists in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$; whether ends of finite-topology $f$-extremal domains are asymptotically Delaunay; and whether the Hélein–Hauswirth–Pacard conjecture holds, that half-planes, ball complements and one explicit domain are the only planar domains where the $f=0$ problem is solvable. ([Ros–Sicbaldi](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1202.5167)) Traizet later settled the finite-connectivity case of the last question: an exceptional planar domain whose boundary has finitely many components is, up to similitude, a half-plane, the exterior of a disc, or the domain $|y|<\pi/2+\cosh x$. ([Traizet, Theorem 12](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1301.6927))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020, 35N](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Nxx): the subject codes and cross-references.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Pompeiu problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeiu_problem): Schiffer's conjecture, Williams's equivalence and recent preprints.
- **Learn:** [Nitsch and Trombetti, The classical overdetermined Serrin problem](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1711.10787): survey of Serrin's, Weinberger's and later proofs.
- **Primary:** [Serrin, A symmetry problem in potential theory (1971)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00250468) and [Weinberger, Remark on the preceding paper of Serrin (1971)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00250469).
- **Primary:** [Krupchyk, Seiler and Tuomela, Overdetermined Elliptic Systems](https://www.mathematik.uni-kassel.de/~seiler/Papers/HTML/Elliptic.html): ellipticity after completion to involution.
- **Primary:** [Catlin and D'Angelo, Subelliptic estimates](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0906.0009): the $\bar\partial$-Neumann problem, Kohn's algorithm and finite type.
- **Further reading:** [Seiler, Involution: The Formal Theory of Differential Equations (Springer)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-01287-7): the formal theory of differential equations and its applications in [computer algebra](node:Computer%20Algebra).
references.MSC 35Pxx - Spectral theory and eigenval:
## Reference
### Overview
Spectral theory for PDEs studies the spectrum of differential operators such as the Dirichlet or Neumann Laplacian on a domain and Schrödinger operators $-\Delta+V$ on $\mathbb R^d$: their eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, essential spectrum and asymptotic distribution. Boundary conditions are part of the operator, and the natural framework is a symmetric, continuous, coercive sesquilinear form on a space compactly embedded in $L^2$, which yields a discrete spectrum. ([Laugesen, Spectral Theory of PDE, ch. 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.2344)) Operator-theoretic background: [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory).

Three kinds of question organize the area: direct asymptotics (Weyl's law and its remainder), optimization and estimates (Faber–Krahn, Pólya, Lieb–Thirring), and inverse problems (what the spectrum determines about the domain, Kac's "Can one hear the shape of a drum?"). The inverse question was answered negatively in the plane by Gordon, Webb and Wolpert in 1992. ([Wikipedia, Hearing the shape of a drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_the_shape_of_a_drum); [Gordon–Webb–Wolpert](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207215))

### Scope
MSC2020 35P lists: 35P05 general topics in linear spectral theory for PDEs; 35P10 completeness of eigenfunctions and eigenfunction expansions; 35P15 estimates of eigenvalues; 35P20 asymptotic distributions of eigenvalues; 35P25 scattering theory for PDEs (see also 47A40); 35P30 nonlinear eigenvalue problems and nonlinear spectral theory; and 35P99. The section header refers operator theory to 47Axx, 47Bxx and 47F05. ([MSC2020, 35P](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Pxx))

- **vs [47A](node:MSC%2047Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20of%20linear%20operators)/[47F](node:MSC%2047Fxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20operators):** the 35P header sends operator theory to 47Axx, 47Bxx and 47F05. ([MSC2020, 35P](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Pxx))
- **Scattering:** 35P25 (scattering theory for PDEs) carries a "see also" cross-reference to 47A40. ([MSC2020, 35P](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Pxx))

### Key concepts
- **Discrete spectrum and min-max (35P05, 35P15).** Let $\mathcal K$ be continuously, densely and compactly embedded in a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, and $a$ a continuous symmetric sesquilinear form on $\mathcal K$ with $a(u,u)\ge c\|u\|_{\mathcal K}^2$, $c>0$. Then there are eigenvectors $u_j\in\mathcal K$ forming an orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H$, with eigenvalues $0<\gamma_1\le\gamma_2\le\dots\to\infty$. The eigenvalues are given by the Poincaré principle $\gamma_j=\min_{\dim S=j}\max_{0\ne f\in S}a(f,f)/\|f\|^2$ ($S\subset\mathcal K$), which gives upper bounds, and the Courant maximin principle $\gamma_j=\max_{\dim S=j-1}\min_{0\ne f\perp S}a(f,f)/\|f\|^2$, which gives lower bounds. ([Laugesen, ch. 4 and 9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.2344)) In finite dimensions this is the Courant min-max characterization of the eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix. ([Wikipedia, Courant minimax principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courant_minimax_principle))
- **Weyl's law (35P20).** For a bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, the Dirichlet counting function satisfies $N_D(\lambda)/\lambda^{d/2}\to\omega_d|\Omega|/(2\pi)^d$, where $\omega_d$ is the volume of the unit ball. ([Wikipedia, Weyl law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_law)) For Dirichlet conditions no boundary hypothesis is needed: Rozenblum proved the law for every open set of finite measure, the problem of minimal assumptions having been emphasized by Birman and Solomyak; Frank extends it to Riesz means of $-h^2\Delta_\Omega+V$ with $V_-\in L^{\gamma+d/2}$. ([Frank, Weyl's law under minimal assumptions](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2202.00323))
- **Two-term asymptotics.** Weyl conjectured $N(\lambda)=(2\pi)^{-d}\omega_d|\Omega|\lambda^{d/2}\mp\tfrac14(2\pi)^{1-d}\omega_{d-1}|\partial\Omega|\lambda^{(d-1)/2}+o(\lambda^{(d-1)/2})$, minus for Dirichlet and plus for Neumann. Courant (1922) obtained remainder $O(\lambda^{(d-1)/2}\log\lambda)$; Duistermaat–Guillemin (1975) gave $o(\lambda^{(d-1)/2})$ when periodic bicharacteristics have measure zero; Ivrii (1980) proved the two-term law for domains whose periodic billiard trajectories have measure zero. ([Wikipedia, Weyl law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_law))
- **Faber–Krahn and Pólya (35P15).** For bounded $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, the first Dirichlet eigenvalue is at least that of the ball of equal volume, with equality only for the ball. ([Wikipedia, Faber–Krahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh%E2%80%93Faber%E2%80%93Krahn_inequality)) Pólya's conjecture asserts $N^D_\Omega(\lambda)\le C_d|\Omega|\lambda^{d}\le N^N_\Omega(\lambda)$ for all $\lambda\ge0$ (in the normalization of eigenvalues $\lambda^2$). Pólya proved it for domains that tile $\mathbb R^d$; the Berezin–Li–Yau inequalities give it up to constants, $(d/(d+2))^{d/2}N^D\le C_d|\Omega|\lambda^d\le\tfrac{d+2}2N^N$; Filonov, Levitin, Polterovich and Sher proved the Dirichlet case for balls in all dimensions and the Neumann case for disks. ([Filonov–Levitin–Polterovich–Sher](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.07696))
- **Nodal domains (35P05).** Courant's theorem: the $n$-th eigenfunction has at most $n$ nodal domains. ([Zelditch, Park City lectures §2.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1310.7888)) Pleijel (1956) sharpened this for planar Dirichlet problems: $\limsup_n N_n/n\le4/j^2\approx0.691$, $j$ the first zero of $J_0$. ([Bourgain, On Pleijel's nodal domain theorem](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1308.4422))
- **[Schrödinger operators](node:Mathematical%20Schrödinger%20Operators).** Weyl's criterion: $\lambda\in\sigma_{\rm ess}(T)$ iff there are unit vectors $\psi_n\rightharpoonup0$ with $(T-\lambda)\psi_n\to0$; the essential spectrum is invariant under compact self-adjoint perturbations, and for $-\Delta$ on $H^2(\mathbb R^n)$ it is $[0,\infty)$. ([Wikipedia, Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum)) The Lieb–Thirring inequality bounds the negative eigenvalues: $\sum_j|\lambda_j|^\gamma\le L_{\gamma,n}\int V_-^{\gamma+n/2}$ for $\gamma\ge\tfrac12$ ($n=1$), $\gamma>0$ ($n=2$), $\gamma\ge0$ ($n\ge3$), and these ranges cannot be relaxed. ([Wikipedia, Lieb–Thirring inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieb%E2%80%93Thirring_inequality))
- **Isospectrality (inverse problems).** Milnor (1964) found isospectral non-isometric 16-dimensional flat tori; Gordon, Webb and Wolpert extended Sunada's method to produce isospectral, simply connected, non-isometric planar domains. Zelditch showed the answer becomes positive for certain convex planar domains with analytic boundary. ([Gordon–Webb–Wolpert](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207215); [Wikipedia, Hearing the shape of a drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_the_shape_of_a_drum)) See [Spectral Geometry](node:Spectral%20Geometry).

### History
Weyl found the leading eigenvalue asymptotics in 1911 for $d=2,3$ and gave a variational proof in 1912. ([Wikipedia, Weyl law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_law)) Rayleigh conjectured the Faber–Krahn inequality, which Faber and Krahn proved independently. ([Wikipedia, Faber–Krahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh%E2%80%93Faber%E2%80%93Krahn_inequality)) Kac's 1966 article, with a phrase due to Bers, popularized the inverse problem, and Lieb and Thirring proved their inequality in 1976 for the stability of matter. ([Wikipedia, Hearing the shape of a drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_the_shape_of_a_drum); [Wikipedia, Lieb–Thirring inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieb%E2%80%93Thirring_inequality))

### Open problems
- **Pólya's conjecture.** For general domains only weakened versions, the Berezin–Li–Yau and Kröger inequalities above, are known; Filonov et al. also state that it "has so far remained open for Euclidean balls, including planar disks", and they settle the Dirichlet case for balls and the Neumann case for disks. ([Filonov–Levitin–Polterovich–Sher](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.07696)) A July 2026 arXiv preprint by Y. Li, with no journal reference listed, reports a proof of the Neumann inequality for balls in every dimension $d\ge2$; this is reported and unconfirmed. ([Li, Pólya's conjecture for the Neumann eigenvalues on Euclidean balls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25958))
- **Two-term Weyl law and Ivrii's conjecture.** The two-term law "remains open in full generality"; Ivrii conjectured that periodic billiard trajectories have measure zero in every bounded Euclidean domain with smooth boundary, which would remove his hypothesis. ([Filonov–Levitin–Polterovich–Sher](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.07696); [Wikipedia, Weyl law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_law))
- **Inverse spectral problems.** It is not known whether two non-convex analytic planar domains can be isospectral. ([Wikipedia, Hearing the shape of a drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_the_shape_of_a_drum))
- **Sharp constants.** Finding the best Lieb–Thirring constant $L_{\gamma,n}$ is "still partly open"; for $n=1$ and $\gamma<\tfrac32$ Lieb and Thirring conjectured an explicit sharp value. For nodal domains it has been conjectured that $2/\pi$ (attained by rectangles) is the optimal Pleijel constant, while Bourgain's bound improves $(2/j)^2$ only by about $3\times10^{-9}$. ([Wikipedia, Lieb–Thirring inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieb%E2%80%93Thirring_inequality); [Bourgain](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1308.4422))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Weyl law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_law): leading and two-term asymptotics, remainder history.
- **Learn:** [Laugesen, Spectral Theory of Partial Differential Equations: Lecture Notes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.2344): discrete spectral theorem via forms, variational principles, Weyl's law and Pólya's conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Gordon, Webb and Wolpert, One cannot hear the shape of a drum](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207215): isospectral planar domains (Bull. AMS 1992).
- **Primary:** [Filonov, Levitin, Polterovich and Sher, Pólya's conjecture for Euclidean balls](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.07696): state of Pólya's conjecture and two-term Weyl law.
- **Primary:** [Frank, Weyl's law under minimal assumptions](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2202.00323): Dirichlet Weyl law on arbitrary open sets.
- **Further reading:** [Henrot, Extremum Problems for Eigenvalues of Elliptic Operators (Birkhäuser, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/3-7643-7706-2): monograph on extremal eigenvalue problems for elliptic operators.
