## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35Qxx collects PDEs of mathematical physics and other areas of application, and is cross-referenced to the model equations 35J05, 35J10, 35K05 and 35L05. Its subcodes name specific equations: Boltzmann (35Q20), Navier–Stokes (35Q30), Euler (35Q31), time-dependent Schrödinger and Dirac (35Q41), transport (35Q49), soliton equations (35Q51), KdV (35Q53), NLS (35Q55), Ginzburg–Landau (35Q56), Maxwell (35Q61), Einstein (35Q76), Vlasov (35Q83) and Fokker–Planck (35Q84). They also name areas of application: fluid mechanics (35Q35), quantum mechanics (35Q40), optics and electromagnetism (35Q60), relativity (35Q75), [Statistical Mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics) (35Q82), mean field games (35Q89), biology and chemistry (35Q92), and control (35Q93). Most named equations carry cross-references to the physics sections, for example 76D05 for Navier–Stokes, 82C40 for Boltzmann, 81Q05 for Schrödinger, and 37K10 for KdV and NLS. ([MSC2020 35Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Qxx))

The analytic questions are those of [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) in general (existence, uniqueness, regularity, long-time behaviour), but each model brings its own structure: incompressibility and energy for fluids, dispersion and [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws) for Schrödinger and KdV, collisions for kinetic equations. Tao's monograph on nonlinear dispersive equations, classified under 35Q53 and 35Q55, organizes that subject around scaling, local existence, conservation laws and global existence, decay, scattering, stability and ill-posedness. ([Tao, Nonlinear dispersive equations, Contents](https://math.ucla.edu/~tao/preprints/chapter.pdf))

### Scope
- **Fluids (35Q30, 35Q31, 35Q35):** the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations $\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=\nu\Delta u-\nabla p+f$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in $\mathbb R^n$ ($n=2,3$), with $\nu>0$; setting $\nu=0$ gives the Euler equations. ([Fefferman, Clay problem description](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf)) See [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations), [Fluid Dynamics](node:Fluid%20Dynamics) and [MSC 76Dxx - Incompressible viscous fluids](node:MSC%2076Dxx%20-%20Incompressible%20viscous%20fluids).
- **Kinetic equations (35Q20, 35Q83, 35Q84):** the [Boltzmann Equation](node:Boltzmann%20Equation) $\partial_tf+\frac pm\cdot\nabla_xf+F\cdot\nabla_pf=(\partial_tf)_{\rm coll}$ is a nonlinear integro-differential equation for a phase-space density $f(r,p,t)$. ([Wikipedia: Boltzmann equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann_equation)) The statistical-mechanics side is [MSC 82Cxx - Time-dependent statistical mechanics (dynamic and nonequilibrium)](node:MSC%2082Cxx%20-%20Time-dependent%20statistical%20mechanics%20%28dynamic%20and%20nonequilibrium%29). ([MSC2020 35Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Qxx))
- **Dispersive and quantum equations (35Q40, 35Q41, 35Q51–35Q55):** NLS $iu_t+\tfrac12\Delta u=\mu|u|^{p-1}u$ with $\mu=+1$ defocusing and $\mu=-1$ focusing, and the nonlinear version of the [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation), $\Box u=\mu|u|^{p-1}u$. ([Tao, §3](https://math.ucla.edu/~tao/preprints/chapter.pdf)) The linear case is the [Schrödinger Equation](node:Schrödinger%20Equation); the relativistic one is the [Dirac Equation](node:Dirac%20Equation). For dynamical-systems aspects of KdV and NLS the entry points to 37K10, see [MSC 37Kxx - Dynamical system aspects of infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian and Lagrangian systems](node:MSC%2037Kxx%20-%20Dynamical%20system%20aspects%20of%20infinite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems). ([MSC2020 35Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Qxx))
- **Fields and geometry (35Q60, 35Q61, 35Q75, 35Q76):** the Maxwell and Einstein equations as PDE problems; see [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations) and [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations). ([MSC2020 35Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Qxx))

### Key concepts
- **Leray weak solutions and the Clay formulation.** Integrating against divergence-free test fields gives a weak formulation that makes sense for $u\in L^2$. Leray (1934) proved that the 3D Navier–Stokes equations always have a weak solution with suitable growth properties; uniqueness of [weak solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) was not known when Fefferman wrote (see Open problems for the forced counterexample). In 2D global smooth solutions have long been known (Ladyzhenskaya). In 3D, smooth solutions exist globally for small data and locally in time for large data, and at a finite blowup time the velocity must become unbounded. ([Fefferman](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf))
- **Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg partial regularity.** For a suitable weak solution of Navier–Stokes, the singular set $E$ (points where $u$ is unbounded in every neighbourhood) has $\mathcal P^1(E)=0$, where $\mathcal P^1$ is the one-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure built from cylinders $B_r\times I_{r^2}$. In particular $E$ contains no space-time curve $x=\varphi(t)$. Such solutions exist for data satisfying the decay conditions. Fefferman calls this "the best partial regularity theorem known so far." ([Fefferman](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf))
- **Euler equations: blowup criteria, non-uniqueness, singularities.** If a smooth Euler solution blows up at $T<\infty$, then $\int_0^T\sup_x|\omega(x,t)|\,dt=\infty$ (Beale–Kato–Majda). Weak Euler solutions are strikingly non-unique: Scheffer and Shnirelman built weak solutions with compact support in space-time. ([Fefferman](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf)) Elgindi proved that $C^{1,\alpha}$ solutions of the 3D Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$, which are locally well posed for suitably decaying data, can form singularities in finite time. ([Elgindi, arXiv:1904.04795](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04795))
- **Onsager's conjecture.** Isett constructed weak solutions of 3D incompressible Euler in $C_tC^\alpha_x$ for every $\alpha<1/3$ that have compact time support and do not conserve kinetic energy. Combined with earlier results that energy is conserved for $\alpha>1/3$, this settles Onsager's conjecture that $\alpha=1/3$ is the threshold. The proof uses convex integration, a gluing technique and Mikado flows. ([Isett, arXiv:1608.08301](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08301)) This connects to [Turbulence](node:Turbulence).
- **Energy-critical NLS.** Colliander, Keel, Staffilani, Takaoka and Tao proved global well-posedness, scattering and global $L^{10}_{t,x}$ bounds for energy-class solutions of the defocusing quintic NLS on $\mathbb R^{1+3}$. This extended the radial results of Bourgain and Grillakis, using induction on energy and an interaction Morawetz estimate. ([CKSTT, arXiv:math/0402129](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0402129))
- **KdV and integrability.** The KdV equation $\phi_t-6\phi\phi_x+\phi_{xxx}=0$ has solitons $\phi=-\tfrac c2\operatorname{sech}^2\!\big(\tfrac{\sqrt c}2(x-ct-a)\big)$ and infinitely many conserved quantities. It has the Lax form $L_t=[L,A]$ with $L=-\partial_x^2+\phi$, so the spectrum of $L$ is time-independent. Gardner, Greene, Kruskal and Miura solved it by the inverse scattering transform (1967). ([Wikipedia: KdV equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation)) Tao's chapter 4 treats its low-regularity existence theory and symplectic non-squeezing. ([Tao, Ch. 4](https://math.ucla.edu/~tao/preprints/chapter.pdf))
- **Boltzmann equation.** DiPerna and Lions proved global existence and weak stability for the Cauchy problem (*Annals of Math.* 1989), and Gressman and Strain constructed global classical solutions without angular cut-off (*JAMS* 2011). ([Wikipedia: Boltzmann equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann_equation))

### History
The Navier–Stokes equations were written in the nineteenth century. ([Clay Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/)) KdV was introduced by Boussinesq in 1877 and rediscovered by Korteweg and de Vries in 1895. Zabusky and Kruskal's 1965 computations revealed solitons, and the inverse scattering transform followed in 1967. ([Wikipedia: KdV equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation)) Leray's weak solutions date from 1934 and Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg from 1982. ([Fefferman, references](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (Clay Millennium Problem).** Prove, for $\nu>0$ and $n=3$, either global existence of smooth finite-energy solutions for all smooth divergence-free data (on $\mathbb R^3$ with decay, or periodic), or a breakdown example. Fefferman states that these problems "are also open and very important for the Euler equations." ([Fefferman](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf)) Elgindi's finite-time singularities concern the $C^{1,\alpha}$ local solutions, not smooth data. ([Elgindi, arXiv:1904.04795](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04795)) The Clay page lists the problem as active and says no proof has been found of the most basic questions of existence and uniqueness. ([Clay Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/))
- **Uniqueness of Leray weak solutions without force.** Whether Leray–Hopf solutions form a uniqueness class has been an open problem since Leray. Albritton, Brué and Colombo answered it in the negative for the forced equations: there are $T>0$, a force $f\in L^1_tL^2_x$ and two distinct suitable Leray–Hopf solutions on $\mathbb R^3\times(0,T)$ with initial data $u_0\equiv0$. They state that removing the force is an open problem. ([Albritton–Brué–Colombo, arXiv:2112.03116](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.03116)) Fefferman adds that going beyond the Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg theorem "appears to be very hard." ([Fefferman](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf))
- **Boltzmann well-posedness.** "The problem of existence and uniqueness of solutions is still not fully resolved." ([Wikipedia: Boltzmann equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann_equation))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 35Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Qxx): official list of subcodes and cross-references.
- **Reference:** [Korteweg–De Vries equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation): solitons, Lax pair, inverse scattering.
- **Learn:** [Tao, Nonlinear dispersive equations: local and global analysis (CBMS lectures)](https://math.ucla.edu/~tao/preprints/chapter.pdf): NLS, NLW, KdV and wave maps from Strichartz estimates to energy-critical global theory.
- **Primary:** [Fefferman, Existence and smoothness of the Navier–Stokes equation (Clay)](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf): official problem statement and survey of partial results.
- **Primary:** [Isett, A proof of Onsager's conjecture (arXiv:1608.08301)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08301): convex integration for Euler.
- **Primary:** [Colliander–Keel–Staffilani–Takaoka–Tao (arXiv:math/0402129)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0402129): energy-critical NLS in $\mathbb R^3$.
- **Further reading:** [Tao, Nonlinear dispersive equations](https://math.ucla.edu/~tao/preprints/chapter.pdf): graduate monograph based on NSF-CBMS lectures (2005).
references.MSC 35Rxx - Miscellaneous topics in part:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35R, "Miscellaneous topics in partial differential equations", is the part of [MSC 35 - Partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations) that collects [PDE](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) topics defined by the setting or the question rather than by equation type. Its codes are PDEs on manifolds (35R01), on graphs and networks (35R02), on Heisenberg, Lie and Carnot groups (35R03), with low-regularity coefficients or data (35R05), with measures (35R06), on time scales (35R07), integro-PDEs (35R09), partial functional-differential equations (35R10), fractional PDEs (35R11), impulsive (35R12) and fuzzy (35R13) PDEs, PDEs on infinite-dimensional spaces (35R15), operator PDEs (35R20), ill-posed problems (35R25), inverse problems (35R30), free boundary (35R35) and moving boundary (35R37) problems, partial differential inequalities (35R45), PDEs of infinite order (35R50), PDEs with randomness and stochastic PDEs (35R60), and PDEs with multivalued right-hand sides (35R70). ([MSC2020 35Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Rxx))

Four of these codes are treated below: inverse problems, where one recovers coefficients from boundary measurements; [free boundary problems](node:Free%20Boundary%20Problems), whose interfaces are a priori unknown and whose central challenge is "to understand the structure and regularity of free boundaries"; nonlocal and fractional equations; and stochastic PDEs. ([Ros-Oton, overview](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00992); [Kwaśnicki](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.07356); [SPDE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_partial_differential_equation))

### Scope
- **Neighbours 58J and 32W.** The 35R heading sends equations on manifolds to 32Wxx and 58Jxx (35R01 is "see also" 53Cxx too), and manifolds of solutions to 58Bxx; see [MSC 58Jxx - Partial differential equations on manifolds; differential operators](node:MSC%2058Jxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20on%20manifolds;%20differential%20operators). ([MSC2020 35Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Rxx))
- **Neighbour 60H.** Stochastic PDEs are cross-referred to 60H15 from both the heading and 35R60; see [MSC 60Hxx - Stochastic analysis](node:MSC%2060Hxx%20-%20Stochastic%20analysis). ([MSC2020 35Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Rxx))
- **Neighbours 45K and 47.** Integro-PDEs (35R09) cross-refer to 34K30 and 45K05; operator PDEs (35R20) cross-refer to 34Gxx and operator-theoretic codes in 47 (47A50, 47D03, 47D06, 47D09, 47H20, 47Jxx). ([MSC2020 35Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Rxx))

### Key concepts
- **Fractional Laplacian (35R11).** For $0<\alpha<2$, the fractional Laplacian on $\mathbb R^d$ can be defined by Fourier multipliers, singular integrals, semigroups, Bochner subordination or harmonic extensions; Kwaśnicki shows that these definitions agree, with common domains and identical action, on $L^p$, on continuous functions vanishing at infinity, and on bounded uniformly continuous functions. ([Kwaśnicki](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.07356)) See also [Fractional Calculus](node:Fractional%20Calculus) and [Integro-Differential Operators](node:Integro-Differential%20Operators).
- **Caffarelli–Silvestre extension.** For $a\in(-1,1)$ and $s=(1-a)/2\in(0,1)$, let $u(x,y)$ solve $\operatorname{div}(y^a\nabla u)=0$ for $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $y>0$, with $u(x,0)=f(x)$. Then
  $$C\,(-\Delta)^sf=\lim_{y\to0^+}\bigl(-y^a u_y\bigr)$$
  for a constant $C=C(n,s)$, so the nonlocal operator becomes a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map of a local degenerate elliptic equation in one more variable; for $s=\tfrac12$ this is the harmonic extension. ([Caffarelli–Silvestre, eqs. 1.4–1.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0608640); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608640))
- **Boundary regularity for the fractional [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem).** Let $s\in(0,1)$, $g\in L^\infty(\Omega)$, and $u\in H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ a weak solution of $(-\Delta)^su=g$ in $\Omega$ with $u\equiv0$ in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega$. If $\Omega$ is bounded Lipschitz with the exterior ball condition, $\|u\|_{C^s(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|g\|_{L^\infty}$. If $\partial\Omega\in C^{1,1}$ and $\delta=\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,\partial\Omega)$, then $u/\delta^s$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$ and lies in $C^\alpha(\overline\Omega)$ for some $\alpha<\min\{s,1-s\}$. ([Ros-Oton–Serra, Proposition 1.1 and Theorem 1.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1207.5985))
- **Obstacle problem (35R35).** Minimize $\int|\nabla v|^2$ over $v$ with given boundary values and $v\ge\varphi$; equivalently $\int\nabla u\cdot\nabla(v-u)\ge0$ for all admissible $v$. The solution is $C^{1,1}$ when the obstacle is (Frehse), and by Caffarelli's theory the free boundary is $C^{1,\alpha}$ outside a set of singular points. ([Obstacle problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstacle_problem)) The singular set can be $(n-1)$-dimensional, but Figalli, Ros-Oton and Serra proved that generically it has zero $\mathcal H^{n-4}$ measure, so for $n\le4$ the free boundary is generically $C^\infty$, solving Schaeffer's conjecture. ([Figalli–Ros-Oton–Serra](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.00714)) The [Stefan Free Boundary Problem](node:Stefan%20Free%20Boundary%20Problem) is the classical moving-boundary (35R37) model.
- **Calderón's inverse problem (35R30).** For a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ and conductivity $\gamma$, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:u|_{\partial\Omega}\mapsto\gamma\partial_\nu u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for $\nabla\cdot(\gamma\nabla u)=0$ is the data; the problem is to recover $\gamma$ from $\Lambda_\gamma$. Sylvester and Uhlmann proved uniqueness for smooth conductivities using complex [geometrical optics](node:Geometrical%20Optics) solutions; Haberman–Tataru reached $C^1$ conductivities and Haberman $W^{1,n}\cap L^\infty$ for $n=3,4$; Caro and Rogers proved uniqueness for Lipschitz conductivities bounded below in all $n\ge3$, which together with Haberman's $n=3,4$ work confirms a conjecture of Uhlmann; counterexamples to unique continuation suggest uniqueness might fail for Hölder conductivities; in two dimensions Astala–Päivärinta solved uniqueness. ([Caro–Rogers, introduction](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1411.8001); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.8001)) The problem, posed by Calderón in 1980 and underlying electrical impedance tomography, is severely ill-posed (35R25). ([Electrical impedance tomography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_impedance_tomography)) Compare [Integral Equation Inverse Problems](node:Integral%20Equation%20Inverse%20Problems) and [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems).
- **Stochastic PDEs (35R60).** The stochastic [heat equation](node:Heat%20Equation) $\partial_tu=\Delta u+\xi$ with space-time white noise $\xi$ has solutions only almost $\tfrac12$-Hölder in space, and less regular in time, in one dimension, but in dimension two and higher solutions are random distributions, so nonlinear terms such as $P(u)$ require renormalisation. ([SPDE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_partial_differential_equation)) Hairer's theory of regularity structures solves such singular semilinear equations by local expansions and renormalisation with diverging counterterms, and constructs a Markov process symmetric for the finite-volume $\Phi^4_3$ measure. ([Hairer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.5113)) See [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus).

### History
Calderón posed the inverse conductivity problem in 1980; in impedance imaging only objects above a size set by the number of electrodes and the measurement precision can be distinguished. ([Electrical impedance tomography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_impedance_tomography)) The obstacle problem grew out of Stampacchia's variational inequalities; Frehse proved $C^{1,1}$ regularity in 1972 and Caffarelli surveyed the free-boundary theory in "The obstacle problem revisited" (1998). ([Obstacle problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstacle_problem)) The Caffarelli–Silvestre extension was posted in 2006, and interest in nonlocal operators has grown since, and Schaeffer's 1974 generic-regularity conjecture was settled for $n\le4$ in 2019. ([Caffarelli–Silvestre](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608640); [Garofalo](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.03347); [Figalli–Ros-Oton–Serra](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.00714))

### Open problems
- **Calderón problem with local partial data.** For a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$, an arbitrary nonempty open $\Gamma\subset\partial\Omega$ and $q_1,q_2\in L^\infty(\Omega)$, show that equality of the Cauchy data sets on $\Gamma$ of $-\Delta+q_1$ and $-\Delta+q_2$ implies $q_1=q_2$; and, for $n\ge2$ with arbitrary disjoint open $\Gamma_D,\Gamma_N\subset\partial\Omega$, the analogous question with Dirichlet data on $\Gamma_D$ and Neumann data on $\Gamma_N$. Kenig and Salo list these as open at the time of writing (2013), noting that the disjoint-sets case is open even for the linearized problem. ([Kenig–Salo, §8 Questions 1–2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.4218))
- **Optimal stability with partial data.** Full-data stability for Calderón-type problems is in general logarithmic, and this is optimal, but the Carleman-estimate approach to partial data gives log-log or weaker moduli; Kenig and Salo ask for the optimal stability of the Kenig–Sjöstrand–Uhlmann partial-data uniqueness result. ([Kenig–Salo, §8 Question 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.4218))
- **Structure of free boundaries.** Understanding the structure and regularity of free boundaries is described as the most important mathematical challenge of the field; the Figalli–Ros-Oton–Serra generic-smoothness result covers dimensions $n\le4$. ([Ros-Oton, overview](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00992); [Figalli–Ros-Oton–Serra](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.00714))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Obstacle problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstacle_problem): variational formulation, regularity of solutions and free boundaries.
- **Learn:** [Garofalo, Fractional thoughts](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.03347): didactic introduction to the fractional Laplacian and the extension method.
- **Primary:** [Kenig–Salo, Recent progress in the Calderón problem with partial data](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.4218): survey ending with a list of open problems.
- **Primary:** [Caro–Rogers, Global uniqueness for the Calderón problem with Lipschitz conductivities](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.8001): state of the art on regularity in $n\ge3$.
- **Further reading:** [Caffarelli–Salsa, A Geometric Approach to Free Boundary Problems (AMS GSM 68, 2005)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/068): standard graduate text on free boundaries.
- **Further reading:** [Isakov, Inverse Problems for Partial Differential Equations (Springer, Applied Mathematical Sciences, 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-51658-5): standard monograph on inverse problems.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 35Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Rxx): official code list.
references.MSC 35Sxx - Pseudodifferential operators:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 35S covers [pseudodifferential operators](node:Pseudodifferential%20Operators) and related generalizations as tools for PDEs, built on [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): pseudodifferential operators as generalizations of differential operators (35S05), initial, boundary and initial-boundary value problems for PDEs with pseudodifferential operators (35S10, 35S15, 35S16), Fourier integral operators applied to PDEs (35S30), topological aspects such as intersection cohomology and stratified sets (35S35), and paradifferential operators (35S50). The heading sends operator theory to 47G30 and 58J40. ([MSC2020 35Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Sxx))

The subject began in the mid-1960s with Kohn, Nirenberg, Hörmander, Unterberger and Bokobza; the class contains differential operators, inverses of elliptic operators and the operators of the second proof of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem via K-theory. ([Pseudo-differential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-differential_operator)) Fourier integral operators extend the calculus to operators that move singularities, such as solution operators of the [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation), and the wave front set, a notion of microlocal analysis, records where and in which direction a distribution is singular. ([Fourier integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_integral_operator); [Wave front set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_front_set))

### Scope
- **Neighbour 47G.** 35S05 is "see also" 47G30 and 47L80: the operator-theoretic study of pseudodifferential operators belongs to [MSC 47Gxx - Integral, integro-differential, and pseudodifferential operators](node:MSC%2047Gxx%20-%20Integral,%20integro-differential,%20and%20pseudodifferential%20operators), while 35S is their use for PDEs. ([MSC2020 35Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Sxx))
- **Neighbour 58J.** 35S05 and 35S30 cross-refer to 58J40, and 35S35 to 58J15, the global-analysis setting on manifolds of [MSC 58Jxx - Partial differential equations on manifolds; differential operators](node:MSC%2058Jxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20on%20manifolds;%20differential%20operators). ([MSC2020 35Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Sxx))
- **Neighbours 32W, 32C, 32S, 43A.** 35S05 also points to 32W25 (several complex variables), 35S35 to 32C38, 32S40, 32S60, and 35S30 to 43A32. ([MSC2020 35Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Sxx))

### Key concepts
- **Symbols and quantization.** For $m\in\mathbb R$, $S^m=S^m_{1,0}$ is the set of $\sigma\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n)$ with $|D_x^\alpha D_\xi^\beta\sigma(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}\langle\xi\rangle^{m-|\beta|}$; for $0\le\delta<\rho\le1$, $S^m_{\rho,\delta}$ allows $\langle\xi\rangle^{m-\rho|\beta|+\delta|\alpha|}$. The operator is $(T_\sigma\varphi)(x)=(2\pi)^{-n/2}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}\sigma(x,\xi)\hat\varphi(\xi)\,d\xi$ on Schwartz functions; polynomial symbols give differential operators, and $T_\sigma:H^s\to H^{s-m}$ is bounded on [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) for $\sigma\in S^m$. ([Ma, Definitions 2.1, 2.4, 2.7, Theorem 2.17](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12839)) The Weyl quantization (in Ma's semiclassical form) uses the midpoint $a\big(\tfrac{x+y}2,\xi\big)$ in the kernel instead of $a(x,\xi)$; it goes back to Weyl (1927) and underlies the phase-space formulation of quantum mechanics of Groenewold and Moyal. ([Ma, Definition 7.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12839); [Weyl quantization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_quantization))
- **Symbolic calculus.** If $a\in S^{m_1}$, $b\in S^{m_2}$, then $T_a\circ T_b=T_{a\#b}$ with $a\#b\in S^{m_1+m_2}$ and
  $$a\#b\sim\sum_\alpha\frac1{\alpha!}\,\partial_\xi^\alpha a\;D_x^\alpha b,\qquad a\#b=ab+\tfrac1i\nabla_\xi a\cdot\nabla_x b \bmod S^{m_1+m_2-2};$$
  the adjoint and transpose of $T_a$ are pseudodifferential operators of the same order, with asymptotic symbol expansions of the same type. ([Ma, Theorems 5.3 and 5.7, eq. 5.11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12839))
- **Ellipticity and parametrices.** $a\in S^m$ is elliptic if $|a(x,\xi)|\ge C\langle\xi\rangle^m$ for $|\xi|\ge R$. Then $T_a$ has a parametrix $S\in\Psi^{-m}$ with $ST_a-I,\ T_aS-I\in\Psi^{-\infty}$, and conversely an operator with a parametrix is elliptic. Pseudodifferential operators are pseudolocal, $\operatorname{sing\,supp}Tu\subset\operatorname{sing\,supp}u$, and microlocal, $\mathrm{WF}(Au)\subset\mathrm{WF}(u)$; for every $A\in\Psi^{+\infty}$ and $u\in\mathcal S'$ one has $\mathrm{WF}(u)\subset\mathrm{WF}(Au)\cup\operatorname{Char}A$, and for elliptic $A$ this becomes $\mathrm{WF}(Au)=\mathrm{WF}(u)$, which is microlocal elliptic regularity (compare [Elliptic Operators on Manifolds](node:Elliptic%20Operators%20on%20Manifolds) and [Hypoelliptic Operators](node:Hypoelliptic%20Operators)). ([Ma, Definition 6.4, Theorems 6.6–6.7, 2.24, 8.17, Corollary 9.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12839))
- **$L^2$ bounds and Gårding.** Order-zero operators ($a\in S^0$) are bounded on $L^2$. The Calderón–Vaillancourt theorem extends this to $a\in S^0_{0,0}$, with $\|T_a\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le C\max_{|\alpha+\beta|\le N}\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta a\|_{L^\infty}$. For strongly elliptic $a\in S^{2m}$, Gårding's inequality gives $\operatorname{Re}(T_a\varphi,\varphi)\ge C\|\varphi\|^2_{H^m}-C_s\|\varphi\|^2_{H^{m-s}}$ for every $s\ge\tfrac12$, and the sharp Gårding inequality gives $\operatorname{Re}(T_a\varphi,\varphi)\ge-C\|\varphi\|^2_{H^{m-1/2}}$ when $\operatorname{Re}a\ge0$ for large $|\xi|$. ([Ma, Theorems 6.12, 6.14, 6.18, 6.21](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12839))
- **Propagation of singularities.** If $P\in\Psi^m$ is classical of real principal type with principal symbol $p_m$, $Pu\in C^\infty$ (for $u\in\mathcal S'$, or $u\in\mathcal D'$ with $P$ properly supported), then each null bicharacteristic of $p_m$ lies entirely inside or entirely outside $\mathrm{WF}(u)$. ([Ma, Theorem 9.13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12839))
- **Fourier integral operators (35S30).** $Tf(x)=\int e^{2\pi i\Phi(x,\xi)}a(x,\xi)\hat f(\xi)\,d\xi$ with $\Phi$ real and homogeneous of degree one in $\xi$, $a$ a symbol compactly supported in $x$, and $\det\partial_x\partial_\xi\Phi\ne0$ on the support of $a$; order-zero FIOs are bounded on $L^2$. Hörmander's "Fourier integral operators I" (Acta Math. 127, 1971) founded the theory. ([Fourier integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_integral_operator); [Hörmander 1971](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392052))
- **Boutet de Monvel calculus (35S15).** On a compact manifold $X$ with boundary $Y$, a pseudodifferential $P$ has the transmission property if its truncation $P_+$ maps $C^\infty(X)$ into $C^\infty(X)$. Boutet de Monvel's algebra consists of matrices $\begin{pmatrix}P_++G&K\\T&S\end{pmatrix}$ acting on $C^\infty(X)\oplus C^\infty(Y)$, with $G$ singular Green, $K$ Poisson, $T$ trace and $S$ a pseudodifferential operator on $Y$; it contains the classical differential boundary value problems together with parametrices of elliptic elements. ([Aastrup–Melo–Monthubert–Schrohe, Introduction and §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611336))

### History
Pseudodifferential operators were developed in the mid-1960s and supplied the second proof of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem. ([Pseudo-differential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-differential_operator)) Hörmander coined the term "wave front" around 1970 and published "Fourier integral operators I" in 1971; the wave front set is treated in Chapter VIII of his treatise. ([Wave front set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_front_set); [Hörmander 1971](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392052)) Calderón and Vaillancourt proved their $L^2$ theorem and then generalized it themselves. ([Ma, §6.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12839))

### Open problems
- **Local smoothing conjecture.** For $n\ge2$, Sogge's conjecture asserts $\big(\int_1^2\|e^{it\sqrt{-\Delta}}f\|^p_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}dt\big)^{1/p}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^p_{s_p-\sigma}}$, $s_p=(n-1)|\tfrac12-\tfrac1p|$, for all $\sigma<1/p$ when $2n/(n-1)<p<\infty$ (and $\sigma<s_p$ for $2<p\le2n/(n-1)$). Guth–Wang–Zhang resolved $n=2$; for $n\ge3$ it is known for $p\ge2(n+1)/(n-1)$ (Bourgain–Demeter) and only improved bounds are known below. ([Gao–Liu–Miao–Xi, Conjecture 1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.06870); [Guth–Wang–Zhang](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.10693)) For general Fourier integral operators, Beltran–Hickman–Sogge's variable-coefficient local smoothing estimates are sharp in odd dimensions at that level of generality; for wave equations on compact Riemannian manifolds, Gan–He–Li–Wu obtain sharp estimates when the spatial dimension is odd and only improved estimates in even dimensions. ([Beltran–Hickman–Sogge](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.06910); [Gan–He–Li–Wu](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05973))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Pseudo-differential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-differential_operator): definitions, properties, history.
- **Learn:** [Ma, Lecture notes for pseudodifferential operators and microlocal analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12839): symbols, calculus, parametrices, Calderón–Vaillancourt, Gårding, wave front sets, propagation of singularities.
- **Primary:** [Hörmander, Fourier integral operators I, Acta Math. 127 (1971) 79–183](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392052): founding paper on FIOs.
- **Further reading:** [Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators III: Pseudo-Differential Operators (Springer)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-49938-1): standard treatise.
- **Further reading:** [Grigis–Sjöstrand, Microlocal Analysis for Differential Operators: An Introduction (CUP, 1994)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511721441): graduate introduction.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 35Sxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Sxx): official code list.

## Reference
### Overview
A dynamical system consists of a phase space of possible states and a law of time evolution, with discrete or continuous, reversible or irreversible time; Katok and Hasselblatt restrict to deterministic, time-invariant laws, where the future depends only on the initial state and the elapsed time. ([Katok–Hasselblatt, Introduction](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-the-modern-theory-of-dynamical-systems/introduction/B1E86AEBAEAD07CF09DAB6443539A310)) Formally a continuous-time system is a tuple $(T,M,\Phi)$ with $T$ a real interval, $M$ a manifold and $\Phi$ continuous; it is a flow when $T=\mathbb R$ and a semiflow when $T=[0,\infty)$. ([Dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system)) See [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems).

[Ergodic theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) studies the statistical properties of deterministic systems through invariant measures; its development was first motivated by statistical physics. ([Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory)) MSC2020 class 37-XX combines both viewpoints and cross-references 26A18, 28Dxx, 34Cxx, 34Dxx, 35Bxx, 46Lxx, 58Jxx and 70-XX. ([MSC2020 37-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37-XX))

The research themes of the field cut across its subfields: hyperbolicity and structural stability (the Palis–Smale and Palis conjectures), entropy and classification of measure-preserving systems, SRB measures for chaotic attractors, KAM theory for nearly integrable Hamiltonian systems, rigidity of homogeneous and higher-rank actions, and renormalization in one-dimensional real and complex dynamics. ([Berger, Lectures on structural stability, arXiv:1703.00092](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092); [Measure-preserving dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_dynamical_system); [SRB measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRB_measure); [KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem); [Ratner's theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratner%27s_theorems); [Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set); [Feigenbaum constants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feigenbaum_constants))

### Scope
- **Measure and topology:** [37Axx ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037Axx%20-%20Ergodic%20theory) (see also 28Dxx) and [37Bxx topological dynamics](node:MSC%2037Bxx%20-%20Topological%20dynamics). ([MSC2020 37-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37-XX))
- **Smooth theory:** [37Cxx smooth systems](node:MSC%2037Cxx%20-%20Smooth%20dynamical%20systems%20-%20general%20theory) (see also 34Cxx, 34Dxx), [37Dxx hyperbolic behavior](node:MSC%2037Dxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20with%20hyperbolic%20behavior), [37Exx low-dimensional systems](node:MSC%2037Exx%20-%20Low-dimensional%20dynamical%20systems), and [37Gxx bifurcation theory](node:MSC%2037Gxx%20-%20Local%20and%20nonlocal%20bifurcation%20theory%20for%20dynamical%20systems) (see also 34C23, 34K18). ([MSC2020 37-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37-XX))
- **Complex, random and arithmetic settings:** [37Fxx](node:MSC%2037Fxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20over%20complex%20numbers) (see also 30D05, 32H50), [37Hxx](node:MSC%2037Hxx%20-%20Random%20dynamical%20systems), and [37Pxx](node:MSC%2037Pxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20and%20non-Archimedean%20dynamical%20systems) (see also 11S82, 37A44). ([MSC2020 37-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37-XX))
- **Hamiltonian and infinite-dimensional:** [37Jxx](node:MSC%2037Jxx%20-%20Dynamical%20aspects%20of%20finite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems) (see also 53Dxx, 70Fxx, 70Hxx), [37Kxx](node:MSC%2037Kxx%20-%20Dynamical%20system%20aspects%20of%20infinite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems), and [37Lxx](node:MSC%2037Lxx%20-%20Infinite-dimensional%20dissipative%20dynamical%20systems) (both see also 35Qxx). ([MSC2020 37-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37-XX))
- **Computation and applications:** [37Mxx](node:MSC%2037Mxx%20-%20Approximation%20methods%20and%20numerical%20treatment%20of%20dynamical%20systems) (see also 65Pxx) and [37Nxx](node:MSC%2037Nxx%20-%20Applications%20of%20dynamical%20systems). ([MSC2020 37-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Poincaré recurrence and ergodic theorems.** If $T$ preserves a finite measure $\mu$ with $0<\mu(X)<\infty$ and $\mu(A)>0$, then almost every point of $A$ returns to $A$ infinitely often (Poincaré 1890; measure-theoretic proof by Carathéodory, 1919). ([Poincaré recurrence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_recurrence_theorem)) $T$ is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or $1$. Birkhoff (1931): for $f\in L^1(\mu)$ the time averages $\frac1N\sum_{n<N}f\circ T^n$ converge almost everywhere, to $\int f\,d\mu$ when $T$ is ergodic. Von Neumann: for a unitary $U$ on a [Hilbert space](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), $\frac1N\sum_{n<N}U^nx\to Px$ in norm, $P$ the projection onto $U$-fixed vectors. ([Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory)) See [Measure-Preserving Transformations](node:Measure-Preserving%20Transformations).
- **Entropy and the isomorphism problem.** For a finite partition $\mathcal Q$, $H(\mathcal Q)=-\sum_{Q}\mu(Q)\log\mu(Q)$, $h_\mu(T,\mathcal Q)=\lim_N\frac1N H\big(\bigvee_{n=0}^{N}T^{-n}\mathcal Q\big)$, and the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy $h_\mu(T)=\sup_{\mathcal Q}h_\mu(T,\mathcal Q)$, attained on generating partitions (Sinai, 1959). Ornstein (1970): Bernoulli shifts with the same entropy are isomorphic, so Bernoulli shifts are classified by entropy. ([Measure-preserving dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_dynamical_system)) Compare [Topological Entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy).
- **Hyperbolicity and stability.** Near a hyperbolic equilibrium (no eigenvalue of the Jacobian on the imaginary axis) a flow is topologically conjugate to its linearization (Hartman–Grobman). ([Hartman–Grobman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem)) For a uniformly hyperbolic compact set $\Lambda$ of a $C^r$ diffeomorphism $f$, the local stable and unstable manifolds of each $z\in\Lambda$ are $C^r$-embedded discs tangent to $E^s(z)$ and $E^u(z)$ and depending continuously on $z$ (stable manifold theorem). Such a set is structurally stable in the sense that every $C^1$-small perturbation $f'$ admits a continuous injection $i:\Lambda\to M$, close to the inclusion, with $f'\circ i=i\circ f$ (Anosov, with a proof by Moser); in particular Anosov diffeomorphisms are structurally stable. Palis and Smale conjectured in 1970 that structural stability is equivalent to Axiom A plus strong transversality, sufficiency being proved by Robbin (1971) and Robinson (1976) and necessity in the $C^1$ topology by Mañé. ([Berger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092)) See [Hyperbolic Dynamical Systems](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems) and [Stable Manifold Theorem](node:Stable%20Manifold%20Theorem).
- **SRB measures.** For a $C^2$ diffeomorphism with an irreducible Axiom A attractor there is a unique invariant probability measure that is SRB (time averages equal space averages for a set of initial points of positive Lebesgue measure), equivalently has absolutely continuous conditionals on unstable manifolds, equivalently has entropy equal to $\int\log\left|\det\big(DT|_{E^u}\big)\right|d\mu$, the integral of the log-Jacobian along unstable directions. ([SRB measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRB_measure)) See [Gibbs Measures](node:Gibbs%20Measures).
- **KAM theory.** Under a small perturbation of a non-degenerate integrable Hamiltonian, invariant tori with sufficiently irrational (Diophantine) frequencies survive, deformed, while resonant ones can break into Cantori; Kolmogorov (1954), Moser (1962) and Arnold (1963). ([KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem)) See [KAM Theory](node:KAM%20Theory).
- **Homogeneous dynamics (Ratner).** For a [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) $G$, a lattice $\Gamma$ and a one-parameter unipotent subgroup $u_t$, the closure of every orbit $xu_t$ in $\Gamma\backslash G$ is homogeneous, each orbit is equidistributed in its closure, and every ergodic invariant probability measure is algebraic (proved around 1990). Unipotent dynamics played a decisive role in Margulis's proof of the Oppenheim conjecture. ([Ratner's theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratner%27s_theorems))
- **Renormalization and universality.** Period-doubling cascades of one-dimensional maps with a quadratic maximum have universal scaling $\delta\approx4.6692016091$ (Feigenbaum 1975–78; computer-assisted proof by Lanford 1982; non-numerical proof by Lyubich). ([Feigenbaum constants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feigenbaum_constants)) MIT 18.353J covers period doubling, strange attractors and universality at the introductory level, linking to [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory). ([MIT OCW 18.353J syllabus](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-353j-nonlinear-dynamics-i-chaos-fall-2012/pages/syllabus/))

### History
Poincaré, often regarded as the founder of the field, wrote *New Methods of Celestial Mechanics* (1892–1899); Lyapunov developed stability methods in 1899; Birkhoff proved Poincaré's "Last Geometric Theorem" in 1913, published *Dynamical Systems* in 1927 and the ergodic theorem in 1931. Sharkovsky's theorem on periods dates from 1964, and Smale's horseshoe spurred much of the later research. ([Dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system)) Sinai's entropy work (1959) and Ornstein's isomorphism theorem (1970) shaped modern ergodic theory. ([Measure-preserving dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_dynamical_system))

### Open problems
- **MLC and density of hyperbolicity.** Local connectivity of the Mandelbrot set is still open (Yoccoz proved it at finitely renormalizable parameters); MLC would imply the density-of-hyperbolicity conjecture, called one of the most important open problems in complex dynamics. ([Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set)) Smale's 11th problem (a) lists hyperbolic density for complex polynomials as unresolved, while part (b), for real interval maps, was solved by Kozlovski, Shen and van Strien (2007). ([Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems))
- **Palis's conjecture.** Every $C^r$ diffeomorphism of a compact manifold can be approximated by a hyperbolic one or by one with a homoclinic tangency or heterodimensional cycle; Crovisier and Pujals prove a $C^1$ version with essential hyperbolicity, and the $C^r$, $r>1$, case is not established. ([Crovisier–Pujals, arXiv:1011.3836](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1011.3836))
- **Furstenberg's ×2×3 conjecture.** An atomless measure on $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ invariant under both $x\mapsto2x$ and $x\mapsto3x$ should be Lebesgue measure (adding ergodicity for the joint action gives an equivalent conjecture). Rudolph (1990) proved this for measures ergodic under the semigroup $\langle p,q\rangle$ (with $p,q>1$ coprime) for which some element has positive entropy, and Johnson extended it to multiplicatively independent $p,q$; in zero entropy "not much is known". ([Tal, Furstenberg's ×2 ×3 conjecture: a short survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2110.05989))
- **Sarnak's conjecture (2010).** Every zero-entropy continuous map $T$ of a compact metric space is Möbius disjoint: $\frac1N\sum_{n\le N}f(T^nx)\mu(n)\to0$ for all continuous $f$ and all $x$. It follows from the Chowla conjecture, which remains open, and the survey reviews results for many classes, including horocycle flows, nilflows, affine automorphisms, substitutions, interval exchanges, rank-one and distal systems, and automatic sequences. ([Ferenczi–Kułaga-Przymus–Lemańczyk, arXiv:1710.04039](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.04039))
- **Smale's 12th and 13th problems.** Density of diffeomorphisms with trivial centralizer is open in $C^r$, $r>1$ (proved for $C^1$ by Bonatti, Crovisier and Wilkinson); a polynomial bound on the number of limit cycles of planar polynomial vector fields is unresolved. The 14th problem, whether the Lorenz attractor is a strange attractor, was settled by Tucker in 2002. ([Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Ergodic theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory): ergodicity and the Birkhoff and von Neumann theorems.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.353J Nonlinear Dynamics I: Chaos](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-353j-nonlinear-dynamics-i-chaos-fall-2012/pages/syllabus/): undergraduate course on nonlinear dynamics and chaos.
- **Learn:** [Berger, Lectures on Structural Stability in Dynamics (arXiv:1703.00092)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092): graduate lectures on hyperbolicity and the stability conjectures.
- **Primary:** [Ferenczi, Kułaga-Przymus and Lemańczyk, Sarnak's Conjecture: what's new (arXiv:1710.04039)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.04039): research survey on Möbius disjointness.
- **Primary:** [Crovisier and Pujals, Essential hyperbolicity and homoclinic bifurcations (arXiv:1011.3836)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1011.3836): research paper on the Palis dichotomy.
- **Further reading:** [Katok and Hasselblatt, Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems (CUP, 1995)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-the-modern-theory-of-dynamical-systems/introduction/B1E86AEBAEAD07CF09DAB6443539A310): standard graduate text.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 37-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37-XX): official code list.

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 37A, "[Ergodic theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory)", is the part of [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory) that studies [measure-preserving transformations](node:Measure-Preserving%20Transformations) and their statistical behaviour. Its codes cover dynamical aspects of measure-preserving transformations (37A05), one-parameter flows (37A10), general group actions (37A15) and homogeneous flows (37A17), algebraic ergodic theory, cocycles and orbit equivalence (37A20), ergodicity and mixing with rates (37A25), ergodic theorems, spectral theory and Markov operators (37A30), entropy, isomorphism and classification (37A35), nonsingular and infinite-measure transformations (37A40), and relations with number theory (37A44), harmonic analysis (37A46), probability (37A50), $C^*$-algebras (37A55) and statistical mechanics (37A60). The section cross-refers to 28Dxx. ([MSC2020 37Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Axx))

A measure-preserving system is $(X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)$ with $\mu(X)=1$, $T$ measurable and $\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)$ for all $A\in\mathcal B$; the Koopman operator $f\mapsto f\circ T$ is an isometry of $L^2(\mu)$, which makes [Hilbert-space](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) and [spectral](node:Spectral%20Theory) methods available. The main themes are recurrence, convergence of averages, the mixing hierarchy, classification up to isomorphism (entropy, spectral invariants), and applications to [combinatorics](node:Combinatorics) and number theory through Furstenberg's correspondence principle. ([Moreira, §§1–3, 5](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf); [Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory))

### Scope
- **Neighbour 28D.** 37A is the dynamical side of measure-theoretic ergodic theory and cross-refers to [MSC 28Dxx - Measure-theoretic ergodic theory](node:MSC%2028Dxx%20-%20Measure-theoretic%20ergodic%20theory). ([MSC2020 37Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Axx))
- **Neighbours 22F and 47A35.** Group actions (37A15) mainly belong to 22Fxx and homogeneous flows (37A17) also to 22Fxx; operator ergodic theory is mainly 47A35 rather than 37A30. ([MSC2020 37Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Axx))
- **Neighbours 11K, 60F, 46L55, 82C.** Interactions with number theory point also to 11Kxx (compare [Equidistribution Modulo One](node:Equidistribution%20Modulo%20One)), with probability to 60Fxx and 60G10, with $C^*$-algebras mainly to 46L55, and with [statistical mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics) to 82Cxx. ([MSC2020 37Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Recurrence.** Poincaré: if $\mu(A)>0$ then $\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A)>0$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$. Khintchine: for every $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{n:\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A)>\mu(A)^2-\varepsilon\}$ is syndetic. ([Moreira, Theorems 2.1.1 and 2.4.4](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf))
- **Ergodic theorems (37A30).** Von Neumann (1932): for an isometry $U$ of a Hilbert space and $P$ the orthogonal projection onto $\ker(I-U)$, $\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U^nx\to Px$ in norm. Birkhoff (1931): if $T$ preserves a probability measure and $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then $\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(T^kx)$ converges almost everywhere to an integrable $T$-invariant $\hat f$, namely $E(f\mid\mathcal C)$ for the $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal C$ of invariant sets; if $T$ is ergodic, $\hat f=\int f\,d\mu$ a.e. ([Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory); [Moreira, Theorem 2.3.4](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf))
- **Mixing hierarchy (37A25).** $T$ is strongly mixing if $\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)\to\mu(A)\mu(B)$, and weakly mixing if the Cesàro averages of $|\mu(A\cap T^{-k}B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|$ tend to $0$; strong mixing implies weak mixing implies ergodicity, and neither converse holds (the Chacon system is weakly but not strongly mixing). ([Mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_%28mathematics%29)) Weak mixing is equivalent to ergodicity of $X\times Y$ for every ergodic $Y$. ([Moreira, Theorem 5.1.5](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf))
- **Spectral classification (37A30).** Two ergodic systems with discrete spectrum are conjugate iff they have the same group of eigenvalues; Bernoulli systems are the other class with a complete conjugacy invariant, and for general systems a useful complete classification is not expected. ([Moreira, Theorem 5.2.4 and Remark 5.2.5](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf))
- **Entropy and isomorphism (37A35).** Kolmogorov and Sinai (1959) introduced measure-theoretic entropy; a Bernoulli scheme $BS(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ has entropy $H=-\sum_ip_i\log p_i$, so schemes of different entropy are not isomorphic. Ornstein (1970) proved the converse: two Bernoulli schemes with the same entropy are isomorphic; factors of Bernoulli shifts are again Bernoulli. ([Ornstein isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornstein_isomorphism_theorem)) Compare [Topological Entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy) and [Symbolic Dynamics](node:Symbolic%20Dynamics).
- **Multiple recurrence and Szemerédi (37A44).** Furstenberg: for $\mu(A)>0$ and $k\in\mathbb N$ there is $n$ with $\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A\cap\dots\cap T^{-kn}A)>0$; in fact $\lim_{N-M\to\infty}\frac1{N-M}\sum_{n=M}^{N}\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A\cap\dots\cap T^{-kn}A)>0$. By the Furstenberg correspondence principle, any $E\subset\mathbb N$ of positive upper density $\bar d(E)$ yields a system and a set $A$ with $\mu(A)=\bar d(E)$ and $\mu(\bigcap_{n\in F}T^{-n}A)\le\bar d(\bigcap_{n\in F}(E-n))$ for finite $F$, so multiple recurrence implies Szemerédi's theorem that such $E$ contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. Furstenberg showed only that the $\liminf$ of the averages is positive; existence of the limit was proved by Host and Kra in 2005. ([Moreira, Lemma 3.2.1, Theorems 3.3.2–3.3.4, Remark 3.3.5](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf); [Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem)) See [Ramsey Theory](node:Ramsey%20Theory); the Green–Tao theorem on progressions in [primes](node:Prime%20Numbers) does not follow from Szemerédi because the primes have density zero. ([Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem))

### History
Birkhoff's pointwise theorem (PNAS 1931) and von Neumann's mean theorem (PNAS 1932) are distinct results; Birkhoff's paper treated systems arising from differential equations on manifolds. ([Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory)) Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy dates from 1959 and Ornstein's isomorphism theorem from 1970. ([Ornstein isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornstein_isomorphism_theorem)) Furstenberg introduced the correspondence principle in his 1977 ergodic-theoretic proof of Szemerédi's theorem. ([Moreira, §3.2](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf); [Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem)) Current research includes measure classification for diagonalizable actions, motivated by conjectures of Furstenberg and Margulis, with Lindenstrauss's partial result under positive entropy. ([Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory))

### Open problems
- **Rokhlin's multiple mixing problem.** It is unknown whether strong 2-mixing implies strong 3-mixing, and more generally whether a mixing automorphism must be mixing of all orders. ([Mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_%28mathematics%29)) Ryzhikov's 2024 survey lists Rokhlin's problem among the open problems on multiple mixing, spectrum, rank and self-joinings. ([Ryzhikov](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03641))
- **Banach's simple Lebesgue spectrum problem.** Whether a measure-preserving transformation can have simple Lebesgue spectrum is listed as open by Ryzhikov, together with the del Junco–Rudolph problem; he observes that a hypothetical automorphism of class $MSJ(2)\setminus MSJ(3)$ with simple Lebesgue spectrum would solve the problems of Banach, Rokhlin and del Junco–Rudolph at once. ([Ryzhikov](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03641))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Ergodic theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory): ergodic theorems, history, current directions.
- **Learn:** [Moreira, Ergodic theory lecture notes (Warwick)](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/moreira/papers/ergodicnotes.pdf): recurrence, ergodic theorems, correspondence principle, mixing and spectra, Furstenberg's multiple recurrence.
- **Primary:** [Ryzhikov, Unsolved problems on joinings, multiple mixing, spectrum, and rank (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03641): survey of open problems (in Russian).
- **Further reading:** [Walters, An Introduction to Ergodic Theory (Springer GTM, 1982)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-5775-2): standard graduate text.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 37Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Axx): official code list.

## Reference
### Overview
Topological dynamics, a branch of [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), studies the long-term behaviour of continuous maps, flows or semigroup actions on [topological spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces), usually compact metric spaces rather than [smooth manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds). Its roots are in the asymptotic behaviour of trajectories of autonomous [ordinary differential equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations), and Birkhoff is considered its founder. It is the topological analogue of [ergodic theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory): topological entropy plays the role of Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy. ([Wikipedia, Topological dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_dynamics))

The standard setting is a pair $(X,T)$ with $X$ a compact [metric space](node:Metric%20Spaces) and $T:X\to X$ continuous; surjectivity and invertibility are extra assumptions. Two systems are isomorphic (conjugate) if a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $\pi:X\to Y$ satisfies $\pi T=S\pi$, and $(Y,S)$ is a factor if $\pi$ is only a continuous surjection. A homeomorphism of phase spaces is a prerequisite for isomorphism, an obstruction that rarely arises in the measurable category. ([Hochman, Definitions 11.1.1–11.1.3](https://math.huji.ac.il/~mhochman/courses/dynamics2014/notes.5.pdf)) Symbolic systems are a large part of the field: MSC files symbolic dynamics, dynamical aspects of cellular automata, multidimensional shifts of finite type and tilings here. ([MSC2020, 37B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Bxx))

### Scope
MSC2020 37B lists: 37B02 dynamics in general topological spaces; 37B05 transformations and group actions with special properties (minimality, distality, proximality, expansivity); 37B10 symbolic dynamics; 37B15 dynamical aspects of cellular automata; 37B20 notions of recurrence; 37B25 stability of topological dynamical systems; 37B30 index theory, Morse–Conley indices; 37B35 gradient-like behaviour, isolated invariant sets, attractors and repellers; 37B40 topological entropy; 37B45 continua theory in dynamics; 37B51 multidimensional shifts of finite type; 37B52 tiling dynamics; 37B55 nonautonomous systems; 37B65 approximate trajectories, pseudotrajectories and shadowing; 37B99. ([MSC2020, 37B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Bxx))

- **vs [37A](node:MSC%2037Axx%20-%20Ergodic%20theory):** 37A works with invariant measures up to null sets; 37B with the topology, where conjugacy requires a homeomorphism. ([Hochman, §11.1](https://math.huji.ac.il/~mhochman/courses/dynamics2014/notes.5.pdf))
- **vs [37C](node:MSC%2037Cxx%20-%20Smooth%20dynamical%20systems%20-%20general%20theory):** smooth structure is not assumed in 37B; phase spaces are general compact metric spaces. ([Wikipedia, Topological dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_dynamics))
- **vs [68Q](node:MSC%2068Qxx%20-%20Theory%20of%20computing):** 37B15 holds dynamical aspects of [cellular automata](node:Cellular%20Automata), while their computational aspects go to 68Q80. ([MSC2020, 37B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Minimality and Birkhoff recurrence (37B05, 37B20).** A system is minimal if it has no nonempty proper closed invariant subset, equivalently every point has a dense orbit. Every topological dynamical system has a minimal subsystem; in a minimal system every point is recurrent ($T^{n_k}x\to x$ along some $n_k\to\infty$), so every system has a recurrent point, a purely topological argument due to Birkhoff. The converse fails: a disjoint union of two minimal systems has all points recurrent but is not minimal. ([Hochman, Lemma 11.3.3, Proposition 11.3.5, Lemma 11.3.12, Corollary 11.3.14](https://math.huji.ac.il/~mhochman/courses/dynamics2014/notes.5.pdf))
- **Multiple recurrence and van der Waerden.** Furstenberg and Weiss (1978) proved the multiple Birkhoff recurrence theorem: if $T_1,\dots,T_N$ are commuting homeomorphisms of a compact metric space $X$, there are $x\in X$ and $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ with $T_i^{n_k}x\to x$ for every $i$. Applying it to $T,T^2,\dots,T^N$ for the shift on the space of colourings gives van der Waerden's theorem: for every $r,k$ there is $N$ such that any $r$-colouring of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ has a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression. This is a basic bridge to [Ramsey Theory](node:Ramsey%20Theory). ([Wikipedia, Van der Waerden's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Waerden%27s_theorem))
- **Topological entropy and the variational principle (37B40).** Adler, Konheim and McAndrew (1965) defined $h_{\rm top}(T)$ through refinements of open covers; Bowen and Dinaburg's definition counts $(n,\varepsilon)$-separated orbit segments. ([Wikipedia, Topological entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_entropy)) The definitions agree, $h_{\rm top}$ does not increase under factors, the full shift on $|A|$ symbols has entropy $\log|A|$, and the variational principle holds: $h_{\rm top}(T)=\sup\{h_\mu(T):\mu\text{ a }T\text{-invariant Borel probability}\}$. For expansive systems the supremum is attained by an ergodic measure. ([Hochman, Theorems 12.1.13, 13.3.4, 14.1.1, Example 12.2.7, Corollary 14.2.7](https://math.huji.ac.il/~mhochman/courses/dynamics2014/notes.5.pdf)) See [Topological Entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy).
- **Distal, proximal and equicontinuous structure (37B05).** A pair $(x,y)$ is proximal if $\inf_g\rho(gx,gy)=0$ and distal otherwise; a system is distal if all pairs of distinct points are distal. The enveloping (Ellis) semigroup $E(X)$ is the closure of the acting maps in $X^X$ with the pointwise topology. Ellis: a system is equicontinuous iff $E(X)$ is a group of homeomorphisms, and a system is distal iff $E(X)$ is a group. Furstenberg's structure theorem: a minimal distal system is an inverse limit of isometric extensions (the Furstenberg tower). ([Qiu–Zhao, §§1.1–1.2, 2.5, 2.7, Theorem 2.11](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1911.05435)) Qiu and Zhao answer Donoso's question: a minimal system is a $d$-step pro-nilsystem iff its enveloping semigroup is a $d$-step top-nilpotent group. ([Qiu–Zhao, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.05435))
- **Symbolic dynamics and SFTs (37B10, 37B51).** A subshift of finite type is a shift space defined by a finite set of forbidden words; every SFT is conjugate by a recoding to an edge shift given by a 0–1 adjacency matrix $A$, sofic shifts are factors of SFTs, the zeta function of an SFT is rational, $\zeta(z)=\det(I-zA)^{-1}$, and for irreducible $A$ the entropy is $\log$ of the largest eigenvalue. ([Wikipedia, Subshift of finite type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subshift_of_finite_type); [Wikipedia, Topological entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_entropy)) Williams conjectured that shift equivalence over $\mathbb Z_+$ implies strong shift equivalence (which is conjugacy); Kim and Roush refuted it in the reducible and then the primitive case. ([Boyle, Open problems in symbolic dynamics, §3](https://math.umd.edu/~mmb/papers/ppost3nov2007.pdf)) See [Symbolic Dynamics](node:Symbolic%20Dynamics).
- **Genericity.** Hochman shows that a property is generic among Cantor homeomorphisms exactly when it is generic among subshifts of a suitably large shift space, that the universal odometer's isomorphism class is generic among transitive Cantor systems, and that minimality, zero entropy, weak and strong mixing and minimal self-joinings are generic among totally transitive ones. ([Hochman, Genericity in topological dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0605386))

### History
Gottschalk and Hedlund's *Topological Dynamics* (1955) and Ellis's *Lectures on Topological Dynamics* (1969) are standard early references, and Furstenberg's early-1960s structure theorem for minimal distal flows inspired much work on classifying minimal flows. ([Wikipedia, Topological dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_dynamics)) Topological entropy dates from 1965, and the Furstenberg–Weiss proof of van der Waerden's theorem from 1978. ([Wikipedia, Topological entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_entropy); [Wikipedia, Van der Waerden's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Waerden%27s_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Classification and decidability of conjugacy for SFTs.** Boyle states the central problem: classify SFTs up to topological conjugacy, and in particular decide when two nonnegative integer matrices $A,B$ define conjugate SFTs (equivalently, are strong shift equivalent over $\mathbb Z_+$); there is "no conjectural solution". His list of open decidability problems also includes conjugacy of sofic shifts and of one-sided sofic shifts; for SFTs and sofic shifts eventual conjugacy is decidable while conjugacy "remains mysterious". ([Boyle, §§3, 19, 32](https://math.umd.edu/~mmb/papers/ppost3nov2007.pdf))
- **Little shift equivalence conjecture.** If a nonnegative integer matrix $A$ has a unique and simple nonzero eigenvalue $n$, then $A$ is strong shift equivalent over $\mathbb Z_+$ to $[n]$. ([Boyle, Conjecture 3.1](https://math.umd.edu/~mmb/papers/ppost3nov2007.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Topological dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_dynamics): scope, history and bibliography.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020, 37B](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Bxx): subject codes.
- **Learn:** [Hochman, Lectures on dynamical systems and entropy, ch. 11–14](https://math.huji.ac.il/~mhochman/courses/dynamics2014/notes.5.pdf): topological systems, minimality, recurrence, entropy and the variational principle.
- **Primary:** [Boyle, Open problems in symbolic dynamics](https://math.umd.edu/~mmb/papers/ppost3nov2007.pdf): problem survey with the SFT classification and decidability problems.
- **Primary:** [Hochman, Genericity in topological dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0605386): generic Cantor systems and subshifts (ETDS 2008).
- **Primary:** [Qiu and Zhao, Top-nilpotent enveloping semigroups and pro-nilsystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.05435): enveloping semigroups and structure of minimal systems.
- **Further reading:** [Lind and Marcus, An Introduction to Symbolic Dynamics and Coding, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2021)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/9781108899727): textbook on symbolic dynamics and coding.
references.MSC 37Cxx - Smooth dynamical systems - g:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 37C, "Smooth dynamical systems: general theory", is the part of [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory) devoted to diffeomorphisms, flows and semiflows of [manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds) studied with the help of their derivatives. It carries see-also references to [34Cxx](node:MSC%2034Cxx%20-%20Qualitative%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations) and [34Dxx](node:MSC%2034Dxx%20-%20Stability%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations), the ODE codes for qualitative and stability theory. ([MSC2020 37Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Cxx))

In the language of [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), the central questions of the area are local (what an orbit looks like near a fixed or periodic point), generic (which properties hold for a dense $G_\delta$ set of systems), and global (which systems are structurally stable, so that every $C^1$-small perturbation is topologically conjugate to the original). The modern theory grew out of the Andronov–Pontryagin "rough systems" of 1937, Peixoto's theorem for surfaces, and Smale's discovery that structurally stable systems are not dense in higher dimensions. ([Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability)) Berger's lectures frame the central task as describing the structurally stable dynamics, a problem that contains some of the hardest conjectures of the field. ([Berger, Lectures on structural stability, arXiv:1703.00092](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092))

### Scope
The MSC2020 entry lists: smooth mappings and diffeomorphisms (37C05); flows and semiflows (37C10); topological and differentiable equivalence, conjugacy, moduli and classification (37C15); generic properties and structural stability (37C20); fixed and periodic points, fixed-point index theory and local dynamics (37C25); periodic orbits of vector fields (37C27); homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits (37C29); functional-analytic techniques, zeta functions and Ruelle–Frobenius [transfer operators](node:Transfer%20Operators) (37C30); orbit growth (37C35); smooth [ergodic theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) and invariant measures (37C40, see also 37Dxx); dimension theory (37C45); pseudotrajectories and shadowing (37C50); periodic and quasi-periodic flows (37C55); nonautonomous systems (37C60); monotone flows (37C65); attractors and repellers (37C70); stability theory (37C75); symmetries, invariants and equivariant systems (37C79, 37C81); systems with singularities such as billiards (37C83); actions of groups other than $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$ (37C85, see mainly 22Fxx); and foliations generated by dynamical systems (37C86). ([MSC2020 37Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Cxx))

- **Versus 37D.** Uniformly and partially hyperbolic systems (Anosov, Axiom A) have their own code [37Dxx](node:MSC%2037Dxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20with%20hyperbolic%20behavior), to which 37C40 points. ([MSC2020 37Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Cxx))
- **Versus 34C/34D.** The 37Cxx heading carries see-also references to 34Cxx and 34Dxx, the ODE codes for qualitative theory and stability theory. ([MSC2020 37Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Cxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Smooth Flows and Diffeomorphisms](node:Smooth%20Flows%20and%20Diffeomorphisms) and local linearization (Hartman–Grobman).** If $f$ is smooth, $f(u^*)=0$, and the Jacobian $Df(u^*)$ has no eigenvalue with zero real part, then near $u^*$ the flow of $\dot u=f(u)$ is topologically conjugate, by a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $h$ with $h(u^*)=0$, to the flow of $\dot U=Df(u^*)U$; the analogous statement holds for hyperbolic fixed points of maps. The conjugacy is in general only Hölder, not smooth or even locally Lipschitz; in dimension 2 it is $C^1$ but need not be $C^2$ (Sternberg). ([Hartman–Grobman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem))
- **[Stable Manifold Theorem](node:Stable%20Manifold%20Theorem).** For a smooth map with a hyperbolic fixed point $p$, the stable set $W^s(p)$ and unstable set $W^u(p)$ are smooth manifolds whose dimensions are those of the stable and unstable spaces of the linearization at $p$. ([Stable manifold theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_manifold_theorem)) Local stable and unstable manifolds of a hyperbolic set are $C^r$-embedded discs depending continuously on the point. ([Berger, Prop. 1.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092))
- **Kupka–Smale theorem (1963).** On a connected compact boundaryless manifold $M$ there is a dense $G_\delta$ subset of $\mathrm{Diff}^1(M)$ whose elements have all periodic points hyperbolic and every intersection of $W^s(O)$ with $W^u(O')$, for hyperbolic periodic orbits $O,O'$, transverse: $T_xM=T_xW^s(O)+T_xW^u(O')$. ([Abdenur–Crovisier, arXiv:1111.4206, §4.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1111.4206)) See [Transversality Theorem](node:Transversality%20Theorem) for the transversality tool behind it.
- **Pugh's closing lemma (1967).** If a diffeomorphism $f$ of a compact manifold has a nonwandering point $x$, then there is a diffeomorphism $g$ arbitrarily $C^1$-close to $f$ for which $x$ is periodic. ([Charles C. Pugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_C._Pugh)) Abdenur and Crovisier summarize it as turning any non-wandering point into a periodic point by a small $C^1$-perturbation, and use it alongside Kupka–Smale and Baire-category arguments in the $C^1$-generic theory. ([Abdenur–Crovisier](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1111.4206))
- **Morse–Smale systems and Peixoto's theorem.** A flow on a compact manifold is Morse–Smale if it has finitely many singular points and periodic orbits, all hyperbolic, every limit set is one of them, and all their stable and unstable manifolds meet transversally. Morse–Smale systems are structurally stable, and Smale (1960) proved Morse inequalities $\sum_{j\le i}(-1)^j m_{i-j}\ge\sum_{j\le i}(-1)^j b_{i-j}$ where $m_i$ is the number of equilibria of index $i$ (dimension of the unstable manifold) plus the number of periodic orbits of index $i$ and $i+1$, and $b_i$ are the Betti numbers; gradient flows of [Morse functions](node:Morse%20Functions%20and%20Handle%20Decompositions) with transverse invariant manifolds are examples. ([Morse–Smale system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse%E2%80%93Smale_system)) Peixoto: a $C^r$ vector field ($r\ge1$) on a compact surface $S$ is structurally stable iff it has finitely many critical elements (singularities and closed orbits), all hyperbolic, no orbit joining two saddles, and nonwandering set consisting only of the critical elements; if $S$ is orientable, these fields are open and dense in the $C^r$ topology. Density on non-orientable surfaces is Peixoto's conjecture, proved for the projective plane, the Klein bottle and the torus with one cross-cap. ([Araújo, arXiv:0804.3616](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0804.3616); [Peixoto's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peixoto%27s_theorem))
- **Stability conjecture.** Palis and Smale (1970) conjectured that a diffeomorphism is structurally stable iff it satisfies Axiom A (the nonwandering set is a finite union of basic sets) and the strong transversality condition. Robbin (1971) and Robinson (1976) proved sufficiency in every $C^r$, $r\ge1$; Mañé proved necessity for $C^1$ diffeomorphisms. ([Berger, Conj. 2.3 and §3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092)) Hayashi's 1997 *Annals* paper solved the $C^1$ stability and $\Omega$-stability conjectures for flows via his connecting lemma; a 1999 correction repaired the proof that $C^1$ $\Omega$-stable vector fields satisfy Axiom A. ([Hayashi, arXiv:math/9907205](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9907205)) Anosov showed that hyperbolic toral automorphisms, and more generally Anosov diffeomorphisms and flows, are structurally stable ([Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability)); see [Hyperbolic Dynamical Systems](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems).

### History
Andronov and Pontryagin introduced rough systems in 1937 and characterized structurally stable $C^1$ flows on the disc and $S^2$: finitely many singular points and periodic orbits, all hyperbolic, and no saddle-to-saddle connections. M. and M. C. Peixoto extended this to surfaces in the late 1950s and early 1960s, the first global characterization. Smale hoped that structurally stable systems would be typical but found higher-dimensional vector fields that cannot be made structurally stable by arbitrarily small perturbations, so such systems are not dense in higher dimensions. ([Structural stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability)) Hartman (1960) and Grobman (1959) proved the linearization theorem. ([Hartman–Grobman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartman%E2%80%93Grobman_theorem)) Kupka and Smale proved their genericity theorem in 1963 and Pugh his closing lemma in 1967. ([Abdenur–Crovisier](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1111.4206); [Charles C. Pugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_C._Pugh))

### Open problems
- **$C^r$ closing lemma, $r>1$ (Smale's 10th problem).** Whether Pugh's closing lemma holds in higher smoothness is listed as unresolved; Asaoka and Irie proved it for Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms of closed surfaces. ([Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems)) Even for vector fields on the 2-torus the problem is open in general; it has been verified for $C^r$ fields, $r\ge4$, with bounded-type rotation number that are area-preserving at saddles. ([arXiv:0811.1089](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.1089))
- **Smale's 12th problem (trivial centralizers).** Density of diffeomorphisms with trivial centralizer is proved in the $C^1$ topology (Bonatti, Crovisier, Wilkinson) and still open in $C^r$ for $r>1$. ([Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems))
- **Palis's density conjecture.** Every $C^r$ diffeomorphism of a compact manifold can be $C^r$-approximated by a hyperbolic one or by one with a homoclinic tangency or heterodimensional cycle. Crovisier and Pujals prove a $C^1$ version with "essentially hyperbolic" in place of hyperbolic; the $C^r$, $r>1$, case is not established. ([Crovisier–Pujals, arXiv:1011.3836](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1011.3836))
- **Stability conjecture in higher regularity.** Berger states that whether structural stability is equivalent to being far from tangencies is "widely open" for $C^r$, $r>1$, and Mañé's 1982 conjecture that every $C^r$-weakly stable diffeomorphism satisfies Axiom A, for every $1\le r\le\infty$, is proved only for $r=1$ (Mañé for surfaces, Aoki and Hayashi in any dimension). ([Berger](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Structural stability (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_stability): definitions, Andronov–Pontryagin, Peixoto, Smale, Anosov.
- **Learn:** [Berger, Lectures on Structural Stability in Dynamics (arXiv:1703.00092)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092): hyperbolicity, stability conjectures and their status.
- **Primary:** [Crovisier and Pujals, Essential hyperbolicity and homoclinic bifurcations (arXiv:1011.3836)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1011.3836): research paper on the $C^1$ Palis dichotomy.
- **Primary:** [Hayashi, Correction to the solution of the $C^1$ stability conjectures for flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9907205): the flow case of the stability conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Katok and Hasselblatt, Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems (CUP, 1995)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-the-modern-theory-of-dynamical-systems/introduction/B1E86AEBAEAD07CF09DAB6443539A310): graduate text covering local analysis, orbit growth, low-dimensional and hyperbolic dynamics.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 37Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Cxx): official code list.
references.MSC 37Dxx - Dynamical systems with hyper:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 37Dxx collects [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) whose derivative splits the tangent space into directions that are contracted and directions that are expanded. For a diffeomorphism $f$ of a manifold $M$, a compact invariant set $\Lambda$ is hyperbolic if $T_\Lambda M=E^u\oplus E^s$ is $Df$-invariant and, for some Riemannian metric and some $\lambda<1$, $\|Df^{-1}|E^u\|<\lambda$ and $\|Df|E^s\|<\lambda$; the splitting is then unique and continuous. If $\Lambda=M$ the map is Anosov. For flows without equilibria one adds a line bundle $E^0$ tangent to the flow. ([Araújo–Viana, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192)) The ambient setting is a diffeomorphism of a compact [smooth manifold](node:Smooth%20Manifolds), and the Anosov diffeomorphisms of such a manifold form a $C^1$-open set and are $C^1$-structurally stable. ([Cooper, abstract](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2021/REUPapers/Cooper.pdf))
