Hyperbolicity is the mechanism that makes chaotic dynamics describable: it yields invariant manifolds, shadowing, symbolic coding through Markov partitions, a complete characterization of structural stability, and physical (SRB) measures on attractors. Uniform hyperbolicity was soon found not to be dense among all systems, which led to the two main extensions classified here: partial hyperbolicity (some directions neutral) and nonuniform hyperbolicity (rates depending on the point). ([Araújo–Viana, §§5–9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192)) The general theory is developed further in [Hyperbolic Dynamical Systems](node:Hyperbolic%20Dynamical%20Systems) and links to [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory) and [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory).

### Scope
MSC2020 lists the following sub-codes under 37Dxx. ([MSC2020 37Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Dxx))
- **37D05, 37D10:** dynamical systems with hyperbolic orbits and sets; invariant manifold theory.
- **37D15, 37D20:** Morse–Smale systems; uniformly hyperbolic systems (expanding, Anosov, Axiom A).
- **37D25, 37D30:** nonuniformly hyperbolic systems (Lyapunov exponents, Pesin theory); partially hyperbolic systems and dominated splittings.
- **37D35:** thermodynamic formalism, variational principles, equilibrium states.
- **37D40, 37D45:** systems of geometric origin (geodesic and horocycle flows); strange attractors and chaotic dynamics of hyperbolic systems.

Nearby classes of MSC 37 include [37Cxx](node:MSC%2037Cxx%20-%20Smooth%20dynamical%20systems%20-%20general%20theory), [37Axx](node:MSC%2037Axx%20-%20Ergodic%20theory), [37Gxx](node:MSC%2037Gxx%20-%20Local%20and%20nonlocal%20bifurcation%20theory%20for%20dynamical%20systems), and [37Jxx](node:MSC%2037Jxx%20-%20Dynamical%20aspects%20of%20finite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems). Two links to them are mathematical: homoclinic tangencies (non-transverse intersections of stable and unstable manifolds of a periodic point) are a mechanism producing open sets of non-hyperbolic systems, and the geodesic flow on manifolds of negative curvature, which preserves Liouville measure, was historically the first important example of uniform hyperbolicity. ([Araújo–Viana, §§6, 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))

### Key concepts
- **[Stable Manifold Theorem](node:Stable%20Manifold%20Theorem) for hyperbolic sets.** If $\Lambda$ is hyperbolic for a $C^k$ diffeomorphism $f$, there are $\varepsilon_0>0$, $\lambda<1$ such that for $x\in\Lambda$ and $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$ the local stable set $W^s_\varepsilon(x)=\{y:d(f^n y,f^n x)\le\varepsilon\ \forall n\ge0\}$ is a $C^k$ embedded disk tangent to $E^s_x$, contracted by $f$ at rate $\lambda$, varying continuously with $x$; likewise for $W^u_\varepsilon$. The global stable manifold $W^s(x)=\{y:d(f^ny,f^nx)\to0\}$ is an immersed submanifold. ([Araújo–Viana, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))
- **Shadowing lemma.** For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $\delta>0$ and a neighbourhood $U$ of the hyperbolic set $\Lambda$ such that every $\delta$-pseudo-orbit in $U$ (a sequence with $d(x_{n+1},f(x_n))\le\delta$) is $\varepsilon$-shadowed by a true orbit in $U$, unique for small $\varepsilon$. Combined with persistence of cone fields, it shows that a hyperbolic maximal invariant set is structurally stable: nearby $g$ have a hyperbolic set $\Lambda_g$ with $f\circ h=h\circ g$ for a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $h$. ([Araújo–Viana, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))
- **Markov partitions and [symbolic dynamics](node:Symbolic%20Dynamics).** Every maximal hyperbolic set admits Markov partitions of arbitrarily small diameter: finite covers by proper rectangles with $W^u(f(x))\cap R_j\subset f(W^u(x)\cap R_i)$ and $f(W^s(x)\cap R_i)\subset W^s(f(x))\cap R_j$. The itinerary map $h$ is a continuous surjection from admissible sequences with $f\circ h=h\circ\sigma$, injective off the orbits meeting rectangle boundaries. ([Araújo–Viana, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))
- **Smale's spectral decomposition.** If $f$ satisfies Axiom A (the non-wandering set $\Omega(f)$ is hyperbolic and periodic points are dense in it), then $\Omega(f)=\Lambda_1\cup\dots\cup\Lambda_N$ is a finite disjoint union of compact, invariant, transitive, maximal invariant basic pieces, and every $\alpha$- and $\omega$-limit set lies in some $\Lambda_i$. ([Araújo–Viana, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))
- **Structural stability theorem.** Hyperbolicity plus strong transversality implies structural stability (Robbin, de Melo, Robinson, 1970s); the converse, that structurally stable systems are hyperbolic, was proved by Mañé for $C^1$ diffeomorphisms and by Hayashi for $C^1$ flows. Hence a $C^1$ diffeomorphism or flow of a compact manifold is structurally stable if and only if it is uniformly hyperbolic and strongly transversal (the Palis–Smale stability conjecture). ([Araújo–Viana, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))
- **SRB measures.** A hyperbolic attractor $\Lambda$ (a basic piece whose stable set $\{x:\omega(x)\subset\Lambda\}$ contains a neighbourhood of $\Lambda$) of a $C^2$ diffeomorphism supports a unique invariant probability $\mu$ with $\frac1n\sum_{j<n}\varphi(f^jz)\to\int\varphi\,d\mu$ for every continuous $\varphi$ and Lebesgue-almost every $z$ in the basin (Sinai, Ruelle, Bowen). ([Araújo–Viana, §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192)) For an irreducible Axiom A attractor this is equivalent to $\mu$ having absolutely continuous conditionals on unstable manifolds, and to its entropy equalling $\int\log|\det Df|_{E^u}|\,d\mu$. ([Wikipedia: SRB measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRB_measure)) Equilibrium states (37D35) and the ergodic theory of Anosov diffeomorphisms are the subject of Bowen's lecture notes. ([Crossref: Bowen, Lecture Notes in Mathematics](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-77695-6)) See [Gibbs Measures](node:Gibbs%20Measures) and [Topological Entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy).
- **Pesin theory (37D25).** For a $C^{1+\alpha}$ diffeomorphism and an invariant measure $\mu$ whose Lyapunov exponents (given by the Oseledets theorem) are all nonzero, for $\mu$-a.e. $x$ there is a $C^1$ local stable disk $W^s_{loc}(x)$ tangent to $E^s_x$ with $d(f^ny,f^nx)\le C_xe^{-n\tau_x}d(y,x)$; $C_x,\tau_x$ depend on $x$, and the stable and unstable laminations are absolutely continuous. If $\mu$ is smooth, Pesin's entropy formula gives $h_\mu(f)=\int\sum_j\max\{0,\lambda_j\}\,d\mu$; Ledrappier and Young characterized the measures for which this holds. ([Araújo–Viana, §§10–11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))
- **Partial hyperbolicity (37D30).** A dominated splitting $E_1\oplus\dots\oplus E_k$ is partially hyperbolic if $Df^\ell$ uniformly contracts $E_1$ or uniformly expands $E_k$. Robustly transitive sets always carry a volume-hyperbolic dominated splitting (Bonatti, Díaz, Pujals, Ures). ([Araújo–Viana, §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))
- **Geodesic flows (37D40).** Anosov proved that the geodesic flow of a compact manifold of negative sectional curvature is ergodic for Liouville measure, by showing it is uniformly hyperbolic and that its stable and unstable foliations are absolutely continuous, although in higher dimensions the invariant subbundles are in general not differentiable; the surface case is due to Hedlund and Hopf. ([Araújo–Viana, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))

### History
Structural stability was introduced by Andronov and Pontryagin in the 1930s. Uniform hyperbolic theory was developed in the 1960s by Smale and collaborators and by Anosov, Sinai, and Arnold; Smale, building on Peixoto, first proposed gradient-like systems as the stable majority, and Levinson's examples showed open sets of systems with infinitely many periodic orbits. ([Araújo–Viana, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.3192)) ([Araújo–Viana, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192)) Smale introduced the hyperbolic set, partly motivated by Anosov toral automorphisms. ([Cooper, §1](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2021/REUPapers/Cooper.pdf)) Newhouse's homoclinic tangencies (in $C^r$, $r\ge2$, on surfaces) and heterodimensional cycles (Abraham–Smale, dimension $\ge3$) showed that hyperbolicity is not dense, motivating partial and nonuniform hyperbolicity, studied since the 1970s by Brin, Pesin, Hirsch, Pugh, and Shub. ([Araújo–Viana, §§8–9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))

### Open problems
- **Classification of Anosov diffeomorphisms.** All known manifolds carrying an Anosov diffeomorphism are infranilmanifolds, and it is conjectured that they are the only ones; it is also not known in general whether Anosov diffeomorphisms are transitive. ([Wikipedia: Anosov diffeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anosov_diffeomorphism))
- **Ergodicity in low regularity.** Every $C^2$ volume-preserving Anosov diffeomorphism is ergodic, but for $C^1$ maps the invariant foliations need not be absolutely continuous and ergodicity is an open problem. ([Araújo–Viana, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192)) ([Wikipedia: Anosov diffeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anosov_diffeomorphism))
- **Density of hyperbolicity for $C^1$ surface diffeomorphisms.** Whether uniform hyperbolicity is dense in the space of $C^1$ diffeomorphisms of a surface is unknown, as is the $C^1$ surface case of the Newhouse phenomenon. ([Araújo–Viana, §8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.3192))
- **Bonatti–Palis conjecture.** There should be a dense open subset of $\mathrm{Diff}^1(M)\setminus\overline{T}$ ($T$ the diffeomorphisms with a homoclinic tangency) whose elements have at most finitely many attractors and quasi-attractors. Crovisier, Potrie, and Sambarino prove, as a step towards it, that an open and dense subset of $C^1$ partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms with one-dimensional centre have at most finitely many quasi-attractors; they announce that a further work will conclude the conjecture in dimension 3. ([Crovisier–Potrie–Sambarino, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.08684))
- **Pugh–Shub stable ergodicity conjecture.** Stable ergodicity should be $C^r$-dense among volume-preserving partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms for all $r>1$; the 2015 survey states that it remains open, while it is proved for one-dimensional centre bundle (Hertz–Hertz–Ures) and in the $C^1$ topology (Avila–Crovisier–Wilkinson). ([Carrasco–Rodriguez-Hertz–Rodriguez-Hertz–Ures, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.00932))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Anosov diffeomorphism (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anosov_diffeomorphism): definitions, examples, and the classification problem.
- **Learn:** [Cooper, Structural Stability of Anosov Diffeomorphisms](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2021/REUPapers/Cooper.pdf): self-contained proof via shadowing and expansiveness.
- **Primary:** [Araújo and Viana, Hyperbolic Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.3192): survey of uniform, partial, and nonuniform hyperbolicity.
- **Primary:** [Carrasco, Rodriguez-Hertz, Rodriguez-Hertz, Ures, Partially hyperbolic dynamics in dimension 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.00932): survey with conjectures on ergodicity and classification.
- **Further reading:** [Katok and Hasselblatt, Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems (CUP, 1995)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511809187/type/book): Part 4 covers hyperbolic sets, equilibrium states, and nonuniform hyperbolicity.
- **Further reading:** [Bowen, Equilibrium States and the Ergodic Theory of Anosov Diffeomorphisms (Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics, 2008 edition with Chazottes and Ruelle)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-77695-6): lecture notes on equilibrium states for Anosov diffeomorphisms.
references.MSC 37Exx - Low-dimensional dynamical sy:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 37E, "Low-dimensional dynamical systems", is the part of [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory) covering maps of the interval, the circle, trees and graphs, homeomorphisms and diffeomorphisms of planes and surfaces, flows on surfaces, twist maps, and the combinatorial, renormalization and rotation-number methods developed for them. ([MSC2020 37Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Exx)) In the theory of [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), low dimension makes possible order-theoretic and topological arguments with no analogue in higher dimensions: a period-3 orbit of a continuous interval map forces orbits of all periods, and an orientation-preserving $C^2$ circle diffeomorphism with irrational rotation number is conjugate to a rotation. ([Sharkovskii's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem); [Denjoy's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denjoy%27s_theorem_on_rotation_number))

The research frontier of the area is the real one-dimensional theory of unimodal and multimodal maps (kneading theory, renormalization, density of hyperbolicity), the smooth theory of circle diffeomorphisms, and the topology of surface homeomorphisms and area-preserving twist maps. Katok and Hasselblatt devote a whole part of their graduate text to "low-dimensional phenomena". ([Katok–Hasselblatt, Introduction](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-the-modern-theory-of-dynamical-systems/introduction/B1E86AEBAEAD07CF09DAB6443539A310)) See also [Interval and Circle Dynamics](node:Interval%20and%20Circle%20Dynamics).

### Scope
The MSC2020 codes are: maps of the interval (37E05); maps of the circle (37E10); combinatorial dynamics, i.e. types of periodic orbits (37E15); universality and renormalization (37E20, see also 37F25); maps of trees and graphs (37E25); homeomorphisms and diffeomorphisms of planes and surfaces (37E30); flows on surfaces (37E35); dynamical aspects of twist maps (37E40); and rotation numbers and vectors (37E45). ([MSC2020 37Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Exx))

- **Versus 37F.** Holomorphic one-dimensional dynamics is [37Fxx](node:MSC%2037Fxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20over%20complex%20numbers); 37E20 cross-refers to 37F25 for renormalization, where real and complex methods meet. ([MSC2020 37Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Exx); [MSC2020 37-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37-XX))
- **Versus 37J.** Twist maps have their own code 37E40, while symplectic and canonical mappings (37J11) and action-minimizing orbits and measures (37J51) of Hamiltonian and Lagrangian systems sit in [37Jxx](node:MSC%2037Jxx%20-%20Dynamical%20aspects%20of%20finite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems). ([MSC2020 37Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Exx); [MSC2020 37Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Jxx)) Aubry–Mather theory, built for twist maps of the annulus in the 1980s, was extended to higher dimensions in that Hamiltonian and Lagrangian setting by Mather, Mañé and Fathi in the 1990s. ([Arnaud, arXiv:1410.1834](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.1834))

### Key concepts
- **Rotation number (37E10, 37E45).** If $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is monotone with $F(x+1)=F(x)+1$, the translation number $\lim_{n\to\infty}(F^n(x)-x)/n$ exists and is independent of $x$. If it is irrational the circle map has no periodic orbit; if it equals $p/q$ in lowest terms, the map has an orbit of period $q$ and no orbit of any other period. ([Milnor, Dynamics notes §14, Theorem 14.10](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~jack/DYNOTES/dn14.pdf))
- **Denjoy's theorem and smooth linearization (37E10).** An orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism $f$ with irrational rotation number $\theta$ and with $f'>0$ of [bounded variation](node:Bounded%20Variation) (e.g. $f\in C^2$) is topologically conjugate to the rotation by $\theta$; every orbit is dense. For each irrational $\theta$ Denjoy built a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with rotation number $\theta$ not conjugate to a rotation. Arnold showed the conjugacy need not be smooth even for analytic $f$; Herman (1979) proved that for analytic diffeomorphisms the conjugacy is analytic for a full-measure set of rotation numbers, with results for $C^r$, $r\ge3$. ([Denjoy's theorem on rotation number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denjoy%27s_theorem_on_rotation_number)) Conjugacy is by a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism).
- **Sharkovskii's theorem (37E15).** Order $\mathbb N$ as $3\prec5\prec7\prec\cdots\prec2\cdot3\prec2\cdot5\prec\cdots\prec4\cdot3\prec\cdots\prec8\prec4\prec2\prec1$. If $f:I\to I$ is a continuous map of an interval with a point of least period $m$ and $m\prec n$, then $f$ has a point of least period $n$. Conversely every tail of the ordering is the set of periods of some continuous interval map. Li and Yorke (1975) showed period 3 also forces uncountably many points that never map to a cycle. ([Sharkovskii's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem))
- **Kneading theory (37E05).** Milnor–Thurston theory (preprints 1977, published 1988) studies iterates of piecewise monotone maps of a closed interval, through properties preserved by topological conjugacy, using the kneading matrix with entries in the ring of integer formal power series and the kneading determinant $D(t)=\sum_k D_kt^k$, a formal power series with odd integer coefficients; for unimodal maps with maximum at $c$ each $D_k=\pm1$ according to whether $f^{k+1}$ has a local maximum or minimum at $c$. Applications include piecewise linear models and the measure of maximal entropy. ([Milnor–Thurston kneading theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor%E2%80%93Thurston_kneading_theory)) [Topological Entropy](node:Topological%20Entropy) is nondecreasing in the real quadratic family; for real cubic families Milnor and Tresser reduce monotonicity (connectedness of isentropes) to a weak form of the Fatou conjecture, proved by Heckman, so real cubic isentropes are connected. ([Milnor–Tresser, arXiv:math/9809096](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9809096))
- **Renormalization and universality (37E20).** For one-parameter families of one-dimensional maps with a single quadratic maximum, the ratios of successive period-doubling intervals converge to $\delta\approx4.6692016091$, with second constant $\alpha\approx2.5029078751$. Feigenbaum announced this in 1975 (published 1978); Lanford gave a computer-assisted proof in 1982, and Lyubich the first complete non-numerical proof. ([Feigenbaum constants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feigenbaum_constants))
- **Density of hyperbolicity.** Kozlovski and co-authors proved density of hyperbolicity for one-dimensional real maps and for non-renormalizable complex polynomials ([Kozlovski–van Strien, Stable maps are dense in dimension one](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/6428)); the resolution of Smale's 11th problem (b), for smooth interval maps, is credited to Kozlovski, Shen and van Strien (2007). ([Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems)) The Fatou conjecture for real quadratic maps was proved by Graczyk–Świątek and Lyubich. ([Berger, arXiv:1703.00092](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.00092))
- **Surface flows: Poincaré–Bendixson (37E35).** For a differentiable flow on an open subset of the plane (or on the cylinder or sphere), a nonempty compact $\omega$-limit set containing finitely many fixed points is a fixed point, a periodic orbit, or a connected set of finitely many fixed points joined by homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits. Schwartz (1963) generalized the classification of minimal sets to every compact connected surface; on the torus a recurrent non-periodic orbit shows the planar trichotomy fails. ([Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem))
- **Surface homeomorphisms: Nielsen–Thurston (37E30).** On a compact orientable surface of genus $\ge2$, every homeomorphism is isotopic to one that is periodic, reducible (preserving a finite union of disjoint simple closed curves), or pseudo-Anosov, with stretched unstable and contracted stable foliations; a pseudo-Anosov map is never periodic or reducible. ([Nielsen–Thurston classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen%E2%80%93Thurston_classification)) See [Mapping Class Groups of Surfaces](node:Mapping%20Class%20Groups%20of%20Surfaces).
- **Twist maps: Aubry–Mather theory (37E40).** For a globally positive symplectic twist map of the 2-dimensional annulus, Mather and Aubry–Le Daeron proved existence of minimizing orbits; each lies on the graph of a Lipschitz function over a closed subset of the circle, and for every rotation number there is a minimizing measure whose support, an Aubry–Mather set, is an invariant loop, a periodic orbit, or a Cantor set. Mather, Mañé and Fathi extended the theory to higher dimensions in the 1990s. ([Arnaud, arXiv:1410.1834](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.1834))

### History
Bendixson completed the proof of the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem in 1901, after Poincaré's weaker 1892 version. ([Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem)) Denjoy's theorem dates from 1932 ([Denjoy's theorem on rotation number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denjoy%27s_theorem_on_rotation_number)), and Sharkovskii published his ordering in 1964. ([Sharkovskii's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem)) Milnor and Thurston's kneading preprints circulated from 1977 ([Milnor–Thurston kneading theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnor%E2%80%93Thurston_kneading_theory)), the same era as Feigenbaum's universality (1975–78). ([Feigenbaum constants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feigenbaum_constants)) Thurston's classification, completing work begun by Nielsen (1944), appeared in the *Bulletin of the AMS* in 1988. ([Nielsen–Thurston classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen%E2%80%93Thurston_classification))

### Open problems
- **Density of hyperbolicity for complex polynomials (Smale's 11th problem (a)).** Whether every complex polynomial can be approximated by one of the same degree all of whose critical points tend to periodic sinks is unresolved, even in the quadratic family parametrized by the Mandelbrot set; the real case is solved. ([Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems))
- **Regularity of Aubry–Mather sets.** For minimizing ergodic measures of symplectic twist maps of the annulus, Arnaud asks whether one with zero Lyapunov exponents can have support that is "not $C^1$ at every point", and whether a measure with nonzero exponents can have support that is not uniformly hyperbolic. ([Arnaud, Questions 1–2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.1834))
- **$C^r$ closing lemma on surfaces.** Pugh's closing lemma in higher smoothness ($C^r$, $r>1$) is unresolved in general, with a proof known for Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms of closed surfaces (Asaoka–Irie). ([Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Sharkovskii's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem): ordering, converse, Li–Yorke.
- **Learn:** [Milnor, Dynamics lecture notes, ch. IV: Degree one circle maps](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~jack/DYNOTES/dn14.pdf): lifts, translation number, periodic orbits.
- **Primary:** [Arnaud, Lyapunov exponents for conservative twisting dynamics: a survey (arXiv:1410.1834)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.1834): survey of Aubry–Mather theory and open questions.
- **Primary:** [Milnor and Tresser, On entropy and monotonicity for real cubic maps (arXiv:math/9809096)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9809096): kneading theory and monotonicity of entropy.
- **Further reading:** [Katok and Hasselblatt, Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems (CUP, 1995)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-the-modern-theory-of-dynamical-systems/introduction/B1E86AEBAEAD07CF09DAB6443539A310): Part 3 treats low-dimensional phenomena.
- **Further reading:** [de Melo and van Strien, One-Dimensional Dynamics (Springer, 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-78043-1): the standard monograph on circle and interval maps.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 37Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Exx): official code list.
references.MSC 37Fxx - Dynamical systems over compl:
## Reference
### Overview
Holomorphic dynamics, the complex-analytic branch of [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), studies iteration of holomorphic maps of a Riemann surface to itself, the central classical case being rational maps of the Riemann sphere $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ of degree at least two. Milnor's introductory lectures set this framework and assume basic complex variable theory and two-dimensional differential geometry. ([Milnor, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9201272)) For a rational map $f$, the Fatou set $F(f)$ is the maximal open subset of $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ on which the family of iterates $\{f^n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ is normal, and the Julia set is $J(f)=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus F(f)$. ([Calegari, Definition 1.7](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf)) See [Julia and Fatou Sets](node:Julia%20and%20Fatou%20Sets); the tools are those of [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) and [Riemann Surfaces](node:Riemann%20Surfaces), above all Montel's theorem and the hyperbolic metric.

The field has two faces. Dynamical-plane questions ask how $J(f)$ and the Fatou components look for one map; parameter-space questions ask how dynamics vary in holomorphic families, with the Mandelbrot set $M=\{c: f_c^n(0)\not\to\infty\}$ for $f_c(z)=z^2+c$ as the model. ([Wikipedia: Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set)) Fatou and Julia showed in the late 1910s that much of the theory of polynomial iteration extends to every rational map of degree greater than one, and the theory has since been developed in all dimensions. ([Wikipedia: Complex dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_dynamics))

### Scope
MSC2020 37Fxx (see also 30D05, 32H50) has these sub-codes. ([MSC2020 37Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Fxx))
- **37F05, 37F10, 37F12:** relations and correspondences; polynomials, rational maps, [entire and meromorphic functions](node:Entire%20and%20Meromorphic%20Functions), Fatou and Julia sets; critical orbits.
- **37F15, 37F20, 37F25:** expanding maps, hyperbolicity and structural stability; combinatorics and topology; renormalization.
- **37F31, 37F32, 37F34:** quasiconformal methods; Fuchsian and Kleinian groups as dynamical systems; Teichmüller theory and [moduli spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces) of holomorphic dynamical systems.
- **37F35, 37F40, 37F44, 37F46:** conformal densities and Hausdorff dimension; geometric limits; holomorphic families and holomorphic motions; bifurcations, parameter spaces, Mandelbrot and Multibrot sets.
- **37F50, 37F75, 37F80:** small divisors, rotation domains and linearization; holomorphic foliations and vector fields; higher-dimensional holomorphic and meromorphic dynamics.

Neighbours: the 37Fxx header cross-references 30D05 in [30Dxx](node:MSC%2030Dxx%20-%20Entire%20and%20meromorphic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable,%20and%20related%20topics) and 32H50 in [32Hxx](node:MSC%2032Hxx%20-%20Holomorphic%20mappings%20and%20correspondences), and 37F75 cross-references 34Mxx; other related classes of MSC 37 include [37Pxx](node:MSC%2037Pxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20and%20non-Archimedean%20dynamical%20systems) and [37Exx](node:MSC%2037Exx%20-%20Low-dimensional%20dynamical%20systems). ([MSC2020 37Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Critical points control attraction.** If $O$ is an attracting or superattracting cycle of a rational map of degree $d\ge2$, its immediate basin contains a critical point; hence there are at most $2d-2$ such cycles. ([Calegari, Lemma 1.18](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf))
- **No wandering domains (Sullivan).** For a rational map of $\widehat{\mathbb C}$, every component of $F(f)$ is eventually periodic. ([Calegari, Theorem 2.1](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf)) Periodic Fatou components are attracting basins, parabolic basins, Siegel disks (where $f$ is conjugate to an irrational rotation of the disk), or Herman rings. ([Wikipedia: Complex dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_dynamics)) The theorem fails for transcendental entire maps: $f(z)=z-\lambda\sin(2\pi z)+1$ with small $\lambda>0$ has wandering Fatou components. ([Calegari, Example 3.15](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf))
- **Connectedness of $M$ (Douady–Hubbard).** For $c\in M$, $J(f_c)$ is connected; for $c\notin M$, $J(f_c)$ is a Cantor set on which $f_c$ is conjugate to the one-sided 2-shift. The Böttcher coordinate gives a conformal isomorphism $\Phi:\mathbb C\setminus M\to\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}$, so $M$ is connected. ([Calegari, Lemma 5.5 and Theorem 5.10](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf)) Interior components of $M$ in which $f_c$ has an attracting cycle are hyperbolic components, each with a centre where $0$ is superattracting. ([Wikipedia: Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set))
- **Thurston's characterization (37F20, 37F34).** A postcritically finite branched cover $f:S^2\to S^2$ with hyperbolic orbifold is equivalent to a rational map if and only if every $f$-stable multicurve $\Gamma$ has Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue $\lambda(\Gamma,f)<1$; the rational map is then unique up to conjugacy. Moreover, $f$ is equivalent to a rational map if and only if an associated self-map $\sigma_f$ of the Teichmüller space of $(S^2,P(f))$ has a fixed point. ([Calegari, Theorem 4.6 and Lemma 4.8](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf)) Thurston obtained it in 1982; Douady and Hubbard circulated a proof in 1984, published in 1993. ([Ohshika–Papadopoulos, holomorphic dynamics](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.06344))
- **Hausdorff dimension (37F35).** The boundary of $M$ has Hausdorff dimension two, and for generic $c\in\partial M$ the Julia set of $z^2+c$ also has dimension two; the proof analyses bifurcations of parabolic periodic points. ([Shishikura, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9201282))
- **Kleinian groups and quasiconformal rigidity (37F31, 37F32).** Flexible Lattès maps come in one-parameter families of quasiconformally conjugate maps whose invariant Beltrami differentials live on $J(f)$, in contrast with Sullivan's theorem that Kleinian groups are quasiconformally rigid on their limit sets. ([Calegari, §3](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf)) Holomorphic motions (37F44), holomorphic families of injections $f_t:X\to\mathbb C$ with $f_0=\mathrm{id}$, were introduced by Mañé, Sad, and Sullivan; Sullivan and Thurston proved that any holomorphic motion of a subset of $\mathbb C$ over the unit disk extends to a holomorphic motion of the whole plane over a smaller disk $|t|<a$, with $a>0$ universal. ([Ohshika–Papadopoulos, holomorphic dynamics](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.06344))
- **Transcendental dynamics (37F10).** For transcendental entire $f$ the escaping set $I(f)=\{z:f^n(z)\to\infty\}$ is nonempty, $\partial I(f)=J(f)$, and every component of $\overline{I(f)}$ is unbounded (Eremenko, 1989). ([Wikipedia: Escaping set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escaping_set)) In the Eremenko–Lyubich class $\mathcal B$ there is a function whose Julia set has only bounded path-components, while for finite-order functions in $\mathcal B$ every escaping point can be joined to $\infty$ by a curve of escaping points. ([Rottenfußer–Rückert–Rempe–Schleicher, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.3213)) Eremenko's conjecture, that every component of $I(f)$ is unbounded, was disproved by a counterexample of Martí-Pete, Rempe, and Waterman (J. Amer. Math. Soc., 2025). ([Martí-Pete–Rempe–Waterman, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.10256))

### History
Fatou and Julia extended polynomial iteration to rational maps in the late 1910s. ([Wikipedia: Complex dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_dynamics)) Douady and Hubbard's work on quadratic polynomials (their foundational paper is cited as 1985) established the connectedness of $M$, and Yoccoz later proved local connectivity of $M$ at all finitely renormalizable parameters. ([Wikipedia: Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set)) Sullivan's no-wandering-domains theorem is the final piece in the classification of Fatou components of rational maps. ([Calegari, §2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf)) Shishikura's dimension result dates from a 1991 Stony Brook preprint. ([Shishikura, arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9201282))

### Open problems
- **MLC conjecture.** The Mandelbrot set is conjectured to be locally connected; Yoccoz proved this at finitely renormalizable parameters, and the full conjecture is still open. ([Wikipedia: Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set))
- **Density of hyperbolicity.** Hyperbolic components are conjectured to be the only interior components of $M$ and to be dense in $M$; this is called one of the most important open problems in complex dynamics, and MLC would imply it. ([Wikipedia: Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set))
- **Area of $\partial M$.** Whether the boundary of the Mandelbrot set has positive planar Lebesgue measure is unsolved. ([Wikipedia: Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Mandelbrot set (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set): definitions, hyperbolic components, MLC and density of hyperbolicity.
- **Learn:** [Calegari, Notes on Complex Dynamics](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/complex_dynamics_2022/complex_dynamics_notes.pdf): graduate course with proofs of Sullivan's and Thurston's theorems and connectedness of $M$.
- **Primary:** [Milnor, Dynamics in One Complex Variable: Introductory Lectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9201272): the standard introduction to rational dynamics.
- **Primary:** [Shishikura, The Hausdorff dimension of the boundary of the Mandelbrot set and Julia sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9201282): research paper.
- **Primary:** [Martí-Pete, Rempe, Waterman, Eremenko's conjecture, wandering Lakes of Wada, and maverick points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.10256): counterexample in transcendental dynamics.
- **Further reading:** [Milnor, Dynamics in One Complex Variable, 3rd ed. (Princeton, Annals of Mathematics Studies, 2006)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691124889/dynamics-in-one-complex-variable-am-160): the graduate text for the area.
references.MSC 37Gxx - Local and nonlocal bifurcati:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 37Gxx is the part of [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory) that classifies [bifurcation theory](node:Bifurcation%20Theory): normal forms, bifurcations of singular points and of periodic orbits, homoclinic orbits of hyperbolic singular points, nontransversal intersections, the infinite nonwandering sets that bifurcations create, bifurcations of attractors, and equivariant bifurcation theory. ([MSC2020 37Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Gxx)) A bifurcation occurs when a small smooth change of parameters in a family of [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) produces a sudden qualitative or topological change in behaviour; Poincaré introduced the word in 1885. ([Bifurcation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifurcation_theory))

The subject divides into local and global (nonlocal) bifurcations. Local bifurcations can be analysed through changes in the stability of equilibria, periodic orbits or other invariant sets and stay inside small neighbourhoods of the bifurcating object; for flows they occur when an eigenvalue of the linearisation has real part zero, for maps when a multiplier has modulus one. Global bifurcations occur when larger invariant sets collide with each other or with equilibria, cannot be detected by stability analysis of fixed points, and affect arbitrarily distant parts of phase space. The codimension of a bifurcation is the number of parameters that must be varied for it to occur. ([Bifurcation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifurcation_theory))

The working method for local problems is reduction: under nondegeneracy conditions the system near a non-hyperbolic equilibrium is restricted to a low-dimensional center manifold and brought to a normal form, whose leading coefficients (such as the first Lyapunov coefficient at a Hopf point) decide the generic picture. ([Shi, Hopf bifurcation lecture (William & Mary)](https://jxshix.people.wm.edu/2013-taiwan/lecture10-taiwan.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists, with a see-also to 34C23 and 34K18 ([MSC2020 37Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Gxx)):
- **37G05** normal forms for dynamical systems.
- **37G10** bifurcations of singular points; **37G15** bifurcations of limit cycles and periodic orbits.
- **37G20** hyperbolic singular points with homoclinic trajectories; **37G25** bifurcations connected with nontransversal intersection.
- **37G30** infinite nonwandering sets arising in bifurcations; **37G35** dynamical aspects of attractors and their bifurcations.
- **37G40** dynamical aspects of symmetries, equivariant bifurcation theory.

Neighbours: 34C23 is bifurcation theory for ordinary differential equations (see also 37Gxx), 34C37 homoclinic and heteroclinic solutions of ODEs, and 34C07 the theory of limit cycles of polynomial vector fields including Hilbert's 16th problem, all in [MSC 34Cxx - Qualitative theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Cxx%20-%20Qualitative%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations). ([MSC2020 34Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Cxx)) Computational methods for bifurcation problems are 37M20 in [MSC 37Mxx - Approximation methods and numerical treatment of dynamical systems](node:MSC%2037Mxx%20-%20Approximation%20methods%20and%20numerical%20treatment%20of%20dynamical%20systems), which points to 65Pxx ([MSC 65Pxx - Numerical problems in dynamical systems](node:MSC%2065Pxx%20-%20Numerical%20problems%20in%20dynamical%20systems)) for numerical analysis. ([MSC2020 37Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Mxx))

### Key concepts
- **Center manifold reduction (37G05, 37G10).** For a $C^r$ vector field, every equilibrium has a neighbourhood containing a unique stable manifold, a unique unstable manifold and a (not necessarily unique) $C^{r-1}$ center manifold, of the same dimension as and tangent to the center subspace spanned by the generalised eigenvectors with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda=0$. If there is no unstable manifold, nearby solutions approach a solution on the center manifold exponentially fast, so the bifurcation analysis reduces to the low-dimensional system on it. ([Center manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_manifold)) At a nondegenerate Hopf point the $n$-dimensional system is locally topologically equivalent to the planar normal form on the center manifold suspended by a standard saddle, $\dot y^s=-y^s$, $\dot y^u=y^u$. ([Shi, Hopf bifurcation lecture (William & Mary)](https://jxshix.people.wm.edu/2013-taiwan/lecture10-taiwan.pdf))
- **Fold (saddle-node).** For a scalar family $\dot x=f(r,x)$ with $f(0,0)=0$, $\partial_xf(0,0)=0$ (a zero eigenvalue), the nondegeneracy condition $\partial_x^2f(0,0)\neq0$ and the transversality condition $\partial_rf(0,0)\neq0$, the family is locally topologically equivalent to $\dot x=r\pm x^2$: for $\dot x=r+x^2$ a stable node at $-\sqrt{-r}$ and an unstable point at $+\sqrt{-r}$ exist for $r<0$, merge at $r=0$, and disappear for $r>0$. ([Saddle-node bifurcation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddle-node_bifurcation)) Saddle-node and Hopf are the only generic local bifurcations that are truly codimension one; transcritical and pitchfork bifurcations are often treated as codimension one only because their normal forms have a single parameter. ([Bifurcation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifurcation_theory))
- **Poincaré–Andronov–Hopf theorem.** Let $x'=f(\lambda,x)$, $x\in\mathbb R^n$, be smooth with a family of equilibria $x_0(\lambda)$ whose Jacobian has one pair of eigenvalues $\mu(\lambda)\pm i\omega(\lambda)$ with $\mu(\lambda_0)=0$, $\omega(\lambda_0)=\omega_0>0$, all other eigenvalues having nonzero real part, and $\mu'(\lambda_0)\neq0$. Then there is a family of periodic solutions $(\lambda(s),x(s))$, $0<s<\delta$, with $\lambda(s)\to\lambda_0$, period $T(s)\to2\pi/\omega_0$ and $x(s)\to x_0(\lambda_0)$. Writing $f(x,0)=A_0x+\tfrac12B(x,x)+\tfrac16C(x,x,x)+O(\|x\|^4)$ with $A_0q=i\omega_0q$, $A_0^Tp=-i\omega_0p$, $\langle p,q\rangle=1$, the first Lyapunov coefficient is
$$l_1(0)=\frac{1}{2\omega_0}\operatorname{Re}\big[\langle p,C(q,q,\bar q)\rangle-2\langle p,B(q,A_0^{-1}B(q,\bar q))\rangle+\langle p,B(\bar q,(2i\omega_0I_n-A_0)^{-1}B(q,q))\rangle\big],$$
and when $l_1(0)\neq0$ its sign decides whether the bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical. ([Shi, Hopf bifurcation lecture (William & Mary)](https://jxshix.people.wm.edu/2013-taiwan/lecture10-taiwan.pdf)) In the Stuart–Landau normal form $\dot z=z((\lambda+i)+b|z|^2)$, $b=\alpha+i\beta$, the cycle exists for $\lambda>0$ and is orbitally stable when $\alpha<0$ (supercritical); for $\alpha>0$ an unstable cycle exists for $\lambda<0$ (subcritical). ([Hopf bifurcation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_bifurcation)) For the Lorenz system the Hopf bifurcation at the nontrivial equilibria, at $r=\sigma(\sigma+b+3)/(\sigma-b-1)$, is subcritical. ([Shi, Hopf bifurcation lecture (William & Mary)](https://jxshix.people.wm.edu/2013-taiwan/lecture10-taiwan.pdf))
- **Bifurcations of cycles and maps (37G15).** For discrete maps (and for the Poincaré map of a periodic orbit) a local bifurcation occurs when a multiplier has modulus one; the codimension-one cases are the fold, the period-doubling (flip) bifurcation, and the Neimark–Sacker (secondary Hopf) bifurcation. ([Bifurcation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifurcation_theory))
- **Bogdanov–Takens point (codimension two).** At an equilibrium whose linearisation has a double zero eigenvalue (with nondegeneracy conditions) the normal form is $\dot y_1=y_2$, $\dot y_2=\beta_1+\beta_2y_1+y_1^2\pm y_1y_2$. Curves of saddle-node, Andronov–Hopf and homoclinic bifurcation all meet at the point, so a local codimension-two singularity forces a global (homoclinic) bifurcation nearby. Bogdanov and Takens described it independently; degenerate codimension-three cases are the Dumortier–Roussarie–Sotomayor bifurcations. ([Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogdanov%E2%80%93Takens_bifurcation))
- **Global bifurcations (37G20, 37G25).** Listed types include homoclinic bifurcation (a limit cycle collides with a saddle), heteroclinic bifurcation (a cycle collides with two or more saddles), infinite-period bifurcation (a saddle and a node appear on a limit cycle and the period tends to infinity), and the blue sky catastrophe (a limit cycle collides with a nonhyperbolic cycle). ([Bifurcation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifurcation_theory))
- **Shilnikov's saddle-focus theorem (37G20, 37G30).** For $\dot x=f(x)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, suppose the hyperbolic equilibrium $z$ has eigenvalues $\beta\pm i\omega$ and $\lambda$ with $0<\beta<-\lambda$, and $q(t)$ is a homoclinic orbit to $z$. Shilnikov (1965) proved that chaotic dynamics exist in every neighbourhood of $q$; he extended the result to higher dimensions in 1970 under the eigenvalue condition plus general-position, asymptotic-tangency and transversality conditions. In the $n$-dimensional statement for analytic $f$, for $1<\rho<-\operatorname{Re}\lambda/\beta$ (all $\lambda$ with negative real part), every neighbourhood of $q$ contains a subsystem of trajectories in one-to-one correspondence with the doubly infinite sequences of symbols $0,1,2,\dots$ satisfying $j_{i+1}<\rho j_i$. ([Coomes–Koçak–Palmer](https://www.math.miami.edu/~hk/publications/files/silnikov4.pdf)) Near the primary Shilnikov homoclinic bifurcation in reflection-symmetric systems, subsequent homoclinics appear in an ordered pattern with universal scaling. ([Xing–Pusuluri–Shilnikov, arXiv:2104.11314](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11314))
- **Melnikov method (37G25).** For a planar Hamiltonian system with a hyperbolic saddle connected to itself by a homoclinic orbit $q_0(t)$, perturbed by $\varepsilon g$ periodic in $t$ with frequency $\omega$, the Melnikov function $M(t_0,\phi_0)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}DH(q_0(t))\cdot g(q_0(t),\omega t+\omega t_0+\phi_0,0)\,dt$ measures to first order the splitting of stable and unstable manifolds. A simple zero ($M=0$, $\partial M/\partial t_0\neq0$) gives a transverse intersection for small $\varepsilon$, hence a Smale horseshoe and chaos; if $M$ never vanishes the manifolds do not intersect. ([Melnikov distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melnikov_distance)) Links to [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory) and [MSC 37Dxx - Dynamical systems with hyperbolic behavior](node:MSC%2037Dxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20with%20hyperbolic%20behavior).
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) and [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): every local test above is a condition on the spectrum of the linearisation at an equilibrium or on the multipliers of a cycle. ([Bifurcation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifurcation_theory))

### History
Poincaré named the phenomenon in 1885. ([Bifurcation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifurcation_theory)) The Melnikov method goes back to Poincaré (1890) and was developed by Melnikov in 1963; Guckenheimer and Holmes (1983) gave a standard textbook treatment. ([Melnikov distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melnikov_distance); [Crossref: Guckenheimer–Holmes](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1140-2)) Shilnikov's saddle-focus theorem dates from 1965, with extensions to four dimensions in 1967 and arbitrary dimension in 1970; Deng (1993) extended it to $C^5$ vector fields. ([Coomes–Koçak–Palmer](https://www.math.miami.edu/~hk/publications/files/silnikov4.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Hilbert's 16th problem (second part).** Determine an upper bound $H(n)$ for the number of limit cycles of planar polynomial vector fields of degree $n$. Whether a finite bound $H(n)$ exists remains unsolved for every $n>1$; Ilyashenko and Écalle proved that each individual polynomial vector field has finitely many limit cycles, and quadratic fields with four limit cycles are known. ([Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem)) MSC files the problem under 34C07. ([MSC2020 34Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Cxx))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bifurcation theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifurcation_theory): local and global types, codimension.
- **Learn:** [Shi, Lecture 9: Hopf bifurcation (William & Mary)](https://jxshix.people.wm.edu/2013-taiwan/lecture10-taiwan.pdf): proof of the Hopf theorem, center manifold reduction, the first Lyapunov coefficient, worked predator-prey and Lorenz examples, Alexander–Yorke global continuation.
- **Reference:** [Center manifold (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_manifold): existence, non-uniqueness and emergence of center manifolds.
- **Primary:** [Coomes, Koçak and Palmer, Shilnikov saddle-focus homoclinic orbits from numerics: higher dimensions](https://www.math.miami.edu/~hk/publications/files/silnikov4.pdf): states Shilnikov's theorem and its conditions (D1)–(D4).
- **Primary:** [Xing, Pusuluri and Shilnikov, Ordered intricacy of Shilnikov saddle-focus homoclinics in symmetric systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11314): research paper on homoclinic bifurcation structure.
- **Further reading:** [Kuznetsov, Elements of Applied Bifurcation Theory (Springer, Applied Mathematical Sciences, 2023)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-031-22007-4) and [Guckenheimer and Holmes, Nonlinear Oscillations, Dynamical Systems, and Bifurcations of Vector Fields (Springer, 1983)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1140-2): bibliographic records of the standard texts.
references.MSC 37Hxx - Random dynamical systems:
## Reference
### Overview
A random dynamical system (RDS) separates the noise from the state. On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ a measurable flow $\theta_t$ preserves $\mathbb P$ (a metric dynamical system), and a measurable map $\varphi:\mathbb T\times\Omega\times X\to X$ is a cocycle over $\theta$:
$$\varphi(0,\omega,\cdot)=\mathrm{id},\qquad \varphi(t+s,\omega,\cdot)=\varphi(t,\theta_s\omega,\varphi(s,\omega,\cdot))$$
for all $\omega$ and $s,t\in\mathbb T$. The RDS is continuous or $C^k$ when $\varphi(t,\omega,\cdot)$ is. ([Engel, Definition 1.1.1](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf)) The cocycle property says that evolving for $s$ and then $t$ with the same noise realization equals evolving for $t+s$; ergodicity of the base is usually not part of the definition. ([Wikipedia: Random dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_dynamical_system)) See [Random Dynamical Systems](node:Random%20Dynamical%20Systems) and, for the deterministic theory it generalizes, [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) and [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory).

RDS arise from products of i.i.d. random maps, from random ODEs, and from stochastic differential equations. For a Stratonovich SDE $dX_t=f(X_t)\,dt+\sum_j g_j(X_t)\circ dW^j_t$ with $f\in C^{k,\delta}_b$ and $g_j\in C^{k+1,\delta}_b$, there is a unique $C^k$ RDS whose orbits solve the SDE; the construction starts from Kunita's two-parameter stochastic flows of $C^k$ diffeomorphisms $\varphi_{st}$ with $\varphi_{rt}\circ\varphi_{sr}=\varphi_{st}$. ([Engel, Theorem 1.4.5](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf)) This makes Lyapunov exponents, attractors, invariant manifolds, and bifurcations available for stochastic models, connecting the subject with [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus) and [stochastic analysis](node:MSC%2060Hxx%20-%20Stochastic%20analysis).

### Scope
MSC2020 37Hxx (see also 15B52, 34Fxx, 47B80, 70L05, 82C05, 93Exx) has these sub-codes. ([MSC2020 37Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Hxx))
- **37H05:** general theory of random and stochastic dynamical systems.
- **37H10:** generation, random and stochastic difference and differential equations (see also 34F05, 34K50, 60H10, 60H15).
- **37H12:** random iteration.
- **37H15:** multiplicative ergodic theory and Lyapunov exponents (see also 34Fxx, 37Axx, 37Cxx, 37Dxx).
- **37H20, 37H30:** [bifurcation theory](node:Bifurcation%20Theory) (see also 37Gxx); stability theory for random and stochastic dynamical systems.

Neighbours named by the MSC entry itself: the 37Hxx header cross-references 15B52, [34Fxx](node:MSC%2034Fxx%20-%20Ordinary%20differential%20equations%20and%20systems%20with%20randomness), 47B80, 70L05, 82C05 and 93Exx; 37H10 points to 60H10 and 60H15 in [60Hxx](node:MSC%2060Hxx%20-%20Stochastic%20analysis); 37H15 points to [37Axx](node:MSC%2037Axx%20-%20Ergodic%20theory), 37Cxx and 37Dxx; and 37H20 points to [37Gxx](node:MSC%2037Gxx%20-%20Local%20and%20nonlocal%20bifurcation%20theory%20for%20dynamical%20systems). ([MSC2020 37Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Hxx))

### Key concepts
- **Invariant measures and the correspondence theorem.** A probability $\mu$ on $\Omega\times X$ is invariant if it is preserved by the skew product $\Theta_t(\omega,x)=(\theta_t\omega,\varphi(t,\omega,x))$ and has marginal $\mathbb P$, so $\mu(d\omega,dx)=\mu_\omega(dx)\mathbb P(d\omega)$. For a Markov RDS on a Polish space, invariant Markov measures correspond bijectively to stationary measures $\rho$ of the associated Markov process: $\rho=\mathbb E[\mu_\omega]$, and conversely $\mu_\omega=\lim_k\varphi(t_k,\theta_{-t_k}\omega,\cdot)_*\rho$. ([Engel, Definition 1.5.1 and Theorem 1.5.6](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf)) See [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains).
- **Furstenberg–Kesten theorem.** For a linear cocycle with generator $A$ and $\log^+\|A^{\pm1}\|\in L^1(\mathbb P)$, the extremal exponents $\lambda_+=\lim\frac1n\log\|A_n(\omega)\|$ and $\lambda_-=\lim\frac1n\log\|A_n(\omega)^{-1}\|^{-1}$ exist almost surely and are invariant and integrable. ([Engel, Theorem 2.3.1](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf))
- **Oseledets multiplicative ergodic theorem (37H15).** Under the same integrability condition, for a.e. $\omega$ there are $k(\omega)$ exponents $\lambda_1>\dots>\lambda_k$ and a flag $\mathbb R^d=V^1_\omega\supsetneq\dots\supsetneq V^k_\omega\supsetneq\{0\}$ with $A(\omega)V^i_\omega=V^i_{\theta\omega}$ and $\lim\frac1n\log\|A_n(\omega)v\|=\lambda_i$ for $v\in V^i_\omega\setminus V^{i+1}_\omega$; if $\mathbb P$ is ergodic these data are a.s. constant. With invertible base one obtains an invariant splitting $\mathbb R^d=\bigoplus E_i(\omega)$ with two-sided growth rates and subexponentially decaying angles. ([Engel, Theorems 2.5.2 and 2.5.3](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf))
- **Furstenberg's positivity theorem.** If $X_k$ are i.i.d. in $SL(d,\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb E\log\|X_1\|<\infty$, and the closed group $G_X$ generated by the support is non-compact with no $G_X$-invariant finite union of proper subspaces, then $\frac1n\log\|X_n\cdots X_1\|\to\lambda_F>0$ almost surely. ([Gorodetski–Kleptsyn, Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.00416)) See [Random Matrices](node:Random%20Matrices).
- **Random attractors.** A compact random set $A$ with $\varphi(t,\omega)A(\omega)=A(\theta_t\omega)$ is a pullback attractor if $\operatorname{dist}(\varphi(t,\theta_{-t}\omega)D(\theta_{-t}\omega),A(\omega))\to0$ a.s. for every $D$ in a class of tempered sets; weak attractors require only convergence in probability, and pullback and forward almost-sure attraction are not equivalent in general. If a continuous RDS on a Polish space has a compact random set absorbing every bounded deterministic set, a random pullback attractor exists, measurable with respect to the past; every forward-invariant random compact set supports an invariant measure. ([Engel, Definition 3.1.2, Theorems 3.1.10 and 3.2.4](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf)) Compare the deterministic [Global Attractors](node:Global%20Attractors).
- **Synchronization by noise.** If the RDS is asymptotically stable on some open set with positive probability, swift transitive, and contracting on large sets, and has a weak random attractor measurable with respect to the past, then the attractor is a single random point a.s. ([Engel, Theorem 3.2.9](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf)) Flandoli, Gess, and Scheutzow show these conditions are essentially necessary for additive-noise SDEs and prove synchronization for a large class including multidimensional double-well potentials. ([Flandoli–Gess–Scheutzow, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.1340)) Conversely, for an SDE-induced ergodic RDS with positive top exponent $\lambda_1>0$, the sample measures $\mu_\omega$ are a.s. atomless. ([Engel, Theorem 3.3.1](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf))

### History
Furstenberg and Kesten proved in 1960 that products of random matrices generated by a stationary process have a well-defined exponential growth rate, and Furstenberg then showed that this exponent is positive in most cases. ([Gorodetski–Kleptsyn, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.00416)) Crauel and Flandoli's "Attractors for random dynamical systems" appeared in Probability Theory and Related Fields 100 (1994). ([Crossref: Crauel–Flandoli 1994](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01193705)) Ludwig Arnold's monograph *Random Dynamical Systems* (Springer, 1998) is one of the three main references of Engel's 2021 course, with Kuksin–Shirikyan's book on two-dimensional turbulence and Viana's lectures on Lyapunov exponents; the notes cite Kunita's monograph on stochastic flows for the first step of the SDE generation theorem. ([Crossref: Arnold 1998](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-12878-7)) ([Engel, references](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Positive exponents for the standard map.** For the Chirikov standard map $\Phi_L(I,\theta)=(I+L\sin\theta,\theta+I+L\sin\theta)$ no one has proved or disproved positivity of its Lyapunov exponents for any single $L$, however large; the best known result gives positivity on sets of Hausdorff dimension 2. Blumenthal, Xue, and Young show that independent random perturbations as small as about $e^{-L^{2-\varepsilon}}$ at each step suffice to give an exponent of order $\log L$, and propose noise as the tractable route; they expect extensions to higher dimensions and weaker hypotheses on the unperturbed map. ([Blumenthal–Xue–Young, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.07583))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Random dynamical system (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_dynamical_system): definition of the cocycle and the pullback viewpoint on random attractors.
- **Learn:** [Engel, Lecture Notes on Random Dynamical Systems (FU Berlin, 2021)](https://irtg.math.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/schools/rds_detailed_lecture_notes.pdf): generation from SDEs, invariant measures, MET, random attractors, Pesin formula, bifurcations.
- **Primary:** [Flandoli, Gess, Scheutzow, Synchronization by noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.1340): necessary and sufficient conditions for singleton random attractors.
- **Primary:** [Blumenthal, Xue, Young, Lyapunov exponents for random perturbations of some area-preserving maps including the standard map](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.07583): Annals paper on noise-induced positive exponents.
- **Further reading:** [Arnold, Random Dynamical Systems (Springer Monographs in Mathematics, 1998)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-12878-7): the standard monograph for the area.
references.MSC 37Jxx - Dynamical aspects of finite-:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 37J covers the dynamics of finite-dimensional Hamiltonian and Lagrangian systems within [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory), with see-also references to [53Dxx](node:MSC%2053Dxx%20-%20Symplectic%20geometry,%20contact%20geometry) (symplectic and contact geometry), [70Fxx](node:MSC%2070Fxx%20-%20Dynamics%20of%20a%20system%20of%20particles,%20including%20celestial%20mechanics) (particle systems and celestial mechanics) and [70Hxx](node:MSC%2070Hxx%20-%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20mechanics) (Hamiltonian and Lagrangian mechanics). ([MSC2020 37Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Jxx))

On a symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$ a smooth function $H$ determines a unique vector field $X_H$ by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; in coordinates with $\omega=\sum_j dq_j\wedge dp_j$ its integral curves solve $\dot q_i=\partial H/\partial p_i$, $\dot p_i=-\partial H/\partial q_i$. The flow of $X_H$ preserves both $\omega$ and $H$. A vector field preserving $\omega$ is symplectic; it is Hamiltonian exactly when $\iota_X\omega$ is exact, and $H^1_{\rm dR}(M)$ measures the obstruction (on $T^2$, $\partial/\partial\theta_1$ is symplectic but not Hamiltonian). ([Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, §18.1–18.2](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf)) See [Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry) and [Hamiltonian Dynamical Systems](node:Hamiltonian%20Dynamical%20Systems).

The dynamical questions of the area sit between two extremes: completely integrable systems, where motion is linear on invariant tori, and their small perturbations, where KAM theory shows that most tori survive while Arnold diffusion describes instability along the gaps. ([Liouville–Arnold theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%E2%80%93Arnold_theorem); [KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem); [Arnold diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_diffusion))

### Scope
The MSC2020 codes are: general theory, structures, symmetries and invariants (37J06); symplectic and canonical mappings (37J11); fixed and periodic points (37J12); bifurcation problems (37J20); stability problems (37J25); obstructions to integrability (37J30); completely integrable systems and integrability tests (37J35); relations with [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) (37J37), with algebraic geometry and [complex analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) (37J38), and with topology and symplectic or Poisson geometry (37J39, see also 53D20); perturbations, normal forms, small divisors, KAM theory and Arnol'd diffusion (37J40); periodic, homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits (37J46); action-minimizing orbits and measures (37J51); contact systems (37J55, see also 53D10); nonholonomic systems (37J60); nonautonomous systems such as Painlevé equations (37J65); and completely integrable discrete systems (37J70). ([MSC2020 37Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Jxx))

- **Versus 37K.** [Infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian systems](node:Infinite-Dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20Systems) are [37Kxx](node:MSC%2037Kxx%20-%20Dynamical%20system%20aspects%20of%20infinite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems). ([MSC2020 37Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Jxx))
- **Versus 53D and 70H.** The 37Jxx heading lists 53Dxx, 70Fxx and 70Hxx as see-also references, and its own codes are phrased as dynamical aspects (periodic orbits, bifurcation, stability, integrability, perturbation theory); 37J39 and 37J55 point to 53D20 and 53D10. ([MSC2020 37Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Jxx))

### Key concepts
- **Liouville–Arnold theorem (37J35).** Let $(M^{2n},\omega,H)$ have $n$ independent integrals $f_1=H,f_2,\dots,f_n$ in involution, and let $c$ be a regular value of $f=(f_1,\dots,f_n)$. Then $f^{-1}(c)$ is a Lagrangian submanifold; if the flows of the $X_{f_i}$ are complete, the component through $p$ is a homogeneous space for $\mathbb R^n$ with angle coordinates in which the flows are linear, and there are complementary action coordinates forming, with the angles, a Darboux chart. Compact components are tori (Liouville tori). ([Cannas da Silva, Theorem 18.12](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf)) Liouville proved the original form in 1853 for $\mathbb R^{2n}$; Arnold generalized it to symplectic manifolds. ([Liouville–Arnold theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%E2%80%93Arnold_theorem)) See [Action-Angle Variables](node:Action-Angle%20Variables).
- **KAM theorem (37J40).** Under a weak perturbation of an integrable Hamiltonian satisfying a non-degeneracy condition, invariant tori whose frequency vector $\omega\in\mathbb R^d$ ($d\ge2$) is Diophantine, $|\langle k,\omega\rangle|\ge\gamma|k|^{-\tau}$ for nonzero integer $k$, deform and survive, while other tori can be destroyed by arbitrarily small perturbations and become invariant Cantor sets (Cantori). Kolmogorov made the original breakthrough in 1954; Moser (1962, smooth twist maps) and Arnold (1963, analytic Hamiltonians) proved and extended it. ([KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem)) See [KAM Theory](node:KAM%20Theory).
- **Nekhoroshev estimates (37J40).** For a nearly integrable system $H(I)+\varepsilon h(I,\theta)$ with $n$ degrees of freedom, under technical assumptions, the actions satisfy $|I(t)-I(0)|<\varepsilon^{1/(2n)}$ for $|t|<\exp\big(c\,\varepsilon^{-1/(2n)}\big)$, so instability, when present, is exponentially slow. ([Nekhoroshev estimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nekhoroshev_estimates))
- **Arnold diffusion (37J40).** For generic nearly integrable systems one expects a fixed $\rho>0$ such that for every small $\varepsilon>0$ some solutions have $\|I(T)-I(0)\|\ge\rho$; the phenomenon occurs with more than two degrees of freedom, where invariant tori no longer separate phase space. Arnold's 1964 example used chains of whiskered tori with transversally intersecting invariant manifolds. ([Arnold diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_diffusion)) Bernard, Kaloshin and Zhang proved that a generic perturbation of a strictly convex integrable $H_0$, with $n\ge2$ degrees of freedom, has orbits whose actions drift by a fixed amount independent of $\varepsilon$ (here $H=H_0(p)+\varepsilon H_1(\theta,p,t)$ with $\theta\in\mathbb T^n$ and the perturbation periodic in $t$), combining normally hyperbolic invariant cylinders with Mather's variational method. ([Bernard–Kaloshin–Zhang, arXiv:1112.2773](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.2773))
- **Poincaré–Birkhoff theorem and Aubry–Mather theory (37J11, 37J51).** An area- and orientation-preserving [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) of an annulus rotating the two boundary circles in opposite directions has at least two fixed points; Poincaré stated it in 1912 and Birkhoff proved it in 1913. ([Poincaré–Birkhoff theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Birkhoff_theorem)) For conservative twist maps, minimizing orbits exist for every rotation number and their supports (Aubry–Mather sets) are invariant loops, periodic orbits or Cantor sets; Mather, Mañé and Fathi extended the theory to higher dimensions (weak KAM). ([Arnaud, arXiv:1410.1834](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.1834))
- **Arnold conjecture (37J12, 37J39).** Strong form: a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of a closed symplectic manifold $M$ has at least as many fixed points as some smooth function on $M$ has critical points. Weak form: a nondegenerate one has at least $\sum_i\dim H_i(M;\mathbb F)$ fixed points; this was proved for $\mathbb F=\mathbb Q$ by Fukaya–Ono (1999), for $\mathbb F_p$ by Abouzaid–Blumberg (2021), and for $\mathbb Z$ by Rezchikov, Bai and Xu (2022). ([Arnold conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_conjecture))
- **Symmetry and reduction (37J06, 37J39).** [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) (1918): if the action $\int L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt$ is invariant under a one-parameter group shifting $t$ by $\varepsilon T$ and $q$ by $\varepsilon Q$, then $(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\dot q-L)T-\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}Q$ is conserved; time invariance gives energy and an ignorable coordinate gives its momentum. ([Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem)) For a Hamiltonian action of a Lie group $G$ with equivariant [moment map](node:Moment%20Maps) $\mu$, if $G$ acts freely and properly on $\mu^{-1}(0)$, then $\mu^{-1}(0)/G$ is a symplectic manifold of dimension $\dim M-2\dim G$ (Marsden–Weinstein, 1974). ([Symplectic reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_reduction)) See [Symplectic Reduction](node:Symplectic%20Reduction) and [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics).

### History
Liouville's integrability theorem dates from 1853 ([Liouville–Arnold theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%E2%80%93Arnold_theorem)); Poincaré's geometric theorem was proved by Birkhoff in 1913 ([Poincaré–Birkhoff theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Birkhoff_theorem)); Noether's theorem appeared in "Invariante Variationsprobleme" in 1918 ([Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem)). KAM theory began with Kolmogorov in 1954 and Arnold hoped to apply it to the Solar System, but it worked only for the three-body problem because of a degeneracy in his formulation for more bodies. ([KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem)) Arnold's diffusion example appeared in 1964 ([Arnold diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_diffusion)), and Aubry–Mather theory in the 1980s. ([Arnaud](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.1834))

### Open problems
- **Analytic Arnold diffusion in a priori stable systems.** Delshams and Zhang write that for real analytic systems "generic Arnold diffusion for a priori stable systems remain wide open", although generic $C^r$ a priori stable systems have seen much progress (Cheng; Kaloshin–Zhang). ([Delshams–Zhang, arXiv:2412.11349](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.11349)) Chen and de la Llave likewise call genericity of Arnold diffusion in the analytic category an open problem, and prove it in the a priori unstable setting. ([Chen–de la Llave, arXiv:2103.03847](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03847))
- **Regularity of Aubry–Mather sets.** For minimizing ergodic measures of symplectic twist maps of the 2-dimensional annulus, Arnaud asks whether one with zero Lyapunov exponents can have support that is "not $C^1$ at every point", and whether one with nonzero exponents can have support that is not uniformly hyperbolic. ([Arnaud, Questions 1–2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.1834))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem): statement, history, Cantori.
- **Learn:** [Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf): Hamiltonian vector fields, integrable systems, moment maps and reduction.
- **Primary:** [Bernard, Kaloshin and Zhang, Arnold diffusion in arbitrary degrees of freedom (arXiv:1112.2773)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.2773): generic diffusion for convex nearly integrable systems.
- **Primary:** [Arnaud, Lyapunov exponents for conservative twisting dynamics: a survey (arXiv:1410.1834)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1410.1834): Aubry–Mather theory and open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics (Springer GTM, 1989)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2063-1): standard graduate text, including Liouville–Arnold and perturbation theory.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 37Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Jxx): official code list.
references.MSC 37Kxx - Dynamical system aspects of:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 37Kxx treats evolution PDEs as Hamiltonian [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), or Lagrangian ones, on infinite-dimensional phase spaces of functions. The Hamilton equations take the form $u_t=\partial_x\,\delta H/\delta u(x)$, with the variational derivative replacing partial derivatives. For KdV with $H[u]=\int_{\mathbb R}(\tfrac12u_x^2+u^3)\,dx$ one has $\delta H/\delta u=-u_{xx}+3u^2$, so $u_t=\partial_x(\delta H/\delta u)$ is $u_t=6uu_x-u_{xxx}$, with integration by parts justified by decay at infinity. ([Dunajski, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.04077)) This places [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) inside the framework of [Infinite-Dimensional Hamiltonian Systems](node:Infinite-Dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20Systems) and [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics).

The area has two halves. The integrable side (Lax pairs, inverse scattering, solitons, bi-Hamiltonian hierarchies) produces exactly solvable models with infinitely many conserved quantities. ([Torrielli, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02946)) The nonintegrable side asks which features survive perturbation: KAM tori, Birkhoff normal forms, invariant Gibbs measures, energy transfer to high frequencies, and long-time asymptotics such as soliton resolution. ([Eliasson–Kuksin, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.2393)) ([Bambusi–Grébert, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0411011)) ([Debussche–Mouzard, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00583)) ([Colliander–Keel–Staffilani–Takaoka–Tao, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0808.1742)) ([Chatterjee, abstract](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1203.4027))

### Scope
MSC2020 37Kxx (see also 35Axx, 35Qxx) has these sub-codes. ([MSC2020 37Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Kxx))
- **37K06, 37K10:** general theory, Hamiltonian and Lagrangian structures, symmetries, conservation laws; completely integrable systems, integrability tests, integrable hierarchies (KdV, KP, Toda).
- **37K15, 37K20, 37K25, 37K30:** inverse spectral and scattering methods; connections with algebraic geometry, [complex analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) and [special functions](node:Special%20Functions); with topology and differential geometry; with infinite-dimensional [Lie algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras).
- **37K35, 37K40:** Lie–Bäcklund and other transformations; soliton theory and asymptotic behaviour of solutions.
- **37K45, 37K50, 37K55, 37K58:** stability problems; bifurcation problems; perturbations and KAM theory; variational principles.
- **37K60, 37K65:** lattice dynamics and integrable lattice equations; Hamiltonian systems on diffeomorphism groups and on manifolds of mappings and metrics.

Neighbours: the 37Kxx header cross-references 35Axx and [35Qxx](node:MSC%2035Qxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20of%20mathematical%20physics%20and%20other%20areas%20of%20application), 37K20 points to 14H70, and 37K60 points to 37L60 in [37Lxx](node:MSC%2037Lxx%20-%20Infinite-dimensional%20dissipative%20dynamical%20systems); the finite-dimensional counterpart is [37Jxx](node:MSC%2037Jxx%20-%20Dynamical%20aspects%20of%20finite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems), and the parent class 37 cross-references 70-XX, which contains [70Hxx](node:MSC%2070Hxx%20-%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20mechanics). ([MSC2020 37Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Kxx))

### Key concepts
- **Lax representation and conservation laws.** If finite square matrices satisfy $\dot L=[M,L]$, then $\operatorname{tr}(L^n)$ is conserved for every $n\ge1$ by cyclicity of the trace, so the eigenvalues of $L$ are conserved. ([Torrielli, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1606.02946)) The review develops the field-theory version through monodromy and transfer matrices up to the classical inverse scattering method. KdV is written as a Lax equation with a Sturm–Liouville operator and has infinitely many conserved quantities. ([Torrielli, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02946)) ([Wikipedia: KdV equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation)) See [Lax Pairs](node:Lax%20Pairs).
- **Bi-Hamiltonian structure and recursion.** KdV is Hamiltonian in two ways: $u_t=D\,\delta H_1/\delta u=E\,\delta H_0/\delta u$ with $D=\partial_x$, $H_1=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2+u^3)dx$, and $E=-\partial_x^3+4u\partial_x+2u_x$, $H_0=\tfrac12\int u^2dx$. If $D$ is non-degenerate and $R=E\circ D^{-1}$ satisfies $R^n(D\,\delta H_0/\delta u)\in\operatorname{im}D$ for all $n$, there are conserved functionals $H_n$ in involution, $\{H_m,H_n\}=\int\frac{\delta H_m}{\delta u}D\frac{\delta H_n}{\delta u}dx=0$, generated by $D\,\delta H_n/\delta u=R^n(D\,\delta H_0/\delta u)$; for KdV, $R=-\partial_x^2+4u+2u_x\partial_x^{-1}$. ([Dunajski, §3.2.1 and Theorem 3.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.04077))
- **KAM for Hamiltonian PDEs (37K55).** For the $d$-dimensional NLS $-i\dot u=-\Delta u+V*u+\varepsilon\,\partial F/\partial\bar u$ on $\mathbb T^d$, with an analytic convolution potential $V$ (real Fourier coefficients) and real analytic $F$, Eliasson and Kuksin show that for $|\varepsilon|$ small, a large set of parameters gives time-quasi-periodic solutions that persist, have all Lyapunov exponents equal to zero, and have reducible linearized equations. ([Eliasson–Kuksin, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.2393)) See [KAM Theory](node:KAM%20Theory).
- **Birkhoff normal form.** Bambusi and Grébert prove an abstract Birkhoff normal form theorem for semilinear Hamiltonian PDEs whose nonlinearity has tame modulus; in the nonresonant case every small-amplitude solution stays close to a torus for very long times, which bounds the growth of high Sobolev norms for NLW and NLS in one dimension and NLS on $\mathbb T^d$. ([Bambusi–Grébert, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0411011))
- **Energy cascade and growth of Sobolev norms.** For defocusing cubic NLS $-iu_t+\Delta u=|u|^2u$ on $\mathbb T^2$, smooth solutions conserve energy and mass, so $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}$ stays bounded. Colliander–Keel–Staffilani–Takaoka–Tao prove: for any $s>1$, $K\gg1$, $0<\delta\ll1$ there is a global smooth solution with $\|u(0)\|_{H^s}\le\delta$ and $\|u(T)\|_{H^s}\ge K$ for some $T$. In one dimension the equation is integrable and $\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$ stays bounded for $s\ge1$. ([CKSTT, §1 and Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0808.1742)) See [Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation](node:Nonlinear%20Schrödinger%20Equation) and [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces).
- **Invariant Gibbs measures.** Bourgain's 1994 paper treats the periodic NLS and its invariant measures. ([Crossref: Bourgain 1994](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02099299)) Continuing the investigations of the periodic NLS started by Lebowitz, Rose, and Speer and by Bourgain, Debussche and Mouzard add a distributional potential and prove global well-posedness for a set of data of full normalized Gibbs measure (after truncation in the focusing case), with the set and the measure invariant under the flow. ([Debussche–Mouzard, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00583)) See [Gibbs Measures](node:Gibbs%20Measures).

### History
Boussinesq introduced the KdV equation in 1877 and Korteweg and de Vries rediscovered it in 1895; Zabusky and Kruskal's 1965 computer simulations revealed solitons, and in 1967 Gardner, Greene, Kruskal, and Miura developed the inverse scattering method. ([Wikipedia: KdV equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation)) Magri's paper "A simple model of the integrable Hamiltonian equation" appeared in the Journal of Mathematical Physics 19 (1978). ([Crossref: Magri 1978](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1063/1.523777)) Bourgain's paper on invariant measures for the periodic NLS appeared in Communications in Mathematical Physics in 1994. ([Crossref: Bourgain 1994](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02099299)) The Eliasson–Kuksin KAM theorem for multidimensional NLS was published in the Annals of Mathematics in 2010. ([Annals: Eliasson–Kuksin](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2010/172-1/p07))

### Open problems
- **Unbounded growth of Sobolev norms.** For the defocusing cubic NLS on tori of dimension two and higher, the 2008 CKSTT paper states that it is unknown whether solutions with unbounded growth in $H^s$, $s>1$, exist, let alone whether such growth is generic; their construction gives arbitrarily large but finite growth. ([CKSTT, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0808.1742)) On the product spaces $\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^d$, $d\ge2$, Hani, Pausader, Tzvetkov, and Visciglia obtained global solutions of the defocusing and focusing cubic NLS with infinitely growing high Sobolev norms.
