([Hani–Pausader–Tzvetkov–Visciglia, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.2275))
- **Soliton resolution.** The conjecture that generic global solutions of the focusing NLS decompose into a dispersing radiation part and a localized soliton part is described as one of the fundamental open problems for nonlinear dispersive equations; Chatterjee proves a statistical version for mass-subcritical nonlinearity in a discrete setting. ([Chatterjee, abstract and §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1203.4027)) For wave-type equations, Duyckaerts, Kenig, Martel, and Merle proved soliton resolution for all times for every energy-space solution of the critical co-rotational wave map equation, and for bounded radial solutions of the energy-critical cubic [wave equation](node:Wave%20Equation) in dimension four. ([Duyckaerts–Kenig–Martel–Merle, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01293))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Korteweg–de Vries equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93De_Vries_equation): the model integrable PDE and its history.
- **Learn:** [Dunajski, Integrable Systems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.04077): lecture notes on inverse scattering, Hamiltonian and bi-Hamiltonian structures, and Lax pairs.
- **Primary:** [Torrielli, Lectures on Classical Integrability (J. Phys. A, 2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02946): review of Lax pairs, r-matrices, and classical inverse scattering.
- **Primary:** [Eliasson and Kuksin, KAM for the Non-Linear Schrödinger Equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.2393): KAM theorem for multidimensional NLS.
- **Primary:** [Colliander, Keel, Staffilani, Takaoka, Tao, Weakly turbulent solutions for the cubic defocusing NLS](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.1742): growth of Sobolev norms via energy cascade.
- **Primary:** [Bambusi and Grébert, Birkhoff normal form for PDEs with tame modulus](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0411011): normal-form theory for Hamiltonian PDEs.
- **Further reading:** [Olver, Applications of Lie Groups to Differential Equations (Springer GTM, 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4350-2): symmetry methods for differential equations; Dunajski cites it for the proof of the recursion-operator theorem above. ([Dunajski, §3.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.04077))

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 37L, "Infinite-dimensional dissipative dynamical systems", is the part of [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory) that treats dissipative evolution equations, chiefly parabolic and damped [partial differential equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations), as [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) on infinite-dimensional phase spaces; it carries see-also references to [35Bxx](node:MSC%2035Bxx%20-%20Qualitative%20properties%20of%20solutions%20to%20partial%20differential%20equations) and [35Qxx](node:MSC%2035Qxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20of%20mathematical%20physics%20and%20other%20areas%20of%20application). ([MSC2020 37Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Lxx))

The solution operators form a semigroup $S(t)$, $t\ge0$, and the central object is the global attractor, a compact invariant set attracting all bounded sets. The guiding theme is that, although the phase space is infinite-dimensional, under mild assumptions the attractor of a dissipative PDE on a bounded domain has finite fractal dimension, so the long-time dynamics is in some sense finite-dimensional; inertial manifolds, exponential attractors and Mañé-type projections make this precise in different ways. ([Zelik, Attractors. Then and now, arXiv:2208.12101](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101)) The model problems are the 2D [Navier–Stokes](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations) and reaction–diffusion equations, and the theory gives rigorous counterparts of heuristic "number of degrees of freedom" arguments in [turbulence](node:Turbulence). ([Robinson, Parametrization of global attractors, J. Fluid Mech. 2007](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/650/1/WRAP_Robinson_Parametrization.pdf))

### Scope
The MSC2020 codes are: general theory, nonlinear semigroups and evolution equations (37L05); normal forms, center manifolds and bifurcation (37L10); stability (37L15); symmetries (37L20); inertial manifolds and other invariant attracting sets (37L25); attractors and their dimensions, Lyapunov exponents (37L30); invariant measures (37L40); hyperbolicity and Lyapunov functions (37L45); noncompact semigroups, dispersive equations and perturbations (37L50); infinite-dimensional [random dynamical systems](node:Random%20Dynamical%20Systems) and stochastic equations (37L55, see also 35R60, 60H10, 60H15); lattice dynamics (37L60, see also 37K60); and special approximation methods such as nonlinear Galerkin (37L65). ([MSC2020 37Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Lxx))

- **Versus 37K.** Conservative (Hamiltonian) infinite-dimensional systems belong to [37Kxx](node:MSC%2037Kxx%20-%20Dynamical%20system%20aspects%20of%20infinite-dimensional%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20systems); 37L60 cross-refers to 37K60 for lattice dynamics. ([MSC2020 37Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Lxx))
- **Versus 35B and 35Q.** The 37Lxx heading lists 35Bxx (qualitative properties of PDE solutions) and 35Qxx (PDEs of mathematical physics) as see-also references; 37L55 points to 35R60, 60H10 and 60H15 for stochastic equations. ([MSC2020 37Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Lxx))

### Key concepts
- **[Global Attractors](node:Global%20Attractors) (37L30).** For a semigroup $S(t)$ on a normed phase space, a global attractor $\mathcal A$ is compact, strictly invariant ($S(t)\mathcal A=\mathcal A$), and attracts every bounded set $B$: each neighbourhood of $\mathcal A$ contains $S(t)B$ for all large $t$. Existence: if each $S(t)$ is continuous and there is a compact set $\mathcal B$ attracting all bounded sets, then a global attractor exists, $\mathcal A=\omega(\mathcal B)\subset\mathcal B$. A dissipative bound alone does not give the compactness needed in infinite dimensions. ([Zelik, Definition 2.3 and Theorem 2.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101)) For the nonlinear [heat equation](node:Heat%20Equation) $u_t=u_{xx}+au-u^3$ on $(0,\pi)$ with Dirichlet conditions, a global Lyapunov function exists and the attractor consists of equilibria and heteroclinic orbits. ([Zelik](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101)) See [Strongly Continuous Operator Semigroups](node:Strongly%20Continuous%20Operator%20Semigroups).
- **Dimension of attractors (37L30).** Finite fractal dimension follows from a squeezing property or from volume contraction (Douady–Oesterlé, Hunt); combined with Lieb–Thirring inequalities, volume contraction gives dimension bounds for the 2D Navier–Stokes attractor. ([Zelik](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101)) Constantin, Foias and Temam (1988) showed that for 2D Navier–Stokes with periodic boundary conditions the attractor's box-counting dimension satisfies $d\le cG^{2/3}(1+\log G)^{1/3}$, where $G=\frac{L^2}{\nu^2}\big(\int_Q|f|^2\big)^{1/2}$ is the Grashof number; for Dirichlet conditions the best bound is only linear, $d\le cG$. ([Robinson, §3.3](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/650/1/WRAP_Robinson_Parametrization.pdf)) See [Mathematical Navier–Stokes Theory](node:Mathematical%20Navier–Stokes%20Theory).
- **Inertial manifolds and the spectral gap (37L25).** An inertial manifold is a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $\mathcal M$ with $S(t)\mathcal M\subset\mathcal M$ for $t\ge0$ that attracts every solution exponentially, $\operatorname{dist}(S(t)u_0,\mathcal M)\le c_1e^{-c_2t}$; it contains the global attractor. ([Inertial manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_manifold)) For $u_t+Au=F(u)$ with $A$ positive self-adjoint with compact inverse and eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots$, and $F:H\to H$ globally Lipschitz with constant $L$, an $N$-dimensional inertial manifold, the graph of a Lipschitz map over the span of the first $N$ eigenvectors, exists if $\lambda_{N+1}-\lambda_N>2L$, and the constant $2$ is sharp; if $F$ loses derivatives, mapping $H$ to $H^{\beta}$ with $-2<\beta\le0$, the condition becomes $(\lambda_{N+1}-\lambda_N)/(\lambda_{N+1}^{-\beta/2}+\lambda_N^{-\beta/2})>L$. ([Zelik, Inertial manifolds and finite-dimensional reduction for dissipative PDEs, arXiv:1303.4457, Thms 2.1, 2.15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1303.4457)) Zelik describes inertial manifolds as globally stable, normally hyperbolic invariant manifolds whose existence is governed by spectral gap conditions on the leading linear part; in general they are only $C^{1+\varepsilon}$-smooth, even for analytic systems. ([Zelik](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101))
- **Mañé projection and embedding (37L30).** Combined with finite fractal dimension of the attractor, the Mañé projection theorem yields a one-to-one homeomorphic projection of the attractor onto a subset of some $\mathbb R^N$. ([Zelik](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101)) Hunt–Kaloshin (1996) with Friz–Robinson (1999): if $d$ is the attractor dimension and $N>2d$, then almost every (in the sense of prevalence) choice of $N$ linear observables distinguishes points of $\mathcal A$, and for smooth forcing the inverse is Hölder with any exponent $\alpha<1-2d/N$. ([Robinson, Theorem 4.1](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/650/1/WRAP_Robinson_Parametrization.pdf))
- **Exponential attractors (37L25).** These enlarge the global attractor (adding points such as metastable states) so that attraction is exponential at a controllable rate while fractal dimension stays finite, keeping Mañé-type projections available. ([Zelik](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101))
- **Determining nodes (37L05).** Foias and Temam (1984) showed that there is a separation $\delta$ such that if a finite set of points $x_1,\dots,x_k$ is $\delta$-dense in the domain, then $\max_j|u(x_j,t)-v(x_j,t)|\to0$ implies $\sup_x|u(x,t)-v(x,t)|\to0$ for 2D Navier–Stokes solutions; Robinson uses the embedding theorem to show that instantaneous point values suffice on the attractor, with the number of points tied to the attractor dimension. ([Robinson, §4](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/650/1/WRAP_Robinson_Parametrization.pdf))

### History
Constantin, Foias and Temam's dimension estimates for 2D Navier–Stokes date from 1985 and 1988; Hunt and Kaloshin's embedding theorem from 1996. Robinson's 2007 review sketches the infinite-dimensional generalization of the Takens time-delay embedding theorem, which it says had been an open problem for a number of years. ([Robinson](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/650/1/WRAP_Robinson_Parametrization.pdf)) The 1988 Foias et al. paper and Temam's 1990 survey are the standard early references for inertial manifolds. ([Inertial manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_manifold)) Zelik's survey traces the subject from classical global attractors to trajectory, pullback and exponential attractors. ([Zelik](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101))

### Open problems
- **Inertial manifolds for Navier–Stokes.** Zelik calls the existence of an inertial manifold for the 2D Navier–Stokes equations "one of the most challenging open problems of the theory". ([Zelik](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101))
- **3D Navier–Stokes and the dimension gap.** Robinson names existence and uniqueness for 3D Navier–Stokes as the most important open problem in the field, and lists further open problems: standard attractor-dimension bounds are very large because they ignore the structure of the forcing, and the 3D attractor-dimension bounds (assuming regularity) should be improved to agree with the Kolmogorov dissipative scale. ([Robinson](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/650/1/WRAP_Robinson_Parametrization.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Inertial manifold (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_manifold): definition and early references.
- **Primary:** [Zelik, Inertial manifolds and finite-dimensional reduction for dissipative PDEs (arXiv:1303.4457)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1303.4457): sharp spectral gap theorems, counterexamples, Mañé-projection approach.
- **Learn:** [Zelik, Attractors. Then and now (arXiv:2208.12101)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2208.12101): minicourse-based survey of attractors, dimension, inertial manifolds and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Robinson, Parametrization of global attractors, experimental observations, and turbulence (J. Fluid Mech. 578, 2007)](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/650/1/WRAP_Robinson_Parametrization.pdf): research review of dimension, embedding and determining nodes for Navier–Stokes.
- **Further reading:** [Temam, Infinite-Dimensional Dynamical Systems in Mechanics and Physics (Springer, Applied Mathematical Sciences, 1997)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0645-3): the standard monograph.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 37Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Lxx): official code list.
references.MSC 37Mxx - Approximation methods and nu:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 class 37Mxx collects work on approximation methods and the numerical treatment of dynamical systems inside [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory): simulation, time series analysis, integrators, and computational methods for bifurcations, invariant manifolds, attractors, and ergodic quantities. The class itself points to 65Pxx for numerical analysis and to 37-04 for software. ([MSC2020 37Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Mxx))

The unifying question is what a computed trajectory says about the true system. Three kinds of answer organize the area. Structure-preserving integrators make the numerical map share a qualitative property of the flow, such as symplecticity, and backward error analysis shows that the exact solution of a modified equation with the same structure closely approximates the numerical flow map at grid points. ([McLachlan–Offen, arXiv:2201.03911](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.03911)) Shadowing results show that, near a hyperbolic set, a computed pseudo-orbit stays close to some true orbit. ([Wikipedia: Shadowing lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadowing_lemma)) Set-oriented and transfer-operator methods avoid long trajectories altogether and approximate attractors and invariant measures by box coverings and Markov chains. ([Dellnitz–Klus–Ziessler, arXiv:1604.07302](https://arxiv.org/html/1604.07302v1))

Rigorous, computer-assisted proofs close the loop between numerics and theorems: Smale's 14th problem, whether the Lorenz attractor is a strange attractor, was answered affirmatively by Warwick Tucker in 2002 with a computer-assisted proof combined with normal form techniques. ([Wikipedia: Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems))

### Scope
- **37M05 Simulation of dynamical systems** and **37M10 Time series analysis of dynamical systems.** ([MSC2020 37Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Mxx))
- **37M15 Discretization methods and integrators (symplectic, variational, geometric, etc.) for dynamical systems.** ([MSC2020 37Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Mxx))
- **37M20, 37M21, 37M22:** computational methods for bifurcation problems, for invariant manifolds, and for attractors. ([MSC2020 37Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Mxx))
- **37M25 Computational methods for ergodic theory** (approximation of invariant measures, computation of Lyapunov exponents, entropy, etc.), and **37M99** for the rest. ([MSC2020 37Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Mxx))
- **Neighbours.** The 37Mxx heading sends numerical analysis to 65Pxx and software to 37-04: 37Mxx is the dynamical-systems view of computation, [MSC 65Pxx - Numerical problems in dynamical systems](node:MSC%2065Pxx%20-%20Numerical%20problems%20in%20dynamical%20systems) the numerical-analysis view, and general ODE solvers sit in [MSC 65Lxx - Numerical methods for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2065Lxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations). ([MSC2020 37Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Mxx)) Continuation and bifurcation computations border [MSC 37Gxx - Local and nonlocal bifurcation theory for dynamical systems](node:MSC%2037Gxx%20-%20Local%20and%20nonlocal%20bifurcation%20theory%20for%20dynamical%20systems).

### Key concepts
- **Symplectic integrators** ([Symplectic Geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry), [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics)). A one-step scheme for a Hamiltonian system is symplectic if it conserves the two-form $dp\wedge dq$, as the exact flow does; the primitive Euler and classical Runge–Kutta schemes are not symplectic. For separable $H=T(p)+V(q)$, symplectic Euler is first order and Verlet (leapfrog) second order, and the coefficients of the fourth-order splitting method can be determined with the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula. ([Wikipedia: Symplectic integrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_integrator)) A UCSD lecture notes that leapfrog is time-reversible. ([UCSD Physics 141, Lecture 2](https://courses.physics.ucsd.edu/2010/Winter/physics141/Lectures/Lecture2/Lecture2.html))
- **Backward error analysis.** If a Hamiltonian ODE is discretized by a symplectic integrator, every truncation of the modified equation is a Hamiltonian system for the original symplectic form with a modified ("shadow") Hamiltonian. The full series does not converge in general, but with optimal truncation the modified flow agrees with the method at grid points up to exponentially small error terms. This is the key ingredient for long-time statements such as oscillatory, non-drifting energy errors over exponentially long time intervals; the standard treatment is Hairer, Lubich and Wanner's *Geometric Numerical Integration*, Ch. IX. Variational methods whose discrete Lagrangian depends on several grid points (multistep methods) are not symplectic but preserve only a modified symplectic structure, given by a formal power series that need not converge. ([McLachlan–Offen, arXiv:2201.03911](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.03911))
- **Shadowing.** An $\varepsilon$-pseudo-orbit of $f$ is a sequence with $x_{n+1}$ within $\varepsilon$ of $f(x_n)$; a computed orbit with rounding errors is one. If $\Lambda$ is a hyperbolic invariant set of a diffeomorphism $f$, there is a neighbourhood $U$ of $\Lambda$ such that for every $\delta>0$ there is $\varepsilon>0$ with every $\varepsilon$-pseudo-orbit in $U$ staying within $\delta$ of a true orbit (Katok–Hasselblatt, Thm 18.1.2). Hammel, Yorke and Grebogi (1988) used this idea to argue that "numerical orbits of chaotic processes represent true orbits". ([Wikipedia: Shadowing lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadowing_lemma)) Links to [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory) and [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems).
- **Delay embedding (37M10).** Takens (1981) showed that delay coordinates of dimension $n\ge 2m+1$ give an embedding of a compact $m$-dimensional manifold without boundary, for generic observation functions and generic vector fields. Sauer, Yorke and Casdagli ("Embedology", 1991) fixed the dynamics, perturbed only the observation function, proved prevalence rather than genericity, and needed only $n>2d$ for an invariant set of box-counting dimension $d$. ([Navarrete–Viswanath, arXiv:1710.00128](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1710.00128); [Wikipedia: Takens's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takens%27s_theorem)) Links to [Submanifolds and Embeddings](node:Submanifolds%20and%20Embeddings).
- **Lyapunov exponents (37M25)** ([Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory)). The maximal exponent is the limit of $\tfrac1t\ln(|\delta Z(t)|/|\delta Z_0|)$ as $t\to\infty$ and $|\delta Z_0|\to0$, and Oseledets' theorem gives the conditions for the limits to exist. The widely used method for smooth systems periodically Gram–Schmidt-orthonormalizes the tangent vectors so they do not all align with the most expanding direction. ([Wikipedia: Lyapunov exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_exponent)) Skokos reviews the maximal-exponent algorithm, the Benettin et al. "standard method", and QR- and SVD-based methods. ([Skokos, arXiv:0811.0882](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.0882))
- **Set-oriented methods (37M22, 37M25).** The Dellnitz–Hohmann subdivision algorithm covers a compact set $Q$ by boxes, repeatedly bisects them, and keeps only boxes hit by the image of the previous collection; for a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $g$, the Dellnitz–Hohmann (1997) result identifies the limit of the nested coverings with the relative global attractor $A_Q=\bigcap_{j\ge0}g^j(Q)$, and the paper generalizes this to systems with parameter uncertainty. Invariant measures are then approximated by the stationary distribution of a Markov chain on the boxes, with transition probabilities estimated from test points; the algorithms are implemented in GAIO. ([Dellnitz–Klus–Ziessler, arXiv:1604.07302](https://arxiv.org/html/1604.07302v1)) Links to [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains).
- **Ulam's method (37M25).** Ulam's 1960 scheme partitions phase space into bins and reads an approximate invariant density from the leading left eigenvector of the bin-to-bin transition matrix. Li (1976, "A solution to Ulam's conjecture") showed that for Lasota–Yorke (piecewise expanding interval) maps the invariant density can be $L^1$-approximated by the step functions obtained from that eigenvector; extensions cover expanding maps in higher dimensions, uniformly hyperbolic maps, nonuniformly expanding interval maps, and random maps. ([Bose–Froyland–González-Tokman–Murray, arXiv:1204.2329](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1204.2329)) Links to [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory).
- **Koopman operators and DMD.** The Koopman family $\mathcal K^t g=g\circ F^t$ acts linearly, but on an infinite-dimensional space of observables $g$. Dynamic mode decomposition fits a best linear operator $A=X'X^{\dagger}$ to snapshot matrices with $X'\approx AX$, approximating the Koopman operator restricted to the measurement subspace. ([Brunton et al., arXiv:2102.12086](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.12086)) Links to [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory).
- **Numerical continuation (37M20).** Continuation computes branches of solutions of parameterized nonlinear equations. Natural-parameter continuation fails at turning points, while pseudo-arclength continuation is a predictor-corrector method that steps along the tangent of the curve and corrects with Newton's method. Software for continuation and bifurcation analysis includes AUTO, MATCONT and DDE-BIFTOOL. ([Wikipedia: Numerical continuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_continuation)) See [Numerical Methods for Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Methods%20for%20Differential%20Equations).

### History
Ronald Ruth found a third-order symplectic integrator in 1983 and a fourth-order one that he distributed privately; Forest and Ruth published the fourth-order method in 1990, and Yoshida (1990) derived coefficients for higher-order integrators. ([Wikipedia: Symplectic integrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_integrator)) Takens's delay-embedding theorem dates from 1981 and the "Embedology" paper of Sauer, Yorke and Casdagli from 1991. ([Wikipedia: Takens's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takens%27s_theorem))

Ulam proposed his discretization in a 1960 problem collection, and Li proved its convergence for Lasota–Yorke maps in 1976. ([Bose et al., arXiv:1204.2329](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1204.2329)) Dellnitz and Hohmann introduced relative global attractors and the subdivision algorithm in 1997. ([Dellnitz–Klus–Ziessler, arXiv:1604.07302](https://arxiv.org/html/1604.07302v1)) Hammel, Yorke and Grebogi's shadowing paper appeared in 1988. ([Wikipedia: Shadowing lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadowing_lemma)) Tucker's 2002 computer-assisted proof for the Lorenz attractor settled Smale's 14th problem. ([Wikipedia: Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems))

### Open problems
- **Finite-dimensional linearizing coordinates.** Brunton, Budišić, Kaiser and Kutz state that obtaining finite-dimensional coordinate systems and embeddings in which nonlinear dynamics appear approximately linear "remains a central open challenge" for Koopman methods. One obstruction they note: systems with multiple simple invariant solutions cannot be represented by a globally uniformly convergent Koopman expansion. ([Brunton et al., arXiv:2102.12086](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12086); [ar5iv full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.12086))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 37Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Mxx): the official code list.
- **Reference:** [Symplectic integrator (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_integrator): definition, splitting methods, history.
- **Learn:** [UCSD Physics 141, Lecture 2](https://courses.physics.ucsd.edu/2010/Winter/physics141/Lectures/Lecture2/Lecture2.html): leapfrog integration and reversibility for Hamiltonian simulation.
- **Primary:** [Skokos, The Lyapunov Characteristic Exponents and their computation (arXiv:0811.0882)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.0882): review, Lect. Notes Phys. 790 (2010).
- **Primary:** [Brunton, Budišić, Kaiser, Kutz, Modern Koopman Theory for Dynamical Systems (arXiv:2102.12086)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12086): survey of Koopman and DMD methods with open challenges.
- **Primary:** [McLachlan and Offen, Backward error analysis for conjugate symplectic methods (arXiv:2201.03911)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03911): modified Hamiltonians and their limits, J. Geom. Mech. 2023.
- **Primary:** [Dellnitz, Klus, Ziessler, A set-oriented numerical approach (arXiv:1604.07302)](https://arxiv.org/html/1604.07302v1): subdivision and transfer-operator algorithms (GAIO).
- **Further reading:** Hairer, Lubich, Wanner, *Geometric Numerical Integration*, Ch. IX on backward error analysis, as cited in [McLachlan–Offen](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.03911).
references.MSC 37Nxx - Applications of dynamical sy:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 class 37Nxx, Applications of dynamical systems, is the part of [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory) for work whose dynamical content is driven by an application: classical and celestial mechanics, fluids and geophysics, solid mechanics, other physics, biology, numerical analysis, control, and optimization and economics. Most codes carry a "see mainly" or "see also" pointer to the application's own MSC class. ([MSC2020 37Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Nxx))

The research mathematics in this class is typically a general theory of [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) applied to a specific model and pushed until it says something rigorous about it. In celestial mechanics this means KAM theory, Arnold diffusion and Nekhoroshev stability for nearly integrable [Hamiltonian systems](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics), together with the algebraic study of central configurations of the $N$-body problem. ([KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem); [Central configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_configuration)) In fluids it includes the finite-time transport geometry of Lagrangian coherent structures, and in biology and physics the synchronization theory of coupled oscillators. ([Lagrangian coherent structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_coherent_structure); [Kuramoto model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuramoto_model))

### Scope
- **37N05** classical and celestial mechanics; see mainly 70Fxx, 70Hxx, 70Kxx ([70Fxx](node:MSC%2070Fxx%20-%20Dynamics%20of%20a%20system%20of%20particles,%20including%20celestial%20mechanics), [70Hxx](node:MSC%2070Hxx%20-%20Hamiltonian%20and%20Lagrangian%20mechanics), [70Kxx](node:MSC%2070Kxx%20-%20Nonlinear%20dynamics%20in%20mechanics)). ([MSC2020 37Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Nxx))
- **37N10** fluid mechanics, oceanography and meteorology; see mainly 76-XX, especially 76D05 and 76F20, and 86A05, 86A10 ([MSC 76 - Fluid mechanics](node:MSC%2076%20-%20Fluid%20mechanics), [MSC 86 - Geophysics](node:MSC%2086%20-%20Geophysics)). ([MSC2020 37Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Nxx))
- **37N15** solid mechanics (see mainly 74Hxx); **37N20** other branches of physics, naming quantum mechanics, [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity) and [laser physics](node:Laser%20Physics). ([MSC2020 37Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Nxx))
- **37N25** biology, see also 92-XX ([MSC 92 - Biology and other natural sciences](node:MSC%2092%20-%20Biology%20and%20other%20natural%20sciences)). ([MSC2020 37Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Nxx))
- **37N30** numerical analysis (see also 65-XX, [MSC 65 - Numerical analysis](node:MSC%2065%20-%20Numerical%20analysis)) and **37N35** control (see also 93-XX, [MSC 93 - Systems theory; control](node:MSC%2093%20-%20Systems%20theory;%20control)). ([MSC2020 37Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Nxx))
- **37N40** optimization and economics, see also 90-XX and 91-XX ([MSC 90](node:MSC%2090%20-%20Operations%20research,%20mathematical%20programming), [MSC 91](node:MSC%2091%20-%20Game%20theory,%20economics,%20finance,%20and%20other%20social%20and%20behavioral%20sciences)). ([MSC2020 37Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Nxx))

### Key concepts
- **KAM theorem (37N05).** For an integrable Hamiltonian system, motion is quasiperiodic on invariant tori. Under a sufficiently small perturbation, and a nondegeneracy condition, the tori whose frequency vector $\omega$ is Diophantine, $|\omega\cdot k|\ge\gamma\|k\|^{-\tau}$ for all nonzero $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ with $\gamma,\tau>0$, survive as deformed invariant tori on which the motion stays quasiperiodic; tori that are destroyed become invariant Cantor sets (named cantori by Percival in 1979), and for larger perturbations the analysis passes to Aubry–Mather theory. Kolmogorov announced the result in 1954, Moser proved a version for smooth twist maps in 1962, and Arnold proved it for analytic Hamiltonians in 1963. Arnold's formulation applied to the three-body problem but was degenerate for more bodies; Pinzari removed the degeneracy with a rotation-invariant version. ([KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem))
- **Arnold diffusion (37N05).** With $N\ge3$ degrees of freedom the $N$-dimensional KAM tori no longer separate the phase space, so orbits can drift. In Arnold's 1964 example (a rotator–pendulum system with a small perturbation), for any $I_+>I_->0$ and small enough perturbation parameters there is an orbit whose action starts below $I_-$ and later exceeds $I_+$; the proof uses transition chains of whiskered tori, the unstable manifold of each meeting the stable manifold of the next. ([Arnold diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_diffusion)) Current work explains the mechanism through stable and unstable manifolds of partially hyperbolic invariant objects and estimates the diffusion speed with normal forms computed at optimal order. ([Efthymiopoulos–Paez, arXiv:2111.03415](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.03415))
- **Nekhoroshev stability (37N05).** For $H(I)+\varepsilon h(I,\theta)$ with $n$ degrees of freedom and suitable technical assumptions on $H$, the actions satisfy $|I(t)-I(0)|<\varepsilon^{1/(2n)}$ for $|t|<\exp\big(c\,\varepsilon^{-1/(2n)}\big)$: orbits stay close to their integrable counterparts for an exponentially long time. ([Nekhoroshev estimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nekhoroshev_estimates)) Giorgilli, Locatelli and Sansottera used computer-algebra expansions to obtain Nekhoroshev-type stability of a Sun–Jupiter–Saturn three-body model over a time comparable with the age of the universe, at the price of strong truncations of the Hamiltonian expansion. ([Giorgilli–Locatelli–Sansottera, arXiv:1303.7395](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.7395))
- **Central configurations (37N05).** A central configuration of point masses is one in which each mass is accelerated directly toward the center of mass with acceleration proportional to its distance from it; such configurations give relative equilibria. For three bodies there are Euler's three collinear configurations and Lagrange's equilateral triangle. Hampton and Moeckel (2006) proved finiteness for four bodies, with between 32 and 8472 configurations depending on the masses. ([Central configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_configuration)) Albouy and Kaloshin proved that the planar five-body problem has finitely many isometry classes of planar central configurations, except possibly for positive masses in a codimension-2 subvariety of mass space. ([Albouy–Kaloshin, Annals 2012](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/176-1/p10))
- **Statistical stability of the Solar System (37N05).** Laskar ran more than 1000 integrations of the secular equations of the Solar System over 5 Gyr and found a probability of about 1–2% that Mercury's eccentricity reaches 0.6, the large excursions being driven by a secular resonance between the perihelia of Mercury and Jupiter; removing general-relativistic corrections makes such orbits more frequent. ([Laskar, arXiv:0802.3371](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.3371))
- **Lagrangian coherent structures (37N10).** LCSs are exceptional material surfaces that most strongly attract, repel or shear nearby trajectories over a finite time interval; they are generally time-dependent even for autonomous flows. A common diagnostic is the finite-time Lyapunov exponent $\mathrm{FTLE}_{t_0}^{t_1}(x_0)=\frac{1}{2(t_1-t_0)}\log\lambda_n(x_0)$, where $\lambda_n$ is the largest eigenvalue of the Cauchy–Green tensor $C=(\nabla F)^T\nabla F$ of the flow map; ridges of the FTLE field are expected near hyperbolic LCSs but are not always reliable markers. Applications include oil spills, drifters and volcanic ash clouds. ([Lagrangian coherent structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_coherent_structure)) Links to [Fluid Dynamics](node:Fluid%20Dynamics) and [Turbulence](node:Turbulence).
- **Lorenz system (37N10, 37N20).** $\dot x=\sigma(y-x)$, $\dot y=x(\rho-z)-y$, $\dot z=xy-\beta z$ was derived in 1963 from Saltzman's convection model and, at $\sigma=10$, $\rho=28$, $\beta=8/3$, has the butterfly-shaped attractor; the same equations model lasers, dynamos, electric circuits and some chemical reactions. Tucker's 2002 computer-assisted proof that the attractor is a strange attractor answered Smale's 14th problem. ([Lorenz system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenz_system)) Links to [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory).
- **Synchronization: the Kuramoto model (37N25, 37N20).** $\dot\theta_i=\omega_i+\frac{K}{N}\sum_j\sin(\theta_j-\theta_i)$ with order parameter $re^{i\psi}=\frac1N\sum_je^{i\theta_j}$ reduces to $\dot\theta_i=\omega_i+Kr\sin(\psi-\theta_i)$. In the limit $N\to\infty$ with a unimodal symmetric frequency density $g$, incoherence ($r=0$) holds for $K<K_c=2/(\pi g(0))$ and partial synchrony appears above $K_c$. Kuramoto proposed the model in 1975, motivated by chemical and biological oscillators. ([Kuramoto model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuramoto_model))

### History
Kolmogorov (1954), Moser (1962) and Arnold (1963) established [KAM theory](node:KAM%20Theory), with Arnold initially hoping to apply it to the Solar System. ([KAM theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem)) Arnold's instability example dates from 1964, and Nekhoroshev's first paper on exponential stability from 1971. ([Arnold diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_diffusion); [Nekhoroshev estimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nekhoroshev_estimates)) The finiteness question for central configurations was posed by Chazy (1918) and Wintner (1941) and put on Smale's 1998 list. ([Central configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_configuration)) Haller and Yuan (2000) introduced Lagrangian coherent structures, and Shadden, Lekien and Marsden (2005) popularized their detection as FTLE ridges. ([Lagrangian coherent structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_coherent_structure))

### Open problems
- **Finiteness of central configurations (Smale's 6th problem).** Smale asked whether the number of relative equilibria (central configurations) of the $n$-body problem is finite for every choice of positive masses $m_1,\dots,m_n$; it is listed as unresolved, with the Albouy–Kaloshin result for almost all five-body masses as partial progress. The Chazy–Wintner question, whether there is always a bounded number of central configurations for five or more masses in two or more dimensions, is likewise unsolved. ([Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems); [Central configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_configuration)) For six bodies in the plane, Chang and Chen reduce finiteness to 117 diagrams by symbolic computation and leave 24 cases unsolved. ([Chang–Chen, arXiv:2303.02853](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.02853))
- **Arnold's conjecture on diffusion.** Arnold conjectured that the transition-chain mechanism of his example produces instability in general nearly integrable systems, citing the three-body problem. The Arnold diffusion problem asks that, for generic a priori unstable or a priori stable systems, there be $\rho>0$ and, for every small $\varepsilon>0$, orbits whose actions drift by at least $\rho$; partial results exist in both settings (in the a priori stable case, for example, Kaloshin–Zhang for smooth systems of two and a half degrees of freedom), and in the elliptic restricted three-body problem there are orbits whose energy changes by an amount independent of the small eccentricity. ([Arnold diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_diffusion))
- **Kuramoto model on networks.** For networks of $n$ identical Kuramoto oscillators in which each oscillator is coupled to at least $\mu(n-1)$ others, there is a critical connectivity $\mu_c$ above which the system converges to the in-phase state for almost all initial conditions; Kassabov, Strogatz and Townsend write that "the precise value of the critical connectivity remains unknown, but it has been conjectured to be $\mu_c=0.75$", and prove $\mu_c\le0.75$. ([Kassabov–Strogatz–Townsend, arXiv:2105.11406](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.11406)) The known bounds are $0.6875\le\mu_c\le0.75$. ([Kuramoto model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuramoto_model))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Arnold%E2%80%93Moser_theorem): statement, Diophantine condition, history.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 37Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Nxx): the official code list with cross-references.
- **Learn:** [Efthymiopoulos and Paez, Arnold diffusion and Nekhoroshev theory (I-CELMECH school lectures)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.03415): lecture notes on mechanisms and speed of diffusion.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.353J Nonlinear Dynamics I: Chaos](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-353j-nonlinear-dynamics-i-chaos-fall-2012/pages/syllabus/): undergraduate course on bifurcations, strange attractors and transitions to chaos, with optional geoscience and biology applications.
- **Primary:** [Albouy and Kaloshin, Finiteness of central configurations of five bodies in the plane (Annals of Mathematics 176, 2012)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/176-1/p10): generic finiteness for five bodies.
- **Primary:** [Laskar, Chaotic diffusion in the Solar System](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.3371): statistical study of planetary orbits over 5 Gyr.
- **Primary:** [Giorgilli, Locatelli and Sansottera, Kolmogorov and Nekhoroshev theory for the problem of three bodies](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.7395): computer-assisted stability estimates for Sun–Jupiter–Saturn.
- **Further reading:** [Arnold, Kozlov and Neishtadt, Mathematical Aspects of Classical and Celestial Mechanics (3rd ed., Springer, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-48926-9) and [Meyer, Hall and Offin, Introduction to Hamiltonian Dynamical Systems and the N-Body Problem (Springer, 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-09724-4): bibliographic records of the research-level monographs.
references.MSC 37Pxx - Arithmetic and non-Archimede:
## Reference
### Overview
[Arithmetic dynamics](node:Arithmetic%20Dynamics) combines [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) and number theory: it studies the number-theoretic properties of integer, rational, $p$-adic or algebraic points under repeated application of a polynomial or rational function, taking part of its inspiration from complex dynamics. ([Wikipedia: Arithmetic dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_dynamics)) In MSC2020 this is class 37Pxx of [MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory), with cross-references to 11S82 and 37A44. ([MSC2020 37Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Pxx))

A guiding dictionary matches Diophantine geometry with dynamics: rational and integral points on [algebraic varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties) correspond to rational and integral points in an orbit, and torsion points on an [abelian variety](node:Abelian%20Varieties) correspond to preperiodic points of a rational map. ([Wikipedia: Arithmetic dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_dynamics)) Silverman's graduate text organizes the subject by ground field and setting: good and bad reduction over local fields, global fields, families, [algebraic groups](node:Algebraic%20Groups) and higher dimension. ([Silverman, The Arithmetic of Dynamical Systems](https://www.math.brown.edu/~jhs/ADSHome.html)) The 2018 survey by Benedetto, DeMarco, Ingram, Jones, Manes, Silverman and Tucker collects the field's motivating conjectures and recent progress. ([Benedetto et al., arXiv:1806.04980](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.04980))

### Scope
- **Maps (37P05, 37P10):** polynomial and rational maps; analytic and meromorphic maps. ([MSC2020 37Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Pxx))
- **Ground fields (37P15, 37P20, 37P25):** global fields, non-Archimedean local fields, [finite fields](node:Finite%20Fields). ([MSC2020 37Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Pxx))
- **Arithmetic invariants (37P30, 37P35):** height functions, Green functions and invariant measures (see also 11G50, 14G40), and arithmetic properties of periodic points. ([MSC2020 37Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Pxx))
- **Non-Archimedean geometry (37P40, 37P50):** non-Archimedean Fatou and Julia sets; dynamics on Berkovich spaces. ([MSC2020 37Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Pxx))
- **Families and higher dimension (37P45, 37P55):** families and [moduli spaces](node:Moduli%20Spaces) of dynamical systems; arithmetic dynamics on general algebraic varieties. ([MSC2020 37Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Pxx))

Neighbours named by the cross-references: 11G50 and 14G40 for heights ([11Gxx](node:MSC%2011Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20algebraic%20geometry%20%28Diophantine%20geometry%29), [14Gxx](node:MSC%2014Gxx%20-%20Arithmetic%20problems%20in%20algebraic%20geometry;%20Diophantine%20geometry)) and 11S82 in [MSC 11Sxx - Algebraic number theory - local and p-adic fields](node:MSC%2011Sxx%20-%20Algebraic%20number%20theory%20-%20local%20and%20p-adic%20fields); complex dynamics, the archimedean model for the theory, is [MSC 37Fxx - Dynamical systems over complex numbers](node:MSC%2037Fxx%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20over%20complex%20numbers). ([MSC2020 37Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=37Pxx); [Wikipedia: Arithmetic dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_dynamics))

### Key concepts
- **Northcott's theorem (37P35).** Let $N\ge1$, $d\ge2$ and $K/\mathbb Q$ a number field. For every degree-$d$ morphism $f:\mathbb P^N\to\mathbb P^N$ defined over $K$, the set $\mathrm{PrePer}(f,\mathbb P^N(K))$ of $K$-rational preperiodic points is finite (Northcott, 1950). ([Benedetto et al., §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))
- **Canonical height (37P30).** For a morphism $f$ of degree $d\ge2$ over $\bar{\mathbb Q}$, $\hat h_f(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}d^{-n}h(f^n(P))$, modeled on Tate's construction of the Néron–Tate height. It satisfies $\hat h_f(f(P))=d\,\hat h_f(P)$, $\hat h_f(P)=h(P)+O(1)$, and $\hat h_f(P)=0$ if and only if $P$ is preperiodic. ([Benedetto et al., §16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980)) Since $\hat h_f$ differs from the naive height by a bounded amount, preperiodic points form a set of bounded height ([Benedetto et al., §16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980)). A course develops absolute and logarithmic heights, a complete proof of Northcott's theorem and Tate's construction of the canonical height. ([Westlake: An Introduction to Arithmetic Dynamics](https://its.westlake.edu.cn/info/1072/3652.htm))
- **Rational periodic points of $x^2+c$ (37P35).** For $c\in\mathbb Q$ and $f_c(x)=x^2+c$: for each $N\in\{1,2,3\}$ infinitely many $c$ give a rational point of exact period $N$; for $N\in\{4,5,6\}$ no $c$ does (Morton 1992; Flynn–Poonen–Schaefer 1997; Stoll 2008, the case $N=6$ conditional on the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture). If Poonen's conjecture holds, then $\sup_{c\in\mathbb Q}\#\mathrm{PrePer}(x^2+c,\mathbb P^1(\mathbb Q))=9$. ([Benedetto et al., §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))
- **Orbits meeting subvarieties (37P55).** The dynamical Mordell–Lang conjecture (Bell, Denis, Ghioca–Tucker) says that for a morphism $f:X\to X$ of a quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb C$, a point $P$ and a subvariety $Y$, the set $\{n\ge0:f^n(P)\in Y\}$ is a finite union of one-sided arithmetic progressions. It is proved when $f$ is unramified, including automorphisms (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker, 2010), and for endomorphisms of $\mathbb A^2$ over $\bar{\mathbb Q}$ (Xie, 2015). Ghioca–Tucker–Zieve (Invent. Math. 2008): if polynomials $f_1,f_2\in\mathbb C[x]$ of degree $>1$ have wandering points $\alpha,\beta$ with $f_1^{n_1}(\alpha)=f_2^{n_2}(\beta)$ for infinitely many $(n_1,n_2)$, then $f_1^{\ell_1}=f_2^{\ell_2}$ for some positive $\ell_1,\ell_2$. Faltings' theorem gives the conjecture for translations on abelian varieties. ([Benedetto et al., §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))
- **Dynamical Manin–Mumford (37P55).** Zhang's conjecture for polarizable endomorphisms, that a subvariety containing infinitely many preperiodic points contains a positive-dimensional periodic subvariety, is false as stated: taking $Y$ to be the diagonal in $E\times E$ for an elliptic curve $E$ with complex multiplication gives a counterexample (Ghioca–Tucker–Zhang). Their modified conjecture adds a condition that tangent spaces of $Y$ at a dense set of preperiodic points are themselves preperiodic under the induced action on the Grassmannian; it is proved for group endomorphisms of abelian varieties and for endomorphisms of $(\mathbb P^1)^n$, where the original form fails. ([Benedetto et al., §8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))
- **Unlikely intersections in moduli (37P45).** Baker–DeMarco (2011): for $a,b\in\mathbb C$ with $a^2\ne b^2$, only finitely many $t\in\mathbb C$ make both $a$ and $b$ preperiodic for $x^2+t$, a dynamical analogue of a Masser–Zannier theorem for elliptic curves. ([Benedetto et al., §11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))
- **Arboreal Galois representations (37P15).** The absolute Galois group of $K$ acts on the tree of iterated preimages $f^{-n}(P)$, giving a map to the automorphism group of the $d$-ary rooted tree (an inverse limit of iterated wreath products of $S_d$). Odoni conjectured (1985) that over a Hilbertian field, for each degree $d\ge2$, some monic polynomial and basepoint $P\in K$ have surjective arboreal representation; Looper proved this over $\mathbb Q$ for prime $d$, and Specter for all number fields. ([Benedetto et al., §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980)) Links to [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory).
- **Non-Archimedean dynamics and Berkovich space (37P40, 37P50).** Over $\mathbb C_p$ the Fatou set is always nonempty while the Julia set may be empty, the reverse of the complex case. ([Wikipedia: Arithmetic dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_dynamics)) $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C_v)$ is totally disconnected and not locally compact, and embeds densely in the compact, Hausdorff, path-connected Berkovich line $\mathbb P^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$. Rivera-Letelier (2000) classified periodic Fatou components: an attracting component is a rational open disk or a domain of Cantor type attracted to a type I attracting periodic point, and an indifferent component is the complement of finitely many disjoint rational closed disks whose boundary points are periodic. Benedetto (2000) showed that if $K$ is a locally compact subfield of $\mathbb C_v$ with $\bar K$ dense in $\mathbb C_v$, $\operatorname{char}K=0$, and $f\in K(z)$ of degree at least $2$ has no wild recurrent type I critical points in its Julia set, then $f$ has no wandering domains. ([Benedetto et al., §17](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980)) Baker and Rumely built a Laplacian, capacity theory and subharmonic functions on the Berkovich line and used them to construct the Lyubich measure of a rational function. ([Baker–Rumely, arXiv:math/0407433](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0407433))

### History
Northcott's theorem dates from 1950 and the Morton–Silverman uniform boundedness conjecture from 1994. ([Benedetto et al., §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980)) Silverman's *The Arithmetic of Dynamical Systems* appeared as Springer GTM 241 in 2007. ([Silverman, ADS home page](https://www.math.brown.edu/~jhs/ADSHome.html)) Baker and Rumely's notes grew out of a 2004 Berkovich-space seminar at the University of Georgia. ([Baker–Rumely, arXiv:math/0407433](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0407433))

### Open problems
- **Uniform boundedness (Morton–Silverman).** For fixed $N\ge1$, $d\ge2$, $D\ge1$ there should be $C(N,d,D)$ with $\#\mathrm{PrePer}(f,\mathbb P^N(K))\le C(N,d,D)$ for all degree-$d$ morphisms over number fields of degree $D$; the survey says very little is known. ([Benedetto et al., §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980)) Doyle and Poonen proved strong uniform boundedness for preperiodic points of $z^d+c$ of bounded eventual period, reducing the full conjecture for this family to periodic points, and proved the function-field version. ([Doyle–Poonen, arXiv:1711.04233](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.04233)) Looper proved the conjecture for unicritical polynomials conditionally on a generalized $abc$ conjecture (the standard $abc$ conjecture suffices in degree at least five), and later for polynomials over number fields conditionally on a standard conjecture. ([Looper, arXiv:1901.04385](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04385); [Looper, arXiv:2105.05240](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05240))
- **Poonen's conjecture.** For all $c\in\mathbb Q$, $x^2+c$ has no rational periodic points of exact period greater than $3$. ([Benedetto et al., §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))
- **Dynamical Mordell–Lang and Zariski-dense orbits.** The general dynamical Mordell–Lang conjecture is open beyond the special cases above, and the weak form of the Amerik–Bogomolov–Rovinsky / Medvedev–Scanlon conjecture (a non-fibered endomorphism has a point with Zariski-dense orbit) "remains very much open, even in the case that $f$ is an automorphism." ([Benedetto et al., §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))
- **Dynamical André–Oort.** Baker–DeMarco conjectured that a subvariety of the moduli space of critically marked maps in which postcritically finite maps are Zariski dense is cut out by critical orbit relations; the one-parameter case was announced for polynomial families by Favre and Gauthier but remains open for rational maps. ([Benedetto et al., §11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))
- **No wandering domains over locally compact fields.** Benedetto conjectured that a rational map of degree at least $2$ defined over a locally compact subfield $K$ of $\mathbb C_v$ with $\bar K$ dense has no wandering domains. ([Benedetto et al., §17](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04980))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Arithmetic dynamics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_dynamics): Diophantine–dynamics dictionary, main theorems and conjectures.
- **Learn:** [Westlake University, An Introduction to Arithmetic Dynamics](https://its.westlake.edu.cn/info/1072/3652.htm): course from orbits through heights, Northcott and canonical heights to uniform boundedness.
- **Primary:** [Benedetto, DeMarco, Ingram, Jones, Manes, Silverman and Tucker, Current trends and open problems in arithmetic dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.04980): the standard survey of open problems.
- **Primary:** [Doyle and Poonen, Gonality of dynatomic curves and strong uniform boundedness of preperiodic points](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.04233): Compositio Math. 156 (2020).
- **Primary:** [Baker and Rumely, Analysis and dynamics on the Berkovich projective line](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0407433): potential theory for non-Archimedean dynamics.
- **Further reading:** [Silverman, The Arithmetic of Dynamical Systems (GTM 241)](https://www.math.brown.edu/~jhs/ADSHome.html): the author's page for the standard graduate text.
- **Further reading:** [Benedetto, Dynamics in One Non-Archimedean Variable (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 198, 2019)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/198): bibliographic record of the graduate text on Berkovich-line dynamics.
references.MSC 39 - Difference and functional equat:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC section 39 covers two linked subjects. [MSC 39Axx - Difference equations](node:MSC%2039Axx%20-%20Difference%20equations) treats equations for sequences or functions of a discrete (or $q$-scaled) variable: linear and nonlinear theory, partial difference equations, oscillation, periodicity, stability, bifurcation and chaos, integrable and lattice equations, stochastic difference equations and difference operators. [MSC 39Bxx - Functional equations and inequalities](node:MSC%2039Bxx%20-%20Functional%20equations%20and%20inequalities) treats equations relating values of an unknown function at related points, including iteration theory, functional inequalities and stability of [functional equations](node:Functional%20Equations). ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx); [MSC2020 39Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Bxx))

A recurrence relation of order $k$ expresses each term of a sequence through the previous $k$ terms; the difference operator $(\Delta a)_n=a_{n+1}-a_n$ turns every recurrence into a difference equation with the same solutions, so the two names are used interchangeably. ([Wikipedia: Recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)) An autonomous recurrence $x_{n+1}=f(x_n)$ is the iteration of $f$, which is why nonlinear [difference equations](node:Difference%20Equations) are studied with the tools of [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), and why MSC sends dynamical systems as such to section 37 ([MSC 37 - Dynamical systems and ergodic theory](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory)). ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx); [Hammond, Warwick lecture notes](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/current/mres/induction/adv-maths/dyneqlects25a.pdf))

The research questions differ sharply from the introductory linear theory: global behaviour of nonlinear rational recurrences, integrability of [birational maps](node:Birational%20Maps), the regularity and stability of solutions of functional equations, and the existence of iterative roots. ([Kulenović–Ladas monograph](https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/math_facpubs/211); [Mase–Willox–Ramani–Grammaticos, arXiv:1810.02693](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02693); [Wikipedia: Hyers–Ulam–Rassias stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyers%E2%80%93Ulam%E2%80%93Rassias_stability); [Tang–Li, arXiv:2109.12747](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12747))

### Scope
- **39Axx, difference equations:** general and linear theory (39A05, 39A06), additive equations (39A10), discrete versions of analysis (39A12), $q$-differences (39A13, see also 33Dxx), partial difference equations (39A14), multiplicative and generalized equations (39A20), oscillation (39A21), growth and boundedness (39A22), periodic and almost periodic solutions (39A23, 39A24), fuzzy equations (39A26), boundary value problems (39A27), bifurcation (39A28), stability (39A30), chaos (39A33), integrable difference and lattice equations and integrability tests (39A36), complex domain (39A45), stochastic equations (39A50), applications (39A60) and difference operators (39A70, see also 47B39). [Dynamic equations on time scales](node:Dynamic%20Equations%20on%20Time%20Scales) go to 34N05 ([MSC 34Nxx - Dynamic equations on time scales or measure chains](node:MSC%2034Nxx%20-%20Dynamic%20equations%20on%20time%20scales%20or%20measure%20chains)). ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx))
- **39Bxx, functional equations and inequalities:** general theory (39B05), iteration theory and iterative and composite equations (39B12), equations for real functions (39B22), complex functions (39B32), matrix and operator equations (39B42), more general domains (39B52), orthogonal additivity and conditional equations (39B55), functional inequalities including subadditivity and convexity (39B62), systems (39B72), and stability, separation and extension (39B82). ([MSC2020 39Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Linear recurrences with constant coefficients (39A06).** For $a_n=c_1a_{n-1}+\dots+c_ka_{n-k}$ with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=\lambda^k-c_1\lambda^{k-1}-\dots-c_k$ and distinct roots $r_1,\dots,r_d$, every solution is $\sum_ik_ir_i^n$; a root of multiplicity $m$ contributes $r^n,nr^n,\dots,n^{m-1}r^n$. Solutions tend to $0$ when all characteristic roots have modulus less than $1$, and a theorem of Schur characterizes this by positivity of a sequence of determinants. ([Wikipedia: Linear recurrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_recurrence_with_constant_coefficients))
- **Global behaviour of rational difference equations (39A20, 39A30).** Kulenović and Ladas's monograph classifies second-order rational equations and studies each for semicycles, invariant intervals, boundedness, periodicity and global stability, with a section of open problems and conjectures in every chapter. ([Kulenović–Ladas monograph](https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/math_facpubs/211)) A representative theorem: for $x_{n+1}=(p+qx_n)/(1+x_{n-1})$ with $p,q>0$, every solution with positive initial values converges to the positive equilibrium; Kocić and Ladas proved the case $q\ge p$ (1993) and Merino the case $q<p$, completing a conjecture of Ladas. ([Merino, arXiv:0812.3398](https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.3398))
- **Lyness recurrence and elliptic curves (39A20, 39A23).** For $x_{n+2}=(a+x_{n+1})/x_n$, every positive solution is $5$-periodic when $a=1$. ([Bastien–Mañosa–Rogalski, arXiv:1201.1027](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.1027)) With rational $a$ and rational initial conditions the only possible prime periods are $1,2,3,5,6,7,8,9,10,12$; infinitely many positive rational $a$ give rational $9$-periodic sequences, and the level sets of the Lyness invariant form a two-parameter family of elliptic curves covering curves with a point of order $n\ge5$. ([Gasull–Mañosa–Xarles, arXiv:1004.5511](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.5511)) For the $2$-periodic equation $u_{n+2}=(a_n+u_{n+1})/u_n$ with $a_n$ alternating between positive $a,b$, every $(a,b)\ne(1,1)$ admits infinitely many periodic initial conditions, almost all even periods occur, and if $a\ne b$ every odd period except $1$ appears. ([Bastien–Mañosa–Rogalski, arXiv:1201.1027](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.1027))
- **Discrete integrable systems (39A36).** The QRT mapping is a multi-parameter family of order-two autonomous maps whose orbits are values of an elliptic function at equidistant points on a line in a complex torus, a dynamical counterpart of the group law on an elliptic curve; discrete Painlevé equations can be regarded as integrable deautonomized QRT mappings. Singularity confinement is a useful but not sufficient detector of integrability. ([Carstea–Takenawa, arXiv:1907.13212](https://arxiv.org/html/1907.13212v1)) The complementary algebraic-entropy test asks for non-exponential growth of the degree of iterates; deautonomizing an integrable map by confinement preserves its degree growth. ([Ohta–Tamizhmani–Grammaticos–Ramani, arXiv:solv-int/9910007](https://arxiv.org/abs/solv-int/9910007)) For birational three-point maps with confinement, integrability and the exact dynamical degree can be read off from the confined singularity patterns. ([Mase–Willox–Ramani–Grammaticos, arXiv:1810.02693](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02693))
- **Cauchy's equation and regularity (39B22).** $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ has only the solutions $f(x)=cx$ on $\mathbb Q$. On $\mathbb R$ an additive $f$ is linear if it is continuous at one point, monotone on some interval, bounded on some interval, or Lebesgue measurable; assuming the axiom of choice, Hamel (1905) showed nonlinear solutions exist, and the graph of every nonlinear solution is dense in $\mathbb R^2$. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_functional_equation))
- **Hyers–Ulam stability (39B82).** Ulam asked in 1940 when a function approximately satisfying a functional equation must be close to an exact solution, starting from approximate group homomorphisms. Hyers (1941) answered for additive maps between [Banach spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces); Aoki (1950) treated an unbounded Cauchy difference, and Rassias (1978) extended Hyers' theorem to an unbounded Cauchy difference under a continuity condition, the first stability result for linear mappings. ([Wikipedia: Hyers–Ulam–Rassias stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyers%E2%80%93Ulam%E2%80%93Rassias_stability); [Wikipedia: Cauchy–Rassias stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Rassias_stability))
- **Iteration theory: Schröder, Abel and Koenigs (39B12).** Schröder's equation $\Psi(h(x))=s\Psi(x)$ is an eigenvalue equation for the composition operator. Koenigs (1884): if $h$ is analytic on the unit disk, $h(0)=0$ and $0<|h'(0)|<1$, there is a nontrivial analytic solution with $s=h'(0)$. Then $\alpha=\log\Psi/\log s$ solves Abel's equation $\alpha(h(x))=\alpha(x)+1$, and $h^t(x)=\Psi^{-1}(s^t\Psi(x))$ defines a continuous group of fractional iterates; the superattracting case $h'(0)=0$ leads to Böttcher's equation. ([Wikipedia: Schröder's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6der%27s_equation))
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) and [Numerical Methods for Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Methods%20for%20Differential%20Equations): Euler's method for $y'=f(t,y)$ is the recurrence $y_{n+1}=y_n+hf(t_n,y_n)$, and time scale calculus unifies difference and differential equations. ([Wikipedia: Difference equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Difference_equation)) The stationary states of an autonomous recurrence $x_{t+1}=f(x_t)$ are exactly the fixed points of $f$. ([Hammond, Warwick lecture notes](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/current/mres/induction/adv-maths/dyneqlects25a.pdf))

### History
Cauchy proved in 1821 that continuous solutions of the additive equation are linear, and Hamel's construction of discontinuous solutions dates from 1905. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_functional_equation)) Koenigs' linearization theorem dates from 1884. ([Wikipedia: Schröder's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6der%27s_equation)) The stability question goes back to Ulam (1940) and Hyers (1941). ([Wikipedia: Hyers–Ulam–Rassias stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyers%E2%80%93Ulam%E2%80%93Rassias_stability)) Quispel, Roberts and Thomson published their family of maps in Physica D in 1989. ([Carstea–Takenawa, arXiv:1907.13212](https://arxiv.org/html/1907.13212v1)) The *Journal of Difference Equations and Applications* has run sections of open problems and conjectures, with submissions directed to Ladas. ([Kulenović–Ladas–Overdeep, JDEA 2003](https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/math_facpubs/200))

### Open problems
- **Characteristic endpoints problem (39B12).** For piecewise monotone (PM) functions of height $1$, continuous iterative roots of every order exist under the characteristic endpoints condition; whether they exist without it is an open question, called the characteristic endpoints problem. It is almost completely solved when the number of forts is at most the order, and Tang and Li give a sufficient condition for continuous iterative roots of order $2$ and height $2$ when the number of forts exceeds the order, a partial answer. ([Tang–Li, arXiv:2109.12747](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12747))
- **Open problems for rational recurrences (39A20).** Each chapter of Kulenović–Ladas closes with a section of open problems and conjectures on the global dynamics of second-order rational equations, and the JDEA problem section collects further ones. ([Kulenović–Ladas monograph](https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/math_facpubs/211); [Kulenović–Ladas–Overdeep, JDEA 2003](https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/math_facpubs/200))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Recurrence relation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation): definitions, linear recurrences, difference operator.
- **Reference:** [Schröder's equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6der%27s_equation): Koenigs' theorem, Abel and Böttcher equations, fractional iterates.
- **Learn:** [Hammond, Dynamic Equations (Warwick lecture notes)](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/current/mres/induction/adv-maths/dyneqlects25a.pdf): first-order and linear difference equations, stationary states and stability.
- **Primary:** [Kulenović and Ladas, Dynamics of Second Order Rational Difference Equations: With Open Problems and Conjectures](https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/math_facpubs/211): the standard monograph on rational recurrences.
- **Primary:** [Gasull, Mañosa and Xarles, Rational periodic sequences for the Lyness recurrence](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.5511): periods and elliptic-curve structure.
- **Primary:** [Mase, Willox, Ramani and Grammaticos, Singularity confinement as an integrability criterion](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02693): integrability tests for birational maps.
- **Further reading:** [Elaydi, An Introduction to Difference Equations (Springer, Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-3110-1); [Aczél and Dhombres, Functional Equations in Several Variables (CUP, 1989)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139086578); [Kuczma, An Introduction to the Theory of Functional Equations and Inequalities (Birkhäuser, 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-7643-8749-5): bibliographic records of standard texts.
references.MSC 39Axx - Difference equations:
## Reference
### Overview
A recurrence relation defines each term of a sequence from earlier terms; its order is the number of previous terms used, and that many initial values are needed to start the sequence. "Recurrence relation" and "[difference equation](node:Difference%20Equations)" are often used interchangeably, and because of the resemblance to differential equations their methods often transfer. ([Wikipedia: Recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)) The linear theory parallels [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations): the Casoratian is the discrete analogue of the Wronskian, and the theorems of Poincaré and Perron describe the asymptotic growth of solutions. ([Chamberland–Straub, §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.03400)) Nonlinear difference equations are discrete-time [dynamical systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems); at the integrable end, discrete Painlevé equations are studied through singularity confinement, algebraic entropy, and the Okamoto–Sakai spaces of initial conditions. ([Alecci–Graffeo–Stokes, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.12647))

MSC2020 class 39Axx sits inside [MSC 39 - Difference and functional equations](node:MSC%2039%20-%20Difference%20and%20functional%20equations). Its header note sends [dynamic equations on time scales](node:Dynamic%20Equations%20on%20Time%20Scales) to 34N05 ([34Nxx](node:MSC%2034Nxx%20-%20Dynamic%20equations%20on%20time%20scales%20or%20measure%20chains)) and dynamical systems to 37-XX ([MSC 37](node:MSC%2037%20-%20Dynamical%20systems%20and%20ergodic%20theory)); the sibling class is [39Bxx](node:MSC%2039Bxx%20-%20Functional%20equations%20and%20inequalities). ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx))

### Scope
- **General and linear theory (39A05, 39A06, 39A10):** general theory, linear difference equations, and additive difference equations. ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx))
- **Variants (39A12, 39A13, 39A14, 39A20):** discrete versions of topics in analysis, $q$-difference (scaling) equations (see also [33Dxx](node:MSC%2033Dxx%20-%20Basic%20hypergeometric%20functions)), partial difference equations, and multiplicative and other generalized equations. ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx))
- **Qualitative theory (39A21–39A33):** oscillation, growth and boundedness, periodic and almost periodic solutions, fuzzy equations, boundary value problems, bifurcation, stability, and chaotic behaviour. ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx))
- **Special settings (39A36–39A70):** integrable difference and lattice equations and integrability tests, the complex domain, stochastic difference equations, applications, and difference operators (see also 47B39). ([MSC2020 39Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Linear constant-coefficient equations.** With difference operator $(\Delta a)_n=a_{n+1}-a_n$, a difference equation in $\Delta$ converts to a recurrence and back. ([Wikipedia: Recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)) For a homogeneous order-$n$ recurrence with distinct characteristic roots $\lambda_i$ the general solution is $\sum_ic_i\lambda_i^t$; a repeated root contributes $c_1\lambda^t+c_2t\lambda^t$. All solutions tend to $0$ if every root has modulus less than $1$, and Schur's criterion decides this by positivity of a sequence of determinants. ([Wikipedia: Linear recurrence with constant coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_recurrence_with_constant_coefficients)) See [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors) and [Generating Functions](node:Generating%20Functions).
- **Casoratian.** For $u(n+d)+p_{d-1}(n)u(n+d-1)+\dots+p_0(n)u(n)=0$ and solutions $u_1,\dots,u_d$, the Casoratian $w(n)=\det\big(u_j(n+i-1)\big)_{i,j=1}^d$ is the discrete Wronskian; it satisfies $w(n+1)=(-1)^dp_0(n)w(n)$, so $w(n)=(-1)^{dn}p_0(0)\cdots p_0(n-1)w(0)$. For $d=2$ a second solution is $u_2(n)=u_1(n)\sum_{k<n}w(k)/(u_1(k)u_1(k+1))$ when $u_1$ never vanishes. ([Chamberland–Straub, §4 and Lemma 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.03400))
- **Poincaré–Perron theorem.** If $p_k(n)\to c_k$ and the roots of $\lambda^d+c_{d-1}\lambda^{d-1}+\dots+c_0$ have distinct moduli, every solution either vanishes for all large $n$ or satisfies $u(n+1)/u(n)\to\lambda_k$ for some root $\lambda_k$ (Poincaré). If moreover $p_0(n)\ne0$ for all $n$, then for each $k$ some solution has $u(n+1)/u(n)\to\lambda_k$ (Perron). ([Chamberland–Straub, Theorem 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.03400))
- **First-order nonlinear maps and stability.** For $x_n=f(x_{n-1})$, a fixed point $x^*$ is locally stable when $|f'(x^*)|<1$, and bounded chaotic recurrences never settle on a fixed point or attracting cycle. ([Wikipedia: Recurrence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation)) The Melbourne cobwebbing applet compares $x_{n+1}=g(x_n)$ with its tangent-line linearization at an equilibrium to motivate this criterion. ([Melbourne applet](https://melbapplets.ms.unimelb.edu.au/2021/07/08/cobwebbing-linear-approximation-and-stability/)) The logistic map $x_{n+1}=rx_n(1-x_n)$ undergoes a period-doubling cascade ending near $r\approx3.56995$, the onset of chaos, with Feigenbaum ratio $\delta\approx4.66920$. ([Wikipedia: Logistic map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_map)) See [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory) and [Bifurcation Theory](node:Bifurcation%20Theory).
- **Sharkovskii's theorem and Li–Yorke.** Order the positive integers as $3\triangleright5\triangleright7\triangleright\dots\triangleright2\cdot3\triangleright2\cdot5\triangleright\dots\triangleright2^2\cdot3\triangleright\dots\triangleright2^3\triangleright2^2\triangleright2\triangleright1$. If a continuous $f:I\to I$ on an interval has a point of least period $m$ and $m\triangleright n$, then $f$ has a point of least period $n$; conversely every upper set of the order is the set of periods of some continuous interval map. Li and Yorke (1975) showed that period three forces all periods and an uncountable set of points that never settle into a cycle. ([Wikipedia: Sharkovskii's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem))
- **Rational difference equations.** Kulenović and Ladas began a systematic study of $x_{n+1}=\frac{\alpha+\beta x_n+\gamma x_{n-1}}{A+Bx_n+Cx_{n-1}}$ with nonnegative parameters, $B+C>0$, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma>0$, and nonnegative initial values, splitting it into 42 cases according to which parameters vanish; the Lyness equation $x_{n+1}=(\alpha+x_n)/x_{n-1}$ is a case whose dynamics differ markedly from the rest. Basu and Merino prove the conjecture of Ladas et al. for two of the hardest cases: when all six parameters are positive, every solution converges to the positive equilibrium or to a prime period-two solution, and the same holds with $A=0$ and positive initial values. ([Basu–Merino, §1 and Theorems 1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.3385))
- **Discrete Painlevé equations and Sakai's classification (39A36).** Discrete analogues of the Painlevé equations can be derived from the standard ones by limits and by deautonomizing simplified mappings. ([Ramani–Grammaticos, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/solv-int/9510011)) Sakai's framework defines discrete Painlevé equations via symmetries of Sakai surfaces: generalized Halphen surfaces $S$ (smooth projective rational surfaces with an effective anticanonical divisor $D=\sum m_iD_i$, $D_i\cdot K_S=0$) with $\dim|-K_S|=0$. Such $S$ has $\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Pic}(S)=10$, the components of $D$ span an affine root lattice, and $h^1(D_{red},\mathbb Z)\in\{0,1,2\}$ separates additive, multiplicative, and elliptic types. ([Alecci–Graffeo–Stokes, §§3.4–3.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.12647)) Sakai's paper "Rational surfaces associated with affine root systems and geometry of the Painlevé equations" appeared in Communications in Mathematical Physics 220 (2001). ([Crossref: Sakai 2001](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/s002200100446)) See [Algebraic Surfaces](node:Algebraic%20Surfaces) and [Root Systems](node:Root%20Systems).

### History
Biologist Robert May popularized the logistic map in a 1976 paper as a discrete-time analogue of Verhulst's logistic equation. ([Wikipedia: Logistic map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_map)) Sharkovskii published his theorem in 1964, and Li and Yorke showed in 1975 that period three implies chaos. ([Wikipedia: Sharkovskii's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkovskii%27s_theorem)) Kulenović and Ladas's monograph on second-order rational difference equations (2001) ends each chapter with open problems and conjectures. ([URI: Kulenović–Ladas](https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/math_facpubs/211)) In 1995 Ramani and Grammaticos derived a range of new discrete Painlevé equations from the standard five, and Sakai's 2001 geometric classification organized them by rational surfaces and affine root systems. ([Ramani–Grammaticos, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/solv-int/9510011)) ([Alecci–Graffeo–Stokes, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.12647))

### Open problems
- **Unresolved cases of the Kulenović–Ladas programme.** Ladas and co-workers posed a series of conjectures on the second-order rational equations; as of 2008, eight normalized cases had resisted complete analysis, among them $x_{n+1}=\frac{\alpha+x_n}{x_n+Cx_{n-1}}$ and $x_{n+1}=\frac{\alpha+\beta x_n+\gamma x_{n-1}}{A+x_{n-1}}$, which the progress Basu and Merino list (including their own theorems) does not settle. ([Basu–Merino, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.3385)) The source monograph is organized around open problems and conjectures. ([URI: Kulenović–Ladas](https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/math_facpubs/211))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Recurrence relation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrence_relation): terminology, difference operator, stability, applications.
- **Learn:** [University of Melbourne: Cobwebbing, linear approximation and stability](https://melbapplets.ms.unimelb.edu.au/2021/07/08/cobwebbing-linear-approximation-and-stability/): interactive applet for first-order equations near an equilibrium.
- **Learn:** [Alecci, Graffeo and Stokes, Classical Algebraic Geometry and Discrete Integrable Systems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.12647): lecture notes on Sakai surfaces, discrete Painlevé equations, and algebraic entropy.
- **Primary:** [Ramani and Grammaticos, Discrete Painlevé equations: coalescences, limits and degeneracies](https://arxiv.org/abs/solv-int/9510011): research paper on integrable nonautonomous difference equations.
- **Primary:** [Basu and Merino, Global behavior of solutions to two classes of second order rational difference equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.3385): proof of a Ladas et al. conjecture, with the list of open cases.
- **Further reading:** [Elaydi, An Introduction to Difference Equations (Springer, Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics, 2005)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/0-387-27602-5): introductory textbook. Author record: [Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=elaydi+introduction+to+difference+equations).
- **Further reading:** [Kelley and Peterson, Difference Equations: An Introduction with Applications](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=kelley+peterson+difference+equations+introduction+applications): text (2nd edition 2001) that Chamberland and Straub cite for the Casoratian identity and Poincaré's theorem. ([Chamberland–Straub, §4 and references](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.03400))
references.MSC 39Bxx - Functional equations and ine:
## Reference
### Overview
