In the narrow sense used by this subfield, a functional equation relates several values of the same unknown function, such as $f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)$ for logarithms; in the broadest sense any equation with unknown functions counts. The typical task is to find all solutions in a given class, and regularity hypotheses decide the answer: without a smoothness or similar condition, most functional equations have highly irregular solutions. ([Wikipedia: Functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation))

The area has three recurring themes. Regularity theory shows that very weak conditions (boundedness on a set of positive measure, measurability) force a solution of Cauchy's equation to be linear. ([Bingham–Ostaszewski, The converse Ostrowski theorem](https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/6832/); [Wikipedia: Cauchy's functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_functional_equation)) Iteration theory studies equations in which the unknown is composed with itself or with a given map, such as iterative roots $g\circ g=f$, an area tied to embedding flows, invariant curves and linearization in dynamics. ([Bhat–Gopalakrishna, arXiv:2105.02171](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.02171)) Stability theory, started by Ulam's 1940 question on approximate homomorphisms, asks whether an approximate solution lies near an exact one. ([Sadeghi, arXiv:1406.1979](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.1979))

### Scope
MSC2020 39Bxx (see also 30D05) has these codes: 39B05 general theory; 39B12 iteration theory, iterative and composite equations (see also 26A18, 30D05, 37-XX); 39B22 equations for real functions (see also 26A51, 26B25); 39B32 equations for complex functions (see also 30D05); 39B42 matrix and operator equations (see also 47Jxx); 39B52 functions with more general domains and/or ranges; 39B55 orthogonal additivity and other conditional equations; 39B62 functional inequalities, including subadditivity and convexity (see also 26A51, 26B25, 26Dxx); 39B72 systems; 39B82 stability, separation, extension and related topics (see also 46A22); 39B99 other. ([MSC2020 39Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Bxx))

Neighbours, following those cross-references: [MSC 39Axx - Difference equations](node:MSC%2039Axx%20-%20Difference%20equations) holds difference equations; [MSC 26Dxx - Inequalities in real analysis](node:MSC%2026Dxx%20-%20Inequalities%20in%20real%20analysis) holds real inequalities and convexity from the real-analysis side; [MSC 30Dxx - Entire and meromorphic functions of one complex variable, and related topics](node:MSC%2030Dxx%20-%20Entire%20and%20meromorphic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable,%20and%20related%20topics) holds complex functional equations via 30D05; and iterative equations border dynamical systems (37-XX). ([MSC2020 39Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Bxx))

### Key concepts
- **Cauchy's equation $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ (39B22, 39B52).** Over $\mathbb Q$ the solutions are exactly $f(x)=cx$. Over $\mathbb R$, continuity (Cauchy 1821), continuity at a single point (Darboux 1875), monotonicity, boundedness above or below on an interval, or Lebesgue measurability each force $f(x)=cx$. Using a Hamel basis of $\mathbb R$ over $\mathbb Q$, Hamel (1905) built nonlinear solutions, and the graph of every nonlinear solution is dense in $\mathbb R^2$. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_functional_equation)) A Berkeley Math Circle handout gives elementary proofs of the rational case, the density of the graph, and the regularity criteria. ([Berkeley Math Circle](https://mathcircle.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/archivedocs/2010_2011//lectures/1011lecturespdf/FunctionalEquationsbmc.pdf)) Links to [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) and [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits).
- **Ostrowski's theorem (regularity).** An additive function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is bounded above (or below) on a set of positive Lebesgue measure is continuous ([Bingham–Ostaszewski, The converse Ostrowski theorem](https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/6832/)), hence of the form $cx$ ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_functional_equation)). Bingham and Ostaszewski derive both the measure and the Baire-category automatic continuity theorems for additive functions from a combinatorial form of this theorem, using combinatorial principles that unify and extend the classical results of Steinhaus and Piccard on interior points of distance sets. ([Bingham–Ostaszewski, Math. Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc. 2011](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/dichotomy-and-infinite-combinatorics-the-theorems-of-steinhaus-and-ostrowski/3E144773AB8A48565A49F2E688EEF311)) Links to [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory).
- **Jensen convexity and the Bernstein–Doetsch theorem (39B62).** A function is Jensen convex if $f\!\left(\tfrac{x+y}{2}\right)\le\tfrac{f(x)+f(y)}{2}$. Bernstein–Doetsch (1915): if $D$ is a nonempty open convex subset of a topological linear space and $f:D\to\mathbb R$ is Jensen convex and locally bounded above at one point of $D$, then $f$ is continuous and convex. Hyers and Ulam (1952) started the study of approximately convex functions. ([Approximately Jensen convex functions, arXiv:2412.05645](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.05645))
- **Other classical equations.** Jensen's equation $f\!\left(\tfrac{x+y}{2}\right)=\tfrac{f(x)+f(y)}{2}$, the quadratic equation $f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2[f(x)+f(y)]$, and d'Alembert's equation $g(x+y)+g(x-y)=2g(x)g(y)$. ([Wikipedia: Functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation)) Cauchy determined the continuous solutions of $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$, $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$, $f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)$ and $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$ as $ax$, $a^x$, $a\log x$ and $x^a$. ([Sadeghi, arXiv:1406.1979](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.1979))
- **The gamma function** ([Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function)). Bohr–Mollerup (1922): the gamma function is the only positive function $f$ on $(0,\infty)$ with $f(1)=1$, $f(x+1)=xf(x)$, and $\log f$ convex. No meromorphy hypothesis is needed. ([Wikipedia: Bohr–Mollerup theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr%E2%80%93Mollerup_theorem))
- **Iterative equations and iterative roots (39B12).** Abel's equation $f(h(x))=h(x+1)$, Schröder's $f(h(x))=cf(x)$, Böttcher's $f(h(x))=(f(x))^c$, and Babbage's involution equation $f(f(x))=x$ (1820) all involve composition. ([Wikipedia: Functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation)) An $n$th iterative root of a continuous $g:X\to X$ is a continuous $f$ with $f^n=g$. For $X=[0,1]$ with the supremum metric, Humke and Laczkovich showed that the maps without a continuous square root are dense in $C([0,1])$, and Simon that the set of iterative squares is nowhere dense; $f(x)=1-x$ has no continuous square root. Bhat and Gopalakrishna show that maps with no square root, even a discontinuous one, are dense in $C(I^m)$ (supremum metric) and in $C(\mathbb R^m)$ (compact-open topology). ([Bhat–Gopalakrishna, arXiv:2105.02171](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.02171)) Links to [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems).
- **Hyers–Ulam–Rassias stability (39B82).** Hyers (1941): if $E_1,E_2$ are real Banach spaces, $\varepsilon>0$, and $\|f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y)\|\le\varepsilon$ for all $x,y$, then there is a unique additive $T$ with $\|f(x)-T(x)\|\le\varepsilon$. Rassias (1978): for $0\le p<1$, the bound $\varepsilon(\|x\|^p+\|y\|^p)$ yields a unique additive $T$ with $\|f(x)-T(x)\|\le\tfrac{2\varepsilon}{2-2^p}\|x\|^p$. Rassias and Šemrl extended this to $p\ge0$, $p\ne1$. For $p=1$ it fails: Gajda (1991) showed that for maps $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and every $\theta>0$ there is no constant $\delta\ge0$ such that every $f$ with $|f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y)|\le\theta(|x|+|y|)$ lies within $\delta|x|$ of an additive function. ([Sadeghi, arXiv:1406.1979](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.1979)) Links to [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces).

### History
Babbage studied the involution equation $f(f(x))=x$ in 1820. ([Wikipedia: Functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation)) Cauchy (1821) showed that continuous additive functions are linear; Darboux reduced the regularity needed to continuity at one point in 1875, and Hamel constructed nonlinear solutions in 1905. ([Wikipedia: Cauchy's functional equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_functional_equation)) Bernstein and Doetsch published their convexity theorem in Math. Ann. 76 (1915). ([arXiv:2412.05645](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.05645))

Ulam posed the stability question for group homomorphisms in a 1940 Wisconsin colloquium talk on unsolved problems, and Hyers answered it for Banach spaces in 1941. ([Sadeghi, arXiv:1406.1979](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.1979)) Aoki (1950) and Rassias (1978) allowed unbounded Cauchy differences, Rassias adding a continuity condition to obtain stability of linear maps. ([Wikipedia: Hyers–Ulam–Rassias stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyers%E2%80%93Ulam%E2%80%93Rassias_stability))

The standard monographs include Aczél and Dhombres, *Functional Equations in Several Variables* (Cambridge, 1989) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139086578)), and Kuczma, *An Introduction to the Theory of Functional Equations and Inequalities* (Birkhäuser, 2009, ed. Gilányi) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-7643-8749-5)). For iteration, Kuczma's *Functional Equations in a Single Variable* (1968) and Kuczma, Choczewski and Ger, *Iterative Functional Equations* (Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications 32) are standard. ([Bhat–Gopalakrishna, references](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.02171))

### Open problems
- **Ulam stability and amenability.** In Ulam's original group setting, a group is Ulam stable if every uniform asymptotic homomorphism into unitary groups (operator norm) is uniformly close to a sequence of true homomorphisms. Kazhdan (1982) proved amenable groups are stable, and Burger–Ozawa–Thom showed groups with non-trivial quasimorphisms are unstable. Fournier-Facio and Rangarajan call it "a well-known open question" whether strong Ulam stability coincides with amenability, and ask whether every countable torsion group, or every countable group without non-abelian free subgroups, is Ulam stable. ([Fournier-Facio–Rangarajan, arXiv:2301.03970](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.03970v2))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Functional equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation): catalogue of classical and iterative equations.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 39Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=39Bxx): official code list with cross-references.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley Math Circle: Functional Equations](https://mathcircle.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/archivedocs/2010_2011//lectures/1011lecturespdf/FunctionalEquationsbmc.pdf): elementary treatment of Cauchy's equation and its pathological solutions.
- **Primary:** [Sadeghi, Cauchy's equations and Ulam's problem (arXiv:1406.1979)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.1979): survey of Hyers, Rassias and Gajda results with new stability theorems.
- **Primary:** [Bhat and Gopalakrishna, Iterative square roots of functions (arXiv:2105.02171)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.02171): density of maps without square roots in spaces of continuous self-maps.
- **Primary:** [Fournier-Facio and Rangarajan, Ulam stability of lamplighters and Thompson groups (arXiv:2301.03970)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.03970): group-theoretic Ulam stability and its open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Kuczma, An Introduction to the Theory of Functional Equations and Inequalities (Birkhäuser 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-7643-8749-5) and [Aczél–Dhombres, Functional Equations in Several Variables (CUP 1989)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139086578): the standard monographs.
references.MSC 40 - Sequences, series, summability:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 section 40-XX, "Sequences, series, summability", collects work on the convergence and divergence of infinite limiting processes and on methods that assign values to sequences and series that need not converge. ([MSC2020 40-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40-XX)) A summation method can be viewed as a function from a set of sequences of partial sums to values; it is regular if it agrees with the actual limit on convergent series, linear, and stable if it respects removing the first term. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series))

The field's core is the comparison of methods with ordinary convergence and with each other. An Abelian theorem says a method sums convergent series correctly; a Tauberian theorem is a partial converse, saying that if a method sums a series and a side condition holds, the series converges. The development of Tauberian theory took a fresh turn with Wiener's very general results; Korevaar's *Tauberian Theory: A Century of Developments* (2004) is the modern monograph. ([Wikipedia: Abelian and Tauberian theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems)) Through the Wiener–Ikehara theorem the field connects directly to [analytic number theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory) and the prime number theorem. ([Wikipedia: Wiener–Ikehara theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Ikehara_theorem))

### Scope
The MSC2020 subclasses are 40Axx (convergence and divergence of infinite limiting processes), 40Bxx (multiple sequences and series), 40Cxx (general summability methods), 40Dxx (direct theorems on summability), 40Exx (inversion theorems), 40Fxx (absolute and strong summability), 40Gxx (special methods of summability), 40Hxx (functional analytic methods in summability), and 40Jxx (summability in abstract structures). 40Fxx and 40Jxx carry the note that papers should also be assigned at least one other classification number in the section, and 40Jxx cross-refers to 43A55, 46A35 and 46B15. ([MSC2020 40-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40-XX))

Leaf codes that locate the main current themes: 40A35 ideal and statistical convergence (see also 40G15) and 40A15 continued fractions ([MSC2020 40Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Axx)); 40E05 Tauberian theorems, 40E10 growth estimates, 40E15 lacunary inversion theorems, 40E20 Tauberian constants ([MSC2020 40Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Exx)); 40G05 Cesàro, Euler, Nörlund and Hausdorff methods, 40G10 Abel, Borel and power series methods, 40G15 summability methods using statistical convergence ([MSC2020 40Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Gxx)).

Neighbouring sections: the Euler–Maclaurin formula goes to 65B15 and continued fractions also to 30B70 ([MSC2020 40Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Axx)); summability on groups and semigroups is 43A55, and summability with bases and frames in Banach spaces is 46B15 ([MSC2020 40Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Jxx)). Almost-everywhere convergence of Fourier series is classified in harmonic analysis: for example, Ashurov's survey of a.e. convergence of multiple Fourier series has primary classification 42B05. ([Ashurov, arXiv:1912.03534](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1912.03534))

### Key concepts
- **Silverman–Toeplitz theorem (40C05).** A matrix $(a_{i,j})$ defines a regular method if and only if every column tends to $0$, the row sums tend to $1$, and the absolute row sums are bounded. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §3.2, Theorem 2](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt); [Wikipedia: Silverman–Toeplitz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverman%E2%80%93Toeplitz_theorem)) Kojima and Schur characterized the matrices sending convergent sequences to convergent ones, and Schur those sending bounded sequences to convergent ones. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §3.2](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) A regular matrix cannot sum all $0$–$1$ sequences (Steinhaus). ([Boos, Filomat 2019](https://web1.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2019/33-14/33-14-16-10677.pdf)) See [Matrix Summability Methods](node:Matrix%20Summability%20Methods).
- **Special methods (40G05, 40G10).** Nörlund means: for $p_n>0$ with $p_n/(p_0+\dots+p_n)\to0$, $t_m=(p_ms_0+\dots+p_0s_m)/(p_0+\dots+p_m)$; Cesàro $(C,k)$ is the case $p_n=\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$. Riesz means: with $A_\lambda(x)=a_0+\dots+a_n$ for $\lambda_n<x\le\lambda_{n+1}$, the sum is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}\frac{\kappa}{\omega^\kappa}\int_0^\omega A_\lambda(x)(\omega-x)^{\kappa-1}dx$. Abelian means: $\lim_{x\to0^+}\sum a_ne^{-\lambda_nx}$, with Abel summation the case $\lambda_n=n$. Borel summation: $\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\sum_n a_nt^n/n!\,dt$. Nörlund means are regular, linear, stable and mutually consistent; Abel summation is consistent with and stronger than Cesàro; Abelian means and Borel summation are not stable. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series)) See [Cesàro and Abel Summation](node:Cesàro%20and%20Abel%20Summation).
- **Tauber and Littlewood (40E05).** If $\sum a_nx^n\to s$ as $x\to1^-$ and $a_n=o(1/n)$, then $\sum a_n=s$ (Tauber, 1897); Littlewood weakened the hypothesis to $a_n=O(1/n)$. ([Wikipedia: Abelian and Tauberian theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems)) See [Tauberian Theorems](node:Tauberian%20Theorems), [Abelian Summability Theorems](node:Abelian%20Summability%20Theorems).
- **Hardy–Littlewood and Karamata.** If $a_n\ge0$ and $\sum a_nx^n\sim1/(1-x)$ as $x\uparrow1$, then $\sum_{k\le n}a_k\sim n$ (Hardy–Littlewood, 1914). Karamata's extension allows a slowly varying factor in the asymptotics, and Karamata (1930) gave a much shorter proof by approximating with polynomials, for which $(1-x)\sum a_nx^ng(x^n)\to\int_0^1g(t)\,dt$ holds directly. ([Wikipedia: Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem)) See [Hardy's Tauberian Theorem](node:Hardy's%20Tauberian%20Theorem).
- **Wiener's Tauberian theorem.** The translates of $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ span a dense subspace of $L^1$ if and only if $\hat f$ has no real zeros. Tauberian form: if $\hat f$ has no real zeros, $h$ is bounded, and $f*h\to A\int f$ at infinity, then $g*h\to A\int g$ for every $g\in L^1$. Gelfand later reformulated the $L^1$ result with Banach algebra methods. ([Wikipedia: Wiener's Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_Tauberian_theorem))
- **Wiener–Ikehara theorem and the prime number theorem.** If $A$ is nonnegative and nondecreasing on $[0,\infty)$, $f(s)=\int_0^\infty A(x)e^{-xs}dx$ converges for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, and $f(s)-c/(s-1)$ extends continuously to $\operatorname{Re}s\ge1$, then $e^{-x}A(x)\to c$. Applied to $-\zeta'/\zeta$, whose Dirichlet coefficients are the von Mangoldt function, it yields the prime number theorem from the nonvanishing of $\zeta$ on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$. ([Wikipedia: Wiener–Ikehara theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Ikehara_theorem)) See [Prime Number Theorem](node:Prime%20Number%20Theorem), [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Mercerian theorems.** These determine the values of $\alpha$ for which summability by $\alpha I+(1-\alpha)A$ is equivalent to convergence; for $\alpha\ne1$ this reduces to finding the spectrum of $A$. Cass and Rhoades showed the spectrum of every weighted mean method $a_{nk}=p_k/P_n$ lies in the disc $|\lambda-\tfrac12|\le\tfrac12$, generalizing results of Mercer, Knopp and others. ([Cass–Rhoades, Pacific J. Math. 1977](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1977.73.63))
- **Ideal and statistical convergence (40A35).** For an ideal $\mathcal I$ on $\mathbb N$, $x$ is $\mathcal I$-convergent to $L$ if $\{n:|x_n-L|\ge\varepsilon\}\in\mathcal I$ for all $\varepsilon>0$; it is regular iff $\mathcal I$ contains the finite sets, and the density-zero ideal gives statistical convergence. An ideal convergence is contained in some matrix summability method if and only if the ideal is not dense. ([Filipów–Tryba, Thm 3.1](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf))
- [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence), [Uniform Convergence of Series](node:Uniform%20Convergence%20of%20Series), [Absolute Summability](node:Absolute%20Summability), [Banach Limits](node:Banach%20Limits), [Multiple Series](node:Multiple%20Series), [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis), [Carleson's Theorem](node:Carleson's%20Theorem), [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), [Summability in abstract structures](node:MSC%2040Jxx%20-%20Summability%20in%20abstract%20structures%20%28should%20also%20be%20assigned%20at%20least%20one%20other%20classification%20number%20from%20Section%2040-XX%29): the ordinary theory, related summability notions, and the harmonic-analysis and Banach-space settings; Parisé's kernel-summability theorem in Banach spaces is classified 40C10/40D05 with 40J05 secondary. ([Parisé, arXiv:2302.06770](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06770v3))

### History
Euler used divergent series freely; Cauchy's rigorous definition of convergent sums led to their neglect, until Poincaré's 1886 work on asymptotic series and Cesàro's explicit 1890 definitions of sums for some divergent series. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series)) Tauber proved the prototype inverse theorem in 1897, and Hardy and Littlewood proved their theorem in 1914. ([Wikipedia: Abelian and Tauberian theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems); [Wikipedia: Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem)) Hardy credits the regularity criterion to Toeplitz (1911) for triangular transformations and its extension to general transformations to Steinhaus, and the convergent-to-convergent characterization to Kojima (1917) and Schur. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, Notes on Ch. III](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Ikehara published his theorem in 1931 and Wiener his general Tauberian theorems in *Annals of Mathematics* in 1932. ([Wikipedia: Wiener–Ikehara theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Ikehara_theorem))

Hardy's *Divergent Series* (Oxford, 1949) is the classical monograph. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Korevaar's *Tauberian Theory: A Century of Developments* appeared in Springer's Grundlehren series in 2004 ([Crossref metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Korevaar+Tauberian+Theory+A+Century+of+Developments&rows=3)), and Boos's *Classical and Modern Methods in Summability* (OUP, 2000) combines classical and functional-analytic methods. ([OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/53786))

### Open problems
- **Ideal convergence and matrix methods.** Filipów and Tryba ask whether some ideal with Mazur's property (M) is not isomorphic to $\mathrm{Fin}$ or $\mathrm{Fin}\oplus P(\mathbb N)$, and whether a non-Borel ideal can have their property GMV. ([Filipów–Tryba, Questions 2–3](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf))
- **Summability of subsequences.** Buck and Pollard showed a bounded sequence is $(C,1)$ summable iff almost all its subsequences are; Boos poses as further problems, unanswered in the paper, whether this extends to unbounded sequences, to positive-density "almost every subsequence", or to arbitrary regular matrices. ([Boos, Filomat 2019, Problems 6.2](https://web1.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2019/33-14/33-14-16-10677.pdf))
- **Boundary with harmonic analysis.** Almost-everywhere convergence of Fourier series is known on $L\log^+L\log^+\log^+\log^+L$ (Antonov), while Konyagin constructed everywhere-divergent Fourier series in a space slightly larger than $L(\log^+L)^{1/2}$. This leaves a gap between the two spaces: whether there is a largest natural space of a.e. convergence is an open question, and $L\log^+L$, which contains Antonov's space, is the simplest candidate consistent with both results. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem)) In MSC2020 such questions fall under 42A20, "Convergence and absolute convergence of Fourier and trigonometric series". ([MSC2020 42Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Axx))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Divergent series (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series): summation axioms and the main classical methods.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 section 40-XX (AMS)](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40-XX): the official subclasses.
- **Learn:** [Abelian and Tauberian theorems (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems) and [Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem): entry points to Tauberian theory with Karamata's proof.
- **Primary:** [Hardy, *Divergent Series* (1949), full text](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt): the classical monograph.
- **Primary:** [Filipów and Tryba, Ideal convergence versus matrix summability](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf): current research on 40A35/40C05 with open questions.
- **Primary:** [Cass and Rhoades, Mercerian theorems via spectral theory](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1977.73.63): Mercerian theorems as spectral problems.
- **Further reading:** [Korevaar, *Tauberian Theory: A Century of Developments* (Springer, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Korevaar+Tauberian+Theory+A+Century+of+Developments&rows=3) and [Boos and Cass, *Classical and Modern Methods in Summability* (OUP, 2000)](https://academic.oup.com/book/53786): the modern monographs.

## Reference
### Overview
MSC 40Axx is the part of [MSC 40 - Sequences, series, summability](node:MSC%2040%20-%20Sequences,%20series,%20summability) about whether infinite limiting processes converge: series and sequences, integrals, continued fractions, infinite products, series of functions, approximation of limiting values, and the generalized notions of ideal and statistical convergence. ([MSC2020 40Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Axx)) Its research content lies past the first-course tests of [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence): the structure of convergence tests and their limits, the convergence theory of continued fractions, rearrangements, and convergence along ideals of subsets of $\mathbb N$. ([Wikipedia: Convergence tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests); [Wikipedia: Convergence problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_problem); [Filipów–Natkaniec–Szuca, Ideal convergence](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/ideal_convergence-survey.pdf))

Two classical facts organize the area. No comparison test is effective for all series: Kummer's test is a complete criterion only because it allows an arbitrary positive auxiliary sequence, and the Abel–Dini theorem builds from any divergent positive series $\sum d_n$ the family $\sum d_n/D_n^{\alpha}$, which changes from divergence to convergence exactly at $\alpha=1$. ([Wikipedia: Convergence tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests); [Knopp, Theory and Application of Infinite Series](https://dn720204.ca.archive.org/0/items/theoryandapplica031692mbp/theoryandapplica031692mbp_djvu.txt)) And conditional convergence is fragile: rearranging a conditionally convergent real series can produce any sum. ([Wikipedia: Riemann series theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_series_theorem))

### Scope
- **40A05** convergence and divergence of series and sequences; **40A10** of integrals; **40A15** of continued fractions (see also 30B70, in [MSC 30Bxx - Series expansions of functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Bxx%20-%20Series%20expansions%20of%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable)); **40A20** of infinite products. ([MSC2020 40Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Axx))
- **40A25** approximation to limiting values (summation of series, etc.), with the Euler–Maclaurin summation formula sent to 65B15. ([MSC2020 40Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Axx))
- **40A30** convergence and divergence of series and sequences of functions; **40A35** ideal and statistical convergence (see also 40G15, in [MSC 40Gxx - Special methods of summability](node:MSC%2040Gxx%20-%20Special%20methods%20of%20summability)). ([MSC2020 40Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Kummer's test and the ratio-test hierarchy (40A05).** For a series of positive terms, $\sum a_n$ converges if and only if there are positive $b_n$ and $c>0$ with $b_k\,a_k/a_{k+1}-b_{k+1}\ge c$, and diverges if and only if there are positive $b_n$ with $b_k\,a_k/a_{k+1}-b_{k+1}\le0$ and $\sum1/b_n=\infty$. Finer tests handle ratio limit $1$: Raabe–Duhamel uses $n(a_n/a_{n+1}-1)$, Bertrand uses $\ln n\,(n(a_n/a_{n+1}-1)-1)$, and Gauss's test says that if $a_n/a_{n+1}=1+\alpha/n+O(n^{-\beta})$ with $\beta>1$, the series converges for $\alpha>1$ and diverges for $\alpha\le1$. ([Wikipedia: Convergence tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests)) Kummer gave the criterion in 1835 with a restrictive condition that Dini recognized as superfluous in 1867. ([Knopp](https://dn720204.ca.archive.org/0/items/theoryandapplica031692mbp/theoryandapplica031692mbp_djvu.txt))
- **Abel–Dini theorem (40A05).** If $\sum d_n$ is a divergent series of positive terms with partial sums $D_n$, then $\sum d_n/D_n^{\alpha}$ converges for $\alpha>1$ and diverges for $\alpha\le1$; Knopp follows it with a refinement due to Pringsheim. ([Knopp](https://dn720204.ca.archive.org/0/items/theoryandapplica031692mbp/theoryandapplica031692mbp_djvu.txt)) Since $1/D_n\to0$, the case $\alpha=1$ produces from any divergent positive series a divergent one with relatively smaller terms.
- **Riemann rearrangement and Lévy–Steinitz (40A05).** A conditionally convergent real series can be rearranged to converge to any real number, to diverge to $\pm\infty$, or to have no limit, while absolutely convergent series are exactly the unconditionally convergent ones. The alternating harmonic series, with sum $\ln2$, can be rearranged in blocks of $p$ positive and $q$ negative terms to reach other sums; Lévy and Steinitz showed that for series in $\mathbb R^n$ the set of sums of convergent rearrangements is an affine subspace, and Sierpiński showed that rearranging only the positive terms reaches every value up to the original sum. ([Wikipedia: Riemann series theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_series_theorem)) Knopp states the theorem as Theorem 187. ([Knopp](https://dn720204.ca.archive.org/0/items/theoryandapplica031692mbp/theoryandapplica031692mbp_djvu.txt))
- **Convergence of continued fractions (40A15).** Śleszyński–Pringsheim: if $|b_n|\ge|a_n|+1$ for all $n\ge1$ (complex $a_n,b_n$), the continued fraction $\mathrm K(a_n/b_n)$ converges to a finite value. Worpitzky: if $|a_i|\le1/4$ for $i\ge2$, then $1/(1+a_2/(1+a_3/(1+\cdots)))$ converges, uniformly when the $a_i$ are complex variables, its value and convergents lie in $|z-4/3|\le2/3$, and $1/4$ is the largest radius that guarantees convergence without exception. Van Vleck: if all $a_i=1$ and $|\arg b_i|<\pi/2-\varepsilon$, the even and odd convergents converge, and the fraction converges if and only if $\sum|b_i|$ diverges. ([Wikipedia: Convergence problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_problem))
- **Infinite products (40A20).** $\prod a_n$ converges if the partial products have a nonzero limit; then $a_n\to1$. Writing $a_n=1+p_n$ with $p_n\ne-1$ for all $n$ (a zero factor forces the limit $0$, which counts as divergence), $\sum|p_n|<\infty$ implies absolute convergence, so factors may be rearranged; convergence of $\sum p_n$ alone does not suffice. For positive $a_n$ the product converges if and only if $\sum\log a_n$ converges. The Euler product $\zeta(z)=\prod_p(1-p^{-z})^{-1}$ converges for $\operatorname{Re}z>1$ ([Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function)). ([Wikipedia: Infinite product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_product))
- **Series of functions (40A30).** Uniform convergence keeps continuity: a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, while $x^n$ on $[0,1]$ converges pointwise to a discontinuous limit. The Weierstrass M-test gives absolute and uniform convergence of $\sum f_n$ on $E$ when $|f_n|\le M_n$ on $E$ and $\sum M_n<\infty$. ([Wikipedia: Uniform convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_convergence))
- **Ideal and statistical convergence (40A35).** For an ideal $\mathcal I$ on $\mathbb N$ containing the finite sets, $(x_n)$ is $\mathcal I$-convergent to $x$ if $\{n:|x_n-x|\ge\varepsilon\}\in\mathcal I$ for every $\varepsilon>0$; the ideal of finite sets gives ordinary convergence. ([Filipów–Natkaniec–Szuca](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/ideal_convergence-survey.pdf)) Fast and Steinhaus introduced statistical convergence independently in 1951 using natural density, and it is $\mathcal I$-convergence for the ideal of sets of natural density zero, introduced in this generality by Kostyrko and coauthors in 2001. ([Shaikh–Datta, arXiv:1911.06548](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.06548)) An ideal has the Bolzano–Weierstrass property if every bounded sequence has an $\mathcal I$-convergent subsequence indexed by a set not in $\mathcal I$; every $F_\sigma$ ideal has it, while no Erdős–Ulam ideal does, in particular not the density-zero ideal, so the [Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem](node:Bolzano–Weierstrass%20Theorem) fails for statistical convergence. ([Filipów–Natkaniec–Szuca](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/ideal_convergence-survey.pdf))

### History
Cauchy observed in 1833 that rearranging a series can change its sum, Dirichlet noted that absolute convergence prevents this, and Riemann gave the full characterization while studying Fourier series. ([Wikipedia: Riemann series theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_series_theorem)) Abel (1826) gave counterexamples to Cauchy's 1821 claim that a convergent sum of continuous functions is continuous; the repairing notion of uniform convergence was named by Weierstrass in 1841 and articulated independently by Seidel and Stokes; Hardy judged in 1918 that Weierstrass alone fully realized its importance. ([Wikipedia: Uniform convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_convergence)) Knopp's *Theory and Application of Infinite Series* first appeared in German in 1921, with the first English edition's preface dated February 1928. ([Knopp](https://dn720204.ca.archive.org/0/items/theoryandapplica031692mbp/theoryandapplica031692mbp_djvu.txt)) Ideal convergence is dual to Cartan's 1937 filter convergence. ([Filipów–Natkaniec–Szuca](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/ideal_convergence-survey.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Flint Hills series.** Whether $\sum_{n\ge1}1/(n^3\sin^2n)$ converges is not known. Alekseyev (2011) related it to the irrationality measure $\mu(\pi)$: the series converges if $\mu(\pi)<2.5$ and diverges if $\mu(\pi)>2.5$. ([Wikipedia: Flint Hills series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint_Hills_series)) The best proven bound is $\mu(\pi)\le7.103205334137\ldots$, obtained by Zeilberger and Zudilin from a variant of Salikhov's proof of $\mu(\pi)\le7.606308\ldots$. ([Zeilberger–Zudilin, arXiv:1912.06345](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06345))

- **Meza-Alcántara's question (40A35).** By a theorem of Meza-Alcántara, an ideal has the finite Bolzano–Weierstrass property (every bounded sequence has an ordinarily convergent subsequence indexed by a set not in $\mathcal I$) if and only if $\mathrm{CONV}\not\le_K\mathcal I$ in the Katětov order, where $\mathrm{CONV}$ is the ideal of subsets of $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$ with finitely many cluster points; every ideal extendable to a proper $F_\sigma$ ideal has the property. ([Filipów–Natkaniec–Szuca](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/ideal_convergence-survey.pdf)) Hrušák asked whether, conversely, every Borel ideal with this property extends to an $F_\sigma$ ideal; Kwela answered this in the negative by constructing a Borel ideal not extendable to any $F_\sigma$ ideal and not Katětov above $\mathrm{conv}$. The localized version asked by Meza-Alcántara (for a Borel ideal $\mathcal I$, either $\mathrm{conv}\le_K\mathcal I|A$ for some $A\notin\mathcal I$, or $\mathcal I$ is contained in a $\Sigma^0_2$ ideal) is stated there to remain open. ([Kwela, arXiv:2106.13053](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.13053))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Convergence tests (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests): Kummer, Raabe, Bertrand, Gauss and the classical tests with hypotheses.
- **Reference:** [Convergence problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_problem): convergence theorems for continued fractions.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.100B Lecture 8: Convergence Tests for Series; Power Series](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100b-real-analysis-spring-2025/mit18_100b_s25_lec08.pdf): comparison, ratio and root tests and the radius of convergence.
- **Primary:** [Filipów, Natkaniec and Szuca, Ideal convergence (survey)](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/ideal_convergence-survey.pdf): ideal convergence of sequences of reals and functions, with open problems.
- **Primary:** [Knopp, Theory and Application of Infinite Series (Internet Archive)](https://dn720204.ca.archive.org/0/items/theoryandapplica031692mbp/theoryandapplica031692mbp_djvu.txt): the classic monograph on tests, rearrangements, products and divergent series.
- **Further reading:** [Knopp, Theory and Application of Infinite Series](https://dn720204.ca.archive.org/0/items/theoryandapplica031692mbp/theoryandapplica031692mbp_djvu.txt): logarithmic scales of comparison tests (§37) and the Abel–Dini and Pringsheim theorems (§39).

## Reference
### Overview
A double series has terms depending on two indices, $\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}$, and multiple sequences and series generalize this to several indices. ([MathWorld: Double Series](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DoubleSeries.html)) The central difficulty is that a two-index array can be passed to the limit in several inequivalent ways: a joint (double) limit and the two iterated limits, which can all differ. ([Wikipedia: Iterated limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterated_limit))

The subject therefore studies which convergence notion is appropriate, when the orders of summation agree, and how summability methods behave on double sequences. Pringsheim's notion of convergence for double series (1900) and Hardy's regular convergence (1916–1919) are the two classical definitions; Bromwich's textbook gave English readers an account of Pringsheim's theory in a chapter on double series. ([Móricz, arXiv:1203.5191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.5191); [Bromwich, *Infinite Series*, Ch. V](https://archive.org/stream/introductiontoth00bromuoft/introductiontoth00bromuoft_djvu.txt)) Recent papers in this code study four-dimensional matrix transformations, double sequence spaces, and Tauberian theorems for double sequences. ([Demiriz–Duyar, arXiv:1501.01113](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.01113); [Önder–Savaş–Çanak, arXiv:2307.00517](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.00517v2))

### Scope
MSC2020 40Bxx has one substantive code, 40B05, "Multiple sequences and series", which should also be assigned at least one other classification number in section 40, and the catch-all 40B99. ([MSC2020 40Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Bxx)) A multi-index paper is therefore paired with another section-40 code naming the convergence or summability question it asks. ([MSC2020 40Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Bxx))

Neighbouring codes in section 40 that such a second code is drawn from include ([MSC2020 40-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40-XX); [MSC2020 40Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Exx)):
- 40Axx, "Convergence and divergence of infinite limiting processes".
- 40Cxx, "General summability methods", and 40Gxx, "Special methods of summability". For example, Patterson and Savaş's paper on RH-regular four-dimensional matrices is classified with primary 40B05 and secondary 40C05. ([Patterson–Savaş, Filomat 2013](https://www.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2013/27-5/F27-5-22.pdf))
- 40Exx, "Inversion theorems", whose code 40E05 is "Tauberian theorems".

Almost-everywhere convergence of multiple Fourier series is classified in harmonic analysis: Ashurov's survey of square, rectangular and spherical partial sums has primary classification 42B05. ([Ashurov, arXiv:1912.03534](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1912.03534))

### Key concepts
- **Pringsheim convergence:** with rectangular partial sums $s_{m,n}=\sum_{j\le m}\sum_{k\le n}u_{jk}$, the series converges to $s$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\kappa$ with $|s_{m,n}-s|<\varepsilon$ whenever $\min\{m,n\}>\kappa$. It implies neither boundedness of the terms nor convergence of the row and column series. ([Móricz, arXiv:1203.5191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.5191)) Boos's example $x_{0n}=n$, $x_{mn}=0$ for $m\ge1$ is a Pringsheim-null double sequence that is unbounded, so the space $C_p$ of P-convergent double sequences is not contained in the space $M_u$ of bounded ones; Móricz showed $C_p$ is complete under the seminorm $\lim_{N}\sup_{m,n\ge N}|x_{mn}|$. ([Tuğ et al., arXiv:2112.09909](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.09909))
- **Regular convergence (Hardy):** a double series converges regularly if it converges in Pringsheim's sense and every row and column series converges. Regular convergence makes the double sum equal to both iterated sums; absolute convergence implies regular convergence but not conversely; for terms of constant sign, Pringsheim convergence is equivalent to absolute convergence. ([Móricz, arXiv:1203.5191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.5191)) Unlike Pringsheim convergence, regular convergence forces boundedness of the double sequence. ([Tuğ et al., arXiv:2112.09909](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.09909))
- **Iterated limits and Moore–Osgood:** for $a_{n,m}=n/(n+m)$ the two iterated limits are $1$ and $0$. If $\lim_n a_{n,m}=b_m$ uniformly in $m$ and $\lim_m a_{n,m}=c_n$ exists for each large $n$, then both iterated limits and the double limit exist and are equal. ([Wikipedia: Iterated limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterated_limit))
- **Positive terms and absolute convergence:** for a double series of positive terms it suffices to test squares; such a series converges if and only if either repeated series converges, and then all sums agree. An absolutely convergent double series inherits these properties, while Bromwich gives counterexamples (including one of Cesàro) for non-absolutely convergent ones. ([Bromwich, *Infinite Series*, Arts. 31–33](https://archive.org/stream/introductiontoth00bromuoft/introductiontoth00bromuoft_djvu.txt)) Absolutely convergent series can be summed over any countable index set independently of order, and the Cauchy product of an absolutely convergent series with a convergent one converges to the product. ([MIT 18.100C, Lecture 10](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100c-real-analysis-fall-2012/3d638d8c60c57cdc610b68a76c01658a_MIT18_100CF12_l10sum.pdf))
- **Robison–Hamilton (RH) regularity:** a four-dimensional matrix $A=(a_{m,n,k,l})$ maps $x$ to $(Ax)_{m,n}=\sum_{k,l}a_{m,n,k,l}x_{k,l}$. Robison's notion of regularity for four-dimensional matrices restricts to bounded sequences: $A$ is RH-regular if it maps every bounded P-convergent sequence to a P-convergent sequence with the same P-limit. The Silverman–Toeplitz-type characterization, due to Robison and Hamilton, is that $A$ is RH-regular if and only if (RH1) $\text{P-}\lim_{m,n}a_{m,n,k,l}=0$ for each $k,l$; (RH2) $\text{P-}\lim_{m,n}\sum_{k,l}a_{m,n,k,l}=1$; (RH3) $\text{P-}\lim_{m,n}\sum_k|a_{m,n,k,l}|=0$ for each $l$; (RH4) $\text{P-}\lim_{m,n}\sum_l|a_{m,n,k,l}|=0$ for each $k$; (RH5) $\sum_{k,l}|a_{m,n,k,l}|$ is P-convergent; and (RH6) there are finite positive integers $\Delta,\Gamma$ with $\sum_{k,l>\Gamma}|a_{m,n,k,l}|<\Delta$. ([Patterson–Savaş, Filomat 2013](https://www.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2013/27-5/F27-5-22.pdf))
- **Cesàro and weighted means of double sequences:** for weights $p_m,q_n$ with $P_m=\sum_{i\le m}p_i$, $Q_n=\sum_{j\le n}q_j$, the $(\overline N,p,q)$ mean is $\sigma_{mn}=\frac{1}{P_mQ_n}\sum_{i\le m}\sum_{j\le n}p_iq_ju_{ij}$; $p_m=q_n=1$ gives the Cesàro means of order $(1,1)$. If $P_m,Q_n\to\infty$, every bounded P-convergent double sequence is $(\overline N,p,q)$ summable to its limit; the converse needs Tauberian conditions: for $(C,1,1)$ the one-sided conditions $m\,\Delta_{10}u_{mn}=O_L(1)$ and $n\,\Delta_{01}u_{mn}=O_L(1)$ suffice for real double sequences, and the two-sided conditions $m\,\Delta_{10}u_{mn}=O(1)$ and $n\,\Delta_{01}u_{mn}=O(1)$ suffice for complex ones. ([Önder–Savaş–Çanak, arXiv:2307.00517](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.00517v2))
- **Almost convergence of double sequences:** Lorentz introduced almost convergence for single sequences and Móricz and Rhoades extended it: $x$ is almost convergent to $L$ if $\text{P-}\lim_{q,q'\to\infty}\sup_{m,n}\bigl|\frac{1}{(q+1)(q'+1)}\sum_{k=m}^{m+q}\sum_{l=n}^{n+q'}x_{kl}-L\bigr|=0$. ([Tuğ, arXiv:1909.00469](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.00469)) Mursaleen and Edely introduced statistical convergence for double sequences and related it to strong Cesàro summability. ([Demiriz–Duyar, arXiv:1501.01113](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.01113))
- **Square, rectangular and spherical partial sums of multiple Fourier series:** for $f\in L^p(\mathbb T^N)$, $p>1$, the square partial sums converge almost everywhere (Tevzadze for $L^2$ in two variables, Sjölin in general), so square sums behave as in one dimension. In contrast C. Fefferman (1971) constructed $f\in C(\mathbb T^2)$ whose rectangular partial sums satisfy $\limsup|R_{k,l}f(x)|=+\infty$ everywhere on $\mathbb T^2$, so a.e. convergence over rectangles fails in every $L^p$. For spherical sums, Fefferman's theorem that they do not converge in $L^p$ for $1\le p<2$ yields divergence on a set of positive measure for some $f\in L^p$. ([Ashurov, arXiv:1912.03534](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1912.03534))
- [Multiple Series](node:Multiple%20Series), [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence), [Fubini's Theorem](node:Fubini's%20Theorem), [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis), [Carleson's Theorem](node:Carleson's%20Theorem), [Matrix Summability Methods](node:Matrix%20Summability%20Methods), [Tauberian Theorems](node:Tauberian%20Theorems): the one-index theory, the integral analogue of interchanging sums, and the methods applied to double sequences. Móricz proves a Fubini-type theorem for locally integrable functions on the quadrant whose double integral converges regularly. ([Móricz, arXiv:1203.5191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.5191))

### History
Móricz attributes convergence in Pringsheim's sense to A. Pringsheim (*Math. Ann.* 53, 1900) and regular convergence to G. H. Hardy (*Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc.* 19, 1916–1919). ([Móricz, arXiv:1203.5191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.5191); [Patterson–Savaş, Filomat 2013](https://www.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2013/27-5/F27-5-22.pdf)) MathWorld lists Hardy's papers "On the convergence of certain multiple series" (1904, 1917), Wilansky's 1947 note on the convergence of double series, and Móricz's 1983 remarks on regular convergence of multiple series. ([MathWorld: Double Series](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DoubleSeries.html)) Bromwich's *Introduction to the Theory of Infinite Series* devotes Chapter V to double series: the definition of the sum, repeated summation, positive terms, absolute convergence and multiplication. ([Bromwich](https://archive.org/stream/introductiontoth00bromuoft/introductiontoth00bromuoft_djvu.txt))

Robison's "Divergent double sequences and series" (*Trans. AMS* 28, 1926) and Hamilton's "Transformations of multiple sequences" (*Duke Math. J.* 2, 1936) gave the multidimensional analogue of the Silverman–Toeplitz characterization of regular matrices for double sequences. ([Demiriz–Duyar, arXiv:1501.01113](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.01113); [Leonetti, arXiv:2201.13059](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.13059); [Patterson–Savaş, Filomat 2013](https://www.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2013/27-5/F27-5-22.pdf)) Tevzadze (1970) extended Carleson's theorem to square partial sums of double Fourier series, and Sjölin (1971) obtained the $L^p$ analogue. ([Ashurov, arXiv:1912.03534](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1912.03534))

### Open problems
- **Pringsheim analogue of uniform convergence of double sine series.** Kórus and Móricz showed that a decay condition such as $jk\,a_{j,k}\to0$ as $\max\{j,k\}\to\infty$ makes the regular convergence of a double sine series uniform in $(x,y)$, with necessity for nonnegative coefficients. Móricz reports that all attempts to prove an analogue for convergence in Pringsheim's sense, with $\max$ replaced by $\min$, have failed so far, and that the sufficiency part seems hopeless. ([Móricz, arXiv:1203.5191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.5191))
- **Luzin's conjecture for spherical partial sums.** Whether the spherical partial sums $S_\lambda f$ of the multiple Fourier series of every $f\in L^2(\mathbb T^N)$, $N\ge2$, converge almost everywhere is unknown; the corresponding question is settled for square sums (positively) and rectangular sums (negatively). ([Ashurov, arXiv:1912.03534](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1912.03534))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Iterated limit (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterated_limit): double and iterated limits, counterexamples, Moore–Osgood theorem.
- **Reference:** [Double Series (MathWorld)](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DoubleSeries.html): examples and the classical references of Hardy, Wilansky and Móricz.
- **Learn:** [Bromwich, *An Introduction to the Theory of Infinite Series*, Ch. V](https://archive.org/stream/introductiontoth00bromuoft/introductiontoth00bromuoft_djvu.txt): the classical textbook account of Pringsheim's theory of double series.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.100C Lecture 10 summary](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100c-real-analysis-fall-2012/3d638d8c60c57cdc610b68a76c01658a_MIT18_100CF12_l10sum.pdf): absolute convergence, reordering and products of series.
- **Primary:** [Móricz, On the convergence of double integrals and a generalized version of Fubini's theorem](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1203.5191): Pringsheim versus regular convergence, with examples and an open problem.
- **Primary:** [Patterson and Savaş, On double sequences of continuous functions having continuous P-limits II (Filomat 2013)](https://www.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2013/27-5/F27-5-22.pdf): states the definition of RH-regularity and the Robison–Hamilton theorem.
- **Primary:** [Önder, Savaş, Çanak, Tauberian conditions for $(\overline N,p,q)$ summability of double sequences](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.00517v2): current Tauberian theory for double sequences.
- **Primary:** [Ashurov, Generalized localization for spherical partial sums of multiple Fourier series](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1912.03534): short survey of almost-everywhere convergence for square, rectangular and spherical sums.
- **Further reading:** [Bromwich, *An Introduction to the Theory of Infinite Series* (Internet Archive)](https://archive.org/stream/introductiontoth00bromuoft/introductiontoth00bromuoft_djvu.txt): the standard classical text; Chapter V covers double series.
references.MSC 40Cxx - General summability methods:
## Reference
### Overview
A summability method assigns a value to some series or sequences that do not converge in the ordinary sense. The basic requirements are regularity (agreeing with the ordinary limit on convergent sequences), linearity, and stability under shifting the sequence; two methods are consistent if they give the same value wherever both are defined, and of two consistent methods the one summing more is stronger. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series)) Abstractly, any function $\Lambda:D\to\mathbb R$ on a set $D$ of real sequences is a summability method, and $\Lambda$ is regular if $c\subseteq D$ and $\Lambda=\lim$ on $c$. ([Filipów–Tryba](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf))

40Cxx is where the general theory lives: which transformations preserve limits, which map bounded or convergent sequences to convergent ones, and how two methods compare. Hardy's *Divergent Series* treats such general theorems on linear transformations alongside the particular Cesàro, Abel and Nörlund methods. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) The modern treatment adds functional-analytic tools: Boos's monograph moves from classical Silverman–Toeplitz-type theorems to FK-spaces, the structure of matrix domains, consistency of matrix methods, and bounded domains via Saks spaces. ([Boos–Cass, *Classical and Modern Methods in Summability*, OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/53786))

### Scope
MSC2020 40Cxx, "General summability methods", has three substantive codes: 40C05 matrix methods, 40C10 integral methods, and 40C15 function-theoretic methods (including power series methods and semicontinuous methods), plus 40C99. ([MSC2020 40Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Cxx))

Neighbouring codes in section 40 ([MSC2020 40-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40-XX)):
- 40Dxx, "Direct theorems on summability", and 40Exx, "Inversion theorems".
- 40Fxx, "Absolute and strong summability", and 40Gxx, "Special methods of summability".
- 40Hxx, "Functional analytic methods in summability". Boos's monograph treats the domains of matrix methods as FK-spaces in a separate functional-analytic part, after the classical Silverman–Toeplitz-type theorems. ([Boos–Cass, OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/53786))

### Key concepts
- **Matrix methods (40C05):** a matrix $(c_{m,n})$ maps $s=(s_n)$ to $t_m=\sum_n c_{m,n}s_n$; the domain $c_A$ is the set of $x$ for which every row series converges and $Ax\in c$. ([Boos, Filomat 2019](https://web1.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2019/33-14/33-14-16-10677.pdf)) The Cesàro $(C,1)$ matrix has $c_{m,n}=1/(m+1)$ for $n\le m$ and $0$ otherwise. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §3.1](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Kojima–Schur theorem (conservative matrices).** The transformation maps every convergent sequence to a convergent one if and only if (i) $\sum_n|c_{m,n}|\le H$ with $H$ independent of $m$; (ii) $c_{m,n}\to\delta_n$ as $m\to\infty$ for each $n$; (iii) $\sum_n c_{m,n}\to\delta$. The limit is then $t=\delta s+\sum_n\delta_n(s_n-s)$. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §3.2, Theorem 1](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Silverman–Toeplitz theorem (regular matrices).** The method is regular if and only if the conditions above hold with $\delta_n=0$ for every $n$ and $\delta=1$: bounded absolute row sums, columns tending to $0$, row sums tending to $1$. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §3.2, Theorem 2](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt); [Wikipedia: Silverman–Toeplitz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverman%E2%80%93Toeplitz_theorem))
- **Schur's theorem (bounded to convergent).** The transformation maps every bounded sequence to a convergent one if and only if $c_{m,n}\to\delta_n$ for each $n$ and $\sum_n|c_{m,n}|$ converges uniformly in $m$. Such a matrix cannot be regular, so the regular class and Schur's class are disjoint. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §3.2 Theorem 3 and §3.5](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Steinhaus's theorem and Hahn's theorem.** A regular matrix cannot sum all sequences of $0$s and $1$s; in particular no regular matrix sums every bounded sequence, which is also a corollary of Schur's theorem. Hahn's theorem says a matrix that sums all $0$–$1$ sequences sums all bounded sequences. Connor gave a short proof of Steinhaus's theorem using the Baire category theorem. ([Boos, Filomat 2019](https://web1.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2019/33-14/33-14-16-10677.pdf))
- **Mazur–Orlicz theorems.** Mazur and Orlicz stated in 1933 that a conservative matrix that sums a bounded nonconvergent sequence must also sum an unbounded sequence; their proof used topological properties of FK-spaces, and Fridy gave a direct proof for regular matrices from the Silverman–Toeplitz conditions alone. ([Fridy 1981, Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc.](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/simple-proof-of-the-mazurorlicz-summability-theorem/82B20967638DF339E79D246EC23872BB)) Comparison on bounded sequences uses b-consistency: two matrices are b-consistent if the bounded sequences summed by both are summed to the same value, and $A$ is b-stronger than $B$ if every bounded $B$-summable sequence is $A$-summable. ([Baker–Petersen 1964](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/A51AC2DEF1CFE14BDB511A5A50C24C1B)) A. K. Snyder and Wilansky's paper "The Mazur–Orlicz bounded consistency theorem" appeared in *Proc. AMS* 80 (1980). ([Wikipedia: Albert Wilansky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Wilansky))
- **Nörlund means:** for weights $p_n>0$ with $P_m=p_0+\dots+p_m$, $t_m=(p_ms_0+p_{m-1}s_1+\dots+p_0s_m)/P_m$ is regular if and only if $p_n/P_n\to0$. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §4.2, Theorem 16](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Nörlund means satisfying this condition are regular, linear and stable, any two of them are consistent, and the Cesàro methods $(C,k)$ are the Nörlund means with $p_n=\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$, with $(C,h)$ stronger than $(C,k)$ for $h>k$. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series))
- **Integral methods (40C10).** For $t(x)=\int c(x,y)s(y)\,dy$ with $s$ bounded, sufficient conditions for regularity are $\int|c(x,y)|\,dy\le H$, $\int_0^Y|c(x,y)|\,dy\to0$ for every finite $Y$, and $\int c(x,y)\,dy\to1$ as $x\to\infty$. For sequence-to-function transformations $t(x)=\sum_n c_n(x)s_n$ with a continuous parameter, Hardy's analogue of the regularity theorem uses a uniform bound on $\sum_n|c_n(x)|$ for large $x$, $c_n(x)\to0$ for each $n$, and $\sum_n c_n(x)\to1$. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §3.5, Theorems 5–6](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Parisé defines kernel-summability methods for Banach-space-valued functions by vector-valued integrals and proves a Silverman–Toeplitz theorem for them; the paper is classified 40C10 and 40D05. ([Parisé, arXiv:2302.06770](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06770v3))
- **Power series methods (40C15).** Abelian means use $\lambda_n\uparrow\infty$ and $f(x)=\sum a_ne^{-\lambda_nx}$, $A_\lambda=\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)$; $\lambda_n=n$ gives Abel summation. Abelian means are regular and linear but not stable, and Abel summation is consistent with and stronger than Cesàro summation. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series))
- **Comparing methods.** Convergence implies $(C,1)$ summability, which implies Abel summability, to the same value; neither implication reverses: $\sum(-1)^{m-1}$ is $(C,1)$ summable to $\tfrac12$ but not convergent, and $\sum(-1)^{m-1}m$ is Abel summable to $\tfrac14$ but not $(C,1)$ summable. ([MIT RES.18-015, Lecture 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/res-18-015-topics-in-fourier-analysis-spring-2024/mitres_18_015_s24_lec04.pdf)) The series $1-2+3-4+\cdots$ is, however, $(C,2)$ summable to $\tfrac14$. ([Wikipedia: 1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_%E2%88%92_2_%2B_3_%E2%88%92_4_%2B_%E2%8B%AF))
- **Matrix methods and statistical convergence.** For a nonnegative regular matrix $A$, $I(A)=\{B\subseteq\mathbb N:\lim_i\sum_{k\in B}a_{i,k}=0\}$ is an ideal; for the Cesàro matrix it is the ideal of density-zero sets, whose ideal convergence is statistical convergence. Khan and Orhan proved that for every nonnegative regular $A$ there is a nonnegative regular $B$ with $I(A)=I(B)$ whose summability coincides with $I(A)$-convergence on bounded sequences, which answers Mazur's Problem 5 of the Scottish Book positively. ([Filipów–Tryba](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf))
- [Matrix Summability Methods](node:Matrix%20Summability%20Methods), [Cesàro and Abel Summation](node:Cesàro%20and%20Abel%20Summation), [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence), [Abelian Summability Theorems](node:Abelian%20Summability%20Theorems), [Tauberian Theorems](node:Tauberian%20Theorems), [Banach Limits](node:Banach%20Limits), [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): the named methods, the baseline every regular method reproduces, and the direct and inverse theorems built on this theory; Hardy calls a method regular when it sums every convergent series to its ordinary sum. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, §1.4](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))

### History
Euler used divergent series freely; after Cauchy made convergence rigorous they were largely set aside, until Poincaré's 1886 work on asymptotic series and Cesàro's 1890 definition of sums for some divergent series. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series)) Hardy's notes credit the substance of the regularity theorem to Toeplitz (1911) for triangular transformations and its extension to general transformations to Steinhaus in the same volume; the conservative-matrix theorem to Kojima (1917, triangular case) and Schur (general case); and the bounded-to-convergent theorem to Schur. ([Hardy, *Divergent Series*, Notes on Ch. III](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Boos cites Schur's paper as *J. reine angew. Math.* 151 (1920) and Steinhaus's as *Prace Mat. Fiz.* 22 (1911). ([Boos, Filomat 2019](https://web1.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2019/33-14/33-14-16-10677.pdf))

Peyerimhoff's *Lectures on Summability* appeared as Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics in 1969, with chapters including matrix transformations and Hausdorff and Nörlund summability. ([Crossref metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Peyerimhoff+Lectures+on+Summability&rows=3)) Boos and P. Cass published *Classical and Modern Methods in Summability* with Oxford University Press in 2000. ([OUP](https://academic.oup.com/book/53786))

### Open problems
- **Summability of almost all subsequences.** Buck and Pollard proved that a bounded sequence is $(C,1)$ summable if and only if almost all of its subsequences (in Lebesgue measure) are $(C,1)$ summable. Boos poses as further problems, unanswered in the paper, whether this holds for unbounded sequences, whether it holds with "almost every subsequence" in the sense of positive density, and whether it holds for an arbitrary regular matrix in place of $(C,1)$. ([Boos, Filomat 2019, Problems 6.2](https://web1.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2019/33-14/33-14-16-10677.pdf))
- **Ideal convergence versus matrix summability.** Filipów and Tryba ask whether there is an ideal with Mazur's property (M) not isomorphic to $\mathrm{Fin}$ or $\mathrm{Fin}\oplus P(\mathbb N)$, and whether some non-Borel ideal has the property that bounded $I$-convergence is the intersection of the matrix methods $A$ with $I\subseteq I(A)$. ([Filipów–Tryba, Questions 2–3](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Divergent series (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series): axioms of summation methods, Nörlund, Riesz, Abelian, Euler and Borel methods.
- **Reference:** [Silverman–Toeplitz theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverman%E2%80%93Toeplitz_theorem): regularity conditions for matrix methods.
- **Learn:** [MIT RES.18-015, Lecture 4: Comparing Summability Methods](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/res-18-015-topics-in-fourier-analysis-spring-2024/mitres_18_015_s24_lec04.pdf): Cesàro implies Abel, with counterexamples to the converses.
- **Primary:** [Hardy, *Divergent Series* (1949), full text](https://dn760003.eu.archive.org/0/items/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt): Kojima–Schur, Silverman–Toeplitz and Schur theorems, integral transformations.
- **Primary:** [Boos, Summability of subsequences of a divergent sequence by regular matrices II (Filomat 2019)](https://web1.pmf.ni.ac.rs/filomat-content/2019/33-14/33-14-16-10677.pdf): Steinhaus, Hahn and Schur theorems in modern form, with open problems.
- **Primary:** [Filipów and Tryba, Ideal convergence versus matrix summability](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf): matrix ideals, the Khan–Orhan theorem, and open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Boos and Cass, *Classical and Modern Methods in Summability* (OUP, 2000)](https://academic.oup.com/book/53786): the modern graduate monograph. Peyerimhoff, *Lectures on Summability* (Springer LNM, 1969), has chapters on matrix transformations and on Hausdorff and Nörlund summability ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Peyerimhoff+Lectures+on+Summability&rows=3)).
references.MSC 40Dxx - Direct theorems on summabili:
## Reference
### Overview
A summability method assigns a value to some sequences or series that need not converge. An Abelian, or direct, theorem for a method $L$ says that whenever a sequence converges to $C$, $L$ also assigns it $C$; partial converses are Tauberian theorems, which MSC2020 places in 40Exx. ([Wikipedia: Abelian and Tauberian theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems); [MSC2020 40Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Exx))

Direct theory asks which methods are regular (agree with the ordinary limit on convergent sequences), which pairs are consistent (agree wherever both apply), and which of two consistent methods is stronger (sums more). ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series)) For matrix methods these questions become conditions on the matrix entries (Silverman–Toeplitz, Kojima–Schur), and Mazur and Orlicz's proof of their theorem on conservative matrices, based on topological properties of FK-spaces, was one of the early applications of functional analysis to summability theory. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, notes on Ch. III](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt); [Fridy 1981](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/simple-proof-of-the-mazurorlicz-summability-theorem/82B20967638DF339E79D246EC23872BB))

### Scope
MSC2020 40Dxx "Direct theorems on summability" contains 40D05 general theorems on summability, 40D09 structure of summability fields, 40D10 Tauberian constants and oscillation limits in summability theory, 40D15 convergence factors and summability factors, 40D20 summability and bounded fields of methods, 40D25 inclusion and equivalence theorems in summability theory, and 40D99 other. ([MSC2020 40Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Dxx))

Neighbours: the methods themselves are defined in [MSC 40Cxx - General summability methods](node:MSC%2040Cxx%20-%20General%20summability%20methods) and particular methods in [MSC 40Gxx - Special methods of summability](node:MSC%2040Gxx%20-%20Special%20methods%20of%20summability); converse (Tauberian) theorems, lacunary inversion and Tauberian constants for inversion are in [MSC 40Exx - Inversion theorems](node:MSC%2040Exx%20-%20Inversion%20theorems) (40E05, 40E15, 40E20); and the Banach-space machinery is in [MSC 40Hxx - Functional analytic methods in summability](node:MSC%2040Hxx%20-%20Functional%20analytic%20methods%20in%20summability). ([MSC2020 40Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Dxx); [MSC2020 40Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Exx))

### Key concepts
- **Silverman–Toeplitz theorem (regularity).** The matrix method $t_i=\sum_j a_{i,j}s_j$ is regular if and only if (i) every column tends to $0$, $\lim_{i}a_{i,j}=0$ for each $j$; (ii) the row sums tend to $1$, $\lim_i\sum_j a_{i,j}=1$; and (iii) the absolute row sums are bounded, $\sup_i\sum_j|a_{i,j}|<\infty$. ([Wikipedia: Silverman–Toeplitz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverman%E2%80%93Toeplitz_theorem)) Hardy credits the theorem in substance to Toeplitz (1911) for triangular matrices, extended by Steinhaus to general ones; the companion characterization of convergence-preserving (conservative) matrices is due to Kojima (1917, triangular) and Schur (1921, general). ([Hardy, Divergent Series, notes on Ch. III](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Links to [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices).
- **Abel's theorem.** If $\sum a_k$ converges then $G(x)=\sum a_kx^k$ satisfies $\lim_{x\to1^-}G(x)=\sum a_k$; for complex $z$ the same holds as $z\to1$ within a Stolz sector $|1-z|\le M(1-|z|)$. There is no exact converse. ([Wikipedia: Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%27s_theorem)) Links to [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence).
- **Cesàro inclusion and Abel's method (40D25).** If a series has a $(C,\alpha)$ sum it has a $(C,\beta)$ sum for every $\beta>\alpha$, with the same value. ([Wikipedia: Cesàro summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ces%C3%A0ro_summation)) Hardy's Theorem 55: if $\sum a_n=A\ (C,k)$ for some $k$, then $\sum a_n=A\ (\mathrm A)$. Theorem 56: some series are Abel summable but not $(C,k)$ summable for any $k$, for instance the coefficients of $e^{1/(1+x)}$, which are not $O(n^k)$ for any $k$; $(-1)^ne^{c\sqrt n}$ with $c>0$ is another example. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §5.12](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) For instance $1-2+3-4+\cdots$ is not $(C,1)$ summable but is $(C,2)$ summable and Abel summable to $\tfrac14$. ([Wikipedia: 1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_%E2%88%92_2_%2B_3_%E2%88%92_4_%2B_%E2%8B%AF))
- **Hausdorff means (40D25).** Hausdorff's transformations $\delta\mu\delta$, with $\delta$ the self-reciprocal difference transformation and $\mu$ diagonal, include the Cesàro, Hölder and Euler means, and any two of them commute (Theorem 197). Theorem 208: $(\mathfrak H,\mu)$ is regular if and only if $\mu_n$ is a regular moment constant, $\mu_n=\int_0^1x^n\,d\chi(x)$ with $\chi$ of bounded variation, $\chi(1)=1$ and $\chi(+0)=\chi(0)=0$; it is convergence-preserving if and only if $\mu_n$ is a moment constant. For regular Hausdorff methods whose moment constants satisfy $\mu_n\ne0$ and $\mu'_n\ne0$ for all $n$, $(\mu')$ includes $(\mu)$ if and only if $\mu'_n/\mu_n$ is a regular moment constant (Theorem 209), and $(C,k)$ and Hölder $(H,k)$ are equivalent for all $k>-1$ (Theorem 211). ([Hardy, Divergent Series, Ch. XI](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Nörlund means.** For positive weights with $p_n/(p_0+\cdots+p_n)\to0$, the means $t_m=(p_ms_0+\cdots+p_0s_m)/(p_0+\cdots+p_m)$ are regular, linear and stable, and any two Nörlund means are consistent; each $(C,k)$ with $k\ge0$ is a Nörlund mean. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series))
- **Mazur–Orlicz theorem (40D09, 40D20).** If a conservative (convergence-preserving) matrix sums a bounded nonconvergent sequence, then it also sums an unbounded sequence. Mazur and Orlicz's proof uses topological properties of FK-spaces; Zeller derived it from his study of the summability of slowly oscillating sequences, and Fridy gave a short direct proof, stated for regular matrices. ([Fridy, Math. Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc. 89 (1981)](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/simple-proof-of-the-mazurorlicz-summability-theorem/82B20967638DF339E79D246EC23872BB)) Links to [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces).
- **Fourier series.** Fejér's theorem (the Fourier series of an integrable $2\pi$-periodic function is Cesàro summable to $f$ at points of continuity) and its Abel analogue via the Poisson kernel are model applications of direct theorems; the Abel result is a particular case of the general fact that every Cesàro summable series is Abel summable to the same limit. ([Cuddy, UChicago REU](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2012/REUPapers/Cuddy.pdf)) Links to [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis).

### History
Abel proved his limit theorem in 1826. ([Wikipedia: Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%27s_theorem)) Hardy records that the $(C,1)$ method was used implicitly by Frobenius (1880) and Hölder (1882) and stated formally by Cesàro in 1890; the regularity theorem goes back to Toeplitz (1911) and Steinhaus, and the conservative-matrix theorem to Kojima (1917) and Schur (1921). ([Hardy, Divergent Series](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Mazur and Orlicz's FK-space proof of their theorem was one of the early applications of functional analysis to summability theory. ([Fridy 1981](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/simple-proof-of-the-mazurorlicz-summability-theorem/82B20967638DF339E79D246EC23872BB))

Hardy's *Divergent Series* (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1949) is the source for many of the classical methods, and Boos and Cass published *Classical and Modern Methods in Summability* (Oxford University Press, 2000). ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series); [Crossref: Boos–Cass](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198501657.001.0001))

### Open problems
None found. Searches tried: arXiv and web searches for "open problem" or "open question" together with summability, Tauberian constants, Mazur–Orlicz, bounded consistency, and summability fields; the MSC2020 40Dxx entry; and the fetched monograph and survey pages above, none of which names an open problem in direct summability theory. ([MSC2020 40Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Dxx))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Divergent series (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series): regularity, consistency, and the main named methods.
- **Reference:** [Silverman–Toeplitz theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverman%E2%80%93Toeplitz_theorem): regularity conditions with proof outline.
- **Learn:** [Cuddy, Convergence of Fourier Series (UChicago REU)](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2012/REUPapers/Cuddy.pdf): Cesàro and Abel summability of Fourier series through Fejér and Poisson kernels.
- **Primary:** [Hardy, Divergent Series (1949), full text](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt): the standard monograph; Ch. III on regular transformations, Ch. V on Cesàro and Abel, Ch. XI on Hausdorff means.
- **Primary:** [Fridy, A simple proof of the Mazur–Orlicz summability theorem (1981)](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/simple-proof-of-the-mazurorlicz-summability-theorem/82B20967638DF339E79D246EC23872BB): statement and context of the theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Boos and Cass, Classical and Modern Methods in Summability (OUP 2000)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198501657.001.0001): modern monograph on summability.
references.MSC 40Exx - Inversion theorems:
## Reference
### Overview
Inversion theorems go from summability back to convergence. An Abelian theorem says a method sums every convergent series to its sum; a Tauberian theorem is a partial converse, giving an extra condition under which summability implies convergence. ([Wikipedia: Abelian and Tauberian theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems)) Abel's theorem has no exact converse: the series of $1/(1+z)$ at $z=1$ is $1-1+1-\cdots$, which diverges although the function tends to $\tfrac12$. ([Wikipedia: Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%27s_theorem))

Hardy explains the principle behind the subject: every useful method fails to sum series that diverge too rapidly, and also fails to sum divergent series whose divergence is too slow; Tauberian theorems make the second half precise, with a condition (for Cesàro methods typically $a_n=O(1/n)$) that limits how slowly a series can diverge. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §6.1](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Since every $(C,k)$-summable series is Abel summable to the same value (Hardy's Theorem 55), a Tauberian theorem for Abel summability implies the corresponding one for every $(C,k)$. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §5.12](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))

The strongest motivation came from number theory: Hardy and Littlewood, Wiener and Ikehara, and later Newman all derived the prime number theorem from Tauberian arguments. ([Wikipedia: Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem); [Wikipedia: Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem))

### Scope
In MSC2020, 40Exx "Inversion theorems" contains 40E05 Tauberian theorems, 40E10 growth estimates, 40E15 lacunary inversion theorems, 40E20 Tauberian constants, and 40E99 other. ([MSC2020 40Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Exx))

Neighbours: direct (Abelian) theorems, inclusion theorems, and Tauberian constants and oscillation limits for direct comparisons of methods are in [MSC 40Dxx - Direct theorems on summability](node:MSC%2040Dxx%20-%20Direct%20theorems%20on%20summability) (40D10, 40D25); the methods themselves are in [MSC 40Cxx - General summability methods](node:MSC%2040Cxx%20-%20General%20summability%20methods). ([MSC2020 40Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Dxx)) Complex-analytic Tauberian theorems for Dirichlet series and Laplace transforms are also used heavily in [MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory) and [MSC 44Axx - Integral transforms, operational calculus](node:MSC%2044Axx%20-%20Integral%20transforms,%20operational%20calculus).

### Key concepts
- **Tauber's and Littlewood's theorems (40E05).** Tauber (1897): if $a_n=o(1/n)$ and $\lim_{x\to1^-}\sum a_nx^n=s$ exists, then $\sum a_n$ converges to $s$. ([Wikipedia: Abelian and Tauberian theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems)) Littlewood (1911) weakened the hypothesis to $a_n=O(1/n)$. ([Wikipedia: Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem))
