- **Tauberian theorems for Cesàro means.** Hardy's Theorem 63: if $\sum a_n=A\ (C,k)$ for some $k$ and $a_n=O(n^{-1})$, then $\sum a_n$ converges, and is even $(C,-1+\delta)$ summable for every $\delta>0$. Theorem 64 (one-sided): if $a_n$ is real, $\sum a_n=A\ (C,k)$, and $na_n>-H$, then $\sum a_n$ converges. These conditions are cases of slow oscillation and slow decrease: $f$ is slowly oscillating if $f(y)-f(x)\to0$ whenever $x\to\infty$, $y>x$, $y/x\to1$, and slowly decreasing if $\liminf\,(f(y)-f(x))\ge0$ under the same conditions; $s_n$ is slowly oscillating when $a_n=O(1/n)$ and slowly decreasing when $a_n\ge-H/n$. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §6.1–6.2](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Mercer's theorem.** Hardy's Theorem 51: if $\alpha>0$ and $\alpha s_n+(1-\alpha)m_n\to s$, where $m_n$ is the arithmetic mean of $s_0,\dots,s_n$, then $s_n\to s$. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §5.9](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Hardy–Littlewood and Karamata.** If $a_n\ge0$ and $\sum a_nx^n\sim\frac1{1-x}$ as $x\uparrow1$, then $\sum_{k\le n}a_k\sim n$; the hypothesis can be weakened to $a_n\ge-K$, but not dropped. Karamata gave a short proof in 1930 by approximating step functions by polynomials. ([Wikipedia: Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem)) In integral form (Karamata's Tauberian theorem; Bingham–Goldie–Teugels Thm 1.7.1): if $U:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous with $U(0)=0$, its Laplace–Stieltjes transform $\hat U(s)=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-st}\,dU(t)$ is finite for $s>0$, $\rho\ge0$ and $L$ is slowly varying, then $\hat U(s)\sim s^{-\rho}L(1/s)$ as $s\to0^+$ if and only if $U(t)\sim t^{\rho}L(t)/\Gamma(\rho+1)$ as $t\to\infty$. ([arXiv:2606.31643, Thm 2.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.31643)) A measurable $L>0$ is slowly varying if $L(ax)/L(x)\to1$ for every $a>0$; the convergence is uniform on compact $a$-intervals, and Karamata's representation theorem writes every such $L$ as $\exp\big(\eta(x)+\int_B^x\varepsilon(t)\,dt/t\big)$ with $\eta$ convergent and $\varepsilon\to0$. ([Wikipedia: Slowly varying function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slowly_varying_function))
- **High indices (40E15).** If $\lambda_{n+1}\ge c\lambda_n$ for some $c>1$ and $S(y)=\sum a_ne^{-\lambda_ny}$, convergent for $y>0$, tends to $s$ as $y\to0^+$, then $\sum a_n$ converges to $s$, with no condition on the size of $a_n$ (Theorem 114). Littlewood conjectured it and Hardy and Littlewood proved it (1926); Hardy gives Ingham's shorter proof. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §7.13 and notes](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Wiener's Tauberian theorem.** For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, the translates of $f$ span a dense subspace of $L^1(\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\hat f$ has no real zeros; equivalently, if $\hat f$ has no real zeros and $f*h\to0$ at infinity for some $h\in L^\infty$, then $g*h\to0$ at infinity for every $g\in L^1$. In $L^2$, translates are dense when the real zero set of $\hat f$ has measure zero. ([Wikipedia: Wiener's Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_Tauberian_theorem)) Links to [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis).
- **Wiener–Ikehara theorem.** Let $A\ge0$ be nondecreasing on $[0,\infty)$, let $f(s)=\int_0^\infty A(x)e^{-xs}\,dx$ converge for $\Re s>1$, and suppose that for some $c\ge0$, $f(s)-\frac{c}{s-1}$ extends continuously to $\Re s\ge1$. Then $e^{-x}A(x)\to c$. Applied to $-\zeta'/\zeta$, whose Dirichlet coefficients are the von Mangoldt function, it yields the prime number theorem given that $\zeta$ has no zeros on $\Re s=1$. ([Wikipedia: Wiener–Ikehara theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Ikehara_theorem)) Newman (1980) observed that only a much easier special case is needed, giving arguably the simplest known proof. ([Wikipedia: Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem)) Links to [Prime Numbers](node:Prime%20Numbers) and [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Remainders and their optimality (40E10).** The Ingham–Karamata theorem: if $\tau$ is Lipschitz on $[0,\infty)$ and its Laplace transform continues analytically across the imaginary axis, then $\tau(x)=o(1)$. Callewaert, Neyt and Vindas show that for every positive $\rho\to0$ there is such a $\tau$, even with entire Laplace transform, with $\limsup|\tau(x)|/\rho(x)=\infty$; so no remainder better than $o(1)$ follows, and the same optimality holds for Wiener–Ikehara. ([Callewaert–Neyt–Vindas, arXiv:2407.15547](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.15547))
- **Abel versus Cesàro.** Hardy's Theorem 56 gives series that are Abel summable but not $(C,k)$ summable for any $k$, such as the coefficients of $e^{1/(1+x)}$ or $(-1)^ne^{c\sqrt n}$, $c>0$. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §5.12](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) A series that is Abel but not $(C,1)$ summable need not be such an example: $1-2+3-4+\cdots$ is not $(C,1)$ summable but is $(C,2)$ summable to $\tfrac14$. ([Wikipedia: 1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_%E2%88%92_2_%2B_3_%E2%88%92_4_%2B_%E2%8B%AF)) Related: [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence).

### History
Tauber published his theorem in 1897 in *Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik*; Wiener's 1932 *Annals* paper "Tauberian theorems" renewed the field, and its central theorem can now be proved by Banach algebra methods. ([Wikipedia: Abelian and Tauberian theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems)) Littlewood extended Tauber's converse in 1911, Hardy and Littlewood used their theorem to prove $\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)\sim x$, and Karamata simplified the proof in 1930. ([Wikipedia: Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem)) Ikehara, Wiener's student, published the Wiener–Ikehara theorem in 1931, and Gelfand reformulated Wiener's theorem through the maximal ideals of the Wiener algebra, giving a new proof. ([Wikipedia: Wiener–Ikehara theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Ikehara_theorem); [Wikipedia: Wiener's Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_Tauberian_theorem))

Book-length treatments include Korevaar's *Tauberian Theory: A Century of Developments* (Springer, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften, 2004) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-10225-1)) and Bingham, Goldie and Teugels's *Regular Variation* (Cambridge University Press, 1987) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511721434)).

### Open problems
None found. Searches tried: arXiv and web searches for "open problem" or "open question" with Tauberian theorem, Tauberian constants, Wiener–Ikehara remainders, and Ingham–Karamata optimality; the recent optimality paper above, which states no open question; and the MSC2020 40Exx entry. ([Callewaert–Neyt–Vindas, arXiv:2407.15547](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.15547); [MSC2020 40Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Exx))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem): statements, Karamata's proof, Littlewood's theorem.
- **Reference:** [Wiener's Tauberian theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_Tauberian_theorem): $L^1$ and $L^2$ forms and Gelfand's proof.
- **Learn:** [Cuddy, Convergence of Fourier Series (UChicago REU)](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2012/REUPapers/Cuddy.pdf): Cesàro and Abel summability via Fejér and Poisson kernels.
- **Primary:** [Hardy, Divergent Series (1949), full text](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt): Ch. VI–VII on Tauberian theorems for Cesàro and power-series methods.
- **Primary:** [Callewaert, Neyt, Vindas, optimality of the Ingham–Karamata theorem (arXiv:2407.15547)](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.15547): recent research on Tauberian remainders.
- **Further reading:** [Korevaar, Tauberian Theory: A Century of Developments (Springer 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-10225-1) and [Bingham–Goldie–Teugels, Regular Variation (CUP 1987)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511721434).
references.MSC 40Fxx - Absolute and strong summabil:
## Reference
### Overview
Absolute and strong summability strengthen ordinary summability. Ordinary summability only asks that a sequence of means of the partial sums converge. Absolute summability asks that the means have bounded variation, possibly with weights and powers. Hardy calls a series $\sum a_n$ absolutely summable $(C,k)$, or summable $|C,k|$, when $\sum_n |C_n^k(A)-C_{n-1}^k(A)|<\infty$, where $C_n^k$ is the $n$th Cesàro mean of order $k$. Summability $|C,0|$ is then absolute convergence, and Hardy attributes the definition to Fekete. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, notes to §§6.5–6](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))

Strong summability instead averages the distances of the partial sums from the limit. For a trigonometric Fourier series with partial sums $S_k(x,f)$, the strong means of order $p>0$ are $\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|S_k(x,f)-f(x)|^p$, and $(H,p)$-summability at $x$ means that these tend to $0$. ([Goginava and Karagulyan, arXiv:1701.08710](https://arxiv.org/html/1701.08710v1)) For a sequence $(x_k)$ in a normed space, strong Cesàro convergence to $L$ means $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\|x_k-L\|=0$. ([Romero de la Rosa, arXiv:2302.10218](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.10218))

Two recurring settings are Fourier series and summability factors. For Fourier series a central question is strong summability almost everywhere. For factors, the question is which multipliers $\lambda_n$ make $\sum a_n\lambda_n$ absolutely summable. ([Goginava and Karagulyan, arXiv:1701.08710](https://arxiv.org/html/1701.08710v1); [Bor, arXiv:1710.00057](https://arxiv.org/html/1710.00057))

### Scope
In MSC2020, 40Fxx "Absolute and strong summability" has one substantive code, 40F05, with the same title, plus 40F99 "None of the above, but in this section". Both 40Fxx and 40F05 carry the instruction that papers here "should also be assigned at least one other classification number in Section 40-XX". ([AMS MSC2020, 40Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Fxx)) So every paper given 40F05 also carries another code from [MSC 40 - Sequences, series, summability](node:MSC%2040%20-%20Sequences,%20series,%20summability). A paper on absolute Cesàro or Riesz summability factors of Fourier series, for example, was classified 26D15, 42A24, 40F05 and 40G99. ([Yıldız, arXiv:1710.06246](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.06246))

Neighbouring codes, one line each:
- [MSC 40Gxx - Special methods of summability](node:MSC%2040Gxx%20-%20Special%20methods%20of%20summability) holds the named methods themselves: 40G05 Cesàro, Euler, Nörlund and Hausdorff methods; 40G10 Abel, Borel and power series methods; and 40G15 summability methods using statistical convergence (see also 40A35). ([AMS MSC2020, 40Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Gxx))
- [MSC 40Dxx - Direct theorems on summability](node:MSC%2040Dxx%20-%20Direct%20theorems%20on%20summability) and [MSC 40Exx - Inversion theorems](node:MSC%2040Exx%20-%20Inversion%20theorems) are the sibling codes for direct and inversion theorems; 40Cxx is "General summability methods" and 40Hxx "Functional analytic methods in summability". ([AMS MSC2020, 40-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40-XX)) Absolute analogues of Hardy's Cesàro theorems were proved by Bosanquet, Fekete and Kogbetliantz. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, notes to §§6.5–6](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- Factor papers on Fourier series pair 40F05 with 42A24 from [MSC 42Axx - Harmonic analysis in one variable](node:MSC%2042Axx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20one%20variable). ([Yıldız, arXiv:1710.06246](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.06246))

### Key concepts
- **Cesàro means.** The $(C,\alpha)$ means iterate arithmetic averaging. If a series has a $(C,\alpha)$-sum, it has a $(C,\beta)$-sum for every $\beta>\alpha$, and the sums agree. ([Wikipedia: Cesàro summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ces%C3%A0ro_summation)) For an integrable $2\pi$-periodic $f$, the Fourier series is Cesàro summable to $f$ at every point of continuity, and uniformly so if $f$ is continuous (Fejér's theorem). ([Cuddy, UChicago REU](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2012/REUPapers/Cuddy.pdf)) This is the base case for [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) and [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence).
- **$|C,\alpha|_k$ summability (Flett, 1957).** Let $k\ge1$ and $\alpha>-1$. Let $u_n^\alpha$ and $t_n^\alpha$ be the $n$th $(C,\alpha)$ means of $(s_n)$ and of $(na_n)$. Then $\sum a_n$ is summable $|C,\alpha|_k$ if $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{k-1}|u_n^\alpha-u_{n-1}^\alpha|^k=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1n|t_n^\alpha|^k<\infty$. ([Yıldız, arXiv:1710.06246](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.06246)) A weighted form, $\varphi$-$|C,\alpha|_k$, requires $\sum n^{-k}|\varphi_nt_n^\alpha|^k<\infty$ and reduces to $|C,\alpha|_k$ when $\varphi_n=n^{1-1/k}$. ([Özarslan, arXiv:math/0310290](https://arxiv.org/html/math/0310290v1))
- **Absolute weighted mean summability $|\bar N,p_n|_k$ (Bor, 1985).** Let $p_n>0$, $P_n=p_0+\dots+p_n\to\infty$, and $w_n=P_n^{-1}\sum_{v\le n}p_vs_v$. The series is summable $|\bar N,p_n|_k$, $k\ge1$, if $\sum_{n\ge1}(P_n/p_n)^{k-1}|w_n-w_{n-1}|^k<\infty$. With $p_n\equiv1$ this is $|C,1|_k$. ([Bor, arXiv:1710.00057](https://arxiv.org/html/1710.00057))
- **Summability factor theorems.** These are the main type of result in the area. One theorem of Bor is a typical example. Let $(X_n)$ be positive and non-decreasing, with $|\Delta\lambda_n|\le\beta_n$, $\beta_n\to0$, $\sum n|\Delta\beta_n|X_n=O(1)$, $|\lambda_n|X_n=O(1)$, $P_n=O(np_n)$, $P_n\Delta p_n=O(p_np_{n+1})$, and $\sum_{n\le m}|s_n|^k/(nX_n^{k-1})=O(X_m)$. Then $\sum a_nP_n\lambda_n/(np_n)$ is summable $|\bar N,p_n|_k$ for $k\ge1$. ([Bor, arXiv:1710.00057](https://arxiv.org/html/1710.00057)) Özarslan proves an analogue: $\sum a_n\lambda_n$ is summable $\varphi$-$|C,\alpha|_k$ for $0<\alpha\le1$, $k\ge1$, $k\alpha+\varepsilon>1$. The hypotheses are an almost increasing $(X_n)$ with $|\lambda_n|X_n=O(1)$, a $\delta$-quasi-monotone $(A_n)$ with $\sum nA_nX_n<\infty$ and $|\Delta\lambda_n|\le|A_n|$, $n^{\varepsilon-k}|\varphi_n|^k$ non-increasing, and $\sum_{n\le m}n^{-k}(w_n^\alpha|\varphi_n|)^k=O(X_m)$, where $w_n^\alpha=|t_n^\alpha|$ for $\alpha=1$ and $w_n^\alpha=\max_{v\le n}|t_v^\alpha|$ for $0<\alpha<1$. ([Özarslan, arXiv:math/0310290](https://arxiv.org/html/math/0310290v1))
- **Absolute summability of factored Fourier series.** Put $\varphi(t)=\frac12\{f(x+t)+f(x-t)\}$ and $\varphi_1(t)=t^{-1}\int_0^t\varphi(u)\,du$. Bor showed that if $\varphi_1\in BV(0,\pi)$ and the factor sequences satisfy his $\delta$-quasi-monotone hypotheses, then $\sum C_n(x)\lambda_n$ is summable $|\bar N,p_n|_k$, $k\ge1$, where $C_n(x)$ are the terms of the Fourier series. Yıldız extends this to absolute matrix summability $|A,p_n|_k$. ([Yıldız, arXiv:1710.06246](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.06246)) Bor, Yu and Zhou prove general theorems on local properties of the absolute summability of factored Fourier series. ([Bor, Yu and Zhou, arXiv:1301.6874](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.6874))
- **Inclusion between absolute weighted means.** For positive $(p_n),(q_n)$ and $1<k\le s<\infty$, Rhoades and Savaş give two explicit conditions that are necessary and sufficient for $|N,p_n|_k$ summability to imply $|N,q_n|_s$ summability. They use Bennett's criterion for a factorable matrix to map $\ell^k$ to $\ell^s$. ([Rhoades and Savaş, arXiv:math/0309419](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309419))
- **Strong summability of Fourier series.** Hardy and Littlewood (1913) proved that for $f\in L^r(\mathbb T)$, $1<r<\infty$, the strong means of order $p$ tend to $0$ almost everywhere. For $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$, Marcinkiewicz (1939) treated $p=2$ and Zygmund the general case $1\le p<\infty$. ([Goginava and Karagulyan, arXiv:1701.08710](https://arxiv.org/html/1701.08710v1))
- **Exponential strong summability.** For continuous increasing $\Phi$ with $\Phi(0)=0$, strong $\Phi$-summability asks that $\frac1n\sum_{k<n}\Phi(|S_k-f|)\to0$. Oskolkov proved it almost everywhere when $\ln\Phi(t)=O(t/\ln\ln t)$. Rodin proved it for every $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ whenever $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\ln\Phi(t)/t<\infty$. For double Fourier series, Gogoladze (1988) proved almost-everywhere strong rectangular $(H,p)$-summability for $f\in L\log L(\mathbb T^2)$. Goginava and Karagulyan prove a.e. rectangular strong $\Phi$-summability, $\frac1{nm}\sum_{i<n}\sum_{j<m}\Phi(|S_{ij}f-f|)\to0$ as $n,m\to\infty$, for every $f\in L\log L(\mathbb T^2)$ when $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\ln\Phi(t)/\sqrt{t/\ln\ln t}<\infty$. In one dimension, Karagulyan showed Rodin's exponential bound is optimal: if $\limsup\ln\Phi(t)/t=\infty$, some $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ has strong $\Phi$-means with $\limsup=\infty$ everywhere. ([Goginava and Karagulyan, arXiv:1701.08710](https://arxiv.org/html/1701.08710v1))
- **Strong Cesàro and statistical convergence.** A sequence is statistically convergent to $l$ if, for each $\varepsilon>0$, $\{k:|x_k-l|\ge\varepsilon\}$ has natural density zero. ([Bhardwaj, Dhawan and Dovgoshey, arXiv:1611.08683](https://arxiv.org/html/1611.08683)) Connor's theorem (1988) relates the two notions. For any $p>0$, strong $p$-Cesàro convergence to $s$ implies statistical convergence to $s$. A *bounded* sequence that is statistically convergent to $s$ is strongly $p$-Cesàro convergent to $s$. Hence the two are equivalent on bounded sequences, and strong $p$- and $q$-Cesàro convergence coincide there. ([Hardtke, arXiv:1011.2365](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.2365))
- **Lacunary strong convergence.** For a lacunary sequence $\theta=(k_r)$, Freedman, Sember and Raphael showed that strong lacunary convergence equals strong Cesàro convergence when $1<\liminf_r k_r/k_{r-1}\le\limsup_r k_r/k_{r-1}<\infty$. ([Romero de la Rosa, arXiv:2302.10218](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.10218))
- **Absolute Borel summability.** Hardy calls $\sum a_n$ absolutely summable $(B)$ when Borel's integral converges absolutely, and notes that Borel's own terminology differs. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §8.6](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))

### History
Fekete (1911) proved that if $A=\sum a_n$ is absolutely summable $(C,r)$ and $B$ is summable $(C,s)$, for integers $r,s$, then their Cauchy product is summable $(C,r+s)$. Kogbetliantz (1925) extended this to general orders. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, notes to §10.3](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Hardy's 1949 book says it "shall not be concerned with absolute summability" for Cesàro means, and records that absolute analogues of its Cesàro factor theorems were proved by Bosanquet, Fekete and Kogbetliantz. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, notes to §§6.5–6](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))

Strong Cesàro convergence for real numbers was introduced by Hardy and Littlewood and by Fekete, in connection with the convergence of Fourier series. ([Romero de la Rosa, arXiv:2302.10218](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.10218)) The Hardy–Littlewood almost-everywhere theorem for $L^r$, $1<r<\infty$, appeared in C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 156 (1913). ([Goginava and Karagulyan, arXiv:1701.08710](https://arxiv.org/html/1701.08710v1)) The definition of the index-$k$ method $|C,\alpha|_k$ is cited to Flett, Proc. London Math. Soc. 7 (1957). ([Özarslan, arXiv:math/0310290](https://arxiv.org/html/math/0310290v1)) The definition of $|\bar N,p_n|_k$ is cited to Bor (1985), "On two summability methods". ([Bor, arXiv:1710.00057](https://arxiv.org/html/1710.00057)) Fast and Steinhaus independently introduced statistical convergence in 1951. Connor's 1988 paper linked it to strong $p$-Cesàro convergence. ([Bhardwaj, Dhawan and Dovgoshey, arXiv:1611.08683](https://arxiv.org/html/1611.08683); [Hardtke, arXiv:1011.2365](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.2365))

A definitional point affects the weighted-mean literature. Sarıgöl's 1994 inclusion theorems used the weight $(P_n/p_n)^{k-1}$ for $|N,p_n|_k$. Rhoades pointed out that the correct condition uses $n^{k-1}$ instead. The two conditions are equivalent when $np_n/P_n$ and $P_n/(np_n)$ are both bounded. ([Rhoades and Savaş, arXiv:math/0309419](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309419))

### Open problems
- **Optimal growth for rectangular strong $\Phi$-summability of double Fourier series.** Goginava and Karagulyan conjecture that $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\ln\Phi(t)/\sqrt t<\infty$ is the optimal condition on $\Phi$ ensuring a.e. rectangular strong $\Phi$-summability for every $f\in L\log L(\mathbb T^2)$; their method proves it only under the stronger condition $\limsup\ln\Phi(t)/\sqrt{t/\ln\ln t}<\infty$. ([Goginava and Karagulyan, arXiv:1701.08710](https://arxiv.org/html/1701.08710v1))
- The question of Bhardwaj and Dhawan on lacunary $f$-strong Cesàro convergence is solved in Romero de la Rosa's paper, so it is not open. ([Romero de la Rosa, arXiv:2302.10218](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.10218))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Cesàro summation, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ces%C3%A0ro_summation): the $(C,\alpha)$ means on which $|C,\alpha|_k$ and strong Cesàro summability are built.
- **Learn:** [Cuddy, Convergence of Fourier Series (UChicago REU)](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2012/REUPapers/Cuddy.pdf): Fejér and Abel kernels and Cesàro summability of Fourier series, the setting for strong summability.
- **Primary:** [Hardy, Divergent Series (1949), full text](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt): the standard monograph on summability, with the historical notes on absolute summability.
- **Primary:** [Goginava and Karagulyan, a.e. exponential strong summability (arXiv:1701.08710)](https://arxiv.org/html/1701.08710v1): survey-style introduction to strong summability of Fourier series from Hardy–Littlewood to Rodin.
- **Primary:** [Rhoades and Savaş, inclusion relations for absolute summability (arXiv:math/0309419)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309419): necessary and sufficient inclusion conditions for absolute weighted means.
- **Further reading:** [Boos and Cass, Classical and Modern Methods in Summability (OUP, 2000)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198501657.001.0001): graduate monograph on summability, including functional-analytic methods. [Zygmund, Trigonometric Series (CUP)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781316036587): the standard reference for summability of Fourier series.
references.MSC 40Gxx - Special methods of summabili:
## Reference
### Overview
This subfield studies named summation methods one at a time: Cesàro, Euler, Nörlund, Hausdorff, Abel, Borel, other power-series methods, and methods based on statistical convergence. ([AMS MSC2020, 40Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Gxx)) Each method assigns values to some divergent series. A method is regular if it gives every convergent sequence its ordinary limit. It is linear if it is a linear functional on its domain, and stable if dropping the first term changes the value in the expected way. Two methods are consistent if they agree wherever both apply, and of two consistent methods the one that sums more series is stronger. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series))

Questions studied for a single method include its regularity, its strength relative to other methods (inclusion and equivalence), Tauberian conditions under which it implies convergence, and the region in which it continues a power series analytically. Hardy's *Divergent Series* has chapters on the methods of Euler and Borel and on Hausdorff means, and sections on Nörlund, Abel, Lindelöf, Mittag-Leffler and Riesz means. ([Hardy, Divergent Series](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists 40G05 Cesàro, Euler, Nörlund and Hausdorff methods; 40G10 Abel, Borel and power series methods; 40G15 summability methods using statistical convergence (see also 40A35); and 40G99. ([AMS MSC2020, 40Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Gxx))

Neighbouring codes, one line each:
- [MSC 40Cxx - General summability methods](node:MSC%2040Cxx%20-%20General%20summability%20methods) covers classes of methods rather than named ones: matrix methods (40C05), integral methods (40C10), and function-theoretic methods, including power series and semicontinuous methods (40C15). ([AMS MSC2020, 40Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Cxx))
- [MSC 40Dxx - Direct theorems on summability](node:MSC%2040Dxx%20-%20Direct%20theorems%20on%20summability) holds general theorems, including inclusion and equivalence theorems (40D25) and summability factors (40D15). ([AMS MSC2020, 40Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Dxx))
- [MSC 40Exx - Inversion theorems](node:MSC%2040Exx%20-%20Inversion%20theorems) holds Tauberian theorems (40E05), growth estimates and Tauberian constants. ([AMS MSC2020, 40Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Exx))
- [40Fxx](node:MSC%2040Fxx%20-%20Absolute%20and%20strong%20summability%20%28should%20also%20be%20assigned%20at%20least%20one%20other%20classification%20number%20in%20Section%2040-XX%29) is "Absolute and strong summability", and papers there must also carry another 40 code. ([AMS MSC2020, 40Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Cesàro and Nörlund means (40G05).** $(C,1)$ assigns $A$ when $\frac1n\sum_{k\le n}s_k\to A$, so Grandi's series $1-1+1-\cdots$ has Cesàro sum $\tfrac12$. A $(C,\alpha)$-summable series is $(C,\beta)$-summable for all $\beta>\alpha$, to the same sum. ([Wikipedia: Cesàro summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ces%C3%A0ro_summation)) Nörlund means $(N,p_n)$ are weighted means $t_m=(p_ms_0+p_{m-1}s_1+\dots+p_0s_m)/P_m$ of the partial sums, with $P_m=p_0+\dots+p_m$; the Cesàro means are a special case. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series)) The method is regular if and only if $p_n/P_n\to0$, and any two regular Nörlund methods are consistent. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §4.2, Theorems 16–17](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Hölder and Riesz means are equivalent to Cesàro means.** The Hölder method $(H,k)$ iterates arithmetic means. Knopp (1907) proved $(H,k)\Rightarrow(C,k)$, Schnee (1909) proved the converse, and Hardy states that $(C,k)$ and $(H,k)$ are equivalent for $k>-1$. Riesz's typical means are $R_k(\omega)=\sum_{n<\omega}(1-n/\omega)^ka_n$, with a continuous parameter $\omega\to\infty$. Summability $(R,n,k)$ is equivalent to $(C,k)$: a series is summable by one if and only if it is summable by the other, to the same sum. Hardy proves this for integral $k$ (Theorem 58) and notes that the general case is harder. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §5.16, notes to §5.8, Theorem 211](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Hausdorff means and Hausdorff's theorem (40G05).** A Hausdorff transformation has the form $\mathfrak H=\delta\mu\delta$, where $\mu$ is a diagonal matrix and $\delta$ is the self-inverse matrix of signed binomial differences. The $(E,q)$ and $(C,1)$ transformations are of this type, and any two Hausdorff transformations commute. Call $\mu_n=\int_0^1x^n\,d\chi(x)$, with $\chi$ of bounded variation on $[0,1]$ and $\chi(0)=0$, a moment constant. It is *regular* if also $\chi(1)=1$ and $\chi(0+)=0$. Hausdorff's theorem has two parts. A sequence is a difference of two totally monotone sequences if and only if it is a moment constant. The transformation $(\mathfrak H,\mu)$ is regular if and only if $\mu_n$ is a regular moment constant. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §§11.3, 11.8–11.9, Theorems 197, 204–208](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Hausdorff's moment theorem states that $(m_n)$ is the moment sequence of a measure on $[0,1]$ if and only if it is completely monotonic. This links the summability theory to [moment problems (44A60)](node:MSC%2044Axx%20-%20Integral%20transforms,%20operational%20calculus). ([Wikipedia: Hausdorff moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_moment_problem))
- **Euler–Knopp means $(E,q)$ (40G05).** If a series is summable $(E,q')$ and $q>q'$, it is summable $(E,q)$ to the same sum. The $r$th Euler transform of the $q$th Euler transform is the $(q+r+qr)$th Euler transform. Every series summable $(E,q)$ is summable by Borel's methods to the same sum (Knopp). ([Hardy, Divergent Series, Theorems 118, 119, 128](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) For $q>0$ the $(E,q)$ methods are strictly weaker than Borel summation and incomparable with Abel summation. ([Wikipedia: Euler summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_summation))
- **Abel and Abelian means (40G10).** $\sum c_k$ is Abel summable to $s$ if $\sum c_kr^k$ converges for $0\le r<1$ and tends to $s$ as $r\to1^-$. Every Cesàro-summable series is Abel summable to the same value, but not conversely. The Fourier series of a continuous $2\pi$-periodic function is uniformly Cesàro and Abel summable to it, a basic fact linking [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence) with [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis). ([Cuddy, UChicago REU](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2012/REUPapers/Cuddy.pdf)) More generally, for $\lambda_n\uparrow\infty$ the Abelian mean is $\lim_{x\to0^+}\sum a_ne^{-\lambda_nx}$. Abelian means are regular and linear but not stable in general, and different $\lambda$ need not be consistent. Abel summation is $\lambda_n=n$, and Lindelöf summation is $\lambda_n=n\log n$. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series))
- **Borel summation and the Borel polygon (40G10).** The integral Borel sum is $\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal BA(tz)\,dt$, where $\mathcal BA(t)=\sum a_kt^k/k!$. The weak and integral forms are both regular. Weak Borel summability implies Borel summability, and the converse needs an extra condition. The method sums $\sum z^k$ to $1/(1-z)$ on $\operatorname{Re}z<1$. ([Wikipedia: Borel summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_summation)) Borel's polygon theorem applies to a power series representing a function regular at the origin. The series is Borel summable inside the Borel polygon of the function, uniformly on closed subregions, and is not summable at any point outside it. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, Theorem 133](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Lindelöf's and Mittag-Leffler's methods sum $\sum z^n$ in its Mittag-Leffler star. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §§4.11, 8.10](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) This is the link with [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis).
- **Borel's Tauberian theorem.** If $\sum a_n=A\ (B)$ and $a_n=O(n^{-1/2})$, then $\sum a_n$ converges to $A$. Hardy calls this "the principal Tauberian theorem" for the Borel method and proves it using Theorems 150 and 151, which compare the Borel method with Valiron's $(e,c)$ methods when $a_n=o(1)$. For example, $(E,q)$ is then equivalent to $(e,c)$ with $c=(q+1)/2q$. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §§9.10–9.13, Theorems 152, 156](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Statistical convergence (40G15).** $(x_k)$ converges statistically to $l$ if every set $\{k:|x_k-l|\ge\varepsilon\}$ has natural density zero. ([Bhardwaj, Dhawan and Dovgoshey, arXiv:1611.08683](https://arxiv.org/html/1611.08683)) By Connor's theorem, strong $p$-Cesàro convergence implies statistical convergence, and the converse holds for bounded sequences. ([Hardtke, arXiv:1011.2365](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.2365))
- **Equivalence under a growth condition.** Vindas proved that if $\sum_{n\le N}n|c_n|=O(N)$, then Lebesgue, Cesàro $(C,\beta)$ for $\beta>0$, Abel, Riemann and $(\gamma,\kappa)$ for $\kappa\ge1$ summability of $\sum c_n$ are all equivalent to one another. The growth condition does not make the series summable. It makes these methods sum exactly the same such series, to the same value. ([Vindas, arXiv:1305.0200](https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0200))

### History
Hutton (1812) summed divergent series by repeatedly averaging partial sums. Frobenius used Cesàro's method implicitly in 1880, and in 1890 Cesàro gave a rigorous definition of the sum of some divergent series. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series)) Émile Borel introduced his method in the 1899 "Mémoire sur les séries divergentes". ([Wikipedia: Borel summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_summation)) Knopp's 1907 Berlin dissertation and Schnee's 1909 paper settled the Hölder–Cesàro equivalence. M. Riesz introduced typical means as a better-behaved alternative to an earlier definition. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §5.16 and notes to §5.8](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Hausdorff's two papers "Summationsmethoden und Momentfolgen" appeared in *Mathematische Zeitschrift* 9 in 1921. ([Wikipedia: Hausdorff moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_moment_problem)) Fast and Steinhaus introduced statistical convergence independently in 1951. ([Bhardwaj, Dhawan and Dovgoshey, arXiv:1611.08683](https://arxiv.org/html/1611.08683))

### Open problems
- **Cesàro and Nörlund means of Walsh–Fourier series on Hardy spaces.** Baramidze, Persson, Tangrand and Tephnadze (2023) study the subsequence $t_{2^n}$ of Nörlund means of Walsh–Fourier series, and the Cesàro means $\sigma^\alpha_n$ as a special case. They list open problems. One (Open Problem 4) asks the following. Let $0<\alpha<1$ and $f$ belong to the martingale Hardy space $H_{1/(1+\alpha)}$. Is there an absolute constant $C_\alpha$ with $\|\sigma^\alpha_{2^n}f\|_{1/(1+\alpha)}\le C_\alpha\|f\|_{H_{1/(1+\alpha)}}$? Open Problem 1 asks whether, for $0.56<\alpha<1$ and $0<p<1/(1+\alpha)$, some martingale $f\in H_p$ has $\sup_n\|\sigma^\alpha_{2^n}f\|_{\text{weak-}L_p}=\infty$. ([Baramidze et al., arXiv:2303.01846](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.01846))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Divergent series, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series): properties of summation methods and definitions of the main named methods.
- **Learn:** [Cuddy, Convergence of Fourier Series (UChicago REU)](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2012/REUPapers/Cuddy.pdf): Cesàro and Abel summability of Fourier series with full proofs.
- **Primary:** [Hardy, Divergent Series (1949), full text](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt): the standard monograph, with Euler, Borel, Hausdorff, Riesz and Tauberian theory.
- **Primary:** [Vindas, Lebesgue summability and other methods (arXiv:1305.0200)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0200): equivalence of several classical methods under a coefficient growth condition.
- **Further reading:** [Boos and Cass, Classical and Modern Methods in Summability (OUP, 2000)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198501657.001.0001): graduate monograph covering the classical methods and their functional-analytic treatment.
references.MSC 40Hxx - Functional analytic methods:
## Reference
### Overview
In this subfield, summability methods are treated as linear maps between spaces of sequences. A regular matrix method is a linear sequence transformation that preserves the limits of convergent sequences. Applied to the partial sums of a divergent series, it can assign that series a generalized sum. ([Wikipedia: Silverman–Toeplitz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverman%E2%80%93Toeplitz_theorem)) FK-spaces are sequence spaces whose topology makes them Fréchet spaces with continuous coordinates, and they are described as important in summability theory. ([Wikipedia: FK-space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK-space))

Functional analysis also supplies nonconstructive limits. A Banach limit is a shift-invariant, positive, continuous linear functional on $\ell^\infty$ that agrees with $\lim$ on convergent sequences. Its existence is usually proved with the Hahn–Banach theorem and is inherently non-constructive. ([Wikipedia: Banach limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_limit)) Banach limits are an established tool in classical summability theory. ([Sofi, arXiv:1906.04168](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.04168))

### Scope
MSC2020 40Hxx "Functional analytic methods in summability" contains 40H05 (same title) and 40H99. ([AMS MSC2020, 40Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Hxx)) Typical work defines new sequence spaces, proves completeness, computes their $\alpha$-, $\beta$- and $\gamma$-duals, and characterizes the matrix transformations between them. ([Manna, Maji and Srivastava, arXiv:1307.6208](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.6208)) Work comparing strong Cesàro and statistical convergence is also classified under 40H05. ([Romero de la Rosa, arXiv:2302.10218](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.10218))

### Key concepts
- **Classical sequence spaces.** These include $c$ (convergent sequences), $c_0$ (null sequences), and $\ell^\infty$ (bounded sequences) with the supremum norm, and $\ell^p$ for $1\le p<\infty$. Each is a Banach space, and the dual of $c_0$ is $\ell^1$. ([Wikipedia: Sequence space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_space))
- **FK- and BK-spaces.** An FK-space is a sequence space with a Fréchet topology in which convergence implies coordinatewise convergence. A BK-space is an FK-space whose topology is normable. The inclusion into the space $\omega$ of all sequences is continuous. ([Wikipedia: FK-space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK-space))
- **Conservative and regular matrices.** Hardy treats the class of transformations that send convergent sequences to convergent sequences and its subclass of regular ones. He gives necessary and sufficient conditions for each. He also shows that regular transformations cannot send every bounded sequence to a convergent one. ([Hardy, Divergent Series, §3.2](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt))
- **Silverman–Toeplitz conditions.** A matrix method is regular if and only if its columns tend to $0$, its absolute row sums are bounded, and its row sums tend to $1$. ([Wikipedia: Silverman–Toeplitz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverman%E2%80%93Toeplitz_theorem))
- **Banach limits and almost convergence.** Every Banach limit assigns $(1,0,1,0,\dots)$ the value $\tfrac12$. A bounded sequence is almost convergent if all Banach limits agree on it. ([Wikipedia: Banach limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_limit)) The Banach limit extends summation to all bounded sequences, but it is nonconstructive. ([Wikipedia: Divergent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series))
- **Banach algebra methods.** Gelfand reproved Wiener's Tauberian theorem with Banach algebra theory. This shows how functional analysis enters Tauberian questions. ([Wikipedia: Wiener's Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_Tauberian_theorem))
- **Operator-theoretic Cesàro means.** Kubrusly and Duggal use Banach limits to study power bounded operators. They show that if the shifted Cesàro means of such an operator converge, at least weakly, uniformly in the shift parameter, then the operator has a Cesàro asymptotic limit. ([Kubrusly and Duggal, arXiv:2010.14740](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.14740))
- Related notes: [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), [Dual Vector Space](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space), [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices), [MSC 46 - Functional analysis](node:MSC%2046%20-%20Functional%20analysis), [MSC 46Bxx - Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices](node:MSC%2046Bxx%20-%20Normed%20linear%20spaces%20and%20Banach%20spaces;%20Banach%20lattices). The MIT functional analysis course covers normed spaces, the Hahn–Banach theorem, duality, and operators. ([MIT OCW 18.102](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/))

### History
Hardy attributes the regularity theorem in substance to Toeplitz (1911) and its extension to general transformations to Steinhaus. He credits the conservative-matrix theorem to Kojima (1917) and Schur (1921). ([Hardy, Divergent Series, notes on Ch. III](https://archive.org/stream/dli.ernet.285939/285939-Divergent%20Series_djvu.txt)) Wiener's 1932 work revived Tauberian theory, and its central theorem can now be proved by Banach algebra methods. ([Wikipedia: Abelian and Tauberian theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_and_Tauberian_theorems)) Gelfand's Banach-algebra papers appeared in 1941. ([Wikipedia: Wiener's Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_Tauberian_theorem))

### Open problems
Sofi's survey of Banach limits covers the structure of the set of Banach limits, vector-valued analogues, and linear selections built from Hahn–Banach extensions. It also includes some open problems that arise naturally in the study. ([Sofi, arXiv:1906.04168](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.04168))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [FK-space, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK-space): definition of FK- and BK-spaces.
- **Reference:** [Banach limit, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_limit): definition, existence, and almost convergence.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102 Introduction to Functional Analysis](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/): normed spaces, Hahn–Banach, duality, and operators.
- **Primary:** [Hardy, Divergent Series (1949), Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.285939): Chapter III on regular and conservative transformations.
- **Primary:** [Sofi, Banach limits: some new thoughts and perspectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.04168): survey with open problems.

## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 40Jxx, "Summability in abstract structures", is the last subdivision of section 40-XX. It has a single substantive code, 40J05, plus 40J99, and papers given it should also receive another number from section 40-XX; the classification cross-refers to 43A55, 46A35 and 46B15. ([MSC2020 40Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Jxx))

Work on summability in abstract structures includes results that characterize completeness of a normed space, or weakly unconditionally Cauchy series, through summability methods ([Moreno-Pulido et al., arXiv:2402.06369](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06369)); extend Silverman–Toeplitz regularity to kernel-summability methods for Banach-space-valued functions ([Parisé, arXiv:2302.06770](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06770v3)); or study Banach limits and their vector-valued analogues ([Sofi, arXiv:1906.04168](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.04168)).

### Scope
- **40J05**, summability in abstract structures, and **40J99**, none of the above. ([MSC2020 40Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Jxx))
- **43A55** (summability methods on groups, semigroups, etc.) is the abstract-harmonic-analysis neighbour and cross-refers back to 40J05. ([MSC2020 43A55](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=43A55))
- **46B15** (summability and bases; functional analytic aspects of frames in Banach and Hilbert spaces) is the Banach-space neighbour, cross-referenced from 40Jxx. ([MSC2020 46B15](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=46B15))
- **40A35** (ideal and statistical convergence) is the section-40 code for those convergence notions, and one possible companion code required by the 40J05 note. ([MSC2020 40Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Axx))

### Key concepts
- **Banach limits:** a Banach limit is a positive, shift-invariant, continuous linear functional $L$ on $\ell^\infty$ with $L(1,1,\dots)=1$. Existence follows from the Hahn–Banach theorem (Day's first proof used the Markov–Kakutani fixed-point theorem). ([Sofi, arXiv:1906.04168](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.04168)) Every Banach limit agrees with $\lim$ on convergent sequences, real Banach limits lie between $\liminf$ and $\limsup$, and Banach limits are not unique. ([Wikipedia: Banach limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_limit))
- **Lorentz's theorem on almost convergence (1948).** A bounded sequence is almost convergent to $s$ (its $F$-limit) if $L(x)=s$ for every Banach limit $L$. Lorentz proved that $x\in\ell^\infty$ is almost convergent to $s$ if and only if
  $$\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}x_{n+j}=s\quad\text{uniformly in }n.$$
  Sucheston showed that the set $\{L(x):L\text{ a Banach limit}\}$ is an interval $[p,q]$ given by the corresponding lower and upper uniform averages. ([Sofi, arXiv:1906.04168](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.04168)) For example $(1,0,1,0,\dots)$ is almost convergent to $\tfrac12$. ([Wikipedia: Banach limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_limit)) Móricz and Rhoades extended almost convergence to double sequences. ([Tuğ, arXiv:1909.00469](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.00469))
- **Unconditional convergence and Dvoretzky–Rogers.** A series converges unconditionally if all of its rearrangements converge to the same sum. In finite-dimensional spaces this is equivalent to absolute convergence, while by the Dvoretzky–Rogers theorem every infinite-dimensional Banach space contains an unconditionally convergent series that is not absolutely convergent. ([Wikipedia: Unconditional convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_convergence))
- **Orlicz–Pettis theorem.** In a Banach space (more generally a Hausdorff [locally convex space](node:Locally%20Convex%20Spaces)), a series that is weakly subseries convergent is subseries convergent in the original topology; equivalently, a weakly countably additive vector measure on a σ-algebra is countably additive. Orlicz proved it in 1929 for weakly sequentially complete spaces, and Pettis (1938) gave a proof in the course of showing weak and strong measures coincide. ([Wikipedia: Orlicz–Pettis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlicz%E2%80%93Pettis_theorem))
- **Bessaga–Pełczyński $c_0$ theorem.** A series $\sum x_n$ in a Banach space $X$ is weakly absolutely convergent if $\sum|x^*(x_n)|<\infty$ for every $x^*\in X^*$; every unconditionally convergent series has this property. $X$ contains no isomorphic copy of $c_0$ if and only if every weakly absolutely convergent series in $X$ is unconditionally convergent. If $X$ is weakly sequentially complete, every weakly unconditionally convergent series is unconditionally convergent. ([Monteiro, arXiv:1501.05196, Proposition A.8, Theorems A.9–A.10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.05196))
- **Statistical and ideal convergence.** For an ideal $\mathcal I$ on $\mathbb N$, a real sequence $x$ is $\mathcal I$-convergent to $L$ if $\{n:|x_n-L|\ge\varepsilon\}\in\mathcal I$ for every $\varepsilon>0$; such convergence is regular exactly when $\mathrm{Fin}\subseteq\mathcal I$, and the ideal of asymptotic-density-zero sets gives statistical convergence. ([Filipów–Tryba](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf)) In normed spaces, Moreno-Pulido and coauthors characterize completeness through strong lacunary ($N_\theta$) and lacunary statistical ($S_\theta$) convergence of series, give a new characterization of wuC series by the same methods, and relate the associated summability spaces to strong $p$-Cesàro convergence. ([Moreno-Pulido et al., arXiv:2402.06369](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06369))
- **Kernel-summability in Banach spaces.** Parisé defines kernel-summability methods for $X$-valued functions with vector-valued integrals, proves a Silverman–Toeplitz theorem for regular methods, and shows that inclusions between scalar methods carry over to $X$-valued functions for every Banach space $X$, with applications to Taylor series in Banach spaces of holomorphic functions on the disc. ([Parisé, arXiv:2302.06770](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06770v3))
- [Banach Limits](node:Banach%20Limits), [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), [Hahn–Banach Theorem](node:Hahn–Banach%20Theorem), [Weak Topologies in Banach Spaces](node:Weak%20Topologies%20in%20Banach%20Spaces), [Vector Measures and Bochner Integration](node:Vector%20Measures%20and%20Bochner%20Integration), [Frames and Wavelet Bases](node:Frames%20and%20Wavelet%20Bases), [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), [Summability in Topological Groups](node:Summability%20in%20Topological%20Groups), [Normed and Banach spaces (46Bxx)](node:MSC%2046Bxx%20-%20Normed%20linear%20spaces%20and%20Banach%20spaces;%20Banach%20lattices), [Abstract harmonic analysis (43Axx)](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis): the functional-analytic setting, the Orlicz–Pettis link to vector measures, frames under 46B15, and the group-theoretic neighbour 43A55. ([MSC2020 46B15](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=46B15))

### History
Lorentz introduced almost convergence in "A contribution to the theory of divergent sequences" (*Acta Math.* 80, 1948), defining it through Banach limits and characterizing it by uniform averages. ([Sofi, arXiv:1906.04168](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.04168)) Banach's 1932 monograph stated the Orlicz–Pettis theorem with credit to Orlicz, and Grothendieck (1953) proved a version covering the locally convex case. ([Wikipedia: Orlicz–Pettis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlicz%E2%80%93Pettis_theorem)) Mazur's Problem 5 of the Scottish Book asked whether statistical convergence of bounded sequences is equivalent to a matrix method; a theorem of Khan and Orhan answers it positively, and Mazur's accompanying claim that the density-zero ideal has property (M) is false. ([Filipów–Tryba](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Vector-valued invariant means.** Sofi asks: if $X$ is a Banach space in which every family of closed balls with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection, does every amenable semigroup $S$ admit an $X$-valued invariant mean on $B(S,X)$? He notes that the converse of the relevant proposition is not known in general, though it holds for spaces not containing $\ell_1$. ([Sofi, arXiv:1906.04168, Problem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.04168))
- **Ideals and matrix summability.** Filipów and Tryba ask whether there is an ideal with Mazur's property (M) that is not isomorphic to $\mathrm{Fin}$ or $\mathrm{Fin}\oplus P(\mathbb N)$, and whether a non-Borel ideal (for instance one generated by a maximal almost disjoint family) can have their property GMV. ([Filipów–Tryba, Questions 2–3](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 40Jxx (AMS)](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=40Jxx): the official codes and cross-references.
- **Reference:** [Unconditional convergence (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_convergence) and [Orlicz–Pettis theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlicz%E2%80%93Pettis_theorem): series in Banach and locally convex spaces.
- **Learn:** [Sofi, Banach limits: some new thoughts and perspectives](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.04168): expository survey from Hahn–Banach existence to Lorentz's theorem, vector-valued Banach limits and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Moreno-Pulido et al., Characterizations of a Banach space through the strong lacunary and lacunary statistical summabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06369): summability methods characterizing completeness and wuC series.
- **Primary:** [Parisé, Kernel-Summability Methods and the Silverman–Toeplitz Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06770v3): a 40J05-classified paper on Banach-space-valued summability.
- **Primary:** [Filipów and Tryba, Ideal convergence versus matrix summability](https://mat.ug.edu.pl/~rfilipow/papers/mazur.pdf): ideal convergence, the Scottish Book problem, and open questions.
- **Primary:** [Monteiro, On functions of bounded semivariation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.05196): its appendix collects the Bessaga–Pełczyński and related series theorems with references to Albiac–Kalton, Diestel's *Sequences and Series in Banach Spaces*, and Kadets–Kadets's *Series in Banach Spaces*.
- **Further reading:** [Albiac and Kalton, *Topics in Banach Space Theory* (Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics, Crossref record)](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Albiac+Kalton+Topics+in+Banach+Space+Theory&rows=3): Monteiro cites it for the Bessaga–Pełczyński theorem and the basic facts on unconditionally convergent series ([Monteiro, arXiv:1501.05196](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.05196)).
references.MSC 41 - Approximations and expansions:
## Reference
### Overview
Approximation theory studies how functions can best be approximated by simpler functions and how to quantify the errors introduced; what counts as "best" and "simpler" depends on the application. A typical goal is to minimize the maximum absolute error of a polynomial approximation over an interval. ([Wikipedia: Approximation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_theory))

In MSC2020, section 41-XX, "Approximations and expansions", has a single research subdivision, 41Axx, alongside the standard reference, exposition, history, software, proceedings, and research-data codes. The section points elsewhere for neighbouring material: approximation in the complex domain (30E05, 30E10), trigonometric approximation and interpolation (42A10, 42A15), and numerical approximation (65Dxx). ([MSC2020 41-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41-XX))

### Scope
The subdivision 41Axx covers interpolation, approximation by polynomials, splines, rational functions and Padé approximants, rates of convergence and inverse theorems, best approximation and Chebyshev systems, approximation by operators, quadratures, series and asymptotic expansions, multidimensional problems, and abstract approximation in normed linear spaces. ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx))

Trefethen's *Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice* illustrates the field's link to computation: it focuses on Chebyshev approximation of nonperiodic functions on an interval, emphasizes topics close to numerical algorithms, and illustrates everything with Chebfun. ([ATAP](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/trefethen/ATAP/))

### Key concepts
- [Approximations and expansions (41Axx)](node:MSC%2041Axx%20-%20Approximations%20and%20expansions): the section's only research subdivision. ([MSC2020 41-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41-XX))
- Weierstrass approximation theorem: for a continuous real-valued $f$ on $[a, b]$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a polynomial $p$ with $|f(x) - p(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $x \in [a, b]$. ([Wikipedia: Stone–Weierstrass theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem))
- Stone–Weierstrass theorem: if $X$ is compact Hausdorff and $A$ is a subalgebra of $C(X, \mathbb{R})$ containing a nonzero constant function, then $A$ is dense in $C(X, \mathbb{R})$ if and only if $A$ separates points. ([Wikipedia: Stone–Weierstrass theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem))
- Bernstein polynomials: $B_n(f)(x) = \sum_{\nu=0}^{n} f(\nu/n) \binom{n}{\nu} x^\nu (1-x)^{n-\nu}$ converges uniformly to continuous $f$ on $[0, 1]$, giving a constructive proof of the Weierstrass theorem. ([Wikipedia: Bernstein polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein_polynomial))
- Equioscillation theorem: for continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$, a polynomial $g$ of degree at most $n$ minimizes $\|f - g\|_\infty$ if and only if the error attains $\pm\|f - g\|_\infty$ with alternating signs at $n + 2$ points. ([Wikipedia: Equioscillation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equioscillation_theorem))
- Jackson's inequality: if $f$ has a continuous $k$-th derivative, the best polynomial approximation error of degree $n$ is bounded by a constant times $(n+1)^{-k}\|f^{(k)}\|$; for merely continuous $f$, convergence can be arbitrarily slow. ([Wikipedia: Stone–Weierstrass theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem))
- Lebesgue constant: the operator norm of polynomial interpolation at given nodes; the interpolant is at most a factor $\Lambda_n + 1$ worse than the best approximation. It grows exponentially for equispaced nodes and logarithmically for Chebyshev nodes. ([Wikipedia: Lebesgue constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_constant))
- Remez algorithm: an iterative algorithm that computes the best polynomial approximation by driving the error to $N + 2$ level extrema. ([Wikipedia: Approximation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_theory))
- [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence) and [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces): series expansions and abstract approximation in normed linear spaces are both classified here. ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx))
- [Numerical analysis](node:MSC%2065%20-%20Numerical%20analysis): numerical approximation is cross-referenced to 65Dxx. ([MSC2020 41-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41-XX))

### History
Weierstrass published his approximation theorem in 1885, and Marshall Stone generalized it and simplified its proof in papers of 1937 and 1948. ([Wikipedia: Stone–Weierstrass theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem)) Bernstein introduced his polynomials in 1912 in a constructive proof of the Weierstrass theorem. ([Wikipedia: Bernstein polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein_polynomial)) The equioscillation characterization of best approximation is attributed to Chebyshev. ([Wikipedia: Equioscillation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equioscillation_theorem))

Computation remains a driver. The AAA algorithm of Nakatsukasa, Sète and Trefethen (2018) computes rational approximations on real or complex point sets by combining a barycentric representation with greedy selection of support points; the paper is classified under 41A20 and 65D15. ([arXiv:1612.00337](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00337))

### Open problems
Optimal interpolation nodes, those minimizing the Lebesgue constant, are not known explicitly in general: optimal nodes are known only for small cases ($n = 2$, Schurer and Rack–Vajda; $n = 3$, Rack and Rack–Vajda), and the general problem is described as still an intriguing topic. ([Wikipedia: Lebesgue constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_constant))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Approximation theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_theory): minimax approximation, Chebyshev expansions, and the Remez algorithm.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 section 41-XX (AMS)](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41-XX): official codes and cross-references.
- **Learn:** [Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/trefethen/ATAP/): book page with the first six chapters online.
- **Primary:** [Nakatsukasa, Sète, Trefethen, The AAA algorithm for rational approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00337): a rational approximation algorithm with Matlab code and applications.
references.MSC 41Axx - Approximations and expansion:
## Reference
### Overview
41Axx is the only research subdivision of MSC2020 section 41-XX. Its codes split approximation theory by the approximating class (polynomials, splines, rational functions, operators), by the question asked (rates, inverse theorems, best approximation, saturation, best constants, widths), and by the setting (multidimensional, weighted, abstract normed spaces). ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx))

The organizing framework is the pairing of direct and inverse theorems. A direct (Jackson) inequality bounds the error of best approximation $E_n(f)_X$ by a smoothness quantity, and an inverse (Bernstein) inequality bounds the smoothness of approximants by their norm; together they identify the functions approximable at a given rate with an interpolation space. ([DeVore, *Nonlinear approximation*, §4.3](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf)) DeVore's survey of nonlinear approximation (from nonlinear manifolds rather than linear spaces) studies what advantages it has over linear methods, measured by the rate of approximation. ([DeVore](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf))

### Scope
The codes are: 41A05 interpolation; 41A10 polynomials; 41A15 splines; 41A17 Bernstein, Jackson and Nikol'skiĭ-type inequalities; 41A20 rational functions; 41A21 Padé approximation; 41A25 rate of convergence, degree of approximation; 41A27 inverse theorems; 41A28 simultaneous approximation; 41A29 approximation with constraints; 41A30 other special function classes; 41A35 approximation by operators; 41A36 approximation by positive operators; 41A40 saturation; 41A44 best constants; 41A45 arbitrary linear expressions; 41A46 arbitrary nonlinear expressions, widths and entropy; 41A50 best approximation, Chebyshev systems; 41A52 uniqueness of best approximation; 41A55 approximate quadratures; 41A58 series expansions (Taylor, Lidstone, not Fourier); 41A60 asymptotic expansions; 41A63 multidimensional problems (with a second 41 code); 41A65 abstract approximation theory; 41A80 remainders; 41A81 weighted approximation; 41A99. ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx))

The heading note of 41Axx sends neighbouring topics elsewhere ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx)):
- approximation theory in the complex domain to 30E05 and 30E10;
- trigonometric approximation and interpolation to 42A10 and 42A15 (41A10 likewise points to 42A10 for trigonometric polynomials, and 41A05 cross-refers to 42A15 and 65D05);
- numerical approximation to 65Dxx.

### Key concepts
- **Chebyshev equioscillation (41A50).** For continuous $f$ on $[a,b]$, a polynomial $g$ of degree at most $n$ minimizes $\|f-g\|_\infty$ if and only if there are $n+2$ points $a\le x_0<\dots<x_{n+1}\le b$ with $f(x_i)-g(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^i\|f-g\|_\infty$, $\sigma=\pm1$. ([Wikipedia: Equioscillation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equioscillation_theorem)) See [Chebyshev Approximation](node:Chebyshev%20Approximation).
- **Jackson's direct theorems (41A17, 41A25).** If $f$ is $2\pi$-periodic and $r$ times differentiable with $|f^{(r)}|\le1$, there are trigonometric polynomials $T_{n-1}$ of degree at most $n-1$ with $\|f-T_{n-1}\|\le C(r)/n^r$, the sharp constant being given by the Akhiezer–Krein–Favard theorem. For continuous periodic $f$ and the $k$-th modulus of smoothness, $E_n(f)\le c(k)\,\omega_k(1/n,f)$; Jackson proved $k=1$, Zygmund and Akhiezer $k=2$, and Stechkin (1967) $k>2$. ([Wikipedia: Jackson's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson%27s_inequality)) The modulus is $\omega_r(f,t)_p=\sup_{|h|\le t}\|\Delta_h^r(f,\cdot)\|_{L_p}$. ([DeVore, §4.5](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf))
- **Bernstein's inverse theorem (41A27).** If $f$ is $2\pi$-periodic and trigonometric polynomials $P_n$ of degree $n$ satisfy $\|f-P_n\|_\infty\le k(f)/n^{r+\alpha}$ for $n\ge n_0$, with $r\in\mathbb N$ and $0<\alpha<1$, then $f=P_{n_0}+\varphi$ where $\varphi^{(r)}$ is bounded and $\alpha$-Hölder continuous. Bernstein proved the first such results in 1912. ([Wikipedia: Bernstein's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_theorem_%28approximation_theory%29))
- **Approximation spaces as interpolation spaces.** Suppose $Y\hookrightarrow X$ and the approximating sets $X_n$ satisfy a Jackson inequality $E_n(f)_X\le Cn^{-r}|f|_Y$ and a Bernstein inequality $|S|_Y\le Cn^r\|S\|_X$ for $S\in X_n$. Then for $0<\gamma<r$ and $0<q\le\infty$, the approximation space $\mathcal A^\gamma_q(X)$ equals the real interpolation space $(X,Y)_{\gamma/r,q}$ with equivalent norms. ([DeVore, Theorem 1](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf))
- **Ditzian–Totik moduli (algebraic polynomials on $[-1,1]$).** With $\varphi(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, the modulus $\omega^\varphi_k(f,\delta)_p$ uses differences $\Delta^k_{h\varphi(x)}f$ with step adapted to the endpoints, and $E_n(f)_p\le C\,\omega^\varphi_k(f,1/n)_p$ for $0<p\le\infty$ and $n>4k$. ([Kolomoitsev–Lomako–Prestin, arXiv:1602.05036](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1602.05036))
- **Korovkin's theorem and Bernstein polynomials (41A36).** If $L_n$ are positive linear operators on $C([0,1])$ and $L_n(g)\to g$ uniformly for $g\in\{1,x,x^2\}$, then $L_n(f)\to f$ uniformly for every $f\in C([0,1])$. The Bernstein operators $B_n(f)(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n f(k/n)\binom nk x^k(1-x)^{n-k}$ satisfy $B_n1=1$, $B_nx=x$, $B_nx^2=\frac{n-1}{n}x^2+\frac1nx$, so $B_nf\to f$ uniformly, a constructive proof of the Weierstrass theorem. ([Altomare, arXiv:1009.2601, Theorems 3.1 and 3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.2601)) Korovkin's 1953 paper is the source of the theory. ([Wikipedia: Korovkin approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korovkin_approximation)) See [Stone–Weierstrass Theorem](node:Stone–Weierstrass%20Theorem).
- **Kolmogorov $n$-widths (41A46).** For compact $K$ in a Banach space $X$, $d_n(K)=\inf_{\dim X_n=n}\sup_{f\in K}E(f,X_n)_X$, the infimum over all $n$-dimensional linear subspaces, measures the best possible linear method. The $n$-width of a Besov ball of smoothness $\alpha$ is never better than $O(n^{-\alpha})$; by Kashin (1977) there are classes in $L_p$, $2<p\le\infty$, with width $\asymp n^{-\alpha}$ that classical linear methods cannot reach. ([DeVore, §9](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf))
- **Nonlinear $n$-term approximation.** On $\mathbb R$, for wavelet bases with enough vanishing moments and smoothness, $1<p<\infty$, $s>0$ and $1/\tau=s+1/p$, the $n$-term error satisfies $\sigma_n(f)_p\le C|f|_{B^s_\tau(L_\tau)}n^{-s}$, with a matching Bernstein inequality. ([DeVore, Corollary 1 and Theorem 6](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf)) See [Frames and Wavelet Bases](node:Frames%20and%20Wavelet%20Bases), [Orthogonal Expansions and Wavelets](node:Orthogonal%20Expansions%20and%20Wavelets).
- **Rational approximation of $|x|$ (41A20).** Bernstein showed $\lim_m m\,E_{m,0}(|x|,[-1,1])=\beta\approx0.28016$ for polynomials. Newman (1964) proved $\tfrac12e^{-9\sqrt n}\le E_{nn}(|x|,[-1,1])\le3e^{-\sqrt n}$ for rational functions of type $(n,n)$, $n\ge4$. Stahl proved $\lim_n e^{2\pi\sqrt{\alpha n}}E_{nn}(x^\alpha,[0,1])=4^{1+\alpha}|\sin\pi\alpha|$ for each $\alpha>0$, which for $|x|$ gives $E_{nn}(|x|,[-1,1])=8e^{-\pi\sqrt n}(1+o(1))$. ([Stahl, arXiv:math/9301217](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/math/9301217)) See [Rational Approximation](node:Rational%20Approximation).
- **Padé approximation (41A21).** For integers $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, the $[m/n]$ Padé approximant of $f$ is the rational function $R=P/Q$ with $\deg P\le m$, $\deg Q\le n$ and $Q(0)=1$ whose Maclaurin series agrees with that of $f$ to the highest possible order, so that $f(x)-R(x)$ begins at order $x^{m+n+1}$. ([Wikipedia: Padé approximant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pad%C3%A9_approximant))
- **Remez algorithm.** To compute a best uniform polynomial approximation of degree $N$, each iteration solves $N+2$ linear equations for the coefficients and the error level at $N+2$ test points, then moves the test points to the actual local extrema of the error; it is usually started from the extrema of the Chebyshev polynomial $T_{N+1}$ and converges to an error with $N+2$ level extrema, as the equioscillation theorem requires. ([Wikipedia: Approximation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_theory))
- **AAA algorithm (41A20, 65D15).** Nakatsukasa, Sète and Trefethen's algorithm for rational approximation on real or complex point sets uses a barycentric representation that interpolates at support points, chosen greedily to avoid exponential instabilities; it needs no user-supplied parameters. ([Nakatsukasa–Sète–Trefethen, arXiv:1612.00337](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00337))
- **Interpolation and Lebesgue constants (41A05).** The interpolant's error is at most $(\Lambda_n+1)$ times the best-approximation error. $\Lambda_n$ grows exponentially for equispaced nodes and lies between $\frac2\pi\log(n+1)+a$ and $\frac2\pi\log(n+1)+1$, $a\approx0.9625$, for Chebyshev nodes. ([Wikipedia: Lebesgue constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_constant)) Kilgore (1978) proved Bernstein's conjecture that optimal nodes are characterized by equioscillation of the local maxima of the Lebesgue function, and de Boor and Pinkus proved Erdős's conjecture, which also gives uniqueness. ([Szokol, arXiv:2508.18029](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.18029v2)) See [Polynomial Interpolation](node:Polynomial%20Interpolation), [Polynomial and Spline Approximation](node:Polynomial%20and%20Spline%20Approximation).
- [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces), [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis), [Numerical approximation (65Dxx)](node:MSC%2065Dxx%20-%20Numerical%20approximation%20and%20computational%20geometry%20%28primarily%20algorithms%29): the settings of abstract approximation (41A65) and of smoothness spaces, the trigonometric neighbour, and the algorithmic neighbour. ([MSC2020 41Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx))

### History
The equioscillation theorem is attributed to Chebyshev. ([Wikipedia: Equioscillation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equioscillation_theorem)) Padé developed his approximants around 1890, though the idea goes back to Frobenius, who studied rational approximations of power series. ([Wikipedia: Padé approximant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pad%C3%A9_approximant)) Remez published his algorithm in 1934. ([Wikipedia: Approximation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_theory)) Bernstein introduced his polynomials to give the first constructive proof of the Weierstrass approximation theorem; Korovkin's theorem dates from 1953, with forerunners by Bohman and Popoviciu. ([Altomare, arXiv:1009.2601](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.2601)) Bernstein's work on best polynomial approximation of $|x|$ and $|x|^\alpha$ appeared between 1909 and 1938, and rational approximation of $|x|$ began with Newman in 1964; Stahl repeats an earlier remark that Newman's bound follows quickly from Zolotarev's 1877 work. ([Stahl, arXiv:math/9301217](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/math/9301217)) DeVore and Lorentz's *Constructive Approximation* appeared in Springer's Grundlehren in 1993. ([Crossref metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=DeVore+Lorentz+Constructive+Approximation+Grundlehren&rows=3)) Trefethen's *Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice* (2013; extended edition 2019) treats Chebyshev approximation with an emphasis on algorithms. ([ATAP](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/trefethen/ATAP/))

### Open problems
- **Explicit optimal interpolation nodes.** Although Kilgore and de Boor–Pinkus characterized optimal nodes by equioscillation, no exact description is known for general $n$. ([Szokol, arXiv:2508.18029](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.18029v2)) Optimal node sets are known for $n=2$ (Schurer; Rack and Vajda) and $n=3$ (Rack; Rack and Vajda), and the search for optimal nodes remains open. ([Wikipedia: Lebesgue constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_constant)) Whether the Bernstein and Erdős characterizations hold for exponential and Hermite weights is also open. ([Szokol](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.18029v2))
- **Bernstein's constant.** Writing $\beta(\alpha)=\lim_m m^\alpha E_{m,0}(|x|^\alpha,[-1,1])$, Stahl (1993) records that no explicit expression for $\beta(\alpha)$ is known; Bernstein asked whether $\beta=\beta(1)$ is expressible in known transcendentals, and his guess $\beta=1/(2\sqrt\pi)$ was disproved by extensive high-precision calculations. ([Stahl, arXiv:math/9301217](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/math/9301217))
- **Widths for highly nonlinear methods.** In his 1998 survey DeVore calls the lack of a concept of widths measuring the performance of $n$-term approximation from dictionaries "an important open problem", and describes the smoothness conditions governing piecewise polynomial approximation on free triangulations as unsolved. ([DeVore](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 41Axx (AMS)](https://mathscinet.ams.org/msc/msc2020.html?t=41Axx): the full list of codes and cross-references.
- **Reference:** [Approximation theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_theory): minimax approximation and the Remez algorithm.
- **Reference:** [Jackson's inequality (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson%27s_inequality) and [Lebesgue constant (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_constant): direct theorems and interpolation.
- **Learn:** [Trefethen, *Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice*](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/trefethen/ATAP/): book page with the first six chapters online.
- **Primary:** [DeVore, Nonlinear approximation (Acta Numerica 1998)](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf): survey of Jackson–Bernstein theory, interpolation spaces, wavelets, widths and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Altomare, Korovkin-type theorems and approximation by positive linear operators](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.2601): survey of 41A36.
- **Primary:** [Nakatsukasa, Sète, Trefethen, The AAA algorithm for rational approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00337): a rational approximation algorithm, classified 41A20 and 65D15.
- **Primary:** [Stahl, Best uniform rational approximation of $x^\alpha$ on $[0,1]$](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/math/9301217): sharp asymptotics for rational approximation and the history from Bernstein to Newman.
- **Further reading:** [DeVore and Lorentz, *Constructive Approximation* (Springer Grundlehren, 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=DeVore+Lorentz+Constructive+Approximation+Grundlehren&rows=3): DeVore's survey refers to it (Chapter 7, Theorem 5.1) for reversing the Jackson estimate with a Bernstein inequality ([DeVore, §4.3](https://people.math.sc.edu/devore/publications/nlacta.pdf)).
references.MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean:
## Reference
### Overview
Harmonic analysis grew out of the study of harmonic functions and their boundary behaviour. It decomposes functions and measures by symmetry, scale, spectrum or oscillation, and proves estimates for the operators those decompositions produce: maximal functions, singular integrals, Littlewood–Paley square functions and spectral decompositions. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis))

Classical Fourier analysis rests on $L^2$ orthogonality and the [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem): the Fourier transform on $L^1\cap L^2$ extends to a unitary operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. ([Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform)) Harmonic analysis often studies Fourier-like decompositions where orthogonality alone is not enough; in Fourier restriction problems the estimates depend on curvature, cancellation, scaling and how wave packets overlap, and advanced restriction problems connect with Kakeya-type geometry. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis)) Decoupling theory combines linear and multilinear restriction estimates and has applications in additive combinatorics, incidence geometry and number theory. ([Bourgain–Demeter, arXiv:1403.5335](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5335); [Bourgain–Demeter–Guth, arXiv:1512.01565](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01565))

### Scope
MSC2020 42-XX, "Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces", has three second-level codes; 42Bxx sends automorphic theory mainly to 11F30. ([MSC2020 42-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 42Axx - Harmonic analysis in one variable](node:MSC%2042Axx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20one%20variable): trigonometric polynomials and approximation, convergence and summability of Fourier series, conjugate functions, lacunary series, uniqueness, almost periodic and positive definite functions. ([MSC2020 42Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Axx&btn=Current))
- [MSC 42Bxx - Harmonic analysis in several variables](node:MSC%2042Bxx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20several%20variables): Fourier transforms and multipliers on $\mathbb{R}^n$, singular and oscillatory integrals, maximal functions and Littlewood–Paley theory, $H^p$ and other function spaces, harmonic analysis and PDE. ([MSC2020 42Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Bxx&btn=Current))
- [MSC 42Cxx - Nontrigonometric harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2042Cxx%20-%20Nontrigonometric%20harmonic%20analysis): orthogonal polynomials and functions, Walsh and other special series, frames, wavelets. ([MSC2020 42Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Cxx&btn=Current))

Neighbouring sections: [MSC 43 - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis) treats locally compact groups, [Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality) and Peter–Weyl, tied to [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) and, via Tate's thesis, to number theory; [MSC 35 - Partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations) shares 42B37; [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) shares maximal inequalities through Calderón transference. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis); [MSC2020 42Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Bxx&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): Fourier series and the Fourier transform; for $f\in L^1$, $\hat f$ is bounded, uniformly continuous and vanishes at infinity. ([Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))
- **Calderón–Zygmund theorem.** An operator bounded on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ whose kernel satisfies $|K(x,y)|\lesssim|x-y|^{-n}$ with Hölder regularity off the diagonal is of weak type $(1,1)$, bounded on $L^p$ for $1<p<\infty$, and maps $L^\infty$ to BMO. The Hilbert and Riesz transforms are the model cases; see [Singular Integral Operators](node:Singular%20Integral%20Operators). ([Tao, 247A Notes 4](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/notes4.pdf))
- [Littlewood–Paley Theory](node:Littlewood–Paley%20Theory): for bumps adapted to dyadic annuli, $\|(\sum_j|\psi_j(D)f|^2)^{1/2}\|_p\sim\|f\|_p$, $1<p<\infty$; it underlies the Hörmander–Mikhlin multiplier theorem. ([Tao, 247A Notes 4](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/notes4.pdf))
- **$H^1$–BMO duality.** BMO is the dual of the Hardy space $H^1$ (Fefferman 1971, Fefferman–Stein 1972); see [Hardy and Bergman Spaces](node:Hardy%20and%20Bergman%20Spaces). ([Wikipedia: Bounded mean oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation))
- **Weights and the $A_2$ theorem.** The maximal operator is bounded on $L^p(w)$ iff $w\in A_p$ (Muckenhoupt).
