([Wikipedia: Muckenhoupt weights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muckenhoupt_weights)) Every Calderón–Zygmund operator satisfies $\|T\|_{L^2(w)\to L^2(w)}\le C(T)[w]_{A_2}$, sharp in $[w]_{A_2}$ (Hytönen). ([arXiv:1007.4330](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1007.4330))
- [Carleson's Theorem](node:Carleson's%20Theorem): Fourier series of $L^2$ functions converge a.e. (1966), extended by Hunt to $L^p$, $p>1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Ball multiplier theorem.** For $n>1$ (Fefferman 1971), partial Fourier integrals over expanding balls need not converge in $L^p$, $p\ne2$; the proof uses Besicovitch sets. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set))
- **Restriction, Bochner–Riesz, Kakeya.** Restriction conjecture: for the sphere or paraboloid, $\|(F\,d\sigma)^\vee\|_{L^{p'}(\mathbb{R}^n)}\lesssim\|F\|_{L^{q'}(S)}$ whenever $p'>2n/(n-1)$ and $(n+1)/p'\le(n-1)/q$; Stein–Tomas proves the $q'=2$ case, and restriction implies Kakeya. ([Tao, arXiv:math/0311181](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0311181)) Bochner–Riesz conjecture: $(1-|\xi|^2)_+^\delta$ is an $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ multiplier iff $\delta>\max(n|1/p-1/2|-1/2,0)$. ([Wikipedia: Bochner–Riesz mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Riesz_mean)) Kakeya conjecture: sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ containing a unit segment in every direction have Hausdorff dimension $n$. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set))
- **Decoupling.** Bourgain–Demeter proved $\ell^2$ decoupling for compact hypersurfaces with positive definite second fundamental form and for the cone (2014). ([arXiv:1403.5335](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5335)) A sharp decoupling inequality for curves gave the main conjecture of Vinogradov's mean value theorem for degrees above three (Bourgain–Demeter–Guth). ([arXiv:1512.01565](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01565))
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) and [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): Riesz potentials and singular integrals give Sobolev embeddings and regularity estimates. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis))

### History
Fourier introduced trigonometric series in 1807 to solve the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation) and published *Théorie analytique de la chaleur* in 1822; Dirichlet (1829) and Riemann (1854, published 1867) made the theory precise. ([Wikipedia: Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series)) In the setting of [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration), Kolmogorov's 1923 $L^1$ function with almost-everywhere divergent Fourier series and Carleson's 1966 $L^2$ theorem bracket the one-dimensional answer. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))

Stein's *Singular Integrals and Differentiability Properties of Functions* (1970), Stein and Weiss's *Introduction to Fourier Analysis on Euclidean Spaces* (1971) and Stein's *Harmonic Analysis: Real-variable Methods, Orthogonality and Oscillatory Integrals* (1993) are the books on which the modern presentation of the subject draws. ([Wikipedia: Elias M. Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_M._Stein)) ([Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis)) Since 2010 the area has seen Hytönen's $A_2$ theorem, Bourgain–Demeter decoupling, and Wang–Zahl's 2025 proof that Kakeya sets in $\mathbb{R}^3$ have Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension 3. ([arXiv:1007.4330](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1007.4330); [arXiv:1403.5335](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5335); [arXiv:2502.17655](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655))

### Open problems
- **Restriction conjecture.** Tao's survey records the restriction conjecture as open; it is solved for the sphere and paraboloid in two dimensions. ([Tao, arXiv:math/0311181](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0311181))
- **Bochner–Riesz conjecture.** Completely resolved for $n=2$ but only partially answered for $n\ge3$. ([Wikipedia: Bochner–Riesz mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Riesz_mean))
- **Kakeya conjecture.** Wikipedia states it remains open for $n>3$ (the case $n=3$ is the February 2025 Wang–Zahl arXiv preprint); it also reports October 2026 OpenAI preprints claiming the four-dimensional case and the local smoothing conjecture, which are reported and unconfirmed. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set); [arXiv:2502.17655](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655))
- **Spherical partial sums.** A.e. convergence of spherical partial sums of multiple Fourier series of $L^2$ functions is open. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **A.e. convergence on $L\log L$ in one variable.** Whether the Fourier series of every $f\in L\log L(\mathbb T)$ converges a.e. is open; Lie states it as a conjecture, with Antonov's $L\log L\log\log\log L$ the best known result. ([Lie, arXiv:1204.6542](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1204.6542))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Harmonic analysis (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis): Euclidean and abstract harmonic analysis and their connections.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 42-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42-XX&btn=Current): official classification.
- **Learn:** [Tao, Math 247A: Fourier analysis (UCLA)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/): graduate course notes on Calderón–Zygmund theory, Littlewood–Paley theory and function spaces, including Sobolev spaces.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.103 Fourier Analysis](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-103-fourier-analysis-fall-2013/): Lebesgue integration, Fourier series and integrals.
- **Primary:** [Tao, Recent progress on the restriction conjecture](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0311181): survey of restriction, Kakeya and bilinear methods.
- **Primary:** [Bourgain–Demeter, proof of the $\ell^2$ decoupling conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5335): the decoupling theorem.
- **Primary:** [Hytönen, The sharp weighted bound for general Calderón–Zygmund operators](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1007.4330): the $A_2$ theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4939-1194-3) and [Modern Fourier Analysis](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4939-1230-8) (GTM, Springer 2014); Stein–Weiss, *Introduction to Fourier Analysis on Euclidean Spaces* (Princeton 1971) ([Wikipedia: Elias M. Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_M._Stein)); [Duoandikoetxea, Fourier Analysis (AMS GSM 29)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/029).
references.MSC 42Axx - Harmonic analysis in one var:
## Reference
### Overview
Harmonic analysis in one variable studies Fourier series on the circle $\mathbb{T}$ and Fourier transforms on the line. For a $P$-periodic integrable function the coefficients are $c_n = \frac1P\int_0^P s(x)e^{-2\pi i n x/P}\,dx$; Parseval gives $\frac1P\int_P|s|^2=\sum|c_n|^2$ for square-integrable $s$, and the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma gives $c_n\to0$ for integrable $s$. ([Wikipedia: Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series))

The research questions are about the sense in which a function is represented by its series. The Dirichlet kernel has $L^1$ norm growing like $\tfrac{4}{\pi^2}\log N$, continuous functions can have divergent Fourier series, and the answers split between pointwise, uniform, norm, and summability convergence. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series)) The Hilbert transform is the prototypical singular integral operator, and Calderón–Zygmund theory extends its $L^2$ boundedness to other $L^p$ spaces. ([Tao, 247A Notes 4 (UCLA)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/notes4.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 42Axx covers: trigonometric polynomials, inequalities and extremal problems (42A05); trigonometric approximation and interpolation (42A10, 42A15); Fourier coefficients and special Fourier series (42A16); convergence and absolute convergence (42A20); summability (42A24); trigonometric series of special types such as positive or monotone coefficients (42A32); Fourier and Fourier–Stieltjes transforms (42A38); multipliers (42A45); conjugate functions, conjugate series and singular integrals (42A50); lacunary series and Riesz products (42A55); probabilistic methods (42A61); uniqueness, Riemann theory and localization (42A63); completeness of sets of functions (42A65); trigonometric moment problems (42A70); classical almost periodic and mean periodic functions (42A75); positive definite functions (42A82); and convolution and factorization (42A85). ([MSC2020 42Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Axx&btn=Current))

Neighbours:
- [MSC 42Bxx - Harmonic analysis in several variables](node:MSC%2042Bxx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20several%20variables): the sibling subfield for several variables. ([MSC2020 42-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 42Cxx - Nontrigonometric harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2042Cxx%20-%20Nontrigonometric%20harmonic%20analysis): expansions in other orthogonal systems, including Walsh functions and wavelets (42C10, 42C40). ([MSC2020 42Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Cxx&btn=Current))
- [MSC 43 - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis): harmonic analysis on general groups; 42A75 (classical almost periodic functions) carries a "See also 43A60". ([MSC2020 42Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Axx&btn=Current))
- [MSC 11 - Number theory](node:MSC%2011%20-%20Number%20theory): 42A16 directs automorphic theory mainly to 11F30. ([MSC2020 42Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Axx&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) on $\mathbb{T}$ and $\mathbb{R}$; in $L^2$ the partial sums converge in norm, and for $1<p<\infty$ they converge in $L^p$, failing for $p=1,\infty$. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series))
- **Fejér's theorem and summability kernels (42A24).** The Cesàro means $\sigma_n f=\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}S_kf = F_n * f$ use the Fejér kernel $F_n(x)=\frac1n\frac{\sin^2(nx/2)}{\sin^2(x/2)}\ge0$, and $\sigma_nf\to f$ uniformly for continuous $2\pi$-periodic $f$. ([Wikipedia: Fejér's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fej%C3%A9r%27s_theorem)) Fejér means also converge in $L^1$ for integrable $f$ and show no Gibbs phenomenon; positivity of the kernel is what partial sums lack. See [Cesàro and Abel Summation](node:Cesàro%20and%20Abel%20Summation). ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series))
- **Conjugate function (42A50).** On $\mathbb{R}$ the Hilbert transform is the principal-value convolution with $1/(\pi t)$, a multiplier operator with symbol $-i\,\mathrm{sgn}\,\omega$, and it produces harmonic conjugates; its circle analogue, with the Hilbert kernel $\cot((x-t)/2)$, is used to study the conjugate function of a Fourier series. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform)) **Kolmogorov:** $f\mapsto\tilde f$ is of weak type $(1,1)$ on $\mathbb{T}$. ([Asmar–Montgomery-Smith, arXiv:math/9401207](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/9401207)) **M. Riesz (1928):** the Hilbert transform is bounded on $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ for $1<p<\infty$. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform)) In Calderón–Zygmund language: every Calderón–Zygmund operator (an $L^2$-bounded operator with a singular kernel satisfying Hölder-type regularity) is of weak type $(1,1)$, and interpolation gives strong type $(p,p)$; writing partial Fourier integrals as modulated Hilbert transforms gives $S_Nf\to f$ in $L^p(\mathbb{R})$, $1<p<\infty$. ([Tao, 247A Notes 4 (UCLA)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/notes4.pdf)) Pichorides found the sharp constant $\tan(\pi/2p)$ for $1<p\le2$ and $\cot(\pi/2p)$ for $p>2$; $H$ maps $L^\infty$ to BMO, not to $L^\infty$. See [Singular Integral Operators](node:Singular%20Integral%20Operators). ([Wikipedia: Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform))
- **Hardy–Littlewood maximal function.** $Mf$ is of weak type $(1,1)$ and bounded on $L^p$, $1<p\le\infty$, and yields the [Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem](node:Lebesgue%20Differentiation%20Theorem). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_maximal_function)) On the line the sharp weak $(1,1)$ constant of the centred operator is the largest root of $12C^2-22C+5=0$, $C\approx1.5675$ (Melas 2003), and the $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ norm of the uncentred operator is known exactly (Grafakos–Montgomery-Smith 1997). ([Annals 157 (2003)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2003/157-2/p08); [arXiv:math/9412218](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9412218))
- **Hardy spaces on the circle.** For $p\ge1$, $H^p(\mathbb{D})$ is identified with the closed subspace of $L^p(\mathbb{T})$ of functions with vanishing negative Fourier coefficients; $H^2$ is unitarily equivalent to $\ell^2(\mathbb{N})$; real $H^1$ is a proper subspace of $L^1$ with dual BMO. See [Hardy and Bergman Spaces](node:Hardy%20and%20Bergman%20Spaces). ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space))
- [Carleson's Theorem](node:Carleson's%20Theorem) (42A20): $S_Nf\to f$ a.e. for $f\in L^p$, $p>1$ (Carleson 1966, Hunt), sharp against Kolmogorov's $L^1$ example and Kahane–Katznelson for continuous functions. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Uniqueness (42A63).** $E\subset\mathbb{T}$ is a set of uniqueness if every trigonometric series converging to $0$ off $E$ has all coefficients zero. The empty set is one (Riemann) and so is every countable closed set (Cantor); Menshov (1916) found a null set of multiplicity; for Cantor-type sets with ratio $\xi$, uniqueness holds iff $1/\xi$ is a Pisot number (Salem–Zygmund). ([Wikipedia: Set of uniqueness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_of_uniqueness)) Piatetski-Shapiro (1954) constructed a compact set of multiplicity that supports no measure with Fourier coefficients tending to zero. ([Lev–Olevskii, arXiv:0908.0447](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0908.0447))

### History
Fourier introduced trigonometric series in his 1807 memoir to solve the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation) and published *Théorie analytique de la chaleur* in 1822; Bessel used them independently for Kepler's equation in 1819; Dirichlet (1829) made the results precise; Riemann's 1854 habilitation (published 1867) began the theory of trigonometric series. ([Wikipedia: Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series))

Cantor's extension of Riemann's uniqueness theorem to countable closed sets led to his development of [set theory](node:Set%20Theory). ([Wikipedia: Set of uniqueness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_of_uniqueness)) [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration) then reframed the convergence problem: du Bois-Reymond (1873) gave a continuous function with a divergent Fourier series, Kolmogorov an $L^1$ function diverging almost everywhere and then everywhere. ([Wikipedia: Convergence of Fourier series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_Fourier_series)) F. Riesz introduced Hardy spaces in 1923, motivated by Hardy's 1915 paper, and M. Riesz proved $L^p$ boundedness of the Hilbert transform in 1928. ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space); [Wikipedia: Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform)) Carleson settled Luzin's $L^2$ conjecture in *Acta Math.* 116 (1966). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392815))

### Open problems
- **A.e. convergence on $L\log L$.** Whether the Fourier series of every $f\in L\log L(\mathbb T)$ converges a.e. is open; Lie states it as a conjecture, with Antonov's $L\log L\log\log\log L$ the best known result. ([Lie, arXiv:1204.6542](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1204.6542)) Konyagin found everywhere-divergent series in a space just beyond $L(\log^+L)^{1/2}$, and $L\log^+L$ is the simplest candidate for a largest natural space consistent with both results. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))
- **Unions of sets of uniqueness.** Whether the union of two Borel sets of uniqueness is a set of uniqueness is listed as open. ([Wikipedia: Set of uniqueness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_of_uniqueness))
- **Maximal constants.** The best constants in the Hardy–Littlewood maximal inequalities are unknown in general, and whether a dimension-independent weak $(1,1)$ bound exists is open; the one-dimensional centred weak $(1,1)$ case is solved (Melas). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_maximal_function); [Annals 157 (2003)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2003/157-2/p08))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fourier series (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series): definitions, convergence, Parseval, history.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 42Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Axx&btn=Current): official codes.
- **Learn:** [Tao, Math 247A Notes 4: Calderón–Zygmund theory (UCLA)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/notes4.pdf): Hilbert transform, weak (1,1) and $L^p$ bounds, $L^p$ convergence of Fourier inversion, BMO, multipliers.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.103 Fourier Analysis (Jerison)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-103-fourier-analysis-fall-2013/): Lebesgue integration, Fourier series and integrals.
- **Primary:** [Melas, The best constant for centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal inequality, Annals 157 (2003)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2003/157-2/p08): sharp one-dimensional weak (1,1) constant.
- **Primary:** [Carleson 1966, Acta Math. 116 (Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02392815): almost-everywhere convergence.
- **Further reading:** [Zygmund, Trigonometric Series, 3rd ed. (CUP 2003)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781316036587) and [Katznelson, An Introduction to Harmonic Analysis, 3rd ed. (CUP 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139165372): the standard monographs.
references.MSC 42Bxx - Harmonic analysis in several:
## Reference
### Overview
Harmonic analysis in several variables studies [Fourier series](node:Fourier%20Analysis) on $\mathbb{T}^n$, the Fourier transform on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the real-variable operators built from them: singular integrals, maximal functions, multipliers, square functions and the function spaces they define. Calderón–Zygmund theory gives conditions under which singular integral operators are bounded on $L^p$, and Littlewood–Paley theory replaces the orthogonality arguments of Fourier theory with almost-orthogonality, which helps when $p\ne2$. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis))

In several variables curvature and geometry enter. In 1967 Stein found that when a measure-zero set such as a sphere has sufficient curvature, the Fourier transform of an $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ function can be restricted to it for some $p>1$, and restriction problems are connected to the Kakeya and Bochner–Riesz conjectures. ([Tao, Recent progress on the restriction conjecture](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0311181)) Besicovitch sets, which contain a unit segment in every direction yet can have measure zero, show that Fourier integrals over expanding balls need not converge in $L^p$ for $p\ne2$ when $n>1$. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set))

### Scope
MSC2020 42Bxx: Fourier series and coefficients in several variables (42B05); summability (42B08); Fourier and Fourier–Stieltjes transforms and other transforms of Fourier type (42B10); multipliers (42B15); singular and oscillatory integrals of Calderón–Zygmund type (42B20); maximal functions and Littlewood–Paley theory (42B25); $H^p$-spaces (42B30); function spaces arising in harmonic analysis (42B35); harmonic analysis and PDEs (42B37, see also 35-XX). Automorphic theory goes mainly to 11F30. ([MSC2020 42Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Bxx&btn=Current))

Neighbours:
- [MSC 42Axx - Harmonic analysis in one variable](node:MSC%2042Axx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20one%20variable): the one-dimensional theory. Partial sums over dilates of a fixed polygon reduce to the one-dimensional Carleson operator of [Carleson's Theorem](node:Carleson's%20Theorem), while over arbitrary rectangles Fefferman's example gives a bounded function whose maximal partial sum is infinite on a set of positive measure. ([Lacey, arXiv:math/0307008](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0307008))
- [MSC 42Cxx - Nontrigonometric harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2042Cxx%20-%20Nontrigonometric%20harmonic%20analysis): non-Fourier expansions (frames in 42C15, wavelets in 42C40), a separate second-level code of 42. ([MSC2020 42Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Cxx&btn=Current))
- [MSC 35 - Partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations): 42B37 is cross-listed with 35-XX; the paraboloid governs the [Schrödinger Equation](node:Schrödinger%20Equation) and the cone the [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation). ([MSC2020 42Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Bxx&btn=Current); [Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis))
- [MSC 43 - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis): Fourier analysis on locally compact groups, [Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality) and Peter–Weyl. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis))
- [Geometric Measure Theory](node:Geometric%20Measure%20Theory): Kakeya problems are questions about Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set))

### Key concepts
- **Calderón–Zygmund theorem (42B20).** A singular kernel satisfies $|K(x,y)|\lesssim|x-y|^{-n}$ and Hölder regularity of order $\sigma>0$ in each variable away from the diagonal. If $T$ is bounded on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $Tf(y)=\int K(x,y)f(x)\,dx$ off the support of $f$, then $T$ is of weak type $(1,1)$, bounded on $L^p$ for $1<p<\infty$, and maps $L^\infty$ to BMO. See [Singular Integral Operators](node:Singular%20Integral%20Operators). ([Tao, 247A Notes 4](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/notes4.pdf))
- **Multipliers and [Littlewood–Paley Theory](node:Littlewood–Paley%20Theory) (42B15, 42B25).** Hörmander–Mikhlin: if $|\nabla^k m(\xi)|\lesssim|\xi|^{-k}$ for $0\le k\le n+2$, then $m(D)$ is bounded on $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. For bumps $\psi_j$ adapted to $|\xi|\sim2^j$ with $\sum|\psi_j|^2\sim1$, $\|(\sum_j|\psi_j(D)f|^2)^{1/2}\|_p\sim_{p,n}\|f\|_p$. ([Tao, 247A Notes 4](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/notes4.pdf))
- **Maximal functions (42B25).** The Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator is weak $(1,1)$ and $L^p$-bounded for $p>1$, with $L^p$ constants independent of dimension for $1<p<\infty$ (Stein). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_maximal_function)) Stein's spherical maximal theorem: for $n\ge3$, $\sup_{t>0}|f*d\sigma_t|$ is bounded on $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ iff $p>n/(n-1)$; Bourgain extended it to $n=2$. ([Gorrell, ANU harmonic analysis lecture 5](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/~plyung/math3349/Noah2.pdf))
- **$H^1$–BMO duality (42B30, 42B35).** Fefferman (1971) and Fefferman–Stein (1972) proved that BMO is the dual of the Hardy space $H^1$; VMO has dual $H^1$; John–Nirenberg gives exponential integrability of BMO functions. See [Hardy and Bergman Spaces](node:Hardy%20and%20Bergman%20Spaces). ([Wikipedia: Bounded mean oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation))
- **Muckenhoupt weights and the $A_2$ theorem.** $w\in A_p$ iff the maximal operator is bounded on $L^p(w)$ (Muckenhoupt 1972), and Calderón–Zygmund operators are bounded on $L^p(w)$ for $w\in A_p$. ([Wikipedia: Muckenhoupt weights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muckenhoupt_weights)) Hytönen proved the sharp linear bound $\|Tf\|_{L^2(w)}\le C(T)\,[w]_{A_2}\|f\|_{L^2(w)}$ for every Calderón–Zygmund operator, hence $[w]_{A_p}^{\max(1,1/(p-1))}$ on $L^p(w)$, by representing $T$ as an average of dyadic shifts. ([Hytönen, arXiv:1007.4330](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1007.4330))
- **Fourier restriction (42B10).** For the sphere or paraboloid $S$ the extension estimate $\|(F\,d\sigma)^\vee\|_{L^{p'}(\mathbb{R}^n)}\lesssim\|F\|_{L^{q'}(S)}$ requires $p'>2n/(n-1)$ and $(n+1)/p'\le(n-1)/q$; the restriction conjecture says these suffice. Stein–Tomas gives the $L^2$ case $q'=2$, $p'\ge2(n+1)/(n-1)$, and the conjecture is solved for $n=2$. ([Tao, arXiv:math/0311181](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0311181)) Guth's polynomial partitioning gives $\|E_Sf\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^3)}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^\infty(S)}$ for $p>3.25$. ([Guth, arXiv:1407.1916](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.1916)) Bourgain–Demeter proved $\ell^2$ decoupling for compact hypersurfaces with positive definite second fundamental form and for the cone, with applications to Strichartz estimates on tori and number theory. ([arXiv:1403.5335](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5335))
- **Ball multiplier and Bochner–Riesz.** Fefferman (1971) used Besicovitch sets to show that partial Fourier integrals over expanding balls need not converge in $L^p$, $p\ne2$, for $n>1$. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set)) The Bochner–Riesz multiplier $(1-|\xi|^2)_+^\delta$ is conjectured bounded on $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ iff $\delta>\max(n|1/p-1/2|-1/2,0)$; necessity is known and $n=2$ is resolved. ([Wikipedia: Bochner–Riesz mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Riesz_mean))

### History
Harmonic analysis emerged from the study of harmonic functions and their boundary behaviour; Calderón–Zygmund theory became a main development in the treatment of singular integral operators, and Littlewood–Paley theory decomposes functions by scale or frequency. ([Wikipedia: Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis)) John and Nirenberg introduced BMO in 1961, Fefferman–Stein identified it as the dual of $H^1$ in 1971–72, and Muckenhoupt characterized maximal-function weights in 1972. ([Wikipedia: Bounded mean oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation); [Wikipedia: Muckenhoupt weights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muckenhoupt_weights))

Fefferman's 1971 ball multiplier theorem linked Fourier analysis to Kakeya sets. Wolff proved that Besicovitch sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ have dimension at least $(n+2)/2$, and Wang and Zahl (2025) proved that Kakeya sets in $\mathbb{R}^3$ have Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension 3. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set); [Wang–Zahl, arXiv:2502.17655](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655)) Hytönen proved the $A_2$ conjecture in 2010, after Petermichl's sharp bounds for the Hilbert and Riesz transforms. ([Hytönen, arXiv:1007.4330](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1007.4330)) Bourgain and Demeter's decoupling theorem (2014) rests on the interplay between linear and multilinear restriction theory and has applications in additive combinatorics, incidence geometry and number theory; Guth's restriction estimate in $\mathbb{R}^3$ uses polynomial partitioning arguments from incidence geometry. ([arXiv:1403.5335](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5335); [arXiv:1407.1916](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.1916))

### Open problems
- **Restriction conjecture.** Tao's survey records the restriction conjecture as open; it is solved for the sphere and paraboloid in two dimensions, and the restriction conjecture implies the Kakeya conjecture. ([Tao, arXiv:math/0311181](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0311181))
- **Bochner–Riesz conjecture.** Completely resolved for $n=2$ but only partially answered for $n\ge3$. ([Wikipedia: Bochner–Riesz mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Riesz_mean))
- **Kakeya conjecture.** Confirmed for $n\le3$ (the case $n=3$ by the February 2025 Wang–Zahl arXiv preprint); Wikipedia reports only partial results in higher dimensions. It also reports two October 2026 OpenAI preprints posted on GitHub, one claiming that every four-dimensional Kakeya set has full Hausdorff dimension and one claiming the local smoothing conjecture, which would imply Kakeya in all dimensions; Wikipedia presents both as claims, so they are reported and unconfirmed here. ([Wikipedia: Kakeya set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakeya_set); [arXiv:2502.17655](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655))
- **Maximal-function constants.** Whether the weak $(1,1)$ bound for the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator can be taken independent of dimension is unknown; in one dimension the sharp centred weak $(1,1)$ constant is the largest root of $12C^2-22C+5=0$ (Melas). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_maximal_function); [Annals 157 (2003)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2003/157-2/p08))
- **Spherical partial sums.** A.e. convergence of spherical partial sums of multiple Fourier series of $L^2$ functions is open. ([Wikipedia: Carleson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleson%27s_theorem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Harmonic analysis (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis): maximal functions, Calderón–Zygmund, Littlewood–Paley, restriction.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 42Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Bxx&btn=Current): official codes.
- **Learn:** [Tao, Math 247A Notes 4: Calderón–Zygmund theory (UCLA)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/247a.1.06f/notes4.pdf): singular kernels, BMO, multipliers, Littlewood–Paley.
- **Learn:** [Tao, Recent progress on the restriction conjecture](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0311181): survey of restriction, Kakeya and bilinear methods.
- **Primary:** [Bourgain–Demeter, The proof of the $\ell^2$ decoupling conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5335): decoupling for curved hypersurfaces and the cone.
- **Primary:** [Hytönen, The sharp weighted bound for general Calderón–Zygmund operators](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1007.4330): the $A_2$ theorem.
- **Primary:** [Wang–Zahl, the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17655): 2025 preprint.
- **Further reading:** [Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis (GTM, Springer 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4939-1194-3) and [Grafakos, Modern Fourier Analysis (GTM, Springer 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4939-1230-8): standard graduate texts.
references.MSC 42Cxx - Nontrigonometric harmonic an:
## Reference
### Overview
Nontrigonometric harmonic analysis studies expansions of functions in systems other than the trigonometric system $\{e^{inx}\}$: general orthogonal polynomials and orthogonal functions, Fourier series in special systems such as Legendre polynomials and Walsh functions, frames and other redundant expansions, and wavelets. MSC2020 places it beside harmonic analysis in one variable (42Axx) and in several variables (42Bxx) inside 42-XX, harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces. ([MSC2020 42Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Cxx); [MSC2020 42-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42-XX))

The unifying setting is a separable Hilbert space, usually $L^2$ of a line, interval or circle, together with a distinguished spanning system. The questions are the classical ones of [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) asked for that system: how coefficients are computed, whether and in what sense expansions converge, which systems are complete, and how stable reconstruction is. Frame theory makes the last question quantitative through frame bounds and the frame operator. ([Frame (linear algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_%28linear_algebra%29); [Casazza, The art of frame theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9910168))

### Scope
The MSC2020 sub-codes are: ([MSC2020 42Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Cxx))
- **42C05** Orthogonal functions and polynomials, general theory of nontrigonometric harmonic analysis (see also 33C45, 33C50, 33D45).
- **42C10** Fourier series in special orthogonal functions (Legendre polynomials, Walsh functions, etc.).
- **42C15** General harmonic expansions, frames.
- **42C20** Other transformations of harmonic type.
- **42C25** Uniqueness and localization for orthogonal series.
- **42C30** Completeness of sets of functions in nontrigonometric harmonic analysis.
- **42C40** Nontrigonometric harmonic analysis involving wavelets and other special systems.
- **42C99** None of the above, but in this section.

Neighbouring codes, one line each:
- [MSC 42Axx - Harmonic analysis in one variable](node:MSC%2042Axx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20one%20variable) and [MSC 42Bxx - Harmonic analysis in several variables](node:MSC%2042Bxx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20several%20variables) are the sibling codes for harmonic analysis in one and in several variables; 42Cxx is the nontrigonometric counterpart within 42-XX. ([MSC2020 42-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42-XX))
- [MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Cxx%20-%20Hypergeometric%20functions): 33C45 covers orthogonal polynomials of hypergeometric type (Jacobi, Laguerre, Hermite, Askey scheme) and refers general orthogonal polynomials to 42C05. ([MSC2020 33Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Cxx))
- [MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis) treats characters of general locally compact groups; Walsh functions fit there as characters of the Cantor group, and in 42C10 as a concrete orthonormal system on $[0,1]$. ([Walsh function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walsh_function))

### Key concepts
- **Frames (42C15).** A family $\{e_k\}$ in a Hilbert space $H$ is a frame if there are $0<A\le B<\infty$ with $A\|v\|^2\le\sum_k|\langle v,e_k\rangle|^2\le B\|v\|^2$ for all $v$. The frame operator $Sv=\sum_k\langle v,e_k\rangle e_k$ is invertible, and with the canonical dual $\tilde e_k=S^{-1}e_k$ one has $v=\sum_k\langle v,e_k\rangle\tilde e_k=\sum_k\langle v,\tilde e_k\rangle e_k$. Tight frames have $A=B$; Parseval frames have $A=B=1$. Duffin and Schaeffer introduced the condition in 1952 in work on nonharmonic Fourier series. ([Frame (linear algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_%28linear_algebra%29))
- **Balian–Low theorem.** Let $g\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ and $g_{m,n}(x)=e^{2\pi i m b x}g(x-na)$ with $ab=1$. If $\{g_{m,n}\}_{m,n\in\mathbb Z}$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb R)$, then $\int x^2|g(x)|^2\,dx=\infty$ or $\int\xi^2|\hat g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi=\infty$: a Gabor orthonormal basis at critical density cannot have a window well localized in both time and frequency. ([Balian–Low theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balian%E2%80%93Low_theorem))
- **Gabor frames for totally positive windows.** Gröchenig and Stöckler proved that for a totally positive function $g$ of finite type, the Gabor system with lattice parameters $\alpha,\beta$ is a frame of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\alpha\beta<1$. Before this result the full set of frame-generating lattice parameters was known for only six windows. ([Gröchenig–Stöckler, arXiv:1104.4894](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.4894))
- **Multiresolution analysis and wavelets (42C40).** An MRA of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ is a nested chain $\cdots\subset V_1\subset V_0\subset V_{-1}\subset\cdots$ of closed subspaces related by dyadic dilation, with $V_0$ invariant under integer shifts and generated by the shifts of a scaling function, $\bigcup_j V_j$ dense and $\bigcap_j V_j=\{0\}$. When the scaling function is compactly supported with orthogonal shifts, the dilates and translates of a mother wavelet spanning $W_0=V_{-1}\ominus V_0$ form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb R)$. Mallat and Meyer introduced the framework in 1988/89. ([Multiresolution analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiresolution_analysis))
- **Daubechies wavelets.** Daubechies constructed orthonormal bases of compactly supported wavelets (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 41 (1988) 909–996); the family has the maximal number of vanishing moments for a given support, with $A$ vanishing moments for a filter of $2A$ coefficients, although maximal vanishing moments do not give the best smoothness. ([Daubechies wavelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daubechies_wavelet); [Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/cpa.3160410705))
- **Favard's theorem (42C05).** If monic polynomials $y_n$ with $\deg y_n=n$, $y_0=1$, satisfy $y_{n+1}=(x-c_n)y_n-d_ny_{n-1}$, then they are orthogonal for a unique linear functional $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda(1)=1$; $\Lambda$ is positive definite if and only if every $c_n$ is real and every $d_n>0$ (Favard 1935, Shohat 1938). ([Favard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Favard%27s_theorem))
- **Verblunsky and Szegő theorems (42C05).** For a nontrivial probability measure $d\mu=w\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}+d\mu_s$ on the unit circle, the monic orthogonal polynomials satisfy $\Phi_{n+1}(z)=z\Phi_n(z)-\bar\alpha_n\Phi_n^*(z)$ with Verblunsky coefficients $\alpha_n\in\mathbb D$. Verblunsky's theorem: $\mu\mapsto(\alpha_n)$ is a bijection onto sequences in $\mathbb D$. Szegő's theorem: $\prod_n(1-|\alpha_n|^2)=\exp\big(\tfrac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log w\,d\theta\big)$, so $\sum|\alpha_n|^2<\infty$ if and only if $\int\log w>-\infty$, independently of $\mu_s$. ([OPUC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal_polynomials_on_the_unit_circle))
- **Walsh system (42C10).** The Walsh functions $W_k$ take values $\pm1$, are products of Rademacher functions, and form an orthonormal basis of $L^2[0,1]$ whose Fourier series converge almost everywhere for $f\in L^2$. In Walsh–Paley order the system is a Schauder basis of $L^p[0,1]$ for $1<p<\infty$, but unlike the Haar system it is not unconditional, and it is not a basis of $L^1$. ([Walsh function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walsh_function))

All of these live in [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) or [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces), and the classical orthogonal polynomials link the area to [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions). ([Frame (linear algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_%28linear_algebra%29); [MSC2020 33Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=33Cxx))

### History
Duffin and Schaeffer's 1952 frame condition came from nonharmonic Fourier series; in the 1980s Mallat, Daubechies and Meyer used frames to analyze wavelets. ([Frame (linear algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_%28linear_algebra%29)) Favard (1935) and Shohat (1938) characterized orthogonal polynomial sequences by three-term recurrences. ([Favard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Favard%27s_theorem)) The Mallat–Meyer multiresolution framework (1988/89) and Daubechies' 1988 compactly supported orthonormal wavelets followed. ([Multiresolution analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiresolution_analysis); [Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/cpa.3160410705)) In 2013 Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava proved Weaver's conjecture $KS_2$ and a paving formulation due to Casazza et al., giving a positive solution of the 1959 Kadison–Singer problem. ([MSS, arXiv:1306.3969](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.3969); [Kadison–Singer problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadison%E2%80%93Singer_problem))

### Open problems
- **HRT conjecture (open).** Any finite set of distinct time-frequency translates $\{e^{2\pi i b_k x}g(x-a_k)\}_{k=1}^N$ of a nonzero $g\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ is linearly independent. First stated in print in 1996, it remains open, with limited partial results. ([Georgia Tech seminar, The HRT Conjecture](https://math.gatech.edu/node/32829624)) Enstad and van Velthoven give a self-contained proof for subsets of arbitrary discrete subgroups via zero divisors in twisted group rings. ([arXiv:2302.01202](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01202)) Gröchenig observes that finite sections of Gabor frames look numerically dependent although they are conjectured to be independent, and studies the decay of their lower Riesz bounds. ([arXiv:1401.1353](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.1353))
- **Frame sets of Gabor systems.** Gröchenig and Stöckler describe their totally positive result as a first positive contribution to a 1990 conjecture of Daubechies on which lattice parameters yield Gabor frames; for general windows the frame set remains undetermined. ([arXiv:1104.4894](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.4894))
- Casazza's survey lists open questions and limitations of abstract frame theory. ([Casazza, arXiv:math/9910168](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9910168))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Frame (linear algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_%28linear_algebra%29): frame bounds, frame operator, dual frames.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.327 Wavelets, Filter Banks and Applications](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-327-wavelets-filter-banks-and-applications-spring-2003/): Strang and Amaratunga's graduate course on wavelets and Mallat's pyramid algorithm.
- **Primary:** [Casazza, The art of frame theory (arXiv:math/9910168)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9910168): survey of abstract frame theory with open questions.
- **Primary:** [Gröchenig–Stöckler, Gabor frames and totally positive functions (arXiv:1104.4894)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.4894): Duke Math. J. 162 (2013); frame set for totally positive windows.
- **Further reading:** [Daubechies, Orthonormal bases of compactly supported wavelets](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/cpa.3160410705): Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 41 (1988) 909–996.
references.MSC 43 - Abstract harmonic analysis:
## Reference
### Overview
Abstract harmonic analysis studies functions on general domains through their symmetries, such as translations or rotations; its core is analysis on [topological groups](node:Topological%20Groups), generalizing the Fourier transform to locally compact Hausdorff groups, and it sits close to representation theory and functional analysis. For [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) the central result is [Pontryagin duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality), and for compact groups the Peter–Weyl theorem produces harmonics from irreducible representations. ([Harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis))

The basic ingredients are a locally compact group $G$, its [Haar measure](node:Haar%20Measure), and the convolution algebra $L^1(G)$, which is commutative exactly when $G$ is abelian. For an abelian group the Fourier transform is the Gelfand transform of $L^1(G)$, an injective map into $C_0(\hat G)$, so the subject is also a chapter of commutative Banach-algebra theory. ([Scalamandre, UChicago REU](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2017/REUPapers/Scalamandre.pdf)) For non-abelian groups the dual object is the space of irreducible unitary representations, and the Plancherel theorem holds for separable unimodular type I groups, with Harish-Chandra's explicit formulas for semisimple Lie groups. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753); [Plancherel theorem for spherical functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem_for_spherical_functions))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 43-XX is titled "Abstract harmonic analysis", with the note that other analysis on topological and Lie groups belongs to 22Exx. Besides the standard form codes (43-00 to 43-11), its only second-level subdivision is [MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis), which carries the same title. ([MSC2020 43-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43-XX&btn=Current))

Within 43Axx the codes cover measures, means and amenable groups, measure algebras, $L^p$ and $L^1$-algebras, multipliers, Fourier and Fourier–Stieltjes transforms on abelian and nonabelian groups, positive definite functions, character groups and dual objects, spectral synthesis, special sets (thin, Kronecker, Helson, Ditkin, Sidon), convergence and summability, almost periodic functions, hypergroups, representations, compact groups, specific Lie groups, homogeneous spaces, spherical functions, and categorical methods. ([MSC2020 43Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43Axx&btn=Current))

Boundaries, from the cross-references in the MSC entry: 43A70 points to 22B05 and 11R56 for specific abelian groups, i.e. to [MSC 22Bxx - Locally compact abelian groups (LCA groups)](node:MSC%2022Bxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20abelian%20groups%20%28LCA%20groups%29); 43A65 points to [MSC 22Dxx - Locally compact groups and their algebras](node:MSC%2022Dxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20groups%20and%20their%20algebras) and 22E45 for representation theory proper; 43A80 and the section note point to [MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups); 43A95 points to 46Mxx. ([MSC2020 43Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43Axx&btn=Current)) Harmonic analysis on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the separate section [MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces](node:MSC%2042%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20on%20Euclidean%20spaces), with subdivisions for one variable, several variables and nontrigonometric harmonic analysis. ([MSC2020 42-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42-XX&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Haar measure.** A locally compact group carries a left-invariant Borel measure, finite on compact sets and suitably regular, unique up to a positive constant; it is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and counting measure on a discrete group. Left and right Haar measures agree exactly for unimodular groups. This is the [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory) underneath the field. ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure))
- **Pontryagin duality and Plancherel.** For locally compact abelian $G$, $\hat G$ is the group of continuous homomorphisms $G\to\mathbb{T}$, the evaluation map $G\to\hat{\hat G}$ is a canonical isomorphism, and for each Haar measure on $G$ there is a dual Haar measure on $\hat G$ making the Fourier transform a unitary $L^2(G)\to L^2(\hat G)$. This is the abstract form of the [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem) and of [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) on $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{T}$, $\mathbb{Z}$. ([Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))
- **Bochner's theorem.** On a locally compact abelian group, the continuous positive-definite functions with $f(e)=1$ are exactly the Fourier transforms $f(g)=\int_{\hat G}\xi(g)\,d\mu(\xi)$ of probability measures $\mu$ on $\hat G$, and $\mu$ is unique. ([Bochner's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%27s_theorem))
- **Wiener's Tauberian theorem and spectral synthesis.** Translates of $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ span a dense subspace if and only if $\hat f$ has no real zeros, and a similar result holds on every locally compact abelian group; Gelfand reproved it via the maximal ideal space of $L^1$. ([Wiener's Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_Tauberian_theorem)) The general question, whether every closed ideal is determined by its zero set, fails: Malliavin proved in 1959 that spectral synthesis fails for $A(G)$ for every non-discrete locally compact abelian $G$. ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06584v1); [Malliavin 1959, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684707))
- **Fourier algebra and amenability.** Eymard (1964) defined the Fourier algebra $A(G)$ and Fourier–Stieltjes algebra $B(G)$ for arbitrary locally compact $G$; for abelian $G$ they are the Fourier images of $L^1(\hat G)$ and $M(\hat G)$. ([Fourier algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_algebra)) Leptin's theorem (1968) ties bounded approximate identities in $A(G)$ to amenability of $G$, and Forrest and Runde proved that $A(G)$ is amenable as a Banach algebra if and only if $G$ has an abelian subgroup of finite index. ([Forrest–Runde, arXiv:math/0211284](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0211284)) A group is amenable when $L^\infty(G)$ has a left-invariant mean; abelian, compact and solvable groups are amenable and the free group on two generators is not. ([Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group))
- **Peter–Weyl theorem.** For a compact group, matrix coefficients of irreducible unitary representations are uniformly dense in $C(G)$, every unitary representation splits as an orthogonal sum of finite-dimensional irreducibles, and the normalized matrix coefficients form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(G)$; every compact [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) therefore has a faithful finite-dimensional representation. This is where the field meets [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory). ([Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))
- **Non-abelian Plancherel theorem.** If $G$ is separable, unimodular and type I with Haar measure $dx$, there is a positive measure $\mu$ on $\hat G$, unique up to a constant, with $\int_G|f|^2\,dx=\int_{\hat G}\|\pi(f)\|_{HS}^2\,d\mu(\pi)$ for $f\in L^1\cap L^2(G)$; the approach was developed by Segal and Mautner from the late 1940s. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753)) For semisimple Lie groups Harish-Chandra found the Plancherel measure explicitly; its support is the tempered representations. ([Plancherel measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_measure)) For $K$-biinvariant functions on a noncompact connected semisimple group with finite center, his spherical Plancherel theorem gives a unitary map onto $L^2(\mathfrak a_+^*,|c(\lambda)|^{-2}d\lambda)$, completed in 1966. ([Plancherel theorem for spherical functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem_for_spherical_functions))
- **Kazhdan's property (T).** A locally compact group has property (T) if the trivial representation is isolated in the unitary dual (Fell topology): almost invariant vectors force a nonzero invariant vector. Introduced by Kazhdan in 1967, it is incompatible with amenability outside the compact case: an amenable group with (T) is compact. $SL(n,\mathbb{R})$ for $n\ge3$ and $Sp(n,1)$ for $n\ge2$ have (T); $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, noncompact solvable groups, and nontrivial free and free abelian groups do not. Connes used discrete property (T) groups to construct type II$_1$ factors whose group of trace-scaling self-similarities is countable. ([Kazhdan's property (T)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhdan%27s_property_%28T%29))
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) and [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory): unitary representations on Hilbert space and the decomposition of the regular representation on $L^2(G)$ are the analytic framework; the Fourier transform on an LCA group is a unitary operator. ([Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))

### History
Peter and Weyl proved their theorem for compact groups in 1927. ([Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem)) Haar proved existence of an invariant measure for second-countable locally compact groups in 1933, and Weil gave the general existence and uniqueness proof. ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure)) Pontryagin set out duality in 1931–1934 for second-countable compact or discrete groups; van Kampen (1935) and Weil (1940) extended it to all LCA groups. ([Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) Von Neumann introduced amenability in 1929, and Day introduced the term "amenable" in 1949. ([Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group))

Segal and Mautner began the non-abelian Plancherel theory in the late 1940s, and Harish-Chandra gave a formula for complex semisimple groups in 1951. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753)) Malliavin's 1959 paper "Impossibilité de la synthèse spectrale sur les groupes abéliens non compacts" appeared in *Publ. Math. IHÉS* 2. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684707)) Eymard introduced the Fourier algebra in 1964 ([Fourier algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_algebra)), Kazhdan property (T) in 1967 ([Kazhdan's property (T)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhdan%27s_property_%28T%29)), and Harish-Chandra completed the spherical Plancherel theorem in 1966. ([Plancherel theorem for spherical functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem_for_spherical_functions))

### Open problems
- **Union problem in spectral synthesis.** Is the union of two sets of spectral synthesis for the Fourier algebra again a set of spectral synthesis? Posed by Herz for abelian groups and restated by Reiter, it is called "an outstanding problem in the field" by Ludwig and Turowska, who state that no solution has been found. ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06584v1))
- **Are sets of synthesis Ditkin sets?** Every Ditkin set is a set of spectral synthesis; the converse is stated to be an open problem, and classifying all sets of spectral synthesis is described as out of reach. ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06584v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Pontryagin duality (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality): dual group, Fourier transform, Plancherel, and history of LCA duality.
- **Learn:** [Scalamandre, Harmonic Analysis on LCA Groups (UChicago REU)](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2017/REUPapers/Scalamandre.pdf): self-contained route from Haar measure through $L^1(G)$ and Gelfand theory to duality and Plancherel.
- **Primary:** [Herb and Sally, The Plancherel formula, the Plancherel theorem, and the Fourier transform of orbital integrals](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.3753): survey of non-abelian Plancherel theory from Segal–Mautner to reductive groups.
- **Primary:** [Forrest and Runde, Amenability and weak amenability of the Fourier algebra](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0211284): Fourier algebras, Leptin's theorem and amenability.
- **Further reading:** [Hewitt and Ross, *Abstract Harmonic Analysis* (Springer, 1963; Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-40409-6); [Rudin, *Fourier Analysis on Groups* (Wiley, 1990; Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/9781118165621); [Folland, *A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis* (CRC, 2016; Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/b19172).
references.MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis:
## Reference
### Overview
43Axx is the only second-level subdivision of [MSC 43 - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis), and it holds every research code of that section, from measures on groups (43A05) to categorical methods (43A95). MSC2020 sends other analysis on topological and Lie groups to 22Exx. ([MSC2020 43Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43Axx&btn=Current))

The mathematics it classifies generalizes [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) from $\mathbb{R}$ to locally compact groups. [Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure) supplies a canonical integral, $L^1(G)$ becomes a [Banach algebra](node:Banach%20Algebras) under convolution, and for an abelian group the Fourier transform is the Gelfand transform of $L^1(G)$, with the dual group (the continuous characters into the circle) playing the role of frequency space. ([Scalamandre, UChicago REU](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2017/REUPapers/Scalamandre.pdf); [Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) For non-[abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) the dual object is the set of irreducible unitary representations, and the analogue of the [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem) is a decomposition of $L^2(G)$ against a Plancherel measure. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753))

### Scope
The 43Axx codes fall into clusters ([MSC2020 43Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43Axx&btn=Current)):
- **Measures and function algebras:** 43A05 measures on groups and semigroups; 43A07 means on groups and amenable groups; 43A10 measure algebras; 43A15 $L^p$-spaces and other function spaces; 43A17 analysis on ordered groups and $H^p$-theory; 43A20 $L^1$-algebras; 43A22 homomorphisms and multipliers of function spaces.
- **Transforms and duality:** 43A25 Fourier and Fourier–Stieltjes transforms on locally compact and other abelian groups; 43A30 the same on nonabelian groups and semigroups; 43A32 other transforms and operators of Fourier type; 43A35 positive definite functions; 43A40 character groups and dual objects.
- **Fine structure of the Fourier image:** 43A45 spectral synthesis; 43A46 special sets (thin, Kronecker, Helson, Ditkin, Sidon sets); 43A50 convergence of Fourier series and inverse transforms; 43A55 summability methods (see also 40J05).
- **Specific settings:** 43A60 almost periodic functions and their generalizations; 43A62 hypergroups; 43A65 representations, in their harmonic-analysis aspects (see also 22A10, 22A20, 22Dxx, 22E45); 43A70 specific locally compact abelian groups (see also 11R56, 22B05); 43A75 and 43A77 specific and general compact groups; 43A80 other specific Lie groups (see also 22Exx); 43A85 homogeneous spaces; 43A90 harmonic analysis and spherical functions (see also 22E45, 22E46, 33C55); 43A95 categorical methods (see also 46Mxx); 43A99 other.

Neighbouring codes named in these cross-references: 43A70 points to 22B05, in [MSC 22Bxx - Locally compact abelian groups (LCA groups)](node:MSC%2022Bxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20abelian%20groups%20%28LCA%20groups%29); 43A65 points to [MSC 22Dxx - Locally compact groups and their algebras](node:MSC%2022Dxx%20-%20Locally%20compact%20groups%20and%20their%20algebras) and to 22A10, 22A20 and 22E45; 43A80 and the section note point to [MSC 22Exx - Lie groups](node:MSC%2022Exx%20-%20Lie%20groups); 43A95 points to 46Mxx. ([MSC2020 43Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=43Axx&btn=Current)) Harmonic analysis on $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself is the separate section [MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces](node:MSC%2042%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20on%20Euclidean%20spaces), with subdivisions for one variable (42Axx), several variables (42Bxx) and nontrigonometric harmonic analysis (42Cxx). ([MSC2020 42-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42-XX&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Haar measure and modular function (43A05).** A locally compact group has, up to a positive constant, a unique nontrivial left-invariant Borel measure that is finite on compact sets and suitably regular. The modular function $\Delta$ is a continuous homomorphism to $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, and $G$ is unimodular when $\Delta\equiv1$, as for abelian, compact, discrete, semisimple and connected nilpotent Lie groups. On the solvable $ax+b$ group the left Haar measure is $a^{-2}\,da\,db$ and the right one is $|a|^{-1}\,da\,db$, so it is not unimodular. This is the [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory) on which every construction in the field rests. ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure))
- **$L^1$-algebras and Gelfand theory (43A20, 43A25).** $L^1(G)$ is commutative if and only if $G$ is abelian, and has a unit if and only if $G$ is discrete. For abelian $A$, the characters of $A$ (the points of $\hat A$) correspond exactly to the nonzero multiplicative functionals of $L^1(A)$, the Gelfand transform is the Fourier transform $L^1(A)\to C_0(\hat A)$, and it is injective; consequently if $A$ is discrete then $\hat A$ is compact. ([Scalamandre, UChicago REU](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2017/REUPapers/Scalamandre.pdf))
- **[Pontryagin Duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality) and Plancherel (43A25, 43A40).** For every locally compact abelian $G$ the evaluation map $G\to\hat{\hat G}$ is a canonical isomorphism. For a Haar measure $\mu$ on $G$ there is a dual Haar measure $\nu$ on $\hat G$ such that the Fourier transform extends from $C_c(G)$ to a unitary $L^2_\mu(G)\to L^2_\nu(\hat G)$. Examples: $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}=\mathbb{T}$, $\hat{\mathbb{T}}=\mathbb{Z}$, $\hat{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}$, and $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is dual to the Prüfer group $\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)$. ([Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))
- **Bochner's theorem (43A35).** On a locally compact abelian group, every continuous positive-definite $f$ with $f(e)=1$ is $f(g)=\int_{\hat G}\xi(g)\,d\mu(\xi)$ for a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\hat G$. ([Bochner's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%27s_theorem))
- **Wiener's Tauberian theorem and spectral synthesis (43A45).** The translates of $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ span a dense subspace of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ if and only if $\hat f$ has no real zeros, and the analogue holds for any locally compact abelian group; Gelfand reproved it by identifying the spectrum of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ with the dual group. ([Wiener's Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_Tauberian_theorem)) Spectral synthesis asks whether a closed ideal is determined by its zero set: a closed set $E$ is a set of synthesis for the Fourier algebra if $k(E)=\overline{j(E)}$. Malliavin proved in 1959 that synthesis fails for $A(G)$ whenever $G$ is a non-discrete locally compact abelian group (equivalently, for $L^1$ of every non-compact LCA group). ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06584v1); [Malliavin 1959, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684707))
- **Fourier algebra (43A30).** Eymard introduced the Fourier algebra $A(G)$ and Fourier–Stieltjes algebra $B(G)$ in 1964. For abelian $G$, $A(G)$ is the image of $L^1(\hat G)$ under the Fourier transform and $B(G)$ is the image of the measure algebra $M(\hat G)$; in general $B(G)$ is the span of continuous positive-definite functions and $A(G)$ is a closed ideal in $B(G)$. ([Fourier algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_algebra)) By Leptin's theorem (1968), $A(G)$ has a bounded approximate identity only when $G$ is amenable, and Forrest and Runde proved that $A(G)$ is amenable as a Banach algebra if and only if $G$ has an abelian subgroup of finite index. ([Forrest–Runde, arXiv:math/0211284](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0211284))
- **Amenability (43A07).** A locally compact group is amenable if $L^\infty(G)$ carries a left-invariant mean. Finite, compact, abelian, solvable, and finitely generated subexponential-growth groups are amenable; the free group on two generators is not. ([Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group))
- **Compact groups (43A75, 43A77).** By the Peter–Weyl theorem, for compact $G$ the matrix coefficients are uniformly dense in $C(G)$, every unitary representation is an orthogonal direct sum of irreducible finite-dimensional ones, and normalized matrix coefficients of the irreducibles form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(G)$; so every compact [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) has a faithful finite-dimensional representation. ([Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))
- **Abstract Plancherel theorem (43A30, 43A65).** For a separable, unimodular, type I group with Haar measure $dx$ there is a positive measure $\mu$ on $\hat G$, unique up to a constant, such that for $f\in L^1\cap L^2(G)$, $\pi(f)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt for $\mu$-a.e. $\pi$ and $\int_G|f|^2\,dx=\int_{\hat G}\|\pi(f)\|_{HS}^2\,d\mu(\pi)$; this grew out of work by Segal and Mautner. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753)) This is the [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) side of the field.
- **Gelfand pairs and spherical functions (43A85, 43A90).** For $G$ finite, or compact, or a Lie group with $K$ compact, $(G,K)$ is a Gelfand pair when the $K$-biinvariant functions (or compactly supported measures) form a commutative convolution algebra, equivalently each irreducible representation has at most a one-dimensional space of $K$-fixed vectors; examples are $(GL(n,\mathbb{R}),O(n))$ and $(\mathrm{Sym}(n+1),\mathrm{Sym}(n))$. ([Gelfand pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_pair)) For $G$ noncompact connected semisimple with finite center and $K$ maximal compact, Harish-Chandra's spherical transform is unitary from $L^2(K\backslash G/K)$ onto $L^2(\mathfrak a_+^*,|c(\lambda)|^{-2}d\lambda)$, completed in 1966. ([Plancherel theorem for spherical functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem_for_spherical_functions))
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) and [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory): the regular representation on $L^2(G)$ and its decomposition are the analytic core of 43A30 and 43A65; the Plancherel measure is supported on the tempered representations for semisimple Lie groups. ([Plancherel measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_measure))

### History
Hurwitz introduced invariant integration for Lie groups in 1897; Haar published the second-countable case in 1933 and Weil proved general existence and uniqueness. ([Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure)) Peter and Weyl proved their theorem for compact groups in 1927. ([Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem)) Pontryagin proved duality for second-countable compact or discrete abelian groups in 1931–1934; van Kampen (1935) and Weil (1940) extended it to all LCA groups. ([Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) Von Neumann introduced amenability in 1929 and Day named it in 1949. ([Amenable group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group))

The non-abelian Plancherel theory began with Mautner and Segal in the late 1940s and Harish-Chandra's 1951 formula for complex semisimple groups. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753)) Malliavin's 1959 paper "Impossibilité de la synthèse spectrale sur les groupes abéliens non compacts" settled the synthesis question negatively ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02684707)), and Eymard's 1964 Fourier algebra moved the commutative Banach-algebra methods to non-abelian groups. ([Fourier algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_algebra))

### Open problems
- **The union problem for spectral sets (43A45).** Whether the union of two sets of spectral synthesis for $A(G)$ is again a set of spectral synthesis was posed by Herz for abelian groups and restated by Reiter; Ludwig and Turowska call it an outstanding problem and state that "to date, no solution has been found". ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06584v1))
- **Synthesis versus Ditkin sets (43A45, 43A46).** Every Ditkin set is a set of spectral synthesis; whether every set of synthesis is a Ditkin set is stated to be open, and classifying the sets of spectral synthesis is described as out of reach for the moment. ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06584v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Pontryagin duality (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality): dual group, Fourier transform, Plancherel, and history of LCA duality.
- **Learn:** [Scalamandre, Harmonic Analysis on LCA Groups (UChicago REU)](https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2017/REUPapers/Scalamandre.pdf): proofs of Pontryagin duality and Plancherel via Banach algebras.
- **Primary:** [Herb and Sally, The Plancherel formula, the Plancherel theorem, and the Fourier transform of orbital integrals](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.3753): survey of non-abelian Plancherel theorems.
- **Primary:** [Ludwig and Turowska, On the structure of spectral sets](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06584v1): current research on spectral synthesis in Fourier algebras.
- **Further reading:** [Hewitt and Ross, *Abstract Harmonic Analysis* (Springer, 1963; Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-40409-6); [Rudin, *Fourier Analysis on Groups* (Wiley, 1990; Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/9781118165621); [Folland, *A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis* (CRC, 2016; Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/b19172): the standard monographs.
references.MSC 44 - Integral transforms, operationa:
## Reference
### Overview
An integral transform maps a function to another function by integration against a kernel of two variables, $(Tf)(u)=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}f(t)K(t,u)\,dt$. Some kernels have an inverse kernel that yields an inverse transform, so a problem can be moved to a domain where it is easier and the answer moved back. Fourier series, and then the Fourier transform, were the precursors of the general theory. ([Wikipedia: Integral transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_transform))

Operational calculus treats differentiation as an operator $p=d/dt$, so that a linear differential equation $F(p)y=g$ is solved by applying an inverse operator. Integration is $p^{-1}$, and the translation formula $e^{ap}f(t)=f(t+a)$ handles delays and difference equations. ([Wikipedia: Operational calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_calculus)) Bromwich justified it rigorously through the Laplace transform, and Mikusiński later gave an algebraic approach. ([Wikipedia: Operational calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_calculus)) The section also contains moment problems (44A60). ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current)) Schmüdgen's lectures treat the one-dimensional and multidimensional moment problem, with emphasis on interactions with real algebraic geometry and polynomial optimization. ([Schmüdgen, Ten Lectures on the Moment Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.12698))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 44-XX "Integral transforms, operational calculus" has a single subfield, [MSC 44Axx - Integral transforms, operational calculus](node:MSC%2044Axx%20-%20Integral%20transforms,%20operational%20calculus), with the same title and cross-references. Its codes are general transforms (44A05), Laplace (44A10), Radon (44A12), special transforms such as Legendre and Hilbert (44A15), transforms of special functions (44A20), multiple transforms (44A30), and convolution (44A35). The rest are Mikusiński and other operational calculi (44A40), classical operational calculus (44A45), discrete operational calculus (44A55), and moment problems (44A60). ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current))

Boundaries with neighbouring sections, one line each ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current)):
- Fourier transforms (42A38, 42B10) belong to [MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces](node:MSC%2042%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20on%20Euclidean%20spaces).
- Transforms in distribution spaces (46F12) belong to [MSC 46Fxx - Distributions, generalized functions, distribution spaces](node:MSC%2046Fxx%20-%20Distributions,%20generalized%20functions,%20distribution%20spaces).
- Fractional calculus goes to 26A33, and numerical methods to 65R10.
- Trigonometric moment problems go to 42A70, and the Radon transform cross-refers to medical imaging (92C55).

### Key concepts
- **Laplace transform.** $(\mathcal Lf)(s)=\int_{0^-}^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the complex $s$ at which it converges. The $0^-$ admits generalized functions containing $\delta(t)$. ([MIT 18.03SC](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-03sc-differential-equations-fall-2011/d40ad07a62996f6dad93b832f8de0e04_MIT18_03SCF11_s27_1text.pdf)) The region of convergence is a half-plane $\operatorname{Re}s>a$. The transform satisfies $\mathcal L\{f'\}=sF(s)-f(0^-)$ and $\mathcal L\{f*g\}=F(s)G(s)$ for $(f*g)(t)=\int_0^tf(\tau)g(t-\tau)\,d\tau$. ([Wikipedia: Laplace transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_transform))
- **Inversion and uniqueness.** Lerch's theorem (1903): an inverse Laplace transform, when it exists, is unique up to functions that differ on a Lebesgue-null set. The Bromwich integral $f(t)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\gamma-iT}^{\gamma+iT}e^{st}F(s)\,ds$ inverts it along a vertical line to the right of all singularities of $F$. ([Wikipedia: Inverse Laplace transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Laplace_transform)) Post's inversion formula, $f(t)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}(k/t)^{k+1}F^{(k)}(k/t)$, holds for continuous $f$ on $[0,\infty)$ of exponential order. ([Wikipedia: Post's inversion formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post%27s_inversion_formula))
- **Bernstein–Widder theorem.** A completely monotone function on $[0,\infty)$ is exactly a Laplace transform $\int_0^\infty e^{-tx}\,dg(x)$ of a non-negative finite Borel measure. Hausdorff had earlier characterized completely monotone sequences, which are the moment sequences of the Hausdorff problem. ([Wikipedia: Bernstein's theorem on monotone functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_theorem_on_monotone_functions))
- **Paley–Wiener theorems.** An $L^2$ function supported in $[-A,A]$ has a Fourier transform that is an entire function of exponential type $A$, square-integrable on horizontal lines. Conversely, every such entire function arises this way. The Fourier–Laplace transform of $F\in L^2(\mathbb R^+)$ is holomorphic in the upper half-plane and gives exactly the Hardy space $H^2$, by [Plancherel](node:Plancherel%20Theorem). Schwartz (1952) characterized Fourier–Laplace transforms of compactly supported distributions by $|F(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^Ne^{B|\operatorname{Im}z|}$. ([Wikipedia: Paley–Wiener theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley%E2%80%93Wiener_theorem))
- **Mellin transform.** The Mellin transform has kernel $t^{u-1}$ on $(0,\infty)$, and its inverse runs along a vertical line in the fundamental strip. $\Gamma(s)$ is the Mellin transform of $e^{-x}$, the transform of $1/(e^x-1)$ is $\Gamma(s)\zeta(s)$, and Perron's formula inverts a Dirichlet series. Mellin methods are used in [asymptotic analysis](node:Asymptotic%20Analysis), and through Perron's formula in the study of Dirichlet series ([Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory)). ([Wikipedia: Mellin transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellin_transform)) The kernels of the Hankel ($tJ_\nu(ut)$) and related transforms are [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions). ([Wikipedia: Integral transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_transform))
- **Titchmarsh convolution theorem and Mikusiński operators.** Let $\varphi,\psi$ be integrable with $\int_0^x\varphi(t)\psi(x-t)\,dt=0$ a.e. on $(0,\kappa)$. Then $\varphi=0$ a.e. on $(0,\lambda)$ and $\psi=0$ a.e. on $(0,\mu)$ for some $\lambda+\mu\ge\kappa$. So convolution on $[0,\infty)$ has no zero divisors. ([Wikipedia: Titchmarsh convolution theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titchmarsh_convolution_theorem)) From the convolution product Mikusiński built a field of fractions whose elements are "Mikusiński operators". ([Wikipedia: Jan Mikusiński](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Mikusi%C5%84ski))
- **Radon transform.** The planar Radon transform integrates $f$ over lines. The projection-slice theorem identifies Fourier transforms of projections with radial slices of the 2D Fourier transform, and filtered back-projection inverts it. Its singular values tend to $0$, so the inverse is unbounded. ([Wikipedia: Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform)) Helgason's support theorem: if $K$ is compact and convex, $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^d\setminus K$ and decays faster than every power of $|x|$, and $Rf$ vanishes on all hyperplanes missing $K$, then $f=0$ outside $K$. ([Boman and Lindskog, arXiv:0802.4373](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0802.4373))
- **Moment problems.** Hamburger: $(m_n)$ is a moment sequence on $\mathbb R$ if and only if the Hankel kernel is positive, $\sum_{j,k}m_{j+k}c_j\bar c_k\ge0$ for every finitely supported complex $(c_j)$. ([Wikipedia: Hamburger moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburger_moment_problem)) Stieltjes, on $[0,\infty)$ with infinite support: both $\det(m_{i+j})_{i,j\le n}$ and the shifted $\det(m_{i+j+1})_{i,j\le n}$ must be positive. ([Wikipedia: Stieltjes moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stieltjes_moment_problem)) Hausdorff, on $[0,1]$: complete monotonicity, with a unique solution. ([Wikipedia: Hausdorff moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_moment_problem)) On unbounded supports determinacy can fail, as for log-normal moments. ([Wikipedia: Moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_problem)) In several variables, Haviland's theorem reduces existence to positivity on polynomials nonnegative on $K$. Schmüdgen's theorem solves the problem on compact semi-algebraic sets via a strict Positivstellensatz. ([Schmüdgen, Ten Lectures on the Moment Problem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.12698))

Related notes: [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis), [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29). The transforms there act on spaces that 44-XX sends to 42 and 46F. ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current))

### History
Euler investigated Laplace-type integrals from 1744, and Laplace began applying such transforms in 1785. ([Wikipedia: Laplace transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_transform)) Heaviside developed operational methods for telegraphy in 1893 without rigor. Bromwich justified them through the Laplace transform, and Carson and Wiener gave other justifications in the mid-1920s. ([Wikipedia: Operational calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_calculus)) That article dates Mikusiński's algebraic approach to the 1930s, but this is wrong. Mikusiński (born 1913) presented the results in 1943 in a secret wartime seminar in Kraków, published a first version as "Hypernumbers" in 1944, and refined it with Titchmarsh's theorem. The book appeared in Polish in 1953, and in English as *Operational Calculus* in 1959. ([MacTutor: Mikusiński](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Mikusinski/)) Titchmarsh's convolution theorem dates from 1926. ([Wikipedia: Titchmarsh convolution theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titchmarsh_convolution_theorem)) Radon introduced his transform with an inversion formula in 1917. ([Wikipedia: Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform)) Stieltjes posed the moment problem in 1894, and Hamburger and Hausdorff treated the line and bounded intervals in 1920. ([Schmüdgen, Ten Lectures on the Moment Problem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.12698))

### Open problems
- **Bivariate truncated moment problem without column relations.** Given a finite bivariate sequence of degree $2k$, when is there a positive measure on $\mathbb R^2$ with exactly those moments? When the moment matrix has no column relations, Zalar states that "for $k>2$ the solution to the TMP is not known", while the case $k=2$ is known. The concretely solved cases he lists include measures on varieties defined by polynomials of degree at most 2 and on the curve $y=x^3$. ([Zalar, arXiv:2212.01645](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.01645))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Integral transform, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_transform): general definition, inverse kernels, and a table of standard transforms.
