- **Learn:** [MIT 18.03SC, Definition of Laplace Transform](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-03sc-differential-equations-fall-2011/d40ad07a62996f6dad93b832f8de0e04_MIT18_03SCF11_s27_1text.pdf): the $0^-$ convention, first examples and linearity.
- **Learn:** [Schmüdgen, Ten Lectures on the Moment Problem (arXiv:2008.12698)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.12698): lectures on one-dimensional, multidimensional and truncated moment problems.
- **Primary:** [Boman and Lindskog, Support theorems for the Radon transform (arXiv:0802.4373)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0802.4373): Helgason's support theorem with Strichartz's proof and exterior-problem extensions.
- **Primary:** [Zalar, The truncated moment problem on curves y=q(x) and yx^ℓ=1 (arXiv:2212.01645)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.01645): current research on bivariate truncated moment problems.
- **Further reading:** [Widder, The Laplace Transform (Princeton)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9781400876457); [Helgason, The Radon Transform (Springer, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-1463-0); [Schmüdgen, The Moment Problem (Springer GTM, 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-64546-9).
references.MSC 44Axx - Integral transforms, operati:
## Reference
### Overview
44Axx is the only subfield of [MSC 44 - Integral transforms, operational calculus](node:MSC%2044%20-%20Integral%20transforms,%20operational%20calculus), and it holds all the research codes of the section, from general integral transforms (44A05) to moment problems (44A60). ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current)) An integral transform has the form $(Tf)(u)=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}f(t)K(t,u)\,dt$, where the kernel $K$ determines the transform. Some kernels have an inverse kernel that yields an inverse transform. ([Wikipedia: Integral transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_transform))

The subfield joins three kinds of mathematics. First come transforms with explicit kernels and their inversion theory (Laplace, Mellin, Hankel, Hilbert, Radon). Second come operational calculi, which turn linear differential equations into algebra by treating $p=d/dt$ as an operator and $F(p)y=g$ as solved by an inverse operator. ([Wikipedia: Operational calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_calculus)) Third come moment problems, the inverse problem of recovering a measure from its moments. These have strong ties to real algebraic geometry and polynomial optimization. ([Schmüdgen, Ten Lectures on the Moment Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.12698))

### Scope
Transform codes: general integral transforms (44A05, see also 42A38), the Laplace transform (44A10), the Radon transform (44A12, see also 92C55), special integral transforms such as Legendre and Hilbert (44A15), integral transforms of special functions (44A20), multiple integral transforms (44A30), and convolution as an integral transform (44A35). ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current))

Operational and moment codes: the calculus of Mikusiński and other operational calculi (44A40), classical operational calculus (44A45), discrete operational calculus (44A55), and moment problems (44A60), with trigonometric moment problems sent to 42A70. ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current))

Boundaries, from the section's cross-references, one line each ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current)):
- Fourier transforms go to 42A38 and 42B10, in [MSC 42Axx - Harmonic analysis in one variable](node:MSC%2042Axx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20one%20variable) and [MSC 42Bxx - Harmonic analysis in several variables](node:MSC%2042Bxx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20several%20variables).
- Integral transforms in distribution spaces go to 46F12, in [MSC 46Fxx - Distributions, generalized functions, distribution spaces](node:MSC%2046Fxx%20-%20Distributions,%20generalized%20functions,%20distribution%20spaces).
- Fractional derivatives and integrals go to 26A33.
- Numerical methods go to 65R10, in [MSC 65Rxx - Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms](node:MSC%2065Rxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20transforms).

### Key concepts
- **Laplace transform and its inversion (44A10).** $(\mathcal Lf)(s)=\int_{0^-}^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the complex $s$ at which the integral converges. The lower limit $0^-$ accommodates generalized functions containing $\delta(t)$. For example, $\mathcal L(1)=1/s$ for $s>0$. ([MIT 18.03SC](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-03sc-differential-equations-fall-2011/d40ad07a62996f6dad93b832f8de0e04_MIT18_03SCF11_s27_1text.pdf)) The region of convergence is a half-plane $\operatorname{Re}s>a$, and $\mathcal L\{f'\}=sF(s)-f(0^-)$. ([Wikipedia: Laplace transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_transform)) Lerch (1903) proved uniqueness: a transform determines its inverse up to a Lebesgue-null set. The Bromwich integral $f(t)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\gamma-iT}^{\gamma+iT}e^{st}F(s)\,ds$ inverts it, with $\gamma$ to the right of all singularities of $F$. ([Wikipedia: Inverse Laplace transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Laplace_transform)) Post's formula $f(t)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}\left(\frac kt\right)^{k+1}F^{(k)}\!\left(\frac kt\right)$ holds for $t>0$ when $f$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and of exponential order. It needs no knowledge of where the poles of $F$ lie, but it is usually impractical. ([Wikipedia: Post's inversion formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post%27s_inversion_formula))
- **Bernstein–Widder theorem (44A10).** A real function on $[0,\infty)$ is completely monotone if and only if it is the Laplace transform $f(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-tx}\,dg(x)$ of a non-negative finite Borel measure on $[0,\infty)$. Widder's 1941 book *The Laplace Transform* is the most cited reference. ([Wikipedia: Bernstein's theorem on monotone functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%27s_theorem_on_monotone_functions))
- **Mellin transform.** The Mellin transform uses the kernel $t^{u-1}$ on $(0,\infty)$ and is the multiplicative form of the two-sided Laplace transform. Its inverse is a line integral inside the fundamental strip, the largest open strip on which the transform is defined. $\Gamma(s)$ is the Mellin transform of $e^{-x}$. The Mellin transform of $1/(e^x-1)$ is $\Gamma(s)\zeta(s)$, and Perron's formula is the inverse Mellin transform of a Dirichlet series. ([Wikipedia: Mellin transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellin_transform)) These connect the subfield with [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function) and [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Special kernels (44A15, 44A20).** The Hilbert transform has kernel $\frac1{\pi(u-t)}$ on $\mathbb R$, and its inverse kernel is the same. The Hankel transform has kernel $tJ_\nu(ut)$ on $(0,\infty)$ and inverse kernel $uJ_\nu(ut)$. The Abel transform has kernel $\frac{2t}{\sqrt{t^2-u^2}}$ on $(u,\infty)$. ([Wikipedia: Integral transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_transform)) Transforms whose kernels are [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions), such as Bessel functions, have their own code, 44A20. ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx&btn=Current))
- **Titchmarsh convolution theorem (44A35, 44A40).** Let $\varphi,\psi$ be integrable with $\int_0^x\varphi(t)\psi(x-t)\,dt=0$ for almost every $x\in(0,\kappa)$. Then there are $\lambda,\mu\ge0$ with $\lambda+\mu\ge\kappa$ such that $\varphi=0$ a.e. on $(0,\lambda)$ and $\psi=0$ a.e. on $(0,\mu)$. In particular, the convolution of two functions on $[0,\infty)$ vanishes identically only if one of them does. Titchmarsh proved it in 1926 by complex-variable methods, and Mikusiński published a new proof in 1953. ([Wikipedia: Titchmarsh convolution theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titchmarsh_convolution_theorem))
- **Mikusiński operational calculus (44A40).** From the convolution product of functions Mikusiński defined what in other contexts is called the field of fractions. Its elements are called Mikusiński operators. ([Wikipedia: Jan Mikusiński](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Mikusi%C5%84ski)) Mikusiński presented the results in 1943 in a secret wartime seminar in Kraków. The first version appeared as "Hypernumbers" in 1944 and was later improved using the Titchmarsh theorem. The book appeared in Polish in 1953, and in English as *Operational Calculus* (Pergamon, 1959). ([MacTutor: Mikusiński](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Mikusinski/))
- **Radon transform (44A12).** In the plane, $Rf$ assigns to each line its integral of $f$. By the projection-slice theorem, the 1D Fourier transform of the projection at angle $\alpha$ is the radial slice of the 2D Fourier transform. Filtered back-projection gives the inversion formula, with separate formulas for odd and even dimension. The singular values of the transform tend to $0$, so the inverse operator is unbounded and inversion is ill-posed. ([Wikipedia: Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform)) Helgason's support theorem is the basic uniqueness result. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact and convex, and let $f$ be continuous on $\mathbb R^d\setminus K$, decaying faster than any power of $|x|$. If $Rf(L)=0$ for every hyperplane $L$ disjoint from $K$, then $f=0$ outside $K$. The decay hypothesis cannot be dropped: for each integer $m\ge d$ there are functions homogeneous of degree $-m$ whose Radon transform vanishes on all hyperplanes missing the origin. ([Boman and Lindskog, arXiv:0802.4373](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0802.4373))
- **Classical moment problems (44A60).** Hamburger's theorem: $(m_n)$ is the moment sequence of a measure on $\mathbb R$ if and only if its Hankel kernel is positive in the sense $\sum_{j,k}m_{j+k}c_j\bar c_k\ge0$ for every finitely supported complex sequence $(c_j)$. ([Wikipedia: Hamburger moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburger_moment_problem)) Stieltjes problem: $(m_n)$ comes from a measure on $[0,\infty)$ with infinite support if and only if both $\det(m_{i+j})_{i,j\le n}>0$ and $\det(m_{i+j+1})_{i,j\le n}>0$ for all $n$. The solution is unique if $\sum_n m_n^{-1/(2n)}=\infty$ (Carleman's condition). ([Wikipedia: Stieltjes moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stieltjes_moment_problem)) Hausdorff problem: $(m_n)$ is a moment sequence on $[0,1]$ if and only if it is completely monotonic, and the solution is then unique. ([Wikipedia: Hausdorff moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_moment_problem)) On unbounded supports uniqueness can fail: log-normal distributions share their moments with other distributions. ([Wikipedia: Moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_problem))
- **Multidimensional moment problems (44A60).** By Haviland's theorem, for closed $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ a linear functional $L$ on $\mathbb R_d[x]$ is a $K$-moment functional if and only if $L(f)\ge0$ for every polynomial $f\ge0$ on $K$. Schmüdgen's theorem covers a compact basic semi-algebraic set $K(\mathsf f)$. There, every functional that is nonnegative on the preordering $T(\mathsf f)$ is a $K(\mathsf f)$-moment functional, and this is equivalent to the strict Positivstellensatz: a polynomial positive on $K(\mathsf f)$ lies in $T(\mathsf f)$. For $d\ge2$ positivity on sums of squares is not enough: as Hilbert noted in 1888, some nonnegative polynomials are not sums of squares, and Motzkin's polynomial in two variables is a prominent example. ([Schmüdgen, Ten Lectures on the Moment Problem, Theorems 1.9, 4.10–4.11, §5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.12698))

### History
Euler studied Laplace-type integrals as solutions of differential equations from 1744, and Laplace began using such transforms in 1785. ([Wikipedia: Laplace transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_transform)) Operator methods run through Arbogast (1800), Servois (1814), Carmichael (1855) and Boole (1859) to Heaviside's non-rigorous 1893 telegraphy work. Bromwich justified them through the Laplace transform, and Carson and Wiener gave other justifications in the mid-1920s. ([Wikipedia: Operational calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_calculus)) Riemann introduced the Mellin transform in 1859, and Mellin treated it rigorously in 1897. ([Wikipedia: Mellin transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellin_transform)) Johann Radon introduced his transform and its inversion in 1917. ([Wikipedia: Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform)) Stieltjes (1894) formulated and solved the moment problem on the half-line and gave the first explicit indeterminate example. Hamburger and Hausdorff studied the real line and bounded intervals later, around 1920. ([Schmüdgen, Ten Lectures on the Moment Problem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.12698)) Mikusiński's algebraic calculus dates from 1943–1944, though the operational-calculus article places it in the 1930s. ([MacTutor: Mikusiński](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Mikusinski/); [Wikipedia: Operational calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_calculus))

### Open problems
- **The bivariate truncated moment problem.** The $\mathbb R^2$ truncated moment problem asks when a finite bivariate sequence $\beta^{(2k)}$ has a representing positive measure on $\mathbb R^2$. Zalar's paper on the truncated moment problem on curves records that when the moment matrix has no relations, "for $k>2$ the solution to the TMP is not known", while the case $k=2$ is known. The concretely solved cases it lists include measures supported on varieties defined by polynomials of degree at most 2 and on the curve $y=x^3$, and moment matrices with special features such as recursive determinateness or extremality. ([arXiv:2212.01645](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.01645))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Integral transform, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_transform): general definition, inverse kernels, and a table of the standard transforms.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.03SC, Definition of Laplace Transform](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-03sc-differential-equations-fall-2011/d40ad07a62996f6dad93b832f8de0e04_MIT18_03SCF11_s27_1text.pdf): course notes with the $0^-$ convention and first examples.
- **Learn:** [Schmüdgen, Ten Lectures on the Moment Problem (arXiv:2008.12698)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.12698): lecture notes on the one-dimensional, multidimensional and truncated moment problems.
- **Primary:** [Boman and Lindskog, support theorems for the Radon transform (arXiv:0802.4373)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0802.4373): statement and Strichartz's proof of Helgason's support theorem, with exterior-problem variants.
- **Primary:** [Zalar, The truncated moment problem on curves y=q(x) and yx^ℓ=1 (arXiv:2212.01645)](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.01645): recent research on bivariate truncated moment problems and what remains unsolved.
- **Further reading:** [Widder, The Laplace Transform (Princeton)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1515/9781400876457); [Helgason, The Radon Transform (Springer, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-1463-0); [Schmüdgen, The Moment Problem (Springer GTM, 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-64546-9).
references.MSC 45 - Integral equations:
## Reference
### Overview
An integral equation is an equation in which the unknown function appears under an integral sign; integral equations are the integral analogue of differential equations. They are classified as linear or nonlinear, homogeneous or inhomogeneous, of the first, second or third kind, Fredholm (fixed limits) or Volterra (variable limit), and regular or singular. ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))

The linear second-kind equation $\lambda\varphi(x)-\int_a^bK(x,y)\varphi(y)\,dy=f(x)$ is the prototype. Its solution theory, created by Fredholm and extended by Hilbert to a complete eigenvalue theory, led directly to the theory of Hilbert spaces; the Fredholm alternative extends to any compact operator. ([MacTutor: Fredholm](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Fredholm/); [Wikipedia: Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) Integral equations arise in boundary-value problems, radiative transfer, ruin theory, option pricing, viscoelasticity and fluid mechanics. ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))

### Scope
MSC2020 section 45 has these subject groups ([MSC2020 45-XX, AMS](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX)):
- Linear theory: [45A linear](node:MSC%2045Axx%20-%20Linear%20integral%20equations), [45B Fredholm](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations), [45C eigenvalue problems](node:MSC%2045Cxx%20-%20Eigenvalue%20problems%20for%20integral%20equations), [45D Volterra](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations), [45E singular](node:MSC%2045Exx%20-%20Singular%20integral%20equations), 45F systems of linear equations, 45H special kernels. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))
- Nonlinear and mixed: [45G nonlinear](node:MSC%2045Gxx%20-%20Nonlinear%20integral%20equations), [45J integro-ODEs](node:MSC%2045Jxx%20-%20Integro-ordinary%20differential%20equations), [45K integro-PDEs](node:MSC%2045Kxx%20-%20Integro-partial%20differential%20equations). ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))
- Theory of solutions: 45L theoretical approximation, [45M qualitative behaviour](node:MSC%2045Mxx%20-%20Qualitative%20behavior%20of%20solutions%20to%20integral%20equations), 45N abstract integral equations in abstract spaces, [45P integral operators](node:MSC%2045Pxx%20-%20Integral%20operators), [45Q inverse problems](node:MSC%2045Qxx%20-%20Inverse%20problems%20for%20integral%20equations), [45R random integral equations](node:MSC%2045Rxx%20-%20Random%20integral%20equations). ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))

Neighbouring codes, one line each, using the cross-references MSC2020 itself gives ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX)):
- 44 (integral transforms, operational calculus) studies transforms as objects; 45 studies equations whose unknown is under the integral. 45E cross-references 44A15 and 44A35, and 45H cross-references 44A15. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))
- 47 (operator theory) studies integral operators as operators; 45P cross-references 47B38 and 47G10, and 45G cross-references 47H30 and 47Jxx for nonlinear operator equations. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))
- 65Rxx holds numerical analysis of integral equations; 45L is restricted to theoretical approximation of solutions. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))
- 34 and 35 hold differential equations; 45J and 45K cross-reference 34K05, 34K30, 35R09, 35R10 and 47G20, and 45C cross-references the eigenvalue codes 34Lxx and 35Pxx. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))
- 60H20 (stochastic integral equations) is the probability-side counterpart of 45R. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Fredholm alternative.** For $\lambda\ne0$ and $K\in L^2([a,b]^2)$, either the homogeneous equation $\lambda\varphi-\int K\varphi=0$ has a nontrivial solution, or the inhomogeneous equation is solvable for every $f$. The same holds for $\lambda I-K$ with $K$ any compact operator on a Banach space. Equivalently, a nonzero $\lambda$ is either an eigenvalue of $K$ or lies in the resolvent set. ([Wikipedia: Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) See [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) and [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces).
- **Volterra equations of the second kind.** For $x(t)=f(t)+\int_0^tK(t,s)x(s)\,ds$ with continuous data there is a unique continuous solution, given by a resolvent kernel that is the limit of a Neumann series. A first-kind equation can be converted to the second kind by differentiation when $K(t,t)\ne0$, and convolution kernels $K(t-s)$ are solved by the Laplace transform. ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation); [Wikipedia: Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)) Integrating an initial value problem for [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) gives a Volterra equation; for example, $u'=2tu$, $u(0)=1$ becomes $u(t)=1+\int_0^t2su(s)\,ds$. ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))
- **Abel's integral equation.** It is the model weakly singular Volterra equation of the first kind, and certain singular first-kind kernels reduce to it. ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation); [Wikipedia: Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation))
- **Wiener–Hopf equations.** The half-line convolution equation $\int_0^\infty k(x-t)f(t)\,dt=g(x)$, $x>0$, introduced in a joint paper of Wiener and Hopf, is solved by factorizing the symbol as $K=K_+K_-$, with factors analytic and invertible in opposite half-planes. Scalar factorization is always possible by Cauchy-type integrals, and the index is the winding number of the symbol. ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))
- **Nonlinear equations.** Urysohn equations $f(x)=g(x)+\int_a^bk(x,y,f(y))\,dy$ and Hammerstein equations $f(x)=g(x)+\int_a^bk(x,y)G(y,f(y))\,dy$ are basic nonlinear classes (45G). ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))
- **Links to PDE.** Fredholm's 1900 preliminary report was titled "Sur une nouvelle méthode pour la résolution du problème de Dirichlet", so the theory began as a method for the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem) for [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations). See also [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions). ([MacTutor: Fredholm](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Fredholm/))
- **Discretization.** Replacing the integral by a quadrature rule turns the equation into a linear system; for Volterra equations the trapezoidal rule gives $x=(I-M)^{-1}f$. ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation); [Wikipedia: Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)) See [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra).

### History
Volterra studied some aspects of integral equations before Fredholm, but little had been done before Fredholm's preliminary report of 1900 and his 1903 Acta Mathematica paper "Sur une classe d'équations fonctionnelles". Holmgren lectured on Fredholm's work at Göttingen in 1901. Hilbert then built a complete eigenvalue theory for Fredholm equations, and this led directly to the theory of [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces). ([MacTutor: Fredholm](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Fredholm/); [Wikipedia: Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) Lalescu studied Volterra equations in his 1908 thesis and wrote the first book on integral equations in 1911. ([Wikipedia: Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation))

### Open problems
- **Matrix Wiener–Hopf factorization.** No constructive factorization procedure is known for general matrix symbols, and in general there is no method to determine the partial indices. The partial indices can change under small perturbations; by Gohberg–Krein they are stable exactly when $\kappa_1-\kappa_n\le1$. Because the indices are unknown, approximate factorizations generally come without guarantees. ([Kisil, Abrahams, Mishuris, Rogosin, arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))
- **Singular stochastic Volterra equations.** For $X_t=x_0+\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}g(s)\,ds+\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}\sigma(X_s)\,dB_s$ with $0<\alpha<1/2$, pathwise uniqueness holds when $\sigma$ is $\gamma$-Hölder with $\gamma>1/(2(1-\alpha))$. Whether uniqueness fails below this threshold is left open. ([Mytnik–Salisbury, arXiv:1502.05513](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1502.05513))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation): classification, Volterra theory, Wiener–Hopf, and numerics.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102 (2009, Melrose), Lecture 19: Fredholm operators](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2009/resources/mit18_102s09_lec19/): lecture notes on Fredholm operators and spectral theory of compact self-adjoint operators.
- **Primary:** [Kisil, Abrahams, Mishuris, Rogosin, The Wiener–Hopf technique, its generalizations and applications (arXiv:2107.06088)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088): research survey including the open matrix problems.
- **Further reading:** [Kress, Linear Integral Equations, Applied Mathematical Sciences, Springer 2014](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4614-9593-2): graduate monograph on linear integral equations.
references.MSC 45Axx - Linear integral equations:
## Reference
### Overview
An integral equation has the unknown function under an integral sign; it is linear when the unknown and its integrals appear linearly. Equations are of the first kind if the unknown appears only inside the integral and of the second kind if it also appears outside; Fredholm equations have fixed limits and Volterra equations a variable limit; an equation is homogeneous if the known function vanishes, and singular if the integral is improper. ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation)) See [Linear Integral Equations](node:Linear%20Integral%20Equations).

The two kinds behave very differently. Second-kind equations $\varphi=f+\lambda K\varphi$ with a compact integral operator $K$ are governed by Riesz–Schauder spectral theory and the Fredholm alternative. ([Wikipedia: Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) First-kind equations $K f=g$ with compact $K$ are ill-posed in Hadamard's sense, because a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is not invertible; regularization methods such as spectral cutoff, Tikhonov and iterative regularization address this. ([Jin, Computational Inverse Problems, CUHK](https://www.math.cuhk.edu.hk/~btjin/math6221/lect1.pdf))

### Scope
In MSC2020, 45Axx ("Linear integral equations") contains 45A05 ("Linear integral equations") and 45A99. ([MSC2020 45Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Axx&btn=Current)) Neighbours within 45:
- [MSC 45Bxx - Fredholm integral equations](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations) and [MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations): the fixed-limit and variable-limit families; 45D is cross-referenced to 34A12. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 45Cxx - Eigenvalue problems for integral equations](node:MSC%2045Cxx%20-%20Eigenvalue%20problems%20for%20integral%20equations): spectral questions, cross-referenced to 34Lxx, 35Pxx, 45P05 and 47A75. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 45Exx - Singular integral equations](node:MSC%2045Exx%20-%20Singular%20integral%20equations) and [MSC 45Pxx - Integral operators](node:MSC%2045Pxx%20-%20Integral%20operators): Cauchy-type kernels (see 30E20, 30E25) and the operators themselves (see 47B38, 47G10). ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 45Qxx - Inverse problems for integral equations](node:MSC%2045Qxx%20-%20Inverse%20problems%20for%20integral%20equations): inverse problems for integral equations. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 45Gxx - Nonlinear integral equations](node:MSC%2045Gxx%20-%20Nonlinear%20integral%20equations) (see 47H30, 47Jxx) and [MSC 65Rxx - Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms](node:MSC%2065Rxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20transforms), to which 45L sends numerical analysis. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Fredholm and Volterra forms.** First kind $g(t)=\int_a^bK(t,s)f(s)\,ds$; second kind $\varphi(t)=f(t)+\lambda\int_a^bK(t,s)\varphi(s)\,ds$, whose iteration gives the Liouville–Neumann series and the resolvent formalism (see [Resolvent Kernels](node:Resolvent%20Kernels)). For convolution kernels on $\mathbb{R}$ the equation is solved formally by Fourier transform. ([Wikipedia: Fredholm integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation)) Volterra equations of convolution type are solved by Laplace transform, and a first-kind Volterra equation becomes second-kind by differentiation when $K(t,t)\ne0$. See [Volterra Integral Equations](node:Volterra%20Integral%20Equations) and [Integral Equations with Convolution Kernels](node:Integral%20Equations%20with%20Convolution%20Kernels). ([Wikipedia: Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation))
- **Contraction solvability.** If $K$ is continuous on $[a,b]^2$ with $c=\max|K|$ and $|\lambda|<1/(c(b-a))$, then $x-\lambda\int_a^bK(\cdot,s)x(s)\,ds=v$ has a unique continuous solution for each continuous $v$, by the [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem). If $K$ is continuous on $a\le s\le t\le b$, the Volterra equation has a unique continuous solution for every real $\lambda$, since $\|T^m x-T^m y\|\le\frac{(|\lambda|c(b-a))^m}{m!}\|x-y\|$. ([Laugesen, Linear Analysis and PDE, Illinois](https://publish.illinois.edu/rlaugesen/files/2023/07/554-Lectures.pdf))
- **Riesz–Schauder theory.** For a compact operator $C$ on a [Banach space](node:Banach%20Spaces), every nonzero point of the spectrum is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional generalized eigenspace, nonzero eigenvalues accumulate only at $0$, the spectrum is at most countable, and $\operatorname{Ran}(I-C)$ is closed. ([Wikipedia: Spectral theory of compact operators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_compact_operators)) See [Compact Integral Operators](node:Compact%20Integral%20Operators) and [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory).
- **[Fredholm Alternative](node:Fredholm%20Alternative).** For a square-integrable kernel on $[a,b]^2$ and $\lambda\ne0$, either the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution or the inhomogeneous equation is solvable for every $f$; results about Fredholm operators generalize this to Banach spaces, and in the boundary-value application the set of $\lambda$ for which solvability fails is a discrete set of eigenvalues. ([Wikipedia: Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative))
- **Hilbert–Schmidt theory.** A kernel $k\in L^2(\Omega\times\Omega)$ defines a compact operator with $\|T\|_{HS}=\|k\|_{L^2}$, self-adjoint if $k(x,y)=\overline{k(y,x)}$. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator)) For compact self-adjoint $B$ on a separable Hilbert space there is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and $\{\beta_k:|\beta_k|>\varepsilon\}$ is finite for each $\varepsilon>0$, so symmetric kernels have eigenfunction expansions; see [Compact and Selfadjoint Operators](node:Compact%20and%20Selfadjoint%20Operators) and [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem). ([Laugesen, Illinois](https://publish.illinois.edu/rlaugesen/files/2023/07/554-Lectures.pdf))
- **[Fredholm Determinants](node:Fredholm%20Determinants).** $\det(I-\lambda K)=\exp\bigl[-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\lambda^n}{n}\operatorname{Tr}K^n\bigr]$. ([Wikipedia: Fredholm theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory)) For trace-class $A$, $z\mapsto\det(I+zA)$ is entire and multiplicative, $\operatorname{Tr}K=\int K(x,x)\,dx$ for integral operators, and Fredholm showed $u+z\int K(x,y)u(y)\,dy=f$ has a unique solution when $\det(I+zA)\ne0$. ([Wikipedia: Fredholm determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_determinant))
- **Ill-posedness and Picard's criterion.** Hadamard calls a problem well-posed if a solution exists, is unique and depends continuously on the data. A compact $A$ has a singular system $Av_n=s_nu_n$, $s_n\downarrow0$; Picard's criterion (1909): $Ax=y$ is solvable iff $y\in\overline{\operatorname{range}A}$ and $\sum_n s_n^{-2}|(y,u_n)|^2<\infty$, with solutions $x_0+\sum_n s_n^{-1}(y,u_n)v_n$, $x_0\in\ker A$. The backward [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation) is the model example. ([Jin, CUHK](https://www.math.cuhk.edu.hk/~btjin/math6221/lect1.pdf)) See [Integral Equation Inverse Problems](node:Integral%20Equation%20Inverse%20Problems).
- **Tikhonov [regularization](node:Regularization).** Minimize $\|Ax-b\|^2+\alpha^2\|x\|^2$; in the singular value decomposition the solution is $\sum_i f_i\,\frac{u_i^{\mathsf T}b}{\sigma_i}v_i$ with Wiener weights $f_i=\sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2+\alpha^2)$ that damp small singular values, and the parameter can be chosen by generalized cross-validation, the discrepancy principle or the L-curve. The method became widely known through its application to integral equations by Tikhonov and Phillips. ([Wikipedia: Tikhonov regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikhonov_regularization); [Wikipedia: Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem))

### History
Fredholm's "Sur une classe d'équations fonctionnelles" (*Acta Math.* 27, 1903, 365–390) introduced the determinant to solve second-kind equations. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02421317); [Wikipedia: Fredholm determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_determinant)) It is considered one of the major landmarks in the establishment of operator theory, and Hilbert developed the abstraction of Hilbert space in association with research on integral equations prompted in part by Fredholm's. ([Wikipedia: Fredholm theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory)) F. Riesz first developed the spectral theory of compact operators. ([Wikipedia: Spectral theory of compact operators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory_of_compact_operators))

Volterra introduced the equations with a variable limit; Lalescu wrote his 1908 thesis on them under Picard and in 1911 the first book on integral equations. ([Wikipedia: Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)) Hadamard's well-posedness criteria date from 1902, and Tikhonov regularization, one of the most commonly used methods for linear ill-posed problems, became widely known through its application to integral equations by Tikhonov and Phillips. ([Wikipedia: Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem); [Wikipedia: Tikhonov regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikhonov_regularization))

### Open problems
- **Regularization theory for first-kind Volterra equations.** Lamm's survey of open problems in inverse-problem solution methods recorded, for local regularization (which unlike Tikhonov's method preserves causality), that convergence theory then covered only a restricted class of kernels (excluding the inverse heat conduction kernel), that numerical evidence suggested stability may fail for some kernel classes although this was not proven, and that no theory was available for choosing the variable regularization parameters. ([Lamm, Some recent developments and open problems in solution methods for mathematical inverse problems](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/lamm/Preprints/Belo_Horizonte_survey/paper.pdf)) Part of this list has since been addressed: Brooks and Lamm (2019) proved stability and convergence of an improved first-order local regularization method for $\nu$-smoothing kernels for every natural number $\nu$, where an earlier version degraded at $\nu=4$ and its convergence theory was unclear for $\nu>4$. ([Brooks–Lamm, J. Math. Anal. Appl. 477 (2019)](https://scholarscommons.fgcu.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/An-improved-first-order-local-regularization/99383431845906570))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Integral equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation): classification by kind, limits, homogeneity and regularity.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current): official field boundaries.
- **Learn:** [Laugesen, Linear Analysis and PDE lecture notes (Illinois)](https://publish.illinois.edu/rlaugesen/files/2023/07/554-Lectures.pdf): fixed-point solution of Fredholm and Volterra equations, compact self-adjoint spectral theorem, Hilbert–Schmidt operators.
- **Learn:** [Jin, Computational Inverse Problems lecture 1 (CUHK)](https://www.math.cuhk.edu.hk/~btjin/math6221/lect1.pdf): Hadamard, compact operators, singular systems, Picard's criterion.
- **Primary:** [Fredholm, Sur une classe d'équations fonctionnelles (Acta Math. 1903)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02421317): the founding paper.
- **Primary:** [Lamm, survey of regularization methods and open problems (MSU)](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/lamm/Preprints/Belo_Horizonte_survey/paper.pdf): regularization of first-kind equations and open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Kress, Linear Integral Equations (Springer, Applied Mathematical Sciences, 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4614-9593-2): the standard graduate monograph.

## Reference
### Overview
A Fredholm integral equation is an integral equation in which both limits of integration are fixed constants; a [Volterra equation](node:Volterra%20Integral%20Equations) is one in which at least one limit is variable. In an equation of the first kind the unknown appears only under the integral sign, $g(t)=\int_a^b K(t,s)f(s)\,ds$; in the second kind it also appears outside, $\varphi(t)=f(t)+\lambda\int_a^b K(t,s)\varphi(s)\,ds$. ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation); [Fredholm integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation))

A principal result is that the kernel yields a compact operator (for instance, any square-integrable kernel does), whose spectrum is a discrete set of eigenvalues tending to $0$. ([Fredholm integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation); [Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator)) For a square-integrable kernel, the Fredholm theorems decide solvability of the second-kind equation by orthogonality of the data to the finitely many independent solutions of the adjoint homogeneous equation. ([Fredholm integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation); [Fredholm's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm%27s_theorem)) For the first kind the same decay of singular values makes the problem ill-posed: the generalized inverse is unbounded and regularization is needed. ([Dong–Cheng–Li, arXiv:2603.20602](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.20602); [Tikhonov regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikhonov_regularization)) Fredholm's 1903 paper is described as a landmark of operator theory, and Hilbert developed Hilbert space partly through work on integral equations prompted by it. ([Fredholm theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory))

### Key concepts
- **Hilbert–Schmidt kernels.** If $k\in L^2(\Omega\times\Omega)$, then $Tf(x)=\int k(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ is a compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator on $L^2(\Omega)$ with $\|T\|_{HS}=\|k\|_{L^2}$; if $k(x,y)=\overline{k(y,x)}$ it is self-adjoint and the [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem) applies. See [Compact Integral Operators](node:Compact%20Integral%20Operators) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces). ([Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator))
- **Fredholm theorems (full alternative).** Let $K\in L^2([a,b]^2)$, with $a$ or $b$ possibly infinite, and fix $\lambda\neq0$. Consider $\lambda\varphi(x)-\int_a^bK(x,y)\varphi(y)\,dy=0$ and its adjoint $\bar\lambda\psi(x)-\int_a^b\overline{K(y,x)}\psi(y)\,dy=0$. (i) Either both have only the trivial solution, or both have the same finite number $n$ of linearly independent solutions $\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n$ and $\psi_1,\dots,\psi_n$. (ii) The inhomogeneous equation $\lambda\varphi-\int_a^bK\varphi=f$ is solvable if and only if $\int_a^b\overline{\psi_j(x)}f(x)\,dx=0$ for every $j$. (iii) Hence either the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution or the inhomogeneous one is uniquely solvable for every $f$; the alternative holds for every compact operator on a Banach space. ([Fredholm's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm%27s_theorem); [Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) Note: [Fredholm Alternative](node:Fredholm%20Alternative).
- **Fredholm operators and index.** A bounded $T:X\to Y$ between Banach spaces is Fredholm if $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{coker}T$ are finite-dimensional; its index $\dim\ker T-\dim\operatorname{coker}T$ is unchanged by compact perturbations, and the Fredholm operators form an open set on which the index is locally constant. $T$ is Fredholm exactly when it is invertible modulo compact operators. Since $I$ has index $0$, every $I+K$ with $K$ compact is Fredholm of index $0$, the abstract form of (i). See [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) and [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory). ([Fredholm operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_operator))
- **Liouville–Neumann series and resolvent kernel.** For $\lambda$ small enough that the series converges, $\varphi=\sum_n\lambda^n\varphi_n$ with $\varphi_n=\int K_n(x,z)f(z)\,dz$, where $K_n$ are the iterated kernels; equivalently $\varphi(x)=\int R(x,z;\lambda)f(z)\,dz$ with $R=\sum_{n\ge0}\lambda^nK_n$. See [Resolvent Kernels](node:Resolvent%20Kernels). ([Liouville–Neumann series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville%E2%80%93Neumann_series))
- **Fredholm determinant.** For trace-class $A$, $\det(I+A)=\sum_{k\ge0}\operatorname{tr}\Lambda^k(A)$ converges absolutely and is multiplicative. For a trace-class integral operator with kernel $K$, $\det(I-\lambda T)=\sum_{n\ge0}(-\lambda)^n\operatorname{tr}\Lambda^nT$, which equals $\exp\!\big(-\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{tr}(T^n)\lambda^n/n\big)$ for small $|\lambda|$, $\operatorname{tr}T=\int K(x,x)\,dx$ and $\operatorname{tr}\Lambda^nT=\frac1{n!}\int\det[K(x_i,x_j)]\,dx$. Fredholm showed $u+z\int Ku=f$ has a unique solution when $\det(I+zA)\ne0$; Widom used Fredholm determinants to give a new proof of Szegő's limit formula, and his singular version of that formula, for symbols supported on an arc, has been applied to the eigenvalue distribution of random unitary matrices. Extends [Determinant](node:Determinant); see [Fredholm Determinants](node:Fredholm%20Determinants). ([Fredholm determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_determinant); [Fredholm theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory))
- **First kind: singular value expansion and Picard's criterion.** Let $A:X\to Y$ be compact and injective between infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces with singular system $(\sigma_j,v_j,u_j)$: $(v_j)$ is an orthonormal basis of $X$, $(u_j)$ is orthonormal in $Y$, $Av_j=\sigma_ju_j$, $A^*u_j=\sigma_jv_j$, $\sigma_j\downarrow0$; the $u_j$ then span a dense subspace of $\overline{A(X)}$. For $g\in\overline{A(X)}$, the equation $Af=g$ is solvable if and only if $\sum_j|\langle g,u_j\rangle|^2/\sigma_j^2<\infty$, and then $f=\sum_j\sigma_j^{-1}\langle g,u_j\rangle v_j$. Because $\sigma_j\to0$, the inverse is unbounded and perturbations of $g$ are amplified by $1/\sigma_j$. Burns and Rust attribute the criterion to Picard via Kress's Theorem 15.18. See [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition). ([Burns–Rust, arXiv:1805.09849](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1805.09849); [Dong–Cheng–Li, arXiv:2603.20602](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.20602))
- **[Regularization](node:Regularization) of first-kind equations.** Hadamard (1902) required existence, uniqueness and continuous dependence on data ([Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems)). ([Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem)) Tikhonov's method replaces $Kx=y$ by the second-kind equation $(\alpha I+K^*K)x_\alpha=K^*y$, which, for a singular system $(\mu_j,x_j,y_j)$ of $K$, is the filter $x_\alpha=\sum_j\frac{\mu_j^2}{\alpha+\mu_j^2}\mu_j^{-1}(y,y_j)x_j$. ([Pang–Wang, arXiv:2504.00209](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.00209)) The method became widely known through Tikhonov's work on integral equations from 1943, with Phillips's contribution (1962). ([Tikhonov regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikhonov_regularization)) See [Integral Equation Inverse Problems](node:Integral%20Equation%20Inverse%20Problems).
- **Nyström method.** Replacing the integral by a quadrature rule $\sum_kw_kK(x,x_k)f(x_k)$ turns a second-kind equation into an $n\times n$ linear system (see [Numerical Quadrature for Integral Equations](node:Numerical%20Quadrature%20for%20Integral%20Equations)), and the same rule interpolates the solution between nodes; Gaussian quadrature is usually a good choice for smooth, nonsingular kernels (Nyström, Acta Math. 54, 1930). ([Nyström method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystr%C3%B6m_method)) MSC2020 classifies theoretical approximation of solutions under [MSC 45Lxx - Theoretical approximation of solutions to integral equations](node:MSC%2045Lxx%20-%20Theoretical%20approximation%20of%20solutions%20to%20integral%20equations), which points to 65Rxx for numerical analysis. ([MSC2020 45Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Lxx&btn=Current))

### History
Ivar Fredholm's "Sur une classe d'équations fonctionnelles" appeared in Acta Mathematica 27 (1903), 365–390. ([Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02421317)) Hadamard introduced well-posedness in 1902, Nyström's quadrature method appeared in 1930, and Tikhonov's regularization of integral equations dates from 1943. ([Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem); [Nyström method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystr%C3%B6m_method); [Tikhonov regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikhonov_regularization)) Groetsch's survey traces the first-kind theory through E. Schmidt's singular functions, Picard's existence criterion and the Moore–Penrose generalized inverse. ([Groetsch 2007](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/73/1/012001)) MIT's graduate course 18.307 (Margetis, 2006) teaches Fredholm theory with the Hilbert–Schmidt theorem, Volterra equations, the Wiener–Hopf method and Cauchy-type singular equations. ([MIT 18.307](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-307-integral-equations-spring-2006/))

### Open problems
- **Eigenfunctions of the Airy integral operator.** Let $A_s$ be the integral operator on $L^2(s,\infty)$ with Airy kernel $\frac{\mathrm{Ai}(\lambda)\mathrm{Ai}'(\mu)-\mathrm{Ai}'(\lambda)\mathrm{Ai}(\mu)}{\lambda-\mu}$; its Fredholm determinant $\det(1-A_s)$ is the edge-scaling distribution of the largest GUE eigenvalue. Deift lists analysing the eigenfunctions of $A_s$, both as $s\to\infty$ and for finite $s$, as an open problem, in parallel with the sine-kernel determinant $\det(1-K_s)$, which gives gap probabilities and is evaluated numerically by Bornemann's method. ([Deift, Some open problems II, arXiv:1703.04931](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1703.04931); [Bornemann, arXiv:0804.2543](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.2543))
- **Kenig's problem on the double-layer operator.** For second-kind boundary integral equations $\pm\frac12I+D$ on a Lipschitz boundary $\Gamma$, Chandler-Wilde and Spence state that it remains open whether the essential spectral radius of the double-layer operator $D$ on $L^2(\Gamma)$ is below $1/2$ for every Lipschitz $\Gamma$; it is known for convex domains, small Lipschitz character, and Lipschitz polyhedra. They settle the related essential-norm and coercivity questions negatively. ([Chandler-Wilde–Spence, arXiv:2105.11383](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.11383); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.11383))

## Reference
### Overview
An eigenvalue problem for an integral equation asks for the numbers $\lambda$ and nonzero functions $\varphi$ with $\int_\Omega k(x,y)\varphi(y)\,dy=\lambda\varphi(x)$. When $k\in L^2(\Omega\times\Omega)$, the operator is a Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator. It is continuous and compact, and its Hilbert–Schmidt norm is $\|k\|_{L^2}$. If moreover $k(x,y)=\overline{k(y,x)}$, the operator is self-adjoint and the spectral theorem applies. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator)) The nonzero spectrum of a compact operator consists of eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity. ([Bornemann, arXiv:0804.2543](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.2543))

A recurring question is how properties of the kernel control the eigenvalues and singular values. The regularity of the kernel forces decay rates of the singular values, and the decay rate relates to how ill-posed the inverse problem is. ([Volkov, arXiv:2309.00153](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.00153)) For concrete operators, above all time-and-band limiting, the distribution of the eigenvalues is studied in detail. ([Kulikov, arXiv:2306.12430](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.12430))

### Key concepts
- **Mercer's theorem (1909).** Let $K$ be continuous, symmetric and positive definite on $[a,b]^2$. Then $L^2[a,b]$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions $e_j$ of $T_K$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j\ge0$, and the eigenfunctions with $\lambda_j>0$ are continuous. Moreover $K(s,t)=\sum_j\lambda_je_j(s)e_j(t)$, with absolute and uniform convergence, so $T_K$ is trace class and $\sum_j\lambda_j=\int_a^bK(t,t)\,dt$. Without continuity, on a $\sigma$-finite space, the expansion converges only in $L^2$. ([Wikipedia: Mercer's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem))
- **Reproducing kernels.** The Moore–Aronszajn theorem says that a symmetric positive definite kernel $K$ on a set $X$ is the reproducing kernel of a unique Hilbert space of functions on $X$. For a continuous kernel on a compact space with a strictly positive finite Borel measure, Mercer's eigen-expansion describes that space explicitly: it consists of the $L^2$ functions $f$ with $\sum_j\langle f,e_j\rangle^2/\lambda_j<\infty$. Every feature map defines a kernel, and every positive definite kernel has infinitely many feature maps, the link used in [Kernel Methods](node:Kernel%20Methods). ([Wikipedia: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducing_kernel_Hilbert_space))
- **Traces, Lidskii's theorem and Carleman's counterexample.** For trace-class $A$, Lidskii's theorem gives $\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_n\lambda_n(A)$, summed with algebraic multiplicity. If an integral operator with continuous kernel is trace class, then $\operatorname{tr}A=\int_a^bK(x,x)\,dx$. Continuity of the kernel alone does not make the operator trace class, as Carleman (1918) showed. ([Bornemann, arXiv:0804.2543](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.2543))
- **Fredholm determinant.** This extends the matrix [Determinant](node:Determinant) to integral operators. Fredholm (1903) attached to $u+z\int K(x,y)u(y)\,dy=f$ an entire function $d(z)$. He proved the equation uniquely solvable if and only if $d(z)\ne0$. ([Bornemann, arXiv:0804.2543](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.2543); [Wikipedia: Fredholm determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_determinant)) For trace-class $A$, $\det(I+zA)=\prod_n(1+z\lambda_n(A))$ is entire, with zeros exactly at $z=-1/\lambda_n(A)$, counting multiplicity. So the nonzero eigenvalues of $A$ correspond to the zeros of an entire function. For example, the probability that an interval of length $s$ contains no eigenvalue of the Gaussian unitary ensemble, in the bulk scaling limit with level spacing 1, is the Fredholm determinant of the sine kernel on $(0,s)$. A Nyström-type quadrature computes such determinants with exponential convergence for analytic kernels. ([Bornemann, arXiv:0804.2543](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.2543))
- **Min-max principle.** For compact self-adjoint $A$ with positive eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$, counted with multiplicity, $\lambda_k=\max_{\dim S=k}\min_{x\in S,\|x\|=1}\langle Ax,x\rangle=\min_{\dim S=k-1}\max_{x\perp S,\|x\|=1}\langle Ax,x\rangle$. ([Wikipedia: Min-max theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Min-max_theorem)) Kulikov's and Bonami–Jaming–Karoui's eigenvalue lower bounds both come from applying it to well-chosen subspaces. ([Kulikov, arXiv:2306.12430](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.12430))
- **Positive kernels: Jentzsch and Krein–Rutman.** Jentzsch (1912): let $k$ be continuous on $[0,1]^2$ with $k(s,t)>0$ everywhere, acting on $L^2[0,1]$. Then the spectral radius is positive and is a simple eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenfunction, and every other eigenvalue has strictly smaller modulus. ([Intissar, arXiv:1910.01120](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.01120)) Krein–Rutman (1948) is the cone version. Let $X$ be a Banach space with a convex cone $K$, $K\cap-K=\{0\}$ and $K-K$ dense. If $T$ is compact, nonzero, maps $K$ into $K$ and has $r(T)>0$, then $r(T)$ is an eigenvalue with an eigenvector in $K\setminus\{0\}$. ([Wikipedia: Krein–Rutman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krein%E2%80%93Rutman_theorem))
- **Eigenvalue decay versus kernel smoothness.** The more regular the kernel, the faster the singular values decay, and the decay rate relates to the ill-posedness of the inverse problem. Volkov's theorem: let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open with Lipschitz boundary, $\Omega'\subset\mathbb R^{d'}$ open, and $k\in L^2(\Omega')\times H^p(\Omega)$. Then the singular values of $K\varphi(x)=\int_\Omega k(x,y)\varphi(y)\,dy$ satisfy $\sum_n n^{2p/d}s_n(K)^2<\infty$, so $s_n(K)=o(n^{-p/d-1/2})$; more precisely $s_n(K)$ is bounded by $Cn^{-p/d}$ times singular values of the operators with kernels $\partial^p_yk$. This estimate is optimal for $C^p$ boundaries and quasi-optimal for Lipschitz ones. If $k$ is analytic in $y$ near $\overline\Omega$, then $s_n(K)\le C\tau^{n^{1/d}}$ for some $\tau\in(0,1)$, and this is sharp. The results recover Ha's bound $s_n(K)=o(n^{-p})$ for $d=1$ and kernels with continuous derivatives, and generalize Little and Reade's one-dimensional analytic results; the relation between regularity and decay was thoroughly understood only in dimension one. ([Volkov, arXiv:2309.00153](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.00153))
- **Karhunen–Loève expansion.** Let $X_t$ be a zero-mean square-integrable process on $[a,b]$ with continuous covariance $K_X$. Then $X_t=\sum_kZ_ke_k(t)$, where the $e_k$ are eigenfunctions of the covariance operator and the $Z_k$ are uncorrelated with variance $\lambda_k$. The convergence is in $L^2$, uniformly in $t$. This makes covariance eigenproblems central for [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes). ([Wikipedia: Karhunen–Loève theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karhunen%E2%80%93Lo%C3%A8ve_theorem))
- **Time–frequency localization.** For sets $T,\Omega$ of finite measure, $S_{T,\Omega}=P_TQ_\Omega P_T$ is a self-adjoint Hilbert–Schmidt operator with eigenvalues $1>\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots>0$. Nazarov proved $\lambda_1\le1-ce^{-C|T||\Omega|}$ with absolute constants. For intervals the eigenvalues depend on $c=|T||\Omega|$. Landau and Widom proved the plunge law $\lambda_{n(c,b)}(c)\to(1+e^b)^{-1}$ for $n(c,b)=[c+\pi^{-2}b\log c]$. Karnik, Romberg and Davenport bounded, for all $c>0$ and $0<\varepsilon<\tfrac12$, the number of eigenvalues in $(\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon)$ by $\frac2{\pi^2}\log(50c+25)\log\frac5{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}+7$. Kulikov proved $\lambda_n(c)\ge1-\delta^c$ for $n=[(1-\varepsilon)c]$, for each $\varepsilon>0$ and large $c$. ([Kulikov, arXiv:2306.12430](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.12430)) The eigenfunctions are the prolate spheroidal wave functions. ([Wikipedia: Prolate spheroidal wave function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prolate_spheroidal_wave_function))
- **No eigenvalues at all.** The Volterra operator $Vf(t)=\int_0^tf(s)\,ds$ on $L^2[0,1]$ is compact with spectrum $\{0\}$, has no nonzero eigenvalues, and has norm $2/\pi$. Compactness alone does not produce nonzero eigenvalues. ([Wikipedia: Volterra operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_operator))

These results are the integral-operator side of [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) and of [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors) in [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces). ([Wikipedia: Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator))

### History
Fredholm's 1903 paper introduced the determinant $d(z)$ and its solvability criterion. Hilbert then wrote six papers (1904–1910) that turned the determinantal approach into the beginnings of the theory of compact operators, later developed by Schmidt, Carleman, Riesz and others. ([Bornemann, arXiv:0804.2543](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.2543)) Mercer's theorem appeared in "Functions of positive and negative type and their connection with the theory of integral equations" (1909). ([Wikipedia: Mercer's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem)) Jentzsch's "Über Integralgleichungen mit positivem Kern" appeared in J. Reine Angew. Math. 141 (1912). ([Intissar, arXiv:1910.01120](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.01120)) Krein and Rutman proved their theorem in 1948. ([Wikipedia: Krein–Rutman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krein%E2%80%93Rutman_theorem)) The time-and-band limiting eigenproblem was opened by Slepian, Landau and Pollak in a series of Bell System Technical Journal papers from 1961 on. ([Wikipedia: Prolate spheroidal wave function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prolate_spheroidal_wave_function)) Bonami, Jaming and Karoui set out to obtain precise non-asymptotic estimates for its eigenvalues within the three main regions of the spectrum. ([Bonami, Jaming and Karoui, arXiv:1804.01257](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.01257))

### Open problems
- **Donoho–Stark conjecture.** Let $T$ be an interval. The conjecture says that among sets $\Omega$ of fixed measure, the top eigenvalue $\lambda_1(T,\Omega)$ of $P_TQ_\Omega P_T$ is largest when $\Omega$ is also an interval. Kulikov (2023) calls it "the famous Donoho–Stark conjecture". The best general bound he cites is Nazarov's $\lambda_1(T,\Omega)\le1-ce^{-C|T||\Omega|}$. ([Kulikov, arXiv:2306.12430](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.12430))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Mercer's theorem, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem): eigen-expansion of positive kernels and the trace formula.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.307 Integral Equations](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-307-integral-equations-spring-2006/): graduate course covering Fredholm theory and the Hilbert–Schmidt theorem.
- **Primary:** [Bornemann, On the numerical evaluation of Fredholm determinants (arXiv:0804.2543)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.2543): survey of trace and determinant theory for integral operators with a general numerical method.
- **Primary:** [Kulikov, Exponential lower bound before the plunge region (arXiv:2306.12430)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.12430): current results on time–frequency localization eigenvalues.
- **Primary:** [Volkov, Optimal decay rates in Sobolev norms for singular values of integral operators (arXiv:2309.00153)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00153): sharp decay versus Sobolev and analytic regularity in any dimension.
- **Further reading:** [Gohberg, Goldberg and Krupnik, Traces and Determinants of Linear Operators (Birkhäuser, 2000)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-8401-3); [König, Eigenvalue Distribution of Compact Operators (Birkhäuser, 1986)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-6278-3); [Kress, Linear Integral Equations (Springer, 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4614-9593-2).
references.MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations:
## Reference
### Overview
A Volterra integral equation has a variable limit of integration. The first kind is $f(t)=\int_a^tK(t,s)x(s)\,ds$ and the second kind is $x(t)=f(t)+\int_a^tK(t,s)x(s)\,ds$, with $x$ unknown. ([Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)) The value at time $t$ depends only on the past, so these are the basic equations for systems with memory. Applications include Lotka's equation in demography, the renewal equation in actuarial science, viscoelastic materials, and fluid mechanics. ([Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation))

Gripenberg, Londen and Staffans treat Volterra integral and integrodifferential equations for $n$-dimensional systems. Their monograph is organized into linear theory (convolution equations, weighted spaces, completely monotone kernels, nonintegrable kernels with integrable resolvents), general nonlinear theory (existence, uniqueness, Lyapunov techniques, asymptotics), and frequency-domain and monotonicity methods. ([Gripenberg–Londen–Staffans, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book)) Brunner's 2017 monograph covers the classical linear and nonlinear theory, equations with vanishing delays, highly oscillatory kernels and non-compact operators. ([Brunner, preface](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/volterra-integral-equations/preface/8556E0E5E4917048D5224C9FBEB6B47D))

### Scope
MSC2020 45Dxx consists of **45D05** Volterra integral equations [See also 34A12] and **45D99** None of the above, but in this section. ([MSC2020 45Dxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Dxx)) It sits in [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations). ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))

Neighbouring codes, one line each:
- [MSC 34Axx - General theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations): 34A12 covers initial value problems, existence, uniqueness, continuous dependence and continuation of solutions, and 34A08 covers fractional ODEs. ([MSC2020 34Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Axx)) Integrating an initial value problem gives a Volterra equation: $u'=2tu$, $u(0)=1$ becomes $u(x)=1+\int_0^x2t\,u(t)\,dt$. ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))
- [MSC 45Bxx - Fredholm integral equations](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations): fixed limits of integration. ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))
- [MSC 45Jxx - Integro-ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2045Jxx%20-%20Integro-ordinary%20differential%20equations): derivatives together with memory terms. [MSC 45Mxx - Qualitative behavior of solutions to integral equations](node:MSC%2045Mxx%20-%20Qualitative%20behavior%20of%20solutions%20to%20integral%20equations): asymptotics, stability, periodicity and positivity. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX); [MSC2020 45Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Mxx))
- [MSC 65Rxx - Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms](node:MSC%2065Rxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20transforms): 65R20 holds numerical methods for integral equations. ([MSC2020 65Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=65Rxx))

### Key concepts
- **Well-posedness and the resolvent.** If $K$ and $g$ are continuous, the second-kind equation has a unique continuous solution $y(t)=g(t)+\int_0^tR(t,s)g(s)\,ds$ with resolvent kernel $R$. ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation)) For convolution equations $u+K\star u=f$ with $K\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R_+,M_n(\mathbb C))$ there is a unique resolvent $R\in L^1_{\rm loc}$ with $R+K\star R=R+R\star K=K$, and for every $f\in L^1_{\rm loc}$ the unique solution is $u=f-R\star f$. ([Coti Zelati–Ertzbischoff–Gérard-Varet, Thm C.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1)) For a nonnegative kernel $h$ the resolvent is the series $a=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n$ with $a_1=h$, $a_{n+1}=h*a_n$. ([Zhang](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0812.0834))
- **Quasinilpotence of the Volterra operator.** $Vf(t)=\int_0^tf(s)\,ds$ on $L^2[0,1]$ has kernel $\mathbf 1_{\{s<t\}}$, so $\|V\|_{HS}^2=\tfrac12$ and $\|V\|_{HS}=1/\sqrt2$. It is compact, has no eigenvalues, has spectrum $\{0\}$, operator norm $2/\pi$ and singular values $((k+\tfrac12)\pi)^{-1}$, $k\ge0$; it is quasinilpotent but not nilpotent. ([Volterra operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_operator)) Since $\sigma(V)=\{0\}$, $I-\lambda V$ is invertible for every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$. This is why second-kind Volterra equations never meet the obstruction that eigenvalues create in the Fredholm alternative (see [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory)).
- **Grönwall's inequality.** Let $\beta\ge0$ and $u$ be continuous on an interval $I$ starting at $a$, and let the negative part of $\alpha$ be locally integrable. If $u(t)\le\alpha(t)+\int_a^t\beta(s)u(s)\,ds$, then $u(t)\le\alpha(t)+\int_a^t\alpha(s)\beta(s)\exp\big(\int_s^t\beta\big)\,ds$. If $\alpha$ is also non-decreasing, then $u(t)\le\alpha(t)\exp\int_a^t\beta$. ([Grönwall's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6nwall%27s_inequality)) This inequality gives uniqueness and continuous dependence for Lipschitz nonlinear Volterra equations, as in [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Half-line Paley–Wiener theorem.** Let $K\in L^1(\mathbb R_+,M_n(\mathbb C))$ with $\det(I+\mathcal L[K](\lambda))\ne0$ for all $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. Then the resolvent $R$ lies in $L^1(\mathbb R_+)$, and for every $f\in L^1$ the solution $u=f-R\star f$ of $u+K\star u=f$ is in $L^1$. ([Coti Zelati et al., Thm C.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1)) By Theorem 2.4.1 of Gripenberg–Londen–Staffans the condition is also necessary for an integrable resolvent, and by Corollary 2.4.2 there, roots of the transform in the right half-plane force exponential growth. ([Abramovich–Pensky–Rozenholc, Remark 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1107.2766)) For $0\le h\in L^1(\mathbb R_+)$ and $x=f+h*x$, the resolvent is integrable iff $\int_0^\infty h<1$. ([Zhang](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0812.0834))
- **Renewal equation.** The renewal function solves $m(t)=F_S(t)+\int_0^tm(t-s)f_S(s)\,ds$, and $m(t)/t\to1/\mathbb E[S_1]$ when $0<\mathbb E[S_1]<\infty$. ([Renewal theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewal_theory)) Key renewal theorem: if the inter-renewal distribution is aperiodic (non-lattice) with finite mean $\mu$ and $z$ is directly Riemann integrable, then $\int_0^tz(t-x)\,dm(x)\to\mu^{-1}\int_0^\infty z$. In the periodic case the limit is taken along multiples of the period, and the theorem is equivalent to Blackwell's theorem. ([IISc lecture 11](https://parimal.ece.iisc.ac.in/courses/spqt/2026/lecture-11.pdf)) See [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes).
- **First kind, Abel and fractional integrals.** A first-kind equation becomes second-kind on differentiation when $K(t,t)\ne0$. With the weakly singular kernel $K(t,s)=(t^2-s^2)^{-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, it can be converted into a classical Abel equation. ([Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)) The Riemann–Liouville integral $I^\alpha f(x)=\Gamma(\alpha)^{-1}\int_a^x(x-t)^{\alpha-1}f(t)\,dt$, $\operatorname{Re}\alpha>0$, is the model weakly singular Volterra operator. It satisfies $I^\alpha I^\beta=I^{\alpha+\beta}$ and uses the [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function). ([Riemann–Liouville integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Liouville_integral))
- **Nonlinear equations and blow-up.** A nonlinear Volterra equation has the form $u(x)=f(x)+\lambda\int_a^xK(x,t)F(x,t,u(t))\,dt$. ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation)) Consider $x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^tW(t-s)f(x(s))\,ds$ with $w=W'$ continuous, nonnegative and $w(0)>0$, and $f$ continuous, positive, asymptotically increasing and superlinear. Appleby and Patterson prove that positive solutions blow up in finite time iff $\int_\eta^\infty du/\sqrt{\int_0^uf(s)\,ds}<\infty$ for some $\eta>0$. ([Appleby–Patterson, Thm 2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- **Convolution quadrature.** Lubich's method takes weights from the power series of $\hat K(\delta(\zeta)/\Delta t)$, where $\hat K$ is the Laplace transform of the kernel and $\delta$ is the generating function of a multistep method. Only $\hat K$ is needed. The error is $O(\Delta t^p)$ for an order-$p$ method, provided the data vanish to sufficient order at $t=0$; otherwise order reduction occurs. ([Achleitner et al., §7.1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.05606)) The original papers appeared in Numer. Math. 52 (1988). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01398686)) See [Numerical Methods for Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Methods%20for%20Differential%20Equations).

### History
Volterra introduced these equations, and Traian Lalescu studied them in his 1908 thesis and wrote the first book on integral equations in 1911. ([Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)) Grönwall proved his inequality in 1919, and Bellman proved a more general integral form in 1943. ([Grönwall's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B6nwall%27s_inequality)) Gripenberg, Londen and Staffans (1990) wrote that the theory had grown rapidly over the previous 25 years, from scattered papers into sizable branches of applied analysis. They noted that most of the asymptotic theory for nonlinear Volterra equations was of fairly recent origin, and that its growth was driven by applications in physics, engineering and biology. ([Gripenberg–Londen–Staffans, preface](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/volterra-integral-and-functional-equations/preface/BC6F7B6BE134B0BE3CCE7D28E273BB82))

### Open problems
- **Uniqueness below the Hölder threshold for singular stochastic Volterra equations.** For $X_t=x_0+\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}g(s)\,ds+\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}\sigma(X_s)\,dB_s$ with $\alpha\in(0,\tfrac12)$, Mytnik and Salisbury prove pathwise uniqueness when $\sigma$ is $\gamma$-Hölder with $\gamma\in(1/(2(1-\alpha)),1]$. They report no counterexample for smaller $\gamma$, so that case is unresolved, and they suggest methods that might settle non-uniqueness. ([Mytnik–Salisbury](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1502.05513)) This links the area to [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus).
- **Blow-up time and growth rates for nonlinear VIEs.** Appleby and Patterson call estimating the blow-up time "an interesting open problem for general nonlinear VIEs". Roberts and Olmstead estimated growth rates of explosive solutions by integral-transform methods that conjecture the leading-order behaviour, and Appleby and Patterson state that "the full proofs of these conclusions remains open". ([Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
### Resources
- **Reference:** [Volterra integral equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation): kinds, convolution case, reduction to second kind, Abel kernels, trapezoidal discretization.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.307 Integral Equations (Margetis, 2006)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-307-integral-equations-spring-2006/): graduate course on Volterra and Fredholm equations with applications.
- **Primary:** [Appleby–Patterson, Blow-up and superexponential growth in superlinear Volterra equations](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583): sharp blow-up criterion for nonlinear convolution equations.
- **Primary:** [Mytnik–Salisbury, Uniqueness for Volterra-type stochastic integral equations](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1502.05513): pathwise uniqueness for singular kernels.
- **Further reading:** [Gripenberg, Londen, Staffans, Volterra Integral and Functional Equations (CUP, 1990)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book): the standard monograph on linear, nonlinear and frequency-domain theory.
- **Further reading:** [Brunner, Volterra Integral Equations: An Introduction to Theory and Applications (CUP, 2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/volterra-integral-equations/preface/8556E0E5E4917048D5224C9FBEB6B47D): classical theory, delays, oscillatory kernels, research problems.
references.MSC 45Exx - Singular integral equations:
## Reference
### Overview
An integral equation is singular when its integral is improper; strongly singular integrals are given meaning by a special procedure such as the Cauchy principal value. ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation)) The classical theory concerns equations with the Cauchy kernel $(\tau-t)^{-1}$ on a contour, and equations of convolution type on a half-line or with Toeplitz structure. Both reduce to boundary value problems for analytic functions: Cauchy-type equations through the Sokhotski–Plemelj formulas and the Riemann–Hilbert problem, convolution equations through Wiener–Hopf factorization. ([MSC2020 45Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Exx); [Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem); [Wiener–Hopf method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Hopf_method))

Singular integral operators are not compact, so the Fredholm alternative is replaced by an index theory in which solvability is governed by a winding number. ([Toeplitz operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toeplitz_operator); [Fredholm operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_operator)) The methods feed into [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) and [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis).

### Scope
MSC2020 45Exx, Singular integral equations (see also 30E20, 30E25, 44A15, 44A35), has the sub-codes: ([MSC2020 45Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Exx))
- **45E05** Integral equations with kernels of Cauchy type (see also 35J15).
- **45E10** Integral equations of the convolution type (Abel, Picard, Toeplitz and Wiener–Hopf type) (see also 47B35).
- **45E99** None of the above, but in this section.

Neighbouring codes, one line each:
- [MSC 30Exx - Miscellaneous topics of analysis in the complex plane](node:MSC%2030Exx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20of%20analysis%20in%20the%20complex%20plane): 30E20 (integrals of Cauchy type) and 30E25 (boundary value problems in the complex plane) both point back to 45Exx; they study the analytic-function side, 45E the equation. ([MSC2020 30Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=30Exx))
- [MSC 44Axx - Integral transforms, operational calculus](node:MSC%2044Axx%20-%20Integral%20transforms,%20operational%20calculus): 44A15 (special transforms such as Hilbert) and 44A35 (convolution as a transform) treat the transforms themselves. ([MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx))
- [MSC 47Bxx - Special classes of linear operators](node:MSC%2047Bxx%20-%20Special%20classes%20of%20linear%20operators): 47B35, cross-referenced from 45E10, is where Toeplitz-type operators are classified as operators. ([MSC2020 45Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Exx))
- [MSC 45Bxx - Fredholm integral equations](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations) covers equations with fixed limits; 45E covers equations whose integrals are improper (singular). ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))
- [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations) is the parent field. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Sokhotski–Plemelj formulas.** For a smooth simple closed curve $C$ and $\varphi$ analytic on $C$, the Cauchy integral $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_C\frac{\varphi(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}d\zeta$ defines analytic functions inside and outside $C$, with boundary values at $z\in C$ equal to $\pm\frac12\varphi(z)+\frac1{2\pi i}\,\mathrm{p.v.}\int_C\frac{\varphi(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}d\zeta$ (plus from inside, minus from outside). Sochocki proved it in 1868; Plemelj rediscovered it in 1908 for the Riemann–Hilbert problem. ([Sokhotski–Plemelj theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokhotski%E2%80%93Plemelj_theorem))
- **Riemann–Hilbert problem.** Given an oriented contour $\Sigma$ and jump matrix $G$, find $M$ holomorphic off $\Sigma$ with $M_+(t)=G(t)M_-(t)$ on $\Sigma$ and $M(z)\to I$ as $z\to\infty$. Scalar problems are solved explicitly by taking logarithms and applying the Cauchy integral, e.g. $G=2$ on $[-1,1]$ gives $M(z)=\big(\tfrac{z-1}{z+1}\big)^{\log2/(2\pi i)}$, with uniqueness from Liouville's theorem under growth conditions at endpoints; matrix problems rarely have explicit solutions. Applications include inverse scattering, Painlevé equations, orthogonal polynomials and random matrices (Deift–Zhou steepest descent, Baik–Deift–Johansson). ([Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem))
- **Hilbert transform.** M. Riesz showed that the Hilbert transform is bounded on $L^p(\mathbb R)$ for $1<p<\infty$; it satisfies $H^2=-I$, and it arose in Hilbert's 1905 work on the Riemann–Hilbert problem. ([Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform)) On the circle $H=i(2P-I)$ with $P$ the Szegő projection onto $H^2(\mathbb T)$, and on the boundary of a smooth simply connected domain the Hilbert transform differs from the circle case by a Hilbert–Schmidt operator with smooth kernel. ([Singular integral operators on closed curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_integral_operators_on_closed_curves))
- **Index theorem for Toeplitz operators.** For continuous $g$ on the circle, $T_g-\lambda$ on the Hardy space $H^2$ is Fredholm if and only if $\lambda\notin g(S^1)$, and then its index is minus the winding number of $g-\lambda$ about $0$ (Krein, Widom, Devinatz); this is a special case of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem. ([Toeplitz operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toeplitz_operator)) Because the Fredholm index is invariant under compact perturbations, smooth-kernel corrections such as the curve-to-circle difference above leave index computations unchanged. ([Fredholm operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_operator); [Singular integral operators on closed curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_integral_operators_on_closed_curves))
- **Wiener–Hopf factorization.** The key step is to split a function $\Phi$ into parts $\Phi_\pm$ analytic in complementary half-planes; scalar kernels are factorized as $K=K_+K_-$ by taking a logarithm and splitting additively, whereas matrix factorizations are much harder because the logarithm is not well defined and factors need not commute.
