([Wiener–Hopf method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Hopf_method))
- **Partial indices and their stability.** A matrix function factorizes with partial indices $\kappa_1\ge\cdots\ge\kappa_n$; by the Gohberg–Krein theorem the system of partial indices is stable under small perturbations if and only if $\kappa_1-\kappa_n\le1$, and by Shubin's theorem, if a matrix function with stable partial indices is factorized, every sufficiently small perturbation admits a factorization with nearby factors, which underlies approximate factorization; in general the partial indices cannot be determined without constructing the factorization. ([Kisil, Abrahams, Mishuris, Rogosin, arXiv:2107.06088](https://arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))

### History
Sochocki's 1868 boundary-value formulas, Plemelj's 1908 rediscovery and Hilbert's 1905 work on Riemann's boundary problem are the starting points. ([Sokhotski–Plemelj theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokhotski%E2%80%93Plemelj_theorem); [Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform)) Wiener and Hopf developed their method to solve systems of integral equations, originally connected with radiative transfer. ([Wiener–Hopf method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Hopf_method); [Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation)) Muskhelishvili's monograph *Singular Integral Equations* appeared in a Springer edition in 1977. ([Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-009-9994-7)) Existence theorems for matrix Riemann–Hilbert problems are credited to Krein, Gohberg and others. ([Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem)) MIT's graduate course 18.307 (2006) teaches the Hilbert problem and singular integral equations of Cauchy type alongside the Wiener–Hopf method. ([MIT 18.307](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-307-integral-equations-spring-2006/))

### Open problems
- **Constructive matrix Wiener–Hopf factorization (open).** Kisil, Abrahams, Mishuris and Rogosin point to the lack of a general exact constructive factorization procedure for matrix functions, with only specific classes solvable exactly, and state that in the general case no method determines the partial indices. Their list of goals includes a systematic test of whether a problem is of Wiener–Hopf type with a unique solution and a unified constructive method for exact or approximate factorization. ([arXiv:2107.06088](https://arxiv.org/html/2107.06088); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06088))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem): scalar and matrix problems, applications.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.307 Integral Equations](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-307-integral-equations-spring-2006/): graduate course on the Wiener–Hopf method and Cauchy-type singular equations.
- **Primary:** [Kisil, Abrahams, Mishuris, Rogosin, The Wiener–Hopf technique, its generalisations and applications (arXiv:2107.06088)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06088): survey of constructive and approximate matrix factorization with open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Muskhelishvili, Singular Integral Equations](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-009-9994-7): Springer Netherlands (1977).
references.MSC 45Fxx - Systems of linear integral e:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 code 45Fxx, "Systems of linear integral equations", has three substantive sub-codes: systems of nonsingular linear integral equations (45F05); dual, triple, etc., integral and series equations (45F10); and systems of singular linear integral equations (45F15), plus 45F99. The MSC entry gives these bare titles and no further notes or cross-references. ([MSC2020 45Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Fxx)) It is part of [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations) and concerns vector-valued versions of [Linear Integral Equations](node:Linear%20Integral%20Equations).

The step from one unknown to a vector of unknowns changes the theory most sharply for singular and convolution equations. A scalar convolution equation on a half-line is solved by an explicit Wiener–Hopf factorization via a logarithm and a Cauchy integral, but for matrix symbols there is no constructive factorization procedure in general and the partial indices that govern solvability cannot in general be computed. ([Kisil–Abrahams–Mishuris–Rogosin, arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088)) Matrix problems arise from coupled multi-modal physics such as elastic waves, where the logarithm is not available to split a matrix problem and the factors can be expected to be non-commutative. ([Wiener–Hopf method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Hopf_method)) Dual and triple integral equations (45F10) are a different kind of "system": one unknown function satisfies different integral equations on complementary intervals, which is how mixed boundary value problems of potential theory present themselves. ([Sneddon 1962](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/dual-integral-equations-with-trigonometrical-kernels/0664361660544EEAF7992AF59AF01621); [Cooke 1963, QJMAM](https://academic.oup.com/qjmam/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/qjmam/16.2.193))

### Scope
- **45F05 Systems of nonsingular linear integral equations.** Fredholm- and Volterra-type systems $u_i(x)-\lambda\sum_j\int K_{ij}(x,y)u_j(y)\,dy=f_i(x)$ with regular kernels. In the scalar theory, an integral operator with square-integrable kernel is Hilbert–Schmidt, hence compact, and the [Fredholm alternative](node:Fredholm%20Alternative) holds. ([Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) Gripenberg, Londen and Staffans treat Volterra equations in $n$ dimensions throughout, rather than scalar equations. ([Gripenberg–Londen–Staffans, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book))
- **45F10 Dual, triple, etc., integral and series equations.** Pairs or triples of integral equations for one unknown holding on complementary ranges, from mixed boundary value problems. ([MSC2020 45Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Fxx); [Sneddon 1962](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/dual-integral-equations-with-trigonometrical-kernels/0664361660544EEAF7992AF59AF01621))
- **45F15 Systems of singular linear integral equations.** Systems with Cauchy-type kernels and the associated vector Hilbert and Riemann boundary problems, studied in Vekua's monograph. ([Heinig, review of Vekua](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/E339EAC396536AB7316B89892A31E4C6/S0008439500030319a.pdf/systems-of-singular-integral-equations-by-n-p-vekua-translated-by-a-g-gibbs-and-g-m-simmons-p-noordhoff-groningen-1967-216-pages.pdf))

Neighbouring codes in section 45 include [MSC 45Bxx - Fredholm integral equations](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations), [MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations), [MSC 45Exx - Singular integral equations](node:MSC%2045Exx%20-%20Singular%20integral%20equations), [MSC 45Gxx - Nonlinear integral equations](node:MSC%2045Gxx%20-%20Nonlinear%20integral%20equations) and [MSC 45Pxx - Integral operators](node:MSC%2045Pxx%20-%20Integral%20operators); the note on 45Lxx sends numerical analysis to [MSC 65Rxx - Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms](node:MSC%2065Rxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20transforms). ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX))

### Key concepts
- **Fredholm theory for regular systems (45F05).** For a square-integrable kernel on $[a,b]^2$ ($a$ or $b$ possibly infinite) the integral operator is Hilbert–Schmidt and compact, and for each $\lambda\neq0$ either the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution or the inhomogeneous equation is solvable for every right-hand side. ([Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) Solvability is organized by the resolvent $(I-\lambda K)^{-1}$, whose expansion in $\lambda$ is the Liouville–Neumann series, and by the Fredholm [determinant](node:Determinant) $\det(I-\lambda K)=\exp\big[-\sum_n\frac{\lambda^n}{n}\operatorname{Tr}K^n\big]$ with $\operatorname{Tr}K=\int K(x,x)\,dx$. ([Fredholm theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_theory)) The determinant requires more than a square-integrable kernel: it is defined when $K$ is trace class, where $\lambda\mapsto\det(I-\lambda K)=\sum_n(-\lambda)^n\operatorname{Tr}\Lambda^n(K)$ is an entire function. ([Fredholm determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_determinant))
- **Matrix Wiener–Hopf factorization and partial indices (45F15).** An $n\times n$ matrix function $G$ on a contour factors as $G=G_+\Lambda G_-$ with $\Lambda(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t^{\kappa_1},\dots,t^{\kappa_n})$; the integers $\kappa_j$ are the partial indices. Left and right factorizations can have different partial indices, but their sum always equals the index of $\det G$. ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))
- **Gohberg–Krein stability theorem.** The system of partial indices $\kappa_1\ge\dots\ge\kappa_n$ is stable under small perturbations of $G$ if and only if $\kappa_1-\kappa_n\le1$; Shubin's theorem adds that in the stable case a sufficiently small perturbation of $G$ gives factors close to the original ones. For the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}\big(\tfrac{t-i}{t+i},\tfrac{t+i}{t-i}\big)$ on the real line, with partial indices $\{1,-1\}$, a small perturbation changes the indices to $\{0,0\}$. ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))
- **Constructive classes.** Explicit factorizations are known for rational matrix functions, analytic and meromorphic ones, triangular matrices (Chebotarev's classical results), functionally commutative matrices including the Khrapkov–Daniele and Jones classes, and matrices with exponential entries. ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))
- **Vector Riemann–Hilbert problem.** Find a holomorphic matrix $M$ off an oriented contour $\Sigma$ with $M_+(t)=G(t)M_-(t)$ on $\Sigma$ and $M\to I$ at infinity. In the scalar case logarithms and the Sokhotski–Plemelj formula give the solution, e.g. $M(z)=\big(\tfrac{z-1}{z+1}\big)^{\log2/(2\pi i)}$ for $G=2$ on $[-1,1]$; explicit solutions are very rare outside the scalar case. This links 45F15 to [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis). ([Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem)) Vekua's monograph solves the homogeneous and inhomogeneous Hilbert problem for several unknown functions (Hölder data, including discontinuous coefficients), proves Noether-type theorems for systems of singular integral equations with Cauchy kernel, introduces the index, and shows that under suitable conditions such a system is equivalent to an essentially regular Fredholm equation. ([Heinig, review of Vekua](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/E339EAC396536AB7316B89892A31E4C6/S0008439500030319a.pdf/systems-of-singular-integral-equations-by-n-p-vekua-translated-by-a-g-gibbs-and-g-m-simmons-p-noordhoff-groningen-1967-216-pages.pdf))
- **Hilbert's twenty-first problem.** The Riemann–Hilbert problem was Hilbert's 21st problem; Plemelj proposed a method of solution and Bolibrukh later showed his proof incomplete. ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088)) Precisely, Plemelj (1908) realized any monodromy by a regular system Fuchsian at all but possibly one point, and Bolibrukh (1989) showed that some monodromy groups are realized by regular systems but not by Fuchsian ones; every irreducible representation is realizable by a Fuchsian system (Bolibrukh–Kostov, 1992). ([Hilbert's twenty-first problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_twenty-first_problem))
- **Dual integral equations (45F10).** For the electrified disc, the unknown $g$ satisfies $\int_0^\infty u^{-1}g(u)J_0(xu)\,du=1$ for $0<x<1$ and $\int_0^\infty g(u)J_0(xu)\,du=0$ for $x>1$, with Titchmarsh's solution $g(u)=\tfrac{2}{\pi}\sin u$ (in the source's variables, $A(u)=\tfrac{2\Phi_0}{\pi}\tfrac{\sin u}{u}$). Sneddon's generalization $\int_0^\infty u^{-2\alpha}(1+\omega(u))g(u)J_\nu(xu)\,du=1$ ($x<1$), $\int_0^\infty g(u)J_\nu(xu)\,du=0$ ($x>1$) reduces to a Fredholm equation of the second kind on $[0,1]$, and the charge density has the edge singularity $(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$. ([Agra–Trizac–Bocquet, App. A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/cond-mat/0407521)) The Bessel functions $J_\nu$ are [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions); Sneddon showed that planar mixed problems lead to trigonometric-kernel pairs reducible to Titchmarsh's form, in a case not covered by Busbridge's general solution. ([Sneddon 1962](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/dual-integral-equations-with-trigonometrical-kernels/0664361660544EEAF7992AF59AF01621))
- **Triple integral equations.** Cooke gave a formal solution of triple integral equations first considered by Tranter, expressed through a Fredholm integral equation of the first kind, and applied it to an electrified disc with a hole, comparing the capacity with Smythe's approximate method. ([Cooke 1963, QJMAM](https://academic.oup.com/qjmam/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/qjmam/16.2.193))
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): Fourier transformation turns a half-line convolution equation into a Wiener–Hopf equation, whose solution requires a multiplicative factorization of the transformed kernel in a strip. ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))

### History
Wiener and Hopf described their method in a joint article treating a convolution-type integral equation on a semi-axis, motivated by an equation governing the radiation equilibrium of stars; it was a single equation, not a system, and was treated with the Laplace transform. ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088)) Plemelj's 1908 work on Hilbert's 21st problem and its 1989 correction by Bolibrukh frame the vector Riemann–Hilbert problem. ([Hilbert's twenty-first problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_twenty-first_problem)) Vekua's *Systems of Singular Integral Equations* appeared in Russian in 1950 and in English (Noordhoff) in 1967. ([Heinig, review of Vekua](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/E339EAC396536AB7316B89892A31E4C6/S0008439500030319a.pdf/systems-of-singular-integral-equations-by-n-p-vekua-translated-by-a-g-gibbs-and-g-m-simmons-p-noordhoff-groningen-1967-216-pages.pdf))

On the dual-equation side, Sneddon (1962) treated trigonometric kernels not covered by Busbridge's general solution, Cooke (1963) triple equations, and Sneddon's monograph *Mixed Boundary Value Problems in Potential Theory* appeared with North-Holland in 1966. ([Sneddon 1962](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/dual-integral-equations-with-trigonometrical-kernels/0664361660544EEAF7992AF59AF01621); [Cooke 1963, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/qjmam/16.2.193); [Cooke, review of Sneddon 1966](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-edinburgh-mathematical-society/article/i-n-sneddon-mixed-boundary-value-problems-in-potential-theory-northholland-publishing-companyamsterdam-1966-viii282-pp-80s/D22E4825F6270C98848107FDD7D69D6B)) Deift and Zhou's 1993 nonlinear steepest descent, building on Its and Manakov, turned matrix Riemann–Hilbert problems into an asymptotic tool. ([Riemann–Hilbert problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem))

### Open problems
- **Constructive matrix factorization.** "Currently, there are no constructive factorisation procedures for matrix functions in general," and "in the general case, there exists no method of determining the partial indices." ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))
- **Approximate factorization.** Whether factors of an approximation $\bar K$ approximate the factors of $K$ has, in general, a negative answer for matrix functions because partial indices are unstable, and the survey notes that one cannot in general determine the partial indices without constructing the factorization, which obstructs applying the stability results. ([Kisil et al., arXiv:2107.06088](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2107.06088))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Riemann–Hilbert problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Hilbert_problem): matrix jump problems, Plemelj formula, nonlinear steepest descent.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.307 Integral Equations (Margetis)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-307-integral-equations-spring-2006/): graduate course on Fredholm theory, the Wiener–Hopf method, and the Hilbert problem for Cauchy-type singular equations.
- **Primary:** [Kisil, Abrahams, Mishuris, Rogosin, The Wiener–Hopf technique, its generalisations and applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06088): survey of matrix factorization, partial indices, constructive classes and approximate methods.
- **Primary:** [Sneddon, Dual integral equations with trigonometrical kernels (1962)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/dual-integral-equations-with-trigonometrical-kernels/0664361660544EEAF7992AF59AF01621): dual equations from planar mixed problems.
- **Further reading:** Vekua, *Systems of Singular Integral Equations* (Noordhoff, 1967), [reviewed by Heinig](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/E339EAC396536AB7316B89892A31E4C6/S0008439500030319a.pdf/systems-of-singular-integral-equations-by-n-p-vekua-translated-by-a-g-gibbs-and-g-m-simmons-p-noordhoff-groningen-1967-216-pages.pdf); Sneddon, *Mixed Boundary Value Problems in Potential Theory* (North-Holland, 1966), [reviewed by Cooke](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-edinburgh-mathematical-society/article/i-n-sneddon-mixed-boundary-value-problems-in-potential-theory-northholland-publishing-companyamsterdam-1966-viii282-pp-80s/D22E4825F6270C98848107FDD7D69D6B); [Gripenberg, Londen, Staffans, *Volterra Integral and Functional Equations* (CUP, 1990)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book).
references.MSC 45Gxx - Nonlinear integral equations:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 code 45Gxx covers integral equations in which the unknown enters nonlinearly. It cross-references 47H30 and 47Jxx. ([MSC2020 45Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Gxx)) The two basic forms are the Urysohn equation $f(x)=g(x)+\int_a^bk(x,y,f(y))\,dy$ and the Hammerstein equation $f(x)=g(x)+\int_a^bk(x,y)\,G(y,f(y))\,dy$. The nonlinear Volterra equation $u(x)=f(x)+\lambda\int_a^xK(x,t)F(x,t,u(t))\,dt$ is the causal analogue. ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation)) Writing $Kv(x)=\int_\Omega k(x,y)v(y)\,dy$ and $Fu(x)=f(x,u(x))$ (the Nemytskii or superposition operator) puts a Hammerstein equation in the operator form $u+KFu=0$. ([Aibinu–Mewomo](https://arxiv.org/html/2008.07851v2)) MSC places these operators in 47H30, "Particular nonlinear operators (superposition, Hammerstein, Nemytskiĭ, Uryson, etc.)". ([MSC2020 47Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Hxx))

The operator-theoretic tools are classified in 47Hxx: monotone operators (47H05), measures of noncompactness and condensing mappings (47H08), fixed-point theorems (47H10) and degree theory (47H11). ([MSC2020 47Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Hxx)) In the fixed-point-index approach, multiplicity comes from the index on cones and nonexistence from growth bounds against constants computed from the kernel. Boundary value problems for ODEs are rewritten as perturbed Hammerstein equations whose kernel is a [Green's function](node:Green's%20Functions). ([Infante–Pietramala–Tojo](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1404.1390))

### Scope
The MSC2020 sub-codes are ([MSC2020 45Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Gxx)):
- **45G05** Singular nonlinear integral equations.
- **45G10** Other nonlinear integral equations.
- **45G15** Systems of nonlinear integral equations.
- **45G99** None of the above, but in this section.

Neighbours ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX); [MSC2020 47Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Hxx)):
- [MSC 45Fxx - Systems of linear integral equations](node:MSC%2045Fxx%20-%20Systems%20of%20linear%20integral%20equations) covers linear systems.
- [MSC 45Nxx - Abstract integral equations, integral equations in abstract spaces](node:MSC%2045Nxx%20-%20Abstract%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20equations%20in%20abstract%20spaces) covers equations posed in abstract spaces.
- [MSC 45Mxx - Qualitative behavior of solutions to integral equations](node:MSC%2045Mxx%20-%20Qualitative%20behavior%20of%20solutions%20to%20integral%20equations) covers asymptotics, stability and positive solutions.
- [MSC 47Hxx - Nonlinear operators and their properties](node:MSC%2047Hxx%20-%20Nonlinear%20operators%20and%20their%20properties) covers the operators themselves: monotone operators (47H05), measures of noncompactness (47H08), fixed-point theorems (47H10), degree theory (47H11) and superposition operators (47H30). The operator-equation side is [MSC 47Jxx - Equations and inequalities involving nonlinear operators](node:MSC%2047Jxx%20-%20Equations%20and%20inequalities%20involving%20nonlinear%20operators).

### Key concepts
- **Superposition operators.** The Nemytskii operator $u\mapsto f(\cdot,u(\cdot))$ is the nonlinear ingredient of every Hammerstein equation. Appell and Zabrejko study when it acts between, and is bounded or continuous on, Lebesgue, Orlicz, symmetric, $C$, $BV$, Hölder, smooth-function and [Sobolev spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces). In spaces of smooth functions a global Lipschitz condition almost never holds, while a local Darbo condition generally does. ([Appell–Zabrejko, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/nonlinear-superposition-operators/superposition-operator-in-spaces-of-smooth-functions/BAEF2B3651B2F83CAB7FB607ADF5425A))
- **Schauder and Leray–Schauder.** If $K$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hausdorff locally convex space and $f:K\to K$ is continuous with $f(K)$ contained in a compact subset of $K$, then $f$ has a fixed point. If $f:X\to X$ is continuous and compact on a Banach space and $\{x:x=\lambda f(x),\ 0\le\lambda\le1\}$ is bounded, then $f$ has a fixed point. ([Schauder fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schauder_fixed-point_theorem)) Applied to a Hammerstein or Urysohn operator with a compact linear part, this reduces existence to an a priori bound (see [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces)).
- **Measures of noncompactness and Darbo's theorem.** The Kuratowski measure is $\beta(X)=\inf\{d>0:X$ is covered by finitely many sets of diameter $\le d\}$. ([Measure of non-compactness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_of_non-compactness)) Darbo's theorem: if $C$ is a nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a Banach space, $T:C\to C$ is continuous, and $\mu(TA)\le k\mu(A)$ for all $A\subset C$ with $k\in[0,1)$, then $T$ has a fixed point. ([Karakaya et al., Thm 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.00188)) Karakaya et al. prove a generalization under an integral condition and apply it to $x(t)=f\big(t,\int_0^tg(t,s,x(s))\,ds,x(t)\big)$ in the space $BC(\mathbb R_+)$ of bounded continuous functions on the half-line. ([Karakaya et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.00188))
- **Contraction methods.** If the nonlinearity is Lipschitz with a small enough constant, the [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem) gives existence and uniqueness. For semilinear Volterra equations with Lipschitz $H$, the solution is $y=y_l+\int_0^tR(t,s)H(s,y(s))\,ds$, where $R$ is the linear resolvent. ([Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation))
- **Monotone-operator methods.** Browder–Minty: a bounded, continuous, coercive, monotone map $T$ from a real separable reflexive Banach space $X$ to $X^*$ is surjective, with no linearity assumed. ([Browder–Minty theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browder%E2%80%93Minty_theorem)) For $u+KFu=0$, existence and uniqueness theorems were proved by Brezis and Browder, Browder and Gupta, and de Figueiredo and Gupta. Recent work builds strongly convergent iterations for $K$ and $F$ strongly monotone. ([Aibinu–Mewomo](https://arxiv.org/html/2008.07851v2))
- **Fixed-point index on cones.** For a compact map $F$ on a cone $K$: if $\mu x\ne Fx$ on $\partial\Omega_K$ for all $\mu\ge1$, the index is $1$; under a suitable perturbation by $e\in K\setminus\{0\}$, it is $0$. Nonzero index forces a fixed point, and indices $1$ and $0$ on nested sets locate one in the difference. ([Infante–Pietramala–Tojo, Lemma 2.5](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1404.1390)) The growth quantities $f^0,f_0,f^\infty,f_\infty$ of the nonlinearity are compared with principal characteristic values $\mu(L)$ of auxiliary linear operators. This gives one, two or three nontrivial solutions, and strict bounds $f(t,u)<m_S|u|$ for $u\ne0$ (or $f(t,u)>M_Su$ on a subinterval for $u>0$) are the hypotheses of the nonexistence result Thm 3.3. ([Infante–Pietramala–Tojo](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1404.1390)) It is the nonlinear counterpart of [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) for positive operators.
- **Nonlinear Volterra equations and blow-up.** Gripenberg, Londen and Staffans devote Part II to perturbed linear equations, existence, continuous dependence and uniqueness, Lyapunov techniques and asymptotics. ([GLS, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book)) Let $x'(t)=\int_0^tw(t-s)f(x(s))\,ds$ with $x(0)>0$, where $w\ge0$ is continuous with $w(0)>0$ and $f$ is continuous, positive, asymptotically increasing with $f(x)/x\to\infty$. Then solutions blow up in finite time iff $\int_\eta^\infty du/\sqrt{\int_0^uf}<\infty$ for some $\eta>0$. The integrated form is the nonlinear VIE $x=x(0)+W\ast f(x)$ with $W'=w$. ([Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- **Chandrasekhar's H-equation.** In radiative transfer, $H(\mu)=1+\mu H(\mu)\int_0^1\frac{\Psi(\mu')H(\mu')}{\mu+\mu'}\,d\mu'$, where $\Psi$ is an even polynomial with $\int_0^1\Psi\le\tfrac12$. In the conservative case the solution is unique and bounded on $[0,1]$. In non-conservative cases where the dispersion function has roots $\pm1/k$, $H(z)(1+kz)/(1-kz)$ is a further solution. ([Chandrasekhar's H-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandrasekhar%27s_H-function))
- **TBA equations.** Let $\mathbf G\in\mathrm{Mat}_{<2}(N)$, the real-diagonalisable $N\times N$ matrices with all eigenvalues in $(-2,2)$, be non-negative and irreducible. Let $\mathbf C\in\mathrm{Mat}_{<2}(N)$, and let $\mathbf a\in BC_-(\mathbb R,\mathbb R)^N$ with $e^{-\mathbf a}$ Hölder continuous. Then the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz system $\mathbf f=\Phi_{\mathbf C}\star(\mathbf G\log(e^{-\mathbf a}+e^{\mathbf f})-\mathbf C\mathbf f)$ has a unique solution $\mathbf f_\star\in BC(\mathbb R,\mathbb R)^N$, independent of $\mathbf C$. If $\mathbf a$ is a valid asymptotics, $\mathbf f_\star$ gives the unique solution of the Y-system $Y_n(x+is)Y_n(x-is)=\prod_m(1+Y_m(x))^{G_{nm}}$ with the stated properties. ([Hilfiker–Runkel, Thms 1.3–1.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1708.00001)) Existence and uniqueness for $\mathbf C=\tfrac12\mathbf G$ follow from the Banach fixed-point theorem (Prop. 3.1). Independence of $\mathbf C$ (Prop. 4.3) comes from rewriting a solution for any $\mathbf C'$ as a solution of a $\mathbf C$-independent functional equation whose solution is unique. For $\mathbf a=0$ the spectral-radius condition is sharp (Rem. 1.6). ([Hilfiker–Runkel](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1708.00001))

### History
Krasnosel'skii's *Topological Methods in the Theory of Nonlinear Integral Equations* (Pergamon, 1964, International Series of Monographs in Pure and Applied Mathematics 45) is the classical monograph for the topological approach. ([Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL18531422W)) Schauder proved his theorem for special cases including Banach spaces in 1930, and Tychonoff proved the compact convex case in a locally convex space. ([Schauder fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schauder_fixed-point_theorem)) Browder and Minty independently proved the surjectivity theorem for monotone operators; Browder's paper appeared in 1967. ([Browder–Minty theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browder%E2%80%93Minty_theorem)) R. K. Miller's *Nonlinear Volterra Integral Equations* (W. A. Benjamin, 1971) was an early monograph on the Volterra case. ([Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL3571205W)) Appell and Zabrejko's *Nonlinear Superposition Operators* (CUP, 1990) systematized the Nemytskii-operator side. ([CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/nonlinear-superposition-operators/superposition-operator-in-spaces-of-smooth-functions/BAEF2B3651B2F83CAB7FB607ADF5425A))

### Open problems
- **TBA equations beyond the proven regime.** For spectral radius of $\mathbf G$ at least $2$, the constant Y-system has no real positive solution. Hilfiker and Runkel write that "it seems likely" this extends to asymptotics $\mathbf a=\mathbf w e^{\pm\gamma x/s}$. They suggest that existence and uniqueness for TBA equations of excited states, with generic root positions, might be provable by similar techniques, and note that a Y-system solution with sufficiently far analytic continuation requires additional constraints (§5). ([Hilfiker–Runkel](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1708.00001))
- **Blow-up time for nonlinear VIEs.** Appleby and Patterson leave blow-up time estimation aside, saying it "represents an interesting open problem for general nonlinear VIEs". They also state that full proofs of the growth rates that Roberts and Olmstead derived by conjecturing leading-order behaviour remain open. ([Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Integral equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation): Urysohn, Hammerstein and nonlinear Volterra forms.
- **Learn:** [Infante–Pietramala–Tojo, Non-trivial solutions of local and non-local Neumann boundary-value problems](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1404.1390): a self-contained worked example of fixed-point index methods for perturbed Hammerstein equations.
- **Primary:** [Hilfiker–Runkel, Existence and uniqueness of solutions to Y-systems and TBA equations](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1708.00001): contraction and analytic arguments for a nonlinear convolution system.
- **Primary:** [Appleby–Patterson, Blow-up and superexponential growth in superlinear Volterra equations](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583): sharp finite-time blow-up criterion.
- **Further reading:** [Krasnosel'skii, Topological Methods in the Theory of Nonlinear Integral Equations (Pergamon, 1964)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL18531422W): the classical monograph.
- **Further reading:** [Appell–Zabrejko, Nonlinear Superposition Operators (CUP, 1990)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/nonlinear-superposition-operators/superposition-operator-in-spaces-of-smooth-functions/BAEF2B3651B2F83CAB7FB607ADF5425A): Nemytskii operators in function spaces.
- **Further reading:** [Gripenberg, Londen, Staffans, Volterra Integral and Functional Equations (CUP, 1990)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book): Part II on nonlinear Volterra theory.
references.MSC 45Hxx - Integral equations with misc:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 code 45Hxx collects integral equations singled out by the specific form of their kernel, with a cross-reference to 44A15, special integral transforms such as the Legendre and Hilbert transforms ([MSC2020 45Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Hxx); [MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx)). Within [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations) it sits beside the structural headings (linear, Fredholm, Volterra, singular, nonlinear) and the qualitative, abstract and inverse-problem headings ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX)).

Examples of equations named for their kernels are Carleman's first-kind equation with logarithmic kernel, solved in closed form in 1922 ([Wikipedia: Carleman's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleman%27s_equation)); dual integral equations with Bessel or trigonometric kernels arising from mixed boundary-value problems ([Sneddon 1960](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/elementary-solution-of-dual-integral-equations/388B274A6E73329389A9451146D8C0D2); [Sneddon 1962](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/dual-integral-equations-with-trigonometrical-kernels/0664361660544EEAF7992AF59AF01621)); and the Love equation with a Lorentzian kernel, whose solution is not known in closed form ([Reichert–Ristivojevic](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.01142)).

### Scope
MSC2020 lists ([MSC2020 45Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Hxx)):
- **45H05** Integral equations with miscellaneous special kernels [See also 44A15].
- **45H99** None of the above, but in this section.

Neighbouring codes ([MSC2020 45Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Exx); [MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX); [MSC2020 44Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=44Axx)):
- [MSC 45Exx - Singular integral equations](node:MSC%2045Exx%20-%20Singular%20integral%20equations): 45E05 for Cauchy-type kernels and 45E10 for convolution-type equations (Abel, Picard, Toeplitz and Wiener–Hopf type), so Abel's equation and Wiener–Hopf equations are classified there, not in 45H.
- [MSC 45Bxx - Fredholm integral equations](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations), [MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations) and [MSC 45Fxx - Systems of linear integral equations](node:MSC%2045Fxx%20-%20Systems%20of%20linear%20integral%20equations): the general theories listed as separate headings (see also [Systems of Integral Equations](node:Systems%20of%20Integral%20Equations)).
- [MSC 44Axx - Integral transforms, operational calculus](node:MSC%2044Axx%20-%20Integral%20transforms,%20operational%20calculus): the transforms themselves, including 44A15 special transforms and 44A20 transforms of special functions.
- [MSC 65Rxx - Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms](node:MSC%2065Rxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20transforms): numerical schemes; 45Lxx covers theoretical approximation of solutions.

### Key concepts
- **Carleman's logarithmic-kernel equation.** The first-kind equation $\int_a^b\ln|x-t|\,y(t)\,dt=f(x)$ has, for $b-a\ne4$, the solution
$$y(x)=\frac{1}{\pi^2\sqrt{(x-a)(b-x)}}\left[\int_a^b\frac{\sqrt{(t-a)(b-t)}\,f'(t)}{t-x}\,dt+\frac{1}{\ln\frac{b-a}{4}}\int_a^b\frac{f(t)\,dt}{\sqrt{(t-a)(b-t)}}\right];$$
for $b-a=4$ it is solvable only if $\int_a^b f(t)/\sqrt{(t-a)(b-t)}\,dt=0$, and then the second term is replaced by an arbitrary constant $C$ ([Wikipedia: Carleman's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleman%27s_equation)).
- **Dual integral equations.** Mixed boundary-value problems treated by [Hankel transforms](node:Hankel%20Transform) lead to pairs of integral equations holding on complementary ranges, with Bessel kernels and prescribed constants $\alpha,\nu$. Titchmarsh first derived the formal solution, using Mellin transforms and essentially a Wiener–Hopf procedure; Sneddon gave an elementary solution suggested by Copson's solution of the electrified disc ($\alpha=-1$, $\nu=0$) ([Sneddon 1960](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/elementary-solution-of-dual-integral-equations/388B274A6E73329389A9451146D8C0D2)). Plane mixed problems give trigonometric-kernel pairs that reduce to the Titchmarsh type with $\alpha=-1$, $\nu=-\tfrac12$, a case not covered by Busbridge's general solution ([Sneddon 1962](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/dual-integral-equations-with-trigonometrical-kernels/0664361660544EEAF7992AF59AF01621)). See [Bessel Functions](node:Bessel%20Functions) and [Laplace and Mellin Transforms](node:Laplace%20and%20Mellin%20Transforms).
- **Wiener–Hopf factorization (technique).** After a Fourier transform one factors the kernel as $K=K_+K_-$, with factors analytic in the upper and lower half-planes (via a logarithm and additive decomposition), splits the known terms the same way, and uses analytic continuation and Liouville's theorem to identify an entire function, usually a polynomial ([Wikipedia: Wiener–Hopf method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Hopf_method)). It is the standard route for the edge problems of special-kernel equations: Hutson, Popov and Pustilnik–Matveev solved the leading Love-equation edge problem this way ([Reichert–Ristivojevic](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.01142)); see [Integral Equations with Convolution Kernels](node:Integral%20Equations%20with%20Convolution%20Kernels).
- **Index transforms.** The Kontorovich–Lebedev transform $g(y)=\int_0^\infty f(x)K_{iy}(x)\,dx$ has the Macdonald function $K_{iy}$ as kernel with the transform variable in the index, so its inversion integrates over the index rather than the argument and is used for the Laplace equation in wedge domains ([Wikipedia: Kontorovich–Lebedev transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kontorovich%E2%80%93Lebedev_transform)); see [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations) and [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions).
- **Love and Lieb–Liniger equations.** The Love equation $f(x)-\frac{\kappa}{\pi}\int_{-1}^1\frac{f(y)\,dy}{\kappa^2+(x-y)^2}=1$ on $|x|\le1$ gives the capacitance $\mathcal C=\frac1{2\pi}\int f\,dx$ of two coaxial unit disks at separation $\kappa$; with $\mathsf L=\ln(16\pi/\kappa)$,
$$\mathcal C=\frac1{4\kappa}+\frac{\mathsf L-1}{4\pi}+\frac{\kappa(\mathsf L^2-2)}{16\pi^2}+\frac{\kappa^2(2\mathsf L^2-1-3\zeta(3))}{64\pi^3}+\cdots,$$
obtained by working with the resolvent, matching bulk and edge solutions through a Laplace transform (Volin's method); for large $\kappa$ a Legendre-polynomial expansion gives $\mathcal C\approx\frac1\pi+\frac2{\pi^2\kappa}+\frac4{\pi^3\kappa^2}-\cdots$ ([Reichert–Ristivojevic](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.01142)). The same equation governs the one-dimensional $\delta$-Bose gas; Tracy and Widom argue by [Matched Asymptotic Expansions](node:Matched%20Asymptotic%20Expansions), not rigorously, that its energy has $\gamma^2$ coefficient $\frac16-\frac1{\pi^2}$ (Takahashi's value, against Kaminaka–Wadati's $\frac18-\frac1{\pi^2}$) ([Tracy–Widom](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.04677)). The $\zeta(3)$ term links to the [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function).
- **Weakly singular kernels in general.** Equations whose kernels are unbounded at a point, so that the integral is improper, are called singular or weakly singular ([Wikipedia: Integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_equation)); the logarithmic kernel above is weakly singular, while strongly singular Cauchy kernels belong to [Cauchy Singular Integral Equations](node:Cauchy%20Singular%20Integral%20Equations).

### History
Kirchhoff derived the leading small-separation capacitance in 1877, Love formulated his equation in 1949, Lieb and Liniger met the same equation for bosons in 1963, the year Hutson proved Kirchhoff's result, and Gaudin linked the problems in 1971; Shaw, Leppington–Levine, Chew–Kong, Tracy–Widom and Paffuti found the next term ([Reichert–Ristivojevic](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.01142)). Carleman solved the logarithmic-kernel equation in 1922 ([Wikipedia: Carleman's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleman%27s_equation)). Kontorovich and Lebedev introduced their transform in the late 1930s ([Wikipedia: Kontorovich–Lebedev transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kontorovich%E2%80%93Lebedev_transform)). Wiener and Hopf developed their method to solve systems of integral equations ([Wikipedia: Wiener–Hopf method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Hopf_method)), and Sneddon's 1960 and 1962 papers treated dual equations by elementary methods ([Sneddon 1960](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/elementary-solution-of-dual-integral-equations/388B274A6E73329389A9451146D8C0D2); [Sneddon 1962](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/dual-integral-equations-with-trigonometrical-kernels/0664361660544EEAF7992AF59AF01621)).

### Open problems
- **Closed-form solution of the Love equation.** Reichert and Ristivojevic state that the explicit solution is not currently known ([Reichert–Ristivojevic](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.01142)).
- **Conjectured constants in the Lieb–Liniger expansion.** Tracy and Widom state conjectural closed forms, for example $\gamma_2=-2/\pi-\pi/4$, checked numerically to over 100 digits, and conjecture that $e(\gamma)$ expands in powers of $\gamma^{1/2}$ ([Tracy–Widom](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.04677)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Carleman's equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleman%27s_equation): the logarithmic-kernel equation and its explicit solution.
- **Reference:** [Wiener–Hopf method (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Hopf_method): kernel factorization.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.307 Integral Equations (Margetis)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-307-integral-equations-spring-2006/): Fredholm theory, Wiener–Hopf method and Cauchy-type singular equations, with physical examples.
- **Primary:** [Reichert–Ristivojevic, Analytical results for the capacitance of a circular plate capacitor](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.01142): high-order expansions of the Love equation.
- **Primary:** [Tracy–Widom, On the ground state energy of the δ-function Bose gas](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1601.04677): Love/Lieb–Liniger asymptotics and conjectures.
- **Primary:** [Sneddon, The elementary solution of dual integral equations](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/glasgow-mathematical-journal/article/elementary-solution-of-dual-integral-equations/388B274A6E73329389A9451146D8C0D2): Bessel-kernel dual equations.
- **Further reading:** [Polyanin and Manzhirov, Handbook of Integral Equations (Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9781420010558): handbook of integral equations (bibliographic record); [Bajnok et al., The complete trans-series for conserved charges in the Lieb–Liniger model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05932): trans-series for Lieb–Liniger moments and the coaxial disk capacitance, checked against high-precision numerics.
references.MSC 45Jxx - Integro-ordinary differentia:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 code 45Jxx covers integro-ordinary differential equations: equations for a function of one variable that involve both its derivatives and integrals of it. It cross-references the general theory of functional-differential equations (34K05), functional-differential equations in abstract spaces (34K30), and integro-differential operators (47G20). ([MSC2020 45Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Jxx); [MSC2020 34Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Kxx); [MSC2020 47Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Gxx)) The general first-order equation, linear only in the derivative term, is $u'(x)+\int_{x_0}^xf(t,u(t))\,dt=g(x,u(x))$, $u(x_0)=u_0$. Closed forms are hard to find; when they exist they often come from integral transforms, which turn the problem into an algebraic one. ([Integro-differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integro-differential_equation)) Applications include the RLC circuit, Wilson–Cowan neural populations, the Whitham equation for dispersive waves, and age-structured epidemic models in the Kermack–McKendrick tradition. ([Integro-differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integro-differential_equation))

The research questions concern resolvents: their integrability, their decay or growth, the stability they encode, and the long-time and blow-up behaviour of nonlinear equations. Gripenberg, Londen and Staffans organize the field around linear integrodifferential convolution equations (their Chapter 3), nonintegrable kernels with integrable resolvents, Lyapunov techniques, and frequency-domain methods. ([GLS, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book))

### Scope
The MSC2020 sub-codes are **45J05** Integro-ordinary differential equations [See also 34K05, 34K30, 47G20] and **45J99** None of the above, but in this section. ([MSC2020 45Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Jxx))

Neighbours, one line each:
- [MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations) covers equations without derivatives. Integrating $x'=ax+k*x$ turns it into one. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX); [Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- [MSC 34Kxx - Functional-differential equations (including equations with delayed, advanced or state-dependent argument)](node:MSC%2034Kxx%20-%20Functional-differential%20equations%20%28including%20equations%20with%20delayed,%20advanced%20or%20state-dependent%20argument%29) covers delay equations; its stability (34K20) and asymptotic (34K25) codes are the delay-equation counterparts. ([MSC2020 34Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=34Kxx))
- [MSC 45Kxx - Integro-partial differential equations](node:MSC%2045Kxx%20-%20Integro-partial%20differential%20equations) adds spatial derivatives, and [MSC 45Mxx - Qualitative behavior of solutions to integral equations](node:MSC%2045Mxx%20-%20Qualitative%20behavior%20of%20solutions%20to%20integral%20equations) is where stability results for integral equations are filed (45M10). ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX); [MSC2020 45Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Mxx))
- [MSC 47Gxx - Integral, integro-differential, and pseudodifferential operators](node:MSC%2047Gxx%20-%20Integral,%20integro-differential,%20and%20pseudodifferential%20operators) covers the operators themselves; 47G20 points back to 45J05. ([MSC2020 47Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Gxx))

### Key concepts
- **Laplace transform solution.** The equation $u'+2u+5\int_0^xu(t)\,dt=\theta(x)$, $u(0)=0$, transforms to $U(s)=1/(s^2+2s+5)$, so $u(x)=\tfrac12e^{-x}\sin(2x)\,\theta(x)$. ([Integro-differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integro-differential_equation)) This links the area to [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) with constant coefficients.
- **Resolvent and variation of constants.** For $x'(t)=ax(t)+\int_0^tk(t-s)x(s)\,ds$, the resolvent $r$ solves $r'=ar+k*r$, $r(0)=1$, and replaces the exponential $e^{at}$. Solutions of the stochastic equation $dX=(aX+k*X)\,dt+\sigma\,dB$ are $X(t)=r(t)X_0+\int_0^tr(t-s)\sigma\,dB(s)$. ([Appleby–Krol, eqs. 1.2, 2.4–2.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.1304)) Its transform is $\hat r(z)=1/h(z)$ with $h(z)=z-a-\hat k(z)$. If $a+\int_0^\infty k>0$, then $r$ grows exponentially. ([Appleby–Krol, Rem. 5.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.1304)) See [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus).
- **Paley–Wiener and shifted spectral conditions.** For $u+K\star u=f$ with $K\in L^1(\mathbb R_+,M_n(\mathbb C))$, the condition $\det(I+\mathcal L[K](\lambda))\ne0$ for $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$ gives a resolvent in $L^1$ and $L^1$ solutions for $L^1$ data. Suppose instead the condition holds on $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge-\delta$ and $|K(t)|\le Ce^{-\gamma_Kt}$. Then $e^{\gamma t}u\in L^1$ for every $0\le\gamma<\min(\gamma_K,\delta)$. ([Coti Zelati–Ertzbischoff–Gérard-Varet, Thms C.2–C.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1)) Integrated, an integro-ODE becomes an equation of this form.
- **Heavy-tailed kernels: exact rates.** Assume $k>0$ is integrable and continuous, $\lambda(t)=\int_t^\infty k$ is log-convex, and $\lambda(t)=L(t)t^{-\alpha}$ with $0<\alpha<1$ and $L$ slowly varying. If $a+\int_0^\infty k=0$, then $r(t)\,t^{1-\alpha}L(t)\to\sin(\alpha\pi)/\pi$ (Thm 3.2). For $0<\alpha<\tfrac12$ the stationary autocovariance satisfies $c(t)L(t)^2t^{1-2\alpha}\to\sigma^2\frac{\Gamma(1-2\alpha)\Gamma(\alpha)}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\frac{\sin^2\pi\alpha}{\pi^2}$, which is long memory (Thm 3.4). ([Appleby–Krol](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.1304))
- **The critical case.** If $k(t)=L(t)t^{-3/2}$ with $\lambda$ log-convex, then $r\in L^2$ iff $\int_1^\infty dt/(tL(t)^2)<\infty$. In that case the autocovariance $c(t)$ is asymptotic to a constant multiple of $\int_t^\infty ds/(sL(s)^2)$, and suitable choices of $L$ give decay at any slowly varying rate, arbitrarily slow (Thm 3.6, Cor. 3.7). ([Appleby–Krol](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.1304))
- **Subexponential regime.** If $k$ is regularly varying of index $-1-\alpha$, $\alpha>0$, and $a+\int_0^\infty k<0$, then $r(t)/k(t)\to1/(a+\int_0^\infty k)^2$, a result of Appleby, Győri and Reynolds. Here $c(t)/k(t)\to\sigma^2/(-a-\int_0^\infty k)^3$, so $c$ is integrable but decays only polynomially. ([Appleby–Krol, §5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.1304))
- **Nonlinear equations: blow-up and growth.** Let $x'(t)=\int_0^tw(t-s)f(x(s))\,ds$ with $x(0)>0$, where $w\ge0$ is continuous with $w(0)>0$ and $f$ is continuous, positive, asymptotically increasing with $f(x)/x\to\infty$. Solutions blow up in finite time iff $\int_\eta^\infty du/\sqrt{\int_0^uf}<\infty$ (Thm 2). When this integral diverges, set $F_U(x)=\int_1^xdu/\sqrt{\int_0^uf}$. For the forced equation $x'=h+w*f(x)$ with $H=\int_0^th\ge0$, and under further hypotheses, $\limsup F_U(H(t))/t\le\sqrt{2w(0)}$ is equivalent to $F_U(x(t))/t\to\sqrt{2w(0)}$ (Thm 10). ([Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- **Non-integrable kernels in kinetic theory.** In linearized active Brownian particle models the density solves a Volterra equation whose non-diffusive kernel decays only like $(1+t)^{-1/2}$. This "forbids to apply the classical theory of Volterra equation", so the authors work directly with the Laplace transform. With rotational diffusion $\nu>0$ and $\nu|k|^{-1}\le\nu_0$, they prove for each Fourier mode $k$ that $\rho_k$ decays like $e^{-\eta_0\nu t}$ with prefactor $C(1+\nu^{-5/4}|k|^{5/4})$ times the norm of the initial datum (Thm 1.4). ([Coti Zelati et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1))

### History
Gripenberg, Londen and Staffans (CUP, Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications 34, 1990) systematized the linear and nonlinear theory for $n$-dimensional systems. Part III covers kernels of positive type and frequency-domain, combined Lyapunov–frequency-domain, and monotonicity methods. ([GLS, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book)) Burton's *Volterra Integral and Differential Equations* (Academic Press 1983; 2nd ed., Elsevier 2005, Mathematics in Science and Engineering 202) is a standard monograph on Volterra integral and integro-differential equations. ([Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL5477665W)) Lakshmikantham and Rama Mohana Rao's *Theory of Integro-Differential Equations* (Gordon and Breach, 1995, Stability and Control 1) is a monograph devoted to integro-differential equations. ([Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL988252W/editions.json)) Volterra's *Theory of Functionals* was published by Blackie in 1930; Dover republished the first English translation in 1959 as *Theory of Functionals and of Integral and Integro-differential Equations*. ([Open Library search](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=theory+of+integro-differential+equations&fields=title,author_name,publisher,first_publish_year,key))

### Open problems
- **Blow-up time.** For $x'=w*f(x)$, Appleby and Patterson prove when finite-time blow-up occurs but do not estimate the blow-up time. They call that estimation "an interesting open problem for general nonlinear VIEs". They also state that the full proofs of the growth rates Roberts and Olmstead obtained by conjecturing leading-order behaviour remain open. ([Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- **Strong forcing.** For $x'=h+w*f(x)$ with $\limsup F_U(H(t))/t>\sqrt{2w(0)}$, Theorem 10 does not apply. Appleby and Patterson "conjecture that the perturbation likely dominates the dynamics" in this regime. ([Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- **Optimal decay with weak diffusion.** For the active Brownian particle equation with $\nu>0$, Coti Zelati, Ertzbischoff and Gérard-Varet conjecture that a decay of the form $(1+\nu^{-3/4})e^{-\varepsilon\nu^{1/2}t}$, an enhanced-dissipation rate, is optimal. They say it "seems out of reach within our approach". They also name nonlinear stability as future work. ([Coti Zelati et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Integro-differential equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integro-differential_equation): forms, Laplace-transform solution, applications.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.307 Integral Equations (Margetis, 2006)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-307-integral-equations-spring-2006/): graduate course on Volterra and Fredholm equations.
- **Primary:** [Appleby–Krol, Long memory in a linear stochastic Volterra differential equation](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.1304): exact resolvent asymptotics for heavy-tailed kernels.
- **Primary:** [Appleby–Patterson, Blow-up and superexponential growth in superlinear Volterra equations](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583): sharp blow-up and growth results for nonlinear integro-ODEs.
- **Further reading:** [Gripenberg, Londen, Staffans, Volterra Integral and Functional Equations (CUP, 1990)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book): the standard monograph.
- **Further reading:** [Burton, Volterra Integral and Differential Equations (2nd ed., Elsevier 2005)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL5477665W): monograph on Volterra integral and integro-differential equations.
- **Further reading:** [Lakshmikantham and Rama Mohana Rao, Theory of Integro-Differential Equations (Gordon and Breach, 1995)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL988252W/editions.json): monograph on integro-differential equations.
