## Reference
### Overview
MSC2020 code 45Kxx covers integro-partial differential equations. It cross-references 34K30, 35R09, 35R10 and 47G20. ([MSC2020 45Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Kxx)) On the PDE side, 35R09 is "Integro-partial differential equations" (pointing back to 45K05), 35R10 is partial functional-differential equations, and 35R11 is fractional PDEs. ([MSC2020 35Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Rxx)) Two large families meet here. The first has operators nonlocal in space, $Lu(x)=\mathrm{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(x+y))K(y)\,dy$ with $K\ge0$, $K(y)=K(-y)$ and $\int\min\{|y|^2,1\}K(y)\,dy<\infty$; the fractional Laplacian is the model. ([Ros-Oton, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1504.04099)) The second has memory in time. Examples are viscoelastic equations $u_{tt}-\Delta u+\int_0^tg(t-s)\Delta u(s)\,ds=\cdots$ ([Peng–Liu](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.01752v1)) and time-fractional diffusion $\partial_t^\alpha(u-u_0)-\operatorname{div}(A\nabla u)=f$. ([Zacher](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503))

Nonlocal operators arise as generators of jump processes. Courrège's theorem says that a linear operator on $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfying the positive maximum principle is the sum of a second-order elliptic differential operator and a nonlocal integral operator. ([Applebaum–Le Ngan](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1902.03836)) Fully nonlinear integro-differential equations come from stochastic control of pure-jump Lévy processes. ([Caffarelli–Silvestre 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.4681)) Both connect the area to [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes).

### Scope
The MSC2020 sub-codes are **45K05** Integro-partial differential equations [See also 34K30, 35R09, 35R10, 47G20] and **45K99** None of the above, but in this section. ([MSC2020 45Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Kxx))

Neighbours ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX); [MSC2020 35Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Rxx); [MSC2020 47Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Gxx)):
- [MSC 45Jxx - Integro-ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2045Jxx%20-%20Integro-ordinary%20differential%20equations) covers memory equations in one variable.
- [MSC 35Rxx - Miscellaneous topics in partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035Rxx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20partial%20differential%20equations) holds 35R09, the PDE-side twin of 45K05, and 35R11 for fractional PDEs; 35R35 covers free boundary problems.
- [MSC 47Gxx - Integral, integro-differential, and pseudodifferential operators](node:MSC%2047Gxx%20-%20Integral,%20integro-differential,%20and%20pseudodifferential%20operators) holds 47G20 integro-differential operators, which points to 45K05.
- [MSC 34Kxx - Functional-differential equations (including equations with delayed, advanced or state-dependent argument)](node:MSC%2034Kxx%20-%20Functional-differential%20equations%20%28including%20equations%20with%20delayed,%20advanced%20or%20state-dependent%20argument%29) holds 34K30 functional-differential equations in abstract spaces.

### Key concepts
- **Fractional Laplacian and its extension.** $(-\Delta)^sf(x)=C_{d,s}\lim_{r\to0^+}\int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus B_r(x)}\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{|x-y|^{d+2s}}\,dy$ with $C_{d,s}=\frac{4^s\Gamma(d/2+s)}{\pi^{d/2}|\Gamma(-s)|}$, equivalently $\mathcal F^{-1}(|\xi|^{2s}\mathcal Ff)$. The definitions in the literature are mostly equivalent. ([Fractional Laplacian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_Laplacian)) Caffarelli and Silvestre realize fractional powers of the Laplacian as Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps of an extension problem in one more variable, so that nonlocal properties can be proved by local arguments. ([Caffarelli–Silvestre 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608640)) See [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) and [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces).
- **Ellipticity classes and interior regularity.** Kernels are taken comparable, $\lambda|y|^{-n-2s}\le K\le\Lambda|y|^{-n-2s}$, or stable, $K(y)=a(y/|y|)|y|^{-n-2s}$ with $0\le a\in L^1(S^{n-1})$. For either class, if $u\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ in $B_1$, $\alpha>0$ and $\alpha+2s\notin\mathbb Z$, then $\|u\|_{C^{2s+\alpha}(B_{1/2})}\le C(\|f\|_{C^\alpha(B_1)}+\|u\|_{C^\alpha(\mathbb R^n)})$ (Thm 6.1). The global $C^\alpha$ norm cannot be replaced by $L^\infty$: for $\alpha\in(0,s]$ and every small $\epsilon>0$ some operator has a solution that is $C^{\alpha-\epsilon}$ but not $C^{2s+\alpha}$ (Prop. 6.2). ([Ros-Oton](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1504.04099)) This is the nonlocal analogue of the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem).
- **Boundary regularity.** For stable operators $u_0=(1-|x|^2)_+^s$ solves $Lu_0=c>0$ in $B_1$ with $u_0=0$ outside, an explicit barrier behaving like $d^s$, with $d$ the distance to the boundary (Lemma 5.4). In a bounded $C^{1,1}$ domain with $f\ge0$, a Hopf lemma gives $u\ge c\,d^s$ or $u\equiv0$, and $u/d^s\in C^{s-\epsilon}(\overline\Omega)$ (Thm 7.4). For comparable kernels only barriers like $d^{\alpha_0}$, $0<\alpha_0<s$, are available, which gives $C^{\alpha_0}$. For any stable operator, solutions are $C^{1+3s-\epsilon}_{\rm loc}$ in convex domains. There is a nonconvex $C^\infty$ domain where a solution is not $C^{3s+\epsilon}_{\rm loc}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ (Thm 8.1). ([Ros-Oton](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1504.04099))
- **Nonlocal De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory.** Kassmann showed by a counterexample that the global positivity assumption in the Harnack inequality cannot be dropped or relaxed, even for the fractional Laplacian, and proposed a version with a nonlocal tail term. Di Castro, Kuusi and Palatucci consider measurable kernels with $\lambda\le K(x,y)|x-y|^{n+sp}\le\Lambda$, modelled on the fractional $p$-Laplacian. For weak solutions $u\in W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ with $u\ge0$ in $B_R$ and balls $B_r\subset B_{R/2}$ they prove $\sup_{B_r}u\le c\inf_{B_r}u+c(r/R)^{sp/(p-1)}\mathrm{Tail}(u_-;x_0,R)$. ([Di Castro–Kuusi–Palatucci](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1405.7842)) Felsinger and Kassmann prove local Hölder estimates and a weak Harnack inequality for parabolic operators of order $\alpha\in(\alpha_0,2)$, robust as $\alpha\to2$, by extending Moser's method. ([Felsinger–Kassmann](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1203.2126)) See [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle).
- **Fully nonlinear equations and the obstacle problem.** Caffarelli and Silvestre prove a nonlocal ABP estimate, a Harnack inequality and interior $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity for fully nonlinear integro-differential equations. The estimates are uniform as the order tends to $2$. ([Caffarelli–Silvestre 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.4681)) Using the extension, Caffarelli, Salsa and Silvestre rewrite the obstacle problem for the fractional Laplacian as a thin obstacle problem. They obtain sharp regularity of the solution and regularity of the free boundary. ([Caffarelli–Salsa–Silvestre](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0702392))
- **Memory and viscoelastic decay.** Dafermos's 1970 paper on asymptotic stability in viscoelasticity ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00251609)) treats the past history as an additional variable governed by its own equation. This turns the memory equation into a system on an extended space. In that history framework, $\mu'+\delta\mu\le0$ is the classical sufficient condition for exponential decay, and $\mu(\sigma+s)\le Ce^{-\delta\sigma}\mu(s)$ is necessary. ([Fabrizio–Giorgi–Pata](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0901.4063)) Peng and Liu consider $u_{tt}-\Delta u+\int_0^tg(t-s)\Delta u\,ds+u_t=\alpha|u|^{p(x)-2}u\log|u|$. Here $g$ is $C^1$, positive and nonincreasing with $\ell=1-\int_0^\infty g>0$, and $g'\le-\xi g^q$ with $\int_0^\infty\xi=\infty$ and $1\le q<2$. Under these hypotheses, (A1) and (A3), together with the paper's conditions on the initial data, the energy decays like $\exp(1-K\int_0^t\xi)$ if $q=1$ and polynomially in $\int_0^t\xi$ if $1<q<2$. ([Peng–Liu, Thm 3.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.01752v1)) This is a memory perturbation of the [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation).
- **Time-fractional diffusion.** The relaxation function solving $s_\mu+\mu\,g_\alpha*s_\mu=1$ is $E_\alpha(-\mu t^\alpha)\ge1/(1+\mu\Gamma(1-\alpha)t^\alpha)$. On bounded domains $\|u(t)\|_{L^2}\le s_{\nu\lambda_1}(t)\|u_0\|_{L^2}$, which is optimal, so decay is algebraic like $t^{-\alpha}$, unlike the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation). A weak Harnack inequality holds for $0<p<(2+d\alpha)/(2+d\alpha-2\alpha)$, but the full Harnack inequality fails for $d\ge2$ even for the Laplacian. ([Zacher](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503))

### History
Caffarelli and Silvestre's extension paper (2006) and their regularity theory for fully nonlinear integro-differential equations (2007) presented nonlocal problems as a continuation of classical elliptic theory. ([Caffarelli–Silvestre 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608640); [Caffarelli–Silvestre 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.4681)) Dafermos's history approach to viscoelasticity dates from 1970; Fabrizio, Giorgi and Pata later proposed an alternative state-space approach to equations with memory. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00251609); [Fabrizio–Giorgi–Pata](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0901.4063)) Bucur and Valdinoci's lecture notes (UMI Lecture Notes 20, Springer 2016) survey nonlocal diffusion in water waves, crystal dislocations, nonlocal phase transitions and nonlocal minimal surfaces. ([Bucur–Valdinoci](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.08292))

### Open problems
- **Harnack inequality for one-dimensional time-fractional diffusion.** For $\partial_t^\alpha(u-u_0)-\operatorname{div}(A(t,x)\nabla u)=0$, the full Harnack inequality fails when $d\ge2$. Zacher writes: "The one-dimensional case is still an open problem", and "It is conjectured that the Harnack inequality is true in this case." ([Zacher, §5](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503))
- **Regularity for comparable kernels.** For kernels comparable to $|y|^{-n-2s}$, only barriers like $d^{\alpha_0}$ with $0<\alpha_0<s$ are known. Ros-Oton writes that "one would expect solutions $u$ to be $C^{1+2s+\alpha_0-\epsilon}$" in the interior of $C^{1,1}$ domains, which is not proved there. ([Ros-Oton, §8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1504.04099))
- **Well-posedness of reaction–subdiffusion models.** Some models couple subdiffusion $\partial_tU=\Sigma e^{At}\mathfrak D_{0,t}^{1-\alpha}(e^{-At}\partial_x^2U)+AU$ with linear creation and annihilation. For these, Achleitner et al. state that "results on well-posedness for these models seem not to be available in the literature". ([Achleitner et al., §3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.05606))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Fractional Laplacian (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_Laplacian): equivalent definitions and normalizing constant.
- **Learn:** [Bucur–Valdinoci, Nonlocal diffusion and applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.08292): introductory lecture notes on the fractional Laplacian and its applications.
- **Primary:** [Ros-Oton, Nonlocal elliptic equations in bounded domains: a survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1504.04099): existence, maximum principles, interior and boundary regularity.
- **Primary:** [Zacher, Time fractional diffusion equations: solution concepts, regularity and long-time behaviour](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503): survey of memory-type diffusion.
- **Further reading:** [Caffarelli–Silvestre, Regularity theory for fully nonlinear integro-differential equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.4681): ABP, Harnack and $C^{1,\alpha}$ estimates.
- **Further reading:** [Fabrizio–Giorgi–Pata, A new approach to equations with memory](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0901.4063): history and state frameworks for viscoelastic memory.
references.MSC 45Lxx - Theoretical approximation of:
## Reference
### Overview
45Lxx collects work on approximating the solutions of integral equations within [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations). Its MSC2020 heading carries the instruction "For numerical analysis, see 65Rxx", so numerical analysis of integral equations is directed to [MSC 65Rxx - Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms](node:MSC%2065Rxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20transforms). ([MSC2020 45Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Lxx&btn=Current)) In practice the two codes overlap: Gonzalez and Li's convergence theorem for Nyström methods is classified primary 65R20, 65N38 and secondary 45B05, 31B20, while Vidunas's mixed Neumann–Fourier approximating series for solutions and resolvents carries 45B05, 45L05, 42A20, 65R20 and 45-01. ([Gonzalez–Li, arXiv:1205.5064](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.5064); [Vidunas, arXiv:2101.00005](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00005v1))

The model problem is a second-kind equation $\lambda u-\mathcal Ku=f$ with $\mathcal K$ an integral operator. One replaces $\mathcal K$ by a finite-rank or discrete operator $\mathcal K_h$ and asks when $\lambda-\mathcal K_h$ is invertible with inverse bounded uniformly in $h$; then $\|u-u_h\|_\infty=\|(\lambda I-\mathcal K_h)^{-1}(\mathcal K-\mathcal K_h)u\|_\infty\le C_s\|(\mathcal K-\mathcal K_h)u\|_\infty$, so the error is controlled by the consistency error on the exact solution. ([Degli Esposti–Sestini, arXiv:2510.17680](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17680)) Atkinson's monograph organizes the classical theory into degenerate kernel methods (Chapter 2), projection methods, including collocation, Galerkin and iterated projection solutions (Chapter 3), and the Nyström method, including collectively compact operator approximations (Chapter 4). ([Cambridge chapter page](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/numerical-solution-of-integral-equations-of-the-second-kind/degenerate-kernel-methods/ED8E730CB5316918888A4139D109B630); [Atkinson, table of contents](https://homepage.divms.uiowa.edu/~atkinson/book-toc.pdf))

### Scope
MSC2020 45Lxx has two codes: **45L05** Theoretical approximation of solutions to integral equations {For numerical analysis, see 65Rxx}, and **45L99** None of the above, but in this section. ([MSC2020 45Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Lxx&btn=Current))

How it differs from its neighbours:
- [MSC 65Rxx - Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms](node:MSC%2065Rxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20transforms) contains 65R10 integral transforms, 65R15 eigenvalue problems in integral equations, 65R20 integral equations, 65R30 ill-posed problems and 65R32 inverse problems; 45L points there for numerical analysis. ([MSC2020 65Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=65Rxx&btn=Current))
- [MSC 45Bxx - Fredholm integral equations](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations) and [MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations) are separate sections; 45Dxx has a cross-reference to 34A12. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 45Cxx - Eigenvalue problems for integral equations](node:MSC%2045Cxx%20-%20Eigenvalue%20problems%20for%20integral%20equations) has cross-references to 34Lxx, 35Pxx, 45P05 and 47A75. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 45Mxx - Qualitative behavior of solutions to integral equations](node:MSC%2045Mxx%20-%20Qualitative%20behavior%20of%20solutions%20to%20integral%20equations) has no cross-reference. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Nyström convergence theorem.** For Degli Esposti and Sestini's decoupled meshless Nyström scheme: if the kernel $k$ and right-hand side $f$ are $C^q$, $\lambda$ is not in the spectrum of $\mathcal K$, and the quadrature and reconstruction schemes are stable of orders $0<q_w\le q$ and $0<q_R\le q$, then for all sufficiently small $\mathbf h=(h_X,h_Y)$ the linear system is uniquely solvable, its $\infty$-norm condition number is bounded independently of $\mathbf h$, and the error is bounded by a stability constant $C_s$ times a quadrature term of order $h_Y^{q_w}$ plus a reconstruction term of order $h_X^{q_R}$. ([Degli Esposti–Sestini, arXiv:2510.17680](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17680)) The method replaces $\int_a^b K(x,x')f(x')\,dx'$ by $\sum_kw_kK(x,x_k)f(x_k)$ and goes back to Nyström's 1930 paper in Acta Mathematica. ([Nyström method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystr%C3%B6m_method)) See [Numerical Quadrature for Integral Equations](node:Numerical%20Quadrature%20for%20Integral%20Equations).
- **Collectively compact operator approximation.** A family $\{A_\gamma\}_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ is collectively compact if $\{A_\gamma\varphi:\varphi\in U,\gamma\in\Gamma\}$ is relatively compact for each bounded $U$. If $I-A$ is invertible and $\|(I-A)^{-1}(A_\gamma-A)A_\gamma\|<1$, then $I-A_\gamma$ is invertible,
  $$\|(I-A_\gamma)^{-1}\|\le\frac{1+\|(I-A)^{-1}A_\gamma\|}{1-\|(I-A)^{-1}(A_\gamma-A)A_\gamma\|},$$
  and $\|\varphi_\gamma-\varphi\|_\infty$ is bounded by the same factor times $\|(A_\gamma-A)\varphi\|_\infty$. An and Wu present this lemma as motivated by Brakhage (1960) and Anselone–Moore (1964), with the full procedure in Kress's monograph, and cite Anselone's 1971 book for collectively compact theory. ([An–Wu, arXiv:2408.14392](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.14392)) That book is Anselone's *Collectively Compact Operator Approximation Theory and Applications to Integral Equations* (Prentice Hall, 1971). ([An–Wu, arXiv:2408.14392](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.14392)) Kloeckner's course teaches the framework as Anselone's theorem. ([UIUC CS 598](https://andreask.cs.illinois.edu/Teaching/IntegralEquationsFall2013/)) Builds on [Compact Integral Operators](node:Compact%20Integral%20Operators) and [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces).
- **Galerkin methods and Céa's lemma.** For a bounded form ($a(u,v)\le C\|u\|\|v\|$) that is elliptic ($a(u,u)\ge c\|u\|^2$) on a Hilbert space and a subspace $V_n$, the Galerkin solution satisfies $a(u-u_n,v_n)=0$ for all $v_n\in V_n$ and $\|u-u_n\|\le(C/c)\inf_{v_n\in V_n}\|u-v_n\|$; Petrov–Galerkin methods use a different test space. ([Galerkin method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galerkin_method)) See [Galerkin Approximation of Integral Equations](node:Galerkin%20Approximation%20of%20Integral%20Equations) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces).
- **Iterated projection and superconvergence.** Chatelin and Lebbar study Sloan's iterated solution of a projection method, with orthogonal projection onto piecewise polynomials or interpolation at Gauss points: they prove global superconvergence for smooth kernels and superconvergence at partition points for kernels of Green's-function type, for both the inhomogeneous equation and eigenvectors. ([Chatelin–Lebbar 1981](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/anziam-journal/article/iterated-projection-solution-for-the-fredholm-integral-equation-of-second-kind/03829C11C7B5718E0AAEA5F6667E69AA)) For collocation $\varphi_n-P_n\mathcal K\varphi_n=P_nf$ with piecewise polynomials of degree $\le2r$ at $2r+1$ equispaced nodes per subinterval, a Green's-function-type kernel and $\varphi\in C^{2r+2}$, the collocation error is $O(h^{2r+1})$ and Sloan's iterate $\varphi_n^S=\mathcal K\varphi_n+f$ is $O(h^{2r+2})$. ([Rakshit–Shukla–Rane, arXiv:2406.12343](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12343)) Kernels of this type arise from [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions).
- **Kulkarni's modified projection method.** Replace $\mathcal K$ by $\mathcal K_n^M=P_n\mathcal K+\mathcal KP_n-P_n\mathcal KP_n$. With interpolatory projection at $2r+1$ distinct points per subinterval and a kernel $\kappa\in C^{2r+1}$, the modified solution and its iterate are $O(h^{4r+2})$ (Kulkarni 2003); with equispaced points, $\kappa\in C^{4r+2}$ and $\varphi\in C^{4r}$ they are $O(h^{4r+3})$ and $O(h^{4r+4})$ (Rane 2017). For Green's-function-type kernels, collocation at $2r+1$ equispaced nodes, $\varphi\in C^{2r+2}$ and $r\ge1$, the modified collocation solution and its iterate have orders $O(h^{2r+2})$ and $O(h^{2r+3})$. ([Rakshit–Shukla–Rane, arXiv:2406.12343](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12343))
- **Weakly singular kernels on surfaces.** Second-kind equations with weakly singular kernels arise from elliptic boundary value problems ([Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations)). Gonzalez and Li prove convergence of Nyström methods with a local polynomial correction on surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$, under minimal regularity consistent with classical potential theory, with rates depending on the regularity, the correction degree and the quadrature order; as a corollary a common singularity-subtraction method converges. ([Gonzalez–Li, arXiv:1205.5064](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.5064))

Kloeckner's course treats compactness of integral operators, Riesz theory and projection error estimates together, linking these methods to [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) of compact operators and [MSC 47 - Operator theory](node:MSC%2047%20-%20Operator%20theory). ([UIUC CS 598](https://andreask.cs.illinois.edu/Teaching/IntegralEquationsFall2013/))

### History
Nyström's quadrature method dates from his 1930 Acta Mathematica paper on integral equations with applications to boundary value problems. ([Nyström method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystr%C3%B6m_method)) Galerkin's method goes back to his 1915 work on rods and plates, with convergence studied by Mikhlin. ([Galerkin method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galerkin_method)) An and Wu trace the collectively compact error lemma to Brakhage's quadrature analysis (1960) and Anselone–Moore (1964), and cite Anselone's 1971 monograph for the general theory. ([An–Wu, arXiv:2408.14392](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.14392)) Chatelin and Lebbar's superconvergence analysis of the iterated projection solution appeared in 1981, and Kulkarni's modified projection method in 2003. ([Chatelin–Lebbar 1981](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/anziam-journal/article/iterated-projection-solution-for-the-fredholm-integral-equation-of-second-kind/03829C11C7B5718E0AAEA5F6667E69AA); [arXiv:2406.12343](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.12343)) In the preface to his 1997 monograph, Atkinson wrote that the 1960–1990 work on compact second-kind Fredholm equations was nearing a stage with few major additions to come, especially for functions of one variable. ([Atkinson, preface](https://homepage.divms.uiowa.edu/~atkinson/book-toc.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Kenig's problem and Galerkin convergence on Lipschitz boundaries.** Galerkin convergence in $L^2(\Gamma)$ for the second-kind boundary integral equations $\pm\frac12I+D$ would follow if the double-layer operator $D$ had essential norm below $1/2$, or if $\pm\frac12I+D$ were compact perturbations of coercive operators. Chandler-Wilde and Spence settle these questions negatively, giving Lipschitz domains and 3-d Lipschitz polyhedra (open-book polyhedra, star-shaped with respect to a ball) with an asymptotically dense sequence of subspaces on which the Galerkin method in $L^2(\Gamma)$ does not converge; they describe whether the essential spectral radius of $D$ on $L^2(\Gamma)$ is below $1/2$ for all Lipschitz $\Gamma$ (Kenig's question) as a long-standing open problem, settled only for convex domains, small Lipschitz character and Lipschitz polyhedra. ([abstract, arXiv:2105.11383](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.11383); [full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.11383))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Nyström method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystr%C3%B6m_method): the quadrature method and choice of rules.
- **Reference:** [MSC2020 45Lxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Lxx&btn=Current): official codes and the pointer to 65Rxx.
- **Learn:** [Kloeckner, Integral Equations and Fast Algorithms (UIUC CS 598, 2013)](https://andreask.cs.illinois.edu/Teaching/IntegralEquationsFall2013/): Riesz theory, Nyström methods, Anselone's theorem, Céa's lemma, singular quadrature.
- **Primary:** [Atkinson, The Numerical Solution of Integral Equations of the Second Kind (CUP 1997)](https://homepage.divms.uiowa.edu/~atkinson/book-toc.pdf): degenerate kernel, projection and Nyström methods, collectively compact approximations, boundary integral equations ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511626340)).
- **Primary:** [Chandler-Wilde and Spence, Coercivity, essential norms, and the Galerkin method for second-kind integral equations on polyhedral and Lipschitz domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.11383): counterexamples and the open essential-spectral-radius problem.
- **Primary:** [Chandler-Wilde, Graham, Langdon, Spence, Acta Numerica 21 (2012)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0962492912000037/type/journal_article): survey of numerical-asymptotic boundary integral methods.
- **Further reading:** [Kress, Linear Integral Equations (Springer, Applied Mathematical Sciences, 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4614-9593-2): graduate text on linear integral equations and their approximation.
- **Further reading:** [Atkinson, The Numerical Solution of Integral Equations of the Second Kind](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511626340): Cambridge University Press (1997), bibliographic record.

## Reference
### Overview
45Mxx collects results on how solutions of integral equations behave: their asymptotics, stability, periodicity and positivity. It is a subfield of [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations). ([MSC2020 45Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Mxx))

For Volterra equations of convolution type, $u+K\star u=f$ with $K\in L^1_{\rm loc}$ has the unique solution $u=f-R\star f$, where the resolvent $R$ solves $R+K\star R=R+R\star K=K$, and its large-time behaviour is read off from the Laplace transform of $K$. Qualitative questions therefore become questions about the resolvent: whether it is integrable, how fast it decays or grows, and what sign it has. ([Coti Zelati–Ertzbischoff–Gérard-Varet, App. C](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1)) Positive solutions of nonlinear Hammerstein systems, by contrast, are often obtained from fixed-point theorems in cones such as the Krasnosel'skiĭ–Precup theorem, which several authors have used for systems of boundary value problems. ([Rodríguez-López](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.10497v1))

### Scope
MSC2020 45Mxx has the codes **45M05** asymptotics of solutions to integral equations, **45M10** stability theory for integral equations, **45M15** periodic solutions of integral equations, **45M20** positive solutions of integral equations, and **45M99** none of the above, but in this section. MSC gives 45Mxx no cross-references. ([MSC2020 45Mxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Mxx))

Neighbouring codes in section 45 ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX)):
- [MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations) and [MSC 45Gxx - Nonlinear integral equations](node:MSC%2045Gxx%20-%20Nonlinear%20integral%20equations) are named by class of equation, whereas the 45M codes are named by property of solutions (asymptotics, stability, periodicity, positivity).
- [MSC 45Jxx - Integro-ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2045Jxx%20-%20Integro-ordinary%20differential%20equations) is the integro-differential counterpart, and [MSC 34Dxx - Stability theory for ordinary differential equations](node:MSC%2034Dxx%20-%20Stability%20theory%20for%20ordinary%20differential%20equations) is the ODE analogue of 45M10.
- [MSC 45Lxx - Theoretical approximation of solutions to integral equations](node:MSC%2045Lxx%20-%20Theoretical%20approximation%20of%20solutions%20to%20integral%20equations) covers approximation of solutions.

### Key concepts
- **Half-line Paley–Wiener theorem.** Let $K\in L^1(\mathbb R_+,M_n(\mathbb C))$ with $\det(I+\mathcal L[K](\lambda))\ne0$ for all $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. Then there is a unique resolvent $R\in L^1(\mathbb R_+)$, and for every $f\in L^1$ the equation $u+K\star u=f$ has a unique solution $u\in L^1$. ([Coti Zelati et al., Thm C.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1)) Gripenberg–Londen–Staffans Theorem 2.4.1 shows the resolvent is integrable iff the transform condition holds. By their Corollary 2.4.2, roots with positive real part make the resolvent grow exponentially. ([Abramovich–Pensky–Rozenholc, Remark 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1107.2766)) For $x=f+h*x$ with $0\le h\in L^1(\mathbb R_+)$, the resolvent $a=\sum_nh^{*n}$ is integrable iff $\int_0^\infty h<1$, and then $\hat a=\hat h/(1-\hat h)$. ([Zhang](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0812.0834))
- **Exponential stability.** If $\det(I+\mathcal L[K](\lambda))\ne0$ on $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge-\delta$ and $|K(t)|\le Ce^{-\gamma_Kt}$, then $e^{\gamma t}u\in L^1$ for every $0\le\gamma<\min(\gamma_K,\delta)$. This holds because $e^{\gamma t}R$ is the resolvent of $e^{\gamma t}K$. ([Coti Zelati et al., Thm C.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1))
- **Renewal asymptotics.** The renewal function solves $m(t)=F_S(t)+\int_0^tm(t-s)f_S(s)\,ds$, and $m(t)/t\to1/\mathbb E[S_1]$ when $0<\mathbb E[S_1]<\infty$. ([Renewal theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewal_theory)) Key renewal theorem: for an aperiodic (non-lattice) inter-renewal law with finite mean and $z$ directly Riemann integrable, $\int_0^tz(t-x)\,dm(x)\to(\mathbb E X_1)^{-1}\int_0^\infty z$. With period $d$, the limit along $t=nd$ is $(d/\mathbb E X_1)\sum_kz(kd)$. The theorem is equivalent to Blackwell's theorem. ([IISc lecture 11](https://parimal.ece.iisc.ac.in/courses/spqt/2026/lecture-11.pdf)) See [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes).
- **Complete positivity.** For $\lambda>0$ define $r_\lambda+\lambda r_\lambda*a=\lambda a$ and $s_\lambda+\lambda s_\lambda*a=1$. A kernel $a\in L^1(0,T)$ is completely positive if $r_\lambda,s_\lambda\ge0$ for every $\lambda>0$, a notion Clément and Nohel introduced to study positivity and asymptotics. A sufficient condition is that $a$ is nonnegative, nonincreasing and log-convex. ([Feng–Li, Def. 2.1, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.00972)) Clément–Nohel (1981, Thm 2.2): $a\not\equiv0$ is completely positive on $[0,T]$ iff there are $\alpha\ge0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing $c\in L^1(0,T)$ with $\alpha a+c*a=1$. Completely monotone kernels are log-convex, hence completely positive. ([Feng–Li, Lemma 2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.00972))
- **Positive solutions via cone compression–expansion.** Krasnosel'skiĭ's theorem: let $K$ be a cone in a normed space, $0<r<R$, and $T:\overline K_{r,R}\to K$ compact. Suppose either $T(u)\not\prec u$ for $\|u\|=r$ and $T(u)\not\succ u$ for $\|u\|=R$ (compression), or the reverse (expansion). Then $T$ has a fixed point with $r\le\|u\|\le R$. ([Rodríguez-López, Thm 2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.10497v1)) Apply this to Hammerstein systems $u_i(t)=\int_0^1k_i(t,s)g_i(s)f_i(u_1,u_2)(s)\,ds$ with continuous $k_i\ge0$, $k_i(t,s)\le\Phi_i(s)$ for all $t,s$, and $c_i\Phi_i(s)\le k_i(t,s)$ for $t\in[a,b]$, $c_i\in(0,1]$. It gives positive solutions in the cone $\{v\ge0:\min_{[a,b]}v\ge c_i\|v\|_\infty\}$. ([Rodríguez-López](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.10497v1))
- **Periodic solutions.** For a Volterra-type equation with infinite heredity, Islam obtains periodic solutions from the Banach contraction principle, from Krasnosel'skii's theorem, and from a Krasnosel'skii–Schaefer theorem. The last needs an a priori bound, which comes from Liapunov's direct method. ([Islam](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-mathematical-bulletin/article/three-fixed-point-theorems-periodic-solutions-of-a-volterra-type-integral-equation-with-infinite-heredity/08ECA470F4B01B69F0ADBE07C06C7569)) See [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem).
- **Algebraic decay for fractional kernels.** For the kernel $g_\alpha$, the solution of $s_\mu+\mu g_\alpha*s_\mu=1$ is $E_\alpha(-\mu t^\alpha)\ge1/(1+\mu\Gamma(1-\alpha)t^\alpha)$. Time-fractional diffusion on bounded domains satisfies $\|u(t)\|_{L^2}\le s_{\nu\lambda_1}(t)\|u_0\|_{L^2}$, optimally, so decay is like $t^{-\alpha}$ rather than exponential. ([Zacher](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503)) Compare the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation).
- **Heavy tails and long memory.** For $r'=ar+k*r$ with $k>0$ integrable, $\int_t^\infty k=L(t)t^{-\alpha}$ log-convex, $0<\alpha<1$ and $a+\int k=0$, one has $r(t)t^{1-\alpha}L(t)\to\sin(\alpha\pi)/\pi$. So $r$ is not integrable, and for $0<\alpha<\tfrac12$ the stochastic equation has a stationary solution whose autocovariance is not integrable (long memory). If instead $a+\int k<0$ and $k$ is regularly varying of index $-1-\alpha$, then $r/k\to(a+\int k)^{-2}$. ([Appleby–Krol](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.1304))
- **Finite-time blow-up.** For $x'=w*f(x)$, $x(0)>0$, with $w\ge0$ continuous, $w(0)>0$, and $f$ positive, continuous, asymptotically increasing and superlinear, solutions blow up in finite time iff $\int_\eta^\infty du/\sqrt{\int_0^uf}<\infty$. ([Appleby–Patterson, Thm 2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- **Lyapunov and frequency-domain methods.** Gripenberg, Londen and Staffans devote chapters to nonintegrable kernels with integrable resolvents (Ch. 6), unbounded and unstable solutions (Ch. 7), Lyapunov techniques and general asymptotics (Chs. 14–15), kernels of positive type (Ch. 16), and frequency-domain and combined Lyapunov–frequency-domain methods (Chs. 17–19). ([GLS, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book)) See [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems).

### History
Lotka's integral equation in demography and the renewal equation in actuarial science are early applications of convolution Volterra equations. ([Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)) Paley and Wiener proved the integrability criterion for resolvents of nonnegative kernels. ([Zhang](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0812.0834)) Clément and Nohel's papers in SIAM J. Math. Anal. (1979, 1981) introduced completely positive kernels to study positivity and asymptotic behaviour of nonlinear Volterra equations. ([Feng–Li](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.00972)) The monographs of Gripenberg, Londen and Staffans (CUP, 1990) and Burton (Academic Press 1983; 2nd ed. 2005) are standard references for stability and asymptotics. ([GLS, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book); [Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL5477665W))

### Open problems
- **Blow-up time.** Appleby and Patterson characterize finite-time blow-up but do not estimate the blow-up time, which "represents an interesting open problem for general nonlinear VIEs". They also state that full proofs of the growth rates of explosive solutions that Roberts and Olmstead obtained by conjecturing leading-order behaviour remain open. ([Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- **Asymptotics under strong forcing.** For $x'=h+w*f(x)$, Theorem 10 of Appleby–Patterson gives the growth rate when $\limsup F_U(H(t))/t\le\sqrt{2w(0)}$. Beyond this threshold they "conjecture that the perturbation likely dominates the dynamics". ([Appleby–Patterson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.07583))
- **Optimal decay rate for a Volterra equation from kinetic theory.** For the density of linearized active Brownian particles with rotational diffusion $\nu>0$, Coti Zelati, Ertzbischoff and Gérard-Varet prove that each Fourier mode $\rho_k$ decays like $e^{-\eta_0\nu t}$ with prefactor $C(1+\nu^{-5/4}|k|^{5/4})$ when $\nu|k|^{-1}\le\nu_0$ (Thm 1.4). They conjecture that a decay of the form $(1+\nu^{-3/4})e^{-\varepsilon\nu^{1/2}t}$ is optimal, a result that "seems out of reach within our approach". ([Coti Zelati et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.17649v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Renewal theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewal_theory): renewal equation and limit theorems.
- **Learn:** [IISc lecture 11: Key renewal theorem](https://parimal.ece.iisc.ac.in/courses/spqt/2026/lecture-11.pdf): Blackwell and key renewal theorems with direct Riemann integrability.
- **Primary:** [Appleby–Krol, Long memory in a linear stochastic Volterra differential equation](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1009.1304): exact resolvent asymptotics.
- **Primary:** [Feng–Li, On the completely positive kernels for nonuniform meshes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.00972): review of Clément–Nohel complete positivity and discrete analogues.
- **Primary:** [Zacher, Time fractional diffusion equations](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503): survey including optimal decay rates.
- **Further reading:** [Gripenberg, Londen, Staffans, Volterra Integral and Functional Equations (CUP, 1990)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511662805/type/book): the standard monograph on stability and asymptotics.
- **Further reading:** [Burton, Volterra Integral and Differential Equations (2nd ed., Elsevier 2005)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL5477665W): monograph on Volterra integral and integro-differential equations.
references.MSC 45Nxx - Abstract integral equations,:
## Reference
### Overview
45Nxx is the subfield of [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations) for integral equations whose unknown takes values in a Banach or Hilbert space, or whose kernel is an operator. Its MSC2020 heading lists the single substantive code 45N05. ([MSC2020 45Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Nxx&btn=Current))

The central model is the abstract Volterra equation
$$u(t)=f(t)+\int_0^t a(t-\tau)\,Au(\tau)\,d\tau,\qquad t\ge0,$$
with a scalar kernel $a\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R_+)$ and a closed, densely defined, unbounded operator $A$ on a separable Hilbert space. ([Karczewska, arXiv 1212.1257](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1212.1257)) With $a\equiv1$ this is the integrated form $u(t)=x+A\int_0^tu(s)\,ds$ that defines mild solutions of the abstract Cauchy problem $u'=Au$, $u(0)=x$, so the theory generalises [$C_0$-semigroup theory](node:MSC%2047Dxx%20-%20Groups%20and%20semigroups%20of%20linear%20operators,%20their%20generalizations%20and%20applications). ([C0-semigroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C0-semigroup)) Prüss's definition of well-posedness via resolvents is described as a direct extension of well-posedness of Cauchy problems and of scalar Volterra equations. ([Karczewska, arXiv math/0509012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0509012)) The standard monograph is Prüss, *Evolutionary Integral Equations and Applications* (Birkhäuser, 1993). ([Crossref: Prüss 1993](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-8570-6))

### Scope
MSC2020 45Nxx has 45N05 (abstract integral equations, integral equations in abstract spaces) and 45N99 (none of the above, but in this section). ([MSC2020 45Nxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Nxx&btn=Current))

How it differs from its neighbours: ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))
- [MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations) covers scalar and finite-dimensional Volterra equations; 45N is used when the state space is infinite-dimensional.
- [MSC 45Kxx - Integro-partial differential equations](node:MSC%2045Kxx%20-%20Integro-partial%20differential%20equations) covers concrete PDEs with memory; abstract Volterra theory is the operator framework used to solve them.
- [MSC 45Pxx - Integral operators](node:MSC%2045Pxx%20-%20Integral%20operators) studies the integral operators themselves rather than equations in abstract spaces.
- [MSC 45Rxx - Random integral equations](node:MSC%2045Rxx%20-%20Random%20integral%20equations) (see also 60H20) takes the stochastic versions, such as Volterra equations driven by a Wiener process in Hilbert space.

### Key concepts
- **Resolvent family.** A family $(S(t))_{t\ge0}$ of bounded operators is a resolvent for the abstract Volterra equation if (i) $S(\cdot)$ is strongly continuous and $S(0)=I$; (ii) $S(t)D(A)\subset D(A)$ and $AS(t)x=S(t)Ax$ for $x\in D(A)$; (iii) $S(t)x=x+\int_0^ta(t-\tau)AS(\tau)x\,d\tau$ for $x\in D(A)$. ([Karczewska, arXiv 1212.1257](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1212.1257)) In Prüss's sense, well-posedness gives existence and uniqueness of the resolvent and of mild solutions, and pseudo-resolvents are always unique. ([Karczewska, arXiv math/0509012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0509012))
- **Generation theorem for completely positive kernels.** A kernel $a\in L^1(0,T)$ is completely positive if for every $\mu\ge0$ the solutions of $s+\mu\,a*s=1$ and $r+\mu\,a*r=a$ are nonnegative. If $A$ generates a $C_0$-semigroup and $a$ is completely positive, then $(A,a)$ admits an exponentially bounded resolvent $S(t)$, and it is the strong limit, uniformly on compacts, of the resolvents for the Yosida approximations $A_n=nAR(n,A)$ (Karczewska–Lizama). ([Karczewska, arXiv 1212.1257](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1212.1257))
- **Difference from semigroups.** Unlike semigroups, resolvents need not be exponentially bounded even when the kernel is in $L^1(\mathbb R_+)$; when well-posedness fails one is led to distribution resolvents (Da Prato–Iannelli). ([Karczewska, arXiv math/0509012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0509012))
- **Equations of nonscalar type.** Operator-valued kernels $A(t)\in B(G,H)$, where $G\hookrightarrow H$, replace $a(t)A$; Prüss's framework of pseudo-resolvents covers these. ([Karczewska, arXiv math/0509012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0509012))
- **Parabolic Volterra equations and time-fractional evolution.** Convolving $\partial_t^\alpha(u-u_0)+Au=f$ with $g_\alpha(t)=t^{\alpha-1}/\Gamma(\alpha)$ gives the abstract Volterra equation $u+g_\alpha*Au=u_0+g_\alpha*f$. For $A=-\Delta$ on $L_q(\mathbb R^d)$, $A$ is sectorial with angle $0$ and $g_\alpha$ is sectorial with angle $\alpha\pi/2$; the angles sum to less than $\pi$, so the equation is parabolic and has a resolvent. ([Zacher, arXiv 1906.08503](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503)) Related: [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation), [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces).
- **Maximal $L_p$-regularity.** For $p,q\in(1,\infty)$ and $\alpha\in(1/p,1)$, the full-space problem $\partial_t^\alpha(u-u_0)-\Delta u=f$ has a unique solution in $H^\alpha_p(J;L_q)\cap L_p(J;H^2_q)$ if and only if $f\in L_p(J;L_q)$ and $u_0\in B^{2-2/(p\alpha)}_{qp}$. ([Zacher, arXiv 1906.08503](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503)) Maximal $L^p$-regularity extrapolates to weighted rearrangement-invariant Banach function spaces, with applications to first-order, second-order, and fractional-order Cauchy problems. ([Chill–Krol, arXiv 1410.3457](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3457))
- **Long-time behaviour.** With $s_\mu=E_\alpha(-\mu t^\alpha)$, the bound $1/(1+\mu\Gamma(1-\alpha)t^\alpha)\le s_\mu(t)$ shows algebraic rather than exponential decay of solutions on bounded domains. ([Zacher, arXiv 1906.08503](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503))

The operator background is in [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces), and [MSC 47 - Operator theory](node:MSC%2047%20-%20Operator%20theory): $A$ is a closed, densely defined, unbounded operator and the solution lives in a separable Hilbert space. ([Karczewska, arXiv 1212.1257](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1212.1257))

### History
Prüss's 1993 monograph (Birkhäuser, Monographs in Mathematics) treats resolvents of evolutionary integral equations, and later work on stochastic Volterra equations in Hilbert space uses its definitions of well-posedness and resolvents. ([Crossref: Prüss 1993](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-8570-6); [Karczewska, arXiv math/0509012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0509012)) Chill and Krol extended maximal $L^p$-regularity, including for fractional-order Cauchy problems, to weighted rearrangement-invariant spaces by extrapolation. ([Chill–Krol, arXiv 1410.3457](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3457))

### Open problems
- **Maximal regularity in general Banach spaces.** For time-fractional evolution equations of order $\alpha\in(0,1)$ in a Banach space with $A$ closed, densely defined, and satisfying a sectorial resolvent bound of order $1/|\lambda|$, maximal regularity for $q=2$ in Hilbert space is known, but whether a source $F\in L^q(0,T;X)$ suffices for $q\ne2$ in a general Banach space is stated as unknown; extension of the Prüss–Simonett approach to small $\alpha$ is also open. ([Floridia–Gölgeleyen–Yamamoto, arXiv 2608.08796](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.08796))
- **Harnack inequality in one space dimension.** For weak solutions of time-fractional diffusion equations, the full Harnack inequality fails in general for $d\ge2$; "the one-dimensional case is still an open problem," conjectured to hold. ([Zacher, arXiv 1906.08503](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.08503))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [C0-semigroup (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C0-semigroup): abstract Cauchy problem and mild solutions, the $a\equiv1$ case.
- **Learn:** [Zacher, Time fractional diffusion equations (arXiv 1906.08503)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08503): survey of the abstract Volterra approach, $L_p$ theory, and decay.
- **Primary:** [Prüss, Evolutionary Integral Equations and Applications (Birkhäuser 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-0348-8570-6): the standard monograph on resolvents and abstract Volterra equations.
- **Primary:** [Karczewska, Stochastic Volterra equations of nonscalar type in Hilbert space (arXiv math/0509012)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0509012): pseudo-resolvents and well-posedness in Prüss's sense.
- **Further reading:** [Gripenberg, Londen, Staffans, Volterra Integral and Functional Equations (CUP 1990)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511662805): text on Volterra equations for $n$-dimensional systems, written to ease generalization to infinite-dimensional spaces.
references.MSC 45Pxx - Integral operators:
## Reference
### Overview
An integral operator acts by $(Tf)(x)=\int K(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ and is determined by its kernel $K$, a function of two variables. The basic questions of the area translate properties of the kernel into properties of the operator: square-integrable kernels give Hilbert–Schmidt, hence compact, operators on $L^2$, and Hermitian kernels give self-adjoint operators to which the spectral theorem applies. ([Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator)) Continuous positive-definite kernels on a compact interval give trace-class operators with uniformly convergent eigenfunction expansions ([Mercer's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem)), and Besov smoothness of the kernel controls how fast the singular numbers decay; there is, however, no sufficiently general estimate of the operator norm in terms of the kernel. ([McDonald–Scheckter–Sukochev, arXiv 2104.06567](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.06567))

If the kernel may be a distribution, the class becomes very large: every continuous linear map $\mathcal D(Y)\to\mathcal D'(X)$ has a unique distributional kernel (Schwartz). ([Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem)) Integral operators are the analytic substrate of [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations): one principal result of Fredholm theory is that the kernel yields a compact operator, whose spectrum is a discrete set of eigenvalues tending to $0$. ([Fredholm integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_integral_equation))

### Scope
MSC2020 45Pxx has two codes: 45P05 "Integral operators [See also 47B38, 47G10]" and 45P99 "None of the above, but in this section"; the classification lists no further subtopics. ([MSC2020 45Pxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Pxx&btn=Current))

Neighbouring codes, one line each:
- [47B](node:MSC%2047Bxx%20-%20Special%20classes%20of%20linear%20operators): 47B38 "Linear operators on function spaces (general)", with compactness (47B07), Schatten–von Neumann and nuclear classes (47B10) and positive operators (47B65) as separate codes. ([MSC2020 47Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Bxx&btn=Current))
- [47G](node:MSC%2047Gxx%20-%20Integral,%20integro-differential,%20and%20pseudodifferential%20operators): 47G10 "Integral operators [See also 45P05]" is the operator-theory twin of 45P05, beside pseudodifferential (47G30) and potential (47G40) operators. ([MSC2020 47Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=47Gxx&btn=Current))
- [42B](node:MSC%2042Bxx%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20in%20several%20variables): Calderón–Zygmund theory is 42B20 "Singular and oscillatory integrals". ([MSC2020 42Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=42Bxx&btn=Current))
- The equations sit in sibling sections such as [45B](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations), [45C](node:MSC%2045Cxx%20-%20Eigenvalue%20problems%20for%20integral%20equations), [45D](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations) and [45E](node:MSC%2045Exx%20-%20Singular%20integral%20equations). ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Hilbert–Schmidt kernels.** If $k\in L^2(\Omega\times\Omega)$, then $T$ is a Hilbert–Schmidt operator on $L^2(\Omega)$ with $\|T\|_{HS}=\|k\|_{L^2}$, hence bounded and compact; the same holds on a locally compact [Hausdorff space](node:Hausdorff%20Space) with a positive Borel measure and separable $L^2$, and $k(x,y)=\overline{k(y,x)}$ makes $T$ self-adjoint. ([Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator)) See [Compact Integral Operators](node:Compact%20Integral%20Operators), [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory).
- **Fredholm alternative.** For $K$ square integrable on $[a,b]^2$ and $\lambda\ne0$, either $\lambda\varphi-\int_a^bK(\cdot,y)\varphi(y)\,dy=0$ has a nontrivial solution or $\lambda\varphi-\int_a^bK(\cdot,y)\varphi(y)\,dy=f$ is solvable for every $f$; the dichotomy holds for every compact operator on a Banach space. ([Fredholm alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_alternative)) See [Fredholm Alternative](node:Fredholm%20Alternative).
- **Volterra operators.** $(Vf)(t)=\int_0^tf$ on $L^2[0,1]$ is Hilbert–Schmidt with $\|V\|_{HS}^2=1/2$ and operator norm $2/\pi$; it has no eigenvalues, so its spectrum is $\{0\}$: it is quasinilpotent but not nilpotent. ([Volterra operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_operator)) See [Volterra Integral Equations](node:Volterra%20Integral%20Equations).
- **Boundedness on $L^p$: Schur test, Young-type bounds, Dunford–Pettis.** If $K\ge0$ and $p,q>0$, $\alpha,\beta>0$ satisfy $\int K(x,y)q(y)\,dy\le\alpha p(x)$ and $\int p(x)K(x,y)\,dx\le\beta q(y)$ a.e., then $\|T\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\sqrt{\alpha\beta}$. For $1\le p\le q\le\infty$ and $1/r=1-(1/p-1/q)$, if $\sup_x\|K(x,\cdot)\|_r+\sup_y\|K(\cdot,y)\|_r\le C$ then $\|T\|_{L^p\to L^q}\le C$. ([Schur test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_test)) **Dunford–Pettis:** if $\Omega$ is $\sigma$-finite with $L^1(\Omega)$ separable, every bounded $T:L^1(\Omega)\to L^\infty(\Omega)$ is an integral operator with kernel $K\in L^\infty(\Omega\times\Omega)$ and $\|T\|=\|K\|_\infty$, and conversely. ([Arhancet, arXiv 2203.06603, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.06603)) See [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces).
- **Mercer's theorem.** If $K$ is continuous, symmetric and positive-definite on $[a,b]^2$, then $L^2[a,b]$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions $e_j$ of $T_K$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$, those with $\lambda_j\ne0$ are continuous, and $K(s,t)=\sum_j\lambda_je_j(s)e_j(t)$ absolutely and uniformly; so $T_K$ is trace class with $\operatorname{tr}T_K=\int_a^bK(t,t)\,dt$. The interval may be replaced by a compact Hausdorff space with a finite Borel measure of full support; for $L^2$ kernels on $\sigma$-finite spaces the expansion holds only in $L^2$. ([Mercer's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem))
- **Singular numbers (Birman–Solomyak).** For a bounded open interval $I$, $0<p\le2$, $1/p=\alpha+1/2$ and $q\ge\max\{2,1/\alpha\}$, a kernel in the vector-valued Besov class $B^\alpha_{q,q}(I,L^2(I))$ gives an operator in the weak Schatten class $\mathcal L_{p,\infty}$; this is a special case of Birman and Solomyak (1977). McDonald, Scheckter and Sukochev strengthen it to the Schatten class $\mathcal L_p$ under a homogeneous Besov condition. ([McDonald–Scheckter–Sukochev, Thms 1.1, 1.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.06567))
- **Fredholm determinant and Lidskii's theorem.** Generalizing the finite-dimensional [Determinant](node:Determinant), for trace-class $A$, $\det(I+A)=\sum_{k\ge0}\operatorname{Tr}\Lambda^k(A)$, convergent since $\|\Lambda^kA\|_1\le\|A\|_1^k/k!$, and $z\mapsto\det(I+zA)$ is entire with $|\det(I+zA)|\le e^{|z|\|A\|_1}$. For an integral operator, $\det(I-\lambda T)=\exp\big(-\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Tr}(T^n)\lambda^n/n\big)$ with $\operatorname{Tr}T=\int K(x,x)\,dx$. ([Fredholm determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_determinant)) **Lidskii's theorem:** the trace of a trace-class operator on a separable Hilbert space equals the absolutely convergent sum of its eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity, and $\det(I+A)=\prod_n(1+\lambda_n(A))$, nonzero iff $I+A$ is invertible. ([Trace class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_class)) See [Fredholm Determinants](node:Fredholm%20Determinants).
- **Positive operators: Krein–Rutman, de Pagter, Perron–Jentzsch.** Krein–Rutman (1948): if $K$ is a total cone in a Banach space and $T$ is compact with $TK\subset K$ and $r(T)>0$, then $r(T)$ is an eigenvalue with an eigenvector in $K\setminus\{0\}$. ([Krein–Rutman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krein%E2%80%93Rutman_theorem)) **De Pagter's theorem** (Math. Z. 192, 1986): on a real Banach lattice of dimension $>1$, a positive compact operator that is ideal irreducible (no nontrivial closed ideal is invariant) has $r(T)>0$, so the spectral-radius hypothesis can be dropped in that setting. ([Gao, arXiv 1208.3495](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.3495)) For positive power-compact $T$ on $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$, with $\rho(T)>0$, $\rho(T)$ is an eigenvalue with nonnegative right and left eigenfunctions; if $T$ is irreducible, Perron–Jentzsch makes it simple with positive eigenfunctions. ([Delmas–Lefki–Zitt, arXiv 2310.15616](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2310.15616))
- **Calderón–Zygmund kernels (boundary with 42B20).** If $K$ is a kernel on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ whose principal-value convolution is bounded on $L^2$ and $\sup_{y\ne0}\int_{|x|\ge2|y|}|K(x-y)-K(x)|\,dx<\infty$ (Hörmander's condition), then the operator is bounded on $L^p$ for $1<p<\infty$ and maps $L^1$ to weak $L^1$; this gives another proof that Riesz transforms and the Beurling transform are $L^p$-bounded. ([Singular integral operators of convolution type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_integral_operators_of_convolution_type)) See [Singular Integral Operators](node:Singular%20Integral%20Operators).
- **Schwartz kernel theorem.** For open $X,Y\subset\mathbb R^n$, every continuous linear $K:\mathcal D(Y)\to\mathcal D'(X)$ is given by a unique $k\in\mathcal D'(X\times Y)$. ([Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem)) See [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29).

### History
Fredholm used his determinant in 1903 to solve an integral equation, and Hilbert's six papers of 1904–1910 helped found the theory of compact operators. ([Fredholm determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredholm_determinant)) Mercer's expansion appeared in 1909. ([Mercer's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer%27s_theorem)) Krein and Rutman proved their cone theorem in 1948. ([Krein–Rutman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krein%E2%80%93Rutman_theorem)) Schwartz published the kernel theorem in 1952, and Grothendieck developed nuclear spaces while studying it (1955). ([Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem)) The monograph of Krasnosel'skii, Zabreiko, Pustylnik and Sobolevskii appeared in 1976 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-010-1542-4)) and Halmos and Sunder's *Bounded Integral Operators on $L^2$ Spaces* in 1978. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-67016-9))

### Open problems
- **Admissible sets under restriction of positive operators.** For positive power-compact $T$ on $L^p(\Omega,\mu)$ with $\rho(T)>0$, a set is admissible if it lies in the $\sigma$-field generated by $T$-invariant sets; let $T'$ be the restriction to $\Omega'$. Delmas, Lefki and Zitt conjecture that if $\Omega'$ is admissible, then $A\subset\Omega'$ is $T'$-admissible iff it is $T$-admissible, which would imply Point 2 of their Proposition 3.32 (atoms of $T'$ are exactly the atoms of $T$ inside $\Omega'$). ([Delmas–Lefki–Zitt, Remark 3.33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2310.15616))

- **Kernel smoothness versus ill-posedness.** Gerth and Hofmann pose as open questions under which conditions an equation $Ax=y$ with a Hilbert–Schmidt operator $A$ from $L^2(0,1)$ into a Hilbert space, with non-closed range, can be severely (exponentially) ill-posed when the kernel of $A^*A$ has limited smoothness, i.e. is not infinitely continuously differentiable on the closed unit square (Open Question 3), and, for the $n\times n$ segments $\mathbb H_n=(1/(i+j-1))_{i,j\le n}$ of the infinite Hilbert matrix $\mathbb H$, whether the singular values satisfy $\sigma_i(\mathbb H_n)\to\pi$ for each fixed $i$ and how $\|\mathbb H-\mathbb H_n\|_{\ell^2\to\ell^2}$ behaves as a function of $n$ (Open Questions 5–6). ([Gerth–Hofmann, arXiv 2206.04127](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2206.04127))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%E2%80%93Schmidt_integral_operator): $L^2$ kernels, compactness, self-adjointness.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.102 Introduction to Functional Analysis (OCW)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/): $L^p$ and Hilbert spaces, compact and self-adjoint operators, spectral theorem.
- **Primary:** [McDonald–Scheckter–Sukochev, Estimates for Schur multipliers and double operator integrals (arXiv 2104.06567)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.06567): Birman–Solomyak Schatten estimates; [Delmas–Lefki–Zitt, Atoms and associated spectral properties for positive operators on $L^p$ (arXiv 2310.15616)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2310.15616): Krein–Rutman and Perron–Jentzsch theory with a conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Krasnosel'skii, Zabreiko, Pustylnik, Sobolevskii, *Integral Operators in Spaces of Summable Functions* (Springer, 1976)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-010-1542-4); [Halmos–Sunder, *Bounded Integral Operators on $L^2$ Spaces* (Springer, 1978)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-67016-9); [Kress, *Linear Integral Equations* (Springer, 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4614-9593-2).
