## Reference
### Overview
45Qxx, "Inverse problems for integral equations", is a subfield of [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations). ([MSC2020 45Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Qxx&btn=Current)) In the most common setting the operator is known and one solves a first-kind equation $Kx=y$ from noisy data $y^\delta$ with $\|y-y^\delta\|\le\delta$. When $K$ is compact with infinite-dimensional range, the pseudoinverse $K^\dagger$ is unbounded, so the problem violates Hadamard's requirement of continuous dependence on the data (see [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems)) and must be regularized. ([Clason, arXiv 2001.00617](https://arxiv.org/html/2001.00617)) A second setting is causal: a first-kind Volterra equation $\int_0^tk(t,s)u(s)\,ds=f(t)$ with a non-degenerate continuous kernel has non-closed range in $L^2(0,T)$, and classical regularization destroys its non-anticipatory structure. ([Lamm, survey of regularization for first-kind Volterra equations](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/lamm/Preprints/Mt_Holyoke_Survey/paper.pdf)) A third recovers the kernel itself, for example a memory kernel or a potential from spectral or boundary data. ([Avdonin–Ivanov–Wang, arXiv 1612.02129](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.02129); [Kravchenko–Torba, arXiv 2010.15275](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2010.15275))

The analytical core is spectral regularization theory for compact operators on [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): singular systems, filter functions, parameter-choice rules, and convergence rates under source conditions. Engl, Hanke and Neubauer's monograph is the standard source for this theory, which Clason's notes specialize to compact operators. ([Clason, arXiv 2001.00617](https://arxiv.org/html/2001.00617); [Crossref: Engl–Hanke–Neubauer 1996](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Engl+Hanke+Neubauer+Regularization+of+Inverse+Problems&rows=3)) See also [Regularization](node:Regularization).

### Scope
MSC2020 45Qxx has 45Q05 "Inverse problems for integral equations" and 45Q99 "None of the above, but in this section", with no cross-references. ([MSC2020 45Qxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Qxx&btn=Current))

How it differs from its neighbours:
- Numerical inversion has its own codes in [MSC 65Rxx - Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms](node:MSC%2065Rxx%20-%20Numerical%20methods%20for%20integral%20equations,%20integral%20transforms): 65R30 "Numerical methods for ill-posed problems for integral equations" and 65R32 "Numerical methods for inverse problems for integral equations". ([MSC2020 65Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=65Rxx&btn=Current))
- Inverse problems for PDEs are 35R30 and integro-partial differential equations 35R09 (see also 45K05), in [MSC 35Rxx - Miscellaneous topics in partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035Rxx%20-%20Miscellaneous%20topics%20in%20partial%20differential%20equations); recovering memory kernels in evolution equations sits on this boundary. ([MSC2020 35Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=35Rxx&btn=Current))
- The direct theory of the same equations is in sibling sections such as [MSC 45Bxx - Fredholm integral equations](node:MSC%2045Bxx%20-%20Fredholm%20integral%20equations) and [MSC 45Dxx - Volterra integral equations](node:MSC%2045Dxx%20-%20Volterra%20integral%20equations), and the operators whose singular values govern ill-posedness are in [MSC 45Pxx - Integral operators](node:MSC%2045Pxx%20-%20Integral%20operators). ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX&btn=Current))

### Key concepts
- **Picard criterion and degree of ill-posedness.** Let $K$ be compact with singular system $(\sigma_n,u_n,v_n)$ and $y\in\overline{R(K)}$. Then $y\in R(K)$ if and only if $\sum_n\sigma_n^{-2}|(y,u_n)|^2<\infty$, and in that case $K^\dagger y=\sum_n\sigma_n^{-1}(y,u_n)v_n$. For the integration operator $(Kx)(t)=\int_0^tx(s)\,ds$ on $L^2(0,1)$ the singular values are $\sigma_n=2/((2n-1)\pi)$, with $v_n(t)=\sqrt2\cos((n-\tfrac12)\pi t)$ and $u_n(t)=\sqrt2\sin((n-\tfrac12)\pi t)$; since $\sigma_n=O(1/n)$, differentiation, which is the inverse of this integral operator, is moderately ill-posed. ([Clason, arXiv 2001.00617](https://arxiv.org/html/2001.00617)) The sideways heat equation is a first-kind Volterra convolution equation with kernel $\kappa(t)=\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}t^{-3/2}e^{-1/(4t)}$ and is severely ill-posed. ([Lamm survey](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/lamm/Preprints/Mt_Holyoke_Survey/paper.pdf)) See [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory), [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation).
- **Tikhonov regularization and saturation.** Tikhonov–Phillips regularization minimizes $\|Kx-y^\delta\|^2+\|\Gamma x\|^2$, giving $x=(K^*K+\Gamma^*\Gamma)^{-1}K^*y^\delta$; for $\Gamma=\alpha I$ the $i$-th singular component is multiplied by $\sigma_i/(\sigma_i^2+\alpha^2)$ instead of $1/\sigma_i$. ([Tikhonov regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikhonov_regularization)) Pang and Wang prove the following for their mixed (fractional weighted) Tikhonov method, which reduces to classical Tikhonov regularization in the case $l=0$, $r=1$: for compact $K$ with infinite-dimensional range and exact solution in the source set $X_{\sigma,E}=\{(K^*K)^{\sigma/2}z:\|z\|\le E\}$, $0<\sigma\le2$, the a priori choice $\alpha=(\delta/E)^{2/(\sigma+1)}$ gives the best rate; for $\sigma=2$ this is $O(\delta^{2/3})$ with $\alpha\propto\delta^{2/3}$. This is the saturation order: if the worst-case error over $\{\|P(y-y^\delta)\|\le\delta\}$ is $o(\delta^{2/3})$, then $x=0$. Their new $m$-fold iterated method reaches $O(\delta^{2m/(2m+1)})$ for $\sigma=2m$. ([Pang–Wang, arXiv 2504.00209](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.00209v2))
- **Landweber iteration.** $x_{k+1}=x_k-\omega K^*(Kx_k-y^\delta)$ with $0<\omega<2/\sigma_1^2$ is gradient descent on $\tfrac12\|Kx-y^\delta\|^2$. For ill-posed problems the iterates semi-converge, so the iteration is stopped early, when the residual reaches the noise level; $1/k$ plays the role of the regularization parameter. Landweber proposed it in 1951 for first-kind Fredholm integral equations. ([Landweber iteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landweber_iteration)) See [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent).
- **Morozov discrepancy principle and Bakushinskii's veto.** The discrepancy principle chooses $\alpha$ as large as possible with $\|KR_\alpha y^\delta-y^\delta\|\le\tau\delta$ for a fixed $\tau>1$; such a choice exists along any strictly decreasing null sequence of parameters (Theorem 4.7). Bakushinskii's veto (Theorem 4.8): if $\{R_\alpha\}$ is a regularization of $K^\dagger$ and some heuristic rule, depending only on $y^\delta$ and not on $\delta$, makes it a convergent regularization method, then $K^\dagger$ is continuous. So noise-level-free parameter choices cannot converge in the worst case for ill-posed problems. ([Clason, arXiv 2001.00617](https://arxiv.org/html/2001.00617))
- **Lavrent'ev regularization of first-kind Volterra equations.** Lavrent'ev's classical method replaces $Au=f^\delta$ by the well-posed second-kind Volterra equation $\alpha u+Au=f^\delta$. For a one-smoothing problem (one differentiation in $t$ turns it into a second-kind equation), $|f-f^\delta|<\delta$ on $[0,T]$ and $\alpha(\delta)$ with $\delta/\alpha(\delta)\to0$, the regularized solutions converge to $\bar u$ uniformly on $[0,T]$ if $\bar u(0)=0$, and uniformly on $[a,T]$ for each $a>0$ otherwise. For the $m$-times iterated method with $m\ge2$ and an accretive Volterra operator, a discrepancy principle $b_0\delta\le\|Au^\delta_\alpha-f^\delta\|\le b_1\delta$ ($b_1\ge b_0>1$) yields convergence. ([Lamm survey](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/lamm/Preprints/Mt_Holyoke_Survey/paper.pdf)) Hofmann, Kaltenbacher and Resmerita prove convergence rates for Lavrent'ev's method for monotone, possibly nonlinear, operators in Hilbert space under variational source conditions. ([Hofmann–Kaltenbacher–Resmerita, arXiv 1506.01803](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.01803))
- **Abel equations.** If $K(t,t)\ne0$, differentiating a first-kind Volterra equation and dividing by $K(t,t)$ gives a second-kind equation; a first-kind equation with kernel $(t^2-s^2)^{-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, reduces to the classical Abel integral equation. ([Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation)) The Abel transform $F(y)=2\int_y^\infty f(r)\,r\,(r^2-y^2)^{-1/2}\,dr$ is inverted, when $f$ decays faster than $1/r$, by $f(r)=-\pi^{-1}\int_r^\infty F'(y)(y^2-r^2)^{-1/2}\,dy$; this recovers axially symmetric emission and absorption profiles, and the data enter through their derivative. ([Abel transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_transform))
- **Gel'fand–Levitan equation for inverse spectral problems.** For $-y''+q(x)y=\rho^2y$ on $(0,\pi)$ with $y'(0)-hy(0)=0$, $y'(\pi)+Hy(\pi)=0$ and real $q\in L_2(0,\pi)$, the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=\rho_n^2$ and norming constants $\alpha_n$ determine
$$F(x,t)=\sum_{n\ge0}\Big(\frac{\cos\rho_nx\cos\rho_nt}{\alpha_n}-\frac{\cos nx\cos nt}{\alpha_n^0}\Big),$$
and the transmutation kernel $G$ in $\varphi(\rho,x)=\cos\rho x+\int_0^xG(x,t)\cos\rho t\,dt$ solves the integral equation $G(x,t)+F(x,t)+\int_0^xF(t,s)G(x,s)\,ds=0$ for $0<t<x<\pi$; then $G(x,x)=h+\tfrac12\int_0^xq$ recovers $q$. ([Kravchenko–Torba, arXiv 2010.15275](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2010.15275)) See [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Kernel identification.** For a one-dimensional Gurtin–Pipkin integro-differential equation, the memory kernel is recovered from the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map by an explicit formula for observations on $t>0$; on a finite time interval a uniqueness theorem analogous to the local Borg–Marchenko theorem holds. ([Avdonin–Ivanov–Wang, arXiv 1612.02129](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.02129))

### History
Tikhonov regularization was invented independently in several contexts; it became widely known through Tikhonov's work on integral equations, with contributions by Phillips, and Hoerl's finite-dimensional version became ridge regression through Hoerl and Kennard's 1970 papers. ([Tikhonov regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikhonov_regularization)) Landweber's iteration dates from 1951. ([Landweber iteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landweber_iteration)) The singular-perturbation (Lavrent'ev) approach to first-kind Volterra equations is attributed to Sergeev and Denisov in the early 1970s, following Lavrent'ev. ([Lamm survey](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/lamm/Preprints/Mt_Holyoke_Survey/paper.pdf)) Engl, Hanke and Neubauer's *Regularization of Inverse Problems* appeared in 1996 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Engl+Hanke+Neubauer+Regularization+of+Inverse+Problems&rows=3)). Kirsch's *An Introduction to the Mathematical Theory of Inverse Problems* first appeared in 1996 in Springer's Applied Mathematical Sciences ([Crossref: Kirsch 1996](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-5338-9)), with a later edition in 2011 ([Crossref: Kirsch 2011](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-8474-6)).

### Open problems
None found that a current source states as open. Searches tried: "open problem inverse problem kernel identification integral equation stability memory kernel", "remains open / open question Abel equation Volterra first kind regularization", and "discrepancy principle local regularization Volterra first kind Lamm". Lamm's survey (whose references stop in the late 1990s) states as open problems the development of a discrepancy principle for the local-regularization parameter and the analysis of standard discretization methods for $\nu$-smoothing Volterra problems with $\nu$ bigger than one or two; the last search returned later work on discrepancy principles for local regularization, and no recent source was found confirming that either is still open. Kravchenko and Torba note that the integrated Gel'fand–Levitan equation is no longer a Fredholm equation of the second kind, so it is unclear whether stability results can be obtained for numerical schemes based on it; this concerns one formulation rather than a posed problem. ([Lamm survey](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/lamm/Preprints/Mt_Holyoke_Survey/paper.pdf); [Kravchenko–Torba, arXiv 2010.15275](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2010.15275))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Tikhonov regularization (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikhonov_regularization): formula, SVD filters, parameter choice, history.
- **Learn:** [Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, lecture notes (arXiv 2001.00617)](https://arxiv.org/html/2001.00617): ill-posedness, Picard criterion, spectral regularization, parameter choice and Bakushinskii's veto.
- **Primary:** [Lamm, A survey of regularization methods for first-kind Volterra equations](https://users.math.msu.edu/users/lamm/Preprints/Mt_Holyoke_Survey/paper.pdf): Lavrent'ev, local and iterative regularization that keeps the causal structure.
- **Primary:** [Kravchenko, Torba, A direct method for solving inverse Sturm–Liouville problems (arXiv 2010.15275)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2010.15275): Gel'fand–Levitan equation and its numerical solution.
- **Further reading:** [Engl, Hanke, Neubauer, Regularization of Inverse Problems (Springer 1996)](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Engl+Hanke+Neubauer+Regularization+of+Inverse+Problems&rows=3); [Kirsch, An Introduction to the Mathematical Theory of Inverse Problems (Springer, 1996; 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-8474-6).
references.MSC 45Rxx - Random integral equations:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 45Rxx collects integral equations whose kernel, forcing term or solution is random, under the single code 45R05 (Random integral equations). MSC2020 cross-references it to 60H20, Stochastic integral equations. ([MSC2020 45Rxx, AMS](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Rxx); [MSC2020 60Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=60Hxx)) It is the probabilistic branch of [MSC 45 - Integral equations](node:MSC%2045%20-%20Integral%20equations).

Two kinds of problem live here. In *random operator equations* the operator depends on a sample point $\omega$, and one seeks a measurable solution $\omega\mapsto x(\omega)$; this is the setting of random fixed point theory. ([Patriche, arXiv:1507.02950](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.02950)) In *stochastic Volterra equations* the integral includes an Itô integral against Brownian motion, $X_t=x+\int_0^tK(t,s)b(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^tK(t,s)\sigma(s,X_s)\,dB_s$, and the kernel $K$ may be singular. ([Coutin–Decreusefond, arXiv:1703.08395](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.08395))

Stochastic Volterra convolution equations arise in [turbulence](node:Turbulence), energy markets and rough volatility modelling, and are linked to fractional Brownian motion and to scaling limits of Hawkes processes; the rough Bergomi model is one model built on them. ([Wikipedia: Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation); [Abi Jaber et al., arXiv:1909.01166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.01166))

### Scope
- **45R05 Random integral equations** (see also 60H20); **45R99** none of the above in this section. ([MSC2020 45Rxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45Rxx))
- Neighbour **60H20 Stochastic integral equations** and **60H25 Random operators and equations** sit in [MSC 60Hxx - Stochastic analysis](node:MSC%2060Hxx%20-%20Stochastic%20analysis); 60H20 is the code that 45R05 explicitly cross-references. ([MSC2020 60Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=60Hxx))
- Neighbour **60H15/60H17** (stochastic and singular stochastic PDEs) is related because existence results for stochastic Volterra equations in Banach spaces apply directly to semilinear SPDEs. ([MSC2020 60Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=60Hxx); [Zhang, arXiv:0812.0834](https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.0834))
- Neighbour **45Dxx (Volterra)** and **45Bxx (Fredholm)** hold the deterministic theory. The deterministic convolution (Riccati–Volterra) equations that arise from affine Volterra processes belong there. ([MSC2020 45-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=45-XX); [Abi Jaber–Larsson–Pulido, arXiv:1708.08796](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.08796))

### Key concepts
- **Random operator and random fixed point.** For a measurable space $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$, a map $T:\Omega\times X\to Y$ is a random operator if $T(\cdot,x)$ is measurable for each $x$. A measurable $\xi:\Omega\to X$ is a random fixed point if $\xi(\omega)=T(\omega,\xi(\omega))$ for every $\omega$. A random operator equation $x=T(\omega,x)$ is thus solved by a measurable family of fixed points, and measurable selections of set-valued maps are the standard device; compare the deterministic [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem). ([Patriche, arXiv:1507.02950](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1507.02950))
- **Well-posedness with singular kernels (Coutin–Decreusefond).** Suppose $K$ is continuous as an operator $L^1\to I_{\gamma,2}$ and $L^2\to I_{\gamma+1/2,2}$ on each $[0,t]$ for some $\gamma>0$. Suppose $b,\sigma$ are Lipschitz in $x$ uniformly in time, with $b(\cdot,x_0),\sigma(\cdot,y_0)\in L^r$ for some $r>\max(2,1/\gamma)$. Then the stochastic Volterra equation has a unique continuous solution, Hölder of every order below $\gamma-1/r$. The fractional Brownian kernel $K_H$ satisfies the hypothesis for every $\gamma<H$. ([Coutin–Decreusefond, arXiv:1703.08395](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.08395))
- **Pathwise uniqueness with Hölder noise (Mytnik–Salisbury).** For $X_t=x_0+\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}g(s)\,ds+\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}\sigma(X_s)\,dB_s$ with $0<\alpha<1/2$, $g$ bounded continuous, and $\sigma$ $\gamma$-Hölder with $\gamma\in\big(\tfrac{1}{2(1-\alpha)},1\big]$, pathwise uniqueness holds. At $\alpha=0$ this matches the Yamada–Watanabe threshold $\gamma\ge1/2$. The proof passes through a degenerate SPDE linked to catalytic super-Brownian motion. ([Mytnik–Salisbury, arXiv:1502.05513](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1502.05513)) Prömel and Scheffels later proved pathwise uniqueness, and hence unique strong solutions, for one-dimensional singular-kernel equations with Hölder diffusion coefficients. ([Prömel–Scheffels, arXiv:2212.08029](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08029v1))
- **Weak existence for convolution equations (Abi Jaber–Cuchiero–Larsson–Pulido).** For $X_t=g_0(t)+\int_{[0,t)}K(t-s)\,dZ_s$, where $Z$ is an Itô semimartingale with characteristics $(b(X),a(X),\nu(X,d\zeta))$, take continuous coefficients with linear growth and a kernel satisfying $L^p$ Sobolev–Slobodeckij-type bounds. Then a weak $L^p$ solution exists, with pathwise uniqueness under Lipschitz conditions. The model kernel is $K(t)=t^{\gamma-1}$ with $\gamma\in(1/2,1)$. ([Abi Jaber et al., arXiv:1909.01166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.01166))
- **Affine Volterra processes.** Solutions of stochastic convolution equations with affine coefficients are generally neither Markov nor semimartingales. Their Fourier–Laplace functional is still exponential-affine, given by solutions of deterministic convolution-type integral equations, which yields existence and uniqueness on specific state spaces. ([Abi Jaber–Larsson–Pulido, arXiv:1708.08796](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.08796))
- **Rough volatility.** High-frequency data indicate that log-volatility behaves like fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent near $0.1$, which motivates singular kernels $t^{H-1/2}$ in stochastic Volterra models. ([Gatheral–Jaisson–Rosenbaum, arXiv:1410.3394](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3394); [Abi Jaber et al., arXiv:1909.01166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.01166))
- **Infinite-dimensional equations.** Stochastic Volterra equations with singular kernels in 2-smooth [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) have unique solutions, and these results apply to semilinear SPDEs driven by Brownian or fractional Brownian motion, including stochastic [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations). ([Zhang, arXiv:0812.0834](https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.0834)) See [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations).
- **Prerequisites**: [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces), [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes), [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus) and [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces); Abi Jaber et al. work by weak convergence in $L^p$ together with a martingale problem. ([Abi Jaber et al., arXiv:1909.01166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.01166))

### History
Early work on random integral equations includes that of A. T. Bharucha-Reid. Crossref lists his paper with L. Arnold, "On Fredholm integral equations with random degenerate kernels" (Applicationes Mathematicae), his monograph *Random Integral Equations* (reviewed by D. A. Dawson in SIAM Review, 1974), a 1964 paper "On random solutions of nonlinear integral equations", and reports on the computational solution of random integral equations (1981) and random equations (1983). ([Crossref search](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Bharucha-Reid+Random+Integral+Equations+1972&rows=5)) His survey "Fixed point theorems in probabilistic analysis" appeared in Bull. AMS 82 (1976), 641–657. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1976-14091-8)) The classical Yamada–Watanabe theorem gives strong uniqueness for $1/2$-Hölder diffusion coefficients in the non-Volterra case. Protter (1985) and Pardoux–Protter (1990) studied Volterra equations driven by semimartingales and with anticipating coefficients. ([Mytnik–Salisbury, arXiv:1502.05513](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1502.05513); [Coutin–Decreusefond, arXiv:1703.08395](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.08395))

### Open problems
- **Sharp uniqueness threshold.** Mytnik and Salisbury prove pathwise uniqueness for $\gamma>1/(2(1-\alpha))$ but have no counterexample below it. Whether uniqueness fails for $\gamma<1/(2(1-\alpha))$ is left open; they suggest non-uniqueness techniques from earlier SPDE work as candidates. ([Mytnik–Salisbury, arXiv:1502.05513](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1502.05513))
- **Non-Lipschitz uniqueness for convolution equations.** Abi Jaber, Cuchiero, Larsson and Pulido obtain weak existence under continuity and growth assumptions but prove uniqueness only under Lipschitz conditions. They describe the non-Lipschitz case as more delicate and do not treat it. ([Abi Jaber et al., arXiv:1909.01166](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.01166))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation): deterministic Volterra theory with a section on stochastic Volterra equations and rough volatility.
- **Learn:** [Hairer, An Introduction to Stochastic PDEs (arXiv:0907.4178)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.4178): lecture notes treating semilinear SPDEs as stochastic evolution equations in Banach and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces).
- **Primary:** [Mytnik and Salisbury, Uniqueness for Volterra-type stochastic integral equations (arXiv:1502.05513)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.05513). [Abi Jaber, Cuchiero, Larsson, Pulido, A weak solution theory for stochastic Volterra equations of convolution type (arXiv:1909.01166)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1909.01166).
- **Further reading:** [Bharucha-Reid, Fixed point theorems in probabilistic analysis, Bull. AMS 82 (1976)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1976-14091-8): classical survey of random operator equations. [Coutin and Decreusefond, Stochastic Volterra equations with singular kernels (arXiv:1703.08395)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.08395).
references.MSC 46Axx - Topological linear spaces an:
## Reference
### Overview
MSC 46Axx covers topological vector spaces in general, beyond normed spaces. Its core is the theory of locally convex spaces: vector spaces whose topology has a base at $0$ of convex balanced sets, or equivalently is generated by a family of seminorms. Such a space is Hausdorff iff its family of seminorms separates points. Von Neumann introduced the general definition in 1935. ([Wikipedia: Locally convex TVS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_convex_topological_vector_space); [nLab: locally convex topological vector space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+convex+topological+vector+space))

The area exists because the spaces of analysis are often not normable. Examples are $C^\infty$ functions, holomorphic functions, the Schwartz space and test functions, together with their duals, the distributions. Fréchet, LF, nuclear and (DF) spaces are the categories in which these spaces and their duality are handled. ([Wikipedia: Locally convex TVS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_convex_topological_vector_space); [Wikipedia: Fréchet space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_space))

### Scope
MSC2020 lists these sub-codes under 46Axx ([MSC2020 46Axx, AMS](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Axx)):
- 46A03 general theory of locally convex spaces; 46A04 locally convex Fréchet spaces and (DF)-spaces; 46A08 barrelled and bornological spaces; 46A11 spaces determined by compactness or summability properties (nuclear, Schwartz, Montel spaces); 46A13 inductive and projective limits (LB, LF). ([MSC2020 46Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Axx))
- 46A16 non-locally-convex spaces (metrizable, locally bounded, quasi-Banach); 46A17 bornologies; 46A19 other "topological" linear spaces such as convergence spaces. ([MSC2020 46Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Axx))
- 46A20 duality theory; 46A22 Hahn–Banach-type theorems; 46A25 reflexivity and semi-reflexivity; 46A30 open mapping, closed graph and completeness; 46A32 operator spaces, topological tensor products and approximation properties; 46A35 bases. ([MSC2020 46Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Axx))
- 46A40 ordered spaces and vector lattices; 46A45 sequence spaces including Köthe spaces; 46A50 compactness and angelic spaces; 46A55 convex sets and Choquet theory; 46A61 graded Fréchet spaces and tame operators; 46A63 topological invariants such as (DN) and $(\Omega)$; 46A70 Saks spaces and strict or mixed topologies; 46A80 modular spaces. ([MSC2020 46Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Axx))

Neighbouring codes, one line each:
- 46Bxx treats normed linear spaces, Banach spaces and Banach lattices; 46Axx is the general and non-normable side. ([MSC2020 46-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46-XX); [Wikipedia: Fréchet space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_space))
- 46Exx and 46Fxx study particular function and distribution spaces; 46Axx supplies the general structures (Fréchet, LF, nuclear) they are instances of. ([MSC2020 46-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46-XX); [Wikipedia: Nuclear space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_space))
- 46Txx holds nonlinear functional analysis; the graded Fréchet spaces and tame operators on which the Nash–Moser theorem is built are classified in 46A61. ([MSC2020 46-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46-XX); [MSC2020 46Axx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Axx); [Wikipedia: Nash–Moser theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash%E2%80%93Moser_theorem))

### Key concepts
- **Hahn–Banach in locally convex spaces.** Every Hausdorff locally convex space has the Hahn–Banach extension property. Conversely (Kalton), a complete metrizable TVS with that property is locally convex. For $0<p<1$, $L^p[0,1]$ has only the zero functional. ([Wikipedia: Locally convex TVS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_convex_topological_vector_space); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+convex+topological+vector+space)) See [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces) and [Dual Vector Space](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space).
- **Fréchet spaces.** These are complete metrizable locally convex spaces, i.e. complete with a countable separating family of seminorms. They include all [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, $C^\infty$ on compact manifolds, and entire functions. The open mapping, closed graph and Banach–Steinhaus theorems hold for them, while the [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem) fails. Eidelheit: a Fréchet space is either isomorphic to a Banach space or has a quotient isomorphic to $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$. Anderson–Kadec: every infinite-dimensional separable real Fréchet space is homeomorphic (not necessarily linearly) to $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$. ([Wikipedia: Fréchet space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_space))
- **Barrelled spaces and Banach–Steinhaus.** A barrel is a closed, absorbing, convex, balanced set; $X$ is barrelled if every barrel is a $0$-neighbourhood (Bourbaki, 1950). If $X$ is barrelled and $Y$ locally convex, a pointwise bounded set of continuous linear maps $X\to Y$ is equicontinuous. Baire TVSs, Fréchet spaces and Hausdorff reflexive locally convex spaces are barrelled. ([Wikipedia: Barrelled space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrelled_space))
- **Nuclear spaces.** Grothendieck introduced them (published 1955) while studying the Schwartz kernel theorem. Examples include smooth functions on a compact manifold, the Schwartz space and [Tempered Distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions), and test functions and [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29). No infinite-dimensional Banach space is nuclear. Every nuclear space has the approximation property, and quasi-complete barrelled nuclear spaces are Montel. The Bochner–Minlos theorem gives a probability measure on the dual from a characteristic functional. ([Wikipedia: Nuclear space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_space))
- **Krein–Milman and Choquet theory (46A55).** In a Hausdorff locally convex space a compact convex set is the closed convex hull of its extreme points (Krein–Milman, 1940). By Choquet–Bishop–de Leeuw, every point of such a set is the barycenter of a probability measure carried by the extreme points. Krein–Milman together with the Boolean prime ideal theorem implies the axiom of choice. ([Wikipedia: Krein–Milman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krein%E2%80%93Milman_theorem)) See [Convex Hull](node:Convex%20Hull).
- **Tame Fréchet spaces and Nash–Moser (46A61).** Let $F,G$ be tame Fréchet spaces, $U\subset F$ open, and $P:U\to G$ smooth tame. If every derivative $dP_f$ is invertible and the inverses form a smooth tame family $U\times G\to F$, then $P$ is locally invertible with smooth tame local inverses (Hamilton, Bull. AMS 1982). Nash's 1956 isometric embedding proof is the origin. ([Wikipedia: Nash–Moser theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash%E2%80%93Moser_theorem)) See [Nash Embedding Theorem](node:Nash%20Embedding%20Theorem).
- **Ambient notions**: [Topological Spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces), [Hausdorff Space](node:Hausdorff%20Space) and [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) supply the axioms. [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) and Banach spaces are Fréchet spaces, and they are barrelled. ([Wikipedia: Fréchet space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_space); [Wikipedia: Barrelled space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrelled_space))

### History
Von Neumann gave the general definition of a (locally) convex space in 1935. Krein and Milman published their extreme-point theorem in Studia Mathematica in 1940, generalizing Minkowski (1911) and Steinitz (1916). Bourbaki introduced barrelled spaces in 1950, and Grothendieck's nuclear spaces appeared in 1955. Nash proved the special case for isometric embeddings in 1956, Moser extended the method in 1966, and Hamilton's 1982 Bulletin AMS paper stated the theorem for tame Fréchet spaces. ([Wikipedia: Locally convex TVS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_convex_topological_vector_space); [Wikipedia: Krein–Milman theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krein%E2%80%93Milman_theorem); [Wikipedia: Barrelled space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrelled_space); [Wikipedia: Nuclear space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_space); [Wikipedia: Nash–Moser theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash%E2%80%93Moser_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Separable quotient problem.** Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have an infinite-dimensional separable quotient? The question is attributed to Mazur (1932) and remains open. Saxon and Wilansky showed it is a 46Axx question: an infinite-dimensional Banach space has a separable quotient iff it contains a dense non-barrelled subspace. Outside local convexity the analogue fails: Popov showed that $L_p([0,1]^{2^{\mathfrak c}})$ for $0<p<1$ has no separable quotient, answering a question of Drewnowski negatively. ([Ferrando et al., arXiv:1709.09646](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09646); [ar5iv text](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1709.09646))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Locally convex topological vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_convex_topological_vector_space): definitions, examples, and properties. [nLab: locally convex topological vector space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+convex+topological+vector+space): seminorm formulation and categorical structure.
- **Learn:** [Garrett, Functional Analysis course notes (UMN)](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/fun/): graduate notes on TVS generalities, seminorms versus local convexity, Hahn–Banach for locally convex spaces, Banach–Steinhaus, Fréchet spaces, quasi-completeness, and nuclear spaces.
- **Primary:** [Ferrando, Kąkol, López-Pellicer, Śliwa, On the separable quotient problem for Banach spaces (arXiv:1709.09646)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09646): survey linking barrelledness and quotients.
- **Further reading:** [Schaefer and Wolff, Topological Vector Spaces, GTM 3, Springer 1999](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1468-7): graduate text on topological vector spaces.
references.MSC 46Bxx - Normed linear spaces and Ban:
## Reference
### Overview
46Bxx is the structure theory of [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces): classifying normed spaces up to isomorphism and isometry, understanding their subspaces, quotients, bases and duals, and studying ordered Banach spaces (Banach lattices). Its guiding questions are how far a general Banach space is from the classical spaces $\ell_p$, $c_0$, $L_p$ and $C(K)$, and which properties single out [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces). Every Banach space is isometric to a subspace of some $C(K)$, and every separable Banach space is isometric to a quotient $\ell^1/M$. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

The modern subject has two strands. The infinite-dimensional ("isomorphic") theory asks about bases, unconditional structure and decompositions, and was transformed by Gowers and Maurey's construction of a space with no infinite unconditional basic sequence. ([Gowers–Maurey, arXiv:math/9205204](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9205204)) The local theory studies finite-dimensional normed spaces with constants independent of dimension; Milman's concentration-of-measure proof of Dvoretzky's theorem was a starting point for asymptotic geometric analysis. ([Wikipedia: Dvoretzky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvoretzky%27s_theorem)) A third strand, the Ribe program, sits between Banach space theory and metric geometry: Naor's Takagi Lectures survey its main results, applications and open problems. ([Naor, arXiv:1205.5993](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.5993))

### Scope
MSC2020 sub-codes of 46Bxx ([MSC2020, 46Bxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Bxx)):
- **46B03** isomorphic theory (including renorming); **46B04** isometric theory; **46B06** asymptotic theory; **46B07** local theory; **46B08** ultraproduct techniques; **46B09** probabilistic methods.
- **46B10** duality and reflexivity; **46B15** summability and bases, functional-analytic aspects of frames; **46B20** geometry and structure of normed spaces; **46B22** Radon–Nikodým, Kreĭn–Milman and related properties.
- **46B25** classical Banach spaces in the general theory; **46B26** nonseparable spaces; **46B28** spaces of operators, tensor products, approximation properties; **46B45** Banach sequence spaces; **46B50** compactness.
- **46B40** ordered normed spaces; **46B42** Banach lattices.
- **46B70** interpolation between normed spaces; **46B80** nonlinear classification and nonlinear quotients; **46B85** embeddings of discrete [metric spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces) into Banach spaces, with applications in topology and computer science; **46B87** lineability; **46B99** other.

Neighbouring codes ([MSC2020, 46-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46-XX)):
- [46Axx](node:MSC%2046Axx%20-%20Topological%20linear%20spaces%20and%20related%20structures) treats non-normable locally convex and topological [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces); 46Bxx needs a norm.
- [46Cxx](node:MSC%2046Cxx%20-%20Inner%20product%20spaces%20and%20their%20generalizations,%20Hilbert%20spaces) treats inner-product structure; 46Bxx asks when a Banach space is or is not Hilbertian.
- [46Exx](node:MSC%2046Exx%20-%20Linear%20function%20spaces%20and%20their%20duals) holds concrete function spaces (e.g. [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces), [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces)); the MSC directs function spaces there.
- 46Hxx–46Lxx add a multiplication (Banach and operator algebras); [47](node:MSC%2047%20-%20Operator%20theory) studies operators on a fixed space; 46Txx is nonlinear functional analysis.

### Key concepts
- **Reflexivity and James's theorem.** A Banach space $X$ is reflexive iff every continuous linear functional attains its norm on the closed unit ball. A space with a Schauder basis is reflexive iff the basis is shrinking and boundedly complete. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Dvoretzky's theorem (46B07).** For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N(k,\varepsilon)$ such that every normed space of dimension $N(k,\varepsilon)$ has a $k$-dimensional subspace $E$ with Banach–Mazur distance $d(E,\ell_2^k)\le1+\varepsilon$; Milman's proof gives $k\ge C(\varepsilon)\log N$, which is sharp. ([Wikipedia: Dvoretzky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvoretzky%27s_theorem))
- **Bases and the approximation property (46B15, 46B28).** $X$ has the approximation property if every compact operator into $X$ is a norm limit of finite-rank operators; every space with a Schauder basis has it. Enflo (1973) constructed a separable Banach space without the approximation property, hence without a basis, and Szankowski showed that $B(H)$ fails it. ([Wikipedia: Approximation property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_property); [Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Hereditarily indecomposable spaces and Gowers's dichotomy (46B03).** Gowers and Maurey constructed a Banach space with no infinite unconditional basic sequence. ([Gowers–Maurey, arXiv:math/9205204](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9205204)) Gowers's dichotomy: every infinite-dimensional Banach space contains a subspace with an unconditional basis or a hereditarily indecomposable subspace; and a Banach space isomorphic to all its infinite-dimensional closed subspaces is isomorphic to $\ell_2$, answering Banach's homogeneous space problem. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Scalar-plus-compact space.** Argyros and Haydon constructed a hereditarily indecomposable $\mathcal{L}_\infty$ space with dual isomorphic to $\ell_1$ on which every bounded operator has the form $\lambda I+K$ with $K$ compact. ([Argyros–Haydon, arXiv:0903.3921](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3921))
- **Characterizations of Hilbert space.** Lindenstrauss–Tzafriri: if every closed subspace of $X$ is complemented, $X$ is isomorphic to a Hilbert space (the proof uses Dvoretzky's theorem). Kwapień: $X$ is isomorphic to a Hilbert space iff it satisfies a two-sided averaged sign-sum inequality with a constant $c\ge1$ for all finite families of vectors. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Topological vs. linear classification (46B80).** Anderson–Kadec: any two infinite-dimensional separable Banach spaces are homeomorphic; Toruńczyk: two Banach spaces are homeomorphic iff they have the same density character. Linear classification is therefore a finer problem than topological classification. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Banach lattices (46B42).** A Banach lattice is a Banach space with a lattice order such that $|x|\le|y|$ implies $\|x\|\le\|y\|$; its continuous dual equals its order dual. An AL-space additionally satisfies $\|f+g\|=\|f\|+\|g\|$ for $f,g\ge0$, and separable AL-spaces are isomorphic to closed sublattices of $L^1[0,1]$. ([Wikipedia: Banach lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_lattice))
- **Isometric theory (46B04).** The Banach–Mazur distance measures how far isomorphic spaces are from isometric; Amir and Cambern extended the Banach–Stone theorem to $C(K)$ spaces at distance below 2. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

### History
Mazur promised a live goose in 1936 for a solution of the approximation problem, and Enflo received it in 1972 after constructing a space without the approximation property, published in 1973. ([Wikipedia: Approximation property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation_property)) Dvoretzky proved his theorem in the early 1960s, answering a question of Grothendieck, and Milman's 1971 proof launched the local theory. ([Wikipedia: Dvoretzky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvoretzky%27s_theorem)) Grothendieck's conjecture that the projective and injective tensor products always differ was disproved by Pisier in 1983, and Bočkarev showed in 1974 that the disk algebra has a basis. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space)) The Gowers–Maurey construction answered the unconditional basic sequence problem, and the Argyros–Haydon space solved the scalar-plus-compact problem. ([Gowers–Maurey, arXiv:math/9205204](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9205204); [Argyros–Haydon, arXiv:0903.3921](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.3921))

### Open problems
- **Separable quotient problem.** Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have an infinite-dimensional separable quotient? The classic problem remains open; the survey collects related results, many relying on complemented copies of $c_0$ and $\ell_p$ ($1\le p\le\infty$), including recent results of Argyros–Dodos–Kanellopoulos and Śliwa. ([Ferrando–Kąkol–López-Pellicer–Śliwa, arXiv:1709.09646](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09646))
- **Mazur rotations problem (46B04).** A Banach space is transitive if its isometry group acts transitively on the unit sphere. Is every separable transitive Banach space isomorphic to a Hilbert space, and is every transitive norm on a Hilbert space Euclidean? Cabello Sánchez states that both questions remain open; the main partial result (Ferenczi–Rosendal) shows separable transitive spaces are strictly convex and smooth with almost transitive dual. ([Cabello Sánchez, arXiv:2109.01906](https://arxiv.org/html/2109.01906))
- **Ribe program (46B80, 46B85).** Naor's survey of the Ribe program, in the 46B80/46B85 area where Banach spaces meet metric geometry, presents its main results, applications and open problems. ([Naor, arXiv:1205.5993](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.5993))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Banach space, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space): classical spaces, reflexivity, bases, characterizations of Hilbert space, Gowers's results.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102, Lecture 1: Basic Banach Space Theory](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/resources/lecture-1-basic-banach-space-theory): lecture notes from an introductory functional analysis course.
- **Primary:** [Gowers and Maurey, The unconditional basic sequence problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9205204): the construction of a space with no unconditional basic sequence.
- **Further reading:** [Albiac and Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory (Springer GTM, 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-31557-7): graduate text; [Lindenstrauss and Tzafriri, Classical Banach Spaces I (Springer, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-66557-8): the classical monograph; [Naor, An introduction to the Ribe program](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.5993): survey of the metric theory.

## Reference
### Overview
46Cxx studies [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) as geometric objects: orthogonality, projections, bases, operator ranges, characterizations of Hilbert space among Banach spaces, and spaces whose inner product is indefinite or only partially defined. A Hilbert space is a complete inner product space; its geometry is governed by the parallelogram identity $\|u+v\|^2+\|u-v\|^2=2(\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2)$, which makes every Hilbert space uniformly convex. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))

The theory began in the first decade of the twentieth century with Hilbert, Schmidt and Riesz; Riesz and Fischer independently proved in 1907 that $L^2$ is complete, and Fréchet and Riesz independently proved the representation theorem for functionals the same year. Von Neumann coined the term "abstract Hilbert space" and gave the first complete axiomatic treatment, in his work on unbounded Hermitian operators. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space)) Every Hilbert space is isometric to $\ell^2(B)$ for a set $B$ whose [cardinality](node:Cardinality) is the Hilbert dimension, so the subfield's codes concern finer structure: characterizations of Hilbert space among [Banach spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), Hilbert subspaces (operator ranges) and their complementation, and spaces with indefinite or generalized inner products. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space); [MSC2020, 46Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Cxx))

### Scope
MSC2020 sub-codes of 46Cxx ([MSC2020, 46Cxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Cxx)):
- **46C05** Hilbert and pre-Hilbert spaces: geometry and topology, including spaces with semidefinite inner product.
- **46C07** Hilbert subspaces (= operator ranges); complementation (Aronszajn, de Branges, etc.); see also 46B70, 46M35.
- **46C15** characterizations of Hilbert spaces.
- **46C20** spaces with indefinite inner product (Kreĭn spaces, Pontryagin spaces, etc.); see also 47B50.
- **46C50** generalizations of inner products (semi-inner products, partial inner products, etc.).
- **46C99** other.

Neighbouring codes ([MSC2020, 46-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46-XX)):
- Hilbert spaces of functions, including reproducing kernel spaces, go to [46Exx](node:MSC%2046Exx%20-%20Linear%20function%20spaces%20and%20their%20duals) (46E20, 46E22): the 46C heading directs function spaces there. ([MSC2020, 46Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Exx))
- [46Bxx](node:MSC%2046Bxx%20-%20Normed%20linear%20spaces%20and%20Banach%20spaces;%20Banach%20lattices) holds general Banach space geometry; 46C15 is where Banach-space properties are used to recognize Hilbert space.
- Operators on Hilbert space belong to [47](node:MSC%2047%20-%20Operator%20theory), and operator algebras on Hilbert space to [46Lxx](node:MSC%2046Lxx%20-%20Selfadjoint%20operator%20algebras%20%28C-star-algebras,%20von%20Neumann%20%28W-star-%29%20algebras,%20etc.%29).

### Key concepts
- **Projection theorem.** If $C$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space $H$ and $x\in H$, there is a unique $y\in C$ minimizing $\|x-y\|$. For a closed subspace $F$, $y$ is characterized by $y\in F$ and $x-y\perp F$; the map $x\mapsto y$ is the linear orthogonal projection, and $F\ne H$ implies $F^\perp\ne\{0\}$. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))
- **Riesz representation theorem.** The map $u\mapsto\varphi_u$, $\varphi_u(x)=\langle x,u\rangle$, is an isometric antilinear isomorphism of $H$ onto its dual $H^*$; consequently Hilbert spaces are reflexive and closed bounded convex sets are weakly compact. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))
- **Orthonormal bases and Hilbert dimension.** Every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis (by Zorn's lemma); any two have the same cardinality, and $H$ is isometrically isomorphic to $\ell^2(B)$ for $B$ of that cardinality. $H$ is separable iff it has a countable orthonormal basis, and every infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space is isometric to $\ell^2$. See [Gram–Schmidt Process](node:Gram–Schmidt%20Process). ([Wikipedia: Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))
- **Characterizations of Hilbert space (46C15).** (i) Parallelogram law: a Banach space whose norm satisfies the parallelogram identity is a Hilbert space, with the inner product recovered by polarization. (ii) Kakutani: a Banach space of dimension at least 3 is isometrically a Hilbert space iff every closed subspace is the range of a norm-one projection. (iii) Lindenstrauss–Tzafriri: a Banach space is isomorphic to a Hilbert space iff every closed subspace has a closed complement. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space)) (iv) Kwapień: a Banach space is isomorphic to a Hilbert space iff a two-sided averaged sign-sum inequality holds for all finite families of vectors, equivalently iff a vector-valued Parseval identity holds for the Fourier transform. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))
- **Kreĭn and Pontryagin spaces (46C20).** A Kreĭn space is a space with a Hermitian form admitting a fundamental decomposition $K=K_+\oplus K_-$ into orthogonal parts that are Hilbert spaces under $\pm\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$; decompositions are not unique but all induce the same topology. A Pontryagin space $\Pi_\kappa$ has finite rank of indefiniteness $\kappa=\min\{\dim K_+,\dim K_-\}$. Applications include the Gupta–Bleuler formalism, the Nehari and bitangential Nevanlinna–Pick problems, and $H^\infty$ filtering. ([Wikipedia: Krein space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krein_space))
- **Reproducing kernels and operator ranges (46C07, 46E22).** A Hilbert space of functions on $X$ with continuous point evaluations has a kernel $K(x,y)=\langle K_x,K_y\rangle$ with $f(x)=\langle f,K_x\rangle$. Moore–Aronszajn: every symmetric positive-definite kernel on a set $X$ is the reproducing kernel of a unique Hilbert space of functions on $X$. ([Wikipedia: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducing_kernel_Hilbert_space)) Aronszajn's paper *Theory of reproducing kernels* appeared in Trans. AMS 68 (1950). ([Crossref: Aronszajn 1950](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1950-0051437-7))
- **Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators.** If $T$ is compact and self-adjoint, $H$ is the orthogonal direct sum of the eigenspaces of $T$ and $T=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda$ in norm; densely defined self-adjoint operators have a spectral resolution $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\int\lambda\,d\langle E_\lambda x,y\rangle$. See [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory). ([Wikipedia: Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space))

### History
Pontryagin spaces ($\Pi_\kappa$-spaces) are named after Lev Pontryagin; standard monographs on indefinite inner product spaces include Bognár (1974) and Azizov–Iokhvidov (1989). ([Wikipedia: Krein space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krein_space)) Reproducing kernels go back to Zaremba (1907) and Mercer, and were systematized by Aronszajn and Bergman in the early 1950s. ([Wikipedia: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducing_kernel_Hilbert_space)) The Lindenstrauss–Tzafriri complemented-subspace characterization relies on Dvoretzky's theorem. ([Wikipedia: Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space))

### Open problems
- **Mazur rotations problem (46C15).** Call a Banach space transitive if its isometry group acts transitively on the unit sphere. Is every separable transitive Banach space isomorphic to a Hilbert space, and is every transitive norm on a Hilbert space Euclidean? Both questions remain open; the main partial result, of Ferenczi and Rosendal, shows that a separable transitive space is strictly convex and smooth with almost transitive dual. ([Cabello Sánchez, arXiv:2109.01906](https://arxiv.org/html/2109.01906))
- **Invariant subspace problem on Hilbert space.** Does every bounded operator on a separable complex Hilbert space of dimension $>1$ have a nontrivial closed invariant subspace? It is open for Hilbert spaces, while Enflo and Read built counterexamples on Banach spaces (Read on $\ell^1$); 2023 preprints by Enflo and by Neville claim solutions for Hilbert space. Known positive results include Aronszajn–Smith (1954: compact operators on any Banach space of dimension at least 2) and Lomonosov (1973: operators commuting with a nonzero compact operator). ([Wikipedia: Invariant subspace problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Hilbert space, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space): projections, Riesz representation, bases, characterizations, spectral theory, history.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102 Introduction to Functional Analysis, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/pages/lecture-notes-and-readings/): lectures on Hilbert space theory, orthonormal bases, Riesz representation, adjoints and the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators.
- **Primary:** [Aronszajn, Theory of reproducing kernels, Trans. AMS 68 (1950)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1950-0051437-7): Aronszajn's paper on reproducing kernels, credited with the Moore–Aronszajn theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Cabello Sánchez, Wheeling around Mazur rotations problem](https://arxiv.org/html/2109.01906): research survey on transitivity and characterizations of Hilbert space; [Albiac and Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory (Springer GTM, 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-31557-7): graduate text on Banach space theory.
