## Reference
### Overview
46Exx, "Linear function spaces and their duals", is the functional analysis of concrete spaces of functions and measures: spaces of continuous, differentiable or analytic functions, [$L^p$](node:Lp%20Spaces) and its generalizations (Orlicz, Köthe, Lorentz, rearrangement-invariant and ideal spaces), [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) with their embedding and trace theorems, reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, spaces of measures, and spaces of vector-valued functions. ([MSC2020, 46Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Exx)) The abstract theory of topological [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces), [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) lives in 46A, 46B and 46C, each of which says "For function spaces, see 46Exx". ([MSC2020, 46-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46-XX))

Typical results identify a dual concretely (the dual of $L^p$ is $L^q$; the dual of $C_0(X)$ is a space of measures; the dual of the Hardy space $H^1$ is BMO), recover a geometric object from a function space (Banach–Stone), or relate two spaces by embedding, trace or interpolation. ([Wikipedia: Lp space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space); [Wikipedia: Riesz–Markov–Kakutani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem); [Wikipedia: Bounded mean oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation); [Wikipedia: Banach–Stone theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach%E2%80%93Stone_theorem)) Real and complex interpolation organize the scales: interpolating $L^1$ and $L^\infty$ gives Lorentz spaces, and interpolating Sobolev spaces gives Besov spaces. ([Wikipedia: Interpolation space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpolation_space)) Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces appear in [complex analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis), harmonic analysis and statistical learning, where the representer theorem reduces empirical risk minimization to finite combinations of kernel evaluations (see [Kernel Methods](node:Kernel%20Methods)); Sobolev spaces are the setting for weak formulations of [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) and [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) supplies the Besov and Hardy scales. ([Wikipedia: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducing_kernel_Hilbert_space))

### Scope
MSC2020 sub-codes of 46Exx ([MSC2020, 46Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Exx)):
- **46E05** lattices, **46E10** topological linear spaces, **46E15** Banach spaces, **46E20** Hilbert spaces, **46E25** rings and algebras, each of continuous, differentiable or analytic functions (46E25: for Banach function algebras, see 46J10, 46J15).
- **46E22** Hilbert spaces with reproducing kernels (functional Hilbert spaces, including de Branges–Rovnyak and other structured spaces); see also 47B32.
- **46E27** spaces of measures; see also 28A33, 46Gxx.
- **46E30** spaces of measurable functions ($L^p$, Orlicz, Köthe, Lorentz, rearrangement-invariant, ideal spaces, etc.).
- **46E35** Sobolev spaces and other spaces of "smooth" functions, embedding theorems, trace theorems; **46E36** Sobolev-type spaces on metric spaces, analysis on [metric spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces); **46E39** Sobolev-type spaces of functions of discrete variables.
- **46E40** spaces of vector- and operator-valued functions; **46E50** spaces of differentiable or holomorphic functions on infinite-dimensional spaces (see also 46G20, 46G25, 47H60); **46E99** other.

Neighbouring codes, as the classification states them: the 46Exx heading carries "See also 30H05, 32A38, 46F05" (spaces of analytic functions of one and several complex variables in [30H](node:MSC%2030Hxx%20-%20Spaces%20and%20algebras%20of%20analytic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable) and [32A](node:MSC%2032Axx%20-%20Holomorphic%20functions%20of%20several%20complex%20variables), and distribution spaces in [46F](node:MSC%2046Fxx%20-%20Distributions,%20generalized%20functions,%20distribution%20spaces)), and the one redirect "For function algebras, see 46J10". ([MSC2020, 46Exx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Exx)) General Banach-space structure is [46Bxx](node:MSC%2046Bxx%20-%20Normed%20linear%20spaces%20and%20Banach%20spaces;%20Banach%20lattices) and inner-product geometry [46Cxx](node:MSC%2046Cxx%20-%20Inner%20product%20spaces%20and%20their%20generalizations,%20Hilbert%20spaces). ([MSC2020, 46-XX](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46-XX))

### Key concepts
- **$L^p$ duality (46E30).** $L^p(\mu)$ is a Banach space for $1\le p\le\infty$ (Riesz–Fischer). For $1<p<\infty$ its dual is $L^q$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$, so $L^p$ is reflexive; for $\sigma$-finite $\mu$ the dual of $L^1$ is $L^\infty$, while the dual of $L^\infty$ consists of bounded finitely additive measures absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$. Clarkson's inequalities make $L^p$ uniformly convex for $1<p<\infty$; for $0<p<1$, $L^p[0,1]$ is not locally convex and has zero dual. ([Wikipedia: Lp space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space)) Background: [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory), [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration).
- **Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem (46E27).** For $X$ locally compact Hausdorff, every continuous linear functional $\psi$ on $C_0(X)$ is $\psi(f)=\int f\,d\mu$ for a unique regular complex Borel measure $\mu$, with $\|\psi\|=|\mu|(X)$, and $\psi\ge0$ iff $\mu\ge0$. ([Wikipedia: Riesz–Markov–Kakutani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem))
- **Banach–Stone theorem (46E15).** For compact Hausdorff $X,Y$, every surjective linear isometry $T:C(X)\to C(Y)$ has the form $(Tf)(y)=g(y)f(\varphi(y))$ with $\varphi:Y\to X$ a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) and $|g|\equiv1$; hence $C(X)\cong C(Y)$ isometrically iff $X$ and $Y$ are homeomorphic. ([Wikipedia: Banach–Stone theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach%E2%80%93Stone_theorem))
- **Orlicz and Lorentz spaces; interpolation (46E30).** For a Young function $\Phi$ and $\sigma$-finite $\mu$, $L^\Phi$ consists of $f$ with $\int\Phi(k|f|)\,d\mu<\infty$ for some $k>0$, with Luxemburg norm $\inf\{k>0:\int\Phi(|f|/k)\,d\mu\le1\}$; $L\log L$ arises with the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function. ([Wikipedia: Birnbaum–Orlicz space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birnbaum%E2%80%93Orlicz_space)) The Lorentz quasinorm of $L^{p,q}$ depends only on the decreasing rearrangement $f^*$ (so $L^{p,q}$ is rearrangement invariant); $L^{p,p}=L^p$, $L^{p,\infty}$ is weak $L^p$, and $L^{p,q}\subset L^{p,r}$ for $q<r$. ([Wikipedia: Lorentz space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_space)) Real interpolation gives $(L^1,L^\infty)_{\theta,q}=L^{p,q}$ with $1/p=1-\theta$, complex interpolation gives $(L^{p_0},L^{p_1})_\theta=L^p$ with $1/p=(1-\theta)/p_0+\theta/p_1$ (the Riesz–Thorin setting), and $(H^{s_0}_p,H^{s_1}_p)_{\theta,q}=B^{s_\theta}_{p,q}$ for $s_0\ne s_1$. ([Wikipedia: Interpolation space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpolation_space))
- **Hardy space $H^1$ and BMO.** The real Hardy space $H^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ consists of [tempered distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions) whose maximal function, built from a Schwartz function $\Phi$ with $\int\Phi=1$, lies in $L^p$; for $1<p<\infty$ it equals $L^p$, while $H^1$ is a proper, non-closed subspace of $L^1$, and for $0<p\le1$ every element has an atomic decomposition. ([Wikipedia: Hardy space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy_space)) Fefferman (1971) showed that the dual of $H^1$ is BMO (proof in Fefferman–Stein, Acta Math. 1972), and $H^1$ is in turn the dual of VMO; BMO functions satisfy the John–Nirenberg exponential-decay estimate for $|\{x\in Q:|f-f_Q|>\lambda\}|$. ([Wikipedia: Bounded mean oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation))
- **Sobolev embeddings, Gagliardo–Nirenberg, traces (46E35).** On $\mathbb{R}^n$: if $k>\ell$, $p<n$, $1\le p<q<\infty$ and $\frac1p-\frac kn=\frac1q-\frac\ell n$, then $W^{k,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)\subseteq W^{\ell,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality)) On a compact Riemannian $n$-manifold, for $1\le p,q<\infty$, $k\ge m$ and $k-\frac np\ge m-\frac nq$ give a continuous embedding $W^{k,p}\subseteq W^{m,q}$, compact when both inequalities are strict (Rellich–Kondrachov); for bounded Lipschitz $\Omega$ the trace maps $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ onto $W^{1-1/p,p}(\partial\Omega)$ for $1<p<\infty$, and $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ has a bounded extension operator to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space)) The Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality $\|D^ju\|_{L^p}\le C\|D^mu\|_{L^r}^\theta\|u\|_{L^q}^{1-\theta}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ holds for $\frac1p=\frac jn+\theta(\frac1r-\frac mn)+\frac{1-\theta}q$, $j<m$, $\frac jm\le\theta\le1$, $1\le q,r\le\infty$, with two exceptional cases: for $j=0$, $q=\infty$, $rm<n$ one needs $u\to0$ at infinity or $u\in L^s$ for some finite $s$, and if $r>1$ and $m-j-\frac nr$ is a non-negative integer then $\theta<1$. ([Wikipedia: Gagliardo–Nirenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagliardo%E2%80%93Nirenberg_interpolation_inequality)) For non-integer $s$, $W^{s,p}=B^s_{p,p}$, and $B^s_{2,2}=H^s$. ([Wikipedia: Besov space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besov_space))
- **Manifold-valued Sobolev maps (46E35).** For a smooth compact connected Riemannian manifold $\mathcal N$ without boundary, $0<s<\infty$, $1\le p<\infty$ and $sp<m$, $C^\infty(\overline{Q}^m;\mathcal N)$ is dense in $W^{s,p}(Q^m;\mathcal N)$ if and only if $\pi_{\lfloor sp\rfloor}(\mathcal N)=\{0\}$; for $sp\ge m$ density always holds. Detaille's theorem completes the cases of Bethuel ($s=1$), Brezis–Mironescu ($0<s<1$) and Bousquet–Ponce–Van Schaftingen (integer $s$). ([Detaille, arXiv 2305.12589](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.12589))
- **Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (46E22).** A Hilbert space of functions on $X$ with continuous point evaluations has a symmetric positive-definite kernel $K$ with $f(x)=\langle f,K_x\rangle$; by Moore–Aronszajn every symmetric positive-definite kernel determines a unique such space. Examples: band-limited functions, kernel $\frac{\sin a(y-x)}{\pi(y-x)}$, and the Bergman space of the disc, kernel $\frac1\pi(1-x\bar y)^{-2}$. ([Wikipedia: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducing_kernel_Hilbert_space)) See also [Gaussian Processes](node:Gaussian%20Processes).
- **Variable-exponent spaces (46E30).** For variable exponent spaces $L^{p(\cdot)}$, boundedness of the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator is a central question; a Muckenhoupt-type condition together with Nekvinda's decay condition implies it even for unbounded exponents. ([Maximal operator on variable exponent spaces, arXiv 2502.10313](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10313))

### History
Riesz's 1909 representation of functionals on $C[0,1]$, extended by Markov (1938) and Kakutani (1941) ([Wikipedia: Riesz–Markov–Kakutani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem)), Banach's isometry theorem for compact metric spaces, extended by Stone ([Wikipedia: Banach–Stone theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach%E2%80%93Stone_theorem)), and Orlicz's 1932 spaces ([Wikipedia: Birnbaum–Orlicz space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birnbaum%E2%80%93Orlicz_space)) identified duals and isometries of concrete function spaces. Lorentz introduced $L^{p,q}$ in 1950 ([Wikipedia: Lorentz space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_space)). Lions introduced complex interpolation in 1960 and Calderón developed it in 1964; Lions and Peetre defined the real method in 1961 ([Wikipedia: Interpolation space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpolation_space)). Gagliardo and Nirenberg announced their inequality at the 1958 ICM ([Wikipedia: Gagliardo–Nirenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagliardo%E2%80%93Nirenberg_interpolation_inequality)), and the $H^1$–BMO duality appeared in Fefferman–Stein (1972) ([Wikipedia: Bounded mean oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_mean_oscillation)). Reproducing kernels go back to Zaremba (1907) and were systematized by Aronszajn and Bergman in the early 1950s ([Wikipedia: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducing_kernel_Hilbert_space)). The strong density problem for manifold-valued Sobolev maps was settled for all $s,p$ by Detaille (arXiv 2023, accepted at JEMS) ([Detaille, arXiv 2305.12589](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12589)).

### Open problems
- **Degree estimates in $W^{1/p,p}(S^1;S^1)$ (46E35).** With $|f|^p_{W^{1/p,p}}=\iint_{S^1\times S^1}|f(x)-f(y)|^p|x-y|^{-2}\,dx\,dy$, one has $|\deg f|\le C_p|f|^p_{W^{1/p,p}}$ for every $1<p<\infty$. Brezis's Open Problem 5.1 asks whether there is a universal $c$ with $|\deg f|\le c\,(p-1)\,|f|^p_{W^{1/p,p}}$ for all $1<p\le2$ and all $f\in W^{1/p,p}(S^1;S^1)$; he records strong evidence for it as $p\searrow1$. ([Brezis, Some of my favorite open problems](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/234.pdf))
- **Nonlocal characterization of $W^{1,p}$ (46E35).** With $\Phi_{\lambda,p}(u)=\operatorname{meas}\{(x,y)\in\Omega^2:|u(x)-u(y)|^p/|x-y|^{p+N}\ge\lambda\}$ on a smooth bounded connected $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$: is $\|\nabla u\|_{L^p}^p\le C\liminf_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda\Phi_{\lambda,p}(u)$ for all measurable $u$ and $1<p<\infty$? (Open Problem 9.2) Poliakovsky proved it with $\limsup$ in place of $\liminf$. ([Brezis, Some of my favorite open problems](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/234.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Lp space, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space): completeness, duality, uniform convexity, embeddings.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102 Introduction to Functional Analysis](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/): normed spaces, duality, Lebesgue measure and integrability, completeness of $L^p$, Hilbert spaces.
- **Primary:** [Detaille, A complete answer to the strong density problem in Sobolev spaces with values into compact manifolds (arXiv 2305.12589)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12589): research paper settling the density problem in 46E35.
- **Primary:** [Brezis, Some of my favorite open problems](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/234.pdf): problem survey including fractional Sobolev maps and nonlocal characterizations of $W^{1,p}$.
- **Further reading:** [Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (Springer, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-70914-7); [Leoni, A First Course in Sobolev Spaces (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics)](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Leoni+A+First+Course+in+Sobolev+Spaces&rows=3).
references.MSC 46Fxx - Distributions, generalized f:
## Reference
### Overview
46Fxx studies [distributions](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29) and their generalizations as objects of functional analysis: the topological [vector spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) of test functions, their duals, and the operations that can be performed on them. A distribution on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a continuous linear functional on $\mathcal{D}(U)=C_c^\infty(U)$; continuity means that for each compact $K\subset U$ there are $C_K,N_K$ with $|T(\varphi)|\le C_K\sup\{|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|:x\in K,\ |\alpha|\le N_K\}$ for $\varphi$ supported in $K$. $\mathcal{D}(U)$ is a complete locally convex space with the Heine–Borel property, and $\mathcal{D}'(U)$ is not metrizable. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))

The standard scale uses three test-function spaces, $\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{E}$ (compact support, rapid decay, all smooth functions), each dense in the next, with duals $\mathcal{E}'\subset\mathcal{S}'\subset\mathcal{D}'$: compactly supported, [tempered](node:Tempered%20Distributions), and general distributions. Derivatives are defined by $(\partial T)(\varphi)=-T(\partial\varphi)$ and multiplication by $g\in C^\infty$ by $(gT)(\varphi)=T(g\varphi)$. ([Ivrii, PDE textbook §11.1](https://www.math.toronto.edu/ivrii/PDE-textbook/Chapter11/S11.1.html)) The area is the functional-analytic infrastructure of linear [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) and [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): the Fourier transform is a continuous linear bijection of $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ onto itself. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) Beyond Schwartz distributions the section covers ultradistributions, hyperfunctions, and algebras of generalized functions built for nonlinear problems. ([MSC2020, 46Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Fxx))

### Scope
The MSC2020 codes, with their cross-references as listed ([MSC2020, 46Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Fxx)); the section heading itself carries "See also 46T30":
- **46F05** topological linear spaces of test functions, distributions and ultradistributions (see also 46E10, 46E35);
- **46F10** operations with distributions and generalized functions;
- **46F12** integral transforms in distribution spaces (see also 42-XX, 44-XX);
- **46F15** hyperfunctions, analytic functionals (see also 32A25, 32A45, 32C35, 58J15);
- **46F20** distributions and ultradistributions as boundary values of analytic functions (see also 30D40, 30E25, 32A40);
- **46F25** distributions on infinite-dimensional spaces (see also 58C35);
- **46F30** generalized functions for nonlinear analysis (Rosinger, Colombeau, nonstandard, etc.);
- **46F99** none of the above, but in this section.

Neighbours: function spaces such as [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) are in [MSC 46Exx - Linear function spaces and their duals](node:MSC%2046Exx%20-%20Linear%20function%20spaces%20and%20their%20duals) (46E35); boundary-value and hyperfunction questions border [MSC 32Axx - Holomorphic functions of several complex variables](node:MSC%2032Axx%20-%20Holomorphic%20functions%20of%20several%20complex%20variables); 58J15 sits in [MSC 58Jxx - Partial differential equations on manifolds; differential operators](node:MSC%2058Jxx%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations%20on%20manifolds;%20differential%20operators). ([MSC2020, 46Fxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Fxx))

### Key concepts
- **Structure theorem.** Every $T\in\mathcal{D}'(U)$ is locally a finite sum of derivatives of continuous functions (globally a locally finite sum); a tempered distribution is $D^\alpha F$ for a single continuous, slowly increasing $F$ and a multi-index $\alpha$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **Schwartz kernel theorem and nuclearity.** For open $X,Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, every continuous linear $K:\mathcal{D}(Y)\to\mathcal{D}'(X)$ comes from exactly one $k\in\mathcal{D}'(X\times Y)$ with $\langle k,u\otimes v\rangle=\langle Kv,u\rangle$ (Schwartz, 1952). ([Wikipedia: Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem)) $\mathcal{D}$, $\mathcal{S}$ and their strong duals are nuclear; Grothendieck introduced nuclear spaces in 1955 while studying the kernel theorem, whose analogue fails for $L^2$, and no infinite-dimensional Banach space is nuclear. The Bochner–Minlos theorem gives, for a continuous positive-definite $C$ on a nuclear space with $C(0)=1$, a unique probability measure on the dual whose Fourier transform is $C$; for $\mathcal{S}$ this yields random tempered distributions. ([Wikipedia: Nuclear space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_space)) See [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces).
- **Convolution and supports (Titchmarsh–Lions).** For $S\in\mathcal{D}'$ and compactly supported $T$, $S*T$ is defined by $\langle S*T,\varphi\rangle=\langle S,\psi\rangle$ with $\psi(x)=\langle T,\tau_{-x}\varphi\rangle$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) Titchmarsh's theorem (1926): for $\varphi,\psi\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, $\inf\operatorname{supp}(\varphi*\psi)=\inf\operatorname{supp}\varphi+\inf\operatorname{supp}\psi$ provided the left-hand side is finite (and likewise for suprema). Lions (1951): for $\varphi,\psi\in\mathcal{E}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$, the [convex hull](node:Convex%20Hull) of $\operatorname{supp}(\varphi*\psi)$ is the sum of the convex hulls of the supports. ([Wikipedia: Titchmarsh convolution theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titchmarsh_convolution_theorem))
- **Paley–Wiener–Schwartz theorem.** An entire $F$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is the Fourier–Laplace transform of a compactly supported distribution iff $|F(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^N e^{B|\operatorname{Im} z|}$ for some $C,N,B>0$, and then the distribution is supported in the closed ball of radius $B$; if the bound holds with $(1+|z|)^{-N}$ for every $N$, the distribution is a smooth function, and conversely. ([Wikipedia: Paley–Wiener theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley%E2%80%93Wiener_theorem))
- **Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem.** Every nonzero constant-coefficient operator $P(\partial)$ has a fundamental solution $E\in\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $P(\partial)E=\delta$, so $P(\partial)u=f$ is solvable for every $f\in\mathcal{E}'$. Ehrenpreis (1954–55) and Malgrange (1955–56) proved it independently, non-constructively; Lewy's example shows it fails for polynomial coefficients. ([Wikipedia: Malgrange–Ehrenpreis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem)) See [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions).
- **Wave front sets and products.** $(x_0,\xi_0)\notin WF(f)$ iff there are $\varphi\in C_c^\infty$ with $\varphi(x_0)\ne0$ and an open cone $\Gamma\ni\xi_0$ with $|\widehat{\varphi f}(\xi)|\le C_N(1+|\xi|)^{-N}$ on $\Gamma$ for all $N$; $WF(f)$ is a closed conic subset of the cotangent bundle whose projection is the singular support. The notion is Hörmander's (around 1970). ([Wikipedia: Wave front set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_front_set)) Hörmander's criterion (Theorem 8.2.10 of his treatise): the product of two distributions is well defined when the sum of their wave front sets does not meet the zero section. ([nLab: wave front set](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/wave+front+set))
- **Ultradistributions (46F05).** For weight sequences $M_p$, $A_p$ (log-convex: $M_p^2\le M_{p-1}M_{p+1}$; with condition (M.2) $M_p\le c_0H^p\min_q M_{p-q}M_q$), the Gelfand–Shilov spaces $\mathcal{S}^{(M_p)}_{(A_p)}$ (Beurling, an (FS)-space) and $\mathcal{S}^{\{M_p\}}_{\{A_p\}}$ (Roumieu, a (DFS)-space) are Montel spaces whose duals are the tempered ultradistributions; the case is quasianalytic when $\sum M_{p-1}/M_p=\infty$, their examples include $M_p=p!^\sigma$ with $0<\sigma<1$, which lies in the quasianalytic range by the criterion just stated, and $A_p=M_p=p!$ gives Fourier hyperfunctions. ([Pilipović–Prangoski–Vindas, arXiv 1507.08331](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1507.08331)) Surjectivity of constant-coefficient ultradifferential operators is tied to minimum-modulus theorems for entire functions. ([Zsidó, arXiv 2101.08329](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.08329))
- **Hyperfunctions and microfunctions (46F15, 46F20).** Sato's hyperfunctions on $\mathbb{R}$ are $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})=H^1_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{C},\mathcal{O})=\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R})/\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{C})$, pairs of holomorphic functions on the half-planes modulo entire functions; distributions embed in them. ([Wikipedia: Hyperfunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperfunction)) Taking one holomorphic function on both half-planes, $\delta=[\tfrac{i}{2\pi z}]$, and $[e^{1/z}]$ is a hyperfunction with support $\{0\}$ equal to an infinite series $\sum_n c_n\delta^{(n)}$ of derivatives of $\delta$ ([nLab: hyperfunction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/hyperfunction)); it is not a distribution, since a distribution supported at a point is a finite combination of derivatives of $\delta$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) On a real-analytic $n$-manifold $M$ with complexification $X$, the sheaf of microfunctions is $\mathcal{H}^n(\mu_M(\mathcal{O}_X)\otimes\mathrm{or}_{M/X})$, and hyperfunctions are by definition its restriction to $M$; this belongs to algebraic analysis, the programme Sato started in 1959. ([Wikipedia: Microfunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microfunction)) Microlocal analysis grew from the 1950s to the 1970s out of hyperfunctions and pseudodifferential operators. ([Wikipedia: Microlocal analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microlocal_analysis)) See [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis).
- **Schwartz impossibility and Colombeau algebras (46F30).** There is no associative product on distributions extending multiplication by smooth functions: $(\delta\cdot x)\cdot\mathrm{p.v.}\tfrac1x=0$ but $\delta\cdot(x\cdot\mathrm{p.v.}\tfrac1x)=\delta$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) Colombeau's algebra is the quotient of moderate nets of smooth functions by negligible ones; it contains $\mathcal{D}'$ via convolution with a $\delta$-net (canonically only in the "full" version) and preserves the product of smooth functions only. ([Wikipedia: Colombeau algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombeau_algebra)) Hairer's regularity structures give a different, problem-specific calculus of multiplication and integration against singular kernels, producing solutions of singular stochastic PDEs as limits of renormalised regularised problems. ([Hairer, arXiv 1303.5113](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.5113))

### History
Green functions used distribution-like objects from the 1830s; generalized functions arose in Sobolev's 1936 work on hyperbolic equations and were developed systematically by Laurent Schwartz in the late 1940s. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) Lions' support theorem appeared in 1951 ([Wikipedia: Titchmarsh convolution theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titchmarsh_convolution_theorem)), the kernel theorem in 1952 and Grothendieck's nuclear spaces in 1955 ([Wikipedia: Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem)), and fundamental solutions for constant-coefficient operators in 1954–56 ([Wikipedia: Malgrange–Ehrenpreis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem)). Sato introduced hyperfunctions in 1958 ([Wikipedia: Hyperfunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperfunction)); Hörmander's wave front set dates from around 1970 ([Wikipedia: Wave front set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_front_set)); Colombeau's book *New Generalized Functions and Multiplication of Distributions* appeared in 1984 ([Wikipedia: Colombeau algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombeau_algebra)). Hörmander's *Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I* is reissued in Springer's Classics in Mathematics ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2)).

### Open problems
None found. Searches tried: "open problem / remains open, ultradistributions, convolution equations, surjectivity, Gelfand–Shilov spaces" and "open problem, division problem, multiplication of distributions, Colombeau, survey 2020–2025". The abstracts and introductions read (Zsidó on surjectivity of ultradifferential operators, Pilipović–Prangoski–Vindas on quasianalytic Gelfand–Shilov convolution) state no open problem; Pilipović–Prangoski–Vindas describe the convolution problem in the non-quasianalytic case as solved. Hairer's paper solves the construction of $\Phi^4_3$ dynamics and states a conjecture about ferromagnets near criticality, which belongs to stochastic PDE rather than to 46F. ([Zsidó, arXiv 2101.08329](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.08329); [Pilipović–Prangoski–Vindas, arXiv 1507.08331](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1507.08331); [Hairer, arXiv 1303.5113](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.5113))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Distribution (mathematics), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29): definitions, topologies, structure theorems, convolution, products.
- **Learn:** [Ivrii, PDE textbook, §11.1 Distributions](https://www.math.toronto.edu/ivrii/PDE-textbook/Chapter11/S11.1.html): test-function spaces, operations, exercises.
- **Primary:** [Pilipović, Prangoski, Vindas, On quasianalytic classes of Gelfand–Shilov type (arXiv 1507.08331)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1507.08331): Gelfand–Shilov spaces, ultradistributions and their convolution.
- **Primary:** [Hairer, A theory of regularity structures (arXiv 1303.5113)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.5113): multiplying distributions in singular SPDE.
- **Further reading:** [Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I: Distribution Theory and Fourier Analysis (Springer, Classics in Mathematics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2): the standard graduate monograph, including wave front sets.
references.MSC 46Gxx - Measures, integration, deriv:
## Reference
### Overview
46Gxx collects the analysis of functions and measures on infinite-dimensional spaces: integrating functions and measures with values in a [Banach space](node:Banach%20Spaces), measures living on infinite-dimensional linear spaces, derivatives of maps between such spaces, liftings, and holomorphic maps and polynomials on them ([MSC2020, 46Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Gxx)). Phenomena that are automatic in $\mathbb{R}^n$ fail here. The Radon–Nikodym theorem fails in general for the Bochner integral and becomes a property that singles out a class of "nice" Banach spaces ([Wikipedia: Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral)). A locally finite Borel measure on a separable Banach space that is quasi-invariant under every translation is zero unless the space is finite-dimensional ([Wikipedia: Cameron–Martin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Martin_theorem)). Gateaux differentiability is strictly weaker than Fréchet differentiability ([Wikipedia: Fréchet derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_derivative)).

Vector measures feed Banach-space geometry through the Radon–Nikodym property, Gaussian measures on Banach spaces carry Wiener measure and [stochastic analysis](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus), and the differentiability theory of Lipschitz maps is used in the nonlinear classification of Banach spaces ([Benyamini, arXiv:math/9406215](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9406215); [Wikipedia: Abstract Wiener space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_Wiener_space)).

### Scope
The MSC2020 sub-codes are ([MSC2020, 46Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Gxx)):
- **46G05** derivatives of functions in infinite-dimensional spaces (see also 46T20, 58C20, 58C25);
- **46G10** vector-valued measures and integration (see also 26E20, 28B05, 46B22);
- **46G12** measures and integration on abstract linear spaces (see also 28C20, 46T12);
- **46G15** functional analytic lifting theory (see also 28A51);
- **46G20** infinite-dimensional holomorphy (see also 32-XX, 46E50, 46T25, 58B12, 58C10);
- **46G25** (spaces of) multilinear mappings, polynomials (see also 46E50, 46G20, 47H60);
- **46G99** none of the above, but in this section.

Neighbouring codes, per those cross-references: the 46Gxx heading points to 28-XX ([Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory)) and 46Txx ([MSC 46Txx - Nonlinear functional analysis](node:MSC%2046Txx%20-%20Nonlinear%20functional%20analysis)). Set functions with values in abstract spaces are 28B05 ([MSC 28Bxx - Set functions, measures and integrals with values in abstract spaces](node:MSC%2028Bxx%20-%20Set%20functions,%20measures%20and%20integrals%20with%20values%20in%20abstract%20spaces)) and measures on spaces with additional structure are 28C20 ([MSC 28Cxx - Set functions and measures on spaces with additional structure](node:MSC%2028Cxx%20-%20Set%20functions%20and%20measures%20on%20spaces%20with%20additional%20structure)); the Radon–Nikodym property as a Banach-space property is 46B22 ([MSC 46Bxx - Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices](node:MSC%2046Bxx%20-%20Normed%20linear%20spaces%20and%20Banach%20spaces;%20Banach%20lattices)); calculus on manifolds and nonlinear operators is 58C20/58C25 ([MSC 58Cxx - Calculus on manifolds; nonlinear operators](node:MSC%2058Cxx%20-%20Calculus%20on%20manifolds;%20nonlinear%20operators)); holomorphy also points to 32-XX and to 58B12 ([MSC 58Bxx - Infinite-dimensional manifolds](node:MSC%2058Bxx%20-%20Infinite-dimensional%20manifolds)). ([MSC2020, 46Gxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Gxx))

### Key concepts
- **Bochner integral (46G10).** A measurable $f:X\to B$ is Bochner integrable if there are integrable simple $s_n$ with $\int_X\|f-s_n\|_B\,d\mu\to0$; a Bochner-measurable $f$ is Bochner integrable iff $\int_X\|f\|_B\,d\mu<\infty$. Dominated convergence holds: if $f_n\to f$ a.e. and $\|f_n\|_B\le g$ with $g$ integrable, then $\int_E\|f-f_n\|_B\,d\mu\to0$. It is the strong analogue of [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration). ([Wikipedia: Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral))
- **Radon–Nikodym property (RNP).** $B$ has the RNP if every countably additive $B$-valued measure of bounded variation that is absolutely continuous with respect to a finite measure $\mu$ has the form $\gamma(E)=\int_E g\,d\mu$ with $g$ Bochner integrable. Equivalent conditions: bounded discrete-time $B$-valued martingales converge a.s.; $B$-valued functions of bounded variation are differentiable a.e.; and every bounded $D\subseteq B$ has slices $\{x\in D: f(x)+\delta>\sup f(D)\}$, $f\in B^*$, $\delta>0$, of arbitrarily small diameter (dentability). Reflexive spaces (so all [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces)), separable dual spaces (the Dunford–Pettis theorem) and $\ell^1$ have the RNP; $c_0$, $L^\infty(\Omega)$, $L^1(\Omega)$ for bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, and $C(K)$ for infinite compact $K$ do not. ([Wikipedia: Bochner integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral)) Dually, $X$ is an Asplund space (every separable subspace has separable dual) iff $X^*$ has the RNP, by Namioka–Phelps (1975) and Stegall (1978). ([Wikipedia: Asplund space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asplund_space))
- **Pettis integral and vector measures.** The weak integral: $f$ is Pettis integrable if every $\varphi\circ f$, $\varphi\in V'$, is integrable and for every measurable $A$ some $e_A\in V$ satisfies $\langle\varphi,e_A\rangle=\int_A\langle\varphi,f\rangle\,d\mu$ for all $\varphi$ ([Wikipedia: Pettis integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pettis_integral)). A vector measure $\mu:\mathcal F\to X$ has variation $|\mu|(A)=\sup\sum_i\|\mu(A_i)\|$ over finite partitions; for $\mu$ of bounded variation, $\mu$ is countably additive iff $|\mu|$ is. Lyapunov's theorem: the range of a non-atomic finite-dimensional vector measure is closed and convex. ([Wikipedia: Vector measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_measure))
- **Gaussian measures and the Cameron–Martin theorem (46G12).** Gross's abstract Wiener space $(H,B)$ is a Hilbert space $H$ densely embedded in a Banach space $B$ carrying a Gaussian measure $\mu$; for infinite-dimensional $H$ the canonical Gaussian cylinder measure on $H$ does not extend to a countably additive measure, and $H$ is $\mu$-null in $B$. Classical Wiener space ($B$ = continuous paths from $0$, $H$ = absolutely continuous paths with $L^2$ derivative) yields Wiener measure, the law of [Brownian motion](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus). ([Wikipedia: Abstract Wiener space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_Wiener_space)) For $h\in H$, translation by $h$ gives an equivalent measure with density $\exp(\langle h,x\rangle^\sim-\tfrac12\|h\|_H^2)$, and $\mu$ is quasi-invariant under translation by $v$ exactly when $v\in H$. ([Wikipedia: Cameron–Martin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Martin_theorem))
- **Extending cylinder measures: Minlos and Sazonov.** Bochner–Minlos: on a nuclear space $A$, every continuous positive-definite functional $C$ with $C(0)=1$ is the Fourier transform $C(y)=\int_{A'}e^{i\langle x,y\rangle}\,d\mu(x)$ of a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the dual $A'$ ([Wikipedia: Bochner–Minlos theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Minlos_theorem)). Sazonov: for Hilbert spaces $G,H$, a bounded $T:G\to H$ pushes the canonical Gaussian cylinder measure on $G$ forward to a genuine measure on $H$ ($T$ is $\gamma$-radonifying) iff $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt ([Wikipedia: Sazonov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sazonov%27s_theorem)).
- **Fréchet versus Gateaux derivatives (46G05).** $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ if a bounded linear $A$ satisfies $\|f(x+h)-f(x)-Ah\|=o(\|h\|)$; Gateaux differentiability asks only for directional limits. If $\varphi$ is a discontinuous linear functional on a Banach space, $f(x)=\|x\|\varphi(x)$ is Gateaux differentiable at $0$ with derivative $0$ but not Fréchet differentiable. See [Differential Calculus](node:Differential%20Calculus). ([Wikipedia: Fréchet derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_derivative))
- **Rademacher-type theorems.** Aronszajn, Christensen and Mankiewicz proved independently that a Lipschitz map from a separable Banach space $X$ into a Banach space $Y$ with the RNP is Gateaux differentiable outside a "null" set; Aronszajn's, Christensen's, Mankiewicz's and Phelps's (Gaussian) notions of null set all serve. The RNP of $Y$ is essential: if $Y$ fails it, some Lipschitz $f:\mathbb{R}\to Y$ is nowhere differentiable. ([Benyamini, arXiv:math/9406215](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9406215)) For Fréchet derivatives, Preiss (1990) proved that a locally Lipschitz function on an open subset of an Asplund space is Fréchet differentiable on a dense set ([Wikipedia: Asplund space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asplund_space)).
- **Γ-null sets (Lindenstrauss–Preiss).** A Lipschitz map between separable Banach spaces is Fréchet differentiable Γ-almost everywhere if it is regularly Gateaux differentiable Γ-a.e. and its Gateaux derivatives lie in a norm-separable space of operators. Where every σ-porous set is Γ-null, as in $C(K)$ for countable compact $K$, Tsirelson space and all subspaces of $c_0$ (but not Hilbert space), every countable family of Lipschitz functions has a common point of Fréchet differentiability. ([Lindenstrauss–Preiss, Ann. Math. 2003](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2003/157-1/p05)) Lipschitz maps from a Hilbert space into the plane have points of Fréchet differentiability ([Lindenstrauss–Preiss–Tišer, Princeton 2012](https://press.princeton.edu/isbn/9780691153568)).
- **Infinite-dimensional holomorphy (46G20, 46G25).** A map between complex Banach spaces is holomorphic if it is Fréchet differentiable at every point; it then has a local expansion $f(x+y)=\sum_n\frac1{n!}D^nf(x)(y)$ in homogeneous polynomials, but the series at the centre of a ball need not converge on the whole ball. On locally convex spaces the notions Gateaux-holomorphic, hypoanalytic (Gateaux holomorphic and continuous on relatively compact sets), holomorphic and locally bounded holomorphic are introduced as successively stronger requirements; by a Hartogs-type theorem, a function separately Gateaux holomorphic in each variable on a product of open sets is Gateaux holomorphic. Compare [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis). ([Wikipedia: Infinite-dimensional holomorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite-dimensional_holomorphy))
- **Liftings (46G15).** A lifting is a linear, multiplicative map $T$ picking a representative from each class $[f]$ of bounded measurable functions, with $T[1]=1$. A complete measure space admits a lifting iff it is a union of mutually disjoint integrable measurable sets; completions of $\sigma$-finite measures always qualify. ([Wikipedia: Lifting theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifting_theory))

### History
Von Neumann introduced liftings in 1931 answering a question of Haar; Maharam (1958) and the Ionescu Tulceas (1961; monograph 1969) developed the theory ([Wikipedia: Lifting theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifting_theory)). Cameron and Martin's paper on translations of Wiener integrals appeared in the Annals of Mathematics in 1944 ([Wikipedia: Cameron–Martin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Martin_theorem)), and Gross recast the theory in 1967 as abstract Wiener spaces ([Wikipedia: Abstract Wiener space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_Wiener_space)). Asplund introduced his spaces in 1968; Namioka–Phelps (1975) and Stegall (1978) tied them to the RNP of the dual, and Preiss's dense-differentiability theorem appeared in 1990 ([Wikipedia: Asplund space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asplund_space)). Diestel and Uhl's monograph *Vector Measures* appeared in the AMS Mathematical Surveys series in 1977 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/015)).

### Open problems
- **Common points of Fréchet differentiability.** Whether every countable collection of Lipschitz functions on a Banach space with separable dual has a common point of Fréchet differentiability is called a long-standing open question; Lindenstrauss and Preiss answer it positively only for some infinite-dimensional spaces. Before their work, the positive answer was known only for finite-dimensional spaces, even for collections of two functions; for a single function it was known in general. ([Lindenstrauss–Preiss, arXiv:math/0402160](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0402160); [Ann. Math. 2003](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2003/157-1/p05))
- **Lipschitz maps into higher-dimensional targets.** The existence of Fréchet derivatives of Lipschitz maps of Banach spaces into higher-dimensional spaces, beyond the Hilbert-to-plane case, and the related theory of porous sets are described as unexpectedly difficult, and the monograph on them raises several open questions on both topics. ([Lindenstrauss–Preiss–Tišer, Princeton 2012](https://press.princeton.edu/isbn/9780691153568))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Bochner integral, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner_integral): Bochner integral, dominated convergence, and the equivalent forms of the Radon–Nikodym property.
- **Learn:** [Rieffel, Measure and Integration lecture notes (Berkeley)](https://math.berkeley.edu/~rieffel/measinteg.html): first-year graduate notes that develop integration with the Bochner integral from the start.
- **Primary:** [Lindenstrauss and Preiss, On Fréchet differentiability of Lipschitz maps between Banach spaces](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2003/157-1/p05): Annals paper introducing $\Gamma$-null sets; [Benyamini, The uniform classification of Banach spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9406215): survey with the Aronszajn–Christensen–Mankiewicz theorem and its proof.
- **Further reading:** [Diestel and Uhl, Vector Measures (AMS, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/surv/015): standard monograph on vector measures and the RNP; [Lindenstrauss, Preiss and Tišer, Fréchet Differentiability of Lipschitz Functions and Porous Sets in Banach Spaces](https://press.princeton.edu/isbn/9780691153568); [Dineen, Complex Analysis on Infinite Dimensional Spaces (Springer, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4471-0869-6): Springer monograph on complex analysis in infinite-dimensional spaces; [Mujica, Complex Analysis in Banach Spaces (North-Holland 1986; Dover 2010)](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780486474663): holomorphic functions and domains of holomorphy in Banach spaces.
references.MSC 46Hxx - Topological algebras, normed:
## Reference
### Overview
46Hxx is the general theory of algebras that carry a compatible topology: Banach algebras, normed algebras, and Fréchet and other topological algebras, together with their ideals, representations, modules, functional calculus and automatic continuity ([MSC2020, 46Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Hxx)). A Banach algebra is an associative algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ that is a [Banach space](node:Banach%20Spaces) with $\|xy\|\le\|x\|\|y\|$; the basic examples are $C_0(X)$ for locally compact Hausdorff $X$, the convolution algebra $L^1(G)$ of a locally compact group, and the algebra of bounded operators on a Banach space $E$, in which the compact operators form a closed ideal ([Wikipedia: Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra)).

The area's recurring questions are structural and topological at once. The Jacobson radical controls how far algebraic structure determines topology: a semisimple Banach algebra has a unique complete norm topology ([Marcos–Velasco, Filomat 2014](https://webapps.math.uci.edu/~brusso/VelascoMarcosFilomat2014.pdf)), while whether homomorphisms from $C(X)$ into Banach algebras are automatically continuous is undecidable in ZFC ([Wikipedia: Kaplansky's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjecture)). Amenability, defined by requiring bounded derivations into dual Banach bimodules to be inner, links the algebra $L^1(G)$ to the amenability of the group $G$ ([Wikipedia: Amenable Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_Banach_algebra)). The spectrum and functional calculus of an element are defined inside the algebra; see [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory).

### Scope
The MSC2020 sub-codes are ([MSC2020, 46Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Hxx)):
- **46H05** general theory of topological algebras;
- **46H10** ideals and subalgebras;
- **46H15** representations of topological algebras;
- **46H20** structure, classification of topological algebras;
- **46H25** normed modules and Banach modules, topological modules (if not placed in 13-XX or 16-XX);
- **46H30** functional calculus in topological algebras (see also 47A60);
- **46H35** topological algebras of operators (see mainly 47Lxx);
- **46H40** automatic continuity;
- **46H70** nonassociative topological algebras (see also 46K70, 46L70);
- **46H99** none of the above, but in this section.

Neighbouring codes, from the classification's own notes: group, convolution and measure algebras go to 43A10 and 43A20 ([MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis)); functional calculus for single operators to 47A60 ([MSC 47Axx - General theory of linear operators](node:MSC%2047Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20of%20linear%20operators)); algebras of operators mainly to 47Lxx ([MSC 47Lxx - Linear spaces and algebras of operators](node:MSC%2047Lxx%20-%20Linear%20spaces%20and%20algebras%20of%20operators)); nonassociative algebras with involution to 46K70 and 46L70 ([MSC2020, 46Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Hxx)). Commutative algebras have their own subfield, [MSC 46Jxx - Commutative Banach algebras and commutative topological algebras](node:MSC%2046Jxx%20-%20Commutative%20Banach%20algebras%20and%20commutative%20topological%20algebras), as do algebras with involution, [MSC 46Kxx - Topological (rings and) algebras with an involution](node:MSC%2046Kxx%20-%20Topological%20%28rings%20and%29%20algebras%20with%20an%20involution), and C*- and von Neumann algebras, [MSC 46Lxx - Selfadjoint operator algebras (C-star-algebras, von Neumann (W-star-) algebras, etc.)](node:MSC%2046Lxx%20-%20Selfadjoint%20operator%20algebras%20%28C-star-algebras,%20von%20Neumann%20%28W-star-%29%20algebras,%20etc.%29).

### Key concepts
- **Spectrum and spectral radius.** In a unital complex Banach algebra the spectrum $\sigma(x)$ of every element is nonempty and compact, and $\sup\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\sigma(x)\}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|x^n\|^{1/n}$. ([Wikipedia: Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra))
- **Gelfand–Mazur theorem.** A complex unital Banach algebra in which every nonzero element is invertible is isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}$; in a commutative unital complex Banach algebra every non-invertible element lies in some maximal ideal. See [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals). ([Wikipedia: Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra))
- **Gleason–Kahane–Żelazko theorem.** A linear functional $\Lambda$ on a complex unital Banach algebra with $\Lambda(1)=1$ that does not vanish on invertible elements is multiplicative, $\Lambda(ab)=\Lambda(a)\Lambda(b)$; it is thus a character. Roitman and Sasane study this GKŻ property for general unital associative algebras and show, for example, that a real or complex algebra with countably many maximal left (or right) ideals has it. ([Roitman–Sasane, Results Math. 2023](https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/117348))
- **Holomorphic functional calculus (46H30).** For $f$ holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\sigma(x)$, $f(x)\in A$ is defined and the spectral mapping theorem $\sigma(f(x))=f(\sigma(x))$ holds. ([Wikipedia: Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra))
- **Jacobson radical and Johnson's uniqueness-of-norm theorem (46H20, 46H40).** The Jacobson radical of an associative Banach algebra is the largest ideal on which the spectral radius of every element vanishes, and the algebra is semisimple when the radical is zero. Johnson (Bull. AMS 1967) proved that a semisimple Banach algebra has a unique complete norm topology, a result Palmer calls a cornerstone of the theory; Rickart's theorem gives continuity of dense-range homomorphisms into strongly semisimple algebras. ([Marcos–Velasco, Filomat 2014](https://webapps.math.uci.edu/~brusso/VelascoMarcosFilomat2014.pdf)) For a unital commutative Banach algebra the radical is exactly the kernel of the Gelfand representation ([Wikipedia: Gelfand representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation)).
- **Automatic continuity and Kaplansky's problem (46H40).** Kaplansky showed every complete algebra norm on $C(X)$, $X$ compact Hausdorff, is equivalent to the uniform norm, and conjectured that every algebra homomorphism from $C(X)$ into a Banach algebra is continuous. Dales and Esterle independently built discontinuous homomorphisms assuming the continuum hypothesis, and in 1976 Solovay, building on Woodin, exhibited a model of ZFC in which the conjecture holds, so it is undecidable in ZFC. ([Wikipedia: Kaplansky's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjecture))
- **Cohen factorization (46H25).** If a Banach algebra $B$ has a bounded left approximate unit $(e_i)$ and $V$ is a left Banach $B$-module, every $v\in V$ with $e_iv\to v$ factors as $v=bw$ with $b\in B$, $w\in V$ (Cohen 1959, Hewitt 1964); in particular every element of $B$ is a product of two elements of $B$. ([Wikipedia: Cohen–Hewitt factorization theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Hewitt_factorization_theorem); [Dixon, Math. Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc.](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/factorization-and-unbounded-approximate-identities-in-banach-algebras/B9C8F9F1B8C746677299DDC86CFE9512))
- **Arens products and Arens regularity.** The bidual $A^{**}$ of a Banach algebra carries two products extending that of $A$, each making it a Banach algebra; $A$ is Arens regular when they coincide; for commutative $A$ this is equivalent to $A^{**}$ being commutative under either product. Young proved that $L^1(G)$ is Arens regular iff the locally compact group $G$ is finite. ([Dabra–Kumar, arXiv:2401.17673](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.17673v1)) For $1<p<\infty$, the Herz algebra $A_p(G)$ is Arens regular iff $G$ is discrete and $A_p(H)$ is Arens regular for every countable subgroup $H$. ([Amini–Rejali, arXiv:1601.04283](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.04283))
- **Fréchet algebras (46H05).** A Fréchet algebra is a Fréchet space with jointly continuous associative multiplication; it is m-convex if the seminorms can be chosen submultiplicative. An m-convex Fréchet algebra is a countable projective limit of Banach algebras, and an element is invertible iff its image in each is invertible. Examples include $C^\infty(S^1)$ and $\mathrm{Hol}(\mathbb{C})$; Arens's algebra $L^\omega[0,1]$ is commutative and not m-convex, with discontinuous inversion. ([Wikipedia: Fréchet algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_algebra))
- **Amenability (46H20, 46H25).** $A$ is amenable if every bounded derivation into a dual Banach $A$-bimodule is inner, equivalently if $A$ has a virtual diagonal. $L^1(G)$ is amenable iff $G$ is amenable; a C*-algebra is amenable iff it is nuclear; and continuous homomorphic images of amenable algebras have amenable closures. ([Wikipedia: Amenable Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_Banach_algebra)) In 1972 Johnson proved that a locally compact group $G$ is amenable iff certain Hochschild cohomology groups of $L^1(G)$ vanish ([Runde, arXiv:math/0206041](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0206041)); his memoir *Cohomology in Banach algebras* appeared the same year ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0127)). Spectral methods reach group theory here: Samei and Wiersma proved every quasi-Hermitian locally compact group is amenable, settling a conjecture about Hermitian groups open since the 1960s, by spectral interpolation across Banach *-algebras between $L^1(G)$ and the reduced group C*-algebra; this ties 46H to [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory) and [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory). ([Samei–Wiersma, arXiv:1805.07908](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07908))

### History
Gelfand's theory gave a much shorter and more conceptual proof of a lemma from Wiener's 1932 paper *Tauberian theorems* on elements of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ and $\ell^1(\mathbb{Z})$ whose translates span dense subspaces, a result of [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) ([Wikipedia: Gelfand representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation)). Bonsall and Duncan's *Complete Normed Algebras* appeared in 1973 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-65669-9)). Cohen's factorization theorem dates from 1959 and Hewitt's module version from 1964 ([Wikipedia: Cohen–Hewitt factorization theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%E2%80%93Hewitt_factorization_theorem)). Johnson's uniqueness-of-norm theorem appeared in 1967 and his cohomology memoir in 1972 ([Marcos–Velasco, Filomat 2014](https://webapps.math.uci.edu/~brusso/VelascoMarcosFilomat2014.pdf); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0127)). Dales and Esterle's continuum-hypothesis counterexamples to Kaplansky's conjecture date from the mid-1970s and Solovay's consistency model from 1976 ([Wikipedia: Kaplansky's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjecture)). Dales's London Mathematical Society monograph *Banach Algebras and Automatic Continuity* was published by Clarendon Press in 2000 ([Lancaster eprints](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/67585/)).

### Open problems
- **Michael's problem.** Is every multiplicative linear functional on an m-convex Fréchet algebra continuous? It has been described as perhaps the most famous open problem in the theory of topological algebras. ([Wikipedia: Fréchet algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_algebra))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Banach algebra, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra): definitions, spectrum, Gelfand–Mazur, functional calculus, semisimplicity.
- **Learn:** [Shirbisheh, Lectures on C*-algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.3404): lecture notes covering elements of Banach algebras, the algebras $L^1(G)$, spectrum and the holomorphic functional calculus.
- **Primary:** [Johnson, Cohomology in Banach algebras (Mem. AMS 127, 1972)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/memo/0127): Johnson's AMS memoir on the cohomology of Banach algebras; [Samei and Wiersma, Quasi-Hermitian locally compact groups are amenable](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07908): recent research paper.
- **Further reading:** [Bonsall and Duncan, Complete Normed Algebras (Springer, 1973)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-65669-9): classical general text; [Dales, Banach Algebras and Automatic Continuity (LMS Monographs, 2000)](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/67585/): comprehensive research monograph; [Runde, Lectures on Amenability (Springer LNM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/b82937): amenability of Banach algebras.
references.MSC 46Jxx - Commutative Banach algebras:
## Reference
### Overview
46Jxx studies commutative Banach and topological algebras, mainly through Gelfand theory, which represents such an algebra as an algebra of continuous functions on its space of characters. For a commutative Banach algebra $A$ the characters (nonzero multiplicative linear functionals) are automatically continuous and, with the weak-* topology, form a locally compact Hausdorff space $\Phi_A$; the Gelfand transform $\hat a(\chi)=\chi(a)$ is a norm-decreasing homomorphism $A\to C_0(\Phi_A)$, in general neither injective nor surjective. When $A$ has an identity, characters correspond to maximal ideals and the kernel of the Gelfand transform is the Jacobson radical, so the transform is injective exactly when $A$ is semisimple. ([Wikipedia: Gelfand representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation))

$\Phi_A$ is compact when $A$ is unital, but a non-unital algebra can also have compact, even empty, character space. A commutative radical Banach algebra has no characters, because $R/M\cong\mathbb{C}$ is impossible for a radical algebra $R$; the Volterra algebra $V=L^1[0,1]$ with truncated convolution $(f\star g)(t)=\int_0^t f(t-s)g(s)\,ds$ is radical and has a bounded approximate identity ([Dales, arXiv:1408.3815](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.3815)). The theory turns analysis into geometry: for $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ under convolution the Gelfand transform is the Fourier transform, for $L^1(\mathbb{R}^+)$ with multiplicative convolution it is the Mellin transform, and for $\ell^\infty$ the character space is the Stone–Čech space $\beta\mathbb{N}$, so the area meets [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis), [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis) and topology ([Wikipedia: Gelfand representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation)).

### Scope
The MSC2020 sub-codes are ([MSC2020, 46Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Jxx)):
- **46J05** general theory of commutative topological algebras;
- **46J10** Banach algebras of continuous functions, function algebras (see also 46E25);
- **46J15** Banach algebras of differentiable or analytic functions, $H^p$-spaces (see also 30H10, 32A35, 32A37, 32A38, 42B30);
- **46J20** ideals, maximal ideals, boundaries;
- **46J25** representations of commutative topological algebras;
- **46J30** subalgebras of commutative topological algebras;
- **46J40** structure and classification of commutative topological algebras;
- **46J45** radical Banach algebras;
- **46J99** none of the above, but in this section.

Neighbouring codes, per the classification's cross-references: function spaces as [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces) are 46E25 ([MSC 46Exx - Linear function spaces and their duals](node:MSC%2046Exx%20-%20Linear%20function%20spaces%20and%20their%20duals)); $H^p$ spaces as spaces of holomorphic functions are 30H10, 32A35–32A38 and 42B30 ([MSC 30Hxx - Spaces and algebras of analytic functions of one complex variable](node:MSC%2030Hxx%20-%20Spaces%20and%20algebras%20of%20analytic%20functions%20of%20one%20complex%20variable), [MSC 32Axx - Holomorphic functions of several complex variables](node:MSC%2032Axx%20-%20Holomorphic%20functions%20of%20several%20complex%20variables)) ([MSC2020, 46Jxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Jxx)). General topological algebras, without commutativity, are [MSC 46Hxx - Topological algebras, normed rings and algebras, Banach algebras](node:MSC%2046Hxx%20-%20Topological%20algebras,%20normed%20rings%20and%20algebras,%20Banach%20algebras). Spectral synthesis in the Fourier algebra $A(G)$ is also studied in abstract harmonic analysis: Ludwig and Turowska's paper on spectral sets has primary classification 43A45 ([MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis)) ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06584)).

### Key concepts
- **Gelfand theory.** In a unital commutative complex Banach algebra, the Gelfand–Mazur theorem makes every quotient by a maximal ideal equal to $\mathbb{C}$, every non-invertible element lies in a maximal ideal, and so the spectrum of $x$ is the range of $\hat x$. See [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals) and [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory). ([Wikipedia: Banach algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra); [Wikipedia: Gelfand representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation)) Every maximal ideal of any commutative Banach algebra has codimension 1, and either $A/M\cong\mathbb{C}$ or $A^2\subset M$ (Dales 2014); in contrast, the Fréchet algebra of entire functions has dense maximal ideals that do not have codimension 1 ([Dales, arXiv:1408.3815](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.3815)).
- **Commutative Gelfand–Naimark theorem.** For a commutative C*-algebra $A$ with spectrum $X$, the Gelfand map is an isometric *-isomorphism $A\cong C_0(X)$; for unital algebras this is a contravariant equivalence with compact [Hausdorff spaces](node:Hausdorff%20Space), and $C(X)\cong C(Y)$ iff $X$ and $Y$ are homeomorphic. ([Wikipedia: Gelfand representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation))
- **Shilov idempotent and Arens–Royden theorems (46J20, 46J40).** For a commutative unital Banach algebra $A$ with maximal ideal space $\Omega$, every clopen $G\subseteq\Omega$ has $\chi_G=\hat c$ for some $c\in A$ (Shilov's idempotent theorem). Arens–Royden: with $G(A)$ the invertibles, $G(A)/e^A\to G(C(\Omega))/e^{C(\Omega)}$, $e^Aa\mapsto e^{C(\Omega)}\hat a$, is an isomorphism, and the right side is the Čech cohomology $H^1(\Omega,\mathbb{Z})$. ([Dawson, arXiv:math/0308226](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0308226))
- **Wiener's Tauberian theorem and spectral synthesis.** For $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, the translates of $f$ span a dense subspace iff $\hat f$ has no real zeros; Gelfand reproved this with Banach algebra theory ([Wikipedia: Wiener's tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%27s_tauberian_theorem)). A closed set $E$ in a locally compact group $G$ is a set of spectral synthesis for the Fourier algebra $A(G)$ (for abelian $G$, $A(G)\cong L^1(\hat G)$) if the ideal $k(E)$ of functions vanishing on $E$ is the only closed ideal with hull $E$. Schwartz (1948) showed synthesis fails for $A(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $n\ge3$, and Malliavin (1959) that it fails for $A(G)$ for every non-discrete locally compact abelian $G$. ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06584))
- **Uniform algebras (46J10).** A uniform algebra on compact Hausdorff $X$ is a uniformly closed subalgebra of $C(X)$ containing the constants and separating points; it is natural if its maximal ideals are exactly $\{f:f(x)=0\}$. A unital commutative Banach algebra with $\|a^2\|=\|a\|^2$ for all $a$ is isomorphic to a uniform algebra. ([Wikipedia: Uniform algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_algebra))
- **Shilov boundary and Gleason parts (46J20).** A closed $F\subseteq\Phi_A$ is a boundary if $\max_{\Phi_A}|\hat x|=\max_F|\hat x|$ for all $x$; Shilov proved the intersection of all boundaries is a boundary, the unique minimal one. It is $X$ for $C(X)$, the unit circle for the disc algebra, and the torus $\mathbb{T}^n$ for the polydisc algebra. ([Wikipedia: Shilov boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilov_boundary)) Gleason parts of a uniform algebra are the classes of the equivalence relation $\varphi\sim\psi\iff\|\varphi-\psi\|<2$ on the maximal ideal space; every point of a nontrivial part is a nonpeak point. ([Ghosh–Izzo, arXiv:2207.11587](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2207.11587))
- **Carleson's corona theorem (46J15, 46J20).** Bounded holomorphic $f_1,\dots,f_n$ on the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$ generate the unit ideal of $H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ iff $|f_1|+\dots+|f_n|\ge\delta>0$ on $\mathbb{D}$; equivalently, $\mathbb{D}$ is dense in the maximal ideal space of $H^\infty$. Kakutani conjectured it in 1941, Carleson proved it in 1962 and introduced Carleson measures, and Wolff gave a simplified unpublished proof in 1979. ([Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem))
- **Radical algebras (46J45).** Commutative radical Banach algebras with $R^2=R$, a class that includes every commutative radical Banach algebra with a bounded approximate identity (such as the Volterra algebra), have no maximal ideals at all, while $R=\{f\in C[0,1]:f(0)=0\}$ with the uniform norm and truncated convolution is radical, but $R^2$ lies in the proper ideal $\{f\in R:f(t)/t\to0\ (t\to0^+)\}$, so $R$ does have maximal ideals, of codimension 1. ([Dales, arXiv:1408.3815](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.3815))
- **Commutative Fréchet algebras and automatic continuity (46J05).** $C(\mathbb{C})$ and $\mathrm{Hol}(\mathbb{C})$, with uniform convergence on compacta, are commutative Fréchet algebras, and every m-convex Fréchet algebra is a countable projective limit of Banach algebras ([Wikipedia: Fréchet algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_algebra)). Every complete algebra norm on $C(X)$ is equivalent to the uniform norm (Kaplansky), but whether every homomorphism from $C(X)$ into a Banach algebra is continuous is undecidable in ZFC (Dales, Esterle; Solovay, Woodin) ([Wikipedia: Kaplansky's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjecture)).

### History
Gelfand used his theory to give a short conceptual proof of a lemma from Wiener's 1932 paper *Tauberian theorems* on when translates span dense subspaces of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ and $\ell^1(\mathbb{Z})$ ([Wikipedia: Gelfand representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation)). Beurling introduced spectral synthesis in the late 1930s; Schwartz found the first failure in 1948 and Malliavin the general failure in 1959 ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06584)). Newman named the corona in 1959 and reduced the problem to interpolation, which Carleson solved in 1962 ([Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem)). Gamelin's *Uniform Algebras* first appeared in 1969 ([Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/books/OL3193225M)), and Dales's *Banach Algebras and Automatic Continuity* appeared with Clarendon Press in 2000 in the LMS Monographs series ([Lancaster eprints](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/67585/)).

### Open problems
- **Union problem for spectral synthesis.** Whether the union of two sets of spectral synthesis is a set of spectral synthesis was posed by Herz for abelian groups, repeated by Reiter, and is described as an outstanding problem with no solution to date; whether every set of spectral synthesis is a Ditkin set is also stated to be open. ([Ludwig–Turowska, arXiv:2412.06584](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06584))
- **Corona problem beyond the disc.** It remains open whether there are versions of the corona theorem for every planar domain or for higher-dimensional domains; Cole showed the result does not extend to all open Riemann surfaces. ([Wikipedia: Corona theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona_theorem)) Partial results include Toeplitz corona theorems for multiplier algebras of Besov–[Sobolev spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) on the unit ball of $\mathbb{C}^n$ ([Sawyer–Wick, arXiv:1410.8862](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.8862)).
- **Point derivations at nonpeak points.** Whether there exist uniform algebras on a metrizable space with no nonzero, possibly unbounded, point derivations at a nonpeak point is called a difficult open question. ([Ghosh–Izzo, arXiv:2207.11587](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2207.11587))
- **Michael's problem.** Whether every multiplicative linear functional on an m-convex Fréchet algebra is continuous is open. ([Wikipedia: Fréchet algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_algebra))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Gelfand representation, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_representation): characters, the Gelfand transform, examples, commutative Gelfand–Naimark.
- **Learn:** [Shirbisheh, Lectures on C*-algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.3404): lecture notes covering spectrum, the Gelfand transform on commutative Banach algebras, and Gelfand duality.
- **Primary:** [Ludwig and Turowska, On the structure of spectral sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06584): research paper on spectral synthesis with a survey of its status; [Dales, Maximal ideals in commutative Banach algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.3815): short research paper with radical-algebra examples.
- **Further reading:** [Kaniuth, A Course in Commutative Banach Algebras (Springer GTM, 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-72476-8): graduate text on commutative Banach algebras; [Gamelin, Uniform Algebras](https://openlibrary.org/books/OL3193225M): standard text on function algebras; [Dales, Banach Algebras and Automatic Continuity (LMS Monographs, 2000)](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/67585/): research monograph.
