## Reference
### Overview
46Kxx studies topological algebras with an involution: Banach *-algebras, normed *-algebras and their representations by operators on [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), in the generality between plain Banach algebras and C*-algebras ([MSC2020, 46Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Kxx)). An involution on a ring is an involutory antiautomorphism, $(x+y)^*=x^*+y^*$, $(xy)^*=y^*x^*$, $x^{**}=x$; on a complex algebra it is conjugate-linear, $(\lambda x)^*=\bar\lambda x^*$. Self-adjoint elements form a Jordan algebra under the symmetrized product and skew-adjoint elements a Lie algebra. Examples are matrix algebras with conjugate transpose, bounded operators with the adjoint, and group algebras with $g\mapsto g^{-1}$. ([Wikipedia: *-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/*-algebra))

The central questions are spectral and representation-theoretic: does a Banach *-algebra have enough *-representations, what is its enveloping C*-algebra, when is the spectrum of every self-adjoint element real, and when are spectra unchanged on passing to a larger algebra (spectral invariance, the abstract form of Wiener's lemma). Thill's text develops the [spectral theory](node:Spectral%20Theory) of Banach *-algebras, including the Shirali–Ford theorem, and constructs the enveloping C*-algebra of a general normed *-algebra ([Thill, arXiv:math/0701306](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0701306)). Hermitian Banach *-subalgebras of C*-algebras are tied to Wiener's lemma and spectral invariance, with uses in time-frequency analysis and noncommutative geometry ([Austad–Ortega, arXiv:2105.14793](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14793)).

### Scope
The MSC2020 sub-codes are ([MSC2020, 46Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Kxx)):
- **46K05** general theory of topological algebras with involution;
- **46K10** representations of topological algebras with involution;
- **46K15** Hilbert algebras;
- **46K50** nonselfadjoint (sub)algebras in algebras with involution;
- **46K70** nonassociative topological algebras with an involution (see also 46H70, 46L70);
- **46K99** none of the above, but in this section.

Neighbouring codes: the 46Kxx heading cross-references 16W10 (rings with involution), and the nonassociative case 46H70 and 46L70 ([MSC2020, 46Kxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Kxx)). Sibling sections of 46 are [MSC 46Hxx - Topological algebras, normed rings and algebras, Banach algebras](node:MSC%2046Hxx%20-%20Topological%20algebras,%20normed%20rings%20and%20algebras,%20Banach%20algebras) (general topological and Banach algebras), [MSC 46Jxx - Commutative Banach algebras and commutative topological algebras](node:MSC%2046Jxx%20-%20Commutative%20Banach%20algebras%20and%20commutative%20topological%20algebras) and [MSC 46Lxx - Selfadjoint operator algebras (C-star-algebras, von Neumann (W-star-) algebras, etc.)](node:MSC%2046Lxx%20-%20Selfadjoint%20operator%20algebras%20%28C-star-algebras,%20von%20Neumann%20%28W-star-%29%20algebras,%20etc.%29); the 46Hxx entry sends group, convolution and measure algebras to 43A10 and 43A20 ([MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis)) ([MSC2020, 46Hxx](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/msc/msc2020.html?t=46Hxx)).

### Key concepts
- **Hermitian and symmetric Banach *-algebras; the Shirali–Ford theorem.** A Banach *-algebra $A$ is Hermitian if $\mathrm{Sp}_A(a)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ for every $a=a^*$, and symmetric if $\mathrm{Sp}_A(aa^*)\subseteq[0,\infty)$ for every $a$ (spectra of non-unital algebras are taken in the minimal unitization). The Shirali–Ford theorem: $A$ is Hermitian iff it is symmetric. ([Austad–Ortega, arXiv:2105.14793](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14793)) In Thill's form, $A$ is Hermitian iff $a^*a\ge0$ for all $a\in A$; in a C*-algebra, consequently, an element is positive iff it equals $c^*c$ for some $c$. ([Thill, arXiv:math/0701306](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0701306))
- **The Pták function.** For a normed *-algebra, $r_\sigma(a):=r_\lambda(a^*a)^{1/2}$, where $r_\lambda$ is the spectral radius; $r_\sigma(a)=r_\lambda(a)$ for Hermitian $a$. For a Banach *-algebra the following are equivalent: $A$ is Hermitian; $i\notin\mathrm{sp}(a)$ for Hermitian $a$; $r_\lambda(a)\le r_\sigma(a)$ for all $a$; $r_\lambda(b)=r_\sigma(b)$ for all normal $b$. Also $A$ is Hermitian iff every unitary of the unitization has spectrum in the unit circle. ([Thill, arXiv:math/0701306](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0701306))
- **Enveloping C*-algebra and spectral invariance (46K05, 46K10).** A Banach *-algebra is reduced if its *-representations separate points; its enveloping C*-algebra $C^*(A)$ is the completion of $A$ in $\|a\|=\sup_\pi\|\pi(a)\|$ over all *-representations $\pi$ (a norm exactly when $A$ is reduced; otherwise one first divides out its null space). For reduced $A$ the following are equivalent: $A$ is Hermitian; $A$ is symmetric; $A$ is spectrally invariant in $C^*(A)$; $r_A(a)=r_{C^*(A)}(a)$ for every $a$. Barnes–Hulanicki theorem: if $\pi:A\to B(H)$ is a faithful *-representation (with $\pi(1_A)=1$ when $A$ is unital), $S$ is a *-subalgebra of $A$, and $r_A(a)=\|\pi(a)\|$ for all self-adjoint $a\in S$, then $\mathrm{Sp}_A(a)=\mathrm{Sp}_{B(H)}(\pi(a))$ for all $a\in S$. ([Austad–Ortega, arXiv:2105.14793](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14793))
- **Automatic continuity of positive functionals (Varopoulos, Shirali).** A positive linear functional on a Banach *-algebra with a bounded one-sided approximate unit has finite variation and is therefore continuous; the proof uses Cohen's factorization theorem. ([Thill, arXiv:math/0701306](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0701306))
- **GNS construction (46K10).** For a state $\rho$ of a C*-algebra there are a *-representation $\pi$ and a unit cyclic vector $\xi$ with $\rho(a)=\langle\pi(a)\xi,\xi\rangle$, unique up to unitary equivalence, and $\pi$ is irreducible iff $\rho$ is pure ([Wikipedia: GNS construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand%E2%80%93Naimark%E2%80%93Segal_construction)). Rickart's B*-algebras, with $\|xx^*\|=\|x\|^2$, are exactly C*-algebras ([Wikipedia: C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebra)).
- **Hermitian groups.** A locally compact group $G$ is Hermitian if $L^1(G)$ is a Hermitian Banach *-algebra; the class includes compact extensions of nilpotent groups and all compactly generated groups of polynomial growth ([Austad–Ortega, arXiv:2105.14793](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14793)). Samei and Wiersma proved every quasi-Hermitian locally compact group is amenable, confirming a conjecture about Hermitian groups open since the 1960s, by spectral interpolation across Banach *-algebras between $L^1(G)$ and the reduced group C*-algebra ([Samei–Wiersma, arXiv:1805.07908](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07908)). For every local field $\mathbb{K}$, the affine group $\mathbb{K}\rtimes\mathbb{K}^*$ is Hermitian; for non-archimedean $\mathbb{K}$ these are totally disconnected Hermitian groups of exponential growth ([Carter, arXiv:2504.06893](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.06893v1)). These results link the area to [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory) and [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory).
- **Hilbert algebras (46K15).** A left Hilbert algebra has an involution $x\mapsto x^\sharp$ and inner product such that left multiplications are bounded, $(xy,z)=(y,x^\sharp z)$, $\sharp$ is preclosed, and products span a dense subspace. Left multiplication generates a von Neumann algebra $\lambda(\mathfrak A)''$, and the closure $S$ of $\sharp$ has polar decomposition $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ (Tomita 1967, Takesaki 1970). If $\sharp$ is isometric (the unimodular case), the generated algebra is a direct sum of type I and type II von Neumann algebras. ([Wikipedia: Tomita–Takesaki theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomita%E2%80%93Takesaki_theory))

### History
Gelfand and Naimark's 1943 paper characterized C*-algebras abstractly, Rickart named B*-algebras in 1946, and Segal introduced the term "C*-algebra" in 1947 ([Wikipedia: C*-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C*-algebra)); Segal also sharpened the GNS construction implicit in Gelfand–Naimark ([Wikipedia: GNS construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand%E2%80%93Naimark%E2%80%93Segal_construction)). Tomita's 1967 theory of left Hilbert algebras became widely known through Takesaki's 1970 account ([Wikipedia: Tomita–Takesaki theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomita%E2%80%93Takesaki_theory)). The second volume of Palmer's *Banach Algebras and the General Theory of *-Algebras*, devoted to *-algebras, appeared from Cambridge University Press in 2001 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511574757)). Whether Hermitian groups are amenable stood from the 1960s until Samei and Wiersma's work ([Samei–Wiersma, arXiv:1805.07908](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07908)), and the case $\mathbb{Q}_p\rtimes\mathbb{Q}_p^*$, stated as open in Palmer's book and in Palma's 2015 paper, was settled by Carter in 2025 as a consequence of a theorem in Leptin's original article ([Carter, arXiv:2504.06893](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.06893v1)).

### Open problems
- **Discrete Hermitian groups of exponential growth.** It is still an open question whether there exists a discrete Hermitian group with exponential growth. ([Carter, arXiv:2504.06893](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.06893v1))
- **Is $\mathbb{Q}_p\rtimes\mathbb{Z}$ Hermitian?** Whether $\mathbb{Q}_p\rtimes\mathbb{Z}$ and certain generalisations are Hermitian is posed as an open question by Palma and by Carter. ([Carter, arXiv:2504.06893](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.06893v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [*-algebra, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/*-algebra): involutions, self-adjoint and skew-adjoint parts, examples.
- **Learn:** [Thill, Introduction to Normed *-Algebras and their Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0701306): book-length notes on Hermitian Banach *-algebras, the Pták function, Shirali–Ford, positive functionals and the enveloping C*-algebra.
- **Primary:** [Samei and Wiersma, Quasi-Hermitian locally compact groups are amenable](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07908): research paper settling the Hermitian-implies-amenable conjecture; [Austad and Ortega, Groupoids and Hermitian Banach *-algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14793): research paper with a compact account of Hermitian theory and spectral invariance.
- **Further reading:** [Palmer, Banach Algebras and the General Theory of *-Algebras, Vol. II (CUP, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511574757): the volume on *-algebras, from general theory through Banach *-algebras to locally compact groups; [Carter, The affine group of a local field is Hermitian](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.06893v1): recent research paper with open questions.
references.Magnetostatics:
## Reference
### Overview
Magnetostatics is the study of magnetic fields produced by steady currents, meaning currents that do not change in time. It is the magnetic analogue of electrostatics. It remains a good approximation for non-static currents as long as they do not alternate rapidly. It is widely used in micromagnetics, including models of magnetic storage, where it can predict switching on nanosecond time scales. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetostatics))

The field equations are Gauss's law for magnetism, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$, and Ampère's law, $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J$. Because $\mathbf B$ is divergence-free it is the curl of a vector potential $\mathbf A$, which for given currents is an explicit integral over $\mathbf J$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetostatics)) The original Ampère law applies only to steady currents in closed circuits. Taking its divergence forces $\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$, which conflicts with charge conservation wherever charge density changes, for instance on a charging capacitor. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amp%C3%A8re%27s_circuital_law))

For a researcher the useful content is the potential theory. In Coulomb gauge each Cartesian component of $\mathbf A$ satisfies a Poisson equation with source $\mu_0\mathbf J$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_vector_potential)). Far from a localized current, the leading term is a magnetic dipole ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dipole)). The Helmholtz theorem gives uniqueness for fields decaying at infinity ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_decomposition)). Energy and inductance are the bilinear forms $\tfrac12\int\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf A$ and Neumann's double line integral ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_energy)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inductance)).

### Formal definition
Magnetostatics is the time-independent truncation of Maxwell's equations for steady currents:
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J,$$
with integral forms $\oint_S\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf S=0$ and $\oint_C\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf l=I_{\rm enc}$. In magnetized media $\mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf M+\mathbf H)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetostatics)) In terms of total current, $\oint_C\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0 I_{\rm enc}$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J$, equivalent by the Kelvin–Stokes theorem. The $\mathbf H$ form involves only free current, while the $\mathbf B$ form includes bound magnetization and polarization currents. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amp%C3%A8re%27s_circuital_law))

**Vector potential and gauge.** $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$. Adding a curl-free field to $\mathbf A$ leaves $\mathbf B$ unchanged. In the Coulomb gauge $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=0$,
$$\nabla^2\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J,\qquad \mathbf A(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d^3r',$$
the analogue of $\nabla^2V=-\rho/\varepsilon_0$. The circulation $\oint_\Gamma\mathbf A\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$ equals the magnetic flux through a surface bounded by $\Gamma$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_vector_potential))

**Magnetic scalar potential.** Where free currents can be ignored, $\nabla\times\mathbf H=0$, so $\mathbf H=-\nabla\Phi_M$ and $\nabla^2\Phi_M=\nabla\cdot\mathbf M$. Here $\nabla\cdot\mathbf M$ plays the role of a magnetic charge density; comparing with $\nabla^2V=-\rho/\varepsilon_0$, the effective density is $\rho_M=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf M$, and $\mathbf J_M=\nabla\times\mathbf M$ is the equivalent current used in the vector-potential method. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetostatics))

### Key results
- **Biot–Savart law.** For a filamentary steady current $I$ along $C$,
$$\mathbf B(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_C\frac{I\,d\boldsymbol\ell\times\mathbf r'}{|\mathbf r'|^3},\qquad\mathbf r'=\mathbf r-\boldsymbol\ell.$$
Writing $\mathbf B$ as a curl shows $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$, and taking the curl again with $\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$ gives $\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J$. Outside magnetostatics the law is superseded by Jefimenko's equations. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biot%E2%80%93Savart_law)) The volume form is $\mathbf B(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\mathbf J(\mathbf r')\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')/|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3\,d^3r'$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetostatics))
- **Uniqueness (Helmholtz).** On $\mathbb R^3$, given a sufficiently smooth scalar $d$ and solenoidal $\mathbf C$ vanishing faster than $1/r^2$ at infinity, there is a field $\mathbf F$ with $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=d$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf F=\mathbf C$. It is unique if additionally $\mathbf F\to0$ as $r\to\infty$. So charge and current densities vanishing at infinity determine the static $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ uniquely. The potentials are not unique, because of gauge freedom. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_decomposition))
- **Dipole moment and far field.** A localized current distribution has magnetic moment $\mathbf m=\tfrac12\int\mathbf r\times\mathbf j\,dV$, which for a planar loop is $\mathbf m=I\mathbf S$. Its far-field vector potential and the point-dipole field are
$$\mathbf A(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{\mathbf m\times\mathbf r}{r^3},\qquad \mathbf B(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\left[\frac{3\hat{\mathbf r}(\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf m)-\mathbf m}{r^3}+\frac{8\pi}{3}\mathbf m\,\delta(\mathbf r)\right].$$
The contact term is the correct one for the current-loop model, and it differs from the fictitious-pole model inside the source. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dipole))
- **Forces, torques and energy of a dipole.** A point dipole $\mathbf m$ in an external field $\mathbf B$ feels force $\mathbf F=\nabla(\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf B)$ and torque $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf m\times\mathbf B$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dipole)). Its potential energy is $U=-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf B$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_energy)).
- **Magnetic energy.** For magnetostatic currents $U=\tfrac12\int\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf A\,dV$, and in linear media $U=\tfrac12\int\mathbf H\cdot\mathbf B\,dV$, with vacuum energy density $B^2/(2\mu_0)$. Neither static expression applies to time-varying sources. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_energy))
- **Inductance and the Neumann formula.** For thin filamentary circuits $C_m,C_n$ the mutual inductance is
$$L_{m,n}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\oint_{C_m}\oint_{C_n}\frac{d\mathbf x_m\cdot d\mathbf x_n}{|\mathbf x_m-\mathbf x_n|}.$$
Energy conservation requires $L_{m,n}=L_{n,m}$, and the stored energy of coupled circuits is $W=\tfrac12\sum_{m,n}i_mL_{m,n}i_n$, reducing to $\tfrac12LI^2$ for one inductor. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inductance))
- **Interface conditions.** With unit normal $\mathbf n_{12}$ from medium 1 to 2, $(\mathbf B_2-\mathbf B_1)\cdot\mathbf n_{12}=0$ and $\mathbf n_{12}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\mathbf j_s$, where $\mathbf j_s$ is free (not polarization) surface current. With $\mathbf j_s=0$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$, $H_{1t}=H_{2t}$ and $\mu_1H_{1n}=\mu_2H_{2n}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interface_conditions_for_electromagnetic_fields))

### Examples
- **Circular loop on its axis.** At distance $x$ along the axis of a loop of radius $R$ carrying $I$, $B=\mu_0IR^2/[2(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}]$ along the axis. Off-axis points need elliptic integrals. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biot%E2%80%93Savart_law))
- **Air-core coils.** In media of relative permeability $1$, Biot–Savart can be integrated piece by piece and superposed, as for air-core inductors. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetostatics))
- **Charging capacitor (counterexample).** Applied to a charging capacitor, the original Ampère law gives inconsistent answers, because $\nabla\cdot\mathbf J\neq0$ there. Adding displacement current resolves this and also permits waves. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amp%C3%A8re%27s_circuital_law))

### History
Ørsted's 1820 observation that a current deflects a compass needle showed that electricity produces magnetism, and Ampère then studied forces between current-carrying wires. Maxwell published a form of the circuital law in 1855, based on a hydrodynamic analogy. He added the displacement current in "On Physical Lines of Force" (1861), at equation 112, and in 1865 generalized the law to account for time-varying currents. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amp%C3%A8re%27s_circuital_law)) "On Physical Lines of Force" appeared in the *Philosophical Magazine* as a four-part paper, and Maxwell used the displacement term in his 1865 paper to derive the electromagnetic [wave equation](node:Wave%20Equation). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Physical_Lines_of_Force)) That paper is "A dynamical theory of the electromagnetic field", *Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond.* 155, 459–512 (1865). ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)) Biot and Savart found their law experimentally in 1820. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biot%E2%80%93Savart_law)) Neumann's formula is from his 1846 paper on induced currents, and Heaviside coined "inductance" in 1884. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inductance))

### Connections
- [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics): the electric static counterpart; $\nabla^2\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J$ mirrors $\nabla^2V=-\rho/\varepsilon_0$.
- [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations): magnetostatics drops the time derivatives.
- [Biot–Savart Law](node:Biot–Savart%20Law): the integral solution for $\mathbf B$ from steady currents.
- [Magnetic Vector Potential](node:Magnetic%20Vector%20Potential): $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$, Coulomb gauge, flux as circulation of $\mathbf A$.
- [Displacement Current](node:Displacement%20Current): the term whose omission defines the magnetostatic regime.
- [Continuity Equation](node:Continuity%20Equation): steady currents require $\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): the scalar and vector potentials solve Poisson equations.
- [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus): Stokes and Helmholtz theorems.
- [Magnetic Monopoles](node:Magnetic%20Monopoles): their absence is what $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$ encodes.
- [Gauge Invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance): freedom $\mathbf A\to\mathbf A+\nabla\lambda$.
- [Electromagnetic Waves](node:Electromagnetic%20Waves): displacement current permits waves.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Steady currents and magnetic fields](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Steady%20currents%20and%20magnetic%20fields)

### Common pitfalls
- **Biot–Savart is magnetostatic.** A uniformly moving point charge is not a steady current, so calling its field a "Biot–Savart law for a point charge" is misleading. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biot%E2%80%93Savart_law))
- **Free versus bound current.** $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f$ uses free current only, whereas $\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J$ uses total current. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amp%C3%A8re%27s_circuital_law)) Likewise the interface jump in tangential $\mathbf H$ is set by free surface current only. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interface_conditions_for_electromagnetic_fields))
- **Gauge choice.** $\nabla^2\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J$ holds in the Coulomb gauge, not in an arbitrary gauge. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_vector_potential))
- **Dipole contact term.** Inside the source, the current-loop and magnetic-pole models give different fields. The $+\frac{8\pi}{3}\mathbf m\delta(\mathbf r)$ term is the current-loop answer. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dipole))
- **Static energy formulas.** $\tfrac12\int\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf A$ and $\tfrac12\int\mathbf H\cdot\mathbf B$ are static expressions and do not apply to time-varying currents. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_energy))

### Open problems
- **Existence of magnetic monopoles.** $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$ encodes the absence of magnetic charge. With magnetic charge density $\rho_m$ it would become $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=\mu_0\rho_m$ in the ampere-metre convention. There is "no known experimental or observational evidence that magnetic monopoles exist", and whether they do remains open. Dirac (1931) showed that a single monopole would force electric charge quantization. MoEDAL at the LHC searches for monopoles with nuclear track detectors and trapping aluminium bars read out by a SQUID, and ATLAS sets cross-section limits for monopoles with one and two Dirac charges. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_monopole))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Magnetostatics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetostatics): field equations, vector and scalar potentials, magnetized media.
- **Reference:** [Magnetic dipole (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dipole): moment, far field, contact term, forces and torques.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 8.07 Electromagnetism II (Guth, Chen, 2012)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-07-electromagnetism-ii-fall-2012/): the [lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-07-electromagnetism-ii-fall-2012/pages/lecture-notes/) include Lecture 10, "Magnetic Multipole Expansion and Magnetic Dipoles", and Lecture 11, "Magnetic Dipoles and Magnetic Fields in Matter".
- **Primary:** [Jackson, *Classical Electrodynamics*, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 1998)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Classical+Electrodynamics,+3rd+Edition-p-9780471309321): standard graduate text; this edition puts Faraday's law and quasi-static fields in Chapter 5 with magnetostatics.
- **Primary:** [Maxwell, "A dynamical theory of the electromagnetic field" (1865)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008): field equations with displacement current.
- **Further reading:** [Jackson, *Classical Electrodynamics* (Wiley)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Classical+Electrodynamics,+3rd+Edition-p-9780471309321), ch. 5.

## Reference
### Overview
Manifold learning, also called nonlinear dimensionality reduction (NLDR), assumes that high-dimensional data lie on or near a curved low-dimensional manifold and seeks low-dimensional coordinates for it, either to visualize the data or to learn the map itself. The methods generalize linear techniques such as principal component analysis to curved structure ([Wikipedia: NLDR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_dimensionality_reduction)).

Most classical algorithms share a pattern: build a neighbourhood graph on the sample, attach local geometric information to it (distances, reconstruction weights, kernel affinities), and solve a global eigenvalue or optimization problem. Isomap keeps estimated geodesic distances, locally linear embedding keeps local reconstruction weights, and Laplacian eigenmaps keep neighbours close; the stochastic neighbour-embedding methods t-SNE and UMAP instead choose embeddings whose pairwise similarity distribution matches that of the input ([Oxford lecture](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~cucuring/CDT_07_Nonlinear_Dim_Red_a__cMDS_ISOMAP_LLE_LapEig_FoDS.pdf); [Wikipedia: NLDR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_dimensionality_reduction)); t-SNE was introduced as a visualization technique ([van der Maaten and Hinton 2008](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v9/vandermaaten08a.html)).

The field's theory connects graph constructions to differential geometry. As sampling density grows, graph shortest paths approximate geodesic distance ([Tenenbaum et al. 2000](https://www.mit.edu/~9.520/spring06/Papers/Tenenbaum-science-00.pdf)), and point-cloud Laplacians approximate the Laplace–Beltrami operator ([Belkin and Niyogi 2006](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2006/file/5848ad959570f87753a60ce8be1567f3-Paper.pdf)). Whether data actually satisfy the manifold hypothesis can itself be tested statistically ([Fefferman, Mitter, Narayanan](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.0425)).

### Formal definition
Given points $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^D$ assumed to lie on a $d$-dimensional embedded manifold $\mathcal{M}$ with $d\ll D$, a manifold-learning algorithm outputs $y_1,\dots,y_n\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ such that nearby points remain nearby and distant points remain distant, measuring distance along $\mathcal{M}$ (geodesic distance) rather than in the ambient space ([Oxford lecture](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~cucuring/CDT_07_Nonlinear_Dim_Red_a__cMDS_ISOMAP_LLE_LapEig_FoDS.pdf)). Standard instances:

**Isomap.** (1) Connect each point to its $K$ nearest neighbours or to all points within radius $\varepsilon$, with edge weights $d_X(i,j)$; (2) estimate geodesic distances $d_{\mathcal M}(i,j)$ by graph shortest-path distances $d_G(i,j)$; (3) apply classical MDS, choosing $y_i$ to minimize $E = \|\tau(D_G)-\tau(D_Y)\|_{L^2}$, where $\tau$ converts distances to inner products; the minimizer is given by the top $d$ eigenvectors of $\tau(D_G)$ ([Tenenbaum et al. 2000](https://www.mit.edu/~9.520/spring06/Papers/Tenenbaum-science-00.pdf)).

**Locally linear embedding.** Find weights minimizing $E(W)=\sum_i \|x_i-\sum_j W_{ij}x_j\|^2$ with $W_{ij}=0$ for non-neighbours and rows summing to one; then, with $W$ fixed, minimize $C(Y)=\sum_i\|y_i-\sum_j W_{ij}y_j\|^2$, a sparse eigenproblem solved by the bottom nonzero eigenvectors ([Wikipedia: NLDR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_dimensionality_reduction)).

**Laplacian eigenmaps.** With affinities $W_{ij}=e^{-\|x_i-x_j\|^2/t}$ on graph edges, degree matrix $D_{ii}=\sum_j W_{ij}$ and Laplacian $L=D-W$, solve
$$\min_{Y^\top D Y = I}\operatorname{tr}(Y^\top L Y),\qquad \text{equivalently } Lf=\lambda Df,$$
discard the constant eigenvector $f_0$, and embed $x_i\mapsto (f_1(i),\dots,f_d(i))$; the objective equals $\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\|y^{(i)}-y^{(j)}\|^2W_{ij}$ ([Oxford lecture](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~cucuring/CDT_07_Nonlinear_Dim_Red_a__cMDS_ISOMAP_LLE_LapEig_FoDS.pdf)).

**t-SNE.** Input similarities $p_{j|i}\propto \exp(-\|X_i-X_j\|^2/2\tau_i^2)$, symmetrized as $p_{ij}=(p_{i|j}+p_{j|i})/2n$ with bandwidths $\tau_i$ set by perplexity; output similarities $q_{ij}\propto(1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)^{-1}$; minimize $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\,\|\,Q)=\sum_{i\neq j}p_{ij}\log(p_{ij}/q_{ij})$ ([Cai and Ma 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.07536)).

### Key results
- **Isomap consistency (Tenenbaum, de Silva, Langford 2000).** For manifolds whose intrinsic geometry is that of a convex region of Euclidean space (however folded in the ambient space), Isomap asymptotically recovers the true dimensionality and geometry: as the number of points grows, $d_G(i,j)\to d_{\mathcal M}(i,j)$, at a rate governed by radius of curvature, branch separation, and sampling density ([Tenenbaum et al. 2000](https://www.mit.edu/~9.520/spring06/Papers/Tenenbaum-science-00.pdf)).
- **Convergence of Laplacian eigenmaps (Belkin–Niyogi 2006).** Let $\mathcal M$ be a compact smooth Riemannian submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^N$ without boundary, with $x_i$ i.i.d. uniform on $\mathcal M$, and let $\hat L^{t}_n$ be the Gaussian-kernel point-cloud Laplacian. There is a sequence $t_n\to0$ such that the $i$-th eigenvalue and eigenfunction of $\hat L^{t_n}_n$ converge in probability to the $i$-th eigenvalue and eigenfunction of the Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta=-\operatorname{div}\nabla$ ([Belkin and Niyogi 2006](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2006/file/5848ad959570f87753a60ce8be1567f3-Paper.pdf)).
- **Testing the manifold hypothesis (Fefferman–Mitter–Narayanan 2013).** For a distribution supported in the unit ball of a separable Hilbert space, there is an algorithm that, from i.i.d. samples and with probability at least $1-\delta$, correctly decides between "some manifold with relaxed volume and reach bounds fits well (in mean-squared distance)" and "no manifold with tightened bounds fits well," where the candidate manifolds have dimension $d$, volume at most $V$ and reach at least $\tau$, and the relaxed and tightened bounds differ by a constant factor $C$ ([Fefferman, Mitter, Narayanan](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.0425)).
- **Provable t-SNE clustering (Arora–Hu–Kothari 2018).** Under a deterministic well-clusterability condition, which holds for mixtures of well-separated log-concave distributions, t-SNE provably produces a visualization that separates the clusters ([Arora, Hu, Kothari](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v75/arora18a.html)).
- **Early exaggeration as power iteration (Cai–Ma 2022).** The early-exaggeration stage of t-SNE is asymptotically equivalent to power iterations driven by the graph Laplacian of the input affinities (an implicit spectral clustering); the analysis exhibits an implicit [regularization](node:Regularization) effect and shows that for weakly clustered data the stage must be stopped early (cf. [early stopping](node:Early%20Stopping)) ([Cai and Ma 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.07536)).

### Examples
- **Faces.** On 698 synthetic $64\times64$ face images, Isomap with $K=6$ finds a three-dimensional embedding whose axes correlate with left-right pose, up-down pose, and lighting direction ([Tenenbaum et al. 2000](https://www.mit.edu/~9.520/spring06/Papers/Tenenbaum-science-00.pdf)).
- **Swiss roll.** On the Swiss roll, where linear methods fail, Isomap's residual variance bottoms out at $d=2$, recovering the intrinsic dimension ([Tenenbaum et al. 2000](https://www.mit.edu/~9.520/spring06/Papers/Tenenbaum-science-00.pdf)).
- **Diffusion maps.** With $K_{ij}=\exp(-\|x_i-x_j\|^2/\sigma^2)$ on neighbours and $P=D^{-1}K$, the diffusion distance $D_t^2(x,y)=\|p_t(x,\cdot)-p_t(y,\cdot)\|^2$ is more robust to noise than geodesic distance ([Wikipedia: NLDR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_dimensionality_reduction)).

### History
Isomap (Tenenbaum, de Silva, Langford) and locally linear embedding (Roweis, Saul) both appeared in 2000; Laplacian eigenmaps (Belkin, Niyogi) followed in 2001, Hessian LLE (Donoho, Grimes) in 2003, local tangent space alignment (Zhang, Zha) in the mid-2000s and diffusion maps (Coifman, Lafon) in 2006; kernel PCA dates from 1998 ([Wikipedia: NLDR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_dimensionality_reduction)). t-SNE, a variant of stochastic neighbour embedding that reduces crowding of points in the centre of the map, was published in 2008 ([van der Maaten and Hinton 2008](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v9/vandermaaten08a.html)). UMAP (McInnes, Healy, Melville, 2018) was built from Riemannian geometry and algebraic topology and is claimed to be competitive with t-SNE in quality while faster and arguably better at global structure ([McInnes et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03426)).

### Connections
- [Principal Component Analysis](node:Principal%20Component%20Analysis): the linear special case; Isomap applies classical MDS, a PCA-like eigendecomposition, to geodesic distances.
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): the model of the data's support.
- [Laplace–Beltrami Operator](node:Laplace–Beltrami%20Operator): the continuum limit of the graph Laplacian in Laplacian eigenmaps.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): Isomap estimates geodesic distance by graph shortest paths.
- [Spectral Clustering](node:Spectral%20Clustering): shares the graph Laplacian eigenvector machinery; t-SNE's early exaggeration behaves like it.
- [Kernel Methods](node:Kernel%20Methods): kernel PCA is the kernelized linear baseline.
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence): the t-SNE objective.
- [Distance Matrices and Metric Embeddings](node:Distance%20Matrices%20and%20Metric%20Embeddings): MDS and metric embedding questions behind distance-preserving methods.
- [Topological Data Analysis](node:Topological%20Data%20Analysis): another family of methods for the shape of point clouds.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): intrinsic distances that the methods try to recover.

### Common pitfalls
- **Short-circuits.** Isomap is sensitive to "shortcuts," graph edges that jump between distant parts of the manifold, and all-pairs shortest paths cost $O(n^3)$ ([Oxford lecture](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~cucuring/CDT_07_Nonlinear_Dim_Red_a__cMDS_ISOMAP_LLE_LapEig_FoDS.pdf)).
- **Non-convex or curved manifolds.** Isomap's guarantee covers manifolds isometric to convex Euclidean regions; for non-Euclidean manifolds such as a hemisphere or a torus it still returns the globally optimal low-dimensional Euclidean representation as measured by its cost function, outside the scope of that guarantee ([Tenenbaum et al. 2000](https://www.mit.edu/~9.520/spring06/Papers/Tenenbaum-science-00.pdf)).
- **Sampling density.** LLE handles non-uniform sampling density poorly, and the neighbourhood size $K$ must be tuned ([Wikipedia: NLDR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_dimensionality_reduction)).
- **Reading t-SNE plots.** For clustered data, t-SNE with random initialization and early exaggeration is reliable for cluster membership but not for the relative position of clusters, and false clusters can appear as artifacts of random initialization, so it helps to run it several times ([Cai and Ma 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.07536)).

### Open problems
- **Limits of neighbour embedding.** Cai and Ma leave open the limiting behaviour of the t-SNE map in its stabilization phase, the interpretation of within-cluster structure, the number of iterations needed, and data-adaptive bandwidth choice; they also pose as future work whether t-SNE must sacrifice global structure to embed local structure well, and what conditions on the data are necessary for a low-dimensional map that is a metric embedding to exist ([Cai and Ma 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.07536)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Nonlinear dimensionality reduction (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_dimensionality_reduction): catalogue of methods with formulas.
- **Learn:** [Cucuringu, Oxford CDT lecture on cMDS, Isomap, LLE, Laplacian eigenmaps](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~cucuring/CDT_07_Nonlinear_Dim_Red_a__cMDS_ISOMAP_LLE_LapEig_FoDS.pdf): derivations of the spectral methods.
- **Primary:** [Tenenbaum, de Silva, Langford 2000, A Global Geometric Framework for Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction](https://www.mit.edu/~9.520/spring06/Papers/Tenenbaum-science-00.pdf): Isomap.
- **Primary:** [Belkin and Niyogi 2006, Convergence of Laplacian Eigenmaps](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2006/file/5848ad959570f87753a60ce8be1567f3-Paper.pdf): spectral convergence to Laplace–Beltrami.
- **Primary:** [Cai and Ma 2022, Theoretical Foundations of t-SNE](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.07536): gradient-flow analysis of t-SNE.
- **Further reading:** [Lee and Verleysen, Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction (Springer, 2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-39351-3): monograph on the field.
references.Manyfold Universe:
## Reference
### Overview
The Manyfold Universe is a 1999 proposal by Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos, Dvali and Kaloper (JHEP 0012 (2000) 010). In it, our world is a brane folded many times inside sub-millimetre extra dimensions, giving a "Manyfold" of parallel sheets with identical microphysics. Matter on another fold is close to us through the bulk and gravitates normally. Its light, however, must travel along the brane around a fold, which can take a cosmological time, so the matter looks dark. ([Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos, Dvali & Kaloper](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9911386); [PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))

The construction lives inside the ADD framework of [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions). Standard Model fields are confined to a 3-brane and gravity propagates in $\delta$ extra dimensions of volume $V_\delta$, so that $M_P^2=V_\delta\bar M_D^{2+\delta}$ and the fundamental scale $M_D$ can be near a TeV. That gives $R\sim0.5$ mm for $\delta=2$. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [Wikipedia: Large extra dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_extra_dimensions)) More broadly, [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology) treats our visible universe as a brane in a higher-dimensional bulk. ([Wikipedia: Brane cosmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brane_cosmology))

The proposal is a single paper with modest follow-up. INSPIRE records 81 citing works. The most cited of these are general braneworld, mirror-matter and dark-matter papers rather than developments of the folded-brane picture. ([INSPIRE record](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=arxiv%3Ahep-ph%2F9911386&fields=citation_count,titles,control_number); [INSPIRE citing works](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=refersto%3Arecid%3A510274&size=100&fields=titles,arxiv_eprints,citation_count&sort=mostcited)) Its cosmology predates the standard $\Lambda$CDM fit, which bears on several of its numbers (see Common pitfalls).

### Formal definition
A *Bifold* is a brane folded once: two parallel 4D sheets joined by a high-curvature "tip". A *Manyfold* has $n_f$ "right" sheets ($R$-branes) next to our "left" brane $L$. Brane-localized fields such as photons travel along the brane, so light from another fold arrives only after going around a tip at distance $\ell$. Gravitons cross the bulk at the sub-millimetre separation. ([Arkani-Hamed et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9911386))

The paper's baseline assumptions are that $\ell\gg H^{-1}$, so the folds are electromagnetically invisible, and that bulk fields such as the dilaton have constant vevs, so that observers on every fold see identical microphysics (for example the same electron-to-proton mass ratio). The dark-matter phenomenology is controlled by two ratios, $T_R/T_L$ (temperatures) and $n_{BR}/n_{BL}$ (baryon densities on $R$-branes versus ours). ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))

### Key results
- **Dark matter is Standard Model matter on other folds.** It is microphysically identical to ours and so can dissipate and clump. It may form dark stars that act as MACHO candidates, and it can raise the rate of collapse events, and hence [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves), seen by LIGO and LISA. ([Arkani-Hamed et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9911386))
- **Dissipation bound.** If $R$-matter tracked ordinary baryons, it would form hybrid stars and globular clusters, which are not observed, and it would collapse to galactic, not halo, scales ([Galaxy Formation](node:Galaxy%20Formation)). The cooling time scales as $t_{\rm cool}\sim n_B^{-1}$, and galaxy formation began at $z\sim4$, so $n_{BR}/n_{BL}\lesssim1/4$ delays $R$-galaxy formation to the present. In the limit $n_{BR}/n_{BL}\to0$, $n_f\to\infty$ with $n_fn_{BR}\simeq30\,n_{BL}$, $R$-matter behaves like ordinary CDM "critically closing the universe". ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))
- **BBN.** Light-element abundances on our fold require $T_R\ll T_L$. The $R$-branes then undergo their own, different nucleosynthesis; the paper cites Wagoner's results that $^4$He rises toward about 80% as the effective number of light species approaches about 10. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))
- **Mirror models.** The same dissipation argument excludes mirror sectors isomorphic to ours if they make up more than about $1/30$ of the critical density, unless there are many copies or an asymmetry, which bulk profiles could generate. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))
- **Gravitational waves.** If violent processes on $R$-branes occur at our rate, gravitational-wave sources increase by about 30, the dark-to-ordinary ratio the paper assumes. If $\ell<H^{-1}$, proximity through the bulk adds a factor of order $(\ell H)^{-1}$. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))
- **Distance to the nearest tip.** Distant matter would then sit on colder folds with different primordial deuterium. Deuterium measured in quasar absorbers out to a fraction of $H^{-1}$ suggests $\ell$ is at least of that order, but the authors note it could be reproduced in other ways, for example by adjusting $n_{BR}$. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))
- **[Sterile Neutrinos](node:Sterile%20Neutrinos).** A single bulk neutrino mixes our $\nu_L$ equally with copies on other folds, and for three folds the mixing is maximal. The nucleosynthesis bound becomes $\Delta m^2<3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{eV}^2/\sin^42\theta$. Since $\sin^42\theta\sim1$, this gives $m_D\lesssim10^{-2}$ eV. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))
- **Supersymmetry breaking.** A folded brane is not a BPS object, which gives a geometric route to [Supersymmetry Breaking](node:Supersymmetry%20Breaking) on our world. ([Arkani-Hamed et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9911386))

### Examples
- **Wall-inflaton initial conditions.** Our fold must be far more baryon-rich than the others, which at first looks like fine tuning. The authors argue that inflation driven by a wall-localized inflaton can naturally produce this asymmetry. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))
- **Horizon problem.** A brane originally crumpled in the bulk allows apparently superluminal communication through the bulk. This gives a possible non-inflationary handle on the horizon problem, though extra dynamics are needed for flatness. ([Arkani-Hamed et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9911386))
- **Crystal Manyfolds.** Kaloper built families of intersecting positive- and negative-tension branes in AdS. Adding connected 3-branes gives a Manyfold example, and bulk gravitons there form Bloch-wave bands (Phys. Lett. B 474 (2000) 269). ([Kaloper](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9912125))

### History
ADD (1998) proposed gravity-only extra dimensions as a resolution of the [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem). Rubakov and Shaposhnikov (1983) had earlier considered confining particles along extra directions, and Randall and Sundrum (1999) introduced warped alternatives. ([Wikipedia: Large extra dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_extra_dimensions); [Wikipedia: Brane cosmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brane_cosmology); [Csaki, TASI lectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0404096)) The Manyfold paper (arXiv November 1999) added the idea that a single ADD brane could be folded. ([Arkani-Hamed et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9911386)) Related later work includes Kaloper's crystal Manyfolds and Dvali and Redi's $10^{32}$ permuted Standard Model copies with a TeV gravity cutoff, a separate model that also uses many hidden copies. Dvali and Redi predict neutron oscillation into dark copies as a low-energy signal. ([Kaloper](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9912125); [Dvali & Redi, PRD 80 (2009) 055001](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.1709))

### Connections
- [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions): the ADD volume relation and sub-millimetre bulk in which the brane folds.
- [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology): Standard Model fields on a brane in a bulk.
- [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions) and [Compactification](node:Compactification): the Manyfold is an embedding of one brane in a compact bulk, not a new compactification.
- [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale): lowered to $M_D\sim$ TeV in ADD.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): here, dissipative Standard Model matter on other folds.
- [Dissipative Dark Matter](node:Dissipative%20Dark%20Matter): the Manyfold's $R$-matter is an early dissipative candidate.
- [Mirror Matter](node:Mirror%20Matter): isomorphic copies; the paper's $1/30$ bound applies to them.
- [Neutron–Mirror-Neutron Oscillations](node:Neutron–Mirror-Neutron%20Oscillations): the signal Dvali and Redi propose for many dark copies.
- [Sterile Neutrinos](node:Sterile%20Neutrinos): neutrinos on odd folds act as sterile partners.
- [Supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry) and [Supersymmetry Breaking](node:Supersymmetry%20Breaking): a non-BPS folded brane breaks it.
- [Tests of the Inverse-Square Law](node:Tests%20of%20the%20Inverse-Square%20Law): sub-millimetre gravity tests bound the bulk size.
- [Gravitational Microlensing](node:Gravitational%20Microlensing): the MACHO data the paper invoked.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model): the modern cosmology against which its numbers must be rescaled.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Extra dimensions and compactification](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Extra%20dimensions%20and%20compactification)

### Common pitfalls
- **The numbers are pre-$\Lambda$CDM.** The factor $\sim30$ (dark-to-ordinary density, with matter "critically closing the universe") reflects the paper's 1999 assumptions. Planck 2018 gives $\Omega_ch^2=0.120\pm0.001$, $\Omega_bh^2=0.0224\pm0.0001$ and $\Omega_m=0.315\pm0.007$, a ratio $\Omega_c/\Omega_b\approx5.4$ in a universe that matter does not close. The source-count enhancement and $n_fn_{BR}$ normalisation should be rescaled accordingly. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386); [Planck 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209))
- **The MACHO motivation has weakened.** The paper cites lensing data favouring sub-solar dark MACHOs. Later EROS-2 did not confirm the MACHO collaboration's signal, and microlensing and Hubble surveys have ruled out MACHOs over a broad mass range as a significant part of the dark matter. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386); [Wikipedia: MACHO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massive_compact_halo_object))
- **ADD is now tightly constrained.** Torsion-balance tests give $R<30\,\mu$m at 95% CL for $\delta=2$, i.e. $M_D>4.0$ TeV. ATLAS (CMS) jet-plus-missing-momentum searches with 139 (137) fb$^{-1}$ at 13 TeV give $M_D>5.9$–$11.2$ ($5.5$–$10.7$) TeV. SN1987A cooling gives $M_D>27$ (2.4) TeV and neutron-star heating $M_D>1700$ (76) TeV for $\delta=2$ (3). These bounds push $M_D$ well beyond a TeV for two extra dimensions. ([PDG Review: Extra Dimensions](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Dark folds are not a second Standard Model sector.** They are parts of one connected brane, so light can in principle arrive after travelling around a tip. ([Arkani-Hamed et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9911386))

### Open problems
- **Existence of large extra dimensions.** No evidence for large extra dimensions has been found. LHC results constrain them severely, while covering only part of the predicted range, and GW170817 gives weak limits. ([Wikipedia: Large extra dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_extra_dimensions); [Wikipedia: Brane cosmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brane_cosmology))
- **Structure formation with $R$-matter.** The authors describe detailed structure formation on $R$-branes, given $T_R/T_L$ and $n_{BR}/n_{BL}$, as a well-defined but challenging programme. It depends on the different chemistry those branes inherit from their BBN. ([PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/9911386))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Large extra dimensions (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_extra_dimensions): the ADD setting and its experimental status.
- **Learn:** [Csaki, TASI Lectures on Extra Dimensions and Branes](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0404096): brane model building, large and warped extra dimensions.
- **Primary:** [Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos, Dvali & Kaloper, "Manyfold Universe", JHEP 0012 (2000) 010](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9911386): the original proposal.
- **Primary:** [PDG Review 85: Extra Dimensions (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf): current laboratory, collider and astrophysical bounds on ADD.
- **Further reading:** [Kaloper, Crystal Manyfold Universes in AdS Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9912125) and [Dvali & Redi, Phenomenology of $10^{32}$ Dark Sectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.1709).
references.Markov Chain Monte Carlo:
## Reference
### Overview
Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a class of algorithms for drawing samples from a probability distribution $\pi$ by constructing a Markov chain whose equilibrium distribution is $\pi$; the states visited by the chain are then used as (correlated) samples. It is used for distributions too complex or too high-dimensional to study with analytic techniques alone ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)). Because the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance rule involves only ratios $\pi(x')/\pi(x)$, the target need only be known up to a normalising constant ([Wikipedia: Metropolis–Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm)).

The basic estimator is the ergodic average $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N h(X_i)$, which converges almost surely to $\pi(h)$ from $\pi$-almost every starting point under $\varphi$-irreducibility and aperiodicity (with $\pi(|h|)<\infty$) and, under further conditions, has Gaussian fluctuations of order $N^{-1/2}$. The price compared with independent [Monte Carlo](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Methods) is autocorrelation between successive states, which increases the variance of estimators ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)). The theory of MCMC is therefore the theory of [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains) on general state spaces: irreducibility, recurrence, ergodicity, rates of convergence, and central limit theorems ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0404033)).

The main algorithm families are Metropolis–Hastings (propose, then accept or reject), Gibbs sampling (update coordinates from their full conditionals), slice sampling, and Hamiltonian (hybrid) Monte Carlo, which uses gradient information and simulated Hamiltonian dynamics to make distant, low-correlation proposals ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo); [Neal 2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.1901)).

### Formal definition
Let $\pi$ be a target distribution on a state space $\mathcal X$. A transition kernel $T$ leaves $\pi$ **invariant** if $\pi(x)=\sum_{x'}T(x',x)\pi(x')$ (an integral on general spaces), and satisfies [detailed balance](node:Detailed%20Balance) (is reversible) with respect to $\pi$ if
$$\pi(x)\,T(x,x')=\pi(x')\,T(x',x)\qquad\text{for all }x,x'.$$
Summing over $x'$ shows that detailed balance implies invariance ([Princeton COS513 notes](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall10/cos513/notes/2010-12-01.pdf)); it is sufficient but not necessary ([Wikipedia: Metropolis–Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm)).

**Metropolis–Hastings.** From the current state $x$, draw a candidate $x'$ from a proposal kernel $B(x,x')$ and accept it with probability
$$A(x,x')=\min\!\left(1,\ \frac{\pi(x')\,B(x',x)}{\pi(x)\,B(x,x')}\right),$$
otherwise keep $x$. Then $\pi(x)B(x,x')A(x,x')=\min\{\pi(x)B(x,x'),\pi(x')B(x',x)\}$ is symmetric in $(x,x')$, which is detailed balance. When $B$ is symmetric the rule reduces to the original Metropolis algorithm, and if each of several component-wise kernels $B_k$ satisfies detailed balance, so does each step of their composition ([Princeton COS513 notes](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall10/cos513/notes/2010-12-01.pdf)).

**Gibbs sampling** updates one coordinate at a time from its full conditional distribution; it is a special case of Metropolis–Hastings whose acceptance probability is always 1 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)).

**Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.** Write $U(x)=-\ln f(x)$ for the target density $f$, add a momentum $p$ with kinetic energy $K(p)=\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p$, and set $H(x,p)=U(x)+K(p)$. Each update resamples $p$ from a Gaussian, runs $L$ leapfrog steps of size $\Delta t$,
$$p\leftarrow p-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\nabla U(x),\quad x\leftarrow x+\Delta t\,M^{-1}p,\quad p\leftarrow p-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\nabla U(x),$$
and accepts the endpoint with probability $\min\{1,\exp(H_{\text{old}}-H_{\text{new}})\}$. The leapfrog map is time-reversible and volume-preserving, so the proposal needs no Jacobian factor ([Wikipedia: HMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_Monte_Carlo); [Neal 2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.1901)).

**General state spaces.** A chain with kernel $P$ is **$\varphi$-irreducible**, for a non-zero $\sigma$-finite measure $\varphi$, if for every measurable $A$ with $\varphi(A)>0$ and every $x$ there is $n=n(x)$ with $P^n(x,A)>0$ ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)); it is **Harris recurrent** if it is $\psi$-irreducible and every set $A$ with $\psi(A)>0$ is Harris recurrent, i.e. the chain started anywhere in $A$ returns to $A$ infinitely often with probability 1 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)). A set $C$ is **small** if there are $n_0$, $\epsilon>0$ and a probability measure $\nu$ with $P^{n_0}(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\,\nu(\cdot)$ for $x\in C$ (a minorisation condition). The chain is **uniformly ergodic** if $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|\le M\rho^n$ with $\rho<1$, $M<\infty$, and **geometrically ergodic** if the same holds with $M=M(x)<\infty$ for $\pi$-a.e. $x$ ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)).

### Key results
- **Finite-space convergence (Neal 1993).** A homogeneous chain on a finite space with invariant distribution $p^*$ and $\nu=\min_x\min_{x':p^*(x')>0}T(x,x')/p^*(x')>0$ is ergodic, with $|p^*(x)-p_n(x)|\le(1-\nu)^n$ ([Princeton COS513 notes](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall10/cos513/notes/2010-12-01.pdf)).
- **Asymptotic convergence on general spaces.** If a chain on a state space with countably generated $\sigma$-algebra is $\varphi$-irreducible and aperiodic with stationary distribution $\pi$, then $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}\to0$ for $\pi$-a.e. $x$, and if $\pi(|h|)<\infty$ then $\frac1n\sum_{i\le n}h(X_i)\to\pi(h)$ almost surely. Convergence can fail on a $\pi$-null set of starting points ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)). For a chain with $\sigma$-finite invariant measure $\pi$, Harris recurrence is equivalent to the ratio-limit law $S_n(f)/S_n(g)\to\int f\,d\pi/\int g\,d\pi$ for all $f,g\in L^1(\pi)$ with $\int g\,d\pi\ne0$, from an arbitrary starting state ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)).
- **Doeblin condition gives uniform ergodicity.** If the whole space is small, $P^{n_0}(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu(\cdot)$ for all $x$, then $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|\le(1-\epsilon)^{\lfloor n/n_0\rfloor}$ for all $x$ ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)).
- **Drift plus minorisation gives geometric ergodicity.** If a $\varphi$-irreducible aperiodic chain with stationary $\pi$ has a small set $C$ and a function $V:\mathcal X\to[1,\infty]$, finite somewhere, with $PV\le\lambda V+b\,\mathbf 1_C$ for some $0<\lambda<1$, $b<\infty$, then it is geometrically ergodic. A symmetric random-walk Metropolis algorithm is geometrically ergodic essentially if and only if $\pi$ has finite exponential moments (Mengersen and Tweedie) ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)).
- **Central limit theorems.** A $\sqrt n$-CLT holds for $h$ if the chain is uniformly ergodic and $\pi(h^2)<\infty$; if geometrically ergodic and $\pi(|h|^{2+\delta})<\infty$ for some $\delta>0$; or if geometrically ergodic, reversible and $\pi(h^2)<\infty$. Without reversibility the last fails: Häggström constructed a geometrically ergodic chain and $h$ with $\pi(h^2)<\infty$ and no CLT under any scaling ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)). For an aperiodic, irreducible, reversible chain the asymptotic variance is $\gamma_h^2=\mathbb E_\pi[\bar h^2(X_0)]+2\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb E_\pi[\bar h(X_0)\bar h(X_k)]$ with $\bar h=h-\pi(h)$, and the effective sample size is $N_{\text{eff}}=N/(1+2\sum_k\rho_k)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)).
- **Optimal scaling (Roberts, Gelman and Gilks).** For a target $\pi(x)=\prod_{i=1}^d f(x_i)$ with smooth $f$, chain started in stationarity, and random-walk Metropolis proposal variance $\ell^2/d$, the first coordinate sped up by a factor $d$ converges weakly as $d\to\infty$ to the Langevin diffusion $dZ_t=h(\ell)^{1/2}dB_t+\tfrac12h(\ell)\nabla\log\pi(Z_t)\,dt$ with speed $h(\ell)=2\ell^2\Phi(-\sqrt I\ell/2)$, $I=\mathbb E[((\log f)'(Z))^2]$. The speed is maximised at $\ell\approx2.38/\sqrt I$, where the asymptotic acceptance rate is $\approx0.234$; the analogous rate for the Langevin (MALA) algorithm with variance $\ell^2/d^{1/3}$ is $\approx0.574$. So RWM costs $O(d)$ and MALA $O(d^{1/3})$ ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)).
- **Non-reversible chains are better (Neal 2004).** From any irreducible reversible Markov chain on a finite state space one can build a non-reversible chain on a related state space that estimates the same expectations with asymptotic variance no larger (typically smaller), by avoiding, where possible, transitions back to the state just left ([Neal 2004](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0407281)); Diaconis's survey describes the improvement in terms of spectral gap ([Diaconis 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.7754)).

### Examples
- **Random-walk Metropolis on $\mathbb R_+$:** for $\pi(x)\propto e^{-x}$ and a symmetric proposal supported in $[x-a,x+a]$, the drift function $V(x)=e^{cx}$ verifies the drift condition and hence geometric ergodicity ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)).
- **Card shuffling and [random walks on groups](node:Random%20Walks%20on%20Groups):** Diaconis and Shahshahani showed that about $\tfrac12 n\log n$ random transpositions are necessary and sufficient to mix $n$ cards, a model case for sharp [mixing-time](node:Mixing%20Times%20of%20Markov%20Chains) analysis ([Diaconis 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.7754)).
- **Lattice gauge theory:** HMC was introduced as "hybrid Monte Carlo" for [Lattice QCD](node:Lattice%20QCD) ([Wikipedia: HMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_Monte_Carlo)).
- **Bayesian computation:** Stan, PyMC and Turing.jl are probabilistic programming languages implementing HMC; its adoption in statistics grew in the mid-2010s when Stan implemented it with [automatic differentiation](node:Automatic%20Differentiation) ([Wikipedia: HMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_Monte_Carlo)).

### History
The Metropolis algorithm appeared in the 1953 paper "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines" by Metropolis, A. and M. Rosenbluth, A. Teller and E. Teller, assuming a symmetric proposal; credit is disputed, with Marshall Rosenbluth stating that he and Arianna Rosenbluth did the work ([Wikipedia: Metropolis–Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm)). Hastings generalised it to asymmetric proposals in 1970, implicitly introducing component-wise updating; Geman and Geman named Gibbs sampling in 1984 for image processing; Green introduced reversible-jump MCMC for variable-dimension models in 1995, and Propp and Wilson introduced perfect sampling in 1996 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)). Duane, Kennedy, Pendleton and Roweth proposed hybrid Monte Carlo in 1987; Neal extended it to broader statistical problems, including neural networks, in 1996, and Hoffman and Gelman's No-U-Turn Sampler (2014) chooses trajectory lengths automatically ([Wikipedia: HMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_Monte_Carlo)). The uniform-ergodicity theorem goes back to Doeblin and Doob ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)).

### Connections
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains): MCMC is applied Markov chain theory; invariance, irreducibility and recurrence are the correctness conditions.
- [Monte Carlo Methods](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Methods): MCMC replaces independent draws with a dependent chain when direct sampling is impossible.
- [Mixing Times of Markov Chains](node:Mixing%20Times%20of%20Markov%20Chains): quantifies how long a chain must run before its law is close to $\pi$.
- [Bayesian Inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference): the dominant application, sampling posteriors known only up to the evidence.
- [Variational Inference](node:Variational%20Inference): the optimisation-based alternative, trading asymptotic exactness for speed.
- [Sequential Monte Carlo](node:Sequential%20Monte%20Carlo): population-based samplers that often use MCMC moves as rejuvenation kernels.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics): supplies the volume-preserving, reversible dynamics behind HMC.
- [Langevin Dynamics](node:Langevin%20Dynamics): the diffusion limit of random-walk Metropolis and the basis of MALA.
- [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model) and [Gibbs Measures](node:Gibbs%20Measures): canonical targets of Metropolis and Gibbs (heat-bath) samplers in [statistical mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics).
- [Markov Chain Critical Slowing Down](node:Markov%20Chain%20Critical%20Slowing%20Down): the growth of autocorrelation times near criticality, the main cost in lattice simulations.
- [Lattice QCD](node:Lattice%20QCD): the original setting for hybrid Monte Carlo.

### Common pitfalls
- **Asymptotic is not quantitative.** The general convergence theorem says nothing about the rate; burn-in length has no general theoretical answer ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033); [Princeton COS513 notes](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall10/cos513/notes/2010-12-01.pdf)).
- **Gelman–Rubin $\hat R$ below 1.1** is a common heuristic for convergence across chains, not a proof ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)).
- **Correlated samples:** reporting $N$ instead of $N_{\text{eff}}$ overstates precision ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo)).
- **Adaptive tuning can break stationarity:** adapting the proposal scale on the fly toward 0.234 must be done carefully, since adaptive strategies can violate the invariance of $\pi$ ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)).
- **Useless constants:** some general convergence theorems give constants as bad as $d^d$ in dimension $d$ ([Diaconis 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.7754)).

### Open problems
- **Generality of optimal scaling.** Roberts and Rosenthal (2004) pose as Open Problem 3: determine the extent to which the 0.234 / 0.574 optimal-scaling results continue to apply when the i.i.d. product assumption fails; they note that the true generality is unknown and that non-stationary starts can behave surprisingly ([Roberts and Rosenthal 2004](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0404033)).
- **Gradient-based samplers on multimodal targets.** For many high-dimensional unimodal targets optimally tuned HMC scales like $d^{1/4}$ versus $d$ for random-walk Metropolis; Mangoubi, Pillai and Smith compute equal spectral gaps for both on a class of multimodal densities and give heuristic arguments that this "may hold quite generally", which they do not prove ([Mangoubi, Pillai and Smith 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.03230)).
- **Sharp mixing of explicit chains.** Diaconis conjectures that the random walk on the alternating group $A_n$ based on any generating pair mixes in at most $n^3\log n$ steps; he asks which element added to the generating set $\{(1\,2),(1\,2\,\cdots\,n)\}$ of $S_n$ ($n$ odd), whose walk needs order $n^3\log n$ steps, would appreciably speed up mixing, and which added edges or weights (Metropolised to keep $\pi$ stationary) best improve mixing or the spectral gap of a random walk on a graph ([Diaconis 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.7754)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Markov chain Monte Carlo (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo): general-state-space LLN, CLT, diagnostics, algorithm survey.
- **Learn:** [Princeton COS513 scribe notes on MCMC sampling](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall10/cos513/notes/2010-12-01.pdf): invariance, detailed balance, finite-space convergence, MH proof.
- **Primary:** [Roberts and Rosenthal, General state space Markov chains and MCMC algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0404033): survey of ergodicity, drift/minorisation, CLTs and optimal scaling, with open problems.
- **Primary:** [Neal, MCMC using Hamiltonian dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.1901): the standard review of HMC and its variants.
- **Primary:** [Diaconis, Some things we've learned (about MCMC)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.7754): survey of rigorous mixing analysis with open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Robert and Casella, Monte Carlo Statistical Methods (Springer, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-4145-2): the standard graduate text.
references.Markov Chains:
## Reference
### Overview
A Markov chain is a random process in which the conditional distribution of the next state, given the whole past, depends only on the present state. For a finite state space the dynamics are encoded by a right-stochastic transition matrix $P$ whose rows sum to one, and the long-run behaviour is governed by stationary distributions, which are left eigenvectors of $P$ with eigenvalue $1$. Markov chains underlie PageRank, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and queueing models such as the M/M/1 queue. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain))

The general theory works on a measurable state space $(S,\mathcal S)$ with a transition probability $p(x,A)$; the chain on path space is built from an initial law and $p$ by Kolmogorov's extension theorem, and on that canonical space one has the Markov and strong Markov properties, the recurrence/transience dichotomy, and the stationary-measure theory. ([Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Sheffield, MIT 18.175 Lecture 30](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture30.pdf))

A second, quantitative theory asks how fast a finite chain approaches equilibrium. It measures distance to stationarity in total variation and studies mixing times through coupling, eigenvalues, and isoperimetry (bottleneck ratios); the cutoff phenomenon, an abrupt transition from "far from" to "close to" equilibrium, is one of its central topics. ([Levin, Peres and Wilmer, *Markov Chains and Mixing Times*](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf))

### Formal definition
A function $p : S\times\mathcal S\to[0,1]$ is a **transition probability** if $A\mapsto p(x,A)$ is a probability measure for each $x\in S$ and $x\mapsto p(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal S$. A sequence $(X_n)$ adapted to a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **Markov chain with transition probability $p$** if
$$P(X_{n+1}\in B\mid \mathcal F_n)=p(X_n,B)\qquad\text{for all } B\in\mathcal S.$$
Given an initial distribution $\mu$, the finite-dimensional laws are
$$P(X_j\in B_j,\ 0\le j\le n)=\int_{B_0}\mu(dx_0)\int_{B_1}p(x_0,dx_1)\cdots\int_{B_n}p(x_{n-1},dx_n),$$
and Kolmogorov's extension theorem gives a measure $P_\mu$ on sequence space. ([Sheffield, Lecture 30](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture30.pdf); [Durrett](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

On a countable state space write $p(x,y)$, $p^n(x,y)$ for $n$-step probabilities, $T_y=\inf\{n\ge1:X_n=y\}$ and $\rho_{xy}=P_x(T_y<\infty)$. A state $y$ is **recurrent** if $\rho_{yy}=1$ and **transient** otherwise; a recurrent $y$ is **positive recurrent** if $E_yT_y<\infty$. The chain is **irreducible** if $\rho_{xy}>0$ for all $x,y$. The period $d_x$ of $x$ is $\gcd\{n\ge1:p^n(x,x)>0\}$ and the chain is aperiodic if all $d_x=1$. A measure $\mu$ is **stationary** if $\sum_x\mu(x)p(x,y)=\mu(y)$ and **reversible** if it satisfies detailed balance $\mu(x)p(x,y)=\mu(y)p(y,x)$. ([Durrett](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain))

For a finite chain with stationary $\pi$, the **total variation distance** is $\|\mu-\nu\|_{TV}=\max_A|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|=\tfrac12\sum_x|\mu(x)-\nu(x)|$, $d(t)=\max_x\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}$, and the **mixing time** is $t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)=\min\{t:d(t)\le\varepsilon\}$, $t_{\mathrm{mix}}=t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)$. The absolute spectral gap is $\gamma_\star=1-\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\ne1 \text{ an eigenvalue of }P\}$ and the relaxation time is $t_{\mathrm{rel}}=1/\gamma_\star$. ([Levin–Peres–Wilmer](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf))

### Key results
- **Chapman–Kolmogorov and the strong Markov property.** $p^{m+n}(x,z)=\sum_y p^m(x,y)p^n(y,z)$. If $N$ is a stopping time and $Y_n$ are bounded measurable functions on path space, then $E_\mu(Y_N\circ\theta_N\mid\mathcal F_N)=E_{X_N}Y_N$ on $\{N<\infty\}$, where $\theta_N$ is the shift. ([Durrett, Thms 5.2.4–5.2.5](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Recurrence criterion.** $y$ is recurrent iff $E_yN(y)=\sum_{n\ge1}p^n(y,y)=\infty$; if $x$ is recurrent and $\rho_{xy}>0$, then $y$ is recurrent and $\rho_{yx}=1$, so recurrence is a class property. Simple random walk on $\mathbb Z^d$ is recurrent for $d\le2$ and transient for $d\ge3$ (Pólya). ([Durrett, Thms 5.3.1, 5.3.2, 5.4.4](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Stationary distributions.** If $p$ is irreducible, the following are equivalent: some state is positive recurrent; a stationary distribution exists; all states are positive recurrent. If an irreducible $p$ has stationary distribution $\pi$, then $\pi(x)=1/E_xT_x$, and an irreducible recurrent chain has a stationary measure unique up to constant multiples. ([Durrett, Thms 5.5.9, 5.5.11, 5.5.12](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Convergence theorem.** If $p$ is irreducible, aperiodic, and has stationary distribution $\pi$, then $p^n(x,y)\to\pi(y)$ for all $x,y$. For finite irreducible aperiodic chains the convergence is geometric: there are $C>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ with $\max_x\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{TV}\le C\alpha^t$. ([Durrett, Thm 5.6.6](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Thm 4.9](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf))
- **Ergodic theorem for occupation times.** If $y$ is recurrent, then for any start $x$, $N_n(y)/n\to\mathbf 1_{\{T_y<\infty\}}/E_yT_y$ $P_x$-a.s., where $N_n(y)$ counts visits to $y$ up to time $n$. ([Durrett, Thm 5.6.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Reversibility (Kolmogorov's cycle condition).** An irreducible $p$ has a reversible measure iff $p(x,y)>0\Rightarrow p(y,x)>0$ and every loop $x_0,\dots,x_n=x_0$ with positive reverse probability satisfies $\prod_i p(x_{i-1},x_i)/p(x_i,x_{i-1})=1$. Any distribution satisfying detailed balance is stationary. ([Durrett, Thm 5.5.6](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Prop. 1.20](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf))
- **Spectral bounds on mixing.** For a reversible irreducible chain with $\pi_{\min}=\min_x\pi(x)$, $t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)\le t_{\mathrm{rel}}\log\!\big(1/(\varepsilon\pi_{\min})\big)$; for an irreducible aperiodic chain and any eigenvalue $\lambda\ne1$, $t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)\ge\big(\tfrac{1}{1-|\lambda|}-1\big)\log(1/(2\varepsilon))$, so for reversible such chains $t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)\ge(t_{\mathrm{rel}}-1)\log(1/(2\varepsilon))$. With bottleneck ratio $\Phi_\star$, the spectral gap $\gamma=1-\lambda_2$ of a reversible chain satisfies $\Phi_\star^2/2\le\gamma\le2\Phi_\star$ (Sinclair–Jerrum, Lawler–Sokal). ([Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Thms 12.4, 12.5, 13.10](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf))
- **Cutoff for the hypercube.** The lazy random walk on $\{0,1\}^n$ has a cutoff at $\tfrac12 n\log n$ with window $O(n)$: on that time scale $d_n(t)$ drops from near $1$ to near $0$. ([Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Thm 18.3](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf))

### Examples
- **Two-state weather chain.** With $P=\begin{pmatrix}.5&.5\\ .2&.8\end{pmatrix}$, solving $\pi P=\pi$ gives $\pi=(2/7,5/7)$, and already $P^{10}$ has both rows within about $10^{-5}$ of $\pi$. ([Sheffield, Lecture 30](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture30.pdf))
- **Standard families.** Random walks on $\mathbb R^d$, branching processes with $p(i,j)=P(\sum_{m=1}^i\xi_m=j)$, renewal chains, card shuffling, and the Ehrenfest chain. ([Sheffield, Lecture 30](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture30.pdf))
- **PageRank** ranks pages by the stationary distribution of a chain on the web graph with damping parameter about $0.85$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain))

### History
Andrey Markov published his first paper on such chains in 1906, aiming to show against Pavel Nekrasov that a weak law of large numbers holds without independence; he later analysed vowel sequences in Pushkin's *Eugene Onegin*. Poincaré studied chains on finite groups in 1912 to model card shuffling, Kolmogorov developed continuous-time Markov processes in a 1931 paper, and Chapman had derived the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation independently in 1928; Feller and Dynkin extended the foundations. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain))

### Connections
- [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): a chain is a sequence of random variables whose joint law is built from an initial distribution and a kernel.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): on a finite state space the chain is the stochastic matrix $P$ acting on row vectors of probabilities.
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): stationary distributions are left eigenvectors for eigenvalue $1$; the spectral gap controls relaxation.
- [Stochastic Processes](node:Stochastic%20Processes): Markov chains are the discrete-time, memoryless case of general processes.
- [Martingales](node:Martingales): harmonic functions of a chain give martingales, used in hitting-probability computations.
- [Random Walks on Groups](node:Random%20Walks%20on%20Groups): card shuffling and hypercube walks are chains on groups, standard examples of cutoff.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory): occupation-time limits are an instance of ergodic averages for the stationary chain.
- [Detailed Balance](node:Detailed%20Balance): the reversibility condition $\mu(x)p(x,y)=\mu(y)p(y,x)$, sufficient for stationarity.
- [Markov Chain Monte Carlo](node:Markov%20Chain%20Monte%20Carlo): designs reversible chains with a prescribed stationary law; mixing times bound its cost.
- [Hidden Markov Models](node:Hidden%20Markov%20Models): an unobserved Markov chain with state-dependent emissions.
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): controlled chains whose kernel depends on an action.
- [Queueing Theory](node:Queueing%20Theory): birth-death chains and the M/M/1 queue.
- [Renewal Processes](node:Renewal%20Processes): return times to a fixed state form a renewal process.

### Common pitfalls
- Irreducibility alone does not give convergence of $p^n(x,y)$: a periodic chain oscillates, and the convergence theorem needs aperiodicity (otherwise only Cesàro averages converge). ([Durrett](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- Recurrence does not imply a stationary *distribution*: for simple random walk on $\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb Z^2$ (recurrent), counting measure is stationary because the kernel is doubly stochastic, and uniqueness up to constants for irreducible recurrent chains then rules out a stationary probability, so these walks are null recurrent. ([Durrett](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- The relaxation time determines the mixing time only up to a logarithmic factor: the spectral upper bound $t_{\mathrm{rel}}\log(1/(\varepsilon\pi_{\min}))$ and lower bound $(t_{\mathrm{rel}}-1)\log(1/(2\varepsilon))$ differ by a factor of order $\log(1/\pi_{\min})$. ([Levin–Peres–Wilmer](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf))
- Modelling with a Markov chain forces geometric holding times in each state, which can be unrealistic (for example durations of social states). ([Sheffield, Lecture 30](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture30.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Cutoff on transitive expanders.** Levin–Peres–Wilmer list as open (Question 5): for a sequence of transitive graphs of fixed degree $\Delta\ge3$ with spectral gap bounded away from zero, must the lazy random walks exhibit cutoff? ([Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Ch. 26](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf)) A 2026 preprint still describes "the long-standing conjecture of cutoff for transitive spectral expanders" as unresolved and claims only intermediate progress. ([Altschuler 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14945))
