- **Card shuffles with pre-cutoff.** The second edition of Levin–Peres–Wilmer poses as open whether cyclic-to-random transpositions, random-to-random insertions, and card-cyclic-to-random shuffles have cutoff; all are known to have pre-cutoff. ([Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Question 6](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf)) The random-to-random case has since been settled: Bernstein and Nestoridi combined Subag's lower bound with an eigenvalue-based upper bound to show cutoff at about $\tfrac34 n\log n-\tfrac14 n\log\log n$ with a window of order $n$. ([Bernstein and Nestoridi 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06210))
- **Glauber dynamics for colourings.** Does Glauber dynamics for proper $q$-colourings mix in time $O(n\log n)$ whenever $q>\Delta+2$? ([Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Question 7](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Markov chain (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain): definitions, classification of states, continuous-time chains, history, applications.
- **Learn:** [Sheffield, MIT 18.175 Lecture 30: Markov chains](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture30.pdf): finite chains, ergodicity and stationarity, general kernels and the Kolmogorov construction (course page [18.175](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/spring2014math175.html)).
- **Primary:** [Levin, Peres and Wilmer, *Markov Chains and Mixing Times*, 2nd ed.](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/mcmt2e.pdf): the standard monograph on mixing, spectral and coupling methods, cutoff, with an open-problems chapter.
- **Primary:** [Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*, Ch. 5](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf): countable-state theory, recurrence, stationary measures, convergence, Harris chains.
- **Further reading:** [Durrett's book page](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/pte.html) and [Levin–Peres–Wilmer book page](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/): author pages for the two graduate texts above.
references.Markov Decision Processes:
## Reference
### Overview
A Markov decision process (MDP) is the standard model of sequential decision-making under uncertainty: at each step a controller in state $s$ picks an action $a$, the system moves to a random next state with a probability that depends only on $(s,a)$, and a reward is collected. Solving an MDP means finding a policy, a rule mapping states to actions, that maximizes an expected cumulative reward, usually discounted by a factor $\gamma$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process)). Once a policy is fixed, the process behaves like a [Markov chain](node:Markov%20Chains), and the optimal value is characterized by the Bellman equation of [dynamic programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process)).

MDPs originated in operations research in the 1950s and are the formal setting of [reinforcement learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning), where the transition probabilities and rewards are unknown and must be learned from interaction ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process)). The mathematical core is an operator view: the Bellman operator is monotone and a sup-norm contraction, so value iteration and policy iteration both converge, and the same structure carries over to arbitrary state spaces with bounded costs ([MIT 6.231](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-231-dynamic-programming-and-stochastic-control-fall-2015/625f95b309b29ae5f2c851f9eab1937c_MIT6_231F15_lec2.pdf)).

Finite MDPs can be solved in polynomial time, but realistic state spaces are often exponentially large (the curse of dimensionality), which motivates approximate and sampling methods such as [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process)). For a fixed discount factor the simplex method (Dantzig's rule) and policy iteration are strongly polynomial, but a strongly polynomial algorithm for general MDPs is an open question at the boundary with the theory of [linear programming](node:Linear%20Programming) ([Post and Ye](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.5083)).

### Formal definition
A (finite) MDP is a tuple $(S, A, P, R)$ with state set $S$, action set $A$, transition probabilities $P_a(s,s') = \Pr(s_{t+1}=s' \mid s_t=s, a_t=a)$, and reward $R_a(s,s')$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process)). A policy $\pi$ maps states to actions (possibly randomly); in the discounted criterion with $0\le\gamma\le1$ (value iteration is guaranteed to converge for $\gamma<1$) its value is
$$V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t R_{a_t}(s_t,s_{t+1}) \,\Big|\, s_0=s,\ a_t=\pi(s_t)\Big].$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process))

The Bellman optimality operator $B$ acts on functions $V:S\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$(BV)(s) = \max_{a}\sum_{s'}P_a(s,s')\big[R_a(s,s') + \gamma V(s')\big],$$
and the action-value (Q-value) form is $Q(s,a)=\sum_{s'}P_a(s,s')[R_a(s,s')+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')]$; an optimal policy is $\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a Q^*(s,a)$ ([Berkeley CS188](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/mdp/value-iteration.html)).

In Bertsekas's cost-minimization notation for a stationary system $x_{k+1}=f(x_k,u_k,w_k)$ with bounded stage cost $g$ and discount $\alpha<1$, the operators are $(TJ)(x)=\min_{u\in U(x)}\mathbb{E}_w[g(x,u,w)+\alpha J(f(x,u,w))]$ and, for a stationary policy $\mu$, $(T_\mu J)(x)=\mathbb{E}_w[g(x,\mu(x),w)+\alpha J(f(x,\mu(x),w))]$; Bellman's equations are $J^*=TJ^*$ and $J_\mu=T_\mu J_\mu$ ([MIT 6.231](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-231-dynamic-programming-and-stochastic-control-fall-2015/625f95b309b29ae5f2c851f9eab1937c_MIT6_231F15_lec2.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Contraction and uniqueness.** For bounded $J,J'$ and any stationary $\mu$, $\|TJ-TJ'\|_\infty\le\alpha\|J-J'\|_\infty$ and $\|T_\mu J-T_\mu J'\|_\infty\le\alpha\|J-J'\|_\infty$. Hence, by the contraction mapping fixed-point theorem, $J^*$ is the unique bounded solution of $J=TJ$, and value iteration $T^kJ\to J^*$ from any bounded $J$. ([MIT 6.231](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-231-dynamic-programming-and-stochastic-control-fall-2015/625f95b309b29ae5f2c851f9eab1937c_MIT6_231F15_lec2.pdf))
- **Optimality of greedy stationary policies.** A stationary policy $\mu$ is optimal if and only if $T_\mu J^*=TJ^*$, i.e. $\mu(x)$ attains the minimum in Bellman's equation for every $x$. When rewards are deterministic, an optimal policy exists that is deterministic and depends only on the current state. ([MIT 6.231](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-231-dynamic-programming-and-stochastic-control-fall-2015/625f95b309b29ae5f2c851f9eab1937c_MIT6_231F15_lec2.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process))
- **Policy iteration improves monotonically and terminates.** Policy iteration alternates evaluation ($J_{\mu^k}=T_{\mu^k}J_{\mu^k}$, which for $n$ states is the $n\times n$ linear system $J_\mu=g_\mu+\alpha P_\mu J_\mu$) and improvement ($T_{\mu^{k+1}}J_{\mu^k}=TJ_{\mu^k}$). Monotonicity of the operators gives $J_{\mu^k}\ge J_{\mu^{k+1}}$, with equality only if $J_{\mu^k}=J^*$; so for finite MDPs the method terminates with an optimal policy. ([MIT 6.231](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-231-dynamic-programming-and-stochastic-control-fall-2015/625f95b309b29ae5f2c851f9eab1937c_MIT6_231F15_lec2.pdf))
- **Approximate policy iteration error bound.** If evaluation errors satisfy $\|J_k-J_{\mu^k}\|\le\delta$ and improvement errors satisfy $\|T_{\mu^{k+1}}J_k-TJ_k\|\le\epsilon$, then $\limsup_k\|J_{\mu^k}-J^*\|\le(\epsilon+2\alpha\delta)/(1-\alpha)^2$; if the generated policies settle on a single $\mu$, then $\|J_\mu-J^*\|\le(\epsilon+2\alpha\delta)/(1-\alpha)$. ([MIT 6.231](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-231-dynamic-programming-and-stochastic-control-fall-2015/625f95b309b29ae5f2c851f9eab1937c_MIT6_231F15_lec2.pdf))
- **Strongly polynomial for fixed discount (Ye).** For discounted MDPs with $n$ states, $m$ actions and a fixed discount $\gamma$, the simplex method with Dantzig's most-negative-reduced-cost rule and Howard's policy iteration are strongly polynomial, with Ye's bound $O\big(\tfrac{nm}{1-\gamma}\log\tfrac{n}{1-\gamma}\big)$. Hansen, Miltersen and Zwick improved the policy-iteration bound to $O\big(\tfrac{m}{1-\gamma}\log\tfrac{n}{1-\gamma}\big)$ and extended it to strategy iteration for two-player turn-based zero-sum discounted stochastic games, the first strongly polynomial algorithm for those games with constant discount. ([Post and Ye](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.5083); [Hansen, Miltersen and Zwick](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.0530))
- **Deterministic MDPs.** The simplex method with the highest-gain pivoting rule solves deterministic MDPs in $O(n^3m^2\log^2 n)$ iterations with a uniform discount, and in $O(n^5m^3\log^2 n)$ iterations when each action has its own discount, so strongly polynomially regardless of the discount factor. ([Post and Ye](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.5083))

### Examples
- **Linear-programming form.** In Post and Ye's formulation the primal LP maximizes total reward over nonnegative "flux" variables $x_a$, one per action, subject to one constraint per state (flux leaving the state equals 1 plus the discounted flux entering it); vertices of its polytope correspond to policies. The dual minimizes the sum of state values $v_s$ subject to $v_s$ being at least each action's reward plus the discounted value of its successor. ([Post and Ye](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.5083))
- **Q-value iteration.** Iterate $Q_{k+1}(s,a)=\sum_{s'}P_a(s,s')[R_a(s,s')+\gamma\max_{a'}Q_k(s',a')]$; storing $Q^*$ lets the optimal action be read off by a single argmax, whereas storing only $V^*$ requires a one-step lookahead. ([Berkeley CS188](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/mdp/value-iteration.html))
- **Constrained MDPs.** With several cost signals and constraints on them, the problem is solved by linear programming rather than dynamic programming, and the optimal policy can depend on the starting state. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process))

### History
MDPs grew out of operations research in the 1950s; Bellman (1957) is credited with value iteration, Howard introduced policy iteration in 1960 (to optimize Sears catalogue mailing), and Shapley's 1953 paper on stochastic games was later recognised to contain value iteration as a special case ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process)). Puterman's monograph brought together many results on discrete-time MDPs previously found only in part in other texts and papers ([Wiley](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Markov+Decision+Processes%3A+Discrete+Stochastic+Dynamic+Programming-p-9780471727828)). Building on Ye's strongly polynomial bound for fixed discount, Hansen, Miltersen and Zwick (2010) gave the first strongly polynomial algorithm for two-player turn-based discounted stochastic games, resolving what they describe as a long-standing open problem ([Hansen, Miltersen and Zwick](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.0530)).

### Connections
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains): fixing a stationary policy turns an MDP into a Markov chain with transition matrix $P_\mu$.
- [Dynamic Programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming): Bellman's equation and backward induction are the solution principle.
- [Value Iteration](node:Value%20Iteration): the fixed-point iteration $V\leftarrow BV$, convergent by contraction.
- [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem): gives existence, uniqueness and geometric convergence of value iteration.
- [Linear Programming](node:Linear%20Programming): finite discounted MDPs are LPs; simplex pivots correspond to policy changes.
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): learning optimal policies when $P$ and $R$ are unknown.
- [Q-Learning](node:Q-Learning): stochastic-approximation version of Q-value iteration.
- [Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes](node:Partially%20Observable%20Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the generalization where the state is seen only through noisy observations.
- [Stochastic Optimal Control](node:Stochastic%20Optimal%20Control): the continuous-time, continuous-state counterpart, governed by the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation.
- [Risk-Sensitive and Constrained Reinforcement Learning](node:Risk-Sensitive%20and%20Constrained%20Reinforcement%20Learning): constrained MDPs and risk measures in place of expected return.
- [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search): online planning when the state space is too large to enumerate.

### Common pitfalls
- Strong polynomiality of policy iteration depends on a fixed discount factor: Fearnley gave an exponential lower bound for policy iteration ([Post and Ye](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.5083)), and Disser, Friedmann and Hopp showed that Zadeh's pivot rule is exponential in the worst case, with exponential lower bounds also for the corresponding policy iteration on MDPs ([Disser, Friedmann and Hopp](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.01074)).
- The simplex method with Dantzig's rule is exponential in the worst case on general LPs (Klee-Minty cube) ([Wikipedia: Simplex algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplex_algorithm)), whereas Ye's strongly polynomial bound for the same rule is specific to discounted MDPs with a fixed discount ([Post and Ye](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.5083)).
- Policy iteration can beat value iteration when the action space is large, but each step solves a linear system and it is usually slower when the state space is large. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process))
- Finite termination of exact policy iteration is a finite-state result; for infinite-state MDPs the lecture establishes only convergence in an infinite number of iterations. ([MIT 6.231](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-231-dynamic-programming-and-stochastic-control-fall-2015/625f95b309b29ae5f2c851f9eab1937c_MIT6_231F15_lec2.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Strongly polynomial algorithm for general MDPs.** Post and Ye call it "another challenging open question" to design a strongly polynomial algorithm for general (stochastic) MDPs, without fixing the discount factor. ([Post and Ye](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.5083))
- **Policy iteration on deterministic MDPs.** Their simplex results do not extend to policy iteration, which they leave as a challenging open question; policy iteration is conjectured to run in $O(m)$ iterations on deterministic MDPs. ([Post and Ye](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1208.5083))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Markov decision process (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process): definition, algorithms, history, extensions (continuous time, constrained MDPs).
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.231 Dynamic Programming and Stochastic Control, Lecture 2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-231-dynamic-programming-and-stochastic-control-fall-2015/625f95b309b29ae5f2c851f9eab1937c_MIT6_231F15_lec2.pdf): Bellman operators, contraction, value and policy iteration, approximate policy iteration bounds.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley CS188 notes: Value iteration](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/mdp/value-iteration.html): introductory treatment with Q-value iteration and policy extraction.
- **Primary:** [Post and Ye, The simplex method is strongly polynomial for deterministic Markov decision processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.5083): complexity of MDP algorithms and the open questions.
- **Primary:** [Hansen, Miltersen and Zwick, Strategy iteration is strongly polynomial for 2-player turn-based stochastic games with a constant discount factor](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.0530): improved policy-iteration bound.
- **Further reading:** [Puterman, Markov Decision Processes: Discrete Stochastic Dynamic Programming (Wiley)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Markov+Decision+Processes%3A+Discrete+Stochastic+Dynamic+Programming-p-9780471727828): the standard monograph on discrete-time MDPs.
references.Mathematical Elasticity:
## Reference
### Overview
Mathematical elasticity is the analysis of the equations that govern how a solid body deforms under loads and stores the work done on it as elastic energy. Its linear branch models small deformations: the displacement $u$ determines an infinitesimal strain, a stiffness tensor converts strain to stress, and balance of momentum gives a linear system of partial differential equations for $u$. The linear theory is a simplification of the nonlinear (finite-strain) theory, valid only for stress states that do not produce yielding. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_elasticity))

The nonlinear theory, in hyperelastic form, describes a deformation $y:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^3$ of a reference body $\Omega$ through a stored-energy function $W(Dy)$ and the energy $I(y)=\int_\Omega W(Dy)\,dx$, whose weak Euler–Lagrange equation expresses equilibrium. Existence is obtained either by the implicit function theorem near a known solution or by the direct method of the [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations), which needs convexity conditions on $W$ such as polyconvexity; quasiconvexity is the weaker condition the theory would prefer. Ball's survey lists open problems from existence, regularity and uniqueness of equilibria through dynamics, atomistic justification and thin structures. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))

The two theories are linked rigorously: linearized elasticity is the Γ-limit of rescaled finite-elasticity energies for Dirichlet and mixed boundary conditions, while for pure traction the limit can differ from linear elasticity unless the loads satisfy a compatibility condition. ([Maddalena, Percivale and Tomarelli](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1810.01339))

### Formal definition
**Linear elasticity.** For a displacement $u$, the infinitesimal strain is $\varepsilon(u)=\tfrac12(\nabla u+\nabla u^{T})$, Hooke's law is $\sigma=C:\varepsilon$, and the equation of motion is $\nabla\cdot\sigma+F=\rho\ddot u$ with body force $F$ and density $\rho$. For a homogeneous isotropic material, $\sigma_{ij}=\lambda\delta_{ij}\varepsilon_{kk}+2\mu\varepsilon_{ij}$ with Lamé parameters $\lambda,\mu$, and $u$ satisfies the Navier–Cauchy equations $\mu\nabla^2u+(\lambda+\mu)\nabla(\nabla\cdot u)+F=\rho\,\partial_t^2u$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_elasticity))

**Stiffness symmetries.** Symmetry of stress gives $c_{ijkl}=c_{jikl}$ and symmetry of strain gives $c_{ijkl}=c_{ijlk}$ (the minor symmetries), leaving 36 constants. If stress derives from a strain-energy density $U$, then $c_{ijkl}=\partial^2U/\partial\varepsilon_{ij}\partial\varepsilon_{kl}=c_{klij}$ (the major symmetry), and only 21 independent components remain. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hooke%27s_law)) See [Anisotropic Elasticity Tensors](node:Anisotropic%20Elasticity%20Tensors).

**Weak form.** With $V=\{v\in[H^1(\Omega)]^3:v=0\text{ on }\Gamma_D\}$, $|\Gamma_D|>0$, seek $u\in V$ with
$$A(u,v):=\int_\Omega 2\mu\,\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)+\lambda\,\operatorname{div}u\,\operatorname{div}v\,dx=\int_\Omega f\cdot v\,dx\quad\forall v\in V,$$
where $2\mu=E/(1+\nu)$ and $\lambda=E\nu/((1+\nu)(1-2\nu))$ for Young's modulus $E$ and Poisson ratio $\nu\in[0,1/2)$. ([Schöberl, iFEM](https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/elasticity/linearized_elasticity.html))

**Nonlinear hyperelasticity.** A hyperelastic material has stress derived from a strain-energy density $W(F)$ of the deformation gradient, with first Piola–Kirchhoff stress $P=\partial W/\partial F$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperelastic_material)) For boundary data $y|_{\partial\Omega_1}=\bar y$ the admissible set is $\mathcal{A}=\{y\in W^{1,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^3):I(y)<\infty,\ y|_{\partial\Omega_1}=\bar y\}$. Frame-indifference requires $W(RA)=W(A)$ for $R\in SO(3)$; non-interpenetration is encoded by $W(A)\to\infty$ as $\det A\to0^+$ and $W(A)=\infty$ for $\det A\le0$. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))

**Convexity notions.** $W$ is *polyconvex* if $W(A)=g(A,\operatorname{cof}A,\det A)$ with $g$ convex; $f$ is *quasiconvex* at $A$ if $\int_\Omega f(A+D\varphi)\,dx\ge\int_\Omega f(A)\,dx$ for all $\varphi\in C_0^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^m)$; it is *rank-one convex* if $t\mapsto f(A+t\,a\otimes n)$ is convex. Quasiconvexity implies rank-one convexity. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf)) See [Quasiconvexity](node:Quasiconvexity).

### Key results
- **[Korn's Inequality](node:Korn's%20Inequality) and linear well-posedness.** On $V$ with $|\Gamma_D|>0$ there is $c_K>0$ with $c_K\|u\|_{H^1}^2\le\|\varepsilon(u)\|_{L^2}^2$, so $A(u,u)\ge2\mu c_K\|u\|_{H^1}^2$; together with boundedness of $A$ on $V$, the [Lax–Milgram Theorem](node:Lax–Milgram%20Theorem) gives a unique weak solution, and Céa's lemma bounds the Galerkin error by the ratio of the continuity constant to $2\mu c_K$ times the best approximation error. The 6 components of $\varepsilon(u)$ thus control all 9 components of $\nabla u$. ([Schöberl, iFEM](https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/elasticity/linearized_elasticity.html))
- **Ball's existence theorem.** If (H1) $W$ is polyconvex, (H2) $W(A)\ge c_0(|A|^2+|\operatorname{cof}A|^{3/2})-c_1$ with $c_0>0$, and $\mathcal{A}\neq\varnothing$, then $I$ has a global minimizer in $\mathcal{A}$; this is Müller, Qi and Yan's refinement of Ball's 1977 theorem. Under (H2) no finite-energy deformation cavitates. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **Šverák's counterexample.** For $n\ge2$, $m\ge3$ rank-one convexity does not imply quasiconvexity, and Kristensen showed quasiconvexity has no local characterization in those dimensions. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **Cavitation (Ball 1982).** For a class of stored energies satisfying (H1) and the growth condition in (H2) with exponents $2\le p<3$ and $q<3/2$ in place of $2$ and $3/2$, e.g. $W(A)=|A|^2+h(\det A)$ with $h''>0$, $h(\delta)/\delta\to\infty$ as $\delta\to\infty$ and $h(\delta)\to\infty$ as $\delta\to0^+$, the energy has a minimizer among radial maps $y(x)=r(|x|)x/|x|$ with $y=\lambda x$ on $|x|=1$, and for $\lambda$ large it has $r(0)>0$ (a hole opens) while still satisfying the weak equilibrium equation. This exhibits a Lavrentiev gap: $\inf_{\mathcal A_1}I<\inf_{\mathcal A_3}I=I(\lambda x)$. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf)) Above a critical stretch $\lambda_{cr}$ the homogeneous solution is unstable and the cavitating minimizer is unique. ([Giesselmann, Miroshnikov and Tzavaras](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1408.0831)) Müller and Spector's existence theory that allows cavitation (*Arch. Rational Mech. Anal.* 131, 1995) ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf)) requires admissible deformations to satisfy condition (INV), a topological condition closely related to invertibility that excludes pathological behaviour and implies almost-everywhere injectivity; Henao's strengthened condition (INV$'$) extends the core-radius approximation of cavitating minimizers from one to several prescribed flaw points. ([Bresciani and Friedrich](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.07546))
- **Local well-posedness of elastodynamics.** If $W$ is strongly elliptic, $D^2W(A)(a\otimes n,a\otimes n)\ge\mu|a|^2|n|^2$ with $\mu>0$, then smooth initial data on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $\det Dy_0>0$ have a unique smooth solution on a short time interval (Hughes, Kato and Marsden 1977), extended to pure displacement conditions by Kato; John (1988) proved almost-global existence for small smooth data on $\mathbb{R}^3$. No short-time result was known for mixed displacement–traction conditions. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **Linearization by Γ-convergence (Dal Maso, Negri and Percivale 2002).** Under frame-indifference, $W(I)=0$, $DW(I)=0$, $C^2$ regularity near $SO(N)$ and coercivity $W(F)\ge C|F^TF-I|^2$, the rescaled energies $\int h^{-2}W(I+h\nabla v)-\int g\cdot v$ Γ-converge to the linear elastic energy for Dirichlet and mixed problems. For pure traction, minimizing sequences may lack compactness, and the limit coincides with linear elasticity only under a compatibility condition on the loads. ([Maddalena, Percivale and Tomarelli](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1810.01339))
- **Geometric rigidity (Friesecke, James and Müller).** For a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\ge2$, there is $C=C(\Omega)$ such that for every $u\in W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^n)$ some $R\in SO(n)$ satisfies $\|\nabla u-R\|_{L^2}\le C\|\operatorname{dist}(\nabla u,SO(n))\|_{L^2}$ (an $L^p$ version holds for $1<p<\infty$). ([Lauteri and Luckhaus](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1703.03288))
- **Hierarchy of plate theories.** If forces scale like $h^\alpha$, minimizers have elastic energy of order $h^\beta$ ($\beta=\alpha$ for $\alpha\le2$, $\beta=2\alpha-2$ otherwise). The Γ-limits of $h^{-\beta}E_h$ are membrane theory for $\beta=0$ (Le Dret and Raoult), nonlinear Kirchhoff bending among isometric immersions for $\beta=2$, von Kármán theory for $\beta=4$, and linear theories for $\beta>4$, all derived from 3D nonlinear elasticity by Γ-convergence. ([Lewicka and Pakzad](https://sites.pitt.edu/~lewicka/preprints/infinite_hierarchy2.pdf))

### Examples
- **Saint Venant–Kirchhoff material.** $W(E)=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}E)^2+\mu\operatorname{tr}(E^2)$ in the Green–Lagrange strain $E$, with $S=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}E)I+2\mu E$; the simplest hyperelastic model, extending geometrically linear elasticity to finite strain. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperelastic_material))
- **Uniaxial stretch.** In isotropic linear elasticity, stress $\operatorname{diag}(E,0,0)$ produces strain $\operatorname{diag}(1,-\nu,-\nu)$. ([Schöberl, iFEM](https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/elasticity/linearized_elasticity.html))
- **Elastic waves.** Plane waves in an anisotropic medium solve the Christoffel equation; isotropic media carry longitudinal (P) and shear (S) waves. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_elasticity))
- **Rubber-like isotropic materials.** Ball showed how (H1)–(H2) can be verified for a class of isotropic materials, including models of natural rubber, via the representation $W(A)=\Phi(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ in principal stretches. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))

### History
Kelvin's point-force solution (1848), Hertz's contact theory (1882) and Boussinesq's half-space solution (1885) belong to the classical linear theory, and Saint-Venant found the compatibility conditions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_elasticity)) Rivlin and Mooney developed the first hyperelastic models. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperelastic_material)) Ball's "Convexity conditions and existence theorems in nonlinear elasticity" (*Arch. Rational Mech. Anal.* 63, 337–403) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00279992)) gave the polyconvexity existence theorem for the direct-method route, later refined by Müller, Qi and Yan. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf)) Ball's cavitation paper (1982), Hughes–Kato–Marsden (1977) and Müller–Spector (1995) followed. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))

### Connections
- [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations): hyperelastic equilibria are minimizers of $\int W(Dy)$, the model vectorial variational problem.
- [Direct Method in the Calculus of Variations](node:Direct%20Method%20in%20the%20Calculus%20of%20Variations): the route to Ball's existence theorem.
- [Quasiconvexity](node:Quasiconvexity): the natural lower semicontinuity condition, still without a usable characterization.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces): deformations live in $W^{1,p}$; the choice of $p$ decides whether cavitation is admissible.
- [Gamma-Convergence](node:Gamma-Convergence): links nonlinear to linear elasticity and 3D bodies to plates and shells.
- [Plate and Shell Equations](node:Plate%20and%20Shell%20Equations): the limit theories of the FJM hierarchy.
- [Finite Element Elasticity](node:Finite%20Element%20Elasticity): Céa's lemma and the Korn constant control discretization error and locking.
- [Young Measures](node:Young%20Measures): describe microstructure when non-quasiconvex energies have no minimizer.
- [Mathematical Models of Martensitic Transformations](node:Mathematical%20Models%20of%20Martensitic%20Transformations): multi-well energies where rigidity and microstructure meet.
- [Bifurcation Theory](node:Bifurcation%20Theory): Ball's Problem 10 asks for bifurcation theories of nonlinear elastostatics.
- [Variational Fracture Models](node:Variational%20Fracture%20Models): energies allowing cracks, where minimizers can differ between function spaces.
- [Continuum Mechanics](node:Continuum%20Mechanics): supplies the balance laws and stress and strain measures.

### Common pitfalls
- **Minimizers are not known to satisfy the equilibrium equations.** Under only $W\to\infty$ as $\det A\to0^+$, it is unclear how to derive the weak [Euler–Lagrange Equations](node:Euler–Lagrange%20Equations) for a minimizer (Ball's Problem 5). ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **Quasiconvex existence theory does not transfer.** It assumes $C_1|A|^p-C_0\le f(A)\le C_2(|A|^p+1)$, incompatible with blow-up as $\det A\to0^+$. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **$\det Dy>0$ a.e. is not invertibility,** not even local invertibility, since $y$ need not be $C^1$. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **Minor symmetries alone give 36 constants, not 21;** the count 21 needs the major symmetry from a strain energy. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hooke%27s_law))
- **Near-incompressibility.** As $\nu\to1/2$, $\lambda\gg\mu$ and the problem degrades (locking); robust mixed discretizations are needed. ([Schöberl, iFEM](https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/elasticity/linearized_elasticity.html))

### Open problems
Problems 1–18 below are numbered as in Ball's 2002 survey, which states them as open. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **Quasiconvex existence (Problem 1)** and **regularity (Problem 3):** existence of minimizers for quasiconvex $W$ blowing up as $\det A\to0^+$, and when the minimizer of Ball's theorem is smooth.
- **Lavrentiev phenomenon (Problem 4).** Can it occur under growth making finite-energy deformations continuous? Foss, Hrusa and Mizel gave 2D examples under 'container' boundary conditions; mixed conditions and interior singularities were open. A 2026 preprint reports a Lavrentiev gap for the 3D neo-Hookean energy, between regular invertible deformations and their weak $H^1$ closure, caused by a dipole-type singularity. ([Barchiesi, Henao, Mora-Corral and Rodiac](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22873))
- **Euler–Lagrange equations (Problems 5–6)**, whether minimizers satisfy weak forms of the equilibrium equations, and **uniqueness (Problem 8)** of smooth equilibria for pure displacement problems for homogeneous bodies with strictly polyconvex $W$ and $\Omega$ homeomorphic to a ball. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **Approximation by diffeomorphisms.** The Ball–Evans problem, motivated by regularity of minimizers, asks whether Sobolev homeomorphisms can be approximated by diffeomorphisms or piecewise affine homeomorphisms; a 2025 survey reports planar results, higher-dimensional counterexamples and open questions. ([Hencl](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01336))
- **Dynamics (Problem 12).** Global existence and uniqueness for dynamic nonlinear elasticity. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf))
- **Atomistic justification (Problem 15).** In 2002 Ball found no atomistic derivation of dynamic theories. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf)) Partial progress since: linear elasticity is derived by Γ-convergence from multi-well atomistic energies with finite-range interactions in the small-deformation regime ([Alicandro, Lazzaroni and Palombaro 2021](https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1137/21M1397179?fields=title,authors,year,venue,abstract)), and the time-dependent von Kármán plate equations from Newtonian particle systems as lattice spacing and thickness vanish ([Buchberger and Schmidt 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10233)).
- **Thin structures (Problem 18).** Ball asked for rod, plate and shell models whose solutions approximate 3D solutions, ideally with error estimates uniform in the loads, and in 2002 found no dynamical results. ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf)) That gap has since closed in part: Abels, Mora and Müller showed that, with suitably scaled forces and initial data, 3D nonlinear elastodynamic solutions converge to the time-dependent von Kármán plate equation ([arXiv:0912.4135](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.4135)), extended to shells of arbitrary geometry by Qin and Yao ([arXiv:1802.00593](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.00593)). For totally clamped plates the regime $5/3\le\beta<2$ remained open as of 2009 and is conjectured to be relevant to the crumpling of elastic sheets, and Lewicka and Pakzad conjecture an infinite hierarchy of shell models, one per scaling range. ([Lewicka and Pakzad](https://sites.pitt.edu/~lewicka/preprints/infinite_hierarchy2.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Linear elasticity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_elasticity): strain, Hooke's law, Navier–Cauchy equations, compatibility, waves.
- **Reference:** [Hooke's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hooke%27s_law): minor and major symmetries of the stiffness tensor.
- **Learn:** [Schöberl, Linearized elasticity (iFEM)](https://jschoeberl.github.io/iFEM/elasticity/linearized_elasticity.html): weak form, Korn, Lax–Milgram, Céa, locking.
- **Learn:** [Lewicka and Pakzad, The infinite hierarchy of elastic shell models](https://sites.pitt.edu/~lewicka/preprints/infinite_hierarchy2.pdf): Γ-convergence derivations of plate and shell theories, with a conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Ball, Some open problems in elasticity (2002)](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf): survey with 18 numbered open problems, in *Geometry, Mechanics, and Dynamics* ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/0-387-21791-6_1)).
- **Primary:** [Ball, Convexity conditions and existence theorems in nonlinear elasticity](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00279992): the polyconvexity existence paper.
- **Primary:** [Abels, Mora and Müller, The time-dependent von Kármán plate equation as a limit of 3d nonlinear elasticity](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.4135): convergence of 3D nonlinear elastodynamics to the dynamic von Kármán plate equation.
- **Further reading:** [Ciarlet, Mathematical Elasticity: Three-Dimensional Elasticity (SIAM, 2021)](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611976786): Ciarlet's three-dimensional elasticity volume.
- **Further reading:** [S. S. Antman, Nonlinear Problems of Elasticity (Springer, Applied Mathematical Sciences 107; DOI of the 2005 edition)](https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-27649-1): monograph, first published 1995, that Ball's survey recommends as background and cites as a survey of rod and shell theories ([Ball 2002](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/ball/Articles%20in%20Conference%20Proceedings%20and%20Books/JMB%202002%20re%20Marsden%2060th.pdf)).
references.Mathematical Induction:
## Reference
### Overview
Mathematical induction proves that a statement $P(n)$ holds for every natural number by proving a base case and an induction step $P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)$. Equivalently, any set of natural numbers that contains $0$ and is closed under successor is all of $\mathbb N$. The same idea underlies definition by recursion: given $a\in A$ and $g$, there is a unique $f$ with $f(0)=a$ and $f(n+1)=g(n,f(n))$. ([Wikipedia: Mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction); [Logic and Proof](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/the_natural_numbers_and_induction.html))

Induction is both a proof technique and an axiom whose logical form matters. In second-order logic it is a single axiom quantifying over all predicates, and it pins down $\mathbb N$ up to isomorphism; in first-order [logic](node:First-Order%20Logic) it becomes a schema with one instance per formula, which admits nonstandard models; in ZFC it is a theorem about sets. How much induction a theory has measures its strength: Gentzen's analysis puts Peano arithmetic at the ordinal $\varepsilon_0$, and weak fragments of induction are the subject of bounded arithmetic. ([Wikipedia: Mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction); [Wikipedia: Peano axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms); [Wikipedia: Gentzen's consistency proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentzen%27s_consistency_proof); [Wikipedia: Bounded arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_arithmetic))

### Formal definition
For a property $P$ of natural numbers:
$$\bigl(P(0)\land\forall n\,[P(n)\to P(n+1)]\bigr)\;\Longrightarrow\;\forall n\,P(n).$$
([Logic and Proof](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/the_natural_numbers_and_induction.html))

In second-order Peano arithmetic this is one axiom, $\forall X\,[(0\in X\land\forall n\,(n\in X\to S(n)\in X))\to\forall n\,(n\in X)]$, quantifying over sets of naturals. First-order Peano arithmetic (PA) replaces it by the schema of all instances $\varphi(0)\land\forall n\,(\varphi(n)\to\varphi(S(n)))\to\forall n\,\varphi(n)$ for first-order formulas $\varphi$; this is weaker, since there are only countably many formulas but uncountably many sets of naturals. ([Wikipedia: Peano axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms))

**Well-founded induction.** If $R$ is a well-founded relation on $X$ and, for every $x$, $P(y)$ for all $y\mathrel{R}x$ implies $P(x)$, then $P$ holds on all of $X$. Ordinary induction is the case of $\mathbb N$ with the successor relation; when $X$ consists of recursively defined [data structures](node:Data%20Structures) it is called structural induction. ([Wikipedia: Well-founded relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-founded_relation))

### Key results
- **Strong (complete) induction.** If $P(n)$ follows from $P(k)$ for all $k<n$, then $P$ holds for all $n$; no separate base case is needed. It is equivalent to ordinary induction: any strong-induction proof can be rewritten as an ordinary one by strengthening the hypothesis to $\forall k\le n\,P(k)$. ([Logic and Proof](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/the_natural_numbers_and_induction.html); [MIT 6.042, ch. 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_session8.pdf))
- **Least element principle.** Every nonempty set of natural numbers has a least element; classically this is equivalent to complete induction. As axioms, however, the relation is subtle: in the context of the other Peano axioms, induction is strictly stronger than the well-ordering principle, which implies induction only with extra axioms such as trichotomy and "every number is $0$ or a successor". ([Logic and Proof](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/the_natural_numbers_and_induction.html); [Wikipedia: Mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction))
- **Transfinite induction.** If, for every ordinal $\alpha$, $P(\beta)$ for all $\beta<\alpha$ implies $P(\alpha)$, then $P$ holds for all ordinals; equivalently one proves a zero case, a successor case and a limit case. It holds for any well-ordered set, and the transfinite recursion theorem gives a unique $F$ with $F(\alpha)=G(F\restriction\alpha)$. ([Wikipedia: Transfinite induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfinite_induction))
- **Dedekind categoricity.** Any two models of the second-order Peano axioms are isomorphic (Dedekind, 1888); no first-order axiomatization has this property. ([Wikipedia: Peano axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms))
- **Nonstandard models of PA.** By compactness and the upward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem, first-order PA has nonstandard models of every infinite [cardinality](node:Cardinality); a countable nonstandard model has order type $\omega+\zeta\cdot\eta$ (the naturals followed by a dense ordering of copies of $\mathbb Z$). Skolem gave an explicit construction in 1933, and by Tennenbaum's theorem (1959) no countable nonstandard model has computable addition or multiplication. Induction forbids any definable proper cut (the overspill lemma). ([Wikipedia: Peano axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms))
- **Gentzen's theorem and the strength of induction.** Gentzen (1936) proved PA consistent assuming primitive recursive arithmetic plus quantifier-free transfinite induction up to $\varepsilon_0$; his work shows that the proof-theoretic ordinal of PA is $\varepsilon_0$, while $I\Sigma_1$ (induction for $\Sigma_1$ formulas only) has ordinal $\omega^\omega$. Kirby and Paris (1982) used it to show Goodstein's theorem is unprovable in PA. ([Wikipedia: Gentzen's consistency proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentzen%27s_consistency_proof); [Wikipedia: Ordinal analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_analysis))
- **Paris–Harrington theorem.** The strengthened finite Ramsey theorem (homogeneous sets $Y$ with $|Y|\ge\min Y$) is true and expressible in PA, but PA proves that it implies the consistency of PA, so by [Gödel's second incompleteness theorem](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems) PA does not prove it (Paris and Harrington, 1977); a proof via a reflection principle can be carried out in second-order arithmetic. ([Wikipedia: Paris–Harrington theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Harrington_theorem))
- **Bounded induction.** $I\Delta_0$ (Robinson arithmetic plus induction for bounded formulas, Parikh 1971) cannot prove that exponentiation is total. ([Wikipedia: Bounded arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_arithmetic))

### Examples
A finite set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets: the empty set has one, and the subsets of an $(n+1)$-element set split into those omitting a fixed element $a$ and those containing it, $2^n$ each. ([Logic and Proof](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/the_natural_numbers_and_induction.html)) Maurolico's 1575 example is $1+3+\dots+(2n-1)=n^2$. ([Wikipedia: Mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction))

The classic fallacy "all horses are the same colour" inducts from $n$ to $n+1$ by overlapping two $n$-element subsets; the step fails at $n+1=2$, where the subsets $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ do not overlap. ([Wikipedia: Mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction); [MIT 6.042, ch. 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_session8.pdf))

### History
Al-Karaji (c. 1000) gave an implicit inductive proof, later cited by al-Samawal al-Maghribi; Bhaskara's "cyclic method" contains early implicit uses; Gersonides (1288–1344) is the earliest rigorous user; Maurolico used the technique in 1575; and Pascal (1665) gave the first explicit formulation. Fermat's infinite descent is a related method. The modern formal treatment came in the nineteenth century with Boole, De Morgan, Peirce, Peano and Dedekind. Acerbi has argued that Plato's *Parmenides* (c. 370 BC) contains traces of an early implicit inductive proof. ([Wikipedia: Mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction)) Dedekind's axiomatization appeared in 1888 (*Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen?*) and Peano's in 1889; Gentzen's consistency proof appeared in *Mathematische Annalen* in 1936. ([Wikipedia: Peano axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms); [Crossref: Gentzen 1936](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01565428))

### Connections
- [Proof Techniques](node:Proof%20Techniques): induction is one general proof pattern, alongside [Proof by Contradiction](node:Proof%20by%20Contradiction).
- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic): the induction step is an implication.
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): the induction schema and nonstandard models.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): successor-closed sets; transfinite induction on ordinals.
- [Structural Induction](node:Structural%20Induction): well-founded induction over recursively defined data.
- [Proof Theory](node:Proof%20Theory): ordinal analysis measures the strength of induction.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): behind Gentzen's and Paris–Harrington's results.
- [MSC 03Hxx - Nonstandard models](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models): nonstandard models of arithmetic.
- [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory): inductive types and their eliminators.

### Common pitfalls
The base case and the step must jointly reach every case claimed; a step that silently needs $n\ge2$ (as in the horses fallacy) leaves a gap. Strong induction is not logically stronger than ordinary induction. Books sometimes state that induction and the well-ordering principle are equivalent without qualification; as axioms over the remaining Peano axioms they are not. First-order induction does not rule out nonstandard numbers. ([MIT 6.042, ch. 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_session8.pdf); [Wikipedia: Mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction); [Wikipedia: Peano axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms))

### Open problems
- **Does bounded induction prove the [pigeonhole principle](node:Pigeonhole%20Principle)?** Paris, Wilkie and Woods showed $I\Delta_0+\Omega_1$ proves the $\Sigma_0$ pigeonhole principle for $n^2$ pigeons into $n$ holes, and with a further construction of Paris–Wilkie–Woods and Thapen this yields the $2n$-into-$n$ version too (where $\Omega_1$ asserts that $x\mapsto x^{\log x}$ is total). Whether $I\Delta_0+\Omega_1$ proves it for $n+1$ pigeons into $n$ holes, first raised by Macintyre, is described by Belanger, Chong, Wang, Wong and Yang as "a fundamental open question in bounded arithmetic"; the question whether $B\Sigma_1+\Omega_1$ proves the $\Sigma_1$ pigeonhole principle for $n+1$ into $n$ is equivalent to it, and no unrelativized separation of the $\Sigma_0$ weak ($2n$) and full ($n+1$) versions is known. ([Belanger et al., §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.03487); [Belanger et al., abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.03487))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Mathematical induction (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction): variants, history, relation to well-ordering.
- **Reference:** [Peano axioms (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms): first- vs second-order induction, nonstandard models, consistency.
- **Learn:** [Logic and Proof, The Natural Numbers and Induction](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/the_natural_numbers_and_induction.html): induction, recursion and complete induction with Lean.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.042, Chapter 5: Induction](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_session8.pdf): ordinary and strong induction, comparison with well ordering.
- **Primary:** [Gentzen, Die Widerspruchsfreiheit der reinen Zahlentheorie, Math. Ann. 112 (1936)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01565428): the consistency proof of PA by induction up to $\varepsilon_0$.
- **Primary:** [Belanger, Chong, Wang, Wong, Yang, Where Pigeonhole Principles meet König Lemmas](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.03487): research paper on pigeonhole principles in weak arithmetic.
- **Further reading:** [Hájek and Pudlák, Metamathematics of First-Order Arithmetic (Springer, 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-662-22156-3): standard monograph on fragments of arithmetic and induction.

## Reference
### Overview
Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) estimates the parameters of an assumed statistical model by maximizing the likelihood function, so that under the model the observed data are as probable as possible. For i.i.d. data the log-likelihood is a sum of log-densities; when it is differentiable, the first-order conditions are the *likelihood equations*, and in general the maximizer must be found by numerical optimization, with possibly several roots in finite samples ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)).

The method's appeal is asymptotic. Under regularity conditions the MLE is consistent and asymptotically normal with variance $1/(nI(\theta^*))$ given by the [Fisher Information](node:Fisher%20Information), and it is often optimal in the sense of having the lowest variance among unbiased estimators with an asymptotic Gaussian limit; for large samples maximizing the likelihood is roughly equivalent to minimizing the [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence) to the true model, an interpretation the method of moments lacks ([CMU 36-700 Lecture 12](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/700/lec12.pdf)). It has, however, no optimality properties for finite samples ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)).

Le Cam's survey stresses that nobody has proved that maximum likelihood estimates are "best" in all circumstances, and collects examples in which the MLE fails to exist, is inadmissible, or is inconsistent, concluding that the procedure "cannot be universally recommended" ([Le Cam 1990](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~rice/LeCam/papers/tech168.pdf)). Much modern theory studies exactly the cases where regularity fails, where the asymptotic theory is not valid (as in high-dimensional statistics, where the number of parameters greatly exceeds the number of data points), or where the MLE is intractable to compute, as in graphical and latent-variable models ([CMU 36-700 Lecture 12](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/700/lec12.pdf)).

### Formal definition
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be i.i.d. with density $f(x,\theta)$ relative to a $\sigma$-finite measure, $\theta\in\Theta$. A maximum likelihood estimate is any $\hat\theta$ with
$$\prod_{j=1}^n f(x_j,\hat\theta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\prod_{j=1}^n f(x_j,\theta).$$
Such a $\hat\theta$ need not exist; when it does it may depend on the version of the densities chosen, and the map $(x_1,\dots,x_n)\mapsto\hat\theta$ need not be measurable ([Le Cam 1990](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~rice/LeCam/papers/tech168.pdf)).

The **score** is $s_\theta(X)=\partial_\theta\log f_\theta(X)$, which has mean zero under $f_\theta$; the **Fisher information** is
$$I(\theta)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta\big(s_\theta(X)\big)=-\,\mathbb{E}_\theta\Big[\tfrac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f_\theta(X)\Big],$$
the second equality holding under mild regularity conditions. The **observed information** is $I_n(\hat\theta)=-\frac1n\sum_i\partial_\theta^2\log f_\theta(X_i)\big|_{\theta=\hat\theta}$ ([CMU 36-700 Lecture 12](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/700/lec12.pdf)).

A model is **identifiable** if $\theta_1\neq\theta_2$ implies $D(f_{\theta_1}\,\|\,f_{\theta_2})>0$, i.e. distinct parameters give distinct distributions ([CMU 36-700 Lecture 12](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/700/lec12.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Consistency.** If the model is identified, $\Theta$ is compact, the log-density is continuous in $\theta$, and a dominance (integrable envelope) condition holds, the MLE converges in probability to the true parameter. Identification is necessary; compactness is sufficient but not necessary ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)). The proof idea: $M_n(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_i\log\frac{f_\theta(X_i)}{f_{\theta^*}(X_i)}\to-D(f_{\theta^*}\|f_\theta)$, uniquely maximized at $\theta^*$, and a uniform law of large numbers upgrades pointwise to uniform convergence ([CMU 36-700 Lecture 12](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/700/lec12.pdf)).
- **Asymptotic normality.** Under regularity conditions (true parameter interior, smooth likelihood), $\sqrt{nI(\theta^*)}\,(\hat\theta-\theta^*)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$, and the same holds with $I(\theta^*)$ replaced by $I(\hat\theta)$ or the observed information $I_n(\hat\theta)$. The proof Taylor-expands the score: $\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta^*)\approx \frac{n^{-1/2}\ell'(\theta^*)}{-n^{-1}\ell''(\theta^*)}$, with the CLT for the numerator and the LLN for the denominator ([CMU 36-700 Lecture 12](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/700/lec12.pdf)).
- **Asymptotic efficiency and bias.** The MLE attains the Cramér–Rao bound asymptotically; its bias is zero to order $n^{-1/2}$ but generally nonzero at order $n^{-1}$, and a bias-corrected MLE is second-order efficient ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)).
- **Functional invariance.** If $\hat\theta$ is the MLE of $\theta$, then $g(\hat\theta)$ is the MLE of $g(\theta)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)).
- **Misspecification.** Even when the model does not contain the true distribution, maximizing likelihood asymptotically finds the model member with minimal KL divergence to the truth, hence minimal cross-entropy ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)).
- **Wilks' theorem (1938).** For nested models with the true parameter in the interior of the parameter space and suitable regularity, $-2\log\Lambda$ converges under $H_0$ to $\chi^2_{k}$ with $k=\dim\Theta-\dim\Theta_0$. On the boundary the limit can instead be a mixture of chi-square laws ([Wikipedia: Wilks' theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilks%27_theorem)).
- **Failure in proportional asymptotics.** For logistic regression with $n,p\to\infty$ at a fixed ratio and independent features, the MLE is biased, its variance is far larger than classical theory predicts, and the likelihood-ratio statistic is not chi-square; the limits depend on the coefficients only through a scalar signal strength ([Sur and Candès 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.06964)).

### Examples
- **Normal and Bernoulli.** For a normal sample, the MLE of the mean is the sample mean and the MLE of the variance divides by $n$, with expectation $\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$. For $s$ successes in $n$ Bernoulli trials the MLE is $s/n$, e.g. $49/80$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)).
- **Uniform$[0,\theta]$.** The MLE is $Z=\max_j X_j$ with $\mathbb E(Z-\theta)^2=\frac{2\theta^2}{(n+1)(n+2)}$, while $\frac{n+2}{n+1}Z$ has mean squared error $\frac{\theta^2}{(n+1)^2}$, smaller for every $n\ge1$ ([Le Cam 1990](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~rice/LeCam/papers/tech168.pdf)).
- **Unbounded likelihood.** In a two-component normal mixture with a free scale $\sigma$, taking $\mu=x_1$ and $\sigma\to0$ makes the likelihood infinite, so no MLE exists; the three-parameter lognormal and shifted gamma behave similarly ([Le Cam 1990](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~rice/LeCam/papers/tech168.pdf)).
- **Neyman–Scott.** With pairs $(X_j,Y_j)\sim N(\xi_j,\sigma^2)$ independent and nuisance means $\xi_j$, the joint MLE is $\hat\sigma^2_n=\tfrac12 s_n^2$ where $s_n^2=\frac1{2n}\sum (X_j-Y_j)^2$ is consistent, so the MLE converges to $\sigma^2/2$: using all the information gives an inconsistent estimate ([Le Cam 1990](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~rice/LeCam/papers/tech168.pdf)).

### History
Early forms of the method were used by Gauss, Laplace, Thiele and Edgeworth; R. A. Fisher created the modern version between 1912 and 1922, and Wilks's 1938 theorem gave the likelihood-ratio test its asymptotic justification ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)). Stigler's history traces the idea back through Lagrange, Bernoulli, Euler, Laplace and Gauss, presents Fisher's unpublished 1930 conditions for consistency and efficiency, and follows the story to Le Cam's dissertation ([Stigler 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.2996)). Counterexamples accumulated in parallel: Neyman and Scott (1948), Bahadur (1958) and Ferguson (1982), the last satisfying all of Wald's (1949) consistency conditions except one while the MLE remains inconsistent ([Le Cam 1990](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~rice/LeCam/papers/tech168.pdf)).

### Connections
- [Fisher Information](node:Fisher%20Information): the asymptotic variance of the MLE is its inverse.
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence): MLE asymptotically minimizes KL divergence from the data distribution to the model.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss): minimizing cross-entropy loss is maximum likelihood for a categorical model.
- [Logistic Regression](node:Logistic%20Regression): fitted by maximum likelihood; the setting of the Sur–Candès high-dimensional theory.
- [Expectation-Maximization Algorithm](node:Expectation-Maximization%20Algorithm): an iterative method for MLE with latent variables.
- [Maximum A Posteriori Estimation](node:Maximum%20A%20Posteriori%20Estimation): adds a prior to the likelihood; MLE is MAP with a flat prior.
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing): likelihood-ratio tests and Wilks' theorem are built on the MLE.
- [Numerical Optimization](node:Numerical%20Optimization): the MLE is usually computed numerically, e.g. by gradient methods.
- [Information Theory](node:Information%20Theory): log-likelihood, entropy and KL divergence share one calculus.

### Common pitfalls
- Finding a stationary point of the likelihood is not the same as finding the maximum: the solution can be a saddle or local minimum, so the Hessian should be checked; on open parameter spaces the likelihood may increase without attaining a supremum ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation)).
- Standard asymptotics assume compact parameter spaces, an interior true parameter and smooth likelihoods, and computing the MLE can in general be intractable ([CMU 36-700 Lecture 12](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/700/lec12.pdf)).
- Rules of thumb such as $n\ge 5p$ or $10p$ do not make classical logistic-regression inference valid when $p/n$ is non-negligible ([Sur and Candès 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.06964)).
- Le Cam's principle: "Never trust an estimate which is thrown out of whack if you suppress a single observation" ([Le Cam 1990](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~rice/LeCam/papers/tech168.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Maximum likelihood threshold of a graph.** The MLT of a graph is the minimum number of samples that almost surely guarantees that the MLE exists in the corresponding Gaussian graphical model. Bernstein et al. characterize it via graph rigidity and conjecture that the MLT of an Erdős–Rényi random graph equals its generic completion rank with high probability; they prove this only for graphs with MLT at most 4 ([Bernstein et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.02185)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Maximum likelihood estimation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation): definition, conditions for consistency, efficiency, KL interpretation, history.
- **Learn:** [CMU 36-700 Lecture 12 (Balakrishnan)](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~siva/teaching/700/lec12.pdf): consistency via KL divergence, Fisher information, and the Taylor-expansion proof of asymptotic normality.
- **Primary:** [Le Cam, Maximum likelihood: an introduction (1990)](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~rice/LeCam/papers/tech168.pdf): counterexamples (Neyman–Scott, Bahadur, Ferguson) and practical principles.
- **Primary:** [Stigler, The Epic Story of Maximum Likelihood (2007)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.2996): history from Lagrange to Le Cam, including Fisher's 1930 conditions.
- **Primary:** [Sur and Candès, A modern maximum-likelihood theory for high-dimensional logistic regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.06964): proportional-asymptotics failure of classical theory.
- **Further reading:** [van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics (CUP, 1998)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/asymptotic-statistics/A3C7DAD3F7E66A1FA60E9C8FE132EE1D): M- and Z-estimators, efficiency, likelihood ratio tests, local asymptotic normality.
references.Maximum Principle:
## Reference
### Overview
A maximum principle says that a function satisfying a second-order elliptic or parabolic differential inequality cannot have an interior maximum unless it is constant, so its size is controlled by boundary (or initial-boundary) values. For harmonic functions this follows from the mean value property: a harmonic function equals its average over every ball and sphere in its domain, and a subharmonic function ($\Delta u\ge0$) that attains its maximum at an interior point of a connected domain is constant. ([MIT 18.156 lecture 1, Theorems 1-2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/2d5342d2f35b2d991e8a284c5ab1e325_lec1.pdf))

The principle holds far beyond the Laplacian. For a general operator $Lu=a^{ij}D_{ij}u+b^iD_iu+cu$ the weak principle needs only strict ellipticity, bounded coefficients and the sign condition $c\le0$; the strong principle of Hopf adds uniform ellipticity and rests on the Hopf boundary point lemma. ([MIT 18.156 lecture 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/d9e0f047d5682a70799331a926d27a11_lec6.pdf)) In the fully nonlinear setting the same idea becomes the comparison principle for viscosity solutions, from which uniqueness and continuous dependence follow. ([Crandall-Ishii-Lions, User's Guide, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207212)) Gilbarg and Trudinger's *Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order* (Springer Classics in Mathematics, 2001) has a chapter titled "The Classical Maximum Principle". ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61798-0_3))

### Formal definition
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded domain and $L=a^{ij}(x)D_{ij}+b^i(x)D_i+c(x)$ with bounded coefficients. $L$ is *elliptic* if $(a^{ij}(x))>\lambda(x)I$ with $\lambda(x)>0$, *strictly elliptic* if moreover $\lambda(x)>\lambda_0>0$, and *uniformly elliptic* if $\Lambda I>(a^{ij})>\lambda_0I$ for constants $\Lambda>\lambda_0>0$. ([MIT 18.156 lecture 6, Definition 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/d9e0f047d5682a70799331a926d27a11_lec6.pdf))

**Weak maximum principle.** If $L$ is strictly elliptic, $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^0(\overline\Omega)$ and $Lu\ge0$ in $\Omega$, then
$$c\equiv0\ \Rightarrow\ \sup_\Omega u=\sup_{\partial\Omega}u,\qquad c\le0\ \Rightarrow\ \sup_\Omega u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^+,$$
where $u^+=\max\{u,0\}$; in particular $Lu=0$ and $c\le0$ give $\sup_\Omega|u|=\sup_{\partial\Omega}|u|$. ([MIT 18.156 lecture 6, Theorems 1-2](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/d9e0f047d5682a70799331a926d27a11_lec6.pdf))

### Key results
- **Comparison and uniqueness.** If $L$ is strictly elliptic with $c\le0$, $u,v\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^0(\overline\Omega)$, $Lu\ge Lv$ in $\Omega$ and $u\le v$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $u\le v$ in $\Omega$; hence the [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem) $Lu=f$, $u=g$ has at most one classical solution. If $L$ is strictly elliptic with $c\le0$, $\Omega$ is bounded and $Lu=f$, then $\sup_\Omega|u|\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}|u|+C\sup_\Omega|f|$ with $C=C(\lambda,\Omega)$. ([MIT 18.156 lecture 6, Corollary 1 and Theorem 3](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/d9e0f047d5682a70799331a926d27a11_lec6.pdf))
- **Hopf boundary point lemma.** Let $L$ be uniformly elliptic with $c=0$ and $Lu\ge0$ in $\Omega$. Suppose $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, $u$ is continuous at $x_0$, $u(x_0)>u(x)$ for all $x\in\Omega$, and $\partial\Omega$ satisfies an interior sphere condition at $x_0$. Then the outer normal derivative, if it exists, satisfies $\partial u/\partial\nu(x_0)>0$. The same holds for $c\le0$ if $u(x_0)\ge0$, and for any $c$ if $u(x_0)=0$. ([MIT 18.156 lecture 6, Lemma 1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/d9e0f047d5682a70799331a926d27a11_lec6.pdf))
- **Hopf strong maximum principle.** Let $L$ be uniformly elliptic, $Lu\ge0$ in a connected $\Omega$, $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^0(\overline\Omega)$. If $c=0$ and $u$ attains its maximum in the interior, $u$ is constant. If $c\le0$, $u$ cannot attain a non-negative interior maximum unless it is constant. ([MIT 18.156 lecture 6, Theorem 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/d9e0f047d5682a70799331a926d27a11_lec6.pdf))
- **Alexandrov-Bakelman-Pucci (ABP) estimate.** Let $Lu=\sum a_{ij}(x)\partial_{ij}u$ with bounded measurable coefficients and $\lambda I\le A(x)\le\Lambda I$, and let $\Omega$ be bounded. If $u\in C(\Omega)$ satisfies $Lu\ge f$ in the $L^n$-viscosity sense with $f\in L^n(\Omega)$ and $u$ is bounded on $\partial\Omega$, then $\sup_\Omega u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u+C\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\|f\|_{L^n(\Omega)}$, with $C$ depending only on $n,\lambda,\Lambda$. ([Torres-Latorre, Theorem 2.12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.15782))
- **Parabolic weak maximum principle.** Let $Q_T=(0,T)\times\Omega$ with parabolic boundary $\partial_pQ_T=\{0\}\times\Omega\cup(0,T]\times\partial\Omega$. If $w\in C^{1,2}(Q_T)\cap C(\overline{Q_T})$ solves $w_t-D\Delta w=f$ with $f\le0$, then $\max_{\overline{Q_T}}w=\max_{\partial_pQ_T}w$. Consequently, if $v_t-Dv_{xx}=f\ge g=w_t-Dw_{xx}$ and $v\ge w$ on $\partial_pQ_T$, then $v\ge w$ on $Q_T$, and $\max|v-w|\le\max_{\partial_pQ_T}|v-w|+T\max|f-g|$. ([Speck, MIT 18.152 class 4, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.0.1](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/da093b7265d1fc4fe9c6edf3e7825661_MIT18_152F11_lec_04.pdf)) The top face $\{T\}\times\Omega$ is excluded from $\partial_pQ_T$. See [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation).
- **Comparison for viscosity solutions.** Call $F(x,r,p,X)$ *proper* if it is nondecreasing in $r$ and nonincreasing in the symmetric matrix $X$ (degenerate ellipticity). If $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^N$ is bounded, $F$ is continuous and proper, $F(x,r,p,X)-F(x,s,p,X)\ge\gamma(r-s)$ for $r\ge s$ with $\gamma>0$, and $F$ satisfies the structure condition (3.14) of the User's Guide, then an upper semicontinuous subsolution $u$ and a lower semicontinuous supersolution $v$ of $F=0$ with $u\le v$ on $\partial\Omega$ satisfy $u\le v$ in $\Omega$. ([Crandall-Ishii-Lions, §0 and Theorem 3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9207212))
- **Phragmén-Lindelöf principle.** On unbounded regions boundary bounds need a growth hypothesis. If $F$ is holomorphic in a sector of opening $\pi/\lambda$, continuous up to the boundary, $|F|\le1$ on the boundary and $|F(z)|\le e^{C|z|^\rho}$ with $\rho<\lambda$, then $|F|\le1$ throughout; a version applies to subharmonic functions. ([Phragmén-Lindelöf principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phragm%C3%A9n%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_principle))

### Examples
The sign condition on $c$ matters: in one dimension $y''+2y=0$ has sinusoidal solutions with interior maxima, whereas $y''-2y=0$ has exponential solutions, and for eigenfunction equations $\Delta u+cu=0$ interior maxima can occur, so the sign of $c$ is relevant. ([Maximum principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_principle)) The growth condition in Phragmén-Lindelöf is sharp: in the strip $|\operatorname{Im}z|<\pi/2$ the function $\exp(\exp z)$ is bounded by 1 on the boundary but unbounded inside. ([Phragmén-Lindelöf principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phragm%C3%A9n%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_principle))

### History
Zaremba found the boundary point lemma for the Laplacian in 1910; Hopf and Oleinik independently proved the general elliptic case in 1952. ([Hopf lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_lemma)) The strong maximum principle for second-order elliptic operators goes back to Hopf (1927); Nirenberg's 1953 paper is titled "A strong maximum principle for parabolic equations", and Protter and Weinberger's monograph (1967, reprinted 1984) collects the classical theory. ([Maximum principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_principle)) Phragmén and Lindelöf formulated their principle in 1908. ([Phragmén-Lindelöf principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phragm%C3%A9n%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_principle)) Crandall, Ishii and Lions surveyed comparison, uniqueness and existence for viscosity solutions in 1992. ([User's Guide, arXiv listing](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207212))

### Connections
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): the harmonic and subharmonic case, via the mean value property.
- [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem): comparison gives uniqueness and $C^0$ bounds.
- [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation): the parabolic version on the parabolic boundary.
- [MSC 35Jxx - Elliptic equations and elliptic systems](node:MSC%2035Jxx%20-%20Elliptic%20equations%20and%20elliptic%20systems): the general elliptic setting.
- [Free Boundary Problems](node:Free%20Boundary%20Problems): boundary nondegeneracy (Hopf-type) estimates feed free-boundary regularity.
- [Partial Differential Operators](node:Partial%20Differential%20Operators): the operator class to which the principle applies.

### Common pitfalls
- The weak principle with $c\le0$ bounds $u$ by $\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^+$, not by $\sup_{\partial\Omega}u$; with $c\le0$ the strong principle only excludes a *non-negative* interior maximum. ([MIT 18.156 lecture 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/d9e0f047d5682a70799331a926d27a11_lec6.pdf))
- The Hopf lemma needs a regularity condition on the boundary, such as an interior sphere at $x_0$. In merely $C^1$ domains one gets a weaker nondegeneracy estimate with an explicit modulus, which becomes the Hopf-Oleinik lemma when the $C^1$ modulus of the boundary is Dini. ([Torres-Latorre, introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.15782))
- The maximum modulus principle cannot be applied directly on an unbounded region; a growth condition such as that of Phragmén-Lindelöf is needed. ([Phragmén-Lindelöf principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phragm%C3%A9n%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_principle))

### Open problems
- **Boundary behaviour in $C^1$ domains and free boundaries.** Torres-Latorre extends the Hopf-Oleinik lemma to $C^1$ domains with an explicit modulus and states the plan to use such finer estimates to understand free boundaries (e.g. those with logarithmic moduli of continuity, as expected for the Stefan problem) "in a future work". ([Torres-Latorre, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.15782))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Maximum principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_principle): statements, history, bibliography.
- **Reference:** [Hopf lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_lemma): boundary point lemma and its history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.156 lecture 6](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-156-differential-analysis-spring-2004/d9e0f047d5682a70799331a926d27a11_lec6.pdf): weak and strong principles, Hopf lemma, $C^0$ estimates with proofs.
- **Learn:** [Speck, MIT 18.152 class 4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/da093b7265d1fc4fe9c6edf3e7825661_MIT18_152F11_lec_04.pdf): the parabolic weak maximum principle.
- **Primary:** [Crandall, Ishii, Lions, User's Guide to Viscosity Solutions](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9207212): comparison principles for fully nonlinear equations (Bull. AMS 1992).
- **Primary:** [Torres-Latorre, Boundary estimates for non-divergence equations in $C^1$ domains](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.15782): ABP and Hopf-Oleinik in rough domains.
- **Further reading:** [Gilbarg, Trudinger, Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order, ch. 3 "The Classical Maximum Principle" (Springer Classics in Mathematics, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61798-0_3).
references.Maxwell's Equations:
## Reference
### Overview
Maxwell's equations are the coupled partial differential equations of classical electromagnetism: they determine the electric field $\mathbf E$ and magnetic field $\mathbf B$ produced by charge density $\rho$ and current density $\mathbf J$, and together with the Lorentz force law they underlie classical optics, circuits and radiation. The microscopic form uses total charge and current; the macroscopic form introduces $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf H$ and only free sources, at the price of constitutive relations for the medium. Since the mid-20th century they have been understood as the classical limit of [Quantum Electrodynamics](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics); they cannot explain photon–photon scattering or phenomena involving individual photons interacting with quantum matter. ([Wikipedia: Maxwell's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations))

Mathematically the system carries constraints: two divergence equations restrict the initial data, and the two curl equations evolve it. In relativistic language they are $dF=0$ and $d{\star}F=\mu_0J$ for the field-strength 2-form $F$, and $F=dA$ for a potential $A$ subject to a topological restriction on spacetime. ([Wikipedia: Maxwell's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations); [Electromagnetic tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_tensor))

### Formal definition
Microscopic equations in SI units:

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf E=-\frac{\partial\mathbf B}{\partial t},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\Big(\mathbf J+\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}\Big)
$$

([Wikipedia: Maxwell's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations))

The macroscopic equations read $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$, $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B$, $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f+\partial_t\mathbf D$, with e.g. $\mathbf D=\varepsilon\mathbf E$, $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$ in linear isotropic media. The term $\varepsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E$ is the [Displacement Current](node:Displacement%20Current). ([Wikipedia: Maxwell's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations))

**Potentials.** The homogeneous equations are solved by $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$, $\mathbf E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$ (see [Magnetic Vector Potential](node:Magnetic%20Vector%20Potential)). The potentials are not unique; imposing the Lorenz condition $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ turns the inhomogeneous equations into $\Box\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\Box\mathbf A=\mu_0\mathbf J$ with $\Box=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\nabla^2$. The Lorenz condition is Lorentz invariant but only partially fixes the gauge (residual $A_\mu\mapsto A_\mu+\partial_\mu f$ with $\Box f=0$); Maxwell himself worked in what is now called the Coulomb gauge. ([Lorenz gauge condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenz_gauge_condition))

**Covariant and differential-form versions.** With $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ and $J^\alpha=(c\rho,\mathbf J)$, the inhomogeneous pair is $\partial_\alpha F^{\beta\alpha}=-\mu_0J^\beta$ (signature $+---$) and the homogeneous pair is the Bianchi identity $\partial_\gamma F_{\alpha\beta}+\partial_\alpha F_{\beta\gamma}+\partial_\beta F_{\gamma\alpha}=0$; both follow from the action $\int\big(-\tfrac{1}{4\mu_0}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}-J^\mu A_\mu\big)d^4x$. In [forms](node:Differential%20Forms), $dF=0$ and $d{\star}F=\mu_0J$. ([Electromagnetic tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_tensor); [Wikipedia: Maxwell's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations))

### Key results
- **Charge conservation and constraint propagation.** Taking the divergence of the Ampère–Maxwell law and using Gauss's law gives $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$ (the [Continuity Equation](node:Continuity%20Equation)). Conversely, the system looks overdetermined (eight equations, six unknowns), but any solution of the two curl equations satisfies both Gauss laws at all times provided the initial data do, charge is conserved and there are no monopoles; uniqueness requires initial and boundary conditions. ([Wikipedia: Maxwell's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations)) See [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems).
- **Waves.** In source-free regions $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ satisfy the [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation) with speed $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$, giving [Electromagnetic Waves](node:Electromagnetic%20Waves). ([Wikipedia: Maxwell's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations))
- **Retarded potentials and Jefimenko's equations.** For arbitrary time-dependent sources, with $r=|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|$, unit vector $\mathbf n$ from source to field point and $[\cdot]$ meaning evaluation at retarded time $t_r=t-r/c$,
  $$\varphi=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\frac{[\rho]}{r}\,dV',\qquad \mathbf E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\Big(\frac{[\rho]\mathbf n}{r^2}+\frac{[\dot\rho]\mathbf n}{cr}-\frac{[\dot{\mathbf J}]}{c^2r}\Big)dV',$$
  $$\mathbf B=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\Big(\frac{[\mathbf J]\times\mathbf n}{c^2r^2}+\frac{[\dot{\mathbf J}]\times\mathbf n}{c^3r}\Big)dV'.$$
  Fields at $(\mathbf r,t)$ depend only on sources at the retarded time. ([Jefimenko's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefimenko%27s_equations); [Lorenz gauge condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenz_gauge_condition))
- **Poynting's theorem (energy).** With $u=\tfrac12(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H)$ in non-dispersive media and $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$, $-\partial_tu=\nabla\cdot\mathbf S+\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$; integrated over a fixed volume, the decrease of field energy equals the outward flux plus the work done on charges (Poynting, 1884). ([Poynting's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poynting%27s_theorem))
