([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%B6wenheim%E2%80%93Skolem_theorem)) Łoś noted in 1954 three ways a complete theory in a countable language with an infinite model could be categorical (countably, uncountably, or totally), and Morley's 1965 theorem showed that categoricity in one uncountable cardinal implies it in all. ([Wikipedia, Morley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morley%27s_categoricity_theorem); [SEP, §5.1](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/)) Vaught proposed his conjecture in 1961. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaught_conjecture))

### Connections
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic) supplies the languages, formulas and quantifiers.
- [Compactness Theorem](node:Compactness%20Theorem) is the basic existence tool.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory) and [Cardinality](node:Cardinality) govern the sizes of models in Löwenheim–Skolem and categoricity.
- [Model Theory of Fields](node:Model%20Theory%20of%20Fields) applies QE and model completeness to ACF, RCF and valued fields; see [Valued Fields](node:Valued%20Fields).
- [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields) are the models of the theory of $\mathbb R$.
- [Ultraproducts of Commutative Rings](node:Ultraproducts%20of%20Commutative%20Rings) uses Łoś's theorem in algebra.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems) contrast with the decidable theories obtained from QE.
- [MSC 03Cxx - Model theory](node:MSC%2003Cxx%20-%20Model%20theory) and [MSC 03Hxx - Nonstandard models](node:MSC%2003Hxx%20-%20Nonstandard%20models) are the subject maps.

### Common pitfalls
A complete theory (one that decides every sentence) differs from the completeness theorem for the proof calculus, and sharing a complete theory does not make structures isomorphic: by Löwenheim–Skolem every complete theory with an infinite model has non-isomorphic models of different infinite cardinalities. ([Pillay, Cor. 1.32](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~apillay/pdf/lecturenotes_modeltheory.pdf)) QE depends on the language: RCF has it in the language of ordered rings but not in the ring language. ([Pillay, Example 3.10](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~apillay/pdf/lecturenotes_modeltheory.pdf)) Do not conflate $A\subseteq B$, $A\equiv B$ and $A\preccurlyeq B$: $A\preccurlyeq B$ implies the other two, but $A\subseteq B$ together with $A\cong B$ does not imply $A\preccurlyeq B$, as the example above shows. ([Weiss–D'Mello, Example 7](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/modeltheory/WeissDMello.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Vaught's conjecture.** For a countable complete first-order theory $T$ with infinite models, the number $I(T,\aleph_0)$ of countable models up to isomorphism cannot satisfy $\aleph_0<I(T,\aleph_0)<2^{\aleph_0}$. Morley showed that if $I(T,\aleph_0)$ is infinite it is $\aleph_0$, $\aleph_1$ or $2^{\aleph_0}$, so the conjecture is settled except for $\aleph_1$ models when CH fails; Harrington, Makkai and Shelah proved it for $\omega$-stable theories. Wikipedia lists it among unsolved problems. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaught_conjecture)) Gonzalez and Montalbán introduce a strengthening of the infinitary Vaught conjecture that they expect a structural proof would also give, and verify it for sentences whose models are linear orders. ([Gonzalez–Montalbán](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02156))
- **Tarski's exponential function problem.** Whether the theory of $(\mathbb R,+,\cdot,\exp)$ is decidable is open; Macintyre and Wilkie (1996) proved decidability assuming the real Schanuel conjecture. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarski%27s_exponential_function_problem)) Wilkie showed that this structure is o-minimal and that its complete theory is model-complete, which is weaker than quantifier elimination. ([SEP, §5.3](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [First-order Model Theory, SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/modeltheory-fo/): compactness, Löwenheim–Skolem, QE, Morley, stability, o-minimality.
- **Learn:** [Pillay, Lecture notes in model theory](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~apillay/pdf/lecturenotes_modeltheory.pdf): ultraproducts, types, QE tests, ACF and RCF; [Weiss and D'Mello](https://people.math.sc.edu/mcnulty/modeltheory/WeissDMello.pdf): introductory examples and exercises.
- **Primary:** [Gonzalez–Montalbán, The ω-Vaught's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02156): current research on Vaught's conjecture; [Hodges, Model Theory](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511551574) (CUP, 1993).
- **Further reading:** [Marker, Model Theory: An Introduction](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b98860) (Springer GTM, 2002) and [Hodges, Model Theory](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511551574): the standard graduate texts.
references.Model-Based Reinforcement Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Reinforcement learning is usually modelled as a Markov decision process with state space $\mathcal S$, action space $\mathcal A$, transition probabilities and rewards. A *model* of the environment is the transition distribution together with the reward function; model-free algorithms such as Q-learning and SARSA estimate neither ([Wikipedia: Model-free RL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model-free_%28reinforcement_learning%29)). Model-based methods first learn (or are given) a model and use it, for example as in Dyna, which generates extra modelled transitions to update a value function alongside real ones, or as in model predictive control, where the model directly drives behaviour. They can be more computationally intensive than model-free methods, and their usefulness is limited by how well the MDP can be learned ([Wikipedia: RL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)).

Moerland et al. define model-based RL as any MDP approach that uses a model, known or learned, and uses learning to approximate a global value or policy function. They separate planning from RL by whether a method stores a local solution (planning) or a global one (RL), giving three subcategories: learned model with learned solution (e.g. Dyna), known model with learned solution (e.g. AlphaZero), and planning over a learned model without a global solution ([Moerland et al., HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16712)). The survey's two halves cover learning dynamics models, with stochasticity, uncertainty, partial observability and temporal abstraction, and the ways planning and learning are integrated ([Moerland et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16712)).

The characteristic trade-off is that learned-model methods tend to have better sample complexity but inferior asymptotic performance, and can be unstable because of model uncertainty and approximation error; they trade extra computation, memory and potential instability for data efficiency ([Moerland et al., HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16712)). Model-based RL is a two-lecture unit of a standard graduate deep RL course ([Berkeley CS 285](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/)).

### Formal definition
Consider a discounted MDP $M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal A,P,r,\gamma)$ with rewards in $[0,1]$. In the *generative model* setting one may query $s'\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ for any $(s,a)$. The plug-in model-based method draws $N$ samples per pair, forms
$$\widehat P(s'\mid s,a)=\frac{\mathrm{count}(s',s,a)}{N},$$
and plans in the empirical MDP $\widehat M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal A,\widehat P,r,\gamma)$, using $|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|N$ samples in total ([Agarwal et al., RL Theory](https://rltheorybook.github.io/rltheorybook_ABJKS.pdf)).

Viewing $P$ as an $|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|\times|\mathcal S|$ matrix and $P^\pi$ as the state-action transition matrix under policy $\pi$, $Q^\pi=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}r$, and analogously $\widehat Q^\pi$ in $\widehat M$ ([Agarwal et al., RL Theory](https://rltheorybook.github.io/rltheorybook_ABJKS.pdf)).

In the deep-RL setting a learned model may predict observations, or only "the quantities most directly relevant to planning: the reward, the action-selection policy, and the value function", as in MuZero ([Schrittwieser et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08265)).

### Key results
- **Simulation lemma.** For any stationary policy $\pi$, $Q^\pi-\widehat Q^\pi=\gamma(I-\gamma\widehat P^\pi)^{-1}(P-\widehat P)V^\pi$; combined with $\|(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}v\|_\infty\le\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\|v\|_\infty$, this gives $\|Q^\pi-\widehat Q^\pi\|_\infty\le\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\|(P-\widehat P)V^\pi\|_\infty$ ([Agarwal et al., RL Theory](https://rltheorybook.github.io/rltheorybook_ABJKS.pdf)).
- **Naive plug-in bound.** There is an absolute constant $c$ such that, for $\epsilon\in(0,\frac1{1-\gamma})$, if $N\ge \frac{c\,|\mathcal S|\log(c|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|/\delta)}{(1-\gamma)^4\epsilon^2}$, then with probability $1-\delta$ every stationary policy has $\|Q^\pi-\widehat Q^\pi\|_\infty\le\epsilon$, and the optimal policy $\widehat\pi^\star$ of $\widehat M$ satisfies $\|Q^{\widehat\pi^\star}-Q^\star\|_\infty\le2\epsilon$ ([Agarwal et al., RL Theory](https://rltheorybook.github.io/rltheorybook_ABJKS.pdf)).
- **Minimax optimality of the model-based approach.** With $|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|N\ge c\frac{|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|}{(1-\gamma)^3}\frac{\log(c|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|/\delta)}{\epsilon^2}$ samples, $\|\widehat Q^\star-Q^\star\|_\infty\le\epsilon$ for $\epsilon\le1$, and $\|Q^{\widehat\pi^\star}-Q^\star\|_\infty\le\epsilon$ for $\epsilon\le1/\sqrt{1-\gamma}$, with probability $1-\delta$. Conversely, there is a class of MDPs such that, for $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ below absolute constants, any algorithm that is $(\epsilon,\delta)$-good on every MDP in the class needs at least $c\,\frac{|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|}{(1-\gamma)^3}\frac{\log(c/\delta)}{\epsilon^2}$ samples. The value bound and the lower bound are due to Azar et al. (2013), and the policy bound for the plug-in estimator to Agarwal et al. (2020) ([Agarwal et al., RL Theory](https://rltheorybook.github.io/rltheorybook_ABJKS.pdf)).
- **R-MAX.** A model-based algorithm that keeps a complete, initially optimistic model and acts optimally for it attains near-optimal average reward in polynomial time, also covering zero-sum stochastic games, and formally justifies "optimism under uncertainty" ([Brafman and Tennenholtz 2002](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/brafman02a.html)).
- **Monotonic improvement with learned models.** Janner et al. analyse a model-based algorithm with a guarantee of monotonic improvement at each step; since the bound is pessimistic, they add an empirical estimate of model generalization, which justifies short model rollouts branched from real data (MBPO) ([Janner et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08253)).

### Examples
- **Dyna.** A learned model plus a learned value function; the agent plans heavily from the model after each real step ([Moerland et al., HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16712)).
- **PILCO.** Differentiates through a Gaussian-process dynamics model and replans after collecting whole episodes ([Moerland et al., HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16712)).
- **MuZero.** Tree search with a learned model that predicts reward, policy and value; it set a state of the art on 57 Atari games and matched AlphaZero in Go, chess and shogi without being given the rules ([Schrittwieser et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08265)).
- **Dreamer.** Learns long-horizon behaviours from images "purely by latent imagination", propagating analytic gradients of learned values through trajectories imagined in a learned latent world model ([Hafner et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01603)).
- **MBPO.** Short model-generated rollouts from real states; more sample-efficient than earlier model-based methods while matching the asymptotic performance of the best model-free algorithms ([Janner et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08253)).

### History
Dyna introduced learning a model from experience and using it to generate additional transitions for value learning ([Wikipedia: RL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)). Polynomial-time guarantees followed with R-MAX in 2002, simpler and more general than Kearns and Singh's $E^3$ ([Brafman and Tennenholtz 2002](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/brafman02a.html)), and Azar et al. (2013) established the minimax sample complexity with a generative model ([Agarwal et al., RL Theory](https://rltheorybook.github.io/rltheorybook_ABJKS.pdf)). Deep model-based RL then produced MBPO and Dreamer in 2019 and MuZero, whose value-equivalent learned model outperformed AlphaGo Zero ([Moerland et al., HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16712); [Schrittwieser et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08265)).

### Connections
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): the parent field; model-based RL uses a model where model-free RL does not.
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the formal setting; the model is the transition kernel and reward.
- [Probabilistic Graphical Models](node:Probabilistic%20Graphical%20Models): dynamics models are often latent-variable or state-space graphical models.
- [Dynamic Programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming), [Value Iteration](node:Value%20Iteration) and [Policy Iteration](node:Policy%20Iteration): planning algorithms run inside a known or learned model.
- [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search): the planner in AlphaZero and MuZero.
- [Model Predictive Control](node:Model%20Predictive%20Control): replanning with a model at every step.
- [World Models](node:World%20Models) and [Latent State-Space Models](node:Latent%20State-Space%20Models): learned latent dynamics used for imagined rollouts, as in Dreamer.
- [Gaussian Processes](node:Gaussian%20Processes): the dynamics model in PILCO.
- [Exploration in Reinforcement Learning](node:Exploration%20in%20Reinforcement%20Learning): R-MAX's optimism is an exploration principle.
- [Options in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning](node:Options%20in%20Hierarchical%20Reinforcement%20Learning): temporal abstraction can reduce search depth.
- [Offline Reinforcement Learning](node:Offline%20Reinforcement%20Learning): model-based methods are one route to learning from fixed data.
- [Q-Learning](node:Q-Learning): the canonical model-free method, estimating values without a transition model.

### Common pitfalls
- Multi-step predictions with a learned model accumulate errors and can diverge from the true dynamics; multi-step losses or per-horizon models are proposed mitigations ([Moerland et al., HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16712)).
- Model-generated data is cheap but biased, so how far to trust the model must be decided explicitly, for instance by limiting rollout length ([Janner et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08253)).
- Comparisons should equalize either total computation or total samples; learning curves plotted against training hours or episodes can mislead ([Moerland et al., HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16712)).
- Bounding the loss of the planned policy through value error alone costs an extra $1/(1-\gamma)$ ("horizon amplification"); avoiding it needs a sharper variance-sensitive argument ([Agarwal et al., RL Theory](https://rltheorybook.github.io/rltheorybook_ABJKS.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Plug-in model-based planning at large accuracy.** The optimal rate is known to be achievable for the full meaningful range of $\epsilon$ (up to about $1/(1-\gamma)$) with a perturbed model-based algorithm, but "it remains an open question" whether the standard unperturbed model-based approach achieves it for large $\epsilon$ ([Agarwal et al., RL Theory](https://rltheorybook.github.io/rltheorybook_ABJKS.pdf)).
- **Matching model-free asymptotic performance.** Moerland et al.'s survey (first posted 2020) lists as a major challenge achieving the asymptotic performance of model-free RL with learned models, together with balancing planning and learning as a function of the data collected, and note that relatively little work benchmarks model-based RL ([Moerland et al., HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16712)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Reinforcement learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning): MDP formulation and model-based algorithms section.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley CS 285 Deep Reinforcement Learning (Levine)](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/): two lectures on model-based RL, plus offline RL and exploration.
- **Primary:** [Moerland, Broekens, Plaat, Jonker, Model-based Reinforcement Learning: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16712): taxonomy, dynamics-model learning, integration of planning and learning, future work.
- **Primary:** [Schrittwieser et al., Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08265): MuZero.
- **Primary:** [Brafman and Tennenholtz, R-MAX (JMLR 2002)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/brafman02a.html): polynomial-time near-optimal model-based RL.
- **Further reading:** [Agarwal, Brantley, Jiang, Kakade, Sun, Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms](https://rltheorybook.github.io/): monograph covering the simulation lemma and minimax sample complexity with a generative model.
references.Modified Newtonian Dynamics:
## Reference
### Overview
Modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) is Milgrom's 1983 proposal that Newtonian dynamics changes at accelerations below a constant $a_0 \approx 1.2\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so that galactic mass discrepancies are explained by the visible baryons alone, without particle [dark matter](node:Dark%20Matter). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics); [Milgrom 1983, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/161130)) The scale appears in several galactic scaling relations, and numerically $a_0 \approx cH_0/2\pi$ and $a_0^2 \sim \Lambda$ in natural units; whether these coincidences are physical is an open question. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))

MOND fits disc-galaxy [rotation curves](node:Galaxy%20Rotation%20Curves) and predicts the [Baryonic Tully–Fisher Relation](node:Baryonic%20Tully–Fisher%20Relation) and the [Radial Acceleration Relation](node:Radial%20Acceleration%20Relation). Its persistent problems are a residual factor-of-two mass discrepancy in galaxy clusters, cosmology (the [CMB Acoustic Peaks](node:CMB%20Acoustic%20Peaks) and matter power spectrum), and high-precision tests in the Solar System and in wide binaries. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics); [Hees et al. 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.6950); [Banik et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03436))

As an algebraic rule MOND is not a theory: it must be derived from an action (AQUAL, QUMOND) to conserve energy and momentum, and from a relativistic action ([TeVeS](node:TeVeS), AeST) to predict lensing and cosmology. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960); [Skordis & Złośnik 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00082))

### Formal definition
**Milgrom's law.** With Newtonian field $\mathbf g_N$ and true field $\mathbf g$ ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960)),
$$
\mu\!\left(\frac{g}{a_0}\right)\mathbf g = \mathbf g_N, \qquad \mu(x)\to 1\ (x\gg1),\quad \mu(x)\to x\ (x\ll1),
$$
or equivalently $\mathbf g = \nu(g_N/a_0)\,\mathbf g_N$ with $\nu(y)\to1$ for $y\gg1$ and $\nu(y)\to y^{-1/2}$ for $y\ll1$. In the deep-MOND limit $g = \sqrt{g_N a_0}$. Outside highly symmetric configurations these algebraic forms cannot be exact, since $\mathbf g$ must remain a conservative field. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960)) The "simple" interpolating function is $\mu(x)=x/(1+x)$, with $\nu(y) = \tfrac12\big[1+(1+4y^{-1})^{1/2}\big]$; the "standard" one is $\mu(x)=x/\sqrt{1+x^2}$. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))

**AQUAL** (Bekenstein & Milgrom 1984). The gravitational action $S_{\rm grav} = -\int \frac{a_0^2}{8\pi G}F\!\left(|\nabla\Phi|^2/a_0^2\right)d^3x\,dt$, with $F$ any dimensionless function and the usual matter coupling to $\Phi$ added, gives the nonlinear [Poisson equation](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations) ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))
$$
\nabla\cdot\Big[\mu\Big(\frac{|\nabla\Phi|}{a_0}\Big)\nabla\Phi\Big] = 4\pi G\rho, \qquad \mu(x) = F'(x^2).
$$
([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960); [Bekenstein & Milgrom 1984, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/162570))

**QUMOND** (Milgrom 2010). First solve $\nabla^2\Phi_N = 4\pi G\rho$, then ([Milgrom 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.5464))
$$
\nabla^2\Phi = \nabla\cdot\Big[\nu\Big(\frac{|\nabla\Phi_N|}{a_0}\Big)\nabla\Phi_N\Big],
$$
so the argument of $\nu$ is $g_N/a_0$, as in Milgrom's law. It needs two linear Poisson solves and one algebraic nonlinear step; it equals Milgrom's law up to a curl-field correction, which differs from AQUAL's, so the two theories agree exactly only in highly symmetric systems. ([Milgrom 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.5464); [Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))

The deep-MOND equations are invariant under $(t,\mathbf r)\to\lambda(t,\mathbf r)$. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))

### Key results
- **Flat rotation curves and the BTFR.** For a test particle around a point mass $M$ in the deep-MOND regime, $V_c^2/r = \sqrt{GMa_0}/r$, so $V_c^4 = V_f^4 = a_0GM$, independent of radius: asymptotically flat curves and a baryonic Tully–Fisher relation $M_b\propto V_f^4$ with no dependence on surface density. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))
- **Acceleration, not length.** The mass discrepancy appears at a characteristic acceleration rather than a characteristic radius, which excludes modifications of gravity that switch on at a fixed length. ([McGaugh lecture notes](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/333s18/lecture27.pdf))
- **External-field effect (EFE).** Because MOND is nonlinear in acceleration, a subsystem's internal dynamics depends on a uniform external field $g_e$: for $g_e<g<a_0$ standard MOND applies, for $g<a_0<g_e$ the system is Newtonian, and for $g<g_e<a_0$ it is Newtonian with a renormalized $G$. This breaks the strong [equivalence principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle). ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))
- **Clusters.** Cluster data follow the MOND slope $M_b\propto T^2$ but not its normalization: roughly a factor of two of missing mass remains, needed even in cluster cores. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))
- **Solar-System constraint.** In the Solar System the Galactic EFE produces an anomalous quadrupole $Q_2$. Nine years of Cassini tracking give $Q_2 = (3\pm3)\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, no deviation from GR, which excludes a large part of relativistic MOND theories. ([Hees et al. 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.6950)) Wikipedia records that this rules out both the simple and standard interpolating functions, and lunar laser ranging rules out the simple one. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))
- **GW170817.** The near-simultaneous gravitational and electromagnetic signals from [GW170817](node:GW170817) rule out "dark matter emulators", theories in which matter couples to a different metric from gravitational waves. ([Boran et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.06168)) TeVeS is of this type: matter couples to a physical metric disformally related to the Einstein metric. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960)) TeVeS appears inconsistent with the measured speed of [gravitational waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))
- **AeST.** Skordis and Złośnik's relativistic theory yields MOND, agrees with the observed CMB and matter power spectra on linear scales, and is ghost-free at second order. ([Skordis & Złośnik 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00082)) It requires several extra fields and does not yet match observed lensing. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))
- **Weak-lensing tests.** KiDS-1000 [weak lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing) extends the radial acceleration relation about two decades lower in acceleration and agrees with MOND, but finds a $\ge 6\sigma$ difference between early- and late-type galaxies of equal stellar mass, which modified-gravity theories without dependence on other galaxy properties cannot explain. ([Brouwer et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11677)) Lensing-derived circular velocities around isolated galaxies stay flat for hundreds of kpc with no clear decline to 1 Mpc, binning to the kinematic BTFR. ([Mistele et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09685))

### Examples
- **Crater 2.** In the EFE regime MOND predicted a velocity dispersion of $2.1^{+0.9}_{-0.6}$ km/s (McGaugh 2016); $2.7\pm0.3$ km/s was observed (Caldwell et al. 2017), while ΛCDM abundance matching anticipated 10–17 km/s. ([McGaugh lecture notes](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/333s18/lecture27.pdf))
- **Wide binaries, the dispute.** Chae used 26,615 Gaia DR3 wide binaries within 200 pc and reported an observed-to-Newtonian acceleration ratio of $1.43\pm0.06$ at $g_N\approx10^{-10.15}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, matching AQUAL with the Galactic EFE. ([Chae 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04613)) Banik et al. analysed 8,611 wide binaries within 250 pc at 2–30 kAU and preferred Newtonian over MOND at $19\sigma$, excluding MOND at $16\sigma$ in an MCMC fit. ([Banik et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03436))
- **Value of $a_0$.** Begeman, Broeils and Sanders (1991) found $a_0\approx1.2\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ optimal for rotation curves, a value that has not changed meaningfully since. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))

### History
Milgrom's first 1983 paper, "A modification of the Newtonian dynamics as a possible alternative to the hidden mass hypothesis", appeared in ApJ 270, 365. ([Milgrom 1983, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/161130)) The modification was suggested only by the asymptotic flatness of rotation curves and the slope of the Tully–Fisher relation. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960)) Bekenstein and Milgrom's 1984 paper "Does the missing mass problem signal the breakdown of Newtonian gravity?" gave AQUAL. ([Bekenstein & Milgrom 1984, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/162570)) Milgrom introduced QUMOND in 2010 ([Milgrom 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.5464)); Bekenstein's TeVeS ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960)) was followed after GW170817 by AeST. ([Skordis & Złośnik 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00082))

### Connections
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): the $g\gg a_0$ limit.
- [Galaxy Rotation Curves](node:Galaxy%20Rotation%20Curves): the original motivation and main test.
- [Radial Acceleration Relation](node:Radial%20Acceleration%20Relation): the $g$–$g_N$ relation MOND predicts.
- [Baryonic Tully–Fisher Relation](node:Baryonic%20Tully–Fisher%20Relation): $V_f^4 = a_0GM_b$.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): the standard alternative.
- [Bullet Cluster](node:Bullet%20Cluster): a lensing–gas offset usually read as collisionless mass.
- [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle): the EFE breaks its strong form.
- [TeVeS](node:TeVeS): the first widely studied relativistic completion.
- [GW170817](node:GW170817): excludes TeVeS-type disformal couplings.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model) and [Large-Scale Structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure): the cosmological arena where MOND is weakest.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): AQUAL and QUMOND are modified Poisson problems.

### Common pitfalls
- **Inverting the $\nu$ argument.** In QUMOND the interpolating function is $\nu(|\nabla\Phi_N|/a_0)$; writing $\nu(a_0/|\nabla\Phi_N|)$ reverses the Newtonian and deep-MOND limits. ([Milgrom 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.5464); [Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))
- **Milgrom's law is exact only in symmetric cases.** AQUAL and QUMOND add different curl-field corrections. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))
- **Modified inertia versus gravity.** Wikipedia reports that laboratory experiments down to accelerations of 0.1% of $a_0$ seem to have ruled out modified-inertia versions, so the modified-inertia reading is experimentally disfavoured. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))
- **Confusing $\mu$ and $\tilde\mu$ functions.** Milgrom's interpolating function $\mu(x)$ and the scalar-field function $\tilde\mu(s)$ of multifield relativistic theories are different functions; confusing them can lead to serious mistakes. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))

### Open problems
- **Cluster residual.** Clusters show a residual mass discrepancy even in MOND, called the most serious problem facing Milgrom's law. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))
- **Wide binaries.** Chae's anomaly and Banik et al.'s strong Newtonian preference disagree; critics attribute the detection to poor quality control and the original authors dispute this. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics); [Banik et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03436)) Banik et al. conclude MOND would need substantial small-scale modification. ([Banik et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03436))
- **Coincidence of $a_0$ with $cH_0$ and $\sqrt\Lambda$.** Whether physically meaningful remains open. ([Famaey & McGaugh 2012](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1112.3960))

> [!warning] Contested
> Brouwer et al. find the lensing RAR consistent with MOND but a $\ge6\sigma$ early/late-type difference that ΛCDM halo-formation history can produce and simple modified gravity cannot. ([Brouwer et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11677)) Mistele et al. report flat lensing circular velocities to hundreds of kpc, matching the BTFR. ([Mistele et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09685))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Modified Newtonian dynamics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics): laws, tests and status.
- **Learn:** [McGaugh, ASTR 333/433 lecture 27 (Case Western)](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/333s18/lecture27.pdf): interpolation, Tully–Fisher, EFE and Crater 2.
- **Primary:** [B. Famaey & S. McGaugh, "Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND): Observational Phenomenology and Relativistic Extensions", Living Rev. Relativ. 15, 10 (2012)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.3960): the standard review.
- **Primary:** [M. Milgrom, "Quasi-linear formulation of MOND", MNRAS 403, 886 (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.5464): QUMOND.
- **Primary:** [J. Bekenstein & M. Milgrom, ApJ 286, 7 (1984)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/162570): AQUAL; and [M. Milgrom, ApJ 270, 365 (1983)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/161130): the original proposal.
- **Further reading:** [Banik et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03436), [Hees et al. 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.6950), [Skordis & Złośnik 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00082): the decisive modern tests and the leading relativistic model.

## Reference
### Overview
Modular arithmetic is the arithmetic of remainders. Two integers $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $m$ when their difference $a-b$ is an integer multiple of $m$, that is, when they leave the same remainder on division by $m$. The congruence classes modulo $m$ form a ring, the ring of integers modulo $m$, written $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$, and this ring is a field exactly when $m$ is prime. Gauss developed the modern approach in *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic))

The subject has two layers. The additive and ring structure of $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ is governed by the Euclidean algorithm and the Chinese remainder theorem, which reduces any modulus to prime powers. The multiplicative group of units $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})^\times$ carries the deeper structure: Fermat's and Euler's theorems, primitive roots, quadratic residues and quadratic reciprocity. ([Stanford, Chinese remainder](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/crt.html); [Stanford, cyclic groups](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/cyclic.html); [Wikipedia, quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_reciprocity))

Modular exponentiation underlies the RSA and Diffie–Hellman cryptosystems, and finite fields built from modular arithmetic are used in elliptic-curve cryptography. On the algorithmic side, linear systems of congruences can be solved in polynomial time, while solving systems of non-linear modular equations is NP-complete. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic))

### Formal definition
For integers $a,b$ and a positive integer $m$,
$$a\equiv b \pmod m \iff m\mid (a-b).$$
Congruence modulo $m$ is an equivalence relation compatible with addition and multiplication, so the classes form the ring $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic))

A class $a$ is a unit (has a multiplicative inverse) modulo $m$ if and only if $\gcd(a,m)=1$. The units form the group $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})^\times$, whose order is Euler's totient
$$\varphi(m)=m\prod_{p\mid m}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr).$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic); [Stanford, units and totients](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/units.html))

The **order** of a unit $a$ modulo $n$ is the least positive $x$ with $a^x\equiv1\pmod n$; it divides $\varphi(n)$. ([Stanford, order of a unit](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/order.html)) A **primitive root** modulo $n$ is an integer $g$ such that every integer coprime to $n$ is congruent to a power of $g$; equivalently, $g$ generates $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$. ([Wikipedia, primitive root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_root_modulo_n))

For an odd prime $p$, the **Legendre symbol** $\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)$ is $0$ if $p\mid a$, $1$ if $a$ is a nonzero quadratic residue modulo $p$, and $-1$ otherwise. ([Stanford, quadratic residues](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/qr.html))

### Key results
- **Linear congruences.** Let $d=\gcd(a,m)$. The congruence $ax\equiv b\pmod m$ is solvable if and only if $d\mid b$, and then it has exactly $d$ solutions modulo $m$, namely $x_0, x_0+m/d,\dots,x_0+(d-1)m/d$. When $d=1$ the unique solution is $x\equiv a^{-1}b$. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LinearCongruenceEquation.html); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic))
- **Chinese remainder theorem.** If $m_1,\dots,m_n$ are pairwise coprime and $M=m_1\cdots m_n$, the system $x\equiv a_i\pmod{m_i}$ has a solution unique modulo $M$, given by $x=\sum_i a_i b_i b_i'$ with $b_i=M/m_i$ and $b_i'\equiv b_i^{-1}\pmod{m_i}$. For coprime $p,q$ the correspondence $\mathbb{Z}_{pq}\to\mathbb{Z}_p\times\mathbb{Z}_q$ is a bijection respecting sums and products componentwise. ([Stanford, Chinese remainder](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/crt.html))
- **Euler and Fermat.** If $a$ and $n$ are coprime positive integers, then $a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n$. The case $n=p$ prime is Fermat's little theorem $a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p$ for $p\nmid a$, equivalently $a^p\equiv a\pmod p$ for all $a$. ([Wikipedia, Euler's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_theorem); [Stanford, order of a unit](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/order.html))
- **Carmichael's theorem.** The Carmichael function $\lambda(n)$ is the least $m>0$ with $a^m\equiv1\pmod n$ for every $a$ coprime to $n$, the exponent of $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$. If $\gcd(a,n)=1$ then $a^{\lambda(n)}\equiv1\pmod n$, and $\lambda(n)\mid\varphi(n)$. One has $\lambda(n)=\varphi(n)$ for $n=1,2,4$ and odd prime powers, while $\lambda(2^r)=\varphi(2^r)/2$ for $r\ge3$; for example $\lambda(8)=2$. ([Wikipedia, Carmichael function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_function))
- **Primitive root theorem.** $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is cyclic, i.e. primitive roots modulo $n$ exist, if and only if $n=1,2,4,p^k$ or $2p^k$ with $p$ an odd prime. When they exist there are $\varphi(\varphi(n))$ of them. Gauss gave the first rigorous proof that primitive roots exist modulo a prime. ([Wikipedia, primitive root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_root_modulo_n); [Stanford, cyclic groups](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/cyclic.html))
- **Structure of the unit group.** For $k>2$, the class of $3$ has order $2^{k-2}$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z})^\times$ and no element has larger order, so $(\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z})^\times\cong C_2\times C_{2^{k-2}}$. Combined with the cyclicity of $(\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z})^\times$ for odd $p$ and the Chinese remainder theorem, this gives $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ as an explicit product of cyclic groups. ([Stanford, cyclic groups](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/cyclic.html))
- **Wilson's theorem.** An integer $n>1$ is prime if and only if $(n-1)!\equiv-1\pmod n$. Gauss's generalization: the product of the positive integers below $m$ coprime to $m$ is $\equiv-1\pmod m$ exactly when $m$ is $4$, an odd prime power, or twice an odd prime power (the moduli with primitive roots), and $\equiv+1$ otherwise. ([Wikipedia, Wilson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson%27s_theorem))
- **Euler's criterion.** For an odd prime $p$ and $p\nmid a$, $a$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$ if and only if $a^{(p-1)/2}\equiv1\pmod p$; hence $\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)\equiv a^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p$, and exactly half of the nonzero residues are squares. ([Stanford, quadratic residues](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/qr.html))
- **Quadratic reciprocity.** For distinct odd primes $p,q$,
  $$\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}\cdot\frac{q-1}{2}},$$
  with supplements $\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=1$ iff $p\equiv1\pmod4$ and $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=1$ iff $p\equiv\pm1\pmod8$. ([Wikipedia, quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_reciprocity)) The same identities hold for the Jacobi symbol with coprime odd positive arguments, which allows quadratic characters to be computed without factoring. ([Stanford, quadratic reciprocity](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/quadrecip.html))
- **Hensel lifting.** Let $f$ be an integer polynomial and $p$ a prime. If $f(r)\equiv0\pmod{p^k}$ and $f'(r)\not\equiv0\pmod p$, then for every $m>0$ there is an $s$, unique modulo $p^{k+m}$, with $f(s)\equiv0\pmod{p^{k+m}}$ and $s\equiv r\pmod{p^k}$; for $m\le k$ one can take explicitly $s=r-f(r)\,a$ with $a\equiv f'(r)^{-1}\pmod{p^m}$, and iterating gives lifts to every power of $p$. ([Wikipedia, Hensel's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hensel%27s_lemma))

### Examples
- **Chinese remainder.** $17\in\mathbb{Z}_{35}$ corresponds to $(2,3)\in\mathbb{Z}_5\times\mathbb{Z}_7$, since $17\equiv2\pmod5$ and $17\equiv3\pmod7$. ([Stanford, Chinese remainder](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/crt.html))
- **A Legendre symbol by reciprocity.** Since $31\equiv103\equiv3\pmod4$, $\left(\frac{31}{103}\right)=-\left(\frac{103}{31}\right)=-\left(\frac{10}{31}\right)=-\left(\frac{2}{31}\right)\left(\frac{5}{31}\right)$. Here $\left(\frac{2}{31}\right)=1$ because $31\equiv7\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{5}{31}\right)=\left(\frac{31}{5}\right)=\left(\frac15\right)=1$, so $31$ is a quadratic nonresidue modulo $103$; the Stanford notes reach the same value by a Jacobi-symbol route. ([Stanford, quadratic reciprocity](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/quadrecip.html); [Wikipedia, quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_reciprocity))
- **Odd squares modulo 8.** Every odd square is $\equiv1\pmod8$, so $\lambda(8)=2<\varphi(8)=4$ and there is no primitive root modulo $8$. ([Wikipedia, Carmichael function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_function))

### History
Ibn al-Haytham stated Wilson's theorem around 1000 AD; Waring announced it in 1770, crediting his student John Wilson, and Lagrange gave the first proof in 1771. ([Wikipedia, Wilson's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson%27s_theorem)) Euler proved Fermat's little theorem in 1736 and the general totient theorem in 1763. ([Wikipedia, Euler's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_theorem))

Gauss's *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801) set out the modern theory. In Article 57 he defined primitive roots, crediting Euler with the term, and he was the first to prove rigorously that they exist modulo a prime. ([Wikipedia, primitive root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_root_modulo_n)) Quadratic reciprocity was conjectured by Euler and Legendre; Gauss first proved it (his diary dates the proof to 8 April 1796) and published his first two proofs in the *Disquisitiones*. Gauss published six proofs in all, and over 240 published proofs now exist. ([Wikipedia, quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_reciprocity))

### Connections
- [Prime Numbers](node:Prime%20Numbers): prime moduli make $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ a field and are the setting of Fermat's and Wilson's theorems.
- [Euclidean Algorithm](node:Euclidean%20Algorithm): computes $\gcd(a,m)$ and modular inverses.
- [Chinese Remainder Theorem](node:Chinese%20Remainder%20Theorem): the reduction of a composite modulus to coprime factors.
- [Quadratic Reciprocity](node:Quadratic%20Reciprocity): the law governing which primes are squares modulo other primes.
- [Hensel's Lemma](node:Hensel's%20Lemma) and [p-adic Numbers](node:p-adic%20Numbers): lifting solutions from $p$ to $p^k$ and passing to the limit.
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory) and [Abelian Groups](node:Abelian%20Groups): $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is a finite abelian group; Euler's theorem is [Lagrange's Theorem](node:Lagrange's%20Theorem) applied to it.
- [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals) and [Finite Fields](node:Finite%20Fields): $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is the quotient of $\mathbb{Z}$ by the ideal $n\mathbb{Z}$, a field when $n$ is prime.
- [Cryptography](node:Cryptography), [Public-Key Cryptography](node:Public-Key%20Cryptography), [Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange](node:Diffie–Hellman%20Key%20Exchange) and [Number-Theoretic Methods in Cryptography](node:Number-Theoretic%20Methods%20in%20Cryptography): modular exponentiation as a one-way operation.
- [Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory): the setting of Artin's conjecture and of primes in residue classes.
- Map: [MSC 11Axx - Elementary number theory](node:MSC%2011Axx%20-%20Elementary%20number%20theory)

### Common pitfalls
- **Cancelling non-units.** From $ac\equiv bc\pmod m$ one may conclude $a\equiv b$ only when $\gcd(c,m)=1$; in general $ax\equiv b$ has $\gcd(a,m)$ solutions or none. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LinearCongruenceEquation.html); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic))
- **Applying Euler's theorem without coprimality.** $a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n$ requires $\gcd(a,n)=1$; only Fermat's form $a^p\equiv a\pmod p$ holds for all $a$, and only for prime moduli. ([Wikipedia, Euler's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_theorem); [Stanford, order of a unit](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/order.html))
- **Assuming every unit group is cyclic.** $(\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is not cyclic for $k\ge3$, and more generally primitive roots exist only for $n=1,2,4,p^k,2p^k$; the exponent $\lambda(n)$, not $\varphi(n)$, is then the sharp universal exponent. ([Stanford, cyclic groups](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/cyclic.html); [Wikipedia, Carmichael function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_function))
- **Hensel without the simple-root hypothesis.** The unique lift needs $f'(r)\not\equiv0\pmod p$. ([Wikipedia, Hensel's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hensel%27s_lemma))

### Open problems
- **Artin's conjecture on primitive roots (1927).** Every integer $a$ that is neither $-1$ nor a perfect square should be a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes, and these primes should have a positive density. When $a$ is not a perfect power and its squarefree part is not $\equiv1\pmod4$, the conjectured density is Artin's constant $A=\prod_q\bigl(1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)}\bigr)=0.3739558136\ldots$, independent of $a$. ([Moree, survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0412262); [Wikipedia, Artin's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%27s_conjecture_on_primitive_roots)) Hooley (1967) proved it assuming the Riemann hypothesis for the number fields $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_k,a^{1/k})$ with $k$ squarefree. Unconditionally, Heath-Brown (1986) showed that the conjecture fails for at most two primes, so at least one of $2,3,5$ is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes, while Moree's survey records that no single integer is known unconditionally to be a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes. ([Moree, survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0412262); [Wikipedia, Artin's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%27s_conjecture_on_primitive_roots))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Modular arithmetic (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic): congruences, the ring $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$, inverses, history, and applications.
- **Learn:** [Ben Lynn, Stanford number theory notes](https://crypto.stanford.edu/pbc/notes/numbertheory/crt.html): short pages on the Chinese remainder theorem, units, orders, cyclic unit groups, quadratic residues and reciprocity.
- **Primary:** [Ireland and Rosen, *A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory*, Springer GTM (1990)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2103-4): graduate text in Springer's Graduate Texts in Mathematics series (bibliographic record).
- **Further reading:** [Moree, Artin's primitive root conjecture: a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0412262): history, Hooley's conditional proof, unconditional results and open problems on multiplicative orders.
