## Reference
### Overview
Monte Carlo methods are computational algorithms that use repeated random sampling to obtain numerical results, often for problems that are deterministic in principle: one defines a domain of inputs, draws inputs at random, runs a deterministic computation on each, and aggregates the results ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)). The justification is the [law of large numbers and central limit theorem](node:Limit%20Theorems%20%28LLN%20and%20CLT%29): sample averages converge to expectations, with an error that falls like $N^{-1/2}$ independent of dimension, which is why Monte Carlo beats grid quadrature in high dimensions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).

In physics the method is used for systems with many coupled degrees of freedom (fluids, disordered materials, strongly coupled solids), for statistical mechanics as an alternative to [molecular dynamics](node:Molecular%20Dynamics), for quantum many-body problems (quantum Monte Carlo), and for radiation transport, detector design and astrophysical modelling ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)). Krauth stresses that *thermodynamic* and *dynamic* Monte Carlo are fundamentally different problems, both built on Markov chains, [detailed balance](node:Detailed%20Balance), rejections and ergodicity ([Krauth, arXiv:cond-mat/9612186](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9612186)).

When independent samples from the target are not available, one builds a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the target; this is [Markov Chain Monte Carlo](node:Markov%20Chain%20Monte%20Carlo), justified by the ergodic theorem for [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).

### Formal definition
Let $X$ be a [random variable](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions) with density $p$ on $\mathbb R^s$ and $f$ a function with $\mathbb E_p|f(X)|<\infty$. For i.i.d. $X_1,\dots,X_N\sim p$, the **crude Monte Carlo estimator** of $I=\mathbb E_p f(X)=\int f\,p$ is
$$\hat I_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f(X_i).$$
It is unbiased, converges almost surely to $I$ by the strong law of large numbers, and if $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}_p f(X)<\infty$ then by the central limit theorem $\sqrt N(\hat I_N-I)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$, so the error is $O(\sigma N^{-1/2})$ regardless of $s$: quadrupling the sample size halves the error ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).

**Importance sampling.** Drawing $X_i$ from a proposal density $q$ instead and weighting by $W=p/q$ gives the unbiased estimator $\hat I_N^{q}=\frac1N\sum_i f(X_i)\,p(X_i)/q(X_i)$. The variance-minimizing proposal is $q^*\propto |f|\,p$, which has zero variance when $f\ge 0$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Importance_sampling)).

**Metropolis–Hastings.** To sample a density $P$ known up to normalization, propose $x'\sim g(\cdot\mid x)$ and accept with probability
$$A(x',x)=\min\!\left(1,\ \frac{P(x')\,g(x\mid x')}{P(x)\,g(x'\mid x)}\right),$$
otherwise stay at $x$. For a symmetric proposal this reduces to $\min(1,P(x')/P(x))$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm)). The target need only be known up to its normalizing constant ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm)); for a Boltzmann weight $P(x)\propto e^{-\beta E(x)}$ the [Partition Function](node:Partition%20Function) therefore never has to be computed.

### Key results
- **Dimension-independent rate.** If $\operatorname{Var}f(X)<\infty$, the crude estimator has root-mean-square error $\sigma/\sqrt N$ for every dimension $s$; Monte Carlo avoids the exponential cost of deterministic quadrature in high dimension ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).
- **Detailed balance implies stationarity; ergodicity gives uniqueness.** If the transition kernel satisfies $\pi(x)P(x'\mid x)=\pi(x')P(x\mid x')$ for all $x,x'$, then $\pi$ is stationary (detailed balance is sufficient, not necessary). If moreover the chain is ergodic (irreducible, with every state aperiodic and positive recurrent), $\pi$ is the unique stationary distribution and the chain converges to it; irreducibility cannot be dropped, since a reducible chain can have several stationary distributions. The Metropolis–Hastings acceptance rule makes $P(x'\mid x)=g(x'\mid x)A(x',x)$ satisfy detailed balance with respect to $P$ ([Wikipedia: Metropolis–Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm); [Wikipedia: Markov chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain)).
- **Hastings's generalization (1970).** The Metropolis method extends from symmetric to general proposal distributions, with theory for applying the method and assessing the error of the resulting estimates ([Hastings, Biometrika 1970](https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article/57/1/97/284580)).
- **Koksma–Hlawka inequality (quasi-Monte Carlo).** For points $x_1,\dots,x_N\in[0,1]^s$ with star discrepancy $D_N^*$ and $f$ of bounded Hardy–Krause variation $V(f)$,
$$\Big|\int_{[0,1]^s}f(u)\,du-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i)\Big|\le V(f)\,D_N^* .$$
Low-discrepancy sequences achieve $D_N^*=O((\log N)^s/N)$, beating $N^{-1/2}$ for large $N$, though the $(\log N)^s$ factor grows with dimension ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-Monte_Carlo_method)).
- **Cluster algorithms beat critical slowing down.** Near a second-order transition the autocorrelation time of local updates grows as $L^z$ with $z\approx 2$ or larger (about $2.125$ for the 2D [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model)); the Swendsen–Wang cluster algorithm (1987), which builds clusters by random bond formation and flips each with probability $1/2$, reduces this to a quoted $z=0.35$ in 2D (and $z=0.75$ versus about $2.0$ in 3D) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swendsen%E2%80%93Wang_algorithm)). See [Markov Chain Critical Slowing Down](node:Markov%20Chain%20Critical%20Slowing%20Down).
- **The fermion sign problem is NP-hard (Troyer–Wiese 2005).** Quantum Monte Carlo for fermions suffers from a negative-sign problem that makes computing time grow exponentially with particle number; the authors prove the sign problem NP-hard, so a generic polynomial-time solution would imply that all problems in NP are solvable in polynomial time, and is "almost certainly unattainable" ([Troyer and Wiese, arXiv:cond-mat/0408370](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0408370)).

### Examples
- **Estimating $\pi$.** Scatter $N$ uniform points in the unit square and count those within distance 1 of the origin; the fraction estimates $\pi/4$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).
- **Ising model.** Metropolis single-spin flips with $P\propto e^{-\beta E}$, or Swendsen–Wang cluster flips near the critical temperature ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swendsen%E2%80%93Wang_algorithm)).
- **Rare-event (tail) probabilities.** Estimating $p_t=\Pr(X\ge t)$ by sampling from a shifted density $f^*$ and weighting by $f/f^*$ gives an unbiased estimator whose variance depends on the choice of $f^*$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Importance_sampling)).

### History
- Fermi experimented with the approach in the 1930s without publishing; Ulam conceived the modern method in 1946 while thinking about solitaire odds, developed it with von Neumann, and Metropolis suggested the code name "Monte Carlo" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).
- Ulam and von Neumann applied the idea to neutron diffusion at Los Alamos; in spring 1948 ENIAC performed the first fully automated Monte Carlo calculation, for a fission weapon core; the method was used in hydrogen-bomb work in the 1950s and spread to physics, chemistry and operations research ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).
- 1953: Metropolis, Rosenbluth, Rosenbluth, Teller and Teller introduced the Metropolis algorithm in "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines"; Hastings generalized it in 1970 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm); [Biometrika](https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article/57/1/97/284580)).
- 1987: Swendsen and Wang introduced cluster updates ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swendsen%E2%80%93Wang_algorithm)).

### Connections
- [Limit Theorems (LLN and CLT)](node:Limit%20Theorems%20%28LLN%20and%20CLT%29): consistency and the $N^{-1/2}$ error rate.
- [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): estimators are functions of random samples.
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains): stationary distributions, ergodicity, detailed balance.
- [Markov Chain Monte Carlo](node:Markov%20Chain%20Monte%20Carlo): Monte Carlo with dependent samples from a constructed chain.
- [Sequential Monte Carlo](node:Sequential%20Monte%20Carlo): particle methods for evolving distributions.
- [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model): the standard benchmark for Metropolis and cluster algorithms.
- [Partition Function](node:Partition%20Function): Monte Carlo samples Boltzmann weights without computing $Z$.
- [Statistical Mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics): thermodynamic averages as high-dimensional integrals.
- [Lattice Field Simulation](node:Lattice%20Field%20Simulation): Monte Carlo evaluation of Euclidean path integrals.
- [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search): random rollouts used in game-tree search.
- [Bootstrap Methods](node:Bootstrap%20Methods): resampling, a statistical use of simulation.

### Common pitfalls
- **Correlated samples.** MCMC draws are autocorrelated, so the effective sample size is smaller than the number of draws; ignoring this underestimates errors ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm)).
- **Burn-in.** Early samples reflect the starting point and are usually discarded ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis%E2%80%93Hastings_algorithm)).
- **Rare events and heavy tails.** Low-probability regions are sampled sparsely; the $N^{-1/2}$ error bar also presumes finite variance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).
- **Random-number quality.** Results depend on pseudo-random generators being "random enough", which must be checked ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method)).
- **Quasi-Monte Carlo in high dimension.** The Koksma–Hlawka bound is only an upper bound and hard to compute, and a poorly chosen sequence can do worse than plain Monte Carlo ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-Monte_Carlo_method)).

### Open problems
- **Sign-problem-free fermionic quantum Monte Carlo.** Since no generic solution is expected (the sign problem is NP-hard), research designs QMC methods that are sign-problem-free for specific model classes, such as Majorana-representation and hot-spot methods; Li and Yao's review discusses possible future directions for designing such methods ([Li and Yao, arXiv:1805.08219](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.08219); [Troyer and Wiese, arXiv:cond-mat/0408370](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0408370)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Monte Carlo method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method): definition, history, error rate, applications and limitations.
- **Learn:** [Krauth, Introduction to Monte Carlo Algorithms (arXiv:cond-mat/9612186)](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9612186): lecture notes on Markov chains, detailed balance, rejection and ergodicity.
- **Primary:** [Hastings, Monte Carlo sampling methods using Markov chains and their applications (Biometrika 1970)](https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article/57/1/97/284580): the general Metropolis–Hastings algorithm.
- **Primary:** [Troyer and Wiese, Computational complexity and fundamental limitations to fermionic QMC (arXiv:cond-mat/0408370)](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0408370): NP-hardness of the sign problem.
- **Further reading:** [Li and Yao, Sign-Problem-Free Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo (arXiv:1805.08219)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.08219): review of sign-free QMC algorithms and applications.
references.Multi-Agent Critique:
## Reference
### Overview
Multi-agent critique covers inference-time schemes in which several language-model agents produce answers and then examine, challenge, or revise each other's work before a final answer is aggregated. The best-known instance is multiagent debate: several instances of a model propose answers and reasoning, read the other agents' responses over several rounds, and converge on a common final answer. The method works on black-box models and uses the same prompts across tasks. ([Du et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325)) In the original experiments debate raised arithmetic accuracy from 67.0% (single agent) to 81.8% and GSM8K from 77.0% to 85.0%. The baselines were mixed: single-agent reflection scored 72.1% on arithmetic but 75.0% on GSM8K, below the single agent, and majority voting over agents scored 69.0% and 81.0%. ([Du et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14325v1))

The motivation is twofold. Single-model self-reflection suffers from "Degeneration-of-Thought": once a model is confident in a solution, reflection no longer produces new ideas, even when the answer is wrong ([Liang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19118)). Intrinsic self-correction without external feedback often fails and can degrade accuracy ([Huang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798)). Separately, AI-safety work proposed zero-sum debate between agents, judged by a human, as a way to supervise tasks too hard to judge directly ([Irving, Christiano, Amodei](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899)), which links the topic to [Scalable Oversight](node:Scalable%20Oversight).

The central design questions are the review topology (who sees whom), how errors are correlated across agents, whether stated confidence is calibrated, when to stop, and how to keep the group from collapsing onto a shared mistake. Analyses find that most of debate's measured gain comes from majority voting rather than the exchange itself ([Choi, Zhu, Li](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536)), and that debate can lower accuracy through conformity ([Wynn, Satija, Hadfield](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.05396v2)). The topic sits inside [LLM Agents](node:LLM%20Agents) and draws on [Uncertainty Quantification](node:Uncertainty%20Quantification) and the epistemology of group judgement ([SEP: Jury Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/jury-theorems/)).

### Formal definition
**Debate protocol.** Fix a question $x$, agents $i=1,\dots,N$, a communication graph with neighbourhoods $\mathcal N(i)$, and rounds $t=0,\dots,T$. At $t=0$ each agent answers independently, $y_{i,0}\sim\pi_i(\cdot\mid x)$. At $t\ge1$ each agent sees its neighbours' previous responses and revises, $y_{i,t}\sim\pi_i(\cdot\mid x,\,y_{i,t-1},\,\{y_{j,t-1}\}_{j\in\mathcal N(i)})$. A final answer comes from an aggregation rule: convergence to a common answer, majority vote $y_{\mathrm{mv}}=\arg\max_k\sum_i\mathbf 1[y_{i,T}=k]$, confidence-weighted voting, or a judge agent. Du et al. use three agents and two rounds in most experiments, and summarize other agents' responses when there are many agents. ([Du et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14325v1); [Choi, Zhu, Li](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536))

**Bayesian belief model.** Choi, Zhu and Li model agent $i$'s belief over $K$ candidate answers by a Dirichlet parameter $\boldsymbol\alpha_{i,t}$: a belief vector $\boldsymbol\theta_{i,t}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha_{i,t})$ is drawn and the response sampled as $y_{i,t}\sim\mathrm{Cat}(\boldsymbol\theta_{i,t})$ (a Dirichlet-compound-multinomial). Debate updates $\boldsymbol\alpha$ with the counts of neighbours' answers, and $p_{i,t}$ denotes agent $i$'s belief in the correct answer. ([Choi, Zhu, Li](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536))

**Debate as a game (oversight setting).** Two agents alternate short statements about a question or proposed action, and a judge decides which agent gave the most true and useful information. The game is zero-sum and agents are trained by self-play. ([Irving, Christiano, Amodei](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899))

**Correlated error.** For two models evaluated on the same items, the relevant statistic is how often they give the *same* wrong answer when both are wrong; on one leaderboard dataset this was about 60% across more than 350 LLMs. ([Kim et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962))

### Key results
- **Condorcet jury theorem.** If voters' correctness events are unconditionally independent and each has the same probability $p>\tfrac12$ of being correct, then the probability that a simple majority is correct increases with (odd) group size and tends to $1$. Common causes such as shared evidence or an opinion leader whom others copy create positive correlations that undermine this. ([SEP: Jury Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/jury-theorems/)) See [Condorcet Jury Theorem](node:Condorcet%20Jury%20Theorem).
- **Majority-vote concentration for LLM agents.** In the Dirichlet-compound-multinomial model with margin $\Delta$ between the mean probabilities of the correct answer and the runner-up, if $N>K/\Delta^2$ then $P(y_{\mathrm{mv}}\text{ correct})\ge1-\exp\!\big(-N(\Delta/\sqrt K-1/\sqrt N)^2\big)$. In the binary case with per-agent accuracy $p_0>\tfrac12$, the majority is correct with probability at least $1-\exp(-2N(p_0-\tfrac12)^2)$. ([Choi, Zhu, Li](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536))
- **Debate is a martingale.** If at every round the average belief of agent $i$'s neighbours in the correct answer equals agent $i$'s own previous belief, then $\mathbb E[p_{i,t}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=p_{i,t-1}$. The condition holds for homogeneous fully connected agents, fully isolated agents, and isolated cliques of homogeneous agents; in these cases debate does not improve expected correctness. Across seven benchmarks the authors conclude that most of debate's gains stem from majority voting. ([Choi, Zhu, Li](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536)) See [Martingales](node:Martingales).
- **Static debate and shared misconceptions.** When models have similar capabilities or produce similar responses, debate dynamics can become static and converge to the majority opinion; if that majority holds a misconception shared through overlapping training data, debate converges to the misconception. ([Estornell and Liu, NeurIPS 2024](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/32e07a110c6c6acf1afbf2bf82b614ad-Abstract-Conference.html))
- **Debate versus self-consistency at equal compute.** On GSM8K with the same number of responses, debate scored 83.2% (6 responses) and 83.0% (9) against 85.3% and 88.2% for self-consistency. Earlier self-correction gains used oracle labels to decide when to stop; without them, GPT-3.5 on CommonSenseQA fell from 75.8% to 41.8% after two rounds. ([Huang et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.01798)) Self-consistency samples diverse reasoning paths and keeps the most frequent answer, improving GSM8K by 17.9 points over chain-of-thought. ([Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171)) A systematic benchmark likewise found that debate systems in their current form do not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling, are sensitive to hyperparameters, and improve when the pressure toward agreement is tuned. ([Smit et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17371))
- **Debate can hurt.** With GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct, debate lowered CommonSenseQA accuracy in every configuration tested. Correct-to-incorrect flips outnumbered the reverse, and they were most likely when no peer agreed with the agent. ([Wynn, Satija, Hadfield](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.05396v2))
- **Model diversity helps.** ReConcile runs a round table of different LLMs with confidence-weighted voting; across seven benchmarks it beat prior single- and multi-agent baselines by up to 11.4%, and the authors find diversity across models critical to the gain. ([Chen, Saha, Bansal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.13007))
- **Complexity of debate as oversight.** With optimal play, debate with a polynomial-time judge can in principle settle any PSPACE question, whereas direct judging covers only NP. ([Irving, Christiano, Amodei](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899)) Doubly-efficient protocols let the honest debater win while simulating only polynomially many steps, even against a dishonest debater with exponentially more computation, and apply to randomized models. ([Brown-Cohen, Irving, Piliouras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.14125))

### Examples
- **Factuality and reasoning debate.** Three agents, two rounds: MMLU 63.9% to 71.1% (reflection: 57.7%), biographies 66.0% to 73.8%, chess move validity 29.3% to 45.2%. On arithmetic, accuracy rose with more agents and with more rounds up to about four. ([Du et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14325v1))
- **Judge-mediated debate.** In MAD, agents argue "tit for tat" and a judge picks the answer; it helped on commonsense machine translation and counter-intuitive arithmetic when the debate ended adaptively and confrontation was moderate, and the judge could be unfair when agents were different LLMs. ([Liang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19118)) ChatEval applies a debating team of LLM referees to evaluating generated text. ([Chan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.07201))
- **Human debate for oversight.** With human debaters on hard reading-comprehension questions, judges who never saw the passage reached 84% accuracy under debate versus 74% under single-expert consultancy. ([Michael et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.08702)) With LLM debaters, non-expert model judges reached 76% versus a 48% baseline and humans 88% versus 60%; optimizing debaters for persuasiveness made judges more accurate. ([Khan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06782))
- **Trained critics.** RLHF-trained critic models writing critiques of code were preferred over human critiques in 63% of cases on naturally occurring bugs; they can hallucinate bugs, and human–critic teams hallucinated less. ([McAleese et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00215)) In prover–verifier games, small verifiers are trained against "helpful" and "sneaky" provers, making solutions more legible to time-constrained humans. ([Kirchner et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13692))
- **Adaptive stopping.** For LLM-as-judge debate, judges' consensus dynamics are modelled as a time-varying mixture of Beta-Binomial distributions, and debate stops when successive distributions are close by a Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic. ([Hu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12697))

### History
Condorcet's 1785 *Essai* gave the jury theorem, the classical root of the idea that aggregating fallible judgements improves accuracy ([SEP: Jury Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/jury-theorems/)). William H. Whyte Jr. coined "groupthink" in 1952, and Irving Janis developed it in 1972 and 1982; his remedies included critical-evaluator roles, independent groups, outside experts and a rotating devil's advocate ([Wikipedia: Groupthink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupthink)). Irving, Christiano and Amodei proposed AI safety via debate in 2018 ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899)). Debate between LLM instances followed in 2023 ([Du et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325); [Liang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19118)), and a critical literature questioned self-correction and debate gains ([Huang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798); [Smit et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17371); [Choi, Zhu, Li](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536)).

### Connections
- [Multi-Agent Debate](node:Multi-Agent%20Debate): the main protocol family this note analyses.
- [LLM Agents](node:LLM%20Agents): critique protocols are an orchestration pattern for agent systems.
- [Scalable Oversight](node:Scalable%20Oversight): adversarial debate as a way to supervise systems stronger than their judges.
- [Uncertainty Quantification](node:Uncertainty%20Quantification): confidence-weighted aggregation and stopping rules need calibrated uncertainty.
- [Human-AI Reliance Calibration](node:Human-AI%20Reliance%20Calibration): a human reading a converged debate must judge how much to trust consensus.
- [Condorcet Jury Theorem](node:Condorcet%20Jury%20Theorem) and [Voting Paradoxes](node:Voting%20Paradoxes): the classical theory of aggregating fallible judgements.
- [Deep Ensembles](node:Deep%20Ensembles): majority voting over agents is an ensemble; correlated members reduce its benefit.
- [Martingales](node:Martingales): under homogeneous topologies debate beliefs form a martingale.
- [Computational Social Choice](node:Computational%20Social%20Choice) and [Mathematical Social Choice](node:Mathematical%20Social%20Choice): aggregation of agent answers is a voting rule.
- [Fine-Tuning and RLHF](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF): trained critics and trained self-correction are alternatives to prompting-only critique.
- [Sharma et al. 2023 - Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548): sycophancy as a mechanism behind conformity.
- [Kumar et al. 2024 - Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12917): SCoRe.
- [Chen et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18005): diversity collapse in open-ended ideation.
- [Evidence-Gated Research Agents](node:Evidence-Gated%20Research%20Agents): gating claims on external evidence counters correlated, unverified consensus.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): shared pretraining data is a source of correlated error.

### Common pitfalls
- **Crediting debate for ensembling.** Compare against majority vote or self-consistency with the same number of samples; at equal compute, voting matched or beat debate in the cited studies. ([Choi, Zhu, Li](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536); [Huang et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.01798))
- **Oracle stopping.** Stopping self-correction once the answer becomes correct uses ground-truth labels; without them the gains vanish. ([Huang et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.01798))
- **Treating agreement as evidence.** Agents from the same model or provider share errors, and larger, more accurate models have highly correlated errors even across providers, so their consensus is weaker evidence than independent votes. ([Kim et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962); [SEP: Jury Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/jury-theorems/))
- **Overconfident consensus.** Converged debate answers were not always correct, and models sometimes confidently affirmed a wrong answer as consistent with the others. ([Du et al., full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14325v1))
- **Sycophancy and conformity.** RLHF assistants are sycophantic across tasks, and humans and preference models sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic answers to correct ones ([Sharma et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548)). In debate, telling agents that correctness pays did not significantly reduce correct-to-incorrect flips, though the authors find no single cause such as sycophancy explains the failures. ([Wynn, Satija, Hadfield](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.05396v2))
- **Dense topologies in open-ended tasks (reported).** A 2026 paper, posted on arXiv and listed as accepted to ACL 2026 Findings, reports that dense communication in larger groups led to premature convergence and that authority-driven groups suppressed semantic diversity. ([Chen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18005))
- **Self-correction by supervised fine-tuning.** SFT on offline correction traces suffers distribution mismatch or collapses to one correction mode; SCoRe instead uses multi-turn online RL on self-generated data. ([Kumar et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12917))

### Open problems
- **Protocols that reward critique over consensus.** Wynn, Satija and Hadfield leave to future debate frameworks mechanisms that promote critical evaluation over consensus: weighting contributions by confidence or credibility, rewarding independent verification, and penalizing unsupported conformity; they do not test these, and their one incentive prompt did not reduce correct-to-incorrect flips. ([Wynn, Satija, Hadfield](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.05396v2))
- **Closing the gap to the oracle.** Interventions that bias updates toward keeping answers (MAD-Conformist, MAD-Follower) improve on vanilla debate but do not reach the oracle-locking upper bound; the authors call closing that gap a promising direction for future work, and call investigating alternative communication protocols an important direction, noting their theory assumes homogeneous agents. ([Choi, Zhu, Li](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536))
- **Modelling dependence among judges.** The SEP entry calls modelling voter dependence in adequate, transparent and tractable ways a central challenge for jury-theorem research. ([SEP: Jury Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/jury-theorems/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Jury Theorems](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/jury-theorems/): Condorcet's theorem, its hypotheses, correlated voters, deliberation and open questions.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Groupthink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupthink): Janis's symptoms and preventive measures.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley CS294/194-196 Agentic AI (Fall 2025)](https://rdi.berkeley.edu/agentic-ai/f25): lectures on multi-agent AI and multi-agent systems in the era of LLMs.
- **Primary:** [Du et al., Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325): the multiagent debate method.
- **Primary:** [Choi, Zhu, Li, Debate or Vote](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.17536): martingale analysis and majority-vote baseline.
- **Primary:** [Irving, Christiano, Amodei, AI safety via debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899): debate as a zero-sum oversight game.
- **Primary:** [Smit et al., Should we be going MAD?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17371): systematic benchmark of debate protocols.
- **Primary:** [Michael et al., Debate Helps Supervise Unreliable Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.08702): human debate experiments.
- **Further reading:** [Landemore and Elster (eds.), Collective Wisdom: Principles and Mechanisms (CUP 2012)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511846427/type/book): edited multidisciplinary volume on when many minds outperform one, including aggregation paradoxes and deliberation.
references.Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is the part of [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning) that studies several learning agents coexisting in a shared environment, each pursuing its own reward, which may conflict with the others' interests. Settings range from pure competition (zero-sum games such as chess and Go), through pure cooperation (identical rewards), to the mixed-sum case that covers most real-world interactions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-agent_reinforcement_learning))

The standard formal model is the Markov (stochastic) game, which extends a [Markov decision process](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes) to joint actions and per-agent rewards. Extensive-form games model sequential imperfect-information interaction such as poker. Theory is organized by task type: fully cooperative, fully competitive and mixed. The theoretical understanding lags well behind empirical successes in Go, poker, robotics and autonomous driving. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.10635))

What makes MARL harder than single-agent RL is a short list of structural problems: non-stationarity (each agent's environment contains other learners), the joint action space growing exponentially with the number of agents, information structures in which agents see different things, non-unique learning goals, multi-agent credit assignment, and equilibrium selection. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635); [Hanna, CS 839 lecture 20](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~jphanna/teaching/25fall_cs839/documents/lec20-marl-II.pdf))

### Formal definition
A **Markov game** is a tuple $(\mathcal N,\mathcal S,\{\mathcal A^i\}_{i\in\mathcal N},P,\{R^i\}_{i\in\mathcal N},\gamma)$ with agents $\mathcal N=\{1,\dots,N\}$, $N>1$, a state space $\mathcal S$ observed by all agents, action sets $\mathcal A^i$ with joint action space $\mathcal A=\mathcal A^1\times\cdots\times\mathcal A^N$, transition kernel $P:\mathcal S\times\mathcal A\to\Delta(\mathcal S)$, rewards $R^i:\mathcal S\times\mathcal A\times\mathcal S\to\mathbb R$ and discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$. Agent $i$ picks a policy $\pi^i:\mathcal S\to\Delta(\mathcal A^i)$, and its value depends on the joint policy $\pi(a\mid s)=\prod_i\pi^i(a^i\mid s)$:
$$V^i_{\pi^i,\pi^{-i}}(s)=\mathbb E\Big[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^tR^i(s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})\,\Big|\,a^i_t\sim\pi^i(\cdot\mid s_t),\ s_0=s\Big].$$
([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))

A **Nash equilibrium** of the Markov game is a joint policy $\pi^*=(\pi^{1,*},\dots,\pi^{N,*})$ such that for every $s\in\mathcal S$, every $i$ and every $\pi^i$, $V^i_{\pi^{i,*},\pi^{-i,*}}(s)\ge V^i_{\pi^i,\pi^{-i,*}}(s)$. The **fully cooperative** case $R^1=\cdots=R^N$ is also called a multi-agent MDP or Markov team game; the **two-player zero-sum** case has $R^1+R^2=0$. With partial observability the general model is the partially observed stochastic game, whose common-reward special case is the decentralized POMDP (Dec-POMDP). ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635)) Other solution concepts are minimax optimality (best worst-case value, usually for two-player zero-sum games) and Pareto optimality, under which no agent's value can be raised without lowering another's. ([Hanna, CS 839 lecture 20](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~jphanna/teaching/25fall_cs839/documents/lec20-marl-II.pdf))

Cooperative methods are classified by information structure into centralized training and execution (CTE), centralized training for decentralized execution (CTDE, the most common), and decentralized training and execution (DTE). ([Amato](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06161))

### Key results
- **Existence of equilibria.** Every finite-state, finite-action, infinite-horizon discounted Markov game has a Nash equilibrium (in stationary policies), but it need not be unique. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- **Shapley's theorem for zero-sum Markov games.** For two-player zero-sum Markov games with finite state and action spaces, $V^*=\max_{\pi^1}\min_{\pi^2}V^1_{\pi^1,\pi^2}=\min_{\pi^2}\max_{\pi^1}V^1_{\pi^1,\pi^2}$. $V^*$ is the unique fixed point of the Bellman operator that solves, at each state, the matrix game with payoff $Q_V(s,a^1,a^2)=\mathbb E_{s'}[R^1+\gamma V(s')]$, and a Nash equilibrium can be built from it. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- **Minimax-Q convergence** (Littman). Tabular minimax-Q, $Q(s_t,a^1_t,a^2_t)\leftarrow(1-\alpha_t)Q+\alpha_t\big(r_t+\gamma\,\mathrm{Value}[Q(s'_t,\cdot,\cdot)]\big)$, converges to $Q^*$ under conditions similar to those for single-agent [Q-Learning](node:Q-Learning). Convergence with even linear function approximation is not well understood. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- **Nash-Q and its limits** (Hu and Wellman). Nash-Q replaces the max in the Bellman operator by the value of a Nash equilibrium of the stage game and converges to a Nash equilibrium under the restrictive assumption that each stage game met during learning has a unique equilibrium. Friend-or-Foe Q-learning converges for two-player zero-sum games and coordination games with a unique equilibrium. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- **Computational hardness.** Finding a Nash equilibrium of a two-player general-sum normal-form game is PPAD-complete, and three-player zero-sum matrix games are PPAD-complete as well. Solving a cooperative Dec-POMDP is NEXP-complete ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635)); the original result of Bernstein, Zilberstein and Immerman is for the finite-horizon problem, even with a small number of agents. ([Bernstein et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3836))
- **Negative results for general-sum learning.** [Value-iteration](node:Value%20Iteration) methods fail to find stationary Nash or [correlated equilibria](node:Correlated%20Equilibrium) of general-sum Markov games. Vanilla policy-gradient play avoids a non-negligible subset of Nash equilibria in general-sum continuous games, including linear-quadratic general-sum games. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- **Independent learners lose guarantees.** An agent that treats others as part of a stationary environment may fail to converge, apart from special settings, although independent learning can work well empirically. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635)) Independent learners running single-agent RL tend to converge to deterministic policies, although optimal play in a Markov game may require a stochastic policy. ([Hanna, CS 839 lecture 20](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~jphanna/teaching/25fall_cs839/documents/lec20-marl-II.pdf))
- **Monotonic value factorization** ([QMIX](node:QMIX)). If the joint action-value is constrained to be monotonic in each agent's local utility, then maximizing the joint value over joint actions is tractable and agrees with each agent greedily maximizing its own utility. This makes centralized and decentralized policies consistent. ([QMIX](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.11485))

### Examples
- **Independent Q-learning and VDN.** In independent Q-learning each agent treats the others as part of the environment, which then becomes a moving target. VDN instead sums per-agent Q-values and trains the sum on the global TD error in cooperative tasks. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-agent_reinforcement_learning))
- **MADDPG.** An actor-critic method in which each agent's critic takes the other agents' policies into account. It addresses the non-stationarity that hampers Q-learning and the variance of policy gradients, which grows with the number of agents. ([Lowe et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02275))
- **MAPPO.** With minimal tuning and no domain-specific changes, PPO-based methods match or beat off-policy baselines on particle worlds, the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge, Google Research Football and Hanabi. ([Yu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01955)) See [Multi-Agent PPO](node:Multi-Agent%20PPO).
- **Fully centralized learning.** Treating the team as one agent with a joint policy avoids credit assignment and non-stationarity, but suffers the curse of multiple agents and needs every agent's observation to choose any action. ([Hanna, CS 839 lecture 20](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~jphanna/teaching/25fall_cs839/documents/lec20-marl-II.pdf))
- **Autocurricula.** In competitive self-play, agents' adaptations to each other produce stacked phases of learning, as in the Hide and Seek experiment. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-agent_reinforcement_learning))

### History
- The Markov game model goes back to Shapley's stochastic games, and a classical overview split MARL algorithms into fully cooperative, fully competitive and mixed settings. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- Early value-based extensions of Q-learning were minimax-Q for zero-sum games, then Nash-Q, Friend-or-Foe Q and correlated Q-learning for general-sum games. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- 2017–2018: deep CTDE methods appear: MADDPG for mixed cooperative-competitive tasks ([Lowe et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02275)), and VDN (2018) and QMIX for cooperative value factorization ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-agent_reinforcement_learning); [QMIX](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.11485)).
- 2021–2022: on-policy PPO is shown to be a strong cooperative baseline. ([Yu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01955))
- 2024: Albrecht, Christianos and Schäfer's textbook with MIT Press, print version scheduled for late 2024. ([Edinburgh](https://informatics.ed.ac.uk/university-of-edinburgh-ellis-unit/multi-agent-reinforcement-learning-foundations-and-modern-0))

### Connections
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): MARL is RL with several simultaneous learners.
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): a Markov game with one agent is an MDP.
- [Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes](node:Partially%20Observable%20Markov%20Decision%20Processes): Dec-POMDPs and partially observed stochastic games generalize POMDPs to many agents.
- [Nash Equilibrium](node:Nash%20Equilibrium): the default solution concept for general-sum Markov games.
- [Correlated Equilibrium](node:Correlated%20Equilibrium): a more general equilibrium concept than Nash equilibrium, used in correlated Q-learning.
- [No-Regret Learning](node:No-Regret%20Learning): no-regret dynamics underlie equilibrium computation in games.
- [Multi-Agent Credit Assignment](node:Multi-Agent%20Credit%20Assignment): attributing a shared reward to individual agents' actions.
- [QMIX](node:QMIX): monotonic value factorization for CTDE.
- [Multi-Agent PPO](node:Multi-Agent%20PPO): the PPO-based cooperative baseline.
- [Policy Gradient Methods](node:Policy%20Gradient%20Methods): their convergence in games is a central open theoretical question.
- [Q-Learning](node:Q-Learning): minimax-Q and Nash-Q extend it to games.
- [Decentralized Coordination](node:Decentralized%20Coordination): execution with local information only.
- [Multi-Robot Coordination](node:Multi-Robot%20Coordination): a main application domain.

### Common pitfalls
- Running single-agent RL independently for each agent discards the convergence guarantees of single-agent RL, because the stationarity assumption fails. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- A Nash equilibrium need not be unique, and convergence to "an equilibrium" does not settle which one is reached (equilibrium selection). ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635); [Hanna, CS 839 lecture 20](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~jphanna/teaching/25fall_cs839/documents/lec20-marl-II.pdf))
- Pareto optimality is not fairness: a Pareto-optimal profile can be very unequal. ([Hanna, CS 839 lecture 20](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~jphanna/teaching/25fall_cs839/documents/lec20-marl-II.pdf))
- Two-player zero-sum results do not transfer to games with more players or general sums, where even computing equilibria is PPAD-hard. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))

### Open problems
Zhang, Yang and Başar (survey first posted in 2019) list the following as open avenues for MARL theory; two of them have since seen partial progress, noted below. ([Zhang, Yang, Başar](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10635))
- **Partially observed stochastic games.** Information states may require beliefs over opponents' policies, not just over states; one suggested route is to extend CTDE for Dec-POMDPs to POSGs.
- **Deep MARL theory.** Extending the global convergence analyses of overparameterized neural TD and neural policy optimization to multiple agents.
- **Model-based MARL.** Very few model-based algorithms exist (R-MAX for zero-sum games is one), and the provable sample-efficiency advantages of model-based single-agent RL had not been carried over. Since then, Zhang, Kakade, Başar and Yang gave a model-based algorithm for two-player discounted zero-sum Markov games with a generative model whose sample complexity is near-optimal, so the open part is beyond that setting. ([Zhang et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.07461))
- **Convergence of policy gradient methods.** Results in general MARL are mostly negative. Global convergence of policy-based methods in general-sum linear-quadratic games is proposed as a starting point. Hambly, Xu and Yang later proved global convergence of the natural policy gradient to the Nash equilibrium in finite-horizon $N$-player general-sum LQ games with stochastic dynamics, under a lower bound on the noise covariance. ([Hambly, Xu, Yang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13090))
- **Robustness and safety.** Constrained Markov games with safety requirements that couple all agents remain largely uncharted.
- **Social dilemmas.** The conflict between individual agents' needs and those of the group is described as a subject of active research. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-agent_reinforcement_learning))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Multi-agent reinforcement learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-agent_reinforcement_learning): settings, non-stationarity, social dilemmas, autocurricula.
- **Learn:** [Hanna, CS 839 Lecture 20: Multi-agent Learning II (UW–Madison)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~jphanna/teaching/25fall_cs839/documents/lec20-marl-II.pdf): stochastic games, solution concepts, independent versus centralized learning.
- **Learn:** [Amato, An Initial Introduction to Cooperative MARL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06161): CTE, CTDE and DTE.
- **Primary:** [Zhang, Yang, Başar, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: A Selective Overview of Theories and Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.10635): survey of MARL theory with open directions.
- **Primary:** [Rashid et al., QMIX](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.11485): monotonic value factorization.
- **Further reading:** [Albrecht, Christianos, Schäfer, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Foundations and Modern Approaches (MIT Press)](https://informatics.ed.ac.uk/university-of-edinburgh-ellis-unit/multi-agent-reinforcement-learning-foundations-and-modern-0): textbook intended as a reference and introduction to the field.

## Reference
### Overview
Multivariable calculus extends single-variable calculus to functions of several variables, covering both differentiation and integration of multivariate functions. Two structural features distinguish it from one dimension: a point can be approached along infinitely many paths, so limits and continuity must be path-independent, and there are several kinds of domains of integration (curves, surfaces, solids), which leads to line, surface and volume integrals tied together by the theorems of Green, Stokes and Gauss. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariable_calculus))

The organizing idea of the differential theory is linear approximation: a map $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is differentiable at a point when it is approximated there by a linear map, whose matrix is the Jacobian. Most theorems of the subject (inverse and implicit function theorems, Taylor's theorem, the second-derivative test, Lagrange multipliers) transfer information from this linear map, or from the quadratic form of second derivatives, to the nonlinear function nearby. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_function); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant)) See [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices).

The integral theory computes multiple integrals as iterated integrals (Fubini) and transforms them by the change-of-variables formula, with the absolute Jacobian determinant as the local volume factor. The subject is the local, coordinate form of calculus on [manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariable_calculus); [MIT OCW notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/53cab862607d9ad1abdab1a10013be9e_MIT18_02SC_MNotes_cv1.pdf))

### Formal definition
A partial derivative of $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ with respect to $x_j$ is the derivative in $x_j$ with all other variables held constant. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariable_calculus))

A map $f:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ is *differentiable* at $x_0$ if there is a linear map $M:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ with
$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(x_0+h)-f(x_0)-M(h)\|}{\|h\|}=0 .$$
Then $M(h)=J_f(x_0)\,h$, where the Jacobian matrix $J_f$ is the matrix of first partials, $(J_f)_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial x_j$. When the matrix is square its determinant is the Jacobian determinant. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_function); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant)) See [Determinant](node:Determinant).

For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ with second partials, the Hessian is the symmetric matrix $\bigl(\partial^2 f/\partial x_i\partial x_j\bigr)$ (symmetric under the hypotheses of Schwarz's theorem below). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_partial_derivative_test))

For a change of variables $x=x(u,v)$, $y=y(u,v)$ the Jacobian is $\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)=x_uy_v-x_vy_u$, and
$$\iint_R f(x,y)\,dx\,dy=\iint_{R'} g(u,v)\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|du\,dv,$$
with $g$ the integrand after substitution and $R'$ the region in $(u,v)$-coordinates. ([MIT OCW notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/53cab862607d9ad1abdab1a10013be9e_MIT18_02SC_MNotes_cv1.pdf))

### Key results
- **Partials versus differentiability.** Existence of all partial and directional derivatives at a point does not imply differentiability there: $f(x,y)=y^3/(x^2+y^2)$, $f(0,0)=0$, is continuous with all directional derivatives at the origin but is not differentiable there. If all partials exist in a neighbourhood of $x_0$ and are continuous at $x_0$, then $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_function))
- **Schwarz–Clairaut theorem.** If $f$ has continuous second partial derivatives on a neighbourhood of $p$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f(p)=\partial_j\partial_i f(p)$. Continuity is needed: for $f(x,y)=xy(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)$, $f(0,0)=0$, the mixed partials at the origin are $1$ and $-1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_of_second_derivatives))
- **Inverse function theorem.** If $f$ is $C^1$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ with values in $\mathbb R^n$ and $J_f(a)$ is invertible, there are open $U\ni a$, $V\ni b=f(a)$ with $f:U\to V$ bijective, $f^{-1}$ of class $C^1$ and $J_{f^{-1}}(b)=J_f(a)^{-1}$; if $f$ is $C^k$ so is $f^{-1}$. The conclusion is local: $F(x,y)=(e^x\cos y,e^x\sin y)$ has Jacobian determinant $e^{2x}\ne0$ everywhere but is $2\pi$-periodic in $y$. The *constant rank theorem* generalizes it: a smooth map of constant rank near a point has a normal form in suitable local charts. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem)) See [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem).
- **Implicit function theorem.** Let $f:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, $f(a,b)=0$, and suppose the Jacobian $J_{f,y}(a,b)$ with respect to the last $m$ variables is invertible. Then there are an open $U\ni a$ and a unique $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ with $g(a)=b$ and $f(x,g(x))=0$ for $x\in U$; $g$ is $C^1$ with $J_g(x)=-J_{f,y}(x,g(x))^{-1}J_{f,x}(x,g(x))$. For the unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$, $y$ is locally a function of $x$ except at $(\pm1,0)$, where $x$ is a function of $y$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implicit_function_theorem)) See [Implicit Function Theorem](node:Implicit%20Function%20Theorem).
- **Taylor's theorem in several variables.** If $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is $k$ times continuously differentiable at $a$, then in multi-index notation $f(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\frac{D^\alpha f(a)}{\alpha!}(x-a)^\alpha+\sum_{|\alpha|=k}h_\alpha(x)(x-a)^\alpha$ with $h_\alpha(x)\to0$ as $x\to a$. If $f$ is $C^{k+1}$ on a closed ball $B$ about $a$, the remainder is $\sum_{|\beta|=k+1}R_\beta(x)(x-a)^\beta$ with $R_\beta(x)=\frac{|\beta|}{\beta!}\int_0^1(1-t)^{|\beta|-1}D^\beta f(a+t(x-a))\,dt$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor%27s_theorem)) See [Taylor's Theorem](node:Taylor's%20Theorem).
- **Second-derivative test.** At a critical point where the Hessian $H$ is invertible: $H$ positive definite gives a local minimum, negative definite a local maximum, and $H$ with eigenvalues of both signs a saddle point (the last conclusion holds even when $H$ is singular); otherwise the test is inconclusive. In two variables with $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$: $D>0,f_{xx}>0$ gives a minimum, $D>0,f_{xx}<0$ a maximum, $D<0$ a saddle, and $D=0$ is inconclusive. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_partial_derivative_test)) See [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices) and [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors).
- **Lagrange multipliers.** If $f$ and $g$ are $C^1$, $(x_0,y_0)$ is a local extremum of $f$ subject to $g=0$, and $\nabla g(x_0,y_0)\ne0$ (the constraint qualification), then there is $\lambda_0$ with $\nabla f=\lambda_0\nabla g$ at that point, i.e. $(x_0,y_0,\lambda_0)$ is stationary for $f-\lambda g$. With several constraints the qualification is linear independence of their gradients. The condition is necessary, not sufficient; candidates are classified by, for example, the bordered Hessian. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_multiplier))
- **Fubini–Tonelli.** For continuous $f$ on a rectangle, the double integral equals either iterated integral. For $\sigma$-finite measure spaces, if $\int_{X\times Y}|f|<\infty$ the two iterated integrals equal the product-measure integral (Fubini); for non-negative measurable $f$ the same holds without the finiteness assumption (Tonelli). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariable_calculus); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem)) See [Fubini's Theorem](node:Fubini's%20Theorem).
- **Sard's theorem.** If $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge\max\{n-m+1,1\}$ and $X$ is the set of points where $J_f$ has rank $<m$, then $f(X)$ has Lebesgue measure zero: almost every value is regular. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem)) See [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory).
- **Classical integral theorems.** The gradient theorem, Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem and the divergence theorem are special cases of the generalized Stokes theorem for differential forms on manifolds. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariable_calculus)) See [Stokes' Theorem](node:Stokes'%20Theorem).

### Examples
For $f(x,y)=x^2y/(x^4+y^2)$ the limit at the origin along every line $y=kx$ is $0$, but along $y=\pm x^2$ it is $\pm1/2$, so no limit exists. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariable_calculus))

Polar coordinates $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ have $\partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)=r$, so $dA=r\,dr\,d\theta$ (with $r\ge0$). For $\iint_R \bigl(\tfrac{x-y}{x+y+2}\bigr)^2\,dx\,dy$ over the square bounded by $x\pm y=\pm1$, the substitution $u=x+y$, $v=x-y$ gives $\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)=-1/2$, so $dA=\tfrac12\,du\,dv$ (here the absolute value is needed), and the region becomes $-1\le u,v\le1$. ([MIT OCW notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/53cab862607d9ad1abdab1a10013be9e_MIT18_02SC_MNotes_cv1.pdf)) In spherical coordinates the Jacobian determinant is $\rho^2\sin\varphi$, giving $dV=\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant))

### History
Bernoulli assumed the symmetry of mixed partials in 1721; Euler and Clairaut published flawed proofs in 1740, and Schwarz gave the first rigorous proof in 1873. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_of_second_derivatives)) Cauchy gave the first rigorous form of the implicit function theorem and Dini extended it to any number of real variables. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implicit_function_theorem)) Picard and Goursat established the inverse function theorem by an iterative scheme; modern proofs use the contraction mapping principle. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem)) The Jacobian is named after C. G. J. Jacobi (1804–1851). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant)) Fubini proved the Lebesgue-integrable case of his theorem in 1907, after Euler's special case for continuous functions and Lebesgue's 1904 result for bounded measurable functions; Tonelli's variant followed in 1909. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem)) A. P. Morse proved Sard's theorem for $m=1$ in 1939 and Sard the general case in 1942. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1942-07811-6))

### Connections
- [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus) and [Differential Calculus](node:Differential%20Calculus): the one-variable special cases.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) and [Determinant](node:Determinant): the derivative is a linear map; its determinant measures volume distortion.
- [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem) and [Implicit Function Theorem](node:Implicit%20Function%20Theorem): local solvability from invertibility of the derivative.
- [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem): the standard modern proof of the inverse function theorem.
- [Taylor's Theorem](node:Taylor's%20Theorem) and [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices): second-order approximation and classification of critical points.
- [Convex Optimization](node:Convex%20Optimization) and [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent): optimization theory built on gradients, Hessians and multipliers.
- [Fubini's Theorem](node:Fubini's%20Theorem), [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration) and [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): iterated integrals and measure-zero critical values.
- [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus), [Stokes' Theorem](node:Stokes'%20Theorem) and [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms): the integral theorems and their unification.
- [Differential Calculus on Manifolds](node:Differential%20Calculus%20on%20Manifolds) and [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): the coordinate-free continuation.
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): equations in partial derivatives.
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits) and [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces): the underlying limits and linear structure.
- Map: [MSC 26 - Real functions](node:MSC%2026%20-%20Real%20functions)

### Common pitfalls
- Inferring a limit from a few paths: every line can give the same value while parabolas do not. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariable_calculus))
- Treating existence of partials as differentiability; continuity of the partials (at the point, with existence nearby) is the usual sufficient condition. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_function))
- Swapping mixed partials without continuity of the second derivatives. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_of_second_derivatives))
- Dropping the absolute value of the Jacobian in a change of variables; it may be omitted only when the Jacobian is known to be non-negative, as for polar $r\ge0$. ([MIT OCW notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/53cab862607d9ad1abdab1a10013be9e_MIT18_02SC_MNotes_cv1.pdf))
- Swapping the order of integration without the Fubini or Tonelli hypotheses: without $\sigma$-finiteness the iterated integrals can differ even for a non-negative indicator function (the diagonal of $[0,1]^2$ with Lebesgue measure on one factor and counting measure on the other gives $0$ and $1$). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem))
- Reading a nonzero Jacobian everywhere as global invertibility, or a Lagrange stationary point as an extremum. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_multiplier))

### Open problems
The Jacobian conjecture (Keller, 1939) asked whether a polynomial map $F:K^n\to K^n$ over a field of characteristic zero whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant must have a polynomial inverse; the converse is automatic. In July 2026 Levent Alpöge presented an explicit three-variable counterexample, with constant Jacobian determinant $-2$ and not injective, which can be checked by [computer algebra](node:Computer%20Algebra) and extends to every $n>2$. The planar case $n=2$ remains open and is problem 16 on Smale's 1998 list. The inverse function theorem already gives a local inverse; the question is a global polynomial one. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_conjecture)) An independent Isabelle/HOL formalization proves that the announced three-dimensional map has determinant identically $-2$ and sends three distinct rational points to the same image, gives counterexamples in every dimension at least three, and makes no claim about $n=2$. ([Archive of Formal Proofs](https://isa-afp.org/entries/Jacobian_Counterexample.html))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Multivariable calculus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariable_calculus), with [Implicit function theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implicit_function_theorem) and [Inverse function theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem).
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.02SC, Mattuck notes on changing variables](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/53cab862607d9ad1abdab1a10013be9e_MIT18_02SC_MNotes_cv1.pdf): Jacobians and worked change-of-variable examples.
- **Primary:** [Sard, The measure of the critical values of differentiable maps, Bull. AMS 48 (1942) 883–890](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1942-07811-6): the original paper on Sard's theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds (Addison-Wesley, 1965)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL3169379W) and [Munkres, Analysis on Manifolds (1991)](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=analysis+on+manifolds+munkres): rigorous texts covering differentiation, the inverse and implicit function theorems, integration and Stokes' theorem.
references.N-body Simulations:
## Reference
### Overview
An N-body simulation follows a system of particles interacting through physical forces, usually gravity, by integrating their equations of motion numerically. In astrophysics it covers scales from few-body systems such as the Earth–Moon–Sun system to the large-scale structure of the universe; a particle may represent a single object such as a star or a bundle of matter such as a gas parcel, and each often stands in for a huge number of real particles ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation)).

Two regimes differ sharply. In a **collisional** system, such as a star cluster with $N\sim10^3$ members, the relaxation time (roughly 100 Myr to 10 Gyr) is not long compared with a typical 10 Gyr lifetime, so encounters between members are significant. In a **collisionless** system, such as a galaxy with $10^6$–$10^{11}$ stars, the relaxation time far exceeds the age of the universe and the stars move in a smooth mean potential ([Wikipedia: Stellar dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_dynamics)). Cosmological dark-matter simulations are of the second kind: they solve the collisionless Boltzmann (Vlasov) equation coupled to Poisson's equation in an expanding Friedmann background, sampling the phase-space density with $N$ particles ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation); [Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165)).

N-body simulations are the main tool for nonlinear structure formation. Navarro, Frenk and White used them to find that cold-dark-matter halos from dwarf galaxies to rich clusters share a "universal" spherically averaged density profile, shallower than $r^{-2}$ near the centre and steeper near the virial radius ([arXiv: Navarro, Frenk, White](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9508025)). State-of-the-art runs follow regions dozens of gigaparsecs across with trillions of particles ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165)).

### Formal definition
**Cosmological Vlasov–Poisson system.** For the phase-space density $f(\mathbf x,\mathbf p,t)$ of particles of mass $m$ in comoving coordinates $\mathbf x$ with canonical momentum $\mathbf p$ and scale factor $a(t)$,
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\frac{p_i}{m a^2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}-m\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}=0,\qquad \nabla^2\phi=4\pi G a^2(\rho-\bar\rho),\qquad \rho=\frac{m}{a^3}\int f\,d^3p .$$
With matter only and $\delta=\rho/\bar\rho-1$, the Poisson equation becomes $\nabla^2\phi=\tfrac32 H_0^2\Omega_m\,\delta/a$ ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165)).

**N-body discretization.** Sample $f$ by $N$ particles of masses $M_i$ in a periodic box of side $L$; the density is $\rho(\mathbf x)=\sum_{\mathbf n}\sum_i M_i W(\mathbf x-\mathbf X_i-\mathbf nL)$ for a softening kernel $W$, and the particles obey
$$\frac{d\mathbf X_i}{dt}=\frac{\mathbf P_i}{M_i a^2},\qquad \frac{d\mathbf P_i}{dt}=-M_i\nabla\phi(\mathbf X_i).$$
([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))

**Softening.** To avoid divergent forces in close encounters the point-mass potential $-1/r$ is replaced by roughly $-1/\sqrt{r^2+\varepsilon^2}$, with softening length $\varepsilon$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation)).

### Key results
- **Relaxation time.** The relaxation time measured in crossing times is $t_{\rm relax}/t_{\rm cross}\approx 0.123\,(N-1)/\ln(N-1)$, which grows roughly like $N/\ln N$; on times much shorter than $t_{\rm relax}$ a system is effectively collisionless. ([Wikipedia: Stellar dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_dynamics))
- **Barnes–Hut tree algorithm (1986).** Store particles in an octree whose internal nodes carry total mass and centre of mass; when computing the force on a particle, treat a node of width $s$ at distance $d$ as a single point mass if $s/d<\theta$, otherwise open it. The cost is $O(N\log N)$ instead of $O(N^2)$ for direct summation, and $\theta=0$ recovers direct summation. ([Wikipedia: Barnes–Hut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnes%E2%80%93Hut_simulation); [Berkeley CS267](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/cs267/lecture26/lecture26.html))
- **Cost of force methods.** Direct particle–particle summation costs $O(N^2)$; particle-mesh solves Poisson's equation by FFT in $O(M\log M)$ for $M$ grid points; tree codes cost $O(N\log N)$; the fast multipole method attains $O(N)$. TreePM and P3M split the force into a long-range mesh part and a short-range tree or direct part, a split pioneered for tree-PM by Bagla (2002). ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))
- **Symplectic leapfrog.** The standard integrator is the second-order drift–kick–drift (or kick–drift–kick) splitting $(I+\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\hat D)(I+\varepsilon\hat K)(I+\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\hat D)$; Angulo and Hahn note that, being symplectic in super-conformal time, it conserves the energy associated with the extended-phase-space Hamiltonian $\tilde{\mathscr H}$. Higher-order symplectic schemes exist (Yoshida, with negative substeps; Chin and Chen, fourth order with positive coefficients), but no production cosmological code is known to use them. ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))
- **Universal halo profile.** Halos in cold-dark-matter simulations, from dwarf to cluster masses, fit a single scaled profile over two decades in radius, and halo concentration correlates strongly with mass, reflecting formation time. ([arXiv: Navarro, Frenk, White](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9508025))

### Examples
- **GADGET-2.** Springel's massively parallel TreeSPH code follows dark matter by N-body and gas by smoothed particle hydrodynamics, optionally as TreePM, with a quasi-symplectic integrator allowing different timesteps for long- and short-range forces; it ran the first cosmological N-body simulation with more than $10^{10}$ particles. ([arXiv: Springel 2005](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0505010))
- **Millennium and Bolshoi.** The Millennium simulation used ten billion particles ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation)); in units of the mean inter-particle separation the Bolshoi simulation uses a softening of 0.016 and the Millennium simulations 0.022, while recent runs exceed a trillion particles, several hundred times the Millennium count ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165)).
- **Initial conditions.** Particles start on a lattice or glass configuration displaced by linear theory or low-order Lagrangian perturbation theory, in comoving coordinates with periodic boundaries. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation); [Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))
- **Star clusters.** Aarseth's direct-summation codes for clusters, planetary systems and galactic nuclei use adaptive timesteps, the Ahmad–Cohen neighbour scheme and regularization of close encounters. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation))

### History
Erik Holmberg ran the first gravitational N-body experiment at Lund Observatory in 1941 using light bulbs and photocells; Sebastian von Hoerner ran the first purely computational simulations at Heidelberg, and Sverre Aarseth at Cambridge developed the efficient direct codes ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation)). Barnes and Hut published their hierarchical $O(N\log N)$ force algorithm in Nature in December 1986 ([Wikipedia: Barnes–Hut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnes%E2%80%93Hut_simulation)). Navarro, Frenk and White's halo-structure paper (arXiv 1995, ApJ 1996) and Springel's GADGET-2 (MNRAS 2005) are landmarks of the cosmological era ([arXiv: NFW](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9508025); [arXiv: Springel](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0505010)). The 2008 edition of Binney and Tremaine's *Galactic Dynamics* added N-body methods to the standard text ([Princeton University Press](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691130279/galactic-dynamics)).

### Connections
- [The N-Body Problem](node:The%20N-Body%20Problem): the underlying dynamical problem that simulations integrate.
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): the pairwise force law being summed.
- [Numerical Methods for Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Methods%20for%20Differential%20Equations): timestepping schemes for the equations of motion.
- [Geometric Numerical Integration](node:Geometric%20Numerical%20Integration): why the symplectic leapfrog is preferred for long integrations.
- [Vlasov Equation](node:Vlasov%20Equation): the collisionless continuum equation that cosmological N-body codes sample.
- [Fast Fourier Transform](node:Fast%20Fourier%20Transform): the Poisson solver of particle-mesh methods.
- [Particle-in-Cell Methods](node:Particle-in-Cell%20Methods): the plasma analogue of particle-mesh gravity.
- [Molecular Dynamics](node:Molecular%20Dynamics): the same particle-integration ideas with short-range forces.
- [Large-Scale Structure](node:Large-Scale%20Structure): the main cosmological output.
- [Dark Matter Halo Profiles](node:Dark%20Matter%20Halo%20Profiles): NFW and successors measured from simulations.
- [Dark Matter Subhalos](node:Dark%20Matter%20Subhalos): substructure whose survival is a resolution-sensitive output.
- [Warm Dark Matter](node:Warm%20Dark%20Matter): a regime where N-body discreteness causes spurious fragmentation.
- [Galaxy Formation](node:Galaxy%20Formation): requires coupling N-body gravity to baryonic physics.
- [High-Performance Computing](node:High-Performance%20Computing): production runs are massively parallel.

### Common pitfalls
- **Softening trade-off.** Each N-body particle stands for an extended piece of phase space, so two-body scattering between particles is artificial and must be suppressed by softening; keeping the softening so large that individual particles are never resolved gives only slow convergence to the correct solution, while force resolution that is too coarse at late times leaves subhalos loosely bound and prone to premature tidal disruption ("overmerging"), which argues for small softening. ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))
- **Discreteness.** When force and mass resolution are mismatched the particle system can depart strongly from the continuum limit; in warm dark matter near the free-streaming scale, discreteness creates spurious low-mass halos that outnumber physical ones by factors of 100–1000, which Angulo and Hahn call a serious shortcoming of the N-body method; the problem is ameliorated only slowly with mass resolution, roughly as $N_{\rm p}^{1/3}$. Hot components such as neutrinos suffer large momentum-space sampling noise. ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))
- **Accuracy of tree codes.** Barnes–Hut is typically used at about 1% force accuracy and can be much worse in the worst case; the fast multipole method can reach machine precision. ([Berkeley CS267](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/cs267/lecture26/lecture26.html))
- **Leapfrog order.** Leapfrog is only second-order accurate in the timestep, yet it remains the most commonly used integrator in cosmological simulations, arguably for its robustness, simplicity, slim memory footprint and easy combination with hierarchical time-stepping. ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))

### Open problems
- **Microhalo survival.** Whether the first WIMP microhalos survive tidal forces inside Milky-Way halos is "still an open question", and their true inner density profiles are "currently unanswered". ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))
- **Two-fluid initial conditions.** Including baryon–CDM relative velocities beyond linear order in the initial conditions of two-fluid simulations is "still an unsolved problem". ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))
- **Verification against non-N-body methods.** Methods that do not rely on N-body discretization now allow its errors to be tested; no significant biases have been found so far for the statistical properties of CDM simulations, but Angulo and Hahn state that many more careful and systematic comparisons will be needed. ([Angulo and Hahn 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [N-body simulation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation): methods, softening, cosmological set-up, history.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley CS267: Barnes–Hut and fast multipole](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~demmel/cs267/lecture26/lecture26.html): tree construction, opening criterion, cost analysis, accuracy.
- **Primary:** [Angulo and Hahn, Large-scale dark matter simulations (Living Reviews in Computational Astrophysics 2022)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.05165): comprehensive review of equations, integrators, force solvers, discreteness and open issues.
- **Primary:** [Springel, The cosmological simulation code GADGET-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0505010): TreePM/SPH code paper.
- **Primary:** [Navarro, Frenk, White, The Structure of Cold Dark Matter Halos](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9508025): universal halo profile from simulations.
- **Further reading:** [Binney and Tremaine, Galactic Dynamics, 2nd ed. (Princeton University Press, 2008)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691130279/galactic-dynamics): described by its publisher as the most widely used advanced textbook on galaxy dynamics; the revised edition covers N-body methods.

## Reference
### Overview
A decision problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. In this sense the NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)). The Cook–Levin theorem showed that such problems exist by proving that Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete. Karp then showed that many other combinatorial problems are NP-complete as well ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness); [Wikipedia: Cook–Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem)).

The notion matters because of [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP). If any NP-complete problem, SAT for instance, has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, then P = NP ([Wikipedia: Cook–Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem)). Practical responses to NP-complete problems include approximation, restriction to structured inputs, parameterization, or heuristics ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).

NP-completeness is the founding example of completeness in [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory). It is refined by finer reductions (logspace), by structural questions (isomorphism, sparseness), by dichotomy theorems for constraint satisfaction, and by the PCP theorem, which extends NP-hardness to approximation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness); [Wikipedia: Berman–Hartmanis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berman%E2%80%93Hartmanis_conjecture); [Wikipedia: PCP theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCP_theorem); [Wikipedia: Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schaefer%27s_dichotomy_theorem)).

### Formal definition
A language $A$ is **polynomial-time many-one (Karp) reducible** to $B$, written $A\le_p B$, if there is a polynomial-time computable $f$ with $x\in A\iff f(x)\in B$ for all $x$. Then:
$$C\ \text{is NP-hard}\iff \forall A\in\mathsf{NP}:\ A\le_p C,\qquad C\ \text{is NP-complete}\iff C\in\mathsf{NP}\ \text{and}\ C\ \text{is NP-hard}.$$
NP-hard problems need not lie in NP ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).

- **Other reductions.** A polynomial-time Turing (Cook) reduction may call the target problem many times as a subroutine. Using Turing reductions gives a class that is not smaller than the NP-complete problems, and whether it is strictly larger is open. All known NP-complete problems remain complete under logspace many-one reductions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).
- **Proof recipe.** To show a problem $C$ is NP-complete, show $C\in\mathsf{NP}$ (a polynomial-time verifier for certificates) and reduce a known NP-complete problem *to* $C$. Karp proved 3-SAT NP-complete this way, by reducing SAT to it ([Wikipedia: Cook–Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem)).

### Key results
- **Cook–Levin theorem.** SAT is NP-complete. Given a nondeterministic Turing machine deciding a problem within a polynomial time bound, one builds a Boolean formula whose variables record tape contents, head position and state at each step. The formula is satisfiable exactly when the machine has an accepting computation, and the reduction is computable even in logarithmic space ([Wikipedia: Cook–Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem)).
- **Karp's 21 problems (1972).** Karp introduced polynomial-time many-one reducibility and proved 21 combinatorial problems NP-complete ([Wikipedia: Cook–Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-2001-2_9)).
