- **Ladner's theorem (1975).** If $\mathsf P\neq\mathsf{NP}$, there are problems in $\mathsf{NP}$ that are neither in $\mathsf P$ nor NP-complete. Hence $\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}$ if and only if $\mathsf{NPI}=\varnothing$ ([Wikipedia: Ladner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladner%27s_theorem)).
- **Mahaney's theorem (1982).** There is no sparse NP-complete language under many-one reductions if and only if $\mathsf P\neq\mathsf{NP}$. Under Turing reductions, a sparse NP-complete language would collapse the polynomial hierarchy ([Wikipedia: Berman–Hartmanis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berman%E2%80%93Hartmanis_conjecture)).
- **Paddability (Berman–Hartmanis).** Any two paddable NP-complete languages are polynomial-time isomorphic ([Wikipedia: Berman–Hartmanis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berman%E2%80%93Hartmanis_conjecture)).
- **Schaefer's dichotomy theorem (1978).** For a finite set $S$ of Boolean relations, $\mathrm{SAT}(S)$ is in $\mathsf P$ if all relations are 0-valid, or all 1-valid, bijunctive, Horn, dual-Horn, or affine. Otherwise it is NP-complete. Equivalently, $\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma)$ is in $\mathsf P$ if $\Gamma$ has one of the polymorphisms constant 0, constant 1, AND, OR, majority or minority, and NP-complete otherwise ([Wikipedia: Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schaefer%27s_dichotomy_theorem)).
- **PCP theorem.** $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{PCP}[O(\log n),O(1)]$: every NP statement has a proof that a randomized verifier checks by reading $O(1)$ bits with $O(\log n)$ random bits. Correct proofs are always accepted, and false claims are rejected with probability at least $1/2$. Equivalently, approximating the maximum fraction of satisfiable constraints of some Boolean CSP within some constant is NP-hard. Consequently, unless $\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}$, MAX-SAT and maximum independent set cannot be approximated efficiently ([Wikipedia: PCP theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCP_theorem)).

### Examples
- SAT, knapsack, Hamiltonian path, decision TSP, subgraph isomorphism, subset sum, clique, vertex cover, independent set, dominating set, graph coloring and (generalized) Sudoku are NP-complete ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).
- Thresholds: 2-SAT is in $\mathsf P$ but 3-SAT is NP-complete. 2-coloring is in $\mathsf P$ but 3-coloring is NP-complete, even on planar graphs ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).
- Special cases of Schaefer's theorem: SAT, 1-in-3 SAT and NAE-3SAT are NP-complete ([Wikipedia: Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schaefer%27s_dichotomy_theorem)).
- Candidates for NP-intermediate status: graph isomorphism and the decision versions of factoring and discrete logarithm. None is proven to be NP-intermediate ([Wikipedia: Ladner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladner%27s_theorem)).

### History
Stephen Cook's "The complexity of theorem-proving procedures" appeared in the *Proceedings of the Third Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing* (1971, pp. 151–158) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/800157.805047)). Richard Karp's "Reducibility among Combinatorial Problems" appeared in *Complexity of Computer Computations* (Springer, 1972, pp. 85–103) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-2001-2_9)). Leonid Levin's "Universal search problems" (1973) independently gave six universal search problems. Cook and Karp each received a Turing Award ([Wikipedia: Cook–Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem)). After a poll run by Knuth, the term "NP-complete" replaced "polynomially-complete" in the galley proofs of Aho, Hopcroft and Ullman's algorithms textbook. Garey and Johnson's *Computers and Intractability* (1979) developed the theory and catalogued problems. The Clay Institute named P versus NP a Millennium Prize Problem in 2000 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)). The PCP theorem was proved by Arora, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy (published 1998; Gödel Prize 2001), and Dinur gave a simpler proof in 2005 ([Wikipedia: PCP theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCP_theorem)).

### Connections
- [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP): an NP-complete problem is in P if and only if P = NP.
- [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory): the general theory of classes, reductions and completeness.
- [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines): the Cook–Levin reduction encodes nondeterministic Turing machine computations.
- [SAT and SMT Solving](node:SAT%20and%20SMT%20Solving): practical solvers for the canonical NP-complete problem.
- [Constraint Satisfaction Problems](node:Constraint%20Satisfaction%20Problems): Schaefer's dichotomy classifies Boolean CSPs.
- [Polynomial Hierarchy](node:Polynomial%20Hierarchy): sparse NP-complete sets under Turing reductions would collapse it.
- [Approximation Algorithms](node:Approximation%20Algorithms): the PCP theorem limits approximation of NP-hard optimization problems.
- [Parameterized Complexity](node:Parameterized%20Complexity): a standard way to cope with NP-hardness.
- [Fine-Grained Complexity](node:Fine-Grained%20Complexity): finer, conditional lower bounds beyond the P/NP split.
- [Graph Colorings](node:Graph%20Colorings): 3-coloring is a classic NP-complete problem.
- [Integer Programming](node:Integer%20Programming): a widely used NP-hard modelling language.
- [Integer Factorization](node:Integer%20Factorization): a candidate NP-intermediate problem.
- [Combinatorial Optimization](node:Combinatorial%20Optimization): decision versions of many optimization problems are NP-complete.

### Common pitfalls
- **Reduction direction.** To prove $C$ hard, reduce a known NP-complete problem to $C$, not $C$ to it ([Wikipedia: Cook–Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem)).
- **"Hardest known problems."** NP-complete problems are not the hardest problems. Presburger arithmetic and the halting problem are harder ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).
- **"Requires exponential time."** That would imply $\mathsf P\neq\mathsf{NP}$, which is unresolved, and some NP-complete problems have subexponential algorithms ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).
- **Quantum computers.** $\mathsf{BQP}$ is not believed to contain $\mathsf{NP}$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).
- **Closure.** The NP-complete problems are not closed under union, intersection, concatenation or Kleene star. Closure under complement holds if and only if $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{coNP}$, which is open ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).
- **NP-hard vs NP-complete.** NP-hard problems need not be in NP ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).

### Open problems
- **P versus NP.** It is unresolved whether any NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm, and the Clay Institute lists it as a Millennium Prize Problem ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).
- **Berman–Hartmanis isomorphism conjecture (1977).** All NP-complete languages are polynomial-time isomorphic, or equivalently all are paddable. This is an open problem, and it would imply that no sparse NP-complete language exists. Evidence is mixed. An analogue holds for AC$^0$ many-one reductions (Agrawal et al. 1997), and under a one-way-function assumption all NP-complete languages have P/poly isomorphisms (Agrawal–Watanabe 2009). The analogue fails relative to a random oracle (Kurtz–Mahaney–Royer 1995), and many complexity theorists believe the conjecture is false ([Wikipedia: Berman–Hartmanis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berman%E2%80%93Hartmanis_conjecture)).
- **Natural NP-intermediate problems.** Whether any natural problem is NP-intermediate is open ([Wikipedia: Ladner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladner%27s_theorem)).
- **Cook vs Karp completeness.** Whether NP-completeness under polynomial-time Turing reductions is a strictly larger class than under many-one reductions is open ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: NP-completeness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-completeness): definition, reductions, examples, misconceptions, history.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Cook–Levin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem): statement and proof sketch.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.404J Theory of Computation (Sipser, Fall 2020)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/): video lectures on computability, complexity and completeness.
- **Primary:** [Cook, The complexity of theorem-proving procedures (STOC 1971)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/800157.805047): the original NP-completeness paper.
- **Primary:** [Karp, Reducibility among Combinatorial Problems (1972)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-2001-2_9): the 21 NP-complete problems.
- **Further reading:** [Arora and Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach (Cambridge University Press)](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/): graduate textbook on computational complexity theory.
references.Nash Equilibrium:
## Reference
### Overview
A Nash equilibrium of a non-cooperative game is a profile of strategies, one per player, in which no player can gain by changing only her own strategy while the others keep theirs; equivalently, each player's strategy is a best response to the strategies of the others. The concept allows players to randomize over their pure strategies (mixed strategies), and a game may have several equilibria, one, or (in pure strategies) none ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)).

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes the concept as the condition that "no player could improve her payoff, given the strategies of all other players in the game", and notes that it is a logically weak solution concept, which is why much of game theory consists of refinements that discard some equilibria ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/game-theory/)). Nash's theorem guarantees existence in every finite game, and this guaranteed existence is what makes the computational question unusual: Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou point out that finding an equilibrium cannot be NP-hard in the usual way, because every instance has a solution ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).

On its computational side the topic belongs to algorithmic game theory, whose standard handbook opens with chapters on the complexity of finding Nash equilibria and on equilibrium computation for two-player games ([Cambridge University Press](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/algorithmic-game-theory/0092C07CA8B724E1B1BE2238DDD66B38)).

### Formal definition
A finite game in normal form consists of players $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, finite pure-strategy sets $S_i$, and payoff functions $u_i : S = S_1 \times \dots \times S_n \to \mathbb{R}$. A profile $s^* \in S$ is a **(pure) Nash equilibrium** if for every player $i$ and every $s_i \in S_i$,
$$u_i(s_i^*, s_{-i}^*) \ \ge\ u_i(s_i, s_{-i}^*),$$
where $s_{-i}$ denotes the strategies of all players other than $i$. The equilibrium is **strict** if every inequality is strict for $s_i \ne s_i^*$, and weak if some player is indifferent between her equilibrium strategy and another ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)).

A **mixed strategy** for player $p$ is a probability vector $x^p = (x^p_j)_{j \in S_p}$. Extending payoffs by expectation, a mixed profile $x$ is a Nash equilibrium if for each player $p$, every pure strategy $j$ in the support of $x^p$ maximizes $p$'s expected payoff
$$\sum_{s \in S_{-p}} u^p_{js}\, x_s$$
against the others' mixed strategies, where $x_s = \prod_{q \ne p} x^q_{s_q}$ ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).

An **$\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium** (in the well-supported sense used for complexity results) requires that whenever pure strategy $j$ earns more than pure strategy $j'$ by more than $\epsilon$ against $x_{-p}$, the strategy $j'$ is played with probability zero ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Nash's existence theorem.** Every finite game (finitely many players, each with finitely many pure strategies) has at least one Nash equilibrium, possibly in mixed strategies. Nash's 1950 paper used Kakutani's fixed-point theorem, and his 1951 paper used the simpler Brouwer fixed-point theorem ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)). The results appeared as "Equilibrium points in $n$-person games", PNAS 36(1), 48–49 (1950) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1073/pnas.36.1.48)) and "Non-Cooperative Games", Annals of Mathematics 54(2), 1951 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1969529)).
- **Existence beyond finite games.** Existence can fail with infinite, non-compact strategy sets (the game "name a larger number" has no equilibrium) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)); in a continuous game, where each pure-strategy set is a compact subset of a metric space and the utilities are continuous, a Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies (Borel probability measures on the strategy sets) exists, by Glicksberg's generalization of the Kakutani fixed-point theorem ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_game)).
- **Oddness theorem (Wilson 1971).** Almost all finite games have an odd number of Nash equilibria ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)).
- **Zero-sum games are easy.** For two-player zero-sum games, von Neumann's work implies that equilibria can be found by linear programming, hence in polynomial time ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).
- **NASH is PPAD-complete (Daskalakis–Goldberg–Papadimitriou).** Computing an $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium of a finite game, with $\epsilon$ inversely exponential in the game size, is complete for the class PPAD, already for three-player games; the proof reduces End-of-the-Line to approximate Brouwer fixed points and Brouwer to Nash ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)). The Brouwer-to-Nash step goes through Arithmetic Circuit SAT, which always has a solution and is PPAD-complete to solve ([Farina, MIT 6.S890](https://www.mit.edu/~gfarina/2024/6S890f24_L18_ppad/L18.pdf)).
- **Two players suffice (Chen–Deng–Teng).** Finding a Nash equilibrium of a two-player (bimatrix) game is PPAD-complete; Bimatrix has no fully polynomial-time approximation scheme unless every PPAD problem is in P; and the smoothed complexity of the Lemke–Howson algorithm, and of any Bimatrix algorithm, is not polynomial unless PPAD is in randomized polynomial time ([Chen, Deng and Teng](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.1678)). This was unexpected because two-player equilibria always have rational probabilities, unlike games with three or more players ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).
- **Quasi-polynomial hardness of approximation (Rubinstein).** There is a constant $\epsilon > 0$ such that, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis for PPAD, computing an $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium of an $n \times n$ bimatrix game requires time $n^{\log^{1-o(1)} n}$, matching the Lipton–Markakis–Mehta algorithm; for $n$-player games, $2^{\Omega(n)}$ payoff queries are needed ([Rubinstein](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04550)).
- **Constant-$\epsilon$ hardness for many players (Rubinstein).** For some constant $\epsilon$, computing an $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium is PPAD-complete even for polymatrix, degree-3 graphical games in which every player has two actions ([Rubinstein, Inapproximability of Nash Equilibrium](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.3322)). This settles the case of general low-degree graphical games, whose complexity Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou had listed as unknown ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).

### Examples
- **Matching pennies** has no pure equilibrium; its unique equilibrium has each player play heads and tails with probability $1/2$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)).
- **Coordination and driving games** have two pure equilibria (both choose A, or both B; both drive left, or both right) and, in the driving game, a 50/50 mixed equilibrium that is unstable, while the pure ones are stable ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)).
- **Prisoner's dilemma** has a unique Nash equilibrium (mutual defection), obtained by iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies, even though mutual cooperation would give both players more ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/game-theory/)).
- **Hi-lo** has two equilibria, and Nash equilibrium alone does not say which one players should choose ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/game-theory/)).
- **Rock-paper-scissors** is a zero-sum game with no pure equilibrium; it has a mixed equilibrium in which both players pick an action uniformly at random ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).

### History
Cournot described the same idea in 1838 for oligopoly, and von Neumann and Morgenstern introduced mixed-strategy equilibria in 1944, restricted to zero-sum games; Nash generalized it to arbitrary finite games in 1950–1951 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)). Selten introduced subgame perfect equilibrium in 1965 to remove equilibria supported by non-credible threats ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)). The Lemke–Howson algorithm for two-player games and Scarf's algorithm for fixed points both follow paths in an "end of the line" graph, and that parity argument inspired the definition of PPAD; the PPAD-completeness of Nash was announced by Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou and extended to two players by Chen and Deng a few months later ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).

### Connections
- [Fixed-Point and Coincidence Theorems](node:Fixed-Point%20and%20Coincidence%20Theorems): Brouwer's and Kakutani's theorems give the existence proof, and approximate Brouwer is the hard core of the PPAD reduction.
- [Linear Programming](node:Linear%20Programming): two-player zero-sum equilibria are the optimal solutions of a linear program.
- [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory): the computational status of Nash is a total-search-problem question, placed in PPAD rather than NP-hardness.
- [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): finding a Nash equilibrium is unlikely to be NP-complete because solutions always exist; finding one with extra properties can be different.
- [Correlated Equilibrium](node:Correlated%20Equilibrium): a relaxation in which players condition on a common signal; every Nash equilibrium is a correlated equilibrium.
- [No-Regret Learning](node:No-Regret%20Learning): decentralized dynamics that converge to coarse correlated rather than Nash equilibria in general games.
- [Algorithmic Mechanism Design](node:Algorithmic%20Mechanism%20Design): designs games so that desirable outcomes are equilibria.
- [General Equilibrium Theory](node:General%20Equilibrium%20Theory): Arrow–Debreu market equilibria are PPAD-hard to compute, by the Chen–Deng–Teng reduction.
- [Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](node:Multi-Agent%20Reinforcement%20Learning): equilibrium concepts define the targets of learning in multi-agent settings.

### Common pitfalls
- A Nash equilibrium need not be Pareto optimal; in congestion networks the equilibrium can be socially suboptimal, and adding a road can make everyone worse off (Braess's paradox) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)).
- In sequential games, Nash equilibria can rest on non-credible threats, because the concept ignores behavior off the path of play; subgame perfection refines it ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/game-theory/)).
- Equilibrium does not by itself predict play: a player has no reason to play a Nash strategy unless she expects the others to, and the SEP describes equilibrium concepts as "tools for analysis, not predictions of what we expect to observe" ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/game-theory/)).
- Pure equilibria need not exist; existence in general requires mixed strategies ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium)).
- Hardness results concern approximate equilibria with specific $\epsilon$ regimes; exact equilibria in games with three or more players can be irrational, which is why exact computation has its own complexity theory (Etessami–Yannakakis) ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Approximation schemes.** Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou called the existence of a PTAS for $\epsilon$-Nash the main open question ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)); for two-player games Rubinstein later showed that, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis for PPAD, some constant $\epsilon$ requires quasi-polynomial time, matching the Lipton–Markakis–Mehta algorithm, so for two players the answer is known only conditionally on that hypothesis ([Rubinstein](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04550)).
- **New equilibrium concepts.** Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou pose, as an overarching research question made more urgent by the hardness of Nash, the identification of novel concepts of rationality and equilibrium suited to the Internet and its computational platforms ([Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Nash equilibrium (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium): definitions, existence, examples, stability and refinements.
- **Reference:** [Game Theory (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/game-theory/): interpretation of equilibrium, refinements, and the multiple-equilibrium problem.
- **Learn:** [Farina, MIT 6.S890 Lecture 18: PPAD-completeness of Nash equilibria](https://www.mit.edu/~gfarina/2024/6S890f24_L18_ppad/L18.pdf): the Brouwer-to-Nash gadget reduction.
- **Primary:** [Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou, The Complexity of Computing a Nash Equilibrium](https://people.csail.mit.edu/costis/simplified.pdf): expository version of the PPAD-completeness result with open problems.
- **Primary:** [Chen, Deng and Teng, Settling the Complexity of Computing Two-Player Nash Equilibria](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.1678): PPAD-completeness for bimatrix games.
- **Primary:** [Nash, Equilibrium points in n-person games (1950)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1073/pnas.36.1.48): the original existence paper (bibliographic record).
- **Further reading:** [Nisan, Roughgarden, Tardos and Vazirani (eds.), Algorithmic Game Theory (CUP 2007)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/algorithmic-game-theory/0092C07CA8B724E1B1BE2238DDD66B38): chapters on the complexity of Nash and two-player equilibrium computation.
references.Navier–Stokes Equations:
## Reference
### Overview
The Navier–Stokes equations are the momentum balance for a viscous Newtonian fluid: Cauchy's momentum equation $\rho\,D\mathbf u/Dt=-\nabla p+\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\tau+\rho\mathbf a$, with material derivative $D/Dt=\partial_t+\mathbf u\cdot\nabla$, closed by a stress tensor $\boldsymbol\tau$ linear in the velocity gradient. Navier developed them from 1822, Stokes refined them between 1842 and 1850, and Poisson reached the same results independently. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations))

They are the working model of nearly all of classical [Fluid Dynamics](node:Fluid%20Dynamics): at high [Reynolds number](node:Reynolds%20Number) they reduce away from walls to the inviscid Euler equations, at low Reynolds number to [Stokes (creeping) flow](node:Stokes%20Flow), and near walls they produce [boundary layers](node:Boundary%20Layers) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics)). Mathematically, their three-dimensional existence and smoothness is one of the Clay Institute's Millennium Prize Problems; the Clay page notes that "our understanding of them remains minimal" ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/)).

### Formal definition
**Incompressible equations.** For constant density $\rho$, kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho$, velocity $\mathbf u$, pressure $p$ and body force $\mathbf f$,
$$\partial_t\mathbf u+(\mathbf u\cdot\nabla)\mathbf u=\nu\Delta\mathbf u-\frac1\rho\nabla p+\frac1\rho\mathbf f,\qquad\nabla\cdot\mathbf u=0,$$
which follows from the Newtonian law $\boldsymbol\tau=\mu(\nabla\mathbf u+\nabla\mathbf u^{\mathsf T})$ with uniform viscosity. The incompressible model rules out density and pressure waves and is typically used up to about Mach 0.3. At solid walls the standard boundary condition is no slip, the fluid velocity vanishing relative to the wall. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations))

**Compressible equations.** The Cauchy stress is
$$\boldsymbol\sigma=-\big[p-\zeta(\nabla\cdot\mathbf u)\big]I+\mu\Big[\nabla\mathbf u+\nabla\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}-\tfrac23(\nabla\cdot\mathbf u)I\Big],$$
with bulk viscosity $\zeta$; the Stokes hypothesis $\zeta=0$ is accurate for monatomic gases but generally not for other gases or liquids. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations))

**Reynolds number.** $\mathrm{Re}=uL/\nu=\rho uL/\mu$ for characteristic speed $u$ and length $L$; it measures inertia against viscosity and governs dynamic similarity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynolds_number))

**Weak and suitable weak solutions.** Leray's global [weak solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions) have finite kinetic energy and finite dissipation energy and satisfy the energy inequality. A *suitable* weak solution $(\mathbf u,p)$ satisfies integrability bounds on $\mathbf u$ and $p$, solves the equations in the sense of distributions, and satisfies the local energy inequality. A point is regular if $\mathbf u$ is bounded (and Hölder continuous) in some parabolic cylinder around it, and singular otherwise. ([arXiv:2210.01783](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01783v1))

### Key results
- **Leray (1934).** For the Cauchy problem in $\mathbb R^3$, global weak solutions with finite kinetic energy and finite dissipation exist and satisfy the energy inequality for almost every $t>0$; Hopf proved the analogous result for bounded domains ([arXiv:2210.01783](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01783v1)). Leray also showed that smooth, globally defined solutions exist when the initial velocity is sufficiently small ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness)).
- **Two dimensions.** Smooth global solutions were proven to exist in two dimensions in the 1960s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness))
- **Maximal existence time.** For any smooth initial velocity there is a maximal time $T$ of smooth existence; the Millennium problem asks whether $T=\infty$ always. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness))
- **Partial regularity (Scheffer; Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg).** For a subclass of Leray–Hopf weak solutions satisfying the local energy inequality, Scheffer showed that the singular set has Hausdorff dimension at most $5/3$. Caffarelli, Kohn and Nirenberg improved this: for a suitable weak solution the singular set $\mathcal S$ has zero one-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure, $\mathcal P^1(\mathcal S)=0$. ([arXiv:2210.01783](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01783v1))
- **Nonuniqueness of weak solutions (Buckmaster–Vicol).** In three dimensions, weak solutions are not unique in the class of weak solutions with finite kinetic energy. ([Buckmaster and Vicol](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.10033))
- **Averaged blowup (Tao).** Replacing the bilinear term $B(u,u)$ in $\partial_tu=\Delta u+B(u,u)$ by an average $\tilde B$ over rotations, zero-order Fourier multipliers and dilations that keeps the cancellation $\langle\tilde B(u,u),u\rangle=0$ (hence the energy identity) yields smooth solutions that blow up in finite time. So any proof of global regularity must use finer structure of the nonlinearity than harmonic-analysis estimates and the energy identity. ([Tao](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.0290))

### Examples
- **Plane Poiseuille flow.** Steady pressure-driven flow between plates $y=\pm h$ with no-slip walls is a degenerate case in which the nonlinear terms vanish; the velocity is the parabola $u=\frac{1}{2\mu}\frac{dP}{dx}(y^2-h^2)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations))
- **Stokes flow.** Dropping the convective (inertial) term gives the linear Stokes equations, a vector diffusion equation valid for creeping flow. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations))
- **Pipe flow transition.** Fully developed pipe flow is laminar below $\mathrm{Re}\approx2300$ and fully turbulent above about $2900$, intermittent in between. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynolds_number))

### History
Navier's work from 1822 and Stokes's refinements of 1842–1850 fixed the equations ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations)). Stokes introduced the Reynolds number in 1851, Reynolds popularized it through his 1883 pipe experiments, and Sommerfeld named it in 1908 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynolds_number)). Leray introduced weak solutions in 1934; in the 1960s finite-difference schemes were shown convergent and two-dimensional global regularity was proved; Tao's averaged blowup appeared in 2016 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness)). The Clay Mathematics Institute posed global existence and smoothness as a Millennium Problem, with an official problem description by Charles Fefferman ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/)).

### Connections
- [Fluid Dynamics](node:Fluid%20Dynamics): the parent subject; Navier–Stokes is its viscous momentum law.
- [Mathematical Navier–Stokes Theory](node:Mathematical%20Navier–Stokes%20Theory): the PDE theory of existence, uniqueness and regularity.
- [Euler Equations for Incompressible Fluids](node:Euler%20Equations%20for%20Incompressible%20Fluids): the inviscid case $\nu=0$.
- [Reynolds Number](node:Reynolds%20Number): the ratio of inertial to viscous forces that sorts flows into regimes.
- [Turbulence](node:Turbulence): the high-Reynolds-number regime of the equations.
- [Stokes Flow](node:Stokes%20Flow) and [Boundary Layers](node:Boundary%20Layers): the low-Re and near-wall limits.
- [Vorticity and Circulation](node:Vorticity%20and%20Circulation): the curl of the equations governs vortex dynamics.
- [Continuum Mechanics](node:Continuum%20Mechanics): supplies Cauchy's momentum equation and constitutive laws.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces), [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29) and [Energy Estimates for PDEs](node:Energy%20Estimates%20for%20PDEs): the functional setting of weak solutions.
- [Computational Fluid Dynamics](node:Computational%20Fluid%20Dynamics): numerical solution of the equations.
- [Constitutive Models of Non-Newtonian Fluids](node:Constitutive%20Models%20of%20Non-Newtonian%20Fluids): what replaces the Newtonian stress law.

### Common pitfalls
- Global regularity is open in three dimensions only; the two-dimensional problem was solved in the 1960s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness))
- Existence of weak solutions is not the Millennium problem: Leray's weak solutions exist globally, and Buckmaster–Vicol showed that weak solutions are not unique in the class of weak solutions with finite kinetic energy, but the Millennium problem asks for smooth solutions. ([Buckmaster and Vicol](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.10033); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness))
- Tao's blowup is for an averaged equation, not for Navier–Stokes itself. ([Tao](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.0290))
- The Stokes hypothesis of zero bulk viscosity is not generally valid outside monatomic gases. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations))

### Open problems
- **Millennium Prize problem.** The Clay formulation has four statements: (A) and (B) assert global smooth solutions with zero force on $\mathbb R^3$ and on $\mathbb T^3$, for smooth divergence-free initial data satisfying derivative bounds (periodic data on $\mathbb T^3$), with solutions of bounded energy $\int|\mathbf u(x,t)|^2dx<E$ for all $t\ge0$; (C) and (D) assert breakdown for some smooth data and smooth force on $\mathbb R^3$ or $\mathbb T^3$. Solving the problem requires settling only one of the four. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness); [Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/))
- **Type I blowup.** The existence and smoothness question is "a question of central importance in the theory of partial differential equations", and ruling out blowup even under Type I bounds is described as "a major open problem in the field"; the paper calls removing the smallness requirement from the CKN criterion "of great importance". ([arXiv:2210.01783](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.01783v1))

> [!warning] Contested
> On 8 September 2026 OpenAI claimed a solution of statement (C), breakdown with a smooth force on $\mathbb R^3$, supported by a Lean formalization; as of 18 September it had not been independently verified. A preprint in October argued that the Lean proof is not a semantically faithful version of the natural-language proof, and a preprint by Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol argued that the method does not extend to real-analytic forcing and therefore cannot settle (A) or (B) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness)). That preprint notes that OpenAI "has recently announced a proof of finite time singularity formation" and proves that solutions with a real-analytic force and two properties of the announced construction are regular at the putative singular point ([arXiv:2609.20803](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20803)). Follow-up work takes the announced blowup solution as its starting point ([arXiv:2609.10262](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10262)). Treat this as reported and unconfirmed; the Clay problem page announces no solution or award ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness): the Clay formulation and known results.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 2.25 Advanced Fluid Mechanics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-25-advanced-fluid-mechanics-fall-2013/): McKinley's graduate course on the Navier–Stokes equation, similarity, boundary layers and vorticity.
- **Primary:** [Tao, Finite time blowup for an averaged three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.0290): the averaged model and its barrier to energy methods.
- **Primary:** [Buckmaster and Vicol, Nonuniqueness of weak solutions to the Navier–Stokes equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.10033): nonuniqueness of finite-energy weak solutions.
- **Further reading:** [Robinson, Rodrigo and Sadowski, The Three-Dimensional Navier–Stokes Equations: Classical Theory (Cambridge University Press, 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139095143): graduate monograph on the classical regularity theory.
- **Further reading:** [Clay Mathematics Institute, Navier–Stokes Equation](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/): the problem page with Fefferman's official problem description.
references.Newtonian Gravity:
## Reference
### Overview
Newton's law of universal gravitation says that any two point masses attract along the line joining them with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation, $F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$. It was published in the *Principia*, first issued on 5 July 1687, and is often called the "first great unification" because it joined terrestrial gravity and planetary motion. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation))

In field form the gravitational field $\mathbf g=-\nabla\phi$ satisfies $\nabla\cdot\mathbf g=-4\pi G\rho$, equivalently Poisson's equation $\nabla^2\phi=4\pi G\rho$. This single equation with no time derivatives implies instantaneous "action at a distance", which is why Newtonian gravity is not relativistic. ([MIT 8.033 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/02415213222b845bbec6e734c64d1718_fieldeqs.pdf)) It is accurate when $\phi/c^2$ and $(v/c)^2$ are both $\ll1$ (about $10^{-8}$ for the Earth–Sun system), and fails, for example, by 43 arcseconds per century in Mercury's perihelion precession, which [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) explains. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation))

Two empirical inputs sit under the theory: the equality of inertial and gravitational mass, now tested to about $10^{-15}$, and the value of $G$, which is difficult to measure with high accuracy and whose published measurements disagree with one another. ([MICROSCOPE 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15487)) ([Wikipedia, Gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_constant))

### Formal definition
The force on point mass 2 due to point mass 1 is the vector law below, with $\hat{\mathbf r}_{12}$ the unit vector from 1 to 2. ([MIT 8.01 ch. 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-01sc-classical-mechanics-fall-2016/mit8_01scs22_chapter8.pdf))
$$
\mathbf F_{12}=-G\frac{m_1m_2}{r_{12}^2}\,\hat{\mathbf r}_{12},\qquad \mathbf F_{21}=-\mathbf F_{12}.
$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation)) The CODATA value is $G=6.67430(15)\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ (relative uncertainty $2.2\times10^{-5}$), unchanged in the 2022 adjustment. ([Wikipedia, Gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_constant))

The field is the force per unit mass; it is conservative, $\mathbf g=-\nabla V$, with $V=-Gm/r$ outside a point or uniform sphere. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation)) For a continuous density $\rho$ the field equations are as follows. ([MIT 8.033 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/02415213222b845bbec6e734c64d1718_fieldeqs.pdf))
$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf g=-4\pi G\rho,\qquad \nabla^2\phi=4\pi G\rho .
$$
The point-mass solution $\phi=-Gm/r$ is the Green's function of this equation. ([Wikipedia, Poisson's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation))

### Key results
- **Shell theorem.** A spherically symmetric body attracts external points as if its mass were at its centre; a spherical shell exerts no net force inside; inside a uniform ball of radius $R$, $|\mathbf g|=GMr/R^3$. ([Wikipedia, Shell theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_theorem)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation))
- **Multipole expansion of the exterior potential.** Outside the sources $\phi$ satisfies Laplace's equation and expands as $u=-\mu/r+\sum_{n\ge2}J_nP_{n0}(\sin\theta)/r^{n+1}+$ tesseral terms ($\mu=GM$). For Earth the oblateness coefficient $J_2$ dominates the corrections; the $J_3$ force is about 2 parts per thousand of the $J_2$ force at 6600 km. ([Wikipedia, Geopotential model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopotential_model))
- **Roche limit (tides).** A rigid spherical satellite of density $\rho_m$ orbiting a primary of radius $R_M$ and density $\rho_M$ is pulled apart by tidal forces inside $d=R_M(2\rho_M/\rho_m)^{1/3}$; Roche's approximate result for a fluid satellite in hydrostatic equilibrium is $d\approx2.44\,R_M(\rho_M/\rho_m)^{1/3}$. ([Wikipedia, Roche limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roche_limit))
- **Virial theorem.** For a stably bound system with bounded positions and velocities, time averages satisfy $2\langle T\rangle=-\sum_k\langle\mathbf F_k\cdot\mathbf r_k\rangle$; for inverse-square gravity this is $2\langle T\rangle=-\langle V\rangle$. A uniform sphere has potential energy $-3GM^2/(5R)$. Zwicky (1933) applied the theorem to the Coma cluster and found a virial mass about 450 times the observed mass. ([Wikipedia, Virial theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virial_theorem))
- **The $N$-body problem.** There is no general closed-form solution of the three-body problem, and for most initial conditions its motion is chaotic. Sundman (1912) gave a power series in $t^{1/3}$ converging for all real $t$ unless the angular momentum is zero, but it converges far too slowly to use; Poincaré showed (1889) that there are no further analytic integrals of the restricted problem. ([Wikipedia, Three-body problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-body_problem)) See [N-body Simulations](node:N-body%20Simulations).
- **Universality of free fall.** Eötvös's torsion-balance experiments (1906–1909, published 1922) showed inertial and gravitational mass equal to about 1 part in $10^8$; torsion balances reached about $2\times10^{-13}$ by 2008. ([Wikipedia, Eötvös experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E%C3%B6tv%C3%B6s_experiment)) The MICROSCOPE satellite's final result for titanium and platinum is $\eta(\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Pt})=(-1.5\pm2.3_{\rm stat}\pm1.5_{\rm syst})\times10^{-15}$, with no violation found. ([MICROSCOPE 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15487)) See [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle).

### Examples
- **Near-surface gravity.** Near Earth's surface the force is $F=mg$ with standard $g=9.80665\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the actual value runs from about $9.78$ at the equator to $9.83\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ at the poles, mainly because of Earth's rotation and flattening. ([MIT 8.01 ch. 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-01sc-classical-mechanics-fall-2016/mit8_01scs22_chapter8.pdf))
- **Hollow shell and solid ball.** Inside a hollow uniform shell $\mathbf g=0$; inside a uniform ball the field grows linearly from zero at the centre. ([Wikipedia, Shell theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_theorem))
- **Coulomb analogy.** Both Coulomb's law and the gravitational law are inverse-square central forces obeying Newton's third law; in field form gravity has $\nabla^2\phi=+4\pi G\rho$ where electrostatics has the opposite sign. ([MIT 8.01 ch. 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-01sc-classical-mechanics-fall-2016/mit8_01scs22_chapter8.pdf)) ([MIT 8.033 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/02415213222b845bbec6e734c64d1718_fieldeqs.pdf)) See [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics).

### History
Newton published the law in the *Principia* (1687); when Book 1 was presented to the Royal Society in 1686, Hooke claimed that Newton had obtained the inverse-square law from him. In the General Scholium (1713) Newton wrote that he had not found the cause of gravity and made no hypotheses about it. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation)) Newton did not compute the constant; Cavendish's 1798 torsion-balance experiment (with Michell's apparatus) made the first laboratory measurement of the attraction between bodies, implying $G\approx6.74(4)\times10^{-11}$, and C. V. Boys introduced the notation $G$ in the 1890s. ([Wikipedia, Gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_constant))

Poisson found that Laplace's equation holds only outside matter; his equation was first published in the *Bulletin de la Société philomatique* in 1813, and Gauss gave a rigorous proof for variable density in 1839. ([Wikipedia, Siméon Denis Poisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sim%C3%A9on_Denis_Poisson))

### Connections
- [Newtonian Mechanics](node:Newtonian%20Mechanics): the force law enters $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$.
- [Gauss's Law for Gravity](node:Gauss's%20Law%20for%20Gravity) and [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): the field form.
- [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus) and [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions): divergence theorem and the kernel $-G/r$.
- [Shell Theorem](node:Shell%20Theorem) and [Spherical Harmonics](node:Spherical%20Harmonics): spherical bodies and multipole expansions.
- [Central Force Motion and the Kepler Problem](node:Central%20Force%20Motion%20and%20the%20Kepler%20Problem): two-body orbits.
- [N-body Simulations](node:N-body%20Simulations): numerical treatment of many-body gravity.
- [Gravitational Constant](node:Gravitational%20Constant): the measured coupling and its discrepancies.
- [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle), [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity), [Newtonian Limit of General Relativity](node:Newtonian%20Limit%20of%20General%20Relativity), [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): the relativistic successor.
- [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics) and [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations): the inverse-square analogue, which unlike gravity has time-dependent field equations.
- [Tests of the Inverse-Square Law](node:Tests%20of%20the%20Inverse-Square%20Law), [Galaxy Rotation Curves](node:Galaxy%20Rotation%20Curves), [Modified Newtonian Dynamics](node:Modified%20Newtonian%20Dynamics), [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter): empirical limits of the theory.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Newtonian gravitational fields and orbits](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Newtonian%20gravitational%20fields%20and%20orbits)

### Common pitfalls
- **Using $GMm/r^2$ inside a body.** Only mass inside radius $r$ contributes; for uniform density $|\mathbf g|\propto r$. ([Wikipedia, Shell theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_theorem))
- **Treating Poisson's equation as relativistic.** Copying Maxwell's equations with $\mathbf E\to\mathbf g$ and $\rho\to\rho_m$ fails because mass density and charge density transform differently under [Lorentz Transformations](node:Lorentz%20Transformations): total charge is a Lorentz scalar, while mass, being equivalent to energy, is not. ([MIT 8.033 notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/02415213222b845bbec6e734c64d1718_fieldeqs.pdf))
- **Quoting $G$ to many digits.** The CODATA relative uncertainty is $2.2\times10^{-5}$, but published values have varied rather broadly at the 0.1% level and some results are mutually exclusive. ([Wikipedia, Gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_constant))
- **Dating Poisson's equation to 1823.** Some accounts give 1823, citing Poisson's memoir on magnetism, ([Wikipedia, Poisson's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation)) but the equation was first published in 1813. ([Wikipedia, Siméon Denis Poisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sim%C3%A9on_Denis_Poisson))

### Open problems
- **Mutually inconsistent measurements of $G$.** Some measurements from the 1980s to 2000s were mutually exclusive; Rosi et al. (2014, atom interferometry) lie about 325 ppm below the 2014 CODATA value with non-overlapping uncertainties, and a 2018 pair of torsion-balance values differing by 2.7 standard deviations suggests unaccounted error sources. ([Wikipedia, Gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_constant))
- **Dark matter or modified gravity.** Stellar orbits in spiral galaxies do not follow Newtonian gravity with the visible mass; Wikipedia lists as an unsolved problem in physics whether this requires a dark-matter particle or a modification of the laws of gravity such as MOND, and calls distinguishing them a subject of current research. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation)) ([Wikipedia, MOND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))

> [!warning] Contested
> MOND fits galaxy-scale data but has not gained widespread acceptance, leaving a residual discrepancy in clusters and struggling with the [Cosmic Microwave Background](node:Cosmic%20Microwave%20Background), while ΛCDM keeps Newtonian gravity at these scales and adds dark matter. ([Wikipedia, MOND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Newton's law of universal gravitation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation): law, field form, validity, history; with [Gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_constant).
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.01SC, Chapter 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-01sc-classical-mechanics-fall-2016/mit8_01scs22_chapter8.pdf): vector form, near-surface gravity, equivalence of masses; [MIT 8.033, Einstein's Field Equations](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/02415213222b845bbec6e734c64d1718_fieldeqs.pdf): Poisson's equation and why it is not relativistic.
- **Primary:** [Touboul et al., MICROSCOPE mission: final results of the test of the Equivalence Principle (PRL 129, 121102, 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15487): the best test of the universality of free fall.
- **Further reading:** [Binney & Tremaine, Galactic Dynamics (2nd ed., Princeton 2008)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691130279/galactic-dynamics); [Poisson & Will, Gravity: Newtonian, Post-Newtonian, Relativistic (CUP 2014)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/cbo9781139507486).
references.Newtonian Limit of General Relativity:
## Reference
### Overview
The Newtonian limit is the regime of [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) in which gravity is weak, fields change slowly (or not at all), and bodies move slowly compared with light. In that regime the geodesic equation becomes $\ddot{\mathbf x}=-\nabla\Phi$ and the $00$ component of the Einstein equation becomes Poisson's equation $\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho$. Matching the two fixes the Einstein coupling constant at $8\pi G/c^4$. ([Wikipedia: Newtonian limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_limit); [Carroll, ch. 4](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March01/Carroll3/Carroll4.html); [Wikipedia: Einstein field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))

The limit is the lowest rung of a systematic expansion. Keeping weak fields but dropping the static and slow-motion assumptions gives linearized gravity and gravitational waves. Keeping slow motion but going one order further in the small parameter gives the post-Newtonian approximation, whose parametrized form (PPN) is the standard framework for solar-system tests. ([Wikipedia: Linearized gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearized_gravity); [Will, 2014 Living Reviews update](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

Whether actual solutions of Einstein's equations converge to Newtonian ones is a separate, rigorous question. Cartan and Friedrichs showed geometrically that Newtonian gravity is a limit of general relativity, and Oliynyk proved that families of Einstein–Euler solutions converge to Newtonian fluids. ([Wikipedia: Newton–Cartan theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%E2%80%93Cartan_theory); [Oliynyk, CMP 276 (2007)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.3744))

### Formal definition
Use signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and $c=1$. Carroll's three hypotheses are: (i) slow particles, $dx^i/d\tau\ll dt/d\tau$; (ii) a weak field, $g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+h_{\mu\nu}$ with $|h_{\mu\nu}|\ll1$; (iii) a static field, $\partial_0 g_{\mu\nu}=0$. Under (i) the geodesic equation reduces to $d^2x^\mu/d\tau^2+\Gamma^\mu_{00}(dt/d\tau)^2=0$. Under (ii)–(iii), $\Gamma^\mu_{00}=-\tfrac12\eta^{\mu\lambda}\partial_\lambda h_{00}$ to first order, so $d^2x^i/dt^2=\tfrac12\partial_i h_{00}$. Newton's law follows with $h_{00}=-2\Phi$, i.e. $g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi)$. ([Carroll, ch. 4](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March01/Carroll3/Carroll4.html); [Carroll, arXiv notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eqs. 4.10–4.21)

For the field equation, write Einstein's equation in trace-reversed form $R_{\mu\nu}=K\bigl(T_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12 Tg_{\mu\nu}\bigr)$. For static dust, $T_{00}\approx\rho c^4$ in the convention $g_{00}\approx-c^2$, and dropping squares of $\Gamma$ and time derivatives gives $R_{00}\approx\Gamma^i_{00,i}$. Poisson's equation is recovered if and only if $\tfrac12K\rho c^4=4\pi G\rho$, so $K=8\pi G/c^4$. In Carroll's $c=1$ form, $R_{00}=\tfrac12\kappa T_{00}$ and $R_{00}\approx-\tfrac12\nabla^2h_{00}$ give $\nabla^2h_{00}=-\kappa T_{00}$, hence $\kappa=8\pi G$. ([Wikipedia: Einstein field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations); [Carroll, arXiv notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eqs. 4.50–4.52)

**Post-Newtonian order counting.** In Will's convention ($G=c=1$), the Newtonian potential is $U(\mathbf x,t)=\int\rho(\mathbf x',t)\,|\mathbf x-\mathbf x'|^{-1}d^3x'$ (so $U=-\Phi$), and the smallness rules are $U\sim v^2\sim p/\rho\sim\epsilon$, $|\partial_t|/|\partial_x|\sim\epsilon^{1/2}$. A consistent post-Newtonian limit needs $g_{00}$ through $O(\epsilon^2)$, $g_{0i}$ through $O(\epsilon^{3/2})$, and $g_{ij}$ through $O(\epsilon)$. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

### Key results
- **Coupling constant.** The Einstein constant is fixed by the Newtonian limit: $K=8\pi G/c^4$, so $G_{\mu\nu}=8\pi G\,T_{\mu\nu}$ at $c=1$. ([Wikipedia: Einstein field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations); [Carroll, ch. 4](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March01/Carroll3/Carroll4.html))
- **Particle action.** With $g_{00}=-1-2\phi/c^2$ and flat spatial components, expanding $S=-mc\int\!\sqrt{-g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\,dt$ and dropping $O(1/c^2)$ terms leaves the rest-energy constant plus the Newtonian action $\int(\tfrac12m\dot{\mathbf x}^2-m\phi)\,dt$. ([Wikipedia: Newtonian limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_limit))
- **Spatial metric at the same order.** The PPN metric has $g_{00}=-1+2U-2\beta U^2+\dots$ and $g_{ij}=(1+2\gamma U)\delta_{ij}+O(\epsilon^2)$, with $\gamma=\beta=1$ in GR. In GR the weak static field is therefore $g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi)$, $g_{ij}=(1-2\Phi)\delta_{ij}$, which Carroll derives from the linearized equations for a star or planet. The spatial part does not affect slow particles at Newtonian order, but it does affect light. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377); [Wikipedia: PPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameterized_post-Newtonian_formalism); [Carroll, arXiv notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eq. 6.29)
- **Light bending and the factor 2.** A ray passing the Sun at distance $d$ is deflected by $\delta\theta=\tfrac12(1+\gamma)\,\tfrac{4M_\odot}{d}\,\tfrac{1+\cos\Phi}{2}$, which is $\approx\tfrac12(1+\gamma)\times1.7505''$ for a grazing ray. The corpuscular (Soldner) and equivalence-principle (Einstein 1911) calculations give only the "1/2" part. Space curvature, measured by $\gamma$, supplies the remaining $\gamma/2$. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))
- **Linearized field equations.** For a general weak field, the harmonic gauge $\partial_\mu h^\mu{}_\nu=\tfrac12\partial_\nu h$ and the trace-reversed perturbation $\bar h_{\mu\nu}=h_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12h\eta_{\mu\nu}$ give $\square\bar h_{\mu\nu}=-2\kappa T_{\mu\nu}$. This is a sourced [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation) whose solutions include gravitational radiation. ([Wikipedia: Linearized gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearized_gravity))
- **PPN parameters.** Ten parameters $(\gamma,\beta,\xi,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\zeta_1,\dots,\zeta_4)$ exhaust the post-Newtonian possibilities for metric theories, under the assumption that only Poisson-like potentials occur. Cassini tracking gives $\gamma-1=(2.1\pm2.3)\times10^{-5}$. Mercury's perihelion shift per orbit is $6\pi m/p$ times $\tfrac13(2+2\gamma-\beta)$ plus preferred-frame and $J_2$ terms. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377); [Wikipedia: PPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameterized_post-Newtonian_formalism))
- **Rigorous Newtonian limit for fluids.** Oliynyk proved that a class of non-stationary Einstein–Euler solutions has a Newtonian limit as $\epsilon=v_T/c\to0$, where $v_T$ is a characteristic fluid velocity. The method is a symmetric hyperbolic formulation with $\epsilon$-independent weighted Sobolev energy estimates. The result is local in time (a "near zone" result). ([Oliynyk](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.3744); [ar5iv text](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0810.3744))
- **Cosmological Newtonian limit.** With $\Lambda>0$ and $p=\epsilon^2K\rho$, $0<K\le1/3$, Liu and Oliynyk constructed future-complete Einstein–Euler solutions on $(0,1]\times\mathbb R^3$. As $\epsilon\to0$ they converge to solutions of the cosmological Poisson–Euler equations, describing nonlinear perturbations of FLRW. ([Liu & Oliynyk, CMP 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10896))

### Examples
- **Point mass.** $\Phi=-GM/r$ gives $g_{00}=-(1-2GM/r)$, the weak-field part of the [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution); matching the Schwarzschild metric at large $r$ to $g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi)$, $g_{rr}=1-2\Phi$ fixes its parameter as $2GM$. ([Carroll, arXiv notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eqs. 7.27–7.29)
- **Gravitational redshift.** The same $g_{00}$ gives $\Delta\lambda/\lambda=\Delta\Phi$ at $c=1$. Pound and Rebka (1960) measured it with the Mössbauer effect on gamma rays sent to the top of Jefferson Labs at Harvard. ([Carroll, ch. 4](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March01/Carroll3/Carroll4.html); [Carroll, arXiv notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eq. 4.7)
- **Solar light deflection.** Newtonian-order $g_{00}$ alone predicts $0.875''$ at the solar limb. GR's $\gamma=1$ doubles it to $1.75''$, and VLBI gives $(1+\gamma)/2=0.99992\pm0.00023$. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

### History
The field equations reduce to Newton's law in the weak-field, low-velocity limit, and the coupling constant is fixed by that correspondence. Einstein's 1916 paper "Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie" (Ann. Phys. 354, 769–822) is the standard primary statement. ([Wikipedia: Einstein field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations); [Crossref: Einstein 1916](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/andp.19163540702)) Cartan (1923) and Friedrichs (1927) gave the geometric Newton–Cartan formulation and used it to show rigorously that Newtonian gravity is a limit of GR; Ehlers extended the correspondence to specific exact solutions. ([Wikipedia: Newton–Cartan theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%E2%80%93Cartan_theory)) Eddington (1922) gave the earliest parametrization, for the vacuum field outside an isolated spherical body; Nordtvedt (1968, 1969) extended it to seven parameters, and the modern ten-parameter version comes from Ni (1972), Will and Nordtvedt (1972), Misner, Thorne and Wheeler (1973) and Will (1981, 1993). ([Wikipedia: PPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameterized_post-Newtonian_formalism)) Ehlers et al. (1976) pointed out that there was no evidence the post-Newtonian approximation was convergent or even asymptotic; by the late 1990s most such criticisms, especially about divergences, had been answered. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

### Connections
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): the $00$ component becomes Poisson's equation.
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): the theory recovered.
- [Linearized Gravity](node:Linearized%20Gravity): the weak-field expansion without staticity or slow motion.
- [Parametrized Post-Newtonian Formalism](node:Parametrized%20Post-Newtonian%20Formalism): the next order, with $\gamma$ and $\beta$.
- [Tests of General Relativity](node:Tests%20of%20General%20Relativity): light deflection, Shapiro delay and perihelion tests probe the post-Newtonian metric.
- [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle): gives the "1/2" of light deflection and the redshift.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): reduce to $\ddot{\mathbf x}=-\nabla\Phi$.
- [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves): weak-field but not Newtonian.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): the Newtonian field equation.
- [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing): requires the spatial metric, not only $g_{00}$.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Weak fields boundaries and classical limits](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Weak%20fields%20boundaries%20and%20classical%20limits)

### Common pitfalls
- **Weak field is not the Newtonian limit.** The Newtonian limit needs weak fields together with slow motion and a static (or slowly varying) field. Keeping only $|h|\ll1$ while allowing time dependence and fast particles gives linearized gravity, which includes gravitational radiation and light deflection. ([Carroll, ch. 4](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March01/Carroll3/Carroll4.html); [Wikipedia: Linearized gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearized_gravity))
- **$g_{00}$ is not the whole metric.** Using $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$ (as in the Newtonian particle action) is fine for slow bodies but gives half the light deflection. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377); [Wikipedia: Newtonian limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_limit))
- **Gauge.** $h_{\mu\nu}\to h_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu\xi_\nu+\partial_\nu\xi_\mu$ is a gauge freedom; harmonic gauge is a choice. ([Wikipedia: Linearized gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearized_gravity))
- **Factors of $c$.** $T_{00}\approx\rho c^4$ goes with $g_{00}\approx-c^2$ and $K=8\pi G/c^4$; with $c=1$, $T_{00}=\rho$ and $\kappa=8\pi G$. ([Wikipedia: Einstein field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations); [Carroll, ch. 4](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March01/Carroll3/Carroll4.html))
- **Formal versus rigorous.** Oliynyk notes that most results rest on formal expansions in $\epsilon$, which leave the question of convergence completely unanswered; his own proof instead uses $\epsilon$-independent energy estimates. ([ar5iv: Oliynyk](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0810.3744))

### Open problems
None found. The textbook reduction to Poisson's equation is settled. Searches tried: "Newtonian limit general relativity open problem", "Oliynyk Newtonian limit perfect fluids", and reviews of post-Newtonian theory. The rigorous results above (Oliynyk 2007; Liu–Oliynyk 2018) and the high-order post-Newtonian programme for compact binaries are active research. None of the fetched sources names a specific problem in the limit itself as open. ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377); [Liu & Oliynyk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10896))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Newtonian limit (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_limit): hypotheses and the particle-action reduction.
- **Learn:** [Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity, ch. 4](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March01/Carroll3/Carroll4.html): derivation of $h_{00}=-2\Phi$ and $\kappa=8\pi G$; full notes at [arXiv:gr-qc/9712019](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/9712019).
- **Primary:** [Will, "The Confrontation between General Relativity and Experiment" (2014 update of the Living Review)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7377): PPN metric, light deflection, and solar-system bounds.
- **Primary:** [Oliynyk, "The Newtonian limit for perfect fluids", CMP 276 (2007)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.3744): rigorous convergence of Einstein–Euler solutions.
- **Primary:** [Einstein, "Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie", Ann. Phys. 354 (1916)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/andp.19163540702): the original field theory.
- **Further reading:** [Wald, General Relativity (Chicago, 1984)](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/G/bo5952261.html): standard graduate text.
references.Newtonian Mechanics:
## Reference
### Overview
Newtonian mechanics is the theory of the motion of bodies under forces built on three laws first stated by Isaac Newton in the *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, originally published in 1687. In modern paraphrase: a body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a force acts on it; the net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration (more generally, the rate of change of its momentum); and two bodies exert forces on each other of equal magnitude and opposite direction. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))

Once a force law is specified as a function of positions, velocities and time, the second law is a second-order system of [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) for the trajectory. Its reformulations in [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics) and [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics) have the same content for standard systems; in the Lagrangian picture the Euler–Lagrange equation is a restatement of the second law, and momentum conservation follows from [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) rather than being assumed through the third law. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))

The laws hold in inertial frames, and the set of inertial frames is permuted by the Galilean group. The theory is the low-velocity approximation of [Special Relativity](node:Special%20Relativity), in which Galilean transformations are replaced by [Lorentz Transformations](node:Lorentz%20Transformations). ([Wikipedia: Galilean invariance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_invariance); [Wikipedia: Galilean transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_transformation))

### Formal definition
For a point particle of mass $m$ with momentum $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v$ in an [inertial frame](node:Inertial%20Frame%20of%20Reference), the laws read as follows. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))

1. **First law.** If the net force vanishes, $\mathbf v$ is constant. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
2. **Second law.** $\mathbf F_{\text{net}}=d\mathbf p/dt$, which for constant $m$ is $\mathbf F_{\text{net}}=m\mathbf a=m\,\ddot{\mathbf r}$. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
3. **Third law.** If body 1 exerts $\mathbf F_{12}$ on body 2, then body 2 exerts $\mathbf F_{21}=-\mathbf F_{12}$ on body 1. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))

Forces add as vectors, and a body with zero net force does not accelerate and is in mechanical equilibrium. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))

**Galilean transformations.** For frames $S,S'$ in standard configuration with relative velocity $v$ along $x$: $x'=x-vt$, $y'=y$, $z'=z$, $t'=t$. Together with spatial rotations and translations in space and time these generate the inhomogeneous Galilean group, of dimension 10, with generators $H$ (time translation), $P_i$ (space translations), $C_i$ (boosts) and $L_{ij}$ (rotations). It arises from the [Poincaré group](node:Poincaré%20Group) by contraction in the limit $c\to\infty$. ([Wikipedia: Galilean transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_transformation))

**Galilean invariance.** Under $\mathbf r'=\mathbf r-\mathbf vt$ with constant $\mathbf v$, velocities shift by $\mathbf v$ and accelerations are unchanged, $\mathbf a'=\mathbf a$; with mass assumed invariant, $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$ keeps its form, so the laws hold in all frames related by a Galilean transformation. ([Wikipedia: Galilean invariance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_invariance))

### Key results
- **Rotating frames and fictitious forces.** Let frame $B$ rotate with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\Omega(t)$ relative to an inertial frame $A$ about a common origin. Then $\mathbf a_A=\mathbf a_B+2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v_B+\dot{\boldsymbol\Omega}\times\mathbf x_B+\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf x_B)$, so an observer in $B$ must add $\mathbf F_{\text{fict}}=-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v_B-m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf x_B)-m\dot{\boldsymbol\Omega}\times\mathbf x_B$: the Coriolis, centrifugal and Euler forces. All are proportional to $m$. ([Wikipedia: Fictitious force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fictitious_force))
- **Existence and uniqueness of motion.** If $f(t,y)$ is continuous in $t$ and Lipschitz in $y$ on a closed rectangle around $(t_0,y_0)$, then $y'=f(t,y)$, $y(t_0)=y_0$ has a unique solution on some $[t_0-\varepsilon,t_0+\varepsilon]$ (Picard–Lindelöf). Writing $\mathbf F=m\ddot{\mathbf r}$ as a first-order system in $(\mathbf r,\dot{\mathbf r})$, Lipschitz forces give locally unique trajectories. Continuity alone gives existence but not uniqueness (Peano); $y'=y^{1/3}$, $y(0)=0$ has several solutions. ([Wikipedia: Picard–Lindelöf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem))
- **Failure of determinism without Lipschitz forces (Norton's dome).** On a frictionless dome of height $h=(2b^2/3g)\,r^{3/2}$ ($r$ the geodesic distance from the apex), the equation of motion is $\ddot r=b^2\sqrt r$. With $r(0)=\dot r(0)=0$, both $r\equiv0$ and $r(t)=\tfrac1{144}\,[b(t-T)]^4$ for $t>T$ (any $T\ge0$) are solutions, because the force is not Lipschitz in $r$ at the apex. ([Wikipedia: Norton's dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norton%27s_dome))
- **Rigid-body dynamics (Euler's equations).** In a body-fixed frame at the centre of mass where the inertia tensor $I$ is constant, $I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}+\boldsymbol\omega\times(I\boldsymbol\omega)=\mathbf M$. Along principal axes, $I_1\dot\omega_1+(I_3-I_2)\omega_2\omega_3=M_1$ and cyclically; $\mathbf M=0$ gives the torque-free Euler top. ([Wikipedia: Euler's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_equations_%28rigid_body_dynamics%29))
- **Centre of mass and conservation laws.** For masses $m_i$ at $\mathbf r_i$ with total mass $M$, $\mathbf R=\sum m_i\mathbf r_i/M$ moves like a particle of mass $M$ under the net external force, since internal forces cancel in third-law pairs. Angular momentum $\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times\mathbf p$ obeys $d\mathbf L/dt=\boldsymbol\tau$. If the force is the gradient of a scalar potential, $\mathbf F=-\nabla U$, and there is no friction, energy is traded between kinetic and potential forms while the total stays constant. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
- **Noncollision singularities (Painlevé conjecture, now proved).** Painlevé showed that every finite-time singularity of the Newtonian three-body problem is a collision. For $n\ge4$, solutions exist in which bodies reach infinity in finite time without collision: Xia proved this for $n\ge5$ (*Annals of Mathematics* 135, 1992), and Xue proved it for the planar four-body problem (arXiv 2014, *Acta Mathematica* 2020), settling the last case. ([Wikipedia: Painlevé conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_conjecture); [Crossref: Xia 1992](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/2946572); [arXiv: Xue](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0048))

### Examples
- **Free fall.** With $F=GMm/r^2$, the mass $m$ cancels and every body falls with $g=GM/r^2$, independent of its mass. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
- **Circular motion and the cannonball.** Uniform circular motion of speed $v$ and radius $r$ requires acceleration $v^2/r$ toward the centre. Newton's cannonball interpolates between projectile motion and a circular orbit. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
- **Harmonic oscillator.** $F=-kx$ gives $m\ddot x=-kx$, oscillating at $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$. See [Oscillations and Normal Modes](node:Oscillations%20and%20Normal%20Modes). ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
- **Rockets.** For a rocket of mass $M(t)$ ejecting matter at velocity $\mathbf u$ relative to it, $\mathbf F=M\,d\mathbf v/dt-\mathbf u\,dM/dt$, with $\mathbf F$ the net external force. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
- **Kepler and three bodies.** An inverse-square central force gives conic orbits (the Kepler problem); the general three-body problem has no exact closed-form solution, and Newtonian systems can be chaotic. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))

### History
Galileo described the relativity of uniform motion in 1632 with a smoothly moving ship, below whose deck an observer could not tell whether it moved. ([Wikipedia: Galilean invariance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_invariance)) Newton stated the three laws in the *Principia* (1687); later developments, including Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, reorganized the theory around energy, action and symmetry. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion)) Painlevé posed the noncollision-singularity question in his 1895 Stockholm lectures; it was resolved for $n\ge5$ by Xia and for $n=4$ by Xue. ([Wikipedia: Painlevé conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_conjecture)) Norton introduced his dome in 2003 as a limiting case of 1997 examples of Bhat and Bernstein. ([Wikipedia: Norton's dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norton%27s_dome))

### Connections
- [Differential Calculus](node:Differential%20Calculus): velocity and acceleration are derivatives; the second law is a second-order ODE.
- [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces): forces, momenta and displacements are vectors and superpose linearly.
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations): Picard–Lindelöf governs when motion is determined by initial data.
- [Inertial Frame of Reference](node:Inertial%20Frame%20of%20Reference): the frames in which the laws hold; the Galilean group acts on them.
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity) and [Central Force Motion and the Kepler Problem](node:Central%20Force%20Motion%20and%20the%20Kepler%20Problem): the inverse-square force and its solved two-body problem.
- [Rigid Body Dynamics](node:Rigid%20Body%20Dynamics): Euler's equations extend the laws to extended rigid bodies.
- [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws) and [Work-Energy Theorem](node:Work-Energy%20Theorem): momentum, angular momentum and energy conservation.
- [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics), [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics), [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem): equivalent reformulations, with conservation laws from symmetries.
- [Special Relativity](node:Special%20Relativity): Newtonian mechanics is the $v\ll c$ limit. Mass stays the invariant $m$; what changes is the momentum, $\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v$ (see [Four-Vectors and Relativistic Momentum](node:Four-Vectors%20and%20Relativistic%20Momentum)).
- [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory), [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems), [N-body Simulations](node:N-body%20Simulations): sensitive dependence in $N$-body systems.
- [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations) and [Continuum Mechanics](node:Continuum%20Mechanics): Newton's second law applied to a continuum.
- Maps: [Physics Subsection - Motion and reference frames](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Motion%20and%20reference%20frames), [MSC 70 - Mechanics of particles and systems](node:MSC%2070%20-%20Mechanics%20of%20particles%20and%20systems).

### Common pitfalls
- The third-law partner of a book's weight is not the table's support force on the book; it is the book's gravitational pull on the Earth. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
- $\mathbf F=d(m\mathbf v)/dt$ applied naively to a body that gains or loses mass is wrong; the rocket equation above tracks the momentum of the ejected matter. ([Wikipedia: Newton's laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion))
- Fictitious forces appear only when a non-inertial frame is used; they arise from the frame's acceleration, not from an interaction. ([Wikipedia: Fictitious force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fictitious_force))
- "Newtonian mechanics is deterministic" holds only under regularity assumptions such as Lipschitz forces; Norton's dome violates them, and critics disagree about which assumption excludes it as unphysical. ([Wikipedia: Norton's dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norton%27s_dome))
- Noncollision singularities in the point-mass $n$-body problem are a theorem for $n\ge4$, not an open question; they are impossible for $n=3$. ([Wikipedia: Painlevé conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painlev%C3%A9_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Finiteness of central configurations (Smale's 6th problem).** Is the number of relative equilibria (central configurations) of the Newtonian $n$-body problem finite for every choice of positive masses? Smale's list records it as unresolved. ([Wikipedia: Smale's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smale%27s_problems)) Albouy and Kaloshin proved that planar five-body central configurations come in finitely many isometry classes except perhaps for masses on a codimension-2 subvariety of mass space. ([Annals 2012](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/176-1/p10))
- **Navier–Stokes regularity.** The Clay Millennium problem concerns only the three-dimensional incompressible [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations) (viscous); the inviscid Euler equations are a separate question. Statements (A)/(B) ask for global smooth solutions with zero external force on $\mathbb R^3$ or the torus; (C)/(D) ask for breakdown with smooth initial data and a smooth force. The Clay Institute's page states that no proof has answered the basic questions of whether solutions exist and are unique. ([Wikipedia: NS existence and smoothness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness); [Clay Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/))

> [!warning] Contested
> On 8 September 2026 OpenAI announced a claimed construction of a smooth external force producing a finite-time singularity (statement (C)), released with a Lean formalization. This is a reported claim, not an accepted solution. ([Wikipedia: NS existence and smoothness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness)) Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen argue that the formalized Lean proof does not correspond to the natural-language proof. ([arXiv:2610.08144](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08144)) Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol prove that solutions with the properties assumed from the OpenAI manuscript are regular at the putative singular point when the force is real analytic, so the force in such constructions cannot vanish identically near that point, as (A)/(B) would require. ([arXiv:2609.20803](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20803))

### Resources
