- **Reference:** [Newton's laws of motion (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_laws_of_motion): the laws, conservation laws, rigid bodies, chaos, and the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian reformulations.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 8.01SC, Week 2: Newton's Laws](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-01sc-classical-mechanics-fall-2016/pages/week-2-newtons-laws/): the three laws, inertial and non-inertial frames, gravity, contact forces and springs; [MIT OCW 8.09 Classical Mechanics III](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/): constraints, rigid-body dynamics, central forces, Hamilton–Jacobi theory, chaos.
- **Primary:** [Xia, The Existence of Noncollision Singularities in Newtonian Systems, *Ann. Math.* 135 (1992)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/2946572): the original proof for five or more bodies; [Xue, Noncollision Singularities in a Planar Four-body Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0048): the four-body case.
- **Further reading:** [Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics* (Springer GTM, 1989)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-2063-1): the standard mathematical treatment from Newtonian mechanics through [symplectic geometry](node:Symplectic%20Geometry).
references.Noether's Theorem:
## Reference
### Overview
Noether's theorem says that if a physical system described by an action has a continuous symmetry, there are corresponding quantities whose values are conserved in time; in field theory, every continuous symmetry generated by local actions gives a conserved current. The symmetry is a one-parameter Lie group of transformations under which the form of the law is unchanged, and the theorem holds on shell: it uses the equations of motion. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))

It is the source of the standard dictionary of conservation laws: time-translation symmetry gives energy, spatial translation gives momentum, rotation gives angular momentum, and a global phase symmetry of a complex field gives a conserved charge. The same argument works for a particle on a line, on manifolds, and in field theory. ([Baez](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/noether.html), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))

Emmy Noether's 1918 paper "Invariante Variationsprobleme" treats variational problems that admit a continuous Lie group, combining the formal calculus of variations with Lie's group theory; it contains two theorems. The first concerns symmetry groups with finitely many parameters and produces conservation laws; the second concerns symmetries depending on arbitrary functions, as in gauge theory and general relativity, and produces identities among the field equations. ([Noether, transl. Tavel](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066), [Wikipedia: second theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_second_theorem))

### Formal definition
**Mechanics.** For an action $I=\int L(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q},t)\,dt$ the Euler–Lagrange equations are $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf q}}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf q}$. For a one-parameter family $q(s)$ with $\frac{d}{ds}L(q(s),\dot q(s))=0$, the quantity
$$C=p\cdot\frac{dq(s)}{ds},\qquad p=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q},$$
is conserved, $\dot C=0$; time-dependent symmetries need a more general version. ([Baez](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/noether.html), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))

**Fields.** For $\mathcal S=\int\mathcal L(\varphi,\partial_\mu\varphi,x^\mu)\,d^4x$ and an infinitesimal transformation $\varphi\mapsto\varphi+\varepsilon\Psi$ under which $\mathcal L\mapsto\mathcal L+\varepsilon\,\partial_\mu\Lambda^\mu$ (a symmetry up to a divergence), the Noether current
$$j^\nu=\Lambda^\nu-\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\nu\varphi)}\cdot\Psi$$
satisfies $\partial_\nu j^\nu=0$ on solutions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))

**Jet-bundle form.** On the variational bicomplex $\Omega^{\bullet,\bullet}(\mathrm{Jet}(E))$ with $d=d_H+d_V$, a local Lagrangian satisfies $d_V\mathbf L=\mathbf E-d_H\Theta$, with $\mathbf E$ the Euler–Lagrange (source) form. An infinitesimal variational symmetry is a vertical vector field $v$ with $\mathcal L_v\mathbf L=d_H\sigma_v$; a conserved current is a horizontal $(n-1)$-form $j$ with $(d_Hj)|_{\mathcal E}=0$ on the shell $\mathcal E$. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Noether%27s+theorem))

### Key results
- **Noether's first theorem (jet-bundle form).** If $v$ is an infinitesimal variational symmetry of a local Lagrangian $\mathbf L$, then $j_v=\sigma_v-\iota_v\Theta$ is a conserved current, because $d_H(\sigma_v-\iota_v\Theta)=\iota_v\mathbf E$, which vanishes on shell. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Noether%27s+theorem))
- **Symplectic (Souriau) version.** If a Lie group $G$ acts on a symplectic manifold $(X,\omega)$ by a Hamiltonian action with moment map $\Phi\in C^\infty(X,\mathfrak g^*)$ and $\{\Phi(\xi),H\}=0$ for all $\xi\in\mathfrak g$, then $\frac{d}{dt}\Phi^\xi=\{H,\Phi^\xi\}=0$; in canonical coordinates $\Phi^\xi=p_i(v_\xi)^i$, the usual Noether charge. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Noether%27s+theorem))
- **Converse (Martínez Alonso–Olver).** For a nondegenerate variational problem, with generalized symmetries (depending on derivatives) allowed, there is a one-to-one correspondence between equivalence classes of nontrivial conservation laws of the Euler–Lagrange equations and equivalence classes of variational symmetries of the action; Olver states it as Theorem 5.42 of his 1986 book. Nondegeneracy excludes the local symmetries of the second theorem. ([Brown](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2010.10909))
- **Noether's second theorem.** If $L$ admits gauge symmetries $\delta_\lambda u^\sigma=\sum_{|I|\le s}R^{a\sigma,I}\lambda_a^{I}$ parametrized linearly by $q$ arbitrary functions $\lambda^a(x)$ and their derivatives, then there are $q$ linear differential relations $\mathcal D_a[E]=\sum F^{a\sigma,I}D_IE_\sigma\equiv0$ among the Euler–Lagrange expressions $E_\sigma$, which are therefore not independent. Conversely, such relations define quasi-symmetries for every $\lambda^a$. ([Wikipedia: second theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_second_theorem))
- **Commutators.** If $Q_1,Q_2$ are symmetry derivations, so is $[Q_1,Q_2]$, so the construction extends to Lie algebras of symmetries. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))

### Examples
- **Energy.** For $L=\frac m2\sum\dot x_i^2-V(x)$ with no explicit time dependence, $H=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{\mathbf q}}\cdot\dot{\mathbf q}-L=\frac m2\sum\dot x_i^2+V(x)$ is conserved. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Momentum and angular momentum.** An ignorable coordinate $q_k$ gives conserved $p_k=\partial L/\partial\dot q_k$; rotation about $\mathbf n$ gives conserved $\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf r\times\mathbf p)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Canonical stress–energy tensor.** Translation invariance of a field theory gives $T_\mu{}^\nu=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\varphi_{,\nu}}\varphi_{,\mu}-\delta_\mu^\nu\mathcal L$ with $\partial_\nu T_\mu{}^\nu=0$; this may differ from the symmetric tensor used in general relativity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Charge.** For the Klein–Gordon field under $\psi\mapsto e^{i\theta}\psi$, the current $j^\nu=i(\partial_\mu\psi\,\psi^*-\partial_\mu\psi^*\,\psi)\eta^{\nu\mu}$ is conserved. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Dilatations.** For $\mathcal L=\frac12\partial_\mu\varphi\partial^\mu\varphi-\lambda\varphi^4$ under spacetime rescaling, $j^\mu=\partial^\mu\varphi(x^\nu\partial_\nu\varphi+\varphi)-x^\mu(\frac12\partial_\nu\varphi\partial^\nu\varphi-\lambda\varphi^4)$ is conserved on shell; for the quantum analogue, a Ward–Takahashi identity, anomalies can intervene. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))

### History
Noether began working on the invariance theorem in 1915 while helping Felix Klein and David Hilbert with problems from Einstein's general relativity, had most of the key ideas by March 1918, and published "Invariante Variationsprobleme" in the Göttingen *Nachrichten* that year (pp. 235–257). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem), [Noether, transl. Tavel](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066)) The abstract credits earlier related work by Hamel, Herglotz, Lorentz, Fokker, Weyl and Klein, and an English translation appeared in 1971. ([Noether, transl. Tavel](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066), [Wikipedia: second theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_second_theorem)) Kosmann-Schwarzbach places the paper in the debate over energy conservation in general relativity and traces how its results were transmitted from 1918 to 1970 before their broad applicability was recognized. ([Kosmann-Schwarzbach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09254)) The modern converse with generalized symmetries is due to Martínez Alonso (1979) and Olver (1986). ([Brown](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2010.10909))

### Connections
- [Lagrangian Mechanics](node:Lagrangian%20Mechanics): the setting of the first theorem; conserved quantities are built from $\partial L/\partial\dot q$.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups) and [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras): the symmetries are one-parameter groups, and their generators close under commutators.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics) and [Poisson Brackets in Mechanics](node:Poisson%20Brackets%20in%20Mechanics): conservation reduces to $\{H,\Phi^\xi\}=0$.
- [Moment Maps](node:Moment%20Maps) and [Symplectic Reduction](node:Symplectic%20Reduction): the conserved charges of a Hamiltonian group action, used to reduce phase space.
- [Jet Bundles and Classical Fields](node:Jet%20Bundles%20and%20Classical%20Fields) and [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations): the variational bicomplex formulation.
- [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws): the output of the first theorem.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): the Noether current of spacetime translations.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory) and [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the second theorem's local symmetries give identities rather than new charges.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): the quantum counterparts are the Ward–Takahashi identities, and anomalies can break classical symmetries.
- [Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking](node:Spontaneous%20Symmetry%20Breaking): concerns symmetries whose conserved currents exist but whose vacuum is not invariant.

### Common pitfalls
- **Not every system has a Lagrangian.** Systems with a Rayleigh dissipation function are outside the theorem, and dissipative systems with continuous symmetries need not have a conservation law. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Boundary terms and falloff.** The derivation assumes no boundary terms, and on non-compact manifolds currents must decay fast enough at infinity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **Invariance of $L$ is stronger than needed.** A symmetry only up to a divergence, $\delta L=\nabla\cdot\sigma$, still yields a current; the WZW model is an example. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Noether%27s+theorem))
- **Gauge symmetries do not give extra physical charges.** Symmetries depending on arbitrary functions yield identities among the field equations (second theorem), not independent conservation laws. ([Wikipedia: second theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_second_theorem))
- **Energy in general relativity.** Global energy, momentum and angular momentum conservation there requires combining the matter stress–energy tensor with the Landau–Lifshitz pseudotensor. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem))
- **The converse needs hypotheses.** It holds for nondegenerate problems with generalized symmetries and equivalence classes modulo trivial conservation laws (those vanishing on shell or holding identically), not for arbitrary systems. ([Brown](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2010.10909))

### Open problems
- **Poisson–Lie symmetries in field theory.** Non-trivial Poisson–Lie symmetries, the classical analogue of quantum-group symmetries, fail to be symplectomorphisms and so go beyond the Noether framework ([Girelli–Pollack–Riello](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14942)). The authors state that they do not know whether a diffeologically meaningful definition of the dual group $G^*$ can be given, call their covariant formulation of localized Poisson–Lie charges "not fully satisfactory", and postpone a formulation via the hypersurface deformation algebra to future work. ([Girelli–Pollack–Riello, full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.14942))
- **Equivalence of converse theorems.** Brown reports that he could not determine whether Vinogradov's 1984 converse theorem is equivalent to the Martínez Alonso–Olver theorem. ([Brown](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2010.10909))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: Noether's theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Noether%27s+theorem): variational bicomplex and symplectic versions, with a bibliography.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Noether's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem): mechanics and field-theory forms, many worked conservation laws.
- **Learn:** [Baez, Noether's Theorem in a Nutshell](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/noether.html): a three-line proof for a particle and the meaning of the conserved quantity.
- **Primary:** [Noether, Invariant Variation Problems (transl. Tavel)](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0503066): English translation of the 1918 paper.
- **Primary:** [Bañados and Reyes, A short review on Noether's theorems, gauge symmetries and boundary terms](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03616): global and local symmetries and asymptotic charges, for students.
- **Primary:** [Brown, Do symmetries "explain" conservation laws? The modern converse Noether theorem vs pragmatism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.10909): the converse, its hypotheses and history.
- **Further reading:** [Kosmann-Schwarzbach, The Noether Theorems: Invariance and Conservation Laws in the Twentieth Century (Springer, 2011; with B. E. Schwarzbach)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-87868-3): a monograph in Sources and Studies in the History of Mathematics and Physical Sciences; and [Olver, Applications of Lie Groups to Differential Equations (Springer GTM, 1993 edition)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-4350-2): generalized symmetries and the converse theorem (Theorem 5.42 in the 1986 edition, per [Brown](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2010.10909)).
references.Nuclear Physics:
## Reference
### Overview
Nuclear physics studies atomic nuclei, their constituents (protons and neutrons) and their interactions, together with other forms of nuclear matter. It is distinct from atomic physics, which treats the whole atom including its electrons, and from the engineering applications of nuclear physics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_physics))

A nucleus with $Z$ protons and $N$ neutrons has mass number $A=Z+N$. Its binding energy is the mass defect, $E_B=(Zm_p+Nm_n-m_{\rm nucleus})c^2$ (electron masses can be included for precision work). Except for the lightest nuclei, $E_B/A$ lies between about $7.5$ and $9\,\mathrm{MeV}$ with a maximum near iron, so both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones can release energy. ([MIT OCW 8.701](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-701-introduction-to-nuclear-and-particle-physics-fall-2020/53e2a7990581aef90a6740f24f8731cf_BCQ9h1PxW08.pdf)) See [Nuclear Fusion](node:Nuclear%20Fusion) and [Nuclear Fission](node:Nuclear%20Fission).

Nuclei are mesoscopic quantum many-body systems: they have too many nucleons to be solved exactly but too few for a purely statistical treatment, and their energy scales run from nucleon momenta ($\sim10^8$ eV) through separation energies ($\sim10^7$ eV) and vibrations ($\sim10^6$ eV) to rotations (as low as $10^4$ eV). Somà's review stresses that, after eighty years of work, the interaction between nucleons remains the most uncertain ingredient of nuclear theory. ([Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978)) Modern theory therefore runs on three levels: phenomenological models (liquid drop, shell model, collective model), energy density functionals across the whole chart of nuclides, and *ab initio* many-body methods built on chiral effective-field-theory forces, with lattice QCD as the ultimate link to quarks and gluons. ([Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978); [Machleidt–Entem](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2919))

### Formal definition
The **semi-empirical (Bethe–Weizsäcker) mass formula** approximates the binding energy by five terms, volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry and pairing:
$$E_B=a_VA-a_SA^{2/3}-a_C\frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{1/3}}-a_A\frac{(N-Z)^2}{A}\pm\delta(N,Z),$$
with coefficients fitted to data and $\delta$ depending on whether $Z$ and $N$ are even or odd. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-empirical_mass_formula)) Variants differ in normalization: Somà writes $E=a_vA-a_sA^{2/3}-a_cZ^2A^{-1/3}-a_a(N-Z)^2/(4A)-\delta A^{-1/2}$, so asymmetry coefficients quoted with and without the factor $1/4$ are not directly comparable. ([Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978)) See [Semi-empirical Mass Formula](node:Semi-empirical%20Mass%20Formula).

The **nuclear shell model** places independent nucleons in a spherically symmetric mean-field potential (between a square well and a harmonic oscillator; Woods–Saxon is the realistic choice) with a strong spin-orbit term, filled according to the Pauli principle. Closed shells occur at the magic numbers $2,8,20,28,50,82,126$; protons and neutrons fill separately, so nuclei can be doubly magic. The *interacting* shell model diagonalizes an effective Hamiltonian for valence nucleons outside an inert core. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_shell_model)) See [Nuclear Shell Model](node:Nuclear%20Shell%20Model) and [Magic Numbers](node:Magic%20Numbers).

### Key results
- **Saturation and short range.** The leading term is $\propto A$, and since $R\propto A^{1/3}$ it is proportional to volume: each nucleon interacts mainly with its neighbours, so the force is short-ranged. The volume coefficient is about $16\,\mathrm{MeV}$, the central density about $0.17$ nucleons/$\mathrm{fm}^3$, and the mean internucleon spacing about $1.8\,\mathrm{fm}$. ([MIT OCW 8.701](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-701-introduction-to-nuclear-and-particle-physics-fall-2020/53e2a7990581aef90a6740f24f8731cf_BCQ9h1PxW08.pdf)) The nucleon–nucleon force is strongly attractive near $0.8\,\mathrm{fm}$, repulsive below about $0.7\,\mathrm{fm}$, negligible beyond about $2.5\,\mathrm{fm}$, spin-dependent with a tensor component, and nearly charge independent. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_force))
- **Peak of binding.** The mass formula predicts $^{58}$Fe as most tightly bound with $^{62}$Ni second; experimentally $^{62}$Ni has the largest binding energy per nucleon. The formula reproduces the smooth trend but not the extra binding at magic numbers. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-empirical_mass_formula))
- **Spin-orbit origin of magic numbers.** A 3D harmonic oscillator without spin-orbit coupling gives shell closures $2,8,20,40,\dots$, matching only the first three; adding a spin-orbit term reproduces $28,50,82,126$. Mayer and Jensen developed the model in 1949 and shared the 1963 Nobel Prize with Wigner. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_shell_model); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_number_%28physics%29)) Spin-orbit coupling is treated in [Angular Momentum and Spin](node:Angular%20Momentum%20and%20Spin).
- **Chiral EFT hierarchy of nuclear forces.** Chiral perturbation theory with power counting in $(Q/\Lambda_\chi)^\nu$ organizes [nuclear forces](node:Nuclear%20Forces) as a hierarchy: at leading order ($\nu=0$) two contact terms and one-pion exchange (which supplies the tensor force); at NLO ($\nu=2$) leading two-pion exchange and seven contacts; at NNLO ($\nu=3$) the first non-vanishing three-nucleon forces appear (the irreducible NLO three-nucleon graphs cancel), so 3NFs are suppressed relative to 2NFs. ([Machleidt–Entem](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2919)) The approach derives forces consistently with the symmetries of QCD and has been applied to light nuclei at various resolution scales. ([Epelbaum–Hammer–Meißner](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.1338)) See [Chiral Nuclear Effective Field Theory](node:Chiral%20Nuclear%20Effective%20Field%20Theory).
- **Energy density functionals.** EDF methods keep all $A$ nucleons active with a simplified (symmetry-breaking) wave function, then restore symmetries by mixing and projection. The zero-range Skyrme and finite-range Gogny functionals date from the 1970s and relativistic functionals from the 1980s; about fifteen parameters are fitted to binding energies and charge radii, and single-reference EDF is the only microscopic method that currently covers the whole nuclear chart. ([Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978)) A density-dependent Skyrme force reproduces basic nuclear properties (Vautherin–Brink). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_structure))
- **Collective motion and deformation.** Rotations and vibrations enter as collective degrees of freedom on top of the mean field; when the self-consistent solution breaks rotational symmetry the nucleus is deformed rather than spherical. Work by Aage Bohr and Ben Mottelson, including on nuclear pairing, contributed to their 1975 Nobel Prize. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_structure)) See [Collective Nuclear Models](node:Collective%20Nuclear%20Models).
- **Decay modes.** Unstable nuclides decay by $\alpha$ emission, $\beta$ decay (interconverting neutrons and protons with emission of an electron or positron), $\gamma$ emission without change of element, internal conversion, and fission. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_physics)) See [Nuclear Beta Decay](node:Nuclear%20Beta%20Decay) and [Alpha Decay and Quantum Tunneling](node:Alpha%20Decay%20and%20Quantum%20Tunneling).

### Examples
$^4$He, $^{16}$O, $^{40}$Ca and $^{208}$Pb are stable doubly magic nuclei; $^{48}$Ca is doubly magic and extremely long-lived (it decays by double beta decay); $^{208}$Pb is the heaviest known stable nuclide. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_number_%28physics%29))

Away from stability magic numbers move: studies of neutron-rich nuclei suggest $N=16$ acts as a magic number there. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_shell_model)) The neutron drip line is now experimentally established through neon ($Z=10$): $^{31}$F and $^{34}$Ne are the heaviest bound fluorine and neon isotopes, while for sodium only the lower bound $^{39}$Na is known. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_drip_line)) Somà's 2018 review still gave the limit as $Z\le8$, which later experiments superseded. ([Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978))

### History
Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896. Geiger and Marsden's alpha-scattering experiments (1909–1911) led to Rutherford's 1911 nuclear atom, and Chadwick identified the neutron in 1932. Yukawa proposed a meson theory of the strong force in 1935. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_physics)) Weizsäcker formulated the semi-empirical mass formula in 1935 on the liquid-drop model first proposed by Gamow and later developed by Bohr, Wheeler and Meitner. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-empirical_mass_formula)) Mayer's 1948 and 1949 *Physical Review* papers established closed shells. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_number_%28physics%29)) Weinberg's non-linear realization of chiral symmetry (late 1960s) and the 1990s effective-field-theory programme of Weinberg, van Kolck and others turned nuclear forces back into a pion theory constrained by chiral symmetry. ([Machleidt–Entem](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2919))

### Connections
- [Postulates of Quantum Mechanics](node:Postulates%20of%20Quantum%20Mechanics): nuclei are quantum many-body systems.
- [Semi-empirical Mass Formula](node:Semi-empirical%20Mass%20Formula), [Nuclear Shell Model](node:Nuclear%20Shell%20Model), [Magic Numbers](node:Magic%20Numbers) and [Collective Nuclear Models](node:Collective%20Nuclear%20Models): the main phenomenological descriptions.
- [Chiral Nuclear Effective Field Theory](node:Chiral%20Nuclear%20Effective%20Field%20Theory) and [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): systematic nuclear forces from QCD symmetries.
- [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics) and [Lattice QCD](node:Lattice%20QCD): the underlying theory and its numerical route to nuclear forces.
- [Nuclear Beta Decay](node:Nuclear%20Beta%20Decay), [Electroweak Theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory) and [Standard Model of Particle Physics](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics): weak decays of nuclei.
- [Neutrinoless Double Beta Decay](node:Neutrinoless%20Double%20Beta%20Decay) and [Neutrino Mass Mechanisms](node:Neutrino%20Mass%20Mechanisms): nuclear matrix elements as the bottleneck for neutrino-mass inference.
- [Nuclear Matter Equation of State](node:Nuclear%20Matter%20Equation%20of%20State) and [Neutron Stars](node:Neutron%20Stars): dense matter from laboratory nuclei to compact stars.
- [Big Bang Nucleosynthesis](node:Big%20Bang%20Nucleosynthesis), [Stellar Nucleosynthesis](node:Stellar%20Nucleosynthesis), [r-Process Nucleosynthesis](node:r-Process%20Nucleosynthesis) and [Stellar Structure](node:Stellar%20Structure): the origin of the elements.
- [Quark–Gluon Plasma](node:Quark–Gluon%20Plasma) and [Heavy-Ion Collisions](node:Heavy-Ion%20Collisions): deconfined matter produced in collisions of heavy nuclei.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): meson exchange and EFT language.
- [Hydrogen Atom](node:Hydrogen%20Atom): atomic shells as contrast to nuclear shells.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Nuclear binding and bulk properties](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Nuclear%20binding%20and%20bulk%20properties)

### Common pitfalls
- Mixing SEMF conventions: $Z^2$ versus $Z(Z-1)$ in the Coulomb term, and $(N-Z)^2/A$ versus $(N-Z)^2/(4A)$ in the asymmetry term, change the fitted coefficients. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-empirical_mass_formula); [Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978))
- Counts of stable nuclides vary by compilation: Wikipedia gives about $251$ stable nuclides across $80$ elements, Somà's 2018 review $253$ stable and about $3100$ unstable isotopes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_physics); [Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978)) Such totals include "observationally stable" nuclides, energetically able to decay but never seen to (105 of the 251), so they change as decays are detected: $^{209}$Bi was reclassified as alpha-active in 2003. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_nuclide))
- Free-particle decay rules do not carry over: the free neutron decays and the free proton does not, but inside nuclei protons can also convert. ([MIT OCW 8.701](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-701-introduction-to-nuclear-and-particle-physics-fall-2020/53e2a7990581aef90a6740f24f8731cf_BCQ9h1PxW08.pdf))
- Treating the no-core shell model with two-body forces only: matching experiment requires three-body interactions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_shell_model))

### Open problems
- **Limits of nuclear existence.** Somà lists as open how many nuclei exist (theory estimates about $6000$–$9000$ bound isotopes), where the drip lines lie, whether a region of superheavy relatively stable nuclei exists beyond the heaviest synthesized element ($Z=118$), and how magic numbers evolve across the chart. ([Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978)) The neutron drip line is still unknown beyond neon. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_drip_line))
- **Origin of heavy elements.** It is not yet clear how and where about half of the elements heavier than iron were produced; neutron-star mergers and type-II supernovae are the leading candidates. ([Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978))
- **Nuclear forces from QCD.** Lattice QCD has produced a two-nucleon potential and applications to light nuclei, but considerable difficulties remain in the three-nucleon sector. ([Somà](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978))
- **Neutrinoless double-beta decay matrix elements.** The rate is $\Gamma=G_{0\nu}|M_{0\nu}|^2\langle m_{\beta\beta}\rangle^2$; observing the decay would show that neutrinos are Majorana particles and that lepton number is violated, but $M_{0\nu}$ must be computed, and different many-body methods disagree by factors of about $2$–$5$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrinoless_double_beta_decay)) Engel and Menéndez review the effort to obtain accurate matrix elements with quantifiable error bars from *ab initio* theory. ([Engel–Menéndez](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.06548))
- **Dense-matter equation of state.** The maximum neutron-star mass depends on the poorly known EOS of dense matter; realistic models give about $2.2$–$2.9\,M_\odot$, and GW170817 constrains it to about $2.01$–$2.17\,M_\odot$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolman%E2%80%93Oppenheimer%E2%80%93Volkoff_limit)) Lattimer and Prakash note that the thermal properties of dense matter, important for [supernovae](node:Supernovae) and mergers, remain far less constrained than cold matter. ([Lattimer–Prakash](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.07820))

- **Learn:** [MIT 8.701 Lecture 9.2, Binding Energies](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-701-introduction-to-nuclear-and-particle-physics-fall-2020/53e2a7990581aef90a6740f24f8731cf_BCQ9h1PxW08.pdf) (Klute): mass defect, the $E_B/A$ curve and the Weizsäcker terms.
- **Primary:** [Somà, From the liquid drop model to lattice QCD (Eur. Phys. J. Plus 133, 434, 2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03978): review of nuclear interactions and many-body methods.
- **Primary:** [Machleidt and Entem, Chiral effective field theory and nuclear forces (Phys. Rept. 503, 2011)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2919) and [Epelbaum, Hammer and Meißner, Modern theory of nuclear forces (Rev. Mod. Phys. 81, 2009)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.1338).

- **Further reading:** [Bohr and Mottelson, Nuclear Structure (1969)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL1274866W); [Ring and Schuck, The Nuclear Many-Body Problem (Springer, 1980)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61852-9); [Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (1987)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL3746671W).
references.Numerical Linear Algebra:
## Reference
### Overview
Numerical linear algebra is the study of how matrix operations can be turned into computer algorithms that approximate answers to problems of continuous mathematics, with the emphasis on accuracy and efficiency in finite-precision arithmetic. It is a subfield of numerical analysis whose core tasks are solving linear systems $Ax=b$, least squares problems, and eigenvalue and singular value problems, organised around a small set of matrix factorisations: LU, QR, the singular value decomposition and the eigendecomposition. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra))

Two ideas separate the subject from exact linear algebra. *Conditioning* is a property of the problem: how much the answer can change under small perturbations of the data. *Stability* is a property of the algorithm: a backward stable algorithm returns the exact answer to a nearby problem, and then the forward error is at most the condition number times the backward error. Householder triangularisation is robust, solving least squares through the normal equations is unstable, and Gaussian elimination is unstable without pivoting. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra)) ([Wikipedia: Numerical stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability))

Direct methods on an $m\times m$ matrix cost $O(m^3)$ operations, and eigenvalue problems for general matrices have no finite direct solution, so iterative methods are essential. For large sparse problems the dominant iterative methods are Krylov subspace projections: conjugate gradients for symmetric positive definite systems, GMRES for nonsymmetric ones, and Lanczos and Arnoldi iterations for eigenproblems. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra))

### Formal definition
For a problem $f: X\to Y$, the (absolute) condition number at $x$ is
$$\hat\kappa = \lim_{\delta\to 0}\ \sup_{\|\delta x\|\le\delta} \frac{\|\delta f\|}{\|\delta x\|},$$
and the problem is ill-conditioned when small perturbations of $x$ produce large changes in $f(x)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra))

For a nonsingular matrix $A$ and a consistent norm, $\kappa(A) = \|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\| \ge 1$; in the 2-norm $\kappa_2(A) = \sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)$, and $\kappa(A)$ is the maximum ratio of the relative error in $x$ to the relative error in $b$ for $Ax=b$. Using the pseudoinverse, $\kappa(A) = \|A\|\,\|A^{+}\|$ extends to rectangular matrices. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condition_number))

If an algorithm computes $y^*$ in place of $y=f(x)$, the forward error is $y^*-y$ and the backward error is the smallest $\Delta x$ with $f(x+\Delta x) = y^*$. The algorithm is **backward stable** when the backward error is small for all inputs, and **mixed stable** when it solves a nearby problem approximately. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability))

The basic factorisations are $A = LU$ (with row permutation, $PA = LU$), $A = QR$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $R$ upper triangular, the singular value decomposition $A = U\Sigma V^*$ with $U,V$ unitary and $\Sigma$ diagonal, and $A = X\Lambda X^{-1}$ for diagonalisable $A$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra))

### Key results
- **Forward error bound.** For a backward stable algorithm, the forward error is at most the condition number times the backward error; with $\kappa(A)=10^k$ up to $k$ further digits can be lost in solving $Ax=b$. ([Wikipedia: Numerical stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability)) ([Wikipedia: Condition number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condition_number))
- **Existence of LU factorisations.** Every square matrix has an $LUP$ (and $PLU$) factorisation; an invertible $A$ has an LU factorisation without pivoting if and only if all its leading principal minors are nonzero. Gaussian elimination costs about $2n^3/3$ operations, is stable for diagonally dominant or positive definite matrices, and is usually stable with partial pivoting, though examples exist where partial pivoting is unstable. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LU_decomposition)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_elimination))
- **Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem.** If $A = \sum_i \sigma_i u_i v_i^T$ is an SVD with $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots$, then $A_k = \sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i u_i v_i^T$ is a best rank-$k$ approximation in both the spectral norm (error $\sigma_{k+1}$) and the Frobenius norm (error $(\sigma_{k+1}^2+\cdots+\sigma_r^2)^{1/2}$), and the Frobenius minimiser is unique if and only if $\sigma_k > \sigma_{k+1}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation))
- **Conjugate gradients.** For real symmetric positive definite $A$, the CG iterate $x_k$ (from $x_0=0$) minimises the $A$-norm of the error over the Krylov space $\operatorname{span}\{b, Ab,\dots,A^{k-1}b\}$, terminates in at most $n$ steps in exact arithmetic, and satisfies
$$\|x-x_k\|_A \le 2\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}\right)^{k}\|x-x_0\|_A,\qquad \kappa=\kappa_2(A).$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_gradient_method))
- **GMRES convergence.** GMRES minimises the residual over the Krylov subspace; with $V$ the matrix of the spectral decomposition $A = V\Lambda V^{-1}$, $\|r_k\|/\|r_0\| \le \kappa_2(V)\min_{p}\max_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}|p(\lambda)|$ over polynomials of degree at most $k$ with $p(0)=1$. Greenbaum, Pták and Strakoš showed that for any nonincreasing residual sequence ending at zero one can find a matrix whose GMRES residuals are exactly that sequence. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_minimal_residual_method))
- **Shifted QR algorithm.** The iteration $A_k = Q_kR_k$, $A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k$ is an orthogonal similarity, hence numerically stable. After reduction to Hessenberg form (about $\tfrac{10}{3}n^3$ operations, or $\tfrac43 n^3$ to tridiagonal form in the symmetric case), each QR step costs $O(n^2)$, and with the shift $\mu = a_{nn}$ convergence is quadratic, so the whole eigenvalue computation takes $O(n)$ steps of $O(n^2)$ work. Modern codes use the implicit double shift with bulge chasing (the Francis algorithm). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_algorithm))
- **Complexity is governed by $\omega$.** Strassen (1969) multiplied $n\times n$ matrices in $O(n^{\log_2 7})$ and showed that inversion, determinants and Gaussian elimination have the same complexity as multiplication up to constants; the current record, $\omega < 2.371177$, is from an August 2026 preprint by Dupont, Eisenberger, Kozlovskii, Mehrabian, Ruiz, See, Zhou, Alman, Vassilevska Williams and Balog, which reformulates the optimisation in the laser method's combination-loss analysis and solves it with machine-learning methods refined by AlphaEvolve. It improves $\omega < 2.371339$ (Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu and Zhou, 2024), which in turn improved $2.371552$ (Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu and Zhou); the revised (v3) abstract of the Alman et al. paper now also states $2.371177$, citing the Dupont et al. optimisation. ([Dupont et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16884)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication)) ([Alman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16349))

### Examples
- **Least squares.** QR by Householder transformations is the stable route; the normal equations $A^TAx = A^Tb$ are unstable, and modified Gram–Schmidt stabilises classical Gram–Schmidt. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra))
- **Well- and ill-conditioned matrices.** Unitary matrices have $\kappa_2 = 1$; for a normal matrix $\kappa_2$ is the ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue magnitudes; a singular matrix is assigned $\kappa = \infty$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condition_number))
- **Krylov eigen-solvers.** Lanczos (symmetric) and Arnoldi (nonsymmetric) iterations approximate a few eigenvalues of a large sparse matrix from its Krylov subspaces. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra))

### History
Pioneers of the field include von Neumann, Turing, Wilkinson, Householder, Forsythe and Rutishauser; von Neumann and Goldstine's 1947 work is described as the first serious attempt to minimise computer error in applying algorithms to real data. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra)) The conjugate gradient method was published by Hestenes and Stiefel in 1952, and the QR algorithm was developed independently by Francis and Kublanovskaya in the late 1950s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_gradient_method)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_algorithm)) Paige and Saunders proposed MINRES in 1975, and Saad and Schultz generalised it to GMRES in 1986. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_minimal_residual_method)) Schmidt solved the low-rank approximation problem for integral operators in 1907, Eckart and Young rediscovered it in 1936, and Mirsky extended it to unitarily invariant norms in 1960. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation))

### Connections
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) and [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): the exact theory whose computation this note studies.
- [Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers](node:Matrix%20Norms%20and%20Condition%20Numbers): the conditioning side in detail.
- [Floating-Point Arithmetic and Numerical Stability](node:Floating-Point%20Arithmetic%20and%20Numerical%20Stability): rounding models behind backward error analysis.
- [QR Factorization](node:QR%20Factorization), [Cholesky Factorization](node:Cholesky%20Factorization) and [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): the core factorisations.
- [Moore–Penrose Pseudoinverse](node:Moore–Penrose%20Pseudoinverse): least squares solutions and condition numbers of rectangular matrices.
- [Krylov Subspace Methods](node:Krylov%20Subspace%20Methods), [Preconditioning](node:Preconditioning) and [Multigrid Methods](node:Multigrid%20Methods): iterative solvers for large sparse systems.
- [Randomized Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Randomized%20Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): sketching-based algorithms for low-rank approximation and least squares.
- [Numerical Methods for Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Methods%20for%20Differential%20Equations): implicit time steps and finite element discretisations generate the large sparse systems solved here.
- [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem): the reason symmetric eigenproblems are well behaved.

### Common pitfalls
- **Conditioning versus stability.** A large error can come from an ill-conditioned problem even with a backward stable algorithm; the condition number belongs to the problem and stability to the algorithm. ([Wikipedia: Numerical stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability))
- **Forming the inverse or normal equations.** Solving least squares via $A^TA$ is unstable; use QR. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra))
- **Clustered eigenvalues are not a guarantee for GMRES.** The eigenvalue bound predicts fast convergence when the eigenvalues are clustered away from the origin only when $A$ is not too far from normality, and by Greenbaum–Pták–Strakoš any nonincreasing residual curve ending at zero is realised by some matrix. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_minimal_residual_method))
- **Unshifted QR.** The unshifted algorithm converges only linearly and is not guaranteed to converge; practical implementations use Hessenberg reduction, shifts and deflation. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_algorithm))

### Open problems
- **Growth factor in Gaussian elimination with complete pivoting.** Edelman and Urschel computed lower bounds on the maximum growth factor for $n\le 75$ and $n=100$, found growth larger than $3n$ at $n=100$ and above $1.0045n$ for $n>10$, against the old conjecture that growth might never exceed $n$, and showed that $\limsup$ of maximum growth over $n$ is at least $3.317$; they consider it likely, but do not prove, that maximum growth divided by $n$ tends to infinity. ([Edelman and Urschel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04892))
- **The matrix multiplication exponent.** Whether $\omega = 2$ is a major open question; since LU factorisation, inversion and determinants share the exponent $\omega$, it governs the asymptotic cost of dense direct methods. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication)) ([Alman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16349))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Numerical linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_linear_algebra): factorisations, conditioning, iterative methods, history.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Numerical stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability): forward, backward and mixed stability.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.335J, Introduction to Numerical Methods (Johnson, 2019)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-335j-introduction-to-numerical-methods-spring-2019/): graduate course on linear systems, eigenproblems, floating point, backward error and stability.
- **Primary:** [Edelman and Urschel, maximum growth factor in Gaussian elimination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04892): new numerical lower bounds for complete pivoting.
- **Primary:** [Alman et al., More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16349): the asymmetric laser-method analysis behind the 2024 bound $\omega<2.371339$.
- **Primary:** [Dupont et al., Improving the matrix multiplication exponent with modern optimization and AlphaEvolve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16884): the 2026 bound $\omega<2.371177$.
- **Further reading:** [Trefethen and Bau, Numerical Linear Algebra (SIAM, 1997)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898719574): the standard graduate textbook.
- **Further reading:** [Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, 2nd ed. (SIAM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898718027): the monograph on rounding-error analysis.

## Reference
### Overview
Numerical methods for differential equations replace an initial or boundary value problem by a finite system of algebraic equations whose solution approximates the true solution. For ordinary differential equations the model problem is the initial value problem $y'(t) = f(t,y(t))$, $y(t_0)=y_0$, which has a unique solution when $f$ is Lipschitz (Picard–Lindelöf); methods march forward in steps of size $h$, either as one-step schemes (Euler, Runge–Kutta) or multistep schemes that reuse past values. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_methods_for_ordinary_differential_equations))

For partial differential equations there are three main families. Finite difference methods replace derivatives by difference quotients on a grid; finite element methods pose the problem in weak form and seek a Galerkin approximation in a space of piecewise polynomials on a mesh, producing sparse systems; spectral methods expand the solution in basis functions that are nonzero over the whole domain, such as Fourier modes, and converge faster than any power of $h$ for smooth solutions. ([Wikipedia: Finite element method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_element_method)) ([Wikipedia: Spectral method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_method))

The organising principle across all of them is that convergence follows from consistency plus stability: the Dahlquist theorem for multistep ODE methods, the Lax equivalence theorem for linear PDE difference schemes, and Céa's lemma for Galerkin methods are three versions of the same idea. Stiff problems, where widely separated time scales force explicit methods to take tiny steps, drive the theory of A-stability and implicit methods. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax_equivalence_theorem)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9a%27s_lemma))

### Formal definition
A **linear $q$-step method** for $y' = f(t,y)$ has the form
$$\sum_{j=0}^{q} \alpha_j\, y_{n+j} = h \sum_{j=0}^{q} \beta_j\, f(t_{n+j}, y_{n+j}),$$
and is explicit when $\beta_q = 0$. It has **order $p$** if its local error is $O(h^{p+1})$, is **consistent** if the local truncation error divided by $h$ tends to $0$, and is **zero-stable** if it satisfies the root condition on its characteristic polynomial. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_methods_for_ordinary_differential_equations))

An **$s$-stage Runge–Kutta method** with Butcher tableau $(A,b,c)$, $A=(a_{ij})$, advances by
$$k_i = f\Big(t_n + c_i h,\; y_n + h\sum_{j=1}^{s} a_{ij} k_j\Big), \qquad y_{n+1} = y_n + h\sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i k_i;$$
it is explicit when $A$ is strictly lower triangular and consistent if and only if $\sum_i b_i = 1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%E2%80%93Kutta_methods))

**A-stability** is defined through the test equation $y' = \lambda y$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda<0$: the method is A-stable when its numerical solution of this equation decays for every step size $h>0$. A Runge–Kutta method applied to the test equation gives $y_{n+1} = R(h\lambda)\,y_n$ with a stability function $R$, which is a polynomial for explicit methods. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method)) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%E2%80%93Kutta_methods))

A **Galerkin method** for a variational problem "find $u\in V$ with $a(u,v)=L(v)$ for all $v\in V$" picks a finite-dimensional subspace $V_h\subset V$ and seeks $u_h\in V_h$ with $a(u_h,v)=L(v)$ for all $v\in V_h$; the finite element method takes $V_h$ to be piecewise polynomials on a mesh, giving a sparse stiffness matrix. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9a%27s_lemma)) ([Wikipedia: Finite element method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_element_method))

### Key results
- **Dahlquist equivalence theorem.** A consistent linear multistep method is convergent if and only if it is zero-stable; a convergent method of order $p$ then has global error $O(h^p)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method))
- **First Dahlquist barrier (1956).** A zero-stable linear $q$-step method cannot have order greater than $q+1$ if $q$ is odd or $q+2$ if $q$ is even; if it is explicit, its order is at most $q$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method))
- **Second Dahlquist barrier (1963).** No explicit linear multistep method is A-stable, and an implicit A-stable linear multistep method has order at most $2$; among order-2 A-stable methods the trapezoidal rule has the smallest error constant. The paper is Dahlquist, "A special stability problem for linear multistep methods", BIT 3 (1963) 27–43. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method)) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01963532))
- **Runge–Kutta stability and stage barriers.** Explicit Runge–Kutta methods are never A-stable because their stability function is a polynomial, while the $s$-stage Gauss–Legendre methods have order $2s$ and are A-stable, their stability function being a diagonal Padé approximant of $e^z$. The minimum number of stages for an explicit method of order $p = 1,\dots,8$ is $1,2,3,4,6,7,9,11$, and Butcher showed no explicit method with $s = p+1$ stages exists for $p>6$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%E2%80%93Kutta_methods))
- **Lax equivalence theorem (Lax–Richtmyer 1956).** For a well-posed linear initial value problem and a consistent linear finite difference approximation, the scheme is convergent if and only if it is stable in the sense of Lax and Richtmyer. Stability is usually easier to establish than convergence, which is how the theorem is used in practice. From Lax and Richtmyer, "Survey of the stability of linear finite difference equations", Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 9 (1956) 267–293. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax_equivalence_theorem)) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/cpa.3160090206))
- **CFL condition (1928).** For explicit time-marching schemes for hyperbolic equations, convergence requires the Courant number $C = u\,\Delta t/\Delta x$ to satisfy $C \le C_{\max}$, typically $C_{\max}=1$; in several dimensions the condition sums over directions, and for systems uses the largest eigenvalue magnitude of the coefficient matrix. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courant%E2%80%93Friedrichs%E2%80%93Lewy_condition))
- **Céa's lemma (1964).** Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, $a$ a bilinear form with $|a(v,w)|\le\gamma\|v\|\|w\|$ and $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$, $L$ a bounded linear functional, $u$ the solution of $a(u,v)=L(v)$ on $V$ and $u_h$ the Galerkin solution in a finite-dimensional $V_h\subset V$. Then
$$\|u-u_h\| \le \frac{\gamma}{\alpha}\inf_{v\in V_h}\|u-v\|,$$
so the finite element error reduces to a question of approximation theory. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9a%27s_lemma))
- **Spectral accuracy.** For smooth solutions, Fourier spectral methods converge faster than any polynomial in the grid size $h$, and with the fast Fourier transform a periodic Poisson solve costs $O(n\log n)$. ([Wikipedia: Spectral method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_method))

### Examples
- **Euler's method.** $y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_n,y_n)$, the explicit one-step method of order 1, published by Euler in 1768. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_methods_for_ordinary_differential_equations))
- **Classical RK4.** $k_1 = f(t_n,y_n)$, $k_2 = f(t_n+\tfrac h2, y_n+\tfrac h2 k_1)$, $k_3 = f(t_n+\tfrac h2, y_n+\tfrac h2 k_2)$, $k_4 = f(t_n+h, y_n+hk_3)$, $y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac h6(k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4)$, with local truncation error $O(h^5)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%E2%80%93Kutta_methods))
- **Adams and BDF families.** $s$-step Adams–Bashforth methods are explicit of order $s$, Adams–Moulton methods implicit of order $s+1$, and backward differentiation formulas are implicit methods used for stiff equations. On $y'=y$, $y(0)=1$, with $h=0.5$, Euler gives $y(2)\approx 5.0625$ and two-step Adams–Bashforth $\approx 6.0234$ against the exact $e^2\approx 7.3891$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method))
- **P1 finite elements in one dimension.** For $u''=f$ on $(0,1)$ with $u(0)=u(1)=0$, the weak form uses $\phi(u,v)=\int_0^1 u'v'\,dx$; continuous piecewise linear "tent" functions give a sparse linear system $-Lu = Mf$ whose stiffness matrix $L$ is symmetric and positive definite, so the conjugate gradient method is a natural solver. ([Wikipedia: Finite element method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_element_method))

### History
Euler's method dates to 1768 and Cauchy proved its convergence in 1824; Bashforth's 1855 letter first mentions Adams's multistep methods, Runge published the first Runge–Kutta method in 1895 and Kutta the popular fourth-order method in 1901, Curtiss and Hirschfelder named stiff equations in 1952, and Dahlquist introduced A-stability in 1963. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_methods_for_ordinary_differential_equations))

Courant, Friedrichs and Lewy published their stability condition in 1928. Hrennikoff (1941) and Courant (1943) anticipated finite elements; the method developed in engineering through Argyris, Clough and Zienkiewicz in the 1960s and 70s, was found independently by Feng Kang in China, and received its rigorous mathematical basis in Strang and Fix (1973). Orszag developed spectral methods in papers beginning in 1969. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courant%E2%80%93Friedrichs%E2%80%93Lewy_condition)) ([Wikipedia: Finite element method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_element_method)) ([Wikipedia: Spectral method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_method))

### Connections
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations): the initial value problems being discretised.
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): the boundary and evolution problems treated by finite differences, elements and spectral methods.
- [Picard–Lindelöf Theorem](node:Picard–Lindelöf%20Theorem): guarantees the well-posedness that convergence theory assumes.
- [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems): a hypothesis of the Lax equivalence theorem.
- [Finite Element Methods](node:Finite%20Element%20Methods): the Galerkin family in detail.
- [Lax–Milgram Theorem](node:Lax–Milgram%20Theorem): existence for the coercive variational problems in Céa's lemma.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the function spaces of the weak formulation.
- [Fast Fourier Transform](node:Fast%20Fourier%20Transform): the algorithm that makes spectral methods fast.
- [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): implicit steps and finite element systems end in large sparse linear solves.
- [Multigrid Methods](node:Multigrid%20Methods), [Krylov Subspace Methods](node:Krylov%20Subspace%20Methods) and [Preconditioning](node:Preconditioning): solvers for those systems.
- [Floating-Point Arithmetic and Numerical Stability](node:Floating-Point%20Arithmetic%20and%20Numerical%20Stability): the rounding-error side of stability.

### Common pitfalls
- **Consistency is not enough.** A consistent multistep method that violates the root condition does not converge; convergence needs zero-stability as well. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method))
- **Order of one-step and multistep methods.** A $p$-th order one-step method has global error $O(h^p)$, but for multistep methods this requires zero-stability in addition to order. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_methods_for_ordinary_differential_equations))
- **$\sum_j a_{ij} = c_i$ is not the consistency condition.** For Runge–Kutta methods consistency is $\sum_i b_i = 1$; the row-sum condition is neither necessary nor sufficient. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%E2%80%93Kutta_methods))
- **Explicit methods on stiff problems.** Explicit schemes can be unstable on stiff problems unless the step is tiny; implicit or exponential integrators are preferred. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_methods_for_ordinary_differential_equations))
- **Von Neumann analysis is not the Lax–Richtmyer condition.** It implies Lax–Richtmyer stability only in certain cases. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax_equivalence_theorem))
- **Spectral methods on non-smooth problems.** Their exponential convergence needs smoothness; for shocks and large non-smooth problems finite elements, with sparse matrices, usually work better. ([Wikipedia: Spectral method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_method))

### Open problems
- **Minimal stages for high-order explicit Runge–Kutta methods.** The precise minimum number of stages $s_{\min}(p)$ for an explicit Runge–Kutta method of order $p$ remains open in general. It is currently solved only for $p\le 8$; for $p>8$ Butcher's bound $s_{\min}(p)\ge p+3$ is known, and for order 10 the stage count has fallen from Curtis's 18 (1975) to Hairer's 17 (1978), Zhang's 16 (2024, order 10 supported numerically but not yet rigorously proved) and Stepanov's 15-stage family. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runge%E2%80%93Kutta_methods)) ([Stepanov](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.17329))
- **Spectral shock capturing.** No three-dimensional single-domain spectral shock-capturing results are known. ([Wikipedia: Spectral method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_method))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Numerical methods for ordinary differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_methods_for_ordinary_differential_equations): methods, stiffness, history.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Linear multistep method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_multistep_method): Dahlquist theory and barriers.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.336, Numerical Methods for PDEs (Seibold, 2009)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-336-numerical-methods-for-partial-differential-equations-spring-2009/): graduate course with lecture notes and problem sets.
- **Primary:** [Lax and Richtmyer, Survey of the stability of linear finite difference equations (1956)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/cpa.3160090206): the equivalence theorem.
- **Primary:** [Dahlquist, A special stability problem for linear multistep methods (1963)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01963532): A-stability and the second barrier.
- **Primary:** [Stepanov, On Runge–Kutta methods of order 10](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17329): 15-stage order-10 methods and the stage-count problem.
- **Further reading:** [Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I (Springer Series in Computational Mathematics, 1993)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-78862-1): the standard monograph on nonstiff ODE integrators.
references.Ontology Induction:
## Reference
### Overview
Ontology induction, usually called ontology learning (also ontology extraction, generation, or acquisition), is the automatic or semi-automatic construction of an ontology from data, mostly text. It extracts a domain's terms, groups them into concepts, arranges the concepts in a taxonomy, and adds non-taxonomic relations and axioms, finally encoding the result in an ontology language. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontology_learning); [Asim et al. 2018](https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/bay101/5116160))

Early landmarks include Maedche and Staab's 2001 article "Ontology learning for the Semantic Web" (IEEE Intelligent Systems 16(2), pp. 72–79) and the 2006 Springer monograph *Ontology Learning and Population from Text*. ([Crossref: Maedche and Staab](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/5254.920602); [Crossref: Springer 2006](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-39252-3)) Its methods are linguistic (lexico-syntactic patterns, parsing), statistical (co-occurrence, clustering, formal concept analysis, association rules), and logical ([inductive logic programming](node:Inductive%20Logic%20Programming) for axioms). ([Asim et al. 2018](https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/bay101/5116160))

Since 2023, large language models have been evaluated on the same subtasks (term typing, taxonomy discovery, relation extraction) and trained to generate whole taxonomic backbones; the LLMs4OL authors conclude that LLMs are best used as assistants, with human experts in the loop. ([Babaei Giglou et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.16648); [Lo et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23584)) For knowledge-graph construction, Chaudhri's Stanford CS520 notes say that enterprise graphs "often require very high accuracy, so human review becomes essential", and that validating extraction outputs at scale remains an unresolved challenge. ([Chaudhri, CS520](https://vchaudhri.github.io/KG_Course/How_To_Create_A_Knowledge_Graph.html); [Chaudhri, CS520 text chapter](https://vchaudhri.github.io/KG_Course/How_To_Create_A_Knowledge_Graph_From_Text.html))

### Formal definition
**Task decomposition.** Ontology learning comprises (1) domain terminology extraction and synonym detection, (2) concept discovery, (3) concept hierarchy derivation, (4) non-taxonomic relation learning, (5) rule/axiom discovery, (6) ontology population with instances, (7) concept hierarchy extension, and (8) frame/event detection. Not every system performs every step. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontology_learning)) The "ontology learning layer cake" orders these stages from terms and synonyms through concepts and taxonomic and non-taxonomic relations to axiom schemata and general axioms. ([Asim et al. 2018](https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/bay101/5116160))

**Taxonomy induction as inference (Snow, Jurafsky and Ng 2006).** A taxonomy $T$ is a set of pairwise relations over a domain $D_T$ of objects, for example word senses. Write $H^n_{ij}$ if $j$ is the $n$-th ancestor of $i$, and $C^{mn}_{ij}$ if $i,j$ are $(m,n)$-cousins (their closest least common subsumer is $m$ and $n$ links away). Admissible taxonomies satisfy
$$H^m_{ij}\wedge H^n_{jk}\Rightarrow H^{m+n}_{ik},\qquad C^{mn}_{ij}\Leftrightarrow\exists k=\mathrm{LCS}(i,j):H^m_{ik}\wedge H^n_{jk}.$$
Given observed evidence $E=\{E^R_{ij}\}$ (for example the lexico-syntactic patterns in which $i$ and $j$ co-occur), the induced taxonomy is $\hat T=\arg\max_T P(E\mid T)$. ([Snow et al. 2006](https://aclanthology.org/P06-1101.pdf))

**Concept formation by formal concept analysis.** A formal context is $K=(G,M,I)$ with objects $G$, attributes $M$, and incidence $I\subseteq G\times M$. For $A\subseteq G$, $A'$ is the set of attributes shared by all of $A$; for $B\subseteq M$, $B'$ is the set of objects having all of $B$. A formal concept is a pair $(A,B)$ with $A'=B$ and $B'=A$ (extent $A$, intent $B$), ordered by $(A_1,B_1)\le(A_2,B_2)\iff A_1\subseteq A_2\iff B_1\supseteq B_2$. ([Wikipedia: Formal concept analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_concept_analysis))

### Key results
- **Concept lattices are complete lattices, and conversely.** The derivation operators $A\mapsto A'$, $B\mapsto B'$ form a Galois connection, so $A\mapsto A''$ and $B\mapsto B''$ are closure operators. The formal concepts of any context form a complete lattice, with meets given by intersecting extents and joins by intersecting intents, and every complete lattice is isomorphic to the concept lattice of some context. ([Wikipedia: Formal concept analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_concept_analysis))
- **Factorization and greedy search for taxonomy induction.** Assume each evidence item is conditionally independent of the others given $T$ and depends on $T$ only through its own relation $R_{ij}$. Then
$$P(E\mid T)=\prod_{R_{ij}\in T}P(E^R_{ij}\mid R_{ij}\in T)\prod_{R_{ij}\notin T}P(E^R_{ij}\mid R_{ij}\notin T),$$
and adding one relation multiplies the likelihood by $\Delta_T(R_{ij})=k\,\frac{P(R_{ij}\in T\mid E^R_{ij})}{1-P(R_{ij}\in T\mid E^R_{ij})}$, where $k$ is the inverse prior odds. To respect the constraints, each step adds the implied set $I(R_{ij})$, scored by $\prod_{R\in I(R_{ij})}\Delta_T(R)$, and the search continues while the best score exceeds $1$. Combining hypernym and coordinate-term classifiers this way added 10,000 novel synsets to WordNet 2.1 at 84% precision. That is a 70% relative error reduction over a non-joint algorithm using the same classifiers, and the resulting taxonomy scored a 23% relative F-score improvement over WordNet 2.1 on an independent hypernym test set. ([Snow et al. 2006](https://aclanthology.org/P06-1101.pdf))
- **Lexico-syntactic patterns for hyponymy (Hearst 1992).** Patterns such as "$NP_0$ such as $\{NP_1,NP_2,\dots,(\text{and}|\text{or})\}\,NP_n$" (yielding hyponym$(NP_i,NP_0)$), "such $NP$ as …", "… or other $NP$", "… and other $NP$", "$NP$, including …", and "$NP$, especially …" are chosen to occur frequently across genres, to indicate the relation reliably, and to be recognizable without prior knowledge. On 8.6M words of encyclopedia text, 7,067 sentences contained "such as" and 152 relations met the strict unmodified-noun criterion. Of the 106 relations whose terms were both in WordNet, 61 were already present in its hierarchy. ([Hearst 1992](https://people.ischool.berkeley.edu/~hearst/papers/coling92.pdf))
- **FCA versus clustering for concept hierarchies (Cimiano, Hotho and Staab 2005).** Representing each term by the syntactic dependencies it occurs in, building a formal context, and converting the concept lattice into a partial order gave higher F-measure against hand-built tourism and finance ontologies than agglomerative clustering and Bi-Section-KMeans ($F'$ = 44.69% vs. at most 38.57% on tourism; 38.85% vs. at most 33.35% on finance). The gain came mainly from higher recall. The lattice can be exponential in the context size in the worst case, but on these sparse contexts (almost 98% zeros for tourism, over 99% for finance) FCA ran faster than agglomerative clustering. The authors rate FCA's traceability as good, because each concept is labelled by its shared attributes; the other methods produce opaque similarity-driven merges. ([Cimiano et al. 2005](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1109.2140))
- **LLMs as ontology learners (LLMs4OL).** Zero-shot prompting of nine LLM families on term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction gave, for example, 78.1% F1 for GPT-4 on UMLS taxonomy discovery and at most 49.5% F1 for relation extraction. Instruction-tuning Flan-T5 on a handful of examples per source raised term typing by about 25% and taxonomy discovery by about 18% on average. The authors conclude that foundation LLMs are not by themselves sufficient for ontology construction but can serve as assistants. ([Babaei Giglou et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.16648))
- **End-to-end generation (OLLM).** Fine-tuning an LLM to generate whole subgraphs of the target ontology, with a regularizer against overfitting to high-frequency concepts, outperformed subtask-composition baselines on Wikipedia categories under new semantic and structural similarity metrics, and transferred to arXiv with few examples. ([Lo et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23584))

### Examples
- From "works by such authors as Herrick, Goldsmith, and Shakespeare", the pattern "such $NP$ as …" yields hyponym(Herrick, author), hyponym(Goldsmith, author), hyponym(Shakespeare, author). ([Hearst 1992](https://people.ischool.berkeley.edu/~hearst/papers/coling92.pdf))
- Adding the synset *microsoft* under *company#n#1* in WordNet forces implied links such as $H^2$(microsoft, institution#n#1) and $C^{11}$(microsoft, dotcom#n#1); the probabilistic score is computed over this whole implied set. ([Snow et al. 2006](https://aclanthology.org/P06-1101.pdf))
- Treating the polysemous term *Bush* as one sense could lead, by transitivity, to inferring that a rose bush is a kind of U.S. president, which is why Snow et al. induce taxonomies over senses rather than words. ([Snow et al. 2006](https://aclanthology.org/P06-1101.pdf))
- A modifier heuristic proposes "eukaryotic cell" as a subclass of "cell"; for weak supervision, labelling functions can also be defined from parse-tree paths or from external resources such as Wikidata and WordNet. ([Chaudhri, CS520 text chapter](https://vchaudhri.github.io/KG_Course/How_To_Create_A_Knowledge_Graph_From_Text.html))

### History
Hearst's 1992 COLING paper described a method for acquiring hyponyms from unrestricted text with lexico-syntactic patterns. ([ACL Anthology: Hearst 1992](https://aclanthology.org/C92-2082/); [Hearst 1992](https://people.ischool.berkeley.edu/~hearst/papers/coling92.pdf)) Maedche and Staab framed ontology learning for the Semantic Web in 2001. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/5254.920602)) Cimiano, Hotho and Staab applied formal concept analysis to concept hierarchies in JAIR in 2005. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.2140)) Snow, Jurafsky and Ng recast taxonomy induction as global probabilistic inference at COLING-ACL 2006. ([ACL Anthology: Snow et al. 2006](https://aclanthology.org/P06-1101/)) LLMs4OL (ISWC 2023) evaluated LLMs on these tasks in a zero-shot setting. ([Babaei Giglou et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16648))

### Connections
- [Knowledge Graphs and Ontologies](node:Knowledge%20Graphs%20and%20Ontologies): the target artefact; induction proposes its schema and taxonomy.
- [Clustering](node:Clustering): hierarchical and divisive clustering are the classical baselines for concept hierarchies.
- [K-Means Clustering](node:K-Means%20Clustering): Bi-Section-KMeans builds a divisive cluster tree used as a taxonomy baseline.
- [Galois Connections](node:Galois%20Connections): the derivation operators of formal concept analysis form one.
- [Lattice Theory](node:Lattice%20Theory): concept lattices are complete lattices, and every complete lattice arises this way.
- [Information Extraction](node:Information%20Extraction): term, entity, and relation extraction supply the raw candidates.
- [Weak Supervision](node:Weak%20Supervision): noisy labelling functions combine pattern and resource evidence for subclass relations.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): now used for term typing, taxonomy discovery, and end-to-end ontology generation.
- [Word Embeddings](node:Word%20Embeddings): distributional similarity underlies clustering-based concept discovery.
- [Description Logics](node:Description%20Logics): the logical formalism (as in OWL) in which induced ontologies and axioms are expressed.
- [Inductive Logic Programming](node:Inductive%20Logic%20Programming): the logical approach to learning axioms from examples and background knowledge.
- [Knowledge Graph Completion](node:Knowledge%20Graph%20Completion): predicts missing facts in an existing graph rather than inducing its schema.
- [Entity Resolution](node:Entity%20Resolution): merges duplicate entities, the instance-level counterpart of synonym and concept discovery.
- [Data Provenance and Lineage](node:Data%20Provenance%20and%20Lineage): recording which evidence produced each induced link makes candidates reviewable.

### Common pitfalls
- Pattern-based extraction finds few relations relative to the text scanned (152 strict relations from 7,067 "such as" sentences), and its output suffers from metonymy (hyponym(king, institution)) and underspecified hypernyms (hyponym(steatornis, species)). ([Hearst 1992](https://people.ischool.berkeley.edu/~hearst/papers/coling92.pdf))
- Errors propagate up the layer cake: a wrong term or concept early on corrupts the taxonomy and relations built from it, and frequent faulty facts can contaminate the knowledge base. ([Asim et al. 2018](https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/bay101/5116160))
- Learning over words instead of senses produces absurd transitive inferences. ([Snow et al. 2006](https://aclanthology.org/P06-1101.pdf))
- Gold-standard evaluation needs a suitable reference ontology, which is often unavailable, and application-based evaluation is hard to generalize. ([Asim et al. 2018](https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/bay101/5116160))
- Cimiano et al. state that they "do not believe in fully automatic ontology construction without any user involvement"; induced structures are candidates for validation, not finished ontologies. ([Cimiano et al. 2005](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1109.2140))

### Open problems
- **Scaling, error propagation, and heavyweight axioms.** Asim et al. list as open challenges the error propagation across layer-cake stages, poor scalability of most tools to large datasets, heavy dependence on human post-processing, the move from lightweight taxonomies to axiom-rich ontologies, and cross-language ontology learning, which they say "has not yet gained enough attention". ([Asim et al. 2018](https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/bay101/5116160))
- **LLM-based ontology learning.** LLMs4OL leaves as future work enhancing LLMs specifically for ontology learning, combining them with pattern mining and clustering, standardizing metrics and benchmarks, handling dynamic ontology evolution, and human-in-the-loop expert involvement. ([Babaei Giglou et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.16648))
- **Validation at scale.** Validating the outputs of entity and relation extraction systems at scale "remains an important and unresolved challenge". ([Chaudhri, CS520 text chapter](https://vchaudhri.github.io/KG_Course/How_To_Create_A_Knowledge_Graph_From_Text.html))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Ontology learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontology_learning): definition, the eight subtasks, pattern- and clustering-based methods.
- **Learn:** [Chaudhri, Stanford CS520 *Knowledge Graphs*: creating a knowledge graph from text](https://vchaudhri.github.io/KG_Course/How_To_Create_A_Knowledge_Graph_From_Text.html): Hearst patterns, bootstrapping, weak supervision, human validation (course index [here](https://vchaudhri.github.io/KG_Course)).
- **Primary:** [Snow, Jurafsky and Ng 2006, *Semantic Taxonomy Induction from Heterogenous Evidence*](https://aclanthology.org/P06-1101.pdf): probabilistic, constraint-respecting taxonomy induction.
- **Primary:** [Cimiano, Hotho and Staab 2005, *Learning Concept Hierarchies from Text Corpora using Formal Concept Analysis*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.2140): FCA versus clustering, with evaluation methodology.
- **Primary:** [Asim et al. 2018, *A survey of ontology learning techniques and applications*](https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/bay101/5116160): survey of techniques, evaluation, and open challenges.
- **Primary:** [Babaei Giglou, D'Souza and Auer 2023, *LLMs4OL*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16648): LLM evaluation on ontology learning tasks.
- **Further reading:** [*Ontology Learning and Population from Text* (Springer, 2006)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-39252-3): Springer monograph (2006) on learning and populating ontologies from text.
references.Operating Systems:
## Reference
### Overview
An operating system is the system software that manages a computer's hardware and software resources and provides common services to programs. Its kernel allocates CPU time and memory among applications, isolates them from one another, creates processes and loads their code, controls access to input/output devices through drivers, and enforces protection between applications and users so that errors and malicious code are contained ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system)).

A standard way to organize the subject is around three ideas: **virtualization** of the CPU and memory (processes, scheduling, address translation, paging, TLBs, swapping), **concurrency** (threads, locks, condition variables, semaphores, concurrency bugs, event-based designs), and **persistence** (I/O devices, disks, RAID, file-system implementation, journaling, log-structured file systems, flash SSDs, data integrity), with security as a further part ([Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/)).

The operating system acts as an intermediary between applications and the hardware described by [Computer Architecture](node:Computer%20Architecture), and kernel design is partly a security question: monolithic kernels remain vulnerable if any part is compromised, while microkernels divide privilege among separate security domains ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system)). Several OS mechanisms have their own theory: page replacement is analysed by competitive ratios ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Page_replacement_algorithm)), and real-time task scheduling by schedulability tests ([Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).

### Formal definition
- **Dual-mode execution.** Most systems run user code in a mode where hardware checks that only legal instructions execute, while the kernel runs in a privileged mode not subject to these checks; applications obtain kernel services through **system calls** (for files: create, delete, open, close, link, read, write) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system)).
- **Interrupts.** An interrupt transfers control of the CPU to an interrupt service routine; hardware interrupts signal events such as I/O completion, and DMA lets devices transfer data to memory and interrupt only when finished ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system)).
- **Virtual memory.** The OS presents scattered RAM and disk space as one contiguous address space; accessing an allocated but unmapped page causes a page fault that the kernel handles, possibly swapping less-used pages to disk ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system)).
- **Periodic task model.** In real-time scheduling a task $\tau_i$ releases a job every $T_i$ time units, each needing at most $C_i$ units of execution; the utilization of a task set is
$$U = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{C_i}{T_i},$$
and deadlines are *implicit* when each job's deadline equals the period ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate-monotonic_scheduling); [Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).
