- **Deadlock.** A set of processes is deadlocked when each waits for another member of the set, for example to release a lock, so none can proceed ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadlock_%28computer_science%29)).

### Key results
- **Liu–Layland bound.** For $n$ independent periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods, free context switches, and preemptive static priorities assigned rate-monotonically (shorter period, higher priority), all deadlines are met if
$$U \le n\left(2^{1/n} - 1\right),$$
a bound that is $0.8284$ for $n = 2$ and decreases to $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$; moreover, if any static-priority assignment meets all deadlines, rate-monotonic does too ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate-monotonic_scheduling)). A tighter sufficient test is the hyperbolic bound $\prod_i (U_i + 1) \le 2$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate-monotonic_scheduling)). The original paper is Liu and Layland, J. ACM 20(1), 46–61 (1973) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/321738.321743)).
- **Uniprocessor optimality.** For preemptive uniprocessor scheduling, rate-monotonic is the optimal fixed task-priority assignment for synchronous periodic or sporadic implicit-deadline task sets, deadline-monotonic is optimal for constrained deadlines, and earliest-deadline-first is the optimal fixed job-priority algorithm for sporadic task sets regardless of deadline constraints ([Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).
- **No optimal online multiprocessor scheduler (Hong–Leung).** For arbitrary collections of jobs with more than one distinct deadline on more than one processor, no online algorithm is optimal: optimality requires knowledge of future arrivals and execution times; Dertouzos and Mok showed knowledge of arrival times is necessary even when execution times are known, and Fisher extended non-existence to sporadic task sets with constrained or arbitrary deadlines ([Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).
- **Coffman conditions.** Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait are the four conditions for deadlock described by Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani (1971); they are sufficient for deadlock when every resource has a single instance and only indicate its possibility when resources have multiple instances. Prevention breaks one condition (for example by a global lock ordering), while avoidance, as in the Banker's algorithm, grants a request only if it is safe, which requires knowing each process's maximum demand in advance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadlock_%28computer_science%29)).
- **Optimal and competitive paging.** Belady's algorithm, which evicts the page whose next use lies farthest in the future, is optimal but not implementable online. Marking and conservative algorithms (LRU is both; FIFO and CLOCK are conservative) with cache size $k$ are $k/(k-h+1)$-competitive against the optimum with cache size $h \le k$, and FIFO exhibits Bélády's anomaly ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Page_replacement_algorithm)).

### Examples
- **UNIX.** Ritchie and Thompson described the UNIX time-sharing system in Communications of the ACM 17(7), 365–375 (1974) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/361011.361061)); UNIX began as a single-user development of MULTICS, and its source code led to System V and BSD ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system)).
- **xv6.** A simple Unix-like teaching operating system, inspired by Unix V6, developed in 2006 and later ported to RISC-V for MIT's Operating System Engineering course ([MIT 6.1810](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.1810/2024/xv6.html)).
- **Monolithic kernels versus microkernels.** General-purpose systems mostly use monolithic kernels, which remain vulnerable if any part of the kernel is compromised; microkernels split kernel privileges into separate security domains to limit the damage of a single breach, and unikernels shrink the kernel further for security and performance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system)).
- **CLOCK page replacement.** Frames sit in a circular list; at a fault the hand evicts the page if its referenced bit is $0$ and otherwise clears the bit and advances; Corbató described it in 1969 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Page_replacement_algorithm)).
- **Rate-monotonic analysis.** A three-task set with utilization above the Liu–Layland bound $3(2^{1/3}-1) \approx 0.7798$ can still be schedulable: in one example the hyperbolic product is $1.995 \le 2$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate-monotonic_scheduling)).

### History
Early computers were programmed directly with plugboards or machine code; mainframe operators were supported by rudimentary systems such as FMS and IBSYS; IBM's OS/360 was the first popular operating system to support multiprogramming; MULTICS aimed to serve hundreds of users; UNIX followed, and MINIX (1987) inspired Linux; microcomputer systems (CP/M, MS-DOS, the Macintosh, Windows NT) and mobile systems (Symbian, iOS, Android) came later ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system)). Dijkstra's account of the "THE" multiprogramming system appeared in Communications of the ACM 11(5), 341–346 (1968) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/363095.363143)). In multiprocessor real-time scheduling, Dhall and Liu's 1978 paper led researchers to favour partitioned over global scheduling for two decades, until Phillips et al. (1997) showed that the "Dhall effect" stemmed from high-utilization tasks rather than global scheduling itself ([Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).

### Connections
- [Computer Architecture](node:Computer%20Architecture): privilege modes, interrupts, MMUs and TLBs are the hardware the OS virtualizes.
- [Virtual Memory](node:Virtual%20Memory): the address-space abstraction and paging machinery.
- [File Systems](node:File%20Systems) and [Log-Structured File Systems](node:Log-Structured%20File%20Systems): the persistence layer.
- [Concurrency and Synchronization](node:Concurrency%20and%20Synchronization): locks, semaphores and condition variables used in and provided by kernels.
- [Deadlock Detection and Avoidance](node:Deadlock%20Detection%20and%20Avoidance): the Coffman conditions and Banker's algorithm.
- [Operating System Scheduling](node:Operating%20System%20Scheduling) and [Real-Time Scheduling](node:Real-Time%20Scheduling): CPU allocation policies and their guarantees.
- [Real-Time and Embedded Systems](node:Real-Time%20and%20Embedded%20Systems): the setting of Liu–Layland and multiprocessor schedulability analysis.
- [Online Algorithms](node:Online%20Algorithms) and [Competitive Analysis](node:Competitive%20Analysis): the theory behind page replacement.
- [Virtualization](node:Virtualization): virtual machines extend [process isolation](node:Process%20Isolation) to whole operating systems.
- [Unikernels](node:Unikernels): a minimal-kernel design point.
- [Memory Safety](node:Memory%20Safety) and [Control-Flow Integrity](node:Control-Flow%20Integrity): kernel hardening against memory corruption.
- [Formal Verification and Proof Assistants](node:Formal%20Verification%20and%20Proof%20Assistants): used to verify microkernels.

### Common pitfalls
- The Liu–Layland bound is sufficient, not necessary: task sets above $n(2^{1/n}-1)$ may still be schedulable, and the tighter hyperbolic test can accept some of them ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate-monotonic_scheduling)).
- Uniprocessor intuitions fail on multiprocessors: because a task's exact response time depends on both the set of higher-priority tasks and their priority order, the greedy approach of Audsley's optimal priority assignment algorithm does not carry over to multiprocessors when the analysis uses exact response times, although it can be combined with some sufficient tests ([Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).
- The four Coffman conditions guarantee deadlock only for single-instance resources ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadlock_%28computer_science%29)).
- Deadlock-recovery schemes can cause livelock, where processes keep changing state in response to each other without progress; in distributed systems, message delays can produce "phantom deadlocks" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadlock_%28computer_science%29)).
- Adding page frames can increase faults under FIFO (Bélády's anomaly) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Page_replacement_algorithm)).

### Open problems
- **Worst-case arrival sequences for global scheduling.** No finite collection of worst-case job arrival sequences has been identified for global scheduling of sporadic task systems; Davis and Burns, whose survey covers research published up to late 2009, call this one of the key open questions of multiprocessor real-time scheduling, and it underlies the large gap between the best sufficient schedulability tests for global fixed-priority scheduling and what feasibility tests suggest is possible ([Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).
- **Utilization limits and overheads.** Fixed job-priority and partitioned algorithms can in the worst case use only 50% of the processing capacity, while global dynamic algorithms that reach 100% have prohibitive overheads; migration, context-switch and run-queue costs on real multicore hardware are named as open issues requiring new algorithms and analysis ([Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).
- **Task models for parallel execution.** Most multiprocessor results use periodic or sporadic models inherited from uniprocessors; models expressing intra-task parallelism and its overheads are identified as needed ([Davis and Burns](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Operating system (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system): kernel functions, modes, interrupts, virtual memory, history and security.
- **Learn:** [Arpaci-Dusseau, Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/): free textbook on virtualization, concurrency and persistence.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.1810 Operating System Engineering: xv6](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.1810/2024/xv6.html): a teaching kernel and its book.
- **Primary:** [Davis and Burns, A Survey of Hard Real-Time Scheduling for Multiprocessor Systems](https://www-users.york.ac.uk/~rd17/papers/MPSurveyv5.0.pdf): survey of multiprocessor scheduling results and open issues.
- **Primary:** [Ritchie and Thompson, The UNIX time-sharing system (CACM 1974)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/361011.361061): the original UNIX paper (bibliographic record).
- **Primary:** [Liu and Layland, Scheduling Algorithms for Multiprogramming in a Hard-Real-Time Environment (J. ACM 1973)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/321738.321743): rate-monotonic and deadline-driven scheduling (bibliographic record).
- **Further reading:** [Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/): the same textbook, free in PDF form, including its newer security chapters by Peter Reiher.
references.Ordinary Differential Equations:
## Reference
### Overview
An ordinary differential equation (ODE) relates an unknown function of one independent variable to its derivatives; "ordinary" distinguishes it from a [partial differential equation](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations). The order is the highest derivative that appears, and the equation is linear when it is a linear combination of the unknown and its derivatives. ([Ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation))

The modern theory has two layers. The classical layer asks when an initial value problem has a solution, whether it is unique, how long it exists, and how it depends on data; for linear systems it describes the full solution space. The qualitative layer treats an autonomous equation $\dot x=f(x)$ as a flow and studies fixed points, stability, periodic orbits and limit sets without solving explicitly, which leads into [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems) and [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory). Teschl's graduate text is organized exactly this way: classical theory, then dynamical systems, then chaos. ([Teschl, contents](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

Existence and uniqueness are not automatic even for smooth-looking equations: solutions can fail to be unique when $f$ is not Lipschitz, and can cease to exist in finite time when $f$ is smooth. ([Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem))

### Formal definition
An ODE of order $n$ is an equation $F(x,y,y',\dots,y^{(n)})=0$ for an unknown function $y$ of $x$. An explicit equation of order $n$ can be rewritten as a system of $n$ first-order equations by introducing $y_i=y^{(i-1)}$. ([Ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation))

The first-order initial value problem (IVP) is
$$\dot x=f(t,x),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0,$$
with $f\in C(U,\mathbb R^n)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ containing $(t_0,x_0)$; a solution is a $C^1$ function on an interval $I\ni t_0$ whose graph lies in $U$. Every solution of a locally Lipschitz IVP extends to a unique maximal interval of existence $(T_-,T_+)$. ([Teschl, Sections 2.2 and 2.6](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

A fixed point $x_0$ of $\dot x=f(x)$ is stable if nearby solutions stay nearby for all $t\ge0$, and asymptotically stable if in addition they converge to $x_0$; it is hyperbolic if the linearization $A=df(x_0)$ has no eigenvalue with zero real part. ([Teschl, Sections 6.5 and 9.2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

### Key results
- **Picard–Lindelöf theorem.** If $f\in C(U,\mathbb R^n)$ is locally Lipschitz in $x$, uniformly in $t$, the IVP has a unique local solution $x\in C^1(I)$. Quantitatively, if $V=[t_0,t_0+T]\times\overline{B_\delta(x_0)}\subseteq U$ and $M=\max_V|f|$, the solution exists at least on $[t_0,t_0+T_0]$ with $T_0=\min\{T,\delta/M\}$. The proof is the contraction principle applied to Picard iteration. ([Teschl, Theorems 2.1 and 2.2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Peano existence theorem.** If $f$ is only continuous on $V$, at least one solution exists on $[t_0,t_0+T_0]$, with the same $T_0$; uniqueness may fail. The proof uses Euler polygons and the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem. ([Teschl, Theorems 2.18 and 2.19](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Gronwall's inequality and continuous dependence.** If $\psi(t)\le\alpha(t)+\int_0^t\beta(s)\psi(s)\,ds$ on $[0,T]$ with $\beta\ge0$, then $\psi(t)\le\alpha(t)+\int_0^t\alpha(s)\beta(s)\exp\big(\int_s^t\beta\big)ds$. Consequently, if $f$ has Lipschitz constant $L$ in $x$ and $x,y$ solve $\dot x=f(t,x)$, $\dot y=g(t,y)$, then $|x(t)-y(t)|\le|x_0-y_0|e^{L|t-t_0|}+\frac{M}{L}(e^{L|t-t_0|}-1)$ with $M=\sup|f-g|$. ([Teschl, Lemma 2.7 and Theorem 2.8](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Blow-up alternative and global existence.** If the maximal existence time $T_+$ is finite, the solution eventually leaves every compact set $C$ with $[t_0,T_+]\times C\subseteq U$; for $U=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ it tends to infinity. If $|f(t,x)|\le M(T)+L(T)|x|$ on $[-T,T]\times\mathbb R^n$ for every $T$, all solutions exist for all $t\in\mathbb R$. ([Teschl, Corollary 2.16 and Theorem 2.17](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Linear systems.** For $\dot x=A(t)x$ with $A$ continuous on $I$, solutions exist on all of $I$ and form an $n$-dimensional vector space; there is a principal matrix solution $\Pi(t,t_0)$ with $x(t)=\Pi(t,t_0)x_0$, and $\Pi(t,t_0)=e^{(t-t_0)A}$ when $A$ is constant, where $\exp(A)=\sum_j A^j/j!$. For constant $A$, every solution tends to $0$ if and only if all eigenvalues have negative real part. ([Teschl, Theorems 3.9, 3.10, Corollary 3.6, Section 3.1](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Floquet theory.** If $A(t)$ is $T$-periodic, $\Pi(t,t_0)=P(t,t_0)\exp((t-t_0)Q(t_0))$ with $P(\cdot,t_0)$ $T$-periodic and $P(t_0,t_0)=I$. The system is asymptotically stable if all Floquet multipliers (eigenvalues of the monodromy matrix) satisfy $|\rho_j|<1$. ([Teschl, Theorem 3.15 and Corollary 3.17](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Lyapunov's theorem.** If a fixed point $x_0$ admits a Lyapunov function, a continuous $L$ on a neighbourhood $U(x_0)$ with $L(x_0)=0$, $L>0$ elsewhere, and $L$ non-increasing along solutions in $U(x_0)\setminus\{x_0\}$, then $x_0$ is stable. If $L$ is not constant on any orbit lying entirely in $U(x_0)\setminus\{x_0\}$ (for example if $L$ is strict, i.e. strictly decreasing along solutions there), $x_0$ is asymptotically stable (Krasovskii–LaSalle principle). ([Teschl, Section 6.6, Theorems 6.13 and 6.14](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Hartman–Grobman theorem.** If $0$ is a hyperbolic fixed point of a $C^1$ vector field $f$ with flow $\Phi_t$ and $A=df_0$, there is a [homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism) $\varphi=\mathrm{id}+h$, $h$ bounded, with $\varphi\circ e^{tA}=\Phi_t\circ\varphi$ in a neighbourhood of $0$: near a hyperbolic point the flow is topologically conjugate to its linearization. ([Teschl, Section 9.2 and Theorem 9.9](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))
- **Poincaré–Bendixson theorem.** Let $M\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and $f\in C^1(M,\mathbb R^2)$. If an $\omega$-limit set $\omega_\sigma(x)$ is nonempty, compact, connected and contains only finitely many fixed points, then it is a fixed point, a regular periodic orbit, or finitely many fixed points joined by orbits whose limit sets are among them. In particular a nonempty compact limit set without fixed points is a regular periodic orbit; this excludes in $\mathbb R^2$ the strange behaviour that already occurs for the Lorenz system in $\mathbb R^3$. ([Teschl, Lemma 7.13, Theorem 7.16 and Section 8.2](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

### Examples
The problem $y'=a\,y^{2/3}$, $y(0)=0$ has the zero solution and also the solution equal to $(at/3)^3$ for $t<0$ and $0$ for $t\ge0$; $y\mapsto y^{2/3}$ is continuous but not Lipschitz at $0$, so Peano applies and Picard–Lindelöf does not. For $y'=y^2$, $y(0)=1$, the solution $y=1/(1-t)$ is not defined at $t=1$ although the right side is smooth everywhere, illustrating the blow-up alternative. ([Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem))

For the scalar periodic equation $\dot x=a(t)x$, $a(t+T)=a(t)$, the monodromy is $e^{T\bar a}$ with $\bar a=\frac1T\int_0^Ta$, so stability is decided by the average of $a$. ([Teschl, Section 3.6](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf))

### History
Newton, Leibniz, the Bernoulli family, Riccati, Clairaut, d'Alembert and Euler contributed early integration methods. Cauchy was the first to appreciate the importance of studying functions defined by differential equations, and Lie's work from 1870 put the theory on a better foundation. ([Ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation)) The existence and uniqueness theorem is named after Picard, Lindelöf, Lipschitz and Cauchy (hence also "Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem"); Lindelöf's 1894 note in *Comptes rendus* generalized an earlier approach of Picard. ([Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem)) Hilbert posed the question of the number of limit cycles in 1900 as the second part of his sixteenth problem; Landis and Petrovsky claimed a solution in the 1950s that was shown wrong in the early 1960s. ([Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem))

### Connections
- [Integral Calculus](node:Integral%20Calculus): separable and linear first-order equations are solved by integration.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): linear systems, the matrix exponential, and Jordan form.
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): stability of linear systems and hyperbolicity.
- [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem): the contraction principle behind Picard–Lindelöf.
- [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems): the qualitative theory of flows.
- [Chaos Theory](node:Chaos%20Theory): chaotic behaviour needs dimension at least three for flows, by Poincaré–Bendixson.
- [Newtonian Mechanics](node:Newtonian%20Mechanics): Newton's equations are second-order ODEs.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics): Hamiltonian flows preserve phase-space volume.
- [Numerical Methods for Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Methods%20for%20Differential%20Equations): Euler polygons and their refinements.
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): equations in several independent variables.

### Common pitfalls
Picard–Lindelöf is local: the existence interval depends on $\delta/M$, and global existence needs extra structure such as linear growth. ([Teschl, Theorems 2.2 and 2.17](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) For a nonautonomous linear system, $x(t)=\exp(\int_{t_0}^tA(s)ds)x_0$ is in general wrong; it holds only when the matrices $A(t)$ commute. ([Teschl, Section 3.4](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)) Smoothness of $f$ does not give global existence: $y'=y^2$ blows up in finite time. ([Picard–Lindelöf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picard%E2%80%93Lindel%C3%B6f_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Hilbert's sixteenth problem, second part.** Bound the number $H(n)$ of limit cycles of a planar polynomial vector field of degree $n$. Écalle and Ilyashenko proved that each polynomial vector field has finitely many limit cycles, but the complete answer is unknown even for $n=2$, and even the existence of a uniform upper bound for quadratic vector fields is not proved. ([Ilyashenko and Llibre, arXiv:0910.3443, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0910.3443); [Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem)) Quadratic vector fields with four limit cycles are known. ([Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Ordinary differential equation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation): classification, history, existence theorems.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.03SC Differential Equations](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-03sc-differential-equations-fall-2011/): free course on first- and second-order equations, linear systems, phase portraits, linearization and limit cycles.
- **Primary:** [Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf): author's preliminary version of the AMS graduate text; existence theory, linear and Floquet theory, stability, planar dynamics, Hartman–Grobman.
- **Further reading:** [Hartman, Ordinary Differential Equations, 2nd ed. (SIAM, 2002)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898719222): the classic research monograph.
- **Further reading:** [Ilyashenko and Llibre, A restricted version of Hilbert's 16th problem for quadratic vector fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.3443): 2009 paper on a restricted form of the open problem.
references.Parallel and Distributed Computing:
## Reference
### Overview
A distributed system is a computer system whose components run on different networked computers and coordinate by passing messages. The traditional distinction is that in parallel computing all processors may access a shared memory, while in distributed computing each processor has private memory and exchanges information only by messages; parallel computing can be viewed as a tightly coupled form of distributed computing and distributed computing as a loosely coupled form of parallel computing ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)).

The two halves ask different questions. Parallel computing asks how fast a problem can be solved with many processors: its measures are work, span, speedup and efficiency, and its complexity class of efficiently parallelizable problems is NC ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_parallel_algorithms); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)). Distributed computing asks what can be computed at all when processes are separated by unreliable, asynchronous communication and may fail: consensus, Byzantine fault tolerance, logical clocks and self-stabilization are its central problems ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)).

Its characteristic results are impossibility theorems. The impossibility of guaranteeing both safety ("nothing bad ever happens") and liveness ("something good eventually happens") in an unreliable system underlies both the FLP theorem and the CAP theorem ([Gilbert and Lynch, Perspectives on the CAP Theorem](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)). In engineering practice the field studies fault tolerance, replication and consistency through case studies of real systems ([MIT 6.5840](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.824/)).

### Formal definition
**Work–span model.** Model a parallel computation as a dependency DAG. Its *work* $T_1$ is the number of operations (the time on one processor), its *span* $T_\infty$ is the length of the longest dependency chain (the time with unboundedly many processors), and $T_p$ is the time on $p$ processors. Speedup is $S_p=T_1/T_p$, efficiency $S_p/p$, and parallelism $T_1/T_\infty$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_parallel_algorithms)).

**Message-passing models.** In the LOCAL model nodes of a network graph compute in synchronous rounds and the cost is the number of rounds; in CONGEST($B$) each message is limited to $B$ bits ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)). In the *asynchronous* model there is no a priori bound on message delivery time ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)).

**Consensus.** Each process $p_i$ starts with a value $v_i$ and must output a value such that (i) *agreement*: all (correct) processes output the same value; (ii) *validity*: every output was some process's input; (iii) *termination*: every (correct) process eventually outputs. Agreement and validity are safety properties and termination is a liveness property ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_%28computer_science%29)).

**Happened-before and logical clocks.** A Lamport clock increments a local counter before each event, attaches it to each message, and on receipt sets the counter to the maximum of its value and the message's timestamp, then increments. It satisfies the *clock condition*: if $a\to b$ ($a$ happened before $b$) then $C(a)<C(b)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamport_timestamp)). See [Logical Clocks](node:Logical%20Clocks).

### Key results
- **Work and span laws; Brent's theorem.** For every $p$, $T_p\ge T_1/p$ and $T_p\ge T_\infty$; with suitable scheduling, $T_1/p\le T_p\le T_1/p+T_\infty$. Hence speedup is below $p$ whenever $p>T_1/T_\infty$, and if the slackness $T_1/(pT_\infty)$ is below 1, perfect linear speedup is impossible ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_parallel_algorithms)).
- **Amdahl's and Gustafson's laws.** For a fixed problem whose parallelizable fraction is $p$, speedup with $N$ processors is $1/((1-p)+p/N)\to 1/(1-p)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)). If instead the problem grows with the machine and the serial fraction $s$ of the run stays fixed, the scaled speedup is $S=N-(N-1)s$, linear in $N$ (Gustafson 1988) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustafson%27s_law)).
- **FLP impossibility (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson 1985).** In an asynchronous message-passing system in which even one process may crash, no deterministic algorithm solves consensus; indeed every protocol guaranteeing agreement and validity has some execution, possibly with no failures, that never terminates ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_%28computer_science%29)). Randomized consensus circumvents FLP, achieving safety and liveness with overwhelming probability ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_%28computer_science%29)).
- **CAP theorem (Brewer's 2000 conjecture).** In a network subject to communication failures, no service can implement an atomic read/write register that guarantees a response to every request. In an asynchronous network the same indistinguishability argument applies even when no message is actually lost. Since consensus is strictly harder than an atomic register, consensus is also impossible under partitions ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)).
- **Byzantine agreement bound.** With oral (unsigned) messages, no algorithm solves consensus with $f$ Byzantine faults when $n\le 3f$, so $n\ge 3f+1$ processes are needed; with unforgeable signatures the bound relaxes. The oral-messages protocol of Pease, Shostak and Lamport and the signed protocol of Dolev and Strong use $f+1$ rounds ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_%28computer_science%29); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_fault)). See [Byzantine Fault Tolerance](node:Byzantine%20Fault%20Tolerance).
- **Locality bound.** In the LOCAL model any computable problem can be solved in about $2D$ rounds on a network of diameter $D$, so interest centres on problems solvable in time polylogarithmic in the network size ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)).

### Examples
- **Replicated state machines.** A service is replicated across servers for availability, and the servers run consensus on every update and its order to stay consistent; this is one of the most common ways to build reliable systems ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)). Paxos and Raft are widely used; they rely on an elected leader and tolerate crash, not Byzantine, failures ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_%28computer_science%29)). See [Raft Consensus](node:Raft%20Consensus).
- **Leader election.** Nodes break symmetry, for instance by electing the node with the largest identifier; LeLann formalized the problem for token rings, and the Gallager–Humblet–Spira algorithm handles general graphs ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)).
- **Distributed graph colouring.** The network is the input graph itself, with one computer per node that initially knows only its neighbours ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)).
- **Weak consistency for availability.** DNS caching gives relatively weak consistency but high availability; systems such as Chubby guarantee consistency with very high availability in the common case ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)).

### History
- Message-passing concurrency goes back to operating-systems research in the 1960s; ARPANET e-mail (early 1970s) was an early large-scale distributed application ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)).
- 1978: Lamport's "Time, clocks, and the ordering of events in a distributed system" in *Communications of the ACM* ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamport_timestamp)); Shostak formalized interactive consistency, and Lamport, Shostak and Pease's Byzantine generals paper followed in 1982 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_fault)).
- The field became a distinct branch in the late 1970s and early 1980s; the PODC conference was first held in 1982 and DISC in 1985 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing)).
- 1985: FLP impossibility; 1988: Gustafson's law; 2000: Brewer's CAP conjecture ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustafson%27s_law)).
- Castro and Liskov's PBFT made Byzantine state-machine replication practical ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_fault)).

### Connections
- [Operating Systems](node:Operating%20Systems): processes, scheduling and message passing on a single machine.
- [Concurrency and Synchronization](node:Concurrency%20and%20Synchronization): shared-memory coordination, mutual exclusion and deadlock.
- [Deadlock Detection and Avoidance](node:Deadlock%20Detection%20and%20Avoidance): a classic coordination problem in both settings.
- [Distributed Consistency and Consensus](node:Distributed%20Consistency%20and%20Consensus): the central fault-tolerance problem.
- [Raft Consensus](node:Raft%20Consensus): a leader-based crash-fault consensus protocol.
- [Byzantine Fault Tolerance](node:Byzantine%20Fault%20Tolerance): consensus with arbitrarily faulty processes.
- [Logical Clocks](node:Logical%20Clocks): ordering events without shared time.
- [Consistency Models](node:Consistency%20Models): the spectrum from [linearizability](node:Linearizability) to eventual consistency.
- [Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types](node:Conflict-Free%20Replicated%20Data%20Types): availability-first replication that converges without consensus.
- [Parallel Algorithms and Scaling](node:Parallel%20Algorithms%20and%20Scaling): work–span analysis and scaling laws.
- [MPI](node:MPI) and [MapReduce](node:MapReduce): programming models for message-passing and data-parallel computation.
- [Computer Architecture](node:Computer%20Architecture): multicore, caches and interconnects are the hardware substrate.
- [Distributed Model Training](node:Distributed%20Model%20Training): large-scale ML as a parallel workload.

### Common pitfalls
- **FLP does not say consensus never happens.** It says no deterministic algorithm can always reach consensus under full asynchrony with a crash; randomized and partially synchronous protocols are used in practice ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_%28computer_science%29)).
- **CAP is a trade-off under partitions, not a free choice of two.** The trade-off is between consistency and availability in a partition-prone system, and under asynchrony consistency cannot be guaranteed even in executions with no actual partition; many real systems guarantee neither fully, segmenting the service instead ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)).
- **Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency.** $C(a)<C(b)$ does not imply $a\to b$; vector clocks are needed for the two-way condition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamport_timestamp)).
- **Amdahl's law assumes a fixed problem size.** When the workload grows with the machine, Gustafson's scaled speedup is the relevant measure ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustafson%27s_law)).

### Open problems
- **Guarantees of segmented services.** Partitioning a system by data, operation or hierarchy into parts with different consistency and availability guarantees is common, but "it remains an open question to better understand these types of partitioning schemes" ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)).
- **Scalability vs. consistency, attacks, and mobile networks.** Gilbert and Lynch call for new theoretical insights: there appear to be inherent trade-offs between scalability and consistency that may explain why strongly consistent protocols like Paxos are hard to scale even within a data centre; denial-of-service and malicious attacks cannot be modelled as partitions; and mobile wireless networks make many of the same trade-offs harder ([Gilbert and Lynch](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Distributed computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing): models, complexity measures, classic problems and history.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Consensus (computer science)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_%28computer_science%29): problem definitions, FLP, Byzantine bounds, Paxos and Raft.
- **Learn:** [MIT 6.5840 Distributed Systems](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.824/): course on fault tolerance, replication and consistency through case studies and labs.
- **Primary:** [Gilbert and Lynch, Perspectives on the CAP Theorem](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf): CAP, its proof, its relation to FLP and the safety–liveness trade-off, and open directions.
- **Further reading:** [Lynch, Distributed Algorithms (Morgan Kaufmann, 1996)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL13538757W): distributed algorithms and impossibility results in an automata-theoretic model, organized by timing model.
references.Partial Differential Equations:
## Reference
### Overview
A partial differential equation (PDE) is an equation for an unknown function of two or more variables involving some of its partial derivatives; a $k$th-order equation has the form $F(D^ku,\dots,Du,u,x)=0$. PDEs are classified as linear, semilinear (linear in the top-order derivatives with coefficients depending only on $x$), quasilinear (top-order coefficients may depend on $u$ and lower derivatives, as for the Navier–Stokes and Einstein equations) or fully nonlinear (as for Monge–Ampère). ([Partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation))

There is no universal theory of PDEs, and specialist knowledge is divided among subfields. A common approach first produces a *weak* solution, defined through distributions or [Sobolev spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces), and then asks about regularity, i.e. whether the [weak solution](node:Weak%20Solutions) is smooth enough to be classical. ([Partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation)) The guiding standard is Hadamard's notion of a [well-posed problem](node:Well-Posed%20Problems) (1902): a solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the data. ([Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem))

### Formal definition
For a second-order equation in two variables with principal part $Au_{xx}+2Bu_{xy}+Cu_{yy}$, the type is elliptic if $B^2-AC<0$ (Laplace), parabolic if $B^2-AC=0$ (heat), hyperbolic if $B^2-AC>0$ (wave); in $n$ variables the signs of the eigenvalues of the coefficient matrix decide, with "ultrahyperbolic" for several positive and several negative eigenvalues and none zero. ([Partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation))

The Sobolev space $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ consists of $u\in L^p(\Omega)$ whose distributional derivatives of order $\le k$ lie in $L^p$; it is a Banach space, and $H^k=W^{k,2}$ is a Hilbert space. $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is the set of $W^{1,p}$ functions with zero trace on $\partial\Omega$ (for bounded Lipschitz $\Omega$). ([Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space)) For $-\Delta u=f$ in $\Omega$, $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, a weak solution is $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ with $\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. ([Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem)) Derivatives here are taken in the sense of [distributions](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29): $\langle T',\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\varphi'\rangle$. ([Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))

### Key results
- **Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem.** For a quasilinear system with analytic coefficients and analytic Cauchy data on the hypersurface $x_n=0$ (in normal form, solved for the $x_n$-derivative), there is a neighbourhood of $0$ on which the problem has a unique analytic solution. The condition on derivative orders cannot be dropped even for analytic data: for $h_t=h_{xx}$ (second order in $x$, first order in $t$) with $h(0,x)=1/(1+x^2)$, the unique formal power series solution diverges for every $t\neq0$. ([Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Kowalevski_theorem))
- **Lewy's non-solvability example (1957).** There is a $C^\infty$ function $F(t,z)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb C$ such that $\partial u/\partial\bar z-iz\,\partial u/\partial t=F$ has no solution on any open set. By contrast, the Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem says every linear PDE with constant coefficients has a solution; Lewy's example shows this fails for polynomial coefficients. ([Lewy's example](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy%27s_example))
- **Lax–Milgram theorem (1954).** If $a$ is a bilinear form on a real Hilbert space $V$ with $|a(u,v)|\le C\|u\|\|v\|$ and $a(u,u)\ge c\|u\|^2$, then for each $f\in V'$ there is a unique $u\in V$ with $a(u,v)=f(v)$ for all $v$, and $\|u\|\le\|f\|_{V'}/c$. With $V=H^1_0(\Omega)$ and $a(u,v)=\int\nabla u\cdot\nabla v$ (coercive by the Poincaré inequality) this gives a unique weak solution of the Dirichlet problem for Poisson's equation. ([Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem))
- **Sobolev embedding and Rellich–Kondrachov.** On a compact $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, if $k\ge m$ and $k-n/p\ge m-n/q$ then $W^{k,p}\hookrightarrow W^{m,q}$ continuously; for $p>n$, $W^{1,p}$ functions are Hölder continuous with exponent $1-n/p$ after modification on a null set. If $k>m$ and $k-n/p>m-n/q$ the embedding is compact; e.g. $H^1_0(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)$ is compact for bounded $\Omega$. ([Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- **Schauder estimates.** If $u\in C^{2,\alpha}$ solves $a_{ij}D_{ij}u+b_iD_iu+cu=f$ with $a_{ij}\xi_i\xi_j\ge\lambda|\xi|^2$ and coefficient Hölder norms bounded by $\Lambda$, then the weighted interior norm satisfies $|u|^*_{2,\alpha;\Omega}\le C(n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda)\,(|u|_{0}+|f|^{(2)}_{0,\alpha})$; on a $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain with $C^{2,\alpha}$ Dirichlet data $\varphi$ there is a global bound by $|u|_0+|f|_{0,\alpha}+|\varphi|_{2,\alpha}$. These estimates drive the method of continuity for the Dirichlet problem. ([Schauder estimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schauder_estimates))
- **De Giorgi–Nash.** A solution of a suitable linear strictly elliptic equation $D_i(a_{ij}(x)D_ju)=0$ with square-integrable first derivatives is Hölder continuous (De Giorgi 1956–57; Nash independently, 1957–58; Moser later gave another proof). This resolved Hilbert's nineteenth problem on analyticity of minimizers of regular variational problems; for elliptic systems the analogue fails (De Giorgi; Giusti–Miranda, 1968). ([Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem))
- **Maximum principles.** Weak: if $u$ is continuous on $\bar\Omega$ ($\Omega$ bounded) and $\Delta u\ge0$, then $\max_{\bar\Omega}u=\max_{\partial\Omega}u$. Parabolic: if $u_t-\Delta u\le0$ in $\Omega_T=(0,T]\times\Omega$, then $u$ attains its maximum on the parabolic boundary $\{t=0\}\cup([0,T]\times\partial\Omega)$; comparison and uniqueness follow. ([Silvestre, Thms 3.2.1, 4.2.1](https://math.uchicago.edu/~luis/pdenotes.pdf)) Hopf's strong form (1927): for $\sum a_{ij}D_{ij}+\sum b_iD_i$ with continuous coefficients and $(a_{ij})$ positive definite, a $C^2$ function with $Lu\ge0$ on a connected open set that attains an interior maximum is constant; for subharmonic functions on connected open sets this is Silvestre's Lemma 4.5.5. ([Maximum principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_principle); [Silvestre, Lemma 4.5.5](https://math.uchicago.edu/~luis/pdenotes.pdf))
- **Energy methods.** For the heat equation on bounded $\Omega$ with Dirichlet or Neumann conditions, $E(t)=\int_\Omega u^2$ is nonincreasing, which gives uniqueness; for $C^2$ solutions of the wave equation on a bounded domain $U$ with piecewise $C^1$ boundary and Dirichlet or Neumann conditions, $\int_U(|\nabla u|^2+u_t^2)$ is conserved, and on the shrinking balls $B_{t_0-t}(x_0)$ it is nonincreasing for smooth solutions on $\mathbb R^d$. ([Silvestre, Prop. 3.1.1, Thms 5.3.1–5.3.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~luis/pdenotes.pdf))
- **Characteristics and shocks.** For first-order equations, characteristic curves reduce the PDE to ODEs. ([Partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation)) For inviscid Burgers $u_t+uu_x=0$, $u(x,0)=f(x)$, characteristics give $u=f(x-ut)$ until they cross at $t_b=-1/\min f'$, after which a shock forms; the viscous equation $u_t+uu_x=\nu u_{xx}$ is linearized to the heat equation by Cole–Hopf, $u=-2\nu\,\partial_x\ln\varphi$. ([Burgers' equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgers%27_equation)) For [Hamilton–Jacobi equations](node:Hamilton–Jacobi%20Equations), Crandall and Lions (1983) introduced viscosity solutions: e.g. for $|u'|=1$ on $(-1,1)$, $u(\pm1)=0$, the function $1-|x|$, which is not differentiable at $0$, is the unique viscosity solution. ([Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution))

### Examples
The model equations are Laplace's $\Delta u=0$ (elliptic), the heat equation $u_t=\Delta u$ (parabolic) and the wave equation $u_{tt}=\Delta u$ (hyperbolic). ([Partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation)) The heat kernel $\Phi(x,t)=(4\pi kt)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/4kt}$ solves $u_t=k\Delta u$ on $\mathbb R^n$, and convolution with the initial data gives the solution; reconstructing earlier temperatures from later ones is very inaccurate except over short times. ([Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation)) In $\mathbb R^3$, $\Phi(x)=1/(4\pi|x|)$ is the [fundamental solution](node:Fundamental%20Solutions) of $-\Delta$: $-\Delta\Phi=\delta$ in the sense of distributions. ([Fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution)) The incompressible Navier–Stokes system $\partial_tu_i+\sum_ju_j\partial_ju_i=\nu\Delta u_i-\partial_ip+f_i$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, is the central quasilinear example from fluid mechanics. ([Fefferman](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf))

### History
Fourier developed the theory of the heat equation, and the series method for solving it, in *Théorie analytique de la chaleur* (1822). ([Heat equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation)) Cauchy proved a special case of the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem in 1842 and Kovalevskaya the full theorem in 1874. ([Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Kowalevski_theorem)) Hadamard introduced well-posedness in 1902; Bernstein (1904) began the regularity theory for nonlinear elliptic equations. ([Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem); [Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem)) Hopf's maximum principle dates from 1927 and Schauder's estimates from 1934. ([Maximum principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_principle); [Schauder estimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schauder_estimates)) Sobolev's generalized functions (1936) and Schwartz's theory of distributions (late 1940s) supplied the function spaces of the modern theory. ([Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) Leray began the theory of weak solutions of Navier–Stokes. ([Fefferman](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf)) Lax–Milgram (1954), De Giorgi–Nash (1956–58), Lewy's example (1957) and Crandall–Lions viscosity solutions (1983) followed. ([Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem); [Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem); [Lewy's example](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy%27s_example); [Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution))

### Connections
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations): characteristics and separation of variables reduce PDEs to ODEs.
- [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus): gradient, divergence, the Laplacian and the divergence theorem behind energy identities.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations), [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation), [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation): the elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic models.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the setting for weak solutions and Lax–Milgram.
- [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29): weak derivatives and fundamental solutions.
- [Maximum Principle](node:Maximum%20Principle) and [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem): uniqueness and comparison for elliptic and parabolic problems.
- [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions) and [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): representation formulas and transform methods.
- [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations): minimizers solve Euler–Lagrange PDEs; Hilbert's 19th problem is their regularity.
- [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems): Hadamard's criteria.
- [MSC 35 - Partial differential equations](node:MSC%2035%20-%20Partial%20differential%20equations): field map.

### Common pitfalls
Existence of a formal or analytic solution says nothing about smooth data: Cauchy–Kovalevskaya needs analyticity, Kovalevskaya's heat example has a divergent formal series, and Lewy's equation with smooth right-hand side has no solution at all. ([Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Kowalevski_theorem); [Lewy's example](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy%27s_example))

Regularity for single equations does not transfer to systems: De Giorgi's and Giusti–Miranda's examples give non-analytic solutions of elliptic systems. Nor do distributions settle nonlinear problems directly: Schwartz's impossibility theorem (1954) says there is no associative product of two distributions extending the product of a distribution by a smooth function. ([Hilbert's nineteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_nineteenth_problem); [Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))

For nonlinear first-order equations classical solutions typically break down (Burgers shocks; the eikonal example), so uniqueness must be stated in a class such as viscosity solutions. ([Burgers' equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgers%27_equation); [Viscosity solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscosity_solution))

### Open problems
- **Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (Clay Millennium Problem).** For $\nu>0$, $n=3$, prove either (A/B) that for every smooth divergence-free $u^\circ$ with rapid decay (or periodic), with $f\equiv0$, there are smooth $p,u$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty)$ (with bounded energy $\int|u|^2\,dx<C$ in the decaying case), or (C/D) that some smooth data and forcing admit no such solution. The 2D analogues are known (Ladyzhenskaya); in 3D, (A) and (B) are known for small data or on a short time interval, and the corresponding questions for the Euler equations ($\nu=0$) are also open. ([Fefferman, official statement](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf); [Clay](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation): classification, weak solutions, well-posedness and regularity.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.152 lecture notes (Speck)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/pages/lecture-notes/): heat, Laplace, wave, Fourier, Schrödinger and transport/Burgers; with [Silvestre, PDE notes](https://math.uchicago.edu/~luis/pdenotes.pdf) for energy methods and maximum principles.
- **Primary:** [Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, 2nd ed. (AMS GSM 19, 2010)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/019): the standard graduate monograph.
- **Further reading:** [Gilbarg and Trudinger, *Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order* (Springer Classics in Mathematics, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61798-0): Schauder theory, maximum principles and De Giorgi–Nash–Moser; [Fefferman, Navier–Stokes problem statement](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf).

## Reference
### Overview
A partial order is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive relation; unlike a total order it allows pairs of elements that are incomparable. A set with such a relation is a partially ordered set (poset). Inclusion of subsets, divisibility of positive integers, and coordinatewise comparison of tuples are the basic models, and in each of them incomparable pairs occur: $2$ and $3$ under divisibility, $\{x\}$ and $\{y\}$ under inclusion. ([Wikipedia: Partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set); [Pong](https://math.csudh.edu/~pong/281Pub/06_Partial_Orders.html))

Order theory studies posets through chains and antichains, linear extensions and dimension, lattices of up- and down-sets, and the incidence algebra with its Möbius function. These tools connect posets to combinatorics (Dilworth's theorem, inclusion–exclusion), to set theory (Zorn's lemma, well-orders), and to finite topologies, which correspond exactly to preorders. ([Britz–Cameron](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))

### Formal definition
A partial order on $X$ is a relation $\le$ with $x\le x$ (reflexivity), $x\le y\wedge y\le x\Rightarrow x=y$ (antisymmetry), and $x\le y\wedge y\le z\Rightarrow x\le z$ (transitivity). A strict partial order $<$ is irreflexive, asymmetric and transitive; removing or adding the diagonal pairs $(a,a)$ gives a bijection between strict and non-strict orders. A total order is a partial order in which every two elements are comparable. ([Wikipedia: Partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set))

A chain is a subset in which every two elements are comparable; an antichain is a subset in which no two distinct elements are comparable. For a finite poset the height is the largest size of a chain and the width $w(X)$ the largest size of an antichain. $b$ covers $a$ if $a<b$ and no element lies strictly between them; the Hasse diagram of a finite poset draws the covering pairs. A poset is locally finite if every interval $[a,b]=\{x:a\le x\le b\}$ is finite. ([Wikipedia: Partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set); [Britz–Cameron, §§4–5](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))

An upper bound of $Y\subseteq X$ is an element of $X$, not necessarily in $Y$, above every element of $Y$; the supremum (join) is the least upper bound when it exists, and the infimum (meet) is defined dually. A greatest element is above every element; a maximal element has nothing strictly above it. ([Pong](https://math.csudh.edu/~pong/281Pub/06_Partial_Orders.html))

A relation is well-founded if every nonempty subset has a minimal element; a well-founded total order is a well-order. ([Wikipedia: Well-founded relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-founded_relation))

### Key results
- **Dilworth's theorem (1950).** A finite poset $X$ can be partitioned into $w(X)$ chains. Since an antichain meets each chain at most once, $w(X)$ is the minimum number of chains in such a partition. ([Britz–Cameron, Thm 4.1](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf); [Wikipedia: Mirsky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirsky%27s_theorem))
- **Mirsky's theorem (1971).** In a finite poset, the height equals the minimum number of antichains in a partition of the set into antichains. It is the dual of Dilworth's theorem and is easier to prove; it amounts to the perfectness of comparability graphs. ([Wikipedia: Mirsky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirsky%27s_theorem))
- **Linear extensions.** If $a,b$ are incomparable in a partial order $R$, then $R\cup(A\times B)$ with $A=\{x:x\le a\}$, $B=\{y:b\le y\}$ is a partial order extending $R$ with $a<b$. Hence every partial order on a finite set extends to a total order, and every finite partial order is the intersection of its linear extensions. ([Britz–Cameron, Prop. 6.2, Thms 6.1, 6.3](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- **Szpilrajn extension theorem (1930).** Every partial order on any set is contained in a total order. The standard proof applies Zorn's lemma to the partial orders extending the given one. Some choice is needed: the statement is not provable in ZF alone, but it is strictly weaker than the axiom of choice. ([Wikipedia: Szpilrajn extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szpilrajn_extension_theorem); [Britz–Cameron, §6](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- **Dimension.** The dimension of a partial order is the least number of total orders whose intersection it is. The crown on $2n$ elements has dimension $n$, so finite dimension is unbounded; by the [compactness theorem](node:Compactness%20Theorem), if every finite restriction has dimension at most $n$, so does the whole order. ([Britz–Cameron, Props 6.4, Thm 6.5](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- **Zorn's lemma.** If $P$ is a nonempty poset and every chain in $P$ has an upper bound in $P$, then $P$ has a maximal element. Over ZF, Zorn's lemma, the axiom of choice and the well-ordering theorem are equivalent. ([Wikipedia: Zorn's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zorn%27s_lemma))
- **Well-founded induction.** If $R$ is well-founded on $X$ and, for every $x$, $P(y)$ for all $y\,R\,x$ implies $P(x)$, then $P$ holds on all of $X$. Assuming dependent choice, well-foundedness is equivalent to the absence of infinite descending chains. ([Wikipedia: Well-founded relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-founded_relation))
- **Cover representation.** In a locally finite poset, $x\le y$ if and only if there is a finite sequence $x=z_0,\dots,z_n=y$ in which each $z_{i+1}$ covers $z_i$. ([Britz–Cameron, Prop. 5.1](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- **Möbius inversion.** For a locally finite poset, the Möbius function is defined by $\mu(x,x)=1$ and $\mu(x,y)=-\sum_{x\le z<y}\mu(x,z)$ for $x<y$; it is the inverse of the zeta function in the incidence algebra, and $f=g\zeta\iff g=f\mu$. On the Boolean lattice $\mu(A,B)=(-1)^{|B\setminus A|}$, which yields inclusion–exclusion; under divisibility $\mu(a,b)=\mu(b/a)$ is the classical Möbius function. ([Britz–Cameron, §8, Thm 8.1](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf); [Wikipedia: Incidence algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_algebra))
- **Birkhoff's representation of finite distributive lattices.** The down-sets of a finite poset form a distributive lattice under union and intersection; conversely, a finite distributive lattice is recovered from the subposet of its nonzero join-irreducible elements, and the two constructions are mutually inverse. ([Britz–Cameron, Thm 10.3](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- **Finite topologies.** On a finite set, topologies correspond one-to-one to preorders (reflexive, transitive relations), with $x\preceq y$ when every open set containing $x$ contains $y$. ([Britz–Cameron, Thm 7.1](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))

### Examples
Divisibility on positive integers, inclusion on a power set, and the product order $(a,b)\le(c,d)\iff a\le c,\ b\le d$ are partial orders that are not total; the lexicographic order on pairs drawn from totally ordered sets is total. The integers with the usual order are locally finite, but $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with the lexicographic order is not. ([Wikipedia: Partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set))

The strict componentwise order on $\mathbb{N}^2$ (both coordinates strictly smaller) and proper divisibility on the positive integers are well-founded but not total; the negative integers and the nonnegative rationals with the usual order are not well-founded. ([Wikipedia: Well-founded relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-founded_relation))

Every poset embeds in $(\mathcal{P}(X),\subseteq)$ via $x\mapsto{\downarrow}x$, and every finite poset embeds in the positive integers under divisibility. ([Pong](https://math.csudh.edu/~pong/281Pub/06_Partial_Orders.html))

A lattice is a poset in which every pair has a least upper bound $x\vee y$ and greatest lower bound $x\wedge y$ (Britz–Cameron also require a top $1$ and bottom $0$). Subsets of a set and subspaces of a vector space are lattices, with join $A\cup B$ and $\operatorname{span}(U\cup V)$ respectively. ([Britz–Cameron, §9](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))

### History
Szpilrajn proved the extension theorem in 1930, Dilworth the chain decomposition theorem in 1950, and Mirsky its dual in 1971. Rota treated incidence algebras and Möbius functions of locally finite posets in a series of papers beginning in 1964 with "On the Foundations of Combinatorial Theory I: Theory of Möbius Functions". ([Wikipedia: Szpilrajn extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szpilrajn_extension_theorem); [Wikipedia: Mirsky's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirsky%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Incidence algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_algebra))

Britz and Cameron wrote their notes in November 2001 as background for study-group talks by Rafael Sorkin on discrete posets and quantum gravity, where a partial order models causal structure. ([Britz–Cameron](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))

### Connections
- [Functions and Relations](node:Functions%20and%20Relations): a partial order is a binary relation with three axioms.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory) and [Axiom of Choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice): Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem are statements about posets.
- [Lattice Theory](node:Lattice%20Theory), [Distributive Lattices](node:Distributive%20Lattices), [Boolean Algebras](node:Boolean%20Algebras): posets with joins and meets.
- [Fixed Points in Complete Lattices](node:Fixed%20Points%20in%20Complete%20Lattices): fixed-point theorems for monotone maps on ordered sets.
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): Hasse diagrams; Dilworth's theorem is equivalent to Hall's and König's theorems.
- [Directed Acyclic Graphs](node:Directed%20Acyclic%20Graphs): the strict order of a finite poset is a transitively closed DAG.
- [Inclusion–Exclusion Principle](node:Inclusion–Exclusion%20Principle): Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice.
- [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics): chain decompositions, linear extensions and Möbius functions.
- [Topological Spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces): finite topologies correspond to preorders.
- [Mathematical Induction](node:Mathematical%20Induction): well-founded induction generalises it.
- [Quantum Gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity): discrete posets as models of causal order.
- [MSC 06Axx - Ordered sets](node:MSC%2006Axx%20-%20Ordered%20sets): subfield map.

### Common pitfalls
- Antisymmetry is not asymmetry: $x\le x$ is allowed; it is the strict order that is asymmetric. ([Wikipedia: Partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set))
- A maximal element need not be greatest; a poset may have many maximal elements and no greatest one, and infinite posets may have none: the positive integers under divisibility have no maximal element. ([Wikipedia: Partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set); [Britz–Cameron, §4](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- The supremum of the empty set is the least element of $X$, if there is one, because every element is an upper bound of $\emptyset$. ([Pong](https://math.csudh.edu/~pong/281Pub/06_Partial_Orders.html))
- The finite linear-extension argument does not give the infinite case without choice; there are models of ZF in which some infinite poset has no linear extension. ([Britz–Cameron, §6](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))
- Describing an infinite order by covers requires local finiteness: $\mathbb{Q}$ has no covering pairs at all. ([Britz–Cameron, Prop. 5.1](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf))

### Open problems
- **The 1/3–2/3 conjecture.** Every finite poset that is not totally ordered has elements $x,y$ such that, in a uniformly random linear extension, $1/3\le\Pr(x<y)\le 2/3$. Kislitsyn formulated it in 1968, and Fredman and Linial later posed it independently. Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter (1995) proved the weaker bound $1/2-\sqrt5/10\approx0.276$, which is optimal for infinite posets; the conjecture remains unsolved. ([Wikipedia: 1/3–2/3 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture))
- **Inequalities for linear extensions.** Chan and Pak survey inequalities for the number of linear extensions of finite posets and discuss open problems in the area. ([Chan–Pak, arXiv:2311.02743](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02743))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Partially ordered set (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set): definitions, examples, intervals, covers.
- **Learn:** [Pong, Partial orders (CSU Dominguez Hills)](https://math.csudh.edu/~pong/281Pub/06_Partial_Orders.html): definitions, embeddings and exercises.
- **Learn:** [Britz and Cameron, Partially ordered sets (QMUL notes)](https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/p.j.cameron/csgnotes/posets.pdf): Dilworth, linear extensions, dimension, Möbius functions, lattices and Birkhoff's theorem.
- **Primary:** [S. H. Chan and I. Pak, Linear extensions of finite posets (arXiv:2311.02743)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02743): research survey of linear-extension inequalities and open problems.
- **Further reading:** [B. A. Davey and H. A. Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press 2002](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511809088): the standard graduate introduction to posets and lattices.

## Reference
### Overview
A partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) generalizes a [Markov decision process](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes) to the case where the controller cannot see the underlying state. The system still evolves by Markov transitions under the chosen actions, but the agent receives only observations drawn from a state-dependent observation model, so it must act on its history or, equivalently, on a probability distribution over states called the belief ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process)). Krishnamurthy describes a POMDP as a controlled [hidden Markov model](node:Hidden%20Markov%20Models) whose belief is updated by an HMM filter ([Krishnamurthy, CUP](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/partially-observed-markov-decision-processes/partially-observed-markov-decision-processes-pomdps/5E831431991E2CFAE4CE162E01D7F129)).

The belief is a sufficient statistic for the history, a fact going back to Aoki and Åström in 1965, and updating it is a [Bayesian](node:Bayesian%20Inference) filtering step ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf)). A POMDP is therefore equivalent to a fully observed "belief MDP" whose state space is the continuous probability simplex over $S$, even when $S$ is finite ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process)). This equivalence explains both the elegance and the difficulty of the model: exact planning is PSPACE-hard for finite horizons and undecidable for some infinite-horizon questions ([Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.04735)).

POMDPs are a very general model of sequential decision-making that allows uncertainty both in action effects and in knowledge of the system state, though only small problems can be solved exactly ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf)). Applications listed in the literature include ischemic heart disease management, assistive handwashing for people with dementia, conservation of Sumatran tigers and aircraft collision avoidance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process)).

### Formal definition
A discrete-time POMDP consists of a state space $S$, action space $A$, observation space $O$, transition kernel $T(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)$, initial-state distribution $T_0$, observation kernel $\mathbb{O}(o_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1},a_t)$, reward $R$, and horizon $N$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process)).

**Belief update.** After taking action $a$ in belief $b$ and observing $o$,
$$b'(s') = \eta\,\mathbb{O}(o\mid s',a)\sum_{s\in S}T(s'\mid s,a)\,b(s),\qquad \eta^{-1}=\Pr(o\mid b,a)=\sum_{s'}\mathbb{O}(o\mid s',a)\sum_{s}T(s'\mid s,a)\,b(s).$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process))

**Belief MDP.** Its states are beliefs $b\in\Delta(S)$, its reward is $r(b,a)=\sum_s b(s)R(s,a)$, and from $b$ under $a$ it moves to $\tau(b,a,o)$ with probability $\Pr(o\mid b,a)$. The optimal value satisfies the Bellman equation
$$V^*(b)=\max_{a\in A}\Big[r(b,a)+\gamma\sum_{o\in O}\Pr(o\mid b,a)\,V^*(\tau(b,a,o))\Big].$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process))

### Key results
- **Sufficiency of the belief state.** Policies based on full histories grow exponentially with the horizon; the belief summarizes the history sufficiently for optimal control (Aoki 1965, Åström 1965), so a POMDP is an MDP over the $(|S|-1)$-dimensional simplex. ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf))
- **Piecewise-linear convexity (Sondik).** For every finite horizon $k$, the optimal value function is piecewise linear and convex in the belief: there is a finite set $\Gamma_k$ of "$\alpha$-vectors" (one value per state) with $V_k(b)=\max_{\alpha\in\Gamma_k}\sum_s \alpha(s)b(s)$. Each $\alpha$-vector is the value of a $k$-step conditional plan, which is linear in $b$. ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process))
- **Hardness of exact and approximate planning.** For finite horizons, computing an optimal policy is PSPACE-hard (Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis); unless PSPACE $=\Sigma_2^P$ optimal policies have no polynomial-space description; computing an $\epsilon$-additive approximation of the optimal value is PSPACE-hard for constant $\epsilon$; and in the infinite-horizon discounted setting, deciding whether some policy achieves value at least a given threshold is undecidable. ([Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.04735))
- **Decidability depends on the objective.** For qualitative $\omega$-regular objectives the picture is mixed: almost-sure Büchi objectives with infinite-memory policies are EXPTIME-complete, while positive Büchi objectives with infinite memory are undecidable (Chatterjee, Chmelík and Tracol 2016). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process))
- **Quasipolynomial planning under observability.** Call the observation matrices $\gamma$-observable if $\|\mathbb{O}_h^\top b-\mathbb{O}_h^\top b'\|_1\ge\gamma\|b-b'\|_1$ for all state distributions $b,b'$. For any $\epsilon,\gamma>0$ there is an algorithm that, given a $\gamma$-observable POMDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions, $O$ observations and horizon $H$, outputs an $\epsilon$-suboptimal policy in time $H(OA)^{C\log(SH/\epsilon)/\gamma^4}$ for a universal constant $C$. Conversely, under the Exponential Time Hypothesis no algorithm for $\gamma$-observable POMDPs runs in time $(SAHO)^{o(\log(SAHO/\epsilon)/\gamma)}$, so quasipolynomial time is necessary, though the $\gamma$-dependence of the two bounds differs. The proof rests on quantitative filter-stability bounds. ([Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.04735); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04735))

### Examples
- **Machine maintenance (Sondik 1973)** and the "crying baby" problem are standard small examples used to illustrate belief-space value functions. ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process))
- **Point-based value iteration (PBVI).** Pineau, Gordon and Thrun approximate exact value iteration by selecting a small set of representative belief points, chosen along stochastic trajectories, and keeping one value hyperplane ($\alpha$-vector) per point; with it they solved an 870-state robot domain, Tag, inspired by laser tag. ([Pineau, Gordon and Thrun](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ggordon/jpineau-ggordon-thrun.ijcai03.pdf))
- **Other approximations.** Grid-based value interpolation, finite-memory controllers, learned value-function representations trained by simulation, and [heuristic search](node:Heuristic%20Search) through belief space from the initial belief. ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf)) Online planners such as [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search) are also used. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process))

### History
Åström introduced the framework in 1965 for discrete state spaces; the acronym POMDP was coined in operations research, and Kaelbling and Littman later brought the model into AI and automated planning ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process)). Sondik introduced value iteration for POMDPs in the 1970s (1971), and numerous authors later refined it ([Pineau, Gordon and Thrun](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ggordon/jpineau-ggordon-thrun.ijcai03.pdf)); Sondik (1973) proved that finite-horizon value functions are piecewise linear and convex ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf)). Pineau, Gordon and Thrun's point-based value iteration attacked the "curse of history", the exponential growth with horizon of the action-observation histories that exact value iteration tracks ([Pineau, Gordon and Thrun](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ggordon/jpineau-ggordon-thrun.ijcai03.pdf)), and Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi later gave a quasipolynomial-time planner for observable POMDPs ([Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04735)).

### Connections
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the special case with perfect state observation; a POMDP is an MDP over beliefs.
- [Hidden Markov Models](node:Hidden%20Markov%20Models): the uncontrolled analogue; belief updating is HMM forward filtering with actions.
- [Bayesian Inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference): the belief update is Bayes' rule applied each step.
- [Value Iteration](node:Value%20Iteration): exact POMDP value iteration backs up sets of $\alpha$-vectors.
- [Sequential Monte Carlo](node:Sequential%20Monte%20Carlo): particle filters approximate beliefs when $S$ is large or continuous.
- [Stochastic Optimal Control](node:Stochastic%20Optimal%20Control): control with imperfect state information is the continuous counterpart.
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): partial observability is a central difficulty when the model is unknown.
- [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search): basis of online POMDP planners.
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains): the latent state process under a fixed policy.

### Common pitfalls
- The belief MDP has a continuous state space even when $S$ is finite, so standard finite-MDP algorithms do not apply directly. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process))
- Piecewise linearity is a finite-horizon statement; the number of $\alpha$-vectors can grow exponentially with the horizon, and each vector has the size of the state space. ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf))
- Implementing a value-function policy requires maintaining the belief online, which itself costs time proportional to the state-space representation. ([Boutilier, CSC2534](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf))
- Since even $\epsilon$-additive approximation of the optimal value is PSPACE-hard for constant $\epsilon$, provable planning guarantees need structural assumptions; Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi's assumption is one-step observability, which can hold only when there are at least as many observations as states. ([Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.04735))

### Open problems
- **Beyond one-step observability.** Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi ask whether there are multi-step generalizations of observability that still allow positive (efficient planning) results. ([Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.04735))
- **Overcomplete POMDPs.** They also ask for natural assumptions under which provable planning guarantees can be established when there are more states than observations. ([Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.04735))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Partially observable Markov decision process (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_observable_Markov_decision_process): definition, belief MDP, approximate methods, decidability table.
- **Learn:** [Boutilier, CSC2534 Lecture 5: Partially Observable MDPs (Toronto)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~cebly/2534/Notes/CSC2534_Lecture5.pdf): belief states, $\alpha$-vectors, exact algorithms, sources of intractability.
- **Primary:** [Golowich, Moitra and Rohatgi, Planning in Observable POMDPs in Quasipolynomial Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04735): survey of hardness results and the observability theorem.
- **Primary:** [Pineau, Gordon and Thrun, Point-based value iteration: An anytime algorithm for POMDPs](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ggordon/jpineau-ggordon-thrun.ijcai03.pdf): the PBVI algorithm.
- **Further reading:** [Krishnamurthy, Partially Observed Markov Decision Processes: From Filtering to Controlled Sensing (Cambridge University Press, 2016)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/partially-observed-markov-decision-processes/partially-observed-markov-decision-processes-pomdps/5E831431991E2CFAE4CE162E01D7F129): graduate monograph treating POMDPs as controlled HMMs, with structural results.
references.Partition Function:
## Reference
### Overview
The partition function $Z$ is the normalizing constant of the canonical ensemble: a system in contact with a heat bath at temperature $T$ occupies microstate $\mu$ with probability $e^{-\beta H(\mu)}/Z$, where $\beta=1/k_BT$ and $Z=\sum_\mu e^{-\beta H(\mu)}$.
