([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)) The symbol comes from the German *Zustandssumme*, "sum over states", and computing $Z$ is equivalent to taking the Laplace transform of the [density of states](node:Density%20of%20States) from energy to $\beta$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28statistical_mechanics%29))

Its importance is that $\ln Z$ is a generating function: the Helmholtz free energy is $F=-k_BT\ln Z$, and the mean, variance and higher cumulants of the energy are derivatives of $\ln Z$ in $\beta$. Every equilibrium thermodynamic quantity therefore follows once $Z$ is known as a function of temperature and the external parameters. ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf))

Beyond physics, partition functions of graphs (the independence polynomial, the Ising and Potts models, the matching and chromatic polynomials) are studied in combinatorics and complexity theory, where zero-free regions in the complex plane yield efficient approximation algorithms, and for some models the presence or absence of zeros corresponds exactly to easiness or hardness of approximation. ([Patel and Regts](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143))

### Formal definition
**Canonical, discrete.** $Z(T,x)=\sum_{\mu}e^{-\beta H(\mu)}$, summed over microstates at fixed external parameters $x$. ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf))

**Canonical, classical continuous.** For $N$ identical particles,
$$Z=\frac{1}{N!\,h^{3N}}\int e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p .$$
**Quantum.** $Z=\operatorname{tr}\big(e^{-\beta\hat H}\big)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28statistical_mechanics%29))

**Grand canonical.** $\mathcal{Z}=\sum_i\exp\big((N_i\mu-E_i)/k_BT\big)=\sum_N z^N Z(N,V,T)$ with activity $z=e^{\mu/k_BT}$, and $\Phi_G=-k_BT\ln\mathcal{Z}$ is the grand potential. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28statistical_mechanics%29))

**Lattice spin models.** For the Ising model $Z_\beta=\sum_\sigma e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}$ over spin configurations, with $P_\beta(\sigma)=e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}/Z_\beta$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model))

### Key results
- **Thermodynamics from $\ln Z$.** $\langle E\rangle=-\partial\ln Z/\partial\beta$, $\langle(\Delta E)^2\rangle=\partial^2\ln Z/\partial\beta^2$, $C_V=\langle(\Delta E)^2\rangle/k_BT^2$, $A=-k_BT\ln Z$ and $S=-\partial A/\partial T$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28statistical_mechanics%29))
- **Cumulant generating function.** $Z(\beta)$ plays the role of a characteristic function for $H$ with $\beta$ in place of $ik$, so $\langle H^n\rangle_c=(-1)^n\partial^n\ln Z/\partial\beta^n$. All cumulants are proportional to $N$, so $\sqrt{\langle H^2\rangle_c}/\langle H\rangle\sim N^{-1/2}$, and $Z\approx e^{-\beta F(E^*)}$ with $E^*$ the most probable energy. ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf))
- **Factorization.** For independent subsystems $Z=\prod_j\zeta_j$; for $N$ identical indistinguishable subsystems $Z=\zeta^N/N!$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28statistical_mechanics%29))
- **Lee–Yang theorem.** Let $H=-\sum J_{jk}S_jS_k-\sum z_jS_j$ with all $J_{jk}\ge0$ (ferromagnetic), and let each single-spin measure be even, decay fast enough that Gaussians are integrable, and have the Lee–Yang property ($\int e^{hS}d\mu_j(S)\neq0$ whenever $\operatorname{Re}h>0$). If every $z_j$ has positive real part, the partition function is nonzero. With a common field $z$, all zeros in $z$ are purely imaginary; for the Ising model, $\rho=e^{\pi z}$ maps them onto the unit circle. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Yang_theorem))
- **Onsager's free energy.** For the zero-field anisotropic square-lattice Ising model,
$$-\beta f=\ln2+\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\ln\big[\cosh2\beta J_1\cosh2\beta J_2-\sinh2\beta J_1\cos\theta_1-\sinh2\beta J_2\cos\theta_2\big]\,d\theta_1d\theta_2 ,$$
with critical point $\sinh(2J_1/kT_c)\sinh(2J_2/kT_c)=1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)) Onsager's original paper also shows the specific heat diverges as $-\log|T-T_c|$. ([Onsager 1944](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117))
- **Barvinok's interpolation method.** If a family of polynomials $P_G$ of degree $d(G)$ is zero-free on $|z|\le R$ and the coefficient $a_i(G)$ can be computed in time $T(|G|,i)$, then a multiplicative $\varepsilon$-approximation of $P_G(z)$ for $|z|<R$ takes time $mT(n,m)+O(m^2)$ with $m=C\ln(d(G)/\varepsilon)$: one truncates the Taylor series of $\ln P_G$. ([Patel and Regts](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143))
- **Zero-free disk for the independence polynomial.** For graphs of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$, $Z_G(\lambda)\neq0$ when $|\lambda|\le(\Delta-1)^{\Delta-1}/\Delta^\Delta$ (Shearer, Dobrushin, Scott and Sokal), and this disk cannot be enlarged in general. For $\Delta\ge3$, zero-freeness on a neighbourhood of $[0,\lambda_c(\Delta))$ with $\lambda_c=(\Delta-1)^{\Delta-1}/(\Delta-2)^\Delta$ yields an FPTAS there, while above $\lambda_c$ no FPTAS exists unless P = NP. ([Patel and Regts](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143))

### Examples
- **Two-dimensional Ising model.** Isotropic couplings $J_1=J_2=J$ give $T_c=2J/\big(k\ln(1+\sqrt2)\big)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model))
- **Three-dimensional Ising model.** No exact solution of the 3D model has been found, though there is no proof that one cannot exist; Istrail's NP-completeness result concerns [spin glasses](node:Spin%20Glasses) with varying couplings on nonplanar lattices, not the uniform ferromagnet. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model))
- **Canonical energy distribution.** $p(E)=\Omega(E)e^{-\beta E}/Z$, which near its peak is Gaussian with variance $k_BT^2C_x$. ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf))
- **Grand canonical gas.** Summing $z^NZ(N,V,T)$ over particle number converts the canonical partition functions into $\mathcal{Z}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28statistical_mechanics%29))

### History
Yang and Lee's 1952 papers in *Physical Review* 87 (pp. 404–409 and 410–419) studied the thermodynamics of an infinitely large sample and proved the unit-circle theorem for the Ising model. ([Yang and Lee 1952](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.87.404); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Yang_theorem)) Asano (1970) extended it to the Heisenberg model with a simpler proof, Simon and Griffiths (1973) to continuous spins, Newman (1974) reduced it to the non-interacting case, and Lieb and Sokal (1981) extended Newman's result to higher-dimensional spins. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Yang_theorem)) Onsager's 1944 paper computed rigorously the zero-field partition function of the 2D Ising model, solving the eigenvalue problem for a strip of finite width and passing to infinite width. ([Onsager 1944](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)) Barvinok introduced the Taylor-interpolation approach, first applied to permanents. ([Patel and Regts](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143))

### Connections
- [Statistical Mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics): the partition function is the normalizer of the canonical ensemble and the bridge to thermodynamics.
- [Microcanonical and Canonical Ensembles](node:Microcanonical%20and%20Canonical%20Ensembles): $Z$ is the Laplace transform of the microcanonical density of states.
- [Grand Canonical Ensemble](node:Grand%20Canonical%20Ensemble): the grand partition function sums canonical ones weighted by activity.
- [Thermodynamic Limit](node:Thermodynamic%20Limit): phase transitions appear as non-analyticity of $\lim N^{-1}\ln Z$, located by limits of complex zeros.
- [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model): the model whose partition function Onsager computed and Lee and Yang analysed.
- [Equipartition Theorem](node:Equipartition%20Theorem): follows from Gaussian integrals in the classical partition function.
- [Generating Functions](node:Generating%20Functions): $\ln Z$ is the cumulant generating function of the energy.
- [Gibbs Measures](node:Gibbs%20Measures): the infinite-volume objects that replace $e^{-\beta H}/Z$ when $Z$ diverges.
- [Path Integral Formulation](node:Path%20Integral%20Formulation): $\operatorname{tr}e^{-\beta\hat H}$ is a path integral in imaginary time.
- [Cluster Expansions](node:Cluster%20Expansions): expansions of $\ln Z$ valid in zero-free regions at high temperature or low density.
- [Thermodynamics](node:Thermodynamics): every equilibrium potential is a logarithmic derivative of $Z$, e.g. the [heat capacity](node:Heat%20Capacity) from $\partial_\beta^2\ln Z$.
- [Approximation Algorithms](node:Approximation%20Algorithms): Barvinok's method gives FPTASs for partition functions inside zero-free regions.
- [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory): approximate evaluation of graph partition functions is a central counting problem.

### Common pitfalls
- **Forgetting $N!$ and $h^{3N}$.** Without $1/N!$ the classical $Z$ overcounts identical particles and the entropy is not extensive (Gibbs paradox). ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf))
- **Transitions need infinite volume.** Phase transitions appear only in the thermodynamic limit, a fact that drives debates about emergence and reduction ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)); accordingly Yang and Lee's theory of condensation is formulated for an infinitely large sample ([Yang and Lee 1952](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.87.404)).
- **Divergent heat capacity.** The Gaussian approximation of $p(E)$ needs care where $C_x$ diverges, as at some continuous transitions. ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf))
- **Additive versus multiplicative error.** A truncated Taylor series of $\ln Z$ gives an additive error, which becomes a multiplicative approximation of $Z$ after exponentiating. ([Patel and Regts](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143))

### Open problems
- **Counting colourings for $q>\Delta$.** It is believed that an FPTAS for counting proper $q$-colourings of graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ exists whenever $q>\Delta$; the survey calls this an active area of research. As of that 2022 survey the deterministic state of the art was an FPTAS for $q\ge2\Delta$ (Liu, Sinclair and Srivastava), while randomized Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms give better bounds. ([Patel and Regts](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143))
- **Optimal zero-containing disk for the chromatic polynomial.** The survey gives a disk of radius $6.91\,\Delta(G)$ containing all zeros of $\chi_G$ and calls the optimal constant unclear. ([Patel and Regts](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143)) The constant has since been lowered to $5.94$ by Jenssen, Patel and Regts and to $4.25$ by Bencs and Regts (preprint, 2025), with $3.60$ for graphs of large girth and $3.81$ for claw-free graphs. ([Bencs and Regts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04366))
- **Zeros versus hardness.** The program of matching the zero-free regions of a model with the boundary of efficient approximability is exact for the matching polynomial and the ferromagnetic Ising model in a field, partial for the Ising model in the edge interaction, and for the independence polynomial established only in the limit $\Delta\to\infty$, with no information yet for any finite $\Delta$. ([Patel and Regts](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Partition function (statistical mechanics), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28statistical_mechanics%29): definitions and thermodynamic identities.
- **Reference:** [Lee–Yang theorem, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Yang_theorem): statement, generalizations and history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.333 Lecture 13 (Kardar)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf): derivation of the canonical ensemble, $F=-k_BT\ln Z$ and energy cumulants.
- **Primary:** [Onsager, Crystal Statistics I (1944)](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117): exact partition function of the 2D Ising model.
- **Primary:** [Yang and Lee, Theory of Condensation (1952)](https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.87.404): equations of state and phase transitions in the infinite-volume limit.
- **Primary:** [Patel and Regts, Approximate counting using Taylor's theorem: a survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.08143): zeros of partition functions and approximation algorithms.
- **Further reading:** [Barvinok, Combinatorics and Complexity of Partition Functions (Springer, 2016)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-319-51829-9): monograph in Springer's Algorithms and Combinatorics series.
references.Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena:
## Reference
### Overview
A phase transition is an abrupt change in the macroscopic state of a system as a control parameter (temperature, pressure, field) is varied: melting, boiling, the onset of ferromagnetism, superconductivity. Mathematically, phase transitions occur where the free energy is non-analytic; this non-analyticity generally stems from interactions among a large number of particles and does not appear in small systems. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition)) The free energy is obtained from the [Partition Function](node:Partition%20Function), which is why that note is a prerequisite.

Transitions are classified into first-order transitions, which involve latent heat and phase coexistence, and continuous (second-order) transitions, which show a divergent susceptibility, an infinite correlation length, and power-law decay of correlations at the critical point. The two phases are distinguished by an order parameter that vanishes in one phase and not in the other, such as the magnetization of a ferromagnet or the density difference between liquid and gas. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition))

Critical phenomena are the singular behaviours near a continuous transition. Observables diverge or vanish as power laws with critical exponents, and these exponents take the same values for very different physical systems: the liquid–gas critical point has the exponents of uniaxial ferromagnets, independent of chemical composition. This universality is explained by the [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group): at criticality the characteristic length scale becomes infinite, and for equilibrium ferromagnets the exponents are believed to depend only on the dimension, the range of the interaction and the spin dimension. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_phenomena); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent))

### Formal definition
Let $\tau=(T-T_c)/T_c$ be the reduced temperature. The standard critical exponents are defined by the asymptotic power laws
$$C\propto\tau^{-\alpha},\quad \Psi\propto(-\tau)^{\beta}\ (\tau<0),\quad \chi\propto\tau^{-\gamma},\quad \xi\propto\tau^{-\nu},$$
$$J\propto\Psi^{\delta}\ \text{at }\tau=0,\qquad \langle\psi(0)\psi(r)\rangle\propto r^{-d+2-\eta}\ \text{at }\tau=0,$$
where $C$ is the heat capacity, $\Psi$ the order parameter, $\chi$ the susceptibility, $\xi$ the correlation length, $J$ the source (e.g. magnetic) field and $d$ the spatial dimension; primed exponents $\alpha',\gamma',\nu'$ describe the ordered side. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent))

In the **Ehrenfest classification** a transition is of order $n$ if the $n$th derivative of the free energy is the lowest discontinuous one. Onsager's 1944 exact solution of the Ising model gave the first transition that does not fit this scheme, since its specific heat diverges logarithmically rather than jumping; the modern classification distinguishes first-order from continuous transitions, and also recognizes infinite-order transitions such as the Kosterlitz–Thouless transition, which are continuous but break no symmetry. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition))

For the nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model) on $\mathbb Z^d$, the critical inverse temperature is $\beta_c=\inf\{\beta:m^\ast(\beta)>0\}$, where $m^\ast(\beta)$ is the spontaneous magnetization. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))

### Key results
- **Scaling relations.** Near criticality only two exponents are independent (e.g. $\nu$ and $\eta$): $\alpha+2\beta+\gamma=2$, $\gamma=\beta(\delta-1)$, $\gamma=\nu(2-\eta)$, the hyperscaling relation $d\nu=2-\alpha$, and $2-\eta=d(\delta-1)/(\delta+1)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent)) Widom's scaling hypothesis and the work of Essam, Fisher and Widom in the 1960s produced these relations, using the 2D and 3D Ising models as checks. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))
- **Mean-field exponents and the upper critical dimension.** Landau theory gives $\alpha=\alpha'=0$, $\beta=1/2$, $\gamma=\gamma'=1$, $\delta=3$, and with gradient terms (Ginzburg–Landau) $\nu=1/2$, $\eta=0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent)) For $d$ above the upper critical dimension $d_u=4$ the saddle-point approximation is valid and these exponents are exact; for $d$ below the lower critical dimension ($d_\ell=2$ for continuous symmetry, $d_\ell=1$ for discrete) fluctuations destroy order; in the intermediate dimensions $d_\ell<d<d_u$, including $d=3$, fluctuations change the exponents without destroying order. ([Kardar, MIT 8.334 Lecture 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/608f0e0b2ffa840d4e51ee0a592ef823_MIT8_334S14_Lec5.pdf)) In $d=4$ the power laws acquire logarithmic corrections. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent))
- **Ginzburg criterion.** Fluctuation corrections to Landau theory become important for reduced temperatures $|t|\ll t_G\simeq(\xi_0^{\,d}\,\Delta C)^{-2/(4-d)}$, with $\xi_0$ the microscopic correlation length (in lattice units) and $\Delta C$ the mean-field specific-heat jump (per $Nk_B$). In $d=3$, $t_G\sim\xi_0^{-6}$: for conventional superconductors with $\xi_0\sim10^3a$ fluctuations are invisible ($t_G<10^{-18}$), while ordinary transitions with $\xi_0$ of a few lattice spacings show them at $t\sim10^{-1}$–$10^{-2}$. ([Kardar, MIT 8.334 Lecture 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/608f0e0b2ffa840d4e51ee0a592ef823_MIT8_334S14_Lec5.pdf))
- **Peierls' argument.** Peierls showed, by mapping Ising configurations on $\mathbb Z^2$ to contours on the dual lattice (the low-temperature expansion), that the Ising model in two and three dimensions has a ferromagnetic phase at low temperature, contradicting extrapolation from Ising's one-dimensional result. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))
- **Onsager's exact solution.** The zero-field free energy of the square-lattice Ising model is
$$-\beta f(\beta,0)=\ln2+\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\ln\!\left[\cosh(2\beta)^2-\sinh(2\beta)(\cos\theta_1+\cos\theta_2)\right]d\theta_1\,d\theta_2,$$
announced in 1942 and published in 1944; the transfer matrices generate a finite-dimensional Lie algebra, i.e. the model is integrable. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))
- **Lee–Yang theorem.** For the ferromagnetic Ising model ($J_{xy}\ge0$) on a finite graph with vertex-dependent complex fields $h=(h_x)$, $Z(G,\beta,h)\ne0$ whenever $\operatorname{Re}h_x>0$ for every $x$; for a uniform field $h$, all zeros of the partition function lie on the imaginary axis. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Yang_theorem)) Consequently the free energy is analytic in a nonzero real magnetic field, with exponential decay of truncated correlations there: phase transitions can only occur at $h=0$. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))
- **Continuity of the 3D Ising transition.** For the nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic Ising model in $d\ge3$, $m^\ast(\beta_c)=0$: the transition is continuous. The proof uses percolation methods on the double random-current representation, adapting the Burton–Keane uniqueness argument. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))
- **Infrared bound.** Reflection positivity (Gaussian domination) gives, for $d>2$ and all $\beta>0$, $\langle\sigma_x\sigma_y\rangle_\beta-m^\ast(\beta)^2\le C\|x-y\|^{2-d}$; at $\beta_c$ spin correlations therefore decay at least as fast as the random-walk Green function. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))

### Examples
- **Ferromagnet.** Curie observed in 1895 that magnets lose spontaneous magnetization above a critical (Curie) temperature, ranging from slightly over 100 °C for some alloys to 769.85 °C for iron: a paramagnet–ferromagnet transition. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))
- **Liquid–gas critical point.** The order parameter is the density difference; its exponents match uniaxial ferromagnets (Ising universality class). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition))
- **Melting.** Cooling a fluid into a crystal breaks continuous translation symmetry; the high-temperature phase usually has more symmetry. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition)) See [Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking](node:Spontaneous%20Symmetry%20Breaking).
- **Percolation.** In percolating networks, the connection probability plays the role of temperature. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition)) See [Percolation in Physical Systems](node:Percolation%20in%20Physical%20Systems).
- **3D Ising exponents from the conformal bootstrap.** The scaling dimensions of the spin and energy operators are $(\Delta_\sigma,\Delta_\varepsilon)=(0.5181489(10),\,1.412625(10))$, more precise than Monte Carlo. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))

### History
Lenz introduced the Ising model in 1920; Ising's one-dimensional analysis found no transition, Peierls' argument established one in higher dimensions, Kramers and Wannier (1941) used duality to predict the 2D critical point, and Onsager's 1944 paper solved the square-lattice model exactly. Kadanoff's block-spin argument justified scaling and universality, and Wilson then put the renormalization group in a general framework. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864)) Lev Landau's phenomenological theory of second-order transitions supplied the mean-field picture. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition))

### Connections
- [Partition Function](node:Partition%20Function): the free energy $-k_BT\ln Z$ is where non-analyticity appears in the thermodynamic limit.
- [Thermodynamic Limit](node:Thermodynamic%20Limit): finite systems have analytic free energies; transitions need infinite volume.
- [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model): the canonical lattice model with a continuous transition in $d\ge2$.
- [Landau Theory of Phase Transitions](node:Landau%20Theory%20of%20Phase%20Transitions): the mean-field order-parameter expansion.
- [Weiss Mean-Field Theory](node:Weiss%20Mean-Field%20Theory): the earliest mean-field theory of ferromagnetism.
- [Critical Exponents and Universality](node:Critical%20Exponents%20and%20Universality): the detailed theory of exponents and classes.
- [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group): explains universality via fixed points.
- [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory): describes critical points; exactly in 2D, numerically via the bootstrap in 3D.
- [Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking](node:Spontaneous%20Symmetry%20Breaking): most ordered phases break a symmetry of the Hamiltonian.
- [Kosterlitz–Thouless Transition](node:Kosterlitz–Thouless%20Transition): infinite-order transition without symmetry breaking in 2D.
- [Finite-Size Scaling](node:Finite-Size%20Scaling): how singularities round off in finite systems and simulations.
- [Markov Chain Critical Slowing Down](node:Markov%20Chain%20Critical%20Slowing%20Down): relaxation times diverge as $\tau\sim\xi^z$ near criticality.
- [Gibbs Measures](node:Gibbs%20Measures): the rigorous framework where phase coexistence means non-unique Gibbs states.
- [Superconductivity](node:Superconductivity): a transition where the Ginzburg criterion makes mean-field theory accurate.

### Common pitfalls
- **No transition in small systems.** The non-analyticity of the free energy that defines a transition comes from interactions of a large number of particles and does not appear in small systems; in the Ising model the free energy is defined as a limit of logarithms of finite-volume partition functions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition); [Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))
- **Mean-field exponents in $d=3$.** Mean-field theory neglects correlations, so critical behaviour usually differs from it below $d_u=4$; apparent mean-field behaviour in an experiment may only mean the resolution does not reach $t_G$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_phenomena); [Kardar, MIT 8.334 Lecture 5](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/608f0e0b2ffa840d4e51ee0a592ef823_MIT8_334S14_Lec5.pdf))
- **Universality is not a theorem.** For equilibrium ferromagnets the exponents are believed to depend only on dimension, interaction range and spin dimension, but universality is believed rather than proven in general. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent))
- **Exponent symbols are overloaded.** The inverse temperature $\beta$ has nothing to do with the magnetization exponent $\beta$ in $m^\ast(\beta)=(\beta-\beta_c)^{\beta+o(1)}$. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))

### Open problems
- **The 3D Ising model.** Dimensions $d\ge4$ are expected to have Gaussian large-scale behaviour and $d=2$ is exactly solvable, which singles out $d=3$ as the remaining challenge; it is not known whether the 3D model is integrable. Determining the CFT data ($\Delta$'s and OPE coefficients) "remains widely open in 3D", and even with bootstrap values for the exponents, proving that the critical 3D Ising model converges to a conformal field theory is "widely open". ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))
- **3D interfaces and roughening.** The fluctuations of the interface between plus and minus phases in 3D are "still widely open", and the roughening transition remains mysterious at a mathematical level. ([Duminil-Copin 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.00864))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Phase transition (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition): classifications, order parameters, universality, examples.
- **Reference:** [Critical exponent (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent): definitions, scaling relations, mean-field values.
- **Learn:** [Kardar, MIT 8.334 Statistical Physics of Fields lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/pages/lecture-notes/): Landau–Ginzburg theory, Ginzburg criterion, scaling, perturbative and position-space RG, exact 2D Ising.
- **Primary:** [Duminil-Copin, 100 Years of the (Critical) Ising Model on the Hypercubic Lattice (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.00864): survey of physical and rigorous results at and near criticality, with open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Kardar, Statistical Physics of Fields (CUP, 2007)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/statistical-physics-of-fields/06F49D11030FB3108683F413269DE945): graduate text on scale invariance, universality and the renormalization group.
references.Plancherel Theorem:
## Reference
### Overview
The Plancherel theorem says that the Fourier transform preserves the $L^2$ norm. With $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx$, if $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})\cap L^2(\mathbb{R})$ then $\int|f|^2=\int|\hat f|^2$, and the transform restricted to $L^1\cap L^2$ extends uniquely to a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, the Plancherel transform, which is unitary. The same holds on $\mathbb{R}^n$. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem); [Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))

The theorem is needed because the defining integral does not converge for a general $f\in L^2$: $\operatorname{sinc}(x)=\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$ lies in $L^2$ but not in $L^1$. On $L^1$ the transform maps into $C_0$, the continuous functions vanishing at infinity (Riemann–Lebesgue lemma), but the transform of an $L^1$ function need not be integrable and there is no easy characterization of the image of $L^1$. On $L^2$, by contrast, the transform is an automorphism. ([UC Davis notes](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/courses/129/ft.pdf); [Wikipedia: Riemann–Lebesgue lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Lebesgue_lemma); [Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))

Plancherel's theorem is the integral counterpart of Parseval's theorem for Fourier series, and it is the $p=2$ endpoint from which the $L^p$ theory (Hausdorff–Young) is built by interpolation. It generalizes to locally compact [abelian groups](node:Abelian%20Groups) via [Pontryagin duality](node:Pontryagin%20Duality), and to many non-abelian groups, where the dual object is the set of irreducible unitary representations and the role of the dual [Haar measure](node:Haar%20Measure) is played by the Plancherel measure. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PlancherelsTheorem.html); [Wikipedia: Hausdorff–Young inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff%E2%80%93Young_inequality); [Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem))

### Formal definition
Fix the convention
$$\hat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i\langle x,\xi\rangle}\,dx,\qquad \check g(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} g(\xi)\,e^{2\pi i\langle x,\xi\rangle}\,d\xi,$$
for $f,g\in L^1$. With this ordinary-frequency convention there is no $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$ factor and the extension to $L^2$ is exactly unitary. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem); [UC Davis notes](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/courses/129/ft.pdf))

**Construction by density (on $\mathbb{R}$).** Let $X=\{f\in L^1:\hat f\in L^1\}$. Every $f\in X$ is bounded and continuous, so $X\subset L^2$, and $X$ is dense in $L^2$. On $X$ one has $\langle f,g\rangle=\langle\hat f,\hat g\rangle$. Given $f\in L^2$, choose $f_k\in X$ with $\|f_k-f\|_2\to0$; then $\|\hat f_k-\hat f_m\|_2=\|f_k-f_m\|_2\to0$, so $(\hat f_k)$ is Cauchy, and $\hat f$ is defined as its $L^2$ limit. ([UC Davis notes](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/courses/129/ft.pdf))

**Construction via Schwartz space (on $\mathbb{R}^n$).** The Fourier transform is a linear automorphism of the [Schwartz space](node:Tempered%20Distributions) $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, which contains $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and is dense in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $1\le p<\infty$. Hence the isometry on $\mathcal{S}$ extends by continuity to $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$; the same unique continuous extension is obtained from the dense subspace $L^1\cap L^2$. ([Wikipedia: Schwartz space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_space); [Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))

### Key results
- **Plancherel theorem on $\mathbb{R}^n$.** If $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\cap L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ then $\hat f\in L^2$ and $\|f\|_2=\|\hat f\|_2$; the map extends uniquely to a unitary operator $\mathcal{F}$ of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem); [Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))
- **Parseval (polarized) form and inverse on $L^2$.** For all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb{R})$, $\langle f,g\rangle=\langle\hat f,\hat g\rangle$. The inverse of the $L^2$ transform is the $L^2$ extension of $g\mapsto\check g$: if $\varphi=\hat f$ with $f\in L^2$, then $\hat\varphi(\xi)=f(-\xi)$, so applying $\mathcal{F}$ twice is reflection and $\mathcal{F}^{-1}=\mathcal{F}^*$. ([UC Davis notes](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/courses/129/ft.pdf); [Wikipedia: Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))
- **Fourier inversion on $L^1$.** If $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ and $\hat f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, then $(\hat f)^\vee=(\check f)^\wedge=f$ almost everywhere. For $f\in L^1$ alone, $\hat f\in C_0$ but need not be integrable. ([UC Davis notes](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/courses/129/ft.pdf); [Wikipedia: Riemann–Lebesgue lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Lebesgue_lemma))
- **Hausdorff–Young inequality.** For $1\le p\le2$ and $1/p+1/p'=1$, $\|\hat f\|_{L^{p'}(\mathbb{R}^n)}\le\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}$. It follows from the Riesz–Thorin interpolation theorem applied between the Plancherel bound $L^2\to L^2$ (norm 1) and the trivial bound $L^1\to L^\infty$ (norm 1, since $|e^{-2\pi i\langle x,\xi\rangle}|=1$). The range $p\in[1,2]$ is essential. ([Wikipedia: Hausdorff–Young inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff%E2%80%93Young_inequality))
- **Sharp constant (Babenko–Beckner).** For $1<p\le2$ the best constant is $\|\hat f\|_{p'}\le\big(p^{1/p}/p'^{1/p'}\big)^{n/2}\|f\|_p$, with equality for Gaussians; Babenko proved a special case in 1961 and Beckner the general case in 1975. ([Wikipedia: Babenko–Beckner inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babenko%E2%80%93Beckner_inequality); [Wikipedia: Hausdorff–Young inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff%E2%80%93Young_inequality))
- **Locally compact abelian groups.** Let $G$ be a locally compact abelian group with Haar measure $\mu$ and Pontryagin dual $\hat G$. There is a dual Haar measure $\nu$ on $\hat G$ such that $\int_G|f|^2\,d\mu=\int_{\hat G}|\hat f|^2\,d\nu$ for continuous compactly supported $f$; the transform extends uniquely to a unitary $L^2_\mu(G)\to L^2_\nu(\hat G)$, whose inverse is its adjoint. ([Wikipedia: Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))
- **Non-abelian Plancherel theorem (Segal, Mautner).** Let $G$ be a separable, unimodular, type I locally compact group with Haar measure $dx$, and let $\hat G$ be the set of equivalence classes of irreducible unitary representations. There is a positive measure $\mu$ on $\hat G$, unique up to a constant depending only on $dx$, such that for $f\in L^1(G)\cap L^2(G)$ the operator $\pi(f)$ is Hilbert–Schmidt for $\mu$-almost every $\pi$ and $\int_G|f(x)|^2\,dx=\int_{\hat G}\|\pi(f)\|_{HS}^2\,d\mu(\pi)$. The approach for separable unimodular groups was pursued by Mautner and Segal from the late 1940s. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753, Thm 1.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753))
- **Finite and compact groups.** In the Hilbert–Schmidt form $\|f\|^2=\sum_{\rho}\dim\rho\,\operatorname{tr}\big(\hat f(\rho)^*\hat f(\rho)\big)$, the Plancherel measure weights each irreducible representation by its dimension; likewise, for compact groups the Plancherel measure of an irreducible representation is proportional to its dimension and the measure need not be finite. For abelian groups it is proportional to the Haar measure of the dual group. Normalizations differ: for a finite group the Plancherel measure article uses $\mu(\pi)=(\dim\pi)^2/|G|$, which is not the weight in the Hilbert–Schmidt formula above. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem); [Wikipedia: Plancherel measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_measure))
- **Harish-Chandra's Plancherel formulas.** For a noncompact connected real semisimple [Lie group](node:Lie%20Groups) $G$ with finite center and maximal compact $K$, the spherical transform $f\mapsto\tilde f$ is unitary from $L^2(K\backslash G/K)$ onto $L^2(\mathfrak a_+^*,|c(\lambda)|^{-2}d\lambda)$, with inversion $f(g)=\int\tilde f(\lambda)\varphi_\lambda(g)|c(\lambda)|^{-2}\,d\lambda$, where $c$ is Harish-Chandra's $c$-function; Harish-Chandra completed this in 1966 after the Gindikin–Karpelevich product formula (1962). He also proved the general Plancherel theorem for semisimple Lie groups, whose Plancherel measure is supported on the tempered representations. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem for spherical functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem_for_spherical_functions); [Wikipedia: Plancherel measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_measure))

### Examples
- **Box and sinc.** For $f=\chi_{(-1/2,1/2)}$, $\hat f(\xi)=\operatorname{sinc}(\xi)=\sin(\pi\xi)/(\pi\xi)\notin L^1$. Conversely, $\operatorname{sinc}\in L^2\setminus L^1$, and its $L^2$ transform is $\chi_{(-1/2,1/2)}$. Plancherel then gives $\int_{\mathbb{R}}\operatorname{sinc}^2=\int\chi_{(-1/2,1/2)}=1$. ([UC Davis notes](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/courses/129/ft.pdf))
- **Gaussians.** $e^{-\pi x^2}$ is its own Fourier transform under this convention; one proof of Plancherel checks the identity on Gaussians and extends by density, and Gaussians are the extremizers of the sharp Hausdorff–Young inequality. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem); [Wikipedia: Hausdorff–Young inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff%E2%80%93Young_inequality))
- **Dual pairs.** $\hat{\mathbb{R}}\cong\mathbb{R}$, $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}\cong\mathbb{T}$, $\hat{\mathbb{T}}\cong\mathbb{Z}$, and $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is self-dual; on $\mathbb{T}$ the transform computes Fourier coefficients, and Plancherel's theorem corresponds to Parseval's theorem for Fourier series. ([Wikipedia: Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality); [MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PlancherelsTheorem.html))
- **Finite groups.** For a finite group $\hat G$ is the set of irreducible characters, and for a class function $f$ the operator $\hat f(\rho)$ is a scalar multiple of the identity, so the Hilbert–Schmidt Plancherel formula becomes a Parseval formula over characters in which each scalar coefficient is weighted by $(\dim\rho)^2$. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem))

### History
Michel Plancherel proved the theorem in 1910 in "Contribution à l'étude de la représentation d'une fonction arbitraire par des intégrales définies", *Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo* 30, 289–335. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/bf03014877)) Rayleigh had used the identity in 1889 in his work on [blackbody radiation](node:Blackbody%20Radiation), and Plancherel first established conditions under which it holds. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PlancherelsTheorem.html)) Parseval's theorem had been proved only for Fourier series, first by Lyapunov. ([Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))

Young stated the series version of the Hausdorff–Young inequality in 1913 and Hausdorff extended it in 1923; Marcel Riesz found his interpolation theorem in 1927. ([Wikipedia: Hausdorff–Young inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff%E2%80%93Young_inequality)) Pontryagin's duality (1931–1934, compact or discrete second-countable groups) was extended to all LCA groups by van Kampen (1935) and Weil (1940). ([Wikipedia: Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality)) The non-abelian theory began with Mautner and Segal in the late 1940s and Harish-Chandra's 1951 formula for complex semisimple groups. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753))

### Connections
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): Plancherel is the $L^2$ cornerstone of the Fourier transform, paralleling Parseval for series.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the theorem says the Fourier transform is a unitary operator on $L^2$.
- [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces): Hausdorff–Young interpolates between the $L^1$ and $L^2$ theories; density of $L^1\cap L^2$ underlies the construction.
- [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration): the transform is a Lebesgue integral on $L^1$ and a limit on $L^2$.
- [Tempered Distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions): the Fourier transform on $\mathcal{S}'$ restricts to the Plancherel transform on $L^2\subset\mathcal{S}'$.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces): $H^s$ norms are weighted $L^2$ norms of $\hat f$ by Plancherel.
- [Carleson's Theorem](node:Carleson's%20Theorem): pointwise a.e. convergence of Fourier series of $L^2$ functions, far deeper than norm convergence.
- [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory) and [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): the non-abelian Plancherel theorem decomposes $L^2(G)$ over irreducible unitary representations.
- [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory): $\mathcal F$ is unitary with $\mathcal F^4=I$.
- Maps: [MSC 42 - Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces](node:MSC%2042%20-%20Harmonic%20analysis%20on%20Euclidean%20spaces); abstract version in [MSC 43Axx - Abstract harmonic analysis](node:MSC%2043Axx%20-%20Abstract%20harmonic%20analysis).

### Common pitfalls
- **The $L^2$ transform is not given by the integral pointwise.** For $f\in L^2\setminus L^1$ the integral need not converge; $\hat f$ is an $L^2$ limit, defined only almost everywhere, and an $L^2$ function's transform cannot be restricted to a set of measure zero. ([UC Davis notes](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/courses/129/ft.pdf); [Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))
- **$L^1$ does not map onto $C_0$-type spaces in any simple way.** The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma gives $\hat f\in C_0$ for $f\in L^1$, but $\hat f$ need not be integrable and the image of $L^1$ has no easy characterization. ([Wikipedia: Riemann–Lebesgue lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Lebesgue_lemma); [Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))
- **No Hausdorff–Young for $p>2$.** For $p>2$, the transform of an $L^p$ function is in general only a tempered distribution, defined by duality. ([Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform); [Wikipedia: Hausdorff–Young inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff%E2%80%93Young_inequality))
- **Normalization.** With kernel $e^{-2\pi i x\xi}$ the identity has constant 1; other conventions put $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$ or $1/(2\pi)$ factors in the transform. On groups, the dual measure must be matched to the chosen Haar measure. ([Wikipedia: Plancherel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem); [Wikipedia: Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality))
- **Non-abelian hypotheses matter.** The Segal–Mautner theorem is stated for separable, unimodular, type I groups; in the semisimple case the Plancherel measure sees only tempered representations, so not every irreducible unitary representation contributes. ([Herb–Sally, arXiv:1101.3753](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.3753); [Wikipedia: Plancherel measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_measure))

### Open problems
- **Stein's restriction conjecture.** For the sphere or paraboloid $S\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ with surface measure $\sigma$, the restriction estimate $\|\hat f|_S\|_{L^q(S,d\sigma)}\le C\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}$ asks when $\hat f$, a priori defined only almost everywhere for $f\in L^p$, $1<p<2$, has a meaningful trace on a measure-zero surface. The conjecture asserts that the known necessary conditions are sufficient; in the dual (extension) form these are $p'>2n/(n-1)$ and $(n+1)/p'\le(n-1)/q$. Tao's survey records that it has been solved for the sphere and paraboloid in two dimensions (the sharp circle range first proven by Zygmund, 1974) and that the full conjecture remains open; the Tomas–Stein argument gives the $L^2$-based range $p\le2(n+1)/(n+3)$. ([Tao, arXiv:math/0303136](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/math/0303136); [Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform)) Progress continues: Wang and Wu propose a two-ends Furstenberg conjecture implying the restriction conjecture and prove a three-dimensional restriction estimate for $p>22/7$. ([Wang–Wu, arXiv:2411.08871](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08871))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Plancherel theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plancherel_theorem): statement on $\mathbb{R}^n$, polarization, LCA and non-abelian versions.
- **Learn:** [Saito, MAT 129 Supplementary Notes II (UC Davis)](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/courses/129/ft.pdf): short construction of the $L^2$ transform by density and completeness.
- **Primary:** [Herb and Sally, The Plancherel formula, the Plancherel theorem, and the Fourier transform of orbital integrals](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.3753): survey of non-abelian Plancherel theorems from Segal–Mautner to reductive groups over local fields.
- **Primary:** [Tao, Some recent progress on the Restriction conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0303136): survey of the restriction problem that sits just beyond Plancherel in $L^p$.
- **Primary:** [Plancherel (1910), Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo 30 (Crossref record)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/bf03014877): bibliographic record of the original paper.
- **Further reading:** [Stein and Weiss, *Introduction to Fourier Analysis on Euclidean Spaces* (Princeton)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691080789/introduction-to-fourier-analysis-on-euclidean-spaces-pms-32-volume-32): standard graduate text on Fourier analysis on $\mathbb{R}^n$; [Folland, *A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis* (Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2016; Crossref record)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/b19172): LCA and non-abelian Plancherel theory.
references.Policy Gradient Methods:
## Reference
### Overview
Policy gradient methods are [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning) algorithms that optimize a differentiable parameterized policy $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ directly by gradient ascent on the expected return $J(\theta)$, instead of deriving the policy from a learned value function as in [Q-Learning](node:Q-Learning). The gradient is estimated from sampled trajectories, so the update is a form of [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent) (ascent) on a non-concave objective. The family runs from REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) through actor-critic methods, the natural policy gradient (Kakade, 2001), TRPO (2015), and PPO (2017), to the critic-free GRPO variant used to train reasoning language models. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method)) ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))

The basic enabling fact is that the gradient of the expected return can be written in a form that can be estimated from experience, without differentiating through the environment dynamics. Sutton, McAllester, Singh and Mansour (1999) proved this for arbitrary differentiable function approximation, showed that an approximate action-value or advantage function can be used in the estimate, and proved that a version of policy iteration with such approximators converges to a locally optimal policy. ([NeurIPS 1999](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1999/hash/464d828b85b0bed98e80ade0a5c43b0f-Abstract.html))

Because $V^{\pi_\theta}$ is non-concave in $\theta$ even for tabular problems, convex optimization tools do not apply directly. A theory developed since 2019 nonetheless shows global convergence for several parameterizations and identifies the distribution mismatch coefficient as the quantity that captures exploration difficulty. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.00261)) The methods sit next to [Actor-Critic Methods](node:Actor-Critic%20Methods), [Natural Gradient Methods](node:Natural%20Gradient%20Methods) and [Proximal Policy Optimization](node:Proximal%20Policy%20Optimization), and their finite-time theory now extends to games and control. ([Cen and Chi survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.05230v1))

### Formal definition
Consider a discounted [Markov decision process](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes) with discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$ and start distribution $\rho$. Write $V^{\pi}(\rho)=\mathbb{E}_{s_0\sim\rho}\,\mathbb{E}_\pi[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r(s_t,a_t)]$, with action-value $Q^\pi$ and advantage $A^\pi=Q^\pi-V^\pi$. The **discounted state visitation distribution** is
$$d^{\pi}_{s_0}(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\Pr\nolimits^{\pi}(s_t=s\mid s_0),\qquad d^\pi_\rho=\mathbb{E}_{s_0\sim\rho}\,d^\pi_{s_0}.$$
A **policy gradient method** updates $\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\alpha_k\widehat{\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)}$, where the gradient estimate is built from sampled trajectories. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))

The **REINFORCE** estimator with reward-to-go (the causality form) and a state baseline $b$ is
$$\widehat{\nabla J}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t}\nabla_\theta\ln\pi_\theta(a^i_t\mid s^i_t)\Big(\sum_{\tau\ge t}\gamma^\tau r^i_\tau-b(s^i_t)\Big);$$
$b\equiv0$ recovers the original REINFORCE. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method)) Two standard parameterizations are the **direct** one, $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=\theta_{s,a}$ with $\theta_{s,\cdot}$ in the simplex, and the **softmax** one, $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\propto\exp(\theta_{s,a})$. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))

The **natural policy gradient** preconditions with the Fisher information matrix $F(\theta)$: $\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\alpha F(\theta_k)^{-1}\nabla_\theta J(\theta_k)$. It is the second-order form of a step constrained in averaged [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence) rather than in Euclidean norm. **TRPO** maximizes a surrogate advantage subject to $\bar D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta_k}\,\|\,\pi_\theta)\le\epsilon$, computing the step by conjugate gradient with a backtracking line search. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method)) **PPO-clip** maximizes, with $r_t(\theta)=\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)/\pi_{\theta_k}(a_t\mid s_t)$,
$$L^{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta)=\hat{\mathbb E}_t\big[\min\big(r_t(\theta)\hat A_t,\ \operatorname{clip}(r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat A_t\big)\big],$$
with $\epsilon$ typically $0.2$. ([Wikipedia: PPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximal_policy_optimization))

### Key results
- **Policy gradient theorem.** For a differentiable policy $\pi_\theta$, $\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi_\theta}_{s_0}}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s)}[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\,Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)]$. If the parameterization keeps $\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s)$ in the simplex for all $\theta$, $Q$ may be replaced by $A$. The advantage form fails for the direct parameterization, while the $Q$ form remains valid. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261); [Sutton et al. 1999](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1999/hash/464d828b85b0bed98e80ade0a5c43b0f-Abstract.html))
- **Baselines are unbiased.** Subtracting any state-dependent baseline $b(s_t)$ leaves the expected gradient unchanged and can reduce variance. The ideal baseline is close to $V^\pi$, which motivates learning a critic. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method); [CS285 lecture 5](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/static/slides/lec-5.pdf))
- **Performance difference lemma** (Kakade and Langford, 2002). For all policies $\pi,\pi'$ and states $s_0$: $V^\pi(s_0)-V^{\pi'}(s_0)=\frac1{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^\pi_{s_0}}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)}A^{\pi'}(s,a)$. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- **Non-concavity.** There is an MDP for which $V^{\pi_\theta}(s)$ is not concave in $\theta$ under both the direct and the softmax parameterization. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- **Gradient domination and projected gradient ascent.** For the direct parameterization and any $\mu,\rho\in\Delta(S)$: $V^\star(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)\le\frac1{1-\gamma}\big\|d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\big\|_\infty\max_{\bar\pi}(\bar\pi-\pi)^\top\nabla_\pi V^\pi(\mu)$. Consequently, projected gradient ascent on $V^\pi(\mu)$ with step $\eta=(1-\gamma)^3/(2\gamma|A|)$ achieves $\min_{t<T}V^\star(\rho)-V^{(t)}(\rho)\le\varepsilon$ once $T>\frac{64\gamma|S||A|}{(1-\gamma)^6\varepsilon^2}\big\|d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\big\|_\infty^2$. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- **Vanishing gradients.** On a chain MDP with $H+2$ states and $\gamma=H/(H+1)$, under the direct parameterization, all derivatives of order $k\le H/(40\log 2H)-1$ have norm at most $(1/3)^{H/4}$ at policies with $\theta_{s,a_1}<1/4$, while the suboptimality is of order $H$. So stationarity alone does not imply optimality without a distribution condition. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- **Softmax policy gradient converges globally.** With exact gradients, step $\eta\le(1-\gamma)^3/8$ and a strictly positive optimization distribution $\mu$, $V^{(t)}(s)\to V^\star(s)$ for every state. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261)) The convergence can nonetheless be very slow: for $\gamma\in(0.96,1)$ and $|S|\ge c_3(1-\gamma)^{-6}$ there is an MDP on which softmax PG needs at least $\frac{c_1}{\eta}|S|^{2^{c_2/(1-\gamma)}}$ iterations to reach $\|V^\star-V^{(t)}\|_\infty\le0.15$ (Li et al.). ([Cen and Chi survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.05230v1))
- **Dimension-free rate for NPG.** For the softmax parameterization with $\theta^{(0)}=0$ and any $\eta>0$, the natural policy gradient satisfies $V^{(T)}(\rho)\ge V^\star(\rho)-\frac{\log|A|}{\eta T}-\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^2T}$. With $\eta\ge(1-\gamma)^2\log|A|$ it finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy within $2/((1-\gamma)^2\varepsilon)$ iterations, independent of $|S|$ and $|A|$. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- **Linear convergence with entropy regularization** (Cen et al.). With entropy weight $\tau$, step $0<\eta\le(1-\gamma)/\tau$, uniform initialization and exact evaluation, $\|V^\star_\tau-V^{(T)}_\tau\|_\infty\le\frac{15(1+\tau\log|A|)}{1-\gamma}(1-\eta\tau)^{T-1}$. ([Cen and Chi survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.05230v1))
- **Linear-quadratic regulator** (Fazel et al.). If $\lambda=\sigma_{\min}(\mathbb{E}[x_0x_0^\top])>0$ and $Q,R\succ0$, the LQR cost of the linear controller $u_t=-Kx_t$ is gradient dominated: $C(K)-C(K^\star)\le\frac{\|\Sigma_{K^\star}\|_2}{\lambda^2\sigma_{\min}(R)}\|\nabla C(K)\|_F^2$, where $\Sigma_K=\mathbb{E}[\sum_t x_tx_t^\top]$ is the state correlation matrix. Gradient descent with a suitable constant step from a stabilizing $K^{(0)}$ therefore converges linearly to the optimal linear controller. ([Cen and Chi survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.05230v1))

### Examples
- **Softmax tabular MDP.** Under the softmax parameterization, $\partial V^{\pi_\theta}(\mu)/\partial\theta_{s,a}=\frac1{1-\gamma}d^{\pi_\theta}_\mu(s)\,\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\,A^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)$. The visitation weight $d_\mu(s)$ and the factor $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ both shrink the update for rarely visited states and for near-deterministic policies, which is the mechanism behind slow convergence. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- **Comparison with maximum likelihood.** The REINFORCE gradient is a maximum-likelihood gradient on the sampled actions, weighted by return. Good trajectories are made more likely and bad ones less likely. ([CS285 lecture 5](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/static/slides/lec-5.pdf))
- **GRPO.** Group relative policy optimization samples a group of $G$ outputs per prompt and uses the within-group standardized reward as the advantage, which removes the learned value function. DeepSeek researchers proposed it for reasoning language models (DeepSeekMath, 2024). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method))

### History
- 1992: Ronald J. Williams introduces REINFORCE, described as the first policy gradient method. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method))
- 1999: Sutton, McAllester, Singh and Mansour show that the gradient can be estimated with function approximation and give the first convergence proof for approximate policy iteration with arbitrary differentiable approximators. ([NeurIPS 1999](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1999/hash/464d828b85b0bed98e80ade0a5c43b0f-Abstract.html))
- 2001: Kakade's natural policy gradient follows the steepest direction under the parameter-space geometry, moving toward the greedy action of a policy-iteration step rather than merely a better one. It was demonstrated on simple MDPs and Tetris. ([NeurIPS 2001](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2001/hash/4b86abe48d358ecf194c56c69108433e-Abstract.html))
- 2015: TRPO (Schulman, Levine, Moritz, Jordan, Abbeel) derives an iterative procedure with guaranteed monotonic improvement and a practical approximation of it. ([arXiv:1502.05477](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.05477)) GAE gives an exponentially weighted advantage estimator, analogous to TD($\lambda$), that trades some bias for much lower variance. ([arXiv:1506.02438](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02438))
- 2017: PPO allows several epochs of minibatch updates on each batch of data and keeps some benefits of TRPO with simpler implementation. ([arXiv:1707.06347](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347)) Wikipedia reports it was OpenAI's default RL algorithm from 2018. ([Wikipedia: PPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximal_policy_optimization))
- 2019 onward: global convergence and agnostic approximation theory for policy gradients (Agarwal, Kakade, Lee, Mahajan). ([arXiv:1908.00261](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.00261))

### Connections
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): policy gradients are the policy-search branch of RL.
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the objective, visitation distributions and advantage are defined on an MDP.
- [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent): the update is stochastic gradient ascent with a score-function estimator.
- [Actor-Critic Methods](node:Actor-Critic%20Methods): a learned critic provides the baseline or advantage in the policy gradient.
- [Natural Gradient Methods](node:Natural%20Gradient%20Methods): NPG is the natural gradient under the Fisher metric of the policy.
- [Fisher Information](node:Fisher%20Information): the preconditioner in NPG and the second-order form of the KL trust region.
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence): the trust-region constraint in TRPO and the penalty in PPO variants.
- [Proximal Policy Optimization](node:Proximal%20Policy%20Optimization): the clipped-surrogate member of the family.
- [Multi-Agent PPO](node:Multi-Agent%20PPO): PPO applied to multiple agents.
- [Fine-Tuning and RLHF](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF): PPO and GRPO are the policy optimizers used in RL fine-tuning of language models.
- [Variance Reduction in Stochastic Optimization](node:Variance%20Reduction%20in%20Stochastic%20Optimization): baselines and control variates address the high variance of score-function estimators.
- [Exploration in Reinforcement Learning](node:Exploration%20in%20Reinforcement%20Learning): the distribution mismatch coefficient quantifies how exploration limits policy gradient guarantees.

### Common pitfalls
- The advantage form of the policy gradient does not hold for the direct (simplex) parameterization; only the $Q$ form does. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- A near-zero gradient does not certify near-optimality. Sparse-reward MDPs have policies with exponentially small gradients that are far from optimal, and sample-based gradients there are typically zero under random exploration. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- In PPO the data become increasingly off-policy as $\theta$ moves away from $\theta_k$ across epochs, and the surrogate objective matches the true objective only near $\theta_k$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method))
- Global convergence results above assume exact gradients and values. In practice these are estimated from noisy samples, which couples statistics and optimization. ([Cen and Chi survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.05230v1))

### Open problems
- **Softmax PG without full-support initial distributions.** Agarwal et al. leave open whether softmax gradient ascent converges globally when the optimization distribution $\mu$ is not strictly positive, since $d_\mu(s)$ then scales down the effective learning rate of some states. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- **Sharper analyses for incremental algorithms.** Whether conservative policy iteration, PSDP and MD-MPI admit analyses that avoid worst-case density-ratio dependence through an approximation/estimation decomposition is posed as a direction for future work. ([Agarwal et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.00261))
- **Policy optimization in Markov games.** Achieving an iteration complexity with better dependence on $|S|$ and $(1-\gamma)^{-1}$ for policy-gradient-type methods in zero-sum Markov games is stated to remain open. ([Cen and Chi survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.05230v1))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Policy gradient method (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method): REINFORCE, baselines, actor-critic, NPG, TRPO, PPO, GRPO, and the mirror-descent view.
- **Learn:** [CS285 Deep RL, UC Berkeley, lecture 5](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/static/slides/lec-5.pdf): derivation of the policy gradient, reward-to-go, baselines, and the link to maximum likelihood. Lectures 6, 9 and 10 cover actor-critic and advanced policy gradients ([course page](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/)).
- **Primary:** [Agarwal, Kakade, Lee, Mahajan, On the Theory of Policy Gradient Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.00261): gradient domination, global convergence, NPG rates, and agnostic approximation bounds.
- **Primary:** [Sutton et al. 1999](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1999/hash/464d828b85b0bed98e80ade0a5c43b0f-Abstract.html): the policy gradient theorem with function approximation.
- **Primary:** [Cen and Chi, Algorithmic foundations of policy optimization](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.05230v1): survey of finite-time convergence for RL, games and control.
- **Further reading:** [Agarwal, Brantley, Jiang, Kakade, Sun, Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms](https://rltheorybook.github.io/): book on the theory of reinforcement learning by the authors of the Agarwal et al. policy gradient paper and others.
references.Polytopes:
## Reference
### Overview
A polytope is a geometric object with flat sides, the generalization of polygons and polyhedra to any dimension $d$. Ludwig Schläfli first described polytopes of more than three dimensions before 1853, calling them *polyschem*; Reinhold Hoppe coined German *Polytop* in 1882, and Alicia Boole Stott introduced the English word *polytope*. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope))

Modern research (MSC 52B) is mostly about **convex polytopes**: convex hulls of finitely many points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, equivalently bounded intersections of finitely many closed half-spaces. They are the feasible regions of linear programs. Their combinatorics is encoded in the face lattice and the $f$-vector, and the central questions are which face lattices and $f$-vectors can occur, how large graph diameters can be, and how to count lattice points and compute volumes. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope); [Ziegler, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411400))

Regular polytopes form the classical, maximally symmetric part of the subject. In every dimension the regular simplex, hypercube, and cross polytope (orthoplex) exist. Dimension $2$ has infinitely many regular polygons, and dimensions $3$ and $4$ have additional exceptional figures; in dimension $4$ these are the $24$-cell, $120$-cell, and $600$-cell. From dimension $5$ on, only the three families remain. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polytope))

### Formal definition
A **V-polytope** is the convex hull $P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\dots,v_m\}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ of a finite set of points; Grünbaum's equivalent definition is a compact convex set with finitely many extreme points. An **H-polyhedron** is a solution set $\{x: Ax\le b\}$ of finitely many linear inequalities. An H-polyhedron need not be bounded; a bounded one is exactly a V-polytope. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope))

A **face** of $P$ is the set of points of $P$ attaining equality in some valid inequality $a^{\top}x\le c$ (one satisfied by every point of $P$). Faces of dimension $0$, $1$, $d-2$, and $d-1$ are vertices, edges, ridges, and facets. Ordered by inclusion, the faces (including $\emptyset$ and $P$) form an Eulerian lattice, the **face lattice**; two polytopes are combinatorially equivalent when their face lattices are isomorphic. The **$f$-vector** is $(f_0,\dots,f_{d-1})$, with $f_j$ the number of $j$-faces. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope))

For a simplicial $d$-polytope (all facets simplices), the **$h$-vector** $(h_0,\dots,h_d)$ is the linear transform of the $f$-vector used to state the Dehn–Sommerville relations, and the **$g$-vector** is $g_0=h_0$, $g_i=h_i-h_{i-1}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehn%E2%80%93Sommerville_equations); [ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.06594))

A polytope is **regular** if its symmetry group acts transitively on flags (maximal chains vertex $\subset$ edge $\subset\cdots$). Regular polytopes carry [Schläfli Symbols](node:Schläfli%20Symbols) $\{p,q,\ldots,z\}$: facets are $\{p,\ldots,y\}$ and vertex figures are $\{q,\ldots,z\}$, and reversing the symbol gives the dual. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polytope))

### Key results
- **Minkowski–Weyl theorem.** $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ is a polyhedron if and only if $E=\Delta+\sigma$ for a polytope $\Delta$ and a convex polyhedral cone $\sigma$. In particular, a bounded intersection of finitely many half-spaces is the [Convex Hull](node:Convex%20Hull) of finitely many points and conversely. Weyl proved in 1935 that a cone is finitely generated if and only if it is a finite intersection of linear half-spaces. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/1008.2608v2); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyhedral_cone); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope))
- **Euler–Poincaré relation.** For a convex $d$-polytope, $f_0-f_1+\cdots+(-1)^{d-1}f_{d-1}=1+(-1)^{d-1}$: the Euler characteristic of the boundary sphere is $0$ for even $d$ and $2$ for odd $d$. For $d=3$ this is $V-E+F=2$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope))
- **Steinitz's theorem (1922).** A graph is the graph ($1$-skeleton) of a convex $3$-polytope if and only if it is planar and $3$-vertex-connected. Every such graph is realized with integer coordinates. No analogous classification is known in dimension $\ge 4$: deciding whether a lattice is the face lattice of a $4$-polytope is complete for the existential theory of the reals (Richter-Gebert's universality theorem), and in higher dimensions some polytopes (built from the Perles configuration) have no realization with integer coordinates. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steinitz%27s_theorem))
- **Graph reconstruction.** The graph determines the face lattice for $3$-polytopes (Whitney) and for simple polytopes of any dimension (Blind and Mani-Levitska; simpler proof by Kalai). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope))
- **Dehn–Sommerville relations.** For a simplicial $d$-polytope, $h_k=h_{d-k}$ for $0\le k\le d$. The relations with $k\le (d-1)/2$ are independent and imply the rest. Stanley interpreted $h_k$ as the dimension of the even intersection cohomology group $IH^{2k}$ of the associated toric variety. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehn%E2%80%93Sommerville_equations))
- **Upper bound theorem.** Among $d$-polytopes with $n$ vertices, the cyclic polytope $C(n,d)$ has the largest number of $i$-faces for every $i$. For $i<\lfloor d/2\rfloor$ it has $\binom{n}{i+1}$ of them, and the total face count is $O(n^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor})$. Motzkin conjectured this in 1957, McMullen proved it in 1970, and Stanley extended it to simplicial spheres in 1975. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_bound_theorem))
- **$g$-theorem.** An integer vector $(h_0,\dots,h_d)$ is the $h$-vector of a simplicial $d$-polytope if and only if (a) $h_i=h_{d-i}$; (b) $1=h_0\le h_1\le\cdots\le h_{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$; and (c) $g_{i+1}\le g_i^{\langle i\rangle}$ for $i\ge1$, the Macaulay bound. Equivalently, $(g_0,\dots,g_{\lfloor d/2\rfloor})$ is an M-sequence. McMullen conjectured this in 1971. Billera and Lee proved sufficiency, and Stanley proved necessity using hard Lefschetz for toric varieties, both around 1980. ([ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.06594))
- **Ehrhart's theorem (1962).** If $P$ is a $d$-dimensional lattice polytope (vertices in $\mathbb{Z}^d$), then $L_P(t)=\#(tP\cap\mathbb{Z}^d)$ for positive integers $t$ agrees with a rational polynomial of degree $d$. Its leading coefficient is $\operatorname{vol}(P)$ and its constant term is $1$. Ehrhart–Macdonald reciprocity gives $L_{\operatorname{int}P}(t)=(-1)^dL_P(-t)$. Pick's theorem is the case $d=2$, $t=1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehrhart_polynomial))
- **Classification of regular convex polytopes.** For $d\ge5$ the regular convex polytopes are the simplex $\{3,\dots,3\}$, the hypercube, and the cross polytope (orthoplex). For $d=4$ there are six: the $5$-cell (4-simplex), the tesseract $\{4,3,3\}$, and its dual the $16$-cell $\{3,3,4\}$, plus the exceptional $24$-cell $\{3,4,3\}$, $120$-cell $\{5,3,3\}$, and $600$-cell. In $\mathbb{R}^3$ there are the five Platonic solids (nine regular polyhedra if the four Kepler–Poinsot star polyhedra are counted). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polytope); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesseract))
- **Volume is hard.** Computing the volume of a polytope exactly is #P-hard even from an explicit list of facets or vertices (Dyer–Frieze 1988). In the membership-oracle model no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximates volume well (Elekes; Bárány–Füredi). Dyer, Frieze, and Kannan (1991) gave a randomized polynomial-time approximation scheme. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_volume_approximation))

### Examples
- **Tesseract** $\{4,3,3\}$: $16$ vertices, $32$ edges, $24$ squares, and $8$ cubes, and the unit tesseract has as vertices all $16$ points with coordinates in $\{0,1\}$. It belongs to the hypercube family. Its dual is the $16$-cell $\{3,3,4\}$. With edge length $s$ it has $4$-volume $s^4$ and boundary $3$-volume $8s^3$. Check: $16-32+24-8=0$, as the Euler–Poincaré relation predicts for $d=4$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesseract); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope))
- **$24$-cell** $\{3,4,3\}$: $24$ vertices (the coordinate permutations of $(\pm1,\pm1,0,0)$), $96$ edges, $96$ triangles, and $24$ octahedral cells. It is self-dual, since its symbol is a palindrome. It and the tesseract are the only regular convex $4$-polytopes whose edge length equals the circumradius. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24-cell))
- **Hirsch counterexample:** a $43$-dimensional polytope with $86$ facets whose graph has diameter greater than $43=n-d$, built from a $5$-dimensional polytope with $48$ facets. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.2814); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirsch_conjecture))

### History
Schläfli's *Theorie der vielfachen Kontinuität* was published in full only in 1901, six years after his death; parts had appeared in 1855 and 1858. Between 1880 and 1900 at least nine other mathematicians rediscovered his results independently. Coxeter's *Regular Polytopes* (1948) is the standard account of regular figures. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polytope))

On the combinatorial side, Hirsch proposed his diameter bound in a 1957 letter to Dantzig, motivated by the simplex method. The upper bound theorem was proved in 1970, the $g$-theorem around 1980, and Santos disproved the Hirsch conjecture in 2010 (*Annals of Mathematics* 176, 2012). Ziegler's *Lectures on Polytopes* (Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics, 1995) is a standard graduate text. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirsch_conjecture); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_bound_theorem); [ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.06594); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.2814); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4613-8431-1))

### Connections
- [Higher-Dimensional Euclidean Geometry](node:Higher-Dimensional%20Euclidean%20Geometry): ambient space for regular and convex polytopes.
- [Convex Hull](node:Convex%20Hull): V-polytopes are convex hulls of finite sets.
- [Schläfli Symbols](node:Schläfli%20Symbols): notation for regular polytopes and their duals.
- [Linear Programming](node:Linear%20Programming) and [Convex Optimization](node:Convex%20Optimization): feasible regions are polyhedra; the Hirsch question bounds simplex-method paths.
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): Steinitz's theorem and graph reconstruction.
- [Combinatorics](node:Combinatorics): $f$-, $h$-, $g$-vectors and lattice-point counting.
- [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders): the face lattice is an Eulerian lattice.
- [Homology](node:Homology): the Euler–Poincaré relation is the Euler characteristic of the boundary sphere.
- [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere): the boundary of a convex $d$-polytope is a $(d-1)$-sphere.
- [Algebraic Varieties](node:Algebraic%20Varieties): toric varieties underlie Stanley's proof of the $g$-theorem.
- Map: [MSC 52Bxx - Polytopes and polyhedra](node:MSC%2052Bxx%20-%20Polytopes%20and%20polyhedra), [MSC 52 - Convex and discrete geometry](node:MSC%2052%20-%20Convex%20and%20discrete%20geometry)

### Common pitfalls
- An intersection of half-spaces is a polytope only if it is bounded. Otherwise it is a polyhedron, the sum of a polytope and a cone. Many texts reserve "polytope" for the bounded case, but some allow polytopes to be unbounded, and some identify a polytope with its boundary. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/1008.2608v2))
- The tesseract is not exceptional. It is the $4$-dimensional member of the hypercube family; the exceptional regular $4$-polytopes are the $24$-, $120$-, and $600$-cells. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polytope))
- $V-E+F=2$ does not hold in every dimension: the alternating face sum of the boundary is $1+(-1)^{d-1}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope))
- The Dehn–Sommerville relations and $g$-theorem as stated apply to simplicial polytopes. For general $4$-polytopes one studies the cone of $f$-vectors instead, where constructing $4$-polytopes of high "fatness" is a key problem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehn%E2%80%93Sommerville_equations); [Ziegler, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411400))

### Open problems
- **Polynomial Hirsch conjecture.** Is there a fixed $k$ with $\operatorname{diam}(P)=O(n^k)$ for every $d$-polytope with $n$ facets? Santos's counterexample does not disprove it, and the problem remains open. Known upper bounds are subexponential, with a quasi-polynomial bound due to Kalai and Kleitman. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirsch_conjecture))
- **Kalai's $3^d$ conjecture (1989).** Every centrally symmetric $d$-polytope has at least $3^d$ nonempty faces, counting $P$ itself. It is proved for $d\le4$ (Sanyal–Werner–Ziegler, 2009) and for simplicial polytopes (via Stanley's 1987 proof of a Bárány–Lovász conjecture), and open in general. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalai%27s_3d_conjecture))
- **Uniform polytopes.** Enumerating the convex and nonconvex uniform polytopes in dimension $\ge4$ "remains an outstanding problem". The convex uniform $4$-polytopes were enumerated by Conway and Guy in 1965. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope))
- **Graphs of $4$-polytopes.** The complexity of recognizing graphs of $4$-polytopes remains open. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steinitz%27s_theorem))
- **$g$-conjecture for spheres.** Do the $g$-theorem's conditions characterize $h$-vectors of all simplicial spheres? This was long one of the main open problems of face enumeration. Adiprasito claims a proof for simplicial rational homology spheres in full generality ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10454)), and Papadakis–Petrotou announced a second proof; a 2020 paper on PL-spheres treats both as announced preprint proofs. ([ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.06594))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Convex polytope (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope) and [Regular polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polytope): representations, faces, and the regular classification.
- **Learn:** Ziegler, [*Convex Polytopes: Extremal Constructions and f-Vector Shapes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411400): PCMI 2004 lecture notes on $3$-polytopes and Koebe–Andreev–Thurston, and on the cone of $f$-vectors of $4$-polytopes.
- **Primary:** Santos, [*A counterexample to the Hirsch conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.2814), Ann. of Math. 176 (2012); and the $g$-theorem survey in [*Weak Lefschetz property of PL-spheres*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2001.06594).
- **Further reading:** Ziegler, [*Lectures on Polytopes*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4613-8431-1) (Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics, 1995), a standard graduate text.
references.Postulates of Quantum Mechanics:
## Reference
### Overview
The Dirac–von Neumann axioms formulate quantum mechanics as a theory of operators on a complex Hilbert space. States are unit vectors up to scalar multiples, observables are (possibly unbounded) self-adjoint operators, and the expectation value of $A$ in state $\psi$ is $\langle\psi,A\psi\rangle$.
