- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 6.1200J Mathematics for Computer Science (Demaine, Abel, Chapman, 2024)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-1200j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2024/): proof techniques, induction and contradiction, counting and discrete probability.
- **Primary:** [Erdős, "Some remarks on the theory of graphs", Bull. AMS 53 (1947)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9904-1947-08785-1): the paper containing Erdős's probabilistic lower bound for $R(r,r)$, a founding example of the probabilistic method.
- **Primary:** [Polya, *How to Solve It* (Princeton University Press; 1945, reissued 2014)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691164076/how-to-solve-it): the classic monograph on heuristics, with a dictionary of strategies such as analogy, induction and working backwards.
- **Further reading:** [Polya, *How to Solve It*](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691164076/how-to-solve-it); for formal proof, the [proof assistant overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_assistant) lists Rocq, Lean, Isabelle and HOL Light.
references.Proof by Contradiction:
## Reference
### Overview
Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) proves a statement $P$ by assuming $\neg P$ and deriving a falsehood. As a principle it is $\neg\neg P\Rightarrow P$, equivalently $(\neg P\Rightarrow\bot)\Rightarrow P$. ([Wikipedia: Proof by contradiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_by_contradiction)) In natural deduction the temporary assumption $\neg P$ is cancelled at the final inference. ([Logic and Proof: Classical Reasoning](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/classical_reasoning.html))

Two patterns share the name. Proving $P$ by refuting $\neg P$ is the classical rule; proving $\neg P$ by assuming $P$ and deriving a falsehood is refutation by contradiction, which is just negation introduction. Classical logic makes them largely interchangeable, so mathematicians call both proof by contradiction, but they differ formally. ([Wikipedia: Proof by contradiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_by_contradiction)) The difference matters because intuitionistic logic keeps the second and rejects the first: there reductio "only proves negative statements". ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/))

The classical rule is the typical source of non-constructive existence proofs: constructively, a proof of $\neg\neg\exists x\,A(x)$ does not automatically allow one to conclude $\exists x\,A(x)$. ([SEP: Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/))

### Formal definition
Let $\Gamma$ be the other undischarged assumptions and $\bot$ falsity.
- **Classical reductio (RAA):** from $\Gamma,\neg P\vdash\bot$ infer $\Gamma\vdash P$, discharging $\neg P$. ([Logic and Proof: Classical Reasoning](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/classical_reasoning.html))
- **Negation introduction:** from $\Gamma,P\vdash\bot$ infer $\Gamma\vdash\neg P$; intuitionistically, $(A\to B)\to((A\to\neg B)\to\neg A)$. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/))
- **Proof by contraposition** is different again: to prove $A\to B$ one gives a direct proof of $\neg B\to\neg A$. It is a direct proof of a different statement, not an indirect argument, though the two can be combined. ([Wikipedia: Contraposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraposition))

### Key results
- **RAA, excluded middle and double-negation elimination.** With RAA one derives $A\lor\neg A$ (assume $\neg(A\lor\neg A)$, derive $\neg A$, then a contradiction) and $\neg\neg A\to A$; conversely excluded middle justifies RAA. $A\to\neg\neg A$ holds intuitionistically; only the other direction is classical. ([Logic and Proof: Classical Reasoning](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/classical_reasoning.html))
- **Contraposition is only half intuitionistic.** $(P\to Q)\to(\neg Q\to\neg P)$ holds intuitionistically; the converse needs $\neg\neg Q\to Q$. ([Wikipedia: Contraposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraposition); [Logic and Proof: Classical Reasoning](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/classical_reasoning.html))
- **Stability of negations.** Intuitionistically $\neg\neg\neg A\leftrightarrow\neg A$ (Brouwer: absurdity of absurdity of absurdity is equivalent to absurdity), so every negated formula is stable. Prime formulas are undecidable in pure intuitionistic predicate logic, but in Heyting arithmetic they (and all quantifier-free formulas) are decidable and stable, and $\neg\neg A\to A$ is provable for negative formulas (those without $\lor$ or $\exists$). Hence RAA is intuitionistically valid when the conclusion is a negation, and in arithmetic when it is a negative formula. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/)) It is also valid for decidable propositions. ([Wikipedia: Proof by contradiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_by_contradiction))
- **Glivenko's theorem (1929).** A propositional formula $A$ is classically provable iff $\neg\neg A$ is intuitionistically provable. This fails for predicate logic, where the double-negation shift $\forall x\neg\neg B(x)\to\neg\neg\forall x B(x)$ is also needed. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/))
- **Gödel–Gentzen negative translation.** There is a translation $A\mapsto g(A)$ with: classical predicate logic proves $A\leftrightarrow g(A)$, intuitionistic logic proves $g(A)\leftrightarrow\neg\neg g(A)$, and if $A$ is classically provable then $g(A)$ is intuitionistically provable. The same results hold for number theory, so Heyting arithmetic has the same consistency strength as Peano arithmetic. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/)) Kolmogorov, Gödel, Gentzen, Kuroda and Krivine translations are all of this kind and can be compared in a single partial order. ([Ferreira and Oliva, On Various Negative Translations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.5442))
- **Disjunction and existence properties.** If intuitionistic logic proves $A\lor B$ (closed), it proves $A$ or proves $B$; if Heyting arithmetic proves $\exists x\,A(x)$ (closed), it proves $A(t)$ for some closed term $t$ (Kleene). ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/))

### Examples
- **$\sqrt2$ is irrational.** Suppose $\sqrt2=a/b$ with $a,b$ integers without common factor. Then $a^2=2b^2$, so $a$ is even; writing $a=2c$ gives $b^2=2c^2$, so $b$ is even, contradicting lowest terms. ([Logic and Proof: Introduction](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/introduction.html)) Logically this proves a negation (irrationality) and is a refutation by contradiction, valid intuitionistically. ([Wikipedia: Proof by contradiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_by_contradiction))
- **Non-constructive existence.** The classical proof that there are irrationals $a,b$ with $a^b$ rational does not say which pair works. ([SEP: Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/))
- **Analysis.** The exact intermediate value theorem implies the lesser limited principle of omniscience (LLPO); constructively one gets $x$ with $|f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for each $\varepsilon>0$, and an exact root under an extra local-nonzero hypothesis. "Every real is $0$ or nonzero" implies LPO. ([SEP: Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/))
- **Hilbert's Nullstellensatz** was proved by assuming no suitable polynomials exist and deriving a contradiction. ([Wikipedia: Proof by contradiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_by_contradiction))

### History
Euclid and Archimedes used reductio in fundamental proofs; Aristotle called it "demonstration to the impossible", and the earliest example is attributed to Xenophanes. Hardy called it "one of a mathematician's finest weapons". ([Wikipedia: Proof by contradiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_by_contradiction)) Brouwer's intuitionism rejected the excluded middle; Glivenko's theorem (1929) and the negative translations of Gödel and Gentzen later showed how classical proofs embed into intuitionistic ones. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/)) Bishop's Foundations of Constructive Analysis (1967) showed much of analysis can be done without these classical principles. ([SEP: Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/))

### Connections
- [Proof Techniques](node:Proof%20Techniques): direct proof, contraposition, contradiction and induction as strategies.
- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic): the natural-deduction rules involved.
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): where Glivenko fails and the double-negation shift is needed.
- [Type Theory](node:Type%20Theory): constructive proof systems where RAA is not a primitive rule.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): apply to both PA and HA.
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): irrationality of $\sqrt2$ and constructive analysis.
- [MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics): the research area.

### Common pitfalls
- **Inconsistent background premises.** By ex falso, $\neg A\to(A\to B)$, so if $\Gamma$ is already inconsistent then $\Gamma,\neg P\vdash\bot$ holds for every $P$: the contradiction does not depend on the temporary assumption and proves nothing specific about $P$; anything obtained along the way is subsumed by the fact that $\bot$ already follows from the hypotheses. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/); [Logic and Proof: Classical Reasoning](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/classical_reasoning.html))
- **Disguised contraposition.** An argument that assumes $A$ and $\neg B$ and then derives $\neg A$ is really a direct proof of the contrapositive $\neg B\to\neg A$; contraposition is a direct proof of a different statement, though the two methods can be combined. ([Wikipedia: Contraposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraposition))
- **Calling a refutation classical.** Proving a negation (irrationality, non-existence) by contradiction is constructively fine; only proving a positive statement from $\neg\neg P$ needs the classical rule. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/))
- **Unrestricted use is too strong for computation.** Under the Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov reading with "method" taken to mean algorithm, accepting the principle universally would yield an algorithm deciding whether an arbitrary Turing machine halts. ([Wikipedia: Proof by contradiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_by_contradiction))

### Open problems
- **Admissible rules of intuitionistic predicate logic.** The SEP states that much less is known about these than in the propositional case and that "they have not been completely classified"; known admissible rules include Markov's rule and the independence-of-premise rule. ([SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/))
- **Constructive reverse mathematics of uniform continuity.** Over Bishop's constructive mathematics, the SEP lists as open finding a form of the fan theorem equivalent to the uniform continuity theorem on $[0,1]$, and whether known implications between them reverse. ([SEP: Constructive Mathematics](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mathematics-constructive/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Intuitionistic Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-intuitionistic/): rejected and retained negation principles, Glivenko, negative translations.
- **Learn:** [Logic and Proof, Classical Reasoning](https://leanprover-community.github.io/logic_and_proof/classical_reasoning.html): natural-deduction and Lean derivations of RAA, excluded middle and double negation.
- **Primary:** [Ferreira and Oliva, On Various Negative Translations (EPTCS 47, 2011)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.5442): the double-negation translations compared.
- **Further reading:** [Troelstra and van Dalen, Constructivism in Mathematics (North-Holland, 1988)](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=constructivism+in+mathematics+troelstra&fields=title,author_name,first_publish_year,publisher,key&limit=5): the standard monograph on intuitionistic logic and constructive mathematics.
references.Propositional Logic:
## Reference
### Overview
Propositional logic studies how whole propositions combine under connectives such as negation, conjunction, disjunction, and the conditional, abstracting from the internal structure of atomic statements. This note uses classical two-valued semantics. ([SEP, Propositional Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/)) It is the base layer of [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic), the language of [Boolean algebra](node:Boolean%20Algebras) and [Boolean circuits](node:Boolean%20Circuits), and the setting of the satisfiability problem SAT, whose complexity is tied to [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP). ([SEP, §§2.1.3, 2.1.6](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/); [Cook–Levin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem))

Its metatheory has a semantic side (valuations, validity, consequence), a deductive side (axiom systems, natural deduction, sequent calculus), and, since the 1970s, a complexity-theoretic side: how hard it is to decide satisfiability and how long proofs of tautologies must be. ([SEP, §§2.1–2.3](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/); [Proof complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity))

### Formal definition
Formulas are built recursively from atomic propositions $p,q,r,\ldots$ by $\neg F$, $F\land G$, $F\lor G$, $F\to G$, $F\leftrightarrow G$. An interpretation $I$ assigns a truth value to each atom, and truth $I\models F$ is defined by recursion: $I\models F\land G$ iff $I\models F$ and $I\models G$; $I\models F\lor G$ iff $I\models F$ or $I\models G$; $I\models\neg F$ iff $I\not\models F$; $I\models F\to G$ iff $I\not\models F$ or $I\models G$. ([CMU 15-414, Lecture 2, Def. 2](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s21/s20/2018/lectures/02-prop.pdf))

A formula is valid (a tautology) if it is true under every assignment and satisfiable if true under at least one. $A$ is a consequence of a set $\Gamma$, $\Gamma\models A$, if no assignment makes every member of $\Gamma$ true and $A$ false; two formulas are equivalent if true under exactly the same assignments. Derivability in a proof system is written $\Gamma\vdash A$. ([SEP, §§2.1, 2.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/))

### Key results
- **Normal forms and functional completeness.** Every classical formula is equivalent to one in disjunctive normal form, a disjunction of conjunctions of atoms and negated atoms (the DNF theorem), and similarly to one in conjunctive normal form. Hence $\{\neg,\land,\lor\}$ is truth-functionally complete: every bivalent truth function is expressed by some formula. Since $A\land B$ is equivalent to $\neg(\neg A\lor\neg B)$, $\{\neg,\lor\}$ and $\{\neg,\land\}$ are complete as well, and Sheffer and Peirce observed that the single connective "not both" suffices. ([SEP, §§2.1.1–2.1.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/))
- **Soundness and completeness.** For the standard classical propositional calculus CPC, $\vdash_{\mathrm{CPC}}A$ if and only if $A$ is a tautology (Completeness Theorem); its "only if" direction is soundness: nothing invalid is provable. Post (1921) also obtained the maximality of the calculus, and Kalmár gave a direct proof of completeness in 1935. ([SEP, §2.2.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/)) The sequent-calculus rules are sound in the same sense: if all premises are valid, so is the conclusion. ([CMU 15-414, Lecture 2](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s21/s20/2018/lectures/02-prop.pdf))
- **Compactness.** If every finite subset of a set $T$ of formulas is satisfiable, then $T$ is satisfiable. As a corollary, classical consequence is finitely determined: $T\models A$ implies $T_0\models A$ for some finite $T_0\subseteq T$. ([SEP, §2.1.7](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/)) See [Compactness Theorem](node:Compactness%20Theorem).
- **Craig interpolation.** If $\models\varphi\to\psi$, there is a formula $\rho$ using only atoms common to $\varphi$ and $\psi$ with $\models\varphi\to\rho$ and $\models\rho\to\psi$. Craig first proved the theorem for first-order logic in 1957; the standard constructive proof for propositional logic can produce an interpolant exponentially larger than $\varphi$. ([Craig interpolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_interpolation))
- **Decidability and the Cook–Levin theorem.** A formula with $n$ atoms has a $2^n$-row truth table, so validity and satisfiability are decidable. ([SEP, §2.1.5](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/)) The Cook–Levin theorem says SAT is NP-complete: it is in NP, and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time (Cook 1971, Levin 1973). Consequently SAT has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm if and only if P = NP. Karp (1972) reduced SAT to 3SAT, showing 3SAT NP-complete, among 21 problems. ([Cook–Levin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem)) See [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness) and [SAT and SMT Solving](node:SAT%20and%20SMT%20Solving).
- **Cook–Reckhow theorem.** A propositional proof system is a polynomial-time checker $P(\varphi,x)$ such that $\varphi$ is a tautology exactly when some $x$ is accepted as a proof of it; it is polynomially bounded if every tautology has a proof of size polynomial in $|\varphi|$. Cook and Reckhow (1979) showed that a polynomially bounded proof system exists if and only if NP = coNP. Haken (1985) proved exponential lower bounds for resolution proofs of the [pigeonhole principle](node:Pigeonhole%20Principle), and Ajtai (1988) a superpolynomial lower bound for constant-depth Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle. ([Proof complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity)) See [Proof Complexity and Certificates](node:Proof%20Complexity%20and%20Certificates).

### Examples
- The interpretation $I=\{q,r\}$ makes $q$ and $r$ true and every other atom, such as $p$, false; formulas are then evaluated by the clauses above. ([CMU 15-414, Lecture 2](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s21/s20/2018/lectures/02-prop.pdf))
- A sequent $\Gamma\vdash\Delta$ means $\bigwedge_{F\in\Gamma}F\to\bigvee_{G\in\Delta}G$; the formula $(p\land q\to r)\land(p\to q)\to(p\to r)$ is proved by starting from the sequent $\vdash(p\land q\to r)\land(p\to q)\to(p\to r)$ and applying the rules backwards until every branch closes by the identity rule. ([CMU 15-414, Lecture 2](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s21/s20/2018/lectures/02-prop.pdf))
- By De Morgan, $A\land B$ is equivalent to $\neg(\neg A\lor\neg B)$, which is why $\land$ can be dropped from a complete set of connectives. ([SEP, §2.1.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/))

### History
Already Aristotle observed that connectives have logical significance, and the entry traces examples such as the disjunctive syllogism to Chrysippus. Frege introduced formal deduction in 1879; Post (1921) obtained maximality results; the first recorded proofs of the deduction theorem are by Herbrand (1930) and Tarski (1933); and Gentzen introduced natural deduction and the sequent calculus in 1934–35. ([SEP, Introduction and §§2.1.4, 2.2, 2.3](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/)) Cook (1971) and Levin (1973) independently placed SAT at the centre of complexity theory, and Cook and Reckhow (1979) began the systematic study of proof complexity. ([Cook–Levin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem); [Proof complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity))

### Connections
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): adds quantifiers and predicate structure; compactness and completeness extend to it.
- [Boolean Algebras](node:Boolean%20Algebras): the algebraic semantics of classical propositional logic.
- [Boolean Circuits](node:Boolean%20Circuits) and [Circuit Complexity](node:Circuit%20Complexity): formulas are circuits of fan-out one.
- [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP) and [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): SAT is the canonical NP-complete problem.
- [Proof Theory](node:Proof%20Theory) and [MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics): sequent calculus and natural deduction.
- [Proof Complexity and Certificates](node:Proof%20Complexity%20and%20Certificates): lengths of propositional proofs.
- [Proof Techniques](node:Proof%20Techniques): informal counterparts of the formal rules.

### Common pitfalls
- Material implication is truth-functional: $F\to G$ is true whenever $F$ is false, so it does not express the causal connection implicit in the word "if", as Frege already noted. ([CMU 15-414, Lecture 2, Def. 2](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s21/s20/2018/lectures/02-prop.pdf); [SEP, §2.1.4](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/))
- Satisfiable is not valid: a formula can be true under one assignment and false under another. ([SEP, §2.1](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/))
- Decidability is not efficiency: truth tables decide validity but take $2^n$ rows, and no polynomial-time method is known. ([SEP, §§2.1.5–2.1.6](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/))
- Frege or extended Frege lower bounds would not by themselves prove NP $\ne$ coNP; that requires showing no proof system is polynomially bounded. ([Pitassi–Tzameret](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1607.00443); [Proof complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity))

### Open problems
- **P versus NP.** The Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as an unsolved Millennium Problem, formulated independently by Stephen Cook and Leonid Levin. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/)) By the Cook–Levin theorem it is equivalent to whether SAT has a polynomial-time algorithm. ([Cook–Levin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem))
- **NP versus coNP and optimal proof systems.** Whether there is a polynomially bounded proof system for classical propositional tautologies (equivalently NP = coNP), and whether a p-optimal or optimal propositional proof system exists, are posed as open questions. ([Proof complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity))
- **Lower bounds for Frege systems.** Proving super-polynomial lower bounds on the size of Frege proofs is "a major open problem in proof complexity" and "seems to be out of reach of current techniques"; no nontrivial lower bound is known for general Frege systems. ([Pitassi–Tzameret](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1607.00443); [Proof complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, Propositional Logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/): semantics, normal forms, compactness, completeness, history.
- **Learn:** [CMU 15-414 Lecture 2, Propositional Logic and Proofs](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15414/s21/s20/2018/lectures/02-prop.pdf): syntax, semantics, sequent calculus.
- **Primary:** [Pitassi and Tzameret, Algebraic Proof Complexity: Progress, Frontiers and Challenges (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00443): survey of proof complexity of strong propositional proof systems and its open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Krajíček, Proof Complexity (CUP, 2019)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/9781108242066): research monograph on propositional proof systems and their lower bounds.
- **Further reading:** [Proof complexity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_complexity): Cook–Reckhow framework and known lower bounds.
- **Further reading:** [Clay Institute, P vs NP](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/): official problem statement.
references.Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
A pseudo-Riemannian (semi-Riemannian) manifold is a differentiable manifold with an everywhere nondegenerate, smooth, symmetric metric tensor $g$. Dropping positive-definiteness lets $g(X,X)$ be positive, negative or zero, so tangent vectors split into spacelike, timelike and null. The Lorentzian case, signature $(1,n-1)$ or $(n-1,1)$, is the geometry of spacetime in [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity), with [Minkowski space](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime) $\mathbb R^{n-1,1}$ as local model. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold); [Wikipedia: Causal structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causal_structure)) nLab treats Riemannian and Lorentzian manifolds as special cases of the same structure. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pseudo-Riemannian+manifold))

The local theory (Levi-Civita connection, curvature, geodesics) carries over from [Riemannian geometry](node:Riemannian%20Metrics) almost verbatim. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Riemannian_geometry)) The global theory is different: existence of a metric is topologically obstructed, Hopf–Rinow fails, compact Lorentzian manifolds are causally pathological, and the central objects become causal structure, Cauchy surfaces, maximal timelike geodesics and singularity theorems. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706); [Wikipedia: Hopf–Rinow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf%E2%80%93Rinow_theorem); [Galloway, Notes on Lorentzian causality](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/vienna-course-notes.pdf))

### Formal definition
A **metric tensor** on an $n$-manifold $M$ assigns to each $p$ a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $g_p$ on $T_pM$, depending smoothly on $p$; nondegeneracy means $g_p(X,Y)=0$ for all $Y$ forces $X=0$. By Sylvester's law of inertia, $g_p$ has a signature $(p,q)$, $p+q=n$, and nondegeneracy plus continuity make it constant on a connected manifold. The flat model of signature $(p,q)$ is $\mathbb R^{p,q}$ with ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold))
$$
g = dx_1^2+\cdots+dx_p^2-dx_{p+1}^2-\cdots-dx_{p+q}^2 .
$$
A **Lorentzian** metric has signature $(1,n-1)$ (or $(n-1,1)$). A nonzero $X$ is timelike if $g(X,X)<0$, null if $g(X,X)=0$, spacelike if $g(X,X)>0$ (signature $-,+,\dots,+$). ([Wikipedia: Causal structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causal_structure)) A Lorentzian manifold is **time-orientable** if the two cones of timelike vectors can be labelled future and past continuously over $M$; a **spacetime** is a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold. A non-time-orientable Lorentzian manifold (e.g. a flat Möbius strip) has a time-orientable double cover. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706))

The **Lorentzian distance** is $d(p,q) = \sup\{L(\sigma)\}$ over future-directed causal curves from $p$ to $q$ if $p<q$, and $0$ otherwise, where $L$ is Lorentzian arc length $\int\sqrt{-g(\dot\sigma,\dot\sigma)}$. It is not a metric-space distance and may be infinite. ([Galloway, Notes on Lorentzian causality](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/vienna-course-notes.pdf))

### Key results
- **Levi-Civita connection.** On any pseudo-Riemannian manifold there is a unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$, given by the Koszul formula, with $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12 g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$; if $g$ is $C^k$ then $\nabla$ is $C^{k-1}$. ([Wikipedia: Fundamental theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_Riemannian_geometry))
- **Existence of Lorentzian metrics.** $M$ admits a time-oriented Lorentzian metric iff it has a nowhere-vanishing continuous vector field $X$; given a Riemannian $h$, $g(Y,Z)=h(Y,Z)-2h(Y,X)h(Z,X)/h(X,X)$ is Lorentzian. Hence every connected noncompact manifold admits a Lorentzian metric, and a connected compact manifold admits one iff $\chi(M)=0$; $S^2$ has none. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706); [MathWorld: Markus's theorem](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/MarcussTheorem.html))
- **Compact spacetimes are acausal (Geroch).** Every compact $C^2$ spacetime contains a closed timelike curve. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706))
- **Reverse inequalities.** For causal $X,Y$ in the same half-cone, $|g(X,Y)|\ge|X||Y|$ and $|X+Y|\ge|X|+|Y|$ with $|X|=\sqrt{-g(X,X)}$; for $p<r<q$, $d(p,q)\ge d(p,r)+d(r,q)$. Within a convex neighbourhood, timelike geodesics maximize Lorentzian length among causal curves. ([Galloway, Notes on Lorentzian causality](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/vienna-course-notes.pdf))
- **Causal ladder.** From weakest to strongest: non-totally vicious, chronological, causal, distinguishing, strongly causal, stably causal (equivalently, admits a time function), causally continuous, causally simple, globally hyperbolic (causal with all $J^+(x)\cap J^-(y)$ compact). ([Wikipedia: Causality conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causality_conditions)) Stable causality is equivalent to existence of a time function, and continuous time functions can be replaced by smooth ones. ([Minguzzi 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.06494))
- **Geroch splitting and its smooth version.** A spacetime is globally hyperbolic iff it has a time function whose level sets are Cauchy surfaces (Geroch, Seifert); then $M\cong\mathbb R\times S$. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706)) Bernal and Sánchez proved a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface exists, giving a smooth splitting. ([Bernal & Sánchez 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0306108))
- **Maximal geodesics.** In a globally hyperbolic spacetime $d$ is finite and continuous, and for $q\in I^+(p)$ there is a timelike geodesic $\gamma$ from $p$ to $q$ with $L(\gamma)=d(p,q)$; global hyperbolicity is the standard condition ensuring such maximal segments exist. ([Galloway, Notes on Lorentzian causality](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/vienna-course-notes.pdf))
- **Penrose singularity theorem.** Let $(M,g)$ be smooth, globally hyperbolic, satisfy the null energy condition $R_{\mu\nu}n^\mu n^\nu\ge0$ for null $n$, and have a noncompact Cauchy surface containing a compact surface that is both inner and outer future-trapped. Then $(M,g)$ is null geodesically incomplete. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706); [Wikipedia: Penrose–Hawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems))
- **Cosmological incompleteness (Geroch's form).** A smooth globally hyperbolic spacetime with the timelike focusing condition and a compact Cauchy surface with strictly negative mean curvature $\operatorname{tr}_hK<0$ is future timelike geodesically incomplete. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706))
- **Kulkarni's theorem.** Sectional curvature $K(X,Y)=g(R(X,Y)Y,X)/(g(X,X)g(Y,Y)-g(X,Y)^2)$ is defined only on nondegenerate planes. Kulkarni proved that if a connected manifold of indefinite metric has sectional curvature bounded from above or from below, it has constant sectional curvature; Harris and Dajczer–Nomizu generalized this using bounds on timelike (or spacelike) planes only. ([Kassabov & Borisov](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1008.1875)) The theorem needs $\dim M\ge3$: in dimension 2 there is one plane per point and $K$ is just the Gauss curvature. Freyn extends it to Lorentzian tame Fréchet manifolds, where a one-sided bound $a\le K$ or $K\le b$ is equivalent to constant $K$. ([Freyn 2011](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1109.2837))
- **Isometric embedding.** Greene and Clarke (1970) extended Nash's theorem to indefinite, even degenerate, metrics: every semi-Riemannian manifold embeds isometrically in some $\mathbb R^N_\nu$. Müller and Sánchez (2011) showed a Lorentzian manifold embeds isometrically in some Minkowski $\mathbb L^N$ iff it admits a steep temporal function, which every globally hyperbolic spacetime does. ([Wikipedia: Nash embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem))

### Examples
- **Minkowski space** $\mathbb R^{n-1,1}$, the flat Lorentzian model. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold))
- **[Warped Products](node:Warped%20Products).** $F\times_f B$ with metric $g\oplus f^2h$; the Schwarzschild solution and Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker models are warped products, as are Randall–Sundrum metrics. ([Wikipedia: Warped product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product))
- **Clifton–Pohl torus.** A Lorentzian metric on the 2-torus that is compact but geodesically incomplete, so Hopf–Rinow fails. ([Wikipedia: Hopf–Rinow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf%E2%80%93Rinow_theorem))
- **$S^1\times\mathbb R$ with $-dt^2+dx^2$**, $t$ periodic: every circle $x=$ const is a closed timelike curve. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706))

### History
Penrose's 1965 theorem was the first modern singularity theorem and introduced closed trapped surfaces. ([Senovilla & Garfinkle 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.5226)) Barrett O'Neill's *Semi-Riemannian Geometry With Applications to Relativity* (Academic Press, 1983) treats manifolds with metrics of arbitrary signature and is a standard reference. ([Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780125267403); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pseudo-Riemannian+manifold)) *Global Lorentzian Geometry* first appeared from Marcel Dekker in 1981, with a second edition by Beem, Ehrlich and Easley in 1996. ([Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL3232616W)) Bernal and Sánchez gave the smooth form of Geroch's splitting in 2003 ([Bernal & Sánchez 2003](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0306108)), and Müller and Sánchez's 2011 embedding theorem also showed that Clarke's technique for the globally hyperbolic case has a gap. ([Wikipedia: Nash embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem))

### Connections
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): the definite special case; every manifold admits one, unlike a Lorentzian metric.
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): the underlying structure.
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives): the Levi-Civita connection exists in any signature.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): sectional curvature is restricted to nondegenerate planes.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): timelike geodesics locally maximize length.
- [Hopf–Rinow Theorem](node:Hopf–Rinow%20Theorem): fails in Lorentzian signature; global hyperbolicity replaces it.
- [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime): the flat model.
- [Light Cone](node:Light%20Cone): the null cone organizes causal structure.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) and [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): spacetime is a Lorentzian 4-manifold.
- [Energy Conditions](node:Energy%20Conditions): curvature hypotheses of singularity theorems.
- [Warped Products](node:Warped%20Products): Schwarzschild and FLRW metrics.
- [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution) and [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): standard warped Lorentzian examples.
- [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space) and [de Sitter Space](node:de%20Sitter%20Space): constant-curvature Lorentzian spaces.
- [Submanifolds and Embeddings](node:Submanifolds%20and%20Embeddings): induced metrics may degenerate on null submanifolds.
- Map: [MSC 53 - Differential geometry](node:MSC%2053%20-%20Differential%20geometry)

### Common pitfalls
- **$g$ is not a distance.** $g(X,X)$ can be negative or zero, and the Lorentzian distance obeys a reverse triangle inequality. ([Galloway, Notes on Lorentzian causality](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/vienna-course-notes.pdf))
- **Compactness is bad, not good.** Compact Lorentzian manifolds need $\chi=0$ and contain closed timelike curves, and need not be geodesically complete. ([Chruściel, Elements of causality theory](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.6706); [Wikipedia: Hopf–Rinow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf%E2%80%93Rinow_theorem))
- **Induced metrics can degenerate.** The metric vanishes on any lightlike curve, so submanifolds need not inherit a pseudo-Riemannian structure. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold))
- **Curvature bounds are not Riemannian-style hypotheses.** For an indefinite metric (dimension at least 3), even a one-sided bound on all sectional curvatures forces constant curvature. ([Kassabov & Borisov](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1008.1875); [Freyn 2011](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1109.2837))

### Open problems
- **Bartnik splitting conjecture.** A globally hyperbolic spacetime with compact Cauchy surfaces satisfying the timelike convergence condition and timelike geodesic completeness should split as $\mathbb R\times S$ with metric $-dt^2+h$. It "has so far been proven under various extra assumptions"; whether the curvature condition forces the needed no-observer-horizon condition remains unresolved. ([García-Heveling 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.07782v2))
- **Markus conjecture.** Markus conjectured in 1962 that a compact affine manifold with parallel volume is complete, $M=\mathbb R^n/\Gamma$ with $\Gamma\subset\operatorname{Aff}(n,\mathbb R)$ discrete. It is "far from being completely resolved", though proved for convex affine manifolds of dimension $\le5$. ([Jo & Kim 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.07918))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Pseudo-Riemannian manifold (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold): definition, signature and Lorentzian case; see also [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pseudo-Riemannian+manifold).
- **Learn:** [G. Galloway, "Notes on Lorentzian causality" (University of Miami, 2014)](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/vienna-course-notes.pdf): causal structure, global hyperbolicity, Lorentzian distance, Penrose's theorem.
- **Primary:** [P. T. Chruściel, "Elements of causality theory"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.6706): monograph-length notes with existence, Geroch splitting and incompleteness theorems.
- **Primary:** [E. Minguzzi, "Causality theory for closed cone structures with applications", Rev. Math. Phys. 31 (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.06494): modern survey-level treatment of the causal ladder and singularity theorems.
- **Primary:** [A. Bernal & M. Sánchez, "On smooth Cauchy hypersurfaces and Geroch's splitting theorem", CMP 243 (2003)](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0306108).
- **Further reading:** [B. O'Neill, *Semi-Riemannian Geometry With Applications to Relativity* (Academic Press, 1983)](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780125267403) and [J. Beem, P. Ehrlich & K. Easley, *Global Lorentzian Geometry* (2nd ed., Marcel Dekker, 1996)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL3232616W): the standard graduate texts.

## Reference
### Overview
Q-learning is a model-free reinforcement-learning algorithm that learns the optimal action-value function $Q^*(s,a)$ of a Markov decision process from sampled transitions, without a model of the transition probabilities. After each transition $(S_t,A_t,R_{t+1},S_{t+1})$ it moves its estimate of $Q(S_t,A_t)$ toward the temporal-difference target $R_{t+1}+\gamma\max_a Q(S_{t+1},a)$. Given unlimited exploration with a partly random policy, it identifies an optimal action-selection policy ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning)).

Q-learning is the standard example of off-policy learning: its target uses the greedy maximum over next actions, so it estimates the optimal policy's values while the agent follows an exploratory behaviour policy. SARSA, the on-policy counterpart, instead bootstraps from the action the agent actually takes next ([Wikipedia: SARSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State%E2%80%93action%E2%80%93reward%E2%80%93state%E2%80%93action); [Wikipedia: Reinforcement learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning); [van Hasselt 2010](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2010/hash/091d584fced301b442654dd8c23b3fc9-Abstract.html)).

Tabular Q-learning applies only to finite state and action spaces. Replacing the table by a deep convolutional network gave the deep Q-network (DQN), which learned to play Atari games from raw pixels; with nonlinear function approximation, however, Q-learning can be unstable or divergent, and its stability with even linear function approximation is a long-standing open question ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning); [arXiv: Mnih et al. 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.5602); [arXiv: Meyn 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02632)).

### Formal definition
For a discounted MDP with discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$, the **Bellman optimality operator** on functions $Q:S\times A\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(HQ)(s,a)=\mathbb E\bigl[R(s,a)\bigr]+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q(s',a'),$$
and $Q^*$ is its fixed point (MIT 2.997 writes the cost-minimizing version with $\min$) ([MIT OCW 2.997 Lecture 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-997-decision-making-in-large-scale-systems-spring-2004/dbd61bc21861760c0e7b7a3fff4d6120_lec_8_v1.pdf)).

The **Q-learning update** with learning rate $\alpha_t\in(0,1]$ is
$$Q_{t+1}(S_t,A_t)=(1-\alpha_t)\,Q_t(S_t,A_t)+\alpha_t\Bigl(R_{t+1}+\gamma\max_{a}Q_t(S_{t+1},a)\Bigr),$$
with all other entries unchanged ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning)). Writing $\alpha_t(s,a)=0$ for pairs not visited at step $t$, it takes the stochastic-approximation form
$$Q_{t+1}=Q_t+\alpha_t\bigl(HQ_t-Q_t+w_t\bigr),\qquad \mathbb E[w_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0,$$
where $w_t$ is the noise from replacing the expectation over $s'$ by the sampled next state ([MIT OCW 2.997 Lecture 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-997-decision-making-in-large-scale-systems-spring-2004/dbd61bc21861760c0e7b7a3fff4d6120_lec_8_v1.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Asynchronous stochastic-approximation theorem.** Let $r_{t+1}(i)=r_t(i)+\alpha_t(i)\bigl((Hr_t)(i)-r_t(i)+w_t(i)\bigr)$. If $\mathbb E[w_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0$, $\mathbb E[w_t(i)^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le A+B\|r_t\|^2$ for some norm, $\sum_t\alpha_t(i)=\infty$ and $\sum_t\alpha_t(i)^2<\infty$ for every $i$, and $H$ is a maximum-norm contraction, then $r_t\to r^*$ with probability 1, where $Hr^*=r^*$. Max-norm contraction allows weaker conditions than a Euclidean-norm contraction. ([MIT OCW 2.997 Lecture 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-997-decision-making-in-large-scale-systems-spring-2004/dbd61bc21861760c0e7b7a3fff4d6120_lec_8_v1.pdf))
- **Convergence of tabular Q-learning (Watkins–Dayan 1992).** As a corollary, if every state–action pair is visited infinitely often and the step sizes satisfy $\sum_t\alpha_t(s,a)=\infty$ and $\sum_t\alpha_t(s,a)^2<\infty$ with probability 1 for all $(s,a)$, then $Q_t\to Q^*$ with probability 1. Watkins and Dayan gave the proof in Machine Learning 8(3–4), 1992; Jaakkola, Jordan and Singh placed Q-learning and TD($\lambda$) in a general stochastic-approximation convergence theorem. ([MIT OCW 2.997 Lecture 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-997-decision-making-in-large-scale-systems-spring-2004/dbd61bc21861760c0e7b7a3fff4d6120_lec_8_v1.pdf); [Crossref: Watkins and Dayan](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00992698); [NeurIPS: Jaakkola, Jordan, Singh](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1993/hash/5807a685d1a9ab3b599035bc566ce2b9-Abstract.html))
- **Sharp sample complexity (Li, Cai, Chen, Wei, Chi).** For synchronous Q-learning on a $\gamma$-discounted MDP with a generative model, about $\frac{|S||A|}{(1-\gamma)^4\varepsilon^2}$ samples (up to logarithmic factors) suffice for $\varepsilon$-accurate $Q$ when $|A|\ge 2$, improving the earlier $(1-\gamma)^{-5}$ dependence; this rate is tight, so Q-learning is strictly sub-optimal relative to the minimax lower bound, whereas for $|A|=1$ (TD learning) the rate $\frac{|S|}{(1-\gamma)^3\varepsilon^2}$ is minimax optimal. The analysis extends to asynchronous Q-learning. ([arXiv: Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06548))
- **Overestimation bias and Double Q-learning.** Q-learning uses the maximum of estimated values as an estimate of the maximum of expected values, which is biased upward and can make it perform very poorly in stochastic environments. Double Q-learning maintains two estimators, one selecting and one evaluating the maximizing action; it may underestimate instead, and it converges to the optimal policy. ([van Hasselt 2010](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2010/hash/091d584fced301b442654dd8c23b3fc9-Abstract.html))
- **The deadly triad.** Combining function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning — all three present in Q-learning with a function approximator — can make learning diverge with unbounded value estimates, although several successful algorithms combine all three. ([arXiv: van Hasselt et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02648); [Wikipedia: Reinforcement learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning))

### Examples
- **DQN.** Mnih et al. trained a convolutional network with a Q-learning variant on raw Atari pixels, outperforming previous approaches on six of seven games and a human expert on three (2013); the 2015 version reported play at roughly the level of a professional human tester on 49 Atari 2600 games using experience replay (training on random samples of past transitions) and targets updated only periodically. ([arXiv: Mnih et al. 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.5602); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning))
- **Double DQN.** DQN substantially overestimates action values on some Atari games; adapting Double Q-learning to deep function approximation reduces the overestimation and improves scores on several games. ([arXiv: van Hasselt, Guez, Silver](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.06461))

### History
Chris Watkins introduced Q-learning in his 1989 PhD thesis *Learning from Delayed Rewards*; Bozinovski's 1981 Crossbar Adaptive Array had a similar memory structure ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning)). Watkins and Dayan's convergence paper "Q-learning" appeared in Machine Learning in 1992 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00992698)), and Jaakkola, Jordan and Singh's stochastic-approximation analysis at NIPS 1993 ([NeurIPS](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1993/hash/5807a685d1a9ab3b599035bc566ce2b9-Abstract.html)). Van Hasselt introduced Double Q-learning at NIPS 2010, Mnih and coauthors' DQN appeared on arXiv in 2013 with a larger study in 2015, and Double DQN followed in 2015 ([NeurIPS](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2010/hash/091d584fced301b442654dd8c23b3fc9-Abstract.html); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.5602); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.06461)).

### Connections
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): Q-learning is a central value-based method of the field.
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the model whose optimal action values Q-learning estimates.
- [Dynamic Programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming): Q-learning is a sampled, model-free form of value iteration on Q-factors.
- [Banach Fixed-Point Theorem](node:Banach%20Fixed-Point%20Theorem): the Bellman operator's sup-norm contraction gives a unique fixed point $Q^*$.
- [Stochastic Approximation](node:Stochastic%20Approximation): the framework of its convergence proofs.
- [Deep Q-Networks](node:Deep%20Q-Networks): Q-learning with neural-network function approximation.
- [Exploration in Reinforcement Learning](node:Exploration%20in%20Reinforcement%20Learning): convergence requires visiting every pair infinitely often.
- [Actor-Critic Methods](node:Actor-Critic%20Methods): policy-based methods that also learn value estimates.
- [Policy Gradient Methods](node:Policy%20Gradient%20Methods): the main alternative to value-based learning.
- [Offline Reinforcement Learning](node:Offline%20Reinforcement%20Learning): Q-learning from fixed data, where overestimation is acute.
- [Kumar et al. 2020 - Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04779): a Q-learning variant for the offline setting.
- [Multi-Armed Bandits](node:Multi-Armed%20Bandits): the one-state special case.

### Common pitfalls
- The convergence theorem is for tabular Q-learning with decreasing step sizes and infinite visitation; it says nothing about function approximation, where learning can be unstable or diverge. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning); [arXiv: van Hasselt et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02648))
- A constant learning rate does not satisfy $\sum_t\alpha_t^2<\infty$; the theorem requires step sizes that decrease to zero. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning); [MIT OCW 2.997 Lecture 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-997-decision-making-in-large-scale-systems-spring-2004/dbd61bc21861760c0e7b7a3fff4d6120_lec_8_v1.pdf))
- Learned Q-values are not unbiased value estimates: the max operator biases them upward in noisy environments. ([van Hasselt 2010](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2010/hash/091d584fced301b442654dd8c23b3fc9-Abstract.html))
- Discretizing continuous spaces to apply tabular Q-learning runs into the curse of dimensionality. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning))

### Open problems
- **Stability and convergence with linear function approximation.** Meyn writes that the stability of Q-learning with linear function approximation "has been an open topic for research for over three decades"; he gives stability conditions for an optimistic training scheme with a modified Gibbs policy, while noting that convergence "remains one of many open topics for research". ([arXiv: Meyn 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02632))
- **Understanding the deadly triad in practice.** That some algorithms combine function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning successfully, despite known divergence, points to at least a partial gap in current understanding. ([arXiv: van Hasselt et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02648))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Q-learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning): update rule, history, variants (Double Q, DQN), limitations.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 2.997 Lecture Note 8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-997-decision-making-in-large-scale-systems-spring-2004/dbd61bc21861760c0e7b7a3fff4d6120_lec_8_v1.pdf): stochastic approximation and the Q-learning convergence theorem.
- **Primary:** [Watkins and Dayan, Q-learning, Machine Learning 8 (1992)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF00992698): the convergence paper (bibliographic record).
- **Primary:** [Li et al., Is Q-Learning Minimax Optimal?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06548): tight sample-complexity analysis.
- **Primary:** [van Hasselt, Double Q-learning (NIPS 2010)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2010/hash/091d584fced301b442654dd8c23b3fc9-Abstract.html): overestimation bias and the double estimator.
- **Further reading:** [Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (MIT Press)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL2691730W): textbook (first edition 1998; bibliographic record).

## Reference
### Overview
Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is the gauge field theory of the strong interaction of colored quarks and gluons; it is the $SU(3)$ factor of the $SU(3)\times SU(2)\times U(1)$ Standard Model. Quarks carry a color index $a=1,\dots,N_c=3$ and transform in the fundamental representation, while the $N_c^2-1=8$ gluon fields transform in the adjoint. Besides the quark masses, the coupling $g_s$ (or $\alpha_s=g_s^2/4\pi$) is the only fundamental parameter. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf))

Neither quarks nor gluons are observed as free particles: hadrons are color-singlet combinations of quarks, antiquarks and gluons. The two ab initio methods are perturbation theory in $\alpha_s$, reliable for hard processes because of asymptotic freedom, and lattice gauge theory for the nonperturbative regime. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)) Spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking together with the conformal anomaly accounts for roughly 99% of the nucleon mass, the explicit light-quark masses for about 1%. ([Wikipedia, Chiral symmetry breaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral_symmetry_breaking))

QCD therefore poses some of the central open questions of quantum field theory: an analytic understanding of confinement, related to the Clay Millennium problem on the Yang–Mills mass gap, and the strong CP problem. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_chromodynamics); [Wikipedia, Strong CP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_CP_problem))

### Formal definition
In the PDG convention,
$$\mathcal L=\sum_q\bar\psi_{q,a}\left(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\delta_{ab}-g_s\gamma^\mu t^C_{ab}A^C_\mu-m_q\delta_{ab}\right)\psi_{q,b}-\tfrac14F^A_{\mu\nu}F^{A\mu\nu},$$
with $F^A_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A^A_\nu-\partial_\nu A^A_\mu-g_sf^{ABC}A^B_\mu A^C_\nu$, $[t^A,t^B]=if^{ABC}t^C$ and $t^A=\lambda^A/2$. The color factors are $C_F=(N_c^2-1)/(2N_c)=4/3$, $C_A=N_c=3$ and $T_R=1/2$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf))

[Gauge Invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance) also allows a CP-violating term $\theta\,\frac{\alpha_s}{8\pi}F^{A}_{\mu\nu}\tilde F^{A\mu\nu}$ with $\tilde F^{A}_{\mu\nu}=\tfrac12\epsilon_{\mu\nu\sigma\rho}F^{A\sigma\rho}$; neutron and mercury electric-dipole-moment limits constrain $|\theta|\lesssim10^{-10}$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)) The physical angle is $\bar\theta=\theta-\arg\det(Y_uY_d)$, with $Y_{u,d}$ the quark Yukawa matrices. ([Wikipedia, Strong CP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_CP_problem))

### Key results
- **Asymptotic freedom and the running coupling.** In $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ with $n_f$ light flavors, $\mu_R^2\,d\alpha_s/d\mu_R^2=-(b_0\alpha_s^2+b_1\alpha_s^3+\cdots)$ with $b_0=(11C_A-4n_fT_R)/(12\pi)=(33-2n_f)/(12\pi)$ and $b_1=(153-19n_f)/(24\pi^2)$; $b_0,b_1$ are scheme-independent, higher coefficients are not. The minus sign is the origin of asymptotic freedom: $\alpha_s\sim0.1$ for momentum transfers of $0.1$–$1$ TeV, while the theory is strongly coupled around and below $1$ GeV. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)) See [Asymptotic Freedom](node:Asymptotic%20Freedom) and [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group).
- **$\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$ and dimensional transmutation.** Keeping only $b_0$, $\alpha_s(\mu_R^2)=1/(b_0\ln(\mu_R^2/\Lambda^2))$, where the integration constant $\Lambda$ is the scale at which the perturbative coupling would diverge and indicates where nonperturbative dynamics dominates. Because $\Lambda$ depends on the approximation used, results are quoted as $\alpha_s(m_Z^2)$; the PDG 2023 world average is $\alpha_s(m_Z^2)=0.1180\pm0.0009$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf))
- **Collinear factorization and DGLAP evolution.** Hadronic cross sections such as deep-inelastic structure functions factorize into perturbative coefficient functions convolved with parton distribution functions $f_{i/p}(x,\mu_F^2)$, up to power corrections $O(\Lambda^2/Q^2)$. The $\mu_F$ dependence obeys the DGLAP equations, at leading order $\mu_F^2\,\partial f_{i/p}/\partial\mu_F^2=\sum_j\frac{\alpha_s}{2\pi}\int_x^1\frac{dz}{z}P_{i\leftarrow j}(z)f_{j/p}(x/z,\mu_F^2)$, e.g. $P_{q\leftarrow g}(z)=T_R(z^2+(1-z)^2)$. Collinear factorization is generally believed valid for sufficiently inclusive hard processes, though the PDG notes that reviews of the proofs are cautious about hadron-collider processes. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)) See [Parton Distribution Functions](node:Parton%20Distribution%20Functions).
- **Spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking.** For massless $u,d,s$ the Lagrangian has an $SU(3)_L\times SU(3)_R$ flavor symmetry; a nonperturbatively induced quark condensate breaks it to the diagonal $SU(3)_V$. The light pseudoscalar mesons, including the pions, are the resulting Nambu–Goldstone bosons, with small masses due to the explicit quark masses; the axial $U(1)_A$ is instead broken by the anomaly via instantons, so the $\eta'$ is much heavier. ([Wikipedia, Chiral symmetry breaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral_symmetry_breaking)) See [Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking](node:Spontaneous%20Symmetry%20Breaking) and [Chiral Nuclear Effective Field Theory](node:Chiral%20Nuclear%20Effective%20Field%20Theory).
- **Lattice QCD.** After Wick rotation the [partition function](node:Partition%20Function) becomes a path integral over $SU(3)$ link variables $U_\mu(x)$ on a four-dimensional lattice, evaluated by Monte Carlo and extrapolated to zero lattice spacing, a limit reached as $g\to0$ by asymptotic freedom. Wilson's 1974 paper "Confinement of quarks" introduced the framework; fermion doubling forces lattice fermions to break an assumption of the Nielsen–Ninomiya theorem, often chiral symmetry. ([Wikipedia, Lattice QCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_QCD)) See [Lattice QCD](node:Lattice%20QCD).
- **Thermal crossover.** At zero baryon [chemical potential](node:Chemical%20Potential), lattice QCD finds a smooth crossover from a hadron resonance gas to quark–gluon matter near $T\sim155$ MeV, rather than a sharp phase transition. ([NNPSS lecture](https://web.mit.edu/2022nnpss/lectures/Lec1HotQCD.pdf)) See [Quark–Gluon Plasma](node:Quark–Gluon%20Plasma).

### Examples
Hadrons are color singlets; protons and neutrons are baryons, pions and kaons are light pseudoscalar mesons whose small masses reflect chiral symmetry breaking. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf); [Wikipedia, Chiral symmetry breaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral_symmetry_breaking)) The need for color itself came from the $\Delta^{++}$, three up quarks with parallel spins, which would violate the Pauli principle without an extra antisymmetric color degree of freedom. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_chromodynamics))

In deep-inelastic scattering, the default scale choice is $\mu_R=\mu_F=Q$, and at zeroth order the gluon coefficient function vanishes while the quark one is $e_q^2\delta(1-z)$, recovering the parton model. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf))

### History
Greenberg, and independently Han and Nambu, proposed color in 1964–65, after Gell-Mann and Zweig's 1963 quark proposal. Gross and Wilczek, and independently Politzer, discovered asymptotic freedom in 1973, sharing the 2004 Nobel Prize; Nambu received the 2008 prize for his work on spontaneous symmetry breaking. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_chromodynamics)) Wilson introduced lattice QCD in 1974. ([Wikipedia, Lattice QCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_QCD)) Peccei and Quinn proposed a chiral solution to the strong CP problem, with which a light pseudoscalar particle, the axion, is associated. ([Peccei](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0607268))

### Connections
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): QCD is the non-Abelian $SU(3)$ gauge theory.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): supplies quantization, perturbation theory and renormalization.
- [Renormalization](node:Renormalization): the running coupling and $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$ are renormalization effects.
- [Standard Model of Particle Physics](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics): QCD is its strong-interaction factor.
- [Axions](node:Axions): the Peccei–Quinn solution of the strong CP problem.
- [CP Violation](node:CP%20Violation): the $\theta$ term is a possible source of CP violation in the strong sector.
- [Hadron Jets](node:Hadron%20Jets): perturbative QCD describes jet production at colliders.
- [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): chiral perturbation theory and heavy-quark theories are QCD effective theories.

### Common pitfalls
Asymptotic freedom and confinement are distinct: weak coupling at short distance does not prove confinement at long distance. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_chromodynamics)) $\Lambda$ is not unique: a value of $\Lambda$ defines $\alpha_s(\mu_R^2)$ only once the particular approximate solution of the RGE is specified, which is why $\alpha_s(m_Z^2)$ is quoted instead. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)) Most of the proton mass does not come from the explicit light-quark masses, which contribute only about 1%. ([Wikipedia, Chiral symmetry breaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiral_symmetry_breaking))

### Open problems
- **Confinement.** Confinement is analytically unproven, though well supported by lattice calculations and experiment; Greensite's monograph states that the confinement problem is far from solved. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_chromodynamics); [Greensite](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-14382-3)) The related Clay Millennium problem asks for a proof that quantum Yang–Mills theory has a mass gap; the Clay Institute states no proof is known. ([Clay](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/))
- **Strong CP problem.** Why is $|\bar\theta|<10^{-10}$ when nothing in QCD requires it to be small? Proposed solutions include the Peccei–Quinn axion, a massless quark (disfavored because lattice calculations show all quarks are massive) and Nelson–Barr models; the problem is sometimes regarded as unsolved, and Peccei's review calls it the strong CP problem because the parameter must be so small to agree with experiment. ([Wikipedia, Strong CP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_CP_problem); [Peccei](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0607268))
- **Dense matter.** The lattice sign problem at nonzero baryon density restricts first-principles lattice studies mainly to low baryon density. ([Wikipedia, Lattice QCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_QCD))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Quantum chromodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_chromodynamics): history, confinement and chiral symmetry overview.
- **Learn:** [Noronha-Hostler, NNPSS 2022 lecture on hot QCD](https://web.mit.edu/2022nnpss/lectures/Lec1HotQCD.pdf): lattice QCD at finite temperature and the crossover.
- **Primary:** [PDG Review of Particle Physics, QCD](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf): conventions, running coupling, factorization and $\alpha_s$ world average.
- **Primary:** [Peccei, The Strong CP Problem and Axions](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0607268): review of $\bar\theta$ and the axion solution.
- **Further reading:** [Greensite, An Introduction to the Confinement Problem](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-14382-3): survey of confinement mechanisms.
references.Quantum Computing:
## Reference
### Overview
Quantum computing is computation in which information is stored in qubits, whose joint state is a unit vector in a tensor product of two-dimensional complex [Hilbert spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), and processed by unitary gates followed by measurement. A qubit measured in the standard basis gives 0 or 1, but before measurement it can be in a superposition $\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle$ with $|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1$, and outcome probabilities follow the [Born rule](node:Born%20Rule); each added qubit doubles the dimension of the state space, so a naive classical simulation of $n$ qubits stores $2^n$ amplitudes. Computations are usually described as circuits of unitary gates, with measurements deferred to the end. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing))

From the complexity-theoretic side, the central object is the class BQP, the decision problems solvable by a uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits with bounded error. It sits between BPP and PP, and its relationship to NP is unknown ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP)). Shor's algorithm factors integers in polynomial time on a quantum computer ([Shor](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9508027)), while factoring is believed infeasible on a classical computer; no proof shows that BQP differs from BPP ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing)).

The field also has an engineering side: [decoherence](node:Decoherence) and gate errors grow with the ratio of operation time to coherence time, and practical machines rely on quantum error correction and the threshold theorem. DiVincenzo's criteria (scalability, initialisable qubits, gates faster than decoherence, a universal gate set, readable qubits) summarise the hardware requirements. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing))

### Formal definition
A **quantum circuit** on $n$ qubits acts on $(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}$ by a product of gates, each a unitary on a constant number of qubits; a standard **universal gate set** is all single-qubit unitaries together with CNOT, $|a,b\rangle\mapsto|a,a\oplus b\rangle$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing))

**BQP.** A language $L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ is in BQP if there is a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits $\{Q_n\}$, $Q_n$ acting on $n$ input qubits (plus ancillas) and outputting one bit, such that
$$x\in L\Rightarrow \Pr[Q_{|x|}(x)=1]\ge \tfrac23,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow \Pr[Q_{|x|}(x)=0]\ge\tfrac23 .$$
The constant $2/3$ is arbitrary: repeating and taking a majority vote reduces the error below any fixed bound, by the Chernoff bound. The promise version, Promise-BQP, is defined the same way for promise problems. ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP))

### Key results
- **Containments.** $\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{AWPP}\subseteq\mathrm{PP}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm{EXP}$; none of these individual inclusions is known to be strict. The PP inclusion is due to Adleman, DeMarrais and Huang (1997), the AWPP inclusion to Fortnow and Rogers (1999), and the PSPACE inclusion (Bernstein and Vazirani 1997) uses Feynman's sum-over-histories technique. BQP is low for itself: $\mathrm{BQP}^{\mathrm{BQP}}=\mathrm{BQP}$. ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP))
- **Complete problem.** APPROX-QCIRCUIT-PROB (given a circuit $C$ and $\alpha>\beta$, decide whether measuring the first output qubit gives 1 with probability $\ge\alpha$ or $\le\beta$, promised one holds) is Promise-BQP-complete; no complete problem for the language class BQP is known. ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP))
- **Shor's algorithm (1994).** Integer factorization and discrete logarithms have randomized quantum algorithms running in a number of steps polynomial in the input size; the paper is the expanded version of the FOCS 1994 paper. Factoring is believed infeasible classically, and a scalable quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break RSA and compromise [Diffie–Hellman key exchange](node:Diffie–Hellman%20Key%20Exchange). ([Shor](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9508027); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing))
- **Grover search and its optimality.** An item among $N$ unsorted entries can be found with $O(\sqrt N)$ oracle queries, with success probability made arbitrarily close to 1 ([Grover](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9605043); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover%27s_algorithm)). Conversely, relative to a random oracle, with probability 1 NP cannot be solved on a quantum Turing machine in time $o(2^{n/2})$, so Grover's quadratic speedup is optimal for black-box search. ([Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard, Vazirani](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9701001))
- **Oracle separation from PH (Raz–Tal 2018).** There is an oracle $A$ with $\mathrm{BQP}^A\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^A$. This does not settle the unrelativized question. ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP))
- **Solovay–Kitaev theorem.** If $\mathcal G\subset SU(2)$ is finite, closed under inverses, and generates a dense subgroup, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ every $U\in SU(2)$ is within operator-norm distance $\varepsilon$ of a product of $O(\log^c(1/\varepsilon))$ elements of $\mathcal G$, for a constant $c$, and such a sequence can be found efficiently; the result extends to $SU(d)$ for fixed $d$. The overhead of approximating a gate to accuracy $\varepsilon$ is therefore polylogarithmic in $1/\varepsilon$; the known general exponent is $c=1.44042\ldots+\delta$ for any $\delta>0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay%E2%80%93Kitaev_theorem))
- **Gottesman–Knill theorem.** Circuits built from computational-basis state preparation, Clifford gates (generated by Hadamard, CNOT and the phase gate $S$), and computational-basis measurement can be simulated in polynomial time on a classical probabilistic computer; so speedups that rely only on the entanglement achievable with Hadamard and CNOT gates give no advantage over classical computers. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottesman%E2%80%93Knill_theorem))
- **Threshold theorem.** Quantum computation can be made robust against errors when the error rate $\eta$ is below a constant threshold $\eta_c$, for a general noise model, and even for one-dimensional nearest-neighbour architectures. ([Aharonov and Ben-Or](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9906129))

### Examples
- **Grover iteration count.** Grover's algorithm on $N=2^n$ items uses approximately $\tfrac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N$ (at most $\lceil \tfrac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N\rceil$) iterations of the oracle followed by the diffusion operator, after which the marked item is output with probability approaching 1 for $N\gg1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover%27s_algorithm))
- **Factoring resources.** One estimate cited in the literature is at least 3 million physical qubits to factor a 2,048-bit integer in five months on a fully error-corrected trapped-ion machine. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing))
- **Sampling experiments.** In 2019 Google and NASA claimed quantum supremacy with a 54-qubit processor, which IBM disputed by estimating a classical simulation of about 2.5 days on Summit; in December 2020 a USTC group reported boson sampling with 76 photons on Jiuzhang. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing))

### History
Benioff introduced a quantum Turing machine in 1980; Manin and Feynman independently proposed quantum hardware for simulating quantum systems, Feynman in 1982; Deutsch's algorithm appeared in 1985; Shor's factoring algorithm in 1994; Grover's search algorithm in 1996; and a two-qubit machine demonstrated feasibility in 1998 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing)). Bernstein and Vazirani (1997) placed BQP inside PSPACE, Adleman, DeMarrais and Huang (1997) inside PP, and Aaronson (2005) showed that postselected BQP equals PP ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP)). Solovay announced the Solovay–Kitaev theorem in 1995 and Kitaev proved it independently in 1997 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay%E2%80%93Kitaev_theorem)).

### Connections
- [Postulates of Quantum Mechanics](node:Postulates%20of%20Quantum%20Mechanics): states, unitary evolution and the Born rule are the computational model.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): gates are unitary matrices on $(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}$.
- [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory): BQP is placed among P, BPP, PP and PSPACE.
- [Polynomial Hierarchy](node:Polynomial%20Hierarchy): the BQP versus PH question and the Raz–Tal oracle separation.
- [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP): the BBBV lower bound shows that, relative to a random oracle, quantum computers cannot solve NP in time $o(2^{n/2})$.
- [Integer Factorization](node:Integer%20Factorization): Shor's algorithm puts factoring in BQP.
- [Quantum Algorithms](node:Quantum%20Algorithms): Shor, Grover and their generalizations.
- [Quantum Query Complexity](node:Quantum%20Query%20Complexity): the oracle model behind Grover's optimality and the Raz–Tal separation.
- [Quantum Error Correction](node:Quantum%20Error%20Correction): needed for the threshold theorem.
- [Quantum Entanglement](node:Quantum%20Entanglement): by Gottesman–Knill, entanglement produced by Clifford circuits alone gives no speedup.
- [Randomized Algorithms](node:Randomized%20Algorithms): BPP is the classical analogue of BQP.
- [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines) and [Boolean Circuits](node:Boolean%20Circuits): the classical models that quantum Turing machines and quantum circuits generalize.
- [Density Matrices](node:Density%20Matrices) and [Quantum Channels](node:Quantum%20Channels): describe noisy, open-system quantum computation.

### Common pitfalls
- Shor's algorithm does not extend to NP in general, and quantum computers are not known to solve NP-complete problems efficiently: relative to a random oracle, NP cannot be solved on a quantum Turing machine in time $o(2^{n/2})$, so black-box search gives only a quadratic speedup. ([Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard, Vazirani](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9701001))
- An oracle separation such as $\mathrm{BQP}^A\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^A$ is not an unconditional separation. ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP))
- Entanglement is not by itself a source of speedup: stabilizer (Clifford) circuits can create entangled states yet are classically simulable in polynomial time. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottesman%E2%80%93Knill_theorem))
- Quantum supremacy demonstrations concern tasks chosen for classical hardness, have been contested, and are not evidence of practical applications. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing))

### Open problems
- **BQP versus PH and NP.** The relationship between BQP and the polynomial hierarchy has been "an open problem since the earliest days of quantum computing"; Aaronson gave evidence that quantum computers can solve problems outside PH and reduced an oracle separation to a circuit-complexity conjecture ([Aaronson](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.4698)). The relationship between BQP and NP is likewise unknown ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP)).
- **Strictness of the containments** $\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{PP}$: none is known to be strict. ([Wikipedia: BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP))
- **Optimal Solovay–Kitaev exponent.** The spectral gap conjecture, if true, would imply that $c=1$ is achievable for a generically chosen gate set; the best known general exponent is about $1.44$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay%E2%80%93Kitaev_theorem))
- **Scalable fault tolerance.** Fully fault-tolerant quantum computing remains out of reach as of 2026. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computing))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [BQP (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP): definition, containments, complete problems, oracle results.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 6.845 Quantum Complexity Theory](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-845-quantum-complexity-theory-fall-2010/): Aaronson's graduate course, from BQP to quantum interactive proofs.
- **Primary:** [Shor, Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9508027): the factoring algorithm.
- **Primary:** [Aharonov and Ben-Or, Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation With Constant Error Rate](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9906129): the threshold theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Aaronson, BQP and the Polynomial Hierarchy](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.4698): research-level account of the BQP versus PH question.
references.Quantum Entanglement:
## Reference
### Overview
Entanglement is the property of a composite quantum system whose joint state cannot be reduced to states of its parts: a pure state is entangled if it is not a product of local pure states, and a mixed state is entangled if it is not a probability mixture of product states ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)). Schrödinger, who introduced the word in 1935, called it "the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics" ([SEP: Quantum Entanglement and Information](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/)).

Entanglement first appeared in the 1935 Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen argument that quantum mechanics is incomplete. Bell showed in 1964 that correlations between measurements on separated entangled systems can violate inequalities that any local hidden-variable theory must satisfy ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/)), and many Bell tests since Aspect's second experiment in 1982 have used the CHSH form of the inequality ([Wikipedia: CHSH inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHSH_inequality)). Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger shared the 2022 Nobel Prize for experiments with entangled photons ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)).

In quantum information theory entanglement is a resource under local operations and classical communication (LOCC): it powers teleportation and entanglement-based key distribution, and can be "measured, transformed, and purified" ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/); [Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)). The Horodeckis' review organizes the field around how entanglement is characterized, detected, distilled and quantified, and why some entangled states (bound entangled states) resist distillation ([Horodecki et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 81, 865](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0702225)).

### Formal definition
Let $\mathcal H_A,\mathcal H_B$ be finite-dimensional [Hilbert spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces). A pure state $|\psi\rangle\in\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_B$ is a **product** (separable) state if $|\psi\rangle=|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle$; otherwise it is **entangled**. A density operator $\rho$ on $\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_B$ is **separable** if
$$\rho=\sum_i p_i\,\rho_i^A\otimes\rho_i^B,\qquad p_i\ge0,\ \sum_ip_i=1,$$
i.e. a probability distribution over product states, and **entangled** otherwise ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)). The **reduced state** is $\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho$ ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)).

**Schmidt decomposition.** For $w\in\mathcal H_1\otimes\mathcal H_2$ with $\dim\mathcal H_1=n\ge m=\dim\mathcal H_2$ there are orthonormal sets $\{u_i\}_{i=1}^m$, $\{v_i\}_{i=1}^m$ and reals $\alpha_i\ge0$, unique up to order, with
$$w=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\,u_i\otimes v_i .$$
It is the singular value decomposition of the coefficient matrix of $w$. The number of nonzero $\alpha_i$ is the **Schmidt rank** ([Wikipedia: Schmidt decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_decomposition)).

**Entanglement entropy.** For a pure state, $E(\psi)=S(\rho_A)=-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A\log\rho_A=-\sum_i\alpha_i^2\log\alpha_i^2$ ([Wikipedia: Schmidt decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_decomposition); [Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)).

### Key results
