- **Pure-state criterion.** A bipartite pure state is entangled iff its Schmidt rank exceeds 1, iff its reduced states are mixed; $\rho_A$ and $\rho_B$ have the same nonzero spectrum $\{\alpha_i^2\}$, and $S(\rho_A)=0$ exactly for product states ([Wikipedia: Schmidt decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_decomposition); [Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)). For pure bipartite states the entanglement entropy is the unique entanglement measure ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)).
- **Nielsen's theorem (1999).** $|\psi\rangle$ can be transformed into $|\phi\rangle$ by LOCC iff $\lambda_\psi\prec\lambda_\phi$, where $\lambda$ is the vector of eigenvalues of Alice's reduced state (squared Schmidt coefficients) and $x\prec y$ means $\sum_{j\le k}x_j^{\downarrow}\le\sum_{j\le k}y_j^{\downarrow}$ for all $k$ with equality at $k=d$ ([Nielsen, PRL 83, 436; arXiv:quant-ph/9811053](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/quant-ph/9811053)).
- **Peres–Horodecki (PPT) criterion (1996).** If $\rho$ is separable, its partial transpose $\rho^{T_B}$ has no negative eigenvalues. For $2\times2$ and $2\times3$ systems the converse holds, so PPT is necessary and sufficient; in higher dimensions there are entangled PPT states, which are bound entangled (not distillable) ([Wikipedia: Peres–Horodecki criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres%E2%80%93Horodecki_criterion)).
- **CHSH inequality and Tsirelson's bound.** For any local hidden-variable model the CHSH combination of four correlation functions satisfies $|S|\le2$ (Clauser, Horne, Shimony, Holt 1969); quantum mechanics with entangled states reaches at most $2\sqrt2$ ([Wikipedia: CHSH inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHSH_inequality)).
- **Separability is computationally hard.** Deciding separability in the general bipartite case is NP-hard, and most [entanglement measures](node:Entanglement%20Measures) are hard to compute for mixed states as the dimension grows ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)).
- **Monogamy.** A particle cannot be maximally entangled with more than one other particle at a time; this underlies the security of entanglement-based key distribution, where no third party can share Alice and Bob's entanglement correlations ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/)).

### Examples
- **Singlet.** $|\Psi^-\rangle=(|01\rangle-|10\rangle)/\sqrt2$ has Schmidt coefficients $(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$; each reduced state is maximally mixed with entropy $\log 2$, the maximum for a qubit ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement); [Wikipedia: Schmidt decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_decomposition)).
- **Two-qubit Werner state.** $\rho_p=p\,|\Psi^-\rangle\langle\Psi^-|+(1-p)\,I/4$. The least eigenvalue of $\rho_p^{T_B}$ is $(1-3p)/4$, so $\rho_p$ is entangled exactly for $p>1/3$ (PPT is sufficient for two qubits) ([Wikipedia: Peres–Horodecki criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres%E2%80%93Horodecki_criterion)). For some parameter values Werner states are entangled yet admit a local hidden-variable model for projective measurements ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)).
- **Teleportation (Bennett et al. 1993).** A shared entangled pair plus two classical bits transfers an unknown qubit state from Alice to Bob; the state remains unknown to both ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/)).

### History
EPR (1935) argued that the wave-function description is incomplete; Schrödinger answered in 1935 and introduced "entanglement" ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/)). Bell's 1964 inequality made the issue experimentally testable; CHSH (1969) gave the form used in many experiments; Aspect's 1982 experiments followed ([Wikipedia: CHSH inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHSH_inequality); [SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/)). Ekert's 1991 key-distribution protocol uses a Bell test to detect eavesdroppers, and teleportation was proposed in 1993 ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/)). Peres and the Horodeckis gave the PPT criterion in 1996 ([Wikipedia: Peres–Horodecki criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres%E2%80%93Horodecki_criterion)); a loophole-free CHSH violation with electron spins 1.3 km apart was reported in 2015 (Hensen et al.) ([Wikipedia: CHSH inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHSH_inequality)).

### Connections
- [Postulates of Quantum Mechanics](node:Postulates%20of%20Quantum%20Mechanics): the tensor-product postulate for composite systems is where entanglement comes from.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): entangled vectors are exactly the non-decomposable tensors.
- [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): the Schmidt decomposition is the SVD of the coefficient matrix.
- [Density Matrices](node:Density%20Matrices): mixed-state entanglement and reduced states.
- [Bell's Theorem](node:Bell's%20Theorem): entanglement produces correlations no local hidden-variable model reproduces.
- [Quantum Teleportation](node:Quantum%20Teleportation): entanglement plus classical communication transmits quantum states.
- [Quantum Information](node:Quantum%20Information) and [Quantum Computing](node:Quantum%20Computing): entanglement as a resource for protocols and algorithms.
- [Quantum Channels](node:Quantum%20Channels): LOCC operations and entanglement-breaking maps are channels.
- [Decoherence](node:Decoherence): entanglement with an environment makes subsystem states mixed.

### Common pitfalls
- **Correlation is not entanglement.** Separable mixed states can be classically correlated; entanglement means not a convex mixture of products ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)).
- **Entanglement does not allow signalling.** Alice's local operations do not change Bob's statistics, because her outcomes are random ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)); teleportation needs two classical bits ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/)).
- **Entanglement is not the same as Bell nonlocality.** Some entangled Werner states admit local hidden-variable models for projective measurements ([Wikipedia: Quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement)).
- **PPT does not imply separable beyond $2\times3$.** Positive partial transpose is only necessary in general ([Wikipedia: Peres–Horodecki criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres%E2%80%93Horodecki_criterion)).

### Open problems
- **NPT bound entanglement.** Do bound entangled states with negative partial transpose exist? Horodecki, Rudnicki and Życzkowski list this among five open problems in quantum information, together with whether a specific two-ququart state is 2-copy distillable ([arXiv:2002.03233](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03233)).
- **Status note: AME(4,6) is no longer open.** The same list included the existence of an absolutely maximally entangled state of four six-level subsystems ([arXiv:2002.03233](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03233)); Rather et al. constructed such a state from orthogonal quantum Latin squares of order six (Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 080507, 2022) ([arXiv:2104.05122](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.05122)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Quantum Entanglement and Information](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-entangle/): history, Bell's theorem, teleportation, monogamy.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Peres–Horodecki criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres%E2%80%93Horodecki_criterion): PPT test and its range of validity.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW MAS.865J Quantum Information Science (Chuang, Shor)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/mas-865j-quantum-information-science-spring-2006/): graduate course including properties of entanglement.
- **Primary:** [Horodecki, Horodecki, Horodecki, Horodecki, "Quantum entanglement" (Rev. Mod. Phys. 81, 865, 2009)](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0702225): comprehensive review of characterization, detection, distillation and measures.
- **Primary:** [Nielsen, "Conditions for a class of entanglement transformations" (PRL 83, 436, 1999)](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9811053): LOCC convertibility and majorization.
- **Further reading:** [Nielsen and Chuang, *Quantum Computation and Quantum Information*, 10th anniversary ed. (CUP, 2010)](https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/quantum-computation-and-quantum-information/01E10196D0A682A6AEFFEA52D53BE9AE): the standard graduate text, covering quantum teleportation and quantum cryptography.
- **Further reading:** [Horodecki, Rudnicki, Życzkowski, "Five open problems in quantum information"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03233): current open questions on entanglement and measurements.
references.Quantum Field Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Quantum field theory (QFT) combines classical field theory, quantum mechanics and [special relativity](node:Special%20Relativity). It is the framework of the [Standard Model](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics) and is also used in condensed matter physics to describe quasiparticles. ([QFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory)) MIT's graduate course 8.323 develops it through applications in both particle and condensed-matter physics. ([MIT 8.323](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/))

The framework has a physical and a mathematical side. Physically, scattering amplitudes are computed from correlation functions of interacting fields, perturbatively via [Feynman Diagrams](node:Feynman%20Diagrams) and the [path integral](node:Path%20Integral%20Formulation), with infinities absorbed by [renormalization](node:Renormalization) and scale dependence governed by the [renormalization group](node:Renormalization%20Group). Structurally, relativistic invariance and locality force general theorems: the spin–statistics and CPT theorems. Mathematically, interacting theories have been constructed rigorously in two and three spacetime dimensions, but there is no proof that any interacting theory in four dimensions satisfies the Wightman axioms. ([QFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory); [Srednicki, contents](https://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~mark/ms-qft-DRAFT.pdf); [Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms))

### Formal definition
In the Lagrangian approach one starts from classical fields $\phi_a(x)$ and an action $S=\int d^4x\,\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a)$; canonical quantization turns the fields into operators, and the path integral gives the correlation functions $\langle0|T\phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_n)|0\rangle$ from which amplitudes follow. ([Srednicki, Sections 3, 8 and 9](https://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~mark/ms-qft-DRAFT.pdf))

An axiomatic definition is given by the Wightman axioms: states are rays in a separable Hilbert space carrying a unitary representation of the [Poincaré group](node:Poincaré%20Group) with energy–momentum spectrum in the forward [light cone](node:Light%20Cone) and a unique invariant vacuum (W0); fields are operator-valued tempered distributions defined on a dense domain containing the vacuum, which is cyclic (W1); fields transform covariantly under a representation of the Lorentz group or $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ (W2); and fields at spacelike separation commute or anticommute (W3). ([Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms)) The Haag–Kastler axioms instead take local algebras of observables as fundamental, and the Osterwalder–Schrader axioms describe Euclidean theories that Wick-rotate to Wightman theories. ([QFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory))

### Key results
- **Wigner's classification.** Positive-energy irreducible unitary representations of the Poincaré group (with $P^\mu\ne0$) are labelled by the Casimirs $P_\mu P^\mu$ (mass squared) and $W_\alpha W^\alpha$ ($W$ the Pauli–Lubanski vector). For $m>0$ the little group is $SU(2)$ and states carry spin $s\in\frac12\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$; for $m=0$ the little group is a double cover of $SE(2)$, and its representations give helicity labels, apart from a separate "continuous spin" family. $P^\mu=0$ gives only the trivial vacuum representation among finite-dimensional unitary ones. Wigner introduced it to classify particles and fields (Annals of Mathematics, 1939). ([Wigner's classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigner%27s_classification))
- **Spin–statistics theorem.** In a Lorentz-invariant theory whose fields transform according to the spin of the particles they create and satisfy microcausality, integer-spin particles are bosons (symmetric states, [Bose–Einstein Statistics](node:Bose–Einstein%20Statistics)) and half-integer-spin particles are fermions (antisymmetric states, [Fermi–Dirac Statistics](node:Fermi–Dirac%20Statistics)). Fierz (1939) and Pauli (1940) gave the first proofs; rigorous proofs within Wightman's framework followed in 1958. Anyons, with fractional statistics, are possible only with fewer than three spatial dimensions. ([Spin–statistics theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin%E2%80%93statistics_theorem))
- **CPT theorem.** Any Lorentz-invariant local quantum field theory with a Hermitian Hamiltonian is invariant under the combined operation of charge conjugation, parity and time reversal; consequently [CP violation](node:CP%20Violation) must be accompanied by T violation. Schwinger (1951) implicitly, Lüders and Pauli (1954) explicitly, Bell independently, and Jost (1958) in axiomatic QFT. ([CPT symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CPT_symmetry))
- **LSZ reduction formula.** For a scalar field normalized so that $\langle0|\phi(x)|0\rangle=0$ and $\langle k|\phi(x)|0\rangle=e^{-ikx}$, the scattering amplitude is
$$\langle f|i\rangle=i^{n+n'}\!\int\! d^4x_1\,e^{ik_1x_1}(-\partial_1^2+m^2)\cdots\int\! d^4x_{1'}\,e^{-ik_{1'}x_{1'}}(-\partial_{1'}^2+m^2)\cdots\langle0|T\phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_{1'})\cdots|0\rangle,$$
in mostly-plus signature, with $m$ the physical mass. Equivalently, S-matrix elements are residues of the on-shell poles of Fourier-transformed correlation functions. Lehmann, Symanzik and Zimmermann published it in 1955; it does not directly handle bound states or massless particles. ([Srednicki, eq. 5.24–5.25](https://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~mark/ms-qft-DRAFT.pdf); [LSZ reduction formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LSZ_reduction_formula))
- **Renormalizability and the renormalization group.** Dyson showed in 1949 that only a limited class of renormalizable theories can have their infinities removed by redefining finitely many parameters; Fermi's weak-interaction theory is non-renormalizable. In Wilson's picture every QFT has a cutoff, renormalizable theories are insensitive to high-energy details, and non-renormalizable ones are low-energy approximations to a more fundamental theory, the basis of [effective field theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory). ([QFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory)) Couplings run with scale according to the renormalization-group function $\beta(g)$; at fixed points the theory is scale invariant, which explains universality classes. ([Renormalization group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group))
- **Asymptotic freedom.** For an $SU(3)$ gauge theory with $n_F$ Dirac quark flavours, $\beta(g)=-\frac{g^3}{16\pi^2}\big(11-\frac23n_F\big)+O(g^5)$, negative for $n_F\le16$, so [QCD](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics) is asymptotically free. In four spacetime dimensions the only asymptotically free theories are non-abelian gauge theories. ([Srednicki, eqs. 78.37 and Section 29](https://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~mark/ms-qft-DRAFT.pdf)) Gross, Wilczek and Politzer established asymptotic freedom of non-abelian gauge theories in 1973. ([QFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory))
- **Anomalies.** An anomaly is a symmetry of the classical action that is not a symmetry of any regularized version of the full quantum theory; the first found was the Adler–Bell–Jackiw chiral anomaly, in which the classically conserved axial current of electrodynamics is broken by quantization. Gauge anomalies must cancel for consistency; in the Standard Model, cancelling the mixed anomaly with two $SU(2)$ generators and one hypercharge requires the charges in each fermion generation to sum to zero, which ties quark charges to lepton charges. ([Anomaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomaly_%28physics%29))
- **Haag's theorem.** The interaction picture relates the interacting field to a free field by an intertwiner, and the theorem's most salient provision is that this intertwiner is unitary. Under that provision, Poincaré invariance and a common vacuum, the first four Wightman functions of the two fields coincide and the "interacting" field must itself be free with the same mass, so the interaction picture cannot describe interactions; renormalisation evades the theorem by violating the unitarity of the intertwiner. ([Klaczynski, arXiv:1602.00662](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.00662); [Haag's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%27s_theorem)) Haag published the argument in 1955 and Hall and Wightman generalized it in 1957, concluding that no single Hilbert-space representation describes both free and interacting fields. ([Haag's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%27s_theorem))
- **Reconstruction and constructive QFT.** Vacuum expectation values with suitable properties suffice to reconstruct a Wightman theory; under technical assumptions a Euclidean theory Wick-rotates to a Wightman theory (Osterwalder–Schrader), and interacting theories satisfying the axioms have been constructed in 2 and 3 dimensions. ([Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms))

### Examples
[Quantum Electrodynamics](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics) describes charged matter coupled to the electromagnetic field; Dirac coined its name in 1927. Yang and Mills generalized gauge symmetry to non-abelian groups in 1954, and 't Hooft later proved such theories renormalizable; [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics) is the non-abelian [gauge theory](node:Gauge%20Theory) of the strong interaction. ([QFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory)) The path integral of the free scalar field, with Hamiltonian density $\frac12\Pi^2+\frac12(\nabla\phi)^2+\frac12m^2\phi^2$, is obtained by generalizing the [harmonic-oscillator](node:Quantum%20Harmonic%20Oscillator) path integral, with $q(t)\to\phi(\mathbf x,t)$. ([Srednicki, Sections 7 and 8](https://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~mark/ms-qft-DRAFT.pdf))

### History
Infinities in QED were highlighted by Oppenheimer in 1930; around 1950 Tomonaga, Schwinger, Feynman and Dyson developed renormalization, making QED agree with experiment. Non-abelian gauge theory (1954), its renormalizability, and asymptotic freedom (1973) led to the Standard Model in the 1970s; the Higgs boson was found at CERN in 2012. ([QFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory)) Wilson gave the renormalization group its computational form in 1971 and received the 1982 Nobel Prize; Callan and Symanzik reformulated it in 1970. ([Renormalization group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)) Wightman formulated his axioms in the early 1950s; they were published with Gårding in 1964. ([Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms))

### Connections
- [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory): the classical action that is quantized.
- [Postulates of Quantum Mechanics](node:Postulates%20of%20Quantum%20Mechanics): states, observables and the Hilbert space.
- [Quantum Harmonic Oscillator](node:Quantum%20Harmonic%20Oscillator): free-field modes.
- [Poincaré Group](node:Poincaré%20Group) and [Lorentz Transformations](node:Lorentz%20Transformations): Wigner's classification and covariance of fields.
- [Angular Momentum and Spin](node:Angular%20Momentum%20and%20Spin): spin labels of particle representations.
- [Klein–Gordon Equation](node:Klein–Gordon%20Equation) and [Dirac Equation](node:Dirac%20Equation): free spin-0 and spin-1/2 fields.
- [Feynman Diagrams](node:Feynman%20Diagrams) and [Path Integral Formulation](node:Path%20Integral%20Formulation): perturbative computation.
- [Renormalization](node:Renormalization), [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group), [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): scale dependence and infinities.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory), [Quantum Electrodynamics](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics), [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics): the main interacting examples.
- [Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking](node:Spontaneous%20Symmetry%20Breaking) and [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): vacua that do not share the symmetry of the action.
- [Tempered Distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions): fields as operator-valued distributions.
- [Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap](node:Yang–Mills%20Existence%20and%20Mass%20Gap): the central open mathematical problem.
- [QFT in Curved Spacetime](node:QFT%20in%20Curved%20Spacetime) and [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory): important variants.

### Common pitfalls
Perturbative success does not establish that a four-dimensional interacting theory exists mathematically; Haag's theorem shows the interaction picture used to motivate perturbation theory is not well defined, yet perturbative predictions such as QCD jet results agree well with experiment. ([Haag's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%27s_theorem)) The Lagrangian parameters are not the physical mass and coupling: LSZ requires field and parameter rescalings fixed order by order. ([Srednicki, Section 5](https://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~mark/ms-qft-DRAFT.pdf)) The field-component representation of the Lorentz group differs from the unitary Poincaré representation on states. ([Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms); [Wigner's classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigner%27s_classification))

### Open problems
- **Yang–Mills existence and mass gap.** Prove that quantum Yang–Mills theory exists on $\mathbb R^4$ and has a mass gap $\Delta>0$; the Clay Institute lists it as unsolved and notes that no proof of the mass gap is known. ([Clay Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/); [QFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory))
- **Interacting Wightman theories in four dimensions.** There is no proof that the Wightman axioms can be satisfied by any interacting theory in dimension 4. ([Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Quantum field theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory): history, renormalization, rigor.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.323 Relativistic QFT I](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/): free graduate course by Hong Liu.
- **Primary:** [Srednicki, Quantum Field Theory (draft of the CUP text)](https://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~mark/ms-qft-DRAFT.pdf): graduate textbook covering spin–statistics, LSZ, renormalization group, effective field theory, anomalies and the Standard Model.
- **Further reading:** [Weinberg, The Quantum Theory of Fields, Vol. I: Foundations (CUP, 1995)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781139644167): graduate monograph on the foundations of QFT.
references.Radial Acceleration Relation:
## Reference
### Overview
The radial acceleration relation (RAR) is an empirical correlation in rotating galaxies. It links the centripetal acceleration $g_{\rm obs}$ measured from the rotation curve with the Newtonian acceleration $g_{\rm bar}$ predicted from the observed stars and gas alone. In the SPARC sample, 2693 points in 153 galaxies of very different morphologies, masses, sizes and gas fractions follow one relation, including where dark matter dominates. McGaugh, Lelli and Schombert concluded that the dark matter contribution is fully specified by the baryons. ([McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05917); [ar5iv text](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1609.05917))

The RAR sits in a family of disk-galaxy regularities with flat rotation curves, the [Baryonic Tully–Fisher Relation](node:Baryonic%20Tully–Fisher%20Relation), Renzo's rule, and the central density relation. McGaugh and collaborators argue that the BTFR, the central density relation and the RAR share one acceleration scale, $g_\dagger\approx g_{\rm CDR}\approx g_{\rm TF}$. ([McGaugh, Lelli, Li & Schombert, IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf))

Its interpretation is contested. The relation has the shape Milgrom's MOND predicted. ΛCDM galaxy-formation models and simulations reproduce a similar relation through baryon–halo coupling, and analyses disagree on whether the acceleration scale is the same in every galaxy. Wikipedia summarises that cosmological ΛCDM simulations produce different relations, some similar to the observed one and some not. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve); [Ludlow et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.07663); [Rodrigues et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.06803))

### Formal definition
For a rotationally supported galaxy with rotation curve $V(R)$, the observed acceleration is $g_{\rm obs}=V^2(R)/R$. The baryonic acceleration is $g_{\rm bar}=|\partial\Phi_{\rm bar}/\partial R|$, where $\nabla^2\Phi_{\rm bar}=4\pi G\rho_{\rm bar}$ is solved numerically for the observed stars and gas. The two axes are measured independently and would agree 1:1 in a universe without dark matter. ([McGaugh et al. IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf); [McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert 2016](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1609.05917))

McGaugh et al. fit the SPARC points with the one-parameter function below. ([ar5iv: McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1609.05917))
$$
g_{\rm obs}=\mathcal F(g_{\rm bar})=\frac{g_{\rm bar}}{1-e^{-\sqrt{g_{\rm bar}/g_\dagger}}},
$$
The fitted scale is $g_\dagger=1.20\pm0.02\,(\text{random})\pm0.24\,(\text{systematic})\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The systematic error is the 20% normalisation uncertainty in the stellar mass-to-light ratio $\Upsilon_\star$, with $\Upsilon_\star^{[3.6]}=0.5\,M_\odot/L_\odot$ for disks and $0.7$ for bulges. The function tends to $g_{\rm bar}$ for $g_{\rm bar}\gg g_\dagger$ and to $\sqrt{g_\dagger g_{\rm bar}}$ for $g_{\rm bar}\ll g_\dagger$. ([ar5iv: McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1609.05917)) In this language the "dark" acceleration is $g_{\rm DM}=g_{\rm obs}-g_{\rm bar}$, a function of $g_{\rm bar}$ alone. ([McGaugh et al. IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf))

### Key results
- **SPARC RAR (2016).** SPARC is a sample of 175 disk galaxies (S0 to Irr) with Spitzer 3.6 μm photometry and H I/Hα rotation curves (Lelli, McGaugh & Schombert, AJ 152, 157). Dropping inclinations below 30°, 12 asymmetric curves, and points with velocity errors above 10% leaves 153 galaxies and 2693 of 3149 points. Fit residuals are Gaussian of width 0.11 dex with rms 0.13 dex. The expected observational scatter is 0.12 dex, leaving little room for intrinsic scatter. ([SPARC data paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.09251); [ar5iv: McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1609.05917))
- **Extension to all types (Lelli et al. 2017, ApJ 836, 152).** 153 late-type galaxies, 25 early-type galaxies (ATLAS$^{3D}$ or Chandra X-ray data) and 62 dwarf spheroidals follow the same RAR over 4 dex. The relation is 1:1 at high acceleration and departs below about $10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Observed scatter is below 0.13 dex, with residuals uncorrelated with baryonic mass, gas fraction or radius. ([Lelli et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.08981))
- **Individual-galaxy fits (Li et al. 2018, A&A 615, A3).** MCMC fits of the mean RAR to 175 SPARC galaxies, marginalising over $\Upsilon_\star$, distance and inclination, leave about 0.057 dex residual scatter. Letting the acceleration scale vary between galaxies does not improve the fits and shows no credible variation. ([Li et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.00022))
- **Counter-analysis (Rodrigues et al. 2018, Nat. Astron. 2, 668).** A Bayesian analysis of 193 SPARC and THINGS disks rejects a single acceleration common to all of them at more than $10\sigma$ ($p<10^{-20}$). It argues the scale is emergent and that MOND-like theories are disfavoured as fundamental at the same level. ([Rodrigues et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.06803))
- **ΛCDM reproductions.** MUGS2 simulations reproduce the SPARC RAR, with less scatter, as a consequence of dissipative baryon collapse (Keller & Wadsley 2017). EAGLE galaxies follow it regardless of feedback prescription, with feedback moving galaxies along the relation (Ludlow et al. 2017, PRL 118, 161103). Navarro et al. (2017) trace it to a narrow halo-mass range, self-similar halo acceleration profiles and tight halo–baryon scalings. Di Cintio & Lelli (MNRAS Letter; arXiv 2015) obtain it semi-empirically with a mass-dependent halo profile. ([Keller & Wadsley](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.06183); [Ludlow et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.07663); [Navarro et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.06329); [Di Cintio & Lelli](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06616))
- **Weak-lensing RAR.** KiDS-1000 lensing around isolated galaxies extends the RAR by about two decades to lower accelerations (Brouwer et al. 2021, A&A 650, A113). At fixed stellar mass, early- and late-type galaxies there differ by at least $6\sigma$. Mistele et al. (JCAP 04 (2024) 020) use consistent stellar masses, a new deprojection formula and strict isolation, and find that lensing continues the kinematic RAR for about 2.5 dex, with early and late types on the same relation. ([Brouwer et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11677); [Mistele et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15248))

### Examples
- **High- versus low-surface-brightness disks.** High acceleration corresponds through Poisson's equation to high surface brightness, where data lie on the 1:1 line. Low-surface-brightness galaxies have low accelerations and large mass discrepancies, peeling away in the same way as in the central density relation. ([McGaugh et al. IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf))
- **A crude halo.** In practice $g_{\rm DM}$ is roughly constant at about $0.3\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (Walker et al. 2010). ([McGaugh et al. IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf))

### History
Rotation curves that fail to fall off in Keplerian fashion became established through work such as Rubin and Ford's 1975 finding that most stars in spirals orbit at roughly the same speed. ([Wikipedia: Galaxy rotation curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve)) Milgrom proposed MOND in 1983. In it the true acceleration tends to $\sqrt{a_Na_0}$ for $a\ll a_0$, with $a_0\approx1.2\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ from rotation-curve fits. ([Wikipedia: MOND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics)) Sanders (1990) found a correlation between mass discrepancy and acceleration at the last measured point; McGaugh (1999) extended it to every resolved point. Spitzer 3.6 μm photometry with a common $\Upsilon_\star$ then removed the outliers caused by optical $\Upsilon_\star$ misestimates. ([McGaugh et al. IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf)) The SPARC RAR appeared in PRL 117, 201101 (2016). ([McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05917))

### Connections
- [Galaxy Rotation Curves](node:Galaxy%20Rotation%20Curves): $g_{\rm obs}=V^2/R$ comes from the rotation curve.
- [Baryonic Tully–Fisher Relation](node:Baryonic%20Tully–Fisher%20Relation): the flat-velocity limit of the same coupling, sharing the scale $g_\dagger$.
- [Modified Newtonian Dynamics](node:Modified%20Newtonian%20Dynamics): predicts a relation of this shape with $a_0\sim g_\dagger$.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter) and [Dark Matter Halo Profiles](node:Dark%20Matter%20Halo%20Profiles): in ΛCDM the RAR constrains how halo acceleration tracks baryons.
- [Lambda-CDM Model](node:Lambda-CDM%20Model) and [Galaxy Formation](node:Galaxy%20Formation): simulations are tested on whether they reproduce the relation and its scatter.
- [Baryonic Feedback in Dark Matter Halos](node:Baryonic%20Feedback%20in%20Dark%20Matter%20Halos): in EAGLE, feedback moves galaxies along the relation.
- [Core-Cusp Problem](node:Core-Cusp%20Problem): Di Cintio & Lelli find a universal profile fits dwarfs poorly, hinting at cores.
- [Weak-Lensing Shear](node:Weak-Lensing%20Shear): extends the RAR to large radii.
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): $g_{\rm bar}$ is the Poisson field of the baryons.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Galaxy dynamics and mass discrepancies](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Galaxy%20dynamics%20and%20mass%20discrepancies)

### Common pitfalls
- **"Acceleration against acceleration" is not circular.** $g_{\rm obs}$ comes from kinematics, $g_{\rm bar}$ from photometry plus Poisson's equation; the two are independent measurements. ([McGaugh et al. IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf))
- **Optical mass-to-light ratios create spurious outliers.** B-band $\Upsilon_\star$ errors made individual galaxies stand out in pre-Spitzer data. ([McGaugh et al. IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf))
- **A tight relation does not by itself choose a theory.** The same SPARC data support a universal scale in Li et al.'s fits and reject one in Rodrigues et al.'s; several ΛCDM simulations reproduce the relation. Conclusions depend on priors on $\Upsilon_\star$, distance and inclination and on the statistical model. ([Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.00022); [Rodrigues et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.06803); [Keller & Wadsley](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.06183))
- **Lensing RARs depend on isolation and baryon accounting.** Brouwer et al.'s early/late difference could come from circumgalactic gas in early types. Mistele et al. find no difference under stricter isolation and consistent masses. ([Brouwer et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11677); [Mistele et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15248))

### Open problems
> [!warning] Contested
> **Is $g_\dagger$ universal?** McGaugh et al. call whether the scale is unique and universal, or has finite intrinsic scatter, critical to its interpretation. Li et al. find no credible galaxy-to-galaxy variation. Rodrigues et al. reject a common scale at more than $10\sigma$. ([McGaugh et al. IAU 353](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf); [Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.00022); [Rodrigues et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.06803))
>
> **Law or emergent relation?** Lelli, Mistele, McGaugh and collaborators (2024) present the RAR as one of the empirical laws of galaxy dynamics and state that these facts were predicted a priori by MOND. Keller & Wadsley, Ludlow et al., Navarro et al. and Di Cintio & Lelli derive it within ΛCDM. ([Lelli et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02499); [Ludlow et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.07663); [Navarro et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.06329))

- **Low-acceleration regime with lensing.** Brouwer et al. state that future lensing surveys could better separate modified gravity from ΛCDM if systematic uncertainties in the baryonic mass around galaxies, especially circumgalactic gas, are reduced. ([Brouwer et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11677))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Galaxy rotation curve (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve): history and the SPARC RAR in context.
- **Learn:** [McGaugh, Lelli, Li & Schombert, Dynamical Regularities in Rotating Galaxies (IAU 353; Case ASTR333)](https://astroweb.case.edu/ssm/ASTR333/LawsofRotation.pdf): the RAR, BTFR, CDR and Renzo's rule.
- **Primary:** [McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert, PRL 117, 201101 (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05917): the SPARC RAR.
- **Primary:** [Rodrigues et al., Nat. Astron. 2, 668 (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.06803) and [Ludlow et al., PRL 118, 161103 (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.07663): the case against a fundamental scale and a ΛCDM reproduction.
- **Further reading:** [Lelli et al. 2017, ApJ 836, 152](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.08981), [SPARC data paper, AJ 152, 157](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.09251), and [Lelli et al. 2024, "The empirical laws of galaxy dynamics: from gas kinematics to weak lensing"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02499).
references.Randall–Sundrum Model:
## Reference
### Overview
Randall–Sundrum (RS) models take a five-dimensional [anti-de Sitter](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space) bulk bounded by, or containing, $(3+1)$-dimensional branes. The geometry is not a product: the four-dimensional metric is multiplied by a warp factor that depends exponentially on the extra coordinate. In RS1 the extra dimension is finite, with a brane at each end; RS2 removes the second brane to infinity, leaving one brane. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall%E2%80%93Sundrum_model); [RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221))

RS1 addresses the [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem): Planck-scale mass parameters on the "visible" brane appear as TeV-scale physical masses because of the warp factor, so no large extra-dimensional volume is needed. RS2 shows that four non-compact dimensions are not implied by Newton's force law: with a single 3-brane in a non-factorizable five-dimensional background, four-dimensional Newtonian and general-relativistic gravity is recovered even though the Kaluza–Klein spectrum has no gap. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221); [RS2](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9906064))

The PDG review places RS one year after the 1998 ADD proposal of two or more flat [large extra dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions), as a warped alternative with an AdS$_5$ bulk and a [compactification](node:Compactification) scale of order $1/$TeV, in which the gravitational redshift factor of the warped metric explains the smallness of the electroweak scale relative to the Planck scale. Through the [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence), warped models are related to four-dimensional strongly coupled theories whose composite states correspond to five-dimensional fields; the PDG review credits this approach with opening new directions on the flavour problem, grand unification, and the origin of electroweak symmetry breaking. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))

### Formal definition
The RS1 line element on an $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ [orbifold](node:Orbifolds) with coordinate $-\pi\le\phi\le\pi$ (identified $\phi\sim-\phi$) is ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221))
$$
ds^2 = e^{-2kr_c|\phi|}\eta_{\mu\nu}\,dx^\mu dx^\nu + r_c^2\, d\phi^2 ,
$$
where $r_c$ sets the size of the extra dimension and $k$ is a scale of order the Planck scale, assumed smaller than the five-dimensional Planck scale $M$. Between the branes the geometry is a slice of AdS$_5$, and the metric is a [warped product](node:Warped%20Products) of Minkowski space with an interval. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221))

The action is $S=S_{\rm gravity}+S_{\rm vis}+S_{\rm hid}$ with ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221))
$$
S_{\rm gravity}=\int d^4x\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\phi\,\sqrt{-G}\,\bigl\{-\Lambda+2M^3R\bigr\},
$$
plus brane terms with vacuum energies $V_{\rm hid}$ at $\phi=0$ and $V_{\rm vis}$ at $\phi=\pi$. The bulk term is the five-dimensional [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action) with cosmological constant $\Lambda$. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221))

Four-dimensional Poincaré invariance of the solution requires the bulk cosmological constant and brane tensions to be tuned against one scale $k$ ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221)):
$$
V_{\rm hid}=-V_{\rm vis}=24M^3k,\qquad \Lambda=-24M^3k^2 .
$$
So the bulk is AdS ($\Lambda<0$), the hidden ("Planck") brane at $\phi=0$ has positive tension, and the visible ("TeV") brane at $\phi=\pi$ has negative tension. RS1 obtains these relations by solving the five-dimensional Einstein equations with the brane vacuum energies as delta-function sources. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221))

RS2 places one brane infinitely far away, leaving a single 3-brane in a non-factorizable five-dimensional background, so the extra dimension is non-compact; Garriga and Tanaka analyse this case as a single positive-tension wall. ([RS2](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9906064); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall%E2%80%93Sundrum_model); [Garriga–Tanaka](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9911055))

### Key results
- **Effective Planck scale.** Integrating the zero-mode graviton action over $\phi$ gives ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221))
  $$M_{\rm Pl}^2=\frac{M^3}{k}\bigl[1-e^{-2kr_c\pi}\bigr],$$
  which depends only weakly on $r_c$ when $kr_c$ is large. The [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale) is therefore set by $M$ and $k$, not by a large volume. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221))
- **Exponential hierarchy.** A mass parameter $m_0$ in the visible-brane action corresponds to the physical mass $m=e^{-kr_c\pi}m_0$. RS1 notes that $e^{kr_c\pi}\sim10^{15}$ turns Planck-scale inputs into TeV-scale masses. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221)) The arithmetic gives $kr_c\pi=\ln 10^{15}\approx 35$, so $kr_c\approx 11$. The letter's own remark that "we only require $kr_c\approx 50$" does not match its $10^{15}$: $kr_c=50$ would give $e^{50\pi}\sim10^{68}$. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221)) The PDG review, writing the warp factor as $e^{-k\pi R}$, states that $M_5\sim k\sim M_P$ gives an IR-boundary scale $ke^{-k\pi R}\sim$ TeV for $R\simeq 11/k$; Csáki, with the proper inter-brane length $r$ in the exponent, writes $rk\sim\log 10^{16}\sim30$. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [Csáki TASI](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0404096))
- **TeV-scale KK gravitons.** In RS1 the masses and couplings of the graviton [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes) are set by the TeV scale, so there is no light, dense KK tower and the gravitational resonances are of order a TeV. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221)) The PDG gives $m_n\simeq(n+\alpha/2-1/4)\,\pi k e^{-\pi kR}$ with $\alpha=1$ for KK gravitons, $0$ for KK gauge bosons, and $|c_f-1/2|$ for KK fermions, so gauge bosons are the lightest KK states and gravitons the heaviest. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **RS2 correction to Newton's law.** For a single positive-tension brane and a static non-relativistic source, Garriga and Tanaka find to linear order
  $$\bar h_{00}=\frac{2GM}{r}\Bigl(1+\frac{2\ell^2}{3r^2}\Bigr),\qquad \bar h_{ij}=\frac{2GM}{r}\Bigl(1+\frac{\ell^2}{3r^2}\Bigr)\delta_{ij},$$
  with $\ell$ the AdS curvature radius and $G=\ell^{-1}G_5$. The Newtonian potential, $\bar h_{00}/2$, is $GM/r\,(1+2\ell^2/3r^2)$, i.e. $1+2/(3k^2r^2)$ with $k=1/\ell$. Einstein gravity is recovered to leading order and the field stays localized near the brane. ([Garriga–Tanaka](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-th/9911055); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9911055)) With two branes of opposite tension, the same paper finds [linearized](node:Linearized%20Gravity) Brans–Dicke gravity on each brane rather than pure Einstein gravity. ([Garriga–Tanaka](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9911055))
- **Goldberger–Wise stabilization.** A bulk scalar with quartic interactions localized on the two 3-branes generates a potential for the modulus that sets the size of the fifth dimension, and its minimum gives a compactification scale solving the hierarchy problem without fine tuning. ([Goldberger–Wise](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9907447)) In Csáki's superpotential treatment, $W(\Phi)=6k/\kappa^2-u\Phi^2$ gives $\Phi_0(y)=\Phi_Pe^{-uy}$ and a stabilized length $r=(1/u)\ln(\Phi_P/\Phi_T)$, so a modest ratio of boundary values produces the large $kr$. ([Csáki TASI](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0404096))
- **Radion.** The fluctuation of the inter-brane distance is the radion. After Goldberger–Wise stabilization its mass satisfies $m^2_{\rm radion}/m^2_{\rm graviton}\sim l^2(u^2/k^2)e^{-2ur}$, so it is likely the lightest new particle of RS1. It couples to matter through $r(x)\,{\rm Tr}\,T/(\sqrt6\,M_{\rm Pl}e^{-kr})$, i.e. to the trace of the energy-momentum tensor with TeV-suppressed strength. ([Csáki TASI](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0404096))
- **Holographic interpretation.** Arkani-Hamed, Porrati and Randall develop the correspondence between warped AdS$_5$ with boundary branes and strongly coupled, broken [conformal field theories](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory) coupled to dynamical gravity, and apply it to radius stabilization, cosmology and unification. ([APR](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0012148)) Rattazzi and Zaffaroni test the conjecture that compact RS is dual to a 4D theory with non-linearly realized conformal symmetry, showing among other things that the radion couples conformally to a background 4d metric, and interpret the Goldberger–Wise mechanism in the dual picture. ([Rattazzi–Zaffaroni](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0012248)) In this picture the TeV-brane KK modes are bound states of the CFT, and RS1 with a brane Higgs is a CFT that becomes strongly coupled and produces a composite Higgs; Csáki summarizes this as the hierarchy problem being solved by Higgs compositeness. ([Csáki TASI](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0404096))
- **Bulk fermions and flavour.** Localizing light fermion zero modes towards the UV brane suppresses their overlap with an IR-localized Higgs, so the Standard Model fermion mass hierarchies follow from order-one bulk mass parameters $c_f$; the top quark is localized near the IR brane. Flavour-changing KK gluon couplings then give constraints and predicted effects in $B$ physics. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)) Agashe, Perez and Soni show that the zero-mode profiles control the flavour structure, and that with KK masses of about $3$ TeV, anarchic 5D Yukawas give a "CP problem": neutron electric-dipole-moment contributions about 20 times the experimental bound. ([Agashe–Perez–Soni](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0408134))
- **Electroweak precision and custodial symmetry.** With bulk gauge fields, the $\hat T$ parameter gives $m_{KK}\gtrsim10$ TeV. A bulk custodial symmetry $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R\times U(1)_{B-L}$ (Agashe, Delgado, May, Sundrum) suppresses $\hat T$, after which $\hat S$ dominates and requires $m_{KK}\gtrsim3$ TeV. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [ADMS](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0308036)) Via AdS/CFT these custodial models are dual to a strongly coupled conformal Higgs sector with a global custodial symmetry. ([ADMS](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0308036))

### Examples
- **Minimal RS1 at the LHC (only gravity in the bulk).** The lightest KK graviton is searched for as a resonance in $\gamma\gamma$ and dilepton final states, parametrized by $k/\bar M_{\rm Pl}$ and $m_1$. With the full $139\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ at 13 TeV, ATLAS excludes $m_{G^*}$ below $2.2$, $3.9$ and $4.5$ TeV for $k/\bar M_{\rm Pl}=0.01$, $0.05$ and $0.1$ in the diphoton channel. ([ATLAS diphoton](https://arxiv.org/html/2102.13405)) CMS dilepton searches with up to $140\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ exclude KK gravitons with masses $2.47$–$4.78$ TeV for $k/\bar M_{\rm Pl}=0.01$–$0.1$. ATLAS (CMS) excludes radions decaying to $WW,ZZ$ below $3.2$ ($3.1$) TeV. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [CMS dilepton](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.02708))
- **Bulk Standard Model.** When SM fields live in the bulk, KK graviton couplings to $ee,\mu\mu,\gamma\gamma$ are suppressed and the limits above do not apply; KK gauge bosons are the better channel. CMS excludes KK gluons (decaying to $t\bar t$) below $4.55$ TeV with $36\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ at 13 TeV. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **RS2 as a non-compact extra dimension.** A single 3-brane in a non-factorizable five-dimensional background reproduces four-dimensional Newtonian and general-relativistic gravity even though the Kaluza–Klein spectrum has no gap; Wikipedia notes the setup is also of interest for studies of the AdS/CFT conjecture. ([RS2](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9906064); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall%E2%80%93Sundrum_model))

### History
Merab Gogberashvili posted related shell-universe papers in 1998–99 (hep-ph/9812296, hep-ph/9812365, hep-ph/9904383). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall%E2%80%93Sundrum_model)) Randall and Sundrum's hierarchy paper (hep-ph/9905221) came a year after the ADD flat-extra-dimension proposal of 1998 ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)), and "An Alternative to Compactification" was submitted on 8 June 1999 and published in *Phys. Rev. Lett.* **83**, 4690–4693 (1999). ([RS2](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9906064))

The 1999 RS1 letter states that the modulus must be stabilized at $r_c$ with a mass of at least $10^{-4}$ eV and that "this problem is not yet solved". ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221)) Goldberger and Wise proposed their bulk-scalar mechanism in July 1999 (*Phys. Rev. Lett.* **83**, 4922). ([Goldberger–Wise](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9907447)) Garriga and Tanaka computed the brane-world Newtonian corrections in November 1999 (*Phys. Rev. Lett.* **84**, 2778). ([Garriga–Tanaka](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9911055)) The holographic reading came in December 2000 from Arkani-Hamed–Porrati–Randall and Rattazzi–Zaffaroni ([APR](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0012148); [Rattazzi–Zaffaroni](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0012248)), and custodial RS1 in 2003. ([ADMS](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0308036))

### Connections
- [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions): RS is the warped five-dimensional realization, in contrast to large flat tori.
- [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions): the ADD alternative; RS1 has no light KK tower, so ADD astrophysical bounds do not apply.
- [Warped Products](node:Warped%20Products): the RS metric is a warped product of Minkowski space with an interval.
- [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space): the bulk is a slice of AdS$_5$.
- [Israel Junction Conditions](node:Israel%20Junction%20Conditions) and [Extrinsic Curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature): fix the brane tensions in terms of $k$.
- [Orbifolds](node:Orbifolds): RS1's extra dimension is $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$.
- [Goldberger–Wise Mechanism](node:Goldberger–Wise%20Mechanism): stabilizes $r_c$ and gives the radion a mass.
- [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes) and [Kaluza–Klein Theory](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Theory): TeV-scale discrete tower in RS1, gapless continuum in RS2.
- [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence), [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory) and [Holographic Principle](node:Holographic%20Principle): the dual reading of RS1 as a composite-Higgs CFT.
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem), [Electroweak Theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory) and [Standard Model of Particle Physics](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics): the phenomenological targets of RS1 and its bulk extensions.
- [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale): $M_{\rm Pl}^2=(M^3/k)(1-e^{-2kr_c\pi})$.
- [Braneworld Cosmology](node:Braneworld%20Cosmology) and [Effective Einstein Equations on the Brane](node:Effective%20Einstein%20Equations%20on%20the%20Brane): cosmology and gravity on RS-type branes.
- [Newtonian Limit of General Relativity](node:Newtonian%20Limit%20of%20General%20Relativity) and [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): RS2 reproduces them up to $\ell^2/r^2$ corrections.
- [Collider Physics](node:Collider%20Physics): KK graviton, KK gluon and radion searches.
- [Einstein–Hilbert Action](node:Einstein–Hilbert%20Action): the bulk gravity action.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Braneworld gravity and cosmology](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Braneworld%20gravity%20and%20cosmology)

### Common pitfalls
- **Product metric.** Writing $g_{\mu\nu}(x)+g_{55}(y)$ without a warp factor loses both the hierarchy and the RS2 bound graviton; both need the $y$-dependent factor $e^{-2kr_c|\phi|}$. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221); [RS2](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9906064))
- **The value of $kr_c$.** The needed warp is $kr_c\pi\approx35$ ($kr_c\approx11$; the PDG's $R\simeq11/k$), not $kr_c\approx50$; check which coordinate convention a source uses, since Csáki's $kr\sim30$ refers to the full proper length. ([RS1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/9905221); [PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [Csáki TASI](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0404096))
- **Graviton limits are model dependent.** Diphoton and dilepton bounds on the KK graviton assume SM fields on the IR brane; with bulk fermions these couplings are suppressed and KK gauge bosons give the relevant limits. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Two branes are not Einstein gravity.** In the unstabilized two-brane setup, linearized gravity on either wall is Brans–Dicke with different BD parameters (greater than 3000 on the positive-tension wall if the separation exceeds four AdS radii; negative but above $-3/2$ on the negative-tension wall), and shadow matter on the other wall gravitates; Einstein gravity is recovered to leading order only for a single positive-tension wall. ([Garriga–Tanaka](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9911055))

### Open problems
- **Little hierarchy.** Agashe, Du, Hong and Sundrum argue that low-energy constraints and the absence of non-standard physics at LHC Run 1 point to a "little hierarchy problem" that remains in warped models, and that the new physics underlying [naturalness](node:Naturalness) may lie beyond LHC reach; they propose extensions in which lighter KK-type resonances remain accessible. ([Agashe–Du–Hong–Sundrum](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.00526)) The tension is quantitative: electroweak precision requires $m_{KK}\gtrsim3$ TeV even with custodial symmetry, Run-2 searches exclude KK gluons below about $4.5$ TeV, and anarchic flavour at $3$ TeV overshoots the neutron EDM bound. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [Agashe–Perez–Soni](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0408134))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Randall–Sundrum model (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall%E2%80%93Sundrum_model): RS1 versus RS2 and the Gogberashvili precursors.
- **Reference:** [PDG Review: Extra Dimensions (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf): warped KK spectra, flavour, electroweak precision bounds and current LHC limits.
- **Learn:** [Csáki, TASI Lectures on Extra Dimensions and Branes](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0404096): derivations of the RS background, gravity localization, Goldberger–Wise, the radion, bulk gauge fields and AdS/CFT.

## Reference
### Overview
A random variable is a measurable function from a probability space to the real line (or to another measurable space), and its distribution is the probability measure it induces on the target: the pushforward $\mu=P\circ X^{-1}$. ([Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution))

On $\mathbb R$ a distribution is determined by its distribution function $F(x)=P(X\le x)$, and the functions that arise are exactly the nondecreasing, right-continuous functions with limits $0$ and $1$ at $\mp\infty$. Every distribution on $\mathbb R$ splits uniquely into a discrete part, an absolutely continuous part (one with a density), and a singular continuous part, such as the Cantor distribution. ([Durrett](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution))

Classifying distributions is not always easy. Bernoulli convolutions, the laws of $\sum_{n\ge0}\pm\lambda^n$ with independent fair signs, are a standard example: the law is absolutely continuous for almost every $\lambda\in(1/2,1)$, but the exact set of parameters for which it is absolutely continuous has not been determined. ([Varjú 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1608.04210))

### Formal definition
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and $(S,\mathcal S)$ a measurable space. A map $X:\Omega\to S$ is a **random element** (a **random variable** when $(S,\mathcal S)=(\mathbb R,\mathcal R)$ with $\mathcal R$ the Borel sets) if
$$X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\}\in\mathcal F\qquad\text{for all }B\in\mathcal S.$$
It suffices to check this for $B$ in a generating class $\mathcal A$ of $\mathcal S$. ([Durrett, Thm 1.3.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Sheffield, MIT 18.175 Lecture 3](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture3.pdf))

The **distribution** (law) of $X$ is $\mu(A)=P(X\in A)$ for Borel $A$; the **distribution function** is $F(x)=P(X\le x)$. $X$ has **density** $f$ if $F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f(y)\,dy$. $X\overset{d}{=}Y$ means $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution. A distribution is **discrete** if it is carried by a countable set, **absolutely continuous** if it has a density, and **singular** if the corresponding measure is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure. ([Durrett, §1.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

The **quantile function** is $F^{-1}(p)=\inf\{x:p\le F(x)\}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution))

### Key results
- **Characterization of distribution functions.** Any distribution function satisfies (i) $F$ nondecreasing, (ii) $F(x)\to1$ as $x\to\infty$ and $F(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$, (iii) right continuity, (iv) $F(x-)=P(X<x)$, (v) $P(X=x)=F(x)-F(x-)$. Conversely, any $F$ satisfying (i)–(iii) is the distribution function of some random variable: on $((0,1),\text{Borel},\text{Lebesgue})$ take $X(\omega)=\sup\{y:F(y)<\omega\}$. ([Durrett, Thms 1.2.1–1.2.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Uniqueness of the Stieltjes measure.** For each right-continuous nondecreasing $F$ with limits $0$ and $1$ there is a unique Borel probability measure with $\mu((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)$; the analogous statement on $\mathbb R^d$ holds for $F$ that is nondecreasing, right continuous, and assigns nonnegative mass to every rectangle. Both follow from Carathéodory's extension theorem. ([Sheffield, Lecture 3](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture3.pdf))
- **Lebesgue decomposition.** Every distribution on $\mathbb R$ is uniquely a mixture of a discrete, an absolutely continuous, and a singular continuous distribution, with weights summing to $1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution))
- **Closure properties.** If $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\mathcal S)$ and $f:(S,\mathcal S)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ are measurable, so is $f(X)$; sums of random variables are random variables; and $\inf_n X_n$, $\sup_n X_n$, $\liminf_n X_n$, $\limsup_n X_n$ are random variables, so $\{\lim_n X_n\text{ exists}\}$ is an event. ([Durrett, Thms 1.3.4–1.3.7](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Sheffield, Lecture 3](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture3.pdf))
- **Inverse transform sampling.** If $U$ is uniform on $(0,1)$, then $F^{-1}(U)$ has distribution function $F$; for example $-\lambda^{-1}\log(1-U)$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution)) Conversely, if $F$ is continuous then $F(X)$ is uniform on $(0,1)$. ([Durrett, Exercise 1.2.4](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Change of variables for densities.** If $X$ has continuous density $f$, $P(\alpha\le X\le\beta)=1$, and $g$ is strictly increasing and differentiable on $(\alpha,\beta)$, then $g(X)$ has density $f(g^{-1}(y))/g'(g^{-1}(y))$ on $(g(\alpha),g(\beta))$. ([Durrett, Exercise 1.2.5](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Convolution.** If $X$ and $Y$ are independent with distribution functions $F$ and $G$, then $P(X+Y\le z)=\int F(z-y)\,dG(y)$; if $X$ has density $f$, then $X+Y$ has density $\int f(x-y)\,dG(y)$. ([Durrett, Thms 2.1.15–2.1.16](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Bernoulli convolutions.** Let $\nu_\lambda$ be the law of $\sum_{n\ge0}\pm\lambda^n$ with independent fair signs. If $1/2<\lambda<1$ and $\lambda^{-1}$ is a Pisot number, $\nu_\lambda$ is singular (Erdős, 1939); for almost every $\lambda\in(1/2,1)$, $\nu_\lambda$ is absolutely continuous with an $L^2$ density (Solomyak, 1995). ([Varjú 2016, Thms 2.1, 2.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1608.04210))

### Examples
- **Normal.** If $X$ is standard normal and $Y=\sigma X+\mu$, then $Y$ has density $(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-(y-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2)$. ([Durrett, Example 1.6.11](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Discrete laws.** Bernoulli: $P(X=1)=p$, $P(X=0)=1-p$; Poisson: $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$; geometric: $P(N=k)=p(1-p)^{k-1}$, $k\ge1$, the number of independent trials until the first success. ([Durrett, Examples 1.6.12–1.6.14](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **Cantor distribution.** The distribution function that is $1/2$ on $[1/3,2/3]$, $1/4$ on $[1/9,2/9]$, $3/4$ on $[7/9,8/9]$, and so on, is continuous but has no density, since its measure gives full mass to the Lebesgue-null Cantor set. ([Durrett, Example 1.2.7](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- **A dense discrete law.** The ratio of two independent Poisson variables is a random rational whose support is dense in $[0,\infty)$. ([Sheffield, Lecture 3](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture3.pdf))
- **Families by mechanism.** Bernoulli, binomial, geometric and negative binomial (yes/no trials); Poisson, exponential, gamma (event rates); categorical and multinomial ($K$ outcomes); beta, Dirichlet, Wishart (conjugate priors). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution))

### History
George Mackey credited Pafnuty Chebyshev as the first person to think systematically in terms of random variables; the modern definition as a measurable function, which, as Wikipedia notes, involves neither randomness nor variability, came with the measure-theoretic foundations. ([Wikipedia: Random variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_variable)) Questions about whether a natural distribution has a density can stay open for decades: Erdős proved singularity of Bernoulli convolutions for Pisot parameters in 1939, and absolute continuity for almost every parameter came only with Solomyak in 1995. ([Varjú 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1608.04210))

### Connections
- [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces): the domain $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ on which random variables are defined.
- [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): distributions are pushforward measures; Carathéodory extension builds them from $F$.
- [Lebesgue Integration](node:Lebesgue%20Integration): densities and probabilities $\int_B f$ are Lebesgue integrals.
- [Radon–Nikodym Theorem](node:Radon–Nikodym%20Theorem): a density is the Radon–Nikodym derivative of an absolutely continuous law.
- [Expectation and Variance](node:Expectation%20and%20Variance): numerical summaries computed from the distribution by the change-of-variables formula.
- [Independence of Random Variables](node:Independence%20of%20Random%20Variables): makes the joint law a product measure and sums convolutions.
- [Multivariate Distributions](node:Multivariate%20Distributions): random vectors and distribution functions on $\mathbb R^d$.
- [Gaussian Distribution](node:Gaussian%20Distribution), [Poisson Distribution](node:Poisson%20Distribution): the two families that arise as limits of sums and of rare events.
- [Limit Theorems (LLN and CLT)](node:Limit%20Theorems%20%28LLN%20and%20CLT%29): convergence in distribution is convergence of the laws.
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains): sequences of random variables built from a transition kernel.

### Common pitfalls
- "Continuous" is not the same as "has a density": the Cantor distribution has a continuous distribution function but no density. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution))
- A density value is not a probability: if $X$ has density $f$ then $P(X=x)=0$ for every $x$, even though $f(x)$ may be positive. ([Durrett, §1.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))
- Equality in distribution says nothing about equality of the random variables: $X\overset{d}{=}Y$ means only that they have the same distribution function, and they need not even be defined on the same probability space. ([Durrett, §1.2](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf); [Wikipedia: Random variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_variable))
- Without right continuity, a nondecreasing $F$ is not a distribution function; the convention $F(x)=P(X\le x)$ (not $<$) fixes it. ([Durrett, Thm 1.2.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Absolute continuity of Bernoulli convolutions.** Varjú's survey states that the main question about $\nu_\lambda$ is to determine the set of parameters for which it is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Singularity is proved when $\lambda^{-1}$ is Pisot (Erdős); absolute continuity is known for almost every $\lambda$ (Solomyak) and for explicit algebraic parameters (Garsia's theorem, Varjú's Theorem 4.11). The only known $\lambda\in(1/2,1)$ with $\dim\nu_\lambda<1$ are inverses of Pisot numbers, and for inverses of Salem numbers the survey notes that the known estimates do not imply singularity. ([Varjú 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1608.04210); [arXiv abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04210))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Probability distribution (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution): pushforward definition, CDF/PMF/PDF, Lebesgue decomposition, families, inverse transform sampling.
- **Learn:** [Sheffield, MIT 18.175 Lecture 3: Random variables and distributions](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/175/Lecture3.pdf): measures on $\mathbb R^d$, measurability, distribution functions (course page [18.175](https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/spring2014math175.html)).
- **Primary:** [Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*, §§1.2–1.3, 2.1](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf): graduate text with the definitions and theorems above.
- **Primary:** [Varjú, *Recent progress on Bernoulli convolutions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04210): survey of singularity versus absolute continuity for a natural family of distributions.
- **Further reading:** [Durrett's book page](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/pte.html): the 5th edition of the standard graduate probability text.
