## Reference
### Overview
The real numbers $\mathbb R$ are the number system of single-variable analysis. Algebraically and order-theoretically they look like the rationals $\mathbb Q$; what distinguishes them is completeness, which fills the "gaps" of $\mathbb Q$ such as the missing square root of $2$ (no rational $x$ satisfies $x^2=2$, while the set $\{x\in\mathbb Q: x^2<2\}$ has supremum $\sqrt2$ in $\mathbb R$). ([Hunter, Theorem 2.4 and §2.6](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf)) Up to unique isomorphism, $\mathbb R$ is the only Dedekind-complete ordered field, so the axiomatic description and the constructions from $\mathbb Q$ (Dedekind cuts, Cauchy sequences) describe the same object. ([Real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number); [nLab, real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/real+number))

Limits turn "approaching a value" into quantified statements, and completeness is what guarantees that limits which ought to exist do exist: bounded monotone sequences converge, Cauchy sequences converge, bounded sequences have convergent subsequences, and closed bounded sets are compact. These facts underlie continuity, the intermediate and extreme value theorems, derivatives, and integrals. ([Hunter, Chapters 3, 5, 7](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf)) The topic is the base of [real functions of one variable](node:MSC%2026Axx%20-%20Functions%20of%20one%20variable) and of [metric-space](node:Metric%20Spaces) analysis.

### Formal definition
$\mathbb R$ is an ordered field satisfying the **least-upper-bound (Dedekind completeness) axiom**: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is bounded above has a supremum (least upper bound) in $\mathbb R$. Applying it to $-A$ gives infima of nonempty sets bounded below; the nonemptiness hypothesis is needed since the empty set is bounded above but has no supremum. Dedekind (1872) showed that the real numbers are characterized as a complete ordered field. ([Hunter, Axiom 2.17 and §2.6](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf))

A real sequence $(x_n)$ **converges** to $x$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with $|x_n-x|<\varepsilon$ for all $n>N$; it is **Cauchy** if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $|x_m-x_n|<\varepsilon$ for all $m,n>N$. ([Hunter, Definition 3.10 and §3.7](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf))

For $f:A\to\mathbb R$ with $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $c$ an accumulation point of $A$, $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L$ means: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $x\in A$ and $0<|x-c|<\delta$ imply $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. The function $f$ is **continuous** at $c\in A$ if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(c)$ there is a neighbourhood $U$ of $c$ with $f(A\cap U)\subseteq V$; at an accumulation point $c\in A$ this is equivalent to $f(x_n)\to f(c)$ for every sequence $(x_n)$ in $A$ with $x_n\to c$. ([Hunter, Definitions 6.1, 7.2 and Theorem 7.6](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf))

### Key results
- **Archimedean property.** For every $x\in\mathbb R$ there is $n\in\mathbb N$ with $x<n$; equivalently, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $n$ with $0<1/n<\varepsilon$. It follows from the least-upper-bound axiom (if $\mathbb N$ were bounded, $M=\sup\mathbb N$ would make $M-1$ an upper bound). ([Hunter, Theorem 2.18](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf))
- **Density of $\mathbb Q$.** If $x<y$ are real, there is $r\in\mathbb Q$ with $x<r<y$. The rationals are countable and dense, the irrationals are also dense but uncountable, and $\mathbb R$ is uncountable. ([Hunter, Theorems 2.5, 2.19, 2.31](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf); [Real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)) See [Cardinality](node:Cardinality).
- **Uniqueness of the complete ordered field.** Any two Dedekind-complete ordered fields are isomorphic, and the isomorphism is unique; every Archimedean ordered field embeds in $\mathbb R$. The nLab notes that this uniqueness uses impredicative foundations. ([Real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number); [nLab, real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/real+number))
- **Monotone convergence theorem.** A monotone real sequence converges if and only if it is bounded; an increasing bounded sequence converges to $\sup_n x_n$, a decreasing one to $\inf_n x_n$. ([Hunter, Theorem 3.29](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf))
- **Cauchy criterion.** A real sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy. ([Hunter, Theorem 3.46](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf)) See [Cauchy Sequences](node:Cauchy%20Sequences).
- **Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem.** Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence; equivalently, a subset of $\mathbb R$ is sequentially compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. The statement extends to $\mathbb R^n$ coordinatewise. ([Hunter, Theorems 3.57, 5.36](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf); [Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolzano%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem)) See [Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem](node:Bolzano–Weierstrass%20Theorem).
- **Heine–Borel theorem.** A subset of $\mathbb R$ (more generally of $\mathbb R^n$) is compact, meaning every open cover has a finite subcover, if and only if it is closed and bounded; hence for subsets of $\mathbb R$ compactness and sequential compactness coincide. In a general metric space compactness is equivalent to being complete and totally bounded. ([Hunter, Theorem 5.56, Corollary 5.57 and Theorem 13.60](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf); [Heine–Borel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heine%E2%80%93Borel_theorem)) See [Heine–Borel Theorem](node:Heine–Borel%20Theorem).
- **Equivalent forms of completeness.** For an ordered field, the least-upper-bound property, Dedekind completeness of cuts, the monotone convergence theorem and the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem are equivalent: a field with one has them all. Cauchy completeness and the nested interval property are strictly weaker for general ordered fields, and each becomes equivalent to the others when combined with the Archimedean property. The intermediate value theorem, taken as an axiom, also implies the least-upper-bound property. ([Completeness of the real numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completeness_of_the_real_numbers))
- **Continuous functions on compact sets.** If $K\subseteq\mathbb R$ is compact and $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, then $f$ is bounded and attains its maximum and minimum (Weierstrass), and $f$ is uniformly continuous. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous with $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ of opposite signs, there is $c\in(a,b)$ with $f(c)=0$ (intermediate value theorem). ([Hunter, Theorems 7.37, 7.42, 7.44](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf)) See [Uniform Continuity](node:Uniform%20Continuity).

### Examples
The interval $(0,1)$ has supremum $1$ and infimum $0$ but contains neither, so a bounded set can have a supremum without a maximum; $\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ has maximum $1$ and infimum $0$ with no minimum. ([Hunter, §2.5](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf)) The sequence $(1/n)$ is strictly decreasing and bounded, hence convergent, while $((-1)^{n+1})$ is bounded but not monotone and does not converge, though it has convergent constant subsequences, as Bolzano–Weierstrass predicts. ([Hunter, §3.5](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf)) In $\mathbb Q$ the set $\{x:x^2<2\}$ is nonempty and bounded above but has no least upper bound in $\mathbb Q$, showing that $\mathbb Q$ is an ordered field that is not complete. ([Hunter, §2.6](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf))

### History
Bolzano proved the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem in 1817 as a lemma for the intermediate value theorem; Weierstrass recognised its importance and reproved it about fifty years later. ([Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolzano%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem)) Dedekind began work on an arithmetic foundation of continuity in autumn 1858 while teaching differential calculus at the Zurich Polytechnic; in *Continuity and Irrational Numbers* he defined a cut of $\mathbb Q$ as a division into two classes $A_1,A_2$ with every element of $A_1$ less than every element of $A_2$, created an irrational number for each cut not produced by a rational, and proved that every cut of the real numbers is produced by exactly one real number. ([Dedekind, Essays on the Theory of Numbers](https://archive.org/stream/essaysontheoryof00dedeuoft/essaysontheoryof00dedeuoft_djvu.txt)) Dedekind and Cantor published their constructions (cuts, and equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences) in 1872, and in 1874 Cantor proved $\mathbb R$ uncountable. ([Real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)) Borel stated a countable-cover version of the Heine–Borel theorem in 1895; Cousin, Lebesgue and Schoenflies extended it to arbitrary covers. ([Heine–Borel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heine%E2%80%93Borel_theorem))

### Connections
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): supplies sets, functions, sequences and the constructions of $\mathbb R$ from $\mathbb Q$.
- [Cauchy Sequences](node:Cauchy%20Sequences): the Cauchy form of completeness, and the basis of completion of metric spaces.
- [Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem](node:Bolzano–Weierstrass%20Theorem) and [Heine–Borel Theorem](node:Heine–Borel%20Theorem): the two compactness forms of completeness.
- [Compactness and Connectedness](node:Compactness%20and%20Connectedness): the topological generalisation of the compactness and intermediate-value results.
- [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence): limits of partial sums.
- [Differential Calculus](node:Differential%20Calculus): derivatives are defined as limits of difference quotients.
- [Hyperreal Numbers](node:Hyperreal%20Numbers): a non-Archimedean ordered field extending $\mathbb R$.
- [Real Closed Fields](node:Real%20Closed%20Fields) and [Ordered Groups and Ordered Rings](node:Ordered%20Groups%20and%20Ordered%20Rings): the algebraic theory of orderings that $\mathbb R$ exemplifies.

### Common pitfalls
- **Quantifier order.** In the definition of convergence $N$ may depend on $\varepsilon$, but a single $N$ must work for all later terms; similarly $\delta$ depends on $\varepsilon$ (and, for continuity, on the point unless the function is uniformly continuous). ([Hunter, Definitions 3.10, 6.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf))
- **Limits ignore the value at the point.** $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)$ only uses $x\ne c$, so $c$ need not be in the domain; it must be an accumulation point of the domain. ([Hunter, Definition 6.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf))
- **Cauchy completeness alone is not enough.** An ordered field can be Cauchy complete without being Dedekind complete; the Archimedean property is needed to recover the full completeness axiom. ([Completeness of the real numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completeness_of_the_real_numbers))
- **Constructions can differ without choice.** Dedekind and Cauchy reals agree assuming weak countable choice, but in some constructive settings, such as internal languages of toposes, they are not equivalent. ([nLab, real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/real+number))

### Open problems
- **Irrationality of specific real numbers.** The foundational theory above is settled, but whether particular real numbers are rational can be very hard: MathWorld states that irrationality "has not yet been established" for $2^e$, $\pi^e$, $\pi^{\sqrt2}$, or the Euler–Mascheroni constant $\gamma$. ([MathWorld, Irrational number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/IrrationalNumber.html))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab, real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/real+number): characterisations, uniqueness, Dedekind versus Cauchy reals and constructive issues.
- **Reference:** [Completeness of the real numbers (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completeness_of_the_real_numbers): the forms of completeness and which are equivalent.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, An Introduction to Real Analysis (UC Davis notes)](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/intro_analysis_pdf/intro_analysis.pdf): free notes with full proofs of every result above.
- **Primary:** [Dedekind, Essays on the Theory of Numbers (Open Court, 1901), part I "Continuity and Irrational Numbers"](https://archive.org/details/essaysontheoryof00dedeuoft): the original construction of the reals by cuts.
- **Further reading:** [Abbott, Understanding Analysis (Springer UTM, 2015)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4939-2712-8): a standard textbook on the axiom of completeness, sequences and continuity.

## Reference
### Overview
A recurrent neural network (RNN) processes a sequence by carrying a hidden state from step to step and applying the same parameters at every step. In the Elman network the update is $h_t=\sigma_h(W_hx_t+U_hh_{t-1}+b_h)$ with output $y_t=\sigma_y(W_yh_t+b_y)$; in the Jordan network the context (state) units are fed from the previous output instead ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network)).

Training uses backpropagation through time (BPTT), which unrolls the network into a feedforward graph with shared weights. The gradient contains long products of Jacobian-like factors, so simple RNNs suffer from vanishing and exploding gradients and learn long-range dependencies poorly ([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/bptt.html)). The LSTM was one of the first and most successful remedies ([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/lstm.html)), and the GRU of Cho et al. (2014) is a streamlined version of the LSTM cell ([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/gru.html)).

RNN encoder–decoders, optionally with attention, were used to build state-of-the-art neural machine translators during 2014–2017 and an instrumental step toward [Transformers](node:Transformers); RNNs remain relevant where computational efficiency or real-time processing matter ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network)). Orvieto et al. (2023) showed that deep RNNs with linearized, diagonalized recurrences (the Linear Recurrent Unit) match deep [state-space models](node:State%20Space%20Models) on Long Range Arena ([Orvieto et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06349)), and linear RNNs such as Mamba and DeltaNet are now pretrained as language models ([Grazzi et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12537)).

### Formal definition
**Simple RNN.** Given inputs $x_1,\dots,x_T$, parameters $(W_h,U_h,b_h,W_y,b_y)$ and $h_0$, set $h_t=\sigma_h(W_hx_t+U_hh_{t-1}+b_h)$ and $y_t=\sigma_y(W_yh_t+b_y)$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network)).

**LSTM (with forget gate).** With sigmoid $\sigma$ and elementwise product $\odot$,
$$\begin{aligned}I_t&=\sigma(X_tW_{xi}+H_{t-1}W_{hi}+b_i),\quad F_t=\sigma(X_tW_{xf}+H_{t-1}W_{hf}+b_f),\quad O_t=\sigma(X_tW_{xo}+H_{t-1}W_{ho}+b_o),\\ \tilde C_t&=\tanh(X_tW_{xc}+H_{t-1}W_{hc}+b_c),\quad C_t=F_t\odot C_{t-1}+I_t\odot\tilde C_t,\quad H_t=O_t\odot\tanh(C_t).\end{aligned}$$
([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/lstm.html)) This is the now-standard cell. The original LSTM block had cells with input and output gates but no forget gate; the forget gate was the first modification of the architecture, introduced by Gers et al. ([Greff et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1503.04069)), published as "Learning to Forget: Continual Prediction with LSTM" (Gers, Schmidhuber, Cummins, *Neural Computation* 12(10), 2000) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1162/089976600300015015)).

**GRU.** With reset gate $R_t=\sigma(X_tW_{xr}+H_{t-1}W_{hr}+b_r)$ and update gate $Z_t=\sigma(X_tW_{xz}+H_{t-1}W_{hz}+b_z)$,
$$\tilde H_t=\tanh\big(X_tW_{xh}+(R_t\odot H_{t-1})W_{hh}+b_h\big),\qquad H_t=Z_t\odot H_{t-1}+(1-Z_t)\odot\tilde H_t .$$
([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/gru.html))

**Echo state network.** $\mathbf x(n+1)=f(\mathbf W\mathbf x(n)+\mathbf W^{in}\mathbf u(n+1)+\mathbf W^{fb}\mathbf y(n))$, $\mathbf y(n)=g(\mathbf W^{out}[\mathbf x(n);\mathbf u(n)])$, with random fixed $\mathbf W,\mathbf W^{in}$ and only $\mathbf W^{out}$ fitted by linear regression ([Scholarpedia](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Echo_state_network)).

**BPTT and RTRL.** BPTT sums each shared parameter's gradient over time steps, costing $O(\#\text{weights})$ per step but storing activations; real-time recurrent learning is online and costs $O(\#\text{hidden}\times\#\text{weights})$ per step ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network); [D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/bptt.html)).

### Key results
- **Vanishing and exploding gradients (Pascanu, Mikolov, Bengio).** For recurrent matrix $W_{\mathrm{rec}}$ and activation with $\|\operatorname{diag}\sigma'\|\le\gamma$ ($\gamma=1$ for $\tanh$, $1/4$ for the logistic sigmoid), the paper states that $\lambda_1<1/\gamma$ is sufficient for vanishing gradients and $\lambda_1>1/\gamma$ is necessary for exploding gradients, $\lambda_1$ being the largest absolute eigenvalue. The proof bounds the 2-norm of each one-step Jacobian by the product of the norms of its factors ([Pascanu et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1211.5063)), so the sufficient condition the argument actually establishes is on the operator 2-norm, i.e. the largest singular value $\|W_{\mathrm{rec}}\|_2<1/\gamma$; since $\rho(W)\le\|W\|_2$ this coincides with the eigenvalue condition only for normal matrices ([Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition)). In the linear case the gradient involves powers of $W_{hh}$ ([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/bptt.html)).
- **Gradient norm clipping.** If $\|\hat g\|\ge$ threshold, replace $\hat g$ by $(\text{threshold}/\|\hat g\|)\hat g$; for vanishing gradients Pascanu et al. add a soft-constraint regularizer $\Omega$ that prefers error signals preserving norm as they travel back in time ([Pascanu et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1211.5063)).
- **Constant error flow.** In the 1997 LSTM the internal state is a node with a self-connected recurrent edge of fixed weight 1, letting gradients pass across many steps ([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/lstm.html)). In the forget-gate cell this self-connection is the learned gate $F_t$; with $F_t=1$ and $I_t=0$ the state is copied unchanged ([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/lstm.html)).
- **Turing completeness (Siegelmann and Sontag).** In the form presented in Yang's lecture slides, which cite Siegelmann and Sontag (1994, 1995): for any Turing machine $M$ there is an RNN with rational weights, ReLU activations and a linear output layer that, fed $w$ followed by blank symbols, accepts or rejects exactly when $M$ halts and accepts or rejects (the slides' construction uses several ReLU layers per step, reducible to one); with real weights such an RNN can decide any language $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$, the theorem the slides credit to Siegelmann and Sontag ([Yang, Notre Dame lecture slides](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~dchiang/teaching/tonn/2024/tm_to_rnn_2_slides.pdf)). The rational-weight result appeared as "On the Computational Power of Neural Nets", *J. Comput. Syst. Sci.* 50(1), 1995 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1006/jcss.1995.1013)). Turing completeness of RNNs relies on infinite precision in the states and unbounded computation time ([Weiss et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04908)).
- **Finite-precision hierarchy (Weiss, Goldberg, Yahav).** With finite precision and time linear in the input length, LSTMs and ReLU Elman RNNs are strictly stronger than squashing-activation RNNs and GRUs, because they can implement counting; trained LSTMs use this mechanism ([Weiss et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04908)).
- **TC⁰ bounds for restricted SSMs (Merrill, Petty, Sabharwal).** Log-precision ($c\log n$ bits) generalized linear SSMs with input-independent matrices (including S4), and SSMs with diagonal or simultaneously diagonalizable transitions (including S6/Mamba), lie in L-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$. Since the $S_5$ word problem is $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete (Barrington), if $\mathsf{TC}^0\neq\mathsf{NC}^1$ no log-precision S4 or S6 model solves it. Adding a nonlinearity to the recurrence, or making the transition matrix an affine function of the input (IDS4), lets a one-layer model recognize any regular language ([Merrill et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08819)).
- **Linear RNNs and state tracking (Grazzi et al.).** Finite-precision linear RNNs whose transition matrices have only nonnegative real eigenvalues cannot solve parity at arbitrary lengths; counting modulo 3 needs non-triangular transitions; and linear RNNs whose transitions are products of generalized Householder (identity-minus-outer-product) matrices with eigenvalues in $[-1,1]$ can recognize any regular language, possibly with width and depth exponential in the automaton's size ([Grazzi et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.12537)). These non-diagonal models fall outside the diagonal classes covered by Merrill et al.
- **Norm-preserving recurrences.** Unitary-evolution RNNs learn a unitary recurrent matrix, so its eigenvalues have modulus exactly 1, avoiding the drift that causes vanishing or exploding gradients ([Arjovsky et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06464)); initializing a ReLU RNN's recurrent matrix to the (scaled) identity performs comparably to LSTMs on four benchmarks ([Le et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.00941)).
- **Echo state property.** A reservoir must asymptotically wash out its initial conditions. For $\tanh$ reservoirs the property fails at zero input if the spectral radius of $\mathbf W$ exceeds 1, and sufficient conditions are stated in terms of singular values; equating it with spectral radius below 1 is a widespread error ([Scholarpedia](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Echo_state_network)).
- **LSTM ablations (Greff et al.).** None of the studied variants improves significantly on the standard LSTM, and the forget gate and output activation are its most critical components ([Greff et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1503.04069)).

### Examples
- **Language modelling.** Mikolov et al. (2010) showed RNN language models substantially outperforming $n$-gram models ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network)).
- **Encoder–decoder translation.** Cho et al. jointly train an encoder RNN mapping a sequence to a fixed vector and a decoder RNN to maximize the [conditional probability](node:Conditional%20Probability) of the target ([Cho et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1078)). Sutskever, Vinyals and Le's deep LSTM sequence-to-sequence model reached 34.8 BLEU on WMT'14 English–French against a 33.3 phrase-based baseline, helped by reversing the source order ([Sutskever et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215)). Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio argued the fixed-length vector is a bottleneck and let the decoder soft-search over source positions, learning alignments between source and target words; see [Attention Mechanism](node:Attention%20Mechanism) ([Bahdanau et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473)).
- **Variable timing.** [Connectionist Temporal Classification](node:Connectionist%20Temporal%20Classification) (Graves, 2006) is a loss for sequence problems with variable timing; bidirectional RNNs (Schuster and Paliwal, 1997) read in both directions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network)).
- **Reservoir computing.** Echo state networks have a sparse random fixed hidden layer and train only output weights ([Wikipedia: Echo state network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echo_state_network)); liquid state machines, developed independently by Maass, share the idea, and both are subsumed under reservoir computing ([Scholarpedia](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Echo_state_network)).

### History
McCulloch and Pitts (1943) considered networks with cycles, and Hopfield (1982) studied networks with binary activations ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network)). Bengio, Simard and Frasconi's "Learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent is difficult" appeared in *IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks* in 1994 ([Pascanu et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1211.5063)). Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's LSTM was published in *Neural Computation* 9(8), 1735–1780, in 1997 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1162/neco.1997.9.8.1735)), and the forget gate followed in Gers et al. 2000 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1162/089976600300015015)). Siegelmann and Sontag's universality paper appeared in 1995 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1006/jcss.1995.1013)). The GRU came from Cho et al. 2014 ([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/gru.html)); sequence-to-sequence LSTMs and attention followed the same year ([Sutskever et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215); [Bahdanau et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473)). Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville's *Deep Learning* devotes chapter 10 to recurrent and recursive nets ([Deep Learning book](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/)).

### Connections
- [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning): RNNs are deep networks unrolled in time.
- [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation) and [Automatic Differentiation](node:Automatic%20Differentiation): BPTT is reverse-mode differentiation through the unrolled graph.
- [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent) and [Stochastic Gradient Descent](node:Stochastic%20Gradient%20Descent): the optimizers whose instability motivates clipping.
- [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): the largest singular value controls one-step gradient growth.
- [Transformers](node:Transformers) and [Attention Mechanism](node:Attention%20Mechanism): attention began as an add-on to RNN translators.
- [State Space Models](node:State%20Space%20Models) and [Selective State-Space Models](node:Selective%20State-Space%20Models): linear recurrences revived for long sequences.
- [Linear Attention](node:Linear%20Attention): a recurrent form of attention with a matrix-valued state.
- [Quasi-Recurrent Neural Networks](node:Quasi-Recurrent%20Neural%20Networks): a convolution–recurrence hybrid.
- [Language Modeling](node:Language%20Modeling) and [Machine Translation](node:Machine%20Translation): the main applications.
- [Circuit Complexity](node:Circuit%20Complexity), [Finite Automata](node:Finite%20Automata) and [Turing Machines](node:Turing%20Machines): yardsticks for RNN expressivity.
- [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems): an RNN is a discrete-time dynamical system driven by its input.
- [Artificial Neural Networks](node:Artificial%20Neural%20Networks): the general framework.

### Common pitfalls
- Truncated BPTT gives an approximate gradient and biases the model toward short-range dependencies ([D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/bptt.html)).
- Turing completeness in theory does not settle practical power: under finite precision and linear time, architectures differ, and GRUs lack LSTM counting ([Weiss et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04908)).
- Linear recurrence is not automatically weak or strong. The $\mathsf{TC}^0$ bound covers input-independent, diagonal and simultaneously diagonalizable SSMs at log precision, and the impossibility of $S_5$ state tracking is conditional on $\mathsf{TC}^0\neq\mathsf{NC}^1$ ([Merrill et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08819)); non-diagonal input-dependent linear RNNs with eigenvalues in $[-1,1]$ recognize all regular languages ([Grazzi et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.12537)).
- Pascanu et al.'s eigenvalue condition for vanishing gradients is proved via norm bounds, so for non-normal $W_{\mathrm{rec}}$ use the largest singular value ([Pascanu et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1211.5063)).
- The "fixed weight 1" carousel describes the 1997 cell; the forget-gate cell gates its own self-connection ([Greff et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1503.04069); [D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/lstm.html)).
- Clipping treats exploding gradients only; vanishing gradients need a regularizer ([Regularization](node:Regularization)), gating or norm-preserving recurrences ([Pascanu et al.](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1211.5063); [Arjovsky et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06464)).

### Open problems
- **Expressivity of deep linear RNNs.** For DeltaNet with eigenvalues in $[-1,1]$ the theoretical expressivity with multiple layers "is still unclear" ([Grazzi et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.12537)).
- **State tracking versus associative recall.** Grazzi et al. hypothesize "a fundamental trade-off between state-tracking and associative recall" and propose to study it in future work ([Grazzi et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.12537)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Recurrent neural network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network): architectures, training, history.
- **Reference:** [Echo state network (Scholarpedia, Jaeger)](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Echo_state_network): reservoir equations and the echo state property.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning: LSTM](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/lstm.html): equations and code; see also the [BPTT chapter](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/bptt.html).
- **Primary:** [Pascanu, Mikolov, Bengio, On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1211.5063): gradient analysis and clipping.
- **Primary:** [Merrill, Petty, Sabharwal, The Illusion of State in State-Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08819): complexity bounds for linear recurrences.
- **Primary:** [Grazzi et al., Unlocking State-Tracking in Linear RNNs Through Negative Eigenvalues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12537): eigenvalue range and regular languages.
- **Primary:** [Greff et al., LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1503.04069): history and ablation of LSTM components.
- **Further reading:** [Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press)](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/): chapter 10, sequence modelling with recurrent and recursive nets.
references.Regularization:
## Reference
### Overview
Regularization is any modification of a learning or estimation problem that converts it into a simpler, better-posed one, most often to prevent overfitting or to stabilize an ill-posed inverse problem. The standard explicit form adds a complexity penalty $R(f)$ with weight $\lambda$ to an empirical loss; implicit forms such as early stopping, robust losses, and discarding outliers change the procedure rather than the objective. An explicit penalty can also make the optimal solution unique. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29))

In the language of the [Bias–Variance Tradeoff](node:Bias–Variance%20Tradeoff), a penalty deliberately introduces bias in exchange for lower variance. Ridge (Tikhonov) regularization adds $\lambda I$ to $X^\top X$ before inversion, which lowers the condition number, shrinks coefficients, and mitigates multicollinearity in [Linear Regression](node:Linear%20Regression). ([Wikipedia: Ridge regression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_regression)) The $\ell_1$ penalty (lasso) additionally performs variable selection by setting coefficients exactly to zero. ([Wikipedia: Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_%28statistics%29))

In [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning), [Dropout](node:Dropout) randomly drops units during training to prevent overfitting ([Srivastava et al. 2014](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/srivastava14a.html)), and the Goodfellow–Bengio–Courville textbook devotes Chapter 7, "Regularization for Deep Learning", to the subject. ([Deep Learning book](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/)) Zhang et al. showed that image classifiers trained with stochastic gradient methods easily fit random labels, even with explicit regularization, and argued that explanations of generalization based on the model family or on regularization do not account for this. ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530))

### Formal definition
Given data $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$, a loss $V$, a regularizer $R$ and $\lambda\ge 0$, explicit regularization solves
$$\hat f \in \arg\min_{f\in\mathcal H}\ \sum_{i=1}^n V(f(x_i),y_i) + \lambda R(f).$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29))

For linear models $f(x)=w^\top x$ the standard penalties are ridge $R(w)=\|w\|_2^2$, lasso $R(w)=\|w\|_1$, and elastic net $R(w)=\alpha\|w\|_1+(1-\alpha)\|w\|_2^2$ with $\alpha\in[0,1]$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29)) The general Tikhonov form is $\min_x \|Ax-b\|^2+\|\Gamma x\|^2$, with $\Gamma$ often a multiple of the identity. ([Wikipedia: Ridge regression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_regression))

The constrained (Ivanov-type) formulation is $\min_w \sum_i V(w^\top x_i,y_i)$ subject to $R(w)\le B$. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote10.html))

### Key results
- **Penalized–constrained equivalence.** For convex loss and regularizer, for every $\lambda\ge0$ there is a $B\ge0$ such that the penalized and constrained problems have the same solutions, and conversely; the map between $\lambda$ and $B$ is data-dependent. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote10.html); [Wikipedia: Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_%28statistics%29))
- **Ridge closed form and spectral filtering.** For the objective $\frac1n\|\hat Xw-Y\|_2^2+\lambda\|w\|_2^2$ with $\lambda>0$ (squared error averaged over the $n$ samples), the minimizer is unique and equals $w=(\hat X^\top\hat X+\lambda n I)^{-1}\hat X^\top Y$; in the SVD of the design matrix the estimator multiplies each component by a filter factor that damps directions with small singular values, and as $\lambda\to0$ it converges to the minimum-norm least-squares solution. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Ridge regression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_regression))
- **Orthonormal design: soft vs. proportional shrinkage.** With the squared error scaled by $1/N$ (objective $\frac1N\|y-X\beta\|_2^2$ plus the penalty) and orthonormal covariates, $X^\top X=I$, the lasso estimate is the soft-thresholded OLS estimate (each coefficient moves toward zero by a constant and is set to zero once it crosses zero), whereas ridge multiplies every OLS coefficient by $1/(1+N\lambda)$ and never produces exact zeros. ([Wikipedia: Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_%28statistics%29))
- **Proximal gradient.** For $\min_w F(w)+R(w)$ with $F$ convex, differentiable, with Lipschitz continuous gradient and $R$ convex, continuous and proper, the iteration $w_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma R}(w_k-\gamma\nabla F(w_k))$, $\operatorname{prox}_R(v)=\arg\min_w\{R(w)+\tfrac12\|w-v\|^2\}$, applies; for $R=\lambda\|\cdot\|_1$ the prox is soft-thresholding, and block soft-thresholding handles non-overlapping group penalties. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29))
- **Bayesian interpretation.** With a Gaussian likelihood, the ridge (Tikhonov) solution is the MAP estimate under a zero-mean Gaussian prior on the coefficients, and the lasso corresponds to a Laplace prior, whose peak at zero is consistent with exact sparsity. ([Wikipedia: Ridge regression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_regression); [Wikipedia: Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_%28statistics%29))
- **Early stopping as regularization in time.** For the least-squares empirical risk $\frac1{2n}\|\hat Xw-\hat Y\|^2$, $T$ steps of [gradient descent](node:Gradient%20Descent) with step size $\gamma$ from $w_0=0$ give $w_T=\frac{\gamma}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{T-1}(I-\frac{\gamma}{n}\hat X^\top\hat X)^i\hat X^\top\hat Y$, a truncated Neumann series for the pseudoinverse, so the iteration count acts like an inverse regularization parameter. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29))
- **Lasso model-selection consistency (Zhao–Yu).** In both fixed-$p$ and growing-$p$ regimes, an Irrepresentable Condition on the predictor covariance (predictors outside the true support are not well represented by those inside) is almost necessary and sufficient for the lasso to select the true sparse model consistently as $n\to\infty$. ([Zhao and Yu 2006](https://jmlr.org/papers/v7/zhao06a.html))
- **Dropout as adaptive $\ell_2$ regularization.** For [generalized linear models](node:Generalized%20Linear%20Models), the dropout regularizer is first-order equivalent to an $\ell_2$ penalty applied after rescaling features by an estimate of the inverse diagonal [Fisher Information](node:Fisher%20Information). ([Wager, Wang and Liang 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.1493))

### Examples
- **Ridge regression** is squared loss plus $\ell_2$; it is strictly convex and dense, and has a closed form. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote10.html))
- **Lasso** is convex but not strictly convex and not differentiable at $0$, so its solution need not be unique; the elastic net restores strict convexity while staying sparsity-inducing. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote10.html)) The elastic net also selects correlated predictors together (a "grouping effect") and helps when $p>n$. ([Wikipedia: Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_%28statistics%29))
- **Dropout** randomly removes units during training, sampling "thinned" networks, and uses the full network with scaled weights at test time as an approximate ensemble average. ([Srivastava et al. 2014](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/srivastava14a.html))
- **$\ell_0$ and $\ell_p$, $p<1$.** Minimizing the $\ell_0$ norm is NP-hard, and $\ell_1$ is its convex relaxation; $\ell_p$ penalties with $0<p<1$ are non-convex and can give sparser but initialization-dependent solutions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29); [Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote10.html))

### History
Tikhonov regularization is one of the earliest uses, named after Andrey Tikhonov, who applied it to integral equations; Tikhonov and David Phillips developed the approach for integral equations, and Hoerl and Kennard introduced ridge regression as a statistical method in 1970. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Ridge regression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_regression)) The lasso was used in geophysics in 1986 and was rediscovered, named and popularized by Robert Tibshirani in 1996, building on Breiman's nonnegative garrote; the elastic net (Zou and Hastie, 2005) and the LARS path algorithm (Efron et al., 2004) followed. ([Wikipedia: Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_%28statistics%29)) Tibshirani's paper, "Regression Shrinkage and Selection via the Lasso", appeared in JRSS Series B, vol. 58, pp. 267–288. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1996.tb02080.x)) Dropout was published in JMLR in 2014 by Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Salakhutdinov. ([JMLR](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/srivastava14a.html))

### Connections
- [Bias–Variance Tradeoff](node:Bias–Variance%20Tradeoff): penalties trade added bias for reduced variance.
- [Linear Regression](node:Linear%20Regression): ridge and lasso are penalized least squares.
- [Kernel Ridge Regression](node:Kernel%20Ridge%20Regression): ridge in a reproducing-kernel feature space.
- [Maximum A Posteriori Estimation](node:Maximum%20A%20Posteriori%20Estimation): penalized likelihood equals MAP under a matching prior.
- [Cross-Validation](node:Cross-Validation): the standard way to choose $\lambda$.
- [Dropout](node:Dropout) and [Early Stopping](node:Early%20Stopping): implicit and stochastic regularizers for networks.
- [Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent](node:Implicit%20Bias%20of%20Gradient%20Descent): regularization supplied by the optimizer instead of the objective.
- [Generalization in Deep Learning](node:Generalization%20in%20Deep%20Learning): why overparameterized networks generalize despite weak explicit regularization.
- [Convex Optimization](node:Convex%20Optimization): proximal and subgradient methods for non-smooth penalties.
- [Sparse Autoencoders](node:Sparse%20Autoencoders): an $\ell_1$ penalty on codes enforces sparse features.

### Common pitfalls
- **Treating $\lambda$ and $B$ as interchangeable numbers.** The penalized and constrained forms share solutions, but the correspondence between $\lambda$ and $B$ depends on the data. ([Wikipedia: Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_%28statistics%29))
- **Expecting a unique lasso solution.** The $\ell_1$ penalty is convex but not strictly convex, so the lasso minimizer need not be unique. ([Cornell CS4780](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote10.html))
- **Reading lasso selection as consistent by default.** Correct support recovery needs the Irrepresentable Condition, which depends on the predictor covariance. ([Zhao and Yu 2006](https://jmlr.org/papers/v7/zhao06a.html))
- **Choosing $\lambda$ on the test set.** Cross-validation, generalized cross-validation, the discrepancy principle, the L-curve and restricted maximum likelihood are the standard selectors. ([Wikipedia: Ridge regression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_regression))

### Open problems
- **Implicit regularization in deep learning.** Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin state as conjectures that overparameterization lets gradient methods find interpolating solutions, that these methods implicitly regularize, and that overparameterization enables benign overfitting; their survey analyzes these phenomena in linear regression and in the linear regime of two-layer networks and closes with the challenges of extending them to realistic deep learning. ([Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09177))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Regularization (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_%28mathematics%29): penalized objective, ridge, lasso, elastic net, early stopping, proximal methods.
- **Reference:** [Lasso (statistics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso_%28statistics%29): forms, orthonormal-design solution, Bayesian and geometric views, history.
- **Learn:** [Cornell CS4780 lecture notes on regularization](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote10.html): penalized vs. constrained forms, $\ell_1$/$\ell_2$/elastic net properties.
- **Primary:** [Zhao and Yu 2006, On Model Selection Consistency of Lasso](https://jmlr.org/papers/v7/zhao06a.html): the Irrepresentable Condition.
- **Primary:** [Srivastava et al. 2014, Dropout](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/srivastava14a.html): the dropout method and its regularization effect.
- **Primary:** [Wager, Wang and Liang 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.1493): dropout as adaptive $\ell_2$ regularization.
- **Further reading:** [Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning (Springer, 2009)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-84858-7): statistics textbook in the Springer Series in Statistics.
- **Further reading:** [Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/): Chapter 7, regularization for deep learning.

## Reference
### Overview
Reinforcement learning (RL) studies how an agent should act in a dynamic environment to maximize a cumulative reward signal. At each step the agent observes a state and reward, chooses an action, and the environment moves to a new state; the environment is usually modelled as a [Markov decision process](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes) but RL algorithms, unlike classical dynamic programming, do not assume knowledge of an exact mathematical model of that MDP ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)). RL is also known as approximate [dynamic programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)).

Unlike [supervised learning](node:Supervised%20Learning), which looks for patterns in labelled data, RL trains an agent through interaction with its environment ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)). The agent must trade off exploration of untried actions against exploitation of current knowledge, and must learn from rewards that arrive with delay. Kaelbling, Littman and Moore's survey organizes the subject around exactly these issues: exploration versus exploitation, learning from delayed reward, building empirical models to speed learning, generalization and hierarchy, and hidden state ([Kaelbling, Littman and Moore](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/9605103)). The exploration-exploitation trade-off has been most thoroughly studied through the [multi-armed bandit](node:Multi-Armed%20Bandits) problem ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)).

With neural-network function approximation ("deep RL") RL has learned Atari games, and applications include Go (AlphaGo) and robot control; and it is now a standard stage in training language models: reinforcement learning from human feedback fine-tunes a model against a reward model learned from human preference rankings ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning); [Ouyang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)). Modern course syllabi cover behavioral cloning ([imitation learning](node:Imitation%20Learning)), policy gradients, actor-critic and value-based methods, model-based and offline RL, exploration, theory and RL for LLMs ([Berkeley CS285](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/)).

### Formal definition
The environment is an MDP $(S,A,P,R)$; a policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ gives action probabilities, and the agent seeks to maximize the expected discounted return $\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t R_{t+1}\big]$ with discount $0\le\gamma<1$. If the state is not fully observed, the problem is a partially observable MDP. The regret of a learning algorithm is the gap between the reward it collects and that of an optimal policy ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)).

**Q-learning** maintains action-value estimates and, after observing $(s_t,a_t,r_{t+1},s_{t+1})$, updates
$$Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha_t\big[r_{t+1}+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')-Q(s_t,a_t)\big];$$
with learning rate $0<\alpha_t\le1$ ([Wikipedia: Q-learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning)). Q-learning is off-policy and SARSA is on-policy ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)).

**Policy-gradient methods** parametrize a differentiable policy $\pi_\theta$ and ascend $J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\big[\sum_{t=0}^T\gamma^tR_t\mid S_0=s_0\big]$ ([Wikipedia: Policy gradient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method)).

### Key results
- **Convergence of tabular Q-learning (Watkins and Dayan 1992).** In a finite controlled Markov domain with discrete (tabular) action-values, Q-learning converges to the optimal action-values with probability 1, provided all actions are repeatedly sampled in all states. ([Watkins and Dayan](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00992698)) The learning rate must decrease to zero under technical conditions. ([Wikipedia: Q-learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning))
- **Policy gradient theorem.** For a differentiable policy $\pi_\theta$,
$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\nabla_\theta\ln\pi_\theta(A_t\mid S_t)\Big(\sum_{\tau=t}^{T}\gamma^\tau R_\tau-b(S_t)\Big)\,\Big|\,S_0=s_0\Big]$$
for any baseline $b:S\to\mathbb{R}$; $b\equiv0$ gives Williams's REINFORCE estimator, and a baseline close to $V^{\pi_\theta}$ can significantly reduce the variance of the gradient estimate. ([Wikipedia: Policy gradient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method)) Sutton, McAllester, Singh and Mansour showed the gradient can be estimated with an approximate action-value or advantage function, and that a version of policy iteration with arbitrary differentiable function approximation converges to a locally optimal policy. ([Sutton et al.](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1999/hash/464d828b85b0bed98e80ade0a5c43b0f-Abstract.html))
- **Minimax regret in communicating MDPs (Jaksch, Ortner and Auer 2010).** For undiscounted RL in an MDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions and diameter $D$ (the largest expected number of steps needed to move between any two states under some policy), their algorithm has total regret $\tilde O(DS\sqrt{AT})$ after $T$ steps, and every algorithm suffers regret $\Omega(\sqrt{DSAT})$ on some MDP; a gap-dependent bound logarithmic in $T$ also holds. ([Jaksch, Ortner and Auer](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/jaksch10a.html))
- **Divergence under the deadly triad.** Combining function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning can make TD value estimates grow without bound; yet several practical algorithms combine all three without diverging. ([van Hasselt et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02648))

### Examples
- **Algorithm families.** [Monte Carlo methods](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Methods) average complete-episode returns; [temporal-difference](node:Temporal-Difference%20Learning) methods bootstrap from the Bellman equation, with a parameter $0\le\lambda\le1$ interpolating between the two in most TD methods; [Q-Learning](node:Q-Learning) and SARSA learn action-values; [policy-gradient](node:Policy%20Gradient%20Methods) and [actor-critic](node:Actor-Critic%20Methods) methods optimize the policy directly; [model-based](node:Model-Based%20Reinforcement%20Learning) methods such as Dyna learn a transition model. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning))
- **Linear and deep function approximation.** Linear methods represent $Q(s,a)=\sum_i\theta_i\phi_i(s,a)$; [deep Q-learning](node:Deep%20Q-Networks) replaces this with a neural network. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning))
- **RLHF.** InstructGPT fine-tunes GPT-3 on human demonstrations, trains a reward model on human rankings of outputs, then optimizes against it with RL; outputs of the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT were preferred to those of 175B GPT-3. ([Ouyang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)) See [Fine-Tuning and RLHF](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF).
- **$\epsilon$-greedy exploration.** Exploit with probability $1-\epsilon$, otherwise act uniformly at random; $\epsilon$ may be fixed, scheduled or adaptive. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning))

### History
Chris Watkins introduced Q-learning in his 1989 Cambridge PhD thesis, *Learning from Delayed Rewards* ([Wikipedia: Q-learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning)), and Williams's REINFORCE (1992) is credited as the first policy-gradient method ([Wikipedia: Policy gradient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method)). Watkins and Dayan published the Q-learning convergence proof in 1992 ([Watkins and Dayan](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00992698)), and Kaelbling, Littman and Moore surveyed the field from a computer-science perspective in 1996 ([Kaelbling, Littman and Moore](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/9605103)). Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis's 1996 *Neuro-Dynamic Programming* is described by its author as historically the first book to fully explain the neuro-dynamic programming/reinforcement learning methodology ([Bertsekas](https://web.mit.edu/dimitrib/www/RLbook.html)). DeepMind's work on learning Atari games increased attention to deep RL, and RLHF (InstructGPT, January 2022; ChatGPT, November 2022) and RL with automatically computed rewards for reasoning (OpenAI o1, 2024; DeepSeek-R1, 2025) brought RL into language-model training ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)).

### Connections
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the formal model; RL solves MDPs from samples.
- [Dynamic Programming](node:Dynamic%20Programming): RL algorithms are sampled, approximate versions of value and policy iteration.
- [Multi-Armed Bandits](node:Multi-Armed%20Bandits): the single-state case isolating exploration versus exploitation.
- [Exploration in Reinforcement Learning](node:Exploration%20in%20Reinforcement%20Learning): optimism, posterior sampling and intrinsic rewards for exploration.
- [Temporal Credit Assignment](node:Temporal%20Credit%20Assignment): the problem of attributing delayed reward to earlier actions.
- [Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes](node:Partially%20Observable%20Markov%20Decision%20Processes): RL under hidden state.
- [Offline Reinforcement Learning](node:Offline%20Reinforcement%20Learning): learning from a fixed dataset without further interaction.
- [Inverse Reinforcement Learning](node:Inverse%20Reinforcement%20Learning): inferring the reward from observed behaviour.
- [Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](node:Multi-Agent%20Reinforcement%20Learning): several learners in a shared environment.
- [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search): sample-based planning used with learned values (AlphaGo).
- [Proximal Policy Optimization](node:Proximal%20Policy%20Optimization): the policy-gradient algorithm used in RLHF.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): RLHF and RL for reasoning are post-training stages of LLMs.

### Common pitfalls
- The Q-learning convergence theorem needs every state-action pair to be visited infinitely often and a tabular representation; it does not cover neural function approximation. ([Watkins and Dayan](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00992698))
- Off-policy TD with function approximation can diverge (the deadly triad), so stability of deep value-based methods is an empirical rather than a guaranteed property. ([van Hasselt et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02648))
- Purely random action selection performs poorly as an exploration strategy. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning))
- Deep RL is sample-inefficient: OpenAI's Dota-playing system used thousands of years of simulated play. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning))
- Policy-gradient convergence results are to local, not global, optima. ([Sutton et al.](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1999/hash/464d828b85b0bed98e80ade0a5c43b0f-Abstract.html))

### Open problems
- **Understanding the deadly triad.** van Hasselt et al. describe the coexistence of the theoretical divergence risk with stable practical algorithms as "at least a partial gap in our understanding." ([van Hasselt et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02648))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Reinforcement learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning): definitions, algorithm families, theory, research directions.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley CS 185/285 Deep Reinforcement Learning (Levine)](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/): lectures from policy gradients to offline RL, LLM RL and RL theory.
- **Primary:** [Kaelbling, Littman and Moore, Reinforcement Learning: A Survey (JAIR 1996)](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/9605103): classical survey.
- **Primary:** [Watkins and Dayan, Q-learning (Machine Learning 1992)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00992698): convergence theorem.
- **Primary:** [Jaksch, Ortner and Auer, Near-optimal Regret Bounds for Reinforcement Learning (JMLR 2010)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/jaksch10a.html): regret upper and lower bounds in terms of the diameter.
- **Primary:** [Sutton, McAllester, Singh and Mansour, Policy Gradient Methods for RL with Function Approximation (NeurIPS 1999)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1999/hash/464d828b85b0bed98e80ade0a5c43b0f-Abstract.html).
- **Further reading:** [Bertsekas, A Course in Reinforcement Learning, and Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, Neuro-Dynamic Programming](https://web.mit.edu/dimitrib/www/RLbook.html): graduate texts connecting RL to approximate dynamic programming.
references.Renormalization:
## Reference
### Overview
Renormalization is the set of techniques in quantum field theory and statistical field theory for dealing with infinities and scale dependence: a regulator (a momentum cutoff, a lattice, or dimensional continuation) makes divergent loop integrals finite, and the regulator-dependent pieces are absorbed into counterterms so that the bare parameters are traded for renormalized parameters fixed by measurements. The two steps are distinct: the regulator alone is not renormalization. ([Wikipedia: Renormalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization))

The modern view, due to Kadanoff's block spins and Wilson's computational renormalization group, treats renormalization as the systematic change of description with scale. Couplings run with the scale, fixed points of the flow are scale-invariant theories, and perturbations of a fixed point are classified as relevant, irrelevant, or marginal; irrelevant ones do not affect long-distance physics, which explains universality of critical exponents. ([Wikipedia: Renormalization group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group))

In this picture a nonrenormalizable theory is not inconsistent: it is an effective theory whose higher-dimension operators are suppressed by inverse powers of a cutoff and can be handled order by order, as in Fermi's theory of the weak interaction. The Standard Model contains only renormalizable operators. ([Wikipedia: Renormalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization))

### Formal definition
**Counterterms and the $\beta$-function.** Write the bare Lagrangian as renormalized Lagrangian plus counterterms, $\mathcal L(\phi_0,g_0,m_0)=\mathcal L(\phi,g,m)+\mathcal L_{ct}$. For a renormalized coupling $g$ defined at scale $\mu$, the $\beta$-function is
$$\beta(g)=\mu\frac{\partial g}{\partial\mu},$$
and a fixed point is a value $g_*$ with $\beta(g_*)=0$. ([Wikipedia: Beta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function_%28physics%29); [Wikipedia: Callan–Symanzik equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callan%E2%80%93Symanzik_equation))

**Anomalous dimension.** With $\gamma_\phi=-\tfrac{\mu}{2}\,d\log Z(\mu)/d\mu$, a field at a fixed point has scaling dimension $\Delta_\phi=d_\phi+\gamma_\phi$, and the two-point function behaves as $\langle\phi(x)\phi(0)\rangle\propto|x|^{-2\Delta_\phi^*}$. ([Hollowood, 6 Lectures on QFT, RG and SUSY](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0859))

**Wilsonian effective action.** Splitting the field into low modes $\varphi$ and modes $\hat\phi$ between cutoffs $\mu$ and $\mu'=\mu+\delta\mu$, the effective action is defined by
$$e^{-S_{\rm eff}[\varphi]}=\int[d\hat\phi]\,e^{-S[\varphi+\hat\phi;\,\mu',g(\mu')]},$$
and requiring $S_{\rm eff}[\varphi]=S[Z^{1/2}\varphi;\mu,g(\mu)]$ defines the flow $g(\mu)$. At one loop $S_{\rm eff}=S+\tfrac12\log\det(-\square+V''(\varphi))$. ([Hollowood](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0859)) A smooth-cutoff version of this flow is Polchinski's exact functional equation. ([Wikipedia: Renormalization group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group); [nLab: renormalization](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/renormalization))

### Key results
- **Callan–Symanzik equation.** Renormalized $n$-point Green functions of a single-coupling theory satisfy
$$\Big[M\frac{\partial}{\partial M}+\beta(g)\frac{\partial}{\partial g}+n\gamma\Big]G^{(n)}(x_1,\dots,x_n;M,g)=0,$$
with $\beta=M\,\delta g/\delta M$ and $\gamma=-M\,\delta\eta/\delta M$ for the field rescaling. In QED the electron and photon fields carry separate functions $\gamma_2,\gamma_3$. Found independently by Callan and Symanzik in 1970. ([Wikipedia: Callan–Symanzik equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callan%E2%80%93Symanzik_equation))
- **Power counting.** In $\phi^4$ theory in $d$ dimensions a graph with $L$ loops and $E$ external legs has superficial degree of divergence $\mathcal D=(d-4)L+4-E$. At $d=4$ this is independent of $L$, so only finitely many Green functions ($E=2,4$) are superficially divergent: the coupling is dimensionless and the theory is renormalizable. ([Hollowood](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0859)) If the Lagrangian contains operators of high enough mass dimension, infinitely many counterterms are required. ([Wikipedia: Renormalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization))
- **BPHZ theorem.** The Bogoliubov–Parasiuk–Hepp–Zimmermann procedure provides a consistent way to renormalise the probability amplitudes associated to Feynman diagrams in perturbative quantum field theory, and the renormalised integrals inherit many natural properties from their unrenormalised counterparts. Hairer gives a self-contained Euclidean formulation for generalised convolutions of functions with a singularity of prescribed order at the origin. ([Hairer, An analyst's take on the BPHZ theorem](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1704.08634)) Zimmermann's forest formula solves Bogoliubov's recursive $R$-operation for subtracting ultraviolet divergences; it sums over restricted forests, sets of UV-divergent subgraphs any two of which are disjoint or nested. ([Herzog, Zimmermann's forest formula](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1711.06121)) In causal perturbation theory, different renormalization schemes are related exactly by vertex redefinitions (the main theorem of perturbative renormalization), which underlies the Stückelberg–Petermann renormalization group. ([nLab: renormalization](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/renormalization))
- **One-loop QED and QCD $\beta$-functions.** $\beta(e)=e^3/(12\pi^2)$, i.e. $\beta(\alpha)=2\alpha^2/(3\pi)$, so the QED coupling grows with energy. For $SU(3)$ with $n_f$ quark flavours, $\beta(g)=-(11-\tfrac{2}{3}n_f)\,g^3/(16\pi^2)$, negative for $n_f\le16$: asymptotic freedom. ([Wikipedia: Beta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function_%28physics%29)) Gross and Wilczek, and independently Politzer, found asymptotic freedom of non-abelian gauge theories in 1973 (Nobel Prize 2004). ([Wikipedia: Asymptotic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_freedom); [Gross and Wilczek 1973](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.30.1343))
- **Landau poles.** For $\lambda\phi^4$ in $d=4$ the one-loop $\beta$-function is $\mu\,d\lambda/d\mu=3\lambda^2/(16\pi^2)$, whose solution $\lambda(\mu')=\lambda(\mu)/\big(1-\tfrac{3}{16\pi^2}\lambda(\mu)\log(\mu'/\mu)\big)$ blows up at the finite ultraviolet scale $\mu_{\rm pole}=\mu\,e^{16\pi^2/(3\lambda(\mu))}$. ([Hollowood](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0859)) For QED the estimated scale is about $10^{286}$ eV; because the pole is found perturbatively, it may only signal that the approximation fails at strong coupling. Asymptotically free theories have no Landau pole. ([Wikipedia: Landau pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_pole); [Wikipedia: Asymptotic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_freedom))
- **Triviality of $\phi^4_4$.** Aizenman and Duminil-Copin proved that scaling limits of critical four-dimensional Ising-type models, and of $\lambda\phi^4$ fields on $\mathbb R^4$ with a lattice ultraviolet cutoff (infinite volume, lattice spacing $\to0$), are Gaussian. ([Aizenman and Duminil-Copin](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.07973))

### Examples
**Wilson–Fisher fixed point.** For $\phi^4$ in $d=4-\epsilon$, with dimensionless $g_4$ and $a=1/(16\pi^2)$, the one-loop flow is $\mu\,dg_4/d\mu=-\epsilon g_4+3a g_4^2+\cdots$, with a nontrivial fixed point $g_4^*=16\pi^2\epsilon/3$, $g_2^*=-\epsilon/6$. There $\phi^2$ has dimension $\Delta_2=2-2\epsilon/3$ (relevant) and $\phi^4$ has $\Delta_4=4$ (irrelevant). ([Hollowood](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0859)) Since $\nu=1/(d-\Delta_\epsilon)$ with $\Delta_\epsilon$ the dimension of the energy operator $\phi^2$ ([Wikipedia: Ising critical exponents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_critical_exponents)), this gives $\nu=1/(2-\epsilon/3)=\tfrac12+\tfrac{\epsilon}{12}+O(\epsilon^2)$. Wilson and Fisher computed exponents to first order in $\epsilon$, including $\gamma=1+\epsilon/6$ for the Ising-like case and $1+\epsilon/5$ for the XY case. ([Wilson and Fisher 1972, INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=t%20%22Critical%20exponents%20in%203.99%20dimensions%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts&size=2)) The same leading anomalous dimensions can be recovered from conformal symmetry alone, using multiplet recombination of $\phi$ and $\phi^3$. ([Rychkov and Tan](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00963)) In $d=3$ the conformal bootstrap gives $\nu\approx0.62997$ and $\eta\approx0.036298$. ([Wikipedia: Ising critical exponents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_critical_exponents))

**Dimensional transmutation.** In an asymptotically free [gauge theory](node:Gauge%20Theory) with $\mu\,dg/d\mu=-bg^3$, $b>0$, the coupling decreases logarithmically, $g(\mu)^2\propto1/\log(\mu/\Lambda)$: a dimensionless coupling is traded for a scale $\Lambda$. ([Hollowood](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0859))

### History
Divergent integrals in QED were met in the 1930s by Born, Heisenberg, Jordan and Dirac; Kramers, Bethe (1947), Tomonaga, Schwinger and Feynman developed methods to handle them, and Dyson systematized these in 1949. Stueckelberg and Petermann (1953) and Gell-Mann and Low (1954) introduced the renormalization group equation; Kadanoff proposed block spins in 1966, and Wilson applied the RG to critical phenomena (1971) and the Kondo problem, receiving the 1982 Nobel Prize. ([Wikipedia: Renormalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization); [Wikipedia: Renormalization group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)) Wilson and Kogut's 1974 Physics Reports review set out the modern RG for critical phenomena and field theory around the expansion in $\epsilon=4-d$. ([INSPIRE: Wilson and Kogut](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=t%20%22The%20renormalization%20group%20and%20the%20epsilon%20expansion%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts&size=3))

### Connections
- [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group): the flow of couplings, fixed points, and universality in their own right.
- [Feynman Diagrams](node:Feynman%20Diagrams): the graphs whose divergences power counting and BPHZ control.
- [Quantum Electrodynamics](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics): the first renormalized theory; positive $\beta$-function and Landau pole.
- [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics): asymptotic freedom and dimensional transmutation.
- [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): nonrenormalizable operators suppressed by a cutoff.
- [Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena](node:Phase%20Transitions%20and%20Critical%20Phenomena) and [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model): the Wilson–Fisher fixed point and critical exponents.
- [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory): fixed points of the flow.
- [Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap](node:Yang–Mills%20Existence%20and%20Mass%20Gap): the nonperturbative construction problem for asymptotically free gauge theory.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): the general setting.

### Common pitfalls
- Renormalization is distinct from introducing a regulator: a regulator makes integrals finite but cutoff-dependent, and counterterms then absorb that dependence. The bare quantities do not correspond to the constants measured in the laboratory, and the renormalization point is not itself a physical quantity. ([Wikipedia: Renormalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization))
- A one-loop Landau pole is a perturbative statement; the $\beta$-function is computed in a truncated expansion and the pole may be an artifact at strong coupling. ([Wikipedia: Beta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function_%28physics%29))

### Open problems
- **Yang–Mills existence and mass gap.** Prove that for every compact simple gauge group a nontrivial quantum Yang–Mills theory exists on $\mathbb R^4$, satisfying axioms at least as strong as Wightman/Osterwalder–Schrader, with mass gap $\Delta>0$. The Clay Institute states no proof is known. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/)) On 26 October 2026 OpenAI announced an AI-generated proof of the existence part only (not the mass gap); the mass gap remains unproven. ([Wikipedia: Yang–Mills existence and mass gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang%E2%80%93Mills_existence_and_mass_gap)) A shepherding committee (Douglas, Gross (chair), Jaffe, Klebanov, Nekrasov) stated on 9 November 2026 that its checks of the submitted Lean code indicate that it proves the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory according to standard problem statements, and announced public repositories for community scrutiny. ([Shepherding Committee, 3rd statement, KITP](https://www.kitp.ucsb.edu/sites/default/files/3rd-Statement-About-Quantum-YangMills-Theory_Nov-9.pdf)) This is a recent claim under community checking; as of this note the Clay Institute still lists the problem as unsolved, and the mass gap is open in any case. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/))
- **Triviality of QED and $\phi^4$.** That both QED and $\phi^4$ are trivial in the continuum limit is described as a widespread belief; lattice results seem to support Landau's conclusion for QED, but another interpretation is possible, and it is unknown whether lattice Higgs fixed points correspond to free theories. ([Wikipedia: Landau pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_pole)) For lattice-regularized $\phi^4_4$ the Gaussian scaling limit is now proved. ([Aizenman and Duminil-Copin](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.07973))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Renormalization (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization): history, counterterms, effective-theory view; [nLab: renormalization](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/renormalization) for the causal (Epstein–Glaser) formulation.
- **Learn:** [Hollowood, 6 Lectures on QFT, RG and SUSY](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0909.0859): Wilsonian effective action, power counting, Wilson–Fisher fixed point, asymptotic freedom.
- **Primary:** [Wilson and Kogut, The renormalization group and the ε expansion (Phys. Rept. 12, 1974)](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=t%20%22The%20renormalization%20group%20and%20the%20epsilon%20expansion%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,abstracts&size=3); [Gross and Wilczek 1973](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.30.1343); [Hairer on BPHZ](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1704.08634).
- **Further reading:** [Collins, Renormalization (Cambridge Monographs on Mathematical Physics, 1984; now open access)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/renormalization/6EA5EEEBB9A02190F7C805856244181B): dimensional continuation of loop integrals, the RG, and the operator-product expansion.

## Reference
### Overview
The renormalization group (RG) is a tool for systematically investigating how a physical system changes when it is viewed at different scales. Couplings become "running" functions of the scale, and at a fixed point, where the beta function vanishes, the couplings stop running and the theory is scale invariant ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)). In statistical physics the RG is a coarse-graining map on the space of Hamiltonians: average over cells of size $b$, rescale lengths, and renormalise the field; critical points are fixed points of this map with infinite correlation length ([Kardar, MIT 8.334 Lec. 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf)).

The RG explains universality. Perturbations of a fixed point split into relevant, irrelevant and marginal directions; the many microscopic details of a system make up the huge space of irrelevant operators, which forms the basin of attraction of the fixed point, so many systems share the same critical exponents. A critical point reached by tuning one parameter must have exactly one relevant operator (two with a magnetic field) ([Kardar, Lec. 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)).

In [quantum field theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory) the same structure appears as the dependence of renormalised couplings on the renormalisation scale $\mu$, encoded in the beta function; a negative beta function makes a coupling weak at high energies, which is asymptotic freedom, as in QCD ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group); [PDG QCD review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)). Monotonicity theorems for RG flows (the $c$- and $a$-theorems) count degrees of freedom that decrease from the UV to the IR ([Wikipedia: c-theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-theorem); [Nakayama](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.0884)).

### Formal definition
**Wilsonian RG.** Start from the most general Hamiltonian allowed by the symmetries, e.g. for an $n$-component field
$$\beta\mathcal H=\int d^dx\Big[\tfrac t2m^2+um^4+vm^6+\cdots+\tfrac K2(\nabla m)^2+\tfrac L2(\nabla^2m)^2+\cdots\Big],$$
a point $S=(t,u,v,\dots,K,L,\dots)$ in parameter space. Coarse-grain by $b$, rescale $x'=x/b$, and renormalise $m'=m/\zeta$; the new Hamiltonian has the same form with parameters $S'=\mathfrak R_bS$. Since rescalings by $b_1$ and $b_2$ compose to $b_1b_2$, the procedure is called a semigroup; the term refers to its action on configurations, where short-scale information is lost ([Kardar, Lec. 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf), eqs. III.41–III.43).

**Fixed points and scaling operators.** A fixed point satisfies $\mathfrak R_bS^*=S^*$. Linearising, the eigenvectors $\mathcal O_i$ of the linearised map have eigenvalues $b^{y_i}$; writing $S=S^*+\sum_ig_i\mathcal O_i$, one has $g_i\mapsto b^{y_i}g_i$, and $\mathcal O_i$ is **relevant** if $y_i>0$, **irrelevant** if $y_i<0$, **marginal** if $y_i=0$, in which case higher-order terms decide its behaviour ([Kardar, Lec. 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf), eqs. III.44–III.46).

**Field-theoretic RG.** Renormalised $n$-point functions obey the Callan–Symanzik equation
$$\Big[M\frac{\partial}{\partial M}+\beta(g)\frac{\partial}{\partial g}+n\gamma\Big]G^{(n)}(x_1,\dots,x_n;M,g)=0,$$
with $\beta=M\,\partial g/\partial M$ the beta function and $\gamma=-M\,\partial\eta/\partial M$ the anomalous dimension from the field rescaling $\phi\to(1+\delta\eta)\phi$ ([Wikipedia: Callan–Symanzik equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callan%E2%80%93Symanzik_equation)).

**Exact (functional) RG.** Polchinski (1984) used a smooth UV cutoff to obtain a functional differential equation in the cutoff scale $\Lambda$ for the interaction part $S_{\mathrm{int},\Lambda}$ of the action, fixed by requiring the partition function to be independent of the cutoff ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group); [Wikipedia: Functional RG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_renormalization_group)). Wetterich (1993) added an infrared regulator $R_k$ to the inverse propagator of a scale-dependent effective action $\Gamma_k$, which obeys
$$k\partial_k\Gamma_k=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{STr}\Big[k\partial_kR_k\,\big(\Gamma_k^{(2)}+R_k\big)^{-1}\Big],\qquad \Gamma_{k\to\Lambda}=S,\quad \Gamma_{k\to0}=\Gamma,$$
the supertrace summing over momenta, internal indices and fields; it follows from the Polchinski equation by a Legendre transformation ([Wikipedia: Functional RG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_renormalization_group)).

### Key results
- **Fixed points and correlation length.** Since $\xi$ decreases under the RG ($\xi'=\xi/b$), a fixed point has $\xi=0$ or $\xi=\infty$; $\xi$ is infinite on the whole basin of attraction of a critical fixed point. Near it, $\xi(g_1,g_2,\dots)=b\,\xi(b^{y_1}g_1,b^{y_2}g_2,\dots)$, so the relevant operators fix the leading singularities and $\nu=1/y_t$ ([Kardar, Lec. 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf), eqs. III.38, III.47).
- **Scaling laws.** With $t'=b^{y_t}t$ and $h'=b^{y_h}h$, the singular free energy obeys $f(t,h)=b^{-d}f(b^{y_t}t,b^{y_h}h)$, giving $\nu=1/y_t$, the gap exponent $\Delta=y_h/y_t$, $\beta=(d-y_h)/y_t$, and the hyperscaling relation $2-\alpha=d\nu$ ([Kardar, Lec. 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf); [Kardar, Lec. 11](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/744468fdc69470176d2835d268bd7837_MIT8_334S14_Lec11.pdf), eq. IV.63).
- **Wilson–Fisher fixed point ($\epsilon$-expansion).** For the $n$-component Landau–Ginzburg model in $d=4-\epsilon$, the Gaussian fixed point is unstable to $u$ and a fixed point with $u^*=O(\epsilon)$ appears, with $y_t=2-\frac{n+2}{n+8}\epsilon+O(\epsilon^2)$ and $y_h=3-\epsilon/2+O(\epsilon^2)$. Hence
$$\nu=\frac12+\frac{n+2}{4(n+8)}\epsilon,\quad \alpha=\frac{4-n}{2(n+8)}\epsilon,\quad \beta=\frac12-\frac{3}{2(n+8)}\epsilon,$$
up to $O(\epsilon^2)$ ([Kardar, Lec. 11](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/744468fdc69470176d2835d268bd7837_MIT8_334S14_Lec11.pdf), eqs. IV.60–IV.63). Wilson and Fisher's abstract gives $\gamma=1+\epsilon/6$ for Ising-like and $1+\epsilon/5$ for XY-like systems ([Wilson and Fisher, PRL 28, 240 (INSPIRE)](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=doi%3A10.1103%2FPhysRevLett.28.240&fields=titles,abstracts,authors.full_name,publication_info)).
- **Running of $\alpha_s$ and asymptotic freedom.** In QCD, $\mu_R^2\,d\alpha_s/d\mu_R^2=\beta(\alpha_s)=-(b_0\alpha_s^2+b_1\alpha_s^3+b_2\alpha_s^4+\cdots)$ with $b_0=(11C_A-4n_fT_R)/(12\pi)=(33-2n_f)/(12\pi)$ and $b_1=(153-19n_f)/(24\pi^2)$; the minus sign is the origin of asymptotic freedom. Keeping only $b_0$ at fixed $n_f$, the equation has the exact solution
$$\alpha_s(\mu_R^2)=\frac{1}{b_0\ln(\mu_R^2/\Lambda^2)},$$
where the integration constant $\Lambda$ is the scale at which the perturbatively defined coupling would diverge; higher-loop solutions are iterative approximations, and a value of $\Lambda$ defines $\alpha_s$ only together with the approximation used ([PDG QCD review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf), eqs. 9.3–9.5).
