- **Zamolodchikov's $c$-theorem (1986).** In a two-dimensional relativistic QFT obeying reflection positivity (unitarity), there is a function $C$ of the couplings that decreases monotonically along the RG flow, $dC/d\log|z|^2=-\tfrac34H\le0$, and agrees with the central charge at fixed points; the sign comes from positivity of the two-point function of the trace $\Theta$ ([Nakayama](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.0884), §5; [Wikipedia: c-theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-theorem)). Reflection positivity is essential to this circle of results: non-conformal scale-invariant theories are known once it is abandoned ([Nakayama](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.0884)).
- **The $a$-theorem in four dimensions.** Komargodski and Schwimmer recast an RG flow as spontaneously broken conformal symmetry and show, from unitarity of dilaton $2\to2$ scattering, that a monotonically decreasing function interpolates between the UV and IR Euler ($a$-)anomalies, so $a_{\rm UV}>a_{\rm IR}$ ([Komargodski and Schwimmer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1107.3987)). Cardy conjectured this in 1988 and Osborn proved it in perturbation theory using the local RG equation ([Wikipedia: c-theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-theorem)).
- **Scale implies conformal in $d=2$ (Zamolodchikov–Polchinski).** Polchinski (1988) completed an argument of Zamolodchikov showing that in two dimensions rigid scale invariance implies local (conformal) invariance under broad conditions, while in three or more dimensions he found neither a proof nor a counterexample ([Polchinski 1988, INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=doi%3A10.1016%2F0550-3213%2888%2990179-4&fields=titles,abstracts,authors.full_name,publication_info)). The assumptions are unitarity, Poincaré invariance, a discrete spectrum of scaling dimensions, existence of a scale current, and unbroken scale invariance ([Nakayama](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.0884), §5).

### Examples
- **Ising model.** Kadanoff's block-spin RG has three fixed points: ordered, disordered, and the critical point between them ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)).
- **Accuracy of the first-order $\epsilon$-expansion.** For $n=1$, $\epsilon=1$ gives $\nu\approx0.58$, $\beta\approx0.33$ against best $d=3$ estimates $\nu\approx0.63$, $\beta\approx0.32$; $\epsilon=2$ gives $\nu\approx0.67$, $\beta\approx0.17$ against the exact two-dimensional values $\nu=1$, $\beta=0.125$. At this order $\alpha$ also has the wrong sign for $n=2,3$ in $d=3$: the first-order formula above gives $0.10$ and $\approx0.05$ at $\epsilon=1$ (Kardar's table lists $0.11$, $0.06$), against experimental $-0.01$, $-0.12$ ([Kardar, Lec. 11](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/744468fdc69470176d2835d268bd7837_MIT8_334S14_Lec11.pdf)).
- **QCD running.** The PDG world average (August 2023) is $\alpha_s(m_Z^2)=0.1180\pm0.0009$; for momentum transfers of 0.1–1 TeV, $\alpha_s\sim0.1$, while the theory is strongly interacting around and below 1 GeV ([PDG QCD review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)).

### History
Stueckelberg and Petermann (1953) anticipated the idea; Gell-Mann and Low (1954) introduced the beta function for scale transformations in QED; Callan and Symanzik (1970) reformulated it in more practical terms ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)). Kadanoff's block-spin paper "Scaling laws for Ising models near $T_c$" appeared in *Physics Physique Fizika* 2, 263 (1966) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysicsPhysiqueFizika.2.263)). Wilson's two papers "Renormalization group and critical phenomena" (I: the Kadanoff scaling picture; II: phase space cell analysis) appeared in *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174 and 3184 (1971) ([INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20K.G.Wilson.1%20and%20date%201971%20and%20j%20Phys.Rev.B&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,dois&size=5)); Wilson and Fisher's "Critical Exponents in 3.99 Dimensions" appeared in *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 28, 240 (1972) ([INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=doi%3A10.1103%2FPhysRevLett.28.240&fields=titles,abstracts,authors.full_name,publication_info)); and K. G. Wilson and J. Kogut's review "The renormalization group and the ε expansion" in *Physics Reports* 12, 75–199 (1974) ([INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=t%20%22renormalization%20group%20and%20the%20epsilon%20expansion%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,dois&size=3)). Wilson received the 1982 Nobel Prize, and asymptotic freedom was found in 1973 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)). Polchinski's "Renormalization and Effective Lagrangians" appeared in *Nucl. Phys. B* 231, 269 (1984) and "Scale and Conformal Invariance in Quantum Field Theory" in *Nucl. Phys. B* 303, 226 (1988) ([INSPIRE](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20Polchinski%2C%20Joseph%20and%20t%20%22Renormalization%20and%20Effective%20Lagrangians%22%20or%20t%20%22Scale%20and%20Conformal%20Invariance%20in%20Quantum%20Field%20Theory%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,dois&size=5)).

### Connections
- [Renormalization](node:Renormalization): the RG organises the scale dependence that renormalisation introduces.
- [Statistical Mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics): coarse-graining partition functions is the Wilsonian RG.
- [Critical Exponents and Universality](node:Critical%20Exponents%20and%20Universality): exponents are functions of fixed-point scaling dimensions.
- [Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena](node:Phase%20Transitions%20and%20Critical%20Phenomena): critical points are RG fixed points with $\xi=\infty$.
- [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model): the standard test case, with ordered, disordered and critical fixed points.
- [Landau Theory of Phase Transitions](node:Landau%20Theory%20of%20Phase%20Transitions): mean-field exponents are those of the Gaussian fixed point.
- [Beta Function](node:Beta%20Function): the generator of the flow in coupling space.
- [Asymptotic Freedom](node:Asymptotic%20Freedom) and [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics): a UV fixed point at zero coupling.
- [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory) and [Wilsonian Effective Actions](node:Wilsonian%20Effective%20Actions): irrelevant operators are suppressed at low energies.
- [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory): fixed points of the flow; the $c$-theorem uses the central charge.
- [Finite-Size Scaling](node:Finite-Size%20Scaling): RG scaling for systems of finite size.
- [Quantum Criticality](node:Quantum%20Criticality): zero-temperature fixed points.
- [Kondo Effect](node:Kondo%20Effect): one of Wilson's applications of the RG.

### Common pitfalls
- **Not a group.** Coarse-graining loses short-distance information, so on configurations the RG has no inverse; "semigroup" is the accurate term ([Kardar, Lec. 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf)).
- **Marginal operators need higher orders.** At $y_i=0$ the linear analysis decides nothing ([Kardar, Lec. 7](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf)).
- **Scheme dependence.** The QCD coefficients $b_2,b_3,\dots$ are renormalisation-scheme dependent; the PDG quotes them in $\overline{\rm MS}$, and $\Lambda$ depends on the approximation used ([PDG QCD review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf)).
- **Low-order $\epsilon$-expansion is rough.** At $\epsilon=1$ the first-order $\beta$ is close to the $d=3$ value while $\nu$ is less reliable; at $\epsilon=2$ both are poor ($\beta$ about 35% high, $\nu$ 0.67 against 1) ([Kardar, Lec. 11](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/744468fdc69470176d2835d268bd7837_MIT8_334S14_Lec11.pdf)).
- **Monotonicity needs its hypotheses.** The $c$-theorem uses unitarity and Poincaré invariance; flow functions also need not force flows to end at fixed points, since cyclic or even chaotic flows are compatible with monotone flow functions when those functions are multivalued in the couplings ([Wikipedia: c-theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-theorem); [Nakayama](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.0884)).

### Open problems
- **Scale versus conformal invariance in $d>2$.** Nakayama calls whether scale invariance implies conformal invariance beyond two dimensions "the outstanding question". In $d=4$ there is no known example of a scale-invariant but non-conformal theory under the assumptions of unitarity, Poincaré invariance, a discrete scaling spectrum, an existing scale current and unbroken scale invariance; a perturbative proof exists, but as of January 2014 the "non-perturbative proof is yet to come" ([Nakayama](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.0884)). Dymarsky, Komargodski, Schwimmer and Theisen show that in unitary scale-invariant 4d theories infinitely many matrix elements vanish in a suitable kinematic configuration, a necessary condition for conformality that they argue is likely also sufficient, and they discuss possible exceptions ([Dymarsky et al., arXiv:1309.2921](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.2921)). Wikipedia describes four-dimensional RG flows and this question as "a field of active research" in which not all questions are settled ([Wikipedia: c-theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-theorem)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Renormalization group (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group): history, block spins, beta functions, fixed points, exact RG equations.
- **Reference:** [PDG Review: Quantum Chromodynamics (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-qcd.pdf): running of $\alpha_s$, beta-function coefficients, world average.
- **Learn:** [Kardar, MIT 8.334 Statistical Physics of Fields, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/85f01760f2ea1193c673baffce5c25e6_MIT8_334S14_Lec7.pdf): conceptual and formal RG, perturbative RG and the $\epsilon$-expansion.
- **Learn:** [Nakayama, Scale invariance vs conformal invariance](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1302.0884): review of the $c$-theorem, the 2d proof and the higher-dimensional question.
- **Primary:** [Wilson and Fisher, Critical Exponents in 3.99 Dimensions (PRL 28, 240, 1972)](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=doi%3A10.1103%2FPhysRevLett.28.240&fields=titles,abstracts,authors.full_name,publication_info): the $\epsilon$-expansion paper.
- **Primary:** [Wilson, Renormalization group and critical phenomena I and II (Phys. Rev. B 4, 1971)](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20K.G.Wilson.1%20and%20date%201971%20and%20j%20Phys.Rev.B&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,dois&size=5): Wilson's founding papers.
- **Primary:** [Kadanoff, Scaling laws for Ising models near $T_c$ (1966)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysicsPhysiqueFizika.2.263): the block-spin paper.
- **Primary:** [Komargodski and Schwimmer, On Renormalization Group Flows in Four Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1107.3987): proof of the $a$-theorem.
- **Primary:** [Polchinski, Scale and Conformal Invariance in QFT and Renormalization and Effective Lagrangians](https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?q=a%20Polchinski%2C%20Joseph%20and%20t%20%22Renormalization%20and%20Effective%20Lagrangians%22%20or%20t%20%22Scale%20and%20Conformal%20Invariance%20in%20Quantum%20Field%20Theory%22&fields=titles,authors.full_name,publication_info,dois&size=5): the 2d scale-implies-conformal theorem and the Polchinski exact RG equation.
- **Further reading:** [Cardy, *Scaling and Renormalization in Statistical Physics*](https://www-thphys.physics.ox.ac.uk/people/JohnCardy/bookdescription.html): introductory text on scaling and the RG, from fixed points and cross-over to conformal symmetry.
- **Further reading:** [Weinberg, *The Quantum Theory of Fields*, Vol. 2 (Cambridge)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781139644174/type/book): chapter 18, renormalization group methods.
references.Representation Similarity Analysis:
## Reference
### Overview
Representational similarity analysis (RSA) compares two systems that respond to the same set of stimuli without mapping one system's units onto the other's. For each system, the dissimilarity between the response patterns to every pair of stimuli is collected in a representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM). Because RDMs are indexed by stimuli, not by neurons, voxels or model units, they can be compared across subjects, regions, modalities (fMRI, MEG, cell recordings), behaviour and models. Kriegeskorte called this the "representational similarity trick". ([Kriegeskorte, RSA workshop slides](https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/www/sites/3/2014/10/Kriegeskorte_Intro-talk_RSA-Workshop_16-Feb-2015_saveas_standard.pdf))

The method came from systems neuroscience. In the 2008 *Neuron* study of man and monkey, single-cell recordings in monkey IT cortex and fMRI in human IT were compared through their RDMs for the same 92 object images instead of a spatial correspondence mapping between species and modalities; the approach is rooted in the similarity analyses of mathematical psychology (Shepard and Chipman 1970) and in Edelman's application of multidimensional scaling to brain-activity patterns. ([Kriegeskorte et al. 2008, Neuron](https://www.cns.nyu.edu/kianilab/papers/Kriegeskorte_Kiani_Bandettini.pdf)) RSA is one of three closely related ways of testing representational models: encoding models, pattern component modelling (PCM) and RSA all depend on the data only through the second-moment matrix of the activity profiles. ([Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte 2017](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005508))

In machine learning, RSA sits among measures for comparing network layers, alongside CCA-based measures, alignment-based measures such as orthogonal Procrustes and shape metrics, and centered kernel alignment (CKA), which is built on representational similarity matrices. ([Klabunde et al. survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.06329); [Kornblith et al. 2019](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/kornblith19a.html))

### Formal definition
Let $R\in\mathbb R^{N\times D}$ and $R'\in\mathbb R^{N\times D'}$ be representations of the same $N$ inputs (rows $R_i$). Given an instance-wise similarity (or dissimilarity) function $s$, the representational similarity matrix is
$$S_{ij}=s(R_i,R_j),\qquad S\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}.$$
RSA computes $S$ and $S'$ with an inner function $s_{\mathrm{in}}$, vectorizes the lower triangle $v(\cdot)$ of each symmetric matrix, and compares the vectors with an outer function $s_{\mathrm{out}}$:
$$\mathrm{RSA}(R,R')=s_{\mathrm{out}}\big(v(S),v(S')\big).$$
The original instantiation used Pearson correlation for $s_{\mathrm{in}}$ and Spearman correlation for $s_{\mathrm{out}}$; Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances were also suggested. ([Klabunde et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.06329)) The 2008 man–monkey study measured dissimilarity by the correlation distance $1-r$, with Pearson $r$ computed across the population of neurons or voxels. ([Kriegeskorte et al. 2008](https://www.cns.nyu.edu/kianilab/papers/Kriegeskorte_Kiani_Bandettini.pdf))

**Crossvalidated distances.** With pattern estimates $p_1,p_2$ from one data set and $p_1',p_2'$ from an independent one, and noise covariance $\Sigma$, the Mahalanobis distance $(p_1-p_2)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(p_1-p_2)$ is replaced by the linear discriminant contrast $(p_1-p_2)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(p_1'-p_2')$, a crossvalidated variant of the Mahalanobis distance. ([Kriegeskorte, RSA workshop slides](https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/www/sites/3/2014/10/Kriegeskorte_Intro-talk_RSA-Workshop_16-Feb-2015_saveas_standard.pdf)) The crossvalidated Mahalanobis ("crossnobis") dissimilarity is the most commonly used crossvalidated distance. ([Schütt et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2112.09200))

**Second-moment matrix.** For $K$ conditions with true activity patterns $U\in\mathbb R^{K\times P}$ over $P$ channels, the second-moment matrix is $G=UU^\top/P$; each cell is the scaled inner product of two activity patterns, and the matrix of squared Euclidean distances is a function of $G$. ([Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte 2017](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005508))

**Noise ceiling.** The noise ceiling is the expected RDM correlation achieved by the unknown true model, given the noise in the data. Its upper bound is the correlation of each subject's RDM with the group-average RDM (overfitted, so an overestimate); its lower bound is each subject's correlation with the average of the other subjects' RDMs (leave-one-subject-out, an underestimate). ([Nili et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003553))

**CKA and alignment measures.** With centering matrix $H_N=I_N-\tfrac1N\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top$ and kernel RSMs $S,S'$,
$$\mathrm{HSIC}(S,S')=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(SH_NS'H_N)}{(N-1)^2},\qquad \mathrm{CKA}(R,R')=\frac{\mathrm{HSIC}(S,S')}{\sqrt{\mathrm{HSIC}(S,S)\,\mathrm{HSIC}(S',S')}}\in[0,1].$$
Linear CKA is equivalent to the RV coefficient ([Klabunde et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.06329)), a multivariate generalization of the squared Pearson correlation that takes values between 0 and 1 and measures the closeness of two sets of points represented as matrices ([RV coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RV_coefficient)). Orthogonal Procrustes is
$$\min_{Q\in O(D)}\|RQ-R'\|_F=\big(\|R\|_F^2+\|R'\|_F^2-2\|R^\top R'\|_*\big)^{1/2},$$
and the angular shape metric of Williams et al., for unit-Frobenius-norm representations and a subgroup $G(D)\le O(D)$, is $m_\theta=\min_{Q\in G(D)}\arccos\langle RQ,R'\rangle_F\in[0,\pi]$. ([Klabunde et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.06329))

### Key results
- **Invariances are set by the inner and outer functions.** With Pearson $s_{\mathrm{in}}$ and Spearman $s_{\mathrm{out}}$, RSA is invariant to scaling and translation; other choices give other invariance classes. Linear CKA is invariant to orthogonal transformations and isotropic scaling (and to permutation and translation) but not to invertible linear maps; the debiased HSIC estimator is recommended, especially when $N<D$. ([Klabunde et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.06329))
- **Limits of invertible-linear invariance (Kornblith et al. 2019).** Neither CCA nor any other statistic invariant to invertible linear transformation can measure meaningful similarities between representations whose dimension exceeds the number of data points. A CKA-equivalent index reliably matches layers across networks trained from different initializations. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/kornblith19a.html))
- **Unification through the second moment (Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte 2017).** Encoding models with regularization, PCM (which models activity profiles as Gaussian with zero mean and second moment $G$) and RSA (which compares observed distances with model-predicted distances that depend only on $G$) all test hypotheses about $G$; RSA and PCM both operate on the inner-product matrix of the activity estimates. ([Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte 2017](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005508))
- **Crossvalidation removes noise bias.** Distance estimates from noisy patterns are positively biased. Crossvalidated distances give an unbiased estimate of the Mahalanobis distance, apart from a multiplicative bias from errors in the noise covariance; if two conditions differ only by noise, the expected value is zero. ([Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte 2017](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005508); [Kriegeskorte, RSA workshop slides](https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/www/sites/3/2014/10/Kriegeskorte_Intro-talk_RSA-Workshop_16-Feb-2015_saveas_standard.pdf)) Such estimators can take negative values, which is what lets them be unbiased. ([Schütt et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2112.09200))
- **Reliability of dissimilarity measures (Walther et al. 2016).** In split-half RDM reliability analyses, multivariate noise normalization significantly enhances the reliability of dissimilarity measures; crossvalidated dissimilarity estimates are unbiased and on a ratio scale with an interpretable zero point; and pairwise classification accuracy is a quantized measure of distinctness that is significantly less reliable than continuous distance measures. ([Walther, RSA workshop slides](https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/www/sites/3/2014/10/rsaworkshop_alex.pdf))
- **Shape metrics are proper metrics (Williams et al. 2021).** CCA-based similarity measures can be modified to satisfy the triangle inequality, giving a family of metric spaces on representations, including a metric that respects the inductive biases of convolutional layers and approximate Euclidean embeddings usable with standard machine-learning methods. ([Williams et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14739))
- **Inference generalizing over subjects and stimuli (Schütt et al.).** Models are evaluated by how accurately they predict representational geometries, with two-factor crossvalidation and a bootstrap over both subjects and conditions. A naive two-factor bootstrap triple-counts the variance contributed by measurement noise; the corrected estimate combines the one-factor and two-factor bootstrap variances. With fewer than about 20 subjects bootstrap variances are biased low, and a $t$-test across subjects is recommended instead. ([Schütt et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2112.09200))

### Examples
- **Human and monkey IT.** For 92 images, monkey IT and human IT RDMs share a categorical structure: dissimilarity is larger when one object is animate and the other inanimate, and faces and bodies form subclusters within the animates. The category-boundary effect is strong in IT and weak in early visual cortex, and a range of low- and intermediate-level computational models could not account for the categorical IT structure. ([Kriegeskorte et al. 2008](https://www.cns.nyu.edu/kianilab/papers/Kriegeskorte_Kiani_Bandettini.pdf))
- **Deep networks and IT (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte 2014).** Of 37 model representations compared with human and monkey IT by RSA, the categorical clustering in IT was largely unexplained by the unsupervised models, and none of the 28 not-strongly-supervised models reached the noise ceiling; a deep convolutional network trained on about 1.2 million labelled ImageNet images matched IT best, and after remixing its features with linear category readouts and reweighting its layers it fell within the human-IT noise ceiling. ([Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003915))
- **Performance-optimized models (Yamins et al. 2014).** Within a class of hierarchical networks, categorization performance correlated strongly with the ability to predict IT neural responses; a high-performing network's top layer predicted IT responses and its intermediate layers predicted V4. ([Yamins et al. 2014, MIT DSpace](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/92787))
- **Comparing network layers.** RSA, CKA and shape metrics compare two networks' activations on the same inputs, e.g. across seeds or NAS-Bench-101 architectures. ([Kornblith et al. 2019](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/kornblith19a.html); [Williams et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14739))

### History
RSA builds on second-order similarity analysis in mathematical psychology (Shepard and Chipman 1970), multidimensional scaling (Torgerson 1958; Kruskal and Wish 1978; Shepard 1980) and Edelman's 1998 similarity analyses of brain activity. ([Kriegeskorte et al. 2008](https://www.cns.nyu.edu/kianilab/papers/Kriegeskorte_Kiani_Bandettini.pdf)) The method was introduced in "Representational similarity analysis – connecting the branches of systems neuroscience" (*Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience*, 2008) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.3389/neuro.06.004.2008)) and applied the same year to man and monkey IT in *Neuron* 60, 1126–1141. ([Kriegeskorte et al. 2008](https://www.cns.nyu.edu/kianilab/papers/Kriegeskorte_Kiani_Bandettini.pdf)) Walther, Nili, Ejaz, Alink, Kriegeskorte and Diedrichsen studied the reliability of dissimilarity measures in *NeuroImage* 137 (2016). ([MRC CBU record](https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/bibliography/articles/8247))

### Connections
- [Centered Kernel Alignment](node:Centered%20Kernel%20Alignment): an RSM-based similarity index with HSIC as the outer comparison.
- [Kernel Methods](node:Kernel%20Methods): kernel RSMs and HSIC come from kernel methods.
- [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): the orthogonal Procrustes solution and the nuclear norm in its closed form come from the SVD.
- [Cross-Validation](node:Cross-Validation): crossvalidated distances and the leave-one-subject-out noise-ceiling bound.
- [Bootstrap Methods](node:Bootstrap%20Methods): inference over subjects and conditions uses one- and two-factor bootstraps.
- [Convolutional Neural Networks](node:Convolutional%20Neural%20Networks): the deep networks compared with IT by RSA.
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): RSA compares geometry, not mechanism.
- [Bansal et al. 2021 - Revisiting Model Stitching to Compare Neural Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07682): a functional alternative that tests whether layers can be swapped.
- [Huh et al. 2024 - The Platonic Representation Hypothesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07987): cross-model convergence measured with such indices.

### Common pitfalls
- **Single-model significance.** A significant correlation between a model RDM and a data RDM shows only that some stimulus information is present; models must be compared with one another and with the noise ceiling. ([Schütt et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2112.09200))
- **Reading the noise ceiling.** If the best model does not reach the noise ceiling, a better model is needed; if it reaches a ceiling well below 1, the experiment should be improved to expose remaining model deficiencies. ([Nili et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003553))
- **Scores are not interchangeable across measures.** Different measures applied to the same pair of models can give materially different results, and a single translated instance can drive the CKA of two identical representations almost to zero without affecting the separability of the representations with respect to their class. ([Klabunde et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.06329))
- **Cost of flexible models under resampling.** Bootstrap-wrapped crossvalidation fits each model thousands of times, which limits model complexity; one workaround is to fit all models on a separate neural data set first, so conclusions hold conditional on that fit. ([Schütt et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2112.09200))

### Open problems
- **Applicability, interpretability and robustness of similarity measures.** Klabunde et al. argue that there is only limited research on which measures capture the differences relevant to an application, that "more research is required to improve the interpretability of measures" (scores generally cannot be read as an intuitive degree of similarity), and that "more research on the robustness of similarity measures is required", citing CKA's sensitivity to single-instance perturbations. ([Klabunde et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.06329))
- **Bayesian population inference for RDMs.** Schütt et al. note that Bayesian generalization to populations of subjects and conditions would need a model of how RDMs vary across both, and "we currently do not have such a model". ([Schütt et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2112.09200))
- **Optimal RDM for rank comparators.** No efficient method is known to find the optimal RDM for a data set under Kendall's $\tau_a$, so the noise ceiling for that comparator is only approximated. ([Schütt et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2112.09200))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Orthogonal Procrustes problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal_Procrustes_problem): the alignment problem behind Procrustes and shape-metric comparisons, with its SVD solution.
- **Learn:** [Kriegeskorte, Introduction to RSA (MRC CBU workshop)](https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/www/sites/3/2014/10/Kriegeskorte_Intro-talk_RSA-Workshop_16-Feb-2015_saveas_standard.pdf): RDMs and crossvalidated distances.
- **Learn:** [Walther, Estimating representational dissimilarity measures (MRC CBU workshop)](https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/www/sites/3/2014/10/rsaworkshop_alex.pdf): noise normalization and crossnobis.
- **Primary:** [Kriegeskorte et al. 2008, Matching categorical object representations in inferior temporal cortex of man and monkey](https://www.cns.nyu.edu/kianilab/papers/Kriegeskorte_Kiani_Bandettini.pdf): the landmark RSA application.
- **Primary:** [Nili et al. 2014, A toolbox for representational similarity analysis](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003553): the toolbox and the noise ceiling.
- **Primary:** [Kornblith et al. 2019, Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/kornblith19a.html): CKA and the limits of CCA-type measures.
- **Primary:** [Williams et al. 2021, Generalized Shape Metrics on Neural Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14739): metric versions of representational comparison.
- **Primary:** [Schütt et al., Statistical inference on representational geometries](https://arxiv.org/html/2112.09200): crossvalidation, bootstrap and noise ceilings.
- **Further reading:** [Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte 2017, Representational models](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005508): the common framework for encoding models, PCM and RSA.
- **Further reading:** [Klabunde et al., Similarity of Neural Network Models: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.06329): unified definitions of RSA, CKA, Procrustes and shape metrics, with open problems.
references.Representation Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Representation theory studies a group through its linear actions: a representation of $G$ on a vector space $V$ over a field $\mathbb F$ is a group homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$, so an abstract multiplication law is realized by invertible linear maps, and questions about $G$ can be attacked with invariant subspaces, traces and decompositions. The same formalism applies to associative algebras, which generalize both group and Lie algebra representations. ([Wikipedia: Representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory))

The subject splits according to the group and the coefficient field. For finite groups over a field whose characteristic does not divide $|G|$, every finite-dimensional representation is a direct sum of irreducibles and the theory is governed by characters. When the characteristic $p$ divides $|G|$, Maschke's theorem fails and one is in modular representation theory, which Brauer developed into a theory of blocks, defect groups and Brauer characters. ([Wikipedia: Representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory); [Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory))

For compact groups, the Peter–Weyl theorem reduces unitary representations to finite-dimensional irreducibles. For compact connected Lie groups and complex semisimple [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras), the finite-dimensional irreducibles are classified by highest weights. ([Wikipedia: Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem); [Wikipedia: Theorem of the highest weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem_of_the_highest_weight))

### Formal definition
A representation of a group $G$ over a field $k$ is a $k$-vector space $V$ together with a homomorphism $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$; equivalently, a module over the group algebra $k[G]$. A subrepresentation is a subspace invariant under every $\rho(g)$, and a nonzero representation is irreducible when its only subrepresentations are $0$ and $V$. ([Etingof et al., §§2.3, 4](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))

An intertwiner (homomorphism of representations) $T:V\to W$ satisfies $T\rho_V(g)=\rho_W(g)T$ for all $g\in G$, and $V\cong W$ when an invertible intertwiner exists. The character of a finite-dimensional representation is $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}\rho_V(g)$; it is a class function. For finite $G$ over $\mathbb C$ the inner product on class functions is
$$(\chi,\psi)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g)\overline{\psi(g)}.$$
([Etingof et al., §§2.3, 4.5](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))

For $H\le G$ and a representation $W$ of $H$, the induced representation $\operatorname{Ind}_H^GW$ is a representation of $G$, and $\operatorname{Res}_H^G V$ denotes restriction of a $G$-representation to $H$. ([Etingof et al., §5.10](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))

### Key results
Unless stated, $G$ is finite and $k$ is algebraically closed, the standing assumption of Etingof et al. from §2.2. ([Etingof et al., §2.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **Maschke's theorem.** If $\operatorname{char}k\nmid|G|$, then $k[G]$ is semisimple and $k[G]\cong\bigoplus_i\operatorname{End}V_i$ over the irreducible representations $V_i$. Hence the regular representation is $\bigoplus_i\dim(V_i)\,V_i$, and $|G|=\sum_i(\dim V_i)^2$. ([Etingof et al., Thm. 4.1.1](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **Schur's lemma.** A nonzero homomorphism between irreducible representations of an algebra over any field is an isomorphism. If $k$ is algebraically closed and $V$ is finite-dimensional irreducible, every intertwiner $V\to V$ is a scalar. This fails over $\mathbb R$, e.g. for $A=V=\mathbb C$ as an $\mathbb R$-algebra. ([Etingof et al., Prop. 2.3.9, Cor. 2.3.10](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **Characters form a basis; counting irreducibles.** If $\operatorname{char}k\nmid|G|$, the irreducible characters form a basis of the space of class functions on $G$. Consequently the number of isomorphism classes of irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$. If $\operatorname{char}k$ divides $|G|$, there are strictly fewer irreducibles than conjugacy classes. ([Etingof et al., Thm. 4.2.1, Cor. 4.2.2, Ex. 4.2.3](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **Orthogonality.** Over $\mathbb C$, $(\chi_V,\chi_W)=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(W,V)$, which is $1$ if $V\cong W$ are irreducible and $0$ if they are non-isomorphic irreducibles. In particular a representation is determined by its character. ([Etingof et al., Thm. 4.5.1, Cor. 4.2.4](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **Frobenius reciprocity.** For groups $H\subset G$, a representation $V$ of $G$ and $W$ of $H$, $\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,\operatorname{Ind}_H^GW)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_H(\operatorname{Res}_H^GV,W)$ naturally. ([Etingof et al., Thm. 5.10.1](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **Frobenius divisibility and Burnside's theorem.** The dimension of an irreducible complex representation of $G$ divides $|G|$. As an application, every group of order $p^aq^b$ ($p,q$ primes) is solvable (Burnside, proved with characters). ([Etingof et al., Thm. 5.3.1, Thm. 5.4.3](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **Brauer's first main theorem and blocks.** In characteristic $p$, $k[G]$ splits into blocks; each simple module lies in exactly one, and each block has a defect group, a $p$-subgroup unique up to conjugacy. The number of blocks of $G$ with defect group $D$ equals the corresponding number for $N_G(D)$. The decomposition matrix $D$ (ordinary irreducibles against irreducible Brauer characters) has nonnegative integer entries, and the Cartan matrix $C=D^{T}D$ has determinant a power of $p$. ([Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory))
- **Peter–Weyl theorem.** For a compact group $G$: matrix coefficients are uniformly dense in $C(G)$; every unitary representation on a Hilbert space is an orthogonal direct sum of finite-dimensional irreducibles; and $L^2(G)$ contains every irreducible with multiplicity equal to its degree, with normalized matrix coefficients forming an orthonormal basis. ([Wikipedia: Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))
- **Theorem of the highest weight.** For a complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, every finite-dimensional irreducible representation has a unique highest weight, which is dominant integral. Two irreducibles with the same highest weight are isomorphic, and every dominant integral $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ occurs. For a compact connected Lie group the same bijection holds with analytically integral weights. ([Wikipedia: Theorem of the highest weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem_of_the_highest_weight))
- **McKay conjecture (now a theorem).** For every prime $\ell$, a finite group $G$ has as many irreducible complex characters of degree prime to $\ell$ as $N_G(P)$ for $P$ a Sylow $\ell$-subgroup. Cabanes and Späth proved it by completing the Isaacs–Malle–Navarro reduction to simple groups. ([Cabanes–Späth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20392))
- **Brauer's height zero conjecture (now a theorem).** For a $p$-block $B$ with defect group $D$, all irreducible characters in $B$ have height zero if and only if $D$ is abelian. Malle, Navarro, Schaeffer Fry and Tiep completed the proof of the conjecture, which dates from 1955. ([Malle, Conj. 3.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145); [Malle–Navarro–Schaeffer Fry–Tiep](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04736))

### Examples
- **$S_4$.** $|S_4|=24$ with five conjugacy classes (of $e,(12),(123),(1234),(12)(34)$), so there are five irreducibles and the sum of squares of their dimensions is $24=1+1+4+9+9$. ([Etingof et al., §4.3](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))
- **$A_4$.** The normal Klein four-subgroup $H$ has $A_4/H\cong\mathbb Z/3$, whose three one-dimensional representations lift to $A_4$. Since $A_4$ has four conjugacy classes, $1^2+1^2+1^2+n_4^2=12$ forces the fourth irreducible to have dimension $3$. ([Singh, §12.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.0462))
- **Finite abelian groups.** Over $\mathbb C$ every irreducible representation of a finite abelian group is one-dimensional, and $G\cong\widehat G$ noncanonically while $G\cong\widehat{\widehat G}$ canonically. ([Etingof et al., §4.3](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))

### History
Etingof et al. date the birth of representation theory to 1896, when Frobenius, prompted by Dedekind's letters about the group determinant (the determinant of the multiplication table of $G$ with entries replaced by variables), developed character theory. Burnside used it to prove his $p^aq^b$ theorem in the early 20th century. ([Etingof et al., Introduction, §§4.10, 5.4](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))

Brauer extended character theory to modular representations from about 1940, and Cartan's 1913 paper proved the theorem of the highest weight for Lie algebras, with Weyl giving the compact-group version. Peter and Weyl published their theorem in 1927. ([Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory); [Wikipedia: Theorem of the highest weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem_of_the_highest_weight); [Wikipedia: Peter–Weyl theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%E2%80%93Weyl_theorem))

McKay stated a limited form of his conjecture (for $p=2$ and simple groups) in 1971, and Isaacs, Malle and Navarro reduced it to simple groups in 2007. Malle and Späth settled $p=2$ in 2016, and Cabanes and Späth announced the general proof in October 2023. ([Wikipedia: McKay conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKay_conjecture))

### Connections
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory): supplies the group; characters prove group-theoretic results such as Burnside's $p^aq^b$ theorem.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): representations are homomorphisms into $\operatorname{GL}(V)$; characters are traces.
- [MSC 20Cxx - Representation theory of groups](node:MSC%2020Cxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20groups): the MSC subfield map for ordinary, modular and integral representations.
- [MSC 16Gxx - Representation theory of associative rings and algebras](node:MSC%2016Gxx%20-%20Representation%20theory%20of%20associative%20rings%20and%20algebras): representations of $G$ are $k[G]$-modules, and modular block theory is representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras.
- [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) and [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): highest-weight classification and the unitary trick.
- [Peter–Weyl Theorem](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem): the compact-group analogue of Maschke plus character orthogonality.
- [Quiver Representations](node:Quiver%20Representations): Gabriel's theorem and Dynkin diagrams in the algebra setting.
- [Finite Simple Groups](node:Finite%20Simple%20Groups): the local-global conjectures are reduced to inductive conditions on simple groups and proved with the classification.
- [Sylow Theorems](node:Sylow%20Theorems): Sylow normalizers are the local subgroups in McKay's conjecture.

### Common pitfalls
- **Irreducible versus indecomposable.** When $\operatorname{char}k=p$ divides $|G|$, a representation can have an invariant subspace with no invariant complement. Singh's exercise: the two-dimensional representation $a\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ of $\mathbb Z/p$ over $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ fixes a line and has no invariant complement, so Maschke's hypothesis cannot be dropped. ([Singh, Ex. 3.13–3.14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.0462))
- **Field hypotheses.** The scalar form of Schur's lemma and the counting "irreducibles = conjugacy classes" need an algebraically closed field (of characteristic prime to $|G|$ for the count). Over $\mathbb R$ an irreducible can have endomorphism algebra $\mathbb C$. ([Etingof et al., Cor. 2.3.10, Remark 2.3.11, Cor. 4.2.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Alperin weight conjecture.** For a $p$-block $B$, the number $|\mathrm{IBr}(B)|$ of irreducible Brauer characters equals the number of $G$-classes of $B$-weights $(Q,\psi)$, with $Q$ a radical $p$-subgroup and $\psi$ a defect-zero character of $N_G(Q)/Q$. Malle's survey lists it as open in general, with a reduction to simple groups (Späth 2013). Feng, Malle and Zhang (2025) present generic weights as "a step towards an eventual proof". ([Malle, Conj. 4.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145); [Feng–Malle–Zhang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22064))
- **Alperin–McKay conjecture.** For a block $B$ with defect group $D$ and Brauer correspondent $b$, the numbers of height-zero characters agree: $|\mathrm{Irr}_0(B)|=|\mathrm{Irr}_0(b)|$. Malle's survey reports it open in general, reduced by Späth to an inductive condition on simple groups. ([Malle, Conj. 2.2](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145))
- **Broué's abelian defect group conjecture.** If $D$ is abelian, the bounded derived categories of $B$ and $b$ are equivalent. Malle's survey records it as open in general and known for $p$-solvable groups, cyclic and Klein-four defect groups, and $S_n$ and $\operatorname{GL}_n(q)$ (Chuang–Rouquier), with no general reduction theorem available. ([Malle, Conj. 6.1](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Modular representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_representation_theory): blocks, defect groups, Brauer characters and the decomposition matrix.
- **Learn:** [Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory (MIT)](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/reprbook.pdf): finite groups, Frobenius reciprocity, quivers, Lie algebras and historical interludes.
- **Learn:** [Singh, Representation Theory of Finite Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.0462): first-course notes with many character-table examples.
- **Primary:** [Malle, Local-global conjectures in the representation theory of finite groups](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1512.01145): survey of McKay, Alperin–McKay, height zero, Alperin weight and Broué conjectures and their reductions.
- **Primary:** [Cabanes–Späth, The McKay Conjecture on character degrees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20392): the proof of McKay's conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups (Springer GTM, 1977)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4684-9458-7): the standard short graduate text, including an introduction to Brauer theory.
references.Reproducible Research Computing:
## Reference
### Overview
Reproducible research computing is the set of practices and tools that let a computational result be regenerated from its inputs. In the narrow, computational sense, reproducibility means rerunning the original data through the same procedures and obtaining the same results; replicability, by contrast, means obtaining consistent results from a new study with new data, and repeatability means repeating an experiment within the same study. Usage of these terms varies, and some fields reverse them ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducibility)). Reproducible research asks that results be documented so their derivation is transparent: detailed methods plus the full data and code, with data and files separated and labeled, operations automated, and work built as a chain of small steps whose outputs feed the next ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducibility)).

The guiding principle is Claerbout's, quoted by Donoho: an article about a computational result is advertising, not scholarship; the actual scholarship is the full software environment, code and data that produced the result. Donoho reports that errors are common in scientific computing and that researchers often misremember or misdescribe their own computations, and argues that projects should be planned from the start so that this full record can be shared and rerun ([Donoho 2010](https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/11/3/385/257703)).

In practice the subject spans version control, explicit dependency and environment capture (lock files, containers), automated pipelines, deterministic builds, notebooks and literate documents, data management, and community policies such as code-submission requirements and checklists ([Wilson et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1609.00037); [Boettiger 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.0846); [Pineau et al. 2021](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-303.html)).

### Formal definition
A useful working model treats a computational result $R$ as the output of a function
$$R = f_{E}(C, D, P),$$
where $C$ is the code, $D$ the input data, $P$ the parameters (including random seeds), and $E$ the execution environment (operating system, libraries, compilers, hardware). The model restates the narrow definition above: computational reproducibility asks that rerunning the same procedure on the same data return the same $R$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducibility)), which requires that every argument be recorded and recoverable, as Claerbout's "full software environment, code and data" demands ([Donoho 2010](https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/11/3/385/257703)).

**Version control (Git's data model).** Git records a project as a sequence of snapshots. A *blob* is file contents, a *tree* maps names to blobs or subtrees, and a *commit* records its parent commits, author, message and top-level tree. Commits form a directed acyclic graph, with merge commits having several parents. Every object is stored under the SHA-1 hash of its content and refers to other objects by hash; mutable *references* (branch names, `HEAD`) point to commits ([MIT Missing Semester](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2020/version-control/)). A commit hash therefore names one exact snapshot of $C$ together with its history.

**Reproducible build.** A build is reproducible (deterministic) if it yields identical output when repeated with the same source code, build environment and build instructions ([Wikipedia: Reproducible builds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducible_builds)).

### Key results
- **Most archived research code does not run as published.** In more than 2,000 replication datasets from Harvard Dataverse (2010–2020), containing over 9,000 unique R files executed in a clean environment, 74% of files crashed on first execution; after automatic cleaning of common coding errors, 56% still crashed. The authors conclude that many failures are preventable by good coding practice, and that journal policy strictness affects re-execution rates. ([Trisovic et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12793))
- **Whole software distributions can be made bit-reproducible.** Debian began making its archive reproducible in July 2013 and passed 90% of packages by July 2017; NixOS claimed 100% reproducibility for its minimal ISO in June 2021. The obstacles are mostly mechanical: embedded timestamps (the largest source), file ordering, build paths and locales, hash-table seeds, address randomization, and unordered data structures. ([Wikipedia: Reproducible builds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducible_builds))
- **Reproducible builds give verifiable provenance.** If source is signed and compilation is deterministic, independent rebuilders can check that a distributed binary came from that source, which exposes binaries altered after compilation. ([Wikipedia: Reproducible builds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducible_builds))
- **Content addressing pins snapshots.** Since Git objects are keyed by the hash of their content and refer to each other by hash, a commit identifier determines the whole tree and history reachable from it. ([MIT Missing Semester](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2020/version-control/))
- **Community policies.** The NeurIPS 2019 reproducibility program combined a code-submission policy, a community reproducibility challenge, and a machine-learning reproducibility checklist completed at submission. ([Pineau et al. 2021](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-303.html))
- **Variation is a main cause of irreproducibility in ML.** Gundersen et al. identify methodological issues and failure to account for variation introduced by the learning algorithms themselves as main causes, and organize the known factors by stage of the scientific method. ([Gundersen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.07610))

### Examples
- **"Good enough" practices** for newcomers ([Wilson et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1609.00037)): keep raw data as originally generated and read-only; record every processing step in scripts; make dependencies explicit (a requirements file); one directory per project with `doc/`, `data/`, `results/`, `src/`, `bin/`; small, frequent changes under a version control system such as Git, with raw data and large files kept out of it; README, LICENSE and CITATION files; manuscripts in a version-controllable plain-text format such as Markdown or LaTeX.
- **Containers.** Docker combines operating-system virtualization, cross-platform portability, reusable modular images, versioning and DevOps practice, which addresses the complex and fast-changing computing environments that stop others from rerunning or extending research code ([Boettiger 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.0846)).
- **Notebooks and literate documents.** R Markdown and Jupyter notebooks, together with version control and the Open Science Framework, are standard tools for keeping code, narrative and results together ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducibility)).

### History
Repetition as the test of experimental facts goes back to Boyle in the seventeenth century, and Popper wrote in 1934 that non-reproducible single occurrences are of no significance to science ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducibility)). Donoho's 2010 invitation to reproducible research in Biostatistics credits the principle to the geophysicist Claerbout and cites reproducibility efforts in signal processing and computational biology ([Donoho 2010](https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/11/3/385/257703)). The GNU project worked on reproducible builds in the early 1990s, Tor adopted them in 2013, and Debian began its archive-wide effort the same year ([Wikipedia: Reproducible builds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducible_builds)). The Software and Data Carpentry workshops informed the "good enough" practices of Wilson et al. ([Wilson et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00037)), and machine learning venues added reproducibility programs from NeurIPS 2019 ([Pineau et al. 2021](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-303.html)).

### Connections
- [Reproducible Builds](node:Reproducible%20Builds): deterministic compilation, the software-distribution side of reproducibility.
- [Containerization](node:Containerization): capturing the execution environment $E$.
- [Interactive Scientific Notebooks](node:Interactive%20Scientific%20Notebooks): literate computing, with hidden-state risks.
- [Computational Workflow Systems](node:Computational%20Workflow%20Systems) and [Workflow Dependency Graphs](node:Workflow%20Dependency%20Graphs): automating the chain of small steps.
- [Computational Experiment Packaging](node:Computational%20Experiment%20Packaging): bundling code, data and environment for re-execution.
- [Data Provenance and Lineage](node:Data%20Provenance%20and%20Lineage) and [FAIR Data Principles](node:FAIR%20Data%20Principles): recording where $D$ came from and making it findable and reusable.
- [Replication across Random Seeds](node:Replication%20across%20Random%20Seeds): accounting for algorithmic variation in $P$.
- [Floating-Point Arithmetic and Numerical Stability](node:Floating-Point%20Arithmetic%20and%20Numerical%20Stability): a source of platform-dependent differences in results.
- [Software Supply-Chain Security](node:Software%20Supply-Chain%20Security): reproducible builds as a supply-chain defense.
- [Machine Learning Evaluation](node:Machine%20Learning%20Evaluation) and [Data Leakage and Temporal Evaluation](node:Data%20Leakage%20and%20Temporal%20Evaluation): reproducible but wrong pipelines are still wrong.
- [Empirical Software Engineering](node:Empirical%20Software%20Engineering): large-scale studies of research code quality.

### Common pitfalls
- **Conflating the terms.** Reproducing a result with the same code and data is a weaker check than replicating it with new data; fields use the words differently, so state the definition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducibility)).
- **Unpinned environments.** Code that ran when published crashes later because the surrounding environment changed; explicit dependencies and captured environments address this ([Boettiger 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.0846); [Trisovic et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12793)).
- **Editing raw data.** Processing steps applied by hand cannot be rerun; keep raw data unchanged and script every step ([Wilson et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1609.00037)).
- **Large data in version control.** Raw data and large files belong outside the repository ([Wilson et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1609.00037)).
- **Ignoring run-to-run variation.** A single run of a stochastic algorithm can support a false finding ([Gundersen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.07610)).

### Open problems
- **A theory of experiment design in ML.** Gundersen et al. note that there is no theoretical framework relating experiment design choices to their effect on the conclusions drawn, and offer a categorized framework of irreproducibility factors as a step toward one ([Gundersen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.07610)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Reproducibility (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducibility): terminology, reproducible research practice, history.
- **Reference:** [Reproducible builds (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducible_builds): deterministic compilation, sources of nondeterminism, adoption.
- **Learn:** [MIT Missing Semester: Version Control (Git)](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2020/version-control/): Git's snapshot and DAG data model.
- **Primary:** [Wilson et al., Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00037): practical recommendations for data, code, collaboration and tracking changes.
- **Primary:** [Trisovic et al., A large-scale study on research code quality and execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12793): re-execution of 9,000 research R files.
- **Further reading:** [Kitzes, Turek and Deniz (eds.), The Practice of Reproducible Research (UC Press 2018)](https://www.github.com/BIDS/practice-repro-research): 31 case studies of reproducible workflows in data-intensive science.
references.Retrieval-Augmented Generation:
## Reference
### Overview
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a language model retrieve information from external sources (databases, uploaded documents, the web) and condition its output on it, supplementing the training data with domain-specific or up-to-date information and allowing responses to cite sources. The process involves *indexing* (convert documents to embeddings and store them in a vector database), *retrieval* (select documents relevant to the query), *augmentation* (insert the retrieved text into the prompt), and *generation*; many systems add reranking or context selection ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation)).

The term comes from Lewis et al. (2020), who combined *parametric memory* (knowledge stored in a pretrained seq2seq model's weights) with *non-parametric memory* (a dense vector index of Wikipedia searched by a neural retriever), and reported state-of-the-art results on three open-domain QA tasks with generations that were more specific, diverse and factual than a parametric-only baseline ([Lewis et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)). A survey by Gao et al. motivates RAG as a remedy for hallucination, outdated knowledge, and opaque reasoning in large language models, and organizes the field into Naive, Advanced and Modular RAG built on retrieval, generation and augmentation components ([Gao et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997)).

RAG is one member of the broader family of *retrieval-based language models*, whose study covers architecture, training, applications, and multilingual and multimodal extensions ([ACL 2023 tutorial](https://acl2023-retrieval-lm.github.io/)). Related designs retrieve at pretraining time (REALM), at the chunk level inside the network (RETRO), or at the token level from a datastore of contexts (kNN-LM) ([Guu et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08909); [Borgeaud et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04426); [Khandelwal et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00172)).

### Formal definition
**Latent-document formulation (Lewis et al.).** Given input $x$ and output $y=(y_1,\dots,y_N)$, a retriever $p_\eta(z\mid x)$ returns a distribution over passages $z$ and a generator $p_\theta(y_i\mid x,z,y_{1:i-1})$ produces tokens. Treating $z$ as latent and truncating to the top-$k$ passages gives two models:
$$p_{\text{RAG-Seq}}(y\mid x)\approx\sum_{z\in\text{top-}k(p_\eta(\cdot\mid x))}p_\eta(z\mid x)\prod_{i}p_\theta(y_i\mid x,z,y_{1:i-1}),$$
$$p_{\text{RAG-Tok}}(y\mid x)\approx\prod_{i}\sum_{z\in\text{top-}k(p_\eta(\cdot\mid x))}p_\eta(z\mid x)\,p_\theta(y_i\mid x,z,y_{1:i-1}).$$
RAG-Sequence uses one passage for the whole output; RAG-Token may use a different passage for each token ([Lewis et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.11401)).

**Dense retriever.** In the DPR bi-encoder, $p_\eta(z\mid x)\propto\exp\big(\mathbf d(z)^\top\mathbf q(x)\big)$ with $\mathbf d,\mathbf q$ BERT-base encoders; top-$k$ retrieval is a maximum inner product search (MIPS). In the original system the index was a December 2018 Wikipedia dump split into 100-word chunks (about 21M passages), searched with FAISS/HNSW; the query encoder and BART-large generator were fine-tuned jointly while the document encoder and index were kept fixed ([Lewis et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.11401)).

**kNN-LM.** With a datastore of pairs $(k_i,v_i)=(f(c_i),w_i)$ of context encodings and next tokens and the retrieved neighbor set $\mathcal N$ of a test context $x$,
$$p_{\text{kNN}}(y\mid x)\propto\sum_{(k_i,v_i)\in\mathcal N}\mathbb 1[y=v_i]\exp(-d(k_i,f(x))),\qquad p(y\mid x)=\lambda p_{\text{kNN}}(y\mid x)+(1-\lambda)p_{\text{LM}}(y\mid x)$$
([Khandelwal et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.00172)).

### Key results
- **Dense retrieval beats BM25 for open-domain QA (DPR).** A dual encoder trained on a modest number of question–passage pairs outperforms a strong Lucene-BM25 baseline by about 9–19 points in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy across several open-domain QA datasets. ([Karpukhin et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906))
- **Retrieval-augmented pretraining (REALM).** A retriever trained without labels, using masked language modeling as the signal and backpropagating through retrieval over millions of documents, improves open-domain QA by 4–16 points of absolute accuracy over prior explicit and implicit knowledge-storage methods on three benchmarks. ([Guu et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08909))
- **Evidence fusion scales with passages (FiD).** A generative reader conditioned on retrieved passages improves significantly as the number of retrieved passages grows, which the authors read as evidence that generative models combine evidence across passages well; it reached state of the art on Natural Questions and TriviaQA. ([Izacard and Grave 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01282))
- **Retrieval substitutes for parameters (RETRO).** Conditioning an autoregressive LM on chunks retrieved from a roughly 2-trillion-token database by similarity to preceding tokens, via a frozen BERT retriever and chunked cross-attention, matches GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile with about 25 times fewer parameters. ([Borgeaud et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04426))
- **Nonparametric interpolation without training (kNN-LM).** Interpolating a pretrained LM with a kNN distribution over its training contexts lowers Wikitext-103 perplexity to 15.79, a 2.9-point gain with no additional training; swapping the datastore adapts the domain. ([Khandelwal et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00172))
- **Position sensitivity ("lost in the middle").** On multi-document QA and key–value retrieval, model accuracy is highest when the relevant information is at the beginning or end of the context and degrades in the middle, including for long-context models. ([Liu et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172))

### Examples
- **Open-domain QA:** retrieve Wikipedia passages with DPR, then generate the answer with BART (the original RAG system) ([Lewis et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.11401)).
- **Hybrid search:** combine vector search with full-text (lexical) search so that key terms missed by embeddings are still found, then rerank the merged list ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation)).
- **Chunking choices:** fixed-length, recursive, or semantic chunking; small chunks are focused but lose context, large chunks keep context but add noise and consume the context budget ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation)).

### History
Sparse vector-space models such as TF-IDF or BM25 were the de facto retrieval method for open-domain QA ([Karpukhin et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906)). In 2020 REALM added learned retrieval to pretraining ([Guu et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08909)) and Lewis et al. introduced the term RAG (NeurIPS 2020) ([Lewis et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)). RETRO (2021) scaled retrieval databases to trillions of tokens ([Borgeaud et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04426)), and by 2023 the field had been surveyed as Naive, Advanced and Modular RAG ([Gao et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997)).

### Connections
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): RAG supplies non-parametric memory to a parametric LLM.
- [Vector Search and Embeddings](node:Vector%20Search%20and%20Embeddings) and [Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search](node:Approximate%20Nearest-Neighbor%20Search): the indexing and MIPS retrieval step.
- [Lexical Retrieval and BM25](node:Lexical%20Retrieval%20and%20BM25) and [Information Retrieval](node:Information%20Retrieval): sparse retrieval baselines and hybrid search.
- [Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation](node:Graph%20Retrieval-Augmented%20Generation): retrieval over knowledge graphs instead of passages.
- [Knowledge Graphs and Ontologies](node:Knowledge%20Graphs%20and%20Ontologies): structured sources that can be indexed for retrieval.
- [In-Context Learning](node:In-Context%20Learning): retrieved text is consumed through the prompt.
- [Long-Context Evaluation](node:Long-Context%20Evaluation): the "lost in the middle" effect and the RAG-versus-long-context question.
- [Agent and Retrieval Security](node:Agent%20and%20Retrieval%20Security) and [Indirect Prompt Injection](node:Indirect%20Prompt%20Injection): poisoned or adversarial retrieved content.
- [LLM Agents](node:LLM%20Agents): agents call retrieval as a tool.
- [Fine-Tuning and RLHF](node:Fine-Tuning%20and%20RLHF): the alternative or complement for injecting knowledge.
- [Language Modeling](node:Language%20Modeling): kNN-LM and RETRO change the next-token distribution itself.

### Common pitfalls
- Assuming retrieval removes hallucination: models can still hallucinate around the retrieved material, misread context, merge conflicting or outdated sources, or answer when evidence is insufficient ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation)).
- Assuming more context is always used: relevant passages placed mid-context are used less reliably ([Liu et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)).
- Forgetting that in the original RAG the document index is frozen; only the query encoder and generator are trained ([Lewis et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.11401)).

### Open problems
- **Robustness to noise and counterfactual evidence.** Gao et al. highlight "the need for further research and exploration into the robustness of RAG" ([Gao et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2312.10997)).
- **RAG versus fine-tuning and super-long contexts.** The optimal integration of RAG with fine-tuning is listed as "ripe for exploration", and new RAG methods for super-long contexts as a future research trend ([Gao et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2312.10997)).
- **Scaling laws for RAG.** The applicability of LLM [scaling laws](node:Scaling%20Laws) to RAG "remains uncertain", and a possible inverse scaling law "merits further investigation" ([Gao et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2312.10997)).
- **Open-ended generation and reasoning.** The ACL 2023 tutorial's "Challenges and opportunities" section lists work reporting that kNN-LM does not improve open-ended text generation and work asking whether retriever-augmented language models can reason ([ACL 2023 tutorial](https://acl2023-retrieval-lm.github.io/)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Retrieval-augmented generation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation): pipeline, chunking, hybrid search, limitations.
- **Learn:** [ACL 2023 tutorial: Retrieval-based Language Models and Applications](https://acl2023-retrieval-lm.github.io/): Asai, Min, Zhong and Chen on architectures, training, applications, challenges.
- **Primary:** [Lewis et al. 2020, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401): the originating paper.
- **Primary:** [Gao et al. 2023, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997): paradigms, components, future directions.
- **Further reading:** [Manning, Raghavan and Schütze, Introduction to Information Retrieval (CUP 2008)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511809071): the standard IR textbook behind indexing and ranking.
references.Riemann Zeta Function:
## Reference
### Overview
The Riemann zeta function is defined for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ by the Dirichlet series $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$ and extends by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ whose only singularity is a simple pole at $s=1$ with residue $1$. Values off the half-plane of convergence are values of the continued function, not sums of a divergent series. ([DLMF §25.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2))

Its importance for number theory comes from the Euler product over primes, which makes the location of its zeros control the distribution of primes. Riemann's 1859 paper "On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude" extended $\zeta$ to complex $s$, proved its continuation and functional equation, and stated the Riemann hypothesis; Euler had earlier proved the product formula (1737). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function); [Riemann hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_hypothesis))

The prime number theorem is equivalent to the absence of zeros on the line $\operatorname{Re}s=1$, and the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to the sharpest expected error term for it, so most of the analytic theory of $\zeta$ is about where its zeros can and cannot lie, how many there are, and how large $\zeta$ is on vertical lines. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function); [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))

### Formal definition
For $s\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, ([DLMF 25.2.1, 25.2.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2))
$$
\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^{s}}=\prod_{p\ \text{prime}}\bigl(1-p^{-s}\bigr)^{-1},
$$
and both the series and the product converge in this half-plane. Near the pole, ([DLMF 25.2.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2))
$$
\zeta(s)=\frac1{s-1}+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n!}\gamma_n(s-1)^n,
$$
where $\gamma_n=\lim_{m\to\infty}\bigl(\sum_{k\le m}(\ln k)^n/k-(\ln m)^{n+1}/(n+1)\bigr)$ are the Stieltjes constants. ([DLMF 25.2.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2))

The completed zeta function is ([Riemann Xi function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_Xi_function))
$$
\xi(s)=\tfrac12\,s(s-1)\,\pi^{-s/2}\,\Gamma(s/2)\,\zeta(s).
$$
It is entire, real for real $s$, and satisfies $\xi(1-s)=\xi(s)$; Riemann's original function is $\Xi(t)=\xi(\tfrac12+it)$. ([Riemann Xi function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_Xi_function))

### Key results
- **Functional equation.** As an identity of meromorphic functions on $\mathbb C$, $\zeta(s)=2^{s}\pi^{s-1}\sin(\pi s/2)\,\Gamma(1-s)\,\zeta(1-s)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function))
- **Special values.** For $n=1,2,3,\dots$: $\zeta(2n)=\dfrac{(2\pi)^{2n}|B_{2n}|}{2\,(2n)!}$, $\zeta(-2n)=0$, and $\zeta(-n)=-B_{n+1}/(n+1)$, so $\zeta(1-2n)=-B_{2n}/(2n)$; also $\zeta(0)=-\tfrac12$. Here $B_k$ are Bernoulli numbers. ([DLMF §25.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.6))
- **Location of zeros.** Apart from the trivial zeros $-2,-4,\dots$, $\zeta(s)\ne0$ for $\operatorname{Re}s\le0$; and $\zeta(s)\ne0$ for $\operatorname{Re}s\ge1$ (for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ by the Euler product, on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ first by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin). The remaining zeros lie in the critical strip $0<\operatorname{Re}s<1$, are infinite in number, and are symmetric about the real axis and about $\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12$. ([DLMF §25.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.10); [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))
- **Non-vanishing on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ (Mertens' argument).** From $3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta=2(1+\cos\theta)^2\ge0$ one gets $|\zeta(\sigma)^3\zeta(\sigma+it)^4\zeta(\sigma+2it)|\ge1$ for $\sigma>1$; a zero at $1+it$ would make the left side tend to $0$ as $\sigma\to1^+$. ([Elkies, Math 259 notes](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~elkies/M259.06/free.pdf); [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))
- **Zero-free regions.** De la Vallée Poussin: there is $C>0$ with no zeros for $1-\sigma\le C/\log t$ (large $t$). Vinogradov–Korobov: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $c>0$ such that $\zeta(\sigma+it)\ne0$ for $\sigma\ge1-c/(\log|t|)^{2/3+\varepsilon}$ and $|t|$ large. ([Riemann hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_hypothesis); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function))
- **Hadamard product.** Over the nontrivial zeros $\rho$, taken in pairs $\rho,\bar\rho$ for convergence, $\xi(s)=\tfrac12\prod_\rho(1-s/\rho)$; equivalently $\zeta(s)=\dfrac{e^{(\log 2\pi-1-\gamma/2)s}}{2(s-1)\Gamma(1+s/2)}\prod_\rho\Bigl(1-\dfrac s\rho\Bigr)e^{s/\rho}$, with $\gamma$ Euler's constant. ([Riemann Xi function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_Xi_function); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function))
- **Riemann–von Mangoldt formula.** If $N(T)$ counts zeros $\rho=\beta+i\gamma$ with $0<\gamma\le T$, then $N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}+O(\log T)$; Trudgian's explicit form is $\bigl|N(T)-\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}\bigr|\le0.112\log T+0.278\log\log T+3.385+0.2/T$ for $T>e$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function))
- **Explicit formula.** For non-integer $x>1$, $\psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)=x-\log(2\pi)-\sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho$, the sum running over all zeros (trivial and nontrivial), the sum over nontrivial zeros converging only conditionally and taken in the principal-value sense; the trivial zeros contribute $-\tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2})$. ([Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))
- **Zeros on the critical line.** Hardy (1914) proved that $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)$ has infinitely many real zeros $t$; Selberg (1942) proved a positive proportion of nontrivial zeros lie on the line; Levinson (1974) raised this to one third and Conrey (1989) to two fifths. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function); [Riemann hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_hypothesis)) Pratt, Robles, Zaharescu and Zeindler raised the proportion to slightly over five twelfths, using a twisted second moment of $\zeta$ with mollifiers built from $\zeta$ and its derivatives. ([Pratt et al., arXiv:1802.10521](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.10521))
- **Prime number theorem and RH.** Von Koch (1901): RH is equivalent to $\pi(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)+O(\sqrt x\log x)$. Unconditionally, de la Vallée Poussin's zero-free region gives $\pi(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)+O\bigl(xe^{-a\sqrt{\log x}}\bigr)$ for some $a>0$. ([Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem))
- **Numerical verification.** Platt and Trudgian proved with interval arithmetic that every zero $\beta+i\gamma$ with $0<\gamma\le3\cdot10^{12}$ has $\beta=\tfrac12$. ([Platt–Trudgian, arXiv:2004.09765](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09765))
- **Odd values.** Apéry proved $\zeta(3)$ irrational (presented in 1978); Rivoal (2000) showed infinitely many $\zeta(2n+1)$ are irrational, by bounding below the dimension of the $\mathbb Q$-span of $1$ and the odd zeta values; Zudilin (2001) showed at least one of $\zeta(5),\zeta(7),\zeta(9),\zeta(11)$ is irrational. ([Apéry's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ap%C3%A9ry%27s_theorem); [Rivoal, arXiv:math/0008051](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0008051))

### Examples
- $\zeta(2)=\pi^2/6$, from the even-value formula with $B_2=1/6$. ([DLMF §25.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.6))
- $\zeta(-1)=-B_2/2=-1/12$. This is a value of the continuation; the series $1+2+3+\cdots$ diverges. ([DLMF §25.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.6); [DLMF §25.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2))
- On the critical line, $Z(t)=e^{i\vartheta(t)}\zeta(\tfrac12+it)$ with $\vartheta(t)=\operatorname{ph}\Gamma(\tfrac14+\tfrac12it)-\tfrac12t\ln\pi$ is real with $|Z(t)|=|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|$, so zeros on the line are found as sign changes of $Z$. The Riemann–Siegel formula $Z(t)=2\sum_{n\le m}n^{-1/2}\cos(\vartheta(t)-t\ln n)+O(t^{-1/4})$, $m=\lfloor\sqrt{t/2\pi}\rfloor$, makes this computable; comparing sign changes with $N(T)$ verifies that no zeros up to height $T$ lie off the line. ([DLMF §25.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.10))

### History
Euler proved the product formula in 1737 and studied the series at positive integers. Riemann's 1859 paper introduced the complex variable, the continuation, the functional equation, and the hypothesis. Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved the prime number theorem independently in 1896 by showing $\zeta(1+it)\ne0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function); [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem)) Montgomery formulated his pair correlation conjecture in 1973, and Odlyzko's computations of zeros, including near height $10^{20}$, matched random-matrix spacing statistics. ([Montgomery's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery%27s_pair_correlation_conjecture))

### Connections
- [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis): continuation, the Hadamard product, and contour integration drive the theory.
- [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence): the Dirichlet series converges only for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$.
- [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function): supplies the archimedean factor in $\xi$ and the functional equation.
- [Jacobi Theta Functions](node:Jacobi%20Theta%20Functions): Riemann's second proof of the functional equation uses theta inversion.
- [Prime Numbers](node:Prime%20Numbers) and [Prime Number Theorem](node:Prime%20Number%20Theorem): the Euler product and explicit formula tie zeros to primes.
- [Analytic Number Theory](node:Analytic%20Number%20Theory) and [L-Functions](node:L-Functions): $\zeta$ is the degree-one prototype of an $L$-function.
- [Entire and Meromorphic Functions](node:Entire%20and%20Meromorphic%20Functions): $\xi$ is entire; Hadamard factorization gives its product.
- [Laplace and Mellin Transforms](node:Laplace%20and%20Mellin%20Transforms): the explicit formula arises from Mellin inversion.
- Map: [MSC 11Mxx - Zeta and L-functions - analytic theory](node:MSC%2011Mxx%20-%20Zeta%20and%20L-functions%20-%20analytic%20theory).

### Common pitfalls
- $\zeta$ has a pole at $1$, while $\xi$ is entire, so statements about zeros or growth must say which function they concern. ([Riemann Xi function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_Xi_function); [DLMF §25.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2))
- The symmetry $\xi(s)=\xi(1-s)$ pairs zeros $\rho\leftrightarrow1-\rho$; it does not place any zero on the critical line. ([DLMF §25.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.10))
- Numerical evidence is not a proof: Clay reports the hypothesis checked for the first $10^{13}$ zeros and still lists it as unsolved, since the statement concerns infinitely many zeros. ([Clay](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/))
- The Euler product formula is stated only for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$; it is not a valid representation in the critical strip. ([DLMF §25.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2))

### Open problems
- **Riemann hypothesis.** Every nontrivial zero has real part $\tfrac12$. It is unsolved and a Clay Millennium Prize Problem. ([Clay](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/))
