## Reference
### Overview
The Schwarzschild solution is the spherically symmetric vacuum solution of the Einstein field equations. It describes the field outside any spherically symmetric, non-rotating body and, maximally extended, the simplest black hole. It is asymptotically flat, reduces to Minkowski space as $M\to0$, and its parameter $M$ is the Newtonian mass measured by distant orbits ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7). It applies only outside the body, $r>R$, where it is matched to an interior solution ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)).

By Birkhoff's theorem it is the unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution, whether or not the source is static, so a spherically symmetric collapse leaves the exterior unchanged and a roughly spherical supernova should emit very little gravitational radiation ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7). Most solar-system tests of general relativity concern its geodesics: light deflection, perihelion precession, gravitational redshift and the Shapiro delay ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7; [Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377), §4).

Its global structure (horizon, Kruskal extension, white hole, second exterior, central singularity) is the template for black-hole physics ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7). Its stability is a central problem of mathematical relativity: linear stability was proved by Dafermos, Holzegel and Rodnianski ([arXiv:1601.06467](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.06467)), and non-linear stability under a codimension-3 condition on the data by Dafermos, Holzegel, Rodnianski and Taylor ([arXiv:2104.08222](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08222)).

### Formal definition
In Schwarzschild coordinates $(t,r,\theta,\phi)$, signature $(-,+,+,+)$, $c=1$:
$$ds^2=-\Big(1-\frac{2GM}{r}\Big)dt^2+\Big(1-\frac{2GM}{r}\Big)^{-1}dr^2+r^2\,d\Omega^2$$
([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eq. 7.29). With $c$ restored and signature $(+,-,-,-)$, $ds^2=(1-r_s/r)c^2dt^2-(1-r_s/r)^{-1}dr^2-r^2d\Omega^2$ with $r_s=2GM/c^2$; $r$ is the circumference of a centred sphere divided by $2\pi$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)).

**Horizon-regular forms.** Ingoing Eddington–Finkelstein: $(1-r_s/r)dv^2-2\,dv\,dr-r^2d\Omega^2$, regular across the future horizon. Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates with $T^2-R^2=(1-r/r_s)e^{r/r_s}$ are regular at $r=r_s$ and cover the maximal extension ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)).

**Geodesics.** Restricting to $\theta=\pi/2$, the Killing fields $\partial_t,\partial_\phi$ give conserved $E=(1-2GM/r)\,dt/d\lambda$ and $L=r^2\,d\phi/d\lambda$, and the radial equation becomes
$$\tfrac12\Big(\frac{dr}{d\lambda}\Big)^2+V(r)=\tfrac12E^2,\qquad V(r)=\tfrac12\epsilon-\epsilon\frac{GM}{r}+\frac{L^2}{2r^2}-\frac{GML^2}{r^3},$$
with $\epsilon=1$ for massive and $0$ for massless particles; the last term is the relativistic correction to the Newtonian potential ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eqs. 7.43–7.48).

### Key results
- **Birkhoff's theorem.** The Schwarzschild metric is the unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7; [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)). The extra Killing field $\partial_t$ is timelike, and the metric static, only for $r>2GM$: for $r<2GM$, $t$ becomes spacelike and $r$ timelike, so the interior is not static ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).
- **Singularities.** The Kretschmann scalar is $R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=48G^2M^2/(c^4r^6)$ ([Wikipedia: Kretschmann scalar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kretschmann_scalar)), so $r=0$ is a curvature singularity; $r=2GM$ is a coordinate singularity removed by Eddington–Finkelstein or Kruskal coordinates ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).
- **Event horizon.** $r=2GM$ is a null hypersurface; no event at $r\le2GM$ can influence any event at $r>2GM$, while infalling observers cross it without incident ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).
- **Circular orbits.** Massive particles have stable circular orbits for $r>6GM$ and unstable ones for $3GM<r<6GM$; $r=6GM$, reached at $L=\sqrt{12}\,GM$, is the innermost stable circular orbit, and $r=3GM$ is the unstable photon orbit ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eqs. 7.51–7.55); no circular orbits exist below $1.5\,r_s$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)).
- **Perihelion precession.** In the PPN framework the advance per orbit is $\Delta\tilde\omega=\frac{6\pi m}{p}\big[\tfrac13(2+2\gamma-\beta)+\frac{J_2R^2}{2mp}\big]$ (dropping a term negligible for Mercury), with $p=a(1-e^2)$ the semi-latus rectum; for Mercury this gives $42.98''\,[\tfrac13(2+2\gamma-\beta)+3\times10^{-4}(J_2/10^{-7})]$ per century, against an observed anomaly of $43''$ per century ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377), eqs. 64–65). General relativity has $\gamma=\beta=1$ ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377), Table 2).
- **Light deflection and Shapiro delay.** A ray passing the Sun at distance $d$ is deflected by $\delta\theta=\tfrac12(1+\gamma)\frac{4M_\odot}{d}\frac{1+\cos\Phi}{2}$, i.e. $\tfrac12(1+\gamma)\,1.7505''$ for a grazing ray. A radar round trip past the Sun is delayed by $\delta t=2(1+\gamma)M_\odot\ln\frac{(r_\oplus+\mathbf x_\oplus\cdot\mathbf n)(r_e-\mathbf x_e\cdot\mathbf n)}{d^2}$, about $\tfrac12(1+\gamma)[240-20\ln(d^2/r)]\,\mu$s near the Sun; Cassini tracking gave $\gamma-1=(2.1\pm2.3)\times10^{-5}$ ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377), eqs. 59–63, §4.1).
- **Gravitational redshift.** For static observers at $r_1,r_2$, a signal's crest intervals obey $\Delta\tau_2=\big[(1-2GM/r_2)/(1-2GM/r_1)\big]^{1/2}\Delta\tau_1$ ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eqs. 7.58–7.60).
- **Linear stability.** The perturbation analysis goes back to Regge and Wheeler, "Stability of a Schwarzschild Singularity", *Phys. Rev.* 108 (1957) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.108.1063)). Dafermos, Holzegel and Rodnianski proved that solutions of the linearised vacuum equations from regular data, in double null gauge, stay bounded on the exterior and decay at inverse-polynomial rates to a linearised Kerr metric after adding a pure-gauge solution controlled by the data; Teukolsky decay follows via Regge–Wheeler-type quantities ([arXiv:1601.06467](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.06467)).
- **Non-linear stability, polarized case.** Klainerman and Szeftel proved non-linear stability of Schwarzschild under axially symmetric polarized perturbations, the first such result for a restricted class of nontrivial perturbations, the restriction ensuring that the final state is again Schwarzschild ([arXiv:1711.07597](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.07597)).
- **Non-linear stability, codimension 3 (DHRT).** Vacuum data close to Schwarzschild and lying on a teleologically constructed codimension-3 submanifold of moduli space evolve to spacetimes with complete future null infinity, a regular future event horizon, closeness to Schwarzschild in the exterior, and convergence to a Schwarzschild member; data off the submanifold are expected to approach Kerr with $a\ne0$ ([arXiv:2104.08222](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08222)). Generic small perturbations are covered by non-linear stability of slowly rotating Kerr, $|a|/m\ll1$, whose proof Giorgi, Klainerman and Szeftel complete with their companion papers ([arXiv:2205.14808](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14808)).

### Examples
- **The Sun.** $R_\odot\approx10^6\,GM_\odot$ ($c=1$), so the horizon would lie deep inside the star, where the vacuum solution does not apply ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), eq. 7.31).
- **Mercury.** The relativistic perihelion advance is $42.98''$ per century for $\gamma=\beta=1$; Messenger-era fits with the Cassini bound on $\gamma$ give $\beta-1=(-4.1\pm7.8)\times10^{-5}$ ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377), §4.2).
- **Flamm's paraboloid.** The equatorial slice at fixed $t$ embeds as $w=2\sqrt{r_s(r-r_s)}$, reproducing spatial distances ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)).
- **Kruskal regions and the Penrose diagram.** The Kruskal diagram has four regions: our exterior I, the black hole II, whose every future-directed path ends at $r=0$, the white hole III (its time reverse, with a past singularity), and a second asymptotically flat exterior IV that cannot be reached from I. Spacelike slices show a wormhole joining I and IV that closes too fast for any observer to cross. In the Penrose diagram the two $r=0$ singularities run between the timelike infinities of the two exteriors, and conformal infinity has the structure of Minkowski space ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).

### History
Schwarzschild found the solution in 1915 and published it in January 1916; Droste found it independently in 1916 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)). The memoir appeared in the *Sitzungsberichte der Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin*, 1916, pp. 189–196, and an English translation is on arXiv ([Schwarzschild, transl. Antoci and Loinger](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/9905030)). Painlevé (1921) and Gullstrand (1922) wrote coordinates regular at $r=r_s$; Eddington (1924) showed the singularity there to be a coordinate artefact and Lemaître (1932) recognised it as unphysical; Robertson (1939) showed that free fall crosses $r_s$ in finite proper time; Synge (1950), then Kruskal and Szekeres (1960), gave the maximal extension ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)). Mercury's perihelion advance, unexplained since Le Verrier's 1859 announcement, was the first test of general relativity ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377), §4.2; [Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).

### Connections
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations): Schwarzschild is their simplest non-trivial exact vacuum solution.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the classical tests are computed in this geometry.
- [Black Holes](node:Black%20Holes): the maximal extension is the static, uncharged black hole.
- [Kerr Black Holes](node:Kerr%20Black%20Holes): the rotating generalisation; generic perturbations of Schwarzschild settle to Kerr.
- [Killing Vectors](node:Killing%20Vectors): $\partial_t$ and $\partial_\phi$ give the conserved $E$ and $L$; $\partial_t$ is timelike only outside the horizon.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): orbits and light rays are geodesics of the metric.
- [Penrose Diagrams](node:Penrose%20Diagrams): the Kruskal extension is the standard conformal-diagram example.
- [Parametrized Post-Newtonian Formalism](node:Parametrized%20Post-Newtonian%20Formalism): the framework in which deflection, delay and perihelion shift measure $\gamma,\beta$.
- [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing): light deflection by a point mass.
- [Tests of General Relativity](node:Tests%20of%20General%20Relativity): perihelion shift, deflection, redshift and Shapiro delay.
- [Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff Equation](node:Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff%20Equation): interior stellar solutions matched to the exterior.
- [Singularity Theorems in Relativity](node:Singularity%20Theorems%20in%20Relativity): the central singularity is not an artefact of symmetry.
- [Black Hole Quasinormal Modes](node:Black%20Hole%20Quasinormal%20Modes): the damped ringing of linear perturbations.
- [Hawking Radiation](node:Hawking%20Radiation) and [Black Hole Thermodynamics](node:Black%20Hole%20Thermodynamics): quantum and thermodynamic properties, simplest in this case.

### Common pitfalls
- **$r=2GM$ is not a curvature singularity.** Only the coordinates fail there ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).
- **The interior is not static.** Birkhoff gives local isometry to Schwarzschild, but inside the horizon $r$ is timelike and motion toward $r=0$ is unavoidable ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).
- **$r$ is circumferential**, not proper radial distance; Flamm's paraboloid shows the difference ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric)).
- **Use the semi-latus rectum.** The perihelion formula involves $p=a(1-e^2)$, not the semi-major axis $a$ ([Will](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377), eq. 64).
- **Light deflection is a weak-field test.** It does not probe the exact form of the geometry ([Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).
- **DHRT is not unconditional.** Its conclusions are proved for data on the codimension-3 submanifold; generic data approach Kerr with $a\ne0$ ([arXiv:2104.08222](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08222)).
- **Fringe readings of the original paper.** The arXiv translators argue that Schwarzschild's memoir "leaves no room" for black holes; this is their view, against the standard account in which $r=r_s$ is a regular null surface ([Schwarzschild, transl. Antoci and Loinger](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/9905030); [Carroll](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019), §7).

### Open problems
- **Kerr stability in the full sub-extremal range.** Since generic perturbations of Schwarzschild settle to Kerr ([arXiv:2104.08222](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08222)), the natural next problem is Kerr stability. Non-linear stability is proved for $|a|\ll M$, but in the full range $|a|<M$ it "remains a major open problem in the subject"; orbital stability for the linearised theory there "remains even more compellingly open", and the extremal case $|a|=M$ "is still open and understood to be far more challenging" ([Benomio and Teixeira da Costa](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.06828), §1).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Schwarzschild metric (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_metric): coordinate forms, singularities, orbits, embedding, history.
- **Learn:** [Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity, ch. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019): Birkhoff's theorem, geodesics and effective potential, classical tests, Kruskal and Penrose diagrams.
- **Primary:** [Schwarzschild 1916, English translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/9905030): the original memoir.
- **Primary:** [Dafermos, Holzegel and Rodnianski, The linear stability of the Schwarzschild solution to gravitational perturbations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.06467).
- **Primary:** [Dafermos, Holzegel, Rodnianski and Taylor, The non-linear stability of the Schwarzschild family of black holes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08222).
- **Primary:** [Klainerman and Szeftel, Global Nonlinear Stability of Schwarzschild Spacetime under Polarized Perturbations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.07597).
- **Further reading:** [Will, The Confrontation between General Relativity and Experiment](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377): review of PPN tests, including deflection, Shapiro delay and perihelion shift.
- **Further reading:** [Wald, General Relativity (University of Chicago Press, 1984)](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/G/bo5952261.html): classic textbook with chapters on the Schwarzschild solution, causal structure, singularities and black holes.
references.Scientific Benchmark Validity:
## Reference
### Overview
A benchmark score is a measurement: a fixed dataset, protocol and metric serve as an indicator of an unobservable quality such as the ability to do research. *Reliability* concerns the variance between repeated i.i.d. measurements; *validity* concerns whether it captures the intended concept, for which there is no simple formal criterion ([Hardt and Recht, Patterns, Predictions, and Actions](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242)). In psychometrics, *construct validity* is how well a set of indicators represents a concept that is not directly measurable; validation accumulates evidence across studies ([Wikipedia: Construct validity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construct_validity)).

For machine-learning benchmarks the question splits into a statistical and a conceptual part. The statistical part asks whether a score reflects population performance rather than noise, test-set reuse, or leakage; here [Statistical Learning Theory](node:Statistical%20Learning%20Theory), [Adaptive Data Analysis](node:Adaptive%20Data%20Analysis) and [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing) apply ([Hardt and Recht](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242); [Kapoor and Narayanan 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048)). The conceptual part asks whether success on the task licenses the broader claim attached to it: Raji et al. argue that reading top scores on a few "general" benchmarks as progress toward general AI has construct-validity problems ([Raji et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.15366)).

Research-competence benchmarks add their own measurement problems: grading relies on rubrics and LLM judges, and pretraining contamination is a known concern ([PaperBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848); [MLE-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095); [Bean et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04703v1)).

### Formal definition
**Holdout estimate.** Let $\mathcal D$ be a distribution over labelled examples, $S=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n$ an i.i.d. test sample and $\ell$ a loss in $[0,1]$. For a classifier $f$ the population risk is $R_{\mathcal D}(f)=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}\,\ell(f(x),y)$ and the empirical (benchmark) risk is $R_S(f)=\frac1n\sum_{i}\ell(f(x_i),y_i)$. If $f_1,\dots,f_k$ are fixed independently of $S$, Hoeffding's inequality and a union bound give
$$\Pr\{\exists t\in[k]:\ |R_S(f_t)-R_{\mathcal D}(f_t)|>\varepsilon\}\le 2k\,e^{-2\varepsilon^2 n}.$$
([Blum and Hardt 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585))

**Leaderboard error.** An adaptive analyst picks $f_t=\mathcal A(f_1,R_1,\dots,f_{t-1},R_{t-1})$ from released scores $R_i$, so Hoeffding's bound no longer applies ([Blum and Hardt 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)). For such $f_1,\dots,f_k$,
$$\operatorname{lberr}(R_1,\dots,R_k)=\max_{1\le t\le k}\Bigl|\min_{1\le i\le t}R_{\mathcal D}(f_i)-R_t\Bigr|,$$
so the leaderboard need only track the true risk of the best model submitted so far ([Blum and Hardt 2015, Def. 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)).

**Model similarity.** Predictors $f_1,\dots,f_k$ with empirical risks $R_i$ are $\zeta$-similar if for every pair with $R_i\le R_j$, $\Pr[\{f_j(x)=y\}\cap\{f_i(x)\ne y\}]\le\zeta$: a lower-risk model rarely errs where a higher-risk model is right ([Hardt and Recht, Def. 11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242)). Mania et al. work with $\{0,1\}$-valued queries $q$ (the 0/1 losses of classifiers) and define a set $M$ to be an *$\eta$-similarity cover* of a query set $F$ if every $q\in F$ has $q',q''\in M$ with $\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[q']\le\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[q]\le\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[q'']$ and $\Pr(q'(z)=q(z))\ge\eta$, $\Pr(q''(z)=q(z))\ge\eta$; $N_\eta(F)$ is the size of a minimal cover ([Mania et al. 2019, Def. 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.12580)).

**Item response model of a benchmark.** The two-parameter multidimensional IRT model used by tinyBenchmarks posits that model $l$ answers item $i$ correctly with probability $p_{il}=\bigl(1+\exp(-\alpha_i^\top\theta_l+\beta_i)\bigr)^{-1}$, where $\theta_l\in\mathbb R^d$ are the model's latent abilities, $\alpha_i\in\mathbb R^d$ selects which abilities item $i$ requires and $\beta_i$ is a difficulty offset ([Polo et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.14992)). Fitting $\theta_l$ with item parameters fixed is a [Logistic Regression](node:Logistic%20Regression) ([Polo et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.14992)).

**Construct validity (Messick).** Messick treats validity as an integrated judgment of how far evidence and theory support inferences from scores, with six aspects: content, substantive, structural, generalizability, external, consequential ([Wikipedia: Construct validity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construct_validity); [Hardt and Recht](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242)). Campbell and Fiske's multitrait-multimethod matrix tests convergent and discriminant validity ([Wikipedia: Construct validity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construct_validity)).

### Key results
- **Adaptive overfitting lower bound.** Choose $k$ random binary predictors, keep those with $R_S(f_i)<1/2$, and output their majority vote. For sufficiently large $k\le n$, with probability $1/3$ the result has $R_S(f)\le\tfrac12-\Omega(\sqrt{k/n})$ while its true risk is $1/2$, a generalization gap of $\Omega(\sqrt{k/n})$, against $O(\sqrt{\log k/n})$ non-adaptively ([Hardt and Recht, Prop. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242)). The same attack works against a leaderboard reporting losses to within $n^{-1/2}$ ([Blum and Hardt, Thm. 5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)).
- **Adaptive holdout upper bound.** For any $k$ adaptively chosen predictors under 0/1 loss, the holdout method satisfies $\max_{t\le k}|R_S(f_t)-R_{\mathcal D}(f_t)|\le O(\sqrt{k\log(n+1)/n})$ with probability $2/3$; the proof bounds the analyst's data-independent query tree by $(n+1)^k$ nodes ([Hardt and Recht, Prop. 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242)).
- **The Ladder mechanism.** Release a new score only when $R_S(f_t)<R_{t-1}-\eta$, rounded to a multiple of $\eta$; otherwise repeat $R_{t-1}$. For any adaptively chosen $f_1,\dots,f_k$, all $t\le k$ and $\varepsilon>0$, $\Pr\{|\min_{i\le t}R_{\mathcal D}(f_i)-R_t|>\varepsilon+\eta\}\le\exp(-2\varepsilon^2n+(1/\eta+2)\log(4t/\eta)+1)$; with $\eta=O(n^{-1/3}\log^{1/3}(kn))$ this gives $\operatorname{lberr}=O(\log^{1/3}(kn)/n^{1/3})$ with high probability. Even for non-adaptive classifiers there is a minimax lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{\log k/n})$ on expected leaderboard error ([Blum and Hardt, Thms. 3.1 and 3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)). A randomized variant improves the rate to $O(n^{-0.4})$ ([Hardt 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02733)).
- **Similarity-aware bounds.** For $k$ queries fixed independently of the test set, the probability of an $\varepsilon$-deviation is bounded by a term proportional to $N_\eta$ plus a term in $k$ that shrinks as $\eta$ grows, improving the $\log k/n$ guarantee even for $\eta$ far below $1-\varepsilon$ ([Mania et al. 2019, Thm. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.12580)). In the adaptive setting, if the analyst's $(n+1)^{k-1}$ possible queries admit a similarity cover with $N_\eta\le(n+1)^{k^{1-\alpha}}$, the plain holdout's error scales with $k^{1-\alpha}$ in place of $k$; for $\alpha=1/2$ this is a quadratic improvement in the number of queries, comparable to the Gaussian mechanism ([Mania et al. 2019, Cor. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.12580)).
- **Reusable holdout.** Perturbing released estimates with privacy techniques allows an exponential-in-$n$ number of adaptively chosen expectations to be estimated accurately, against a linear number for plain empirical averages ([Dwork et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.2664)); see [Differential Privacy](node:Differential%20Privacy). Under a standard hardness assumption no computationally efficient estimator achieves $o(1)$ error on more than $n^{2+o(1)}$ adaptively chosen functions ([Blum and Hardt 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)).
- **Paired comparison and power.** Treating questions as draws from a super-population, two models scored on the same questions have $\operatorname{SE}_{A-B}=\sqrt{\operatorname{SE}_A^2+\operatorname{SE}_B^2-2\operatorname{SE}_A\operatorname{SE}_B\operatorname{Corr}(s_A,s_B)}$; questions sharing a passage need clustered standard errors. Detecting a difference $\delta$ at level $\alpha$ with power $1-\beta$ needs $n=(z_{\alpha/2}+z_\beta)^2(\omega^2+\sigma_A^2/K_A+\sigma_B^2/K_B)/\delta^2$ questions, $K_M$ being resampled answers per question; with $\omega^2=1/9$, $\delta=0.03$, $\alpha=0.05$, $\beta=0.2$ this is about 969 ([Miller 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.00640v1)). See [Bootstrap Methods](node:Bootstrap%20Methods).
- **IRT-based small benchmarks.** Using item parameters fitted on many models, tinyBenchmarks' IRT++ estimator predicts recent LLMs' accuracy on all 14K MMLU examples from 100 curated examples to within 1.9% on average; correctness-based example selection is the strategy most affected when the evaluated models differ in distribution from those used for fitting ([Polo et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.14992)).

### Examples
- **CIFAR-10.1 and ImageNetV2.** Fresh test sets built by the original process showed drops of 3–15% on CIFAR-10 and 11–14% on ImageNet, yet gains on the old test sets translated into larger gains on the new ones; the authors conclude the drops are not caused by adaptivity but by somewhat harder images ([Recht et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10811)).
- **Kaggle meta-analysis.** Over a hundred Kaggle competitions showed little evidence of substantial overfitting from holdout reuse ([Roelofs et al. 2019](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/hash/ee39e503b6bedf0c98c388b7e8589aca-Abstract.html)).
- **Underpowered NLP comparisons.** On several GLUE tasks most comparisons to state-of-the-art models are underpowered, and a typical 2,000-sentence translation test set has about 75% power to detect a 1 BLEU difference ([Card et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.06595)).
- **Dynamic benchmarking.** Dynabench has annotators write examples that a target model gets wrong but a human would answer correctly ([Kiela et al. 2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.naacl-main.324/)). Bowman and Dahl argue the opposite: adversarial, out-of-distribution test sets ensure poor model performance but obscure the abilities a benchmark should measure ([Bowman and Dahl 2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.naacl-main.385/)).
- **Research-competence benchmarks.** PaperBench asks agents to replicate 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers, with 8,316 rubric items scored by an LLM judge that is itself checked on a judge benchmark; the best agent averaged 21.0%, and models did not beat a baseline set by top ML PhD students ([Starace et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848)). MLE-bench uses 75 Kaggle competitions with human baselines from public leaderboards and studies the effect of pretraining contamination ([Chan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095)).

### History
Cronbach and Meehl introduced construct validity in 1955 with the nomological network; Campbell and Fiske's multitrait-multimethod matrix (1959) and Messick's unified view (1989, 1995) followed ([Wikipedia: Construct validity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construct_validity)). Goodhart's 1975 law became, in Strathern's 1997 wording, "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" ([Wikipedia: Goodhart's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law)). In machine learning, adaptive data analysis ([Dwork et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.2664)) and the Ladder ([Blum and Hardt](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)) formalized test-set reuse, followed by the 2019 reproduction studies ([Recht et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10811)) and a 2025 review of 445 LLM benchmarks ([Bean et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04703v1)).

### Connections
- [Machine Learning Evaluation](node:Machine%20Learning%20Evaluation): the practice whose inferential limits are studied here.
- [Statistical Learning Theory](node:Statistical%20Learning%20Theory), [Concentration of Measure](node:Concentration%20of%20Measure), [Covering Numbers and Metric Entropy](node:Covering%20Numbers%20and%20Metric%20Entropy): union, concentration and covering arguments behind holdout and similarity bounds.
- [Adaptive Data Analysis](node:Adaptive%20Data%20Analysis), [Differential Privacy](node:Differential%20Privacy): test-set reuse theory and the stability tool behind the reusable holdout.
- [Hypothesis Testing](node:Hypothesis%20Testing), [Multiple Testing and False Discovery Control](node:Multiple%20Testing%20and%20False%20Discovery%20Control): significance, power and selection across compared models.
- [Bootstrap Methods](node:Bootstrap%20Methods), [Cross-Validation](node:Cross-Validation): resampling estimates of uncertainty and generalization.
- [Logistic Regression](node:Logistic%20Regression): the fitting step of IRT ability estimation.
- [Benchmark Contamination Detection](node:Benchmark%20Contamination%20Detection), [Data Leakage and Temporal Evaluation](node:Data%20Leakage%20and%20Temporal%20Evaluation): threats that break the i.i.d. holdout assumption.
- [Adversarial Robustness](node:Adversarial%20Robustness): adversarial test construction.

### Common pitfalls
- **Ignoring reuse.** After selection on released scores the worst-case gap is $\Omega(\sqrt{k/n})$, not $O(\sqrt{\log k/n})$ ([Hardt and Recht](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242)).
- **Conflating distribution shift with overfitting.** A drop on a fresh test set can come from a harder data distribution even when adaptive overfitting is small ([Recht et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10811)).
- **Comparing point estimates without uncertainty.** Only 16.0% of the 445 reviewed LLM benchmarks conducted any statistical testing ([Bean et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04703v1)); on Atari 100k, point estimates led to conclusions that interval estimates did not support ([Agarwal et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.13264)).
- **Benchmark-choice effects.** Choosing different benchmark tasks can significantly alter the relative performance of algorithms ([Dehghani et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07002)).
- **Leakage.** Leakage errors have been found in 17 fields, affecting 329 papers; Kapoor and Narayanan give an eight-type taxonomy and propose model info sheets ([Kapoor and Narayanan 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048)).
- **Contamination despite good faith.** Bean et al. state that benchmark contamination is likely even when developers act in good faith ([Bean et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04703v1)).
- **Unvalidated scoring.** 81.3% of reviewed LLM benchmarks used exact match at least partly (40.7% exclusively) and 17.1% used an LLM judge at least partly (3.1% exclusively) ([Bean et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04703v1)). Judges need their own validation: GPT-4 as judge reached over 80% agreement with human preferences on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, the level humans reach with each other, but showed position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases and limited reasoning ability ([Zheng et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)).

### Open problems
- **Optimal adaptive leaderboard error.** A gap separates the $\Omega(\sqrt{\log k/n})$ lower bound from the $O(n^{-0.4})$ randomized-Ladder rate; Hardt shows that improving the upper bound would give asymptotic improvements for general adaptive estimation, which "have remained elusive" ([Hardt 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02733); [Blum and Hardt 2015](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)).
- **Why adaptivity is benign in practice.** Hardt and Recht state that model similarity and the leaderboard principle do not explain the entirety of why overfitting is not observed ([Hardt and Recht](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242)). Mania et al. list as future work explaining why classifiers are so similar, whether similarity arises beyond image classification, and a statistical procedure that exploits model structure to give reliable bounds under test-set reuse ([Mania et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.12580)).
- **Hard leakage types.** Kapoor and Narayanan's taxonomy of leakage ranges "from textbook errors to open research problems" ([Kapoor and Narayanan 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Construct validity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construct_validity): psychometric validity theory.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Goodhart's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law): Goodhart's statement and Strathern's formulation.
- **Learn:** [Hardt and Recht, Patterns, Predictions, and Actions (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.05242): Chapter 8 "Datasets" on holdout reuse and measurement validity.
- **Learn:** [Empirical Foundations of Machine Learning (University of Washington, Autumn 2021)](https://mlfoundations.github.io/au21/): Ludwig Schmidt's course on benchmarks, confidence intervals and test-set overfitting.
- **Primary:** [Blum and Hardt 2015, The Ladder](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04585): leaderboard error and the Ladder.
- **Primary:** [Mania et al. 2019, Model Similarity Mitigates Test Set Overuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.12580): similarity-aware holdout bounds.
- **Primary:** [Polo et al. 2024, tinyBenchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14992): IRT models of benchmarks.
- **Primary:** [Zheng et al. 2023, Judging LLM-as-a-Judge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685): LLM-judge validation.
- **Primary:** [Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04703v1): construct validity in 445 LLM benchmarks.
- **Further reading:** [Hardt and Recht, Patterns, Predictions, and Actions (Princeton University Press, 2022)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691233734/patterns-predictions-and-actions): graduate textbook with a chapter on benchmarks and datasets.
references.Self-Supervised and Contrastive Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Self-supervised learning (SSL) trains a model on a task whose supervisory signal is generated from the data itself, typically by augmenting inputs into related pairs. Three families are usually distinguished: autoassociative (reconstruct the input, e.g. autoencoders), contrastive (pull positive pairs together and push negatives apart, e.g. with InfoNCE), and non-contrastive (use only positives and avoid trivial solutions by other means, e.g. BYOL's predictor with no backpropagation through the target side) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-supervised_learning)). Liu et al. group methods by objective into generative, contrastive and generative-contrastive (adversarial) approaches across vision, language and graphs, and file autoregressive language models such as GPT, trained by next-word prediction, under generative SSL ([Liu et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2006.08218)).

In language, BERT's masked language model selects 15% of tokens, replaces 80% of those with `[MASK]`, 10% with a random token and leaves 10% unchanged, and predicts the originals with a cross-entropy loss; unlike left-to-right models, the representation fuses left and right context ([Devlin et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1810.04805)). In vision, SimCLR showed that composed augmentations, a nonlinear projection head and large batches give a linear probe of 76.5% top-1 on ImageNet, matching a supervised ResNet-50 ([Chen et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2002.05709)); BYOL drops negatives and reaches 74.3% ([Grill et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.07733)); masked autoencoders hide 75% of image patches and reconstruct them with an asymmetric encoder–decoder ([He et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.06377)); and joint-embedding predictive architectures predict masked content in latent space ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-supervised_learning)).

The central failure mode of joint-embedding methods is *collapse*, where the network maps every input to the same vector. Contrastive objectives block it by repelling negatives; clustering methods such as SwAV use an equipartition constraint enforced by Sinkhorn–Knopp ([NYU Deep Learning notes](https://atcold.github.io/NYU-DLSP21/en/week10/10-1/)). MoCo keeps a FIFO queue of keys from a momentum encoder, decoupling the number of negatives from batch size, and contrasts this with the memory bank of Wu et al. 2018 ([He et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.05722)). A milder failure, *dimensional collapse* (embeddings spanning a low-dimensional subspace), occurs even in contrastive learning ([Jing et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.09348)).

### Formal definition
**InfoNCE.** Given context $c_t$ and $X=\{x_1,\dots,x_N\}$ containing one positive from $p(x_{t+k}\mid c_t)$ and $N-1$ negatives from $p(x_{t+k})$, with positive score $f_k$,
$$\mathcal L_N=-\mathbb E_X\left[\log\frac{f_k(x_{t+k},c_t)}{\sum_{x_j\in X} f_k(x_j,c_t)}\right],$$
the cross-entropy of identifying the positive. CPC uses $f_k = \exp(z_{t+k}^\top W_k c_t)$, and the optimal $f_k$ is proportional to $p(x_{t+k}\mid c_t)/p(x_{t+k})$ ([van den Oord et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1807.03748)).

**NT-Xent (SimCLR).** $N$ images, each augmented twice, give $2N$ examples; with $z=g(h)=W^{(2)}\sigma(W^{(1)}h)$, cosine similarity $\mathrm{sim}$ and temperature $\tau$,
$$\ell_{i,j}=-\log\frac{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(z_i,z_j)/\tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{2N}\mathbb 1_{[k\neq i]}\exp(\mathrm{sim}(z_i,z_k)/\tau)},$$
so the other $2(N-1)$ examples are negatives ([Chen et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2002.05709)).

**MoCo.** Queries from encoder $\theta_q$ are contrasted by InfoNCE against one positive key and $K$ queued negative keys from a key encoder updated as $\theta_k \leftarrow m\theta_k + (1-m)\theta_q$, with $m=0.999$ and $\tau=0.07$ by default ([He et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.05722)).

**SwAV.** For two views with features $z_t, z_s$ and codes $q_t, q_s$, $L(z_t,z_s)=\ell(z_t,q_s)+\ell(z_s,q_t)$ with $\ell(z,q)=-\sum_k q^{(k)}\log p^{(k)}$ and $p^{(k)}\propto\exp(z^\top c_k/\tau)$ over $K$ prototypes. Codes maximize $\operatorname{Tr}(Q^\top C^\top Z)+\varepsilon H(Q)$ over a transportation polytope (equal use of prototypes per batch), solved as $Q^*=\operatorname{Diag}(u)\exp(C^\top Z/\varepsilon)\operatorname{Diag}(v)$ by a few Sinkhorn–Knopp iterations ([Caron et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2006.09882)).

**Barlow Twins.** With $\mathcal C_{ij}$ the cross-correlation between dimensions $i$ and $j$ of the two views' batch-centred embeddings,
$$\mathcal L_{BT}=\sum_i(1-\mathcal C_{ii})^2+\lambda\sum_i\sum_{j\ne i}\mathcal C_{ij}^2,$$
an invariance term plus a redundancy-reduction term ([Zbontar et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.03230)).

**VICReg.** For embedding batches $Z,Z'$ of size $n$ and dimension $d$: variance $v(Z)=\frac1d\sum_j\max(0,\gamma-\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(z^j)+\epsilon})$, covariance $c(Z)=\frac1d\sum_{i\ne j}[C(Z)]_{ij}^2$, invariance $s(Z,Z')=\frac1n\sum_i\lVert z_i-z_i'\rVert_2^2$, and loss $\lambda s+\mu[v(Z)+v(Z')]+\nu[c(Z)+c(Z')]$ with defaults $\gamma=1$, $\lambda=\mu=25$, $\nu=1$ ([Bardes et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.04906)).

**Alignment and uniformity.** For $f:\mathbb R^n\to S^{m-1}$, $\mathcal L_{\text{align}}(f;\alpha)=\mathbb E_{p_{\text{pos}}}\lVert f(x)-f(y)\rVert_2^\alpha$ and $\mathcal L_{\text{uniform}}(f;t)=\log\mathbb E_{x,y\sim p_{\text{data}}}e^{-t\lVert f(x)-f(y)\rVert_2^2}$, $\alpha,t>0$ ([Wang and Isola 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.10242)).

### Key results
- **InfoNCE bounds mutual information.** $I(x_{t+k};c_t)\ge\log N-\mathcal L_N$, tighter as $N$ grows ([van den Oord et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1807.03748)). The bound is itself at most $\log K$ for batch size $K$, so it is loose when $I(X;Y)>\log K$; the NWJ bound becomes tight with the optimal critic but has high variance, and an interpolated bound $I_\alpha$ trades the two with ceiling $\log(K/\alpha)$ ([Poole et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.06922)).
- **No distribution-free MI lower bound beats $O(\ln N)$ (McAllester–Stratos, Thm 1.1).** If $B$ maps $N$ i.i.d. samples to a number with $I(X;Y)\ge B$ with probability $\ge 0.99$ for every $p_{XY}$, then for any $q_{XY}$ and $N\ge 50$, $B\le 2\ln N+5$ with probability $\ge 0.96$ ([McAllester and Stratos 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1811.04251)).
- **Asymptotics of the contrastive loss (Wang–Isola, Theorem 1).** For fixed $\tau>0$, encoders onto $S^{m-1}$, symmetric $p_{\text{pos}}$ with marginals $p_{\text{data}}$, and $M$ i.i.d. negatives, $\mathcal L_{\text{contrastive}}-\log M$ converges as $M\to\infty$ to $-\tfrac1\tau\mathbb E_{p_{\text{pos}}}[f(x)^\top f(y)]+\mathbb E_x\big[\log\mathbb E_{x^-}e^{f(x^-)^\top f(x)/\tau}\big]$. The first term is minimized iff $f$ is perfectly aligned; perfectly uniform encoders, if they exist, minimize the second; the deviation decays as $O(M^{-1/2})$. Perfectly uniform encoders exist when $n\ge m-1$ and $p_{\text{data}}$ has bounded density ([Wang and Isola 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.10242)).
- **Downstream guarantees under latent classes.** If semantically similar points are sampled from the same latent class, minimizing a contrastive loss gives provable guarantees on average classification over subsets of those classes, with a generalization bound showing reduced labelled sample complexity ([Arora et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.09229)).
- **Spectral contrastive loss (HaoChen et al.).** On the augmentation graph with $w_{xx'}=\mathbb E_{\bar x}[A(x\mid\bar x)A(x'\mid\bar x)]$, the loss $\mathcal L(f)=-2\,\mathbb E[f(x)^\top f(x^+)]+\mathbb E[(f(x)^\top f(x^-))^2]$ factorizes the normalized adjacency matrix. If labels are recoverable from augmentations with error $\alpha$, the hypothesis class contains a minimizer and $k\ge 2r$, the linear-probe error of the population minimizer is $\tilde O(\alpha/\rho^2_{\lfloor k/2\rfloor})$, with $\rho$ a Dirichlet-conductance sparsest-partition quantity; Rademacher-complexity bounds transfer this to the empirical minimizer. No conditional independence of views is assumed ([HaoChen et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2106.04156)).
- **Non-contrastive dynamics (Tian, Chen and Ganguli).** In a linear model of SimSiam (no negatives, online and target weights identical), removing the stop-gradient gives a gradient flow $\tfrac{d}{dt}\operatorname{vec}(W)=-H(t)\operatorname{vec}(W)$ with $H(t)$ positive semidefinite, so $W(t)\to0$ (collapse) whenever $\lambda_{\min}(H(t))$ stays bounded below by a positive constant; with stop-gradient, under stated conditions the predictor's eigenspaces align with those of the input correlation matrix $F$, and each mode has a collapsed and a non-collapsed fixed point, with weight decay and predictor learning rate shaping the collapse basin. Setting the predictor directly from $F$'s eigendecomposition (DirectPred) reaches 72.4% top-1 on ImageNet at 300 epochs, matching BYOL's two-layer predictor (72.5%) ([Tian et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.06810)).
- **Negatives do not prevent dimensional collapse.** Contrastive embeddings can span a lower-dimensional subspace; DirectCLR, which optimizes the representation without a trainable projector, outperforms SimCLR's linear projector on ImageNet ([Jing et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.09348)).

### Examples
- **CPC** predicts future latents with an autoregressive context model and InfoNCE, evaluated on speech, images, text and 3D [reinforcement learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning) ([van den Oord et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1807.03748)).
- **SimCLR** reaches 85.8% top-5 on ImageNet with 1% of labels; random crop plus colour distortion is critical ([Chen et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2002.05709)).
- **MoCo** reaches 60.6% top-1 linear accuracy with ResNet-50 and beats supervised pretraining on 7 detection and segmentation tasks ([He et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.05722)).
- **SwAV** reaches 75.3% top-1 with ResNet-50 using multi-crop ([Caron et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2006.09882)); **Barlow Twins** 73.2% with no predictor, stop-gradient or momentum encoder ([Zbontar et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.03230)).
- **MAE** with ViT-Huge reaches 87.8% on ImageNet-1K and trains at least three times faster because the encoder sees only visible patches ([He et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.06377)).
- **Pretext tasks** such as relative patch position, jigsaw puzzles and rotation prediction preceded contrastive methods; PIRL instead seeks invariance to the data augmentation (for example the jigsaw permutation) rather than predicting it ([NYU Deep Learning notes](https://atcold.github.io/NYU-DLSP21/en/week10/10-1/)).
- **Multimodal:** CLIP pretrains a text encoder and an image encoder so matching image–text pairs have high cosine similarity ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-supervised_learning)).

### History
Precursors include Kramer's autoassociative networks (1991) and Becker and Hinton's networks maximizing agreement between inputs (1992); context-prediction pretext tasks appeared in 2015, BYOL in 2020, Barlow Twins and VICReg in 2021, and LeCun's JEPA proposal in 2022 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-supervised_learning)). CPC introduced the InfoNCE loss ([van den Oord et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1807.03748)), and MoCo's queue replaced the memory bank of Wu et al. 2018 ([He et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.05722)). The 2023 Cookbook was written because SSL has a high barrier to entry and many design choices ([Balestriero et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.12210)).

### Connections
- [Deep Learning](node:Deep%20Learning): SSL is the main pretraining regime when labels are scarce.
- [Contrastive Collapse and Negative Sampling](node:Contrastive%20Collapse%20and%20Negative%20Sampling): collapse and negative selection in depth.
- [Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures](node:Joint-Embedding%20Predictive%20Architectures): latent-prediction branch (I-JEPA, V-JEPA).
- [Masked Autoencoders](node:Masked%20Autoencoders) and [Masked Representation Learning](node:Masked%20Representation%20Learning): the reconstruction branch.
- [Language Model Pretraining Objectives](node:Language%20Model%20Pretraining%20Objectives): masked and next-token prediction as self-supervision for text.
- [Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining](node:Contrastive%20Language-Image%20Pretraining): InfoNCE across modalities.
- [Information Theory](node:Information%20Theory): InfoNCE as a mutual-information lower bound and its $\log N$ ceiling.
- [Information Bottleneck](node:Information%20Bottleneck): Barlow Twins is presented as an approximate instance.
- [Optimal Transport](node:Optimal%20Transport): SwAV's codes solve an entropy-regularized transport problem.
- [Spectral Clustering](node:Spectral%20Clustering): the spectral contrastive loss factorizes the augmentation-graph adjacency.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss): InfoNCE and NT-Xent are cross-entropies over one positive among $N$.
- [Semi-Supervised Learning](node:Semi-Supervised%20Learning): SSL representations are fine-tuned with few labels.
- [Knowledge Distillation](node:Knowledge%20Distillation): BYOL-style target networks resemble self-distillation.
- [Vision Transformers](node:Vision%20Transformers): the backbone for MAE and JEPA.

### Common pitfalls
- **Reading InfoNCE as an MI estimator.** It is capped at $\log K$, and no distribution-free high-confidence lower bound can exceed $O(\ln N)$, so small batches cannot certify large mutual information ([Poole et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.06922); [McAllester and Stratos 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1811.04251)).
- **Evaluating the projection-head output.** SimCLR's pre-head representation transfers better than the post-head one ([Chen et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2002.05709)).
- **Assuming negatives rule out collapse.** Dimensional collapse still occurs ([Jing et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.09348)).
- **Over-reading alignment and uniformity.** When positives are augmentations of a finite dataset, no encoder is both perfectly aligned and perfectly uniform, since alignment forces all augmentations of a sample to one feature; in general the paper says only that the two are "likely hard to simultaneously achieve in practice" ([Wang and Isola 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.10242)).
- **Calling MoCo's dictionary a memory bank.** MoCo uses a queue of momentum-encoded keys; its ablation finds it 2.6% more accurate than a memory bank ([He et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.05722)).
- **Dropping stop-gradient in BYOL-style methods.** In the linear SimSiam analysis this leads to collapse of the weights to zero ([Tian et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.06810)).

### Open problems
- **Theoretical foundations and sampling strategies.** Liu et al.'s future-directions section calls for more theory of why SSL works, better transfer of pretrained representations to downstream tasks and across datasets, exploring sampling strategies with many negatives and augmented positives, and avoiding early degeneration of contrastive objectives; elsewhere the survey calls the role of negatives "not clear enough" and the theory of augmentation "still quite ambiguous" ([Liu et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2006.08218)).
- **Non-contrastive dynamics beyond the linear symmetric case.** Tian et al. assume a symmetric linear predictor, leave the asymmetric case to future work, give only an intuition for two-layer predictors and leave a thorough analysis of that setting to future work ([Tian et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.06810)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Self-supervised learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-supervised_learning): families, JEPA, timeline.
- **Learn:** [NYU Deep Learning, SSL in computer vision](https://atcold.github.io/NYU-DLSP21/en/week10/10-1/): pretext tasks, PIRL, SimCLR, MoCo, SwAV, collapse.
- **Primary:** [Chen et al. 2020, SimCLR](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2002.05709); [van den Oord et al. 2018, CPC](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1807.03748): InfoNCE; [He et al. 2019, MoCo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.05722); [Wang and Isola 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2005.10242): alignment and uniformity.
- **Primary:** [Tian, Chen and Ganguli 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2102.06810): non-contrastive learning dynamics; [Zbontar et al. 2021, Barlow Twins](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2103.03230).
- **Further reading:** [Bishop and Bishop, Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (Springer 2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-45468-4); [Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics (MIT Press 2023)](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book2.html); [Balestriero et al. 2023, A Cookbook of Self-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.12210): survey of recipes; [Liu et al., Self-supervised Learning: Generative or Contrastive](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2006.08218): survey.
references.Series and Convergence:
## Reference
### Overview
An infinite series $\sum a_n$ is assigned a value through its sequence of partial sums: the series converges when that sequence converges. Convergence is therefore a question about limits of sequences, and every criterion for series is ultimately a statement about the sequence $s_N=\sum_{n\le N}a_n$. Numerical series, power series, and series of functions share this framework, but each raises its own convergence questions. ([Lebl, series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_series.html); [Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Series_%28mathematics%29))

Two distinctions organise the subject. For numerical series, absolute convergence behaves like a finite sum (it survives rearrangement and multiplication), while conditional convergence is fragile: a conditionally convergent real series can be rearranged to have any sum. For series of functions, pointwise convergence does not justify exchanging the sum with limits, integrals, or derivatives; uniform convergence, typically certified by the Weierstrass M-test, supplies the needed control. ([Riemann series theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_series_theorem); [Lebl, interchange of limits](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_liminter.html))

A third theme is the relation between ordinary convergence and weaker summation methods. Abel's theorem says that a convergent series is Abel summable to the same value; Tauberian theorems give conditions under which the converse holds. These ideas are used well beyond elementary analysis, for instance in the Hardy–Littlewood approach to the prime number theorem. ([Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%27s_theorem); [Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem))

### Formal definition
For real or complex $a_n$ put $s_N=\sum_{n=1}^N a_n$. The series converges to $s$ if $s_N\to s$; it converges absolutely if $\sum|a_n|$ converges, and conditionally if it converges but not absolutely. Absolute convergence implies convergence. ([Lebl, series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_series.html))

**Cauchy criterion.** $\sum a_n$ converges if and only if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $M$ such that $\left|\sum_{i=n+1}^{k}a_i\right|<\varepsilon$ for all $k>n\ge M$. In particular $a_n\to 0$ is necessary for convergence. ([Lebl, series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_series.html); [Convergence tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests))

For functions $f_n$ on a set $A$, $\sum f_n$ converges uniformly on $A$ if its partial sums converge uniformly; it converges normally if $\sum\sup_A|f_n|<\infty$. ([Weierstrass M-test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_M-test))

### Key results
- **Comparison and limit comparison.** If $0\le a_n\le b_n$ and $\sum b_n$ converges, so does $\sum a_n$. If $a_n,b_n>0$ and $\lim a_n/b_n$ exists, is finite and nonzero, then $\sum a_n$ and $\sum b_n$ converge or diverge together. The $p$-series $\sum n^{-p}$ converges iff $p>1$. ([Lebl, series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_series.html); [Convergence tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests))
- **Ratio and root tests.** Let $L=\limsup_n|a_n|^{1/n}$. If $L<1$ the series converges absolutely; if $L>1$ it diverges; $L=1$ is inconclusive. For nonzero terms with $\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|=L$, the same conclusions hold. ([Lebl, more on series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_moreonseries.html); [Lebl, series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_series.html))
- **Integral and condensation tests.** If $f:[1,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is nonincreasing with $f(n)=a_n$, then $\sum a_n$ converges iff $\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx<\infty$. If $a_n\ge 0$ is nonincreasing, $A=\sum_{n\ge1} a_n$ converges iff $A^*=\sum_{n\ge0} 2^n a_{2^n}$ converges, and then $A\le A^*\le 2A$. ([Convergence tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests))
- **Alternating series, Dirichlet and Abel tests.** If $x_n>0$ decreases to $0$, then $\sum(-1)^n x_n$ converges. (Dirichlet) If $a_n$ is real, nonincreasing with $a_n\to0$, and the partial sums of $\sum b_n$ are bounded, then $\sum a_nb_n$ converges. (Abel) If $\sum a_n$ converges and $(b_n)$ is monotone and bounded, then $\sum a_nb_n$ converges. ([Lebl, more on series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_moreonseries.html); [Convergence tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests))
- **Rearrangements (Riemann).** Every rearrangement of an absolutely convergent series converges absolutely to the same sum. If a real series converges conditionally, then for every $M\in\mathbb R$ some rearrangement converges to $M$, and others diverge to $+\infty$, to $-\infty$, or oscillate. In $\mathbb R^d$ the Lévy–Steinitz theorem says the set of sums of convergent rearrangements is an affine subspace. ([Lebl, more on series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_moreonseries.html); [Riemann series theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_series_theorem))
- **Cauchy products (Mertens, Cesàro).** With $c_n=\sum_{i=0}^n a_ib_{n-i}$: if $\sum a_n=A$, $\sum b_n=B$ and at least one converges absolutely, then $\sum c_n=AB$. Convergence of both is not enough: for $a_n=b_n=(-1)^n/\sqrt{n+1}$ one has $|c_n|\ge1$, so $\sum c_n$ diverges. Without absolute convergence the product is still Cesàro summable to $AB$. ([Lebl, more on series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_moreonseries.html); [Cauchy product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy_product))
- **Weierstrass M-test.** If $|f_n(x)|\le M_n$ for all $x\in A$ and $\sum M_n<\infty$, then $\sum f_n$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $A$. ([Weierstrass M-test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_M-test))
- **Uniform limits.** A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, and a uniform limit of Riemann integrable functions on $[a,b]$ is integrable with $\int f=\lim\int f_n$. If $f_n\in C^1$ on a bounded interval $I$, $f_n'\to g$ uniformly, and $f_n(c)$ converges for one $c\in I$, then $f_n$ converges uniformly to a $C^1$ function $f$ with $f'=g$. ([Lebl, interchange of limits](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_liminter.html))
- **Cauchy–Hadamard and power series.** The radius of convergence of $\sum c_n(z-a)^n$ is given by $1/R=\limsup|c_n|^{1/n}$; the series converges for $|z-a|<R$ and diverges for $|z-a|>R$. A real power series converges uniformly on $[a-r,a+r]$ for $0<r<R$ and may be integrated termwise there; the termwise derivative series has the same radius $R$ and represents the derivative. ([Cauchy–Hadamard theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Hadamard_theorem); [Lebl, interchange of limits](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_liminter.html))
- **Abel's theorem.** If $\sum a_k$ converges (real coefficients), then $G(x)=\sum a_kx^k$ satisfies $\lim_{x\to1^-}G(x)=\sum a_k$. In the complex case the same holds as $z\to1$ inside a Stolz sector $|1-z|\le M(1-|z|)$. The converse fails: $1/(1+x)\to1/2$ although $1-1+1-\cdots$ diverges. ([Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%27s_theorem))
- **Tauberian theorems (Littlewood, Hardy–Littlewood).** If $a_n=O(1/n)$ and $\sum a_nx^n\to s$ as $x\uparrow1$, then $\sum a_n=s$ (Littlewood, 1911). If $a_n\ge0$ and $\sum a_nx^n\sim 1/(1-x)$ as $x\uparrow1$, then $\sum_{k\le n}a_k\sim n$ (Hardy–Littlewood, 1914). ([Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_Tauberian_theorem))

### Examples
The geometric series $\sum_{n\ge0}r^n$ equals $1/(1-r)$ for $|r|<1$ and diverges for $|r|\ge1$. The harmonic series diverges although its terms tend to zero (indeed $s_{2^k}\ge1+k/2$), so $a_n\to0$ is necessary but not sufficient. The alternating harmonic series converges conditionally and is the standard example for Riemann's rearrangement theorem. ([Lebl, series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_series.html); [Riemann series theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_series_theorem))

For series of functions, $f_n(x)=\sin(nx)/n$ converges uniformly to $0$ while $f_n'(x)=\cos(nx)$ fails to converge at $x=\pi$, showing why the differentiation theorem asks for uniform convergence of the derivatives. ([Lebl, interchange of limits](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_liminter.html))

### History
Oresme proved the divergence of the harmonic series in the fourteenth century, and the Kerala school studied series for trigonometric functions between about 1350 and 1530. James Gregory introduced the terms "convergence" and "divergence" in 1668. Gauss's 1812 memoir on hypergeometric series gave convergence criteria; Cauchy in 1821 insisted on strict convergence tests and showed that the product of two convergent series need not converge; Abel's 1826 memoir on the binomial series corrected certain of Cauchy's conclusions. Seidel and Stokes first treated uniform convergence successfully in 1847–48. ([Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Series_%28mathematics%29))

The root-test formula for the radius of convergence appeared in Cauchy's 1821 *Analyse algébrique* and was rediscovered by Hadamard in 1888. Cauchy observed in 1833 that rearranging the alternating harmonic series can change its sum, Dirichlet noted that absolute convergence rules this out, and Riemann gave the full characterization while studying Fourier series. ([Cauchy–Hadamard theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Hadamard_theorem); [Riemann series theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_series_theorem))

### Connections
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): partial sums are sequences, and completeness underlies the Cauchy criterion.
- [Cauchy Sequences](node:Cauchy%20Sequences): the Cauchy criterion for series is the Cauchy condition for partial sums.
- [Uniform Convergence of Series](node:Uniform%20Convergence%20of%20Series): the M-test and interchange theorems in more detail.
- [Taylor's Theorem](node:Taylor's%20Theorem) and [Laurent Series](node:Laurent%20Series): power-series expansions governed by Cauchy–Hadamard.
- [Abelian Summability Theorems](node:Abelian%20Summability%20Theorems), [Tauberian Theorems](node:Tauberian%20Theorems) and [Hardy's Tauberian Theorem](node:Hardy's%20Tauberian%20Theorem): summation methods and their converses.
- [Matrix Summability Methods](node:Matrix%20Summability%20Methods): Cesàro and related methods as regular transformations of sequences.
- [Prime Number Theorem](node:Prime%20Number%20Theorem): Hardy and Littlewood applied Tauberian methods to it.
- [Diophantine Approximation](node:Diophantine%20Approximation): the convergence of the Flint Hills series is tied to the irrationality measure of $\pi$.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): trigonometric series, where Riemann's rearrangement theorem originated.

### Common pitfalls
Rearranging or regrouping a conditionally convergent series can change its value; only absolutely convergent series can be rearranged freely. Multiplying two series by the Cauchy product needs absolute convergence of at least one factor (Mertens). The ratio and root tests say nothing when the limit is $1$: $\sum 1$ diverges and $\sum1/n^2$ converges, yet both give $L=1$. Pointwise convergence of functions preserves neither continuity nor integrals, and uniform convergence of $f_n$ alone does not justify differentiating termwise. ([Lebl, more on series](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_moreonseries.html); [Cauchy product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy_product); [Ratio test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratio_test); [Lebl, interchange of limits](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_liminter.html))

### Open problems
- **Flint Hills series.** Whether $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2 n}$ converges is stated by Alekseyev to be not known. He shows that convergence would imply $\mu(\pi)\le 2.5$ for the irrationality measure of $\pi$, much stronger than the best bound known at the time ($\mu(\pi)\le 7.6063\ldots$). MathWorld adds that Meiburg (2022) proved $\mu(\pi)<2.5$ implies convergence, so the boundary case is unsettled, and it reports a 2026 claim of $\mu(\pi)=2$ that, as of October 2026, had not been independently verified. ([Alekseyev 2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.5100); [Flint Hills series](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FlintHillsSeries.html))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Convergence tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests): catalogue of tests with hypotheses, alongside [Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Series_%28mathematics%29) for history.
- **Learn:** [Lebl, Basic Analysis, §2.5–2.6](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_series.html) and [§6.2](https://jirilebl.github.io/ra/html/sec_liminter.html): open textbook proofs of the tests, rearrangement, Mertens, and interchange of limits.
- **Primary:** [Alekseyev, On convergence of the Flint Hills series](https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.5100): research paper linking a convergence question to the irrationality measure of $\pi$.
- **Further reading:** [Knopp, Theory and Application of Infinite Series](https://archive.org/details/theoryandapplica031692mbp) (Blackie, 1954 edition): the classical monograph on convergence, rearrangement, and summability.
references.Set Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Set theory studies collections and membership, with infinite sets as its central concern, and it also serves as a foundation in which essentially all of mathematics can be encoded. It grew out of Cantor's 1873 discovery that the real line is not countable; Russell's paradox (the "set" of all sets that are not members of themselves) then showed that unrestricted set formation is inconsistent, and Zermelo gave the first axiomatization in 1908. ([SEP, Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))

Modern set theory is driven by the incompleteness phenomenon. By [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems), if ZFC is consistent then some propositions are undecidable in it, and the continuum hypothesis (CH) turned out to be such a proposition: Gödel's constructible universe $L$ (1938) shows CH is consistent with ZFC, and Cohen's forcing (1963) shows its negation is too. The research programme since then has two sides: the technical study of models (inner models such as $L$, forcing extensions, large cardinals, determinacy, descriptive set theory of the reals) and the search for new axioms that would decide questions like CH, which the SEP calls "Gödel's Program". ([SEP, Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [SEP, Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))

Set theory sits in [MSC 03Exx - Set theory](node:MSC%2003Exx%20-%20Set%20theory) beside [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory) and proof theory, and it uses the language and deductive calculus of [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic). A comprehensive monograph is T. Jech, *Set Theory*, 3rd edition (Springer Monographs in Mathematics, 2003). ([Crossref record for Jech](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/3-540-44761-X); [SEP, Set Theory, Bibliography](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))

### Formal definition
ZFC is Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice, a first-order theory whose only non-logical symbol is membership $\in$. Its axioms are: **Extensionality** (if two sets have the same elements they are equal, $\forall A\,\forall B\,[\forall x\,(x\in A\leftrightarrow x\in B)\to A=B]$); **Separation** (for every set $A$ and every property expressible by a formula, there is a set of exactly the elements of $A$ with that property); Pairing, Union, Power Set, Infinity, Foundation, the **Replacement** schema, and **Choice**. Separation and Replacement are schemas, one axiom per formula. ([SEP, Set Theory §2.1](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))

The axiom of choice states that every set $X$ of nonempty sets has a choice function $f$ with $f(x)\in x$ for every $x\in X$. Over ZF it is equivalent to Zorn's lemma (a statement about [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders)) and to the well-ordering theorem. ([Wikipedia, Axiom of choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_choice))

**Ordinals and cardinals.** Von Neumann ordinals are generated from $\varnothing$ by taking successors $\alpha\cup\{\alpha\}$ and unions; they satisfy the principle of transfinite induction, and Replacement yields transfinite recursion. A **cardinal** is an ordinal not in bijection with any smaller ordinal; cardinals measure the [Cardinality](node:Cardinality) of sets. ([SEP, Set Theory §3](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/)) Transfinite induction extends [Mathematical Induction](node:Mathematical%20Induction) past $\omega$: a property that holds of $\alpha$ whenever it holds of all $\beta<\alpha$ holds of every ordinal. ([SEP, Set Theory §3](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))

**The cumulative hierarchy.** Define $V_0=\varnothing$, $V_{\alpha+1}=\mathcal P(V_\alpha)$, and $V_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$ for limit $\lambda$. ZFC proves that the universe $V$ of all sets is $\bigcup_\alpha V_\alpha$, and the Reflection Principle states that for a formula $\varphi$ there are ordinals $\alpha$ such that, for all $a_1,\dots,a_n\in V_\alpha$, $\varphi(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ holds in $V$ if and only if it holds in $V_\alpha$. ([SEP, Set Theory §4](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))

### Key results
- **Cantor's theorem (1891).** For every set $A$, $|\mathcal P(A)|>|A|$. Proof: for any $f:A\to\mathcal P(A)$, the diagonal set $B=\{x\in A: x\notin f(x)\}$ is not in the range of $f$, while $x\mapsto\{x\}$ is an injection. Iterating gives an unbounded chain of infinite cardinals, and applied to a universal set it gives Cantor's paradox, so there is no set of all sets. ([Wikipedia, Cantor's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor%27s_theorem))
- **Gödel's constructible universe (1938).** Let $L_0=\varnothing$, $L_{\alpha+1}=\operatorname{Def}(L_\alpha)$ (the subsets of $L_\alpha$ first-order definable over it with parameters), and take unions at limits; $L=\bigcup_\alpha L_\alpha$. Gödel proved that $L$ is an inner model of ZF in which AC and the generalized continuum hypothesis hold. Hence if ZF is consistent, so is ZF + AC + GCH. ([Wikipedia, Constructible universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructible_universe); [SEP, Set Theory §7](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))
- **Cohen's forcing (1963).** Given a forcing poset $(\mathbb P,\le,\mathbf 1)$ and a filter $G$ meeting every dense subset of $\mathbb P$ in the ground model, the generic extension $V[G]$ again satisfies ZFC. Forcing with finite partial functions from $\omega\times\omega_2$ to $2$ adds $\aleph_2$ distinct subsets of $\omega$ without collapsing cardinals (the poset is ccc), so $2^{\aleph_0}\ge\aleph_2$ in $V[G]$. With Gödel's result this proves CH independent of ZFC, assuming ZFC is consistent; Cohen likewise obtained a model of ZF with AC false, so AC is independent of ZF. Cohen's announcement is "The Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis", *PNAS* 50(6) (1963), 1143-1148. ([Wikipedia, Forcing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forcing_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia, Axiom of choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_choice); [Crossref record for Cohen 1963](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1073/pnas.50.6.1143))
- **Easton's theorem.** For regular cardinals, monotonicity of $\kappa\mapsto 2^\kappa$, Cantor's theorem, and König's theorem are the only restrictions on the continuum function provable in ZFC; Easton realized any other assignment by class forcing. ([Wikipedia, Forcing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forcing_%28mathematics%29))
- **Large cardinals and consistency strength.** A large cardinal axiom asserts the existence of a cardinal with some strong property (inaccessible, measurable, Woodin, supercompact, ...). Such an axiom implies the consistency of ZFC, so by Gödel's second incompleteness theorem ZFC cannot prove it consistent with ZFC (if ZFC is consistent). The known axioms appear to be linearly ordered by consistency strength, but this is "an observation, not a theorem". ([Wikipedia, Large cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_cardinal)) Scott showed in 1961 that a measurable cardinal implies $V\ne L$; Woodin cardinals lie between strong and supercompact cardinals. Large cardinals cannot settle CH, by results of Lévy and Solovay. ([SEP, Set Theory §10](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [SEP, Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))
- **Determinacy.** For $A\subseteq\omega^\omega$, the game $G_A$ has two players alternately choosing natural numbers for $\omega$ moves, player I winning iff the play lies in $A$; $A$ is determined if one player has a winning strategy. Martin proved in ZFC that every Borel set is determined. Martin and Steel (1989) proved that every projective set is determined if there are infinitely many Woodin cardinals. ([SEP, Set Theory §6.2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/)) Projective determinacy implies that all projective sets of reals are Lebesgue measurable and have the Baire and perfect set properties. ([Wikipedia, Projective determinacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_determinacy)) The full axiom of determinacy contradicts AC, and ZF + AD is equiconsistent with ZFC + infinitely many Woodin cardinals (Woodin). ([Wikipedia, Axiom of determinacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_determinacy))
- **Forcing axioms.** Martin's Axiom is consistent with $\neg$CH (Martin and Solovay, 1970), and MA + $\neg$CH implies Suslin's Hypothesis. The proper forcing axiom PFA and Martin's Maximum MM are consistent relative to a supercompact cardinal and imply $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$. ([SEP, Set Theory §11](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/)) MM was introduced by Foreman, Magidor and Shelah (1988); it also makes the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ $\aleph_2$-saturated. ([Wikipedia, Martin's maximum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin%27s_maximum))

### Examples
The empty set $\varnothing$ has no members, while $\{\varnothing\}$ has one; the finite von Neumann ordinals are $0=\varnothing$, $1=\{0\}$, $2=\{0,1\}$, and $\omega$ is the first infinite ordinal. Cantor's theorem applied to $\omega$ gives $|\mathcal P(\omega)|=2^{\aleph_0}>\aleph_0$, the cardinality of the continuum, so the reals of [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits) are uncountable; CH is the assertion $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1$. ([SEP, Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [Wikipedia, Cantor's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor%27s_theorem))

Choice has strong consequences in analysis: choosing one point from each orbit of the circle under rational rotations gives a set that no rotation-invariant countably additive measure can measure, a basic example for [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory), and the Banach-Tarski decomposition of a ball into finitely many pieces that reassemble into two balls, each congruent to the original, uses non-measurable pieces built with AC. ([Wikipedia, Axiom of choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_choice))

### History
Cantor proved the uncountability of the reals in 1873 and formulated CH in 1878; Zermelo axiomatized set theory in 1908, and Ulam discovered measurable cardinals in 1930. Gödel's consistency proof for AC and GCH via $L$ appeared in 1938, and Cohen introduced forcing in 1963 and proved the consistency of $\neg$CH and of $\neg$AC relative to ZF. ([SEP, Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/)) The theory of AD was proposed by Mycielski and Steinhaus in 1962. ([Wikipedia, Axiom of determinacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_determinacy)) Woodin's 2017 *Bulletin of Symbolic Logic* memoir argues that a solution of the inner model problem for one supercompact cardinal would yield an "ultimate version of $L$". ([Woodin, In Search of Ultimate-L](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-symbolic-logic/article/in-search-of-ultimatel-the-19th-midrasha-mathematicae-lectures/BDBD4F26AC73B54AA7CD76CD5808B957))

### Connections
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): ZFC is a first-order theory; independence results are statements about provability in it.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): guarantee undecidable statements in ZFC and underlie the consistency-strength hierarchy.
- [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory): inner models, forcing extensions and $L$ are models of ZFC studied with model-theoretic tools.
- [Cardinality](node:Cardinality): cardinals formalize size; Cantor's theorem gives the first non-trivial comparison.
- [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders): Zorn's lemma, equivalent to AC, and forcing posets.
- [Mathematical Induction](node:Mathematical%20Induction): transfinite induction is its extension to the ordinals.
- [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): AC yields non-measurable sets; determinacy restores measurability for definable sets.
- [Functions and Relations](node:Functions%20and%20Relations): encoded as sets of ordered pairs.

### Common pitfalls
Separation only carves subsets out of an existing set; unrestricted comprehension yields Russell's paradox, and Cantor's theorem rules out a set of all sets. Independence of CH means neither CH nor its negation is provable from ZFC (if ZFC is consistent); it is not a missing proof that ingenuity could supply within ZFC. Consistency-strength comparisons between large cardinals need not match the size of their least instances: the first huge cardinal is smaller than the first supercompact, yet hugeness is stronger. ([SEP, Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/); [Wikipedia, Cantor's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia, Large cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_cardinal))

### Open problems
- **The continuum problem.** The SEP calls CH "one of the most central open problems in set theory": independence from ZFC is settled, but whether new, justified axioms decide it is not, and the SEP entry on set theory states "to this day, the CH remains open". ([SEP, Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/); [SEP, Set Theory §9](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/))
- **Woodin's $\Omega$ Conjecture.** $\Omega$-logic is sound, but "it is open whether the corresponding completeness theorem holds"; this is Woodin's $\Omega$ Conjecture. ([SEP, Continuum Hypothesis §3](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/))
- **Ultimate-L and the HOD Conjecture.** The SEP describes a candidate inner model $L_\Omega$ whose axiom $V=L_\Omega$ is compatible with all large cardinal axioms, with rival candidates, so the programme's outcome is unresolved. ([SEP, Continuum Hypothesis §6](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/)) Aguilera, Bagaria and Lücke show that new "exacting" large cardinals imply $V\ne\mathrm{HOD}$ and that the consistency of an exacting cardinal above an extendible would refute Woodin's HOD Conjecture and Ultimate-L Conjecture. ([arXiv:2411.11568](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11568))
- **Why consistency strength is linear.** The apparent linear ordering of large cardinal axioms is unexplained; Shelah asked whether some theorem explains it. Woodin derives the ordering from his $\Omega$ Conjecture, which the same source describes as unsolved. ([Wikipedia, Large cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_cardinal))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP, Set Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/): axioms, ordinals, $L$, forcing, large cardinals, determinacy, forcing axioms.
- **Reference:** [SEP, The Continuum Hypothesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/continuum-hypothesis/): independence, $\Omega$-logic, Ultimate-L, and the case for and against new axioms.
- **Learn:** [Cornell MATH 6870, Set Theory](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~justin/6870): Spring 2022 course (J. Moore) covering ordinals, transfinite recursion, Martin's Axiom, forcing and the consistency of $\neg$CH.
- **Primary:** [Cohen, The Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis, PNAS 1963](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1073/pnas.50.6.1143): the original announcement of forcing.
- **Primary:** [Woodin, In Search of Ultimate-L, Bull. Symb. Logic 23 (2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-symbolic-logic/article/in-search-of-ultimatel-the-19th-midrasha-mathematicae-lectures/BDBD4F26AC73B54AA7CD76CD5808B957): the Ultimate-L programme.
- **Primary:** [Aguilera, Bagaria, Lücke, Large cardinals, structural reflection, and the HOD Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11568): recent work on the HOD dichotomy.
- **Further reading:** [Jech, Set Theory (Springer, 2003)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/3-540-44761-X): T. Jech's comprehensive monograph (3rd edition).
references.Sim-to-Real Transfer and Domain Randomiz:
## Reference
### Overview
