Sim-to-real transfer trains a policy or perception model in simulation and deploys it on a physical system. Simulators provide training data that is cheaper and safer than real-world collection. Policies trained there often degrade on real robots because of the *reality gap*, the mismatch between simulated and real dynamics, sensing and appearance. The Zhao–Peña Queralta–Westerlund survey groups the main remedies into domain randomization, domain adaptation, [imitation learning](node:Imitation%20Learning), meta-learning and [knowledge distillation](node:Knowledge%20Distillation). ([Zhao et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13303)) Most simulators model friction, impact and deformation inaccurately, especially on the actuation side, and sensing differs between simulation and the real world. ([Berkeley EE 290-005 Lecture 15](https://pages.github.berkeley.edu/ee290-005/sp21-site/assets/scribe/week15_scribed.pdf))

Domain randomization (DR) does not try to make the simulator exact. It randomizes simulator parameters during training so widely that the real world looks like one more sample. Tobin et al. randomized rendering (textures, object positions, distractor objects) and trained an object detector purely on non-realistic synthetic images. Peng et al. randomized the simulator's physical dynamics for control. ([Tobin et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06907); [Peng et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.06537)) DR sits beside *system identification*, which fits simulator parameters to measured input–output behaviour, and *domain adaptation*, which transfers a model from a source domain to a related target domain. ([Berkeley EE 290-005 Lecture 15](https://pages.github.berkeley.edu/ee290-005/sp21-site/assets/scribe/week15_scribed.pdf); [Wikipedia: Domain adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_adaptation))

Domain randomization has worked well in robotics and autonomous driving, while its theoretical basis was long limited. Chen et al. model the simulator as a set of MDPs with tunable parameters, such as friction, that stand in for unknown physical properties, and bound the resulting sim-to-real gap. ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.03239))

### Formal definition
**Domain shift.** Source and target are distributions $\mathcal D_S,\mathcal D_T$ on $X\times Y$. The aim is a hypothesis with small error under $\mathcal D_T$ when training draws on $\mathcal D_S$. Common cases are covariate shift (input marginals differ, $P(y\mid x)$ fixed), prior shift (label proportions differ), and concept shift ($P(y\mid x)$ changes). ([Wikipedia: Domain adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_adaptation))

**Simulator as an MDP family.** Let $\mathcal U$ be a set of MDPs sharing state space $\mathcal S$, action space $\mathcal A$ and horizon $H$ but differing in transition dynamics, indexed by latent physical parameters such as friction. The real system is some unknown $\mathcal M^{\star}\in\mathcal U$. Domain randomization with distribution $\nu$ on $\mathcal U$ returns
$$\pi_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\star}=\arg\max_{\pi}\ \mathbb E_{\mathcal M\sim\nu}\big[V^{\pi}_{\mathcal M,1}(s_1)\big],$$
optimized over history-dependent policies, so that $\pi$ is optimal for the latent MDP $(\mathcal U,\nu)$. Its sim-to-real gap is
$$\mathrm{Gap}(\pi)=V^{\star}_{\mathcal M^{\star},1}(s_1)-V^{\pi}_{\mathcal M^{\star},1}(s_1),$$
and no real-world samples are used. ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2110.03239))

**Robust (risk-averse) variant.** EPOpt draws simulator parameters $p\sim P$ and optimizes the conditional value at risk (CVaR) of the return $\eta_{\mathcal M}(\theta,p)$ at risk level $\epsilon$, so that poorly handled model instances are sampled more often. It then adapts $P$ to target-domain trajectory data by [Bayesian inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference) with a particle filter. ([Berkeley EE 290-005 Lecture 15](https://pages.github.berkeley.edu/ee290-005/sp21-site/assets/scribe/week15_scribed.pdf))

### Key results
Chen, Hu, Jin, Li and Wang analyse $\pi_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\star}$ with $\nu$ uniform on $\mathcal U$. ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2110.03239))
- **Necessity of mixing.** Without the assumption that every MDP in $\mathcal U$ has diameter at most $D$ (communicating MDPs), the gap can be $\Omega(H)$, the worst possible.
- **Finite simulator class, $\delta$-separated.** Suppose $|\mathcal U|=M$, every MDP has diameter at most $D$, and any two MDPs differ by at least $\delta$ in $\ell_1$ next-state distribution at some state-action pair. Then $\mathrm{Gap}(\pi_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\star})=O\!\big(D M^3\log(MH)\log^2(SMH/\delta)/\delta^4\big)$, which is polylogarithmic in $H$.
- **Finite class without separation.** $\mathrm{Gap}(\pi_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\star})=O\big(D\sqrt{M^3H\log(MH)}\big)=\tilde O(\sqrt H)$. The $\sqrt H$ rate cannot be improved: under stated conditions on $S,A,M,D,H$, every history-dependent policy has gap $\Omega(\sqrt{DMH})$ on some $M$-element class.
- **Infinite classes.** If the value of $\pi_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\star}$ is $L$-Lipschitz near $\mathcal M^{\star}$, then for $0\le\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, $\mathrm{Gap}=O\!\big(D\sqrt{d_eH\log(H\,\mathcal N(\mathcal F,1/H))}/\nu(\mathcal C_{\mathcal M^{\star},\varepsilon})+L\varepsilon\big)$, where $d_e$ is an eluder dimension and $\mathcal N$ a covering number. Without smoothness, even low-rank classes can force an $\Omega(H)$ gap. The authors conclude that history-dependent (memory-using) policies matter for domain randomization.
- **Empirical milestones.**
  - Rendering randomization alone gave a real-world object detector accurate to 1.5 cm, robust to distractors and partial occlusion, trained only on simulated RGB images. The authors report it as the first successful transfer of such a network to real-world robotic control. ([Tobin et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06907))
  - Dynamics randomization gave pushing policies, trained only in simulation, that performed at a similar level on a real arm and were robust to significant calibration error. ([Peng et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.06537))
  - Automatic domain randomization (ADR) grows a distribution of increasingly difficult environments. It enabled a humanoid robot hand to solve a Rubik's Cube, and memory-augmented policies trained with it showed signs of emergent meta-learning at test time. ([OpenAI et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07113))

### Examples
- *Visual randomization.* Tobin et al. vary the number and shape of distractor objects, the positions and textures of all objects, and the textures of table, floor, skybox and robot. This removes the need for accurate real-world calibration. ([Berkeley EE 290-005 Lecture 15](https://pages.github.berkeley.edu/ee290-005/sp21-site/assets/scribe/week15_scribed.pdf))
- *Closing the loop.* The "Closing the Sim-to-Real Loop" method uses domain randomization to represent stochastic dynamics, evaluates the discrepancies between simulated and executed trajectories, and iteratively updates the randomization distribution to match real dynamics. This combines DR with system identification. ([Berkeley EE 290-005 Lecture 15](https://pages.github.berkeley.edu/ee290-005/sp21-site/assets/scribe/week15_scribed.pdf))

### History
Tobin et al. (2017) proposed domain randomization of rendering for transferring deep networks trained on simulated images ([Tobin et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06907)). Peng et al. extended randomization to dynamics for control (ICRA 2018) ([Peng et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.06537)). OpenAI's ADR (2019) made the randomization range adaptive ([OpenAI et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07113)). Zhao et al. surveyed the field in 2020 ([Zhao et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13303)), and Chen et al. gave sim-to-real gap bounds (2021, revised 2022) ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.03239)).

### Connections
- [Robotics and Embodied Intelligence](node:Robotics%20and%20Embodied%20Intelligence): the main deployment setting.
- [Generalization in Deep Learning](node:Generalization%20in%20Deep%20Learning): DR trains for [out-of-distribution generalization](node:Out-of-Distribution%20Generalization) by widening the training distribution.
- [Domain Adaptation](node:Domain%20Adaptation): the alternative family that adapts to the target instead of covering it.
- [System Identification for Sim-to-Real Transfer](node:System%20Identification%20for%20Sim-to-Real%20Transfer): fits simulator parameters instead of randomizing them, and is often combined with DR.
- [Markov Decision Processes](node:Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the simulator is formalized as a family of MDPs.
- [Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes](node:Partially%20Observable%20Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the latent simulator parameter makes the real problem partially observed, which is why memory helps.
- [Meta-Learning](node:Meta-Learning): memory-based policies trained under ADR adapt at test time.
- [Reinforcement Learning](node:Reinforcement%20Learning): the usual training method for DR policies.
- [Distributionally Robust Optimization](node:Distributionally%20Robust%20Optimization): EPOpt's CVaR objective is a robust counterpart of DR's expectation.
- [Simulator Misspecification](node:Simulator%20Misspecification): the reality gap seen from the inference side.
- [Differentiable Simulation](node:Differentiable%20Simulation): an alternative route to calibrating simulators.
- [World Models](node:World%20Models): learned simulators as a source of training data.
- [Transfer Learning](node:Transfer%20Learning): the umbrella notion.

### Common pitfalls
- **Randomization does not replace real feedback.** In the lecture discussion, Prof. Ma remarks that however the domain is randomized, some discrepancy remains that only policy execution reveals, so a mechanism for adapting on the fly from real-world feedback is still needed. ([Berkeley EE 290-005 Lecture 15](https://pages.github.berkeley.edu/ee290-005/sp21-site/assets/scribe/week15_scribed.pdf))
- **Memoryless policies.** The $\tilde O(\sqrt H)$ guarantees are proved for $\pi_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\star}$ optimized over history-dependent policies, and the authors stress that memory matters. ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2110.03239))
- **Non-communicating dynamics.** If some simulated MDP can trap the agent, the worst-case gap is $\Omega(H)$. ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2110.03239))

### Open problems
- **Tight dependence on class size and separation.** Chen et al. note that their dependence on $M$ and $\delta$ may not be tight. ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2110.03239))
- **Theory with real-world fine-tuning.** Their framework excludes real-world samples, and they leave combining simulation training with real data to future research. ([Chen et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2110.03239))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Domain adaptation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_adaptation): source and target distributions and types of shift.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley EE 290-005 (Spring 2021) Lecture 15 scribe notes](https://pages.github.berkeley.edu/ee290-005/sp21-site/assets/scribe/week15_scribed.pdf): sim-to-real overview, DR, EPOpt, SimOpt.
- **Primary:** [Chen, Hu, Jin, Li, Wang, Understanding Domain Randomization for Sim-to-real Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.03239): gap bounds and lower bounds.
- **Primary:** [Tobin et al., Domain Randomization for Transferring Deep Neural Networks from Simulation to the Real World](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06907): the original visual DR paper.
- **Primary:** [Zhao, Peña Queralta, Westerlund, Sim-to-Real Transfer in Deep RL for Robotics: a Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13303): taxonomy of methods.
- **Further reading:** [Peng et al., Sim-to-Real Transfer of Robotic Control with Dynamics Randomization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.06537); [OpenAI et al., Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07113).
references.Singular Value Decomposition:
## Reference
### Overview
The singular value decomposition (SVD) factors every real or complex $m\times n$ matrix as $M=U\Sigma V^*$ with $U,V$ unitary and $\Sigma$ rectangular diagonal with non-negative entries, the singular values. Unlike the eigendecomposition, it exists for every matrix, square or not; for normal matrices the two can be related, but in general they differ ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).

Geometrically the SVD says that every linear map between inner product spaces is, after orthonormal changes of basis in domain and codomain, a coordinate scaling. The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $M^*M$, the number of nonzero singular values is the rank, and the largest equals the operator 2-norm, so the SVD exposes rank, norm, conditioning, range and null space at once ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).

Its most used consequence is optimal low-rank approximation: truncating the SVD gives the best rank-$k$ approximation in every unitarily invariant norm (Eckart–Young–Mirsky) ([Wikipedia: Low-rank approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation)). It also underlies large-scale randomized algorithms that use random sampling to find a subspace capturing most of the action of a matrix, compress the matrix to that subspace, and factor the small matrix deterministically ([Halko, Martinsson, Tropp, arXiv:0909.4061](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.4061)).

### Formal definition
**Theorem (existence).** For every $M\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ there are unitary $U\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}$, $V\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and a rectangular diagonal $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with diagonal entries $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\dots\ge0$ such that
$$M=U\Sigma V^* .$$
The $\sigma_i$ (singular values) are uniquely determined by $M$; for real $M$, $U,V$ can be taken real orthogonal. Columns of $V$ (right singular vectors) are eigenvectors of $M^*M$, columns of $U$ (left singular vectors) are eigenvectors of $MM^*$, and the nonzero $\sigma_i$ are the square roots of the nonzero eigenvalues of $M^*M$. Equivalently, $\sigma\ge0$ is a singular value iff there are unit vectors $u,v$ with $Mv=\sigma u$ and $M^*u=\sigma v$ ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).

**Reduced forms.** With $r=\operatorname{rank}M$, the *compact* SVD is $M=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^*$ with $\Sigma_r$ the $r\times r$ diagonal of nonzero singular values; the *thin* SVD uses $k=\min(m,n)$; the *truncated* SVD $M_t=U_t\Sigma_tV_t^*$ keeps only the $t$ largest singular values ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).

**Variational characterization.** For real $M$, $\sigma_1=\max_{\|u\|=\|v\|=1}u^{\mathsf T}Mv$, attained at a pair $(u_1,v_1)$ with $Mv_1=\sigma_1u_1$, $M^{\mathsf T}u_1=\sigma_1v_1$; later singular values are maxima over vectors orthogonal to the earlier ones ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).

### Key results
- **Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem.** Let $A_k$ be the rank-$k$ truncated SVD of $A$. Then for every $B$ with $\operatorname{rank}B\le k$,
  $$\|A-B\|_2\ge\|A-A_k\|_2=\sigma_{k+1},\qquad \|A-B\|_F^2\ge\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 .$$
  Mirsky extended optimality to all unitarily invariant norms; in the Frobenius norm the minimizer is unique iff $\sigma_k>\sigma_{k+1}$ ([Wikipedia: Low-rank approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation)).
- **Weyl perturbation bound.** For any $M,\Delta$ of the same size, $|\sigma_k(M+\Delta)-\sigma_k(M)|\le\sigma_1(\Delta)=\|\Delta\|_2$; it follows from Weyl's eigenvalue inequality $\lambda_{i+j-1}(A+B)\le\lambda_i(A)+\lambda_j(B)$ for Hermitian $A,B$ ($i+j\le n+1$) applied to an augmented Hermitian matrix ([Wikipedia: Weyl's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl%27s_inequality)).
- **Pseudoinverse and polar decomposition.** $M^+=V\Sigma^+U^*$, where $\Sigma^+$ inverts the nonzero diagonal entries and transposes; and, for square $M$, $M=SR$ with $S=U\Sigma U^*$ positive semidefinite and $R=UV^*$ unitary ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).
- **Norms from singular values.** The Ky Fan $k$-norm is $\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i$ (so the Ky Fan 1-norm is the operator 2-norm), the nuclear norm is $\sum_i\sigma_i$, and $\|M\|_F=(\sum_i\sigma_i^2)^{1/2}$ ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).
- **Compact operators.** If $M$ is a compact operator between [Hilbert spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces), $M\psi=\sum_i\sigma_i\langle\psi,Ve_i\rangle\,Ue_i$ with norm convergence; $M$ is compact iff $M^*M$ is ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).
- **Randomized range finder (Halko–Martinsson–Tropp).** Let $A$ be real $m\times n$, target rank $k\ge2$, oversampling $p\ge2$ with $k+p\le\min(m,n)$. Draw a standard Gaussian $n\times(k+p)$ test matrix $\Omega$ and let $Q$ be an orthonormal basis of the range of $A\Omega$. Then
  $$\mathbb E\,\|A-QQ^*A\|\le\Big[1+\tfrac{4\sqrt{k+p}}{p-1}\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\Big]\sigma_{k+1},$$
  and with probability at least $1-6p^{-p}$ the error is at most $[1+11\sqrt{k+p}\sqrt{\min(m,n)}]\sigma_{k+1}$ ([Halko, Martinsson, Tropp, arXiv:0909.4061](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0909.4061)).

### Examples
- **Schmidt decomposition.** Writing $w\in\mathcal H_1\otimes\mathcal H_2$ as $\sum_i\alpha_iu_i\otimes v_i$ is the SVD of the coefficient matrix of $w$; the Schmidt rank is the matrix rank ([Wikipedia: Schmidt decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_decomposition)).
- **Rank-$k$ compression.** Keeping only $U_k,\Sigma_k,V_k$ of an $m\times n$ matrix gives its best rank-$k$ approximation, with spectral-norm error exactly $\sigma_{k+1}$ by Eckart–Young ([Wikipedia: Low-rank approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation)).
- **Cost of computation.** For $m\ge n$ the standard algorithm (Householder bidiagonalization followed by an iterative bidiagonal SVD) costs $O(mn^2)$ flops; the Householder reduction to bidiagonal form takes about $4mn^2-4n^3/3$ flops when only singular values are needed ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)); randomized methods with structured test matrices reach $O(mn\log k)$ for a rank-$k$ approximation of a dense matrix ([Halko, Martinsson, Tropp, arXiv:0909.4061](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0909.4061)).

### History
Beltrami (1873) and Jordan (1874) independently found singular values as a complete set of invariants of bilinear forms; Sylvester (1889) called them "canonical multipliers"; Schmidt (1907) introduced the analogue for integral operators and Picard (1910) named them "singular values"; Autonne (1915) derived the SVD via the polar decomposition; Eckart and Young (1936) proved it for rectangular and complex matrices; and Golub–Kahan (1965) and Golub–Reinsch (1970) developed the algorithms still in use ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)). Eckart and Young's paper, "The Approximation of One Matrix by Another of Lower Rank", appeared in *Psychometrika* 1, 211–218 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02288367)); Schmidt had already solved the infinite-dimensional approximation problem ([Wikipedia: Low-rank approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation)).

### Connections
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): the SVD is a canonical form for a linear map under independent unitary changes of basis.
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors) and [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem): singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of $M^*M$; the SVD applies the spectral theorem to $M^*M$ and $MM^*$.
- [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces): orthonormality of singular vectors needs an inner product.
- [Moore–Penrose Pseudoinverse](node:Moore–Penrose%20Pseudoinverse) and [Least-Squares Problems](node:Least-Squares%20Problems): $M^+=V\Sigma^+U^*$ gives minimum-norm least-squares solutions.
- [Principal Component Analysis](node:Principal%20Component%20Analysis): principal directions are right singular vectors of the centred data matrix.
- [Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers](node:Matrix%20Norms%20and%20Condition%20Numbers): the 2-norm, Frobenius and nuclear norms are functions of singular values; $\kappa_2=\sigma_1/\sigma_n$.
- [Positive Definite Matrices](node:Positive%20Definite%20Matrices): the polar factor $S=U\Sigma U^*$ is positive semidefinite.
- [QR Factorization](node:QR%20Factorization) and [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): Householder reductions are the first stage of SVD algorithms.
- [Randomized Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Randomized%20Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): sketching-based approximate SVDs.
- [Quantum Entanglement](node:Quantum%20Entanglement): the Schmidt decomposition of bipartite states.

### Common pitfalls
- **SVD is not the eigendecomposition.** For non-normal $M$ the two decompositions differ; even for normal $M$, the unitary diagonalization $M=UDU^*$ is an SVD only when $M$ is positive semidefinite, and otherwise becomes one after moving the phase of each eigenvalue into one of the unitary factors ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).
- **Non-uniqueness of singular vectors.** Singular values are unique but $U,V$ are not; with repeated singular values the subspaces, not the vectors, are determined, and the best rank-$k$ approximation in the Frobenius norm is unique only if $\sigma_k>\sigma_{k+1}$ ([Wikipedia: Low-rank approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation)).
- **Forming $M^*M$ explicitly.** The eigenvectors of $M^*M$ give $V$ in exact arithmetic, but practical algorithms bidiagonalize $M$ directly with Householder transformations ([Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition)).
- **Weighted problems lose the closed form.** With entrywise weights, low-rank approximation has no analytic solution via the SVD, and local optimization gives no guarantee of a global optimum ([Wikipedia: Low-rank approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation)).

### Open problems
- **Guarantees for structured sketches.** Randomized SVD uses random embeddings; Martinsson and Tropp note that for sparse sign matrices "it is conjectured that improvements are still possible" in subspace-embedding bounds, that the common practical embedding dimension for subsampled trigonometric transforms has "no rigorous justification", and that structured embeddings "lack the precise guarantees" available for Gaussians ([Martinsson and Tropp, arXiv:2002.01387](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2002.01387)).
- **Analysis of non-Gaussian test matrices.** The same survey remarks that "the rigorous analysis of other types of embeddings tends to be difficult", which limits sharp error bounds for fast randomized SVD variants ([Martinsson and Tropp, arXiv:2002.01387](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2002.01387)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Singular value decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition): existence, reduced forms, norms, operators, algorithms, history.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Low-rank approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rank_approximation): Eckart–Young–Mirsky and weighted variants.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.06SC Lecture 29: Singular Value Decomposition (Strang)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/resources/lecture-29-singular-value-decomposition/): video lecture with transcript.
- **Primary:** [Eckart and Young, "The Approximation of One Matrix by Another of Lower Rank" (Psychometrika, 1936)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02288367): the optimal low-rank approximation theorem.
- **Primary:** [Halko, Martinsson, Tropp, "Finding structure with randomness" (SIAM Review, 2011)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.4061): randomized algorithms for approximate SVD with error analysis.
- **Primary:** [Martinsson and Tropp, "Randomized numerical linear algebra: foundations and algorithms"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.01387): survey of sketching and randomized low-rank approximation; published in *Acta Numerica* 29 (2020), 403–572 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/S0962492920000021)).
- **Further reading:** [Horn and Johnson, *Matrix Analysis* (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/matrix-analysis/9CF2CB491C9E97948B15FAD835EF9A8B): standard graduate reference on matrix norms and perturbation.
references.Smooth Manifolds:
## Reference
### Overview
A smooth manifold is a space locally modelled on $\mathbb{R}^n$ in which the changes of coordinates are $C^\infty$, so that derivatives, vector fields, differential forms and integrals can be defined globally. Smoothness is extra structure on a topological manifold, not a property of it: some topological manifolds admit no smooth structure, and some admit several inequivalent ones. ([Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold); [Wikipedia: Smooth structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_structure))

The basic toolkit is local: the inverse function theorem makes a map with invertible differential a local diffeomorphism, the regular value theorem produces submanifolds as level sets, Sard's theorem says regular values are plentiful, and transversality makes intersections generic. Global results then follow by gluing with partitions of unity, for example Whitney's embedding of every manifold in Euclidean space. MIT 18.965 follows this order, from inverse and implicit function theorems through vector bundles, Sard, transversality, Whitney embedding, Morse theory, the Lie derivative and de Rham cohomology. ([MIT OCW 18.965](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-965-geometry-of-manifolds-fall-2004/pages/lecture-notes/); [Wikipedia: Inverse function theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem))

nLab describes smooth manifolds as the differential-geometric analogue of schemes, and notes that relaxing the requirement of local Euclidean models leads to diffeological spaces and smooth sets. ([nLab: smooth manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+manifold); [Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold))

### Formal definition
A chart on a topological space $M$ is a homeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open $U\subseteq M$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Charts $(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)$, $(U_\beta,\varphi_\beta)$ are smoothly compatible if the transition map $\varphi_\alpha\circ\varphi_\beta^{-1}:\varphi_\beta(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta)\to\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta)$ is $C^\infty$. A smooth atlas is a cover by pairwise compatible charts, and a maximal smooth atlas is a smooth structure. A smooth $n$-manifold is a Hausdorff, second-countable space with a smooth structure. ([Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold); [nLab: smooth manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+manifold))

A map $f:M\to N$ is smooth if $\psi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$ in charts. A point $p$ is regular if $df_p:T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N$ is surjective; $q\in N$ is a regular value if every point of $f^{-1}(q)$ is regular, and otherwise $q$ is a critical value. $f$ is a submersion if $df_p$ is surjective everywhere and an immersion if it is injective everywhere. ([Wikipedia: Submersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersion_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Sard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem))

A smooth real vector bundle of rank $k$ is a smooth map $\pi:E\to M$ with local trivializations $\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times\mathbb{R}^k$ whose transition functions $g_{UV}:U\cap V\to GL(k,\mathbb{R})$ are smooth and satisfy the cocycle condition. The tangent bundle $TM$, of dimension $2n$, is the basic example, and vector fields are its sections. ([Wikipedia: Vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle); [Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold))

### Key results
- **Partitions of unity.** Every open cover of a $C^k$ manifold ($0\le k\le\infty$) admits a subordinate $C^k$ partition of unity; analytic and holomorphic manifolds generally do not. Hausdorffness and second countability are essentially equivalent to the existence of bump functions and partitions of unity. ([Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold))
- **Inverse function theorem.** If $F:M\to N$ is $C^1$ and $dF_p$ is a linear isomorphism, then $F$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from an open neighbourhood of $p$ onto its image. More generally, the constant rank theorem: if $F$ has constant rank near $p$, then in suitable charts $F$ coincides with its (linear) differential. ([Wikipedia: Inverse function theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_function_theorem))
- **Submersions and the regular value theorem.** Near a point where $f$ is a submersion there are coordinates in which $f$ is the projection $(x_1,\dots,x_m)\mapsto(x_1,\dots,x_n)$. If $q$ is a regular value of $f:M\to N$, then $f^{-1}(q)$ is empty or a smooth manifold of dimension $\dim M-\dim N$. ([Wikipedia: Submersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersion_%28mathematics%29))
- **Sard's theorem.** If $f:N\to M$ is $C^k$ between manifolds of dimensions $n$ and $m$ with $k\ge\max\{n-m+1,1\}$, the set of critical values has measure zero in $M$. Morse proved the case $m=1$ in 1939 and Sard the general case in 1942; Smale proved a version for infinite-dimensional [Banach manifolds](node:Banach%20Manifolds). ([Wikipedia: Sard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem); [MIT OCW 18.965, lectures 10–11, 18–19](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-965-geometry-of-manifolds-fall-2004/pages/lecture-notes/))
- **Transversality.** Submanifolds $X,Y\subseteq M$ are transverse if $T_pX+T_pY=T_pM$ at every $p\in X\cap Y$; a transverse intersection is a submanifold whose codimension is the sum of the codimensions. If $f$ is transverse to a submanifold $Z$, then $f^{-1}(Z)$ is a submanifold. Parametric transversality: if $F:X\times S\to Y$ and $\partial F$ are transverse to $Z$, then $f_s=F(\cdot,s)$ and $\partial f_s$ are transverse to $Z$ for almost every $s$; Thom's theorem gives density of transverse maps. ([Wikipedia: Transversality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transversality_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Transversality theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transversality_theorem))
- **Whitney embedding.** Every smooth $m$-manifold ($m>0$, Hausdorff, second-countable) embeds smoothly in $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$; this is the best linear bound, since $\mathbb{RP}^m$ does not embed in $\mathbb{R}^{2m-1}$ when $m$ is a power of two. The weak version: a continuous map from an $n$-manifold to an $m$-manifold can be approximated by an embedding if $m>2n$ and by an immersion if $m>2n-1$. ([Wikipedia: Whitney embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_embedding_theorem))
- **Flows and the Lie derivative.** A smooth vector field $X$ has a local flow $\Phi_t$, the unique solution of $\tfrac{d}{dt}\Phi_t(p)=X(\Phi_t(p))$, $\Phi_0(p)=p$. The Lie derivative of a tensor field is $\mathcal{L}_XT=\tfrac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^{*}T$; it gives $\mathcal{L}_Xf=X(f)$, $\mathcal{L}_XY=[X,Y]$, and on forms Cartan's formula $\mathcal{L}_X\omega=i_X\,d\omega+d(i_X\omega)$. ([Wikipedia: Lie derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_derivative))
- **Exotic spheres.** Milnor (1956) found smooth manifolds homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to $S^7$. In dimensions other than 4, oriented homotopy spheres form a finite abelian group under connected sum; Kervaire and Milnor showed the group in dimension 7 is cyclic of order 28. Spheres of dimensions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 12, 56 and 61 have no exotic smooth structures. ([Wikipedia: Exotic sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_sphere))
- **Smoothing in low and high dimensions.** In dimension 3 and lower every topological manifold admits an essentially unique PL structure, and in dimensions at most 6 a PL structure can be smoothed in an essentially unique way; in every dimension other than 4 a compact topological manifold has only finitely many essentially distinct PL or smooth structures. The Kirby–Siebenmann class $\kappa(M)\in H^4(M;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ of a topological manifold vanishes whenever $M$ admits a PL structure. ([Wikipedia: 4-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4-manifold); [Wikipedia: Kirby–Siebenmann class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirby%E2%80%93Siebenmann_class))
- **Dimension four.** $\mathbb{R}^4$ has uncountably many exotic smooth structures; the $E_8$ manifold admits no smooth structure; and for a simply connected compact 4-manifold the Kirby–Siebenmann class must vanish for a smooth structure to exist; if moreover the intersection form is definite, Donaldson's work shows a smooth structure exists if and only if the form is diagonalizable. ([Wikipedia: 4-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4-manifold); [Wikipedia: Smooth structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_structure))

### Examples
- **Spheres.** $S^n$ is covered by two charts, copies of $\mathbb{R}^n$ glued by the inversion $x\mapsto x/\|x\|^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$; it is also a level set of $x_1^2+\dots+x_{n+1}^2$ with nonvanishing gradient, which is the implicit-function-theorem definition of a submanifold that Poincaré used. ([Wikipedia: Manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold))
- **Level sets.** For $f(x,y,z)=x^4+y^4+z^4$ the only critical point is the origin, so $f^{-1}(t)$ is a smooth surface for every $t>0$. ([Wikipedia: Submersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersion_%28mathematics%29))
- **Projective spaces** $\mathbb{RP}^n$ arise as quotients of $S^n$ identifying antipodal points. ([Wikipedia: Manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold))
- **Lie groups** are manifolds with smooth group operations; every Lie group is parallelizable, and even-dimensional spheres of positive dimension admit no Lie group structure. ([Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold))
- **Bundles.** The Möbius bundle is a nontrivial line bundle over $S^1$; by the hairy ball theorem $TS^2$ is nontrivial. ([Wikipedia: Vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle))

### History
Riemann introduced $n$-dimensional manifolds in his habilitation lecture; Weyl gave a modern definition of 2-dimensional manifolds in 1913; and the widely accepted general definition by atlases is due to Whitney. ([Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold)) Morse (1939) and Sard (1942) proved Sard's theorem; Milnor's 1956 exotic 7-spheres showed that smooth structure is not determined by topology. ([Wikipedia: Sard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem); [Wikipedia: Exotic sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_sphere))

### Connections

### Common pitfalls
- A topological space does not "be" a smooth manifold; one must specify a smooth structure, and some topological manifolds, such as the $E_8$ manifold, have none. ([Wikipedia: Smooth structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_structure))
- Sard's theorem is about critical values: it says the image $f(X)$ of the critical set $X$ has measure zero, not that $X$ itself is small. ([Wikipedia: Sard's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sard%27s_theorem))
- An immersion can self-intersect; an embedding is an immersion that is a homeomorphism onto its image. ([Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold))
- Partitions of unity exist in the smooth category but not in the analytic or holomorphic ones, so gluing arguments do not transfer. ([Wikipedia: Differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold))

### Open problems
- **Smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.** The Poincaré conjecture is known in every dimension except the smooth (equivalently PL) case in dimension 4, whose truth is unknown. Freedman, Gompf, Morrison and Walker studied potential counterexamples and showed the conjecture is equivalent to a generalization of Property R for knots. ([Wikipedia: 4-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4-manifold); [Freedman–Gompf–Morrison–Walker, arXiv:0906.5177](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.5177); [Wikipedia: Exotic sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_sphere))
- **Classifying smooth 4-manifolds.** For simply connected compact 4-manifolds, which topological ones are smoothable is almost settled, the main gap being the 11/8 conjecture, an inequality between the second Betti number and the signature of smooth spin 4-manifolds of which Furuta proved a weaker 10/8 form; by contrast, there is not a single smoothable 4-manifold whose smooth structures are fully known. ([Wikipedia: 4-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4-manifold)) Hopkins, Lin, Shi and Xu attack the 11/8 conjecture through Furuta's question on Pin(2)-equivariant stable maps and prove a "10/8+4" theorem. ([Hopkins–Lin–Shi–Xu, arXiv:1812.04052](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.04052))

references.Sobolev Spaces:
## Reference
### Overview
Sobolev spaces are Banach spaces of functions whose weak (distributional) derivatives up to some order lie in $L^p$; for $p<\infty$ they are separable. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space)) They are the spaces in which weak formulations of [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations) are posed: the right-hand side of a weak Dirichlet problem may be any element of the dual space $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ of $H^1_0(\Omega)$; for $\Omega$ bounded in some direction the Riesz representation theorem gives a unique weak solution $u\in H^1_0$ of $-\Delta u=f$, and the Lax–Milgram theorem does the same for non-symmetric uniformly elliptic operators. ([Hunter, Elliptic PDEs, ch. 4](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch4.pdf)) Embedding theorems convert integrability of derivatives into integrability or Hölder continuity of the function, and on bounded domains and compact manifolds some of these embeddings are compact. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality))

Sergei Sobolev introduced the spaces in the 1930s, building on the variational method for elliptic boundary value problems, and proved norm inequalities that became central to the theory of embeddings of function spaces. ([MacTutor: Sobolev](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Sobolev/)) Current research questions include sharp constants and their stability, nonlocal characterizations of $W^{1,p}$, and spaces of maps into manifolds, where topology decides whether smooth maps are dense. ([Nobili, arXiv 2412.05935](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.05935); [Brezis, Some of my favorite open problems](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/234.pdf); [Detaille, arXiv 2305.12589](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.12589))

### Formal definition
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$$W^{k,p}(\Omega)=\{u\in L^p(\Omega): D^\alpha u\in L^p(\Omega)\ \text{for all }|\alpha|\le k\},$$
where $D^\alpha u$ is the weak derivative, with norm
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}=\Big(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p}^p\Big)^{1/p}\quad(p<\infty),\qquad \|u\|_{W^{k,\infty}}=\max_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty}.$$
$H^k=W^{k,2}$ is a Hilbert space, and $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in $H^1(\Omega)$. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space)) See [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29), [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces).

**Negative order.** $H^{-1}(\Omega)=H^1_0(\Omega)^*$ with norm $\|f\|_{H^{-1}}=\sup\{|\langle f,\phi\rangle|/\|\phi\|_{H^1_0}:\phi\ne0\}$. It consists exactly of the distributions $f=f_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_if_i$ with $f_0,f_i\in L^2(\Omega)$, and $\|f\|_{H^{-1}}$ is the infimum of $(\sum_{i=0}^n\|f_i\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$ over such representations. ([Hunter, Elliptic PDEs, ch. 4](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch4.pdf))

**Fractional order.** For $s\in\mathbb{R}$ the Bessel-potential space is $H^{s,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)=\{f\in\mathcal{S}':\mathcal{F}^{-1}[(1+|\xi|^2)^{s/2}\mathcal{F}f]\in L^p\}$ (see [Tempered Distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions)); for integer $k$ and $1<p<\infty$ it agrees with $W^{k,p}$ up to equivalent norms. For $0<\theta<1$ the Sobolev–Slobodeckij space uses the Gagliardo seminorm
$$[f]_{\theta,p}^p=\iint\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^p}{|x-y|^{\theta p+n}}\,dx\,dy.$$
([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space)) These spaces sit in the Besov scale: $B^s_{2,2}=H^s$, and for non-integer $s$, $B^s_{p,p}$ is the Sobolev–Slobodeckij space $W^{s,p}$. ([Wikipedia: Besov space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besov_space))

### Key results
- **Meyers–Serrin.** For $1\le p<\infty$ and any open $\Omega$, every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ can be approximated in norm by smooth functions. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- **Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality.** For $1\le p<n$ there is $C=C(n,p)$ with $\|u\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^n)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}$ for all $u\in C^1_c(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where $\frac1{p^*}=\frac1p-\frac1n$. Sobolev proved $1<p<n$ (1938); Gagliardo and Nirenberg independently proved $p=1$. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality))
- **Sobolev embedding on $\mathbb{R}^n$.** If $k>\ell$, $p<n$, $1\le p<q<\infty$ and $\frac1p-\frac kn=\frac1q-\frac\ell n$ (such $q$ exists when $(k-\ell)p<n$), then $W^{k,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)\subseteq W^{\ell,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ continuously. If $n<pk$ and $r+\alpha=k-\frac np$ with $\alpha\in(0,1)$, then $W^{k,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)\subset C^{r,\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality))
- **Embedding on compact manifolds.** On a compact Riemannian $n$-manifold, for $1\le p,q<\infty$: if $k\ge m$ and $k-\frac np\ge m-\frac nq$, then $W^{k,p}\subseteq W^{m,q}$ continuously; if $k>m$ and $k-\frac np>m-\frac nq$, the embedding is compact (Rellich–Kondrachov). ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space)) The compact-manifold form allows $q<p$ only because the measure is finite: for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ neither inclusion between $L^p$ and $L^q$ holds. ([Wikipedia: Lp space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space)) For bounded $\Omega$, $H^1_0(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)$ is compact. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space)) See [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds), [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics).
- **Morrey's inequality.** For $n<p\le\infty$ there is $C=C(n,p)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{0,\gamma}(\mathbb{R}^n)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)}$ for $u\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\cap L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $\gamma=1-\frac np$. At $p=n$, $u\in W^{1,n}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ has bounded mean oscillation with $|u|_{BMO}\le C\|Du\|_{L^n}$. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality))
- **Trudinger's theorem.** Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain satisfying the cone condition, $mp=n$, $p>1$. Then $W^{m,p}(\Omega)$ embeds in the Orlicz space $L_A(\Omega)$ defined by $A(t)=\exp(t^{n/(n-m)})-1$. Trudinger proved it in 1967; Moser (1971) gave a sharp form and Adams (1988) a sharp version for higher derivatives. ([Wikipedia: Trudinger's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trudinger%27s_theorem))
- **Sharp Sobolev constant (Aubin, Talenti).** For $1<p<d$, $\|u\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le S_{d,p}\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)}$ for all $u\in\dot W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with the explicit constant
$$S_{d,p}=\frac1d\Big(\frac{d(p-1)}{d-p}\Big)^{\frac{p-1}p}\Big(\frac{\Gamma(d+1)}{d\,\omega_d\,\Gamma(d/p)\,\Gamma(d+1-d/p)}\Big)^{\frac1d},\quad\omega_d=\frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)},$$
computed by Aubin and Talenti; equality holds exactly for the bubbles $a(1+b|x-z_0|^{p/(p-1)})^{-(d-p)/p}$, $a\in\mathbb{R}$, $b>0$, $z_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Because these form a non-compact family, Lions' concentration-compactness principle is what shows that a sequence nearly attaining $S_{d,p}$ converges, up to translation, dilation and scaling, to a bubble. Bianchi and Egnell gave the first quantitative result, for $p=2$ with an implicit constant $C_d$: $\inf\|\nabla(u-u_{a,b,z_0})\|_2/\|\nabla u\|_2\le C_d(\|\nabla u\|_2/\|u\|_{2^*}-S_{d,2}^{-1})^{1/2}$. ([Nobili, arXiv 2412.05935](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.05935)) Dolbeault, Esteban, Figalli, Frank and Loss proved stability with explicit constants of the correct large-dimension behaviour. ([Dolbeault et al., arXiv 2209.08651](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.08651)) See [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function).
- **Hardy's inequality.** For $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (hence $f\in W^{1,p}$ by density), $\|f/|x|\|_{L^p}\le\frac p{n-p}\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}$, with sharp constant; in one dimension, for $p>1$, $\int_0^\infty\big(\frac1x\int_0^xf\big)^p\,dx\le\big(\frac p{p-1}\big)^p\int_0^\infty f^p$ for nonnegative measurable $f$. ([Wikipedia: Hardy's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%27s_inequality))
- **Poincaré inequality.** For bounded $\Omega$ there is $C=C(\Omega)$ with $\int_\Omega|f|^2\le C^2\int_\Omega|\nabla f|^2$ for $f\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- **Traces and extension.** For bounded Lipschitz $\Omega$ there is a bounded $T:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\to L^p(\partial\Omega)$ with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for $u\in W^{1,p}\cap C(\overline\Omega)$; for $1<p<\infty$ it maps onto $W^{1-1/p,p}(\partial\Omega)$, and $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is its kernel. For Lipschitz $\Omega$ there is a bounded extension operator $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\to W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- **Bourgain–Brezis–Mironescu formula.** $\lim_{s\nearrow1}(1-s)\iint_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^p}{|x-y|^{sp+n}}=K_{n,p}\int_\Omega|\nabla f|^p$ with $K_{n,p}=\frac{2\pi^{(n-1)/2}\Gamma((p+1)/2)}{p\,\Gamma((p+n)/2)}$, and, for $1<p<\infty$ and $\Omega$ smooth and bounded, finiteness of the $\limsup$ characterizes $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ among $L^p$ functions. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- **Density of smooth maps into manifolds (Detaille).** Let $\mathcal N$ be a smooth compact connected Riemannian manifold without boundary, $0<s<\infty$, $1\le p<\infty$, $Q^m$ the unit cube. If $sp\ge m$, smooth maps are always dense in $W^{s,p}(Q^m;\mathcal N)$. If $sp<m$, $C^\infty(\overline{Q}^m;\mathcal N)$ is dense if and only if $\pi_{\lfloor sp\rfloor}(\mathcal N)=\{0\}$. This completes Bethuel ($s=1$), Brezis–Mironescu ($0<s<1$) and Bousquet–Ponce–Van Schaftingen (integer $s\ge2$); non-integer $s>1$ was the new case. ([Detaille, arXiv 2305.12589](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.12589))

### Examples
- In one dimension, $W^{1,1}(0,1)$ consists of absolutely continuous functions and $W^{1,\infty}(I)$ of bounded Lipschitz functions; $|x|^{-1}\in W^{1,1}$ of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is unbounded. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- $W^{k,\infty}$ is a normed algebra, while $W^{k,p}$ for $p<\infty$ need not be: $|x|^{-1/3}$ is in $L^2$ near $0$ but its square is not. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- Nash's inequality $\|u\|_{L^2}^{1+2/n}\le C\|u\|_{L^1}^{2/n}\|Du\|_{L^2}$ for $u\in L^1\cap W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is proved by splitting the Fourier integral at a radius $\rho$ and using Parseval. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality)) See [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis), [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem).
- Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev: for $0<\alpha<n$, $1<p<q<\infty$, $\frac1q=\frac1p-\frac\alpha n$, the Riesz potential $I_\alpha=(-\Delta)^{-\alpha/2}$ satisfies $\|I_\alpha f\|_q\le C\|f\|_p$; Sobolev's original proof of the embedding used this. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality))

### History
Sobolev introduced his spaces in the 1930s; by 1935 he headed the differential equations department of the Steklov Institute, and his 1950 book on applications of functional analysis in mathematical physics was translated by the AMS in 1963. ([MacTutor: Sobolev](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Sobolev/)) Sobolev's inequality for $1<p<n$ dates from 1938 and the $p=1$ case is due to Gagliardo and Nirenberg. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality)) Trudinger's exponential embedding appeared in 1967 and Moser's sharp form in 1971. ([Wikipedia: Trudinger's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trudinger%27s_theorem)) The density problem for manifold-valued maps, opened by Schoen and Uhlenbeck's example of a map from the 3-ball to the 2-sphere, was settled for all $s$ and $p$ by Detaille (arXiv 2023, accepted at JEMS). ([Detaille, arXiv 2305.12589](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12589); [Detaille, arXiv 2305.12589 (HTML)](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.12589))

### Connections
- [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces): $W^{k,p}$ is the subspace of $L^p$ with derivatives in $L^p$; $W^{0,p}=L^p$.
- [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29) and [Tempered Distributions](node:Tempered%20Distributions): weak derivatives are distributional derivatives; $H^{-1}$ is a space of distributions and $H^s$ for real $s$ lives in $\mathcal{S}'$.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): $H^k$ and $H^1_0$ are Hilbert spaces; Riesz representation and Lax–Milgram give weak solutions.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations) and [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem): the weak Dirichlet problem is posed in $H^1_0$, with data in $H^{-1}$.
- [Calculus of Variations](node:Calculus%20of%20Variations): Rellich–Kondrachov compactness and concentration compactness drive the direct method.
- [Well-Posed Problems](node:Well-Posed%20Problems) and [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation): energy estimates are $H^k$ estimates.
- [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces): each $W^{k,p}$ is a Banach space.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): homotopy groups of the target decide density of smooth maps.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): Sobolev inequalities on manifolds with Ricci lower bounds.
- [MSC 46Exx - Linear function spaces and their duals](node:MSC%2046Exx%20-%20Linear%20function%20spaces%20and%20their%20duals): the MSC home (46E35).

### Common pitfalls
- The embedding $k-\frac np\ge m-\frac nq$ with $k\ge m$ is a compact-manifold statement. On $\mathbb{R}^n$ the theorem is stated for $p<q<\infty$ with equality of the scaling exponents. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space); [Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality))
- The Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality needs $p<n$; at $p=n$ its substitutes are a BMO bound on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and Trudinger's exponential integrability on bounded domains, not boundedness. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_inequality); [Wikipedia: Trudinger's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trudinger%27s_theorem))
- Traces of $W^{1,p}$ functions are not in $W^{1,p}(\partial\Omega)$: "taking the trace costs $1/p$ of a derivative." ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- $H^{-1}$ is larger than $L^2$: each $f\in L^2$ defines an element of $H^{-1}$ with $\|f\|_{H^{-1}}\le\|f\|_{L^2}$, but $H^{-1}$ also contains first-order distributional derivatives of $L^2$ functions, so weak formulations allow such right-hand sides. ([Hunter, Elliptic PDEs, ch. 4](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch4.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Nonlocal characterization of $W^{1,p}$ (Brezis–Van Schaftingen–Yung).** For $\lambda>0$, $p\ge1$ and measurable $u$ on a smooth bounded connected $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^N$, let $\Phi_{\lambda,p}(u)=\operatorname{meas}\{(x,y)\in\Omega\times\Omega:|u(x)-u(y)|^p/|x-y|^{p+N}\ge\lambda\}$. If $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda\Phi_{\lambda,p}(u)=0$ then $u$ is constant. Open Problem 9.1: does $\liminf_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda\Phi_{\lambda,p}(u)=0$ suffice? Open Problem 9.2: for $1<p<\infty$, is $\|\nabla u\|_{L^p}^p\le C\liminf_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda\Phi_{\lambda,p}(u)$ for all measurable $u$ (with the BV analogue for $p=1$)? Poliakovsky proved this with $\limsup$ in place of $\liminf$. ([Brezis, Some of my favorite open problems](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~brezis/PUBlications/234.pdf))
- **Quantitative stability of the Sobolev inequality on manifolds.** On non-compact $d$-manifolds with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge0$ and positive asymptotic volume ratio, functions nearly saturating the sharp Sobolev inequality are close to Euclidean bubbles, but only qualitatively, by concentration compactness. Nobili poses as open (Question 4.5) whether a quantitative version can be proved, notes that the compactness approach would have to be changed or complemented by a quantitative local analysis around bubbles, and expects it to be considerably harder than his Question 4.6 because the underlying manifold is non-compact. ([Nobili, arXiv 2412.05935](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.05935))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Sobolev space, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space): definitions, approximation, embeddings, traces, extension, fractional spaces.
- **Learn:** [Hunter, Elliptic PDEs, chapter 4 (UC Davis)](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/ch4.pdf): $H^1_0$, $H^{-1}$, weak solutions and Lax–Milgram; [MIT OCW 18.155 Differential Analysis, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-155-differential-analysis-fall-2004/pages/lecture-notes/): tempered distributions, Fourier inversion and Sobolev embedding.
- **Primary:** [Detaille, A complete answer to the strong density problem in Sobolev spaces with values into compact manifolds (arXiv 2305.12589)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12589): the density theorem for all $s,p$.
- **Primary:** [Nobili, An overview of the stability of Sobolev inequalities on Riemannian manifolds with Ricci lower bounds (arXiv 2412.05935)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.05935): sharp constants, bubbles, concentration compactness, stability, open questions.
- **Further reading:** [Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (Springer, 2011)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-0-387-70914-7); [Leoni, A First Course in Sobolev Spaces (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics)](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Leoni+A+First+Course+in+Sobolev+Spaces&rows=3).

## Reference
### Overview
A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is an autoencoder whose hidden code is pushed to be sparse, so that each input is reconstructed from a few active units. In the classical formulation of the Stanford UFLDL tutorial, a penalty keeps the average activation of each hidden unit close to a small target $\rho$ such as $0.05$, so most units are inactive most of the time. ([UFLDL](http://ufldl.stanford.edu/tutorial/unsupervised/Autoencoders/)) With a linear decoder, training an SAE is a form of sparse [dictionary learning](node:Dictionary%20Learning): the decoder directions form a dictionary, usually overcomplete, and each input is approximated as a sparse combination of them. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_dictionary_learning); [Cunningham et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.08600))

In [mechanistic interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability), SAEs are used to disentangle neural-network activations into sparse representations whose dimensions often correspond to human-understandable concepts. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability)) The motivation is polysemanticity, neurons that respond to several unrelated concepts, which toy models explain by [superposition](node:Feature%20Superposition): a network stores more sparse features than it has dimensions, along non-orthogonal directions. ([Elhage et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652)) An SAE trained on the residual stream or an MLP layer is meant to recover those directions as dictionary atoms ("features" or "latents") that are more interpretable than neurons. ([Cunningham et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.08600); [Templeton et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29358))

The method has two structural limits. Reconstruction is imperfect, so substituting the SAE output for the true activations degrades the model; and the learned dictionary is not unique, so features change with the random seed. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093); [Paulo and Belrose 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615)) The classical identifiability theory of dictionary learning is strongest for square dictionaries, while interpretability SAEs are heavily overcomplete, where provable guarantees need extra assumptions such as incoherence. ([Spielman et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.5882); [Arora, Ge and Moitra 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.6273))

### Formal definition
**Sparse dictionary learning.** Given data $x_1,\dots,x_K \in \mathbb R^d$, find a dictionary $D \in \mathbb R^{d\times n}$ with norm-constrained atoms and codes $r_i$ minimizing
$$\sum_i \lVert x_i - D r_i\rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert r_i\rVert_0 .$$
With the $\ell_0$ penalty the problem is non-convex and NP-hard; with $\ell_1$ it is convex in $D$ or in $R$ when the other is fixed, but not jointly. The dictionary is overcomplete when $n > d$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_dictionary_learning))

**Classical sparse autoencoder.** With $\hat\rho_j = \frac1m\sum_i a_j(x^{(i)})$ the mean activation of hidden unit $j$ over the training set,
$$J_{\text{sparse}}(W,b) = J(W,b) + \beta \sum_j \Big[\rho\log\frac{\rho}{\hat\rho_j} + (1-\rho)\log\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho_j}\Big],$$
where $\beta$ weights the KL sparsity penalty. ([UFLDL](http://ufldl.stanford.edu/tutorial/unsupervised/Autoencoders/))

**ReLU (L1) SAE for activations.** For an activation $x \in \mathbb R^{d}$, $c = \mathrm{ReLU}(Mx + b)$, $\hat x = M^\top c$, with rows of $M$ normalized as dictionary features, trained on $\lVert x - \hat x\rVert_2^2 + \alpha\lVert c\rVert_1$ (tied weights). ([Cunningham et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.08600)) Bricken et al. (2023) used ReLU autoencoders with an $\ell_1$ penalty, unit-norm decoder columns and geometric-median bias initialization; this became the baseline for later work. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093); [Rajamanoharan et al. 2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.16014))

**Gated SAE.** With $\pi_{\text{gate}}(x) = W_{\text{gate}}(x-b_{\text{dec}})+b_{\text{gate}}$, the encoder is
$$\tilde f(x) = \mathbf 1[\pi_{\text{gate}}(x)>0]\odot \mathrm{ReLU}\big(W_{\text{mag}}(x-b_{\text{dec}})+b_{\text{mag}}\big),\qquad (W_{\text{mag}})_{ij} = e^{(r_{\text{mag}})_i}(W_{\text{gate}})_{ij},$$
trained on $\lVert x-\hat x(\tilde f(x))\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathrm{ReLU}(\pi_{\text{gate}}(x))\rVert_1 + \lVert x - \hat x_{\text{frozen}}(\mathrm{ReLU}(\pi_{\text{gate}}(x)))\rVert_2^2$, where $\hat x_{\text{frozen}}$ uses a frozen copy of the decoder. Separating which latents fire from their magnitudes removes the shrinkage the $\ell_1$ penalty causes. ([Rajamanoharan et al. 2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.16014))

**TopK SAE.** $z = \mathrm{TopK}(W_{\text{enc}}(x - b_{\text{pre}}))$, $\hat x = W_{\text{dec}} z + b_{\text{pre}}$, trained on reconstruction error alone; $k$ sets $L_0$ directly. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093))

**JumpReLU SAE.** Replaces ReLU with a discontinuous JumpReLU and trains an $\ell_0$ penalty directly with straight-through estimators, avoiding $\ell_1$ shrinkage. ([Rajamanoharan et al. 2024b](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14435)) With tied gate and magnitude weights, a Gated SAE is itself a JumpReLU SAE with threshold $\theta = b_{\text{mag}} - e^{r_{\text{mag}}}\odot b_{\text{gate}}$. ([Rajamanoharan et al. 2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.16014))

**Variants.** Transcoders are wider, sparsely activating MLPs trained to approximate a dense MLP sublayer rather than reconstruct its input. ([Dunefsky et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11944)) Crosscoders allow a wider class of inputs and outputs, potentially reconstructing many layers' activations at once. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))

### Key results
- **Identifiability of square dictionaries (Spielman–Wang–Wright, Theorem 3).** Let $Y = AX$ with $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ nonsingular and $X$ Bernoulli($\theta$)-subgaussian. If $1/n \le \theta \le 1/C$ and $p > Cn\log n$, then with probability at least $1-C'n\exp(-c\theta p)$ any other factorization with no denser rows than $X$ equals $(A, X)$ up to a permutation and a nonsingular diagonal scaling. Their two-column ER-SpUD linear-programming algorithm recovers all rows of $X$ with high probability when $p > c_1 n^2\log^2 n$ and $2/n \le \theta \le \alpha/\sqrt n$ (Theorem 9); the single-column version fails once $\theta \ge \sqrt{\beta\log n/n}$ (Theorem 10). They conjectured the sample requirement could drop to $O(n\log n)$. ([Spielman et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.5882)) Adamczak proved that a version of ER-SpUD recovers $A$ and $X$ exactly with high probability once $p \ge Cn\log n$, optimal up to the constant. ([Adamczak 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.02049))
- **Overcomplete recovery (Arora–Ge–Moitra).** For a $\mu$-incoherent overcomplete dictionary (pairwise column inner products at most $\mu/\sqrt n$) and random codes with $k \le c\min\big(\sqrt n/(\mu\log n),\ m^{1/2-\eta}\big)$ (any $\eta>0$) nonzeros, a polynomial-time algorithm learns the dictionary; in the noiseless case running time and sample complexity depend on $\log(1/\varepsilon)$. This was the first provable algorithm for overcomplete dictionaries, previous guarantees covering the full-rank case. ([Arora, Ge and Moitra 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.6273)) Agarwal, Anandkumar and Netrapalli give a clustering-style procedure that approximately recovers sparsely used overcomplete dictionaries, refinable to high accuracy, for example by $\ell_1$-regularized regression. ([Agarwal et al. 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.1952)) These results concern generative sparse models and specific algorithms, not SAEs trained by gradient descent.
- **[Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws) for TopK SAEs.** Reconstruction MSE follows a power law in compute, with fits improved by an irreducible-loss term; a joint law in $n$ and $k$ holds for small $k$; at fixed $k$ larger subject models need more latents for the same MSE. Tied initialization plus an auxiliary loss kept dead latents to about 7% in a 16-million-latent SAE on GPT-4, against up to 90% without them. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093))
- **Reconstruction gap.** Substituting the 16M-latent SAE into GPT-4 gave the loss of a model trained with about 10% of GPT-4's pretraining compute; in Pythia-70M, substituting a layer-2 residual reconstruction raised Pile perplexity from 25 to 40. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093); [Cunningham et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.08600))
- **Shrinkage and the Pareto frontier.** Gated SAEs remove $\ell_1$ shrinkage and need about half as many firing features for comparable reconstruction fidelity, at similar interpretability, on models up to 7B parameters; JumpReLU SAEs on Gemma 2 9B reach higher fidelity at a given sparsity than Gated and TopK SAEs. ([Rajamanoharan et al. 2024a](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16014); [Rajamanoharan et al. 2024b](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14435))
- **Seed dependence.** SAEs differing only in initialization seed learn different features: in a 131K-latent SAE on a Llama 3 8B feedforward layer only about 30% of features were shared, and ReLU/$\ell_1$ SAEs were more stable than TopK SAEs at matched sparsity. ([Paulo and Belrose 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615))
- **Proxy metrics do not predict usefulness.** Across eight metrics and over 200 SAEs from eight architectures, gains on unsupervised proxy metrics did not reliably translate into practical performance; Matryoshka SAEs did slightly worse on proxies but much better on feature disentanglement. ([Karvonen et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09532)) Under data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise and covariate shift, ensembles adding SAE probes did not consistently beat baseline-only ensembles. ([Kantamneni et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16681))

### Examples
- **Pythia residual stream.** Tied ReLU SAEs on Pythia-70M and Pythia-410M score higher on automated interpretability than PCA, ICA, neurons and random directions in early layers (the gap shrinks in later layers), and an apostrophe feature whose ablation mainly lowers the logit of a following "s". ([Cunningham et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.08600))
- **Claude 3 Sonnet.** Templeton et al. trained SAEs with up to 34 million features on the middle-layer residual stream of a production model; features were multilingual and multimodal, included safety-relevant ones (deception, sycophancy, bias), and steered behaviour when clamped. ([Templeton et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29358)) Only about 12M of the 34M latents were alive, illustrating the dead-latent problem. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093))
- **GPT-4.** A 16-million-latent TopK SAE trained on GPT-4 activations for 40 billion tokens, evaluated by downstream loss, probe loss on 61 tasks, explainability and ablation sparsity. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093))
- **Gemma Scope.** An open suite of JumpReLU SAEs on all layers and sub-layers of Gemma 2 2B and 9B, with selected layers of 27B. ([Lieberum et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05147))
- **Transcoder circuits.** Transcoders on models of 120M–1.4B parameters matched SAEs on sparsity, faithfulness and interpretability and were used to reverse-engineer the greater-than circuit in GPT-2 small. ([Dunefsky et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11944))

### History
Sparse autoencoders with a KL sparsity penalty were taught as unsupervised feature learners in the UFLDL tutorial. ([UFLDL](http://ufldl.stanford.edu/tutorial/unsupervised/Autoencoders/)) In signal processing, learned dictionaries give sparser representations than fixed Fourier or wavelet bases and are trained by MOD, K-SVD and online dictionary learning. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_dictionary_learning); [Mairal et al. 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.3230)) The toy-model account of superposition appeared in September 2022. ([Elhage et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652)) Sharkey et al. (2022) did early work applying dictionary learning to transformer activations, which Cunningham et al. build on. ([Rajamanoharan et al. 2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.16014); [Cunningham et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.08600)) In 2023 Cunningham et al. on Pythia and Bricken et al. at Anthropic brought SAEs into language-model interpretability; Anthropic's scaling to Claude 3 Sonnet (Templeton et al.), Gated, TopK and JumpReLU SAEs, Gemma Scope and transcoders followed in 2024, and SAEBench in 2025. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanistic_interpretability); [Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496); [Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093); [Templeton et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29358); [Rajamanoharan et al. 2024a](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16014); [Rajamanoharan et al. 2024b](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14435); [Dunefsky et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11944); [Lieberum et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05147); [Karvonen et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09532))

### Connections
- [Dictionary Learning](node:Dictionary%20Learning): an SAE with a linear decoder learns a sparse dictionary, with an encoder computing the codes amortized.
- [Feature Superposition](node:Feature%20Superposition): the hypothesis that motivates decomposing activations into overcomplete sparse features.
- [Feature Stability and Absorption](node:Feature%20Stability%20and%20Absorption): seed dependence, splitting and absorption of SAE features.
- [Linear Representation Hypothesis](node:Linear%20Representation%20Hypothesis): SAEs assume features are linear directions.
- [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): the research program that uses SAEs to decompose activations.
- [Circuit Tracing](node:Circuit%20Tracing): builds attribution graphs from transcoder and crosscoder features.
- [Activation Steering](node:Activation%20Steering): SAE features supply candidate steering directions.
- [Principal Component Analysis](node:Principal%20Component%20Analysis): a dense, orthogonal baseline that SAEs are compared against.
- [Regularization](node:Regularization): the $\ell_1$, KL and $\ell_0$ sparsity penalties.
- [Artificial Neural Networks](node:Artificial%20Neural%20Networks): the autoencoder architecture and the networks whose activations are decomposed.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models): the main subject models of current SAE work.
- [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): SAE reconstruction error obeys power laws in latents and compute.

### Common pitfalls
- **Reading interpretability off sparsity.** Under enough optimization pressure sparsity stops being a proxy for interpretability, producing feature splitting, absorption and composition. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))
- **Ignoring the error term.** The reconstruction residual holds everything the dictionary misses, and its effect on model loss can be large. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093); [Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))
- **Treating one run's features as canonical.** Features vary with the seed; they are better seen as a pragmatically useful decomposition than a complete list of the model's features. ([Paulo and Belrose 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615))
- **Borrowing identifiability theorems.** Uniqueness results for square dictionaries do not transfer to overcomplete SAEs; overcomplete guarantees need incoherence and sparsity assumptions and apply to specific algorithms. ([Spielman et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1206.5882); [Arora, Ge and Moitra 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.6273))
- **Optimizing proxies, skipping baselines.** Proxy metrics do not predict downstream value, and usefulness claims need strong non-SAE baselines. ([Karvonen et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09532); [Kantamneni et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16681))

### Open problems
- **Reconstruction error, cost and the linear representation hypothesis.** Sharkey et al. list as open that SDL reconstructions may not be faithful enough, that SDL assumes the linear representation hypothesis in nonlinear models, that SDL is expensive for large models, and that SDL latents may not contain the concepts needed downstream. ([Sharkey et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16496))
- **Better sparsity constraints and explanations.** Gao et al. note that TopK forcing exactly $k$ latents per token is likely suboptimal, suggest constraining $\mathbb E[L_0]$ instead, and list better optimization and explanation methods as future work. ([Gao et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2406.04093))
- **Completeness and faithfulness.** Templeton et al. state that their feature set is incomplete and that rigorous methods for checking whether features faithfully capture model computation are lacking. ([Templeton et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29358))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Sparse dictionary learning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_dictionary_learning): problem statement, overcompleteness, MOD, K-SVD, online algorithms.
- **Learn:** [Stanford UFLDL tutorial, Autoencoders](http://ufldl.stanford.edu/tutorial/unsupervised/Autoencoders/): the KL-penalized sparse autoencoder and its gradient.
- **Primary:** [Cunningham et al. 2023, Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.08600): the tied ReLU SAE on Pythia.
- **Primary:** [Templeton et al., Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29358): SAEs with up to 34M features on a production model.
- **Primary:** [Gao et al. 2024, Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04093): TopK SAEs, scaling laws and evaluation metrics.
- **Primary:** [Rajamanoharan et al. 2024, Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16014): the Gated SAE.
- **Primary:** [Arora, Ge and Moitra, New Algorithms for Learning Incoherent and Overcomplete Dictionaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.6273): provable overcomplete dictionary learning.
- **Further reading:** [Sharkey et al. 2025, Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16496): survey including the limits of sparse dictionary learning.
- **Further reading:** [Mairal, Bach and Ponce, Sparse Modeling for Image and Vision Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.3230): monograph on learned dictionaries and sparse coding.
references.Special Functions:
## Reference
### Overview
"Special functions" is a term defined by consensus rather than by a formal definition: it names the functions (gamma, Bessel, Legendre, hypergeometric, elliptic and others) whose identities and applications recur often enough to deserve a theory and tables. In the nineteenth century the high point was the theory of [elliptic functions](node:Elliptic%20Functions), with a detailed theory of spherical harmonics by the end of the century; later the Bateman Manuscript Project under Erdélyi aimed at an encyclopedic collection, and from 1950 onward much of the classical theory was recast in terms of [Lie groups](node:Lie%20Groups). ([Wikipedia, Special functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_functions))

The organizing principle of the classical part of the subject is the hypergeometric function. Bessel functions, complete elliptic integrals, incomplete beta functions, Legendre functions and the classical orthogonal polynomials (Jacobi, Legendre, Chebyshev, Gegenbauer) are special or limiting cases of the Gauss function ${}_2F_1$ or its confluent forms. ([Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function); [DLMF §10.16](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.16); [DLMF §18.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.5))

In physics the same functions appear through separation of variables: Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates separates into a radial equation and the Legendre equation, giving Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics, while cylindrical separation leads to Bessel's equation. ([Dine, Physics 212 lecture](https://scipp-legacy.pbsci.ucsc.edu/~dine/ph212/212_special_functions_lecture.pdf))

### Formal definition
The generalized hypergeometric function is
$$ {}_pF_q(a_1,\dots,a_p;b_1,\dots,b_q;z)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(a_1)_k\cdots(a_p)_k}{(b_1)_k\cdots(b_q)_k}\frac{z^k}{k!}, $$
with $(a)_k$ the Pochhammer symbol and no $b_i$ a nonpositive integer. For $p\le q$ the series defines an entire function; for $p=q+1$ the radius of convergence is $1$; for $p>q+1$ it diverges for all $z\ne0$ unless a top parameter is a nonpositive integer, when it is a polynomial. ([DLMF §16.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/16.2))

The Gauss function $F(a,b;c;z)={}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)$ is defined by this series for $|z|<1$ and by analytic continuation elsewhere; its principal branch is analytic in the plane cut along $[1,\infty)$, and the regularized function $\mathbf F=F/\Gamma(c)$ is entire in $a,b,c$. It solves the hypergeometric equation $z(1-z)w''+[c-(a+b+1)z]w'-abw=0$, which has regular singularities at $0,1,\infty$ with exponent pairs $\{0,1-c\}$, $\{0,c-a-b\}$, $\{a,b\}$. ([DLMF §15.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.2); [DLMF §15.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.10))

Confluent forms arise by merging singularities: replacing $z$ by $z/b$ in the equation for $F(a,b;c;z)$, letting $b\to\infty$, and then renaming $c$ as $b$ gives Kummer's equation $zw''+(b-z)w'-aw=0$, with an irregular singularity at $\infty$ and solution $M(a,b,z)={}_1F_1(a;b;z)$. Bessel functions, solutions of $z^2w''+zw'+(z^2-\nu^2)w=0$, are expressible through these functions (DLMF 10.16.5 writes $J_\nu$ via $M$), and also as a ${}_0F_1$:
$$J_\nu(z)=\frac{(z/2)^\nu}{\Gamma(\nu+1)}\,{}_0F_1\!\left(-;\nu+1;-\tfrac14z^2\right)=(z/2)^\nu\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-z^2/4)^k}{k!\,\Gamma(\nu+k+1)}.$$
([DLMF §13.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/13.2); [DLMF §10.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.2); [DLMF §10.16](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.16))

The basic (q-) hypergeometric series ${}_{r+1}\phi_s$ replaces Pochhammer symbols by $q$-shifted factorials $(a;q)_n$; for $|q|<1$ it converges for all $z$ when $s>r$ and for $|z|<1$ when $s=r$, and as $q\to1^-$, with parameters $q^{a_j},q^{b_j}$ and argument $(q-1)^{s-r}z$, it tends to ${}_{r+1}F_s$. ([DLMF §17.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/17.4))

### Key results
- **Riemann's characterization.** Every second-order linear ODE with exactly three regular singular points can be transformed to the hypergeometric equation; Kummer found a group of 24 transformations of its solutions, isomorphic to the symmetric group on four points. The monodromy representation maps $\pi_1(\mathbb C\setminus\{0,1\})$ to $GL(2,\mathbb C)$; when the exponent differences $1-c$, $c-a-b$, $a-b$ are non-integer rationals with denominators $k,l,m$, the monodromy group is finite iff $1/k+1/l+1/m>1$, and Schwarz's list identifies the cases with algebraic solutions. ([Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function); [DLMF §15.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.10))
- **Gauss's summation and Chu–Vandermonde.** If $\Re(c-a-b)>0$ then $F(a,b;c;1)=\dfrac{\Gamma(c)\Gamma(c-a-b)}{\Gamma(c-a)\Gamma(c-b)}$; for $n=0,1,2,\dots$, $F(-n,b;c;1)=(c-b)_n/(c)_n$. ([DLMF §15.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.4))
- **Integral representations.** Euler: for $\Re c>\Re b>0$ and $|\arg(1-z)|<\pi$, $\mathbf F(a,b;c;z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(b)\Gamma(c-b)}\int_0^1t^{b-1}(1-t)^{c-b-1}(1-zt)^{-a}\,dt$. A Mellin–Barnes integral $\mathbf F(a,b;c;z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i\,\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\int_{-i\infty}^{i\infty}\frac{\Gamma(a+t)\Gamma(b+t)\Gamma(-t)}{\Gamma(c+t)}(-z)^t\,dt$ holds for $|\arg(-z)|<\pi$, $a,b\notin\{0,-1,\dots\}$. ([DLMF §15.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.6))
