- **Asymptotics by saddle points.** If $\Re(zp(t))$ attains its minimum on the path at an interior simple saddle $t_0$ ($p'(t_0)=0$), then $\int_a^be^{-zp(t)}q(t)\,dt\sim2e^{-zp(t_0)}\sum_{s\ge0}\Gamma(s+\tfrac12)b_{2s}z^{-s-1/2}$, with $b_0=q/(2p'')^{1/2}$ at $t_0$. A standard large-argument example is Hankel's expansion $J_\nu(z)\sim(2/\pi z)^{1/2}(\cos\omega\sum_k(-1)^ka_{2k}(\nu)z^{-2k}-\sin\omega\sum_k(-1)^ka_{2k+1}(\nu)z^{-2k-1})$, $\omega=z-\tfrac12\nu\pi-\tfrac14\pi$, valid for $|\arg z|\le\pi-\delta$; for real $\nu\ge0$, $z>0$ the remainder is bounded in absolute value by the first neglected term, and has its sign, once the truncation index $\ell\ge\max(\tfrac12\nu-\tfrac14,1)$. ([DLMF §2.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.4); [DLMF §10.17](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.17))
- **Stokes phenomenon.** In compound asymptotic expansions the form of the expansion changes discontinuously across Stokes lines, where one contribution maximally dominates another, although the function is analytic; exponentially small terms are switched on smoothly through complementary error functions, and repeated re-expansion of remainders gives hyperasymptotic expansions. ([DLMF §2.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.11))
- **Orthogonal polynomials and Favard's theorem.** Polynomials orthogonal for a weight $w\ge0$ on $(a,b)$ with $0<\int w<\infty$ and all moments finite satisfy a three-term recurrence $p_{n+1}=(A_nx+B_n)p_n-C_np_{n-1}$; conversely polynomials generated by such a recurrence with $A_nA_{n-1}C_n>0$ are orthogonal for some measure (Favard). The Jacobi polynomials are $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)=\frac{(\alpha+1)_n}{n!}{}_2F_1(-n,n+\alpha+\beta+1;\alpha+1;\tfrac{1-x}{2})$ and the Laguerre polynomials are $L_n^{(\alpha)}(x)=\frac{(\alpha+1)_n}{n!}{}_1F_1(-n;\alpha+1;x)$. ([DLMF §18.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.2); [DLMF §18.5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.5))
- **Askey scheme.** The hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials form a hierarchy linked by limits: the number of free parameters rises from zero for Hermite to four for Wilson and Racah, e.g. Hahn $\to$ Jacobi, Meixner $\to$ Laguerre, Charlier $\to$ Hermite. Wilson polynomials are ${}_4F_3$ series: $W_n(y^2)=(a+b)_n(a+c)_n(a+d)_n\,{}_4F_3(-n,n+a+b+c+d-1,a+iy,a-iy;a+b,a+c,a+d;1)$. Koekoek and Swarttouw catalogue the scheme and its $q$-analogue, with limit relations and the $q\to1$ recovery of the classical families. ([DLMF §18.21](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.21); [DLMF §18.26](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.26); [Koekoek–Swarttouw](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9602214))

### Examples
Legendre polynomials have generating function $(1-2xt+t^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{\ell\ge0}P_\ell(x)t^\ell$, which arises from expanding the Coulomb potential $1/|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|$; from it one derives $\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)^2dx=2/(2n+1)$. ([Dine, Physics 212 lecture](https://scipp-legacy.pbsci.ucsc.edu/~dine/ph212/212_special_functions_lecture.pdf)) Bessel functions are confluent hypergeometric: $J_\nu(z)=\frac{(z/2)^\nu e^{\mp iz}}{\Gamma(\nu+1)}M(\nu+\tfrac12,2\nu+1,\pm2iz)$. ([DLMF §10.16](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.16))

### History
Wallis used the term "hypergeometric series" in 1655; Euler studied such series and Gauss gave the first systematic treatment in 1813. Kummer's study followed in 1836, Riemann characterized the function by its three regular singularities in 1857, and Schwarz determined the algebraic cases. ([Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function)) Klein stressed the importance of hypergeometric series for astronomy and mathematical physics, and electronic computation later changed the role of printed tables. ([Wikipedia, Special functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_functions))

### Connections
- [Hypergeometric Functions](node:Hypergeometric%20Functions): the unifying family for most classical special functions.
- [Basic Hypergeometric Series](node:Basic%20Hypergeometric%20Series): the $q$-analogues and the $q$-Askey scheme.
- [Bessel Functions](node:Bessel%20Functions): confluent hypergeometric functions from cylindrical separation.
- [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function) and [Beta Function](node:Beta%20Function): they appear in Gauss's summation and Euler's integral.
- [Spherical Harmonics](node:Spherical%20Harmonics): Legendre functions on the sphere.
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations): regular and irregular singular points classify the families.
- [Complex Analysis](node:Complex%20Analysis): branch cuts, analytic continuation, Mellin–Barnes integrals and saddle points.
- [Laplace and Mellin Transforms](node:Laplace%20and%20Mellin%20Transforms): Mellin–Barnes representations.
- [Numerical Evaluation of Special Functions](node:Numerical%20Evaluation%20of%20Special%20Functions): computation from series, recurrences and asymptotics.
- [Orthogonal Expansions and Wavelets](node:Orthogonal%20Expansions%20and%20Wavelets): expansions in orthogonal polynomial bases.
- [MSC 33Cxx - Hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Cxx%20-%20Hypergeometric%20functions) and [MSC 33Dxx - Basic hypergeometric functions](node:MSC%2033Dxx%20-%20Basic%20hypergeometric%20functions): the corresponding MSC subfields.

### Common pitfalls
- Branches: for non-integer $\nu$, $J_\nu$ is taken on the plane cut along $(-\infty,0]$, and ${}_2F_1$ on the plane cut along $[1,\infty)$; identities valid on principal branches can fail after continuation. ([DLMF §10.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.2); [DLMF §15.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.2))
- $F(a,b;c;z)$ has poles at $c=0,-1,-2,\dots$; the regularized $\mathbf F$ avoids them, and formulas in references may use either normalization. ([DLMF §15.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.2))
- Asymptotic expansions such as Hankel's are generally divergent and hold only in stated sectors; crossing Stokes lines changes the expansion. ([DLMF §10.17](https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.17); [DLMF §2.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.11))
- Orthogonality is relative to a specific weight and interval (or a discrete measure); changing it changes the polynomials. ([DLMF §18.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.2))

### Open problems
- **Positivity of a Gegenbauer integral.** Conjecture 6.1 of the OPSFA13 problem session (Beatson, zu Castell, Xu) asserts that a certain integral $F_n^{\lambda,\delta}(t)$ of Gegenbauer polynomials is positive on $(0,\pi]$ iff $\delta\ge\lambda+1$; at the time of the 2015 report the case $\delta=\lambda+1$ was proved only for $\lambda=(d-2)/2$, $d=4,6,8$. ([Cohl, OPSFA13 report](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1607.06196)) Xu (Proc. AMS 2018) later proved the sufficiency direction for $\lambda\in\mathbb N$, and for real $\lambda>0$ under the stronger condition $\delta\ge\lceil\lambda\rceil+1$, leaving open whether this can be improved to $\delta\ge\lambda+1$. ([Xu, arXiv 1701.00787](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1701.00787)) A 2026 preprint of Feng and Ge reports results that "can verify" the conjecture; this is not yet refereed and its scope is unconfirmed. ([Feng–Ge, arXiv 2604.11187](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11187))
- **Linearization and other problems.** The same report lists generalized linearization formulas for hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials (Cohl) as open in general, and Chihara's question whether orthogonal polynomial systems of the Blumenthal–Nevai type other than Meixner–Pollaczek exist with spectrum the whole real line. ([Cohl, OPSFA13 report](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1607.06196); [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06196))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia, Hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function): special cases, Riemann's characterization, monodromy, history.
- **Reference:** [NIST DLMF, chapter 15](https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.2): definitions, summation formulas, integrals and connection formulas for ${}_2F_1$.
- **Learn:** [Dine, Physics 212 lecture on special functions (UC Santa Cruz)](https://scipp-legacy.pbsci.ucsc.edu/~dine/ph212/212_special_functions_lecture.pdf): Legendre, spherical harmonics and Bessel functions from separation of variables.
- **Primary:** [Koekoek and Swarttouw, The Askey-scheme of hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials and its q-analogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9602214): definitions, orthogonality, recurrences and limits for every family in the scheme.
- **Primary:** [Cohl, Report from the open problems session at OPSFA13 (SIGMA 2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06196): current open problems.
- **Further reading:** [Andrews, Askey and Roy, Special Functions (Cambridge University Press, 1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9781107325937): graduate monograph on the subject.
- **Further reading:** [Whittaker and Watson, A Course of Modern Analysis (5th ed., ed. Moll, Cambridge University Press, 2021)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/9781009004091): classical analysis text, edited fifth edition.
references.Special Relativity:
## Reference
### Overview
Special relativity is the theory of physics in flat spacetime without gravitation. It rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers regardless of the motion of source or observer. Together these replace the absolute time of [Newtonian Mechanics](node:Newtonian%20Mechanics) with Lorentz transformations between inertial frames, so that time intervals, lengths, and simultaneity become frame-dependent while the spacetime interval is invariant. ([Special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity))

Geometrically, special relativity is the statement that the symmetry group of physics is the isometry group of [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime), the ten-dimensional [Poincaré Group](node:Poincaré%20Group) of translations and Lorentz transformations. Physical laws are written as relations between four-vectors and tensors, which makes their frame independence manifest; Maxwell's equations take this form, and in quantum theory the unitary representations of the Poincaré group classify particles by mass and spin. ([Poincaré group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_group); [Covariant electromagnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_formulation_of_classical_electromagnetism))

Special relativity is restricted to flat (Minkowski) spacetime; it is the approximation to [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) that holds for weak gravitational fields and small regions, and it is the most accurate model of motion at any speed when gravitational and quantum effects are negligible. ([Special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity))

### Formal definition
For frames in standard configuration with relative velocity $v$ along $x$, let $\beta=v/c$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$. The Lorentz boost is
$$t'=\gamma\left(t-\frac{vx}{c^2}\right),\qquad x'=\gamma(x-vt),\qquad y'=y,\qquad z'=z.$$
With rapidity $\zeta$ defined by $\beta=\tanh\zeta$, it reads $x'=x\cosh\zeta-ct\sinh\zeta$, $ct'=ct\cosh\zeta-x\sinh\zeta$: a hyperbolic rotation. ([Lorentz transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_transformation); [Special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity))

In signature $(+,-,-,-)$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$, the interval $ds^2=c^2dt^2-dx^2-dy^2-dz^2$ is invariant. The Lorentz group $O(1,3)$ consists of the linear maps preserving it, and the Poincaré group is the semidirect product $\mathbb R^{1,3}\rtimes O(1,3)$, a ten-dimensional noncompact Lie group. A four-vector is a quantity whose components transform by the Lorentz transformation; the four-momentum is $P=(E/c,\mathbf p)$. ([Poincaré group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_group); [Covariant electromagnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_formulation_of_classical_electromagnetism); [Special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity))

### Key results
- **Time dilation and length contraction.** A clock moving uniformly at speed $v$ runs slow by the factor $\gamma$: proper time $\Delta\tau$ between two of its ticks corresponds to coordinate time $\Delta t=\gamma\,\Delta\tau$. A rod of rest length $L_0$ moving along its length has length $L=L_0/\gamma$, measured with simultaneous endpoint positions in the observer's frame. ([Lorentz transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_transformation))
- **Velocity addition and rapidity.** For collinear motion a velocity $u$ in one frame becomes $u'=(u-v)/(1-uv/c^2)$ in a frame moving at $v$; equivalently rapidities add, $\zeta=\zeta_1+\zeta_2$. Two boosts in different directions compose to a boost followed by a rotation (Wigner rotation, the origin of Thomas precession). ([Special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity); [Lorentz transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_transformation))
- **Relativistic Doppler effect.** For source and receiver receding at $\beta>0$, $f_r=f_s\sqrt{(1-\beta)/(1+\beta)}$. In the receiver frame with angle $\theta_r$, $f_r=f_s/[\gamma(1+\beta\cos\theta_r)]$; at $\theta_r=90^\circ$ this gives the purely relativistic transverse redshift $f_r=f_s/\gamma$. ([Relativistic Doppler effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_Doppler_effect))
- **Energy–momentum relation.** For a free particle of invariant mass $m$, $\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v$, $E=\gamma mc^2$, and $E^2=(pc)^2+(mc^2)^2$, which is the invariant $P\cdot P=(mc)^2$. Massless particles have $E=pc$. For $v\ll c$, $E\approx mc^2+\tfrac12mv^2$. The invariant mass $M$ of a system satisfies $(\sum E_n)^2=(\sum\mathbf p_nc)^2+(Mc^2)^2$ and is not the sum of the constituent masses unless all are at rest. ([Energy–momentum relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy%E2%80%93momentum_relation))
- **Lorentz covariance of electrodynamics.** With four-potential $A^\alpha=(\phi/c,\mathbf A)$, field tensor $F_{\alpha\beta}=\partial_\alpha A_\beta-\partial_\beta A_\alpha$, and four-current $J^\alpha=(c\rho,\mathbf j)$, Maxwell's equations are $\partial_\alpha F^{\alpha\beta}=\mu_0J^\beta$ and $\partial_\sigma F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\sigma}+\partial_\nu F_{\sigma\mu}=0$; the Lorentz force is $dp^\alpha/d\tau=qF^{\alpha\beta}u_\beta$. ([Covariant electromagnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_formulation_of_classical_electromagnetism))
- **Stress–energy and conservation.** The electromagnetic stress–energy tensor is $T^{\alpha\beta}=\frac1{\mu_0}\left(\eta^{\alpha\nu}F_{\nu\gamma}F^{\beta\gamma}-\tfrac14\eta^{\alpha\beta}F_{\gamma\nu}F^{\gamma\nu}\right)$, and the field equations imply $\partial_\beta T^{\alpha\beta}=-F^{\alpha\beta}J_\beta$, expressing energy–momentum exchange between field and charges. ([Covariant electromagnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_formulation_of_classical_electromagnetism))
- **Wigner classification.** Positive-energy unitary irreducible representations of the Poincaré group are labelled by mass $m\ge0$ and spin (integer or half-integer); the Casimirs are $P_\mu P^\mu$ and $W_\mu W^\mu$, with $W$ the Pauli–Lubanski pseudovector. ([Poincaré group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_group))

### Examples
Fast muons produced by [cosmic rays](node:Cosmic%20Rays) in the upper atmosphere survive longer than slow muons produced and decaying in a laboratory, because their lifetimes in the Earth frame are dilated. ([Special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity); [Tests of special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_special_relativity))

The Ives–Stilwell experiment (1938) observed the Hβ line from fast hydrogen-ion canal rays both directly and in a mirror, one image blueshifted and one redshifted. Averaging the two isolated the second-order shift predicted by the relativistic Doppler formula, the first direct quantitative confirmation of the time-dilation factor. Modern storage-ring versions with lithium ions bound the deviation parameter to $\hat\alpha\le2\times10^{-8}$ (2014), and aluminium-ion optical clocks detected time dilation at speeds below 36 km/h (2010). ([Ives–Stilwell experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ives%E2%80%93Stilwell_experiment))

### History
Einstein's paper "Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper" appeared in *Annalen der Physik* in 1905 (pp. 891–921). He applied to mechanics the Lorentz transformations already known to be compatible with Maxwell's electrodynamics. Poincaré showed that Lorentz transformations form part of what is now called the Poincaré group, and the theory became essentially complete in 1907 with Minkowski's papers on spacetime; Minkowski defined the Poincaré group in 1908. ([Crossref, Einstein 1905](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/andp.19053221004); [Special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity); [Poincaré group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_group))

The Michelson–Morley experiment (1887) found no aether wind, testing the direction-independence of light speed; Kennedy–Thorndike experiments test its independence of the apparatus velocity, and Ives–Stilwell tests time dilation. Such experiments are analysed in test theories such as the Robertson–Mansouri–Sexl framework, which has three testable parameters, and the much larger Standard-Model Extension. ([Tests of special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_special_relativity))

### Connections
- [Lorentz Transformations](node:Lorentz%20Transformations): the coordinate changes between inertial frames.
- [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime): the geometric arena; boosts are hyperbolic rotations.
- [Poincaré Group](node:Poincaré%20Group): the full symmetry group, and Wigner's particle classification.
- [Four-Vectors and Relativistic Momentum](node:Four-Vectors%20and%20Relativistic%20Momentum) and [Four-Velocity](node:Four-Velocity): the covariant kinematics.
- [Electromagnetic Field Tensor](node:Electromagnetic%20Field%20Tensor) and [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations): the first Lorentz-covariant field theory.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): energy and momentum densities and their conservation.
- [Doppler Effect](node:Doppler%20Effect): its relativistic form includes time dilation.
- [Galilean Relativity](node:Galilean%20Relativity) and [Newtonian Mechanics](node:Newtonian%20Mechanics): the low-velocity limit.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): curved-spacetime generalization reducing to special relativity locally.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): built on Poincaré-invariant fields.
- [Quantum Gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity): models in which Lorentz invariance might be broken at high energy.

### Common pitfalls
Length contraction refers to endpoint positions measured simultaneously in the observer's frame, and simultaneity itself is frame-dependent. The transverse Doppler shift is a blueshift $f_r=\gamma f_s$ at geometric closest approach (analysed in the source frame) but a redshift $f_r=f_s/\gamma$ when the receiver sees the source at closest approach. Rest energy $mc^2$ is not the total energy of a moving particle, and the mass of a composite system is not the sum of constituent masses. The Hafele–Keating clock experiment also involves general-relativistic effects, so it is not a pure test of special relativity. ([Lorentz transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_transformation); [Relativistic Doppler effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_Doppler_effect); [Energy–momentum relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy%E2%80%93momentum_relation); [Tests of special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_special_relativity))

### Open problems
- **Is Lorentz invariance exact at all energies?** Mattingly's review reports theoretical suggestions that Lorentz invariance may not be an exact symmetry at all energies, investigated in several quantum-gravity models, although no quantum-gravity model predicts violation conclusively; it found no experimental evidence of violation and listed further experiments to come. Kostelecký and Russell maintain tables of bounds on Lorentz- and CPT-violating coefficients of the Standard-Model Extension across the matter, photon, neutrino, and gravity sectors, most recently revised in 2026. ([Mattingly, Modern tests of Lorentz invariance](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0502097); [Kostelecký–Russell data tables](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.0287); [Tests of special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_special_relativity))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_relativity): postulates, kinematics, four-vectors, and tests.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.033 Relativity](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-033-relativity-fall-2006/): undergraduate course on Einstein's postulates, the Lorentz transformation, paradoxes, and applications to electromagnetism and particle physics.
- **Primary:** [Einstein, Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper (1905)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/andp.19053221004): the founding paper; and [Mattingly, Modern tests of Lorentz invariance](https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0502097), a *Living Reviews* survey of experimental tests.
- **Further reading:** [Gourgoulhon, Special Relativity in General Frames](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-37276-6): Springer Graduate Texts in Physics monograph, from particles to astrophysics.
references.Spectral Theorem:
## Reference
### Overview
The spectral theorem says when a linear operator can be diagonalized. In finite dimensions a Hermitian operator has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues, and a matrix is unitarily diagonalizable exactly when it is normal. In infinite dimensions eigenvectors may not exist, so the theorem is restated: a self-adjoint or normal operator is unitarily equivalent to a multiplication operator, or equivalently is an integral of the identity function against a projection-valued measure on its spectrum. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))

The bounded formulations continue to hold for unbounded self-adjoint operators after technical changes for domains, and this version, due to von Neumann, is described as perhaps the most important result of operator theory. It underlies the functional calculus $f(A)$, Stone's theorem identifying self-adjoint operators with generators of unitary time evolution, and so the Hilbert-space formulation of quantum mechanics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem), [Wikipedia: Self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator))

### Formal definition
A densely defined operator $A$ on a Hilbert space is **symmetric** if $A\subseteq A^*$, **self-adjoint** if $A=A^*$ (symmetric with $\mathrm{Dom}\,A=\mathrm{Dom}\,A^*$), and **essentially self-adjoint** if it is symmetric and its closure is self-adjoint. ([Wikipedia: Self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator))

A **projection-valued measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal M)$ is a map $\pi$ from $\mathcal M$ to bounded operators on $H$ such that each $\pi(E)$ is an orthogonal projection, $\pi(\emptyset)=0$, $\pi(X)=I$, $\pi(E_1\cap E_2)=\pi(E_1)\pi(E_2)$, and for disjoint $E_j$, $\pi(\bigcup_jE_j)v=\sum_j\pi(E_j)v$ for every $v\in H$. For bounded measurable $f$ there is a unique bounded $T=\int f\,d\pi$ with $\langle T\xi,\xi\rangle=\int f\,d\mu_\xi$, where $\mu_\xi(E)=\langle\pi(E)\xi,\xi\rangle$. ([Wikipedia: Projection-valued measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projection-valued_measure))

### Key results
- **Finite-dimensional theorem.** A Hermitian operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, all eigenvalues real; a matrix is unitarily diagonalizable iff it is normal. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))
- **Compact self-adjoint operators.** A compact self-adjoint operator on a real or complex Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, with real eigenvalues; for compact operators the nonzero spectrum consists of eigenvalues accumulating only at $0$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem), [Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))
- **Multiplication-operator form.** If $A$ is self-adjoint (possibly unbounded) on a separable Hilbert space $H$, there are a finite measure space $(X,\mu)$, a unitary $U:H\to L^2(X,\mu)$ and a real a.e.-finite measurable $f$ such that $v\in\mathrm{Dom}\,A$ iff $f\cdot Uv\in L^2(X,\mu)$ and $UAU^{-1}g=fg$ on $U(\mathrm{Dom}\,A)$. Bounded normal operators admit the same form with complex-valued $f$. ([Wikipedia: Self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator), [Argoty, after Reed–Simon](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1102.2454), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))
- **Projection-valued-measure form.** For bounded self-adjoint $A$ there is a unique projection-valued measure $\pi_A$ on the Borel sets of $\sigma(A)$ with $A=\int\lambda\,d\pi_A(\lambda)$; the integral extends to unbounded $A$, and $g(A)=\int g(\lambda)\,d\pi_A(\lambda)$ for Borel $g$. ([Wikipedia: Projection-valued measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projection-valued_measure))
- **Borel functional calculus.** Every self-adjoint $T$ has a unique Borel functional calculus: a unit- and involution-preserving homomorphism $\pi_T$ from bounded Borel functions on $\mathbb R$ to $B(H)$, normalized by $\pi_T((\eta+i)^{-1})=(T+i)^{-1}$, with $\|\pi_T(h)\|\le\|h\|_\infty$; and if bounded Borel $h_n\to x$ pointwise with $|h_n(x)|\le|x|$ then $\pi_T(h_n)v\to Tv$ for $v\in\mathrm{Dom}\,T$. ([Wikipedia: Borel functional calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_functional_calculus), [Argoty, after Reed–Simon](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1102.2454))
- **Stone's theorem.** For every strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group $(U_t)$ there is a unique self-adjoint $A$ with $U_t=e^{itA}$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$, and conversely; $A$ is bounded iff $t\mapsto U_t$ is norm-continuous. On separable spaces, von Neumann showed strong continuity can be weakened to weak measurability. ([Wikipedia: Stone's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%27s_theorem_on_one-parameter_unitary_groups))
- **Multiplicity theory.** On a separable Hilbert space every projection-valued measure on a standard Borel space is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by $1_E$ on a direct integral $\int^\oplus H_x\,d\mu(x)$, determined up to unitary equivalence by the measure class of $\mu$ and the multiplicity function $x\mapsto\dim H_x$. ([Wikipedia: Projection-valued measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projection-valued_measure))

### Examples
- **Multiplication by $t$ on $L^2([0,1])$** is bounded self-adjoint with spectrum $[0,1]$ and no eigenvectors, so compactness cannot be dropped from the eigenbasis version. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))
- **Constant-coefficient differential operators** are diagonalized by the Fourier transform, which supplies the unitary $U$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))
- **Momentum and translations.** The translation group $T_t\psi(x)=\psi(x+t)$ has generator extending $-i\,d/dx$, the momentum operator. ([Wikipedia: Stone's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%27s_theorem_on_one-parameter_unitary_groups))
- **Boundary conditions matter.** On $L^2[0,1]$, $-i\,d/dx$ with Dirichlet conditions is symmetric but not essentially self-adjoint; with periodic conditions it is essentially self-adjoint. The negative Laplacian on $\mathbb R^n$ has uniform multiplicity 2 for $n=1$ and countably infinite multiplicity for $n\ge2$. ([Wikipedia: Self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator))
- **Square root of $-\Delta$** is defined by the functional calculus. ([Wikipedia: Borel functional calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_functional_calculus))

### History
Cauchy proved the theorem for symmetric matrices. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem)) Hilbert's 1906 work introduced bounded and compact operators and discovered continuous spectra; Riesz (1913) recast it with operators on $\ell^2$. Von Neumann established the spectral theorem for possibly unbounded self-adjoint operators in 1930–1932, Stone independently developed parts of the theory, and Stone's theorem was found independently by Stone and von Neumann. ([Landsman](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.06630)) Von Neumann's paper "Allgemeine Eigenwerttheorie Hermitescher Funktionaloperatoren" appeared in *Mathematische Annalen* 102 (1930), 49–131. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01782338)) Stone's own proofs of his theorem date from 1930 and 1932. ([Wikipedia: Stone's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%27s_theorem_on_one-parameter_unitary_groups)) According to Landsman, von Neumann told Bargmann around 1948 that self-adjointness of atomic Hamiltonians, even for hydrogen, was difficult and open; Kato's 1951 work addressed it. ([Landsman](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.06630))

### Connections
- [Spectral Theory](node:Spectral%20Theory): the general study of spectra, of which the spectral theorem is the central structure result.
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): the finite-dimensional diagonalization it generalizes.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the setting; separability is needed for the finite-measure multiplication form.
- [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): projection-valued measures and spectral measures $\mu_\xi$.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): the Fourier transform diagonalizes constant-coefficient operators.
- [C-Star Algebras and von Neumann Algebras](node:C-Star%20Algebras%20and%20von%20Neumann%20Algebras) and [Gelfand Representation](node:Gelfand%20Representation): the algebraic form of the theorem for commutative algebras.
- [Postulates of Quantum Mechanics](node:Postulates%20of%20Quantum%20Mechanics): observables are self-adjoint operators, measurement probabilities come from spectral measures, and dynamics is $e^{-itH}$ by Stone's theorem.
- [Sturm–Liouville Problems](node:Sturm–Liouville%20Problems): eigenfunction expansions for self-adjoint ODE operators.
- [Mathematical Schrödinger Operators](node:Mathematical%20Schrödinger%20Operators): self-adjointness and spectral type of quantum Hamiltonians.

### Common pitfalls
- **Eigenbasis needs compactness (or finite dimension).** Bounded self-adjoint operators need not have any eigenvectors; the general theorem is about multiplication operators or spectral measures. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))
- **Symmetric is not self-adjoint.** The spectral theorem and Stone's theorem need $A=A^*$, including equality of domains; the self-adjoint extensions of a symmetric differential operator are parametrized by unitary maps between the solution spaces of $Pu=\pm iu$. ([Wikipedia: Self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator))
- **Normal is the right finite-dimensional condition.** Normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable but may have non-real eigenvalues; real spectrum characterizes self-adjointness among bounded normal operators. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem), [Wikipedia: Self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator))

### Open problems
- **Invariant subspaces beyond normal operators.** The spectral theorem gives nontrivial invariant subspaces for normal operators, but whether every bounded operator on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space has one is open; operators without nontrivial invariant subspaces are known on certain Banach spaces (Enflo's example, and Read's on $\ell^1$). ([Wikipedia: Invariant subspace problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace_problem))

> [!warning] Contested
> Enflo's preprint (arXiv May 2023, revised April 2024, no journal reference listed) claims every bounded operator on a Hilbert space has a closed non-trivial invariant subspace ([Enflo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15442)); Wikipedia lists it among claimed solutions without confirming it ([Wikipedia: Invariant subspace problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace_problem)). Reported and unconfirmed.

- **Spectral type of random operators.** For the Anderson model $-\Delta+\lambda V_\omega$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)$, a 2017 survey calls a proof of delocalization (extended states) on the square lattice the biggest open problem in the field, and lists localization at every disorder strength in two dimensions as an open problem. ([Rojas-Molina](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.02293))

> [!warning] Contested
> An October 2026 abstract by Jakšić and Last refers to "the recent OpenAI preprint on the weak-disorder Anderson model on $\mathbb Z^d$", $d\ge3$, and its final passage "from boundary positivity to purity" ([Jakšić–Last](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11611)). The abstract does not identify that preprint or state its status; any claimed resolution of the $d\ge3$ weak-disorder problem is reported and unconfirmed here.

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem): finite-dimensional, compact, bounded, normal and unbounded versions.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Projection-valued measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projection-valued_measure): definitions, the PVM form and multiplicity theory.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102 Introduction to Functional Analysis](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/pages/lecture-notes-and-readings/): lecture 22 proves the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators.
- **Primary:** [von Neumann, Allgemeine Eigenwerttheorie Hermitescher Funktionaloperatoren (Math. Ann. 1930)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01782338): the original unbounded spectral theorem.
- **Primary:** [Landsman, Quantum theory and functional analysis](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.06630): historical survey from Hilbert to von Neumann, Stone and Gelfand–Naimark.
- **Further reading:** [Hall, Quantum Theory for Mathematicians (Springer GTM, 2013)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4614-7116-5): graduate text on the mathematics of quantum theory.
references.Spectral Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Spectral theory extends eigenvalue theory from matrices to linear operators on infinite-dimensional spaces. For an operator on a finite-dimensional space the spectrum is exactly its set of eigenvalues, but in infinite dimensions the spectrum can contain points that are not eigenvalues, so the theory studies where $T-\lambda I$ fails to be invertible rather than only where it fails to be injective. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))

The name was introduced by David Hilbert in his Hilbert-space theory, framed through quadratic forms and developed, in his words, from purely mathematical interests; the link to atomic spectra and the Schrödinger equation came about two decades later. The theory also extends beyond Hilbert spaces to Banach spaces and Banach algebras, where the commutative case leads to the Gelfand representation. ([Wikipedia: Spectral theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theory))

The central result for Hilbert spaces is the spectral theorem: self-adjoint and normal operators are unitarily equivalent to multiplication operators, and the spectral measure splits the spectrum into absolutely continuous, pure point and singular parts. Much of mathematical physics, from Schrödinger operators to random media, is a study of which of these parts occur. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29), [Wikipedia: Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))

### Formal definition
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex Banach space $X$. Then $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ lies in the **spectrum** $\sigma(T)$ if $T-\lambda I$ has no bounded inverse (for bounded $T$, if $T-\lambda I$ is not bijective). The **resolvent set** is $\rho(T)=\mathbb C\setminus\sigma(T)$, on which the **resolvent** $R(\lambda)=(T-\lambda I)^{-1}$ is defined and holomorphic. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))

The spectrum is the disjoint union of the point, continuous and residual spectra; the approximate point spectrum is an overlapping subset ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29)):
- **point spectrum** $\sigma_p(T)$: $T-\lambda I$ not injective (eigenvalues);
- **continuous spectrum** $\sigma_c(T)$: $T-\lambda I$ injective with dense range but not surjective;
- **residual spectrum** $\sigma_r(T)$: $T-\lambda I$ injective with non-dense range;
- **approximate point spectrum**: there are unit vectors $x_n$ with $\|Tx_n-\lambda x_n\|\to0$.

For a self-adjoint $T$ on a Hilbert space, the **essential spectrum** $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(T)$ is the set of real $\lambda$ for which $T-\lambda I$ is not Fredholm, and the **discrete spectrum** is $\sigma_{\mathrm{disc}}(T)=\sigma(T)\setminus\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(T)$, the isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity. ([Wikipedia: Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum))

For an unbounded operator, $\lambda\in\rho(T)$ only if $T-\lambda I$ has a bounded, everywhere-defined inverse; for closed $T$ boundedness of the inverse is automatic, and a non-closed operator has spectrum $\mathbb C$. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))

### Key results
- **Non-emptiness and compactness.** Every bounded operator on a complex Banach space has a non-empty, closed and bounded (hence compact) spectrum. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))
- **Spectral radius formula (Gelfand).** For bounded $T$, $r(T):=\sup\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\sigma(T)\}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|T^n\|^{1/n}$. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))
- **Compact operators (Riesz).** If $T$ is compact, $\sigma(T)$ is countable, $0$ is its only possible accumulation point, and every nonzero point of $\sigma(T)$ is an eigenvalue. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))
- **Self-adjoint operators.** The spectrum of a self-adjoint operator is real ([Wikipedia: Self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator)), and a compact self-adjoint operator has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues. ([Wikipedia: Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem))
- **Weyl's theorem.** For self-adjoint $T$ and compact self-adjoint $K$, $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(T+K)=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(T)$. ([Wikipedia: Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum))
- **Weyl's criterion.** For self-adjoint $T$, $\lambda\in\sigma(T)$ iff there are unit vectors $\psi_n$ with $(T-\lambda)\psi_n\to0$, and $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(T)$ iff the $\psi_n$ can in addition be chosen with $\psi_n\rightharpoonup0$ weakly. ([Wikipedia: Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum))
- **Lomonosov's theorem (1973).** Every operator on a complex Banach space that commutes with a nonzero compact operator has a nontrivial closed invariant subspace; for compact operators themselves this is due to von Neumann (Hilbert spaces of dimension at least 2, unpublished) and Aronszajn–Smith (Banach spaces). ([Wikipedia: Invariant subspace problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace_problem))

### Examples
- **Multiplication by $t$ on $L^2([0,1])$.** No eigenvectors, yet the spectrum and the essential spectrum are $[0,1]$; narrow bumps concentrating at $\lambda$ form Weyl sequences. ([Wikipedia: Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem), [Wikipedia: Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum))
- **Right shift on $\ell^2$.** No eigenvalues, but $0\in\sigma$; the bilateral shift is unitary and its spectrum lies on the unit circle. ([Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))
- **Differential operators.** $-i\,d/dx$ on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ has essential spectrum $\mathbb R$, and $-\Delta$ on $H^2(\mathbb R^n)$ has essential spectrum $[0,\infty)$. ([Wikipedia: Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum))
- **Anderson model.** $H_\omega=-\Delta+\lambda V_\omega$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)$ with i.i.d. random site potentials $V_\omega$; in one dimension it typically localizes across the whole spectrum for every disorder strength, and in $d\ge2$ it localizes at high disorder and near band edges. ([Rojas-Molina](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.02293))

### History
Hilbert's 1906 work introduced bounded and compact operators and spectral theory, including continuous spectra; Riesz in 1913 recast these results with operators on $\ell^2$ and gave the modern definition of the spectrum, and in 1918 developed the spectral theory of compact operators on Banach spaces. ([Landsman](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.06630)) Weyl introduced the essential spectrum in 1910 for a differential operator, as the part of the spectrum independent of boundary conditions. ([Wikipedia: Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum)) Von Neumann (1930–1932) proved a spectral theorem for possibly unbounded self-adjoint operators, Stone independently developed parts of the abstract theory, and Gelfand and Naimark's 1943 paper founded the theory of C*-algebras. ([Landsman](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.06630))

### Connections
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): the setting of the spectral theorem and of quantum mechanics.
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](node:Eigenvalues%20and%20Eigenvectors): the finite-dimensional case, where the spectrum is the set of eigenvalues.
- [Spectral Theorem](node:Spectral%20Theorem): diagonalization of self-adjoint and normal operators by projection-valued measures.
- [Banach Algebras](node:Banach%20Algebras) and [Gelfand Representation](node:Gelfand%20Representation): the spectrum of an element of an abstract algebra, and the commutative theory.
- [C-Star Algebras and von Neumann Algebras](node:C-Star%20Algebras%20and%20von%20Neumann%20Algebras): the operator-algebraic setting founded by Gelfand–Naimark and von Neumann.
- [Fredholm Alternative](node:Fredholm%20Alternative): the solvability theory for compact perturbations of the identity, underlying the essential spectrum.
- [Sturm–Liouville Problems](node:Sturm–Liouville%20Problems) and [Laplace–Beltrami Operator](node:Laplace–Beltrami%20Operator): spectral theory of differential operators.
- [Mathematical Schrödinger Operators](node:Mathematical%20Schrödinger%20Operators) and [Anderson Localization](node:Anderson%20Localization): the main source of spectral-type questions in mathematical physics.
- [Spectral Theory in Physics](node:Spectral%20Theory%20in%20Physics) and [Hydrogen Atom](node:Hydrogen%20Atom): the physical counterpart and a classic computation of discrete and continuous spectrum.
- [Spectral Geometry](node:Spectral%20Geometry): recovering geometry from the spectrum of the Laplacian.

### Common pitfalls
- **Spectrum is not the set of eigenvalues.** Multiplication by $t$ on $L^2([0,1])$ and the right shift on $\ell^2$ have spectrum but no eigenvalues. ([Wikipedia: Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem), [Wikipedia: Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29))
- **Self-adjoint is not the same as symmetric for unbounded operators.** Self-adjointness requires $\mathrm{Dom}\,A=\mathrm{Dom}\,A^*$: $-i\,d/dx$ on $[0,1]$ with Dirichlet conditions is symmetric but not essentially self-adjoint, while with periodic conditions it is essentially self-adjoint. ([Wikipedia: Self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator))
- **"Essential spectrum" has several meanings.** On Banach spaces five definitions (via normally solvable, semi-Fredholm, Fredholm, index-zero Fredholm, and isolatedness conditions) are nested and any of the inclusions can be strict; for self-adjoint operators on Hilbert spaces all but the first coincide. ([Wikipedia: Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum))
- **Naive numerics can mislead.** Traditional methods for computing spectra can fail, for example through spectral pollution; Colbrook and Hansen demonstrate new algorithms on such problems and use the Solvability Complexity Index hierarchy to classify which spectral problems can be solved and what kinds of algorithms they need. ([Colbrook–Hansen](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09592))

### Open problems
- **Invariant subspace problem.** Does every bounded operator on a separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space have a nontrivial closed invariant subspace? It is open for separable Hilbert spaces; counterexamples exist on certain Banach spaces (Enflo, Read), and normal operators are settled by the spectral theorem. ([Wikipedia: Invariant subspace problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace_problem))

> [!warning] Contested
> Enflo's arXiv preprint (May 2023, revised April 2024) claims that every bounded operator on a Hilbert space has a closed non-trivial invariant subspace, and has no journal reference listed ([Enflo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15442)); Wikipedia lists it and a July 2023 preprint by Neville as claimed solutions without confirming either ([Wikipedia: Invariant subspace problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_subspace_problem)). Treat the claim as reported and unconfirmed.

- **Delocalization in the Anderson model.** A 2017 survey calls a proof of delocalization (extended states) for the Anderson model on $\mathbb Z^d$ "the biggest open problem in the field", with bulk extended states proven only on the Bethe lattice, and notes that two-dimensional localization at every disorder strength is also open. ([Rojas-Molina](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.02293))

> [!warning] Contested
> An October 2026 abstract by Jakšić and Last refers to "the recent OpenAI preprint on the weak-disorder Anderson model on $\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge3$" and its passage "from boundary positivity to purity" ([Jakšić–Last](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11611)). The abstract does not identify that preprint or state its status; any claimed resolution of the $d\ge3$ weak-disorder problem is reported and unconfirmed here.

- **Computing spectral features.** Colbrook states that there remain no general methods able to compute geometric features of spectra of infinite-dimensional operators (measure-theoretic and fractal quantities, spectral radii, numerical ranges, essential spectral gaps), gives the first algorithms for many of these problems, which he calls longstanding, and classifies them in the Solvability Complexity Index hierarchy. ([Colbrook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09598))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Spectrum (functional analysis)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_%28functional_analysis%29): definitions, parts of the spectrum, basic theorems and examples.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Essential spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_spectrum): Weyl's criterion, compact perturbations, Banach-space variants.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.102 Introduction to Functional Analysis (Rodriguez, Spring 2021)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/pages/lecture-notes-and-readings/): lectures 20–22 on the spectrum, compact self-adjoint operators and the spectral theorem.
- **Primary:** [Colbrook and Hansen, The foundations of spectral computations via the Solvability Complexity Index hierarchy](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09592): which spectral problems are computable and how.
- **Primary:** [Rojas-Molina, Random Schrödinger operators on discrete structures](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1710.02293): survey of localization and delocalization.
- **Primary:** [Landsman, Quantum theory and functional analysis](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1911.06630): history of spectral theory from Hilbert to Gelfand–Naimark.
- **Further reading:** [Schmüdgen, Unbounded Self-adjoint Operators on Hilbert Space (Springer GTM, 2012)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-94-007-4753-1): graduate text on the unbounded theory.
references.Spherical Harmonics:
## Reference
### Overview
Spherical harmonics are special functions on the sphere. Equivalently they are restrictions to the unit sphere of harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree $\ell$ in three variables. Separating variables in Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates produces them as the angular factor, with separation constant $\ell(\ell+1)$ and integer order $|m|\le\ell$; the radial factor is $r^\ell$ or $r^{-\ell-1}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))

They form a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2)$, so every square-integrable function on the sphere expands in them with mean-square convergence, in analogy with Fourier series on the circle. Each degree-$\ell$ space is an irreducible representation of $SO(3)$ of dimension $2\ell+1$, which ties the subject to angular momentum in quantum mechanics and to harmonic analysis on the homogeneous space $S^2=SO(3)/SO(2)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics); [Marinucci–Peccati, Ch. 3](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/random-fields-on-the-sphere/representations-of-so3-and-harmonic-analysis-on-s2/D13AA81EA339FDC99AE1766E42C1AB6B))

The theory extends to higher-dimensional spheres: the spaces of degree-$\ell$ harmonics are the eigenspaces of the spherical Laplacian, with eigenvalue $-\ell(\ell+n-2)$ on the $(n-1)$-sphere, and the zonal harmonics are constant multiples of Gegenbauer polynomials. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics)) Frye and Efthimiou treat spherical harmonics and Legendre polynomials in any dimension with nearly all proofs written out. ([Frye–Efthimiou](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.3548))

### Formal definition
For integers $\ell\ge0$, $|m|\le\ell$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$, $0\le\phi\le2\pi$:
$$Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi)=\sqrt{\frac{(2\ell+1)(\ell-m)!}{4\pi(\ell+m)!}}\;e^{im\phi}\,\mathsf P_\ell^m(\cos\theta),$$
with $\mathsf P_\ell^m$ the Ferrers function of the first kind. ([DLMF 14.30](https://dlmf.nist.gov/14.30))

Coordinate-free: $\mathcal H^\ell$ is the space of harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree $\ell$ on $\mathbb R^3$ (i.e. $\Delta H=0$), and the degree-$\ell$ spherical harmonics are $\{H|_{S^2}:H\in\mathcal H^\ell\}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))

### Key results
- **Orthonormality.** $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi \overline{Y_{\ell_1m_1}}Y_{\ell_2m_2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=\delta_{\ell_1\ell_2}\delta_{m_1m_2}$. ([DLMF 14.30](https://dlmf.nist.gov/14.30))
- **Completeness.** The $Y_{\ell m}$ form a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2)$; expansions converge in mean square. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))
- **Addition theorem.** If $\gamma$ is the angle between directions $(\theta_1,\phi_1)$ and $(\theta_2,\phi_2)$, then $P_\ell(\cos\gamma)=\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\theta_1,\phi_1)}\,Y_{\ell m}(\theta_2,\phi_2)$. Setting the directions equal gives Unsöld's theorem $\sum_m|Y_{\ell m}|^2=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}$. ([DLMF 14.30](https://dlmf.nist.gov/14.30); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))
- **Irreducibility under $SO(3)$.** For every $\ell\ge0$, $\mathcal P^\ell=\mathcal H^\ell\oplus r^2\mathcal P^{\ell-2}$ (with $\mathcal P^\ell$ the homogeneous polynomials of degree $\ell$), and $\mathcal H^\ell$ is an irreducible representation of $SO(3)$ of dimension $2\ell+1$. ([Durham notes, Thm 3.16.7](https://www.maths.dur.ac.uk/users/jamie.j.mason/RepresentationTheoryNotes-epiphany/Ch3.S16.html))
- **Rotations.** A rotation $R$ maps each $Y_{\ell m}$ to a linear combination of the $Y_{\ell m'}$ of the same degree $\ell$; the coefficients are complex conjugates of entries of the Wigner D-matrix $D^{(\ell)}(R)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))
- **Higher dimensions.** On $S^{n-1}\subset\mathbb R^n$ the space $\mathcal H_\ell$ of degree-$\ell$ harmonics has dimension $\binom{n+\ell-1}{n-1}-\binom{n+\ell-3}{n-1}$ (which is $2\ell+1$ for $n=3$); the $\mathcal H_\ell$ are mutually orthogonal in $L^2(S^{n-1})$ and their sum is dense there. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))
- **Angular-momentum eigenfunctions.** $L^2Y_{\ell m}=\hbar^2\ell(\ell+1)Y_{\ell m}$ and $L_zY_{\ell m}=\hbar mY_{\ell m}$, with $L_z=-i\hbar\,\partial/\partial\phi$; solid harmonics $\rho^\ell Y_{\ell m}$ solve Laplace's equation. ([DLMF 14.30(iv)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/14.30))
- **Triple-product (Gaunt) integral.** $\int Y_{\ell_1m_1}Y_{\ell_2m_2}Y_{\ell_3m_3}\,d\Omega=\sqrt{\tfrac{(2\ell_1+1)(2\ell_2+1)(2\ell_3+1)}{4\pi}}\begin{pmatrix}\ell_1&\ell_2&\ell_3\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\ell_1&\ell_2&\ell_3\\m_1&m_2&m_3\end{pmatrix}$ in terms of Wigner 3j-symbols. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SphericalHarmonic.html))
- **Symmetries.** $Y_{\ell,-m}=(-1)^m\overline{Y_{\ell m}}$ and $Y_{\ell m}(\pi-\theta,\phi+\pi)=(-1)^\ell Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi)$. ([DLMF 14.30](https://dlmf.nist.gov/14.30))

### Examples
$Y_{00}=1/\sqrt{4\pi}$ and $Y_{1,-1}=\sqrt{3/8\pi}\,\sin\theta\,e^{-i\phi}$; for $m=0$, $Y_{\ell0}=\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/4\pi}\,P_\ell(\cos\theta)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics); [MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SphericalHarmonic.html))

Functions with $m\ne0$ are called tesseral for $|m|<\ell$ and sectorial for $|m|=\ell$. ([DLMF 14.30](https://dlmf.nist.gov/14.30))

### History
Laplace introduced these functions in 1782 through the Newtonian potential; Thomson and Tait introduced solid harmonics and the name "spherical harmonics" in 1867. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))

### Connections
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations): harmonic potentials separate into radial and angular parts.
- [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions): associated Legendre functions give explicit formulas.
- [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory): each degree is an irreducible $SO(3)$-module.
- [Peter–Weyl Theorem](node:Peter–Weyl%20Theorem): yields the $L^2(S^2)$ decomposition via $S^2=SO(3)/SO(2)$.
- [Angular Momentum and Spin](node:Angular%20Momentum%20and%20Spin): $Y_{\ell m}$ are orbital angular momentum eigenfunctions.
- [Laplace–Beltrami Operator](node:Laplace–Beltrami%20Operator): $Y_{\ell m}$ are eigenfunctions on $S^2$ with eigenvalue $-\ell(\ell+1)$.
- [Wigner–Eckart Theorem](node:Wigner–Eckart%20Theorem): Gaunt integrals are built from 3j-symbols.
- [Hydrogen Atom](node:Hydrogen%20Atom): angular part of the bound states.
- [Multipole Green-Function Expansions](node:Multipole%20Green-Function%20Expansions): expansions in $Y_{\ell m}$.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): spherical analogue of Fourier series.

### Common pitfalls
Conventions differ. The Condon–Shortley phase $(-1)^m$ is included in $P_\ell^m$ in the Wikipedia/NIST convention and common in quantum mechanics, but geodesy and magnetics often omit it, and use $4\pi$ or Schmidt semi-normalization. Fix one convention before comparing formulas. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))

"Harmonic" refers to the ambient polynomial: a polynomial $f$ is harmonic when the ambient Laplacian gives $\Delta f=0$ ([Durham notes](https://www.maths.dur.ac.uk/users/jamie.j.mason/RepresentationTheoryNotes-epiphany/Ch3.S16.html)), while on $S^2$ the degree-$\ell$ functions are Laplace–Beltrami eigenfunctions with eigenvalue $-\ell(\ell+1)$, nonzero for $\ell\ge1$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics))

### Open problems
Nodal sets of eigenfunctions generalize spherical harmonics' zero sets. Yau's conjecture asserts $\lambda\lesssim\mathcal H^{n-1}(Z_{\varphi_\lambda})\lesssim\lambda$ on compact smooth Riemannian manifolds ($\lambda$ the square root of the eigenvalue). The lower bound is proved by Logunov and the sharp upper bound is proved in the real-analytic case (Donnelly–Fefferman). ([Zelditch survey](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1808.03342)) For $C^\infty$ metrics only a polynomial upper bound is known, and Logunov and Malinnikova call the conjectured upper bound still a challenging problem even in dimension two. ([Logunov–Malinnikova review](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.01639))

Related: in dimension two, for $\Delta u+\lambda u=0$ (so $\lambda$ is now the eigenvalue and the conjectured bound is of order $\lambda^{1/2}$), $H^1(\{u=0\})\le C\lambda^{3/4-\beta}$ for some universal $\beta\in(0,1/4)$, with $C$ depending on the manifold, refining the Donnelly–Fefferman estimate. ([Logunov–Malinnikova](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.02595); [Logunov–Malinnikova review](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.01639))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Spherical harmonics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_harmonics): definitions, addition theorem, representation theory, conventions.
- **Reference:** [DLMF §14.30](https://dlmf.nist.gov/14.30): definition, orthogonality, addition theorem.
- **Learn:** [Durham representation theory notes, Lecture 16](https://www.maths.dur.ac.uk/users/jamie.j.mason/RepresentationTheoryNotes-epiphany/Ch3.S16.html): harmonic polynomials and irreducible $SO(3)$ representations.
- **Primary:** [Frye–Efthimiou, Spherical Harmonics in p Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.3548): full proofs in arbitrary dimension.
- **Primary:** [Logunov–Malinnikova, nodal sets of Laplace eigenfunctions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.02595): Hausdorff measure estimates.
- **Further reading:** [Marinucci–Peccati, Random Fields on the Sphere (CUP, 2011)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/random-fields-on-the-sphere/representations-of-so3-and-harmonic-analysis-on-s2/D13AA81EA339FDC99AE1766E42C1AB6B): $SO(3)$ representations and Fourier analysis on $S^2$ via Peter–Weyl.
references.Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking:
## Reference
### Overview
Spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) occurs when the laws of a system are invariant under a symmetry but its stable state, such as the vacuum of a field theory or the equilibrium state of a magnet, is not. In Goldstone's "Mexican hat" potential the minima form a circle, so there are infinitely many degenerate vacua and selecting one breaks the $U(1)$ symmetry ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_symmetry_breaking)). Beekman, Rademaker and van Wezel stress that a state need not share the symmetries of the theory describing it, and that SSB is signalled by singular limits: limits that fail to commute, such as an infinitesimal symmetry-breaking perturbation and the [thermodynamic limit](node:Thermodynamic%20Limit) ([Beekman et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01820), §2).

Breaking a continuous global symmetry produces gapless Nambu–Goldstone modes, which govern low-energy physics across high-energy, condensed-matter, and atomic physics ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00569)). Examples include magnons in magnets, phonons in solids and fluids, and pions, which are pseudo-Goldstone bosons of approximately broken chiral symmetry in QCD ([Goldstone boson, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstone_boson)). Chiral symmetry breaking accounts for over 99% of the nucleon mass ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_symmetry_breaking)).

When the symmetry is gauged, the would-be Goldstone modes are absorbed by gauge fields, which become massive: the Higgs mechanism, responsible for the $W$ and $Z$ masses in the Standard Model ([Higgs mechanism, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_mechanism)). Strictly, a local gauge symmetry cannot be spontaneously broken (Elitzur's theorem), so "breaking of a gauge symmetry" is a convenient but technically incorrect description ([Higgs mechanism, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_mechanism)).

### Formal definition
Let a symmetry group $G$ act on a system by unitary operators, and let $|\psi\rangle$ be a stable state. The **residual (unbroken) subgroup** is $H=\{g\in G: g|\psi\rangle=e^{i\phi}|\psi\rangle\}$; the symmetry is spontaneously broken if $H\neq G$. Assuming some translational invariance, distinct broken-symmetry states are orthogonal in the thermodynamic limit, and the inequivalent ones are labelled by the cosets $gH\in G/H$ ([Beekman et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01820), §2.5.1).

Breaking of a generator $Q_i$ (the Noether charge $Q_i=\int d^3x\,q_i$) is detected by a nonzero order parameter $\langle[Q_i,\Phi_\alpha(x)]\rangle$ for some local field $\Phi_\alpha$; the number of broken generators is
$$n_{\rm BG}=\dim G/H=\dim G-\dim H$$
([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), eqs. 5–6).

**Example Lagrangian.** The abelian Higgs model
$$S=\int d^4x\Big[-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}+|(\partial_\mu-iqA_\mu)\phi|^2-\lambda(|\phi|^2-\Phi^2)^2\Big]$$
has its potential minimum on the circle $|\phi|=\Phi$ rather than at $\phi=0$ ([Higgs mechanism, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_mechanism)). For an ungauged complex scalar normalised as $\mathcal L=\tfrac12(\partial_\mu\phi^*)(\partial^\mu\phi)-\cdots$, freezing $|\phi|=v$ and writing $\phi=ve^{i\theta}$ leaves the massless field $\theta$ with Lagrangian $\tfrac{v^2}{2}(\partial\theta)^2$ up to a constant ([Goldstone boson, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstone_boson)).

### Key results
- **Goldstone's theorem (relativistic).** In Lorentz-invariant systems, spontaneous breaking of a continuous global symmetry $G\to H$ produces one massless Nambu–Goldstone boson per broken generator: $n_{\rm NGM}=n_{\rm BG}$ ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), eq. 7; [Goldstone boson, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstone_boson)). If the symmetry is also broken explicitly, the modes are light pseudo-Goldstone bosons instead ([Goldstone boson, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstone_boson)).
- **General counting rule.** Without Lorentz invariance one has only $n_{\rm NGM}\le n_{\rm BG}$. Define the real antisymmetric matrix $\rho_{ij}=-i\lim_{V\to\infty}V^{-1}\langle[Q_i,Q_j]\rangle=\sum_k f^k_{ij}\langle Q_k\rangle/V$. Then $n_{\rm NGM}=n_{\rm BG}-\tfrac12\operatorname{rank}\rho$, with $n_A=n_{\rm BG}-\operatorname{rank}\rho$ type-A modes (typically $E\propto k$) and $n_B=\tfrac12\operatorname{rank}\rho$ type-B modes (typically $E\propto k^2$), so $n_A+2n_B=n_{\rm BG}$. The rule assumes unbroken (at least discrete) translations and internal symmetries; in Lorentz-invariant systems $\rho=0$ and all modes are type A ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), eqs. 8–12). The formula was conjectured and later proved in work reviewed by Watanabe; it refines the Nielsen–Chadha inequality $n_{\rm I}+2n_{\rm II}\ge n_{\rm BG}$ of 1976 ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §2.2–2.3).
- **Coleman–Mermin–Wagner theorem.** In an infinite system with sufficiently short-range interactions in spatial dimension $d\le2$, there is no phase with spontaneously broken continuous symmetry at $T>0$; Coleman's QFT version is that there are no Goldstone bosons in two spacetime dimensions. Discrete symmetries (2D Ising) and quasi-long-range BKT order in the XY model are not excluded ([Mermin–Wagner theorem, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mermin%E2%80%93Wagner_theorem)).
- **Elitzur's theorem.** Local gauge symmetries can never be spontaneously broken; after gauge fixing, a remaining global symmetry (or redundancy) can break in a way that formally resembles spontaneous symmetry breaking ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_symmetry_breaking)).
- **No SSB in finite quantum systems.** Spontaneous symmetry breaking cannot happen in quantum mechanics of finite-dimensional systems; it requires infinitely many degrees of freedom, as in QFT or the thermodynamic limit ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_symmetry_breaking)). Even so, symmetric states of large finite systems are unstable and symmetry-broken states can be stable, the thermodynamic limit foreshadowing finite-size behaviour ([Beekman et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01820), §2.5).
- **Higgs mechanism.** In the abelian Higgs model, in the gauge where the condensate has constant phase, the term $|(\partial_\mu-iqA_\mu)\phi|^2$ evaluated on $|\phi|=\Phi$ becomes a Proca mass term for $A_\mu$, with mass proportional to $q\Phi$ (the numerical factor depends on how the scalar kinetic term is normalised); in the [electroweak theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory) three of the four Higgs components mix with the $W$ and $Z$ bosons instead of appearing as Goldstone bosons, the remaining one is the Higgs boson, and the photon, associated with unbroken electric charge, stays massless ([Higgs mechanism, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_mechanism)).
- **Higher-form symmetries.** Photons can be viewed as type-A Nambu–Goldstone modes of a spontaneously broken one-form symmetry; Watanabe listed an extended counting formalism for higher-form symmetries as future work ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §5). Hidaka, Hirono and Yokokura then built effective theories for these modes by a generalised coset construction and derived a formula for the number of gapless Nambu–Goldstone modes in terms of expectation values of commutators of conserved charges, including charges of different degrees ([Hidaka, Hirono and Yokokura](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.15901)).
- **Time translations cannot be broken in equilibrium.** Time-translation symmetry cannot be spontaneously broken in any ground state or thermal equilibrium state, which rules out equilibrium quantum time crystals; discrete time crystals arise only in driven non-equilibrium systems ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §4.1).

### Examples
- **Superfluid.** $G=U(1)$ phase rotations broken to $H=\{e\}$; broken states are labelled by $e^{i\phi}$ and distinguished by Josephson currents ([Beekman et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01820), §2.5.1). The single Nambu–Goldstone mode is the type-A superfluid phonon ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §2.4.1).
- **Ferromagnet vs antiferromagnet.** Both break $SO(3)\to SO(2)$ with $n_{\rm BG}=2$. In the ferromagnet the magnetisation gives $\operatorname{rank}\rho=2$ and a single type-B magnon with quadratic dispersion; in the antiferromagnet $\rho=0$ and there are two linear type-A magnons ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §2.4.2 and Fig. 1).
- **Pencil on its tip.** The limits of perfect balance and infinitely sharp tip do not commute, $\lim_{b\to0}\lim_{\theta\to0}y>0$ but $\lim_{\theta\to0}\lim_{b\to0}y=0$, the elementary model of SSB as a singular limit ([Beekman et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01820), eq. 2.1).
- **Crystals.** Breaking continuous translations in $d$ dimensions gives $n_{\rm BG}=d$ and $d$ acoustic phonons, matching the count of broken generators ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §3.1).

### History
Nambu identified the effect in BCS superconductivity in 1960; Goldstone elucidated it in 1961; and Goldstone, Salam and Weinberg generalised it in quantum field theory in 1962 ([Goldstone boson, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstone_boson)), in "Broken Symmetries", *Phys. Rev.* 127, 965–970 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.127.965)). Anderson proposed the gauge-field mass mechanism non-relativistically in 1962, and Brout and Englert, Higgs, and Guralnik, Hagen and Kibble gave relativistic models in 1964; Higgs and Englert received the 2013 Nobel Prize ([Higgs mechanism, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_mechanism)). Mermin and Wagner proved the absence of SSB in 1D and 2D isotropic Heisenberg models in 1966, Hohenberg published a general proof in 1967, and Coleman gave the QFT version in 1973 ([Mermin–Wagner theorem, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mermin%E2%80%93Wagner_theorem)). Nambu shared the 2008 Nobel Prize for spontaneous symmetry breaking in subatomic physics ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_symmetry_breaking)).

### Connections
- [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory): SSB is a property of the vacuum of a symmetric Lagrangian.
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory): broken states are classified by the coset space $G/H$.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem): the conserved charges $Q_i$ whose commutators define order parameters and the matrix $\rho$.
- [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): SSB in a gauge theory, with Goldstone modes eaten by gauge bosons.
- [Landau Theory of Phase Transitions](node:Landau%20Theory%20of%20Phase%20Transitions): order parameters and symmetry-breaking patterns at phase transitions.
- [Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena](node:Phase%20Transitions%20and%20Critical%20Phenomena): SSB distinguishes ordered from disordered phases.
- [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model): the prototype of discrete symmetry breaking, allowed in two dimensions.
- [Superconductivity](node:Superconductivity): Nambu's original setting and the condensed-matter Higgs mechanism.
- [Bose–Einstein Condensation](node:Bose–Einstein%20Condensation): breaks a global $U(1)$, with a gapless excitation.
- [Supersymmetry Breaking](node:Supersymmetry%20Breaking): spontaneously broken fermionic symmetries give Nambu–Goldstone fermions.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): Elitzur's theorem forbids breaking local gauge symmetry itself.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): SSB needs infinitely many degrees of freedom, as in QFT.
- [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): Goldstone modes are described by low-energy effective theories on $G/H$.

### Common pitfalls
- **Gauge symmetries are not broken.** By Elitzur's theorem, only global symmetries break; the Higgs mechanism has a gauge-invariant reformulation (Fröhlich–Morchio–Strocchi) giving the same physics ([Higgs mechanism, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_mechanism)).
- **Counting is not $\dim G/H$ in general.** Outside Lorentz-invariant systems, the symmetry-breaking pattern alone does not fix the number of Nambu–Goldstone modes; densities of conserved charges (the matrix $\rho$) are needed ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §2.2).
- **Space-time symmetries break the simple counting.** In a 2D crystal, rotations $J_z$ are broken along with translations $P_x,P_y$, but the relation $q_z=xq_y-yq_x$ among Noether densities means rotations give no independent mode; in general one Nambu–Goldstone fluctuation is lost for each linear combination $\sum_a c_a(x)q_a(x)$ that annihilates the ground state (related to the inverse-Higgs effect) ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §3.2.1).
- **Finite systems.** The classification of broken states by $G/H$ holds only in the thermodynamic limit; in finite systems distinct broken states are not exactly orthogonal ([Beekman et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01820), §2.5.1).

### Open problems
- **Never-broken space-time symmetries.** Time translation is the single known global symmetry that can never be spontaneously broken in equilibrium; Watanabe calls pinning down a general criterion for space-time symmetries of this type "an interesting future work" ([Watanabe](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00569), §4.1).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Spontaneous symmetry breaking (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_symmetry_breaking): overview with Mexican-hat, ferromagnet, chiral-symmetry and Elitzur discussions.
- **Reference:** [Goldstone boson (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstone_boson): Goldstone's theorem, examples, history.
- **Learn:** [Beekman, Rademaker and van Wezel, An Introduction to Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.01820): graduate lecture notes (SciPost Physics Lecture Notes) on singular limits, towers of states, Goldstone modes and gauge fields.
- **Primary:** [Watanabe, Counting Rules of Nambu–Goldstone Modes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00569): Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics review of the general counting formulas.
- **Primary:** [Goldstone, Salam and Weinberg, Broken Symmetries (1962)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.127.965): the field-theoretic Goldstone theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Weinberg, The Quantum Theory of Fields, Vol. 2 (Cambridge)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781139644174/type/book): chapters 19 and 21 on spontaneously broken global and gauge symmetries.
references.Standard Model of Particle Physics:
## Reference
### Overview
The Standard Model (SM) is the quantum field theory that classifies all known elementary particles and describes three of the four known fundamental forces: electromagnetism and the weak and strong interactions. It excludes gravity. Its current form was finalized in the mid-1970s, after quarks were confirmed experimentally. The top quark (1995), the tau neutrino (2000), and the Higgs boson (2012) were observed later. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))

Its matter content is twelve spin-$\tfrac12$ fermions: six quarks and six leptons, arranged in three generations. The spin-$1$ gauge bosons are eight gluons, the photon, and $W^\pm$ and $Z$. There is one spin-$0$ Higgs boson, which gives mass to the $W$, $Z$, and fermions while the photon and gluons stay massless. Higgs and electroweak precision data show that there are precisely three sequential fermion families. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model); [PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))

The SM is known to be incomplete. Its classic form has massless neutrinos, it has no viable dark-matter particle, it does not fully explain the matter–antimatter asymmetry, and it does not include general relativity. It is the base on which extensions are built. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))

### Formal definition
The gauge group is $\mathrm{SU}(3)_c\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_L\times\mathrm{U}(1)_Y$, for the strong, weak-isospin, and hypercharge interactions. The theory is the most general renormalizable Poincaré- and gauge-invariant Lagrangian built from the field content below. Its dynamics then depends on $19$ experimentally fixed parameters: masses, mixing angles, the three gauge couplings, the QCD vacuum angle, and the Higgs parameters. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))

**Electroweak sector.** $\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{U}(1)$ has gauge fields $W^i_\mu$ ($i=1,2,3$) and $B_\mu$ with couplings $g$ and $g'$. Left-handed leptons and quarks of family $i$ are doublets $(\nu_i,\ell_i^-)_L$ and $(u_i,d'_i)_L$, where $d'_i=\sum_j V^{\mathrm{CKM}}_{ij}d_j$. Right-handed fields are singlets. Electric charge is $Q=T^3+Y/2$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))

**Quantum numbers of one generation** ($Q=T^3+Y_W/2$): ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_hypercharge))

| Field | $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ | $T^3$ | $Y_W$ | $Q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $u_L$, $d_L$ | $\mathbf 3$ | $+\tfrac12$, $-\tfrac12$ | $+\tfrac13$ | $+\tfrac23$, $-\tfrac13$ |
| $u_R$ | $\mathbf 3$ | $0$ | $+\tfrac43$ | $+\tfrac23$ |
| $d_R$ | $\mathbf 3$ | $0$ | $-\tfrac23$ | $-\tfrac13$ |
| $\nu_L$, $e_L$ | $\mathbf 1$ | $+\tfrac12$, $-\tfrac12$ | $-1$ | $0$, $-1$ |
| $e_R$ | $\mathbf 1$ | $0$ | $-2$ | $-1$ |
| Higgs doublet | $\mathbf 1$ | $\pm\tfrac12$ | $+1$ | $+1$, $0$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_hypercharge); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model)) |

**Higgs sector (PDG convention).** A complex scalar doublet $\phi=(\phi^+,\phi^0)^T$ has potential
$$V(\phi)=\mu^2\phi^\dagger\phi+\frac{\lambda^2}{2}(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2 .$$
For $\mu^2<0$ it acquires $\langle\phi\rangle=(0,v/\sqrt2)^T$ with $v=\sqrt2|\mu|/\lambda\approx246$ GeV. This breaks $\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{U}(1)_Y$ to $\mathrm{U}(1)_{\mathrm{em}}$. Three of the four real components become the longitudinal $W^\pm$, $Z$ polarizations, leaving one neutral scalar $H$. The physical fields are
$$A_\mu=B_\mu\cos\theta_W+W^3_\mu\sin\theta_W,\quad Z_\mu=-B_\mu\sin\theta_W+W^3_\mu\cos\theta_W,\quad W^\pm_\mu=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(W^1_\mu\mp iW^2_\mu),$$
with $\theta_W\equiv\tan^{-1}(g'/g)$ and $e=g\sin\theta_W$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))

**Strong sector.** QCD is $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ Yang–Mills theory coupled to quarks. With $D_\mu=\partial_\mu-ig_s\tfrac12\lambda^aG^a_\mu$, the Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{QCD}}=\bar\psi\,i\gamma^\mu D_\mu\psi-\tfrac14G^a_{\mu\nu}G_a^{\mu\nu}.$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))

### Key results
- **Tree-level boson masses.** In the convention above, $M_H=\sqrt2|\mu|=\lambda v$, $M_W=\tfrac12gv$, $M_Z=\tfrac12\sqrt{g^2+g'^2}\,v=M_W/\cos\theta_W$, and $M_\gamma=0$. At momenta well below $M_W$, $W$ exchange gives the Fermi interaction with $G_F/\sqrt2=1/(2v^2)=g^2/(8M_W^2)$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))
- **Yukawa sector and fermion masses.** Gauge-invariant Yukawa terms (3×3 coupling matrices) give Dirac masses $m_i$ to the charged fermions after symmetry breaking. In the minimal model the $H\bar\psi_i\psi_i$ coupling is flavor diagonal and equals $gm_i/(2M_W)=m_i/v$. Fermion couplings to the Higgs are therefore proportional to mass. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model); [PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))
- **CKM mixing and CP violation.** Diagonalizing the quark mass matrices leaves a unitary mixing matrix $V^{\mathrm{CKM}}$ in the charged current. For $N$ generations it has $(N-1)^2$ physical parameters: $N(N-1)/2$ angles and $(N-1)(N-2)/2$ phases. For $N=3$ that is three angles and one phase, and this single phase is the SM's source of CP violation in the weak interaction. Kobayashi and Maskawa (1973) noted that CP violation could not be explained in a four-quark model, which motivated a third generation; they shared half of the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabibbo%E2%80%93Kobayashi%E2%80%93Maskawa_matrix); [PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))
- **Neutral currents.** The $Z$ couples to fermion $i$ with $g_V^i=T^3_i-2Q_i\sin^2\theta_W$ and $g_A^i=T^3_i$. The $W$ couples only to left-handed doublets, through $\gamma^\mu(1-\gamma^5)$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))
- **Gauge anomaly cancellation.** Gauge anomalies would make the theory inconsistent. In the SM they cancel generation by generation through relations among the fermion quantum numbers; for example the mixed $\mathrm{SU}(2)^2\mathrm{U}(1)_Y$ anomaly requires the charges in a generation to sum to zero, which balances quarks against leptons. The hypercharges are fixed up to a twofold ambiguity by requiring all anomalies to cancel. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomaly_%28physics%29); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_hypercharge); [PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))
