- **No neutrino mass in the minimal SM.** With no right-handed neutrinos there is no Dirac neutrino mass term, and [gauge invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance) plus renormalizability forbid Majorana masses. Observed oscillations therefore require new physics. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))
- **Leptonic mixing (PMNS).** With massive neutrinos, flavor states are related to mass states by the unitary PMNS matrix. It has three angles $\theta_{12},\theta_{23},\theta_{13}$ and a Dirac phase $\delta_{\mathrm{CP}}$, plus two more phases if neutrinos are Majorana. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontecorvo%E2%80%93Maki%E2%80%93Nakagawa%E2%80%93Sakata_matrix))

### Examples
- **Higgs discovery.** On 4 July 2012 ATLAS and CMS reported a particle with mass near $125$ GeV consistent with the Higgs boson; it was confirmed as the Higgs on 13 March 2013. Since $M_H=\lambda v$ with $\lambda$ free, the mass had to be measured rather than predicted. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model); [PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))
- **$W\to e\nu$ vertex.** The coupling is $-\dfrac{e}{2\sqrt2\sin\theta_W}\big[W^-_\mu\bar e\gamma^\mu(1-\gamma^5)\nu+W^+_\mu\bar\nu\gamma^\mu(1-\gamma^5)e\big]$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf))
- **Hypercharge check.** For $e_R$: $Q=0+(-2)/2=-1$. For $u_R$: $Q=0+(4/3)/2=2/3$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_hypercharge))

### History
Yang and Mills extended gauge theory to nonabelian groups in 1954. Glashow combined electromagnetism and the weak interaction in 1961, and Weinberg and Salam added the Higgs mechanism. Gell-Mann and Zweig introduced quarks in 1964. Neutral weak currents were found at CERN in 1973, the same year asymptotic freedom of nonabelian gauge theories was established. Glashow, Salam, and Weinberg shared the 1979 Nobel Prize, and the $W$ and $Z$ were discovered in 1983. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))

Weinberg's "A Model of Leptons" appeared in *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 19, 1264–1266 on 20 November 1967. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1264))

### Connections
- [Electroweak Theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory), [Weak Mixing Angle](node:Weak%20Mixing%20Angle), and [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): the broken $\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{U}(1)$ sector.
- [Quantum Chromodynamics](node:Quantum%20Chromodynamics) and [Lattice QCD](node:Lattice%20QCD): the $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ sector and its nonperturbative treatment.
- [Quantum Electrodynamics](node:Quantum%20Electrodynamics): the unbroken $\mathrm{U}(1)_{\mathrm{em}}$.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory), [Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking](node:Spontaneous%20Symmetry%20Breaking), [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory), [Renormalization](node:Renormalization): the framework.
- [CKM Matrix](node:CKM%20Matrix): quark mixing and CP violation.
- [Neutrino Oscillations](node:Neutrino%20Oscillations) and [Sterile Neutrinos](node:Sterile%20Neutrinos): evidence for, and models of, neutrino mass.
- [Axions](node:Axions): the Peccei–Quinn solution of the strong CP problem.
- [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): the SM viewed as the renormalizable part of SMEFT.
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem), [Naturalness](node:Naturalness), [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter), [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale): motivations for physics beyond the SM.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the force the SM leaves out.
- [Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap](node:Yang–Mills%20Existence%20and%20Mass%20Gap): the mathematical status of the nonabelian sector.
- [Feynman Diagrams](node:Feynman%20Diagrams) and [Collider Physics](node:Collider%20Physics): perturbative computation and tests.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Electroweak symmetry and mass generation](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Electroweak%20symmetry%20and%20mass%20generation)

### Common pitfalls
- **Mixing Higgs-potential conventions.** In the PDG convention, $V=\mu^2\phi^\dagger\phi+\tfrac{\lambda^2}{2}(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2$ with $\mu^2<0$, one gets $M_H=\sqrt2|\mu|=\lambda v$. In Wikipedia's convention, $V=-\mu^2\phi^\dagger\phi+\lambda(\phi^\dagger\phi)^2$ with $\mu^2>0$, the same physics reads $m_H=\sqrt2\mu=\sqrt{2\lambda}\,v$. The two $\lambda$s differ: $\lambda_{\mathrm{Wiki}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{PDG}}^2/2$. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))
- **Hypercharge normalization.** Some texts use $Y_W=Q-T^3$ instead of $Y_W=2(Q-T^3)$, which halves every entry in the table. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_hypercharge))
- **Neutrino masses are beyond the minimal SM.** The minimal SM forbids them, and the "19 parameters" count excludes them. ([PDG](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))
- **Chiral structure.** The $W$ couples only to left-handed fermions and right-handed antifermions, so parity is maximally violated. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))

### Open problems
- **Strong CP problem.** QCD allows a CP-violating angle $\bar\theta=\theta-\arg\det(Y_uY_d)$. Neutron electric-dipole-moment limits require $\bar\theta\lesssim10^{-10}$, although any value in $[0,2\pi)$ is allowed, with no SM reason for it to be small. Proposed solutions are the Peccei–Quinn axion, a massless quark (disfavored by lattice results), and Nelson–Barr models. It is often listed among the unsolved problems in physics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_CP_problem))
- **Neutrino mass: Dirac or Majorana?** Neutrinos have mass, but whether they are Dirac or Majorana fermions is not settled. Neutrinoless double beta decay would prove Majorana nature and lepton-number violation; it has not been observed, and the best half-life limits exceed $10^{26}$ years. The PMNS phase $\delta_{\mathrm{CP}}$ has not been measured directly. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majorana_fermion); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrinoless_double_beta_decay); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontecorvo%E2%80%93Maki%E2%80%93Nakagawa%E2%80%93Sakata_matrix))
- **Mathematical consistency.** The SM has not been proved mathematically self-consistent; the Yang–Mills existence and mass gap problem is a key open question. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))
- **Hierarchy problem.** If new physics coupling to the Higgs exists at high scales, keeping the weak scale far below them requires fine-tuning. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))
- **Dark matter, baryon asymmetry, gravity.** The SM has no viable dark-matter particle, does not fully explain the matter–antimatter asymmetry, and does not include gravity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Standard Model (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Model): particle content, Lagrangian, history, and challenges.
- **Learn:** Quevedo and Schachner, [*Cambridge Lectures on The Standard Model*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09211): Part III notes building the SM from first principles, with Yukawas, CKM and GIM, neutrino oscillations, anomaly cancellation, and SMEFT.
- **Primary:** PDG, [*Electroweak Model and Constraints on New Physics*](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-standard-model.pdf) (de Blas, Dittmaier, Kogler, 2025): the current review of the electroweak Lagrangian, renormalization, and global fits. Weinberg, [*A Model of Leptons*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1264) (1967).
- **Further reading:** Peskin, [*An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9780429503559) (CRC Press, 2018). Langacker, [*The Standard Model and Beyond*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/b22175) (2nd ed., CRC Press, 2017).
references.Statistical Learning Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Statistical learning theory is the mathematical framework, drawing on statistics and functional analysis, for choosing a predictive function from data. Inputs lie in a space $X$, outputs in $Y$, and training pairs are drawn from an unknown joint distribution; a learner searches a hypothesis space $H$ for a function with small expected loss, although it can only measure the average loss on its sample ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_learning_theory)). The central question is when, and how fast, minimizing the empirical risk also makes the true risk small.

Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory, developed by Vapnik and Chervonenkis between 1960 and 1990, answers this for empirical risk minimization through uniform laws of large numbers over the hypothesis class, measured by combinatorial capacity (the growth function and VC dimension) ([Wikipedia: VC theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapnik%E2%80%93Chervonenkis_theory)). Valiant's 1984 PAC model adds computational efficiency to the statistical requirement ([Wikipedia: PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probably_approximately_correct_learning)). Data-dependent measures such as Rademacher and Gaussian complexity give risk bounds that apply to decision trees, neural networks and SVMs ([Bartlett and Mendelson 2002](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/bartlett02a.html)); stability and PAC-Bayes arguments give bounds that depend on the algorithm or on a distribution over hypotheses rather than on the class alone ([Bousquet and Elisseeff 2002](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v2/bousquet02a.html); [Alquier 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.11216)).

Two regimes should be kept apart. Without restricting the class, convergence to the Bayes risk is possible for every distribution ([Wikipedia: k-NN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-nearest_neighbors_algorithm)), but no rate is uniform over distributions ([Berner et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.04026)); for a class of finite VC dimension, uniform finite-sample rates hold relative to the best hypothesis in the class ([MIT gradml](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/)). The classical picture of capacity control as the explanation of generalization is under pressure from overparameterized networks that fit random labels yet generalize well ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530); [Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09177)).

### Formal definition
**Risk.** Given a distribution $\mathbb P$ on $X\times Y$, a loss $V$, and a sample $S=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n$ drawn i.i.d. from $\mathbb P$,
$$I[f]=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\mathbb P}\,V(f(x),y),\qquad I_S[f]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n V(f(x_i),y_i).$$
Empirical risk minimization (ERM) returns $\hat f\in\arg\min_{f\in H} I_S[f]$. Tikhonov regularization adds a norm penalty, which ensures existence, uniqueness and stability of the solution ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_learning_theory)).

**Bayes risk.** The Bayes risk $R^*=\inf_f R(f)$ is the infimum of the risk over all measurable functions; for classification it is attained by the Bayes classifier $f^*(x)=\operatorname{sgn}\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]$ ([Berner et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.04026)). A rule whose risk converges to $R^*$ for every joint distribution of $(X,Y)$ is consistent for all distributions (universally consistent); the $k$-NN classifier is the standard example ([Wikipedia: k-NN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-nearest_neighbors_algorithm)).

**PAC learnability.** For binary $H\subseteq\{0,1\}^X$ with 0–1 loss $L_{\mathbb P}$, $H$ is (realizable) PAC learnable if there are a function $N_H(\epsilon,\delta)$ and a learner such that for all $\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$ and every $\mathbb P$ realizable by $H$, given $N\ge N_H(\epsilon,\delta)$ samples, the learner returns $h$ with $L_{\mathbb P}(h)\le\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. $H$ is agnostic PAC learnable if, for every distribution on $X\times Y$, the output satisfies $L_{\mathbb P}(h)\le\inf_{h'\in H}L_{\mathbb P}(h')+\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$ ([MIT gradml](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/)).

**Shattering and VC dimension.** A finite $C\subseteq X$ is shattered by $H$ if $|H_C|=2^{|C|}$, where $H_C$ is the set of restrictions to $C$. The VC dimension is the largest size of a shattered set (infinite if there is none). The growth function $\tau_H(N)=\max_{|C|=N}|H_C|$ counts labelings of an $N$-point set ([MIT gradml](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/)).

**Littlestone dimension.** A tree of depth $d$ whose internal nodes are labelled by points of $X$ is shattered by $H$ if every root-to-leaf path is realized by some $h\in H$. $\mathrm{Ldim}(H)$ is the largest $d$ such that $H$ shatters a tree of depth $d$ ([UMass CS690M notes](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~akshay/courses/cs690m/files/lec14.pdf)).

**Rademacher complexity.** For a sample $S=(z_1,\dots,z_m)$ and i.i.d. uniform signs $\sigma_i\in\{\pm1\}$,
$$\mathrm{Rad}_S(\mathcal F)=\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\Big[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\Big|\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i f(z_i)\Big|\Big]$$
([Wikipedia: Rademacher complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher_complexity)).

**Uniform stability.** An algorithm has uniform stability $\beta$ if for every training set $S$ of size $m$ and every index $i$, $\sup_z|V(f_S,z)-V(f_{S^{\setminus i}},z)|\le\beta$, where $S^{\setminus i}$ removes the $i$-th example; it is called stable when $\beta=O(1/m)$ ([Wikipedia: Stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_%28learning_theory%29)).

### Key results
- **Sauer–Shelah lemma.** If $\mathrm{VCdim}(H)\le d<\infty$ then $\tau_H(N)\le\sum_{i=0}^d\binom Ni$ for all $N$, and $\tau_H(N)\le(eN/d)^d$ for $N>d+1$, so the growth function is polynomial in $N$. ([MIT gradml](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/); [Wikipedia: Rademacher complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher_complexity))
- **VC inequality.** For binary classification with 0–1 loss and growth function $S(\mathcal F,n)$,
$$\Pr\Big(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|\hat R_n(f)-R(f)|>\epsilon\Big)\le 8\,S(\mathcal F,n)\,e^{-n\epsilon^2/32}.$$
The proof symmetrizes with a ghost sample: for nondecreasing convex $\Phi$, $\mathbb E\,\Phi(\|\mathbb P_n-P\|_{\mathcal F})\le\mathbb E\,\Phi(2\|\mathbb P_n^0\|_{\mathcal F})$, with $\mathbb P_n^0$ the Rademacher process. ([Wikipedia: VC theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapnik%E2%80%93Chervonenkis_theory))
- **Fundamental theorem of statistical learning.** For $H\subseteq\{0,1\}^X$ with 0–1 loss the following are equivalent: $H$ has the uniform convergence property; every ERM rule is a successful agnostic PAC learner; $H$ is agnostic PAC learnable; $H$ is PAC learnable; every ERM rule is a successful PAC learner; $\mathrm{VCdim}(H)<\infty$. If $d=\mathrm{VCdim}(H)<\infty$, there are absolute constants $C_1,C_2$ with agnostic sample complexity between $C_1\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\epsilon^2}$ and $C_2\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\epsilon^2}$, and realizable sample complexity between $C_1\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\epsilon}$ and $C_2\frac{d\log(1/\epsilon)+\log(1/\delta)}{\epsilon}$. ([MIT gradml](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/))
- **Optimal realizable sample complexity (Hanneke 2016).** Hanneke gives an upper bound on the realizable PAC sample complexity that matches the known lower bounds up to numerical constants, solving a long-standing open problem ([Hanneke 2016](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v17/15-389.html)). Combined with the lower bound above, the realizable sample complexity is $\Theta\big((d+\log(1/\delta))/\epsilon\big)$, so the $\log(1/\epsilon)$ factor in the ERM upper bound is not needed ([MIT gradml](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/); [Hanneke 2016](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v17/15-389.html)).
- **Universal consistency.** The $k$-nearest-neighbour classifier is consistent for every joint distribution of $(X,Y)$ provided $k=k_n\to\infty$ and $k_n/n\to0$ ([Wikipedia: k-NN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-nearest_neighbors_algorithm)). An analogous strong-consistency result holds for weighted nearest-neighbour classifiers, for which Wikipedia cites Stone ([Wikipedia: k-NN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-nearest_neighbors_algorithm)), "Consistent Nonparametric Regression", *Annals of Statistics* 5(4), 1977 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aos/1176343886)).
- **No free lunch for rates (Devroye, Györfi and Lugosi 1996, Thm 7.2).** Let $a_m\in(0,\infty)$ be monotonically decreasing with $a_1\le1/16$. For every learning algorithm $A$ of a classification task there is a distribution $P_Z$ such that for every $m$ and $S\sim P_Z^m$, $\mathbb E\,R(A(S))\ge R^*+a_m$. So universally consistent rules exist, but the rate of convergence to the Bayes risk must depend on the distribution. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.04026))
- **Rademacher generalization bound.** For a class $\mathcal F$ of 0–1 loss functions and any $\delta>0$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample of size $m$, $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\big(L_{\mathbb P}(f)-L_S(f)\big)\le 2\,\mathrm{Rad}_S(\mathcal F)+4\sqrt{2\ln(4/\delta)/m}$. For VC dimension $d$ and $m>d+1$, Massart's lemma with Sauer–Shelah gives $\mathrm{Rad}\le\sqrt{2d\log(em/d)/m}$, and Dudley's entropy bound with Haussler's packing bound improves this to $C\sqrt{d/m}$. ([Wikipedia: Rademacher complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher_complexity))
- **Stability implies generalization.** For symmetric algorithms with bounded loss, uniform stability implies generalization ([Wikipedia: Stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_%28learning_theory%29)); Bousquet and Elisseeff derive bounds on the generalization error in terms of empirical and leave-one-out error from stability, and apply them to regularization in Hilbert spaces and to SVM regression and classification ([Bousquet and Elisseeff 2002](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v2/bousquet02a.html)).
- **PAC-Bayes (Catoni form).** Let $\pi$ be a prior on parameters $\Theta$ fixed before seeing the data, let the loss take values in $[0,C]$, and let the $n$ observations be i.i.d. Then for any $\lambda>0$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for all posteriors $\rho$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta\sim\rho}R(\theta)\le\mathbb E_{\theta\sim\rho}r(\theta)+\frac{\lambda C^2}{8n}+\frac{\mathrm{KL}(\rho\|\pi)+\log(1/\delta)}{\lambda},$$
with $R$ the risk and $r$ the empirical risk ([Alquier 2021, Thm 2.1.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2110.11216)). Alquier presents such bounds as improvements of the original PAC-Bayes bounds of McAllester ([Alquier 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.11216)).
- **Compression.** PAC learnability is equivalent, under regularity conditions, to finite VC dimension (Blumer, Ehrenfeucht, Haussler and Warmuth 1989) and to compressibility in the sense of Littlestone and Warmuth ([Wikipedia: PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probably_approximately_correct_learning)). Littlestone and Warmuth (1986) showed compression implies learnability and asked for the converse; Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every class of VC dimension $d$ has a sample compression scheme of size exponential in $d$ ([Moran and Yehudayoff 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.06960)).
- **Universal learning rates.** Without realizability, the universal rates of ERM for binary classification fall into a trichotomy: exponential, $o(n^{-1/2})$, or arbitrarily slow ([Hanneke and Xu, COLT 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v291/hanneke25b.html)). This extends the realizable trichotomy of optimal universal rates of Bousquet et al. ([Bousquet et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.04483)). For optimal (not necessarily ERM) learners, a January 2026 preprint by Hanneke and Moran reports a complete agnostic theory with a tetrachotomy of rates (exponential, $e^{-o(n)}$, $o(n^{-1/2})$, arbitrarily slow); it is reported here as a preprint, not yet a refereed result ([Hanneke and Moran 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20961)).
- **Online learnability (Littlestone).** In realizable online classification every algorithm can be forced to make at least $\mathrm{Ldim}(H)$ mistakes, and a halving-type algorithm makes at most $\mathrm{Ldim}(H)$; so $H$ is online learnable iff $\mathrm{Ldim}(H)<\infty$. Always $\mathrm{VCdim}(H)\le\mathrm{Ldim}(H)$, with arbitrarily large separation possible ([UMass CS690M notes](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~akshay/courses/cs690m/files/lec14.pdf)).
- **Private learnability equals online learnability.** An approximately differentially private learner for a class of Littlestone dimension $d$ needs $\Omega(\log^* d)$ examples, so thresholds over $\mathbb N$ are not privately learnable ([Alon, Livni, Malliaris and Moran 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.00949)); conversely, every class of finite Littlestone dimension is learnable by an approximately differentially private algorithm, with sample complexity doubly exponential in the dimension ([Bun, Livni and Moran 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.00563)).

### Examples
- Linear classifiers (halfspaces) in $\mathbb R^d$ have VC dimension $d+1$; on the line they shatter two points but not three, and in the plane three but not four ([MIT gradml](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/)).
- Thresholds over $\mathbb N$ have VC dimension 1 but cannot be learned by any approximately differentially private algorithm, a consequence of the $\Omega(\log^* d)$ lower bound ([Alon et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.00949)).
- Practical deep networks fit random labels and random-noise images with SGD, and a simple two-layer network can fit a finite sample perfectly once its parameter count exceeds the number of data points ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530)).

### History
Vapnik and Chervonenkis obtained their uniform convergence results in draft in 1966, announced them in *Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR* in 1968, and published the full paper in *Teoriya Veroyatnostei i ee Primeneniya* in 1971 ([Wikipedia: VC theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapnik%E2%80%93Chervonenkis_theory)); the English version is "On the Uniform Convergence of Relative Frequencies of Events to Their Probabilities", *Theory of Probability & Its Applications* 16(2), 1971 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1116025)). Valiant proposed the PAC model in 1984 and Blumer et al. connected it to VC dimension in 1989 ([Wikipedia: PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probably_approximately_correct_learning)). Bousquet and Elisseeff introduced uniform stability in 2002 ([Wikipedia: Stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_%28learning_theory%29)). Data-dependent Rademacher bounds followed in 2002 ([Bartlett and Mendelson 2002](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/bartlett02a.html)), and Hanneke settled the realizable sample complexity in 2016 ([Hanneke 2016](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v17/15-389.html)).

### Connections
- [Supervised Learning](node:Supervised%20Learning): the setting whose generalization the theory analyzes.
- [Limit Theorems (LLN and CLT)](node:Limit%20Theorems%20%28LLN%20and%20CLT%29): uniform laws of large numbers over function classes generalize the LLN.
- [Concentration of Measure](node:Concentration%20of%20Measure): Hoeffding-type inequalities drive every bound.
- [PAC Learning](node:PAC%20Learning) and [VC Dimension](node:VC%20Dimension): the core definitions; the fundamental theorem ties them together.
- [Rademacher Complexity](node:Rademacher%20Complexity): the data-dependent capacity measure.
- [Empirical Risk Minimization](node:Empirical%20Risk%20Minimization) and [Regularization](node:Regularization): the algorithms whose consistency the theory characterizes.
- [PAC-Bayesian Bounds](node:PAC-Bayesian%20Bounds): bounds for posterior distributions over hypotheses.
- [Nearest-Neighbor Learning](node:Nearest-Neighbor%20Learning): the standard universally consistent rule.
- [Online Learning](node:Online%20Learning): Littlestone dimension governs mistake bounds.
- [Differential Privacy](node:Differential%20Privacy): private PAC learnability is equivalent to finite Littlestone dimension.
- [Generalization in Deep Learning](node:Generalization%20in%20Deep%20Learning), [Double Descent](node:Double%20Descent) and [Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent](node:Implicit%20Bias%20of%20Gradient%20Descent): where classical capacity bounds fall short.

### Common pitfalls
- **Consistency is not a rate.** Universally consistent rules such as $k$-NN with $k\to\infty$, $k/n\to0$ converge to the Bayes risk for every distribution ([Wikipedia: k-NN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-nearest_neighbors_algorithm)), but no algorithm has a rate uniform over all distributions ([Berner et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.04026)).
- **VC dimension is not parameter count.** Halfspaces in $\mathbb R^d$ have VC dimension $d+1$ by a shattering argument, not by counting ([MIT gradml](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/)).
- **Bounds for a fixed hypothesis do not apply to ERM.** The chosen hypothesis depends on the data, so a uniform bound over $H$ is required ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_learning_theory)).
- **PAC learnable does not mean online learnable.** Finite VC dimension does not imply finite Littlestone dimension ([UMass CS690M notes](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~akshay/courses/cs690m/files/lec14.pdf)).
- **Uniform convergence can be vacuous.** Uniform-convergence bounds for overparameterized networks are often numerically large and can grow with the training set size ([Nagarajan and Kolter 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04742)).

### Open problems
- **Explaining generalization of overparameterized models.** Zhang et al. show that explanations based on the model family or on regularization fail to explain why large networks generalize ([Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530)). Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin conjecture that interpolation by gradient methods, implicit regularization and benign overfitting underlie these phenomena, focus their analysis on the linear regime, and close by discussing the challenges in extending these insights to realistic deep learning ([Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09177)).
- **Limits of uniform convergence.** Nagarajan and Kolter construct overparameterized models trained by gradient descent for which two-sided uniform convergence, even restricted to the algorithm's outputs, gives only vacuous bounds although test error is small ([Nagarajan and Kolter 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04742)).
- **Interpolating kernel machines.** For smooth kernels the norm of zero-loss solutions grows nearly exponentially with sample size, none of the existing bounds give non-trivial results for interpolating solutions, and the authors call for new theory ([Belkin, Ma and Mandal 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.01396)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapnik%E2%80%93Chervonenkis_theory): uniform convergence, growth function, VC inequality, symmetrization.
- **Learn:** [MIT gradml: Learnability and VC dimension](https://gradml.mit.edu/supervised/learnability_and_vc/): PAC definitions, Sauer's lemma, fundamental theorem with sample complexity.
- **Learn:** [UMass CS690M, Lecture 14: online learning](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~akshay/courses/cs690m/files/lec14.pdf): mistake bounds and Littlestone dimension.
- **Learn:** [Berner, Grohs, Kutyniok and Petersen, The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026): learning-theory chapter with the no-free-lunch theorem and the generalization puzzle.
- **Primary:** [Vapnik and Chervonenkis, On the Uniform Convergence of Relative Frequencies of Events to Their Probabilities (1971)](https://doi.org/10.1137/1116025): the founding uniform convergence paper.
- **Primary:** [Bartlett and Mendelson, Rademacher and Gaussian Complexities (JMLR 2002)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/bartlett02a.html): data-dependent risk bounds and structural results.
- **Primary:** [Bousquet and Elisseeff, Stability and Generalization (JMLR 2002)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v2/bousquet02a.html): stability-based bounds.

- **Further reading:** [Alquier, User-friendly introduction to PAC-Bayes bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.11216): survey of PAC-Bayes from McAllester's bounds onward.
references.Statistical Mechanics:
## Reference
### Overview
Statistical mechanics applies probability theory to large assemblies of microscopic constituents in order to explain the aggregate properties of matter from the laws of atomic motion. Its central device is the ensemble, a probability distribution over microstates: a distribution over phase points in classical mechanics, evolving by the Liouville equation, or a density matrix in quantum mechanics, evolving by the von Neumann equation ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics)).

Two frameworks coexist. Boltzmannian statistical mechanics partitions phase space into macro-regions and assigns a macrostate the entropy $S_B=k\log\mu(X_M)$, so the equilibrium macrostate is the one with the largest macro-region. Gibbsian statistical mechanics puts a probability density on phase space, identifies equilibrium with stationarity, and equates measured values with phase averages. How the two relate is called a "pressing and yet understudied question" ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)).

Equilibrium theory covers ensembles, partition functions, phase transitions and exactly solvable models; non-equilibrium theory covers the Boltzmann equation, the BBGKY hierarchy, fluctuation–dissipation and Green–Kubo relations; Metropolis–Hastings Monte Carlo was first used to sample the canonical ensemble ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics)). Near continuous transitions, the renormalization group explains why different systems share critical exponents ([Wikipedia: Renormalization group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)).

### Formal definition
Let $\mu$ range over microstates of a system with Hamiltonian $H$ and macroscopic constraints $x$, and set $\beta=1/k_BT$ ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)).

- **Microcanonical** $(E,x)$: $p(\mu)=\delta\big(H(\mu)-E\big)/\Omega(E,x)$, with $S(E,x)=k_B\ln\Omega(E,x)$. **Canonical** $(T,x)$: $p(\mu)=e^{-\beta H(\mu)}/Z$, $Z(T,x)=\sum_\mu e^{-\beta H(\mu)}$, $F(T,x)=-k_BT\ln Z$ ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)).
- **Grand canonical** $(T,\mu_c,V)$: $\mathcal Z=\sum_k e^{-(E_k-\mu_cN_k)/k_BT}$ and $\Omega_G=-k_BT\ln\mathcal Z$, with $\mu_c$ the [chemical potential](node:Chemical%20Potential) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics)).
- **Classical measure.** For $N$ identical particles $d\Gamma_N=\frac{1}{h^{3N}N!}\prod_{i=1}^N d^3q_i\,d^3p_i$; the $N!$ removes the overcounting of permutations ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)).
- **Quantum ensembles.** The canonical state is the density matrix
$$\rho=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}},\qquad \langle A\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho),\qquad Z=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}=\sum_n e^{-\beta E_n},$$
and the grand canonical state is $\rho\propto e^{\beta(\sum_i\mu_iN_i-H)}$; the entropy is $S=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\ln\rho)$ ([Wikipedia: Quantum statistical mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_statistical_mechanics)).

A system is *ergodic* if, for almost all initial conditions, the long-run fraction of time spent in a region equals that region's share of the state space ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)).

### Key results
- **Boltzmann distribution.** If $S$ exchanges energy with a reservoir $R$ large enough that its temperature is fixed, and $R\oplus S$ is microcanonical at $E_{\rm tot}$, then $S_R(E_{\rm tot}-H_S)\approx S_R(E_{\rm tot})-H_S/T$ gives $p(\mu_S)\propto e^{-\beta H_S(\mu_S)}$ ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)).
- **Cumulants, fluctuations and equivalence of ensembles.** Canonically $\langle H^n\rangle_c=(-1)^n\partial^n\ln Z/\partial\beta^n$, so $\langle H^2\rangle_c=k_BT^2C_x$; all cumulants are proportional to $N$, the relative width vanishes as $1/\sqrt N$, and in the thermodynamic limit canonical and microcanonical probabilities become indistinct, with care needed where $C_x$ diverges ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)). Equivalence can fail for small systems, at phase transitions and with long-range interactions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics)).
- **Maximum entropy (Jaynes 1957).** MaxEnt thermodynamics began with two 1957 *Physical Review* papers by Jaynes; it views equilibrium statistical mechanics as inference, each ensemble being the distribution of maximum uncertainty given the known expectation values, and holds that time averages and the ergodic hypothesis are strictly not relevant to the probability assignment ([Wikipedia: Maximum entropy thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_entropy_thermodynamics)). Concretely, the Gibbs density matrix maximizes the von Neumann entropy at fixed mean energy, and the grand canonical one at fixed mean energy and particle number ([Wikipedia: Quantum statistical mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_statistical_mechanics)). There is no consensus on the principle's significance or even its cogency ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)).
- **Quantum occupation numbers.** For non-interacting fermions in the grand canonical ensemble, $\bar n_i=1/(e^{(\varepsilon_i-\mu)/k_BT}+1)$ ([Wikipedia: Fermi–Dirac statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi%E2%80%93Dirac_statistics)); for bosons, $\bar n_i=g_i/(e^{(\varepsilon_i-\mu)/k_BT}-1)$ with $\varepsilon_i>\mu$ ([Wikipedia: Bose–Einstein statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bose%E2%80%93Einstein_statistics)).
- **Phase transitions need the thermodynamic limit.** A phase transition is a non-analyticity of the free energy in some thermodynamic variable ([Wikipedia: Phase transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_transition)). A finite system's partition function is a finite sum of analytic exponentials, so its free energy has no singularities; singularities can arise only in the infinite-volume limit ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)).
- **Lee–Yang circle theorem (1952).** For a ferromagnetic Ising model ($J_{jk}\ge0$) with spins $\pm1$, $H=-\sum J_{jk}S_jS_k-\sum z_jS_j$, the partition function is nonzero whenever all $z_j$ have positive real part; for a uniform field its zeros in $z$ are purely imaginary, which after a change of variable puts them on the unit circle ([Wikipedia: Lee–Yang theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Yang_theorem)). The lattice gas maps onto the Ising model with a magnetic field ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)), the subject of Lee and Yang's paper "Statistical Theory of Equations of State and Phase Transitions. II. Lattice Gas and Ising Model" (*Phys. Rev.* 87, 1952) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.87.410)).
- **Onsager's solution (1944).** Onsager obtained the free energy of the zero-field square-lattice Ising model analytically; with couplings $J_1,J_2$ the critical point satisfies $\sinh(2J_1/kT_c)\sinh(2J_2/kT_c)=1$, and it was the first model to exhibit a continuous phase transition at positive temperature ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)). The paper is "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition", *Phys. Rev.* 65 (1944) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)).
- **Critical exponents, scaling and the renormalization group.** With $\tau=(T-T_c)/T_c$: $C\propto\tau^{-\alpha}$, order parameter $\propto(-\tau)^\beta$, $\chi\propto\tau^{-\gamma}$, critical isotherm $J\propto\Psi^\delta$, $\xi\propto\tau^{-\nu}$, correlations $\propto r^{-(d-2+\eta)}$. Scaling relations such as $\alpha+2\beta+\gamma=2$, $\gamma=\nu(2-\eta)$ and $d\nu=2-\alpha$ leave only two independent exponents (e.g. $\nu$ and $\eta$); mean-field (Landau) theory gives $\alpha=0,\beta=\tfrac12,\gamma=1,\delta=3$, and with gradient terms $\nu=\tfrac12,\eta=0$, valid only above an upper critical dimension, which varies with the system ([Wikipedia: Critical exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent)). Kadanoff's block spins (1966) and Wilson's 1971 RG explain universality: microscopic differences are carried by irrelevant operators, so systems sharing relevant ones share exponents ([Wikipedia: Renormalization group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)).
- **Lanford's theorem.** In the Boltzmann–Grad limit, hard-sphere Hamiltonian dynamics and the Boltzmann equation stay close for most initial points on $[0,t^*]$, with $t^*$ about two fifths of the mean free time, and the result needs a measure-theoretic Stosszahlansatz ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)). Deng, Hani and Ma derive the Boltzmann equation from hard spheres for as long as the Boltzmann solution exists (arXiv preprint, 2024, revised 2025) ([Deng, Hani and Ma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07818)).
- **H-theorem.** For the spatially homogeneous Boltzmann equation, $H$ decreases monotonically; the derivation rests on the Stosszahlansatz ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)).

### Examples
- **Ideal gas.** $\Omega(E,V,N)\propto V^N(2mE)^{(3N-1)/2}$ gives $E=\tfrac32Nk_BT$, $C_V=\tfrac32Nk_B$, $PV=Nk_BT$, and the one-particle marginal tends to the Maxwell–Boltzmann law $(2\pi mk_BT)^{-3/2}e^{-p_1^2/2mk_BT}$ ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)).
- **Gibbs paradox.** Without the $1/N!$ the entropy is not extensive and predicts a spurious mixing entropy $\Delta S_{\rm mix}=-Nk_B\sum_\alpha(N_\alpha/N)\ln(V_\alpha/V)$ for identical gases ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)).
- **Square-lattice Ising model.** Isotropically $T_c=2J/(k\ln(1+\sqrt2))\approx2.269\,J/k$, and $\nu=1$ ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model); [Wikipedia: Critical exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent)). In 3D no exact solution is known; exponents come from the RG, Monte Carlo and the conformal bootstrap ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)).

### History
Daniel Bernoulli's *Hydrodynamica* (1738) founded kinetic theory; Maxwell's 1859 velocity distribution was the first statistical law in physics; Boltzmann developed entropy as a function of microstates; Gibbs coined "statistical mechanics" in 1884 and published *Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics* in 1902 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics)). Loschmidt's reversibility and Zermelo's recurrence objections led to Boltzmann's statistical reading of the H-theorem ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)). Fermi and Dirac derived Fermi–Dirac statistics independently in 1926 ([Wikipedia: Fermi–Dirac statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi%E2%80%93Dirac_statistics)); Bose introduced his statistics for photons in 1924 and Einstein extended it to atoms ([Wikipedia: Bose–Einstein statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bose%E2%80%93Einstein_statistics)). Onsager solved the 2D Ising model in 1944 ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)); Yang and Lee's 1952 papers "I. Theory of Condensation" and "II. Lattice Gas and Ising Model" appeared in *Phys. Rev.* 87 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.87.404); [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.87.410)); Wilson received the 1982 Nobel prize for the RG theory of critical phenomena ([Wikipedia: Renormalization group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renormalization_group)).

### Connections
- [Thermodynamics](node:Thermodynamics): statistical mechanics derives its potentials, e.g. $F=-k_BT\ln Z$ and $S=k_B\ln\Omega$.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics): supplies the phase space and dynamics whose invariant measures are the ensembles.
- [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces): ensembles are probability measures on microstates.
- [Liouville's Theorem in Mechanics](node:Liouville's%20Theorem%20in%20Mechanics): makes the microcanonical measure invariant.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory): the traditional, contested justification for phase averages.
- [Partition Function](node:Partition%20Function), [Microcanonical and Canonical Ensembles](node:Microcanonical%20and%20Canonical%20Ensembles) and [Grand Canonical Ensemble](node:Grand%20Canonical%20Ensemble): the Gibbs ensembles.
- [Thermodynamic Limit](node:Thermodynamic%20Limit): where ensembles agree and singularities can appear.
- [Lee–Yang Theorem](node:Lee–Yang%20Theorem): locates partition-function zeros, the mechanism of phase transitions.
- [Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena](node:Phase%20Transitions%20and%20Critical%20Phenomena), [Critical Exponents and Universality](node:Critical%20Exponents%20and%20Universality) and [Renormalization Group](node:Renormalization%20Group): the theory of continuous transitions.
- [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model) and [Landau Theory of Phase Transitions](node:Landau%20Theory%20of%20Phase%20Transitions): the paradigm model and its mean-field description.
- [Quantum Statistical Mechanics](node:Quantum%20Statistical%20Mechanics) and [Density Matrices](node:Density%20Matrices): the quantum ensembles.
- [Fermi–Dirac Statistics](node:Fermi–Dirac%20Statistics) and [Bose–Einstein Statistics](node:Bose–Einstein%20Statistics): ideal quantum gases.
- [Boltzmann Equation](node:Boltzmann%20Equation) and [Kinetic Theory of Gases](node:Kinetic%20Theory%20of%20Gases): kinetic theory, linked to mechanics by Lanford's theorem.
- [Gibbs Measures](node:Gibbs%20Measures): the rigorous infinite-volume equilibrium states.
- [Markov Chain Monte Carlo](node:Markov%20Chain%20Monte%20Carlo): Metropolis sampling of the canonical ensemble.
- [Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem](node:Fluctuation-Dissipation%20Theorem): near-equilibrium response from equilibrium fluctuations.

### Common pitfalls
- **Mean versus most probable energy.** $F=-k_BT\ln Z$ is suggested by the most probable energy and $\langle H\rangle=-\partial_\beta\ln Z$ by the mean; they can be used interchangeably only because the width grows as $N^{1/2}$ ([MIT 8.333, Lec. 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf)).
- **Ergodicity is not the whole justification.** Many systems of interest, including the ideal gas and solids, are not ergodic ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)).
- **Gibbs entropy does not increase.** The fine-grained Gibbs entropy is a constant of motion, so approach to equilibrium needs coarse-graining or another mechanism ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)).
- **Lanford's time scale is short.** $t^*$ is a fraction (about two fifths) of the mean free time between collisions, far below macroscopic relaxation times ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)).
- **No transitions in finite systems.** Sharp singularities in a finite-size simulation are artefacts; they exist only in the infinite-volume limit ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)).
- **Universality is not proved in general.** Critical exponents are believed, not proved, to be universal ([Wikipedia: Critical exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_exponent)).

### Open problems
- **Crystallization conjecture.** Show that interacting particles under suitable conditions minimize energy in periodic arrangements, breaking translation invariance; Blanc and Lewin's review calls this "still largely open" and mentions several related open problems ([Blanc and Lewin](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.01153)).
- **Exact solution of the 3D Ising model.** No exact solution has been found, "although there is no proof that it may not exist" ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)).
- **Boltzmann versus Gibbs.** Their relation is "pressing and yet understudied", and in some contexts they do not give empirically equivalent predictions ([SEP](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Philosophy of Statistical Mechanics (SEP)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-statmech/): Boltzmann and Gibbs frameworks, ergodicity, Lanford's theorem, maximum entropy.
- **Reference:** [Statistical mechanics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics): ensembles, history, non-equilibrium methods, solvable models.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.333 Statistical Mechanics I, Lecture 13](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-333-statistical-mechanics-i-statistical-mechanics-of-particles-fall-2013/0cdb670a825c6aaea7e229ac40776cbf_MIT8_333F13_Lec13.pdf): ideal gas, Gibbs paradox, canonical ensemble.
- **Learn:** [MIT 8.334 Statistical Physics of Fields, lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/pages/lecture-notes/): Landau–Ginzburg theory, scaling, perturbative and position-space RG.
- **Primary:** [Onsager, Crystal Statistics I (Phys. Rev. 65, 117, 1944)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117): exact solution of the 2D Ising model ([Wikipedia: Ising model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ising_model)).
- **Primary:** [Lee and Yang, Statistical Theory of Equations of State and Phase Transitions II (Phys. Rev. 87, 410, 1952)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.87.410): lattice gas and Ising model; with paper I, the source of the Lee–Yang theorem ([Wikipedia: Lee–Yang theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Yang_theorem)).
- **Primary:** [Jaynes, Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics (Phys. Rev. 106, 620, 1957)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1103/PhysRev.106.620): one of the two papers that began MaxEnt thermodynamics ([Wikipedia: Maximum entropy thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_entropy_thermodynamics)).
- **Primary:** [Deng, Hani and Ma, Long time derivation of the Boltzmann equation from hard sphere dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07818): long-time extension of Lanford's theorem (preprint).
- **Further reading:** [Blanc and Lewin, The crystallization conjecture: a review](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.01153): review article on a central open problem.
- **Further reading:** [Kardar, Statistical Physics of Particles (CUP, 2007)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/CBO9780511815898): textbook on the statistical physics of particles.
- **Further reading:** [Ruelle, Statistical Mechanics: Rigorous Results (1999)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1142/4090): the rigorous monograph.
- **Further reading:** [Friedli and Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems (CUP, 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/9781316882603): mathematical introduction to lattice systems.
references.Stirling's Formula:
## Reference
### Overview
Stirling's formula says that $n!$ is asymptotic to $\sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^n$: the ratio of the two sides tends to $1$ as $n\to\infty$. In logarithmic form $\ln n! = n\ln n - n + O(\ln n)$, and the approximation is accurate even for small $n$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling%27s_approximation))

The same leading behaviour holds for the [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function) of a complex variable, $\Gamma(z)\sim\sqrt{2\pi}\,z^{z-1/2}e^{-z}$ as $|z|\to\infty$ in a sector avoiding the negative real axis, and the leading term sits at the head of a full asymptotic series with Bernoulli-number coefficients. ([DLMF §5.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11)) That series has zero radius of convergence, so it must be read as an asymptotic expansion rather than a convergent one. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling%27s_approximation))

Standard proofs include Euler–Maclaurin summation of $\ln n!=\sum\ln j$, Laplace's method on the gamma integral, saddle-point methods, and a central-limit argument for the [Poisson distribution](node:Poisson%20Distribution). ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling%27s_approximation)) In the Euler–Maclaurin route the constant $\sqrt{2\pi}$ is fixed by Wallis' product. ([Rutgers Math 571 notes](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~tunnell/courses/571/571-f19/stir.pdf))

### Formal definition
For positive integers,
$$n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}\left(\frac ne\right)^n\quad(n\to\infty),\qquad\text{i.e. } \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n!\,e^n}{n^n\sqrt{2\pi n}}=1.$$
([Stirling's Series Revisited](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.09873))

For fixed $\delta>0$, as $z\to\infty$ in $|\mathrm{ph}\,z|\le\pi-\delta$, with $B_{2k}$ the Bernoulli numbers and $\operatorname{Ln}$ the general logarithm,
$$\operatorname{Ln}\Gamma(z)\sim\left(z-\tfrac12\right)\ln z-z+\tfrac12\ln(2\pi)+\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{B_{2k}}{2k(2k-1)z^{2k-1}},$$
$$\Gamma(z)=e^{-z}z^z\sqrt{2\pi/z}\;\Gamma^*(z),\qquad \Gamma^*(z)\sim\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{g_k}{z^k},$$
with $g_0=1,\ g_1=\tfrac1{12},\ g_2=\tfrac1{288},\ g_3=-\tfrac{139}{51840},\ g_4=-\tfrac{571}{2488320}$. ([DLMF §5.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11))

### Key results
- **Robbins bounds.** For every integer $n\ge1$, $\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n e^{1/(12n+1)}<n!<\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n e^{1/(12n)}$. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/StirlingsApproximation.html))
- **Euler–Maclaurin form with explicit constant.** For $N\ge1$, $\ln N!=C+(N+\tfrac12)\ln N-N+\theta(N)/(12N)$ with $0<\theta(N)<1$, and $C=\ln\sqrt{2\pi}$, the constant being identified from Wallis' formula $\sqrt{\pi/2}=\lim_{n}\frac{(2^n n!)^2}{(2n)!\sqrt{2n}}$. The proof applies the trapezoidal/Hermite rule to $\ln x$ on $[1,N]$; the remainder integral is positive and at most $1/(12N)$. ([Rutgers Math 571 notes](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~tunnell/courses/571/571-f19/stir.pdf))
- **Euler–Maclaurin summation.** If $f$ has $m$ continuous derivatives on $[M,N]$, then $\sum_{j=M}^{N-1}f(j)=\int_M^N f\,dx+\sum_{k=1}^{m}\big[f^{(k-1)}(x)\big]_M^N\frac{B_k}{k!}-R_m$ with $R_m=(-1)^m\int_M^N f^{(m)}(x)\frac{B_m(\{x\})}{m!}dx$ and $B_1=-\tfrac12$. ([Rutgers Math 571 notes](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~tunnell/courses/571/571-f19/stir.pdf))
- **Error bounds for the Stirling series.** If the sum in the series for $\operatorname{Ln}\Gamma(z)$ is truncated at $k=n-1$ with $z>0$ real, the remainder has the sign of, and is bounded in magnitude by, the first neglected term; for complex $z$ the bound is multiplied by $\sec^{2n}(\tfrac12\mathrm{ph}\,z)$. ([DLMF §5.11(ii)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11))
- **Divergence.** The Stirling series is not convergent (zero radius of convergence); Bayes showed this in 1763, and Binet's formulas give exact representations for $\operatorname{Re}z>0$. ([Wikipedia: Gamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling%27s_approximation))
- **Coefficient formula.** The coefficients $a_k$ in $n!\sim\frac{n^n\sqrt{2\pi n}}{e^n}\sum a_k n^{-k}$ satisfy $a_k=\frac1{2^kk!}\frac{d^{2k}}{dz^{2k}}\Big[\big(\tfrac{z^2}{2(e^z-1-z)}\big)^{k+1/2}\Big]_{z=0}$; replacing $a_k$ by $(-1)^ka_k$ gives the expansion of $1/n!$, and $\sum_{k=0}^m(-1)^ka_ka_{m-k}=0$ for $m\ge1$. ([Stirling's Series Revisited](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.09873))
- **Shifted arguments.** For fixed $a>0$ and $b$, $\Gamma(az+b)\sim\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-az}(az)^{az+b-1/2}$, and $|\Gamma(x+iy)|\sim\sqrt{2\pi}|y|^{x-1/2}e^{-\pi|y|/2}$ as $y\to\pm\infty$ uniformly for bounded real $x$. ([DLMF §5.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11))

### Examples
- Gosper's refinement $n!\approx\sqrt{(2n+\tfrac13)\pi}\,n^ne^{-n}$ approximates, rather than truncates, the series; as $n\to0^+$ it gives $\sqrt{\pi/3}\approx1.0233$ for $0!$. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/StirlingsApproximation.html))
- Binet's first formula, for $\operatorname{Re}z>0$: $\ln\Gamma(z)=(z-\tfrac12)\ln z-z+\tfrac12\ln 2\pi+\int_0^\infty\big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1t+\tfrac1{e^t-1}\big)\frac{e^{-zt}}{t}dt$. ([Wikipedia: Gamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function))
- Laplace's method: write $n!=\int_0^\infty e^{-x}x^n\,dx$, whose integrand peaks near $x=n$; expanding the logarithm of the integrand to second order about the peak leaves a Gaussian integral equal to $\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n$. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/StirlingsApproximation.html)) This is Laplace's method applied to the gamma integral. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling%27s_approximation))

### History
De Moivre found the form $n!\sim c\,n^{n+1/2}e^{-n}$ in 1721; Stirling's 1730 contribution was identifying $c=\sqrt{2\pi}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling%27s_approximation)) Stirling's *Methodus differentialis* appeared in London in 1730. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/StirlingsApproximation.html))

### Connections
- [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function): Stirling's formula is its large-argument asymptotics; $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.
- [Series and Convergence](node:Series%20and%20Convergence): the Stirling series is the standard example of a divergent asymptotic series.
- [Special Functions](node:Special%20Functions): large-argument expansions with error bounds are a recurring theme.
- [Beta Function](node:Beta%20Function): ratios of gamma functions, hence Stirling asymptotics, control its large-parameter behaviour.
- [Laplace and Mellin Transforms](node:Laplace%20and%20Mellin%20Transforms): the gamma integral is a Laplace transform, and Binet's formula is a Laplace transform representation.
- [Asymptotic Analysis](node:Asymptotic%20Analysis): Laplace's method and the divergent Stirling series are standard examples.
- [Riemann Zeta Function](node:Riemann%20Zeta%20Function): Bernoulli numbers appear in both Stirling's series and zeta values at negative integers.

### Common pitfalls
- Asymptotic equivalence $f_n\sim g_n$ means $f_n/g_n\to1$, not that $f_n-g_n\to0$; $n!-\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n$ grows without bound. (follows from the Robbins bounds: [MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/StirlingsApproximation.html))
- The crude form $\ln n!\approx n\ln n-n$ omits the $\tfrac12\ln(2\pi n)$ term. ([MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/StirlingsApproximation.html))
- $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$, so the gamma form $\sqrt{2\pi}z^{z-1/2}e^{-z}$ and the factorial form $\sqrt{2\pi n}\,n^ne^{-n}$ differ by the shift $z=n+1$; keep the argument convention explicit. ([Wikipedia: Gamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function))
- Validity of the complex form requires a fixed margin $\delta$ from the negative real axis. ([DLMF §5.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11))

### Open problems
- **Transcendence of Stirling-type constants.** The Stirling–Ramanujan constants include the Euler–Mascheroni, Stirling, and Glaisher–Kinkelin constants; Muñoz and Pérez-Marco (2024) give integral representations showing they are exponential periods and conjecture that all of them are transcendental, which is not proved there. ([arXiv:2402.02660](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02660))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stirling's approximation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling%27s_approximation): statement, bounds, derivations, history.
- **Reference:** [DLMF §5.11](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11): asymptotic expansions, coefficients $g_k$, error bounds in the complex plane.
- **Learn:** [Rutgers Math 571: Euler–Maclaurin summation and Stirling's formula](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~tunnell/courses/571/571-f19/stir.pdf): full derivation with the $\sqrt{2\pi}$ constant via Wallis.
- **Primary:** [Nemes, On the coefficients of the asymptotic expansion of n!](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.2907): explicit coefficient formulas (J. Integer Seq. 13, 2010).
- **Primary:** [Stirling's Series Revisited](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.09873): elementary derivation of the full series and coefficient formula.
- **Primary:** [Borwein and Corless, Gamma and Factorial in the Monthly](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.05349): survey of about fifty American Mathematical Monthly papers on $\Gamma$ and Stirling's formula.
- **Further reading:** [Olver, Asymptotics and Special Functions (A K Peters/CRC Press)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1201/9781439864548): Frank Olver, A K Peters/CRC Press, 1997 (bibliographic record).
references.Stochastic Gradient Descent:
## Reference
### Overview
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is an iterative method for objectives with a sum structure, $Q(w)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Q_i(w)$, the form of empirical risk in machine learning. Each step replaces the full gradient by an estimate computed from a randomly selected subset of the data, as in $w\leftarrow w-\eta\nabla Q_i(w)$. It is a stochastic approximation of gradient descent. Computing the estimate on a minibatch of several samples is a compromise that exploits vectorized hardware and gives smoother convergence. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_gradient_descent))

The appeal is cost. A full gradient over $n$ examples costs $O(n)$ per iteration, while a single-example stochastic gradient costs $O(1)$. If the index is drawn uniformly, $\mathbb{E}_i\nabla f_i(x)=\nabla f(x)$, so the step is right on average. The price is noise: with a constant learning rate the trajectory stays noisy even near the minimum, so the learning rate is reduced as optimization progresses. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/sgd.html))

Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal argue that large-scale machine learning is a setting where SGD has played the central role while conventional gradient-based nonlinear optimization tends to falter. They give a unified convergence theory for a general SG algorithm and survey the noise-reduction and second-order methods that build on it. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))

### Formal definition
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be the objective. The SG method is given an initial $w_1$, step sizes $\alpha_k>0$, and a stochastic direction $g(w_k,\xi_k)$ that depends on a random seed $\xi_k$. It iterates
$$w_{k+1}=w_k-\alpha_k\,g(w_k,\xi_k).$$
The direction can be a single-sample gradient $\nabla f(w_k;\xi_k)$, a minibatch average $\frac1{n_k}\sum_{i\in S_k}\nabla f(w_k;\xi_{k,i})$, or such a gradient multiplied by a positive-definite scaling matrix. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))

The standard analysis uses three assumptions ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838)):
1. **(4.1) Smoothness.** $F$ is continuously differentiable and $\nabla F$ is $L$-Lipschitz.
2. **(4.3) Moment bounds.** (a) $F$ is bounded below by $F_{\inf}$ on an open set containing the iterates. (b) There are $\mu_G\ge\mu>0$ with $\nabla F(w_k)^\top\mathbb{E}_{\xi_k}[g(w_k,\xi_k)]\ge\mu\|\nabla F(w_k)\|_2^2$ and $\|\mathbb{E}_{\xi_k}[g(w_k,\xi_k)]\|_2\le\mu_G\|\nabla F(w_k)\|_2$. (c) There are $M,M_V\ge0$ with $\mathbb{V}_{\xi_k}[g(w_k,\xi_k)]\le M+M_V\|\nabla F(w_k)\|_2^2$. An unbiased estimate satisfies (b) with $\mu=\mu_G=1$. Together these give $\mathbb{E}_{\xi_k}\|g\|_2^2\le M+M_G\|\nabla F(w_k)\|_2^2$ with $M_G:=M_V+\mu_G^2$.
3. **(4.5) Strong convexity.** There is $c>0$ with $F(\bar w)\ge F(w)+\nabla F(w)^\top(\bar w-w)+\tfrac c2\|\bar w-w\|_2^2$.

The classical Robbins–Monro step-size conditions are
$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty\alpha_k=\infty,\qquad\sum_{k=1}^\infty\alpha_k^2<\infty.$$
([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))

### Key results
- **Strongly convex, fixed step: linear convergence to a noise ball.** Under (4.1), (4.3), and (4.5) with $F_{\inf}=F^*$, a fixed step $0<\bar\alpha\le\mu/(LM_G)$ gives $\mathbb{E}[F(w_k)-F^*]\le\frac{\bar\alpha LM}{2c\mu}+(1-\bar\alpha c\mu)^{k-1}\big(F(w_1)-F^*-\frac{\bar\alpha LM}{2c\mu}\big)$. The gap therefore converges linearly to the floor $\bar\alpha LM/(2c\mu)$, which scales with the step and the gradient noise $M$. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))
- **Strongly convex, diminishing steps: $O(1/k)$.** Under the same assumptions, with $\alpha_k=\beta/(\gamma+k)$ for some $\beta>1/(c\mu)$ and $\gamma>0$ such that $\alpha_1\le\mu/(LM_G)$, one has $\mathbb{E}[F(w_k)-F^*]\le\nu/(\gamma+k)$ with $\nu=\max\{\beta^2LM/(2(\beta c\mu-1)),\,(\gamma+1)(F(w_1)-F^*)\}$. With stochastic gradients, acceleration can improve only the constants in this rate, not the rate itself. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))
- **Nonconvex, fixed step.** Under (4.1) and (4.3) with $0<\bar\alpha\le\mu/(LM_G)$, for all $K$: $\mathbb{E}\big[\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\|\nabla F(w_k)\|_2^2\big]\le\frac{\bar\alpha LM}{\mu}+\frac{2(F(w_1)-F_{\inf})}{K\mu\bar\alpha}$. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))
- **Nonconvex, diminishing steps.** Under (4.1) and (4.3) with Robbins–Monro steps, $\liminf_{k\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(w_k)\|_2^2=0$. More precisely, $\lim_{K}\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k\|\nabla F(w_k)\|_2^2\big]<\infty$, so the step-weighted average of squared gradient norms tends to $0$. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))
- **Convex, bounded gradients: $O(1/\sqrt T)$.** If the objective is convex, stochastic gradients have norm at most $L$, and $\|x_0-x^*\|\le r$, the averaged iterate $\bar x$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[R(\bar x)]-R^*\le\big(r^2+L^2\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t^2\big)/\big(2\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t\big)$. The constant step $\eta=r/(L\sqrt T)$ gives $rL/\sqrt T$. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/sgd.html))
- **Almost-sure convergence.** With learning rates decreasing at an appropriate rate and under mild assumptions, SGD converges almost surely to a global minimizer when the objective is convex or pseudoconvex, and otherwise almost surely to a local minimizer. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_gradient_descent))

### Examples
- **Learning-rate schedules.** Common choices are piecewise constant, exponential decay $\eta_0e^{-\lambda t}$ (which can stop before convergence), and polynomial decay $\eta_0(\beta t+1)^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha=\tfrac12$ a popular choice. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/sgd.html))
- **Sampling with or without replacement.** Drawing $n$ indices with replacement selects a given example at least once with probability about $1-e^{-1}\approx0.63$. Practice therefore samples without replacement and reshuffles each epoch. ([d2l.ai](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/sgd.html))
- **Variants.** Momentum adds a fraction of the previous update, and Polyak–Ruppert averaging returns the average of the iterates. AdaGrad (2011), RMSProp, and Adam (2014) adapt per-parameter step sizes. Later analysis showed that Adam can fail to converge on some convex objectives. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_gradient_descent))

### History
Robbins and Monro's "A Stochastic Approximation Method" appeared in the Annals of Mathematical Statistics in 1951. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aoms/1177729586)) It introduced the earliest stochastic approximation methods, which preceded SGD. Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1952) gave a close relative that approximates the gradient by central differences, and Rosenblatt used SGD-type updates for the perceptron later in the 1950s. Backpropagation and momentum came in 1986, and Ruppert and Polyak independently introduced averaging in the late 1980s. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_gradient_descent)) Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal describe the Robbins–Monro paper as a landmark in the history of numerical optimization. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))

### Connections
- [Gradient Descent](node:Gradient%20Descent): the deterministic method SGD approximates.
- [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): the sampled index and gradient noise are random variables.
- [Expectation and Variance](node:Expectation%20and%20Variance): unbiasedness and the variance bound drive every rate above.
- [Martingales](node:Martingales): the probabilistic tool behind almost-sure convergence of stochastic approximation.
- [Variance Reduction in Stochastic Optimization](node:Variance%20Reduction%20in%20Stochastic%20Optimization): methods that remove the noise floor of fixed-step SGD.
- [Adaptive Optimizers](node:Adaptive%20Optimizers): AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam as rescaled SGD.
- [Empirical Risk Minimization](node:Empirical%20Risk%20Minimization): the finite-sum objective SGD is designed for.
- [Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent](node:Implicit%20Bias%20of%20Gradient%20Descent): which solutions gradient-based training selects.
- [Generalization in Deep Learning](node:Generalization%20in%20Deep%20Learning): batch size and gradient noise affect test performance.
- [Federated Optimization](node:Federated%20Optimization): distributed SGD-type methods with local updates.
- [Backpropagation](node:Backpropagation): computes the minibatch gradients in neural-network training.
- [Regularization](node:Regularization): explicit penalties that SGD's implicit effects are compared against.

### Common pitfalls
- With a constant step, SGD does not converge to the minimizer. In the strongly convex case the expected gap converges to a floor proportional to $\bar\alpha M$, and a smaller step brings the iterates closer to the optimum but worsens the contraction constant. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))
- The nonconvex guarantees concern expected (weighted average) squared gradient norms, not convergence to a minimizer. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))
- Small finite learning rates are not equivalent to gradient flow on the original loss: for SGD with random shuffling, the mean SGD iterate follows gradient flow on a modified loss that penalizes the norms of minibatch gradients, with strength proportional to the ratio of learning rate to batch size (for small batches, under mild assumptions); adding this regularizer explicitly can improve test accuracy at small learning rates. ([Smith et al., arXiv:2101.12176](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12176))

### Open problems
- **Large batches and sharp minima.** Large-batch training generalizes worse and tends to converge to sharp minimizers, while small-batch SGD finds flatter ones. Keskar et al. list as open questions whether one can prove that large-batch methods typically converge to sharp minimizers, the relative density of sharp and flat minima, and how to steer large-batch methods away from sharp minimizers. ([Keskar et al., arXiv:1609.04836](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04836))
- **Next-generation methods.** Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal organize the next generation of large-scale methods around two research streams, noise reduction in the stochastic directions and second-order derivative approximations, and raise open questions along the way. For example, they state that it remains an open question whether randomized coordinate descent is more effective than cyclic coordinate descent in typical applications, despite its better theoretical properties. ([Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, arXiv:1606.04838](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stochastic gradient descent (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_gradient_descent): definition, history, and variants from momentum to Adam.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, Stochastic Gradient Descent](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/sgd.html): cost per step, schedules, a convex convergence proof, and sampling.
- **Primary:** [Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, Optimization Methods for Large-Scale Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04838): review with the general SG convergence theory used above.
- **Primary:** [Robbins and Monro, A Stochastic Approximation Method (1951)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aoms/1177729586): the founding paper of stochastic approximation.
- **Primary:** [Keskar et al., On Large-Batch Training for Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04836): generalization gap and sharp minima.
- **Further reading:** [Bubeck, Convex Optimization: Algorithms and Complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.4980): monograph covering SGD, mini-batching, and random coordinate descent alongside deterministic methods.
references.Stochastic Processes:
## Reference
### Overview
A stochastic process is a collection of random variables $\{X(t):t\in T\}$ defined on a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, indexed by a set $T$ (usually time) and taking values in a common state space $S$. Fixing $\omega$ gives a sample path (realization) $t\mapsto X(t,\omega)$, so a process is either a family of random variables or a random function; its law is the pushforward measure on the function space, and its finite-dimensional distributions are the joint laws of $(X(t_1),\dots,X(t_n))$. The main classes are random walks, martingales, Markov processes, Lévy processes, Gaussian processes, random fields, renewal processes and branching processes ([Wikipedia: Stochastic process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process)).

Construction goes through Kolmogorov's extension theorem, whose measure lives on the rather coarse product $\sigma$-algebra; for Brownian motion, path continuity comes instead from a continuous modification given by the Kolmogorov continuity theorem ([Wikipedia: Kolmogorov extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov_extension_theorem)). Discrete-time limit theory: martingale convergence, ergodic theorems and convergence of Markov chains to equilibrium ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)). Continuous time: Markov processes described by operator semigroups and generators ([Wikipedia: Feller process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feller_process)), Lévy processes classified by the Lévy–Khintchine formula ([Wikipedia: Lévy process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy_process)), and stochastic integration against Brownian motion and martingales ([Wikipedia: Itô calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It%C3%B4_calculus)).

Brownian motion is a centred Gaussian process, a martingale and a Lévy process ([Wikipedia: Wiener process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_process)), and by Donsker's theorem the scaling limit of every random walk with i.i.d. mean-zero, finite-variance steps ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).

### Formal definition
**Process, modification, indistinguishability.** A process with index set $T$ and state space $S$ is a family $X=\{X(t):t\in T\}$ of $S$-valued random variables on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. $Y$ is a *modification* of $X$ if $P(X_t=Y_t)=1$ for every $t$; $X$ and $Y$ are *indistinguishable* if $P(X_t=Y_t\ \forall t)=1$. Almost surely continuous modifications are indistinguishable ([Wikipedia: Stochastic process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process)).

**Stationarity.** $X$ is strictly stationary if its finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under time translations ([Wikipedia: Stochastic process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process)). It is *wide-sense (weakly) stationary* if all three hold:
$$m_X(t)=m_X(t+\tau)\ \ \forall t,\tau,\qquad K_{XX}(t_1,t_2)=K_{XX}(t_1-t_2,0)\ \ \forall t_1,t_2,\qquad E|X_t|^2<\infty\ \ \forall t,$$
that is, constant mean, autocovariance depending only on the lag, and finite second moments ([Wikipedia: Stationary process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary_process)).

**Filtrations, martingales, stopping times.** A filtration is an increasing family of $\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal F_s\subseteq\mathcal F_t$ for $s\le t$ ([Wikipedia: Stochastic process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process)). An adapted sequence of integrable $X_n$ is a martingale if $E(X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n)=X_n$ (submartingale $\ge$, supermartingale $\le$) ([Lalley, Conditional Expectation and Martingales](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/Martingales.pdf)). A random variable $N$ with values in $\{0,1,2,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ is a stopping time if $\{N=n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for all $n<\infty$; the value $\infty$ is allowed, which is why optional stopping below is stated for $N\le\infty$ ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)). In continuous time Durrett calls a $[0,\infty]$-valued $S$ a stopping time if $\{S<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for all $t\ge0$; this is equivalent to $\{S\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for all $t$ when the filtration is right continuous, whereas $\{S\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ always implies $\{S<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).

**Poisson process.** $N_t$, $t\ge0$, is a rate-$\lambda$ Poisson process if for $0=t_0<\dots<t_n$ the increments $N(t_k)-N(t_{k-1})$ are independent and $N(t)-N(s)\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))$ ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).

**Lévy process.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ with $X_0=0$ a.s., independent increments over disjoint intervals, stationary increments ($X_t-X_s\overset d=X_{t-s}$ for $s<t$), and continuity in probability: $\lim_{h\to0}P(|X_{t+h}-X_t|>\varepsilon)=0$ for all $\varepsilon>0$, $t\ge0$ ([Wikipedia: Lévy process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy_process)).

**Feller semigroup and generator.** Let $X$ be locally compact Hausdorff with a countable base and $C_0(X)$ the continuous functions vanishing at infinity with the sup norm. A Feller semigroup is a family $(T_t)_{t\ge0}$ of positive linear contractions on $C_0(X)$ with $T_0=\mathrm{Id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_tT_s$, strongly continuous at $t=0$; a Feller process is a Markov process whose transition function gives such a semigroup. Its generator is $Af=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(T_tf-f)/t$ (uniform limit) on the domain $D(A)$ where the limit exists; the resolvent $R_\lambda=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}T_t\,dt$ equals $(\lambda-A)^{-1}$ ([Wikipedia: Feller process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feller_process)).

### Key results
- **Kolmogorov's extension theorem.** Sequence form: if probability measures $\mu_n$ on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal R^n)$ are consistent, $\mu_{n+1}(A\times\mathbb R)=\mu_n(A)$ for rectangles $A$, there is a unique $P$ on $(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N},\mathcal R^{\mathbb N})$ with these marginals. It fails for arbitrary measurable spaces (Andersen–Jessen 1948) but extends trivially to *nice* (standard Borel) spaces, which include every Borel subset of a complete separable metric space ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)). General form: for any index set $T$, Hausdorff spaces $\Omega_t$, and measures $\mu_F$ on $\Omega_F$ ($F\subset T$ finite) that are inner regular and consistent, $\mu_F=(\pi_{FG})_*\mu_G$ for $F\subset G$, there is a unique $\mu$ on the product $\sigma$-algebra of $\Omega_T$ with $\mu_F=(\pi_{FT})_*\mu$. Borel probability measures on Polish spaces are automatically Radon, so the theorem holds for Polish state spaces and uncountable $T$ ([Wikipedia: Kolmogorov extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov_extension_theorem)).
- **Separable and continuous modifications.** If the state space $\Xi$ is a compact metric space and $T$ a separable metric space, every $\Xi$-valued process on $T$ has a separable modification; if $\Xi$ is not compact, the separable modification exists with values in a compactification of $\Xi$ (for real-valued processes, the extended reals $[-\infty,\infty]$), though at each fixed $t$ it lies in $\Xi$ almost surely ([Shalizi, 36-754 lecture notes, ch. 8](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/754/notes/lecture-08.pdf)). Under moment conditions on increments, Kolmogorov's continuity theorem gives a modification with almost surely continuous paths ([Wikipedia: Stochastic process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process)).
- **Martingale convergence and maximal inequalities.** A submartingale with $\sup_nEX_n^+<\infty$ converges a.s. to $X$ with $E|X|<\infty$. With $\bar X_n=\max_{0\le m\le n}X_m^+$: $\lambda P(\bar X_n\ge\lambda)\le EX_n\mathbf 1_{\{\bar X_n\ge\lambda\}}\le EX_n^+$, and $E\bar X_n^p\le(\tfrac p{p-1})^pE(X_n^+)^p$ for $1<p<\infty$. If $E|X_n|<\infty$ and $X_n\to X$ in probability, then uniform integrability, $L^1$ convergence, and $E|X_n|\to E|X|<\infty$ are equivalent ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).
- **Optional stopping and Wald.** For a stopping time $\tau$ the stopped process $X_{\tau\wedge n}$ of a martingale (sub-, super-) is again one, so $EX_{\tau\wedge n}=EX_0$ for martingales ([Lalley, Conditional Expectation and Martingales](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/Martingales.pdf)). For a uniformly integrable submartingale and any stopping time $N\le\infty$, $EX_0\le EX_N\le EX_\infty$; for a nonnegative supermartingale, $EX_0\ge EX_N$ without uniform integrability. Wald: if $\xi_i$ are i.i.d., $E|\xi_1|<\infty$ and $E\tau<\infty$, then $ES_\tau=E\tau\,E\xi_1$; if moreover $E\xi_i=0$, $\operatorname{var}\xi_i=\sigma^2$, then $ES_\tau^2=\sigma^2E\tau$ ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).
- **Birkhoff's ergodic theorem; Markov chain convergence.** If $\varphi$ preserves $P$ with invariant $\sigma$-field $\mathcal I$, then for $X\in L^1$, $\frac1n\sum_{m<n}X(\varphi^m\omega)\to E(X\mid\mathcal I)$ a.s. and in $L^1$. If a countable-state transition kernel $p$ is irreducible, aperiodic and has a stationary distribution $\pi$, then $p^n(x,y)\to\pi(y)$ ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).
- **Strong Markov property of Feller processes.** An adapted right-continuous Feller process on a filtered probability space satisfies the strong Markov property with respect to $(\mathcal F_{t+})$. Hille–Yosida characterizes their generators.
