Brownian motion, the Poisson process and every Lévy process are Feller processes ([Wikipedia: Feller process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feller_process)).
- **Lévy–Khintchine formula and Lévy–Itô decomposition.** If $X$ is a Lévy process on $\mathbb R$, then
$$E e^{i\theta X_t}=\exp\Big(t\Big(ia\theta-\tfrac12\sigma^2\theta^2+\int_{\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}}\big(e^{i\theta x}-1-i\theta x\mathbf 1_{|x|<1}\big)\,\Pi(dx)\Big)\Big)$$
with $a\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$ and a Lévy measure $\Pi$ satisfying $\int\min(1,x^2)\,\Pi(dx)<\infty$. Pathwise, $X_t=\sigma B_t+at+Y_t+Z_t$ with $Y$ compound Poisson (jumps of size $>1$) and $Z$ a zero-mean martingale of compensated small jumps ([Wikipedia: Lévy process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy_process)).
- **Donsker's invariance principle.** Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with mean $0$ and variance $1$, $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$, and $S(u)$ the linear interpolation of $k\mapsto S_k$. Then $S(n\cdot)/\sqrt n\Rightarrow B(\cdot)$ as measures on $C[0,1]$, hence $\psi(S(n\cdot)/\sqrt n)\Rightarrow\psi(B)$ for $\psi$ continuous at a.e. Brownian path ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)). The step-function version converges in the Skorokhod space $D[0,1]$; the empirical-process version says $\sqrt n(F_n-F)$ converges to $B(F(\cdot))$ with $B$ a Brownian bridge, covariance $\min\{F(s),F(t)\}-F(s)F(t)$ ([Wikipedia: Donsker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donsker%27s_theorem)).
- **Itô integral.** For Brownian motion $B$, $\int_0^tH\,dB$ is defined for every predictable $H$ with $\int_0^tH_s^2\,ds<\infty$: for left-continuous adapted $H$ as the in-probability limit of left-endpoint Riemann sums, and in general by approximating $H$ with such processes; it satisfies the Itô isometry $E[(\int_0^tH\,dB)^2]=E\int_0^tH_s^2\,ds$ when the right side is finite; if $M$ is a local martingale and $H$ is locally bounded and predictable, $H\cdot M$ is a local martingale; and for $f\in C^2$ and an Itô process $X$, $f(X_t)$ is an Itô process whose differential carries an extra second-derivative term from quadratic variation (Itô's lemma) ([Wikipedia: Itô calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It%C3%B4_calculus)).
- **Strong solutions of SDEs.** Fix $T>0$. If $\mu,\sigma$ are measurable with $|\mu(x,t)|+|\sigma(x,t)|\le C(1+|x|)$ and $|\mu(x,t)-\mu(y,t)|+|\sigma(x,t)-\sigma(y,t)|\le D|x-y|$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n$, and $Z$ is independent of $B$ with $E|Z|^2<\infty$, then $dX_t=\mu(X_t,t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t,t)\,dB_t$, $X_0=Z$, has an a.s. unique $t$-continuous solution, adapted to the filtration of $Z$ and $B$, with $E\int_0^T|X_t|^2dt<\infty$ ([Wikipedia: Stochastic differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation)).

### Examples
- **Brownian motion.** The centred Gaussian process with covariance $\min(s,t)$ and continuous paths; $W_t$, $W_t^2-t$ and $e^{\theta W_t-\theta^2t/2}$ are martingales, and a continuous local martingale with $W_0=0$ is Brownian motion iff its quadratic variation is $t$ (Lévy's characterization) ([Wikipedia: Wiener process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_process)).
- **Poisson process.** Characterized by independent stationary arrival counts with $P(N(0,h)=1)=\lambda h+o(h)$ and $P(N(0,h)\ge2)=o(h)$; equivalently $N_t=\sup\{n:T_n\le t\}$ for partial sums $T_n$ of i.i.d. exponential($\lambda$) times. Independently labelling arrivals $j$ with probability $P(Y=j)$ yields independent Poisson processes of rates $\lambda P(Y=j)$ (thinning) ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).
- **Galton–Watson and Pólya martingales.** With mean offspring $\mu>0$ and $\zeta$ the smallest fixed point in $[0,\infty)$ of the offspring generating function, $Z_n/\mu^n$ and $\zeta^{Z_n}$ are martingales, as is the red-ball fraction of a Pólya urn ([Lalley, Conditional Expectation and Martingales](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/Martingales.pdf)).

### History
Bachelier used the Wiener process for Paris Bourse prices and Erlang the Poisson process for telephone calls. Edgeworth used "random process" in 1888; Lévy's 1925 book was the first to use measure theory; Kolmogorov gave a measure-theoretic foundation in 1929 and used the German term in 1931; in 1934 Khinchin gave the first definition as a family of random variables indexed by the real line and Doob introduced the English term ([Wikipedia: Stochastic process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process)). Birkhoff proved the ergodic theorem in 1931, Paley, Wiener and Zygmund the nondifferentiability of Brownian paths in 1933, and Donsker the invariance principle in 1951 ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).

### Connections
- [Random Variables and Distributions](node:Random%20Variables%20and%20Distributions): a process is an indexed family of random variables.
- [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces) and [Measure Theory](node:Measure%20Theory): path-space measures.
- [Markov Chains](node:Markov%20Chains) and [MSC 60Jxx - Markov processes](node:MSC%2060Jxx%20-%20Markov%20processes): Markov dynamics in discrete and continuous time.
- [Martingales](node:Martingales), [Stopping Times](node:Stopping%20Times), [Conditional Expectation](node:Conditional%20Expectation): the martingale toolkit.
- [Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus](node:Brownian%20Motion%20and%20Stochastic%20Calculus) and [Itô Integration](node:Itô%20Integration): the central continuous process and its integral.
- [Strongly Continuous Operator Semigroups](node:Strongly%20Continuous%20Operator%20Semigroups): the analytic side of Feller processes.
- [Characteristic Functions](node:Characteristic%20Functions): the language of the Lévy–Khintchine formula.
- [Limit Theorems (LLN and CLT)](node:Limit%20Theorems%20%28LLN%20and%20CLT%29): Donsker's theorem is the functional CLT.
- [Gaussian Processes](node:Gaussian%20Processes), [Poisson Point Processes and Stochastic Geometry](node:Poisson%20Point%20Processes%20and%20Stochastic%20Geometry), [Renewal Processes](node:Renewal%20Processes): further classes of processes.
- [Ergodic Theory](node:Ergodic%20Theory) and [Mixing Times of Markov Chains](node:Mixing%20Times%20of%20Markov%20Chains): convergence to equilibrium.
- [Numerical Stochastic Differential Equations](node:Numerical%20Stochastic%20Differential%20Equations), [Queueing Theory](node:Queueing%20Theory), [Statistical Time Series](node:Statistical%20Time%20Series), [Random Dynamical Systems](node:Random%20Dynamical%20Systems): applications.

### Common pitfalls
- Wide-sense stationarity needs a constant mean as well as a lag-only covariance ([Wikipedia: Stationary process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary_process)).
- Path questions for uncountable $T$ need separability (sample functions essentially determined by a countable dense set of indices) or a càdlàg (Skorokhod) construction ([Wikipedia: Stochastic process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process)); a separable modification of a real-valued process may take values $\pm\infty$ ([Shalizi, 36-754 lecture notes, ch. 8](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/754/notes/lecture-08.pdf)).
- Almost sure martingale convergence does not give $L^1$ convergence; uniform integrability is exactly what is needed. Optional stopping at unbounded times needs hypotheses; both Wald identities require $E\tau<\infty$ ([Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Zero-one law for directional transience of RWRE.** For $\ell\ne0$ let $A_\ell=\{\lim_nX_n\cdot\ell=\infty\}$. Kalikow proved $P_0[A_\ell\cup A_{-\ell}]\in\{0,1\}$ for i.i.d. uniformly elliptic environments; the stronger $P_0[A_\ell]\in\{0,1\}$ was settled for $d=2$ by Merkl and Zerner (2001), while Zerner (2007) calls the 0-1 law one of the major open questions for RWRE and the case $d\ge3$ still wide open, as of that paper ([Zerner 2007](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0706.0745)).
- **Curves in planar Brownian paths.** Pemantle showed the range of planar Brownian motion a.s. covers no line segment; which curves can be covered is, per Mörters and Peres (2008 draft), in general open, and the minimal Hausdorff dimension of curves in the range is unknown, though the outer boundary is a curve of dimension $4/3$ ([Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Stochastic process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process): definitions, classes, modifications, history.
- **Learn:** [S. Lalley, Conditional Expectation and Martingales (University of Chicago)](https://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/385/Martingales.pdf): martingales, optional sampling, Wald identities, convergence.
- **Learn:** [C. Shalizi, 36-754 Advanced Probability, ch. 8 "More on Continuity" (CMU)](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/754/notes/lecture-08.pdf): separable and measurable modifications.
- **Learn:** [R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples (author's PDF)](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf): graduate text, martingales through Donsker's theorem.
- **Primary:** [M. P. W. Zerner, The zero-one law for planar random walks in i.i.d. random environments revisited (2007)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.0745): RWRE and the open 0-1 law.
- **Further reading:** [P. Mörters and Y. Peres, Brownian Motion (monograph, 2008 draft)](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205B/bmbook.pdf): sample-path theory of Brownian motion.
- **Further reading:** [R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 2019)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/9781108591034).
- **Further reading:** [I. Karatzas and S. E. Shreve, Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus (Springer GTM)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-0949-2): continuous-time martingales, stochastic integration, SDEs.
references.Stress-Energy Tensor:
## Reference
### Overview
The stress–energy tensor $T^{\mu\nu}$ is a symmetric rank-2 tensor field that packages energy density, momentum density, energy flux and stress into one frame-independent object. In an inertial frame, $T^{00}$ is the energy density, $T^{0k}=T^{k0}$ the momentum density (equivalently energy flux), and $T^{kl}$ the flux of the $k$-th momentum component across a surface of constant $x^l$: diagonal entries are normal stresses (pressures), off-diagonal ones shears. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor); [Carroll, §1](https://arxiv.org/html/gr-qc/9712019))

It is the source term of the [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations), $G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\kappa T_{\mu\nu}$ with $\kappa=8\pi G/c^4$, so that in [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) matter and radiation enter gravity only through $T_{\mu\nu}$. The contracted Bianchi identity $\nabla_\nu G^{\mu\nu}=0$ then forces $\nabla_\nu T^{\mu\nu}=0$. ([Einstein field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))

Two constructions coexist: the canonical tensor from [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) for spacetime translations, which need not be symmetric, and the metric (Hilbert) tensor obtained by varying the matter action with respect to the metric, which is symmetric and is the one that couples to gravity. The Belinfante–Rosenfeld procedure reconciles them. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor); [Belinfante–Rosenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinfante%E2%80%93Rosenfeld_stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))

### Formal definition
Use signature $(-,+,+,+)$. For a matter action $S_M=\int\mathcal L_M\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$, the Hilbert (metric) stress–energy tensor is ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))
$$
T_{\mu\nu}=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta S_M}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}=-2\frac{\partial\mathcal L_M}{\partial g^{\mu\nu}}+g_{\mu\nu}\mathcal L_M .
$$
It is symmetric by construction and gauge invariant. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor)) Hawking and Ellis likewise obtain the energy–momentum tensor of matter fields from a Lagrangian. ([Hawking–Ellis, ch. 3](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/large-scale-structure-of-spacetime/general-relativity/08A6F56F77A32678F8CF16FB1FDFFE84))

For fields $\Psi_\ell$ in flat spacetime the canonical (Noether) tensor of translations, in the form Weinberg gives (mostly-plus signature), is ([Belinfante–Rosenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinfante%E2%80%93Rosenfeld_stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))
$$
T_{\mathrm{can}}^{\mu\nu}=\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathcal L-\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\Psi_\ell)}\,\partial^\nu\Psi_\ell .
$$
The stress–energy article writes the same tensor with the opposite overall sign, $\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\varphi_\alpha)}\partial_\nu\varphi_\alpha-\delta^\mu_\nu\mathcal L$, which has positive energy density in the $(+,-,-,-)$ signature, so compare signs only within one convention. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))

A perfect fluid with rest-frame energy density $\rho$, pressure $p$ and four-velocity $U^\mu$ ($U^\mu U_\mu=-1$, $c=1$) has $T^{\mu\nu}=(\rho+p)U^\mu U^\nu+p\,g^{\mu\nu}$, diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(\rho,p,p,p)$ in its rest frame. ([Carroll, eq. 1.110](https://arxiv.org/html/gr-qc/9712019))

### Key results
- **Local conservation.** In [special relativity](node:Special%20Relativity) $\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$ holds for matter obeying its equations of motion; the $\nu=0$ component is energy conservation and $\nu=k$ momentum conservation. In general relativity it becomes $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$. ([Carroll, eq. 1.113](https://arxiv.org/html/gr-qc/9712019); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))
- **Belinfante–Rosenfeld symmetrization.** If the canonical tensor fails to be symmetric because of a spin current $S_{\mu\nu\lambda}$, then $T^B_{\mu\nu}=T_{\mu\nu}+\tfrac12\partial^\lambda\bigl(S_{\mu\nu\lambda}+S_{\nu\mu\lambda}-S_{\lambda\nu\mu}\bigr)$ is symmetric yet still conserved, the added term being a divergence interpreted as bound momentum from gradients of intrinsic angular momentum. Belinfante and Rosenfeld (1940) showed it coincides with the Hilbert tensor that sources gravity. ([Belinfante–Rosenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinfante%E2%80%93Rosenfeld_stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))
- **Energy conditions.** NEC: $T_{ab}k^ak^b\ge0$ for all null $k$; WEC: $T_{ab}X^aX^b\ge0$ for all timelike $X$; DEC: WEC plus no faster-than-light energy flow; SEC: $(T_{ab}-\tfrac12Tg_{ab})X^aX^b\ge0$ for timelike $X$. For a perfect fluid these read NEC $\rho+p\ge0$; WEC $\rho\ge0,\ \rho+p\ge0$; DEC $\rho\ge|p|$; SEC $\rho+p\ge0,\ \rho+3p\ge0$. They are imposed assumptions, not laws. ([Energy condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_condition))
- **Hawking–Ellis classification.** In $3+1$ dimensions, $T^\mu{}_\nu$ is of type I if it has a timelike eigenvector, so $T^\mu{}_\nu\sim\operatorname{diag}(-\rho,p_1,p_2,p_3)$; type II has a double eigenvalue with only a null eigenvector (a $2\times2$ Jordan block); type III a triple eigenvalue with a single null eigenvector; type IV complex eigenvalues $-\rho\pm if$ and no causal eigenvector. The cores of types III and IV violate the NEC, WEC, SEC and DEC; types II and III are unstable under perturbation while I and IV are stable; type IV arises semiclassically in renormalized expectation values. ([Martin-Moruno–Visser](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1802.00865); [arXiv:1802.00865](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.00865))
- **Quantum energy inequalities.** [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory) violates all the classical pointwise energy conditions, but satisfies weaker averaged bounds, the quantum energy inequalities (QEIs), a programme begun by Ford in 1978; Fewster derives them for the free scalar field and for unitary positive-energy two-dimensional CFTs. ([Fewster, arXiv:1208.5399](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.5399))
- **Averaged null energy condition.** ANEC requires $\int_C T_{ab}k^ak^b\,d\lambda\ge0$ along a complete null geodesic $C$. Hartman, Kundu and Tajdini argued from microcausality that the averaged null energy is positive in interacting QFTs in more than two dimensions (Minkowski space). ([Energy condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_condition); [Hartman–Kundu–Tajdini, arXiv:1610.05308](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.05308))
- **Gravitational energy pseudotensors.** Gravitational energy–momentum has no local tensor; the [Landau–Lifshitz pseudotensor](node:Landau–Lifshitz%20Pseudotensor) $t_{LL}^{\mu\nu}$ is symmetric and satisfies the ordinary conservation law $\partial_\mu\bigl[(-g)(T^{\mu\nu}+t_{LL}^{\mu\nu})\bigr]=0$, but it vanishes at any chosen point in a locally inertial frame. ([Landau–Lifshitz pseudotensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93Lifshitz_pseudotensor))

### Examples
- **Dust:** $T^{\mu\nu}=\rho U^\mu U^\nu$, the pressureless perfect fluid. ([Carroll, eq. 1.106](https://arxiv.org/html/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Electromagnetic field (SI):** $T^{\mu\nu}=\frac1{\mu_0}\bigl(F^{\mu\alpha}g_{\alpha\beta}F^{\nu\beta}-\tfrac14g^{\mu\nu}F_{\delta\gamma}F^{\delta\gamma}\bigr)$, the Hilbert tensor of Maxwell theory. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))
- **Real scalar field** of mass $m$ in flat spacetime: $T^{\mu\nu}=\partial^\mu\phi\,\partial^\nu\phi-\tfrac12\eta^{\mu\nu}\bigl(\partial^\lambda\phi\,\partial_\lambda\phi+m^2\phi^2\bigr)$. ([Carroll, eq. 1.112](https://arxiv.org/html/gr-qc/9712019))
- **Casimir plates:** for ideal plates at separation $a$ the energy per unit area is $-\hbar c\pi^2/(720a^3)$, so the field energy density between them is $-\pi^2\hbar c/(720a^4)$, a standard violation of the WEC. ([Casimir effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casimir_effect); [Energy condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_condition))
- **Vacuum energy and dark energy** with $w=p/\rho=-1$ violate the SEC, which needs $w\ge-1/3$. ([Energy condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_condition))

### History
Einstein published the field equations, with the energy–momentum tensor of matter as the source, in 1915, and gave the full account in his review "Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie," *Annalen der Physik* 354 (1916) 769–822; his original publication wrote the coupling constant as $8\pi G/c^2$, putting $T_{\mu\nu}$ in mass-density units. ([Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/andp.19163540702); [Einstein field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations)) Belinfante and Rosenfeld independently gave the symmetrized tensor in 1940, and Landau and Lifshitz's pseudotensor is cited to the 1951 edition of *The Classical Theory of Fields*. ([Belinfante–Rosenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinfante%E2%80%93Rosenfeld_stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor); [Landau–Lifshitz pseudotensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93Lifshitz_pseudotensor))

### Connections
- [Four-Vectors and Relativistic Momentum](node:Four-Vectors%20and%20Relativistic%20Momentum) and [Four-Velocity](node:Four-Velocity): $T^{\mu\nu}$ is the continuum version of particle four-momentum, built from $U^\mu$ for fluids.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): index placement, eigenvector (Hawking–Ellis) structure of $T^\mu{}_\nu$.
- [Einstein Field Equations](node:Einstein%20Field%20Equations) and [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): $T_{\mu\nu}$ is the source of curvature.
- [Energy Conditions](node:Energy%20Conditions) and [Singularity Theorems in Relativity](node:Singularity%20Theorems%20in%20Relativity): inequalities on $T_{\mu\nu}$ used as hypotheses.
- [Noether's Theorem](node:Noether's%20Theorem) and [Lagrangian Field Theory](node:Lagrangian%20Field%20Theory): the canonical tensor is the Noether current of translations.
- [Electromagnetic Field Tensor](node:Electromagnetic%20Field%20Tensor) and [Klein–Gordon Equation](node:Klein–Gordon%20Equation): standard field examples.
- [Casimir Effect](node:Casimir%20Effect): negative energy density from boundary conditions on quantum fields.
- [Conservation Laws](node:Conservation%20Laws): local divergence identities versus global charges.

### Common pitfalls
- $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$ is not an ordinary conservation law for total energy in curved spacetime: including gravity requires a pseudotensor, which can be made to vanish at a point by a coordinate choice. ([Landau–Lifshitz pseudotensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93Lifshitz_pseudotensor))
- The canonical tensor need not be symmetric (it fails when fields carry spin); only the Belinfante/Hilbert tensor sources gravity. ([Belinfante–Rosenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinfante%E2%80%93Rosenfeld_stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor))
- Signature and unit conventions change signs and factors: with $(+,-,-,-)$ the cosmological term flips sign, and Einstein's original constant differs from $8\pi G/c^4$. ([Einstein field equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations))
- "Strong" does not imply "weak": the SEC and WEC are independent conditions on a perfect fluid. ([Energy condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_condition))

### Open problems
- **ANEC beyond flat space.** Extending the averaged null energy condition results beyond the settings where they are established is described as an open problem. ([Energy condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_condition)) Graham and Olum proposed the weaker achronal ANEC for curved spacetimes, which has no known violations and would suffice to rule out wormholes and closed timelike curves; it is proposed, not proved. ([Graham–Olum, arXiv:0705.3193](https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.3193))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Stress–energy tensor (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor): components, canonical and Hilbert definitions, field examples.
- **Learn:** [Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity](https://arxiv.org/html/gr-qc/9712019): dust, perfect fluids, electromagnetic and scalar tensors, conservation.
- **Primary:** [Fewster, Lectures on quantum energy inequalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.5399): survey of QEIs; [Martin-Moruno and Visser, Essential core of the Hawking–Ellis types](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.00865): the algebraic classification of $T^{\mu\nu}$.
- **Further reading:** [Hawking and Ellis, The Large Scale Structure of Space-Time (CUP)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/large-scale-structure-of-spacetime/general-relativity/08A6F56F77A32678F8CF16FB1FDFFE84): energy–momentum tensors from a Lagrangian (ch. 3) and the singularity theorems (chs. 8–10).
references.String Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
String theory replaces point particles by one-dimensional strings whose vibrational modes play the role of particle species. One of these modes is a massless spin-2 state with the properties of the graviton, which is why the theory is studied as a candidate for [Quantum Gravity](node:Quantum%20Gravity) and for a unified description of gravity and gauge interactions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory)). Consistency of the quantum theory fixes the spacetime dimension: 26 for the bosonic string and 10 for the superstring, with an eleven-dimensional theory, [M-Theory](node:M-Theory), appearing at strong coupling ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory)).

In its perturbative formulation, string theory replaces the sum over Feynman graphs of [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory) by a sum over two-dimensional surfaces (worldsheets) of correlators of a two-dimensional QFT; in simple cases this worldsheet theory is a sigma-model whose target is spacetime, and summing the correlators produces an S-matrix. Each admissible choice of worldsheet theory, called a "vacuum", determines an effective spacetime geometry and particle content ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory)). The Polyakov action is an action of the two-dimensional [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory) describing the worldsheet ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyakov_action)); a standard first course assumes [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory) and [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) and treats conformal field theory as one of its core topics ([Tong, arXiv:0908.0333](https://arxiv.org/abs/0908.0333)).

It is not known in general how to define string theory non-perturbatively, nor whether any principle selects its vacuum state, and there is to date no connection to experimental phenomenology, although conceptual insights from string theory have helped analyze quantum field theory ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory)).

### Formal definition
A string sweeps out a worldsheet $X^\mu(\sigma^0,\sigma^1)$ in a target spacetime with metric $g_{\mu\nu}$. In the mostly-plus signature $(-,+,\dots,+)$, the **Nambu–Goto action** is minus the tension times the worldsheet area:
$$S_{\mathrm{NG}} = -T\int d^2\sigma\,\sqrt{-\det G_{ab}},\qquad G_{ab}=g_{\mu\nu}(X)\,\partial_a X^\mu\,\partial_b X^\nu ,$$
with $T=1/(2\pi\alpha')$ the string tension ([Wikipedia: Nambu–Goto action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nambu%E2%80%93Goto_action)). The **Polyakov action** introduces an independent auxiliary worldsheet metric $h_{ab}$; in the same conventions, normalized so that it reduces to $S_{\mathrm{NG}}$,
$$S_{\mathrm{P}} = -\frac{T}{2}\int d^2\sigma\,\sqrt{-h}\,h^{ab}\,g_{\mu\nu}(X)\,\partial_a X^\mu\,\partial_b X^\nu .$$
The action is invariant under target-space Poincaré transformations, worldsheet diffeomorphisms, and Weyl rescalings $h_{ab}\mapsto e^{2\omega(\sigma)}h_{ab}$; eliminating $h_{ab}$ by its equation of motion returns the Nambu–Goto action, so the two are classically equivalent, and the Polyakov form is the more easily quantized ([Wikipedia: Polyakov action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyakov_action); [Wikipedia: Nambu–Goto action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nambu%E2%80%93Goto_action)). (Overall signs depend on the signature convention; the Wikipedia Polyakov article writes both actions with a $+$ sign in a mostly-minus convention.)

**Critical dimension.** Quantizing the Polyakov action produces a conformal (Weyl) anomaly depending on the target dimension $d$ and the dilaton. For vanishing dilaton the anomaly vanishes exactly for $d=26$ (bosonic string) and $d=10$ (superstring); these are the critical string theories, and non-critical models are studied separately ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory)).

**Perturbative amplitudes.** A string vacuum is a choice of worldsheet QFT; scattering amplitudes are sums over worldsheet topologies of correlators of that QFT, which together define an S-matrix ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory)). A one-semester treatment of this construction (classical and quantum string, D-branes, CFT, Polyakov path integral and ghosts, interactions, low-energy effective action, [compactification](node:Compactification) and T-duality) is in [Tong's lectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/0908.0333) ([arXiv:0908.0333](https://arxiv.org/abs/0908.0333)).

### Key results
- **Five consistent superstring theories.** In ten dimensions there are five supersymmetric string theories: Type I, Type IIA, Type IIB, heterotic $SO(32)$ and heterotic $E_8\times E_8$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory)).
- **Green–Schwarz anomaly cancellation (1984).** In type I string theory the gauge and gravitational anomalies cancel through an extra classical contribution from a 2-form field, provided the gauge group has dimension 496; for $SO(32)$ and $E_8\times E_8$ the anomaly polynomial factorizes and the anomaly can be cancelled by a tree diagram. This discovery started the first superstring revolution ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Schwarz_mechanism)).
- **T-duality.** A string on a circle of radius $R$ is equivalent to a string on a circle of radius $\alpha'/R$, with $\alpha'$ the inverse string tension; momentum and winding numbers are exchanged, leaving the spectrum unchanged. Type IIA is T-dual to Type IIB, and the two heterotic theories are T-dual to each other ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-duality)). See [String Dualities](node:String%20Dualities).
- **Strong coupling and eleven dimensions (Witten 1995).** The strong-coupling limit of ten-dimensional Type IIA string theory has eleven-dimensional [Supergravity](node:Supergravity) as its low-energy limit; the paper also relates heterotic–Type II duality to strong-coupling dynamics in five, six and seven dimensions, implying S-duality for heterotic and Type II strings ([Witten, arXiv:hep-th/9503124](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9503124)).
- **D-branes carry Ramond–Ramond charge (Polchinski 1995).** Dirichlet-branes, defined by mixed Dirichlet–Neumann boundary conditions for open strings, break half the supersymmetry of type II string theory and carry the full set of electric and magnetic Ramond–Ramond charges, with the charge quantum required by string duality; they are therefore intrinsic objects of type II theory ([Polchinski, arXiv:hep-th/9510017](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9510017)). See [D-Branes](node:D-Branes).
- **Microscopic black-hole entropy (Strominger–Vafa 1996).** For a class of five-dimensional extremal supersymmetric [black holes](node:Black%20Holes) in string theory, counting the degeneracy of BPS soliton bound states (configurations of D-branes) reproduces the Bekenstein–Hawking area–entropy relation $S_{BH}=A/4$ exactly, including the factor $1/4$ ([Strominger and Vafa, arXiv:hep-th/9601029](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9601029); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory)). See [Black Hole Thermodynamics](node:Black%20Hole%20Thermodynamics).
- **AdS/CFT (Maldacena 1997).** The large-$N$ limit of certain conformal field theories contains a sector describing supergravity on products of anti-de Sitter spaces with compact manifolds; in particular the 't Hooft limit of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=4$ super-Yang–Mills contains Type IIB strings, and compactifications of string/M-theory on AdS spaces are conjectured to be dual to specific CFTs ([Maldacena, arXiv:hep-th/9711200](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9711200)). See [Holographic Principle](node:Holographic%20Principle).

### Examples
- **Toroidal compactification.** Compactifying one direction on a circle gives the momentum/winding spectrum and the $R\leftrightarrow\alpha'/R$ symmetry described above ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-duality)).
- **Compactification.** Choosing a worldsheet theory (a vacuum) amounts to choosing an effective target-space geometry, including any compact internal directions, and with it the effective particle content ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory)). Related: [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds).
- **KKLT de Sitter construction.** Warped Type IIB compactifications with NS and RR three-form fluxes, plus non-perturbative superpotential corrections (Euclidean D-brane instantons or gaugino condensation), fix all moduli in a supersymmetric AdS vacuum; adding a few anti-D3-branes lifts it to a proposed metastable de Sitter vacuum ([Kachru, Kallosh, Linde and Trivedi](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0301240), [arXiv:hep-th/0301240](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0301240)).

### History
- **1968:** Veneziano wrote down the dual-resonance amplitude; in 1969–1970 Nambu, Nielsen and Susskind interpreted it as describing vibrating strings, as a model of the strong force ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_string_theory)).
- **1971:** Ramond, and Neveu and Schwarz, added fermions ("spinning strings"); Claud Lovelace discovered the critical dimension 26 in 1971 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_string_theory)).
- **1974:** Scherk and Schwarz, and independently Yoneya, identified a string mode with the graviton, recasting the theory as one of gravity ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_string_theory)).
- **1976–1981:** the Polyakov action was introduced by Deser and Zumino and independently by Brink, Di Vecchia and Howe (1976); Polyakov used it to quantize the string in 1981 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyakov_action)).
- **1977:** the GSO projection gave the first tachyon-free superstring theories ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_string_theory)).
- **1984:** Green–Schwarz anomaly cancellation launched the first superstring revolution ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Schwarz_mechanism)).
- **About 1994–1995:** the second superstring revolution, sparked by Witten's evidence that the superstring theories are limits of an eleven-dimensional M-theory, brought new dualities and Polchinski's D-branes (1995); Maldacena's AdS/CFT conjecture followed in 1997 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_string_theory); [arXiv:hep-th/9711200](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9711200)).

### Connections
- [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory): the worldsheet theory of a string vacuum is a 2d (super)conformal field theory.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): perturbative string amplitudes generalize Feynman-graph sums to sums over surfaces; low-energy limits are QFTs.
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the massless spin-2 mode reproduces Einstein gravity at low energy.
- [Supergravity](node:Supergravity): the low-energy effective theory of superstrings and of M-theory.
- [M-Theory](node:M-Theory): the eleven-dimensional theory whose limits are the five superstring theories.
- [String Dualities](node:String%20Dualities): T- and S-dualities relating the five theories.
- [D-Branes](node:D-Branes): extended objects on which open strings end; sources of RR charge.
- [Holographic Principle](node:Holographic%20Principle): realized concretely by AdS/CFT.
- [Black Hole Thermodynamics](node:Black%20Hole%20Thermodynamics): string theory gives a microscopic count of entropy for some black holes.
- [String Landscape](node:String%20Landscape): the large space of vacua and the problem of vacuum selection.
- [Supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry): the five ten-dimensional superstring theories are spacetime supersymmetric.
- [Kaluza–Klein Theory](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Theory): compactification of [extra dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions) generalizes the Kaluza–Klein idea.
- [Loop Quantum Gravity](node:Loop%20Quantum%20Gravity): a competing approach to quantum gravity.
- [Gauge Theory](node:Gauge%20Theory): gauge fields arise from open strings on D-branes and from compactification.

### Common pitfalls
- **"String theory predicts ten dimensions" is only half the statement.** The critical dimension follows from cancelling the worldsheet Weyl anomaly at vanishing dilaton; non-critical strings exist, and the bosonic theory needs 26 ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory)).
- **Perturbative vs. complete theory.** The worldsheet construction defines a perturbative series; there is no full non-perturbative definition in all backgrounds, and a rigorous theory of 2d QFT exists only in special cases ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory)).
- **Black-hole entropy counting is not for realistic black holes.** Strominger–Vafa applies to extremal, supersymmetric five-dimensional black holes ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory); [arXiv:hep-th/9601029](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9601029)).
- **Nambu–Goto vs. Polyakov.** They agree classically, but the Polyakov action is the more easily quantized of the two ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyakov_action)).

### Open problems
- **Non-perturbative definition and vacuum selection.** No satisfactory non-perturbative formulation exists in all circumstances, and it is unclear whether any principle selects the vacuum describing our universe ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory)).
- **Does string theory have de Sitter vacua?** Constructions such as KKLT propose metastable de Sitter vacua ([arXiv:hep-th/0301240](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0301240)), while Danielsson and Van Riet, reviewing about twenty years of such attempts, argue that the results could suggest string theory has no de Sitter vacua at all ([arXiv:1804.01120](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.01120)).
- **The Swampland program.** A research program aiming to distinguish effective field theories that can be completed into quantum gravity from those that cannot; the review covers conjectures such as the Weak Gravity Conjecture and the de Sitter conjecture ([Palti, arXiv:1903.06239](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06239)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: string theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory): worldsheet formulation, critical dimension, vacua, and the status of non-perturbative questions.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: String theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory): overview of the five theories, dualities, M-theory, AdS/CFT and criticisms.
- **Learn:** [Tong, Lectures on String Theory (arXiv:0908.0333)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0908.0333): one-semester graduate course on the bosonic string through T-duality.
- **Primary:** [Witten, String Theory Dynamics in Various Dimensions (hep-th/9503124)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9503124): strong coupling, eleven dimensions and S-duality.
- **Primary:** [Maldacena, The Large N Limit of Superconformal Field Theories and Supergravity (hep-th/9711200)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9711200): the AdS/CFT conjecture.
- **Primary:** [Palti, The Swampland: Introduction and Review (arXiv:1903.06239)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06239): survey of the swampland conjectures.
- **Further reading:** [Polchinski, String Theory, Vol. 1 (Cambridge University Press)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511816079/type/book): standard graduate text on the bosonic string, CFT, the Polyakov path integral, T-duality and D-branes.
references.Submanifolds and Embeddings:
## Reference
### Overview
A submanifold of a manifold $M$ is a subset that is itself a manifold, with conditions on the inclusion. An *immersed* submanifold is the image of an immersion; it may self-intersect, and when the immersion is injective its own topology can be finer than the subspace topology. An *embedded* (regular) submanifold is one whose inclusion is a topological embedding, so its topology is the subspace topology. Lie subgroups are the standard example of naturally immersed submanifolds. ([Wikipedia: Submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold))

Two questions organise the subject. The topological one asks when and in what dimension a manifold can be embedded or immersed in another, with answers from Whitney's theorems, transversality and the h-principle. ([Wikipedia: Whitney embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_embedding_theorem); [Wikipedia: Homotopy principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_principle)) The geometric one asks how a submanifold of a Riemannian manifold bends: the induced metric, the second fundamental form, the normal connection, and the Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci equations linking them. ([Chen, Riemannian submanifolds: a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.1875))

Nash's theorems join the two: every Riemannian manifold can be isometrically embedded in some Euclidean space, flexibly in class $C^1$ and with explicit dimension bounds in class $C^k$, $k\ge3$. ([Wikipedia: Nash embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem))

### Formal definition
A smooth map $F:X\to Y$ is an *immersion* if its differential is injective at every point; $F$ itself need not be injective. ([Wikipedia: Immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_%28mathematics%29)) A *smooth embedding* is an immersion that is a topological embedding, i.e. a homeomorphism onto its image; its domain is then diffeomorphic to its image. ([Wikipedia: Embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embedding)) See [Homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism).

**Slice charts.** A $k$-dimensional embedded submanifold $S$ of an $n$-manifold $M$ has, around each $p\in S$, a chart $\varphi:U\to\mathbb R^n$ of $M$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)$ equal to the intersection of a $k$-dimensional plane with $\varphi(U)$; the restricted charts form the smooth atlas of $S$. ([Wikipedia: Submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold)) The plane is a hyperplane only in codimension one, although nLab's version of this proposition (citing Lee, Thm. 5.8) says "rectilinear hyperplane". ([nLab: submanifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/submanifold))

**Induced metric and second fundamental form.** For a surface in $\mathbb R^3$ the first fundamental form is the Euclidean inner product restricted to each tangent plane. ([Galloway, Ch. 4](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/dgnotes/chpt4.pdf)) For an isometric immersion $f:(M,g)\to(\tilde M,\tilde g)$ with Levi-Civita connections $\nabla,\tilde\nabla$, the Gauss formula $\tilde\nabla_XY=\nabla_XY+h(X,Y)$ defines the second fundamental form $h$, a symmetric normal-bundle-valued tensor; the Weingarten formula $\tilde\nabla_X\xi=-A_\xi X+D_X\xi$ defines the shape operator $A_\xi$, with $g(A_\xi X,Y)=\tilde g(h(X,Y),\xi)$, and the normal connection $D$. ([Chen survey, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

### Key results
- **Regular value theorem.** If $q$ is a regular value of a smooth $f:M\to N$, then $f^{-1}(q)$ is empty or a manifold of dimension $\dim M-\dim N$; near a point where $f$ is a submersion, $f$ is a coordinate projection in suitable charts. ([Wikipedia: Submersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersion_%28mathematics%29)) More generally, submanifolds $L_1,L_2\subset M$ are transverse if their tangent spaces span $T_pM$ at each common point, and then $L_1\cap L_2$ is a manifold of dimension $\ell_1+\ell_2-m$; submanifolds can be perturbed into transverse position without changing their homology class. ([Wikipedia: Transversality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transversality_%28mathematics%29))
- **Tubular neighbourhood theorem.** An embedded submanifold $S\subset M$ has an open neighbourhood modelled on its normal bundle: there is a smooth map from the normal bundle into $M$ sending the zero section to $S$ that restricts, on an open neighbourhood of the zero section, to a diffeomorphism onto an open neighbourhood of $S$, and the tubular neighbourhood deformation retracts onto $S$. ([Wikipedia: Tubular neighborhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubular_neighborhood)) See [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles).
- **Whitney embedding and immersion theorems.** Every smooth Hausdorff second-countable $m$-manifold, $m>0$, embeds in $\mathbb R^{2m}$; this is the best linear bound, since $\mathbb{RP}^{2^k}$ does not embed in $\mathbb R^{2\cdot2^k-1}$. Maps from an $n$-manifold to an $m$-manifold can be approximated by embeddings if $m>2n$ and by immersions if $m>2n-1$. Haefliger: a compact $k$-connected $n$-manifold embeds in $\mathbb R^{2n-k}$ when $2k+3\le n$. ([Wikipedia: Whitney embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_embedding_theorem)) See [Whitney Embedding Theorem](node:Whitney%20Embedding%20Theorem).
- **Cohen's immersion theorem.** Every compact smooth $n$-manifold ($n\ge2$, the range of Whitney's $\mathbb R^{2n-1}$ immersion theorem) immerses in $\mathbb R^{2n-\alpha(n)}$, where $\alpha(n)$ is the number of ones in the binary expansion of $n$, and this bound is best possible. ([Wikipedia: Ralph Louis Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Louis_Cohen); [Spring, The golden age of immersion theory, §§1, 6](https://arxiv.org/html/math/0307127v1)) This immersion conjecture was proved by Ralph Cohen (1985), after Massey (1960) showed that the Stiefel–Whitney classes of the stable normal bundle vanish above degree $n-\alpha(n)$, a bound realised by real projective space. If $M$ is compact, an injective immersion of $M$ is an embedding. ([Wikipedia: Immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_%28mathematics%29))
- **Smale–Hirsch and the h-principle.** Smale expressed the regular homotopy classes of immersions of spheres in Euclidean space as homotopy groups of a Stiefel manifold, with sphere eversion as a striking consequence, and Hirsch generalised this to a homotopy-theoretic description of immersions of any $m$-manifold in any $n$-manifold. Gromov's h-principle abstracts this: a relation satisfies it if every non-holonomic (formal) solution can be deformed to a holonomic one, and Gromov's convex integration is based on the work of Nash and Kuiper. ([Wikipedia: Homotopy principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_principle); [Wikipedia: Immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Nash embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem))
- **Nash–Kuiper $C^1$ theorem.** If $(M,g)$ is an $m$-dimensional Riemannian manifold and $f:M\to\mathbb R^n$ is a short smooth embedding (or immersion) with $n\ge m+1$, then $f$ is a uniform limit of $C^1$ isometric embeddings (or immersions). Nash proved it for $n\ge m+2$ (1954) and Kuiper for $n\ge m+1$. ([Wikipedia: Nash embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem))
- **Nash $C^k$ theorem.** For a $C^k$ metric, $3\le k\le\infty$, there is a $C^k$ isometric embedding in $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\le m(3m+11)/2$ if $M$ is compact and $n\le m(m+1)(3m+11)/2$ otherwise (1956); Günther (1989) simplified the proof. ([Wikipedia: Nash embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem)) See [Nash Embedding Theorem](node:Nash%20Embedding%20Theorem).
- **Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci equations.** For an isometric immersion with second fundamental form $h$, shape operators $A_\xi$ and normal curvature $R^D$,
  $$\langle R(X,Y)Z,W\rangle=\langle\tilde R(X,Y)Z,W\rangle+\langle h(X,W),h(Y,Z)\rangle-\langle h(X,Z),h(Y,W)\rangle,$$
  $$(\tilde R(X,Y)Z)^\perp=(\bar\nabla_Xh)(Y,Z)-(\bar\nabla_Yh)(X,Z),\qquad \langle\tilde R(X,Y)\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle R^D(X,Y)\xi,\eta\rangle-\langle[A_\xi,A_\eta]X,Y\rangle.$$
  ([Chen survey, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))
- **Fundamental theorem of submanifolds (Bonnet).** If $(M,g)$ is a simply connected Riemannian $n$-manifold carrying a Riemannian vector bundle $\nu$ of rank $m$ with a metric connection and a $\nu$-valued symmetric tensor $h$ satisfying the Gauss, Codazzi and Ricci equations for constant curvature $c$, then $M$ admits an isometric immersion into the simply connected complete space form $R^{n+m}(c)$ with normal bundle $\nu$ and second fundamental form $h$; such an immersion is unique up to ambient isometry. Bonnet gave the first proof. ([Chen survey, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))

### Examples
- **Klein bottle.** An immersion is precisely a local embedding, and the Klein bottle immerses in $\mathbb R^3$ but does not embed there. ([Wikipedia: Immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_%28mathematics%29))
- **Sphere of radius $r$.** In geographic coordinates the induced metric is $ds^2=r^2d\theta^2+r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$. ([Galloway, Ch. 4](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/dgnotes/chpt4.pdf)) With the outward normal, the unit sphere has $\mathrm{I\!I}=-du^2-\sin^2u\,dv^2$, while a plane has $\mathrm{I\!I}=0$. ([Wikipedia: Second fundamental form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_fundamental_form)) See [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere).
- **Round sphere, rigid and flexible.** A $C^1$ isometric immersion of the round $S^2$ can lie in an arbitrarily small ball of $\mathbb R^3$; it cannot be $C^2$, since the Theorema Egregium would force Gauss curvature $1$. ([Wikipedia: Homotopy principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_principle))

### History
Gauss introduced the second fundamental form for surfaces (1827); Mainardi (1856) and Codazzi (1860; see also Codazzi 1868) found the Codazzi equation; Bonnet (1867) recognised the importance of these formulas and proved the fundamental theorem; Voss (1880) gave the Gauss and Codazzi equations for general submanifolds; and Ricci gave the Ricci equation in 1888. ([Chen survey, §3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875)) Whitney's embedding theorem unified chart-based and extrinsic definitions of manifolds. ([Wikipedia: Whitney embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_embedding_theorem)) Nash's isometric embedding theorems date from 1954 and 1956; Smale and Hirsch's immersion theory from 1959; Gromov's *Partial Differential Relations* appeared in 1986. ([Wikipedia: Nash embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem); [Wikipedia: Homotopy principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_principle))

### Connections
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): slice charts give submanifolds their smooth structure.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): the induced metric is the pullback of the ambient metric.
- [Tangent Spaces and Vector Fields](node:Tangent%20Spaces%20and%20Vector%20Fields): immersions are injective on tangent spaces; transversality is a tangent-space condition.
- [Extrinsic Curvature](node:Extrinsic%20Curvature): the second fundamental form and shape operator.
- [Gauss–Codazzi Equations](node:Gauss–Codazzi%20Equations): the compatibility conditions above.
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives): $h$ and the normal connection come from splitting $\tilde\nabla$.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): the Gauss equation compares intrinsic and ambient curvature.
- [Whitney Embedding Theorem](node:Whitney%20Embedding%20Theorem) and [Nash Embedding Theorem](node:Nash%20Embedding%20Theorem): the two basic existence theorems.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): Lie subgroups are immersed, not always embedded, submanifolds.
- [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles): normal bundles and tubular neighbourhoods.
- [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere): the model hypersurface.
- [MSC 53 - Differential geometry](node:MSC%2053%20-%20Differential%20geometry) and [MSC 57Rxx - Differential topology](node:MSC%2057Rxx%20-%20Differential%20topology).

### Common pitfalls
- **Immersion versus embedding.** An immersion is only locally an embedding; injectivity is not enough without compactness, since an injective immersion's image can carry a finer topology. ([Wikipedia: Immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold))
- **Flexibility versus rigidity.** $C^1$ isometric embeddings are flexible and often pathological. Smooth ones are not rigid in general (Nash's $C^k$ theorem is itself an existence result in high codimension), but rigidity appears in low codimension: a smooth isometric hypersurface immersion of the round sphere is round, and Hilbert's theorem forbids a smooth isometric immersion of the hyperbolic plane in $\mathbb R^3$. ([Wikipedia: Nash embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem)) Cohn-Vossen (1929) proved closed convex surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ rigid, and Pogorelov (1951) removed the smoothness assumption; yet $S^n$, rigid in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ for $n\ge2$, is not rigid in $\mathbb R^{n+2}$. ([Chen survey, §4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.1875))
- **Slice dimension.** The slice $\varphi(S\cap U)$ is a $k$-plane, not a hyperplane, unless $S$ has codimension one. ([Wikipedia: Submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold))

### Open problems
- **Optimal embedding dimension.** Let $e(n)$ be the least integer such that every compact connected $n$-manifold embeds in $\mathbb R^{e(n)}$. Whitney gives $e(n)\le2n$, with equality for $n=1,2$ and for $n$ a power of 2; otherwise $e(n)\le2n-1$ (Haefliger–Hirsch for $n>4$, Wall for $n=3$). $e(n)$ is not known in closed form for all $n$, in contrast to the immersion bound $2n-\alpha(n)$ from the immersion conjecture proved by Cohen. ([Wikipedia: Whitney embedding theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_embedding_theorem); [Wikipedia: Immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_%28mathematics%29))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Submanifold (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold): immersed versus embedded submanifolds and slice charts.
- **Reference:** [Nash embedding theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_embedding_theorem): $C^1$ and $C^k$ isometric embeddings and rigidity contrasts.
- **Learn:** [Galloway, differential geometry notes, Ch. 4 (Miami)](https://www.math.miami.edu/~galloway/dgnotes/chpt4.pdf): first fundamental form and induced metric with worked examples.
- **Primary:** [B.-Y. Chen, Riemannian Submanifolds: A Survey (arXiv:1307.1875)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.1875): fundamental equations and theorems, Nash's theorem, rigidity.
- **Further reading:** [J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed. (Springer GTM, 2012)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-9982-5): standard graduate text on submanifolds, transversality and Whitney's theorem.
references.Supersymmetry:
## Reference
### Overview
Supersymmetry (SUSY) is a proposed symmetry between particles of integer spin (bosons) and half-integer spin (fermions): each particle has a superpartner whose spin differs by a half-integer, and in unbroken supersymmetry partners share their mass and all internal quantum numbers other than spin. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry))

Mathematically, supersymmetry is invariance under the action of a supergroup or super Lie algebra; in the stricter physics sense it means a super-extension of the isometry algebra of spacetime, for Minkowski space the super-Poincaré algebra. Odd elements are the supersymmetry generators, irreducible unitary representations organize particles into supermultiplets, and gauging supersymmetry gives supergravity. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/supersymmetry)) The Haag–Łopuszański–Sohnius theorem relaxes the Coleman–Mandula theorem by allowing anticommuting generators, and shows that supersymmetry is then the only way to nontrivially mix spacetime and internal symmetries. ([Wikipedia: HLS theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%E2%80%93%C5%81opusza%C5%84ski%E2%80%93Sohnius_theorem))

Phenomenologically, weak-scale supersymmetry was motivated by the hierarchy problem (superpartner loops cancel quadratic corrections to the Higgs mass), by gauge coupling unification near $10^{16}$ GeV, and by a heavy stable dark matter candidate such as the neutralino, whose existence is closely related to R-parity. The LHC has found no evidence for superpartners. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry)) Supersymmetric field theories are also a laboratory for exact results, through nonrenormalization theorems and indices. ([Wikipedia: Nonrenormalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry_nonrenormalization_theorems))

### Formal definition
A **super Lie algebra** is a $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space $\mathfrak s=\mathfrak s_0\oplus\mathfrak s_1$ with a bilinear bracket that is graded skew-symmetric and satisfies the graded Jacobi identity. A **super-extension** of an ordinary Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is equivalent to a $\mathfrak g$-representation $S$ with a $\mathfrak g$-equivariant symmetric bilinear map $S\otimes S\to\mathfrak g$ satisfying $\rho_{(\phi,\phi)}(\phi)=0$ for all $\phi\in S$. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/supersymmetry))

The four-dimensional $\mathcal N$-extended **super-Poincaré algebra** adds $\mathcal N$ pairs of Weyl-spinor supercharges $Q^L_\alpha$, $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha R}$ to the Poincaré algebra, commuting with $P_\mu$, with
$$\{Q_\alpha^L,\bar Q_{\dot\beta R}\}=\delta^L_R(\sigma^\mu)_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu,\qquad \{Q^L_\alpha,Q^M_\beta\}=\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{LM},$$
where the central charges $Z^{LM}$ commute with all generators. For $\mathcal N=1$ the central charges vanish and the R-symmetry is $U(1)$; for $\mathcal N>1$ the R-symmetry is $U(\mathcal N)$. ([Wikipedia: HLS theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%E2%80%93%C5%81opusza%C5%84ski%E2%80%93Sohnius_theorem), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry))

The **Witten index** is $\operatorname{Tr}\big[(-1)^Fe^{-\beta H}\big]$, with $F$ the fermion number. ([Wikipedia: Witten index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witten_index))

### Key results
- **Coleman–Mandula.** Under S-matrix assumptions, the symmetry Lie algebra of the S-matrix is a direct sum of the Poincaré algebra and a compact internal algebra. ([Wikipedia: HLS theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%E2%80%93%C5%81opusza%C5%84ski%E2%80%93Sohnius_theorem), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry))
- **Haag–Łopuszański–Sohnius (1975).** With the same hypotheses (analytic scattering amplitudes, every two-particle state scattering at almost all energies and angles, finitely many particle types below any mass) but allowing anticommuting generators, the only possible extension is the super-Poincaré algebra above: odd generators must be spin-$\tfrac12$, and spin-$\tfrac32$ or higher generators are excluded. With massless particles the algebra enlarges to the superconformal algebra, $\mathfrak{su}(2,2|\mathcal N)$ in four dimensions. The theorem holds in dimensions above two and does not apply to spontaneously broken or discrete symmetries, which are not symmetries of the S-matrix. ([Wikipedia: HLS theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%E2%80%93%C5%81opusza%C5%84ski%E2%80%93Sohnius_theorem))
- **Bounds on extended supersymmetry.** The minimal number of supersymmetry generators in four dimensions is four; more than 32 would force massless fields of spin above 2, theories with 32 supercharges automatically contain a graviton, and supersymmetry can exist in up to eleven dimensions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry))
- **Witten index and breaking.** States of nonzero energy pair bosons with fermions, so the Witten index is independent of $\beta$ and equals the number of bosonic minus fermionic zero-energy vacua. Spontaneous supersymmetry breaking leaves no zero-energy ground state, so the index then vanishes; a nonzero index therefore rules out spontaneous breaking. ([Wikipedia: Witten index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witten_index))
- **Nonrenormalization.** In 4D $\mathcal N=1$ theories the superpotential is not renormalized in perturbation theory (instantons can renormalize it); in $\mathcal N=2$ there are no perturbative beta-function corrections beyond one loop and the Higgs-branch hyper-Kähler metric is not renormalized; $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills has vanishing beta function for all couplings and is conformal. ([Wikipedia: Nonrenormalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry_nonrenormalization_theorems))

### Examples
- **Superpartners and the MSSM.** Martin's primer develops supersymmetric Lagrangians, superspace and superfields, soft supersymmetry-breaking terms, the MSSM and R-parity, the MSSM mass spectrum and sparticle decays. ([Martin](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9709356))
- **Neutralino dark matter.** In many supersymmetric extensions such as the MSSM a heavy stable particle such as the neutralino is a WIMP dark matter candidate; its existence is closely related to R-parity. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry))
- **Worldline and worldsheet supersymmetry.** The Dirac spinning particle has worldline supersymmetry and the spinning string has worldsheet supersymmetry. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/supersymmetry))
- **Supergravity.** Local supersymmetry gives supergravity, with Killing spinors playing the role Killing vectors play in gravity. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/supersymmetry))

### History
Miyazawa proposed a baryon–meson supersymmetry in 1966, but it was internal rather than spacetime and largely ignored. Gervais–Sakita and Golfand–Likhtman (1971) and Volkov–Akulov (1972) rediscovered supersymmetry in field theory, while Ramond, Neveu and Schwarz (1971) introduced a graded structure in early string theory. Wess and Zumino (1974) identified the renormalization properties of 4D supersymmetric field theories, and Fayet (1977) proposed the first realistic supersymmetric Standard Model. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry)) The HLS classification dates from 1975 ([Wikipedia: HLS theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%E2%80%93%C5%81opusza%C5%84ski%E2%80%93Sohnius_theorem)), the first nonrenormalization theorem is credited to Grisaru, Roček and Siegel (1979), and Witten's index appeared in "Constraints on Supersymmetry Breaking" (1982). ([Wikipedia: Nonrenormalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry_nonrenormalization_theorems), [Wikipedia: Witten index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witten_index))

### Connections
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory): supersymmetric QFTs, their Lagrangians and nonrenormalization theorems.
- [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras) and [Poincaré Group](node:Poincaré%20Group): supersymmetry algebras are super-extensions of the Poincaré algebra.
- [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras): the supercharges are spinors, and $\{Q,\bar Q\}\propto\sigma^\mu P_\mu$ is a spinor bilinear.
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem) and [Naturalness](node:Naturalness): the original motivation for weak-scale SUSY.
- [Grand Unification](node:Grand%20Unification): improved gauge coupling unification with superpartners.
- [Weakly Interacting Massive Particles](node:Weakly%20Interacting%20Massive%20Particles): the neutralino as a dark matter candidate.
- [Standard Model of Particle Physics](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics) and [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): extended by the MSSM.
- [Supergravity](node:Supergravity) and [String Theory](node:String%20Theory): local supersymmetry and its role in superstrings.
- [Conformal Field Theory](node:Conformal%20Field%20Theory) and [AdS-CFT Correspondence](node:AdS-CFT%20Correspondence): superconformal theories such as $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills.
- [Atiyah-Singer Index Theorem](node:Atiyah-Singer%20Index%20Theorem): the Witten index is an index-theoretic invariant.

### Common pitfalls
- **Superpartners are not known particles.** Unbroken SUSY would give partners equal masses; since none are observed, SUSY must be broken, spontaneously by a separate sector, with its effects parametrized by soft breaking terms. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry))
- **"Excluded" usually means a simplified model.** Run 2 limits such as gluinos up to about 2.2 TeV assume specific decays and a massless lightest neutralino; sensitivity drops for compressed spectra (none for gluinos above about 1.3 TeV when the gluino–LSP gap is small), and complex spectra with many decay modes may evade simplified-model limits. ([Adam–Vivarelli](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.10180))
- **HLS does not forbid all extra symmetry.** It applies to S-matrix symmetries, not to discrete or spontaneously broken ones, and its analyticity assumptions fail in two or fewer dimensions. ([Wikipedia: HLS theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%E2%80%93%C5%81opusza%C5%84ski%E2%80%93Sohnius_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Is there weak-scale supersymmetry?** The LHC has found no evidence for supersymmetry ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry)). Adam and Vivarelli report that SUSY models considered mainstream before the LHC have been completely excluded, while compressed electroweakino spectra, stau final states, long-lived particles and R-parity violation pose experimental challenges for the searches. ([Adam–Vivarelli](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.10180))
- **The Little Hierarchy problem.** Baer et al. argue that Run 2 limits may exacerbate a so-called Little Hierarchy problem, and that from a stringy-naturalness viewpoint the HL-LHC has only begun to probe the relevant parameter space. ([Baer et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10879))
- **Naturalness after the LHC.** Many physicists hold that the MSSM, though not ruled out, can no longer fully resolve the hierarchy problem, and Shifman urged the community to look for new ideas. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersymmetry))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: supersymmetry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/supersymmetry): super Lie algebras, super-extensions and supermultiplets.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Haag–Łopuszański–Sohnius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haag%E2%80%93%C5%81opusza%C5%84ski%E2%80%93Sohnius_theorem): hypotheses and the allowed superalgebras.
- **Learn:** [Krippendorf, Quevedo and Schlotterer, Cambridge Lectures on Supersymmetry and Extra Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.1491): Part III course notes on 4D supersymmetry.
- **Primary:** [Martin, A Supersymmetry Primer](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9709356): the standard introduction to the MSSM and SUSY breaking.
- **Primary:** [Adam and Vivarelli, Status of searches for electroweak-scale supersymmetry after LHC Run 2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2111.10180): experimental review.
- **Further reading:** [Wess and Bagger, Supersymmetry and Supergravity (Princeton University Press)](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691025308/supersymmetry-and-supergravity): a widely acclaimed introduction to $\mathcal N=1$ supersymmetry and supergravity.
references.Supervised Learning:
## Reference
### Overview
Supervised learning is the machine-learning paradigm in which an algorithm learns a map from inputs to outputs using labeled example pairs, with the goal of predicting outputs for new, unseen inputs. Common tasks are classification, regression, and conditional density estimation. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning)) Given a training set $\{(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^n$, the learner outputs a function $h:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$, called a hypothesis, that should be a good predictor of $y$; the problem is regression when $y$ is continuous and classification when $y$ takes finitely many values. ([CS229 notes](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf))

The standard workflow is to gather a representative labeled set, choose features, select a model class and algorithm, tune hyperparameters on a validation set or by cross-validation, and report performance on a held-out test set. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning)) The mathematical theory, statistical learning theory, assumes training and test examples are i.i.d. draws from one unknown distribution and studies how far the true risk of the learned function can be from the best achievable. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

Supervised learning is where the bias–variance trade-off, empirical risk minimization, and capacity bounds were developed, and where modern overparametrized models most visibly break the classical picture: rich models such as neural networks are trained to fit (interpolate) their training data exactly, can fit even random labels, and still often achieve high test accuracy, including when the training data are noisy. ([Belkin et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118); [Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530); [Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

### Formal definition
Let $\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $\mathcal Y$ an output space, $\mathcal L(f,(x,y))$ a loss (e.g. squared loss $(f(x)-y)^2$ for regression, 0-1 loss $\mathbf 1_{(-\infty,0)}(yf(x))$ for $\mathcal Y=\{\pm1\}$), and $\mathcal F$ a hypothesis set. Training data $S=(Z^{(i)})_{i=1}^m$ with $Z^{(i)}=(X^{(i)},Y^{(i)})$ are i.i.d. copies of $Z=(X,Y)\sim P_Z$. ([Berner et al. 2021, Def. 1.2, Assump. 1.10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

- **Risk:** $\mathcal R(f)=\mathbb E[\mathcal L(f,Z)]$; for classification with 0-1 loss, $\mathcal R(f)=\mathbb P[f(X)\neq Y]$. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Empirical risk:** $\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(f)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathcal L(f,Z^{(i)})$. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Empirical risk minimization (ERM):** choose $\hat f_S\in\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal F}\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(f)$. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Bayes risk:** $\mathcal R^*=\inf_f\mathcal R(f)$ over all measurable $f$; a minimizer is Bayes-optimal. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

Structural risk minimization adds a complexity penalty $\lambda\,\Omega(f)$ to the empirical risk, with $\lambda$ typically chosen by cross-validation. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning))

### Key results
- **Bayes-optimal predictors.** For regression with $\mathrm{Var}[Y]<\infty$, $\mathcal R(f)=\mathbb E[(f(X)-\mathbb E[Y\mid X])^2]+\mathcal R^*$, so the regression function $f^*(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]$ is optimal; for binary classification the Bayes classifier $f^*(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x])$ is optimal. ([Berner et al. 2021, Lemma 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **No free lunch.** For any decreasing sequence $a_m>0$ with $a_1\le1/16$ and any learning algorithm $\mathcal A$ for classification, there is a distribution $P_Z$ with $\mathbb E[\mathcal R(\mathcal A(S))]\ge\mathcal R^*+a_m$ for all $m$; useful guarantees therefore need prior assumptions on $P_Z$. ([Berner et al. 2021, Thm 1.13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Error decomposition.** With $f^*_{\mathcal F}\in\arg\min_{\mathcal F}\mathcal R$ and learned $f_S$, $\mathcal R(f_S)-\mathcal R^*\le\varepsilon_{\rm opt}+2\varepsilon_{\rm gen}+\varepsilon_{\rm approx}$, where $\varepsilon_{\rm opt}=\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(f_S)-\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(\hat f_S)$ is the optimization error, $\varepsilon_{\rm gen}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|\mathcal R(f)-\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(f)|$ and $\varepsilon_{\rm approx}=\mathcal R(f^*_{\mathcal F})-\mathcal R^*$. ([Berner et al. 2021, §1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Finite hypothesis classes.** If $|\mathcal H|=k$, then with probability at least $1-\delta$ the ERM hypothesis satisfies $\varepsilon(\hat h)\le\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\varepsilon(h)+2\sqrt{\tfrac1{2n}\log\tfrac{2k}{\delta}}$, so $n\ge\frac1{2\gamma^2}\log\frac{2k}{\delta}$ samples suffice for excess error $2\gamma$. ([CS229 notes §8.3](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf))
- **VC bound.** If $D=\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal H)<\infty$, then with probability at least $1-\delta$, $|\varepsilon(h)-\hat\varepsilon(h)|\le O\big(\sqrt{\tfrac Dn\log\tfrac nD+\tfrac1n\log\tfrac1\delta}\big)$ for all $h\in\mathcal H$; hence sample complexity is linear in [VC Dimension](node:VC%20Dimension). ([CS229 notes §8.3.3](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf)) A bound without the logarithmic factor, $\sup_f|\mathcal R(f)-\widehat{\mathcal R}_S(f)|\le c\sqrt{(\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal F)+\log(1/\delta))/m}$, also holds. ([Berner et al. 2021, Thm 1.19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Bias–variance decomposition (regression).** If $y=h^\star(x)+\xi$ with $\xi\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ and $h_{\rm avg}(x)=\mathbb E_S[h_S(x)]$, then $\mathbb E[(y-h_S(x))^2]=\sigma^2+(h^\star(x)-h_{\rm avg}(x))^2+\mathrm{Var}(h_S(x))$: irreducible noise, squared bias, and variance. ([CS229 notes §8.1.1](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf))

### Examples
- **Housing prices.** Predicting price from living area is a regression problem; [Linear Regression](node:Linear%20Regression) fits $h_\theta(x)=\theta^\top x$ by least squares. ([CS229 notes](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf))
- **Standard algorithms.** Support-vector machines, linear and [logistic regression](node:Logistic%20Regression), naive Bayes, linear discriminant analysis, decision trees, $k$-nearest neighbours, and neural networks. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning))
- **Generative versus discriminative.** Generative training fits a joint model of $(x,y)$ (naive Bayes, LDA, with closed-form solutions); discriminative training fits a function that separates classes directly. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning))
- **Interpolating networks.** CNNs with about 1.6 million parameters reach zero training error on the 50,000 CIFAR-10 images, and also on random labels, so parameter-count bounds are vacuous for them. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026); [Zhang et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03530))

### History
The model-wise double-descent phenomenon perhaps dates back to Opper (1995, 2001) and was popularized by Belkin et al. (2020) and Hastie et al. (2019); Nakkiran (2019) observed sample-wise double descent. ([CS229 notes §8.2](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf)) Belkin, Hsu, Ma, and Mandal proposed the double-descent curve as an extension of the classical U-shaped bias–variance curve. ([Belkin et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118))

### Connections
- [Probability Spaces](node:Probability%20Spaces): data are modeled as i.i.d. draws from an unknown distribution.
- [Empirical Risk Minimization](node:Empirical%20Risk%20Minimization): the default learning rule.
- [Statistical Learning Theory](node:Statistical%20Learning%20Theory), [PAC Learning](node:PAC%20Learning), [VC Dimension](node:VC%20Dimension), [Rademacher Complexity](node:Rademacher%20Complexity): tools for bounding generalization error.
- [Bias–Variance Tradeoff](node:Bias–Variance%20Tradeoff): the classical model-selection principle.
- [Cross-Validation](node:Cross-Validation) and [Regularization](node:Regularization): practical control of complexity.
- [Conditional Expectation](node:Conditional%20Expectation): the Bayes-optimal regression function is $\mathbb E[Y\mid X]$.
- [Linear Regression](node:Linear%20Regression), [Logistic Regression](node:Logistic%20Regression), [Support Vector Machines](node:Support%20Vector%20Machines), [Decision Trees and Ensembles](node:Decision%20Trees%20and%20Ensembles), [Nearest-Neighbor Learning](node:Nearest-Neighbor%20Learning), [Artificial Neural Networks](node:Artificial%20Neural%20Networks): standard hypothesis classes.
- [Generalization in Deep Learning](node:Generalization%20in%20Deep%20Learning): the modern overparametrized regime.
- [Semi-Supervised Learning](node:Semi-Supervised%20Learning) and [Active Learning](node:Active%20Learning): variants with fewer labels.

### Common pitfalls
- **Tuning on the test set.** Parameters of the learner are adjusted on a validation subset of the training data or by cross-validation, and final performance is measured on a test set separate from the training set. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning))
- **Noisy labels and overfitting.** With noisy outputs the learner should not try to match the training examples exactly, since fitting the data too carefully leads to overfitting; [early stopping](node:Early%20Stopping) and detecting and removing noisy examples before training are remedies. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning))
- **Assuming the U-curve always holds.** Test error can rise near the interpolation threshold and then fall again in the overparametrized regime; the peak can be mitigated by tuned regularization. ([CS229 notes §8.2](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf))
- **The i.i.d. assumption.** The bounds above are proved under the assumption that training and test examples are i.i.d. draws from the same distribution $P_Z$, so they do not by themselves cover test data from a different distribution (see [Out-of-Distribution Generalization](node:Out-of-Distribution%20Generalization)). ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))

### Open problems
- **Why overparametrized models generalize.** CS229, discussing the second descent, states that "the theoretical understanding of overparameterized models is an active research area"; a typical explanation is implicit regularization by the optimizer (for linear models with $n\ll d$, [gradient descent](node:Gradient%20Descent) from zero initialization finds the minimum-norm solution that fits the data). ([CS229 notes §8.2](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf)) Berner et al. list it among the open questions of deep-learning theory. ([Berner et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04026))
- **Bias–variance for classification.** For classification there have been several proposals but "as yet no agreement" on the right bias–variance formalism. ([CS229 notes §8.1.1](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Supervised learning, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning): workflow, issues, ERM and SRM, algorithms.
- **Learn:** [Stanford CS229 lecture notes (Ma and Ng)](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf): supervised learning, bias–variance, double descent, sample-complexity bounds.
- **Primary:** [Berner, Grohs, Kutyniok, Petersen, The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04026): survey with the formal learning setup, no-free-lunch, error decomposition, and open questions.
- **Primary:** [Belkin, Hsu, Ma, Mandal, Reconciling modern machine learning practice and the bias-variance trade-off](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118): the double-descent curve.
- **Further reading:** [Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms (CUP 2014)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/understanding-machine-learning/3059695661405D25673058E43C8BE2A6): graduate text on learning theory and algorithms.
references.Symplectic Geometry:
## Reference
### Overview
Symplectic geometry studies symplectic manifolds: smooth manifolds equipped with a closed, nondegenerate 2-form. It grew out of the Hamiltonian formulation of classical mechanics, whose phase spaces carry this structure, and the symplectic form plays a role analogous to a Riemannian metric except that it measures oriented areas rather than lengths and angles. Hermann Weyl introduced the word "symplectic" in 1939 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_geometry)).

Unlike Riemannian geometry, symplectic geometry has no local invariants: by Darboux's theorem every symplectic manifold is locally isomorphic to the standard $(\mathbb R^{2n},\sum dx_i\wedge dy_i)$, so all invariants are global ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_geometry); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold)). The subject took its modern shape with Arnold's conjectures in the 1960s and Weinstein's foundational work in the 1970s; Gromov's 1985 paper introduced pseudoholomorphic curves, which led to Gromov–Witten invariants and, through Floer, to Floer homology ([Cannas da Silva, Lectures](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_geometry); [Crossref: Gromov 1985](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01388806)).
