The subject combines local normal forms (Darboux, Moser, Weinstein), moment maps, symplectic reduction and the classification of toric manifolds ([Cannas da Silva](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf)) with rigidity phenomena invisible to volume: Gromov's nonsqueezing theorem, the most fundamental manifestation of symplectic rigidity, shows that some volume-preserving maps cannot be approximated by symplectic ones and gave rise to symplectic capacities ([Wikipedia: Non-squeezing theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-squeezing_theorem); [Schlenk 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.03317)).

### Formal definition
A **symplectic manifold** is a smooth manifold $M$ of dimension $2n$ with a 2-form $\omega$ that is closed, $d\omega=0$, and nondegenerate, i.e. $\omega^{\wedge n}$ is nowhere zero ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold)). A **symplectomorphism** is a diffeomorphism $\varphi:(M_1,\omega_1)\to(M_2,\omega_2)$ with $\varphi^*\omega_2=\omega_1$ ([Cannas da Silva](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf)).

For $H\in C^\infty(M)$ the **Hamiltonian vector field** $v_H$ is the unique vector field with
$$dH=\omega(v_H,-),$$
and the **Poisson bracket** $\{F,H\}=\iota_{v_F}\iota_{v_H}\omega$ makes $C^\infty(M)$ a Poisson algebra. A vector field preserves $\omega$ exactly when it is locally Hamiltonian ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold)). A subspace $W$ of a symplectic vector space is **Lagrangian** if $W=W^{\perp_\omega}$; a submanifold $Y\subset M^{2n}$ is Lagrangian if $i^*\omega=0$ and $\dim Y=n$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold); [Cannas da Silva](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf)).

### Key results
- **Darboux theorem.** If $(M,\omega)$ is $2n$-dimensional and $p\in M$, there is a chart $(U,x_1,\dots,x_n,y_1,\dots,y_n)$ centred at $p$ with $\omega|_U=\sum_{i=1}^n dx_i\wedge dy_i$. ([Cannas da Silva, Thm 8.1](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf))
- **Moser stability.** Let $M$ be compact and $\omega_t$, $0\le t\le1$, a smooth family of symplectic forms with $[\omega_t]\in H^2(M)$ independent of $t$. Then there is an isotopy $\rho_t$ with $\rho_t^*\omega_t=\omega_0$. ([Cannas da Silva, Thm 7.3](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf))
- **Weinstein tubular neighbourhood theorem.** If $X\subset(M,\omega)$ is a compact Lagrangian submanifold, a neighbourhood of $X$ in $M$ is symplectomorphic to a neighbourhood of the zero section in $T^*X$ with its canonical form, by a map restricting to the identity on $X$. ([Cannas da Silva, Thm 9.3](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf))
- **Marsden–Weinstein–Meyer reduction.** If a compact Lie group $G$ acts on $(M,\omega)$ in a Hamiltonian way with moment map $\mu$ and acts freely on $\mu^{-1}(0)$, then $M_{\rm red}=\mu^{-1}(0)/G$ is a manifold, $\pi:\mu^{-1}(0)\to M_{\rm red}$ is a principal $G$-bundle, and there is a symplectic form $\omega_{\rm red}$ with $i^*\omega=\pi^*\omega_{\rm red}$. ([Cannas da Silva, Thm 23.1](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf))
- **Convexity theorem (Atiyah; Guillemin–Sternberg).** For a Hamiltonian action of a torus $T^m$ on a compact connected symplectic manifold with moment map $\mu$, the levels of $\mu$ are connected and $\mu(M)$ is the convex hull of the images of the fixed points. Delzant's theorem then classifies compact symplectic toric manifolds bijectively by their moment polytopes (Delzant polytopes). ([Cannas da Silva, Thms 27.1, 28.2](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf))
- **Arnold–Liouville theorem.** For an integrable system with integrals $f_1=H,\dots,f_n$ and a regular value $c$ of $f=(f_1,\dots,f_n)$, the level $f^{-1}(c)$ is Lagrangian, and if the flows are complete each component is an $\mathbb R^n$-homogeneous space with angle coordinates in which the flows are linear. ([Cannas da Silva, Thm 18.12](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf))
- **Gromov nonsqueezing (1985).** If the ball $B^{2n}(r)$ embeds symplectically into the cylinder $Z^{2n}(R)=B^2(R)\times\mathbb R^{2n-2}$, then $r\le R$; Lalonde and McDuff extended this to $B^2(R)\times M$ for any symplectic $(2n-2)$-manifold $M$. Equivalently, there is a symplectic capacity $c$ with $c(B^{2n}(1))=c(Z^{2n}(1))=\pi$. ([Wikipedia: Non-squeezing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-squeezing_theorem); [Schlenk 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.03317))
- **Arnold conjecture, homological version.** For a nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of a closed symplectic manifold, the number of fixed points is at least the sum of the Betti numbers over a field $\mathbb F$; this is proved over $\mathbb Q$ (Fukaya–Ono 1999), over $\mathbb F_p$ (Abouzaid–Blumberg, via Floer homology with Morava K-theory coefficients), and with integer coefficients (Rezchikov; Bai–Xu, 2022). ([Wikipedia: Arnold conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_conjecture); [arXiv: Abouzaid and Blumberg](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01507))
- **Ellipsoid embeddings (McDuff–Schlenk; McDuff–Hutchings).** The function $c(a)=\inf\{A: E(1,a)\hookrightarrow B^4(A)\}$ is given by the Fibonacci staircase on $[1,\tau^4]$, $\tau=(1+\sqrt5)/2$, and equals $\sqrt a$ for $a\ge(17/6)^2$; more generally $E(a,b)$ embeds in $E(c,d)$ iff the ECH capacities satisfy $N_k(a,b)\le N_k(c,d)$ for all $k$. ([Schlenk 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.03317))

### Examples
- **Standard space.** $(\mathbb R^{2n},\omega_0=\sum dx_i\wedge dy_i)$ is the local model of every symplectic manifold. ([Cannas da Silva](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf))
- **Cotangent bundles.** $T^*X$ carries a canonical symplectic form, the model near any compact Lagrangian by Weinstein's theorem. ([Cannas da Silva](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf))
- **Kähler manifolds.** Every Kähler manifold is symplectic, but most symplectic manifolds are not Kähler; Thurston gave the first compact non-Kähler example, and Gompf showed every finitely presented group is the fundamental group of a symplectic 4-manifold. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_geometry))
- **Spheres.** Among spheres only $S^2$ admits a symplectic form; more generally a closed symplectic manifold is even-dimensional, orientable, and has nontrivial second cohomology. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_geometry))
- **Reduced phase spaces.** In field theory, nLab presents the critical locus of a local action functional, after dividing out symmetries, as a symplectic manifold, the reduced phase space; this is a heuristic statement, not a theorem with stated hypotheses. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold))

### History
Weyl named the symplectic group in 1939, replacing the term "line complex group" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_geometry)). Arnold's 1966 fixed-point conjecture generalized the Poincaré–Birkhoff theorem ([Cannas da Silva](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf)); Weinstein posed his periodic-orbit conjecture in 1978, Viterbo proved it for contact hypersurfaces of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ (paper dated 1987), and Taubes proved it for all closed 3-manifolds in 2007 ([Wikipedia: Weinstein conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weinstein_conjecture)). Gromov's "Pseudo holomorphic curves in symplectic manifolds" (Inventiones 82, 1985) proved nonsqueezing ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01388806); [Wikipedia: Non-squeezing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-squeezing_theorem)). McDuff constructed simply connected non-Kähler symplectic manifolds (1984) and cohomologous but non-isotopic symplectic forms (1987), and in 1990 showed that a closed symplectic 4-manifold containing a symplectic sphere of non-negative self-intersection is $\mathbb{CP}^2$, ruled, or a blow-up of one of these ([Schlenk 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.03317)). In 2024 Haim-Kislev and Ostrover found a counterexample to Viterbo's volume–capacity conjecture, showing that symplectic capacities do not coincide on convex domains in $\mathbb R^{2n}$ ([arXiv: Haim-Kislev and Ostrover](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16513)).

### Connections
- [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms): the symplectic form is a closed nondegenerate 2-form.
- [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology): the class $[\omega]$ governs Moser stability.
- [Hamiltonian Mechanics](node:Hamiltonian%20Mechanics): phase spaces are symplectic and Hamiltonian flows are symplectomorphisms.
- [Poisson Brackets in Mechanics](node:Poisson%20Brackets%20in%20Mechanics): the bracket induced by $\omega$.
- [Hamiltonian Dynamical Systems](node:Hamiltonian%20Dynamical%20Systems): fixed-point and periodic-orbit questions (Arnold, Weinstein).
- [Symplectic Reduction](node:Symplectic%20Reduction): Marsden–Weinstein–Meyer quotients.
- [Moment Maps](node:Moment%20Maps): Hamiltonian group actions, convexity, toric geometry.
- [Toric Varieties](node:Toric%20Varieties): symplectic toric manifolds correspond to Delzant polytopes.
- [Kähler and Calabi–Yau Manifolds](node:Kähler%20and%20Calabi–Yau%20Manifolds): Kähler manifolds are the integrable symplectic examples.
- [Special Lagrangian Submanifolds](node:Special%20Lagrangian%20Submanifolds): Lagrangians in Calabi–Yau manifolds.
- [Geometric Quantization](node:Geometric%20Quantization): passes from symplectic manifolds to Hilbert spaces.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): symmetry groups acting by symplectomorphisms.
- [Integrable Physical Systems](node:Integrable%20Physical%20Systems): Arnold–Liouville action-angle coordinates.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): the contrasting geometry with local curvature invariants.

### Common pitfalls
- Symplectomorphisms preserve volume, but volume preservation is far weaker: a ball can be squeezed into a thin cylinder by volume-preserving maps but not symplectically. ([Wikipedia: Non-squeezing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-squeezing_theorem))
- Moser's theorem needs a path of symplectic forms in a fixed cohomology class; cohomologous symplectic forms need not be isotopic (McDuff 1987), and in dimension 8 can even fail to be diffeomorphic. ([Cannas da Silva](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf); [Schlenk 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.03317))
- Nondegenerate but non-closed 2-forms give only almost symplectic structures ($Sp(2n)$-structures); closedness is the integrability condition. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold))
- The proved Arnold bounds are the homological version for nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms; the strong version bounds fixed points by the minimal number of critical points of a smooth function. ([Wikipedia: Arnold conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Packing stability in dimension 6.** Schlenk asks "Is it true that $p(B^6)=8$?", where the packing-stability number $p(M)$ is the index from which every packing number $p_k$ of $M$ by $k$ equal balls equals 1; the known bounds are $8\le p(B^6)\le 21$. In dimension 4, $p(B^4)=9$. ([Schlenk 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.03317))
- **Ellipsoids into polydiscs.** Embeddings of $E(1,a)$ into $B^2(A)\times B^2(bA)$ are intricate enough that "we shall probably never know the answer for all $b$." ([Schlenk 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.03317))
- **McDuff–Salamon problem list.** The third edition of *Introduction to Symplectic Topology* adds a chapter of open problems (54 according to Schlenk). ([Crossref: McDuff–Salamon](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198794899.001.0001); [Schlenk 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.03317))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Symplectic manifold (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold): definitions, Hamiltonian vector fields, Poisson brackets, Darboux, $G$-structure viewpoint.
- **Learn:** [Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry (ETH)](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~acannas/Papers/lsg.pdf): standard lecture notes from Darboux–Moser–Weinstein to reduction, convexity and Delzant.
- **Primary:** [Schlenk, Dusa McDuff and symplectic geometry (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.03317): survey of symplectic embedding problems, packing, capacities and 4-manifolds, with open questions.
- **Primary:** [Abouzaid and Blumberg, Arnold Conjecture and Morava K-theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01507): Arnold bound in characteristic $p$.
- **Primary:** [Gromov, Pseudo holomorphic curves in symplectic manifolds (1985)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01388806): founding paper of hard symplectic topology (bibliographic record).
- **Further reading:** [McDuff and Salamon, Introduction to Symplectic Topology, 3rd ed. (OUP 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/oso/9780198794899.001.0001): graduate monograph whose third edition adds a chapter of open problems (bibliographic record).
references.Tangent Spaces and Vector Fields:
## Reference
### Overview
The tangent space $T_pM$ of a manifold at a point generalizes the tangent line of a curve and the tangent plane of a surface; physically it is the space of possible velocities of a particle passing through $p$. The tangent spaces glue into the [Tangent Bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle) $TM$, a manifold of twice the dimension. ([Wikipedia: Tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space))

A vector field is a smooth section of $TM$, equivalently a derivation of the algebra $C^\infty(M)$. Its integral curves assemble into a flow, defined on a flow domain in general and, for a complete field, a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms. Algebraically, the sections of $TM$ form a finitely generated projective $C^\infty(M)$-module, and by the smooth Serre–Swan theorem vector bundles and such modules correspond. ([nLab: derivations are vector fields](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derivations+of+smooth+functions+are+vector+fields); [nLab: flow](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/flow+of+a+vector+field); [nLab: Serre–Swan theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Serre-Swan+theorem))

The Lie bracket $[X,Y]$ is the derivative of $Y$ along the flow of $X$. It makes vector fields an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra and measures whether flows commute. Brackets govern integrability of distributions (Frobenius), and the topology of $M$ constrains which vector fields exist (Poincaré–Hopf, hairy ball, Adams). ([Wikipedia: Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields); [Wikipedia: Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_theorem_%28differential_topology%29); [Wikipedia: Vector fields on spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_fields_on_spheres))

### Formal definition
**Curves.** On a $C^k$ manifold ($k\ge1$), curves $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ through $p$ are equivalent if $(\varphi\circ\gamma_1)'(0)=(\varphi\circ\gamma_2)'(0)$ in a chart $\varphi$; $T_pM$ is the set of classes. ([Wikipedia: Tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space))

**Derivations.** On a smooth manifold, a tangent vector at $p$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear $V:C^\infty(M)\to\mathbb{R}$ with $V(fg)=f(p)V(g)+g(p)V(f)$. The curve $\gamma$ gives $f\mapsto(f\circ\gamma)'(0)$, an isomorphism between the two definitions. ([MIT 18.965, Def. 1.8](https://www.mit.edu/~anser/files/18_965.pdf); [Wikipedia: Tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space))

**Cotangent ideal.** If $I\subset C^\infty(M)$ is the ideal of functions vanishing at $p$, then $T_pM\cong(I/I^2)^*$. ([Wikipedia: Tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space))

**Vector fields.** A vector field assigns $X(p)\in T_pM$ with smooth coefficients in every chart; equivalently it is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear $X:C^\infty(M)\to C^\infty(M)$ with $X(fg)=fX(g)+gX(f)$. ([MIT 18.965, Def. 1.21](https://www.mit.edu/~anser/files/18_965.pdf))

**Bracket, Lie derivative, interior product.** $[X,Y](f)=X(Yf)-Y(Xf)$; in coordinates
$$[X,Y]=\sum_{i,j}\bigl(X^j\partial_jY^i-Y^j\partial_jX^i\bigr)\partial_i .$$
For a tensor field $T$, $\mathcal L_XT=\tfrac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*T$ with $\Phi_t$ the flow of $X$; then $\mathcal L_Xf=X(f)$ and $\mathcal L_XY=[X,Y]$. The interior product $i_X$ contracts a $p$-form with $X$; it is the unique antiderivation of degree $-1$ extending this, and $i_X\circ i_X=0$. ([Wikipedia: Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields); [Wikipedia: Lie derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_derivative); [Wikipedia: Interior product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_product))

**Related fields.** For smooth $F:M\to N$, a field $W$ on $N$ is $F$-related to $V$ on $M$ if $W\circ F=dF\circ V$. A manifold is parallelizable if there are vector fields $V_1,\dots,V_n$ forming a basis of every tangent space, i.e. $TM$ is trivial. ([Wikipedia: Vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_field); [Wikipedia: Parallelizable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallelizable_manifold))

### Key results
- **Basis theorem.** In a chart, every $V\in T_pM$ equals $\sum_iV(x^i)\,\partial_i|_p$, so $\dim T_pM=n$; the proof writes $u(x)=u(p)+\sum_i(x^i-p^i)w_i(x)$ with $w_i$ smooth (Hadamard lemma). The same lemma shows every derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ comes from a unique smooth vector field: $\Gamma(TM)\cong\operatorname{Der}(C^\infty(M))$. ([MIT 18.965, Lemmas 1.11–1.12](https://www.mit.edu/~anser/files/18_965.pdf); [nLab: derivations are vector fields](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derivations+of+smooth+functions+are+vector+fields))
- **Smooth Serre–Swan theorem.** For a smooth manifold $M$, $E\mapsto\Gamma(E)$ is an equivalence between finite-rank smooth vector bundles over $M$ and finitely generated projective $C^\infty(M)$-modules. It is stated for every smooth manifold, whereas Swan's topological version is for compact Hausdorff spaces and modules over the continuous functions $C(X)$. ([nLab: Serre–Swan theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Serre-Swan+theorem))
- **Differential and inverse function theorem.** A smooth $\varphi$ induces linear $d\varphi_p:T_pM\to T_{\varphi(p)}N$, the Jacobian in coordinates; if $\varphi$ is $C^1$ and $d\varphi_p$ is an isomorphism, $\varphi$ is a local diffeomorphism near $p$ (the [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem)). ([Wikipedia: Tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space))
- **Fundamental theorem on flows.** A smooth vector field $v$ on a smooth manifold has a unique maximal flow $\phi:O\to M$, where $O\subset M\times\mathbb{R}$ is open and each slice $O\cap(\{x\}\times\mathbb{R})$ is an open interval containing $0$. ([nLab: flow](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/flow+of+a+vector+field)) On a compact manifold without boundary every smooth vector field is complete, and compactly supported fields are complete on any manifold; on $\mathbb{R}$, $\dot x=x^2$ has solution $x_0/(1-tx_0)$, which blows up at $t=1/x_0$. ([Wikipedia: Vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_field))
- **Straightening theorem.** If $X(p)\neq0$ there are coordinates $y^1,\dots,y^n$ near $p$ with $X=\partial/\partial y^1$, built by flowing a hypersurface transverse to $X$; Frobenius's theorem is its higher-dimensional generalization. ([Wikipedia: Straightening theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straightening_theorem_for_vector_fields))
- **Lie algebra structure and calculus identities.** The bracket is $\mathbb{R}$-bilinear, antisymmetric and satisfies Jacobi, with $[X,fY]=X(f)Y+f[X,Y]$ and $[fX,Y]=f[X,Y]-Y(f)X$. Further $\mathcal L_{[X,Y]}=[\mathcal L_X,\mathcal L_Y]$, Cartan's formula $\mathcal L_X=d\,i_X+i_X\,d$ on forms, and $i_{[X,Y]}=[\mathcal L_X,i_Y]=[i_X,\mathcal L_Y]$. If $V_i$ is $F$-related to $W_i$, then $[V_1,V_2]$ is $F$-related to $[W_1,W_2]$. ([Wikipedia: Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields); [MIT 18.965, Lemma 1.24](https://www.mit.edu/~anser/files/18_965.pdf); [Wikipedia: Lie derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_derivative); [Wikipedia: Interior product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_product); [Wikipedia: Vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_field))
- **Commuting flows.** $[X,Y]=0$ iff the flows of $X$ and $Y$ commute locally. ([Wikipedia: Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields))
- **Frobenius theorem.** A subbundle $E\subset TM$ is integrable (tangent to a regular foliation) iff it is involutive: $[X,Y]$ takes values in $E$ whenever $X,Y$ do. ([Wikipedia: Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_theorem_%28differential_topology%29))
- **Poincaré–Hopf theorem.** Let $M$ be compact and $v$ a continuous vector field with isolated zeros, pointing outward with no zeros along $\partial M$ if there is a boundary. Then the sum of the indices of the zeros equals $\chi(M)$. ([Wikipedia: Poincaré–Hopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Hopf_theorem))
- **Hairy ball theorem.** $S^{2n}$ has no nowhere-vanishing continuous tangent field; odd spheres do, by pairing coordinates: $v(x)=(x_2,-x_1,\dots,x_{2n},-x_{2n-1})$ on $S^{2n-1}$. ([Wikipedia: Hairy ball theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_ball_theorem))
- **Vector fields on spheres (Adams 1962).** Write $n=(2a+1)2^{4d+c}$ with $0\le c<4$ and $\rho(n)=2^c+8d$. Then $S^{n-1}$ admits exactly $\rho(n)-1$ pointwise linearly independent vector fields; Clifford-algebra constructions give the lower bound and Adams proved optimality with topological K-theory. ([Wikipedia: Vector fields on spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_fields_on_spheres))
- **Parallelizability.** Lie groups are parallelizable (translate a basis at the identity), products of parallelizable manifolds are parallelizable, every parallelizable manifold is orientable, and every orientable closed 3-manifold is parallelizable. Among spheres only $S^0,S^1,S^3,S^7$ are parallelizable (Hirzebruch, Kervaire, Bott–Milnor 1958), matching the unit spheres of the normed division algebras. ([Wikipedia: Parallelizable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallelizable_manifold))

### Examples
- **Non-commuting fields spanning an integrable distribution.** On $\mathbb{R}^2$, $X=\partial_x$ and $Y=e^x\partial_y$ span every tangent plane, yet the coordinate formula gives $[X,Y]=e^x\partial_y=Y\neq0$: Frobenius needs only $[X,Y]\in\operatorname{span}\{X,Y\}$. ([Wikipedia: Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields); [Wikipedia: Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_theorem_%28differential_topology%29))
- **Matrix Lie groups.** Left-invariant fields are closed under the bracket, which for matrix groups is the commutator $XY-YX$. ([Wikipedia: Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields))
- **Torus versus sphere.** $\chi(T^2)=0$ and the torus has a nowhere-zero field; $\chi(S^2)=2$, so every field on $S^2$ vanishes. $S^3=SU(2)$ is parallelizable, while $S^{n-1}$ for $n$ odd has $\rho(n)-1=0$ independent fields. ([Wikipedia: Hairy ball theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_ball_theorem); [Wikipedia: Parallelizable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallelizable_manifold); [Wikipedia: Vector fields on spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_fields_on_spheres))

### History
Embedded pictures of tangent planes, still common in relativity texts, gave way to intrinsic definitions via curves, derivations, or $I/I^2$. ([Wikipedia: Tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space)) The Frobenius theorem was first proved by Deahna and Clebsch; Frobenius applied it to Pfaffian systems in 1877. ([Wikipedia: Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_theorem_%28differential_topology%29)) Poincaré (1885) and Brouwer (1912) proved the hairy ball theorem, Hopf proved the index theorem in 1926, and Adams published "Vector Fields on Spheres" in the Annals of Mathematics 75 (1962). ([Wikipedia: Hairy ball theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_ball_theorem); [Wikipedia: Poincaré–Hopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Hopf_theorem); [Crossref: Adams 1962](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1970213)) Serre (1955) and Swan (1962) proved the algebraic and compact topological forms of the bundle–module correspondence. ([nLab: Serre–Swan theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Serre-Swan+theorem))

### Connections
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): $T_pM$ requires a smooth structure.
- [Tangent Bundle](node:Tangent%20Bundle) and [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles): vector fields are sections of the prototypical vector bundle.
- [Inverse Function Theorem](node:Inverse%20Function%20Theorem): invertibility of $d\varphi_p$ gives local diffeomorphisms.
- [Ordinary Differential Equations](node:Ordinary%20Differential%20Equations) and [Dynamical Systems](node:Dynamical%20Systems): integral curves, flows, limit cycles.
- [Frobenius Integrability Theorem](node:Frobenius%20Integrability%20Theorem): involutive distributions are integrable.
- [Lie Derivative](node:Lie%20Derivative): differentiation along flows; $\mathcal L_XY=[X,Y]$.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups) and [Lie Algebras](node:Lie%20Algebras): left-invariant fields and their bracket; Lie groups are parallelizable.
- [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms), [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology) and [Dual Vector Space](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space): $T^*_pM=(T_pM)^*$, interior products, Cartan's formula.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): vector fields as $(1,0)$-tensor fields.
- [Connections and Covariant Derivatives](node:Connections%20and%20Covariant%20Derivatives): torsion and curvature involve $[X,Y]$.
- [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere), [Homology](node:Homology) and [Topological K-Theory](node:Topological%20K-Theory): Euler characteristic, Poincaré–Hopf, Adams's theorem.
- [Modules over Commutative Rings](node:Modules%20over%20Commutative%20Rings): Serre–Swan identifies bundles with projective modules.
- [Three-Manifold Topology](node:Three-Manifold%20Topology): orientable closed 3-manifolds are parallelizable.
- [Submanifolds and Embeddings](node:Submanifolds%20and%20Embeddings): immersions are maps with injective differential.
- Map: [MSC 58Axx - General theory of differentiable manifolds](node:MSC%2058Axx%20-%20General%20theory%20of%20differentiable%20manifolds), [MSC 58 - Global analysis, analysis on manifolds](node:MSC%2058%20-%20Global%20analysis,%20analysis%20on%20manifolds)

### Common pitfalls
- **Commuting is stronger than integrable.** $[X,Y]=0$ is sufficient but not necessary for $\operatorname{span}\{X,Y\}$ to be integrable; it is the condition for local commuting flows. ([Wikipedia: Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_theorem_%28differential_topology%29); [Wikipedia: Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields))
- **The bracket is not $C^\infty$-linear.** $[fX,Y]=f[X,Y]-Y(f)X$, so $[X,Y](p)$ depends on $X,Y$ near $p$. ([MIT 18.965, Lemma 1.24](https://www.mit.edu/~anser/files/18_965.pdf))
- **Compactness alone is not completeness.** The completeness theorem is for compact manifolds *without boundary* (or for compactly supported fields); a smooth field on a non-compact manifold need not be complete, as $x^2\,\partial_x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ shows. ([Wikipedia: Vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_field))
- **Physics sign conventions.** Rosenfeld's local variation is $\delta^*A=-\mathcal L_XA$. ([Wikipedia: Lie derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_derivative))
- **Affine versus linear tangent space.** The plane touching an embedded surface is an affine tangent space, distinct from the vector space $T_pM$. ([Wikipedia: Tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space))
- **Immersion is not embedding.** The figure-eight curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is an immersion but not an embedding. ([MIT 18.965, Ex. 1.20](https://www.mit.edu/~anser/files/18_965.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Hilbert's sixteenth problem, second part.** Is there a bound $H(n)$ on the number of limit cycles of a planar polynomial vector field of degree $n$? Whether a finite $H(n)$ exists is open for every $n>1$ ($H(1)=0$); quadratic fields with four limit cycles are known. Ilyashenko and Écalle (1991/92) proved that each individual planar polynomial vector field has finitely many limit cycles; Dulac had claimed this in 1923, but a gap in his proof was found in 1981. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_sixteenth_problem))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Tangent space (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space) and [nLab: flow of a vector field](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/flow+of+a+vector+field): definitions, differentials, and the maximal flow.
- **Learn:** [Minicozzi, MIT 18.965 Geometry of Manifolds I (notes by S. An)](https://www.mit.edu/~anser/files/18_965.pdf): derivations, the basis theorem with proof, vector fields, and the Lie bracket.
- **Primary:** [J. F. Adams, Vector Fields on Spheres, Annals of Mathematics 75 (1962)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1970213): the original solution of the vector-fields-on-spheres problem.
- **Further reading:** [Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (Springer GTM, 2012)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-9982-5): graduate text; nLab cites its chapter "Integral curves and flows" for the fundamental theorem on flows. ([nLab: flow](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/flow+of+a+vector+field))
- **Further reading:** [Warner, Foundations of Differentiable Manifolds and Lie Groups (Springer GTM, 1983)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4757-1799-0): alternative Springer GTM graduate text.
references.Tempered Distributions:
## Reference
### Overview
A tempered distribution is a continuous linear functional on the Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ of smooth functions that decay rapidly at infinity together with all their derivatives. The space $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ of tempered distributions generalizes the bounded or slowly growing locally integrable functions; it contains every compactly supported distribution and every square-integrable function, and the Fourier transform is a continuous linear bijection of $\mathcal{S}'$ onto itself. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) It is a subspace of the space of all [distributions](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29).

The construction works because the Fourier transform is an automorphism of $\mathcal{S}$, so it can be transported to the dual by $\langle\widehat T,\psi\rangle=\langle T,\widehat\psi\rangle$. This puts $\delta$, polynomials, all $L^p$ functions and their derivatives in one space on which [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) is a bijection. In particular, for $p>2$ there are $L^p$ functions whose Fourier transform is not a function, and $\mathcal{S}'$ is where their transforms live. ([Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform); [Wikipedia: Schwartz space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_space)) This is why $\mathcal{S}'$ is the setting for constant-coefficient [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations), Bessel-potential [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces), [pseudodifferential operators](node:Pseudodifferential%20Operators), and the Wightman axioms of [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory). ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space); [Wikipedia: Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms))

The topic belongs to [MSC 46Fxx - Distributions, generalized functions, distribution spaces](node:MSC%2046Fxx%20-%20Distributions,%20generalized%20functions,%20distribution%20spaces). The space $\mathcal{S}$ is a nuclear Fréchet space, and its strong dual $\mathcal{S}'$ is nuclear, Montel and reflexive, so $\mathcal{S}'$ is a well-behaved locally convex space. ([Wikipedia: Schwartz space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_space))

### Formal definition
The Schwartz space is
$$\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)=\Big\{\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n):\ p_{\alpha,\beta}(\varphi)=\sup_{x}|x^\alpha D^\beta\varphi(x)|<\infty\ \text{for all multi-indices }\alpha,\beta\Big\},$$
a complete topological vector space under the seminorms $p_{\alpha,\beta}$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))

A **tempered distribution** is a linear map $T:\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)\to\mathbb{C}$ such that $T(\varphi_m)\to0$ whenever $p_{\alpha,\beta}(\varphi_m)\to0$ for all $\alpha,\beta$; equivalently there are $C>0$ and integers $M,N$ with
$$|T(\varphi)|\le C\sum_{|\alpha|\le M,\ |\beta|\le N}p_{\alpha,\beta}(\varphi)\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal{S}).$$
$\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is the continuous dual of $\mathcal{S}$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Spaces of test functions and distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaces_of_test_functions_and_distributions))

Operations are defined by duality: $\langle D^\alpha T,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle T,D^\alpha\varphi\rangle$, $\langle\mathcal{F}T,\psi\rangle=\langle T,\mathcal{F}\psi\rangle$, and multiplication by a smooth slowly increasing function $\psi$ maps $\mathcal{S}'$ to itself. The derivative of a tempered distribution is tempered. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Spaces of test functions and distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaces_of_test_functions_and_distributions))

### Key results
- **Fourier isomorphism and convolution theorem.** $\mathcal{F}$ is a linear automorphism of $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and, by transposition, a TVS isomorphism of $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ onto itself. If $\psi$ is smooth and slowly increasing and $T\in\mathcal{S}'$, then $\psi T\in\mathcal{S}'$ and $\mathcal{F}(\psi T)=\mathcal{F}\psi*\mathcal{F}T$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Spaces of test functions and distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaces_of_test_functions_and_distributions))
- **Structure theorem.** For every $T\in\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ there exist a continuous slowly increasing (polynomially bounded) function $F$ and a multi-index $\alpha$ with $T=\partial^\alpha F$. Conversely every such derivative is tempered, so $\mathcal{S}'$ is exactly the space of finite-order derivatives of continuous functions of polynomial growth, and each derivative of $T$ grows at most polynomially. ([Wikipedia: Spaces of test functions and distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaces_of_test_functions_and_distributions); [Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **$L^p$ inside $\mathcal{S}'$.** Every product of a polynomial with an $L^p$ function, $p\ge1$, is tempered. For $1\le p\le2$ the Fourier transform maps $L^p$ into $L^{p'}$ with $\|\hat f\|_{p'}\le\|f\|_p$ (Hausdorff–Young); for $2<p<\infty$ there are $L^p$ functions whose transform is not a function, only a tempered distribution. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Hausdorff–Young inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff%E2%80%93Young_inequality); [Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))
- **Paley–Wiener–Schwartz theorem.** An entire function $F$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is the Fourier–Laplace transform of a compactly supported distribution $v$ if and only if there are $C,N,B>0$ with $|F(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^Ne^{B|\operatorname{Im}z|}$ for all $z$; then $\operatorname{supp}v$ lies in the closed ball of radius $B$. Moreover $v$ is smooth if and only if for every $N$ there is $C_N$ with $|F(z)|\le C_N(1+|z|)^{-N}e^{B|\operatorname{Im}z|}$. ([Wikipedia: Paley–Wiener theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley%E2%80%93Wiener_theorem))
- **Bochner–Minlos theorem.** If $A$ is a nuclear space and $C:A\to\mathbb{C}$ is a continuous positive-definite functional with $C(0)=1$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $A'$ whose Fourier–Stieltjes transform is $C$. With $A=\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and a Gaussian characteristic functional this yields the white-noise measure, a probability measure on random tempered distributions. ([Wikipedia: Bochner–Minlos theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bochner%E2%80%93Minlos_theorem))
- **Schwartz kernel theorem.** For open $X,Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, each $k\in\mathcal{D}'(X\times Y)$ defines a continuous linear $K:\mathcal{D}(Y)\to\mathcal{D}'(X)$ by $\langle k,u\otimes v\rangle=\langle Kv,u\rangle$, and every such map has exactly one kernel $k$. ([Wikipedia: Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem))
- **Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem.** Every nonzero linear differential operator $P(\partial)$ with constant coefficients has a [fundamental solution](node:Fundamental%20Solutions) $E$ with $P(\partial)E=\delta$, so $P(\partial)u=f$ is solvable for every compactly supported distribution $f$; this fails for polynomial coefficients by Lewy's example. ([Wikipedia: Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem))
- **Homogeneous distributions.** $x_+^\alpha$ ($x^\alpha$ for $x>0$, $0$ otherwise) is locally integrable on $\mathbb{R}$ only for $\operatorname{Re}\alpha>-1$; $\alpha\mapsto x_+^\alpha$ is holomorphic from the right half-plane into $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R})$ and extends uniquely to a meromorphic family with simple poles at $\alpha=-1,-2,\dots$, staying homogeneous of degree $\alpha$ whenever $\alpha$ is not a negative integer. The related extensions at negative integers generalize the principal value $\mathrm{p.v.}\,1/x$. ([Wikipedia: Homogeneous distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_distribution))

### Examples
- **Principal value and the Hilbert transform.** $\mathrm{p.v.}\,\frac1{\pi t}$ is a tempered distribution, and convolution with it is the Hilbert transform, whose Fourier multiplier is $-i\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)$. It is bounded on $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ for $1<p<\infty$ (M. Riesz, 1928), maps $L^1$ only into weak $L^1$, and, suitably regularized, maps $L^\infty$ into BMO. ([Wikipedia: Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform))
- **Bessel-potential spaces.** For $s\in\mathbb{R}$, $H^{s,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)=\{f\in\mathcal{S}':\mathcal{F}^{-1}[(1+|\xi|^2)^{s/2}\mathcal{F}f]\in L^p\}$, a Hilbert space when $p=2$; negative-order Sobolev spaces are spaces of tempered distributions. ([Wikipedia: Sobolev space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobolev_space))
- **Test functions.** $x^\alpha e^{-a|x|^2}$ ($a>0$) and all of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ lie in $\mathcal{S}$, and $\mathcal{S}$ is dense in $L^p$ for $1\le p<\infty$, which is how [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces) embed in $\mathcal{S}'$. ([Wikipedia: Schwartz space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_space))
- **Pseudodifferential operators.** An operator $P(x,D)u(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}P(x,\xi)\hat u(\xi)\,d\xi$ with symbol in Hörmander's class $S^m_{1,0}$ (smooth, with $|\partial_\xi^\alpha\partial_x^\beta P|\le C_{\alpha\beta}(1+|\xi|)^{m-|\alpha|}$) is defined through the Fourier transform and acts on distributions; such operators are pseudo-local, creating no singularity where the input is smooth. Their study began in the mid-1960s with Kohn, Nirenberg, Hörmander and others. ([Wikipedia: Pseudo-differential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-differential_operator))
- **Wave front sets.** A pair $(x_0,v)$ lies outside the wave front set of a distribution $f$ exactly when there are a test function $\phi\in C_c^\infty$ with $\phi(x_0)\neq0$ and an open cone $\Gamma\ni v$ on which $\widehat{\phi f}$ decays faster than every power of $|\xi|$; the wave front set is the complement of such pairs, and its projection to $x$ is the singular support. Hörmander coined the term around 1970. ([Wikipedia: Wavefront set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavefront_set))
- **Quantum fields.** In the Wightman axioms, fields are operator-valued tempered distributions, and the vacuum expectation values suffice to reconstruct the theory. ([Wikipedia: Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms))

### History
Generalized functions originate in Sobolev's 1936 work on hyperbolic equations, and Laurent Schwartz developed the theory in extended form in the late 1940s. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29)) Schwartz published the kernel theorem in 1952, and Grothendieck developed much of the theory of nuclear spaces while studying it, publishing in 1955. ([Wikipedia: Schwartz kernel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwartz_kernel_theorem)) Schwartz's distributional Paley–Wiener theorem dates from 1952. ([Wikipedia: Paley–Wiener theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley%E2%80%93Wiener_theorem)) Ehrenpreis (1954–55) and Malgrange (1955–56) independently proved existence of fundamental solutions. ([Wikipedia: Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgrange%E2%80%93Ehrenpreis_theorem)) Pseudodifferential operators date from the mid-1960s and the wave front set from about 1970, both building microlocal analysis on $\mathcal{S}'$. ([Wikipedia: Pseudo-differential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-differential_operator); [Wikipedia: Wavefront set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavefront_set))

### Connections
- [Distributions (Generalized Functions)](node:Distributions%20%28Generalized%20Functions%29): $\mathcal{S}'\subset\mathcal{D}'$; tempered distributions are those of polynomial growth.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis): $\mathcal{S}'$ is the space on which the Fourier transform is a bijection on generalized functions.
- [Plancherel Theorem](node:Plancherel%20Theorem): the $L^2$ isometry is the restriction of the $\mathcal{S}'$ transform to $L^2\subset\mathcal{S}'$.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces): $H^s$ and $H^{s,p}$ are subspaces of $\mathcal{S}'$ defined by Fourier multipliers.
- [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions): fundamental solutions of constant-coefficient operators are distributions.
- [Lp Spaces](node:Lp%20Spaces) and [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): $L^p\subset\mathcal{S}'$; $L^2$ is the Hilbert space on which $\mathcal F$ is unitary.
- [Quantum Field Theory](node:Quantum%20Field%20Theory) and [Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap](node:Yang–Mills%20Existence%20and%20Mass%20Gap): Wightman fields are operator-valued tempered distributions.
- [Gaussian Processes](node:Gaussian%20Processes): white noise is a Gaussian random element of $\mathcal{S}'$.
- [MSC 35Sxx - Pseudodifferential operators and other generalizations of partial differential operators](node:MSC%2035Sxx%20-%20Pseudodifferential%20operators%20and%20other%20generalizations%20of%20partial%20differential%20operators): the microlocal theory built on $\mathcal{S}'$.
- [MSC 46Fxx - Distributions, generalized functions, distribution spaces](node:MSC%2046Fxx%20-%20Distributions,%20generalized%20functions,%20distribution%20spaces): the MSC home of the topic.

### Common pitfalls
- **Not every distribution is tempered.** $\mathcal{S}'$ is a proper subspace of $\mathcal{D}'$, and the structure theorem forces polynomial growth of the primitive $F$. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **Products are restricted.** On $\mathcal{S}'$ one may multiply by smooth slowly increasing functions, but there is no associative product of two distributions extending multiplication by smooth functions (Schwartz, 1950s). Convolution of two distributions is defined when one has compact support. ([Wikipedia: Distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29))
- **$\hat f$ for $f\in L^p$, $p>2$, need not be a function.** Hausdorff–Young stops at $p=2$. ([Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))
- **Normalization.** Formulas such as $\widehat{\delta}=1$ or the multiplier of the Hilbert transform depend on the Fourier convention; the ordinary-frequency convention $e^{-2\pi ix\xi}$ has no normalizing constant, while definitions based on other units differ from it by various constants. ([Wikipedia: Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform))

### Open problems
- **Interacting Wightman fields in four dimensions.** Wightman fields are operator-valued tempered distributions, and interacting theories satisfying the axioms have been constructed in two and three dimensions, but "there is no proof that the Wightman axioms can be satisfied for interacting theories in dimension 4"; one Millennium Problem asks to realize the axioms for Yang–Mills fields, with a mass gap. ([Wikipedia: Wightman axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_axioms)) The Clay Mathematics Institute lists the Yang–Mills problem as unsolved and states that no proof of the mass gap property is known. ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/yang-mills-the-maths-gap/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Distribution (mathematics), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_%28mathematics%29): definitions, Fourier transform on $\mathcal{S}'$, structure theorem, products.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.155 Differential Analysis (Melrose), lecture notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-155-differential-analysis-fall-2004/pages/lecture-notes/): lectures on test functions, tempered distributions, Fourier inversion, Sobolev embedding, wave front sets and homogeneous distributions.
- **Primary:** [Hörmander, *The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I: Distribution Theory and Fourier Analysis* (Springer, Classics in Mathematics; Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2): the standard graduate monograph on distributions, Fourier analysis and wave front sets.
- **Further reading:** [Gel'fand and Shilov, *Generalized Functions*, Volume 2 (AMS, 2016 edition; Crossref)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/chel/378): spaces of test and generalized functions, translated by Friedman, Feinstein and Peltzer.
references.Tensors and Multilinear Algebra:
## Reference
### Overview
A tensor is an algebraic object describing a multilinear relationship among vectors, covectors, and other tensors attached to a vector space. Three standard definitions describe the same object: an array of components obeying a transformation law, a multilinear map, and an element of a tensor product of copies of $V$ and $V^*$. Tensors do not depend on a basis, though they are usually computed with components. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor))

The tensor product is the representing object for bilinear and multilinear maps. This works for vector spaces and, more generally, for modules over a ring, where its failure to be left exact leads to flatness and the Tor functors of homological algebra. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tensor+product); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product_of_modules); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tor_functor))

Much of the modern theory concerns the rank of a single tensor, for example in $V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3$. Tensor rank generalizes matrix rank but behaves very differently: it depends on the field, its computation is NP-hard, and best low-rank approximations may not exist. The complexity of matrix multiplication is governed by the rank and border rank of one specific tensor. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.1393); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.00857))

### Formal definition
**Tensor product.** For vector spaces $V,W$ over a field $K$, $V\otimes W$ comes with a bilinear map $\varphi(v,w)=v\otimes w$. For every bilinear $h:V\times W\to Z$ there is a unique linear $\tilde h:V\otimes W\to Z$ with $h=\tilde h\circ\varphi$. If $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional, then $\dim(V\otimes W)=\dim V\cdot\dim W$, with basis $\{e_i\otimes f_j\}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product))

**Type $(p,q)$ tensors.** A type $(p,q)$ tensor on $V$ is an element of $V^{\otimes p}\otimes(V^*)^{\otimes q}$. Equivalently it is a multilinear map taking $p$ covectors and $q$ vectors to a scalar. Its order is $p+q$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor))

**$k$-tensors (Guillemin).** For $n$-dimensional real $V$, $L^k(V)$ is the space of $k$-linear maps $V^k\to\mathbb{R}$, with $L^1(V)=V^*$ and $L^0(V)=\mathbb{R}$. The tensor product is $(T_1\otimes T_2)(v_1,\dots,v_{k+\ell})=T_1(v_1,\dots,v_k)\,T_2(v_{k+1},\dots,v_{k+\ell})$. Tensors $\ell_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\ell_k$ with $\ell_i\in V^*$ are called decomposable. ([MIT 18.952](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.952/spring2011/chapter1.pdf))

**Tensor, symmetric, and exterior algebras.** $T(V)=\bigoplus_kV^{\otimes k}$ is the tensor algebra, graded by order. The exterior power is a quotient, e.g. $V\wedge V=V\otimes V/\langle v\otimes v\rangle$, and the symmetric algebra is the quotient in which adjacent factors may be swapped. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product)) Dually, the alternating $k$-tensors $A^k(V)\subset L^k(V)$ have dimension $\binom nk$ for $1\le k\le n$ and are $0$ for $k>n$. ([MIT 18.952](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.952/spring2011/chapter1.pdf))

**Modules.** For a commutative ring $R$, $M\otimes_RN$ is defined by the same universal property for $R$-bilinear (balanced) maps. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product_of_modules); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tensor+product))

**Tensor rank.** The rank of $T\in V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes V_d$ is the least $R$ with $T=\sum_{r=1}^R v^{(r)}_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v^{(r)}_d$. The border rank is the least $r$ such that $T$ is a limit of tensors of rank $\le r$; equivalently, $T$ lies in the $r$-th secant variety of the Segre variety. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/cs/0703059v1))

### Key results
- **Basis of $L^k(V)$.** If $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is a basis with dual basis $e^*_i$, the decomposable tensors $e^*_I=e^*_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^*_{i_k}$ form a basis of $L^k(V)$, so $\dim L^k(V)=n^k$. ([MIT 18.952](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.952/spring2011/chapter1.pdf))
- **Hom–tensor identities.** For finite-dimensional $U,V$, $U^*\otimes V\cong\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)$ via $f\otimes v\mapsto(u\mapsto f(u)v)$. In general $\operatorname{Hom}(U\otimes V,W)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(U,\operatorname{Hom}(V,W))$, so $-\otimes V$ is left adjoint to $\operatorname{Hom}(V,-)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tensor+product))
- **Right exactness and flatness.** If $0\to N'\to N\to N''\to0$ is exact, then $M\otimes_RN'\to M\otimes_RN\to M\otimes_RN''\to0$ is exact, but the left map need not be injective. A module $T$ is flat when $T\otimes_R-$ is exact. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product_of_modules))
- **Tor.** $\operatorname{Tor}^R_i(-,B)$ are the left derived functors of $-\otimes_RB$, with $\operatorname{Tor}_0=\otimes$. They extend the right-exact sequence to a long exact sequence. If $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(A,B)=0$ for all $B$ then $A$ is flat. $\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/n,A)$ is the $n$-torsion of $A$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tor_functor))
- **Transformation law and contraction.** Under a change of basis, the $p$ contravariant indices transform with the inverse of the change-of-basis matrix and the $q$ covariant indices with the matrix itself. Contracting one upper with one lower index maps type $(p,q)$ to $(p-1,q-1)$; the trace of a $(1,1)$ tensor is the basic case. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor))
- **Metric isomorphisms.** A metric gives $v_i=g_{ij}v^j$ and $\alpha^i=g^{ij}\alpha_j$, the musical isomorphisms $\flat,\sharp$ between $TM$ and $T^*M$. The metric trace $g^{ij}X_{ij}$ of a $(0,2)$ tensor does not depend on which index is raised. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_and_lowering_indices))
- **Tensor rank is NP-hard.** Hillar and Lim show that determining the rank of a $3$-tensor is NP-hard, as are its best rank-$1$ approximation, eigenvalues, singular values, and spectral norm. Restricting to symmetric tensors does not remove the hardness. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.1393))
- **Rank pathologies.** Rank depends on the field: some real tensors have complex rank $2$ but real rank $3$, and both $2$ and $3$ are typical ranks of real $2\times2\times2$ tensors. Border rank can be strictly less than rank, though for matrices they coincide. Best rank-$R$ approximations may not exist because the set of rank-$\le R$ tensors is not closed. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition))
- **Matrix multiplication as tensor rank.** The minimum number of multiplications in a noncommutative bilinear algorithm for matrix multiplication is the rank of the matrix-multiplication tensor. The exponent $\omega$ can be defined through rank or through border rank of $M_{\langle n,n,n\rangle}$. Strassen's algorithm shows the $2\times2$ case has rank $\le7$, and Winograd proved it equals $7$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/cs/0703059v1))

### Examples
- **Low-type tensors.** Scalars, vectors, covectors, and linear operators have types $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(1,1)$. The last matches $V^*\otimes V\cong\operatorname{End}V$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product))
- **Torsion kills tensor products.** $\mathbb Z/m\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n\cong\mathbb Z/\gcd(m,n)$ and $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n=0$. Tensoring $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$ with $\mathbb Z/n$ gives a sequence that is not exact. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product_of_modules))
- **Decompositions in data analysis.** The CP (CANDECOMP/PARAFAC) decomposition writes a tensor as a sum of $K$ rank-one terms. The Tucker decomposition (Tucker 1966; idea from Hitchcock 1927) writes it as a small core tensor multiplied by a factor matrix in each mode; CP is the case of a diagonal core. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucker_decomposition))
- **Physics.** In [Continuum Mechanics](node:Continuum%20Mechanics) the Cauchy stress tensor is a second-order tensor. In [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity) the stress–energy and Riemann tensors are central. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor))

### History
Hamilton introduced the word "tensor" in 1846 with a different meaning; Voigt introduced the modern usage in 1898. Ricci-Curbastro developed tensor calculus around 1890 as absolute [differential calculus](node:Differential%20Calculus). Einstein learned it from Grossmann, and Levi-Civita corrected Einstein's errors in 1915–17. Whitney popularized the tensor product. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor)) Ricci and Levi-Civita's memoir "Méthodes de calcul différentiel absolu et leurs applications" appeared in *Math. Ann.* 54 (1900), 125–201 ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01454201)). Whitney's "Tensor products of Abelian groups" appeared in *Duke Math. J.* 4 (1938), 495–528 ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tensor+product)). Strassen's 1969 algorithm, with exponent $\log_27\approx2.807$, began the study of $\omega$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication)).

### Connections
- [Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces) and [Dual Vector Space](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space): the factors of $V^{\otimes p}\otimes(V^*)^{\otimes q}$.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices): $\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)\cong V^*\otimes W$; matrix rank is the $d=2$ case of tensor rank.
- [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces), [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics), [Musical Isomorphism](node:Musical%20Isomorphism): raising and lowering indices.
- [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms): alternating tensors and the exterior algebra.
- [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras): quotients of the tensor algebra by a quadratic form.
- [Homological Algebra](node:Homological%20Algebra) and [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals): tensor products of modules, flatness, Tor.
- [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): universal property and tensor–hom adjunction.
- [Tangent Spaces and Vector Fields](node:Tangent%20Spaces%20and%20Vector%20Fields) and [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): tensor fields on manifolds.
- [Stress-Energy Tensor](node:Stress-Energy%20Tensor): a symmetric rank-$2$ tensor field.
- [Numerical Linear Algebra](node:Numerical%20Linear%20Algebra): CP and Tucker decompositions.
- Map: [MSC 15 - Linear and multilinear algebra; matrix theory](node:MSC%2015%20-%20Linear%20and%20multilinear%20algebra;%20matrix%20theory)

### Common pitfalls
- **"Rank" means two things.** Many texts use "rank" for the order $p+q$, but tensor rank (fewest rank-one summands) is a different invariant. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition))
- **Pseudotensors.** The cross product and the Levi-Civita symbol change sign under orientation-reversing transformations, so they are not tensors in the strict sense. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor))
- **Matrix intuition fails.** For $d\ge3$, rank depends on the field, border rank can be smaller than rank, and best low-rank approximation can be ill-posed. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition))
- **Symmetric rank versus rank.** Comon conjectured that a symmetric tensor's rank equals its symmetric rank. Shitov gave a counterexample: an $800\times800\times800$ complex symmetric tensor that is a sum of $903$ rank-one tensors but not of $903$ symmetric ones. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08740))
- **Finite-dimensionality.** $V^*\otimes W\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$ is stated for finite-dimensional spaces. In infinite dimensions, different topologies give inequivalent tensor products. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor))

### Open problems
- **Is $\omega=2$?** The trivial bound is $\omega\ge2$, and the best upper bound the source lists is $\omega<2.371177$. Whether $\omega=2$ "is a major open question in theoretical computer science". Landsberg states the central conjecture as "the exponent of matrix multiplication is two". ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_of_matrix_multiplication); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/cs/0703059v1))
- **Maximum rank.** The maximum rank of tensors of a given format is unknown in general; only upper bounds in terms of the generic rank are known. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank_decomposition))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Tensor (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor) and [nLab: tensor product](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tensor+product): definitions, universal property, and history.
- **Learn:** [Guillemin, *Multilinear algebra* (MIT 18.952)](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.952/spring2011/chapter1.pdf): $k$-tensors, decomposable tensors, the basis theorem, alternating tensors, and wedge products.
- **Primary:** Hillar and Lim, [*Most tensor problems are NP-hard*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.1393); Landsberg, [*Secant varieties and the complexity of matrix multiplication*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.00857) (survey, 2022).
- **Further reading:** Landsberg, [*Tensors: Geometry and Applications*](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/128) (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 128): research-level geometry of tensor rank and border rank.
references.Tests of General Relativity:
## Reference
### Overview
Tests of general relativity compare Einstein's theory with experiment. Einstein proposed three classical tests in 1916: the anomalous perihelion precession of Mercury, the deflection of light by the Sun, and the gravitational redshift. Mercury's anomaly was already known, light bending was measured at the 1919 eclipse, and a redshift measurement accurate enough to test the theory came only in 1954 (white dwarf) and, in the laboratory, with Pound and Rebka in 1960. ([Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity); [Wikipedia: Pound–Rebka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound%E2%80%93Rebka_experiment))

From the 1960s a systematic weak-field programme used the parameterized post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism to compare GR with alternative metric theories. Solar-system experiments (Shapiro delay, light deflection, perihelion advance, lunar laser ranging, frame-dragging) and clock experiments now bound the PPN parameters and the equivalence principle at high precision. Binary pulsars, starting with Hulse–Taylor in 1974, tested gravitational radiation damping; gravitational-wave detection since 2015 and black-hole imaging since 2019 probe the dynamical strong field. ([Will, Living Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7377); [Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity); [LIGO/Virgo, arXiv:1602.03837](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.03837))

A rough measure of field strength is $\epsilon\sim GM/Rc^2$: about $1$ near a black-hole horizon, $0.2$ for neutron stars, and below $10^{-5}$ in the Solar System. ([Will, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

### Formal definition
The PPN formalism expands the metric of a slow-motion, weak-field system in post-Newtonian potentials and replaces the fixed coefficients of GR by parameters. It applies to metric theories in which all bodies obey the Einstein equivalence principle. In the Will–Nordtvedt notation there are ten parameters, with GR values
$$\gamma=\beta=1,\qquad \alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha_3=\zeta_1=\zeta_2=\zeta_3=\zeta_4=\xi=0.$$
$\gamma$ measures how much space curvature unit rest mass produces, $\beta$ the nonlinearity in the superposition law for $g_{00}$, the $\alpha_i$ preferred-frame effects, and the $\zeta_i$ violations of conservation of energy, momentum and angular momentum. ([Wikipedia: PPN formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameterized_post-Newtonian_formalism))

In the standard PPN gauge (units $G=c=1$), the metric begins
$$g_{00}=-1+2U-2\beta U^2+\cdots,\qquad g_{ij}=(1+2\gamma U)\,\delta_{ij}+O(\epsilon^2),$$
where $U=\int\rho'/|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'|\,d^3x'$ is the Newtonian potential and the omitted terms in $g_{00}$ involve further post-Newtonian potentials multiplied by combinations of the other parameters. ([Will, §3.2, Box 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

The Nordtvedt effect is a violation of the weak equivalence principle for self-gravitating bodies: a body of gravitational self-energy $-E_g$ has $m_p/m=1-\eta_N E_g/m$, with $\eta_N=4\beta-\gamma-3-\tfrac{10}{3}\xi-\alpha_1+\tfrac23\alpha_2-\tfrac23\zeta_1-\tfrac13\zeta_2$, which vanishes in GR. ([Will, §4.3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

### Key results
- **Mercury perihelion.** After subtracting $532.3035''$ per Julian century from other bodies and $0.0286''$ from solar oblateness, the remaining GR (gravitoelectric) contribution is $42.9799''$ per Julian century; the GR shift per orbit is approximately $\sigma=24\pi^3L^2/\bigl(T^2c^2(1-e^2)\bigr)$. The PPN bound from the perihelion shift is $|\beta-1|<8\times10^{-5}$. ([Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity); [Will, Table 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))
- **Light deflection and Shapiro delay.** GR predicts $1.75''$ for a ray grazing the Sun, twice the 1911 equivalence-principle value; VLBI confirms it at the $0.03\%$ level. Radar time delays to Mercury and Venus agreed with GR at $5\%$, and Cassini tracking gave $|\gamma-1|<2.3\times10^{-5}$. ([Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity); [Wikipedia: PPN formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameterized_post-Newtonian_formalism))
- **Lunar laser ranging.** Ranging to the Apollo retroreflectors since 1969, now approaching mm accuracy, finds no Nordtvedt effect: the Earth and Moon fall toward the Sun alike to about $1.4$ parts in $10^{13}$. Combined with laboratory composition tests this gives $\eta_N=(4.4\pm4.5)\times10^{-4}$, and assuming $\eta_N=4\beta-\gamma-3$ Will's table lists $|\beta-1|<2.3\times10^{-4}$ from the Nordtvedt effect. ([Will, §4.3.1, Table 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377); [Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity))
- **Gravitational redshift.** Pound and Rebka used the Mössbauer effect in $^{57}\mathrm{Fe}$ over $22.5\,\mathrm{m}$ at Harvard (1960, $10\%$), and Pound and Snider reached $1\%$ in 1964. Gravity Probe A (1976), a hydrogen maser rocketed to about $10\,000\,\mathrm{km}$, bounded the redshift anomaly by $|\alpha|<2\times10^{-4}$. Aluminium-ion optical clocks resolved the shift over a height of $1/3\,\mathrm{m}$. ([Wikipedia: Pound–Rebka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound%E2%80%93Rebka_experiment); [Will, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))
- **Galileo satellites.** Two Galileo navigation satellites left in eccentric orbits gave, from 1008 days of clock data, a fractional redshift deviation $(+0.19\pm2.48)\times10^{-5}$, a factor of about $5.6$ better than Gravity Probe A. ([Delva et al., arXiv:1812.03711](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.03711))
- **Frame-dragging.** Gravity Probe B measured geodetic and frame-dragging drifts of $-6601.8\pm18.3$ and $-37.2\pm7.2\,\mathrm{mas\,yr^{-1}}$ against GR predictions $-6606.1$ and $-39.2\,\mathrm{mas\,yr^{-1}}$ (final results 2011). ([Wikipedia: Gravity Probe B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity_Probe_B))
- **Binary pulsars.** Radiation damping in the Hulse–Taylor pulsar agrees with GR to better than half a percent. The double pulsar PSR J0737−3039A/B, timed for 16 years, has seven measured post-Keplerian parameters and tests the quadrupole formula for gravitational-wave emission to $1.3\times10^{-4}$ (95% confidence). ([Will, Living Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7377); [Kramer et al., arXiv:2112.06795](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.06795))
- **GW150914 tests.** Final mass and spin estimated separately from the inspiral and from the post-inspiral signal agree; the post-peak signal matches the least-damped quasinormal mode of the remnant; parametrized deviations of post-Newtonian phase coefficients were bounded for the first time; and the graviton Compton wavelength exceeds $10^{13}\,\mathrm{km}$ (90%). ([LIGO/Virgo, arXiv:1602.03841](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.03841))
- **Catalog tests.** For the 15 confident signals (false-alarm rate below $10^{-3}$ per year) from the second half of the third observing run (O3b), residuals, parametrized post-Newtonian deformations, spin-induced quadrupoles, dispersion, non-GR polarizations, echoes, and ringdown frequencies are all consistent with GR, with $m_g\le2.42\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{eV}/c^2$ (90%). ([LVK, arXiv:2112.06861](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.06861))
- **Speed of gravity.** GW170817 and GRB 170817A arrived $1.74\pm0.05\,\mathrm{s}$ apart, constraining $-3\times10^{-15}\le(v_{\rm GW}-c)/c\le+7\times10^{-16}$. ([LIGO/Virgo/Fermi/INTEGRAL, arXiv:1710.05834](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05834))
- **Black-hole shadow.** The Event Horizon Telescope image of M87* shows a ring of diameter $42\pm3\,\mu\mathrm{as}$, consistent with the shadow of a Kerr black hole of mass $(6.5\pm0.7)\times10^9M_\odot$. ([EHT, arXiv:1906.11238](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11238))

### Examples
- **Eddington 1919.** Eclipse plates taken at Sobral (Brazil) and Príncipe measured the shift of stars near the Sun. ([Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity))
- **PSR B1913+16.** Its mean rate of periastron advance is $4.226598(5)^\circ$ per year. ([Will, Table 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377); [Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity))
- **GW150914.** Detected on 14 September 2015 with signal-to-noise ratio 24, sweeping from 35 to 250 Hz; black holes of $36^{+5}_{-4}$ and $29^{+4}_{-4}M_\odot$ merged into $62^{+4}_{-4}M_\odot$, radiating $3.0\pm0.5\,M_\odot c^2$, at $410^{+160}_{-180}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$. ([LIGO/Virgo, arXiv:1602.03837](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.03837))
- **GPS.** Satellite clocks run fast relative to ground clocks by about $39\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ per day ($46\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ gravitational redshift, $-7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ time dilation), which the system must correct. ([Will, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

### History
Einstein explained Mercury's perihelion in 1915; light bending made the theory famous in 1919. Will divides the history into a genesis (1887–1919), a period of hibernation (1920–1960), a golden era of technology-driven tests (1960–1980), and the present quest for strong gravity. Nordtvedt pioneered the PPN formalism, Will generalized it to perfect fluids, and Will and Nordtvedt developed a unified version. The EHT observed M87 in 2017 and released its image in April 2019; the first image of Sagittarius A* followed in May 2022. ([Will, §1 and §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377); [Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity))

### Connections
- [General Relativity](node:General%20Relativity): the theory under test.
- [Parametrized Post-Newtonian Formalism](node:Parametrized%20Post-Newtonian%20Formalism): the weak-field framework that organizes Solar-System bounds.
- [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle): underlies redshift tests and the Nordtvedt effect.
- [Scalar-Tensor Gravity](node:Scalar-Tensor%20Gravity): the main alternative that predicts $\gamma\neq1$ and a Nordtvedt effect.
- [Newtonian Limit of General Relativity](node:Newtonian%20Limit%20of%20General%20Relativity) and [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution): perihelion, deflection and delay in the static metric.
- [Binary Pulsars](node:Binary%20Pulsars) and [Quadrupole Formula](node:Quadrupole%20Formula): radiation-damping tests.
- [Linearized Gravity](node:Linearized%20Gravity) and [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation): gravitational waves as solutions of the linearized field equations.
- [Gravitational Waves](node:Gravitational%20Waves), [Gravitational-Wave Detectors](node:Gravitational-Wave%20Detectors), [GW170817](node:GW170817): dynamical strong-field and propagation tests.
- [Black Hole Quasinormal Modes](node:Black%20Hole%20Quasinormal%20Modes) and [Kerr Black Holes](node:Kerr%20Black%20Holes): ringdown and shadow tests of the Kerr metric.
- [Atomic Clocks](node:Atomic%20Clocks): redshift tests from towers to satellites.
- [Gravitational Lensing](node:Gravitational%20Lensing): astrophysical light deflection.
- [Black Holes](node:Black%20Holes) and [Neutron Stars](node:Neutron%20Stars): strong-gravity sources.
- [Tests of the Inverse-Square Law](node:Tests%20of%20the%20Inverse-Square%20Law): short-distance probes of new forces.
- [Falsifiability and Theory Assessment](node:Falsifiability%20and%20Theory%20Assessment): GR is tested by named, repeatable experiments.
- [Physics Subsection - Relativistic observations and precision tests](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Relativistic%20observations%20and%20precision%20tests): field map.

### Common pitfalls
- **Newtonian light bending is half the GR value.** Einstein's 1911 equivalence-principle calculation, like Soldner's 1801 Newtonian one, gives half of the full GR value $1.75''$, i.e. $0.875''$. ([Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity))
- **PPN is not a strong-field framework.** Near neutron stars and black holes $\epsilon\sim1$ and the post-Newtonian approximation breaks down, and the 1PN metric contains no radiation reaction, so for such systems the simple 1PN approximation of the PPN framework is no longer appropriate. ([Will, §5.1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))
- **Absence of extra polarizations is weak evidence.** Detecting any mode beyond GR's two transverse quadrupolar ones would be disastrous for GR, but a missing breathing mode does not rule out scalar–tensor gravity, since its strength depends on the source. ([Will, §7.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))
- **Cassini systematics.** Later studies found a gravitomagnetic contribution that affects the measured $\gamma$, and suggest the true uncertainty may be about ten times larger than claimed; LAGEOS frame-dragging analyses also remain controversial. ([Wikipedia: Tests of GR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity))

### Open problems
Will lists the questions that motivate tests in GR's second century: whether astrophysical black holes are truly the black holes of GR; whether gravitational waves propagate at the speed of light with only two polarization states; whether GR holds on cosmological scales; whether Lorentz invariance is exact; whether the equivalence principle breaks down at some level; and whether quantization of gravity has testable effects. ([Will, Living Review](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.7377))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Tests of general relativity (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity): classical tests, PPN, pulsars, gravitational waves, EHT.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 8.962 General Relativity (Scott Hughes, Spring 2020)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-962-general-relativity-spring-2020/): graduate course including experimental tests of GR.
- **Primary:** [C. M. Will, The Confrontation between General Relativity and Experiment (arXiv:1403.7377)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7377): Living Review of equivalence-principle, PPN, pulsar and gravitational-wave tests.
- **Primary:** [Kramer et al., Strong-field gravity tests with the double pulsar (arXiv:2112.06795)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.06795): the most precise test of quadrupolar radiation damping.
- **Primary:** [LVK, Tests of General Relativity with GWTC-3 (arXiv:2112.06861)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.06861): catalog-wide gravitational-wave tests.
- **Further reading:** [C. M. Will, Theory and Experiment in Gravitational Physics, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press 2018](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/9781316338612): the standard monograph.
references.Tests of the Inverse-Square Law:
## Reference
### Overview
An inverse-square law states that an observed intensity falls off as the inverse square of the distance from a source; the geometric reason is that the flux from a point source is spread over a sphere of area $4\pi r^2$. For gravity it is Newton's law $F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$. ([Inverse-square law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-square_law); [Newton's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation))

Tests of the gravitational inverse-square law (ISL) look for a departure from $1/r^2$ over some range of distances. Adelberger, Heckel and Nelson review the motivations for testing at the sub-millimetre scale: extra dimensions, light moduli and other new bosons, and the length $\sim100\,\mu$m associated with the observed vacuum (dark-energy) density. In 2003 gravitational-strength deviations were excluded down to $\lambda=200\,\mu$m, and many square decades of Yukawa parameter space had been ruled out between $20$ nm and $4$ mm. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284))

Today the strongest laboratory bounds near $50\,\mu$m come from torsion balances of the Eöt-Wash group and of Tan et al. at HUST; micro-cantilevers, Casimir-subtraction force measurements and neutron scattering extend the search down to micron, nanometre and sub-nanometre ranges, and lunar laser ranging gives the tightest constraint at astronomical range. ([Lee et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2002.11761); [Tan et al. 2020](https://ngl.hust.edu.cn/info/1238/4626.htm); [Geraci et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.2350); [Chen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.7267); [Haddock et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.02984); [Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284))

### Formal definition
Newton's law for point masses is $F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$, with $G=6.67430(15)\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ (CODATA 2022). By the [shell theorem](node:Shell%20Theorem), a spherically symmetric distribution acts on an exterior point as if its mass were at the centre, and exerts no net force from shells outside the point. ([Newton's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation))

ISL tests are reported in two parametrizations of a modified potential ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284)):
$$
V(r)=-\frac{Gm_1m_2}{r}\Bigl[1+\alpha\,e^{-r/\lambda}\Bigr],\qquad
V(r)=-\frac{Gm_1m_2}{r}\Bigl[1+\alpha_N\Bigl(\frac{r_0}{r}\Bigr)^{N-1}\Bigr].
$$
The Yukawa term is the static limit of the exchange of a boson of mass $m_b=\hbar/(\lambda c)$, with $\alpha$ its strength relative to gravity. The power-law terms arise from simultaneous exchange of two massless particles: $N=2$ from two scalars, $N=3$ from two pseudoscalars, and $N=5$ from two axions or a massless neutrino–antineutrino pair. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284))

For $n$ flat extra dimensions compactified on a torus of radius $R_*$, the lowest Kaluza–Klein graviton mode gives a Yukawa term with $\lambda=R_*$ and $\alpha=8n/3$; the PDG quotes $\alpha=16/3$, $\lambda=R$ for a $2$-torus. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284); [PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)) Well below $R$ the force law itself changes; for two extra dimensions it becomes $1/r^4$. ([Large extra dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_extra_dimension))

### Key results
- **Kapner et al. (2007).** Three Eöt-Wash torsion-balance experiments at separations from $9.53$ mm down to $55\,\mu$m showed, at 95% confidence, that the ISL holds for gravitational-strength ($|\alpha|=1$) Yukawa interactions down to $\lambda=56\,\mu$m, below the dark-energy length $\lambda_d=\sqrt[4]{\hbar c/\rho_d}\approx85\,\mu$m; a single extra dimension must have size $R\le44\,\mu$m. ([Kapner et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0611184))
- **Tan et al. (HUST, 2016 and 2020).** The PDG takes its two-extra-dimension bound $R<30\,\mu$m (95% CL), corresponding to $M_D>4.0$ TeV, from Tan et al., *Phys. Rev. Lett.* **116**, 131101 (2016). ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)) The 2020 HUST result, obtained by suppressing vibration of the electrostatic shielding membrane, shows at 95% CL that the ISL holds ($|\alpha|\le1$) down to $\lambda=48\,\mu$m, gives the strongest bound on $\alpha$ for $40$–$350\,\mu$m (up to a factor 3 better near $\lambda\approx70\,\mu$m), and improves power-law bounds by about a factor 2 for $k=4,5$. ([Tan et al. 2020](https://ngl.hust.edu.cn/info/1238/4626.htm))
- **Lee et al.
