(2020).** With platinum test bodies carrying $18$-fold and $120$-fold azimuthal patterns, at separations from $52\,\mu$m to $3.0$ mm, Newtonian gravity gave an excellent fit: any gravitational-strength Yukawa must have $\lambda<38.6\,\mu$m, and the largest extra dimension has toroidal radius below $30\,\mu$m. ([Lee et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2002.11761); [Eöt-Wash](https://www.npl.washington.edu/eotwash/))
- **Micro-cantilevers.** Geraci, Smullin, Weld, Chiaverini and Kapitulnik used cryogenic attonewton-sensitive cantilevers to give the best bound in the $5$–$15\,\mu$m range, excluding $|\alpha|>14{,}000$ at $\lambda=10\,\mu$m (95% CL). ([Geraci et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.2350))
- **Casimir-subtraction measurements.** Chen, Tham, Krause, López, Fischbach and Decca measured differential forces between a test mass and rotating gold and silicon source masses, a technique that subtracts the otherwise dominant Casimir force at the outset, and improved Yukawa limits by up to a factor $10^3$ over $40$–$8000$ nm. ([Chen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.7267)) Adelberger et al. note that most earlier Casimir-based limits assumed a Yukawa force could not exceed the difference between measurement and Casimir theory, and that a rigorous simultaneous fit would give significantly weaker limits. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284))
- **Neutron scattering.** Haddock et al. compared the momentum-transfer dependence of slow-neutron scattering on xenon and helium with known forms, improving bounds for $\lambda<0.1$ nm and remaining competitive at larger $\lambda$. ([Haddock et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.02984))
- **Long range.** At astronomical ranges the tightest constraint on $\alpha$ comes from lunar laser ranging (anomalous lunar precession $\delta\omega/\omega<1.6\times10^{-11}$ at 95% CL), limited by tidal distortion and atmospheric and ocean loading of the Earth; planetary radar and microwave ranging are limited by target definition and solar-plasma delay. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284))

### Examples
- **Eöt-Wash torsion pendulum.** A pendulum with bored-out holes hangs above a rotating attractor; the hole patterns produce torques at harmonics of the rotation frequency, and the attractor is designed so that the inverse-square torque cancels, leaving any non-Newtonian residual. ([Burrage & Sakstein](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1709.09071)) Lee et al. used platinum detector and attractor plates $54$ and $99\,\mu$m thick with two patterns at once, $18$-fold and $120$-fold. ([Lee et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2002.11761))
- **Chameleon fields.** In chameleon theories the scalar's mass increases with the ambient density, so it is short-ranged in dense environments and evades classic fifth-force tests. Eöt-Wash-type balances still constrain chameleons, but whether the gold-coated beryllium–copper membrane between pendulum and attractor has a thin shell depends on the parameters, which makes modelling difficult. ([Burrage & Sakstein](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1709.09071))

### History
Bullialdus argued for an inverse-square weakening of gravity in 1645, Hooke wrote to Newton that attraction is in "duplicate proportion" to distance (1679–80), and Newton derived the law in the *Principia*. ([Inverse-square law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-square_law)) Cavendish's 1798 torsion-balance experiment, 111 years after the *Principia*, was the first laboratory test of Newton's law of gravitation between masses. ([Newton's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation)) The 1998 ADD proposal allowed extra dimensions as large as about a millimetre, which sub-millimetre tests of Newton's law constrain ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)), reviewed by Adelberger, Heckel and Nelson in 2003 ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284)); the torsion-balance bound then moved from $56\,\mu$m (2007) to $48\,\mu$m (HUST, 2020) and $38.6\,\mu$m (Eöt-Wash, 2020). ([Kapner et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0611184); [Tan et al. 2020](https://ngl.hust.edu.cn/info/1238/4626.htm); [Lee et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2002.11761))

### Connections
- [Newtonian Gravity](node:Newtonian%20Gravity): the $1/r^2$ law under test; [Gravitational Constant](node:Gravitational%20Constant): a long-range Yukawa only renormalizes $G$.
- [Gauss's Law in n Dimensions](node:Gauss's%20Law%20in%20n%20Dimensions) and [Gauss's Law for Gravity](node:Gauss's%20Law%20for%20Gravity): in $d$ spatial dimensions the flux argument gives $F\propto1/r^{d-1}$, so with $n$ extra dimensions $F\propto1/r^{n+2}$ well below the compactification radius.
- [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions) and [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions): ADD predicts $\alpha=8n/3$ at $\lambda=R$ and a $1/r^{n+2}$ force at $r\ll R$; ISL tests bound $R$ directly.
- [Compactification](node:Compactification) and [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes): the graviton KK tower produces the Yukawa term.
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model): RS1's KK gravitons lie at the TeV scale, so it is not testable with feasible ISL probes; RS2's infinite warped dimension instead adds a correction of relative size $\sim1/(r^2k^2)$ to the Newtonian potential at distances above $1/k$. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284))
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem) and [Planck Scale](node:Planck%20Scale): bounds on $R$ translate into bounds on the fundamental scale $M_D$.
- [Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant](node:Dark%20Energy%20and%20the%20Cosmological%20Constant): the dark-energy length $\lambda_d\approx85\,\mu$m is an independent motivation.
- [Equivalence Principle](node:Equivalence%20Principle): composition-dependent forces are tested by a different class of torsion balances.
- [Tests of General Relativity](node:Tests%20of%20General%20Relativity) and [Parametrized Post-Newtonian Formalism](node:Parametrized%20Post-Newtonian%20Formalism): Solar-System tests probe complementary ranges.
- [Electrostatics](node:Electrostatics): patch potentials are the main systematic at tens of microns.
- [Kapner et al. 2006 - Tests of the Gravitational Inverse-Square Law below the Dark-Energy Length Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0611184): source note for the 2007 result.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Modified gravity and screening](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Modified%20gravity%20and%20screening)

### Common pitfalls
- **Yukawa versus power-law bounds.** Results are reported separately in the two parametrizations: Yukawa bounds on $\alpha$ as a function of $\lambda$, and power-law bounds for each exponent, as in the HUST improvement for $k=4,5$. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284); [Tan et al. 2020](https://ngl.hust.edu.cn/info/1238/4626.htm))
- **Planetary tests compare orbits.** Long-range planetary bounds are typically Keplerian tests comparing the values of $G(r)M_\odot$ deduced for different planets. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284))
- **Force law versus Yukawa term.** For two extra dimensions of size $d$ the force law is $1/r^4$ for $r\ll d$ and $1/r^2$ for $r\gg d$, while sub-millimetre experiments report their bounds in the Yukawa form, with $\alpha=16/3$, $\lambda=R$ for a 2-torus. ([Large extra dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_extra_dimension); [PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **Electrostatic and Casimir backgrounds.** Electrostatic potential differences, patch fields and the Casimir force are major backgrounds at short range; torsion balances use a shielding membrane whose vibration limits the smallest separation, and Casimir-range experiments must cancel or model the Casimir force. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284); [Tan et al. 2020](https://ngl.hust.edu.cn/info/1238/4626.htm); [Lee et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2002.11761); [Chen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.7267))
- **Screened forces.** A null ISL result does not exclude chameleon-type forces, which are suppressed in dense test masses; their bounds require separate modelling. ([Burrage & Sakstein](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1709.09071))

### Open problems
- **Screened scalar parameter space.** Burrage and Sakstein conclude that commonly studied chameleon models are well constrained, but less commonly studied models have large regions of parameter space that are still viable; for symmetrons there is a "desert" between two scales where the model is unconstrained; and few bounds exist for $f(R)$ theories with higher powers of $R$. ([Burrage & Sakstein](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09071))
- **Gravitational strength at $20\,\mu$m.** Adelberger, Heckel and Nelson estimate that testing gravitational-strength Yukawas at a $20\,\mu$m scale needs a background-free increase in sensitivity of at least $10^3$, and note that many proposed ideas remain viable because their predicted effects lie below current limits. ([Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284)) The 2020 bound for gravitational-strength Yukawas, $\lambda<38.6\,\mu$m, has not reached that scale. ([Lee et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2002.11761))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Inverse-square law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-square_law): geometric origin and history of $1/r^2$ laws.
- **Reference:** [PDG Review: Extra Dimensions (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf): Yukawa parametrization of KK gravitons and the torsion-balance bound on two extra dimensions.
- **Learn:** [The Eöt-Wash Group (University of Washington)](https://www.npl.washington.edu/eotwash/): programme and publications on inverse-square and equivalence-principle tests.
- **Primary:** [Adelberger, Heckel & Nelson, Tests of the Gravitational Inverse-Square Law](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0307284): review of theory motivations, parametrizations and experiments from nanometres to the Solar System.
- **Primary:** [Lee et al., New Test of the Gravitational $1/r^2$ Law at Separations down to $52\,\mu$m](https://arxiv.org/html/2002.11761): current Eöt-Wash bound.
- **Further reading:** [Burrage & Sakstein, Tests of Chameleon Gravity (Living Reviews in Relativity)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09071): screened scalar forces and the laboratory searches that constrain them.
references.Topological K-Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
Topological K-theory studies vector bundles over [topological spaces](node:Topological%20Spaces) by turning their isomorphism classes, under direct sum, into an abelian group: $K(X)$ is the Grothendieck group of the monoid of vector bundles on $X$, whose elements are virtual bundles $[E_+]-[E_-]$ ([nLab: topological K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory)). Hatcher describes it as the first generalized cohomology theory to be studied thoroughly, introduced around 1960 by Atiyah and Hirzebruch on the basis of Bott's periodicity theorem ([Hatcher, *Vector Bundles and K-Theory*](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).

Complex K-theory $KU$ and real K-theory $KO$ are generalized cohomology theories represented by spectra, periodic of period 2 and 8 by Bott periodicity ([nLab: topological K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory)). K-theory is tied to index theory: the index of a continuous family of Fredholm operators parametrized by $X$, kernel minus cokernel, is a class in $K(X)$ ([nLab: topological K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory)).

K-theory gave short solutions to classical problems in homotopy theory: with Adams operations it settles the Hopf invariant one problem, hence the classification of real division algebras and parallelizable spheres, and it gives the upper bound in the vector-fields-on-spheres problem ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf); [Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory)). Through operator K-theory and Kasparov's KK-theory it connects to noncommutative geometry, notably in the Baum–Connes conjecture ([Wikipedia: KK-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KK-theory); [Wikipedia: Baum–Connes conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture)).

### Formal definition
Let $X$ be compact Hausdorff and $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb C}(X)$ the commutative monoid of isomorphism classes of finite-rank complex vector bundles under Whitney sum. Then
$$K(X)=K^0(X)=\operatorname{Gr}\big(\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb C}(X)\big),$$
and tensor product makes $K(X)$ a commutative ring ([Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory)). In a Grothendieck group, $[a]-[b]=[c]-[d]$ iff $a+d+k=b+c+k$ for some $k$; the extra $k$ is needed because cancellation can fail ([Wikipedia: Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group)). The real version $KO(X)$ uses real bundles ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory)).

For pointed $X$, $\tilde K(X)$ measures bundles modulo trivial ones, and higher groups are defined by suspension,
$$\tilde K^{-n}(X)=\tilde K(S^nX).$$
Over a compact Hausdorff base every bundle is a direct summand of a trivial bundle, and $K(X)\cong[X_+,\mathbb Z\times BU]$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory); [Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory)).

**Clutching.** A map $f:S^{k-1}\to GL_n(\mathbb C)$ glues trivial bundles over the two hemispheres $D^k_\pm$ into a bundle $E_f\to S^k$, and $[S^{k-1},GL_n(\mathbb C)]\to\mathrm{Vect}^n_{\mathbb C}(S^k)$, $f\mapsto E_f$, is a bijection (Hatcher, Prop. 1.11) ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).

**Equivariant K-theory.** For a group $G$ acting on $X$, $K_G(X)$ is built from virtual $G$-equivariant bundles; a $G$-bundle over a point is a representation, so $K_G(\mathrm{pt})=R(G)$, the representation ring ([nLab: equivariant K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivariant+K-theory)).

**KK-theory.** Kasparov (1980) defined a bivariant group $KK(A,B)$ for separable $C^*$-algebras as homotopy classes of triples $(H,\rho,F)$ with $H$ a graded Hilbert $B$-module, $\rho$ a representation of $A$ and $F$ an odd operator; $KK(\mathbb C,B)\cong K_0(B)$, $KK(C_0(\mathbb R),B)\cong K_1(B)$, and the Kasparov product $KK(A,B)\times KK(B,C)\to KK(A,C)$ is bilinear ([Wikipedia: KK-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KK-theory)).

### Key results
- **Bott periodicity.** $\pi_i(U)\cong\pi_{i+2}(U)$ with $\pi_0(U)=0$, $\pi_1(U)=\mathbb Z$, and $\pi_i(O)$ is 8-periodic with $\pi_0,\dots,\pi_7(O)=\mathbb Z/2,\mathbb Z/2,0,\mathbb Z,0,0,0,\mathbb Z$; equivalently $\Omega^2BU\simeq\mathbb Z\times BU$ and $\Omega^8BO\simeq\mathbb Z\times BO$ ([Wikipedia: Bott periodicity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bott_periodicity_theorem)). In K-theory: the external product $K(X)\otimes\mathbb Z[H]/(H-1)^2\to K(X\times S^2)$ is a ring isomorphism for all compact Hausdorff $X$ (Hatcher, Thm 2.2), and $\beta:\tilde K(X)\to\tilde K(S^2X)$, $a\mapsto(H-1)*a$, is an isomorphism (Thm 2.11), where $H$ is the canonical line bundle on $S^2=\mathbb{CP}^1$ ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).
- **Cohomology theory and representability.** $K^*$ is a multiplicative generalized cohomology theory represented by the spectrum with spaces $\mathbb Z\times BU$ ([Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory)).
- **Even cell complexes.** If $X$ is a finite cell complex with $n$ cells, $K^*(X)$ is finitely generated with at most $n$ generators; if all cells have even dimension, $K^1(X)=0$ and $K^0(X)$ is free abelian with one basis element per cell (Hatcher, Prop. 2.23) ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).
- **Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence (1961).** For a CW complex $X$ and generalized cohomology theory $E$ there is a spectral sequence $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(X;E^q(\mathrm{pt}))$ converging conditionally to $E^{p+q}(X)$. For K-theory of a finite complex the odd rows vanish, and $d_3=\beta\circ Sq^2\circ r$, with $r$ reduction mod 2 and $\beta$ the Bockstein ([Wikipedia: AHSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Hirzebruch_spectral_sequence)).
- **Chern character.** $\mathrm{ch}(V)=\mathrm{rk}\,V+c_1+\tfrac12(c_1^2-2c_2)+\tfrac16(c_1^3-3c_1c_2+3c_3)+\cdots$ satisfies $\mathrm{ch}(V\oplus W)=\mathrm{ch}V+\mathrm{ch}W$ and $\mathrm{ch}(V\otimes W)=\mathrm{ch}V\,\mathrm{ch}W$, a ring homomorphism to (the completion of) rational cohomology ([Wikipedia: Chern character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chern_character)); for a finite CW complex it is a rational isomorphism on $K^0$ (Atiyah–Hirzebruch) ([Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory)).
- **Thom isomorphism.** If a rank-$n$ bundle $V\to X$ is $E$-oriented, cup product with a Thom class gives $E^\bullet(X)\cong\tilde E^{\bullet+n}(\mathrm{Th}(V))$ ([nLab: Thom isomorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Thom+isomorphism)); for $E=KU$, an oriented manifold $X$ is generalized-oriented ($X\to *$ is $KU$-oriented) precisely when it carries a $\mathrm{Spin}^c$-structure, which any almost complex structure induces ([nLab: spin^c structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin%5Ec+structure)).
- **Atiyah–Segal completion theorem (1969).** For a compact Lie group $G$ and a $G$-CW-complex $X$, the projection $X\times EG\to X$ induces an isomorphism of pro-rings $K^*_G(X)^\wedge_I\cong K^*((X\times EG)/G)$, completion at the augmentation ideal $I\subset R(G)$; in particular $K^*(BG)\cong R(G)^\wedge_I$. Atiyah proved the case of finite groups in 1961 ([Wikipedia: Atiyah–Segal completion theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Segal_completion_theorem)).
- **Vector fields on spheres (Adams 1962).** Write $n=(2a+1)2^{4d+c}$ with $0\le c<4$ and $\rho(n)=2^c+8d$. The maximal number of pointwise linearly independent vector fields on $S^{n-1}$ is exactly $\rho(n)-1$; Clifford-algebra constructions give the lower bound and K-theory the upper bound ([Wikipedia: Vector fields on spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_fields_on_spheres)).
- **Hopf invariant one (Adams; Adams–Atiyah).** A map $S^{4n-1}\to S^{2n}$ of Hopf invariant $\pm1$ exists only for $n=1,2,4$ (Hatcher, Thm 2.19), so $\mathbb R^n$ is a division algebra and $S^{n-1}$ is parallelizable only for $n=1,2,4,8$ (Thm 2.16) ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)). Adams proved it in 1960; Adams and Atiyah gave the K-theory proof in 1966 ([Wikipedia: Hopf invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_invariant)).

### Examples
- **Point.** $K(\mathrm{pt})\cong\mathbb Z$, since bundles over a point are classified by rank ([Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory)).
- **Spheres.** $K(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z[H]/(H-1)^2$ (Hatcher, Cor. 2.3), and repeated periodicity gives $\tilde K(S^n)=\mathbb Z$ for $n$ even and $0$ for $n$ odd; in particular $\tilde K^0(S^{2k+1})=0$, while $\tilde K^1(S^{2k+1})\cong\tilde K(S^{2k+2})\cong\mathbb Z$ since $\tilde K^1(Y)\cong\tilde K(SY)$ ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)). Real K-theory gives $\widetilde{KO}(S^n)=\mathbb Z_2,\mathbb Z_2,0,\mathbb Z,0,0,0,\mathbb Z$ for $n\equiv1,\dots,8\pmod 8$ ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).
- **Complex projective space.** $\mathbb{CP}^n$ has one cell in each dimension $0,2,\dots,2n$, so $K^1(\mathbb{CP}^n)=0$ and $K^0(\mathbb{CP}^n)\cong\mathbb Z^{n+1}$; as a ring $K(\mathbb{CP}^n)\cong\mathbb Z[L]/(L-1)^{n+1}$ with $L$ the canonical line bundle (Hatcher, Prop. 2.24) ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)).
- **Collapse of the AHSS.** Collapse can be checked on every $\mathbb{CP}^n$, on algebraic curves, and on spaces with nonzero cohomology only in even degrees; it follows that the sequence collapses for all complex even-dimensional smooth complete intersections in $\mathbb{CP}^n$ ([Wikipedia: AHSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Hirzebruch_spectral_sequence)).
- **Vector fields.** For odd $n$, $\rho(n)=1$, so $S^{n-1}$ has no nowhere-zero field; $\rho(16)=9$, so $S^{15}$ carries 8 independent fields ([Wikipedia: Vector fields on spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_fields_on_spheres)).

### History
Bott announced periodicity in 1957 and gave the full proof, by Morse theory, in 1959 ([Wikipedia: Bott periodicity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bott_periodicity_theorem)). Atiyah and Hirzebruch's "Vector bundles and homogeneous spaces" (Proc. Symp. Pure Math. 3, 1961, 7–38) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/pspum/003/0139181)) introduced their spectral sequence ([Wikipedia: AHSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Hirzebruch_spectral_sequence)). Adams's "Vector Fields on Spheres" appeared in *Annals of Mathematics* 75 (1962) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1970213)); Adams and Atiyah's "K-theory and the Hopf invariant" (Quart. J. Math. 1966) and Atiyah's book *K-Theory* (Benjamin, 1967) are listed in Hatcher's bibliography ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf)). Atiyah and Segal's "Equivariant K-theory and completion" appeared in *J. Differential Geom.* 3 (1969) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.4310/jdg/1214428815)). Kasparov introduced KK-theory in 1980 ([Wikipedia: KK-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KK-theory)); Baum and Connes proposed their conjecture in a 1982 IHES preprint, and the general precise statement is Baum–Connes–Higson 1994 ([Gomez Aparicio, Julg, Valette](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.10081)).

### Connections
- [Bott Periodicity](node:Bott%20Periodicity): makes $K^*$ 2-periodic and $KO^*$ 8-periodic.
- [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles) and [Holomorphic Vector Bundles](node:Holomorphic%20Vector%20Bundles): K-theory is built from vector bundles.
- [Characteristic Classes](node:Characteristic%20Classes): Chern classes and the Chern character map K-theory to rational cohomology.
- [Spectral Sequences](node:Spectral%20Sequences): the Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence computes $K^*(X)$ from cohomology.
- [Adams Operations](node:Adams%20Operations) and [Steenrod Operations](node:Steenrod%20Operations): Adams operations play in K-theory the role Steenrod operations play in cohomology.
- [Clifford Algebras](node:Clifford%20Algebras): Clifford modules construct vector fields on spheres and mirror Bott periodicity.
- [Atiyah-Singer Index Theorem](node:Atiyah-Singer%20Index%20Theorem): the index of an elliptic operator is a K-theory class.
- [Operator Algebra K-Theory](node:Operator%20Algebra%20K-Theory) and [C-Star Algebras and von Neumann Algebras](node:C-Star%20Algebras%20and%20von%20Neumann%20Algebras): KK-theory and the Baum–Connes assembly map live here.
- [Representation Theory](node:Representation%20Theory): $K_G(\mathrm{pt})=R(G)$ and the completion theorem.
- [Equivariant Topology](node:Equivariant%20Topology): equivariant K-theory is a basic equivariant cohomology theory.
- [Grassmannians](node:Grassmannians): $BU$ is a colimit of Grassmannians.
- [Topological Insulators](node:Topological%20Insulators): band structures are classified by (twisted, equivariant) K-theory.

### Common pitfalls
- **Monoid vs. group.** $\mathrm{Vect}(X)$ is not a group; group completion adds formal differences, and the stabilizing summand is needed because cancellation can fail ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory); [Wikipedia: Grothendieck group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_group)).
- **Compactness matters.** The bundle definition and the summand-of-trivial lemma are for compact Hausdorff $X$; in general one uses the represented theory $[X_+,\mathbb Z\times BU]$ ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory)).
- **Even cohomology is sufficient, not necessary, for collapse.** The AHSS collapses for spaces with nonzero cohomology only in even degrees, but also for algebraic curves; and the collapse stated for smooth complete intersections is for even complex dimension ([Wikipedia: AHSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Hirzebruch_spectral_sequence)).
- **Rational vs. integral.** The Chern character identifies K-theory with cohomology only after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$; integrally the differential $d_3=\beta Sq^2r$ involves mod-2 operations ([Wikipedia: AHSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiyah%E2%80%93Hirzebruch_spectral_sequence)).
- **Orientability.** The Thom isomorphism needs an orientation for the theory: for $KU$ a $\mathrm{Spin}^c$-structure, not merely an ordinary orientation ([nLab: spin^c structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin%5Ec+structure)).

### Open problems
- **Baum–Connes conjecture.** For a locally compact group $G$, the assembly map $\mu_r:K_*^{\mathrm{top}}(G)\to K_*(C^*_r(G))$, $*=0,1$, from the $G$-equivariant K-homology of the classifying space $\underline EG$ for proper actions (defined via Kasparov's equivariant KK-theory) to the K-theory of the reduced group $C^*$-algebra, is conjectured to be an isomorphism. The version with coefficients holds for groups with the Haagerup property (Higson–Kasparov) and for hyperbolic groups (Lafforgue), but is false in general, and the groupoid version is false; for the conjecture without coefficients the survey says "For BC without coefficients we don't know", and surjectivity is open for $SL_3(\mathbb Z)$ ([Gomez Aparicio, Julg, Valette](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1905.10081)). Wikipedia lists the conjecture without coefficients as open, with $SL_3(\mathbb Z)$ the simplest unresolved group; surjectivity would imply the Kadison–Kaplansky conjecture for torsion-free discrete groups, and injectivity is closely related to the Novikov conjecture ([Wikipedia: Baum–Connes conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baum%E2%80%93Connes_conjecture)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: topological K-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+K-theory): definitions, $KU$/$KO$ spectra, index theory.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Topological K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_K-theory): properties, Bott periodicity, Chern character, applications.
- **Learn:** [Hatcher, *Vector Bundles and K-Theory*](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VBpage.html): free partial book; clutching, product theorem, complex Bott periodicity, $K(\mathbb{CP}^n)$, Adams operations and Hopf invariant one.
- **Learn:** [Gomez Aparicio, Julg, Valette, "The Baum–Connes conjecture: an extended survey"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10081): KK-theory, assembly map, known cases and counterexamples.
- **Primary:** [Atiyah and Hirzebruch, "Vector bundles and homogeneous spaces" (1961)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/pspum/003/0139181): founding paper of topological K-theory and its spectral sequence.
- **Primary:** [Adams, "Vector Fields on Spheres" (Ann. Math. 75, 1962)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1970213): the K-theoretic solution of the vector-fields problem.
- **Primary:** [Atiyah and Segal, "Equivariant K-theory and completion" (J. Diff. Geom. 3, 1969)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.4310/jdg/1214428815): the completion theorem.
- **Primary:** [Higson and Kasparov, "E-theory and KK-theory for groups which act properly and isometrically on Hilbert space" (Invent. Math. 144, 2001)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/s002220000118): Baum–Connes with coefficients for Haagerup groups.
- **Further reading:** [Karoubi, *K-Theory: An Introduction* (Springer, Classics in Mathematics)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-540-79890-3): book-length introduction to K-theory.
