## Reference
### Overview
A topological space is a set with a structure, its topology, that formalizes closeness without a numeric distance. The usual axiomatization specifies the open sets. Equivalent formulations use neighbourhoods, closed sets, Kuratowski closure operators, or convergence of nets. Topological spaces are the general setting for continuity, limits, compactness, and connectedness, and they include Euclidean spaces, metric spaces, and manifolds. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space))

Hatcher describes topology as qualitative geometry: two objects are the same if one can be continuously transformed into the other, i.e. if they are homeomorphic. A circle and a square are homeomorphic. A figure-eight is not homeomorphic to a circle, since removing its crossing point leaves two pieces. ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf))

General (point-set) topology studies which properties a topology can have and how they interact. These include separation axioms, countability axioms, compactness, connectedness, and metrizability. Some of its questions, such as whether every normal Moore space is metrizable, cannot be settled in ZFC set theory alone. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore_space_%28topology%29))

### Formal definition
**Open sets.** A topology on $X$ is a family $\tau\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ containing $\varnothing$ and $X$ that is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. Its members are open, and their complements are closed. Infinite intersections need not be open: $\bigcap_n(-1/n,1/n)=\{0\}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space); [Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf))

**Bases and countability.** A base $\mathcal B\subseteq\tau$ is a family such that every open set is a union of members of $\mathcal B$; the open intervals form a base for $\mathbb R$. $X$ is second-countable if it has a countable base, and first-countable if every point has a countable local base. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-countable_space))

**Continuity and homeomorphism.** $f:X\to Y$ is continuous if $f^{-1}(U)$ is open for every open $U\subseteq Y$. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism))

**Constructions.** In the subspace topology on $A\subseteq X$, the open sets are the $U\cap A$ with $U$ open. The product topology on $\prod_iX_i$ is generated by inverse images of open sets under the projections; its basic open sets are $\prod_iU_i$ with $U_i=X_i$ for all but finitely many $i$. For a surjection $f:X\to Y$, the quotient topology is the finest topology on $Y$ making $f$ continuous. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space); [Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf))

**Separation axioms.** $T_0$: distinct points are topologically distinguishable. $T_1$: distinct points are separated, equivalently points are closed. $T_2$ (Hausdorff): distinct points have disjoint neighbourhoods. Regular: a point and a closed set not containing it have disjoint neighbourhoods. Completely regular: they can be separated by a continuous function. Normal: disjoint closed sets have disjoint neighbourhoods. $T_3$ is $T_0$ plus regular, $T_{3\frac12}$ is $T_0$ plus completely regular, and $T_4$ is $T_1$ plus normal. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_axiom))

**Compactness and connectedness.** $X$ is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. $X$ is connected if it is not a union of two disjoint nonempty open sets, and path-connected if any two points are joined by a path. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connected_space))

**Nets.** A net is a function from a directed set into $X$. Every sequence is a net indexed by $\mathbb N$. Nets and filters give equivalent theories of convergence. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_%28mathematics%29))

### Key results
- **Nets characterize the topology.** A set is closed if and only if it contains the limits of all nets in it. $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only if it preserves limits of nets converging to $x$. $X$ is compact if and only if every net has a convergent subnet. Limits of nets are unique if and only if $X$ is Hausdorff. Sequences do not suffice in general. They do suffice to detect closed sets in sequential spaces, which include all first-countable and metric spaces. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_%28mathematics%29))
- **Compactness.** Continuous images of compact spaces are compact, closed subsets of compact spaces are compact, and compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed. Heine–Borel: a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. A continuous real function on a **nonempty** compact space is bounded and attains its supremum. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space))
- **Tychonoff's theorem.** Any product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology. Tychonoff proved this for powers of $[0,1]$ in 1930 and in general in 1935. The full theorem is equivalent to the axiom of choice (Kelley); the Hausdorff case is equivalent to the strictly weaker Boolean prime ideal theorem. The box topology does not preserve compactness: an infinite box product of finite discrete spaces with at least two points is discrete and infinite. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tychonoff%27s_theorem); [Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf))
- **Connectedness.** Continuous images of connected spaces are connected, which generalizes the intermediate value theorem. Path-connected spaces are connected, but the topologist's sine curve is connected and not path-connected. The connected subsets of $\mathbb R$ are exactly the intervals and rays. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connected_space))
- **Urysohn's lemma.** $X$ is normal if and only if for all disjoint nonempty closed $A,B$ there is a continuous $f:X\to[0,1]$ with $f|_A=0$ and $f|_B=1$. It generalizes to the Tietze extension theorem. Compact Hausdorff spaces and metric spaces are normal. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urysohn%27s_lemma); [Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf))
- **Metrization theorems.** Urysohn–Tikhonov: every second-countable regular Hausdorff space is metrizable. Urysohn's posthumous 1925 paper treated the normal case, and Tikhonov proved the regular form in 1926. Nagata–Smirnov: $X$ is metrizable if and only if it is regular, Hausdorff, and has a $\sigma$-locally finite base. Smirnov: a locally metrizable space is metrizable if and only if it is Hausdorff and paracompact. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrization_theorem))
- **Countability.** Second-countable spaces are separable and Lindelöf. For metric spaces, second-countable, separable, and Lindelöf are equivalent. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-countable_space))
- **Invariance of dimension.** $\mathbb R^m$ and $\mathbb R^n$ are not homeomorphic for $m\neq n$; the usual proof uses invariance of domain. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism))

### Examples
- **Discrete, trivial, cofinite.** In the discrete topology every set is open, and in the trivial topology only $\varnothing$ and $X$ are. The cofinite topology, with open sets $\varnothing$ and sets of finite complement, is the smallest $T_1$ topology on an infinite set. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space))
- **Lower-limit topology.** The lower-limit topology on $\mathbb R$, with base $[a,b)$, is strictly finer than the Euclidean topology. It is first-countable, separable, and Lindelöf but not second-countable, so it is not metrizable. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-countable_space))
- **A continuous bijection that is not a homeomorphism.** $[0,2\pi)\to S^1$, $\varphi\mapsto(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$, has an inverse that is discontinuous at $(1,0)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism))
- **Cantor set.** It is homeomorphic to the product $\{0,2\}^{\mathbb N}$ of discrete two-point spaces, and it is compact by Tychonoff. ([Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf))
- **Dowker spaces.** A Dowker space is $T_4$ but not countably paracompact. Rudin constructed the first one (1971), of size $\aleph_\omega^{\aleph_0}$; Balogh (1996) gave a ZFC example of [cardinality](node:Cardinality) $\mathfrak c$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowker_space))

### History
Euler solved the Königsberg bridge problem in 1736. He stated the polyhedron formula $v-e+f=2$ in a 1750 letter to Goldbach; MacTutor dates its publication, in two papers, to 1752, while the Euler characteristic article cites *Elementa doctrinae solidorum* in the *Novi Commentarii* under 1758. ([MacTutor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Topology_in_mathematics/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_characteristic)) Listing published *Vorstudien zur Topologie* in 1847. Poincaré's *Analysis Situs* appeared in 1895 in the *Journal de l'École Polytechnique*, followed by five supplements (1899–1904). ([MacTutor](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Topology_in_mathematics/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_Situs_%28paper%29)) Fréchet introduced metric spaces and the term compactness in 1906. Hausdorff defined topological spaces by four neighbourhood axioms in 1914 and included the $T_2$ axiom. Alexandrov and Urysohn developed the open-cover form of compactness. Moore and Smith introduced nets in 1922, and Cartan introduced filters in 1937. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_%28mathematics%29))

### Connections
- [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces): every metric induces a topology; metrization theorems characterize which topologies arise.
- [Hausdorff Space](node:Hausdorff%20Space): the $T_2$ axiom and uniqueness of limits.
- [Homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism): the isomorphisms of the category of topological spaces.
- [Compactness and Connectedness](node:Compactness%20and%20Connectedness): the two central topological properties.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): Tychonoff versus choice and ZFC-independence of metrization questions.
- [Partial Orders](node:Partial%20Orders): the topologies on a set form a complete lattice; nets are indexed by directed sets.
- [Functions and Relations](node:Functions%20and%20Relations): continuity of maps between spaces.
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): the standard topology on $\mathbb R$ and Heine–Borel.
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): second-countable Hausdorff locally Euclidean spaces with a smooth atlas.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group) and [Homology](node:Homology): algebraic invariants of homeomorphism type.
- [Polytopes](node:Polytopes): Euler's $v-e+f=2$ was an early topological invariant.
- [Graph Theory](node:Graph%20Theory): the Königsberg bridge problem.
- Map: [MSC 54 - General topology](node:MSC%2054%20-%20General%20topology), [MSC 54Axx - Generalities in topology](node:MSC%2054Axx%20-%20Generalities%20in%20topology), [MSC 54Dxx - Fairly general properties of topological spaces](node:MSC%2054Dxx%20-%20Fairly%20general%20properties%20of%20topological%20spaces)

### Common pitfalls
- **The open-cover definition is the definition of compactness.** Sequential compactness differs in general, though it agrees for second-countable spaces. Bourbaki and much of algebraic geometry reserve "compact" for Hausdorff spaces and say "quasi-compact" otherwise. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-countable_space))
- **Separation-axiom conventions vary.** "Regular" and "$T_3$", and "normal" and "$T_4$", are sometimes used interchangeably, and authors differ on whether $T_1$ is included. Hatcher includes Hausdorff in "normal". ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_axiom); [Hatcher](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf))
- **Quotients can lose separation.** Subspaces and products of Hausdorff spaces are Hausdorff, but quotients need not be. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_space))
- **Sequences are not enough.** Outside sequential spaces (for example, first-countable spaces), closed sets cannot in general be detected by sequences, and nets or filters must be used. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_%28mathematics%29))
- **Metric properties are not topological.** Homeomorphic metric spaces can differ in completeness. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism))

### Open problems
- **Efimov's problem.** Does every infinite compact Hausdorff space contain either a nontrivial convergent sequence or a copy of $\beta\mathbb N$? Brian and Dow call it "a longstanding open problem of set-theoretic topology". A negative answer has been known to be consistent with ZFC since the 1970s (Fedorčuk), and it is unknown whether a positive answer is consistent. ([ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.06055); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.06055))
- **Bing–Borsuk conjecture (1965).** Every $n$-dimensional homogeneous absolute neighbourhood retract is a topological manifold. It is proved for $n=1,2$ and unsolved in general. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bing%E2%80%93Borsuk_conjecture))
- **Context: independence.** The normal Moore space conjecture, that every normal Moore space is metrizable, is not open in the usual sense but cannot be decided in ZFC alone: it fails under CH and under MA$+\neg$CH, and holds under PMEA, which needs a large cardinal. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore_space_%28topology%29))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Topological space (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) and [Separation axiom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_axiom): axioms, constructions, and conventions.
- **Learn:** [Hatcher, *Notes on Introductory Point-Set Topology*](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf): Cornell notes on bases, subspaces, products, connectedness, compactness, normal spaces, infinite products, and quotients.
- **Primary:** Brian and Dow, [*Small cardinals and small Efimov spaces*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.06055): a research paper on Efimov's problem with a survey of known consistency results.
- **Further reading:** Munkres, [*Topology*](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=topology+munkres&fields=title,author_name,first_publish_year,publisher&limit=5) (Prentice Hall); Willard, [*General Topology*](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=general+topology+willard&fields=title,author_name,first_publish_year,publisher&limit=5) (1970; Dover reprint); Engelking, [*General Topology*](https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=general+topology+engelking&fields=title,author_name,first_publish_year,publisher&limit=5), originally *Topologia ogólna*.
references.Transformers:
## Reference
### Overview
A Transformer is a neural sequence model built entirely from [attention](node:Attention%20Mechanism) and position-wise feed-forward layers, with no recurrence or convolution. The original model, introduced for [machine translation](node:Machine%20Translation) in "Attention Is All You Need" (2017), stacks $N=6$ encoder and $N=6$ decoder layers; each layer combines multi-head self-attention with a two-layer MLP, wrapped in residual connections and layer normalization. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))

Three families descend from it: encoder-only models (BERT, 2018) with bidirectional self-attention for representation learning; decoder-only models (the GPT series, from 2018) with causal self-attention for generation; and encoder–decoder models (T5) that connect the two with cross-attention. Vision transformers treat image patches as tokens. ([Wikipedia: Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29)) Decoder-only Transformers, used for text generation, underlie [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models) such as the GPT series. ([Wikipedia: Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29))

The architecture's advantage over recurrent networks is parallelism: a self-attention layer connects every pair of positions in $O(1)$ sequential steps, at a cost quadratic in sequence length. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7)) Empirically, the cross-entropy loss of Transformer language models scales as a power law in model size, dataset size and training compute. ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361))

### Formal definition
Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_{\text{model}}}$ be the sequence of token embeddings plus positional encodings. With multi-head attention
$$\operatorname{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1,\dots,\mathrm{head}_h)W^O,\quad \mathrm{head}_i=\operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QW_i^Q (KW_i^K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)VW_i^V,$$
and position-wise feed-forward network $\operatorname{FFN}(x)=\max(0,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2$, the original (post-LN) encoder layer computes
$$X' = \operatorname{LayerNorm}\big(X + \operatorname{MultiHead}(X,X,X)\big),\qquad X''=\operatorname{LayerNorm}\big(X'+\operatorname{FFN}(X')\big).$$
A decoder layer inserts a masked self-attention sublayer (scores of future positions set to $-\infty$) and an encoder–decoder attention sublayer whose queries come from the decoder and keys/values from the encoder output. Positions enter through sinusoidal encodings $PE_{(pos,2i)}=\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})$, $PE_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})$ added to the embeddings. The base model uses $d_{\text{model}}=512$, $d_{\text{ff}}=2048$, $h=8$, $d_k=d_v=64$. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))

The pre-LN variant moves layer normalization inside the residual branch, $X' = X + \operatorname{MultiHead}(\operatorname{LN}(X))$, and was found easier to train, needing no learning-rate warm-up. ([Wikipedia: Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29)) The output layer ("unembedding") is a linear map followed by a softmax over the vocabulary, often tied to the transposed embedding matrix. ([Wikipedia: Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29))

### Key results
- **Universal approximation.** Transformers are universal approximators of continuous permutation-equivariant sequence-to-sequence functions with compact support; with positional encodings they approximate arbitrary continuous sequence-to-sequence functions on a compact domain. Self-attention layers computing "contextual mappings" are the key ingredient. ([Yun et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.10077))
- **Circuit upper bound.** Log-precision softmax Transformer encoders recognize only languages in DLOGTIME-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ (Merrill and Sabharwal), extending the $\mathsf{TC}^0$ upper bound shown earlier for average-hard attention (Merrill et al. 2022). ([Strobl et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.00208v3))
- **Chain of thought increases power.** A decoder with $O(\log(n+T(n)))$ precision and $O(T(n))$ intermediate decoding steps can simulate a $T(n)$-step Turing machine, and with polynomially many steps recognizes exactly $\mathsf P$ (Merrill and Sabharwal 2024); with arbitrary precision and unboundedly many steps, encoder–decoders recognize any recursively enumerable language (Pérez et al. 2021). ([Strobl et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.00208v3))
- **Quadratic lower bound for self-attention.** The time complexity of self-attention is necessarily quadratic in the input length unless the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) is false; the argument holds even if attention is computed only approximately, and for a variety of attention mechanisms. ([Keles, Wijewardena and Hegde 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04881))
- **Post-LN instability.** For post-LN Transformers at initialization, mean-field analysis shows the expected gradients of parameters near the output are large, which explains why warm-up is needed; pre-LN keeps gradients well-behaved and trains without warm-up. ([Xiong et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745))
- **Neural scaling laws.** Language-model cross-entropy follows power laws in parameters, dataset size and compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude, while width and depth matter little within a wide range. ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)) Fitting over 400 models from 70M to over 16B parameters, Hoffmann et al. find instead that compute-optimal training scales parameters and tokens equally; their 70B Chinchilla, trained on 4x more data than the 280B Gopher with the same compute, outperformed it. ([Hoffmann et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556))

### Examples
- **WMT 2014 translation.** The big Transformer reached 28.4 BLEU on English–German newstest2014, at a training cost of about $2.3\cdot10^{19}$ FLOPs. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))
- **Decoder-only language models.** GPT-style models use only causal self-attention and generate text autoregressively; the feed-forward width is typically larger than the embedding width ($4\times$ in GPT-2 and BERT), and where the original Transformer used ReLU, GPT-1 and BERT used GELU and Llama and PaLM used SwiGLU. ([Wikipedia: Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29))

### History
Recurrent models such as LSTMs were the standard for long sequences until 2017; attention was first added to recurrent seq2seq models, and in 2016 decomposable attention applied self-attention to feed-forward networks. ([Wikipedia: Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29)) Vaswani et al. posted "Attention Is All You Need" on 12 June 2017 ([arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)), replacing recurrence with an attention-only encoder–decoder for translation. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7)) BERT and the GPT series followed in 2018. ([Wikipedia: Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29))

### Connections
- [Attention Mechanism](node:Attention%20Mechanism): the core operation; multi-head scaled dot-product attention.
- [Residual Networks](node:Residual%20Networks) and [Normalization in Neural Networks](node:Normalization%20in%20Neural%20Networks): each sublayer is a residual block with layer normalization.
- [Recurrent Neural Networks](node:Recurrent%20Neural%20Networks): the architecture the Transformer replaced for sequence modeling.
- [Large Language Models](node:Large%20Language%20Models), [Language Modeling](node:Language%20Modeling) and [Language Model Pretraining Objectives](node:Language%20Model%20Pretraining%20Objectives): decoder-only and encoder-only Transformers trained at scale.
- [Subword Tokenization](node:Subword%20Tokenization): produces the token sequence the model consumes.
- [Rotary Positional Embeddings](node:Rotary%20Positional%20Embeddings): a later positional scheme replacing sinusoidal encodings.
- [Vision Transformers](node:Vision%20Transformers), [Graph Transformers](node:Graph%20Transformers), [Decision Transformer](node:Decision%20Transformer): the architecture applied to images, graphs and trajectories.
- [Linear Attention](node:Linear%20Attention), [State Space Models](node:State%20Space%20Models), [Mixture of Experts](node:Mixture%20of%20Experts): efficiency-motivated variants and alternatives.
- [Scaling Laws](node:Scaling%20Laws): power-law loss curves were measured mainly on Transformers.
- [In-Context Learning](node:In-Context%20Learning) and [Mechanistic Interpretability](node:Mechanistic%20Interpretability): behaviors of trained Transformers and methods for reverse-engineering them.

### Common pitfalls
- Without positional information a Transformer encoder cannot see token order: the functions it computes are permutation-equivariant (permuting the input permutes the output), which is why positional encodings are needed to approximate arbitrary sequence-to-sequence functions. ([Wikipedia: Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29); [Yun et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.10077))
- Layer normalization, not batch normalization, is standard: it normalizes across the feature dimension and so is independent of batch size, and batch normalization is usually empirically less effective in NLP, where inputs are often variable-length sequences. ([Dive into Deep Learning, §11.7](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/transformer.html))
- "Quadratic cost" refers to sequence length $n$: a self-attention layer costs $O(n^2 d)$ against $O(n d^2)$ for a recurrent layer, so it is the cheaper of the two when $n<d$. ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7))
- Kaplan et al.'s compute-optimal allocation (large models, modest data) was revised by Hoffmann et al., who recommend scaling tokens and parameters equally. ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361); [Hoffmann et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556))

### Open problems
- **Expressivity of real Transformers.** Strobl et al. list as open whether softmax-attention Transformers can be characterized exactly by a logic, how positional encodings, softmax versus average-hard attention, pre- versus post-norm, and BOS/EOS/CLS tokens affect expressivity, and what circuits and logic can say about Transformer decoders. ([Strobl et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.00208v3))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Transformer (deep learning architecture), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_%28deep_learning_architecture%29): variants, components, history.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning, §11.7 The Transformer Architecture](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/transformer.html): encoder and decoder blocks implemented step by step.
- **Primary:** [Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7): the original architecture.
- **Primary:** [Kaplan et al., Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361): power-law scaling of Transformer language models.
- **Further reading:** [Strobl, Merrill, Weiss, Chiang and Angluin, What Formal Languages Can Transformers Express? (TACL 2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.00208v3): survey of the theory of Transformer expressivity.
references.Turing Machines:
## Reference
### Overview
A Turing machine is a finite-state control attached to an unbounded tape of symbols, read and written one cell at a time by a head that moves left or right. Turing introduced these "automatic machines" in "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem" (*Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society* s2-42, 230–265, 1937) to make precise which real numbers are computable; Church named them "Turing machines" in his 1937 review ([SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/), [Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.230)).

The model matters for two reasons. In computability theory, it gave a universal machine, a single machine that simulates any other from its description, and it gave a negative answer to Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem: no general method decides derivability in [first-order logic](node:First-Order%20Logic) ([SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/)). In complexity theory, it is the reference model for measuring time and space, which is how a theory-of-computation course moves from decidability and reducibility to complexity classes, completeness and the hierarchy theorems ([MIT OCW 18.404J](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/)).

The Church–Turing thesis asserts that the Turing-computable functions are exactly the effectively calculable ones. The λ-definable, general recursive and Turing-computable functions on the positive integers provably coincide, but the thesis itself is not a theorem, because "effectively calculable" is an informal notion ([SEP: The Church-Turing Thesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/church-turing/)).

### Formal definition
Following the Stanford Encyclopedia, a Turing machine is a quadruple
$$T=(Q,\Sigma,s,\delta),\qquad \delta:Q\times\Sigma\rightharpoonup \Sigma\times\{L,R\}\times Q,$$
where $Q$ is a finite set of states, $\Sigma$ a finite tape alphabet containing a blank, $s\in Q$ the initial state, and $\delta$ the transition function. At each step the machine, in state $q$ reading symbol $a$, writes $b$, moves the head one cell in direction $D$, and enters state $q'$ where $\delta(q,a)=(b,D,q')$. In Post's formulation the tape is infinite in both directions and the machine halts when $\delta$ is undefined on the current pair; Turing's original tape was one-way infinite ([SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/)).

A configuration records the state, tape contents and head position; a computation is the sequence of configurations from the initial one. A partial function $f:\mathbb N\rightharpoonup\mathbb N$ is Turing-computable if some machine started on an encoding of $n$ halts with an encoding of $f(n)$ exactly when $f(n)$ is defined. For complexity, $\mathrm{DTIME}(t(n))$ is the class of languages decided by a deterministic multitape machine in $O(t(n))$ steps, and $\mathrm{NTIME}(t(n))$ is the nondeterministic analogue ([Wikipedia: Time hierarchy theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_hierarchy_theorem)).

### Key results
- **Universal machine (Turing 1936).** There is a single machine $U$ which, given the standard description of any machine $T$ on its tape, simulates $T$ by writing out $T$'s successive complete configurations; Post later corrected a defect in Turing's construction. ([SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/))
- **Efficient universal simulation (Hennie–Stearns 1966).** If machine $M_\alpha$ halts on input $x$ within $N$ steps, a multitape universal machine halts on $(\alpha,x)$ within $CN\log N$ steps, where $C$ depends on $M$'s alphabet size, number of tapes and number of states but not on the input length. ([Wikipedia: Universal Turing machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Turing_machine))
- **Undecidability of halting.** No machine decides, for every machine $T$ and input, whether $T$ halts; the proof is a diagonal argument from a hypothetical halting decider. Turing proved the closely related PRINT? problem undecidable and used it to show the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable; Church obtained the Entscheidungsproblem result independently in 1936. ([SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/))
- **Rice's theorem (1951/1953).** For an admissible numbering $\varphi$ of the partial computable functions, every index set $P\subseteq\mathbb N$ that is non-trivial ($\emptyset\ne P\ne\mathbb N$) and extensional ($\varphi_i=\varphi_j$ implies $i\in P\Leftrightarrow j\in P$) is undecidable; the only decidable index sets are $\emptyset$ and $\mathbb N$. ([Wikipedia: Rice's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice%27s_theorem))
- **Robustness of the model.** Two symbols suffice given enough states, and states can be exchanged for symbols (Shannon 1956); non-erasing machines compute the same functions (Wang 1957); any $n$-tape machine reduces to a single-tape machine (Hartmanis–Stearns 1965); higher-dimensional tapes reduce to one dimension; nondeterminism does not enlarge the class of computable functions. ([SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/), [Wikipedia: Universal Turing machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Turing_machine))
- **Equivalence of formalisms (1936).** Church and Kleene proved that the λ-definable functions of positive integers are exactly the recursive ones, and Turing proved λ-definability equivalent to Turing computability. ([SEP: The Church-Turing Thesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/church-turing/))
- **Time hierarchy theorem.** For time-constructible $f$, $\mathrm{DTIME}(o(f(n)))\subsetneq\mathrm{DTIME}(f(n)\log f(n))$ (Hartmanis–Stearns 1965); for time-constructible $g$ with $f(n+1)=o(g(n))$, $\mathrm{NTIME}(f(n))\subsetneq\mathrm{NTIME}(g(n))$ (Cook 1972; refined by Seiferas, Fischer and Meyer in 1978 and given a simpler proof by Žák in 1983). In particular $\mathrm P\subsetneq\mathrm{EXPTIME}$. ([Wikipedia: Time hierarchy theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_hierarchy_theorem))
- **Busy beaver $S(5)$.** Let $S(n)$ be the maximum number of steps taken by a halting $n$-state, 2-symbol machine started on the all-zero tape. The bbchallenge Collaboration proved $S(5)=47{,}176{,}870$, with the proof formalized in Coq, the first new Busy Beaver value in over 40 years. ([arXiv:2509.12337](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.12337))

### Examples
- **Small universal machines.** Minsky found a 7-state, 4-symbol universal machine in 1962 using 2-tag systems; universal machines are known for state–symbol pairs including $(15,2),(9,3),(6,4),(5,5),(4,6),(3,9),(2,18)$, Rogozhin's $(4,6)$ machine using 22 instructions; no one-state universal machine exists (Shannon). ([Wikipedia: Universal Turing machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Turing_machine))
- **Weak universality.** Neary and Woods gave weakly universal machines simulating the Rule 110 cellular automaton for $(6,2),(3,3),(2,4)$, where weak universality allows an infinitely repeated word on the tape. ([Wikipedia: Universal Turing machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Turing_machine))
- **Undecidable word problem.** Post (1947) showed the word problem for semigroups (Thue's problem) unsolvable. ([SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/))

### History
Turing's paper of 1936–37 introduced the machines, the universal machine, and the undecidability of the Entscheidungsproblem; Church named the machines in his 1937 review ([SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/)). Church's thesis of 1936 identified effective calculability with λ-definability or recursiveness; Kleene introduced the names "Church's thesis" (1952) and "Church-Turing thesis" (1967) ([SEP: The Church-Turing Thesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/church-turing/)). Stearns and Hartmanis first proved the deterministic time hierarchy theorem in 1965 ([Wikipedia: Time hierarchy theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_hierarchy_theorem)), and Cook and Levin independently formulated P versus NP in 1971 ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/)).

### Connections
- [Automata and Formal Languages](node:Automata%20and%20Formal%20Languages) and [Finite Automata](node:Finite%20Automata): Turing machines add an unbounded read-write tape to finite-state control.
- [Computability Theory](node:Computability%20Theory): the theory of what Turing machines can and cannot compute.
- [Lambda Calculus](node:Lambda%20Calculus): an equivalent model of computation, by the 1936 equivalence theorems.
- [Rice's Theorem](node:Rice's%20Theorem): the general undecidability of semantic properties of programs.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems) and [Hilbert's Tenth Problem](node:Hilbert's%20Tenth%20Problem): other undecidability results reducible to halting.
- [Computational Complexity Theory](node:Computational%20Complexity%20Theory), [P versus NP](node:P%20versus%20NP), [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): complexity classes are defined by resource-bounded Turing machines.
- [Kolmogorov Complexity](node:Kolmogorov%20Complexity): description length relative to a universal machine.
- [Cellular Automata](node:Cellular%20Automata): Rule 110 underlies the smallest weakly universal machines.
- [Circuit Complexity](node:Circuit%20Complexity) and [Descriptive Complexity](node:Descriptive%20Complexity): alternative characterizations of Turing-machine complexity classes.

### Common pitfalls
- The Church–Turing thesis is not a theorem and cannot be proved in the ordinary sense; the equivalence of formalisms is evidence for it, and the source notes that equivalence alone is not conclusive ([SEP: The Church-Turing Thesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/church-turing/)).
- The classical thesis concerns what a human computer can do by rule; Turing's 1936 version is about numbers that "would naturally be regarded as computable", not about what any physical device can compute ([SEP: The Church-Turing Thesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/church-turing/)).
- Model variants are equivalent in what they compute but not in how fast: the hierarchy theorem and the $N\log N$ universal simulation are stated for multitape machines ([Wikipedia: Time hierarchy theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_hierarchy_theorem), [Wikipedia: Universal Turing machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Turing_machine)).
- Rice's theorem needs both hypotheses: the property must be non-trivial and extensional, i.e. depend only on the function computed, not on the program text ([Wikipedia: Rice's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice%27s_theorem)).

### Open problems
- **P versus NP.** Whether every problem whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time is unsolved and is a Clay Millennium Prize Problem ([Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/)).
- **$S(6)$ and the Cryptids.** The bbchallenge paper reports that the 6-state champion halts after more than $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow5$ steps, that about 2,600 six-state holdouts remain, and predicts that $S(6)$ "will never be proved". The 6-state machine Antihydra is a "Cryptid": its behaviour is governed by a Collatz-like iteration, the associated conjecture (that there are never more than twice as many odd as even numbers in the iteration) is open, and the authors write that properly proving Antihydra does not halt is believed mathematically hard ([arXiv:2509.12337 (HTML)](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.12337v1)).
- **Five-state questions.** The same paper lists as future work characterizing all 5-state counters, finding the biggest loop among 5-state machines with no halting transitions, and whether there is a universal Turing machine with 5 states ([arXiv:2509.12337 (HTML)](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.12337v1)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Turing Machines](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/): definitions, Turing's 1936 paper, universality, undecidability, variants.
- **Reference:** [SEP: The Church-Turing Thesis](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/church-turing/): formulations, equivalence results, status of the thesis.
- **Learn:** [MIT OCW 18.404J Theory of Computation (Sipser)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/): decidability, reducibility, time and space complexity, hierarchy theorems.
- **Primary:** [bbchallenge Collaboration, Determination of the fifth Busy Beaver value](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.12337): formal proof of $S(5)$ and a list of open questions.
- **Primary:** [Turing 1937, On Computable Numbers (Crossref record)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.230): the founding paper.
- **Further reading:** [Arora and Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach (Cambridge University Press)](https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/): graduate text building complexity theory on the Turing machine model.
references.Type Theory:
## Reference
### Overview
A type theory is a formal system in which every term carries a type, and the typing rules restrict which terms can be combined; a function can be applied only to an argument of its domain type. Russell introduced the first such system to block the paradoxes of naive set theory, and Church reformulated simple type theory using the lambda calculus in 1940. Later systems added polymorphism (Girard, Reynolds), dependent types and universes (Martin-Löf), and the univalence axiom (Voevodsky). ([SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/))

Martin-Löf's dependent type theory, also called intuitionistic type theory, was developed to support constructive mathematics. It interprets first-order intuitionistic logic by reading propositions as types, and its intensional form has enough computational content to serve as a programming language. ([nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory)) The reading of propositions as types is the Curry–Howard correspondence: a proof is a program, and the formula it proves is the program's type. ([Wikipedia: Curry–Howard correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence))

Type theories underlie proof assistants. The calculus of constructions was developed alongside the Rocq (formerly Coq) proof assistant, and variants of it are used in Matita and Lean. ([Wikipedia: Calculus of constructions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_constructions)) On the semantic side, Seely proposed locally cartesian closed categories as the basic models of dependent type theory, and Hofmann and Dybjer refined this to categories with families. ([Wikipedia: Intuitionistic type theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuitionistic_type_theory))

### Formal definition
Martin-Löf type theory has three basic judgment forms: $\Gamma\ \mathsf{ctx}$ (a well-formed context), $\Gamma\vdash A\ \mathsf{type}$ (a type in context $\Gamma$), and $\Gamma\vdash a:A$ (a term of type $A$), together with judgmental (definitional) equality $a\equiv b:A$. Each type former is given by formation, introduction, elimination, and computation rules, with an optional uniqueness rule. ([nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory))

**Dependent products.** If $\Gamma\vdash A\ \mathsf{type}$ and $\Gamma,x{:}A\vdash B\ \mathsf{type}$, then $\Gamma\vdash\prod_{x:A}B\ \mathsf{type}$. Introduction: from $\Gamma,x{:}A\vdash b:B$ infer $\Gamma\vdash\lambda x.b:\prod_{x:A}B$. Elimination: from $f:\prod_{x:A}B$ and $a:A$ infer $f\,a:B[a/x]$. Computation ($\beta$): $(\lambda x.b)\,a\equiv b[a/x]$. When $B$ does not depend on $x$ this is the function type $A\to B$. ([nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory))

**Dependent sums.** Under the same premises, $\sum_{x:A}B$ is a type whose introduction rule pairs $a:A$ with $b:B[a/x]$; its elimination and computation rules recover the components. When $B$ is constant this is the product $A\times B$ with projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$. ([nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory))

**Identity types.** Formation: from $\Gamma\vdash A\ \mathsf{type}$ infer $\Gamma,a{:}A,b{:}A\vdash a=_A b\ \mathsf{type}$. Introduction: $\mathsf{refl}_A(a):a=_A a$. Elimination ($J$): given a family $C(a,b,p)$ over $a,b:A$ and $p:a=_Ab$, and $t:C(c,c,\mathsf{refl}(c))$ for $c:A$, one gets $J(t,a,b,p):C(a,b,p)$. Computation: $J(t,c,c,\mathsf{refl}(c))\equiv t$. The theory is *extensional* if it adds the reflection rule that $p:a=_Ab$ yields $a\equiv b:A$, and *intensional* otherwise. ([nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory))

**Natural numbers.** $\mathbb N$ has introduction rules $0:\mathbb N$ and $s(n):\mathbb N$; its eliminator $\mathrm{ind}^C_{\mathbb N}(n,c_0,c_s):C[n/x]$ satisfies $\mathrm{ind}(0,c_0,c_s)\equiv c_0$ and $\mathrm{ind}(s(n),c_0,c_s)\equiv c_s(n,\mathrm{ind}(n,c_0,c_s))$. ([nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory)) General inductive types are defined via W-types, the types of well-founded trees, and universes form a predicative hierarchy; Martin-Löf's original theory had to be changed to account for Girard's paradox. ([Wikipedia: Intuitionistic type theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuitionistic_type_theory))

**Univalence.** For a universe $U$, the univalence axiom says that the canonical map $\mathrm{Id}_U(A,B)\to\mathrm{Equiv}(A,B)$ is an equivalence; it implies function extensionality. ([SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/))

### Key results
- **Strong normalization of simple types.** Every typable term of the simply typed lambda calculus is strongly normalizing: every reduction sequence terminates. The standard proof is Tait's reducibility method: show by induction on types that reducible terms are strongly normalizing, and by induction on terms that every typable term is reducible. Consequently $\beta$-equality of typable terms is decidable (reduce both to normal form and compare) and there are no fixed-point combinators in the simply typed system; via the principal type algorithm, both type checking and typability are decidable. ([Ker, Lambda Calculus and Types, Ch. 7–8](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/andrew.ker/docs/lambdacalculus-lecture-notes-ht2009.pdf); [SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/))
- **Girard's normalization theorem for System F.** Girard proved normalization for his impredicative polymorphic system (System F, $\lambda2$ in the lambda cube) by extending Tait's 1967 reducibility method; the circularity of impredicativity does not produce non-normalizing terms. ([SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/))
- **Normalization in the lambda cube.** Every term well-typed in one of the eight systems of Barendregt's lambda cube ($\lambda{\to}$, $\lambda2$, $\lambda\underline\omega$, $\lambda P$, $\lambda P2$, $\lambda\omega$, $\lambda P\underline\omega$, $\lambda C$) is strongly normalizing. This property fails for pure type systems in general, and no system in the cube is Turing complete. The calculus of constructions $\lambda C$ is strongly normalizing and hence consistent (Coquand–Gallier 1990). ([Wikipedia: Lambda cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_cube); [Wikipedia: Calculus of constructions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_constructions))
- **Girard's paradox.** A type of all types is inconsistent. Girard proved in 1972 that System U is inconsistent: one can construct a term of type $\forall p{:}\ast.\,p$, so every type is inhabited and every proposition provable. The result led to the realization that Martin-Löf's original 1971 theory, which also had a "type in type", was inconsistent. It is the type-theoretic analogue of the Burali-Forti paradox (Coquand 1986), and Hurkens (1995) gave a simplified version. ([Wikipedia: System U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_U); [SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/))
- **Curry–Howard correspondence.** Implication corresponds to the function type, conjunction to the product, disjunction to the sum, truth and falsity to the unit and empty types, and $\forall$ and $\exists$ to $\Pi$- and $\Sigma$-types. Curry observed (1934) that the types of combinators can be seen as axiom schemes of intuitionistic implicational logic; Curry and Feys (1958) note that the simplest types of $K$ and $S$ are the schemes $\alpha\to(\beta\to\alpha)$ and $(\alpha\to(\beta\to\gamma))\to((\alpha\to\beta)\to(\alpha\to\gamma))$. Howard's manuscript of 1969 (published 1980) made explicit the analogy between natural-deduction proofs and simply typed lambda terms; the current formulation of the isomorphism is due to Martin-Löf. The Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov interpretation reads intuitionistic proofs as functions without fixing a class of functions; taking that class to be the lambda terms gives Howard's correspondence. ([Wikipedia: Curry–Howard correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence))
- **Decidability of type checking.** Type checking is decidable in intensional Martin-Löf type theory but undecidable in extensional type theory, where programs might not terminate. The price of intensionality is that some constructions need setoids or similar devices: integers and rationals can be represented without setoids but are awkward to work with, and Cauchy reals cannot.  ([Wikipedia: Intuitionistic type theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuitionistic_type_theory))
- **Consistency strength of simple type theory.** Church's simple type theory is equiconsistent with the bounded version of Zermelo set theory. ([SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/))
- **Categorical semantics.** Models of extensional Martin-Löf type theory are locally cartesian closed categories; Seely introduced these as the basic models, and Hofmann and Dybjer refined them to categories with families. ([Wikipedia: Intuitionistic type theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuitionistic_type_theory)) Faithful models of the intensional theory with identity types are certain $(\infty,1)$-categories, notably $(\infty,1)$-toposes presented by simplicial model categories, which is the basis of homotopy type theory. ([nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory)) Awodey's natural models of type theory agree exactly with Dybjer's categories with families, and he gives conditions under which they interpret $\Sigma$-, $\Pi$-, and intensional identity types; many settings for homotopy theory admit such models. ([Awodey, arXiv:1406.3219](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3219))

### Examples
- The combinator $K=\lambda x.\lambda y.x$ has type $\alpha\to(\beta\to\alpha)$, which read as a formula is the propositional axiom "$\alpha$ implies ($\beta$ implies $\alpha$)". ([Wikipedia: Curry–Howard correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence))
- In Curry-style simple types, $x$, $\lambda x.x$, $K$, $S$, $(\lambda x.x)(\lambda x.x)$ and the Church numerals are typable, while $xx$, $\lambda x.xx$, $\Omega$ and the fixed-point combinator $Y$ are not; an untypable term can be detected by exhibiting an infinite reduction path, since typable terms are strongly normalizing. ([Ker, Lambda Calculus and Types, Ch. 7](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/andrew.ker/docs/lambdacalculus-lecture-notes-ht2009.pdf))
- In System U the inhabitant of $\forall p{:}\ast.\,p$ given by Girard's paradox is equivalent to an inhabitant of $\bot$, so every type is inhabited. ([Wikipedia: System U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_U))

### History
Russell set out the doctrine of types in Appendix B of *The Principles of Mathematics* (1903) and presented type theory as a foundation in "Mathematical logic as based on the theory of types" (1908); the ramified theory of *Principia Mathematica* needed the axiom of reducibility. Church's "A formulation of the simple theory of types" (1940) built simple type theory on the lambda calculus. Martin-Löf (1970) suggested the axiom $U:U$, a type of all types, which Girard's 1972 thesis showed inconsistent; predicative universes replaced it, and Martin-Löf introduced identity types in 1975 [1973]. Girard's motivation for his polymorphic system was to extend Gödel's Dialectica interpretation to second-order arithmetic, and Reynolds independently introduced a similar system in 1974. Voevodsky's univalent foundations added the univalence axiom. ([SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/))

Barendregt introduced the lambda cube to organize systems from the simply typed calculus to the calculus of constructions, and generalized it to pure type systems. ([Wikipedia: Lambda cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_cube)) The homotopy type theory book was written during the Univalent Foundations program at the Institute for Advanced Study in 2012–13. ([HoTT book repository](https://github.com/HoTT/book))

### Connections
- [Lambda Calculus](node:Lambda%20Calculus): simple type theory is the typed lambda calculus; strong normalization separates it from the untyped calculus.
- [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): propositions-as-types interprets intuitionistic first-order logic in Martin-Löf type theory.
- [Propositional Logic](node:Propositional%20Logic): the implicational fragment corresponds to simple types under Curry–Howard.
- [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory): the competing foundation; simple type theory is equiconsistent with bounded Zermelo set theory.
- [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): locally cartesian closed categories, categories with families, and $(\infty,1)$-toposes model dependent types.
- [Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems](node:Gödel's%20Incompleteness%20Theorems): normalization proofs for strong systems need principles beyond the system, consistent with incompleteness.
- [Type Systems](node:Type%20Systems): the programming-language side of the same calculi.
- [Functional Programming](node:Functional%20Programming): typed lambda calculi are the core of typed functional languages.
- [Formal Verification and Proof Assistants](node:Formal%20Verification%20and%20Proof%20Assistants): Rocq and Lean are built on variants of the calculus of constructions.
- [MSC 03Fxx - Proof theory and constructive mathematics](node:MSC%2003Fxx%20-%20Proof%20theory%20and%20constructive%20mathematics) and [MSC 03Bxx - General logic](node:MSC%2003Bxx%20-%20General%20logic): where normalization and constructive foundations are classified.
- [MSC 55Qxx - Homotopy groups](node:MSC%2055Qxx%20-%20Homotopy%20groups): synthetic computations of homotopy groups of spheres are a target of homotopy type theory.

### Common pitfalls
- **Definitional versus propositional equality.** In the intensional theory $a\equiv b$ is a judgment, decided by computation, while $a=_Ab$ is a type whose elements are proofs; only the extensional theory, via equality reflection, collapses them, and it pays with undecidable type checking. ([nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory); [Wikipedia: Intuitionistic type theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuitionistic_type_theory))
- **Type in type.** A universe containing itself ($U:U$) is inconsistent, so practical systems use a hierarchy of universes; the Rocq system extends $\lambda C$ with a linear universe hierarchy and inductive types. ([Wikipedia: System U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_U); [Wikipedia: Lambda cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_cube))
- **Not all type theory is homotopy type theory.** Univalence is an extra axiom on universes, not part of Martin-Löf type theory, and it implies function extensionality. Strong normalization also fails for some pure type systems, so metatheorems must be checked system by system. ([SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/); [Wikipedia: Lambda cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_cube))

### Open problems
- **Semi-simplicial types.** Defining infinitary structures such as semi-simplicial types in plain homotopy type theory, or showing this is impossible, is listed as open. Known constructions use extensions: Voevodsky's Homotopy Type System, two-level type theory (Altenkirch–Capriotti–Kraus), computational higher-dimensional type theory, and Kolomatskaia–Shulman's displayed type theory (2023); the nLab notes that none of these approaches are currently possible in plain dependent type theory. ([nLab: open problems in HoTT](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/open+problems+in+homotopy+type+theory); [nLab: semi-simplicial type](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/semi-simplicial+type))
- **Proof-theoretic strength.** The proof-theoretic strength of univalent type theory with higher inductive types, and whether univalence is consistent with induction-recursion, are listed as open metatheory problems. ([nLab: open problems in HoTT](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/open+problems+in+homotopy+type+theory))
- **Cubical metatheory.** Whether cubical type theory with regularity has canonicity and normalization is listed as open. ([nLab: open problems in HoTT](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/open+problems+in+homotopy+type+theory))
- **Higher categories internally.** Defining a weak $\omega$-category, and calculating further homotopy groups of spheres, inside type theory are listed as open. ([nLab: open problems in HoTT](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/open+problems+in+homotopy+type+theory))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [SEP: Type Theory](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/): history from Russell to univalence, with normalization and consistency results.
- **Reference:** [nLab: Martin-Löf dependent type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory): complete inference rules and categorical semantics.
- **Learn:** [Ker, Lambda Calculus and Types (Oxford lecture notes)](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/andrew.ker/docs/lambdacalculus-lecture-notes-ht2009.pdf): simple types, Tait-style strong normalization, principal types.
- **Primary:** [Awodey, Natural models of homotopy type theory (arXiv:1406.3219)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3219): natural models coincide with categories with families and interpret Σ, Π, and identity types, Math. Struct. Comp. Sci. 2016.
- **Further reading:** [Barendregt, Dekkers, Statman, Lambda Calculus with Types (Cambridge, 2013)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/lambda-calculus-with-types/simply-typed-lambda-calculus/D4F02BC85E57F8C26DCA692C1D357FAC): the standard monograph on simple, recursive, and intersection types.
- **Further reading:** [Homotopy Type Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics (source repository)](https://github.com/HoTT/book): the IAS 2012–13 textbook, CC BY-SA.
- **Further reading:** Martin-Löf, *Intuitionistic Type Theory* (Bibliopolis, 1984), and Nordström, Petersson, Smith, *Programming in Martin-Löf's Type Theory* (OUP, 1990), both listed in the [nLab references](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Martin-L%C3%B6f+dependent+type+theory).
