## Reference
### Overview
Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is the science of quantitatively characterizing and estimating uncertainties in computational and real-world applications: how likely particular outcomes are when some aspects of a system are not exactly known. In scientific computing it is organized into forward problems (propagating uncertain inputs through a model to the distribution, mean, variance or reliability of the outputs) and inverse problems (using data to calibrate unknown parameters and estimate the discrepancy between model and reality), the inverse problem being considerably harder. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty_quantification)) The Bayesian approach to inverse problems for differential equations treats the unknown as a function, and the posterior measure on function space both regularizes the ill-posed problem and quantifies the remaining uncertainty. ([Stuart 2010, Acta Numerica](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/71949); [Dashti and Stuart](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.6989))

Sources of uncertainty (parameters, input variability, model inadequacy, numerical error, experimental noise, interpolation) are grouped into **aleatoric** uncertainty, inherent randomness that differs from run to run, and **epistemic** uncertainty, which comes from things one could in principle know but does not in practice. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty_quantification)) Hüllermeier and Waegeman review attempts to formalize this distinction in machine learning. ([Hüllermeier and Waegeman 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.09457))

In statistics and machine learning, predictive UQ is judged by **calibration** (statistical consistency between forecasts and outcomes), **sharpness** (concentration of the predictive distributions), and **coverage** of prediction sets; the goal is to maximize sharpness subject to calibration, assessed with proper scoring rules. ([Gneiting and Raftery 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf)) Modern deep networks are often poorly calibrated ([Guo et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599)), and calibration of many UQ methods degrades under dataset shift ([Ovadia et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.02530)). Conformal prediction gives distribution-free finite-sample coverage around any pretrained model ([Angelopoulos and Bates 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511)), under the assumption that calibration and test points are exchangeable ([Tibshirani, lecture notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/statlearn-s23/lectures/conformal_ds.pdf)).

### Formal definition
**Proper scoring rules.** For a forecast $P$ and outcome $\omega$, a scoring rule assigns a reward $S(P,\omega)$; write $S(P,Q)=\int S(P,\omega)\,dQ(\omega)$. $S$ is *proper* relative to a class $\mathcal P$ if $S(Q,Q)\ge S(P,Q)$ for all $P,Q\in\mathcal P$ and *strictly proper* if equality forces $P=Q$. Examples: the logarithmic score $\log p(\omega)$; the continuous ranked probability score $\mathrm{CRPS}(F,x)=-\int_{-\infty}^\infty(F(y)-\mathbf 1\{y\ge x\})^2\,dy=\tfrac12\mathbb E_F|X-X'|-\mathbb E_F|X-x|$ for $F$ with finite first moment; and, for a central $(1-\alpha)$ prediction interval $[l,u]$, the negatively oriented interval score $S^{\mathrm{int}}_\alpha(l,u;x)=(u-l)+\tfrac2\alpha(l-x)\mathbf 1\{x<l\}+\tfrac2\alpha(x-u)\mathbf 1\{x>u\}$. ([Gneiting and Raftery 2007](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf))

**Calibration of a classifier.** A classifier with predicted label $\hat Y$ and confidence $\hat P$ is calibrated when $\Pr(\hat Y=Y\mid\hat P=p)=p$ for all $p\in[0,1]$; post-hoc calibration maps raw scores to probabilities, e.g. Platt scaling (a logistic fit), isotonic regression, or temperature scaling. ([Guo et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599); [Wikipedia: Calibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calibration_%28statistics%29))

**Coverage.** Given data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ and a test point $(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})$, a set-valued predictor $\hat C_n$ has **marginal coverage** $1-\alpha$ if $\Pr\{Y_{n+1}\in\hat C_n(X_{n+1})\}\ge1-\alpha$ over all $n+1$ points, and **conditional coverage** if $\Pr\{Y_{n+1}\in\hat C_n(X_{n+1})\mid X_{n+1}=x\}\ge1-\alpha$ for almost all $x$; a property is distribution-free if it holds for every distribution $P$. ([Barber et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.04684)) **Training-conditional coverage** asks that, for most draws of the training set, the fitted set covers future test points at the nominal rate. ([Bian and Barber 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03647))

**Split conformal prediction.** Fit any model on a proper training set; on a calibration set of size $n$ compute nonconformity scores $R_i$ (e.g. $|Y_i-\hat\mu(X_i)|$); output $\hat C(x)=\{y:R(x,y)\le\hat q\}$, where $\hat q$ is the $\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil/n$ empirical quantile of $R_1,\dots,R_n$. ([Barber et al., jackknife+](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.02928); [Tibshirani, lecture notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/statlearn-s23/lectures/conformal_ds.pdf)) Full conformal refits the model on the training data augmented with $(X_{n+1},y)$ for each candidate $y$, which is prohibitively expensive outside special cases such as ridge regression and the lasso; the variants trade statistical accuracy against computation. ([Barber et al., jackknife+](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.02928); [Lei et al. 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.04173))

**Jackknife+.** With leave-one-out fits $\hat\mu_{-i}$ and residuals $R_i^{\mathrm{LOO}}=|Y_i-\hat\mu_{-i}(X_i)|$, the interval is $\bigl[\hat q^-_{n,\alpha}\{\hat\mu_{-i}(X_{n+1})-R_i^{\mathrm{LOO}}\},\ \hat q^+_{n,\alpha}\{\hat\mu_{-i}(X_{n+1})+R_i^{\mathrm{LOO}}\}\bigr]$, where $\hat q^-_{n,\alpha}$ is the $\lfloor\alpha(n+1)\rfloor$-th smallest value and $\hat q^+_{n,\alpha}$ the corresponding upper quantile; CV+ is the $K$-fold analogue. ([Barber et al., jackknife+](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.02928))

**Bayesian inverse problem.** For data $y=\mathcal G(u)+\eta$, define the potential (negative log-likelihood) $\Phi(u;y)$. With prior $\mu_0$ on a separable Banach space $X$, the posterior is
$$\frac{d\mu^y}{d\mu_0}(u)=\frac1{Z(y)}\exp(-\Phi(u;y)),\qquad Z(y)=\int_X\exp(-\Phi(u;y))\,\mu_0(du).$$
([Dashti and Stuart](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.6989))

**Model discrepancy (Kennedy–O'Hagan).** Inverse UQ models experimental output as $y_e(x)=y_m(x,\theta^*)+\delta(x)+\varepsilon$, with simulator $y_m$, true parameters $\theta^*$, discrepancy $\delta$ and noise $\varepsilon$, often with Gaussian-process priors on $y_m$ and $\delta$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty_quantification))

### Key results
- **Quantile lemma and split conformal coverage.** If $R_1,\dots,R_{n+1}$ are exchangeable, then for any $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$\Pr\Bigl\{R_{n+1}\le\mathrm{Quantile}\Bigl(\tfrac{\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil}{n};\ \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{R_i}\Bigr)\Bigr\}\ge1-\alpha,$$
which gives split conformal prediction finite-sample marginal coverage $\ge1-\alpha$ for any model and distribution. ([Tibshirani, lecture notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/statlearn-s23/lectures/conformal_ds.pdf); [Lei et al. 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.04173))
- **Impossibility of informative distribution-free conditional coverage (Vovk 2012; Lei and Wasserman 2014).** If $\hat C_n$ satisfies $(1-\alpha)$ conditional coverage for every distribution $P$, then for all $P$, $\mathbb E[\mathrm{leb}(\hat C_n(x))]=\infty$ at almost all points $x$ other than the atoms of $P_X$. The trivial set $\hat C_n\equiv\mathbb R$ has conditional coverage, so the theorem rules out *informative* sets, not conditional coverage as such. Coverage over every subgroup of probability $\ge\delta$ in a sufficiently limited class $\mathcal X$ is achievable nontrivially. ([Barber et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.04684))
- **Jackknife+ and CV+.** For i.i.d. data and a fitting algorithm invariant to the ordering of the data, the jackknife+ interval satisfies $\Pr\{Y_{n+1}\in\hat C^{\text{jackknife+}}_{n,\alpha}(X_{n+1})\}\ge1-2\alpha$ with no assumption on the distribution or the algorithm; jackknife-minmax attains $\ge1-\alpha$; $K$-fold CV+ attains $\ge1-2\alpha-2(1-1/K)/(n/K+1)$. ([Barber et al., jackknife+](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.02928))
- **Weighted conformal prediction.** If $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$ are *weighted exchangeable*, with joint density $\prod_iw_i(z_i)\,g(z_1,\dots,z_{n+1})$ for permutation-invariant $g$, a correspondingly weighted quantile of the scores restores coverage $\ge1-\alpha$. With fixed weights $w_i\in[0,1]$ and no assumption on the joint distribution, the weighted conformal set satisfies $\Pr(Y_{n+1}\in\hat C^w_n(X_{n+1}))\ge1-\alpha-\sum_{i=1}^n\tilde w_i\,\mathrm{TV}(R(Z),R(Z^i))$, where $Z^i$ swaps the $i$-th and test points. ([Tibshirani, lecture notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/statlearn-s23/lectures/conformal_ds.pdf); [Barber et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13415))
- **Adaptive conformal inference.** For any sequence of nested set-valued predictors that are empty at level $\beta\le0$ and everything at $\beta\ge1$, the update $\alpha_{t+1}=\alpha_t-\eta(\mathrm{err}_t-\alpha)$ satisfies $\bigl|\frac1T\sum_{t=t_0+1}^{t_0+T}\mathrm{err}_t-\alpha\bigr|\le\frac{1+2\eta}{T\eta}$, so long-run miscoverage equals $\alpha$ for every data sequence, even an adversarial one. ([Tibshirani, lecture notes](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/statlearn-s23/lectures/conformal_ds.pdf))
- **Well-posedness of Bayesian inverse problems.** Suppose $\Phi$ is continuous on $X'\times Y$ with $\Phi(u;y)\ge-M_1(r,\|u\|_X)$ and $|\Phi(u;y_1)-\Phi(u;y_2)|\le M_2(r,\|u\|_X)\|y_1-y_2\|_Y$ for $y$'s in the ball $B_Y(0,r)$, that $\mu_0(X')=1$ with $\mu_0(X'\cap B)>0$ for some bounded $B$, and that $\exp(M_1)(1+M_2^2)\in L^1_{\mu_0}$. Then there is $C(r)$ with $d_{\mathrm{Hell}}(\mu^y,\mu^{y'})\le C(r)\|y-y'\|_Y$ for all $y,y'\in B_Y(0,r)$: unlike the ill-posed inverse map, the posterior depends Lipschitz-continuously on the data. ([Dashti and Stuart](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.6989))
- **Non-identifiability of the calibration parameter (Kennedy–O'Hagan).** In $y_e(x)=y_m(x,\theta)+\delta(x)+\varepsilon$, the distribution of the physical data does not in general determine $\theta$ uniquely given the computer model: writing the physical system as $y_m(x,\theta)+\delta(x)$ with $\delta$ fully nonparametric, the pair $(\theta,\delta)$ is not determined by it. This was raised in the discussion of Kennedy and O'Hagan (2001). Brynjarsdóttir and O'Hagan (2014) gave a concrete example in which a constrained Gaussian-process prior encoding derivative information about $\delta$ improved estimation of $\theta$. Tuo and Wu instead define the true parameter as the $L^2$ projection $\theta^*=\arg\min_\theta\|\eta-y_m(\cdot,\theta)\|_{L^2}$ of the physical system $\eta$, which is identifiable and admits frequentist guarantees, and Xie and Xu give a Bayesian projected-calibration analogue. ([Xie and Xu 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.01231))
- **Modern networks are miscalibrated; temperature scaling repairs much of it.** Unlike networks from a decade earlier, modern deep classifiers are poorly calibrated, with depth, width, weight decay and batch normalization all affecting calibration; one-parameter temperature scaling was effective on most datasets. ([Guo et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599)) Under dataset shift, post-hoc calibration falls short while ensembles did surprisingly well. ([Ovadia et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.02530))

### Examples
- **Deep ensembles.** Independently trained networks give calibration as good as or better than approximate Bayesian neural networks and higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution inputs. ([Lakshminarayanan et al. 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.01474))
- **Polynomial chaos.** A random output $Y$ is expanded in polynomials of the random inputs orthogonal with respect to their distribution: Wiener (1938) used Hermite polynomials for Gaussian inputs, and Xiu and Karniadakis (2002) generalized to the Askey scheme for other distributions. It can outperform Monte Carlo but becomes expensive with many random variables. ([Wikipedia: Polynomial chaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_chaos))
- **Cold posteriors.** With careful MCMC, the Bayes posterior predictive of deep networks gave systematically worse predictions than SGD point estimates, while a "cold" posterior that overcounts the evidence did significantly better, a departure from the Bayesian paradigm. ([Wenzel et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.02405))

### History
Gammerman, Vovk and Vapnik introduced a transductive form of conformal prediction in 1998; Saunders et al. gave the p-value version in 1999; inductive (split) conformal prediction followed in 2002 (Papadopoulos et al.). ([Wikipedia: Conformal prediction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_prediction)) Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer's monograph *Algorithmic Learning in a Random World* appeared in a 2022 Springer edition. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-031-06649-8)) Stuart's 2010 *Acta Numerica* survey set out the function-space Bayesian framework for inverse problems. ([Caltech record](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/71949))

### Connections
- [Conformal Prediction](node:Conformal%20Prediction): the main distribution-free route to coverage guarantees.
- [Proper Scoring Rules](node:Proper%20Scoring%20Rules): the basis for evaluating probabilistic predictions.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss): the negative logarithmic score, used to train and evaluate probabilistic classifiers.
- [Bayesian Inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference): the standard framework for epistemic uncertainty and inverse UQ.
- [Bayesian Neural Networks](node:Bayesian%20Neural%20Networks): posterior over weights as a model of epistemic uncertainty.
- [Deep Ensembles](node:Deep%20Ensembles): a non-Bayesian ensemble baseline for predictive uncertainty.
- [Gaussian Processes](node:Gaussian%20Processes): priors for simulators and discrepancy in Kennedy–O'Hagan calibration.
- [Markov Chain Monte Carlo](node:Markov%20Chain%20Monte%20Carlo): sampling posteriors in inverse problems and Bayesian deep learning.
- [Monte Carlo Methods](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Methods): the default tool for forward propagation.
- [Scientific Surrogate Models](node:Scientific%20Surrogate%20Models): cheap emulators used for forward and inverse UQ.
- [Simulation-Based Calibration](node:Simulation-Based%20Calibration): checking that Bayesian inference software produces calibrated posteriors.
- [Out-of-Distribution Generalization](node:Out-of-Distribution%20Generalization): dataset shift is where UQ methods most often fail.
- [Cross-Validation](node:Cross-Validation): CV+ turns $K$-fold residuals into prediction intervals.

### Common pitfalls
- **Marginal is not conditional.** A $1-\alpha$ conformal guarantee averages over $X_{n+1}$; informative sets with distribution-free conditional coverage are impossible (they must have infinite expected length at non-atoms), though the trivial set has it. ([Barber et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.04684))
- **Marginal is not training-conditional.** A marginal guarantee averages over training sets; split conformal has training-conditional coverage, but for some other methods it cannot be guaranteed without further assumptions. ([Bian and Barber 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03647))
- **Exchangeability is a real assumption.** Drift over time or asymmetric fitting breaks the standard conformal guarantee. ([Barber et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13415))
- **Ignoring model discrepancy, or trusting calibrated parameters as physical.** Identifiability problems arise when different parameter combinations give the same prediction ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty_quantification)), and Kennedy–O'Hagan-calibrated models can give poor approximations to the physical system. ([Xie and Xu 2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.01231))

### Open problems
- **Relaxed conditional coverage.** Barber, Candès, Ramdas and Tibshirani state that many open questions remain: which classes $\mathcal X$ of subgroups are most meaningful for approximate conditional coverage, how to compute the corresponding split conformal intervals efficiently, and whether conditional coverage can hold at an adaptive tolerance $\delta(P)$ that is small for well-behaved distributions; they leave these for future work. ([Barber et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.04684))
- **The cold-posterior effect.** Wenzel et al. put forward and test several hypotheses for why cold posteriors outperform the Bayes posterior in deep networks, and argue that the field should now focus on understanding the origin of this improved performance. ([Wenzel et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.02405)) Izmailov et al., using full-batch Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, found that tempering is not required for near-optimal performance and attributed the cold-posterior effect largely to data augmentation, so the explanation remains debated rather than settled. ([Izmailov et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14421))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Uncertainty quantification (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty_quantification): sources of uncertainty, forward and inverse problems, Kennedy–O'Hagan.
- **Reference:** [Polynomial chaos (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_chaos): Wiener and generalized polynomial chaos.
- **Learn:** [Tibshirani, Conformal Prediction Under Distribution Shift (Berkeley lecture notes)](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/statlearn-s23/lectures/conformal_ds.pdf): quantile lemma, weighted exchangeability, adaptive conformal inference.
- **Learn:** [Dashti and Stuart, The Bayesian Approach to Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.6989): lecture notes on function-space Bayesian inversion and well-posedness.
- **Learn:** [Angelopoulos and Bates, A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511): hands-on tutorial with code.
- **Primary:** [Gneiting and Raftery 2007, Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf): calibration, sharpness, CRPS, interval score.
- **Primary:** [Barber et al. 2019, The limits of distribution-free conditional predictive inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.04684): marginal vs conditional coverage.
- **Primary:** [Barber et al., Predictive inference with the jackknife+](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.02928): jackknife+, CV+.
- **Primary:** [Stuart 2010, Inverse problems: a Bayesian perspective (Acta Numerica)](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/71949): survey of Bayesian inversion.
- **Primary:** [Guo et al. 2017, On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599): miscalibration and temperature scaling.
- **Further reading:** [Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer, *Algorithmic Learning in a Random World* (Springer, 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-06649-8): the monograph on conformal prediction.
- **Further reading:** [Sullivan, *Introduction to Uncertainty Quantification* (Springer, Texts in Applied Mathematics, 2015)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-23395-6): textbook on uncertainty quantification.
references.Universal Algebra:
## Reference
### Overview
Universal algebra studies algebraic structures in general: the possible *types* of structure and the relations between them, rather than one type such as groups or rings. An algebra is a set with a family of finitary operations. Classes of algebras defined by identities (equational laws) are called *varieties*, and the subject's basic constructions are homomorphic images, subalgebras and products. ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))

The nLab describes the field as "the study of algebraic theories and their models or algebras". Classically the models live in the category of sets. Categorical universal algebra moves them into other categories using Lawvere theories, monads or [type theory](node:Type%20Theory). For example, [Hopf algebras](node:Hopf%20Algebras) are models of the theory of groups in vector spaces, and computational side effects are described by free algebras over a monad. On the nLab's account, the categorical approach mainly unifies previously separate viewpoints. ([nLab: universal algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+algebra))

Universal algebra also reaches into computer science: it provides a natural language for the constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra)) The Feder–Vardi dichotomy conjecture on the complexity of finite-template CSPs was proved in 2017, with tractability characterized by a polymorphism condition. ([Bulatov](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03021); [Zhuk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01914))

### Formal definition
A **signature** (type) is a set of operation symbols $f$, each with an arity $n_f\in\mathbb N$. An **algebra** of that signature is a set $A$ with an operation $f^A:A^{n_f}\to A$ for each symbol. A $0$-ary operation is a constant. ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))

An **identity** is a universally quantified equation $s\approx t$ between terms built from variables and operation symbols. A **variety** (equational class) is the class of all algebras of a signature that satisfy a given set of identities. For example, groups form a variety once the signature contains a binary product, a nullary identity element and a unary inverse. Fields do not form a variety, because inversion cannot be a total operation. ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))

A **subdirect product** of algebras $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is a subalgebra $A\le\prod_i A_i$ such that every projection $A\to A_j$ is surjective. $A$ is **subdirectly irreducible** if in every subdirect representation of $A$ some projection is an isomorphism. ([Wikipedia: Subdirect product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdirect_product))

**Categorical form.** A **Lawvere theory** is a category $\mathbf T$ with finite products, together with an identity-on-objects functor $J:\mathbb F^{op}\to\mathbf T$ that strictly preserves powers. Here $\mathbb F$ is a skeleton of finite sets, so every object is a power $x^n$ of a generic object. A **model** is a product-preserving functor $A:\mathbf T\to\mathbf{Set}$, with underlying set $A(1)$. Each $\varphi\in\mathbf T(n,1)$ acts as an $n$-ary operation on $A(1)$. ([nLab: Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory))

### Key results
- **Birkhoff's HSP theorem (1935).** For a signature of single-sorted finitary operations, a class of algebras is a variety (the models of some set of identities) if and only if it is closed under homomorphic images (H), subalgebras (S) and arbitrary products (P). ([nLab: Birkhoff's HSP theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Birkhoff%27s+HSP+theorem); [Wikipedia: Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29))
- **Free algebras.** Every non-trivial variety $\mathcal V$ contains a free algebra $F_{\mathcal V}(S)$ on every set $S$, and every member of $\mathcal V$ is a homomorphic image of a free algebra in $\mathcal V$. ([Wikipedia: Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29))
- **Birkhoff's subdirect representation theorem (1944).** Every algebra whose operations all have finite arity is isomorphic to a subdirect product of subdirectly irreducible algebras. For instance, every distributive lattice is a subalgebra of a power of the two-element lattice, and every reduced commutative Noetherian ring is a subdirect product of integral domains. ([Wikipedia: Subdirect product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdirect_product))
- **Mal'cev's theorem (1954).** For a variety $\mathcal V$ the following are equivalent: (1) every algebra in $\mathcal V$ has permuting congruences, $\alpha\circ\beta=\beta\circ\alpha$; (2) the free algebra on three generators in $\mathcal V$ has permuting congruences; (3) there is a ternary term $q$ with $\mathcal V\models q(x,y,y)\approx x\approx q(y,y,x)$. In groups, $q(x,y,z)=xy^{-1}z$ is such a term. ([Wikipedia: Congruence-permutable algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence-permutable_algebra))
- **Lawvere theories and monads.** Lawvere theories correspond to finitary monads on $\mathbf{Set}$, and infinitary Lawvere theories to arbitrary monads. Every Lawvere theory gives a monad on $\mathbf{Set}$, and every finitary monad on $\mathbf{Set}$ arises this way. ([nLab: Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory); [Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))
- **Finite basis theorems.** A variety has a *finite residual bound* if its subdirectly irreducible members have bounded finite size. Baker proved in the early 1970s that a finite algebra in a finite language that generates a congruence-distributive variety is finitely based (its identities follow from finitely many). For varieties in a finite language with a finite residual bound, McKenzie (1987) proved finite basedness in the congruence-modular case and Willard (2000) in the congruence-meet-semidistributive case, extending Baker's theorem in two different directions. Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard found a common generalization: a variety in a finite language that has a difference term and a finite residual bound is finitely based. ([Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard, preprint](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf); [Moore, full text](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1304.4659))
- **Undecidability.** McKenzie showed, using an algebra $\mathbb A(\mathcal T)$, that it is undecidable whether a finite algebra generates a variety with a finite residual bound. Willard used the same algebra to give a second proof that Tarski's finite basis problem is undecidable. ([Moore, full text](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1304.4659))
- **CSP dichotomy (Bulatov; Zhuk, 2017).** For a finite constraint language $\Gamma$: if $\Gamma$ has a weak near-unanimity polymorphism, then $\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma)$ is solvable in polynomial time; otherwise it is NP-complete. This settles the Feder–Vardi dichotomy conjecture. ([Zhuk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01914); [Bulatov](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03021))

### Examples
- **Groups, rings, lattices.** Groups and rings are congruence-permutable varieties. Fields are not a variety. ([Wikipedia: Congruence-permutable algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence-permutable_algebra); [Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))
- **Subdirect decompositions.** Every semilattice is a subdirect power of the two-element semilattice. Every vector space ([Vector Spaces](node:Vector%20Spaces)) over a field $K$ is subdirectly represented by the one-dimensional space $K$. $(\mathbb Z,+)$ is subdirectly represented by arbitrarily large finite cyclic groups. ([Wikipedia: Subdirect product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdirect_product))
- **Lawvere theory of groups.** $\mathbf T_{\mathrm{Grp}}$ is the opposite of the category of finitely generated free groups, and its models are exactly groups. ([nLab: Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lawvere+theory))
- **Graph colouring as a CSP.** $n$-colouring is $\mathrm{CSP}(\{0,\dots,n-1\},\neq)$. ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))
- **Finite semigroups and languages.** No general finitary analogue of Birkhoff's theorem exists for classes of finite algebras. Reiterman instead characterized pseudovarieties of finite monoids by profinite identities, and Eilenberg's variety theorem links pseudovarieties of finite semigroups with varieties of regular languages. ([Wikipedia: Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29))

### History
Whitehead's *A Treatise on Universal Algebra* (1898) used the term roughly in its modern sense, though it had no general results. Birkhoff and Ore began publishing on universal algebras in the early 1930s. Birkhoff's paper "On the Structure of Abstract Algebras" appeared in the *Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society* 31 (1935), 433–454. ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra); [Crossref record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/S0305004100013463)) Between 1935 and 1950 most papers followed the lines suggested by Birkhoff's papers. Mal'cev's 1940s results went unnoticed during the war. Tarski's 1950 ICM lecture opened a model-theoretic period, and Marczewski emphasized free algebras in the late 1950s. Lawvere's 1963 thesis introduced categorical methods. ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra)) Park stated his finite-basis conjecture in 1976. ([Moore, full text](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1304.4659)) The CSP dichotomy was proved by Bulatov and by Zhuk in 2017. ([Bulatov](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03021); [Zhuk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01914))

### Connections
- [Birkhoff's Variety Theorem](node:Birkhoff's%20Variety%20Theorem): the HSP characterization of equational classes.
- [Equational Classes of Algebras](node:Equational%20Classes%20of%20Algebras) and [Quasivarieties](node:Quasivarieties): classes defined by identities, and by quasi-identities (implications between equations).
- [Congruence Relations on Algebras](node:Congruence%20Relations%20on%20Algebras): congruences are the kernels of homomorphisms, and congruence-lattice conditions (permutable, distributive, modular) organize the structure theory.
- [First Isomorphism Theorem](node:First%20Isomorphism%20Theorem): holds for arbitrary algebras, with congruences in place of normal subgroups or ideals.
- [Monads and Algebraic Theories](node:Monads%20and%20Algebraic%20Theories) and [Category Theory](node:Category%20Theory): Lawvere theories and finitary monads give the categorical form.
- [Lattice Theory](node:Lattice%20Theory), [Distributive Lattices](node:Distributive%20Lattices) and [Boolean Algebras](node:Boolean%20Algebras): classical varieties, and the congruence lattices of algebras.
- [Group Theory](node:Group%20Theory), [Rings and Ideals](node:Rings%20and%20Ideals), [Semigroups and Monoids](node:Semigroups%20and%20Monoids) and [Loops and Quasigroups](node:Loops%20and%20Quasigroups): the standard varieties.
- [Model Theory](node:Model%20Theory) and [First-Order Logic](node:First-Order%20Logic): varieties are the equationally axiomatized classes, and Tarski's school developed the field model-theoretically.
- [Constraint Satisfaction Problems](node:Constraint%20Satisfaction%20Problems) and [NP-Completeness](node:NP-Completeness): polymorphism algebras classify the complexity of finite-template CSPs.
- [Automata and Formal Languages](node:Automata%20and%20Formal%20Languages): Eilenberg's theorem links pseudovarieties of finite semigroups to varieties of regular languages.

### Common pitfalls
- **"Closed under products" means arbitrary products.** Classes of finite algebras are closed only under finite products, and for them Birkhoff's theorem has no general finitary analogue. ([Wikipedia: Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28universal_algebra%29))
- **The signature matters.** Groups form a variety only when the identity and the inverse are included as operations. With just a binary operation and quantified axioms, the class is not defined by identities. ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))
- **Operads are more restrictive than varieties.** Operads allow only identities in which the same variables occur on each side, without duplication or omission. Rings fit, groups do not. ([Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra))

### Open problems
- **Park's conjecture (1976), or Jónsson's problem.** If a variety in a finite language has a finite residual bound, must it be finitely based? (Moore states it for finitely generated varieties.) Moore says the conjecture "is still open", and Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard say Jónsson's problem remains open. The congruence-distributive, congruence-modular, congruence-meet-semidistributive and difference-term cases are proved. ([Moore, full text](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1304.4659); [Kearnes, Szendrei and Willard, preprint](https://math.colorado.edu/~kearnes/Papers/diffterm-july2014.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: universal algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+algebra): algebraic theories and their models, categorical approaches; with [Wikipedia: Universal algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_algebra) for definitions, HSP, CSP and history.
- **Learn:** [Bergman, Math 245 / An Invitation to General Algebra and Universal Constructions](https://math.berkeley.edu/~gbergman/245/): Berkeley course notes turned textbook, with free PDF versions.
- **Primary:** [Zhuk, A Proof of the CSP Dichotomy Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01914): the polymorphism-based algorithm that completes the dichotomy.
- **Primary:** [Moore, The Variety Generated by A(T): Two Counterexamples](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1304.4659): residual bounds, finite basis theorems and Park's conjecture.
- **Further reading:** [Bergman, An Invitation to General Algebra and Universal Constructions (Springer Universitext)](https://math.berkeley.edu/~gbergman/245/): graduate text grown from the Berkeley course Math 245, General Theory of Algebraic Structures.
