## Reference
### Overview
Universal extra dimensions (UED) are models in which *all* Standard Model fields propagate in one or more flat compact extra dimensions, in contrast to the ADD model, where Standard Model fields are confined to a four-dimensional brane and only gravity propagates in the bulk. The Kaluza–Klein (KK) resonances of Standard Model fields then appear at $M_{\mathrm{KK}}\approx R^{-1}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_extra_dimensions)) Appelquist, Cheng and Dobrescu (2001) showed that momentum conservation in the extra dimensions implies KK-number conservation, so KK modes affect electroweak observables only through loops and the compactification scale can be as low as a few hundred GeV. ([Appelquist, Cheng & Dobrescu](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012100))

The standard five-dimensional model lives on the orbifold $S^1/Z_2$ with an extra $Z_2$, KK parity, that interchanges the two boundaries. The lightest KK-odd state is stable and is a dark-matter candidate; at colliders KK particles are pair-produced and cascade to it, giving jets or leptons plus missing $p_T$, as in $R$-parity-conserving supersymmetry. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)) In the minimal model (mUED) the spectrum is fixed by only two parameters, $R$ and the cutoff $\Lambda$; the PDG reports that mUED is ruled out once LHC data are combined with the dark-matter relic density, while extensions that include boundary terms can be compatible with experiment. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [Avnish et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15137))

### Formal definition
Start from the minimal Standard Model in $d=4+\delta$ dimensions, an effective theory valid below a cutoff $M_s$, with the extra dimensions compactified at $1/R<M_s$. For $\delta=2k$ the compactification is $[(S^1\times S^1)/Z_2]^k$ and for $\delta=2k+1$ it is $[(S^1\times S^1)/Z_2]^k\times S^1/Z_2$. Gauge components polarized along $x^\mu$ are even (their zero modes are the SM gauge bosons), components along the extra coordinates are odd (no massless adjoint scalars), and the Higgs is even. Tree-level KK masses are $M_j=p_j/R$ with $p_j^2=j_1^2+\dots+j_\delta^2$. ([Appelquist, Cheng & Dobrescu](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0012100))

KK-number conservation means there are no vertices involving only one non-zero KK mode, so non-zero modes are produced in pairs or larger groups. ([Appelquist, Cheng & Dobrescu](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0012100)) Radiative effects break KK number to KK parity $P=(-1)^n$, which still forces pair production of level-one states and makes the lightest KK particle (LKP) stable. ([Kong & Matchev](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0610057))

In 5D, at tree level $m^2_{X^{(n)}}=n^2/R^2+m^2_{X^{(0)}}$, so each level is nearly degenerate. Bulk loops and boundary-localized kinetic terms split it; with boundary terms assumed to vanish at $\Lambda$, the one-loop corrections include
$$\delta m^2_{B^{(n)}}=\frac{g'^2}{16\pi^2R^2}\Big(-\frac{39}{2}\frac{\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}-\frac{n^2}{3}\ln\Lambda R\Big),\qquad \delta m^2_{g^{(n)}}=\frac{g_3^2}{16\pi^2R^2}\Big(-\frac32\frac{\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}+23\,n^2\ln\Lambda R\Big),$$
$$\delta m_{e^{(n)}}=\frac{n}{16\pi^2R}\,\frac92 g'^2\ln\Lambda R .$$
([Hooper & Profumo, §2.2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0701197))

**Non-minimal UED (nmUED)** adds KK-parity-preserving bulk fermion masses $M_\Psi(y)=-M_\Psi(-y)$ and boundary-localized operators $r\,[\delta(y-L)+\delta(y+L)]\,\mathcal O$ (gauge, fermion, Higgs and Yukawa terms) to the 5D action. ([Flacke, Kong & Park](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1408.4024))

### Key results
- **Electroweak bounds (2001).** Because KK number is conserved, SM observables receive KK contributions only through loops. One universal extra dimension could have $1/R$ as low as about $300\,\mathrm{GeV}$, the main constraint being weak-isospin violation; for two extra dimensions the bound depends logarithmically on the cutoff and was estimated at $400$–$800\,\mathrm{GeV}$. ([Appelquist, Cheng & Dobrescu](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012100))
- **Higgs-mass dependence of the precision bound.** Including subleading new-physics contributions and two-loop SM corrections to $\rho$, Gogoladze and Macesanu found $R^{-1}>600\,\mathrm{GeV}$ at 90% CL for one extra dimension and $m_h=115\,\mathrm{GeV}$, a bound that is significantly relaxed for heavier Higgs masses (down to $300\,\mathrm{GeV}$). ([Gogoladze & Macesanu](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0605207))
- **Radiative spectrum (Cheng–Matchev–Schmaltz).** The complete one-loop corrections to KK masses in 5D and 6D are finite for loops winding the extra dimension and are needed for any meaningful UED phenomenology. ([Cheng, Matchev & Schmaltz](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0204342)) The KK gluon is the heaviest level-one state; for $\Lambda=20R^{-1}$ the KK quark and gluon masses shift by about 20% and the other level-one states by a few percent or less. The KK photon gets a small negative correction and is the LKP under these corrections; at level one it is nearly pure $B^{(1)}$ (for $R^{-1}=1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ the level-one Weinberg angle has $\sin^2\theta_{W,1}\approx10^{-3}$). ([Hooper & Profumo](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0701197)) $B^{(1)}$ is the LKP naturally obtained in minimal UED. ([Kong & Matchev](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0610057))
- **LKP relic density and coannihilation.** Servant and Tait found that a TeV-scale KK photon can have a suitable annihilation cross section to be the dark matter. ([Servant & Tait](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0206071)) Because the level-one spectrum is nearly degenerate, coannihilations matter. ([Kong & Matchev, relic density](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0509119)) For $B^{(1)}$ alone the WMAP abundance needs $m_{B^{(1)}}\approx850$–$900\,\mathrm{GeV}$; three KK-lepton families $1\%$ heavier shift this to $550$–$650\,\mathrm{GeV}$, while quasi-degenerate KK quarks push it to $1500$–$2000\,\mathrm{GeV}$. ([Hooper & Profumo, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0701197)) Including level-two resonances and all coannihilations raises the preferred mUED scale to $R^{-1}\approx1.3\,\mathrm{TeV}$; a sub-TeV candidate requires the non-minimal model. ([Belanger, Kakizaki & Pukhov](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.2577))
- **LHC exclusion of mUED.** Recasting SUSY missing-energy searches with CheckMATE gives $1/R>1.4$–$1.5\,\mathrm{TeV}$ for $\Lambda R=5$–$35$. ([Deutschmann, Flacke & Kim](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.00410); [PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf)) The relic-density-allowed region of mUED has been ruled out by the ATLAS 13 TeV multijet $+E_T^{\mathrm{miss}}$ search with $139\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$; with boundary-localized terms the same search gives stringent bounds on the BLT parameters. ([Avnish et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15137))
- **Six-dimensional proton stability.** In 6D UED, SM [gauge invariance](node:Gauge%20Invariance) and $SO(1,5)$ Lorentz symmetry make the lowest-dimension baryon-number-violating operator nine-dimensional in the 4D theory, giving $\tau_p\sim10^{35}\,\mathrm{yr}\,(R^{-1}/500\,\mathrm{GeV})^{12}(\Lambda R/5)^{22}$, well above Super-Kamiokande limits. ([Hooper & Profumo, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0701197))

### Examples
- **Minimal 5D UED.** One extra dimension on $S^1/Z_2$, all SM fields in the bulk, boundary terms vanishing at $\Lambda$; the only new parameters are $R$ and $\Lambda$. ([Avnish et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15137); [Hooper & Profumo](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0701197)) Its level-one and level-two KK particles outside the Higgs sector are implemented in CalcHEP/CompHEP with the one-loop spectrum computed from $R$ and $\Lambda$. ([Datta, Kong & Matchev](https://arxiv.org/abs/1002.4624))
- **Level-two resonances.** Second-level KK states can decay to SM particles without missing energy, so dilepton resonance searches constrain them; Edelhäuser, Flacke and Krämer obtained $R^{-1}>715\,\mathrm{GeV}$ for mUED and level-two masses above about $1.4\,\mathrm{TeV}$. Such resonances have no $N=1$ SUSY analogue. ([Edelhäuser, Flacke & Krämer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.6076); [Kong & Matchev](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0610057))
- **KK gluon cascade.** $g^{(1)}$ decays almost always to a KK quark and a quark, with $\mathrm{BR}(g^{(1)}\to Q^{(1)}Q)\approx\mathrm{BR}(g^{(1)}\to q^{(1)}q)\approx0.5$; singlet KK quarks then decay to a quark and $B^{(1)}$. ([Hooper & Profumo](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0701197))

### History
Kaluza (1919) extended [general relativity](node:General%20Relativity) to five dimensions; Klein (1926) proposed compactifying the fifth dimension on a small circle. ([Hooper & Profumo](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0701197)) Appelquist, Cheng and Dobrescu introduced UED in 2001, with the then-current Tevatron bound in the few-hundred-GeV range. ([Appelquist, Cheng & Dobrescu](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012100)) Cheng, Matchev and Schmaltz computed the radiative spectrum in 2002, and Servant and Tait proposed the KK photon as dark matter the same year. ([Cheng, Matchev & Schmaltz](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0204342); [Servant & Tait](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0206071)) Split and non-minimal UED extend the model with fermion bulk masses and boundary-localized terms, which are allowed by all symmetries and are induced at loop level even if absent at tree level. ([Flacke, Kong & Park](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1408.4024)) LHC Run 2 analyses excluded the minimal model. ([Avnish et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15137))

### Connections
- [Kaluza–Klein Modes](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Modes): the 4D towers obtained by compactifying the extra dimensions.
- [Kaluza–Klein Theory](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Theory): the historical all-fields-in-the-bulk idea that UED modernizes.
- [Kaluza–Klein Dark Matter](node:Kaluza–Klein%20Dark%20Matter): the $B^{(1)}$ LKP as a thermal relic.
- [Standard Model of Particle Physics](node:Standard%20Model%20of%20Particle%20Physics), [Electroweak Theory](node:Electroweak%20Theory) and [Higgs Mechanism](node:Higgs%20Mechanism): every SM field has a KK partner; precision and Higgs-mass constraints bound $1/R$.
- [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions), [Large Extra Dimensions](node:Large%20Extra%20Dimensions) and [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model): UED is the flat, universal branch, unlike ADD (brane-confined SM) and warped RS.
- [Compactification](node:Compactification) and [Orbifolds](node:Orbifolds): $S^1/Z_2$ and $T^2/Z_2$ geometries.
- [Effective Field Theory](node:Effective%20Field%20Theory): UED is non-renormalizable and valid only below $\Lambda$.
- [Collider Physics](node:Collider%20Physics) and [Supersymmetry](node:Supersymmetry): pair-produced cascades with missing energy mimic SUSY.
- [Dark Matter](node:Dark%20Matter), [Weakly Interacting Massive Particles](node:Weakly%20Interacting%20Massive%20Particles) and [Dark Matter Direct Detection](node:Dark%20Matter%20Direct%20Detection): the LKP is a WIMP-like candidate.
- [Hierarchy Problem](node:Hierarchy%20Problem): not UED's original target.
- Map: [Physics Subsection - Extra dimensions and compactification](node:Physics%20Subsection%20-%20Extra%20dimensions%20and%20compactification).

### Common pitfalls
- **UED is not ADD.** In ADD only gravity is in the bulk; in UED every SM field has a KK tower. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_extra_dimensions))
- **KK number versus KK parity.** KK number is broken by loops to KK parity $(-1)^n$; level-two states can couple singly to SM pairs. ([Kong & Matchev](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0610057); [Edelhäuser, Flacke & Krämer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.6076))
- **Dated bounds.** Early estimates ($\sim300\,\mathrm{GeV}$ from electroweak data, the "about $1\,\mathrm{TeV}$" LHC figure quoted on Wikipedia) are superseded for mUED by $1/R>1.4$–$1.5\,\mathrm{TeV}$ from 13 TeV searches. ([Appelquist, Cheng & Dobrescu](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012100); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_extra_dimensions); [PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf))
- **"UED is excluded" is model-dependent.** The exclusion applies to the minimal model; boundary terms change both spectrum and relic density. ([PDG review](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf); [Hooper & Profumo](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0701197))

### Open problems
- **Full nmUED parameter space.** The Flacke–Kong–Park review states that existing nmUED studies use reasonable but "certainly-not-most-general" parameter choices and that "further studies are definitely required to probe the full parameter space" with electroweak-precision, collider and dark-matter data. ([Flacke, Kong & Park](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1408.4024))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Universal extra dimensions (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_extra_dimensions): contrast with ADD, scales, early bounds.
- **Reference:** [PDG, Extra dimensions review (2024)](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-extra-dimensions.pdf): current status of UED among extra-dimension models.
- **Learn:** [Kong & Matchev, Phenomenology of Universal Extra Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/html/hep-ph/0610057): KK parity, LKP, and UED-versus-SUSY discrimination.
- **Primary:** [Appelquist, Cheng & Dobrescu, Bounds on Universal Extra Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0012100): the defining paper.
- **Primary:** [Cheng, Matchev & Schmaltz, Radiative Corrections to Kaluza-Klein Masses](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0204342): the mUED spectrum.
- **Primary:** [Avnish, Ghosh, Jha & Niyogi, mUED and nmUED in the light of 13 TeV LHC data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15137): exclusion of the relic-density-allowed mUED region.
- **Further reading:** [Hooper & Profumo, Dark Matter and Collider Phenomenology of UED (Phys. Rept. 453)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0701197): the standard review; and [Flacke, Kong & Park, A Review on Non-Minimal UED](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1408.4024).
references.Variational Inference:
## Reference
### Overview
Variational inference (VI) approximates an intractable probability density, typically a Bayesian posterior $p(z\mid x)$, by optimisation rather than sampling: one posits a family $\mathcal Q$ of tractable densities and finds the member closest to the target in Kullback–Leibler divergence. Blei, Kucukelbir and McAuliffe present it as an alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo that tends to be faster and suits large data sets and rapid model exploration, while MCMC suits smaller data sets where precise samples are worth the cost ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670)).

The key identity is the decomposition of the log evidence into the evidence lower bound (ELBO) plus the KL gap, so maximising the computable ELBO is equivalent to minimising the uncomputable divergence. Variational Bayes can be seen as an extension of the EM algorithm that returns full posterior approximations rather than point estimates, and the ELBO is called the negative variational free energy by analogy with thermodynamics ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variational_Bayesian_methods)).

In the broader sense of Wainwright and Jordan, any procedure that approximates a density by optimisation is variational inference; this includes expectation propagation, belief propagation, and even the Laplace approximation ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670)). Wainwright and Jordan use the conjugate duality between the cumulant (log partition) function and the entropy of exponential families to show that sum-product, expectation propagation, mean-field methods and related algorithms can all be understood as exact or approximate forms of one variational representation ([Wainwright and Jordan](https://groups.seas.harvard.edu/courses/cs281/papers/WaiJor08_FTML.pdf)).

### Formal definition
Given observations $x$, latent variables $z$, and a variational family $\mathcal Q$, KL variational inference solves
$$q^*=\arg\min_{q\in\mathcal Q}\mathrm{KL}\big(q(z)\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\big).$$
Since $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(\cdot\mid x))=\mathbb E_q[\log q(z)]-\mathbb E_q[\log p(z,x)]+\log p(x)$, one maximises instead
$$\mathrm{ELBO}(q)=\mathbb E_q[\log p(z,x)]-\mathbb E_q[\log q(z)]=\mathbb E_q[\log p(x\mid z)]-\mathrm{KL}(q(z)\|p(z)),$$
and
$$\log p(x)=\mathrm{KL}\big(q(z)\|p(z\mid x)\big)+\mathrm{ELBO}(q)\ \ge\ \mathrm{ELBO}(q)$$
([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), eqs. 10–14).

The **mean-field family** consists of fully factorised densities $q(z)=\prod_j q_j(z_j)$ ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670)). For an unnormalised model $\tilde p$ with partition function $Z$, the same bound reads $\log Z\ge\mathbb E_q[\log\tilde p(x)-\log q(x)]$, with gap exactly $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$ ([Stanford CS228 notes](https://ermongroup.github.io/cs228-notes/inference/variational/)).

### Key results
- **ELBO bound.** For every density $q$ with $q\ll p(\cdot\mid x)$, $\log p(x)\ge\mathrm{ELBO}(q)$, with equality iff $q=p(\cdot\mid x)$, because the gap is a KL divergence and KL is nonnegative ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), eq. 14).
- **Coordinate-ascent (CAVI) update.** In the mean-field family, holding $q_\ell$ fixed for $\ell\ne j$, the ELBO-optimal factor is $q_j^*(z_j)\propto\exp\{\mathbb E_{-j}[\log p(z_j\mid z_{-j},x)]\}\propto\exp\{\mathbb E_{-j}[\log p(z_j,z_{-j},x)]\}$; iterating these updates climbs the ELBO to a local optimum ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), eqs. 17–18). Only factors in the Markov blanket of $z_j$ enter the update ([Stanford CS228 notes](https://ermongroup.github.io/cs228-notes/inference/variational/)).
- **Exact variational principle for exponential families.** For an exponential family with log partition function $A$, mean-parameter set $\mathcal M$ and conjugate dual $A^*$: $A^*(\mu)=-H(p_{\theta(\mu)})$ for $\mu$ in the interior $\mathcal M^\circ$ and $A^*(\mu)=+\infty$ for $\mu\notin\overline{\mathcal M}$; $A(\theta)=\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\{\langle\theta,\mu\rangle-A^*(\mu)\}$; and the supremum is attained uniquely at $\mu=\mathbb E_\theta[\phi(X)]$ ([Wainwright and Jordan](https://groups.seas.harvard.edu/courses/cs281/papers/WaiJor08_FTML.pdf), Theorem 3.4).
- **Mean-field lower bound.** Any $\mu\in\mathcal M^\circ$ gives $A(\theta)\ge\langle\theta,\mu\rangle-A^*(\mu)$, with equality iff $\mu=\mathbb E_\theta[\phi(X)]$; mean-field methods restrict $\mu$ to the means realisable by a tractable (e.g. product) subfamily, so they produce lower bounds on $A(\theta)$ ([Wainwright and Jordan](https://groups.seas.harvard.edu/courses/cs281/papers/WaiJor08_FTML.pdf), Proposition 5.1).
- **Variational [Bernstein–von Mises theorem](node:Bernstein–von%20Mises%20Theorem).** Under the paper's regularity conditions, the variational Bayes posterior converges to the Kullback–Leibler minimiser of a normal distribution centred at the true parameter, and the corresponding variational expectation of the parameter is consistent and asymptotically normal; the result covers Bayesian mixture models, generalised linear mixed models, and stochastic block models ([Wang and Blei](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03439)).
- **Covariance underestimation.** For Bayesian mixtures of Gaussians with [conjugate priors](node:Conjugate%20Priors), the mean-field variational posterior mean is consistent and approaches the MLE at rate $O(1/n)$, but the asymptotic variational posterior covariance is "too small": it differs from the inverse [Fisher information](node:Fisher%20Information) by a positive-definite matrix (Wang and Titterington, as summarised by [Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), §5.2).
- **Stochastic and black-box VI.** Stochastic variational inference combines natural gradients of the ELBO with Robbins–Monro stochastic optimisation to scale conditionally conjugate models to massive data ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), §4.3). For non-conjugate models, Monte Carlo estimates of the ELBO gradient give model-agnostic "black box" methods ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), §5.3); a reparameterisation of the bound yields a lower-bound estimator optimisable by standard stochastic gradient methods, and fitting a recognition model with this estimator makes approximate posterior inference efficient for i.i.d. data sets with continuous latent variables ([Kingma and Welling](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114)).

### Examples
- **Two-dimensional Gaussian.** The optimal mean-field approximation to a correlated bivariate Gaussian posterior is a product of two Gaussians with the correct mean but decoupled covariance, and its marginal variances under-represent those of the target ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), Figure 1).
- **Gaussian with unknown mean and precision.** With conjugate Gaussian–gamma priors and the factorisation $q(\mu,\tau)=q(\mu)q(\tau)$, the optimal $q(\mu)$ is Gaussian and $q(\tau)$ is gamma, with parameters updated in an EM-like loop, whereas the true posterior is Gaussian–gamma (not a product) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variational_Bayesian_methods)).
- **Bayesian mixture of Gaussians.** CAVI alternates closed-form updates of the cluster-assignment responsibilities and of Gaussian factors for the cluster means ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), §3).
- **Naive mean field for the Ising model.** For the Ising model, the naive mean-field algorithm replaces the random spin flips of the Gibbs sampler with deterministic updates of each mean parameter $\mu_s$ from its neighbours' parameters; mean-field methods arise from restricting the exact variational principle to a tractable (e.g. product) subfamily ([Wainwright and Jordan](https://groups.seas.harvard.edu/courses/cs281/papers/WaiJor08_FTML.pdf), §2 and §5).

### History
Peterson and Anderson (1987) is arguably the first variational procedure for a particular model, a neural network; together with insights from statistical mechanics this led to a flurry of variational procedures for a wide class of models, among them Jordan et al. (1999). In parallel, Hinton and van Camp (1993) proposed a variational algorithm for a similar network, and Neal and Hinton (1999, first published in 1993) connected these ideas to the EM algorithm ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670)). Wainwright and Jordan's monograph *Graphical Models, Exponential Families, and Variational Inference* appeared in *Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning* 1(1–2), 1–305 (2008) ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1561/2200000001)). Kingma and Welling's reparameterised estimator was posted in December 2013 ([Kingma and Welling](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114)).

### Connections
- [Bayesian Inference](node:Bayesian%20Inference): VI approximates the posterior that Bayes' rule defines but cannot normalise.
- [Kullback–Leibler Divergence](node:Kullback–Leibler%20Divergence): the objective is the reverse divergence $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$, which explains the mode-seeking behaviour.
- [Expectation-Maximization Algorithm](node:Expectation-Maximization%20Algorithm): EM is coordinate ascent on the same lower bound with a point estimate for parameters.
- [Markov Chain Monte Carlo](node:Markov%20Chain%20Monte%20Carlo): the main alternative; sampling is asymptotically exact, VI is biased but fast.
- [Variational Autoencoders](node:Variational%20Autoencoders): amortised VI with reparameterised gradients and a neural recognition model.
- [Probabilistic Graphical Models](node:Probabilistic%20Graphical%20Models): mean-field updates are local message passing over Markov blankets.
- [Information Geometry](node:Information%20Geometry): natural-gradient SVI uses the Fisher geometry of the variational family.
- [Amortized Bayesian Inference](node:Amortized%20Bayesian%20Inference): learning a map from data to variational parameters.
- [Statistical Mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics): mean-field theory and variational free energy originate there.
- [Ising Model](node:Ising%20Model): naive mean field for the Ising model is the prototype of product-family VI.
- [Belief Propagation](node:Belief%20Propagation): another approximation to the same exponential-family variational principle.
- [Partition Function](node:Partition%20Function): the ELBO is a lower bound on the log partition function.

### Common pitfalls
- **Variance underestimation.** Because $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$ penalises mass of $q$ where $p$ is small more than the reverse, mean-field solutions tend to be too narrow ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670)). The exclusive divergence is zero-forcing and typically under-estimates the support of $p$; fit to a multimodal target, a unimodal $q$ locks onto one mode ([Stanford CS228 notes](https://ermongroup.github.io/cs228-notes/inference/variational/)).
- **Local optima.** CAVI is guaranteed only to reach a local optimum of the non-convex ELBO ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670)).
- **Model selection by the ELBO.** Using the bound as a proxy for the marginal likelihood sometimes works in practice but is not justified in theory ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670)).
- **Direction of the divergence.** Minimising $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$ (as in expectation propagation) needs expectations under $p$, which are usually intractable; standard VI uses $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$ precisely because it needs only expectations under $q$ ([Stanford CS228 notes](https://ermongroup.github.io/cs228-notes/inference/variational/)).

### Open problems
Blei, Kucukelbir and McAuliffe list the following as open research avenues ([Blei et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670), §5.4):
- **Alternative divergences.** Developing VI methods that optimise other measures, such as $\alpha$-divergences or bounds tighter than the ELBO, which may be harder to optimise but give better approximations.
- **Richer families.** Building variational families more expressive than mean field (structured, full-covariance, hierarchical) while keeping optimisation efficient.
- **VI and MCMC.** The interface between the two is "relatively unexplored"; a principled analysis of when to use or combine them is called a ripe area for future research.
- **Statistical theory.** Understanding VI as an estimator and its statistical profile relative to the exact posterior; the relative accuracy of VI and MCMC is described as still unknown (§1).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Variational Bayesian methods (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variational_Bayesian_methods): ELBO, mean-field derivation, relation to EM, Gaussian–gamma example.
- **Learn:** [Stanford CS228 notes: Variational inference](https://ermongroup.github.io/cs228-notes/inference/variational/): ELBO from the partition function, exclusive vs inclusive KL, mean-field coordinate ascent.
- **Primary:** [Blei, Kucukelbir and McAuliffe, Variational Inference: A Review for Statisticians](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.00670): survey with CAVI, SVI, theory, and open problems.
- **Primary:** [Wang and Blei, Frequentist Consistency of Variational Bayes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03439): variational Bernstein–von Mises theorem.
- **Further reading:** [Wainwright and Jordan, Graphical Models, Exponential Families, and Variational Inference](https://groups.seas.harvard.edu/courses/cs281/papers/WaiJor08_FTML.pdf): the standard monograph on exact and approximate variational principles via convex duality.
references.Vector Calculus:
## Reference
### Overview
Vector calculus studies differentiation and integration of scalar and vector fields, mainly in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Its operators are the gradient, divergence, curl, and Laplacian, and its integral theorems (gradient, Green, Kelvin–Stokes, and divergence theorems) extend the fundamental theorem of calculus to curves, surfaces, and solids. ([Vector calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_calculus))

All of these integral theorems are special cases of one statement about differential forms on manifolds, the generalized Stokes theorem $\int_\Omega d\omega=\int_{\partial\Omega}\omega$. In that language, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{grad}=0$ and $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}=0$ are both $d^2=0$, and whether a curl-free field is a gradient becomes a question about the topology of its domain, measured by de Rham cohomology. ([Generalized Stokes theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Stokes_theorem); [Closed and exact forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_and_exact_differential_forms))

The cross-product form of the curl is special to three dimensions (a cross product exists only in dimensions 3 and 7), which is why differential forms or geometric algebra are used in higher dimensions. ([Vector calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_calculus))

### Formal definition
In Cartesian coordinates $\nabla=(\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z)$. For a differentiable scalar $f$ and field $\mathbf F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$:
$$\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf),\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z,$$
$$\nabla\times\mathbf F=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x),\qquad \Delta f=\nabla\cdot\nabla f.$$
([Vector calculus identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_calculus_identities); [Vector calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_calculus))

In spherical coordinates $(r,\theta,\varphi)$ with $\theta$ the polar angle, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=\frac1{r^2}\partial_r(r^2A_r)+\frac1{r\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(A_\theta\sin\theta)+\frac1{r\sin\theta}\partial_\varphi A_\varphi$ and $\Delta f=\frac1{r^2}\partial_r(r^2\partial_rf)+\frac1{r^2\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f)+\frac1{r^2\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi^2f$. In cylindrical coordinates $(\rho,\varphi,z)$, $\Delta f=\frac1\rho\partial_\rho(\rho\,\partial_\rho f)+\frac1{\rho^2}\partial_\varphi^2f+\partial_z^2f$. ([Del in cylindrical and spherical coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Del_in_cylindrical_and_spherical_coordinates))

### Key results
- **Identities.** For $C^2$ scalar $\varphi$ and field $\mathbf A$: $\nabla\times(\nabla\varphi)=\mathbf 0$, $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf A)=0$, and $\nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf A)=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf A)-\nabla^2\mathbf A$. Product rules include $\nabla\cdot(\psi\mathbf A)=\psi\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+\mathbf A\cdot\nabla\psi$ and $\nabla\cdot(\mathbf A\times\mathbf B)=(\nabla\times\mathbf A)\cdot\mathbf B-\mathbf A\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf B)$. ([Vector calculus identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_calculus_identities))
- **Gradient theorem and its converse.** If $\varphi$ is continuously differentiable on open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $\gamma$ is a piecewise smooth curve in $U$ from $\mathbf p$ to $\mathbf q$, then $\int_\gamma\nabla\varphi\cdot d\mathbf r=\varphi(\mathbf q)-\varphi(\mathbf p)$. Conversely, a continuous path-independent field on an open path-connected set is a gradient. ([Gradient theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_theorem))
- **Green's theorem.** If $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise smooth, simple closed curve bounding $D\subset\mathbb R^2$, and $L,M$ have continuous partial derivatives on an open set containing $D$, then $\oint_C(L\,dx+M\,dy)=\iint_D(\partial_xM-\partial_yL)\,dA$. In particular $\operatorname{Area}(D)=\tfrac12\oint_C(x\,dy-y\,dx)$. ([Green's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_theorem))
- **Kelvin–Stokes theorem.** For a smooth oriented surface $\Sigma\subset\mathbb R^3$ with boundary $\partial\Sigma$ oriented by the right-hand rule, and $\mathbf F$ with continuous first partial derivatives on $\Sigma$, $\iint_\Sigma(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S=\oint_{\partial\Sigma}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$. ([Kelvin–Stokes theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin%E2%80%93Stokes_theorem))
- **Divergence theorem.** If $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ is compact with piecewise smooth boundary $S$ and $\mathbf F$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $V$, then $\int_V\nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV=\oint_S\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dS$ with outward normal. Applying it to $g\mathbf F$ with $\mathbf F=\nabla f$ gives Green's identities. ([Divergence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergence_theorem))
- **Generalized Stokes theorem.** For a smooth compactly supported $(n-1)$-form $\omega$ on an oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $\Omega$, $\int_\Omega d\omega=\int_{\partial\Omega}\omega$; the [fundamental theorem of calculus](node:Fundamental%20Theorem%20of%20Calculus), Green, Kelvin–Stokes, and divergence theorems are the cases of a segment, a planar region, a surface in $\mathbb R^3$, and a solid in $\mathbb R^3$. ([Generalized Stokes theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Stokes_theorem))
- **Poincaré lemma and conservative fields.** On a contractible open set every closed $p$-form with $p>0$ is exact. In vector language: if $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ is open and simply connected and $\nabla\times\mathbf F=0$, then $\oint_c\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=0$ for every piecewise smooth loop $c$ in $U$, so $\mathbf F$ is a gradient. ([Closed and exact forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_and_exact_differential_forms); [Kelvin–Stokes theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin%E2%80%93Stokes_theorem))
- **Helmholtz decomposition.** If $\mathbf F$ is $C^2$ on a bounded domain $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ with boundary $S$, then $\mathbf F=-\nabla\Phi+\nabla\times\mathbf A$ with
$$\Phi(\mathbf r)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_V\frac{\nabla'\cdot\mathbf F(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}dV'-\frac1{4\pi}\oint_S\frac{\hat{\mathbf n}'\cdot\mathbf F(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}dS',$$
and $\mathbf A$ given by the same formula with $\nabla'\times\mathbf F$ and $\hat{\mathbf n}'\times\mathbf F$. On all of $\mathbb R^3$, for fields decaying faster than $1/r$, the surface terms vanish and the two components are unique when the potentials also decay. ([Helmholtz decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_decomposition))

### Examples
The field $\mathbf F=\left(\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2},\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\right)$ on the punctured plane has zero curl, yet its line integrals around unit circles winding different numbers of times about the origin take different values, so it is not conservative. This does not contradict the zero-curl theorem, because no simply connected region containing the circle avoids the origin. In form language, $d\theta=(-y\,dx+x\,dy)/(x^2+y^2)$ is closed but not exact, since the angle $\theta$ is not single-valued there. ([Millersville notes](https://sites.millersville.edu/rumble/Math.311/simply-connected.pdf); [Closed and exact forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_and_exact_differential_forms))

In three dimensions, a closed $1$-form corresponds to an irrotational field and an exact one to a conservative field; a closed $2$-form corresponds to a divergence-free (solenoidal) field. ([Closed and exact forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_and_exact_differential_forms))

### History
Green stated a similar result in his 1828 essay, which was almost forgotten until Thomson (Kelvin) rediscovered the essay in 1845; Cauchy stated the theorem in 1846, and Riemann gave the first proof in 1851. Ostrogradsky gave the first proof of the general divergence theorem in 1826, after special cases by Lagrange (1762) and Gauss (1813). Kelvin communicated the curl theorem to Stokes in a letter of 2 July 1850, Stokes set it on the 1854 Smith's Prize examination, Hankel published the first proof in 1861, and Cartan gave the modern differential-form version in 1945. ([Green's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%27s_theorem); [Divergence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergence_theorem); [Generalized Stokes theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Stokes_theorem))

Stokes described the three-dimensional decomposition in 1849 and Helmholtz published his hydrodynamic version in 1858. Modern notation was shaped by Gibbs and Heaviside, and Gibbs and Wilson's 1901 *Vector Analysis* fixed most of it. ([Helmholtz decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_decomposition); [Vector calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_calculus))

### Connections
- [Multivariable Calculus](node:Multivariable%20Calculus): derivatives and multiple integrals in several variables.
- [Fundamental Theorem of Calculus](node:Fundamental%20Theorem%20of%20Calculus): the one-dimensional case of every integral theorem here.
- [Stokes' Theorem](node:Stokes'%20Theorem): the general theorem in its own note.
- [Differential Forms](node:Differential%20Forms) and [Differential Calculus on Manifolds](node:Differential%20Calculus%20on%20Manifolds): the coordinate-free setting of the generalized Stokes theorem.
- [De Rham Cohomology](node:De%20Rham%20Cohomology): measures the failure of closed forms to be exact, e.g. on the punctured plane.
- [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group): simple connectivity is the hypothesis making curl-free fields conservative.
- [Hodge Theory](node:Hodge%20Theory): generalizes the Helmholtz decomposition to forms on Riemannian manifolds.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations) and [Newtonian Potential Theory](node:Newtonian%20Potential%20Theory): the scalar potential solves a Poisson equation.
- [Green's Functions](node:Green's%20Functions): the kernel $1/(4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|)$ in the Helmholtz potentials.
- [Maxwell's Equations](node:Maxwell's%20Equations): written with divergence and curl, equivalent integral forms via Gauss and Stokes.
- [Euler Equations for Incompressible Fluids](node:Euler%20Equations%20for%20Incompressible%20Fluids): divergence-free velocity fields and vorticity.

### Common pitfalls
Zero curl does not imply conservative unless the domain is simply connected; the punctured-plane field above is the standard counterexample. In Stokes' theorem the boundary orientation must match the surface normal by the right-hand rule. The Helmholtz potentials are never unique (gauge freedom), and the gradient and rotational parts are unique only under decay or boundary conditions, since a harmonic gradient $\nabla H$ can be moved between them. The Hodge decomposition is not strictly a generalization of Helmholtz's theorem on $\mathbb R^3$, because most formulations assume compactness. Physics and mathematics texts swap the roles of $\theta$ and $\varphi$ in spherical coordinates. ([Millersville notes](https://sites.millersville.edu/rumble/Math.311/simply-connected.pdf); [Kelvin–Stokes theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin%E2%80%93Stokes_theorem); [Helmholtz decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_decomposition); [Del in cylindrical and spherical coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Del_in_cylindrical_and_spherical_coordinates))

### Open problems
None found. The classical theorems above are settled under their hypotheses; current work extends them, for example Glötzl and Richters construct Helmholtz decompositions in $\mathbb R^n$ with antisymmetric matrix-valued rotation potentials, including fields growing at infinity and an existence proof for all analytic fields, but present these as results rather than open questions. Searches tried: "Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition survey open problems boundary conditions", and "Helmholtz decomposition n-dimensional vector fields". ([Glötzl–Richters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09556))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Vector calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_calculus) and [Generalized Stokes theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Stokes_theorem): scope, history, and the unifying theorem.
- **Learn:** [Millersville Math 311, Why simply connected?](https://sites.millersville.edu/rumble/Math.311/simply-connected.pdf): a worked note on the zero-curl theorem and the winding-number counterexample.
- **Primary:** [Glötzl and Richters, Helmholtz decomposition and potential functions for n-dimensional analytic vector fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09556): research paper (J. Math. Anal. Appl. 2023) extending the Helmholtz decomposition.
- **Further reading:** [Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4419-9982-5): Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics; differential forms, Stokes's theorem, and de Rham cohomology.
references.Vector Search and Embeddings:
## Reference
### Overview
Vector search retrieves, from a large collection of vectors, those closest to a query vector under a similarity or distance function. In modern systems the vectors are embeddings: learned representations of text, images or audio in spaces of a few hundred to tens of thousands of dimensions, produced by models such as word-embedding methods or deep networks so that similar items lie close together ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_database)). A vector database stores such embeddings and answers queries by approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search rather than exact matching; it is a common retrieval component in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where documents relevant to a prompt are retrieved and added to a language model's context ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_database)).

The underlying problem is nearest-neighbor search (NNS), which Knuth called the "post-office problem". In high-dimensional Euclidean space no general-purpose exact method is known with polynomial preprocessing and polylogarithmic query time, and tree indexes degrade as dimension grows (the curse of dimensionality) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search)). Practical systems therefore accept approximation, using locality-sensitive hashing, proximity graphs such as HNSW, and compressed codes such as product quantization, often in combination ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_database)).

Dense retrieval showed that learned embeddings can beat classical sparse retrieval: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) learns question and passage embeddings with a dual-encoder and outperforms a strong Lucene-BM25 baseline by 9-19 points absolute in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy for open-domain question answering ([arXiv:2004.04906](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906)). The design space of a vector index is a trade-off among accuracy, search speed and memory, with build time and I/O as secondary constraints ([arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.08281)).

### Formal definition
Given database vectors $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^d$ and a query $q$, **$k$-NN search** returns the indices of the $k$ vectors closest to $q$, i.e. the first $k$ entries of $\operatorname{argsort}_i\|q-x_i\|$; **range search** returns $\{n:\|q-x_n\|\le\varepsilon\}$. Cosine similarity reduces to $L_2$ search by normalizing the vectors, and inner-product search reduces to $L_2$ search by adding an extra dimension ([arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.08281)).

**Approximate NN.** A $c$-approximate nearest neighbor of $q$ is a point whose distance to $q$ is at most $c$ times the distance from $q$ to its true nearest neighbor ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search)).

**Locality-sensitive family.** For a metric space $(M,d)$, threshold $r>0$, approximation factor $c>1$ and probabilities $p_1>p_2$, a family $\mathcal F$ of functions $h:M\to S$ is $(r,cr,p_1,p_2)$-sensitive if for $h$ drawn at random from $\mathcal F$,
$$d(a,b)\le r\Rightarrow\Pr[h(a)=h(b)]\ge p_1,\qquad d(a,b)\ge cr\Rightarrow\Pr[h(a)=h(b)]\le p_2$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality-sensitive_hashing)).

**Product quantization (PQ).** Split $x\in\mathbb R^d$ into $M$ sub-vectors and quantize each with its own $k$-means codebook of $K$ centroids; the code $(c_1,\dots,c_M)\in\{1..K\}^M$ takes $M\lceil\log_2K\rceil$ bits and can represent $K^M$ distinct vectors. In asymmetric distance computation the query is left uncompressed and distances to codes are computed from per-query lookup tables ([arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.08281)).

### Key results
- **Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.** For every $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and every $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ with $|X|=n$, there is a map $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m$ with $m=O(\log n/\epsilon^2)$ such that $\|x-y\|_2\le\|f(x)-f(y)\|_2\le(1+\epsilon)\|x-y\|_2$ for all $x,y\in X$. The proof uses the linear map $f(x)=Ax$ with $A$ an $m\times d$ matrix of independent $N(0,1/m)$ entries: for $m>17\log n/\epsilon^2$, with constant probability $\|f(x)-f(y)\|_2=(1\pm\epsilon)\|x-y\|_2$ for all pairs, and rescaling gives the one-sided form. ([Stanford CS265 notes](https://theory.stanford.edu/%7Evaliant/teaching/CS265/lectureNotes/l9.pdf))
- **LSH for approximate near neighbors (Indyk-Motwani).** Given an $(R,cR,P_1,P_2)$-sensitive family, let $\rho=\log P_1/\log P_2$; concatenating $k=\lceil\log n/\log(1/P_2)\rceil$ hash functions per table in $L=\lceil P_1^{-k}\rceil$ tables gives a structure with space $O(n^{1+\rho}P_1^{-1})$ plus the data and query time $O(n^{\rho}P_1^{-1}(kt+d))$ (with $t$ the cost of one hash evaluation), which returns a point within distance $cR$ with probability at least $1-(1-P_1^k)^L$ whenever a point within distance $R$ exists. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality-sensitive_hashing); [MIT 6.851 notes](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring07/scribe/lec10.pdf))
- **Random-hyperplane hashing (Charikar).** For $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ and $k$ independent Gaussian hyperplanes, $\Pr[\operatorname{sign}(Ax)=\operatorname{sign}(Ay)]=(1-\theta(x,y)/\pi)^k$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $x$ and $y$; this is an LSH family for cosine distance. ([Stanford CS265 notes](https://theory.stanford.edu/%7Evaliant/teaching/CS265/lectureNotes/l9.pdf); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality-sensitive_hashing))
- **Guarantees for graph indexes (Indyk-Xu).** If the DiskANN graph is built with the slow preprocessing so that it is $\alpha$-shortcut reachable ($\alpha>1$), greedy search from any vertex returns an $\big(\tfrac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}+\varepsilon\big)$-approximate nearest neighbor in $O\big(\log_\alpha\tfrac{\Delta}{(\alpha-1)\varepsilon}\big)$ steps, each of cost $O((4\alpha)^{d}\log\Delta)$, where $\Delta$ is the aspect ratio and $d$ the doubling dimension. ([arXiv:2310.19126](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.19126))
- **Worst cases for practical graph indexes (Indyk-Xu).** For DiskANN with fast preprocessing, HNSW and NSG there are instances on which reaching reasonable accuracy requires query time linear in the instance size; for DiskANN, queries can take at least $0.1n$ steps before reaching any of the 5 nearest neighbors. ([arXiv:2310.19126](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19126))
- **Exact NN in low dimension.** For $n$ points in fixed dimension, all nearest neighbors can be found in $O(n\log n)$ time, and $k$-d trees answer queries in $O(\log N)$ average time on random points. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search))

### Examples
- **HNSW.** A stack of proximity graphs over nested subsets of the data; each element's top layer is drawn at random with exponentially decaying probability, and search descends from the top layer, which the authors report gives logarithmic complexity scaling ([arXiv:1603.09320](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320)). Its main search parameter (efSearch) trades exploration steps for accuracy; the Faiss HNSW index does not support deletion or mutation of vectors, while HNSWlib and FreshDiskANN handle mutation by graph-rebuilding heuristics ([arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.08281)).
- **IVF-PQ.** An inverted-file index partitions the data with a coarse quantizer of $K_{\mathrm{IVF}}$ centroids and visits only the $P_{\mathrm{IVF}}$ nearest lists (nprobe); a simple cost model suggests $K_{\mathrm{IVF}}\approx\sqrt{P_{\mathrm{IVF}}N}$, and residuals are encoded with PQ ([arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.08281)).
- **Brute force.** Linear scan costs $O(dN)$ per query with no index and can beat space partitioning in high dimension ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search)).
- **Systems.** Vector databases include Chroma, Milvus, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate and pgvector for PostgreSQL ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_database)).

### History
Knuth named nearest-neighbor search the post-office problem in *The Art of Computer Programming* (1973) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search)). Johnson and Lindenstrauss introduced their random dimension reduction in 1984, and Indyk and Motwani introduced locality-sensitive hashing in the late 1990s ([Stanford CS265 notes](https://theory.stanford.edu/%7Evaliant/teaching/CS265/lectureNotes/l9.pdf)); Charikar's random-projection method dates from 2002 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality-sensitive_hashing)). Malkov and Yashunin proposed HNSW in 2016 ([arXiv:1603.09320](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320)), and DPR (EMNLP 2020) showed a dense dual-encoder retriever outperforming BM25 for open-domain QA ([arXiv:2004.04906](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906)). The Faiss library paper (2024) documents the index families used in practice ([arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08281)).

### Connections
- [Word Embeddings](node:Word%20Embeddings): the original learned embeddings searched by similarity.
- [Information Retrieval](node:Information%20Retrieval): vector search is the dense counterpart of inverted-index retrieval.
- [Lexical Retrieval and BM25](node:Lexical%20Retrieval%20and%20BM25): the sparse baseline DPR is compared against.
- [Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search](node:Approximate%20Nearest-Neighbor%20Search): the algorithmic core.
- [Product Quantization](node:Product%20Quantization): vector compression used in IVF-PQ indexes.
- [Johnson–Lindenstrauss Lemma](node:Johnson–Lindenstrauss%20Lemma): dimension reduction underlying random-projection LSH.
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation](node:Retrieval-Augmented%20Generation): vector search supplies the retrieved context.
- [Self-Supervised and Contrastive Learning](node:Self-Supervised%20and%20Contrastive%20Learning) and [Metric Learning](node:Metric%20Learning): how embedding spaces are trained so that distance reflects similarity.
- [Hash Tables](node:Hash%20Tables): LSH replaces exact hashing with collision-seeking hashing.
- [Nearest-Neighbor Learning](node:Nearest-Neighbor%20Learning): $k$-NN classifiers use the same search primitive.
- [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces): NNS and LSH are defined over a metric.

### Common pitfalls
- **Metric mismatch.** Cosine and inner-product search reduce to $L_2$ search only after preprocessing (normalization, or an extra dimension for inner product), and the added dimension makes the data anisotropic and harder to quantize ([arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.08281)).
- **Empirical speed is not a guarantee.** Popular graph indexes can need linear query time on adversarial instances ([arXiv:2310.19126](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19126)).
- **Distribution drift.** IVF and PQ indexes lose efficiency when insertions and deletions change the data distribution, and out-of-distribution queries are not addressed by standard benchmarks ([arXiv:2401.08281](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.08281)).
- **Embedding space matters.** Nearest-neighbor search is only useful if the feature space and comparison metric are appropriate to the task ([Stanford CS265 notes](https://theory.stanford.edu/%7Evaliant/teaching/CS265/lectureNotes/l9.pdf)).

### Open problems
- **Guarantees for fast graph indexes.** Whether there is a fast preprocessing algorithm and query procedure that is empirically fast and also has worst-case query-time and approximation guarantees is posed as an open question, together with testing the lower-bound phenomena on real data ([arXiv:2310.19126](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.19126)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Nearest neighbor search (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search): exact and approximate NNS, curse of dimensionality, index families.
- **Reference:** [Locality-sensitive hashing (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality-sensitive_hashing): definitions, amplification and the $n^\rho$ algorithm.
- **Learn:** [Valiant, CS265 Lecture 9: Dimension Reduction and Nearest Neighbor Search (Stanford)](https://theory.stanford.edu/%7Evaliant/teaching/CS265/lectureNotes/l9.pdf): JL lemma, random-hyperplane LSH, open questions.
- **Primary:** [Douze et al., The Faiss library](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08281): design space of vector search, PQ, IVF and graph indexes.
- **Primary:** [Malkov and Yashunin, HNSW](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320): the hierarchical navigable small world index.
- **Primary:** [Indyk and Xu, Worst-case Performance of Popular ANN Implementations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19126): guarantees and lower bounds for graph indexes.
- **Primary:** [Karpukhin et al., Dense Passage Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906): dual-encoder dense retrieval for QA.
- **Further reading:** [Manning, Raghavan, Schütze, Introduction to Information Retrieval (CUP 2008)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/introduction-to-information-retrieval/669D108D20F556C5C30957D63B5AB65C): standard IR textbook covering indexing, search and evaluation.
references.Vector Spaces:
## Reference
### Overview
A vector space over a field $F$ is a set $V$ with an addition and a scalar multiplication $F\times V\to V$ satisfying eight axioms; equivalently, it is a module over a field. Vector spaces are the objects of linear algebra, and linear maps are their morphisms. Kernels and images of linear maps are subspaces, and subspaces, quotients, direct sums and products, duals and tensor products are all again vector spaces. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space))

What makes the theory rigid is that a vector space is classified up to isomorphism by one cardinal, its dimension: every space has a basis, all bases have the same cardinality, and two $F$-spaces are isomorphic exactly when their dimensions agree. In infinite dimensions both existence of bases and the comparison of bases depend on choice principles, and the algebraic dual is strictly larger than the space. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space); [Dimension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_theorem_for_vector_spaces); [Dual space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space))

### Formal definition
Let $F$ be a field. A vector space over $F$ is a nonempty set $V$ with maps $+:V\times V\to V$ and $F\times V\to V$ such that for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in F$: $u+(v+w)=(u+v)+w$; $u+v=v+u$; there is $0\in V$ with $v+0=v$; each $v$ has $-v$ with $v+(-v)=0$; $a(bv)=(ab)v$; $1v=v$; $a(u+v)=au+av$; $(a+b)v=av+bv$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space))

A subspace is a nonempty subset closed under addition and scalar multiplication; intersections of subspaces are subspaces, and the span of $G\subseteq V$ is the smallest subspace containing $G$, the set of finite linear combinations of elements of $G$. A basis is a linearly independent spanning set, and the dimension is the common cardinality of all bases. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space))

Constructions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space); [Quotient space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_space_%28linear_algebra%29); [Direct sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_sum_of_modules); [Tensor product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product)):
- **Quotient:** for a subspace $U$, $V/U$ is the set of cosets $v+U$, with $v+U=v'+U$ iff $v-v'\in U$; the quotient map $V\to V/U$ is surjective with kernel $U$, and $\dim V/U$ is the codimension of $U$.
- **Direct product and direct sum** of a family $(V_i)_{i\in I}$: $\prod_iV_i$ is all tuples, $\bigoplus_iV_i$ the tuples with only finitely many nonzero entries; they agree for finite $I$. The direct sum is the coproduct: maps $f_i:V_i\to W$ extend uniquely to a linear map $\bigoplus V_i\to W$.
- **Dual:** $V^*=\operatorname{Hom}_F(V,F)$; a linear $f:V\to W$ induces the transpose $f^*:W^*\to V^*$, $\lambda\mapsto\lambda\circ f$.
- **Tensor product:** $V\otimes W$ with bilinear $(v,w)\mapsto v\otimes w$ such that every bilinear $h:V\times W\to Z$ factors through a unique linear map $V\otimes W\to Z$.

### Key results
- **Steinitz exchange lemma.** If $U$ is a finite linearly independent set and $W$ a finite spanning set of $V$, then $|U|\le|W|$, and there is $W'\subseteq W$ with $|W'|=|W|-|U|$ such that $U\cup W'$ spans $V$. Consequently any two bases of a finite-dimensional space have the same number of elements. ([Steinitz exchange lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steinitz_exchange_lemma))
- **Dimension theorem.** In any vector space, a linearly independent set is no larger than a generating set, so any two bases have the same cardinality. The infinite case is proved by writing each element of one basis as a finite combination of the other; it uses choice, and the invariance requires only the ultrafilter lemma. ([Dimension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_theorem_for_vector_spaces))
- **Existence of bases.** Applying Zorn's lemma to linearly independent subsets ordered by inclusion gives a maximal independent set, which spans; hence every vector space has a basis, every independent set extends to a basis, and every spanning set contains one. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/basis+theorem); [Axiom of choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_choice))
- **Blass's theorem.** Over ZF, "every vector space has a basis" is equivalent to the axiom of choice (Blass, 1984). In every model of ZF + ¬AC there is a vector space with no basis, and without AC a vector space can have two bases of different cardinalities. ([Axiom of choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_choice); [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/basis+theorem)) Fernandes, Mezabarba and Rodrigues prove the implication from bases to AC in ZF without the axiom of foundation and in set theory with atoms. ([arXiv:2609.20140](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20140))
- **Classification.** Two vector spaces over the same field are isomorphic iff they have the same dimension; every $n$-dimensional $F$-space is isomorphic, non-canonically, to $F^n$, and every vector space is isomorphic to a direct sum $\bigoplus_{i\in B}F$ indexed by a basis. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space); [Direct sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_sum_of_modules); [Dual space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space))
- **Rank–nullity.** For linear $T:V\to W$ with $V$ finite-dimensional, $\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T$; no finiteness is needed on $W$. It is the vector-space case of the [first isomorphism theorem](node:First%20Isomorphism%20Theorem) $V/\ker T\cong\operatorname{im}T$, and in finite dimension $\dim V/U=\dim V-\dim U$. For an $m\times n$ matrix, $\operatorname{rank}+\operatorname{nullity}=n$. ([Rank–nullity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank%E2%80%93nullity_theorem); [Quotient space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_space_%28linear_algebra%29))
- **Duality in finite dimension.** A basis of $V$ determines a dual basis of $V^*$, so $\dim V^*=\dim V$, and the canonical map $V\to V^{**}$ is an isomorphism; $V\cong V^*$ holds but not naturally. ([Dual space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space))
- **Duality in infinite dimension (Erdős–Kaplansky).** If $V$ is infinite-dimensional over $F$ with basis $I$, then $V^*\cong F^I$ and $\dim V^*=|F^I|=|F|^{|I|}$, which exceeds $|I|$ by Cantor's theorem; so $V\not\cong V^*$ and $V\to V^{**}$ is injective but not surjective. ([Erdős–Kaplansky theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Kaplansky_theorem); [Dual space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_space)) The dual of a direct sum is the direct product of the duals. ([Direct sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_sum_of_modules))
- **Tensor products.** If $B_V,B_W$ are bases, $\{v\otimes w:v\in B_V,w\in B_W\}$ is a basis of $V\otimes W$, so $\dim(V\otimes W)=\dim V\cdot\dim W$ in finite dimension; and $V^*\otimes W\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$ for finite-dimensional $V,W$ via $f\otimes w\mapsto(u\mapsto f(u)w)$. ([Tensor product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product))

### Examples
- $F^n$ with componentwise operations; $\mathbb C$ is a $2$-dimensional real space; a field extension $E\supseteq F$ is an $F$-space. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space))
- The polynomial ring $F[x]$ has countably infinite dimension, while many function spaces have the dimension of the continuum. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space))
- $\mathbb R$ over $\mathbb Q$ is infinite-dimensional; Hamel's 1905 basis for it was obtained from the well-ordering theorem, and no explicit basis is known. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/basis+theorem); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space))
- $\mathbb R^n$ modulo the span of the first $m$ standard basis vectors is isomorphic to $\mathbb R^{n-m}$. ([Quotient space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_space_%28linear_algebra%29))
- The vectors $(1,1,2),(2,2,5)$ span a plane in $\mathbb R^3$ but are not a basis of $\mathbb R^3$; $n$ vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ form a basis when they are the columns of an invertible matrix, and $\operatorname{rank}A=\dim C(A)$ is the number of pivot columns. ([MIT 18.06SC, Ses. 1.9](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/0bbc30e3f1d7933ea07a2d2e9ab050d9_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses1.9sum.pdf))

### History
Grassmann's 1844 *Ausdehnungslehre* contains linear independence and dimension. Peano gave the modern axioms for vector spaces and linear maps in 1888, calling them "linear systems" and allowing infinite dimension; Pincherle studied infinite-dimensional spaces in 1897, and Banach and Hilbert formalized function spaces around 1920. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)) Hamel's basis of $\mathbb R$ over $\mathbb Q$ appeared in 1905, and Blass proved in 1984 that the general basis theorem implies AC. ([nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/basis+theorem); [Blass 1984, Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/conm/031/763890))

### Connections
- [Functions and Relations](node:Functions%20and%20Relations): the operations and linear maps are functions.
- [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory): scalars form a field, and field extensions are vector spaces.
- [Modules and Bimodules](node:Modules%20and%20Bimodules): a vector space is a module over a field.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) and [Rank–Nullity Theorem](node:Rank–Nullity%20Theorem): morphisms, kernels and images.
- [Dual Vector Space](node:Dual%20Vector%20Space): $V^*$, transposes, and the double dual.
- [Quotient Groups](node:Quotient%20Groups): $V/U$ is the quotient of the additive group with induced scalars.
- [Tensors and Multilinear Algebra](node:Tensors%20and%20Multilinear%20Algebra): tensor products and multilinear maps.
- [Axiom of Choice](node:Axiom%20of%20Choice), [Set Theory](node:Set%20Theory) and [Cardinality](node:Cardinality): existence and size of bases.
- [Matroids and Geometric Closure](node:Matroids%20and%20Geometric%20Closure): the exchange property generalizes to matroids (Steinitz–Mac Lane).
- [Inner Product Spaces](node:Inner%20Product%20Spaces), [Banach Spaces](node:Banach%20Spaces), [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces): vector spaces with extra structure.
- Map: [MSC 15 - Linear and multilinear algebra; matrix theory](node:MSC%2015%20-%20Linear%20and%20multilinear%20algebra;%20matrix%20theory).

### Common pitfalls
- Three vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ are independent exactly when they do not lie in a common plane; algebraically, the columns of $A$ are independent exactly when $Ax=0$ has only the zero solution, so independence is tested by elimination rather than by inspecting coordinates. ([MIT 18.06SC, Ses. 1.9](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/0bbc30e3f1d7933ea07a2d2e9ab050d9_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses1.9sum.pdf))
- A Hamel basis allows only finite linear combinations; it is not an orthonormal (Hilbert) basis. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space))
- Direct sum and direct product differ for infinite families, and so $V^*$ for $V=\bigoplus_{I}F$ is the much larger $F^I$. ([Direct sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_sum_of_modules); [Erdős–Kaplansky theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Kaplansky_theorem))
- Rank–nullity in the form $\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T$ needs $V$ finite-dimensional. ([Rank–nullity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank%E2%80%93nullity_theorem))

### Open problems
- **Choice principles for families of subspaces.** In ZF without AC, the deductive strength of statements asserting the existence of almost disjoint and maximal almost disjoint (MAD) families of infinite-dimensional subspaces of an infinite-dimensional vector space, and the extension of almost disjoint families to MAD families, is an open problem investigated by Tachtsis, whose paper records further open questions, for example whether countable choice $\mathrm{AC}^{\aleph_0}$ implies $\mathrm{MA}(\aleph_0)$. ([Tachtsis, J. Symbolic Logic 87 (2022)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-symbolic-logic/article/almost-disjoint-and-mad-families-in-vector-spaces-and-choice-principles/A3A63D81C69F6FDA28E41FC12B8499F8))
- The existence of bases itself is settled: it is equivalent to AC over ZF. ([Axiom of choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_choice))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [nLab: basis theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/basis+theorem): Zorn's lemma proof, Hamel, Blass; [Wikipedia: Vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space): axioms, constructions, history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.06SC, Independence, basis, and dimension](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/0bbc30e3f1d7933ea07a2d2e9ab050d9_MIT18_06SCF11_Ses1.9sum.pdf): Strang's treatment of independence, bases, rank and nullspace.
- **Primary:** [Blass, Existence of bases implies the axiom of choice, Contemp. Math. 31 (1984) 31–33](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/conm/031/763890); [Fernandes, Mezabarba, Rodrigues, a foundation-free proof](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20140).
- **Further reading:** [Halmos, Finite-Dimensional Vector Spaces (Springer Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics, 1974)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-6387-6): standard textbook on finite-dimensional linear algebra.
references.Warped Products:
## Reference
### Overview
A warped product is a product manifold whose metric is a product metric except that the metric of one factor is scaled by a function of the other. Wikipedia writes the metric as $g\oplus(f^2\cdot h)$ on $F\times_f B$ with warping function $f:B\to\mathbb{R}$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product)) Bishop and O'Neill's paper "Manifolds of negative curvature" appeared in *Transactions of the American Mathematical Society* **145** (1969), pages 1–49. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1969-0251664-4))

The same idea organizes many exact solutions of Einstein's equations. Wikipedia lists the Schwarzschild metric, the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) cosmologies, and the Randall–Sundrum models as warped geometries; separation of variables is often available for PDEs on such backgrounds. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product)) Randall and Sundrum's 1999 metric is $ds^2=e^{-2kr_c\phi}\eta_{\mu\nu}\,dx^\mu dx^\nu+r_c^2 d\phi^2$, a warped product of Minkowski 4-space with an interval. ([Randall & Sundrum](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9905221))

### Formal definition
Let $F=(F,h)$ and $B=(B,g)$ be Riemannian (or pseudo-Riemannian) manifolds and $f:B\to\mathbb{R}$ a function. The *warped product* $F\times_f B$ is the product space with metric tensor $g\oplus(f^2\cdot h)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product)) Equivalently, writing $\pi$ and $\eta$ for the projections onto the base $B$ and fibre $F$, the metric is $\pi^*g+(f\circ\pi)^2\eta^*h$. The fibre metric is scaled by $f^2$, so lengths on the fibre scale by $|f|$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product))

A one-dimensional base is the most common special case: on an interval $I$ times a Riemannian manifold $(N,h)$,
$$g=dr^2+\varphi(r)^2 h,\qquad \varphi>0\text{ on }I.$$
A metric $\psi(r)^2 dr^2+\varphi(r)^2 h$ reduces to this form by $d\rho=\psi(r)\,dr$. ([Petersen notes](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf))

The construction extends to pseudo-Riemannian (semi-Riemannian) metrics. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product))

### Key results
- **Surfaces of revolution.** Revolving an embedded curve in the $rz$-plane (with $r>0$) about the $z$-axis yields a warped product. ([Stanford notes](https://web.stanford.edu/~lindrew/math215C.pdf))
- **Hessian characterization.** If smooth functions $f$ and $\lambda$ on a Riemannian manifold satisfy $\operatorname{Hess} f=\lambda g$, then the metric is a warped product in a neighbourhood of any point where $\nabla f\neq 0$. If also $\nabla f|_p=0$ and $\lambda(p)\neq 0$, the same holds around $p$, with spherical fibres. ([Petersen notes](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf))
- **Model spaces.** With $f(p)=0$ and $\nabla f|_p=0$: $\operatorname{Hess} f=g$ gives Euclidean space locally; $\operatorname{Hess} f=(1-f)g$ gives the unit sphere; $\operatorname{Hess} f=(1+f)g$ gives hyperbolic space. The corresponding warped products are $dr^2+r^2 ds^2_{n-1}$, $dr^2+\sin^2 r\,ds^2_{n-1}$, and $dr^2+\sinh^2 r\,ds^2_{n-1}$. ([Petersen notes](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf))
- **Smoothness at a pole.** If $\varphi(r_0)=0$ and $h$ is the round sphere metric, smoothness at the corresponding point requires $\varphi'(r_0)=\pm 1$ and vanishing even derivatives of $\varphi$ at $r_0$. If $h$ is not round, the singularity cannot be removed. ([Petersen notes](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf))

### Examples
- **Polar coordinates.** $dr^2+r^2 ds^2_{n-1}$ on $(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1}$ is the Euclidean metric. ([Petersen notes](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf))
- **Hyperbolic space.** $dr^2+\sinh^2(r)\,ds^2_{n-1}$ on $(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1}$, equivalently the half-space form $ds^2+e^{2s}\mathrm{can}_{\mathbb{R}^{n-1}}$. ([Petersen notes](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf))
- **FLRW.** The cosmological metric $-c^2 d\tau^2=-c^2 dt^2+a(t)^2 d\mathbf{\Sigma}^2$ warps a space of constant curvature by the scale factor $a(t)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedmann%E2%80%93Lema%C3%AEtre%E2%80%93Robertson%E2%80%93Walker_metric))
- **Randall–Sundrum.** The five-dimensional metric $ds^2=e^{-2kr_c\phi}\eta_{\mu\nu}\,dx^\mu dx^\nu+r_c^2 d\phi^2$ on a slice of $\mathrm{AdS}_5$ is a warped product of Minkowski 4-space with an interval. ([Randall & Sundrum](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9905221))

### History
Bishop and O'Neill's paper "Manifolds of negative curvature" appeared in *Transactions of the American Mathematical Society* **145** (1969), pages 1–49. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0002-9947-1969-0251664-4)) O'Neill's later textbook *Semi-Riemannian Geometry* is Wikipedia's second source for the pseudo-Riemannian definition. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product)) Randall and Sundrum used a warped extra dimension in 1999 to generate the weak/Planck hierarchy from an exponential warp factor. ([Randall & Sundrum](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9905221))

### Connections
- [Pseudo-Riemannian Geometry](node:Pseudo-Riemannian%20Geometry): the natural setting; the definition works for indefinite metrics.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): a warped product is a special Riemannian (or pseudo-Riemannian) structure on a product manifold.
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): the underlying manifold is an ordinary product.
- [n-Sphere](node:n-Sphere): polar coordinates present Euclidean space as a warp of $S^{n-1}$.
- [Curvature Tensors](node:Curvature%20Tensors): Petersen's Hessian criterion $\operatorname{Hess} f=\lambda g$ is the local recognition tool for warped products.
- [Geodesics](node:Geodesics): polar-coordinate warped products include the standard model-space metrics $dr^2+r^2 ds^2_{n-1}$, $dr^2+\sin^2 r\,ds^2_{n-1}$, and $dr^2+\sinh^2 r\,ds^2_{n-1}$.
- [Schwarzschild Solution](node:Schwarzschild%20Solution) and [FLRW Cosmology](node:FLRW%20Cosmology): standard GR metrics that are warped products.
- [Randall–Sundrum Model](node:Randall–Sundrum%20Model): physics built on a warped interval times Minkowski space.
- [Anti-de Sitter Space](node:Anti-de%20Sitter%20Space): the RS bulk is a slice of $\mathrm{AdS}_5$.
- [Extra Dimensions](node:Extra%20Dimensions): warping is an alternative to large volume as a way to hide a fifth dimension.
- [MSC 53 - Differential geometry](node:MSC%2053%20-%20Differential%20geometry): the field map.

### Common pitfalls
- **Which factor is warped.** The warping function lives on the *base* $B$ and scales the *fibre* $F$. Wikipedia's $F\times_f B$ notation puts the fibre first. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product))
- **$f$ versus $f^2$.** The fibre metric is multiplied by $f^2$, not by $f$: lengths on the fibre scale by $|f|$. A conformal factor written without the square is a different convention. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product))
- **Not every product-looking metric is warped.** A doubly warped product $dr^2+\varphi_1(r)^2 h_1+\varphi_2(r)^2 h_2$ is a further generalization; Petersen discusses it under transnormal functions. ([Petersen notes](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf))

### Open problems
No major open problems are specific to the local theory of warped products as developed in Petersen's notes: a Hessian criterion $\operatorname{Hess} f=\lambda g$ identifies a warped product in a neighbourhood of any point where $\nabla f\neq 0$. ([Petersen notes](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Warped product (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warped_product): definition and the main spacetime examples.
- **Learn:** [P. Petersen, Warped Products (UCLA lecture notes)](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~petersen/warpedproducts.pdf): polar-coordinate examples, Hessian characterization, and model-space recognition.
- **Primary:** [R. L. Bishop & B. O'Neill, Manifolds of negative curvature, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 145 (1969)](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1969-0251664-4): original paper (bibliographic record: volume 145, pages 1–49).

## Reference
### Overview
The wave equation $\partial_t^2u-c^2\Delta u=0$ is the prototype hyperbolic partial differential equation. It models small transverse vibrations of a string, sound, and other propagating disturbances, and in units with $c=1$ its operator $\Box=-\partial_t^2+\Delta$ is the d'Alembertian of Minkowski spacetime, so its geometry is that of [special relativity](node:Special%20Relativity). ([Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation); [MIT 18.152, lecture 12](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/940561a138578640826f762b5a57bcad_MIT18_152F11_lec_12.pdf))

Its defining qualitative features are finite speed of propagation (the solution at $(t,x)$ depends only on data in the ball of radius $ct$ about $x$), conservation of energy, and a dimension-dependent sharp Huygens principle: in odd dimensions $n\ge3$ the solution depends only on data on the sphere of radius $ct$, while in $n=1$ and in all even dimensions it depends on the solid ball. This contrasts with the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation), whose solutions spread instantly. ([MIT 18.152, lecture 12](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/940561a138578640826f762b5a57bcad_MIT18_152F11_lec_12.pdf); [Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation))

Linear theory is classical; the research frontier concerns nonlinear wave equations $\Box u=\pm|u|^{p-1}u$ and the question of whether smooth data give global smooth solutions. ([Tao 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.08059))

### Formal definition
For $u:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ and $c>0$, the homogeneous equation is $\partial_t^2u-c^2\Delta u=0$. The global Cauchy problem prescribes $u(0,x)=f(x)$ and $\partial_tu(0,x)=g(x)$; on a bounded spatial region one also prescribes boundary conditions. Rescaling time by $c$ reduces to $c=1$. The inhomogeneous equation is $\partial_t^2u-c^2\Delta u=F$. ([MIT 18.152, lecture 10](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/ccd4ae63858e855c18c96ce96a797b9b_MIT18_152F11_lec_10.pdf); [Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation))

The energy of a solution on a ball $B$ at time $t$ is $\tfrac12\int_B\left((\partial_tu)^2+|\nabla_xu|^2\right)dx$ (with $c=1$); it is the time component of the energy–momentum tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$, which is divergence-free for solutions. ([MIT 18.152, lectures 13–14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/ad3a71c522df2396b6248cf9b35aedea_MIT18_152F11_lec_13_14.pdf))

### Key results
- **d'Alembert's formula ($n=1$).** If $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and $g\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, the Cauchy problem for $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}=0$ has a unique $C^2$ solution
$$u(t,x)=\tfrac12\left[f(x-ct)+f(x+ct)\right]+\frac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g(z)\,dz,$$
a superposition of left- and right-moving waves; $u(t,x)$ depends only on data in $[x-ct,x+ct]$. Odd reflection solves the half-line problem with $u(t,0)=0$. ([MIT 18.152, lecture 10](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/ccd4ae63858e855c18c96ce96a797b9b_MIT18_152F11_lec_10.pdf))
- **Duhamel's principle.** With zero initial data, the solution of $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}=F$ is
$$u(x,t)=\frac1{2c}\int_0^t\int_{x-c(t-s)}^{x+c(t-s)}F(\xi,s)\,d\xi\,ds,$$
obtained by superposing, for each time $s$, homogeneous solutions started with zero displacement and velocity $F(\cdot,s)\,ds$. ([Duhamel's principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duhamel%27s_principle))
- **Kirchhoff's formula ($n=3$).** If $f\in C^3(\mathbb R^3)$ and $g\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$, the unique solution with $c=1$ is $C^2$ and
$$u(t,x)=\frac1{4\pi t^2}\int_{\partial B_t(x)}\left[f(\sigma)+\nabla f(\sigma)\cdot(\sigma-x)+t\,g(\sigma)\right]d\sigma .$$
The solution is one derivative less regular than the data, unlike d'Alembert's formula. ([MIT 18.152, lecture 12](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/940561a138578640826f762b5a57bcad_MIT18_152F11_lec_12.pdf))
- **Two dimensions by descent from $n=3$.** Treating a planar solution as a 3D solution independent of the third coordinate turns Kirchhoff's sphere integral into an integral over the disc of radius $ct$, so in two dimensions the solution depends on the whole disc and a wake trails the wavefront; Kirchhoff-type formulas with spherical or ball means exist for all odd $n\ge3$ and even $n\ge2$. ([Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation))
- **Sharp Huygens principle.** Data influence $u(t,x)$ only through the sphere $\partial B_{ct}(x)$ exactly when $n\ge3$ is odd; it fails for $n=1$ and for every even $n$, though finite speed of propagation still holds.
