([MIT 18.152, lecture 12](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/940561a138578640826f762b5a57bcad_MIT18_152F11_lec_12.pdf))
- **Energy estimate in a cone and uniqueness.** For a $C^2$ solution in $\mathbb R^{1+n}$, the energy on $B_{R-t}(p)$ is non-increasing for $0\le t\le R$: $E(t)\le E(0)$. Hence two $C^2$ solutions with the same data on $B_R(p)$ agree in the backward [light cone](node:Light%20Cone) $\{(\tau,y):0\le\tau\le R,\ |y-p|\le R-\tau\}$, which gives uniqueness and finite speed of propagation. ([MIT 18.152, lectures 13–14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/ad3a71c522df2396b6248cf9b35aedea_MIT18_152F11_lec_13_14.pdf))
- **Nonlinear defocusing equations.** For defocusing equations and systems such as $\Box u=|u|^{p-1}u$ in $\mathbb R^{1+d}$, global smooth solutions exist for arbitrary smooth data in the energy-subcritical and energy-critical cases ($d\le2$, or $d\ge3$ and $p\le1+\tfrac4{d-2}$), at least for $d\le7$, using conservation of the (non-negative) energy and Morawetz estimates. Tao constructed finite-time blowup for a defocusing supercritical *system* ($m=40$ components, $p>5$) in $d=3$. ([Tao 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.08059))
- **Supercritical blowup (complex-valued).** Shao, Wei and Zhang proved that for odd integers $p$ with $d=4$, $p\ge29$, or $d\ge5$, $p\ge17$, there is a smooth complex-valued solution of the defocusing equation that blows up in finite time ([Shao–Wei–Zhang, Forum Math. Pi](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/9E6EB9B2641FF3F4CA38D6DED0780B90/core-reader)); Buckmaster and Chen's preprint proves finite-time blowup for the septic ($p=7$) defocusing equation in $\mathbb R^{4+1}$, lowering the order from $29$ to $7$, again for complex-valued solutions. ([Shao–Wei–Zhang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19674); [Buckmaster–Chen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15619))

### Examples
For a string with tension $T$ and linear density $\mu$, small-amplitude vibrations satisfy the wave equation with speed $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$. With both ends of a string of length $L$ fixed, separation of variables $u=T(t)v(x)$ leads to a trigonometric eigenvalue problem; the standing waves have nodes at the ends, fundamental frequency $f_1=\frac1{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}$, and harmonics $f_n=nf_1$. ([String vibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_vibration); [Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation))

A profile $F(x-ct)$ translates rightward unchanged; by d'Alembert, initial data with compact support in $[a,b]$ produce a solution supported in $[a-ct,b+ct]$. ([MIT 18.152, lecture 10](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/ccd4ae63858e855c18c96ce96a797b9b_MIT18_152F11_lec_10.pdf))

### History
D'Alembert discovered the one-dimensional wave equation, and Euler treated the three-dimensional case. Strichartz's 1977 paper on restriction of the Fourier transform to quadratic surfaces and decay of solutions of wave equations arose from connections to the Fourier restriction problem and gave the Strichartz estimates used in modern dispersive theory. ([Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation); [Strichartz estimate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strichartz_estimate))

### Connections
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): the hyperbolic member of the classical trio with the [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation) and [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations).
- [Method of Characteristics](node:Method%20of%20Characteristics): the lines $x\pm ct=\text{const}$ carry the d'Alembert solution.
- [Fourier Analysis](node:Fourier%20Analysis) and [Sturm–Liouville Problems](node:Sturm–Liouville%20Problems): mode expansions on bounded domains.
- [Vector Calculus](node:Vector%20Calculus): the Laplacian and the divergence theorem behind energy identities.
- [Minkowski Spacetime](node:Minkowski%20Spacetime) and [Light Cone](node:Light%20Cone): the d'Alembertian and light cones govern domains of dependence.
- [Klein–Gordon Equation](node:Klein–Gordon%20Equation): the wave equation with a mass term.
- [Huygens–Fresnel Principle](node:Huygens–Fresnel%20Principle): the optical counterpart of the sharp Huygens principle.
- [Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation](node:Nonlinear%20Schrödinger%20Equation): the dispersive analogue where defocusing supercritical blowup was also studied.
- [Compressible Euler Equations](node:Compressible%20Euler%20Equations): self-similar imploding Euler solutions underlie the supercritical NLW blowup constructions.
- [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces): the natural setting for energy and well-posedness.

### Common pitfalls
A second-order-in-time equation needs both initial position and initial velocity. Finite speed of propagation and the sharp Huygens principle are different: the first holds in every dimension, the second only in odd $n\ge3$, so its failure is an even-dimension (and $n=1$) phenomenon, not a low-dimension one. Kirchhoff's formula loses a derivative, so $C^2$ data need not give a $C^2$ solution in three dimensions. The whole-line d'Alembert formula does not enforce boundary conditions on an interval; reflection or separation of variables is needed. ([MIT 18.152, lecture 12](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/940561a138578640826f762b5a57bcad_MIT18_152F11_lec_12.pdf); [MIT 18.152, lecture 10](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/ccd4ae63858e855c18c96ce96a797b9b_MIT18_152F11_lec_10.pdf))

### Open problems
- **Scalar defocusing supercritical NLW.** Shao, Wei and Zhang state that "the blow-up for the scalar defocusing supercritical wave equation remains open"; their construction gives complex-valued blowup only. Tao had noted that lowering the number of components in his blowup system to one would be needed to settle the scalar equation, and that any global regularity proof must use a special property of the scalar equation. ([Shao–Wei–Zhang, Forum Math. Pi](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/9E6EB9B2641FF3F4CA38D6DED0780B90/core-reader); [Tao 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.08059))
- **Three space dimensions.** The same paper states that "the existence of blow-up solutions for $d=3$ remains open" for the supercritical defocusing problem, and that $d=3$ is not amenable to their analysis. ([Shao–Wei–Zhang, Forum Math. Pi](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/9E6EB9B2641FF3F4CA38D6DED0780B90/core-reader))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wave equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation): solutions in all dimensions, Huygens' principle, and history.
- **Learn:** [MIT 18.152 (Speck), lectures 10, 12, 13–14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-152-introduction-to-partial-differential-equations-fall-2011/940561a138578640826f762b5a57bcad_MIT18_152F11_lec_12.pdf): d'Alembert, Kirchhoff, Minkowski geometry, and geometric energy estimates.
- **Primary:** [Shao, Wei, Zhang, On blow-up for the supercritical defocusing nonlinear wave equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19674) (Forum Math. Pi 2025) and [Tao, Finite time blowup for a supercritical defocusing nonlinear wave system](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.08059).
- **Further reading:** [Evans, Partial Differential Equations](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/gsm/019): AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics vol. 19, the standard graduate text.
references.Well-Posed Problems:
## Reference
### Overview
A problem is well-posed in Hadamard's sense when a solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the data; Hadamard introduced these criteria in 1902. A problem that fails any of them is ill-posed. The heat equation with given initial data is the standard well-posed example, and running it backward to recover an earlier temperature from later data is the standard ill-posed one, because the solution is highly sensitive to the final data. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem))

For a PDE the equation alone does not determine well-posedness. The domain, the initial or boundary conditions, the class of admissible data, and the notion of solution are all part of the problem: Hadamard's operator formulation asks for surjectivity, injectivity, and a continuous inverse between specified spaces. ([Srinivasamurthy, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.5323)) Ill-posed problems usually have to be reformulated before they are solved numerically, typically by adding assumptions such as smoothness of the solution. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem))

Continuous dependence is always measured in chosen norms. For hyperbolic evolution equations the standard requirement is an $L^2$ energy estimate, and well-posedness of the initial value problem is then equivalent to an algebraic condition on the principal symbol, strong hyperbolicity. For nonlinear problems, linearization and frozen coefficients give only local-in-time results; long-time existence needs much more sophisticated methods. ([Hilditch, §1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1309.2012))

### Formal definition
Write the problem as an operator equation $Au=f$ with $A:X\to Y$ between normed spaces. It is well-posed if (1) it is solvable for every $f\in Y$ ($A$ surjective), (2) the solution is unique ($A$ injective), and (3) the solution depends continuously on $f$ ($A^{-1}$ continuous). ([Srinivasamurthy, §1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.5323))

For the linear constant-coefficient Cauchy problem $\partial_tu=A^p\partial_pu+Bu$, $u(0,\cdot)=f$ on $\mathbb R^3$, Hilditch calls the problem well-posed if there are constants $K,\alpha$ such that every solution with $L^2$ data satisfies
$$\|u(t,\cdot)\|_{L^2}\le Ke^{\alpha t}\|f\|_{L^2}.$$
For an initial–boundary value problem on a half-space, strong well-posedness additionally bounds the $L^2$ norm of the solution on the boundary, and the right-hand side includes the forcing and boundary data. ([Hilditch, eqs. 2, 18](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1309.2012))

### Key results
- **Well-posed $\iff$ strongly hyperbolic.** For the constant-coefficient system above, with principal symbol $P_s=A^ps_p$ for unit vectors $s$: the system is weakly hyperbolic if every $P_s$ has real eigenvalues, and strongly hyperbolic if moreover each $P_s$ has a complete set of eigenvectors with $|T_s|+|T_s^{-1}|\le K$ uniformly in $s$, where $T_s$ is the eigenvector matrix. The initial value problem is well-posed in $L^2$ if and only if the system is strongly hyperbolic. Sufficiency uses the symmetrizer $H_s=T_s^{-\dagger}T_s^{-1}$. For necessity, a nonreal eigenvalue gives growth like $e^{\omega\,\mathrm{Im}\lambda\,t}$ and a missing eigenvector gives frequency-dependent polynomial growth; the uniform bound on $T_s$ comes from the Kreiss matrix theorem. ([Hilditch, §1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1309.2012))
- **Symmetric hyperbolic systems.** If one Hermitian positive definite $H$, independent of $s$, makes $HA^ps_p$ Hermitian for all $s$, the system is symmetric hyperbolic. Every symmetric hyperbolic system is strongly hyperbolic, but not conversely. With maximally dissipative boundary conditions, symmetric hyperbolicity gives the initial–boundary value problem an energy estimate. Kreiss's symmetrizer theorem makes boundary stability sufficient for strong well-posedness in the generalized sense for symmetric hyperbolic systems, or strongly hyperbolic systems of constant multiplicity. ([Hilditch, §1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1309.2012))
- **Hille–Yosida theorem.** A closed, densely defined operator $A$ on a Banach space generates a strongly continuous semigroup with $\|T(t)\|\le Me^{\omega t}$ if and only if every real $\lambda>\omega$ is in the resolvent set and $\|(\lambda I-A)^{-n}\|\le M/(\lambda-\omega)^n$ for all $n\ge1$. It gives necessary and sufficient conditions for the semigroup solution of the Cauchy problem $u'=Au$ to exist. ([Hille–Yosida theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hille%E2%80%93Yosida_theorem); [Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem))
- **Lax–Milgram theorem.** If $a$ is a bounded, coercive bilinear form on a real Hilbert space $V$ ($|a(u,v)|\le C\|u\|\|v\|$ and $a(u,u)\ge c\|u\|^2$), then for every $f\in V'$ there is a unique $u\in V$ with $a(u,v)=f(v)$ for all $v$, and $\|u\|\le c^{-1}\|f\|_{V'}$. All three of Hadamard's conditions follow at once. For $-\Delta u=f$ with $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ this gives a unique weak solution in $H^1_0(\Omega)$. ([Lax–Milgram theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem))
- **Lax equivalence theorem.** For a linear, consistent finite-difference method approximating a well-posed linear initial value problem, the method converges if and only if it is stable (Lax–Richtmyer, 1956). ([Lax equivalence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax_equivalence_theorem))
- **Tikhonov regularization.** For a bounded, linear, injective $A$ with discontinuous inverse, a solvable equation $Au=f$ (so $f\in R(A)$), and noisy data with $\|f-f_\delta\|\le\delta$, the minimizer of $\|Au-f_\delta\|^2+\alpha\|u\|^2$ is $u_{\alpha,\delta}=(A^*A+\alpha)^{-1}A^*f_\delta$. It converges to the minimal-norm solution when $\alpha(\delta)\to0$ and $\delta/\alpha(\delta)\to0$; the discrepancy principle chooses $\alpha$ by solving $\|Au_{\alpha,\delta}-f_\delta\|=C\delta$, $C>1$. ([Srinivasamurthy](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.5323))

### Examples
**Hadamard's example.** On $y>0$, solve $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ with $u(x,0)=0$ and $u_y(x,0)=A_n\sin(nx)$, $A_n\to0$. The unique solution is $u=(A_n/n)\sin(nx)\sinh(ny)$; with $A_n=1/n$ the data tend to zero uniformly while the solution grows without bound for every $y>0$. So the Cauchy problem for the Laplace equation fails continuous dependence in the sup norm, even though uniqueness holds. ([Srinivasamurthy](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.5323))

**Weakly but not strongly hyperbolic.** If $P_s$ has real eigenvalues but lacks an eigenvector, the eigensolution $e^{i\omega\lambda t}[1+i\omega t(P_s-\lambda)]v$ grows linearly in the frequency $\omega$. No estimate of the form $\|u(t)\|\le Ke^{\alpha t}\|f\|$ can hold, so the problem is ill-posed in $L^2$. ([Hilditch, eq. 16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1309.2012))

**Low-regularity ill-posedness.** Nonlinear wave and Schrödinger equations with power nonlinearities, focusing or defocusing, are ill-posed in $H^s$ when $s$ is below the threshold predicted by scaling or Galilean invariance, or when the regularity is too low to support distributional solutions. ([Christ–Colliander–Tao](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0311048))

### History
Hadamard introduced the three criteria in 1902. Inverse problems, such as recovering earlier temperatures from later heat data, are often ill-posed, and Tikhonov regularization is one of the most commonly used treatments of linear ill-posed problems. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem)) The variational regularization method is credited to Phillips (1962) and Tikhonov (1963). ([Srinivasamurthy](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.5323)) Lax and Milgram proved their theorem in 1954, and Lax and Richtmyer published the equivalence theorem in 1956. ([Lax–Milgram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax%E2%80%93Milgram_theorem); [Lax equivalence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lax_equivalence_theorem))

### Connections
- [Partial Differential Equations](node:Partial%20Differential%20Equations): equations need domains, data, and solution spaces before well-posedness is a question.
- [Hilbert Spaces](node:Hilbert%20Spaces) and [Sobolev Spaces](node:Sobolev%20Spaces): the norms in which continuous dependence is measured.
- [Lax–Milgram Theorem](node:Lax–Milgram%20Theorem): the standard well-posedness tool for elliptic boundary value problems.
- [Strongly Continuous Operator Semigroups](node:Strongly%20Continuous%20Operator%20Semigroups) and [Evolution Equations in Banach Spaces](node:Evolution%20Equations%20in%20Banach%20Spaces): the Hille–Yosida framework for evolution problems.
- [Heat Equation](node:Heat%20Equation): well-posed forward, ill-posed backward.
- [Laplace and Poisson Equations](node:Laplace%20and%20Poisson%20Equations) and [Dirichlet Problem](node:Dirichlet%20Problem): well-posed Dirichlet problem, ill-posed Cauchy problem.
- [Weak Solutions](node:Weak%20Solutions): the solution concept for which Lax–Milgram gives well-posedness.
- [MSC 35Lxx - Hyperbolic equations and hyperbolic systems](node:MSC%2035Lxx%20-%20Hyperbolic%20equations%20and%20hyperbolic%20systems) and [Wave Equation](node:Wave%20Equation): strong and symmetric hyperbolicity.
- [Regularization](node:Regularization) and [Integral Equation Inverse Problems](node:Integral%20Equation%20Inverse%20Problems): how ill-posed problems are treated.
- [Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers](node:Matrix%20Norms%20and%20Condition%20Numbers): a well-posed problem can still be ill-conditioned.
- [Mathematical Navier–Stokes Theory](node:Mathematical%20Navier–Stokes%20Theory), [Navier–Stokes Equations](node:Navier–Stokes%20Equations) and [Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation](node:Nonlinear%20Schrödinger%20Equation): global well-posedness questions for nonlinear PDE.

### Common pitfalls
- **Well-posed is not well-conditioned.** A well-posed problem can be ill-conditioned: small data errors can still produce much larger errors in the answer, which a large condition number indicates. Chaotic systems are an example. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem))
- **The norm is part of the statement.** Hadamard's example fails continuous dependence in the sup norm. Hilditch's equivalence with strong hyperbolicity is for constant coefficients and $L^2$ data, and extends to variable coefficients only when a smooth symmetrizer can be built. For nonlinear problems the conclusions become local in time. ([Srinivasamurthy](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.5323); [Hilditch](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1309.2012))
- **Two notions of boundary well-posedness.** Strong well-posedness for initial–boundary value problems is sometimes defined without the boundary term on the left of the estimate. Hilditch notes that the two variants are distinct notions, even though they are sometimes given the same name. ([Hilditch, §1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1309.2012))

### Open problems
- **Global well-posedness of the 3D Navier–Stokes equations.** For smooth, divergence-free initial data on $\mathbb R^3$ or the torus, smooth solutions exist up to some maximal time, and Leray (1934) proved global existence for small data and of weak solutions. Whether smooth solutions always exist globally is a Millennium Prize Problem (2000), which the Clay Institute lists as active. With zero or real-analytic external force the problem remains unsolved; a 2026 claimed finite-time singularity with smooth forcing is reported as not yet independently verified. ([Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_existence_and_smoothness); [Clay Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Well-posed problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-posed_problem): Hadamard's criteria, inverse problems, conditioning.
- **Learn:** [Hilditch, An introduction to well-posedness and free-evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.2012): lecture notes on strong and symmetric hyperbolicity, boundary conditions, and the Kreiss theory.
- **Primary:** [Christ–Colliander–Tao, Ill-posedness for nonlinear Schrödinger and wave equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0311048): sharp low-regularity ill-posedness results.
- **Further reading:** [Kreiss–Lorenz, Initial-Boundary Value Problems and the Navier–Stokes Equations (SIAM, 2004)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1137/1.9780898719130): the monograph that Hilditch follows for boundary well-posedness. Also [Srinivasamurthy, Methods of solving ill-posed problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.5323): a survey of regularization methods.
references.Word Embeddings:
## Reference
### Overview
A word embedding represents each word of a vocabulary as a real-valued vector such that words close together in the [vector space](node:Vector%20Spaces) are expected to have similar meanings. Embeddings can be learned by neural networks, by dimensionality reduction of word co-occurrence matrices, or by probabilistic models ([Wikipedia: Word embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_embedding)). They replace one-hot vectors, which cannot encode similarity because any two distinct one-hot vectors have cosine similarity 0, with dense, fixed-length vectors that can reflect semantic similarity and analogies ([Dive into Deep Learning §15.1](https://d2l.ai/chapter_natural-language-processing-pretraining/word2vec.html)).

The theoretical basis is the distributional hypothesis, associated with Firth's 1957 dictum that a word is characterized by the company it keeps ([Wikipedia: Word embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_embedding)). Count-based methods such as latent semantic analysis compress sparse word–context matrices; predictive methods such as word2vec learn vectors by predicting words from their contexts. Levy and Goldberg showed that the two families are closely linked: skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a word–context matrix of pointwise mutual information shifted by a global constant ([Levy and Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2014/hash/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Abstract.html)).

Static embeddings assign one vector per word type, so all senses of a polysemous word share one vector; contextual models such as ELMo and BERT instead give each occurrence of a word its own vector ([Wikipedia: Word embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_embedding)). What counts as a "word" is itself a modelling choice: subword units such as byte-pair encoding, introduced for open-vocabulary neural [machine translation](node:Machine%20Translation), became the default tokenization for most [large language models](node:Large%20Language%20Models) ([ACL Anthology: Sennrich et al. 2016](https://aclanthology.org/P16-1162/), [Mielke et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10508)).

### Formal definition
An embedding is a map $E:\mathcal V\to\mathbb R^d$ from a vocabulary $\mathcal V$ to $d$-dimensional vectors, with $d$ typically between 100 and 1,000 for word2vec ([Wikipedia: Word2vec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2vec)). Similarity is usually measured by the cosine $\cos(u,v)=u^\top v/(\|u\|\,\|v\|)$ ([Dive into Deep Learning §15.1](https://d2l.ai/chapter_natural-language-processing-pretraining/word2vec.html)).

**Skip-gram.** Each word $w$ has a centre vector $v_w$ and a context vector $u_w$. The probability of context word $w_o$ given centre word $w_c$ is
$$P(w_o\mid w_c)=\frac{\exp(u_o^\top v_c)}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal V}\exp(u_i^\top v_c)},$$
context words are assumed conditionally independent given the centre word within a window of size $m$, and training minimizes the negative log-likelihood; CBOW instead predicts the centre word from the average of the context vectors ([Dive into Deep Learning §15.1](https://d2l.ai/chapter_natural-language-processing-pretraining/word2vec.html)).

**Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS).** With $\sigma$ the logistic function, $k$ negative samples drawn from the unigram distribution $P_D(c)=\#(c)/|D|$, and $\#(w,c)$ the count of the pair in corpus $D$, SGNS maximizes
$$\ell=\sum_{w}\sum_{c}\#(w,c)\Big(\log\sigma(\vec w\cdot\vec c)+k\,\mathbb E_{c_N\sim P_D}\big[\log\sigma(-\vec w\cdot\vec c_N)\big]\Big)$$
([Levy and Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014 (PDF)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2014/file/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Paper.pdf)).

**Pointwise mutual information.** $\mathrm{PMI}(w,c)=\log\frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)P(c)}$, estimated as $\log\frac{\#(w,c)\,|D|}{\#(w)\,\#(c)}$; shifted positive PMI is $\mathrm{SPPMI}_k(w,c)=\max(\mathrm{PMI}(w,c)-\log k,0)$ ([Levy and Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014 (PDF)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2014/file/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Paper.pdf)).

**GloVe.** Given the co-occurrence matrix $X$, GloVe minimizes the weighted least-squares objective
$$J=\sum_{i,j=1}^{V}f(X_{ij})\big(w_i^\top\tilde w_j+b_i+\tilde b_j-\log X_{ij}\big)^2,\qquad f(x)=\begin{cases}(x/x_{\max})^{\alpha}&x<x_{\max}\\1&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$
with $x_{\max}=100$ and $\alpha=3/4$ in the paper's experiments ([Pennington, Socher, Manning, EMNLP 2014 (PDF)](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1162.pdf)).

### Key results
- **SGNS as implicit matrix factorization (Levy–Goldberg 2014).** If the dimension $d$ is large enough that each product $\vec w\cdot\vec c$ can take its value independently of the others, the SGNS objective is maximized at $\vec w\cdot\vec c=\mathrm{PMI}(w,c)-\log k$. Thus for $k=1$ SGNS factorizes the PMI matrix and for $k>1$ the shifted matrix $M^{\mathrm{PMI}}-\log k$, under a weighting that penalizes errors on frequent pairs more; noise-contrastive estimation similarly factorizes a shifted log-conditional-probability matrix. ([Levy and Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014 (PDF)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2014/file/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Paper.pdf))
- **Spectral alternative.** SVD of the shifted PPMI matrix outperforms SGNS on the word-similarity tasks studied but lags it on analogy questions; the authors conjecture the gap comes from SGNS's weighted factorization. ([Levy and Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014 (PDF)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2014/file/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Paper.pdf))
- **GloVe's log-bilinear derivation.** Requiring a function of $(w_i-w_j)^\top\tilde w_k$ to equal the ratio of co-occurrence probabilities $P_{ik}/P_{jk}$, and to be a homomorphism between the additive and multiplicative groups, is solved by $F=\exp$, giving $w_i^\top\tilde w_k=\log P_{ik}=\log X_{ik}-\log X_i$; absorbing $\log X_i$ into a bias $b_i$ and adding $\tilde b_k$ gives $w_i^\top\tilde w_k+b_i+\tilde b_k=\log X_{ik}$, which the weighted objective $J$ fits by least squares. ([Pennington, Socher, Manning, EMNLP 2014 (PDF)](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1162.pdf))
- **Generative explanation of PMI embeddings and analogies (Arora et al. 2016).** A dynamic log-linear topic model yields closed-form expressions for word co-occurrence statistics that justify PMI-based methods, word2vec and GloVe, and explains why low-dimensional embeddings exhibit the linear-algebraic structure used to solve analogies, under an assumption, supported experimentally, that latent word vectors are fairly uniformly dispersed in space. ([ACL Anthology: Arora et al., TACL 2016](https://aclanthology.org/Q16-1028/))
- **Bias is linear (Bolukbasi et al. 2016).** In word2vec embeddings trained on news text, gender stereotypes are captured by a single direction, and gender-neutral words are linearly separable from gender-definitional words; their debiasing algorithm, evaluated by crowd workers and standard benchmarks, substantially reduces measured stereotypes while preserving [clustering](node:Clustering) quality and analogy-solving ability. ([arXiv:1607.06520](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06520))
- **Debiasing is superficial (Gonen–Goldberg 2019).** After such debiasing, gender information remains recoverable from distances between "neutralized" words, so existing bias-removal techniques mostly hide bias rather than remove it. ([ACL Anthology: Gonen and Goldberg 2019](https://aclanthology.org/N19-1061/))

### Examples
- **Vector-offset analogies.** In word2vec embeddings, vector arithmetic such as "brother" − "man" + "woman" lands closest to "sister" ([Wikipedia: Word2vec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2vec)); the same arithmetic produces stereotyped analogies such as "man is to computer programmer as woman is to homemaker" ([Wikipedia: Word embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_embedding)).
- **Training cost.** The full softmax requires a probability for every vocabulary word, so each gradient requires the conditional probabilities of all words in the dictionary ([Dive into Deep Learning §15.1](https://d2l.ai/chapter_natural-language-processing-pretraining/word2vec.html)); hierarchical softmax and negative sampling avoid this, and subsampling frequent words speeds training and yields more regular representations ([arXiv:1310.4546](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546)).
- **Recommended windows.** The word2vec authors recommend context window 10 for skip-gram and 5 for CBOW; skip-gram handles infrequent words better while CBOW is faster ([Wikipedia: Word2vec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2vec)).

### History
Latent semantic analysis (late 1980s) applied dimensionality reduction to word–context matrices; Bengio and colleagues proposed neural probabilistic language models learning a distributed representation for words in 2000 (journal version 2003) ([Wikipedia: Word embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_embedding)). Mikolov, Chen, Corrado and Dean introduced the skip-gram and CBOW architectures in January 2013, reporting high-quality vectors from a 1.6-billion-word corpus in under a day ([arXiv:1301.3781](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781)); the follow-up paper added negative sampling, subsampling and phrase vectors ([arXiv:1310.4546](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546)) and received the 2023 NeurIPS Test of Time Award ([Wikipedia: Word2vec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2vec)). GloVe appeared at EMNLP 2014 ([ACL Anthology: Pennington et al. 2014](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1162/)), Levy and Goldberg's factorization analysis at NeurIPS 2014, and subword BPE for translation at ACL 2016 ([ACL Anthology: Sennrich et al. 2016](https://aclanthology.org/P16-1162/)).

### Connections
- [Language Modeling](node:Language%20Modeling): word2vec is a simplified predictive language model; neural language models learn embeddings as their first layer.
- [Linear Maps and Matrices](node:Linear%20Maps%20and%20Matrices) and [Singular Value Decomposition](node:Singular%20Value%20Decomposition): count-based embeddings are low-rank factorizations of co-occurrence matrices.
- [Information Theory](node:Information%20Theory): PMI is the pointwise form of mutual information.
- [Subword Tokenization](node:Subword%20Tokenization) and [Byte-Level Language Modeling](node:Byte-Level%20Language%20Modeling): choices of the units that get embedded.
- [Transformers](node:Transformers) and [Attention Mechanism](node:Attention%20Mechanism): produce contextual embeddings, one per token occurrence.
- [Rotary Positional Embeddings](node:Rotary%20Positional%20Embeddings): a positional encoding used alongside token embeddings in transformers.
- [Vector Search and Embeddings](node:Vector%20Search%20and%20Embeddings): nearest-neighbour retrieval in embedding spaces.
- [Algorithmic Fairness](node:Algorithmic%20Fairness): bias measured and mitigated in embedding geometry.
- [Cross-Entropy Loss](node:Cross-Entropy%20Loss): the training objective of skip-gram and CBOW softmax models.
- [Distance Matrices and Metric Embeddings](node:Distance%20Matrices%20and%20Metric%20Embeddings): the mathematical theory of embedding finite sets in vector spaces.

### Common pitfalls
- Analogy arithmetic does not show that embeddings "understand" meaning; why word2vec works is described as poorly understood, and Goldberg and Levy call the distributional explanation "very hand-wavy" ([Wikipedia: Word2vec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2vec)).
- The PMI characterization of SGNS assumes dimension large enough for perfect reconstruction; with small $d$ SGNS is a weighted low-rank approximation, not an exact factorization ([Levy and Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014 (PDF)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2014/file/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Paper.pdf)).
- A static embedding conflates senses: "club" gets one vector for sandwich, clubhouse and golf club ([Wikipedia: Word embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_embedding)).
- Lower measured bias after debiasing does not mean bias is gone ([ACL Anthology: Gonen and Goldberg 2019](https://aclanthology.org/N19-1061/)).

### Open problems
- **Removing, not hiding, bias.** Gonen and Goldberg conclude that existing bias-removal techniques are insufficient and should not be trusted for gender-neutral modelling, leaving open how to remove bias encoded throughout embedding geometry ([ACL Anthology: Gonen and Goldberg 2019](https://aclanthology.org/N19-1061/)).
- **Explaining why embeddings work.** The reasons word2vec succeeds are described as poorly understood; Arora et al.'s generative model is one candidate explanation resting on modelling assumptions ([Wikipedia: Word2vec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2vec), [ACL Anthology: Arora et al., TACL 2016](https://aclanthology.org/Q16-1028/)).
- **Choice of units.** A survey of open-vocabulary modelling and tokenization concludes that there is, and likely will never be, a single tokenization solution for all applications, and that thinking seriously about tokenization remains important ([Mielke et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10508)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Word embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_embedding): definition, history, contextual embeddings, polysemy, bias.
- **Reference:** [Wikipedia: Word2vec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2vec): CBOW, skip-gram, training tricks, hyperparameters.
- **Learn:** [Dive into Deep Learning §15.1 Word Embedding (word2vec)](https://d2l.ai/chapter_natural-language-processing-pretraining/word2vec.html): skip-gram and CBOW derivations with gradients.
- **Primary:** [Levy and Goldberg, Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization (NeurIPS 2014)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2014/hash/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Abstract.html): SGNS as shifted-PMI factorization.
- **Primary:** [Mikolov et al., Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546): negative sampling and subsampling.
- **Primary:** [Pennington, Socher, Manning, GloVe (EMNLP 2014)](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1162/): the GloVe model.
- **Further reading:** [Goldberg, Neural Network Methods for Natural Language Processing (Springer, 2017)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-3-031-02165-7): graduate monograph covering word embeddings within neural NLP.
references.World Models:
## Reference
### Overview
A world model is a learned system that builds an internal representation of an environment and predicts how that environment changes in response to actions, so that an agent can plan and simulate instead of relying only on real trial and error; the term describes an approach rather than a specific architecture ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_model_%28artificial_intelligence%29)). Ha and Schmidhuber's 2018 agents learned "a compressed spatial and temporal representation of the environment" without supervision, fed its features to a small policy, and could be trained entirely inside the model's own "hallucinated dream" before transferring to the real environment ([Ha and Schmidhuber](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.10122)).

What a world model must predict depends on the agent's interface. In [model-based reinforcement learning](node:Model-Based%20Reinforcement%20Learning) with images, the problem is high-dimensional, redundant and partially observed, so practical systems learn a latent state-space model with an observation model, a latent dynamics model and a reward model ([Berkeley CS 285](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse-fa23/static/slides/lec-11.pdf)). Other systems predict only what planning needs: MuZero's learned model predicts the quantities most directly relevant to planning (reward, policy and value) ([Schrittwieser et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08265)). [Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures](node:Joint-Embedding%20Predictive%20Architectures) encode observations into embeddings and train a predictor by minimizing prediction error in embedding space, predicting future representations rather than pixel-by-pixel reconstructions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_model_%28artificial_intelligence%29)).

The definition is still debated: one camp treats a world model as an internal representation for understanding how the world works, the other as a simulator for predicting future states to guide decisions, with video generators leaning to the second ([Ding et al. survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.14499v4)).

### Formal definition
In the embodied-AI survey of Li et al., interaction is a [POMDP](node:Partially%20Observable%20Markov%20Decision%20Processes): at step $t$ the agent sees $o_t$, takes $a_t$, and the true state $s_t$ is hidden; a world model infers a latent $z_t$ with a dynamics prior $p_\theta(z_t\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1})$, a filtered posterior $q_\phi(z_t\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_t)$ and a decoder $p_\theta(o_t\mid z_t)$, giving
$$p_\theta(o_{1:T},z_{0:T}\mid a_{0:T-1})=p_\theta(z_0)\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(z_t\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1})\,p_\theta(o_t\mid z_t).$$
Training maximizes an evidence lower bound that splits into per-step reconstruction terms and KL terms pulling the posterior toward the dynamics prior ([Li et al. survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16732v2)).

Ha and Schmidhuber's architecture has three parts: a VAE "V" encoding each frame to $z_t$; an MDN-RNN "M" modelling $P(z_{t+1}\mid a_t,z_t,h_t)$ as a mixture of Gaussians; and a linear controller "C", $a_t=W_c[z_t\ h_t]+b_c$, trained by CMA-ES ([worldmodels.github.io](https://worldmodels.github.io/)). PlaNet's recurrent state-space model combines deterministic and stochastic transition components and is trained with a multi-step [variational inference](node:Variational%20Inference) objective called latent overshooting ([Hafner et al., PlaNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.04551)).

### Key results
- **General agents contain world models (Richens, Abel, Bellot, Everitt, ICML 2025).** Let the environment be a finite, communicating, stationary, fully observed controlled Markov process with at least two actions, and let $\pi$ be a deterministic goal-conditioned policy achieving every composite goal of depth at most $n>1$ with probability at least $(1-\delta)$ times optimal. Then $\pi$ determines a transition model $\hat P$ with
$$|\hat P_{ss'}(a)-P_{ss'}(a)|\le\sqrt{\frac{2P_{ss'}(a)(1-P_{ss'}(a))}{(n-1)(1-\delta)}},$$
i.e. error $O(\delta/\sqrt n)+O(1/n)$ for small $\delta$, large $n$; myopic agents ($n=1$) need not learn transitions. ([Richens et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.01622))
- **Robust agents learn causal models (Richens and Everitt, ICLR 2024).** Any agent that satisfies a regret bound under a large set of distributional shifts must have learned an approximate causal model of the data-generating process, which converges to the true causal model for optimal agents. ([Richens and Everitt](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10877))
- **Planning with a learned model (MuZero).** Tree search with a learned model that predicts reward, policy and value set a new state of the art on 57 Atari games and matched AlphaZero's superhuman play in Go, chess and shogi without being given the rules. ([Schrittwieser et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08265))
- **Fixed-hyperparameter imagination training (DreamerV3).** Learning a world model and improving behaviour by imagining futures, with normalization, balancing and transformation techniques for robustness, outperformed specialized methods on over 150 tasks with one configuration and was the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without human data or curricula. ([Hafner et al., DreamerV3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04104))
- **Learning to plan from pixels (PlaNet).** A purely model-based agent planning online in a learned latent space solved continuous-control tasks with contact dynamics, partial observability and sparse rewards from pixels, using substantially fewer episodes than model-free methods. ([Hafner et al., PlaNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.04551))

### Examples
- **CarRacing and VizDoom.** Ha and Schmidhuber's full V+M+C agent scored $906\pm21$ on CarRacing over 100 tracks (solved threshold 900); a controller seeing only $z_t$ scored $632\pm251$. In VizDoom a policy trained only in the dream at temperature $\tau=1.15$ survived $1092\pm556$ steps in the real game. ([worldmodels.github.io](https://worldmodels.github.io/))
- **Genie.** An 11B-parameter "foundation world model" trained without action labels on unlabelled Internet videos, combining a spatiotemporal video tokenizer, an autoregressive dynamics model and a latent action model, so users can act frame by frame in generated environments. ([Bruce et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15391))
- **Board-state models in sequence models.** A GPT variant trained only to predict legal Othello moves developed an internal nonlinear representation of the board that interventions show is causally used ([Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13382)); a closely related linear "mine vs. theirs" encoding allows steering by vector arithmetic ([Nanda, Lee, Wattenberg](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00941)).
- **[Model predictive control](node:Model%20Predictive%20Control) with ensembles.** CS 285 presents the loop: fit a dynamics model, plan, execute, replan every $N$ steps, and add bootstrap ensembles so planning accounts for model uncertainty ([Berkeley CS 285](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse-fa23/static/slides/lec-11.pdf)).

### History
Schmidhuber introduced the term world model in machine learning in 1990, with recurrent networks that predict future states ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_model_%28artificial_intelligence%29)). Ha and Schmidhuber revived it in 2018 ([Ha and Schmidhuber](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.10122)); PlaNet (2018) and DreamerV3 (2023) extended latent-dynamics agents ([Hafner et al., PlaNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.04551); [Hafner et al., DreamerV3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04104)). LeCun advanced the idea in a 2022 position paper, *A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence*, and Genie (2024) learned interactive environments from unlabelled video ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_model_%28artificial_intelligence%29)).

### Connections
- [Model-Based Reinforcement Learning](node:Model-Based%20Reinforcement%20Learning): world models are the learned dynamics in model-based RL.
- [Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes](node:Partially%20Observable%20Markov%20Decision%20Processes): the formal setting for latent-state world models.
- [Latent State-Space Models](node:Latent%20State-Space%20Models): the probabilistic structure (prior, posterior, decoder) of recurrent world models.
- [Variational Autoencoders](node:Variational%20Autoencoders): the ELBO training objective and the "V" component of Ha–Schmidhuber.
- [Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures](node:Joint-Embedding%20Predictive%20Architectures): predict in embedding space instead of reconstructing observations.
- [Latent Predictive Planning](node:Latent%20Predictive%20Planning): planning by rolling out learned latent dynamics.
- [Monte Carlo Tree Search](node:Monte%20Carlo%20Tree%20Search): MuZero searches over its learned model.
- [Sim-to-Real Transfer and Domain Randomization](node:Sim-to-Real%20Transfer%20and%20Domain%20Randomization): transferring dream-trained policies faces the same model-gap problem.
- [Nanda et al. 2023 - Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00941): evidence for world representations inside sequence models.

### Common pitfalls
- **Exploiting model errors.** In VizDoom the controller found an adversarial policy that stopped the simulated monsters from firing; at low temperature the agent scored about 2,000 in the dream but about 190 in reality. Raising $\tau$ makes such exploits harder but the dream harder to learn in. ([worldmodels.github.io](https://worldmodels.github.io/))
- **Distribution shift.** A model fit to data from one policy is wrong where the planner drives the system; the problem worsens with more expressive model classes, motivating iterative data collection and replanning ([Berkeley CS 285](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse-fa23/static/slides/lec-11.pdf)).
- **Pixel fidelity is not physical consistency.** Evaluation should measure physical consistency over pixel fidelity ([Li et al. survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16732v2)); video-prediction accuracy and robot success rates do not always predict real-world performance ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_model_%28artificial_intelligence%29)).
- **Reading "contains a world model" as "uses it to plan".** Richens et al. prove a model is encoded in the policy, not that the agent plans with it or "knows" it ([Richens et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.01622)).

### Open problems
- **Partially observed environments.** The world-models-are-necessary theorem covers only fully observed environments; what an agent must learn about latent variables, and what causal knowledge a regret bound requires, are left open, as are scalable model-recovery algorithms ([Richens et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.01622)).
- **Long-horizon consistency and evaluation.** The embodied-AI survey names the scarcity of unified datasets, metrics for physical consistency, the trade-off between accuracy and real-time efficiency, and long-horizon temporal consistency with error accumulation as open challenges ([Li et al. survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16732v2)).
- **Physical rules and counterfactual simulation.** Ding et al. list physical rules and counterfactual simulation, benchmarks, simulation efficiency, sim-to-real bridging and safety as future directions ([Ding et al. survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.14499v4)).

### Resources
- **Reference:** [World model (artificial intelligence), Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_model_%28artificial_intelligence%29): definition, history, JEPA-style and generative variants.
- **Learn:** [Berkeley CS 285, Lecture 11: Model-Based RL](https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse-fa23/static/slides/lec-11.pdf): learning dynamics, distribution shift, ensembles, latent state-space models.
- **Learn:** [Ha and Schmidhuber, World Models (interactive article)](https://worldmodels.github.io/): V–M–C architecture and dream training.
- **Primary:** [Ha and Schmidhuber 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.10122): the paper that revived the term.
- **Primary:** [Hafner et al., DreamerV3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04104): general imagination-based RL across 150+ tasks.
- **Primary:** [Richens et al., General agents contain world models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01622): formal necessity result.
- **Further reading:** [Ding et al., Understanding World or Predicting Future? A Comprehensive Survey of World Models](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.14499v4): survey organized around the understanding-vs-prediction split.
- **Further reading:** [Li et al., A Comprehensive Survey on World Models for Embodied AI](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16732v2): POMDP formalism and taxonomy.
references.n-Sphere:
## Reference
### Overview
The $n$-sphere $S^n$ is the set of points of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ at a fixed distance from a centre: $S^1$ is the circle, $S^2$ the ordinary sphere, and the solid region it bounds is the $(n+1)$-ball. It is a smooth $n$-manifold of constant positive curvature, and stereographic projection identifies $S^n$ minus a point with $\mathbb R^n$, so $S^n$ is $\mathbb R^n$ with a single point at infinity added. ([Wikipedia: n-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere)) In the standard convention (Hocking–Young, Maunder) the index is the intrinsic dimension; Coxeter instead indexes by the ambient dimension, calling the circle a 2-sphere, which matters when reading older literature. ([MathWorld: Hypersphere](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Hypersphere.html))

Spheres matter at two levels. Metrically, the area $2\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2)$ of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^n$ is the factor that appears whenever a radially symmetric quantity is integrated in $n$ dimensions, from Gauss's law to the density of states in [Statistical Mechanics](node:Statistical%20Mechanics). ([Wikipedia: n-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere); [Chemla, Phys 427 notes](https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys427/sp2012/Lectures/Hypersphere_volume_deriv.pdf)) Topologically, spheres are the basic test spaces of algebraic topology: their homology is as simple as possible, while their homotopy groups are "surprisingly complex and difficult to compute". ([Wikipedia: Homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Homotopy groups of spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_groups_of_spheres))

In differential topology, spheres are where smooth and topological categories first come apart: Milnor's exotic 7-spheres are homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to $S^7$, and the generalized Poincaré conjecture asks which homotopy spheres are spheres. ([Wikipedia: Exotic sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_sphere); [Wikipedia: Generalized Poincaré conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Poincar%C3%A9_conjecture))

### Formal definition
$$S^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:\ \|x\|=1\},\qquad S^n_r(c)=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:\ \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(x_i-c_i)^2=r^2\}.$$
$S^0$ is a pair of points. ([Wikipedia: n-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere); [nLab: n-sphere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-sphere))

As homogeneous spaces of compact Lie groups,
$$S^n\cong O(n+1)/O(n)\cong SO(n+1)/SO(n)\cong \mathrm{Spin}(n+1)/\mathrm{Spin}(n),\quad S^{2k+1}\cong SU(k+1)/SU(k),\quad S^{4k-1}\cong Sp(k)/Sp(k-1),$$
with exceptional cases such as $S^6\cong G_2/SU(3)$ and $S^{15}\cong\mathrm{Spin}(9)/\mathrm{Spin}(7)$. ([nLab: n-sphere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-sphere)) See [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups).

A *homotopy $n$-sphere* is a closed $n$-manifold homotopy equivalent to $S^n$; an *exotic sphere* is a smooth manifold homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to the standard $S^n$. ([Wikipedia: Generalized Poincaré conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Poincar%C3%A9_conjecture); [Wikipedia: Exotic sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_sphere))

### Key results
- **Area and volume.** With $S_{n-1}$ the area of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^n$ and $V_n$ the volume of the unit $n$-ball,
  $$S_{n-1}=\frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)},\qquad V_n=\frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2+1)},\qquad V_{n+1}=\frac{S_n}{n+1},\quad S_{n+1}=2\pi V_n,$$
  and the ratio of $V_n$ to the volume of the enclosing cube tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$. ([Wikipedia: n-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere)) Among integer ambient dimensions the unit sphere area is largest in $\mathbb R^7$. ([MathWorld: Hypersphere](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Hypersphere.html)) Equating $\int_{\mathbb R^D}e^{-|k|^2}d^Dk=\pi^{D/2}$ with $\int_0^\infty g_De^{-k^2}k^{D-1}dk$ gives the solid angle $g_D=2\pi^{D/2}/\Gamma(D/2)$. ([Chemla, Phys 427 notes](https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys427/sp2012/Lectures/Hypersphere_volume_deriv.pdf))
- **Homology and degree.** $H_k(S^n)\cong\mathbb Z$ for $k=0,n$ and $0$ otherwise. ([Wikipedia: Homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29)) A map $f:S^n\to S^n$ acts on $H_n(S^n)\cong\mathbb Z$ by multiplication by an integer $\deg f$; by Hopf's theorem two maps from a closed connected oriented $n$-manifold to $S^n$ are homotopic iff they have the same degree, so $\pi_n(S^n)\cong\mathbb Z$, and a self-map of $S^n$ extends over the $(n+1)$-ball iff its degree is $0$. ([Wikipedia: Degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_a_continuous_mapping))
- **Brouwer fixed-point theorem.** Every continuous $f:D^n\to D^n$ has a fixed point. Otherwise the ray from $f(x)$ through $x$ defines a retraction $D^n\to S^{n-1}$, which would inject $H_{n-1}(S^{n-1})\cong\mathbb Z$ into $H_{n-1}(D^n)=0$. ([Wikipedia: Brouwer fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brouwer_fixed-point_theorem))
- **Hairy ball theorem.** Every continuous tangent vector field on an even-dimensional sphere $S^{2m}$ vanishes somewhere, while odd-dimensional spheres carry nowhere-vanishing fields. Poincaré proved the case $S^2$ (1885) and Brouwer the higher even dimensions (1912). ([Wikipedia: Hairy ball theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_ball_theorem))
- **Parallelizability and Hopf invariant one.** The only parallelizable spheres are $S^0,S^1,S^3,S^7$; that no other sphere is parallelizable was proved in 1958 by Hirzebruch and Kervaire and, independently, by Bott and Milnor. ([Wikipedia: Parallelizable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallelizable_manifold)) Adams proved that a map $S^{2n-1}\to S^n$ of Hopf invariant one exists only for $n=1,2,4,8$, matching $\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H,\mathbb O$; Adams and Atiyah later gave a K-theory proof. ([Wikipedia: Hopf invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopf_invariant)) Among spheres only $S^0,S^1,S^3$ are Lie groups. ([nLab: n-sphere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-sphere))
- **Homotopy groups.** $\pi_i(S^n)=0$ for $0<i<n$. The Freudenthal suspension $\pi_i(S^n)\to\pi_{i+1}(S^{n+1})$ is an isomorphism for $i<2n-1$ and onto for $i=2n-1$, so $\pi_{n+k}(S^n)$ is independent of $n$ for $n\ge k+2$ (the stable stems). Serre: every $\pi_i(S^n)$ is finite except $\pi_n(S^n)$ and $\pi_{4n-1}(S^{2n})$. The Hopf fibrations $S^1\to S^3\to S^2$, $S^3\to S^7\to S^4$, $S^7\to S^{15}\to S^8$ give in particular $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z$. Nishida (1973): every element of positive degree in the stable homotopy ring is nilpotent. ([Wikipedia: Homotopy groups of spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_groups_of_spheres)) See [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles) and [Fundamental Group](node:Fundamental%20Group).
- **Exotic spheres.** Milnor (1956) constructed exotic 7-spheres as $S^3$-bundles over $S^4$; Kervaire–Milnor showed the oriented smooth structures on $S^7$ form a cyclic group $\Theta_7$ of order 28 under connected sum. $\Theta_n$ has the subgroup $bP_{n+1}$ of spheres bounding parallelizable manifolds, and $\Theta_n/bP_{n+1}$ injects into the stable stems modulo the image of $J$. Spheres of dimensions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 12, 56 and 61 have no exotic smooth structures. ([Wikipedia: Exotic sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_sphere)) The Gromoll–Meyer sphere realises an exotic 7-sphere as a double coset space of a compact Lie group. ([nLab: n-sphere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-sphere))
- **Generalized Poincaré conjecture.** Every topological homotopy $n$-sphere is homeomorphic to $S^n$: Smale proved $n\ge5$, Freedman $n=4$ (1982), Perelman $n=3$ (2003). The smooth version fails in general (first in dimension 7) and is open in dimension 4. ([Wikipedia: Generalized Poincaré conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Poincar%C3%A9_conjecture))

### Examples
- **Low dimensions.** $S_0=2$, $V_1=2$; $S_1=2\pi$, $V_2=\pi$; $S_2=4\pi$, $V_3=\tfrac43\pi$. ([Wikipedia: n-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere))
- **Hyperspherical coordinates.** In $\mathbb R^n$, $d^nV=r^{n-1}\sin^{n-2}\varphi_1\cdots\sin\varphi_{n-2}\,dr\,d\varphi_1\cdots d\varphi_{n-1}$; the area element on the sphere of radius $R$ drops $dr$ and sets $r=R$. ([Wikipedia: n-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere))
- **Phase space.** For $N$ particles in three dimensions the states of energy $E$ lie on a hypershell in $D=3N$-dimensional $k$-space, whose volume $g_Dk^{D-1}dk$ gives the multiplicity of an ideal gas. ([Chemla, Phys 427 notes](https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys427/sp2012/Lectures/Hypersphere_volume_deriv.pdf))
- **The Hopf map.** $S^3\to S^2$ with fibre $S^1$, from complex numbers, generates $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z$; there is no analogous fibration with base $S^{16}$. ([Wikipedia: Homotopy groups of spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_groups_of_spheres))

### History
Poincaré's 1885 vector-field theorem for $S^2$ and Brouwer's work of 1909–1912 are early topological results about spheres. ([Wikipedia: Hairy ball theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_ball_theorem); [Wikipedia: Brouwer fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brouwer_fixed-point_theorem)) nLab credits Montgomery and Samelson (1943) with the coset-space classification of compact Lie groups acting effectively and transitively on spheres, and also cites Borel–Serre (1953) and Gray–Green (1970) for coset structures on spheres. ([nLab: n-sphere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-sphere)) Milnor's 1956 exotic spheres and the 1958 parallelizability theorems were followed by Smale's proof of the high-dimensional Poincaré conjecture, Freedman's in dimension 4 (1982) and Perelman's in dimension 3 (2003). ([Wikipedia: Exotic sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_sphere); [Wikipedia: Parallelizable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallelizable_manifold); [Wikipedia: Generalized Poincaré conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Poincar%C3%A9_conjecture)) Isaksen, Wang and Xu computed the stable stems from dimension 0 to 90 by motivic methods, with a few listed uncertainties. ([arXiv:2001.04511](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.04511))

### Connections
- [Higher-Dimensional Euclidean Geometry](node:Higher-Dimensional%20Euclidean%20Geometry): $S^n$ is the round hypersurface of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$.
- [Gamma Function](node:Gamma%20Function): $\Gamma(n/2)$ appears in $S_{n-1}$ and $V_n$.
- [n-Ball](node:n-Ball): the solid that $S^{n-1}$ bounds; Brouwer's theorem is about it.
- [Gauss's Law in n Dimensions](node:Gauss's%20Law%20in%20n%20Dimensions): flux through a sphere is the area factor $S_{n-1}$ times the radial field.
- [Smooth Manifolds](node:Smooth%20Manifolds): $S^n$ is the basic closed manifold, and exotic spheres show a topological manifold can carry several smooth structures.
- [Exotic R4](node:Exotic%20R4): the four-dimensional counterpart of exotic smoothness; exotic $S^4$ is the open case.
- [Homology](node:Homology): $H_*(S^n)$ is the model computation, used for degree and fixed-point theorems.
- [Fiber Bundles](node:Fiber%20Bundles): the Hopf fibrations and Milnor's $S^3$-bundles over $S^4$.
- [Lie Groups](node:Lie%20Groups): $S^n$ as homogeneous spaces; $S^1,S^3$ as groups.
- [Riemannian Metrics](node:Riemannian%20Metrics): the round metric of constant positive curvature.
- [Submanifolds and Embeddings](node:Submanifolds%20and%20Embeddings): the standard embedding $S^n\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$.
- [Spherical Harmonics](node:Spherical%20Harmonics): harmonic analysis on $S^{n-1}$.
- [Homeomorphism](node:Homeomorphism): exotic spheres are homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to $S^n$.
- Map: [MSC 51 - Geometry](node:MSC%2051%20-%20Geometry), [MSC 55Qxx - Homotopy groups](node:MSC%2055Qxx%20-%20Homotopy%20groups).

### Common pitfalls
- **Intrinsic versus ambient dimension.** $S^n$ is $n$-dimensional and sits in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$; Coxeter's convention names the ambient dimension. ([MathWorld: Hypersphere](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Hypersphere.html))
- **"Volume of the $n$-sphere".** It may mean the ball volume $V_n$ or the $n$-dimensional measure of $S^n$ itself ($S_n$ in Wikipedia's notation); check which. ([Wikipedia: n-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere))
- **Homology does not see homotopy.** Spheres have homology only in degrees $0$ and $n$, yet higher homotopy groups need not vanish, e.g. $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z$. ([Wikipedia: Homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_%28mathematics%29); [Wikipedia: Homotopy groups of spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_groups_of_spheres))
- **Topological versus smooth Poincaré.** The topological generalized Poincaré conjecture holds in all dimensions; the smooth one is false in dimension 7 and open in dimension 4. ([Wikipedia: Generalized Poincaré conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Poincar%C3%A9_conjecture))

### Open problems
- **Hopf problem.** Does $S^6$ admit a complex structure? Agricola, Bazzoni, Goertsches, Konstantis and Rollenske describe this as an unsolved question, the subject of a 2017 conference on (non-)existence of complex structures on $S^6$. ([arXiv:1708.01068](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01068))
- **Smooth Poincaré conjecture in dimension 4.** Whether exotic 4-spheres exist, and how many, is unsolved; candidates such as Cappell–Shaneson and Gluck-twist spheres have been studied and many ruled out. ([Wikipedia: Exotic sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_sphere))
- **Homotopy groups of spheres.** The stable stems have been computed only up to dimension 90, with a few carefully enumerated uncertainties, and are unknown beyond (as of 2023), and the unstable groups have been tabulated only for $k<19$. ([Wikipedia: Homotopy groups of spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_groups_of_spheres); [Isaksen–Wang–Xu, arXiv:2001.04511](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.04511))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [n-sphere (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere): definitions, area and volume formulas, coordinates.
- **Reference:** [n-sphere (nLab)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-sphere): homogeneous-space presentations, parallelizability, exotic examples.
- **Learn:** [Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (free online edition, CUP 2002)](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html): homology of spheres, degree, homotopy groups and the Hopf invariant.
- **Learn:** [Chemla, Phys 427 notes (Illinois)](https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys427/sp2012/Lectures/Hypersphere_volume_deriv.pdf): Gaussian derivation of the area of the unit sphere.
- **Primary:** [Isaksen, Wang, Xu, Stable homotopy groups of spheres: from dimension 0 to 90 (arXiv:2001.04511)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.04511): current computations of the stable stems.
- **Primary:** [Agricola et al., On the history of the Hopf problem (arXiv:1708.01068)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01068): complex structures on $S^6$.
- **Further reading:** [Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (Cambridge University Press)](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html): the standard graduate text for the topology of spheres.
references.p-adic Numbers:
## Reference
### Overview
For a prime $p$, the field $\mathbb Q_p$ of $p$-adic numbers is the completion of $\mathbb Q$ with respect to the $p$-adic absolute value, under which a rational number is small when it is divisible by a high power of $p$. Every element has a unique expansion as a $p$-adic series $\sum_{i\ge v}a_ip^i$, and the $p$-adic integers $\mathbb Z_p$ can also be described as the inverse limit of the rings $\mathbb Z/p^n\mathbb Z$, i.e. as compatible systems of congruences. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))

Kurt Hensel introduced them in 1897, and about twenty years later Ostrowski explained in retrospect why the idea is natural: every nontrivial absolute value on $\mathbb Q$ is a power of the ordinary one or of a $p$-adic one, so the only completions of $\mathbb Q$ are $\mathbb R$ and the $\mathbb Q_p$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number); [Conrad, Ostrowski's theorem for Q](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/ostrowskiQ.pdf)) The $\mathbb Q_p$ therefore stand on an equal footing with $\mathbb R$, and arithmetic questions over $\mathbb Q$ can be studied one prime at a time: Hensel lifting turns solutions modulo $p$ into $p$-adic solutions, and the Hasse principle asks when solutions everywhere locally give a rational solution. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))

They are the setting for $p$-adic analysis and for $p$-adic Hodge theory, which classifies $p$-adic Galois representations of characteristic-$0$ local fields with residual characteristic $p$; for a number field, Ostrowski's theorem identifies the non-Archimedean absolute values with those attached to primes of its ring of integers (see [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields)). Since 1987 they have also been used in mathematical physics, beginning with attempts at a non-Archimedean description of spacetime and strings at the Planck scale. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number); [Dragovich et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.04758))

### Formal definition
Every nonzero $x\in\mathbb Q$ can be written $x=p^{v}\,n/d$ with $n,d$ integers coprime to $p$; the exponent $v=v_p(x)$ is the **$p$-adic valuation**, with $v_p(0)=\infty$. The **$p$-adic absolute value** is
$$|x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)}\ (x\neq0),\qquad |0|_p=0.$$
It satisfies the strong (ultrametric) triangle inequality $|x+y|_p\le\max(|x|_p,|y|_p)$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))

$\mathbb Q_p$ is the metric completion of $(\mathbb Q,|\cdot|_p)$. Equivalently its elements are $p$-adic series
$$x=\sum_{i=v}^{\infty}a_ip^i,\qquad a_i\in\{0,1,\dots,p-1\},$$
with $v_p(x)$ the index of the first nonzero digit. The $p$-adic integers are $\mathbb Z_p=\{x:v_p(x)\ge0\}$, and
$$\mathbb Z_p\cong\varprojlim_n\mathbb Z/p^n\mathbb Z.$$
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))

### Key results
- **Ostrowski's theorem (1916).** If $|\cdot|$ is a nontrivial absolute value on $\mathbb Q$, there is $t>0$ such that $|\cdot|=|\cdot|_\infty^t$ or $|\cdot|=|\cdot|_p^t$ for some prime $p$. Hence every completion of $\mathbb Q$ at a nontrivial absolute value is $\mathbb R$ or some $\mathbb Q_p$. ([Conrad, Ostrowski's theorem for Q](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/ostrowskiQ.pdf))
- **Product formula.** For every $x\in\mathbb Q^\times$, $\prod_v|x|_v=1$, the product over $|\cdot|_\infty$ and all $|\cdot|_p$ (only finitely many factors differ from 1). ([Conrad, Ostrowski's theorem for Q](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/ostrowskiQ.pdf))
- **Hensel's lemma (simple roots).** If $f\in\mathbb Z_p[X]$ and $a\in\mathbb Z_p$ satisfy $f(a)\equiv0\pmod p$ and $f'(a)\not\equiv0\pmod p$, there is a unique $\alpha\in\mathbb Z_p$ with $f(\alpha)=0$ and $\alpha\equiv a\pmod p$. ([Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf)) See [Hensel's Lemma](node:Hensel's%20Lemma).
- **Hensel's lemma (strong form).** If $f\in\mathbb Z_p[X]$ and $a\in\mathbb Z_p$ satisfy $|f(a)|_p<|f'(a)|_p^2$, there is a unique root $\alpha\in\mathbb Z_p$ of $f$ with $|\alpha-a|_p<|f'(a)|_p$; moreover $|\alpha-a|_p=|f(a)/f'(a)|_p$ and $|f'(\alpha)|_p=|f'(a)|_p$. This covers multiple roots mod $p$. ([Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf))
- **Roots of unity and units.** The roots of unity in $\mathbb Q_p$ are the $(p-1)$th roots of unity for odd $p$ and $\pm1$ for $p=2$. For all $p$, $\mathbb Z_p^\times=\mu_{p-1}\times(1+p\mathbb Z_p)$ and $\mathbb Q_p^\times=p^{\mathbb Z}\times\mu_{p-1}\times(1+p\mathbb Z_p)$; for $p=2$, $\mathbb Z_2^\times=\{\pm1\}\times(1+4\mathbb Z_2)$. ([Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf))
- **Power criteria.** A unit $u\in\mathbb Z_2^\times$ is a square in $\mathbb Q_2$ iff $u\equiv1\pmod 8$. For $p\ne2$ and $u\in\mathbb Z_p^\times$, $u$ is a $p$th power in $\mathbb Q_p$ iff it is a $p$th power modulo $p^2$; this fails for $p=2$ (5 is a square mod 4 but not a 2-adic square). ([Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf))
- **Topology and algebra.** $\mathbb Z_p$ is a discrete valuation ring whose units are the elements of valuation $0$; $\mathbb Z_p$ is compact and $\mathbb Q_p$ is locally compact; both have the cardinality of the continuum; $\mathbb Q_p$ has characteristic $0$ and cannot be ordered. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))
- **Algebraic closure.** $\overline{\mathbb Q}_p$ has infinite degree over $\mathbb Q_p$ and is not complete; its completion $\mathbb C_p$ is algebraically closed. Every finite Galois extension of $\mathbb Q_p$ has solvable Galois group. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))
- **Mahler's theorem.** Mahler's theorem characterizes every continuous $p$-adic function in terms of polynomials, and the Volkenborn integral gives a method of integrating $p$-adic functions. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))

### Examples
- **A 3-adic square root of 7.** $f(X)=X^2-7$ has $f(1)=-6\equiv0\pmod3$ and $f'(1)=2\not\equiv0$, so there is a unique $\alpha\in\mathbb Z_3$ with $\alpha^2=7$, $\alpha\equiv1\pmod3$; $\alpha\equiv1+3+3^2+2\cdot3^4\pmod{3^5}$. ([Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf))
- **A multiple root that lifts and one that does not.** $10$ is a 3-adic cube (apply the strong form to $X^3-10$ at $a=4$) but $5$ is not, since $5$ is not a cube mod $9$ (the cubes mod 9 are 0, 1, 8), even though $X^3-5$ has a root mod 3. ([Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf))
- **Torsion.** The torsion subgroup of $\mathbb Q_p^\times$ is cyclic of order $p-1$ for $p>2$ and is $\{\pm1\}$ for $p=2$. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))
- **Local-global.** For quadratic forms, a rational solution exists exactly when real and $p$-adic solutions exist for every $p$ (the Hasse principle); this fails for higher-degree polynomials in several variables. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number)) See [Quadratic Forms over Number Fields](node:Quadratic%20Forms%20over%20Number%20Fields).

### History
Hensel introduced the $p$-adic numbers in 1897, though some of Kummer's earlier work can be read as implicitly using them. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number)) Ostrowski's 1916 classification of absolute values on $\mathbb Q$ explained in retrospect why Hensel's idea was natural. Hensel himself found the roots of $X^2+1$ in $\mathbb Q_5$ to four digits. ([Conrad, Ostrowski's theorem for Q](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/ostrowskiQ.pdf); [Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf)) $p$-adic mathematical physics began in 1987 and later extended to other areas, including biology. ([Dragovich et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.04758))

### Connections
- [Hensel's Lemma](node:Hensel's%20Lemma): the Newton-method lifting of roots that makes $p$-adic fields computable.
- [Algebraic Number Fields](node:Algebraic%20Number%20Fields): completions of a number field at its primes are finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_p$.
- [Adic Completion](node:Adic%20Completion): $\mathbb Z_p$ is the $p$-adic completion of $\mathbb Z$.
- [Real Numbers and Limits](node:Real%20Numbers%20and%20Limits): $\mathbb R$ is the other completion of $\mathbb Q$ allowed by Ostrowski's theorem.
- [Cauchy Sequences](node:Cauchy%20Sequences): $\mathbb Q_p$ is built from Cauchy sequences for $|\cdot|_p$.
- [Metric Spaces](node:Metric%20Spaces): $|\cdot|_p$ gives an ultrametric.
- [Local Rings](node:Local%20Rings): $\mathbb Z_p$ is a complete discrete valuation ring.
- [Topological Groups](node:Topological%20Groups): $\mathbb Q_p$ is a locally compact abelian group with compact open subgroup $\mathbb Z_p$.
- [Haar Measure](node:Haar%20Measure): the additive Haar measure on $\mathbb Q_p$ underlies $p$-adic integration.
- [Quadratic Forms over Number Fields](node:Quadratic%20Forms%20over%20Number%20Fields): Hasse–Minkowski reduces rational solvability to real and $p$-adic solvability.
- [Fields and Galois Theory](node:Fields%20and%20Galois%20Theory): Galois groups of finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_p$ are solvable.

### Common pitfalls
- **Strong triangle inequality changes geometry.** Because $|x+y|_p\le\max(|x|_p,|y|_p)$, convergence of infinite series is simpler than over $\mathbb R$, and intuitions from the real line (such as ordering) do not carry over: $\mathbb Q_p$ cannot be made an ordered field. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))
- **Hensel needs the right hypothesis.** A root mod $p$ need not lift when it is a multiple root: $X^3-5$ has a root mod 3 but none in $\mathbb Q_3$. ([Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf))
- **$p=2$ is special.** Squares in $\mathbb Z_2^\times$ are detected mod 8, not mod 4, and the unit group splits off $\{\pm1\}$ with $1+4\mathbb Z_2$ rather than $1+2\mathbb Z_2$. ([Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf))
- **$\overline{\mathbb Q}_p$ is not complete.** Analysis over an algebraically closed complete field requires $\mathbb C_p$; the abstract field isomorphism $\mathbb C_p\cong\mathbb C$ uses the axiom of choice and is not explicit. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number))

### Open problems
- **Leopoldt's conjecture.** For a number field $K$ and prime $p$, the Leopoldt regulator map, induced by the diagonal embedding of the global units into the $p$-adic completions of $K$, is conjectured to be injective (Leopoldt defect $\delta^L_K=0$). It is known for abelian extensions of $\mathbb Q$ or of an imaginary quadratic field (Ax's method with Brumer's $p$-adic Baker theorem) and the same method handles an imaginary $A_4$-extension case over $\mathbb Q$; in general the best bound is Waldschmidt's $\delta^L_K\le(|S_\infty(K)|-1)/2$. ([Maksoud 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.08203))
- **Gross–Kuz'min conjecture.** Gross's finiteness conjecture, stated by Maksoud as the surjectivity of Gross's $p$-adic regulator map (vanishing of Gross's defect); it was proved by Greenberg for abelian $K/\mathbb Q$ and by Kleine for fields with at most two $p$-adic primes, and Maksoud proves new cases beyond the classical abelian case and shows Gross's regulator has at least half its conjectured rank. ([Maksoud 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.08203); [Maksoud 2023, full text](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2201.08203))

### Resources
- **Reference:** [p-adic number (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_number): construction, valuation, algebraic and topological properties, history.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Hensel's lemma](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/hensel.pdf): both forms of Hensel's lemma, units, roots of unity, squares and $p$th powers, with many examples.
- **Learn:** [Conrad, Ostrowski's theorem for Q](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/ostrowskiQ.pdf): proof of Ostrowski's theorem and the product formula.
- **Primary:** [Dragovich, Khrennikov, Kozyrev, Volovich, Zelenov, p-Adic mathematical physics: the first 30 years (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.04758): review of $p$-adic methods in physics and applications.
- **Primary:** [Maksoud, On the rank of Leopoldt's and Gross's regulator maps (Doc. Math. 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.08203): current state of Leopoldt's conjecture and defect bounds.
- **Further reading:** [Koblitz, p-adic Numbers, p-adic Analysis, and Zeta-Functions (Springer GTM, 1984)](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/978-1-4612-1112-9): standard graduate introduction.
